analysis.label: Using the Queen to deliver check or capture on a square where the Rook should go instead, destroying the Queen's critical role covering escape squares.
analysis.description: In 8/9 positions, the correct move was to use a Rook to check or capture on the EXACT same square where the Queen went (Re7+ not Qe7+, Rxe6+ not Qxe6+, Rg2+ not Qg2+, Rf4+ not Qf4+, Re6# not Qe6+, Rxc3+ not Qxc3+). The remaining position involved a move-order error where the Rook needed to check first on a different square before the Queen followed. In every case, the Queen was already perfectly placed to seal the opponent's king escape routes (covering critical ranks, files, or diagonals), and moving it to deliver the check catastrophically opened those escape paths. The Rook delivering the blow preserved the Queen's coordinating role, maintaining the mating net. Average cp_loss was 8371, typically converting forced checkmates into merely large advantages.
analysis.move_pattern: Queen delivers check or capture-with-check on a square where a Rook could deliver the same check, always toward the opponent's exposed king in the center
analysis.why_bad: The Queen is already covering the opponent king's escape squares from its current position; moving it to deliver the check removes that coverage, allowing the king to flee. The Rook can deliver the same check while the Queen maintains its stranglehold.
sub_patterns: Queen captures piece with check where Rook should capture (Qxe6+ vs Rxe6+)
Queen checks on open file/rank where Rook should check (Qe7+ vs Re7+)
Queen captures defender with check instead of Rook capturing for immediate mate (Qxc3+ vs Rxc3#)

analysis.label: The losing side captures/exchanges their only remaining active piece, eliminating all counterplay and making the position trivially convertible for the opponent.
analysis.description: In 10/10 positions, the side making the move is already significantly losing (avg eval ~600+ cp disadvantage) and plays a capture that exchanges their last meaningful active piece—almost always a rook (9/10 are Rx captures). The analyses unanimously identify that the best moves all preserve the piece and maintain activity: Position 1 (Ra2/Ra1 keep the rook), Position 2 (Rc2/Re2/Rh2 dodge the exchange), Position 6 (Ra1 preserves the rook), Position 8 (Rf2/Re2 keep the rook active), Position 9 (Rb2/Rc2 maintain the rook on the 7th rank), Position 11 (Rh1/Rb1/Ra1 keep harassing). In 8/10 cases the position is an endgame where that single piece was the sole source of defensive resources—blockading passed pawns, targeting weaknesses, or generating counterplay. After the trade, the winning side faces zero resistance: passed pawns promote freely (positions 1, 3, 6, 8, 13), the superior side's king dominates unchallenged (positions 2, 7, 9, 11), or both.
analysis.move_pattern: Rook (or minor piece) captures an opponent's piece of equal/greater value, resulting in a piece exchange that removes the capturer's last active piece from the board
analysis.why_bad: The losing side's only practical chance lies in maintaining piece activity to create complications, blockade passed pawns, or harass the opponent's king—trading that piece removes all resistance and transforms a difficult-but-defensible position into a trivially won endgame for the opponent
sub_patterns: Rook exchange leaving bare king vs rook + passed pawns
Rook exchange freeing an unstoppable passed pawn to promote
Trading into a hopeless pawn endgame by exchanging the last piece
Exchanging the only piece capable of blockading a passed pawn

analysis.label: Playing quiet repositioning moves that abandon critical squares or files when an immediate concrete action (capture, forced defense, or active move) was urgently required.
analysis.description: All 5 positions share a pattern where the player chose a 'building' or preparatory move over an immediately necessary tactical action. In 5/5 cases, the move played was a non-forcing repositioning (no check, no capture, no direct threat) that abandoned a critical defensive or offensive duty: Kc6 left c5 abandoning c4 defense (should have played Ne5), Qa5 left the center abandoning f5 (should have played Qd7), Ng8 retreated from active f6 post losing tempo (should have played Ne4), Kf1 walked into a mating net instead of blocking with Rg2, and Rdh7 doubled rooks slowly instead of immediately capturing the hanging Nh4. In 4/5 positions the 'missed_tactic' tag applies, and in 4/5 'tempo_loss' is flagged. The average cp_loss of ~1984 reflects how catastrophic it is to play slowly when the position demands concrete action. Each position had very few good moves available (avg 1.8), indicating critical moments where precision—not plans—was required.
analysis.move_pattern: Non-forcing quiet moves (no check/capture/threat) that reposition a piece away from its current useful post—kings stepping sideways, queens moving to flanks, knights retreating, rooks shifting files
analysis.why_bad: These moves abandon immediate tactical obligations (defending hanging pieces, capturing unprotected material, blocking mating threats) in favor of slow strategic plans, giving the opponent time to exploit the newly undefended squares, files, or pieces
sub_patterns: King advancing/stepping away from pawn defense duties
Queen moving to a flank while leaving central material hanging
Knight retreating to starting square losing critical tempo
Rook abandoning a contested file for slow doubling on another

analysis.label: Choosing a superficially aggressive or active-looking move that abandons a critical defensive or stabilizing function, when only one precise (often quieter) move maintains the advantage.
analysis.description: In all 5/5 positions, the player chose a move that appeared purposeful or aggressive but fatally abandoned a critical positional or defensive responsibility. In 3/5 cases, a piece was moved from a square where it performed an essential function (Ne7 removed the defender of f6; Nf5 abandoned the dominant d4 outpost; Qb8 left the queen disconnected from key squares c6 and the long diagonal). In 2/5 cases, a move looked thematically active but created exploitable vulnerabilities (f5 released central tension prematurely; Qc5 placed the queen on a square vulnerable to Bd4 tempo gains). A defining characteristic is that only ~1 good move existed on average (1.4 good moves), meaning these were high-precision moments where the player defaulted to intuitive-looking 'active' play rather than finding the one correct continuation. The average cp_loss of 321 reflects that the abandoned function was truly critical—once relinquished, the opponent's refutation directly exploited the gap (Qxf6 capturing the undefended bishop, a4 exploiting the unguarded b5, dxe5 punishing the released tension, Bf8 neutralizing the displaced knight, Be2-Bd4 trapping the misplaced queen).
analysis.move_pattern: A piece (queen, knight, or pawn) moves to an apparently aggressive or active square, typically forward or laterally toward an opponent's piece, while vacating a square or role that was performing a critical defensive or stabilizing function.
analysis.why_bad: The move abandons a critical duty (defending a piece, controlling a key square, maintaining pawn tension, or occupying a dominant outpost) for a superficially attractive but easily refuted aggressive idea, and the opponent exploits the abandoned function immediately.
sub_patterns: Removing a defender by moving a piece that protects another (Ne7 unguards f6 bishop)
Abandoning a dominant outpost for a challengeable aggressive square (Nf5 leaves unassailable d4)
Queen misplacement to seemingly active but tactically vulnerable square (Qc5 falls to Bd4 tempo)
Premature pawn advance releasing critical central tension (f5 allows dxe5 with tempo)
Passive queen retreat abandoning coordination with active pieces (Qb8 loses c6 control)

analysis.label: Playing an instinctive check (or active-looking move) that misses a far superior forcing continuation, often another check or tactical blow on a different square.
analysis.description: In 6/7 positions, Black delivers a check that appears forcing but is actually the wrong forcing move. The pattern shows checks to peripheral squares (Qg2+, Qg6+, Qb2+, Qb2+, Rd1+, R4d5+) when a different check or capture decisively wins—often delivering immediate checkmate (3/7 positions missed mate-in-1 or mate-in-2). The one non-check (Bg6, position 4) shares the same underlying error: choosing an instinctively 'active' move that actually retreats from a critical function. In every case, the played move removes a piece from a square where it was performing essential work (controlling escape squares, supporting a mating net, pressuring a key piece) and relocates it to a square where it accomplishes nothing beyond the superficial threat. The average cp_loss of ~5494 reflects that most of these positions had forced wins available. The consistent tag across analyses is 'pointless_check' or 'wrong_check'—the player's impulse to give check overrides precise calculation of which check (or non-check) actually wins.
analysis.move_pattern: Queen or rook delivers check (usually to b2, g2, g6, or d1/d5) moving AWAY from the square where checkmate or a decisive fork exists
analysis.why_bad: The check carries no secondary threat beyond forcing one king move—the opponent's king escapes to safety, an interposition neutralizes the attack, or a critical piece leaves a square where it controlled escape routes needed for the actual mating pattern
sub_patterns: Queen checks on wrong square when mate exists on adjacent square (Qg6+ instead of Qe2#, Qb2+ instead of Qe3+)
Wrong piece gives check, releasing control of escape squares (R4d5+ instead of R8d5#)
Check with no follow-up when a different check creates a fork or mating net (Rd1+ instead of Rf4+, Qb2+ instead of Re2+)
Piece retreats from functional diagonal/square removing pressure on key squares (Bg6 releasing f3 control)

analysis.label: Moving a piece or pawn away from a square where it performed an essential defensive or blocking function, leaving a critical vulnerability immediately exploitable.
analysis.description: In 7/9 positions, the blundering move removes a piece from a square where it was performing an irreplaceable defensive role: Be3 leaves b2 unguarded by blocking the queen's protection (1/9); c4 advances the pawn from c5 that was the sole defender of d4 (2/9); Nd2 removes the f3-knight that was the only piece keeping g2 defensible (3/9); Nc6 moves the knight off e7 where it blocked the enemy rook's lateral path along the 7th rank (4/9); Bf5 moves the bishop to a wrong square instead of blocking the d-file, leaving the c4-knight tactically hanging (5/9); Rg8 abandons the dominant open e-file where the rook was enabling a winning queen trade (6/9); O-O moves the king into the tactical zone where an existing pin on f3 becomes immediately exploitable (7/9). In each case, the player intended an 'active' or 'improving' move but overlooked that the piece's current function was essential and its departure creates an immediate tactical exploit.
analysis.move_pattern: Any piece type moving away from a square where it guards a pawn, blocks a file/rank, or shields the king; typically sideways or backward relative to the critical defensive axis
analysis.why_bad: The moved piece was performing an irreplaceable defensive function (guarding a hanging pawn, blocking an enemy piece's path to the king, or maintaining structural integrity), and its departure creates an immediate tactical vulnerability the opponent can exploit in one move
sub_patterns: Removing a pawn or piece that guards another pawn, leaving it hanging (Be3/b2, c4/d4, Nd2/g2)
Moving a piece off a blocking square, opening a file or rank for enemy invasion (Nc6 unblocks 7th rank, Rg8 vacates e-file, Bf5 fails to block d-file)
Castling or king movement into a zone where an existing pin or tactical motif becomes lethal (O-O into Nxd4/Nxf3+ exploitation)

analysis.label: Playing a natural-looking active move (development, centralization, or capture) when the position demands one specific concrete tactical solution.
analysis.description: This feature fires when a player makes a piece move that appears active or logical by general principles but misses the position's singular critical tactical need. In 6/6 positions, there was essentially only one truly good move (avg 1.5 good moves), yet the player chose a 'reasonable' alternative: capturing with the wrong piece (Bxd3 instead of cxd3, 1/6), developing passively while ignoring tactical vulnerability (Bb7, 1/6), checking on the wrong square (Qg5+ instead of Qf6+, 1/6), placing the queen on a seemingly active square while missing a decisive knight jump (Qf3 missing Ne4, 1/6), centralizing the queen to an exposed square instead of making a prophylactic retreat (Qe3 missing Bf7, 1/6), or abandoning a dominant centralized piece to chase a queen that easily sidesteps (Nc6 missing Nxf5, 1/6). In every case, the played move would be reasonable in a general context but fails the specific tactical test of the position. The average cp_loss of 278 reflects that these narrow-margin positions punish generic activity harshly.
analysis.move_pattern: Piece move (bishop, queen, or knight) to an open/active-looking square—captures, checks, or centralization—when a different specific tactical move was required
analysis.why_bad: The moves prioritize general principles (activity, development, captures, checks) over the one concrete tactical solution demanded by the position, squandering advantages because the position has very few good alternatives (typically only 1) and the 'natural' move allows the opponent to exploit a specific vulnerability that the correct move would have addressed.
sub_patterns: Capturing with wrong piece (retaining strong piece vs creating passed pawn)
Developing a piece while ignoring existing piece vulnerability to tempo attacks
Queen moving to exposed/suboptimal square when prophylaxis or precise Knight move required
Abandoning a dominant centralized piece for an apparently active but fruitless relocation

analysis.label: Moving a piece to a seemingly natural/safe square when the position demands immediate concrete action, sacrificing initiative or defensive function.
analysis.description: This feature fires when a player makes a quiet repositioning move—typically to a 'safe' or 'natural-looking' square—instead of taking the concrete action the position demands. In 3/5 cases the destination square is f3 (Bf3, Qf3, Nf3), suggesting the feature strongly activates on moves to this 'default development' square. In 4/5 positions, the critical requirement was either a tactical strike (Bxg6 in Position 4), active counterplay (Qd7 in Position 5), an aggressive queen placement (Qh4 in Position 7), or maintaining a piece's defensive function (O-O/keeping Nd2 in Position 8). In all 5/5 cases, the chosen move looks reasonable to a casual observer but fatally surrenders tempo or removes a piece from a critical role, allowing the opponent to consolidate (f6 solidifying in Position 4), launch counterplay (e4 gaining tempo in Position 7, Qa5+ exploiting the vacated diagonal in Position 8), or seize the initiative (e5 creating an unassailable pawn chain in Position 5). The average cp_loss of 251 reflects positions where one or two precise moves existed but the player defaulted to a 'safe' choice.
analysis.move_pattern: Piece (any type) moves to a natural-looking square (especially f3, or back-rank squares d1/b1), typically a non-capture, non-check repositioning move
analysis.why_bad: These moves prioritize abstract piece placement over concrete positional demands—missing tactical strikes, surrendering tempo that allows opponent consolidation, or removing pieces from critical defensive duties, all because the chosen square 'looks right' without calculating consequences.
sub_patterns: Piece retreat/move to f3 instead of attacking (3/5 cases)
Piece placed on back rank for passive defense instead of active counterplay
Developing move that removes a key defender from its post

analysis.label: Natural-looking moves that waste a critical tempo in positions where only one specific move avoids catastrophe.
analysis.description: This feature fires on positions with extremely narrow margins (avg 1.3 good moves available) where the player makes a plausible, 'autopilot' move instead of the single required action. In 9/11 positions, the analyses identify 'tempo_loss' as the core failure mechanism. The played moves all appear reasonable by general principles—centralizing a bishop (Be5, position 1), contesting an open file (Rhe8, Rc2, positions 12/2), reinforcing a kingside attack (Ndf6, Ne3, positions 7/8), prophylactic king moves (Kh8, Kh4, positions 5/9), or addressing a passed pawn (Rd7, position 13)—but each ignores the ONE urgent demand: attacking a bishop before a5 advances, marching a king to escort a pawn, capturing a critical f6 pawn, or maintaining a rook on a promotion-guarding square. The catastrophic average cp_loss of 2717 reflects that these 'routine' moves gift the opponent exactly the tempo needed to execute a winning plan (pawn promotion, mating attack, piece trap) that the one correct move would have prevented.
analysis.move_pattern: Diverse piece types moved to seemingly logical squares (centralization, open files, development) rather than the one tactically demanded destination
analysis.why_bad: Each move wastes a critical tempo in a position where the opponent has an immediate concrete threat or the position has one narrow saving/winning resource; the 'natural' move allows the opponent to execute their plan uncontested.
sub_patterns: King retreat/sidestep when immediate pawn advance or capture is demanded
Rook moves to open files that abandon critical defensive duties
Piece development that blocks own retreat squares or ignores tactical shots
Pawn advances that ignore immediate opposing tactical threats

analysis.label: Premature material captures or slow pawn moves in the opening that ignore tactical vulnerabilities created by the king remaining in the center.
analysis.description: This feature fires on opening blunders where the player makes a greedy capture or a slow positional move while both kings remain uncastled in the center, allowing the opponent to exploit newly opened lines with devastating tactical blows. In 3/7 positions, dxe7 captures a knight but opens the d-file, permitting the deflection sacrifice Bxf2+ followed by Qxd1 winning the queen. In 2/7 positions, premature pawn advances (b3, b6) open diagonals that allow a queen check or invasion to win the rook on a1/a8. In the remaining cases, Bc4 ignores central tension leading to a fork, and Nxe5 miscalculates a pin that is blocked by interposition. All 7/7 positions feature at least one king still on its starting square (e1 or e8), and in every case, simple developing moves (Nc3, Nf3, d4, Be3) were available that maintained the advantage without tactical risk.
analysis.move_pattern: Captures (pawn takes on e7, knight takes on e5) or non-developing pawn pushes (b3, b6), all in early opening positions with kings on e1/e8
analysis.why_bad: These moves prioritize material gain or slow plans over development, opening critical lines (d-file, a1-e5 diagonal, a8-d5 diagonal) that the opponent exploits with forcing moves (checks, deflections, forks) against the uncastled king to win back more material than was gained.
sub_patterns: dxe7 opening d-file allowing Bxf2+ deflection winning queen (3 cases)
Pawn advance (b3/b6) opening diagonal to undefended rook, punished by queen invasion with check
Premature capture miscalculating opponent's interposition or fork resource

analysis.label: Making a forward-looking advance or repositioning that squanders a critical tempo when the position demands precision, restraint, or a more urgent action.
analysis.description: This feature fires on moves that appear active or logical—pushing pawns forward (h6, a5, d4, c5), developing pieces to natural-looking squares (Nf5, Nf6, Na6), or placing pieces on seemingly useful posts (Ra1, Ba1)—but fatally waste a critical tempo or relinquish control of key squares. In 5/9 positions, the error involves a premature pawn advance (h6 allows blockade, a5 gives up b5 control, d4 surrenders e4, c5 wastes tempo in a drawn endgame). In 4/9 positions, piece moves go to suboptimal squares when a more efficient alternative exists (Ra1 instead of Bc3, Ba1 instead of Bb2, Nf5/Nf6 abandoning defensive duties, Na6 ignoring castling urgency). The common refutation in 7/9 cases involves the opponent immediately exploiting the wasted tempo—seizing a vacated square (Ke4 after d4, Kc4 after a5), capturing an undefended pawn (Kxf5 after c5), or launching a tactic against the weakened position (e5! after Nf6, Qe5+ after Nf5). The average cp_loss of 359 reflects positions where the margin for error was extremely thin (avg 2.1 good moves available).
analysis.move_pattern: Forward advances—pawn pushes or piece moves to seemingly active squares—typically one square past the optimal destination or to a functionally inferior square compared to the correct alternative
analysis.why_bad: The move squanders a critical tempo by committing to an advance that either relinquishes control of a key square (enabling opponent king/piece infiltration), creates a tactical target, or simply wastes time when a more urgent positional need (king safety, piece coordination, blockade maintenance) must be addressed first
sub_patterns: Pawn pushed one square too far, abandoning control of critical square (a5 vs a6, d4 vs keeping d5)
Piece placed on wrong square requiring costly repositioning (Ba1 vs Bb2, Ra1 vs Bc3)
Piece moved from vital defensive post to apparently active but functionally useless square (Nf5, Nf6, Na6)
Premature passed pawn advance when piece improvement was needed first (h6, c5)

analysis.label: Moves that appear active or purposeful (checks, pawn advances, piece activation) but waste a critical tempo by failing to address the position's most urgent demand.
analysis.description: This feature detects moves that look energetic or forcing on the surface but fundamentally misallocate the player's tempo in positions requiring precise, concrete action. In 9/9 positions, the played move appears to 'do something' — give check (d5+, Rd1+, Qb6+), advance pawns aggressively (d4, h5, g4), or activate pieces (Ra6, Rd7, Kg3) — yet each fails to address what the position actually demands. In 7/9 cases, the position had an urgent tactical or defensive need (forced mate to deliver, back-rank to address, passed pawns to block, attacking pieces to neutralize) that the played move completely ignores. The best moves in these positions are typically more precise or less superficially attractive — a knight check instead of a pawn push (Position 1), capturing a key defender before giving a rook check (Position 5), trading off dangerous attacking pieces rather than advancing the center (Position 2), or giving check on a square that restricts the king rather than drives it to safety (Position 11). The common denominator is prioritizing general-looking activity over the specific concrete demand of the position.
analysis.move_pattern: Mixed piece types (pawn advances 4/9, rook moves 3/9, checks 3/9, king move 1/9); all moves are forward/aggressive-looking in direction; none involve captures of critical pieces or precise tactical operations
analysis.why_bad: Each move wastes a tempo on a secondary objective while the position's primary demand — whether delivering a forced mate, neutralizing immediate threats, supporting a critical pawn race, or maintaining proper move order — goes unaddressed, allowing the opponent to escape, consolidate, or accelerate their own plans.
sub_patterns: Pointless checks that drive the enemy king toward safety rather than restricting it (Qb6+, d5+)
Ambitious pawn advances that ignore urgent defensive needs (d4, h5, g4)
Rook moves to non-critical squares when the position demands addressing specific threats (Ra6, Rd7)
Move-order errors where the sequence of forcing moves matters critically (Rd1+ before Rxe6+)
King moves to squares that block own piece coordination (Kg3 blocking Ng3)

analysis.label: Playing a plausible-looking but non-urgent move that ignores the position's most critical demand, allowing the opponent to execute a decisive pawn advance or key plan.
analysis.description: This feature fires on moves that pursue a secondary objective (file occupation, flank pawn push, routine development, a check) while the position urgently demands addressing a specific critical threat. In 4/6 positions, the refutation involves a crushing pawn advance that the move failed to prevent: d5-d6 gaining tempo on a piece (positions 7, 12), b5 displacing a knight (position 2), and b8 promotion with interposition (position 15). In the remaining cases, the opponent executes a dominant piece centralization (Nd4 in position 5) or devastating queen placement (Qe2 in position 11). All 6 positions share the 'tempo_loss' tag - the played move effectively gives the opponent a free move to execute their winning plan. The moves are typically on the periphery or address non-primary concerns: flank pawn pushes like a4, b6, g5 (3/6), a rook to an open file ignoring piece repositioning needs (1/6), bishop development allowing d6 with tempo (1/6), and a check through the promotion square (1/6). Most occur in the opening (4/6) with kings uncastled, where tempo is most critical.
analysis.move_pattern: Diverse piece types and directions, typically peripheral or flank-oriented moves (pawn pushes on a/b/g files, rook to wing file, routine bishop development, queen check) while the critical action demands central or anti-pawn-advance response
analysis.why_bad: The move ignores the position's #1 priority (preventing a crushing pawn advance, addressing a vulnerable piece, or maintaining drawing mechanism), giving the opponent a free tempo to execute their decisive plan uncontested
sub_patterns: Flank pawn push ignoring central pawn advance threat (b6, g5, a4)
Routine development allowing d5-d6 with tempo (Be7)
Active-looking rook move ignoring piece vulnerability (Rad8)
Pointless check through promotion square (Qf8+)

analysis.label: Moves that appear logical or purposeful but catastrophically ignore the position's most urgent tactical demand, typically involving king safety.
analysis.description: This feature fires on moves that seem natural or actively constructive—pawn advances to gain space (d5, f3, e4, f6 in 4/8 positions), checks that appear forcing (Rf2+, Qxe2+ in 2/8), rook moves attacking key pawns (Rg7), or king moves toward a logical goal (Ke8)—but which fatally ignore an immediate tactical vulnerability. In every case, the position required precise attention to a critical concrete threat (king safety in 7/8, hanging pieces in 2/8, back-rank weakness in 1/8), yet the player chose a move driven by a general plan rather than calculating forced consequences. The positions share extremely low margins for error (avg 2.1 good moves available) and catastrophic punishment (avg 3958 cp loss), indicating that the feature captures moments where tactical precision is mandatory but the player defaults to 'obvious-looking' continuation instead.
analysis.move_pattern: Mixed piece types and directions; predominantly pawn advances (4/8) or seemingly active piece moves (checks, captures, rook lifts) that neglect defensive requirements in the player's own position
analysis.why_bad: Each move either creates a new tactical vulnerability (weakened diagonal via f3, self-blocked escape via Rg7, abandoned critical square via e4) or fails to address an already-existing one (exposed king with d5/Ke8, hanging piece with f6, wrong capturing piece with Qxe2+), allowing the opponent an immediate devastating tactical refutation that was entirely avoidable.
sub_patterns: Pawn advances that weaken king position or abandon critical squares (f3, e4, f6, d5)
Checks or captures that look forcing but lead to unfavorable forced sequences (Rf2+, Qxe2+)
Piece moves that self-block king escape or choose wrong path to a goal (Rg7, Ke8)

analysis.label: Non-forcing moves that waste a critical tempo when the position demands immediate concrete action to address king safety, pawn tension, or tactical opportunities.
analysis.description: This feature fires on positions where the player makes a natural-looking, non-forcing move (developing, repositioning, or consolidating) while ignoring the position's most urgent demand. In 7/9 cases, the moving side has an uncastled or exposed king, yet plays a slow move instead of addressing king safety directly. In 8/9 cases, the best alternatives involve concrete, forcing play: resolving critical pawn tension (positions 3, 14), completing development/castling (positions 1, 2, 5, 7), generating immediate counterplay (position 15), or executing a specific tactic (position 12). The common punishment is that the opponent gains a decisive tempo to execute a concrete plan—typically a central pawn breakthrough (e5-e6 in position 1, e4 in positions 2 and 5), a tactical strike exploiting the unresolved vulnerability (Bg6+ in position 3, Nxc5 fork in position 15), or seizing dominant piece placement (Bf4/Bd4 in positions 9, 14). The moves themselves look reasonable in isolation but fatally misjudge the position's urgency level.
analysis.move_pattern: Various piece types (queen, rook, knight, bishop, pawn) moved to seemingly natural squares; all are non-checking, non-threatening moves that neither resolve existing tension nor create concrete threats
analysis.why_bad: Each move wastes a critical tempo in a position where the opponent has a concrete plan ready to execute—the delay allows a forcing sequence (pawn break, tactical combination, or piece invasion) that the correct move would have prevented or preempted
sub_patterns: Queen repositioning to wing/back rank instead of resolving central tension (Qa5, Qe2, Qe8)
Piece development to passive square instead of castling or generating counterplay (Rb1, Bd7, Nc4)
Generic central pawn push missing a specific concrete tactic or opening lines for opponent (d4, e5, fxg5)

analysis.label: Playing a natural-looking or tempting move that abandons the single critical positional/tactical requirement in a position where very few good options exist.
analysis.description: This feature fires on positions where the player makes a superficially logical move (a check, a capture, a development, a defense) that fundamentally ignores or violates the one critical demand of the position. In 5/6 cases, the move either self-obstructs a key square/line or abandons a critical defensive/tactical function: Qa6+ drives the king to safety eliminating Rf3+ (1/6), Bb6 abandons the g5-d8 diagonal allowing queen trap (2/6), Kf3 walks into a check+deflection on the a8-h1 diagonal (3/6), Ra8 passively defends instead of seeking active counterplay (4/6), Nc3 blocks the c-pawn from supporting the d4 bishop (5/6), and Nxh7 blocks the king's escape square enabling back-rank tactics (6/6). The positions average only 2.0 good moves available, indicating critical moments demanding precise calculation rather than general principles. The average cp_loss of 271 reflects how severely these 'plausible' moves are punished.
analysis.move_pattern: Various piece types moving to seemingly logical squares (checks, captures, developments, retreats) that create self-obstruction or abandon a critical line/square
analysis.why_bad: Each move prioritizes a surface-level goal (giving check, winning material, defending a pawn, centralizing) while abandoning or obstructing the ONE specific tactical/strategic requirement that the position demands, in situations where accuracy is critical and few alternatives work.
sub_patterns: Piece captures/moves that block own king's escape or critical squares (Nxh7, Nc3)
Retreats/checks that abandon a critical defensive diagonal (Bb6, Qa6+)
King/rook moves to tactically vulnerable squares allowing deflection or passivity (Kf3, Ra8)

analysis.label: Playing natural-looking developing or consolidating moves that waste a critical tempo in positions demanding immediate concrete action.
analysis.description: This feature fires on positions where a time-sensitive strategic or tactical element exists (a critical pawn advance, a decisive outpost occupation, a forced attacking sequence, or an urgent king safety move) but the player instead chooses a 'sensible' routine move. In 9/11 positions, the played move is tagged as a tempo loss. In 8/11 positions, a specific tactic or forcing continuation is missed. The best moves typically involve aggressive pawn advances (d3 in positions 1 and 6), forceful queen maneuvers (Qg4/Qh5+ in position 10, Qe4 in position 5, Qd1/Qf4 in position 11), seizing critical outposts (Nd6 in position 14), or contesting key files (Rg1 in position 3). Instead, the players chose fianchetto preparations (g6, Bg2), standard development (Be3, O-O, Qe2), passive repositioning (Ne6, Nf5, Ng3, f3), or wrong execution of the right concept (Bxe5, Bb4+). The average cp_loss of 1087 with only 1.8 good moves available confirms these are narrow, critical moments where one specific action is required.
analysis.move_pattern: Various piece types moved to seemingly reasonable squares (developing, consolidating, repositioning) rather than the one forcing/concrete continuation the position demands
analysis.why_bad: The position contains a time-critical element (advanced passed pawn needing to push, exposed king needing exploitation, outpost needing immediate occupation, or key file needing contestation) and the routine move surrenders the exact tempo the opponent needs to neutralize or reverse the advantage — typically by allowing a key defensive resource (like d3 blocking a passed pawn, consolidation of king safety, or piece trades) that was previously unavailable.
sub_patterns: Missed critical pawn advance (d3) while developing pieces instead
Passive piece repositioning when king escape or file contest is urgent
Routine development (Be3, O-O) ignoring forcing tactical opportunities
Knight retreating from dominant outpost to seemingly safe but tactically vulnerable square
Wrong piece/direction for a capture or check when one specific execution wins

analysis.label: Aggressive-looking moves (captures, piece activations, pawn breaks) that ignore a concrete tactical vulnerability in the player's own position, allowing the opponent to win material.
analysis.description: This feature fires on moves where the player pursues a secondary objective—capturing a pawn, activating a piece, or executing a pawn break—while failing to notice that one of their own pieces is undefended or about to become tactically exploitable. In 6/8 analyzed positions, the primary tactical motif is 'hanging_piece': Nxg5 leaves a rook en prise (positions 1, 7), exd6 ignores a hanging knight on f3 (position 4), Bb2 places a bishop on an undefended square exploitable via a rook check (position 8), Qb5 moves the queen away from defending f3 (position 11), Nd5 invites an exchange that leaves the f5 pawn hanging (position 12), and Rxg7 captures a pawn while leaving a knight on c6 unprotected (position 13). In all cases, the correct moves addressed the defensive necessity FIRST (retreating a threatened piece, moving the king to safety, or challenging the opponent's active piece), with the average good alternatives being 2.1—meaning safe options were readily available but ignored in favor of the tempting active move.
analysis.move_pattern: Any piece type making a capture, forward development, or pawn break that neglects an existing undefended or forkable piece in the player's own camp
analysis.why_bad: The player prioritizes an offensive or positional goal (pawn grab, piece activation, structural advance) without first checking whether their own pieces are tactically secure, allowing the opponent to exploit hanging pieces, forks, discovered attacks, or deflections to win material immediately.
sub_patterns: Pawn captures that ignore own hanging pieces elsewhere (Nxg5, exd6, Rxg7)
Piece placements that create fork or deflection vulnerabilities (Re3, Bb2, Rc7)
Piece activations that abandon defense of a critical square or piece (Bf4, Qb5, Nd5)
Premature pawn breaks that weaken squares protecting key material (c5)

analysis.label: Plausible-looking moves that address secondary concerns while neglecting the position's one critical tactical vulnerability, allowing immediate concrete punishment.
analysis.description: This feature fires on positions where a player makes a reasonable-seeming move (centralizing, repositioning, capturing) that fatally ignores an immediate tactical requirement. In 5/6 positions, king safety was the critical factor being neglected. In 5/6 cases, the punishment involved a check, fork, or direct attack on the king/major piece. The positions typically had very few good moves (avg 2.0), demanding precise play. The blunders share a common structure: the player addresses a secondary concern (advancing the king in Kc4/Kd2, centralizing the queen in Qf5, defending passively in R4d2, grabbing material in fxe5, 'activating' the knight in Nb5) while the position actually required addressing one specific tactical vulnerability - often the only correct approach being unintuitive (retreating in Kc4/Nb5, attacking in R4d2, developing in fxe5, repositioning a different piece in Kd2).
analysis.move_pattern: Various piece types moving to squares that seem natural/active but abandon critical defensive coordination or expose tactical vulnerabilities - no single geometric direction, but pieces leaving key squares or entering unsafe ones
analysis.why_bad: Each move creates or exposes an immediate tactical exploit (fork, back-rank attack, check sequence, promotion threat) by abandoning the one piece or pawn that was preventing the opponent's concrete threat, in positions where the tactical vulnerability was the overriding concern demanding attention
sub_patterns: King advancing into fork/check vulnerability instead of retreating (Kc4, Kd2)
Piece abandoning critical defensive post enabling opponent activation (Nb5, Qf5)
Choosing passive defense over decisive tactical blow (R4d2)
Pawn capture opening dangerous lines against own king (fxe5)

analysis.label: Non-forcing piece repositions or general-purpose moves that overlook a specific, concrete tactical demand in the position—whether a free capture, critical pawn break, or urgent defensive need.
analysis.description: This feature activates on moves that appear natural or positionally reasonable but fatally ignore the position's concrete tactical requirement. In 3/9 positions, the best move was a simple capture of hanging or inadequately defended material that was missed in favor of a repositioning move (Nf5 instead of Nexd5, Qc7 instead of Qxc5, Rb3 instead of Rxb6). In 3/9 positions, the played move placed a piece on a square creating a new tactical vulnerability—typically on an open file where an opponent's bishop sacrifice (Bh2+) enables a discovered attack or deflection winning the piece back with interest (Qd2 walked into Bh2+/Rxd2, Qf3 walked into Bh2+/Rxf3, Bd1 left the f1-rook undefended for ...Bd3). In 2/9 positions, the move ignored an urgent opponent threat that demanded immediate attention (fxg6 opening the a2-g8 diagonal instead of hxg6, Rd8 ignoring Qh5+). In 1/9, a vague aggressive gesture (Ng5) was played instead of the one concrete attacking break (e5) that maintained the initiative. The average cp_loss of 358 reflects positions where only 1-3 good moves existed, making the failure to find the concrete action catastrophic.
analysis.move_pattern: Non-forcing piece moves (queen repositions, knight jumps, rook slides, bishop retreats) to squares that serve a general purpose but are not the specific concrete action demanded
analysis.why_bad: The moves prioritize vague improvement (piece coordination, file control, attack buildup) over the position's concrete tactical demand, either missing free material, creating new vulnerabilities by placing pieces on tactically exposed squares (especially open files with lurking discovered attacks), or ignoring immediate opponent threats that require prophylaxis
sub_patterns: Missing a free/hanging piece capture in favor of repositioning (3/9)
Placing queen/piece on an open file where Bh2+ deflection or discovered attack wins it (3/9)
Ignoring an immediate tactical threat while pursuing a general positional plan (2/9)
Generic aggression (knight jump) instead of the one concrete forcing break (1/9)

analysis.label: Playing a non-forcing developing or positional move when an enemy piece is completely undefended and can be captured immediately for free.
analysis.description: In 9/9 positions, an opponent's piece (bishop, knight, rook, or queen) is sitting completely undefended and capturable in one move, yet the player makes a quiet non-tactical move instead—typically a routine developing move (Bb7, Be2, Be7, Bg7), a positional pawn push (c6, d6), castling (O-O), a rook lift (Rf6), or a queen reposition (Qd6). In every case, the best move was a simple one-move capture of hanging material (Nxb5, Qxc7, Bxa6, Rxa2, Kxf7, Rxa5, Bxg5, Bxf5, Bxh6). The positions are overwhelmingly in the opening (8/9) and played by Black (8/9), suggesting players on autopilot following general opening principles rather than checking for immediate tactical opportunities. The average cp_loss of 633 reflects that these blunders typically cost a full piece or more. The refutation in each case is straightforward: the opponent either saves or trades the previously-hanging piece, or captures the player's piece that was left vulnerable by the wasted tempo.
analysis.move_pattern: Any quiet non-capture (bishop development, pawn push, castling, piece repositioning) played in a direction unrelated to the hanging enemy piece
analysis.why_bad: The player follows general positional or developmental instincts on autopilot instead of performing a basic tactical scan that would reveal an undefended enemy piece available for immediate capture, wasting a critical tempo that allows the opponent to save or trade the hanging material.
sub_patterns: Bishop develops to natural square ignoring hanging piece (Bb7, Be2, Be7, Bg7)
Pawn push prepares something already achievable by capture (c6, d6)
King move (castling/O-O) ignores fork or hanging piece
Piece repositions to active square while free capture exists (Rf6, Qd6)

analysis.label: Developing or repositioning a piece to an active-looking square while the own king remains dangerously uncastled in the center, when castling or king-safety moves were urgently needed.
analysis.description: This feature fires on moves where the player makes a seemingly natural developing or repositioning move (bishop, knight, or queen) while their king remains exposed on e1/e8. In 9/9 positions, the moving side's king is uncastled in the center. The best alternatives consistently involve castling directly (positions 2, 3, 7, 9, 12 all have O-O among top moves) or moves immediately preparing castling. The blundering moves look plausible—Be6 developing a bishop (3/9), Ne5 placing a knight on an outpost (2/9), Qe2 centralizing the queen (2/9)—but they all fatally delay king safety. The punishments exploit the central king through checks (Bb4+, Bxf2+, Bxc6+), e-file pressure (Re8 pinning queen to king), central pawn breaks (d4 opening lines against the uncastled king), or tactical forks targeting the exposed monarch. Average cp_loss of 277 reflects the severity of leaving the king in the center one move too long.
analysis.move_pattern: Minor piece or queen move (B, N, Q) to a central/active square (e5, e6, f4, e2) while own king sits on e1/e8 uncastled
analysis.why_bad: Each move delays castling by one critical tempo, allowing the opponent to exploit the central king through tactical motifs (checks, pins on the e-file, central pawn breaks, forks) that wouldn't work if the king were already safe
sub_patterns: Be6 bishop development allowing d4-d5 pawn fork or central break (3/9)
Ne5 aggressive knight outpost allowing checks or counterplay on vacated squares (2/9)
Qe2 queen development on e-file creating pin/tempo targets with Re8 (2/9)
Piece repositioning (Bf4) losing tempo with king in center (1/9)
Wrong recapture (Qxd2) leaving pieces hanging with king exposed (1/9)

analysis.label: Playing a quiet, non-forcing move in a critical position where only one specific concrete action addresses an urgent tactical or structural threat.
analysis.description: This feature activates on positions where the player makes a passive, slow, or non-urgent move (king walk, prophylactic pawn push, wrong-flank rook development, passive queen retreat) in situations demanding immediate concrete action. In 8/10 positions, only 1 good move existed (avg 1.3), indicating these are razor-thin decision points. The common thread is tempo loss: 7/10 analyses explicitly tag 'tempo_loss' as the tactical motif or primary tag. In positions 1-2, the king retreats passively (Kf8) instead of centralizing (Ke6) to prevent a fork. In positions 5, 7, 9, 10, quiet moves (h5, Rab1, Kg2, h3) ignore urgent needs like blockading a passed pawn, making a central strike, or defending a weak pawn. In position 3, a greedy pawn grab removes the queen from the critical sector. The opponent consistently punishes by executing the specific tactical/strategic plan that the wasted tempo allowed (fork execution 2/10, passed pawn advance 3/10, piece activation/attack 5/10).
analysis.move_pattern: Quiet non-forcing moves: king walks (Kf8, Kg5, Kg2), slow pawn pushes (h5, h3), passive piece repositioning (Rab1, Qb8, Nfd2), or greedy captures (Qxh7) - all non-urgent alternatives to the one critical move
analysis.why_bad: Each position has exactly one urgent concrete need (blockade a passed pawn, prevent a fork, make a central strike, defend a key square) and the chosen move wastes the tempo needed to address it, giving the opponent a free move to execute their winning plan
sub_patterns: Passive king retreat walking into tactical vulnerability (Kf8 into fork, Kg5 losing pawn coordination)
Prophylactic pawn push (h5, h3) ignoring opponent's advanced passed pawn that needs immediate restraint
Wrong-flank play (Rab1, Qxh7) while critical action is needed in the center or on the other wing
Aimless king move (Kg2) when a specific piece reroute is the only defense
Passive piece retreat (Qb8, Nfd2) surrendering initiative or defensive coordination

analysis.label: Quiet, non-forcing pawn pushes or piece retreats played in positions that demand immediate dynamic or concrete action.
analysis.description: This feature fires on moves that are slow, consolidating, or prophylactic in positions where the engine identifies a critical need for immediate dynamic play. The most common pattern is small pawn advances (h3 appears 2/8 times, plus c3, e6, d4, g5) or piece retreats to passive squares (Bf4, Nc3). In 6/8 positions, the player chose a non-threatening one-square pawn move; in 2/8 positions, a piece was voluntarily retreated from an active square. All 8 moves share the property of being non-forcing (no checks, captures, or direct threats) in positions where the best moves involved active piece deployment, forcing sequences, or exploiting concrete tactical opportunities. The average number of good moves was only 1.8, indicating these are critical moments with narrow paths to maintaining the evaluation, yet the players treated them as routine positions suitable for quiet improvement. The refutations consistently show that the tempo loss allowed the opponent to seize the initiative through pawn breaks (5/8), piece activation (6/8), or direct tactical exploitation of created weaknesses (4/8).
analysis.move_pattern: One-square non-capturing pawn advances (especially h3, c3, e6) or minor piece retreats to passive squares (Bf4, Nc3), all non-forcing with no check or threat
analysis.why_bad: These moves waste a critical tempo in positions requiring immediate action, allowing the opponent to resolve tension favorably, activate pieces, launch attacks, or exploit the newly created weaknesses/passivity. The player misjudges the position's urgency, treating a dynamic/sharp moment as calm.
sub_patterns: Prophylactic h3 creating kingside hook/weakness (2/8)
Piece retreat from dominant centralized square releasing positional pressure (2/8)
Self-blocking pawn advance that entombs own pieces (e6, d4)
Quiet queenside pawn move ignoring back-rank or tactical vulnerability (c3)

analysis.label: Quiet developing or repositioning moves played when the position has one critical demand requiring immediate concrete action.
analysis.description: This feature fires on positions where the player makes a routine, non-forcing developing or repositioning move while ignoring an urgent tactical or strategic demand. In 4/4 cases, the played move was a quiet piece development or retreat (Nc3, Qd1, Be7, Bd7) when the position had essentially one correct plan: address an immediate concrete threat or tension. Position 1: developing Nc3 instead of capturing a dangerous e3-pawn threatening ...exf2+ check. Position 2: retreating Qd1 from f3, abandoning its critical role guarding g2 and h1. Position 3: passively developing Be7 instead of capturing the d5 pawn before White dictates the tension resolution. Position 4: passively developing Bd7 instead of the active Bc5 enabling immediate castling. All positions had only ~1 good move available (avg 1.2), indicating these were critical moments demanding precision, not calm positions allowing routine play. The average cp_loss of 218 reflects the severity of choosing 'autopilot' over urgency.
analysis.move_pattern: Quiet non-capturing, non-checking piece development or retreat to a passive square (back rank, 7th rank, or standard development square) that does not address the position's critical tension point
analysis.why_bad: These moves waste the one tempo needed to address an immediate concrete demand—whether capturing a threatening pawn, maintaining a critical defensive piece placement, or resolving central tension before the opponent dictates terms. The opponent then exploits the tempo gift with forcing moves (checks, captures, or seizing the center).
sub_patterns: Developing a piece while ignoring a dangerous advanced pawn requiring capture
Retreating a piece from a critical defensive post it was guarding
Passive bishop development instead of resolving urgent central pawn tension
Slow defensive development instead of active development enabling castling

analysis.label: White makes an active-looking move that fatally neglects a critical defensive responsibility, leaving a pawn or square undefended for immediate exploitation.
analysis.description: In all 6 positions, White has an exposed or vulnerable king and the position demands prioritizing defensive integrity, yet the played move abandons a critical defensive duty for an apparently constructive but ultimately counterproductive action. In 5/6 cases, the move directly leaves a specific pawn undefended (a2 in Rxc1, c3 in Nb2, the a1 rook via line-opening in Kd3, structural pawns after c4, b3 in Nc3), allowing the opponent to win material through immediate tactical exploitation. The e6 push similarly sacrifices structural integrity for illusory attacking chances. In every case, multiple better alternatives existed (avg 2.5 good moves) that addressed the defensive requirement first—whether capturing with the correct piece (Kxc1 vs Rxc1), retreating the king to safety (Kb3), or eliminating a critical threat (Bxd3). The common thread is that White's king situation demanded caution and structural maintenance, but the player chose a move that appeared active or improving while creating a concrete, exploitable vulnerability.
analysis.move_pattern: Diverse piece types (rook capture, knight moves, king advance, pawn pushes) that share the characteristic of moving a piece away from a defensive duty or creating a new structural weakness in the vicinity of an already-exposed king
analysis.why_bad: Each move removes or fails to provide defense of a critical pawn or square, allowing the opponent to immediately exploit the newly created weakness through tactical means (checks along opened files, captures of undefended pawns, forks, or discovered attacks) that win material or create decisive positional advantage.
sub_patterns: Wrong recapture that opens a file toward the exposed king (Rxc1 leaving a2 undefended)
Knight displacement from key defensive post leaving pawns hanging (Nb2 abandoning c3, Nc3 abandoning b3/d3)
King advance into concrete tactical shot with discovered attack (Kd3 allowing e4+)
Premature pawn break that self-destructs own structure when defense was needed (c4, e6)

analysis.label: Quiet piece-improving moves (predominantly knight repositioning) played when the position urgently demands a concrete tactical action, typically a capture.
analysis.description: This feature fires on positions where the player makes a quiet developing or repositioning move—most often a knight move (6/9 positions)—instead of addressing an urgent tactical demand. In Position 1, Nd2 develops while leaving g1 hanging for a mating attack. In Position 6, Ne2 removes the only defender of e4, allowing a crushing pawn fork. In Position 7, Nf5 moves to an 'attractive' outpost while missing Qxf4 winning a free pawn. In Position 12, Nf6 develops naturally while missing Qxg5 capturing a completely unguarded bishop. In Position 13, g3 is prophylactic while exd4 was urgently needed. In Position 15, Ne2 blocks the king's escape square enabling immediate checkmate. The correct moves were overwhelmingly concrete actions—captures like Bxd4, Qxf4, Qxg5, exd4, dxc5—that the player passed over in favor of 'improving' piece placement. The average cp_loss of ~2305 reflects how catastrophically wrong these aesthetic choices are when calculation is required.
analysis.move_pattern: Non-capturing, non-forcing piece moves (especially knights) to seemingly natural or improving squares; no checks, no captures, no pawn breaks
analysis.why_bad: The player prioritizes general piece development or repositioning aesthetics over urgent concrete tactical demands (hanging pieces, forced captures, mating threats, or critical defensive needs), often simultaneously creating new vulnerabilities like removing key defenders or blocking escape squares.
sub_patterns: Knight repositioning that removes a key defender
Knight development that misses a free capture
Knight move that blocks own king's escape
Quiet pawn move ignoring central tactical urgency
Piece placement on vulnerable diagonal/square

analysis.label: Making a secondary or misdirected move when the king is tactically vulnerable, allowing the opponent to exploit king exposure with immediate tactical threats.
analysis.description: In all 5 positions, the player makes a move that ignores the critical vulnerability of a king (usually their own). The punishments consistently involve king-targeting tactics: discovered check exploiting the e-file (Position 5), knight fork involving the exposed king on f7 (Position 2), bishop sacrifice on f7 (Position 10), queen infiltration to f2 against exposed king (Position 6), and tempo-gaining attacks exploiting undeveloped kingside (Position 1). The tag 'king_safety' appears in 5/5 positions, 'tempo_loss' in 4/5, and 'development' in 4/5. In every case, the player had alternatives that either addressed king safety directly (castling, covering key squares) or gained active counterplay, but instead chose a passive, peripheral, or greedy move that left the king's vulnerability unresolved. The moves range from prophylactic flank pawns (a6), to piece development to tactically unsafe squares (Bd7), to pawn pushes opening lines against one's own king (f6), to capturing material with the wrong piece (Qxa4 instead of Rxa4).
analysis.move_pattern: Various piece types making non-defensive moves (flank pawn pushes, queen captures on the wing, bishop/queen moves to vulnerable squares, pawn pushes opening central files) while the player's king lacks shelter or is exposed to tactical motifs
analysis.why_bad: The moves waste a critical tempo or displace a defender in positions where the king is under latent tactical fire, allowing the opponent to execute immediate tactical punishments (forks, discovered attacks, sacrifices, infiltrations) that exploit the king's exposure before the player can consolidate.
sub_patterns: Queen displaced to wing when king needs nearby defense (Qd2, Qxa4)
Flank/prophylactic pawn move wasting tempo with uncastled king (a6)
Piece placed on square creating fork/pin vulnerability involving king (Bd7)
Pawn push opening lines against own centrally-placed king (f6)

analysis.label: Moves that prioritize capturing or attacking queenside pawns while neglecting a more urgent positional or tactical necessity.
analysis.description: In all 4/4 positions, the played move targets queenside material (capturing a7, b7 pawns, attacking a4 pawn, or attacking the c4 bishop) while a critical strategic priority is ignored. In Position 1, Qxa7 grabs a pawn but displaces the queen where Ra8 traps it. In Position 4, Nb6 attacks the a4-pawn but allows a5 to trap the knight. In Position 8, c5 superficially attacks the c4 bishop but grants White tempo to play Ra1 and eliminate Black's dominant a2 bishop. In Position 11, Rxb7 captures the b7-pawn but abandons c-file control, allowing the c3 passed pawn to equalize. In each case, the correct move involved piece coordination or addressing the critical threat (Qc6, Nb8, Bf6, Rc7) rather than material acquisition. The average cp_loss of 229 reflects how severely these peripheral captures are punished when the opponent exploits the resulting positional concession.
analysis.move_pattern: Piece moves to a-file or b-file (a7, b6, b7) or pushes c-pawn, targeting queenside pawns/pieces rather than maintaining central coordination
analysis.why_bad: Each move wastes a critical tempo on peripheral material gain while the opponent exploits the real imbalance—whether that's an open file toward the king, a trapped piece, an unstoppable passed pawn, or a dominant piece that needed to be challenged immediately
sub_patterns: Queen displaced to corner capturing edge pawn
Knight moves to attack flank pawn and gets trapped by pawn advance
Pawn push attacks enemy piece but gives tempo for opponent to exploit embedded piece
Rook captures wrong pawn instead of controlling critical file to stop passed pawn

analysis.label: Knight captures the f-pawn (f7 or f2) in the opening as a premature sacrifice that is refuted by the king simply recapturing.
analysis.description: All 8/8 positions feature a knight capturing the opponent's f-pawn (f7 for White in 6 cases, f2 for Black in 2 cases) during the opening with both kings still in the center. In every case, the sacrifice is immediately refuted by the king recapturing (Kxf7 or Kxf2), leaving the sacrificing side down a full piece for just one pawn with no compensation. The critical shared failure is that the attacking side's remaining pieces are almost entirely undeveloped — bishops, knights, and rooks sit on starting squares, providing zero follow-up threats against the displaced king. In positions 1, 2, 4, 7, and 8 (White's Nxf7), the knight typically jumps from g5 or e5; in positions 3 and 6 (Black's Nxf2), the knight strikes from e4. The average cp_loss of 317 confirms these are full-piece-value blunders. Players are consistently seduced by Fried Liver Attack patterns (king exposure, fork potential on queen/rook) without verifying they have the developed pieces necessary to sustain the attack.
analysis.move_pattern: Knight captures the f-pawn (f7 or f2), typically jumping from g5/e5 to f7 or from e4 to f2, targeting the square defended only by the king
analysis.why_bad: The king simply recaptures the knight, and the attacker has no developed pieces to generate follow-up threats against the displaced king, leaving them down a full piece for one pawn with no compensation
sub_patterns: Ng5xf7 hoping for king/rook fork
Ne4xf2 hoping for queen/rook fork
Ne5xf7 exploiting fianchetto weakness

analysis.label: Playing a superficially active or attractive move that squanders critical tempo when the position demands one specific concrete continuation.
analysis.description: This feature fires on moves that appear purposeful—checks, captures, pawn advances, piece redeployments—but actually waste the tempo needed to execute the position's one critical idea. In 3/7 positions, the error is a pointless check (Rc7+, Rg3+, Re8+) that either displaces the checking piece from an optimal square or drives the enemy king to a better square. In 2/7 positions, the queen is misplaced via a greedy capture (Qxb2) or an infiltration to a square immediately attacked (Qd2), losing tempo to forced retreats. In 2/7 positions, a slow non-forcing move (a5, Kf3) ignores the opponent's imminent tactical opportunity. All 7 positions share the characteristic that only 1-3 good moves existed (avg 1.7), meaning precise calculation was required, and the chosen move—despite looking natural—gifted the opponent the single tempo needed to equalize, consolidate, or execute a winning tactic.
analysis.move_pattern: Various piece types (rooks, queens, kings, pawns) making apparently forcing or active moves—especially checks and captures—that fail to accomplish anything concrete and lose a critical tempo
analysis.why_bad: The position demanded one specific concrete continuation (a pawn break, a tactical combination, a piece maneuver to a key square, or castling), but the player chose a move that looks active without improving the position, allowing the opponent to use the gifted tempo to neutralize threats, centralize their king, execute a counter-tactic, or trap the displaced piece.
sub_patterns: Pointless rook/piece checks that displace the attacker from a dominant square or improve the defender's king (3/7)
Queen misplacement via greedy captures or infiltrations to immediately-attacked squares (2/7)
Slow non-forcing moves that ignore the opponent's concrete tactical threats (2/7)

analysis.label: Playing superficially aggressive or active-looking moves that ignore the single most urgent defensive or prophylactic necessity in the position.
analysis.description: This feature fires on positions where the player has ONE critical requirement (addressing a passed pawn, preventing a fork, securing a piece, or maintaining correct move order) but instead plays a forward-looking, 'active' move that loses a decisive tempo. In 4/7 positions, the ignored threat involves an opponent's advanced passed pawn or promotion (Kc3 ignoring c8=Q+ with check, c7 leaving the pawn undefended for Rxc7, Nf4 ignoring the d6 passer, g4 allowing c4+ break). In 2/7 positions, the player places a piece on an aggressive-looking square that is immediately refuted by a simple response (Bg4 allows Qg5 winning the piece, Ng4 allows f3 kicking with tempo enabling Nxc7+ fork). In 1/7 positions, a natural-looking exchange (Nxd4) allows a recapture with tempo that dissolves the entire advantage. All 7 positions share extremely low good-move counts (avg 1.4), meaning the position demanded a single precise response and the player instead chose superficial activity.
analysis.move_pattern: Forward-moving pieces or pawns (often to g4/f4 squares or advancing passed pawns), typically looking aggressive or active, frequently knights or bishops deployed to seemingly threatening squares
analysis.why_bad: The move wastes a critical tempo on a threat the opponent can easily neutralize (sidestep, capture, or ignore), meanwhile the opponent executes their own far more dangerous plan (promotion with check, winning hanging material, decisive pawn break, or fork) that the player's move failed to prevent or address.
sub_patterns: Piece deployment to g4/f4 creating superficial threats while ignoring hanging material or king safety (Bg4, Ng4, Nf4)
Premature pawn advance without preparation or correct move order (c7, g4)
King or piece move that stays in the path of opponent's tactical blow (Kc3 on c-file allowing promotion check)
Exchange that grants opponent tempo via recapture attacking a piece (Nxd4 allowing cxd4)

analysis.label: Playing a plausible-looking move that wastes the one critical tempo in a narrow position where only 1-2 moves address the urgent tactical requirement.
analysis.description: All 5 positions share an extremely narrow solution space (avg 1.6 good moves) where ONE specific tactical demand dominates - yet the player chooses a natural-looking alternative that ignores it. In Position 3, Qe3 centralizes the queen but leaves the rook on e6 hanging to Nxe6 (4/5 involve missed tactics). In Position 9, a5 chases a bishop while the critical f2 weakness goes undefended against Bf2+. In Position 10, Kg6 approaches the promotion square via the wrong path when only Kf6 (king IN FRONT of pawn) draws. In Position 11, Qg3 repositions for attack but abandons the f2 square where the queen supported the decisive Bg5 pin. In Position 14, bxc5 grabs material instead of the sole equalizing resource Ne7-Nf5-Ng3+. The 'tempo_loss' tag appears in 4/5 positions, and 'missed_tactic' in 4/5, confirming that these moves all squander the one tempo that mattered in tactically critical moments.
analysis.move_pattern: No consistent geometric pattern - includes queen centralizations, flank pawn pushes, king moves, and captures - unified by being the 'second-best idea' that ignores the position's actual priority
analysis.why_bad: Each move pursues a secondary objective (centralization, material gain, piece chasing, natural-looking improvement) while fatally ignoring the one concrete tactical demand the position requires immediate attention to, wasting the critical tempo in positions where no margin for error exists.
sub_patterns: Queen repositioning that abandons a critical defensive/offensive square
Pawn moves on wrong flank while tactical crisis brews elsewhere
Materialistic captures that surrender the only dynamic counterplay
King moves to plausible but imprecise squares in technical positions

analysis.label: Queen captures a piece with check adjacent to the enemy king, allowing the king to recapture and eliminating the queen's dynamic attacking or defensive value.
analysis.description: In all 8/8 positions, the player's queen captures a piece (usually the opponent's queen, sometimes a rook) with check, and the enemy king recaptures the queen. This pattern represents a premature queen liquidation where the queen's continued presence on the board was essential to maintaining the position's advantage. In 3/8 cases (positions 1, 3, 11), the player missed forced checkmate (including a mate-in-one) while trading. In 1/8 cases (position 7), the player missed a perpetual check draw and traded into a losing endgame. In 4/8 cases (positions 2, 5, 13, 14), the player traded away their most dominant piece when the advantage stemmed entirely from the queen's superior activity, pressure against weak pawns, or attacking potential against the exposed enemy king. The average cp_loss of 3664 reflects how catastrophic these trades are, often converting brilliantly won positions into merely better or drawn ones.
analysis.move_pattern: Queen captures a piece on a square adjacent to the enemy king, giving check; the king recaptures the queen (Qx_+ Kxq pattern)
analysis.why_bad: The queen is the player's most active and powerful piece generating all winning threats (checkmates, perpetual checks, pressure on weak points), and voluntarily exchanging it removes the entire basis of the advantage while allowing the opponent's king to centralize or escape danger.
sub_patterns: Missing forced checkmate while capturing material with queen (mate-in-1 to mate-in-8 available)
Missing perpetual check drawing resource by trading queens into losing endgame
Premature simplification trading dynamic queen dominance for inferior endgame
Queen captures opponent's queen with check but resulting queenless position favors opponent's king activity

analysis.label: Playing a quiet b/c-file move (pawn push, king walk, or rook shift) that ignores an immediate tactical vulnerability requiring urgent defensive attention.
analysis.description: All 5 positions share the pattern of making a positional-looking queenside move on the b or c file while a concrete tactical threat goes unaddressed. In 5/5 cases the move is on the b-file or c-file (c6, Kb6, b4, c4, Rc7). In 4/5 cases the position demanded urgent king safety measures or piece protection. In 3/5 cases the move directly enabled a discovered attack or opened a critical line for the opponent. The best moves consistently involved addressing the immediate crisis first (king evacuation in positions 1/5, staying off tactical alignments in positions 2/3, piece activation before pawn advances in position 4). The played moves all appear 'reasonable' from a positional standpoint—blocking diagonals, gaining space, repositioning—but catastrophically miss that the position requires concrete tactical awareness rather than slow strategic maneuvers.
analysis.move_pattern: Quiet move on b-file or c-file (pawn advance to b4/c4/c6, king to b6, rook to c7) — no checks, no captures, no threats
analysis.why_bad: Each move prioritizes a secondary positional concern (queenside space, diagonal control, piece repositioning) while ignoring an immediate tactical vulnerability — typically a hanging piece, discovered attack alignment, or undefended king — allowing the opponent to exploit the concrete threat with a forcing sequence.
sub_patterns: Pawn push to c6/c4 removing structural protection or ignoring hanging material
King walking to b6 into a discovered check alignment on an open file
Pawn advance b4 enabling opponent's discovered attack by opening a file
Rook repositioning to c7 while a piece hangs on the opposite wing

analysis.label: Moves that prioritize active-looking play (captures, development, centralization, checks) while leaving a piece or pawn fatally undefended.
analysis.description: This feature fires on moves where a player makes a natural-looking 'active' move—a capture, development, centralization, or check—while failing to notice that the move abandons a critical defensive duty, leaving material hanging. In 6/10 positions, a piece moves away from protecting another piece or pawn: Qxd7 instead of Nxd7 leaves Nf6 undefended on the open f-file (Position 1), Kc7 abandons defense of Na7 on the open a-file (Position 3), Qb6 abandons defense of Be7 on the open e-file (Position 4), Qe6 abandons defense of the a7 pawn (Position 14). In 2/10 positions, a piece is developed to an undefended square vulnerable to a fork or capture: Bb5 allows Qa5+ winning it (Position 11), Bb5 ignores the hanging g1-knight (Position 15). In 1/10, a piece is developed into a tactical shot exploiting king exposure (Nf6 allows Qxg7+ winning the knight, Position 5). The average cp_loss of 1263 reflects that these are catastrophic oversights where the refutation is typically a simple one-move tactic.
analysis.move_pattern: Any piece type moving to a seemingly active/natural square (capture, development, centralization, check) while leaving another piece or pawn undefended on an open file or vulnerable diagonal
analysis.why_bad: The moves abandon a critical defensive function (guarding a piece, blocking an open file, covering a fork square) in favor of an optically active but tactically catastrophic alternative, allowing the opponent to win material with a simple capture, fork, or file exploitation.
sub_patterns: Queen moves away from back rank leaving a bishop/piece hanging on an open file
King moves abandoning defense of a piece on an adjacent square
Bishop develops to an undefended square vulnerable to a queen fork with check
Piece develops ignoring an immediately hanging piece elsewhere
Wrong piece captures, leaving the correct capturer as a tactical target

analysis.label: Playing any other move instead of immediately promoting a pawn that sits one square from queening.
analysis.description: In 11/12 positions, the player has a pawn on the 7th rank (or 2nd rank for Black) that can promote immediately, yet plays a different move—king moves (Kf1, Kc1, Ke1, Kg7), rook moves (Ra6, Re1+, Rc7, Ra8), or other pawn advances (a4, d6, gxh4). In every case, the best move was to promote immediately (g8=Q, d8=Q, c8=Q, a8=Q, h8=Q, b8=Q, d1=Q, a1=Q, e8=Q). The played moves represent preparatory actions, peripheral captures, pointless checks, or overprotection of the promotion square—all unnecessary when the promotion itself was immediately decisive. The average cp_loss of ~4795 reflects that many of these positions had forced checkmates via immediate promotion that were squandered.
analysis.move_pattern: Any move (king, rook, or pawn) played INSTEAD of an immediately available pawn promotion on the 8th/1st rank
analysis.why_bad: Delaying promotion by one tempo allows the opponent to establish blockades on the promotion square, deliver discovered checks, counter-promote with check, advance their own passed pawns, or activate pieces—converting forced mates or easily won positions into merely advantageous or even drawn ones.
sub_patterns: King moves near promotion square (Kf1, Ke1, Kg7, Kc1)
Rook moves that 'support' the pawn instead of promoting (Ra6, Ra8, Rc7)
Pointless checks before promoting (Re1+)
Unrelated pawn advances (a4, d6, gxh4)

analysis.label: Playing a quiet, non-forcing move that wastes a critical tempo in a position demanding immediate aggressive action, typically a pawn break or tactical strike.
analysis.description: This feature fires on moves that squander time-critical attacking momentum by choosing slow, prophylactic, or repositioning moves when concrete forcing play is required. In 6/10 positions the center is closed with a kingside pawn storm in progress, and in at least 5/10 the best move is h5 (the decisive kingside break) while the player instead plays a quiet move (a3, b3, g3, Qb1, or a piece relocation). In 8/10 positions the moving side's king remains uncastled or on the back rank, making tempo even more precious. The average cp_loss is 225 with only 1.9 good moves available on average, confirming these are critical junctures where one specific forcing continuation maintains the advantage and any passive alternative allows the opponent to neutralize threats (often via ...h6/...g5 locking the kingside, or ...d5/...f6 counter-breaking in the center). The 'tempo_loss' tactical motif appears in 7/10 analyses as the primary diagnosis.
analysis.move_pattern: Non-forcing moves (quiet pawn pushes a3/b3/g3/f6/g4/g5, piece repositioning Ng5/Bb4/Nc4/Qb1) in positions where a specific aggressive pawn break or tactical shot was required
analysis.why_bad: In time-critical positions with attacking momentum (often a kingside pawn storm against a castled king), wasting even one tempo on a non-essential move allows the defender to execute a neutralizing counter-break, lock the position, or seize the initiative—the attacker's advantage evaporates because it was built entirely on having the tempo to strike first.
sub_patterns: Quiet prophylactic pawn move (a3/b3/g3) instead of decisive h5 break in kingside pawn storms
Premature piece sally (Ng5/Nc4) to aggressive-looking but concretely ineffective square
Passive queen/bishop repositioning (Qb1/Bb4) ignoring hanging material or critical tactical tension
Weakening pawn advance (f6/g5/g4) that creates targets rather than threats while king is uncastled

analysis.label: Active-looking moves (captures, checks, attacks) played before the necessary preparatory or intermediate move, failing tactically due to wrong sequencing.
analysis.description: This feature fires on positions where the player executes what appears to be the natural 'action move' but fatally skips a required preparatory step. In 11/11 positions, there exists a specific move that needed to be played FIRST: Bxc6 before Nxc6 (preserving the knight for Nf7 fork), Qb6+ before Nxh3+ (forcing Rf2 to enable Nxg2), a3 before Bxd6 (gaining tempo so Qxd6 is impossible), exd6 en passant before anything else, Rxf3 before moving the queen, Bh3 before committing the rook, and Bb6/Kb8 instead of b6 (keeping the b7 pawn shielding the king). The average cp_loss of 1254 with only 1.5 good moves available confirms these are critical junctures requiring precise sequencing. Move-order errors are explicitly identified in 4/11 positions, and the 'preparatory move first' pattern applies to all. The moves chosen look aggressive or logical (checks in 3/11, captures in 4/11, attacks in 4/11) but each removes a critical resource or creates a vulnerability before the supporting structure is in place.
analysis.move_pattern: Forcing moves (captures, checks, piece relocations) that appear to advance an attacking or active plan but are played one tempo too early, before a necessary intermediate move establishes the required preconditions
analysis.why_bad: The player executes the 'second move' of a combination or plan before playing the 'first move' that makes it work - either removing the very piece needed for a follow-up tactic, abandoning a critical defensive post before alternative coverage exists, or creating a vulnerability that the opponent exploits with a specific tactical reply
sub_patterns: Wrong capture piece order (Nxc6 vs Bxc6, removing tactical piece)
Check/sacrifice before forcing preparatory move (Nxh3+ before Qb6+)
Trade before gaining tempo (Bxd6 before a3)
Pawn move removing critical defensive shield (b6 opening 7th rank, c5 collapsing center)
Pointless check that hangs the piece (Bd7+ captured by queen)

analysis.label: Playing quiet, non-forcing moves when the position demands an immediate forcing response to address a critical tactical threat.
analysis.description: In all 4 positions, the player chose a move that appears reasonable or 'improving' but fails to address the most urgent tactical priority. In position 9 (Bb6), the player repositioned a passive piece instead of directly confronting White's deadly kingside rooks (3/4 positions involve ignoring immediate king safety threats). In position 11 (Kf3), the king moved to a suboptimal square requiring a later correction (tempo detour). In position 12 (Bxe6), the player captured a threatening-looking piece instead of winning the hanging rook with Qxe5. In position 15 (Qg6), the queen moved to an apparently active square but delivered no check/threat, allowing immediate Re1#. All 4 positions share the 'tempo_loss' tag, and 3/4 share 'missed_tactic'. The consistent pattern is choosing secondary objectives (piece repositioning, removing apparent threats) over the position's primary tactical demand.
analysis.move_pattern: Quiet piece moves (no check, no critical capture) to seemingly active or logical squares, when forcing alternatives (checks, critical captures, or direct defensive moves) were required
analysis.why_bad: These moves waste a critical tempo in sharp positions where the opponent has immediate tactical threats (back-rank mates, hanging pieces, kingside attacks). By not playing a forcing move, the player allows the opponent to execute their plan unimpeded, converting latent threats into concrete advantages.
sub_patterns: Repositioning a piece away from the critical zone while under attack
Capturing a secondary target instead of the primary hanging piece
Moving to an active-looking square that delivers no forcing threat
