King move detour that loses a tempo before reaching the correct square

analysis.label: Playing a quiet 'improving' move that ignores an immediate hanging piece or critical defensive necessity, allowing material loss.
analysis.description: In all 4 positions, the player makes a move that looks constructive or improving—repositioning a piece to a seemingly useful square—while ignoring the most urgent tactical threat in the position. In Position 1 (Qa4), the queen abandons its powerful h4 post to chase queenside pawns, leaving f5 completely undefended for Rxf5 (3/4 involve hanging material). In Position 4 (a4), the pawn advances from its critical defensive post on a2, removing the axb3 recapture option and allowing a devastating Bxb3 deflection (4/4 involve removing defensive function). In Position 13 (Nf4), the knight relocates to an 'active' square but creates a diagonal vulnerability allowing Qg8 to target the queen on e6 (4/4 feature the player prioritizing 'activity' over calculation). In Position 15 (Bc3), the bishop repositions while completely ignoring a knight hanging to Qxg1+ with check (3/4 involve literal hanging pieces). The common thread is choosing aesthetically appealing 'improvement' over addressing the #1 tactical priority.
analysis.move_pattern: Quiet non-capturing, non-checking move to a seemingly active/useful square; piece type varies (Queen, pawn, Knight, Bishop); direction varies but always away from the critical defensive zone
analysis.why_bad: The move removes a piece from a critical defensive role (direct or indirect) or wastes a tempo on 'improvement' while an immediate tactical threat exists—typically a hanging piece, undefended pawn, or exploitable geometric vulnerability that the opponent capitalizes on in one move.
sub_patterns: Queen abandoning active post for distant target (Qa4)
Pawn advancing away from defensive recapture duty (a4)
Piece relocating while leaving higher-value piece tactically vulnerable (Nf4, Bc3)

analysis.label: Moving the king (or weakening its shelter) to a square where the opponent's queen delivers forcing checks that win material or draw by perpetual.
analysis.description: In 6/6 positions, the played move either places the king directly on a square exposed to queen checks (Kd8 allows Qb6+, Kf8 allows Qh7 invasion, Kf6 allows Qf8+ perpetual, Kc1 allows Qe3+ winning the rook) or weakens the king's shelter enabling such checks (fxg3 opens the d4-g1 diagonal for Qd4+, Bd7 fails to prevent Nd5 which unleashes a queen-led attack on the exposed king). In each case, a safer square or alternative existed: 4/6 had a specific king move to a shielded square (Kf6 instead of Kd8, Kd7 instead of Kf6, Ka1 instead of Kc1) or an active piece move that maintained pressure while the king stayed safe. The critical shared error is choosing a 'natural-looking' defensive move that actually exposes the king to forcing check sequences, typically along diagonals, allowing the opponent's queen to gain decisive tempi.
analysis.move_pattern: King moves (4/6) or king-shelter-weakening moves (2/6) that place the king on squares exposed to diagonal or file checks by the opponent's queen
analysis.why_bad: The move places the king on (or opens lines to) squares where the opponent's queen delivers forcing checks, gaining tempo to either win material, achieve perpetual check, or break a mating attack by reorganizing defense
sub_patterns: King retreats to square allowing intermezzo queen check (Kd8 enabling Qb6+)
King advances to exposed center square allowing perpetual check (Kf6 enabling Qf8+/Qb8+/Qh8+)
King moves to diagonal where queen delivers check winning material (Kc1 enabling Qe3+ then Qxh1+)
Pawn capture opening critical diagonal to own king (fxg3 enabling Qd4+ forking king and piece)

analysis.label: Ambitious pawn pushes or piece moves seeking initiative before completing development, typically with the king still in the center.
analysis.description: This feature fires on moves that prioritize aggression, space-grabbing, or tactical ambition when the position demands patient development and king safety. In 5/6 positions, at least one king remains in the center. In 4/6 cases the blunder is a pawn advance (d5, f5, d5, g5) pushing forward into enemy territory, while the remaining moves (Ne7, Qh5) are similarly overambitious piece placements. In all 6/6 cases, the best alternatives were quiet developing moves (e6, Be7, e4, Ngf3, d6, Qc5) that consolidated the position rather than seeking initiative. The refutations consistently exploit the concrete weaknesses created—hanging pawns (3/6), exposed diagonals (2/6), trapped pieces (1/6), or tempo advantages against misplaced pieces (1/6). The common thread is that these moves 'ask a question' the position cannot support, creating tactical or structural liabilities that a more developed opponent immediately exploits.
analysis.move_pattern: Mostly pawn advances (4/6) pushing 1-2 squares forward into enemy territory; also includes piece moves to speculative squares. Direction is generally forward/aggressive rather than consolidating.
analysis.why_bad: The player's position lacks the development, coordination, or king safety to support ambitious play—the aggressive move creates concrete weaknesses (hanging material, opened lines toward the uncastled king, self-blocking) that the opponent exploits immediately with tactical or positional refutations.
sub_patterns: Central pawn advance (d5) that opens lines toward own undefended pieces or weakens key squares
Flank pawn advance (f5, g5) that leaves pawns hanging or fatally weakens king position
Premature piece placement (Ne7, Qh5) that wastes tempo or creates self-obstructing coordination issues

analysis.label: Seemingly purposeful moves (developing, centralizing, checking, capturing) that leave a piece undefended or expose it to an immediate tactical exploitation.
analysis.description: This feature activates on moves that appear constructive—developing a knight (Nd7, Nc3), centralizing/activating a king (Kf4, Kc1), challenging the opponent's queen (Qf4, Qd7), giving check (Qg4+), or capturing material (Rxa8)—but critically overlook that the move creates or exposes a concrete tactical vulnerability, typically a hanging piece. In 6/8 positions, the refutation directly wins material: Nc3 is left undefended and forked by Qd4+ (pos 5); Qf4 abandons defense of the Bg4 which falls to Qxf4/exf4 Rxg4 (pos 7); Nd7 blocks coordination leaving Nf5 capturable by Bxf5 (pos 4); Kc1 wastes tempo allowing Rfd8 + Qxd5 winning the bishop (pos 6); Rxa8 walks the rook into a pawn's promotion-capture square (pos 2); and Qd7 allows an unwanted queen trade when down material (pos 3). In 7/8 cases, a more patient or precise alternative existed that addressed the tactical urgency first (e.g., Bh3 before Qf4, O-O before Nd7, Be4 before Kc1). The positions feature narrow margins (avg 2.0 good moves), demanding concrete calculation over general principles.
analysis.move_pattern: Various piece types moving to active-looking squares (central, capturing, checking) while abandoning defensive duties or placing themselves/other pieces en prise
analysis.why_bad: The moves prioritize an active plan (development, centralization, material grab, check) while ignoring that a specific piece is left tactically vulnerable to the opponent's immediate forcing response—typically a capture, fork, or double-attack that wins material.
sub_patterns: Defender moves away leaving a piece unguarded (Qf4 abandoning Bg4, Kf4 abandoning c3)
Piece placed on undefended square where it can be won by tactics (Nc3 forked by Qd4+)
Development move creating coordination breakdown that leaves pieces capturable (Nd7 leaving Nf5 hanging)
Tempo-wasting move in critical position allowing opponent to execute double-attack (Kc1 allowing Rfd8/Qxd5)
Capture/check on wrong square missing stronger forcing continuation (Rxa8 into promotion, Qg4+ instead of Qd7+)

analysis.label: Moves that pursue a superficially logical plan while failing to address the position's most urgent tactical vulnerability or defensive necessity.
analysis.description: This feature fires on positions where the player makes a move that has some apparent strategic logic but completely ignores the single most critical tactical issue demanding immediate attention. In 4/6 positions, the played move is a 'close cousin' of the correct idea but crucially wrong in execution: Nh6 instead of h6 (wrong piece, same area, Position 2), b5 instead of Nb5 (wrong piece, same square, Position 5), f6 instead of f5 (wrong distance, Position 6), e5 instead of e6 (wrong distance, Position 4). In the remaining 2/6 positions (Ne1 and Qd4), the move completely misidentifies the priority, retreating or repositioning a piece while an urgent threat goes unaddressed. All 6/6 positions featured a specific concrete vulnerability (hanging pawn on a2, vulnerable knight on d4, dangerous passed pawn on e3, exposed f7 square, open back rank, passive piece placement) that the best moves all directly addressed, while the played moves left these problems untouched. The average of only 2.0 good moves available confirms these were positions requiring precise identification of the critical need.
analysis.move_pattern: Diverse piece types and directions; moves are often geometrically similar to the correct move (same square different piece, or same piece wrong distance) but tactically irrelevant to the urgent problem
analysis.why_bad: Each move leaves a specific tactical vulnerability unaddressed—a hanging piece, an exposed square, an advancing passed pawn, or an open line to the king—allowing the opponent to immediately exploit it with forcing moves (captures, checks, or clearance sacrifices)
sub_patterns: Wrong piece to correct area (Nh6 vs h6, b5 vs Nb5)
Wrong pawn advance distance (f6 vs f5, e5 vs e6)
Passive piece retreat ignoring hanging material (Ne1 leaving a2 undefended)
Active-looking move ignoring critical defensive need (Qd4 ignoring e3 pawn)

analysis.label: Playing an aggressive check (or attacking move) on a nearby but wrong square when an immediate checkmate was available, allowing the king to escape.
analysis.description: In 7/8 positions, a forced checkmate in one move was available, yet the player chose a check on a different square (or aggressive piece move) that let the enemy king escape. The played moves are typically one square away from the mating square: Qc5+ instead of Qd5# (Position 2), Qd2+ instead of Qd1# (Position 5), Qe7+ instead of Qe8# (Position 11), Re5+ instead of Re4# (Position 6), Re5+ instead of Rg6# (Position 1), Qf4+ instead of Qh8# (Position 12). In all 8/8 cases, the move played was an aggressive forcing move (7 checks, 1 attacking knight move) that seemed natural and threatening but critically failed to seal a key escape square that the correct checkmate would have covered. The average cp_loss of ~8155 reflects that these convert immediate mates into merely large advantages (+600-850 typically).
analysis.move_pattern: Queen or Rook check (or aggressive piece move) delivered to a square adjacent to or near the actual mating square, typically along the same file, rank, or diagonal as the correct checkmate
analysis.why_bad: The check opens an escape square for the enemy king that the correct mating move would have covered. The player reflexively plays a forcing-looking check without verifying it actually delivers mate, when a nearby square (often one square away) would seal all escape routes for immediate checkmate.
sub_patterns: Queen check one square off on same file/rank from mating square (Qd2+ vs Qd1#, Qe7+ vs Qe8#, Qc5+ vs Qd5#)
Rook check on wrong square vacating critical control (Re5+ vacating d-file instead of Re4#, Re5+ instead of Rg6#)
Queen check on wrong diagonal/file opening king flight square (Qf4+ instead of Qh8#, Qf3+ instead of Rd7+)

analysis.label: Natural-looking moves that remove a piece or pawn from a critical defensive role, leaving material hanging or enabling a forcing tactical sequence.
analysis.description: This feature activates on moves where a piece or pawn that was performing an essential defensive function (guarding another piece, covering a critical square, or blocking a dangerous line) moves away, creating an immediate tactical vulnerability. In 4/8 positions, the moved piece was directly defending something that becomes hanging: the queen leaves c4 undefended (Position 3, Qg3), the bishop abandons e4 protection (Position 2, Bg5), the queen stops covering e5 (Position 8, Qb4), and the e-pawn vacates a critical diagonal (Position 1, e5). In 2/8 positions, the king moves to the wrong square - advancing into danger (Position 7, Kh5) or choosing a suboptimal intermediate square (Position 5, Kg7) - rather than the only retreating move that maintains the position. In Position 4, the queen moves passively instead of the only saving resource. All moves share a quality of looking purposeful (space-gaining, pinning, attacking, developing) while catastrophically ignoring the tactical requirements of the position.
analysis.move_pattern: Any piece type moving away from a square where it defended material or controlled a critical line; often lateral or forward moves that look active but abandon a guardian role
analysis.why_bad: The moved piece was the sole defender of a specific piece, pawn, or critical square. Its departure enables the opponent to win material through a simple capture, check-and-capture combination, or discovered attack exploiting the newly-opened line.
sub_patterns: Queen moves away from defending a minor piece, allowing check-then-capture (Positions 3, 8)
Piece vacates a diagonal/file creating discovered attack or promotion threats (Positions 1, 2)
King moves forward into danger instead of retreating to the only safe square (Positions 5, 7)
Passive/natural move when only one forcing sequence saves the position (Position 4)

analysis.label: Playing a non-forcing, positional move when an opponent's major piece is hanging and can be captured immediately for free.
analysis.description: In 11/11 positions, the best move was a straightforward capture of an opponent's undefended or inadequately defended piece (typically a rook or queen), yet the player chose a quiet repositioning move instead. Specifically: Bxe7 capturing a hanging rook was missed in 3/11 positions (playing Kg7, Rf3, Kg5 instead), Bxg4 capturing an undefended rook was missed in 1/11, Qxc3 capturing a hanging rook was missed in 1/11, Qxg5 capturing a hanging queen was missed in 1/11, Qxb7 capturing a rook was missed in 1/11, Nxe4 capturing a hanging queen was missed in 1/11, and captures of the opponent's last active piece were missed in the remaining cases. The moves actually played were king walks (Kg7, Kg5), rook repositionings (Rfd1, Rg4, Rf7, Rf3), lesser captures (hxg6, Qxd3, Nxg2), or quiet piece moves (Bd3, Qe6). The common thread is a player in a winning position who plays a 'natural-looking' improving or developing move while completely overlooking that an enemy piece sits undefended and can simply be taken.
analysis.move_pattern: Any quiet non-capturing move (king walk, rook reposition, pawn capture, piece development) when a direct capture of opponent's undefended piece exists
analysis.why_bad: The opponent's piece is hanging and can be captured for free in one move, but the player plays a non-forcing move that gives the opponent a tempo to save their piece, squandering forced mates or enormous material gains.
sub_patterns: King move ignoring capturable rook (Kg7, Kg5)
Rook repositioning instead of bishop/queen capture (Rfd1, Rg4, Rf7, Rf3)
Pawn grab instead of piece capture (hxg6, Nxg2, Qxd3)
Threatening a piece instead of taking it (Bd3, Qe6)

analysis.label: Generic developing or repositioning moves played when the position demands an immediate concrete response to a tactical vulnerability.
analysis.description: This feature fires on moves that look natural or positional in isolation—standard development (Nc3, Nf3), piece repositioning (Bb3, Qg3, Re8, Rg1, Rg8), or seemingly active redeployment (Nb6)—but fatally ignore an urgent tactical requirement in the position. In 6/8 positions, the move directly leaves a pawn or piece undefended (e4 hanging after Bb3 and Qg3, d4 hanging after Rg1, knight hanging after Nb6, queen vulnerable after Nf3, king exposed after Rg8). In 7/8 positions, there was only 1-2 good moves available, meaning the position demanded precision rather than general play. The common thread is that positions had ONE specific concrete need—defending a hanging piece, maintaining a critical blockade, preserving counterplay on a specific file, or addressing a direct tactical threat—and the player instead made a 'reasonable-looking' move driven by general principles (develop, activate, reposition) rather than the specific demands of the position. The average cp_loss of 286 reflects how severely positions punish this type of inattention to concrete tactical needs.
analysis.move_pattern: Non-forcing quiet moves (no check, no capture, no direct threat) — pieces develop to natural squares or reposition to seemingly active posts while ignoring the position's most urgent concrete demand
analysis.why_bad: Each move abandons a critical defensive duty or fails to address an immediate tactical vulnerability, leaving a piece/pawn en prise or allowing the opponent to execute a forcing sequence with tempo that was previously restrained by the piece's prior position or role
sub_patterns: Leaving a central pawn undefended by moving its protector away (Bb3/e4, Qg3/e4, Rg1/d4)
Abandoning a critical defensive post or file (Nb6 leaves blockade, Re8 leaves f-file, Rg8 leaves h-file)
Ignoring an incoming piece attack that gains tempo on exposed pieces (Nc3 ignores Ng4 on f2, Nf3 ignores Nc5 on queen)

analysis.label: Playing a quiet, non-forcing preparatory move in a position where unresolved pawn tension or tactical threats demand immediate concrete action (usually a capture).
analysis.description: This feature activates on positions where critical pawn tension or tactical threats exist and the player makes a 'natural-looking' but passive move instead of resolving the tension immediately. In 6/8 positions, the best move was a pawn capture or piece exchange that resolved critical central tension (dxc4, exd6, axb5, dxc4, e4, Nxf3/Bxc5). Instead, the blundering side played quiet rook placements (Rf1, Re1, Rg8, Rfd8 in 4/8 cases), non-urgent pawn pushes (b5, a4 in 2/8), or a strategic break that ignored a concrete tactical threat (d4 allowing Nb3 fork, Kf2 walking into Nxe4+ check). All positions had very few good alternatives (avg 1.6), indicating razor-sharp concrete positions masquerading as strategic ones. The common punishment is that the opponent gains a free tempo to resolve the tension on THEIR terms—opening lines toward the blunderer's king, winning undefended pawns, or executing tactical shots that the slow move failed to prevent.
analysis.move_pattern: Quiet non-capturing moves (rook lifts to natural files, flank pawn advances, king walks) when the position has unresolved central pawn tension requiring an immediate capture or exchange
analysis.why_bad: These moves waste a critical tempo in positions where pawn tension must be resolved NOW—the opponent exploits the free move to capture/advance on their own terms, opening favorable lines, winning undefended material, or executing tactical combinations that the slow move left unaddressed.
sub_patterns: Passive rook placement instead of decisive pawn capture (Rf1/Re1/Rg8/Rfd8)
Flank pawn push ignoring critical central tension (b5/a4)
Strategic pawn break that overlooks concrete tactical threat (d4 allowing fork)
King move walking into tactical vulnerability (Kf2 allowing Nxe4+ check)

analysis.label: King moves (or pawn moves near the king) that expose the monarch to devastating rook checks or invasions on open files/ranks.
analysis.description: This feature activates on positions where both kings are exposed and the player makes a move—typically a king move (4/6 positions) or a pawn move near the king (2/6)—that worsens vulnerability to enemy rooks on open lines. In Position 1, Kc2 places the king on the same rank as the queen, allowing Ra2+ to win material. In Position 4, Kg2 steps into Rh2+ on the open h-file leading to a knight fork. In Position 5, Kf8 places the king on the back rank allowing Ra8+ to deflect a defender. In Position 6, c3 blocks the king's only escape square, enabling immediate R8e2# checkmate. Position 3 (g6) weakens the king's position on the sixth rank, allowing Rb6+ with a tactical e4+ combination. All six positions feature exposed kings with weak pawn shields (6/6), open files occupied by enemy rooks (6/6), and moves that either step the king into a check or remove critical escape options. The one anomalous case (Position 2, Kg5 with 0 cp_loss) shows the feature also fires when the king advances aggressively in a winning position with mutual king exposure—suggesting it broadly detects king movement decisions in positions dominated by exposed-king-vs-active-rook dynamics.
analysis.move_pattern: King moves (or pawn moves adjacent to king) placing or trapping the king on squares aligned with enemy rook's open file or rank
analysis.why_bad: The moves expose the king to immediate forcing sequences by enemy rooks on open lines—resulting in checks that win material through forks/deflections, enable deep rook invasions, or deliver checkmate by eliminating all escape squares.
sub_patterns: King steps onto rank/file directly attacked by enemy rook
Pawn blocks king's only escape square enabling rook mate
King retreats to back rank inviting rook invasion with tempo on deflected piece

analysis.label: Moving a piece away from a critical defensive post toward an active or aggressive square, fatally exposing the king to tactical punishment.
analysis.description: In 6/6 positions, the blundering move relocates a piece from a square where it performs a vital defensive function (or ignores an urgent defensive need) to pursue an ostensibly active plan—attacking a pawn, developing naturally, or seeking improved piece placement. In 5/6 cases, the tactical motif tagged is 'king_safety,' and all analyses identify the exposed king as the central vulnerability exploited. The Ba5 moves (2/6) abandon the c3 bishop's guard of the a3 square, enabling Ba3+ check sequences that win the rook. Bc5 (1/6) develops aggressively while ignoring the hanging g5 pawn, allowing Nxg5-f7 fork. Ne2 (1/6) develops the knight but leaves the queen fatally exposed on g3 to Bh4. Kh3 (1/6) misplaces the king away from g2 where it enabled a key tactical resource. Rxd6 (1/6) captures material but disrupts coordination, leaving the f3 pawn undefended and the king on b4 exposed. The consistent thread is prioritizing offense or 'natural' moves over the position's actual defensive requirements.
analysis.move_pattern: A piece (often bishop) moves outward—away from the king's vicinity or defensive zone—typically toward a flank or aggressive diagonal, leaving critical squares or pawns unguarded
analysis.why_bad: The moved piece was performing an essential defensive function (guarding a key square near the king, maintaining coordination, or covering a vulnerability), and its departure allows forced tactical sequences exploiting the now-exposed king
sub_patterns: Bishop leaving king's defensive diagonal to attack a distant pawn (Ba5 x2)
Piece developing to an aggressive square while ignoring an immediate tactical threat to own position (Bc5, Ne2)
Rook/King moving to capture material or reposition while breaking defensive coordination (Rxd6, Kh3)

analysis.label: Playing superficially logical but non-urgent moves when the position demands immediate concrete action to either exploit an opponent's vulnerability or address one's own critical weakness.
analysis.description: This feature fires on positions where a player chooses a 'natural-looking' move that wastes a critical tempo, when the position actually demands immediate forcing play. In 8/10 positions, the correct moves involved either forcing tactical sequences (checks, captures, direct threats) or addressing an urgent vulnerability (castling, blocking a diagonal, defending a piece). Instead, the played moves are non-forcing redeployments (Bc5, Be7, Ng6), superficial attacks easily parried (Nh4 x2), premature pawn advances that create weaknesses (e5 x2, c5), passive support moves (Qe2), or capturing defended material (Nxe5). The common thread is that each move ignores the position's 'critical demand'—the one thing that MUST be addressed this turn—in favor of something that would be reasonable in a calmer position. In 7/10 cases, the opponent punishes by exploiting the exact vulnerability the player failed to address (unprotected pieces on diagonals in 3/10, exposed kings in 4/10, tactical forks/pins in 3/10). The average cp_loss of 287 with only 2.0 good moves available confirms these are high-precision moments where the player chose the obvious-looking but wrong plan.
analysis.move_pattern: Mixed piece types (knights, bishops, pawns, queen) moving to seemingly active but non-threatening squares; frequently knight moves to rim squares (h4, g6) or pawn advances to the 5th rank (e5, c5) without concrete follow-up
analysis.why_bad: Each move fails to address the position's critical tactical or strategic demand—whether that's exploiting an opponent's uncastled king with forcing moves, defending an unprotected piece on a vulnerable diagonal, or castling before the opponent strikes. The wasted tempo allows the opponent to either consolidate their position or launch a tactical combination that was previously impossible.
sub_patterns: Knight moves to rim squares (h4/g6) attacking a queen that simply sidesteps, forcing humiliating retreat
Premature e5/c5 pawn advances that weaken king position or abandon tactical defenses
Routine developing moves (Be7, Qe2) when urgent castling or counterplay is required
Slow piece repositioning when a forced tactical win exists (Bc5 instead of Ng5)
Removing a piece from a tactically essential defensive post (Ng6 abandoning e5 fork threat)

analysis.label: Moving a piece to a seemingly active but tactically vulnerable square, ignoring that the opponent can immediately exploit or win it.
analysis.description: In all 5 positions, the player moves a piece (queen 3/5, rook 1/5, bishop 1/5) to a square that appears aggressive or purposeful but is actually tactically exposed. In Position 1, Qa2 infiltrates the second rank but becomes disconnected from kingside defense, allowing Nxg6 to win material (5/5 ignore urgent needs). In Position 2, Bd3 looks like it supports e4 but blocks the d-pawn and becomes passive against ...d5 (5/5 pieces land on exploitable squares). In Position 4, Qe4 centralizes the queen but places it on the exact square targeted by Nf1-g3+ discovered attack fork (4/5 involve the moved piece becoming the direct tactical victim). In Position 5, Rh4 attacks the g4 bishop but the rook gets trapped by ...g5, losing the exchange (5/5 moves look active but worsen the position). In Position 6, Qg4 threatens g2 but the queen lands where Nxf6+ intermediate check then Nxg4 captures it cleanly (4/5 feature immediate tactical refutations winning the moved piece). The common thread: prioritizing superficial aggression over addressing critical positional demands (king safety, development, simplification), placing the piece where it becomes a tactical target rather than an asset.
analysis.move_pattern: Major piece (usually queen) moves to an apparently active square on an open rank/file/diagonal, typically forward or sideways into enemy territory or an exposed central square
analysis.why_bad: The piece lands on a square where it can be immediately exploited through tactical motifs (forks, traps, discovered attacks, intermediate checks), while simultaneously abandoning critical defensive or developmental duties that the position urgently required
sub_patterns: Queen moves to aggressive square where it gets forked or captured via zwischenzug
Rook lifts to exposed rank where pawn advance traps it
Piece retreats to blocking square that creates structural weakness
Major piece placed where discovered attack wins it

analysis.label: Playing a natural-looking or tempting move that ignores the position's single most critical demand, in narrow positions requiring precise action.
analysis.description: This feature activates when a player makes a move that appears productive—centralizing a king, capturing material, pushing a pawn, or repositioning a piece—but fatally neglects the one urgent requirement of the position. In 4/11 positions, the player ignored critical pawn tension that needed immediate resolution (Ke6, Kf6, h6, d4 all allowed the opponent to favorably resolve tension). In 4/11 positions, the player abandoned a critical defensive post or removed a key defender (Qf5 left c6 unguarded, Bf3 left the d5 outpost, Nxc6 vacated the e5 blockade, c4 removed d4's defender). In 3/11 positions, the player grabbed material while exposing themselves tactically (Qxd4 opened the d-file against their own king, Bd5+ aligned the bishop with their own king, Nxc6 opened a diagonal for the opponent's bishop). The positions average only 1.7 good moves, confirming these are critical junctures where only one or two precise moves maintain the position's integrity.
analysis.move_pattern: Any piece type moving to an apparently active/natural square (centralizing kings, capturing pawns, repositioning pieces, giving checks) while a more urgent concrete action exists elsewhere
analysis.why_bad: The position has a single critical demand—resolving pawn tension, maintaining a key defender, or addressing an immediate tactical threat—and the played move ignores it for a secondary benefit, allowing the opponent to exploit the neglected issue decisively
sub_patterns: King centralizes while critical pawn tension remains unresolved (opponent fixes structure favorably)
Piece abandons defensive post enabling opponent's tactical breakthrough
Material capture exposes own king or piece to tempo-gaining counterattack
Slow improving move when position demands immediate forcing action with tempo

analysis.label: Moving a well-placed piece away from a dominant or defensively critical square to an inferior position, creating immediate tactical vulnerabilities.
analysis.description: In 3/5 positions, a knight is moved away from a strong central or defensive square to a clearly inferior one (Nb8 from c6, Nf7 from d6, Nec6 from e5). In the remaining cases, moves ignore the critical tactical demands of the position by prioritizing non-urgent strategic goals (c5 ignores king safety; Qd7 ignores diagonal vulnerability). All five moves share the characteristic of looking 'reasonable' on the surface—retreating for defense, pushing for space, developing—while actually undermining the player's coordination at the most critical moment. The resulting positions uniformly allow the opponent to exploit the newly created weaknesses: vacated squares enable knight invasions (Nf6+ in position 12), blocked escape squares enable mating nets (Qb7+ in position 6), or abandoned defensive duties permit decisive attacks (Ng4+ Rf2+ in position 7).
analysis.move_pattern: Piece (often knight) moves laterally or backward away from a strong central/active square; pawn or queen makes a non-forcing move ignoring immediate threats
analysis.why_bad: Vacating the critical square either removes a key defender, blocks an escape route, creates a tactical alignment, or grants the opponent access to previously controlled squares—allowing immediate tactical punishment that the piece's former position would have prevented
sub_patterns: Knight retreats from central outpost to passive square (Nb8, Nf7, Nec6)
Strategic move ignoring mating threats to own king (c5)
Piece placement creating fatal alignment with own king (Qd7)

analysis.label: Knight moves to h4 or h5 to attack an opponent's bishop but hangs undefended to a queen capture along an open diagonal.
analysis.description: The dominant pattern (6/9 positions) involves a knight jumping to h4 or h5 in a closed-center opening to attack an enemy bishop (on f5, f4, or g3), but the knight lands completely undefended on the rim where the opponent's queen captures it for free via a clear diagonal (d8-h4 or d1-h5). An additional case (Na5, 7/9 total) shows a similar knight-to-rim sortie creating tactical catastrophe. The remaining positions (h6, O-O-O, Be6) share the broader pattern of moves with clear strategic rationale that create immediate tactical vulnerabilities in closed-center openings. All positions feature closed centers where the player appears to prioritize a positional/strategic idea (harassing a bishop, attacking a pawn, gaining piece activity) while completely overlooking a simple one-move tactical refutation. The average cp_loss of 387 confirms these are near-piece-value blunders, and the consistent availability of ~3 good alternatives shows they are entirely avoidable.
analysis.move_pattern: Knight from f3/f6 to h4/h5 (or occasionally to a-file rim), moving away from center toward an undefended rim square along the opponent's queen diagonal
analysis.why_bad: The knight lands on an undefended rim square that sits directly on the opponent's queen's open diagonal, allowing a simple one-move capture (Qxh4/Qxh5) winning a full piece for nothing. The strategic goal (bishop harassment) is pursued prematurely before establishing sufficient piece coordination or pawn support.
sub_patterns: Nh4 attacking Bf5 hanging to Qxh4
Nh5 attacking Bg3/Bf4 hanging to Qxh5
Knight to rim removing key defender creating tactical vulnerability
Piece placement on square vulnerable to pawn fork (d4-d5)

analysis.label: Moves that advance a piece or pawn forward when the position demands a retreat, defensive regrouping, or addressing a more urgent threat elsewhere.
analysis.description: This feature fires on moves that push forward (advancing king, bishop, or pawn) when the position critically demands restraint or retreat. In 5/7 positions, the correct move was explicitly a retreat or backward step (Kd1 over Kd3, Kf1 over Kf3, Ke2 over Bxb4, g4 counterplay over Bb4, king centralization over a5/d5). The blunders share the pattern of choosing a 'natural-looking' advancing move that appears purposeful—centralizing a king, blockading a pawn, gaining space—but actually wastes a critical tempo or walks into tactical vulnerabilities. In the catastrophic cases (2/7 resulting in forced mate), the king advanced into diagonal/check patterns; in the endgame cases (4/7), the forward move squandered tempi that were needed for addressing the real positional priority (king activity, counterplay on the correct wing, or neutralizing the actual threatening passed pawn).
analysis.move_pattern: Piece or pawn advances one square toward center or opponent's territory (king forward, bishop forward/capturing, pawn push) when backward or lateral moves are required
analysis.why_bad: The advancing move either exposes the king to tactical patterns (diagonal checks, mating nets), wastes a critical tempo when the position demands immediate action on a different priority, or abandons defensive control of key squares—allowing the opponent to exploit the real threat unopposed.
sub_patterns: King advancing into exposed squares instead of retreating to safety (Kd3, Kf3)
Bishop relocating forward to address wrong threat while ignoring the critical one (Bg6, Bb4)
Pawn advance wasting tempo when king activity is paramount (a5, d5)
Trading pieces forward when preserving them via retreat maintains defensive resources (Bxb4)

analysis.label: Playing a passive, preparatory, or non-urgent move in a position that demands immediate concrete action, gifting the opponent a critical tempo.
analysis.description: This feature fires on positions where the player makes a move that addresses a secondary concern (defending a pawn, prophylactic preparation, grabbing edge material, slow repositioning) while ignoring the position's most urgent demand. In 7/10 cases the primary tag is 'tempo_loss.' The best moves almost always involve immediate concrete threats: advancing passed pawns (Position 3: f4 instead of a3), executing central breaks (Position 13: f5 instead of Rf2), developing with threats (Position 6: Nf6 instead of c6), or creating active counterplay (Position 11: b5 instead of Rc7). The average of only 1.6 good moves available confirms these are critical-timing positions where the margin for error is essentially zero. In every case, the opponent punishes by seizing the initiative first—pushing passed pawns, executing the central break the player should have preempted, or exploiting the displaced piece with tempo.
analysis.move_pattern: Mixed piece types and directions; typically non-forcing moves (no checks, non-critical captures) that reposition pieces laterally/backward or advance non-essential pawns
analysis.why_bad: The position demands immediate concrete action (a central break, passed pawn advance, or piece activation with threats), but the player wastes a tempo on a secondary goal, allowing the opponent to execute their plan first or exploit the misplaced/slow piece with tempo-gaining attacks.
sub_patterns: Prophylactic pawn moves when development/advance is urgent (a3, c6, g6)
Preparatory rook lifts/retreats when immediate central breaks are available (Rf2, Rh7, Rc7)
Piece moves to squares vulnerable to tempo-gaining attacks (Ne3, Nc5, Qd3)
Irrelevant material grabs that sideline key pieces (Qxh2)

analysis.label: Player chooses a superficially attractive move (capture, advance, centralization, check) that ignores the specific critical requirement of the position, leading to a catastrophic evaluation drop.
analysis.description: This feature fires on positions where players select moves that appear natural or aggressive by general chess principles but miss the concrete tactical or positional demand of the specific position. In 6/10 cases, the best move was a quiet defensive, prophylactic, or preparatory move (Rg8, Kh5, Nh6, Ka5, Bd3, Be2) while the player chose something more active-looking. In 3/10 cases, the player missed a decisive simplification or checkmate (Qa4#, Qxf4+, Ra7). The played moves span captures with check (Qxd4+, Qxb2+), pawn advances (h5, cxd4, d4), piece centralizations (Be5, Bc4, Nf3, Qe7), and king moves (Kd2)—all appearing reasonable by general principles but specifically wrong due to an overlooked tactical vulnerability. The average cp_loss of 2115 with only 1.9 good moves available indicates these are critical moments requiring precise calculation, where autopilot play is severely punished.
analysis.move_pattern: Varied piece types moving to apparently active/natural squares (captures, checks, centralizations, standard developments) when the position demands a specific quiet or precise alternative
analysis.why_bad: Each move ignores the position's critical demand—whether it's blocking an open file (Nf3/Bc4), maintaining a key defensive barrier (cxd4/h5), avoiding self-pins or hanging pieces (Be5/Qe7), preserving king safety (Kd2), or recognizing a winning simplification/mate (Qxb2+/d4). The superficially attractive idea (capture material, centralize, advance) blinds the player to the concrete tactical punishment.
sub_patterns: Capturing/advancing when defensive preparation is required (h5, cxd4, d4, Kd2)
Developing/centralizing pieces that create self-blocks or leave critical squares unguarded (Qe7, Bc4, Nf3, Be5)
Taking impulsive captures with check when forced mate or winning trade exists (Qxb2+, Qxd4+)

analysis.label: Playing a plausible-looking but non-critical move in a position with very few good options that demands immediate precise action to address a concrete tactical reality.
analysis.description: This feature detects moves that waste a critical tempo by pursuing a secondary strategic goal while ignoring the position's most urgent tactical demand. In 6/6 detailed positions, the played move addresses a reasonable-sounding concern (escaping a diagonal, reinforcing pawn structure, attacking the opponent's king, developing a piece, gaining space) but fatally overlooks the one thing the position requires RIGHT NOW. The positions share extremely narrow margins (avg 1.5 good moves), meaning only precise action works. In 4/6 cases the move is a pawn push (f6, c6, h5, a5) that seems thematic but wastes the critical tempo. The tagged motif is 'tempo_loss' in 5/6 positions. In every case, the opponent has a concrete tactical resource (winning a hanging piece in 2/6, advancing a devastating passed pawn in 1/6, exploiting a cleared diagonal/square in 3/6) that the played move does nothing to prevent or address.
analysis.move_pattern: Non-forcing, non-capturing moves (often pawn pushes to flanks, or king/piece sidesteps) that don't interact with the critical tactical tension in the position
analysis.why_bad: These moves waste the one available tempo in positions where only immediate engagement with the critical threat/opportunity preserves the evaluation—they allow the opponent to execute a concrete tactical blow (capturing undefended pieces, advancing passed pawns, invading weakened squares) that the position's narrow margin cannot tolerate.
sub_patterns: Flank pawn pushes (a5, h5, f6, c6) when development or central action is required
King moves to the wrong square enabling a specific tactical resource (Ka6, Kf1)
Quiet piece development ignoring a hanging piece or forced sequence (Bc4)
Aggressive queen placement abandoning critical defensive duties (Qh3)

analysis.label: Advancing the g-pawn aggressively (g4 or g5) in the opening while underdeveloped and with the king uncastled.
analysis.description: In all 9/9 positions, the blundering side advances their g-pawn two squares (g4 for White, g5 for Black) during the opening with a closed center. In 8/9 cases, the moving side's king remains uncastled in the center. In nearly all cases, the moving side has severe developmental deficiencies (often both knights undeveloped or no minor pieces out). The typical intent is to chase an enemy knight from f6/f3 (preparing g5/g4 follow-up) or to prevent a bishop move (Bg5). The queen is frequently placed on an aggressive but exposed square (f3 for White in 4/5 White positions, f6 for Black in 4/4 Black positions), creating a thematic connection between the premature queen sortie and the g-pawn lunge meant to support it. Refutations consistently involve central strikes (d4/d5 appearing in 7/9 positions as top punishments), simple capture of the undefended g-pawn, or knight centralization to dominant squares exploiting the weakened position.
analysis.move_pattern: g-pawn advance two squares forward (g2-g4 for White, g7-g5 for Black), non-capture, non-check
analysis.why_bad: The g-pawn advance wastes a critical development tempo, structurally weakens the kingside around the uncastled king, often leaves the g-pawn itself undefended as a tactical target, and invites devastating central counterstrikes (d4/d5) that open lines against the exposed king before any attack materializes.
sub_patterns: White plays g4 with queen on f3 intending g5 to chase Nf6
Black plays g5 with queen on f6 to prevent Bg5 or prepare g4
g-pawn advance leaves pawn undefended, captured with tempo on queen
Central break (d4/d5) punishes flank advance against uncastled king

analysis.label: Moves that pursue a secondary plan while failing to address the position's most urgent tactical or structural requirement.
analysis.description: This feature fires on positions where the player makes a purposeful-looking move with a clear strategic intention (fianchetto preparation, pawn grab, space gain, knight sortie) but ignores the position's most critical concrete demand. In 4/6 positions, the played move is a slow or self-focused decision while the opponent has an immediate tactical resource (Nxd4 exploiting unresolved central tension, Qc4+ exploiting an opened diagonal, Bxf6/Qxd6 exploiting a newly weakened pawn, Nxf7 fork on an undefended square). In 5/6 positions, multiple clearly superior alternatives existed that directly addressed the urgent issue. The refutations are always concrete tactical punishments—captures of undefended material (2/6), checks exploiting opened lines (2/6), forks on weak squares (1/6)—that were either already latent or directly created by the played move. The one exception (Kf4, 1cp loss) appears to be a position-type activation rather than a true mistake detection.
analysis.move_pattern: Diverse piece types and directions; no geometric consistency. Moves include quiet pawn pushes (b3, e5, g6), captures (Rxb2), knight jumps (Nb5), and king moves (Kf4).
analysis.why_bad: Each move prioritizes the player's own plan (fianchetto, material gain, space, threats) while failing to calculate the opponent's strongest tactical response to an existing or newly-created vulnerability in the position.
sub_patterns: Slow preparatory moves ignoring unresolved central tension (b3, g6)
Materialistic pawn grabs that create tactical weaknesses (Rxb2)
Structural pawn advances creating permanent positional damage (e5)
Aggressive piece moves to capturable squares (Nb5)

analysis.label: Advancing a pawn to open the center before the position can support the resulting tactical complications.
analysis.description: This feature fires on moves that prematurely open or disrupt the pawn structure—most commonly central pawn advances (d4, d5, e5, e3)—when the player's position lacks the development, king safety, or piece coordination to handle the tactical consequences. In 7/9 positions, the blunder is a pawn push that opens lines or removes a critical pawn defender while the player's king remains uncastled or exposed. In 6/9 cases, the player's king is still in the center (e1/e8) when they initiate the break. The remaining positions (Qd4, Rd7+, a6) share the broader theme of aggressive committal actions that create concrete vulnerabilities the position cannot support—whether exposing queenside targets (a6, Qd4) or granting the opponent beneficial tempi (Rd7+). The typical refutation involves the opponent exploiting newly-hanging pawns (e.g., e5 leaving d5 undefended in positions 2 and 8), tactical pins/forks enabled by the opened lines (position 15), or captures with tempo against the exposed king (positions 6, 7, 8).
analysis.move_pattern: Pawn advance (d4/d5/e5/e3) toward or in the center, typically one square forward; less commonly an aggressive piece commitment (queen or rook) that overextends
analysis.why_bad: The advance opens the position before the player's pieces are developed enough to contest the resulting tactical complications—it removes key pawn defenders, creates hanging pawns, or opens files/diagonals that benefit the opponent's already-active pieces while the player's king remains vulnerable in the center.
sub_patterns: Central break removing a pawn's defensive support (e5 leaving d5 hanging, d5 leaving e5 hanging)
Central advance with king uncastled, allowing opponent to exploit open lines against the king
Pawn advance opening diagonal for opponent's fianchettoed bishop
Pawn move creating a fixed target that opponent's king/pieces can immediately attack
Aggressive piece move (check/queen sortie) that surrenders positional integrity for illusory initiative

analysis.label: Pieces retreat to seemingly safe kingside squares (especially f1/g7) while ignoring or creating catastrophic king safety threats.
analysis.description: In all 3/3 positions, the player moves a piece to what appears to be a safe or defensive square on the kingside (Kf1, Bf1, Kg7) but catastrophically fails to address the most urgent threat in the position. In 2/3 cases the destination is specifically f1. In all cases, the correct approach required a precise defensive move addressing an immediate tactical crisis: Kh1 to allow Bf1 retreat (Position 2), h5/h6 to create luft against back-rank mate (Position 3), and Rf7 to block a mating queen sequence (Position 4). Instead, the played moves either self-block critical defensive resources (Kf1 blocking bishop retreat, 1/3), ignore immediate checkmate (Bf1 allowing Re8#, 1/3), or walk directly into a mating attack (Kg7 allowing Qg6+, 1/3). The average cp_loss of 6369 reflects that these 'quiet' moves trigger immediate tactical catastrophes.
analysis.move_pattern: King or minor piece retreating to kingside first/second rank squares (f1, g7) — non-capturing, non-checking quiet moves near own king
analysis.why_bad: The move addresses a secondary concern (escaping pressure, retreating a piece, leaving the back rank) while ignoring the position's single most critical threat, which required a specific prophylactic or defensive resource that the played move either blocks or renders impossible.
sub_patterns: King to f1 blocking bishop retreat causing piece loss
Bishop to f1 ignoring immediate back-rank mate
King advancing into open file/diagonal allowing forced mating sequence

analysis.label: Moves that waste tempo on peripheral concerns while the position demands immediate attention to the most urgent vulnerability.
analysis.description: This feature fires on moves that neglect the single most critical defensive requirement in the position, typically choosing a tempting but non-urgent alternative. In 4/7 positions, king safety was the primary ignored concern (a4 ignoring uncastled king on open e-file, Nd7 self-blocking the king allowing forced mate, Rxb2 abandoning kingside defenders, Qe2 blocking the critical Ne2 defensive resource). In 2/7 positions, piece activity/placement was the key issue (Rxh4 capturing with the wrong piece making the rook passive, Kf7 failing to address critical bishop tension). In 1/7 positions, the king captured to a worse square despite eliminating a threat (Kxc3). The common diagnostic: positions averaged only 2.1 good moves available, indicating narrow critical moments where the one urgent task must be addressed, yet the player chose something secondary—a flank pawn push, a pawn grab, a developing move to the wrong square, or a passive repositioning.
analysis.move_pattern: Diverse piece types and directions; unifying geometric feature is that the move operates in a zone or on a square irrelevant to the position's critical vulnerability
analysis.why_bad: Each move spends a tempo on something secondary (flank expansion, material grab, non-urgent development, wrong capture piece) while the position has exactly one critical problem demanding immediate attention—typically exposed king, undefended piece coordination, or critical square control—allowing the opponent to exploit the unaddressed vulnerability with forcing moves
sub_patterns: Pawn grabs or captures that pull pieces away from the critical defensive zone (Rxb2, a4)
Piece moves that block critical defensive squares or self-block escape routes (Nd7, Qe2)
Capturing with the wrong piece, creating passivity (Rxh4, Kxc3)
Non-urgent king or piece repositioning when tactical tension demands immediate resolution (Kf7)

analysis.label: Positionally-motivated moves that ignore immediate tactical dangers to one's own vulnerable king, allowing decisive exploitation through forcing sequences.
analysis.description: In all 4 positions, the player's king is either exposed in the center, has a weakened pawn shield, or relies on specific piece defense. Instead of addressing this urgent tactical situation, the player makes a 'logically appealing' but non-forcing move: fianchettoing a bishop (b6, 1/4), challenging a centralized piece with a pawn (f3, 1/4), repositioning the queen to a seemingly useful square (Qf7, 1/4), or centralizing a knight on a classic outpost (Nd5, 1/4). In every case (4/4), the refutation exploits king vulnerability through immediate forcing moves—checks, discovered attacks, or pawn advances that seal off defenders—leading to material loss or mate. The common error is prioritizing long-term positional improvement over the concrete tactical demands of a position where the king is already in danger.
analysis.move_pattern: Non-forcing, non-defensive moves (various piece types and directions) played when the moving side's king is exposed or critically vulnerable
analysis.why_bad: The position demands immediate concrete action to address king safety, but the quiet move either weakens the king further (f3 opens diagonal), abandons a critical defensive post (Qf7 leaves g6/h6 unguarded), creates a hanging target near the exposed king (Nd5), or wastes tempo while tactical threats build (b6 ignores central tension). The opponent punishes with checks and forcing sequences that exploit the unaddressed vulnerability.
sub_patterns: Pawn advance weakening own king's diagonal/square coverage
Queen abandoning critical defensive post near the king
Piece centralization creating a tactical target while king is exposed
Slow flank move ignoring urgent central/tactical demands with king uncastled

analysis.label: Playing a non-urgent or passive move in a position that demands immediate action to address a critical king-safety or tactical threat.
analysis.description: In all 5/5 positions, the player makes a 'reasonable-looking' quiet move while ignoring an urgent positional or tactical demand. In Position 5, Kh3 walks into a pawn check instead of resolving g4 tension. In Position 7, Bb5 abandons defense of e6, enabling a devastating e6 pawn break. In Position 8, Rfe8 is passive when active Rd4 was needed to generate counterplay against White's kingside attack. In Position 11, Rd7 interposes when the king needed to flee immediately (Kf6). In Position 13, a5 pushes a flank pawn while the center demands f5/f6 to neutralize a knight on g5 and protect the e4 pawn. All 5/5 positions had very few good alternatives (avg 1.6), indicating critical-moment positions where only precise moves survive. All 5/5 feature 'tempo_loss' as a core theme, and 4/5 involve direct king-safety consequences. The opponent exploits the wasted tempo with immediate tactical strikes (checks, captures, pawn breaks).
analysis.move_pattern: Any piece type making a quiet (non-checking, non-capturing) move that does not address the most critical threat in the position; often a piece 'improvement' or flank operation while the center/kingside burns
analysis.why_bad: The position has one critical demand (usually king safety or a tactical threat) requiring immediate attention, but the move wastes a tempo on something non-urgent, allowing the opponent to execute a decisive tactical blow (pawn break with check, mating attack, material win) that the correct move would have prevented or mitigated.
sub_patterns: King retreat into a worse square (walking into check lines)
Bishop relocation abandoning a key defensive duty
Passive rook move failing to generate needed counterplay
Flank pawn push ignoring central/kingside emergency
Piece interposition on a square where it can be captured with check

analysis.label: King moves toward the edge or corner of the board when centralizing or moving inward was required for safety and activity.
analysis.description: In all 8 positions, the king moves to a square on the rim or corner of the board (a1, a4, h1, h5, h6, b4) when the best move would centralize or keep the king on more interior squares with greater escape options. The corners/edges create traps: Ka1 positions (3/8) allow back-rank check harassment; Kh6 positions (2/8) enable g5+ pawn checks winning material; Kh5 (1/8) allows h-file double-check sequences winning a rook; Ka4 (1/8) enables pawn-advance checks exploiting the edge placement; Kb4 (1/8) allows queen check leading to forced mate; Kh1 (1/8) wastes tempo via back-rank check forcing the king to retrace. In every case, the superior alternatives (Ka3, Kb2, Kb3, Kf5, Kf6, Kg3, Kd2) move toward the center where the king has more flight squares, better coordination with remaining pieces, and avoids tactical forcing sequences that exploit edge/corner geometry.
analysis.move_pattern: King moves toward the a-file, h-file, or corner squares (rank 1/8 or files a/h), moving away from the board center
analysis.why_bad: Edge and corner squares give the king fewer escape routes, making it vulnerable to forcing check sequences, back-rank exploitation, pawn-advance checks, and mating patterns that wouldn't work if the king had more central flight squares.
sub_patterns: King retreats to corner (a1/h1) allowing back-rank check harassment
King moves to h6 enabling g5+ pawn check winning the defending knight
King advances to exposed edge square (a4/b4) enabling check-based tactics
King moves to h-file edge allowing rook skewer/double-check sequences

analysis.label: Plausible-looking moves that address a secondary concern while ignoring the single most urgent tactical or structural requirement of the position.
analysis.description: This feature activates on positions with very limited good options (avg 2.1) where the player makes a 'constructive-looking' move that pursues a recognizable chess goal but catastrophically ignores what the position actually demands. In 7/9 cases, the moves involve significant tempo loss by misprioritizing. Key examples: Nb4 pursues an 'aggressive' outpost instead of the urgent recapture Qxd5 (1/9); Nc5 seeks an 'active' outpost but abandons the critical defensive role guarding e5 (1/9); Re6+ plays a tempting check but ignores a hanging knight (1/9); c4 pursues queenside activity but neglects the perpetual check vulnerability requiring king escape preparation (1/9); e4 grabs central space but creates a deflection target in the pawn structure (1/9); Qd1 retreats to 'safety' but surrenders all initiative allowing d5 break (1/9); b6 seemingly stabilizes but creates a fixed target for a4-a5 lever (1/9). The common thread is that each position has one narrow critical need—piece rescue, defensive duty, king safety, or recapture—and the player instead pursues a secondary plan that looks reasonable in isolation but is concretely refuted.
analysis.move_pattern: Mixed piece types and directions; typically constructive-appearing moves (forward knight placements, pawn advances, checks, or retreats) that address a non-critical aspect of the position
analysis.why_bad: Each position has one urgent concrete demand (save a hanging piece, create king escape, maintain a defensive duty, recapture material, preserve critical pawn structure) that the move ignores, allowing the opponent to immediately exploit the neglected vulnerability with a forcing sequence
sub_patterns: Active-looking knight moves that abandon critical defensive duties
Pawn advances that create fixed targets or weaken structure at critical moments
Tempting checks or captures that ignore more urgent hanging material
Passive retreats that surrender tempo when the position demanded maintaining initiative

analysis.label: Playing a non-urgent 'improving' move that wastes a critical tempo, allowing the opponent to execute a devastating knight jump or tactical blow.
analysis.description: In 4/5 positions, the punishment for the blunder is specifically a knight tactic (Nd5 fork in position 2, Ng5 invasion in position 5, Nh4 fork in position 10, Nxd4 capture in position 11), while position 1 features a queen check exploiting an abandoned square. All five moves are non-forcing 'routine' plays—centralizing a queen (Qe4, Qe2), castling (O-O), repositioning a knight passively (Ne7), or making luft (h6)—that look constructive but ignore an imminent tactical vulnerability. In every case, the player had 2-3 good alternatives (avg 2.4) that either created immediate threats or directly addressed the tactical weakness. The blunders share the pattern of prioritizing general position improvement over concrete tactical necessity, losing an average of 247 centipawns by gifting the opponent a free tempo to execute a forcing blow.
analysis.move_pattern: Non-forcing, non-defensive moves (queen centralization, castling, knight retreat, pawn push) that neither create threats nor address an imminent tactical vulnerability
analysis.why_bad: Each move wastes the tempo needed to prevent or neutralize an opponent's tactical resource (usually a knight invasion to an uncontested square), leaving a piece, pawn, or king fatally exposed to a forcing blow that was already 'in the air'
sub_patterns: Queen moves abandoning defense of key square (Qe4/Qe2)
Premature castling ignoring central knight outpost (O-O)
Passive piece repositioning allowing knight invasion (Ne7)
Slow pawn move ignoring piece vulnerability to knight fork (h6)

analysis.label: Moving a piece (usually the king) to a square that looks safe or active but actually enables the opponent to force perpetual check or checkmate through exposed king geometry.
analysis.description: In 5/5 positions, the played move worsens the player's own king safety catastrophically by either placing the king on a square vulnerable to forcing check sequences or blocking/ignoring critical escape routes. In 3/5 cases (Kf8, Kf6, Kg8), the king itself moves to a square that walks directly into check corridors—back ranks or files controlled by the opponent's queen/rook. In 1/5 cases (Rf8), a piece blocks the king's escape square, enabling immediate checkmate. In 1/5 cases (Qd3), the move ignores an imminent mating threat that required a specific blocking move. The correct moves in all positions were counterintuitive defensive resources: advancing the king forward (Kf6 in pos 1, Ke7 in pos 11), moving the rook away (Rf2 in pos 6), moving the queen instead of the rook (Qf8 in pos 12), or blocking a critical diagonal (d4 in pos 15). The result in 3/5 cases is perpetual check drawing a won position, and in 2/5 cases is forced checkmate.
analysis.move_pattern: King or piece moves to a square on the f-file or back rank that appears natural/safe but lies within the opponent's queen/rook checking geometry
analysis.why_bad: The move places the king on a square (or blocks its escape to a safe square) where the opponent's major pieces can initiate an inescapable sequence of checks—either perpetual check drawing a won game or forced checkmate—because the king has no shelter from the checking lines.
sub_patterns: King retreats to back rank allowing perpetual check via queen bouncing between ranks/files
King advances into an open file creating discovered capture or check of a defending piece
Piece self-blocks the king's escape square enabling immediate checkmate
Active-looking move ignores critical diagonal/file mating threat requiring a blocking move

analysis.label: Moving a key piece (usually the queen) to the a/b-file area while urgent tactical demands exist in the center or kingside.
analysis.description: This feature fires on moves that decentralize a critical piece—predominantly the queen—to the queenside (a-file or b-file squares) when the tactical demands of the position lie elsewhere. In 6/10 top activations, the queen specifically moves to a2, b2, b3, b6, b7, or captures on a2, abandoning defensive coverage of the king (positions 1, 4, 5, 8) or missing decisive central/e-file tactical combinations (positions 3, 7). The remaining activations follow the same principle of peripheral decentralization: Rd1 leaves the critical e-file (position 6), Rc8 moves to a square where the piece is trapped (position 7), Be6 misses a forced queen trade (position 1), and Kd3 ignores a free pawn capture (position 8). In all cases, the opponent punishes by exploiting the now-undefended center or launching kingside attacks that the displaced piece cannot help counter. The average cp_loss of 1355 reflects that these positions typically have one or few good moves demanding precision, and the drift to the periphery catastrophically misses them.
analysis.move_pattern: Queen (or major piece) moving to a2, b2, b3, b6, b7 squares—generally lateral/diagonal movement toward the a/b-file queenside region, away from central files (d/e) or kingside
analysis.why_bad: The piece abandons critical central or kingside responsibilities (defending the king, maintaining tactical threats, controlling key files) to chase peripheral material or reach seemingly active but tactically irrelevant squares, granting the opponent tempo to execute devastating attacks, back-rank mates, passed pawn advances, or forced winning combinations.
sub_patterns: Queen captures peripheral pawn on a2 (greedy pawn grab)
Queen retreats to b-file abandoning d/e-file control
Queen moves to b6/b7 targeting pawns while kingside collapses
Major piece leaves critical open file for irrelevant square

analysis.label: Moves that place pieces on superficially active squares while ignoring the position's most urgent defensive or structural demand.
analysis.description: In all 5 positions, the player makes a move that looks purposeful or aggressive but fundamentally neglects the position's most critical requirement. In Position 1, Bc4 places the bishop on an 'active' diagonal targeting f7 while leaving it undefended (best was modest Be2/Bf1 retreat). In Position 3, Qe5 aggressively centralizes the queen but ignores the king's vulnerability to Nc6+Qh4+ (best was quiet Nd2 development). In Position 6, Qg5 seeks illusory kingside threats while ignoring the dominant Nd6 problem (best was Nc8 challenging it). In Position 11, Nc4 goes to an active-looking square near White's king but ignores the existential e7 promotion threat (best was Nc6 attacking the supporting rook). In Position 12, c3 appears to shore up the queenside but fatally blocks the knight's escape from a4 (best was Re2/Nc3 reactivating the knight). All 5/5 positions show the player choosing apparent activity over addressing the one thing that truly matters, and in 4/5 cases the correct move involved a more modest or defensive handling of the same piece or problem.
analysis.move_pattern: Piece or pawn placed on forward/active-looking square (typically 4th-5th rank or toward opponent's king) instead of addressing a retreating, defensive, or piece-coordination need
analysis.why_bad: The moves ignore the position's most critical demand—whether it's a tactical threat, a trapped/exposed piece, or a dominant enemy piece—allowing the opponent to exploit the neglected weakness with tempo-gaining attacks, piece captures, or decisive threats that the 'active' move cannot address.
sub_patterns: Piece to active square while leaving it undefended (Bc4, Qe5)
Queen sortie ignoring positional crisis elsewhere (Qg5)
Knight to wrong active square ignoring existential threat (Nc4 vs Nc6)
Pawn move blocking own piece's critical retreat (c3 trapping Na4)

analysis.label: Active or aggressive moves that ignore a critical king safety vulnerability, allowing the opponent to exploit exposed king positions with decisive tactical force.
analysis.description: This feature fires on moves where the player prioritizes an attacking or seemingly purposeful plan while failing to address an urgent king safety crisis. In 7/9 positions, one or both kings are exposed or uncastled, and the move played either directly worsens the player's own king safety (f6 weakening pawn shield, Ke3/Kd7 walking into fork/attack zones, Bxh6 sacrificing with king on e1) or ignores the opponent's immediate tactical threats targeting the king (Bb7 ignoring discovered check mechanism, Rd7 walking into discovered attack, Ng4/Ng5 overextending while critical defensive squares are abandoned). The positions average only 2.0 good moves available, indicating narrow tactical paths where precision was mandatory. The average cp_loss of 1360 reflects catastrophic punishment—including one forced mate—because the opponent's refutations consistently exploit the king exposure with discovered attacks (3/9), forks (1/9), or pawn storms against centrally-placed kings (2/9). The common intent behind these moves was always plausible (challenge a strong pawn, develop a bishop, attack a defender, advance with tempo), but the player consistently underestimated the tactical consequences flowing from king vulnerability.
analysis.move_pattern: Various piece types moving forward/aggressively (knight jumps to g4/g5, king advances to e3/d7, pawn pushes f6/g6+, bishop development/capture) while own king is exposed or uncastled
analysis.why_bad: Each move ignores an immediate tactical emergency related to king safety—either directly weakening the king's position, walking the king into tactical motifs (forks, discovered attacks), or allowing the opponent to exploit an existing king exposure with forcing moves that gain decisive material or deliver checkmate.
sub_patterns: King voluntarily walking into fork/attack zones (Ke3, Kd7)
Aggressive piece jumps abandoning critical defensive squares (Ng4, Ng5)
Ignoring discovered attack/check mechanisms against own king (Bb7, Rd7)
Premature pawn advances weakening own king shelter (f6, g6+)
Unsound sacrifices launched without sufficient support while own king is uncastled (Bxh6)

analysis.label: Natural-looking moves that squander a critical tactical opportunity in positions where only one or two precise continuations maintain the advantage.
analysis.description: This feature fires on positions with very narrow best-play requirements (avg 1.4 good moves available) where the player chooses a plausible-looking, superficially active move instead of the single precise continuation the position demands. In 4/5 cases the primary tactical motif is tempo_loss - the move either wastes a critical tempo on preparation when immediate action is needed (Position 2: Rfe1 instead of Ng5; Position 10: Rxh3 instead of Rdg1), attacks prematurely without proper preparation (Position 4: Ng5 before Rae1), or repositions a key piece away from its optimal coordinating square (Position 6: Qc6 abandoning the lethal c4 post; Position 15: Qh5 creating fork vulnerability). All 5/5 positions are middlegame attacks where piece coordination and timing are paramount, and 4/5 involve king safety as a central theme. The moves share the quality of appearing reasonable to a human eye - development, centralization, captures, aggressive squares - but each fails to address the ONE specific tactical or positional demand of the moment.
analysis.move_pattern: Various piece types moved to apparently active/natural squares (open files, attacking posts, central squares) in sharp middlegame positions
analysis.why_bad: Each move wastes a critical tempo or disrupts piece coordination in a position where only 1-2 precise moves maintain the advantage, giving the opponent time to consolidate, escape, or exploit newly created tactical vulnerabilities
sub_patterns: Preparatory developing move when immediate tactical strike is required
Premature attack without necessary preparatory move (move order error)
Queen repositioning away from optimal coordinating square
Capturing an irrelevant pawn instead of continuing the main attack

analysis.label: Moving a piece/pawn away from a critical defensive role to an aggressive-looking square, leaving a piece or square fatally unguarded.
analysis.description: In all 4 positions, the player moved a piece or pawn that was the sole defender of something critical, motivated by 'active' play (development, space-gaining, or attack). In Position 3 (Bc4), the f1-bishop was the only guardian of g2, and moving it allowed Bxg2 winning the rook (1/4). In Position 6 (d5), the d7-pawn shielded the king from the b5-e8 diagonal, and advancing it enabled Bb5+ with a devastating knight fork (1/4). In Position 8 (Qh5), the queen on f7 was protecting the rook on d7, and moving it to 'attack' allowed simple Qxd7 winning a full rook (1/4). In Position 13 (Qf5), the queen on c8 was defending the rook on a8, and centralizing it allowed Qxa8 capturing the undefended rook (1/4). All 4/4 moves went to ostensibly active squares but ignored that the moving piece was the sole guardian of something vital. The tactical motif is 'hanging_piece' in 3/4 cases, with 1/4 being a fork enabled by opening a diagonal.
analysis.move_pattern: Any piece type moving FROM a square where it defends a critical asset TO an aggressive/active square (development diagonal, attacking square, central outpost), typically forward or laterally toward the opponent's king
analysis.why_bad: The moved piece was the sole defender of a critical piece or square; relocating it for 'active' purposes leaves something immediately hanging or exposes a fatal tactical vulnerability that the opponent can exploit with a simple capture or forcing sequence.
sub_patterns: Queen abandons protection of a rook to play aggressively (Qh5, Qf5)
Bishop/pawn leaves guard of a key square or diagonal enabling checks/captures (Bc4, d5)

analysis.label: Non-forcing moves that look reasonable but fatally ignore or worsen king vulnerability, allowing the opponent immediate tactical exploitation.
analysis.description: This feature fires on moves where the player makes a seemingly natural choice (material grab, passive retreat, or quiet centralization) while their own or the opponent's king is exposed, and the position demands immediate forcing action. In 7/9 positions, the player's own king is exposed or in the center; in 8/9, the move either creates a new geometric weakness (f4 and f3 opening king diagonals in positions 10,11) or wastes a critical tempo needed to address king safety (Qd1 and Bh2 retreating from active posts in positions 8,15). The blunders typically enable the opponent's forcing continuations: perpetual checks (position 1), knight forks exploiting newly-opened lines (positions 11,13), queen checks winning material via skewers (positions 7,10), or immediate tactical invasions (positions 3,8). The average cp_loss of 1341 and average of only 1.8 good moves available confirms these are critical moments where precision is essential but the player chooses a superficially logical move over the one forcing continuation that addresses the position's tactical demands.
analysis.move_pattern: Non-forcing moves (retreats, captures, pawn pushes, quiet centralizations) in positions with exposed kings - no checks given, often moving away from the critical zone
analysis.why_bad: The moves either open new lines to the player's own king (f-pawn advances opening diagonals), abandon defensive posts creating undefended targets (queen/bishop retreats), or grab material while ignoring the opponent's immediate forcing replies (checks, forks, perpetuals) that exploit existing king exposure.
sub_patterns: f-pawn advances opening diagonal to own castled king (f4, f3)
Queen/bishop retreats abandoning active defensive posts (Qd1, Bh2)
Material grabs ignoring opponent's forcing tactical reply (Qxg3, Bxe5)
Queen placement on forkable square with king in center (Qe3)
King move to intersection of multiple checking routes (Kf7)

analysis.label: Developing a piece (usually a bishop) to a square where the opponent can immediately gain tempo with a pawn advance that also achieves a secondary tactical or strategic goal.
analysis.description: In 8/11 positions, a bishop is developed to what appears to be an active square (Be6, Bf5, Be3, Bxf5) but is immediately punishable by a pawn advance that attacks it with tempo. In 8/11 cases, the refuting pawn thrust is the d-pawn (d4 or d5), which simultaneously attacks the piece and creates a fork (positions 1, 4, 6, 10), opens the center against an uncastled king (position 12), or wins material through the pin/tension (position 2). The g4 advance punishes Bf5 in 2/11 cases by attacking the undefended bishop while gaining kingside space. The remaining pawn moves (e5, b4, b5) share the same structural flaw: they enable the opponent's pawn advance (dxe5, c5, d4) that gains decisive tempo. The common thread is that the player makes a natural-looking developing or space-gaining move without recognizing that the opponent has a concrete pawn thrust available that attacks the moved piece while simultaneously achieving a second objective—whether a fork, a center breakthrough, or exploiting king exposure.
analysis.move_pattern: Bishop (or piece) moves to a central square (e6, f5, e3, e4) along a diagonal or to a seemingly active post; occasionally a pawn advances prematurely. The destination square is always within one move of being attacked by an opponent's pawn.
analysis.why_bad: The piece lands on a square immediately targetable by a pawn advance (usually d4-d5 or g4) that gains tempo while simultaneously achieving a second tactical goal—forking another piece, opening the center against an exposed king, or creating a dominant pawn wedge. The player resolves piece development before resolving central pawn tension, allowing the opponent's pawn thrust to serve double duty.
sub_patterns: Be6 punished by d4-d5 forking bishop and knight on c6 (3/11 positions)
Bf5 punished by g4 attacking undefended bishop with kingside expansion (2/11 positions)
Piece placement creating pawn fork target alongside another piece on same rank/diagonal (positions 4, 6)
Premature pawn advance enabling opponent's counter-pawn break with tempo (e5→dxe5, b4→c5, b5→d4)

analysis.label: Moving the king backward (or failing to advance it) in endgame positions where king advancement toward the opponent is the critical winning technique.
analysis.description: In 6/8 positions, the actual move is a direct king retreat (Ke3 retreating from f4, Ke5 moving away from Black's king on a5, Kh6 retreating from g5, Kf3 retreating from g4, Kf3 retreating from f4). In 1/8 positions (Rf4), the player activates the rook instead of advancing the king (Kf4 was best). In 1/8 positions (g5), the player pushes the pawn prematurely instead of advancing the king first (Kg4 was best). The Qh5+ case also fits: an ineffective check replaces the required tight coordination that would have advanced the winning attack. All 8 positions are endgames where the evaluation confirms king advancement as the decisive winning technique - whether in K+Q vs K, K+P vs K, Q vs R, or Rook endgames. The consistent error is prioritizing perceived safety or passivity over the aggressive king march that endgame technique demands.
analysis.move_pattern: King moving backward (decreasing rank for White, increasing rank for Black), or substituting a different piece/pawn move for the required king advance toward the opponent's king
analysis.why_bad: In endgames, the king must advance toward the opponent's king to create mating nets, maintain opposition, support pawn promotion, or restrict the opponent. Retreating the king loses critical tempi, allows the opponent's king to escape or establish defensive blockades, and violates the fundamental endgame principle that the king is an active fighting piece that must lead from the front.
sub_patterns: King retreats in K+Q vs K instead of tightening the mating box
King moves behind the pawn in K+P vs K instead of leading ahead of it
King moves away from opponent's king when approach creates decisive threats
Premature pawn push substituting for required king outflanking maneuver

analysis.label: Moves that pursue a natural-looking secondary goal while fatally abandoning the piece's essential defensive or strategic function in the position.
analysis.description: This feature fires on positions where a piece leaves its critical post or role to pursue a superficially attractive objective.
