In 8/10 positions, the played move removes a piece from a square or function that was preventing the opponent's primary threat: Bg4 abandons e6 where it prevented e4-e5 (allowing a fork), Na5 abandons c6 central control (allowing d3/d4 breaks), Kg7 abandons central activity (allowing opponent's king march), Kxc4 abandons b1-square control (failing to blockade promotion), Re2 leaves the g-file where Rg5 attacked the queen (and hangs on the diagonal), Rd1 chooses passive blockade over active Rf1+ forcing play, Kd7 fails to reach d5 for direct blockade, and c8=N abandons queen-promotion's mating potential for insufficient material. In 9/10 cases, the move has clear purposeful logic (capturing material, pinning, invading, blockading, promoting) that would satisfy a surface-level assessment but catastrophically misreads which function matters most. The average cp_loss of 1141 reflects that these errors convert winning/holdable positions into lost ones.
analysis.move_pattern: Any piece type moving away from a square or role where it performed a critical defensive/blocking/controlling function, typically toward an attractive-looking but strategically inferior destination
analysis.why_bad: The moved piece was the sole guardian of a critical positional requirement (blockading a pawn, preventing a central break, maintaining activity, providing sufficient mating material), and its departure allows the opponent an immediate tactical or strategic breakthrough that the 'attractive' goal cannot compensate for
sub_patterns: Piece abandons defense of key central square enabling pawn fork/break
King moves to wrong square failing to blockade passed pawn
Active piece retreats passively when forcing moves were required
Piece pursues rim/material when central presence was essential

analysis.label: Moving a rook (or piece) to the deepest possible rank seeking maximum penetration when a more restrained intermediate placement maintains superior coordination or avoids favorable simplification for the opponent.
analysis.description: In 5/7 positions, the blunder is a rook moving directly to the 1st or 8th rank (Rb8, Rb1, Rf8, Rd1, Rb8), appearing to maximize penetration or create back-rank threats, but actually backfiring. In Position 2, Rb8 allows a simplifying exchange that dissipates White's entire kingside attack (Rb5 was correct, keeping the rook on an intermediate rank). In Position 3, Rb1 overextends the rook deep into White's position but leaves the c5-bishop undefended for Rxc5. In Position 5, Rf8 goes to the 8th rank instead of the far superior Rf7 (7th rank) which would form a lethal battery trapping the king. In Position 9, Rd1 invites a rook exchange that favors White's passed f-pawn endgame. In Position 11, Rb8 ignores a hanging knight while pursuing a meaningless exchange. The remaining two positions show related patterns: e2 pushes a pawn to maximum depth where it's easily blockaded (6/7), and Rxf3 captures with the wrong piece, overcommitting the rook from its defensive post (7/7). The common thread is choosing the most visually aggressive/deepest square when restraint preserves decisive advantages.
analysis.move_pattern: Rook moving to the 1st or 8th rank (back rank), typically along an open file, sometimes a pawn push to the 2nd/7th rank or a capture that overextends the rook
analysis.why_bad: The maximally deep placement invites exchanges that simplify away the player's advantage, removes the piece from intermediate squares where it maintained coordination or defensive duties, or wastes a tempo pursuing illusory threats while real problems go unaddressed
sub_patterns: Rook to 8th rank allowing simplifying exchange (Positions 2, 5, 11)
Rook to 1st rank inviting favorable trade for opponent (Positions 3, 9)
Piece/pawn overextension to deepest rank creating blockadeable or exploitable target (Position 6, 12)

analysis.label: Moves that pursue apparent piece activity or material gain while neglecting the position's critical strategic or defensive requirement.
analysis.description: This feature fires on positions where the player chooses a move that appears constructive (capture, centralization, attack) but fails to address the position's most pressing need. In 4/5 positions, the mistake involves prioritizing a secondary objective over the primary one: Qxh3 captures a peripheral pawn but abandons queen-rook coordination against an exposed king (Position 2); f4 attacks the enemy queen but fatally weakens the king shelter when h4 achieved the same goal safely (Position 13); Bd4 centralizes the bishop but creates no counterplay while allowing a devastating exchange on b1 (Position 15); h5 advances two squares instead of one, giving the opponent critical king-infiltration tempo (Position 3). In 3/5 cases, a clearly superior move existed that addressed the real strategic priority (maintaining coordination, preserving king safety, creating passed pawn counterplay). The common thread is choosing moves that look active on the surface while missing the deeper positional or tactical requirement.
analysis.move_pattern: Various piece types moving to seemingly active squares or making captures; no single geometric direction, but typically toward central or attacking positions while leaving a critical vulnerability unaddressed
analysis.why_bad: These moves sacrifice positional integrity (king safety, piece coordination, counterplay potential) for superficial gains or activity, allowing the opponent to exploit the newly created vulnerability with tactical shots (discovered attacks, exchange combinations, passed pawn advances)
sub_patterns: Capturing peripheral pawns while abandoning piece coordination
Pawn advances that weaken king shelter when safer alternatives achieve the same goal
Bishop/piece centralization that ignores concrete counterplay needs
Tempo-losing pawn advances in critical endgame positions

analysis.label: Playing a slow, non-forcing pawn push or piece retreat when the position demands immediate concrete tactical action to maintain or exploit an advantage.
analysis.description: In all 3/3 positions, Black had a significant tactical opportunity available (Ne5 fork winning material, Qb4/Nd7 defending hanging pawns, Be7 exploiting a trapped knight) but instead played a quiet, non-forcing move that prioritized vague structural goals over concrete calculation. In position 5, g5 aimed to solidify a pawn chain while missing a devastating fork combination. In position 12, b4 pushed a queenside pawn while leaving g4/h3 pawns completely undefended. In position 13, Bg6 retreated the bishop to 'preserve' it but actually rescued White's otherwise-trapped Nh4 by offering a favorable exchange. All 3/3 moves are non-forcing (no checks, captures, or immediate threats), and all 3/3 positions had very few good alternatives (avg 1.3), indicating critical moments where precision was essential. The average cp_loss of 279 confirms these are severe mistakes where tactical awareness would have been decisive.
analysis.move_pattern: Non-forcing quiet moves: pawn advances (g5, b4) or bishop retreats (Bg6) with no check, no capture, no direct threat — played by Black in the middlegame
analysis.why_bad: These moves waste tempo on structural or prophylactic goals while the position contains a concrete tactical solution that is time-sensitive; the opponent gains time to either collect undefended material, seize the initiative, or escape from a tactically lost situation
sub_patterns: Kingside pawn push ignoring central tactical combination
Queenside pawn push leaving own pieces/pawns hanging
Bishop retreat that rescues opponent's trapped piece

analysis.label: Playing a slow, non-forcing improving move when the position demands immediate exploitation of a hanging piece or forced winning sequence.
analysis.description: This feature activates on positions where a player makes a positional or developmental move while ignoring a critical tactical opportunity, typically an undefended piece that can be captured or a forced winning sequence. In 6/10 cases, the tactical motif is explicitly a hanging piece (positions 1, 2, 4, 6, 9, 10). In 8/10 positions, there are very few good moves available (1-2), indicating narrow critical moments demanding precision. The moves themselves vary in type—pawn pushes (c4, h4), bishop developments/retreats (Bf3, Bd6, Bd2, Be5), knight repositioning (Ng6), queen relocation (Qf2), wrong rook captures (Raxd6), and slow king moves (Kb5)—but all share the quality of being non-forcing 'improving' moves that prioritize piece placement over concrete material or mating threats. The average cp_loss of 2090 reflects that these quiet moves squander decisive advantages.
analysis.move_pattern: Non-forcing piece repositioning, development, or pawn advance (no checks, no captures of hanging material) in positions with immediate tactical wins available
analysis.why_bad: The player prioritizes general piece improvement or positional concepts over concrete tactics, missing hanging pieces, forks, or forced mating sequences that demand immediate exploitation before the opponent can consolidate or create counterplay.
sub_patterns: Bishop development/retreat ignoring hanging material (Bf3, Bd6, Bd2, Be5)
Slow pawn push leaving own piece undefended (c4, h4)
Piece repositioning instead of capturing free material (Ng6, Qf2)
Slow king/rook move missing forced mate or critical defense (Kb5, Raxd6)

analysis.label: Moves that voluntarily remove a piece or pawn from a critical defensive function to pursue a secondary objective, creating an immediate tactical exploitation.
analysis.description: This feature fires on moves where the player relocates a piece/pawn that was performing an essential defensive task (guarding a piece, blocking a line, shielding the king, maintaining a blockade), motivated by a plausible but secondary goal. In 6/11 positions, the moved piece/pawn was directly defending against a tactical shot: Bf2 leaves g5 pawn en prise (pos 5), d4 removes pawn defense of c4 knight (pos 6), both Bxg5 captures remove the e7 bishop allowing devastating knight invasions (pos 3, 14), dxe5 opens a diagonal for a skewer (pos 15), and axb4 opens lines toward the exposed king (pos 8). In 3/11 positions, the player moves the king to a newly vulnerable square or in the wrong direction: Kg2 creates a diagonal check vulnerability (pos 2), Kf8 abandons a critical blockade square (pos 11), and f6 ignores an immediate checkmate threat (pos 7). The remaining positions show the same fundamental error of prioritizing an 'improvement' while overlooking the critical defensive requirement. The average of only 1.7 good moves available confirms these are narrow positions demanding precise defensive awareness.
analysis.move_pattern: Any piece type moving away from a square where it performed a critical defensive function (guarding a piece, blocking a line/diagonal, shielding the king), often captures or retreats that look purposeful
analysis.why_bad: The moved piece/pawn was performing an irreplaceable defensive function - guarding another piece, blocking a dangerous line, or maintaining a fortress/blockade. Removing it creates an immediate tactical exploitation (fork, skewer, capture of undefended piece, line opening to the king, or promotion) that the opponent can execute in one move.
sub_patterns: Removing pawn/piece defense of another piece (d4, Bf2)
Capturing a bishop that was shielding the king from knight invasions (Bxg5 x2)
Opening a diagonal/file toward own king or pieces (dxe5, axb4, Kg2)
Abandoning a critical blockade or escape square (Kf8, f6)
Moving to a square creating a fork/tactical target (Qg4)

analysis.label: Playing a non-urgent or peripheral move in a critical position where the player's own exposed king demands immediate precise action.
analysis.description: In all 7/7 positions, the player's king is critically exposed or facing immediate tactical threats, yet the move played is passive, peripheral, or self-weakening rather than addressing the crisis. The positions share extremely narrow margins (avg 1.3 good moves available) where only one precise response survives. In 4/7 cases the move abandons a critical defensive function (Qe3 leaves king unguarded, Rg8 blocks escape square, gxh4 removes shield pawn, Bg5 wastes tempo with king on d7). In 2/7 cases the move is a slow prophylactic (a6, g5) when immediate tactical action was required. In 1/7 cases the move retreats when a capture was available (Kd2 instead of Kxf3). The devastating punishment always exploits the exposed king through checks, rook invasions, or mating attacks that the 'correct' move would have prevented.
analysis.move_pattern: Quiet non-forcing moves (pawn pushes, piece retreats, peripheral development) that neither give check, address immediate threats, nor improve king safety
analysis.why_bad: The position is at a critical tipping point where the player's exposed king can only survive through one precise move (forcing sequence, blockade, or elimination of attacker), and any tempo spent on non-essential activity allows the opponent to launch a decisive attack exploiting the king's vulnerability.
sub_patterns: Prophylactic pawn push ignoring hanging piece or tactical shot
Piece relocation abandoning critical defensive post near exposed king
Self-blocking or self-weakening move removing king's escape route or pawn shield
King retreat missing available capture of attacking piece

analysis.label: Positions with lethal open-file threats against the king where only 1-2 moves survive, and the player typically chooses the wrong direction or fails to address the critical threat.
analysis.description: This feature fires on middlegame positions at extreme decision points where open files create devastating threats against an exposed king, and the margin for error is virtually zero (avg 1.2 good moves). In 3/5 positions, the correct move was specifically to move the king AWAY from the dangerous open file (Kd8 was best in positions 1 and 3), but the player moved toward or stayed on the file (Kc7 on the b-file, Kf8 on the f-file). In position 2, the player abandoned defensive duties (Qg5 instead of Rd1) leaving the back rank exposed. In position 5, the player made a slow pawn move (b6) when only active piece play (Rcd8) could neutralize open-file pressure. Position 4 (Nd5, 0 cp loss) confirms the positional signature: exposed king on open files with narrow best play. The common thread is open-file artillery (rooks/queens) pointed at the king creating near-forced wins if the defender chooses incorrectly.
analysis.move_pattern: Piece moves toward (or failing to move away from) an open file where opponent's heavy pieces create lethal threats; king moves into open files, queen abandoning back-rank defense, or slow moves when active defense required
analysis.why_bad: The moves either place/leave the king on an open file where opponent's rooks/queen deliver checks initiating unstoppable sequences, or abandon critical defensive posts allowing back-rank/open-file invasions. The opponent's heavy pieces on open files create immediate tactical refutations (Qxb7+, Rxf6!, b5! creating passed pawns).
sub_patterns: King moving toward open file instead of away (Kc7/Kf8 instead of Kd8)
Abandoning defense for pseudo-attacking moves when back rank is weak
Slow pawn moves when only active piece play contests critical open files

analysis.label: Pawn advances (or piece moves abandoning defense) that create structural weaknesses around an already-exposed king when active piece play was required.
analysis.description: In 5/7 positions, the player pushes a pawn forward (f5, h6, c5, g6, plus Rc6 abandoning a pawn-defended piece) that creates a fixed structural weakness or removes a critical defender precisely when the king is already exposed. In 6/7 cases the king lacks adequate pawn shelter or sits in the center. The correct alternatives universally involve active piece play: captures (hxg3), rook activations (Rc4, Rb8), queen trades (Qxg5+), or knight repositioning (Nc2). The refutations exploit the newly-created weakness through tactical strikes: Bxf5/Bxg6+ exploiting the opened diagonal (Position 1), Re5+ entering a winning pawn ending targeting h6 (Position 2), g5+ tempo-gaining check exposing c5 (Position 3), Qe7+/Rxe6 exploiting the weakened dark squares after g6 (Position 5), and Nh4 winning the undefended knight after Rc6 abandoned its guard (Position 7). The average cp_loss of ~1497 reflects that these self-weakening moves in already-precarious positions often prove catastrophic.
analysis.move_pattern: Single-step pawn advances (especially f-, g-, h-file) or piece moves away from defensive duties, typically by Black, in positions with exposed kings
analysis.why_bad: These moves create new fixed targets or abandon critical defensive roles in positions where the king is already vulnerable, allowing the opponent to combine existing pressure with exploitation of the freshly-created weakness through tactical strikes on the weakened squares/diagonals/files.
sub_patterns: Kingside pawn push weakening king shelter (f5, g6, h6)
Pawn advance creating isolated target (c5)
Piece relocation abandoning key defensive duty (Rc6, Qe6)

analysis.label: Moves that place pieces on seemingly strong or central squares but create immediate tactical vulnerabilities allowing the opponent to gain decisive tempo.
analysis.description: This feature fires on moves where a piece is placed on an apparently active, centralizing, or aggressive square that is immediately exploitable by the opponent through tempo-gaining attacks. In 6/8 positions, the moved piece goes to a prominent central square (e4, e6, e6, e5, c6, d5) that appears strong but can be immediately challenged. The refutations consistently involve the opponent attacking the newly-placed piece or exploiting the vulnerability it created: Qf3/Qd5 attacks Ne4 (Position 2), Nd8+ forks Ke6 (Position 4), Nc7/Bg5+ attacks Be6 (Position 5), Bxg7+fxg6 exploits the removed defender after Nxe5 (Position 6), a2 exploits the bishop leaving its critical diagonal after Bc6 (Position 7), Ne4 occupies the square vacated by dxc4 (Position 9), Qxd5 captures the queen after Qd5+ (Position 13), and Qa4 forks after Nc6 (Position 15). The 'tempo_loss' tag appears in 7/8 positions, and 'missed_tactic' in 7/8, confirming that these are moves that look purposeful but hand the opponent a concrete tactical resource that gains material or decisive initiative.
analysis.move_pattern: Various piece types moving to central or prominent squares (especially e4, e5, e6, c6, d5) where they appear active but are immediately targetable or create exploitable weaknesses
analysis.why_bad: The piece lands on a square where it can be immediately attacked with tempo (check, threat, or fork), or the move abandons control of a critical square/diagonal, allowing the opponent to gain material or decisive positional concessions in 1-2 moves
sub_patterns: Piece centralizes on unstable outpost immediately challenged by queen or minor piece
King advances to exposed square vulnerable to check/fork
Piece abandons critical defensive diagonal or square control
Wrong capture order exposes key squares to opponent occupation
Check that places piece on capturable square dissolving winning advantage

analysis.label: Seemingly active or aggressive moves (usually queen moves, often checks) that place a piece on a tactically exploitable square or abandon a critical defensive function, allowing the opponent an immediate concrete punishment.
analysis.description: This feature fires on moves that appear natural, active, or aggressive—particularly queen moves to central or checking squares—but which contain a hidden tactical flaw that the opponent can immediately exploit. In 8/11 positions the move is a queen move, and in 4/11 it is a check. The core issue is that the moved piece either lands on a square where it becomes vulnerable to interposition-with-tempo (positions 1, 3: checks that allow counter-interpositions), direct attack/fork/skewer (positions 7, 10, 11: queen trapped on b2, queen forked by Ne8, king skewered on 4th rank), or the move abandons a critical defensive post that was the only thing preventing the opponent's tactical resource (positions 2, 4, 5, 9: removing back-rank guard, removing Rg4+ interposition capability, abandoning h8 coverage, abandoning bishop defense). The purposeless check sub-pattern (positions 6, 12) drives the opponent's king toward safety with no follow-up. Average cp_loss of 2107 with only 1.7 good moves available confirms these are narrow tactical positions demanding precision, where the 'natural-looking' move is catastrophically wrong.
analysis.move_pattern: Queen (or occasionally king/rook) moves to apparently active squares—centralization, checking squares, open files/diagonals—typically forward or lateral moves that look improving
analysis.why_bad: The move either places the piece on a square where the opponent gains a forcing tempo (interposition with check, fork, skewer, direct attack on the piece) or abandons a critical defensive function that was preventing the opponent's key tactical resource, allowing immediate concrete punishment
sub_patterns: Purposeless checks that drive the enemy king to safety or allow tempo-gaining interpositions
Queen centralization/relocation that abandons defense of a key piece or square
Piece moves creating geometric alignments (same rank/file/diagonal) exploitable by skewer, fork, or pin
Removing a piece from a square where it served as sole guardian against a specific tactical threat

analysis.label: Playing a quiet or positional move that either creates or fails to prevent a devastating knight fork of two high-value pieces.
analysis.description: In all 10/10 positions, the played move either actively places a piece on a square vulnerable to a knight fork (Ke2 enables Nc3+ forking king+rook; Rd2 enables Nf3+ forking king+rook; O-O places king on g8 enabling Ne7+ forking king+queen in 2 cases; Qc3 enables Ne2+ forking king+queen; Rxe2 enables Nc3 forking queen+rook) or is a slow non-urgent move that ignores an already-existing knight fork threat (a4 ignores Ne2+ forking king+rook; bxc3 leaves queen exposed to Nc2+ triple fork; Rf1 ignores Ne2+ forking king+rook; e6 ignores Nd7+ beginning a fork sequence winning the queen). In every case, the best moves specifically address the fork vulnerability—typically by moving the king off the forkable square (Kh1, Kd1, Ke1), covering the knight's landing square, or recapturing with the piece that would otherwise be forked (Qxe2 instead of Rxe2). The punishment is always a knight delivering check while simultaneously attacking a queen or rook, winning major material.
analysis.move_pattern: Quiet non-forcing moves (pawn pushes, castling, piece repositioning) that leave the king and another high-value piece geometrically aligned on squares a knight can simultaneously attack from one square
analysis.why_bad: They ignore or create a geometry where the opponent's knight can land on a square that simultaneously attacks the king (delivering check) and a second undefended high-value piece (queen or rook), winning material through a forced fork sequence.
sub_patterns: Moving king TO a forkable square (Ke2, O-O to g8)
Moving a piece TO a square forkable with the king (Rd2, Qc3, Rxe2)
Playing a slow pawn/rook move ignoring existing fork threat (a4, Rf1, e6, bxc3)

analysis.label: Playing a superficially attractive move (capture, centralization, development, or pawn advance) that wastes a critical tempo by failing to address the position's most pressing tactical obligation.
analysis.description: This feature fires on moves that look reasonable in isolation—pawn captures (Nxc4, Nxb3), flank advances (a4, g5), piece centralization (Nd5, Qd6), development (Bd3, Na3), or 'active' rook play (Ra1)—but catastrophically ignore the #1 concrete need in the position. In 9/9 cases, the position demanded specific urgent action: addressing an exposed king (positions 1, 5, 9), maintaining piece coordination (position 6), prioritizing development over material rescue (position 3), activating pieces centrally rather than on the flank (position 4), avoiding self-blocking (position 12), or creating compensation before material is lost (position 15). Instead, the player pursued a secondary objective—grabbing a pawn, reaching an 'outpost,' pushing a pawn storm—that the position simply didn't have time for. The refutations consistently exploit the wasted tempo with immediate tactical strikes: forks (3/9), captures of hanging/trapped pieces (4/9), or decisive king attacks (3/9). The average cp_loss of 1340 with only 2.1 good moves available confirms these are critical junctures where precision is mandatory.
analysis.move_pattern: No single geometric pattern; diverse piece types (knights, pawns, rooks, queens, bishops) moving to squares that serve a secondary strategic purpose while leaving the primary tactical obligation unaddressed
analysis.why_bad: The move wastes a tempo that the position cannot afford, allowing the opponent to execute an immediate tactical blow (fork, piece capture, mating attack, deflection, or pawn break) that exploits the specific vulnerability the move failed to address—exposed king, undefended piece, trapped piece, or loss of coordination.
sub_patterns: Capturing material while leaving own king exposed to tactical exploitation
Flank pawn moves when central piece activity is urgently required
Piece development to undefended or tactically vulnerable squares
Self-blocking moves that trap own pieces or remove retreat squares
Simplifying exchanges that deflect pieces from critical defensive duties

analysis.label: Playing a quiet, non-forcing move (typically a pawn push or passive piece repositioning) in a position that demands immediate concrete action to maintain or address a critical tactical/positional need.
analysis.description: This feature fires on positions where the player makes a 'preparatory' or 'improving' move that fatally wastes tempo in a position requiring urgent concrete play. In 9/9 positions, the played move is non-forcing (no check, no capture, no direct threat). In 5/9 cases, it's a quiet pawn move (g3, h3, a4, b6, e6) and in 4/9 it's a passive piece relocation (Nb5, Bh6, Rg8, Rc1). The positions consistently feature one clear urgent need: supporting passed pawns before they're captured (positions 1, 3, 5), exploiting an exposed enemy king (position 10), preventing a critical pawn break (position 9), maintaining defensive coverage of a key square/pawn (position 8), or addressing an immediate tactical vulnerability (positions 4, 7, 15). In 8/9 positions, the refutation directly exploits what the slow move failed to address—typically the opponent seizes the d-file against passed pawns, executes the thematic break, or exploits a newly undefended piece/square. The average cp_loss of 394 with only 1.6 good moves available confirms these are high-urgency positions where the wasted tempo is catastrophic.
analysis.move_pattern: Non-forcing moves (no checks, captures, or direct threats): quiet pawn advances (g3, h3, a4, b6, e6) or non-threatening piece repositioning (Nb5, Bh6, Rg8, Rc1) that fail to interact with the critical tension in the position.
analysis.why_bad: The positions demand immediate concrete action—either activating pieces to support vulnerable assets (passed pawns, exposed kings), preventing an opponent's forcing break, or executing a time-sensitive tactic. The slow move gifts the opponent a free tempo to execute exactly the plan the player needed to prevent or preempt, causing the position's dynamic balance to collapse.
sub_patterns: Quiet kingside pawn moves while central passed pawns need piece support (g3, h3)
Slow queenside pawn advances creating weaknesses instead of activating pieces (a4, b6)
Passive piece repositioning ignoring forcing tactical opportunities (Bh6, Nb5, Rg8)
Premature pawn advance breaking a strong formation without coordination (e6)
Rook placement on a file without addressing the critical positional need (Rc1)
categories: wasted tempo enabling opponent's concrete threat

analysis.label: Placing a piece on a seemingly strong or aggressive square that creates an immediate tactical vulnerability (hanging, fork, pin, or trap).
analysis.description: This feature fires on moves where the player makes a natural-looking, 'active' piece placement that ignores concrete tactical flaws of the destination square. In 10/13 positions, the moved piece goes to a square that appears strong (central outpost, aggressive post, contested file) but is immediately exploitable: Bg4 places the bishop where Bxg4/Qxg4 wins it (pos 1); Nf5 jumps aggressively but leaves e4 undefended for Nxe4/Qxf5 (pos 4); Qxd4 centralizes the queen but it becomes a tempo target (pos 8); Ng6 repositions but creates a target on an open diagonal for Bh5 (pos 9); Re2 contests the 2nd rank but Bd3 traps it (pos 10); Rxf7 grabs a pawn but leaves c3 undefended for Ne2+ fork (pos 11); Ne4 occupies a 'strong' square that multiple pieces can capture favorably (pos 14); Rc4 centralizes but aligns with f1 on a fork diagonal for Bb5 (pos 15); Be4 centralizes instead of delivering forced mate with Bg3 (pos 13); Kf5 advances 'actively' into a mating net (pos 6). The common thread is prioritizing apparent piece activity over concrete calculation of the destination square's tactical safety.
analysis.move_pattern: Any piece type moving to a central, advanced, or seemingly active square; no single direction or capture pattern, but the destination creates an exploitable geometric alignment (diagonal, file, or knight-fork square) for the opponent
analysis.why_bad: The destination square has a concrete tactical flaw: the piece can be captured profitably, trapped, forked with another piece, or its departure leaves something else undefended. The player mistakes 'looking active' for 'being safe' and fails to calculate the opponent's forcing reply.
sub_patterns: Piece placed on undefended square attackable by opponent's piece (Bg4, Re2, Be4, Rc4)
Piece moves aggressively but leaves a critical square/piece undefended behind it (Nf5→e4 hangs, Rxf7→c3 hangs)
Capture with wrong piece creating tempo targets (Qxd4, Bxf3 move order)
King advancing to seemingly active square that walks into mating geometry (Kf5)
Piece repositioned to square that creates exploitable diagonal/fork alignment (Ng6, Rc4)

analysis.label: Playing a preparatory move (usually a king move) instead of executing an immediately required pawn break in a time-critical endgame.
analysis.description: In 9/9 positions, the player is in an endgame where an immediate pawn advance or pawn break is the only correct move (f5, b5, e4, e5, f4, h4), but instead plays a 'preparatory' or 'improving' move that delays the critical pawn push by one tempo. In 7/9 cases the played move is a king move (Kc5, Ke5, Ke3, Kb4, Kg6, Kg7, Kf3), while the remaining cases are a slow pawn advance (f6 instead of f5) and a rook repositioning (Ra7 instead of h4). The correct moves share a common theme: they are decisive pawn breaks that resolve structural tension immediately (e.g., f5 challenging g4, b5 creating a passed pawn, e5 eliminating a weakness, f4 initiating a promotion race). The errors look natural—centralizing the king, winning material, or 'preparing'—but in these razor-thin pawn race positions, a single wasted tempo allows the opponent to either equalize a pawn race, execute a counter-break, or invade with their king.
analysis.move_pattern: King moves (or slow preparatory moves) in various directions, played instead of an immediate forward pawn advance/break
analysis.why_bad: In critical pawn endgame positions where timing is razor-thin, one wasted tempo allows the opponent to launch their own pawn race, execute a counter-break (e.g., c4, d6, h4), or invade with the king to win a key pawn, flipping the promotion race outcome.
sub_patterns: King approaches a pawn instead of pushing it immediately (Kc5/Kb4/Kf3 instead of b5/f4)
King retreats from defending a pawn instead of eliminating it via a break (Kg6/Kg7 instead of e5)
Pawn advances one square preparatorily instead of two-square break (f6 instead of f5)
Piece repositioning instead of urgent pawn counterplay (Ra7 instead of h4)

analysis.label: A move that removes the sole defender of the e5 pawn (typically retreating the queen from e7 to d8), allowing the opponent to simply capture it.
analysis.description: The dominant pattern across these positions is a move that abandons the defense of a critical central pawn on e5. In 7/10 positions, the e5 pawn becomes immediately capturable after the mistake. The most specific recurring motif (positions 2, 3, 5, 7) involves the queen retreating from e7 back to d8, where it was the sole defender of e5 along the e-file—after Qd8, the opponent wins the pawn with Nxe5. In position 6, the d5 push removes the d6 pawn's protection of e5 after exchanges. In position 12, Bb4 ignores that Nxe5 wins the hanging pawn. Position 9 (Qd1) follows the same tempo-losing retreat pattern. The remaining positions (11, 13, 15) share the broader theme of making a move that ignores a critical tactical obligation in favor of routine or cosmetically active play. All occur in the opening phase with underdeveloped positions where maintaining central control is paramount.
analysis.move_pattern: Piece retreat (usually queen from e7 to d8, or queen to d1) or pawn advance that removes the only defender of the e5 pawn
analysis.why_bad: The moved piece was the sole defender of e5 (or the pawn structure supporting e5), and removing it allows immediate capture of the central pawn, often with additional positional gains like central domination or initiative against an uncastled king.
sub_patterns: Queen retreats e7→d8 leaving e5 en prise (most common, 4/10)
Pawn advance (d5 or f5) that removes structural support of e5
Bishop development (Bb4) that ignores hanging e5 pawn
Queen retreat to starting square (Qd1) losing critical tempo

analysis.label: A natural-looking, non-forcing move that squanders a critical tempo when the position demands concrete or urgent action.
analysis.description: This feature activates on positions where the player makes a quiet, 'reasonable-looking' move (development, king repositioning, or prophylaxis) that fatally wastes tempo when the position demands immediate concrete action. In 6/6 cases, the move played was non-forcing (no check, no capture, no direct threat) and placed a piece on a seemingly logical square while missing the tactical urgency. The positions share the characteristic that only 1-3 good moves existed and the window for correct play was narrow. Examples include: king moves abandoning critical squares (Kb7 leaving the center in a pawn race, Kh5 drifting from centralization, Kf8 undefending h7), slow development when sharp tactics existed (Be3 missing Ne5/Ng5 tactics, Nc3 walking into a fork sequence), and passive rook shuffles when active counterplay was essential (Rb1 when f4 was needed). In every case, the opponent gains a decisive tempo to execute their plan—whether pushing a passed pawn, winning undefended material, or seizing a key square.
analysis.move_pattern: Quiet piece repositioning (king, minor piece, or rook) to a seemingly logical square—no checks, no captures, no direct threats—when the position has one narrow correct path requiring concrete play.
analysis.why_bad: These moves gift the opponent a free tempo to execute a plan that was previously impossible or preventable, whether it's seizing a dominant square (Kf4/Ke5), capturing an undefended pawn (Qxh7), launching a tactical combination (Nxc3/Ne2+), or initiating a decisive pawn break (b4). The 'natural' appearance of the move masks that the position had a ticking clock requiring immediate action.
sub_patterns: King drifting away from critical defensive/blocking duties in endgames
Slow development when sharp tactical exploitation of opponent's weaknesses was available
Passive piece repositioning when active counterplay (pawn breaks, central thrusts) was the only way to maintain balance

analysis.label: White makes a move that leaves their queen capturable by an enemy bishop along a diagonal.
analysis.description: In 5/6 positions, the immediate punishment is an enemy bishop capturing White's queen along an unobstructed diagonal (Bxd2, Bxc4, Bxg3, Bxf5, Bxe4). The remaining case (Bd4) removes a blocking piece on a rank, allowing queen capture by Black's queen. The blunders split into two sub-patterns: in 3/6 cases (Qxc4, Qxf5, Qxe4), White's queen greedily captures a pawn, landing directly on a square controlled by an enemy bishop's diagonal. In the other 3/6 cases (c3, Bb1, Bd4), White moves a piece that was shielding/blocking the queen from attack, exposing it to immediate capture. The average cp_loss of 510 reflects that these are essentially queen-losing blunders. The overlooked bishop is typically a fianchettoed or centralized piece controlling a long diagonal (b7-h1, c8-h3, f7-a2, e5-g3 diagonals appear).
analysis.move_pattern: Mixed piece types (queen captures, bishop retreats, pawn pushes) that all result in White's queen being left undefended on a square attacked by an enemy bishop along a diagonal
analysis.why_bad: White overlooks that their queen sits on (or will sit on) a diagonal controlled by an enemy bishop with no intervening blockers, resulting in immediate queen loss for insufficient compensation
sub_patterns: Queen captures a pawn on a bishop-defended diagonal square (Qxc4, Qxf5, Qxe4)
Piece moves away from a blocking/shielding role, exposing queen to diagonal capture (c3, Bb1, Bd4)

analysis.label: Moving a piece (usually the king) forward or actively when the position demanded a retreat toward safety.
analysis.description: In 7/7 positions, the blunder moves a piece forward, toward the center, or toward the opponent's forces when the critical need was to retreat toward the player's own back rank or maintain defensive positioning. The clearest sub-pattern is king advances (4/7: Kh3 from g2 twice, Kf3 from f2, Kd6 from e7) where the correct move was always retreating the king backward (Kh1, Kh1, Kg1, Kd8 respectively). In 2/7 positions, the queen greedily captures on d4 instead of making quiet developmental moves (c6/e6) that maintain defensive coverage of the queenside. In 1/7, a rook moves laterally away from its defensive station. The common thread is choosing an 'active' or materialistically greedy move over the necessary defensive retreat, resulting in catastrophic exposure of the king to mating attacks, forks, or decisive material loss.
analysis.move_pattern: King advancing one square toward the center/opponent (h3, f3, d6) or queen/rook moving forward to capture/activate instead of retreating; correct move was always toward own back rank
analysis.why_bad: The forward move places the king on a tactically vulnerable square (exposed to checks, diagonals, knight forks, or mating nets) or removes a key defender's coverage, allowing the opponent to exploit the newly created weakness with immediate tactical blows—often checkmate or winning material via discovered attacks, forks, or queen invasions.
sub_patterns: King advancing forward instead of retreating to back rank (Kh3/Kf3/Kd6 vs Kh1/Kg1/Kd8)
Queen greedily capturing central pawn (Qxd4) instead of quiet development, exposing queenside to Qxb7
Defender abandoning king zone for active posting elsewhere (Rc6 leaving kingside unguarded)

analysis.label: Playing a natural-looking active move that wastes a crucial tempo in positions where only one or two precise continuations maintain the evaluation.
analysis.description: This feature fires on moves that appear superficially logical or active—seizing a file (Rc1), grabbing a pawn (Qxg2), centralizing the king (Kf5, Kd5)—but critically waste a tempo in positions demanding extreme precision. In all 4/4 positions, the correct move addressed a specific concrete obligation (challenging a dominant piece, protecting a vulnerable piece, attacking with tempo, or interposing with gain), while the played move pursued a 'natural' plan that ignored that obligation. The positions share extremely low good-move counts (avg 1.5), meaning the player had essentially one correct continuation. The tempo loss manifests differently—leaving a piece/pawn undefended (2/4: Rc1 leaves a3 hanging, Qxg2 leaves Bg4 hanging), choosing the wrong adjacent square (1/4: Kf5 vs Kf6), or moving the wrong piece entirely (1/4: Kd5 vs Be6)—but in each case, the opponent gains one critical tempo to execute a tactical blow that was not available had the correct move been played.
analysis.move_pattern: Non-forcing 'improving' moves (rook to open file, queen captures undefended pawn, king steps to adjacent square) that fail to address the single most urgent tactical obligation in the position
analysis.why_bad: Each move ignores a concrete tactical necessity—defending a hanging piece/pawn, attacking an enemy piece with tempo, or blocking a dangerous line—giving the opponent one free tempo to exploit an existing vulnerability (capturing undefended material, launching a king hunt, or advancing a decisive pawn).
sub_patterns: Rook move that abandons defense of a weak pawn
Greedy pawn capture that leaves own piece undefended
King move to wrong adjacent square losing critical tempo
King advance into open lines when interposition was required

analysis.label: King moves to the wrong square in a pure pawn endgame, abandoning the opposition or critical central positioning.
analysis.description: This feature fires on king moves (8/9) or tempo-wasting pawn moves (1/9) in pure king-and-pawn endgames where the player sends the king in the wrong direction, losing the opposition or abandoning the critical sector of the board. In all 9 positions, the correct move required placing the king on a very specific square to maintain opposition (positions 1, 2, 4, 10) or to contest the critical central/active zone (positions 6, 8, 11, 12, 15). The played moves instead go sideways or backward relative to where the king is needed—e.g., Kb6 instead of Ka5, Kc5 instead of Ke4, Kg2 instead of Ke2, Kb5 instead of Kd5, Kc2 instead of Kd3. These positions are characterized by extremely narrow margins (avg 1.6 good moves available) and locked/fixed pawn structures where king maneuvering is the only resource, making a single directional error catastrophic (avg 486cp loss).
analysis.move_pattern: King move (or rare pawn move) going in the wrong direction—away from opponent's king, away from the critical opposition square, or toward the wrong flank—in locked pawn endgame positions
analysis.why_bad: In pawn endgames with fixed structures, the position is determined entirely by king placement relative to the opponent's king (opposition) or relative to the critical breakthrough sector. Moving the king one square in the wrong direction loses a decisive tempo, surrenders the opposition, and allows the opponent's king to infiltrate or outflank, converting drawn positions into losses or worsening already difficult positions.
sub_patterns: King abandons direct vertical/horizontal opposition (Kb6, Kc5, Kg2, Kf2)
King moves toward wrong flank away from decisive sector (Kb5, Kc2, Kb2)
King stops one square short of the critical blocking square (Kf7 vs Kf6)
Pawn move wastes tempo when king move was essential (g6 vs Kf6)

analysis.label: Aggressive-looking moves that ignore a critical defensive vulnerability, leaving own material undefended or unsupported.
analysis.description: This feature fires on positions where the player makes a forward/active-looking move (centralizing a queen, jumping a knight to an outpost, advancing a passed pawn, activating the king) while neglecting that something in their position requires immediate attention. In 5/7 positions, the blunder specifically leaves a piece or pawn undefended: Qd5 abandons defense of g2 (Position 1), Ne6 places a knight without any protection (Position 2), Qb5 deserts the threatened f3 knight (Position 4), h6 leaves the g4 pawn hanging (Position 10), and b3 advances without king support allowing blockade (Position 6). The Kg4 endgame (Position 14) follows the same logic—king activates before locking the structure with f5, leaving e5 vulnerable to f6. These positions typically have only 1-2 good moves (avg 1.7), indicating high tactical urgency that demands a specific preparatory action. The correct moves consistently address the vulnerability first: developing a piece to defend (Nd2/Na3/Nc3), playing the critical sacrifice (Nxh7), protecting the attacked piece (Nce5), or locking the structure (f5/h5).
analysis.move_pattern: Forward piece/pawn moves to active-looking squares (centralizing queens, outpost jumps, pawn advances, king activation) - diverse piece types but consistently aggressive/improving in appearance
analysis.why_bad: The position contains a specific tactical vulnerability (undefended piece, hanging pawn, structural weakness) that requires immediate attention; the active-looking move ignores this urgency, and the opponent simply captures the undefended material or exploits the unresolved tension
sub_patterns: Queen centralization abandoning pawn defense
Knight outpost jump without any protection
Queen repositioning while own piece is attacked
Premature pawn advance without king support
King activation before locking critical pawn structure

analysis.label: Making quiet moves (usually king moves) instead of capturing undefended enemy pieces or pawns that would draw or decisively improve the position.
analysis.description: This feature fires on endgame positions where the player makes a non-capturing move—overwhelmingly a king move (8/12 positions)—when a critical capture was immediately available. In 8/12 positions, the best move was capturing an undefended or hanging piece/pawn: capturing a queen (positions 2, 4, 5), a rook (position 6), or a critical pawn (positions 1, 3, 10, 12). In many of these cases (5/12), the capture would have resulted in insufficient mating material and an immediate draw. The remaining positions (7, 8, 11) show the inverse: making moves that leave one's own pieces undefended. The common thread is a failure to recognize that material must be captured or protected THIS move—the player instead plays a developing/repositioning move as if the critical capture will still be available later, when in fact the one-tempo difference is catastrophic.
analysis.move_pattern: Quiet king moves (or other non-capturing piece moves) played when a piece capture or critical pawn capture was available on an adjacent/attacked square
analysis.why_bad: The moves ignore immediately available captures of undefended material (or leave own material hanging), missing that the capture was the sole resource to draw/equalize. The quiet move allows the opponent to either retain decisive material advantage, achieve promotion, or win the now-undefended piece.
sub_patterns: King move instead of capturing hanging queen/rook/pawn
Giving check instead of capturing hanging piece
Moving piece to square where own material becomes undefended
Tempo-losing king move when pawn capture prevents promotion

analysis.label: Superficially active or developing moves that bypass the position's one urgent requirement, losing material or crucial tempo.
analysis.description: This feature fires on moves that look natural or aggressive in isolation but critically fail to address the position's most urgent demand. In 3/5 positions, there was essentially only one good move available, yet the player chose a 'reasonable-looking' alternative. Two positions (4/5 and 5/5) feature Bg4 developing a bishop to an undefended square where the queen captures it for free. Position 3/5 shows b4 (a seemingly aggressive pawn storm) that actually blocks the knight from the b4 square needed for the winning tactic. Position 2/5 shows Rxg6 grabbing a pawn instead of the crushing Re7 infiltration. Position 1/5 shows Be7 (passive development) ignoring urgent central pawn tension requiring dxc4. All 5 positions share the pattern of a 'looks active/normal' move failing against a forcing refutation the player didn't consider.
analysis.move_pattern: Piece development or pawn/rook move to seemingly active square (especially bishops to g4 or e7, pawns forward, rook captures) that ignores the position's forcing requirements
analysis.why_bad: The moves fail because they don't address the position's primary tactical demand — either leaving pieces undefended in capture range (Bg4 x2), blocking critical tactical resources (b4), surrendering dominant piece placement for trivial material (Rxg6), or allowing the opponent to execute a forcing sequence that was only preventable by the one correct move (Be7 allowing Nf4 + Qb3 fork).
sub_patterns: Bishop developed to undefended square capturable by queen (Bg4)
Pawn advance that blocks own tactical resource
Grabbing material instead of maintaining crushing positional pressure
Passive development ignoring urgent central pawn tension

analysis.label: Playing a passive repositioning move when the position demands an immediate concrete action (capturing or defending hanging material).
analysis.description: In all 6/6 positions, the player chose a quiet, non-forcing piece maneuver—seemingly improving placement for strategic reasons—while ignoring an urgent tactical obligation. In 3/6 cases (Nb6, Bf2, Qe6), the moved piece was the sole defender of vulnerable material (e6 pawn, f4 pawn, d3 knight respectively), and relocating it left that material hanging. In 2/6 cases (Qb8, Rc7), the player missed an available capture of undefended enemy material (c4 pawn, d5 rook). In 1/6 cases (Kd1), the passive move left the player's own undeveloped piece (g1 knight) completely undefended while failing to make the one freeing break available. The average cp_loss of 337 reflects that these are not subtle positional inaccuracies but severe tactical oversights disguised as reasonable-looking moves. Each position had 1-3 good alternatives that addressed the immediate tactical reality through captures, defensive reinforcement, or forced breaks.
analysis.move_pattern: Non-capture, non-check piece repositioning to a new square (knight, king, bishop, queen, or rook maneuver sideways/backward) rather than addressing immediate tactical obligations
analysis.why_bad: The player prioritizes a strategic plan (piece improvement, king safety, attacking an unrelated target) while overlooking that a piece or pawn is either left undefended by the move or available for immediate capture. The opponent punishes by simply taking the hanging material.
sub_patterns: Moving the sole defender of a piece/pawn to a different task, leaving material hanging
Playing a passive repositioning move instead of capturing undefended enemy material
Making a slow preparatory move when the position demands an immediate concrete response

analysis.label: Pursuing a secondary goal (material, slow improvement, or strategic plan) while catastrophically ignoring the position's single most urgent tactical or safety demand.
analysis.description: This feature fires on positions where very few good moves exist (avg 1.7) and the player makes a move motivated by a completely different plan than what the position demands. In 8/10 cases, king safety is the ignored critical factor: b3 ignores the open e-file requiring castling, Nexg2 grabs a pawn while dismantling defensive coordination against back-rank threats, Na5 attacks a bishop while f7 is under lethal dual assault, Nxe4 captures material with the king exposed on e2, Nf7 retreats passively when counterplay was essential, Ke6 centralizes into a discovered checkmate, d5 closes the center when the opponent's king exposure demanded opening it, and Rg2 passively defends when active piece play was required. In all cases, the position had ONE critical priority that demanded immediate attention, and the player chose a move motivated by an entirely different consideration—resulting in average losses of 2136 centipawns.
analysis.move_pattern: Mixed piece types and directions—pawn advances (b3, b6, d5), knight moves to various squares (Na5, Nf7, Nexg2, Nxe4), rook/queen retreats (Rg2, Qb8), king walk (Ke6)—united by being moves aimed at secondary objectives rather than the position's urgent demand
analysis.why_bad: Each move fails because it addresses something irrelevant while a concrete, immediate tactical or safety demand goes unmet, allowing the opponent to exploit the neglected vulnerability with devastating effect—often involving king exposure, hanging pieces, or mating patterns that the 'correct' moves would have neutralized.
sub_patterns: Material grabs ignoring own king exposure (Nexg2, Nxe4)
Slow pawn moves wasting critical tempo (b3, b6, d5)
Passive piece retreats surrendering initiative (Nf7, Qb8, Rg2)
King walking into tactical danger (Ke6)
Attacking opponent's pieces while own king is under assault (Na5)

analysis.label: Playing a natural-looking improving or active move when the position demands an immediate concrete/forcing continuation.
analysis.description: This feature fires on positions where the player selects a move that appears sensible—developing a piece (Bb7), centralizing a rook (Re3, Rd7, Rc3, Rc2), targeting a weakness (Na5), or capturing a pawn (Nxe5, Nxd4)—but critically fails to address the position's most urgent tactical demand. In 6/8 cases, a forcing tactical sequence was available (Rxe2 exploiting overloaded defender, Nge3 securing the knight, Nd7 removing a tactical target, dxe5/dxc6 resolving tension correctly, Nf4 creating direct threats). In all 8 positions, the played move gives the opponent a crucial tempo to either consolidate (Re3 allowing ...f5 trapping a knight, Rc3 allowing ...Ng6 activating a piece, Rc2 allowing Qe3 consolidation) or execute their own tactical blow (Rd7 enabling Rxf6+Nxf6+ fork, Na5 enabling ...exd4 creating passed pawn, Nxd4 inviting c5-c4 tempo gains). The average position had only 1.8 good moves available, indicating narrow critical moments where precision was essential.
analysis.move_pattern: Non-forcing piece moves (development, repositioning, or materialistic captures) to seemingly active/useful squares, avoiding the position's most forcing continuation
analysis.why_bad: These moves surrender the initiative or create new vulnerabilities by failing to play the position's concrete forcing sequence—giving the opponent time to activate pieces, exploit trapped/exposed pieces, or resolve tension on their own terms
sub_patterns: Slow positional development missing a concrete tactical shot (Bb7, Rc2)
Piece placement that blocks or strands own pieces (Re3 self-blocking knight)
Piece moves creating new fork/sacrifice targets (Rd7 becoming fork target)
Decentralizing moves when center demands resolution (Na5)
Greedy captures creating piece vulnerabilities (Nxe5, Nxd4)
Purposeless rook moves when forcing piece improvements exist (Rc3)

analysis.label: Playing a quiet positional move instead of capturing an undefended rook on a1 or a8 along an open diagonal.
analysis.description: In 7/8 positions, the best move was capturing an undefended enemy rook sitting on a corner square (a1 or a8) via an open diagonal with a queen or bishop (Qxa8, Qxa1, or Bxa8). Instead, the player chose a slow, non-forcing move—quiet pawn pushes (c4), knight developments/retreats (Na3, Nb1, Ne7), bishop repositioning (Be4, Ba7), king moves (Ke7), or rook lifts (Rab1). The hanging rook was always capturable along the a1-h8 or a8-h1 diagonal, but the player failed to recognize the open line to the undefended piece. After the quiet move, the opponent simply defended the rook (via castling, bishop development to b7/b2, or moving the rook), permanently closing the tactical window. Average cp_loss of 283 reflects losing roughly a full exchange worth of advantage.
analysis.move_pattern: Quiet non-capturing, non-checking move (any piece type) played instead of a diagonal capture of an undefended rook on a1 or a8
analysis.why_bad: The moves waste a critical tempo on slow positional ideas while an undefended corner rook sits en prise along an open diagonal—giving the opponent time to defend the rook or castle, permanently eliminating the free material.
sub_patterns: Quiet development ignoring Qxa8
Slow repositioning ignoring Qxa1
Bishop centralization missing Bxa8
King move missing queen capture of corner rook

analysis.label: Aggressive or forward-directed moves (pawn advances, king marches, greedy captures) in critical positions that demand defensive restraint or the one precise continuation.
analysis.description: This feature fires on positions where the player makes an actively forward-looking move—advancing a pawn (g5, h5, e4), pushing the king forward (Kf7, Kh5, Kf2), grabbing material (Qxd4), or deploying a piece toward an undefended square (Nc3, Rb8)—when the position urgently required restraint, retreat, or a specific forcing move. In 7/9 cases, the played move is clearly forward-directed while the best move involved retreat or defensive consolidation (Kf5 not Kf7, Kh3 not Kh5, Kh2 not Kf2, Kg6 not h5, b5 not g5, Nce7 not Rb8, c6 not Qxd4). The positions share extremely narrow margins with only 1.6 good moves on average, meaning the player faced a critical juncture where one precise move worked and the natural-looking aggressive option catastrophically failed. The resulting punishments span multiple tactical motifs—forks (4/9), hanging pieces (3/9), skewers (1/9), pins (1/9)—but the common cause is identical: the forward move either exposes the king to tactical sequences, leaves pieces undefended, or wastes the critical tempo needed for survival.
analysis.move_pattern: Pieces or pawns moving forward/aggressively (king advances, pawn pushes toward opponent, captures toward center) when retreat or solid defense was required
analysis.why_bad: The forward move either walks into a concrete tactic (fork, skewer, pin), leaves a critical piece/square undefended by addressing a secondary concern, or wastes the one tempo needed to maintain a tenable position—all in situations where only 1-2 moves avoid catastrophe.
sub_patterns: King advancing into fork/skewer vulnerability (Kh5, Kf7)
Kingside pawn pushes weakening own king shelter (g5, h5)
Greedy captures abandoning defensive duties (Qxd4, Rb8 addressing wrong problem)
Non-forcing advances when forcing moves demanded (e4 instead of Bb5+, Kf2 instead of Kh2)

analysis.label: Moves that execute a superficially logical plan prematurely, before addressing the one specific tactical demand the position requires.
analysis.description: This feature fires on moves that look natural or tempting but are done at the wrong moment, directly enabling a concrete opponent punishment in positions with very few good alternatives (avg 1.9). The pattern manifests as: premature pawn captures that open critical king diagonals (fxe5 enabling Qh4+, fxe4 enabling Qh5+, f6 enabling Nxe5/Ng6 fork — 3/10), prophylactic or reinforcing pawn moves that waste critical tempo (f3 blocking Nf3, h6 ignoring hanging e5 pawn — 2/10), premature material grabs ignoring strategic priorities (Qxd4 exposing queen to Rd2+ — 1/10), premature promotion without removing the defender (b8=Q into Nxb8 — 1/10), passive piece retreats abandoning active positions (Rdd1 surrendering d5 outpost — 1/10), and imprecise pawn advances missing forcing tactical sequences (d4 missing d3! with check, Rfe1 enabling ...d5 break — 2/10). In all cases, the position demanded ONE precise action, and the player chose an 'obvious' alternative that directly created or failed to prevent the opponent's tactical blow.
analysis.move_pattern: Diverse piece types and directions, but predominantly pawn moves (7/10) including f-pawn advances, flank pawn pushes, and captures; remaining are piece moves to 'natural' squares or retreats
analysis.why_bad: Each move executes a secondary objective (reinforcement, material gain, prophylaxis, promotion, consolidation) before addressing the position's primary tactical demand, directly enabling the opponent's one clear punishment in positions with extremely limited good alternatives
sub_patterns: Pawn captures that fatally open king diagonals (fxe5, fxe4, f6)
Tempo-wasting pawn moves ignoring immediate tactical threats (f3, h6)
Premature captures/promotions without necessary preparation (Qxd4, b8=Q)
Passive piece moves abandoning active play (Rdd1, Rfe1)
Wrong pawn advance missing a forcing tactical sequence (d4 instead of d3)

analysis.label: Quiet, non-forcing moves that ignore the position's most urgent concrete demand, wasting a critical tempo.
analysis.description: This feature fires on positions where the player chooses a slow, 'improving' or preparatory move while the position urgently demands a concrete, forcing response. In 12/12 cases, the player pursued a non-urgent plan (knight repositioning to the rim, pawn pushes for space, piece doubling, passive retreats) while ignoring an immediate tactical or structural vulnerability. The best moves consistently involved direct action—challenging the center (positions 1, 2), securing a critical piece (position 4), defending a hanging pawn (positions 11, 15), retreating the king (positions 10, 14), or making a tactical strike (position 12). Instead, the played moves were all quiet and non-forcing, granting the opponent a free tempo to execute devastating concrete plans: pawn advances cracking open the position (6/12), piece invasions to critical squares (4/12), or simple captures of undefended material (5/12). The average cp_loss of 328 reflects how severely a single wasted tempo punishes in positions at a tipping point.
analysis.move_pattern: Any piece type moving to a non-forcing square (no check, no capture, no immediate threat) — typically repositioning moves, flank pawn pushes, or passive retreats
analysis.why_bad: The position has reached a critical tipping point where one specific concrete action (defending a weakness, challenging a structure, or making a tactical strike) is required immediately; the quiet move wastes the tempo needed to address this urgency, allowing the opponent to execute a forcing plan that exploits the neglected vulnerability.
sub_patterns: Knight maneuvers to rim squares ignoring central tension (Na6, Na5)
Piece retreats to passive squares abandoning active pressure (Bd7, Qa5)
Rook moves abandoning critical file control (Rce8, Rhd8, Rh7)
Flank pawn pushes creating weaknesses instead of addressing central demands (h5, a5, d6)
Routine development ignoring urgent tactical weakness (Nf3, Bd6)

analysis.label: White plays a natural-looking or seemingly constructive move that completely ignores the position's most critical concrete requirement, wasting a decisive tempo.
analysis.description: This feature fires on positions where White makes a move that appears reasonable in isolation—developing a piece, giving a check, pushing a pawn, or repositioning—but catastrophically ignores the ONE thing the position demands. In 5/6 positions, king safety is the dominant neglected factor: either White's own king needs urgent protection (Na3 ignoring kingside mating threats, Nd2 leaving king exposed to Re2+, g4 ignoring the lethal d3 pawn, Kh4 walking into h-file checks) or the opponent's king vulnerability offers a concrete winning tactic that goes unexploited (Bb4+ missing Qc5+ queen trap, Qe3 missing Nb5/Nc7+ fork, Qc7+ missing Qf5+ forced queen trade). In all cases, the position demanded precise calculation targeting a specific tactical motif, but the player instead made a 'general improvement' move that addresses the wrong sector of the board. The average cp_loss of ~2800 reflects that these are critical moments where one tempo decides between winning/surviving and losing/getting mated.
analysis.move_pattern: Varied piece types (K, B, N, Q, pawn) moving to squares disconnected from the board's critical sector—often away from the file/diagonal where the decisive action occurs
analysis.why_bad: Each move wastes a critical tempo in a position with urgent concrete demands—either failing to defend against immediate threats to one's own king, or failing to execute a available winning tactic against the opponent's vulnerable king/pieces, allowing the opponent to consolidate or deliver a devastating blow
sub_patterns: Developing/repositioning a piece to the wrong side of the board while the kingside burns (Na3, Qc7+)
Moving a piece to an undefended square while the king remains exposed to checks (Nd2, Kh4)
Pushing an irrelevant pawn instead of addressing lethal threats (g4)
Playing a purposeless check instead of executing the winning combination (Bb4+)
Retreating the queen passively when a knight fork tactic wins material (Qe3)

analysis.label: Playing slow, non-forcing repositioning moves in positions demanding immediate checks or captures that maintain a winning attack.
analysis.description: In all 4 positions, the player had a decisive advantage (forced mate in 3/4 cases) but chose a quiet, non-forcing 'improving' move instead of a concrete forcing continuation. Position 1: e2 (pawn push) instead of Qg5+ (check leading to mate in 4). Position 2: Re8 (quiet rook repositioning) instead of Qxd6+ (capture with check leading to mate in 6). Position 3: Bb6 (bishop repositioning) instead of Rg6+ (tempo-gaining check), though this was 0cp loss. Position 4: Rd1 (rook to open file) instead of Ke7 or Rf1+ (maintaining forced mate). In 4/4 cases the played move was non-forcing—no check, no capture, no direct threat. In 3/4 cases the best move involved an immediate check. The common error is prioritizing abstract piece improvement (occupying open files, advancing passed pawns, placing bishops on diagonals) over concrete calculation of forcing sequences against exposed kings.
analysis.move_pattern: Quiet piece repositioning to open files/diagonals without check or capture, in positions where forcing moves (especially checks) win immediately
analysis.why_bad: The non-forcing move surrenders the initiative by giving the opponent a free tempo to mount counterplay (Rd8+ in pos 1, Qxd5 in pos 2, g4 in pos 4), allowing them to escape mating nets or neutralize decisive threats that required immediate forcing action to maintain.
sub_patterns: Pawn push toward promotion instead of delivering check
Rook to open file instead of capturing with check
Bishop repositioning instead of tempo-gaining check
Quiet centralization losing forced mating sequence

analysis.label: Active-looking moves that leave the player's own piece or pawn undefended, allowing simple capture or exploitation.
analysis.description: In 8/10 positions, the player makes a natural-seeming or greedy move that creates or ignores a hanging piece in their own camp. The pattern manifests in three ways: (1) moving a piece's defender away, exposing it (Ba3 abandons d4 pawn, dxc6 removes d5 pawn protecting Bc4, Nxd7 vacates e5 exposing the queen on the long diagonal); (2) placing a piece on an unprotected square where it can be immediately captured (Bb4 allows simple Bxb4, Bf4 allows Nxf4 hitting the queen, Qh5 leaves Bc4 completely unguarded); (3) developing while ignoring an already-hanging piece (Nf6 ignores the undefended Ne5). These are predominantly opening-phase moves (6/10) where the player prioritizes activity, development, or material gain over basic piece safety, resulting in an average loss of ~290cp. The positions typically feature uncastled kings and sharp tactical tension where one tempo of defensive neglect is immediately punishable.
analysis.move_pattern: Any piece type moves to an active/capturing square while leaving own material (bishop, pawn, knight, or queen) undefended or newly exposed to capture
analysis.why_bad: The move removes a critical defender, places a piece where it lacks protection, or ignores an existing undefended piece—allowing the opponent to win material through simple capture, discovered attack, or capture-with-tempo on a higher-value piece behind it.
sub_patterns: Moving defender away from a pawn or piece (Ba3, dxc6)
Placing piece on unprotected square capturable with tempo (Bf4, Bb4)
Premature queen sortie leaving minor piece undefended (Qh5)
Greedy capture that exposes own piece to tactics (Nxd7, Qxd4)
Developing while ignoring own hanging piece (Nf6)

analysis.label: Playing an aggressive-looking or natural move that misses the one forcing continuation that wins material or maintains a decisive advantage.
analysis.description: In 5/5 positions, the player had a significant advantage (or needed to minimize damage) with only ~1 good move available, yet chose a superficially attractive alternative. In 3/5 cases (Positions 1, 14 with Qg5, and Position 10 with Bxe6), the player moved a piece toward seemingly active squares while missing a concrete capture of hanging material (Bxf2+ fork winning a piece, Qxb2 grabbing a free pawn, Qxe5 taking an undefended rook). In Position 9, the player grabbed a pawn (Kxa2) when king safety demanded staying away from the corner. In Position 11, an aggressive pawn push (d5) was played instead of the one retreat (Ne2) that preserved the full center. The common thread is prioritizing perceived threats, piece removal, or activity over the single precise forcing move that was required in a tactically narrow position.
analysis.move_pattern: Piece moves to aggressive-looking square (often kingside or captures) while a more forcing capture or combination goes unplayed
analysis.why_bad: These moves fail because they ignore the one concrete winning continuation (usually a hanging piece, tactical combination, or forced sequence) in favor of a move that looks active but is non-forcing, allowing the opponent to consolidate, counter-attack, or exploit the piece's new placement with tempo
sub_patterns: Queen moves to g5 for kingside aggression while free material exists elsewhere
Capturing a threatening piece instead of the actually hanging one
Greedy pawn capture walking into a tactical refutation
Aggressive pawn push ignoring that it creates more weaknesses than threats

analysis.label: Playing a positionally attractive or 'improving' move when the position demands immediate concrete tactical action or defense.
analysis.description: This feature fires on moves that look natural or positionally desirable but critically ignore urgent tactical demands. In 6/8 positions, the moved piece either abandoned a vital defensive role or was deployed to a seemingly strong square while a forcing tactical sequence was available to the opponent. Key examples: Nd5 left f6 unguarded enabling Bxh6/Rxf7 (Position 15), Bg7 removed the Bh4+ checking resource allowing Qb7+/Nc7+ winning the queen (Position 9), Nc6 failed to block the f-file with Ne7 enabling Qf8+ back-rank destruction (Position 13), and a3 wasted a critical tempo allowing ...f6 to trap a bishop (Position 4). In each case, the player chose a move motivated by general principles (centralization, prophylaxis, development, restricting pieces) rather than calculating the concrete tactical consequences. The positions were under extreme tension (avg 1.9 good moves available), meaning only specific moves maintained the balance, but the players defaulted to pattern-based 'improving' moves instead of addressing the urgent concrete needs.
analysis.move_pattern: Piece moves to a natural/attractive square (outpost, fianchetto, centralization) or quiet pawn advance, rather than addressing an immediate forcing tactical demand
analysis.why_bad: The positions required concrete calculation due to acute tactical tension; the 'improving' moves either abandoned critical defensive duties (removing key defenders/checking resources) or wasted tempo, allowing the opponent to execute forcing tactical sequences (checks, sacrifices, back-rank attacks) that the position had been holding in balance only through specific counter-resources.
sub_patterns: Knight moves to attractive outpost but leaves kingside fatally unguarded (Nd5, Nc6)
Piece repositions to 'better' square but removes key tactical resource (Bg7 removes check, Qd6 removes perpetual)
Slow prophylactic move wastes tempo in position requiring immediate action (a3, h5)
Active-looking move ignores hanging material or forced wins (Rg4 instead of Qxh4)
Knight commits to premature exchange that destroys own structure (Nc5)

analysis.label: Playing a slow positional or developmental move while immediate material (own or opponent's pieces/pawns) is tactically vulnerable or freely capturable.
analysis.description: This feature fires on positions where the player makes a non-forcing, repositioning move while concrete tactical material is hanging somewhere on the board. In 5/10 positions, the player's own piece is left undefended and immediately capturable (Nc7 hangs to Nxc7, Bd5 hangs to exd5, Nh3 leaves Rf5 hanging, Rf5 hangs to Bxf5, Qd2 allows Bb4 attacking the queen). In 2/10 positions, the player misses capturing an opponent's undefended material (Bd3 instead of Nxb5, b6 instead of Nxg4). In the remaining cases, the player ignores critical forcing threats (a3 allows Qxd8#, Ne5 ignores Nxc7+ fork, Qxa5 nets queen-for-rook loss). Nearly all positions feature both kings in the center (8/10), creating tactical tension that demands immediate concrete action rather than slow maneuvering. The average cp_loss of 1267 reflects that these quiet moves are catastrophically inappropriate for the tactical demands of the position.
analysis.move_pattern: Non-capturing, non-checking piece repositioning moves to seemingly natural squares (development squares, central outposts, or prophylactic positions) - diverse piece types including bishops, knights, rooks, queens, and pawns
analysis.why_bad: The position demands immediate tactical action (capturing hanging material, defending en prise pieces, or addressing forced threats), but the player instead makes a slow positional move that either leaves own material undefended, misses free captures, or ignores forcing sequences - a fundamental failure to prioritize concrete tactics over abstract positional goals.
sub_patterns: Own piece moved to undefended square where it hangs (Nc7, Bd5, Rf5)
Developing move that abandons defense of another piece (Nh3 leaving Rf5, Qd2 allowing Bb4)
Slow pawn move ignoring free material capture (b6 missing Nxg4, a3 missing back-rank)
Knight centralization ignoring opponent's fork/forcing sequence (Ne5 ignoring Nxc7+)

analysis.label: Playing a slow or non-urgent move in positions with unresolved e4/f5 or e5/f4 pawn tension, allowing the opponent's f-pawn advance to seize the initiative.
analysis.description: In 6/7 positions, a critical pawn tension exists on the e/f-file axis (e4 vs f5, or e5 vs f4), and the player makes a slow, non-essential move instead of resolving or addressing it. The punishment in 6/7 cases is the opponent's f-pawn advance (f4 or f5) gaining tempo against a piece (typically attacking a bishop or knight) while simultaneously seizing massive kingside space. Position 1: Ng3 allows ...f4 attacking the knight. Position 3: a3 allows ...f4 displacing the g3-knight. Position 4: ...Bg7 removes restraint, allowing f5 attacking the e6-bishop. Position 7: Nd5 allows ...f4 attacking the e3-bishop. Position 12: Rxb7 ignores the f5/e4 tension allowing ...f4 with tempo. Position 14: ...f5 itself creates the exploitable pawn weakness. All best moves involve either resolving the tension immediately (exf5, fxe5) or first preparing for the opponent's advance. The closed-center structure (6/7 positions) amplifies the importance of this pawn lever as the primary source of dynamic play.
analysis.move_pattern: Any slow or repositioning move (piece retreat, wing pawn push, or pawn grab) that neglects the f4/f5 vs e4/e5 central pawn tension
analysis.why_bad: The opponent's f-pawn advance comes with tempo (attacking a piece that must move), simultaneously gaining crushing kingside space, activating dormant pieces, and seizing the initiative in a closed structure where this pawn lever is the decisive dynamic element.
sub_patterns: Wing pawn move (a3, b6) while f-pawn tension demands resolution
Piece repositioning (Ng3, Bg7, Nd5) leaving a piece vulnerable to f-pawn attack
Material grab (Rxb7) ignoring central tension urgency
Premature f-pawn advance (f5) creating structural weakness instead of resolving tension properly

analysis.label: Advancing a king or pawn to the 4th rank in endgames that appears active but concedes critical squares, tempo, or ignores urgent priorities.
analysis.description: All 4/4 positions involve moves landing on the 4th rank (f4, Kd4, Kc4, Kf4) in endgames where the advance looks centralizing or space-gaining but actually backfires. In position 1, the pawn push f4 relinquishes control of e4, allowing White's king to centralize decisively. In position 2, Kd4 allows Black to seize the opposition with Kd6, locking White's king into passivity. In position 3 (minimal 6cp loss), Kc4 permits White a tempo-gaining b3+ check that Kc5 would have avoided. In position 4, Kf4 ignores the urgent passed c-pawn while exposing the king to bishop checks. In 3/4 cases the error is significant (avg 162cp loss), and in all cases the opponent exploits the overextended position through tempo gains, opposition, or tactical shots directed at the advanced piece.
analysis.move_pattern: King or pawn advancing to the 4th rank (d4/c4/f4 squares) in endgame positions
analysis.why_bad: The forward advance looks active but concedes key squares to the opponent's king, allows tempo-gaining responses (checks, pawn advances with check, opposition), or neglects more urgent positional/tactical priorities like eliminating passed pawns or maintaining square control.
sub_patterns: King advance to 4th rank allowing opponent's opposition (Kd4 vs Kd6)
Pawn push to 4th rank releasing key square control (f4 opening e4)
King advance to 4th rank exposing to checks or tempo-gaining pawn pushes (Kc4 allowing b3+, Kf4 allowing Bg5+)

analysis.label: Retreating a major piece (Queen or Rook) to the player's own back ranks, surrendering an active position for false safety.
analysis.description: In all 4/4 positions, the player retreats a major piece to their own 1st or 2nd rank (Rc6→c2, Qd4→d8, Q→c7, Qf5→f1), abandoning an active or critical post in favor of perceived safety or consolidation. In position 2, the Rook leaves a dominant c6 outpost for passive c2, missing the decisive Rxf6 sacrifice. In position 6, the Queen retreats from a powerful centralized d4 to the congested back rank d8, wasting a critical developmental tempo. In position 10, the Queen moves to c7 away from the kingside where Qf4 was the only move challenging White's mating attack. In position 11, the Queen retreats from active f5 to passive f1, surrendering control of infiltration squares. All retreats moved the piece toward the player's own camp (rank 1-2 from their perspective) when the position demanded either maintaining the advanced post or executing a forward-looking action.
analysis.move_pattern: Major piece (Queen or Rook) retreating backward along a file to the player's 1st or 2nd rank
analysis.why_bad: Surrenders active piece placement and tempo, allowing the opponent to seize the initiative—either executing tactical threats the retreated piece could have challenged, infiltrating squares the piece previously controlled, or developing with gain of time against the now-passive piece.
sub_patterns: Queen retreating to back rank when forward defense/attack was required
Rook retreating from advanced outpost to second rank missing a tactical shot
Major piece fleeing imagined danger rather than maintaining pressure
