analysis.label: Moves pursuing a plausible secondary strategic idea while missing the single critical concrete requirement of the position.
analysis.description: This feature fires on positions where the player makes a 'reasonable-looking' move addressing a secondary concern while ignoring the one urgent tactical or concrete need. In 2/8 positions, the player chose a fianchetto preparation (b3, b6) when the center demanded immediate reinforcement. In 2/8 positions (Kc3, Kb2), the player moved the king toward a secondary target when h4 was the only move preserving a pawn race advantage. In 2/8 positions (Bxc5, e5), the player made aggressive/greedy moves (captures, space-gaining) while their own pieces were tactically vulnerable. In 2/8 positions (Qd4+, Qd5+), the player chose an imprecise check allowing the opponent defensive resources when a more forcing alternative existed. The average good moves available is only 2.1, confirming these are narrow positions demanding precision. The common thread is that the played move addresses something real but non-urgent (fianchetto, material, centralization, a check) while the position has a single critical concrete requirement (defending a hanging piece, pushing a pawn in a race, delivering precise mate, evacuating from a file).
analysis.move_pattern: Varied piece types and directions; typically a move toward a flank/secondary target (b-file pawns, king toward queenside) when the critical action is elsewhere (center, kingside pawn race, e-file defense)
analysis.why_bad: These moves fatally misprioritize: they address a secondary strategic concern while a narrow tactical window closes. The position demands one specific concrete action (defend a hanging piece, advance a pawn in a tempo-critical race, find a precise forcing sequence), and the played move wastes the critical tempo on something less urgent.
sub_patterns: Fianchetto preparation ignoring central pawn vulnerability (b3/b6)
King approach toward decoy pawn instead of critical h-pawn push (Kc3/Kb2)
Greedy capture leaving own pieces/king tactically exposed (Bxc5/e5)
Imprecise check allowing defensive interposition or king escape to safety (Qd4+/Qd5+)

analysis.label: Queen moves to squares where the opponent can trade queens, dissipating the player's dynamic or attacking advantage.
analysis.description: In all 7/7 positions, the player makes a queen move that allows the opponent to exchange queens, which devastates the player's position because their advantage was built on dynamic factors requiring the queen's presence. In 4/7 cases (positions 5, 9, 10, 13), the primary refutation is the opponent simply accepting a queen trade (Qxb4, Qxd4, Qxb4, Qxe4), instantly neutralizing kingside attacks or piece coordination. In 2/7 additional cases (positions 1, 8), queen trading is the second-strongest refutation. In 2/7 cases (positions 1, 2), the error is specifically capturing with the queen instead of another piece, placing it on a vulnerable square where trades or tactical counterblows follow. The common thread is that positions with attacking potential, open files aimed at the opponent's king, or coordinated piece pressure all require the queen as the linchpin—and these moves either offer or enable its removal.
analysis.move_pattern: Queen moves (captures or relocations) to squares where the opponent can immediately trade queens—includes wrong-piece captures (Qxg6/Qxe5 instead of Bxg6/Nxe5) and voluntary approaches toward the opponent's queen (Qb4, Qf6, Qxd4, Qe4)
analysis.why_bad: The player's advantage derives from dynamic attacking potential (piece coordination against the opponent's king, open files, advanced pawns) that depends critically on the queen's presence; trading it off converts a dynamic advantage into a static position where the opponent can consolidate or even gain structural/positional superiority.
sub_patterns: Capturing with the queen when another piece should capture, misplacing the queen and enabling counterplay (positions 1, 2)
Offering queen trade in positions with active kingside attacks using coordinated rooks, bishops, and pawns (positions 5, 9)
Queen trade that displaces well-placed pieces or surrenders outposts to the opponent (position 10)
Queen centralization that invites simplification when a concrete tactical blow exists (position 13)

analysis.label: Passive major piece repositioning to a natural-looking square when the position demands a concrete tactical response to an immediate threat or opportunity.
analysis.description: In all 4 positions, the player moved a major piece (queen or rook) to a seemingly logical square—centralizing, developing, or defending—while ignoring a specific tactical demand. In Position 3 (Rd8), Black 'developed' a rook to an open file instead of addressing a knight fork vulnerability (Na4). In Position 4 (Qc2), White retreated the queen to a passive square instead of seizing the open d-file with Rad1. In Position 13 (Qe3), White 'centralized' the queen but walked into a knight tempo (Ng4) that required prophylaxis (h3). In Position 14 (Qe7), Black placed the queen on a 'defensive' square that blocked the e-file, preventing the critical Rfe8 resource while failing to create counterplay against White's queen (Qd7 was needed). In 4/4 cases, the best moves either created a direct counter-threat against the opponent's pieces, seized a key open file, or played prophylaxis against an imminent tactical blow—all concrete actions rather than general improvements.
analysis.move_pattern: Major piece (queen or rook) moved to an open or central square in a non-forcing, repositioning manner without creating threats or addressing vulnerabilities
analysis.why_bad: The moves prioritize general piece placement over addressing the position's most urgent tactical demand—whether that's neutralizing a fork, seizing a contested file first, preventing a tempo-gaining attack, or creating a forcing counter-threat. The opponent then exploits the missed tactical element with a concrete punishing move.
sub_patterns: Queen repositioned to passive square when file occupation was critical
Major piece 'develops' while ignoring an imminent fork or tactical shot
Queen placed on square that blocks own rook or creates self-interference
Quiet move when position demands forcing counter-threat against opponent's queen

analysis.label: Aggressive captures or advances that remove a piece from a critical defensive role, allowing immediate tactical exploitation.
analysis.description: In all 5 positions, the player makes a superficially attractive move—capturing material, advancing a pawn, or repositioning—while ignoring that the moved piece was performing a critical defensive function. In Position 1 (exf4), the e5 pawn defended e4, and its removal allows Ne4+ forking the king and queen. In Position 3 (d3), the pawn advance ignores that the f6 knight is attacked by exf6. In Position 5 (Bxh3), the bishop leaves f5 where it defended the f6 pawn, allowing Qxf6+ with a devastating check. In Position 4 (f6), the pawn push weakens the king's dark-square shelter, enabling Bxf6 winning the exchange. Position 2 (Nf1) fits the broader pattern of pursuing a tempting slow plan instead of the immediately demanded tactical action (5/5 positions show moves prioritizing a 'plan' over the position's tactical requirements). The average cp_loss of 359 reflects how these oversights typically surrender between a piece and a full piece worth of material.
analysis.move_pattern: A piece or pawn moves away from a square where it was defending a critical point, typically via a capture or forward advance toward the opponent's position
analysis.why_bad: The moved piece was the sole defender of a critical square or piece; its departure allows the opponent an immediate tactical blow (fork, capture of hanging piece, check along cleared line) that wins material or decisively shifts the initiative
sub_patterns: Pawn capture removes guard of key knight-landing square
Pawn advance ignores hanging piece under attack
Bishop capture abandons defense of adjacent pawn enabling check
Pawn push to challenge active pieces weakens king shelter

analysis.label: Playing a non-forcing developing or repositioning move in a position that demands urgent attention to king safety threats.
analysis.description: This feature fires on quiet, non-tactical moves (no checks, no captures, no direct threats) played in positions where critical king safety issues require immediate resolution. In 6/7 positions, the player's own king faces an exploitable vulnerability (back-rank mate in positions 5 and 9, diagonal exposure in positions 2, 7, and 12, and positional collapse in position 1), while in position 10 the player misses a decisive counterattack against the opponent's exposed king by playing passively defensive. The moves are typically 'plan-based' - fianchetto preparation (b3), central expansion (c5), queen centralization (Qe6, Qd7, Qf5), piece repositioning (Ba4), or material preservation (Rb8) - but all ignore that the position has crossed a tactical threshold where only 1-2 moves survive (avg good moves: 1.7). The catastrophic average cp_loss of 3143 reflects that these quiet moves allow forced mates or decisive material loss.
analysis.move_pattern: Quiet non-forcing moves (no check, no capture): pawn pushes, queen repositioning, bishop development, or rook relocation - all lacking immediate tactical purpose
analysis.why_bad: The position demands urgent concrete action (king evacuation, blocking a dangerous diagonal, counterattacking an exposed king, or prophylactic defense against mating threats), but the player instead pursues a secondary strategic goal, either ignoring the threat entirely or actively worsening their vulnerability by removing defensive resources
sub_patterns: Pawn advance removing key defensive square (c5 removing c6 block, b3 wasting tempo)
Queen centralization creating tactical vulnerability (Qe6 enabling fork, Qd7 enabling pin, Qf5 abandoning back rank)
Piece improvement ignoring forced mate (Ba4 instead of king evacuation)
Passive material defense missing decisive counterattack (Rb8 instead of Nxe4)

analysis.label: Moving a piece to a seemingly improved or natural square while vacating a position where it served an essential defensive or tactical function, allowing immediate exploitation.
analysis.description: This feature fires on moves where a player repositions a piece to what appears to be a better square — often centralizing, activating, or retreating — but in doing so abandons a critical defensive duty or tactical resource. In 4/10 cases, a knight is moved from a square where it provided an essential defensive function (Nb2 abandoning center defense, Ng3 removing the f1 knight needed for Be3/Nxe3, Ne1 abandoning the Na3+ fork from c2, Nd4 placing it where Be3 wins tempo). In 2/10 cases, the king walks to a seemingly active square but exposes itself to tactical exploitation (Kf5 into a mating net, Kf7 abandoning g5 control). In 2/10 cases, the queen moves for apparent counterplay but abandons defensive coverage (Qc3 uncovering c7 invasion, Qd2 placing it on a controlled square). The remaining cases show a rook placed on a fork-vulnerable square (Rf3) and a capture that misses a much stronger tactical opportunity (Bxf3 instead of gxf4 winning the queen). The positions demand tactical precision (avg 1.6 good moves available) but players choose 'natural-looking' piece improvement moves instead.
analysis.move_pattern: Piece (especially knight) moved to seemingly natural/active square; mostly non-captures; various directions; pieces leave functionally critical squares for apparently improved but tactically inferior ones
analysis.why_bad: The moved piece was serving a critical but non-obvious defensive or tactical function on its original square — blocking discovered attacks, controlling key invasion squares, enabling defensive combinations, or maintaining fork threats — and relocating it creates immediate tactical vulnerabilities the opponent can exploit
sub_patterns: Knight retreats from active defensive post (Nb2, Ng3, Ne1)
King advances/retreats abandoning key square control (Kf5, Kf7)
Queen moves for counterplay abandoning defensive coverage (Qc3, Qd2)
Piece placed on tactically vulnerable square creating fork/attack target (Rf3, Nd4)

analysis.label: Playing a slow repositioning or secondary-objective move while an immediate tactical crisis (usually a mating threat or critical piece removal) demands urgent attention.
analysis.description: In all 7/7 positions, the player made a move pursuing a non-urgent strategic goal—piece repositioning (Bd8, Nh5), slow pawn push (a6), queenside counterplay (Na5, Rab1), or attacking a secondary target (Rh7, Rd7)—while an immediate, concrete tactical threat existed that demanded priority. In 5/7 cases, the threat involved direct king safety (mating nets, back-rank mates, kingside attacks). In 4/7 cases, the blundering move actively removed a piece from a critical defensive post or abandoned control of a key square (Nh5 leaving f4, Na5 leaving c6, Rh7 abandoning f7, Rd7 abandoning f1's defensive coordination). The positions all featured exposed kings and dynamic imbalances where tempo was critical, yet the played moves behaved as if the position were quiet and positional improvement could proceed at leisure. The average cp_loss of ~4192 reflects that these 'slow' moves often enabled immediate forced wins for the opponent.
analysis.move_pattern: Diverse piece types moving toward periphery/secondary targets (knight to rim, rook to side file, bishop retreat, flank pawn push) - away from the critical sector of the board where threats exist
analysis.why_bad: Each move ignores an immediate concrete threat (usually a mating attack or tactical shot) in favor of a slow strategic plan, giving the opponent a free tempo to execute a winning combination that was only preventable by addressing the threat directly
sub_patterns: Removing a key defensive piece from its post enabling checkmate (Na5, Nh5)
Slow pawn push or repositioning while facing forced mate (a6, Bd8)
Rook pursuing secondary target while abandoning critical file/square (Rh7, Rd7, Rab1)

analysis.label: Piece relocations that look active (often giving check or developing) but permanently abandon the position's one critical tactical or strategic resource.
analysis.description: This feature activates on moves where a piece leaves a strong or essential station for a superficially attractive but fundamentally inferior square, destroying the position's key resource. The clearest sub-pattern (3/7 positions) involves Na6+ instead of Nb5+ in identical perpetual-check structures: the knight abandons c7 for the rim square a6, breaking the perpetual mechanism because from a6 it cannot answer ...Kc8 (unlike Nb5 which threatens Nd6+). The remaining positions (4/7) show the same conceptual error in different forms: Ne2 places a knight where it's immediately traded away, surrendering a crushing space advantage; dxe5 releases central tension in the wrong direction, missing a devastating d5 pawn fork; Bf5 retreats a bishop from its powerful g4 post to become a tempo-gaining target; Rde1 abandons the contested d-file, leaving a rook tactically hanging. In all cases, the position demanded one precise continuation (avg 1.3 good moves) to maintain the critical resource, and the player chose a move that permanently eliminated it.
analysis.move_pattern: Piece moves away from optimal square to inferior one - knights to rim/tradeable squares, rooks abandoning key files, bishops retreating from active diagonals - often while giving check or appearing to develop
analysis.why_bad: The move permanently destroys the position's sole key resource (perpetual check mechanism, central tension, piece coordination, file control) by relocating the critical piece to a square from which it cannot sustain tactical pressure or fulfill its essential function
sub_patterns: Knight to a6 (rim) instead of b5 (perpetual-enabling), breaking discovered check perpetual
Piece development to easily-traded square that invites simplification neutralizing advantages
Premature tension release capturing in wrong direction instead of advancing for breakthrough
Rook/bishop abandoning critical file/diagonal creating immediate tactical vulnerability

analysis.label: Choosing a slow, passive, or purposeless move (retreat, aimless check, slow advance) when the position demands immediate forcing action, catastrophically wasting a critical tempo.
analysis.description: All four positions share a common thread: the player chose a 'comfortable' or seemingly safe move that wastes a decisive tempo in a position demanding urgency. In 4/4 cases the move is tagged as a tempo loss, and in 4/4 cases piece activity is compromised. Position 1: Rg3+ gives a purposeless check that improves White's king and traps the rook. Position 2: Ka1 retreats to the corner when the a-pawn must advance immediately in a promotion race. Position 3: Kc5 plays a slow king march when Qxf6 delivers forced mate in 8. Position 4: Qd2 retreats the queen from a dominant d8 post to a passive square, allowing b2 to become unstoppable. In each case, 1-2 clearly superior forcing/active moves existed, and the error gave the opponent time to execute their own plans (promote a pawn, escape a mating net, advance a passed pawn). The positions are predominantly endgames (3/4) where single tempi are often the difference between winning and losing.
analysis.move_pattern: Any piece type moving to a less active square: retreats, corner moves, purposeless checks, or slow positional moves when immediate tactical solutions exist
analysis.why_bad: The move wastes a critical tempo in a position where urgency is paramount—allowing the opponent to advance a passed pawn, escape a mating net, or seize the initiative, converting what was manageable into catastrophe
sub_patterns: Purposeless check that improves opponent's king
King retreat to corner in promotion race
Slow positional move missing immediate forced mate
Queen retreat from dominant post enabling opponent's passed pawn

analysis.label: Playing a seemingly purposeful move that directly addresses a secondary concern while wasting critical tempo and creating self-inflicted weaknesses in positions demanding immediate dynamic action.
analysis.description: This feature fires on moves where the player identifies a real positional concern (an opponent's strong piece, advanced pawn, or structural target) and attempts to address it directly, but the chosen approach backfires by creating new vulnerabilities or wasting irreplaceable tempo. In 5/6 positions, the played move had clear intent: c3 challenged the d4-pawn, h6 tried to create a passed pawn, Rbb1 attempted back-rank pressure, a5 challenged the b4-pawn, and Nf5 targeted the d6-knight. However, in each case the correct approach was indirect—pawn breaks (f4, f6, g5 recommended in 4/6 positions), king centralization (1/6), or maintaining existing piece pressure (1/6). The blunders share a critical mechanism: the 'purposeful' move removes a defensive resource (c3 removed the d3-guard in 1/6), invites a favorable exchange that damages structure (Nf5 in 1/6), abandons an active post (Rbb1 in 1/6), or simply wastes tempo allowing opponent reorganization (a5, h6 in 2/6). Tempo loss appears as a tag in 4/5 mistake positions, and piece_activity in all 6. The average of 2.2 good alternatives shows these weren't desperation positions—multiple sound options existed that maintained active play.
analysis.move_pattern: Mixed piece types (pawns, rooks, knights, queen); typically non-forcing moves (no checks or captures) directed at an opponent's asset; often single-step pawn pushes (3/6) or piece repositioning toward the opponent's strength
analysis.why_bad: The move addresses a secondary concern while ignoring the primary strategic demand, and in doing so either removes a key defensive function, invites a structurally favorable exchange for the opponent, abandons critical counterplay, or wastes tempo that allows the opponent to achieve ideal piece placement—all when more dynamic, forcing alternatives were available
sub_patterns: Pawn push that removes a defensive guard of a critical square (c3 unguarding d3)
Advancing the wrong pawn in a connected passer pair (h6 instead of f6)
Retreating an active piece from a dominant post to pursue a phantom plan (Rbb1)
Flank pawn push when king centralization is the priority (a5 instead of Kc6)
Piece move challenging opponent's strength that invites structurally damaging exchange (Nf5 inviting Nxf5 exf5)

analysis.label: Playing a routine non-urgent move when an enemy pawn advance is ready to trap or decisively attack a piece (usually a bishop) that lacks safe retreat squares.
analysis.description: In 9/12 positions, a bishop sits on an exposed square (Bc4, Bb6, Bc5, Bf5) vulnerable to an enemy pawn advance (b5, a5, b4, or g4) that wins material. The moves played are non-forcing, routine actions—castling (2x), prophylactic pawn moves (h3, d3, e6, d6), normal development (Nc6, Bb6), or premature breaks (d5, b3)—that address secondary concerns while ignoring the concrete tactical emergency. In 10/12 cases, the punishment is a single pawn advance that either traps the piece outright or creates a tactical combination winning material. The best moves in each position either (a) prevent the pawn advance directly (a4, a5, a6), (b) move the vulnerable piece to safety (Be7, Bd6), (c) open the center to create counterplay before the pawn strikes (d4, d5, e5), or (d) maintain retreat squares by NOT blocking them with own pawns. The pattern is strongest when own pawns block the piece's escape diagonal—d6 blocks Bc5's retreat (2/12), e6 blocks Bf5 (1/12), d3 blocks Bc4 (1/12)—or when the piece simply has nowhere to go due to board geometry.
analysis.move_pattern: Quiet non-forcing moves (pawn pushes, castling, piece development) that do not address a piece's lack of retreat squares against an impending enemy pawn advance
analysis.why_bad: Each move wastes a critical tempo on a secondary objective, giving the opponent time to execute a pawn advance that traps or wins a piece—the position demanded either preventing the pawn thrust, moving the vulnerable piece, or blocking its own pawns from cutting off escape routes.
sub_patterns: Bc4/Nc3 vulnerable to ...b5 winning knight for pawns (positions 1-3)
Bishop on b6 trapped by a4-a5 advance (positions 8, 9, 12, 14)
Own pawn blocking bishop retreat diagonal (d6 blocks Bc5, e6 blocks Bf5, d3 blocks Bc4)
Routine castling/development ignoring queenside pawn storm
Wrong-sector move when opponent's flank attack is one tempo away

analysis.label: Moving a piece to a square where it can be exchanged (or enabling an exchange), transitioning into a hopelessly lost pawn endgame where the opponent's passed pawns or structural advantage become decisive.
analysis.description: In 9/10 positions, the blundering move either places a major piece directly where it can be captured/exchanged (Rf2, Rg8, Rc1, Rc6, Rd3), captures a piece inviting a recapture exchange (Rxh4), offers a piece trade (Qf4), enables an exchange by moving the king adjacent to the rook (Kg3 enabling Rxf3+), or fails to prevent a forced exchange (f5 leaving the queen on d5 for Qxd5). The resulting simplified position—almost always a pure pawn endgame—is catastrophically lost because the opponent has advanced passed pawns, superior king activity, or structural advantages that only become decisive once the defending side's last major piece is removed. The common strategic thread is that the losing side's only practical chance was to keep pieces on the board for counterplay/checking potential, but instead they facilitated the exact simplification their opponent needed. Position 14 (Kh3) is a partial outlier where the king walks into a mating net rather than enabling an exchange, though the theme of self-confinement still applies.
analysis.move_pattern: Major piece (usually rook) moves to a square directly confronting or adjacent to opponent's piece, or king/pawn move enables forced exchange; typically on an open file where pieces face each other
analysis.why_bad: The move removes the last major piece from the board (via exchange) in a position where the resulting pawn endgame is trivially won for the opponent due to passed pawns, superior king position, or material advantage that only pieces could compensate for
sub_patterns: Rook moves to same file/rank as opponent's rook, allowing immediate Rx exchange into lost pawn endgame
Queen offered on square where opponent gladly accepts trade into winning pawn structure
King moves adjacent to own rook, enabling opponent to capture with check and force exchange
Pawn move wastes tempo instead of relocating the piece that will be exchanged
Rook moves to back rank where opponent can capture with check

analysis.label: Retreating a piece to the back rank or second rank when the position demands counterintuitive forward/active placement.
analysis.description: All 4 positions share a common pattern: the player retreats a piece backward (to rank 1/8 or rank 2/7) when the correct move was to go forward or stay active. In Position 6, Kd8 retreats to the back rank instead of the correct Ke7 (forward). In Position 8, Rd8 goes to the back rank instead of the king advancing with Kg7. In Position 10, Ke1 retreats to the first rank when the counterintuitive Kf3 (forward) was correct. In Position 12, Qf2 drops to the passive second rank when Qg3 (forward/active) maintained control. In all 4/4 cases, the best move was more forward or active than the move played, and in 4/4 cases the retreat surrendered critical tempo or control that allowed the opponent to seize the initiative with tactical threats.
analysis.move_pattern: Any piece retreating backward toward ranks 1-2 (White) or 7-8 (Black), away from the action
analysis.why_bad: The passive retreat wastes critical tempo and/or places the piece on a square where it becomes vulnerable to tactics (back-rank mates, forks, diagonal exploitation) or fails to control key squares that the opponent immediately exploits with central breaks or attacking maneuvers.
sub_patterns: King retreating to back rank when forward centralization is correct (Kd8/Ke1 vs Ke7/Kf3)
Piece retreating to passive square instead of addressing urgent king safety needs
Queen retreating to second rank surrendering control of active squares

analysis.label: Playing a reasonable-looking move that ignores the single most critical demand of the position, wasting an irreplaceable tempo.
analysis.description: This feature activates when players make moves that look 'logical' or 'improving' in isolation but catastrophically ignore the one urgent requirement of the position. In 7/7 cases, the position had very few good moves (avg 1.6), indicating narrow paths where precision was essential. The blunders share a common structure: each addresses a secondary concern (activating a bishop in Position 15, supporting a pawn chain in Position 13, centralizing the king in Position 10, challenging an enemy piece in Position 6) while ignoring the single critical demand (blockading a passed pawn, castling immediately, resolving pawn tension, developing). In 6/7 positions, the correct moves were restrained or defensive (Rd5, Re8, Rg8, Ne2, Nc3, Qc7+), while the blunders appeared 'active' or 'improving.' The tempo waste is uniformly punished because the opponent exploits the specific vulnerability the move creates or fails to prevent—trapped pieces (1/7), forks enabled (1/7), exposed kings (3/7), and removed defenders (1/7).
analysis.move_pattern: Various piece types making short-range 'improving' moves (pawn pushes, bishop developments, king steps, queen repositioning) that look natural but miss the critical action
analysis.why_bad: The position demands one specific urgent action (castling, blockading, maintaining initiative, resolving tension), and the chosen move wastes the one available tempo on a secondary concern, allowing the opponent to exploit the actual critical factor of the position with immediate tactical or strategic punishment.
sub_patterns: Aggressive pawn advance when consolidation is needed (e5, f4+)
Piece 'improvement' that removes a critical defender or blocks development (Bf3, Bd7, c3)
Premature repositioning when concrete action is required (Qh5, Kg7)

analysis.label: Moving a critical attacking piece away from the enemy king when forced checkmate is available through that piece's current position.
analysis.description: In all 3/3 positions, White had a forced checkmate (ranging from mate-in-1 to mate-in-12) but instead moved the key attacking piece AWAY from the enemy king's zone to a passive or irrelevant square. In Position 1, the knight retreated from the dominant e5 outpost back to f3 when checks and captures from e5 delivered mate. In Position 2, the queen retreated from g8 (one square from delivering Qg6#) all the way back to b3. In Position 3, the queen left f3—where it commanded the critical diagonal toward the exposed king on g6—and moved to c3 where it had no attacking function. All 3/3 positions featured fatally exposed enemy kings (center or open board), all 3/3 had the moved piece as the linchpin of the mating combination, and all 3/3 moves went toward the queenside or backward, abandoning the attack entirely.
analysis.move_pattern: Major or minor piece retreating/relocating away from enemy king's vicinity (toward queenside or back rank) when it occupies a critical attacking square
analysis.why_bad: The moved piece was the essential component of a forced mating attack—removing it from its optimal attacking square gives the opponent critical tempo to develop, escape, or capture undefended pieces, converting an immediate forced mate into merely a large advantage.
sub_patterns: Knight retreating from advanced outpost to passive home square
Queen retreating from deep enemy territory to own queenside
Queen sliding laterally away from attacking diagonal/file toward inactive square

analysis.label: Moves that pursue secondary objectives (peripheral captures, passive repositioning, or premature attacks) while ignoring an opponent's advanced passed pawn or most urgent concrete threat.
analysis.description: In 6/8 positions, the opponent has a dangerous advanced passed pawn (c6, d6, e4, b6) that demands immediate concrete action—blockading, capturing, or racing against it. Instead, the blundering side pursues an attractive but non-critical objective: Rb4 attacks the b2 pawn instead of blockading with Rd4 (Position 2); Re1 targets the wrong pawn e6 instead of the lethal d6 (Position 3); h6 is a cosmetic king-luft move ignoring d6 which needs Rd8 (Position 4); Rxh4 grabs the peripheral h-pawn instead of eliminating the b6 passer with Bxb6 (Position 14); Ke5 advances aggressively instead of eliminating the e4 passer with g4 (Position 15); Rc2 invades prematurely enabling White's d5 breakthrough creating a passer (Position 12). The remaining positions (Bd7, g5) follow the same structural error—pursuing a secondary improvement while ignoring the position's most concrete existential threat. The average cp_loss of ~1466 reflects how devastating it is to give a passed pawn one extra tempo.
analysis.move_pattern: Piece moves directed toward peripheral targets (wing pawns, secondary files, cosmetic improvements) rather than toward the opponent's advanced passed pawn's file or promotion path
analysis.why_bad: Advanced passed pawns create concrete, time-critical threats where one tempo often means the difference between survival and promotion. These moves waste the critical tempo needed to blockade, capture, or race against the pawn, allowing it to advance to an unstoppable promotion.
sub_patterns: Capturing a peripheral pawn instead of eliminating the dangerous passed pawn
Attacking the wrong passed pawn when two exist (targeting less dangerous one)
Making a passive/cosmetic move (h6, g5, Bd7) when only concrete anti-pawn action survives
Premature rook invasion before neutralizing opponent's central/passed pawn threat
King advance that abandons control of the enemy pawn's promotion corridor

analysis.label: Moves that squander time by going to ineffective squares, allowing the opponent to consolidate or gain counterplay.
analysis.description: All 4/4 positions feature moves explicitly tagged as 'tempo_loss' in their tactical motif. The pattern connects moves where a piece goes to a square that either (a) must be immediately vacated (Kf5 then Ke6, Ne4 allowing Nf7+ forcing king retreat), (b) is passive compared to available active alternatives (Bc1 instead of a5/Be5+), or (c) gives the opponent a constructive defensive resource (Qa6+ allowing Qb7 simplification instead of Qa8+ forcing a winning fork). In each case, the player chose a superficially reasonable-looking move that appears active or aggressive but actually hands the initiative or a crucial tempo to the opponent. The average cp_loss of 2364 reflects that these tempo losses are particularly costly in positions (especially endgames, 3/4) where precise timing is critical.
analysis.move_pattern: Piece moves to a square that provides no lasting benefit - either requiring immediate retreat, abandoning a dominant post, or giving a check that allows the opponent to consolidate
analysis.why_bad: The moves waste a critical tempo, allowing the opponent to either gain a tempo-gaining response (check/fork), simplify into a more defensible position, or escape from a mating net/dominant setup that required one more precise move to complete.
sub_patterns: Piece retreats to passive square when active options exist
Piece abandons dominant outpost allowing opponent tempo-gaining check
Imprecise check that permits defensive simplification
King advances to square requiring immediate retreat

analysis.label: Moves that waste a crucial tempo by addressing non-urgent concerns while ignoring the position's most critical immediate tactical demand.
analysis.description: This feature fires on positions where the player makes a seemingly purposeful move—a queen relocation, king walk, pawn advance, or capture—that completely ignores the single most urgent tactical need of the position. In 9/9 cases, the position had very few good moves (avg 1.9), meaning one highly specific action was required. The blunders include: ignoring a hanging piece that could be captured (positions 1, 4, 6 where d4-pawn, queen on b6, or recapturing with the right piece was critical), making passive queen retreats when active centralization was demanded (positions 3, 7, 11 with Qe8 retreating instead of Nd5/Qc6), moving a king to the wrong square by one tempo (positions 5, 8, 12 where Kg1/Ke5/Kc5 missed blockade or stalemate by exactly one square), or playing slow flank moves ignoring center threats (position 10 with a5). All 9/9 positions share the 'tempo_loss' tag, and the average cp_loss of 335 reflects positions where the margin for error was essentially zero.
analysis.move_pattern: Mixed piece types (queen retreats, king walks to adjacent squares, flank pawn pushes, wrong-piece captures) that appear constructive but address a secondary concern rather than the position's critical demand
analysis.why_bad: Each move wastes the one tempo needed to address an immediate tactical emergency (capturing hanging material, blockading a passed pawn, maintaining a dominant piece's central post, or creating stalemate), allowing the opponent to execute a concrete tactical sequence that was previously prevented
sub_patterns: Passive queen retreat to e8 abandoning key defensive duties (3 instances)
King stepping to adjacent square that is exactly one tempo too far from the critical square
Speculative flank moves ignoring central hanging material or threats
Capturing with the wrong piece, abandoning a dominant centralized post

analysis.label: Moves that place or leave the king on a square where the opponent can execute a forcing check-based sequence that wins material or decisive tempo.
analysis.description: This feature fires on moves where the player creates or ignores a tactical vulnerability exploitable through checks. In 5/7 positions, the refutation involves a direct check winning material: Bd4+ exploiting the exposed b2 king (position 5), Bxc3+ exploiting the unresolved pin (position 4), Nxe8+ capturing with check because the king remained on g7 (position 3), Rf8+ back-rank mating pattern with king on h8 (position 2), and d3+ advancing with check against Ke2 (position 7). The remaining positions involve the move allowing the opponent to gain critical tempo through forcing sequences. In every case, the best move involved either advancing the king to a square immune to these checks (Kc5, Kg8, Kf6, Kc4 in positions 1,2,3,7), capturing the threatening piece (Nxb6 in position 5), or resolving the tactical tension before it could be exploited (Bd2 in positions 4,6). The average of only 1.6 good moves confirms these are high-precision positions where the one correct resource must be found.
analysis.move_pattern: King retreats/sidesteps to a square on a vulnerable geometric line (diagonal, file, back rank), or a non-king move ignores an existing check-based threat; the common direction is retreating/passive rather than advancing toward the threat
analysis.why_bad: The move places the king on (or leaves it on) a square where the opponent can deliver a check that simultaneously wins material, gains tempo for a passed pawn advance, or enables a forcing tactical sequence — the opponent's check-based resource either didn't exist or was neutralizable before the blunder
sub_patterns: King retreats into diagonal check (Kxb2→Bd4+, Ke2→d3+)
King retreats to back rank allowing file-based check (Kh8→Rf8+)
Non-king move ignores existing check vulnerability (e3 allows Nxe8+, Bg5 allows Bxc3+)
King moves passively when advancing eliminates the threat source (Kc7 vs Kc5, Ke2 vs Kc4)

analysis.label: King moves in pawn endgames with passed pawns that waste critical tempo or go to the wrong part of the board relative to the pawn race.
analysis.description: This feature fires on king moves in endgame positions (11/11 endgame) where passed pawns are present and pawn promotion races are the dominant strategic concern. Nearly all positions are pure pawn endgames (10/11) with exposed kings navigating relative to passed pawns. The king moves typically represent tempo inefficiencies: moving toward the wrong target (Position 10: Ka3 chasing the a2 pawn instead of blockading the c-pawn), approaching the wrong side of the board (Position 3: Kh5 abandoning the center while a passed e-pawn advances), moving to a square that loses a critical tempo in the pawn race (Position 4: Ke4 instead of Ke6, arriving one move too late for the draw), or choosing king activity over immediate pawn advancement (Position 12: Kb3 instead of pushing the a-pawn). Several activations show 0 cp loss (3/11), indicating the feature fires on the pattern of king maneuvering in passed-pawn endgames generally, with the mistakes being the extreme cases where the tempo cost is decisive.
analysis.move_pattern: King move (any direction) in pawn endgames with passed pawns present; king navigating toward or around the pawn structure rather than retreating to a defensive/blockading post
analysis.why_bad: The king wastes a critical tempo by moving to a square that doesn't efficiently address the passed pawn race—either chasing an irrelevant target, going to the wrong side of the board, or moving when a pawn push was more urgent, allowing the opponent's passed pawn(s) to advance with decisive speed advantage.
sub_patterns: King approaches wrong side while passed pawn advances on opposite wing
King moves when immediate pawn push was needed for race timing
King chases material (pawn capture) while critical blockade square is abandoned
King centralizes aimlessly instead of heading to specific drawing/blockading square
King leaves critical support square for own pawn breakthrough

analysis.label: Non-forcing, natural-looking moves played in positions that demand immediate concrete action (captures, sacrifices, or forcing continuations).
analysis.description: This feature activates on quiet, non-tactical moves—piece developments, king repositionings, and gentle pawn advances—that ignore urgent tactical demands in the position. In 9/11 positions, the best move was a concrete forcing continuation (capture, sacrifice, or decisive pawn break): Bxf7+ (pos 5), Qe7 invasion (pos 7), f4 pawn support (pos 8), d4 central break (pos 9), Nxe4 tactical capture (pos 12), bxc6 deflection capture (pos 13). The played moves instead 'improve' pieces to seemingly natural squares (Bd7, Nbd7, Nc6, Bf4, Qh3) or make prophylactic gestures (Kh1, g3, Kh5) that waste the critical tempo needed to exploit opponent vulnerabilities. Even the 0-cp-loss positions (1, 3) fit the pattern of choosing a quiet continuation over more forcing alternatives. The average 2.0 good moves available confirms these are narrow positions with specific tactical solutions.
analysis.move_pattern: Any non-forcing move (no captures, no checks): piece development to natural squares, king repositioning, quiet pawn advances, or piece retreats
analysis.why_bad: These moves squander a critical tactical window by giving the opponent a free tempo to neutralize threats, exchange key attackers, consolidate weaknesses, or execute their own tactical ideas—the position demanded an immediate forcing continuation that the quiet move fails to deliver.
sub_patterns: Passive piece development ignoring tactical sacrifice (Bd7, Nbd7, Nc6, Bf4)
King moves that waste tempo or create vulnerability (Kh1, Kh5, Kf4)
Pawn moves that open lines for opponent or miss captures (g3, b6)
Queen repositioning that is too slow (Qh3)

analysis.label: Playing a superficially active or purposeful-looking move while ignoring a concrete tactical need or abandoning a critical sector of the board.
analysis.description: In all 6 positions, the player chose a move that appears active or ambitious—penetrating enemy territory, developing a piece to a 'natural' square, or seeking counterplay—but fundamentally ignores the position's concrete demands. In 2/6 cases (Qb2, Qa5), a queen is relocated away from the critical kingside sector where it was either attacking or defending, leaving the king fatally exposed. In 2/6 cases (Qd7, Rc7), a major piece penetrates deep into the opponent's position only to become a tactical target—vulnerable to a discovered attack/fork (Be5+ forking king and rook) or a pawn break (d4 hitting the queen on the open file). In 2/6 cases (Kf6, Bc4), the player makes a 'general principles' move (centralizing the king, developing the bishop classically) while missing a specific concrete tactic (Nc4+ fork winning a pawn, or d4/exf5 exploiting central tension). The unifying thread is prioritizing the appearance of purposeful play over calculating what the position actually requires.
analysis.move_pattern: Various pieces (mostly queen 3/6, also king, bishop, rook) moved to squares that appear active or penetrating but are either too far from the critical sector or tactically exposed
analysis.why_bad: The moves prioritize superficial activity or general principles over concrete positional/tactical demands—either abandoning a critical zone where the piece was needed, placing it on a square where it becomes a tactical target, or ignoring a forcing tactical resource that required immediate attention
sub_patterns: Queen abandoning critical kingside sector for illusory queenside counterplay (Qb2, Qa5)
Piece penetrating enemy position only to become a fork/discovery target (Qd7, Rc7)
Natural-looking move ignoring a concrete forced tactic (Kf6 missing Nc4+, Bc4 ignoring central tension)

analysis.label: Major piece (queen or rook) abandons an active file or post for a passive square, surrendering tempo and initiative.
analysis.description: All three positions feature a major piece voluntarily leaving a key active position for a passive square: Qd1 retreats the queen to the back rank instead of keeping it aggressively placed (3/3 involve tempo loss); Rc7 pulls the rook from the active first rank to a defensive seventh-rank post; Rg8 slides the rook off the critical open d-file to the g-file. In each case (3/3), the opponent immediately exploits the lost tempo—White launches a kingside pawn storm (Position 5), White infiltrates with Rh7+ winning a pawn (Position 10), or White executes a devastating Ne4+ fork on the now-undefended rook (Position 14). All three analyses explicitly tag 'tempo_loss' and 'piece_activity' as core issues (3/3), and in each position the active alternative (Qc8, b5/Rd1, Ba8) maintained pressure on critical lines. The average cp_loss of 290 reflects how severely passivity is punished when the opponent has concrete tactical resources.
analysis.move_pattern: Major piece (Q or R) moves away from an active file or aggressive post to a passive/retreating square, often along a rank or to the back rank
analysis.why_bad: Surrendering tempo allows the opponent to activate decisively—either launching pawn storms, infiltrating on open files, or executing tactical shots against pieces left undefended by the retreat
sub_patterns: Queen retreating to back rank when aggressive queen placement available
Rook leaving open file for lateral defensive move
Rook abandoning doubled-rook coordination on key file

analysis.label: Playing a slow positional/strategic move that completely ignores the position's most urgent tactical requirement (hanging piece, exposed king, or critical defender needed).
analysis.description: In all 4/4 positions, the player chose a move motivated by long-term strategic thinking while a critical tactical crisis demanded immediate attention. In Position 13 (g4), the player tried to undermine a pawn chain while their rook was attacked by two pieces. In Position 12 (Nb6), the player moved a knight to attack d5 while it was the sole defender of the critical f8 square near their exposed king. In Position 2 (Kd4), the player centralized the king as in a pawn endgame, ignoring that the opponent's queen demanded king shelter. In Position 5 (Ne2), the knight moved to an undefended square where it could be captured for free while abandoning its central post. All 4/4 moves are quiet (no checks, captures, or direct threats) played in positions where immediate forced/defensive action was required. The average cp_loss of ~4700 reflects the catastrophic nature of these oversights.
analysis.move_pattern: Quiet non-forcing move (no check, no capture, no direct threat) - typically a piece relocation or pawn push with strategic intent, played when a piece is hanging or a critical defense is required
analysis.why_bad: The move addresses a secondary positional concern (centralization, pawn attack, file blockade) while ignoring the position's most critical tactical requirement - either saving an attacked piece, maintaining a key defender, or keeping the king sheltered from immediate threats
sub_patterns: Pawn push ignoring a hanging piece that needs immediate rescue
Knight relocation abandoning critical defensive duty (removing the defender of a key square)
King advance into exposed square when retreat to shelter was essential
Piece placement on undefended square while failing to address urgent threats

analysis.label: Natural-looking but passive moves that allow the opponent to gain tempo through checks, captures, or forcing piece invasions.
analysis.description: This feature fires on moves that address an immediate concern (developing a piece, removing a threat, blockading a pawn) in the most obvious but suboptimal way, resulting in a critical tempo loss. In 3/7 positions, Nh3 develops the knight to a rim square that fails to cover the critical d4 outpost, allowing the opponent's knight to invade with tempo against the queen. In 3/7 positions, king moves (Kxf7, Kc2, Ke7) either expose the king to checks/forks (4/7 involve the opponent gaining tempo via check or piece attack), retreat when active counterplay was needed, or abandon defense of material. In 1/7, a rook capture enters a theoretically lost simplified position. All 7/7 positions share the tag 'tempo_loss' in their analysis, and 6/7 involve 'piece_activity' issues. The correct moves in each case were more dynamic: Ne2 covering d4 (3 cases), active king moves toward threats rather than away (Ke5 vs Ke7, Kd3 vs Kc2), or maintaining pieces on the board rather than trading into worse endings.
analysis.move_pattern: Piece moves to a passive or peripheral square (knight to h-file rim, king retreating/sideways, rook exchanging into worse endgame) rather than an active central square
analysis.why_bad: The move fails to address the critical positional requirement (usually controlling a key central square or maintaining activity), allowing the opponent to gain a forcing tempo through checks, attacks on undefended pieces, or tactical invasions that weren't possible before
sub_patterns: Knight to h3 leaving d4 uncontrolled (3/7)
King move exposing itself to checks or abandoning pawn defense (3/7)
Capture that enters a losing simplified position (1/7)

analysis.label: Playing a slow, peripheral, or misdirected move in a position that demands immediate, forcing action to address a critical threat or maintain coordination.
analysis.description: This feature fires on moves that waste a crucial tempo by prioritizing a secondary objective over the position's primary tactical or strategic demand. In 7/8 analyzed positions, 'tempo_loss' was explicitly tagged as the core error. The moves fall into sub-categories but share the same fundamental flaw: pawn grabs that displace the queen (Qxb7, Qxa2 - positions 3, 12), slow pawn pushes when active piece play is urgent (b3, g6, a5 - positions 4, 5, 11), king moves in the wrong direction (Kf1, Kg7 - positions 2, 10), and piece moves that abandon critical duties or invite immediate challenge (Rxe7, Ng6, Bd4 - positions 1, 6, 7). In all cases, the opponent punishes by executing their plan one tempo faster - whether that's a promotion (positions 10, 11), a pawn break (position 5's a5), a fork (position 12's Nc4), or a structural collapse (position 1's d5 loss). The average cp_loss of 1146 and average of only 2.1 good moves confirm these are critical decision points where precision was essential.
analysis.move_pattern: Any piece type; typically non-forcing (no check, often not a capture except peripheral pawn grabs); moves directed away from the critical sector of the board or toward irrelevant objectives
analysis.why_bad: The position demands immediate, forcing action to neutralize a concrete threat or maintain piece coordination, but the played move ignores this urgency, giving the opponent a free tempo to execute their plan (promotion, tactical strike, structural destruction, or decisive piece activation)
sub_patterns: Queen captures peripheral pawn, becoming displaced from critical defense
Slow pawn push in tactically critical position ignoring opponent's threats
King moves in wrong direction exposing it to files or missing recapture squares
Piece repositioned to exposed square immediately challenged with tempo gain
Critical defender moved away allowing tactical exploitation of unguarded piece

analysis.label: Playing general piece-improvement moves (rooks to open files, bishops to diagonals, queen centralizing) while ignoring an immediate concrete tactical threat demanding urgent action.
analysis.description: In 8/8 positions, the player makes a move that looks positionally reasonable in isolation—placing a rook on an open file (Rac8, Rd8), repositioning a bishop to an active diagonal (Bc4 x2, Ba7), centralizing the queen (Qd5), or advancing a pawn for space (c4)—but critically ignores an urgent tactical emergency. In 6/8 cases, the position featured an immediate tactical threat (promotion on c7/c8, knight fork via Ne7+, mating attack via f5 break, en passant creating passed pawns, back-rank vulnerability) that required concrete defensive action. In 7/8 cases, the best moves involved addressing the immediate threat directly (capturing the dangerous pawn, escaping with the king, creating counterplay against the opponent's king). The average cp_loss of 3626 reflects that many of these 'quiet improvement' moves walked into forced mates or decisive material loss.
analysis.move_pattern: Piece relocation to a conventionally desirable square (open file, long diagonal, center) rather than addressing the most forcing line in the position
analysis.why_bad: The position demands an immediate concrete response to a tactical threat (promotion, fork, mating attack, en passant), but the player makes a general positional improvement move that loses critical tempo, allowing the opponent to execute their threat unimpeded.
sub_patterns: Rook to open file while king needs escape route (Rac8, Rd8)
Bishop repositioned to active diagonal while hanging piece/promotion unaddressed (Bc4, Ba7)
Queen centralized while king faces mating threats (Qd5, Qe1)
Pawn advance creating tactical vulnerability (c4 allowing en passant)

analysis.label: Queenside castling (O-O-O) directly into an opponent's advanced pawns or ready-made pawn storm that immediately opens lines against the king.
analysis.description: In 9/10 positions, the move is O-O-O (the outlier Rab8 prioritizes queenside counterplay while ignoring immediate threats). The consistent error is placing the king on the c1/c8 square when the opponent already has advanced queenside pawns acting as battering rams. In positions 1, 4, and 15, Black has advanced b/c pawns (b5, c5) ready to push forward with ...b4 or ...c4 to rip open files. In positions 3, 5, and 6, White has an advanced b4 pawn and prepared a4-a5 break that cracks open the a-file within 2 moves. In position 7, Black's pieces already target the c-file with knight-to-b4 fork threats. In position 10, the a-file becomes an invasion route via ...Rxa2. All 10/10 positions share the king_safety tactical motif, and in 9/10 cases the opponent's castled king was on the opposite wing, meaning the player castled away from where safety actually existed. The average cp_loss of 1143 reflects catastrophic consequences.
analysis.move_pattern: King castles queenside (Ke1→c1 or Ke8→c8) via O-O-O; opponent has pre-advanced pawns on the b/c/a files or immediate pawn-lever access to open lines toward c1/c8
analysis.why_bad: The opponent already has advanced pawns (typically on b5/b4/c5 or b6 as a hook for a4-a5) that can immediately open files against the freshly castled king, turning latent queenside pressure into a concrete, often unstoppable attack. The king walks directly into the opponent's strongest sector of play.
sub_patterns: O-O-O into opponent's advanced b5/b4 pawn ready to push and open the b/a-file
O-O-O into opponent's a4-a5 pawn break with b6 pawn serving as a hook
O-O-O into open/semi-open c-file with opponent's pieces already targeting queenside squares
O-O-O giving tempo to opponent for central pawn breaks that expose the king
O-O-O instead of exploiting immediate tactical opportunities (tempo loss)

analysis.label: Moving the king (or key piece) away from an opponent's dangerous passed pawn that urgently needs to be blockaded or restrained.
analysis.description: In 10/11 positions, the blunder involves a move that neglects an opponent's advanced passed pawn by moving a defending piece in the wrong direction. The dominant pattern is king moves away from the promotion path (8/11 are king moves: Kf4, Ke2, Kc5, Kd5, Ke5, Ke5, Kc1, Kxb7), but also includes a bishop abandoning a blockading diagonal (Bd2 in position 2) and a pawn capture removing a sentry restraining a passer (gxf6 in position 8). In every case, the correct move involved either racing the king toward the passed pawn's promotion square, maintaining a piece on a blockading square, or immediately eliminating the passed pawn. The player typically chose centralization, own-pawn support, piece activation, or material capture over the singular defensive priority of containing the opponent's passer.
analysis.move_pattern: King (or bishop) moving away from opponent's passed pawn's promotion path; typically moving laterally or in the opposite direction from where blockade is needed
analysis.why_bad: The opponent's passed pawn advances unopposed to promotion because the only piece capable of restraining it has moved away, and the resulting promotion threat or promotion itself is faster than whatever counterplay the misguided move intended to create.
sub_patterns: King marching toward wrong flank (Kc5, Ke5, Kc1, Ke2, Kd5)
King capturing material instead of blockading (Kxb7)
Bishop abandoning blockade diagonal (Bd2)
Pawn capture removing sentry pawn (gxf6)
Piece activation wasting critical tempo (Ba6, Kf4)

analysis.label: Playing seemingly active or purposeful moves that ignore the position's single most critical tactical or defensive demand.
analysis.description: This feature fires on moves that appear constructive—queen raids (Qa5, Qb7, Qd3), piece repositioning (Bf3, Ne5), pawn advances (e5, d6, f3), or rook penetration (Rb7)—but catastrophically ignore the one critical demand of the position. In 7/9 positions, the best move addressed a concrete defensive need or secured a vulnerability before acting (e.g., Rf1 to defend back rank, Rh8 to challenge the attacker, Rd2 to expel an infiltrating queen, Qd3 to defend a hanging knight, d5 to block a diagonal). In 8/9 cases the blunder allowed immediate tactical exploitation of the ignored vulnerability: king checks with piece capture (3/9), hanging pieces won with tempo (2/9), devastating infiltrations on abandoned files/diagonals (3/9). The extremely low average of 1.7 good moves confirms these are critical-precision positions where only one correct idea existed, yet the player chose a 'side quest' instead.
analysis.move_pattern: Various piece types moving to active-looking squares (flanks, center, 7th rank) or pawn advances that attack opponent pieces, all directed AWAY from the position's critical sector
analysis.why_bad: The position has a single urgent need (defending the king, securing a hanging piece, blocking a critical diagonal/file) and the move ignores it to pursue irrelevant activity, giving the opponent a tempo to exploit the unaddressed vulnerability with checks, captures, or forced tactical sequences
sub_patterns: Queen abandoning king defense for flank raids (Qa5, Qb7)
Pawn advances that weaken structure or open lines for opponent (f3, e5, d6)
Piece moves to undefended or premature aggressive squares (Ne5, Rb7, Bf3)
Centralizing moves that miss the single tempo-critical advance (Qd3 instead of e5)

analysis.label: Moves that appear active or forcing (especially checks, captures, and aggressive queen moves) but actually waste a critical tempo, allowing the opponent to escape or improve their position.
analysis.description: This feature fires on moves where the player selects an apparently aggressive or forcing continuation—typically a check, capture, or assertive queen relocation—that actually squanders the initiative. In 3/8 positions the blunder is a premature check (Qh6+, Qh8+, Be5+) that drives the opponent's king toward safety instead of maintaining pressure with a more precise move. In 2/8 positions (Nxh6, Qh8+) the error is specifically a move-order mistake where the forcing move needed a preparatory step first. In 3/8 positions (Qg6, Qb6, Qb1) the queen moves to an apparently active square but actually abandons critical duties or allows the opponent a favorable simplification. The consistent thread across all 8 positions is that the player chose a natural-looking, aggressive move over a subtler or differently-ordered alternative that was objectively far stronger. The average cp_loss of 2564 reflects that these positions had very narrow winning paths (avg 1.4 good moves), making the tempo waste catastrophic—often converting forced mates into mere advantages, or winning positions into equality.
analysis.move_pattern: Primarily queen moves (5/8) or other piece moves that appear forcing; often checks or captures directed at the opponent's king sector; the piece moves toward the opponent but to the wrong square or in the wrong sequence
analysis.why_bad: These moves waste a critical tempo by forcing the opponent's pieces/king to squares that actually improve their position, or by committing to a sequence in the wrong order, allowing the opponent an escape route or defensive resource that a more precise (often quieter) move would have denied
sub_patterns: Premature checks that drive king to safety (checking disease)
Move-order errors where preparation was needed before the forcing move
Queen relocations that abandon critical defensive/offensive duties
Captures that leave key pawns/squares undefended

analysis.chip: Active piece lands on doomed square
analysis.label: Moving a piece to a seemingly purposeful square where it becomes immediately capturable, forkable, or tactically exploitable, while ignoring the position's critical need.
analysis.description: This feature fires on moves that appear to serve a clear purpose (checking, defending, developing, attacking) but place a piece on a square with a fatal tactical flaw. In 4/7 positions, the moved piece itself becomes immediately capturable or forkable (Re3+ captured by queen, Rf7 captured with check leading to mate, Bc4 forked by d5, Qb8 'defending' a rook that's actually blocked by own knight). In 3/7 positions, the piece moves away from the critical sector, leaving key squares/pawns undefended (Ba6 abandoning kingside defense, Ng4 abandoning b2 defense, Ke3 retreating into check vulnerability). The common thread is that each move has an obvious surface-level rationale but ignores a concrete tactical refutation that exploits the piece's new position. The average cp_loss of 1543 reflects how catastrophic these misjudgments can be, and the low average of 1.9 good alternatives shows these arise in already-demanding positions where precise calculation was required.
analysis.move_pattern: Various piece types moved to squares that appear active or defensive but are tactically compromised; no consistent direction, includes checks, developments, and retreats
analysis.why_bad: The destination square has a critical tactical vulnerability (can be captured with tempo, forked by a pawn, or is blocked from fulfilling its intended defensive purpose), while the move simultaneously abandons a more urgent positional or tactical priority in the position.
sub_patterns: Piece moves to a square where it can be immediately captured with devastating follow-up (Rf7, Re3+)
Piece develops to a square where a pawn fork wins it (Bc4 forked by d5)
Piece appears to defend but is obstructed by own pieces (Qb8 blocked by Nb5)
Piece relocates pursuing speculative threats while abandoning critical defensive duties (Ng4, Ba6, Ke3)

analysis.label: Moves that address a non-urgent concern while ignoring the position's critical demand (development, king safety, or king activation).
analysis.description: In all 5 positions, the player makes a move that appears purposeful—centralizing a piece (Nd4), chasing an enemy piece with a pawn (g6 x2), creating 'counterplay' (f5), or attacking a pawn (Rb3)—but fatally wastes a tempo when the position urgently demands something else. In 3/5 positions, the critical need is piece development with the king still in (or vulnerable in) the center. In 4/5, the move is a non-developing action when urgent threats exist. In 4/5, the opponent punishes the wasted tempo by exploiting weakened squares or seizing the initiative on the neglected front. The tagged tactical motif is 'tempo_loss' across all 5 positions, and the average cp_loss of 193 reflects that one wasted move in these tense positions hands the opponent a decisive advantage. The best alternatives in all cases involve addressing the primary positional need directly: developing pieces (3/5), activating the king in the endgame (1/5), or repositioning pieces without weakening the pawn structure (1/5).
analysis.move_pattern: Any piece or pawn move (often a kingside pawn push like g6/f5 or a piece relocation) that pursues a secondary objective rather than the most urgent positional task
analysis.why_bad: The position has one critical demand (development, king safety, or king activation) that tolerates no delay; the played move ignores this demand, giving the opponent a free tempo to exploit the existing weaknesses with tactical strikes on undefended squares, diagonals, or files.
sub_patterns: Prophylactic kingside pawn push (g6/f5) that weakens king's pawn shield or key squares while development is incomplete
Piece repositioning to an 'ideal' square that gets immediately challenged with tempo (Nd4 met by ...c5)
Attacking a peripheral target (Rb3 vs e3 pawn) instead of executing the winning plan (king march)

analysis.label: Mistakes in positions where both kings are exposed and vulnerable, leading to critical navigational or defensive errors.
analysis.description: This feature fires on positions where BOTH kings simultaneously have weak pawn shields and are exposed (10/10 positions explicitly note both kings' vulnerability). The resulting mutual tension creates high-stakes decision points where the player navigates incorrectly. Common errors include moving the king to the wrong square when multiple directions exist (Kd2 instead of Kb2 in positions 4-5, Kf5 instead of Kg7 in position 1), removing a critical defender from near the vulnerable king (Ra7 in position 8 removes the g-file blockader), creating structural weaknesses near the exposed king (b5 in position 7), and giving premature checks instead of quiet winning moves that exploit the opponent's king exposure (Rb1+ in position 13 missing a forced mate via quiet bxa5). The mutual vulnerability amplifies the cost of errors—average cp_loss is 1188—because in these positions, a single wrong move can flip which exposed king becomes the fatal liability.
analysis.move_pattern: Diverse piece types (king, rook, queen, pawn) moving in various directions; the unifying geometric context is both kings on exposed squares with weak/absent pawn shields, often on the same rank or in open/semi-open positions
analysis.why_bad: The moves fail to correctly prioritize which king's exposure matters most—either abandoning a defensive duty that protects their own vulnerable king, moving the king toward danger rather than safety, or failing to exploit the opponent's exposed king with the most precise continuation (often a quiet move rather than a flashy check).
sub_patterns: King moves to wrong square when multiple escape routes exist
Piece/rook leaves critical defensive post near exposed king
Premature check allowing opponent's exposed king to escape to safety
Pawn advance creating new weaknesses around already-exposed king

analysis.label: Endgame moves that appear active or purposeful but fatally compromise piece coordination, allowing the opponent to win material through a short forcing sequence.
analysis.description: This feature fires on endgame positions (9/9) where a player makes a move that looks natural or productive—capturing a pawn (Rxc6), centralizing a rook (Rd4, Rd3), attacking a piece (Ra3), advancing a pawn (g4), repositioning a knight (Nb3), or activating the king (Kh5, Kg8)—but in reality creates a concrete tactical vulnerability exploitable through a forcing sequence. In 7/9 cases, the punishment involves checks or attacks along open lines that win material (typically a rook via skewer, separation from the king, or trapping). The positions share open centers with exposed kings (9/9 have at least one exposed king), and the blunder typically abandons a critical defensive responsibility or places a piece on a square where geometric relationships (same file as king creating skewers in position 9, blocking escape squares in position 4, vulnerability along a rank in position 2) allow immediate tactical punishment. The average cp_loss of 1300 reflects that these are catastrophic errors despite 2.3 good alternatives being available on average.
analysis.move_pattern: Piece (usually rook or king) moves to an apparently active square in an open endgame position, but lands on a tactically compromised square vulnerable to checks, skewers, or direct attacks along open lines/ranks/files
analysis.why_bad: The moves prioritize apparent activity or secondary goals (material gain, centralization, pawn advance) while creating a geometric vulnerability that allows the opponent to win decisive material through a short forcing sequence—typically involving checks that separate pieces, skewers along shared lines, or attacks on undefended pieces that can no longer be rescued.
sub_patterns: Rook moved to square where it's attacked/trapped along a rank or file (Rd4, Rxc6, Ra3, Rd3)
King moved to square exposed to check sequences that separate it from its rook or create skewers (Kh5, Kg8)
Move blocks own king's escape squares or abandons critical defensive duties (g4, Rg1, Nb3)

analysis.label: Playing repositioning or 'improving' moves in sharp positions that demand one specific immediate concrete action.
analysis.description: This feature fires on moves that look purposeful (centralizing, repositioning, or creating apparent threats) but fatally waste the one critical tempo available in a position with very narrow margins (avg 1.8 good moves). In 6/7 analyzed positions, the correct move was a specific forcing action: a sacrifice to expose the king (Bxa6 in pos 1), capturing a hanging piece (Qxe7 in pos 3), challenging an attacking piece (d6 in pos 4), penetrating with the correct piece (Rxc7+ in pos 5), a tactical knight strike (Nc4 in pos 7), or maintaining a key piece on its critical square (Bg3/keeping rook on c4 in pos 12-14). Instead, the player chose moves like slow pawn pushes (a4), bishop 'improvements' (Bg7), knight 'centralization' (Ne6), king walks (Ke7), queen repositioning to irrelevant wings (Qa5), or rook redeployment away from critical files (Rf4). The 'tempo_loss' tag appears in 7/7 positions, and 'missed_tactic' in 6/7, confirming the pattern of squandering a one-move window for optimal action.
analysis.move_pattern: Various piece types repositioned to 'better-looking' squares; non-forcing moves (or wrong forcing moves) in positions demanding one specific concrete action
analysis.why_bad: These moves waste the single available tempo in razor-sharp positions where only 1-2 moves maintain the evaluation, allowing the opponent to consolidate, trade off attacking pieces, advance passed pawns, or launch counter-attacks that the displaced/repositioned piece can no longer defend against
sub_patterns: Slow preparatory pawn moves when immediate sacrificial tactics are available
Piece repositioning that abandons critical file or defensive duty
Natural-looking knight/king centralization that ignores concrete forcing moves
Queen moved to irrelevant wing while kingside attack becomes unstoppable
Choosing flashy but wrong forcing move over correct one with same theme

analysis.label: Moving a piece away from a square where it performs an essential tactical or strategic function, in favor of a superficially active or natural-looking move.
analysis.description: This feature fires on positions where a player displaces a piece from a critical role—whether defensive blocking, mating net construction, piece protection, or controlling a key line—to make a move that appears active but fundamentally ignores the position's urgent tactical demand. In 8/10 cases, the moved piece was performing an irreplaceable function on its original square: the knight on e4 controlled c5 for the mating net (Nc5+), the knight on d2 blocked the b4-e1 diagonal (Ndf3), the knight on d6 controlled the center and queenside (Nxf7), the queen protected a hanging piece (Qb2 abandoned Re7, Qh6 abandoned Nf3), the rook needed to pin the g4-pawn (Rb3 instead of Ra4), and the rook on a7 needed preparatory moves before checking (Ra8+). The positions uniformly feature very few good alternatives (avg 1.7), meaning precision was mandatory, yet the players chose moves that LOOK forcing or logical—often checks (4/10), captures, or standard development—while catastrophically misallocating their most important piece.
analysis.move_pattern: Any piece type moving away from a critical square/function; often checks, captures, or developing moves that displace the piece from an essential role
analysis.why_bad: The moved piece was performing an irreplaceable tactical or strategic function on its original square (blocking a diagonal, completing a mating net, protecting a hanging piece, pinning an enemy pawn), and relocating it allows the opponent to exploit the newly created vulnerability—whether capturing an undefended piece, breaking through with a passed pawn, escaping a mating net, or delivering a devastating check on the vacated line.
sub_patterns: Giving a check that removes a piece from a mating/attacking construction (Nc5+, Ng3+)
Moving a queen away from protecting a hanging piece (Qb2, Qh6)
Relocating a knight from a critical blocking/controlling square (Ndf3, Nxf7)
Moving a rook away from its only effective defensive post (Rb3, Ra8+)
Developing a piece while ignoring an urgent central/tactical crisis (Bb4, Rf8)

analysis.label: Giving non-constructive checks (or passive moves) in tempo-critical endgames instead of the one purposeful move that addresses the critical threat.
analysis.description: This feature fires on endgame positions where the player gives a check or makes a natural-looking move that wastes a critical tempo, when the position demands an immediate purposeful action (king advance, pawn blockade, or precise rook placement). In 5/7 positions the move is a check (Qf6+, Qb7+, Qe4+, Qa6+, Ne5+), and in 6/7 the analysis identifies 'tempo_loss' as the core tactical motif. The best moves in these positions are consistently quiet, constructive moves: king centralization (Kb4, Kc6, Ke5), direct pawn blockade (Qe3, Qh2), or precise rook placement (Rd4/Rd7). The checks drive the opponent's king to squares it wanted to reach anyway or fail to address the critical positional demand (stopping a promotion, winning a race, or approaching with the king). Average cp_loss of 1583 reflects that several positions involve converting forced mates into draws.
analysis.move_pattern: Queen or knight check along open lines toward exposed king, or passive piece move on an open file, in positions where a quiet king/piece approach was critical
analysis.why_bad: In tempo-critical endgames (pawn races, promotion threats, stalemate patterns), one wasted move gives the opponent exactly the tempo needed to draw or equalize—the check accomplishes nothing the quiet move wouldn't achieve more efficiently, or actively improves the opponent's king position
sub_patterns: Queen check that allows opponent king to improve (Qf6+, Qb7+, Qa6+)
Check that drives king toward promotion support square (Ne5+ letting Kg7)
Check before eventual blockade wastes tempo (Qe4+ before Qe3)
Passive piece move in critical pawn race (Rd3 instead of Rd4)

analysis.label: Quiet, routine moves that ignore the urgent demand to address king vulnerability, either by failing to relocate an exposed king or by missing concrete exploitation of an opponent's exposed king.
analysis.description: In 6/6 analyzed positions, the critical factor was king safety—either the player's own king was on a tactically vulnerable square (exposed to forks, checks, rook invasions) or the opponent's king was exposed and demanded immediate exploitation. Instead of addressing this urgent need, the player chose quiet, natural-looking moves: repositioning pieces (Be7, Rc7, Rc8), pushing pawns (c5), making routine recaptures (Nxf3), or moving the king to the wrong square (O-O, Kb2). In 5/6 positions, the best move involved either physically relocating the king to a safer square (Ka8, Kc8, Kd2) or launching a concrete tactical strike against the opponent's vulnerable king (Nb5). The tag 'king_safety' appears in 5/6 tactical motif labels, and 'exposed_king' or 'king_in_center' appears across all positions. The average cp_loss of 1558 reflects how catastrophically these quiet moves fail when king vulnerability is the dominant positional factor.
analysis.move_pattern: Quiet non-forcing moves (piece repositioning, pawn pushes, routine recaptures, castling) that do not address king vulnerability on an exposed file/rank/diagonal
analysis.why_bad: The position demands immediate concrete action for king safety (relocating the king, contesting a critical file, or exploiting opponent's king exposure), but the player addresses a secondary concern (material defense, piece development, general principles), leaving the king on a square where it is subject to devastating tactical blows (forks, checks, rook invasions, deflections).
sub_patterns: Defending material while own king remains on tactically exposed square (Rc8, Rc7)
Quiet piece repositioning ignoring open-file pressure against own king (Be7, c5)
Moving king to wrong square creating new tactical vulnerabilities (Kb2, O-O)
Routine recapture that strips king's defensive structure (Nxf3)

analysis.label: Playing a plausible-looking but non-urgent move at a critical moment when the position demands immediate concrete action.
analysis.description: This feature fires on positions where the player spends a crucial tempo on a secondary concern while ignoring the position's most pressing demand. In 4/11 cases, slow pawn moves (a3, a6, c5) or preparatory pawn pushes (Kd5 missing h5) are played when development or tactical precision is urgent. In 3/11 cases, king moves (Ke7 twice, Kd5) waste critical tempo in races or expose the king unnecessarily. In 4/11 cases, piece moves that seem logical (Bd7 developing, Qd2 repositioning, Bf3 challenging a piece, Nd8 rerouting) address non-critical concerns while enabling devastating tactical responses. The common thread across all positions is that exactly one tempo separates a manageable position from a catastrophic one, and the chosen move squanders that tempo on something that looks reasonable but is the wrong priority. The best alternatives in every case address the position's primary urgency—whether castling immediately, fixing pawn structure, keeping a key defender in place, or retreating to a safe square.
analysis.move_pattern: Any piece type; typically quiet non-forcing moves (no checks, no captures except Nxd5); moves to seemingly natural squares that address secondary positional concerns rather than the primary tactical/strategic demand
analysis.why_bad: These moves waste an irreplaceable tempo at a critical juncture, allowing the opponent to execute a concrete plan (central break, tactical combination, pawn race win, or piece invasion) that was previously held at bay by exactly one tempo of defensive action or immediate counter-action.
sub_patterns: Slow prophylactic pawn moves when piece development is urgent (a3, c5)
Preparatory pawn advances when immediate advance is required (a6 instead of a5)
King moves that lose tempo in pawn races or expose to tactics (Ke7, Kd5)
Piece rerouting/repositioning that removes key defenders or enables forks (Nd8, Qd2, Bf3)
Developing moves that ignore castling urgency (Bd7)

analysis.label: Quiet, reasonable-looking moves that miss the one critical requirement in narrow positions with very few good alternatives.
analysis.description: This feature fires on positions where the player makes a quiet (non-checking, non-capturing) move that appears plausible but fails to address the position's most urgent tactical or strategic demand.
