In 9/9 cases, the played move involves no check or capture. The positions typically have very few good moves (avg 1.8), meaning one narrow correct path exists and the player chose a 'neighboring' alternative. Common failure modes include: moving the wrong piece to the right square (R8g7 vs R5g7, Rb2 vs Kb1), moving the right piece to the wrong square (Kb4 vs Kb2, Qc7 vs Qa5+, Rd3 vs Rh5), or moving in the wrong direction entirely (O-O-O vs O-O, Be4 vs Qd1). In 5/9 positions, the move creates an immediate tactical vulnerability (hanging piece, exposed king, or exploitable check). The remaining cases involve critical tempo losses in endgame races or forced-mate positions.
analysis.move_pattern: Quiet piece repositioning moves (no checks, no captures), predominantly to b/c-file squares (6/9), typically one square or direction off from the correct destination
analysis.why_bad: These moves address a secondary concern (defense, development, piece activity) while ignoring the position's primary demand—whether that's a hanging piece, a critical pawn race tempo, an immediate check opportunity, or a king safety emergency. The narrowness of correct options (avg 1.8 good moves) means even small deviations from the optimal plan are catastrophic.
sub_patterns: Wrong piece to correct destination (R8g7 instead of R5g7, Rb2 instead of Kb1)
Right piece to wrong square/no check (Qc7 instead of Qa5+, Kb4 instead of Kb2)
King moves toward danger instead of safety (O-O-O, Kb4 toward edge)
Piece placed on undefended/tactically vulnerable square (Be4, Rd3)

analysis.label: Playing a non-forcing move (no check/capture) in a desperate position where an immediate check was required to survive or maximize resistance.
analysis.description: In all 5 positions, the player made a quiet, non-forcing move when a check (or forcing defensive move) was essential to survival. In Position 3 (Qb4), White needed Qe7+ for perpetual check to draw but played a quiet queen move. In Position 8 (Qf3), Black needed Qd1+ as an intermediate check before Qf3 to prevent promotion. In Position 13 (Qb6), Black needed Qa8+ to force White into a defensive response. In Position 2 (Kf2), the king walked into the center allowing checks instead of retreating to h2 to avoid them. In Position 9 (Kc8), the king walked onto the c-file enabling a devastating check via Rac7+. In 5/5 cases, the move gave the opponent a free tempo to execute a winning plan (promotion, mating attack, piece capture). The average cp_loss of 5656 reflects that these tempo losses are immediately fatal in positions where every move counts.
analysis.move_pattern: King or Queen moves to a quiet square without delivering check, capture, or immediate threat, typically in positions where a check was available
analysis.why_bad: In critical positions (forced mates, promotion races, desperate defenses), failing to play the forcing move gives the opponent a free tempo to execute their winning plan — promote a pawn, construct a mating net, or win decisive material via discovered attacks
sub_patterns: Queen retreats when perpetual check was available
King walks onto open file enabling discovered/direct checks
Missing intermediate check before playing intended move

analysis.label: Playing slow repositioning moves (retreats, king shuffles, passive development) when an immediate capture of undefended material or exploitation of a tactical vulnerability was available.
analysis.description: This feature fires on positions where the player chose a non-forcing, quiet move while a concrete material-winning opportunity existed. In 4/7 positions (Ke7, Nb1, Na3, Qb3), the player missed capturing a completely undefended rook or exploiting a pin to win material — choosing instead to reposition a piece slowly. In position 12 (Qf3), the queen relocated to an 'active' square while leaving a pawn completely undefended for the opponent to grab. In position 11 (Kb8), the player shuffled the king instead of developing to maintain a file advantage. In position 1 (d4), a premature pawn advance ignored the tactical consequences of leaving pieces undefended. The unifying thread is prioritizing abstract positional improvement (knight rerouting, king safety shuffles, queen centralization) over immediate concrete tactical exploitation of hanging or poorly defended material.
analysis.move_pattern: Non-capturing, non-checking moves — typically retreats (Nb1, Qb3), sideways shuffles (Kb8, Ke7), rim development (Na3), or quiet queen relocation (Qf3) — all moving away from or ignoring the critical tactical square
analysis.why_bad: These moves waste a critical tempo in positions where an undefended piece can be captured or a forcing tactical sequence (pin exploitation, discovered attack) wins material immediately; the opponent uses the gifted tempo to defend the hanging piece or consolidate, permanently closing the tactical window.
sub_patterns: Knight retreat/rim move missing hanging rook (Nb1, Na3)
King shuffle instead of capturing material (Ke7, Kb8)
Queen relocation abandoning pin or leaving pawn undefended (Qb3, Qf3)
Premature pawn advance ignoring piece vulnerabilities (d4)

analysis.label: Moves that sacrifice critical dynamic resources (attacking coordination, defensive function, or checking potential) for superficially attractive but ultimately counterproductive short-term goals like captures, pointless checks, or passive safety.
analysis.description: This feature fires on moves where players prioritize immediately 'concrete' actions—material gains, giving check, or tucking the king away—while abandoning the position's essential dynamic requirements. In 4/6 positions, the move is tagged with tempo_loss as the core motif, and in 5/6 positions piece_activity is compromised. Captures with the wrong piece remove queens from critical defensive/attacking posts (Qxd5 abandons kingside defense in Position 1; Qxd6 abandons perpetual check resources in Position 7). Checks that look forcing actually allow defensive interpositions or simply misplace the checking piece (Rc1+ misplaces the rook from the active e-file in Position 6; Rf3+ allows the saving Rf2 interposition in Position 9). Passive moves seeking safety backfire immediately (Kh1 allows Rb1+ forcing the king back in Position 5). Piece rerouting abandons defensive duties (Nfd2 removes the d4 defender in Position 10). The common thread is choosing the 'obvious' move over the position's true demand, wasting the one critical tempo needed to maintain dynamic superiority.
analysis.move_pattern: Mixed piece types (queen captures, rook checks, king retreats, knight rerouting) that all share the quality of being immediate/concrete-looking actions (checks, captures, safety moves) that misplace the moving piece relative to the position's true demands
analysis.why_bad: These moves sacrifice essential positional or tactical resources—perpetual check potential, piece coordination against an exposed king, defensive coverage of critical squares, or rook placement on active files—for gains that prove illusory because the opponent immediately exploits the abandoned resource with a tempo-gaining response
sub_patterns: Greedy queen captures that remove the queen from defensive/attacking coordination
Pointless or premature checks that misplace the checking piece or allow saving interpositions
Passive king moves that invite immediate tempo-gaining checks
Piece rerouting that abandons a critical defensive function

analysis.label: Plausible-looking moves that neglect a critical prophylactic requirement in positions with very few safe options, enabling a forcing tactical punishment.
analysis.description: This feature fires on positions where the player makes a natural-seeming move (king development, recapture, material grab, rook repositioning) while overlooking that it specifically enables the opponent to execute a forcing sequence - typically starting with a check or tempo-gaining attack. In 6/6 positions, very few moves were safe (avg 1.5 good moves), creating a narrow tactical path the player missed. In 4/6 cases (Ke7, Kg8, Rbb1, Nxd5), the move abandons a defensive resource or exposes to checks along a newly-accessible line. In 2/6 cases (exf4, Qxf2), the move makes a wrong capture that creates immediate tactical vulnerabilities. The refutations consistently exploit the specific weakness created: Bf6+ exploits Ke7's diagonal exposure (pos 4), Qd5+ exploits Kg8's diagonal (pos 11), Bd4 exploits exf4's removed blocker (pos 8), Rd2 traps the queen after Qxf2 (pos 10), Qd7-Qxf7+ exploits Rbb1's abandoned counterplay (pos 14), and Rfe8 with tempo exploits Nxd5's back-rank vulnerability (pos 15).
analysis.move_pattern: Various piece types making natural-looking moves (king walks, recaptures, material grabs, rook repositioning) that expose to immediate forcing sequences on newly-accessible lines
analysis.why_bad: Each move neglects the ONE critical defensive/prophylactic requirement in a position with almost no margin for error, specifically enabling a forcing tactical sequence (check, tempo-gaining attack, or piece trap) that the opponent can immediately execute to convert a significant advantage
sub_patterns: King moving to a square exposed on a diagonal to checks (Ke7, Kg8)
Wrong recapture that removes a key defensive pawn/blocker (exf4)
Greedy capture ignoring a simpler winning move (Qxf2)
Abandoning an active piece from its critical post (Rbb1)
Premature material grab that can't be maintained due to tempo/back-rank issues (Nxd5)

analysis.label: In endgames with passed pawns, making a natural-looking improving move instead of the one urgent forcing advance that creates an immediate promotion threat or gains a critical tempo.
analysis.description: This feature fires on endgame positions where only one good move exists and that move is a forcing, time-sensitive action (usually a specific pawn advance creating a promotion threat), but the player instead makes a 'logical' but non-forcing improving move. In 6/6 positions, the blunder is tagged as tempo_loss; in 6/6 positions, passed pawns are the central strategic element. The correct move in 4/6 cases was a specific pawn push (f6 in three cases, e4 in one), while the played moves were king repositioning (Kg3, Kc7, Kg4), wrong pawn advances (g5, h6), or piece improvement (Be5). The common thread is that the best move FORCES the opponent into a specific response (covering promotion, retreating a piece), gaining a tempo that is then used to execute the secondary plan; the played move gives this tempo away, allowing the opponent to reorganize or launch counterplay. In 3/6 positions, the specific error was advancing the wrong pawn of a connected pair (g5/h6 instead of f6), failing to create the immediate promotion threat that pins the opponent's pieces to defensive duties.
analysis.move_pattern: Non-forcing king moves, bishop repositioning, or wrong pawn advances in positions where one specific forcing pawn push (often f6) was required
analysis.why_bad: These moves gift the opponent a critical tempo in razor-sharp endgames where move order determines the outcome - the opponent uses that tempo to reposition pieces optimally, start counterplay, or blockade the passed pawn that should have been advanced first
sub_patterns: Advancing wrong pawn of connected pair (g5/h6 instead of f6) - no immediate promotion threat
King repositioning before critical pawn push (Kg4/Kc7 instead of f6/e4)
Piece improvement move instead of tempo-gaining king attack (Be5 instead of Kd6)
King to aesthetic square instead of escort square (Kg3 instead of Ke3)

analysis.label: Passive piece repositioning moves that squander critical timing when the position demands immediate concrete action (typically advancing passed pawns or executing forcing tactics).
analysis.description: In all 4/4 positions, the player chose a quiet, non-forcing piece reposition to a seemingly useful square (Kd7 toward the center, Ng2 to target h-pawn, Ra2 to the second rank, Rfc8 to the open file) when the position urgently demanded an immediate concrete action. In 3/4 cases, the best move involved advancing or addressing passed pawns (b3 push in position 12, Kc8 to flexibly contest the b-pawn in position 1, Rab1 targeting the b4-pawn in position 6). In 4/4 cases, the opponent exploited the gifted tempo to reorganize or create new threats (e6+ with check, Nc6 hitting the rook, Rc2 invasion, rook repositioning). The common 'tempo_loss' tag appears in all 4 analyses, and the average cp_loss of 289 reflects how severely these positions punish one wasted move.
analysis.move_pattern: Non-forcing piece move (any piece type) to a seemingly natural/useful square, with no check, no capture, and no immediate threat created
analysis.why_bad: The position demands immediate concrete action (advancing passed pawns, executing forks, or creating forcing threats), but the quiet repositioning move gifts the opponent a critical tempo to stabilize, create counterplay, or execute tactical resources that exploit the moved piece's new position
sub_patterns: Piece retreat from active square when forcing continuation exists
Rook reposition instead of pawn advance in passed-pawn positions
King move to wrong square allowing opponent check/tempo gain

analysis.label: Playing a plausible-looking move that addresses a secondary concern while missing the position's single critical tactical opportunity or urgent requirement.
analysis.description: This feature fires on positions where the player chooses a 'natural' or 'obvious-seeming' move in a narrow critical position (avg 1.8 good moves available) that demands precise concrete play. In 5/8 cases, the missed opportunity was a material-winning tactic: capturing a hanging piece (Qxh1 in pos 1, Qxa8 in pos 4, Qxb2 in pos 7), a preliminary exchange sacrifice (Rxc6! in pos 6), or winning material before the opponent stabilizes (Bxa6 in pos 2). In 3/8 cases, the error involved a king move to an exposed square that allows immediate tactical punishment (Kh6 walking into Rh7# in pos 3, Kg7 walking into Ndf5+ fork in pos 5, Kf6 allowing the opponent to play h6 first in pos 8). The common thread is that each position had one specific non-obvious move that was essential, while the played move addressed something that looked important (eliminating a passed pawn, developing a piece, 'activating' the king, prophylaxis) but was strategically secondary to the actual tactical demand.
analysis.move_pattern: Mixed piece types and directions; no single geometric pattern - the moves span queens capturing centrally, knights developing, kings stepping forward/sideways, pawn captures and pushes
analysis.why_bad: These moves fail because they address a visible but secondary concern (removing a threat, developing, prophylaxis, king activation) while ignoring the position's single critical demand - typically an unexpected material-winning shot or a forced refutation that the new piece placement allows
sub_patterns: Missing a hanging/undefended piece capture (Qxh1, Qxa8, Qxb2)
King walking into tactical vulnerability (checks, forks, or mating nets)
Wrong move order in a forced sequence (dxe5 before Rxc6, Kf6 before h6)
Slow positional move when concrete action is demanded (Ng3, g6)

analysis.label: Moving a piece toward an opponent's unstoppable passed pawn instead of generating counterplay elsewhere on the board.
analysis.description: This feature fires on endgame positions where a dangerous passed pawn (usually the opponent's) is close to promotion, and the player wastes critical tempo by moving a piece toward that pawn in a futile attempt to stop or blockade it. In 7/9 positions, there is a passed pawn within 1-2 squares of promotion that the played move cannot actually stop. The correct plans universally involve ignoring the unstoppable pawn and instead generating counterplay in the opposite wing (attacking kingside pawns in positions 1, 9, 10; heading queenside in position 3), finding shelter in enemy pawn structures (position 13), or targeting concrete material (position 15). The average cp_loss of 2113 reflects several catastrophic cases where the tempo loss converts a survivable position into forced mate. The positions are exclusively endgames (9/9) with passed pawns as the central tension, and the key diagnostic is that the best moves always direct energy AWAY from the passed pawn toward alternative counterplay.
analysis.move_pattern: King or knight moving toward an opponent's advanced passed pawn (approaching the promotion square or its file), typically 1-2 squares closer to the pawn
analysis.why_bad: The passed pawn is unstoppable regardless of the approach, so the move wastes irreplaceable tempo in a pawn race; the piece must later reverse direction to generate counterplay, falling fatally behind in the race or allowing promotion with check/forced mate.
sub_patterns: King approaching opponent's far-advanced a/b/c pawn instead of attacking kingside pawns
King moving adjacent to promotion square allowing promotion with check
Knight centralizing abstractly instead of capturing a concrete hanging pawn
King moving to exposed open terrain instead of sheltering in enemy pawn mass

analysis.label: Black plays a superficially active-looking move that ignores the position's concrete tactical requirement, leaving a piece/pawn misplaced while a straightforward response neutralizes all threats.
analysis.description: In all 3/3 positions, Black chose a move that appeared aggressive or developmental but failed to address the position's single most critical concrete need. In position 4, f2 pushed toward promotion but ignored the winning exchange fxg2 that secured a draw. In position 8, Bd6 developed a piece to an 'active' diagonal but ignored the need for Nbd7 to create a queen-trapping threat, allowing White to simply capture the hanging rook. In position 13, Qa4 placed the queen on an apparently active square but moved it away from the center where Qc3 was needed to attack the e3 weakness, allowing White to equalize with Qg3. All 3/3 moves share the property that they look natural or threatening at a glance but are trivially refuted by a single straightforward response (Kxf2, Qxa8, Qg3), after which the piece/pawn is either lost or stranded on an irrelevant square. The correct moves in each case required concrete calculation rather than general principles of activity.
analysis.move_pattern: Piece or pawn moved to an apparently aggressive/active square (forward pawn push, piece development to open diagonal, queen to active-looking file) that is actually peripheral to the position's critical demands
analysis.why_bad: The move creates an illusion of activity or threat that is neutralized by one simple response, while the position's actual concrete requirement (exchanging to simplify, developing a specific piece to create a trap, centralizing to attack a weakness) goes unmet, resulting in material loss or complete dissipation of advantage.
sub_patterns: Pawn advance toward promotion when exchange was needed
Piece development to 'active' square while ignoring hanging material
Queen relocation to peripheral square abandoning central pressure

analysis.label: Major piece moves to directly confront an enemy pawn in an endgame, losing tempo or flexibility when indirect methods (king advancement, rook-behind-pawn, flexible file placement) are required.
analysis.description: This feature fires on endgame positions where a player moves a rook or queen to directly attack or confront an enemy pawn, typically landing on a square where the piece can be challenged by the target pawn's advance or by the enemy king. In 6/10 positions, the piece moves to a square adjacent to or directly confronting an enemy pawn (Rf4 vs f5 pawn, Qg3 vs g4/f5 pawns, Rf5 vs g5 pawn, Rg5 vs g6 pawn, Rd7 attacking d6 knight/pawn, Rb4 pressuring f4). The correct moves in these positions consistently involve king advancement (5/10 positions list king moves as best), rook placement on distant open files for flexibility (Ra8/Ra6/Ra7 patterns in positions 5, 9, 15), or rook repositioning to the 8th rank for blockade duties (position 4). The errors share a common tactical consequence: the piece on its 'attacking' square either gets kicked with tempo (positions 1, 2), falls into a tactical trap (position 4), ignores a more urgent passed pawn threat (position 5), or loses critical flexibility needed for defense (position 15).
analysis.move_pattern: Rook or queen moves to a middle rank (3rd-7th) square that directly targets or confronts an enemy pawn, often on the f/g files in kingside pawn endgames
analysis.why_bad: Direct frontal attacks on pawns in endgames violate core endgame principles: the piece lands on a square where it can be challenged by the pawn's advance or the enemy king, costing tempo; it abandons flexible positioning (open files, back rank) needed for indirect pressure; and it often ignores more urgent priorities like king centralization, passed pawn management, or promotion prevention.
sub_patterns: Rook moves in front of a passed pawn that can advance with tempo (Rf4 kicked by Ke5, Qg3 kicked by f4)
Rook attacks a pawn that is tactically poisoned due to discovered/fork threats (Rf5 vs g5 with Kh6 trap)
Rook leaves flexible open file to attack defended piece, allowing counterplay break (Rd7 allows e5)
Rook moves to a less flexible rank when maintaining open-file distance preserves defensive resources (Rb4 vs Ra8/Ra6/Ra7)

analysis.label: Moving a piece or pawn that was performing a vital blocking, defending, or restraining role, immediately allowing the opponent to exploit the vacated function.
analysis.description: This feature fires on moves where a piece or pawn abandons a critical static function—blocking an enemy king's advance, maintaining protective pawn tension, defending a key square, or restraining enemy pieces—in favor of a seemingly active but ultimately self-destructive plan. In 6/8 positions, the moved piece was specifically performing a blocking/restraining duty: the e5 pawn restrained Black's king (Position 1), the king on d7 blocked White's king from c6 (Position 3), the bishop on g5 maintained dark-square pressure (Position 5), the rook's original post defended f2 (Position 6), the king on d4 blocked the e7-a3 diagonal (Position 7), and the bishop on g4 maintained pressure without conceding the e4 pawn structure (Position 8). In Position 2, the e5 pawn protected the knight on f3, and in Position 11, the king walked into a knight's checking range. All moves share the pattern of looking purposeful (breakthrough attempt, material win, centralization, aggressive placement) while catastrophically releasing a restraint the opponent immediately exploits.
analysis.move_pattern: Any piece type moving away from a square where it performed a critical blocking/defending/restraining role; often advancing toward the opponent or repositioning 'actively'
analysis.why_bad: The piece's static function (blocking a king path, protecting a piece, maintaining pawn tension, guarding a diagonal) was far more valuable than any active idea the move pursues; the opponent immediately exploits the vacated role through tempo-gaining tactics, captures, or king advances.
sub_patterns: Premature pawn tension release (e6, exf4)
King abandoning a blocking square (Kc8, Kc5, Kg6)
Piece moving to a square where it's easily captured/exploited (Bf6, Bf3, Re1)

analysis.label: Playing slow, non-forcing developing or repositioning moves in positions that demand immediate tactical exploitation of a concrete, time-sensitive advantage.
analysis.description: This feature fires on positions where the player chooses a passive, preparatory, or 'natural-looking' piece move instead of seizing an immediate tactical opportunity that will disappear if not acted upon now. In 9/10 cases, the move is non-capturing and non-checking, creating no direct threats. The missed opportunities include exploiting pins (Nxe4 in position 7), capturing hanging pawns (Nxg5 in position 5), leveraging powerful outpost pieces (Nd5/Nb5 in positions 4, 8, 13), and maintaining critical defensive coverage (position 12). The played moves typically look reasonable in the abstract—developing a bishop (Bd3), centralizing a queen (Qe5, Qf6), connecting rooks (Qe2, Qc2, Rhe8)—but ignore specific positional demands. With an average of only 1.3 good moves available, these positions required precision, yet the player chose generic improvement over concrete action. All 10/10 positions share the 'tempo_loss' motif where the wasted move allows the opponent to consolidate, escape danger, or neutralize the advantage.
analysis.move_pattern: Non-forcing piece moves (predominantly queen moves 7/10) to natural-looking squares; no captures, no checks, no direct threats; often retreats (Nf3, Nh2) or lateral/forward repositioning to central squares
analysis.why_bad: The position contains a concrete, time-sensitive tactical resource (pin exploitation, hanging material, forcing sequence, or attacking breakthrough) that will disappear once the opponent gets a free tempo to consolidate, develop, castle, or trade queens—the quiet move gifts that crucial tempo.
sub_patterns: Queen development blocking a bishop's critical deployment (Qe2 blocking Bf1-b5)
Knight retreat abandoning a dominant outpost (Nf3 from d4, Nh2 from f3)
Queen repositioning abandoning defensive duties (Qe5 leaving f7 unguarded)
Preparatory queen moves when queenside attack demands immediate execution (Qc2 instead of Nb3/b4)
Passive rook move instead of aggressive piece redeployment (Rhe8 instead of Bc5+Rd2)

analysis.label: Moves that block critical squares/lines needed by the player's own pieces or abandon restraint of the opponent's primary threat while pursuing secondary objectives.
analysis.description: This feature fires on moves that appear purposeful (development, centralization, pawn capture, creating luft) but critically undermine the player's own defensive coordination. The dominant pattern is self-obstruction: in 4/10 positions the move physically blocks a critical resource (Nc3 blocks c-pawn support, Qe6 blocks king escape routes, Kd7 blocks bishop retreat to d7, g3 removes the pawn shield blocking the second rank). In the remaining positions, the move abandons restraint of the opponent's primary threat: Ka3 and Kf3 both send the king to grab irrelevant pawns while abandoning blockade of dangerous passed pawns (3/10 involve passed pawn neglect), Re2 ignores lethal passed pawns to activate the rook on an irrelevant file, Qe4 delays an urgent fork exploitation giving the opponent time to reorganize, and Rxb3+ commits to an exchange before optimizing king position. The average 2.0 good moves available confirms these are narrow positions demanding precise responses to a single critical factor, which the player neglected.
analysis.move_pattern: Piece moves to apparently active/purposeful squares (central squares, captures, king moves forward/sideways) that physically obstruct friendly piece coordination or abandon the critical defensive zone
analysis.why_bad: The move addresses a secondary concern while either physically blocking a critical square/retreat path needed by the player's own pieces, or removing/abandoning the one resource that restrains the opponent's primary threat (passed pawn promotion, mating attack, tactical sequence)
sub_patterns: King blocking own piece retreat squares (Kd7/bishop, Qe6/king escape)
King abandoning passed pawn blockade for irrelevant material (Ka3, Kf3)
Pawn move removing critical defensive shield (g3 opening second rank)
Premature action without preparation (Rxb3+ before Kf2, Qe4 before Nxf3)
Development to square that creates tactical vulnerability (Nc3 allowing d4/e5)

analysis.label: Impulsive captures that appear to win material or eliminate threats but catastrophically open lines, remove defenders, or ignore more urgent threats, allowing devastating tactical exploitation.
analysis.description: This feature fires on positions where the player makes a natural-looking capture that seems to win material or address an immediate concern, but the act of capturing itself creates a far worse vulnerability. In 9/9 positions, the blunder move is a capture. The consequences typically involve opening a critical file or diagonal (positions 1, 2, 3, 4, 6, 8 show captures that open lines directly to the player's king or undefended pieces) or removing a piece that was performing essential defensive duty (positions 1, 7, 10 show captures that eliminate key defenders). In most cases (7/9), the best alternative was a quiet non-capturing move - retreating, repositioning, or developing - that maintained tension rather than resolving it. The average cp_loss of ~2494 reflects that these captures often allow forced mates (positions 3, 8) or massive material loss. Back-rank exploitation specifically features in 4/9 positions. The common psychology is a player grabbing something attractive without calculating the opponent's forcing response to the newly opened line or undefended piece.
analysis.move_pattern: Captures (all types: piece takes piece, pawn takes piece/pawn) that open a file, rank, or diagonal toward the capturer's own king or undefended material
analysis.why_bad: The capture opens a critical line (file/diagonal/rank) or removes a piece that was guarding key squares, allowing the opponent an immediate forcing sequence (typically involving checks along the opened line) that wins back far more material or delivers checkmate
sub_patterns: Capture opens file/rank enabling back-rank mate or rook invasion (4/9 positions)
Capture removes piece that was defending another piece or critical square (3/9 positions)
Capture of attractive target while ignoring more urgent positional threat like passed pawn (2/9 positions)
Capture with wrong piece when order matters for maintaining back-rank defense (2/9 positions)
Capture opens diagonal to uncastled/exposed king allowing queen check with tempo (1/9 positions)

analysis.label: Moving a piece away from its sole defensive duty or to a tactically vulnerable square, creating an immediate one-move exploitation for the opponent.
analysis.description: This feature fires on moves where a piece abandons an irreplaceable defensive function, instantly creating a concrete tactical vulnerability. In 4/8 positions, the moved piece was the sole defender of a critical asset: the king guarding g2 (Ke1), the queen defending d2 against a pin (Qxf3), the knight guarding invasion squares b5/d6 (Nec6), and the king needing to reach the h8 blockade square (Kf8). In 3/8 positions, the piece moves FROM a safe square TO one where it becomes immediately capturable: bishop to c5 where Nxc5 wins it (Bxc5), knight to f6 where Rf5+ deflects its defender (Nf6), and bishop to d5 where it aligns with own king allowing Qxd5+ (Bd5+). In 1/8 (Kd5), the king walks into an open file facing immediate devastating checks. All moves share the property of looking superficially active or reasonable (centralizing, capturing, checking) while fatally ignoring a one-move tactical refutation. The average 1.6 good moves available confirms these are critical precision moments with almost no margin for error.
analysis.move_pattern: Any piece type moving away from a square where it performed a unique defensive function, or moving to a square where it becomes immediately tactically exploitable (capturable, forkable, or subject to deflection)
analysis.why_bad: Each move removes the sole defender of a critical asset or places a piece where a simple one-move tactic (capture, deflection check, fork, or pin exploitation) immediately wins material or creates a decisive positional collapse
sub_patterns: King moves away from defending a pawn or blockade square (Kf8, Ke1, Kd5)
Piece moves to square where it becomes immediately hanging or capturable (Bxc5, Nf6, Bd5+)
Overloaded defender leaves its post via capture (Qxf3)
Piece vacates guard of invasion square (Nec6)

analysis.label: Natural-looking moves that abandon a critical defensive responsibility in positions where only 1-2 moves hold, allowing a forcing tactical punishment.
analysis.description: This feature activates on moves that appear logical or developing but fatally ignore the one critical requirement of the position. In 5/8 cases (Qh5, Rad8, Qb1, Rad1, Kg8), the move removes a piece from a defensive duty or misplaces it, allowing an immediate forcing sequence. In 2/8 cases (Kd8, Kd8), the king retreats to the wrong square, walking into back-rank tactics. In 1/8 cases (Bxh6), an unsound sacrifice is launched without sufficient support. The unifying thread is that positions have extremely narrow defensive requirements (avg 1.6 good moves available), the player selects a move that looks reasonable in general terms but specifically fails to address the most forcing threat, and the opponent punishes with a check, capture, or mating threat that wins decisive material. The refutations typically involve a two-move forcing sequence: a tempo-gaining move (check or threat) followed by exploitation of the abandoned defensive point.
analysis.move_pattern: Diverse piece types moving to 'logical' squares (aggressive queen placements, rook development to open files, king retreats toward center/back rank) that abandon coverage of a tactically critical square or piece
analysis.why_bad: Each move removes a piece from its essential defensive function or places the king on a square vulnerable to forcing tactics, while the position demands precision because only 1-2 moves adequately address the opponent's most threatening continuation. The opponent then exploits the abandoned point with checks, captures, or mating threats.
sub_patterns: Queen moves to aggressive square abandoning back-rank/second-rank coverage (Qh5, Qb1)
Rook develops to natural file removing defense of a pawn or piece (Rad1, Rad8)
King retreats to wrong square enabling back-rank or diagonal mating patterns (Kd8, Kg8)
Unsound sacrifice launched without sufficient piece coordination (Bxh6)

analysis.label: Reasonable-looking developing or repositioning moves played in critical positions that demand one specific concrete action, resulting in large evaluation swings.
analysis.description: This feature activates when a player makes a move that follows general chess principles (developing pieces, centralizing, gaining space, giving checks) but fails to address the one critical concrete requirement of the position. In 8/10 positions, only 1-2 good moves existed (avg 1.4), indicating these are demanding moments requiring precise calculation rather than routine play. The moves appear purposeful—Be2 develops, Bf5/Bd6/Bc5 develop bishops to active diagonals, Qf3 centralizes, Rd5 activates, b4 gains space, Na8+ gives check—but each ignores a specific tactical vulnerability. Common consequences include enabling favorable exchanges for the opponent (Be2→Qxf3, b4→Qxf3, Qg6→Qxg6 in 3/10), trapping own pieces (Qf3 blocking Nh4, Na8+ self-trapping in 2/10), abandoning critical restraining posts (Rd5 leaving g5, f4 fixing structure in 2/10), or blocking own key resources (Bd6 blocking d4 advance, Bf5 before repositioning queen in 2/10). The average cp_loss of 363 reflects that these positions had razor-thin margins where generic moves catastrophically fail.
analysis.move_pattern: Diverse piece types (bishops 4/10, queens 2/10, rook/knight/pawns 4/10) moved to seemingly logical developing or active squares, typically non-capturing and non-checking quiet moves
analysis.why_bad: The position demands one specific concrete move (tactical strike, capture, or preservation of a key piece/post), but the player substitutes a generically 'good' move that either creates a new vulnerability, enables a favorable simplification for the opponent, traps their own piece, or abandons a critical defensive/offensive function
sub_patterns: Bishop development blocking own critical pawn advance (Bd6 blocks d4, Bf5 before Qg6)
Piece move enabling damaging queen exchange (Be2→Qxf3, b4→Qxf3, Qg6 offering trade)
Self-obstruction trapping own piece (Qf3 blocking Nh4, Na8+ trapping knight)
Abandoning restraining post for 'active' centralization (Rd5 leaving g5, f4 fixing structure)

analysis.label: Black plays ...Qe7 with king uncastled, creating a self-pin on the open e-file that White exploits with O-O + Re1.
analysis.description: This feature fires most strongly on positions where Black plays ...Qe7 in the opening with the king still on e8, placing the queen on an open or semi-open e-file where it becomes a devastating pin target. In 6/11 top activations, the exact move is ...Qe7, and in all of these the king remains on e8, both kings are uncastled, and White punishes with O-O followed by Re1 creating a lethal pin along the e-file. The queen on e7 simultaneously blocks the f8-bishop from developing and often obstructs the knight's access to e7, compounding the developmental damage. The remaining activations (5/11) share the broader pattern of pieces moving to squares that create tactical vulnerabilities on open files or abandon critical defensive posts—such as Re3 walking into a knight fork, Rh1 abandoning g-file control, or Ra5 leaving the king exposed to checks. The common thread is choosing superficially active piece placements that catastrophically ignore alignment-based tactical threats (pins, forks, file exploitation).
analysis.move_pattern: Queen to e7 (Black, from d8 or d-file), non-capture, non-check, with king on e8 and e-file open/semi-open
analysis.why_bad: The queen on e7 sits on the same open file as the king on e8, creating an immediate pin target once White castles and plays Re1. It also blocks the f8-bishop and often the knight's path to e7, preventing castling and crippling development—all while accomplishing nothing that addresses the position's actual needs (development, capturing free material, or king safety).
sub_patterns: Qe7 blocking f8-bishop and preventing castling
Qe7 creating Re1 pin with king on e8
Qe7 obstructing knight development to e7
Piece moving to file where it becomes fork/pin target due to king alignment
Rook abandoning critical file control for superficial activity

analysis.label: Playing a visually impressive or centralizing piece move that neglects concrete tactical obligations, leaving a piece or pawn undefended for the opponent to exploit.
analysis.description: In all 5 positions, the player chose a move that places a piece on an apparently strong or active square (Rd4 centralizing, Rf1 developing, Nf5 attacking, Qd5 dominating the center, Rh8 activating on the back rank), but each move critically abandons a defensive duty or concrete forcing plan. In 4/5 cases, the move directly leaves a piece or pawn tactically undefended (Rd4 hangs itself to Rxd4; Nf5 leaves the a6-bishop unguarded for Qa3/Qxa6; Qd5 leaves the c1-rook unprotected against Qe3+/Qxc1+; Rh8 abandons the a2-pawn). In 5/5 cases, superior forcing moves were available (checks, immediate pawn advances, or moves maintaining tactical threats) that would have preserved the advantage. The common failure mode is prioritizing piece aesthetics over concrete calculation.
analysis.move_pattern: Major piece (or knight) moved to an imposing central or distant square, typically non-forcing (no check, no capture), abandoning defense of another piece or pawn
analysis.why_bad: The move abandons a critical defensive or tactical obligation—either leaving a piece/pawn en prise, removing a key threat that constrained the opponent, or misplacing the piece away from the winning plan—allowing the opponent to win material or neutralize the advantage through captures or checks.
sub_patterns: Piece moves to square where it can be directly captured (Rd4 hanging to Rxd4)
Queen centralizes leaving back-rank/first-rank pieces undefended against check sequences (Qd5 leaving Rc1 hanging)
Rook placed on wrong file/rank missing critical tactical pressure (Rf1 missing Re8+ threat, Rh8 abandoning a2)
Aggressive piece advance leaving distant pieces unprotected (Nf5 leaving Ba6 hanging after Qa3)

analysis.label: Voluntarily relocating a critically-placed piece from its most active/threatening square to a seemingly attractive but less effective position.
analysis.description: In all 3/3 positions, the player moves a piece that was performing a vital dynamic function (creating threats against the opponent's king or deeply infiltrating enemy territory) to a different square that appears strong but serves a lesser purpose. In Position 1, the Queen leaves h2 (where it anchored a lethal kingside attack with Qh1+ threats) to go to b2 chasing queenside pawns. In Position 2, the Knight leaves c3 (where it provided essential defensive coverage of e2 and the center) to jump to d5 for apparent centralization, immediately vulnerable to ...c6. In Position 3, the Rook abandons the deeply infiltrated e2 square (where it paralyzed White's back rank and threatened f2) to go to e6 for passive pawn defense. All three moves prioritize a superficially appealing goal (attacking distant pawns, centralization, defending a weakness) over maintaining the piece's critical dynamic role, and in each case the opponent exploits the absence of that pressure with a king attack or tactical combination.
analysis.move_pattern: Active piece (Q/N/R) voluntarily moved away from its most threatening/functional square to a different part of the board that appears attractive
analysis.why_bad: The relocated piece was performing an irreplaceable dynamic function (threatening the opponent's king, providing counterplay, or maintaining defensive coverage); once removed, the opponent gains a free hand to execute tactical blows against the now-unprotected king or exploit the loss of coordination.
sub_patterns: Queen abandons kingside mating attack for queenside pawn targets
Knight leaves defensive post for flashy centralization vulnerable to pawn kicks
Rook retreats from deep infiltration square to passive defense

analysis.label: Natural-looking moves in narrow positions that neglect the single most critical tactical requirement, typically leaving a piece undefended or walking into a simple refutation.
analysis.description: This feature fires on positions where the player makes a superficially reasonable move—one that addresses a secondary concern or appears to improve piece placement—but fatally overlooks the position's primary tactical demand. In 5/7 positions, only 1-2 good moves existed (avg 1.6), creating a narrow path where one precise move was required. The blunders consistently share the pattern of ignoring a concrete tactical vulnerability: in Position 1, Qc7 leaves the b7 bishop undefended (hanging piece); in Position 3, Rde1 removes tactical protection from the h6 bishop (hanging piece); in Position 5, h6 wastes a critical tempo allowing Rxd3 winning the queen; in Position 12, Qg4 walks into a pawn fork with f3; in Position 15, Kc6 fails to block the f-file when Be7 was the singular solution. The correct moves in each case directly addressed the most urgent issue—saving an endangered piece (Bf4), targeting the critical weakness (Rc8, Ra4), or maintaining dynamic pressure (Qe4/Qh5/Be7). The blunders instead pursue plausible secondary ideas (doubling rooks, creating luft, centralizing the king, maintaining queen activity) while a simple 1-2 move refutation exists.
analysis.move_pattern: Various piece types moving to seemingly active/useful squares; no consistent geometric direction, but moves tend to address a secondary positional goal rather than the primary tactical imperative
analysis.why_bad: Each move neglects the single most urgent tactical requirement of the position—typically leaving a piece tactically undefended, walking into a fork, or wasting a tempo in a position where the opponent has an immediate forcing sequence that wins material
sub_patterns: Piece moves away from defending another piece, leaving it hanging (Positions 1, 3)
Queen moves to square vulnerable to pawn fork or attack (Positions 6, 12)
Quiet/passive move wastes critical tempo in dynamically tense position (Positions 5, 11)
King move to exposed square when piece development solves structural problem (Position 15)

analysis.chip: Ignoring Critical Threat for Tangible Gain
analysis.label: Moves that pursue a secondary objective (material capture, development, or slow threat) while catastrophically ignoring the position's most urgent tactical or strategic demand.
analysis.description: This feature fires on positions where the player makes a superficially reasonable move—often a pawn/piece capture (Rxg3, Bxb4, Kxg3, Qxf8: 4/12), a developing/repositioning move (Nc6, Ba6, Re8, Rb6: 4/12), or a pawn push creating threats (h3, g4, Qg4, Qa5+: 4/12)—but fatally ignores the single most critical demand in the position. The positions share extremely low good-move counts (avg 1.7), meaning only one or two moves maintain the evaluation, and the chosen move addresses a tangible but secondary concern while an existential threat (promotion in 3/12, king exposure in 6/12, piece invasion in 3/12) goes completely unaddressed. The catastrophic average cp_loss of 2545 reflects that these are 'one right answer' positions where the player's plausible-looking alternative walks into a devastating tactical punishment that was already latent in the position.
analysis.move_pattern: Various piece types and directions; no consistent geometric pattern—captures, developments, pawn pushes, and checks all appear. The unifying element is that the move pursues a concrete secondary goal while leaving the critical square/file/diagonal undefended.
analysis.why_bad: Each move fails because it allocates a tempo toward a lower-priority goal (grabbing material, creating a slow threat, developing routinely) while the position contains an urgent, often existential threat that requires immediate attention—and with so few good moves available (avg 1.7), any deviation from addressing the critical need is catastrophically punished.
sub_patterns: Material capture ignoring promotion or mating threat (Rxg3, Kxg3, Bxb4)
Routine development/repositioning ignoring tactical emergency on critical square (Nc6, Ba6, Re8, Rb6)
Creating own slow threat while opponent has faster/lethal counter (Qg4, h3, g4)
Check or capture with wrong piece/direction allowing opponent's key escape or counter (Qa5+, Qxf8)

analysis.label: King moves in pawn endgames that fatally lose the opposition or critical tempo by moving the king in the wrong direction.
analysis.description: This feature fires on positions where a player makes a king move (or tempo-committing move) in a pawn endgame that abandons the critical opposition or outflanking position. In 12/12 cases the position is a simplified endgame with locked or fixed pawns where king maneuvering is paramount. In 11/12 cases the mistake is a king move; the remaining case (h5) is a premature pawn push that eliminates a reserve tempo needed for opposition battles. The key errors include: moving the king laterally away from the file where vertical opposition must be maintained (Kf6, Kd4, Kd3, Kc5, Kg2), retreating the king from an ideal outflanking square (Ke4, Ke1), or making a king/pawn move that gives the opponent a free tempo to improve their king (Kc7, h5, Ka5). In every case, the locked pawn structure means only king activity determines the outcome, and a single wrong directional choice permanently cedes penetration squares to the opponent.
analysis.move_pattern: King moves (any direction) in simplified endgames that move away from the file or rank where direct opposition must be maintained against the opponent's king
analysis.why_bad: In locked pawn endgames, the opposition (keeping kings directly facing each other with an odd number of squares between them) is the sole drawing/winning mechanism. Moving the king sideways, backward, or to the wrong flank permanently surrenders the opposition, allowing the opponent's king to outflank and penetrate to attack fixed pawns.
sub_patterns: King retreats from ideal outflanking position (Ke4 from f5, Ke1 from d2)
King moves laterally away from critical opposition file (Kd4 instead of Kf4, Kg2 instead of Ke2, Kd3 instead of Kb3)
King moves toward pawns instead of maintaining opposition (Kf6, Kc5, Kc7)
Premature pawn push eliminating reserve tempo for opposition (h5)

analysis.label: King (or key piece) retreats toward the back rank, corner, or board edge when it should centralize or advance, landing on a tactically vulnerable square.
analysis.description: In 6/8 positions, the blunder is a king move that retreats or drifts toward a passive square (back rank or edge) instead of centralizing or advancing: Kd8 retreats to the 8th rank onto a fatal diagonal, Kf1 retreats to the 1st rank exposing a diagonal check, Kd1 retreats to the back rank where promotion tactics trap it, Ka6 drifts to the edge abandoning pawn defense, Kg3 moves sideways losing a critical tempo instead of advancing to g2, and Kb1 retreats to the corner (trivial loss). In 2/8 positions, Ncb5 removes a centralized defensive knight from its optimal post (c3), which is functionally the same error—moving a piece away from its critical central defensive role toward the edge. The consistent punishment pattern is that the retreated piece lands on a square that is either tactically exploitable (falls on a checking diagonal/file, enables forks, allows promotion tactics) or abandons a defensive duty that the opponent immediately exploits. The best moves consistently involved centralizing (Ke3, Kd2), advancing (Kg2), or maintaining the defensive piece in place (Ndb5 instead of Ncb5).
analysis.move_pattern: King retreating one square toward the 1st/8th rank, corner, or board edge; or knight moving from center toward edge, vacating a critical defensive square
analysis.why_bad: The retreated piece lands on a tactically vulnerable square (exposed diagonal, back rank geometry, edge passivity) or abandons a defensive function that the opponent immediately exploits with checks, forks, or promotion threats
sub_patterns: King retreats to back rank exposing fatal diagonal (Kd8, Kf1)
King retreats to back rank allowing promotion tactics (Kd1, Kb1)
King drifts to edge abandoning pawn defense (Ka6)
King takes indirect route losing critical tempo (Kg3)
Wrong knight moved to same square, evacuating defensive post (Ncb5 x2)

analysis.label: Playing a plausible-looking move that wastes a decisive tempo in a position where urgency demands immediate action on the critical front.
analysis.description: This feature fires on moves that appear reasonable or active (king centralization, checks, captures, pawn advances) but fatally waste tempo in positions where time is the decisive factor. In 9/13 positions, the phase is endgame—mostly pawn endgames where a single tempo determines promotion races. The 'tempo_loss' tag appears in 12/13 analyses. The pattern manifests as: choosing the wrong king direction in a pawn race (Ke5 instead of Ke4, Kc8 instead of f4 push, Kb4 instead of h4 push—positions 2, 6, 8); making an irrelevant pawn move instead of the critical action (h3 instead of Bd1, h6 instead of Kd5, b5 prematurely—positions 5, 7, 9); delivering the wrong check that allows escape (Nf5+ instead of Nh5+, Ng4+ instead of Bd4+—positions 3, 11); capturing irrelevant material while forfeiting the decisive tactic (Nxa6 missing Ne6+ fork—position 12); or overextending a piece into tactical vulnerability (Qd3 allowing Ne5 fork—position 10). In all cases, the opponent needs only one simple response to exploit the wasted tempo.
analysis.move_pattern: Any piece type moving to a seemingly active/aggressive square (checks, captures, centralizing moves, pawn advances) rather than the precise square demanded by the position's urgency
analysis.why_bad: These moves lose a critical tempo in time-sensitive positions—the player chooses a 'natural' or 'active' looking option over the one precise move that addresses the position's most urgent demand (racing a pawn, executing a forced combination, repositioning to the critical defensive square)
sub_patterns: Wrong king direction in pawn race (one square off the optimal diagonal path)
Wrong piece check that allows king escape/capture of key attacker
Irrelevant pawn push when piece repositioning is urgent
Capturing secondary material while missing a decisive fork/mate
King advance to square that allows opponent to gain tempo with check

analysis.label: Moving a piece (usually a knight) to a square where it is inadequately defended and gets captured or traded unfavorably, often lured by an attractive-looking destination (check, capture, or apparent outpost).
analysis.description: This feature fires on moves where a piece is relocated to a square where it becomes tactically vulnerable to immediate capture or unfavorable exchange. In 6/8 positions, a knight is the piece that moves; in 5/8 cases the piece is directly captured on its destination square (Ne5+→Bxe5, Nxc6→deflection then capture, Ne6→Bxe6, Ne8→Bxe8, Bxd5→eventually recaptured with tempo via g6). The moves consistently look superficially attractive—they involve checks (Ne5+), captures (Nxa6, Nxc6, Bxd5), or seemingly dominant outpost squares (Ne6, Ne8)—but each destination is directly attacked by an opponent's piece (often a bishop on a diagonal covering the landing square). In 4/8 positions, the tactical motif is explicitly 'hanging_piece.' The better alternatives consistently involve maintaining the piece on its current strong square or improving it to a genuinely safe position. Position 4 (Ne1) represents the retreating variant where the piece moves to safety but sacrifices control of critical squares, enabling the opponent's breakthrough.
analysis.move_pattern: Minor piece (predominantly knight) moves to a square directly covered by an opponent's piece, typically a bishop on a diagonal or a rook on an open file; destinations include captures, checks, and apparent outposts
analysis.why_bad: The destination square is inadequately defended, allowing the opponent to capture the piece outright or force an unfavorable exchange that eliminates the player's best-placed piece, often losing the positional cornerstone of their position for insufficient material compensation
sub_patterns: Knight moves to square directly attacked by opponent's bishop (Ne6→Bxe6, Ne8→Bxe8, Ne5+→Bxe5)
Piece captures a pawn but lands on undefended/vulnerable square (Nxa6, Nxc6, Bxd5)
Knight retreats to passive square abandoning critical square control (Ne1)

analysis.label: Playing a quiet developing or consolidating move instead of a critical central pawn advance (d4/d5/e4) that forks two enemy pieces.
analysis.description: In all 7/7 positions, the best move was a central pawn thrust (d5 in 3 cases, e4 in 2 cases, d4 in 2 cases) that simultaneously attacks a bishop and a knight sitting on adjacent squares. Instead, the player chose a quiet, non-forcing move: routine development (Nf3 twice), queen centralization (Qd6), a routine recapture (cxd5), a slow prophylactic pawn move (b3), consolidation (c6), or castling (O-O). In every case, the enemy had a bishop and knight aligned vulnerably to a pawn advance — e.g., Be6+Nc6 vulnerable to d5 (3/7), Bd3+Nf3 vulnerable to e4 (2/7), Nc3+Be3 vulnerable to d4 (2/7). The quiet moves gifted the opponent time to reposition these pieces off the vulnerable squares, permanently closing the tactical window. Average centipawn loss was 269, and in all 7 positions only one move was within 50cp of optimal.
analysis.move_pattern: Any quiet/non-forcing move (knight development, castling, pawn consolidation, queen repositioning) played INSTEAD of a central pawn advance to the 4th or 5th rank
analysis.why_bad: The opponent has a bishop and knight sitting on squares simultaneously attacked by a central pawn advance (d4/d5/e4); the quiet move gives the opponent a free tempo to retreat one or both pieces, permanently eliminating the pawn fork opportunity.
sub_patterns: d5 forking bishop on e6 and knight on c6
e4 forking bishop on d3 and knight on f3
d4 forking knight on c3 and bishop on e3

analysis.label: Moving a piece to a seemingly logical square where it immediately becomes a tactical target through captures, checks, or deflections.
analysis.description: In all 5 positions, the player repositions a piece to a square that appears active or useful but is tactically compromised. In 3/5 cases (Nf3, Ne2, Rad8), the piece moves directly into a square where it can be captured or trapped by an opponent's piece already bearing down on that square. In 2/5 cases (Rf1, Qd2), the piece moves to address one threat but gets deflected away by forcing moves (checks), failing to accomplish its intended purpose. The common thread is that the destination square is already in the opponent's tactical crosshairs: Bxf3 exploits the knight walking into the bishop's line, Qh1+ forces Ne2 to block on g1 where it's trapped, Rxd8 exploits the rook entering a dominant piece's territory, Qd5+ deflects the rook from f1, and Rb7 invades because Qd2 abandoned kingside defense. All moves had constructive intent (centralize, challenge, block, defend, reposition) but failed to account for the opponent's concrete forcing response.
analysis.move_pattern: Quiet piece repositioning (non-capture, non-check) of any piece type to a central or semi-central square that falls within an opponent's existing tactical scope
analysis.why_bad: The destination square is already controlled or targeted by an opponent's piece, enabling an immediate tactical exploitation (capture, deflection, or piece trapping) that the player failed to calculate before committing the move.
sub_patterns: Knight moved into line of enemy bishop/queen (Nf3, Ne2)
Major piece moved to square inviting favorable exchange/deflection (Rad8, Rf1)
Queen repositioned away from critical defensive zone (Qd2)

analysis.label: Queen checks that waste tempo by driving the opponent's king to a safer square or abandoning pressure on critical targets, when a more forcing alternative (often a different check direction or a capture with check) was available.
analysis.description: In all 12/12 positions, the played move is a Queen delivering check that fails to achieve anything concrete. The consistent pattern is that a stronger alternative existed—either a check from a better direction that trapped the king (positions 1, 2, 7, 9, 14), a capture with check winning material (positions 4, 5, 15), or a quiet move maintaining overwhelming pressure (positions 8, 12). In 10/12 cases, the check drives the enemy king to a safer square (e.g., Kc6 instead of being forced to block with Qc6 in position 1; Kf7 gaining shelter in position 4; Ka7 reaching safety in positions 3 and 6; Kd4 centralizing in position 7). In 9/12 positions, the analyses explicitly tag 'tempo_loss' as the primary motif—the check burns a move without improving White/Black's attacking geometry. The average cp_loss of 3367 reflects that many of these convert forced mates into merely winning positions (positions 1, 6, 9, 14 all lose forced mates). The 'patzer sees check, patzer gives check' syndrome is the unifying behavioral pattern.
analysis.move_pattern: Queen check to any square, typically to edge/back-rank squares (b8, a8, h8, d8, c8) or peripheral squares, where the check is non-capturing and non-forcing
analysis.why_bad: The check either drives the opponent's king to a safer square, allows a defensive interposition that breaks the attacking geometry, or abandons the queen's pressure on critical squares/pawns—when a more precise check direction, a capture with check, or a quiet building move would have maintained or increased the advantage.
sub_patterns: Wrong check direction allowing king escape to safety (Qb8+ instead of Qb6+, Qb7+ instead of Qd5+)
Non-capturing check when capture-with-check wins material (Qh8+/Qh6+ instead of Qxf6+)
Check that abandons pressure on key pawn or square (Qg3+ leaving e3, Qe1+ leaving e3)
Check to back rank allowing interposition that breaks mating net (Qb8+ allowing Rc7 block)
Queen placed on wrong attacking square losing coordination with supporting pieces (Qa5+ instead of Qc5+)

analysis.label: Playing a natural-looking active move (often a check or capture) in razor-sharp positions where only ONE specific continuation works, missing the precise saving or winning resource.
analysis.description: This feature fires on positions with essentially a single correct move (avg 1.2 good moves available) where the player chooses a plausible-looking alternative that catastrophically fails. In 8/12 positions, the played move is a check or capture that appears forcing. The correct move often involves the same tactical theme but with a different piece (wrong rook: positions 1, 11; wrong piece capture: positions 2, 6), a different target square (positions 4, 9 - wrong check direction), or a fundamentally different approach like forcing simplification instead of passive play (positions 7, 8, 9). The astronomical average cp_loss of 4357 reflects that these positions are knife-edge moments where one move draws/wins and everything else loses catastrophically. In 6/12 cases the blunder involves choosing the wrong piece or wrong square for essentially the correct idea.
analysis.move_pattern: Primarily checks and captures (8/12) directed at seemingly logical targets; also includes passive king moves (2/12) and piece repositions (2/12). The common geometric error is choosing an adjacent-but-wrong execution of the correct tactical theme.
analysis.why_bad: In positions with only one correct continuation, these moves fail because they select the wrong piece for a capture (destroying coordination needed for perpetual/mate), check in a direction that allows the king to escape toward safety, remove a critical piece from a key defensive/attacking square for trivial material, or waste tempo on passive moves when concrete tactical strikes are required immediately.
sub_patterns: Wrong piece captures on same square (Rbxb2 vs Rhxb2, Rxb4 vs Qxb4)
Wrong check direction allowing king escape (Qd1+ vs Qb5+, Qxg5+ vs Qf6+)
Greedy check/capture missing immediate checkmate (Qxd3+ vs Qxf2#)
Passive king moves when concrete tactics required (Kg1 vs Qf3, Kb1 vs Rxf7)
Removing critical piece from key square for trivial gain (Rxg3+ abandoning e3, Qg5 abandoning h4)

analysis.label: Playing a natural-looking or 'improving' move that wastes critical tempo when the position demands immediate concrete forcing action.
analysis.description: This feature fires on positions where players make seemingly reasonable moves—piece centralizations, 'active' development, material captures, or king safety moves—that catastrophically squander a decisive advantage by failing to play the one forcing continuation the position demands. In 6/6 detailed positions, the correct move was a more forcing option (Bxh3 capturing a hanging piece, Rd7 penetrating the 7th rank, Bc4+ exploiting a king on an open diagonal, Rxf7 executing a tactical capture, Ng4 maintaining attack, Qe5+ delivering check). The played moves instead either relocated pieces to kickable squares (Nf5, Ne5, Bf5, Qg4 in 4/6 cases), made passive king retreats (Kg8, Kf7 in 2/6 cases), or made captures that broke critical piece coordination (exf3, Qxc7). All share the common thread of being non-forcing moves that give the opponent a free tempo to reorganize, escape danger, or seize the initiative. The average cp_loss of 2685 reflects how these positions had razor-thin margins between winning brilliantly and squandering everything.
analysis.move_pattern: Various piece types (knights, bishops, queens, kings, pawns) moving to aesthetically appealing or seemingly natural squares; no single geometric direction but consistently NON-forcing (no checks, no captures of hanging material, no immediate threats)
analysis.why_bad: The moves waste critical tempo in tactically demanding positions, allowing the opponent to reorganize defenses, kick the misplaced piece, capture with check, or seize the initiative—the position demanded an immediate forcing continuation (check, capture, or direct threat) that was missed.
sub_patterns: Piece 'improvement' to aggressive but kickable squares (Nf5, Ne5, Bf5, Qg4)
Passive king retreats that waste tempo and/or walk into tactics (Kg8, Kf7)
Pawn/piece captures that break critical coordination with attacking pieces (exf3, Qxc7)

analysis.label: Moving a piece to a seemingly useful square while missing the one urgent action the position demands, wasting an irreplaceable tempo.
analysis.description: This feature fires on positions where the player makes a 'reasonable-looking' repositioning move (rook, queen, or king) that addresses a secondary concern while the position demands one specific immediate action. In 9/11 positions, the correct move involved either maintaining a piece's critical function (keeping rook on 6th rank cutting off king, keeping queen on restraining square), making an immediate forcing move (capture, pawn advance, attacking a key piece), or addressing a direct tactical threat (hanging piece, diagonal check). Instead, the played moves reposition to squares that seem active or useful—blockading a pawn already covered (Rc1 in positions 7 and 3), retreating a queen from a dominant post (Qh5, Qe7), moving a rook from a critical file/rank to attack secondary targets (Rg5 twice, Rf7), or advancing the king when urgent tactics exist (Ke3, Kg2). The positions average only 1.7 good moves available, meaning these are narrow decision points where a single tempo waste is catastrophic.
analysis.move_pattern: Major piece (rook/queen) or king move to a non-forcing square that appears purposeful but abandons a critical function or ignores the position's one urgent demand
analysis.why_bad: The position has extremely few good moves (avg 1.7), meaning only one specific action works. The played move wastes the critical tempo needed for that action—whether it's advancing a pawn in a race, attacking a key piece, maintaining a rank/file barrier, or addressing an immediate tactical threat. The opponent exploits the tempo by activating their king, advancing passed pawns, or executing the tactic that was left unaddressed.
sub_patterns: Rook abandons critical rank (6th rank king cut-off) to attack secondary targets
Queen retreats from dominant restraining/attacking post to seemingly active but passive square
Rook moves to blockade a pawn already controlled from its current square (redundant defense)
King moves forward ignoring immediate tactical threats (hanging pieces, diagonal checks)
Rook leaves active file to passively block an advancing pawn

analysis.label: Playing a natural-looking, non-forcing move in a position that demands immediate concrete precision, where very few moves maintain the evaluation.
analysis.description: This feature fires on positions where the player selects a move that appears reasonable in a general sense (centralizing a queen, contesting a file, gaining space, making a prophylactic pawn move) but catastrophically fails because the position is on a knife's edge requiring specific, often forcing or defensive precision. In 6/6 cases, the position had very few good moves available (avg 1.8), and the chosen move ignored a concrete tactical or tempo-critical demand: abandoning a defensive duty (Rac1 leaving a2 undefended, Qe6 leaving g7/g5 unguarded: 2/6), losing a critical tempo when only one move order works (a3 instead of h4, Qc7 instead of forcing Qe1+: 2/6), or choosing the wrong square/idea for what looks like the right concept (Qd1+ instead of Qg1+ for perpetual, e4 ignoring a tactical refutation: 2/6). All moves share the characteristic of being 'generic improving' moves that a player might make without deep calculation, in positions where only concrete analysis reveals the narrow winning or drawing path.
analysis.move_pattern: Quiet, non-forcing moves (pawn pushes, queen relocations, rook lifts) that look positionally or strategically motivated but lack tactical justification in the specific position
analysis.why_bad: The position demands immediate precision (forcing sequences, prophylaxis against a specific threat, or maintaining a critical defensive function) and the chosen move either abandons a vital defensive task, loses a tempo that allows the opponent to execute their plan, or misses the only geometric path that maintains the evaluation.
sub_patterns: Abandoning a defensive post/guard duty for an 'improving' move
Playing a slow prophylactic move when an urgent tempo-critical action is required
Choosing the wrong square for a correct strategic idea (e.g., wrong checking square)
Making a general space-gaining or centralizing move that ignores a concrete tactical refutation

analysis.label: Making a natural-looking active move that squanders the one tempo needed to address the position's most urgent concrete threat.
analysis.description: This feature fires on positions where the player chooses a move that appears reasonable or active but fatally wastes a tempo in a position where timing is paramount. In 8/8 analyzed positions, the tag 'tempo_loss' appears, and in 7/8 positions there were only 1-2 good moves available, indicating critical decision points. The pattern manifests in endgames (6/10) as king moves to wrong squares (Kg5 instead of Rb3 first; Ke8 instead of Kg6; Kb4 instead of Kc2), rook moves that abandon critical squares or go to the wrong rank (Rd3 leaving a1 unguarded; Rg3 instead of king activation; Rh7 instead of Rh8), and in middlegames as pieces relocating to seemingly active squares while abandoning essential defensive functions (Qb6 leaving d8 unguarded; Re4 instead of Ne4; Bc4 to an undefended square; f6 removing a key pawn defender). The opponent consistently exploits the tempo gift with a concrete forcing sequence—typically a passed pawn advance, discovered attack, or promotion threat that arrives exactly one move faster than the defender can handle.
analysis.move_pattern: Any piece type moving to a seemingly active or natural square; no consistent geometric direction; characterized by looking reasonable but being one tempo too slow for the position's demands
analysis.why_bad: The moves prioritize general activity or naturalness over the single urgent concrete requirement of the position, gifting the opponent exactly the tempo needed to execute a decisive threat (promotion, tactical strike, or piece redeployment) that the correct move would have prevented or preempted.
sub_patterns: Endgame king moving to active-looking square instead of creating immediate counterplay against opponent's passed pawn
Rook moving to wrong rank or file, abandoning control of a critical promotion square or losing one tempo in a pawn race
Middlegame piece relocation that abandons a key defensive function, allowing tactical exploitation of the vacated squares

analysis.label: Playing peripheral wing moves (knight-to-rim or flank pawn pushes) when the position urgently demands central development or piece coordination.
analysis.description: All 4 top-activating positions share a striking geometric pattern: the moves played (Ng5, Na5, g4, b6) are all directed toward the edge of the board—files a, b, g, or h—while the best alternatives in every case involve central action or piece development (Qe1/Qd2 in position 5, Nxd5 in position 9, Qh4 in position 10, Nc6 in position 14). In 4/4 cases, the position had very few good moves available (avg 1.5), meaning these were critical decision points requiring precision. The flank moves address secondary concerns—attacking f7 prematurely, keeping a knight 'safe' on the rim, launching a kingside pawn storm, or prophylactically defending a pawn—while ignoring the single urgent priority: completing development, capturing a central pawn, maintaining piece coordination, or resolving king safety. In 3/4 cases the opponent exploits the tempo loss by seizing central control or infiltrating through the squares the flank move left unattended. The average cp_loss of 339 reflects how punishing these positions are when the player's attention drifts to the periphery.
analysis.move_pattern: Pieces or pawns moving to edge files (a/b/g/h columns or 1st/8th rank squares like a5, g5, g4, b6) away from the center
analysis.why_bad: The flank move wastes a critical tempo on a secondary goal while the position demands immediate central development, key captures, or piece coordination—giving the opponent time to resolve their own weaknesses or exploit the resulting misplacement/structural damage.
sub_patterns: Knight retreating or advancing to rim square (a5/g5) abandoning central duties
Flank pawn push (g4/b6) weakening king position or wasting tempo on prophylaxis
Aggressive wing action when own development is incomplete

analysis.label: Moving the king or queen to an apparently active square while ignoring a critical tactical threat or defensive requirement, resulting in catastrophic punishment.
analysis.description: This feature fires on positions where a player moves their king or queen to a square that appears natural or active, but fatally abandons a critical defensive duty or walks into a tactical vulnerability. In 6/11 cases, the king moves to an exposed square allowing checkmate or mating nets (Kf4 into R5d4+/g6#, Kb4 into Bd7/Ra4+, Ke7 onto the open e-file, Kg4 into Ra4#/Re4#, Ka3 into rook mating net). In 5/11 cases, the queen relocates away from a square where it performed an essential defensive function: Qe2 abandoned defense of the b3 bishop, Qc2 disconnected from the f7/f8 rooks, Qd2 missed the life-saving Rxg2 sacrifice, Qb3 left the a7 pawn hanging, and Qe5 abandoned control of b5 allowing Rxb3+. All positions share extremely narrow margins (avg 1.5 good moves) and catastrophic punishment (avg 3575cp loss), indicating positions where concrete calculation was mandatory but the player defaulted to a 'natural-looking' improving move instead.
analysis.move_pattern: King or queen moves one or two squares to a seemingly active/central square, typically lateral or forward, abandoning its current defensive post
analysis.why_bad: The moved piece abandons a specific critical defensive function (guarding a piece, controlling a key square, or staying safe from checks/mates) in favor of an apparently improving relocation, while the position demands finding a precise tactical resource or maintaining exact piece coordination
sub_patterns: King advances into mating net formed by rooks and own pawns
Queen relocates leaving piece/pawn undefended to capture
King steps onto open file allowing decisive rook check
Queen moves away from only drawing resource (sacrifice/perpetual)
King walks to square exposed to coordinated piece attacks

analysis.label: Plausible-looking developing or active moves played in narrow critical positions that demand a specific concrete tactical action.
analysis.description: In 6/6 analyzed positions, the played moves follow general principles—developing pieces (Bd6, Rd1, Qd3, Ba6), repositioning for attack (Qh4, Rb8), expanding aggressively (g5), or capturing material (Qxd3)—but each catastrophically ignores the position's concrete demands. The average of only 1.4 good moves available confirms these are extremely narrow critical moments where principled play fails. The correct moves are consistently specific tactical sequences: Ba3 exploiting diagonal immunity (pos 1), Re1 penetrating the first rank (pos 12), Ne5-Bh5+ forcing a combination (pos 6), Nh5-Nxg3 exploiting pawn weaknesses (pos 8), Nc6-Ne5 seizing outposts (pos 9), and Ra1 doubling rooks on the 8th rank (pos 11). The played moves create concrete vulnerabilities: trapped pieces (2/6), abandoned coordination allowing counterplay (3/6), and collapsed attacks from premature exchanges (1/6). Most positions feature both kings in or near the center (5/8 in the opening phase), where concrete accuracy trumps routine development.
analysis.move_pattern: Mixed piece types moving to apparently logical squares (central files, active diagonals, attacking targets); no consistent geometric direction but consistently non-forcing, non-tactical choices
analysis.why_bad: Each move prioritizes a general principle (develop, attack a target, gain material) over a specific concrete action the position demands, allowing the opponent to exploit a transient tactical vulnerability—whether a trapping sequence, a central pawn break, an undefended piece, or a collapsing attack coordination
sub_patterns: Natural developing moves that create piece trapping vulnerabilities (Bd6, Rd1)
Repositioning moves that abandon critical defensive coordination (Qh4, Rb8)
Slow moves that miss immediate forcing tactical sequences (Qd3, Ba6, g5)
Material captures that collapse a dominant attacking position (Qxd3)

analysis.label: Aggressive piece moves to kingside attacking squares (g5, h6, f7, g3) that pursue speculative attacks while ignoring more concrete positional or tactical needs.
analysis.description: This feature fires on moves that aggressively deploy pieces to kingside attacking squares when the position doesn't support the attack. In 5/6 positions, the player moved a piece toward the opponent's kingside (Ng5 targeting f7 in positions 1 and 5, Nxf7 in position 2, Bh6 in position 6, Rg3 in position 4), while in position 3, Black weakened their own kingside with g6. The common thread is that 4/6 involve opening positions where kings remain in the center and the attacking player lacks sufficient development to justify aggression. In positions 1 and 5, Ng5 abandoned defense of a central pawn to pursue an f7 attack. In position 2, Nxf7 was an unsound sacrifice mimicking Fried Liver patterns. In position 6, Bh6 skipped necessary preparation (Ra4). In each case, concrete alternatives existed—capturing hanging material (positions 1, 5), retreating soundly (position 2), or preparing first (position 6)—but the player chose the flashy kingside move instead.
analysis.move_pattern: Pieces moving to kingside squares (g5, h6, f7, g3, g6) — typically minor pieces or rooks advancing toward the opponent's king position
analysis.why_bad: The attacks are unsupported by sufficient development or preparation, typically abandoning defensive duties (leaving pawns/pieces hanging), ignoring concrete tactical opportunities, or weakening one's own king position while the center remains unresolved
sub_patterns: Ng5 targeting f7 while leaving central pawn undefended
Unsound Nxf7 sacrifice mimicking Fried Liver patterns in wrong positions
Bh6 bishop exchange without preparatory moves to ensure compensation
Kingside pawn advance weakening own king shelter

analysis.label: Proactive pawn advances or piece repositioning that ignore an immediate tactical vulnerability, typically resulting in catastrophic king safety failures.
analysis.description: This feature fires on moves where the player prioritizes their own plans—usually a pawn advance for space (g3, d3, c4, h4, g5, a5, b4, c6 = 8/13) or a piece repositioning for activity (Nc5, Ne5, Rc3, Ka4×2 = 5/13)—while completely overlooking an immediate tactical threat to their king or a critical defensive necessity. In 10/13 cases, the refutation directly exploits king safety (checkmates in positions 3, 4, 11, 12; mating attacks in 1, 5, 9, 10; king exposure in 2, 14). The moves frequently REMOVE a defensive guard from a specific square: g3 unguards f3, b4 unguards c3, Rc3 unguards e2, Nc5 abandons f4 control, c6 creates a target exploitable with check. The average cp_loss of 3175 reflects that many positions (5/13) result in immediate forced checkmate. The average of only 1.9 good moves available confirms these are razor-sharp positions demanding precise defensive solutions rather than proactive play.
