analysis.move_pattern: Typically one-square pawn advances (often flank pawns) or piece moves away from defensive duties; no captures or checks; the move addresses the player's own agenda rather than the opponent's threats
analysis.why_bad: The move removes a critical defensive guard from a key square (or walks into a mating net), enabling the opponent to immediately exploit the created weakness—usually through a check, fork, or mating combination that was previously impossible
sub_patterns: Pawn advance weakening king shelter (g3, g5, h4, c6)
Pawn advance removing guard of key square (b4→c3, c4→overextension)
King walking into mating geometry (Ka4×2, Ne5 leaving king on mating file)
Piece abandoning critical defensive post (Nc5 leaving f4, Rc3 leaving e2)
Passive development ignoring concrete tactical threat (d3 ignoring Bxf2+)

analysis.label: Playing a slow, non-urgent move when the king (or queen) is dangerously exposed on an open file and needs immediate evacuation.
analysis.description: In 8/10 positions, the player's king sits directly on an open or semi-open file where an enemy rook exerts pressure, and the best move is a king move or castling to escape (Kf2, Kc8, Kc8, Kf7, Kf3, O-O, Kb8, Kd8). In the remaining 2 cases, a queen on an open file needs evacuation (position 14) or a tactical blunder occurs in a king-exposed context (position 9). Instead of addressing this existential threat, the player makes a visually reasonable but non-urgent move: a pawn push (h4, g6, b4, a6), piece development (Nc6, Bd7), piece centralization (Ne5), rook activation (Rge8, Rf8), or a material grab (Nxc5). The 'tempo_loss' tag appears in 9/10 positions and 'king_safety' in 8/10. The common punishment involves the opponent doubling rooks, executing forks/pins, or winning material along the open file that was left unaddressed.
analysis.move_pattern: Any non-king move (pawn push, piece development, rook repositioning, capture) played when the king sits on a file controlled by an enemy rook
analysis.why_bad: The king's exposure on an open file is an immediate tactical emergency; wasting a tempo on anything else allows the opponent to exploit the file with decisive tactical blows (doubled rooks, pins, forks, material wins) before the king can escape.
sub_patterns: Pawn push ignoring king on open file (h4, g6, b4, a6)
Piece development instead of castling or king escape (Nc6, Bd7, Ne5)
Rook activation while king remains exposed (Rge8, Rf8)
Material grab leaving king vulnerable (Nxc5)

analysis.label: Non-forcing moves that waste a critical tempo when the position demands one specific urgent action to address the primary threat.
analysis.description: This feature fires on positions where a player makes a quiet, non-forcing move (no check, no capture, no concrete threat) while the position has an extremely narrow set of correct continuations (avg 1.6 good moves). In 7/10 positions, the critical factor is a passed pawn that needs immediate attention—either blockading it (Kf8 away from g8, Bb2 instead of blockading c5, Kh6 instead of Nd3), maintaining perpetual check against it (Kg1, Rh2 away from checking distance), or exploiting a tactical opportunity before the opponent advances (Be7, e6). In 3/10 positions, the key piece is removed from a critical defensive post (Nh2 from f3, Bf4 as exchangeable defender, Ng5 to unstable square). All moves share the characteristic of addressing a secondary concern (king centralization, attacking a side pawn, passive development) while catastrophically ignoring the position's singular concrete demand.
analysis.move_pattern: Quiet non-forcing moves (no checks/captures/threats): king retreats, piece retreats to rim, passive piece development, or pawn pushes that don't address the critical factor
analysis.why_bad: The position demands one specific urgent concrete action (blockade, perpetual check, tactical strike, maintaining key defensive post), and the quiet move gifts the opponent a free tempo to execute their winning plan—usually advancing a passed pawn to promotion or seizing a dominant square/structure
sub_patterns: King moves away from critical blockading/defensive square (Kf8, Kg1, Kh6)
Piece retreats from key defensive post (Nh2 from f3, Rh2 from checking file)
Passive development when tactical strike was available (Be7, e6, Bf4)
Attacking secondary target instead of addressing primary threat (Bb2, Ng5)

analysis.label: Superficially forcing or active moves (checks, captures, outpost jumps, aggressive advances) that waste tempo by directing energy toward the wrong square or driving the opponent's pieces/king to better locations.
analysis.description: This feature fires on moves that appear active, forcing, or aggressive but are concretely misdirected. The pattern manifests in several ways: checks that drive the opponent's king toward its ideal square rather than away from it (Bh6+ allows Ke2 supporting promotion 1/7, Qg8+ allows Kh1 creating defensive oscillation 1/7), piece placements to apparently powerful squares that create vulnerabilities (Nd3 overextends into a trapped-piece geometry 1/7, Rf8 develops but ignores the critical g4 break 1/7), pawn advances that go one square too far (h5 instead of h6, giving wrong timing 1/7), captures of apparently free material that trigger devastating zwischenzugs (Nxd4 falling into Bb5+ 1/7), and rook placements on seemingly active ranks that are less effective than alternative squares (Rb6 instead of Rb8 1/7). In all 7/7 cases, the player chose what looks like the 'active' or 'forcing' option over a more precise move that was often quieter, more prophylactic, or even sacrificial. The average cp_loss of 250 with only 2.1 good moves available indicates these are critical decision points where precision was essential but the player was seduced by apparent activity.
analysis.move_pattern: Mixed piece types making apparently forcing moves (checks, captures, deep outpost placements, aggressive advances) that direct energy to the wrong square or in the wrong direction
analysis.why_bad: The moves invest tempo in something superficially attractive (a check, a capture, an outpost, an advance) but fail to address the position's concrete demands—the correct move was typically more precise in direction (driving the king the other way), more modest in ambition (h6 not h5, Rb8 not Rb6), or more prophylactic (preventing the opponent's key break rather than pursuing one's own plan). The forcing appearance masks that the move actually helps the opponent.
sub_patterns: Checks that drive opponent's king toward ideal defensive/promotional squares
Piece overextension to deep outposts that create trapped-piece geometry
Pawn advances that overshoot by one square, giving wrong timing
Captures of apparently free material that trigger tactical refutations
Rook placements to active-looking ranks when more distant placement was superior

analysis.label: Natural-looking or instinctive moves that squander a winning tactical opportunity in positions where only 1-2 moves maintain the advantage.
analysis.description: This feature fires on positions where the player chooses a superficially reasonable move—castling (O-O), giving check (Bxf7+, Rb6+, d5+, R8e3+), centralizing a piece (Qd3, Qf6, Kd4, Kf7), or pushing a passed pawn (a2, e3)—in a position that secretly demands one very specific tactical continuation. The positions share extremely narrow corridors of correct play (avg 1.6 good moves), meaning they are critical decision points disguised as normal positions. In 10/11 cases, the player misses a concrete tactic; in 9/11, the move results in tempo loss; in 9/11, king safety is a central theme. The moves all have intuitive justification (routine development, checking, centralization, pawn promotion threats) but catastrophically fail because they either block critical lines for the player's own pieces (Kf7 blocks e-file, e3 blocks d-pawn, R8e3+ removes rook from ideal post), walk into tactical vulnerabilities (Kd4 allows c5+, Qd3 creates diagonal weakness, Qf6 allows Be5 trap), or choose an inferior forcing sequence over the optimal one (Bxf7+ misses Qxg6+ mate, Rb6+ misses Rxe7+ material win, d5+ misses Rbe1+ attack).
analysis.move_pattern: Mixed piece types (king moves, checks, queen relocations, pawn pushes) that appear to follow general chess principles—all are moves a player could justify with standard reasoning but that miss the single critical tactical continuation.
analysis.why_bad: The position demands one specific concrete move (a precise tactic, the correct discovered check, or an exact piece placement), but the player defaults to a 'natural-looking' alternative that either self-blocks critical lines, exposes their own pieces to tactics, drives the opponent's king to safety, or trades a forced win for a lesser advantage.
sub_patterns: Patzer checks that ruin mating geometry (R8e3+, d5+, Bxf7+)
King/piece moves that block own critical files or diagonals (Kf7, e3, O-O)
Piece placements to seemingly active squares that create immediate tactical vulnerabilities (Qd3, Qf6, Kd4)
Pawn pushes that waste tempo when piece activity is urgent (a2, e3)

analysis.label: Moving a piece to an apparently active square that is immediately tactically exploitable by the opponent, resulting in material loss.
analysis.description: This feature fires on moves where a piece is placed on a square that looks purposeful (developing, attacking, advancing) but is immediately tactically vulnerable on arrival. In 4/9 positions, the moved piece lands on a square directly controlled by an enemy piece and is captured outright (e5 captured by Rxe5, Bb5 by Nxb5, Bd2 by Nxd2, Nc3 trapped after Qc2). In 3/9 cases, the move creates a geometric vulnerability—a skewer (Qxb3 allows Ba4 skewering queen and rook), a back-rank weakness (Rb2 abandons defense allowing Qa1+), or king exposure (Kg1 allows Rg3+ check). In 2/9 cases the piece departure removes a critical defender (Nb6 abandons d6 defense) or loses essential tempo (Nd3 fails to give check unlike Ng6+). The unifying thread is that in positions with very few good alternatives (avg 1.7), players choose natural-looking moves that immediately create concrete tactical targets, typically resulting in catastrophic material loss averaging 1326 centipawns.
analysis.move_pattern: Any piece type moving to a destination square that is directly attacked, trapped, or tactically poisoned by opponent forces already in position
analysis.why_bad: The destination square is concretely controlled or exploitable by enemy pieces already in place—the moved piece is immediately captured, trapped, skewered, or its departure removes a critical defensive function, resulting in instant material loss.
sub_patterns: Piece moves to square attacked by enemy minor piece (Bb5/Bd2 captured by knight)
Piece moves to square creating geometric tactic against itself (Qxb3 skewer, Rb2 back-rank)
Piece abandons critical defensive duty for apparently active purpose (Nb6 removing d6 guard)
Knight reaches aggressive-looking square but becomes trapped (Nc3 after Qc2)

analysis.label: Queen checks on suboptimal squares that allow the enemy king to escape toward safety rather than into a mating net.
analysis.description: This feature fires on queen checks that are tactically misguided—the player gives check with the queen but selects the wrong square, wrong queen, or wrong move order, allowing the opponent's king to flee to a square that the correct alternative would have controlled. In 6/8 positions, the best move was a different check (often from a nearby square like Qf4+ instead of Qf2+, or Qg5+ instead of Qf2+, or Qh8+ instead of Qd8+) that covered the critical king escape route. In 2/8 positions, a non-queen piece should have checked first (Bb4+ or Ne5+) to cut off escape squares before the queen delivers the decisive blow. The average cp_loss of ~4950 reflects that these positions typically feature forced mates or decisive attacks that evaporate because the premature/misdirected queen check grants the king exactly one extra escape square. Positions 2 and 4 show the identical error (Qf2+ vs Qf4+ failing to control c1), while positions 14 and 15 show move-order errors where another piece needed to restrict the king first.
analysis.move_pattern: Queen delivers check (often with capture) on a square adjacent to or near the optimal check square, failing to cover the king's key escape diagonal or file
analysis.why_bad: The check fails to control the critical escape square that the correct check/move would block, allowing the king to flee toward safety (typically sideways to the queenside or forward to a sheltered square) and defusing the entire mating attack
sub_patterns: Qf2+ instead of Qf4+/Qg5+ failing to cover c1 escape (positions 2, 4)
Wrong move order: queen checks before a minor piece restricts escape (positions 14, 15)
Check to back rank allowing bishop interposition (position 12)
Checking with wrong queen/piece displacing it from critical file (position 10)
Aimless back-rank check driving king to better square (position 11)

analysis.label: Playing an instinctive check or aggressive-looking move that wastes tempo instead of finding the truly effective continuation.
analysis.description: This feature fires on moves that appear active or forcing but fail to achieve anything concrete. The dominant sub-pattern is giving pointless checks, especially with rooks (5/9 moves are rook moves, 6/9 are checks: Rb8+, h2+, Re5+, Rd1+, Ra4+, Re8+). In multiple cases (positions 4, 6, 8), the check simply allows the opponent's king to choose a favorable escape square while the checking piece must retreat to its original file. In position 15, Re8+ misses a checkmate in one (Qf3#). In position 5, h2+ prematurely advances a pawn with check that paradoxically shelters the enemy king. The non-check moves (b3, g5, Nf6) follow the same underlying error: choosing a 'natural-looking' or instinctive move instead of calculating the critical tactical need. Analyses repeatedly cite 'tempo_loss' (7/9 positions), 'missed_tactic' (6/9), and 'piece_activity' (8/9) as key tags, confirming the pattern of squandering initiative on non-productive forcing moves.
analysis.move_pattern: Primarily rook checks along open files/ranks; also pawn advances with check and 'natural' developing moves that ignore concrete tactical demands
analysis.why_bad: The move wastes tempo because it either forces the opponent's king to a square it wanted to reach anyway, requires the checking piece to return to its original position, blocks the player's own pieces, or simply misses a stronger tactical continuation that was available
sub_patterns: Rook check on open file that achieves nothing (Rb8+, Re5+, Rd1+, Re8+)
Premature pawn check/advance that helps opponent (h2+, g5)
Natural-looking move that ignores immediate tactical threat (b3, Nf6)

analysis.label: Black plays an impulsive pawn promotion to queen with check (or aggressive capture) when the newly created/moved piece is immediately capturable or a key piece is left undefended.
analysis.description: This feature fires on hasty aggressive moves by Black—predominantly pawn promotions to queen with check on the first rank (4/7 positions: a1=Q+, f1=Q+, d1=Q+, e1=Q+), but also captures/moves to the third rank (3/7: Rg3, Bxc3, Bxf3). The common thread is that Black plays the most visually forcing move available (a promotion with check or a material-grabbing capture) but ignores a critical tactical vulnerability created by the move. In the promotion cases (positions 2, 7, 9), the new queen lands on a square directly controlled by a White rook on the same file, allowing immediate recapture that liquidates Black's advantage. In position 2, a simple Qb1# was missed in favor of the flashy promotion. In the capture cases (positions 5, 15), the bishop move removes a key defensive relationship—in position 15, Bxf3 abandoned defense of the queen on g3, and in position 5, Bxc3 surrendered Black's best attacking piece while activating White's dormant knight. Position 4's Rg3 placed the rook on an undefended square allowing a two-move tactical combination. The one exception (position 3, f1=Q+) was actually correct (0 cp loss), representing the pattern's boundary case where promotion with check IS the right move because proper follow-up exists.
analysis.move_pattern: Piece moves to rank 1 (promotion) or rank 3 (capture/placement) in White's territory; typically promotions to queen with check on the back rank, or bishop/rook captures on the third rank
analysis.why_bad: The promoted queen or moved piece lands on a square directly controlled by a White rook (or other piece) that can immediately capture it, or the move removes a defensive relationship protecting a more valuable piece, allowing the opponent to win material through simple recapture or exploitation of the newly-undefended piece.
sub_patterns: Pawn promotes to queen with check but new queen is on same file as opponent's rook
Bishop capture removes defense of own queen, leaving it hanging
Piece moves to aggressive but undefended square allowing two-move tactical refutation
Promotion when a simpler winning move (like checkmate) already exists

analysis.label: Advancing wing pawns (a/b/h files) in endgames when king activity or central pawn breaks are more urgent.
analysis.description: This feature activates on flank pawn advances in endgame positions with exposed kings. In 7/7 positions, the move is a pawn advance or capture on the a, b, or h files during an endgame with both kings exposed. The critical error pattern (seen in 5/7 positions with actual cp loss) is prioritizing a wing pawn push when king centralization (Position 2: Kf6 best, Position 10: Kf6 best) or a more forcing central pawn break (Position 9: c5 best instead of b5) would be superior. The flank advances typically either waste a critical tempo (Position 4: h6 provokes g6), weaken structure (Position 10: h4 creates passed pawns for the opponent), enable tactical resources for the opponent (Position 9: b5 allows c5+), or represent a move-order error (Position 15: a3 before h4). Two positions (3, 7) show 0 cp loss, suggesting the feature also fires on correct flank pawn moves in similar endgame structures.
analysis.move_pattern: Pawn advance or capture on files a, b, or h (wing/flank), typically one square forward, in king-and-pawn or bishop endgames with exposed kings
analysis.why_bad: Flank pawn advances spend a tempo on a non-forcing move that either weakens the pawn structure, provokes favorable transformations for the opponent, or wastes critical time when king centralization or central pawn breaks would generate more forcing counterplay in the endgame race.
sub_patterns: h-pawn advances when king centralization needed (h5/h4/h6)
a/b pawn advances that enable opponent tactical resources
move-order errors where a different flank pawn should come first

analysis.label: Playing a strategically natural-looking move that squanders a concrete advantage by being too slow or releasing tension when the position demands urgent forcing play.
analysis.description: This feature fires on positions where the player has a significant concrete advantage (or near-equality requiring precision) but chooses a move that looks principled by general chess standards—centralizing a piece, capturing material, making a prophylactic move, or gaining space—but actually squanders the position's tactical demands. In 6/8 positions, the player had a meaningful advantage that was largely or entirely thrown away. The good alternatives were consistently active, forcing moves: rook invasions to the 7th/8th rank (positions 1, 6), knight advances to aggressive squares (positions 1, 4), pawn storms toward the enemy king (position 8), and piece development prioritizing king safety (positions 10, 11). By contrast, the actual moves chosen were either passive knight maneuvers to seemingly strong squares (3/8: Nd5, Nf6, Nb3), pawn captures that released critical central tension and opened squares/diagonals for the opponent (3/8: exd5, exf5, gxh5), or slow pawn pushes ignoring tactical urgency (2/8: h6, d5). In every case, the opponent gained a specific tactical resource (pin, fork, passed pawn, piece invasion) that didn't exist before the blunder.
analysis.move_pattern: Mixed piece types (knights, pawns) making non-forcing moves: knight repositioning to squares that become targets, pawn captures releasing central tension, or prophylactic pawn pushes in positions requiring concrete action
analysis.why_bad: These moves fail because they prioritize abstract strategic goals (centralization, material, prophylaxis, space) over concrete tactical demands—the position invariably required maintaining pressure through forcing moves, and the chosen move either creates new vulnerabilities (targets for forks/pins), opens lines benefiting the opponent, or simply wastes a critical tempo allowing the opponent to seize the initiative.
sub_patterns: Pawn captures releasing central tension that open squares/diagonals for opponent pieces (exd5, exf5, gxh5)
Knight repositioning to seemingly strong squares that become tactical targets (Nd5, Nf6, Nb3)
Slow prophylactic or space-gaining pawn moves in positions requiring urgent counterplay (h6, d5)

analysis.label: Playing a slow or non-urgent move when the position requires immediate concrete action to address critical pawn tension, hanging material, or tactical threats.
analysis.description: This feature fires on moves that appear superficially reasonable (quiet development, flank pawn pushes, piece repositioning) but fatally ignore the position's immediate tactical demands. In 7/8 positions, the move is explicitly tagged as a tempo loss. In 5/8 positions (Nf3, Bf4, Bc4, Qh5, a6), the player ignores critical central pawn tension or allows the opponent to execute a tactical combination (forks in 3/8, hanging pieces in 2/8). The best moves consistently involve resolving tension through captures (positions 4, 7: dxe5/cxd5), executing forcing tactical sequences (position 2: Rf2 sacrifice), or addressing immediate threats (positions 8, 11: castling or neutralizing fork setups). The played moves share the characteristic of being appropriate in calm positions but catastrophically inappropriate given the concrete tactical urgency—they give the opponent a free tempo to execute their plan, whether that's a knight fork (Qh5, a6, Bc4), a pawn advance with tempo (Nf3: e4 kicks the knight), material grab (Bf4: dxe4 wins a pawn), or a direct attack (h5: Qxh5 wins material).
analysis.move_pattern: Non-forcing moves (flank pawn advances a3/a6/h5/c3, quiet piece development Nf3/Bf4/Bc4, premature queen sortie Qh5) played when a forcing move was required
analysis.why_bad: The move wastes a critical tempo in a position where the opponent has an immediate tactical resource (fork, capture of undefended material, tempo-gaining pawn advance, or decisive combination) that becomes available or cannot be prevented because the player spent their move on something non-urgent.
sub_patterns: Developing a piece instead of capturing a hanging/tension pawn (Nf3, Bf4)
Flank pawn push ignoring central/tactical emergency (h5, a3, a6, c3)
Moving a piece to a square that enables opponent's tactic (Bc4 uncovering e3, Qh5 allowing Nc2+ forks)
Premature aggressive move when basic development was essential (Qh5)

analysis.label: Playing slow, non-forcing moves (typically queenside pawn pushes or peripheral maneuvers) in positions that demand immediate concrete tactical action.
analysis.description: In 7/7 positions, the player chose a non-urgent move that ignored the critical tactical demands of the position. The most common manifestation is a queenside pawn push or peripheral piece maneuver (b4, a4, a5, Na5 in 4/7 cases) when the position screams for immediate action elsewhere — addressing a mating threat, exploiting a tactical opportunity, or defending against a sacrifice. In 6/7 positions, the analyses tagged 'tempo_loss' as a core issue, and in 7/7 'missed_tactic' appeared. The positions typically had very few good moves available (avg 1.7), meaning they demanded precision, yet the player chose generic-looking positional moves. The consequences were catastrophic: allowing Greek Gift sacrifices (position 13), back-rank invasions (position 6), pawn promotions (position 4), mating nets (position 2), or unstoppable passed pawns (position 15). The moves share an appearance of logical positional thinking — gaining space, targeting weaknesses, consolidating — applied at moments where only concrete tactical solutions could maintain the position.
analysis.move_pattern: Quiet non-forcing moves, predominantly queenside pawn advances (a4, a5, b4) or peripheral piece maneuvers (Na5, Rdd3), with no immediate tactical purpose
analysis.why_bad: The position demands immediate concrete action (defending against a tactical threat or exploiting a narrow window), but the slow move wastes the critical tempo needed, allowing the opponent to execute a decisive combination that was already 'loaded and ready to fire'
sub_patterns: Queenside pawn pushes ignoring kingside attacks (b4, a4, a5)
Piece decentralization away from critical squares (Na5, Rdd3)
Pointless checks that help opponent reorganize (Qf8+)
King moves into tactical danger zones (Kf7)

analysis.label: A bishop sacrifice capturing the f-pawn with check (Bxf7+ or Bxf2+) in the opening that lacks sufficient tactical follow-up after the king simply accepts the material.
analysis.description: All 10/10 positions feature a bishop capturing the opponent's f-pawn with check (8 Bxf7+ by White, 2 Bxf2+ by Black), sacrificing a full piece for a single pawn in the opening. In every case, the opponent's strongest response is to simply accept the sacrifice (Kxf7 or Kxf2), after which the king either retreats to safety within 1-2 moves (e.g., Kg8 in positions 1, 6, 9) or remains stable on the f-file while the sacrificing side has no coordinated follow-up. The positions consistently show that the attacker's remaining pieces are insufficiently developed or poorly coordinated to generate real threats: undeveloped knights on starting squares (positions 2, 9, 10), no open lines for rooks, and no secondary attackers ready to join. In 10/10 cases, calm developing alternatives (castling, piece development, central play) maintained the existing evaluation. The average cp_loss of 344 reflects losing approximately a full minor piece for no compensation. These moves are inspired by classical patterns like the Fried Liver Attack or Greek Gift, but fail because the essential prerequisites (coordinated supporting pieces, open attacking lines, vulnerable king position) are absent.
analysis.move_pattern: Bishop captures f-pawn (f7 for White, f2 for Black) with check, sacrificing a piece for one pawn
analysis.why_bad: After the king accepts the sacrifice, it finds safety quickly (retreating to g8/e8 or staying on f7/f2) while the sacrificing side lacks coordinated pieces to sustain an attack, leaving them down a full minor piece with no compensation.
sub_patterns: Bxf7+ with undeveloped pieces and no follow-up attack
Bxf7+ when opponent's king retreats to g8 immediately
Bxf2+ as a move-order error missing essential preparation
Bxf7+ from Bc4/Bb3 in Italian-style openings against uncastled king

analysis.label: Playing routine developing or repositioning moves in critical positions where exactly one urgent defensive or attacking task demands immediate attention.
analysis.description: This feature fires when a player faces a position with extremely narrow best-move options (avg 1.4 good moves) and ignores an immediate tactical emergency to play a 'normal-looking' move. In 11/13 positions, an enemy or friendly queen creates a decisive threat (infiltrated to h1/a1, or capable of delivering devastating checks like Qh5+ or Qxg1+) that the player completely overlooks. The blundered moves are diverse in type (bishop development 5/13, king moves 4/13, pawn pushes 2/13, knight retreats 2/13) but share the common error of addressing a secondary concern while the position's single most critical task goes unaddressed. Hanging pieces are left en prise (positions 1, 2, 3, 8), open diagonals to the king are ignored (positions 4, 7, 13), defensive pieces are moved away from critical posts (positions 9, 10, 15), and weakening moves create new tactical vulnerabilities (positions 5, 11, 12). The king remains in the center in 10/13 cases, amplifying the consequences.
analysis.move_pattern: No consistent geometric pattern - diverse piece types and directions (Bb5, Ke2, Bxc2, Kf7, f4, O-O-O, Bd6, Be5, Ngf1, Ne2). All are non-forcing moves (no checks, no critical captures) played when a forcing defensive or attacking response was required.
analysis.why_bad: The position has exactly one urgent priority (defending a hanging piece, blocking a lethal diagonal, or executing a winning tactical blow) and the player plays a move addressing a secondary concern, allowing the opponent to exploit the unaddressed threat - typically winning material through captures with check, forks, or initiating mating attacks against an exposed king.
sub_patterns: Developing a piece while leaving another piece hanging to an infiltrated queen (positions 1, 2, 11)
Grabbing material while ignoring a queen's access to an undefended piece along an open diagonal (position 3)
Moving a defending piece away from its critical post, enabling a pawn breakthrough or piece capture (positions 9, 10, 13)
Making a king move that exposes it to diagonal checks or tempo-gaining attacks (positions 4, 12, 14)
Missing a winning tactical blow (check/mate) to play a positional or weakening move (positions 5, 7, 8)

analysis.label: Playing an aggressive-looking move when the position demands one specific quiet/prophylactic move to neutralize a critical positional factor.
analysis.description: This feature fires on positions where a single quiet move (typically a b-pawn or g-pawn advance) is urgently required to address the most critical positional element—usually an enemy piece that must be restricted or a trapped piece that must be kept entombed—but the player instead chooses a flashy, aggressive action. In 6/12 positions, the correct move was specifically b3 or b4 (addressing an enemy bishop on a2/a3 in positions 4, 5, 6, 14, or exploiting piece placement in positions 3, 7). In 2/12 positions the correct move was g6 (denying a square in position 1, maintaining a trapped bishop in position 9). The remaining positions required other quiet improvements (Kc2 for king safety, Bb6 for piece improvement, Kg4 to exploit a misplaced piece). The blunders are universally 'active' moves—knight jumps to central squares, rook lifts, kingside pawn storms, aggressive king advances—that look purposeful but waste the critical tempo needed for the one essential quiet intervention. Positions average only 1.3 good moves, creating a narrow precision requirement that punishes the instinct toward aggression.
analysis.move_pattern: Forward/aggressive piece deployments (knight jumps, rook lifts, bishop redeployments, king advances, pawn pushes) directed toward opponent's king or center, ignoring the defensive/restrictive quiet move required
analysis.why_bad: These moves waste the critical tempo needed to address the single most important positional factor (usually restricting an enemy piece via a quiet pawn advance like b3/g6), allowing the opponent to consolidate, escape, or seize central dominance with the free time gifted by the misguided aggression.
sub_patterns: Ignoring b3/b4 when an enemy bishop on a2/a3 demands restriction (4/12 positions share this exact scenario)
Premature kingside attack (rook lifts, pawn storms) while critical queenside issues are unaddressed
Aggressive knight jumps to central squares that invite favorable exchanges or leave defensive posts unguarded
King advances into knight-fork geometry when quiet piece improvement was needed

analysis.label: Moving a piece away from a square where it performs an essential defensive, blocking, or coordinating role, enabling an immediate tactical exploitation.
analysis.description: These moves share a common pattern of voluntarily displacing a piece from a critical function. In 4/11 cases, a rook or knight is moved away from a square that was blocking an opponent's tactical resource (Nc4 removes e-file blockade enabling back-rank mate; Rc8 undefends the d7 rook; Rge7 abandons the mating attack and allows rook exchange; Rc8 leaves f1-rook undefended for a fork). In 3/11 cases, a pawn or piece move removes control of a critical square (f5 abandons e6 control enabling a fork; b6 ignores back-rank/promotion threat; Qd6 places the queen where Nb5 creates a fork). In 3/11 cases, a piece retreats to a passive square or the wrong piece moves entirely (Qf2 abandons the active f5 post; Kg3 is likely a mouse-slip moving king instead of queen; Kf8 wastes a tempo needed to prevent Nh4). All positions feature very few good alternatives (avg 1.5), indicating critical moments requiring precision where the player chose a natural-looking but functionally catastrophic relocation.
analysis.move_pattern: Any piece type moving away from a square where it performs a blocking, defending, or coordinating function; typically relocating to an apparently active but tactically inferior square
analysis.why_bad: The moved piece was performing a hidden critical role (blockading a file, defending another piece, controlling a key square, or maintaining attacking coordination), and its relocation creates an immediate tactical vulnerability—typically a fork, back-rank threat, hanging piece, or unstoppable passed pawn—that the opponent can exploit with one precise move.
sub_patterns: Removing a piece that blocks an open file, enabling back-rank or infiltration tactics
Moving a piece that was defending another piece, leaving it hanging
Pushing a pawn that controlled a critical square, enabling a knight outpost or fork
Retreating an active piece to a passive square, surrendering tempo and initiative
Making a slow positional move in a position requiring immediate tactical attention

analysis.label: Moves that appear reasonable but inadvertently create an immediate tactical vulnerability the opponent exploits with a forcing response.
analysis.description: This feature fires on moves where the player attempts something logical (defending a pawn, developing a piece, escaping pressure) but overlooks that their move creates a worse tactical problem than it solves. In 5/5 positions, the blunder enables a forcing opponent response (check, capture, or pin) that wasn't available before the move. Specifically: b5 allows en passant creating an unstoppable passed pawn (1/5), Bd3 places a bishop where two pieces can capture it destroying pawn structure (1/5), Rd8 abandons castling rights leaving the king on an open e-file for a battery (1/5), Kh2 walks into a capture-with-check sequence that wins the rook (1/5), and Qd7 self-blocks development while creating a pin vulnerability on the b5-e8 diagonal (1/5). All 5 positions share the 'missed_tactic' tag, and 4/5 involve 'tempo_loss' where the opponent's refutation gains a free move through a check or threat. The average cp_loss of 2085 reflects catastrophic self-harm from ostensibly sensible moves.
analysis.move_pattern: Various piece types moving to squares that create immediate tactical vulnerabilities (captures-with-check, pins, en passant, batteries against own king)
analysis.why_bad: Each move gives the opponent a forcing response (check, en passant, pin, or file battery) that wasn't previously available, allowing the opponent to gain decisive material or positional advantage with tempo. The player overlooks that their 'solution' to one problem creates a worse problem.
sub_patterns: Piece placed en prise to multiple attackers creating structural damage
King moving onto a file/diagonal where capture-with-check wins material
Pawn advance allowing en passant or leaving adjacent pawns undefended
Self-blocking move that creates pin or battery vulnerability
Voluntary loss of castling rights exposing king to open-file tactics

analysis.label: Playing a slow, quiet, or passive move in a position where only one or two concrete actions maintain the evaluation, wasting a decisive tempo.
analysis.description: This feature fires on positions where the player makes a natural-looking but non-forcing move (quiet pawn push, king retreat, or generic development) when the position urgently demanded immediate concrete action. In 9/9 cases, the move played was quiet and non-forcing, while the correct moves involved active king advances (positions 1,2,3,7), addressing hanging material (positions 4,8), decisive captures (position 6), avoiding tactical alignments (position 5), or setting up unstoppable tactical sequences (position 9). The average number of good moves was only 1.6, indicating these are narrow critical moments. The common thread is tempo: in 8/9 positions the 'tempo_loss' tag applies, as the wasted move gives the opponent exactly the time needed to neutralize a threat, capture an unsupported piece, activate their king in a race, or exploit a tactical alignment. The moves look strategically sensible (advance a passed pawn, improve the king, double rooks) but fatally miss that the position has crossed into a concrete-tactics-required phase where only one specific action works.
analysis.move_pattern: Quiet non-forcing moves: king retreats (Ke1, Kf1, Kh7), slow pawn pushes (b2, d7, f3), passive piece development (Rf8, Rae1), or king walks into danger (Kb6)
analysis.why_bad: The position demands one specific concrete action (active king advance, capture, or tactical redeployment), and the quiet move wastes the critical tempo that separates winning from drawing or drawing from losing, allowing the opponent to activate, neutralize threats, or exploit tactical vulnerabilities.
sub_patterns: Premature passed pawn advance that immobilizes supporting pieces (b2, d7)
King retreating backward when forward king activation is critical (Ke1 vs Kg3, Kf1 vs Kf3, Kh7 vs Rh1)
Quiet pawn/piece move ignoring an immediate tactical threat on the board (f3, Rae1, Rf8)
King walking into a tactical alignment without recognizing the geometry (Kb6)

analysis.label: Slow, non-forcing repositioning moves that inadvertently create new tactical weaknesses in positions demanding immediate concrete action.
analysis.description: This feature fires on quiet, non-forcing moves (no checks, captures, or direct threats) that appear to 'improve' the position but actually introduce fresh tactical vulnerabilities that the opponent can immediately exploit. The common thread across all 8 positions is a player choosing a passive repositioning move when the position required urgent concrete play. These moves self-inflict new problems: Kg2 exposes the king on the a8-h1 diagonal (1/8), f3 fatally opens the a7-g1 diagonal to the king (1/8), Kg5 exposes the king to checks on the d8-g5 diagonal (1/8), Be1 blocks the f1-rook and leaves Ne2 hanging (1/8), Ne7 blocks the bishop's only retreat creating a trapped piece (1/8), both Qb5 moves abandon critical squares the queen needed to control (2/8), and b4 ignores immediate central threats for slow flank expansion (1/8). In all cases, the average number of good moves was only 1.9, indicating positions requiring precision where the player defaulted to a 'looks useful' move rather than finding the necessary concrete solution.
analysis.move_pattern: Non-forcing moves of any piece type (king, bishop, queen, knight, pawn) to seemingly purposeful squares with no immediate threat, check, or capture
analysis.why_bad: These moves ignore immediate tactical demands in critical positions, and the chosen square/move itself creates a new geometric vulnerability (exposed diagonal, blocked retreat, hanging piece, abandoned key square) that the opponent exploits with forcing play
sub_patterns: King moves to squares exposed on long diagonals or checking lines (Kg2, Kg5)
Piece retreats that block friendly piece coordination or create hanging pieces (Be1, Ne7)
Queen repositioning that abandons control of critical tactical squares (Qb5 x2)
Pawn moves weakening king position or ignoring central threats (f3, b4)

analysis.label: Black plays a quiet, non-forcing preparatory move when the position demands immediate tactical action or urgent counterplay.
analysis.description: In all 5 positions, Black plays a natural-looking but passive move (pawn advance, bishop development, queen repositioning) that ignores a critical tactical window. In 4/5 positions the best move involved an immediate forcing sequence - a check (Bg5+ in position 10), a tactical thrust (Ng4/Qh4+ in position 6), urgent piece activation (Rb8 in positions 2 and 11), or piece centralization preserving pawn integrity (Bd4 in position 15). The played moves are all tagged as 'tempo_loss' in 4/5 cases, and the analyses consistently identify the error as wasting a critical tempo on a slow move while the opponent has a concrete plan about to execute (h4 kingside break, f3 trapping a piece, developing a dormant knight, capturing an undefended pawn). The positions all featured dynamic imbalances where Black needed to act NOW - opposite-side castling attacks, exposed enemy kings, vulnerable pieces, or delicate pawn structures requiring maintenance rather than disturbance.
analysis.move_pattern: Non-forcing move (pawn push, piece development, queen repositioning) to a square that creates no immediate threat, check, or tactical problem for the opponent
analysis.why_bad: These moves squander a critical tempo in positions where the opponent has an imminent concrete plan (kingside pawn break, piece development, material capture); the quiet move gives the opponent exactly the time needed to execute their threat, converting a dynamic advantage into equality or worse.
sub_patterns: Flank pawn advance ignoring central/tactical urgency (a5, h5)
Passive piece development when forcing moves available (Bd7, Bd4)
Queen repositioning that fails to address piece vulnerability (Qc7)

analysis.label: Playing superficially active or aggressive-looking moves that ignore the single critical tactical requirement of the position, resulting in significant material or positional loss.
analysis.description: In all 8 positions, the player makes a move that appears active or ambitious—an aggressive queen placement (Qe7, Qa7), a rook lift (Rf3), a flashy check (Qd8+, Bg5+), an advancing king (Kg6), an outpost-seeking knight (Nc5), or a space-gaining pawn push (c5)—while ignoring the one concrete tactical demand of the position. In 5/8 cases, the moved piece immediately becomes a target (Qe7 attacked by Nf5, Kg6 attacked by Nh4+, Rf3 forked by Ne5, Bg5+ kicked by f6, Nc5 captured by Bxc5/d6). In 2/8 cases, the move abandons a critical defensive assignment (Qa7 leaves e7 bishop unguarded, c5 ignores the Bxe7/Bxd8 tactical sequence). In 1/8 cases, the check leads to a dead end (Qd8+ after Kg7 loses perpetual check resources). The average of only 1.8 good moves confirms these are positions demanding precise play rather than general improvement, and the average 325cp loss shows catastrophic consequences for pursuing secondary goals over the primary tactical obligation.
analysis.move_pattern: Various piece types moving to superficially active squares (forward, checking, attacking) while the position has a specific narrow tactical requirement
analysis.why_bad: The moves prioritize vague strategic ambition (7th rank penetration, rook lifts, outpost occupation, checks) over the single concrete tactical necessity of the position—either placing the moved piece where it can be immediately attacked/forked, abandoning a critical defensive duty, or burning the only forcing sequence available (perpetual check)
sub_patterns: Piece moves to square where opponent's knight delivers fork or tempo-gaining attack (Qe7/Rf3/Kg6/Nc5)
Purposeless check that is easily blocked, losing tempo and position (Qd8+/Bg5+)
Moving a defender away from its critical protective role, leaving material hanging (Qa7/c5)

analysis.label: Natural-looking or routine moves that ignore the position's most critical tactical or defensive demand, giving the opponent a crucial tempo.
analysis.description: This feature fires on moves that appear logical in a vacuum—natural development (Nf6, Nc6), rook centralization (Re8, Re6, Rf7, Rf1), passed pawn advances (d2, a6), or solidifying pawn moves (c6, a5)—but critically fail to address the ONE urgent demand of the position. In 8/10 cases, the best move involved either a forcing tactical sequence (Rxc6+, Ra7+, Rg1+), proactive king safety (Kg7, Kh7, Kg3), or addressing a specific vulnerability (defending e5 against a pin, preventing Qh5+). The played moves all surrender tempo to the opponent: allowing simplification that dissipates an attack (1/10), enabling a passed pawn advance (2/10), permitting a devastating queen check on an open diagonal (2/10), creating a target the opponent immediately exploits (2/10), or removing a critical defender (1/10). The average centipawn loss of 1120 and average of only 2.1 good moves available confirms these are critical-moment positions where precision was required but the player defaulted to a 'looks reasonable' move instead of calculating the position's concrete demands.
analysis.move_pattern: Diverse piece types and directions (rook lifts, knight development, pawn pushes); all are non-forcing, non-checking moves in positions demanding forcing play
analysis.why_bad: These moves waste a critical tempo by pursuing a secondary goal (development, infiltration, pawn advance, centralization) while the position demands immediate attention to a specific tactical vulnerability or forcing opportunity, allowing the opponent to execute their primary threat unchallenged
sub_patterns: Non-developing pawn push ignoring king diagonal weakness (a5, Nc6 in From's Gambit)
Rook repositioning that abandons a critical defensive file (Re8, Rf1)
Premature passed pawn advance before neutralizing opponent's counter-threat (d2, a6)
Natural infiltration instead of decisive tactical sacrifice (Rf7 instead of Rxc6+)
Structural pawn move creating immediate target (c6 allowing d5)

analysis.label: Playing a rook check when a queen check or queen move would have created a superior mating geometry or maintained decisive pressure.
analysis.description: In all 4/4 positions, the player delivered a rook check (+) when the correct move was a queen move (3/4 specifically a queen check like Qc5+ or Qb5+, 1/4 a non-checking queen move Qxe3 creating unstoppable threats). The rook checks all allowed the opposing king to step to a safer square (Kf2, Kd1/Kc1, Kf3), whereas the queen's superior reach would have either forced the king to a worse square or created an inescapable mating coordination between queen and rook. In 3/4 positions this converted forced checkmate into merely winning positions (avg ~5000cp loss), and in 3/4 there was only 1 good move available, showing these are narrow tactical moments requiring precise piece-selection for the checking sequence.
analysis.move_pattern: Rook move delivering check (various files/ranks: a1, g4, e8, c2) when queen check was geometrically superior
analysis.why_bad: The rook check drives the king to a square where it finds safety, whereas a queen check would have controlled more escape squares, forced the king into a lethal corridor, or set up a subsequent rook check/queen-rook mating net that the king cannot survive. The player reflexively checks with the piece already on an active file rather than calculating which piece's check creates the deadlier geometry.
sub_patterns: Rook check allows king to escape when queen check would force king into mating net
Wrong move order: rook check first when queen check should precede to restrict king
Checking with the less powerful piece when queen covers more escape squares

analysis.label: Playing a routine developing move when Nb5 (knight to b5) threatens a devastating fork against the opponent's uncastled king.
analysis.description: In 4/5 positions, the single best move was Nb5, jumping the knight to b5 to threaten Nc7+ or Nd6+ forking the king and rook. Instead, the player chose passive minor piece developing moves (Bg5, Be2, Bb5, Ne2, Bc4) that ignore the concrete tactical opportunity. Position 7 is especially illustrative: the player sent the wrong piece to b5 (Bb5 instead of Nb5), achieving only a superficial pin easily broken by ...a6. In Position 8, Nb5 threatened Nc7+ winning the exchange outright. In Position 10, Nb5 threatened Nd6+ against Black's completely undeveloped army. Position 2 shares the broader theme of choosing development over addressing/exploiting knight fork vulnerabilities against a centralized king. All 5 positions feature an opponent king stuck in the center, and in every case the played move allows the opponent to consolidate or develop with tempo, squandering a significant advantage.
analysis.move_pattern: Minor piece development (bishop or knight) to a natural square instead of Nc3-b5 exploiting uncastled king
analysis.why_bad: These passive developing moves waste the critical tempo needed to execute Nb5 with unstoppable fork threats (Nc7+/Nd6+) against the opponent's king stuck in the center, allowing the opponent to consolidate, castle, or neutralize the tactical opportunity.
sub_patterns: Bishop to wrong square on b5 instead of knight (Bb5 vs Nb5)
Bishop development ignoring Nb5-Nc7+ fork
Knight retreat (Ne2) missing Nb5 invasion
Natural bishop development (Bc4/Be2) when Nb5 is crushing

analysis.label: Pieces moved to apparently active or aggressive squares where they become immediate tactical targets or leave critical vulnerabilities behind.
analysis.description: This feature fires on moves that place pieces on forward-looking, seemingly active squares that are actually tactically exploitable. In 6/9 positions, the piece that moves ends up directly vulnerable to attack—trapped by pawn advances (Nh5 punished by g4, Rg4 punished by h5), captured via geometric tricks (Bc5 lost to Qh5+/Qxc5+), or exposed on open lines (Ke5 punished by rook pressure on the e-file). In the remaining cases, the aggressive move removes a critical defender (Ncxe7 vacates c6 allowing Nb5 invasion), hangs material to simple recapture (Bxf4 lost to gxf4), or misplaces a piece allowing the opponent to seize the initiative (Ba4 enables Ba6 preventing castling, Nh4 leaves c2 undefended for a fork). The correct alternatives are typically quieter retreats or consolidating moves (Bh2, Rd3, Kg7, Bd3, Ne3) that prioritize concrete safety over illusory activity. The average cp_loss of 293 reflects that these aggressive placements create one-move tactical refutations the player overlooked.
analysis.move_pattern: Piece (often knight, bishop, rook, or king) moves forward or to an aggressive-looking square on the rim/center, typically not a capture, prioritizing apparent activity over safety
analysis.why_bad: The destination square is tactically vulnerable—the piece can be attacked by pawns, trapped due to lack of retreat squares, captured via checks/discovered attacks, or its departure from its original square leaves critical defensive gaps that are immediately exploited
sub_patterns: Knight to rim square (h4/h5) where it is attacked by pawn advances or has no productive continuation
Piece advances to exposed square where it is trapped by pawn push (Rg4 trapped by h5, Nh5 attacked by g4)
Bishop/piece develops to active-looking diagonal that is tactically exploitable via queen check geometry
King advances aggressively into open position where rooks/queen exploit open files
Wrong piece captures/moves, removing a key defender from a critical square

analysis.label: Playing a non-forcing, seemingly constructive move in a tactically critical position that demands immediate concrete action.
analysis.description: This feature fires on positions where the player makes a quiet, 'improving' move (development, repositioning, or a non-threatening pawn push) instead of the required forcing continuation. In 7/9 positions, the primary tactical motif is tempo_loss, and in 8/9 the error is tagged as missed_tactic. The positions characteristically have very few good moves (avg 1.8), indicating narrow critical moments requiring precision. The correct moves are always forcing—advancing passed pawns with tempo (Position 1: d3, Position 4: Qd4+), executing sacrifices (Position 5: Rf2), opening the center tactically (Position 6: exd5), neutralizing mate threats (Position 7: Qxc3+), or making aggressive pawn breaks (Position 13: f5). Instead, the blunder moves are universally non-forcing: piece repositioning (Ne4, Qg5, Qb6, Nb4, Nge2), flank pawn pushes (b5, a3, b5), or passive consolidation (f6). The opponent then exploits the gifted tempo with captures of hanging pieces (2/9), forks (2/9), back-rank mates (1/9), or decisive counterplay that neutralizes the player's advantage.
analysis.move_pattern: Non-forcing moves (no check, no capture, no immediate threat): piece repositioning to seemingly active squares, slow flank pawn pushes, or passive defensive moves
analysis.why_bad: The position demands immediate forcing play (a tactical combination, a check, a critical pawn advance, or addressing an urgent threat), and the quiet move gives the opponent a free tempo to either exploit a tactical vulnerability (hanging piece, fork, mate), neutralize the player's winning advantage, or seize the initiative entirely.
sub_patterns: Piece placed on undefended square within tactical capture range (Ne4, Nb4)
Slow flank pawn push when center demands immediate action (b5, a3, b5)
Queen relocation ignoring urgent mating or forking threats (Qg5, Qb6)
Development move that allows opponent's central fork or counterattack (Nge2)
Passive pawn move instead of aggressive break maintaining initiative (f6 instead of f5)

analysis.label: Moves that squander a critical tempo by ignoring the most urgent tactical demand of the position, allowing the opponent to execute a decisive plan unchallenged.
analysis.description: This feature fires on moves that fail to address the single most pressing tactical or positional demand in the position, wasting a crucial tempo when precision is required (avg 1.9 good moves available). The moves appear superficially purposeful—king centralizing (Kd5, Kc6), prophylaxis (h6), attacking (Qa6), repositioning (Na7, Ng8), or seeking safety (O-O-O)—but all catastrophically misread the position's priorities. In 6/7 cases, the position has an explicit urgent tension (hanging piece on f5, h-file battle, queenside pawn storm, mating threat requiring exact square, queen check geometry, f7 weakness) that the move ignores entirely. The 'tempo_loss' tag appears in all 7 positions, 'king_safety' in 6/7, and 'piece_activity' in 6/7, confirming that these moves both fail to address immediate threats AND degrade the player's piece coordination. The resulting punishment is severe (avg 444cp loss) because the opponent gains a free move to execute their critical plan—whether capturing a hanging piece, launching a pawn storm, sacrificing on an open file, or delivering a mating sequence.
analysis.move_pattern: Mixed piece types moving to passive, exposed, or misdirected squares—often retreats to back rank (Ng8, Na7), king moves to tactically vulnerable squares (Kd5, Kc6), or slow non-developing moves (h6, O-O-O into attack)
analysis.why_bad: Each move grants the opponent a free tempo to execute an already-prepared tactical or strategic plan, because the move neither addresses the position's most critical tension (hanging piece, open file control, mating geometry, pawn storm) nor creates a sufficiently urgent counter-threat.
sub_patterns: King advancing/moving into tactical vulnerability (checks, pins, forks)
Passive piece retreat abandoning critical defensive post
Slow prophylactic move ignoring immediate tactical hanging
Castling directly into a prepared pawn storm
Piece moving to nearly-correct but fatally wrong square

analysis.label: Endgame moves that waste critical tempo for king penetration toward the opponent's weaknesses, either by moving the king in the wrong direction or by making passive non-king moves.
analysis.description: This feature fires on endgame positions where aggressive king penetration toward a specific target is the decisive factor, but the player instead wastes the crucial tempo. In 6/8 positions, the best move was an aggressive king advance toward the opponent's vulnerable pawns or critical squares (Kd6, Ke4, Kd4, Ke5, Kg5, Kc5). The mistakes take three forms: (1) king moves in the wrong direction, away from the critical sector (Kb5 toward the rim instead of Kd6 toward center in Position 1; Kc6 toward queenside instead of Ke4 toward kingside in Position 2; Kc4 away from kingside defense in Position 3), (2) king moves that are too conservative or one square short of the optimal penetration square (Kd4 instead of Kc5 in Position 15; Ke6 retreating instead of Kd4 advancing in Position 5), and (3) non-king moves when king activation was urgent (Bf8 instead of Ke5 in Position 6; f4/g5 pawn pushes instead of Kg5/Kg4 in Positions 8 and 13). All 8/8 positions are endgames where a single tempo determines whether the king reaches the decisive square in time.
analysis.move_pattern: King moves to wrong/passive squares (wrong direction or insufficient penetration depth), or pawn/bishop moves played instead of critical king advances in endgames
analysis.why_bad: These moves waste the single tempo needed for king penetration to a decisive square, allowing the opponent to either activate their own king, establish a defensive fortress, or create counterplay against abandoned sectors of the board
sub_patterns: King moves toward the wrong flank (away from targets)
King retreats or stays conservative when aggressive advance wins
Passive pawn or piece moves played when king activation is urgent
King advances one square short of the winning penetration square

analysis.label: Moves that waste a decisive tempo by pursuing a secondary objective when the position demands immediate action on the most urgent threat or opportunity.
analysis.description: This feature fires on positions with extremely narrow margins (avg 1.9 good moves available) where the player chooses a move that looks purposeful but fatally misorders priorities. The common thread across all 12 positions is tempo loss in time-critical situations: capturing wing pawns when development is urgent (gxh5, Bxg4, gxh4 - 3/12), moving pieces to passive/wrong squares when tactical shots exist (Rb3, Rc7, Rg6, Nh2 - 4/12), premature pawn advances that lose control of critical squares (d5, b5 - 2/12), king moves that walk into tactics or waste time (Kf2, Kb3 - 2/12), and purposeless checks (Qc8+ - 1/12). In every case, the correct moves address the position's primary demand first - whether that's a forced mating sequence (Position 3: Ra4+ vs Rc7), maintaining piece coordination for defense (Position 2: Rb8 vs Rb3), preserving initiative over material (Position 6: Qf6 vs Bxg4), or executing a winning tactical motif (Position 8: Nh4 vs Rg6). The 'tempo_loss' tag appears in 11/12 analyses, confirming this as the unifying mechanism.
analysis.move_pattern: Diverse piece types and directions; the geometric commonality is moves directed toward secondary targets (wing pawns, peripheral squares, purposeless checks) rather than the critical sector of the board where the position's primary tension exists
analysis.why_bad: These moves surrender a critical tempo in positions that only tolerate 1-2 correct continuations, allowing the opponent to either execute a decisive tactic, generate unstoppable counterplay, consolidate a defense, or escape a losing position - the wasted move creates a priority inversion where the secondary objective is achieved at the cost of the primary one
sub_patterns: Pawn captures that open lines against own king or create structural weaknesses (gxh5, gxh4)
Pawn grabs that sacrifice initiative or abandon key square control (Bxg4, b5)
Piece redeployments to passive squares when active tactics exist (Nh2, Rc7, Rg6)
Abandoning defensive duties for irrelevant attacks (Rb3 leaving f8 undefended)
Purposeless checks that improve opponent's position (Qc8+)
King moves that walk into forks or waste pawn-race tempo (Kf2, Kb3)

analysis.label: Playing a reasonable-looking move that completely ignores the single most critical tactical demand of the position.
analysis.description: This feature activates on moves that appear purposeful—developing pieces, making captures, preparing plans—but fatally miss the position's most urgent tactical requirement. In 4/6 positions, the critical issue involved undefended or vulnerable pieces that needed immediate attention (Positions 4, 8, 9, 11). In 4/6 positions, an exposed or uncastled king was the exploitable factor (Positions 6, 9, 11, 15). The common thread is that each move addresses a secondary concern (fianchetto preparation in b3, prophylaxis in g3, flashy captures in Rxc6+, pawn-grabbing in Nxe4, development in Re1, piece repositioning in Nc4) while a concrete tactical vulnerability goes unaddressed—whether that's a mate-in-one available, a piece about to be won via discovered attack, a queen fork on undefended rooks, or a bishop sacrifice exploiting an uncastled king. The moves would often be perfectly fine one tempo earlier or in a slightly different configuration, but the position has crossed a tactical threshold that demands immediate, specific action.
analysis.move_pattern: Varied piece types and directions; the commonality is choosing any non-critical move (captures, quiet pawn pushes, piece development, knight repositioning) when one specific forcing continuation was required
analysis.why_bad: Each move fails to address the position's single most urgent tactical issue—whether that's an available checkmate, an undefended piece about to be forked, a piece about to be trapped by pawn advances, or king exposure enabling sacrificial combinations—allowing the opponent to exploit the unaddressed vulnerability with a concrete tactical sequence.
sub_patterns: Flashy capture with check when quiet move delivers checkmate
Slow preparatory pawn move when pieces are undefended and forkable
Development move that ignores central tension allowing piece to be won
Premature abandonment of key outpost without tactical preparation
Pawn grab that ignores king safety and enables sacrifice-plus-fork

analysis.label: Natural-looking developing or improving moves that neglect a concrete, immediate tactical vulnerability requiring prophylactic or forcing action.
analysis.description: This feature fires on moves that follow general chess principles (develop pieces, centralize, castle, control files) but critically fail to address an immediate tactical demand in the position. In 5/7 positions, the move is a standard developing or repositioning move (Nc6, Rhe8, Rc8, Qe2, O-O) played during the opening or early middlegame when only 1-3 good alternatives exist. The correct moves are consistently either prophylactic (a6 preventing Nb5 in 2/7, h3/h5 preventing kingside invasions in 2/7) or tactically exploitative (Nxe4 grabbing a free pawn in 1/7, Ba3 preventing castling in 1/7, Nd7 clearing a rank for piece coordination in 1/7). The blunders share the characteristic that they allow the opponent a concrete tactical shot—forks (2/7), hanging pieces via exposed diagonals (2/7), king safety exploitation (2/7), or pawn capture with initiative (1/7)—that the prophylactic alternative would have prevented.
analysis.move_pattern: Non-forcing, non-capturing developing or repositioning moves (knights to natural squares, rooks to open files, castling, queen centralization, pawn advances) that neither create threats nor address existing ones
analysis.why_bad: Each move fails because it prioritizes general positional improvement over an immediate, concrete tactical vulnerability—either an unguarded square enabling a fork (Nb5-Nc7+), an abandoned defensive post (rook leaving h8 or a8 unprotected), a king walking into an existing pawn storm, or a slow move granting the opponent a free tempo to resolve their only weakness.
sub_patterns: Knight development to c6 allowing Nb5-Nc7+ fork motif
Rook repositioning that abandons critical defensive duty on home rank/file
Castling into an advanced pawn storm
Slow queen development when forcing moves exploit exposed king
Unsupported central pawn advance losing material

analysis.label: Playing a plausible but insufficiently forcing move when the position demanded immediate concrete action on a time-critical opportunity.
analysis.description: In all 6 positions, the player chose a 'reasonable-looking' move that addressed a secondary concern while missing the position's true tactical urgency. In 5/6 cases, only 1 good move existed (avg 1.5), indicating extremely narrow margins requiring precise calculation. The pattern: Kb2 prioritized proximity to promotion square over king safety in the queening race; Qc8 pursued back-rank infiltration while abandoning kingside defense; d4 gained space while releasing critical central tension and allowing piece activation; Bxf8 removed a blockader while trading away the only piece capable of stopping a passed pawn; c3 challenged a knight while ignoring the one-move-window Bxf7+ sacrifice; Kf8 fled perceived danger while stepping into a knight-fork attack radius. Each position contained a fleeting tactical resource (a sacrifice, a precise king square, maintaining dual-purpose piece placement) that required immediate exploitation, and the played move was 'one tempo too slow' or addressed the wrong problem entirely.
analysis.move_pattern: Various piece types; moves appear positionally reasonable (retreats, captures, pawn pushes) but are non-forcing when the position demands concrete/forcing action
analysis.why_bad: The position has a narrow tactical window requiring immediate concrete action (sacrifice, precise placement, maintaining tension), and the played move squanders this time-sensitive opportunity by addressing a secondary positional concern, allowing the opponent to neutralize or exploit the changed circumstances.
sub_patterns: King moves to exposed/vulnerable square instead of optimal safety square in pawn race
Queen relocates far from critical defensive sector to pursue illusory attack
Pawn advance releases tension and activates opponent's dormant pieces
Piece trade removes own dual-function piece that was restraining multiple threats
Slow pawn move when forcing sacrifice exploiting uncastled king was available

analysis.label: Superficially reasonable positional moves that ignore the position's most critical tactical or defensive demand, wasting decisive tempo.
analysis.description: This feature fires on moves that look like normal positional play—piece repositioning, pawn expansion, pawn grabs, rook lifts—but catastrophically ignore the position's most urgent requirement. In 6/7 analyzed positions, the move either removes a piece/pawn from a square where it performed a critical defensive function (Qd6 abandons f7 defense, d4 removes d5's protection of e4, Qh4 surrenders e3 control, Qxc3 leaves a dominant post, Qb3 disconnects from king defense) or wastes a tempo on a secondary goal when survival demands immediate action (Be2 delays king escape via g3+Kg2, Rc1 delays king centralization, c5 ignores a back-rank mating threat). The best moves in each position address the critical need directly—king safety moves, maintaining defensive piece placement, or capturing attacked pieces. The common thread is that the played moves are all plausible-looking ideas that a player might choose when failing to identify what the position truly demands.
analysis.move_pattern: Various piece types (queen, bishop, rook, pawn) moved to seemingly active or natural squares, but away from where they were performing essential defensive/structural duties
analysis.why_bad: These moves waste critical tempo on non-urgent goals while the position demands immediate attention to a tactical threat, defensive duty, or survival plan—the opponent exploits the abandoned responsibility (undefended pawns, back-rank weakness, infiltration squares, hanging pieces) with one precise response
sub_patterns: Queen abandons critical defensive guard duty (f7, e3, king proximity)
Pawn push removes protection of another key pawn
Slow piece repositioning when king safety requires immediate pawn moves
Rook sidesteps to open file when king centralization is the priority
Greedy pawn capture abandons a dominant piece position

analysis.label: Natural-looking developing or retreating moves played on autopilot when a specific forcing tactical opportunity (check, capture, or concrete sequence) was the only way to maintain the position.
analysis.description: This feature activates when players make moves that appear principled by general opening standards—developing pieces to natural squares, castling, connecting rooks, retreating to safe positions—but catastrophically miss a concrete tactical opportunity that was uniquely available in the position. In 5/5 cases, the played move looks like reasonable 'textbook' chess (Qd2 to connect rooks, Nc6 to develop, O-O-O for king safety, Nxe2 to develop while capturing, Qd7 as a safe retreat), yet each position demanded specific calculation rather than general principles. The average number of good moves available was only 1.6, indicating these are critical junctures with very narrow paths to success. In 4/5 positions, a forcing move (Nxe4 winning a pawn, Qb4+ winning material via check, Qxe2 as the only correct recapture, O-O as the urgent safety move) was the sole good option. The average cp_loss of 268 reflects that these auto-pilot decisions occur at moments where the tactical opportunity, once missed, cannot be recovered.
analysis.move_pattern: Quiet piece moves to natural/routine squares (development, retreat, castling) rather than forcing moves (checks, captures, tactical strikes)
analysis.why_bad: These moves surrender a unique tactical opportunity that required concrete calculation—the position demanded a specific forcing move (check, pawn capture, or precise recapture) that was the only path to maintain the evaluation, and the routine alternative gives the opponent time to neutralize the threat or exploit new vulnerabilities.
sub_patterns: Passive queen retreats missing check-based tactics (Qd7 instead of Qb4+, Qd2 instead of O-O)
Natural knight development walking into tempo/pin tactics (Nc6 enabling Nc4 tempo)
Castling into an attack instead of capturing a free pawn (O-O-O instead of Nxe4)
Wrong piece recapture leaving critical squares undefended (Nxe2 instead of Qxe2)

analysis.label: Plausible-looking moves in critical positions where only one specific continuation maintains the position, resulting in large evaluation drops.
analysis.description: This feature activates on positions with extremely narrow margins—averaging only 1.4 good moves available—where the player fails to find the single critical continuation. In 7/9 positions, there was exactly one good move. The mistakes vary in form (passive king retreats like Kf1/Ke1/Kc1, aimless piece moves like Bb8, premature pawn advances like d7/h5/g6, speculative checks like Qd2+, and greedy captures like Qxh5) but all share the trait of addressing the WRONG positional priority while ignoring the one urgent demand. Notably, 3/9 positions come from the same game where the player repeatedly fails to find Bc7 (the only move attacking a critical target), instead making natural-looking but irrelevant alternatives. The average cp_loss of 308 confirms these are severe failures at critical junctures.
analysis.move_pattern: Mixed piece types and directions; no single geometric pattern. King retreats (3/9), pawn advances (3/9), queen moves (2/9), bishop retreat (1/9). All are 'reasonable-looking' moves that fail to address the position's singular requirement.
analysis.why_bad: Each move prioritizes a secondary concern (king centralization, material gain, pawn advancement, speculative tactics) over the ONE critical positional/tactical requirement—whether that's attacking a specific target (Bc7 in positions 1-3), addressing king safety timing (position 4), maintaining coordination (position 5), preserving piece mobility (position 6), managing structural threats (position 7), maintaining pressure without liquidation (position 8), or defending a key pawn (position 9).
sub_patterns: Passive king retreats when active piece play is critical (Kf1, Ke1, Kc1)
Premature pawn advances that weaken or self-obstruct (h5, g6, d7)
Speculative tactics or greedy captures with clear refutations (Qd2+, Qxh5)
Piece retreats to passive squares when active deployment is essential (Bb8)

analysis.label: Routine developing moves played without first neutralizing a concrete piece-invasion threat that requires immediate prophylaxis.
analysis.description: All 10 positions share a common pattern: the player makes a 'natural' or 'textbook' developing move (developing a piece, fianchettoing, castling) while ignoring a specific, concrete tactical threat that required prophylactic attention first. In 6/10 cases, the needed move was a small pawn push (a6/a3/h3) to control a critical invasion square. The Nb5 invasion pattern dominates: in 5/10 positions (Positions 1, 4, 8, 12 with ...Nc6, and Position 13 with Bb5+), the player needed ...a6 to prevent a knight or bishop landing on b5 with devastating consequences (typically Nc7+ fork). In other cases (Positions 2, 5, 6, 7, 11), the player needed to prevent a piece from reaching a specific attacking square (g4, b4) or avoid blocking a retreat path. The average cp_loss of 253 reflects that these 'obvious' developing moves walk into concrete tactical sequences. The positions are exclusively in the opening phase (10/10), split evenly between sides (5 White, 5 Black), confirming this is a move-order/prophylaxis failure rather than a piece-specific or side-specific pattern.
analysis.move_pattern: Any natural developing move (piece development, castling, fianchetto) played instead of a required prophylactic pawn push or queen retreat
analysis.why_bad: The move ignores a concrete one-move tactical threat (piece invasion to an uncontrolled square), allowing the opponent to exploit an unguarded invasion point with forks, skewers, deflections, or tempo-gaining attacks that win material or destroy king safety.
sub_patterns: ...Nc6 played without ...a6, allowing Nb5-Nc7+ fork (4 cases)
Fianchetto/development ignoring Bb4 or Bb5+ on open diagonal (2 cases)
Castling that removes a key defender or creates diagonal/file alignment (2 cases)
Developing move that blocks own queen retreat, allowing trapping (1 case)
Pawn move ignoring Ng4 tactical sequence against f2 (1 case)

analysis.label: Playing a natural-looking but insufficiently concrete move in a position where only one precise action maintains the evaluation.
analysis.description: This feature fires on positions where the player makes a reasonable-seeming move that fundamentally ignores the single critical demand of the position. In 9/11 cases, there were ≤2 good moves available, indicating knife-edge positions requiring precision. The errors share a common quality: the played move addresses a secondary concern (centralizing a piece, capturing material, advancing a pawn) while missing the one concrete action the position demanded. Examples include capturing with the wrong piece (Rxe5 instead of Qxe5, position 4), advancing the king before securing pawn structure (Kg4 before f5, position 11), pushing the wrong pawn of a duo (e6 instead of f6, position 9), retreating a piece to a passive square abandoning counterplay (Bf8, position 6), and opening the center with an exposed king (e4, position 3). In 8/11 positions, the refutation involves the opponent gaining a concrete forcing response (check, capture, or tempo-gaining attack) that the played move either enabled or failed to prevent. The moves are characteristically 'almost right' — often the correct piece type or general direction but wrong square, wrong timing, or wrong piece selection.
analysis.move_pattern: Diverse piece types and directions; no single geometric pattern. Moves tend to be non-forcing (no checks/captures) quiet moves that look developmental or positional.
analysis.why_bad: These moves waste the critical tempo needed to address the position's one concrete requirement — whether that's maintaining piece control of a key square, locking a pawn structure before king activation, choosing the most forcing capture, or preserving dynamic counterplay. The opponent punishes by exploiting the one-move window to seize initiative with a forcing response.
sub_patterns: Wrong piece captures (right target, wrong attacker)
Premature king activation before pawn preparation
Wrong pawn advance from a pawn duo
Passive piece retreats abandoning active counterplay
Offside piece maneuvers ignoring urgent positional needs
Opening the center with an exposed king

analysis.label: Playing a move that belongs later (or not at all) in the correct tactical sequence, skipping the critical first step.
analysis.description: All three positions feature critical move-order errors in sharp tactical positions where one specific move needed to come FIRST. In 2/3 cases (Re2+ and Rxh6+), the move played actually appears in the best continuation but at a later point in the sequence — after a quiet winning move (Qxc4 or Qxg5) should have been played first to set it up as decisive. In position 4 (a3), the player ignores the only saving move (Re1+ check) entirely, spending a tempo on an irrelevant pawn push. All three analyses explicitly identify 'tempo_loss' (3/3) and 'move_order' errors as the core issue, and all occur in positions with exposed kings (3/3) where precise sequencing determines whether the position is winning, drawn, or lost. The common thread is prioritizing the flashy, secondary, or irrelevant action over the quiet but critical preparatory move.
analysis.move_pattern: Any piece/pawn move that disrupts the correct tactical sequence — often premature rook checks (2/3) or quiet moves when an immediate forcing move is required (1/3)
analysis.why_bad: These moves skip the essential first step in the winning sequence, either allowing the opponent to neutralize the subsequent tactic (Re2+ lets Bxe2 trade favorably; Rxh6+ lets Qxh6 block the mate) or gifting a critical tempo (a3 allows Black to castle into a crushing position)
sub_patterns: Premature rook check before capturing undefended piece
Flashy sacrifice before quiet queen capture enables mate
Quiet peripheral move when only a forcing check saves the position

analysis.label: Playing a slow, non-forcing move in a critical position where only one specific saving move exists to address an immediate tactical threat.
analysis.description: In all 6/6 positions, the player makes a quiet, non-forcing move (pawn push or passive piece repositioning) while the position demands finding one specific critical resource. The average number of good moves available is just 1.2, meaning these are razor-sharp positions with essentially a single correct answer. In 5/6 cases, the played move completely ignores an immediate tactical crisis: a mating threat (Ke7 walks into Re1+ Re6#; a6 ignores g6/Rxh7+; b5 ignores Re7+), a hanging piece (h5 ignores Rg8+/Rxa8), or the need for a dynamic counter-blow (Ne6 misses e4; Rf1 fails to contest Black's rooks).
