The moves share the character of being 'reasonable in a vacuum' — developing, gaining space, or consolidating — but catastrophically inappropriate given the urgency of the position. The average cp_loss of 3312 reflects that many of these transform survivable positions into forced checkmates.
analysis.move_pattern: Non-forcing moves (quiet pawn pushes to a6/h5/b5, passive piece retreats/repositions like Ne6/Rf1/Ke7) — no checks, no captures, no direct threats created
analysis.why_bad: The position has only one critical saving move addressing an immediate threat (mating attack, hanging piece, file invasion), and the quiet move wastes a tempo allowing the opponent to execute their tactical plan unimpeded
sub_patterns: Irrelevant pawn push while under mating attack (a6, b5, h5)
Passive piece retreat/reposition ignoring dynamic requirement (Ne6, Rf1)
King steps into tactical danger rather than away from it (Ke7)

analysis.label: Playing a positionally reasonable or natural-looking move that squanders a concrete forcing opportunity by giving the opponent a critical tempo to consolidate or find a defensive resource.
analysis.description: This feature fires on positions where a player had a specific forcing continuation available (fork, promotion, mating attack, or decisive combination) but instead chose a 'sensible-looking' move—typically a piece development, centralization, or standard-looking maneuver. In 6/7 positions, the player moved the WRONG piece: they should have moved the queen (positions 4, 6), promoted a pawn (position 7), or executed a knight fork (position 5), but instead developed/repositioned a different piece to a textbook square. In 2/7 cases (positions 2, 12), the player actively WITHDREW or RELOCATED a piece that was the linchpin of their attack (knight from e5 to f3, knight from f7 to d6), surrendering the key attacking asset. The common mechanism is tempo loss: each move gives the opponent exactly the time needed to neutralize the threat—blocking a promotion square (Be6 in position 7), forcing a queen trade (Qc7 in position 6), escaping to safety (Ke7 in positions 4, 6), or repositioning the queen (Qg3 in position 5). All 7 moves look plausible to an intuition-guided player but fail under concrete calculation.
analysis.move_pattern: Piece moves to a standard/natural square (central outpost, developing diagonal, prophylactic block, centralizing check) rather than executing the critical forcing move in the position
analysis.why_bad: Each move surrenders a crucial tempo that allows the opponent to neutralize a concrete tactical threat—whether by blocking a promotion, forcing simplification, escaping the king, or repositioning defensively—converting winning/mating positions into merely better ones.
sub_patterns: Retreating/relocating a piece that anchors the attacking position (Nf3 from e5, Nd6 from f7)
Developing a different piece when one specific piece delivers a decisive tactic (Bc5 instead of Nd4 fork, Be4 instead of Qa6 reroute)
Giving check on the wrong square allowing the king safe escape (Qd4+ instead of Qb4+)
Prophylactic defense when immediate forcing action wins (Ke1 instead of g8=Q promotion)

analysis.label: Playing an active-looking or positionally motivated move that squanders a critical tempo when the position demands immediate concrete action.
analysis.description: This feature fires on moves that appear to improve piece placement, gain space, or create activity, but actually waste the decisive tempo in positions where urgent concrete demands exist. In 9/10 positions, the blunder involves choosing a 'generally good idea' (centralizing a piece, gaining space, giving a check, repositioning) over the one move that addresses the position's critical concrete requirement. The missed requirements include: stopping passed pawns (2/10), maintaining back-rank defense (1/10), exploiting hanging material immediately (2/10), preserving control of critical squares (2/10), and winning the pawn promotion race (2/10). The average cp_loss of 1209 and average of only 2.0 good moves available confirms these are narrow positions where the single wasted tempo is catastrophic. The tempo_loss tag appears in all 10 analyzed positions, and piece_activity/missed_tactic appear in 9/10 each.
analysis.move_pattern: Any piece type moving to an apparently active or central square (no consistent direction/piece); includes king centralization, rook activation, queen repositioning, pawn pushes, and checks that appear purposeful but are concretely irrelevant
analysis.why_bad: The position has one urgent concrete demand (stopping a promotion, defending a back rank, capturing hanging material, winning a tactical sequence, maintaining blockade), and spending a tempo on anything else—no matter how 'improving'—allows the opponent to execute their critical threat or consolidate their advantage unchallenged.
sub_patterns: Active-looking piece moves that abandon critical defensive duties (Re2, Rd4, Qc2)
Slow positional repositioning when immediate tactics exist (Nf1, Kf3, Ke6)
Pawn pushes or checks that gift the opponent a crucial tempo (h5, c4, Bc4+, Qf5)

analysis.label: Knight jumps to a seemingly strong central outpost defended only by the d-pawn, but a two-step exchange sequence wins the recapturing pawn.
analysis.description: In all 10/10 positions, the player moves a knight to an apparently powerful central square (e4, e5, d6, or c5) that is defended primarily by the d-pawn. The opponent then initiates a capture sequence: first a piece takes the knight (Nxe4, Bxe4, Bxe5, etc.), the d-pawn is forced to recapture (dxe4 or dxe5), and then a second piece captures the now-undefended advanced pawn. In 7/10 cases the move is Ne4 with dxe4 leaving the e4-pawn hanging to a bishop or queen; in 2/10 cases it's Ne5 with dxe5 falling similarly; and in 1/10 case each for Nd6 and Nc5 with analogous pawn-loss sequences. The resulting pawn loss averages ~208cp with no compensation, as the knight's 'outpost' was illusory — it could not be maintained because the supporting pawn structure collapses upon exchange.
analysis.move_pattern: Knight forward to central square (e4/e5/d6/c5), non-capturing, defended only by d-pawn
analysis.why_bad: The knight is defended only by the d-pawn; after an exchange on that square (piece takes knight, d-pawn recaptures), the advanced pawn lands on an undefended square where a second enemy piece captures it, netting a clean pawn.
sub_patterns: Ne4 with dxe4 falling to Bxe4 or Qxe4 (7 cases)
Ne5 with dxe5 falling to Bxe5 or Nxe5 (2 cases)
Nd6/Nc5 with recapturing pawn similarly undefended (1 case each)

analysis.label: Advancing pawns aggressively when the position demands development, castling, or preservation of pawn-chain integrity, creating immediate tactical vulnerabilities.
analysis.description: This feature fires on positions where the player pushes a pawn forward aggressively (9/10 are pawn advances, with f5 appearing 3 times) when safer developmental or consolidating moves are available. The common thread is that these advances create immediate concrete weaknesses: opening diagonals against an uncastled king (positions 2, 4, 6 feature f5 enabling Qh4+), leaving pawns or pieces undefended after chain-breaking (positions 3, 8 where g5 and h5 destroy mutual pawn protection), creating hanging material (positions 5, 7 where c5 and e4 leave pawns capturable), or squandering tempo on the wrong plan (positions 9, 10 where e5 and a4 miss tactical opportunities). In 7/10 positions the player's king remains uncastled in the center, yet the player chooses aggression over safety. The best alternatives consistently involve development, castling, or maintaining structural integrity (avg 2.5 good moves available).
analysis.move_pattern: Single-step pawn advance forward (f5, g5, h5, e4, e5, c5, a4) or aggressive piece reposition, typically on kingside or center files, pushing toward opponent's territory
analysis.why_bad: The advances sacrifice structural integrity (breaking pawn chains, opening diagonals, or leaving material undefended) without the positional prerequisites to justify aggression — usually an uncastled king, undeveloped pieces, or insufficient piece support means the opponent can immediately exploit the newly created weaknesses tactically.
sub_patterns: f-pawn advance opening h4-e1 diagonal against own uncastled king
Pawn chain break (h5 or g5) leaving adjacent pawn undefended
Unsupported pawn push to a square where it can be captured for free
Space-gaining advance that misses a concrete tactical opportunity
Flank pawn push ignoring urgent central/developmental needs

analysis.label: Playing preparatory or non-forcing moves when the position demands immediate concrete action, losing a critical tempo.
analysis.description: This feature fires on positions where the player makes a natural-looking 'improving' or 'preparatory' move but the position actually demands urgent, concrete action. In 4/6 positions, the analyses explicitly identify 'tempo_loss' as the core error. In Position 2, Kb3 wastes a tempo preparing king centralization when b7/c6 immediately wins the pawn race. In Position 4, Ng5 is an aggressive lunge that abandons defense of c4, requiring a retreat that loses two tempi. In Position 5, b4 creates a structural weakness when Rc3 was needed to contest the file immediately. In Position 6, Rf3 passively places the rook when Rh4 maintains the dynamic balance in a pawn race. In Position 7, d4 is a generic central break when Bd3 wins material tactically. In Position 8, Ka2 is a move-order error where Ne1 was urgently needed first to protect the knight from ...e4. All 6 positions share high dynamic tension (pawn races, hanging pieces, tactical shots) where one tempo decides the evaluation. The average cp_loss of 257 reflects how severely timing matters in these critical moments.
analysis.move_pattern: Mixed piece types and directions; typically non-capturing, non-checking moves that reposition pieces or advance pawns without creating immediate threats
analysis.why_bad: The positions all contain a time-critical dynamic element (pawn race, available tactic, hanging material, forced sequence) where spending one tempo on preparation allows the opponent to execute their threat first, converting a won/equal position into a drawn/lost one.
sub_patterns: King moves for safety/preparation when pawns need pushing (Kb3, Ka2)
Pawn advances creating weaknesses instead of active piece play (b4, d4)
Piece moves to seemingly active but tactically flawed squares (Ng5, Rf3)

analysis.label: Playing a slow, non-forcing move when the position demands immediate concrete tactical action to exploit or defend against a critical threat.
analysis.description: In all 6 positions, the player chose a quiet, non-forcing move (pawn push, routine development, king walk, passive rook lift) when the position specifically demanded a concrete forcing action. In 5/6 cases, the best move involved either a tactical shot (Qd1+ check, Bc6 attacking a trapped piece, d4 central break threatening fork), forced development to neutralize a specific threat (Ne7 to block f5), or prophylaxis against an imminent attacking move (Qc7/a5 to preempt White's a5). The played moves all serve some superficial positional logic—h5 provides queen retreat squares, Qb4 attacks b2, d5 challenges the center, Re6 centralizes the rook, Nbc3 develops a piece, Kd6 centralizes the king—but each fatally ignores the one concrete demand the position imposes. The punishment in 5/6 cases involves the opponent exploiting the wasted tempo to execute the very tactical threat the best move would have prevented (f5 breakthrough, Nd5 fork, a5 queen displacement, Rf7#, castling to safety, Nxe7 liquidation).
analysis.move_pattern: Quiet non-forcing moves (no check, no capture, no direct threat) of various piece types, typically moving to squares that serve a vague positional purpose rather than addressing a specific tactical demand
analysis.why_bad: Each move wastes a critical tempo in a position where the tactical clock is ticking—either failing to exploit the opponent's vulnerability (exposed king, trapped piece, uncastled position) before they can consolidate, or failing to address an imminent concrete threat that gains overwhelming force with one extra move.
sub_patterns: Non-developing pawn moves when piece development neutralizes a tactical threat
Routine development when an explosive central break exploits king exposure
Slow king/piece repositioning when a forcing tactical shot wins material
Self-blocking defensive moves that create worse tactical vulnerabilities

analysis.label: Player makes an alternative move (developing, attacking, or lesser capture) while a simple winning capture of an enemy rook is available.
analysis.description: In 6/7 positions, the best move was directly capturing an enemy rook (Nxd8, Nxf8, Nxd1, Bxd1, Bxf8, Bxf1), and in the remaining position the best move began with capturing a piece protecting a rook. Instead, players chose: lesser captures of pawns/pieces (positions 1, 2, 3), aggressive-looking piece moves (positions 5, 7), quiet developing/preparatory moves (positions 4, 6), or unsound sacrifices (position 5). The common thread is a vulnerable rook sitting on the back rank (d1, d8, f1, f8) within capture range of an existing piece, yet the player's attention is drawn elsewhere—to checks, pawn grabs, positional ideas, or kingside attacks. The average cp_loss of 314 reflects that missing a rook capture typically squanders a full exchange or more of advantage.
analysis.move_pattern: Any piece type, any direction; the played move is NOT the available capture of a hanging/underdefended rook on the back rank (d1/d8/f1/f8)
analysis.why_bad: A rook (or the exchange) is freely available via a simple one-move capture by an already-placed piece, but the player is distracted by other ideas (checks, pawn captures, development, attacks) and allows the opponent a tempo to rescue the vulnerable rook.
sub_patterns: Playing a lesser capture (pawn/minor piece) instead of taking the rook
Making a forcing check that trades away the attacking piece for less value
Playing a quiet preparatory/developing move while a tactical shot exists
Moving a piece aggressively toward the king instead of cashing in material

analysis.label: Playing a seemingly active or forcing move (often a check or threat) before the necessary preparatory step, allowing the opponent a critical tactical counter.
analysis.description: In 6/6 positions, the player executes a move that appears logical and aggressive—centralizing a piece, giving check, or pushing an attacking pawn—but does so before completing essential preparation. In 4/6 cases, the exact move played actually appears in the best continuation but at a later point in the sequence (Re8+ is move 3 in the best line after Qb5+/Qd5+; h3 is move 2 after Bxf4; c4+ works after Qe1). In 5/6 positions the blunder is tagged 'tempo_loss' because the premature action grants the opponent a free tempo to deploy a devastating counter-resource: a checking sequence harvesting pawns (Position 3), a promotion with mate (Position 5), a king escape to safety (Positions 6, 10, 11), or a bishop capture with check neutralizing the attack (Position 8). The common diagnostic is that the played move fails to address the position's primary tension first—removing a key defender, forcing an enemy piece off a dangerous square, or eliminating a tactical resource—before launching the aggressive action.
analysis.move_pattern: Varied piece types (knight, bishop, rook, pawn); typically aggressive-looking moves toward the center or giving check; often the exact move that belongs later in the correct tactical sequence
analysis.why_bad: The move is played before a critical preparatory step (eliminating a defender, repositioning a piece, or forcing an interposition), giving the opponent a tempo to execute a tactical counter (check with gain, king escape, or structural refutation) that would not exist if the correct move order were followed.
sub_patterns: Premature check allowing king to escape to safety (Re8+, Rd7+, c4+)
Premature pawn push before eliminating defending piece (h3 before Bxf4)
Piece move removing critical counter-threat coverage (Ne4 removing c3 control, Bf8 abandoning diagonal)

analysis.label: Playing the correct second move of an optimal sequence prematurely, without the necessary preparatory move that makes it work.
analysis.description: This feature detects moves that appear in the best continuation but are played too early, without critical preparation. In 7/10 positions, the blunder move literally appears in the engine's top line but at a later point: Nc7 appears after Bxe6 in Position 6, Rxf7 appears after Bxb7 in Position 5, Be8 appears after Kd8-Kc7 in Position 8, and Kg4 appears after f5 or gxh3 in Positions 11-12. The remaining positions (f3, Rf1, Ke5) show the related pattern of pursuing a reasonable longer-term goal while skipping an immediate concrete necessity. The common thread is that the preparatory move either removes a tactical vulnerability (hanging piece, promotion threat, pawn break), locks a structure, or creates a precondition that makes the subsequent move safe. Without it, the opponent gets a one-move window to exploit the exposed weakness. Average cp_loss of 2219 reflects that these positions typically have only 1-2 good moves (avg 1.5), making the move-order precision absolutely critical.
analysis.move_pattern: Various piece types moving to squares that appear in the best line's continuation but executed one move too early; often king advances (Kg4×2, Ke5), knight jumps (Ne6, Nc7), or piece repositions (Be8, Rf1, Rxf7)
analysis.why_bad: The preparatory move serves a concrete tactical function (eliminating a defender, capturing a key piece, locking pawn structure, neutralizing a passed pawn) that makes the subsequent move safe. Skipping it leaves a critical vulnerability exposed for exactly one tempo, which the opponent exploits with a forcing move (capture of hanging piece, check, pawn promotion, pawn break).
sub_patterns: Knight jump to aggressive square before preparatory exchange (Ne6, Nc7)
King advance before essential pawn move that locks structure (Kg4 before f5 or gxh3)
Piece repositioning before urgent king march (Be8 before Kd8)
Capture before preparatory exchange that removes counterplay (Rxf7 before Bxb7)
Passive defense when immediate concrete action was the prerequisite (f3, Rf1)

analysis.label: Player makes an attractive-looking move (pawn grab, centralization, or preparation) that wastes a critical tempo when the position demands one specific urgent action.
analysis.description: This feature fires on moves that appear reasonable—centralizing a piece, grabbing material, or 'improving' placement—but catastrophically ignore the position's single most urgent demand. In 11/11 positions, the player chose a superficially attractive move over the ONE thing the position required: seizing the 7th rank (Position 1), repositioning the king (Position 2), playing a discovered check first (Position 4), occupying the open d-file (Position 6), addressing king safety (Position 7), preparing with a knight exchange before pushing e5 (Position 8), supporting passed pawns (Position 10), rescuing a trapped piece (Positions 12, 14), creating counterplay with f5 (Position 13), or launching a kingside pawn storm (Position 15). The average good moves available was only 1.5, meaning these are razor-thin decision points where only the critical action works. The average cp_loss of 2029 reflects that these tempo wastes occur at tipping points where one lost tempo is catastrophic.
analysis.move_pattern: Any piece type moving to a plausible-looking square (captures of flank pawns, centralizations, file-doubling, piece activations) rather than the position's one critical action
analysis.why_bad: The move abandons or delays the position's single urgent requirement—whether rescuing a trapped piece, maintaining a mating net's move order, occupying a critical file, or supporting passed pawns—giving the opponent exactly the tempo needed to neutralize the threat, establish a blockade, achieve a defensive sacrifice, or launch a decisive counter-blow.
sub_patterns: Grabbing a peripheral pawn when attack/defense is critical (Nxb2, Bxa2, Rxg5)
Centralizing a piece away from its essential defensive post (Nd5, Kf6, Ref1, Re1)
Choosing a passive improvement over the one forcing continuation (Rd2, Rb5, Nb4, e5)

analysis.label: Moves that remove a piece from its essential defensive or restraining function, allowing the opponent to execute a decisive breakthrough.
analysis.description: This feature fires on moves where a piece abandons its most critical positional duty—whether defending a key pawn, guarding a mating square, restraining a passed pawn, or maintaining time-sensitive priorities. In 6/9 positions, the moved piece was the sole defender of a critical square or threat (Ng6 leaves d5 unguarded, Qc5 abandons g7 defense, Rb2 leaves the a-file allowing promotion, Qxa4 removes the queen from kingside defense, Qc4 fails to control the promotion path, Rf4 abandons the critical 3rd rank). In 3/9 cases, the move involves material greed that creates tactical vulnerabilities (Qxa4 grabs a pawn while the king is under attack, Bxg6 wins a pawn but traps the piece, f6 tries to challenge center but weakens the king). The resulting punishments are severe (avg cp_loss 2374), often enabling forced mates, promotions, or decisive material gains that were previously restrained by the piece's presence on its original square.
analysis.move_pattern: Any piece type moving away from a square where it performs an irreplaceable defensive or restraining function—no consistent geometric direction, but typically moving toward the wing or away from the critical zone
analysis.why_bad: The moved piece was the sole restrainer of a critical opponent threat (promotion, mating attack, pawn capture), and its departure gives the opponent a free hand to execute a decisive tactical sequence that was previously impossible
sub_patterns: Queen leaving kingside when king is under attack (Qxa4, Qc5)
Rook abandoning critical file that restrains a passed pawn (Rb2)
Knight/piece abandoning protection of a key central pawn (Ng6)
Greedy captures that open lines toward own king (Bxg6, f6)
Wrong move order losing critical tempo in pawn race (Kg4, Qc4)

analysis.label: Superficially logical but passive moves that waste critical tempo in positions demanding concrete tactical action.
analysis.description: This feature fires on moves that appear purposeful on the surface—defending a pawn (Bf1, h3), centralizing a piece (Ne4, Ng4), gaining space (h4), developing (Qe2), or giving check (Qc2+)—but fundamentally waste a critical tempo in positions where concrete forcing play was required. In 6/7 positions, the primary tactical motif is tagged as 'tempo_loss.' The best alternatives consistently involve active, forcing moves: sacrificing material for development (Position 1), capturing free pawns (Position 6: Bxg4), castling immediately (Position 4: cxd5 then O-O), active piece repositioning (Position 5: Bb5), or checking with the correct piece to maintain mating coordination (Position 7: Rc2+ not Qc2+). The blundered moves all share the quality of addressing a secondary or imaginary concern while ignoring the position's urgent concrete demand, resulting in an average cp_loss of 1532.
analysis.move_pattern: Non-forcing quiet moves (retreats, pawn pushes, piece relocations) or inefficient checks; typically lack captures or direct threats
analysis.why_bad: They squander a crucial tempo in tactically demanding positions, allowing the opponent to seize the initiative through development, concrete captures, or tactical blows that the quiet move failed to prevent or address
sub_patterns: Backward piece retreat blocking own development (Bf1)
Preventive h-pawn push that doesn't actually prevent the tactic (h3, h4)
Piece centralization ignoring a concrete capture (Ne4, Ng4)
Check with wrong piece disrupting winning coordination (Qc2+)

analysis.label: Playing a natural-looking capture, check, or developing move without first executing a necessary intermediate or preparatory move that would make it far stronger.
analysis.description: This feature fires on positions where the player has a significant advantage but squanders it by executing a reasonable-looking move in the wrong sequence. In 4/4 cases, a critical preparatory move existed that should have preceded the played move: Position 2 needed f5 before Bxc3 (to displace the e4 knight from its ideal recapture square), Position 3 needed the quiet Rh7 before any knight move (to maintain the mating net), Position 4 needed Bxf1 or e5 before Nbd7 (to resolve the a6 bishop tension while the b8 knight still defended it), and Position 5 needed Qh4+ before Nxd4 (to displace White's king before capturing). In 3/4 positions, the analyses explicitly tag 'move_order' or 'tempo_loss' as the core error. All 4 positions feature the player holding a significant advantage (avg eval around -300+ for their side) that collapses due to the sequencing error.
analysis.move_pattern: Piece moves (3/4 knight moves, 1 bishop capture) that are captures (3/4) or development moves, played prematurely before a forcing intermediate move (check, pawn thrust, or exchange)
analysis.why_bad: By playing the 'second move' of the optimal sequence first, the player allows the opponent to reorganize defensively—recapturing on an ideal square, escaping a mating net, or winning an undefended piece—because the preparatory move that would have prevented these defensive resources was never played.
sub_patterns: Capturing before driving away a recapturing piece (f5 then Bxc3)
Checking with a piece that abandons a dominant post (Ng7+ leaving f5)
Developing a defender away from its defensive duty (Nbd7 leaving Ba6 hanging)
Capturing material before forcing intermediate checks (Nxd4 before Qh4+)

analysis.label: Playing a non-forcing or secondary move when the position demands immediate concrete action to address a critical tactical or strategic necessity.
analysis.description: This feature fires on positions where the player makes a move that appears purposeful—a pawn advance, piece repositioning, prophylactic defense, or speculative sacrifice—but fundamentally fails to address the position's most urgent concrete demand. In 7/8 positions, there existed a specific forcing or decisive action (check sequences to save a hanging piece, a critical breakthrough like Ra7, king activation toward a weak pawn, or preparatory exchanges before a pawn break) that the player bypassed in favor of something secondary. The blunders share a common computational signature: the player correctly identifies *a* plan or concern in the position but misjudges its priority relative to an immediate tactical or timing requirement. In Position 1, e6+ ignores a hanging bishop when check-tempo could save it. In Position 5, Nf3 blocks the critical f-pawn lever. In Position 9, h4 fixes pawns when king activation was winning. In Position 15, g3 addresses a phantom threat while Ra7 wins immediately. The average cp_loss of 316 with only 2.1 good moves available indicates these are critical decision points where the position has one narrow path to maintain the advantage.
analysis.move_pattern: Diverse piece types (pawns 4/8, knights 2/8, rook 1/8, bishop 1/8); typically non-capturing, non-forcing moves that address a secondary positional concern rather than the primary tactical demand
analysis.why_bad: The moves waste a critical tempo on a non-urgent concern, allowing the opponent to seize the initiative, exploit an unaddressed vulnerability, neutralize a winning advantage, or lock the position into a drawable structure. The position demanded immediate concrete action (forcing checks, decisive breakthroughs, piece safety) that couldn't wait one move.
sub_patterns: Pawn advance that ignores hanging piece or creates exploitable weakness (e6+, e5, h4, g3)
Piece repositioning that blocks own key plan or walks into tactics (Nf3, Nc7, Rf3)
Speculative sacrifice without sufficient attacking force (Bh3)

analysis.label: Player makes a quiet non-capturing move while the opponent's queen is hanging and capturable.
analysis.description: In all 6/6 positions, the opponent's queen was en prise (directly capturable) and the player instead made a passive or irrelevant move, ignoring the queen capture entirely. In positions 1, 5, and 7, a pawn could capture the queen (fxe6, dxc5, dxc5) but the player pushed a different pawn or moved the king. In positions 6 and 9, a rook could capture the queen (Rxa4, Rxe7) but the player moved the rook elsewhere (Rc5, Rd8). In position 15, a knight could capture the queen (Nxd7) but the player retreated a rook (Rf8). The average cp_loss of 3354 reflects the catastrophic nature of missing a free queen capture. The played moves are uniformly quiet—pawn advances (f6, f3), a king move (Kh2), or rook repositioning moves (Rc5, Rd8, Rf8)—none involving captures or checks, suggesting a complete failure to scan for available captures before committing to a positional idea.
analysis.move_pattern: Quiet non-capturing moves (pawn pushes, king retreats, rook repositioning) when the enemy queen is directly attacked and capturable
analysis.why_bad: The opponent's queen is undefended and directly capturable by a piece or pawn, but the player overlooks this elementary material win and plays a passive move instead, allowing the queen to escape or remain active with devastating consequences.
sub_patterns: Pawn advances past a capturable queen (f6, f3 instead of fxe6/dxc5)
Rook retreats away from attacking the queen (Rd8, Rf8, Rc5 instead of Rxe7/Rxa4)
King safety moves ignoring hanging queen (Kh2 instead of dxc5)

analysis.label: Positional-looking piece repositions or pawn advances that ignore a more urgent concrete tactical need in the position.
analysis.description: This feature fires on moves that appear reasonable from a general improvement standpoint but fatally ignore the position's most pressing demand. In 4/7 cases, a free or nearly free capture was available (Qxh4, Qxf4, gxh5, and the king-before-pawn principle in the endgame), but the player chose a repositioning or 'improving' move instead. In 3/7 cases, the move actively created a target or displaced a defender that the opponent exploited with tempo (h5 allowed Bg5 winning a pawn, Bf5 allowed g4 with tempo, Qxa2 allowed perpetual check). The recurring theme across all positions is tempo loss: the played move either wastes time on a non-urgent improvement while a concrete opportunity exists, or it invites the opponent to gain time by attacking the moved piece/exposed weakness. The average cp_loss of ~199 reflects positions where one critical action was needed but a 'plausible alternative' was chosen instead.
analysis.move_pattern: Piece repositions (bishop retreats, knight relocations, rook lifts to non-critical files) or pawn advances to seemingly active squares, typically away from the key tactical sector of the board
analysis.why_bad: Each move prioritizes the player's own plan (piece improvement, space, material) over the position's concrete tactical demand—whether that's capturing an undefended piece, defending an exposed king, or optimizing king position before advancing. The opponent then exploits the lost tempo with a forcing move (check, attack on the displaced piece, or pawn break).
sub_patterns: Positional piece move missing a free capture (Rc8/Nf5 miss hanging pieces)
Bishop retreat from active square creating tempo targets (Bf5/Bd8 invite g4/Qh5+)
Premature pawn advance before piece/king optimization (h5/c5)
Greedy pawn grab displacing queen from defensive duties (Qxa2)

analysis.label: Natural-looking moves that pursue a reasonable strategic goal while catastrophically ignoring the position's most urgent tactical or defensive demand.
analysis.description: This feature fires on moves that follow a plausible plan—pushing a passed pawn (d2), castling for king safety (O-O), repositioning a piece to a 'better' square (Bb3, Ng5, Ne7), developing (Na6), or fleeing the king to 'safety' (Kf1, Kb1)—but critically fail to address the position's most urgent concrete need. In 6/8 positions, the move abandons a critical defensive function or creates a new tactical vulnerability: Ne7 removes the defender of f6, Bb3 abandons a blockade allowing a4 with tempo, Kf1 walks into a mating pattern, Kb1 creates back-rank vulnerability, O-O ignores a hanging bishop, and d2 converts a permanent positional threat into an easily captured target. In 7/8 positions, a specific tactic was missed. The average cp_loss of 1447 is extreme, with only 1.9 good moves available on average, indicating these are critical-moment positions where only precise play preserves the evaluation. The moves share the quality of being 'the move you'd play if you weren't looking at what's really going on'—strategically motivated but tactically catastrophic.
analysis.move_pattern: Diverse piece types (pawns, knights, bishops, kings) making repositioning, development, or safety-seeking moves; no single geometric direction but all involve moving a piece according to a 'plan' rather than addressing concrete board demands
analysis.why_bad: Each move prioritizes a general strategic principle (advance passers, castle early, reposition pieces, flee king) over the specific tactical reality, either abandoning a critical defensive function, leaving pieces undefended, walking into forced sequences, or allowing the opponent to neutralize the position's key advantage with tempo
sub_patterns: Removing a defender from its post (Ne7 leaves f6 hanging, Bb3 abandons blockade)
King moves to 'safe' squares that are actually dangerous (Kf1 into mating net, Kb1 into back-rank, O-O ignoring hanging piece)
Aggressive-looking moves that allow forced simplification (Ng5 allows Qg4 queen trade, d2 allows easy blockade/capture)
Piece development to passive/wrong squares when critical threats demand immediate attention (Na6 to rim instead of Nd7 addressing passed pawn)

analysis.label: Playing a slow, non-urgent move (pawn push, piece retreat, or passive development) when the position critically demands immediate central tactical action such as occupying an outpost, capturing a central pawn, or executing a pawn break.
analysis.description: This feature fires when a player makes a peripheral, prophylactic, or repositioning move while ignoring the single most critical demand of the position—almost always involving the center (d4/d5/e4/e5). In 9/11 positions, the best move involved direct central action: occupying d4/d5 outposts (positions 5,6,7,15), capturing hanging/attackable central pawns (positions 2,11,12), or executing decisive pawn breaks (position 1). The blunders instead feature passive alternatives: flank pawn pushes (h6, g4, h5, c4, d5 in wrong context), piece retreats/repositions away from the action (Nd3, Nd7×2, Nc6 to wrong square), or slow development (Bd6, Be3). The average cp_loss of 266 reflects how catastrophic it is to ignore the central crisis—the opponent immediately exploits the unresolved tension via pawn breaks (d5 in positions 7,11,12), captures of undefended pawns (positions 11,12,15), or devastating tactical sequences enabled by the lost tempo (positions 2,3,9). With only 2.0 good moves available on average, these are critical-moment positions where the center demanded immediate attention.
analysis.move_pattern: Non-capturing, non-checking moves directed peripherally (flank pawns, piece retreats, sideways development) rather than toward the contested central squares d4/d5/e4/e5
analysis.why_bad: By failing to resolve critical central tension (capturing contested pawns, occupying dominant outposts, or executing pawn breaks), the player cedes the initiative and allows the opponent to exploit the unresolved center—typically through pawn breaks that open lines, captures of suddenly undefended central pawns, or piece invasions into the abandoned outposts.
sub_patterns: Removing a key central defender (Nf6→d7) leaving d5 pawn undefended
Playing flank pawn moves (h6/h5/g4) instead of resolving e5/d5 tension
Retreating a piece from a strong outpost to a passive square (Nf4→d3)
Routine development missing a dominant central knight jump (Be3/Nc6 instead of Nd5)
Prophylactic moves losing critical tempo in sharp central positions

analysis.label: Playing a quiet, non-forcing move (capture, retreat, or exchange) when the position urgently demands immediate active or forcing play.
analysis.description: In all 4/4 positions, the player chose a non-forcing, passive move when the position demanded urgent active play. In Position 1, fxe4 grabbed a pawn instead of exploiting a dominant knight with Nh6+ (forcing checks). In Position 4, Kg6 shuffled the king instead of activating the dormant bishop with Be6 (gaining tempo on a rook). In Position 5, Bh7 passively retreated an already-adequate bishop instead of developing with e6. In Position 15, gxh5 exchanged pawns instead of centralizing the king with Kf3/Kd3/Ke3. All best moves in these positions involved piece/king activation or forcing sequences, while the chosen moves all prioritized material gain, perceived safety, or unnecessary prophylaxis. The average cp_loss of 307 with only 1.8 good moves available shows these are critical moments where one active plan exists and passivity is severely punished.
analysis.move_pattern: Quiet pawn captures (2/4), piece/king retreats or sidesteps (2/4); all non-checking, non-forcing moves that fail to improve piece activity
analysis.why_bad: They waste a critical tempo on a non-urgent action, allowing the opponent to consolidate, activate pieces, or neutralize the player's existing tactical/positional advantages that require immediate exploitation
sub_patterns: Materialistic pawn captures instead of exploiting existing tactical advantages
Passive piece retreats when development or activation is urgent
Pawn exchanges that release tension the opponent was tied down by

analysis.label: Playing a move that follows a familiar positional principle (rook on 7th, advance passed pawn, attack a piece) while missing an urgent forcing continuation that the position demands.
analysis.description: This feature activates on moves where a player defaults to a known strategic principle rather than calculating the concrete tactical demands of the position. In 4/9 positions, the played move puts a rook on the 7th rank or an active-looking rank (Re7, Rg7, Rc3, Ra7) when a forcing check or tactical shot was required. In 2/9 positions, the player advanced a passed pawn prematurely (d2, c7) when the threat of advancement was more valuable than the advance itself. In 2/9 positions, the player made a 'natural' developing/attacking move (Na6, Kg4) while ignoring an immediate checkmate threat. In the opening case (cxd6), a routine recapture was chosen over a tactical check winning material. The best moves across all positions tend to be forcing (checks like Rc5+, Qxe4+, Bd4+; captures like Nxd5; or precise prophylactic moves like Nf3 blocking a key pawn). The average cp_loss of 3172 reflects that several positions (Na6, Kg4, Rc3) allowed immediate or near-immediate checkmate.
analysis.move_pattern: Quiet non-forcing moves (rook lifts to active ranks, pawn advances, piece repositioning) in positions requiring checks, captures, or urgent defensive responses
analysis.why_bad: The position demands a concrete forcing response—a check that wins material, a move that tightens a mating net, a capture that addresses an immediate threat, or a prophylactic move preventing an opponent's tactic—but the player instead makes a 'template' move based on general principles, losing critical tempo or walking into tactical punishment.
sub_patterns: Rook to 7th rank instead of a forcing check or passed pawn creation
Premature passed pawn advance removing a latent threat that was more powerful as potential
Piece repositioning that ignores an immediate checkmate threat on the board
Routine recapture missing a tactical intermediate move (check winning material)

analysis.label: Playing an active-looking move that overlooks a concrete tactical vulnerability (typically an undefended piece) in positions where both kings remain centralized.
analysis.description: This feature fires on moves that prioritize an aggressive or purposeful-looking plan while ignoring an immediate tactical problem in the position. In 5/5 cases, both kings are still in (or just leaving) the center with closed/semi-closed pawn structures. In 4/5 cases, the blunder directly leaves a piece undefended or capturable (Ne4 leaves Bb4 hanging, Nc4 is itself undefended on arrival, O-O removes tactical threats protecting Bc5, f4 leaves e4 unguarded and opens diagonals). The remaining case (Qh5) is a premature queen sortie that allows development with tempo. All moves appear purposeful—centralizing knights, attacking pawns, castling for safety, launching kingside initiatives—but catastrophically overlook that a simple capture refutes them. The average cp_loss of 393 reflects that these are not subtle positional errors but outright tactical oversights where the refutation is typically a one-move capture of undefended material.
analysis.move_pattern: Various piece types moved to seemingly active squares; no single geometric direction, but all involve repositioning a piece or pawn while leaving another piece unprotected
analysis.why_bad: The moves ignore that a piece is undefended or becomes capturable, because the player is focused on their own 'plan' (centralization, attack, king safety) rather than checking what the opponent can simply take on the next move
sub_patterns: Knight moves to active square leaving another piece hanging (Ne4/Nc4)
Aggressive pawn/queen advance creating tactical weakness (f4/Qh5)
Routine developing move removing tactical protection of a piece (O-O)

analysis.label: Playing a slow positional move when a single forcing check would immediately win the opponent's rook.
analysis.description: In 9/9 positions, the best move was a check (or short forcing check sequence) that directly won the opponent's rook - via skewer (positions 1, 2, 7), discovered attack (position 8), fork (positions 3, 9), or capturing an undefended rook after forcing the king away (positions 4, 5, 6). Instead, the player chose a non-forcing 'improving' move: king centralizations (Kg6, Ke6, Ke4, Kg5 in 4/9), quiet piece repositioning (Re5, Ng7 in 2/9), a pawn capture (Rxf7), a quiet pawn move (a3), or a check to the wrong square (Rb5+ instead of Rf1+). All positions featured exposed kings on both sides with rooks on open files, creating tactical geometries where a single check exploited the alignment of king and rook. The average cp_loss of 375 reflects that each miss squandered the equivalent of winning a full rook.
analysis.move_pattern: Any non-optimal move (king advance, quiet piece move, pawn move, or wrong-square check) played instead of a check that exploits king-rook alignment on a rank, file, or diagonal
analysis.why_bad: These moves fail because they surrender a one-move tactical opportunity to win the opponent's rook via a forcing check (skewer, fork, or discovered attack), allowing the opponent time to reposition and eliminate the geometric vulnerability that made the tactic possible.
sub_patterns: King advance instead of rook skewer check (4/9)
Quiet piece move instead of fork/skewer check (3/9)
Greedy capture instead of back-rank/file check winning rook (2/9)

analysis.label: Playing an indirect, slow, or preparatory move when an immediately forcing or capturing continuation was available, effectively gifting the opponent a free tempo.
analysis.description: This feature activates on moves that waste critical tempo through indirectness. In 8/10 positions, the analysis explicitly identifies 'tempo_loss' as the tactical motif. The pattern manifests in several ways: repositioning an already well-placed piece (Bb3 moving bishop away from optimal a4 square, losing a forced mate-in-6), threatening instead of executing (Qg7 threatens f7 when Qxh7 captures immediately, costing 302cp), taking indirect king paths (Kg3 instead of direct Kg4, Kg2 instead of centralizing Kg4), retreating pieces passively when aggressive options existed (Ne3 retreating when Ne5/Nh6/Nf6 attacked), wrong move order giving opponent defensive resources (Bc4+ before Rd1 allowing Kd7 escape), and placing pieces on tactically vulnerable squares (Qd3 getting hit by ...dxe4, Qb4 getting forked by Nd5). The positions are overwhelmingly winning (avg eval heavily favoring the player's side), making these 'lazy' tempo losses in positions demanding precision.
analysis.move_pattern: Any piece type moving to a seemingly useful square that accomplishes less than the most forcing alternative - no consistent piece or direction, but consistently indirect/slow vs. immediate/forcing
analysis.why_bad: The move gives the opponent a crucial tempo to organize defenses, escape threats, or advance counterplay - whether by threatening instead of capturing, retreating instead of attacking, checking prematurely (wrong move order), or taking an indirect path when a direct one existed
sub_patterns: Threatening instead of capturing material
Premature check before preparation
Passive piece retreat in winning position
Indirect king path losing tempo
Repositioning already-optimal piece

analysis.label: Moves that appear active or purposeful (checks, captures, aggressive-looking relocations) but waste critical tempo by failing to address the position's actual demands.
analysis.description: This feature fires on moves that prioritize superficial goals over the position's critical needs. In 10/10 positions, the played move was tagged as 'tempo_loss' - the piece moved to a square that looked attractive but didn't serve the position's fundamental requirements. Common manifestations include: pointless checks that allow the opponent to reorganize (Qe6+, Rh6+), piece relocations away from dominant posts for trivial material (Rxb4 leaving the crushing b2 square for a pawn), aggressive-looking bishop/knight lunges that get immediately refuted (Be6 allowing ...h6 driving the g5 knight, Ng5 hanging to Rxg5+), passive queen retreats surrendering initiative (Qf7), king moves in the wrong direction missing critical pawn breaks or walking into forks (Kc5 missing e5, Ke2 allowing Ng3+/Nxe4+), and rook placement on slightly wrong files (Rh1 vs Rg1). In each case, 2-3 alternative moves maintained the position's true strategic thread - usually piece coordination, central control, or a specific tactical resource - but the player chose the move that looked 'active' without calculating whether it created genuine threats.
analysis.move_pattern: Any piece type moving to a square that appears active/aggressive (often a check, capture, or forward move) but is misaligned with the position's critical tactical or strategic requirement
analysis.why_bad: These moves waste tempo by not addressing what the position actually demands - whether that's a critical pawn break, maintaining a piece on a dominant square, or keeping coordination for a mating attack. The opponent gains time to reorganize, exploit the misplaced piece, or execute their own plan unimpeded.
sub_patterns: Pointless checks that gain no real tempo (Qe6+, Rh6+)
Piece captures/relocations abandoning dominant posts (Rxb4, Rb1)
Aggressive-looking moves to unprotected/refutable squares (Be6, Ng5)
King moves in wrong direction missing critical resources (Kc5, Ke2)
Passive retreats surrendering initiative when active play exists (Qf7)

analysis.label: Playing an ambitious pawn expansion move while a central pawn is directly attacked and undefended, allowing the opponent to win material.
analysis.description: In all 4 positions, the player makes a pawn advance aimed at expanding or building their position (d4, c4, or b6) while a critical central pawn tension exists that demands immediate resolution. In 3/4 positions, White's e4 pawn is directly attacked by Black's f5 pawn with no defender, and White plays d4 or c4 instead of capturing (exf5), defending (d3/Nc3), or advancing (e5). In 1/4 positions, Black ignores the e5 vs d6 tension where dxe5 wins a clean pawn tactically, instead playing the quiet b6 fianchetto. All positions share closed centers with both kings still on their original squares, and all feature exactly one clearly best move that resolves the tension. The refutation in every case is the simple capture of the hanging/vulnerable pawn (fxe4 in 3 cases, dxe5 in 1 case), often with tempo or additional tactical benefits.
analysis.move_pattern: Pawn advance (to d4, c4, or b6) expanding territory while ignoring an existing pawn-vs-pawn central tension where own e-pawn is undefended
analysis.why_bad: The expansion move does nothing to address the immediately hanging central pawn, which the opponent can simply capture, winning clean material and often gaining additional tempo or tactical advantages in the process.
sub_patterns: d4 leaving e4 en prise to f5-pawn
c4 leaving e4 en prise to f5-pawn
Quiet flank move ignoring favorable central capture

analysis.label: Playing quiet developing or strategic moves instead of the simple h-pawn capture (hxg4 or hxg5) that wins a hanging piece on the g-file.
analysis.description: In 5/6 positions, the clearly best move was an h-pawn capturing a piece on g4 or g5 (hxg4 or hxg5), winning material outright. Instead, players chose quiet, non-forcing moves: bishop developments (Bf4, Bd2), a rook lift (Rb1), a knight retreat (Nh7), or a pawn push (d4). In Position 7, Position 12, and Position 15, a bishop sat on g4 attacked by a pawn on h3, and the simple hxg4 won it. In Positions 1 and 14, a knight sat on g5 attacked by an h-pawn, and hxg5 won it cleanly. The one outlier (Position 5, Kd4 walking into checkmate) shares the broader pattern of playing an aimless quiet move when a forcing tactical resolution was required. The average cp_loss of 1748 reflects catastrophic consequences of ignoring immediately available material.
analysis.move_pattern: Quiet non-capturing moves (bishop/rook development, knight retreat, pawn push) played instead of h-pawn capturing a piece on the g4 or g5 square
analysis.why_bad: The h-pawn can simply capture a piece (bishop or knight) sitting on g4/g5, winning material with a one-move tactic requiring no calculation, but players get distracted by positional plans and overlook the immediate free capture
sub_patterns: hxg4 winning bishop on g4
hxg5 winning knight on g5
Quiet development ignoring hanging piece

analysis.label: Natural-looking 'improving' moves that ignore urgent tactical demands of the position, allowing immediate exploitation.
analysis.description: This feature fires on positions where the player chooses a superficially reasonable move—centralizing a piece, 'supporting' something, or making a general improvement—while missing a concrete tactical obligation. In 4/5 positions, the best move involved a forcing or specific tactical action (Na3 rerouting to capture e3 pawn, Rg7+ forcing a won pawn endgame, Qh5 defending the bishop, d5 central break), but the player instead made an intuitive move based on general principles (Qd3 centralizing, Re3 centralizing, h5 'anchoring', Rd7 'improving', f6 'challenging'). In 3/5 cases this created an immediate tactical vulnerability: a hanging piece (Re3 captured by Ra3, bishop on g4 captured by hxg4) or a critical square/diagonal weakness (f6 opening a2-g8 diagonal). The average cp_loss of 308 with only 1.8 good moves available indicates these are critical-precision positions where the natural move is catastrophically wrong.
analysis.move_pattern: Mixed piece types and directions; typically piece centralization moves (to d3, e3, d7) or pawn pushes (h5, f6) that appear to improve the position or challenge the opponent
analysis.why_bad: These moves bypass concrete calculation in favor of intuition—they either leave pieces undefended on their new squares, abandon critical defensive duties, open lines toward their own king, or miss available forcing sequences that would have been decisively superior.
sub_patterns: Piece centralizes to square where it hangs or loses defensive function
Pawn push intended to support/challenge that creates tactical vulnerability
Generic rook placement missing forcing check/transition opportunity

analysis.label: Playing a natural-looking active move (check, advance, capture, or development) in a critical position where only one specific action addresses the position's true urgent demand.
analysis.description: This feature fires on positions where the player makes a plausible, 'active' move that fundamentally ignores the position's most critical requirement. These positions typically have very few good options (avg 1.7 good moves), creating narrow paths where precision is essential. The blunders include pointless checks that waste time (Qf1+, Rd1+, Rdf8+ - 3/11), premature pawn advances that create targets or get blockaded (h4, d3, e3, g4 - 4/11), and piece moves/captures that abandon critical defensive or positional duties (Kf2, Rc8, Nf3, Bxc4 - 4/11). In every case, the correct move required addressing a specific concrete necessity: eliminating a passed pawn (Position 1), activating the king (Positions 3, 10), maintaining piece coordination for a mating attack (Positions 4, 8), keeping a pawn in place as a strategic clamp (Positions 5, 9), executing a precise forcing sequence (Position 6), maintaining a rook's cutting function (Position 7), avoiding an attacked square (Position 11), or preserving a piece for defensive duties (Position 14). The played moves all share the quality of looking reasonable or productive in isolation but catastrophically missing what the position actually demands.
analysis.move_pattern: Mixed piece types and directions; predominantly active moves (checks, pawn advances forward, captures, piece development) rather than defensive or restraining moves
analysis.why_bad: These moves prioritize apparent activity or a superficial plan over the position's true concrete demand—they either create exploitable new weaknesses (pawn advances becoming targets/blockaded), waste critical tempo on non-constructive forcing moves (checks the opponent easily sidesteps), or remove pieces from essential posts (abandoning defensive duties or piece coordination), all while the position required one specific non-obvious action to maintain the evaluation.
sub_patterns: Purposeless checks that give the opponent time to consolidate or escape
Premature pawn advances that create targets or enable blockade
Piece moves/captures that abandon critical defensive or coordination duties
Choosing general 'improvement' over addressing the one concrete threat

analysis.label: A knight or bishop captures or moves to an apparently attractive square, but the resulting recapture or response creates devastating tactical consequences that outweigh the apparent gain.
analysis.description: This feature fires on positions where a player makes a minor piece capture or centralization that looks superficially appealing but catastrophically backfires. The unifying pattern is that the player focuses on eliminating a target piece or occupying a strong square while failing to calculate the consequences of the recapture. In 3/8 positions (Bxe4, Nxd4-pos11, Nxe4), a pawn recapture forks or attacks another white piece (queen or knight). In 3/8 positions (Nxc3, Nxh5, Bxe5), removing the minor piece from its original post leaves another piece or square fatally undefended (kingside dark squares, the e5 knight, the b7 bishop respectively). In 1/8 (Nd4-pos7), the piece moves to a square directly controlled by an opposing piece and is simply captured. In 1/8 (Bxd4), the wrong piece is exchanged, losing a critical strategic asset. All moves share the characteristic of being knight or bishop moves that appear to simplify favorably but actually destabilize the position.
analysis.move_pattern: Minor piece (knight or bishop) captures toward center/active square, or moves to an apparently strong outpost; 7/8 are captures, targets concentrated on central squares (c3, d4, e4, e5, h5)
analysis.why_bad: The recapture (usually by a pawn) creates secondary threats - either forking remaining pieces, attacking another minor piece that must retreat passively, or the removal of the moved piece from its original post exposes a critical defensive vulnerability that the opponent exploits with tempo
sub_patterns: Pawn recapture forks queen and remaining knight (Nxd4→exd4, Nxe4→fxe4, Bxe4→dxe4)
Piece removal exposes undefended ally (Nxh5 leaves Ne5 hanging, Bxe5 leaves Bb7 hanging, Nxc3 weakens dark squares)
Piece moves to square directly controlled by opponent's minor piece (Nd4 captured by Be3)
Wrong piece exchanged sacrificing strategic trump (Bxd4 trades promotion-supporting bishop)

analysis.label: Playing a non-urgent or self-weakening move in a critical position where the king is exposed and immediate precise action is demanded.
analysis.description: This feature fires when a player makes a slow, passive, or counterproductive move in a position where their king (or their opponent's tactical threats against it) requires immediate attention. The positions share extremely narrow margins (avg 1.7 good moves available) and high consequences (avg 1289cp loss). In 7/9 cases, the move directly ignores or worsens king safety: quiet pawn moves like b3, a3, a6 waste tempo while the king sits exposed (positions 1, 8, 12); self-weakening pawn moves like gxh5 and g5 rip open files/diagonals in front of the castled king (positions 6, 14); natural-looking but irrelevant developing moves like Re1 ignore forcing threats against the king (position 4); and king moves like Ke8 walk directly into mating nets (position 13). In 8/9 cases the move constitutes a decisive tempo loss that allows the opponent to execute a tactical combination. The refutations typically involve immediate forcing sequences (checks, pins, file-opening sacrifices) exploiting the king's vulnerability that the played move failed to address.
analysis.move_pattern: Quiet non-forcing moves (pawn pushes to a3/a6/b3/e5/g5, rook development, king retreat) in positions requiring immediate defensive precision
analysis.why_bad: These moves waste a critical tempo in positions with very few good options, allowing the opponent to execute a forcing tactical sequence (checks, sacrifices, file/diagonal openings) against the already-exposed king that the played move completely failed to address or actively worsened.
sub_patterns: Quiet a/b-file pawn moves ignoring central/kingside king exposure (b3, a3, a6)
Kingside pawn moves opening lines against own castled king (gxh5, g5)
Natural-looking developing moves that ignore imminent tactical threats to the king (Re1)
King moves walking into forcing mating sequences (Ke8)
Counterproductive checks driving opponent's king to ideal squares (Na5+)

analysis.label: Passive or seemingly reasonable quiet moves in positions demanding one specific defensive action, where the move abandons or overlooks the single resource preventing immediate collapse.
analysis.description: This feature fires on positions where the player makes a non-forcing, superficially reasonable move while ignoring the one critical tactical resource that holds the position together. In 5/7 positions, the correct move involved either capturing a key attacking piece (Rxd5, fxe6), forcing simplification (Qd2), or securing a specific defensive structure (Rf1 to guard back rank, Ra7 to defend f7). Instead, the played moves are all quiet — king walks (Kh7, Kd2), rook repositions (Re2, Re1), pawn advances (f6, b6), or queen development (Qc7) — that fail to address the single most urgent threat. The positions share extremely narrow margins with an average of only 1.6 good moves available, meaning one specific resource was critical. In 4/7 cases, the move directly abandons a defensive function: Re2 leaves Bd3 undefended, Re1 abandons the Rxd5 capture, b6 makes Nc6 vulnerable to Bxc6 (pawn can't recapture), and Kd2 walks into a check enabling back-rank exploitation. The catastrophic average cp_loss of 4128 reflects positions tipping from 'difficult but defensible' to 'immediately terminal.'
analysis.move_pattern: Quiet, non-forcing moves (king walks, rook repositions, pawn advances, queen development) — no checks, no captures, no direct engagement with the critical threat
analysis.why_bad: Each move abandons or ignores the single tactical resource preventing immediate collapse — whether that's a defensive capture, a forcing simplification, or maintenance of a key piece's protective function — in positions where almost no other moves are acceptable
sub_patterns: Rook/piece moves away from defending a critical piece (Re2, Re1)
Pawn advances weakening key defensive structures (b6, f6)
King moves into worse tactical patterns (Kd2, Kh7)
Piece placement on tactically vulnerable squares (Qc7)

analysis.label: Quiet piece moves to non-forcing squares when immediate tactical action (captures, checks, or forced sequences) was available.
analysis.description: In all 4 positions, the player chose a quiet, non-forcing piece repositioning move instead of executing an immediately available tactical strike. In Position 1, Qd7 pursued a peripheral counterattack instead of retreating to defend the kingside (Qe2/Qe3). In Position 2, Qa1 retreated the queen to the corner instead of capturing a hanging knight (Qxd4). In Position 3, Be2 passively retreated an actively-placed attacking bishop instead of executing a crushing pawn capture (Bxh6). In Position 4, Qa7 passively repositioned a queen instead of playing a forcing check sequence (Qbc1). All 4/4 positions featured immediate tactical opportunities that were foregone in favor of 'improving' moves that granted the opponent a critical tempo to consolidate, escape threats, or launch counterplay. The moved pieces uniformly went to less active squares (a1 corner, a7 edge, e2 retreat, d7 peripheral).
analysis.move_pattern: Queen or bishop moving to passive/peripheral square (a-file corners, back ranks, retreat squares) without delivering check or capture
analysis.why_bad: These non-forcing moves gift the opponent a tempo in positions requiring immediate tactical action—allowing them to save hanging pieces, develop dormant defenders, execute forks/checks, or neutralize attacking formations that demanded exploitation NOW.
sub_patterns: Queen retreat to corner/edge (a1, a7) missing hanging material
Piece retreat from active attacking diagonal missing forced wins
Counterattack on peripheral target abandoning critical defensive duties

analysis.label: Choosing an indirect or secondary action instead of the single most urgent direct move (capture, advance, or centralize) in simplified endgame positions with passed pawn dynamics.
analysis.description: This feature fires on endgame positions (11/12) where the critical decision involves whether to execute the most direct, urgent action immediately or pursue a seemingly active but ultimately tempo-wasting alternative. The blunders consistently involve: giving pointless checks instead of capturing critical pawns (Na8+, Nd3+ — 2/12), attacking secondary targets instead of advancing/eliminating passed pawns (Ra5, Ra2, Rg5 — 3/12), moving pieces when king centralization was paramount (Bc2, Ke2 — 2/12), or pushing pawns when the king should lead first (g5, g4 — 2/12). The common thread across 10/12 positions is identified as 'tempo_loss' in analysis tags. Passed pawn themes appear in 8/12 positions, and exposed kings feature in virtually all positions. The zero-loss activations (Kxb6, Ka3) represent the 'correct' version of the same positional pattern — directly addressing pawn capture/elimination — confirming the feature detects this specific decision-point structure rather than strictly mistakes.
analysis.move_pattern: Diverse piece types (king, rook, knight, bishop, pawn) making moves that address secondary objectives — checks that don't constrain, attacks on non-critical targets, piece repositioning — when one immediate action (capture, advance passed pawn, or centralize king) was required
analysis.why_bad: These moves waste a critical tempo in positions where only one action matters, allowing the opponent to either establish a blockade/opposition, activate their king, advance their own passed pawn, or escape a mating net — converting won positions into draws or draws into losses
sub_patterns: Pointless checks driving pieces to trapped/ideal squares (Na8+, Nd3+)
Attacking secondary targets instead of advancing decisive passed pawns (Ra5, Ra2)
Piece/pawn moves before essential king centralization (Bc2, g5, Ke2)
Wrong capture/move order breaking coordination (Rxh6, g4, Rg5)

analysis.label: King moves (or tempo-wasting moves) by the losing side in pure pawn endgames where a single passed pawn is racing to promote.
analysis.description: This feature fires on moves in minimalist pawn endgames (typically K+P vs K or K+Ps vs K+Ps) where one side has a decisive passed pawn advantage and the losing side makes a move—almost always a king move. In 9/10 positions the phase is endgame, and 9/10 involve pure pawn endgames with a single critical passed pawn. The evaluations cluster around +/-530-570 cp in most cases, indicating positions that are already decisively won. When the moves are actual blunders (4/10 with significant cp_loss: h6 at 276cp, Kc1 at 9298cp, Ke5 at 348cp, Ke4 at 546cp), the error is specifically moving the king in the wrong direction or wasting a tempo on a pawn move, leaving the king one square too far from the critical defensive zone needed to contest the passed pawn. When the moves are NOT blunders (5/10 with cp_loss 0-2), the position is already hopelessly lost and multiple king moves offer equivalent futile resistance. The outlier (Bh7+, middlegame) shares the tempo-loss theme of ignoring a critical positional requirement.
analysis.move_pattern: King moves (any direction) in open positions with minimal material; occasionally pawn moves or piece moves that waste a tempo
analysis.why_bad: The king moves in the wrong direction relative to the critical defensive squares needed to blockade or intercept a passed pawn, losing a decisive tempo in positions where every single move counts for the pawn race
sub_patterns: King retreating/advancing away from passed pawn's path
Pawn move (h6) instead of urgent king repositioning
King blockading instead of capturing a passed pawn (Kc1)
King one diagonal square wrong (Ke4 vs Ke6, Ke5 vs Kf6)

analysis.label: Playing a non-forcing repositioning move (typically king retreat to g-file corner or knight centralization) when the position demands an immediate tactical response.
analysis.description: This feature fires on positions where the player makes a 'natural-looking' quiet move—repositioning a piece to an apparently safe or strong square—while ignoring an immediate concrete tactical requirement. In 4/8 cases, the king retreats to the back rank (g1 or g8) where it becomes trapped, lands on a vulnerable diagonal, or loses contact with critical pawns (Positions 1, 6, 8 with Kg1/Kg8). In 3/8 cases, a knight moves to a central square that either hangs to a simple capture or ignores an urgent threat like an opponent's passed pawn about to promote (Positions 2, 5, 7 with Ne5/Ne4/Nf3). In all cases, the player had a concrete forcing alternative—a capture (Rxf3+, Bxe7, Bxe4), an active king move (Kf3, Kg6), or piece activation (Ba3, Nc5)—that would have addressed the position's tactical demands. The enormous average cp_loss (2552) reflects that these quiet moves allow opponents to execute devastating tactical blows: mating nets, piece captures on undefended squares, back-rank exploitation, or pawn promotions.
analysis.move_pattern: Non-forcing piece repositioning: king retreating one square toward g1/g8 corner, or knight jumping to central square (e4, e5, f3), with no capture or check
analysis.why_bad: The move ignores an immediate tactical emergency (hanging piece, promotion threat, mating pattern, or need to capture), allowing the opponent to execute a concrete tactical blow that exploits the piece's new vulnerability—trapped king on back rank, knight hanging on an unprotected square, or critical tempo lost while opponent's threat materializes.
sub_patterns: King retreating to g1/g8 back-rank corner becoming trapped or landing on exploitable diagonal
Knight centralizing to square where it hangs to pawn or bishop capture
Developing/improving move when position demands immediate capture of threatening piece/pawn
Abandoning defensive post to make an offensive-looking move (Qb7 leaving kingside unguarded)

analysis.label: Moves that pursue irrelevant plans instead of addressing the opponent's dominant piece or critical positional demand when already worse.
analysis.description: This feature fires on middlegame positions where the side already at a disadvantage plays a move that fails to address the most urgent demand of the position. In 4/5 cases, the correct move was a pawn advance challenging the opponent's dominant piece (g4 hitting a bishop in positions 2 and 10, c4 hitting a bishop in position 9, b4 challenging a knight in position 14), yet the played moves pursued unrelated plans—aggressive pawns (f4), routine captures (exd5), passive retreats (Bf8), rook lifts to vulnerable squares (Rab1), or knight relocations from strong to exposed squares (Nc4). All 5 positions feature the losing side (avg eval already ~+200 against them), and all result in significant deterioration (avg 227cp loss) because the opponent's key pieces remain unchallenged and the initiative compounds. The critical commonality is that precisely one narrow path maintained the position (avg 1.8 good moves), and the player chose a plausible-looking but fundamentally misdirected alternative.
analysis.move_pattern: Various piece types; no consistent geometric direction; moves away from the critical sector of the board where the opponent's dominant piece operates
analysis.why_bad: By failing to challenge the opponent's most active/dominant piece (usually via pawn advance), the player wastes a critical tempo, allowing the opponent to consolidate or increase pressure on the position's decisive weakness—often resulting in material loss or positional collapse.
sub_patterns: Aggressive pawn push that ignores opponent's threats (f4)
Routine central capture when dynamic play is required (exd5)
Passive piece retreat when counterplay is essential (Bf8)
Placing piece on tactically vulnerable square (Rab1)
Abandoning strong outpost for exposed square (Nc4)

analysis.label: Playing a slow or non-forcing move in a narrow position that demands immediate concrete action to address an urgent tactical requirement.
analysis.description: This feature fires on moves that waste a critical tempo when the position has one specific urgent demand. In 7/10 positions, the analysis explicitly identifies 'tempo_loss' as the primary tactical motif. The positions share extremely narrow best-move windows (avg 1.8 good moves available), meaning precision was essential. The pattern spans quiet pawn pushes ignoring hanging pieces (a3 missing Qxd5, b5 ignoring d7 promotion), piece repositioning when the king needed immediate attention (Rg8 when Kg1 was critical), self-blocking moves (Kh2 blocking the h-pawn's promotion path), irrelevant flank moves while passed pawns advance (h4 ignoring d2), circuitous piece routing (Nd1 instead of direct Nd3), rim development missing free central pawns (Nh6 missing Qxd4), self-weakening pawn moves (f6 opening a diagonal), and captures creating exposed pieces (Rxe4). In all cases, the position had one concrete requirement that went unaddressed.
analysis.move_pattern: Any piece type; typically non-forcing (no check/no immediate threat); often peripheral or retreating direction; occasionally a capture that misplaces the piece
analysis.why_bad: The position demands one specific immediate action (capturing a free piece, fleeing with the king, blockading a passer, or exploiting a tactical shot), and the move played addresses a secondary or irrelevant concern, giving the opponent a free tempo to consolidate, promote, or launch a decisive attack
sub_patterns: Quiet pawn push ignoring a hanging piece or tactical opportunity
Piece repositioning when king safety requires immediate king movement
Pawn move ignoring an opponent's advanced passed pawn about to promote
Circuitous piece routing when a direct path exists
Self-weakening move that opens lines toward own king

analysis.label: Playing a forward-advancing move (pawn push, king march, or piece advance) when the position demands retreat, consolidation, or immediate concrete action.
analysis.description: In 6/6 positions, the blunder involves advancing something forward—pawns (c5, b5, g6), king (Kf2, Kg5), or a piece (Nge2)—when the position's critical demand is for consolidation or retreat. In Position 2, Nge2 advances a knight forward but blocks the bishop's retreat, allowing it to be trapped. In Position 4, c5 advances a pawn prematurely releasing tension. In Position 8, b5 pushes a pawn forward instead of supporting the passed d-pawn with king approach or checks. In Position 9, Kf2 walks the king forward instead of developing normally. In Position 11, g6 advances a pawn to chase the queen instead of retreating the king to f8. In Position 15, Kg5 advances the king into danger instead of retreating to h7. In 5/6 cases, the best move involved either retreating (Kf8, Kh7, Qf3) or quiet development (Nf3, Bg2, d5), showing a systematic pattern of choosing forward motion when backward motion was critical.
analysis.move_pattern: Any unit (pawn, king, or piece) advancing forward/toward the opponent's side, typically one rank forward or toward the center/opponent
analysis.why_bad: The forward move either creates new vulnerabilities (exposed king, trapped pieces, weakened pawns), wastes a critical tempo when immediate action is needed, or releases tension that was advantageous to maintain—while the position specifically demands retreat, consolidation, or addressing an existing critical threat.
sub_patterns: Pawn advance that weakens king position or wastes tempo (g6, b5, c5)
King march forward into tactical vulnerability (Kf2, Kg5)
Piece development that blocks a critical retreat path (Nge2)

analysis.label: Playing a passive, non-forcing move that leaves a piece undefended or removes a critical defender, allowing the opponent to win material through a concrete tactical shot.
analysis.description: This feature fires on positions where a player makes a 'natural-looking' quiet move (retreat, prophylactic pawn push, or slow development) while ignoring an immediate tactical vulnerability in the position. In 6/9 cases, the move directly leaves a piece en prise or removes its only defender: Ng3 abandons defense of Bd3 (captured via fork), Rxd2 leaves Bc4 hanging, b6 ignores the unprotected Bd6, Qd2 removes the queen from the d1-h5 diagonal allowing Bxf3, Bf8 removes the bishop from guarding f6 enabling Bxf6/Qg4+, and Bd7 disrupts coordination allowing Bxe4 profitably. The remaining cases (Re1, h6, Nd1) share the same character of tempo-wasting quiet moves that allow the opponent to execute concrete threats. All moves are non-forcing (no checks, captures, or direct threats) and appear superficially reasonable, but catastrophically fail to address the position's most urgent tactical demand.
analysis.move_pattern: Non-forcing moves (retreats to back rank, prophylactic pawn pushes, passive repositioning) with no check or capture, typically moving a piece away from a critical defensive duty
analysis.why_bad: Each move either removes a defender from a critical square, leaves a piece with no protection, or wastes a crucial tempo in a position requiring immediate concrete action—allowing the opponent to win material through a simple capture or short tactical sequence
sub_patterns: Piece retreat that abandons defense of another piece (Ng3, Bf8, Qd2, Bd7)
Slow pawn move ignoring an undefended piece (b6, h6)
Wrong recapture or passive developing move leaving material hanging (Rxd2, Re1, Nd1)

analysis.label: Playing slow consolidating or repositioning moves when immediate captures or forcing tactical shots are available.
analysis.description: In 5/6 positions (excluding the 0cp-loss example), the player chose a quiet, non-forcing move—often a king walk (Ka6, Kb5) or passive piece repositioning (R4f2, c6)—when concrete tactical action was demanded. In Position 10, Kb5 ignored a completely hanging rook capturable by three different pieces (Nxc6/Bxc6/bxc6). In Position 11, c6 was a structural pawn push that missed Rxg2 winning a pawn with ongoing threats. In Position 9, Ka6 wandered the king away from the center when Re2 attacked an active enemy piece. In Position 6, R4f2 chose passive defense over Qd4's active counterplay with queen exchange. In Position 2, Rb3+ checked with the wrong rook, allowing the opponent's king to step forward with tempo. The common thread is prioritizing vague positional goals (king safety, consolidation, structure) over urgent concrete action, gifting the opponent a free tempo to stabilize or launch counter-threats.
analysis.move_pattern: Non-capturing quiet moves (king walks to a6/b5/b3, passive rook retreats to f2, structural pawn pushes to c6) when captures or stronger forcing moves exist
analysis.why_bad: These moves waste a critical tempo on consolidation or repositioning, allowing the opponent to save hanging pieces, secure weaknesses (e.g., g3 stabilizing g2), or generate counterplay (e.g., Nc3+ forks, Kc4 advancing with tempo) that would not have been possible had the player taken immediate concrete action.
sub_patterns: King walks ignoring hanging material (Ka6, Kb5)
Passive rook defense instead of active queen counterplay (R4f2)
Structural pawn moves missing tactical captures (c6 instead of Rxg2)
Checking with wrong piece allowing opponent king to activate with tempo (Rb3+ vs Ra3+)

analysis.label: King moves backward or toward the edge/corner in pawn endgames instead of advancing actively toward the critical action.
analysis.description: All 13/13 positions are pure pawn endgames where the played move is a king retreat — moving toward the back rank, corner, or away from the center. In every case, the best move required the king to advance toward enemy pawns (to attack or blockade them), toward the center (for maximum mobility), or forward along a race path. The retreats lose critical tempi: in Position 1, Kf1 retreats when Kf3 advances toward queenside counterplay; in Position 3, Kc2 retreats into a check diagonal when Kc4 attacks a pawn; in Position 4, Kd2 retreats from kingside counterplay when Ke4 heads toward f5; in Positions 5-6, king retreats to the first rank allow passed pawns to promote by force; in Position 7, Kf7 retreats from an attackable pawn when Kf5 captures it; in Positions 2, 11, 13, and 14, kings retreat toward corners/edges and allow forced mates or drastically shortened resistance. The average cp_loss of 3710 reflects the catastrophic consequences of passive king play in simplified positions where every tempo decides the race.
analysis.move_pattern: King moves backward (toward own back rank, toward corner/edge, or away from center) in pawn-only endgames
