analysis.why_bad: In pawn endgames, the king is the only piece and must be maximally active — retreating loses irreplaceable tempi in king races, allows passed pawns to advance unopposed, surrenders opposition/key squares, and often places the king on squares vulnerable to checks or where it cannot reach blockading positions in time.
sub_patterns: King retreats to back rank instead of advancing to contest passed pawns
King retreats toward corner allowing forced mating nets
King moves away from attackable enemy pawns instead of approaching them
King retreats onto checking diagonal of advancing passed pawn
King moves sideways/backward losing opposition in king race

analysis.label: Plausible-looking improving or developing moves in narrow positions that ignore the single most critical tactical requirement, creating or exposing a decisive vulnerability.
analysis.description: This feature activates on positions where very few moves are acceptable (avg 1.5 good moves) and the player chooses a natural-looking alternative that either disrupts their own piece coordination or ignores an immediate tactical threat. In 8/10 cases, the move addresses a secondary concern (development, repositioning, pawn advancement, material grab) while missing the one urgent tactical requirement. Common sub-themes include self-interference where a piece blocks its own ally's defense (Ne2 blocking queen's diagonal defense of f3 in Position 1, Ne8 removing a critical diagonal blocker in Position 11), moves that expose the player's own king to checks or discovered attacks (Bg3 allowing capture with check in Position 2, Be2 allowing Bxg3+ in Position 9, Qe7 creating a pin on the e-file in Position 7, Qxc2 allowing Qa3+ in Position 10), and tempo-wasting piece moves when one specific action was demanded (Bb5 when Kd3 was required in Position 4, a3 when the bishop needed saving in Position 3). All positions share the hallmark of having one clear punishment available to the opponent.
analysis.move_pattern: Various piece types making lateral/retreating repositioning moves, pawn advances, or captures that look like improvements but disrupt defensive coordination or ignore alignment threats
analysis.why_bad: The moves actively create or expose tactical vulnerabilities (self-pins, unblocked diagonals, hanging pieces, check opportunities) in positions that demand the one specific move addressing the most urgent threat rather than any secondary plan
sub_patterns: Self-blocking moves that cut off defensive communication between own pieces
Piece repositioning that removes a critical defender from a key diagonal or square
Routine development moves ignoring king-safety emergencies (checks with tempo)
Greedy captures or pawn advances that ignore opponent's forcing replies
Tempo-wasting bishop/piece moves when king activation or immediate tactics are required

analysis.label: Moves that leave a corner rook (usually a8) undefended on the long diagonal, allowing capture by a bishop or queen.
analysis.description: In 9/9 positions, the played move creates or fails to address a tactical vulnerability where a rook sitting on a corner square (a8 in 7/9 cases, a1 in 2/9 cases) becomes capturable along the long diagonal (a8-h1 or a1-h8) by an opposing bishop or queen. The mechanisms vary: pawn moves opening the diagonal (g3, b6 - 2/9), piece retreats removing protection of the rook (Bb1, Rf3, Qe7 - 3/9), failure to block the diagonal when it was the critical defensive necessity (Nf6, Nh5 - 2/9), choosing the wrong rook to move leaving the other exposed (Rfd8 - 1/9), or removing piece coordination that made capturing the rook tactically unfavorable (Bf7 - 1/9). In every case, the refutation involves a simple capture of the undefended rook along the long diagonal, typically by a fianchettoed bishop (Bxa8/Bxa1) or a queen (Qxa8/Qxa1). The tactical motif is consistently 'hanging piece' with the long diagonal as the geometric axis of exploitation.
analysis.move_pattern: Any piece type moving in any direction; the unifying geometry is that the move leaves a rook undefended on a1 or a8, exposed to capture along the a1-h8 or a8-h1 diagonal
analysis.why_bad: The move removes a pawn blocker, piece defender, or diagonal interposer that was the sole protection keeping a corner rook safe from an enemy bishop or queen operating on the long diagonal
sub_patterns: Pawn moves that open the long diagonal (removing b7/g2 pawn blocker)
Piece retreats that abandon defense of the corner rook (bishop/rook/queen moves away)
Knight moves that fail to block or vacate the only piece that could block the diagonal
Moving the wrong rook to an active square while leaving the other exposed on the diagonal
Removing piece coordination that made the diagonal capture tactically unsound

analysis.chip: King Move Instead of Pawn Push
analysis.label: In pawn endgames with a far-advanced passed pawn, playing a king move when the only winning/correct move was to immediately push the pawn (typically to the 7th rank).
analysis.description: This feature fires on pawn endgame positions where the player has a passed pawn on or near the 6th rank ready for a critical advance, but instead plays a king move that allows the opponent to blockade, capture, or achieve stalemate. In 11/12 positions, the correct move was an immediate pawn push (to the 7th rank: b2, c7, e7, f2, g7, or c6), while the player chose a king move instead. The positions share a common structure: a far-advanced passed pawn requiring one precise timing-dependent push, an opponent's king directly blocking or about to blockade, and a window of exactly one move where the pawn advance works. The king moves played (Kd3, Ka4, Kg6, Kc5, Kf5, Kf4, Kb4, Kc5, Kc5, Ke6, Ke5, Ke6) all represent the same conceptual error—temporizing with the king when the pawn demanded immediate attention. Average cp_loss of 5117 reflects that many of these convert forced mates into draws.
analysis.move_pattern: King move (any direction) in a pawn endgame when a passed pawn on the 5th-6th rank should have been pushed to the 7th rank instead
analysis.why_bad: The king move wastes the critical tempo needed to advance the passed pawn before the opponent's king can establish a blockade, reach a drawing square, or trigger a stalemate mechanism. Once the opponent occupies the square directly in front of the pawn, the win evaporates into a theoretical draw.
sub_patterns: King retreats when pawn push to 7th rank forces enemy king aside (c7/e7/g7 positions)
King moves laterally instead of pushing b-pawn to b2 to imprison opponent's king
King abandons escort duty of advanced pawn, allowing blockade or capture

analysis.label: Endgame positions where the critical decision revolves around pawn promotion, and the typical error is underpromoting or mismanaging passed pawns.
analysis.description: This feature fires on endgame positions where pawn promotion is the decisive factor. The strongest activations involve catastrophic underpromotions: promoting to a knight when queen wins instantly (2/10), promoting to a bishop when queen or rook mates faster (1/10), and promoting to a rook when queen is superior (1/10). The remaining mistake positions involve mishandling pawn advancement that relates to promotion potential: capturing with the wrong unit to fail creating a passed pawn (1/10), pushing a pawn that removes tactical protection from a piece (1/10), and a premature pawn break that permanently freezes the structure preventing any future passed pawn (1/10). The non-mistake activations (3/10, cp_loss 0-1) occur in queen-vs-pawns endgames where the critical theme is preventing Black's g2 pawn from promoting, confirming the feature's focus on promotion-critical decisions rather than exclusively on errors.
analysis.move_pattern: Pawn promotion to suboptimal piece (knight/bishop/rook instead of queen), or pawn/king moves that destroy passed pawn creation potential in endgames with advanced pawns
analysis.why_bad: Underpromotions create insufficient mating material (K+N vs K is drawn), drastically slower checkmates (K+R vs K instead of K+Q vs K), or useless pieces that cannot generate threats. Non-promotion errors destroy the winning asset (passed pawn potential) through premature exchanges, wrong capture methods, or move-order mistakes that remove tactical protection.
sub_patterns: Underpromotion to knight creating drawn insufficient material
Underpromotion to rook/bishop when queen delivers faster mate
Wrong capture method failing to create passed pawn
Pawn push that removes indirect protection of a piece
Premature pawn break that freezes structure and eliminates breakthrough potential

analysis.label: Strategically motivated forward moves (pawn breaks, king advances, piece sorties) that ignore an immediate concrete tactical vulnerability in the position.
analysis.description: This feature activates on positions where the player makes a move that appears positionally principled—centralizing the king, pushing a pawn break, developing a piece to an active square—but fatally ignores an urgent tactical demand. In 7/13 cases the move is a pawn advance (d5×2, d4, d3×2, a3, f6), in 5/13 it's a king move to a vulnerable square (Kf4, Kd4, Ke6, Kd7, Kg7), and in 1/13 it's a piece sortie (Bb4). The common thread is that each move addresses a secondary strategic goal while leaving the position's primary tactical problem unresolved: an exposed king (positions 1, 7, 8, 12, 13), an undefended pawn (positions 3, 5), a premature break creating recapture problems (positions 4, 10, 11, 15), or a king walking into a fork/check (positions 2, 12, 13). The positions are overwhelmingly early-game (8/13 opening phase) and played by Black (10/13), with an average of only 2.4 good alternatives available, indicating narrow decision points where concrete calculation trumps general principles.
analysis.move_pattern: Forward-moving pawn advances (especially d-pawn) and king steps toward center/opponent, typically one-square advances that look natural but leave a critical defensive duty unfulfilled
analysis.why_bad: Each move wastes the tempo needed to address the position's most urgent tactical threat—whether that's preventing a check/fork (Qh5+, Nf5+, Rxb4+), blocking an attacking piece (Ng4 hitting f2), or maintaining a defensive pawn recapture (axb3). The opponent exploits the tempo with an immediate forcing sequence that wins material or destroys coordination.
sub_patterns: Premature d-pawn central break before completing development (d5, d4)
King stepping onto tactically vulnerable square (Nf5+ fork, Rxb4+ check)
Slow positional pawn move ignoring piece attack on f2 (d3 × 2)
Pawn advance removing critical defensive resource (a3 removing axb3 recapture, f6 blocking Nf6)

analysis.label: Playing a slow piece relocation (usually king or queen) in a critical position demanding one specific immediate tactical or prophylactic action.
analysis.description: This feature fires on positions where there is essentially only one good move available (avg 1.3 good moves) and the player instead plays a quiet repositioning move—typically a king walk or queen retreat—that addresses a secondary concern while ignoring the position's immediate tactical demand. In 5/10 cases the move is a king relocation (Kb3, Kh2, Kg3, Kf6, Ke3), and in 3/10 it is a queen retreat or repositioning (Qd1, Qd1, Qg3). The critical commonality is that each move looks 'reasonable' (improving king safety, centralizing, launching an attack) but squanders a tempo in a position where the opponent has one specific forcing threat or where one specific concrete action was required. In 3/10 cases (Kh2, Kg3, Ke3) the king walks directly onto a vulnerable diagonal allowing a devastating bishop check. In 3/10 cases (Kb3, Qd1, Kf6) the move releases pressure on a hanging or threatened enemy piece, granting a free tempo. The average cp_loss of 369 reflects that these are catastrophic errors in narrow positions with no margin for non-forcing play.
analysis.move_pattern: Non-forcing piece relocation (predominantly king moves or queen retreats) to squares that appear safe or useful but are tactically vulnerable, typically one square in a new direction
analysis.why_bad: The position demands exactly one concrete action (capturing a hanging piece, blocking a critical diagonal, maintaining pressure on a threatened piece, or finding the one safe square), and the quiet repositioning move wastes the critical tempo, allowing the opponent to execute a decisive tactical blow—usually a diagonal check, material capture, or forcing sequence that wasn't possible one move earlier.
sub_patterns: King walks onto vulnerable diagonal allowing check (Kh2→Qf4+, Kg3→Bd6+, Ke3→Bc5+)
Queen/piece retreats missing an immediately winning tactic (Qd1 missing Qd5 winning rook)
Moving piece away from defensive/offensive duty leaving another piece hanging (Nb4 unguarding bishop, Kf6 releasing pressure on rook)
Premature aggression when a defensive consolidation is the only good move (Qg3, g5)

analysis.label: Playing a non-forcing move when the only good continuation was an immediate queen trade or queen capture.
analysis.description: In all 5/5 positions, the single best move (or only good move) was a queen exchange or queen capture: Qxc5 (pos 1), Qxe4 (pos 2), Nxb6 capturing queen (pos 5), Qxe4 (pos 11), and Qxc4 (pos 14). Instead, the player made a different move—typically a king move (3/5: Kg8, Ka1, Kxb2) or a piece development/capture (2/5: Rxd6, Bh6)—that ignored the critical queen tension. With an average of only 1.4 good moves available, these were narrow positions where the queen exchange was the singular resource to defuse tactical threats. The played moves left queens undefended (2/5: Kg8 left Qf5 hanging, Bh6 left Qg4 hanging), exposed the king to discovered attacks (Kxb2), wasted critical tempo (Ka1), or got move order wrong by not resolving queens first (Rxd6).
analysis.move_pattern: Non-queen piece move (often king retreat/capture or quiet piece development) when mutual queen tension demands immediate queen-level resolution
analysis.why_bad: The position contained critical queen tension (opposing queens threatening each other, undefended queens, or forced exchange sequences) that required immediate resolution. By playing a different move, the player either left their own queen hanging, allowed the opponent to force a structurally damaging queen trade, or missed the only tactical resource that kept the position manageable.
sub_patterns: King moves ignoring hanging queen (Kg8, Ka1, Kxb2)
Piece moves leaving own queen undefended (Bh6)
Wrong move order—capturing material before trading queens (Rxd6)

analysis.label: Moving a piece away from its essential blocking or shielding duty on an open file, rank, or diagonal, exposing a tactical vulnerability behind it.
analysis.description: In 3/5 positions (positions 1, 2, and 4), the moved piece was serving as a critical blocker or shield on an open line between an enemy attacker and a friendly target. In position 1, Qe7 removed the queen from d7 where it could interpose after Bxc6+ Qxc6+, leaving the a8 rook exposed. In position 2, Nd5 removed the knight from e7 where it blocked White's queen from capturing Black's queen on e8 along the open e-file. In position 4, Rh1 removed the rook from g1 where it guarded the g-file, allowing Rxh3+/Rg3+/Rxh1+ to win material. Position 3 (Nb1) is a related variant where the piece moves INTO the attack line of an enemy rook on a1. Position 5 (Qc8+, 0cp loss) represents the offensive exploitation of the same open-line principle — using the queen to check along an open file. The common thread is that pieces are moved without recognizing their essential function as shields along open lines.
analysis.move_pattern: Piece (queen, knight, or rook) moves along or away from an open file/rank, either vacating a blocking square between attacker and target, or landing on a square attacked along that open line
analysis.why_bad: The moved piece was performing a critical but non-obvious defensive function — blocking an enemy piece's access along an open line to a vulnerable target (undefended queen, rook, or king). Removing it allows the opponent to exploit the now-open line with captures, checks, or attack sequences.
sub_patterns: Knight/Queen vacates blocking square on open e-file
Rook abandons defensive post on adjacent file allowing check sequences
Piece placed directly on square attacked along open rank/file

analysis.label: Moves that voluntarily surrender a critical positional function (defensive piece, pawn barrier, king safety, or geometric advantage) to pursue a plausible but incorrect secondary plan.
analysis.description: This feature fires on positions where the player abandons a critical positional asset in favor of a natural-looking but strategically wrong alternative. In 3/8 cases, a piece retreats from a vital defensive post (Ne8 and Nd7 both remove knights from f6 where they guarded kingside dark squares; Qe1 retreats from an active h4 post). In 2/8 cases, the player captures non-urgent material while ignoring a more pressing need (Rxa4 grabs a queenside pawn while kingside pawns advance unchecked; exd4 captures with the wrong pawn, removing a barrier to the opponent's f4 break). In 2/8 cases, the move directly exposes the player's own king to tactical exploitation (Kg6 walks into a skewer via Ra6+; g4 weakens the pawn shield). In 1/8 cases, a check drives the opponent's king in the wrong direction, forfeiting a winning geometric fork (Qf5+ instead of Qc6+). The unifying thread is that all positions had a narrow critical requirement (avg 1.9 good moves) and the player chose a superficially reasonable move that surrendered the one thing keeping their position viable.
analysis.move_pattern: Piece retreats to passive squares, captures on non-critical wings, pawn pushes weakening own structure, or checks in wrong direction — all removing a piece/pawn from where it performed a vital function
analysis.why_bad: Each move voluntarily eliminates a critical positional resource (defender, pawn barrier, king safety, or geometric advantage), allowing the opponent to immediately execute a specific threat that was previously prevented — resulting in tactical exploitation (forks, skewers, pawn breakthroughs, or attacking combinations)
sub_patterns: Knight retreat from f6 removing kingside dark-square defense (Ne8, Nd7)
Queen/piece retreat from active post wasting critical tempo (Qe1)
Wrong capture direction removing key pawn barrier (exd4)
Pawn/king move exposing own king to tactical shots (g4, Kg6)
Capturing non-urgent material while ignoring critical timing (Rxa4)
Check in wrong direction losing winning geometric motif (Qf5+)

analysis.label: Playing a positional non-capture (pawn push or piece relocation) when a concrete capture was clearly the strongest move available.
analysis.description: In 5/7 positions, the best move was a concrete capture (cxd4, cxd4, Nxa2, dxe5, Qxh4) but the player chose a 'strategic' non-capturing alternative instead. The played moves—c4, Bg4, Nd3, d5, f5—are all positional-looking moves motivated by general principles (gaining space, developing pieces, centralizing knights, challenging the center). In position 2, c4 pushed for queenside space instead of capturing cxd4. In position 4, Bg4 developed a piece instead of capturing cxd4. In position 8, Nd3 centralized the knight instead of capturing Nxa2 (winning the exchange via a fork). In position 12, d5 challenged the center instead of simply capturing the hanging e5 pawn with dxe5. In position 13, f5 attacked the queen instead of capturing the undefended knight with Qxh4. The remaining positions (b3, Kh1) similarly chose quiet moves over the most forcing continuation. The pattern reveals a systematic preference for 'looks good' positional play over calculating concrete material-winning tactics.
analysis.move_pattern: Non-capturing moves (pawn advances to c4/d5/f5/b3, piece relocations Bg4/Nd3/Kh1) when a pawn capture or piece capture was available on adjacent squares or nearby
analysis.why_bad: These moves release tactical tension or ignore free/cheaply available material, allowing the opponent to stabilize or counterattack; concrete captures would have won material, opened decisive lines, or simplified into winning positions.
sub_patterns: Pawn push instead of pawn capture on adjacent file (c4 vs cxd4, d5 vs dxe5)
Knight centralization instead of knight capture winning material (Nd3 vs Nxa2)
Piece development/pawn push instead of capturing hanging piece (f5/Bg4 vs Qxh4/cxd4)
Weakening pawn push instead of prophylactic pawn move (b3 vs c3)

analysis.label: Moves that pursue non-urgent objectives (material, pawn advances, repositioning) while a critical king safety crisis demands immediate attention.
analysis.description: This feature fires on positions where an acute king safety issue exists—either the player's own king is under immediate tactical threat or the opponent's king is ripe for a decisive attack—but the player makes a move addressing something else entirely. In 8/11 positions, the primary tactical motif is king_safety or back_rank vulnerability. The pattern manifests in several ways: peripheral pawn captures while the center demands attention (bxa5 ignoring knight vulnerability, c5 ignoring back rank), weakening own king shelter (h5 creating a mating pattern, c4 exposing d3 to checks, Ke3 walking into pawn forks), abandoning defensive posts (Qa4 leaving kingside unguarded against Rxh7+ mate), missing king-targeting tactics in favor of material (Rb4 missing Re3-Re5# mate in 2, Qxd8+ missing Bf7+ deflection), and wasting tempo when king activity is critical (Bf8 instead of Ke5). The average cp_loss of 2821 is extremely high, with three positions involving missed forced mates (9570, 9979, 9998 cp loss), indicating the feature captures moments where king safety is not merely important but existentially urgent.
analysis.move_pattern: Diverse piece types and directions; the common geometric feature is that the move is directed AWAY from the critical king-safety sector (often toward queenside/periphery when kingside/center has the crisis)
analysis.why_bad: The position contains an immediate king safety crisis (exposed king, mating threat, back rank weakness, tactical vulnerability) that requires urgent defensive or offensive action, but the played move ignores this crisis to pursue a secondary objective, giving the opponent time to execute or escape the decisive king-targeting tactic.
sub_patterns: Peripheral pawn captures/advances while king is exposed (bxa5, c5, c4)
Weakening own king shelter allowing forced mates (h5, Ke3)
Queen abandoning defensive duties near threatened king (Qa4)
Missing immediate checkmate patterns for material (Rb4 missing Re5#)
Premature simplification missing king-targeting combination (Qxd8+ missing Bf7+)
Tempo-wasting piece moves when king advance is critical (Bf8 instead of Ke5)

analysis.label: Plausible-looking moves that ignore the single most pressing tactical or strategic demand in positions requiring precise responses.
analysis.description: This feature fires on positions where very few good moves exist (avg 1.5) and the player makes a 'natural' or 'active-looking' move that completely bypasses the one critical concrete obligation. In 10/12 positions, only 1-2 good moves were available, indicating extreme precision was required. The played moves often appear purposeful—giving checks (Ng5+ x2, Nf5+), counterattacking (Qg4, Rg1), prophylactic defense (Kc2, a6, c6), or pursuing activity (Ra5, Rc8, f5, Bg6)—but each ignores the specific urgent demand: winning material via a fork instead of a flashy check (positions 1, 5), defending a hanging piece (positions 4, 11), maintaining a latent threat rather than executing it prematurely (position 2), preserving piece coordination (positions 3, 9, 10), or protecting a critical square/piece (positions 6, 7, 8, 12). The correct moves in every case address the ONE most pressing concrete need rather than pursuing secondary goals.
analysis.move_pattern: No single geometric pattern; varied piece types and directions (knight checks, rook repositions, pawn pushes, king/queen/bishop moves) that all share the property of pursuing a secondary agenda
analysis.why_bad: These moves fail because they address a secondary concern while the position has exactly one critical obligation—a hanging piece to defend, a specific escape square to cover, a threat to maintain rather than execute, or a capture to make—and ignoring it allows the opponent a concrete refutation that was not available against the correct move.
sub_patterns: Flashy checks that miss material-winning alternatives (Ng5+, Nf5+ instead of fork/covering escape)
Active-looking moves that leave own pieces undefended (Rg1, Kc2, Qg4, a6)
Premature execution of threats better left latent (Ng5+ position 2)
Piece repositioning that destroys coordination in critical positions (Ra5, Rc8, Bg6)
Pawn moves that ignore the urgent concrete demand (f5, c6, a6)

analysis.label: Non-capturing piece moves to aggressive-looking squares that ignore more urgent concrete needs (captures, development, or king safety).
analysis.description: This feature fires when a player places a piece (typically queen or bishop) on an ambitious attacking square while ignoring what the position concretely demands. In 4/8 positions, the player chose speculative attacks (targeting f7 or threatening mate) over completing development or castling their exposed king (Positions 1, 4, 5, 7). In 2/8 positions, the player missed free piece captures in favor of repositioning the queen to a 'threatening' square (Positions 8, 13 - both Qd3 missing hanging knights). In 2/8 positions, a bishop was placed on a tactically vulnerable central square (d6) where it immediately became a target of pawn forks or open-file tactics (Positions 2, 9). The unifying thread is prioritizing aspirational piece placement - making a move that 'looks good' positionally or creates a speculative threat - over addressing the position's immediate tactical reality. The avg cp_loss of 369 reflects how severely this mismatch between ambition and calculation is punished.
analysis.move_pattern: Non-capturing piece move (usually Queen or Bishop, occasionally Knight) forward to a central or attacking square (c4, d3, d6, e4, c6, g5) that creates speculative pressure
analysis.why_bad: The piece's new square either becomes immediately vulnerable to tempo-gaining attacks, or the move wastes time on speculative threats that are easily parried while ignoring concrete opportunities (hanging pieces, urgent development, or castling an exposed king)
sub_patterns: Queen placed on attacking diagonal for speculative mate threat while opponent has hanging piece (Qd3 x2)
Piece moved aggressively toward f7 before completing development with king in center (Bc4, Ng5)
Queen centralized to exposed square where it gets attacked with tempo (Qe4, Qc6)
Bishop placed on open file or pawn-fork-vulnerable square (Bd6 x2)

analysis.label: King (or queen) moves onto an open file or diagonal where the opponent immediately exploits the alignment with checks, pins, or captures.
analysis.description: In 7/8 positions, the blundering move is a king move (including castling) that places the king on or adjacent to an open line controlled by the opponent's pieces, creating an immediate tactical vulnerability. The exploitation takes several forms: the king walks onto an open file allowing rook/queen checks (positions 3, 4, 8 with Re2+, Qe2+, Rd1+), the king steps onto a diagonal allowing a bishop fork or discovery (position 1 with Bc4+), castling leaves a piece undefended on a file where the opponent has a battery (positions 2, 6 with Qxe4/Rxe4 and Qxe7), the queen moves onto a diagonal creating a pin alignment (position 5 with Bb5 pinning Nc6 to Qd7), and the king moves to the wrong wing abandoning pieces to invasion (position 7 with Qc2 winning material). All moves share the common thread of being motivated by positional reasoning (centralization, safety, development) while overlooking a concrete one-move tactical shot that exploits the new placement on an open geometric line.
analysis.move_pattern: King move (or castling/queen move) to a square sitting on an open file or diagonal controlled by opponent's long-range pieces
analysis.why_bad: The moved piece lands on an open line where the opponent can immediately deliver a check, pin, or capture that wins material—the player prioritizes general positional goals (king safety, centralization) over the concrete tactical threat created by the new alignment on the open line.
sub_patterns: King walks onto open file, punished by rook/queen check winning material
King walks onto open diagonal, punished by bishop check/fork
Castling leaves a piece undefended on an open file against enemy battery
Queen moves creating pin alignment with another piece on a diagonal
King moves to wrong wing, abandoning defense of trapped/hanging pieces

analysis.label: Playing a purposeful-looking move that ignores a critical tactical vulnerability the opponent can immediately exploit.
analysis.description: This feature fires on moves where the player pursues an active plan (pawn development, material capture, piece centralization, king activation) while overlooking a more urgent tactical priority. In 5/5 positions, the move creates or fails to address a critical vulnerability: Position 3 ignores a knight fork on f7 to play d6; Position 4 removes the key f6 knight defender to grab a g4 pawn; Position 11 places the rook on f7 blocking its own knight's retreat, allowing it to be trapped; Position 12 walks the king to c6 where Rc4+ forces a losing rook exchange; Position 15 advances the king to g4 where it's harassed by Rg2+ instead of advancing the winning e-pawn. In 4/5 cases, the opponent's refutation involves a check or forced capture exploiting the newly created vulnerability. In 5/5 cases, the correct move addressed the critical tactical demand first (capturing the fork, retreating the bishop, keeping f7 clear, avoiding the c-file, pushing e4).
analysis.move_pattern: Various piece types (pawn, knight, rook, king) moving to active-looking squares that either ignore an existing threat or create a new geometric vulnerability (check line, fork square, blocked retreat path)
analysis.why_bad: Each move prioritizes the player's own agenda (development, material gain, centralization) over the position's most critical tactical demand, allowing the opponent to exploit a check, fork, piece trap, or forced exchange
sub_patterns: Ignoring an existing fork/threat to play a quiet developing move
Removing a key defensive piece to grab material
Self-blocking a piece's escape route with another piece
Walking the king onto a file/rank where it faces a decisive check or forced exchange

analysis.label: Endgame moves that prioritize apparent activity over pawn defense, leaving material unprotected for immediate capture.
analysis.description: In 8/9 positions (all endgames), the player makes a move that appears active or purposeful—repositioning a piece, advancing a pawn, or seeking piece activity—but critically abandons the defense of one or more pawns that the opponent immediately captures. In Position 4 (Ke7), g6 becomes undefended and Rxg6 wins it. In Position 5 (Ra3), c5 is left unprotected and Rxc5 takes it. In Position 6 (f4), both c4 and the new f4 pawn become hanging targets collected by the opponent's rook. In Position 7 (Rd7), the rook leaves the back rank allowing Kxb3 then Kxa4 harvesting two pawns. In Position 1 (Bg5), the bishop abandons coverage allowing Rc7+ winning a7. In Position 2 (Bc7), the bishop abandons blockade of d7 allowing immediate promotion. In Position 3 (d5), the pawn itself becomes an unsupported target captured by the approaching king. In Position 9 (f3), the pawn becomes a direct target capturable by Rxf3. The correct alternatives (7/9 cases involving king activation or maintaining defensive posts) all share the common thread of first securing material before seeking activity.
analysis.move_pattern: Mixed piece types and directions; common thread is moving a piece/pawn AWAY from defending own pawns, or advancing a pawn to an undefended square
analysis.why_bad: The move exposes or creates undefended pawns that the opponent can immediately capture, converting positional/material advantage into concrete material loss. In endgames where pawns are the primary winning resource, losing even one pawn is often decisive.
sub_patterns: Piece abandons pawn defense (Bg5, Bc7, Ke7, Rd7)
Pawn advance creates new undefended target (d5, f4, f3)
Premature pawn exchange allows blockade/equalization (a5)
Rook repositions without creating adequate counter-threat (Ra3)

analysis.label: Pieces retreat to passive back-rank squares in endgames when active, centralized placement is required to handle passed pawns or king activity.
analysis.description: This feature fires on endgame positions where the player moves a piece backward to a passive square (typically their own back rank) when the position demands forward activity. In 5/8 positions, the move literally places a piece on rank 1 or 8 (Ke1, Kd1, Rg1, Qb8, Kd8), abandoning critical areas. The remaining positions share the theme of tempo loss through aimless repositioning (Nf3 retreats instead of advancing pawns, Rd8+ is an aimless check, Kc6 walks into a fork requiring retreat). The correct moves consistently involve maintaining active/centralized placement: king advancing toward passed pawns (6/8), rook staying on aggressive ranks (2/8), or queen centralizing (1/8). The tactical motif 'tempo_loss' appears in 6/8 analyses, and 'piece_activity' tags appear in all 8 positions. The average cp_loss of 1302 reflects that endgame passivity is catastrophic when passed pawns or king races are the decisive factor.
analysis.move_pattern: Any piece moving backward toward own back rank (rank 1 for White, rank 8 for Black) or retreating to passive squares away from the critical theater
analysis.why_bad: In endgames, tempo is critical - retreating pieces to passive squares wastes moves needed to stop/advance passed pawns, maintain king centralization, or keep rooks on aggressive ranks, allowing the opponent to advance their winning plan uncontested
sub_patterns: King retreating to back rank instead of staying centralized
Rook abandoning active rank for passive first-rank position
Queen/piece moving to back rank instead of centralizing
Aimless checks that drive opponent's king to better squares

analysis.label: Quiet, non-threatening developing or repositioning moves that waste a critical tempo in positions where the opponent has an immediate forcing continuation available.
analysis.description: This feature activates on moves that look natural or routine but fatally ignore the dynamic urgency of the position. In 10/13 positions the phase is the opening, where tempo is paramount. The most common pattern involves placing a bishop on a passive square (Be7 ×3, Bd6, Bd7, Be2) or making a slow preparatory/retreating move (b6, Qd8, Nge7, Nge2, Kh1, Re8) when the opponent has a concrete forcing reply ready. In 6/13 cases, the opponent punishes with an immediate pawn advance gaining tempo (d6 hitting Be7 in positions 1-3, c5 hitting Bd6 in position 6, d5 pushing with tempo in positions 4-5). In 4/13 cases the opponent exploits a tactical vulnerability the move created or left unaddressed (fork via Nb4/Nxc2+ in position 11, Qd5 fork in position 10, Ne4 fork in position 8, diagonal attack in position 12). The best moves in these positions were consistently active—Bb4 creating pins/pressure was optimal in 6/13 positions—demonstrating that the positions demanded concrete, forcing play rather than generic development.
analysis.move_pattern: Piece (usually bishop) developing to a quiet, non-attacking square; or piece retreating/repositioning passively without creating threats. No checks, no captures, no forcing element.
analysis.why_bad: The move wastes a tempo in a position where the opponent has an immediate forcing continuation (pawn advance with tempo, fork, or tactical strike) that exploits the passivity. The played move neither creates counter-threats nor defends against the opponent's concrete plan, giving them a free move to execute their tactical or dynamic idea.
sub_patterns: Bishop developing to a square immediately hit by opponent's pawn advance (Be7 hit by d6, Bd6 hit by c5)
Slow preparatory move ignoring opponent's central pawn breakthrough (b6/Qd8 allowing d5-d6)
Piece placement that blocks own coordination or creates tactical vulnerability (Nge2 blocking king escape, Nge7 blocking bishop, Kh1 entering diagonal)
Non-urgent rook/piece repositioning when tactical intervention was required (Re8, Bc4 abandoning key square control)

analysis.label: Pieces or pawns moving from the d-file to f-file squares (f3/f5/f6) in positions where the original central post served a critical defensive function.
analysis.description: In all 4 positions, the move involves relocating a piece or pawn from the d-file to the f-file: Nd7-f6 (Position 2), f2-f3 (Position 5), Qd7-f5 (Position 7), and Nd4-f3 (Position 9). In 3/4 cases, these moves appear aggressive or structurally sound—attacking an enemy piece, reinforcing a pawn, activating the queen—but they abandon critical defensive duties at the original square. In Position 2 (212cp loss), the knight left d7 which was blocking a diagonal and controlling e5. In Position 5 (224cp loss), f3 unblocked the a6-f1 diagonal exposing the rook. In Position 7 (249cp loss), the queen left d7 allowing White's knight to activate with tempo via Ne3. Position 9 (0cp loss) was a legitimate endgame move where the defensive considerations were minimal, suggesting this feature fires on the geometric pattern itself and the mistakes occur when the context demands staying on the d-file.
analysis.move_pattern: Piece or pawn moving from d-file (d7, d4, f2) to f-file squares (f3, f5, f6), typically a knight or queen shifting laterally toward the kingside
analysis.why_bad: The original d-file position served a crucial blocking, guarding, or covering function (blocking a diagonal, defending a piece, controlling a key square), and abandoning it for an aggressive-looking f-file square creates immediate tactical vulnerabilities that the opponent exploits with tempo-gaining moves or discovered attacks.
sub_patterns: Knight from d7 to f6 abandoning diagonal blockade
Pawn f2-f3 exposing back-rank piece on f1
Queen from d-file to f5 allowing knight activation with tempo
Knight from d4 to f3 in endgame (benign variant)

analysis.label: Moving a piece to a passive or peripheral square when the position demands active, coordinating play, surrendering dynamic advantage for an illusory benefit.
analysis.description: This feature fires on moves that displace pieces to inferior squares—often the rim, corner, or a non-functional file—when active alternatives maintaining coordination and initiative were available. In 5/7 positions, the moved piece lands on an edge/corner square (Kh1, Nh2, Nxa2+, a5, Rb8) where it becomes passive or stranded. In 6/7 cases, the move breaks a critical piece coordination or defensive function (Nh2 abandons f3 control, Rb8 breaks rook-bishop coordination, Re4 misses the c-file, Kh1 enters a check corridor). In all 7 positions, the player chose a superficially logical goal—apparent king safety (Kh1, Nh2), material gain (Nxa2+, Qxg6, a5 attacking the rook), or 'textbook' placement (Rb8 behind passer, Re4 centralizing)—over dynamic requirements. The average cp_loss of 321 with 2.3 good alternatives shows these are avoidable errors where active play was clearly available but rejected in favor of passive/materialistic thinking.
analysis.move_pattern: Various pieces (K, N, R, Q, P) moving to passive, peripheral, or tactically vulnerable squares—frequently rim/corner squares (h1, h2, a2, a5, b8)—away from central activity or key defensive posts
analysis.why_bad: The moved piece abandons its active function (defending key squares, maintaining coordination, generating counterplay) for a perceived benefit that proves illusory, leaving it passive/stranded while the opponent exploits the resulting gap in defensive coverage or coordination
sub_patterns: Knight retreating to rim square (h2, a2) losing central influence
King retreating to corner creating check corridors instead of addressing threats
Rook placed on wrong file/rank missing critical counterplay axis
Pawn advance self-blocking a key square needed by own pieces
Queen capturing peripheral material while landing on tactically exploitable square

analysis.label: Moving a piece away from a square where it performs a vital defensive or coordinating function, creating an immediately exploitable weakness.
analysis.description: This feature fires on moves that relocate a piece from a critical square—typically one providing defense, coordination, or central control—to a peripheral, passive, or tactically vulnerable square. In 4/7 positions, the moved piece directly abandoned defense of a key pawn or square (Qa4 left the king unshielded, Qb3 left c6 undefended, Kh1 left e4 unprotected, d4 released tension needed to keep the queen's escape routes open). In 4/7 positions, the piece moved to a square where it became trapped or immediately attackable by enemy pawns (Bg6 fell to h5+Nh4, Rf5 was won by g4, Nxe5 allowed dxe5 forking two pieces, d4 allowed Nxc3 sealing the queen). The common thread is that each move looks superficially purposeful (targeting a pawn, centralizing, prophylaxis) but fatally neglects the most urgent positional requirement. In 6/7 cases, tempo loss was a key tag, as the opponent gained time to exploit the newly created weakness with forcing moves.
analysis.move_pattern: Any piece type moving away from a coordinating/defensive square, often toward the board's edge or to a tactically exposed square; no consistent direction or piece type
analysis.why_bad: The move abandons a critical function (defending a pawn, shielding the king, maintaining central coordination, or keeping escape routes) and the opponent immediately exploits the resulting weakness through tempo-gaining attacks, captures of undefended material, or trapping the displaced piece with pawn advances.
sub_patterns: Queen retreats to rim/edge abandoning defense of key pawns or king coverage
Piece moves to a square where it gets trapped by enemy pawn advances
Passive king move wastes tempo when active piece play was required to maintain advantage
Wrong piece captures, leaving remaining pieces vulnerable to forks or traps

analysis.label: Superficially active or forcing moves (checks, pins, advances) played in critical positions where only one specific move holds, resulting in catastrophic tactical loss.
analysis.description: This feature fires on moves that appear purposeful—giving check (Na3+, Nb3+), creating a pin (Bg5), advancing aggressively (Kc6), or seeking activity (Qb6, Kf8)—but catastrophically ignore the position's single critical tactical requirement. In 5/6 positions, the move lands the piece on a square where it becomes immediately vulnerable: Na3+ leaves the knight trapped by Kb3 (trapped piece), Nb3+ allows cxb3 capturing the knight outright, Kc6 walks into a Bd5+ skewer winning the rook, Kf8 enters a mating net, Bg5 ignores the hanging a1 rook, and Qb6 fails to prevent a Bxb8/Bxc6+ fork combination. All positions had extremely narrow margins (avg 1.2 good moves available), meaning only one precise move held the position, yet players chose instinctive-looking 'active' moves instead. The average cp_loss of ~1896 reflects the catastrophic nature: these aren't subtle inaccuracies but position-destroying blunders disguised as purposeful play.
analysis.move_pattern: Piece moves to apparently active/forcing squares (checks, pins, attacks, advances) where the piece becomes tactically vulnerable or fails to address an immediate concrete threat
analysis.why_bad: The moved piece lands on a square where it can be captured, trapped, skewered, or where its placement enables a devastating opponent combination—all because the player chose apparent activity over the one constructive move that addressed the position's critical tactical demand
sub_patterns: Purposeless knight checks that lose the knight (Na3+/Nb3+ captured or trapped)
King moves to exposed squares enabling skewers or mating nets (Kc6/Kf8)
Slow 'threatening' piece moves that ignore hanging material (Bg5/Qb6)

analysis.label: Playing a natural-looking but non-urgent move in a critical position where exactly one move addresses an immediate tactical obligation.
analysis.description: This feature fires when players fail to find the single good continuation in positions of extreme tactical tension (avg 1.1 good moves available). In 6/7 positions, the played move ignores an immediate tactical necessity—whether it's saving a hanging piece (Rf1 ignoring Bxb1 threat), eliminating a critical threat (a5 ignoring Nxf3, Nc6 ignoring the d6 pawn), or avoiding a geometric trap (Kb8/Kf4/Kf5 walking into diagonal checks or mating nets, Kb2 decentralizing when only Kd3 works). The blundering moves all appear 'reasonable' on the surface—developing pieces, advancing pawns, repositioning kings—but catastrophically miss the ONE task the position demands. The tempo_loss tag appears in 6/7 cases, and missed_tactic in 6/7, confirming these are positions where a single wasted tempo allows the opponent a decisive tactical exploitation.
analysis.move_pattern: Any piece type moving to a plausible square; predominantly king moves (5/7) to rim squares or exposed squares, plus quiet developing/pawn moves that ignore immediate threats
analysis.why_bad: Each move wastes the critical tempo needed to address the ONE urgent tactical obligation in the position—whether defending a hanging piece, eliminating a dangerous threat, or avoiding a geometric vulnerability—allowing the opponent a forcing tactical sequence that was previously preventable.
sub_patterns: King retreating to rim instead of centralizing (Kb8, Kb2)
King advancing into tactical danger zone (Kf4, Kf5)
Slow flank/developing moves ignoring immediate captures (a5, Rf1, Nc6)

analysis.label: Moving a King or Rook to an exposed square in endgames where the opponent's active Queen immediately exploits the placement through checks, forks, or direct capture.
analysis.description: In all 7/7 positions, the opponent possesses an active Queen, and the blunder moves either a King (3/7: Kf4, Kc6, Kc4) or a Rook (4/7: Rb8, Rb7, Rh7, Rb8) to a square where the Queen can punish it. The exploitation mechanisms include: Queen checks that drive the King away from the Rook and then capture it (2/7: positions 5 and 8), Queen forks attacking King and Rook simultaneously (1/7: position 3), Queen delivering immediate checkmate on the King's new square (1/7: position 6), Queen directly capturing the Rook on its destination square (1/7: position 9), Queen checks harassing the King into worse positions after the Rook abandons defense (1/7: position 7), and Queen checks exploiting the King's forward placement to gain tempo (1/7: position 1). The best moves consistently keep the piece within a defensive coordination zone—Rooks staying near the King to interpose checks, or Kings retreating toward safer squares away from the Queen's active lines.
analysis.move_pattern: King or Rook moves to an exposed square (often forward for Kings, to edge files b/h for Rooks) away from its defensive post, in positions with an active enemy Queen
analysis.why_bad: The moved piece abandons its defensive coordination, landing on a square within the enemy Queen's tactical reach—either directly attackable, forkable with the King, or removing a critical interposition resource that leaves the King naked against checks
sub_patterns: Rook moves to b8/b7 away from King, Queen wins it via checks or direct capture
Rook leaves defensive file, Queen exploits exposed King with unstoppable check sequences
King advances forward into Queen fork or mating net
King moves to square where all escape routes are sealed by own/opponent pawns

analysis.label: Routine-looking developing or active moves that ignore an urgent tactical vulnerability or opponent's devastating reply.
analysis.description: This feature fires on moves that appear natural or purposeful in isolation (piece development, castling, central pawn pushes, rook activation) but critically fail to address the most urgent demand of the position. In 6/7 cases, the position required addressing a specific tactical vulnerability FIRST—an undefended piece (Ke8 leaves queen hanging, Nc6 leaves bishop on a6 unprotected), an unstoppable pawn advance (Nf6 allows d6, e4 allows fxe4 without recapture), a fork vulnerability (Bc5 allows d4 pawn fork), or a critical prophylactic resource (Rc6 misses Be2 first). In 5/7 cases the move was a 'developing' or 'improving' move (Bc5, Nf6, Nc6, O-O-O, e4) that looks thematic but overlooks the opponent's concrete tactical shot. The positions typically had only 1-3 good alternatives (avg 2.3), indicating the urgency of the threat being ignored. The average cp_loss of 308 reflects catastrophic consequences from a single tempo of negligence.
analysis.move_pattern: Mixed piece types (knights, bishops, kings, rooks, pawns) moving to seemingly active or natural squares; no consistent geometric direction but all are non-forcing moves that fail to address a forcing threat
analysis.why_bad: Each move ignores an urgent concrete threat or vulnerability in the position—either leaving a piece undefended, allowing a devastating pawn advance, creating a fork target, or missing a critical defensive resource that must be played NOW before the opponent executes their tactical blow
sub_patterns: Developing a piece while leaving another piece undefended (Nc6, Ke8)
Premature pawn break allowing uncapturable pawn gain (e4 with fxe4)
Placing piece on square creating fork vulnerability (Bc5 allows d4)
Castling into unresolved pawn tension (O-O-O with axb4)
Ignoring critical pawn advance opportunity for opponent (Nf6 allows d6)
Missing tempo-critical prophylactic move (Rc6 instead of Be2)

analysis.label: Playing a passive piece repositioning move when a concrete material-winning capture was available.
analysis.description: In all 4/4 positions, the player made a quiet, non-forcing piece move (repositioning a knight, rook, or bishop to a different square) when the position demanded an immediate tactical capture. The missed best moves were ALL captures: Qxa2 (position 2), Qxf7 (position 3), Bxf2 (position 7), and Nxd4 (position 8). In each case, the player had a narrow tactical window to exploit a concrete weakness through a forcing capture, but instead chose a 'natural-looking' piece relocation that wasted the critical tempo needed to strike. The positions all featured attacking stances with significant advantages (avg eval before move: ~-280 for the side to move) and very few good alternatives (avg 1.2 good moves), indicating these were sharp positions demanding precise calculation rather than positional maneuvering.
analysis.move_pattern: Non-capturing piece repositioning (knight, bishop, or rook moving to a new square without capturing) when a piece capture on an enemy-occupied square was optimal
analysis.why_bad: Wastes a critical tempo in a tactically demanding position, allowing the opponent to consolidate defenses, neutralize attacking pressure, or launch counterplay. The quiet move closes a narrow tactical window where only a forcing capture maintained the advantage.
sub_patterns: Knight retreat from dominant outpost instead of queen capture
Slow rook development instead of queen taking hanging pawn
Passive rook shuffle instead of bishop capturing weak pawn
Bishop retreat to passive square instead of knight fork/capture

analysis.label: Playing a non-forcing 'natural' move that neglects an urgent concrete tactical demand, such as a hanging piece, a critical capture, or a defensive necessity.
analysis.description: This feature fires when players choose passive, repositioning, or 'improving' moves while ignoring immediate tactical necessities in the position. In 4/9 cases, the move directly leaves a piece undefended or breaks critical piece coordination (Re8 abandoning the d4 bishop, Bg4 leaving the a8 rook hanging, Nf6 leaving the c5 bishop en prise, Bb4 allowing knight redeployment). In 3/9 cases, the move misses a concrete winning capture or forcing continuation (Bc8 missing Bxb2 winning a free pawn, Kd7 missing 17...e5 central break, a5 ignoring the Nf8+ discovered check threat). In 2/9 cases, the move places a piece where it can be attacked with tempo, surrendering initiative (Bd5 allowing Nd4 with tempo on the queen, Kd7 allowing c4-c5 gaining space with tempo). The common thread is that positions demanded concrete, forcing action but the player chose something that 'looks reasonable' without addressing the most pressing tactical reality.
analysis.move_pattern: Various piece types; typically non-captures, non-checks, and non-forcing moves (retreats, lateral repositions, quiet development, pawn pushes) when the position demands an immediate tactical response
analysis.why_bad: The move wastes a critical tempo on a non-urgent action while the position contains an immediate concrete demand—either a piece needs defending, a free capture is available, or a tactical threat must be neutralized—allowing the opponent to exploit the neglected tactical element (capturing hanging pieces, executing discovered attacks, or seizing tempo-based initiative).
sub_patterns: Moving a defender away from its coordination role, leaving a piece hanging
Retreating an active piece when a forcing capture was available
Playing a slow positional move while ignoring a concrete tactical threat
Placing a piece on a square where it can be attacked with tempo

analysis.label: Playing a general-looking improving or active move in a critical position that demands an immediate concrete response to an urgent tactical threat.
analysis.description: In 9/9 positions, the player chose a move that appears reasonable in general terms—centralizing, activating, developing, or checking—but completely fails to address the single most urgent concrete requirement of the position. In Position 1, Qc8+ gives a check but misses Qd5# (checkmate in one). In Position 7 (Bd6), the bishop 'activates' but ignores the g6 pawn threatening promotion via gxf7+. In Position 8 (Nd5), the knight 'centralizes' but abandons the winning g3 passed pawn promotion path. In Position 9 (Re8), the rook goes to a 'natural' file but leaves f7 fatally undefended. In Position 3 (Nf4), an aggressive outpost move abandons back-rank defense of d8. In Position 5 (Bg8), the bishop repositions but has zero relevance to the critical d-pawn race. The average cp_loss of 3483 and average of only 2.0 good moves confirm these are razor-sharp positions where only precise concrete responses work, yet the player defaults to positionally 'reasonable' but tactically catastrophic choices.
analysis.move_pattern: Mixed piece types moving to seemingly active/natural squares (outposts, open files, active diagonals, checks) rather than addressing the position's most urgent tactical demand
analysis.why_bad: The moves ignore an immediate concrete threat (promotion, checkmate, fork, back-rank invasion, piece hanging) in favor of general piece improvement, costing decisive material or allowing forced wins because the position required only-move precision, not general activity
sub_patterns: Giving a showy check when a stronger forcing move exists (Qc8+ missing Qd5#)
Activating a piece that vacates a critical defensive square (Bd6 vacating f8, Nf4 vacating e6, Re8 vacating f8)
Centralizing/repositioning when a pawn race demands immediate concrete action (Nd5, Bg8)
Making a positional move when only one tactical resource draws/wins (Qc2 vs Raf2, Bxh5 vs Qxc6)

analysis.label: Playing an aggressive or routine move that ignores a critical immediate tactical vulnerability requiring defensive attention.
analysis.description: In all 4 positions, the player makes a move pursuing their own plan (attacking, developing, or centralizing) while a concrete tactical threat demands immediate attention. In Position 5 (Bh6), White attacks the kingside but ignores the a6-f1 diagonal threatening the rook. In Position 7 (Nc3), White develops routinely but fails to address the Ng4/f2 weakness. In Position 12 (Kg5), Black advances the king into check range (h4+) making it a pure tempo loss. In Position 13 (Nb5), White plays an aggressive knight jump but abandons the f2 square, allowing Nf2+ with discovered check winning the queen. The common thread in 4/4 positions is that a specific defensive move was available and necessary, but the player chose an optimistic/active move instead, losing between 98-489 cp. The feature particularly fires when the ignored threat involves a critical weak square (f2 in 2/4, f1 in 1/4) or king vulnerability (4/4).
analysis.move_pattern: A piece or king moves to an aggressive/active square (forward or to the flank) away from the square or sector that requires immediate defense
analysis.why_bad: The move abandons a critical defensive duty (usually protecting a weak square like f2/f1 or the king's safety), allowing the opponent to execute an immediate tactical combination that wins material or forces a decisive advantage
sub_patterns: Knight jumps to aggressive outpost abandoning key defensive square (Nc3, Nb5)
Bishop deployed to attacking square while own piece hangs on undefended diagonal (Bh6)
King advances into check/tempo-loss territory rather than maintaining defensive post (Kg5)

analysis.label: Non-forcing positional or flank moves played when the position demands an immediate concrete response to a central tactical vulnerability.
analysis.description: In 3/4 positions, the player chose a quiet, strategically-motivated move (b3 to attack a knight, b4 to start a pawn storm, Qg3 for kingside pressure) while the position contained an urgent tactical issue requiring concrete resolution—an undefended pawn on c3, a central pawn defended only by a pinned piece, or a discovered attack opportunity on the e-file. In each mistake case, the move either created a new vulnerability (b3 unguarded c3) or failed to address an existing one (b4 ignored the pin on d4, Qg3 missed Bd3 discovered attack), and the punishment involved an enemy knight exploiting the neglected weakness (Nxc3, Nxd4, Ne4 with tempo). The 4th position (Ke3, 0cp loss) represents the feature firing on a similar-looking quiet centralizing move that happened to be correct in a technically won endgame where no tactical urgency existed.
analysis.move_pattern: Non-forcing White moves—typically pawn advances on flanks (b3, b4) or quiet piece repositioning (Qg3, Ke3)—that don't address the most critical file or piece interaction in the position
analysis.why_bad: These moves neglect an immediate tactical demand (undefended square, pin exploitation, discovered attack), allowing enemy knights to exploit the created or unaddressed weakness with tempo-gaining maneuvers
sub_patterns: b-pawn advances that weaken central pawn chains
Queen repositioning that leaves e-file tactics unexploited
Flank operations while center is tactically unstable

analysis.label: Moves that pursue a plan or idea while overlooking that a piece becomes immediately capturable or tactically exploitable.
analysis.description: This feature fires on positions where the player makes a seemingly reasonable move—developing, attacking, capturing, or repositioning—while failing to notice that a piece (their own or a key defender) becomes en prise or tactically vulnerable to a short forcing sequence. In 6/8 positions, the blunder directly creates a hanging piece: Bh6 places the bishop where Nf7 fork wins it (Position 2), Nd2 leaves the d4 pawn undefended for Nxd4 (Position 5), Nf5 puts the knight in direct capture by Kxf5 (Position 7), Nxg5 leaves the Rd5 undefended for Nxd5 (Position 14), Qh6 abandons f6 allowing Ng4 tempo to win material (Position 6), and Qa6 removes queen defense enabling Nxd7/Ne5+ fork (Position 12). In the remaining cases, the move ignores an already-hanging piece (a4 ignores Nc3 capturable by Kxc3, Position 3) or exposes the king to material-winning tactics (Kf2 allows Rxc1/Qxb5, Position 9). The average cp_loss of 272 (~minor piece value) and average of only 1.5 good moves confirms these are critical junctures requiring tactical awareness.
analysis.move_pattern: Various piece types moving to seemingly active/purposeful squares while leaving own material undefended or within opponent's capture radius
analysis.why_bad: Each move pursues a secondary goal (development, attack, pawn grab, king safety) while overlooking that a piece is or becomes immediately capturable through a simple capture or short tactical sequence (fork, removal of defender, unprotected piece)
sub_patterns: Moving a piece TO a square where it hangs (Bh6 to fork, Nf5 to king capture)
Moving a defender away, leaving another piece hanging (Nd2 leaves d4, Nxg5 leaves Rd5, Qa6 leaves Nd7)
Ignoring an already-hanging piece to play an unrelated move (a4 ignores Nc3 en prise)
Moving to a square where opponent gains decisive tempo against the piece (Qh6 allows Ng4)

analysis.label: Player makes a seemingly purposeful move addressing a secondary concern while ignoring the position's actual critical demand, losing a decisive tempo.
analysis.description: In 7/8 positions, the player makes a move that appears active or logical (attacking a pawn, centralizing the king, capturing material, posting a piece aggressively) but fundamentally misidentifies the position's primary requirement. In Position 1, Rh8 attacks the h-pawn instead of controlling the h1 promotion square. In Position 3, Bxg8 wins material but trades away the sole blockading piece. In Position 5, Ke6 centralizes instead of rushing toward the critical kingside. In Position 6, Nf5 seeks an aggressive outpost instead of simple development. In Position 10, h6 makes a pawn move instead of activating the king. In Position 13, Rd1 attacks an intruder while leaving c3 undefended. In Position 15, Ke3 centralizes the king forward into tactical fire instead of resolving f3 vulnerability. The 'tempo_loss' tag appears in 7/8 analyses, confirming that the wasted move on a secondary goal is the unifying error.
analysis.move_pattern: Any piece type moving to an aggressive, forward, or active-looking square (captures, centralization, attacks) rather than the required defensive/precise alternative
analysis.why_bad: The move addresses a secondary goal (attacking a pawn, winning material, centralizing, seeking an outpost) while the position's actual critical demand (blocking promotion, preserving a key defensive piece, activating the king toward the right flank, resolving a tactical vulnerability) goes unmet, and the lost tempo allows the opponent to execute the real threat.
sub_patterns: King centralizes toward wrong sector in pawn endgame
Piece captures material but trades away sole defensive resource
Rook/piece attacks secondary target while real threat is promotion or hanging piece
Forward king move walks into tactical checks/captures
Aggressive piece placement on undefended or irrelevant square

analysis.label: A slow, non-forcing 'improving' move played when the position demands immediate attention to a concrete tactical vulnerability.
analysis.description: This feature fires on quiet, positional-looking moves made in positions with urgent tactical problems. In all 8/8 cases, the player chose a non-forcing move (no check, no capture, no direct threat) while an immediate tactical issue demanded attention. The failures manifest in several ways: leaving a piece undefended on an open file (positions 1, 5 with bishop hanging on d7 after Bxf6), blocking a friendly piece's critical retreat square (position 3 with Bd7 blocking the knight from retreating when f4 comes), creating a self-pin or alignment vulnerability (position 7 with Qe3 in front of own rook), placing a piece on the terminal square of an opponent's forcing sequence (position 8 with Rh8 enabling Qxh8#), placing a piece where an intermediate check removes its defender (position 12 with Bg5 met by Nxf3+), or ignoring a pawn thrust that traps a piece (position 13 with Kf1 allowing g4 to win the bishop). The common thread is prioritizing strategic ideas (development, centralization, structure) over calculating the opponent's concrete tactical resources.
analysis.move_pattern: Non-forcing quiet moves (bishop development, pawn pushes, king walks, queen repositioning) - no checks, no captures, no direct threats - in tactically sharp positions
analysis.why_bad: The moves ignore immediate tactical threats (hanging pieces, discovered attacks, removing-the-defender motifs, pawn thrusts trapping pieces) that the opponent can exploit with forcing moves, turning a reasonable or advantageous position into a losing one.
sub_patterns: Quiet development leaving a piece undefended on an open file (Bd7/b6 with Bxf6+Rxd7)
Blocking own piece's retreat square creating a trapped piece (Bd7 blocking knight)
Placing piece in front of own piece creating self-pin (Qe3 in front of Re1)
King move ignoring pawn thrust that traps a minor piece (Kf1 allowing g4)
Piece placement where intermediate forcing move removes its defender (Bg5 met by Nxf3+)

analysis.label: Natural-looking moves that voluntarily surrender a critical defensive or positional foundation in pursuit of a superficially attractive but less important objective.
analysis.description: In all 6 positions, the player makes a move that follows obvious surface logic (capture the queen, castle for safety, remove a threatening pawn, attack the king, defend pawns, advance a passer) but fatally abandons the position's most critical structural requirement. In 2/6 cases, rooks leave dominant files or essential back-rank coverage (Rg8 abandons e-file, Ra7 abandons back rank). In 2/6 cases, pawn moves break a vital protective structure (fxe6 opens tactical vulnerabilities on d5, e4 separates connected passers). In 2/6 cases, the king or a major piece moves to an apparently logical square that walks directly into the opponent's attacking lines (O-O-O into c-file pressure, Rxg1 allowing a more active promotion). The unifying thread is that each move addresses a secondary concern while neglecting the primary positional truth that the position's evaluation depends on.
analysis.move_pattern: Various piece types making captures, advances, or repositionings that remove a piece/pawn from a square where it performs an essential structural or defensive function
analysis.why_bad: Each move sacrifices the position's most critical asset (file control, back-rank defense, pawn coordination, king safety zone) for a superficially appealing but strategically inferior objective, allowing the opponent to exploit the newly created weakness with forcing moves
sub_patterns: Rook abandoning critical file or rank for speculative attack
Pawn capture/advance that breaks mutual pawn protection
King or piece voluntarily entering opponent's active zone
Choosing wrong capture target when defensive priority exists

analysis.label: Moves that fatally compromise defensive structure in positions with only one or two acceptable continuations, enabling immediate tactical exploitation.
analysis.description: This feature activates on moves that voluntarily weaken the player's position in moments where very few moves are acceptable (avg 1.5 good moves). In 5/6 positions, the move removes a piece or pawn from a critical defensive role: f5 (Position 12) removes the f7 pawn blocking the a2-g8 diagonal enabling Qc4+; Rh8 (Position 3) places the rook on a vulnerable diagonal enabling Bd4+ discovered attack; Ka6 (Position 2) walks the king into c5+ tempo gaining tactics; c5 (Position 6) weakens the d6 outpost enabling a knight fork on f7; Rf1 (Position 8) misses the counter-intuitive Kf7 that neutralizes the promotion threat. In each case, the player chose a 'natural-looking' or 'active' move (contesting a file, defending a pawn, gaining space, attacking a piece) while missing the singular critical defensive resource that the position demanded.
analysis.move_pattern: Diverse piece types (king, rook, pawn) moving to seemingly active or natural squares, typically within the player's own camp or toward the flanks, that create new tactical vulnerabilities
analysis.why_bad: Each move either removes a piece/pawn from a critical defensive function (blocking a diagonal, controlling a key square, restraining an enemy passed pawn) or places the moved piece on a tactically vulnerable square, enabling immediate exploitation via checks, discovered attacks, forks, or mating threats that did not exist before the move
sub_patterns: Pawn advances opening critical diagonals to own king (f5, c5)
King walking into tactical vulnerability on edge squares (Ka6)
Rook repositioning that misses a single counter-intuitive defensive resource (Rf1, Rh8)
Developing moves that ignore an imminent tactical break (Rc1)

analysis.label: Playing a natural developing or improving move that ignores critical unresolved central pawn tension, leaving a pawn (usually on e4 or e5) undefended.
analysis.description: In 3/5 positions, the player develops a knight to f6 or advances d4 while their central e-pawn (e4 or e5) is in direct tension with the opponent's d-pawn, and the move played does nothing to protect, exchange, or support that pawn—allowing the opponent to simply capture it with dxe5 or dxe4. In the remaining 2/5 positions, the same underlying error manifests: the player makes a routine improving move (centralizing a knight to e5, or tucking the king to g7) that ignores the position's most urgent tactical demand—in one case disrupting h-file coordination and allowing a favorable rook trade, in the other walking into a pawn-advance tactic that wins the exchange. The common thread across all five is prioritizing a 'natural-looking' move over addressing the position's critical tension point, resulting in immediate material loss or decisive positional deterioration.
analysis.move_pattern: Minor piece development (knight to natural square like f6/e5) or king/pawn improvement, ignoring an undefended central pawn or critical file tension
analysis.why_bad: The move ignores unresolved pawn tension or a tactical vulnerability that demands immediate resolution; the opponent simply captures the hanging material or exploits the abandoned tension with a forcing sequence
sub_patterns: Nf6 leaving e5 pawn undefended against dxe5 (3 instances)
d4 bypassing d3 leaving e4 pawn undefended against dxe4
Piece centralization abandoning defensive coordination on critical file

analysis.label: Advancing a pawn prematurely in the endgame when a preparatory king move or piece repositioning was required first.
analysis.description: This feature fires on endgame positions (9/10) where the player makes a hasty forward pawn advance instead of the required preparatory move. In 8/10 cases, the blunder is a pawn push (g4, f5+, c6, a5, d4, c5, g3+, g6+) that is strategically the right idea but critically wrong in timing. The correct moves consistently involve king activation first (Positions 1, 10, 14: king should lead the pawn), piece repositioning before the advance (Positions 2, 4, 6: rook/bishop needed to prepare), or precise move-order with supporting pawns (Position 12: h3 before g3+). The common punishment is that the premature advance either hangs the pawn (2/10), abandons control of a critical square allowing opponent king penetration (3/10: a5→b5, d4→e4, c6→blockade), or gives the opponent tempo to consolidate/blockade (5/10). The average cp_loss of 465 reflects catastrophic evaluation swings, typically converting wins into draws.
analysis.move_pattern: Pawn advance (usually 1 square forward, occasionally with check), predominantly on semi-open or open files/diagonals, in endgame positions with passed pawns
analysis.why_bad: The pawn advance wastes a critical tempo or abandons key square control, allowing the opponent's king to centralize, blockade, capture the pawn, or achieve a drawn fortress—when a quieter preparatory move (king activation, piece repositioning, or supporting pawn advance) would have maintained the winning advantage.
sub_patterns: Pawn advances before king in K+P endgames (king should lead pawn)
Pawn pushes to squares where they are immediately capturable
Pawn advances that abandon control of critical blockade squares
Premature pawn checks that give opponent tempo to reach drawing squares
Advancing the wrong pawn first in connected passer positions

analysis.label: Playing a check or aggressive move on the wrong square when only one specific square delivers the winning tactical blow.
analysis.description: This feature fires on positions where the player has a narrow tactical solution (avg 1.3 good moves available) but chooses a superficially similar forcing move on the wrong square or from the wrong direction, resulting in catastrophic evaluation swings (avg 2861 cp loss). In 5/11 positions, the error is explicitly giving check on the wrong square: Qa1+ instead of Qe1+ (allowing interposition vs. forcing back-rank mate), Ne4+ instead of Ng4+ (knight can't reach the fork square), Bf6+ instead of Bf2+ (wrong diagonal, failing to control the escape square), Qd5+ instead of Qg5+ (allows productive block vs. targeting the weakness), and Be3+ instead of Ba3+ (drives king toward safety instead of setting up discovered attack). In the remaining 6/11 cases, the player similarly misses the ONE precise move by choosing a 'close but wrong' alternative: routine development (Nc6) instead of a discovered attack (e4+), natural king move (Kg7) walking into a fork (Nf5+), passive queen placement (Qe2) leaving the queen on a forkable square, or retreating (Nd7) from a dominant attacking position. The positions share extreme narrowness—typically only one move maintains the advantage or avoids disaster.
analysis.move_pattern: A piece moves to a square that appears aggressive/natural (often delivering check) but is geometrically wrong—the correct destination is typically a different square on the same rank, file, or one diagonal over that enables a specific tactical motif.
analysis.why_bad: The chosen square fails to support the critical tactical mechanism: it allows interposition where the correct square doesn't, it places a piece where it can't reach the necessary fork/follow-up square, it fails to control the opponent's escape route, or it permits a simplifying trade that the correct move prevents. The 'close but wrong' square looks equally forcing on the surface but lacks the precise geometric relationship needed for the combination to work.
sub_patterns: Wrong checking square allowing interposition (Qa1+ vs Qe1+, Qd5+ vs Qg5+)
Wrong discovered check square preventing follow-up fork (Ne4+ vs Ng4+)
Wrong checking diagonal failing to control escape square (Bf6+ vs Bf2+, Be3+ vs Ba3+)
Routine move missing discovered attack/pawn thrust (Nc6 vs e4+, Kg7 vs Kh8)
Removing a critical defender for seemingly active play (Bg2, Nd7, Qe2)

analysis.label: Moves that pursue a secondary plan (attacking, centralizing, or breaking the center) while ignoring the position's most urgent concrete tactical need.
analysis.description: This feature fires on moves where the player chooses a plausible-looking action—pawn breaks, queen relocations, or piece maneuvers—but fatally ignores a concrete tactical vulnerability that required immediate attention. In 6/8 positions, straightforward developing or consolidating moves (Nf3, Bb7, Be4, Ke1, Bc3+, Qf2) would have maintained the position, but instead the player pursues a secondary objective. The punishment consistently involves a forcing reply (pawn advance with tempo in 5/8 cases: e4+, e5, dxc4, exf3, Qh4+) that exploits what the blunder left undefended. Common scenarios include: premature pawn breaks before piece preparation (c4, c5 in positions 5 and 7), queen moves to tactically vulnerable squares (Qe2 hit by exf3, Qb3 allowing Qh4+, Qc3+ blocked by d4), and piece placements ignoring open lines (Kd3 on an unprotected diagonal, Bc2 abandoning d4 support). The average 2.6 good alternatives suggests these aren't narrow decisions but fundamental plan-selection errors.
analysis.move_pattern: Mixed piece types (queen moves most common: 3/8) placed on squares vulnerable to opponent's forcing pawn advances or checks; includes premature c-file pawn breaks and misdirected piece centralization
analysis.why_bad: Each move ignores the position's most urgent concrete demand (development, covering a critical diagonal, defending a key pawn/piece) in favor of a secondary plan, allowing the opponent to respond with a forcing move that gains decisive tempo or material against the misplaced piece or exposed vulnerability
sub_patterns: Premature pawn breaks before piece preparation (c4, c5)
Queen placed on square immediately exploited by pawn capture with tempo (Qe2, Qb3, Qc3+)
Piece moved to square exposed on an undefended diagonal (Kd3, Bc2, Nf6)

analysis.label: Non-developing flank pawn advances or peripheral moves that waste a critical tempo while the king remains vulnerable to immediate tactical exploitation.
analysis.description: This feature activates on moves that prioritize flank action over urgent development or king safety needs. In 4/6 positions, the blunder is a wing pawn advance (g5, a4, h4, a5) when the best moves involved development or castling. In 5/6 positions, the player's king is exposed or uncastled, making tempo critically important. The remaining moves (Bb5, Kf2) share the same fundamental error: ignoring an immediate tactical vulnerability to make a peripheral or non-essential move. In all 6 cases, the opponent punishes by exploiting the tempo loss—either opening the center against the uncastled king (positions 1, 2, 6), winning material via a fork or hanging piece (positions 4, 5), or executing a central pawn break that wins material (position 3). The best moves in all 6 positions focused on piece development, castling, or active centralization rather than flank expansion.
analysis.move_pattern: Pawn advances to wing squares (a/g/h files) or piece/king moves to peripheral squares that don't address central or king-safety priorities
analysis.why_bad: These moves waste a tempo on non-urgent flank action while the king is vulnerable, allowing the opponent to exploit the center, execute forks, or win undefended material through immediate tactical strikes that the tempo loss enables.
sub_patterns: Wing pawn push with king uncastled (g5, a4, a5)
Kingside pawn storm enabling central pawn fork (h4 allowing ...e5-e4)
Piece placed on undefended square ignoring diagonal checks (Bb5)
King walking into pawn fork (Kf2 allowing g3+)

analysis.label: Moving a piece to a seemingly active square where the opponent immediately gains tempo by attacking it or exploiting what it left undefended.
analysis.description: In all 6 positions, the player makes a non-forcing move (no check, no capture) placing a piece on a square that appears useful but is immediately punished by a tempo-gaining response. In 4/6 cases, the piece is directly attacked on its new square: Re3 gets hit by Bc5, Bd4 by Ne6, Ra4 by b5, and Ka5 allows the unstoppable g5 advance. In 2/6 cases, the move abandons a critical defensive post: Rg3 leaves the d-file allowing Rxd7, and Rh7 leaves d3 undefended enabling Nxd3+ fork.
