The correct moves in each case were either direct actions (capturing with Rxc4, Bxf6) or prophylactic moves (Kf1, Kc1, h5) that addressed the primary positional demand without creating new vulnerabilities. The common error is choosing an indirect, aesthetically appealing piece placement over the most urgent concrete need.
analysis.move_pattern: Non-capturing, non-checking piece move (mostly rooks 4/6) to an open file/rank targeting a pawn or central square, often lateral repositioning
analysis.why_bad: The piece lands on a square where the opponent gains a free tempo by attacking it (or exploits the abandoned post), allowing the opponent to execute their critical plan one move faster than expected, turning a manageable position into a losing one.
sub_patterns: Rook moves laterally to attack a pawn, gets attacked by minor piece with tempo (Re3/Bc5, Ra4/b5)
Piece abandons defensive duty to pursue secondary target, key square/pawn falls (Rg3 leaves d-file, Rh7 leaves d3)
King moves toward peripheral pawn while critical breakthrough happens on opposite flank (Ka5 vs g5)
Centralizing piece move allows opponent knight activation with tempo (Bd4/Ne6)

analysis.label: Moves that pursue superficially active piece placement while fatally abandoning critical defensive responsibilities, enabling tactical exploitation.
analysis.description: This feature fires on positions where the player chooses a move that appears to follow sound chess principles (piece activation, checks, seventh-rank invasion, centralization, captures) but actually abandons a critical defensive duty in the position. In 5/6 cases, the move relocates a piece FROM a necessary defensive post TO an exposed or ineffective square: Rb7 abandons back-rank defense (Position 12), Ke2 exposes the king to second-rank invasion (Position 5), Bf4 releases restraint from g5 enabling ...d5 (Position 2), Bxe4 places the bishop on a tactically vulnerable central square (Position 15), and Qd7+ checks from the wrong square missing perpetual geometry (Position 1). In 4/6 positions, the opponent's refutation directly exploits the abandoned defensive post (back-rank mates, rook invasions, checks along vacated diagonals). The average cp_loss of 294 reflects severe consequences, and the average 2.0 good moves available indicates alternatives existed that maintained defensive integrity while still being constructive.
analysis.move_pattern: Various piece types moved to apparently active/aggressive squares (7th rank, central squares, checking squares) that abandon their defensive station or expose their own position
analysis.why_bad: The moves create or expose tactical vulnerabilities (back-rank weakness, exposed king, undefended pieces, diagonal access) that the opponent can immediately exploit with concrete tactical sequences, because the relocated piece no longer fulfills its essential defensive function
sub_patterns: Rook leaving first rank for seventh-rank activity while back rank is vulnerable
King moving to exposed central square instead of staying sheltered
Bishop retreating from actively restraining square to passive diagonal
Piece attacking opponent's queen that actually invites it to a stronger square
Capturing a pawn to activate bishop but placing it on a tactically exposed square

analysis.label: Playing a seemingly purposeful move (attacking, developing, or repositioning) while a concrete tactical vulnerability in one's own position demands urgent attention.
analysis.description: This feature fires on moves where the player pursues a plausible-looking plan but catastrophically ignores an immediate tactical threat. In 5/7 positions, the refutation involves a check or back-rank invasion that the blunder either enables or fails to prevent (Rh1+ in Position 1, Ba3/exf6+ discovered attack in Position 2, Ra7+ in Position 4, Rb8+ in Position 5, Qb2# in Position 7). In 6/7 cases, the blundering move either abandons a critical defensive function (Re2 leaves back rank, Nd7 abandons kingside defense, Rb5 stops guarding bishop) or creates a new vulnerability (f5/f6 weaken pawn structure, Qd2 blocks escape square). The moves all share a 'looks reasonable' quality—Re2 appears to contest the 2nd rank, Nd7 attacks a rook, Rb5 attacks a knight, f5/f6 strengthen pawn chains—but each ignores a concrete, calculable punishment that the opponent has available immediately. The average 1.6 good moves available confirms these are critical positions requiring precise defensive awareness.
analysis.move_pattern: Various piece types moving to apparently useful squares (attacking enemy pieces, gaining space, repositioning) while abandoning defensive duties or creating vulnerabilities on own back rank/king position
analysis.why_bad: The moves abandon critical defensive responsibilities or create new weaknesses while the opponent has an immediate concrete tactical exploitation available—typically a back-rank invasion, discovered attack, or exploitation of a newly undefended piece. The player prioritizes a 'plan' over addressing the position's most urgent demand.
sub_patterns: Piece leaves back rank allowing invasion with check (Re2, f6)
Piece abandons defensive post to chase material (Nd7, Rb5)
Pawn advance weakens structure enabling immediate tactic (f5, f6)
Piece self-blocks king escape route (Qd2)
Development ignoring explosive central tension (Nh6)

analysis.label: Pawn advances giving check to an exposed king that paradoxically help the opponent's king escape or dismantle the attacker's own winning structure.
analysis.description: All 6 positions feature a pawn advance delivering check (+) to a king that is already exposed or vulnerable. In 5/6 cases this is a significant mistake (avg cp_loss 3311). The core problem is that the irreversible pawn push, while superficially aggressive, actually undermines the attacker's position: in Position 5 (b6+), the pawn removes a c6 pawn that was caging the king; in Position 6 (f4+), the pawn opens the h4 escape square, severing perpetual check; in Position 14 (b4+), the check allows Kd2 escaping the Nf2# mating geometry; in Position 2 (f6+), the pawn blocks the attacker's own queen from the critical f6 square; in Position 1 (c4+), it weakens the pawn chain for no compensation. In 5/6 cases, calm non-checking moves (piece repositioning, captures, or quieter checks with pieces) were vastly superior. The pattern exemplifies 'patzer sees a check' syndrome specifically with pawns, where the irreversibility of the advance makes the error permanent.
analysis.move_pattern: Pawn advance one square forward delivering check to an exposed enemy king (various files: b, c, f), typically in positions where the opponent's king is already in danger
analysis.why_bad: The irreversible pawn advance either opens escape squares for the enemy king, removes constraining pawns from the attacker's own cage structure, blocks the attacker's own pieces from critical squares, or grants the defender a tempo to consolidate—all while better moves (quiet piece improvements, perpetual checks, or forcing captures) were available to maintain or convert the advantage.
sub_patterns: Pawn check removes own pawn that was trapping the enemy king
Pawn check opens an escape square the king can use
Pawn check blocks own queen/piece from a critical attacking square
Pawn check disrupts mating geometry by pushing king to a safe square
Pawn check squanders perpetual check or forced mate opportunity

analysis.label: Active-looking moves that remove a piece from a vital defensive duty, creating an immediate tactical vulnerability.
analysis.description: In 6/7 positions analyzed, the player made a move that appeared purposeful (contesting a file, attacking a piece, capturing material, gaining space) but critically removed a piece from a square where it was performing an essential defensive function. In Position 1, Rb4 abandoned the a-file allowing a passed pawn promotion. In Position 3, Nc4 left f7 unguarded, enabling Bxf7+ winning a piece. In Position 6, d4 severed the bishop's support chain, leaving it hanging. In Position 10, Rd1 vacated the back rank, allowing Nxe4 since fxe4 Rxd1+ would be catastrophic. In Position 11, Rxg5 captured with the wrong piece, exposing the rook to a queen attack. In Position 2, Kc7 moved to a square allowing a tempo-gaining check. The consistent thread across all 7 positions is that the moved piece was silently performing a critical defensive role the player failed to recognize, and the punishment was a swift tactical blow exploiting the newly created weakness.
analysis.move_pattern: Diverse piece types moving away from a square where they performed a latent defensive function; often toward an apparently active square or target
analysis.why_bad: The piece was silently guarding a critical square, defending a key piece, or preventing a tactical motif (promotion, fork, back-rank); removing it creates an immediate exploitable vulnerability that the opponent punishes with a forcing sequence
sub_patterns: Rook leaves file/rank that was preventing a passed pawn advance or back-rank tactic
Knight/piece moves away from defensive post leaving a hanging piece or weak square
Pawn push disconnects a piece from its support chain, leaving it en prise
King moves to a square allowing a tempo-gaining check that enables invasion
Capturing with the wrong piece, leaving the capturing piece tactically exposed

analysis.label: Moving a piece to an aggressive-looking square while missing a concrete tactical opportunity, creating or allowing vulnerabilities.
analysis.description: In all 6 positions, the player moves a piece (knights 3/6, queens 2/6, bishop 1/6) to a square that appears dominant or aggressive but is actually non-forcing and either creates a tactical vulnerability or wastes the tempo needed for a concrete continuation. In Position 1, Ng4 targets h2/f2 but lands where Bh3 attacks it with tempo. In Position 3, Qe3 'centralizes' but misses the forcing Rxh7+ sacrifice. In Position 5, Ba4 maintains diagonal pressure but is immediately vulnerable to ...b5. In Position 6, Ne4 occupies a 'central outpost' but opens the a3-f8 diagonal for a skewer. In Position 10, Qf6 appears active but passes up capturing the free f4-pawn. In Position 13, Nd3 infiltrates deeply but aligns the queen on g6 with White's bishop via Bc2. The common thread is prioritizing aggressive-looking piece placement over concrete calculation, with the chosen square proving tactically flawed.
analysis.move_pattern: Piece (knight, queen, or bishop) moves forward or laterally to an apparently active/aggressive square that is non-forcing
analysis.why_bad: The move wastes a critical tempo on a non-forcing 'improvement' when the position demands concrete action; the piece either becomes a target on its new square, opens lines/diagonals that create tactical vulnerabilities, or simply passes up a forcing tactical continuation that would have been decisive.
sub_patterns: Knight moves to outpost that creates alignment vulnerability (Ne4/Nd3/Ng4)
Queen repositions to 'active' square instead of capturing or forcing (Qe3/Qf6)
Bishop relocates to seemingly strong diagonal but is immediately attackable by pawn (Ba4)

analysis.label: Quiet, non-forcing moves that neglect critical king vulnerability, allowing the opponent to launch devastating tactical sequences targeting the exposed king.
analysis.description: This feature fires on positions where a player makes a quiet, non-urgent move (no check, no capture, no direct threat) while their own king is critically vulnerable—typically uncastled or exposed in the center. In 7/9 positions, the moving side's king is uncastled or on an exposed square. The moves include flank pawn pushes (b5), pawn moves that weaken the king's shield (f3, f6), piece developments to tactically exploitable squares (Be6, Be7), queen relocations that abandon defensive duties (Qg3), king walks to dangerous squares (Ke3, Kc3), and castling into an exposed wing (O-O-O). All share the critical flaw of addressing a secondary concern—space, development of a non-critical piece, or positional goals—while the position demands immediate attention to king safety. The punishment consistently involves forcing sequences (checks, discovered attacks, forks) that exploit the king's vulnerability, with an average centipawn loss of 288.
analysis.move_pattern: Non-forcing moves (no check/capture) of any piece type, often pawn pushes or quiet piece repositions, played when the player's own king is in the center or on an exposed square
analysis.why_bad: The position's critical factor is king safety, but the player addresses a secondary concern instead; the opponent exploits the tempo gap with forcing moves (checks, attacks on the king) that win material or create decisive threats against the exposed/uncastled king.
sub_patterns: Flank pawn moves ignoring central king exposure (b5, f6)
Pawn advances weakening own king shield (f3, f6)
Piece placement on squares immediately exploitable with tempo (Be6→Ng5, Be7→d6, Qg3→Nh5)
King walks to tactically vulnerable squares (Ke3→Rxc3+, Kc3→Ba5+)
Castling into an exposed/opening file structure (O-O-O→dxc3, cxb2+)

analysis.label: Playing a slow positional or improving move when the position demands an immediate forcing tactical blow, allowing the opponent to seize initiative.
analysis.description: In all 5 positions, the player chose a quiet, non-forcing 'improving' move (centralizing a knight, pushing a flank pawn, castling, or repositioning the king) when a concrete tactical opportunity existed that demanded immediate execution. In Position 2 (Ne4), the player centralized a knight instead of relocating the queen to an attacking square (Qh5), allowing a simplifying queen trade. In Position 3 (a4), a slow pawn push replaced an active knight jump (Nf5), allowing Nxd4 with a trapped bishop. In Position 4 (O-O), routine castling replaced resolving central tension (dxe5), allowing Qxd4+ winning material. In Position 7 (Ke6), the king centralized passively instead of capturing a free pawn (Kxf4), allowing f5+ tempo. In Position 11 (Ne4), a knight retreated from its attacking post instead of executing a winning sacrifice (Nxf7), allowing d3-d2 counterplay. In 5/5 cases the best move was forcing (capture, sacrifice, or direct attack), while the played move was positional/quiet. The average cp_loss of 344 reflects these being critical moments where tempo was everything.
analysis.move_pattern: Non-capturing, non-checking piece repositioning or quiet move (knight centralization, pawn push, castling, king walk) instead of a forcing capture or sacrifice
analysis.why_bad: The quiet move surrenders the initiative by giving the opponent time to activate counterplay (passed pawns, simplifying captures, tactical shots) that the forcing best move would have prevented; the position demanded concrete action but received a passive response.
sub_patterns: Knight retreating from active attacking square to e4
Flank pawn push ignoring central tactical vulnerability
Routine king safety move when tactical resolution required
King repositioning missing immediate pawn capture

analysis.label: Playing forward/aggressive moves (advances, captures, checks) when the position demands defensive retreat due to the player's own exposed king.
analysis.description: In all 5/5 positions, the player's own king was already dangerously exposed with a weak or non-existent pawn shield. The correct move involved retreating or consolidating defensively (Ka6 retreat in position 5, Ne3 centralization in position 6, Kh3 retreat in position 9, Bxf5 maintaining pawn structure in position 12, Qf4+ addressing the real threat in position 14). Instead, the player chose forward/aggressive moves: Kxa4 (king advances to capture), Nb4 (knight advances to exposed square), Kg5 (king advances into danger), gxf5 (pawn capture removing own king's shield), Qh7+ (check driving opponent's king to safety while ignoring the actual threat). In every case, the refutation exploited the player's own king exposure that the aggressive move either created or failed to address: forced mates against the king on a4 (position 5), piece loss leaving bare king (position 6), Bf6+ winning the queen (position 9), Rh6+ exploiting the opened file (position 12), and opponent king reaching safety allowing pawn promotion (position 14).
analysis.move_pattern: Various piece types moving forward (advancing, capturing, checking) rather than retreating or consolidating - specifically king advances (3/5), forward captures (1/5), and misdirected checks (1/5)
analysis.why_bad: The player's own king is already critically exposed and the position demands defensive consolidation, but the aggressive move either worsens king exposure (advancing into attacks, removing pawn shield) or ignores the real positional threat, allowing the opponent to exploit the existing king vulnerability with checks, mating attacks, or unstoppable threats.
sub_patterns: King advances into mating nets instead of retreating
Pawn captures that strip own king's shelter
Checks in wrong direction that let opponent reach safety
Piece moves to exposed squares abandoning defensive duties

analysis.label: Playing a non-urgent, natural-looking move when the position demands one specific concrete action, squandering a critical tempo that allows the opponent to seize the initiative.
analysis.description: This feature fires on positions where the player makes a 'reasonable-looking' but non-forcing move in a position that has very few acceptable continuations (avg 1.9 good moves). In 7/9 positions, the core tagged motif involves tempo loss. The blundered moves look superficially logical—contesting a file (Re1, Rc3), advancing pawns (d5, c3, g6), improving the king (Kf2, Kg3), or repositioning the queen (Qa2, Qe4+)—but each neglects the position's ONE urgent demand: maintaining a critical defensive connection (Qa2 abandons e2 defense, Re1 abandons g3 defense), executing an immediate breakthrough (Kf2 instead of c5, d5 instead of h5, c3 instead of c4), or avoiding self-obstruction (Kg3 blocks own pawn, g6 traps own bishop). The opponent then exploits the wasted tempo with a concrete tactical or strategic blow that was previously impossible. Positions typically swing 200-800cp because the narrow margin for correct play (often 1 good move) means any tempo waste is catastrophic.
analysis.move_pattern: Any piece type; typically a non-forcing, non-checking, non-capturing move that looks positionally reasonable (centralizing, contesting files, advancing pawns, improving king) but addresses a secondary concern rather than the position's primary urgent need
analysis.why_bad: The position requires one specific concrete action (breakthrough, defensive maintenance, or piece rescue), and the chosen move wastes the final tempo available before the opponent executes a tactical idea—whether exploiting an undefended piece, seizing an outpost, launching a counter-attack on the exposed king, or establishing a permanent positional advantage
sub_patterns: Moving a defender away from its critical post (Qa2, Re1)
Passive pawn move instead of dynamic breakthrough (c3 instead of c4, d5 instead of h5)
Unnecessary king move when immediate pawn action is required (Kf2, Kg3)
Self-obstructing advance that blocks own pieces (g6 traps bishop, Kg3 blocks pawn)
Check on wrong line allowing decisive interposition (Qe4+)

analysis.label: Playing a slow, non-forcing move in a critical position where an immediate check, capture, or forcing continuation was required.
analysis.description: This feature fires on positions where the player chose a quiet, strategically-motivated move (pawn advance, piece retreat, rook repositioning) when the position demanded an immediate forcing continuation. In 7/8 positions, a check or capture was the best move (c3+ check, Qxg8 capture, Be5+ check, Qb5+ check, Nxd4 tactical capture, Kg2 defending f3 against checks, or Rh1 maintaining activity). The played moves all look superficially reasonable—contesting a file, advancing a passer, retreating to safety—but critically waste the tempo needed to execute the winning tactic or maintain a forcing sequence. The average number of good moves available was only 1.6, indicating these are narrow positions requiring precision where the single correct continuation was a forcing move. The enormous average cp_loss (2424) reflects that many positions involved missed forced mates (positions 8 and 12) or missed material-winning captures (position 6).
analysis.move_pattern: Any piece type moving to a non-threatening square (no check, no capture, no direct threat) when a forcing alternative exists
analysis.why_bad: The quiet move surrenders the initiative by wasting a critical tempo, allowing the opponent to execute their own plans (escape the mating net, capture an undefended piece, advance counterplay pawns, or stabilize a lost position) that the forcing move would have prevented.
sub_patterns: Slow pawn advance instead of check or promotion sequence
Piece retreat to passive square missing a hanging piece capture
Queen relocation to irrelevant square instead of delivering forcing checks
Pawn capture on wrong square missing a tactical fork/combination
Rook repositioning inviting unfavorable exchange instead of maintaining pressure

analysis.label: Choosing aggressive-looking moves (captures, forward piece jumps, queen decentralizations) when the position demands quiet preparation or prophylactic defense, allowing the opponent to gain decisive tempo.
analysis.description: This feature fires on positions where the player selects a superficially active or aggressive move while ignoring a more critical quiet/prophylactic need. In 6/6 positions, the correct move was patient and non-aggressive: regrouping a knight (Nbd8, Ne7), prophylactic pawn moves (h6), defensive queen repositioning (Qf1), preparatory queen moves (Qa5), or king safety (Kb8). Instead, the played moves were all 'flashy': capturing an apparently free pawn (Nxe5, 1/6), jumping a knight aggressively forward (Nb4, 2/6), decentralizing the queen to a peripheral 'attacking' square (Qc5, Qh3, 2/6), or making a slow structural move ignoring urgency (b6, 1/6). In every case, the opponent punishes by gaining tempo against the misplaced piece or exploiting the vacancy left behind — the knight gets kicked with a3 (2/6), the queen is challenged by opponent piece centralization (2/6), or a tactical sequence exploits the piece's absence from defense (2/6). The average cp_loss of 308 confirms these are serious blunders that transform advantageous or equal positions into losing ones.
analysis.move_pattern: Pieces (knights or queens) move forward to seemingly active squares, or captures are made on tempting targets, when the correct move involves quiet retreats, regrouping, or prophylactic preparation
analysis.why_bad: The 'active' move neglects a more urgent positional or prophylactic need, and the opponent exploits the misplacement by gaining tempo (kicking the piece, challenging the queen) or by executing tactics made possible by the piece's absence from its proper defensive post
sub_patterns: Knight jumps to forward squares prematurely (Nb4) when preparation is needed first
Queen decentralizes to peripheral attacking square abandoning central coordination
Capturing a poisoned/tactically defended pawn instead of patient regrouping
Ignoring an opponent's imminent pawn advance that requires prophylactic response

analysis.label: Playing a slow or non-urgent move instead of actively challenging the opponent's powerful bishop on the a2-g8 diagonal with a knight.
analysis.description: This feature fires when a player makes a passive or non-urgent move (typically a flank pawn push like a6/b3, a piece retreat like Bf8, or a move that abandons a key defensive post) while the opponent has a strong light-squared bishop stationed on the a2-g8 diagonal (Bc4 or Bb3) creating tactical pressure against f7. In 7/8 positions, the opponent's bishop sits on c4 or b3 bearing down on f7, and in 6/8 cases the best move explicitly involves a knight challenging that bishop (Na5 in positions 1, 3, 5; Nb6 in position 7; Na4 in position 14; Nd4 centralizing in position 12). The played moves all ignore this dominant piece, wasting a critical tempo that allows the opponent to execute devastating breakthroughs (e5 central breaks, Bxf7+ sacrifices, or piece coordination exploiting the unchallenged diagonal). The king is typically uncastled (6/8 positions), making the diagonal pressure even more lethal when left unaddressed.
analysis.move_pattern: Non-forcing moves (flank pawn pushes a6/b3, passive retreats Bf8/Rfe8, or piece relocations away from key squares) that fail to interact with the opponent's active bishop on the long diagonal
analysis.why_bad: The opponent's bishop on the a2-g8 diagonal (Bc4/Bb3) creates imminent tactical threats against f7 and the king; failing to challenge it with a knight gives the opponent a free tempo to execute central breakthroughs (e5, d6, Bxf7+) or consolidate the bishop's dominance, turning the diagonal pressure into a decisive attack.
sub_patterns: Slow flank pawn push (a6, b3) instead of Na5/Nb6 challenging the bishop
Passive piece retreat (Bf8, Rfe8) ignoring the diagonal threat
Moving knight away from key blocking/attacking square (Nf6 from d5, Nxd5 from f6, Nb4 from c6) exposing f7

analysis.label: Playing a tempting but incorrect check when a different move (different square, different piece, or preparatory move) was required for the tactical idea to work.
analysis.description: All 7/7 positions feature the player delivering a check that is either on the wrong square (Qd7+ instead of Qe7+ for perpetual; Qe2+ instead of Qc4+ to win material), with the wrong piece (Qd3+ instead of Bd3+ for forced mate; Ne6+ discovered check instead of Nxf7+ direct check for mate-in-3), in the wrong move order (Rd1+ before the critical Qf8+ deflection), or a check that actively helps the opponent's king escape to safety (Rf8+ allowing Ke2 to a sheltered position; Rxg3+ allowing Kf1 escaping all threats). The common thread is the player recognizing that a check exists and playing it reflexively without verifying it achieves the tactical goal—the 'right idea, wrong execution' pattern where the forcing nature of check creates a false sense of progress.
analysis.move_pattern: Any piece delivering check (+) — queen, rook, or knight checks in all directions, typically toward the enemy king
analysis.why_bad: The check either drives the enemy king to a safer square (breaking attacking geometry), allows the opponent to interpose/capture favorably, uses the wrong piece (leaving a stronger piece misplaced), or skips a necessary preparatory move that would have made the check decisive
sub_patterns: Check on wrong square misses perpetual or tactical geometry (Qd7+ vs Qe7+, Qe2+ vs Qc4+)
Wrong piece delivers check on correct square (Qd3+ vs Bd3+, Ne6+ vs Nxf7+)
Check that improves opponent's king position (Rf8+ allowing Ke2, Rxg3+ allowing Kf1)
Correct check played in wrong move order without preparatory deflection (Rd1+ without Qf8+ first)

analysis.label: King moves forward (usually toward the h-file) into an exposed position where it becomes trapped or mated, when retreating to safety would have drawn or maintained resistance.
analysis.description: In 6/6 positions, the king advances one rank forward (toward the opponent's side) instead of retreating to a safer square. The moves are predominantly to the h-file (5/6: Kh5 x3, Kh3, Kh4) with one to f3. In every case, the correct move was a king retreat: Kh7 (3/6), Kg1 (1/6), Kg2 (1/6), or Kd3/Kd1 (1/6). The advancing king walks into positions where it becomes entombed by its own pawns, the board edge, and opposing queen coverage—allowing forced checkmate (4/6 positions result in mate) or devastating tactical sequences. The positions typically feature queen endgames or queen-heavy positions where the opponent's queen can exploit diagonals and files once the king lands on the exposed forward square. In 4/6 cases, the correct retreat would have maintained a draw (often via perpetual check), making these blunders cases of refusing or failing to recognize drawing resources.
analysis.move_pattern: King moves one square forward (away from own back rank) toward the h-file flank, advancing into an exposed square rather than retreating to shelter
analysis.why_bad: The king advances onto a square where it is trapped by its own pawns, the board edge, and opposing queen diagonal/file coverage, allowing forced checkmate patterns or decisive check sequences. Retreating would have maintained safety or perpetual check draws.
sub_patterns: Kh5 walking into queen diagonal mate with own g/h pawns entombing
King advancing to h3/h4 allowing g5 pawn mate or diagonal checks
King stepping onto diagonal allowing bishop/queen discovered check sequences
Refusing perpetual check draw by advancing king forward

analysis.label: Moving a piece away from a critical defensive or controlling role, immediately creating an exploitable tactical vulnerability.
analysis.description: This feature fires on moves where a piece that was performing a vital protective function (guarding a square, shielding another piece, or blockading a line) relocates to a seemingly reasonable square, instantly leaving a tactical hole. In 5/6 positions, the moved piece was directly defending a specific square or piece: the Nd5 blocked pin diagonals (Position 4, Nf6 allows Bg5 pin), the Kf7 guarded g7 (Position 5, Ke8 allows Qg7 invasion winning the h8 rook), the Ke8 protected the f8 bishop (Position 9, O-O-O allows Rxf8), the Ne5 blockaded the h2-b8 diagonal and defended f4 (Position 10, Nxc6 allows Bxf4), and the Qg7 was safe but Qd4 placed it undefended on a square vulnerable to clearance sacrifice (Position 12, Bxh2+ discovers the queen). The remaining positions show passive moves that ignore the position's concrete demands (Position 6, Qd7 misses en passant; Position 7, Kh7 worsens king exposure). All moves appear superficially logical—retreating, castling, capturing material, centralizing—but catastrophically ignore the specific tactical responsibility the piece was fulfilling.
analysis.move_pattern: Piece relocates from a functionally critical square to a 'natural' or 'safe' square; includes retreats (Nf6, Ke8, Kh7), castling (O-O-O), captures that vacate outposts (Nxc6), and centralizations to undefended squares (Qd4)
analysis.why_bad: The moved piece was the sole guardian of a key square, piece, or diagonal; its departure immediately creates a concrete tactical exploitation (pin, invasion, hanging piece, clearance sacrifice) that the opponent can capitalize on within 1-2 moves.
sub_patterns: Knight retreats from dominant outpost, allowing pin or line-opening (Nf6, Nxc6)
King moves away from piece it was physically shielding (Ke8 leaves g7, O-O-O leaves f8)
King sidesteps to square creating new tactical vulnerabilities (Kh7)
Passive developing move ignores fleeting tactical window (Qd7)
Queen placed on undefended square exploitable by clearance (Qd4)

analysis.label: Moves that waste a critical tempo in razor-sharp positions where only 1-2 moves correctly address an advanced passed pawn or forcing tactical threat.
analysis.description: This feature fires on catastrophic blunders in positions requiring extreme precision (avg 1.8 good moves available). The overwhelming pattern is failing to properly address an urgent threat—most commonly an advanced passed pawn about to promote (7/11 positions involve passed pawns on the 7th rank or creating unstoppable promotion). Position 1: check through the promotion square allowing promotion-with-interposition. Position 3: bishop placed on wrong diagonal, failing to cover c8 promotion square. Position 4: knight blockades instead of capturing a g7 pawn, allowing promotion with check. Position 14: rook abandons blockade of b2 pawn, allowing immediate promotion. Position 8: slow flank move allows d5-d6 creating a crushing advanced passer. Even non-promotion positions share the same core mistake: Position 7 wastes a tempo with Kd7 allowing c4-c5 breakthrough; Position 10 gives a premature check driving the enemy king to a better square; Position 13 walks into immediate checkmate. In every case, the player makes a superficially reasonable move while missing the ONE action the position demands.
analysis.move_pattern: Various piece types moving to plausible but critically wrong squares; often king/piece moves that fail to capture, block, or control a specific promotion-related square
analysis.why_bad: The move wastes the single available tempo to address an urgent forcing threat (usually an advanced passed pawn), allowing the opponent to execute an unstoppable tactical sequence—promotion with check, pawn advance to create a wedge, or immediate checkmate
sub_patterns: Blocking/blockading a passed pawn instead of capturing it outright
Giving a check that passes through the promotion square, allowing promotion-with-interposition
Moving a piece to the wrong square/diagonal to 'stop' promotion
Abandoning blockade duty of an enemy passed pawn
Wasting tempo with aimless king moves when one specific action is required

analysis.label: Playing ambitious or peripheral moves while the player's king remains dangerously exposed in the center, ignoring critical development or simplification needs.
analysis.description: In all 7/7 positions, the player's king (or both kings) remains uncastled in the center, yet the move played pursues a non-urgent agenda—chasing pieces (a3), advancing pawns aggressively (e5, e4), centralizing pieces for attack (Ne4, Qc3), seeking queenside activity (Qb6), or grabbing material (Bxf4)—instead of addressing the critical vulnerability. The best moves in every case involve simplifying exchanges (Nxg6, Nxb6, Bxe5, Bxc3), quiet development (Nd2, Bd3), or castling (O-O). The played moves all create new tactical vulnerabilities—undefended pawns, hanging pieces, loss of coordination—that the opponent exploits specifically because the king's central position makes the position tactically fragile. The refutations consistently involve tactical strikes (forks, discovered attacks, captures with tempo) that are only possible because the king blocks its own rook, sits on open files, or cannot escape to safety.
analysis.move_pattern: Diverse move types (pawn advances, queen repositioning, knight centralization, bishop capture) that share the property of being non-developmental or non-simplifying while the player's king sits on e1/e8
analysis.why_bad: With the king in the center, the position demands development, simplification, or castling—these moves instead waste tempo on secondary goals, leaving the king exposed to tactical exploitation through forks, hanging pieces, and open-file attacks that wouldn't work if the king were safely castled.
sub_patterns: Aggressive pawn advances (e4, e5) that overextend while undeveloped
Queen repositioning (Qb6, Qc3) that ignores central tension
Quiet prophylactic moves (a3) that leave critical squares undefended
Material grabs (Bxf4) that prioritize pawns over king safety
Piece centralization (Ne4) that destroys defensive coordination

analysis.label: Non-forcing, preparatory, or repositioning moves played in positions that demand immediate decisive action, squandering a critical tempo.
analysis.description: In 7/8 positions, the played move wastes a critical tempo on a non-urgent action when the position demands immediate tactical execution. The pattern manifests as: king moves to exposed or purposeless squares instead of breakthrough moves (Kd4 instead of f5, Ke8 instead of Nd7 - 2/8), piece retreats from active posts or to passive squares (Bc2 retreating a well-placed bishop, Rff1 abandoning the dominant f5 square - 2/8), slow pawn moves in tactically urgent positions (c3 instead of O-O, h4 instead of Kg3 - 2/8), and a non-lethal check when immediate checkmate exists (Qg4+ instead of Bd5# - 1/8). In every case, the best moves involve immediate forcing action (pawn breakthroughs, sacrifices, checkmates, piece activation toward targets), while the played moves give the opponent time to consolidate, counter-attack, or neutralize the critical threats. The positions uniformly feature high urgency where one specific tempo cannot be wasted.
analysis.move_pattern: Any piece type moving to a non-forcing, non-attacking square (retreats, sidesteps, non-urgent advances) when a forcing continuation exists
analysis.why_bad: The position has a narrow tactical window requiring immediate action (breakthrough, sacrifice, checkmate, or piece activation toward a target), and the played move hands the opponent a crucial tempo to consolidate defenses, activate counterplay, lock pawn structures, or escape danger
sub_patterns: King moves to exposed squares instead of executing pawn breakthroughs
Piece retreats from dominant active squares to passive positions
Non-urgent pawn moves in tactically critical positions requiring piece activity
Non-lethal checks when immediate checkmate or stronger forcing moves exist

analysis.label: Advancing a pawn (typically on the wing) in an endgame position where immediately activating or marching the king is the urgent priority, wasting a critical tempo.
analysis.description: This feature fires on endgame positions (9/10) where the player makes a non-urgent pawn advance instead of the more pressing king activation. In 7/10 positions the move is a pawn push (h4, h5, a3, a6, b4, b5, f5), predominantly on wing files (a/b/h in 6 cases). The core pattern: in tempo-critical endgames with exposed kings and open centers, the player commits a pawn forward when the king should be marching first. Position 4 (a6 instead of Ke4, costing 592cp), Position 6 (b4 instead of Kb2, costing 659cp), and Position 1 (h4 instead of Kg7, costing 136cp) are the clearest examples where king activation was urgent but a wing pawn was pushed. Even mild activations (Positions 2, 7, 8 with 0-34cp loss) show the same structural pattern of pawn-before-king in endgames. The two rook moves (Positions 5, 10) represent the related error of slow piece repositioning instead of addressing the position's most urgent demand.
analysis.move_pattern: Pawn advance (especially a, b, f, h files) in king-and-pawn or simple piece endgames; occasionally a slow rook repositioning move
analysis.why_bad: In tempo-critical endgames, every move counts in pawn races and king marches. Advancing a pawn that could wait wastes the one tempo needed for the king to reach a critical square (capturing an enemy pawn, establishing a blockade, or escorting a passed pawn), allowing the opponent's king to arrive at its optimal defensive/offensive square first.
sub_patterns: Wing pawn advance instead of king march toward enemy pawn (h4/a3 type)
Prophylactic pawn move instead of decisive king penetration (a6/b4 type)
Pawn structure commitment before king is optimally placed (f5/exd4 type)
Rook repositioning abandoning critical defensive duty (Re8 type)

analysis.label: Playing a plausible-looking attacking move when an immediate checkmate or crushing forced combination was available.
analysis.description: This feature fires on positions where the player has a forced mate or immediately decisive tactical shot but instead plays a non-forcing move that merely looks aggressive. In 4/7 positions, the missed best move involved Qxh2 as either an immediate mate or the start of a mating sequence (Positions 1, 4, 6, 8). In 5/7 positions, the played move was a queen or bishop repositioning to a square that appears to increase pressure but lacks forcing power (Bg5, Qh3, Qa1+, Qa6, Qa3). The average cp_loss of 5844 reflects that these are overwhelmingly won positions where only 1.1 good moves existed on average, meaning the position demanded precise calculation rather than general improvement. The blunders share the quality of choosing 'atmosphere' over concrete threats—moving pieces toward the enemy king without delivering the decisive blow that was already available.
analysis.move_pattern: Queen or bishop moves to non-optimal aggressive squares (h3, a1, a6, a3, g5) instead of immediate captures/sacrifices on h2, g3, or b6 that deliver forced mate or win decisive material
analysis.why_bad: These moves waste the critical tempo needed to execute an immediately available forced mate or crushing combination, giving the opponent time to organize defense (interpose, deflect, simplify) when no defense existed against the correct continuation
sub_patterns: Queen repositioned near enemy king instead of delivering Qxh2# or Qxh2+ mate
Bishop 'improved' instead of executing a mating combination already in progress
Positional pawn capture instead of recognizing an existing one-move checkmate
Flashy check on wrong square instead of simple decisive queen capture

analysis.label: Moves that pursue a secondary objective (material gain, piece activation, aggression) while conceding decisive tempo to the opponent's primary tactical or strategic threat.
analysis.description: This feature fires on positions where the player makes a natural-looking, often tempting move that fatally neglects the position's most urgent demand. In 6/8 cases, the best move involved addressing a concrete defensive need or maintaining a critical piece function (Rg2 maintaining king shelter, Qc6/Ne8 defending key squares, Qe5 staying centralized, Qd4 blockading a passer, Qxf3 preserving pawn shield), while the played move pursued something tangential — grabbing material (Rxb2, Bxd4), aggressive piece activation (Bd6, Qe7), or impulsive pawn advances (f5, e5, gxf3). In 7/8 positions, the core consequence is tempo loss: the opponent gains a free move to execute their primary plan, whether that's a rook check on the opened e-file (f5), a knight attack gaining tempo on an exposed queen (Qe7), pushing a pawn to promotion (Qa1), exploiting an opened g-file (gxf3), or harvesting unprotected pieces (Rxb2, Bd6). The average 1.6 good moves available confirms these are critical decision points demanding precision.
analysis.move_pattern: Diverse piece types and directions; typically captures, forward pawn pushes, or piece moves to 'active-looking' squares that abandon a key defensive function or ignore an immediate threat
analysis.why_bad: Each move concedes a critical tempo or removes a key defensive function, allowing the opponent to execute their primary threat unimpeded — whether exploiting an opened file toward the king, attacking a now-exposed piece, advancing a passed pawn, or launching a tactical combination against abandoned weaknesses
sub_patterns: Pawn grab on the wing while kingside threats are critical (Rxb2, Bxd4)
Aggressive pawn push that weakens own king shelter or opens lines for opponent (f5, gxf3, e5)
Piece placed on exposed/wrong square losing tempo to opponent's attack (Qe7, Qa1, Bd6)

analysis.label: Playing a plausible-looking but non-forcing 'improving' move in a position that demands immediate concrete action, wasting a decisive tempo.
analysis.description: This feature fires when a player makes a non-urgent repositioning or 'improving' move in a position where immediate forcing play is critical. In 6/9 positions, the correct move involved advancing or exploiting a passed pawn (Rf1+ enabling b2 promotion, Nc2+ stopping Black's f-pawn, a7 locking Black's queen, d2 with Qxe5+ check). In 3/9 positions, the error was moving a piece away from a critical defensive duty (Nd5 removing the e7 blocker, Rd5 abandoning f5 kingside defense, Nf5 removing the g3 king shield). The average cp_loss of 2160 and only 1.8 good moves available confirms these are razor-sharp positions where one specific action was required NOW, yet the player chose something that appeared active or useful—centralizing a queen, repositioning a bishop, delivering a purposeless check, making a premature pawn break—that fatally squandered the critical tempo. The opponent then exploits the gift by advancing their own threats, reorganizing defensively (as in position 6 where Rg1 becomes possible), or launching tactical counters (as in position 8 where Qg4+/Nd7+ wins material).
analysis.move_pattern: Mixed piece types (knight, rook, queen, bishop, king, pawn) making non-capturing, non-threatening repositioning moves in positions requiring immediate forcing play
analysis.why_bad: The position has a narrow tactical window or tempo-critical race (usually involving passed pawns, exposed kings, or one-move tactical threats) where a single wasted tempo allows the opponent to reorganize, advance counter-threats, or close the window entirely
sub_patterns: Failing to advance a critical passed pawn when promotion is within reach
Removing a piece from a vital defensive post for an 'active' redeployment
Delivering a purposeless check that forces the piece to retreat, losing two tempi
Making a preparatory move before a forcing sequence that works better immediately
Premature pawn break that opens lines favoring the opponent's better-placed pieces

analysis.label: Aggressive-looking moves (captures, penetrations, pawn pushes) played before necessary preparatory steps, leaving the moved piece trapped, hanging, or stranded.
analysis.description: This feature fires on positions where a player makes an ambitious, active-looking move that appears to gain material, space, or piece activity, but is premature because critical prerequisites haven't been met. In 3/8 positions, pieces are literally trapped after the aggressive move (Bxh7 trapped by g6, h4 removing the bishop's retreat, Rd2 hanging to Bxd2). In 3/8 positions, pieces become stranded or useless after the opponent easily parries the threat (Ra3 accomplishes nothing once Qb2 defends, Rb4 is neutralized by b3, Qxf4 is driven away by Rf1). In 2/8 positions, pawn advances create permanent structural weaknesses (f4 creates an e4 outpost, d5 allows en passant winning material). In nearly all cases (6/8), the correct approach involved patient preparation—developing pieces, addressing prerequisites, or using a different move order that would have made the aggressive idea viable later. The average cp_loss of 292 reflects the severity of these overextensions.
analysis.move_pattern: Various piece types making forward/aggressive moves—rook penetrations to active ranks, pawn pushes gaining space, captures grabbing material—that skip preparatory steps
analysis.why_bad: The aggressive move is played before prerequisites are met (removing defenders, securing retreat squares, controlling key diagonals), so the 'active' piece becomes trapped, hanging, or stranded, or the advance creates permanent weaknesses that the opponent exploits with simple responses
sub_patterns: Piece penetration to active square where it hangs or becomes trapped (Rd2, Bxh7, Ra3)
Pawn advance removing retreat squares or creating permanent holes (h4, f4, d5)
Premature capture that exposes the capturing piece to tempo attacks (Qxf4, Rb4)

analysis.label: Playing a non-urgent, peripheral, or tempo-wasting move in an already worse position that demands immediate attention to king safety or piece development.
analysis.description: In all 5/5 positions, the side making the move is already at a disadvantage and faces urgent demands (king safety, development, maintaining a critical defensive post). Instead of addressing these priorities, the player makes a slow or peripheral move: a flank pawn push (a4, b4, f5 in 3/5), a queen retreat to a vulnerable square (Qd2 in 1/5), or a king move abandoning a key blockading square (Kg5 in 1/5). In 5/5 cases, king safety is a critical factor that the move ignores. In 3/5 positions, severe development lag exists that the move fails to address. In 4/5 cases, the refutation exploits the wasted tempo to penetrate with superior pieces against the exposed king. The common thread is prioritizing a secondary plan (queenside expansion, attacking a pawn, seeking activity) over the position's primary demand, which results in the opponent gaining decisive time to exploit existing vulnerabilities.
analysis.move_pattern: Non-developing moves (pawn pushes to flanks, piece moves to passive/vulnerable squares) that do not address central or king-side urgency
analysis.why_bad: These moves waste a critical tempo in positions where the opponent already has superior piece activity or the player's king is vulnerable, allowing the opponent to exploit the existing weaknesses with decisive tempo-gaining attacks (checks, forks, piece invasions against the exposed king).
sub_patterns: Flank pawn push ignoring undeveloped pieces
King walking away from critical blockading square
Pawn push removing own king's defensive shield
Queen move to square vulnerable to tempo-gaining attack

analysis.label: Playing a superficially attractive move in a critical position where only one narrow tactical resource saves the game.
analysis.description: This feature fires on positions with extremely limited good options (avg 1.3 good moves) where the player selects a natural-looking active move—attacking, checking, capturing, or advancing—but misses the single critical tactical resource. In 6/7 positions, only 1 move was within 50cp of optimal. The correct moves are typically counterintuitive: a quiet bishop development (Bc5), a specific check direction (Qa5+ not Qg2+), a rook sacrifice for perpetual (Rxg2), a tempo-gaining intermediate check (Re8+), or targeting a different pawn than expected (Rd1 vs b2). The blunders all share the quality of looking plausible—Ne3 attacks multiple pieces, Rxc6 wins material, b2 advances a passer, Qe7 appears defensive—but each fatally misjudges what the position actually requires, whether that's maintaining a defensive piece (3/7), finding a drawing resource (2/7), or avoiding creating a tactical target (5/7).
analysis.move_pattern: Mixed piece types and directions; moves are typically forward/aggressive (attacks, checks, captures, pawn advances) rather than defensive or retreating
analysis.why_bad: The moves create immediate-looking threats or grab material but miss the one precise resource the position demands, typically because they either abandon a critical defensive function, place a piece on a tactically vulnerable square, or allow the opponent an improving interposition/recapture that transforms the position.
sub_patterns: Greedy capture leaving piece undefended to checks
Wrong check direction allowing improving interposition
Abandoning key defensive piece for illusory attack
Advancing passed pawn when rook activity was critical
Missing sacrifice that forces perpetual or draw

analysis.label: Playing a king move or quiet pawn advance instead of making a time-critical pawn capture to resolve central/kingside tension on favorable terms.
analysis.description: This feature fires on positions where the player makes a king move (or non-capturing pawn push) when the position demands an immediate pawn capture to resolve critical pawn tension. In 8/11 positions, the best move is a specific pawn capture (dxe3, fxg5, gxf5, exf3, exf4, bxc6, bxa5, gxf4) that resolves tension on the player's terms, but instead the player makes a king move that appears active or centralizing. The opponent then resolves the tension on THEIR terms—often with check or creating a passed pawn—gaining a decisive tempo advantage. The pattern overwhelmingly occurs in pawn endgames (9/11 positions) where a single tempo determines whether a position is drawn or lost. In positions 12 and 13, the same error manifests as a quiet pawn push (b5+, g4) instead of the correct pawn capture. The average cp_loss of 389 reflects how catastrophic this timing error is in simplified positions.
analysis.move_pattern: King moves in any direction (or non-capturing pawn advances) in endgame positions where a specific pawn capture is urgently required
analysis.why_bad: By delaying the critical pawn capture, the player allows the opponent to resolve the pawn tension on their own terms—typically capturing with check, creating a passed pawn, or centralizing their king to a dominant square that was previously blocked by the tension.
sub_patterns: King move ignoring adjacent pawn tension
Pawn push past capture square instead of taking
King centralization when pawn exchange resolves position

analysis.label: Playing a routine developing or structural move while failing to block the opponent's queen bearing down the open e-file toward the player's uncastled king.
analysis.description: In 5/7 positions, the opponent's queen sits on the open e-file aimed directly at the player's uncastled king (e1 or e8), and the player makes a 'normal' move (d6, Nf3, Bf4, Qc6, b5) that completely ignores this critical pressure. In every case, the best move involves interposing a piece on e2 (for White: Qe2, Be2, Ne2, or O-O) or e6/e7 (for Black: Qe7, Qe6) to neutralize the pin/x-ray. Position 12 (Rfe1+) is a wrong-rook error that also revolves around e-file piece coordination, and Position 14 (b5) features a king stuck in the center vulnerable to a central break while the player ignores development urgency. The common thread across 6/7 positions is an uncastled king on the e-file with the opponent's queen exploiting it, and the played move fails to address this single most critical positional demand.
analysis.move_pattern: Miscellaneous developing/structural moves (pawns, minor pieces, queen) that do NOT interpose on the e-file between opponent's queen and player's king
analysis.why_bad: The opponent's queen controls the open e-file aimed at the uncastled king, creating latent pins, x-rays, or tactical threats. By not interposing (placing a piece on e2/e6/e7), the player allows the opponent to exploit the file with pawn breaks, piece challenges, or discovered attacks that win material or collapse the position.
sub_patterns: White plays Nf3/Bf4 instead of Qe2/Be2/Ne2/O-O to block Black's queen on e-file
Black plays d6/b5 instead of Qe7/Bb4+ to neutralize White's queen on e-file
Black plays Qc6 instead of Qe6 to defend e4-bishop while blocking the e-file
Wrong rook sent to e-file destroying critical f-file mating coordination

analysis.label: Quiet, non-forcing moves that waste a critical tempo by ignoring an immediate tactical vulnerability the position demanded be addressed first.
analysis.description: This feature fires on positions where the player makes a natural-looking but non-urgent move (retreat, quiet development, passive pawn push) while an immediate tactical problem exists that required attention. In 10/12 positions, the correct move involved either active engagement (Kd2 not Kd1, Kf3 not Ke1, Kc3 not Kc1, Rb7 not g3, Nxg4 not Bxc6, Rb1+ not Rd4+) or addressing a specific vulnerability (saving Bg5 not developing Be2, keeping Nc6 defending d5 not playing Na5, moving Be2 off a fork diagonal not developing Bd2). The blunder pattern is consistent: the played move addresses no immediate need while the opponent gets a 'free move' to execute their primary threat—whether that's capturing a hanging piece (Be2 ignoring Bg5 en prise, g3 allowing Nc6xBb4), exploiting a removed defender (Na5 leaving Nd5 unprotected, Qd7 unguarding the f8-Ba3 diagonal), or winning material through a newly enabled tactic (Bd2 allowing fork on d4, Qe6 allowing cxd5). The average cp_loss of 274 with only 2.1 good moves available confirms these are positions demanding precise, active responses where passive play is catastrophically punished.
analysis.move_pattern: Quiet retreats (king to back rank), passive developments (bishop to 2nd rank), non-forcing pawn pushes, or aimless piece repositioning—moves that go backward or sideways rather than addressing the critical tactical tension
analysis.why_bad: These moves waste the one tempo needed to address an immediate tactical vulnerability (hanging piece, undefended key defender, exposed piece on exploitable square), giving the opponent a free move to execute their primary threat—typically winning material through capture, fork, pin, or removal of a critical defender
sub_patterns: King retreating to back rank when active centralization was needed (Kd1/Ke1/Kc1 vs Kd2/Kf3/Kc3)
Developing a different piece while one piece is en prise (Be2 ignoring hanging Bg5)
Moving a key defender away from its defensive duty (Na5 abandoning defense of Nd5)
Quiet pawn moves in positions requiring immediate piece action (g3/b4 when Rb7/Nxc6 needed)
Queen repositioning that creates new tactical vulnerabilities (Qd7 enabling pin, Qe6 enabling capture)

analysis.label: Playing seemingly natural or active piece moves that neglect the position's most urgent priority, typically king safety or a concrete tactical opportunity.
analysis.description: In 4/5 positions, the played move was a piece deployment to a seemingly active square (Bc5, Qxe5, Rf8, Qe7) that looked natural or developing but missed the critical urgency of the position. In 3/5 positions (Qxe5, Rf8, Qe7), the best move was castling (O-O) or directly addressing king safety, and the king remained dangerously in the center. In position 12, Rf8 actually forfeited castling rights entirely, enabling a diagonal exploitation tactic. In position 14, Qe7 blocked the f8-bishop and allowed Nd5 with tempo. In position 2, Bc5 was a slow repositioning when Ng5 delivered a decisive tactical blow. The common thread is choosing a move that 'looks active' (piece to a central/useful-looking square, or a material grab) while being blind to the position's true critical demand - usually the exposed king's vulnerability or a concrete forcing sequence.
analysis.move_pattern: Piece (bishop, queen, or rook) moves to a seemingly active central square (c5, e5, e7, f6, f8) without addressing king vulnerability
analysis.why_bad: These moves prioritize superficial piece activity or material gain over the position's most urgent need (castling, king safety, or exploiting a concrete tactic), allowing the opponent to punish the exposed king or seize a lasting initiative through tempo-gaining threats.
sub_patterns: Pawn grab that permanently prevents castling
Quiet piece repositioning when a forcing tactical sequence exists
Rook/queen move that forfeits castling rights or blocks development
Queen placement that allows knight fork/tempo gains

analysis.label: Playing a non-forcing move (often targeting a pawn) when an immediate check or forcing continuation would maintain a decisive advantage.
analysis.description: In 6/7 analyzed positions, the player chose a quiet repositioning move—typically a rook sliding to attack a pawn, a slow pawn push, or a passive king/queen move—when the position demanded an immediate forcing move, almost always a check. In positions 5, 6, and 7 (Rd5, R7c6, Re7), White moved a rook to target a pawn instead of delivering a rook check that would have been decisive (Rf5+, Rc8+, Rb7+ respectively). In positions 2 and 3 (g3, b4), slow pawn pushes were played when active piece play was urgent. In positions 1 and 4 (Qe4, Kh8), passive piece/king moves lost the critical tempo needed to maintain control. The universal consequence is that the single lost tempo allows the opponent to escape (king flees back rank 3/7), generate counterplay (pawn breaks equalizing 2/7), or establish perpetual check (1/7). The average cp_loss of 1661 reflects how catastrophic even one tempo can be in these sharp positions.
analysis.move_pattern: Non-checking piece repositioning (especially rooks laterally or to central squares) targeting pawns instead of delivering available checks
analysis.why_bad: The quiet move surrenders the initiative by giving the opponent one free tempo, which is enough for the king to escape a mating net, for counterplay to equalize, or for a perpetual check mechanism to activate—positions where forcing moves (checks) would have maintained an irresistible attack.
sub_patterns: Rook targets pawn instead of giving check (Rd5/R7c6/Re7 vs Rf5+/Rc8+/Rb7+)
Slow pawn push when active piece play needed (g3/b4)
Passive king or queen move losing critical tempo (Kh8/Qe4)

analysis.label: Playing a superficially logical but non-forcing move in a position that demands the single precise tactical response.
analysis.description: This feature activates when a player makes a 'plan-based' or positionally-motivated move in a position where only ONE good move exists (avg 1.1 good moves available) and tactical precision is required. In 7/8 positions, the played move either wastes a critical tempo on a flank pawn push (f4, a4, h4) or repositions a piece to a seemingly active square (Ba6, Qg8, Qg4, Rg6, Kf6) while ignoring the single urgent tactical demand. The moves look reasonable from a strategic standpoint—expanding on the flank, activating pieces, centralizing the king—but catastrophically miss that the position has an immediate tactical vulnerability requiring attention. In 5/8 cases, the move actively removes a critical defensive element (f-pawn shielding a diagonal, king proximity protecting a piece, queen deterring an invasion) rather than merely wasting time. The average cp_loss of 475 reflects positions where the gap between the one correct move and all alternatives is enormous.
analysis.move_pattern: Non-forcing, non-capturing moves—typically flank pawn advances (a4, f4, h4) or piece relocations to seemingly active but tactically vulnerable squares (Ba6, Qg4, Qg8, Rg6, Kf6)
analysis.why_bad: The position has exactly one critical tactical need (defending a key square, resolving central tension, maintaining a tactical relationship between pieces) and the chosen move ignores this need entirely, either wasting the tempo on a secondary plan or actively dismantling a tactical defense the player didn't recognize existed.
sub_patterns: Flank pawn push ignoring central/tactical crisis (f4, a4, h4)
Removing a piece from its critical defensive function without recognizing the tactical linkage (Kf6, Qg8)
Placing a piece on a square where it becomes vulnerable to tempo-gaining attacks (Qg4, Ba6, Rg6)

analysis.label: Moves that abandon critical defensive coordination in positions where one or both kings are dangerously exposed, often choosing an active-looking alternative over a necessary defensive duty.
analysis.description: This feature fires on positions where kings are exposed with weak or absent pawn shields (11/11 positions feature at least one exposed king, and 7/11 feature both kings exposed). The moves played typically abandon a critical defensive function: pieces leave protective posts for seemingly active squares (Nf5 abandoning d6 defense 1/11, Bg5 abandoning g7 coverage 1/11, Nxe5 removing the f3 kingside guardian 1/11), kings retreat to the wrong square (Kd7 and Kh6 both should have been Kf7, 2/11), queens leave control of key fork squares (Qb6 instead of Qc7 covering e5, 1/11), or material is grabbed at the cost of initiative against an exposed king (Bxb5 and Bxh6, 2/11). The positions share an extremely low average of 1.9 good moves available, indicating critical decision points where only precise defensive choices maintain the balance. Notably, the few correctly-played moves that activate this feature (Bxf3 at 0cp, b6 at 36cp, Kc6 at 7cp) occur in the same exposed-king positional archetype, confirming the feature identifies the position type rather than exclusively the error type.
analysis.move_pattern: Diverse piece types (king, knight, bishop, queen, pawn) moving to squares that appear active or natural but fail to address the critical defensive requirement of the position—often lateral king retreats, piece moves to the 5th rank, or captures on wing files
analysis.why_bad: In positions with exposed kings and very few adequate moves, the player prioritizes apparent piece activity, material gain, or instinctive king retreat over the one specific defensive coordination needed—abandoning a key defender, sending the king toward the wrong flank, or grabbing material while a tactical refutation (fork, invasion, passed pawn breakthrough) becomes available
sub_patterns: King retreating to wrong square when only one direction is safe (Kd7/Kh6 instead of Kf7)
Piece abandoning a critical defensive post for an active-looking square (Nf5, Bg5, Nxe5)
Material grab that squanders attacking initiative against exposed king (Bxb5, Bxh6)
Queen misplacement leaving tactical holes around vulnerable king (Qb6 not covering fork square)

analysis.label: Playing a natural-looking quiet move when a specific forcing continuation was required to exploit a time-sensitive tactical opportunity.
analysis.description: In all 4/4 positions, the player chose a 'reasonable' non-forcing move (centralizing a queen, developing a bishop, castling, targeting a pawn) when a precise concrete move was urgently needed. In Position 1, Qc5 centralized the queen instead of Rc8 which tactically won a knight. In Position 5, O-O was 'safe' development instead of Ne5 which exploited a pin to win material. In Position 11, Qc4 targeted pawns instead of Qb4 which created unstoppable back-rank threats. In Position 2, Bg4 repositioned a bishop instead of Bc4 which exploited Black's uncastled king. All positions featured very narrow best-move counts (avg 1.5 good moves), indicating critical moments demanding calculation, and all actual best moves were forcing/concrete (attacking pinned pieces, creating unstoppable threats, executing double attacks). The blundered moves are the type of moves a player makes when treating a sharp position as a 'normal' one.
analysis.move_pattern: Quiet piece repositioning (queen centralization, bishop development, castling) - no checks, no captures, no direct threats
analysis.why_bad: These moves surrender a time-sensitive tactical window; once the opponent gets one free move, they consolidate (break a pin, centralize a queen, castle to safety) and the concrete opportunity vanishes permanently.
sub_patterns: Queen repositioning when a different queen square created mating/back-rank threats
Piece development when a forcing attack on a pinned/overloaded piece was available
Castling when the opponent's vulnerability demanded immediate exploitation

analysis.label: Piece moves to an aggressive square targeting a specific pawn, but the piece becomes vulnerable to counter-attack or the target is easily removed, losing critical tempo.
analysis.description: In all 3/3 positions, the played move sends a piece to an attacking square that targets a specific pawn in the opponent's camp (Rh3 targets a3, Nb5 targets c7, Bc4 targets f7), but in each case the opponent can either remove the target (a4 pushing past the attack), counter-attack the piece with tempo (Ba6/Bd7 hitting the knight, b5 hitting the bishop), or both. The analyses consistently tag 'tempo_loss' (3/3) and 'piece_activity' (3/3) as core motifs. In all cases, 2-3 good alternatives existed that focused on flexible piece placement or immediate development rather than committing to a single-target attack. The common thread is that the piece leaves a superior square for an apparently aggressive but committal one, giving the opponent a concrete way to improve their position while neutralizing the threat.
analysis.move_pattern: Any piece moving to an aggressive square targeting a specific opponent pawn (rank/file/diagonal), committing to one function
analysis.why_bad: The targeted pawn can be defended, pushed away, or the attacking piece itself becomes a counter-target, meaning the opponent gains tempo while deflecting the threat and simultaneously improving their own position.
sub_patterns: Rook moving laterally to attack a wing pawn that can simply advance
Knight jumping to outpost where it becomes a target for bishop activation
Bishop developing to active diagonal where it's hit by a pawn advance

analysis.label: Playing slow, non-forcing positional moves in positions that demand immediate tactical action (capturing hanging pieces, addressing mating threats, or resolving critical tension).
analysis.description: All 5 positions share a critical pattern: the player chose a quiet, non-threatening move while an urgent tactical opportunity or defensive necessity was screaming for attention. In 2/5 cases (Nb1, Na3), the player made slow knight maneuvers while an undefended rook on a8 was freely capturable by the queen. In 2/5 cases (Kg5, b6), the player ignored immediate king safety emergencies—walking into pawn checks or ignoring a mating attack involving Nxh6+. In 1/5 cases (f3), a slow pawn support move was played when the position demanded immediate central resolution to exploit a forced queen trade stripping castling rights. The average cp_loss of 2023 and only 1.6 good moves available confirm these are critical moments where one specific action was required. All played moves are non-forcing (no check, no capture, no direct threat), and all represent the player treating a tactically explosive position as though it were calm and strategic.
analysis.move_pattern: Non-forcing, non-capturing moves (knight retreats/rim moves, quiet pawn pushes, or king walks) that neither create threats nor address existing ones
analysis.why_bad: These moves waste a critical tempo in positions where an immediate tactic exists (hanging piece capture, mating threat to address, or forced favorable exchange), allowing the opponent to consolidate, defend the hanging piece, or execute their own tactical threat unopposed
sub_patterns: Knight retreating/repositioning while enemy piece hangs
Slow flank pawn push ignoring kingside mating attack
King walking into pawn-check minefield instead of addressing pawn tension
Quiet pawn move blocking development in sharp opening position

analysis.label: Choosing a superficially attractive move that abandons the position's critical active element, wasting decisive tempo.
analysis.description: In all three positions, the player had a significant positional asset (ability to eliminate a key attacking piece, development tempo advantage, or 7th-rank rook pressure) but chose a move that looked appealing on the surface while abandoning that critical resource. In position 2 (gxh3), Black captured a worthless h-pawn instead of eliminating the crucial f3 knight with gxf3 (1/3 positions showing wrong capture direction). In position 3 (Ne5), White lunged a knight to a 'strong' outpost that was immediately refutable, instead of developing naturally with Nc3/h4/Qe1+ (1/3 showing premature piece placement). In position 12 (Raa8), White retreated an actively-placed rook from the 7th rank to the passive 8th rank, surrendering the counterplay that kept the position defensible (1/3 showing retreat from active position). All 3/3 positions were tagged 'tempo_loss' and 'piece_activity' in analysis, confirming the unifying theme: each move wastes a critical tempo at a moment when precision was essential (avg 1.7 good moves available).
analysis.move_pattern: Various piece types making moves that look aggressive or natural but abandon the one active element that matters - captures toward the edge, knight jumps to unsupported outposts, or rook retreats from active ranks
analysis.why_bad: Each move squanders the position's key tactical or positional resource (attacking piece elimination, development coordination, or rank pressure) in favor of something superficially appealing, giving the opponent time to consolidate or counterattack against the newly passive setup.
sub_patterns: Wrong capture direction (toward rim instead of toward key piece)
Premature outpost occupation on unsustainable square
Rook retreat from active rank to passive position

analysis.label: Playing a preparatory or seemingly reasonable move that weakens one's own king position when an immediately decisive action was available.
analysis.description: This feature fires on positions where the player holds a significant advantage but chooses a slow, self-weakening move instead of the immediately decisive continuation. In 5/6 positions, the move directly compromised the player's own king safety: f3 and g3 weakened kingside pawn shelters (positions 1, 4), f6 opened the critical a2-g8 diagonal toward the castled king (position 2), Kb6 placed the king on an exposed square vulnerable to checks along files and diagonals (position 3), and Nf5 invited g4 which blows open lines against the player's own king (position 6). In all 6 cases, clearly superior immediate actions existed (b5/Rf7/Bxe7/Be8/Kd7) that would have maintained or increased the advantage, but the player chose a plausible-looking alternative that either lost critical tempo (4/6 positions had avg 1.7 good moves, demanding precision) or created new vulnerabilities the opponent could exploit. The average cp_loss of 233 reflects positions where advantages of +192 to +454 were squandered to near-equality or worse.
analysis.move_pattern: Pawn advances near own king (f3/f6/g3) or piece placements to tactically vulnerable squares (Kb6/Nf5/Nxc6), typically appearing preparatory or defensive rather than immediately decisive
analysis.why_bad: These moves waste a critical tempo and/or create structural weaknesses around the player's own king, giving the opponent time to either consolidate their king's safety, open attacking lines against the player's weakened position, or exploit newly created tactical vulnerabilities—all in positions where immediate decisive action would have been conclusive.
sub_patterns: f/g-pawn advances weakening own castled king shelter when queenside/7th-rank invasion was available
King moving to exposed square instead of safe centralization
Piece placement on insecure outpost inviting pawn storm against own king
Wrong exchange trading dominant piece instead of exploiting tactical blow

analysis.label: Moves motivated by pawn capture or defense that fatally abandon a critical positional responsibility, allowing the opponent's most dangerous resource to become decisive.
analysis.description: In 5/6 positions, the player chooses a move oriented toward material gain (Nxf2 captures pawn, Qxc7 captures pawn) or pawn-related defense/support (Ra4 supports passed a-pawn, Rg5 defends g4 pawn, h5 attempts to stabilize pawn structure) while ignoring the critical strategic imperative. In each case, the correct move addresses the opponent's most dangerous threat: Re1 restrains the e-pawn (pos 4), Bxg5/hxg5 captures free material (pos 6), Rc8 eliminates dangerous knights (pos 1), f4 addresses f2 weakness (pos 4/Qxc7), Kh8 avoids the fatal diagonal (pos 2), and Kg5 maintains rook activity on e-file (pos 5). The abandoned duties include: e-file control (2/6: Ra4, Rg5), guard of critical squares (Nxf2 removes g4 knight guarding f6), kingside defense (Qxc7 displaces queen), and diagonal awareness (Kg8). All positions featured multiple strong alternatives (avg 2.0 good moves) making these avoidable errors.
analysis.move_pattern: Mixed piece types moving to capture or support pawns, typically lateral rook moves or piece captures away from the critical zone of action
analysis.why_bad: The moves abandon a critical restraining or defensive obligation—file control, key square coverage, or proximity to the opponent's most dangerous threat—in exchange for secondary material gain or pawn defense, allowing the opponent to activate a decisive tactical or positional resource (passed pawn advance, knight fork, discovered check, rook dominance)
sub_patterns: Greedy pawn captures removing a piece from a defensive role (Nxf2, Qxc7)
Rook abandoning a critical open file to support/defend pawns (Ra4, Rg5)
Passive pawn moves declining free captures or ignoring dynamic priorities (h5)
King moves that appear safe but walk into geometric vulnerabilities (Kg8)

analysis.label: Making a rook move (or pawn push) when the position urgently demands a king relocation to escape tactical danger.
analysis.description: In 12/12 positions, the best move was a king move to address an exposed/vulnerable king, but instead the player made a rook move (10/12) or a quiet pawn push (2/12). The rook moves (Rd3, Rd6, Rf7, Rd7, Re6, Rf6, Re7) all place the rook on squares that become tactically vulnerable—either undefended on an open file/diagonal, blocking the king's own escape route, or within reach of the opponent's queen and advancing king. The correct king moves (Kf2, Ke1, Ke6, Kd6, Kf5, Kg8, Kh7, Kd7, etc.) all prioritize evacuating the monarch from exposed central or open-file squares. The blunders share the characteristic that the position appears to need 'consolidation' or 'activity' from the rook, but in reality the king's safety is the single most urgent priority, and delaying it by even one tempo allows devastating tactical exploitation.
analysis.move_pattern: Rook moves along open files/ranks (or quiet pawn pushes) when the king sits exposed on an open file, diagonal, or central square needing immediate relocation
analysis.why_bad: The king is critically exposed and needs to move immediately; the rook move wastes the crucial tempo, often placing the rook on an undefended/trappable square or blocking the king's own escape, allowing the opponent to exploit the still-exposed king with checks, file seizure, or mating attacks.
sub_patterns: Rook blocks own king's escape square (Rd7 blocking Ke7, Re7 blocking Ke7)
Rook moves to undefended square on open file/diagonal, gets captured (Rd3, Rd6, Rf6)
Rook retreats passively instead of king relocating (Rf7, Re6, Re7)
Quiet pawn push ignores urgent king safety (g4, h3)

analysis.label: Active-looking moves (checks, advances, development) that abandon a critical tactical responsibility or miss a concrete opportunity in the position.
analysis.description: This feature fires on moves that appear purposeful or aggressive—delivering checks (Rf8+, Rb3+), centralizing the king (Ke3), advancing pawns for space (c4, e4, g4), developing pieces (Bg5), or repositioning (Rc2)—but concretely worsen the position by ignoring a specific tactical demand. In 5/8 positions, a forcing tactical shot was available but missed (Rxf6 sacrifice, Rg2+ king hunt, Nxf3+ structure destruction, Bxc3+ pin exploitation). In 3/8 positions, the move directly abandoned defense of a piece or critical square (Ke3 leaving Bf1 hanging, Rf8+ leaving Rg3 en prise, Rc2 abandoning the dominant c6 outpost). In 3/8 positions, pawn advances prematurely released tension that held the position together (c4 freeing dxe5, e4 losing a pawn to fxe4, g4 gifting a pawn). The average cp_loss of 279 reflects that these positions typically had few good moves (avg 2.2) and demanded precise calculation rather than general principles.
analysis.move_pattern: Diverse piece types and directions (rook retreats/checks, king advances, pawn pushes, bishop development); unified by being 'proactive' moves that pursue a plan rather than address the position's concrete tactical demands
analysis.why_bad: Each move prioritizes a general strategic goal (activity, space, centralization, development, checks) over a specific tactical requirement—either exploiting a concrete combination or maintaining defense of a critical piece/square. The player follows heuristics ('checks are good,' 'centralize the king,' 'gain space') instead of calculating the position's forcing lines.
sub_patterns: Pointless checks that misplace attacking pieces away from optimal squares (Rf8+, Rb3+)
Premature pawn breaks that release tension and lose material (c4, e4, g4)
Piece moves that abandon defense of unprotected pieces (Ke3 leaving Bf1, Rc2 leaving c6 outpost)
Aggressive development that ignores existing tactical vulnerabilities (Bg5 ignoring c3 pin)

analysis.label: Quiet repositioning or retreating moves that miss immediate captures or concrete tactical solutions the position demands.
analysis.description: This feature fires on positions where the player makes a passive, repositioning, or prophylactic move when the position requires immediate concrete action—typically a capture or forcing move.
