In 4/7 positions, the best move was a direct capture (Qxc3 winning a free pawn in position 3, Bxg5 capturing an undefended pawn in position 4, Nxe4 trading equal material in position 12) or an active piece centralization (Ke6 in position 5, Qe3 in position 6). Instead, the moves played retreat pieces to passive squares (Bg7 retreating to a blocked diagonal, Nh2 burying the knight in the corner, Kf8 moving toward the edge) or make non-urgent pawn moves (g6 addressing a non-immediate threat). In position 7, d4 advances a pawn into tactical vulnerability rather than playing patient consolidation. The common thread across 5/7 positions is that the player perceived a positional need (improving piece placement, prophylaxis, freeing the position) while overlooking that the position's concrete tactical features demanded immediate resolution—either a forcing capture or an active centralization that maintains control.
analysis.move_pattern: Pieces retreat toward back rank/rim or pawns advance non-forcingly, ignoring available captures on central/active squares
analysis.why_bad: These moves spend tempo on cosmetic improvements or address non-urgent concerns, allowing the opponent to stabilize a weakness, escape tactical pressure, or exploit the newly passive piece placement through forcing continuations
sub_patterns: Bishop/knight retreating to passive rim squares (Bg7, Nh2) instead of capturing available targets
Defensive pawn moves (g6) ignoring immediate tactical captures
King moving toward edge/corner instead of centralizing (Kf8 vs Ke6)
Wrong piece capturing when correct piece maintains material equality (Rxe4 vs Nxe4)
Pawn advance creating an undefended target in enemy piece territory (d4)

analysis.label: Checks that drive the enemy king to a safer square, when a different check square or a non-checking move would maintain the attack or drawing resource.
analysis.description: All 11/11 positions feature a check (queen check in 8 cases, rook check in 3) that worsens the attacker's position by allowing the enemy king to escape to safety. The recurring failure mode is that the check either (a) targets the wrong square, missing a geometrically superior check that maintains critical pressure (e.g., Qf2+ instead of Qf4+ which controls c1; Qc2+ instead of Qc4+ which keeps the king exposed; Qd2+ instead of Qe4+ which lines up a capture on g4), seen in ~6/11 positions, or (b) is a premature forcing move when a quiet non-checking move would be stronger (e.g., Ra1+ instead of Qxe3 preserving back-rank mate threats; Qe8+ instead of b5 advancing a passer), seen in ~5/11 positions. In 5/11 positions, the correct move was specifically a perpetual check mechanism that the played check abandoned. The average cp_loss of 1131 reflects how catastrophically these checks backfire—typically converting wins or draws into losses by gifting the king one critical escape tempo.
analysis.move_pattern: Queen or rook delivering check (any direction), typically moving to a square that fails to control the enemy king's best escape route
analysis.why_bad: The check allows the enemy king to reach a fundamentally safer square (e.g., back rank, behind pawns, or off a dangerous diagonal/file), after which the attacker's threats dissipate and the checking piece often ends up misplaced—meanwhile the correct alternative either kept the king confined, maintained a perpetual check geometry, or created unstoppable threats without needing to check.
sub_patterns: Wrong check square: correct check controls the escape route the played check misses (Qf4+ vs Qf2+, Qc4+ vs Qc2+, Qe4+ vs Qd2+, Qe5+ vs Rf3+)
Premature check: quiet move creates stronger threats than the forcing check (Ra1+ vs Qxe3, Qe8+ vs b5, Rd7+ vs Qd5+)
Abandoned perpetual: check breaks the only drawing shuttle pattern (Qb1+ vs Qd4+, Rf3+ vs Qe5+)
Speculative trap check: check hoping opponent blunders into mate but trivially refuted (Qe8+ hoping for Bf8??)

analysis.label: Black plays a slow flank pawn move (usually ...b6 for fianchetto) when behind in development, ignoring immediate central threats that punish the tempo loss.
analysis.description: In 6/6 positions, Black plays a non-developing flank pawn move (b6 in 5/6, h6 in 1/6) intended to prepare a bishop deployment (fianchetto to b7 or challenging a g5 bishop), but in each case the position demands immediate central action. The best moves consistently involve central pawn play (d5, d6, f6) or piece development (Be7, Ne7). In 5/6 cases both kings are still in the center during the opening, and Black is already slightly worse with underdeveloped pieces. The refutations exploit the tempo loss via central pawn thrusts (e5 in positions 5 and 13, d6 in position 14) displacing Black's pieces, or queen invasions along weakened diagonals (Qd5 exploiting the a8-h1 diagonal in positions 1 and 7). The average cp_loss of 262 reflects how severely these slow moves are punished when concrete central action was available.
analysis.move_pattern: Black pawn advances one square on the b-file (b7-b6) or h-file (h7-h6) — non-developing flank pawn push
analysis.why_bad: The flank pawn move wastes a critical tempo in an underdeveloped position, allowing White to exploit the center with immediate pawn advances (e5, d6) that gain tempi on Black's pieces, or to invade on diagonals weakened by the pawn's departure (a8-h1 after b6, dark squares after h6).
sub_patterns: b6 exposes a8 rook on long diagonal, allowing Qd5 invasion
b6 ignores e4-e5 pawn thrust displacing Nf6
b6 ignores d5-d6 advanced pawn creating a paralyzing wedge
h6 weakens dark squares allowing Bf6 crushing bind

analysis.label: Playing a non-defensive or secondary-purpose move when the position demands an immediate, specific response to a lethal king-safety threat.
analysis.description: In 7/9 positions, the player faces an immediate tactical crisis involving their king's safety (forced mate threats, discovered checks, or devastating infiltration) where only 1-3 moves survive. Instead of addressing this crisis, the player makes a move with an unrelated purpose: pawn advances for 'counterplay' (h4, f4, e6, g3, c5, a6 — 6/9 are pawn pushes), a king move to the wrong square (Kg1, Kh7 — 2/9), or an aggressive piece placement that creates a target (Bh5). In every case, the position had very few surviving moves (avg 2.2), and the chosen move fatally ignores the primary threat — whether it's diagonal queen checks (positions 1, 2, 14), discovered attacks (position 8), removal of a critical defensive barrier (positions 3, 7), or rook invasion on an open rank (position 5). The catastrophic average cp_loss of 6243 reflects that these moves typically convert defensible-but-bad positions into immediate forced checkmates.
analysis.move_pattern: Mostly pawn advances (6/9) or king moves to wrong squares (2/9); non-forcing, non-checking moves in positions requiring a precise defensive response
analysis.why_bad: The move wastes the critical tempo needed for the one defensive resource that prevents immediate checkmate or decisive tactical exploitation, while often actively worsening the position by removing defenders, opening lines toward the king, or stepping into tactical patterns
sub_patterns: Pawn push that removes critical defensive barrier (g3, f4)
Pawn push ignoring existing mating diagonal/rank threat (a6, h4, e6)
King move to square with worse tactical exposure (Kg1, Kh7)
Premature strategic advance in tactically critical position (c5, e6)

analysis.label: Non-forcing piece improvements (especially rook/king moves) that waste critical tempo when an immediate concrete action—capturing a target, advancing a passer, or delivering a forcing blow—was required.
analysis.description: Across all 10 positions, the played moves share a common thread: they reposition a piece to a 'reasonable-looking' square without creating an immediate forcing threat, while the position demanded direct, concrete action. In 7/10 cases, a rook is moved to a square that appears active but misses the critical target (Rb7, Rg5, Rb4, Re7, Re3, Rd6, and implicitly Rb7's lateral nature). In 3/10 cases, a king or pawn move wastes a tempo (Kh5 chasing a pawn the rook could win, Kf6 approaching when c3 was urgent, Ke3 abandoning blockade duty, a6 as prophylaxis missing a fork). The best moves in each case were sharply forcing: back-rank skewers (Rh8+ in pos 2), immediate pawn captures (Rh5 hitting g5 in pos 6, Ra5 hitting a4 in pos 7), passed pawn advances (c3 in pos 3), checkmate (Rd4 in pos 9), or tactical combinations (Ndb4 in pos 13). The average of only 1.5 good moves available confirms these are narrow positions demanding precision over general improvement. All 9 endgame positions feature time-sensitive elements (pawn races, back-rank threats, exposed kings) where one tempo of non-forcing play allows the opponent to consolidate or generate counterplay.
analysis.move_pattern: Piece (usually rook or king) moves to a square that appears reasonable/active but does not directly attack a target, deliver check, capture material, or advance a passed pawn—often moving laterally or up/down a file to a non-threatening square
analysis.why_bad: These moves squander critical tempo in positions with urgent concrete demands (pawn races, back-rank vulnerabilities, undefended targets, or mating nets), allowing the opponent to escape, consolidate, advance their own threats, or generate counterplay that would have been impossible had the forcing continuation been played immediately.
sub_patterns: Rook repositioning away from the critical sector/target (Rb4 away from kingside, Rg5 missing back-rank check, Rd6 abandoning lateral attack on h4)
King walking toward a target that the rook could attack faster (Kh5 chasing h4 pawn, Kf6 approaching instead of pushing c3)
Rook moving to the 7th rank for general pressure but exposing the back rank or missing forced mate (Re7, Re3)
Prophylactic/positional pawn move ignoring concrete tactical combination (a6 missing Ndb4 fork)
King move abandoning a critical blockading square for passed pawns (Ke3 leaving c3 unguarded)

analysis.label: Playing a non-forcing, preparatory or repositioning move when the position demands immediate concrete action, squandering a decisive tempo.
analysis.description: This feature detects positions where the player chooses a quiet, non-forcing move—a pawn push, piece repositioning, or material grab—in a critical moment that demands urgent tactical or strategic precision. In 6/7 positions, the analyses explicitly tag 'tempo_loss' as the core motif, and the average number of good moves is only 1.4, indicating extremely narrow positions where one wasted tempo is catastrophic. The moves share a common character: they address secondary concerns (prophylaxis, structure, material) while ignoring the primary urgent need. In Position 8 and 12, slow h5 pawn pushes ignore the need for immediate central action or defensive queen repositioning. In Position 13, a structural c4 push ignores a crushing Re7 seventh-rank invasion. In Position 6, grabbing a pawn with Nxc4 abandons a dominant knight outpost. In Position 2, Be6 retreats an already-active piece. In all cases, the opponent exploits the gifted tempo to seize the initiative decisively.
analysis.move_pattern: Quiet, non-checking, non-forcing moves (pawn advances to 4th/5th rank, piece retreats/repositions, captures of non-critical material) in positions requiring immediate forcing play
analysis.why_bad: The position has a very narrow set of correct moves (avg 1.4 good options) requiring immediate concrete action—the quiet move wastes a critical tempo, allowing the opponent to execute threats, activate pieces, or exploit newly created weaknesses before the player can recover
sub_patterns: Slow flank pawn push (h5) when center demands immediate breakthrough
Structural pawn advance (c4) when piece activity (7th rank invasion) is decisive
Voluntary piece retreat from an active square to a passive/target square
Material grab (Nxc4) that abandons a dominant piece outpost
King move in wrong direction ignoring urgent defensive duties

analysis.label: Moves that squander a vital tempo in positions with razor-thin margins, allowing the opponent to execute a decisive threat.
analysis.description: This feature fires on moves that ignore the position's most urgent tactical demand in critical positions where very few acceptable moves exist (avg 1.8 good moves). The played moves take various forms: passive retreats to useless squares (Bg1 to corner, Bf8 abandoning e5 control, Kc1 moving away from a promotion threat - 3/10), 'attacking' moves that abandon critical defensive duties (Qe7 leaving g2 unguarded, Qg6 releasing control of f8 escape square - 2/10), moves that appear logical but miss the concrete necessity (Re1 weakening f2, Rd4 abandoning the superior d2 post, a5 ignoring the Rb8 invasion, Ne4 landing on an immediately capturable square - 4/10), and capturing with the wrong piece (Rxc5 when Qxc5 was required - 1/10). In all cases, the position demanded a very specific response to an imminent threat, and the played move addressed a secondary concern instead, resulting in catastrophic evaluation swings (avg 2124cp loss).
analysis.move_pattern: Any piece type, any direction; the unifying geometric trait is moving a piece AWAY from the square or zone where it is most critically needed for the position's primary tactical demand
analysis.why_bad: These moves waste the one tempo the player cannot afford to lose—the position has an immediate concrete threat (passed pawn promotion, king invasion, piece capture, mating attack) that requires a precise response, and the played move either retreats to passivity, attacks a non-priority target, or abandons a crucial defensive post, giving the opponent a free move to execute their decisive plan.
sub_patterns: Passive piece retreat to dead square when active defense needed (Bg1, Bf8, Kc1)
Queen attacks secondary target while abandoning king defense (Qe7, Qg6)
Piece leaves optimal defensive post for inferior one (Re1 from f1, Rd4 from d2)
Flank pawn push ignoring central/tactical emergency (a5)
Piece lands on tactically vulnerable square (Ne4 hanging, Rxc5 targetable by Ba3)

analysis.label: Seemingly purposeful moves that fatally overlook the opponent's immediate forcing reply (usually a check or attack on an undefended piece) that wins material or delivers mate.
analysis.description: This feature fires on moves where the player pursues a plausible-looking idea—active development, aggressive piece placement, or spatial gains—while catastrophically ignoring that the move allows the opponent an immediate forcing tactical response. In 5/9 positions, the punishment is a direct check (Qa4+, Qb3+, e5+, Rf2+, Qa5+) that wins material or creates a mating attack. In 7/9 positions, the move either abandons defense of a specific piece/pawn (Qg4 abandons b7, e5 abandons d5, Rb4 abandons the dominant 2nd rank) or places a piece on a square directly exposed to a forcing shot (Kf4 walks into e5+, Kf1 walks into Rf2+, d3 allows Qa5+). The best moves in these positions are typically prophylactic (Kf8, Kf2, O-O), defensive repositions (Be2, Qd7), or address the tactical issue directly before executing the plan (Bxc6+ before d3, Nc5 before Rb4). The average cp_loss of 1276 reflects that these are catastrophic oversights where tactical reality is completely ignored in favor of strategic intent.
analysis.move_pattern: Diverse piece types (kings, queens, bishops, rooks, pawns) moving to seemingly active or natural squares while leaving a critical tactical vulnerability (exposed king diagonal, undefended piece, or file/rank exposure) for the opponent to exploit with a forcing response
analysis.why_bad: Each move creates or fails to address a concrete tactical vulnerability that the opponent exploits with an immediate forcing sequence—typically a check, fork, or capture—winning material or delivering checkmate. The player prioritizes a strategic idea while being blind to the opponent's one-move tactical refutation.
sub_patterns: King advances to square exposed to pawn/piece check (Kh5, Kf4, Kf1)
Piece abandons defense of key pawn/square allowing check+capture (Qg4, e5)
Premature piece development ignoring diagonal/file exposure to king (Bb4, d3)
Rook moves to inferior square abandoning dominant position or losing tempo (Rb4 x2)

analysis.label: Quiet king retreat to h8 corner (or equivalent passive move) when the position demands exactly one urgent concrete action, typically a capture.
analysis.move_pattern: King retreating to h8 (4/6) or quiet piece repositioning to a non-forcing square, always moving AWAY from engagement rather than toward the critical action
analysis.why_bad: These moves waste a critical tempo in positions with only ~1 good move available, ignoring an urgent tactical necessity (a mandatory capture, a specific safe square, or a hanging piece) and allowing the opponent to execute a devastating tactical blow—back rank mate, mating attack, knight check gaining tempo, or simple piece capture.
analysis.description: This feature fires on positions where a player makes a quiet, seemingly safe, non-committal move—most commonly Kh8 (4/6 positions)—when the position urgently demands one specific concrete action. In position 9, Kh8 avoids capturing an attacking bishop on h7 (the ONLY good move was Kxh7), allowing a forced mate in 4. In position 4, Kh8 instead of Kg8 places the king on a square vulnerable to Qh5+ check after a piece capture. In position 15, Kh8 wastes tempo while a knight on b8 hangs to a simple bishop capture. In position 2, Rc4 ignores the critical need to capture on e4, allowing Nf2+ back rank mate. In position 13, Be6 passes up a free pawn capture (Bxd4) while abandoning defense of e4. In position 12, Kh5 instead of Kh4 walks into a knight fork check. All 6 positions averaged only 1.2 good moves, indicating extremely narrow critical moments where the player chose avoidance over engagement.
sub_patterns: Kh8 declining a mandatory king capture (Kxh7/Kxg8)
Kh8 allowing check sequences unavailable on g8
Kh8 wasting tempo while pieces hang
Quiet piece move ignoring free capture of undefended pawn/piece
King moving to adjacent square that falls in enemy piece's attack range

analysis.label: Playing a quiet preparatory or improving move instead of the immediate concrete tactical blow the position demands.
analysis.description: In all 4/4 positions, the player chose a natural-looking, non-forcing move (developing a piece, repositioning the queen, advancing a pawn) when the position demanded an immediate concrete strike with a narrow tactical window. In Position 3, Nef6 was routine development instead of the crushing c5-c4 pawn advance winning material. In Position 8, Qc3 repositioned the queen 'strategically' instead of g3 which would trap/win the enemy bishop. In Position 11, Bf3 'prepared' g4 instead of playing g4 immediately while the enemy bishop was vulnerable. In Position 12, h6 advanced past the critical pawn tension instead of hxg6 which would blow open lines with the devastating gxf7+ follow-up. All 4/4 positions had exactly 1 good move available, indicating narrow tactical windows. The average cp_loss of 272 reflects that these moments punish hesitation severely.
analysis.move_pattern: Quiet non-forcing moves (piece development, queen repositioning, pawn advance) to natural/useful squares without creating immediate threats or captures
analysis.why_bad: The position has a narrow tactical window requiring immediate forcing action; the quiet move hands the opponent a crucial tempo to consolidate, reposition defensively, or neutralize the threat before it can be executed, permanently closing the window of opportunity.
sub_patterns: Developing a piece to a natural square instead of a concrete pawn break
Repositioning queen to a strategic diagonal instead of a piece-winning pawn push
Bishop preparation instead of immediate pawn attack on exposed enemy piece
Pawn advance past tension instead of capturing to blow open lines

analysis.label: Active-looking moves that catastrophically compromise an already-vulnerable king, when only precise defensive play could survive.
analysis.description: This feature fires on moves that fatally expose the king in positions where king safety is already precarious. The pattern manifests in three ways: (1) King moves directly into mating nets or perpetual checks (Kh5 into Rh4#, Kb5 into a6+/b5+ pawn storm, Kg8 into Rf8+/Ng5+ perpetual - 3/9 positions), (2) Removing critical defensive pieces from the king's vicinity (Bxc5 removing the e3 bishop shielding the king, R1b2 abandoning the back rank, Re5 leaving f2 undefended, Ne5 removing knight from f3 defense - 4/9 positions), and (3) Structural weakening near the king (h4 eliminating the hxg3 recapture, enabling ...Bxg3/fxg3 devastation against the uncastled king - 1/9). In all 9 positions, the played move appears natural or active (centralizing, capturing material, advancing) but ignores the single critical defensive requirement. The extremely low average good moves (1.7) and astronomical average cp_loss (3366) confirm these are positions demanding precise defensive awareness where any alternative is catastrophic.
analysis.move_pattern: Various piece types moving away from king defense, or king moving to exposed squares; captures and centralizations that abandon defensive duties
analysis.why_bad: Each move ignores an imminent king safety crisis—the position demanded the ONE defensive move, but the player chose an active/greedy alternative that allows immediate tactical exploitation of the exposed king (checkmates, perpetuals, back-rank invasions, or winning material via discovered attacks on the unshielded king area).
sub_patterns: King walks into mating net or perpetual check (Kh5, Kb5, Kg8)
Key defensive piece removed from king proximity (Bxc5, R1b2, Re5, Ne5)
Pawn advance weakens king shelter irreparably (h4)
Material capture opens lines to own king (Nxe4 opens d-file)

analysis.label: Retreating the king (or pushing a pawn prematurely) when a critical forward king advance was the only way to maintain a winning advantage.
analysis.description: This feature fires on positions where the player makes a catastrophic tempo-losing move—typically retreating the king backward—when a single forward step was required to win. In 4/6 positions, the king physically retreats (Kf4 from g3, Kb3 from a4, Kf3 from g4) or moves away from a critical blocking/outflanking square, allowing the opponent to seize opposition or establish an unbreakable blockade. In 1/6 positions (b5), the pawn advances prematurely when the king should have advanced first—the same strategic error of failing to lead with the king. The middlegame positions (Bf4, f3) share the pattern of choosing the superficially active but strategically wrong advancing move while abandoning the critical square/tempo. All 6/6 positions convert decisive advantages (~+550cp) into draws or equality, with an average loss of 539cp. The common thread is a fundamental violation of endgame tempo principles: one forward king step wins, but the player retreats or misdirects, giving the opponent exactly the tempo needed to draw.
analysis.move_pattern: King retreating one square backward (toward own back rank or away from opponent's position), or pawn advancing when king should advance instead
analysis.why_bad: By retreating or misdirecting, the player surrenders the critical tempo needed to maintain outflanking/opposition/blockade, allowing the opponent's king to reach the drawing square (opposition, frontal blockade, or stalemate setup) in exactly the one move gifted to them.
sub_patterns: King retreats from critical outflanking square in pawn endgame (Kb3, Kf3, Kf4)
Premature pawn advance when king must lead (b5)
Wrong pawn/piece advance ignoring king safety or tempo (f3, Bf4)

analysis.label: Knight jumps to an aggressive-looking square while abandoning a critical defensive role, allowing devastating tactical exploitation.
analysis.description: In all 3/3 positions, a knight makes an attractive-looking forward move to an active square (Nc5 attacking a queen, Nxe4 grabbing a pawn, Nf5 attacking a bishop) while neglecting a crucial defensive responsibility. In 2/3 cases (Nc5 and Nxe4), the knight was directly guarding a key square (e7 and g7 respectively) whose abandonment allows immediate tactical devastation along open files or against the king. In 1/3 cases (Nf5), the knight move prioritized offense while a mating threat (Nxf3+/Qxh2#) went completely unaddressed. All three positions feature open files (e-file in 3/3) and vulnerable kings, creating the tactical preconditions that make the defensive role of the knight irreplaceable. The refutations all exploit the newly created weakness within 1-2 moves, often with checks or captures that give no time to recover.
analysis.move_pattern: Knight moves forward to an active/aggressive central square (outpost or capture), away from a square where it performed defensive duties near the king or along a critical file
analysis.why_bad: The knight was the linchpin defender of a critical square or the position needed an urgent defensive response; moving it to an 'active' square removes the guard on a key weakness, allowing the opponent to exploit open files, deliver checks, or execute mating combinations that the knight previously prevented.
sub_patterns: Knight leaves guard of square on open file allowing exchange/invasion
Knight captures pawn while king is uncastled, exposing kingside weaknesses
Aggressive knight jump ignores opponent's forced mating threat

analysis.label: Moves that remove a piece or pawn from a critical defensive function, immediately creating an exploitable tactical vulnerability.
analysis.description: This feature fires on moves where a piece or pawn is relocated for seemingly constructive purposes (space-gaining, centralization, repositioning) but fatally abandons a critical defensive role, allowing immediate tactical punishment. In 3/6 positions, a pawn advance removes the guard of a crucial square (c4 unguards d4 allowing Qd4+ check; b3 unguards c3 leaving the knight exploitable via Bb4; h4 leaves the pawn itself undefended for Bxh4). In 2/6 positions, a piece move abandons a restraining function (Qd6 removes the queen's attack on f2, freeing White's bishop to play Bxd4; Bf5 places the bishop on an undefended square in the rook's firing line). In 1/6, a capture with the wrong piece (Qxe5 instead of dxe5) exposes the queen to tempo-gaining pawn advances. All positions featured very few good alternatives (avg 1.5), indicating critical moments demanding precision, and in each case the refutation is a simple one-move exploitation (check, capture, or direct attack on the newly-created weakness).
analysis.move_pattern: Piece or pawn moved forward/sideways from a square where it performed a critical defensive or restraining function; mixed piece types (pawns 3/6, queens 2/6, bishop 1/6)
analysis.why_bad: The moved piece/pawn was performing an invisible but essential defensive role (guarding a square, restraining an enemy piece, maintaining its own safety), and its departure creates an immediate concrete vulnerability that the opponent exploits with a simple forcing move—typically a check, capture of the now-undefended unit, or invasion of the now-unguarded square.
sub_patterns: Pawn advance removing guard of a critical central square (c4 unguards d4, b3 unguards c3)
Pawn advance to an undefended square capturable by a minor piece (h4 taken by Bxh4)
Piece repositioned to undefended square in enemy piece's firing line (Bf5 met by Rf8)
Queen moved from a square where it restrained a key enemy piece (Qd6 frees Bxd4)
Capturing with the wrong piece, exposing it to tempo-gaining attacks (Qxe5 met by f4)

analysis.label: Aggressive-looking moves that prioritize attacking or capturing enemy pawns while abandoning critical defensive responsibilities or exposing pieces to tactical exploitation.
analysis.description: This feature fires on moves where a piece advances to a seemingly strong, active square—often targeting enemy material—while neglecting a more urgent positional or defensive priority. In 4/6 positions, the move directly targets or captures an enemy pawn (Qxd6 grabs a passed pawn, Rxc6 captures a weak pawn, Kc4 aims at b2, Rb6 attacks a6). In 5/6 cases, the piece that moved becomes tactically vulnerable on its new square or the move abandons a critical defensive duty (Ng5 leaves the Bf4 hanging, Be5 gets trapped by f4, Qxd6 walks into a Ne4+ fork, Rxc6 abandons kingside against g4, Kc4 abandons passed pawn blockade). The moves all share surface-level appeal—they look active, materialistic, or centralizing—but ignore that the position demanded attention to a specific vulnerability. The best moves in all positions share the opposite quality: they address the concrete defensive need first (Bg5 blocks the g-file, Nc8 reroutes safely, Bxh6 eliminates an attacker, Kc5 blockades, Qxc6 keeps coordination, Rb8 maximizes checking distance).
analysis.move_pattern: Piece advances forward or laterally to attack/capture an enemy pawn or occupy an aggressive-looking square, typically moving away from where defensive coordination is needed
analysis.why_bad: The move abandons a critical defensive responsibility (blockade, piece protection, king safety) or places the piece on a square where it becomes tactically exploitable (trapped, forked, overloaded), while the opponent has a concrete punishing resource that exploits the newly created vulnerability.
sub_patterns: Piece activation that leaves another piece undefended (Ng5 leaving Bf4 hanging)
Centralization to a square where the piece becomes trapped or attacked by pawns (Be5 trapped by f4)
Pawn capture that places a piece on a tactically exploitable square (Qxd6 into Ne4+ fork)
King advance that abandons restraint of enemy passed pawn (Kc4 instead of Kc5)
Heavy piece commitment to one flank while opponent breaks through on the other (Rxc6 ignoring g4)

analysis.label: Pieces move to active-looking squares where they are immediately driven back or exploited by simple tempo-gaining responses from the opponent.
analysis.description: This feature fires on moves that appear aggressive or purposeful but immediately invite a tempo-gaining refutation. In 7/9 positions, the moved piece lands on a square that is instantly challenged by a simple pawn advance (b3 kicks Nc4, c6 hits Qb5, b4 hits Qc5) or creates a tactical vulnerability the opponent exploits with tempo (Bg5 attacks the queen after O-O, Qe2 becomes possible after Bg6 vacates h5, Qf6 attacks both Nd4 and the exposed f2). The common thread is investing a tempo in an 'improvement' that actually loses a tempo (or more) because the opponent's response simultaneously develops their position AND addresses the threat. In positions 1, 8/14, the piece abandons a critical defensive duty to reach the aggressive square. In positions 2, 3, 9/15, the piece reaches a square immediately challenged by pawn advances. The average cp_loss of 1289 (inflated by one walk-into-mate) reflects how severely these tempo losses compound when the position demands precise coordination rather than superficial activity.
analysis.move_pattern: Pieces (especially knights and queens) move to central or queenside squares (c4, d4, b5, c5) that appear active but lack support; also includes committal moves (castling, pawn advances, bishop retreats) that create immediate targets
analysis.why_bad: The move places a piece where it is immediately attacked by a simple pawn advance or exploits a newly-abandoned defensive function, allowing the opponent to gain one or more tempi while simultaneously improving their position—the 'active' piece must retreat or the created weakness proves decisive
sub_patterns: Knight moves to outpost immediately kicked by pawn (Nc4→b3, Nd4→attacked by queen)
Queen moves to exposed square hit by tempo-gaining pawn advance (Qb5→c6, Qc5→b4)
Piece abandons critical defensive square enabling opponent's key move (Bg6 vacates h5 allowing Qe2, Nd4 vacates f3 exposing f2)
Premature committal move without prophylaxis (O-O without h6, b4 creating weak target, Kf5 into mating net)

analysis.label: Greedy or aggressive moves (especially queen sorties) in the opening while the king remains uncastled in the center, ignoring development priorities.
analysis.description: This feature fires on moves that prioritize local objectives—material gains, flank attacks, or piece trades—over the fundamental need to develop and castle. In 9/9 positions, the moving side's king remains uncastled in the center. Queen moves dominate (5/9: Qe2, Qa4, Qe7, Qxd5, Qb6), typically placing the queen on an exposed or tactically vulnerable square. The remaining moves involve pieces venturing to the rim or flank prematurely (Bh3, Nxa3, Rxh7) or natural-looking development that ignores an immediate central tactical refutation (Nc6). The best alternatives consistently involve quiet development or castling preparation (e.g., Ne2/Be2 preparing O-O in Position 2, Nf6/Be7 developing while blocking the e-file in Positions 8/3). The punishments exploit the resulting discoordination through diverse tactical motifs: forks (2/9), hanging pieces (4/9), trapped pieces (1/9), and tempo-gaining central advances (2/9), but all share the common precondition that the uncastled king creates latent vulnerabilities the opponent exploits.
analysis.move_pattern: Piece (usually queen) moves to an exposed, aggressive, or greedy square away from the center while king remains on e1/e8
analysis.why_bad: The moves leave the king uncastled while creating tactical vulnerabilities (undefended pieces, forkable squares, trapped pieces), allowing opponents to exploit the discoordination with concrete tactical blows that punish the premature aggression.
sub_patterns: Queen sortie to exposed/undefended square (Qe2, Qa4, Qe7, Qxd5, Qb6)
Piece capture or advance to rim/flank ignoring development (Bh3, Nxa3, Rxh7)
Natural-looking development that ignores immediate central pawn tempo (Nc6 allowing d5)

analysis.label: Playing an active-looking move (check, threat, or minor capture) when a more decisive forcing capture was available, losing critical tempo.
analysis.description: This feature fires on positions where the player selects a seemingly active or threatening move instead of the most materially or tactically decisive option. In 4/6 positions, the correct move involved a capture (often capture-with-check) that the player skipped: Qxd6+ instead of Rg8+ (position 3), Bxh8 instead of Rxc3 (position 10), Qxf5+ instead of Qf8+ (position 13), and Bf7 winning the rook instead of R3d6 merely threatening it (position 4). In the remaining cases, the player chose a repositioning move that vacated a critical defensive square (Rd2, position 11) or pushed a pawn insufficiently far (h3 vs h4, position 14). The unifying error is prioritizing a move that LOOKS purposeful—delivering check, threatening a piece, removing an immediate annoyance—over the move that actually WINS the most material or maintains the tightest tactical grip, giving the opponent a crucial tempo to escape or reorganize.
analysis.move_pattern: Rook moves (4/6), queen checks, or pawn pushes that appear active but miss a more forcing capture or capture-with-check by a different piece
analysis.why_bad: These moves give the opponent a tempo to escape (king flees to uncontrolled square), save a hanging piece, or exploit a newly vacated defensive square, because the player failed to execute the most forcing continuation (typically a capture or capture-with-check) first
sub_patterns: Check before capture-with-check (move order error losing mating net)
Capturing lesser material when a bigger capture is freely available
Threatening a piece when a different piece could win it outright
Repositioning when the vacated square creates back-rank vulnerability
Insufficient pawn advance failing to control critical escape squares

analysis.label: Playing a natural-looking positional or improving move when the position demands an immediate forcing continuation or critical defensive priority.
analysis.description: This feature fires on positions where the player chooses a 'reasonable-looking' non-forcing move—centralizing a piece, developing a rook to an open file, pushing a pawn—while missing that the position urgently requires a forcing tactical blow or defensive necessity. In 6/9 positions, the best move was a forcing move (check, capture, or direct threat): Be4+ wins a piece (Position 5), Nxg4+ forks (Position 9), fxe4 wins material (Position 4), Qf2+ wins a pawn with check (Position 14), Rd4 challenges an active enemy piece (Position 2), Qc1 defends a critical weakness (Position 1). In the remaining cases (Positions 7, 12, 15), the best moves prevent an immediate opponent plan (a5 advance, diagonal check-capture, h5 pawn break). The played moves instead are all 'improving' moves—Nd6 (outpost), Rd3 (centralization), Rac8 (development), c4/f4 (space), Nf3 (attack), Rb7 (contesting rank)—that would be perfectly reasonable in quieter positions but critically waste the tempo needed to address the position's tactical demands. Average cp_loss of 217 with only 1.6 good moves available confirms these are narrow critical moments.
analysis.move_pattern: Non-forcing piece/pawn moves to natural-looking squares (outposts, open files, central squares, pawn advances) rather than checks, captures, or urgent defensive moves
analysis.why_bad: The position contains an immediate tactical opportunity (discovered check, fork, capture of hanging material) or urgent defensive need (undefended pawn, imminent opponent break) that the slow improving move fails to address, giving the opponent time to consolidate or execute their own threat.
sub_patterns: Knight to impressive outpost ignoring hanging material
Rook to open file instead of preventing critical pawn advance
Pawn push closing position instead of forcing capture that wins material
Piece development when a forcing check/fork wins immediately
King move to natural square allowing check+capture

analysis.label: Playing a reasonable-looking move that neglects an urgent tactical vulnerability, allowing the opponent to immediately exploit a hanging piece, undefended pawn, or exposed king.
analysis.description: Across all 6 positions, the played moves pursue a superficially logical plan (pawn advance, piece development, rook activation) while critically ignoring that something is left undefended or exposed to immediate exploitation. In 3/6 cases the tactical motif is a hanging piece/pawn (f4 abandons g4's defense, e5 pushes an unguarded pawn, Rhg8 leaves Bd5 vulnerable to Nxd5). In 2/6 cases king safety is immediately exploited (Ke8 walks into Bh5#, Nc6 allows Qh5+). In 1/6 a key central pawn is left undefended (Bg5 leaves d4 capturable). The positions average only 1.7 good moves available, indicating critical moments requiring precise concrete calculation rather than general principles. The average cp_loss of 1738 (skewed by a mate) reflects catastrophic consequences of ignoring the board's most urgent demand.
analysis.move_pattern: Diverse piece types and directions (pawn pushes, king moves, piece development, rook lifts) — no geometric commonality; unified by being 'own-plan' moves that don't address the position's critical vulnerability
analysis.why_bad: Each move fails to address the single most urgent tactical need in the position — whether defending a hanging piece, protecting the king from a forcing sequence, or maintaining a critical pawn's defensive role — allowing the opponent an immediate concrete exploitation
sub_patterns: Pawn advance abandoning defensive duty of guarding adjacent piece/pawn
King move walking into a forcing check or mating pattern
Development move that leaves a critical piece/pawn undefended for capture
Rook activation that removes defensive coverage from a key square or piece

analysis.label: Leaving the last remaining bishop undefended on a square where a queen or rook can immediately capture it in the endgame.
analysis.description: In all 4 positions, the critical error involves a bishop being left en prise to a major piece (queen or rook) along a rank or file. In 3/4 cases the bishop itself moves to the vulnerable square (Be4 captured by Qxe4, Bb7 captured by Rxb7, Bxb2 captured by Qxb2), while in 1/4 cases a different move (h3) is played while ignoring the already-hanging bishop. In every case, the bishop is the player's ONLY remaining piece in a material-depleted endgame, making its loss immediately catastrophic—converting defensible losing positions into forced checkmates (3/4 positions) or eliminating all defensive resources (4/4). The capturing major piece always takes the bishop along a straight line (rank or file), and the loss triggers either immediate mating attacks against exposed kings (positions 6, 11, 12) or trivially won technical endgames (position 10).
analysis.move_pattern: Bishop placed/left undefended on a square aligned with an enemy queen or rook along a rank or file; the bishop is the sole remaining minor piece
analysis.why_bad: The bishop is the player's only surviving piece providing defensive coverage or material balance; placing it where a major piece captures it for free immediately collapses the position because no other piece remains to offer resistance or shield the king.
sub_patterns: Bishop actively moves to unguarded square on major piece's line (3/4)
Non-bishop move played while bishop remains hanging (1/4)
Queen captures undefended bishop along rank (3/4)
Rook captures undefended bishop along file (1/4)

analysis.label: Moving a piece toward a tempting target or square while fatally abandoning a critical defensive responsibility.
analysis.description: In all 5/5 positions, the blunder involves a piece leaving a critical protective role to pursue an attractive but insufficient goal. In Position 4, Ke2 chases the f2 pawn but abandons defense of e4. In Position 5, Kxb5 captures a pawn but moves away from blockading the lethal a-pawn. In Position 6, Rg1 seeks g-file play but abandons f-file support and leaves e3 fatally exposed. In Position 9, Ne1 attempts blockade duty but unlike Re1 fails to control f1, allowing devastating back-rank invasion. In Position 15, Nc5 centralizes aggressively but moves the defender away from the hanging h5 bishop. In each case, the player was drawn to a visually appealing idea (capturing material, creating threats, centralizing) while overlooking that the moved piece was performing an essential defensive function—guarding a pawn (3/5), controlling an invasion square (1/5), or shielding a piece (1/5).
analysis.move_pattern: Various piece types moving toward seemingly productive squares (captures, centralization, or file placement) while vacating a defensive assignment
analysis.why_bad: The moved piece was the sole guardian of a critical asset (pawn, square, or piece), and its departure allows the opponent to immediately exploit the newly undefended element—often via a simple capture, pawn race, or back-rank/infiltration tactic.
sub_patterns: King chases material but abandons pawn defense in K+P endgame
Piece moves to attractive square but fails to control critical invasion square
Piece develops/centralizes while leaving another piece tactically hanging

analysis.label: King moves backward to the 1st/8th rank in pawn endgames when forward centralization was essential to maintain resistance.
analysis.description: This feature fires on positions where the king retreats toward its own back rank (or edge) instead of advancing toward the center or toward the opponent's passed pawn. In 8/11 positions, the king explicitly moves to the 1st or 8th rank (Kd1, Ke8, Kc1, Kd8, Ke1, Kf1, Kf1, Kf1) when the correct move involved stepping forward (Kc3, Ke6, Kb3, Kd6, Kd3, Ke3, Kf3). The catastrophic consequence is typically allowing the opponent's passed pawn to advance with check or gain a decisive tempo in the promotion race. In 7/11 positions the evaluation shifts from 'losing but no forced mate' to 'forced checkmate,' with an average cp_loss over 4000. The pattern also captures edge cases where the king moves to an exposed/rim square losing tempo (Ka6) or where a piece develops passively when an urgent defensive move was needed (Nf6, Kc6). The unifying thread is choosing the passive/retreating direction over the active/advancing one in tempo-critical positions.
analysis.move_pattern: King moving backward toward own back rank (rank 1 for White, rank 8 for Black), typically one square retreat along a file or diagonal
analysis.why_bad: In pawn endgames with passed pawns, retreating the king to the back rank loses a critical tempo - it allows the opponent's pawn to advance (often with check), converts drawn/slow losses into forced mates, and abandons the king's ability to blockade, intercept, or race to counterattack distant pawns.
sub_patterns: King retreats to 1st rank allowing pawn advance with check (Kd1, Ke1, Kc1)
King retreats to 8th rank allowing immediate pawn promotion (Ke8, Kd8)
King retreats to back rank losing king-race tempo (Kf1 variants)
King moves to rim/edge square disconnecting from central action (Ka6, Kc6)

analysis.label: Castling (O-O or O-O-O) played as a routine developing move before necessary prophylaxis, walking the king into a specific tactical vulnerability.
analysis.description: All 9/9 positions feature castling moves (5 kingside O-O, 4 queenside O-O-O) played prematurely, before a critical prophylactic or developing move was needed to neutralize a concrete tactical threat. In every case, the castling creates a new geometric relationship that the opponent immediately exploits: in Position 1, O-O exposes c2 to Nd4 fork; in Position 3, O-O places the rook on f8 where Bc5 creates dual threats; in Position 4, O-O means the rook (not king) recaptures on d8 leaving the queenside undefended; in Position 9, O-O leaves the queen vulnerable to Bg5; in Position 5, O-O-O places the king on the h3-c8 diagonal where the queen already sits; in Position 13, O-O-O aligns king on c8 with queen on d7 allowing Bf5 with check. In 9/9 cases, simple prophylactic moves (h6, c3, g6, Be6, etc.) were available that would have prevented the punishment. The average cp_loss of 272 reflects that these aren't subtle positional errors but concrete tactical oversights disguised as principled play.
analysis.move_pattern: Castling move (O-O or O-O-O), moving king to wing before addressing a specific tactical precondition
analysis.why_bad: Castling creates new geometric alignments (king on diagonal, rook exposed on f8/d8, pieces suddenly undefended) that enable immediate tactical exploitation; a prophylactic move was needed first to deny the opponent's concrete resource
sub_patterns: O-O placing rook on f8 where a bishop can attack it (Bc5/Bxf6)
O-O-O placing king on c8/c1 on a vulnerable diagonal (h3-c8, f5-d7)
O-O-O castling into pre-existing pawn storm or piece pressure on that wing
O-O removing king from center defensive duties (no longer guarding c2, d-file pieces)
Castling before h6/g6 prophylaxis against Bg5/Bf5 bishop deployments

analysis.label: Playing a quiet repositioning or preparatory move when an immediately available forcing continuation (check, capture, or decisive advance) was demanded by the position.
analysis.description: In 8/8 analyzed positions, the player chose a non-forcing 'improving' move (piece repositioning, quiet pawn push, or centralizing maneuver) while a concrete, immediately winning tactical blow was available — typically a check, pawn capture, or forcing advance that exploited an existing vulnerability. For example, Bd4 (slow centralization) instead of Rd7+ (decisive 7th-rank invasion with check), Re3 (preparatory rook lift) instead of Rxe5 (winning a hanging pawn), Rf5 instead of g5+ (forced mate in 3), h4 (aimless pawn push) instead of Rxf7 (capturing a weak pawn), and Ke4 instead of g5 (the only winning advance). The played moves all appear reasonable in a slow positional sense — they centralize pieces, gain space, or prepare future plans — but they catastrophically waste the critical tempo needed to execute the concrete tactical opportunity that the position presented. The average cp_loss of 2086 reflects how devastating these tempo losses are: the opponents consistently exploit the extra move to neutralize threats, escape danger, or activate counterplay.
analysis.move_pattern: Quiet piece repositioning (knight/bishop/rook/king moves to central or 'improved' squares) or non-threatening pawn advances, typically lacking check or capture, in positions where a forcing alternative (check, capture of hanging/weak material, or decisive pawn advance) exists
analysis.why_bad: The position demanded immediate tactical execution of an available forcing continuation, but the player wasted a critical tempo on a preparatory move, allowing the opponent to defend, escape, or generate counterplay that neutralizes the advantage
sub_patterns: Slow piece centralization instead of immediately available check/invasion (Bd4 vs Rd7+, Ke4 vs g5)
Preparatory rook lift instead of capturing hanging material (Re3 vs Rxe5)
Aimless pawn push instead of decisive capture (h4 vs Rxf7, hxg6 vs Qxf3)
Passive knight retreat instead of tactical knight route (Na3 vs Qf4, Nd7 vs Nb7-Nd6+)
Self-weakening pawn move instead of quiet consolidation (h3 trapping own bishop, g6 weakening king)

analysis.label: Playing a plausible-looking move that misidentifies the position's most critical tactical requirement, typically abandoning a piece's essential function or targeting the wrong objective.
analysis.description: This feature fires on positions where the player makes a move that appears reasonable (a capture, an attack, a relocation) but fundamentally misidentifies which element of the position demands attention. In 5/7 positions, a well-placed piece abandons its optimal post: Nxd5 removes the f6-knight from kingside defense, Qxc2 abandons the queen's dominant e4 centralization, Nd7 retreats from the powerful e5 outpost, Qg3 relocates the queen to a square where it no longer defends the g5 knight, and Bh6 commits the bishop to an undefended square. In 6/7 positions, the player ignores a more urgent tactical obligation (capturing the correct target, addressing an immediate threat, or maintaining critical coordination). The positions share extremely narrow correct paths (avg 1.6 good moves), meaning the player faced a position demanding one specific priority but chose a secondary goal that looked attractive on the surface.
analysis.move_pattern: Any piece type moving to a plausible-looking square or making a plausible capture, but targeting the wrong objective or abandoning a critical defensive/offensive role; no consistent geometric direction
analysis.why_bad: These moves disrupt the player's own piece coordination by removing or misusing the piece that was the linchpin of their position's advantage or defensive requirements, giving the opponent tempo to exploit the resulting tactical gaps (hanging pieces, forks, loss of central control, or exposed king).
sub_patterns: Capturing the wrong target when multiple captures exist (Nxd5 vs Nxe5, Nxa8 vs Nxd4, Qxc2 vs Bxf3)
Moving a piece away from a dominant outpost to a passive square (Nd7 from e5, Qxc2 from e4)
Choosing the wrong retreat square that loses defensive coordination (Qg3 instead of Qd2)
Ignoring an immediate tactical threat to pursue a secondary plan (g3 ignoring Bxe2, Bh6 ignoring overloaded queen)

analysis.label: Non-forcing repositioning moves played in positions that demand immediate concrete tactical action.
analysis.description: This feature fires when players make quiet, non-forcing moves (no checks, no captures, no direct threats) in positions where a specific tactical blow is available. In 6/6 positions, the move played was a passive repositioning or slow pawn advance when a concrete winning or equalizing tactic existed. In 4/6 cases, the move involved retreating or passively placing a piece (Rf8 retreating from active f5, Rg8 abandoning powerful g2, Be2 misplacing bishop, Qg6 losing tempo), while 2/6 were non-forcing pawn advances (f5, h4) that created weaknesses. The best moves in all cases involved concrete tactical actions: capturing hanging material (Rxb2 in position 11), forcing pawn advances (f3 in position 3), tactical queen sacrifices (Qd3 in position 6), or active piece centralization (Nb5 in position 12, Re2 in position 14). The average cp_loss of 1752 reflects that these quiet moves squander positions with sharp tactical demands.
analysis.move_pattern: Non-capturing, non-checking piece repositioning or pawn advance; often pieces moving to back ranks (f8, g8) or passive squares (e2, g6)
analysis.why_bad: These moves waste critical tempo in tactical positions, allowing opponents to stabilize defenses, seize open files, or exploit the abandoned active piece positions, while the concrete tactical opportunity (capture, pawn breakthrough, sacrifice) disappears.
sub_patterns: Rook retreating from active rank to back rank (Rf8, Rg8)
Piece repositioning to apparently aggressive but tactically irrelevant square (Qg6, Be2)
Slow pawn advance creating weaknesses when captures/tactics exist (f5, h4)

analysis.label: King relocates (usually via castling) to a wing where the opponent already has attacking pieces, pawns, or tactical resources aimed at that side.
analysis.description: In 7/8 positions, the blunder is a castling move (O-O or O-O-O) or king move that places the monarch directly into a pre-existing attacking configuration. Positions 1 and 2 show classic Greek Gift setups where Black castles kingside despite a bishop aimed at h7 and a knight ready for g5+ (2/8). Position 15 shows castling into an advanced h6 pawn that rips open the g-file (1/8). Position 13 shows castling queenside into White's already-advanced a4/b4 pawn storm (1/8). Position 7 shows White castling queenside where Black's fully-developed pieces immediately generate b-file and central pressure (1/8). Position 8 shows Kg7 exposing the king to open-file and knight-fork tactics after gxf5 (1/8). Position 14 shows castling that inadvertently removes tactical counter-resources protecting a piece (1/8). The consistent theme is that the opponent's attacking infrastructure is already in place BEFORE the king arrives, making the relocation a trigger rather than a target.
analysis.move_pattern: King relocation moves (O-O, O-O-O, or Kg7/Kg8) moving the king toward a wing where opponent has pre-aimed attacking pieces or advanced pawns
analysis.why_bad: The king moves to a square where the opponent already has a coordinated attacking setup (bishops on diagonals, advanced pawns ready to open files, knights ready to jump to attacking squares), converting latent potential energy into an immediate concrete attack without the opponent needing any preparation moves.
sub_patterns: Kingside castling into Greek Gift sacrifice (Bxh7+/Ng5+/Qh5)
Queenside castling into advanced pawn storm (a4/b4/b5 breaks)
Castling into advanced pawn that tears open the king's shelter (hxg7)
King move exposing monarch on newly-opened file or to fork tactics
Castling that removes indirect tactical protection from other pieces

analysis.label: Player makes a materialistic pawn move or capture when the position urgently demands a piece-based tactical, developmental, or defensive solution.
analysis.description: This feature fires on positions where the player chooses a pawn advance, pawn capture, or material-grabbing move while ignoring a critical piece-based need. In 10/13 positions, the played move is a pawn move while the best move is a piece move (tactic, development, repositioning, or defense). Examples include: capturing pawns while under mating attack (dxc3, Position 11), pushing pawns instead of capturing a hanging piece (e5 instead of Qxd4, Position 6; d3 ignoring exf6, Position 4), making pawn captures that open files toward one's own king (gxh5, hxg4, Positions 10/12), advancing pawns that weaken defensive structure (g3 exposing f3 knight, Position 5; g4 allowing Bxg4 pin, Position 13), and grabbing material while abandoning defensive coordination (Qxg6, Position 15). The correct moves consistently involve piece activity: tactical captures (Nxf3, Qxd4, Qxe8), piece development (Bg4, O-O), defensive repositioning (Ne1, Be8, Re3), or prophylactic consolidation (a3, Qe3). The average cp_loss of 1753 reflects how catastrophically wrong pawn-level thinking becomes when piece-level demands are paramount.
analysis.move_pattern: Pawn advances or pawn captures (especially on kingside files g/h/f), occasionally piece captures grabbing material; typically lateral pawn captures (gxh, hxg, dxc) or single-step pawn pushes
analysis.why_bad: These moves prioritize material gain, space, or pawn structure when the position demands immediate piece action—whether exploiting a tactic, defending against threats, developing pieces, or maintaining defensive coordination. The pawn moves either remove defenders, open files toward the player's own king, waste critical tempo, or ignore hanging/threatened pieces.
sub_patterns: Pawn capture that opens file toward own king (gxh5, hxg4, gxh4)
Pawn push ignoring hanging piece or free capture (d3, e5, f6)
Pawn advance weakening own king shelter (g3, g4, h5)
Material grab abandoning defensive coordination (Qxg6, dxc3)
Piece relocation removing key defender (Nd2, Kf2)

analysis.label: Moving a major piece (usually queen) to a visually impressive central square while missing a more forcing continuation or creating an exploitable tactical vulnerability.
analysis.description: This feature activates when a player makes a 'natural-looking' major piece move—typically a queen centralization—that appears active but squanders a significant advantage. In 5/6 positions, the blunder is a queen move (Qe6, Qe2, Qe5, Qg2+, Qb4), and in 5/6 the player had a substantial advantage (+294 to +432) that was thrown away. The correct moves were consistently MORE forcing: a decisive check (Qb2+ in position 5, Qa5+ in position 9), maintaining targeted pressure (Qg3 in position 1), safe retreats preserving winning chances (Qb5 in positions 6 and 14), or active development with concrete purpose (Bc4 in position 7). The blundered moves share the trait of LOOKING strong while IGNORING the opponent's concrete tactical responses—back-rank shots (3/6 positions), forks (1/6), interpositions improving the opponent (1/6), or counterplay on open files (1/6). The average cp_loss of 374 reflects how these moves transform winning positions into equal or lost ones.
analysis.move_pattern: Major piece (5/6 queen) moved to an apparently active/central square, often on the e-file (3/6 to e2/e5/e6), without forcing sequences
analysis.why_bad: The moves prioritize visually impressive piece placement over concrete tactical requirements—missing forcing checks that win material, ignoring back-rank vulnerabilities, or placing the piece where it becomes a tactical target on open files
sub_patterns: Queen centralization blocking own rook coordination on open file
Non-forcing queen move when a decisive check was available
Queen placement ignoring back-rank deflection tactics
Major piece move walking into capture-with-check followed by fork

analysis.label: Playing a tempting check (or forcing-looking move) that squanders a winning position by giving the opponent a defensive resource that the truly best move would have denied.
analysis.description: In 6/7 positions, the player chose a check that appeared strong but was inferior to the actual best continuation. In Position 6, Nxf7+ was played when Qh7# was mate in one. In Position 2, Rxg7+ was the right idea but in the wrong move order (Qh6+ first enables the mate). In Position 10, Bg5+ gave a pointless check when Nxb6 led to forced mate in 9. In Position 3, Bh4+ allowed an interposing bishop trade that eliminated the key attacking piece needed for Bc7+. In Position 4, Nf2+ was a flashy fork-check that allowed recapture by the very piece that should have been captured (Qxe4). In Position 1, Nxe7+ was the wrong knight capture with check when Nxf6+ set up a devastating discovered attack. The outlier (a3) shares the tempo-loss quality—a preparatory move when immediate action was critical. The common thread is prioritizing a superficially forcing move over the genuinely strongest continuation.
analysis.move_pattern: Check (any piece type, any direction) that captures material or attacks the king, when a stronger non-check or differently-forcing move exists
analysis.why_bad: The check gives the opponent a tempo to block, recapture, or escape to a better square, neutralizing the actual winning threats that the correct (often quieter or differently-timed) move would have maintained
sub_patterns: Wrong move order in mating sequence (check before setup move)
Flashy check when simple mate/material win exists
Knight fork-check allowing recapture by the target piece
Check that allows defensive interposition trading key attacker
Premature capture-check choosing wrong target square

analysis.label: Superficially attractive aggressive or active moves that ignore the position's most critical tactical requirement, allowing the opponent to exploit what was left unaddressed with a forcing reply.
analysis.description: This feature activates on moves that appear purposeful—centralizing a piece, capturing material, or launching an attack—but fatally overlook the position's most pressing tactical demand. In 7/8 positions, the played move loses tempo because the opponent responds with a forcing reply (check, attack on the moved piece, or capture of what was left hanging). In 5/8 cases, a piece moves to an apparently strong square but is immediately attacked with tempo (Qh4 met by Ng6, Qf6 allowing Nh5, Qe5 hit by Nd7, Nf4 captured by Bxf4, Nxe4 allowing Rxd4). In 6/8 positions, king safety concerns (either the player's own or an opportunity to exploit the opponent's) are ignored in favor of the active-looking move. The common thread is that positions demanded addressing an urgent specific problem (a hanging piece in 3/8, a defensive duty in 2/8, a mating threat in 1/8, a unique tactical opportunity in 2/8), but the player chose a generically 'good-looking' alternative that crumbles to a concrete tactical response.
analysis.move_pattern: Pieces moving to apparently active/central/aggressive squares (queen centralizations, knight jumps, captures) or pawn advances seeking counterplay, generally forward-oriented moves that look strong in isolation
analysis.why_bad: The moves ignore the position's single most critical tactical element—whether a hanging piece, a defensive duty being abandoned, or a unique winning resource being forfeited—in favor of a generically aggressive action. The opponent exploits the oversight with a forcing reply (tempo attack, capture, or check) that nets material or decisive positional advantage.
sub_patterns: Queen centralizing to square immediately vulnerable to a knight tempo attack (Qh4/Ng6, Qf6/Nh5, Qe5/Nd7)
Piece capture or move that leaves another piece undefended (Nxe4 leaving Bd4 hanging, Nf4 hanging to bishop)
Pawn advance on wrong side of the board ignoring critical king safety threats (b5 ignoring kingside mate)
Materialistic capture that creates self-pin or vulnerability along a file shared with own king (Bxc4 on c-file)

analysis.label: Minor piece jumps aggressively to a central/advanced square before addressing king safety or structural obligations, creating tactical vulnerabilities.
analysis.description: In 6/6 positions, the player moves a minor piece (5/6 knights, 1/6 bishop) to an apparently imposing central or advanced square (d4, d5, c5, e4, f3) that looks like a strong outpost, while neglecting a more urgent positional need. In 4/6 positions, the player's king remains uncastled and the best moves all involve castling or preparing to castle first. The piece placement creates concrete tactical problems: in 3/6 cases the piece can be favorably captured (Ne4→Nxe4 ruining pawn structure, Bf3→Nxf3 winning key pawn, Nd5→e4 winning material), and in 3/6 cases the piece's departure abandons a critical defensive duty (Nd4 leaves e5 hanging, Nc5 abandons king defense, Nd5 leaves b2 undefended). The best alternatives consistently involve patient development, castling, or quiet consolidation rather than flashy centralization.
analysis.move_pattern: Minor piece (usually knight) jumping forward to central square on ranks 4-5 (d4, d5, c5, e4, f3) - aggressive centralization/outpost occupation
analysis.why_bad: The aggressive piece placement either abandons a defensive duty (leaving pawns/squares unguarded), invites a favorable exchange that damages pawn structure, or neglects the urgent need to castle—creating immediate tactical refutations that exploit the very weaknesses left behind by the premature advance.
sub_patterns: Knight to outpost while own king remains uncastled (Nc5, Nd5, Nd5)
Knight centralization that invites favorable capture ruining pawn structure (Ne4, Nd4)
Piece overextension to square where it can be captured with structural/material gain (Bf3)

analysis.label: Moves that voluntarily remove a well-placed piece from its strongest square for an immediate but strategically inferior gain (check, capture, or repositioning).
analysis.description: This feature fires on moves where a player abandons a dominant piece position that was the cornerstone of their advantage. In 5/8 positions, a piece leaves a powerful outpost or key square: knight leaves e5 (Nd7), knight leaves f5 for a superficial check (Ng7+), knight leaves g4 to capture (Nxe3), queen abandons its central/defensive post for a pawn grab (Qxg6), and queen commits prematurely instead of placing a piece on an outpost (Qa3 instead of Nc5). In the remaining 3/8 cases, the same principle of surrendering positional assets applies: releasing central tension that benefited the player (dxe5), prematurely advancing a restraining pawn (e6), and wasting critical development tempo (Kf8). All moves share the characteristic that the piece/pawn was generating more strategic value in its current role than whatever the move aimed to achieve, and the opponent's refutation consistently exploits the vacancy left behind.
analysis.move_pattern: Piece (especially knight) moves away from a central/dominant square, often backward, sideways, or to the edge; includes captures and checks that remove the piece from its optimal post
analysis.why_bad: The piece was the positional linchpin generating multi-directional threats or restraining the opponent; removing it eliminates tactical resources, grants the opponent free tempi to consolidate or counterattack, and collapses the coordination that justified the player's advantage
sub_patterns: Knight retreats from central outpost (e5, f5, g4) losing control of key squares
Queen leaves defensive/central post for a pawn grab exposing own king
Premature pawn advance sacrificing restraining/blocking value
Tempo-wasting move that allows opponent to seize initiative
Capture that surrenders a powerful attacking piece for insufficient return

analysis.label: Playing quiet, non-forcing moves in positions where a single concrete tactical blow is required to maintain a large advantage.
analysis.description: This feature fires on positions where the player holds a significant advantage (typically +3 to forced mate) but chooses a 'reasonable-looking' quiet move instead of the one decisive tactical shot. In 7/8 positions, the best move was a concrete forcing operation (Bg5 gaining tempo, Nxd4 fork, Nxf5 winning material, d5 central break with Bb5+ check, Rc7 forcing mate, f5 pawn storm, Nxg5 discovered attack), but the player instead chose non-forcing alternatives: passive repositioning (Qd2, Qf3, Bd6), a slow flank pawn push (a4), prophylactic castling (O-O-O), a tempo-wasting capture (Qxh6), or a knight move without real follow-through (Nc6). In 6/8 positions there was only 1 good move available, indicating razor-sharp tactical moments demanding precise calculation rather than general principles. The average cp_loss of 1406 reflects how catastrophic these 'natural' moves are when concrete action is demanded.
analysis.move_pattern: Diverse piece types (Q, B, N, R, pawn, castling) but all share the quality of being non-forcing repositioning or consolidation moves rather than captures, checks, or concrete threats
analysis.why_bad: These moves waste the critical tempo needed to exploit a tactical opportunity, giving the opponent time to consolidate, escape danger, or generate counterplay. The position demanded immediate forcing action (typically a capture or sacrifice creating an unavoidable threat), and the quiet move hands back the initiative.
sub_patterns: Queen repositioning to passive square (Qd2, Qf3)
Piece retreat from active position (Bd6, Nc6 from d4)
Slow prophylactic moves ignoring forced mate (O-O-O, a4)
Material grab over mating attack (Qxh6)

analysis.label: Slow pawn moves (especially d3) that open or fail to guard a critical diagonal to the uncastled king, enabling queen checks that fork undefended pieces.
analysis.description: The dominant pattern across these positions is a quiet, structurally-motivated pawn advance played while the king remains in the center, which fatally opens or neglects a diagonal leading to the king. In 7/13 positions (1, 3, 4, 7, 11, 15, and 5), the refutation is a queen check along a newly-exposed diagonal (typically a5-e1 or a4-e8) that simultaneously attacks an undefended minor piece, winning material by force. Four positions specifically feature d3 opening the a5-e1 diagonal while a bishop sits undefended on b5 (positions 1, 4, 7, 11). The remaining positions extend the pattern to other pawn moves that create similar geometric vulnerabilities: e6 blocking a bishop's retreat allowing Qa4+ (position 5), b6 opening the a8-h1 diagonal for a discovered attack (position 8), f6 weakening the back rank (position 2), c3 ignoring a diagonal-opening knight capture (position 13), and b4 pushing into a piece's capture range (position 14). In all 13 cases, the player chose a slow positional move while an immediate tactical threat existed involving exposed geometry.
analysis.move_pattern: Pawn advance (predominantly d2-d3, also d4, e6, f6, b6, c3, b4) that opens or weakens a diagonal line to the player's uncastled/exposed king or undefended piece
analysis.why_bad: These moves prioritize long-term structural goals (supporting center, preparing bishop development) while ignoring that the pawn advance opens a critical diagonal or removes a defensive barrier, allowing a queen check/fork that wins an undefended piece outright. The king's presence in the center makes these diagonal vulnerabilities lethal.
sub_patterns: d3 opening a5-e1 diagonal allowing Qa5+ to fork king and undefended Bb5 (positions 1, 4, 11)
d-pawn advance exposing king to queen check that forks a hanging piece (positions 3, 7, 15)
Pawn move blocking a minor piece's only retreat square, trapping it (positions 2, 5)
Pawn move opening a long diagonal for opponent's fianchettoed bishop or enabling discovered attacks (positions 8, 13)
Quiet move creating or ignoring a pawn fork / piece-capture geometry (positions 9, 14)

analysis.label: Non-forcing prophylactic or passive moves played in positions demanding immediate concrete tactical action.
analysis.description: This feature fires when players choose quiet, non-urgent moves—typically flank pawn pushes or passive piece placements—in positions where sharp tactical action is required. In 5/7 positions, the player's king was uncastled or inadequately safe, making tempo especially precious. In 4/7 cases, the move was a slow rim/support pawn push (a6, a6, a3, c3) that addressed no immediate threat and created no concrete pressure. The remaining moves (Rc1, Re8, Qg5) similarly chose vague positional 'improvement' over decisive tactical continuation. In every case, the opponent punished the tempo loss with an immediate central break (e5 or d4 in 5/7 positions) or piece invasion that exploited the wasted move. The 'tempo_loss' motif was tagged in 6/7 positions, confirming this as the dominant thread.
analysis.move_pattern: Non-forcing, non-capturing moves—typically edge pawn pushes (a-file, c-file) or quiet piece relocations to open files—that lack immediate threats
analysis.why_bad: These moves treat sharp, tactically loaded positions as if they are calm, giving the opponent a free tempo to execute decisive central breaks, pawn forks, or piece invasions that exploit the player's existing vulnerabilities (uncastled king, fragile piece coordination, available winning tactics).
sub_patterns: Flank pawn push (a6/a3) when center is about to break open against uncastled king
Slow support pawn (c3) leaving piece duo vulnerable to central pawn fork
Passive rook development (Re8/Rc1) instead of urgent counterplay or defense
Vague attacking queen move instead of concrete winning combination

analysis.label: Playing an aggressive-looking move that neglects a critical defensive obligation, leaving a piece or square fatally unguarded.
analysis.description: All three positions share a common mistake profile: the player chooses a superficially attractive, forward-looking move (central pawn advance, queen centralization, bishop pin) when the position demands a single precise response to an urgent concrete need. In 3/3 cases, the played move removes protection from or fails to address a critically vulnerable piece/square: e5 abandons control of d5 allowing Bd5 domination, Qf6 leaves f5 tactically undefended for Nxf5, and Bg5 abandons the e3 post leaving Nc3 hanging to dxc3. In all cases only ~1 good move existed (avg 1.7), meaning these are critical junctures where the single correct plan had to be found. The refutations in 3/3 cases exploit the newly undefended target immediately. The common thread is prioritizing general positional improvement (space, activity, pins) over concrete tactical demands.
analysis.move_pattern: Piece or pawn moves forward to an active-looking square (advancement, centralization, or pin) away from its defensive duties
analysis.why_bad: The move removes defense from a critical piece or square, creating an immediate tactical exploitation (undefended piece captured, dominant outpost occupied, or material won) in positions where only one precise continuation maintains the balance
sub_patterns: Pawn advance weakening key square control
Queen misplacement leaving pawns tactically vulnerable
Bishop relocation abandoning piece defense

analysis.label: Natural-looking developing or consolidating moves played in positions where an immediate tactical crisis (hanging piece, trapped piece, or mating threat) demands urgent attention.
analysis.description: This feature fires on moves that look reasonable in isolation—rook centralizations, pawn pushes, captures, or king moves—but critically fail to address an urgent tactical problem requiring immediate action. In 6/9 positions, the player's own piece is hanging or about to be captured/trapped (Position 1: knight vulnerable to ...c5; Position 3: knight attacked by rook; Position 5: e4 needed immediate play; Position 9: bishop left exposed to ...f6; Position 12: e4 pawn undefended; Position 13: knight on e4 capturable). In the remaining cases, the moves either give a pointless check that aids the opponent's king (Position 4) or walk into immediate checkmate (Position 14). The average good moves available is only 1.6, indicating these are narrow critical moments. The common thread is that positions demand one specific action (save/relocate a vulnerable piece, or exploit a fleeting tactical window), but the player instead makes a generic-looking move—typically a rook to an open file (5/9 are rook moves), a pawn advance, or a king retreat—that ignores the crisis entirely.
analysis.move_pattern: Mostly rook moves to open/semi-open files (Rd1, Rd8+, Rc3, Rd3, Rfe1), plus generic king moves and captures, all directed at improving general piece placement rather than addressing the specific square where a tactical crisis exists
analysis.why_bad: These moves fail because they prioritize general positional improvement (file control, piece development, space) over the one urgent tactical problem in the position—typically a piece that is hanging, trapped, or about to be captured with tempo, leaving the opponent a simple tactical refutation that wins material or delivers checkmate.
sub_patterns: Rook-to-open-file ignoring hanging piece (Rd1, f4, Rfe1)
Passive rook placement missing dynamic piece maneuver (Rc3, Rd3)
Pointless check/move aiding opponent's king escape (Rd8+, Kc8)
Wrong recapture exposing piece to tempo gain (Bxe5)

analysis.label: Playing a natural-looking improving move that fails to address the single most urgent tactical or structural demand of the position.
analysis.description: This feature fires on positions where a critical tension or threat exists that must be addressed immediately, but the player instead makes a 'reasonable-looking' move that ignores it. In 8/12 positions, a specific pawn tension (g4 vs h3, f4 vs e3, f5 vs g6, d4 vs c3, h6 vs g7, f5 advancing to f6) demanded immediate resolution, but the player played a centralizing (Nd5, Kf7), developing (Bf3, Rab8, O-O, O-O-O), retreating (Ba7, Qb6), or materialistically capturing (Nxg4, Nxd7) move instead. The average number of good moves was only 1.9, indicating these are narrow critical moments where only the urgent response works. The moves themselves look logical in isolation—centralizing a knight, tucking a king, activating a rook, winning material—but each catastrophically fails because it allows the opponent one free tempo to execute their threatened plan (pawn break, discovered check, kingside advance, etc.).
analysis.move_pattern: Various piece types making non-forcing moves (quiet development, centralizing, castling, retreating, or non-critical captures) when a forcing or defensive response to an immediate threat was required
analysis.why_bad: These moves waste the one critical tempo needed to address an imminent threat or exploit a fleeting tactical opportunity, allowing the opponent to execute a pawn break, discovered attack, advanced passed pawn creation, or kingside assault that was preventable on the previous move.
sub_patterns: Castling into an existing pawn storm or advanced pawn (O-O into h6 pawn, O-O-O into d4/c3 break)
Quiet king moves when pawn tension demands tactical resolution (Kg1, Kb7, Kf7)
Material grabs that remove a key defensive piece (Nxg4 abandons f6, Nxd7 ignores c3 pawn threat)
Piece retreats from dominant squares abandoning critical pressure (Ba7 from d4, Qb6 from c6)
Natural-looking development when a forcing tactical blow exists (Bf3 instead of Nxa6+, Rab8 ignoring f6 break)

analysis.label: Playing slow, passive, or misdirected moves in critical positions that demand immediate precise forcing action.
analysis.description: This feature fires on positions where there is one specific urgent tactical requirement — an immediate threat to neutralize, a forcing sequence to execute, or a critical piece to maintain — but the player instead plays a non-urgent, 'natural-looking' move that ignores the position's demands. In 6/9 positions, only 1 good move existed (avg 1.9), indicating positions requiring extreme precision.
