The errors include: retreating a dominant piece from a key outpost (Nf6 abandoning e4, Nde7 removing the d5 blockader), playing in the wrong sector of the board (a5 on the queenside when the kingside demanded f5/f6), choosing passive development over untangling (Bb2 instead of Nc2), executing wrong move orders (Nxc1 before Nxd5), giving counterproductive checks (Ra1+ driving the king to f2 where it blocks promotion), and making slow preparatory moves when decisive tactics exist (Rhf3 instead of the winning Ra1+ check sequence). The unifying thread is that each position had a narrow tactical solution the player missed in favor of a superficially reasonable but strategically irrelevant alternative.
analysis.move_pattern: Various piece types; typically retreats, flank moves, or captures away from the critical zone; moves directed away from the position's tactical epicenter
analysis.why_bad: These moves waste critical tempo in positions demanding immediate action, allowing the opponent to execute threats (pawn breaks, piece activations, king attacks) that the correct move would have prevented or preempted. The positions have very few good continuations, so any deviation from the precise path results in severe punishment.
sub_patterns: Retreating pieces from dominant outposts (Nf6, Nde7)
Flank play when center demands attention (a5)
Wrong check direction helping opponent (Ra1+)
Wrong capture order exposing tactical vulnerabilities (Nxc1)
Slow moves when forcing wins exist (Rhf3, Bb2)

analysis.label: Aggressive-looking moves (predominantly checks) that waste tempo by allowing the opponent's king to reach a safer square or displacing the attacker from its optimal post.
analysis.description: This feature fires on positions where the player makes a forcing or active-seeming move—most often a check—that actually worsens their position. In 6/11 positions, the blunder is a direct check (Qc6+, Qc5+, Qe7+, Rf6+, Rd7+, Qe5+) that drives the opponent's king to a better square or strands the checking piece away from where it's needed. In the remaining cases, the moves are similarly 'active-looking' but counterproductive: Re7 places the rook one square off from the only correct file, Nf3 blocks the queen's critical path, Rd4 centralizes aggressively while ignoring a king-safety need, a3 attacks the queen but creates a target exploitable by an intermediate exchange, and Rxc3 grabs a pawn but walks into a clearance sacrifice. The unifying thread is that the player prioritizes apparent forcing quality or surface-level activity over the position's actual demand—typically a quieter or more precise move (Re1+, Rc1+, Qh4+, Rh1+, Rf7, Kg2, Qf3) that addresses the real tactical or strategic issue. The consistent tag across analyses is 'tempo_loss' (appearing in 9/11 positions), confirming these moves hand the initiative to the opponent rather than maintaining it.
analysis.move_pattern: Major piece (queen or rook) delivering check or making an aggressive-looking centralization/capture, typically moving to a square one step away from the correct one
analysis.why_bad: The check or forcing move allows the opponent's king to reach a safer square (escaping the danger zone), displaces the attacker from critical defensive or offensive duties, or triggers an intermediate tactical response that exploits the commitment. The truly best move is usually quieter, more precise, and addresses a specific vulnerability.
sub_patterns: Queen check that lets king escape to safety (Qc6+/Qc5+/Qe7+/Qe5+)
Rook check along wrong rank/file allowing capture or escape (Rf6+/Rd7+)
Piece placed on wrong adjacent square missing key attack (Re7 vs Rf7, Nf3 blocking Qf3)
Active-looking move neglecting critical prophylaxis or allowing intermediate tactic (Rd4/a3/Rxc3)

analysis.label: Playing quiet, natural-looking improving moves (repositioning pieces, advancing pawns) when the position demands a specific concrete response to an immediate tactical danger.
analysis.description: This feature fires on moves that appear positionally reasonable—activating a piece, advancing a pawn for space, repositioning for a better diagonal—but fatally ignore the position's concrete tactical requirements. In 5/7 positions, the player needed either a specific defensive move to parry an immediate threat or active counterplay to challenge a key attacking piece, but instead chose a 'general improvement' move. In Position 1, Nc5 removes a critical d-file blocker allowing back-rank devastation. In Position 3, Bc5 wastes a tempo when only h5 disrupts the converging attack. In Position 6, Qg7 repositions passively when g4 was urgently needed to challenge the f3-knight. In Position 7, Re8 places the rook on a fork-vulnerable square instead of contesting the critical d-file. In Position 14, Kf8 walks into immediate checkmate when only Qf6 (queen trade) survived. The positions typically had very few good moves available (avg 2.0), meaning these were critical moments demanding precision, not quiet maneuvering.
analysis.move_pattern: Non-forcing moves (no checks, no captures, no direct threats) - piece repositioning, pawn advances, or king moves that appear to improve coordination but address no immediate threat
analysis.why_bad: These moves spend a critical tempo on non-urgent improvement while the opponent has access to (or gains access to) a concrete tactical blow—back-rank mates, knight forks, overwhelming piece coordination against the king, or passed pawn exploitation. The positions demanded either a precise defensive resource or immediate counterplay, and the quiet move allows the opponent's latent threats to become decisive.
sub_patterns: Removing a key defensive piece for 'activity' (Nc5 unblocking the d-file)
Repositioning when only a tempo-gaining defensive move survives (Bc5 instead of h5)
Passive piece relocation when active pawn counterplay is required (Qg7 instead of g4)
Placing a piece on a tactically vulnerable square (Re8 into fork territory)
Premature pawn advance creating a fixed target or tactical vulnerability (c5, g4)

analysis.label: Playing a non-forcing move when a knight jump (usually Ne5) attacking the opponent's queen was available to gain decisive tempo.
analysis.description: In 6/6 positions, the best move available was a forcing move that directly attacked the opponent's queen to gain tempo—specifically a knight jump to e5 in 4/6 cases (positions 5, 7, 10, 13 with Ne5 or Nxg5), a knight jump to c5 attacking the queen in 1/6 (position 1), and a pawn push attacking the queen in 1/6 (position 15 with a5). Instead, the player chose a slow, non-threatening move: pawn pushes (c3, d5, d4, hxg5) or quiet piece development (Rc1, Qa5). In all cases, the opponent was underdeveloped or had a king in the center, making tempo critical—the non-forcing move allowed the opponent to consolidate (develop, castle, or defend hanging pieces) while the forcing queen-attack would have maintained or increased the initiative. The average cp_loss of 279 reflects how catastrophic a single wasted tempo is in these dynamic positions.
analysis.move_pattern: Non-forcing move (pawn push or quiet piece development) played instead of a knight jump to e5/g5/c5 that attacks the opponent's queen
analysis.why_bad: The opponent's queen is exposed to a tempo-gaining knight attack that would simultaneously develop/centralize the knight and force the queen to retreat, maintaining initiative against an underdeveloped position; the quiet move gives the opponent a free tempo to solve their coordination problems.
sub_patterns: Pawn push instead of Ne5 attacking queen
Wrong recapture (pawn vs knight) missing queen attack
Quiet queen/rook move ignoring forcing knight centralization

analysis.label: Making routine positional or developing moves that ignore an immediate tactical crisis requiring concrete calculation.
analysis.description: This feature fires on moves that appear strategically reasonable in isolation—placing rooks on open files (5/10 positions: Re1, Rad1, Rhf1, Ra3, Re1), repositioning knights to 'active' squares (2/10: Nc5, Na5), or making prophylactic king/pawn moves (3/10: Kf1, b6, f3)—but catastrophically ignore a concrete tactical demand in the position. In every case, the position required urgent action: defending a hanging piece (Rad1 ignoring Nxf4, Kf1 ignoring hanging d4), relocating a threatened piece (Rhf1 instead of Bf1), preventing a fork (Re1 creating Nf3+ target), exploiting a trapped piece (Re1 missing Ra4), or avoiding creating vulnerabilities (f3 allowing Bh4-Bf2+, Na5 removing kingside defender, b6 enabling c6 advance). The average cp_loss of 309 reflects that these positions had narrow best play (avg 2.0 good moves) where only concrete calculation could identify the critical move, but the player defaulted to general positional principles instead.
analysis.move_pattern: Quiet piece-improving moves (especially rooks to open files, knights to outposts, prophylactic king moves) that don't address the position's concrete tactical demands
analysis.why_bad: The position contains an immediate tactical threat, vulnerability, or opportunity that requires urgent concrete attention, but the player makes a 'standard' positional move based on general principles, either leaving an existing problem unaddressed or creating a new tactical vulnerability that the opponent can immediately exploit.
sub_patterns: Rook to open file while own piece hangs or creates fork target
Knight redeployment to rim/outpost that loses tempo or abandons defensive duties
Pawn push or king move that weakens own position or ignores hanging material

analysis.label: Playing a natural-looking developing, activating, or prophylactic move while an immediate tactical threat (fork, invasion with check, or piece capture) goes unaddressed.
analysis.description: In all 6 positions, the player chose a 'reasonable-looking' move that aims to improve their position generally (develop a piece, activate a rook, chase an enemy piece, retreat a bishop) but fatally ignores a concrete, forcing tactical threat from the opponent. In 4/6 cases, the refutation involves a check or fork that wins material immediately (Nxd6+ in position 2, Nc7+ in position 7, Qxd5+ in position 15, Qxa6+ in position 5). In 5/6 cases, the position featured very few good moves available (avg 1.8), indicating critical moments where only precise responses survive. The moves span piece types (bishops 3/6, knights 1/6, rooks 1/6, pawns 1/6) but share the quality of being non-forcing improvements that waste the single crucial tempo needed to parry the opponent's tactical shot. The avg cp_loss of 242 reflects how punishing these oversights are—positions that demanded emergency measures received routine treatment.
analysis.move_pattern: Non-forcing piece improvement (development, activation, retreat, or prophylactic pawn push) that neither captures, gives check, nor blocks the opponent's immediate tactical sequence
analysis.why_bad: The position is at a critical tactical inflection point where the opponent has a concrete forcing sequence (check, fork, piece capture) available on the very next move, and the played move neither prevents nor complicates this threat, effectively giving the opponent a free tempo to execute their combination.
sub_patterns: Developing a minor piece while a knight fork/invasion with check goes unblocked (Bd7, Be2)
Activating a piece away from a critical defensive post, leaving back-rank or key pieces unguarded (Rf5, Ng6)
Prophylactic pawn push to chase a piece that can jump forward with check instead of retreating (a6)
Bishop retreat to a square vulnerable to tempo-gaining pawn advance (Bf4)

analysis.label: Moves that abandon a key positional asset (file control, piece placement, pawn structure) for a superficially active but concretely pointless continuation, losing critical tempo.
analysis.description: This feature fires on moves where a player holds a concrete positional asset—active file control, optimal piece placement, or a critical structural pawn—and discards it for a move that *appears* purposeful (a check, a pawn break, development, a rook lift) but actually accomplishes nothing concrete. In 5/7 positions, the move directly abandons control of a key file or square (Rdg8 leaves the d-file, Rg1 leaves the b-file, exd5 removes the e4 sentry pawn, d5 opens lines toward own king, Nf6 ignores a hanging piece). In 2/7 positions, the move is a pointless check (Ra3+, Qe6+) that grants the opponent a useful king move while misplacing the checking piece. The common thread is that all moves prioritize a general principle (attack the king, develop, break in the center, give check) over the specific concrete demand of the position, and the opponent immediately exploits the tempo loss or structural weakening. The average cp_loss of 181 and average of only 1.9 good moves available confirms these are precision-demanding positions where the player chose the 'natural-looking' move over the required one.
analysis.move_pattern: Diverse piece types moving to superficially active squares (checks, lateral rook shifts, pawn advances, developing moves) that abandon their current optimal function
analysis.why_bad: Each move wastes tempo or surrenders a concrete positional asset (open file, structural pawn, piece coordination) without extracting any concession from the opponent, allowing immediate exploitation through file invasion, central breaks, or tactical shots.
sub_patterns: Pointless checks that misplace the checking piece (Ra3+, Qe6+)
Rook abandoning open file for passive square (Rdg8, Rg1)
Pawn capture/advance that removes critical structural sentry (exd5, d5)
Routine development missing a concrete tactical opportunity (Nf6)

analysis.label: King moves toward the wrong sector or retreats passively in the endgame when it should race actively toward counterplay.
analysis.description: In 12/12 positions, all in the endgame phase, the player makes a king move that heads in the wrong direction—either retreating passively or marching toward the wrong flank. The analyses consistently identify the same error: in positions 1, 3, 6, 7, and 11, the king retreats or moves queenside when kingside counterplay (attacking pawns or supporting a passed pawn) was essential. In positions 2, 9, and 12, the king retreats when it should advance actively (Kg7 toward pawns it can't stop, Ke7 losing tempo, Kc7 instead of Kb5). In positions 4, 7, and 10, the king heads toward passive defense of pawns rather than creating threats elsewhere. The 'wrong direction' manifests as abandoning a pawn race (6/12), failing to centralize (4/12), or walking into danger (1/12, position 10 with Kc5 into mate). Tags across analyses overwhelmingly cite 'tempo_loss' (11/12), 'king_activity' (9/12), and 'counterplay_abandonment' or 'wrong_king_direction' as the core strategic failure.
analysis.move_pattern: King move in any direction, typically retreating or moving laterally toward the wrong flank, away from the critical sector of the board
analysis.why_bad: The king wastes critical tempo by heading toward a sector where it cannot generate counterplay or meaningfully stop threats, while abandoning the direction where active king participation (supporting a passed pawn race, attacking weak pawns, or maintaining centralization) was the only source of resistance or winning chances.
sub_patterns: King retreats toward queenside abandoning kingside pawn race
King moves toward opponent's passed pawns it cannot actually blockade
King retreats passively when advancing creates necessary counterplay
King commits to wrong flank allowing opponent free hand on the critical side

analysis.label: Non-urgent 'improving' moves that leave a piece or pawn undefended, allowing the opponent to capture it immediately.
analysis.description: This feature fires on moves where the player prioritizes a seemingly constructive plan over addressing an immediate tactical vulnerability. In all 6/6 positions, the played move leaves (or creates) a hanging piece or pawn that the opponent can capture immediately: a3 leaves Bg5 tactically loose after Nxd4 (position 2), fxg3 opens the g-file and a7-g1 diagonal for devastating Qxg3+ (position 6), Qe6 abandons defense of the a7 pawn allowing Qxa7 (position 7), g6 leaves h6 completely undefended for Bxh6 (position 9), Kg2 allows Qxg5+ capturing the g5 pawn with check (position 13), and Rh6 leaves c7 unprotected for Rxc7 (position 15). In each case, the best moves either directly defend the vulnerable piece/pawn or preemptively resolve the tension, while the blundering move ignores the concrete threat in favor of a secondary objective like prophylaxis, king consolidation, piece 'activation,' or creating luft.
analysis.move_pattern: Various piece types making non-forcing, non-defensive moves while a pawn or piece remains unprotected on another part of the board
analysis.why_bad: The moves fail to address an immediately capturable piece or pawn, allowing the opponent to win material (or force a devastating attack) on the very next move. The player prioritizes their own agenda over concrete tactical calculation.
sub_patterns: Pawn moves creating new weaknesses (g6 leaving h6, fxg3 opening king)
Piece relocations abandoning defensive duties (Qe6 leaving a7, Rh6 leaving c7)
King moves enabling captures with check (Kg2 allowing Qxg5+)
Prophylactic moves ignoring central tactical tension (a3 ignoring Nxd4)

analysis.label: A quiet piece relocation that neglects a concrete tactical vulnerability, leaving a central pawn or piece undefended and capturable.
analysis.description: This feature fires on positions where the player makes a seemingly logical 'improving' move—relocating a piece to what appears to be a better square—while failing to address an immediate tactical vulnerability. In 5/9 positions, the d4 pawn specifically becomes capturable (Positions 1, 9, 12, 13, 14), often with check or tempo. In 2/9 positions, a misplaced knight on h3 is left hanging (Positions 4, 11). The remaining cases involve abandoning central oversight for a non-threatening aggressive move (Position 7: Qh4) or a slow developing move when material is hanging (Position 3: Rg4 instead of Qxh4). All 9 moves are non-capturing, non-checking quiet moves that prioritize abstract piece placement over concrete defensive needs. The resulting punishments typically involve capturing the abandoned pawn/piece with check or tempo, often swinging the evaluation by 200+ centipawns.
analysis.move_pattern: Non-capturing, non-checking piece relocation (knight, rook, queen, or king) moving away from a square that defended a critical central pawn or piece, typically involving moves to the d-file/center or periphery
analysis.why_bad: The moved piece was performing a critical defensive function (defending d4, covering a hanging piece, or maintaining central control), and its relocation allows the opponent to capture undefended material, often with check or an additional tempo-gaining threat that makes recovery impossible.
sub_patterns: Knight leaves f3 abandoning d4 pawn defense (Nd2, Nd4, Nc3)
Rook/King move to d-file exposes d4 to capture with check (Kd2, Rg1)
Queen relocation abandons defense of hanging piece or central control (Qe1, Qh4)
Slow developing move when opponent material is hanging (Rg4, Rd1)

analysis.label: Quiet developing or repositioning moves that neglect the position's most critical tactical demand, allowing the opponent to win material through a concrete tactical exploitation.
analysis.description: All 6 positions share a common thread: the player makes a natural-looking, non-forcing move (developing a piece or repositioning it to a seemingly logical square) while the position urgently demands concrete tactical action. In 4/6 positions, the move develops or repositions a minor piece to what appears to be a standard square (Bd3 twice, Ne2, Nc6). In 6/6 cases, there exists a specific tactical vulnerability that the move fails to address: a trapped piece (position 6 - Bd3 blocks Bf4 retreat), a critical pin (positions 4 and 8 - unresolved pressure on pinned pieces), removal of essential counterplay (position 12 - Nc6 removes fork threat), abandonment of a defensive post (position 15 - Ne2 leaves center unsupported), or failure to neutralize active enemy pieces (position 10 - Bd3 ignores Bg4). In 5/6 cases, the refutation involves winning material through a concrete tactical shot (piece capture, fork, or trapped piece). The average cp_loss of 284 reflects that these moves typically allow decisive material gain.
analysis.move_pattern: Quiet non-forcing moves (no check, no capture, no direct threat) - typically minor piece development or repositioning to natural-looking squares in the opening/early middlegame
analysis.why_bad: Each move ignores the position's most critical tactical issue - whether a pin, trapped piece vulnerability, undefended square, or removal of defensive/counterplay resources - allowing the opponent to execute a concrete combination that wins material
sub_patterns: Bishop developed to d3 when e2 was needed to address specific pressure (2 cases)
Piece moved away from critical active/defensive post, removing counterplay or support (Nc6 from b4, Ne2 from c3)
Developing move made before addressing urgent pin or tactical pressure (Qc2 ignoring d4 collapse, e6 ignoring c6 pin)

analysis.label: Quiet preparatory or repositioning moves played in positions that demand immediate forcing tactical action (captures, sacrifices, or direct attacks).
analysis.description: In all 4/4 positions, the player chose a non-forcing, quiet move (king retreat, pawn advance, bishop repositioning) when a concrete tactical blow was available. In Position 1, Ke2 was a passive king approach when Nf1 blockaded the critical pawn. In Position 4, c4 was a slow pawn push when Bg8+ sacrificed the bishop to win the rook. In Position 6, Be2 was a slow bishop redeployment when Rfxf2 crashed through on the weak f2 pawn. In Position 15, d5 was a premature central advance when dxc5 cleanly resolved tension in Black's favor. The common thread is that each chosen move is 'improving' or 'preparatory' in nature—solidifying structure or repositioning pieces—while the position demanded immediate exploitation of a concrete vulnerability through forcing sequences. The tagged motifs across positions include 'missed_tactic' (4/4), 'tempo_loss' (4/4), and 'piece_activity' (3/4).
analysis.move_pattern: Quiet non-capturing, non-checking moves (various piece types) to central/near-central squares, chosen over available forcing captures or sacrifices
analysis.why_bad: These moves surrender the initiative by allowing the opponent time to neutralize a concrete tactical vulnerability or reorganize defensively, when an immediate forcing sequence would have decisively exploited the position's critical weakness.
sub_patterns: Slow pawn advance missing a piece sacrifice that wins material
Passive piece repositioning missing a direct capture on a weak point
King move creating overloading when a piece move solves the problem
Premature central advance creating weaknesses instead of favorable exchange

analysis.label: Moves that displace a piece from an essential defensive or blocking role to a superficially attractive square, allowing immediate tactical exploitation.
analysis.description: This feature fires on moves where a piece performing a critical but non-obvious defensive function (blocking a file, defending another piece, maintaining an escape route, or preventing a pawn advance) is voluntarily moved to a 'better-looking' square. In 2/10 positions, a knight on f3 moved to d4 seeking centralization but abandoned defense of the e4 knight, which fell immediately. In 1/10 positions, a knight left e5 (where it blocked the e-file) for c4, allowing devastating rook checks. In 2/10 positions, the king advanced toward the opponent (Kf7) when it needed to retreat or go sideways, walking into skewers or moving away from critical passed pawns. In 1/10 positions, Kb7 moved the king in the wrong direction instead of challenging a rook on e6. In 1/10 positions, g6 blocked the king's own escape square, enabling immediate checkmate. In 1/10 positions, Bxb3 used the wrong piece (bishop instead of rook), losing crucial tempo. In 1/10 positions, Qg6 failed to give check, allowing h7 to establish a drawing fortress. The moves universally appear logical (centralizing, capturing, 'improving') but fatally ignore the displaced piece's essential current function.
analysis.move_pattern: A piece (knight, king, bishop, queen, or pawn) moves away from a square where it performs a critical blocking, defending, or access-maintaining role to a seemingly attractive but non-essential destination
analysis.why_bad: The moved piece was performing an essential defensive function (blocking a file/rank, defending another piece, maintaining escape routes, or preventing a pawn advance) that the player failed to recognize; once removed, the opponent exploits the newly created vulnerability with checks, captures of undefended pieces, or unstoppable pawn advances
sub_patterns: Knight leaves defensive coordination to centralize, leaving partner piece undefended (Nd4 x2)
Piece removed from file-blocking duty allows devastating checks (Nc4, Kf7)
King moves in wrong direction, away from the critical theater of operations (Kb7, Kf7 x2)
Self-blocking move cuts off own king's escape route (g6)
Tempo-insensitive move allows opponent to reach a critical threshold (Qg6 allowing h7, Bxb3 losing tempo)

analysis.label: A knight moves to d2/e2 (White) or d7/e7 (Black), abandoning a critical defensive function and self-obstructing piece coordination.
analysis.description: In all 9/9 positions, a knight moves to the player's second rank on the d or e file (d7/e7 for Black, d2/e2 for White), typically intending to challenge an opponent's strong centralized piece or 'develop' toward the center. However, these moves catastrophically abandon a critical defensive function. In 3/9 positions (Positions 1, 2, 3), Nd7 blocks the queen's access to escape/defensive squares, enabling Nc6 forks or trapping the queen. In 2/9 positions (Positions 5, 9), Ne7 removes a key pawn defender or fails to challenge the opponent's center, allowing tactical exploitation. In 4/9 positions (Positions 7, 10, 12, 13), Nd2/Ne2 removes a knight from active defensive duty (guarding diagonals, supporting c3, maintaining outpost potential), allowing opponent piece invasions or pawn breaks. The average cp_loss of 258 reflects that these moves look logical but have a hidden tactical or structural cost that the opponent can immediately exploit.
analysis.move_pattern: Knight moves to d2 or e2 (White) / d7 or e7 (Black) — one square behind the center on the d/e files, always on the player's second rank
analysis.why_bad: The knight abandons a critical guard duty (controlling a key square, protecting a piece, or preventing an invasion) to reach a self-obstructing interior square where it blocks the queen, bishop diagonals, or piece coordination, allowing the opponent to exploit the newly undefended weakness immediately
sub_patterns: Nd7 blocking queen escape routes, enabling Nc6 fork/queen trap
Nge7/Ne7 removing pawn defense, allowing Nxf6 or Nf4 tactics
Nd2/N1d2 abandoning active square potential, allowing positional invasion or pawn breaks
Ne2 removing knight from defensive post (c3), allowing bishop infiltration on light squares

analysis.label: Non-urgent developing or preparatory moves played when the king urgently needed to castle or address central safety.
analysis.description: In 13/13 positions, the moving side has an uncastled king stuck in the center (e1 or e8), typically facing an opponent who has already castled or has pieces trained on the open/semi-open e-file. The blundering moves are diverse in piece type (pawns: b3, h3, c6, a4, g3; pieces: Nd2, Qe2, Qd7, Bc4, Bf4, Nc3, Nh6) but share the critical flaw of being 'one more preparatory move' when castling or an immediate king-safety measure was the singular priority. In 11/13 positions, castling itself (O-O or O-O-O) was the best or second-best move. The refutations consistently exploit the exposed king through central pawn breaks opening the e-file (positions 4, 9, 10), pins along diagonals to the king (positions 5, 8), checks exploiting weakened squares (positions 7, 15), or piece coordination against the stranded monarch (positions 3, 12, 14). The average cp_loss of 238 reflects the catastrophic cost of a single wasted tempo when the king's safety is critical.
analysis.move_pattern: Any piece type or pawn move; no common geometric direction; the unifying feature is that the move is NOT castling and NOT a direct king-safety measure when the king remains on e1/e8
analysis.why_bad: Each move wastes a critical tempo on a non-urgent objective (prophylaxis, development of peripheral pieces, pawn structure) while the uncastled king on the open or semi-open e-file is one or two moves from being fatally exploited through central breaks, pins, checks, or coordinated attacks.
sub_patterns: Pawn moves on flanks (h3, b3, a4, g3) ignoring central king vulnerability
Piece development to passive squares (Nd2, Nc3, Bf4, Nh6) when castling was available
Queen repositioning (Qe2, Qd7) that blocks retreat squares or key defensive paths
Bishop development (Bc4) that enables opponent's pin tactics against uncastled king

analysis.label: Moves that prioritize material gain or piece repositioning while catastrophically ignoring immediate threats to the player's own exposed king.
analysis.description: In all 4/4 positions, the player's king is already critically vulnerable (exposed on open files, diagonals, or lacking pawn shelter), yet the move played ignores this vulnerability in favor of a superficially logical action—a passive retreat (Bc8), an aggressive rook centralization (Rf6), a greedy capture (Nxe7), or a recapture with the wrong piece (Qxe2). In every case, the best moves specifically address king safety: blocking critical diagonals (2/4), keeping the king mobile (1/4), or using the king itself to capture and escape a danger square (1/4). The refutations universally exploit the unaddressed king weakness through back-rank attacks (1/4), forced mating nets via queen checks (1/4), diagonal checks leading to mate (1/4), and sequential knight fork-checks destroying the pawn shield (1/4). The average cp_loss of 4875 reflects that these are catastrophic oversights, often converting defensible positions into forced mate.
analysis.move_pattern: Any piece type moving away from king defense or capturing when the player's own king requires immediate attention; often removes a key blocking/defending piece from a critical line
analysis.why_bad: The move removes or misplaces a piece that was either actively defending the king, blocking a critical attacking line, or needed to relocate the king to safety, allowing the opponent to exploit the now-unguarded king with checks, pins, or mating attacks
sub_patterns: Removing a piece that blocks a mating diagonal/file (Nxe7, Bc8)
Recapturing with wrong piece leaving king on vulnerable square (Qxe2 instead of Kxe2)
Moving a piece far from king defense when king is in a checking net (Rf6)

analysis.label: Moves that pursue the player's own slow plan while ignoring the position's most critical and time-sensitive tactical or defensive requirement.
analysis.description: This feature fires on moves where a player wastes a critical tempo by pursuing their own agenda (pawn advances, material grabs, piece repositioning) while the position demands an urgent response to a concrete threat. In 8/10 positions, analyses explicitly tag 'tempo_loss' as the key error. The pattern manifests in several ways: advancing pawns when king activity is paramount (h4 instead of Kg7, g3 ignoring a passed pawn on a3, c7 ignoring Qh4#); grabbing material without preparation (Qxf4 without first removing the f5 knight, Qxd4 allowing Bb5+ intermezzo); retreating/repositioning pieces away from the critical sector (Nb8 to starting square, Qc2 abandoning kingside defense, Kd6 walking away from needed defensive zone); or developing naturally while ignoring concrete tactical demands (Bc5 ignoring pressure on e4). In every case, the opponent punishes the wasted tempo with an immediate tactical or strategic exploitation—whether a mating attack (3/10), winning material via intermezzo (2/10), advancing an unstoppable passed pawn (2/10), or seizing a critical file/diagonal (3/10).
analysis.move_pattern: Any piece or pawn move directed toward the player's own plan rather than the position's most urgent demand; no consistent geometric direction but consistently moves away from or ignores the critical sector of the board
analysis.why_bad: The move wastes a tempo that the opponent exploits to execute their own concrete threat—whether a mating attack, promotion, material-winning tactic, or positional domination—because the position was at a critical tipping point where one tempo determined whether the threat could be neutralized or would become decisive.
sub_patterns: Pawn advances on non-critical flank while opponent has urgent threats elsewhere
Material captures that ignore tactical intermezzos or prerequisite exchanges
Piece retreats or repositionings that abandon the critical defensive sector
Natural development moves that ignore concrete hanging-piece or king-safety tactics
Passed pawn advances that ignore immediate mating threats

analysis.label: Playing a quiet developing, repositioning, or improving move when the position urgently demands a single specific concrete action to address an imminent tactical vulnerability.
analysis.description: This feature fires on moves that appear reasonable or constructive in isolation—knight development (Nc6, Ne7), queen repositioning (Qg5, Qe6, Qc1), king sidesteps (Kf1), pawn captures (exd4), or pawn pushes (h5)—but fatally ignore the one critical demand of the position. In 8/8 positions, the player had very few acceptable alternatives (avg 2.0 good moves), indicating these are sharp moments requiring precision. The correct moves consistently involved concrete, forcing actions: preventing a specific pawn break (f5 in position 2), challenging a dominant piece via trade (Qe7 in position 7, Qf2 in position 12), forcing simplification (Qg4/Qg3 in position 9), maintaining a critical defensive function (keeping the queen on the 7th rank in position 10), confronting attacking pieces (h6 in position 13), or addressing an immediate tactical vulnerability (Ka8 preventing a fork in position 15, Na5 creating threats in position 14). The blundered moves all share the quality of being 'one move too slow'—tempo-wasting non-forcing moves in positions where the opponent has a concrete threat ready to execute on the very next move.
analysis.move_pattern: Non-forcing quiet moves (piece development, repositioning, non-critical captures, flank pawn pushes) that fail to interact with the critical tactical element of the position
analysis.why_bad: Each move wastes the one tempo needed to address a specific concrete threat, allowing the opponent to execute an immediate tactical operation (pawn break, knight fork, piece trap, material capture, attacking invasion) that was only preventable on that exact move
sub_patterns: Knight development ignoring opponent's imminent pawn break
Queen repositioning abandoning critical defensive duty
Passive king move creating worse tactical geometry than forcing queen trade
Materialistic pawn capture ignoring attacking threats against exposed king
Flank pawn push ignoring central tactical vulnerability

analysis.label: Playing a natural positional or material move without first delivering an available check that was essential to the position's tactical demands.
analysis.description: In all 5/5 positions, the best move was to deliver check first (e5+ in P2, f5+ in P3, g5+ in P8, Nc5+ in P9, d3+ in P10), but the player instead played a 'natural' move—capturing material (Nxa4), gaining space (g5), activating a piece (Ra7), advancing the king (Kc5), or centralizing a knight (Nc4). The intermediate check was critical because it either displaced the enemy king to neutralize a mating threat (3/5 positions: P2 prevents g5#, P8 prevents Rh8#, P3 prevents g4 seal), or it forced the enemy king to a worse square making the subsequent move far more effective with tempo (P9: Nc5+ forces Kf7 before e5; P10: d3+ forces Ke5 making Nc4+ come with check). All positions feature mutually exposed kings in open/semi-open structures (5/5), making the check-first tempo uniquely powerful. The average cp_loss of 4120 reflects that 3/5 positions involved allowing immediate checkmate by skipping the check.
analysis.move_pattern: Various piece types (knight, pawn, rook, king) making non-checking moves when a check with a different piece/pawn was available as an intermediate forcing move
analysis.why_bad: Skipping an available check allows the opponent to execute a lethal threat (often checkmate) or seize a critical tempo that the check would have denied—the intermediate check either neutralizes the opponent's tactical resource or forces their king to a square where the player's subsequent move gains additional tempo.
sub_patterns: Material grab before neutralizing mate threat (Nxa4, Ra7)
Positional pawn move before tempo-gaining check (g5)
Piece development without preparatory check (Nc4, Kc5)

analysis.label: Moves that pursue a plausible-looking plan while ignoring the opponent's immediate ability to exploit a resulting tactical or structural vulnerability.
analysis.description: This feature fires on moves where the player commits to a seemingly logical idea—gaining space, developing, castling, or repositioning—but critically fails to account for the opponent's concrete resources to punish. In 5/7 positions, the move either creates a new weakness or abandons an existing strength that the opponent immediately exploits: a4 creates a chronic pawn target (Position 1), b4 allows Bxb4+ with check against an uncastled king (Position 3), g6 traps the player's own rook via g4 (Position 7), O-O-O places the king in front of an already-advanced pawn storm (Position 10), and Rd1 abandons the critical open e-file allowing consolidation (Position 12). In 5/7 cases the tags include 'tempo_loss', and in 5/7 cases 'king_safety' is implicated. The average cp_loss of 211 reflects that these aren't subtle inaccuracies but significant positional or tactical oversights where 2-3 clearly better alternatives existed (avg 2.4 good moves available).
analysis.move_pattern: Diverse piece types and directions (flank pawn pushes, knight development, castling, rook repositioning); no single geometric pattern—the connection is functional rather than geometric
analysis.why_bad: Each move ignores the opponent's most threatening concrete response—whether a pawn break, piece capture with check, piece trap, or file exploitation—while committing to an irreversible action (pawn advance, castling direction, abandoning a file, removing a centralized piece) that either creates a new exploitable vulnerability or surrenders an existing positional asset.
sub_patterns: Flank pawn advances creating chronic weaknesses (a4, b4, g6)
Castling or placing king toward opponent's pre-loaded pawn storm (O-O-O, b4)
Abandoning a critical open file or outpost (Rd1, Ndf5)
Routine development ignoring urgent central tension (Nf6)

analysis.label: Knight moves (often checks or captures) that look aggressive but abandon superior plans by losing tempo or removing the knight from a dominant position.
analysis.description: This feature fires on positions where a player makes a knight move (7/9 positions) that appears active—frequently giving check (4/9: Ne5+, Ne4+, Ne3+, Ng6+) or capturing material (Nxa3)—but actually worsens the position significantly. The common mechanism is that the knight leaves a dominant square where it exerted pressure (e.g., g4 threatening the king in Position 2, c5 supporting the attack in Position 5, f8 covering critical squares in Position 10) and lands on a square where it is immediately driven back (Nf6→Ng8 via Rf7), captured (Nxa3 by bxa3), or triggers simplification (Ne3+ allowing Qxe3). The 2/9 non-knight moves (Kg7, fxg3) share the broader pattern of choosing a superficially active continuation over the position's true requirement. In all cases, the best moves were quieter or differently-directed, prioritizing piece coordination and concrete threats over flashy-looking activity.
analysis.move_pattern: Knight moved to active-looking square (usually with check or capture), often jumping forward/sideways 1-2 squares toward opponent's king or a pawn target
analysis.why_bad: The knight abandons a superior post or coordination, allowing the opponent to gain a defensive resource (king escape, queen trade, immediate counter-attack) or simply driving the knight back with tempo—the 'check' or 'capture' is a distraction from the position's true winning plan
sub_patterns: Knight check that allows king to find safe square (Ne5+, Ne4+, Ng6+)
Knight check that enables simplifying queen trade (Ne3+)
Knight capture on square immediately recaptured (Nxa3)
Knight activation immediately driven back with tempo (Nf6→Ng8)
Knight development ignoring urgent tactical threat (Nc3)

analysis.label: White plays a natural-looking move instead of the one precise knight maneuver that the position demands.
analysis.description: In all 4/4 positions, the best move was a specific knight maneuver (Nb5 tactical strike, Nd3 prophylactic retreat, Ne3 attacking queen on safe square, Nxf2 capturing with correct piece), yet White chose a more routine-looking alternative: castling, a pawn capture, a knight to the wrong square, or a bishop capture. The positions share extremely narrow margins (avg 1.5 good moves available) where only the precise knight move maintained the evaluation. The played moves all have clear surface logic — O-O for king safety, hxg4 for material, Ng3 to attack the queen, Bxf2 to remove an intruder — but each ignores the critical tactical requirement that only the correct knight placement could address. The refutations typically exploit opened files or diagonals (3/4 involve d-file or central file exploitation), while the missed knight moves would have blocked those very lines or created overriding tactical threats.
analysis.move_pattern: Various piece types (king, pawn, knight, bishop) played as natural/routine alternatives when a specific knight move to a non-obvious square was required
analysis.why_bad: The played moves address secondary concerns (king safety, material gain, piece development) while ignoring the one critical tactical need that only a precise knight maneuver could solve, leaving lines open or pieces vulnerable to immediate exploitation
sub_patterns: Natural developing move instead of knight tactical strike (O-O vs Nb5)
Materialistic capture instead of knight prophylactic retreat (hxg4 vs Nd3)
Knight to wrong square ignoring piece safety (Ng3 vs Ne3)
Capture with wrong piece removing critical blocker (Bxf2 vs Nxf2)

analysis.label: Moves that squander an essential tempo through premature checks, non-urgent pawn pushes, or piece repositioning when the position demands immediate precise action on the primary threat.
analysis.description: This feature fires on positions with extremely narrow margins (avg 1.7 good moves) where the player wastes a critical tempo. The most prominent sub-pattern is premature/counterproductive queen checks (4/10 positions: Qd2+, Qh1+, Qc7+, Qc1+) that either allow simplifying trades, free the opponent's king, displace the queen from its ideal post, or move it away from defensive duties. A secondary sub-pattern involves non-essential pawn moves (3/10: c5, c6, a6) that address secondary positional concerns while ignoring urgent tactical demands like mating threats or king centralization. The 'tempo_loss' tag appears in 8/8 of the substantive blunders analyzed. In every case, the position required one specific action—maintaining attacking coordination (2/10), forcing a favorable trade (2/10), centralizing the king (2/10), or blocking a mating diagonal (1/10)—and the played move addressed something else entirely.
analysis.move_pattern: Mixed piece types (mostly queen moves with check, also pawn advances and bishop/king moves) that fail to address the position's primary demand; checks that are forcing but counterproductive, or quiet moves that waste the critical tempo needed for the one saving/winning plan.
analysis.why_bad: These moves lose the initiative by spending a tempo on something non-essential: premature checks liberate the opponent's king or allow simplification; prophylactic pawn moves ignore urgent tactical threats; piece moves abandon critical squares. In all cases, the opponent gains the tempo needed to solve their problems (escape perpetual, trade queens, invade with the king, or deliver mate).
sub_patterns: Premature queen checks that help the opponent's king reach safety or allow simplifying queen trades (Qd2+, Qh1+, Qc7+, Qc1+)
Non-essential pawn moves ignoring urgent tactical/strategic demands (c6 ignoring mate, a6 ignoring king centralization, c5 allowing en passant fork)
Piece moves to geometrically inferior squares (Kh7 where Nf5 isn't check vs Kg7 where it is; Bxf6 ignoring back-rank mate)

analysis.label: Moving a piece away from a square where it performs an essential function to pursue a seemingly attractive but far less important goal (pawn grab, centralization, space).
analysis.description: This feature fires on moves where a piece voluntarily leaves a critical post—where it controlled key squares, maintained pressure on vital pawns, or preserved escape routes—to pursue a secondary objective that appears logical on the surface. In 8/10 positions, the moved piece was performing an irreplaceable function: the bishop on g3 pinned the e3 pawn protecting a dominant knight (Position 1); the bishop on g6 was a dominating outpost that would become trapped on h7 (Position 2); the knight on e6 controlled mating squares g7/f8 (Position 11); the rook's absence from h8 blocked the king's escape to f8 (Position 9). The 'temptation' varies—grabbing an h-pawn (Positions 1, 2), gaining space with pawn advances (Positions 5, 6, 7, 10), centralizing the king (Position 15), or repositioning a piece (Positions 4, 9)—but in every case the move prioritizes a secondary goal while catastrophically undermining the position's primary tactical or structural requirement. The tag 'tempo_loss' appears in 9/10 positions and 'piece_activity' in 10/10, confirming the core pattern of self-inflicted positional degradation.
analysis.move_pattern: Any piece type moving away from an active/critical square to a seemingly attractive destination (captures on wing pawns, retreats, advances, centralizations); no single geometric direction but destination is always less functionally important than the origin square
analysis.why_bad: The piece was performing an essential function on its original square (controlling mating squares, pressuring key pawns, maintaining defensive coverage, keeping escape routes open), and removing it collapses the position's tactical or strategic infrastructure—the opponent immediately exploits the vacated function with concrete threats that far outweigh whatever the move gained.
sub_patterns: Bishop captures wing pawn (h2/h7) abandoning active diagonal pressure
Piece retreats to passive square losing critical tempo for opponent's centralization
Pawn advance weakens king shelter or opens center with exposed king
Piece blocks own king's escape route enabling perpetual/mate
King moves to seemingly logical square walking into tactical shot

analysis.label: Moving a piece away from a square where it was performing a vital defensive/protective function, leaving material or a critical square undefended.
analysis.description: This feature fires on moves where the player relocates a piece that was serving an essential guarding role, directly causing a tactical vulnerability. In 6/8 positions, the move explicitly removes protection from a piece or critical square: Kb4 leaves the d4-knight unguarded (position 1), d4 removes the d-pawn's protection of e4 (position 2), b4 wastes tempo while c2 remains undefended by the distant king (position 3), Kb8 steps onto the b-file enabling a discovered attack that wins the knight (position 4), Kc4 moves the king to where the a4-pawn falls with check (position 5), and Bxe5 leaves the e4-knight completely unprotected (position 6). The remaining cases involve choosing a passive/misdirected move over the single active option needed to maintain coordination: Kh7 retreats when only Kh5-g4 provides counterplay (position 7), and Qf6 places the queen where it becomes an immediate target for tempo-gaining attacks (position 8). These positions average only 1.5 good moves, indicating extremely narrow defensive requirements where one critical coordination had to be maintained.
analysis.move_pattern: Any piece type moving away from a square where it guarded another piece, pawn, or critical square; most commonly king moves (5/8) but also pawn advances and piece relocations
analysis.why_bad: The move severs a critical defensive link in the player's position—typically removing protection from a piece that becomes immediately capturable, or vacating a key square that allows the opponent's passed pawn breakthrough or tactical exploitation (discovered attacks, captures with check)
sub_patterns: King moves away from protecting its own piece (Kb4, Kb8, Kc4)
Pawn advance removes defense of adjacent pawn (d4 unguards e4, b4 wastes tempo leaving c2 exposed)
Piece capture/move leaves another piece hanging (Bxe5 unguards Ne4)
King/Queen moves to passive or targetable square instead of the one active defensive option (Kh7, Qf6)

analysis.label: Slow or greedy moves that leave a piece (or critical square) tactically exploitable by a forcing opponent reply.
analysis.description: In 8/8 positions, the player makes a move with a superficially logical purpose (grabbing a pawn, pushing a pawn for positional reasons, or pursuing a slow plan) while completely overlooking that the opponent has an immediate forcing response—typically a check, capture, or piece trap—that wins material or delivers a decisive blow. In Position 3, b3 ignores Qxc6+ winning a bishop with check. In Position 4, Nxh5 leaves the knight hanging to Qa5+ with tempo. In Position 6, Ba1 places the bishop directly where the king captures it. In Position 7, h3 ignores Bg4+ leading to forced mate. In Position 15, Bxa7 walks into the classic b6 trapping pattern. In Positions 2 and 14, f4 advances leave critical squares unguarded allowing the opponent to seize them with tempo. In Position 1, Kc5 places the king one crucial tempo too far from the defensive resource. The consistent error is prioritizing a non-urgent plan over checking whether the opponent's most forcing reply devastates the position.
analysis.move_pattern: Non-forcing moves (pawn pushes, quiet piece moves, or greedy edge captures) made while a piece or critical square is left tactically undefended against an opponent's check, capture, or trap
analysis.why_bad: The player fails to verify that their pieces remain safe after their move, allowing the opponent to exploit a hanging piece, deliver a forcing check that wins material, or spring a piece trap—all of which could have been prevented by addressing the immediate tactical obligation first.
sub_patterns: Greedy captures on the wing leaving the capturing piece trapped or hanging (Nxh5, Bxa7, Ba1)
Slow pawn pushes ignoring opponent's forcing tactical shot (b3, h3)
Premature pawn advances abandoning key defensive squares and giving opponent tempo (f4, f4)
King placement error missing critical one-tempo defensive window (Kc5)

analysis.label: Non-developing pawn advances (especially flank/c-pawn pushes) that waste critical tempo when the position urgently demands piece development, king safety, or concrete tactical action.
analysis.description: This feature fires on positions where the player makes a slow, non-forcing pawn advance (or generic quiet move) while their king remains vulnerable or concrete tactical opportunities exist. In 6/8 positions, the moving side's king is uncastled and stuck in the center. In 7/8 cases, the move is a pawn push (c5 appears 4 times, a-pawn pushes twice, h4 once). The best alternatives consistently involve piece development (Nf6, Be7, Nd7 in positions 3-4), concrete tactical exploitation (Qd7/Nxg2 in position 1, e5 in position 6), or prophylactic king safety measures (castling preparation, h3 preventing Ng4 in position 7). The punishment typically involves the opponent exploiting the wasted tempo to attack the exposed king via diagonal checks/sacrifices (5/8), invade weak squares abandoned by the pawn push (Bd5 in positions 3-4), or open the center against the uncastled monarch.
analysis.move_pattern: Single-square pawn advances (primarily c5, a4/a5, h4) or passive non-forcing moves, played from the moving side's 2nd-5th rank, non-capturing, non-checking
analysis.why_bad: These moves waste a critical tempo on non-urgent positional goals (space, structure) while the position demands immediate attention to king safety, piece development, or concrete tactical opportunities—the opponent punishes the lost tempo by attacking the exposed king or exploiting newly created weaknesses
sub_patterns: c5 push abandoning d5 control, allowing bishop invasion on d5 (positions 3, 4, 10)
Flank pawn push (a5/a4/h4) ignoring uncastled king vulnerability and concrete threats (positions 1, 2, 7)
Generic quiet move (Re1) missing forcing central breakthrough while opponent's king is still in center (position 6)
c5 pawn push ignoring tactical threats on diagonal with uncastled king (position 8)

analysis.label: Playing a quiet, defensive, or routine move when the position urgently demands immediate concrete/active play, resulting in a devastating tempo loss.
analysis.description: In 7/7 positions, the player chose a non-forcing, seemingly safe or natural move (retreating king, defensive rook placement, routine development, quiet pawn push) when the position critically required immediate aggressive action — whether king advancement (2/7 Kh2 instead of Kh4), king centralization (1/7 h4 instead of Ke2), immediate capture of a tactical target (2/7 Rf1/Rhf1 instead of Bxd5 or Kg3), or addressing a concrete threat (1/7 Nf6 ignoring Bxb7, 1/7 Rg8 allowing d6). Every analysis explicitly identifies 'tempo_loss' as the core motif, and in each case the wasted tempo allowed the opponent to execute a forcing sequence (perpetual check, passed pawn advance, piece activation, castling) that completely neutralized or reversed the evaluation.
analysis.move_pattern: Quiet non-forcing moves: king retreats toward back rank, lateral/defensive rook placements to first rank, routine minor piece development, passive pawn advances — all avoiding captures, checks, or direct threats
analysis.why_bad: The position demanded an immediate concrete action (aggressive king advance, tactical capture, centralization) and the quiet move surrendered a critical tempo, allowing the opponent to execute their plan — whether initiating perpetual check, advancing a passed pawn decisively, castling to safety, or seizing the initiative with active pieces.
sub_patterns: King retreating to 'safe' square instead of counterintuitively advancing (Kh2 vs Kh4)
Defensive rook move to first rank instead of active king/pawn play in endgame
Slow preparatory rook lift instead of immediate tactical capture
Routine development ignoring concrete tactical vulnerability
Purposeless pawn push when king activity is the only priority

analysis.label: Playing non-urgent a/b-file pawn advances (or equivalent slow moves) when the position demands immediate central action, development, or tactical defense.
analysis.description: In 6/7 positions, the blunder is a queenside flank pawn move (a5, a5, a6, a4, b5) or a slow queenside piece repositioning (Bb2), while in 1/7 the move (e5) locks the center similarly wasting a crucial tempo. All positions share the critical feature that the player ignores an urgent demand—whether it's resolving central tension (positions 4, 6, 10), completing development (positions 4, 10, 13), addressing immediate tactical threats to the king (position 8 with Greek Gift), or maintaining dynamic piece pressure (positions 2, 3). In every case, the opponent exploits the wasted tempo with forcing central breaks (c4, d4, e5), piece activation (Ne5, Bd3), or direct tactical strikes (Bxh2+). The average cp_loss of 240 reflects how severely a single tempo waste is punished in positions of high tactical or strategic urgency.
analysis.move_pattern: a-file or b-file pawn advances (5/7), or slow queenside piece/pawn moves that do not address central tension or immediate threats
analysis.why_bad: These moves waste a critical tempo in positions where the opponent can immediately exploit the delay with forcing central pawn breaks, tactical strikes against the king, or piece activation that the slow flank move does nothing to prevent or address.
sub_patterns: a-pawn advance ignoring uncastled king or undeveloped pieces
b-pawn 'attacking' a bishop that improves by retreating
queenside pawn push ignoring kingside tactical threats
flank play when center demands immediate resolution

analysis.label: Playing a slow, non-forcing, or misguided move when an immediate decisive tactical sequence (usually a mating attack against an exposed king) is available.
analysis.description: This feature fires on positions where the player has a forced winning combination—typically a mating attack exploiting king exposure—but instead plays a quiet developing move, a retreat, a peripheral capture, or a misguided check. In 9/11 positions, the opponent's king is critically exposed or trapped, and the best move involves an immediate forcing sequence (checks, mating patterns, diagonal/file exploitation). The chosen moves include passive piece development (Nd2, d3, Ng1), queen retreats from attacking positions (Qb3, Qd1), material grabs away from the real action (Rxc6, Nxh5, exd5), unnecessary piece repositioning (Ba6 in position 3), a pawn push ignoring mate-in-one (c3), and a flashy but wrong check that disrupts the mating mechanism (Ba6+). The unifying error is choosing a 'useful-looking' quiet or tangential move over calculating the immediately available forcing lines. The average cp_loss of 4375 reflects that most cases involve missed forced mates (7/11 positions have mate evaluations), with the position typically having very few good alternatives (avg 1.9), indicating narrow tactical moments demanding precise calculation.
analysis.move_pattern: Diverse piece types and directions; typically quiet moves (non-checks, non-captures toward the opponent's king), retreats, or captures/checks directed away from the critical attacking zone around the exposed enemy king
analysis.why_bad: These moves surrender a time-critical tactical opportunity—the position demands immediate forcing action (checks, mating sequences) against a vulnerable king, but the chosen move gives the opponent one or more tempi to escape the mating net, cover critical squares, or consolidate their king's position.
sub_patterns: Queen retreats from active attacking position when mate is available (Qb3, Qd1)
Quiet piece development ignoring immediate mating checks (Nd2, d3, Ng1)
Material-grabbing captures away from the critical king attack (Rxc6, Nxh5, exd5)
Moving a piece off its ideal tactical square needed for the combination (Ba6 from b7, Ba6+ from b5)
Pawn advance toward promotion ignoring immediate checkmate (c3)

analysis.label: Playing a tempting but passive/non-urgent move when a more forcing continuation (mate, decisive tactic, or maximum pressure) was available in a winning position.
analysis.description: This feature fires on moves where the player has a significant advantage (often a winning attack or exposed enemy king) but chooses a visually appealing, 'natural-looking' move over the most forcing continuation. In 7/9 positions, the analyses tag 'tempo_loss' as the primary motif. In 8/9 cases, the move reduces piece activity or coordination against the opponent's vulnerable king. In 4/9 cases, a forced checkmate was available but missed (Bd4 missed mate-in-2, Bg2 had mate-in-15 vs mate-in-12, Qxe7+ lost a mate-in-9, Nxc2+ missed mate-in-3). The remaining positions involve choosing comfortable centralization (Qe5, Qb6), slow prophylaxis (a6, Kc6), or wrong-direction checks (Qh7+) when concrete forcing moves maintained overwhelming pressure. The average cp_loss of 2338 reflects how devastating these errors are—each move converts a dominating/winning position into one that is merely better or even lost.
analysis.move_pattern: Diverse piece types moving to 'attractive' squares (centralization, development, material gain, or check) but in wrong direction or with wrong urgency relative to the critical forcing continuation
analysis.why_bad: Each move reduces the forcing nature of the position by giving the opponent time to escape, consolidate, or counter-attack. The player prioritizes general chess principles (centralization, development, material) over concrete calculation of the most forcing line, allowing the opponent to address the critical vulnerability that the best move would have exploited immediately.
sub_patterns: Centralizing piece to 'nice' square instead of maintaining pressure on exposed king (Qe5, Bd4, Bg2, Qb6)
Capturing with wrong piece or in wrong direction, losing coordination (Qxe7+, Qh7+, Nxc2+)
Slow pawn/king move when urgent tactical action required (a6, Kc6)

analysis.label: Superficially reasonable piece-improving moves that miss the position's concrete, forcing demands and waste critical tempo.
analysis.description: This feature activates when a player makes a move that appears positionally logical or improving—placing a piece on an 'active' square, centralizing, or creating apparent pressure—but fails to execute the specific concrete action the position demands. In 8/11 positions, the best move was a direct forcing move (capture, precise check, or immediate threat) while the played move was a general improvement. For example, Qf3 instead of the forcing Qh5 (position 13), Nd4+ instead of the material-winning Nxe5+ (position 11), Rd3 centralizing instead of Rh4 engaging the passed pawn (position 12), Bf4 'attacking' the queen instead of Nb5 creating concrete threats (position 15), and Bd5 'centralizing' instead of Qb6 or Rxe1+ addressing real needs (position 10). The pattern also includes premature non-forcing advances like f4 blocking development (position 6), c5 creating weaknesses (position 7), and Kh8 being passive when active counterplay was available (position 3). In all cases, the opponent gains time to solve their problems—castling safely (positions 6, 13), capturing undefended material (positions 3, 7, 12), or generating tactical counterplay (positions 1, 15).
analysis.move_pattern: Piece placement to seemingly active/central square (any piece type, any direction) that is non-forcing — not a capture, not a meaningful check, and not addressing an immediate concrete threat
analysis.why_bad: The position requires a specific concrete action (forcing capture, precise check, addressing an immediate tactical threat, or preventing opponent's consolidation), but the played move is merely 'improving' — it gives the opponent a free tempo to castle, capture hanging material, create counterplay, or neutralize the position's tactical energy
sub_patterns: Queen to attractive-but-less-forcing square vs. the one that creates immediate threats (Qf3 vs Qh5, Qc4 vs Qxg6+, Qb2 vs Bb2)
Piece centralization that creates a target or abandons a critical task (Bd5 getting captured, Rd3 abandoning g-pawn duty)
Flashy check that only leads to exchanges vs. direct material-winning move (Nd4+ vs Nxe5+)
Premature pawn advance that neglects development or exposes own king (f4, c5)
Developing/improving move that ignores an immediate hanging piece or tactical vulnerability (Bb4 allowing Qxg7, Kh8 dropping g5)

analysis.label: Moving a piece away from its essential defensive or strategic duty, immediately allowing the opponent to exploit the vacated sector.
analysis.description: This feature fires on moves where a piece leaves a square where it was performing a vital function—defending a pawn, controlling a critical file, maintaining pressure, or keeping the king safe—and relocates to an irrelevant or inferior post. In 7/9 positions, the moved piece was directly guarding something that immediately becomes exploitable: the queen leaves c3 undefending b2 (Qe3), the queen leaves d8 undefending b7 (Qe7), the rook leaves the b-file allowing a decisive b-pawn break (Re1), the rook abandons the h-file attack (Rg8), the bishop releases pressure on f6 allowing central counterplay (Bf4). In 2/9 positions, the piece moves toward danger rather than away: the king walks into a mating net (Kd3) or into pawn-check attacks (Kg5). In the remaining cases, the piece ignores the critical threat entirely: capturing a peripheral h4 pawn while a b6 passed pawn promotes (Rxh4), or placing a rook where advancing pawns gain tempo against it (Rb3). The average cp_loss of 1266 and average of only 2.1 good moves confirms these are critical moments requiring precision.
analysis.move_pattern: Any piece type moving away from the critical sector (file, diagonal, or rank where the main battle is occurring) to an irrelevant or dangerous square
analysis.why_bad: The piece was performing an essential function (guarding a pawn, controlling a file, maintaining pressure, or shielding the king), and its departure creates an immediate tactical or strategic vulnerability that the opponent exploits within 1-2 moves—typically winning material, creating unstoppable passed pawns, or delivering checkmate.
sub_patterns: Queen leaves defensive post, hanging a pawn to a double attack
Rook abandons critical open file, allowing opponent's pawn break
Bishop/piece retreats releasing tension, giving opponent a free tempo to strike
King advances into exposed square vulnerable to checks or mating nets
Piece captures peripheral material while ignoring existential positional threat

analysis.label: Active-looking moves that prioritize secondary objectives (material, centralization, or activity) while ignoring the position's most urgent tactical demand.
analysis.description: This feature fires on positions where a player makes an aggressive or ambitious-looking move while neglecting a critical tactical vulnerability in their own position. In 6/9 positions, king safety is the ignored concern (Kg3 walks into Rf3+ mating net, Bc4 leaves king exposed on e1-h4 diagonal, cxb5 opens the c-file toward own king, Qd5 ignores Re7+ devastating the exposed king, d5 opens the b4-e1 diagonal for a check). In 3/9 positions, the error involves choosing the wrong target or wrong piece (Qxh7 captures a pawn when the knight on g8 was available, Rxf2 captures with the rook leaving the knight hanging on e4, Kb5 pursues the a5-pawn instead of the immediate g7 promotion). The common thread is that the played move looks natural or active in isolation but completely misreads the position's priorities, resulting in an average 1352cp loss. The best moves in each position tend to be quieter, more defensive, or more precisely targeted at the real tactical demand.
analysis.move_pattern: Piece moves to active/central/aggressive-looking square or makes materialistic capture, typically forward or toward opponent's territory, while own position contains an unaddressed critical vulnerability
analysis.why_bad: These moves ignore the position's most urgent tactical demand—whether it's defending an exposed king, promoting an advanced pawn, capturing the correct target, or using the right piece for a capture—in favor of a secondary objective that looks appealing but allows a tactical refutation exploiting the neglected vulnerability.
sub_patterns: King advances into tactical danger instead of retreating to safety (Kg3, Kd4)
Materialistic captures that miss a bigger tactical opportunity (Qxh7 vs Qxg8, Kb5 vs g7)
Active piece placement on undefended squares ignoring diagonal/file exposure (Bc4, Qd5)
Pawn captures that open lines toward own king (cxb5, d5)
Capturing with wrong piece leaving other pieces hanging (Rxf2 vs Nxf2)

analysis.label: Playing a slow preparatory move while the opponent has an immediately decisive pawn break (axb5 or hxg6) that rips open critical lines.
analysis.description: In 6/6 positions, the player makes a quiet, non-forcing move (pawn push or passive rook repositioning) while the opponent has a concrete pawn capture or advance ready to execute with devastating effect. In 5/6 cases, a specific pawn tension exists (axb5 in positions 1-2, hxg6 in positions 4-5, or g4 in position 6) that the played move completely fails to address. The refutations in all cases involve the pawn break proceeding immediately—creating advanced passed pawns (2/6), opening the h-file toward the king (3/6), or winning material via removing key defenders (1/6). The best moves in each position either directly address the tension (c6, Nh6, g5 reinforcing the critical pawn), generate immediate counterplay against the opponent's king (Qb6, Rah8), or win material that changes the calculus (Qxd4). The common thread is wasting the final critical tempo on a 'planning' move when the position demands immediate tactical response.
analysis.move_pattern: Quiet pawn pushes (b5, g6, g3, b6) or passive rook moves to back rank (Rb8, Rf8), typically on flanks, never addressing the critical pawn tension
analysis.why_bad: The opponent has an imminent pawn break (axb5, hxg6, or g4) that creates decisive structural damage or opens lethal attacking lines, and these moves waste the one tempo needed to prevent or neutralize it
sub_patterns: Queenside pawn push ignoring axb5 breaking the chain and winning material
Slow fianchetto preparation while hxg6 opens the h-file against uncastled/castled king
Passive rook move while kingside pawn storm delivers mating attack
Pawn move that self-weakens by enabling opponent's capture to open lines

analysis.label: Slow preparatory or repositioning moves that miss available immediate captures or one-time tactical opportunities.
analysis.description: In 5/7 positions, the best move was an immediate concrete capture (Bxa6, Rxg2, dxc3 en passant, Kxh5, Qxc3), but the player chose a slower approach or repositioning move instead. The pattern is especially striking in positions 4 and 6, where the king literally moves TOWARD the capture target (Kf2 approaching g2, Kg5 approaching h5) without actually taking. Similarly in position 8, the queen moves to b6 (near c3) instead of capturing on c3, and in position 5, a pawn advances on the queenside (b5) instead of executing the time-limited en passant capture (dxc3). In position 3, the king approaches the a6-pawn (Kb6) instead of maintaining defensive coordination (Kd7). The moves share a 'one square short' quality—they orbit the critical action without completing it, giving the opponent a decisive tempo to create threats (connected passers, mating nets, or simply winning undefended material).
analysis.move_pattern: Various pieces (King, Queen, Knight, pawn) moving toward or near a critical target square without executing the available capture on that target
analysis.why_bad: These moves forfeit a critical tempo when an immediate capture or concrete action is available, allowing the opponent to either create unstoppable threats (passed pawns advancing, mating attacks) or stabilize a position that was about to collapse. The one-move delay transforms winning/defensible positions into lost ones.
sub_patterns: King advancing toward a pawn without capturing it (Kf2/Kg5 instead of Rxg2/Kxh5)
Queen repositioning near a capturable pawn instead of taking it (Qb6 vs Qxc3)
Missing time-limited captures like en passant (b5 vs dxc3)
Retreating/regrouping when a forcing capture resolves the position (Nf1 vs Bxa6)

analysis.label: Moves that follow general principles or obvious ideas while completely ignoring the position's single most urgent tactical demand.
analysis.description: This feature activates on moves where the player chooses a 'reasonable-looking' or 'routine' action that fails to address the one critical requirement of the position. In 6/9 cases, a specific tactic was missed (free piece capture on g4, mate in 2 via Nxb3+, forced mate via Bd3, immediate Bb4# checkmate, Ng6+ fork setup, b7 advance winning material). In 5/9 cases, the move was explicitly passive or prophylactic (h3, g3, h5, Rb8, Nd7) when sharp concrete action was demanded. The common thread is that each position had exactly one pressing demand — whether offensive (exploiting a tactic) or defensive (blocking a passed pawn, maintaining a critical defender on a file) — and the player instead played a move addressing a secondary concern: 'kicking' a bishop that could simply be captured (h3), creating 'luft' that opens a fatal diagonal (g3), grabbing material when mate exists (Qxa1+), passively blocking instead of actively controlling (Rb8), repositioning when blockade is needed NOW (Nd7), or abandoning a critical defensive post for pawns (Qb3). The average cp_loss of 4310 reflects that ignoring the position's singular demand typically leads to catastrophic consequences.
analysis.move_pattern: Any piece type or direction; no geometric consistency — the pattern is functional (addressing a secondary concern) rather than spatial
analysis.why_bad: Each move ignores the ONE thing the position urgently demands — a winning capture, a critical blockade, maintaining a defensive piece, or finding the correct escape route — choosing instead a generically reasonable but specifically catastrophic alternative
sub_patterns: Routine prophylactic pawn push when a direct tactical win exists (h3 instead of Bxg4)
Greedy material capture when forced checkmate is available (Qxa1+ instead of Nxb3+)
Passive piece placement when active counterplay is the only defense (Rb8, Nd7, h5)
Removing a critical defensive piece for offensive purposes (Qb3 abandoning e-file, Bd4 leaving e3)
King retreating to wrong square that allows perpetual checks (Kd2 instead of Kf2 or Bd3)

analysis.label: Moves that pursue the correct tactical or strategic concept but fatally misexecute by choosing the wrong piece, wrong square, or wrong timing in razor-sharp positions.
analysis.description: This feature fires on positions where the player demonstrates correct pattern recognition but fails in precise execution, typically in narrow positions with very few good moves (avg 1.7). In 6/6 cases, the played move closely resembles the best move conceptually: Rdg8 mirrors Rhg8 (wrong rook, Position 1), Rf6+ mirrors Rf7+ (wrong rank for discovered check, Position 4), Kb5 goes in a similar direction as Kc7 (wrong king retreat square, Position 2), Qa5 is a queen relocation like Qd3 (wrong destination, Position 5), Nb5 is a knight move when Nxb7 was needed (wrong knight action, Position 6), and b5 pushes on the queenside when Qf3 maintains the bind (premature release, Position 3). The catastrophic nature of these 'near-misses' is evident in the average cp_loss of 3392, with two positions converting from winning to forced mate against. The narrow margin (avg 1.7 good moves) confirms these are critical junctures where only exact play succeeds.
analysis.move_pattern: Various piece types moving to an adjacent or conceptually similar square compared to the correct move; often one rank/file off from the winning continuation, or the wrong piece executing the same geometric idea
analysis.why_bad: Each move abandons control of a critical square or line that the opponent immediately exploits: the d-file vacancy allows Qd4 (Pos 1), the b5 square allows a6+/b5+ pawn checks (Pos 2), releasing tension opens a6 for knight development (Pos 3), f6 instead of f7 lets the king escape to g7 (Pos 4), leaving c3 abandons c5 control allowing Rc5 (Pos 5), and Nb5 fails to engage any critical threat (Pos 6)
sub_patterns: Wrong rook or piece executing the correct idea
One-square-off errors in checks/attacks missing forced mate
Queen/king relocating to a plausible but fatally imprecise square
Premature pawn breaks releasing tension that was the source of advantage

analysis.label: Moves that remove a piece from its critical defensive role (or capture with the wrong piece) to pursue an aggressive or improving plan, leaving material undefended.
analysis.description: This feature fires on moves where the player abandons a critical defensive function to pursue some other goal—attacking, advancing, or repositioning—resulting in a piece being left undefended or a key square collapsing. In 5/8 positions, the move directly removes the sole defender of an important piece (Qc4 abandons Ne6 in position 1; f4 removes the bishop's retreat from Ng4 in position 8; Nh7 removes the knight from f6 where it defended d5 in position 14; Nc6 abandons defensive duties for a speculative attack in position 7; d5 weakens the e7 knight's pawn support in position 6). In 2/8 positions, the player captures with the wrong piece, leaving a more valuable piece stranded and undefended (bxc3+ instead of Qxc3+ in position 9; bxc3 prematurely in position 10). In 1/8 positions, a piece is placed on an undefended square where it can simply be taken (Nb4 in position 15). The average cp_loss of 314 reflects that the punishment is typically winning a full piece through a straightforward capture or short forcing sequence.
analysis.move_pattern: A defender (queen, knight, or pawn) moves away from its protective role—or a capture is made with the wrong piece—leaving a piece/square fatally unprotected
analysis.why_bad: The move removes the sole defense of a piece or critical square, allowing the opponent to win material through a simple capture or short tactical sequence that exploits the newly undefended target
sub_patterns: Queen/piece moves away from defending a knight or minor piece, leaving it hanging
Pawn advance removes defensive support (retreat square or pawn shield) for a piece
Capturing with the wrong piece (pawn instead of queen) strands a valuable piece
Knight repositioned from strong central square to passive/edge square, collapsing defense
Knight placed on an unsupported outpost where it can be captured for free

analysis.label: Playing a passive, indirect move in a position where an immediately available capture or direct confrontation was essential to maintain the evaluation.
analysis.description: In 4/7 positions, the best move was a concrete capture (fxe5, Nxe3, dxe5, cxb6) that the player ignored in favor of a quiet maneuver. In the remaining cases, the best move was still a direct, forcing action (king centralization, defensive queen reposition, pawn lock) that addressed the critical tension in the position. The played moves instead pursued secondary strategic goals: flank pawn pushes (a5, c6), piece retreats to passive squares (Bb1, Kg1), queen sorties to the wing (Qa5 × 2), or quiet development (Qd7). All 7 positions had very few good moves available (avg 1.3), indicating critical moments where the margin for error was razor-thin and only concrete resolution of the central tension maintained the evaluation. The feature fires when a player sidesteps the position's most urgent demand in favor of an indirect improvement.
