analysis.move_pattern: Non-capturing, non-forcing moves (pawn pushes to a/c files, piece retreats toward a1/g1 corners, queen deployments to a5/d7) avoiding available captures or direct central confrontations
analysis.why_bad: These moves waste a critical tempo ignoring available captures or urgent tension-resolution, allowing the opponent to reorganize (centralize king/knight, castle safely, invade open files, or execute a tactical blow) that would have been impossible had the concrete action been taken immediately.
sub_patterns: Flank queen deployment (Qa5) instead of capturing centrally (Nxe3, dxe5)
Passive pawn move (a5, c6) instead of king centralization or pawn capture
Piece retreat for strategic aim (Bb1, Kg1) instead of immediate material gain or defensive coverage

analysis.label: Quiet, non-forcing moves that waste a critical tempo when the position demands immediate concrete action.
analysis.description: This feature fires on moves that appear 'useful' or 'natural' in isolation but fatally ignore the position's urgent tactical or strategic demands. In 5/6 positions, the analysis explicitly identifies 'tempo_loss' as the core tactical motif. The pattern spans prophylactic pawn moves when king safety is critical (h3, c3 in openings with uncastled kings: 2/6), piece retreats that remove defenders from key squares (Nd8 abandoning f7 control: 1/6), king moves in the wrong direction during razor-sharp pawn races (Ke3 instead of Ke4 or f4: 1/6), checks that drive the opponent's king to favorable squares (Qg8+ allowing Kh1 oscillation: 1/6), and development that ignores immediate mate threats (Nc3 allowing Qh4#: 1/6). In every case, the opponent punishes by executing the concrete action the slow move failed to prevent—central breakthroughs (e4-e5), pawn races won by one tempo, or direct mating attacks.
analysis.move_pattern: Quiet non-forcing moves (pawn pushes, piece retreats, development, wrong-direction checks) that don't address the position's most critical demand
analysis.why_bad: They squander a tempo on an irrelevant or low-priority objective while the opponent has a concrete tactical threat or breakthrough that the wasted move fails to prevent, allowing the opponent to execute their plan with decisive timing advantage.
sub_patterns: Prophylactic pawn moves (h3/c3) when king safety demands castling
Piece retreats removing critical defenders from key squares
King moves in wrong direction during pawn endgame races
Checks that drive opponent's king to safer squares
Standard development ignoring immediate mating threats

analysis.label: Moving a king or queen to a square that appears purposeful but is fatally exposed on an open file, rank, or diagonal, enabling immediate tactical exploitation.
analysis.description: This feature fires on moves where a high-value piece (king or queen) is voluntarily placed on a square that lies on an exploitable geometric line. In 7/9 cases, the king or queen directly moves to the dangerous square: king castles into an attackable queenside (O-O-O), king steps onto a lethal diagonal (Ke8 allowing Bh5#), king advances into pawn-check exposure (Kb4 allowing a3+), king lands on its own rook's file creating a skewer (Kd4 allowing Rd5+), queen retreats to a rank attackable by rook (Qf3 allowing Re3), queen abandons a defensive diagonal (Qh7 allowing Qxg6+), and queen moves to a square enabling back-rank forced queen trade (Qe7 allowing Qg8+). In 2/9 cases, the move indirectly creates the open-line vulnerability (Bxg5 opens the h-file against own king, gxh5 allows an intermezzo knight fork exploiting the king's position on an open file). The average centipawn loss is catastrophic (~2336), with multiple positions going from playable to forced mate, yet an average of 2.8 good alternatives existed in each case.
analysis.move_pattern: King or queen moves to a square on an open file, rank, or diagonal; or a capture/exchange opens a line against the player's own king position
analysis.why_bad: The moved piece lands on a geometric line (file, rank, or diagonal) already controlled or immediately accessible by the opponent's active pieces, enabling a forcing tactical response (check, skewer, back-rank mate, or winning attack) that the player failed to foresee.
sub_patterns: King moves to exposed square on open file/diagonal (Ke8, Kb4, Kd4, O-O-O)
Queen moves to square attackable along rank/file or abandons critical defensive duty (Qf3, Qe7, Qh7)
Capture/exchange that opens a line against own king (Bxg5 opens h-file, gxh5 allows intermezzo)

analysis.label: Early queen sortie to an aggressive forward square (usually f3) aimed at f7, which becomes a target for tempo-gaining minor piece attacks.
analysis.description: This feature fires on premature queen developments to exposed attacking squares in the opening, overwhelmingly Qf3 (7/10 positions) but also Qh5, Qf6, and Qxd5. In every case, the queen is placed on a forward square targeting f7 or centralizing aggressively before piece development is complete. The punishment consistently involves minor pieces attacking the queen with tempo: Nd4 forks (positions 7, 12), Bg4 pins/attacks (position 10), Bd5 diagonal attacks (position 5), Nf6 tempo (position 11), Nd5 attacks (position 6), c4 pawn thrusts (position 3), and Qb4+ exploiting the exposed king diagonal (position 14). The average cp_loss of 258 reflects how severely these moves are punished. In 9/10 cases the position is in the opening phase with kings uncastled, and the queen move both wastes tempo AND blocks critical development squares (especially f3 for the knight). All positions had 2-3 solid developing alternatives available.
analysis.move_pattern: Queen moves forward to f3 (or h5/f6/d5) in the opening, typically eyeing f7 pressure, before minor piece development is complete
analysis.why_bad: The queen on an exposed forward square becomes a target for tempo-gaining attacks by developing minor pieces (Nd4, Bg4, Bd5, Nf6), costing multiple tempi while simultaneously blocking critical development squares (especially Nf3) and leaving the king vulnerable in the center.
sub_patterns: Qf3 blocking knight's natural f3 square and allowing Nd4 fork
Qf3/Qh5 attacked by bishop developing to g4 or d5 with tempo
Qxd5 centralized queen chased by pawn advances (c4, b5)
Queen sortie leaving undefended pieces vulnerable to discovered attacks/checks

analysis.label: Moves that waste critical tempo on secondary goals (checks, pawn grabs, flank pushes, premature actions) when the position demands immediate attention to the primary strategic or tactical need.
analysis.description: This feature fires on moves that pursue a superficially reasonable but fundamentally misdirected plan at a critical moment. The common thread is tempo loss: the player makes a move that looks active or logical but gives the opponent a crucial beat to solve their problems or exploit weaknesses. In 9/11 positions, the analyses explicitly tag 'tempo_loss' as a core issue. Specific manifestations include: premature attacks without preparation (Qb3 before hxg6, Position 1), pointless checks that drive the king to safety (Ba4+ allowing Ke1, Position 13), greedy pawn grabs that squander development time (Rxh7 with bishop round-trip, Position 14), flank pawn pushes when central action is critical (h4 letting Black castle, Position 8; b4 weakening the center, Position 9), and pushing pawns to undefended squares (c4, Position 7). In all cases, the position offered 2-3 good alternatives that addressed the primary need (development, central action, piece coordination), yet the player chose a tangential action. The average cp_loss of 1049 reflects that these tempo-wasting moves occur at critical moments where the position demands precision.
analysis.move_pattern: Diverse piece types and directions, but typically sideways/peripheral moves (flank pawns, rim squares, non-central queen relocations, captures on the edge) rather than moves toward the center of action
analysis.why_bad: Each move gives the opponent a critical tempo to resolve their main vulnerability (castle to safety, escape the king, consolidate development, capture free material, break the center) - the player prioritizes a secondary goal while the opponent uses the gifted time to neutralize or reverse the position's demands.
sub_patterns: Pointless/premature checks that improve the opponent's king position
Greedy rim captures that waste multiple tempi for marginal material
Flank pawn pushes when central development/action is urgent
Premature execution of the right plan without necessary preparation moves
Passive retreats that abandon critical defensive duties

analysis.label: Moving a piece to a seemingly active square while abandoning critical defensive responsibilities, leaving key squares or the king unguarded.
analysis.description: In 7/7 positions, the played move places a piece on a square that appears active or natural but neglects the position's actual defensive requirements. The best moves are consistently more modest or retreating (Be6 over Bb7, Qd2 over Qg2, Qb8 over Qa5, Kc4 over Kb4, Kd2 over Kb3, h4 over Nf4, Qc1 over Qc5). In 5/7 cases, the move directly abandons coverage of critical squares near the player's own king, allowing immediate tactical punishment via checks, invasions, or piece traps. In 6/7 positions, king_safety is the primary concern being neglected. The punishments range from forced mate (Qg2 allowing Qc3+, Qc5 allowing Qda7+) to open-file invasions (Bb7 allowing Rd6+) to piece trapping (Qa5 trapped by Be3-Bb6). The feature appears to detect the strategic error of choosing cosmetic piece activity over functional defensive placement.
analysis.move_pattern: Piece (queen, bishop, knight, or king) moves away from the critical defensive zone toward a peripheral, forward, or seemingly aggressive square
analysis.why_bad: The move abandons coverage of critical squares near the player's own king or leaves the piece tactically vulnerable (trapped/exposed), while the position demanded consolidation, retreat, or defensive reinforcement of key files/diagonals
sub_patterns: Queen moves to exposed/distant square abandoning king defense (Qg2, Qa5, Qc5)
Piece developed to wrong square ignoring open-file invasion (Bb7 instead of Be6)
King moves toward the wing away from the critical action zone (Kb4, Kb3)
Piece placed on tactically vulnerable square becoming a tempo target (Nf4 hit by g5)

analysis.label: Active-looking moves that ignore the single most urgent tactical or defensive requirement of the position, resulting in severe punishment.
analysis.description: This feature fires on moves that appear purposeful—centralizing a piece, making a capture, delivering a check, or repositioning the king—but fatally neglect the one critical demand of the position. In 5/5 cases, the position had very few good alternatives (avg 1.8), meaning precision was essential. In 4/5 cases the player chose aggression or activity over addressing an immediate vulnerability: Nd5 centralized instead of castling (leaving b2 hanging), Qf2 repositioned instead of covering e3 (allowing forced mate), Bxd5 captured a pawn but broke the Bc4-Ng5 battery (leaving the knight hanging), Bxf6+ won a rook with check but missed Qxf7# (checkmate in one), and Kg8 moved the king 'safely' without defending the back rank (losing the c8 bishop). King safety was the underlying critical issue in 5/5 positions, and tempo loss appears as a tag in 4/5. The common thread is that each move pursues a secondary objective while the position screams for one specific response.
analysis.move_pattern: Mixed piece types (N, Q, B, B, K) making seemingly productive moves—centralizations, captures, checks, repositions—that address a lower-priority concern than what the position demands
analysis.why_bad: Each move leaves the most critical tactical vulnerability unaddressed (exposed king, hanging piece, undefended back rank, or available checkmate), and the opponent punishes by exploiting that exact vulnerability with forcing moves
sub_patterns: Aggressive centralization neglecting castling priority
Captures that break essential piece coordination leaving pieces hanging
Winning checks/captures that miss immediately decisive alternatives
Repositioning moves that fail to address back-rank or defensive emergencies

analysis.label: Retreating or non-forcing moves in positions where only one or two aggressive continuations maintain a winning advantage.
analysis.description: This feature fires on positions where the player has a significant (often winning) advantage but with an extremely narrow path to maintain it (avg 1.4 good moves available). In 7/9 positions, the best move involved aggressive piece infiltration (Rb3, Rd1, Re1, Nd6) or a critical space-gaining pawn advance (c4), but the player instead chose a passive, retreating, or misdirected move. In 5/9 cases, the played move was explicitly a retreat toward the back rank or board edge (Rb1, Qc8, Nf8, Ka6, Kb7). In 2/9 cases, the player captured the wrong target (Qxd3 trading the attacking queen, Rxc4 taking a passive bishop instead of the critical defending rook). The common thread is that these positions were time-sensitive — the advantage stemmed from dynamic factors like piece activity, king exposure, or initiative — and the passive move allowed the opponent to consolidate, seize a key square, or execute a tactical resource (e5 fork in 2/9 positions, b4 space grab, Rg2 defensive consolidation). The average cp_loss of 1411 reflects how catastrophically these advantages evaporate when tempo is wasted.
analysis.move_pattern: Retreating, sideways, or non-forcing piece moves (especially to back rank or board edge); also misdirected captures that trade attacking pieces or miss the critical target
analysis.why_bad: The position demands urgent aggressive action (infiltration, invasion, or critical pawn advance) because the advantage is dynamic and time-sensitive; passive moves surrender the initiative and allow the opponent to neutralize threats, seize key squares, or execute tactical counters that were previously impossible
sub_patterns: Piece retreats to back rank when infiltration available (Rb1/Qc8/Nf8)
King walks into exposed square allowing pawn fork or check sequences (Kb7/Kc6/Ka6)
Capturing wrong target when removing key defender forces mate (Rxc4/Qxd3)
Generic improving move instead of critical one-move tactical window (Qf3)

analysis.label: Player makes a quiet repositioning move instead of simply capturing an undefended enemy piece that is freely available.
analysis.description: In all 8/8 positions, an enemy piece (queen, rook, or bishop) is completely undefended and capturable for free, yet the player makes a quiet non-capturing move instead. The missed captures include: Qxd4 winning an undefended rook (pos 1), Bxa6 capturing a hanging queen (pos 2), Rxd8 taking an undefended queen (pos 3), Nxc5 winning an unprotected bishop (pos 4), Bxh3 capturing a hanging rook (pos 5), Rxd5 taking an undefended bishop (pos 6), Qxb3 capturing a hanging queen (pos 7), and Nxg4 taking an undefended queen (pos 8). In several cases, the player actually moves the very piece that should make the capture AWAY from the target (Be2 moves bishop away from h3; Be4 moves bishop off the a6-capturing diagonal). The average cp_loss of 3756 reflects that 5/8 positions involved missing a queen capture or forced mate. All played moves are quiet repositioning moves with no checks, captures, or direct threats.
analysis.move_pattern: Quiet non-capturing piece repositioning (any piece type, any direction) when an immediate free capture of an undefended enemy piece exists
analysis.why_bad: The player fails to recognize that a major or minor enemy piece is completely undefended and immediately capturable, instead making a positional or developmental move that wastes the critical tempo needed to collect free material—often allowing the opponent to save the hanging piece on the next move.
sub_patterns: Moving the capturing piece AWAY from its target (bishop leaves capturing diagonal)
Moving an irrelevant piece while a different piece has a free capture available
King move wasting tempo when a piece capture delivers checkmate-level advantage
Pawn push ignoring that own piece is simultaneously hanging and can capture instead

analysis.label: Playing a slow non-forcing move while leaving a piece (often a queen) undefended and immediately capturable.
analysis.description: In 5/5 positions, the player makes a quiet, non-tactical move (king walk, pawn push, or passive development) while a major or minor piece is en prise or left undefended on the board. In Position 1, Kc6 abandons defense of the queen on d4, allowing Rxd4. In Position 2, Ne2 ignores the hanging rook on h1, allowing Bxh1. In Position 3, Kf3 places the king where recapturing on e4 creates a fork, losing material. In Position 4, Kf5 abandons defense of the queen on d6, allowing Rxd6. In Position 5, h5 is a slow pawn push while the knight on c5 hangs to Bxc5. All correct alternatives involved either saving the threatened piece, resolving the tactical tension first, or making a concrete forcing move. The blunders average 338cp loss, consistent with losing roughly a full piece.
analysis.move_pattern: Quiet non-capturing, non-checking move (3/5 king moves, 1 knight retreat, 1 pawn push) that fails to address an immediately capturable piece
analysis.why_bad: The move ignores an urgent tactical reality—a piece is hanging or about to be captured—in favor of a slow positional or developmental idea, allowing the opponent to simply win material on the next move.
sub_patterns: King move abandoning defense of own queen (Kc6, Kf5)
Quiet development while rook/piece hangs (Ne2, h5)
King move creating tactical vulnerability for piece recapture (Kf3)

analysis.label: Playing a plausible-looking piece improvement or repositioning move in a position that demands exactly one urgent forcing action, squandering the critical tempo.
analysis.description: In all 5/5 positions, exactly one good move existed (avg good moves = 1.0), indicating razor-sharp positions demanding precise concrete action. The played moves are all non-forcing 'improvements' — Qd3 centralizes the queen, Ka4 repositions the king, Nb4 develops a knight to an 'active' square, Bxh6 grabs a pawn, Rf8 doubles rooks — that look natural but waste the one tempo needed for the position's urgent demand. In 4/5 cases, the best move was a pawn advance or tactical strike (d5, a4, e4, Bh4) that exploited concrete tension before the opponent could resolve it favorably. The 'tempo_loss' tag appears in 5/5 analyses. The blunders average 317cp loss, transforming winning/equal positions into lost/drawn ones because the opponent gains exactly the time needed to execute their own plan (passed pawn advance, kingside attack, piece coordination).
analysis.move_pattern: Non-forcing piece moves (repositioning, development, or minor captures) rather than checks, critical pawn advances, or forcing tactical strikes
analysis.why_bad: These moves waste the single critical tempo in positions where only one urgent action maintains the evaluation — allowing the opponent to resolve tension on their terms, advance passed pawns, or exploit newly created vulnerabilities
sub_patterns: Piece repositioning instead of critical pawn advance (Qd3/Ka4 vs d5/a4)
Pawn capture instead of piece-winning tactical strike (Bxh6 vs e4)
Piece development to vulnerable square creating geometric weakness (Nb4 allowing fork)
Rook improvement ignoring opponent's unstoppable passed pawn (Rf8 vs Bh4)

analysis.label: Moves that pursue a secondary objective while ignoring the single most urgent demand of the position.
analysis.description: This feature fires on moves that spend a critical tempo addressing a non-urgent concern while the position demands immediate action on something else entirely. In 8/8 positions, the player chose a move that looked reasonable in isolation—capturing a pawn (bxa6, Rxe6), attacking a piece (Nf4), repositioning (Rb5, Re3), or moving the king (Kh4, Kf1, Ke6)—but completely ignored the PRIMARY positional necessity: sealing the kingside (Position 1), delivering forced checkmate (Position 4), activating the king in a rook endgame (Position 7), eliminating dangerous passed pawns (Position 8), keeping the king safe (Positions 9, 11, 12), or capturing an immediately available pawn for tempo (Position 14). The analyses unanimously tag 'tempo_loss' across all 8 positions, confirming that the shared error is wasting a move on something that doesn't matter while the opponent's critical threats proceed unimpeded. The average cp_loss of 2554 reflects how punishing this mistake is—positions with one urgent demand tolerate zero wasted moves.
analysis.move_pattern: Diverse piece types and directions; typically captures of non-critical material, piece repositionings to secondary squares, or king moves toward non-critical zones—all moving AWAY from the primary battlefield or urgent threat
analysis.why_bad: Each move wastes a critical tempo on a secondary objective (capturing a harmless pawn, attacking non-urgent material, repositioning passively) while the position has exactly one urgent demand—whether defensive (stopping a mating attack, blocking passed pawns) or offensive (delivering forced mate, capturing the critical pawn)—that cannot be delayed by even one move.
sub_patterns: Capturing a static/harmless pawn while ignoring dynamic threats (bxa6, Rxe6)
Attacking a piece while missing forced checkmate (Nf4)
King move to wrong square ignoring the one correct destination (Kh4, Kf1, Ke6)
Passive piece repositioning instead of the urgent active move (Rb5, Re3)

analysis.label: Playing an obvious forcing move (usually a rook check) before a quieter preparatory move that would have been far more devastating.
analysis.description: This feature fires on positions where the player chooses a flashy forcing move—overwhelmingly a rook check (6/9 positions)—instead of a stronger quiet or intermediate move that would maintain a tighter mating net or winning tactical sequence. In 5/9 cases, forced checkmates were missed (positions 5, 6, 7, 8, and 4's mate-in-15). The premature check gives the opponent an escape square or interposition that was blocked by the stronger continuation: Rc6+ lets the king flee the fork zone (pos 1), Rg3+ lets the king reach h7 without concession (pos 3), Rxe6+ lets the king use f7 which Bg6+ would control (pos 5), Rb5+ pushes the king to a4 destroying the Nc4+/Ra6# geometry (pos 6), Rg7+ blocks the bishop's control of h8 (pos 7), Rf2+ allows Qe2 interposition that Bh6+ would prevent (pos 8). The average cp_loss of 3206 and average good moves of only 1.3 confirm these are narrow tactical moments where one precise move was required.
analysis.move_pattern: Rook moves delivering check (or pawn moves/captures) played before a stronger quiet move that controls escape squares or sets up a more lethal continuation
analysis.why_bad: The premature forcing move gives the opponent an escape route, interposition square, or defensive resource that the correct preparatory move would have eliminated—essentially alerting the opponent's king before the trap is fully set
sub_patterns: Rook check before quiet piece move that controls escape squares
Move-order error: check delivered before intermediate move cuts off flight
Pawn advance/capture before piece activation in winning position
Wrong piece to the same square (Rg7+ vs Rg1#)

analysis.label: A piece is repositioned to a seemingly logical square, abandoning a critical function or missing a forcing/counterintuitive move that the position demands.
analysis.description: This feature fires when players make 'natural-looking' piece moves that fail to address the position's actual concrete requirement. In 6/8 positions, the best move was counterintuitive or forcing (Kf7 paradoxically unblocking a promotion in positions 1-2, Rf2 immediate invasion in position 4, Rxf7 exchange sacrifice in position 7, Nc2 preparation in position 6, Rad1 activation in position 12). Instead, the played moves appear purposeful—rooks shift along ranks to seemingly active squares (Rf1, Rh1, Re8), queens relocate to apparently aggressive posts (Qb4, Qf3, Qg3), or pieces reposition defensively (Ne7, Kc3)—but all abandon the critical tactical function the position requires. In 5/8 cases, the piece moved to a square where it was either immediately attacked with tempo or became tactically irrelevant, while in 4/8 cases a critical file or defensive post was abandoned, allowing the opponent a concrete tactical shot.
analysis.move_pattern: Major or minor piece moves to a seemingly active/useful square (often along a rank, to the wing, or toward the king), typically a non-forcing repositioning move rather than a check, capture, or direct threat
analysis.why_bad: The move abandons the piece's critical current or potential function (file control, fork prevention, tactical resource) in favor of a superficially logical but concretely inferior square, missing a counterintuitive or forcing move that the position's tactical structure actually demands
sub_patterns: Rook abandons critical file to go to seemingly active square (positions 1,2,4)
Queen moves to aggressive-looking square but becomes tactically vulnerable or abandons defense (positions 5,7,12)
Piece repositions near king but to wrong square, missing actual defensive requirement (positions 6,13)

analysis.label: Playing slow, natural-looking developing moves (especially bishop placements and pawn pushes) in tactically critical positions demanding immediate concrete action.
analysis.description: This feature activates on positions where the player makes a non-forcing, 'autopilot' developing move while the position screams for tactical precision. In 5/7 positions, the move is a quiet bishop development (Bd3, Bf4, Be6, Be3) or quiet pawn push (g3, b3) in positions with only 1-2 acceptable moves. Two positions (5, 11) feature missed mate-in-one where the player made purposeless improving moves instead of delivering Qb8#/Rb8#. In the remaining positions, the quiet moves either place pieces on tactically vulnerable squares where they can be captured with structural damage (positions 8, 12, 14), remove critical defenders (position 15 where b3 unguards the c3 knight), or abandon defensive duties (position 13 where Qxf6 exposes the king to Qa4+). The average cp_loss of 2961 and average of only 1.3 good moves confirms these are knife-edge positions requiring calculation, not positional intuition.
analysis.move_pattern: Non-forcing, non-checking moves—predominantly bishop developments to natural squares (d3, f4, e6, e3) and quiet pawn advances (g3, b3)—with no immediate threat created
analysis.why_bad: The positions demand immediate tactical action (delivering checkmate, initiating forced sequences, or addressing concrete threats), but the player defaults to general-principle moves that either miss winning tactics entirely or create new vulnerabilities by placing pieces on undefended/exchangeable squares or removing key defenders
sub_patterns: Missing forced checkmate in 1 for purposeless developing moves
Placing bishop on undefended square creating tactical targets after captures
Quiet pawn moves removing defenders of pieces
Offering piece exchanges where recapture creates structural catastrophe

analysis.label: Wasting a critical tempo on a pawn advance (or passive move) in a losing endgame where king centralization is the only defensive resource.
analysis.description: This feature fires on positions where the losing side plays a non-essential move—overwhelmingly a pawn push—when every tempo should be devoted to king activity and centralization. In 8/10 positions, the phase is endgame and the side is already losing (often facing forced mate). In 6/10 cases the actual move is a pawn advance (b4, h4, g6, c4, a4, exd5) when the best moves involve immediate king centralization (Kb3/Kc6/Kd3/Ke2 etc.). The remaining cases involve the king moving in the wrong direction (Ka7 instead of Kc6) or passive piece play (Rge8 instead of dynamic a3). The analyses unanimously identify 'tempo_loss' as the tactical motif (9/10 positions), and all best-move alternatives prioritize king activity. The positions share the feature of a dominant opponent (usually rook + pawns vs bare king + pawns) where resistance duration is measured in tempi, making each wasted move catastrophic to survival timelines.
analysis.move_pattern: Pawn advances (any direction, non-capturing or capturing) or king/piece moves in passive/wrong directions, when the position demands immediate king centralization toward the center
analysis.why_bad: In desperate endgame positions, the only defensive resource is king mobility and centralization. Pawn pushes waste irreplaceable tempi, often create new targets for the opponent's pieces, remove defensive pawn shields, and accomplish nothing that king activity wouldn't do better—shortening resistance by multiple moves toward forced checkmate.
sub_patterns: Queenside/kingside pawn push instead of king centralization in rook endgame
King retreating away from center when centralization shortens opponent's winning path
Passive piece move abandoning dynamic counterplay that maintained equality

analysis.label: Playing a slow, passive, or imprecise move in a position demanding immediate tactical action, allowing the opponent to exploit a pre-existing vulnerability.
analysis.description: This feature fires on positions where the player wastes a critical tempo by choosing a non-forcing or slightly imprecise move when the position requires an immediate tactical blow or precise forcing sequence. In all 6/6 positions, the correct move was a sharp, forcing action (Qxd5 capturing a hanging pawn, Qxd4 recapturing with the right piece, Bh4 winning the exchange, Bxe5 eliminating a dangerous attacker, Qh3+ setting up a discovered check, Ne3 keeping the knight alive via fork threats), but instead the player chose something passive (a6, g6, f5), imprecise (Qh2+ instead of Qh3+, Rxd4 instead of Qxd4), or self-destructive (Nc3 hanging the piece). In 6/6 cases the opponent immediately seized the initiative by exploiting a tactical vulnerability that the correct move would have neutralized. The average cp_loss of 1804 with only 1.5 good moves available confirms these are razor-sharp positions where a single wasted tempo is catastrophic.
analysis.move_pattern: Any piece/pawn move that is non-forcing (or forcing but to the wrong square) when an immediate tactical resolution exists; includes quiet pawn advances, wrong-piece captures, wrong-square checks, and moves to undefended squares
analysis.why_bad: The position contains a latent tactical vulnerability (hanging piece, fork possibility, promotion threat, or combinative sequence) that the correct move would address immediately; the played move wastes the one tempo needed to act, giving the opponent time to exploit the vulnerability with a counter-tactic (fork, capture, sacrifice, or promotion).
sub_patterns: Slow pawn push ignoring immediate tactical opportunity (f5, a6, g6)
Capture with wrong piece leaving it vulnerable to fork (Rxd4)
Check on adjacent wrong square destroying forcing mechanism (Qh2+ vs Qh3+)
Piece placed on undefended square in queen's line of fire (Nc3)

analysis.label: Pieces or pawns advance to c/d file squares that appear active or centralizing but are actually tactically vulnerable or strategically misplaced.
analysis.description: All 6/6 moves land on the c-file or d-file (c4, Kc2, Kd4, Kc6, Kd4, Rd6), creating an illusion of central activity or purposeful advancement. In 2/6 positions, the piece moves to a square directly controlled by an enemy piece and is immediately capturable (Rd6 captured by knight, c4 pawn captured by rook). In 3/6 endgame positions, the king chooses the wrong central square when a more aggressive alternative existed (Kc2 instead of Kc4 in Position 2, Kd4 instead of Kc5 in Position 3, Kc6 instead of Ke4 in Position 5). The common thread across both middlegame and endgame cases is that the player selects a 'reasonable-looking' central square that fails to address the actual critical requirement—whether that's avoiding a hanging piece or optimally engaging passed pawns. Tempo loss appears as a tag in 5/6 positions, and piece/king activity issues appear in 5/6 positions, confirming the pattern of moves that waste time by going to ineffective squares.
analysis.move_pattern: Any piece type moving to c-file or d-file squares (ranks 2-6), appearing to centralize or advance but landing on a tactically or strategically inferior square
analysis.why_bad: The moves prioritize apparent centralization over addressing the position's actual demands—either landing on undefended squares capturable by the opponent, or choosing the wrong central square when a more aggressive alternative (capturing a pawn, advancing further, or going toward the correct flank) was required.
sub_patterns: King moves to wrong c/d file square in pawn endgames when a more aggressive square captures or blockades pawns
Pieces/pawns advance to c/d file squares directly controlled by enemy pieces (hanging)
King retreats to passive central square instead of advancing toward critical targets

analysis.label: Quiet, non-forcing moves (typically flank pawn advances) played in positions that demand immediate concrete tactical action.
analysis.description: This feature fires on positions where players choose slow, plan-oriented moves—predominantly flank pawn advances—when the position urgently requires concrete, forcing play. In 6/10 cases the move is a wing pawn push (h4, h5, f6, f5, g5, a3) that either weakens the player's own structure or wastes a critical tempo. The remaining piece moves (Kf6, Qd3, Qa5) similarly prioritize repositioning over addressing immediate tactical demands. In every case, the best move was a concrete piece action: a centralization (Ne5), a tactical strike (Rg1), a defensive activation (Rf6, Rh2), or a capture eliminating threats (gxf5). The blunders share the pattern of choosing long-term 'strategic-looking' moves while ignoring that the position is tactically critical—positions averaged only 2.0 good moves, indicating razor-sharp situations with narrow correct paths. The tempo wasted consistently allows the opponent to execute a specific tactical blow: a fork (3/10), a king attack (4/10), or exploitation of a newly-created weakness.
analysis.move_pattern: Predominantly flank pawn advances (h, f, g, a files) or piece moves to non-urgent squares; non-forcing, non-capturing moves that don't address the position's tactical tension
analysis.why_bad: These moves waste a critical tempo in tactically sharp positions, either removing a pawn/piece from a key defensive duty (creating immediate vulnerabilities like open diagonals, fork squares, or unguarded pieces) or failing to seize a one-move tactical opportunity that the opponent can then neutralize
sub_patterns: Flank pawn advance weakening own king shelter (h4, f6, g5)
Slow pawn push missing immediate tactical strike (h5, f5, a3)
Piece retreat/repositioning abandoning defensive duties (Qa5, Kf6, Qd3)

analysis.label: Blunders in positions with essentially one correct continuation, where the player makes a plausible-looking but catastrophic alternative move.
analysis.description: This feature fires on positions where the path to success is extremely narrow (avg 1.3 good moves available) and the player fails to find it, resulting in massive evaluation swings (avg 1152cp loss). The positions span all phases and both colors, unified by the critical constraint that only ONE move maintains the evaluation. In 11/13 positions, exactly one good move existed. The errors are typically 'near-miss' choices that appear reasonable: wrong king square on the same file (Ka6 vs Ka8, position 5), wrong queen check direction (Qd8+ vs Qb4+, position 10), advancing instead of capturing (a6 vs axb6, position 15), wrong pawn advance blocking own king (c4 vs a4, position 3), or passive queen placement when a tactical shot existed (Qc8 vs Qe4, position 1). The moves share a surface-level plausibility—checks that look aggressive (4/13 are checks), pawn advances that look purposeful, piece moves that look active—but each fatally fails to address the position's ONE critical requirement.
analysis.move_pattern: No single geometric pattern; mix of queen moves (5/13), pawn advances (4/13), checks (4/13), king moves (1/13), rook moves (2/13), and castling (1/13). The moves tend to be 'almost right'—same piece to wrong square, same pawn advancing instead of capturing, or superficially forcing moves (checks) that lack concrete follow-through.
analysis.why_bad: Each move fails because it doesn't address the position's singular critical demand: a specific tactical shot (deflection mate, back-rank exploit, pin avoidance), precise king geometry (triangulation, opposition), exact capture timing (axb6 not a6, hxg6 not h6), or the need to avoid unfavorable simplification. The common thread is that the position offers only one narrow correct path and the played move—despite looking reasonable—falls off the cliff into the vast space of losing alternatives.
sub_patterns: Purposeless checks that allow favorable simplification or drive the opponent's king to safety
Pawn advances that self-block king infiltration paths or lose critical tempo
Queen moves to squares that create tactical vulnerabilities (pins, hanging pieces, lost back-rank defense)
Near-correct moves on wrong squares (same piece, wrong destination)

analysis.label: Advancing a passed pawn toward promotion (often with check) instead of improving king or piece positioning first.
analysis.description: All 5/5 positions involve pushing a passed pawn forward toward the promotion square—d6+, g6+, g7, b6+, and a2 are all single-square pawn advances of passed pawns. In 3/5 cases the advance gives check, exploiting the instinct to gain tempo. The analyses consistently identify that preparatory moves (king advancement in front of the pawn, prophylactic moves, or piece activity) were superior: Position 4 shows the textbook case where Kf7 (king in front) wins but g6+ draws; Position 11 shows Ra4 (piece play) was decisive while a2 left d5 undefended; Position 6 shows h5 (rear pawn coordination) was marginally better than g7 which boxed in the king. The feature captures the universal instinct to push a passed pawn one square closer to queening rather than investing in preparation, ranging from catastrophic (553cp loss) to negligible (0cp loss).
analysis.move_pattern: Pawn advance forward one square along a file, typically a passed pawn moving toward the 8th/1st rank, frequently giving check
analysis.why_bad: Advancing the passed pawn prematurely gives the opponent time/squares to blockade or reach drawing positions, restricts the friendly king behind its own pawn, or neglects other positional needs (defending other pawns, activating pieces) that should come first
sub_patterns: Pawn check that gifts opponent a tempo to reach blockade square
Pawn to 7th rank trapping own king behind it
Pawn push ignoring piece/king coordination needs

analysis.label: Plausible-looking active moves that neglect the position's most critical defensive or developmental need, creating an immediate tactical vulnerability.
analysis.description: This feature fires on moves that appear purposeful or aggressive but fatally ignore the position's most pressing requirement. In 6/8 positions, the best move addressed an urgent need (castling in position 8, developing the knight in position 15, central break d5 in position 1, retreating to safety in positions 3 and 7, maintaining active piece placement in position 4), while the played move pursued a secondary plan that created a concrete exploitable weakness. The resulting vulnerabilities take various tactical forms—hanging pieces (Rc1 captured by bishop, Nd4 undefended, Kc2 leaving rook on e7 unprotected: 4/8), forks (Qb6 allowing Na4: 1/8), trapped/targetable pieces (Qf6 enabling Bc2 to win the rook: 1/8), pawn structure collapse exposing king/pieces (g5, e5: 2/8)—but the common thread is that each move has a superficially logical rationale yet miscalculates the opponent's specific tactical refutation.
analysis.move_pattern: Various piece types (king, queen, rook, knight, pawn) moving to apparently active or purposeful squares; no single geometric direction dominates, but moves tend toward forward/flanking rather than consolidating
analysis.why_bad: Each move creates a specific tactical vulnerability (undefended piece, fork target, exposed king, or structural weakness enabling forcing sequences) while failing to address the position's most critical need (king safety, development, piece defense, or central control)
sub_patterns: Pawn advances that leave other pawns/pieces undefended (e5 exposes f5, g5 weakens dark squares)
Pieces placed on tactically vulnerable squares (Nd4 undefended, Rc1 on bishop diagonal, Qb6 forkable)
King moves that expose the king to checks or leave pieces unprotected (Kh1 allows f2 without check, Kc2 allows Bxe7)
Queen moves that prioritize activity over addressing development lag or piece safety (Qf6 ignoring Nd7, Qb6 ignoring O-O)

analysis.label: Active-looking moves that abandon a critical defensive function, leaving pieces or squares tactically vulnerable.
analysis.description: In all 5 positions, the player makes a move that appears aggressive or constructive (advancing a pawn, developing a piece, repositioning the queen to an 'active' square, marching the king forward) but fatally abandons a defensive obligation. In 3/5 cases (Qg3, Qg6, e4), the moved piece was directly protecting another piece that becomes hanging after the move. In 4/5 cases, the opponent punishes with an immediate tactical blow exploiting the newly undefended piece or weakened square. In 5/5 cases, the player had safer alternatives that maintained the defensive function while still making progress. The consistent error is misjudging the relative importance of offense vs. defense—choosing apparent activity over maintaining a piece's guardian role, which the opponent exploits with checks, captures, or pawn thrusts that win material.
analysis.move_pattern: Various piece types moving to seemingly active squares (forward advances, queen relocations to g-file, piece development) that vacate a critical defensive post
analysis.why_bad: The moved piece was performing an essential defensive function (guarding another piece, blocking an attack line, or controlling a critical square), and its relocation leaves material or the king tactically exposed to immediate exploitation.
sub_patterns: Queen leaves defense of a piece to relocate to 'active' square (Qg3, Qg6)
Pawn advance abandons protection of adjacent pawn and opens diagonal (e4)
King advances aggressively but walks into a tempo-gaining check (Kg5)
Piece develops passively instead of challenging the immediate tactical threat (Nge2)

analysis.label: Quiet, non-forcing moves played at critical decision points where immediate concrete action (captures, pawn advances, or king evacuations) was the only way to maintain the position.
analysis.description: This feature fires on positions where the player makes a 'reasonable-looking' but ultimately aimless or misdirected move at a moment demanding immediate, forcing action. The positions share extremely narrow correct paths (avg 1.8 good moves available), meaning the window for the right move is small. In 9/12 positions, the correct move was a concrete action: an immediate capture (Bxg2, Kxh7, Nxb2 in 3 cases), a critical pawn advance (c6 in 2 cases), or urgent king evacuation (Kg1, Kg8 in 2 cases). Instead, the player chose a passive alternative that appears logical—blockading with the wrong piece (Ng6 instead of Kg8), quiet pawn pushes when captures were available (h6 instead of Bxg2, a6 instead of Rac8), premature attacks before completing priorities (Ng5 instead of Bg5, g5 instead of f5), or king moves before forced pawn pushes (Kh4 instead of c6). The devastating consequence in all cases is that the opponent exploits the wasted tempo with a forcing tactical blow: deflection checks (Position 1), diagonal pins (Position 15), pawn storms (Position 2), or initiative-seizing attacks (Positions 6, 9, 12).
analysis.move_pattern: Mixed piece types (king moves 4x, knight moves 5x, pawn moves 3x), generally non-forcing and non-capturing moves that are quiet or misdirected when a specific forcing action was required
analysis.why_bad: Each move wastes a critical tempo at a moment when the position's tactical demands are urgent and narrow—the opponent immediately exploits the lost tempo with concrete threats (promotions, pins, infiltrations, or initiative seizure) that were preventable only by the one correct forcing move.
sub_patterns: Wrong piece used for a task the king/other piece should handle (Ng6 blockading instead of Kg8)
Quiet pawn moves ignoring available immediate captures (h6 instead of Bxg2, a6 instead of Rac8)
Premature knight lunges before completing development or king safety (Ng5, Ne5)
King moves that miss critical move-order (Kh4 before c6, Kg7 walking into pin)
Piece repositioning that ignores king safety crisis (Ne2 instead of Kg1)

analysis.label: Moves that catastrophically compromise king safety by opening lines toward a vulnerable king or failing to exploit an exposed opponent king.
analysis.description: This feature fires on moves where the player makes a superficially reasonable or natural-looking move (a pawn capture, castling, material grab, or king move) that catastrophically misjudges king safety. The dominant pattern involves opening files directed at a vulnerable king: in 4/8 positions (exd4 ×2, gxf3, g3), the move opens or weakens a file (e-file or g-file) pointing directly at an underprotected king. In 2/8 positions (Kf8, O-O-O), the king physically moves onto or toward a dangerous open line where the opponent has attacking resources. In 2/8 positions (Qxg4+, Rxc4), the player captures material greedily instead of exploiting the opponent's fatally exposed king with a winning attack. The average cp_loss of 1382 reflects the catastrophic nature of these errors—several convert winning positions into losing ones or miss forced checkmates. In 5/8 positions, the king in danger was uncastled or exposed in the center, making the open-line creation doubly devastating.
analysis.move_pattern: Varied move types (pawn captures, castling, king moves, piece captures, pawn pushes) that share the consequence of opening or failing to exploit open files/diagonals directed at a vulnerable king
analysis.why_bad: These moves open critical files or diagonals toward a king with inadequate shelter (often uncastled or with weakened pawn cover), allowing devastating tactical exploitation via rook lifts, queen invasions, or piece sacrifices along the newly opened lines—or they miss winning such attacks against the opponent's exposed king by grabbing lesser material instead.
sub_patterns: Opening the center (exd4) while own king remains on e8, exposing it to e-file attacks
Opening the g-file toward own castled king (gxf3/g3) allowing rook and queen invasion
Moving king onto an open file controlled by opponent (Kf8 onto f-file, O-O-O into b-file pressure)
Capturing material instead of delivering decisive king attacks (Qxg4+ instead of Qb1+, Rxc4 instead of Rxg1)

analysis.label: Capturing or targeting a central pawn (or making materialistic/consolidating moves) when the position demands maintaining dynamic tension, piece activity, or king safety.
analysis.description: This feature fires on moves that prioritize material gain or static considerations over urgent dynamic requirements. In 6/8 positions, the move is a direct capture of a central pawn (d3, d5, e5, c4), while the remaining 2 (Nf3 retreat, c4 advance) share the same materialistic/consolidating spirit. The best moves in all positions instead demand aggressive action (Ng6 tactical strike, h4 pawn storm), prophylactic defense (c3 securing a blocker, Kg7 addressing king safety), or completing development (Bg7, Nb4). The common punishment across all positions is that the opponent seizes the initiative through tempo-gaining responses exploiting king safety (6/8 positions tagged king_safety) or piece activity (7/8 positions tagged piece_activity). The average cp_loss of 285 with only 1.8 good moves available confirms these are critical moments demanding specific non-materialistic solutions.
analysis.move_pattern: Piece or pawn captures on central squares (d3/d5/e5/c4), typically knights capturing pawns, or retreat/advance moves with materialistic rather than dynamic intent
analysis.why_bad: The captures remove pieces from critical defensive or attacking functions, give the opponent crucial tempo to generate attacks against exposed kings, or create structural weaknesses that the opponent exploits before the material advantage can be consolidated. The player trades dynamic potential for static material when the position's character demands initiative.
sub_patterns: Knight captures central pawn but removes itself from key defensive/attacking duties (Nxd5, Nxe5, Nfxd5)
Capture removes a piece blocking a critical line or diagonal (Rxd3 unblocking bishop's path to rook)
Material grab before addressing king safety allows opponent's tempo-gaining counterattack (Qxc4 before Kg7)
Wrong recapture creates structural weaknesses that enable opponent's piece coordination (fxe5 vs Nxe5)
Consolidating move ignores immediate tactical crisis requiring defensive attention (c4 ignoring Nxf3+, Nf3 abandoning outpost)

analysis.label: Moves that advance a piece (usually the king) to an overextended or misplaced square, wasting a critical tempo in positions where precise move order determines the outcome.
analysis.description: This feature fires on positions where a player advances a piece to a square that appears natural or aggressive but is actually suboptimal due to tempo loss or misplacement. In 8/12 positions, this occurs in endgames with exposed kings and passed pawns where the king advances prematurely (Kg7, Kh7, Kh3, Ka6, Kg4) before the position is ready—the piece goes too far forward, too far to the edge, or to a square it must retreat from. The tempo loss pattern is explicitly identified in 9/12 analyses. In the middlegame examples, the same principle manifests as pieces going to intuitively appealing but disconnected squares (Qa5 leaving pawns undefended, Qd8 leaving rook hanging, Bc4 ignoring king threats). Even the 0cp-loss positions (Ka8, g3) share the positional signature: simplified positions with passed pawns where the key question is whether to advance king or pawn first.
analysis.move_pattern: King or piece moving forward/sideways to an edge or advanced square, typically away from the critical zone of action; often king moves toward the rim (h-file, a-file, 7th/8th rank) in endgame positions
analysis.why_bad: The piece arrives on a square where it is either overextended (must retreat), disconnected from the critical action (e.g., far from a passed pawn's path or the opponent's threats), or premature (the correct preparatory move was needed first), resulting in a wasted tempo that the opponent exploits to improve their position or execute a tactical blow.
sub_patterns: King overextension past optimal opposition square in pawn endgames
Premature pawn push before king secures support position
King retreat to rim/corner disconnecting from center
Queen/piece displacement to passive wing leaving key squares undefended

analysis.label: Playing a natural-looking 'improving' move (centralizing, attacking, or repositioning a piece) while ignoring an urgent tactical requirement in the position.
analysis.description: This feature fires on moves that appear strategically reasonable—centralizing pieces, placing them on 'ideal' squares, going to open files, or creating threats—but fatally ignore the position's concrete tactical demands. In 5/7 positions, the piece moved to a central square (e4, d4, d5, d8, d2) that looked attractive but was either en prise to a pawn (Nd4 captured by cxd4, Bd5 captured by cxd5: 2/7), exposed to counterattack (Bxe4 becoming a target: 1/7), or simply wasted a critical tempo when a specific tactical response was required (Rd8 ignoring queen vulnerability, Qh5 allowing knight forks, Nd2 abandoning an outpost: 3/7). In each case, a precise tactical move was available (Nf2+ fork, Nf5 to challenge a dominant knight, h3 to challenge an active knight, etc.) but the player chose a 'general improvement' move instead. The positions typically had very few good options (avg 2.1), meaning the tactical demands were narrow and specific, punishing imprecise play severely (avg 275cp loss).
analysis.move_pattern: Piece moves to apparently strong/active square (usually central d/e files or attacking position) — bishop, knight, rook, queen, or king to squares that look textbook-good but are tactically flawed
analysis.why_bad: The position demands a specific tactical response (exploiting a fork, challenging a dominant piece, addressing a vulnerability), but the player instead makes a 'natural-looking' positional/strategic move that either places the piece where it can be captured by a pawn, wastes a critical tempo while an opponent's threat goes unanswered, or abandons an important defensive post
sub_patterns: Piece placed on central square capturable by pawn (Nd4/cxd4, Bd5/cxd5)
Bishop leaves safe fianchetto for exposed central square where it becomes a target
Rook/Queen makes routine-looking move while ignoring urgent tactical vulnerability
Knight retreats from active outpost to passive square, enabling structural damage
Premature queen sortie ignoring development and allowing knight forks

analysis.label: Playing a slow, non-forcing repositioning move when the position demands immediate concrete action to address a critical tactical or time-sensitive threat.
analysis.description: In all 7 positions, the player chose a quiet, non-forcing move (piece repositioning, prophylactic pawn push, or slow development) when the position contained an urgent tactical demand requiring immediate concrete action. In 5/7 cases, a passed pawn was the critical dynamic element being mishandled—either failing to advance one's own (h3 instead of b7, Position 12) or passively blockading instead of actively controlling (Rb8 instead of Ne5, Position 1). In 4/7 cases, the quiet move directly created a tactical vulnerability exploited by a fork or forcing sequence (Re2 allowing Nd3+, Bd2 enabling Qd4+, Kb4 permitting Nc6+, Rd3 leaving c4 hanging). The average of only 1.9 good moves confirms these are narrow, concrete positions disguised as positional ones—the players consistently misjudged the position as requiring slow improvement when it actually demanded a specific forcing solution.
analysis.move_pattern: Quiet non-forcing moves (piece repositioning to seemingly reasonable squares, prophylactic pawn pushes, or lateral piece shifts) with no check, capture, or direct threat
analysis.why_bad: These moves waste a critical tempo in positions with urgent concrete demands (advanced passed pawns, hanging pieces, available forcing sequences), allowing the opponent to execute a tactical resource (fork, capture, promotion combination, or piece reactivation) that would not have been possible had the player addressed the position's primary tension immediately.
sub_patterns: Passive rook repositioning instead of active piece centralization (Rb8, Re2, Rc8, Rd3)
Prophylactic pawn move instead of executing forced winning combination (h3)
Piece development to vulnerable square enabling forcing check/fork (Bd2, Kb4)

analysis.label: Playing non-forcing, natural-looking moves when the position demands an immediate concrete/forcing response to a critical threat or opportunity.
analysis.description: This feature fires on positions where the player makes a superficially reasonable move (developing a rook to an open file, repositioning a queen, capturing a pawn, advancing a passed pawn) while missing that the position has reached a critical inflection point requiring immediate forcing play. In 6/8 positions, there was only 1 good move available (avg 1.5), indicating razor-thin margins where routine play fails. The mistakes share a pattern of prioritizing general improvement or material over urgency: Rae8 and Rc8 'develop' rooks when tactical breaks (e4) or piece safety (a7 pawn) demand attention; Nxg4 and Rxh4 grab pawns when maintaining tension (f3) or blockading (Kd7) is critical; Qg8 and Qb7 reposition queens when move-order precision or forcing checks (Qd8+) are required; Nf5 looks active but walks into a tactical refutation; h5 pushes a pawn when king mobility is the only survival factor. In 7/8 cases the position demanded either an immediate tactical strike, a forced sequence beginning with a check, or urgent prophylaxis against a concrete threat.
analysis.move_pattern: Various piece types making quiet, non-forcing moves (rook development to files, queen repositioning, pawn captures, pawn advances) instead of checks, forcing pawn breaks, or prophylactic moves addressing immediate tactical threats
analysis.why_bad: The position has a critical tactical or strategic feature (hanging piece, unstoppable passed pawn, forcing check available, piece needing urgent relocation) that requires immediate attention, but the player defaults to a 'natural' or 'greedy' move that ignores the urgency, allowing the opponent to exploit the unaddressed threat
sub_patterns: Rook development to open file ignoring hanging/undefended pawns
Pawn capture releasing tension when maintaining it is crushing
Queen repositioning when a forcing check sequence wins material
Move-order error: repositioning one piece when another needs urgent relocation first
Pawn advance blocking own king's escape squares

analysis.label: Pieces leave critical defensive duties to pursue active/offensive goals, immediately allowing tactical exploitation of the vacated responsibility.
analysis.description: In all 6 positions, the blundering move relocates a piece to a seemingly purposeful or active square while fatally abandoning a defensive necessity. In Position 2 (Nc4), the knight leaves d2 where it blockaded a passed c-pawn, allowing promotion (1/6). In Position 5 (Rxc2), the rook leaves the g-file where it provided counterplay, enabling a Nd5+ fork (2/6). In Position 6 (Qf5), the queen abandons coverage of b5, permitting a devastating knight fork via Na7+ (3/6). In Position 7 (Nc3), the knight leaves proximity to the exposed king, allowing Rf7+ 7th-rank invasion (4/6). In Position 9 (Qd7), the queen ignores the urgent g7/h8 diagonal vulnerability, allowing Bxg7-Bxh8 winning a trapped rook (5/6). Even Position 4 (Nxf7), while a sacrifice, represents abandoning sound piece deployment for an unjustified aggressive concept (6/6). The average cp_loss of 423 with only 1.5 good moves available confirms these are critical moments requiring defensive precision rather than active play.
analysis.move_pattern: Knight or queen/rook moves to an active-looking square (captures or development), moving AWAY from the sector requiring defensive attention
analysis.why_bad: The moved piece was performing an indispensable defensive function (blockading, covering a key square, providing counterplay, or needing to address an immediate threat), and its departure creates an immediate tactical vulnerability that the opponent exploits within 1-2 moves via forks, promotions, invasions, or piece traps.
sub_patterns: Removing a blockader from a passed pawn's path allowing promotion
Greedy captures that remove a piece from its counterplay-generating post
Queen abandoning defensive coverage of critical squares enabling knight forks
Knight leaving king proximity allowing rook invasions on 7th rank
Ignoring existing tactical vulnerabilities (trapped pieces, diagonal threats)

analysis.label: Making an apparently productive or aggressive move that neglects a critical tactical vulnerability the opponent can immediately exploit with a forcing response.
analysis.description: This feature fires on moves where the player pursues a natural-looking plan (advancing pawns for space, centralizing pieces, repositioning) while ignoring the position's most urgent tactical demand. In 5/6 positions, the opponent punishes with a forcing tempo-gaining response (check, capture, or double attack): e5 allows Qh4+ exploiting the weakened king (1/6), Rae1 self-blocks allowing Bxc3+Ba6 winning the exchange (2/6), Bb5 leaves the bishop undefended for Qa5+ fork (5/6), b7 ignores e1 promotion-with-check leading to a discovered attack winning the rook (6/6). In the remaining cases, the moves waste critical tempo: Bb6 (3/6) repositions an already-effective bishop when Kd5 delivers forced mate, and Kg5 (4/6) retreats from a crushing attacking post when Kf3 paralyzes the opponent. The common thread is that all 6/6 moves prioritize the player's strategic agenda over addressing the position's most critical tactical obligation, with an average cp_loss of 1877.
analysis.move_pattern: Mixed piece types and directions; moves tend to be forward/aggressive (pawn advances, piece development to active-looking squares) or passive repositioning, all sharing the quality of being 'the wrong priority' in a tactically demanding position
analysis.why_bad: Each move leaves a specific vulnerability unaddressed (undefended piece, exposed king diagonal, critical square uncontrolled, promotion with check) that the opponent immediately exploits with a forcing tactical response that gains decisive material or tempo.
sub_patterns: Premature pawn advance leaving pieces/squares undefended (e5, b7)
Piece placement that creates self-blocking or leaves pieces hanging (Rae1, Bb5)
Tempo-wasting repositioning when immediate king advancement delivers decisive advantage (Bb6, Kg5)

analysis.label: White moves a piece away from the decisive area of the board, wasting a critical tempo to address a secondary concern while the primary strategic or tactical priority goes unattended.
analysis.description: This feature fires on positions where White plays a move that directs a piece to an irrelevant or suboptimal sector of the board, losing a crucial tempo in a position that demands immediate action on the primary front. In 9/9 positions, the played move either retreats/redirects a piece away from where it's most needed (Rh8 away from the c-pawn defense, Ra8 away from the e-file, Kb2 away from center, Kf3 away from the knight, Bg5 away from the back rank) or addresses a secondary target instead of the critical one (cxd3+ capturing a pawn instead of promoting, Nxc3 capturing instead of Bxg7, Rh1 defending h2 instead of striking with Bxf6). In 7/9 cases the analysis explicitly identifies the error as giving the opponent a free tempo to execute their winning plan (passed pawn advance, king infiltration, piece activation). The best moves in all positions share the trait of directly engaging with the position's most urgent demand.
analysis.move_pattern: Any piece type moving away from the critical sector; often king/rook moving to the wrong side of the board, or captures/defenses addressing secondary targets
analysis.why_bad: The move wastes a decisive tempo by misdirecting a piece from the critical battle, allowing the opponent to execute their primary plan (promote a passed pawn, infiltrate with king, activate pieces) unopposed while White's piece must often return or becomes irrelevant
sub_patterns: Rook moving to wrong end of file or irrelevant file (Rh8, Rh1, Ra8)
King retreating/moving toward wrong flank (Kf3, Kb2)
Capturing secondary material while ignoring the primary threat (Nxc3, cxd3+)
Defensive move protecting unimportant material instead of attacking (Bg5, Rh1)

analysis.label: Playing a non-urgent, secondary move that abandons responsibility for the position's most critical element, typically allowing capture of a passed pawn or exploitation of an immediate tactical threat.
analysis.description: All 5 positions share a common pattern: the player makes a slow, non-forcing move (no check, no capture, no immediate threat) that addresses a secondary concern while the position demands immediate action on its most critical feature. In 3/5 cases (Ng2, Qg1, f4), the critical element is a passed pawn—either the player's own that becomes undefended (c3 pawn in Qg1, c5 pawn in Ng2) or the opponent's that is about to promote (a2 pawn in f4). In the remaining 2/5 cases (h3, Na4), the critical element is hanging material or an imminent tactical threat that the slow move fails to address. In all cases, the moved piece or pawn was either directly guarding the critical asset or should have been used to neutralize the urgent threat. The refutations are consistently simple: the opponent takes the undefended asset (Kxc3, Bxc5, Nxf8, a1=Q) or launches the now-unopposed tactical blow (Nf5, Rb3). Average cp_loss of 2259 reflects the catastrophic cost of this one-tempo neglect.
analysis.move_pattern: Non-forcing moves (quiet pawn pushes or piece retreats/repositions) directed away from the critical zone of action, typically toward the periphery or a passive square
analysis.why_bad: The move squanders a critical tempo by addressing a secondary concern while the position's most urgent feature (a passed pawn needing defense/capture, a hanging piece, or an imminent tactical threat) goes unattended, allowing the opponent to exploit it immediately
sub_patterns: Knight retreat abandoning passed pawn support (Ng2)
Queen leaving critical defensive diagonal (Qg1)
Slow kingside pawn push ignoring hanging material (h3, f4)
Knight repositioning to rim abandoning prophylaxis (Na4)

analysis.label: Moves that either worsen king exposure or squander critical tempo when the king's vulnerability is the decisive positional factor.
analysis.description: This feature fires on positions where king safety is the overriding concern and the player makes a move that either actively worsens the king's position or neglects the urgency of the king's vulnerability. In 2/5 positions, the king itself moves to the wrong square (Ke1 toward the open center instead of Kg2 to shelter; Kf6 into a tactical corridor instead of Kh7 behind pawns). In 1/5 positions, a pawn advance (c6 instead of c5) creates a new tactical weakness enabling a sacrifice with check against the king. In 2/5 positions (Qd3, a3), the player ignores the critical urgency of king safety—failing to address a pin/development needed for castling, or wasting tempo on a prophylactic flank move while the king remains dangerously in the center. All 5 positions share the characteristic of having very few good moves (avg 1.2), indicating critical decision points where king safety demanded specific attention. The punishments consistently involve queen invasions, checks, and tactical exploitation of the exposed king.
analysis.move_pattern: King moves toward center/open lines instead of retreating to shelter, OR non-king moves that waste tempo/create weaknesses when the king is already vulnerable
analysis.why_bad: The moves fail because they misjudge where the king needs to be or how urgent addressing king safety is—either walking the king into tactical corridors (checks, forks, file pressure) or giving the opponent the tempo needed to launch devastating attacks against the exposed king.
sub_patterns: King moves toward center/exposed square instead of retreating to pawn shelter (Ke1, Kf6)
Pawn advance creates new tactical weakness near king (c6 enabling Rxb7/Qxc6+)
Slow/prophylactic move squanders tempo while king remains dangerously uncastled (a3, Qd3)

analysis.label: Moves that look purposeful or aggressive but fundamentally misread the position's concrete demands, allowing the opponent to exploit a specific tactical or structural vulnerability.
analysis.description: This feature detects positions where the player makes a plausible-looking move—often with clear intent like attacking a piece, developing, or gaining space—but fatally ignores the position's most urgent requirement. In 6/8 cases, the move either allows the opponent to solve their problems with tempo (Bb4 attacked a queen that simply sidesteps; Ng5 allowed ...Bg7 developing with tempo against the exposed queen; Nc6 attacked a queen that escapes while the knight is captured) or fails to prevent a critical opponent resource (Bb7 ignored the Nxd5 fork combination; Re8 left the c-file uncontested for Rc7; d3 surrendered all initiative when d4 was required). In 3/8 positions the move abandons a strong positional asset (Ne4 left a dominant f6 outpost; g5 weakened the king position irreparably). The best moves consistently demanded either addressing tactical vulnerabilities directly, maintaining pressure through pawn breaks (e5, d4, f5), or contesting critical files/squares—concrete actions the played moves all neglect.
analysis.move_pattern: Varied piece types and directions—often knight/bishop moves to seemingly active squares (Bb4, Ng5, Nc6, Ne4), or routine developing/placing moves (Bb7, Re8, d3, g5)—all pursuing a generic or superficial plan rather than the position's specific concrete requirement
analysis.why_bad: Each move prioritizes a secondary goal (attacking something, developing, gaining space) while ignoring the position's critical demand—whether that's a defensive obligation, a tactical vulnerability to address, a pawn break to execute, or an outpost to maintain. The opponent then exploits the neglected factor to seize initiative, win tempo, or execute a combination that was previously impossible.
sub_patterns: Piece moves to aggressive-looking squares easily parried with tempo (Bb4, Ng5, Nc6)
Routine developing moves that ignore urgent tactical vulnerabilities (Bb7, Re8, d3)
Abandoning dominant piece placement for phantom activity (Ne4 leaving f6 outpost)
Premature flank action when center/king safety demands attention (g5)

analysis.label: Quiet, non-forcing piece retreats or repositioning moves played in positions that urgently demand active counterplay or forcing continuation.
analysis.description: This feature fires on positions where the player makes a passive move—typically a piece retreat or aimless king walk—instead of the active, forcing play the position demands. In 8/9 positions, the best move involved creating immediate threats (c5/f5 central breaks, Ne6/Ne4 centralization, c6+ forcing advances, Qh4 kingside attacks), but the player chose quiet repositioning instead. The played moves share the geometric pattern of pieces retreating toward back ranks or quiet squares (Bh8, Kg8, Be2, Qg8, Qd1, Qd7, Kf2×2), surrendering the initiative and granting the opponent a crucial tempo. In 7/9 positions the opponent punishes by executing a tactical or forcing plan that was previously too slow—pawn storms (g4 in pos 1, g3+ in pos 14), passed pawn advances (c6 in pos 2, Re6/d6 in pos 13), or exploitation of newly created weaknesses (Qc5+ diagonal in pos 3, Qh5 winning rook in pos 5). The average cp_loss of 221 reflects positions where one wasted tempo proves catastrophic.
analysis.move_pattern: Piece (King, Queen, or Bishop) retreats to back rank or second rank square; non-forcing, no check, no capture, no immediate threat created
analysis.why_bad: The position requires active forcing play (threats, counterplay, or initiative-seizing moves), but the passive retreat wastes a critical tempo, allowing the opponent to execute tactical plans that were previously too slow or to exploit newly created weaknesses (open diagonals, undefended squares, passed pawn advances)
sub_patterns: King walks to quiet square instead of creating counterplay
Queen retreats from active post abandoning attack or defensive coverage
Bishop retreats to passive square creating tactical vulnerability
Premature quiet move when forcing continuation available

analysis.label: Player makes an unrelated move while their own queen is or becomes capturable by an opponent's piece.
analysis.description: In all 10/10 positions, the played move results in the player's queen being immediately capturable by the opponent. The mechanisms vary: sometimes a defender of the queen is moved away (Position 1: Nxf4 leaves Qd7 undefended for Nxd7; Position 10: Ne7 leaves Qg6 hanging to Rxg6), sometimes the queen is moved to an attacked square (Position 4: Qxf4 lands on rook's file allowing Rxf4; Position 3: Qd6 places queen on bishop's diagonal allowing Bxd6; Position 9: Qh2 allows Rxh2+), and sometimes an existing attack on the queen is simply ignored in favor of a greedy or developmental move (Position 5: exd5 ignores Rf8 attacking Qf3; Position 6: Bg7 ignores Rd1 x-raying Qd6; Position 8: dxc6 ignores Bg4 attacking Qf3; Position 7: Bxg6 ignores Rf8 attacking Qf3; Position 2: O-O ignores Nf4 attacking Qd5). The captures are most commonly by rooks along open files (7/10) but also by bishops on diagonals (2/10) and knights (2/10). The average cp_loss of ~488 corresponds to losing a queen for the capturing piece.
analysis.move_pattern: Any piece type or move direction; the unifying geometric feature is that the player's queen sits on a rank, file, or diagonal attacked by an enemy piece with no intervening blocker
analysis.why_bad: The move either removes a defender of the queen, places the queen on an attacked square, or ignores an existing direct attack on the queen, allowing the opponent to capture it outright or win it for insufficient material
sub_patterns: Ignoring a rook's open-file x-ray on the queen
Moving a piece that was shielding or defending the queen
Moving the queen onto a square attacked by an enemy piece
Ignoring a minor piece's direct attack on the queen

analysis.label: Passive piece repositioning moves played when the position demands immediate forcing action (checks, captures, or critical defensive moves).
analysis.description: In all 3/3 positions, the player chose a 'reasonable-looking' piece move to a seemingly useful square—reinforcing center, blockading a pawn, or activating a piece—while the position urgently demanded forcing, high-priority moves. In Position 9, Rfe1 reinforced the e-file instead of rushing the queen back to h2 via Qd6/Qc7 to neutralize Black's attacking queen. In Position 10, Rd1 passively blockaded the d2 pawn instead of giving check with Rf1+ or capturing material with Kxb6. In Position 11, Bf6 'activated' the bishop but removed it from b2 where it performed an irreplaceable blocking function against Qb3. All three moves share the signature of prioritizing a slow positional idea over the one forcing continuation that addresses the position's critical demand, surrendering a decisive tempo to the opponent.
analysis.move_pattern: Non-forcing, non-checking piece move to a seemingly useful central or active square (back-rank rook centralization or bishop repositioning)
analysis.why_bad: These moves waste a critical tempo on a slow 'improving' plan while the position has an urgent tactical or defensive need that requires immediate forcing action; the opponent exploits the lost tempo with a decisive combination (king attacks, fork checks, or sacrificial breakthroughs).
sub_patterns: Passive rook centralization to back rank (e1/d1) when checks or queen redeployment are needed
Removing a piece from a critical defensive post to an 'active' square, enabling opponent's forcing sequence

analysis.label: Moves that are conceptually similar to the best continuation but choose the wrong piece, square, or direction, exposing an immediate tactical vulnerability in positions where only 1-2 moves work.
analysis.description: This feature fires on catastrophic blunders in critical positions where very few good moves exist (avg 1.6). In 5/7 positions, the played move is structurally similar to the correct one but misses a critical geometric detail: Qe8+ instead of Qf5+ (wrong check square, missing mate in 2), Ke8 instead of Kf8 (wrong retreat square, landing on vulnerable diagonal), Nh6 instead of Nf5 (wrong knight, leaving Ne7 hanging on open file), Kf7 instead of Kd5 (wrong king direction, abandoning passed pawn), h6 instead of d6 (wrong pawn, ignoring central vulnerability). In all 7/7 cases, the move immediately creates or exposes a tactical weakness: a hanging piece (Rgg2→Bxg2, Nh6→Rxe7+, h6→Nxe5), a diagonal vulnerability (Ke8→Qh5+, Rgg2 on bishop diagonal), an escape route for the opponent's king (Qe8+ fails to control g5/f6), or an interposition resource (Rd3+→Be3). The common thread is that these are 'almost right' moves that demonstrate correct strategic intuition but catastrophically wrong tactical execution.
analysis.move_pattern: Various piece types moving to squares adjacent to or near the correct destination, often one square off from optimal (wrong file, wrong diagonal, wrong direction)
analysis.why_bad: Each move creates an immediate tactical vulnerability (hanging piece, exposed diagonal, uncontrolled flight square) that the opponent can exploit with a single forcing response, because the chosen square fails to control the critical geometric lines that the correct move would have covered.
sub_patterns: Wrong check square - delivers check but fails to control enemy king's escape routes (Qe8+ vs Qf5+, Rd3+ vs Qh1+)
Wrong king retreat - moves king to a square that falls on an attacking diagonal or abandons critical sector (Ke8 onto h5-e8 diagonal, Kf7 away from queenside)
Wrong piece/square leaving material hanging - moves a piece while leaving another undefended on an open line (Nh6 abandoning Ne7, Rgg2 onto bishop diagonal, h6 ignoring e5)

analysis.label: Black plays a natural-looking move that leaves a specific pawn undefended, allowing simple capture.
analysis.description: In 3/4 positions, Black makes a move that appears constructive (castling, centralizing, regrouping) but critically fails to address a vulnerable pawn that the opponent can immediately capture. In Position 1, O-O leaves the e4-pawn hanging for Nxe4/Qxe4. In Position 2, Ne4 creates an illusory dual attack but after forced exchanges leaves the resulting e4-pawn hanging for Qxe4. In Position 3, Qe8 is a slow regrouping move that leaves the h5-pawn for Bxh5. In Position 4, capturing with the wrong rook (Rhxf3+ instead of Rfxf3+) misses a tactical sequence to recover material on h7 via d3. The common thread across all positions is prioritizing general concepts (king safety, centralization, repositioning) over the concrete need to defend or address a specific tactical vulnerability, resulting in clean material loss with no compensation.
analysis.move_pattern: Various piece types making 'routine' moves (king castle, knight centralization, queen retreat, rook capture) while a specific pawn remains or becomes undefended
analysis.why_bad: The moves ignore a concrete hanging pawn that the opponent can capture in one or two moves, turning a positional/developmental idea into immediate material loss with no compensation
sub_patterns: Castling while central pawn hangs
Knight centralization creating exchangeable hanging pawn
Quiet regrouping while wing pawn is en prise
Wrong piece capture missing coordination sequence

analysis.label: Black repositions a piece to an apparently useful square but allows the opponent a forcing response (check or trade) that boomerangs the tempo advantage.
analysis.description: In all 3/3 positions, Black moves a piece that was performing a critical function (defending the 7th rank, maintaining attacking pressure, or controlling a key diagonal) to what appears to be a more active or purposeful square, but the new placement allows White a forcing response that exploits the abandoned duty.
