In Position 11, Rb6 'attacks' the queen but abandons 7th-rank defense, allowing Qa7+ with check. In Position 10, Qc8 repositions the queen but allows Qxc8+ forcing a trade that kills the attack. In Position 8, Be2 appears flexible but allows Rb2 without check (whereas Bh5 would have forced Rb2+), losing a critical tempo in a pawn race. Each move superficially looks purposeful but creates a tactical vulnerability the opponent exploits with tempo.
analysis.move_pattern: Non-forcing piece repositioning (bishop, queen, or rook) to a square that enables opponent's forcing response (check or capture)
analysis.why_bad: The piece abandons a critical defensive or strategic function, and its new square allows the opponent a forcing move (check or forced trade) that gains decisive tempo, reversing the initiative.
sub_patterns: Abandoning 7th-rank defense allowing queen check
Retreating queen to back rank allowing forced simplification
Choosing a bishop route that fails to force opponent's response with check

analysis.label: Pieces moved to the 7th rank (or near-equivalent) in an aggressive-looking manner when a more immediately decisive move exists elsewhere.
analysis.description: In 4/5 positions, the played move lands on the 7th rank (Re7, Qc7+, Rg7+, Kc7), and the fifth (Rc2) targets the 2nd rank — White's equivalent of 'dominating' a rank. In 3/5 cases, a forced checkmate (often mate-in-1) was available via a different square or piece: Qc6# instead of Qc7+ (Position 3), Rg1# instead of Rg7+ (Position 4), and Bg7+ leading to mate-in-4 instead of Re7 (Position 2). In all positions, the 7th-rank move appears naturally strong — occupying the penultimate rank, often with check or threatening material — but is slightly imprecise compared to the optimal continuation. The best moves consistently operated on different files or ranks (e-file in Position 1, g1 in Position 4, c6 in Position 3, toward e6 in Position 5), showing the player was attracted to the 7th-rank idea over the truly forcing blow.
analysis.move_pattern: Any piece moves to the 7th rank (ranks 7 or 2 from White's perspective), often delivering check, when the optimal move uses a different square or piece
analysis.why_bad: The 7th-rank move looks aggressive and 'standard strong' but either blocks a critical line (4/5 - Rg7+ blocks bishop diagonal), allows the king an escape square not covered from the 7th rank (Qc7+ vs Qc6#), or diverts the piece from a more forcing function (Re7 when Bg7+ forces mate, Rc2 when Re2 forces exchanges), consistently trading immediate decisiveness for superficially attractive placement.
sub_patterns: Check on the 7th rank missing adjacent-square checkmate (Qc7+ vs Qc6#, Rg7+ vs Rg1#)
Rook to 7th rank missing faster forced mate via different piece or square
King advancing to 7th rank away from optimal centralization path

analysis.label: In endgames with a dangerous enemy passed pawn near promotion, the player makes a move that ignores the pawn threat in favor of an irrelevant objective.
analysis.description: This feature fires on endgame moves where one side has an advanced passed pawn (typically 1-2 squares from promotion) that demands immediate attention, but the player instead pursues an unrelated goal. In 14/14 positions, a critical passed pawn exists that is the dominant factor in the position. The blundering moves include rook moves abandoning the critical file (Rh2, Rb8, Rb2, Rg4+, Ra8 — 5/14), irrelevant pawn advances (f5, g5, h4, h4 — 4/14), captures of unimportant material while ignoring the pawn (fxe4, Rxh7 — 2/14), and piece moves that waste tempo or fail to restrain the passer (Ke2, Kd4, Rb4 — 3/14). The correct moves consistently prioritize direct engagement with the passed pawn: getting the rook behind it, blockading on the promotion file, or capturing it immediately. The average cp_loss of 1628 reflects that ignoring an advanced passer in an endgame is typically catastrophic.
analysis.move_pattern: Any piece type moving AWAY from the file or area of an advanced passed pawn, or making a non-forcing move (pawn push, peripheral capture, pointless check) when the pawn is 1-2 squares from promotion
analysis.why_bad: Advanced passed pawns in endgames require immediate attention — every tempo spent elsewhere allows the pawn to advance or enables tactical combinations (promotion with check, rook sacrifices clearing the promotion square, deflection). The opponent punishes by promoting or executing a forcing sequence that was only possible because the defender's piece abandoned its critical restraining post.
sub_patterns: Rook abandons the critical file allowing promotion (Rh2, Rb8, Rb2, Rg4+, Ra8)
Irrelevant kingside pawn advance while queenside pawn races to promote (f5, g5, h4, h4)
Capturing a peripheral pawn while the passed pawn needs restraint (fxe4, Rxh7)
King/rook move wastes tempo allowing pawn advance or promotion tactic (Ke2, Kd4, Rb4)

analysis.label: Playing a slow, peripheral, or non-essential move in a closed center with unresolved pawn tension when immediate central action or development was required.
analysis.description: All 5 positions share a closed or tense center with unresolved pawn tension (e4 vs d5, c4 vs d5, d4 vs c5) and at least one king still in the center. In every case, the player makes a 'luxury' move—whether a flank pawn push (h3, f3: 2/5), a premature queen sortie to attack peripheral targets (Qb6: 2/5), or repositioning a developed piece to an exposed square (Bf4: 1/5)—instead of directly resolving the central tension or completing development. The punishment consistently involves the opponent either opening the center with tempo (e5 hitting a knight in position 15, dxc5/exd5 blowing open lines in positions 8/12, cxd4 forcing humiliating queen moves in position 10) or exploiting the tempo loss with tactical motifs like forks (Bxf3 + d4 in position 2, Nb5-Nc7+ in position 12). All 5 positions had 2-3 good alternatives that addressed the center directly, making these unforced errors.
analysis.move_pattern: Any non-central move (flank pawn, queen to wing, piece to exposed peripheral square) played while central pawn tension remains unresolved and king is uncastled
analysis.why_bad: Unresolved central tension is a ticking clock when kings are uncastled—spending a tempo on anything other than center resolution or development allows the opponent to blow open the center with tempo-gaining moves, exploiting undeveloped pieces, exposed kings, and the wasted move to gain decisive material or positional advantages.
sub_patterns: Flank pawn moves (h3/f3) that block development or provoke unfavorable exchanges
Premature queen moves (Qb6) attacking peripheral targets while ignoring central urgency and allowing knight forks
Piece repositioning (Bf4) to exposed squares where tempo-gaining pawn advances drive them back

analysis.label: Pieces voluntarily leave their optimal or critical squares for seemingly active but actually inferior placements, losing tempo and abandoning key functions.
analysis.description: In 8/8 positions, the blundering move relocates a well-placed piece (or king) from a square where it performs a critical function to a square that appears active but actually abandons that function. In 6/8 positions, the piece leaves a defensive duty (Qb7 abandons kingside defense, Ra6 leaves the f6 shield, Ra7 abandons back-rank coverage, Kd3 walks away from queenside infiltration path, Ra4 leaves the critical f-file, Nc5 leaves the dominant e6 outpost). In 7/8 positions, 'tempo_loss' is explicitly tagged as the piece must eventually return or be rerouted. In 5/8 positions, the opponent exploits the gap with immediate tactical shots (Bc7 winning the queen, Nd4 fork, Qe5+ check, Ng3+ fork, Qg3+ followed by e4+). The moves share the common intent of seeking 'activity' (attacking a target, centralizing, occupying an open file) but misjudge which function of the piece matters most in the position.
analysis.move_pattern: Any piece type moving away from its critical square (defensive post, dominant outpost, or key file) to a seemingly active but actually inferior square, typically moving laterally or toward the periphery
analysis.why_bad: The piece abandons its most important function (shielding the king, controlling a key diagonal/file, maintaining a dominant outpost), and the opponent immediately exploits the newly created gap with checks, forks, or accelerated plans that the piece's presence had previously prevented.
sub_patterns: Queen moving away from king defense to a distant square
Rook leaving critical file/rank for seemingly active but misplaced square
Knight leaving dominant central outpost for peripheral square
King walking toward open center instead of toward safety or infiltration path

analysis.label: Playing a non-urgent move when aggressively-placed pieces deep in enemy territory need immediate retreat or consolidation to avoid being trapped or captured.
analysis.description: In 9/11 positions, the player has piece(s) aggressively planted deep in the opponent's territory (typically a Bishop on f7/h7 combined with a Knight on g5/e5) that are tactically unstable and require immediate retreat. Instead of pulling back the overextended piece(s) to safe squares (the engine's top recommendations are nearly always bishop retreats like Bb3, Bc4, Bd3, or Be4), the player makes a different 'useful-looking' move—developing another piece (Nc3 in 3/11 cases), castling (O-O in 2/11), pushing a central pawn (d4), centralizing the queen (Qe4), blocking a retreat square (h3), or moving the wrong piece in a combination (Nxe4, Nxf3, Nd4, Rb2). In every case, the opponent punishes by directly challenging the overextended piece(s) with simple moves like ...h6 (attacking Ng5), ...d6 (attacking Ne5), ...g6 (trapping Bh7), or ...Qa5+ (exploiting removed defenders), winning material. The average cp_loss of 398 reflects that these positions typically involve losing a full piece.
analysis.move_pattern: Any non-retreat move (development, castling, pawn push, capture, queen centralization) when an aggressively-posted minor piece deep in enemy territory requires immediate withdrawal
analysis.why_bad: The overextended piece(s) are only temporarily safe and depend on precise timing to retreat; any tempo spent on other business allows the opponent to challenge them with simple pawn advances or piece attacks, resulting in the piece being trapped or captured for insufficient compensation.
sub_patterns: Castling instead of retreating bishop from f7 (allows ...h6 trapping Ng5)
Developing a new piece instead of saving an overextended one (Nc3 ignoring Bf7/Ng5 crisis)
Moving the wrong piece in a tactical sequence (Nxe4/Nd4 removing a defender of another overextended piece)
Pawn moves that block retreat squares (h3 blocking Nh3 escape)
Move-order errors leaving a coordinating piece undefended (Nxf3 before Rxf3, Rb2 before Qc5)

analysis.label: Superficially aggressive moves (checks, threats, piece repositioning) that waste critical tempo by ignoring the position's true concrete demands.
analysis.description: This feature fires on moves that appear active or aggressive on the surface but fundamentally waste tempo by failing to address the position's actual priorities. In 6/8 positions, the player had a concrete tactical solution available (capturing a key pawn with check, eliminating a passed pawn, or addressing a specific structural weakness) but instead chose a vague 'improving' gesture. Pointless checks appear in 2/8 cases (Rd1+, Ba4+) where the check displaces the opponent's king to a better square or misplaces the checking piece. Premature/misdirected pawn advances appear in 3/8 cases (f6, a4, b6) where the push either weakens the king position or commits to a plan without proper preparation. Piece repositioning to 'active' but actually worse squares appears in 3/8 cases (Bh3, Nh4, Nh4) where a well-placed piece is moved to seemingly threaten something but abandons critical defensive or positional duties. The average cp_loss of 1555 and average of only 1.6 good moves available confirms these are critical moments demanding precision where the player chose flash over substance.
analysis.move_pattern: Mixed piece types moving to aggressive-looking squares, giving non-forcing checks, or advancing pawns toward the opponent - all appearing to create initiative without concrete follow-through
analysis.why_bad: These moves squander tempo in positions that demand concrete solutions (capturing key pawns, addressing passed pawns, neutralizing specific threats), allowing the opponent to consolidate advantages, exploit newly created weaknesses, or seize the initiative that was voluntarily abandoned
sub_patterns: Purposeless checks that misplace the checking piece or improve the opponent's king (Rd1+, Ba4+)
Piece repositioning from functional squares to seemingly active but actually worse squares (Bh3, Nh4)
Premature or misdirected pawn advances that ignore the real positional priority (f6, a4, b6)

analysis.label: Playing a non-urgent, slow move in a position that demands immediate forcing or prophylactic action, allowing the opponent a free tempo to execute their plan.
analysis.description: This feature fires on moves that squander a critical tempo in sharp or dynamic positions. The played moves appear superficially logical (repositioning a piece, making a pawn push, grabbing material) but ignore the position's most urgent demand. In 9/11 positions, the analyses explicitly identify 'tempo_loss' as a key tag. The best moves in all cases were either forcing (checks, threats, attacks on hanging pieces) or prophylactic (addressing king safety before capturing, developing before pushing). Instead, the blunders include passive pawn pushes that don't create threats (c3 in position 9, f3 in position 14, b4 in position 10), piece relocations to irrelevant squares abandoning critical files or diagonals (Rc8 abandoning the d-file in position 1, Bh6 ignoring the passed pawn in position 2, Rb1 abandoning e4 defense in position 8, Qb6 leaving the central outpost in position 12), premature material grabs before addressing defense (Qxc4 before Kg7 in position 7), and a king walk into a tactical vulnerability (Kg6 onto a check diagonal in position 5). In all 11 cases, the opponent exploits the gifted tempo with an immediate forcing response (pawn break, check, capture of undefended material, or launching a decisive attack).
analysis.move_pattern: Non-forcing move (quiet pawn push, lateral piece shuffle, premature capture, or king walk) that fails to address the position's most urgent tactical or strategic demand
analysis.why_bad: Grants the opponent a free tempo to execute a concrete plan (passed pawn advance, central break, piece activation, or king attack) that the correct move would have neutralized or pre-empted, turning dynamic equilibrium into a decisive advantage for the opponent.
sub_patterns: Passive pawn push (c3, f3, b4, e4) ignoring development or king safety needs
Piece relocation to irrelevant square (Rc8, Bh6, Rb1, Rh8, Qb6) abandoning a critical file/diagonal/post
Capturing material before addressing king safety (Qxc4 before Kg7)
King move into tactical vulnerability (Kg6 onto bishop diagonal)

analysis.label: Moving the queen (or king) to a plausible-looking square that voluntarily abandons its essential defensive or offensive function in the position.
analysis.description: In 9/10 positions, the player relocates their queen from a square where it performs a critical task (defending the king, pressuring a weakness, controlling an invasion square, or maintaining deep infiltration) to a square that appears reasonable but fails to address the position's concrete demands. In Position 2, the queen leaves king defense allowing a diagonal check mating attack. In Position 8, the queen retreats from a devastating e2 infiltration to a toothless e4. In Position 12, the queen abandons g6 king defense allowing forced mate. In Positions 5 and 14, the queen sidesteps when capturing an undefended b7 pawn was the only good move. In Position 6, the queen retreats from f5 where it blocked Qe4+ checks. In Position 1, the queen retreats passively when it needed to contest the d3 invasion square. The consistent thread across all 10 positions is that the move looks purposeful (centralization, regrouping, creating threats) but concretely abandons the one function the position demanded, with an average of only 1.6 good alternatives available—indicating critical decision points requiring precision rather than general repositioning.
analysis.move_pattern: Queen (9/10) or king (1/10) moves to a seemingly logical square 1-3 squares away, typically a retreat or sideways shift, without capturing or giving check
analysis.why_bad: The queen was performing an irreplaceable function (king defense, invasion, pressure on a weakness, blockade of a key square) and its relocation creates a vacuum that the opponent immediately exploits through checks, invasions, material captures, or mating attacks that the queen previously prevented
sub_patterns: Queen retreats from deep infiltration square (e2→e4, giving opponent consolidation time)
Queen leaves king defensive post (g6→h5, c8→c4, exposing king to checks/mates)
Queen sidesteps when concrete capture was the only good move (f3→g3 instead of Qxb7)
Queen relocates to 'active' square that creates no immediate threats while abandoning real pressure
King voluntarily walks into tactical vulnerability (Kf2 exposing to Rd2+ discoveries)

analysis.label: Playing a non-urgent or misdirected piece move instead of the one critical capture that exploits or addresses immediate king vulnerability.
analysis.description: In all 3/3 positions, there was exactly one good move available (a specific tactical capture: Bxd6, Nxf1, or Qxd4), and the player instead made a seemingly reasonable but catastrophically wrong piece move that failed to address the position's urgent demands. In 3/3 cases, king safety was the central issue (exposed/uncastled king), and the best move was a capture that either exploited the opponent's king vulnerability or addressed one's own defensive needs. The played moves—Nc3 (slow development), Nh5 (passive repositioning away from a critical square), and Bxa8 (greedy capture far from the critical theater)—all share the trait of being plausible-looking moves that ignore the one-tempo window before the opponent consolidates or launches a decisive counterattack. The average cp_loss of 486 reflects positions on a knife's edge where only precision maintains the advantage.
analysis.move_pattern: Minor piece moves (knight or bishop) to non-critical squares or captures far from the tactical center, when the position demands an immediate specific capture near the vulnerable king
analysis.why_bad: These moves waste the critical tempo needed to exploit king vulnerability or address mating threats; the opponent then escapes danger (Kd7), launches a winning counterattack (Qxh7), or forces a perpetual (Bh2+), collapsing the player's entire advantage.
sub_patterns: Quiet development ignoring a hanging pawn/piece capture
Repositioning an active piece away from its critical tactical post
Material greed on the rim while ignoring mating threats near own king

analysis.label: A pawn advance attacking a well-placed enemy knight that doesn't need to retreat, wasting a critical tempo.
analysis.description: In all 7/7 positions, the blunder is a pawn push (a6, f3, c3, b5, f5, b5, b4) aimed at chasing an enemy knight from a strong square (b5, e4, d4, c4, e4, c4, c5 respectively). In every case, the knight has a superior forward destination rather than needing to retreat: in 3/7 cases the knight jumps forward with check or fork (Nc7+ in position 2, Ne2+ in position 4, Ne5 in position 10), in 2/7 cases it advances to a dominant outpost (Na5-Nc6 in position 6, Nd2 attacking a key piece in position 9), and in the remaining cases the tempo loss allows the opponent to consolidate or the attacker misses a far more urgent plan. The pawn move creates no real threat because the knight was never trapped—it was actively positioned with escape routes that improve its placement. Meanwhile, the tempo spent should have gone toward king safety (positions 2, 3), piece development (positions 3, 4, 12), or maintaining tactical pressure (positions 9, 10, 12).
analysis.move_pattern: Pawn advance one square to attack an enemy knight on an adjacent diagonal square (b/c/f-pawns targeting knights on b5/c4/c5/d4/e4)
analysis.why_bad: The knight doesn't need to retreat—it has a stronger forward square (often with check, fork, or outpost creation), so the pawn move wastes a tempo in a position demanding immediate action on development, king safety, or attack.
sub_patterns: Pawn attacks knight that jumps forward with check/fork (Nc7+, Ne2+, Ne5)
Pawn attacks knight that advances to a permanent outpost (Na5-Nc6)
Pawn attacks knight when the tempo should address king exposure or piece activation

analysis.label: Moving a piece away from a square where it performs an essential restraining, blocking, or coordinating function, allowing the opponent to exploit the vacated coverage.
analysis.description: In all 5 positions, the player moves a piece away from a square where it was performing a vital function—blocking a rank, pressuring key squares, coordinating an attack, or maintaining escape routes—for an ostensibly purposeful but ultimately inferior goal. In Position 5 (Rc2), the rook abandons the back rank zone to seek counterplay, allowing Ra7# (1/5 immediate mate). In Position 6 (Nh7), the knight leaves its powerful g5 outpost to the rim, freeing Black's center and leaving the knight stranded (1/5 piece trapped on rim). In Position 9 (Nxe7+), the key attacking knight on d5 is traded off for material instead of continuing the mating attack via Nxf6+ (1/5 wrong capture removing coordinator). In Position 12 (Be6), the bishop retreats from g4 where it restrained White's knight and supported kingside play, gifting White a free tempo in an opposite-side castling race (1/5 tempo loss in race). In Position 14 (Kg7), the king moves to a square that blocks its own knight's escape route, allowing a tactical fork combination (1/5 self-obstruction). All 5/5 cases share the common thread of voluntarily vacating a critical post for an illusory benefit.
analysis.move_pattern: Any piece type moving away from an active/restraining square to a less functional square; no consistent direction or capture pattern
analysis.why_bad: The piece was performing an essential function at its current square (blocking mating lines, pressuring key squares, coordinating attack, restraining opponent's pieces, or maintaining escape routes), and its departure allows the opponent to immediately exploit the abandoned function via tactical or positional means.
sub_patterns: Rook/piece abandoning rank-blocking duty allowing back-rank/file mate
Knight moving from powerful central post to rim square becoming trapped/useless
Capturing with the wrong piece removing key attacking coordinator
Retreating active piece from restraining square losing critical tempo in a race
King blocking own piece escape route enabling tactical forks

analysis.label: Moving a piece to a seemingly natural or active square where it is immediately captured or tactically exploitable by the opponent.
analysis.description: This feature fires on moves where a piece is placed on a square that appears positionally desirable (centralizing, blockading, developing, or challenging a file) but is tactically compromised—the piece either hangs directly or becomes exploitable via a simple tactic. In 5/9 positions, the moved piece is immediately capturable: Bd6 hangs to Rxd6 (pos 2), Ne4 hangs to Nxe4 (pos 12), Rdc3 allows Rxc3 winning the exchange (pos 9, 10), and Rg8 is won by a deflection check Rf5+ (pos 11). In 2/9 positions, the piece walks into checkmate or a mating net: Ke7 allows Qc5# (pos 1). In 1/9, moving the piece abandons a critical defensive duty: Re8 leaves f7 undefended for Bxf7+ (pos 4). The remaining cases involve tempo-wasting moves that allow decisive tactical breakthroughs. The common thread is that each move has clear positional motivation (blockading, centralizing, doubling rooks, challenging files) but overlooks an immediate one-move tactical refutation.
analysis.move_pattern: Any piece type moving to a seemingly active/central square that is directly attacked or tactically exploitable by an enemy piece; no consistent direction but often toward the center or onto open files/diagonals controlled by the opponent
analysis.why_bad: The destination square is directly controlled by an enemy piece that can immediately capture, or moving to that square creates a deflection/removal-of-guard tactic allowing the opponent to win material in one or two moves. The player focuses on positional intent while missing simple tactical threats.
sub_patterns: Piece moves onto open file controlled by enemy rook (Bd6, Rdc3)
Piece moves to square attacked by enemy knight/queen (Ne4, Ke7)
Piece abandons defense of critical square enabling sacrifice (Re8, Rg8)
King walks toward danger rather than safety (Ke7, Kc6)

analysis.label: Positional or space-gaining moves that create immediate tactical vulnerabilities exploitable by the opponent's forcing responses (checks, attacks, captures).
analysis.description: This feature fires on moves motivated by general strategic goals—space-gaining pawn advances, piece centralization, or king activation—that ignore concrete tactical consequences. In 10/12 positions, the refutation involves a tempo-gaining forcing move: checks (Rc2+ in pos 3, Rb7+ in pos 12, Ba4+ in pos 15, Nxf3+ in pos 9, Re8+ in pos 2), attacks on pieces (Nb5 hitting queen in pos 7, e4 hitting queen in pos 6/8), or captures of undefended material (Qxd4 in pos 4). The played moves all have a recognizable strategic intent (f4 for space, Ke7 for centralization, Qd3 for multi-purpose posting, c5 for central control) but each creates or exposes a vulnerability the opponent immediately exploits with tempo. King safety tags appear in 9/12 positions, and tempo_loss tags in 10/12, confirming the core pattern: the player loses a critical tempo by making a non-forcing self-weakening move when the position demanded concrete awareness.
analysis.move_pattern: Non-forcing moves (pawn advances, piece repositioning, or king moves) that create a new target or weakness on the square/file/diagonal just vacated or exposed
analysis.why_bad: These moves prioritize a vague strategic improvement while ignoring that the opponent has an immediate forcing response (check, piece attack, or capture) that exploits the newly created vulnerability with tempo, converting a manageable position into a significantly worse one
sub_patterns: Pawn advances (f4/g4/f6/c5) weakening king shelter or abandoning defensive control of critical squares
Queen moves to squares immediately attackable by knight jumps or pawn thrusts with tempo (Qd6→Nb5, Qf3→Nxf3+, Qd3 blocking retreat)
King moves to exposed squares vulnerable to rook checks along ranks/files (Kf2→Rc2+, Ke7→Rb7+)
Central pawn breaks releasing tension and allowing opponent's pieces to activate with tempo (d4→e4!)

analysis.label: Endgame king moves that waste a crucial tempo by moving away from a key defensive or counterplay responsibility.
analysis.description: This feature fires on endgame positions where the player makes a king move (7/8 cases) or pawn commitment (1/8) that squanders a critical tempo by abandoning an essential duty. In 8/8 positions, the move allows the opponent to execute a plan one tempo faster than would otherwise be possible. The specific failure modes include: moving the king away from a piece it was defending (Positions 7, 11 - king leaves knight/pawn unguarded), retreating passively when urgent pawn advances are needed (Positions 2, 4), moving the king toward the wrong flank when counterplay exists elsewhere (Position 1), committing structure prematurely and eliminating flexibility (Position 3), advancing the king while leaving a pawn hanging (Position 6), and choosing the wrong adjacent square when only one preserves the position (Position 8). All 8 positions are endgames, and the analyses consistently identify 'tempo_loss' as the core motif in 7/8 cases.
analysis.move_pattern: King moving one square in the wrong direction (away from a critical square or defensive duty), predominantly lateral or retreating moves in endgame positions
analysis.why_bad: The king abandons defense of a key piece/pawn or moves away from the critical sector of the board, giving the opponent a free tempo to advance passed pawns, capture undefended material, execute a kingside break, or activate pieces—turning winning positions into draws or defensible positions into lost ones.
sub_patterns: King retreats passively when urgent pawn advances are needed (Kd8, Kb1)
King moves to wrong flank away from counterplay (Kf7 positions)
King advances aggressively but leaves key pawn/piece undefended (Kc4, Kc5)
King moves to wrong adjacent square when only one holds the position (Kc3 vs Kd3)

analysis.label: Moves that remove the only blocker or defender on a bishop's diagonal, allowing it to capture a hanging rook (or place a rook directly on an undefended diagonal square).
analysis.description: This feature fires on moves that expose a rook to capture by an enemy bishop along a diagonal. The dominant pattern (at least 13/15 positions) involves a fianchettoed bishop on the long diagonal (b2 or g2) that threatens a corner rook (h8 or a8). The blunder either removes the pawn blocking the diagonal (g6 exposing Rh8 to Bb2: positions 2, 4, 7, 10), removes the piece defending the critical square (Bd6/Be7 moving the f8-bishop away from guarding g7 against Bb2: positions 6, 8, 12, 14), removes the blocking piece on the other long diagonal (b6 exposing Ra8 to Bg2: position 5; Bd3 leaving g2 undefended against Bb7: position 11), or places a rook directly on an undefended diagonal square (Ra3 on f8-bishop's diagonal: positions 1, 3; Ra6 on Bc4's diagonal: position 13). In virtually every case, the immediate punishment is a bishop simply capturing a completely undefended rook for free, winning a full exchange or more.
analysis.move_pattern: Any piece/pawn move that vacates or fails to occupy the one square blocking an enemy bishop's diagonal line to a hanging rook; alternatively, a rook move to an undefended square on a bishop's active diagonal
analysis.why_bad: The move removes the sole blocker or defender on a bishop's diagonal, allowing the bishop to capture an undefended rook outright—typically winning a full exchange (rook for bishop) or the entire rook for free when it was the only piece on the now-open diagonal.
sub_patterns: Moving g-pawn (g6) when opponent's Bb2 aims at Rh8 on the long diagonal
Moving dark-squared bishop away from f8, leaving g7 undefended against Bb2
Moving b-pawn or f1-bishop, exposing rook on the h1-a8 long diagonal
Placing a rook on an undefended square within a bishop's active diagonal (Ra3, Ra6)
Playing a non-blocking move when rook is already exposed on a bishop's open diagonal

analysis.label: Playing a quiet, seemingly natural piece move to e7 (or e-file) that ignores concrete tactical demands and creates vulnerabilities.
analysis.description: The dominant pattern is pieces being placed on the e7 square (or analogous e-file squares like e8/e1). A striking 7/11 positions feature a piece literally moving to e7 (Ne7 x3, Be7 x2, Nge7, Qe7), and 9/11 involve e-file piece placement. These moves appear 'natural' or 'developing' but catastrophically ignore the position's concrete tactical requirements. In positions 2, 4, and 10, Ne7 blocks the d-pawn advance while leaving f7 fatally weak to diagonal attacks (Qh5+, Ng5, Bxf7+). In positions 6 and 7, Be7 is passive development allowing tactical sacrifices on f7 or queen infiltration via h5. In position 11, Qe7 enables the crushing f5-f6 pawn break. The outlier moves (c5, a5, Ba4 in 3/11 positions) share the same conceptual error: choosing a 'routine' or 'standard-looking' move when immediate tactical action is required. The average cp_loss of 1127 reflects how severely these quiet moves are punished.
analysis.move_pattern: Piece (knight, bishop, queen, or rook) moving to e7 square (Black) or e1/e2 (White) — quiet, non-capturing, non-checking repositioning moves
analysis.why_bad: These moves are too slow and passive for the position's tactical demands — they typically block the d-pawn or f8-bishop's development, leave f7 critically under-defended against diagonal/knight attacks, or waste tempo on generic 'improving' when concrete tactical opportunities or threats require immediate attention.
sub_patterns: Ne7 blocking d-pawn and exposing f7 to Qh5+/Ng5/Bxf7+ tactics
Be7 passive development allowing sacrificial combinations on f7 or queen infiltration
Qe7 passive retreat enabling devastating pawn breaks (f5-f6)
Rook to e-file generic improvement missing concrete tactical wins
Slow pawn/bishop moves ignoring forced tactical sequences

analysis.label: Quiet piece or pawn repositioning moves that abandon critical defensive duties or ignore urgent tactical requirements of the position.
analysis.description: All 7 positions share a common pattern: the player makes a non-forcing, 'improving' move (no checks, no captures, no direct threats) when the position demands precise concrete action to address immediate dangers. In 6/7 cases, the move either removes a piece from a critical defensive square (Bb2 abandons e3 guard, Qc5 abandons e6/f7 defense, Bf6 loses defensive tempo) or places a piece on a tactically vulnerable square (Rf3 walks into Nf4 fork, Rd5 allows Qe4 tempo, Ra3 leaves Nb1 undefended). In position 7 (g3), a pawn advance fatally weakens the king shelter. In every case, the best moves address the actual urgent need: developing undeveloped pieces (4/7), covering critical squares (5/7), or continuing attacks with concrete threats (3/7). The played moves all look like reasonable positional improvements in isolation but catastrophically fail to engage with the position's tactical reality.
analysis.move_pattern: Quiet piece/pawn repositioning to seemingly improved squares - no checks, no captures, no direct threats. Pieces move to 'active' squares (rook lifts to 3rd/5th rank, bishop to long diagonal, queen to attacking square) or pawns advance to 'solidify'.
analysis.why_bad: The moves remove pieces from squares where they performed critical (often non-obvious) defensive functions, or place pieces on squares where they become tactical targets. This creates immediate exploitable vulnerabilities - unguarded squares for queen infiltration, fork targets, weakened king shelter, or lost tempo allowing opponent's threats to become unstoppable.
sub_patterns: Removing a defensive piece from a key square allowing enemy queen infiltration (Bb2→Qe3, Qc5→Bxe6)
Rook lift/centralization to a square attackable with tempo (Ra3→Qd3, Rd5→Qe4, Rf3→Nf4)
Pawn advance weakening king shelter when rooks already on 2nd/7th rank (g3→Qh5)
Premature piece repositioning losing critical defensive tempo (Bf6 allowing d6-d7)

analysis.label: Plausible-looking moves that waste a critical tempo in positions where only 1-2 precise moves maintain the evaluation, failing to address the most urgent tactical or king-safety requirement.
analysis.description: This feature activates on positions with extremely limited good options (avg 1.6 good moves) where the player chooses a move that appears reasonable—developing a piece (Rhe8), advancing pawns (c4, b4, fxe6), repositioning (Bb6, Qe2, Qf6), moving the king (Kh6, Kf5), or giving a check (Nc5+)—but catastrophically fails to address the single most critical requirement of the position. In 8/8 analyzed positions, king safety is a dominant factor that the move ignores. In 7/8 cases, the move constitutes a decisive tempo loss in positions where one tempo is the difference between holding and collapse. The positions share a pattern of precarious tactical balance where only precise defensive or exploitative moves maintain coordination, but the player opts for something that looks constructive while leaving the key vulnerability (exposed king, hanging piece, undefended pawn, critical pin) completely unaddressed. The very high average cp_loss (1165) reflects that these are 'only move' moments where the wrong choice is immediately punished.
analysis.move_pattern: Various piece types and directions; no single geometric pattern—the commonality is that the move addresses a SECONDARY positional goal rather than the position's PRIMARY tactical requirement
analysis.why_bad: Each move ignores the one critical vulnerability or urgent requirement of the position (king safety, pinned piece, hanging material, critical defensive coordination), wasting a tempo on something that would be fine in a calmer position but is catastrophic in these razor-sharp situations where the opponent can immediately exploit the neglected weakness.
sub_patterns: Piece retreat/repositioning abandoning a critical defensive post (Bb6, Qe2, Kh6)
Natural developing moves when immediate tactical action is required (Rhe8, c4, b4)
Premature checks that drive opponent's king to better squares (Nc5+)
Captures that open lines against own king (fxe6)
Piece placement to squares where it can be exchanged/captured (Qf6)

analysis.label: Quiet, non-forcing piece repositioning moves that waste critical tempo when the position demands immediate tactical action.
analysis.description: This feature fires on positions where the player chooses a slow, preparatory, or seemingly reasonable quiet move instead of the forcing continuation the position demands. In 4/5 positions, the move is explicitly tagged as 'tempo_loss' and 'missed_tactic.' The blunders share a pattern of passive piece shuffling—Bb1 retreats the bishop pointlessly (allowing Nf4 fork), Re2 prepares what should be done immediately (allowing Rb2 invasion), Bc5 develops when concrete tactics like Ng4/Nd3 win material, and Kd3 repositions the king into a mating net instead of fleeing laterally. In each case (4/5), significantly stronger forcing alternatives existed—captures (Rxe7), aggressive jumps (Ng4), or urgent king flights (Kb5)—that the player bypassed in favor of a 'reasonable-looking' quiet move. The common punishment is that the opponent seizes the initiative with a tactical blow that the slow move failed to prevent or preempt.
analysis.move_pattern: Non-forcing piece moves (no check, no capture, no direct threat) to passive or vulnerable squares, often retreats or lateral repositioning
analysis.why_bad: Wastes a critical tempo in a position requiring immediate forcing action, allowing the opponent to execute tactical strikes (forks, invasions, mates) that the slow move neither prevents nor preempts
sub_patterns: Bishop retreat to passive back-rank square (Bb1)
Rook repositioning instead of immediate capture (Re2 vs Rxe7)
Developing to undefended square when concrete tactics available (Bc5)
King walking toward open file/center instead of fleeing (Kd3)

analysis.label: Moving a piece away from its critical defensive or tactical role to a peripheral square while an urgent concrete threat or opportunity demands immediate attention.
analysis.description: This feature fires on positions where the player makes a seemingly purposeful but non-urgent move (often to a wing or rim square) while the position demands an immediate concrete response. In 10/12 positions, the played move sends a piece to the periphery (a-file, b-file, h-file, or rim squares like h5, a3, b4, a5, b5, h6) instead of addressing the actual tactical emergency. The urgent need varies: capturing a dangerous pawn (Positions 1, 9), defending a hanging piece (Positions 2, 8, 11), executing a winning tactic (Position 3), addressing kingside threats (Position 14), maintaining king safety (Positions 4, 5), or avoiding a fork (Position 6). In every case, the player's move looks like a reasonable strategic idea (queenside pressure, piece activation, pawn advance) but fatally ignores that the position has only 1-3 adequate moves. The average cp_loss of 1139 reflects that these are positions of extreme tactical urgency where slow moves are catastrophically punished.
analysis.move_pattern: Diverse piece types (Q, B, N, K, pawns) relocating laterally or to peripheral files (a, b, h) and rim squares, moving AWAY from the center of tactical tension or abandoning defensive responsibilities
analysis.why_bad: The position contains an urgent tactical obligation (a hanging piece, a critical capture, a mating threat, or a must-address pawn) that requires immediate concrete action. The played move instead pursues a non-urgent strategic objective elsewhere on the board, losing critical tempo and allowing the opponent to exploit the unaddressed threat—typically winning material, breaking through with a pawn, or launching a decisive attack.
sub_patterns: Queen abandons defensive post for wing activity (Qa5, Qb4, Qh6, Qd7)
Minor piece goes to rim ignoring central tactical shot (Ba3, Nh5, Nb5, Bb4)
Pawn/piece move ignores hanging material (a6, Bxb7)
King moves into danger instead of to safety (Kf8)

analysis.label: Playing a slow, obvious move (usually a king move) to directly address a passed pawn when a more concrete tactical action was urgently needed.
analysis.description: In 6/6 positions, the player makes a 'natural-looking' endgame move that directly attends to a passed pawn—either moving toward it to blockade (Ke2, Rg7), support it (Kg3), capture it (Kxe3), or centralize near it (Ke3, Ng3)—when the position demanded a more dynamic, non-obvious action. The correct moves involve tactical precision: capturing an undefended piece (Rxc5 in position 5), repositioning a piece to a dominant square (Ng5, Nd4 in positions 1-2), executing a prophylactic pawn push (h4 in position 12), a critical move-order exchange (bxc5 in position 13), or an active rook maneuver creating a tactical threat (Ra1 in position 15). In all cases, the blunder wastes a crucial tempo in positions where every move counts, allowing the opponent to advance connected passed pawns (4/6), activate pieces decisively (3/6), or exploit tactical sequences like checks/captures that the slow move enabled.
analysis.move_pattern: King moves to ranks 2-3 (4/6), or piece retreat/redirection toward a passed pawn rather than executing a concrete action elsewhere
analysis.why_bad: These moves waste a critical tempo in razor-sharp endgame positions by addressing passed pawns through slow, direct means (blockade, escort, capture) when the position required immediate tactical action; the lost tempo allows the opponent to create unstoppable connected passers, advance pawns to the seventh rank, or consolidate a previously precarious position.
sub_patterns: King moves to blockade/support a passed pawn when a piece maneuver solves the problem more efficiently
Grabbing a pawn before executing a necessary preparatory exchange (move-order error)
Rook passively blockading a pawn instead of capturing an undefended piece
Retreating an active piece from an outpost to a passive square near the king

analysis.label: Playing a non-urgent or retreating move that wastes a decisive tempo when the position demands immediate action to maintain control of a key square, file, or zone.
analysis.description: In 9/9 positions, the played move abandons a critical positional responsibility by moving a piece away from where it's needed most, wasting a tempo that the opponent immediately exploits. In Position 3 (Kf6), Position 11 (h3), and Position 12 (Ke5), the king fails to seize or stay near a critical square, losing a king-activity race. In Position 1 (Rf1), Position 4 (Rgf3), and Position 5 (Qd7), a major piece moves away from a key defensive file/zone, allowing opponent invasion. In Position 2 (Ke8), the king abandons blockading duty against passed pawns. In Position 7 (Bf1), a piece retreats to a passive square when development was urgent. In Position 8 (Kxe7), the wrong piece captures, exposing the king. The common thread in all cases is that exactly one or very few good moves existed (avg 1.9), the position was at a critical inflection point requiring precise action, and the player chose a seemingly reasonable but ultimately non-forcing move that conceded the initiative.
analysis.move_pattern: Piece moves to a passive or irrelevant square (often retreating or sideways), frequently abandoning an open file, key central square, or defensive station; includes king retreats, rook redeployments away from critical files, and quiet pawn pushes in time-critical positions
analysis.why_bad: The move wastes a decisive tempo in positions where the opponent can immediately seize the vacated square/file/zone or exploit the loss of time to advance passed pawns, launch a mating attack, or establish a dominant piece on the now-uncontested outpost
sub_patterns: King retreating or moving away from a critical blockade/race square in endgames
Rook/Queen abandoning control of an open file, allowing opponent invasion
Non-forcing pawn or piece move in a tempo-critical promotion or king race
Retreating a piece to a passive square when aggressive action maintains the advantage

analysis.label: Moves that pursue a secondary objective while neglecting the single most urgent tactical or strategic requirement of the position.
analysis.description: This feature activates when a player makes a move that appears purposeful or active but fundamentally misses the position's critical priority. In 6/6 cases, the position demanded one specific action (capturing a free pawn, exploiting a forcing tactic, blocking an invasion file, or maintaining a piece on a critical defensive square), yet the player chose a move addressing a less important concern. In positions 2 and 3, available captures/wins were ignored in favor of passive consolidation (g3 instead of Nh4 winning a piece; Qc7 instead of Qxc6 capturing a free passed pawn). In positions 9, 14, and 15, the player launched premature aggression (Nd3 attacking a rook, Ng5 attacking f7, Qb4 seeking queenside pressure) while ignoring that the opponent had immediate forcing refutations exploiting exposed kings or development advantages. In position 12, the player withdrew a critically-placed rook from its defensive post (Rdd8), abandoning 7th-rank control. All 6 positions had very few good options (avg 1.5), indicating narrow critical moments where only addressing the primary demand was acceptable.
analysis.move_pattern: Piece or pawn move to a square that serves a secondary purpose (prophylaxis, attack on non-critical target, repositioning) while the position's critical lane/square/capture goes unaddressed
analysis.why_bad: The opponent has an immediate forcing response (check, capture, invasion, fork) that exploits the neglected critical factor, gaining tempo or material because the played move neither creates a sufficient counter-threat nor addresses the primary vulnerability
sub_patterns: Passive prophylaxis when a forcing tactical win exists (g3, Qc7 - missing captures/wins)
Premature aggression ignoring opponent's forcing refutation against exposed king (Nd3, Ng5, Qb4)
Withdrawing piece from critical defensive post, allowing invasion (Rdd8)

analysis.label: Quiet developing or repositioning moves played in positions that demand immediate concrete tactical action.
analysis.description: This feature fires on positions where players make natural-looking, principled moves (typically piece development or repositioning) while ignoring urgent tactical demands. In 7/9 positions, the played move was a minor piece development or quiet repositioning (Bc4 x2, Ne3, Nc3 x2, Bc6, Nbc3, Qh6) when the position required a specific forcing response — such as capturing a hanging piece (Position 1: Nxg5 needed), exploiting an exposed king with a central break (Position 13: d4 needed), capturing with the correct piece for maximum effect (Position 9: Qxe5 over Rxe5), or defending against an immediate checkmate threat (Position 8: Bg7 to prevent Nf6#). The average number of good moves available was only 1.7, confirming these are narrow positions where precision is critical. The average cp_loss of 1321 reflects the catastrophic consequences of missing the position's tactical requirements. The 'tempo_loss' tag appears across 8/9 positions, confirming the central issue: these moves waste critical time in positions where every tempo matters.
analysis.move_pattern: Quiet piece development, retreat, or repositioning (especially bishops to diagonals, knights to central squares, queen shuffles) — non-forcing, non-capturing moves in sharp positions
analysis.why_bad: These moves follow general principles (develop pieces, centralize) but ignore specific tactical requirements — hanging pieces, forced captures, mate threats, or central breaks that would exploit the opponent's vulnerabilities. The quiet move gifts the opponent a crucial tempo to consolidate, defend, or escape.
sub_patterns: Bishop development to active diagonal ignoring hanging material (Bc4 instead of capturing)
Knight development to natural square ignoring central break or tactical threat (Nc3/Nbc3 instead of d4 or dxe4)
Piece retreat/shuffle instead of aggressive forward action (Ne3 instead of Ne5, Qh6 instead of Qe7)
Wrong piece capture when a more powerful piece should take (Rxe5 instead of Qxe5)
Ignoring immediate mating threats for positional moves (Bc6 instead of Bg7)

analysis.label: Moving a piece away from a critical coordinating or defensive square to pursue a superficially attractive but tactically flawed objective (check, capture, or advance).
analysis.description: This feature fires when a player removes a piece from a square where it performs an essential function—defending material, controlling key squares, or maintaining coordination—in order to pursue something that appears active (a check, capture, pawn grab, or advance) but actually leaves a fatal weakness. In 7/11 positions, the moved piece was the sole defender of something critical: Qg6+ abandons control of escape squares allowing the king to flee (2 cases), Qd8 removes defense of the e5 pawn, Na5 decentralizes a knight from c4 leaving e4 and c5 unguarded, Nxh5 removes a defensive knight allowing queen invasion, b3 unguards the c3 knight, and Ne8+ places the only active piece where it can be captured. In 3/11 cases the wrong piece was used for a task another piece could accomplish better (Bxf6+ instead of exf6+, Bxh6 as an unsound sacrifice, Qg6+ instead of Bg6#). In 2/11 cases a pawn advance creates targets or overextension (b5, Qd3). The common thread across all positions is that quiet, restraining alternatives were available (avg 1.9 good moves) that maintained the piece's critical function while preserving or improving the position.
analysis.move_pattern: Any piece type moving away from a coordinated/defensive square, frequently involving checks, captures, or pawn advances that appear forcing but abandon essential positional duties
analysis.why_bad: The moved piece was performing a critical function (defending material, controlling escape squares, guarding key points, or maintaining central coordination) that cannot be replaced once it leaves, and the superficially attractive objective (check/capture/advance) provides insufficient compensation for the structural or tactical damage caused by the vacancy.
sub_patterns: Queen check that abandons control of critical squares (Qg6+ leaving e8 unguarded)
Pawn move that removes defense of a piece (b3 unguarding Nc3)
Knight decentralization from powerful outpost to rim or capturable square (Na5, Ne8+, Nxh5)
Using the wrong piece for a capture when another piece achieves the same goal more efficiently (Bxf6+ vs exf6+)
Queen retreat/advance abandoning a defensive assignment (Qd8, Qd3)

analysis.label: Moving the king or queen to an exposed square in a critical position where only one precise move avoids tactical catastrophe.
analysis.description: This feature fires on positions where the player moves their king or queen (8/10 cases) to a seemingly natural or active square that is immediately punished by a tactical refutation. The positions are characteristically narrow, with an average of only 1.4 good moves available, meaning the player needed to find one specific continuation. King moves to the f-file are especially prominent (Kf5, Kf3, Kf6, Kf2 = 4/10), all placing the king on squares exposed to diagonal or file-based attacks. Queen moves (Qg4, Qa3, Qh8 = 3/10) similarly place the queen where it can be won or rendered useless by forcing sequences. In every case, the correct move was qualitatively different from what was played—often a retreat to safety (Kf1, Kh1, Kf8, Qd8), a pawn advance (e3, a6, d3), or a tactical strike (Rxh2, Bxf2+). The common thread is choosing a move that looks reasonable but ignores concrete tactical consequences in a position demanding precision.
analysis.move_pattern: King or queen moves to an exposed square (especially king to f-file: f2, f3, f5, f6), typically forward or central rather than retreating to safety
analysis.why_bad: The piece lands on a square vulnerable to immediate tactical exploitation (checks, captures, mating patterns, or forced sequences that win material), and the position required finding the single precise alternative that avoided these consequences.
sub_patterns: King moves to f-file squares exposed to diagonal/file attacks (Kf2, Kf3, Kf5, Kf6)
Queen moves to squares where it can be captured or trapped by forcing sequences (Qg4 via back-rank, Qh8 via Qxh8+)
Active-looking moves in positions requiring defensive precision
Forward king marches when pawn advances were the critical resource

analysis.label: Natural-looking moves that place pieces (especially the king) on squares immediately exploitable by opponent's checks, forks, or tactical strikes.
analysis.description: This feature fires on moves that appear routine or logical in isolation but catastrophically ignore the opponent's most forcing tactical reply. In 6/9 positions, the move is a king move to a square that falls on a dangerous attacking line (Kf3 onto the a8-f3 diagonal, Ke8 onto the h5-e8 diagonal, Ke1 onto the h4-e1 diagonal, Kd7 onto a knight-fork square from c5, Kc7 allowing Qe5+ with tempo). The remaining 3/9 positions involve piece moves that similarly ignore urgent threats: Be7 ignores the e5 central break with tempo, Nc4 ignores the lethal Ne6+ fork, Nf3 fails to block the critical e-file allowing Rae8+ with devastation, and Qxe7 removes defensive coverage from c8. The common thread across all 9 positions is that the player selects a move that seems purposeful (centralizing, developing, retreating to a 'safe' square) while the opponent has an immediate forcing response—typically a check or fork—that exploits the new piece placement with decisive tempo gain. The average cp_loss of 1386 reflects that these are severe tactical oversights where the position demanded threat-awareness over general principles.
analysis.move_pattern: Piece (usually king) moves to a square on an open diagonal, file, or knight-attack square; non-king moves ignore immediate forcing threats to pursue routine development or activation
analysis.why_bad: The moves place pieces on squares immediately targetable by the opponent's forcing continuations (checks along diagonals/files, knight forks), granting the opponent decisive tempo to launch attacks, win material, or achieve checkmate—the player prioritizes 'natural' placement over calculating the opponent's most forcing reply.
sub_patterns: King retreating to a square on a vulnerable diagonal allowing queen checks (Ke8, Ke1, Kf3)
King moving to a knight-fork square allowing decisive discovered or direct fork (Kd7, Kc7)
Piece activation ignoring immediate tactical threat (Nc4 ignoring Ne6+ fork, Nf3 failing to block e-file)
Routine development allowing opponent's central/tactical break with tempo (Be7 allowing e5)
Capturing with wrong piece removing defensive duty from critical square (Qxe7 abandoning c8-Bishop)

analysis.label: Playing a visually appealing piece development or centralization move when the position demands immediate tactical execution of a forcing continuation.
analysis.description: In all 5 positions, the player chooses a move that looks 'natural' or 'improving' from a general principles standpoint—centralizing a piece, developing to an active square, or making a routine capture—while missing a critical tactical opportunity with a narrow window. In Position 1 (Nf4), the knight goes to a central outpost instead of the forcing Qf5. In Position 2 (cxd4), a routine pawn capture replaces the brilliant Nxf2 tactical strike. In Position 3 (Be5), the bishop centralizes impressively but becomes a tactical target. In Position 4 (Bc4), the bishop develops to a 'textbook' diagonal instead of the structurally necessary d5. In Position 5 (Rac1), the rook activates on a 'logical' file instead of executing the devastating Rxf7+ sacrifice. All 5/5 positions feature a concrete forcing continuation that must be played immediately before the opponent neutralizes the key vulnerability, and all 5/5 played moves are non-forcing improvements that squander this window. The average cp_loss of 235 and average of only 1.6 good moves confirms these are critical-precision moments disguised as quiet positions.
analysis.move_pattern: Non-forcing piece moves to classically attractive squares (central outposts, active diagonals, open files) or routine captures, bypassing an available forcing sequence
analysis.why_bad: The position has a narrow tactical window requiring immediate execution of a forcing continuation (sacrifice, fork, pin), and the 'improving' move wastes the crucial tempo, allowing the opponent to escape the tactical vulnerability, consolidate their king, or exploit the piece's new placement as a target.
sub_patterns: Centralizing a minor piece to an attractive square that creates a tactical target
Developing a rook to an open file when a sacrifice on a different file wins immediately
Making a routine pawn capture instead of a tactical piece strike first (move-order error)
Developing a bishop to an active diagonal that leaves it or other pieces undefended

analysis.label: In pure pawn endgames, the king moves (or a tempo is spent) toward the wrong sector of the board, losing a critical pawn race.
analysis.description: This feature fires on pawn endgame positions where the player directs their king toward a sector that appears active or aggressive but is strategically irrelevant, while the decisive battle occurs on the opposite flank. In 11/11 positions, the game is a pure king-and-pawn endgame. In the high-loss examples, the king marches toward the kingside when the queenside race is decisive (Position 1: Kf4, Position 3: Kf4, Position 2: Ke5), toward the rim when centralization is needed (Position 4: Ka4), captures a pawn on the wrong side (Position 7: Kxc3 captures queenside when Ke4 toward kingside wins), or abandons defense of critical pawns (Position 9: Kd5 abandoning b6, Position 10: Kg5 abandoning e6). Position 12's a3 represents the pawn-move variant: wasting a tempo on an irrelevant pawn advance instead of the urgent king move Ke5. Position 15's Kd6 prioritizes a king move over a time-sensitive pawn advance (b5). The average cp_loss of 411 reflects that in pawn endgames, a single tempo in the wrong direction is often the difference between winning and losing.
analysis.move_pattern: King move (or tempo-wasting pawn move) directed away from the critical sector in a pure pawn endgame; the king goes toward the wrong flank or captures on the wrong side
analysis.why_bad: In pawn endgames, the king is the only piece and tempo is everything—moving toward the wrong sector means arriving too late to stop an opponent's passed pawn, defend a critical pawn, or win a decisive pawn race, often swinging the result by a full point
sub_patterns: King moves toward kingside when queenside pawn race is decisive
King moves toward queenside/rim when kingside or central pawns need attention
King captures material on wrong flank, getting lured away from the critical sector
Irrelevant pawn move wastes the tempo needed for an urgent king march
King centralizes or develops when a defensive retreat to guard a specific pawn is required

analysis.label: Playing a seemingly active or forcing move (check, capture, centralization) that misses a much stronger alternative on a nearby square or targeting a different piece.
analysis.description: This feature fires on positions where the player has a decisive or critical advantage but squanders it by choosing the wrong forcing move. The most prominent sub-pattern is wrong check direction: 3/10 positions involve checking on the wrong square when an adjacent square delivers immediate checkmate (Qb1+ vs Qc2#, Qh7+ allowing Qg7 interposition vs Qh5+ which prevents it, Qd3+ vs Qe3#). Another 2/10 involve capturing the wrong target (Qxb7 grabbing a distant pawn instead of Qxd5 maintaining king defense; Rxf2 capturing the knight instead of Qxf3 eliminating the dangerous bishop). The remaining 5/10 involve moving a piece to a plausible-looking square that abandons a critical duty or creates a fatal vulnerability (Rb8 passive retreat vs Ng6 counter-sacrifice; Nd6 leaving defensive c8 post; Kb1 walking onto back rank; Ra1 abandoning the f-file; d4 overextension). All share the thread of choosing a move that appears natural or aggressive but is tactically one step off from the correct solution, with devastating consequences (avg cp_loss 4034).
analysis.move_pattern: Piece moves to a square that appears active or forcing (often a check or capture) but is one square away from, or a different target than, the truly decisive move
analysis.why_bad: The chosen move either allows a defensive resource that the correct alternative would have prevented (interposition, king escape to an uncovered square), abandons a critical file/diagonal/defensive duty, or captures the wrong target leaving the real threat alive - all because the player selected the most obvious-looking forcing move rather than the precisely correct one.
sub_patterns: Wrong check direction allowing escape/interposition (3/10)
Capturing wrong target leaving key threat alive (2/10)
Piece abandons critical defensive/offensive post for seemingly active square (3/10)
Premature advance creating exploitable weakness (1/10)
King moves to wrong safe square creating back-rank vulnerability (1/10)

analysis.label: Playing a purposeful-looking developing, capturing, or advancing move while ignoring an urgent king safety crisis that demands an immediate quiet/prophylactic response.
analysis.description: In 5/6 positions, the player's king faces an existential threat (back-rank mates, sacrificial attacks on f7, queen infiltration along open files) that requires an immediate quiet defensive move—most often a simple king sidestep (Kb7/Kb8 in positions 3, 4, 5; e6 blocking a diagonal in position 14). Instead, the player makes a 'normal' active move: activating a rook (Rhe8), blocking with a bishop (Bc7), pushing a central pawn break (d5), repositioning the queen (Qf4), grabbing material (Nxb7), or preparing a fianchetto (b6). In 5/6 cases, king safety is the primary tactical motif. In 4/6, the king is castled queenside on c8 and the best move is literally Kb7 or Kb8. The positions share extremely narrow best-move margins (avg 1.3 good moves), meaning the one correct defensive/prophylactic move is the only way to survive. The blunders average 3533cp loss, often resulting in forced mates.
analysis.move_pattern: Any piece type; non-king moves (developing, capturing, or advancing) played instead of required king walk or critical diagonal-blocking pawn move
analysis.why_bad: The moves ignore an immediate existential threat to the player's king—typically a queen check/invasion along an open file, a back-rank mate, or a sacrifice on f7—where only a quiet prophylactic response (usually a king sidestep like Kb7/Kb8) would neutralize the danger. The 'active' move neither defends nor provides escape routes, allowing devastating forced sequences.
sub_patterns: Queenside-castled king on c8 needs Kb7/Kb8 but player activates pieces instead
Central king on e8 needs pawn block (e6) but player plays flank move
Grabbing material while own attacking coordination collapses
Queen repositioning ignoring opponent's unstoppable passed pawns

analysis.label: Moving a piece to a square where it immediately faces a tempo-gaining attack (check, fork, or pawn advance) from the opponent.
analysis.description: In all 5 positions, the moved piece lands on a square that is directly in the attack range of an enemy piece or pawn, granting the opponent a critical free tempo. In Position 1 (Kh5), the king walks into the range of Nf4+ check. In Position 4 (Kd2), the king walks into Ne4+ fork range. In Position 5 (Kd7), the king steps onto a square where c8=Q+ comes with check. In Position 3 (Rb3), the rook moves to a square immediately attacked by ...b4 pawn advance. In Position 2 (Ne4+), the knight lands on a square where it's captured (Nxe4) and the intended follow-up check sequence is refuted. All 5/5 positions feature 'tempo_loss' in their tags, and all involve a nearby alternative square (Kh4, Kxd3, Kxe8, Rc2, c5) that avoids giving the opponent this exploitable target. The average cp_loss of 2194 reflects how catastrophic a single gratuitous tempo can be in sharp positions.
analysis.move_pattern: Piece (usually King) moves one square to an adjacent square that falls in the direct attack range of an enemy knight check, pawn advance, or promotion-with-check
analysis.why_bad: The piece moves to a square where the opponent immediately attacks or checks it, gaining a tempo that accelerates their winning plan (passed pawn promotion, mating attack, or material win). A nearby alternative square was immune to this tactical response.
sub_patterns: King steps onto knight-check square (Kh5 into Nf4+, Kd2 into Ne4+)
King moves onto file/diagonal allowing promotion with check (Kd7 into c8=Q+)
Rook moves in front of advancing pawn, allowing tempo-gaining pawn push (Rb3 into ...b4)
Piece gives check but lands on capturable square where follow-up is refuted (Ne4+ into Nxe4)

analysis.label: Pawn advances giving check in endgames that permanently damage the player's own pawn structure for a meaningless tempo.
analysis.description: This feature fires on positions where a player advances a pawn to give check in an endgame, trading permanent structural damage for a single tempo that doesn't meaningfully improve their position. In 9/9 positions, the move is a pawn push delivering check. In 7/9 cases the check breaks a connected pawn chain or duo (d5/e5 broken by d4+, f6/g5/h5 broken by g4+, b4/c4 broken by b5+, g5/h5 broken by h4+, b6 structure broken by b5+, queenside majority frozen by c5+). The opponent's king typically reaches a superior square after the check (e.g., White's king reaches the blockading d3 square after d4+, reaches f4 after g4+, reaches b4 attacking both pawns after b5+). The average cp_loss of 213 reflects that these structural concessions often convert winning positions into draws or near-equality. The checks appear to stem from a 'checking is free' heuristic that ignores the irreversible cost of pawn commitments.
analysis.move_pattern: Pawn advance one square forward delivering check to the opposing king, typically on the g, b, c, d, or h files
analysis.why_bad: The pawn advance permanently breaks a connected pawn structure (chain, duo, or majority) for a single tempo that merely relocates the opponent's king to an equal or superior square, often granting the opponent access to blockading squares or enabling capture of the now-isolated pawns.
sub_patterns: g-pawn check breaking kingside chain (g4+ appears 4 times)
b-pawn check exposing queenside pawns (b5+ appears 2 times)
central pawn check breaking pawn duo (c5+, d4+)

analysis.label: Natural-looking moves that lose exactly one critical tempo by choosing the wrong piece, wrong square, or wrong priority in positions requiring surgical precision.
analysis.description: This feature activates on moves that appear reasonable or active on the surface but waste a decisive tempo in positions where precision is paramount (avg 2.0 good moves available). The pattern manifests in several forms: choosing the wrong square that's adjacent to the correct one (Kc3 instead of Kc5 in position 2; Kc5 instead of Kc6 in position 5), moving the wrong piece when another should act (Rbc2+ instead of Rdc2+ in positions 11-12; Bb3 instead of Bf4 in position 8), developing to a square that immediately gets kicked (Nf6 in position 13), or prioritizing a capture/attack when prophylaxis is needed (Kxa2 in position 6; a5 in position 7). In 10/12 positions, analyses explicitly tag 'tempo_loss' as the core error. The common outcome is that the opponent gains exactly one forcing move to seize control—whether creating unstoppable passed pawns (positions 2, 4, 5), forcing checkmate (position 6), trapping pieces (position 7), or exploiting newly-created tactical vulnerabilities (positions 8, 9, 14). These positions are characterized by being tempo-critical moments where the margin between holding and losing collapses to a single move.
analysis.move_pattern: Any piece type moving to a plausible but subtly wrong square or capturing when another action is urgent; no consistent geometric direction but consistently one square/one tempo away from the correct choice
analysis.why_bad: The move fails to address the single most urgent positional or tactical priority, granting the opponent a free tempo to execute a forcing plan (promotion race, mating attack, piece trap, passed pawn advance) that would have been prevented by the correct move
sub_patterns: Wrong rook delivers check (vacates critical file)
King moves one square short of the drawing/winning square
Piece develops to immediately kickable square
Bishop abandons critical defensive diagonal for apparent attack
Capture/pawn push ignores imminent tactical threat

analysis.label: Quiet, preparatory, or retreating moves that neglect the position's immediate tactical demands, leaving critical pieces or squares fatally undefended.
analysis.description: This feature fires on middlegame moves that appear logical in isolation (retreating a piece, advancing a pawn to 'solidify,' centralizing a knight, or repositioning a rook) but catastrophically ignore the most urgent tactical requirement of the position. In 4/5 cases, the opponent controls or threatens to exploit an open file (h-file in position 2, e-file in positions 5, 9, and 10), and the blunder either fails to contest that file or creates a new vulnerability that compounds with existing pressure. In 3/5 cases (Ng8, Nd4, Rg2), the move directly removes a defender or creates a fork/tactical target. In 2/5 cases (both f3 moves), a pawn advance weakens the king's pawn shield and creates structural targets. The best moves in all positions share the quality of addressing the immediate concrete threat—contesting the open file, reinforcing a key defender, or developing pieces to active squares—rather than pursuing secondary plans. The average centipawn loss of 384 reflects the catastrophic nature of these oversights.
analysis.move_pattern: Non-forcing moves (retreats, pawn advances on f3, quiet piece redeployments) that ignore an immediate tactical vulnerability on an open file or weak square complex
analysis.why_bad: Each move abandons a critical defensive duty or creates a new tactical vulnerability (fork target, hanging piece, dark-square weakness) while the opponent has concrete attacking resources (open file rook, centralized knight, active minor piece) ready to exploit the neglected vulnerability immediately.
sub_patterns: Knight retreat abandoning file defense (Ng8)
f3 pawn advance weakening king structure against open-file pressure
Piece redeployment creating fork/tactical target (Rg2, Nd4)
Removing the only defender of a piece on an open file

analysis.label: King moves toward the wrong wing or edge in endgames, losing critical tempo in the race to reach decisive squares.
analysis.description: In 6/7 positions, the played move is a king move that heads in the wrong direction relative to the critical theater of action. The pattern is strikingly consistent: Kb7 retreats from center when Kc5 centralizes (Position 2); Kd5 stays central-passive when Kf4 attacks kingside pawns (Position 3); Kc6 drifts queenside when Ke6 contests centralization (Position 4); Kb6 goes further from advancing kingside passers when Kd5 approaches them (Position 11); Kc3 retreats queenside when Ke4 supports the d5 passer (Position 15); Kxh2 commits to the corner when active squares exist (Position 9). Even the non-king move (a3) follows the same logic—investing tempo on the wrong flank. In all 7/7 cases, the best move involved approaching the critical zone (center or opponent's advancing pawns) more directly, and the error gave the opponent free tempo to advance pawns or achieve positional goals unopposed.
analysis.move_pattern: King moves laterally or backward toward the a/b/c files or board edge, away from center or opponent's advancing pawns; occasionally a tempo-wasting pawn move on the inactive wing
analysis.why_bad: Loses critical tempo in endgame king races—the king moves away from the only squares that matter (blockading opponent's passers, supporting own passers, or contesting centralization), allowing the opponent to advance pawns or achieve positional dominance unopposed
sub_patterns: King retreats toward queenside when centerization needed
King moves to passive square instead of aggressively targeting opponent pawns
Tempo wasted on inactive wing while opponent advances passed pawns
King captures material on wrong side of board at cost of decisive tempo

analysis.label: Playing a plausible-looking improving move that completely ignores the position's most urgent tactical demand, whether an offensive opportunity to seize or a defensive necessity to address.
analysis.description: This feature fires on positions where the player makes a move with clear positional motivation (piece activation, centralization, prophylaxis, or structural improvement) but catastrophically neglects the single most critical tactical reality of the position. In 5/10 cases, the player moved a piece to a seemingly 'active' square while ignoring lethal threats (Nc4 opening a mating diagonal, Nc3 ignoring gxh7+ mate, Nd3 placing a piece en prise, Ke7 walking into Bxd6+ discovery, Qb6 exposing the queen to a trap). In 3/10 cases, slow pawn moves were played in tactically critical positions (g3 and e6 missing forcing wins, g6 fatally weakening the king). In 2/10 cases, 'improving' moves replaced the one forcing tactical blow available (Rf6 instead of Bxg6 winning material, Qd6 instead of developing the bishop for castling). The positions share extremely narrow margins (avg 2.0 good moves), meaning only specific moves address the critical issue, and any 'general improvement' fails catastrophically.
analysis.move_pattern: Piece or pawn moved to an ostensibly useful square (centralizing, activating, or prophylactic) while the position demands addressing one specific critical tactical issue
analysis.why_bad: The position contains a single dominant tactical requirement (a forcing combination to execute, a mating threat to parry, or a piece safety issue to resolve) and ANY move that doesn't address it - no matter how reasonable it looks - leads to catastrophe because the opponent's tactical resources are too concrete and immediate to ignore
sub_patterns: Missing a forcing tactical opportunity in favor of a slow improving move (Rf6/g3)
Moving a piece that was performing a critical defensive function, opening lines against own king (Nc4/Ke7)
Activating a piece on the wrong side of the board while lethal threats exist on the other (Nc3/Nd3)
Making a structural pawn move that creates immediate tactical weaknesses (g6/e6)
Repositioning the queen to an exposed square where it becomes a tactical target (Qb6/Qd6)

analysis.label: Playing a secondary-purpose move when the position urgently demands addressing king vulnerability through castling, king relocation, or defensive consolidation.
analysis.description: In 9/11 positions, the king (own or opponent's exploitation thereof) is critically exposed or uncastled, and the best move directly addresses this vulnerability (castling in positions 5, 8, 12; specific king moves in positions 1, 2, 10, 14; defensive consolidation in 3, 11, 15). Instead, the played moves pursue secondary objectives: pawn advances (e3, h5, f3), passive piece retreats (Bd8, Rg7, Rf1), misguided king moves to wrong squares (Kf8×2, Kg1), piece relocation for material (Nf7), or aggressive queen sorties (Qg5). The punishment consistently exploits the neglected king vulnerability through diagonal checks (Bc5+ after f3, Bh6+ after Kf8, Bc5+ after Kg1), file invasions, or tactical combinations that only work because the king was left unattended. The average 1.7 good moves available confirms these are positions demanding precise prioritization where only addressing the king survives.
analysis.move_pattern: Varied piece types and directions; moves that address a secondary positional concern (attack, material, specific square defense) rather than the most urgent king safety requirement
analysis.why_bad: The move ignores the position's most critical demand—securing the king—allowing the opponent to exploit king vulnerability through tactical resources (diagonal checks, file attacks, piece invasions) that the correct defensive moves would have neutralized
sub_patterns: King walking onto exposed diagonal (Kf8, Kg1)
Pawn advance weakening king shelter or wasting tempo (e3, f3, h5)
Passive piece move when castling is urgent (Bd8, Rf1, Rg7)
Abandoning key defensive piece placement for material (Nf7)
Aggressive move when defensive retreat needed (Qg5)

analysis.label: Moving a piece away from its essential blocking or restraining role to a seemingly active but strategically disconnected square, allowing the opponent to execute their primary threat.
analysis.description: In all 5/5 positions, a piece leaves a square where it performed a vital restraining function—blockading a passed pawn, guarding a key invasion square, or defending the king—and relocates to a square that appears purposeful but creates no concrete threat. In Position 2, the knight abandons c5 (blocking e6) for d3 (attacking pawns), allowing e6+ with tempo. In Position 4, the bishop leaves b5 for d7, unguarding c4 and allowing rook penetration on the d-file. In Position 10, the rook moves from f6 (threatening e3) to f5 (attacking nothing), giving White time for Rh4 and b3 to destroy the passed pawn. In Position 11, the queen goes to g8 where Ne7 forks it and the critical g6 pawn. In Position 15, the queen abandons e8 (guarding the e6 invasion square and king) for b8, allowing Qe6+ with devastating checks. All 5/5 moves share the pattern of prioritizing apparent activity over essential restraint, with the opponent then exploiting the abandoned post with tempo.
analysis.move_pattern: Any piece type moving away from a critical blocking/guarding square to a different square that lacks concrete threats; non-capturing, non-checking repositioning moves
