analysis.why_bad: The piece was performing an irreplaceable restraining function (blockading a passed pawn, guarding an invasion square, or shielding the king), and its departure allows the opponent to execute their primary winning plan—typically a pawn advance with check, queen invasion with check, or piece penetration—with decisive tempo gains
sub_patterns: Knight abandons pawn blockade for pawn attacks
Bishop/Queen repositions away from key diagonal coverage
Rook moves to passive rank abandoning attack on weak pawn
Queen retreats far from exposed king allowing invasion checks

analysis.label: Defensive moves that intend to improve king safety but actually expose the king to tactical exploitation.
analysis.description: This feature fires on moves where the player attempts to improve their defensive setup or king safety but fundamentally misjudges which direction is safe, creating worse king vulnerability. In 5/7 positions, the king itself moves or castles to a square that becomes tactically exploitable (Kf8 walks into Ne6#, Kd7 allows Ne5+ discovered attack, Kf1 exposes king to queen infiltration on g3, O-O-O places king behind already-pressured c3-pawn). In the remaining 2/7 positions, a key piece relocates defensively (Nd8 retreats abandoning c7 defense, Qf3 abandons kingside threats) leaving the position's actual defensive needs unmet. All 7 positions share the 'king_safety' tag, and 6/7 feature 'exposed_king' or 'central_king' issues. The common thread is that each move SEEMS like a reasonable safety-seeking or reorganizing decision but actually worsens the king's tactical situation, typically because the chosen square falls on a vulnerable line (file, diagonal, or fork pattern) that the opponent immediately exploits.
analysis.move_pattern: King or defensive piece moving to a seemingly safe square (often one square away from origin), frequently toward f-file or back rank, without capturing or giving check
analysis.why_bad: The destination square is actually more tactically vulnerable than the origin due to discovered attacks, mating patterns, forks, or open lines that the opponent can immediately exploit - the player misjudges the direction of danger
sub_patterns: King walking into mating net on apparently quieter square (Kf8, Kd7)
Castling into already-compromised pawn structure (O-O-O)
Unnecessary king move creating exposure when active piece play was needed (Kf1)
Piece retreat abandoning critical defensive duties for illusory safety (Nd8, Qf3)
Capture removing defender from key square and enabling check along opened line (Nxf6)

analysis.label: Moving a piece away from a crucial defensive or structural role to pursue an indirect, non-urgent goal when concrete action was demanded.
analysis.description: In all 5 positions, the player moved a piece away from a square or role where it performed a critical function—guarding key squares, pressuring a target, or controlling the opponent's main threat—in favor of a seemingly logical but indirect plan. In Position 1, f5 abandoned f7's guard of e6, fatally weakening the pawn chain. In Position 2, Nb4 left the dominant d5 outpost for a peripheral square when Nxf4 won material immediately. In Position 4, Nxe4 removed the c3 knight from its diagonal-guarding duty for a greedy pawn grab. In Position 6, Kg2 passively retreated instead of boldly capturing the attacking piece with Kxe4. In Position 9, Bc2 repositioned the bishop irrelevantly while ignoring the existential b6 passed-pawn threat. In 5/5 cases, the best move involved concrete, forcing action (captures, sacrifices, or direct confrontation), while the blunder chose an indirect maneuver. The positions averaged only 2.0 good moves available, indicating critical moments requiring precision that the player met with strategic drift.
analysis.move_pattern: A piece (any type) leaves a square where it performs a key defensive/structural function, moving to a less relevant square—often appearing logical (gaining space, threatening, retreating to safety) but disconnecting from the position's central demand.
analysis.why_bad: The moves fail because they prioritize indirect goals (space, vague threats, material, safety) over the one concrete action the position demands, allowing the opponent to exploit the abandoned defensive role—whether through tactical strikes on weakened squares, promoting passed pawns, or maintaining dangerous attacking pieces that should have been eliminated.
sub_patterns: Pawn advance weakening key square protection (f5 abandoning e6)
Knight decentralization from dominant outpost (Nb4 leaving d5)
Piece removal from critical defensive square for greedy capture (Nxe4 leaving c3)
Passive king retreat when bold king capture eliminates the threat (Kg2 vs Kxe4)
Slow bishop maneuver ignoring existential passed-pawn threat (Bc2 ignoring b6)

analysis.label: Pieces (especially knights) voluntarily retreat to passive or starting squares when the position demands active development or tactical engagement.
analysis.description: This feature fires on moves that surrender critical tempo by retreating or passively placing pieces when forward development or tactical action is urgently needed. The strongest sub-pattern involves knights retreating to inferior squares: Ng1 and Nb1 return knights to their starting squares (2/10), Nh2 and Nh7 retreat knights to passive rim squares (2/10), Ne2 develops a knight passively instead of actively to c3 (1/10), and Ncxe7 removes a knight from an active post (1/10). The remaining moves share the broader tempo-loss theme: Rc1 makes a quiet rook move when an immediate tactical combination existed, b4 pushes a pawn when all pieces need development, Rf6 moves a rook to a square where it becomes a target giving the opponent escape with tempo, and Qe7+ gives a suboptimal check that improves the opponent's king position. In 8/10 positions, the analyses identify 'tempo_loss' as a primary tag, and the average cp_loss of 218 reflects the severe cost of voluntarily making active pieces passive during critical moments.
analysis.move_pattern: Pieces (predominantly knights) moving backward toward starting squares, rim squares (h-file), or passive positions; also rook/pawn moves that waste tempo when tactical action is available
analysis.why_bad: Surrendering tempo allows opponents to seize initiative through immediate tactical strikes (forks, checks, pawn captures), exploit undefended pieces/squares vacated by the retreat, or complete development/attack unopposed while the retreating side falls further behind
sub_patterns: Knight retreating to starting square (Ng1, Nb1)
Knight retreating to passive rim square (Nh2, Nh7)
Knight developing to suboptimal passive square (Ne2 instead of Nc3)
Quiet rook/pawn move when immediate tactical action exists (Rc1, b4)
Removing an active piece from a key defensive post (Ncxe7, Rf6)

analysis.label: Moving the king or queen to a square where the opponent gains a critical tempo through a check, fork, or forcing move targeting that piece.
analysis.description: In all 6 positions, the player moves their most important piece (king in 3/6, queen in 3/6) to a square that appears active or logical but is tactically flawed because the opponent can immediately gain tempo by attacking it. In Position 1 (Kc1), the king steps onto the c-file allowing Rxb3 followed by Rxd3+ and Rc2+. In Position 2 (Kb4), the king walks into a Nc6+ check that activates Black's dormant knight. In Position 5 (Ke5), the king steps into Nf3+ which activates White's passive knight from g1 with tempo. In Position 3 (Qa1+), the queen checks from a1 instead of e1, allowing Rd1 interposition that blocks the mating idea. In Position 4 (Qf8+), the queen checks from f8 which fails to control d7, giving the king an escape square. In Position 6 (Qb6), the queen moves away from the kingside, allowing Bxc6+ exploiting the uncastled king. The common thread across all 6/6 positions is that the piece's destination allows a tempo-gaining response (check or decisive threat) that fundamentally shifts the position's dynamics.
analysis.move_pattern: King or queen moves to an apparently active square (often lateral/diagonal) that is tactically vulnerable to opponent's forcing response (check, fork, or interposition)
analysis.why_bad: The destination square allows the opponent to gain a free tempo via check, fork, or interposition, either activating dormant pieces, executing a tactical combination, or neutralizing an attack that would otherwise be decisive.
sub_patterns: King stepping onto open file/diagonal where it faces checks or combinations
King walking into knight fork square
Queen checking from wrong square allowing interposition or escape
Queen moving away from critical defensive/attacking zone

analysis.label: Choosing the structurally passive or inferior piece/pawn for a task when a more active alternative maintains better piece coordination and square control.
analysis.description: In all 3/3 positions, Black faces a choice between multiple ways to accomplish the same goal (recapturing a piece or improving position) and selects the option that sacrifices piece activity for apparent simplicity. In Position 1, cxd6 captures with a pawn creating an isolated weakness when Qxd6 or Bxd6 would activate a piece. In Position 2, Ncxe7 removes a knight from its powerful defensive post on c6 when Ngxe7 would develop the idle g8-knight while preserving c6's guard duty. In Position 3, Kf6 passively advances the king when Nd3/Nc6/Nc2 would generate active knight infiltration with concrete counterplay. All 3/3 cases involve the opponent immediately exploiting the resulting positional holes (unguarded squares, tempo gains against exposed pieces/king) that the passive choice created.
analysis.move_pattern: Any piece type moving to accomplish a goal (capture or reposition) where a more active alternative piece could perform the same function; no consistent geometric direction
analysis.why_bad: The passive choice removes active piece influence from key squares or fails to generate counterplay, allowing the opponent to exploit resulting weaknesses (invasion squares, tempo attacks against exposed king, piece dominance) that the active alternative would have prevented.
sub_patterns: Wrong recapture removing key defender from post
Pawn capture when piece capture activates development
Passive king move when knight infiltration creates counterplay

analysis.label: Materialistic or passive moves that ignore critical king safety vulnerabilities, allowing tactical punishments via diagonals, discovered attacks, or pins.
analysis.description: This feature fires on positions where a player's king (or opponent's king) is critically exposed—stuck in the center, lacking pawn shield, or on a vulnerable diagonal—and the player makes a move prioritizing material gain or defense over addressing this vulnerability. In 6/9 positions, the move involves capturing or targeting a pawn (Kxh4, Nxf5, Rxd5, Ng4 attacking e5, Bxf3, Rxe5+). In 7/9 positions, at least one king is explicitly exposed in the center or on an open diagonal. The punishments typically exploit this king exposure through diagonal tactics (Bxg8 in Position 1, Bh3+ zwischenzug in Position 13, Bb5 pin in Position 15), discovered attacks (Kf3+ in Position 6), or piece forks exploiting the misplaced piece (f4 in Position 2). The two 0-cp-loss positions (Bxf3, Rxe5+) represent cases where the materialistic capture IS correct because the player's king is safe and they're converting a winning advantage—but the same positional signature (exposed kings, material captures) is present.
analysis.move_pattern: Captures of pawns (Kxh4, Nxf5, Rxd5, Bxf3, Rxe5+) or moves targeting/defending pawns (Ng4, b6, Qd7, Qe3) across various piece types; no single geometric direction but typically moving toward material while leaving the king's diagonal or file unguarded.
analysis.why_bad: The moves prioritize winning or defending a pawn over addressing an urgent king safety crisis, enabling the opponent to exploit the exposed king via discovered attacks, zwischenzugs, pins, or forks that recover far more material than the pawn was worth.
sub_patterns: Pawn capture that displaces king from active square (Kxh4, Nxf5)
Pawn capture that leaves a major piece hanging to a check/zwischenzug (Rxd5)
Move-order error allowing unfavorable queen exchange that exposes own king (Ng4)
Passive pawn defense that neglects development and enables pins (Qd7, b6)
Piece placement on tactically vulnerable square near exposed king (Qe3)

analysis.label: Playing passive or non-confrontational moves (especially aimless king moves) when the position urgently requires one specific concrete piece action to address a critical threat or opportunity.
analysis.description: This feature fires on positions where the player makes a quiet, repositioning move instead of the one urgent action the position demands. In 4/8 top activations, the blunder is specifically a king move (Kh8, Kf2, Kf2, Kf1) that accomplishes nothing toward addressing the critical tactical requirement - whether that's blocking a mating attack (Position 2), defending against an open-file pin (Position 3), eliminating a passed pawn (Position 5), or generating essential counterplay (Position 7). The remaining cases share the same prioritization failure: wrong recapture that squanders a dominant piece (Position 1), queen to a geometrically vulnerable square (Position 4), and grabbing an irrelevant pawn while ignoring a promotion threat (Position 8). In all cases, the best move involves active piece play addressing the single most pressing demand of the position (Nf7 blocking, Rf2 defending, Rxd3 eliminating, Re3 counterattacking, Rfc2 blockading), while the played move is either passive repositioning or misdirected activity.
analysis.move_pattern: King moves to adjacent squares (f1, f2, h8) or other quiet non-forcing moves, typically not addressing an existing piece on a critical square or file
analysis.why_bad: These moves waste a critical tempo when the position has exactly one urgent requirement (blocking a threat, eliminating a passed pawn, preserving a key piece, generating counterplay). The quiet move allows the opponent to execute their primary threat unimpeded, often resulting in the position collapsing entirely because the single defensive/active resource is no longer available next turn.
sub_patterns: King stepping forward into exposed position (Kf2/Kf1) when rook defense needed
King retreating to corner (Kh8) worsening tactical geometry
Material grab (Rxa2) ignoring passed pawn promotion
Wrong piece recapture trading away strongest piece (Nxg5)
Queen to geometrically trapped square (Qd5)

analysis.label: Moving a critically-placed defensive piece to an aggressive queenside square when a different piece (or capture) should have been used instead.
analysis.description: In 5/5 positions, the player makes an aggressive-looking move toward the queenside (b5, b3, a5, or d5 capture) that removes a piece from a critical defensive post, when a clearly superior alternative existed. In 2/5 cases, the player moved the WRONG knight to b5 (Ncb5 instead of Ndb5), evacuating the c3 knight which was guarding key diagonals and central pawns. In 1/5, cxd5 removed the pawn that was defending a bishop on e5. In 1/5, Qb3 placed the queen on a square vulnerable to a knight fork. In 1/5, Na5 declined an obvious capture (Nxd5) to place a knight on the rim. The common thread is choosing an outwardly threatening move that actually undermines the player's own defensive structure, with the correct alternative typically being either using a different piece for the same purpose or taking an available capture.
analysis.move_pattern: Piece (usually knight) moves to queenside square (a5/b3/b5), abandoning central defensive duties
analysis.why_bad: The moved piece was performing a critical defensive function (guarding key squares, blocking diagonals, or supporting other pieces), and its removal allows immediate tactical exploitation—forks, checks along opened diagonals, or pieces left hanging.
sub_patterns: Wrong knight to b5 (Ncb5 vs Ndb5)
Pawn capture removing defender of own piece
Queen placement creating fork vulnerability
Knight to rim declining obvious central capture

analysis.label: Forward-moving, plan-oriented moves that fail to address the position's critical tension point, allowing opponents to exploit the unresolved vulnerability with immediate tactical or structural gains.
analysis.description: This feature fires on moves that pursue the player's own agenda (pawn breaks, piece advances, development) while ignoring the position's most critical demand. In 5/6 positions, the player had at least 2 good alternatives that directly addressed the key tension (Ne2/Be3 addressing Bg5 vulnerability, c3 stabilizing d4, Bb4 maintaining pressure, Ba2 activating the bishop, Bc5 exploiting a pin). Instead, the played moves (a3, c4, c5, Bd3, Rc4, dxe6) were all committal, forward-moving actions that either overextended pawn structure (c4 removing d4 support, c5 losing a pawn to dxc5, dxe6 removing a restraining pawn), wasted tempo (a3 ignoring hanging Bg5), misplaced pieces (Bd3 failing to neutralize Bg4, Rc4 exposing rook to tempo attacks), or released tension that was holding the position together. In 5/6 cases, the opponent punished with immediate material-winning tactics: Nxd4/Qxg5 fork, dxc4+cxd4 double pawn win, dxc5 pawn grab, b5 tempo gain on the rook, and Nc4 knight fork.
analysis.move_pattern: Forward pawn pushes (4/6), piece advances to exposed/wrong squares (2/6) - all committal moves that alter or ignore the existing central/piece tension
analysis.why_bad: These moves release or ignore critical tension that was maintaining positional equilibrium, creating immediate tactical vulnerabilities (undefended pieces, exposed targets, opened key squares) that the opponent exploits with tempo-gaining combinations
sub_patterns: Premature pawn breaks that overextend and lose material (c4, c5, dxe6)
Quiet tempo-wasting moves that ignore tactical threats (a3)
Piece moves to exposed/incorrect squares that become tempo targets (Rc4, Bd3)

analysis.label: In rook endgames with advanced passed pawns, the player makes an indirect or preparatory move instead of urgently advancing their own passed pawn.
analysis.description: This feature fires on endgame positions—almost exclusively rook endgames (12/13)—where both sides have advanced passed pawns creating a promotion race, and the player fatally wastes a tempo by playing an indirect move rather than the critical direct pawn advance. The most common error is failing to push one's own passed pawn when it's one or two squares from queening (positions 6, 8, 10, 15 all required an immediate pawn push like a2, b7, or g2). Other manifestations include placing a rook ON the square the pawn needs (position 1: Ra2 blocking own a-pawn), placing a rook IN FRONT of own pawn (position 4: Rb7 blocking b-pawn advance), using the rook to attack the opponent's passer instead of advancing one's own (positions 8, 14: Rc1/Ra1 targeting enemy pawn), moving the king in the wrong direction or to the wrong square in the promotion race (positions 2, 3, 6: Ke4/Ke3/Kf2), or playing an irrelevant prophylactic move (position 10: h3 instead of winning b7/Rh8+/b8=Q+). In 11/13 positions, 'tempo_loss' was identified as a key tag, and 'passed_pawn' was the tactical motif in 11/13 cases.
analysis.move_pattern: Rook moves to inactive squares, king moves in wrong direction, or prophylactic pawn pushes—all in endgames where an immediate passed pawn advance was required
analysis.why_bad: In pawn race endgames, a single wasted tempo allows the opponent to either advance their own counter-passer to equality, eliminate the player's passed pawn, or establish a defensive fortress. The indirect move (attacking opponent's pawn, 'improving' king position, or blocking own pawn) gives the opponent exactly the time needed to neutralize the player's primary winning/drawing asset.
sub_patterns: Rook physically blocks own passed pawn's advance square
Rook attacks opponent's passed pawn instead of pushing own passer
King moves to wrong square/direction in pawn race
Prophylactic pawn move when forced winning combination exists
Using rook instead of king to address opponent's passer, abandoning support of own passer

analysis.label: Slow, non-forcing preparatory moves played in positions where urgent king safety issues or critical tactical tensions demand immediate concrete action.
analysis.description: This feature activates on quiet, non-forcing moves (no checks, captures, or direct threats) played at moments when the position demands immediate concrete action to address king safety or resolve critical tensions. In 7/8 positions, at least one king is exposed or uncastled, creating tactical urgency. The mistakes share a common pattern: g6, h6, and b3 are slow preparatory pawn moves ignoring central/tactical crises; Bf8 and Be2 are passive piece repositioning moves that neglect immediate threats; Ke1 and Nc6 are natural-looking moves that overlook tactical vulnerabilities. In each case, the best move involved either resolving a critical pawn tension (fxg4, cxd4), castling immediately (O-O-O), generating concrete counterplay (b4, Ng3), or addressing a tactical vulnerability (Bc6 protecting d7). The refutations consistently exploit the lost tempo to open files against exposed kings (fxe6/Qg6+, gxf5/Rg1, Ng4/Bb4+) or win material from unresolved tactical weaknesses.
analysis.move_pattern: Non-forcing quiet moves (pawn advances, passive retreats, slow development) - no checks, captures, or threats created
analysis.why_bad: These moves waste a critical tempo in positions with urgent tactical demands (unresolved king safety, critical pawn tension, or piece vulnerability), allowing the opponent to execute forcing plans that exploit the exposed king or hanging pieces before the preparatory plan can materialize.
sub_patterns: Slow prophylactic pawn moves (g6/h6/b3) when central tension or castling demands attention
Passive piece retreats/repositioning (Bf8/Ke1) abandoning critical defensive posts
Natural development moves (Nc6/Be2) ignoring immediate tactical vulnerabilities requiring specific defensive responses

analysis.label: Moves that look natural but go to the wrong square or choose the wrong piece, losing a critical tempo and allowing the opponent to consolidate.
analysis.description: This feature fires on moves that represent a 'close but wrong' choice — the player selects a plausible-looking square, piece, or direction when a more precise alternative was available. In 9/11 positions, 'tempo_loss' is the explicit tactical motif. The pattern manifests as: kings moving toward the rim instead of the center (Kh2 instead of Kf1, Kc7 instead of Kb5, Kc6 instead of Kc4) in 5/11 cases; knights retreating or repositioning to inferior squares (Ne1 instead of Ne5, Nf6 instead of Nxe3, Ne5 abandoning queen defense) in 3/11 cases; and choosing the wrong file, square, or piece for what seems like the right idea (Qa4+ instead of Qa2+, Rad8 instead of Rae8, Rxd1 instead of Nxd1) in 3/11 cases. The consistent thread is that the move played addresses a real concern (supporting promotion, centralizing, attacking a target, recapturing) but does so one square off, one piece wrong, or one tempo too slow, allowing the opponent to execute their critical plan unchallenged.
analysis.move_pattern: Any piece type moving to a plausible but suboptimal square, often one square away from the correct destination or choosing the wrong piece for a natural-looking action (recapture, centralization, check)
analysis.why_bad: These moves waste a critical tempo by choosing the wrong direction, wrong piece, or wrong square, allowing the opponent to consolidate their position, execute a key plan (double rooks on 7th, push passed pawn, escape to safety, block with optimal timing), or exploit the misdirected piece's absence from its ideal post.
sub_patterns: King moving toward the rim/edge instead of centralizing
Knight retreating passively when an active jump was available
Checking or placing a piece on the wrong square of two similar-looking options
Recapturing with the wrong piece leaving something undefended
Move-order errors where an intermediate forcing move was needed first

analysis.label: Moves that appear to improve piece activity or centralization but ignore an immediate tactical vulnerability they create or allow.
analysis.description: In 8/8 positions, the player chose a move that looks purposeful and active—centralizing a queen (Qd6, Qf3, Qg4, Qd3), developing a knight (Nf6, Nc7), activating a king (Kf5), or attacking a pawn (Rc4)—but each move either places the piece on a square where it becomes tactically exploitable or blocks critical coordination of friendly pieces. In 5/8 positions, the moved piece itself becomes a direct tactical target (Qg4 on a clearance diagonal, Qf3 attacked by Nxd4, Rc4 capturable after deflection, Qd6 attracted to g6, Nf6 entering a pin). In 2/8 positions, the move blocks the player's own piece from reaching a critical square (Nc7 blocking the rook from c7, Qd3 blocking the knight's retreat to d3). In 1/8, the king walks into a pawn check (Kf5 allowing g4+). The common thread is prioritizing superficial piece 'improvement' while missing the position's critical tactical requirement—whether that's capturing a hanging piece (Nf6 missed Qxg5), addressing king safety (Qd6/Kf5), or maintaining piece coordination (Nc7/Qd3).
analysis.move_pattern: Various pieces (queen, knight, rook, king) moving to central or seemingly active squares—typically to files d/f/c or ranks 3-6—that appear purposeful but create immediate tactical liabilities
analysis.why_bad: The move places the piece on a square where it becomes vulnerable to opponent tactics (forks, discovered attacks, deflections, clearance combinations, pins) or blocks essential coordination of friendly pieces, while ignoring the position's actual critical need
sub_patterns: Queen moved to a square on an opponent bishop's firing line (Qg4 on Be2 diagonal, Qd6 enabling Bh5 capture)
Piece occupies a square needed by a friendly piece (Nc7 blocking rook, Qd3 blocking knight retreat)
Active-looking piece placement creates a deflection/fork target (Rc4 deflected by Rd2+, Qf3 enabling Nxd4+ fork)
Natural development misses free material or creates a pin (Nf6 missing Qxg5, entering Bg5 pin)
King centralization walks into tactical checks or attacks (Kf5 allowing g4+ and Nc2)

analysis.label: Natural-looking moves that squander a decisive tempo in narrow positions where both kings are exposed and precise timing determines the evaluation.
analysis.description: This feature fires on positions characterized by exposed kings on both sides (11/12 positions explicitly note exposed kings) with extremely narrow correct paths (avg 2.0 good moves). The dominant shared error is tempo loss, tagged in 10/12 positions. The played moves appear logical—advancing passed pawns (h2, g6), capturing material (fxg2, bxa5), attacking pieces (Rb3), giving checks (Qg4+), repositioning (Rb1, Qg4)—but each wastes the single critical tempo that determines whether the position is winning, drawn, or lost. In pawn endgames (5/12), the tempo loss involves king overextension or premature pawn advances when opposition/restraint was needed. In middlegames, the tempo loss involves pursuing secondary targets while the opponent seizes the initiative on the primary front. The average cp_loss of 1782 reflects that these positions sit on knife-edges where one wasted move collapses the evaluation catastrophically.
analysis.move_pattern: Diverse piece types (kings, pawns, rooks, queens) moved forward, toward flanks, or capturing material—appearing aggressive/natural but failing to address the position's single most critical demand
analysis.why_bad: Each move pursues a secondary goal (material gain, piece attack, pawn advance, premature check) while ignoring the one critical positional requirement—whether maintaining opposition, preventing a pawn break, keeping a file closed, or restricting escape squares—in positions where a single wasted tempo flips the evaluation
sub_patterns: King overextension in pawn endgames losing opposition/tempo (Kf5, Kg7, Ka6)
Premature passed pawn advance when restraint preserves decoy value (h2, g6)
Materialistic captures that open critical lines for opponent (fxg2, bxa5)
Piece moves attacking secondary targets while primary threat goes unaddressed (Rb3, Rb1, Qg4)

analysis.label: In razor-thin positions where only one precise move survives, the player makes a natural-looking active move that fatally ignores an immediate tactical threat to their king or position.
analysis.description: This feature fires on positions where exactly ~1 good move exists (avg 1.1 good moves) and the player instead chooses a seemingly purposeful move—an offensive queen deployment, a piece 'attack,' or a passed pawn advance—while overlooking the position's single critical defensive requirement. In 7/8 positions, king safety is the primary concern being ignored. The best moves are typically quiet or defensive (h4 creating an escape square, Be1 covering f2, Rc8 defending the back rank, Kxc2 capturing an unguarded piece, Qe6 blocking a file, Qc6 maintaining perpetual check resources), while the blunders pursue active plans (Qc7 attacking g7, Nd2 attacking a rook, Qf6 centralizing, d2 advancing a passer, a3 pushing a pawn). The refutations are devastating (avg 3836 cp loss), often involving forced checkmate sequences that exploit the exact vulnerability the one correct move would have addressed.
analysis.move_pattern: Varied pieces (queen 4/8, knight 2/8, pawn 2/8) moving to active-looking squares or making captures, bypassing the position's singular defensive necessity
analysis.why_bad: Each move abandons the one critical task the position demands—whether that's creating a king escape square, blocking an open file, maintaining perpetual check resources, or capturing an undefended piece—allowing the opponent an immediate devastating tactical response (usually a mating attack or decisive material gain exploiting king vulnerability)
sub_patterns: Queen moved offensively while own king faces mating net (Qc7, Qf6, Qc5, Qe2)
Pawn advanced toward promotion while neglecting back-rank/piece safety (d2, a3)
Piece moved 'attacking' something while enabling opponent's superior tactical sequence (Nd2, Nxe4)

analysis.label: Moving a piece away from its key defensive duty to a passive or rim square, leaving a critical pawn or piece undefended.
analysis.description: In 5/6 positions, the played move removes a piece from a square where it was performing an essential defensive function—guarding a pawn or piece—and relocates it to a passive, rim, or back-rank square. In Position 4 (Ne1), the knight leaves f3 for passive e1, surrendering second-rank control. In Position 6 (c3), the c2 pawn advances, removing its diagonal defense of d3. In Position 9 (Rh2), the rook abandons d2 where it guarded d3, relocating to the passive h-file. In Position 10 (Rcd1), the c-file rook abandons defense of the c3 knight, allowing it to be captured via Qc5+. In Position 13 (Nh8), the knight retreats from g6 to the dead corner, unable to contest any kingside advance. The common geometric thread is pieces moving backward or toward the rim (e1, h8, h2, leaving the c-file) while opponents immediately exploit the now-undefended target.
analysis.move_pattern: Piece (knight, rook, or pawn) moves backward toward back rank, corner, or rim, away from a central or active defensive square
analysis.why_bad: The moved piece was the sole or critical defender of a key pawn (d3 in 3/6 cases) or piece (Nc3 in 1/6), and relocating it to a passive square allows the opponent to immediately exploit the undefended target via tactical or positional means (rook invasion, pawn break, queen fork).
sub_patterns: Knight retreating to back rank or corner (Ne1, Nh8) abandoning active central post
Rook leaving open/central file for rim file (Rh2, Rcd1) removing piece/pawn defense
Pawn advance removing support from neighboring pawn (c3 undefending d3)

analysis.label: Moves that appear active or rewarding (queen infiltrations, captures, checks) but allow the opponent to gain decisive tempo through forced improving responses.
analysis.description: This feature fires on moves that prioritize immediate gratification—material gain, aggressive-looking placement, or checking—but fatally surrender tempo or defensive coordination. In 5/8 positions the move is a queen relocation to a seemingly active but actually exposed square (Qxc2, Qc7, Qg2+, Qf5, Qg5), where the opponent responds with a tempo-gaining attack on the queen or exploits the queen's abandonment of critical defensive duties. The remaining moves (f6, Rg2, c5) share the same core error: making a move that looks purposeful but hands the opponent a forced improving response. The tagged motif 'tempo_loss' appears explicitly in 5/8 positions and implicitly in all. Characteristically, positions have very few good alternatives (avg 1.8), meaning precision was required but the player chose the 'flashy' option. The refutations consistently involve the opponent making improving moves with tempo—interpositions that activate pieces (Rf2 in Position 7), back-rank checks exploiting abandoned defense (Rd8+ in Position 6), or attacks forcing the moved piece to retreat passively (Re8-e7 in Position 2).
analysis.move_pattern: Primarily queen moves to aggressive/exposed squares (captures, checks, infiltrations); also includes pawn/rook moves that appear purposeful but concede tempo
analysis.why_bad: The move allows the opponent to respond with a tempo-gaining threat (attack on the piece, interposition improving coordination, or exploitation of abandoned defensive duty), effectively giving the opponent a free improving move while the player's piece ends up misplaced or exchanged unfavorably
sub_patterns: Queen captures loose pawn but lands on exposed/trappable square
Queen check that allows improving interposition
Queen centralizes but abandons back-rank or key defensive coverage
Passive move that surrenders initiative when concrete action was required
Pawn/piece move enabling forced favorable exchange for opponent

analysis.label: Moves that look purposeful but ignore the single critical tactical demand in razor-sharp positions with very few correct options.
analysis.description: This feature fires on positions where very few moves are correct (avg 1.5 good moves available) and the player chooses a superficially reasonable move that fails to address the position's urgent tactical requirement. In 10/13 positions, the best move involved a specific forcing sequence (check, capture, sacrifice, or addressing a critical pawn tension) while the played move was either a quiet repositioning (Kg1, Rb6, Bg6, Nc6, Nd6, Qd7), a misdirected forcing move (Qf4+, Qa1+ - checks on the wrong square), or a weakening/irrelevant pawn advance (g3, b4, f4). The common thread is that each position had ONE specific demand - a diagonal to defend (5/13 positions involved newly-opened diagonal exploitation), a piece that needed to stay on its post for tactical justification (Rb6 abandoning b1 counterplay, Nc6 abandoning b4 pressure, Qd7 abandoning f5 defense), or a concrete winning combination to execute (Qe1+ deflection, Qc3+ forcing Qxf1, Bxf2 sacrifice) - and the player instead pursued a secondary goal.
analysis.move_pattern: Any piece type moving to a seemingly logical square (centralization, check, pawn advance) in positions requiring one specific forcing response; no consistent geometric direction
analysis.why_bad: These moves waste the critical tempo needed to address the position's one urgent demand - whether that's defending a newly-exposed diagonal, maintaining a piece on its tactically-justified post, or executing a concrete forced sequence. With only ~1.5 good moves available, any deviation from the narrow correct path results in catastrophic evaluation loss (avg 1761cp).
sub_patterns: Pointless/wrong-square checks that drive the opponent's king to safety or allow interposition (Qf4+, Qa1+)
Retreating pieces from active posts that provided critical counterplay or defensive coverage (Rb6, Nc6, Qd7)
Pawn advances that weaken king shelter or open dangerous diagonals (g3, b4, f4)
Piece repositioning to 'impressive' squares that threaten nothing concrete (Nd6, Bg6, Qh4, Qb4)

analysis.label: Playing a natural-looking quiet or routine move in a position where only one specific concrete tactical action maintains the evaluation.
analysis.description: This feature fires on positions where the player chooses a 'general principle' move—developing, castling, centralizing, repositioning—while ignoring a narrow tactical obligation. In 9/9 positions, the played move follows a standard positional heuristic (e3 supports center, O-O castles for safety, Bg5 develops with pin, Bg4 repositions bishop, Qc4 centralizes, d4 pushes center) rather than addressing the ONE concrete tactical requirement. The average number of good moves is only 1.2, confirming these are razor-sharp positions with essentially a single correct path. Examples include: O-O when Nxe5 wins a pawn with a crushing attack (7/9 positions feature a hanging piece or immediate tactic), Bg5 when Nxe5-Nxf7 wins material by force, Qxe2 when Kxe2 was the only way to avoid a knight-check combination, and e3 when h5/Nxd5 exploited a tactical target. The catastrophic average cp_loss of 2366 reflects that these 'natural' moves uniformly squander critical one-move tactical windows.
analysis.move_pattern: Quiet non-forcing moves (development, castling, pawn pushes, piece repositioning) when the position demands an immediate capture, check, or forcing sequence
analysis.why_bad: These moves waste the one critical tempo needed to exploit a concrete tactical vulnerability (hanging piece, mating attack, forced combination), allowing the opponent to stabilize, escape, or counterattack on the very next move
sub_patterns: Developing/castling instead of capturing hanging material
Repositioning pieces instead of executing a combination
Moving defensive pieces away from critical duties
Quiet king moves walking into checking diagonals/files

analysis.label: Moves that voluntarily relocate a piece away from a square where it was performing a critical (often latent) restraining or defensive function, immediately enabling a tactical blow.
analysis.description: In 7/7 positions, the played move removes a piece from a square where it was preventing a specific opponent resource. In Position 1, g5 vacates g4's control of f5, allowing Nf5 with tempo. In Position 2, Nf6 removes the d7-knight's coverage of c5, enabling Nc4 to deflect the queen. In Position 3, Bg6 removes pressure from f3, unleashing Ne5 to a dominant outpost. In Position 6, Nc6 invites d5 with tempo gain on the misplaced knight. In Position 8, Bd7 removes the bishop from the b5-c6 interposition diagonal, enabling Rxb6+ sacrifice into forced mate. In Position 9, Kxf4 walks the king into a mating net by abandoning its safe square. In Position 12, Rdd1 retreats the active rook, enabling Bf4+/Qa1# back-rank mate. All moves appear natural (developing, centralizing, or material-winning) but miss that the piece was performing an invisible defensive duty. The average cp_loss of 4278 reflects that the consequences are often catastrophic (3/7 lead to forced mate).
analysis.move_pattern: Any piece type voluntarily moving away from a square that was restraining an opponent's tactic; diverse directions but always abandoning rather than maintaining tension
analysis.why_bad: The moved piece was the sole restraint preventing a specific opponent resource (outpost occupation, pawn break with tempo, sacrifice, or mating pattern). Once the restraint is removed, the opponent immediately exploits the released constraint with a forcing sequence.
sub_patterns: Bishop/knight retreating from pressure on key square, enabling opponent outpost (Bg6, Nf6)
Piece moving off a defensive interposition line, enabling sacrificial breakthrough (Bd7, Rdd1)
Pawn advance releasing square control, gifting opponent tempo (g5, Nc6 inviting d5)
King capturing into exposed position, abandoning safe square (Kxf4)

analysis.label: Moving a piece away from an irreplaceable defensive or restrictive function to a superficially active but concretely ineffective square.
analysis.description: This feature activates when a player relocates a piece that is performing a sole, irreplaceable defensive or restrictive function to a square that appears active or aggressive but generates no concrete threats. In 7/9 positions (endgames), the moved piece was the only one preventing a critical breakthrough: in positions 1&2, the knight on f2 was restricting White's king and supporting g5+, but Ng4 looked aggressive yet was toothless; in position 4, the king on d7 was the sole guard against Ke7 invasion; in position 7, the knight left f5 to attack a bishop instead of playing prophylactic a3; in position 8, the knight abandoned f3 (guarding h2) for passive e1; in position 9, the bishop left the critical a1-h8 diagonal allowing unstoppable promotion. In each case, the opponent immediately exploited the now-unguarded function—king invasion, pawn promotion, or material win—causing an average 265cp loss.
analysis.move_pattern: Piece (most often knight: 5/9) moves away from a functionally critical square, typically one step sideways or backward, to a square that appears aggressive or purposeful but lacks concrete follow-through
analysis.why_bad: The piece was the sole guardian of a critical function (restricting enemy king, guarding a promotion square, defending a weak point), and no other piece can substitute; moving it allows an immediate breakthrough that the opponent exploits with one precise response
sub_patterns: Knight abandoning dominant outpost for aggressive-looking but toothless square (f2→g4, f5→g3)
Knight retreating from defensive post removing key guard function (f3→e1)
King moving away from invasion-blocking square prematurely (d7→c6)
Bishop leaving critical diagonal allowing pawn promotion (c3→d2)
Check to wrong square allowing king escape to safe haven (Qe6+ allowing Ka5)

analysis.label: Non-urgent improving moves in closed-center positions that waste the critical tempo needed to address an imminent pawn break or attack.
analysis.description: This feature fires on quiet, 'natural-looking' moves (piece development, repositioning, castling, or wrong-flank pawn pushes) that ignore the position's most urgent concrete demand. In 6/6 positions the center is closed, creating a deceptive sense of slowness, but a critical pawn break or attack is one tempo away from execution. The blundering moves are all non-forcing (no checks, captures, or direct threats) and appear to improve piece placement or king safety in isolation, but they hand the opponent the tempo needed to execute a devastating plan: White's c5 break after O-O (Position 13), White's e5 break after Be7 (Position 6), White's f5 break after Ng6 (Position 10), Black's queenside storm after Rde1 (Position 2), the lethal hxg6/g7 advance after Nd4 (Position 14), and Black's bxa3 counter after a4 (Position 7). King safety is compromised in 6/6 cases, with uncastled kings (4/6) or opposite-side castling (2/6) amplifying the punishment.
analysis.move_pattern: Non-forcing piece development, knight repositioning, castling, or flank pawn push - all lacking checks, captures, or direct threats
analysis.why_bad: The move wastes the last available tempo to prevent or preempt the opponent's critical pawn break/advance, which then crashes through against a vulnerable king position that the closed center had been masking
sub_patterns: Quiet piece development when central tension must be resolved immediately (Be7, O-O)
Knight repositioning to a tactically vulnerable square that invites a tempo-gaining pawn advance (Ng6, Nd4)
Wrong-side operation abandoning the critical sector (a4, Rde1)

analysis.label: Choosing the seemingly natural/direct move that blocks one's own critical file, rank, or tactical resource, when a counterintuitive or indirect move was needed.
analysis.description: This feature fires on moves that look like logical 'direct progress' toward a goal but actually create self-obstruction or allow devastating tactics. In 3/6 positions (positions 3, 4, and 2), the player moves a king or rook directly toward a logical destination but allows an intermediate check that drives the piece to a worse square or wins material (Kc1 allows Rdc2+ in two cases; Rd2 allows Re2+ winning the rook). In position 6, Kf7 blocks the f-file preventing the crushing Rf8-into-Nxe6+ fork. In position 10, h2 pushes a pawn one square from queening but permanently entombs it since the opponent's king blockades h1 forever. In position 14, Qc3 occupies an 'active' square but wastes the critical tempo needed for the e4 central breakthrough. All 6/6 positions share the theme of a visually progressive move that undermines the player's own winning resource, when a subtler alternative (often a retreat or preparatory move) would have maintained the advantage.
analysis.move_pattern: Any piece type moving to a seemingly active/progressive square that blocks own critical file, rank, diagonal, or promotion path
analysis.why_bad: The 'direct' move occupies a square that obstructs the player's own tactical resource (blocks a file for a rook, allows an intermediate check by being on the wrong square, or self-blocks a promotion path), when an indirect or retreating move would have preserved the critical tactical threat.
sub_patterns: King moving directly toward destination allowing intermediate check (Kc1 enabling Rdc2+)
Piece blocking own critical file (Kf7 blocking Rf8, Rd2 creating Re2+ vulnerability)
Premature pawn push that permanently self-blocks promotion (h2 with king on h1)
Active-looking piece move that wastes tempo for critical breakthrough (Qc3 instead of e4)

analysis.label: Playing a tempting but irrelevant move that neglects the position's single most critical tactical obligation, leaving something vital undefended or miscoordinated.
analysis.description: This feature fires on moves where the player pursues a secondary objective (peripheral material grab, piece repositioning, development, pawn advance) while ignoring the position's most urgent tactical requirement. In 11/13 cases, the move either removes a piece from a critical defensive post (Ng3 abandons f2 defense, Na7 abandons c6 coverage, Kb7 exposes king to checks) or places a piece on a tactically vulnerable/irrelevant square (Bb5 hangs to Qa5+, Bb4 hangs to Qa4+, Qc3 illusorily defends c6 through an obstructing pawn). In 4/13 cases, the player captures the wrong target or with the wrong piece (Nxa6 grabs a pawn instead of delivering Ne6+ fork, Nxd6 wrong move-order, Rxf4 instead of exf4, d4 ignores hanging h5-pawn). The consistent thread is that one clear urgent task exists (recapture, defend a hanging piece, execute a forcing sequence) and the player chooses something else entirely, resulting in catastrophic punishment averaging 1696cp loss.
analysis.move_pattern: Any piece type moving to a peripheral, undefended, or tactically irrelevant square instead of addressing the position's critical obligation - often pieces leaving defensive posts, capturing wrong targets, or developing to hanging squares
analysis.why_bad: The position has one urgent tactical demand (defend a hanging piece, execute a forced sequence in correct order, maintain a critical defender) that the player ignores in favor of a tempting but non-essential action, allowing the opponent to exploit the neglected vulnerability with checks, forks, or simple captures
sub_patterns: Removing a defensive piece from its post while the defended target is under active pressure
Capturing a peripheral/irrelevant target while missing a forcing tactical sequence at the critical point
Placing a piece on an undefended square vulnerable to a discovered attack or fork
Wrong move-order that squanders a forced combination by doing steps out of sequence
Advancing a pawn while ignoring that a different pawn or piece is hanging elsewhere

analysis.label: Capturing or advancing against central d-pawns while underdeveloped, leaving pieces or pawns undefended.
analysis.description: In all 3/3 positions, the player makes a greedy move targeting a central d-file pawn (Nxd4, Nxd5, or c4 attacking d5) while their king remains uncastled and development is incomplete. In 2/3 cases, the move is a knight capture on d4/d5 that leaves the knight itself or other pieces/pawns immediately hanging (tagged 'hanging_piece'). In the remaining case, the pawn advance undermines the player's own center, opening lines against their uncastled king. All 3/3 positions feature the moving side's king still on its starting square (e1 or e8), and the refutations in every case exploit the resulting undefended material—the d4 knight captured freely (Position 7), the e5 pawn left hanging (Position 9), or the d4 pawn collapsing with tempo against exposed pieces (Position 3). The common error is prioritizing central pawn captures/attacks over completing development.
analysis.move_pattern: Piece or pawn capture/advance targeting d4 or d5 central pawn, typically knight captures on d-file
analysis.why_bad: Resolving central tension prematurely while underdeveloped leaves the capturing piece or other pawns/pieces undefended, and the uncastled king means the resulting open lines become immediately exploitable.
sub_patterns: Knight capture on d4/d5 leaving knight en prise or other pawns hanging
Pawn advance undermining own d-pawn support while king is in center

analysis.label: Pieces or pawns moved from critical defensive posts to seemingly active squares, allowing immediate tactical exploitation of the abandoned function.
analysis.description: This feature fires on moves that appear to improve piece placement (centralizing, repositioning, recapturing, or checking) but fatally neglect a specific defensive responsibility the moved piece/pawn was fulfilling. In 5/6 detailed positions, the moved piece was covering a critical invasion square or blocking a dangerous line: Bd8 abandoned coverage of d6 allowing Nd6+ (Position 5), cxd5 removed the c6 pawn from the a4-e8 diagonal exposing the uncastled king (Position 10), Qc6 abandoned h8/g7 defense allowing a mating Rh8+ sequence (Position 12), c5 surrendered c6's pressure on d5 giving White an unchallenged space advantage (Position 3), and Bd4 blocked the knight's ideal d4 outpost creating self-interference (Position 2). The remaining cases follow the same logic: Be2 placed a piece on an exposed square attackable with tempo (Position 1), Nd5 centralized before preventing Nf5+ (Position 6), and Rh6+ broke a mating net for an aimless check (Position 8). All moves are surface-level 'improving' moves that ignore an underappreciated defensive requirement.
analysis.move_pattern: Piece or pawn moves away from a square where it was guarding a critical entry point, blocking a dangerous line, or maintaining structural pressure—typically to a central or active-looking destination
analysis.why_bad: The moved piece/pawn was the sole guardian of a critical square, diagonal, or file; removing it immediately allows the opponent to invade, deliver checks, or execute tactical combinations that were previously impossible, resulting in catastrophic material or positional loss.
sub_patterns: Pawn moves that open diagonals to own uncastled king (cxd5, c5)
Bishop retreats/repositioning that abandon coverage of invasion squares (Bd8, Bd4)
Queen moves away from kingside allowing mating attacks (Qc6)
Piece centralization before addressing immediate tactical threats (Nd5, Be2)
Breaking coordinated attacking formations for superficial checks (Rh6+)

analysis.label: King moves in endgames that lose a critical tempo when an immediate pawn advance was required to win or draw a pawn race.
analysis.description: This feature activates on king moves (9/10 positions) in endgame positions (9/10) where the correct action was to immediately push a passed pawn or execute a pawn break. In Position 1, Ke7 lost the pawn race that g4 would have won. In Position 2, Ke3 retreated when Ke5 would have captured g5. In Position 4, Kd3 wasted time when Rf5 was needed to advance the f-pawn. In Position 8, Ke6 delayed queenside pawn pushes (a5/b5/c5). In Position 12, Kf3 delayed the critical f4 breakthrough. In Position 15, Kf2 retreated instead of advancing with Ke4 or pushing d5. The common error across all positions is choosing a seemingly useful king repositioning move over the time-critical pawn advance, costing exactly the one tempo that determines the outcome of a promotion race. Even the one non-king move (Qg3, Position 9) shares the theme of a piece repositioning that wastes tempo when immediate action was needed.
analysis.move_pattern: King moves (sideways or backward) in open-center endgames, typically one square laterally or in retreat, when a forward pawn push was the critical alternative
analysis.why_bad: In pawn endgames and pawn races, every single tempo determines whether a pawn promotes first or a king catches a runner. These king moves waste the critical tempo needed to win the promotion race, allowing the opponent to equalize the timing or flip the race outcome entirely.
sub_patterns: King retreat instead of forward king march toward enemy pawns
King move instead of immediate passed pawn advance in pure pawn race
King move instead of critical pawn break (f4, g4) that creates a passed pawn
King move to a square vulnerable to tempo-gaining checks
Piece repositioning instead of addressing the most urgent tactical need

analysis.label: Moves that worsen own piece harmony by blocking retreats, abandoning critical duties, or displacing pieces from where they're needed, leaving material tactically vulnerable.
analysis.description: This feature fires on moves that actively damage the player's own piece coordination, creating tactical vulnerabilities. The pattern manifests in three sub-types: (1) Self-blocking, where a piece or pawn occupies a square needed by another piece for retreat or function (g6 traps bishop in position 1, Be2 blocks queen's retreat in position 2, Re3 blocks knight's retreat in position 10 — 3/10 clear self-blocks); (2) Critical role abandonment, where a piece leaves a square or task it was uniquely performing (Re1 abandons c3 pawn defense in position 8, Ne6 abandons d4 outpost in position 5, Qxa7 displaces queen from defensive zone in position 9 — 3/10); (3) Piece placement on tactically vulnerable squares (Bd7 on fork-vulnerable square in position 6, Ng4+ on hanging square in position 7, Ka6 self-cornering in position 3 — 3/10). All 10 positions share the characteristic that the player makes a seemingly natural or improving move while ignoring how it catastrophically worsens their own piece interactions, with opponents punishing via forks (3/10), trapped pieces (2/10), hanging material (2/10), or initiative seizure against the exposed king (3/10).
analysis.move_pattern: Any piece type moving to a square that obstructs, abandons, or undermines the function of another friendly piece; typically quiet non-forcing moves (no captures/checks in 8/10 cases)
analysis.why_bad: The move prioritizes a secondary goal (development, centralization, pawn capture) while ignoring how it disrupts the player's own piece coordination — blocking retreat squares, removing defensive guardians, or creating fork/entrapment vulnerabilities that the opponent immediately exploits
sub_patterns: Self-blocking: piece/pawn occupies square needed by another piece for retreat
Role abandonment: piece leaves critical defensive or controlling duty
Self-placement on tactical weakness: piece moves to square vulnerable to fork or capture
Queen displacement: queen chases material while abandoning defensive responsibilities

analysis.chip: Piece Move Instead Of Pawn Break
analysis.label: Playing a passive or non-forcing piece move in a critical position where only an immediate pawn break or tactical strike maintains the advantage.
analysis.description: This feature fires on positions where exactly one good move exists (avg good moves: 1.0) and the player makes a plausible-looking piece relocation instead of the required concrete action. In 4/7 cases, the best move was a central pawn break (e3, f5, d5, f5) that the player ignored in favor of piece moves. In the remaining 3/7 cases, the best move was a precise tactical piece capture (Rg5, Bxg5, Nxd6) while the player chose a less forcing alternative. The common thread is tempo loss at a critical inflection point: the played moves look reasonable (developing bishops to active diagonals, centralizing knights, doubling rooks, grabbing pawns) but allow the opponent to consolidate or escape. Every position featured a narrow tactical window that demanded immediate forcing action, and the piece moves uniformly squander that window by being one tempo too slow.
analysis.move_pattern: Non-pawn piece moves (R, N, B) relocating to natural-looking squares or making non-critical captures, when the position demands an immediate pawn advance (f5, d5, e3) or specific tactical capture
analysis.why_bad: These moves waste the single critical tempo available in razor-sharp positions where only one continuation works. They allow the opponent to consolidate king safety (play ...g6 blocking f5, escape with ...Kf8-g7), neutralize threats prophylactically, or simplify favorably. The positions are at inflection points where dynamic energy must be converted immediately or it dissipates permanently.
sub_patterns: Bishop repositioning instead of pawn break (Bh3, Bc4 instead of f5/d5)
Passive rook move instead of pawn thrust (Re2 instead of f5)
Peripheral pawn capture losing piece activity (Rxh3)
Premature check giving king escape squares (Rh3+)
Knight retreat from active outpost (Nc3 instead of Nxd6)
Wrong piece recapture trading key positional asset (Nxg5 instead of Bxg5)

analysis.label: Quiet piece relocations that abandon an essential defensive, blocking, or guarding role in favor of seemingly reasonable but non-urgent repositioning.
analysis.description: This feature fires on moves where a piece is relocated from a square where it performs a critical function (guarding, blocking a line, or demanding urgent action) to a seemingly reasonable but ultimately catastrophic new square. In 6/8 positions, the moved piece was serving as a vital defender or blocker: Nh7 removed the knight from f6, unblocking the h4-e7 diagonal and leaving the queen hanging; Qd4 pulled the queen away from defending the e7 bishop; Kg7 placed the king on the same rank as the rook, enabling Qxe7+ with check; Kg8 moved the king to a square where it gets trapped on the h-file after Qe8+; Qg1 entombed the queen passively, surrendering control of the second rank; Ba4 chased the opponent's queen to a superior square while abandoning the decisive Bxa6 sacrifice. In the remaining 2/8 cases (b4, Qe5), the error is choosing a non-urgent relocation over an immediately decisive action (f5 lockdown, e7 pawn advance). All moves share the quality of being quiet, non-forcing relocations that superficially look like consolidation or improvement.
analysis.move_pattern: Any piece type, non-capturing and non-checking quiet moves, typically moving away from the center of tactical action or off a critical line/diagonal/rank
analysis.why_bad: The piece was performing an invisible but essential function on its original square (blocking a line, guarding a piece, or the position demanded an urgent concrete action), and the relocation abandons that function, creating immediate tactical vulnerabilities or surrendering decisive advantages.
sub_patterns: Removing a piece that blocks a critical diagonal/rank, exposing hanging pieces
King moves to geometrically worse squares enabling forcing checks or trapping
Queen retreats/relocations that surrender activity and invite opponent invasion
Non-urgent pawn/piece moves when position demands immediate concrete action

analysis.label: Queenside castling (O-O-O) when the opponent has a ready-made or imminent pawn storm and/or piece attack targeting that wing.
analysis.description: In 7/8 positions, the blunder is specifically O-O-O (the 8th involves a wasted tempo with the king already exposed on the queenside). The defining pattern is that in every case, the opponent has pawns (a4, b5, c4, or similar levers) and/or open/semi-open files (a-file, c-file) already positioned to immediately attack the queenside king. In 6/8 positions, the opponent has already castled kingside, creating opposite-side castling where the pawn storm is one-directional. In 7/8 positions, the center is closed or semi-closed, which likely deceived the player into thinking queenside castling was safe—but the closed center protects the OTHER king (on the kingside) while the queenside remains vulnerable to direct pawn breaks. The refutations consistently involve pawn advances (a4-a5, b5, c4+b5) that rip open files pointing directly at the freshly castled king within 1-3 moves, often combined with piece jumps (Nb5, Nc2) that create tactical threats. Better alternatives in all positions involved kingside castling, keeping the king in the center, or pure development.
analysis.move_pattern: King castles queenside (O-O-O), moving from e1/e8 to c1/c8, into the direction of opponent's prepared pawn advance
analysis.why_bad: The king is placed directly in the path of the opponent's already-prepared or easily-launched queenside pawn storm (a4/b5/c4 breaks), which rips open files and diagonals against the king within 1-3 moves, while the closed center that made castling seem safe actually protects the opponent's king on the other wing.
sub_patterns: O-O-O into opponent's a4-a5 pawn lever breaking the b-pawn shield
O-O-O into opponent's b5/c4 pawn avalanche targeting the c-file
O-O-O into semi-open c-file with opponent's pieces ready to exploit
O-O-O when kingside castling offered natural safety behind fianchetto or solid pawn shield

analysis.label: Moves that pursue a reasonable-looking plan but go in the wrong direction or to the wrong square in positions with essentially only one correct continuation.
analysis.description: This feature activates on moves that appear purposeful—a check, a development, a pawn advance, a king march—but critically waste tempo in razor-sharp positions demanding immediate concrete action. In 6/7 positions, there were only 1-2 good moves available, yet the played move addresses a secondary concern or executes the right general idea on the wrong square/direction. Qg4+ checks toward the wrong side when Qe2+ forces perpetual (4/7). e6 advances the wrong pawn when f6 creates real threats (4/7). Kf3 marches the king toward h2 when the critical battle is on the queenside (7/7 have the king/piece going away from the critical zone). Be3 and Bh3 develop bishops to immediately vulnerable squares (5/7 place pieces on tactically exploitable squares). h6 and Qd2 are passive/misplaced when urgent concrete action is required (7/7 positions punish the tempo loss with an opponent advance—passed pawn promotion, king escape, pawn fork). The common thread is that the opponent exploits the single wasted tempo to achieve a decisive positional or material gain.
analysis.move_pattern: Mixed piece types moving to seemingly active/purposeful squares that are actually the wrong target square or wrong direction relative to the critical action in the position
analysis.why_bad: In positions with only 1-2 correct moves, these moves waste the critical tempo needed to address the primary threat or exploit the single saving resource, allowing the opponent to execute their plan (advance passed pawns, escape to safety, fork pieces, invade on key files) one move faster than the player can recover.
sub_patterns: Check to the wrong square allowing king escape to safety (Qg4+ vs Qe2+)
Bishop development to a tactically vulnerable square that becomes a target (Be3 forked, Bh3 captured)
King marching to wrong flank in pawn race endgames (Kf3 away from queenside passers)
Wrong pawn advance that dissolves attacking potential (e6 instead of f6)
Passive/waiting moves when immediate concrete defense is demanded (h6, Qd2)

analysis.label: Playing a plausible, principled-looking move that pursues a secondary objective while ignoring the single critical tactical or strategic priority the position demands.
analysis.description: In all 8 positions, the player makes a move that follows reasonable general chess principles (rook to open file, piece centralization, pawn advance, material capture) but completely misses that the position has exactly ONE critical priority that must be addressed immediately. In Position 1 (b4), the player pushes a queenside pawn instead of addressing the deadly f-file threat via Na6/Rc8 (7/8 positions show only 1-2 good moves available). In Position 3 (Re8), the player 'develops' a rook to the e-file instead of securing the a-pawn with a5. In Position 4 (f4), a pawn attacks a bishop instead of the urgent central strike d4. In Position 6 (Ne6), a knight 'centralizes' to an attractive square instead of addressing White's active pieces with b5/Ne7. In Position 7 (Qb3), the queen repositions instead of the critical O-O. In Position 9 (c5), a pawn creates 'connected passers' instead of the essential king activation Kf4. In Position 12 (Rac8), a rook doubles on a file without first removing the queen from tactical danger. In Position 15 (Nxb3), material is captured instead of prioritizing urgent development with Nf6. The average of only 1.6 good moves confirms these are narrow, demanding positions where one specific idea dominates.
analysis.move_pattern: Mixed piece types and directions; the unifying geometric thread is that the move operates on a different sector or addresses a different concern than where the critical action is — often a wing move when the center/king demands attention, or a positional/material move when a specific tactical threat requires resolution.
analysis.why_bad: These moves waste the one critical tempo needed to address the position's most urgent demand (king safety, threat neutralization, piece vulnerability), allowing the opponent to immediately exploit the unaddressed weakness. The positions are extremely narrow (avg 1.6 good moves), so any deviation from the single correct priority is catastrophically punished.
sub_patterns: Queenside/wing pawn advance ignoring kingside tactical threat (b4, c5)
Rook to open file without first securing vulnerable piece/pawn (Re8, Rac8)
Piece repositioning instead of addressing king safety (Qb3, f4)
Attractive piece centralization walking into tactical combination (Ne6)
Material capture instead of urgent development (Nxb3)

analysis.label: White fails to execute a Bxe6 tactical combination when the bishop on c4 and a supporting knight create a forcing sequence involving fxe6 Nxe6 with forks.
analysis.description: In at least 7/10 positions, the best move is specifically Bxe6, exploiting a bishop on c4 aligned against Black's e6 pawn combined with a knight on d4 or g5 ready to recapture on e6 with devastating tactical consequences (typically fxe6 Nxe6 creates a fork on the queen, or enables a subsequent Nxg7+/Nxc7 fork). The remaining positions still feature the Bc4 as a critical piece. Instead of this forcing tactical strike, the player makes quiet moves—retreating pieces (Nb3, Bb3, Nf3), pushing pawns (b3, b4, e5), premature queen sorties (Qh5), or castling (O-O)—all of which squander the narrow tactical window. The positions share a common structure: Sicilian/Italian-type formations where Black has an e6/d6 pawn chain, the king often uncastled, and the Bc4+Knight battery is the key attacking resource.
analysis.move_pattern: Any quiet or non-forcing White move (pawn push, piece retreat, castling, queen sortie) when the Bc4 is aimed at e6 with a knight ready to exploit fxe6
analysis.why_bad: The player misses that Bxe6 is tactically sound because fxe6 allows Nxe6 with a knight fork (on queen/king/rook), meaning the e6 pawn capture is essentially free or wins material by force. Playing any quiet move instead gives Black time to consolidate, castle, or neutralize the tactical configuration.
sub_patterns: Knight retreat from d4 (Nb3/Nf3) abandoning the Nxe6 support
Slow pawn moves (b3/b4/e5) ignoring the tactical urgency
Premature queen moves (Qh5) allowing development with tempo
Castling (O-O) when a forcing strike is available

analysis.label: Playing a slow, non-urgent move in a position that demands one specific immediate action, allowing the opponent to execute a decisive threat.
analysis.description: This feature fires on moves that waste a critical tempo by addressing a secondary concern (or pursuing a misguided plan) when the position has exactly one urgent demand. In 9/10 positions, the analyses explicitly tag 'tempo_loss' as a key motif. The positions share a narrow margin: on average only 1.8 good moves exist, meaning precision is essential. The pattern manifests as: retreating a piece when development is urgent (Nb1, 1/10), advancing a flank pawn when a central move is required (h6, f5, b3 — 3/10), moving the king when a pawn advance is time-critical or vice versa (Kd3 vs a6 needed, Kg7 vs Bf8 needed — 2/10), pushing a pawn before the necessary preparatory move (f7 before Rd8, fxe5 opening center with exposed king — 2/10), or moving a piece sideways instead of penetrating immediately (Rg5 vs Rf2, Na5 without d6 first — 2/10). In every case, the one wasted tempo allows the opponent to execute a concrete tactical or positional blow: e5 trapping a piece, e6 breaking through, Bc3+ winning a queen, Rh2 neutralizing an invasion, or bxa5 capturing a critical pawn.
analysis.move_pattern: Any piece type; non-forcing quiet moves (non-checks, non-captures in 9/10); moves to peripheral squares or backward directions; pawn advances on flanks or non-critical files
analysis.why_bad: The position has exactly one critical demand (preventing a breakthrough, maintaining a threat, or executing an immediate tactic), and these moves ignore it, giving the opponent a free tempo to execute a devastating concrete plan that was previously preventable.
sub_patterns: Prophylactic flank pawn move ignoring central breakthrough (h6, f5)
Piece retreat/sideways move when penetration or development is urgent (Nb1, Rg5, Na5)
King move when a time-sensitive pawn advance is required, or vice versa (Kd3 vs a6, b3 vs Kd3)
Premature pawn advance before necessary preparatory move (f7 before Rd8, fxe5 with exposed king)
King move onto a tactical vulnerability (Kg7 onto diagonal)

analysis.label: Playing a slow, non-forcing move when a rook check would gain decisive tempo and material.
analysis.description: In all 3/3 positions, the critical best move was a rook delivering check (Rd1+, Rb8+, Re2+) that would exploit the opponent's exposed king to gain tempo and win material or activate pieces. Instead, the player chose a quiet, non-forcing move (a king retreat, a pawn push, or a passive rook redeployment) that failed to create immediate threats. Each missed check would have forced the opponent's king to an inferior square while the rook simultaneously attacked key targets (winning pawns on b2, cracking open the kingside, or capturing f2). The passive alternatives in all cases allowed the opponent to exploit a tactical vulnerability that the tempo-gaining check would have preempted—a bishop capturing a hanging rook (Position 8), counterplay against an undefended d4 pawn (Position 11), or simplification winning the a5 pawn (Position 12).
analysis.move_pattern: Any quiet non-forcing move (king, pawn, or passive rook) when a rook check along a rank or file was available
analysis.why_bad: The slow move wastes a critical tempo, allowing the opponent to seize the initiative or exploit a tactical vulnerability that the forcing check would have neutralized by keeping the opponent's king under duress.
sub_patterns: Quiet king move ignoring rook check with tempo gain
Slow pawn push instead of rook invasion with check
Wrong rook to passive square missing check that wins material

analysis.label: King moves to the wrong adjacent square in a critical pawn endgame, losing opposition or tempo by exactly one file/rank.
analysis.description: In 14/14 positions, the king moves to a square adjacent to the single correct square in a razor-thin pawn endgame, catastrophically losing the opposition, blockade, or stalemate resource. The pattern is remarkably consistent: the king retreats or sidesteps one file away from the only drawing/best square (e.g., Kf1 instead of Kg1, Kd1 instead of Ke1, Ke8 instead of Kf8, Kh8 instead of Kg8, Ka1 instead of Kb1, Kb8 instead of Kc8). In 13/14 cases only 1 good move existed within 50cp of best. The positions all feature advanced passed pawns 1-2 squares from promotion where the defending king must maintain precise contact with the promotion square while preserving opposition or stalemate tricks. The error uniformly results from choosing a plausible-looking adjacent square that appears equivalent but fatally concedes the critical tempo in the opposition battle.
analysis.move_pattern: King moves one square to an adjacent file or rank, landing on a square neighboring the single correct square in a K+P endgame
analysis.why_bad: Moving the king one square away from the correct square loses the opposition (wrong side to move in the critical king face-off), abandons stalemate resources, or breaks the blockade timing, allowing the opponent's passed pawn to promote or the opponent's king to achieve the decisive escort position.
sub_patterns: King retreats to wrong back-rank square away from pawn's queening file (Kf1/Kh1 vs Kg1, Ke1 vs Kf1)
King moves to wrong blockading square behind opponent's pawn (Kb8/Kd8 vs Kc8, Ke8 vs Kf8)
King retreats to corner instead of adjacent square preserving stalemate (Ka1 vs Kb1)
King sidesteps to wrong file losing opposition tempo (Kd1 vs Ke1, Kh8 vs Kg8)

analysis.label: An apparently active or centralizing move that places a piece on (or exposes a piece to) a square where the opponent can favorably capture it.
analysis.description: In 3/4 positions, the player moves a piece to an aggressive-looking square that is directly controlled by an opponent's piece, allowing an immediate favorable capture: Nc5 walks into Bxc5 which removes a key blocker of the passed d-pawn; Bd6 walks into Nxd6+ which wins with check and saddles Black with doubled isolated pawns; Rde1 removes the rook's support from d4, allowing Bxd4 cxd4 which rips open the c-file against White's king. The g4 case is a milder variant where premature pawn advance removes flexibility. In each case, safer preparatory moves (Nb4, Be7, Bh6, Kf4) were available that addressed the position's actual demands. The common thread is prioritizing superficially active piece placement over concrete tactical awareness of which squares the opponent controls.
analysis.move_pattern: Piece moves to a central or advanced square that is directly attacked by an opponent's minor piece or opens a line allowing favorable capture of a now-undefended piece
analysis.why_bad: The destination square (or the abandoned defensive relationship) allows the opponent to make a favorable capture—often with check, structural damage, or opening of attacking lines—that the player overlooked while pursuing a 'natural' improving move.
sub_patterns: Piece moves to square attacked by opponent's minor piece (Nc5, Bd6)
Rook leaves defensive post exposing key piece to capture (Rde1)
Premature pawn advance when preparation needed (g4)

analysis.label: A rook moves to a seemingly active central square where it becomes tactically vulnerable to attacks by minor pieces or pawn advances.
analysis.description: In all 8/8 positions, a rook is moved to an open or central square (typically the 3rd-6th rank) that appears active but creates a critical tactical vulnerability. The rook becomes a target for bishop attacks via pins or direct threats (positions 2, 4, 8, 14: Bg4 attacks Rf3, Bh6 attacks the king through Rd4's absence, Bh6 pins Rd2, Bg5 attacks Rf6), for pawn forks exploiting the rook's placement near other pieces (positions 5, 7: f5-f4 forks Re3 and Ng3), for back-rank exploitation when the rook vacates its defensive post (position 6: Rxf5 leaves 8th rank unguarded for Qd5+ fork), or for wrong-piece recapture leaving the king exposed (position 3: Rxf3 instead of Nxf3). The common thread is that the player prioritizes apparent rook activity over concrete tactical safety, placing the rook where it lacks adequate support or creates geometric alignment with other vulnerable pieces.
analysis.move_pattern: Rook moves to an open/central square on the 2nd-6th rank (lifts, captures, or advances), typically on the d/e/f files
analysis.why_bad: The rook's new square creates an exploitable tactical relationship—it can be pinned, forked with another piece by a pawn advance, attacked by a bishop along an unguarded diagonal, or its departure from the back rank leaves critical defensive gaps. The 'active' placement actually makes the rook a liability rather than an asset.
sub_patterns: Rook placed on square pinnable or attackable by enemy bishop along diagonal (Rf3/Rd2/Rf6 targeted by Bg4/Bh6/Bg5)
Rook on 3rd rank forked with nearby knight by pawn advance (Re3 + Ng3 forked by f4)
Rook leaves back rank creating fork/invasion vulnerability (Rxf5 allows Qd5+)
Rook abandons kingside defense allowing dark-square attack (Rd4 permits Bh6/Qg5)
Wrong recapture with rook instead of piece that provides defensive coverage (Rxf3 vs Nxf3)

analysis.label: Playing a positionally-motivated or developing move that ignores the critical concrete tactical demands of the position, wasting a vital tempo.
analysis.description: This feature fires on moves that look superficially reasonable (developing pieces, gaining space, consolidating structure) but catastrophically fail to address urgent tactical requirements. In 6/6 positions, the played move ignored an immediate tactical need—whether an available attacking combination (positions 3, 7), a hanging piece (position 9), overloaded defenders (position 10), or exposed pieces becoming targets (positions 4, 5). The positions all featured tactical tension requiring concrete resolution: king safety crises (6/6), piece activity imbalances (5/6), and development emergencies (4/6). In every case, the best move was a concrete, forcing continuation while the blunder was a non-forcing 'improving' move. The average cp_loss of 216 with only 2.0 good moves available confirms these are critical moments where only precise tactical play suffices, yet the player chose a generic positional gesture instead.
analysis.move_pattern: Non-forcing, non-capturing moves (pawn pushes, piece repositioning to seemingly active squares, development to passive squares) in positions with immediate tactical tension
analysis.why_bad: These moves waste a critical tempo in positions where tactical urgency demands concrete action—either executing an available tactic, defending a hanging piece, or maintaining attacking momentum. The tempo loss allows the opponent to seize the initiative, exploit existing vulnerabilities, or neutralize the player's advantages.
sub_patterns: Passive consolidation when attack available (e6, c4)
Piece repositioning to inferior/exposed square (Bf6, Qg4, Bg5)
Development to passive square ignoring hanging material (Na3)
