analysis.label: Playing aesthetically appealing or generally principled moves in critical positions that demand one specific concrete solution to an urgent tactical problem.
analysis.description: This feature fires on positions where the player chose a 'natural-looking' move—piece centralization, standard development, prophylactic pawn pushes, or routine improvement—while ignoring the ONE concrete action the position demands. In 6/8 positions, there was only 1 good move available (avg 1.5), indicating critical moments requiring precision. The ignored urgent needs include: eliminating a dangerous attacking piece (Bf3 instead of Bxe2, Position 1), blocking a tactical diagonal against f7 (h6/g6 instead of e6, Positions 2-3), capturing a lethal passed pawn (Kd2 instead of Kxd3, Position 4), capturing a dangerous advanced pawn (Nc6 instead of cxd6, Position 8), preventing a crushing pawn advance (Nd6 instead of b6, Position 10), and executing a concrete tactical combination (Ne5 instead of Nd4, Position 7). In several cases (5/8), the 'natural' move also placed the piece on a tactically vulnerable square—hanging to captures with check, forks, or pawn attacks—compounding the error.
analysis.move_pattern: Non-capturing piece moves to seemingly active/natural squares (central outposts, development squares, prophylactic positions); no checks or captures; diverse piece types (knights, bishops, king, pawns)
analysis.why_bad: The position has one urgent concrete problem (a tactical threat, a dangerous passed pawn, an exposed diagonal, an immediate combination) that requires the ONE specific solution, and these moves address general positional improvement instead, often placing the piece on a newly vulnerable square that creates additional tactical problems.
sub_patterns: Knight development to central square that abandons a critical defensive duty or walks into a pawn attack (Nc6, Nd6, Ne5)
Bishop/piece placement on undefended or tactically exploitable square (Bf3, Bb4)
Slow prophylactic pawn moves when blocking a dangerous diagonal or developing is urgent (h6, g6)
King move to seemingly safe square that walks into forks or fails to address passed pawn (Kd2)

analysis.label: In narrow endgame positions with only one winning move, the player chooses a natural-looking but non-forcing alternative that surrenders critical tempo.
analysis.description: This feature activates in endgame positions (8/8) where the correct move is highly specific and forcing, but the player instead makes a plausible-seeming move that fails to directly address the most urgent need. The common failure modes include: generic king centralization when a specific king attack on an enemy piece was required (Kd3 instead of Kf5 in Position 1; Kd5 instead of a2 in Position 2; g5 instead of Kf5 in Position 14), advancing the wrong pawn without tempo (d2 instead of e2+ in Position 5), decentralizing a piece for material instead of advancing a decisive pawn (Nxb6 instead of g4 in Position 13), moving a piece far from the critical target (Rc8 instead of Rd3 in Position 9), and placing a piece on a tactically vulnerable square (Bg8 allowing Nf6+ fork in Position 15). In 6/7 mistake positions, only 1 good move maintained the advantage (avg good moves 1.4), confirming these are extremely narrow decision points. The average cp_loss of ~293 reflects the catastrophic cost of losing a single tempo in these simplified positions.
analysis.move_pattern: Diverse piece types and directions; the unifying geometric thread is that the chosen move moves AWAY from or fails to directly engage the critical target (enemy piece or promotion square), while the correct move directly attacks/advances toward it
analysis.why_bad: In simplified endgame positions with few pieces, a single tempo often determines the outcome of a race, blockade, or attack. These moves all gift the opponent a free tempo to organize a defense (establish blockade, coordinate pieces, create counterplay) that the forcing alternative would have prevented.
sub_patterns: King moves to wrong side of board, abandoning passed pawns or missing direct attacks on enemy pieces
Advancing the wrong pawn without check/tempo when the alternative pawn gives check
Material greed (capturing a peripheral pawn) instead of advancing decisive passed pawns
Moving a piece far from the critical square/target instead of directly engaging it
Placing a piece on a tactically vulnerable square (fork/trap)

analysis.label: Plausible-looking moves that inadvertently allow the opponent to exploit with a forcing check, pin, or fork that wins material.
analysis.description: This feature fires on moves that appear to serve a reasonable purpose (defending, developing, creating counterplay, or activating the king) but critically overlook that they enable the opponent's forcing tactical combination—almost always involving check or pin. In 7/8 positions, the refutation involves a check or pin to the king: Qe2 enables Nf4-Nxd3+ fork (check); Qb6 abandons d7's defense allowing Bxd7+ (check); Kg6 exposes king to Qxc6+ (check winning bishop); Qe7 is bypassed by exf7+ (pawn check); Nc6 enables Bb5 pin to king; f4 opens the diagonal for Bxe3+ (check); Kf4 allows Rc4+ perpetual checks. The moves all look natural—defending, developing, centralizing—but miss that they create a vulnerability specifically exploitable by a forcing move (check/pin) that prevents the defender from addressing the material loss.
analysis.move_pattern: Various piece types (Queen, King, Knight, pawn) moving to seemingly useful squares but creating tactical vulnerabilities to opponent's checks, pins, or forks along newly opened lines or exploited alignments
analysis.why_bad: Each move either removes a piece from a critical defensive duty, places a piece/king on a tactically exploitable square, or opens a line that enables the opponent to win material through a forcing sequence starting with check or pin—the check gains tempo that prevents the defender from saving the threatened material.
sub_patterns: Queen abandoning defense of a piece, allowing capture with check (Qb6, Qe7)
King moving to square exposed to discovered or direct check (Kg6, Kf4)
Pawn advance opening critical line toward own king (f3, f4)
Piece development to square immediately exploitable by pin or fork (Nc6, Qe2)

analysis.label: A piece moves away from a square where it provided essential defense, leaving a pawn, piece, or key square fatally unguarded for immediate exploitation.
analysis.description: This feature fires on moves where a piece relocates (often via capture or seemingly active move) but in doing so removes critical defensive coverage, leaving a target immediately exploitable. In 5/7 positions, the moved piece was directly defending something vital: the queen leaves e7 exposing the e-file to the uncastled king (Position 1), the queen abandons d8 leaving d5 en prise to Nxd5 (Position 3), the knight departs d7 leaving a7 undefended for Rxa7 (Position 5), the queen enters d7 walking into a forced exchange sequence (Position 6), and the knight retreats from c6 uncovering e5/g5 squares enabling Ng5 attacking queen and f7 (Position 7). In Position 4, a slow queen move ignores the hanging g4 pawn (Bxg4), and Position 2 exchanges the rook needed for a mating combination. All 7 share the pattern of making a move that appears purposeful—a capture, development, or active placement—while critically leaving something undefended that the opponent exploits within 1-2 moves. Average cp_loss of 1559 and only 1.6 good alternatives confirm these are narrow positions requiring precise defense.
analysis.move_pattern: Queen or knight moves away from a central/defensive square, often via capture or to an apparently active square, leaving a previously-defended pawn or square unguarded
analysis.why_bad: The moved piece was the sole or critical defender of a pawn, square, or coordination point; removing it creates an immediate tactical target (hanging pawn, open file against king, exploitable square) that the opponent seizes within 1-2 moves
sub_patterns: Wrong piece captures (queen/knight used instead of simpler pawn recapture that maintains coverage)
Queen leaves back rank abandoning defense of central pawn or e-file coverage
Knight retreats/relocates removing control of squares opponent immediately occupies
Premature exchange removes a piece needed for the primary tactical plan

analysis.label: Piece (usually king) vacates a critical controlling square, allowing the opponent to immediately exploit the vacated territory.
analysis.description: This feature fires on moves where White's piece—overwhelmingly the king (6/9 positions)—leaves a square where it performed a vital blocking, defending, or controlling function, enabling the opponent to exploit the newly unguarded zone. In Position 14 (Kf4), the king retreats from g5 allowing Black's king to reach f7 unchallenged. In Position 15 (Kb5), the king retreats from a6 allowing Black's king to race to the a8 drawing corner. In Position 1 (Kf5), the king moves forward but abandons the shelter behind its pawns, exposing both g5 and h4 to queen harassment. In Position 4 (Ng5), the knight abandons f3 leaving h2 undefended for a devastating Bh2+ sacrifice. In Position 12 (Rgf3), the rook abandons the g-file allowing immediate invasion via Rg1. In Position 10 (Kxh5), capturing a pawn displaces the king from h4 where it controlled the g3 advance. In Position 6 (Ba8), the bishop abandons its active d5 post to become trapped in the corner. In Position 7 (Rh4), the rook moves to a square immediately targetable by ...hxg5. All 9/9 positions share the pattern of a piece leaving a square whose controlling function was more important than the intended gain.
analysis.move_pattern: Piece (predominantly king) moves away from a square where it controlled opponent's key plan—includes diagonal retreats, sideways shifts, greedy captures, and apparent centralization attempts
analysis.why_bad: The vacated square or line performed a critical function (blocking opponent's king path, defending a key square, controlling a file, shielding pawns). Leaving it gives the opponent an immediate tempo or invasion route that more than compensates for any positional or material gain the move intended.
sub_patterns: King retreats from advanced outpost when it should maintain or advance (Kf4, Kb5)
King advances into tactical vulnerability abandoning shelter (Kf5, Kxh5, Kf3)
Piece abandons defensive duty for aggressive but unsound sortie (Ng5, Rgf3)
Piece retreats to passive/trapped square losing critical influence (Ba8, Rh4)

analysis.label: Quiet, passive, or misdirected moves that waste a critical tempo when the position demands immediate forcing action.
analysis.description: This feature fires on moves that are slow, preparatory, or peripheral when the position demands an immediate active response. In 7/7 positions, the analyses identify 'tempo_loss' as a core theme. The played moves share the characteristic of being non-forcing repositions (Be8 retreating to back rank, Qd7 passively consolidating, a4 pushing a flank pawn, Kb6 going to the rim, Kf2 approaching instead of capturing) while the correct moves were forcing or directly addressed the critical positional demand (Rd8 contesting the open file, Qb4+ winning material with check, Rxg2 eliminating a promotion threat, c4 creating connected passers, Kd6 centralizing). In 5/7 cases the best move was either a capture, a check, or a direct contest of the critical file/square. The played moves look reasonable superficially—they develop, approach targets, or prophylactically defend—but they gift the opponent a tempo to seize the initiative or execute a tactical blow (h3 creating connected passers in position 10, a5+ exploiting the decentralized king in position 15, Ne4-c5 exploiting passivity in position 4).
analysis.move_pattern: Non-capturing, non-checking quiet moves: piece retreats to back rank, king moves to periphery, slow pawn pushes, approaching without capturing
analysis.why_bad: The position requires an immediate forcing move (capture, check, or direct contest of critical squares), but the played move wastes a tempo on preparation or passive repositioning, allowing the opponent to execute a tactical resource or seize the initiative first.
sub_patterns: Piece retreats to passive back-rank square (Be8, Qd7)
King moves away from center/critical zone (Kb6, Kf2 approaching instead of capturing)
Slow flank pawn push ignoring dynamic central demands (a4)
Piece development to tactically flawed square (Bb4)

analysis.label: Choosing a reasonable-looking but non-forcing move in a razor-sharp position that demands one specific precise continuation, wasting a critical tempo.
analysis.description: This feature fires on positions where only 1-2 moves maintain the evaluation (avg 1.5 good moves), but the player makes a 'natural' or 'logical' alternative that squanders a critical tempo. In 8/11 positions, the correct move involved either a forcing continuation (check, direct threat, or precise prophylactic) while the played move was passive or addressed a secondary concern. Examples include: retreating a knight to b1 when active play was needed (Pos 4), passively blockading a pawn instead of counterattacking with f5 (Pos 5), playing a routine exchange (exd4) when Ne7+ with check was winning (Pos 7), doubling rooks 'naturally' while ignoring the king's vulnerability on an open file (Pos 9), developing a bishop that overloads a defender (Pos 10), and capturing with the wrong piece/direction destroying coordination (Pos 1, 12, 15). The tempo_loss tag appears in 8/11 analyses, and 'missed_tactic' in 8/11, confirming that these are positions demanding urgent action where the player defaulted to a plausible-looking move.
analysis.move_pattern: Various piece types making non-forcing moves (no checks, no immediate threats) — retreats, passive captures, wrong-direction captures, natural development, or blockading moves when forcing alternatives exist
analysis.why_bad: The positions demand one precise forcing or prophylactic move (often involving check, a pawn break, or addressing a critical vulnerability), but the played move wastes the tempo needed to maintain the position's tactical balance, allowing the opponent to execute a tactical blow, advance passed pawns, or exploit exposed king positions
sub_patterns: Capturing with wrong piece/direction, destroying defensive coordination (Bxh1, Bxd5, dxc6)
Passive retreat or development when forcing moves exist (Nb1, Nc3, Be6)
Natural 'improving' moves ignoring critical tactical vulnerability (Re8, Red8, h4)
Non-forcing exchange surrendering initiative (exd4, Kg1)

analysis.label: Knight moves to edge or peripheral squares without concrete purpose, losing tempo and activity.
analysis.description: All three positions feature a knight moving to a peripheral or exposed square (Ng5, Nh3, Na4) where it lacks concrete follow-up and becomes passive or easily challenged. In 3/3 cases, the knight move prioritizes a speculative tactical idea (attacking f7, targeting g3/f4 pawns, or hitting the c5 bishop) over more fundamental positional needs like king centralization, castling, or maintaining central control. The analyses consistently identify 'tempo_loss' and 'piece_activity' as core issues (tagged in 3/3 positions), with the knight either needing to retreat (Position 7: Ng5-f3), being stranded on the rim (Position 8: Nh3 completely out of play), or creating tactical vulnerabilities through decentralization (Position 13: Na4 allowing ...b5 double attack). In all cases, the best moves involved centralization or advancing strategic plans rather than speculative knight sorties.
analysis.move_pattern: Knight moving away from center to edge/peripheral square (a-file, h-file, or exposed advanced square), non-capturing, non-checking
analysis.why_bad: The knight reaches a square without concrete threats or stability, wasting tempo while neglecting urgent positional priorities; opponents exploit the misplaced knight by gaining time to centralize, strike in the center, or launch counterattacks against the resulting structural weaknesses.
sub_patterns: Knight to rim square (a4, h3) becoming passive
Premature knight sortie to advanced square (g5) with forced retreat
Speculative knight attack on pawns instead of king centralization in endgame

analysis.label: Playing a non-forcing, passive move when the position demands immediate tactical or forcing action, gifting the opponent a critical tempo.
analysis.description: This feature activates when a player makes a slow, non-forcing move in a position that requires urgent action. In 7/10 positions, the primary tagged motif is 'tempo_loss.' The played moves are consistently described as passive or non-addressing the critical threat: Qc5 centralizes instead of counterattacking the exposed king (Position 1), Qd7 retreats passively instead of the aggressive Qh4 (Position 4), h4 is a slow pawn push instead of the tactical g4 breakthrough (Position 8), a4 pushes an irrelevant pawn instead of clearing for promotion (Position 11), Ra4 places the rook unproductively instead of playing the crushing f6 break (Position 12), Rc2 retreats from an active post instead of generating counter-threats with Qd7 (Position 14), and Bd6 places a bishop where c5 gains tempo (Position 15). In 8/10 positions, at least one king is exposed, creating mutual urgency. The best moves in nearly all cases are forcing (checks, pawn breaks, tactical shots, or immediate piece activation), while the played moves are quiet improvements that ignore the position's tactical demands.
analysis.move_pattern: Quiet piece repositioning, pawn push, or retreat to a non-forcing square; no checks, no direct threats, no captures of strategic importance
analysis.why_bad: In positions with exposed kings, advanced passed pawns, or imminent tactical threats, wasting a single tempo allows the opponent to execute a decisive plan—whether launching a mating attack, advancing a passed pawn, or gaining a tempo-gaining pawn break that reshapes the position irreversibly.
sub_patterns: Quiet queen centralization ignoring king safety threats
Slow pawn push missing a tactical pawn breakthrough
Piece retreat to passive square when active placement was critical
Grabbing material while walking into a forcing sequence
Irrelevant pawn push delaying a critical promotion or forcing plan

analysis.label: Superficially attractive aggressive moves (checks, attacks, active placements) that waste the one tempo needed for the position's actual tactical or positional demand.
analysis.description: This feature fires on moves that LOOK active or forcing—often checks (Rf6+, Qf4+, Qa6+, Bxg7+), attacks on pieces (Bf2 hitting Re1, Bf4 hitting Qc7, Bh6 hitting Bg7), or seemingly active placements (Rg8, Bd3, Qb2)—but critically waste the tempo needed for the position's real requirement. In 7/11 positions the primary tag is 'tempo_loss.' The pattern manifests as: the player is seduced by an immediately forcing-looking move while ignoring what the position actually demands—whether that's maintaining a mating net (Position 6: Rg1 sealed the net, Rf6+ let the king escape), preserving a perpetual check mechanism (Position 10: Qxd4+ drew, Qf4+ first lost), exploiting a specific tactic (Position 11: Rf3+ won White's queen, Qa6+ just drove the king to safety), or maintaining a critical defensive duty (Positions 8, 9, 14: pieces abandoned key squares for 'active' alternatives). The common thread is choosing apparent activity over actual necessity.
analysis.move_pattern: Piece moves (bishop, queen, rook) toward opponent's pieces or king, frequently with check or attacking intent, away from their positionally/tactically critical current duty
analysis.why_bad: The 'active' move squanders the critical tempo that the position's unique tactical or positional demand requires—either driving the opponent's king to safety, abandoning defense of a key square/piece, or disrupting a precise forced sequence that only works in the correct move order
sub_patterns: Pointless or counterproductive checks that drive the king to safety (Rf6+, Qa6+, Bxg7+)
Checks in wrong move order that break a forced drawing/winning mechanism (Qf4+ before Qxd4+)
Bishop moves that abandon critical defensive squares for illusory attacks (Bf4, Bh6, Bf2)
Piece placements to active-looking squares that miss the position's real demand (Rg8, Qb2, Bd3)

analysis.label: Checks or active-looking moves played on the wrong square or in the wrong order, wasting tempo and allowing the opponent to consolidate or escape.
analysis.description: This feature fires on positions where the player delivers a seemingly forcing move (usually a check) that actually loses critical tempo. In 4/6 positions, the error is a queen check on the wrong square: Qf8+ instead of Qe8+ (2/6 positions, identical wrong-square error), Qe1+ instead of Qh2+ (1/6), and Qf3+ before the preparatory Rxe3+ (1/6). In 1/6 positions, an active-looking developing move (Be6) allows the opponent to gain tempo with Bb5+ and a subsequent fork. The common thread is that these moves APPEAR forcing or active but fail to create the necessary follow-up threats, allowing the opponent's king to reach safety or pieces to consolidate. The average cp_loss of 3273 reflects how catastrophic it is to waste initiative in sharp attacking positions. All positions are tagged with 'tempo_loss' (6/6) and 'king_safety' (6/6), confirming the pattern of squandering attacking momentum against exposed kings.
analysis.move_pattern: Queen checks (or active piece moves) delivered to squares adjacent to but distinct from the optimal checking/forcing square, typically along the same rank or file but missing the critical pivot point
analysis.why_bad: The move wastes a tempo by placing the piece on a square where it lacks follow-up threats (e.g., Qf8 cannot pivot to Qc6 with mate threats, unlike Qe8), allowing the opponent's king to escape to a safer square or enabling the opponent to consolidate defenses. The initiative, once lost in these sharp positions, cannot be recovered.
sub_patterns: Queen check on adjacent wrong square (Qf8 vs Qe8, Qe1 vs Qh2)
Premature check before required preparatory capture (Qf3+ before Rxe3+)
Active development that enables opponent's tempo-gaining reply (Be6 allowing Bb5+)

analysis.label: Non-forcing, preparatory moves played in critical positions where the opponent gains a decisive tempo to execute their own plan.
analysis.description: This feature fires on moves that are slow, non-forcing (no check, no capture, no immediate threat), played in positions that demand immediate tactical or strategic action. In 9/9 positions, the blunder is a quiet, apparently reasonable move that wastes a critical tempo: flank pawn pushes (g4, h4, f4 in 3/9), bishop retreats to passive squares (Bc1 in 2/9), slow preparatory rook moves (Rcd3, Rg1 in 2/9), or misdirected piece moves (Rh6, Kd8 in 2/9). The common consequence is that the opponent gets one free move to execute a plan that was previously preventable—whether king infiltration (4/9), capturing an undefended pawn or piece (3/9), or escaping a mating net (1/9). The positions feature very few good alternatives (avg 1.8), indicating these are critical junctures where precision is demanded. The tagged tactical motif is 'tempo_loss' in 8/9 cases, confirming the unifying thread is the catastrophic waste of time rather than any specific geometric error.
analysis.move_pattern: Any quiet, non-forcing move (pawn push, piece retreat, preparatory repositioning) - no check, no capture, no direct attack on opponent's pieces
analysis.why_bad: The position demands immediate forcing action (advancing a passed pawn, exploiting an exposed king, winning material via tactics), but the slow move cedes a critical tempo, allowing the opponent to execute counterplay (c5 breaks, king infiltration to d3/c2, escaping mating nets, capturing undefended pawns) that was previously preventable with one more move of delay.
sub_patterns: Kingside pawn pushes (g4/h4/f4) ignoring urgent queenside or central action
Bishop retreats to c1 losing control of critical infiltration squares
Preparatory rook moves when immediate forcing wins exist (Rcd3 missing mate, Rg1 missing Qf6)
Piece moves to tactically vulnerable squares allowing trapping or counterattack

analysis.label: Developing a piece to a square where an enemy central pawn advance creates a devastating fork against it and another friendly piece.
analysis.description: In 10/11 positions, the player develops a piece (usually a bishop) to a square that aligns with another friendly piece such that both sit on the forward diagonals of an advanceable enemy central pawn. The consistent pattern: two friendly pieces end up two files apart on the same rank, and an enemy d- or e-pawn advances one square to the file between them, forking both diagonally. Specific sub-patterns include: Be6+Nc6 forked by d5 (positions 1, 7), Be3+Nc3 forked by d4 (positions 4, 5), Bd6+Nf6 forked by e5 (positions 6, 9), Bf5+Nd5 forked by e4 (position 10), Bf4+Nd4 forked by e5 (position 2), Nf3+Bd3 forked by e4 (position 3), and Bf4+Qd4 attacked by e5 (position 11). Position 8 (e6) is a variant where the pawn blocks the bishop's retreat square, enabling the fork. In all cases, the player makes a natural-looking developing move while overlooking that a single enemy pawn thrust wins material.
analysis.move_pattern: Piece (predominantly bishop) developed to a square on ranks 3-6 that is diagonally adjacent to an advanceable enemy central pawn, while another friendly piece already occupies the other forward diagonal of that same pawn
analysis.why_bad: The move creates a two-piece alignment where both friendly pieces sit on the capture diagonals of an enemy d- or e-pawn that can advance with tempo, winning material through an unavoidable pawn fork or double attack
sub_patterns: Bishop to e6 with knight on c6 enabling d4-d5 fork
Bishop to e3 with knight on c3 enabling d4 fork
Bishop to d6 with knight on f6 enabling e4-e5 fork
Bishop to f5 with knight on d5 enabling e2-e4 fork
Bishop to f4 with knight/queen on d4 enabling e5 double attack
Knight to f3 with bishop on d3 enabling e4 fork
Pawn to e6 blocking bishop retreat enabling e4 fork on f5+d5

analysis.label: Choosing a natural-looking but fatally flawed move in narrow positions where only one specific continuation maintains the evaluation.
analysis.description: This feature fires on critical positions with extremely narrow margins (avg 1.4 good moves available) where the player selects a plausible-seeming alternative that catastrophically fails. In 7/9 cases the move wastes a critical tempo, and in 7/9 cases a concrete tactic is missed. The blunders share a pattern of ABANDONING the position's single critical requirement: abandoning development for a queen sortie (Qa4), abandoning a free pawn for routine castling (O-O), abandoning piece coordination for a queen reposition (Qf3), abandoning correct move order for a premature capture (Bxb3), abandoning active counterplay for passive repositioning (Bh6), abandoning a crushing pawn advance for a superficial fork (Ng6), abandoning a dominant outpost for piece harassment (Nd7), abandoning defensive structure for knight rerouting (Na5), and abandoning a safe king path for an exposed square (Ke1). Each move has a surface-level justification that appears reasonable (attacking, developing, castling, capturing) but ignores the ONE thing the position demands.
analysis.move_pattern: Non-forcing piece relocations (rarely checks or captures) that move pieces to apparently purposeful but tactically refutable squares, away from where the position's critical action lies
analysis.why_bad: The position has essentially only one correct continuation, and the chosen move ignores that critical requirement—whether it's a concrete tactic to execute, a piece to keep centralized, material to capture, or a specific king escape route—allowing the opponent to exploit the resulting tactical vulnerability with a single clear refutation.
sub_patterns: Queen sorties abandoning development or coordination duties
Knight moves abandoning dominant central outposts or landing undefended
Passive/routine moves (castling, quiet repositioning) when concrete action is demanded
King moves to exposed squares allowing perpetual check or tactical exploitation
Premature captures or wrong move-order allowing decisive intermediate moves

analysis.label: Moves that voluntarily relocate a piece from a square where it was performing an essential defensive, blockading, or controlling function, enabling the opponent's decisive tactical breakthrough.
analysis.description: This feature detects positions where a player moves a piece that was serving a critical positional or tactical role (blockading, defending, controlling key squares) in favor of a seemingly active or logical plan. In 5/8 positions, the moved piece was directly preventing the opponent's key idea: Kc7 abandoned a d6 blockade enabling d6+ (Position 13), Ne2 removed the knight from c3 enabling Black's ...c5 liberation (Position 14), Qb6 abandoned c-file/kingside defense enabling Rxc8 (Position 3), g5 wasted the critical tempo needed to address Nxb3+ (Position 1), and Bc4 ignored development allowing Nd4 fork (Position 15). In 6/8 cases, the opponent's refutation directly exploits the vacated square or abandoned duty. The moves all share a surface-level attractiveness (attacking, gaining material, repositioning for 'improvement') but fundamentally misread which aspect of the position demands priority attention. Positions average only 1.9 good moves, indicating these are tense, critical moments requiring precise responses rather than plan execution.
analysis.move_pattern: Any piece type voluntarily moving away from a square where it controlled, blocked, or defended something critical; no consistent geometric direction but typically moves toward the player's 'desired' plan rather than the position's urgent need
analysis.why_bad: The piece was performing an irreplaceable function (blockading a pawn, controlling a critical square, defending against a tactical shot, or maintaining piece coordination), and its removal allows the opponent to execute a previously impossible breakthrough—often a fork, passed pawn advance with check, tactical capture on the abandoned file, or tempo-gaining attack on the misplaced piece
sub_patterns: King abandoning blockade enabling passed pawn advance
Knight leaving c3 enabling central breaks or opponent occupation
Queen relocating away from defensive duties to queenside
Aggressive piece move ignoring development/king safety priorities
Material grab missing a more crushing positional continuation

analysis.label: Playing a reasonable-looking move that wastes a decisive tempo by failing to address the position's single most urgent tactical demand.
analysis.description: This feature fires on moves where the position has one critical, time-sensitive priority that demands immediate attention, but the player instead makes a plausible-looking move addressing a secondary concern. The urgent priorities being ignored include: trapped pieces needing rescue (Be7 ignores trapped Bh5, Ba1 ignores vulnerable Rh4 - 2/9), king safety demanding immediate defense (Nxg7 grabs material while own king faces mate, Qd4 ignores lethal e3 pawn - 2/9), available forced wins being overlooked (Nc4+ dismantles own mating net when Qf3# exists, Rxh6 grabs a pawn when Bxf6 wins immediately - 2/9), and tempo-sensitive races requiring king activation over peripheral activity (Rc2 and h5 waste time while passed pawns or king centralization demand attention, Ng6 weakens a critical defensive point - 3/9). The common thread across all 9 positions is that there were very few good moves available (avg 2.0) making these high-precision moments, and the played moves all look like normal chess (captures, checks, development, centralization) but catastrophically misread what the position actually requires.
analysis.move_pattern: Diverse piece types and directions - queen centralizing, rook shuffling, knight checks/captures, bishop retreats, pawn pushes - all sharing the property of being directed at a non-critical target or square while the critical sector is elsewhere
analysis.why_bad: Each move wastes a tempo that the position cannot afford to lose, because a single urgent tactical or strategic demand (trapped piece, mating threat, tempo-sensitive pawn race, immediately winning tactic) requires action THIS move. The played move addresses something secondary, giving the opponent the one tempo needed to solve their problem or execute their threat.
sub_patterns: Material grabs on the wing while own king faces mating attack (Nxg7, Rxh6)
Passive piece repositioning while a trapped/vulnerable piece needs saving (Ba1, Be7)
Peripheral pawn pushes or rook shuffles while king activation or passed pawn race demands priority (Rc2, h5)
Seemingly forcing checks that dismantle own coordination (Nc4+ removing mating piece)
Knight 'improvements' that fatally weaken critical defensive squares (Ng6)

analysis.label: Aggressive-looking moves that squander critical tactical opportunities at narrow decision points where only one precise continuation maintains the advantage.
analysis.description: This feature fires on positions where very few good moves exist (avg 1.2 acceptable moves) and the player makes a forward/aggressive-looking move that appears natural but catastrophically misses the one precise winning continuation. In 6/6 cases, the played move is active and threatening (a king advance, a capture on the 7th rank, pawn pushes, a developing move with tempo, a queen check) yet each ignores the position's key tactical feature. The correct moves tend to exploit a specific concrete vulnerability: trapping a bishop with g4-f4-f5 (Position 9), delivering discovered check via Qf6+ (Position 10), invading with Ne4 after Qd3 (Position 8), blockading a passed pawn with Rc7 (Position 3), or capturing material that generates counterplay with Kxf6 (Position 1). The blunders share the characteristic of pursuing a secondary objective (development, material, general activity) when only a narrow, concrete tactical path preserves the position's full value. Average cp_loss of 2042 reflects that these are often game-decisive moments.
analysis.move_pattern: Forward/aggressive moves (pawn pushes, captures, checks, developing moves) that target the wrong square or wrong objective; no single geometric direction but always a proactive piece/pawn commitment
analysis.why_bad: Each move wastes the critical tempo needed to exploit a concrete tactical feature (trapped piece, forced mate, knight outpost, passed pawn blockade), allowing the opponent to neutralize the position's key advantage or consolidate
sub_patterns: Pawn advance when piece precision required (d5, g5)
Wrong check square missing forced mate (Qg6+ vs Qf6+)
Material grab ignoring urgent positional threat (Rxb7 vs Rc7)
Developing move vacating critical defensive square (Bf4 exposing d2)
King to wrong square missing capture (Ke6 vs Kxf6)

analysis.label: Playing a superficially attractive move (often a check, capture, or natural development) that squanders the one critical tempo needed for the position's unique precise solution.
analysis.description: This feature fires on positions where there is typically only one correct move (avg 1.7 good moves available) and the player chooses something that looks forcing or natural but catastrophically misses the point. In 5/11 cases the mistake is a check on the wrong square or a greedy check/capture (Qa8+ instead of Qc8+, Qxg4+ instead of f5+, Qd7+ instead of Qh4+, Ng1+ trapping own knight, Qxe5+ missing Qh4#). In the remaining cases, it's a natural-looking move that addresses a secondary concern while ignoring the critical one (h3 addressing Ng4 instead of f4 solving f2 weakness, Nc6 developing instead of d3 advance, d5 pushing center instead of defending king, Kg1 fleeing wrong direction, fxg3 opening invasion lines, a5 wasting time while invasion looms). The common thread is that each move ENABLES the opponent's key resource: Qa8+ allows Kd7 protecting the rook, Ng1+ allows Kf2 trapping the knight, h3 allows Rxf2+ sacrifice, fxg3 opens e1 for queen infiltration. Average cp_loss of 2058 reflects the razor-thin margin in these positions.
analysis.move_pattern: Various piece types and directions; predominantly queen checks/captures (5/11), pawn moves (4/11), and king/knight moves (2/11) - all appearing forcing or natural but missing the one precise alternative
analysis.why_bad: Each move wastes the critical tempo that the position uniquely demands, allowing the opponent a specific defensive or counterattacking resource (escape square, interposition, infiltration route, piece trap) that would not have been available after the correct move
sub_patterns: Wrong checking square allowing king escape (Qa8+, Qd7+)
Greedy check/capture missing stronger tactical shot (Qxg4+, Qxe5+)
Natural development ignoring concrete tactical urgency (Nc6, a5, d5)
Addressing secondary threat while critical vulnerability remains (h3, fxg3)
Moving piece to square where it becomes trapped or useless (Ng1+, Kg1)

analysis.label: Plausible-looking moves in narrow positions that allow the opponent a devastating forcing response (check, promotion, or capture with tempo).
analysis.description: This feature activates on positions where very few good moves exist (avg 1.8) and the player selects a natural-looking move that specifically enables the opponent to execute a forcing tactical blow. In 8/10 cases, the punishment involves a check or promotion: Rxa8 allows bxa8=Q promotion (1/10), Rxc1 allows dxc1=Q+ promotion with check (2/10), Rxc1 allows dxc1=Q# promotion with mate (1/10), Kb2 allows Rb4+ check winning the queen (1/10), Ke7 allows d6+ advance with check (1/10), Rg2 allows Qf4+ deflection check (1/10), Kh2 allows Qe5+ check winning a piece (1/10). The remaining cases (Ng6, e5, Nxg5) allow the opponent captures with tempo or positional domination. The moves played span captures (4/10), king moves (3/10), and piece/pawn moves (3/10), but all share the critical trait of being the 'obvious' or 'natural' choice in a position where only one specific alternative preserves the evaluation.
analysis.move_pattern: Mixed piece types and directions; predominantly captures of seemingly free material, king moves to seemingly safe squares, or active-looking piece maneuvers—all in positions with only 1-2 viable alternatives
analysis.why_bad: Each move overlooks that it specifically enables a forcing opponent response (check, promotion-with-check, fork, or deflection) that was not available before the move was played, catastrophically worsening the position in what are razor-thin critical moments
sub_patterns: Captures that remove critical blockaders enabling pawn promotion
King moves to squares exposed to diagonal/file checks that win material
Piece moves abandoning defensive duties allowing forced tactical sequences

analysis.label: Playing a plausible-looking move in a critical position where exactly one precise move maintains the evaluation.
analysis.description: This feature activates on positions with extremely narrow margins—exactly 1 good move available (7/7 positions show good_moves=1)—where the player chooses a natural or intuitive alternative instead of the single correct option. The correct moves tend to be concrete and forcing: captures (Kxe2 in position 14, bxc3 in position 5), direct attacks on pieces (Ke6 attacking knight in position 15, Ne2 forking in position 4), or prophylactic queen moves addressing tactical threats (Qe3 in position 7). The played moves instead are quieter, 'reasonable' alternatives: developing moves (Rad1), king centralizations that miss free captures (Ke3 instead of Kxe2), pawn advances instead of captures (b3 instead of bxc3), or moves one tempo too slow (Ke7 instead of Ke6). The average cp_loss of 332 reflects the severity of deviating when there's no margin for error. The feature spans all game phases (4 endgame, 3 middlegame) and both sides, suggesting it detects the structural property of positional narrowness rather than a specific piece pattern.
analysis.move_pattern: Diverse piece types (K, R, B, pawn) making quiet non-forcing moves when a concrete capture, check, or direct piece attack was the sole correct option
analysis.why_bad: In positions where only one move works, any alternative—regardless of how natural or principled it appears—leads to catastrophic evaluation loss because the opponent gains a critical tempo, escapes a tactical threat, or reaches a drawing resource
sub_patterns: King moves near a piece without capturing it (Ke3 vs Kxe2, Ke7 vs Ke6)
Pawn advance instead of pawn capture (b3 vs bxc3)
Developing moves ignoring tactical threats (Rad1 ignoring Nf4 fork)
King to wrong square in pawn endgame (Kh4 vs Kf4)

analysis.label: Natural-looking moves that waste a critical tempo in positions with very few good alternatives, allowing the opponent to seize the initiative.
analysis.description: This feature fires on positions where the player makes a plausible-looking move that loses a decisive tempo in a position with extremely narrow margins (avg 1.7 good moves available). In 8/10 positions, the analyses explicitly identify 'tempo_loss' as the core tactical motif or tag. The moves often go to a square one step away from the correct destination (Kd1 instead of Ke1, Kg2 instead of Kf1, Kf3 instead of Kd3 — 4/10 are king moves to adjacent-but-wrong squares), or make a thematically similar but imprecise pawn push (h6 instead of g6, h5 instead of activating the king). The common consequence is that the opponent exploits the wasted tempo to invade with rooks (positions 1, 3), force unfavorable exchanges (positions 6, 8), advance/create passed pawns (positions 9, 14), or execute forks against misplaced pieces (position 15). These are not random blunders but rather 'almost-correct' moves in positions demanding surgical precision.
analysis.move_pattern: King, piece, or pawn moving to a plausible but suboptimal square — often one square adjacent to the correct destination or a similar-looking but wrong pawn advance
analysis.why_bad: The move wastes a critical tempo in a position with essentially only one correct move, allowing the opponent to immediately exploit the lost time through invasion, forced exchanges, passed pawn advances, or tactical strikes against the now-misplaced piece
sub_patterns: King to wrong adjacent square (Kd1/Ke1, Kg2/Kf1, Kf3/Kd3)
Wrong pawn pushed (h6 instead of g6, h5 instead of king move)
Piece placed on tactically vulnerable square (Bd3 captured, Re7 exchanged, Ndf6 blocks retreat)

analysis.label: Playing a non-urgent move when an undefended piece (usually a bishop) can be captured for free.
analysis.description: In 7/8 positions, the best move was capturing an undefended or hanging piece—overwhelmingly a bishop (positions 3, 4, 5, 6, 7, 8, 11 all feature a hanging bishop as the key target). Instead, the player chose a quiet repositioning move (Kg2, Qd3, b6, b5), a speculative attack (Qxf2, Bh4), or captured the wrong piece (Rxc6 taking a pawn instead of the bishop, Rxe6 taking a knight instead of the bishop). The positions typically have only 1 good move available (avg 1.2), creating a narrow critical decision point where the free material must be taken immediately before the opponent rescues the piece. The feature fires when a player's attention is drawn to secondary concerns—king safety improvements, queenside pawn breaks, attacking ideas—while a concrete, simple capture goes unnoticed.
analysis.move_pattern: Diverse piece types and directions (king shuffle, queen repositioning, bishop development, pawn pushes, wrong rook captures); no single geometric thread—the pattern is defined by what the move FAILS to do rather than what it does.
analysis.why_bad: The move wastes a critical tempo, allowing the opponent to rescue an undefended piece (usually a bishop) that could have been captured for free. Once saved, that piece often becomes actively dangerous—counterattacking, winning other material, or escaping to a dominant square.
sub_patterns: Quiet/slow moves ignoring hanging piece (Kg2, Qd3, b6, b5)
Speculative attacks instead of simple capture (Qxf2, Bh4)
Wrong capture—taking inferior target while better one hangs (Rxc6 pawn vs bishop, Rxe6 knight vs bishop)

analysis.label: Ambitious moves (usually central pawn pushes or piece relocations) made before the position's coordination can support them, leaving pieces or pawns tactically vulnerable.
analysis.description: This feature fires on moves where a player makes an aggressive or ambitious action—most commonly a central pawn advance—before their pieces are adequately developed or coordinated to sustain the resulting tension. In 5/9 positions, the blunder is a premature central pawn push (e4, e4, d5, e5, c4) that overextends the pawn structure and creates multiple weaknesses that cannot be simultaneously defended, typically because the king is uncastled (7/9 positions involve an uncastled king or exposed king) and supporting pieces are undeveloped. In the remaining 4/9 positions, a piece is moved to an ostensibly active square (Ng7, Qxe7, Rf7, Qe7) but in doing so abandons a critical defensive function, leaving another piece or pawn hanging. The common thread is that the move looks thematically reasonable or aggressive in isolation, but the position lacks the coordination to support it, resulting in immediate tactical exploitation through captures with check, forks, pins, or simple material wins averaging 294cp loss.
analysis.move_pattern: Central pawn advances (e4, d5, e5, c4) or piece relocations that break defensive coordination; typically forward/aggressive in nature
analysis.why_bad: The position's pieces are insufficiently developed or coordinated to support the aggression—the resulting tension exposes hanging pieces, undefended pawns, or the uncastled king to immediate tactical exploitation through forcing sequences.
sub_patterns: Premature central pawn break while king is uncastled (e4, e4, d5, e5, c4)
Piece relocation that abandons defense of another piece, leaving it hanging (Ng7, Qxe7, Qe7)
Passive move ignoring urgent tactical obligations (Rf7)

analysis.label: Moving a piece to a seemingly purposeful square that immediately enables a concrete tactical punishment (fork, check, capture, or decisive tempo gain) due to abandoning a defensive duty or landing on a vulnerable square.
analysis.description: This feature fires on moves where a piece is relocated with apparent logic (centralization, material gain, attacking intent, or defense) but critically creates an immediate tactical vulnerability. In 3/9 positions, a king walks to a square where it is hit by a check or fork (Kc7 into Nb5+, Kd5 exposing f7 to Qxf7+, Ke4 into Re2+). In 3/9 positions, a knight moves to an active-looking square but either abandons a critical guard duty (Nb5 removing defense of b3 allowing a fork, Ndf2 failing to prevent Ng3+ fork) or invites a counter-battery (Nc4 enabling Qd3 mating threat on h7). In 2/9 cases, a rook or queen chases material or appears active but becomes tactically exposed (Rb3 leaving itself undefended for Qxb3, Qxa5 stranding the queen on the edge while f4 breaks through). In 1/9 cases (Rd3), the piece goes to a nearly-correct but critically wrong square, losing the single tempo needed for the opponent to draw. All positions share low good-move counts (avg 2.2) indicating narrow tactical paths where a single misstep is immediately punished.
analysis.move_pattern: Various piece types moved to apparently active/logical squares; often one square away from the correct destination; includes king moves into open files/diagonals, knight jumps abandoning guard duties, and pieces chasing material on the board periphery
analysis.why_bad: Each move either (1) places the moved piece on a square where it is immediately exploitable via check, fork, or capture, or (2) removes a piece from a critical defensive function, allowing the opponent an immediate tactical shot that was previously prevented. The player pursues a secondary strategic goal while overlooking a concrete, forcing tactical response.
sub_patterns: King walking into check/fork on open lines
Knight leaving a guarded square enabling opponent's fork
Piece chasing material while abandoning kingside defense
Rook/piece on wrong square losing critical tempo

analysis.label: Opening moves that catastrophically misplace or neglect king safety, most often O-O-O directly into the opponent's pre-positioned queenside pawn storm or piece attack.
analysis.description: This feature fires strongly on opening-phase moves that fatally misjudge king safety. The dominant pattern (6/10 positions) involves queenside castling directly into the opponent's advanced pawns or active pieces that can immediately rip open files toward the king — Positions 2, 4, 7, and 11 show White O-O-O into Black's ready b5/c4 pawn storms or open c-files, while Position 6 shows Black O-O-O into White's c5+b4 advance. The secondary pattern (4/10) involves passive or irrelevant moves while the king remains dangerously in the center: Position 3 (h6 wasting tempo while e5 hangs), Position 5 (Be7 ignoring Bxf7+ sacrifice), Position 8 (g4 weakening kingside with king on e1), and Position 13 (Qe2 unguarding d4 while king is exposed). In all cases, the correct moves involved either kingside castling, concrete development addressing the king's vulnerability, or launching attacks on the side where the OPPONENT's king sits.
analysis.move_pattern: King castling queenside (O-O-O) or quiet developing/pawn moves made while own king is vulnerable; no captures or checks
analysis.why_bad: The king is placed directly in the path of the opponent's pre-existing pawn majority, advanced pawns, open files, or active pieces that can immediately generate a devastating attack with pawn storms (b4-b5, c4-b5) or piece invasions along newly opened files targeting the exposed monarch.
sub_patterns: O-O-O into opponent's advanced queenside pawn chain ready to storm with b5/b4
O-O-O into opponent's pieces controlling open or semi-open c-file
Passive tempo moves (h6, Be7) ignoring concrete tactical threats to uncastled king
Premature aggressive pawn advances (g4, d6) weakening position while king is in center

analysis.label: Captures (mostly bishop takes knight) that prematurely release tension when a stronger non-exchanging move would maintain or exploit the advantage.
analysis.description: This feature fires on positions where a player makes a premature exchange—overwhelmingly bishop captures knight (9/11 positions involve Bx capturing a knight, plus 1 NxN and 1 QxQ). In every case, the captured/exchanged piece was performing critical work: creating pins, supporting pawn breaks, enabling tactical combinations, or maintaining pressure that restricted the opponent. The best move in each position was instead a non-exchanging continuation—a central pawn break like d5 (positions 1, 4), a powerful knight centralization like Nd5 (positions 7, 8), a space-gaining advance like f5 (position 5), a preparatory developing move (positions 9, 11), or capturing a hanging pawn first (positions 6, 10). The common thread is that tension was the player's most valuable asset, and the exchange dissipated it. In 10/11 positions, only 1 good move existed, indicating these are critical-precision moments where the 'natural-looking' exchange is a trap.
analysis.move_pattern: Piece captures piece (primarily bishop captures knight on various squares), simplifying the position by exchanging an active piece for a less active one
analysis.why_bad: The exchanged piece was performing essential tactical or strategic work—maintaining pins, supporting pawn breaks, enabling knight forks, or restricting the opponent's coordination. Trading it releases tension, gives the opponent time to consolidate, and forfeits concrete tactical opportunities that depended on the piece remaining in play.
sub_patterns: Bishop captures knight that was supporting a pending central pawn break (d5/f5)
Bishop captures knight on c6 when the Bb5 pressure was enabling a tactic (Nxd5 fork, Qxd5 pawn grab)
Move-order error: exchanging before forcing the opponent to commit a tempo (Bxf3 before h3, Bxd2 before e4)
Exchanging an active pressure piece when maintaining tension would preserve a dominant position
Queen exchange that allows opponent's trapped/misplaced piece to escape with tempo

analysis.label: Playing a non-forcing, non-critical move (typically a flank pawn push or routine action) when the position demands immediate concrete measures to address tactical vulnerabilities or king safety.
analysis.description: This feature fires on positions where a player wastes a critical tempo on a peripheral or routine move while the position screams for urgent action. In 8/10 positions, at least one king is exposed or uncastled, creating tactical tension that demands precision. The played moves are overwhelmingly quiet (7/10 are pawn moves, often on the b or g files: bxa5, g6, g4, b3, g3, c5), while the best alternatives consistently involve piece activity, development, file-blocking, or concrete tactical operations. The common punishment pattern involves the opponent exploiting the wasted tempo to launch a decisive attack on the exposed king, execute a tactical combination, or consolidate a material/positional advantage. The average cp_loss of 1192 reflects that these tempi are squandered in positions where the margin for slow play is zero.
analysis.move_pattern: Quiet pawn moves (especially on b/g files) or non-forcing piece moves in positions with high tactical tension and exposed kings
analysis.why_bad: The position has concrete tactical demands (development completion, file blocking, piece coordination against an exposed king) that require immediate attention; the slow move cedes the initiative, allowing the opponent to exploit existing vulnerabilities with forcing moves like checks, captures, or central breaks that the tempo loss can no longer be parried.
sub_patterns: Peripheral pawn captures ignoring central threats (bxa5)
Quiet kingside pawn moves wasting tempo (g6, g4, g3)
Preparatory queenside pawn moves delaying development (b3, c5)
Pointless checks that improve the opponent's king (Ra2+)
Routine castling/king moves into tactical danger (O-O, Ke1)

analysis.label: Choosing a natural-looking active move (check, capture, centralization) over a more precise forcing continuation that demands specific calculation.
analysis.description: This feature fires on positions where the player selects a superficially attractive move—often a check, capture, or centralizing piece placement—instead of the uniquely correct forcing continuation. In 7/10 positions, only one move was within 50cp of the best, indicating these are positions demanding tactical precision. The errors include: choosing the wrong square for a knight (Ne5 instead of Ng5+ in Position 1), the wrong open file for a rook (Re1 vs Rd1 in Position 5), an inefficient check (Qf8+ vs Rd1+ in Position 10), a materialistic check that surrenders positional compensation (Ng2+ vs Qe4+ perpetual in Position 11), abandoning defensive duties for illusory attacking chances (Qc2 vs Qxa2 in Position 14), and a premature capture violating move order (Nxg7 vs Be4 in Position 15). The played moves share a common 'attractiveness'—they look aggressive, active, or logical at first glance—but miss the one precise move that maximizes the forcing nature of the position.
analysis.move_pattern: Various piece types moving to natural/active-looking squares, often involving checks, captures, or centralizations that are the second-best version of the correct idea
analysis.why_bad: The move allows the opponent time to stabilize, escape, or exploit the imprecision—whereas the correct move was more forcing (a better check sequence, a sacrifice, a precise move order, or a specific square) that left no room for the opponent to recover
sub_patterns: Knight to wrong attacking square (centralizing vs checking)
Rook to wrong open file
Inefficient check when a stronger forcing sequence exists
Premature capture violating correct move order
Abandoning defensive duties for illusory second-rank pressure

analysis.label: Playing a superficially purposeful move that ignores the position's single critical tactical requirement, in positions where only 1-2 moves maintain the evaluation.
analysis.description: This feature fires on positions where the player faces a critical decision point (average only 1.6 good moves available) and chooses a move with clear superficial logic—attacking a piece, giving check, centralizing, advancing—but catastrophically misses the position's actual tactical demand. In 7/9 positions, the move constitutes a tempo loss; in 7/9, a specific tactic is missed. The played moves look active or purposeful: Nb4 attacks a bishop (Position 5), Rg1+ and h2+ give check (Positions 12, 13), e5 and c5 grab space (Positions 14, 2), Qe6 centralizes (Position 8), Kb7 targets a pawn (Position 7). But in each case, the position demanded one specific response: a capture (Nxd4, dxe5, Qxf3), a preparatory move before the obvious one (Nf5+ before Rg1+, Kf6 before h2), or simple development (Nd5, Nf6). The average cp_loss of 1287 reflects that these are not subtle positional inaccuracies but catastrophic oversights of concrete tactical consequences—forks created (Qe6 allows d5), pieces left hanging (Kb7 leaves Ng6, c5 leaves d4), self-obstruction (Qe7 blocks Bf8, h2+ shelters White king), or escape routes granted (Rg1+ without Nf5+ allows Kf7).
analysis.move_pattern: Mixed piece types and directions; no single geometric pattern. Moves tend to be forward/aggressive-looking (advances, checks, attacks on pieces) played when the position requires a different move entirely.
analysis.why_bad: Each move pursues a secondary plan while ignoring the one critical tactical requirement of the position, creating or exposing a concrete vulnerability (hanging piece, fork target, self-obstruction, or escape route) that the opponent exploits immediately.
sub_patterns: Premature checks without necessary preparation (wrong move order)
Abandoning a strong post to chase a superficial target
Self-blocking moves that obstruct own piece coordination
Pawn advances that leave pieces/squares undefended
Queen moves that create fork or pin targets

analysis.label: Quiet piece relocations that inadvertently create new tactical vulnerabilities (fork targets, mating squares, removed defenders, blocked escape routes) in positions with high tactical tension.
analysis.description: Across all 6 positions, the blundered moves are non-forcing piece relocations that appear natural or defensive but each creates a specific exploitable vulnerability. In 3/6 cases (Rh8, Kc6, Qf8), the moved piece lands on a square where it becomes a direct tactical target — Rh8 provides Qxh8# as a mating finish, Kc6 walks into Bb5+ discoveries, and Qf8 becomes a Ne6+ fork target. In 2/6 cases (Bb2, Rc1), the move removes a critical defender or blocks the king's escape — Bb2 abandons the e3 square allowing queen infiltration with mate threats, while Rc1 blocks the c1 escape square worsening diagonal check sequences. In 1/6 cases (Qb3), the premature queen commitment gives the opponent a key tempo to reorganize defenses. All positions had 2-3 good alternatives that addressed the tactical urgency (king evacuation, active counterplay, maintaining defensive coordination), but the player chose a quiet repositioning move instead.
analysis.move_pattern: Non-forcing piece relocations (no checks, no captures) — rook/king/bishop/queen moving to back rank squares, retreat squares, or apparently active diagonals
analysis.why_bad: Each move ignores the position's tactical urgency and places a piece on a square that becomes part of the opponent's tactical combination — either as a direct target (fork/mate square) or by removing a key defensive function, allowing the opponent a forcing sequence that was previously impossible.
sub_patterns: Piece moves to square where it becomes a mating/fork target (Rh8, Qf8, Kc6)
Piece vacates critical defensive post enabling opponent infiltration (Bb2 leaves e3 unguarded)
Piece blocks own king's escape route (Rc1 blocks c1 square)
Premature commitment gives opponent tempo for reorganization (Qb3 allows ...Bf8)

analysis.label: Moves that spend a tempo on a secondary objective while ignoring the position's most urgent demand (king safety, development, or a tactical vulnerability).
analysis.description: This feature fires on moves that pursue a plausible but non-urgent goal while the position critically demands addressing a specific vulnerability. In opening positions (6/11), players waste tempo on preparatory pawn moves (g6, e5, f4), misguided development (Bg4 twice, Bc4), or piece placement to passive squares (Na5) when immediate development or blocking a critical diagonal (especially f7/f2) was essential. In endgame positions (4/11), players move their king in the wrong direction (Kb7, Kc1, Kg8) or grab material that isn't truly free (Rxa7) instead of activating the king toward where it's needed. The common punishment involves the opponent exploiting the unaddressed weakness with concrete tactics—bishop sacrifices on f7 (positions 7, 9, 15), diagonal attacks (position 6), mating nets (position 10), or simply winning the misplaced piece (position 14). The average of only 2.3 good moves available confirms these are critical decision points where precision matters most.
analysis.move_pattern: Diverse piece types and directions—pawn pushes, bishop developments to exposed squares, knight retreats to rim, king moves away from center/safety—unified by moving to a square that serves a secondary purpose rather than the position's primary demand
analysis.why_bad: Each move ignores the position's single most critical requirement (usually defending f7/f2, completing development, or centralizing the king) in favor of a secondary plan, giving the opponent a free tempo to exploit the unaddressed vulnerability with forcing tactics
sub_patterns: Developing bishop to active-looking square while leaving f7 undefended (Bg4 x2, Bc4)
Preparatory pawn moves when piece development is urgent (g6, e5, f4)
King moving in wrong direction away from safety/activity (Kg8, Kb7, Kc1)
Piece/rook moving to tactically vulnerable square (Na5 rim, Rxa7 hanging)

analysis.label: Moving king or major piece to an exposed square that enables immediate forcing sequences (mates, perpetuals, pins) instead of addressing the critical defensive need.
analysis.description: In all 5 positions, the player makes a natural-looking repositioning move (often with the king) that voluntarily places a high-value piece on a tactically vulnerable square. In 3/5 cases the king itself moves to an exposed position (Kd4 into the center, Ke7 onto a diagonal target, Kf8 into a perpetual-check zone). In 1/5 the queen moves to e7 creating a pin vulnerability along the h4-e7 diagonal, and in 1/5 the bishop retreats to c7 ignoring the critical need to defend h7 and the e-file. All positions featured extremely narrow defensive paths (avg 1.2 good moves), and in each case the correct move addressed the most urgent safety concern (retreating to safety, defending a weakness, or challenging an opponent's strong piece) rather than repositioning. The punishments are all forcing sequences: forced mate in 2/5, perpetual check in 1/5, decisive pin in 1/5, and winning battery/file seizure in 1/5. All 5 share the 'king_safety' and 'tempo_loss' tags, confirming the pattern of wasting a critical tempo on an aesthetically reasonable but tactically catastrophic piece placement.
analysis.move_pattern: King, queen, or bishop moving to an undefended or exposed central/back-rank square (d4, e7, e7, c7, f8) where it becomes a target for checks, pins, or forcing sequences
analysis.why_bad: The piece voluntarily enters a square vulnerable to immediate tactical exploitation (diagonal pins, perpetual checks, mating nets), while the position demanded addressing a specific defensive priority - the one critical tempo is squandered on a misguided repositioning rather than the sole defensive resource
sub_patterns: King advances into center with no pawn cover, enabling queen mating nets
King/queen moves to e7 square exposed to dark-square diagonal attacks (Bg5+, Bh4 pin)
King moves to back rank square enabling perpetual check patterns
Passive piece retreat ignoring critical open-file or battery threats

analysis.label: Tempting aggressive moves (checks or captures) that result in the moving piece or a key piece becoming trapped with no escape squares.
analysis.description: This feature activates on positions where a player makes an aggressive-looking move—typically a check, capture, or space-gaining push—that ultimately leads to a piece being trapped or stranded. In 4/6 positions, the explicit tactical motif is 'trapped_piece': positions 1&2 feature queen checks (Qa4+) that drive the opponent's king toward safety while the queen runs out of checking squares and is captured on f1; position 3 (Bxa2) places the bishop on a corner square where b3+Ra1 entombs it; position 5 (a5) wastes a tempo allowing c4 to trap the d5 knight. Position 4 (Rxf2) overloads the queen leaving the knight hanging, and position 6 (Qf8+) places the queen on a back-rank square lacking follow-up threats, allowing the opponent's counter-tactics to equalize. The common thread is that the piece moves to an apparently attractive square (edge, corner, or check square) but lacks subsequent escape routes or useful continuations, while the opponent has a clear punishing response exploiting the stranded piece.
analysis.move_pattern: Piece (usually queen or bishop) moves aggressively to edge/corner square (a-file, 1st/8th rank) via check or capture, ending up with limited escape squares
analysis.why_bad: The piece reaches a square where it runs out of safe follow-up squares—either trapped by pawns/rooks controlling its escape diagonals, or left without productive checking/attacking continuations, allowing the opponent to win material or neutralize the advantage.
sub_patterns: Queen gives check sequence that dead-ends on 1st/8th rank where it is captured (positions 1&2)
Bishop captures pawn on corner square (a2) and is entombed by b3+Ra1 (position 3)
Tempo-wasting pawn move allows opponent to challenge and trap a centralized piece (position 5)
Queen check to wrong square lacks follow-up threats enabling defensive counter-tactics (position 6)

analysis.label: Playing a quiet, natural-looking move (often a pawn push or passive piece move) when the position critically demands immediate active play, a forcing capture, or a tactical strike.
analysis.description: This feature fires on positions where the player defaults to a 'routine' or 'autopilot' move—one that looks reasonable in the abstract position type—while missing the specific urgent demand of the concrete position. In 5/8 cases the blunder is a pawn push (b5, b4, d5, h6, hxg4) chosen over critical piece activation or tactics. In 2/8 cases a hanging piece or free pawn capture was missed in favor of a passive alternative (Qd8 missing Qxd6; d5 missing Bxc6). In 1/8 case a piece was misdirected to a passive square (Rc8 in front of passed pawns). The unifying thread is tempo loss (tagged in 7/8 positions) and insufficient piece activity (tagged in 8/8 positions). The best moves consistently involve immediate active operations—captures of undefended material, piece activation to dominant squares, or forcing moves that exploit the position's tactical features—while the played moves address secondary concerns (prophylaxis, space-gaining, structural ideas) that the position cannot afford.
analysis.move_pattern: Quiet pawn advances (b5, b4, d5, h6), passive retreats (Qd8), wrong captures (hxg4), or piece moves to suboptimal squares (Rc8, Rxh6) when forcing alternatives exist
analysis.why_bad: These moves waste a critical tempo on non-urgent concerns while the position demands immediate active play—either capturing hanging material, activating pieces to dominant squares, or opening key lines. The opponent is given time to consolidate, activate, or execute their own plan, causing the window for the best continuation to close permanently.
sub_patterns: Pawn push when piece activation is critical (b4, h6, b5)
Missing a free capture of hanging material (Qd8 missing Qxd6, d5 missing Bxc6)
Greedy material grab that deflects a key piece (Rxh6 deflecting rook from f6)
Wrong capture that fails to open the critical file (hxg4 instead of fxg4)
Piece placement violating positional principles under time pressure (Rc8 in front of passed pawns)

analysis.label: Knight (or minor piece) makes an aggressive jump to attack an enemy piece or weak square in the opening, but lands on an undefended square or abandons a critical defensive duty.
analysis.description: This feature fires on positions where a player launches a premature attacking piece sortie—almost always a knight jump—during the opening phase. The most common pattern (5/9) involves a knight jumping to a rim square (h4, h5, g4, a5) to attack an enemy bishop, but landing completely undefended where the opponent's queen can simply capture it along an open diagonal. In 3/9 cases (Nh4 x3), the knight moves from f3 to h4 targeting a bishop on f5, but the queen captures via the d8-h4 diagonal. In other cases (2/9), the knight abandons its defensive post (Nc6) to jump aggressively (Na5, Nd4), leaving the e5 pawn undefended and allowing immediate capture. The remaining cases (2/9) involve unsound piece sacrifices on f7 (Bxf7+, Nxf7) without sufficient supporting pieces developed. All 9/9 positions occur in the opening with both kings still in the center, and the average cp_loss of 367 confirms these are severe blunders uniformly motivated by attacking a target while ignoring that the attacking piece itself is vulnerable.
analysis.move_pattern: Knight (occasionally bishop) jumps aggressively forward to rim or exposed square (h4, h5, g4, a5, d4, f7) to attack enemy piece or weak point; no capture on the move in most cases (7/9 are non-capturing knight moves)
analysis.why_bad: The attacking piece lands on or moves to a square where it is completely undefended, allowing simple capture (usually by the queen along an open diagonal), or the move removes a piece from a critical defensive role (guarding e5/central pawn), allowing the opponent to win material immediately with a simple recapture or tactical blow.
sub_patterns: Nh4/Nh5 attacking bishop on f5/f4, queen captures along open diagonal
Na5/Nd4 abandoning defense of e5 pawn, allowing Nxe5 or Bxf7+ tactics
Ng4 attacking f2 but hanging to Qxg4 on open diagonal
Unsound sacrifice on f7 (Bxf7+/Nxf7) without supporting piece development

analysis.label: Superficially active or aggressive moves that waste critical tempo by failing to address the position's singular urgent requirement.
analysis.description: This feature activates on positions where the player makes a move that appears purposeful—giving a check (Nb2+, 1/7), advancing a pawn aggressively (h5, b6, 2/7), centralizing a piece (Qd2, Qe3, Rb2, 3/7), or 'improving' the king (Kh3, 1/7)—but which fundamentally wastes tempo in a position demanding precision. In 6/7 positions, only 1-2 good moves exist (avg 1.4), making these critical decision points. The common thread is that each move looks active but accomplishes nothing toward the position's primary task: blockading a passed pawn (b6 ignores d5-d6), maintaining piece pressure (Rb2 releases pressure on e3), executing a winning combination (Qe3 misses Qxa7+ mate), or converting efficiently (Nb2+ returns knight to its starting square after two moves). The opponent exploits the wasted tempo to advance their own plan—pushing passed pawns, centralizing their king, or neutralizing threats.
analysis.move_pattern: Varied piece types moving to seemingly active squares (checks, attacks on pawns, centralizing moves) that do not address the position's primary strategic/tactical requirement
analysis.why_bad: Each move wastes a critical tempo in a position where only 1-2 continuations work, allowing the opponent to execute their primary plan (advance a passed pawn, centralize their king, liquidate favorably with tempo) or neutralize the player's advantage
sub_patterns: Pointless checks where piece returns to original square (Nb2+-Ka3-Nc4+-Ka2)
Pawn advances that ignore opponent's passed pawn threat (b6 ignoring d5-d6)
Piece relocations that abandon critical pressure (Rb2 releasing e3 pressure, Qe3 abandoning c5)
King moves that must immediately be reversed (Kh3 then Kg2)
Aggressive pawn pushes that allow forced liquidation with tempo (h5 allowing fxg6+ and gxh5+)

analysis.label: Quiet developing or repositioning moves that waste a critical tempo in positions demanding immediate concrete action.
analysis.description: This feature fires on positions where a player makes a natural-looking, non-forcing move (piece repositioning, preparatory pawn advance, or seemingly active development) while ignoring an urgent tactical or strategic requirement. In 12/13 positions, the core tag is 'tempo_loss' — the move gives the opponent exactly the time needed to exploit a vulnerability. The positions share a common structure: there exists either a critical pawn break available (f6 in position 5, g4 in position 10), an undefended square/piece needing protection (f7 in positions 2, 3, 6; e5 in position 12), or an opponent's king safety issue that must be exploited immediately (positions 5, 9). Instead of seizing the moment, the played moves prepare future plans (fianchetto setups with g6/b6, bishop repositioning to Bg4/Be4/Bc6/Ba5, knight centralizing with Nd4/Nxc6) that would be fine in quiet positions but here squander the window of opportunity. The opponent then uses the gifted tempo to castle to safety (positions 3, 5), execute a tactical blow (Bxf7+ in positions 3, 6), or seize permanent positional advantage through central expansion (positions 10, 13).
analysis.move_pattern: Quiet non-forcing moves: bishop slides to seemingly active squares (Bg4, Be4, Bc6, Ba5), preparatory pawn pushes (g6, g3, b6, c4), or knight repositioning (Nd4, Nxc6) — all lacking checks, captures, or direct threats
analysis.why_bad: These moves waste a critical tempo in positions where the opponent has a specific vulnerability (exposed king, hanging piece, weak pawn) or where an immediate concrete action (pawn break, piece sacrifice, forcing move) would maintain/exploit the advantage. The gifted tempo allows the opponent to neutralize the vulnerability — castling to safety, completing development, or executing a tactical refutation that wasn't possible one move earlier.
sub_patterns: Preparatory pawn moves (g6, b6, g3, c4) that weaken structure or remove defenders while ignoring tactical obligations
Bishop repositioning to active-looking but wrong squares (Bg4, Be4, Bc6, Ba5) that ignore f7 weakness or urgent pawn breaks
Knight maneuvers (Nd4, Nxc6) that remove pieces from critical defensive duties or waste tempi on round-trips
Rook moves (Re8) that abandon defense of critical squares

analysis.label: Quiet, non-forcing repositioning moves in tactically demanding positions where only one or two precise moves prevent catastrophic loss of advantage.
analysis.description: This feature fires on positions where the player makes a passive, non-forcing move (retreat, quiet repositioning, or slow development) when the position urgently demands either a concrete tactical blow or precise prophylaxis. In 9/9 positions, the move played was quiet (no check, no capture, no direct threat) while the best move was either forcing (Bxe6 in pos 7, f4 in pos 1, Bb3 in pos 3) or addressed a critical vulnerability. The average good moves available was only 1.8, indicating these are razor-sharp moments with essentially one correct path. In 7/9 cases, the move is explicitly tagged as 'tempo_loss' — the player wastes a move on reorganization while the opponent gains a decisive tactical blow. King moves feature prominently (Ke2, Kf7, Kf8 — 3/9), as do piece retreats/shuffles (Ne2, Qe8, Rc6 — 3/9), and non-committal quiet moves (e3, Rc4 — 2/9). The refutations typically exploit the abandoned defensive duty or vacated square control to win material through forks, deflections, or file-opening sequences.
analysis.move_pattern: Quiet, non-capturing, non-checking moves — often king steps, piece retreats, or lateral repositioning — that fail to address the position's critical tactical demand
analysis.why_bad: These moves waste a critical tempo in positions requiring immediate action, allowing the opponent to execute a forcing tactical sequence (fork, deflection, file-opening combination) that the correct move would have prevented or preempted
sub_patterns: King moves (Ke2/Kf7/Kf8) exposing the king to tactical motifs like checks, forks, or diagonal attacks
Piece retreats (Ne2/Qe8) abandoning control of critical squares the opponent immediately occupies
Rook repositioning (Rc4/Rc6) leaving a defensive post unguarded, allowing material-winning combinations
Quiet pawn moves (e3) when a forcing sacrifice or tactical blow was available

analysis.label: Moves that waste a critical tempo by addressing a secondary objective before the time-sensitive primary task in endgames.
analysis.description: In 6/6 positions, the player squanders a decisive tempo by prioritizing a less urgent concern over the truly time-critical task. In Position 4, h4 pushes a pawn instead of activating the king (Kd1). In Position 6, Kd4 grabs at a pawn without first preparing with ...a6. In Position 7, Kb3 chases the a3 pawn before securing the kingside with f3. In Position 9, dxc3 creates a passed pawn the opponent can blockade instead of immediately advancing the king. In Position 12, Kc7 blockades a pawn the rook already controls instead of sending the king kingside. In Position 13, Kg6 prepares pawn support when h6 needed to be pushed immediately in a pawn race. All 6/6 positions involve razor-sharp timing where one tempo determines the outcome, and all 6/6 feature the player choosing to address something that could wait (or was already handled) while neglecting the action that could not wait.
analysis.move_pattern: King moves toward a secondary objective (wrong flank/already-defended pawn) or pawn moves replacing urgent king activation; diverse piece types but consistently directed away from the time-critical sector
analysis.why_bad: In endgames with razor-thin tempo margins, addressing a secondary concern (capturing a distant pawn, blockading an already-blockaded pawn, making preparatory moves before a forced race) costs exactly the one tempo needed to accomplish the truly decisive task—typically king infiltration defense, pawn race promotion, or prophylactic pawn structure fixes.
sub_patterns: King marches toward less-urgent pawn instead of contesting critical sector (Kb3, Kc7, Kd4)
Preparatory king move before pawn push when immediate push wins the race (Kg6 instead of h6)
Pawn push or capture instead of urgent king centralization (h4, dxc3)

analysis.label: Playing a non-forcing or positional move when the position demands an immediate concrete tactical action through a narrow window of opportunity.
analysis.description: This feature fires on positions where a single critical forcing move exists (avg 1.8 good moves) but the player instead chooses a quiet, slow, or imprecise alternative.
