In 8/11 positions, a forcing tactic (check, sacrifice, or winning capture) was available but missed: Bxh2+ Greek Gift (Position 3), Bxa8 capturing a hanging rook (Position 14), Qh5+ exploiting an exposed king (Position 15), Nxg6 initiating a forced combination (Position 1), Nxe4 winning a pawn (Position 13). In 9/11 positions the opponent's king was exposed or vulnerable, creating a narrow tactical window. The played moves are characteristically 'reasonable-looking' alternatives—quiet development (Be7, Be4), structural pawn moves (d5, c4, h4), speculative piece relocations (Ng5, Ng4, Qb4), or misguided defensive moves (Rf1)—that fail because they waste the critical tempo needed to exploit the position's concrete features. The average cp_loss of 340 reflects positions where the difference between the ONE right move and any alternative is enormous.
analysis.move_pattern: Diverse piece types (knights, bishops, rooks, pawns, queens) making non-forcing moves—quiet centralization, pawn advances, piece repositioning, or greedy captures away from the critical sector—instead of the available check, sacrifice, or forcing capture.
analysis.why_bad: These moves waste the one tempo that the position's tactical window allows. The opponent either escapes king danger (castles to safety), consolidates a weakness, or gains counterplay that was previously unavailable. The position's concrete advantage evaporates because it depended on immediate forcing action, not gradual improvement.
sub_patterns: Quiet development move missing a sacrifice/combination (Be7, Be4)
Slow structural pawn push ignoring forcing checks against exposed king (c4, d5)
Speculative knight aggression abandoning a critical defensive or attacking function (Ng5, Ng4)
Greedy capture removing a piece from its attacking post (Rxc2)
Wrong move order executing a sequence's later move first (Nxd6, h4)

analysis.chip: Passive piece retreat to inferior square
analysis.label: Retreating an active piece (predominantly a knight) to a passive or starting square when the position demands maintaining or increasing activity.
analysis.description: In 8/10 positions, the blunder involves retreating a knight from an active or functional square to a clearly inferior one: Ne1 (f3→e1), Ng1 (e2→g1, starting square), Ne2 (g3→e2), Nd1 (c3→d1, back rank), Nd2 (e4→d2, abandoning outpost), Nb1 (b3→b1, starting square), Nh2 (f3→h2, rim). The remaining cases involve a rook abandoning the powerful 7th rank (Rf8 retreating from f7, Rf7 sliding laterally from e7) and one bishop placement to an undefended square (Ba6). In every case, the best move required maintaining or increasing piece activity—typically the same piece needed to leap forward to an aggressive outpost (Ne5 in positions 1 and 15, Rxd6 in position 4, Nc5 in position 12, Nd4 in position 14, Na4 in position 13). The average cp_loss of 279 reflects how severely these tempo-wasting retreats are punished. All 10 positions are middlegame, and 9/10 are White moves, suggesting a defensive/consolidation mindset misapplied in positions requiring initiative.
analysis.move_pattern: Piece (predominantly knight) retreats backward toward own back rank, starting square, or rim; also rook retreating from 7th rank
analysis.why_bad: The retreat wastes critical tempo and abandons piece activity precisely when the position demands forward action, allowing the opponent to seize the initiative, activate their own pieces, or execute concrete tactical threats that the retreated piece can no longer prevent or counter.
sub_patterns: Knight retreats to back rank or starting square (Ng1, Nd1, Nb1, Ne1)
Knight abandons central outpost for passive square (Nd2 from e4, Ne2 from g3)
Knight retreats to rim (Nh2 from f3)
Rook abandons dominant 7th-rank placement (Rf8, Rf7 from e7)

analysis.label: Bishop develops to g4 or g5 in the opening where it is undefended or insufficiently protected, hanging to immediate captures or remove-the-defender tactics.
analysis.description: All 8 positions involve a bishop moving to g4 (6/8) or g5 (2/8) during the opening phase where the piece is tactically vulnerable. In 4/8 cases, the bishop is completely undefended and immediately capturable by a queen (Qxg4/Qxg5) or knight already controlling that square (Nxg4). In 2/8 cases, the bishop's sole defender (typically a knight on f6) can be removed with a forcing capture-check, leaving the bishop hanging. In the remaining 2/8 cases, intermediate forcing moves (Nxf3+ or Bxf6) exploit the bishop's lack of protection through tactical sequences. Players typically intend these moves as 'developing with purpose'—pinning an anticipated Nf3, pressuring the queen along a diagonal—but the pin or pressure doesn't actually exist because the expected target piece isn't there, or a piece already controls the destination square.
analysis.move_pattern: Bishop (either color) moves to the g-file 4th or 5th rank (g4 for Black, g5 for White) as a development move in the opening
analysis.why_bad: The bishop lands on g4/g5 without adequate protection—either completely undefended, or defended only by one piece that can be forcibly removed—allowing immediate material loss through simple captures or remove-the-defender tactics
sub_patterns: Bishop directly hangs to a knight already on e5 controlling g4 (Nxg4)
Bishop hangs to queen with clear diagonal access (Qxg4/Qxg5)
Bishop's sole defender (Nf6) removed with check (Nxf6+) leaving bishop en prise
Intermediate forcing move (Nxf3+/Bxf6) removes coordination before capturing the bishop

analysis.label: Black makes a seemingly reasonable but misguided move that abandons the position's most important strategic demand, allowing the opponent a tempo-gaining or position-transforming response.
analysis.description: In all 3/3 positions, Black had a clear winning or best plan involving central/active play (exploiting a passed pawn and piece activity in Position 4, maintaining central king flexibility in Position 6, and queen infiltration via the open d-file in Position 14), but instead chose a move that addressed a secondary concern or pursued a suboptimal goal. In each case, the chosen move (f6, Kb7, Bg4) created a specific exploitable weakness or lost critical tempo: 3/3 positions show the opponent gaining a powerful response that wasn't available before (queen invasion via f7 after f6 weakens the diagonal, e5 creating an unstoppable passed pawn after Kb7 abandons the center, f3 chasing the bishop with tempo enabling Nxh5). The correct moves in all cases were notably more active and directly addressed the position's primary demand: Nc5/e2 pushing the initiative, Kd7 maintaining central flexibility, Qd3 infiltrating the open file.
analysis.move_pattern: Various Black piece types (pawn, king, bishop) moving to squares that seem natural/prophylactic but are tactically exploitable, typically away from the position's critical theater of operations
analysis.why_bad: The moves abandon the position's most critical strategic demand (passed pawn advancement, central king activity, open file exploitation) for a secondary objective, while simultaneously creating a concrete weakness or tempo opportunity that the opponent immediately exploits with a forcing response
sub_patterns: Pawn advance weakening king shelter when initiative is elsewhere
King moving to wrong flank when central flexibility is required
Bishop relocation to attackable square when infiltration on open file is available

analysis.label: Aggressive pawn advances (mostly a- or h-file) that waste a critical tempo while ignoring immediate tactical threats or superior piece moves.
analysis.description: All 5 positions feature non-capturing pawn advances to the 3rd or 6th rank (a3, e6, h6, h6, a3) aimed at disrupting the opponent's pawn structure or king shelter. In 4/5 cases the push is on the a- or h-file (rook pawn). Every move attempts to create threats on one wing while a concrete tactical shot exists elsewhere: Position 7 allows Nxf6 winning a piece (5/5 tempo loss), Position 11 allows Black to seize the center with d4 (premature sacrifice), Position 12 misses Nh4 trapping a bishop, Position 13 ignores central tension with king uncastled, and Position 15 allows Nxf7+ queen-winning fork. All analyses tag 'tempo_loss' and 'missed_tactic' (5/5), and 4/5 tag 'premature_attack' or 'king_safety'. The moves share the psychological signature of prioritizing a slow structural plan over an immediate concrete need.
analysis.move_pattern: Single-square pawn advance on the a-file or h-file (or deep e-file push to 6th rank), non-capture, directed toward opponent's king or queenside shelter
analysis.why_bad: These pawn advances waste a tempo on a slow structural/attacking plan while the position demands immediate tactical action—either exploiting an existing opportunity (trapped piece, fork, piece maneuver) or defending against a concrete threat that the opponent can now execute.
sub_patterns: a-pawn thrust against queenside-castled king ignoring central/tactical vulnerability
h-pawn advance for kingside attack missing superior piece tactics
premature central pawn sacrifice before completing development

analysis.label: Choosing a slow, non-forcing piece redeployment or positional move when the position demands an immediate concrete tactical strike or central break.
analysis.description: This feature fires on positions where the player selects a quiet piece maneuver, retreat, or non-urgent repositioning move when a sharp, forcing continuation was critically available. In 8/8 positions, the best move was a concrete tactical action (captures like Bxh6, Bxe5, Qxd6; central breaks like e5 or d4; or forcing attacks like Ng5), while the actual move played was invariably non-forcing—piece shuffles (Ne2, Ng4, Ng5 to wrong square), bishop retreats (Bh4, Bd2), premature pawn advances (g4), or passive king moves (Kf2). The positions typically feature a narrow tactical window (avg 1.4 good moves available) where only 1-2 moves maintain the advantage, and the slow alternative allows the opponent to equalize or seize the initiative. The common thread across all analyses is 'tempo_loss' (tagged in 7/8 positions) and 'missed_tactic' (7/8 positions)—the player's move looks reasonable in isolation but catastrophically wastes the one critical tempo needed to exploit a concrete vulnerability.
analysis.move_pattern: Non-forcing piece redeployments (knight hops, bishop retreats to passive squares, king shuffles, or slow pawn advances) that create no immediate threat, replacing an available forcing capture, sacrifice, or central pawn break
analysis.why_bad: The position has a narrow tactical window requiring immediate concrete action; the quiet move wastes the critical tempo, allowing the opponent to neutralize threats, counterattack in the center, or exploit newly created weaknesses (exposed pieces, abandoned defense of key squares, lost initiative)
sub_patterns: Knight redeployment to aggressive-looking but achievementless square (Ng5, Ng4) when central break available
Bishop retreat from active post when tactical capture/sacrifice wins (Bh4 instead of Bxh6, Bd2 instead of Bxe5)
Passive king move addressing minor threat while ignoring winning tactical continuation
Wrong piece captures the target (Nxd6 vs Qxd6), leaving other pieces exposed
Premature flank pawn advance with king uncastled when central break demands attention

analysis.label: Slow preparatory pawn moves or passive king retreats that squander a decisive tempo in razor-thin endgame positions where immediate king activation was required.
analysis.description: This feature fires on endgame positions (9/10) where the player makes a non-forcing, non-urgent move—typically a peripheral pawn push or passive king retreat—when the position demanded immediate, decisive action (usually aggressive king centralization). In 8/10 cases the blunder is a pawn move (h3, h4, f4, f5, b3, a4, a6, g6) and in 2/10 cases it's a passive king retreat (Ke7, Kg7). The correct moves were overwhelmingly king activations toward critical squares: Kf5 in pos.1, Kc4 in pos.3, Kg3 in pos.4, Kf4 in pos.5, Kh5 in pos.10, Ke4 in pos.11, and Kd6 in pos.15. The average number of good moves available was only 1.7, indicating these are narrow positions where precision is essential. The average cp_loss of 288 confirms these are catastrophic errors—often converting wins to draws or draws to losses—because a single wasted tempo allows the opponent to establish a fortress (pos.15, pos.2), create/advance passed pawns (pos.1, pos.3), lock the pawn structure favorably (pos.4), or achieve critical king infiltration (pos.7, pos.11).
analysis.move_pattern: Non-capturing, non-checking pawn advances (usually one square, on a flank away from the critical action) or king retreats moving away from optimal active squares
analysis.why_bad: In endgame positions where the outcome is determined by a single tempo, these moves waste that tempo on non-urgent tasks (prophylaxis on a frozen wing, preparatory moves, or passive retreats), allowing the opponent to establish a defensive blockade, seize key squares, or advance decisive passed pawns before the player can act
sub_patterns: Irrelevant flank pawn push when king centralization is critical (h3, h4, a4, a6)
Premature pawn advance that creates a fixed target or blocks own king (f4, f5, b3)
Passive king retreat away from active attacking square (Ke7 instead of Kf5, Kg7 instead of Kh5)
Non-forcing pawn move giving opponent tempo for king infiltration (g6)

analysis.label: Moves that attempt to address a positional concern using the wrong piece or approach, leaving the actual critical vulnerability unresolved.
analysis.description: This feature fires on moves that appear defensively motivated but fatally misidentify which piece should execute the plan. In 3/9 cases, the correct move was sending a DIFFERENT piece to the same or nearby square (Position 1: Rf2 instead of Kf2; Position 8: Rf2 instead of Bf2; Position 7: Rf7 when Kd7 was needed). In 3/9 cases, the king retreats or moves in the wrong direction when it should advance or go the opposite way (Kd5 instead of Kf3, Kg1 instead of Ke2, Kg3 instead of Ke5). In 2/9 cases, a piece is moved away from its strong post leaving it or another piece undefended (Nb7 leaving itself hanging, d3 not supporting the knight on e5). The common thread is that each move looks purposeful—defending a square, centralizing, or retreating to apparent safety—but addresses the wrong problem while the actual tactical threat (a pin, hanging piece, mating attack, or promotion race) goes unmet.
analysis.move_pattern: Piece moves to a seemingly useful defensive/repositioning square, often the same square or adjacent to where the correct piece belongs, typically non-capturing and non-checking
analysis.why_bad: The move leaves a critical tactical vulnerability unaddressed—either a piece remains undefended (3/9 hanging piece), creates a new pin/weakness (2/9), walks into a mating net (1/9), or loses a decisive tempo in a pawn race (2/9)—because the player used the wrong piece or moved in the wrong direction to address the position's actual demands.
sub_patterns: Rook goes to square where king or bishop needed to be (f2)
King retreats when it should advance toward critical action
Piece leaves dominant outpost to unprotected square
Defensive rook move when king evacuation was required
Quiet pawn move ignoring tactical emergency

analysis.label: Non-progressive moves in technically won endgames that fail to execute the winning plan, losing tempo by repositioning pieces without restricting the opponent or advancing passed pawns.
analysis.description: This feature fires on moves in won endgames that waste time instead of executing the correct winning technique. The dominant pattern is tempo loss: 12/14 positions are explicitly tagged with 'tempo_loss' as the primary motif. In KR vs K endgames (positions 1, 2, 3, 4, 6, 9), the error is typically moving the rook to a passive square (Ra8, Rb8, Rh3) that abandons a critical rank or file cut-off, or moving the king when the rook should restrict first. In pawn-race positions (10, 11, 12), the error is making a non-forcing piece move (Bf1, Ke3, Qb8) instead of immediately advancing the winning passed pawn. In positions with material dominance (5, 14, 15), the error is giving purposeless checks (Nc2+, Qd1+) or retreating active pieces (Qc8) that allow the opponent to improve their position for free. All 14 positions are endgames, and the average of 2.4 good moves available confirms these are positions where the winning technique demands specific action rather than flexible maneuvering.
analysis.move_pattern: Any piece type moving to a passive or non-restrictive square; often rooks to corner/back rank, kings sideways instead of forward, or pieces giving non-forcing checks
analysis.why_bad: These moves fail to make progress toward the conversion goal—they don't restrict the opponent's king, don't advance passed pawns, and don't maintain optimal piece coordination. The opponent gains a free tempo to escape restriction, centralize their king, or improve defensive coordination, extending the game significantly or even losing the forced win.
sub_patterns: Rook abandons rank/file cut-off in KR vs K (Ra8, Rb8, Rh3)
King moves when pawn advancement is urgent (Ke3, Kg5, Bf1)
Purposeless checks that improve opponent's king position (Nc2+, Qd1+)
Active piece retreats to passive square losing initiative (Qc8, Qb8)

analysis.label: Moves that appear active or purposeful but catastrophically ignore the single most urgent defensive or tactical requirement in the position.
analysis.description: This feature fires on moves where the player makes a seemingly constructive or active decision—centralizing a king (Kd6, Kc4, Ke2), pushing a flank pawn (h4), contesting a file (Re8), or rerouting a piece (Bc8)—while completely ignoring the one critical tactical or positional requirement that the position demands. In 5/6 positions, the move enables an immediate concrete tactical punishment: a skewer on the c-file (Kc4), a mating attack via diagonals (Ke2), capture of a hanging piece on an open file (Re8 allows Rxe7), exploitation of an overloaded defender (h4 allows Rd6-Rxd3-Nxd3), or an unstoppable passed pawn (Kd6 abandons d4 blockade). In 6/6 positions, the best moves address a specific urgent issue (evacuate a bishop, blockade a pawn, trade queens, avoid exposed squares) that the played move ignores entirely. The average cp_loss of 1841 reflects that these aren't marginal inaccuracies but catastrophic oversights where the player's attention was directed at the wrong aspect of the position.
analysis.move_pattern: Mixed piece types (king 3/6, bishop 1/6, rook 1/6, pawn 1/6) moving to squares that create or maintain tactical vulnerabilities—typically advancing/relocating to squares that produce fatal alignments on open files or diagonals
analysis.why_bad: Each move ignores the single most critical concrete requirement in the position (defending a hanging piece, blockading a passer, avoiding a skewer/mating pattern), allowing the opponent an immediate decisive tactical exploitation that the 'active' move fails to prevent or even worsens
sub_patterns: King advancing into tactical alignment (skewer/mating net)
Piece retreating from active post abandoning critical pressure
Slow pawn push ignoring hanging/overloaded piece
Contesting a file while leaving another piece tactically unprotected

analysis.label: Playing quiet preparatory or repositioning moves when the position demands immediate tactical action or addressing a critical vulnerability.
analysis.description: This feature fires on moves that look 'natural' or 'improving' in isolation but catastrophically ignore the position's most urgent demand. In 10/12 positions, the best alternative involved either an active capture (Qxf5, cxb6, Rxb1), immediate development to address a concrete threat (Nc6 blocking a diagonal, Nf6 defending kingside, O-O for king safety), or creating an immediate forcing threat (Qa5 with check invasion). Instead, the played moves are passive preparations (b3, c6, Rb1), pawn weakeners (g6, g3, f6, c4), piece repositions to 'better' squares that remove critical defenders (Be3 abandoning b2, Be5 abandoning g7/h6), or routine moves that ignore specific threats (O-O ignoring c2, Rad8 choosing wrong rook). In 8/12 cases, the refutation directly exploits a weakness created or exposed by the tempo wasted. The average cp_loss of 259 confirms these are severe errors despite the moves appearing reasonable at a superficial level.
analysis.move_pattern: Diverse piece types and directions - pawn pushes (6/12), piece repositions (4/12), rook lifts (2/12), castling (1/12) - all sharing the quality of being non-forcing and non-addressing of the position's critical tactical demand
analysis.why_bad: These moves waste a critical tempo in positions where an immediate tactical vulnerability exists or concrete action is required, allowing the opponent to execute a tactical blow (diagonal exploitation, fork, removal of defender, pawn breakthrough) that the slow move failed to prevent or preempt.
sub_patterns: Pawn moves that weaken key squares/diagonals (g6, g3, f6, c4 - weakening light squares, king diagonals, or abandoning defense of key squares)
Piece moves that remove critical defenders (Be3 leaving b2 unguarded, Be5 leaving h6/dark squares exposed)
Slow rook repositions when immediate forcing play is available (Ra1/Rb1/Rad8 instead of queen activity or castling)
Passive blocking instead of active capturing (c6 instead of cxb6, f6 instead of Qxf5)
Routine development ignoring specific tactical obligations (O-O into fork, Rb1 when castling urgent)

analysis.label: Moving a piece to an apparently natural/active square while ignoring the critical tactical demand of the position, allowing the opponent to gain decisive tempo or exploit a new vulnerability.
analysis.description: This feature fires on moves that look reasonable or aggressive to a human eye—approaching targets, capturing pawns, developing to open files, centralizing—but fatally ignore the specific concrete requirement of the position. In 5/9 positions, the piece moves toward the kingside/opponent's pawns when central action was needed (Kg4 vs Ke4, Kg5 vs Ke5, Qg5 vulnerable to h4, Qxg6 abandoning defense, Rd6 vs Rd7). In 6/9 positions, the move creates or ignores a tactical vulnerability that allows the opponent to win tempo or material (Kd4 blocks own rook enabling a skewer, Rae1 ignores the hanging knight on g3, Bb5 allows the pin Bg4, Qg5 walks into h4 tempo gain, Qxg6 leaves Re1 hanging). The common thread is choosing a 'natural-looking' move over one requiring concrete calculation of the position's tactical specifics. The average good moves available (2.2) confirms these are positions with narrow correct paths where superficial reasoning fails.
analysis.move_pattern: Piece (king, queen, rook, or bishop) moves to a square that appears active or aggressive—often toward opponent's weaknesses or onto open files—but is tactically misplaced relative to the position's concrete demands
analysis.why_bad: The move prioritizes apparent activity over the position's critical tactical requirement, either placing the piece where it becomes vulnerable to tempo-gaining attacks (h4 against Qg5, Rd5+ skewering Kd4/Rd1, Qc8+ separating king from Rd6) or ignoring an urgent threat that needed immediate attention (Rxg3 capturing undefended knight, Qh4 attacking abandoned rook)
sub_patterns: King marches toward wing pawns when central penetration was decisive (pawn endgames)
Piece placed on same file/rank as own piece, enabling skewer or fork
Queen/piece captures pawn while abandoning critical defensive coordination
Slow development move ignoring immediate hanging piece or tactical crisis
Piece moved to square vulnerable to a tempo-gaining pawn advance

analysis.label: Moving a piece away from a critical defensive duty or ignoring an existing checkmate threat, allowing immediate or near-immediate forced mate.
analysis.description: This feature fires on catastrophic blunders where the player makes a move that either removes a key defender from a critical post or completely ignores an existing mating threat. In 3/6 positions (Nh8, Rh3, dxe6), the blunder allows checkmate in exactly one move. In 4/6 positions, forced mate follows within a few moves (including Kf6 allowing mate in 22). The moves themselves often appear to have some surface logic—attacking a piece (Rh3 targeting Bf3), capturing material (dxe6), retreating defensively (Nh8), or giving check (Qd7+)—but all fatally neglect the single most critical requirement of the position: preventing checkmate or preserving the only defensive resource keeping the king alive. The positions are typically already difficult (avg 1.5 good moves available), meaning the margin for error is razor-thin, and the played move represents a complete failure to prioritize the most urgent threat.
analysis.move_pattern: Various piece types moving away from defensive posts or making irrelevant captures/checks while back-rank or king-proximity mate threats exist
analysis.why_bad: The move abandons the one piece or function preventing immediate checkmate—whether a rook guarding the back rank, a knight defending a key square near the castled king, or a bishop controlling an invasion square—or plays an irrelevant move while an existing mate-in-one threat goes unaddressed.
sub_patterns: Rook lifts off back rank allowing back-rank mate (Rh3 → Rd1#)
Piece abandons guard of square adjacent to king enabling queen mate (Nh8 removes g7 defense → Qxg7#)
Irrelevant pawn capture ignoring existing one-move checkmate (dxe6 ignores Qxb2#)
Piece moves from defensive post exposing king to forcing tactical sequence (Bf3 unguards d3)
King walks into checking pattern creating mating net (Kf6 allows Qd8+)

analysis.label: Playing a slow, non-forcing move (typically a pawn push or piece repositioning) when the position demands immediate attention to a concrete tactical threat or opportunity.
analysis.description: Across all positions, the player makes a move that looks superficially useful—gaining space, centralizing, capturing material, or advancing a passed pawn—but completely ignores the single most critical demand of the position. In 5/10 cases the blunder is a pawn push (h4, f6, a4, d2, b4) that addresses a secondary concern while a concrete tactical necessity goes unmet. In the remaining cases, piece moves pursue 'improvement' (Ka5 fleeing, Bxh4 grabbing material, Nf6/Nd4 repositioning, Be4 centralizing) while ignoring immediate checkmate threats (2/10), free captures available (1/10), hanging pieces (2/10), or activation opportunities for the opponent (3/10). The average cp_loss of 2026 reflects that these positions were critical moments where only 1-3 moves were acceptable, and the chosen move falls catastrophically outside that narrow window. The recurring theme in all refutations is that the opponent exploits the wasted tempo with an immediate concrete tactical blow—checkmate, fork, piece capture, or decisive activation.
analysis.move_pattern: Non-forcing moves (pawn advances to non-critical squares, piece repositioning away from critical sector, greedy captures of peripheral material) when the position contains an immediate tactical obligation
analysis.why_bad: The move wastes a critical tempo on a secondary goal while the position contains an immediate concrete demand—either a defensive necessity (preventing mate, protecting a piece) or an offensive opportunity (free capture, winning tactic)—that goes unaddressed, allowing the opponent to execute a punishing tactical blow on the very next move.
sub_patterns: Pawn push ignoring checkmate threat (Ka5, a4)
Peripheral capture ignoring strategic priority (Bxh4)
Pawn advance past capturable piece (f6 instead of fxe6)
Piece repositioning leaving tactical vulnerability (Nf6, Nd4)
Piece placement on undefended square allowing fork (Be4)
Premature passed pawn advance giving opponent tempo (d2)
Slow pawn push in sharp position requiring immediate action (b4, h4)

analysis.label: Active-looking moves that abandon a critical defensive or positional responsibility, allowing the opponent to gain decisive tempo or exploit the created weakness.
analysis.description: This feature fires on moves that appear aggressive or purposeful (knight sorties, captures, pawn advances) but fatally neglect a more important positional obligation. In 3/5 positions, a knight leaves a crucial post or arrives on a tactically vulnerable square (Nb4 abandons blockade on c6, Ne1 attacks pawns in wrong move order, Nf6 walks into capture with check). In 4/5 positions, the move directly creates a tempo-gaining opportunity for the opponent (a3 kicks the knight, Ke3 centralizes with tempo, Nxf6+ comes with check, Rxc4+ captures with check). In 5/5 cases, a more patient or defensive move (Be6, Kd4, Nd7, Qxc3, Kd3) would have preserved a critical structural or positional asset—blockade, passed pawn, king centralization—that the played move sacrificed for an illusory gain. The average cp_loss of ~1955 reflects that these 'active' moves often catastrophically misread the position's priorities.
analysis.move_pattern: Piece moves to an aggressive-looking but exposed/premature square (often knight sorties forward, captures, or pawn advances) rather than maintaining a key defensive post or proper move order
analysis.why_bad: The move abandons a critical positional responsibility (blockade, passed pawn defense, king centralization priority) for a short-term tactical idea, and the opponent exploits the abandoned duty or the piece's exposed placement to gain tempo and decisive material/positional advantage.
sub_patterns: Knight sortie to exposed square that gets kicked with tempo
Capture that surrenders a more valuable positional asset than what is gained
Pawn advance creating tactical vulnerability when king activity was needed
Correct tactical idea executed in wrong move order

analysis.label: Rook captures a piece in the endgame, simplifying the position when maintaining the rook's attacking activity would preserve a faster or more decisive win.
analysis.description: This feature fires on endgame positions where a rook captures a piece, leading to simplification/exchange. In 2/3 positions, the rook capture is a significant error because it trades away the rook's crucial attacking function: in Position 3, Rxc5 captures with the wrong piece (bishop should take, preserving the rook for a forced mate-in-5 against an exposed king), and in Position 7, Rxf8 captures the queen but allows gxf8 promotion with recapture, collapsing a mate-in-7 into a mere -552 pawn endgame. Position 5's Rxf7 is actually correct (the simplification IS the winning plan), suggesting the feature detects the structural pattern of rook-captures-piece-in-endgame rather than purely detecting errors. The common thread is that in positions with exposed kings and mating potential (2/3 positions), the rook's dynamic attacking value far exceeds the material gained by capturing, yet the player opts for the simplifying capture.
analysis.move_pattern: Rook captures a piece (knight, rook, or queen) on an open file in endgame positions, triggering material exchange and simplification
analysis.why_bad: The rook is the primary attacking/checking piece needed to exploit an exposed enemy king, and capturing with it allows the opponent to either recapture (neutralizing the attack) or promote/simplify, eliminating the mating geometry that required the rook's continued activity
sub_patterns: Rook captures when bishop should capture (wrong piece order)
Rook captures allowing pawn promotion recapture
Rook exchange simplifying a won mating attack into a technical grind

analysis.label: Playing a passive developing move or pawn push instead of a forcing check (usually Qa4+) that exploits the opponent's uncastled king to win material.
analysis.description: In 6/7 positions, the best move was a check (Qa4+ in 4/7, Qe1+ in 1/7, Bb5+ in 1/7) that exploited the opponent's king remaining in the center to win material—typically an undefended bishop on b4 or a piece forced to interpose. In all 7 positions, Black's king was still on e8. The played moves were uniformly quiet and non-forcing: passive bishop retreats (Bd3, Bb3, Bd2 in 3/7), pawn pushes that chase pieces or grab space (f3, f3, e4 in 3/7), or a defensive queen move (Qc2 in 1/7). The average number of good moves was only 1.3, indicating these are narrow tactical moments requiring precise calculation. The recurring Qa4+ pattern (4/7) specifically targets positions where Black has an undefended bishop on b4 pinning Nc3 while the king sits on e8—the check forces an interposition (usually ...Nc6 or ...c6), after which the hanging piece is captured.
analysis.move_pattern: Quiet non-forcing move (bishop retreat, pawn push, or queen defense) instead of a check along the a4-e8 diagonal or e-file
analysis.why_bad: The quiet move gives the opponent time to castle or consolidate, removing the tactical vulnerability (uncastled king + hanging piece) that the check would have exploited to win material immediately.
sub_patterns: Qa4+ exploiting undefended Bb4 with king on e8 (most common)
Queen check on e-file against uncastled king winning hanging piece on rim
Bishop check (Bb5+) forcing structural concessions before consolidation

analysis.label: Black plays a superficially logical or instinctive move (check, capture, promote, advance) that ignores the position's most critical urgency, losing decisive tempo.
analysis.description: This feature fires when Black selects a move that appears purposeful—promoting a pawn (a1=Q), capturing an attacking piece (Kxg7), giving check (Nc5+), advancing passed pawns (f5, b6), blockading (Rd5), or tucking the king to safety (Kg8)—but catastrophically misses the position's true priority. In 7/8 positions, the error is fundamentally a tempo loss: the 'obvious' action allows the opponent to seize the initiative with a tempo-gaining response (checks, pawn advances, piece attacks). In 5/8 positions, passed pawns are the critical factor being mishandled—either failing to advance them when racing (Rd5 instead of a4), creating them incorrectly (hxg4 before a1=Q), or failing to blockade them (Kg8 instead of Bf8-h6). In 5/8 positions, the correct move required addressing king safety or piece coordination before the 'natural' action. The common thread is that the played moves would be reasonable in a less urgent context but are wrong specifically because the position demands precise move-ordering, and one lost tempo converts winning/equal positions into lost ones.
analysis.move_pattern: Various piece types (pawns, knights, kings, rooks) making moves that look active or purposeful—checks, captures, promotions, advances—but ignoring a more urgent alternative
analysis.why_bad: The moves waste a critical tempo in time-sensitive positions (pawn races, mating attacks, blockade setups), allowing the opponent to advance passed pawns, activate pieces with tempo, or escape threats that were one move from decisive
sub_patterns: Promoting immediately when an intermediate capture creates a second passer
Capturing the wrong piece when a more valuable one hangs
Giving purposeless check that removes a piece from a mating net
Passive pawn advance that creates targets when active piece play was needed
King move to apparent safety when piece repositioning was urgent for blockade
Blockading with a piece when racing with pawns was critical

analysis.label: King moves backward or sideways instead of advancing to blockade an opponent's passed pawn in a pawn endgame.
analysis.description: This feature fires on endgame positions where the king retreats passively or steps sideways rather than occupying the critical blockading square directly in front of a passed pawn. In 10/11 positions the blunder is a king move, and in at least 8/11 cases the correct move required the king to advance toward or stand directly in front of a passed pawn (e.g., Ke2 blocking e3, Kf7 blocking f6, Ke7 blocking e6, Kf2 blocking f3, Kc3 blocking c4, Kd5 blocking c5/e5). The catastrophic examples (positions 1-4, 8) show draws converted to forced mates by abandoning the blockade square, while milder activations (positions 6, 9-12) show tempo losses that worsen already lost/won positions. The common thread is a king that retreats toward its own back rank or sidesteps off the pawn's file, violating the fundamental endgame principle that the defending king must blockade directly in the pawn's path.
analysis.move_pattern: King moves backward (toward own back rank) or laterally off the file of an enemy passed pawn, away from the critical blockading square
analysis.why_bad: In king-and-pawn endgames, the defending king MUST stand directly in front of a passed pawn to maintain blockade and opposition; any retreat or sidestep cedes the critical square, allowing the opponent's king to outflank or the pawn to advance with decisive tempo gain.
sub_patterns: King sidesteps off the pawn's file (Kf1 instead of Ke2, Kf8 instead of Ke7)
King retreats to back rank instead of advancing to blockade (Kc1 instead of Kc3, Kb1 instead of Kc2)
King retreats passively instead of challenging the pawn directly (Kd2 instead of Kd4)
King moves one square too far from optimal blockade (Kd7 instead of Kd5)

analysis.label: Playing a superficially reasonable move that wastes tempo by failing to address the position's single most urgent tactical or strategic requirement.
analysis.description: This feature fires on positions where the player makes a plausible-looking move—often appearing active or constructive—but completely misses the ONE specific action the position demands. In 6/8 positions, the best moves involve seizing a critical open file (Rad1, Rc1, Rf3) or executing a precise forcing sequence (Qc5+, d5, Nh4), while the played moves address secondary concerns: prophylactic king shuffles (Kg1, Kh1 in 2/8), superficial piece repositioning (Be3, Nd5, Bb4+ in 3/8), or premature/misdirected pawn advances (e5, c4, g4 in 3/8). The positions are characteristically narrow (avg 1.9 good moves), meaning the critical action is specific and non-obvious. In every case, the played move either destroys the player's key strategic asset (connected pawns in positions 2 and 8), removes a critical defensive/attacking piece from its ideal post (knight from e7 in position 9), or squanders the window for a decisive tactical blow (d-file occupation in position 12, Qc5+ combination in position 7, c-file contest in position 15). The common punishment pattern involves the opponent exploiting exactly what was left unaddressed—capturing an undefended pawn (Nxh5), delivering a check on the newly-exposed square (Qe3+), or consolidating a position that should have been hit with immediate force.
analysis.move_pattern: Diverse piece types and directions (king moves, pawn pushes, piece developments/checks); no single geometric pattern—the commonality is that the move addresses a secondary concern rather than the critical one
analysis.why_bad: The position demands one specific concrete action (seizing a file, executing a forcing combination, maintaining a structural asset, or addressing an immediate tactical tension), and the played move ignores this critical demand in favor of something that looks natural but is beside the point, typically losing a tempo that allows the opponent to consolidate, exploit a new weakness, or neutralize the advantage
sub_patterns: Premature pawn exchanges that destroy winning connected pawn structures
Quiet king moves that expose to immediate tactical punishment (checks/forks)
Piece repositioning that superficially attacks but misses a more forcing combination
Irrelevant pawn pushes that ignore the critical open file needing immediate contest
Moving a key piece from its ideal square to a seemingly strong but actually inferior post

analysis.label: Moves that appear purposeful or aggressive but directly create a concrete tactical vulnerability the opponent can immediately exploit.
analysis.description: This feature fires on moves that seem to accomplish something useful (attacking a piece, winning material, gaining space, centralizing) but actually self-inflict a tactical problem. In 8/8 positions, the played move itself is what ENABLES the opponent's refutation: f5 blocks the queen's own defensive path to g6 and enables Bh5+; Qc2 abandons kingside defense enabling Nf3+ forks; Qb7 abandons the Bxe4+ combination and leaves e5 undefended; Qb8+ lures the queen into a trap; Re5 leaves the a5 knight hanging to Nxa5; h5 weakens g6 enabling Nxg6; hxg4 opens the h-file into Black's doubled rooks enabling Rxh1; g4 leaves the pawn en prise to Bxg4. In all cases, a precise move (often tactical or prophylactic) was required instead, with only 1.5 good moves available on average. The positions are critical junctures where the player follows a plausible strategic rationale but ignores the concrete tactical reality.
analysis.move_pattern: Mixed piece types (pawns: f5/h5/g4/hxg4, queens: Qc2/Qb7/Qb8+, rook: Re5); typically advancing/repositioning toward seemingly useful squares or captures; no consistent direction but all are 'active-looking' moves
analysis.why_bad: Each move directly creates or exposes a concrete tactical vulnerability (hanging piece, open line into opponent's prepared forces, trapped piece, abandoned defensive alignment) that did not exist before the move was played, allowing the opponent an immediate tactical exploitation
sub_patterns: Pawn advances that weaken king position or leave the pawn itself hanging (f5, h5, g4, hxg4)
Queen moves to seemingly active squares that abandon critical defensive duties or enter traps (Qc2, Qb7, Qb8+)
Piece repositioning that leaves another piece undefended (Re5 abandoning knight on a5)

analysis.label: Playing a standard-looking piece development move when the position demands an immediate concrete tactical action like capturing hanging material or exploiting a specific vulnerability.
analysis.description: All three positions share the pattern of choosing a 'textbook' developing move (piece to a natural square) when the position urgently demanded concrete action. In position 6 (3/3), Bc4 develops the bishop to an active diagonal but ignores a completely hanging g5 pawn that Nxg5 wins with devastating follow-up. In position 3 (3/3), Qd7 appears to attack a vulnerable knight on c6 from a natural square, but Qc7/Qd6 attacked it from squares that properly handled the tactical interplay of pins and open files. In position 7 (3/3), Nc3 places a knight on its standard central development square but blocks the c-pawn, misplaces the piece where it gets driven to the rim, and ignores the bishop's vulnerability to ...e5. All three moves would be perfectly reasonable in generic positions but fail catastrophically because each position had a specific, forcing opportunity (capture, superior attack angle, or prophylactic requirement) that trumped general development principles. The average cp_loss of 253 reflects the severity of ignoring concrete demands.
analysis.move_pattern: Non-forcing piece development to a standard square (queen/bishop/knight to natural central or active squares) without captures or checks
analysis.why_bad: The position demands a specific concrete action (capturing hanging material, exploiting a tactical vulnerability, or addressing an immediate positional threat) but the player defaults to general development principles, giving the opponent time to consolidate or exploit the neglected tactical opportunity.
sub_patterns: Developing bishop to active diagonal while material hangs elsewhere
Moving queen to seemingly attacking square that tactically fails to concrete responses
Developing knight to standard square that blocks own pawns and gets driven away

analysis.label: Rook repositioning moves that abandon a key file, rank, or defensive duty, leaving pawns or squares tactically vulnerable.
analysis.description: In 5/6 positions, a rook is moved to a seemingly purposeful square but in doing so abandons a critical responsibility—whether defending a pawn, maintaining file control, or sustaining rank pressure. In Position 2, Rc6 leaves the powerful 2nd rank and abandons defense of the a7 pawn. In Position 3, Rg3 slides laterally along the 3rd rank but abandons the b-file where the rook was effectively cutting off the enemy king. In Position 6, Rg8 targets the g5 pawn which simply advances with g4, leaving the rook misplaced. In Position 7, Rb4 moves laterally from g4, abandoning the g-file and leaving the g5 pawn hanging to Rxg5. In Position 13, Rfd8 passively doubles on the d-file instead of creating immediate threats, gifting tempo for counterplay. The common thread (5/6 rook moves, 5/6 endgames) is repositioning that looks active or logical but concretely leaves something undefended that the opponent can immediately exploit.
analysis.move_pattern: Rook lateral or file repositioning away from a critical file/rank, typically along the same rank (b3→g3, g4→b4) or retreating/advancing along a file (c2→c6), abandoning defense of a pawn or critical square
analysis.why_bad: The rook abandons its current critical duty (defending a pawn, controlling a key file, maintaining rank pressure) for a less urgent purpose, allowing the opponent to immediately exploit the undefended target—either capturing a free pawn, advancing a targeted pawn away, or generating decisive counterplay in the vacated zone.
sub_patterns: Lateral rook slide along a rank that abandons a critical file (Rg3, Rb4)
Rook targets a mobile pawn that can simply advance away (Rg8 vs g5→g4)
Rook leaves active 2nd/7th rank position for a less threatening square (Rc6)
Passive rook doubling instead of immediate concrete threats (Rfd8)

analysis.label: Moves that pursue superficially attractive goals (material, attack, prophylaxis) while abandoning a critical positional or defensive requirement, enabling a devastating tactical refutation.
analysis.description: This feature fires on moves that look reasonable or even aggressive on the surface but fundamentally misidentify the position's primary demand. In 4/9 positions, the move was a greedy capture or pawn advance that displaced a well-placed piece from its optimal post (Rxb4 abandoning b2 dominance, Qxe4 abandoning rook protection, gxh3 choosing the wrong capturing unit, a7 pushing a pawn already blockaded). In 3/9 positions, the move was a speculative attacking gesture that left critical squares undefended (Qh6 abandoning c2 control, Qg4 creating a fork target, Nd5 losing tempi to refutation). In 2/9 positions, the move was a misguided piece relocation that ignored the position's urgent requirement (Kh8 walking into Rxh7+ sacrifice, Nh3 going to the rim when king centralization was essential). The average good moves available was only 1.7, confirming these are narrow critical moments requiring precision, yet players consistently chose the attractive-looking option over the one demanded by concrete calculation.
analysis.move_pattern: Piece moves toward opponent's camp or captures material, typically moving away from where it performs a critical function (defending a square, protecting another piece, maintaining centralization)
analysis.why_bad: The move abandons a critical defensive or positional function—protecting a piece, controlling a key square, maintaining a dominant placement, or addressing the position's primary requirement—giving the opponent a free tempo to execute a concrete tactic (fork, sacrifice, breakthrough, hanging piece exploitation)
sub_patterns: Queen captures/attacks abandoning protection of other pieces (Qxe4, Qh6, Qg4)
Piece leaves dominant post for material gain (Rxb4, gxh3)
Piece moves to peripheral/vulnerable square ignoring central priority (Nh3, Kh8, Nd5)
Premature pawn advance wasting critical tempo (a7)

analysis.label: Moves that voluntarily worsen the player's own king safety in positions where the king is already vulnerable, walking into tactical punishments.
analysis.description: This feature fires on moves that fatally compromise the player's own king position in already-sharp situations. In 4/7 positions, the king itself moves to a tactically worse square (Kg8 walks into h7+ promotion, Ke7 walks into Qg7 attacking f7, Kf6 exposes the king to g5+ and Rxf7+). In 2/7 positions, a knight that was shielding the king is moved away (Nd7 abandons the f6 outpost releasing the opponent's king, Nf5 removes the d4 shield allowing Re6+ and Qc4#). In 1/7 positions, a pawn advance (g3) weakens the light-square complex around the king. The common thread is that all moves look superficially logical (centralizing the king, attacking a piece, consolidating the pawn structure) but catastrophically ignore concrete tactical vulnerabilities of the king. Nearly all positions feature both kings already exposed (6/7 have 'exposed king' or 'weak pawn shield' noted), and the blunder tips the delicate balance by making one's own king significantly worse. The average cp_loss of 2939 reflects the catastrophic nature of self-inflicted king exposure in tactical positions.
analysis.move_pattern: King moving to a more exposed square, knight moving away from a king-shielding post, or pawn advancing to weaken the king's shelter
analysis.why_bad: These moves ignore concrete tactical threats against the player's own king—walking into checks, discoveries, promotion sequences, or mating nets—by prioritizing general principles (centralization, piece activity, aggression) over the immediate safety calculation required by the sharp position.
sub_patterns: King stepping onto a square where an enemy pawn/piece delivers check with tempo
Knight abandoning a square that was blocking enemy access to the king
Pawn advance creating light/dark square holes in the king shelter

analysis.label: Choosing a natural-looking repositioning move in a narrow position where only one specific forcing continuation maintains the advantage.
analysis.description: This feature fires on positions where a player makes a move that appears purposeful—developing, defending, supporting a passed pawn, or attacking—but misses the single critical forcing move the position demands. In 6/8 positions, the average good moves available is only 1.8, indicating extreme narrowness. The correct moves are consistently more CONCRETE and FORCING (e.g., g5! trapping a bishop, cxd3 capturing a hanging piece, Ke6 directly attacking a blockader, Kb4 ensuring king safety post-promotion, Ba3 winning material via queen displacement, cxd4 removing a key attacker). Instead, the played moves are repositioning or natural-looking (Bf6 'developing,' Bxg1 capturing a peripheral piece, Kb2 'approaching the promotion square,' Kc6 'supporting from behind,' Qf3/Qf6 'increasing pressure/defending'). In 5/6 blunders, the refutation exploits a newly-created tactical vulnerability—checks on opened files, forks, tempo-gaining intermezzo captures, or knight invasions into squares the moved piece previously controlled.
analysis.move_pattern: Piece (queen, king, or bishop) repositions to a square that looks active/purposeful but is either tactically vulnerable or abandons critical defensive duties, when one forcing alternative (pawn thrust, direct capture, or king advance toward enemy pieces) was required
analysis.why_bad: The positions demand a single concrete, forcing move (a tactical shot, direct capture, or precise king route), but the player chooses a plausible-looking alternative that either exposes their piece to tempo-gaining counterattacks, abandons control of critical squares allowing enemy piece invasions, or selects a secondary target over the primary tactical demand.
sub_patterns: Piece repositioning that abandons control of key squares, allowing knight outpost invasions (Bf6 → c5/d6 weakness)
Capturing a peripheral piece instead of the primary tactical target (Bxg1 vs cxd3)
King moving to an exposed square vulnerable to file/diagonal checks instead of the optimal approach route (Kc6, Kb2)
Queen moving to an aggressive/defensive square that walks into tempo-gaining forks or discovered attacks (Qf3 → Nf4, Qf6 → Bxg7+Nf5)

analysis.label: Playing a slow, retreating, or peripheral move when the position demands immediate decisive action to maintain or convert an advantage.
analysis.description: In 6/8 positions, the player held a significant advantage that required one precise, active continuation to maintain. Instead, they played moves that appeared reasonable—prophylactic pawn pushes (h3), king retreats (Kg3, Kh1), queen relocations to peripheral squares (Qh4, Qa5, Qxg6), or premature rook repositioning (Rc3, Rb3)—but fundamentally wasted the critical tempo needed to execute the winning plan. In 7/8 cases, the analyses identify 'tempo_loss' as a core tag. The positions typically featured passed pawns needing support (4/8), exposed enemy kings requiring immediate exploitation, or piece activity that needed to be maintained on a dominant square. The blunders allowed opponents to seize the initiative through counterattacks, perpetual checks, or consolidation that was previously impossible. The average of only 1.6 good moves confirms these were narrow decision points where only decisive action succeeded.
analysis.move_pattern: Moving king, queen, or rook in a retreating/peripheral/lateral direction (toward edges, corners, or backward ranks) rather than advancing toward the critical zone of action
analysis.why_bad: These moves address secondary concerns (king safety, pawn targets, prophylaxis) while abandoning the position's primary strategic requirement—whether advancing a passed pawn, maintaining paralyzing pressure on an exposed king, or capturing available material. The wasted tempo allows the opponent to neutralize the advantage through active counterplay, perpetual checks, piece consolidation, or seizing the initiative.
sub_patterns: King retreating when it should advance toward or capture near a passed pawn (Kg3, Kh1)
Queen moving to peripheral square abandoning critical defensive or paralyzing duties (Qh4, Qa5, Qxg6)
Rook or pawn moves addressing secondary targets before completing the required preparatory move (Rc3 before Kf4, Rb3 before Bc8, h3 before Qe6)

analysis.label: Making superficially attractive piece moves (developing, centralizing, attacking) that neglect a concrete tactical vulnerability, typically an undefended pawn or piece that the opponent exploits with tempo.
analysis.description: This feature consistently fires on positions where players make 'natural-looking' or aesthetically pleasing moves—centralizing knights (Nd5, Nf4, Nd3), developing bishops (Bg5 x2), repositioning queens (Qd6, Qb8, Qxg4+), advancing pawns (f3, f6)—while overlooking a specific, concrete tactical vulnerability in the position. In 5/12 cases, the move directly leaves a pawn undefended that gets captured with tempo (Bg5 leaving e4 hanging in positions 5 and 13, Nf4 leaving c4 undefended in position 15, Nd3 unguarding f3 in position 10, f3 failing to challenge e4 while weakening diagonals in position 3). In 4/12 cases, the piece moves to a square where it immediately becomes a target with tempo (Nd5 kicked by Ke6, Qd6 attacked by Nb5, Qb8 giving White tempo for a6, Nfd7 removing a critical blocking function). The average cp_loss of 1071 confirms catastrophic consequences, while the average of 2.0 good alternatives shows these were avoidable—simple prophylactic or defensive moves existed in every case.
analysis.move_pattern: A piece moves to an apparently strong or active square (central outpost, developing square, attacking position) while failing to address or actively creating a tactical vulnerability elsewhere on the board
analysis.why_bad: The move prioritizes 'general principles' (activity, centralization, development, material gain) over the concrete tactical demands of the position—typically leaving a pawn/piece undefended, removing a critical defender, or placing a piece where it becomes a target with tempo, allowing the opponent an immediate tactical exploitation that more than offsets any positional gain.
sub_patterns: Piece development leaving a center pawn undefended (Bg5 with e4 hanging)
Knight repositioning that removes guard of critical square (Nd3 unguarding f3, Nfd7 unblocking diagonal)
Queen placement on square immediately attackable with knight tempo (Qd6 allowing Nb5)
Pawn advance weakening king position without achieving its target (f3, f6)
Material grab missing a stronger forcing continuation (Qxg4+ missing f5+)

analysis.label: Playing a passive repositioning move when a simple capture of undefended material (pawn or piece) was available.
analysis.description: In 4/4 positions, the player made a quiet, non-capturing piece repositioning move while a concrete material-winning opportunity existed. In 3/4 cases (positions 1, 2, 4), the best move was directly capturing undefended material: Qxb2 winning a free pawn, Rxe7 capturing a completely hanging knight, and Qxb7 taking an undefended pawn. In position 3, the best move (Qf5) leveraged the queen's active position to force a favorable trade rather than retreating it to an irrelevant square. Instead, the players chose developing-looking moves (Bc5, Re4, Qb6, Qe2) that improved piece placement in abstract terms but surrendered concrete advantages ranging from 198 to 464 centipawns. All positions had exactly 1 good move available, indicating critical decision points where calculation was essential but the players defaulted to positional intuition.
analysis.move_pattern: Quiet non-capturing piece development or repositioning (bishop, rook, or queen) to a natural-looking square, ignoring an available capture on the same file or diagonal
analysis.why_bad: The moves prioritize vague positional improvement (development, centralization, piece activity) over concrete material gains, giving the opponent time to defend previously hanging material or launch counterplay that erases the squandered advantage.
sub_patterns: Developing a piece to an active square while a queen can capture a free pawn
Centralizing a rook on a file instead of capturing a hanging piece on that same file
Relocating the queen to a new sector while abandoning a dominant active post

analysis.label: A non-urgent 'improving' move played in a position that demands specific concrete action to address a tactical vulnerability.
analysis.description: This feature fires on positions where the player chose a superficially reasonable positional or developmental move while ignoring an urgent tactical demand. In 8/8 analyzed positions, the move played was non-forcing and aimed at generic improvement (developing a piece, pushing a pawn, placing a rook on an open file) while a concrete vulnerability went unaddressed. The positions share extremely low margins for error (avg 1.7 good moves), meaning only one or two specific moves maintained the evaluation. Common ignored problems include: hanging/undefended pieces (positions 1, 13), pieces about to be trapped (positions 6, 10), critical passed pawns needing immediate advance (positions 3, 12), king safety emergencies (positions 5, 7, 14), and weakening of key squares/diagonals (position 9). The tempo spent on the 'improving' move gives the opponent exactly the time needed to exploit the vulnerability.
analysis.move_pattern: Non-forcing, non-capturing moves to apparently reasonable squares (pawn pushes, piece repositioning, rook-to-open-file, development) that do not address the position's critical tactical demand
analysis.why_bad: Each position has one specific urgent problem (a hanging piece, a piece about to be trapped, a pawn needing advance, a king needing safety) that requires immediate concrete action. The played move wastes the crucial tempo needed to address this problem, allowing the opponent to execute a tactic that was previously only a threat.
sub_patterns: Slow pawn push while a piece hangs or a tactic is available (a4, b3, b6)
Piece development/repositioning while own queen is about to be trapped (Bf5, Qb6)
Rook placed on open file instead of advancing critical passed pawn (Rfe1, Rg7, Re1)
Knight/piece abandons key defensive square for 'active' one (Nc4, Bc1)
Wrong piece captures, exposing king to tactical sequence (Qxe5, Ke7)

analysis.label: Moves that pursue a secondary objective (material, centralization, apparent safety, or flashy attack) while abandoning the piece's critical role in the position's primary battle.
analysis.description: All 5 positions share a pattern where the player makes a natural-looking move that ignores the position's urgent demand. In 5/5 cases, the move diverts a piece away from its most important function: Rxa2 pulls the rook off the dominant c-file for a pawn grab (Position 2); Be4 centralizes the bishop onto an undefended square within reach of an enemy rook (Position 3); Kg8 removes the king from a square where a defensive tactical trick (Qd2 intercepting on h6) was the only saving resource (Position 6); Rdg1 abandons the d-file and center to launch a slow kingside attack while the opponent has an immediate queenside breakthrough (Position 11); Qh4 repositions the queen from h6—where it coordinated a lethal R8f7-Rh7 battery—to h4, leaving c7 hanging and breaking the mating setup (Position 15). In all cases the opponent exploits the abandoned area immediately, and the positions averaged only 1.4 good moves available, meaning these were critical decision points demanding the one precise continuation over the tempting alternative.
analysis.move_pattern: Any piece type moving to a seemingly active or natural square, diverting away from its critical defensive or coordinative post; no consistent geometric direction but always involves relocating a piece from where it's most needed
analysis.why_bad: The move neglects the position's primary demand—whether maintaining file control, preserving a defensive tactic, or sustaining attacking coordination—in favor of a secondary goal (material, centralization, king safety, or attack on the wrong flank), allowing the opponent to exploit the newly unattended vulnerability immediately
sub_patterns: Premature pawn-grab diverting active piece from critical file
Piece centralization onto tactically undefended square
King move eliminating a critical defensive interposition resource
Rook redeployment to wrong flank ignoring faster opponent counterplay
Queen repositioning that breaks coordinated mating battery

analysis.label: Playing an apparently natural or position-improving move that ignores or creates an immediate concrete tactical vulnerability, typically allowing a fork or piece-winning shot.
analysis.description: This feature fires on moves where the player prioritizes apparent piece improvement, space-gaining, or positional goals while overlooking a concrete tactical refutation. In 3/9 positions, the move directly walks into a knight or pawn fork (Nf5 allows g4 pawn fork, Qc5 allows Ne6 knight fork, Kd7 allows Nxf6+ fork). In 2/9 positions, a king moves to a vulnerable square on an open file/diagonal (Kf7 into f-file combination, Kd7 into fork geometry). In 2/9 positions, a passive non-forcing move is played when only immediate active counterplay could hold (a5 instead of Ba5, Rc7 instead of Qh6). In 1/9, a defender is removed from a critical piece (Rc6 abandons defense of Ne4). In 1/9, a pawn advance ignores a hanging queen (f5 allows Nxd1). The average cp_loss of 1284 reflects catastrophic consequences, and the average of only 2.1 good moves shows these are critical positions where precision was required. All moves share the trait of looking 'reasonable' or 'natural' at a glance but failing a basic tactical safety check.
analysis.move_pattern: Any piece type moving to an apparently active/natural square without checking opponent's immediate tactical responses; no single geometric direction dominates
analysis.why_bad: The moves create or ignore an immediate tactical vulnerability (fork, hanging piece, open-file exploitation) because the player focused on their own plan rather than verifying concrete opponent responses
sub_patterns: Piece/King walks into fork geometry (3/9)
Passive pawn/rook move when only forcing play holds (3/9)
Removing a key defender while threats exist (1/9)
Ignoring an immediately hanging piece (1/9)
King stepping onto dangerous open file (1/9)

analysis.label: Black plays a seemingly natural developing or repositioning move that leaves a piece (the moved piece or another) undefended and tactically exploitable.
analysis.description: In all 4/4 positions, Black plays what appears to be a reasonable developing or repositioning move (Nc6 as classical development, Rb8 to protect the b-file, Qc5 for central activity) but critically ignores that the move creates or fails to address an undefended piece vulnerability. In 3/4 cases, the moved piece itself becomes the direct tactical target (Nc6 targeted by Qa4 fork or d5 pawn advance; Rb8 capturable via Bxd6+ discovered geometry). In 1/4 cases (Qc5), the queen abandons defensive duties leaving the king fatally exposed. All positions feature White having a concrete forcing response (fork, discovered capture, or mating attack) that exploits the newly created geometric vulnerability. In all 4/4 cases, better alternatives existed that addressed the position's actual tactical demands—securing undefended pieces, castling, or maintaining critical defensive coverage—rather than making routine-looking moves.
analysis.move_pattern: Black piece (knight, rook, or queen) moves to a seemingly natural square where it becomes undefended on a line exploitable by the opponent's forcing response
analysis.why_bad: The moves prioritize generic development or apparent activity over the position's concrete tactical demands, leaving pieces undefended on squares where the opponent has a forcing shot (fork, diagonal capture sequence, or mating attack) that wins material or delivers checkmate.
sub_patterns: Knight to c6 creating fork/tempo target (Qa4 or d5 exploiting the piece)
Piece repositioning to undefended square on opponent's tactical diagonal
Queen abandoning critical defensive square for apparent activity

analysis.label: Pawn advances (or passive moves) in critical endgame pawn-race positions that waste a vital tempo or prematurely fix the structure, when a different pawn push or immediate action was needed.
analysis.description: This feature fires on endgame positions (10/11) — predominantly pure pawn endgames (8/11) — where the player makes a move that either advances a pawn on the wrong wing, fixes the pawn structure prematurely, or wastes a critical tempo when precise move order is essential. The positions share razor-thin evaluations hinging on single tempi, with both kings typically exposed and centralized. In Position 1, a4 was played when h4 was needed to freeze White's kingside; in Position 15, h4 was played allowing ...h5 to permanently lock the kingside; in Position 12, a4 allowed ...a5 to freeze the queenside. Positions 3 and 5 show king moves that waste tempo instead of urgent pawn pushes (e4). Position 13 shows a prophylactic pawn push (g3) when pieces needed immediate activation. The common thread is a move-order/priority error: the player addresses a secondary concern while the opponent seizes the initiative on the critical front. Nearly all positions (8/11) are tagged with 'tempo_loss' as the core tactical motif.
analysis.move_pattern: Predominantly flank pawn advances (a-file, h-file, g-file, f-file) or passive king retreats; rarely captures or checks; moves typically push a pawn one square on a wing where the structure should remain flexible
analysis.why_bad: In pawn endgames where every tempo decides the race, these moves either fix the structure on one wing (allowing the opponent to lock it with a responding pawn push), waste a tempo on a non-urgent front (letting the opponent's king centralize or their critical pawn advance first), or commit to a plan in the wrong move order — all allowing the opponent to seize the initiative on the decisive front
sub_patterns: Pawn advance that allows opponent to lock that wing permanently (h4 answered by ...h5, a4 answered by ...a5)
Wrong-wing pawn push when the other side of the board demands immediate action
Passive king move instead of urgent passed pawn advance (Kc7/Kd7 instead of e4)
Prophylactic pawn move wasting tempo when piece activity is critical
Premature pawn structure commitment eliminating future breakthrough potential

analysis.label: Quiet repositioning or prophylactic moves in advantageous positions where resolving pawn tension or making a concrete forcing move was more precise.
analysis.description: This feature fires on non-forcing, non-capturing moves—typically piece repositioning (Bb7, Bc4, Nc4), king improvement (Ka6, Kc2, Kf7), or prophylactic pawn moves (g3)—in positions where the player holds a significant advantage. In 5/8 positions, the evaluation exceeded +345 before the move. The critical thread is that these are all quiet 'improving' moves made when a more concrete action was available: resolving pawn tension with a capture (exd5 in position 6, exd6 in position 8, Bxe6 in position 7), advancing a passed pawn (a5 in position 6), or directly defending a weakness (Ra8 in position 4). The actual blunders (4/8 positions with avg 253cp loss) occur when the quiet move gives the opponent a critical tempo to execute a defensive resource (d4 break, Bg4 pin, c5+ fork) that wouldn't have been possible had the forcing move been played first. The 0cp-loss activations (4/8) represent positions where the quiet approach was viable but suboptimal in timing.
analysis.move_pattern: Non-capturing, non-checking quiet moves: piece repositioning along diagonals (Bb7, Bc4), knight relocation to central square (Nc4), king steps (Ka6, Kc2, Kf7), or prophylactic pawn advances (g3, c6)
analysis.why_bad: The quiet improving move squanders a tempo that the opponent uses to execute a concrete defensive resource (pawn break, tactical shot, or simplification) that eliminates the advantage; resolving pawn tension or making a forcing capture first would have denied the opponent that opportunity.
sub_patterns: Bishop repositioning instead of capturing material (Bb7/Bc4 vs Bxe6/exd6)
King improving instead of resolving pawn tension (Kc2 vs exd5)
Piece relocation abandoning defensive duties (Nc4 leaving e4 unguarded)
King wandering into tactical vulnerability (Ka6 allowing c5+)

analysis.label: Premature advances that release pawn tension or alter a structure that was protecting the player's existing advantage, allowing the opponent to equalize through exchanges or blockades.
analysis.description: In all 4/4 positions, the player held a significant advantage (avg eval favoring them by ~300cp) but made a forward move that fundamentally changed the position's structure to their own detriment. In 3/4 cases these are pawn advances (f4, f6, a5) and in 1/4 a king move that self-obstructs. The key thread: the existing structure (closed center in position 13, queenside tension in position 15, compact pawns in position 8, bishop escape routes in position 5) was actively benefiting the player, and the move destroyed that structural advantage. In each case, the best alternatives involved either improving piece activity without structural change (Rc3, Bd2, g4, Rb6) or maintaining pawn tension (b5, h4+). The refutations in 4/4 cases show the opponent exploiting the newly created weaknesses: isolated pawns becoming fork targets, opened files activating opponent's pieces, exchanges leading to dead-drawn structures, or pieces becoming trapped.
analysis.move_pattern: Pawn advances (especially f-pawn) or king moves forward that irreversibly alter a favorable pawn structure or self-obstruct
analysis.why_bad: The moves release structural tension that was protecting the player's advantage, allowing the opponent to exchange into simplified/fortress positions, create blockades, exploit newly isolated pawns, or trap pieces that lose their escape squares
sub_patterns: f-pawn advance opening position for opponent's rooks
Queenside pawn advance allowing liquidation into drawn structure
King move blocking own piece's retreat square
Center break releasing tension that favored the breaker's opponent

analysis.label: Natural-looking moves that pursue a non-urgent goal while abandoning defense of a critical square or piece, enabling immediate tactical exploitation.
analysis.description: This feature fires on moves that appear logical or thematic but fatally neglect a defensive obligation. In 5/7 positions, the moved piece was either defending a critical square/piece or needed to address the opponent's most forcing continuation. Position 5 (Re8) removes the rook from f7-defense, allowing Bxf7+ sacrifice into a fork. Position 15 (Qg2) abandons queen's defense of c2, permitting Nb4 forking both rooks. Position 4 (Kd4) places the king in alignment with its own rook, enabling Nf3+ fork. Position 14 (Qd2) blocks own knight development while leaving Bg5 undefended against Ne4. Position 10 (c6) is a passive pawn move that doesn't address the critical e4-e5 advance, losing tempo. Position 7 (Kc5) marches the king toward a non-threat while abandoning the kingside. Position 2 (bxc6) captures with the wrong unit, creating structural weaknesses. All moves share the pattern of having a superficially logical purpose while ignoring the opponent's strongest reply.
analysis.move_pattern: Short-distance quiet moves (1-2 squares) to seemingly purposeful squares; no captures of enemy pieces, no checks given; diverse piece types but typically non-forcing repositioning moves
analysis.why_bad: Each move abandons a critical defensive function (guarding a piece, controlling a key square, or maintaining piece coordination) to pursue a secondary goal, allowing the opponent an immediate tactical shot—most commonly a fork (3/7) or a tempo-gaining central advance that exploits the newly undefended target.
sub_patterns: Queen relocates to passive square, leaving pawn/piece undefended (Qd2, Qg2)
King moves into tactical danger or away from critical zone (Kd4, Kc5)
Piece/pawn moves abandon defense of f7 or key square (Re8, c6)
Wrong recapture creates structural weaknesses enabling opponent's breakthrough (bxc6)

analysis.label: Playing an intuitive-looking but non-forcing move in a critical position where only one precise, concrete continuation maintains the advantage.
analysis.description: This feature fires on positions where the player selects a 'natural' or 'obvious-looking' move—often a check, centralization, or seemingly active piece play—but misses the single forcing continuation that the position demands. In 6/7 positions, the error is tagged as tempo_loss: the played move gives the opponent exactly the tempo needed to consolidate or create counterplay. In 5/7 positions, only 1 good move existed (avg 1.1), meaning these are narrow critical moments. The best moves are typically concrete tactical blows: pawn checks (b3+, d3+, h3+ in positions 3, 10, 15), pins (Bb4 in position 5), rook placement (Ra1 in position 8), or forcing queen threats (Qh5 in position 13). The played moves instead look reasonable—centralizing queens, advancing passed pawns, repositioning kings—but lack the forcing character needed. The common thread is that the position had one precise resource requiring calculation, and the player defaulted to an instinctive move.
analysis.move_pattern: Various pieces (Q/K/B/pawn) making plausible-looking active moves; frequently checks (3/7) or centralizing/advancing moves, but all non-forcing relative to the position's demands
analysis.why_bad: These moves surrender the critical tempo that was needed to maintain a forcing sequence, allowing the opponent to consolidate their position, create counterplay, or escape tactical danger—typically the best move was a more concrete forcing blow (pawn check, pin, or specific threat) that the natural move fails to replicate
sub_patterns: Premature/purposeless queen checks (Qa4+, Qe4+) when a pawn check or pin was stronger
King moves abandoning optimal squares (Kg3, Kd3) when forcing pawn advances were available
Developing/repositioning pieces (Bf4, a6) that set traps or look active but miss the one forcing continuation

analysis.label: Moving a piece to an apparently strong central/kingside square (often f5/f6) that is actually tactically exposed or fails to address the position's critical requirement.
analysis.description: In 3/4 positions, the piece moves to f5 or f6 (Qxf6, Kf5, Nf6), with the fourth (Qe3) going to a nearby central square. All moves share the characteristic of appearing aggressive and centralizing while actually being tactically flawed. In position 12, Nf6 places the knight on a 'strong' outpost but it hangs after the deflection check Rf5+. In position 6, Qxf6 captures actively but abandons the a4-e8 diagonal, allowing Qa4+. In position 10, Kf5 centralizes the king but fails to protect h6 (unlike Kf6) and allows the tempo-gaining Qe6+. In position 3, Qe3 attacks the rook but critically fails to control c4, enabling the decisive d7 push. In all 4/4 cases, a more modest alternative (often just one square different—Kf6 vs Kf5, Qe2 vs Qe3, Nh2 vs Nf6) was vastly superior because it addressed a concrete tactical or defensive requirement.
analysis.move_pattern: Various piece types moving to central-kingside squares (primarily f5, f6, e3), appearing to centralize aggressively
analysis.why_bad: The piece on its new 'active' square becomes a tactical target (hanging, deflectable) or creates a vulnerability elsewhere (exposed king, unguarded pawn, loss of critical square control) that is immediately exploited by forcing moves
sub_patterns: Knight to f6 hanging after deflection check
Queen capture on f6 exposing king to diagonal check
King to f5 instead of f6 failing to support passed pawn
Queen to e3 instead of e2/f1 losing critical square control

analysis.label: Natural-looking moves in sharp positions that catastrophically ignore the one essential tactical requirement for survival.
analysis.description: This feature fires on positions where the player makes a move that appears reasonable or addresses a real concern, but fatally misses the single critical action the position demands. In 4/5 positions, king safety is the dominant theme, and in 5/5 cases the position has very few good moves (avg 1.8), meaning precision is absolutely essential. The pattern shows: Rf2 blocks the king's own escape square instead of moving the king there (Position 2); Ne4 centralizes but ignores a hanging rook (Position 6); Rf7 'defends' f7 but places the rook on a doubly-attacked square allowing mate in 2 (Position 7); Bxf2 grabs a pawn but skips the essential preparatory Rg6 that enables the whole attack (Position 10); Kh6 'avoids' a fork but walks into a worse tactical net with Qe3+ (Position 14). In 5/5 cases, the move addresses a secondary concern while missing the position's true critical point.
analysis.move_pattern: Various piece types moving to squares that appear active or defensive but that either self-block escape routes, land on fatally attacked squares, or waste tempo on secondary objectives
analysis.why_bad: Each move ignores the ONE essential action the position demands (king escape, forcing promotion, precise rook placement, preparatory tempo move, or active counterplay), choosing instead a superficially logical alternative that fails to meet the position's critical tactical requirement, resulting in catastrophic evaluation swings (avg 2265cp loss).
sub_patterns: Self-blocking king escape routes with pieces (Rf2)
