Ignoring hanging pieces for cosmetic development (Ne4)
Placing piece on multiply-attacked square enabling checkmate (Rf7)
Greedy captures that skip essential preparatory moves (Bxf2)
King moves that increase rather than decrease tactical exposure (Kh6)

analysis.label: Playing a preparatory or developing move while an enemy knight threatens to profitably capture a bishop, resulting in material or positional loss.
analysis.description: In all 5/5 positions, an enemy knight directly threatens (or is poised to capture) a bishop, and the move played fails to adequately address this threat. In Position 1, the Nb3 attacks Bc5 and Black plays c6 instead of saving it. In Position 9, White places the Bd2 directly into the powerful Nc4's capture range. In Position 11, Na4 attacks Bb6 and Black plays c6, removing the crucial cxb6 recapture. In Position 12, Ng5 attacks Be6 and Black plays Qe7 which pseudo-defends but makes Nxe6+ devastatingly strong. In Position 14, Nb5 attacks Bd6 and Black plays Nd5 instead of retreating the bishop. The consistent pattern is a 'constructive' move (pawn push, development, centralization) that ignores the tactical urgency of a knight bearing down on a bishop, allowing the opponent to execute the capture favorably.
analysis.move_pattern: Non-capture, non-defensive moves (pawn pushes to c6, piece development Bd2/Qe7, piece centralization Nd5) played while an enemy knight has a direct attacking relationship with a friendly bishop
analysis.why_bad: The moves ignore an immediate tactical threat where an enemy knight can profitably capture a bishop, either winning material outright, creating a devastating follow-up (fork/tempo gain), or removing a key defensive resource from the position.
sub_patterns: Slow pawn push while bishop hangs to knight (c6 x2)
Placing a piece on a square controlled by an embedded enemy knight (Bd2)
Pseudo-defending a bishop in a way that makes the knight capture more powerful (Qe7)
Centralizing another piece while bishop remains en prise to knight (Nd5)

analysis.label: Catastrophic blunders in razor-sharp positions where only one move works, choosing a natural-looking alternative that allows immediate tactical punishment.
analysis.description: This feature fires on positions with extreme tactical narrowness (avg 1.3 good moves available) where the player makes a plausible-looking move that catastrophically fails. In 6/7 positions, there was essentially only ONE correct move, and in all cases the chosen move either ignores a one-move tactical refutation or misses a forcing tactical opportunity. The mistakes manifest in diverse ways—removing a defender from the back rank (Re2 allowing Rh1+, 1/7), capturing the wrong target (Qxd6 instead of Nxd8, 1/7), retreating into perpetual check (Kf8, 1/7), wasting tempo while a piece is trapped (h6 allowing b4, 1/7), playing positionally when a forcing sacrifice wins (Rd7 instead of Rxg7+, 1/7), abandoning a critical defensive post (Ng5 instead of Ng3, 1/7), or placing a piece on a tactically vulnerable square (Qf8 into Bg8+ discovered check, 1/7)—but all share the signature of choosing a 'reasonable' move in a position demanding extreme precision.
analysis.move_pattern: Mixed piece types and directions; moves tend to be positionally plausible (rook to 7th rank, piece development, king retreating, prophylactic pawn push, material capture) but tactically catastrophic
analysis.why_bad: Each move ignores the single critical tactical element of the position—either a one-move refutation by the opponent or a forcing continuation available to the player—choosing routine logic over concrete calculation in a position that allows no margin for error
sub_patterns: Removing a key defender allowing immediate tactical invasion (Re2, Ng5)
Missing a forcing sacrifice/capture that wins decisively (Rd7, Qxd6)
Walking into an immediate tactical shot (Kf8 perpetual, Qf8 discovered check, h6 piece trap)

analysis.label: Playing a slow, non-forcing move when the position urgently demanded an immediate capture, defensive placement, or concrete tactical response.
analysis.description: In 9/9 positions, the player chose a passive, routine-looking, or 'improving' move while ignoring a critical tactical obligation. In 3/9 cases (Nd2, Rb2, Nf6), the player retreated or repositioned a piece instead of capturing a powerful enemy piece that was available (Nxd4, Rxd6, Qxe5). In 3/9 cases (Bg4, Bd7, b5), the player moved a piece away from a key defensive post, leaving pawns or squares fatally unguarded (b7 twice, and the e-file/king exposure). In 2/9 cases (Kg8, Kg5), the king moved to a seemingly natural square but abandoned a critical post (g7 allowing Ne7#, f5 allowing Ke5 infiltration). In 1/9 cases (Re1), a rook abandoned its file-guarding duty, enabling a crushing pawn break. The common thread is choosing a non-urgent, positionally motivated action when only 1-3 precise moves maintained the evaluation, and the resulting tactical punishment was severe (checks, forks, discovered attacks, or immediate checkmates).
analysis.move_pattern: Non-capturing, non-checking moves - typically retreats, sideways shuffles, or pawn pushes - away from the critical tactical zone where immediate action was required
analysis.why_bad: These moves abandon an urgent tactical duty (capturing a hanging/dominant enemy piece, guarding a critical square, or contesting a key file), giving the opponent a tempo to execute a forcing tactical blow - typically a knight fork/check, discovered attack, or exploitation of newly undefended material.
sub_patterns: Retreating a piece when a capture was required (Nd2/Nf6/Rb2)
Moving a defender away from a key pawn or square (Bg4/Bd7/Re1)
Moving the king away from a critical restraining or safe square (Kg8/Kg5)
Pushing a pawn while ignoring opponent's forcing checks (b5)

analysis.label: Playing a slow, non-forcing preparatory move instead of executing the critical pawn break (f5, d5, c5, e4) that the dynamic position urgently demands.
analysis.description: This feature fires on positions where the player makes a passive or preparatory move—quiet rook repositioning, knight retreats, prophylactic pawn pushes, or bishop maneuvers—when the position demands an immediate central or flank pawn break. In 8/11 positions, the best move was a concrete pawn break (f5, d5, c5, e4, or f6) that would exploit the opponent's temporary weakness (underdevelopment, exposed king, unresolved central tension). The blunder moves are consistently non-forcing: Rfe8 instead of f6, Rd1 instead of defending g3, h6 instead of f5, Nh7 instead of d5, Qe3 blocking e4, Be3 instead of f5, Rac8 instead of d5, g5 instead of f5, Nd4 instead of Qd5, g6 instead of development. The common consequence is that the opponent gains a critical tempo to consolidate, reorganize defensively, or launch their own initiative—turning what was a dynamic advantage into a lasting disadvantage. The positions share a characteristic of having a narrow window for concrete action before the opponent stabilizes.
analysis.move_pattern: Quiet non-forcing moves (rook to open file, knight retreat/reposition, prophylactic pawn push, bishop/queen relocation) played instead of an available forcing pawn break or tactical strike
analysis.why_bad: These moves waste the critical tempo needed to execute an urgent pawn break or forcing action; the opponent uses the gifted time to consolidate their center, complete development, defend the key weakness, or seize the initiative with their own plans, permanently closing the window for the correct break.
sub_patterns: Quiet piece repositioning (Rfe8, Rd1, Nh7, Be3, Rac8, Nd4, Qe3) instead of central pawn break
Wrong pawn push that weakens structure (g5, g6, f5, h6) instead of the correct break direction
Moving a rook away from where it defends a critical weakness or supports the needed break

analysis.label: Black plays an active-looking or natural move that overlooks a tactical vulnerability, leaving a piece (often the moved piece itself) insufficiently defended and capturable.
analysis.description: In all 5/5 positions, Black plays a middlegame move that appears to serve a logical purpose—gaining space (e5), attacking a piece (Rg6), targeting a pawn (Qg6), grabbing material (Nxe5), or consolidating (Rf7)—but each overlooks that the move creates or exposes a hanging piece. In 4/5 cases the moved piece itself becomes the tactical victim: the rook on g6 is capturable by the knight (Position 9), the rook on f7 is attacked by two pieces and captured with check enabling a fork (Position 11), the knight on e5 is won through a Bxe5/Rxe5 X-ray sequence (Position 13), and in Position 6 the queen's departure from f6 leaves the d6 bishop undefended against e5. In Position 2, the pawn push creates structural weaknesses exploited by Ne4. In every case, quieter alternatives (piece repositioning, pawn breaks, or capturing different targets) maintained Black's advantage, but the player was drawn to the more visually appealing move. The average cp_loss of 369 reflects that these are concrete material-losing oversights rather than subtle positional errors.
analysis.move_pattern: Various pieces (pawn/queen/rook/knight) moving to active-looking squares on the e-g files, typically toward the center or kingside, where they become tactically exposed
analysis.why_bad: The move either places the moving piece on a square where it can be captured by the opponent's coordinating pieces, or abandons the defense of another piece that immediately becomes a tactical target, allowing a simple material-winning combination.
sub_patterns: Moving piece lands on square attacked by multiple opponent pieces (Rf7, Rg6)
Piece leaves defensive duty exposing a hanging piece (Qg6 abandoning Bd6)
Capturing an apparently free pawn that is tactically defended via X-ray/discovered attack (Nxe5)
Aggressive pawn push creating tactical weakness exploited by piece invasion (e5 allowing Ne4)

analysis.label: Natural-looking consolidating or positional moves played when the position demanded immediate forcing action, squandering a critical tempo.
analysis.description: This feature fires on quiet, reasonable-looking moves that fail because the position required immediate forcing play. In 6/6 positions, the player chose a 'natural' move (developing, centralizing, gaining space) while a more urgent action existed: a forcing pawn break (f5 instead of g5 in position 3; d5 instead of c5 in position 5), a check (Qa5+ instead of e6 in position 1), active king/piece play (Kg2 instead of f4 in position 4; g5 instead of Kd5 in position 7), or a critical pawn advance (f4 instead of Rfd1 in position 10). The common mechanism is tempo loss—5/6 positions explicitly identify tempo_loss as the tactical motif or key tag. The played moves all appear logical by general principles (consolidate pawns, centralize the king, support pieces, gain space) but allow the opponent to consolidate, activate, or neutralize the position in ways that wouldn't have been possible after the correct forcing continuation. Avg cp_loss of 184 with only 1.8 good moves available indicates these are critical decision points where precision was essential.
analysis.move_pattern: Non-forcing, non-capturing, non-checking moves (mostly pawn advances or quiet piece repositioning) that look positionally motivated but are too slow for the position's tactical demands
analysis.why_bad: The position required immediate forcing action (a pawn breakthrough, a check, or an active piece move) to maintain/exploit dynamic advantages, but the quiet move gifts the opponent a tempo to consolidate, neutralize threats, or seize the initiative—converting winning positions to equal or worsening already difficult ones.
sub_patterns: Wrong pawn advanced when adjacent pawn break was critical (g5 vs f5, c5 vs d5)
Premature pawn advance creating fixed target when restraint was needed (f4 vs f3)
King centralization losing tempo to opponent's counter-activation (Kd5 repelled by Kf4)
Passive piece placement abandoning support of critical pawn break (Rfd1 abandoning f4)

analysis.label: Pieces move to seemingly logical or active squares while ignoring concrete tactical vulnerabilities they create or defensive duties they abandon.
analysis.description: This feature fires on moves that appear positionally reasonable—centralizing a piece, blockading a pawn, giving a check, challenging an enemy piece—but critically fail because they overlook immediate tactical consequences. In 4/9 positions, the moved piece lands on a square where it becomes directly capturable or forkable (Nd5 allowing Rd4+ fork, Bc7 walking into Bxc7 opening the a4-e8 diagonal, Kd4 allowing Qxc3+ winning material, Nd3 becoming a target on the open d-file). In 3/9 positions, the move abandons a critical defensive duty (Qd2 leaving the back rank unguarded for Rc8, Qc2 vacating e4 allowing queen invasion on d2, Nd3 ignoring the Rg2+ infiltration threat). In 2/9 positions, the move gives tempo to the opponent or drives their king toward safety (Qb6+ enabling Kc2 escape, Kh5 allowing the opposing king to reach a blockading square). The common thread is that each move has a surface-level justification but catastrophically neglects a concrete tactical refutation.
analysis.move_pattern: Various piece types (K, N, Q, B) moving to central or seemingly purposeful squares, often along files/diagonals where they become exposed to immediate tactical exploitation
analysis.why_bad: The moves prioritize a superficial positional goal (centralization, blockading, piece exchange, checking) over the position's concrete tactical demands—either placing the piece where it becomes vulnerable to double attacks/captures, or vacating a square whose defensive function was critical to hold the position together.
sub_patterns: Piece centralizes onto a tactically exposed square (fork/capture)
Queen/piece abandons critical file/rank defense
Check drives enemy king toward safety rather than danger
Bishop/knight moves to challenged square where immediate capture is devastating
King advances when retreating or repositioning was needed

analysis.label: Advancing a pawn (or king) prematurely in the endgame, wasting a critical tempo or self-blocking the king's optimal path.
analysis.description: This feature fires on positions where players make premature forward pawn advances (5/6 are pawn moves, 1/6 is a king advance with equivalent intent) in endgame or late-game positions that squander a significant advantage. The common thread is that each advance commits to a structural or positional decision one tempo too early: in Position 3, f4 blocks the king from the critical f4 square; in Position 8, f6 permanently blocks the king from the winning f6 outpost (self-blocking, 531cp loss); in Position 10, g3 wastes a tempo allowing the opponent to lock the kingside with ...g5; in Position 14, g5 prematurely fixes the kingside pawns, eliminating dynamic potential; in Position 7, d4 creates a target instead of exploiting a knight fork; in Position 6, Kh4 advances before the supporting g5 push, exposing the king to tempo-gaining checks. All 6/6 positions involve tempo loss as a key factor, and 4/6 explicitly involve the king being denied or displaced from a critical square as a direct consequence of the premature advance.
analysis.move_pattern: Single-square forward pawn advances (f, g, or d-file) or one-square king advances in endgame positions; no captures or checks involved
analysis.why_bad: The advance wastes a critical tempo by committing to a structure prematurely—either blocking the king from occupying the square the pawn now occupies, locking the pawn structure allowing the opponent to equalize, or creating a fixed target that the opponent's active king/pieces can exploit before the intended plan materializes.
sub_patterns: Pawn advances to square the king needed to occupy (self-blocking)
Preparatory pawn moves that allow opponent to lock the position
Premature structural commitment giving opponent time to activate king
Unnecessary advance creating a fixed pawn target

analysis.label: Quiet repositioning moves that ignore urgent king safety demands, allowing the opponent to launch or intensify a devastating tactical attack.
analysis.description: This feature fires on positions where a player makes a slow, routine-looking move (piece maneuver, castling, or pawn advance) while the position urgently demands concrete action related to king safety. In 5/6 positions, king_safety is the dominant theme—the played move either removes a defender from the critical sector (Qc7 abandoning g7 coverage, Na2 removing a knight from center/kingside defense), walks the king into an existing attack (O-O into Bc5+Ng4 battery, Ka2 into Rxb2+ mating threats), or ignores the opponent's exposed king when tactical exploitation was available (f5 missing Nxe5 winning a pawn against an uncastled king, Nf6 creating a tactical vulnerability near the g-file). In all 6/6 cases, the player had concrete best moves available (captures, defensive king moves, or forcing continuations) but chose a 'planning' move instead, suffering an average 1740cp loss. The refutations consistently involve immediate tactical explosions targeting king safety that the slow move enabled.
analysis.move_pattern: Quiet non-forcing moves (piece repositioning, castling, pawn advances) that move away from or ignore the critical sector where king safety demands immediate attention
analysis.why_bad: The position demands urgent concrete action (capturing hanging pieces, defending critical squares near the king, or moving the king from danger) but the player makes a slow developmental or repositioning move, giving the opponent a free tempo to launch or intensify a tactical attack against the vulnerable king.
sub_patterns: King walking into existing attack (O-O, Ka2)
Piece retreating to rim when center/kingside defense needed (Na2, Nf6 allowing Ne4)
Queen/piece leaving critical defensive post (Qc7 abandoning g7)
Positional pawn advance ignoring concrete tactical win (f5 missing Nxe5)

analysis.label: Moves that waste a critical tempo by choosing a seemingly constructive action (king advance, capture, check, piece repositioning) instead of the one urgent time-sensitive move the position demands.
analysis.description: This feature fires on positions where a single time-critical action—almost always an immediate passed pawn advance—is required, but the player instead makes a 'reasonable-looking' alternative move that squanders the tempo advantage. In 6/10 positions, the correct move was an immediate pawn push (d6, g4, g7, a5, or similar), but the player chose a king move or capture instead. The king moves (Ke6, Kg3, Kg7, Kb4, Kxh5) all represent attempts to 'improve' or 'escort' before pushing, losing the critical tempo. The middlegame examples (Nf7, Nd2, Re6+, Nd4) follow the same principle—the player makes a superficially attractive move (a fork, a development, a check, a centralization) instead of the one move exploiting a time-sensitive advantage. Nearly all positions (8/10) are tagged with 'tempo_loss' in analysis. The average good moves available is only 1.9, confirming these are narrow positions demanding precision.
analysis.move_pattern: King advances, pawn captures, piece repositioning, or checks played INSTEAD of an immediate passed pawn advance or decisive tactical blow; often king steps forward one square toward a pawn it should be pushing rather than escorting
analysis.why_bad: These moves lose a critical tempo in positions where the race/clock is the deciding factor—typically allowing the opponent to either start their own pawn race (Ke6 allows b4, Kb4 allows c5+), escape a mating net (Re6+ frees Kg7), unblock their own passers (fxe4 frees f3), or force simplification that eliminates the attacker's advantage (Kxh5 allows promotion+trade, Nf7 allows Qd7 queen trade)
sub_patterns: King advances in front of or beside own passed pawn instead of pushing it (Ke6, Kg7, Kb4)
Capture that removes own pawn-blocking structure and frees opponent's passers (fxe4, Kxh5)
Aimless check or piece move that releases winning pressure (Re6+, Nd4, Nf7)
Passive king move without creating pawn tension when counterplay is needed (Kg3, Nd2)

analysis.label: Playing natural-looking, non-forcing moves in critical positions where only one precise tactical continuation maintains the evaluation.
analysis.description: This feature fires on positions where the player selects a 'normal' or 'improving' move—developing a piece, pushing a pawn for space, or repositioning a rook—when the position demands a single concrete, often forcing continuation. In 7/7 cases, the average number of good moves available was only 1.1, meaning these are razor-sharp positions disguised as quiet ones. The played moves all look reasonable on the surface: pawn advances for space (e5, f4, c5 in 3/7), knight development to natural squares (Nf6 in 2/7), or rook repositioning (Ra7, Ra3 in 2/7). But each ignores a critical tactical obligation—whether it's an immediate capture that wins/maintains material (Nxe5, Rxc6, Rd3), a forcing check that exploits a weakness (Qh4+), or a pawn storm that must continue immediately (g4). The blunders either create new vulnerabilities (abandoning key squares, leaving pieces undefended) or waste irreplaceable tempo in positions where the opponent can seize the initiative with checks and tactical threats.
analysis.move_pattern: Quiet, non-forcing moves (no checks or captures): pawn advances, knight developments to classical squares, or rook lateral moves to seemingly active positions
analysis.why_bad: These positions have only ~1 correct move and demand concrete calculation, but the player defaults to a generic positional improvement that either creates a tactical vulnerability (undefended piece, abandoned square, weakened king shelter) or wastes critical tempo allowing the opponent to consolidate or counter-attack
sub_patterns: Pawn advances that abandon key squares or leave other pawns undefended (e5, f4, c5)
Knight development to natural squares that become tactically vulnerable or waste attacking tempo (Nf6, Nf6)
Rook repositioning to passive or exposed squares when direct action on a critical file/pawn is required (Ra7, Ra3)

analysis.label: Piece (usually a rook) abandons a critical controlling or restraining post to pursue a secondary target, allowing the opponent to exploit the vacated control.
analysis.description: In 6/8 positions, the moved piece was performing a vital restraining function—controlling an open file (positions 1, 2), blockading a dangerous passed pawn (positions 6, 7), or occupying a dominant outpost (position 10)—and was redirected to attack a less important target. In positions 1 and 2, the rook left the c-file to attack f5, enabling a crushing d5 central break. In position 6, the rook abandoned d-pawn restraint to attack the f5 bishop, allowing d3 to advance decisively. In position 7, the rook left the back rank to go to the 7th, allowing c2 with an unstoppable promotion threat. In position 10, the knight left e6 to capture on g5, opening the f-file fatally. In positions 5 and 12, pieces abandoned active central/coordinated positions for passive or peripheral squares. The common thread is prioritizing a visible but secondary target over the piece's invisible but critical restraining duty, with the opponent immediately exploiting the abandoned control via a pawn advance (d5, d3, c2, fxe4) in 6/8 cases.
analysis.move_pattern: Piece (predominantly rook) moves away from a file, rank, or square where it was restraining a critical threat, often toward the f-file to attack the f5 square/pawn
analysis.why_bad: The piece was performing a crucial restraining function (controlling an open file, blockading a passed pawn, or occupying a dominant outpost), and its departure allows the opponent to immediately exploit the vacated control with a decisive pawn advance or piece activation that cannot be contained.
sub_patterns: Rook leaves c-file/back rank to attack f5, enabling central d-pawn break
Rook abandons pawn-stopping duty allowing promotion threats
Knight/Queen leaves dominant central post for peripheral capture/retreat

analysis.label: Moves that address a secondary concern while ignoring the single most critical positional demand, typically king centralization in endgames or maintaining pressure on a key target.
analysis.description: This feature fires on moves where the player makes a seemingly reasonable but strategically misguided choice that neglects the position's #1 priority. In endgames (7/11 positions), the error is almost always failing to centralize the king when that is the decisive factor—instead playing a piece repositioning (Bc2 in position 4, Rc7 in position 11) or premature pawn advance (f5 in position 3, h3 in position 5). In openings/middlegames (4/11), the error involves moving a piece away from its essential function—abandoning defense of a key pawn (Ba3 leaving d4 unguarded in position 15), placing a piece on a passive/attacked square rather than the attacking one (Qe7 instead of Qc7 in position 14, Ng4 into capture in position 10), or creating weaknesses while ignoring existing vulnerabilities (e5 in position 2). The unifying thread is that only 1-2 good moves existed on average (1.8), meaning these are positions with a narrow correct path that the player missed by addressing a less important concern.
analysis.move_pattern: Any piece type; typically a piece repositioning, pawn advance, or king move that addresses a secondary goal rather than the position's primary demand; no consistent geometric direction
analysis.why_bad: The move neglects the single most urgent positional requirement—usually king centralization in endgames, or maintaining a critical defensive/offensive function of a piece—allowing the opponent to seize the initiative, capture undefended material, or establish a decisive positional advantage that was previously preventable
sub_patterns: Pawn advance before king centralization in endgame
Piece repositioning when king activation is urgent
Moving a piece away from its essential defensive duty
Placing piece on passive/attacked square instead of optimal attacking square

analysis.label: Moving a piece such that the player's queen is left undefended and directly capturable by the opponent's queen along a clear line.
analysis.description: In all 4/4 positions, the blundering move results in the player's queen being captured by the opponent's queen with no possible recapture. In 3/4 cases, the queen itself moves to a fatally undefended square (Qe6+ hangs to Qa2 along the diagonal, Qg5+ hangs to Qd2 along the diagonal, Qd2 hangs to Qd5 along the d-file). In 1/4 cases (Rxa2), the wrong piece captures, leaving the queen en prise on b3 to the opponent's queen on d1 via the diagonal. The common thread is a clear queen-to-queen line (diagonal in 3/4 cases, file in 1/4) with no intervening pieces or defenders. In 2/4 positions, the blunder is disguised as an aggressive check, making the hanging queen harder to notice due to the forcing appearance of the move. Average material loss is 752cp, consistent with losing a queen outright.
analysis.move_pattern: Queen (or supporting piece) moves to a square leaving own queen undefended on a clear diagonal or file controlled by the opponent's queen
analysis.why_bad: The queen ends up on an unprotected square with a direct, unobstructed line (diagonal or file) to the opponent's queen, allowing immediate capture with no recapture available—resulting in catastrophic material loss.
sub_patterns: Queen gives check but lands on a square capturable by enemy queen along a diagonal (Qe6+, Qg5+)
Queen moves to undefended square on same file as enemy queen (Qd2 captured by Qd5)
Wrong piece captures, exposing queen to capture by enemy queen along a diagonal (Rxa2 leaves Qb3 hanging)

analysis.label: Active-looking moves that address a secondary concern while ignoring the single most critical positional or tactical priority in the position.
analysis.description: This feature fires on moves that pursue a plausible but non-urgent objective—typically a material grab, piece activation, or counterplay attempt—while the position demands immediate attention to one dominant factor. In 6/7 positions, the error is tagged as 'tempo_loss' because the critical tempo is spent on the wrong plan. In 4/7 cases, the ignored priority involves a passed pawn (supporting one's own or neutralizing the opponent's). In 5/7 cases, king safety is a key neglected factor. The positions characteristically offer very few good moves (avg 1.6), indicating a narrow decision point where only one priority matters. Examples: Rf4 harasses a queen instead of supporting the c7 passed pawn (Position 1); Rhd8 reinforces an already-strong d-pawn instead of capturing the a5 pawn to prevent a lethal breakthrough (Position 7); bxa5 grabs material instead of repositioning the queen to address a passed pawn threat (Position 8); Re8 seeks e-file counterplay but removes the defender of a critical piece (Position 12); Qa5 pursues queenside pressure but abandons control of d5, allowing a devastating fork (Position 15).
analysis.move_pattern: Mixed piece types (rooks, queen, knight, pawn captures) moving to active-looking but strategically irrelevant squares, typically away from the critical sector of the board
analysis.why_bad: These moves waste the one critical tempo needed to address the position's dominant priority (passed pawn support, threat neutralization, piece defense, or key-square control), allowing the opponent to execute a decisive plan that the correct move would have prevented.
sub_patterns: Material captures (Nxf5, bxa5, Rxd3) that ignore a more urgent positional need or allow tactical refutation
Rook moves to active-looking files (Re8, Rhd8, Rf4) that abandon defensive duties or miss the critical file/rank
Queen relocation (Qa5) that abandons control of a critical central square enabling tactical exploitation

analysis.label: Non-constructive moves that ignore the position's most urgent demand, giving the opponent a free tempo to execute a decisive tactical or strategic strike.
analysis.description: In 6/7 positions, the played move wastes a critical tempo on a secondary goal while the position demands immediate constructive action. The common thread: each position has one clearly urgent need (development in 4/7, blocking a dangerous file in 2/7, maintaining piece coordination in 1/7), yet the player chooses a plausible-looking but non-addressing move—a flank pawn push (b5, h6), a king retreat to a vulnerable square (Kd8 x2, Kf3), a greedy capture that abandons a critical post (Rxa3), or a piece placement that creates new weaknesses (Qe2). In all cases, the opponent punishes by immediately executing the tactical operation that the wasted tempo enabled: central pawn breaks (e5, c5+d5), captures of now-undefended material (Rxh3, Nxb7+), devastating pins (Re8), or checks exploiting the newly exposed king (Rd7+, Rxd4/Qe4+). The average cp_loss of 293 reflects that these are positions at a tipping point where one tempo separates defensible from lost.
analysis.move_pattern: Any piece type; typically sideways/backward king moves, quiet flank pawn advances, or captures away from the critical zone—all sharing the property of not addressing the board's most urgent demand
analysis.why_bad: The position has a critical tactical or developmental vulnerability that requires immediate attention; the played move ignores this demand, giving the opponent a free tempo to launch a concrete tactical operation (central break, fork, pin, or decisive invasion) that the missing tempo would have prevented
sub_patterns: Flank pawn pushes (b5, h6) when piece development or central action is urgent
King moves to tactically vulnerable squares (Kd8 into d-file checks/forks, Kf3 into discovered attacks)
Greedy captures that abandon a piece's critical defensive function (Rxa3 releasing pressure on d2-knight)
Queen/piece placement creating new pin or x-ray vulnerabilities (Qe2 on same file as king)

analysis.label: Plausible-looking moves that squander a critical tempo by addressing a secondary concern instead of the position's single most urgent demand.
analysis.description: This feature fires on positions where the player makes a move that looks constructive—attacking a pawn, developing a piece, capturing material, advancing a passed pawn—but fatally ignores the ONE critical priority the position demands. In 7/7 cases, the analyses identify 'tempo_loss' as a core theme. The pattern manifests as: a knight attacking wing pawns instead of centralizing the king (Nh3, Position 1); a king marching to escort a passer instead of advancing connected passers (Kc4, Position 2); a pawn break releasing tension instead of developing pieces (c5, Position 3); a rook capturing an irrelevant pawn instead of promoting a queen (Rxb3+, Position 4); a bishop developing to a passive square instead of preparing castling (Bd2, Position 5); a pawn push when the king is one move from checkmate (h5, Position 6); and the wrong piece capturing when only the queen enables a winning tactic (Rxd5, Position 7). In all cases, the correct move addresses an urgent, singular priority—king safety (4/7), pawn promotion (2/7), or a specific tactical sequence (3/7)—while the played move pursues something that merely appears useful.
analysis.move_pattern: Any piece type or direction; characteristically a move that 'does something' (captures, develops, advances) but toward a non-critical target while the position has one urgent demand
analysis.why_bad: Each position has a single critical priority (escaping a mating net, advancing a decisive pawn, enabling a tactical combination, or centralizing the king) and exactly 1-3 moves that address it. The played move wastes the tempo on a secondary objective, allowing the opponent to execute their primary threat or consolidate a decisive advantage.
sub_patterns: Piece moves to peripheral square ignoring central king activity needs
Pawn push on a wing while critical center/king issues demand attention
Wrong piece captures (rook instead of queen) missing tactical combinations
Piece develops passively when castling preparation is urgent
Material capture that trades away a decisive advantage for something trivial

analysis.label: Playing a plausible-looking but non-urgent move in a razor-sharp position where only 1-2 moves correctly address the critical demand (usually king safety).
analysis.description: This feature fires on moves that appear reasonable by general chess principles but catastrophically ignore the single most urgent requirement of the position. In 6/8 cases, the urgent need involves king safety—either the player's king needed to move to a specific safe square but they played something else (h6 instead of Kc7, Ng6 instead of Kg8, c4/b4 instead of developing), or the king moved to the wrong square making it more vulnerable (Ke2 walking into a mating net, Kf2 retreating away from defensive duties, Kf5 without first disrupting the opponent). In 1/8 cases (Ng2+), the player abandoned their only drawing mechanism (perpetual check from f3) for a tempting but self-destructive tactical trick. The positions share an extremely narrow margin for error (avg 2.0 good moves), meaning these are critical junctures where only precise action maintains the position, yet the players chose moves motivated by secondary goals: centralization, space gains, piece activity, or material winning.
analysis.move_pattern: Mixed piece types and directions (king moves 3/8, pawn pushes 3/8, knight moves 2/8); no geometric unity—the pattern is conceptual: moves pursuing secondary objectives while the position demands one specific urgent action
analysis.why_bad: These moves waste a critical tempo on non-essential goals while the position has ONE requirement that must be met immediately—typically evacuating an exposed king to the correct square, maintaining a key defensive configuration, or addressing an imminent tactical threat. The resulting tempo loss allows the opponent to execute a devastating tactical blow (mating nets, passed pawn promotions, piece coordination attacks) that was previously impossible.
sub_patterns: King moving to wrong square (exposed to forks/mating nets): Ke2, Kf2, Kf5
Pawn push ignoring urgent defensive need: h6, c4, b4
Active piece move abandoning critical defensive resource: Ng6 (abandoning Kg8), Ng2+ (abandoning perpetual)

analysis.label: Playing a slow, non-forcing move in a critical position that demands immediate tactical precision, surrendering initiative to the opponent.
analysis.description: This feature fires on positions where the player makes a non-urgent move—often a slow pawn push (c6, e3, b6), a king move to a dubious square (Ke2, Ke7), or a piece relocation to a non-threatening square (Qg5)—when the position demands immediate forcing play. In 6/8 positions, the analysis explicitly identifies 'tempo_loss' as the tactical motif or primary tag. The critical commonality is that the position required a forcing continuation (check, attack on a key piece, or immediate development addressing a threat), but instead the player chose a move that gave the opponent a free hand. For example, c6 failed to attack a hanging queen (3/8), e3 advanced a pawn instead of castling to safety (4/8), Ke2 exposed the king instead of repositioning the queen (7/8), and Ke7 walked to the wrong square allowing a knight to find a superior retreat (8/8). The average cp_loss of 1312 and narrow good-move count (avg 1.9) confirm these are high-stakes positions where the tempo squandered was decisive.
analysis.move_pattern: Any piece type; non-capturing, non-checking moves that fail to create an immediate threat or address an urgent opponent's plan; often pawn pushes or king walks
analysis.why_bad: The position demands forcing play (checks, captures, direct threats to key pieces) but the player makes a quiet move that gives the opponent a free tempo to execute their own tactical plan—whether that's consolidating a defensive piece, launching a counterattack on the exposed king, or capturing a critical pawn that was left undefended.
sub_patterns: Slow pawn pushes ignoring development or tactical urgency (c6, e3, b6)
King moves to exposed squares when queen repositioning was needed (Ke2, Ke7)
Piece placed on non-forcing square when check/attack was available (Qg5)
Capturing material on the rim instead of continuing a forcing attack (Nxh1)

analysis.label: Playing a non-threatening, passive or retreating move when the position demands immediate forcing/active play, resulting in critical tempo loss.
analysis.description: This feature fires on positions where a player chooses a passive, non-forcing move when the position urgently demands active, forward play. In 6/7 positions, the move either retreats a piece or places it on a non-threatening square while a clearly stronger forcing alternative exists. The best moves consistently involve aggressive penetration (Rh3 attacking a bishop in 2/7, Rf7 penetrating to 7th rank in 1/7, Qh8+ delivering checks in 1/7, Ka5 advancing toward center in 1/7, or castling/counterplay in 1/7). The played moves instead choose lateral/backward placement (Rh5 staying passive on 5th rank, Rf2 retreating to 2nd rank, Ka3 retreating toward corner, Bc2 slow development, d6 non-urgent pawn push). All analyses tag 'tempo_loss' (7/7) and 'piece_activity' (6/7) as central issues, with the common thread being that the passive move grants the opponent a free tempo to execute their plan (advancing a passed pawn in 3/7, launching an attack, or coordinating pieces).
analysis.move_pattern: Piece placed on passive/lateral/retreating square instead of forward-attacking square; no check, no capture, no direct threat created
analysis.why_bad: The position requires forcing moves (attacks on pieces, penetration to active ranks, checks) to maintain tempo parity; passive moves grant the opponent a free tempo to advance passed pawns, coordinate attacks, or execute tactical sequences that were previously preventable
sub_patterns: Rook staying on 5th rank instead of attacking piece on 3rd rank
Rook retreating to 2nd rank instead of penetrating to 7th
King retreating toward corner instead of advancing toward center
Slow positional development ignoring available forcing checks/sequences
Non-urgent pawn move when concrete threats demand immediate reaction

analysis.label: Moving a piece (usually the king) to a square where the opponent gains a decisive tempo through a check, pawn advance, or tactical shot that forces a permanent concession.
analysis.description: This feature fires on endgame positions where the player makes a move—predominantly a king move (6/10 positions)—that exposes their piece to an immediate tempo-gaining tactical response. In 6/10 cases, the king walks to a square where it can be checked, and the check either forces a structural concession (Kg3 allowing Rc3+ forcing f3), creates a skewer (Kc2 allowing Rh2+→Rh3+ winning the rook), enables a pawn advance with check (Ke3 allowing f4+), or walks into a mating net (Kb6 allowing Rd7+a5#). In the remaining positions, the move ignores a critical passed pawn's ability to advance with tempo (Kd4 ignoring a2, Ra3 ignoring g3, Rc6 ignoring e2). The best alternatives typically involve rook activity (keeping range and flexibility) or keeping the king on a safe square. All 10/10 positions are endgames, 9/10 feature 'tempo_loss' as a key tag, and 8/10 involve king safety failures. The average cp_loss of ~2016 reflects that these tempo gifts are often catastrophic in simplified positions where a single tempo decides the game.
analysis.move_pattern: King (or piece) advances to a square on an open rank/file/diagonal where opponent can deliver check or advance a pawn with tempo; typically king moves one square forward or sideways into the path of an enemy rook check or pawn advance
analysis.why_bad: The move places the king (or piece) on a square where the opponent gains a free tempo through check, skewer, or pawn advance with threat, forcing either a structural weakness (pushing a pawn to block), loss of material (skewer), allowing an unstoppable passed pawn to advance, or walking into a mating construction—all while the correct moves maintain safety or use rook activity instead
sub_patterns: King walks onto rank/file allowing rook check that forces pawn weakness (Kg3→Rc3+/f3, Ke3→f4+)
King moves creating geometric skewer vulnerability along a rank (Kc2→Rh2+→Rh3+ skewering rook)
King advances ignoring critical passed pawn one tempo from decisive advance (Kd4 ignoring a2)
King walks into mating net formed by rook and pawns (Kb6 allowing Rd7+a5#)
Piece moves to inactive square while opponent's pawn gains tempo (Ra3/Rc6 allowing passed pawn push)

analysis.label: Retreating or passively repositioning a piece in a position that demands aggressive continuation, wasting critical tempo.
analysis.description: This feature fires on moves where the player makes a passive retreat, backward move, or non-forcing repositioning when the position demands maintaining or increasing pressure. In 9/11 positions, the player had the initiative or a significant advantage. The moves include clear piece retreats (Ne1 from active f3, Be2 from attacking d3, Nd2 from critical f3, Rdd1 retreating a well-placed rook, Bg3 retreating from h4) and passive relocations (Qb6 moving the queen away from the attacking zone, Bd4 placing the bishop on the wrong square instead of the aggressive Bh6). Even the non-retreat examples (Kxf1, Rd5, Qg6, Rc6) share the theme of choosing a non-forcing, suboptimal piece placement over a concrete attacking continuation. In every case, the best move involved sharp tactical action (Nxe5, Rxf1, Rhg8, Ng5, f4, Qe6, Be4, Bf3, Bh6, Nd5) that maintained pressure, while the played move gave the opponent a free tempo to consolidate, reorganize defenses, or launch counterplay.
analysis.move_pattern: Piece moves backward, sideways, or to a passive square rather than forward/aggressively; typically retreating from the 3rd-5th rank toward the 1st-2nd rank or away from the opponent's king
analysis.why_bad: The retreat removes a piece from a critical function (blocking a diagonal, supporting a tactic, maintaining attacking pressure) and wastes a tempo in a position where the opponent can immediately exploit the respite to solve defensive problems, centralize pieces, or launch tactical counterplay
sub_patterns: Knight retreats from active f3 square (Ne1, Nd2)
Bishop retreats from attacking diagonal (Be2, Bg3)
Rook retreats or moves to passive square (Rdd1)
Queen relocates away from the attacking zone (Qb6, Qg6)
Piece placed on wrong square when a more aggressive option exists (Bd4 instead of Bh6, Rc6 without preparation)

analysis.label: Moving pieces (especially kings) away from central/active squares toward the board's edge or back rank when maintaining centralization or activity was critical.
analysis.description: This feature fires on moves that voluntarily retreat pieces toward passive positions—particularly the board's edges or back rank—when the position demands active centralization or constructive defense. The clearest sub-pattern is king retreats toward the edge in KR vs K endgames (3/10 positions: Kd6, Kc6, Kc6), where the fundamental defensive principle requires staying centralized. Additional examples include Kd8 retreating to the back rank instead of blocking the e-file with development (1/10), Qe1 retreating to a passive back-rank square instead of the prophylactic Kh2 (1/10), Rhh1 abandoning a critical defensive post on h3 for an illusory back-rank attack (1/10), Nde7 retreating a vital defensive knight from its central post (1/10), and f3/c5 weakening moves that create passivity or structural vulnerability instead of addressing the real problem through active piece play (2/10). The common thread across 8/10 meaningful activations is choosing a non-constructive, retreating, or passivity-inducing move when the position required maintaining activity, centralization, or defensive resilience.
analysis.move_pattern: Various piece types (predominantly kings, but also queens, knights, rooks) moving away from the center or from active squares toward the board's edge, back rank, or passive positions
analysis.why_bad: These moves abandon critical active piece placement in favor of perceived safety or escape, but the resulting passivity allows the opponent to advance decisively—kings get corralled to edges for checkmate, defensive pieces lose influence over critical squares, and opponents gain free tempi to execute winning plans.
sub_patterns: King retreating toward edge in KR vs K (violating centralization principle)
King retreating to back rank instead of developing/blocking
Queen/rook retreating to passive first-rank square
Removing a key defensive piece from its critical post
Self-weakening pawn/piece moves that create passivity over activity

analysis.label: Moves that focus on addressing an opponent's active piece (chasing, capturing, or attacking it) while inadvertently leaving a more critical piece or square fatally undefended.
analysis.description: This feature fires on moves where the player targets an opponent's active piece but neglects a more important defensive requirement. In 3/6 positions, a pawn advances to chase an enemy bishop (f6 chasing Bg5, g6 chasing Bh5, gxh4 removing a threatening pawn) but in doing so removes a pawn from a critical defensive duty—leaving the f6 knight hanging after g6 (Position 14), the d5 pawn indefensible after f6 (Position 2), and the king's shield shattered after gxh4 (Position 6). In 2/6 positions, a piece move targets an enemy piece while ignoring that something else is hanging—Qh8 attacks the g8 knight but strands the queen in a corner (Position 15), and Rf2 addresses the e2 bishop but leaves the queen on h4 completely undefended (Position 10). In Position 5, e4 looks like an aggressive central advance but removes the e3 pawn from defending d4, creating an overloaded knight that allows Black to win the queen. All moves share the common error of tunnel-visioning on a secondary tactical concern while a larger vulnerability goes unaddressed.
analysis.move_pattern: Pawn advances (4/6) or piece moves (2/6) directed toward an opponent's active piece, typically on the kingside; the moved unit abandons a critical defensive post
analysis.why_bad: The move addresses a local/cosmetic issue (enemy piece activity) while removing a pawn or piece from a defensive role that was holding the position together, allowing the opponent to exploit the newly undefended piece, pawn, or square with immediate tactical blows
sub_patterns: Pawn advances chasing enemy bishops that remove defense of own knight (f6, g6)
Pawn advances that remove critical support of a central point (e4 removing defense of d4)
Pawn captures that destroy own king's pawn shield (gxh4)
Piece moves targeting enemy pieces while own queen hangs (Rf2, Qh8)

analysis.label: Moving a piece onto or off a critical square that fatally exposes the king (or queen) to an immediate check-based combination along an open file or diagonal.
analysis.description: In all 3/3 positions, the blundering move creates a fatal geometric vulnerability on an open line that the opponent immediately exploits with check. In Position 1, Ke2 places the king directly on the open e-file, allowing Re8+ to win the queen via a forced interposition and capture. In Position 3, Kd4 places the king on a square exposed to both a diagonal check (Qb2+) and a file check (Rd2+), creating a mating net. In Position 4, Nxe5 removes the knight from c6 which was shielding the queen on d7 from the bishop on b5, allowing Bxd7+ to win the queen. All three share the pattern of voluntarily creating exposure on a previously blocked or avoided line, with the punishment being an immediate check (3/3 positions) that leads to decisive material loss or forced mate. The positions had very few good moves available (avg 1.3), indicating razor-sharp situations where one specific geometric constraint had to be respected.
analysis.move_pattern: Piece (usually king) moves onto an open file/diagonal, or a shielding piece moves off a critical line, exposing a high-value target to immediate check
analysis.why_bad: The move ignores a critical open line (file or diagonal) that the opponent controls, allowing an immediate check-based tactic that wins decisive material or forces mate through the newly created geometric vulnerability
sub_patterns: King steps onto open file allowing rook/queen check
King steps onto square exposed to multiple check directions creating mating net
Shielding piece moves off diagonal allowing discovered check/attack on queen

analysis.label: Purposeful-looking moves that fatally ignore the position's most urgent tactical or structural demand, typically king safety.
analysis.description: This feature fires on moves that appear active or purposeful (aggressive knight jumps, checks, pawn advances, flanking moves) but catastrophically fail to address the critical requirement of the position. In 7/8 positions, king safety was the dominant concern that went unaddressed. The blunders include: moving a knight aggressively while leaving pieces hanging on an open file (Nd4, Position 3); walking the king into a pawn storm (Kh3, Position 5); playing a queenside pawn move while facing forced mate on the kingside (b6, Position 7); giving a pointless check that loses tempo while the knight abandons a critical square (Nf4+, Position 8); moving the king toward the edge into a mating net (Kh6, Position 9); escaping the king in the wrong direction into perpetual check (Kg8, Position 11); locking pawns to create a permanently bad bishop (e5, Position 12); and advancing a pawn that becomes frozen and structurally indefensible (g5, Position 14). All share the quality of being 'doing something' moves when the position demanded addressing a specific urgent threat or maintaining a specific structural feature.
analysis.move_pattern: Diverse piece types and directions; moves are characteristically forward/aggressive (advancing pawns, jumping knights forward, moving kings toward the edge) rather than retreating or defensive
analysis.why_bad: These moves ignore the position's critical demand—usually an immediate king safety threat or structural necessity—in favor of a secondary plan. The opponent then exploits the unaddressed vulnerability with forcing tactics (captures on open files, pawn storms with check, sacrificial attacks, establishment of permanent outposts, or perpetual check sequences).
sub_patterns: King walking into exposed squares (Kh3/Kh6/Kg8)
Irrelevant flank moves while kingside collapses (b6/g5)
Tempo-losing aggressive moves that abandon critical defensive duties (Nd4/Nf4+)
Pawn advances that create permanent structural concessions (e5/g5)

analysis.label: Knights abandon strong central posts for aggressive-looking peripheral squares that leave them hanging or allow the opponent to seize central control.
analysis.description: In 6/7 positions, a knight moves from a useful central square (typically f3 or c6) to an edge square (g5, g4, h4, b4) motivated by speculative attacking ideas like targeting f7, threatening forks, or attacking bishops. In 3/7 cases (positions 1, 3, 4), the knight specifically moves Ng5 in Fried Liver-style attacks on f7 that fail because the knight abandons defense of d4 or lands undefended. In 2/7 cases (positions 4, 5), the knight lands on a completely unprotected square and is simply captured by queen (Qxg5 or Qa4+/Qxb4). In position 7, Nh4 leaves the critical e4 square unguarded, allowing Black's knight to occupy it. Position 2 shows a knight retreating to the rim (Ng4) instead of making a central capture (Nxe4). The single non-knight move (Kh6, position 6) shares the pattern of moving to the edge for speculative reasons while losing tempo. All moves prioritize aggressive fantasies over concrete central requirements.
analysis.move_pattern: Knight moves from central file (c/f) to rim squares (b4, g4, g5, h4) - typically 2 squares outward from center
analysis.why_bad: The knight abandons critical central defensive duties (guarding d4, controlling e4/e5) or lands on an undefended square, allowing the opponent to either capture the hanging piece directly, exploit undefended central pawns, or seize dominant central control with tempo
sub_patterns: Ng5 Fried Liver-style attack on f7 that abandons d4 defense
Knight lands on undefended peripheral square captured by queen check
Knight retreats to rim instead of making available central capture
Knight moves to edge chasing a bishop while leaving key squares uncontrolled

analysis.label: Player uses an inferior piece to address a positional need, blocking or ignoring the correct piece's urgent role.
analysis.description: In all 3/3 positions, the player makes a move with the wrong piece that either blocks or ignores the critical piece needed for the position's demands. In Position 11, f3 (pawn) permanently blocks the knight from reaching its ideal f3 square, stranding it on d2 when Ndf3 was winning. In Position 12, Bxb3 uses the bishop to capture when the rook needed to attack via b3 (Ra3→Rxb3+ with check was decisive). In Position 2, Rc3 moves the rook passively when the knight on f3 urgently needed relocation before ...g4 drives it away. The common error is choosing a superficially logical piece/pawn to handle a task while the truly critical piece goes unused or becomes obstructed, resulting in massive tempo loss (tagged in 3/3 positions) and loss of piece coordination.
analysis.move_pattern: Quiet move (rook lateral, pawn push, or bishop capture) to the 3rd rank that ignores or blocks the key piece's optimal routing
analysis.why_bad: The move wastes a critical tempo or permanently obstructs the correct piece from fulfilling its urgent role, allowing the opponent to seize the initiative with concrete threats (pawn storms, development with tempo, or promotion threats) that the misplaced/blocked piece can no longer counter.
sub_patterns: Pawn push blocking knight's ideal square
Bishop capture where rook attack was needed
Passive rook move ignoring urgent knight relocation

analysis.label: Moving a queen or rook to a superficially aggressive square that creates no concrete threat, abandoning critical duties and allowing the opponent to seize initiative with tempo.
analysis.description: In 10/11 positions, the blundering move involves a major piece (queen in 7/11, rook in 4/11) relocating to a square that appears active—targeting a pawn, occupying an open file, entering the 7th rank, or pressuring the opponent's king—but generates no forcing continuation. The best moves in these positions all involve either immediate concrete action (perpetual checks in Position 1, Rc7 invasion in Position 6, the e5 central break in Position 3, Bxf6 combination in Position 12) or maintaining the piece on a critical square for defensive coordination (Qg6 in Position 13, Queen on c7 in Position 15, Rook on f1 in Position 14). Instead, the played moves drift to non-urgent targets: Qb3 chases b7, Rh7 enters the 7th rank against nothing, Rb6 attacks a6, Qa3 threatens the already-escaping king, Rb1 envisions b-file counterplay. The 'tempo_loss' tag appears in 10/11 positions because these moves uniformly grant the opponent a free move to either attack the relocated piece (Nh5 hitting Qg3/Qg5 in 2/11), exploit the vacancy left behind (Nf3+ forking Rb1, ...Re6 hitting displaced queen in 2/11), or simply escape danger (Kf7/Kd8 evading in 3/11).
analysis.move_pattern: Queen or rook moves laterally or to a new file/rank, appearing to create an attack or occupy an active square, but not delivering check or making a forcing capture
analysis.why_bad: The moved piece creates no concrete threat that the opponent must address, granting them a free tempo to either attack the now-exposed piece, exploit the abandoned square/defensive duty, or consolidate their own position—the 'threat' is easily sidestepped while the player loses coordination or critical counterplay resources.
sub_patterns: Queen moves away from kingside when perpetual/attack resources require it there (Qb3, Qa3, Qb6)
Queen repositions to exposed square inviting tempo-gaining attacks (Qg5, Qg3, Qh5)
Rook occupies open file/rank prematurely or self-blocks behind own pieces (Rc1, Rh7, Rb6)
Rook abandons king defense for illusory counterattack (Rb1, Rb6)

analysis.label: Moving a piece to a seemingly active square instead of addressing the most critical passed pawn threat in the endgame.
analysis.description: This feature fires on endgame positions where the player makes a 'general improvement' or 'activating' move (typically placing a rook on an open file/rank or centralizing the king) while ignoring the single most urgent concrete threat in the position, almost always involving a passed pawn. In 7/9 positions, the critical issue is a passed pawn that needs to be immediately blockaded, captured, or promoted against. In Position 2, Ra6 abandons the f-file needed to blockade the g-pawn; in Position 7, Rf2 fails to challenge the a8 promotion square (Rf8 needed); in Position 9, Ra7 abandons control of the c1 promotion square; in Position 3, Kf2 ignores the a3/b4 pawn tension; in Position 8, Rhf3 plays a slow consolidation when Ra1+ wins material immediately. The consistent error is choosing a move that 'looks good' positionally (7th rank rook, centralized king, doubled rooks) while the position demands one specific concrete action within the next 1-2 tempi.
analysis.move_pattern: Rook or King moved to a seemingly active but non-critical square (often rook to open file/rank, king centralizing), away from the square needed to address the most urgent pawn threat
analysis.why_bad: These moves waste a critical tempo in positions where the opponent's passed pawn (or pawn break) creates an immediate promotion/tactical threat that cannot be deferred; the 'active' square chosen is irrelevant to the position's concrete demands, allowing the opponent to advance unstoppably or deliver an immediate tactical blow.
sub_patterns: Rook leaves back rank/key file allowing unstoppable promotion
King centralizes instead of resolving critical pawn tension
Slow rook doubling/consolidation when forcing tactical blow exists
Rook activates on wrong file/rank while passed pawn advances

analysis.label: Moving a piece or pawn away from a critical king-defense function for a seemingly improving but tactically punished move.
analysis.description: This feature fires on moves where the player voluntarily removes a piece or pawn from a vital defensive post protecting their king (or neglects an urgent king-safety priority), choosing instead a 'natural-looking' improving move. In 5/7 positions, king_safety is the primary tactical motif of the refutation. Specific manifestations include: removing a rook from a critical guarding square (Rfd3 abandons f3, enabling the f3 pawn break, Position 4), pushing an f-pawn away from its shielding role (f6 removes the f7 shield allowing Rc7 7th-rank invasion, Position 7), moving the king onto a vulnerable diagonal (Kg2 enables Qd5+ tempo, Position 3), moving the queen away from defensive rerouting capacity (Qc7 prevents Qe8 defense of f7, Position 5), and making non-urgent captures/improvements while the king sits exposed (Bxb6 ignores open e-file discovered check, Position 1). In 6/7 cases the opponent punishes with a direct tactical blow against the weakened king. The moves all appear reasonable superficially—centralizing, capturing, 'improving'—but fatally ignore that the moved unit was performing an irreplaceable defensive function.
analysis.move_pattern: Piece or pawn moves AWAY from king-adjacent defensive square; diverse piece types (R, Q, K, B, f-pawn) leaving squares that shield or cover the king area
analysis.why_bad: The moved piece/pawn was performing a critical defensive function for king safety; its removal allows the opponent a tactical breakthrough (discovered attack, 7th-rank invasion, diagonal check, pawn storm) against the now-exposed king
sub_patterns: f-pawn advance removing king shield pawn (f6, f5)
Rook/Queen leaving king-defense square for seemingly active post (Rfd3, Qc7)
King walking onto vulnerable line (Kg2 onto diagonal)
Non-urgent capture while king remains on open file (Bxb6)
Tempo-wasting improvement ignoring opponent's advancing threat (Be5)

analysis.label: Playing a non-forcing repositioning or preparatory move when the position demands immediate concrete action (typically a pawn break or tactical shot).
analysis.description: This feature fires on positions where a player chooses a quiet, seemingly reasonable 'improving' move while ignoring a critical forcing opportunity. In 6/9 cases, the best move was an immediate pawn break (h3, e4, b5, h3, g4, Rf8-enabling-Bxf6+), yet the player chose piece repositioning (Be6, Nf5, Ne4, Re6, Ra3) or slow pawn pushes (c3, c4, Kf5, Ke7) instead. The positions share a common urgency: a narrow window exists for concrete action before the opponent stabilizes or launches their own threats. The average of only 1.9 good moves available confirms these are critical-moment positions where only forcing play maintains the evaluation. In every case, the played move looks purposeful (centralizing a piece, defending a pawn, attacking something) but fatally ignores the position's tactical demands, allowing the opponent to execute plans that should have been preempted.
analysis.move_pattern: Non-capturing, non-checking piece repositioning or quiet pawn advance; no specific geometric direction—moves are diverse in piece type but uniformly non-forcing
analysis.why_bad: These moves waste a critical tempo in positions with concrete tactical demands. The opponent gains time to execute their own plan (kingside break, back-rank invasion, piece capture) that the best move would have preempted or rendered impossible. The quiet move either abandons a key defensive duty (4/9: removing defenders from critical squares like d5, d1, g4, e8) or forgoes an immediate pawn break that would seize the initiative.
sub_patterns: Piece retreats away from attacking/defending post (Be6, Nf5, Re6, Ra3)
Defensive pawn moves instead of offensive pawn breaks (c3 instead of g4, c4 instead of Rf8)
King wandering when pawn action is required (Kf5, Ke7)
Removing sole defender of key pawn or square (Ne4 leaving d5, Ra3 leaving d1)

analysis.label: Moves that pursue a secondary or superficially logical objective while neglecting the position's most urgent tactical or king-safety requirement.
analysis.description: This feature fires on moves that have a plausible rationale but fatally ignore the position's most critical demand, resulting in catastrophic punishment. In 5/6 positions, king safety is the urgent requirement being neglected: f3 weakens the king's diagonal while trying to attack a knight (Position 3), Qc2 delays castling preparation in favor of queen repositioning (Position 8), Kc1 walks directly into a forced mating corridor instead of fleeing to the a-file (Position 10), Nh5 decentralizes a knight to the rim instead of countering centrally with d5 while both kings are uncastled (Position 14), and Ne4 jumps aggressively without first neutralizing the opponent's bishop with d5 (Position 13). In 4/6 positions, development urgency is ignored in favor of a lower-priority action. The blunders share the characteristic of having very few good alternatives (avg 1.8), indicating positions that demand precise responses to a single critical factor, yet the player addresses a secondary concern instead. The refutations consistently exploit the neglected vulnerability—checks along weakened diagonals, queen checks exploiting exposed kings, forced mating patterns, and piece captures after removing defenders.
analysis.move_pattern: Diverse piece types and directions; no geometric commonality. Functionally: moves that address a secondary positional concern (contesting a file, attacking a piece, repositioning) rather than the critical tactical requirement.
analysis.why_bad: Each move fails to address the position's single most urgent need (usually king safety or a direct tactical vulnerability), allowing the opponent to exploit that neglected weakness immediately with checks, sacrifices, or forcing sequences that the played move neither prevents nor mitigates.
sub_patterns: Pawn moves that weaken king position while attacking enemy pieces (f3 opening diagonal)
Queen repositioning that abandons defensive coverage of critical squares (Qc2 allowing Qa5+)
King moves toward danger instead of away from mating patterns (Kc1 into king march)
Premature piece jumps without essential preparatory moves (Ne4/Nh5 without d5 first)
Contesting files/squares while ignoring that own piece is tactically vulnerable (Rd1 ignoring threatened bishop)

analysis.label: Plausible-looking developing or aggressive moves that fail to address a critical undefended line or piece, allowing immediate tactical exploitation.
analysis.description: This feature fires on moves that appear natural, developing, or active but critically neglect the position's most urgent tactical requirement—typically an unguarded diagonal, open file, or exposed piece. In 5/7 positions, the key vulnerability is a long diagonal left unblocked or undefended (Bd7 leaves b7 exposed on the long diagonal; f5 opens e1-h4 for Qh4+; Neg5 abandons e4 creating fork vulnerability; Bd6 fails to block a8-h1 diagonal; Kf1 walks into a mating net along diagonals). In 6/7 cases, the correct alternatives all specifically address the critical vulnerability (keeping the c8-bishop to guard b7, playing Nc6 to block the diagonal, developing pieces to cover exposed lines, or fleeing toward safety). The blunder moves all share the quality of looking like reasonable chess (developing a bishop, centralizing a piece, advancing aggressively) while being tactically oblivious to a concrete geometric threat that the opponent exploits within 1-2 moves.
analysis.move_pattern: Minor piece development (bishops to d4/d6/d7, knights to g4/g5) or pawn/king moves to seemingly natural squares, typically moving AWAY from the critical line or removing a piece from a needed defensive post
analysis.why_bad: Each move either removes a defender from a critical line, fails to block a dangerous diagonal/file, or self-blocks coordination—while correct alternatives all specifically neutralize the position's most pressing geometric vulnerability. The opponent punishes by immediately exploiting the undefended line (Bf3xa8, Bxb7, Qh4+ on open diagonal, Nf4 with tempo, Rbe1 challenging uncoordinated pieces).
sub_patterns: Removing a defender from a long diagonal (Bd7 unguards b7, Neg5 abandons e4)
Failing to block a critical diagonal when multiple alternatives do (Bd6 vs Nc6)
Self-blocking piece coordination (Bd4 blocks knight's ideal d4 square)
Aggressive piece placement that creates counter-tempo (Ng4 allows Nf4 hitting queen)
King moving toward danger rather than away from geometric threats (Kf1 into mating diagonal)

analysis.label: Playing a quiet positional or preparatory move when the position demands immediate tactical resolution of a critical tension.
analysis.description: This feature fires on positions where a player makes a non-forcing 'improving' move (king centralization, bishop repositioning, quiet pawn advance) while a critical tactical tension demands instant resolution. In 5/7 positions, the correct move was a concrete capture (Nxf3, Rxc8, Nxd4, Rxc4, bxc6) that the player ignored in favor of a 'planning' move. In 6/7 cases, the blunder gave the opponent a tempo to resolve the tension in THEIR favor—capturing an undefended piece first (positions 1, 2), exploiting an overextended king with tempo-gaining checks (positions 3, 7), or winning a critical passed pawn (positions 4, 6). The positions share extremely low good-move counts (avg 1.7), indicating sharp moments where only precise forcing play maintained the evaluation, yet the player chose the strategic-looking but concretely wrong continuation.
analysis.move_pattern: Quiet non-forcing moves (piece repositioning, king walks, pawn pushes) in positions requiring immediate captures or pawn breaks to resolve mutual tension
analysis.why_bad: The wasted tempo allows the opponent to resolve the critical tension in their favor—capturing an undefended piece, exploiting king exposure with tempo-gaining checks/advances, or winning a key passed pawn that was previously contested
sub_patterns: Slow move leaves own piece hanging while mutual tension exists (a5, Bb4)
Repositioning piece instead of capturing opponent's undefended piece (Be7 misses Rxc8)
King overextension into exposed square allowing tempo-gaining pawn checks (Kg4, Ke4)
King chases secondary target while abandoning critical pawn (Kb5)
Wrong capture that ignores survival-critical forcing sequence (Qxf4)

analysis.label: Playing a seemingly reasonable piece-improving move that completely ignores the position's critical tactical demand, resulting in catastrophic loss.
analysis.description: This feature fires on positions where a player makes a 'looks-good' piece move—developing, centralizing, or grabbing material—in a position that has very few viable options (avg 1.3 good moves) and demands a specific concrete/forcing response. In 6/6 positions, the played move appears superficially reasonable (Ng5 activating a knight, Nxd4 capturing centrally, Qd6 centralizing, Rxh2 winning a pawn, Bd6 developing, Bd1 repositioning) but fatally ignores the most urgent tactical issue. The correct moves were always concrete and addressing the specific threat: blocking a file (Bg5), creating counterattack with check (Qa5 in 2/6 cases), or defending the king (Qh2/Qf1). The blunders consistently prioritize general chess principles over the immediate tactical reality, resulting in massive cp_loss (avg 1839) from fork exploits (2/6), hanging/trapped pieces (2/6), or checkmate (1/6).
analysis.move_pattern: Any piece type moving to an apparently logical square (development, centralization, or pawn capture) without addressing an immediate tactical vulnerability
analysis.why_bad: The position demands a specific forcing or defensive response to an urgent threat (fork, hanging piece, mating attack, discovered attack), but the player operates on general principles—improving pieces, grabbing material—while the critical tactical issue goes unaddressed, allowing the opponent to exploit the vulnerability catastrophically.
sub_patterns: Piece development/centralization into a fork (Qd6, Nxd4)
Pawn grab walking into discovered attack (Rxh2)
Piece activation leaving own piece hanging (Ng5)
Quiet development instead of mandatory counterattack (Bd6)
Piece repositioning ignoring immediate checkmate (Bd1)

analysis.label: Pieces move to the 2nd-3rd rank (often h-file) abandoning active duties for illusory plans.
analysis.description: This feature fires on moves where pieces relocate to low-rank squares (2nd or 3rd rank from White's perspective) in pursuit of plans that appear aggressive but are actually passive or self-defeating. In 2/3 positions, the move targets the h-file specifically (Rh2, Bxh3), attempting to generate kingside pressure against the opponent's king. In Position 1, the rook abandons its critical defensive post on d2 to go to the passive h2 square. In Position 2, the bishop trades itself on h3 to 'open lines' but actually removes Black's best attacking piece. Position 3 (Kc2, 0 cp loss) represents a king retreating to the 2nd rank in a hopeless position. The common geometric signature is pieces moving to squares on the second or third rank near the board edge, often leaving critical central or defensive tasks unattended.
analysis.move_pattern: Piece moves to 2nd-3rd rank squares (h2, h3, c2), often laterally or backward, frequently targeting h-file
analysis.why_bad: The moves abandon active piece placements or trade key attacking pieces for insufficient compensation, sacrificing concrete positional duties (central control, pawn defense) for illusory flank activity that the opponent easily neutralizes
sub_patterns: Rook slides to h2 abandoning central defense
Bishop sacrifices itself on h3 for a pawn removing key attacker
King retreats to passive 2nd rank square

analysis.label: Playing a natural-looking developing or advancing move instead of recognizing a concrete tactical opportunity involving capturable or forkable pieces.
analysis.description: This feature fires on positions where the player makes a 'routine' or 'obvious-looking' move (development, pawn push, or straightforward capture) while missing a much stronger concrete tactical resource. In 4/4 positions, the correct move involved an immediate capture or forcing move that exploited piece vulnerability: Bxe6 winning a queen for a bishop (position 5), Nxe5 starting a devastating combination (position 3), c4/Nxe4 preventing a fork (position 4), and Qc5 addressing queen safety before a pin materializes (position 2). In 3/4 cases, the blunder either created a tactical vulnerability (fork target on e2, trapped queen after e5) or failed to exploit one (hanging e5 pawn, queen capturable by bishop). The common error is prioritizing superficially reasonable 'improving' moves over the tactical demands of the position, particularly failing to see that pieces are capturable or about to become capturable by less valuable pieces.
analysis.move_pattern: Quiet developing or advancing moves (bishop development to natural squares, central pawn pushes, or captures with the wrong/more valuable piece) when a concrete capture or forcing move was available
analysis.why_bad: These moves ignore that a key piece (often a queen) is currently capturable, about to become forkable, or that an opponent's piece can be won through a short tactical sequence - the player defaults to 'natural' play instead of calculating concrete tactics
sub_patterns: Bishop development creating fork vulnerability (Be2 allowing Nc3)
Pawn push exposing previously safe piece (e5 allowing Bb5 attack on queen)
Quiet development missing immediate combination (Bg5 instead of Nxe5-Nxf7)
Capturing with wrong piece losing value differential (Qxe6 instead of Bxe6)

analysis.label: Playing a quiet repositioning move when the position demands immediate concrete/tactical action, surrendering a critical tempo to the opponent.
analysis.description: In all 6/6 positions, Black plays a non-forcing 'improving' move (piece repositioning, quiet king move, or structural pawn move) when the position urgently demands a concrete tactical response. In Position 1, g6 is a passive pawn move instead of the devastating Ne3 fork. In Position 2, Nf5 repositions a knight instead of the critical d3 pawn advance. In Position 6, Ng6 repositions a knight instead of capturing with Qxf3. In Position 11, Kh8 tucks the king into a vulnerable corner instead of active defense with Ng6/Kg8. In Position 13, Kd7 centralizes the king into a mating net instead of staying safer. In Position 14, Be7 repositions a bishop instead of Ne7 which uses the correct piece. The 'tempo_loss' tag appears in 6/6 positions and 'missed_tactic' in 5/6, confirming the consistent pattern of squandering urgency on comfort.
analysis.move_pattern: Quiet non-forcing moves (piece repositioning, king shuffles, structural pawns) with no check, no capture, and no immediate threat
analysis.why_bad: These moves gift the opponent a free tempo to consolidate, reorganize passive pieces, block passed pawns, launch attacks, or execute back-rank/mating patterns that the immediate tactical alternative would have prevented or exploited
sub_patterns: Knight repositioning to seemingly active square (Nf5, Ng6)
Passive king moves to worse squares (Kh8, Kd7)
Structural pawn moves ignoring tactics (g6)
Wrong piece to correct square (Be7 instead of Ne7)

analysis.label: Moves that squander a vital tempo in positions where an urgent race, threat, or defensive task demands immediate precise action.
analysis.description: This feature fires on moves that lose a critical tempo in time-sensitive positions. The pattern manifests in several ways: capturing material when there's no time for it (Kxc4, Kxh2, Qxb7 in 3/10 positions), taking an indirect route when a direct one is required (Ka6 instead of Ka5, Kc7 instead of Ke6 in 2/10), displacing a key defensive piece to an irrelevant square (Qb5, Rd8 in 2/10), making preparatory moves when immediate action is needed (g6 instead of developing, Kb3 instead of routing the knight in 2/10), and removing a critical defensive barrier for dubious positional 'improvements' (c5 opening the diagonal in 1/10). In all cases, the position demands precise, urgent action—blockading a passed pawn, defending an exposed king, racing to a key square—and the played move appears reasonable but is fatally slow. The 'tempo_loss' tag appears in 8/8 analyzed positions, and 'king_safety' in 7/8, reflecting that the lost tempo typically allows the opponent to execute a decisive attack or promotion.
analysis.move_pattern: Any piece type; moves that go to a non-urgent square, capture non-critical material, or take an indirect path when a direct one exists—often king moves to wrong squares or queen/rook moves away from the critical sector
analysis.why_bad: The position contains a time-critical race or threat (promotion race, mating attack, key square contest) where every tempo counts, and the played move wastes one or more tempi by prioritizing material gain, preparation, or natural-looking placement over addressing the single most urgent requirement of the position.
