sub_patterns: Greedy captures that divert pieces from defensive duties (Kxc4, Kxh2, Qxb7)
Indirect king routing losing a crucial tempo (Ka6 vs Ka5, Kc7 vs Ke6)
Displacing defensive pieces to irrelevant squares (Qb5, Rd8 abandoning king defense)
Preparatory moves when immediate action is required (g6, Kb3 instead of knight move)
Pawn advances removing critical defensive barriers (c5 opening diagonal to exposed king)

analysis.label: Playing natural-looking improving moves in overwhelmingly won positions where forced checkmate exists, converting a decisive win into merely a large advantage.
analysis.description: This feature activates in positions where White has an overwhelming advantage—typically forced checkmate—but plays a 'natural' or 'comfortable' move instead of finding the precise killing blow. In 3/4 positions, forced checkmate was available (mate in 1, mate in 16, mate in 32), yet the player chose moves that look reasonable on the surface: centralizing a bishop (Be4), activating the king (Kf3), or capturing material with check (Qxe6+). These moves follow sound general principles—piece centralization, king activity in endgames, material gain with tempo—but catastrophically fail to deliver the forced win. The common thread is that the position demands a specific, often non-obvious precise move (Qc7#, Bc5, Rd6) while the player defaults to generic 'improving' technique appropriate for normal winning positions. Position 4/4 (Kc7, 0cp loss) represents the baseline pattern—a won endgame with advanced passed pawn—where such a move happens to be correct, suggesting the feature detects the positional archetype rather than exclusively the mistake.
analysis.move_pattern: Various piece types making centralizing, capturing, or activating moves that appear to generically improve White's already dominant position
analysis.why_bad: These moves apply routine winning technique (centralization, material gain, king activation) in positions that demand specific tactical precision—the 'improving' move abandons the key square, file, or diagonal needed for the forced mating pattern, giving the opponent time to establish defensive resources or escape the mating net.
sub_patterns: Centralizing a piece to a square needed by another piece (blocking coordination)
King activation when piece activity is more urgent
Capturing with check instead of delivering checkmate
Applying general endgame principles when concrete calculation is required

analysis.label: Apparently active moves that abandon positional control and inadvertently open a critical diagonal for the opponent to exploit.
analysis.description: In all 3/3 positions, the player makes a move that appears productive (centralizing a piece, capturing material, or gaining space) but critically opens or exposes a diagonal that the opponent immediately exploits with a forcing response. In position 1, Qc4 places the queen on the b5-f1 diagonal alongside the undefended Rf1, allowing Bb5 to fork both. In position 3, Rxb4 abandons the dominant b2 rook post for a pawn, freeing White to play f5 attacking the bishop on e6 along the newly relevant diagonal. In position 6, e4 pushes the pawn off e5, directly opening the h3-c8 diagonal for White's fianchettoed bishop to relocate to h3 and pressure the queen on e6. All 3/3 moves share the theme of prioritizing immediate material or space over maintaining piece coordination, with the punishment arriving via diagonal-based tactics (bishop redeployment or fork).
analysis.move_pattern: Piece or pawn moves to 4th rank (c4/b4/e4) that opens or exposes a critical diagonal
analysis.why_bad: The move abandons a defensive function or positional asset, opening a diagonal that allows the opponent's bishop (or piece along that diagonal) to deliver a tempo-gaining tactical blow—fork, attack on queen, or breakthrough.
sub_patterns: Queen centralization onto undefended diagonal (Qc4 allowing Bb5 fork)
Rook captures pawn abandoning dominant post (Rxb4 allowing f5 tempo)
Pawn push opening bishop diagonal against own queen (e4 allowing Bh3)

analysis.label: Non-forcing moves (especially slow pawn advances or non-urgent captures) in positions with exposed kings, gifting the opponent a critical tempo to exploit king vulnerability with checks or tactical blows.
analysis.description: This feature fires on positions where the player makes a passive, non-forcing move—typically a kingside pawn advance (f5 appears twice, h5, h4) or a peripheral material capture (Bxh3, Rxd5)—when the position's key characteristic is mutual king exposure demanding immediate tactical action. In 7/9 positions, the opponent's primary refutation involves delivering a check that gains a decisive tempo. The played moves uniformly fail to address the most urgent positional demand: in Position 1, Kf7 walks onto a check diagonal; in Position 6, h5 ignores a forced mate via checks; in Position 14, Rxd5 allows Bh3+ zwischenzug; in Position 3, Bxh3 removes the key defender of the king's diagonal. All 9 positions feature at least one exposed king, and 8/9 feature the playing side's own king being tactically vulnerable. The better alternatives (available in 7/9 cases with 2-3 good moves) consistently involved immediate forcing play: checks (Qxc2+, Rg1+), piece activation (Nf4, Rg7, b4), or prophylactic king moves (Ke7, Ke8) that addressed the tactical vulnerability first.
analysis.move_pattern: Non-checking, non-threatening pawn advances (especially f5, h5, h4) or captures of peripheral material (pawns on d5, h3), predominantly on the kingside, made by the side whose own king is exposed
analysis.why_bad: These moves waste a critical tempo in positions where king exposure creates immediate tactical urgency—the opponent exploits the gifted tempo with a check or forcing move that gains material, escapes a trap, or delivers a mating attack. The played move neither creates a threat nor addresses the position's central tactical vulnerability.
sub_patterns: Kingside pawn advance (f5/h5/h4) when checks or piece activity wins immediately
Capturing a non-essential pawn while abandoning a key defensive post
Pawn/piece move that walks into or enables a discovered/direct check
Materialistic capture that allows a zwischenzug check

analysis.label: King retreats to the h-file (or a defensive pawn push) as a perceived safety measure when active defense or piece coordination was required.
analysis.description: In 4/5 positions, the player moved the king to the h-file (Kh7, Kh1, Kh3, Kh7), and in the remaining case played a pawn move (f6) motivated by king safety. All moves share the intent of prophylactically improving king security by tucking it toward the edge, but each time the move either wastes a critical tempo (3/5 positions explicitly tagged as tempo_loss), abandons a defensive duty (Position 15: Kh7 leaves f7 undefended; Position 3: Kh1 leaves Bd2 hanging), or creates new tactical vulnerabilities (Position 14: Kh3 allows perpetual via Qg2+; Position 11: f6 self-blocks the king's escape route). The correct alternatives in each case involved active piece moves (Qf2, Rf3, Bf8, Be6) that addressed concrete threats rather than vaguely improving king placement. The average cp_loss of ~2027 (skewed by the forced mate case) reflects how catastrophic these seemingly quiet retreats can be.
analysis.move_pattern: King moves one square toward the h-file (Kg7-h7, Kg1-h1, Kg4-h3, Kg8-h7), or a pawn advance on the f-file meant to shield the king
analysis.why_bad: These moves waste tempo on vague king safety when concrete tactical obligations exist—leaving pieces/pawns undefended, self-blocking escape squares, or walking into perpetual check patterns—while the position demanded active piece coordination instead.
sub_patterns: King abandons defense of adjacent pawn (Kh7 losing f7)
King retreat leaves piece hanging (Kh1 losing Bd2)
King walks into perpetual check corridor (Kh3)
Defensive pawn push self-blocks king escape (f6)

analysis.label: Slow, natural-looking moves played in tactically critical positions where an immediate threat or vulnerability demands urgent attention.
analysis.description: This feature activates on moves that appear positionally reasonable or 'improving' but catastrophically ignore an urgent tactical crisis. In 9/9 positions, the player made a move focused on general improvement (castling, developing, centralizing, creating luft) while the position demanded immediate concrete action. The blunders include: castling into a diagonal check (O-O, Position 1), moving a defensive piece away from hanging material (Ne5, Position 4), pushing pawns that destroy drawn structures or create hanging pawns (g5+, g6, b6 in Positions 5, 12, 10), developing pieces that obstruct key defensive squares (Be6, Bg4 in Positions 11, 6), stepping the king into a pawn fork (Kf2, Position 13), and making a passive rook move allowing forced mate (Re3, Position 14). The average cp_loss of 1331 and average good moves of only 2.0 confirm these are critical-moment positions with very narrow correct paths. In all cases, the opponent had an immediate tactical punishment (fork 2/9, hanging piece 2/9, king attack 3/9, pawn structure collapse 2/9) that the played move completely failed to address.
analysis.move_pattern: Mixed piece types and directions; all are non-forcing quiet moves (no captures, only 1 check) that fail to address the most critical tactical element
analysis.why_bad: The player treats a tactically critical position as if it were quiet, making a 'normal' improving move without calculating the opponent's immediate forcing response. The position demands either neutralizing a specific threat, maintaining a precise defensive structure, or generating immediate counterplay—but instead the player plays on autopilot.
sub_patterns: Castling/developing into a tactical vulnerability (O-O, Bg4, Be6, Re3)
Pawn moves creating new weaknesses or destroying key structures (g5+, g6, b6)
King/piece moves stepping into forks or removing defensive coverage (Kf2, Ne5)

analysis.label: Quiet piece development or repositioning moves (especially bishops) that neglect an immediate tactical or defensive necessity in the position.
analysis.description: In 7/7 positions, the player makes a non-forcing 'developing' or repositioning move—most commonly placing a bishop on a seemingly natural square (5/7 are bishop moves: Bb7, Bb5, Be2, Bb2, plus Rf1/Re1/a4)—while the position demands an urgent defensive action or the move creates a new exploitable vulnerability. In 4/7 cases, the moved piece was either defending a critical point (Re1 abandons f2, Be2 abandons g2) or needed to go to a specific defensive square (Bb7 should be Be6 to block f7 pressure, Rf1 should be Be3 to block f2 diagonal). In 2/7 cases, the piece lands on a square that becomes an immediate tactical target (Bb2 falls to Rd2 invasion, Bb5 allows Qa5+ exploiting the diagonal). The opponent consistently punishes with forcing tactics—checks, invasions, or captures—that exploit the neglected weakness within 1-2 moves.
analysis.move_pattern: Quiet piece repositioning (mostly bishops) to natural-looking development squares; non-forcing, non-capturing moves along diagonals or files
analysis.why_bad: The move addresses a low-priority positional goal (piece development, long diagonal control, file occupation) while ignoring a specific high-priority defensive requirement—either removing a piece from a critical defensive post, failing to block a dangerous attacking diagonal/file, or placing a piece on an immediately exploitable undefended square.
sub_patterns: Bishop developed to long diagonal while key pawn (f7/g2/h3) left undefended
Rook moved off f-file abandoning f2 defense against converging pieces
Bishop placed on undefended square exploitable via open file invasion
Slow flank move (a4) ignoring imminent kingside attack
Development to aggressive but irrelevant square exposing king diagonal

analysis.label: Moving a piece away from the critical sector to a passive, peripheral, or exposed square when the position demands urgent active play.
analysis.description: This feature fires on moves that voluntarily relocate pieces to ineffective squares—typically toward the rim, back rank, or away from the main battleground—wasting critical tempo in positions that demand immediate action. Knights to the rim appear in 4/13 cases (Na5, Nh4×2, Nd7 leaving f6), pieces retreating to passive squares in 5/13 (Bd8, Be7, Qa6, Rxe7, Nd7), and king/pawn moves in the wrong direction in 4/13 (Kg7, Kxh2, a5, cxb3). The unifying thread is that every move goes in the opposite direction from what the position requires: instead of challenging the center, addressing immediate threats, or maintaining active posts, the player moves toward the periphery or passivity. The positions typically have sharp demands (open files toward the king, critical central tension, advancing passed pawns) where a single wasted tempo is catastrophic—reflected in the extremely high average cp_loss of 1651 and low average good-move count of 2.2.
analysis.move_pattern: Any piece type moving away from optimal activity toward the board edge, back rank, or non-critical sector; often knights to a/h files, pieces retreating from dominant posts, or wrong-direction captures
analysis.why_bad: These moves waste critical tempo in positions with urgent demands (central challenges, king safety threats, passed pawns), placing pieces on squares where they accomplish nothing while the opponent exploits the lost time to seize the initiative, win material, or deliver a mating attack.
sub_patterns: Knight retreating to rim (a/h file) from active central square
Piece moving away from dominant outpost to passive square
King moving to more exposed position on the edge
Wrong capture target (peripheral vs central)
Queen/piece decentralizing to pursue irrelevant threats

analysis.label: Playing natural-looking or attractive moves (centralizing, grabbing material, giving checks) in critical positions that demand specific concrete tactical action.
analysis.description: This feature fires on moves that appear 'generally good' by standard chess principles but catastrophically ignore the position's urgent concrete requirement. The pattern manifests as: knight centralizations to outposts (Ne5, Nd5, Nc5 - 3/10), greedy pawn captures on the wing (Bxa3, Qxa7 - 2/10), seemingly active rook/piece moves (Rb6, Bd6+ - 2/10), and premature king walks or pawn pushes (Ke7, b5, Kf4 - 3/10). In every case, the position had extremely limited good options (avg 1.7 good moves), indicating critical junctures demanding precise calculation. The missed tactical themes include queen traps (Nd5), deflection sacrifices (Ne5), 7th-rank invasions (b5), mating patterns (Bd6+), and hanging pieces (Bxa3). The moves all share the characteristic of being 'the kind of move you'd play if you weren't looking deeply' - they follow general principles (centralize, capture, gain activity) rather than addressing the one thing the position actually requires.
analysis.move_pattern: Piece/pawn moves to 'attractive' squares - knight centralizations, wing captures, forward king/rook moves - that appear actively improving but miss urgent tactical demands
analysis.why_bad: These moves waste a critical tempo in positions demanding immediate concrete action, allowing the opponent to execute a tactical blow (deflection, invasion, piece trap, passed pawn creation) that the 'natural' move failed to prevent or preempt
sub_patterns: Knight centralizations ignoring urgent tactical threats (Ne5, Nd5, Nc5)
Greedy captures displacing pieces from critical sectors (Qxa7, Bxa3)
Premature king/pawn moves ignoring invasion vulnerabilities (Ke7, b5, Kf4)
Checks that drive the opponent to safety rather than maintaining pressure (Bd6+)

analysis.label: Moving a piece away from a square where it served a vital blocking or shielding function, into a seemingly active but tactically vulnerable position.
analysis.description: In 7/7 positions, the blundering move relocates a piece (king, rook, or pawn) from a square where it was performing a crucial defensive function—blocking a diagonal (3: Kg3 vacates g4 blocking bishop from h3), restraining a passed pawn (4: Rd6 abandons f-file blockade; 7: Re4 allows exchange that doesn't eliminate the e3 pawn), shielding the king (6: g4 opens lines; 1: Kxe6 leaves safety for exposed square), or maintaining safe distance from tactical patterns (2: Kd7 walks into knight fork; 5: Rg8 enters a file where forced exchange gives opponent tempo). The better alternatives in all cases involve either staying on the functional square, preparing with an indirect improving move (developing a piece, blocking a diagonal with a pawn), or approaching the problem from a different angle. The refutations all exploit the newly created gap within 1-2 moves: forks (2/7), piece captures on newly unblocked lines (2/7), forced exchanges that favor the opponent (2/7), and mating attacks through opened lines (2/7).
analysis.move_pattern: King, rook, or pawn moves away from a functionally critical square (blocking, shielding, or restraining) toward a seemingly more active but tactically poisoned square
analysis.why_bad: The piece was performing an invisible but essential defensive task on its original square; the 'active' destination exposes an immediate tactical vulnerability (fork, unblocked diagonal/file, unfavorable forced exchange, or king exposure) that the opponent exploits within 1-2 moves
sub_patterns: King vacates a blocking square that shielded a piece from diagonal/file attack
King moves to capture material on a square dominated by enemy queen/knight checks
Rook abandons a file where it was restraining a dangerous passed pawn
Rook enters an open file where forced exchange gives opponent tempo/initiative
Pawn advance weakens own king position by opening lines toward it

analysis.label: Making a tempting capture, pawn advance, or king move toward material while ignoring the position's single most urgent tactical or structural requirement.
analysis.description: This feature fires on moves where the player pursues a secondary objective—usually material gain or positional pawn play—while the position demands addressing one critical task. In 3/10 positions, Kb4 abandons escort duty of a passed pawn near promotion to chase enemy a-pawns. In 3/10 positions (dxe7 x2, dxc6), greedy pawn captures fatally open the d-file, exposing the queen to capture via deflection or direct attack. In 1/10 (Bxb4), a piece capture ignores an advanced pawn that delivers a deflection check winning the queen. In 3/10 (b6, h4, d3), slow pawn moves ignore urgent needs: b6 weakens the knight's support allowing a crushing b5 advance; h4 wastes tempo while a piece is trapped; d3 ignores mate-in-2. All positions share extremely narrow margins (avg 2.1 good moves) where only 1-3 moves address the critical requirement, making the greedy/slow alternative catastrophic (avg 443cp loss).
analysis.move_pattern: Captures (especially d-pawn captures opening files), king moves toward enemy pawns, or quiet pawn advances—all directed away from the critical sector of the board
analysis.why_bad: The move fails because it addresses a secondary concern (material, pawn structure, slow improvement) while the position has ONE overriding requirement: supporting a promotion race, preventing a deflection tactic on an open file, addressing an immediate mating threat, or rescuing a trapped piece. The opponent gains a free tempo to execute their primary threat unchallenged.
sub_patterns: King abandons passed pawn escort to chase enemy pawns (Kb4 x3)
D-pawn capture opens file exposing own queen to deflection/capture (dxe7 x2, dxc6)
Greedy piece capture ignores advancing pawn with check (Bxb4)
Slow pawn advance ignores immediate tactical crisis (b6, h4, d3)

analysis.label: Non-forcing preparatory or generic moves played when the position demands immediate concrete action, tactical exploitation, or urgent development.
analysis.description: All 5 positions share a common pattern: the player chooses a quiet, non-threatening move—often 'reasonable-looking'—when the position urgently demanded something forcing or concrete. In 3/5 cases (c5, h3, b3), these are slow pawn moves that neither develop pieces nor create threats; in 2/5 cases (Bc5, Qd2), pieces are moved to seemingly active squares that miss far stronger tactical continuations. The 'tempo_loss' tag appears in all 5 positions, and 'missed_tactic' appears in 4/5. The critical shared element is that the opponent has a specific vulnerability or the position has a narrow window for action (uncastled king in 3/5, tactical fork in 1/5, initiative preservation in 1/5), and the played move gives the opponent time to consolidate or launch their own attack. The average cp_loss of 328 reflects how costly these wasted tempi are when positions are sharp.
analysis.move_pattern: Non-forcing, non-capturing, non-checking moves (pawn pushes to non-central squares or piece relocations to unthreatening squares) that fail to interact with the opponent's position
analysis.why_bad: These moves squander a tempo-sensitive moment—they allow the opponent to either execute a threatened plan (pawn storm, consolidation), escape a tactical vulnerability (exposed queen, uncastled king), or seize the initiative, because the position demanded immediate concrete action rather than preparation.
sub_patterns: Slow flank pawn pushes (b3, h3, c5) ignoring central/developmental urgency
Generic developing moves (Bc5) missing specific tactical shots
Queen relocation to tactically vulnerable square (Qd2) allowing tempo-gaining attack

analysis.label: Passive moves (often Nd7 or blocking pawn pushes) when active knight repositioning was urgently required.
analysis.description: This feature fires on positions where the player makes a move that fundamentally mishandles knight coordination. In 2/4 positions, the knight is moved to the passive d7 square (abandoning a strong c5 outpost in one case, walking into a bishop capture in another). In the other 2/4 positions, pawn pushes (h4, f3) are played when the knight urgently needed repositioning — f3 specifically blocks the knight's natural development square, while h4 wastes tempo when Ne2 was critical. In all cases, the best move involved placing the knight on an active square (Nb7 enabling Nd6+ fork, keeping Nf6 for defense, Ne2 for endgame activity, Nf3 for development and castling). The common thread is choosing a slow/passive/counterproductive move when the position's demands centered on optimizing knight placement.
analysis.move_pattern: Knight moved to d7 (passive square) or pawn pushed to f3/h-file when knight needed active repositioning
analysis.why_bad: These moves either place the knight on a passive/tactically vulnerable square (d7), or delay/block necessary knight activation with irrelevant pawn pushes, allowing the opponent to seize initiative through piece activity, central control, or tactical exploitation of the resulting coordination failure.
sub_patterns: Knight retreating/moving to passive d7 square
Pawn push blocking knight's natural development square
Slow pawn move ignoring urgent knight repositioning need

analysis.label: Moving a piece to a seemingly attractive square where it immediately becomes a tactical target or creates an exploitable vulnerability.
analysis.description: This feature fires on moves where a piece (or king) relocates to a square that looks purposeful—giving check, centralizing, capturing material, attacking a target—but actually makes the moved piece (or the position) immediately exploitable through a concrete tactical response. In 5/11 cases the piece moves directly to a square where it can be captured by an opponent's minor piece (Bd4+ captured by Nxd4, Nd4 by Bxd4, Bc4 attacked by Be6 fork, Nd3 by Bxd3, Kd7 enabling Bh3+ clearance). In 4/11 cases the king walks to a square creating fatal tactical exposure (Ke7 into knight forks, Kf5 into mating net, Kd6 abandoning a critical pawn to capture, Kd7 onto a diagonal enabling discovered attack). The remaining cases involve ignoring a concrete threat for an aggressive-looking but ultimately losing capture (fxe3 ignoring Nxc6), or choosing passivity over the one active defense (Rf2 instead of Rf7). The positions share an extremely narrow margin for error (avg 1.6 good moves available) and very high punishment (avg 1161 cp_loss), indicating critical moments where precise calculation was required but the player chose the move that 'looked right' over the one that 'was right.'
analysis.move_pattern: Piece (knight, bishop, king, rook, or pawn) moves to a central or seemingly active square that is directly covered or exploitable by an opponent's piece, often involving moves to the d-file/center ranks
analysis.why_bad: The destination square is tactically vulnerable—either directly capturable by an opponent's minor piece, exposed to a fork/discovered attack, or removes the piece from a position where it was providing critical tactical resources, allowing the opponent an immediate concrete exploitation.
sub_patterns: Minor piece moves to square directly capturable by opponent's bishop or knight (Nd4, Bd4+, Nd3, Bc4)
King walks to square creating diagonal/fork vulnerability (Ke7, Kd7, Kf5, Kd6)
Piece abandons critical tactical resource for superficially attractive target (Ba6 losing Bf3 resource, fxe3 ignoring hanging piece)
Passive piece retreat when only active play survives (Rf2 instead of Rf7)

analysis.label: Moves that pursue a secondary active plan while neglecting the position's single most urgent requirement, allowing concrete tactical punishment.
analysis.description: This feature fires on positions where there is essentially one correct plan (average only 1.7 good moves available) but the player chooses an active-looking or purposeful move that addresses a secondary concern. In 8/10 positions, the player's king remains uncastled or inadequately sheltered, and the best move involves resolving this (Ne2 to block a pin and prepare castling in position 2, Qd2 to prepare O-O in position 3, Be7 to enable castling in positions 11 and 12). The blunder moves appear logical—a3 tries to kick a knight, Rc1 tries to defend a pinned piece, Qg5/Qg6 attempt kingside aggression, Bc5 develops aggressively—but all ignore the position's critical demand. The punishments exploit what was neglected: hanging pieces (positions 1, 5), knight forks against exposed kings (positions 2, 3, 12), tempo-gaining attacks against misplaced queens (positions 8, 11), or positional domination (positions 7, 13). The average cp_loss of 292 reflects that these narrow positions brutally punish the wrong priority.
analysis.move_pattern: Various piece types (queen, rook, bishop, pawn) moving to seemingly active or purposeful squares, often aggressive-looking moves toward the flanks or attacking positions, rather than the required defensive/developmental move
analysis.why_bad: The position has one critical requirement (usually completing development, castling, resolving a pin, or defending a specific piece) and only 1-2 moves satisfy it. The played move ignores this requirement, leaving a tactical vulnerability (hanging piece, fork target, penetration square) that the opponent can immediately exploit with a concrete tactic.
sub_patterns: Queen sortie to exposed square while king remains in center (Qb6, Qg5, Qg6)
Quiet pawn move when piece development/activity is urgent (a3, h3)
Rook move that creates a fork target or abandons critical post (Rc1, Rc1+, Rb3)
Aggressive piece development that creates a fork vulnerability (Bc5, Qg3)

analysis.label: Piece moves that pursue irrelevant plans while an enemy pawn one square from queening goes uncontested.
analysis.description: In all 5/5 positions, there is an enemy pawn exactly one square from promotion (c2→c1, h7→h8, b2→b1, a2→a1, a7→a8), and the played move completely ignores this threat. Instead of contesting the promotion square (which in every case required placing a rook on the back rank—Rh1, Rb8, Rb7, Rd1, Rf8), the player makes an 'active' move elsewhere: centralizing a piece (Be4, Re4), attacking a different target (Rb6 hitting a knight), pushing an irrelevant pawn (h5), or activating laterally (Rf2). In each case exactly 1 move was within 50cp of best, and the average cp_loss exceeds 9200—reflecting the shift from a losing-but-defensible endgame to forced checkmate in 8-12 moves once the pawn promotes unopposed.
analysis.move_pattern: Piece moves (rook, bishop, or pawn push) directed toward the center or middle ranks, away from the back rank where the promotion square needs to be contested
analysis.why_bad: The moves abandon control of the critical promotion square, allowing the enemy pawn to queen immediately with devastating effect—the new queen combined with existing pieces creates an instant mating attack against the exposed king that cannot be survived.
sub_patterns: Rook centralization to e4 instead of back-rank defense (Re4, positions 1 and 4)
Rook lateral move attacking irrelevant piece instead of blocking promotion square (Rb6)
Slow pawn advance while opponent's pawn queens in one move (h5)
Rook to second rank for counterplay instead of eighth rank to contest promotion (Rf2)

analysis.label: Natural-looking repositioning moves that ignore urgent concrete demands (king safety, development, or available tactics), creating exploitable vulnerabilities.
analysis.description: This feature fires on moves that appear to improve piece placement or gain space but are poorly timed because they ignore the position's actual critical needs. In 4/6 cases, the moved piece or pawn was serving an important (often unrecognized) defensive or structural function: the e6 pawn blocked a diagonal protecting an undefended bishop (Position 2), the f6 knight defended f7 and controlled the center (Position 6), the g7-pawn shielded dark squares around the king (Position 4), and the c2-bishop was actively disrupting White's coordination (Position 14). In 5/6 positions, the analyses explicitly identify tempo loss as a key factor. In 4/6 cases, the best moves involved addressing more urgent priorities—completing development, ensuring king safety, or executing available concrete tactics (Position 15's d5 pawn break). The average cp_loss of 246 with an average of 2.2 good alternatives indicates these are significant blunders where clearly better moves existed, making this a pattern of prioritizing abstract positional 'improvement' over concrete positional demands.
analysis.move_pattern: Piece or pawn moved to a seemingly active/central square (often forward or toward center), typically not a capture or check—repositioning moves that appear to improve placement
analysis.why_bad: The moved piece/pawn was serving a critical structural or defensive function (blocking diagonals, defending key squares, maintaining piece coordination), and its displacement creates immediate tactical vulnerabilities or cedes tempo to the opponent while ignoring more urgent needs like development, king safety, or available decisive tactics
sub_patterns: Pawn advances that open critical lines toward own undefended pieces (e5, g6)
Knight/bishop repositioning to seemingly active squares that are immediately challenged or captured (Nd4, Be4, Nh7)
Slow bishop maneuvers when concrete tactical breakthroughs exist (Bc3)

analysis.label: Choosing a natural-looking move that directly targets an enemy piece but neglects the position's true strategic or tactical priority.
analysis.description: In all 4/4 positions, the player selected a move that directly attacks or captures an enemy piece in an apparently active manner, but missed a more precise or urgent alternative. In Position 4, Qf3 looked aggressive but blocked the knight's critical access to f3 (Qf2 was needed). In Position 9, Bxg5 removed a threatening knight but surrendered the dark-squared bishop when an exchange sacrifice (Rxf4!) was far stronger. In Position 11, Rd4 attacked the knight on e4 but ignored the urgent c3 passed pawn (Kd3 was needed). In Position 14, Kb6 attacked the b7 knight directly but from the wrong square, allowing Nd6 escape (Kc6 dominated the center). All 4/4 moves appear 'logical' on the surface—they attack enemy pieces—but all miss that the position's real demand lies elsewhere. The average cp_loss of 278 reflects how costly this 'obvious aggression' pattern is.
analysis.move_pattern: Any piece type moving to directly attack or capture an enemy piece, often one square away from the correct square or selecting the wrong method of engagement
analysis.why_bad: The player prioritizes direct, obvious aggression against an enemy piece rather than addressing the position's true critical need (blocking a passed pawn, maintaining a key tactical resource, finding a deeper combination, or choosing the geometrically superior approach square).
sub_patterns: Placing piece on wrong square that blocks own tactical resource (Qf3 blocking Nf3)
Capturing threatening piece when exchange sacrifice or indirect defense is stronger
Attacking secondary target while ignoring urgent passed pawn or king-approach priority
Approaching enemy piece from wrong direction allowing escape with counterplay

analysis.label: Moving a piece away from a square where it was performing a vital defensive function—guarding a piece, controlling an invasion square, or maintaining a threat that restrained the opponent.
analysis.description: In 7/9 positions, the played move removes a piece from a square where it was performing an indispensable protective role, immediately allowing the opponent to exploit the newly unguarded target. The clearest cases: Nb4 removes the knight from d5 which was the sole piece controlling e7, permitting R2e7+ leading to mate in 3 (9/9); Kg2 moves the king from f1 where it defended the e2 bishop, allowing the trivial Rxe2 winning a piece (6/9); Nxg4 removes the knight from f6 which guarded h7, permitting Qxh7 invasion (2/9); Bg3 moves the bishop from c7 whose threatening presence kept Black's queen occupied, allowing Qxa6 capturing an undefended piece (4/9); Be1 moves the bishop passively away from guarding back-rank squares, enabling Bf6 with unstoppable Rd8 mate threats (3/9). In the remaining cases (Re7, Ng6, Re1, f3), pieces abandon active posts for passive squares, surrendering control of key lines or creating structural weaknesses that the opponent immediately exploits. The common thread is a self-deflection: the player voluntarily removes their own guard from a critical function.
analysis.move_pattern: Any piece type moving away from a defended/controlled square; typically retreats or lateral repositioning moves rather than forward attacking moves; not checks or captures (except Nxg4 pawn grab)
analysis.why_bad: The moved piece was the sole defender of a critical square or piece; its departure creates an immediate tactical exploitation—either winning undefended material, enabling an invasion/mating attack on the newly unguarded square, or permanently degrading the position of the displaced piece
sub_patterns: Removing defender of a piece → that piece is captured (Kg2→Rxe2, Bg3→Qxa6)
Removing controller of an invasion square → enemy piece invades with decisive threats (Nb4→R2e7+ mate, Nxg4→Qxh7, Be1→Bf6/Rd8 mate)
Abandoning an active outpost for a passive square → opponent seizes initiative (Ng6 leaving f4, Re7 leaving a7, Re1 leaving g-file)

analysis.label: Natural-looking moves that waste a crucial tempo in precision-demanding positions (usually endgames) where only one or two moves maintain the evaluation.
analysis.description: This feature fires on moves that appear reasonable—attacking a piece, capturing material, repositioning the king, or pushing a pawn—but fatally waste a tempo in positions requiring extreme precision (avg 1.4 good moves available). In 11/13 positions, the phase is endgame where every tempo is magnified. The blunders share a consistent mechanism: the player prioritizes a secondary concern while the opponent gains one critical tempo to execute their plan. Examples include Rf4 attacking a bishop instead of the urgent d5 pawn break first (Position 5, move order), h4 pushing a pawn instead of Kd2 to contest a lethal passed pawn (Position 14), Kxe3 capturing out of order instead of bxc5 first (Position 12), Ra6 attacking a knight while allowing Ne4+ fork (Position 6), and Kf7/Kd3 king moves that get immediately punished by the opponent seizing initiative (Positions 1, 7, 11). In every case, the opponent exploits the gifted tempo via passed pawn advancement (8/13 positions), piece activation, or tactical shots. The extremely high average cp_loss (1038) reflects that these are positions balanced on a knife's edge where one wasted move is catastrophic.
analysis.move_pattern: Diverse piece types and directions; typically a seemingly active/natural move (capture, attack, repositioning) that addresses a non-urgent concern
analysis.why_bad: These moves give the opponent one critical tempo to execute their primary plan—advancing a passed pawn, delivering a fork/check, or activating pieces—in positions where the single most urgent action was the only way to maintain the evaluation.
sub_patterns: Move-order errors: capturing/attacking before necessary preparatory move (Rf4 before d5, Kxe3 before bxc5)
King moves to exposed/irrelevant square giving opponent activation tempo (Kf7, Kd3)
Piece attacks secondary target while opponent exploits exposed king (Ra6, Rc7)
Pawn pushes ignoring urgent positional demand (h4, b5)
Checks/captures that allow devastating counter-tactics (Qf5+ allowing Qd5+, Qxe6+ allowing Kb7 escape)

analysis.label: Aggressive captures or piece advances to seemingly active squares that immediately become tactical liabilities, when a more patient alternative maintained the advantage.
analysis.description: This feature fires on moves that appear to gain material or activity but place the moved piece (or pawn) on a square where it is immediately exploited by the opponent. In 4/6 positions, a piece captures a pawn or advances to an 'active' square only to be captured or trapped (Rxh2 trapped by bishop diagonal in Position 4, Ng4 immediately captured by bishop in Position 5, Re7 captured by bishop on d6 in Position 11, Rgxh2 abandons dominant infiltration for a worthless pawn in Position 10). In 5/6 positions, a better move existed that either targeted a different square (Rxb2 instead of Rxh2, Rxf2 instead of Rgxh2) or prepared the same idea with proper coordination (Bf6 before Ng4, e6 instead of Nxe4). The common thread is choosing an 'obvious' aggressive continuation over a subtler move that maintains positional integrity, resulting in the opponent having a simple forcing refutation.
analysis.move_pattern: Piece or pawn moves to an apparently active square (captures on wing pawns, advances to 7th rank, knight jumps to central/attacking squares) where the piece is immediately vulnerable to capture or exploitation
analysis.why_bad: The moved piece lands on a square controlled by the opponent's existing pieces, allowing a simple tactical refutation (intermediate check + capture, direct capture by bishop, favorable exchanges) that either wins the moved piece outright or converts the position through forced simplification that favors the opponent.
sub_patterns: Rook captures wing pawn but lands on bishop's diagonal (Rxh2 variants)
Piece advances to active square before support is in place (Ng4, Re7)
Capture removes own key positional piece for lesser material (Nxe4)
Pawn break allows opponent to exchange into drawn/simplified position (g5)

analysis.label: Moving a piece (often the king) to an apparently active central square that is immediately punished by forcing moves along open files or diagonals.
analysis.description: In all 3/3 positions, the player moves a piece to a seemingly desirable central or active square while ignoring that the destination is fatally exposed to the opponent's forces on open lines. In Position 1, Bc5 develops to an 'active' diagonal but ignores the e4-e5 advance that gains tempo and opens lines against the uncastled king. In Position 4, Ke3 attempts king centralization but walks into Rf3+ on the open f-file, allowing rook infiltration with check tempo. In Position 9, Ke7 moves toward the center but steps directly into discovered check mechanisms along the e-file and diagonals, resulting in forced mate in 5. The common thread is that each move prioritizes apparent piece activity or centralization while the opponent's pieces already dominate the relevant open lines, and the refutations all exploit this with immediate tempo-gaining forcing moves (checks, pawn advances attacking pieces).
analysis.move_pattern: Piece (king or bishop) moves to a central square (c5/e3/e7) that sits on open files or diagonals controlled by opponent's active pieces
analysis.why_bad: The destination square is dominated by the opponent's forces on open lines, allowing immediate tempo-gaining attacks (checks, discovered checks, pawn thrusts) that exploit the exposed piece or king before any benefit is realized
sub_patterns: King walks into check sequences on open files
Piece develops to active square ignoring opponent's central pawn break
Centralization into discovered attack geometry

analysis.label: Playing developing or preparatory moves while a central pawn is under direct attack and demands immediate resolution, allowing the opponent to win material.
analysis.description: This feature fires on opening moves that neglect urgent central pawn tension. In 6/8 positions, the player makes a non-critical developing or preparatory move (c6, g6, Bb4, Be7, Bc5, Nc3) while their central pawn (typically e5 or d5) is directly attacked and insufficiently defended, allowing the opponent to simply capture it with dxe5 or exd5/cxd5. In the remaining 2/8 positions (both fxe5), the player resolves the tension with the wrong capture, removing a pawn that was protecting a critical diagonal or square, creating tactical vulnerabilities (Qh4+ or dxe4 attacking the knight). In all 8 cases, the position featured a closed/tense center with both kings uncastled, and the correct approach was to immediately resolve or reinforce the central tension (typically via exd4, d6, dxe4, or d4) before pursuing other plans. The punishments consistently involve winning the abandoned central pawn and achieving a massive development/space advantage.
analysis.move_pattern: Non-forcing moves (flank pawn pushes, bishop/knight development to non-defensive squares, or wrong pawn captures) played while a central pawn on e5 or d5 is directly attacked by an opposing d4 or c4/e4 pawn
analysis.why_bad: The central pawn is hanging or under-defended, and the move played neither captures the attacking pawn, defends the threatened pawn, nor creates a tactical counter-threat, allowing the opponent to win material cleanly while gaining tempo and development advantage.
sub_patterns: Flank pawn moves (c6, g6) preparing long-term plans while e5 hangs to dxe5
Bishop development (Bb4, Be7, Bc5) ignoring undefended central pawn
Wrong pawn capture (fxe5) removing a key defensive pawn from the king's diagonal
Natural piece development (Nc3) missing a time-sensitive tactical capture (cxd5 with e4 fork)

analysis.label: Moving the queen (or key piece) to an aggressive-looking square while abandoning a critical defensive or functional role, allowing the opponent to exploit the vacancy.
analysis.description: In 5/6 positions, the queen moves to a seemingly active or centralized square (Qd4, Qg5, Qd7, Qf4, Qb6) while in 1/6 a knight makes the analogous error (Nh5). The common thread is that the piece was performing a vital defensive or coordinating function on its current square (or should have stayed/retreated defensively), but is seduced by an apparently attractive destination. In 4/6 cases the queen moves forward into enemy territory or to an aggressive central post (Qd4, Qg5, Qd7, Qf4). In 5/6 cases the refutation directly exploits the piece's absence from its defensive station—allowing queenside infiltration (Pos 1), fork via diagonal check (Pos 2), tempo-gaining attacks on the exposed piece (Pos 3), capturing a now-undefended piece (Pos 4), favorable simplification (Pos 5), or a sacrificial combination against the weakened king (Pos 6). The average cp_loss of 298 reflects how severely these 'tempting but irresponsible' moves are punished.
analysis.move_pattern: Queen (5/6) or knight moving to an aggressive/forward square, typically centralized (d4, d7, f4) or wing-attacking (g5, h5, b6), abandoning its current defensive post
analysis.why_bad: The piece abandons a critical defensive or coordinating role—guarding key squares, protecting hanging pieces, or maintaining king safety—for an attractive-looking but ultimately less important aggressive function, allowing the opponent to exploit the defensive vacuum with infiltration, tactics against undefended pieces, or simplification.
sub_patterns: Queen moves aggressively to central square when it should maintain defensive coverage of the king
Queen infiltrates enemy camp while leaving own pieces undefended
Queen invites favorable trade by moving to a square where opponent's queen can capture with follow-up tactics
Piece abandons defensive guard duty to attack an enemy piece, allowing sacrificial combination against exposed king

analysis.label: King shuffles between f3/g3 instead of playing the immediately winning f5 pawn break in rook endgames.
analysis.description: In 7/9 positions, the feature fires on nearly identical rook endgame structures where White has a rook on g5, pawns on e4/f4 facing Black's g6/h5, and should play the immediate f5 break to create a winning passed pawn while Black's king is far away. Instead, White plays a preparatory king move (Kf3 or Kg3) shuffling on the third rank, which grants Black exactly the tempo needed to march the king toward f7 to blockade. Position 10 (Ne2) shares the theme of a preparatory/developing move that blocks the critical piece action (rook on the e-file), and Position 15 (g2) similarly represents premature action when the status quo was superior. The overwhelming commonality is choosing a 'improving' move over the time-critical breakthrough.
analysis.move_pattern: King moves laterally on the third rank (f3↔g3) or nearby piece development, delaying an immediate pawn break
analysis.why_bad: The single wasted tempo allows the opponent's king to march 2-3 squares closer (typically c6/c8→d7→e7→f7), arriving just in time to blockade the passed f-pawn that would have been unstoppable with the immediate f5 push.
sub_patterns: Kf3 instead of f5 (king from e3/g3)
Kg3 instead of f5 (king from f3)
Preparatory piece move blocking critical action (Ne2 blocking e-file)

analysis.label: Playing an aggressive-looking move (check, capture, or centralization) that displaces a critically-placed piece from the exact square enabling a winning combination or mating attack.
analysis.description: In 5/7 positions, the player had a forced checkmate available but played a tempting aggressive move that converted the win into a merely large advantage. The core pattern is a piece voluntarily leaving its optimal square—where it enabled a decisive tactical sequence—in favor of a superficially active destination. In Position 1, the knight abandons its dominant g4 post (covering escape squares) to give a purposeless check on e5. In Position 7, the bishop leaves b5 (enabling Qc2+ mating mechanism) to give a check on a6. In Position 5, the knight captures on e3 instead of the queen, which on that square would have created an unstoppable mating net. In Position 2, the rook abandons back-rank duty to attack a pawn. In Position 4, the queen moves to f4 without first inserting the critical intermediate check Qf7+ that would gain a tempo. In Position 6, the queen leaves h6 (coordinating with rooks for a mating battery) for h4 where it leaves c7 hanging. In Position 3, the bishop captures instead of the pawn, placing itself where it can be won by the opponent's knight. All moves share the quality of looking active while actually dismantling the player's own winning coordination.
analysis.move_pattern: Any piece type moving to an apparently aggressive square (often delivering check or making a capture) but away from a critical square where it enabled a forcing sequence
analysis.why_bad: The piece was already optimally placed to support a winning tactical combination, and moving it—even to deliver check or win material—disrupts the coordination needed for the decisive continuation, giving the opponent escape routes or counterplay that didn't previously exist.
sub_patterns: Giving a purposeless check that removes a piece from a dominant attacking post (Ne5+, Ba6+)
Capturing with the wrong piece, missing that the other capturer creates a mating attack (Nxe3 instead of Qxe3, Bxc5 instead of bxc5)
Repositioning an attacking piece without first inserting a critical intermediate forcing move (Qf4 without Qf7+ first)
Abandoning a defensive/coordinating function to pursue a less important target (Rd6 abandoning back rank, Qh4 breaking battery)

analysis.label: Playing natural-looking but too-slow moves in sharp positions that demand immediate concrete action, wasting critical tempo.
analysis.description: This feature fires on positions where the player makes a plausible, routine-seeming move that catastrophically ignores the position's primary tactical or strategic demand. In 7/8 cases, the position features exposed kings or critical passed pawn dynamics requiring precise concrete play. The best moves in each position are forcing and address the central crisis: winning combinations (Qxb3 in pos 12, Qd7 in pos 1), immediate checkmate (Re6# in pos 5), prophylactic prevention of opponent plans (Re8/a5 in pos 13, b5 in pos 6), or correct promotion races (gxh3 in pos 14). Instead, the player chooses something that addresses a secondary concern — blocking a pawn (Re3), giving an aimless check (R1f5+), pushing a flank pawn (a5 in pos 9 and 11), centralizing passively (Qc5), making a passive defensive rook move (Rb7), or capturing the wrong pawn (fxe6). The avg good moves of only 1.6 confirms these are narrow positions, and the avg cp_loss of 1772 confirms the punishment is severe. The tempo_loss tag appears in 7/8 positions, and missed_tactic/piece_activity in 5-6/8.
analysis.move_pattern: Mixed piece types and directions — pawn advances (especially flank a/c-pawns: 4/8), passive piece retreats/repositioning to seemingly logical squares, and captures that address secondary concerns rather than the critical threat
analysis.why_bad: These moves waste a critical tempo in positions with razor-thin margins, allowing the opponent to execute their primary threat (king attack, passed pawn advance, promotion race) or escape from a losing/mated position. The position demanded forcing, concrete action but the player chose something routine.
sub_patterns: Flank pawn push (a5/c5) ignoring central/kingside crisis
Passive piece move when a winning combination exists
Aimless check when an immediate mate is available
Wrong capture/move-order allowing opponent's passed pawn breakthrough
Self-blocking a key piece with a pawn advance

analysis.label: Superficially active or constructive moves that waste a crucial tempo by addressing a secondary concern while ignoring the position's most urgent requirement.
analysis.description: In all 6/6 analyzed positions, the player made a move that appears reasonable on the surface—advancing a passed pawn (b4, h2), occupying an open file (Rd8, Re8), giving a check (Ng6+), or placing a piece on an 'active' square (Ba5, Kd8)—but fatally ignores the position's most critical demand. In 6/6 cases, the correct move required addressing the opponent's primary threat FIRST (blockading with Be6, counterattacking with Re3/Qf5, advancing the correct pawn with a4, maintaining piece influence with Be7/Bd6, or keeping the king off a vulnerable file). The common thread is a move-order or priority error: the played move might even be correct one move later, but doing it NOW gives the opponent a decisive tempo to execute their plan—whether promoting passed pawns (h2, b4), forcing favorable exchanges (Kd8, Re8), exploiting abandoned squares (Ba5), or stranding pieces on useless squares (Ng6+). Passed pawn dynamics feature in 6/6 positions, and tempo_loss is tagged in all 6 analyses.
analysis.move_pattern: Various piece types moving to plausible-looking squares (open files, forward advances, checks) but away from the position's critical sector
analysis.why_bad: Each move surrenders a crucial tempo in positions where the opponent has an immediate concrete plan (passed pawn advance, tactical strike, piece invasion); the opponent exploits the wasted move to execute their threat one tempo faster than the player can complete their secondary objective
sub_patterns: Advancing the wrong passed pawn first allowing blockade (b4, h2)
Placing rook on open file that becomes a tactical target (Rd8, Re8, Kd8)
Moving piece to inactive square abandoning defense of critical pawn (Ba5, Ng6+)

analysis.label: Passive queen (or piece) repositioning move that wastes a critical tempo in a position demanding immediate concrete action.
analysis.description: This feature fires on positions where a player makes a non-forcing 'improving' move—overwhelmingly a queen move to a second/third-rank square (8/10 positions involve queen or major piece repositioning: Qc2, Qd2, Qe2, Qe3, Qe7, Qc7, Re2)—when the position contains a time-sensitive tactical or dynamic opportunity that demands immediate exploitation. In every case, the position features a concrete vulnerability (exposed king 4/10, tactical target like a trapped piece or weak pawn 6/10, open file to seize 4/10) that requires forcing play (pawn breaks like b4/a4/h4, file occupation, or direct tactical strikes). The quiet moves look reasonable—connecting rooks, centralizing pieces, supporting pawns—but they grant the opponent a free tempo to consolidate their weakness, castle to safety, or execute their own threats. The average cp_loss of 226 reflects the catastrophic cost of missing the narrow tactical window.
analysis.move_pattern: Queen (or major piece) moved to a second/third-rank square (c2, d2, e2, e3, e7, c7) without creating any immediate threat—non-forcing repositioning rather than attacking, capturing, or checking.
analysis.why_bad: The position has a time-sensitive concrete opportunity (exposed king, piece vulnerability, pawn break, open file) that evaporates in one tempo. The quiet move creates zero threats, giving the opponent exactly the tempo needed to castle, consolidate, retreat a vulnerable piece, or launch their own counterplay.
sub_patterns: Queen to back rank instead of initiating pawn break (b4, a4, h4 needed)
Queen/rook repositioning that blocks own piece activation (Qe2 blocking Re1, Re2 abandoning d-file)
Passive queen move ignoring opponent's uncastled king
Queen placed on tactically vulnerable square (forkable, pinnable)
Piece move that removes control of critical square (c4 weakening d4, Re2 abandoning d4)

analysis.label: Moves that look natural or active but waste a crucial tempo in time-sensitive positions where the opponent can immediately exploit the lost time.
analysis.description: This feature activates on moves that appear reasonable—developing checks (Bb5+), piece repositionings (Bd4, Bb5, Bc5), pawn advances (a4), or king moves to seemingly safe squares (Kh1, Kh2)—but critically waste a tempo in positions where timing is paramount. In 7/8 analyzed positions, 'tempo_loss' was identified as a primary motif. The positions typically involve passed pawn races (5/8 tagged with passed_pawn), exposed kings, or urgent tactical demands. The common thread is that the player makes a move that looks active or logical on its own but fails to address the position's critical demand: blocking a pawn advance (Bd4 instead of Bd2), centralizing the king (Kh2 instead of Kf2, a4 instead of Kg8), or maintaining a defensive guardian (Bb5 abandoning e6 defense). The opponent then exploits the single lost tempo to execute a decisive pawn breakthrough, pawn promotion, or tactical strike that was preventable one move earlier.
analysis.move_pattern: Piece or king moves to apparently active or safe squares (bishop diagonals, king to edge/corner, checking moves, pawn grabs) that don't address the position's urgent tactical demand
analysis.why_bad: Each move wastes exactly the tempo the opponent needs to execute a decisive breakthrough—whether advancing a passed pawn to promotion, creating a pawn fork, trapping the moved piece, or generating a mating attack. The position's critical timing demand goes unaddressed while the opponent exploits the free move.
sub_patterns: Bishop to wrong diagonal/square when specific diagonal control was critical
King retreating to edge/corner instead of centralizing or staying active
Pawn or piece moves that ignore an urgent passed pawn race
Developing checks that are easily neutralized, wasting the initiative
Piece abandoning a critical defensive post for an apparently active square

analysis.label: Moving a piece away from its one essential task to pursue a superficially attractive but secondary objective, losing decisive tempo.
analysis.description: This feature fires on moves where a piece abandons its critical positional responsibility to chase a tempting but ultimately inferior goal. In 7/9 positions, the move involves a piece moving away from the square or task that the position demands: kings leave passed pawn escort duty to grab distant pawns (Positions 2, 9), a bishop abandons kingside defense for a peripheral square (Position 5), knights leave dominant central outposts for aesthetically pleasing but tactically hollow squares (Positions 4, 6, 14), a king takes an indirect route losing a crucial tempo (Positions 11, 12), and a bishop grabs a pawn instead of making the one essential intermediate move (Position 15). The positions are characteristically narrow (avg 1.6 good moves), meaning the correct continuation is usually singular and non-obvious, while the blunder is the 'obvious' or 'natural-looking' alternative. In all cases, the opponent exploits the lost tempo to neutralize or seize the initiative, typically through immediate tactical strikes at the now-undefended weakness.
analysis.move_pattern: Piece (king/knight/bishop) moves away from its functionally critical square toward a secondary target, often sideways or toward opponent's material
analysis.why_bad: The piece was performing an irreplaceable function (supporting a passed pawn, guarding a weakness, controlling a key file/outpost); abandoning that duty gives the opponent a tempo window to exploit the newly undefended asset or seize the initiative with checks/threats
sub_patterns: King retreating from passed pawn escort to grab distant material
Knight leaving dominant outpost for peripheral/trappable square
Bishop/piece capturing a pawn instead of making an essential tempo move
King choosing indirect route when only the direct path maintains advantage

analysis.label: Playing a routine developing or repositioning move while an undefended piece hangs to a central pawn advance (d4/d5/e4/e5).
analysis.description: This feature fires on moves that ignore the tactical vulnerability of an undefended piece (most commonly a bishop on c4 or c5) to a central pawn thrust. In 9/13 positions, the refutation is a d-pawn or e-pawn advance that directly attacks or wins an unprotected piece: d4 wins Bc5 (positions 1, 2), d5 wins Bc4 or exploits exposed queens on the c8-h3 diagonal (positions 3, 4, 8, 10, 15), e5 wins Nf4 (position 13), and e3 opens the diagonal against Qc4 (position 14). The blundered moves themselves are varied—knight developments, queen repositionings, bishop moves, even castling—but share the property of being 'routine' or 'natural-looking' moves that ignore an urgent tactical reality. The position typically features an early/middle opening with both kings near center, an undefended piece sitting on an open diagonal or exposed square, and the opponent having a ready-made central pawn break to exploit it.
analysis.move_pattern: Any developing/repositioning move (knight, queen, bishop, or castling) that fails to address an undefended piece on the c4-f7 or c5-f2 diagonal vulnerable to a d/e-pawn advance
analysis.why_bad: The moves waste a critical tempo on non-urgent development while an undefended piece (typically a bishop on c4/c5 or exposed queen) sits en prise to a central pawn advance. The opponent's d4/d5/e4/e5 push attacks the hanging piece with tempo, often simultaneously opening lines or creating additional threats, winning material outright.
sub_patterns: Developing a knight while bishop on c5 hangs to d4
Moving the queen to an exposed square while bishop on c4 hangs to d5
Playing a slow pawn move while opponent's central break wins a piece
Placing a piece on c4/c5 without pawn support, immediately punished by d5/d4
Castling or developing while a minor piece on the 4th rank is undefended against a pawn attack

analysis.label: Moves that remove a piece from its essential defensive or attacking role, typically for material gain, allowing catastrophic king-safety punishment.
analysis.description: This feature fires on moves where a piece abandons a critical function in the position—usually guarding a key square near an exposed king or maintaining a winning attack—in favor of a seemingly attractive alternative (material gain, centralization, or peripheral activity). In 5/8 positions, the moved piece was the sole guardian of a critical square enabling mating threats (Nb4 abandons d5 guarding e7, Rxa2 neglects bringing the knight to e7, Nxh1+ removes the mating piece from f2, Be4 removes the bishop shielding the king from d-file checks). In 6/8 positions, the error directly enables forced checkmate or devastating king attacks. The positions share extremely narrow margins (avg 2.0 good moves) and massive punishment (avg ~4941cp loss), with exposed kings on both sides creating hair-trigger tactical environments where a single misplaced priority is fatal.
analysis.move_pattern: Any piece type moving away from a critical defensive/offensive square, often toward the edge or toward material capture; no consistent direction but always AWAY from the position's dominant tactical axis
analysis.why_bad: The moved piece was performing an irreplaceable function (blocking a mating lane, guarding an invasion square, maintaining a mating net, or contesting a critical file/diagonal), and its relocation leaves no other piece able to fulfill that role, resulting in immediate tactical catastrophe—usually forced mate or decisive material loss via the now-unguarded squares.
sub_patterns: Knight leaves square guarding key invasion point (Nb4, Ne5)
Piece captures material instead of addressing mating threat (Rxa2, Nxh1+)
Bishop/piece vacates critical defensive file/diagonal (Be4)
Tempo wasted on peripheral move while critical task is urgent (h4)
King moves to slightly suboptimal square in endgame race (Kc4, Kxc3)

analysis.label: Routine-looking developing or repositioning moves that waste a critical tempo when the position demands urgent concrete action to defend a specific vulnerability.
analysis.description: This feature fires on positions where players choose quiet, natural-looking moves (piece development, pawn pushes, rook repositioning) while ignoring a concrete tactical emergency. In 5/6 cases, the played move leaves a critical pawn or square undefended: Be2 and Bb2 both leave advanced d5 pawns en prise to knight captures (positions 2 and 6), Nxe2 leaves the d3 pawn undefended leading to a devastating fork (position 5), h6 ignores an open diagonal to the king (position 1), and Qe6 abandons the critical defensive post guarding g5/g7 (position 4). The average good moves available is only 1.5, meaning these are precision-critical positions where only one or two moves maintain the evaluation. In each case, the best move addresses the specific urgent demand—defending the hanging pawn (c4), exploiting the diagonal (Qa2), maintaining defensive coverage (Kh7), or capturing with the correct piece (Qxe2)—while the played move prioritizes a general improvement that the position cannot afford.
analysis.move_pattern: Quiet non-forcing moves (bishop development to long diagonals, pawn pushes, rook retreats, queen repositioning) that don't address the most critical square or piece in the position
analysis.why_bad: Each move wastes a tempo that the opponent immediately exploits to capture an undefended pawn, execute a tactical combination, or seize a critical diagonal/file, because the played move fails to address the single most pressing concrete need in the position (typically an undefended advanced pawn or exposed king)
sub_patterns: Developing bishop to blocked diagonal while advanced pawn hangs (Be2/Bb2 leaving d5 undefended)
Premature pawn advance instead of piece development when king is exposed (h6)
Passive piece repositioning instead of active development in lost positions (Rh7)
Moving queen away from critical defensive square enabling opponent's tactical break (Qe6)
Capturing with wrong piece leaving key pawn undefended (Nxe2 vs Qxe2)

analysis.label: Moving a key piece (usually the queen) away from the side where the king needs defense, ignoring an urgent tactical crisis around the monarch.
analysis.description: This feature fires on moves that relocate a critical defensive piece—most often the queen—to the wrong flank or an irrelevant square, abandoning the king's defensive perimeter at a moment when immediate threats demand attention. In 8/10 positions, the blunder directly worsens king safety: the queen leaves the kingside for the queenside while the king faces a kingside storm (Qb6, Qc2×2), the queen abandons queenside defense while the king sits there (Qg7, Qg5), a rook leaves the critical f-file exposing a breakthrough (Rfb8), or the king walks into exposure (Ke2). The remaining cases involve placing pieces on tactically vulnerable squares (Qe6 allowing Ng5 fork, Rxd4 allowing e5 fork). The consistent thread is a disconnect between where the player sends their piece and where the actual danger lies—pursuing slow positional ideas (queenside pressure, queen centralization, pawn pushes) while an opponent's attack is one or two moves from breaking through.
analysis.move_pattern: Queen (7/10) or rook/king moved away from the flank where own king is located or under attack; typically lateral repositioning to the opposite wing, non-capturing, non-checking
analysis.why_bad: The moved piece was the last line of defense against an imminent attack (blocking a file, covering a critical square, or guarding a weak pawn near the king), and its departure grants the opponent tempo to launch a decisive breakthrough—typically involving pawn storms, sacrificial file-openers, discovered attacks, or direct piece invasions against the now-unguarded king.
sub_patterns: Queen retreats to queenside while kingside king faces open-file/pawn-storm attack
Queen moves to kingside while own queenside-castled king loses b-file/c-file defense
Rook leaves critical defensive file (f-file) to pursue slow queenside counterplay
Slow positional move (pawn push, king walk) when immediate defensive emergency exists
Piece placed on square tactically vulnerable to fork or discovered attack

analysis.label: Playing a reasonable-looking move that pursues a secondary goal when the position has essentially one critical requirement that must be addressed immediately.
analysis.description: This feature fires on positions where very few good moves exist (avg 1.5) and the player chooses a move that appears purposeful but fatally neglects the position's most urgent obligation. In 4/11 cases, players pushed pawns (b4, a5, f5, f6) pursuing space or breaks while ignoring immediate tactical needs. In 3/11 cases, players made developing-style moves (Be2, Na6, Qe7) that looked natural but missed critical tactical vulnerabilities. In 2/11 cases, pieces abandoned essential defensive duties (Bc7 left a blockade, Rce8 abandoned a file). In 1/11, a king moved to the wrong square (Kb2 onto a file where it was exposed to check). In 1/11, material was grabbed in wrong move order (Nxc1 before neutralizing a more dangerous piece). All share the defining characteristic: the position demanded one specific response—defending a hanging piece, maintaining a blockade, addressing an attacking threat, or completing development urgently—and the player instead pursued a plausible but non-critical plan, resulting in catastrophic evaluation drops (avg 404cp).
analysis.move_pattern: Diverse piece types and directions; typically quiet/repositioning moves (pawn advances, piece development, retreats) rather than forcing moves, played in positions requiring precise/forcing responses
analysis.why_bad: The position has essentially one critical task (defend a tactical vulnerability, maintain a blockade, address an immediate threat, or complete development before the opponent opens the position), and the chosen move ignores that task entirely, giving the opponent a tempo or opportunity to execute a decisive tactical blow
sub_patterns: Non-developing pawn pushes when development/tactics are urgent (b4, a5, f6)
Abandoning critical defensive duties for repositioning (Bc7 leaves blockade, Rce8 leaves file)
Natural-looking development that ignores tactical counting problems (Be2, Na6)
Wrong move-order when capturing (grabbing material before neutralizing the bigger threat)
King moves to exposed squares when a safer alternative exists

analysis.label: Moves that look active or natural but critically fail to address or worsen the player's exposed king position, allowing tactical punishment via checks, skewers, or attacks along opened lines.
analysis.description: This feature fires on positions where the player's king is already exposed or vulnerable, and the player makes a move that either opens lines toward their own king (Position 1: dxc3 opens d-file/diagonals for Qd5+ sequence), moves the king into greater danger (Position 2: O-O-O into open d-file; Position 3: Kg4 creating skewer on g-file), removes a critical defensive piece from the king's vicinity (Position 9: Ne6 abandons f8 where it guarded g6/h7), or ignores the king's need for safety by pursuing a tangential plan (Position 4: Bg4 ignores d5 tempo gaining attack; Position 13: Qe2 wastes tempo with king in center). In 6/8 positions, the direct punishment involves checks or attacks exploiting the weakened king. The positions overwhelmingly feature exposed kings (noted in 7/8 position features) and very few good alternatives (avg 1.6), indicating critical defensive moments where precision was required but the player chose an 'active-looking' move instead.
analysis.move_pattern: Various piece types moving to apparently active squares or making captures/developments, but all in positions where the player's king is exposed and the move fails to address or worsens that exposure
analysis.why_bad: These moves prioritize apparent activity (capturing material, developing, centralizing, castling) over the critical defensive requirement of protecting an exposed king, allowing the opponent to exploit opened lines, undefended squares, or geometric alignments (skewers, discovered attacks, check sequences) targeting the vulnerable king
sub_patterns: Removing a blocking pawn/piece that shielded the king from checks
Moving the king onto a file/diagonal shared with own piece (skewer)
Castling into an open file where opponent has a rook
Developing a piece while ignoring a tempo-gaining central advance aimed at the king
Removing a knight/piece from a defensive post guarding king's pawn shield

analysis.label: Quiet or repositioning moves that waste a critical tempo by ignoring the position's most urgent tactical or strategic demand.
analysis.description: This feature fires on moves that look superficially purposeful (repositioning, developing, challenging) but fatally ignore the position's single most critical requirement. In 10/11 positions, the move is tagged as 'tempo_loss' in the analysis. The pattern manifests as: abandoning defense of a key pawn enabling a tactic (Qd8 abandons e6 in Position 1; Bc3 abandons e3 in Position 3; Bc4 abandons the h7-counter-tactic in Position 8), moving a king away from a critical blockading duty (Kf6/Kc6 in Positions 4-5 abandon passed pawn blockade), placing pieces on undefended squares (Rf5 in Position 12, Nh3 leaving Rf5 hanging in Position 14), choosing passive over active play (Rc8 instead of queen activity in Position 10), weakening a key defensive square (h5 abandoning g5 control in Position 11), or using the wrong piece to capture (Qxc7+ destroying mating coordination in Position 6). All moves share the characteristic of being non-forcing or misdirected in positions where only ~2 good moves existed (avg 2.0), resulting in catastrophic average losses of 1162cp.
analysis.move_pattern: Quiet non-forcing moves (retreats, repositioning, development, pawn pushes) in positions requiring immediate precise action; no consistent piece type or geometric direction
analysis.why_bad: Each move wastes the one tempo needed to address the position's critical demand—whether defending a specific square, blockading a passed pawn, maintaining piece coordination, or preserving counterplay—allowing the opponent to execute a concrete tactical punishment that was previously prevented.
sub_patterns: Piece retreats/repositions abandoning a defensive duty (Qd8, Bc3, Bc4)
King moves away from passed pawn blockade (Kf6, Kc6)
Piece placed on undefended square (Rf5, Nh3 leaving Rf5)
Passive move surrendering active counterplay (Rc8, h5)
Wrong piece captures destroying coordination (Qxc7+)

analysis.label: Natural-looking but non-urgent moves played in positions that demand immediate tactical action, resulting in critical tempo loss.
analysis.description: This feature fires on moves that appear reasonable or 'textbook' in isolation but fatally ignore the position's urgent tactical or dynamic demands. In 6/6 positions, the played move wastes a tempo on a non-forcing action (developing a knight to a natural square, pushing a flank pawn, repositioning a piece) when the position requires immediate exploitation of a temporary advantage or neutralization of an opponent's threat. In Position 1, Nf3 is a standard developing move that walks into ...g4 with tempo. In Position 2, Nf6 develops naturally but ignores the Ng5+Bc4 battery. In Position 5, b4 is a slow pawn push when Nxe5 wins material immediately. In Position 9, Kc5 drifts away from critical squares. In Position 13, Nc7 abandons a dominant central outpost (e6) when forced mate exists via Rg2. The common thread (tagged 'tempo_loss' in 6/6 analyses) is that all positions featured a fleeting dynamic advantage requiring immediate forceful play, and the chosen move squanders that window.
analysis.move_pattern: Quiet, non-forcing moves (piece development, repositioning, or pawn pushes) to seemingly natural squares, avoiding captures and checks when they are available
analysis.why_bad: The position contains a temporary dynamic advantage (development lead, exposed enemy king, tactical target) that requires immediate forceful exploitation; the quiet move gives the opponent a free tempo to neutralize the threat, develop, reach safety, or advance passed pawns
sub_patterns: Knight development to natural square ignoring pawn attack (Nf3/Nf6)
Slow flank pawn push ignoring central tactics (b4)
King/piece drifting away from critical zone (Kc5, Nc7)
Rook repositioning when more forcing options exist (Ra8)

analysis.label: Playing natural-looking but non-forcing moves in positions that demand immediate concrete action, wasting the one tempo needed to maintain the position's balance.
analysis.description: This feature fires on positions where the player chooses a quiet, 'reasonable-looking' move—often a king walk (Ke2, Kb2, Kg5, Kb8), pawn push (f4, f6, fxe5), or piece repositioning (Qg7, Rc3, Rhg1)—when the position contains a narrow tactical or strategic requirement that cannot be delayed by even one tempo. In 8/10 positions, the critical need was concrete and urgent: a forcing tactic that only works now (Ng8+ in Position 1, Qxh7 in Position 3), an immediate pawn capture by the correct piece (Rg3/Rxg2 in Position 4, Bxe5 in Position 15, Kxg6 in Position 11), or addressing king safety before the opponent exploits it (Kf2 in Position 10, Rhf1 in Position 14). The blunders share the common trait of being 'one-tempo-too-slow'—the move played would often be fine in a quieter position but fatally misjudges the urgency of the moment. The average number of good moves (2.1) confirms these are narrow positions with almost no margin for imprecision, yet the players consistently chose moves that look sensible but address the wrong priority.
analysis.move_pattern: Quiet non-forcing moves (king walks, pawn pushes, piece repositioning without check/capture) in positions requiring immediate tactical resolution
analysis.why_bad: Each move wastes the critical tempo needed to execute a forcing tactic, address an immediate threat, or prevent the opponent from consolidating/advancing—allowing the opponent to either escape a tactical net, create an unstoppable threat, or seize the initiative that was available only for one move.
sub_patterns: King moves toward a target when another piece should handle it (Ke2, Kg5)
Threatening a piece/pawn instead of immediately capturing it (Qg7 vs Qxh7)
Unnecessary prophylactic king shuffles when development/action is urgent (Kb8)
Piece repositioning that blocks own king's escape route (Rhg1)
Wrong capture method that weakens own king shelter (fxe5 vs Bxe5, f6 vs g6)

analysis.label: Playing a natural-looking or principled move that ignores a concrete tactical vulnerability requiring immediate attention.
analysis.description: This feature fires on positions where the player makes a move with clear strategic justification (gaining space, developing, capturing material, castling) but fails to address the single most critical tactical element in the position. In 9/9 cases, the played move has a plausible general-purpose motivation: a5 aimed for a4+ check (Position 2), e5 fought for center control (Position 3), Be3 centralized the bishop (Position 6), e6 solidified the pawn chain (Position 7), Nxh5 won the bishop pair (Position 9), g5 chased a bishop (Position 10), Bc5 activated the bishop (Position 12), Nxe4 won a free pawn (Position 13), and O-O sought king safety (Position 14). Yet in every case, a concrete tactical issue demanded priority: a self-blocking problem (2/9), a trapped/undefended piece (3/9), removing a critical defender (2/9), or walking into a forcing sequence (3/9). The average cp_loss of 1294 and only 2.2 good alternatives confirm these are narrow, calculation-critical moments where autopilot fails catastrophically.
analysis.move_pattern: Diverse piece types and directions (pawn pushes, bishop retreats, knight captures, castling) - no geometric unity; the commonality is strategic-looking moves in tactically acute positions
analysis.why_bad: The moves prioritize a general strategic goal (development, space, material, king safety) over the concrete tactical demand of the position, allowing the opponent to exploit an immediate vulnerability (fork, trapped piece, back rank, removed defender, self-block) within 1-2 moves
sub_patterns: Self-blocking own piece from critical square (a5 blocks Ba5+ check)
Failing to save or provide escape for a trapped piece (e6 allows g4 trapping bishop)
