Removing a key defender to grab material (Nxh5 removes Nf6 from defending Ne5)
Walking king into a forcing tactical sequence (O-O enables Nxf3+ fork)
Pawn advance enabling en passant or diagonal exploitation (g5, e5)
Capturing wrong target when a superior tactical capture exists (Nxe4 vs Nxe5)

analysis.label: Making an apparently active or routine move while leaving own material completely undefended and capturable by a simple tactic.
analysis.description: This feature activates when a player executes a move that looks purposeful—castling for safety, capturing material, giving check, building the center, or repositioning a piece—while critically ignoring that one of their own pieces is (or becomes) undefended and freely winnable. In 6/6 positions, the blunder leaves material en prise: Position 1 (O-O leaves Ne5 hanging for capture), Position 2 (Qxd4 exposes Bf5 to capture), Position 4 (Nc7 places the knight where it gets trapped by Ra7), Position 6 (d4 leaves e4 pawn completely undefended), Position 8 (Ng7 places knight on same rank as king allowing Rf7+ fork), Position 15 (Nc5+ puts knight where Bxc5 simply captures it). The average cp_loss is enormous (1866), and only 1.8 good moves were typically available, indicating critical moments demanding tactical alertness rather than 'plan execution.' The unifying error is prioritizing a strategic goal or superficially attractive idea over the concrete tactical reality of undefended material.
analysis.move_pattern: Any piece type or direction; the moved piece itself lands on an undefended/vulnerable square OR another piece is left hanging because the move fails to address its vulnerability
analysis.why_bad: The move ignores that a piece is completely undefended—either the piece moved lands where it can be captured/trapped/forked, or an existing undefended piece is left hanging while the player pursues a different plan, allowing the opponent to win material with a simple capture or one-move tactic.
sub_patterns: Castling or developing while leaving another piece hanging (positions 1, 6)
Moving a piece to a square where it is immediately capturable or trappable (positions 4, 5, 15)
Capturing material that removes defensive coverage from another piece (position 2)

analysis.label: Developing or moving a piece to an undefended square while the king is exposed on an open line, allowing the opponent to exploit the king vulnerability with check and then capture the hanging piece.
analysis.description: In 7/8 positions, the player moves a piece (predominantly a bishop) to an aggressive-looking but completely undefended square while their king sits exposed on an open diagonal or file. The opponent then exploits the king weakness with a forcing move (check), and on the follow-up captures the hanging piece. In 5/8 cases, a bishop is developed to c5 or b4 while a critical diagonal to the king (h5-e8 or a3-f8) is open, allowing Qh5+/f7+ followed by Qxc5 or a fork winning the bishop. In position 3, the knight leaves f4 (where it shielded the h3 bishop) to capture on g2, exposing the bishop to immediate capture. In position 6, the queen abandons all defensive duties to grab b2, leaving the king defenseless against checks on the c-file. The common thread across all 8 positions is: the moved piece becomes a free target because a forcing king attack (check or unstoppable threat) gives the opponent a tempo to collect the undefended piece.
analysis.move_pattern: Piece (usually bishop) moves to an undefended square 2+ squares from the king, typically along an active diagonal (c5, b4, f4), while the player's king is vulnerable on an open line
analysis.why_bad: The piece lands on an undefended square while the king is exposed on an open diagonal/file; the opponent delivers check first (exploiting the king weakness), then captures the hanging piece on the next move, winning material through the tempo gained by the check.
sub_patterns: Bc5 with missing f-pawn allows Qh5+ then Qxc5 (positions 1, 2, 7)
Bc5 abandoning guard of g7 allows Rxg7 (position 4)
Bb4 creating fork target with queen already on exposed square (position 8)
Bishop/queen moves to aggressive square ignoring pin/fork vulnerability on a5-e1 diagonal (position 5)
Piece captures material while abandoning defensive duty near exposed king (positions 3, 6)

analysis.label: Playing a quiet, non-forcing preparatory move when the position demands immediate concrete action to address a critical tactical or strategic need.
analysis.description: This feature fires on positions where the player makes a slow, non-forcing move (pawn push, piece repositioning, or quiet development) while ignoring the single most urgent demand of the position. In 5/8 cases, the move is a flank pawn push or peripheral piece maneuver (e6, a5, Ba5, b5, Rc3) when the center or king safety requires immediate attention. In Positions 1&2, e6 ignores the critical need to cover d6, enabling Ndb5-Nd6 invasion. In Position 5, a5 ignores the need to capture on d5 before d6 crushes. In Position 6, Ba5 wastes time repositioning when Kc7 was essential to support the passed pawn. In Position 9, b5 ignores king vulnerability allowing Re7+. In Position 11, Rc3 abandons a strong post without securing king safety. In Position 12, Kd6 abandons the blockade of a passed pawn. In Position 14, Be3 develops to a tactically vulnerable square instead of eliminating the critical centralized knight. All positions feature low good-move counts (avg 1.6), indicating sharp situations with one right answer that the player misses in favor of a generically reasonable but positionally irrelevant move.
analysis.move_pattern: Quiet, non-forcing moves (pawn advances, bishop/rook repositioning, king walks) that don't capture, check, or directly address the opponent's primary threat
analysis.why_bad: The position has one critical, concrete need (blocking an invasion square, capturing a threatening pawn, addressing king safety, maintaining a blockade) and the played move spends a tempo on a secondary objective, giving the opponent time to execute their primary tactical or strategic plan unchallenged
sub_patterns: Flank pawn push ignoring central crisis (e6/a5/b5)
Piece repositioning when direct action required (Ba5/Rc3/Be3)
King move abandoning critical duty (Kd6)

analysis.label: Moving a piece away from a square where it performed an essential defensive or controlling function, immediately allowing opponent exploitation of the vacancy.
analysis.description: In all 5 positions, the player moves a piece (or pawn) away from a critical post where it was performing an essential function—defending a pawn, controlling a key square, or blocking an invasion route—in pursuit of a superficially logical but ultimately counterproductive plan. In 4/5 cases, the opponent's queen immediately exploits the gap: Qxa7 grabs an undefended pawn (Position 1), Qxc6 captures the abandoned pawn (Position 3), Qh3 infiltrates toward the exposed king (Position 8), and Qe2+ launches a devastating infiltration (Position 14). In Position 13, the pawn push e5 abandons control of e6, enabling a queen trade into a knight fork. The key diagnostic is that multiple good alternatives existed (avg 2.2 good moves) that maintained the piece's critical function while making useful improvements, but the player chose an 'active' move that neglected the position's primary requirement.
analysis.move_pattern: Various piece types moved away from squares performing critical defensive/controlling functions; no single geometric direction but often toward the queenside (3/5 to b-file squares)
analysis.why_bad: The moved piece was the sole guardian of a critical pawn, square, or invasion route; removing it gives the opponent an immediate tactical exploitation (usually via the queen) that was previously impossible
sub_patterns: Queen abandoning pawn defense (Qb3 leaving c6)
Bishop abandoning dominant central post (Bb3 from d5)
King failing to block invasion square (Kb2 instead of Kd2)
Piece placed on suboptimal square missing threats (Re4 instead of Re3)
Pawn push opening opponent outpost (e5 vacating e6)

analysis.label: A piece (usually a knight) moves to an aggressive-looking square but abandons a critical defensive responsibility, allowing the opponent to immediately exploit the newly undefended pawn or square.
analysis.description: In 5/6 positions, a knight leaves a square where it was performing a vital defensive function (guarding a key pawn or square) to occupy an apparently active but premature square. In Position 2, Nf3 leaves f2 unguarded → Bxf2+ devastates. In Position 6, Nc6 leaves e5 undefended → Nxe5 wins material with a king attack. In Position 7, the knight moves to c3 where it hangs on the queen's diagonal. In Position 8, Nc6 decentralizes to a5, abandoning defense of the a6-pawn and queenside → a4 exploits. In Position 9, Nc6 jumps to d4 prematurely before development is complete → Nxd4 followed by e5 tears open the center against the uncastled king. In Position 10, Bg4 develops the bishop while leaving f7 fatally unguarded → Bxf7+ sacrifice wins material. The common thread across 6/6 positions is that a piece abandons guard duty for an aggressive-looking placement, and the opponent immediately punishes the newly created weakness. In 5/6 cases, the uncastled king's safety is the ultimate factor exploited.
analysis.move_pattern: Knight (or minor piece) moves from a defensive square to an aggressive central/active square (d4, e5, c3, a5, g4), typically forward or sideways, leaving a previously guarded pawn or square undefended
analysis.why_bad: The moved piece was the sole or primary defender of a critical pawn or square (f2, e5, a6, f7, or itself on a safe square); removing it creates an immediate tactical target that the opponent exploits through captures, sacrifices, or forks against the typically uncastled king
sub_patterns: Knight leaves f3/c6, unguarding a pawn that gets immediately captured or sacrificed upon
Knight jumps to d4 prematurely in the opening before development is complete, getting exchanged to open the center against uncastled king
Piece moves to a square where it hangs on a diagonal or is tactically vulnerable
Minor piece develops aggressively but exposes f7/f2 weakness with king in center

analysis.label: Playing a quiet defensive or prophylactic move that loses a decisive tempo when the position demanded immediate tactical action.
analysis.description: In all 3/3 positions, the player chose a quiet, non-forcing move motivated by vague defensive or prophylactic concerns (g3 for king safety, Kc1 for king relocation, Qf8 for passive defense) while ignoring an urgent tactical necessity that required immediate attention. In each case, a forcing or active alternative existed (f3 to control a critical square, Nh6 to blockade a passed pawn, Nd3+ to fork king and bishop) that addressed the position's primary demand. The quiet moves allowed the opponent to seize the initiative: in Position 6, the Queen invaded e4 to win a hanging piece; in Position 7, the g-pawn advanced unopposed to forced mate; in Position 8, White's king escaped to safety eliminating all counterplay. All three analyses explicitly identify 'tempo_loss' as a central tag, and each blunder transformed a manageable position into a catastrophic one (avg cp_loss: 3233).
analysis.move_pattern: Quiet non-forcing moves (pawn push, king step, queen retreat) that address secondary king-safety concerns rather than the position's primary tactical demand
analysis.why_bad: The quiet move wastes the one tempo needed to address the critical tactical requirement of the position, allowing the opponent to execute their threat uncontested - whether that's a queen invasion to win material, a pawn promotion march, or safe king consolidation that eliminates counterplay.
sub_patterns: King-area pawn move ignoring hanging piece
King relocation ignoring passed pawn advance
Passive queen move missing forcing fork/tactic

analysis.label: Playing slow, non-urgent moves (typically weakening pawn advances) in positions requiring immediate concrete or forcing action.
analysis.description: This feature fires on positions where the player ignores the most urgent demand of the position in favor of a secondary, non-forcing move that wastes a critical tempo. In 8/12 cases, the mistake is a pawn advance (g5, f6, h4, f4, c6, b3, b3, d4) that either weakens the player's own structure or addresses a peripheral concern. The remaining cases involve passive piece moves (Rae1 missing Rf8, Bh7 retreating to passivity, Nh4 misplacing a piece) or a move-order error (Rxd7+ before Bg5+). In every case, the position demanded a specific forcing continuation—a development move, a concrete threat, or a precise tactical sequence—and instead the player chose something that looks reasonable but gives the opponent a free tempo to solve their problems, activate pieces, or exploit the newly-created weakness. The average good moves available is only 1.8, indicating these are narrow-path positions where precision is critical, yet the player defaults to generic 'improving' moves.
analysis.move_pattern: Non-forcing moves (predominantly single-step pawn advances, also passive piece retreats or non-threatening piece repositioning) that neither check, capture, nor create an immediate threat
analysis.why_bad: They waste a critical tempo in positions where the opponent can immediately exploit either a pre-existing vulnerability (exposed king, undefended piece, open file) or a new weakness created by the move itself (opened diagonal, unsupported pawn, misplaced piece), allowing the opponent to seize the initiative or solve their defensive problems for free
sub_patterns: Weakening flank pawn advances when piece activity is needed (g5, f6, h4, f4)
Slow pawn moves ignoring immediate tactical threats (b3, c6, d4)
Passive piece moves missing a forcing opportunity (Rae1, Bh7, Nh4)
Move-order errors playing the non-forcing move first (Rxd7+ before Bg5+)

analysis.label: Playing natural-looking checks or aggressive moves that fail to exploit a winning attacking position, often using the wrong piece or targeting the wrong square.
analysis.description: This feature fires on positions where the player has a strong attacking position (typically against an exposed king) and plays a move that appears aggressive but fails to be the precise winning continuation. The most striking sub-pattern is checks with the wrong piece: 3/8 positions explicitly involve using the wrong piece (Qf6+ instead of Bf6+, Qxf1+ instead of Rxf1#, Rf8+ instead of Ng5+). Additionally, 5/8 moves are checks or captures that look forcing but actually allow the opponent to escape or neutralize the attack. The positions share extremely low counts of good moves available (avg 1.6), indicating critical decision points requiring calculation rather than intuition. Tags across positions consistently include 'missed_tactic' (5/8), 'tempo_loss' (6/8), and 'king_safety' (7/8). The underlying error pattern is prioritizing the appearance of aggression (giving check, making captures) over calculating which specific move maintains the attacking geometry.
analysis.move_pattern: Pieces (especially Queen) moving to give check or capture, frequently landing on f-file squares (5/8 moves target f1/f3/f5/f6/f8), in positions with exposed enemy kings
analysis.why_bad: The checks/captures allow the opponent's king to escape to a safer square or enable defensive resources (captures of undefended attacking pieces, interpositions), while the correct move maintains the mating net or attacking pressure through a less obvious but more precise piece placement that preserves coordination.
sub_patterns: Wrong piece gives check (Qf6+ vs Bf6+, Qxf1+ vs Rxf1#, Rf8+ vs Ng5+)
Purposeless queen checks to passive squares (Qa8+)
Active piece retreats abandoning key function (Bf5 from g4, Qe1)
Ignoring prophylaxis in favor of irrelevant advance (c4 vs g5)

analysis.label: Moves that remove the last defender or open the critical invasion square on the back rank, enabling immediate checkmate.
analysis.description: All 4/4 positions feature a player making a move that fatally compromises their own back rank, allowing forced checkmate in 1-2 moves. In 2/4 cases (Rb5, Rbc4), a rook is moved away from the back rank, removing the only piece that could interpose against a rook invasion on the 8th rank. In 2/4 cases (f3, b4), a pawn is advanced that was the sole guardian of a first-rank entry square (c1 in both cases), opening the gate for an enemy rook to deliver mate. In all cases, the opponent has a long-diagonal bishop or advanced pawn sealing off king escape squares (g7 controlled in positions 5, 10, 12; knight controlling f2/h2 in position 7), making the back-rank threat lethal once the last defensive resource is removed. The average cp_loss of ~9800 reflects that these moves convert playable positions into immediate forced checkmate.
analysis.move_pattern: Piece or pawn moves away from the first/eighth rank, either laterally repositioning a rook or advancing a pawn forward, abandoning defense of a critical back-rank square
analysis.why_bad: Each move removes the single remaining resource (interposing rook or guarding pawn) protecting against back-rank invasion, while a bishop or pawn already seals the king's escape squares, enabling immediate forced checkmate
sub_patterns: Rook moved laterally/forward away from back rank, leaving no interposer against doubled-rook or rook invasion
Pawn advanced from first/second rank, opening c1 or f1 as an unguarded entry point for enemy rook mate

analysis.label: Playing a non-forcing, seemingly improving move that wastes a critical tempo in a position demanding immediate concrete action.
analysis.description: This feature fires on positions where the player makes a quiet, plausible-looking move while ignoring an urgent tactical or strategic demand. In 7/10 positions, the analyses explicitly tag 'tempo_loss' as the core error. The moves vary widely in piece type (kings, bishops, knights, rooks, pawns) but share the characteristic of being non-forcing 'improvements' when the position requires immediate action: missing a saving tactic like Nh6+ (Position 11, 471cp loss) or Nxf7 (Position 5, 544cp loss), playing passive repositioning moves like Rc7 or Bh3 when active queen moves or concrete threats are needed (Positions 8, 9), pushing irrelevant flank pawns like a4 or c4 while ignoring critical central/tactical issues (Positions 11, 13), or making king moves that waste time or create new vulnerabilities (Positions 1, 2). In 8/10 positions, exposed kings or king safety issues create the urgency that the played move ignores. The average cp_loss of 1120 reflects that these tempo losses are catastrophic precisely because the positions are razor-sharp and demand specific concrete play.
analysis.move_pattern: Any piece type; non-capturing, non-forcing moves; often repositioning or advancing without creating immediate threats
analysis.why_bad: The position has one urgent concrete demand (a tactical shot, addressing an immediate threat, or maintaining a pawn race tempo) and the played move ignores it entirely, giving the opponent a free tempo to execute their winning plan or consolidate an advantage
sub_patterns: Missing a critical one-move tactic (sacrifice/fork) in favor of a quiet move
Passive piece retreat or repositioning when active forcing play is required
Irrelevant flank pawn push ignoring central/tactical crisis
King move that wastes tempo or walks into a target square
Natural developing move that ignores a concrete tactical vulnerability

analysis.label: Moving a piece away from its essential defensive duty, leaving material or king fatally unguarded.
analysis.description: This feature fires on moves where a piece that was performing a critical defensive function (guarding another piece, blocking an attack line, or maintaining counterplay) is relocated, catastrophically neglecting its obligation. In 3/6 positions (Qe1, Qd2, Qa7), the queen was the sole defender of a piece (Nf3, Rf1, Be7 respectively) and its departure allowed immediate material capture. In 1/6 (Bd3), the bishop abandoned its critical counterplay trajectory (Ba6) while simultaneously blocking its own king's escape route. In 1/6 (Rf6), the rook was moved instead of addressing the only critical threat (h6 to neutralize g6 pawn), losing a crucial tempo. In 1/6 (Kd8), the king walked to a worse square that increased vulnerability to checking patterns. All moves appear to be reasonable repositioning moves but fatally ignore the piece's hidden defensive role in the current position.
analysis.move_pattern: Quiet piece relocation (no capture, no check) away from a square where it performed a sole defensive function
analysis.why_bad: The moved piece was the only thing preventing an immediate tactical catastrophe (hanging piece, mating attack, or unopposed threat), and its departure creates an irrecoverable tactical vulnerability that the opponent exploits within one move.
sub_patterns: Queen abandons defense of minor piece/rook (3 cases)
Piece blocks own escape route or abandons counterplay line
Tempo-wasting move ignores immediate critical threat

analysis.label: Knight moves to a tempting central square (d5/e5/e4) where it is immediately captured or exchanged, with the resulting recapture creating devastating tactical or structural consequences.
analysis.description: All 4/4 positions involve a knight moving to a prominent central square (d5, e5, or e4) that appears attractive but where the opponent can immediately exchange it with severe consequences. In 2/4 cases (positions 1 and 12), a knight captures the d5 pawn only for the opponent's knight to recapture on d5 and generate powerful follow-up tactics (attacking e7 with check/fork). In 1/4 cases (position 3), the knight moves to e5 where Nxe5 forces dxe5, ruining pawn structure, opening the d-file, and empowering the opponent's pieces. In 1/4 cases (position 4), the knight repositions from an aggressive square (g5) to e4, where the opponent captures it and eliminates the only active attacking piece. The common thread is that the player is seduced by the apparent power of a centralized knight without calculating what happens after the forced exchange on that square.
analysis.move_pattern: Knight moves inward to central square (d5/e5/e4), typically a capture or centralization, where it is immediately recaptured or exchanged
analysis.why_bad: The exchange on the central square favors the opponent—the recapture either creates new tactical threats (forks, attacks on weak pieces), ruins the player's pawn structure, or eliminates the player's most active piece while giving the opponent superior coordination and initiative.
sub_patterns: Knight captures poisoned central pawn where recapture creates fork/attack
Knight centralizes to square where trade ruins own pawn structure
Active knight retreats to exchangeable square losing initiative

analysis.label: Non-urgent, non-forcing moves played in positions demanding immediate attention to a critical tactical or king-safety vulnerability.
analysis.description: This feature activates on positions where the player makes a quiet, secondary-objective move (typically a pawn push or piece repositioning) while the position screams for immediate action on a specific critical need. In 8/10 positions, king safety is the ignored crisis. The positions share extremely low good-move counts (avg 1.5), meaning precision is essential, yet the player wastes tempo on irrelevant plans. Examples include: b4 ignoring a mating net (Position 1), g4 weakening king shelter enabling back-rank mate (Position 5), Re5 abandoning b-file back-rank defense (Position 9), Rf4 leaving back rank unguarded (Position 13), b5 ignoring c-file/back-rank tension (Position 11), Qb6 abandoning e-file defense (Position 14), and h4 allowing d6 counterplay (Position 15). In 7/10 cases, the refutation involves a forcing sequence (check, capture, or invasion) on the exact square/file/rank that was left unattended. The moves look purposeful in isolation but catastrophically misjudge positional priorities.
analysis.move_pattern: Quiet, non-forcing moves (predominantly pawn pushes 5/10 or piece relocations away from critical defensive posts) that are neither checks nor captures in positions requiring immediate tactical precision
analysis.why_bad: These moves waste the single critical tempo available in razor-sharp positions (avg 1.5 good moves), allowing the opponent to exploit an unaddressed vulnerability—typically a back-rank weakness, exposed king, or undefended piece—with an immediate forcing sequence that was previously prevented by the piece/tempo now squandered.
sub_patterns: Pawn push on opposite flank while king is under direct attack (b4, b5, h4, g4)
Piece abandons critical defensive file/rank allowing back-rank invasion (Re5, Rf4, Qb6)
King or queen retreats to tactically vulnerable square (Ke8 onto diagonal, Qg5 abandoning defense)
Wrong recapture opening file toward own uncastled king (exd5)

analysis.label: Playing a seemingly purposeful move that wastes the one critical tempo in a position where very few moves maintain the evaluation.
analysis.description: This feature fires on positions where there are extremely few good moves (avg 1.5) and the player makes a move that appears active or purposeful but fatally squanders the one available tempo. In 7/8 positions, the move places a piece on a square where it immediately becomes a target for tempo-gaining attacks: Kf5 gets confined by ...Kf7/g6 (1/8), Qb5 gets kicked by ...a6/b5 (2/8), Rxf4 gets exploited by Nd5 tempo on the queen (3/8), Nc5 allows Qc2 infiltration (4/8), Rh3 fails to prevent the f5 break (5/8), Kh2 walks into Rxh3+ sacrifice (6/8), Qh4 gets kicked by g3 (7/8), and a3 wastes the one tempo needed for ...h4 to lock the kingside (8/8). All positions feature a single critical action the position demands—neutralizing a queen (Qg3), locking a pawn structure (h4), exploiting a file (Rac1), or centralizing (Kd5)—and the played move ignores it in favor of a plausible-looking but irrelevant improvement.
analysis.move_pattern: Various piece types moved to apparently active/useful squares that don't address the position's one critical requirement; pieces often land where they become exposed to tempo-gaining attacks
analysis.why_bad: These moves waste the one critical tempo in razor-thin positions where only 1-2 moves work, allowing the opponent to execute a decisive tactical or positional blow (pawn breaks, piece infiltration, sacrificial combinations) that the correct move would have prevented or preempted
sub_patterns: Piece moved to square where it gets attacked by pawn advances (Qb5→a6/b5, Qh4→g3)
King moved to square creating tactical vulnerability (Kf5→confinement, Kh2→Rxh3+ sacrifice)
Active-looking piece placement that abandons critical defensive duty (Nc5 leaves b3, Rh3 blocks king escape)
Tempo-wasting move when position requires immediate structural action (a3 instead of h4)

analysis.label: Non-forcing moves that appear to strengthen an attack but squander a position demanding an immediate concrete tactical blow (sacrifice, check, or forced combination).
analysis.description: In all 7 positions, the player had a decisive forcing continuation available (often a sacrifice with check or a forced mating sequence) but instead played a move that merely 'looks attacking' or 'improving' without delivering the knockout. In 6/7 cases, the played move involves placing a piece on a kingside square (h5, g4, f4, h3, f4, g2) that appears aggressive but is non-forcing. In 5/7 cases, the missed best move was a sacrifice or capture with check (Bxf2+, Nxf5+, Ng5→Qb3+, Rxf7!, Qg3→Rxg2+). In 6/7 positions, the player was already winning or had a mating attack, meaning the error converted a decisive advantage into merely a good or even position. The average cp_loss of ~3000 reflects that these are catastrophic misses where forced mates or queen-winning combinations existed. The common thread is choosing a 'building' move in a position that demanded immediate tactical execution.
analysis.move_pattern: Piece moves (especially to kingside squares f4/g4/h3/h5/g2/e2) that appear attacking or active but lack forcing character (no check, no immediate threat that must be answered)
analysis.why_bad: The position demanded an immediate concrete forcing blow (sacrifice with check, forced mating sequence, or decisive capture) but the player chose a non-forcing 'improving' move that gives the opponent time to consolidate, defend critical squares, or generate counterplay that neutralizes the attack.
sub_patterns: Queen centralization to f4 missing a tactical combination (2 cases)
Piece repositioning away from a dominant square (Ng4 from f6, Re2 from e5)
Slow pawn push or bishop development when forced mate exists (h5, Bh3)
Greedy material capture that abandons critical file/geometry (Rxg2)

analysis.label: Quiet repositioning moves that waste a critical tempo when the position demands immediate tactical or concrete action.
analysis.description: All 5/5 positions feature non-forcing, non-capturing moves (Be7, Kb1, Kg4, Qc3, Kg2) that appear to 'improve' a piece's placement but fatally ignore the position's urgent tactical demands. In 5/5 cases the opponent gains a devastating tactical opportunity on the very next move (e5 breakthrough, Rxc3 exchange sacrifice, discovered check, Bc5 activation). The 'missed_tactic' tag appears in 5/5 positions, 'tempo_loss' in 4/5, and 'king_safety' in 4/5. The best moves in each position were concrete actions: castling immediately (Position 4), creating an active threat with Bh6 (Position 6), prophylactic h6 (Position 10), tactical capture Nxe5 (Position 12), or the precise retreat Kf1 (Position 15). The played moves instead prioritize vague piece improvement — natural development, king tucking, queen centralization — that is one tempo too slow for the position's tactical reality.
analysis.move_pattern: Quiet, non-forcing moves (no check, no capture, no direct threat) that reposition a piece or king to a seemingly natural/improved square
analysis.why_bad: The position requires immediate concrete action (tactical strike, castling, prophylaxis against a specific threat), and the quiet move allows the opponent to execute a decisive tactical blow — discovered attacks, sacrificial combinations, or central breakthroughs — that were not possible one move earlier.
sub_patterns: King moves to tactically vulnerable squares (3/5: Kb1, Kg4, Kg2)
Quiet development/repositioning when a forcing capture wins (Qc3 instead of Nxe5, Be7 instead of O-O-O)
Placing pieces on squares that create new geometric weaknesses (diagonals, files, discovered check lanes)

analysis.label: Moves that waste tempo on irrelevant plans while a critical tactical vulnerability (hanging piece, exposed king, imminent threat) demands immediate attention.
analysis.description: This feature fires on moves where the player makes a 'reasonable-looking' developing, activating, or capturing move while completely ignoring the single most urgent tactical or structural need in the position. In 6/7 cases, the analyses explicitly identify 'tempo_loss' as a core issue. In 2/7 positions (Positions 1&2), the player makes developing moves (Qe1, Rd1) instead of playing f3 to address an identically stranded knight on h3. In 2/7 cases (Ng4, Be5+), the player physically removes a piece from a critical defensive post—the f6-knight guarding h7 or the d6-bishop guarding f8—allowing immediate material gain. In 2/7 cases (g6, Ba3), the player makes a slow preparatory/flanking move while an existential tactical threat demands immediate action. In 1/7 (gxh5), the player opens lines directly against their own king. The common evaluation pattern shows massive drops (avg 2958cp) because the opponent can immediately exploit the neglected weakness, often winning material outright or creating forced checkmate.
analysis.move_pattern: Any piece type moving to an irrelevant square/direction while a critical defensive duty is abandoned or an emergency goes unaddressed
analysis.why_bad: Each move fails to address the position's most critical vulnerability—a hanging piece, an exposed king, or an imminent unstoppable threat—giving the opponent a free tempo to exploit the weakness decisively, typically winning material or creating a mating attack.
sub_patterns: Developing moves instead of rescuing/rerouting a misplaced hanging piece (Qe1, Rd1 ignoring knight on h3)
Removing a critical defensive piece from its guardian role (Ng4 abandoning h7, Be5+ abandoning f8 coverage)
Slow preparatory moves ignoring an imminent tactical blow (g6 ignoring d5-d6, Ba3 ignoring kingside crisis)
Pawn captures that fatally weaken own king shelter (gxh5 opening g-file)

analysis.label: Moves that abandon control of critical invasion squares on open files, allowing the opponent's rook to penetrate to the 6th or 7th rank.
analysis.description: In 9/10 positions, the blundered move directly enables the opponent's rook to invade the 6th or 7th rank (or equivalently, the 2nd/3rd rank from the attacker's perspective) along an already-open file. The punishing responses are: Rf3/Rf2 invasion (Position 1), Re3 invasion (Position 2), rook domination after piece removal (Position 3), Re6+ with tempo (Position 4), Rd6→Rd7 penetration (Position 5), Re7 invasion (Position 6), Rc6 invasion (Position 7), Rf2+ forcing trade (Position 8), Rc7+ invasion (Position 9). The blundered moves themselves are diverse—bishop moves, knight moves, king moves, rook moves, captures—but they all share the structural consequence of vacating a piece that controlled the invasion square, moving the king to where it can be checked with tempo on the open file, or abandoning a strong post that contested the critical file. The best moves in each position specifically maintain file blockade or invasion-square control (e.g., Bf4 blocking f-file, Kf2 guarding e2/e3, Bd5 blocking d-file, Ne4 centralizing with counterplay, Bc4 challenging the rook).
analysis.move_pattern: Any piece type moving away from (or failing to occupy) squares that control an open file's 6th/7th rank penetration points; includes king moves to check-vulnerable squares on open files
analysis.why_bad: The moves surrender control of the critical entry squares on open files, allowing the opponent's rook to reach the 6th or 7th rank where it attacks pawns laterally, restricts the king, dominates the position, and often wins material immediately through dual threats or back-rank/rank pressure.
sub_patterns: King walks into open file check allowing rook invasion with tempo (Kg6→Re6+, Kh7→Re7, Kf6→Rf2+, Kb5→Rd6)
Piece abandons defensive post that was blocking file penetration (Ba3, Nf3, Nd2, Rd1)
Trading away the only piece preventing rook dominance (Bxg5 removing sole defender)

analysis.label: Non-developing flank pawn advances in the opening that create tactical or structural vulnerabilities while neglecting urgent development or central play.
analysis.description: This feature fires on positions where a player advances a flank pawn (b, c, f, or g file) instead of developing pieces or executing central play. All 11 moves are pawn advances on non-central files (b-pawn in 7/11, c-pawn in 2/11, f/g-pawn in 3/11). The resulting weaknesses typically involve exposed long diagonals for opponent's fianchettoed bishops (positions 4, 5, 6, 7, 10 all feature Bxa1 or Bxa8 tactics after the b-pawn vacates), undefended pawns becoming targets (positions 2, 15), or weakened king positions (positions 11, 14). In every case, simple developing moves (Nf3, Bd6, Bb7, O-O, etc.) or central breaks (d5, e5) were available and clearly superior. The average cp_loss of 260 reflects that these tempo-wasting flank moves consistently allow concrete tactical exploitation of the newly created weaknesses.
analysis.move_pattern: Pawn advance on b, c, f, or g file (non-central flanks); no captures or checks; predominantly 1-2 squares forward
analysis.why_bad: These moves waste a critical development tempo to advance a flank pawn that either exposes a long diagonal (allowing bishop captures on a1/a8), creates an undefended pawn target, or weakens key squares around the king—all while the opponent can exploit the tempo loss with immediate tactical strikes against the newly created vulnerability.
sub_patterns: b-pawn advance exposing long diagonal to fianchettoed bishop (b3/b6 allowing Bxa1/Bxa8)
Queenside pawn expansion creating structural targets (b4/b5/c4/c5)
Kingside pawn advance weakening king shelter or squares (f6/g6/g4)

analysis.label: Aggressive-looking piece relocations (often queen to g4/h4/h5 area) that abandon critical defensive or coordinative functions, allowing the opponent to seize initiative through tempo-gaining responses.
analysis.description: This feature fires on moves that appear aggressive or threatening but actually sacrifice essential positional responsibilities for illusory activity. In 5/7 positions, the queen is the piece moved, typically to kingside squares (Qh5, Qh4, Qg4, Qd5+) that look threatening but create no real concrete threats. The common thread across all 7 positions is that the move abandons control of a critical line or square: Qh5 abandons the second rank (1/7), Qh4 loses queen coordination for a mating attack (2/7), Kg5 walks into check combinations on open diagonals (3/7), Qg4 abandons the c5-g1 diagonal allowing Bc5+ (4/7), Bh2 wastes a tempo needed to attack the f6 pawn (5/7), Qd5+ allows an interposition with check (6/7), and f4 blocks development while weakening squares (7/7). In every case, the opponent exploits the abandoned function with a tempo-gaining response (check, invasion, forced trade). The tag 'tempo_loss' appears explicitly in 6/7 analyses, confirming the unifying mechanism.
analysis.move_pattern: Piece (usually queen) relocates toward g/h files at ranks 4-5, or forward into apparently active but functionally disconnected squares
analysis.why_bad: The move creates no concrete threats while abandoning control of a critical line, square, or defensive duty, allowing the opponent a tempo-gaining response (check, invasion, or forced simplification) that exploits the vacated function
sub_patterns: Queen to kingside rim square (h4/h5/g4) abandoning central/rank control
Giving check that allows interposition with counter-check
Piece retreat to passive edge square losing critical tempo
Forward king/pawn move creating tactical vulnerabilities on opened lines

analysis.label: Slow positional moves that ignore an opponent's queen check winning an undefended piece.
analysis.description: In all 5/5 positions, White plays a quiet, non-forcing move (pawn push or bishop development) prioritizing long-term positional goals while an undefended piece is vulnerable to being won by a queen check. The refutations all follow the same template: the opponent's queen delivers check (Qa5+ in 2/5, Qb6+ in 1/5, Qc1+ in 1/5, Qc2+ in 1/5), and after the king moves, the queen captures the hanging piece on the next move. The played moves either open a diagonal to the king (d3 opens a5-e1, g3 weakens back rank), place a piece on an undefended square reachable after a check (Bb5, Bb2), or block the king's escape route so a check forces separation from a hanging piece (f3). In all cases, 3+ good alternatives existed that addressed the tactical vulnerability first.
analysis.move_pattern: Quiet non-forcing moves (pawn advances g3/d3/f3 or bishop development Bb2/Bb5) that ignore diagonal/rank vulnerability to the opponent's queen
analysis.why_bad: Each move either opens a line for an enemy queen check, places a piece where it hangs after a queen check, or blocks the king's escape route allowing a queen check to win a hanging piece - the player prioritizes positional structure over immediate tactical safety of undefended pieces.
sub_patterns: Pawn move opens diagonal allowing Qa5+ winning hanging bishop (d3, Bb5 positions)
Bishop development to undefended square attackable after queen check (Bb2, Bb5)
Pawn move blocks king escape allowing queen check to disconnect king from rook (f3, g3)

analysis.label: Moving the king (or piece) to a seemingly safe square that actually lies on an enemy piece's critical attacking line, enabling immediate forced mate or devastating tactics.
analysis.description: This feature activates on positions where the player selects the wrong square for a piece (usually the king) when only one specific square survives. In 6/9 cases, the king directly steps onto a diagonal or file controlled by an enemy bishop or queen, enabling discovered checks or mating sequences (Kh1 onto Bxg2+ check line, Kg1 onto d4-g1 bishop diagonal twice, Kd2 onto queen's checking diagonal, Kf3 exposing to f-file checks, Kh6 onto f8-h6 bishop diagonal). The remaining 3/9 cases involve non-king moves that similarly waste the one critical tempo or block the one defensive resource (Be7 blocking the queen's access to the saving e7 square, c3 ignoring mating construction, Rbc1 allowing opponent to seize initiative). The astronomical average cp_loss of 6307 and average of only 1.2 good moves confirm these are razor-thin positions where choosing the wrong square—often differing by a single square from survival—results in immediate catastrophe.
analysis.move_pattern: King moves (or piece moves) to an adjacent square that lies on an enemy bishop/queen's diagonal or rook/queen's file, typically one square away from the only surviving alternative
analysis.why_bad: The chosen square sits on a critical enemy attacking line (diagonal or file), enabling discovered checks, direct checks, or mating sequences that would not be possible if the piece were placed on the one alternative safe square
sub_patterns: King steps onto bishop's diagonal enabling discovered check via knight move
King retreats to corner where sacrifice comes with check (back rank trap)
King walks onto queen's checking diagonal allowing forced mate in 2-3
King retreats passively abandoning centralization and exposing to file checks
Non-king move blocks the one defensive resource or wastes critical tempo

analysis.label: Catastrophic blunders in positions where exactly one move is acceptable, with the player choosing a natural-looking but fatally flawed alternative.
analysis.description: This feature fires on positions where exactly ONE good move exists (avg good moves = 1.0 across all 8 positions) and the player makes a catastrophic error (avg cp_loss = 2618). The moves look purposeful—Nc2 appears to attack a piece (Position 1), Ng2 looks defensive (Position 2), Rcc2 seems to create a powerful battery (Position 6), Qc4+ and Qf1+ are active checks (Positions 5, 7)—but each fatally ignores the single critical factor that makes only one move work. In 6/7 detailed positions, the blunder ignores a specific concrete tactical vulnerability: a piece landing on a controlled square (Rfe1 into bishop's diagonal, Nc2 where it's captured), a check allowing interposition/forced trade (Qc4+ allows Qf4 trade, Qf1+ allows b1=Q interposition), or an unaddressed threat (Rcc2 ignores hxg6, f5 strips king cover). The positions span all piece types and both sides but uniformly demand precise calculation over natural-looking moves.
analysis.move_pattern: Diverse piece types moving to squares or along lines that appear active/purposeful but are concretely refuted by one specific opponent resource
analysis.why_bad: Each move ignores the single critical concrete factor (a tactical shot, geometric vulnerability, or forced response) that makes only one move survivable, resulting in catastrophic material or positional collapse
sub_patterns: Checks along lines allowing interposition or forced queen trade (Qf1+, Qc4+)
Pieces moving to squares controlled by opponent (Nc2, Rfe1)
Ignoring critical opponent threats to pursue own plans (Rcc2, f5)
King moving to geometrically wrong square by one step (Kb2 vs Kb3)
Defensive retreat abandoning crucial tactical resource (Ng2)

analysis.label: A piece repositions to a seemingly reasonable square but fatally abandons a critical defensive duty, allowing immediate tactical exploitation of the unguarded point.
analysis.description: In all 5/5 positions, the player makes a quiet, non-forcing repositioning move (no checks, no captures) that looks developmental or purposeful but removes a piece from a critical defensive role. In Position 12 (Ne2), the knight leaves c3 unblocking the a1-d4 diagonal and leaving the a1-rook hanging to Qxa1+. In Position 13 (Qh5), the queen abandons coverage of f2 and the a7-g1 diagonal, enabling Qc5+/Nf2+ fork combinations. In Position 8 (Bf3), the bishop retreats to a square that fails to cover c4, leaving the f1-rook defended only by the overloaded queen, exploitable via Bc4. In Position 6 (Kh1), the king sidesteps onto the h-file directly into a back-rank checkmate pattern. In Position 5 (Bd6), the bishop blocks the queen's flexible positioning, allowing a forced deflection sequence (Rxe8+ Qxe8 Bxf6). The common thread is that each move serves a plausible strategic purpose (piece development, king safety, attacking ideas) but catastrophically ignores an existing defensive obligation that the opponent immediately exploits.
analysis.move_pattern: Quiet piece repositioning (bishop retreat, knight reroute, king sidestep, queen sortie) to a non-forcing square that removes coverage from a critical line, square, or piece
analysis.why_bad: The moved piece was performing a hidden defensive function (guarding a piece, controlling a diagonal/file, or preventing a tactical motif) that the player failed to recognize; removing it creates an immediate tactical vulnerability (hanging piece, fork, mate, or forced sequence) that the opponent exploits in 1-2 moves.
sub_patterns: Knight/piece vacates square that unblocks a dangerous diagonal, leaving a piece hanging (Ne2 → Qxa1+)
Queen sortie to aggressive square abandons defense of critical squares, enabling check-then-fork (Qh5 → Qc5+/Nf2+)
Bishop retreats to wrong square failing to control key invasion point (Bf3 fails to cover c4 → Bc4 wins exchange)
King sidesteps onto an open file controlled by enemy heavy piece (Kh1 → Rxh2#)
Piece development self-blocks queen flexibility, enabling forced deflection sequence (Bd6 → Rxe8+ deflection)

analysis.label: Moves that look purposeful but fatally expose the player's own king to immediate tactical exploitation through checks and queen invasions.
analysis.description: In 9/9 positions, the played move either places the king on an exposed square (Kf2, Kxg2, Kf6, Kd7 — 4/9 are direct king moves to vulnerable squares) or removes/misplaces a piece that was performing a critical defensive role shielding the king (Bc4 vacates f1 allowing Qg1+ back-rank invasion, Bd6 ignores the open e8-h5 diagonal allowing Qh5+, Ne7 fails to cover f7, Nh5 abandons queenside leaving a7 hanging while the reroute accomplishes nothing defensively, Nxf2+ trades the key attacking piece and exposes own king to perpetual). In every case, the opponent's refutation involves an immediate forcing sequence starting with a queen check or invasion (Qc2+, Qg3+, Qh5+, Qg1+, Qg4+, Qe4+). The average cp_loss of 361 and average of only 1.7 good moves available confirms these are critical moments where the correct alternative specifically prioritized king safety (castling queenside, retreating to sheltered squares, blocking dangerous diagonals). The moves all appear natural or aggressive on the surface — capturing material, developing pieces, centralizing the king — but ignore the singular most important positional factor: the monarch's vulnerability.
analysis.move_pattern: King moves to exposed central/flank squares (f2, g2, f6, d7), or minor pieces move away from squares defending the king's zone (Bf1→c4, Nf6→h5/e7), allowing diagonal/file-based queen checks
analysis.why_bad: Each move abandons a critical defensive function (blocking a check diagonal, covering an invasion square, or keeping the king sheltered) in favor of an apparently purposeful but ultimately self-destructive goal, enabling the opponent to launch immediate forcing sequences with queen checks that win material or create devastating attacks against the exposed king.
sub_patterns: King voluntarily walks to square exposed to queen checks (Kf2, Kxg2, Kf6, Kd7)
Piece vacates critical defensive square near king allowing back-rank or diagonal invasion (Bc4, Bd6)
Knight reroute abandons defensive duties and wastes tempo (Nh5, Ne7, Nxf2+)

analysis.label: Moving a piece away from its critical active or defensive role to a peripheral or passive square, often motivated by a tempting but flawed tactical idea.
analysis.description: This feature fires on moves where a piece abandons a crucial central or functional post in favor of a peripheral, rim, or passive square. In 4/7 positions, knights specifically drift to rim squares (Ng1+, Nf3 instead of e2, Nh6, Nh7) where they become trapped, stranded, or lose coordination. In 2/7 positions, queens relocate to less effective squares (Qe3 leaving e5 centralization, Qg5 abandoning e4 defense). The moves are typically motivated by superficially attractive ideas—delivering a check (Ng1+), attacking a pawn (Nh7 targeting f8, Qg5 targeting h4, Nh6 targeting h7), or forcing a trade (Qe3)—but they sacrifice the piece's critical functional role. The common outcome is the piece becomes ineffective on its new square: trapped (Ng1+ leads to Kxh3, Nh7 becomes stranded), losing defensive coordination (Nf3 fails to block e-file, Qg5 leaves e4 hanging), or entering an inferior position (Qe3 allows knight fork after trade).
analysis.move_pattern: Piece (especially knight) moves from central/active square toward the edge of the board (g/h files, back ranks), often with a superficially forcing idea like check or attack
analysis.why_bad: The piece abandons a critical defensive or coordinative function at its current location, and on its new peripheral square it becomes trapped, stranded, or unable to fulfill any meaningful role—allowing the opponent to exploit the abandoned duty or capture the misplaced piece
sub_patterns: Knight retreating/advancing to h-file rim (Nh6, Nh7, Ng1)
Queen leaving centralized post for less effective peripheral square
Developing to wrong square when specific blocking/defensive square was required
Slow moves ignoring urgent tactical demands of the position

analysis.label: Black plays a committal move (usually a pawn advance) seeking activity while neglecting an urgent positional or structural priority that the correct move would address first.
analysis.description: This feature detects positions where Black makes an irreversible committal move—typically a pawn advance or piece reposition—that looks active but ignores a more urgent concrete need. In 5/7 positions, the blunder is a pawn advance (a5, h4, a4, g4, plus the failure to play b4 in position 1). The correct moves consistently address a specific priority FIRST: fixing critical pawn tension before king moves (1/7), placing the bishop on the exact square that controls the opponent's pawn break (2/7), supporting a pawn advance with the rook beforehand (1/7), maintaining structural tension rather than dissolving it (1/7), advancing the kingside majority on the correct flank (1/7), and blockading a passed pawn instead of seeking illusory counterplay (1/7). In all cases, the opponent punishes by exploiting the specific vulnerability the correct move would have addressed—creating passed pawns (5/7), winning material on the newly-weakened square (1/7), or inflicting permanent structural damage (1/7). The average cp_loss of 280 reflects how severely these preparation errors are punished.
analysis.move_pattern: Mostly one-square pawn advances on flanks (a- or g/h-file) or piece moves to suboptimal squares; no consistent geometric direction, but always committal/irreversible moves
analysis.why_bad: The move ignores a concrete urgent priority (fixing pawn tension, supporting an advance, blockading a passer, or avoiding a tactical vulnerability), giving the opponent a one-tempo window to exploit the neglected weakness—typically creating unstoppable passed pawns or winning material from the structural collapse.
sub_patterns: Flank pawn advance without piece support (a5, a4, g4)
Pawn advance dissolving favorable tension (h4)
Piece move before resolving critical pawn structure (Kf6, Bd4)
Active move abandoning required defensive blockade (g4 vs Kb8)

analysis.label: A piece (usually a rook) leaves its strategically ideal post for an intermediate, active-looking but less effective square, violating key endgame principles like rook-behind-passed-pawn or maximum checking distance.
analysis.description: This feature fires on positions where a piece abandons its optimal strategic position in favor of a superficially active but fundamentally inferior square. In 6/8 positions, a rook moves to an intermediate rank (3rd, 6th, or 7th) when the correct placement was either behind a passed pawn, at maximum checking distance (back rank), or maintaining the powerful 2nd/7th rank. In Position 1, the rook leaves c8 (behind the passed c2 pawn) for c3, freeing White's king to approach. In Position 2, the rook leaves the dominant 2nd rank (b2) for the passive b3. In Positions 3 and 8, rooks go to rank 6 when rank 8 provides critical checking distance. In Position 7, the rook abandons blockade duty on a7 by moving to c7, releasing three connected passers. In Position 6, a rook penetrates to c7 missing a quieter bishop move that forced mate. The 2/8 king moves (Kf5, Kf4) share the same principle: advancing forward into exposed positions when retreating or staying put was essential. The common thread is sacrificing a piece's structurally optimal position for an intermediate square that appears aggressive but reduces strategic effectiveness.
analysis.move_pattern: Rook moving along a file to an intermediate rank (3rd, 6th, 7th) or laterally away from a critical file; king advancing forward one square into exposed central positions
analysis.why_bad: These moves violate fundamental positional principles: they remove rooks from behind passed pawns (allowing the opponent's king to approach), reduce checking distance (allowing faster interposition), abandon critical restraining duties (releasing passed pawns to advance), or expose kings to mating attacks. The 'active' square provides less real influence than the position being abandoned.
sub_patterns: Rook leaves file behind passed pawn for active-looking lateral rank
Rook moves to rank 6 instead of rank 8 (insufficient checking distance)
Rook abandons 2nd/7th rank for the 3rd/6th rank
King advances forward into exposed center instead of retreating
Rook leaves blockade/restraint position for superficially aggressive penetration

analysis.label: Playing a plausible-looking but non-urgent quiet move when the position demands immediate concrete action to address a pressing tactical or developmental need.
analysis.description: In 6/7 positions, the primary tag is 'tempo_loss' — the played move is a non-forcing, preparatory, or routine-looking move that squanders a critical tempo. The moves include slow pawn pushes (b3, g6, d6 in 3/7 positions), piece relocations to suboptimal squares (Bg4, Qb5 in 2/7), development to the 'wrong' natural square (Nf6 in 1/7), and a king retreat when capturing was available (Kd5 in 1/7). In each case, the position had a concrete demand — developing pieces urgently (positions 1, 3, 7), maintaining defensive coordination (position 4), rescuing a trapped piece (position 5), or capturing free material (position 6) — and the played move instead addressed a secondary or non-existent concern. The opponent then exploits the gifted tempo to execute a concrete plan (Ne5xg6, g4 pawn break, Ra1 winning trapped piece, f5 breakthrough, etc.) that the correct move would have prevented.
analysis.move_pattern: Non-forcing quiet moves (no checks, no captures, no direct threats) — pawn pushes, piece repositioning to passive/unstable squares, or retreats away from action
analysis.why_bad: The position has a concrete urgent demand (development, piece safety, material capture, preventing opponent's plan) that requires immediate action; the quiet move wastes the one tempo needed to address it, allowing the opponent to execute a winning tactical or positional plan unimpeded.
sub_patterns: Slow preparatory pawn moves when piece development is critical (b3, g6, d6)
Piece placed on superficially active but unstable square that will be challenged with tempo (Bg4, Qb5)
Developing to a natural square that fails to address the key positional requirement (Nf6 not controlling e5)
King retreating from active position instead of capturing available material (Kd5 instead of Kxf4)

analysis.label: Moving a piece to a b/c-file square for speculative queenside activity while it was performing a critical defensive or tactical function elsewhere.
analysis.description: In all 4 positions, the player moves a piece (bishop or queen) to a queenside square (b2, b5, c4, c7) seeking material gain or positional pressure, but in doing so removes that piece from a vital defensive role. In Position 3 (Bb2), the bishop abandons f6 kingside defense for an a3 pawn grab, allowing g4 to expose the king (1/4). In Position 4 (Qb5), the queen chases queenside targets while the f3 knight is critically attacked by Bg4, leaving it hanging (2/4). In Position 11 (Bc4), the bishop leaves f1 to attack Black's queen, abandoning the guard of g2 which falls immediately to Qxg2 winning the rook (3/4). In Position 13 (Qc7), the queen shifts one square from c6 to c7, removing the Qxc3 counter-threat that was the tactical justification for the entire e4 knight outpost (4/4). All four share the pattern of prioritizing peripheral/speculative gains over maintaining a piece's hidden but essential defensive contribution.
analysis.move_pattern: Queen or bishop moving to b-file or c-file (ranks 2-7), generally lateral or retreating, non-capturing
analysis.why_bad: The moved piece was a 'removed defender'—it was guarding a key square, piece, or providing a tactical counter-threat that made the opponent's combinations unplayable. Once relocated to the queenside, the opponent immediately exploits the newly undefended target.
sub_patterns: Bishop leaves kingside for queenside pawn grab
Queen moves to b/c file abandoning tactical counter-threat
Developing move that vacates a critical guard square

analysis.label: Giving a check (or pseudo-forcing move) that allows the opponent to improve their position with the forced response, when a more precise move would maintain or increase pressure.
analysis.description: This feature fires on moves—overwhelmingly checks—that appear aggressive but actually grant the opponent a constructive tempo. In 4/5 positions the move is a check, and in 4/5 cases the opponent's best reply simultaneously addresses the threat AND improves their position (interposing a piece to a stronger square or walking the king toward safety). Position 1: Qf6+ allows Nf3 blocking the check while saving the hanging knight. Position 2: Qf6+ allows Nd6 interposing while transforming a passive knight into a powerfully centralized defender. Position 4: Bc2 wastes a tempo on bishop repositioning, letting White's king seize the critical d4 square. Position 6: Qe6+ lets the king escape to h2 when Qh1# was mate-in-one. Position 14: Rd8+ pushes White's king along the escape route e3→f2→g1 to total safety. In all 5/5 cases, only one good move existed (avg good moves = 1.0), and the correct alternative either delivered check on a line the opponent couldn't exploit (Position 1: Qh4+ on a diagonal Nf3 can't block), won material with precision (Position 2: Qc8+ forcing the king without helping the knight), or prioritized positional urgency over piece activation (Position 4: Kc5 before Bc2).
analysis.move_pattern: Queen or rook check (4/5) along a file or diagonal where the opponent can interpose a piece to a stronger square or step the king toward safety; one case is a bishop move that similarly gifts the opponent a critical tempo
analysis.why_bad: The check/forcing move allows the opponent to solve two problems with one response: they address the immediate threat (block or sidestep) while simultaneously improving their position (centralizing a piece, activating a knight, or walking the king to safety). The correct alternative delivers threats on lines where no constructive interposition/escape exists.
sub_patterns: Check allows piece interposition that saves/activates the blocking piece
Check drives opponent king along an escape route toward safety
Missed immediate checkmate in favor of a non-mating check
Quiet piece move wastes tempo when king centralization was urgent

analysis.label: Moving a piece or pawn away from a vital defensive role, allowing the opponent to exploit the vacated square or unguarded piece with forcing moves.
analysis.description: In all 7 positions, the player moves a piece/pawn away from a square or function that was performing a critical (often non-obvious) defensive task. In 5/7 cases, the abandonment directly enables the opponent to deliver check or win material through newly accessible squares (Rfb1 clears the back rank for Rxb1+; Rh2 vacates g1 for Qg1+; Qe1 removes queen coverage enabling Ne7+ fork; d3 leaves Be2 hanging with check; Qf6 exposes e3 to a devastating queen check). In 6/7 cases, the move appears purposeful - attacking something, controlling a file, or pursuing an 'active' plan - but ignores the tactical emergency. The positions average only 1.7 good moves, indicating critical moments requiring precise defense rather than exploration. In 5/7 cases, the opponent's refutation involves an immediate check or capture that gains decisive tempo.
analysis.move_pattern: Various piece types (Q, R, N, pawn) moving away from a square that was covering a back rank, blocking a check diagonal, defending a hanging piece, or maintaining coordination - no single geometric direction but always a departure from a defensive station
analysis.why_bad: The moved piece was performing a hidden defensive function (guarding a check square, covering a back rank, defending a hanging piece, or maintaining coordination). Its departure allows the opponent to deliver forcing moves (checks, captures, forks) that gain decisive material or tempo, typically exploiting the exact square/file/diagonal the piece just vacated.
sub_patterns: Rook leaves back rank allowing queen infiltration with check
Queen leaves active central post allowing knight fork or check
Knight abandons key defensive square allowing tactical exploitation of coordination gaps
Pawn move blocks the correct piece move that would address the hanging/vulnerable piece
Kingside pawn advance weakens shelter without addressing central tactical demands

analysis.label: Black moves a piece/pawn from an invisible defensive post to a seemingly active square, allowing White to exploit the vacated defensive function.
analysis.description: In all 3/3 positions, Black plays a forward/centralizing move that looks natural and improving but fatally removes a piece from a critical defensive role it was performing invisibly. In Position 2, c5 advances the pawn from c7, removing its ability to recapture on d6 after Nd6+/exd6, allowing White a devastating passed pawn. In Position 5, Rd7 moves the rook forward from d8, abandoning back-rank coverage and allowing Qe8+ leading to forced mate in 3. In Position 6, Be5 pulls the fianchettoed bishop from g7 to a central square where it blocks its own e4 pawn and becomes a tactical target after c4, dissolving Black's entire pawn center. In each case (3/3), the moved piece appeared passive on its original square but was fulfilling an essential prophylactic function, and the 'active' destination proves to be tactically exploitable.
analysis.move_pattern: Black piece/pawn moves forward or toward center from a defensive square (c7→c5, d8→d7, g7→e5), leaving a critical square or function unguarded
analysis.why_bad: The piece was performing an invisible defensive duty (guarding a square, maintaining recapture rights, or supporting pawn structure) that only becomes apparent once removed, allowing White a concrete tactical exploitation of the vacated function
sub_patterns: Pawn advance removing recapture/defensive coverage of invasion square
Rook leaving back rank allowing queen penetration with check
Bishop leaving fianchetto blocking own pawns and becoming tactical target

analysis.label: Capturing material or moving a key piece away from the mating zone when a short forced checkmate (mate in 1-3) was available.
analysis.description: In all 5/5 positions, a forced checkmate in 1-8 moves was available, yet the player chose to capture material or reposition away from the mating attack. In 4/5 cases (Qxf5, Qxb1, Kxd6, Rxe1+), the move is a capture that wins substantial material (a rook or piece) but removes the attacking force from the critical mating zone. In 1/5 cases (Qd3), the queen is moved off the file where the mating combination existed. The common mechanism is that a tempting material gain or seemingly strong move draws the player's attention away from the mating pattern, which typically involves a queen or rook delivering check on the opponent's vulnerable back rank or exposed king position. The average cp_loss of 5471 reflects that most positions went from forced mate to merely a large advantage.
analysis.move_pattern: Key attacking piece (usually queen or rook) captures material or moves away from the opponent's king, abandoning the square/file/diagonal needed for the mating combination
analysis.why_bad: The move removes the very piece that enables the forced checkmate from its critical attacking position—either by capturing on an irrelevant square, trading itself off, or repositioning to a non-mating diagonal/file—giving the opponent time to escape the mating net.
sub_patterns: Queen captures distant piece instead of delivering mate (Qxf5, Qxb1)
King captures material instead of using another piece to mate (Kxd6)
Trading the rook that supports the queen's mating square (Rxe1+)
Queen moves off the critical file/diagonal where mate exists (Qd3)

analysis.label: Non-urgent moves that squander a critical tempo while the position demands immediate attention to king safety, a tactical threat, or a key positional obligation.
analysis.description: This feature fires on moves that appear reasonable in isolation (developing a piece, advancing a pawn, making a capture) but fatally ignore the position's most urgent demand. In 7/10 positions, king safety was the primary concern being neglected—either the player's own king was exposed and needed castling (Na6, Bd2, f4 all delayed castling; O-O-O castled into the attack), or defensive measures against an imminent kingside storm were required (b5 ignored g5 one tempo away; b6 enabled a c-file opening against the king). In 2/10 cases, a specific defensive obligation was abandoned (Be3 left b2 hanging; Bxg6 removed a paralyzing piece). In 1/10 cases, a tactical vulnerability was left unaddressed (Be6 allowed Qxb7 winning a rook). The common thread is that all moves pursue secondary objectives—rim development, slow pawn advances, premature captures—while the opponent needs just one more tempo to execute a decisive threat. The average cp_loss of 275 reflects how one wasted tempo in a critical moment can swing the entire position.
analysis.move_pattern: Quiet, non-forcing moves (no checks; mostly non-captures) directed at a secondary objective while ignoring the board's critical sector—often a pawn push or piece development to a suboptimal square
analysis.why_bad: The position has an imminent one-tempo threat (pawn break opening a file against the king, tactical shot exploiting an undefended piece, or attack breakthrough) that the played move fails to prevent or address, giving the opponent the critical tempo needed to execute their plan
sub_patterns: Delaying castling for slow development (Na6, Bd2, f4)
Queenside pawn pushes ignoring kingside attack (b5, b6)
Castling into the wrong side where opponent has pawn levers (O-O-O)
Removing a well-placed piece or abandoning a defensive duty (Bxg6, Be3)
Development that ignores hanging material (Be6)

analysis.label: Non-forcing 'improving' moves played in positions demanding immediate concrete action, allowing the opponent a decisive tactical opportunity.
analysis.description: This feature fires on moves that appear natural or positionally motivated (repositioning pieces, pushing flank pawns, developing quietly) but critically ignore the position's immediate tactical demands. In 6/8 positions, the player had a significant advantage or near-equality that was squandered by choosing a slow move. The correct alternatives consistently involved more concrete, forcing actions: capturing key pieces (Bxc4 in Position 12, hxg4 in Position 6), placing pieces on tactically critical squares (Rab8 in Position 1, Rc7 in Position 8), or developing with immediate threats (Bb5 with pin in Position 10, Nh6 attacking g4 in Position 4). The blunders instead chose quiet repositioning (Bf6, Qa5, Nd7), premature pawn advances (d7, f5, a5), or slow preparatory moves (c3, Qd3) that either placed pieces on vulnerable squares, vacated critical defensive squares, or simply wasted tempo while the opponent gained a tactical resource. The average cp_loss of 318 with only 2.1 good moves available confirms these are sharp positions with narrow correct paths that punish non-forcing play severely.
analysis.move_pattern: Diverse piece types and directions; unifying pattern is non-capturing, non-checking, non-forcing moves (repositioning, advancing, developing without threats) in tactically critical positions
analysis.why_bad: Each move either places a piece/pawn on a square where it becomes tactically vulnerable (Nd7 hangs to Bxd7, Qd3 allows Nb4/Nc2+ fork, d7 allows capture/liquidation), vacates control of a critical square (Qa5 abandons c5 control, Bf6 fails to put rook on b8), or wastes tempo on non-urgent business (c3 blocks Nc3, a5/f5 push pawns when development is critical), allowing the opponent one clear tactical shot.
sub_patterns: Piece repositioning that vacates critical defensive control
Premature pawn advances allowing captures or counterstrikes
Quiet development moves placing pieces on tactically vulnerable squares
Preparatory moves blocking own piece coordination

analysis.label: Playing a reasonable-looking move that addresses a secondary concern while ignoring the position's most critical and urgent demand.
analysis.description: In all 4/4 positions, the player chose a move that appeared logical in isolation—doubling rooks on a file (Rdf8), challenging the center (c4), capturing material (Bxf5), or blockading a passed pawn (Ra1)—but each ignored the single most important demand of the position. In Position 4, Black played a slow preparatory rook move when three immediate tactical strikes exploited White's uncastled king. In Position 5, White pushed a strategic pawn that blocked a critical defensive escape square (c2 for the queen), enabling a fork tactic. In Position 7, Black grabbed a pawn while leaving White's monstrous invading bishop on f8 alive, the one piece demanding immediate removal. In Position 11, White used its most powerful mobile piece (the rook) as a passive blockader when a bishop could perform that duty, surrendering all active pressure. The common thread: each move addresses something plausible but secondary while the position's primary requirement—exploiting king vulnerability, neutralizing a dominant piece, or maintaining piece coordination—goes unmet, granting the opponent a critical tempo to consolidate or counterattack.
analysis.move_pattern: Diverse piece types (rook, pawn, bishop) moving to address peripheral concerns; no single geometric direction but typically moves toward non-critical sectors or targets
analysis.why_bad: The position has one overwhelmingly important demand (tactical exploitation, threat neutralization, or piece coordination), but the move spends a tempo on a secondary objective, giving the opponent time to resolve their critical weakness or launch a counterattack that exploits the misallocation of resources.
sub_patterns: Slow preparatory moves when concrete tactics demand immediate action
Material grabs that ignore a more dangerous positional/tactical threat
Passive defensive moves when active solutions address both attack and defense
Strategic pawn pushes that inadvertently create tactical vulnerabilities

analysis.label: Playing a non-urgent move (material grab, passive repositioning, or structural play) when the position demands immediate attention to a critical tactical threat or opportunity.
analysis.description: This feature fires on positions where the player makes a move that pursues a secondary objective while completely ignoring the single most urgent element of the position. In 3/6 cases, the player ignores an immediate mating threat or allows a devastating attack on their king (Bf1 allows Re8#, Qxb2 leaves the f8-king totally undefended, Nb6 fails to prevent promotion leading to forced mate). In 2/6 cases, the player misses a powerful tactical opportunity in favor of a slow move (d6 misses the Ne3 fork, Ng6 abandons an active knight post allowing Rxf7). In 1/6 cases, the aggressive move backfires by trapping their own piece (h6 entombs the bishop). The common thread is that all positions had very few good moves (avg 1.8) and demanded a specific, urgent response, but the player chose something that 'looks reasonable' on the surface while catastrophically missing the point of the position.
analysis.move_pattern: Piece moves toward a secondary target or passive square, directed away from the critical tactical zone (usually away from own king's defensive needs or away from the opponent's key vulnerability)
analysis.why_bad: These moves fail because they address non-urgent concerns (grabbing a pawn, repositioning a piece, making a structural move) in positions where a single immediate threat dominates everything else - either a mate threat requiring prophylaxis, a promotion that must be correctly handled, or a concrete tactic that must be executed NOW before it disappears.
sub_patterns: Queen/piece moves away from own king, allowing devastating attack on undefended monarch
Slow positional/structural move missing a concrete forcing sequence (fork, capture with check)
Piece repositioning that abandons active post, surrendering critical tempo
Attempted defensive move that miscalculates piece geometry and fails at its purpose

analysis.label: Playing a quiet, non-forcing positional move when the position demands immediate concrete action to protect or exploit a tactical vulnerability.
analysis.description: This feature activates on moves that are quiet, natural-looking developments, repositionings, or pawn pushes played in positions that urgently require concrete action. In 5/7 analyzed positions, the moved piece or another piece is left tactically vulnerable, allowing the opponent to win material (Bc3 allows Nxe4/Nxc3 winning a piece, Qe2 leaves Ng3 capturable by Rxg3, a4 leaves Be4 undefended to ...f5, Nf6 leaves Bd3 hanging to Re3, Kc3 enables a check+pin winning material). In the remaining cases, the tempo waste allows the opponent to execute a critical pawn break (Bd2 permits ...c4 activating all Black's pieces) or self-blocks a winning plan (c3 blocks the a-pawn advance). The best moves in these positions consistently involve either immediate piece activation toward concrete threats (Ng3→knight maneuver in 2/7, queen-to-kingside in 1/7), addressing a critical pawn break (b3 in 1/7), or simply moving to a safe square (Ka3/Ka1 in 1/7). Average cp_loss of 1516 (inflated by one forced mate) reflects positions where one quiet tempo is the difference between winning and losing.
analysis.move_pattern: Non-forcing quiet moves (piece repositioning, development, pawn pushes) - no checks, no captures, no immediate threats created
analysis.why_bad: The position contains an immediate tactical demand (a hanging piece, a critical timing issue, or a concrete threat requiring attention) that the quiet move completely ignores, giving the opponent a free tempo to exploit the vulnerability and win material or achieve a decisive positional transformation.
sub_patterns: Piece repositioning that leaves another piece undefended (Bc3, Qe2, a4, Nf6)
Slow development that blocks own king's escape or walks into tactical motifs (Nd7, Kc3)
Passive pawn move that self-blocks winning plan or allows opponent's pawn break (c3, Bd2)

analysis.label: Piece (usually queen) moves to a plausible-looking aggressive square that's near but critically different from the optimal one, losing a key tactical resource.
analysis.description: In 5/7 positions the blunder is a queen move to an aggressive square adjacent to or on the same file/rank as the correct one (Qg5 vs Qh5, Qxh3+ vs Qh1+, Qh6+ vs Qh8+, Qa3+ vs Qa1+, Qf5 vs development). In 6/7 cases, the chosen square fails because it loses control of a critical escape square, allows an interposition, or can be attacked with tempo. The 'tempo_loss' tag appears in 6/7 analyses and 'missed_tactic' in 5/7. The moves all appear natural and forcing but miss a precise geometric requirement: Qh3+ doesn't control g1 (unlike Qh1+), Qh6+ allows Qg7 interposition (unlike Qh8+), Qa3+ loses the d4 diagonal (unlike Qa1+), Qg5 abandons the 6th-rank Qd6+ resource (unlike Qh5), and Nd4 creates only one threat (unlike Nb4's dual threats). Each position had 1-3 good alternatives available.
analysis.move_pattern: Queen (or knight) moves to an aggressive/checking square on the same file or nearby rank as the correct destination, typically one or two squares away from optimal
analysis.why_bad: The subtly wrong square choice eliminates a critical geometric property - control of an enemy king's escape square, prevention of an interposition, maintenance of a defensive x-ray, or creation of dual threats - converting winning attacks into equal or losing positions
sub_patterns: Queen check on wrong square of same file (h3 vs h1, h6 vs h8, a3 vs a1)
Queen to wrong aggressive square abandoning hidden defensive duty (Qg5 losing Qd6+ resource)
Premature queen sortie to attackable square instead of development (Qf5 hit by ...e6)
Knight to center creating single threat instead of dual-threat square (Nd4 vs Nb4)

analysis.label: Advancing a passed pawn prematurely in the endgame before coordinating pieces to support it, allowing the opponent to blockade or generate counterplay.
analysis.description: In 9/10 positions, the player advances a passed pawn (or creates a premature pawn commitment) without first establishing proper piece coordination. The correct moves consistently involve preparatory steps: placing a rook behind the passer (positions 5, 11 with Rf1/Ra1), centralizing the king (positions 9, 12 with Kd5/Kf3), creating pawn support structures (position 3 with c4 before b6), or prophylactic restraint of counterplay (position 1 with h4). In every case, the premature pawn push allows the opponent to either blockade the pawn (positions 5, 12 with ...Rf4/...Re4), capture it with tempo (positions 3, 14 with ...Rxb6+/...Qxc5), or remove the target and generate counterplay (position 9 with ...c4). The average cp_loss of 198 reflects that these positions typically had only 1-2 good moves available, making the preparation-before-advance principle critical. The endgame phase (9/10) is characteristic because passed pawn conversion requires precise coordination rather than raw speed.
