analysis.move_pattern: Pawn advance forward (one square) on any file, typically pushing a passed or advanced pawn in the endgame without prior piece preparation
analysis.why_bad: The pawn advance commits to an irreversible structural decision before pieces are optimally coordinated to support it, allowing the opponent to blockade, capture with tempo, or generate sufficient counterplay to neutralize the advantage.
sub_patterns: Pushing pawn without rook behind it (f6, a6 - should be Rf1/Ra1 first)
Pushing pawn without king penetration (h5, e5 - should be Kd5/Kf3 first)
Pushing pawn without creating connected support (b6 - should be c4 first)
Pushing pawn leaving it tactically vulnerable (c5 in queen endgame - drops to check+capture)
Pushing pawn instead of prophylaxis against counterplay (b5 - should be h4 first)

analysis.label: Aggressive captures, sacrifices, or forward-lunging moves that lack the necessary piece support to justify the commitment.
analysis.description: This feature fires on moves that attempt to force aggression—especially unsound piece sacrifices—without adequate positional prerequisites. The clearest sub-pattern is the unsound Nxf7 knight sacrifice (3/7 positions), where a knight captures on f7 attempting a Fried Liver-style king exposure but with zero supporting pieces developed to sustain the attack. The remaining positions share the same underlying error: Bxe5 captures aggressively with the wrong piece leaving it tactically exposed (1/7), Bd6 develops forward but ignores immediate tactical threats requiring resolution (1/7), R6d5+ gives a check that merely helps the opponent's king centralize (1/7), and Ka5 moves the king to a more exposed square vulnerable on two axes (1/7). In all cases, the move looks purposeful or aggressive to the player but ignores the concrete tactical reality that the position cannot support the forward commitment.
analysis.move_pattern: Piece moves forward/toward opponent, typically a capture or check; most commonly knight captures on f7, but also bishop captures on central squares, rook checks, or king advances toward exposed positions
analysis.why_bad: The position lacks sufficient supporting piece coordination to justify the aggressive commitment—the player's other pieces are undeveloped, misplaced, or unable to follow up, allowing the opponent to simply collect the offered material or exploit the resulting tactical weakness with no compensation.
sub_patterns: Unsound Nxf7 sacrifice without developed supporting pieces
Pointless check that improves opponent's king position
Capturing with the wrong piece leaving tactical vulnerabilities
Slow forward development ignoring immediate tactical threats

analysis.label: Black makes a queenside-oriented move involving the b4-b6 squares while ignoring a critical kingside tactical vulnerability.
analysis.description: In all 3/3 positions, Black plays a move focused on the b4 or b6 square on the queenside (a5 attacking a bishop on b4, Nxb4 capturing a pawn, Bb6 retreating a bishop) while a far more urgent kingside threat demands attention. In each case, the move either removes a critical defensive piece from its post (2/3: the knight from d5 blocking the e-file, the bishop from f2 disrupting White's coordination) or wastes a tempo on an irrelevant queenside attack (1/3: a5 vs. the g7 promotion threat). The opponent's refutation in all cases is a forcing kingside sequence involving checks or captures (Ne4+ fork, Nxb6/Bxh7+ Greek gift, Be7 supporting promotion). Average cp_loss of 337 reflects positions where Black had a significant advantage (-204 to -356) that was squandered by one misguided queenside tempo.
analysis.move_pattern: Black piece or pawn moves to/captures on b4 or b6 squares on the queenside
analysis.why_bad: These moves abandon critical defensive responsibilities or active piece placements for low-priority queenside material/activity, giving the opponent a free tempo to execute a devastating kingside tactical combination.
sub_patterns: Pawn advance attacking piece on b4
Knight capture on b4 removing key defender
Bishop retreat to passive b6 square from active post

analysis.label: A piece moves to the 7th rank (or back rank for White) creating self-obstruction or removing defensive coordination that fatally exposes the king.
analysis.description: In 4/5 positions, Black places a piece on the 7th rank (Bc7, Bb7, Rb7, Ne7), while the White example (Kh1) places the king on the equivalent back rank. The common failure mode is that these moves either block the king's escape squares (Bc7 in position 1 blocks c7 flight square allowing back-rank mate, Ne7 in position 5 blocks the bishop's retreat enabling a fork), trap the king against the edge (Kh1 in position 4 allows Rf1+ mating net), or remove defensive piece coordination from the king's vicinity (Rb7 in position 13 strands the rook away from interposition duty, Bb7 in position 5 ignores the uncastled king). In 3/5 cases the tactical motif is explicitly back-rank related, and in 4/5 cases the tag 'king_safety' appears. These moves all appear natural or developing but catastrophically undermine the player's own king position through self-obstruction or abandonment.
analysis.move_pattern: Piece (bishop, rook, knight, or king) moves to the 7th rank for Black or 1st rank for White, typically to the b/c/e columns, often appearing as a retreat or quiet development move
analysis.why_bad: The piece placement creates self-obstruction that blocks the king's escape routes or removes a critical defensive resource from the king's vicinity, allowing forced mating attacks, back-rank exploitation, or decisive tactical blows (forks/pins) that exploit the king's newly created vulnerability
sub_patterns: Bishop to c7/b7 blocking king escape on queenside back rank
King retreating to corner where own pawns seal escape
Knight to e7 blocking bishop retreat enabling fork
Rook to b7 abandoning interposition duties near king

analysis.label: Major piece repositioned to a seemingly useful square while abandoning the critical sector where forcing tactical continuations exist.
analysis.description: This feature fires on positions where a rook (5/6) or queen (1/6) is moved to an apparently purposeful square—targeting a pawn, occupying an open file, or centralizing—but actually relocates away from where the decisive action lies. In 5/6 cases, a concrete forcing tactical sequence was missed (Ne1+ forced mate, Rg7+ winning transition, Bd5 exploiting a battery, Re7 dominating the 7th rank, Ke2 consolidation). The played moves look natural (Rd8 'activates' on d-file, Qa8 'targets' a-pawn, Rd1 'pressures' d6, Ra6 'attacks' the knight, Re1 'controls' e-file, Rd7 'centralizes') but each abandons coordination with the actual winning mechanism. In all 6 positions, the opponent gained tempo to reorganize—via counterattacking checks (2/6), pawn breaks (2/6), or piece activation (2/6). Average cp_loss of 1796 reflects several positions where forced mates or winning transitions were squandered.
analysis.move_pattern: Rook or queen moving along file or rank to an open line or target square, typically 1-4 squares, non-capturing, non-checking
analysis.why_bad: The piece leaves the sector where it coordinates with tactical threats (mating nets, forcing checks, critical file pressure), giving the opponent a crucial tempo to neutralize the position's winning features or generate counterplay
sub_patterns: Rook retreats from deep penetration to passive back-rank square
Major piece decentralizes to corner/edge chasing minor targets
Rook switches to wrong file, abandoning coordination with bishop or passed pawn
Rook moves laterally when a forcing check along the same file wins

analysis.label: Making a plausible-looking preparatory or 'improving' move that fatally ignores the position's most urgent tactical demands.
analysis.description: All 5/5 positions share a common error pattern: the player makes a move with a superficially logical purpose (giving a check, attacking a bishop, developing a piece, improving the worst piece, preparing a fianchetto) while ignoring what the position actually demands. In 5/5 cases, the chosen move wastes critical tempo - tagged as 'tempo_loss' in every analysis. The positions typically feature unresolved tactical tension (open files with enemy king exposed 2/5, uncastled king needing immediate shelter 3/5, enemy passed pawns requiring blockade 1/5). The best moves in all cases involve direct, concrete action: captures (Rxe1, Nxe4), central challenges (d4, c4, f6), or forcing moves (Qf2+). Instead, the player makes a 'planning' move that either abandons a critical defensive duty (Nh4 leaving e4 unguarded, Bd7 leaving b7 undefended, b6+ removing the mating-net pawn), walks into a tactic (Nc7 allowing b5!), or simply does nothing urgent (b3 while the king sits on e1).
analysis.move_pattern: Non-forcing, non-capturing piece relocations or pawn pushes away from the critical sector of the board; varied piece types but all directed toward secondary objectives rather than the main battlefield
analysis.why_bad: These moves waste a critical tempo in positions where the opponent can immediately exploit the delay - either by seizing a tactical opportunity that didn't exist before (Ng4, b5!, Qb3), by gaining an escape route that was previously blocked (Kxc6-c7), or by establishing permanent positional dominance (Ne4 occupying the abandoned outpost). The position demanded immediate concrete action but received a slow preparatory move instead.
sub_patterns: Impulsive check that dismantles own attacking structure (b6+)
Peripheral knight excursion abandoning central guard duty (Nh4)
Slow bishop development creating undefended pawn targets (Bd7)
Piece relocation walking into a tactical refutation (Nc7 into b5!)
Preparatory pawn move with king uncastled in a sharp position (b3)

analysis.label: Moves in overwhelmingly won endgames (~+7-8 pawns) where the winning side plays quiet positional advances rather than seeking the most incisive continuation.
analysis.description: This feature activates on positions where one side holds a massive endgame advantage (evaluations ranging from ±650 to ±850 cp) with both kings exposed and weak pawn shields. In 5/5 positions, the game is in a late endgame with exposed kings. In 4/5 cases the moves are essentially optimal (0 cp loss), representing routine conversion moves like king marches (Kc5, Ka4), piece centralization (Nc4), or pawn structure fixes (g4). The one actual blunder (f4, 568 cp loss) reveals the danger: playing a slow positional pawn push when an immediate tactical win (check + capture of hanging piece) was available. The feature appears to detect the position type - heavily won endgames requiring conversion - where the risk is autopiloting with quiet improvements when sharper solutions may exist.
analysis.move_pattern: Forward-advancing moves (king marches, pawn pushes, piece centralization) in won endgames with both kings exposed; non-forcing, non-checking moves
analysis.why_bad: When these moves ARE mistakes, it's because a slow positional advance wastes a critical tempo, allowing the opponent to rescue hanging pieces or reposition defensively - the winning side plays strategically when an immediate tactical blow (typically a check or capture) would have been decisive
sub_patterns: King march toward passed pawn (Ka4, Kc5)
Pawn push to fix structure (g4, f4)
Knight centralization to pressure weak pawns (Nc4)

analysis.label: Pieces moved to seemingly purposeful squares while catastrophically ignoring the position's most urgent tactical vulnerability.
analysis.description: This feature fires on moves where the player makes a natural-looking, strategically motivated piece move—development, centralization, a capture, or repositioning—while completely missing an immediate tactical crisis. In 7/10 positions, the blunder directly compromises king safety (Qd2 ignores Nf3+ sacrifice, Nc6 ignores Ng5/Bxh7+, Ne5 removes the f6 defender, Qxb3 abandons kingside for a pawn, Be7/Rb8 ignore exposed king emergencies). In 3/10 positions, the move places or leaves a piece undefended (Nd5 hangs to Rxb8+Bxd5, Bg5 leaves itself and central pawns tactically loose, Ba4 allows Nxd4 winning it). The common thread is a disconnect between strategic intent (improving piece placement) and tactical reality (opponent has a concrete, devastating response). The average cp_loss of 1133 reflects moves that look reasonable on the surface but walk into one-move tactical refutations, typically with 2-3 safer alternatives clearly available.
analysis.move_pattern: Any piece type moving to an apparently active/purposeful square; no consistent direction or piece type, but typically non-forcing moves (not checks/captures) that ignore opponent's forcing reply
analysis.why_bad: The moves prioritize positional improvement or piece activity while failing to recognize the opponent's immediate tactical opportunity—whether a forcing combination exploiting king exposure, a simple capture of the now-undefended piece, or punishment of a removed critical defender.
sub_patterns: Piece moves away from critical defensive duty, enabling king attack (Ne5, Qd2, Qxb3, Nc6)
Piece placed on undefended square where it can be won tactically (Nd5, Ba4, Bg5)
Move blocks escape route or wastes tempo with king exposed (Be7, Rb8)
Rook repositions releasing pressure on key pawn/square (Rb2)

analysis.label: Playing a natural-looking 'improving' move that ignores the position's concrete tactical demand—typically a winning capture, forced sequence, or critical defensive necessity.
analysis.description: These moves share a common error pattern: the player makes an active, purposeful-looking move (centralizing a queen, advancing a king, developing a piece, pushing a pawn for space) while ignoring a specific concrete tactical requirement. In 5/8 positions, the best move was a capture or forcing move that the player bypassed: Qxh2+ sacrifice for mate (Position 1), Nxh4 removing a dangerous piece before advancing (Position 3), dxc3 winning a knight for free (Position 8), O-O securing king safety before tactics (Position 7). In the remaining cases, the played move creates a tactical vulnerability by abandoning a defensive duty: g4 removes the g-pawn defending f3 (Position 3), Kg5 walks away from controlling the f-file (Position 4), Qc5 overloads the queen leaving the rook undefended (Position 15), exd5 opens the e-file against the player's own uncastled king (Position 2). The average cp_loss of 1584 reflects how catastrophically expensive these 'reasonable-looking' moves are when the position demanded precision. The low average of 2.1 good moves confirms these are sharp positions where only specific solutions work.
analysis.move_pattern: Non-forcing piece/pawn moves to apparently active squares (queen centralization, king advance, bishop development, pawn pushes for space) when a capture, forcing sequence, or prophylactic move was required
analysis.why_bad: These moves prioritize general positional improvement or piece activity while missing that the position has a concrete tactical demand—either a winning capture/forcing line is available, or moving the piece/pawn removes a critical defender or creates a vulnerability that the opponent can immediately exploit for material or a decisive attack.
sub_patterns: Missing a winning capture or queen sacrifice (Qg6 instead of Qxh2+, Bc5 instead of dxc3)
Advancing when the position requires removing an opponent's piece first (g4 instead of Nxh4, Ne4 instead of O-O)
Moving a piece to an 'active' square that overloads or disconnects it from defensive duties (Qc5 leaving rook undefended)
King advancement into tactical vulnerability when holding position was correct (Kg5 allowing Rf1 cutoff)
Premature pawn exchanges that open lines against the player's own king (exd5 opening e-file)

analysis.label: Moves that prioritize material gain, centralization, or repositioning over the urgent need to address critical king safety when the player's king is exposed.
analysis.description: This feature fires on moves where the player ignores a critical king safety problem—either their own exposed king or their defensive obligations—in favor of material gain, piece repositioning, or seemingly natural moves. In 8/8 positions, the player's king is significantly exposed or vulnerable at the moment of the blunder. The mistakes take various forms: walking the king into danger (Kg6 into open territory, Kd3 onto an open file leading to immediate mate), removing defensive pieces for material (Nxd4 taking the f3-knight that guards the king, fxg2 capturing a pawn instead of castling), abandoning defensive posts (Rd3 leaving the f-file unguarded, Qf2 vacating the queen from critical defensive coordination), or retreating attacking pieces that provided indirect king safety through pressure (Qg3 retreating from a dominant g8 post). In all cases, the refutations exploit the king directly—through queen infiltration (5/8), back-rank or open-file mates (3/8), or piece coordination against the exposed monarch (7/8). The average cp_loss of 1428 reflects the catastrophic nature of ignoring king safety at critical moments.
analysis.move_pattern: Various piece types moving away from king defense or toward exposed squares; no single geometric direction but moves consistently reduce king protection or increase king exposure
analysis.why_bad: These moves fail because they ignore the position's most urgent demand—king safety—allowing the opponent to exploit open files, diagonals, or weak squares around the king with devastating tactical blows (checks, infiltrations, mates) that the abandoned defensive pieces could have prevented.
sub_patterns: King voluntarily walking into open files or exposed squares (Kg6, Kd3)
Removing a key defensive piece for material gain (Nxd4, fxg2)
Queen retreating from active/defensive post abandoning critical squares (Qf2, Qg3)
Piece repositioning that opens lines to own king (Rd3 vacating f-file)

analysis.label: Moves that voluntarily place a key piece (especially king or queen) on a square where it immediately becomes exploitable through checks, forks, or discovered attacks along newly-activated lines.
analysis.description: This feature fires on moves that create self-inflicted tactical vulnerability by placing pieces on geometrically exploitable squares. In 4/9 cases, kings step onto open files or into discovered check patterns (Kd8 onto the open d-file/g5-d8 diagonal, Ke2 onto the open e-file, Kc6 into a discovered check on the c-file, Kxb4 moving away from the critical sector). In 2/9 cases, queens are placed on squares that create fork targets or tempo-gaining pawn attacks (Qf3 where Nd4 forks queen+bishop, Qe7 where dxe5/exd6 hits the queen). In 2/9 cases, moves open critical lines to the king (cxd5 removes the c6 pawn guarding the a4-e8 diagonal, Be2 fails to prevent Ne4-Nxf2+ fork against the king on d1). The remaining case (g5) is a non-forcing move that grants the opponent a free tempo for a king march. All share the core thread: the played move looks natural or routine but creates or fails to prevent an immediate forcing sequence that the opponent exploits with tempo-gaining threats.
analysis.move_pattern: King/queen/piece moves to a square aligned with enemy attacking pieces along open files, diagonals, or fork patterns; or pawn moves that open such lines to the player's own king
analysis.why_bad: The moves create geometric alignments (open file checks, diagonal checks, discovered checks, knight forks, tempo-gaining pawn attacks) that the opponent immediately exploits with forcing sequences, gaining material or mating attacks before the intended benefits of the move can be realized
sub_patterns: King stepping onto open file allowing rook/queen checks (Kd8, Ke2, Kc6)
Pawn capture/move opening critical line to own uncastled king (cxd5, Qe7 enabling dxe5)
Piece placement creating fork geometry with another friendly piece (Qf3 forkable with Bb5)
King moving away from critical pawn race sector (Kxb4)
Development move ignoring imminent tactical threat on exposed king (Be2)

analysis.label: Playing an alternative move (usually a check or wrong capture) instead of simply taking an undefended enemy piece in the endgame.
analysis.description: This feature fires on endgame positions where an enemy piece is clearly hanging (undefended and capturable) but the player chooses a different move instead. In 8/10 positions, the best move was a simple capture of an unprotected piece (usually a rook, sometimes a bishop), but the player was distracted by other options. In 5/10 cases, the player gave a check instead of taking the free piece (Ra1+, Ra2+, Rc2+, f4+, Rg3+), embodying the 'patzer sees a check, patzer gives a check' syndrome. In other cases, players targeted the wrong piece (Rg8 targeting a pawn instead of the rook), moved without purpose (Ke2, Be3), or captured with the wrong piece (Rxb2 instead of Kxb3). The positions share structural similarities: rook endgames with passed pawns near promotion, mutual threats on ranks/files, and exposed kings. The critical error is consistently a failure to prioritize the immediate concrete capture over seemingly active or forcing alternatives.
analysis.move_pattern: Diverse moves (checks, quiet moves, wrong captures) that all share the property of NOT being the available capture of a hanging enemy piece
analysis.why_bad: The alternative move gives the opponent time to save the hanging piece (retreat it, exchange it, or promote a pawn), converting a winning material advantage into a draw or even a loss. Checks drive the enemy king to squares that actually defend the hanging piece, quiet moves allow piece retreats, and wrong captures lead to simplification into drawn endgames.
sub_patterns: Unnecessary check that drives enemy king to defend the hanging piece
Targeting wrong material (pawn instead of rook)
Capturing with wrong piece allowing forced trade into drawn endgame
Quiet developing move ignoring free capture

analysis.label: King moves that squander a critical tempo in endgame pawn races or time-sensitive positions where a pawn push or more direct king path was essential.
analysis.description: This feature fires on king moves that lose tempo in positions where every move counts, overwhelmingly in endgames (10/12 positions). The pattern manifests in three sub-types: (1) moving the king when an immediate pawn push was more urgent (positions 1, 2, 4, 5, 13 — e.g., Kb4 instead of pushing the a-pawn in a pawn race), (2) choosing a less efficient king path that requires an extra move to reach the ideal square (positions 7, 8 — e.g., Kg6 instead of Kh7, adding one extra move to reach g8), and (3) moving the king to a square where it becomes exposed to tempo-gaining checks or attacks (positions 6, 10, 12 — e.g., Kb3 allowing Rb6+ or Kg3 allowing Ra3+). In 9/12 positions, the analyses explicitly identify 'tempo_loss' as the primary tactical motif. The average cp_loss of 927 reflects that in pawn races, a single lost tempo is often decisive, converting draws into losses or advantages into equality.
analysis.move_pattern: King moves (single-square orthogonal/diagonal) in any direction, overwhelmingly in endgames, that fail to take the most direct path or defer to a more urgent pawn advance
analysis.why_bad: In pawn race endgames, every tempo is critical — these king moves waste a beat by either going to an intermediate square when a direct path exists, moving when a pawn push would advance the race faster, or stepping onto a rank/file where the opponent gains tempo with checks, ultimately allowing the opponent's passed pawn to promote first or neutralize the player's counterplay.
sub_patterns: King moves when an immediate pawn push was more time-critical
King takes indirect path (extra move) to its ideal destination square
King steps onto rank/file where it becomes vulnerable to tempo-gaining checks
King moves toward opponent's pawns instead of supporting own passed pawn

analysis.label: Playing a natural-looking but ineffective move in a sharp endgame where only one specific concrete action (usually a precise pawn advance) holds or wins the position.
analysis.description: This feature fires on endgame positions where very few good moves exist (avg 2.1) and the player makes a plausible-looking move that catastrophically fails to address the position's critical demand. In 5/8 positions, the correct move was a specific pawn advance (h5 fixing structure in Position 3, f2 forcing promotion in Position 10, f5 creating counterplay in Position 15, a5 forcing exchanges in Position 2, c5 generating counterplay in Position 4) but instead the player made a king move, wrong pawn push, or piece relocation. In 3/8 positions, the player advanced a pawn when king activation or piece safety was paramount (b3 instead of Ke4 in Position 6, Kf5 abandoning d5 in Position 5, Rf8+ hanging the rook in Position 12). The unifying thread is that positions with razor-thin margins (often only 1 truly good move) punish 'reasonable' moves with massive evaluation swings because a single concrete tactical resource is the entire foundation of the position's evaluation.
analysis.move_pattern: Various piece types and directions - no single geometric pattern; moves tend to be king advances, slow pawn pushes, or centralizing piece moves in open endgame positions with exposed kings
analysis.why_bad: The move fails to execute the one specific concrete action the position demands - typically a precise pawn advance that fixes structure, forces promotion, or creates counterplay. Instead, the player makes a 'natural' move (centralizing, advancing generally) that either leaves a critical pawn/piece undefended, allows the opponent to lock the structure favorably, or wastes the crucial tempo needed to hold or win.
sub_patterns: Missing a critical pawn-fixing advance (h5, f5) that neutralizes opponent's threats
Failing to push a passed pawn at the critical moment (f2 for promotion)
Wrong move order in pawn advances (b4 before a5, a5 when c5 needed)
King moving away from protective duty of a key pawn (Kf5 abandoning d5, Ke2 abandoning f4)
Passive pawn move creating weaknesses when king activation required (b3 instead of Ke4)

analysis.label: Quiet, non-forcing moves (especially h-pawn pushes and piece retreats) played in positions requiring the one precise active/forcing move to survive.
analysis.description: This feature fires on positions where the player makes a 'natural-looking' passive move—typically a prophylactic pawn push or a piece/king retreat—in a position that demands immediate tactical action with extremely narrow margins (average 1.3 good moves available). The most common manifestation is h3/h5 pawn pushes (4/9 positions), which are classic 'I don't know what to do' moves that waste a critical tempo. King retreats to seemingly safe squares that are actually dangerous appear in 3/9 positions (Kg1, Kd2, Kg7), and passive queen retreats (Qd1, Qe7) appear in 2/9 positions. In every case, the position required one specific forcing move—often a queen trade (Position 5), a central pawn advance (Position 1), a king centralization counter-intuitively forward (Position 9), or a check sequence (Position 8)—but the player instead chose the quiet prophylactic option. The catastrophic average cp_loss of 2444 reflects how these tempo losses are immediately exploitable by forcing continuations.
analysis.move_pattern: Non-forcing, non-capturing quiet moves: h-pawn advances (h3/h5), king retreats toward the corner or onto exposed files, queen retreats to passive squares
analysis.why_bad: These moves waste a critical tempo in positions with razor-thin margins, allowing the opponent to execute forcing tactical sequences (discovered attacks, file invasions, mating nets) that the one correct active move would have prevented or preempted.
sub_patterns: h3/h5 prophylactic pawn push ignoring urgent tactical needs (4/9)
King retreat to 'safe' square that actually increases vulnerability (Kg1, Kd2, Kg7 — 3/9)
Queen retreat surrendering initiative when checks or active play was required (Qd1, Qe7 — 2/9)

analysis.label: Moves that send a piece away from the critical zone of the position, abandoning essential defensive or positional duties.
analysis.description: This feature fires on moves where a piece travels in the wrong direction relative to the position's demands, wasting a critical tempo. In 6/7 positions, king safety is the primary concern being neglected. In 6/7 positions, the move constitutes a clear tempo loss in a time-sensitive situation. The pattern manifests as: kings marching toward the edge when centralization is needed (Kh4 away from center, Kf7 abandoning g6, Kb4 taking wrong geometric path), defensive pieces leaving critical posts (Be3 removing g-file guard, Rf5 abandoning first-rank defense), or playing on the wrong side of the board entirely (c4 pushing queenside while kingside collapses, Qd6 centralizing into a fork). In each case, the player's move appears purposeful on the surface but fundamentally addresses the wrong aspect of the position.
analysis.move_pattern: Any piece type moving away from the critical sector (usually king safety zone or optimal geometric path), typically toward the edge or wrong flank
analysis.why_bad: The move abandons a critical defensive or positional function, wasting an irreplaceable tempo in a position where the opponent has immediate threats or a time-sensitive plan, allowing tactical exploitation of the newly undefended squares/files/diagonals
sub_patterns: King moving toward board edge instead of centralizing
Defensive piece relocating away from its critical guard duty
Playing on the wrong side of the board while immediate threats exist on the other
Taking a geometrically suboptimal path in a tempo-critical race

analysis.label: Quiet moves that lose critical tempo against passed pawn threats by directing pieces away from the sector where the decisive pawn breakthrough will occur.
analysis.description: This feature fires on moves that fatally misdirect forces in positions where passed pawn timing is critical. In 4/5 positions, the tactical motif is 'passed_pawn' and the tag 'tempo_loss' appears in 4/5. The pattern manifests as: king walking away from the critical kingside pawn break (Position 3, Kc7 allowing f5); wrong rook abandoning a key file (Position 6, Rfb8 losing coordination); irrelevant pawn push ignoring an opponent's advanced passer (Position 7, f4 ignoring d2); king retreating passively instead of centralizing to prevent a pawn advance (Position 10, Ke7 instead of Kf5 to stop b5); and subtle king mis-routing in a pawn race (Position 14, Kg2 vs Kg1). All 5/5 moves are non-forcing (no checks, no captures) and all allow the opponent to execute a pawn advance that becomes unstoppable due to the wasted tempo.
analysis.move_pattern: Non-forcing piece/king moves (often retreats or lateral moves) directed away from the sector where a critical pawn break or passed pawn advance is imminent
analysis.why_bad: The moves waste a critical tempo in positions where the opponent's passed pawn (or potential passed pawn) requires immediate containment — by moving the wrong direction, the player allows the opponent to advance pawns past the point of no return, creating unstoppable passers that the misdirected pieces cannot reach in time.
sub_patterns: King retreating away from critical pawn break sector
Pawn push on wrong flank ignoring opponent's advanced passer
Wrong rook/piece moved, abandoning key defensive post
Passive king move allowing opponent's breakthrough tempo

analysis.label: Retreating or passively relocating pieces (especially knights to back-rank squares) when the position demands immediate concrete action.
analysis.description: This feature fires on moves that waste critical tempo by retreating or passively developing pieces when the position requires urgent aggressive play. The strongest activations (4/6 positions) involve pieces moving backward to passive or starting squares: Ng8 and Ng1 are literal knight retreats to home squares, Nbd2 places a knight on a blocking passive square, and even e4 is a 'natural-looking' but non-forcing advance that misses concrete tactical shots. In all significant cases (cp_loss 173-283), the player had a large positional or tactical advantage that demanded immediate exploitation of the opponent's weaknesses (exposed kings in 4/4 significant cases, open files, weak pawns), yet chose consolidation over action. The tagged tactical motif is 'tempo_loss' in 4/4 major positions, and all feature analyses emphasize that the move surrendered initiative allowing the opponent to equalize or consolidate.
analysis.move_pattern: Pieces (predominantly knights) moving backward toward back rank or to passive interior squares; non-forcing moves replacing required tactical strikes
analysis.why_bad: These moves waste tempo in positions where the opponent has concrete vulnerabilities (exposed king, weak pawns, open files) that demand immediate exploitation. The retreat gives the opponent time to consolidate, neutralize threats, or generate counterplay that wasn't previously available.
sub_patterns: Knight retreating to starting square (g1/g8)
Knight developing to passive blocking square (Nbd2)
Natural-looking pawn push ignoring concrete tactical opportunity
Piece relocation when exchange sacrifice or forcing continuation exists

analysis.label: Moving a piece away from its essential coordinating or defensive role, leaving key squares or pieces unprotected and allowing immediate tactical punishment.
analysis.description: This feature fires on moves where a piece that was performing a vital defensive or coordinating function is moved away, breaking the position's integrity. In 6/7 analyzed positions, the moved piece was directly protecting another piece or critical square: Bf4 abandoned defense of Nc3 (Position 11), Qxd7 abandoned defense of Bd4 and Nd5 (Position 13), Bxa3 removed the dark-squared bishop from any kingside defensive role (Position 7), Kf3 placed the king on an exposed diagonal without proper shielding (Position 6), Na6 developed to a rim square while ignoring the need to address central tension and castling (Position 1), and Kd6 walked into multiple check diagonals (Position 15). The moves are often motivated by secondary goals—material grabs (Bxa3, Bxg5, Qxd7), apparent development (Na6, Bf4), or perceived centralization (Kf3, Kd6, Kb4)—while the position actually demanded maintaining the piece's current function. The extremely low average of 1.2 good moves available confirms these are positions with razor-thin margins where only careful, often defensive-minded moves preserve the position's integrity.
analysis.move_pattern: Any piece type moving away from a cluster of defended/coordinating squares, often toward the board periphery or onto exposed lines, frequently involving captures of peripheral material or stepping onto tactically vulnerable squares
analysis.why_bad: The moved piece was the linchpin of a defensive coordination—guarding another piece, blocking a check diagonal, or maintaining tension—and its departure allows immediate tactical exploitation via checks, captures of now-undefended pieces, or pawn advances that seize the initiative
sub_patterns: Bishop/Queen captures peripheral material, abandoning central defense
King steps onto exposed square allowing check sequences
Piece develops to passive square while ignoring urgent defensive need

analysis.label: Playing an aggressive-looking move (check, pawn thrust, or active piece move) that wastes tempo while ignoring an urgent concrete tactical obligation in the position.
analysis.description: This feature fires on moves that appear proactive or threatening but actually waste critical tempo by ignoring the position's concrete demands. The most common manifestations are: pointless or counterproductive checks that allow the opponent's king to escape or consolidate (4/11 positions: Re8+, Re5+, Bb3+, Rdf8+), prophylactic or aggressive flank pawn advances when central tension demands immediate resolution (5/11: g4, h6×3, e5), and queen/king moves that look centralizing but leave material hanging (2/11: Qg4, Ke3). In every case, the player chose a move that 'looks like it's doing something' over the position's actual requirement—whether that was capturing an undefended pawn, finding a forced mating sequence, or keeping a piece on a critical defensive square. The average cp_loss of 2061 and average of only 1.4 good moves available confirms these are critical juncture positions where precision was mandatory but the player defaulted to superficially attractive aggression.
analysis.move_pattern: Forward-moving or checking moves (pawn advances toward enemy king, piece checks, centralizing moves) across all piece types and directions; no single geometric pattern but consistently outward/attacking in appearance
analysis.why_bad: These moves waste a crucial tempo on superficial threats while the position demands immediate concrete action—capturing hanging material, resolving urgent central tension, executing forced tactical sequences, or maintaining pieces on critical defensive squares. The 'aggressive' move either helps the opponent (giving their king escape routes, removing own pieces from key posts) or ignores a far more valuable tactical opportunity.
sub_patterns: Pointless checks that help opponent's king escape mating nets
Prophylactic h6/flank pawn pushes ignoring central pawn tension
Choosing wrong forcing move when precise check/capture order is critical
Aggressive pawn advances that weaken own king position
Piece moves that abandon defense of hanging material

analysis.label: Moving a piece/king to a square where the opponent immediately gains a critical tempo through a pawn advance (often with check) or exploiting a vacated defensive duty.
analysis.description: This feature fires on moves that directly enable the opponent to gain a decisive tempo, typically by placing the king or piece on a square immediately attackable by an enemy pawn advance with check, or by vacating control of a square the opponent instantly exploits. In 4/6 positions, the moved piece is immediately hit by a forcing pawn advance: Kf2 walks into e3+ check, Kh3 walks into g4+ check, f5 allows Kf4 seizing the key square, and Kd4 allows Kf4 invading the abandoned zone. In 2/6 positions, the move vacates a critical defensive duty: Bf2 no longer controls d4 enabling the ...d4 break, and Qd1 removes the queen from e2 enabling Bg3+ check. All share the critical feature of being non-urgent moves in positions where tempo is decisive (avg cp_loss 316), with the opponent immediately punishing via a forcing response that was previously impossible. Most occur in endgames (4/6) where single tempi determine the game's outcome.
analysis.move_pattern: King, queen, bishop, or pawn moved to a square in the direct path of an enemy pawn advance or piece attack that gains tempo (frequently via check)
analysis.why_bad: The move places the piece on a square immediately exploitable by the opponent's forcing response (pawn check, pawn break, or piece invasion of vacated square), gifting the opponent a critical tempo that converts to a winning advantage or decisive positional gain
sub_patterns: King stepping into path of enemy pawn check (Kf2→e3+, Kh3→g4+)
King abandoning defensive zone allowing opponent king invasion (Kd4→Kf4, f5→Kf4)
Piece retreat vacating control of critical square enabling opponent's break (Bf2→...d4, Qd1→...Bg3+)

analysis.label: Pieces (usually queens) move to seemingly natural or active squares while abandoning critical defensive functions or ignoring immediate tactical threats.
analysis.description: This feature activates when a player makes a move that looks superficially reasonable—developing, centralizing, or grabbing material—but catastrophically neglects the position's most urgent demand. In 4/6 cases, the queen is moved to an apparently active square (b2, g3, f5, b2) while leaving something critical undefended. In Position 1, Qxb2 grabs a pawn but abandons a forced mating attack on the exposed king. In Position 3, Qg3 aims at kingside targets but leaves c2 undefended, allowing Nxc2+ fork. In Position 5, Qf5 centralizes but places the queen on a square where it's immediately forked by Nh4+. In Position 13, Qb2 leaves the e1 rook completely unguarded, allowing Qxe1. The non-queen examples follow the same logic: Bf4 (Position 2) develops but leaves the g5 knight vulnerable to ...h6, and Nc6 (Position 6) is natural development that ignores the immediate exf6 capture winning a piece. The average of only 1.7 good moves available confirms these are positions demanding precise responses where 'normal' moves fail.
analysis.move_pattern: Pieces (predominantly queens, 4/6) move to natural-looking active squares (b2, g3, f5, f4, c6) that are away from where the piece is critically needed for defense or attack coordination
analysis.why_bad: The moves abandon the piece's essential function in the position—whether that's defending a hanging piece (3/6), maintaining attacking coordination (1/6), or addressing an immediate tactical threat (2/6)—in favor of superficially attractive placement that ignores the position's most urgent demand.
sub_patterns: Queen leaves defense of a hanging piece (Qg3 abandons c2, Qb2 abandons e1 rook)
Piece moves to square creating tactical vulnerability for itself (Qf5 allows Nh4+ fork, Nc6 allows exf6)
Queen leaves critical attacking zone for peripheral material (Qxb2 grabs pawn, abandons mating attack)
Piece development to wrong square ignoring immediate positional needs (Bf4 instead of Be3)

analysis.label: Playing a quiet, non-forcing move in a critical position where an immediately decisive or forcing continuation was required to maintain the evaluation.
analysis.description: This feature fires on positions where the player chooses a slow, non-urgent move (pawn advance, piece repositioning, passive king move) when the position demands immediate tactical precision. In 8/8 cases, the position had very few good moves available (avg 1.4), indicating a critical juncture. In 5/8 positions, the correct move involved a forcing tactical idea (Bf6 threatening mate, Bh7+ sacrifice, Qc1/Qd2 enabling Qh6 mate, Rf2 penetration, Ra1 preparing doubled rooks on 8th rank) while the played move addressed a secondary concern. Pawn advances account for 3/8 moves (b4, fxg5, a4), piece repositioning to non-optimal squares accounts for 4/8 (Qf4, Qe2, Rc8, Rb8), and a passive king move accounts for 1/8 (Kg1). The average centipawn loss is extraordinarily high (1393), reflecting how these positions punish passivity with drastic evaluation swings. The common thread is that every move looks 'reasonable' in isolation but squanders a narrow tactical window that the position offered.
analysis.move_pattern: Any piece type; non-forcing quiet moves (no checks, no critical threats); often lateral/backward repositioning or non-urgent pawn advances
analysis.why_bad: These moves waste a critical tempo in positions where only 1-2 forcing continuations work, giving the opponent time to consolidate defenses, activate dormant pieces, or exploit newly created weaknesses (hanging pawns, abandoned files, king exposure).
sub_patterns: Pawn advance ignoring piece activity demands (b4, a4)
Queen repositioning missing a decisive tactical blow (Qf4, Qe2)
Rook abandoning critical file/rank for secondary target (Rc8, Rb8)
Routine capture missing a brilliant sacrifice (fxg5 vs Bh7+)
Passive king move in a position demanding active piece play (Kg1)

analysis.label: Playing an improving or active move while leaving a pawn undefended against an opponent's rook that immediately captures it.
analysis.description: In all 6/6 positions, the player makes a move that looks active or improving (king centralization, piece repositioning, greedy capture elsewhere, doubling rooks) while ignoring a specific pawn that is directly attacked or accessible by the opponent's rook. The refutation in every case is the opponent's rook simply capturing the abandoned pawn: Rxg6 (Position 1), Rxc6 (Position 2), Rxe6 (Position 3), Rxd3 (Position 4), Rxe4+ (Position 5), and Rxc5 (Position 6). In each case, the best move instead addressed the defensive obligation first—Kg7 defended g6, Rc8 defended c6, Bd7 defended e6, Ne1 defended d3, Bd2 prepared to hold e4/b4, and Rd8 created a counter-capture on d3. The opponent's rook was already positioned on the relevant open file or rank, making the capture immediate and devastating.
analysis.move_pattern: Various piece types move to seemingly active squares (centralization, repositioning, capturing elsewhere) while a critical pawn sits undefended on a file/rank controlled by opponent's rook
analysis.why_bad: The move ignores an immediate concrete threat—an opponent's rook already aimed at an undefended pawn—in favor of a slower positional improvement or greedy capture, allowing a clean pawn win (often with additional structural or tactical consequences) in one move.
sub_patterns: King moves abandoning pawn defense (Ke7, Kh2)
Bishop/Rook repositioning that leaves pawn en prise (Bc2, Rfe8, Ra3)
Greedy capture elsewhere while home pawns hang (Nxb7)

analysis.label: Knight moves that remove the critical e4 blocker from the e-file, enabling a devastating discovered check from the opponent's queen aligned against the uncastled king.
analysis.description: In 9/9 positions, a queen is aligned on the open e-file against the opposing uncastled king (typically White's Qe2 vs Black's Ke8 in Petroff Defense structures). In 7/9 cases, Black's knight on e4 serves as the sole blocker preventing discovered check, and the blunder move directly removes it (Nf6 in 4 cases, Ng5, Nxf2, Nxd2). In 1/9 cases (Position 2), White ignores Black's already-loaded discovered check mechanism. In 1/9 cases (Position 9), Black develops Nc6 ignoring White's Nf6+ discovered check leading to forced mate. The refutation in 8/9 cases involves the opposing knight leaving e5 with discovered check (typically Nc6+ or Ng6+), simultaneously attacking a high-value piece (usually the queen on d8). The average cp_loss of 1451 reflects that queen loss or checkmate typically follows. All positions occur in the opening with both kings centralized.
analysis.move_pattern: Knight moving away from e4 (or making any knight move that ignores the Qe2/Ke8 e-file alignment), typically to f6, g5, f2, d2, or c6
analysis.why_bad: The knight on e4 is the sole piece blocking the queen's X-ray down the e-file to the king; removing it allows the opponent's knight on e5 to move with discovered check, simultaneously attacking the queen or delivering checkmate
sub_patterns: Ne4-f6 retreat to 'natural' square (4 cases)
Ne4 captures away from e-file greedily (Nxf2, Nxd2)
Ne4-g5 aggressive but wrong knight relocation
Routine development (Nc6) ignoring imminent Nf6+ discovered mate
White Nf3 ignoring Black's Nxc3+ discovered check

analysis.label: Playing a natural-looking move that neglects unresolved tactical pressure from a piece on g4 or g5 (usually a bishop pinning a knight on f3/f6), allowing immediate exploitation.
analysis.description: In 10/10 positions, there is a piece (almost always a bishop) on g4 or g5 creating a pin or pressure on a knight on f3 or f6 (or analogous tactical tension involving those squares). The blundering move is a 'natural' developing, advancing, or repositioning move that fails to address this critical tension. In positions 1, 5, 7, 9, and 12, a Bg4 pins a Nf3 and the player ignores it. In positions 2, 5, 8, and 14, a Bg5 pressures Nf6/Ne7 and the player ignores it. Position 4 attempts to address the Bg4 pin with Be2 but walks into a tactical refutation (d3). Position 11 has Ng4 pressure on f2 that Be3 fails to handle. The best moves in nearly all positions involve directly confronting the g4/g5 piece (h3 kicking it, Bb3/Bd3 reinforcing the target, or Qa4+ creating counterplay) rather than playing elsewhere.
analysis.move_pattern: Any piece move or pawn advance that does NOT address an enemy bishop/knight sitting on g4 or g5; varied piece types (pawns, bishops, knights, rooks, queens) moving in various directions
analysis.why_bad: The g4/g5 piece creates latent tactical energy (pin on f3/f6, pressure on central pawns like e4, or threats against f2/f7) that compounds when ignored - the opponent exploits the unresolved tension through captures, forks, intermediate moves, or pawn thrusts that the pinned/pressured pieces cannot defend against
sub_patterns: Central pawn advance (d5/e4) that removes protection from e4/e5 while pin on f3/f6 persists
Bishop/piece development (Be2/Be3) that blocks own coordination or creates new tactical targets under the existing pin
Queen/rook repositioning (Qd7/Re3) that removes a critical defensive resource while pressure on f3/f6 remains

analysis.label: Choosing a slow piece-repositioning move in a critical position that demanded immediate concrete tactical action (usually a capture or forcing move).
analysis.description: In all 5/5 positions, the player chose to reposition or 'improve' a piece rather than execute the one correct forcing move. The best moves were overwhelmingly concrete actions: tactical captures (Nf7 fork, Rxh6, Bxh6 in 3/5 positions), a defensive queen trade (Qf5), or an immediate pawn advance (h6). Instead, the played moves were all passive piece maneuvers—Na4 (knight to rim), Qc6 (queen repositioning), Rdh1 (doubling rooks), Bf4 (bishop retreating), Qg5 (queen advancing)—that looked like 'preparation' for an attack or improvement but ignored the position's razor-sharp tactical demands. The average good moves available was only 1.2, confirming these were critical moments requiring precision. In 4/5 cases the piece ended up vulnerable (hanging on f4, trappable on g5, ineffective on a4/h1) or abandoned a critical function (c3 knight guarding e4, queen defending kingside). The catastrophic average cp_loss of 2111 reflects how a single 'slow' move in a position with one right answer leads to total collapse.
analysis.move_pattern: Any piece type moving to a non-forcing square (no check, no capture, no direct threat) when immediate captures or forcing moves were available
analysis.why_bad: The position demanded exactly one concrete action (usually a capture on h6 or a tactical strike), and the repositioning move either created a specific vulnerability (hanging piece, trapped queen, exposed king) or abandoned a critical defensive/attacking function, allowing the opponent to seize the initiative with a forcing response.
sub_patterns: Bishop/rook retreat or reposition when capture on h6 was winning (Bf4, Rdh1 vs Bxh6, Rxh6)
Piece decentralization abandoning critical square control (Na4 losing e4 control)
Queen repositioning to a square where it can be attacked or trapped (Qg5, Qc6)
Doubling/preparation when one-move tactical solution existed

analysis.label: Playing a plausible-looking move that addresses a secondary concern when the position demands exactly one specific critical action.
analysis.description: All three positions share a crucial characteristic: exactly 1 good move existed (avg good moves = 1.0), yet the player chose a 'reasonable' alternative addressing a non-critical concern. In Position 1 (3/3 critical coordination), Qg4 pursued kingside attacking ideas but abandoned the queen's coordination with the f6-rook that enabled the winning Rxf7 tactic. In Position 2 (3/3 ignoring existential threat), c6 attacked the d5 bishop positionally while completely ignoring the Qg7# mating pattern requiring Qf6 to block. In Position 3 (3/3 abandoning key square), Qb6 sought peripheral targets but surrendered the queen's dominant central post on d4, which was the only thing holding the position together. Each move looks purposeful in isolation but catastrophically misreads what the position actually requires.
analysis.move_pattern: Active piece (usually queen) moved away from its critical coordination square, or a non-urgent pawn move played instead of the one defensive requirement
analysis.why_bad: The position demanded one specific action (tactical execution, blocking a mating diagonal, or maintaining a key piece placement), and the move played addressed a secondary concern instead, allowing the opponent to exploit the now-undefended critical vulnerability
sub_patterns: Queen abandoning coordination with attacking rook
Positional pawn move ignoring forced mating threat
Queen decentralization from dominant post when only that post held the position

analysis.label: Playing a quiet, non-forcing move when the position demands immediate concrete tactical action, wasting a critical tempo.
analysis.description: This feature activates when a player chooses a slow, positionally-motivated or 'improving' move in a position that requires immediate concrete action. In 6/7 positions, the analyses explicitly tag 'tempo_loss' as a key factor. The moves share no geometric similarity (queen moves, pawn pushes, king move, bishop move) but are united by their non-forcing nature: Qh4 chases phantom kingside pressure while b2 hangs (Position 1), g4 tries to 'block' an attack instead of prophylactic Kf1 (Position 6), h5 pushes a pawn instead of the decisive Nd8 exploiting an overloaded queen (Position 7), c6 solidifies structure while ignoring the immediate f4 threat (Position 10), Kf6 consolidates instead of generating counterplay with d3 (Position 14), and Bg5 'develops' instead of the crushing Nd5 (Position 15). In 4/7 cases, a specific tactical blow was missed (Nd5, Nd8, d3, Qe5), and in all cases the opponent gains time to neutralize the position's critical imbalance.
analysis.move_pattern: Any piece type; quiet non-capturing non-checking move; often pawn advances or piece relocations to seemingly active but non-threatening squares
analysis.why_bad: These moves squander a critical tempo in positions where the dynamic balance demands immediate forcing action—either exploiting a tactical vulnerability (hanging piece, overloaded defender, exposed king) or addressing an urgent defensive need. The opponent uses the gifted tempo to stabilize, trade queens, cover weaknesses, or launch their own concrete threats.
sub_patterns: Slow pawn pushes (g4/h5/c6) that weaken structure or miss decisive piece tactics
Piece moves to seemingly aggressive but tactically toothless squares (Qh4/Bg5)
Passive consolidation moves (Qc8/Kf6) when active counterplay was required to survive

analysis.label: Playing natural-looking positional or centralizing moves in narrow positions that demand immediate concrete/forcing action.
analysis.description: This feature fires when players choose seemingly reasonable 'improving' moves—centralizing pieces, repositioning bishops, advancing pawns—in positions that critically require one specific forcing move. In 6/7 positions, the correct move was a forcing action: a tactical shot (Bxf6 in pos 1), a critical pawn break (exd5 in pos 7), a tempo-gaining check (Qc5+ in pos 10), immediate counterplay (Qg4/f5 in pos 6), or piece activation targeting weaknesses (Ng3 in pos 8). Instead, players chose quiet moves (Bd4, Be1, Kc2, c3, Rd6, Ne6) that look like standard positional improvements but ignore that the position is on a knife's edge with only 1-3 good moves available (avg 1.9). In 4/7 cases, the 'improving' move directly left a piece undefended or created a tactical vulnerability (Rxe5 left rook en prise to queen; Bd4 abandoned b3 knight; Be1 left e2 knight hanging; Ne6 placed knight on open file enabling fork). The positions share extremely narrow margins where one tempo of inactivity allows the opponent to seize the initiative irreversibly.
analysis.move_pattern: Various piece types making non-forcing repositioning moves (bishop retreats/centralization, knight redeployment, king walks, quiet pawn pushes, rook lifts) rather than checks, critical captures, or pawn breaks
analysis.why_bad: These moves surrender the critical tempo needed to exploit or maintain an advantage in tactically demanding positions; by choosing a slow improvement over the one forcing continuation, the player either leaves pieces undefended, allows the opponent a decisive counter-break, or walks into a tactical refutation that the 'natural' move fails to anticipate.
sub_patterns: Centralizing a piece to a square where it becomes tactically vulnerable (Ne6, Rxe5)
Repositioning a defender that was indirectly protecting another piece (Bd4 abandoning b3, Be1 leaving e2 hanging)
Slow king/pawn moves when an immediate pawn break or exchange resolves tension (Kc2 instead of exd5, c3 instead of Ng3)
Passive rook move losing a critical forcing check resource (Rd6 instead of Qc5+)

analysis.label: Playing a check (or attack) with queen/rook/bishop that can be interposed or captured, when an unblockable knight check or fork was the winning forcing move.
analysis.description: In 5/6 positions, the correct best move involved a knight check or fork (Ne6+ in positions 4 and 7, Nb4+ in position 14, Nf4+ in position 13, Nc2+ as third-best in position 3), yet the player chose a check with a different piece that could be neutralized. In position 14, Rd8+ was blocked by Bd5 when Nb4+ delivered an unblockable mating net. In position 7, Bc7+ was interposed by Ne5 (which then won the bishop) when Ne6+ gave an immediate fork. In position 13, Rxf2+ sacrificed material for mere equality when Nf4+ won the exchange cleanly through proper move order. In position 3, Qe1+ was simply captured by Rxe1. Position 9 (Bd3+, cp_loss 0) is the exception that proves the rule—it's the correct check precisely because it leads to the knight coordination (Ne5, Nxf7+) that delivers forced mate. The pattern is consistently choosing a visually flashy line-piece check over the tactically superior knight check.
analysis.move_pattern: Check delivered by queen, rook, or bishop along a file/diagonal toward an exposed king, when a knight had an available check or fork from a different angle
analysis.why_bad: Line-piece checks (along files/diagonals) can be interposed or the checking piece can be captured, neutralizing the threat. Knight checks cannot be blocked—only evaded—making them far more forcing. The player consistently chose the 'obvious' check over the geometrically superior knight jump that created unblockable forks or mating nets.
sub_patterns: Rook check on open file blocked by bishop interposition (Rd8+ blocked by Bd5, Bc7+ blocked by Ne5)
Queen check that hangs to simple capture (Qe1+ taken by Rxe1)
Rook sacrifice check as wrong move order when knight check first wins material cleanly (Rxf2+ vs Nf4+)
Non-forcing piece attack missing available knight fork/check (Nf7 missing Ne6+)

analysis.label: Piece abandons a critical defensive duty for a seemingly active/purposeful move, leaving material or key squares immediately vulnerable.
analysis.description: This feature fires on moves where a piece that was performing an essential protective function (directly or indirectly defending another piece, pawn, or critical square) relocates to an apparently active square, immediately creating a concrete tactical vulnerability. In 4/6 positions, the moved piece was clearly the defender of specific material: Ng3 (Position 1) abandons indirect defense of g4 via the Nf6+ fork threat; Bg5 (Position 6) removes the sole defender of the e5 knight; Rxe1 (Position 2) is the wrong capture that leaves the e3 bishop unprotected; Kc7 (Position 4) walks into a forced check enabling a discovered attack along a newly-opened diagonal. In the remaining cases, the moved piece abandons a positional obligation: Rf8 (Position 3) surrenders counterplay and self-blocks the queen, while Nd5 (Position 5) neglects development leaving the king fatally exposed. All 6 moves appear purposeful (attacking a queen, creating a pin, centralizing, capturing an intruder, activating a rook) but fatally ignore that the piece's current placement was holding the position together. The average of only 1.2 good alternatives confirms these are positions demanding precise awareness of defensive obligations.
analysis.move_pattern: Any piece type moves away from its current square to a seemingly active destination, vacating defense of a piece, pawn, or critical square
analysis.why_bad: The moved piece was the sole or primary defender of something important; its relocation immediately creates a hanging piece, enables a capture with check, or opens a devastating tactical sequence that the opponent can exploit.
sub_patterns: Moving a piece that indirectly defended material via a counter-threat (e.g., knight leaving a square where it could fork)
Choosing the wrong capturing piece, leaving another piece undefended
Bishop/knight relocating to an 'aggressive' square while abandoning defense of a centralized piece
King moving to a square vulnerable to check that enables a discovered attack or combination
Piece moving to a square that self-blocks escape routes for another piece

analysis.label: Pieces moved to attractive-looking squares (central posts, checks, captures) that miss a more concrete tactical continuation or create immediate vulnerabilities.
analysis.description: This feature fires on moves where a player makes a superficially active or aggressive-looking piece placement—centralizing a bishop (Bd5, Bd4, Be4: 3/11), giving a check (Nd4+, Nc5+, Rf2+, Rg8+: 4/11), capturing on an exposed square (Rxe3: 1/11), or repositioning to an 'active' post (Qf3, Ra2: 2/11)—when the position demanded a more concrete tactical solution. In nearly every case, the played move either lands the piece on a square where it can be captured or challenged with tempo (Nc5+ captured by Bxc5, Be4 captured by Nxe4, Bd4 kicked by c3, Rxe3 exploited by fxe3), gives a check that doesn't accomplish the critical objective (Rf2+ vs Rg3+ for rook exchange, Rg8+ vs Rh5+ hitting the target directly, Nd4+ vs Nxe5+ winning material), or abandons a vital function (Qf3 leaving e4, Ra2 leaving d7 undefended). The average of only 1.7 good moves available confirms these are critical positions requiring precision, and the massive avg cp_loss (1992) reflects how severely these 'looks good' moves squander the position.
analysis.move_pattern: Any piece type moving to a central, forward, or seemingly aggressive square—often with check or capture—landing on a square that is tactically vulnerable or strategically suboptimal compared to a more forcing alternative
analysis.why_bad: The move prioritizes superficial piece activity (impressive square, check, capture) over the position's concrete tactical demand, either placing the piece where it can be profitably challenged/captured, giving a purposeless check that gains no material or positional concession, or abandoning a critical function that the opponent immediately exploits
sub_patterns: Checks that fail to accomplish the critical objective (wrong check direction/target)
Piece centralized on a square where it can be immediately captured or kicked with tempo
Wrong piece sent to the right square (Bd5 instead of Nd5, fxe3 needed instead of Rxe3)
Active-looking rook move that abandons defense of a hanging piece or key square
Queen repositioning that surrenders initiative by leaving an optimal post

analysis.label: Developing or space-gaining moves that ignore immediate tactical vulnerabilities of undefended pieces.
analysis.description: All three positions share the same core error: the player makes a move that appears to improve their position (development, centralization, or space-gaining) while leaving a piece completely unprotected and tactically exploitable. In 3/3 positions the tactical motif is 'hanging_piece.' In Position 9, Qf6 looks active but ignores the undefended a8 rook on an open diagonal (Qxa8). In Position 10, e5 appears aggressive but creates an undefended pawn whose capture triggers a chain that loses the dominant d6 bishop and d2 knight. In Position 14, Nh6 aims to develop the dormant knight but places it on an unprotected rim square where Bxh6 wins it after the supporting c4 knight is exchanged. In all cases (3/3), the position demanded concrete tactical action or piece protection rather than slow improvement, and only 1-2 good alternatives existed. The opponent's refutation in each case is straightforward material capture of the hanging piece.
analysis.move_pattern: Piece or pawn moves to an undefended square (or ignores an existing undefended piece) without creating a forcing threat to compensate
analysis.why_bad: The move fails to create any immediate threat or check, giving the opponent a free tempo to exploit the hanging/undefended piece via a simple capture or two-move tactical sequence
sub_patterns: Knight developed to unprotected rim square (Nh6)
Pawn pushed without adequate support creating removal sequence (e5)
Queen placed passively while rook hangs on open diagonal (Qf6)

analysis.label: Ill-timed pawn advances that open a closed position, creating tactical vulnerabilities in the player's own camp.
analysis.description: This feature fires on positions where a player makes a pawn break (or tempo-wasting move) that prematurely opens a closed or semi-closed position to their own detriment. In 7/8 cases, the mistake is a direct single-square pawn advance (e4, c4, c4, c5, f5, e5, f5) that ruptures the pawn structure; in 1/8 cases (Kh2), it's a tempo loss that allows the opponent to open favorably. The positions share closed centers (6/8 explicitly noted) where patience and quiet piece improvement were required. In every case, the better alternatives involved maintaining the closed structure through piece repositioning or prophylaxis (avg 2.8 good moves available). The punishments consistently exploit newly opened lines—diagonals to undefended pieces (2/8), files against uncastled kings (2/8), weakened squares around the player's own king (2/8), or structural collapse creating isolated/hanging pawns (2/8). The average cp_loss of 256 reflects how catastrophically these breaks backfire.
analysis.move_pattern: Single-square pawn advances (typically c, e, or f pawns) pushing into enemy pawn chain, or passive non-pawn moves when pawn tension demands immediate resolution
analysis.why_bad: Opening the position creates lines (diagonals, files, weak squares) that the opponent exploits tactically—against an uncastled king, undefended pieces on cleared diagonals, or a destabilized pawn structure that collapses under tactical pressure.
sub_patterns: Central pawn break with king still uncastled (e4, e5 with king on e1/e8)
Pawn break removing key defender of adjacent pawn (c4 unguarding d4)
Pawn break destroying own supportive pawn chain (c5 breaking c6-d5)
Kingside pawn break opening lines against own exposed king (f5 with king on g7)
Pawn break clearing diagonal to own undefended piece (f5 opening a8-h1)
Tempo loss allowing opponent to open position favorably (Kh2 permitting ...exf4)

analysis.label: Choosing the wrong piece or direction for a move that superficially achieves the same goal as the best move but critically fails in execution.
analysis.description: In 4/4 positions, the player makes a move that appears to accomplish the same objective as the best move but uses the wrong piece, captures with the wrong unit, or moves in the wrong direction. In Position 2, gxf5 captures the same pawn that Bxf5 would, but with the wrong unit (pawn vs bishop), destroying the king's shield. In Position 4, Rd3+ delivers check on the same file as the correct Rd7+, but with the wrong rook, failing to control d5. In Position 6, Bc4 repositions a piece when the direct h2 pawn push was winning by force—wrong piece entirely. In Position 11, Kd7 moves the king on the d-file but in the wrong direction (backward vs. forward to d5). All 4 moves share the critical consequence of surrendering control of a key square (h-file in P2, d5 in P4, promotion square in P6, d4 in P11), allowing the opponent to seize initiative. Tagged as tempo_loss in 3/4 positions.
analysis.move_pattern: A natural-looking move (capture, check, piece repositioning, or king move) that parallels the best move's type or file but uses the incorrect piece or direction
analysis.why_bad: The move fails to control the critical square that the correct alternative would have dominated, allowing the opponent to immediately exploit the vacuum with a forcing response (check, central occupation, or tempo-gaining attack on the misplaced piece)
sub_patterns: Capturing with wrong unit (pawn vs piece) destroying pawn structure
Checking with wrong rook failing to cut off king's retreat square
Moving a non-critical piece when a passed pawn should advance immediately
Moving king backward when forward centralization was essential

analysis.label: King moves to an apparently active or central square that exposes it to tactical exploitation, when a different king move (often to an adjacent square) was needed for safety or to create a specific threat.
analysis.description: In all 11 positions, the player moves their king to a square that appears natural or centralizing but lacks tactical justification while creating critical vulnerabilities. In 4/11 cases (Ke5, Ke3→Kc3, Kg7→Kf5, Kc4→Kd4), the correct move attacked or threatened an enemy rook, while the played move failed to create that threat. In 5/11 cases (Ke4, Kd3, Kf4, Kc5, Kd7), the chosen square placed the king on an open file or rank where immediate checks won material or delivered mate. In 3/11 cases (Ka5, Kb6, Kd4), the king moved passively when a counter-intuitive direction (forward to create threats, or blocking a file) was required. The average cp_loss of ~1952 reflects that many of these are catastrophic (including two walk-into-mate positions), with typically only 1-2 good alternatives available. The consistent error is prioritizing abstract king activity over concrete tactical safety and threats.
analysis.move_pattern: King move to adjacent square, typically toward center or forward, bypassing a safer or more threatening adjacent square
analysis.why_bad: The chosen square fails to create a necessary threat against enemy pieces (especially rooks) while simultaneously placing the king on an open line or vulnerable diagonal where it can be checked, forked, or mated—the correct adjacent square either attacked an enemy piece or avoided tactical exposure.
sub_patterns: King advances when correct square attacks an enemy rook (Ke5 vs Ke6, Kc3 vs Ke3, Kf5 vs Kg7, Kd4 vs Kc4)
King walks onto open file/rank allowing devastating check sequences (Kd7 on d-file, Kf4 on 4th rank, Kc5 near c4 pawn)
King walks into mating net created by coordinated enemy rooks (Ke4 into Ra4#)
King retreats passively when forward move creates counterplay (Ka5 vs Kb3)

analysis.label: Quiet developing or flank moves that ignore a free knight capture of an undefended central e-pawn (Nxe4 or Nxe5).
analysis.description: In all 7/7 positions, the best move was a knight capture of an undefended central e-pawn (Nxe4 in positions 1, 4, 5, 6; Nxe5 in positions 2, 3, 7), yet the player instead chose a slow, non-tactical move. The played moves include fianchetto preparations (b6, b3), passive bishop development (Bd3, Be7, Be3), prophylactic pawn moves (h6), and speculative pawn advances (g5). All occur in the opening phase where central tension between e4 and e5 pawns exists, and in every case the opponent's e-pawn is tactically undefended or insufficiently protected, making it capturable by a knight for free or with significant advantage. The players appear to be following general opening principles (develop pieces, prevent threats, expand on flanks) without checking whether the opponent's central pawn is actually defended.
analysis.move_pattern: Non-captures (bishop development, flank pawn pushes, prophylactic moves) played instead of Nxe4 or Nxe5 knight captures on undefended central pawns
analysis.why_bad: They waste a critical tempo on a non-urgent move while a free central pawn capture (Nxe4 or Nxe5) is available, allowing the opponent to either defend the pawn on the next move or exploit the tempo loss by seizing the initiative themselves.
sub_patterns: Fianchetto prep (b6/b3) ignoring hanging e-pawn
Passive bishop development (Be7/Bd3/Be3) ignoring hanging e-pawn
Prophylactic/aggressive pawn moves (h6/g5) ignoring hanging e-pawn

analysis.label: Moves that address a secondary concern while ignoring the position's primary tactical urgency, leaving a critical weakness unresolved.
analysis.description: This feature fires on positions where the player makes a purposeful-looking move that addresses a real but secondary concern, while failing to address the most urgent tactical demand. In 6/6 cases, the position had very few good options (avg 1.7 good moves), meaning precise play was required. The blunders include flank pawn pushes ignoring king safety or piece vulnerability (b5 ignoring Qh5+Bxg6, a4 ignoring Nd4-Nxf3+ fork), wrong-order captures that leave pieces hanging (Bxf3 leaving Bd6 undefended 1/6, Bxe6 abandoning the Ne4's defender 1/6), passive retreats surrendering initiative when attacking moves were critical (Qe7 instead of d4+ exploiting uncastled king), and premature pawn advances removing defensive barriers (e4 eliminating a pawn shield). In every case, the best move addressed the PRIMARY tactical need (defending the king, correct capture sequence, maintaining piece protection), while the blunder addressed something less urgent.
analysis.move_pattern: Various piece types and directions (pawn pushes, bishop captures, queen retreats), unified by being non-forcing moves in positions requiring immediate concrete action
analysis.why_bad: The move leaves the most critical tactical vulnerability unaddressed—whether that's an exposed king (2/6), a hanging piece (3/6), or a lost initiative (1/6)—giving the opponent a tempo to exploit the primary weakness with forcing moves
sub_patterns: Flank pawn advances ignoring kingside/tactical crisis (b5, a4)
Wrong capture order leaving another piece undefended (Bxf3, Bxe6)
Passive consolidation surrendering critical initiative (Qe7, e4)

analysis.label: Playing a slow, non-essential move that ignores a critical positional demand, giving the opponent a free tempo to execute a decisive plan.
analysis.description: This feature fires on moves that squander a tempo when the position contains an urgent tactical or structural demand. In 5/7 positions, the blunder allows the opponent to execute a concrete central action (cxd5 winning a pawn in positions 1 and 4, d5-d6 advance in positions 6 and 11, dxc4 exploiting overextension in position 9). The played moves include prophylactic flank pawn pushes (h6 appearing 2/7 times), passive king moves (Kh7), aimless rook relocations (Rd8, Re5), a structurally damaging pawn capture (dxe5), and a premature pawn advance (c4). In all cases, 6/7 positions feature tempo_loss as a primary tag, and the opponent's refutation exploits the gifted move to push pawns forward or launch a tactical strike that was previously held in check. The average cp_loss of 267 reflects that these are positions where one wasted tempo is catastrophic because a concrete threat or tension point demands immediate resolution.
analysis.move_pattern: Any piece type; typically non-forcing moves (no check, no capture, no direct threat) that don't address the board's critical tension point
analysis.why_bad: The position contains an urgent demand (unresolved central pawn tension, an imminent pawn break, or a tactical vulnerability) that requires immediate action; the played move ignores this demand, gifting the opponent a free tempo to execute their key plan (win a pawn, advance a passed pawn, or exploit a newly created weakness)
sub_patterns: Prophylactic h6 ignoring central pawn tension (cxd5 wins material)
Passive king/rook move allowing opponent's passed pawn advance (d5-d6)
Rook relocation that abandons defense of a critical pawn (f7)
Overextending pawn push that creates more weaknesses than threats
Wrong recapture method that destroys key structural pawn

analysis.label: Moving a piece that serves a critical defensive function around your own king to an aggressive square, fatally exposing the king to tactical exploitation.
analysis.description: In 7/7 positions, the blundering side moved a piece away from a defensive role protecting their own king in favor of an active or attacking placement. In positions 2 and 7, rooks left defensive files (g-file, e-file) to attack the opponent's king on the 7th rank, leaving the moving side's king exposed to devastating queen checks and mating attacks. In position 4, a bishop vacated d2 (key king-shielding square) for an active f4 post, enabling a fatal discovered-check sequence along the d-file. In position 13, the queen—the sole piece holding the defensive position together—gave a check on a square where it was immediately capturable, removing the defensive anchor. In positions 6 and 8, piece placement on f8 exposed the king to back-rank/file tactics. In position 12, a pawn push weakened the king's cover while neglecting development. The common thread is choosing visually active moves (attacking pawns, contesting files, giving checks) over maintaining the critical defensive infrastructure around one's own king.
analysis.move_pattern: Piece (usually rook, bishop, or queen) moves away from squares adjacent to or shielding own king, typically toward opponent's side of the board or to an aggressive square
analysis.why_bad: The moved piece was the linchpin of king defense—its removal opens files, diagonals, or squares that allow the opponent's pieces (especially queens) to deliver unstoppable checks, pins, or mating attacks against the now-undefended king
sub_patterns: Rook leaves defensive file to attack on 7th rank, allowing queen infiltration
Minor piece vacates king's defensive perimeter for active square, enabling discovered/file attacks
Queen gives check on exposed square where it can be captured, removing key defender
Pawn advance or king move weakens own pawn shield/king position on critical file

analysis.label: Moving the king (or piece) to a square on an open file/rank where it becomes an immediate target for a tempo-gaining check or attack.
analysis.description: This feature fires on moves that place the king or a key piece onto a tactically vulnerable square—predominantly an open file—allowing the opponent to gain decisive tempo through a check, capture, or forcing attack. In 7/12 positions, the played move is a king move (Kc6, Ke6, Kg6, Ke7, Ke2) that steps onto or near an open file where the opponent immediately exploits it with a rook check (Rc4+ in positions 1,2; Re1+ in position 5; d6+ in position 7; Rd8 penetration in position 9). The remaining positions share the same structural error: a piece moves to a square where the opponent gains a free tempo (Qxa7 gets attacked by Ra8; Bf4 enables Re7 attacking the queen; Rab1 leaves a2 undefended for Qxa2). In all cases, the played move looks like natural 'improvement' (centralizing, capturing) but neglects a more concrete continuation (typically a pawn advance like d5 or g4, or prophylactic control of the critical file). The average cp_loss of 939 reflects how devastating these tempo gifts are—the opponent converts the free move into penetration, promotion acceleration, or material gain.
analysis.move_pattern: King (or queen/piece) moves to a square on an open file or rank, typically toward the center, without controlling that file first
