analysis.why_bad: The destination square is exposed to an immediate tempo-gaining check or attack along the open file/rank, allowing the opponent to seize the initiative, penetrate with heavy pieces, or accelerate passed pawn promotion while the blundering piece is forced backward
sub_patterns: King advances onto open file allowing rook check (Kc6→Rc4+, Ke6→Re1+)
King steps onto promotion diagonal allowing pawn advance with check (Ke7→d6+)
Premature king activation before prophylactic pawn move (Ke2 before g4)
Queen/piece goes to edge square vulnerable to tempo-gaining attack (Qxa7→Ra8)
Removing defensive sentry pawn that controlled key squares (exd5 releasing f5)

analysis.label: Seemingly natural or active moves that fatally leave material undefended or place pieces on tactically vulnerable squares, enabling immediate exploitation.
analysis.description: This feature fires on positions where the player makes a move that appears active, natural, or attractive (developing a piece, grabbing material, giving a check, approaching a target) but catastrophically ignores that the move creates or exposes hanging material. In 7/9 positions, the played move either places a piece on a square where it can be immediately captured (Rc5 hangs to Bxc5; Be6 allows Bc5+ skewer winning the exchange), moves a defensive piece away from its critical guard duty (Qxb2 and Qxf2 abandon queen defense of key pieces/king, enabling captures of undefended material like Nd7 or Rc8), or neglects a critical vulnerability (Bg4 leaves b7/a8 hanging; Kf4 leaves g2 uncontrolled enabling promotion; c4 removes a defensive pawn barrier). The positions typically have very few good moves available (avg 2.0), demanding precise calculation rather than natural play, and the punishment is usually devastating (avg cp_loss 5353) with one clear tactical refutation winning material through a forcing sequence.
analysis.move_pattern: Piece or pawn moves to active-looking squares or captures peripheral material, while leaving critical squares, pieces, or defensive alignments unguarded; no consistent piece type or direction, but always creating or exposing an immediately exploitable hanging target
analysis.why_bad: Each move prioritizes the player's own active plan (development, material gain, king activity, checking) over addressing the position's critical tactical vulnerability, leaving material en prise to forcing responses (captures with check, skewers, or immediate piece wins) that the opponent can exploit in 1-2 moves
sub_patterns: Queen grabs distant pawn, abandoning defense of king/pieces (Qxb2, Qxf2)
Piece develops to active square that is tactically compromised (Bg4 leaves diagonal open, Be6 allows skewer, Rc5 hangs to bishop)
King moves to wrong square missing critical control (Kf4 doesn't control g2, Kf7 allows tempo-gaining check)
Pawn/piece move removes defensive barrier or drives opponent to safety (c4 removes restraint, Qd8+ gives king escape)

analysis.label: Playing a routine developing or preparatory move while a minor piece (usually a knight) is directly attacked by an enemy pawn, allowing a simple pawn capture to win material.
analysis.description: In all 10/10 positions, a minor piece (knight in 9/10, bishop in 1/10) is directly en prise to an enemy pawn, and the player makes a routine move (development, castling, prophylaxis, or pawn push) that completely ignores this threat. In 8/10 cases, the piece is already on the attacked square and the player fails to move it away (e.g., knight on c6 attacked by d5 pawn in positions 1, 2, 3; knight on c3 attacked by d4 pawn in positions 7, 11; knight on f6 attacked by e5 pawn in position 10; knight on f3 attacked by e4 pawn in position 15; bishop on d4 attacked by e5 pawn in position 5). In 2/10 cases (positions 6, 14), the player actively moves a piece ONTO a square controlled by an enemy pawn. The moves played are universally 'normal-looking' opening moves — Nf6, O-O, h6, d3, a6, Nc3, c4, Nf3 — that would be reasonable in other contexts but catastrophically ignore the immediate material threat. The refutation in every case is the trivial pawn capture (dxc6, bxc6, exf6, dxc3, exf3, exd4), winning a full piece for at most one pawn.
analysis.move_pattern: Any routine move (knight development, castling, pawn push, prophylactic) that ignores a pawn directly attacking an undefended minor piece
analysis.why_bad: The player fails to recognize or prioritize that an enemy pawn directly attacks their minor piece, allowing a simple pawn capture that wins a full piece for free or for one pawn — the most basic form of hanging piece oversight.
sub_patterns: Knight on c6 ignored while attacked by d5/b5 pawn
Knight on c3/f3 ignored while attacked by d4/e4 pawn
Knight moved onto a square controlled by an advanced enemy pawn
Bishop left on a square attacked by an enemy pawn while castling

analysis.label: In rook endgames with advanced enemy passed pawns, making a passive non-checking move when an immediate rook check was the only way to disrupt the opponent's pawn-promotion coordination.
analysis.description: In all 8/8 positions, the opponent has dangerous advanced passed pawns (typically connected, on the 3rd-4th rank) threatening imminent promotion. In 7/8 cases, the engine's best move is an immediate rook check (Rf8+, Rb3+, Rc2+, Re4+) or king blockade that directly disrupts the opponent's king-pawn coordination. Instead, the player makes a passive rook move (Rb8, Rg8, Rh6, Rh5, Rh1, Rxh4) or an aimless king move (Ke6, Ke7) that wastes the critical tempo. The check is essential because it forces the opponent's king to a worse square (blocking its own pawn, moving away from pawn support), but the passive alternative gives the opponent a free move to advance the pawn or improve king position, after which the promotion becomes unstoppable. All 8/8 positions are tagged 'tempo_loss' and 'passed_pawn' in the analysis, and 7/8 had only 1 good move available, demonstrating razor-thin margins where a single wasted tempo is catastrophic.
analysis.move_pattern: Rook moves to non-checking squares (lateral repositioning, retreat to back rank, or irrelevant capture) or king moves, when the rook could deliver an immediate check along a file
analysis.why_bad: Against advanced passed pawns in rook endgames, a single tempo is often the difference between holding and losing. The immediate check disrupts the opponent's king-pawn coordination (forcing the king onto the pawn's square or away from support), but the passive move grants a free pawn advance that creates an unstoppable promotion threat.
sub_patterns: Rook repositioning to wrong file instead of checking (Rb8, Rg8, Rh6, Rh5)
Rook retreating to back rank passively (Rh1)
Capturing an irrelevant/blocked pawn instead of checking (Rxh4)
King moves when immediate rook check was required (Ke6, Ke7)

analysis.label: Playing a less-forcing move when the position demands maximum urgency, wasting a decisive tempo in a time-critical situation.
analysis.description: This feature fires on positions where the player makes a move that wastes a critical tempo in a razor-sharp position that demands the most forcing continuation available. In 5/5 positions, the correct move exploited tempo precisely (pushing a promotion-race pawn immediately, capturing with check before recapturing a loose piece, or delivering the one precise check leading to mate), while the played move looked active or reasonable but was fundamentally one tempo too slow. In 2/5 cases the player moved their king when they should have pushed a passed pawn to start/maintain a pawn race (Ke1 instead of h6, Kc8 instead of f4). In 1/5 cases the player captured with the wrong piece, missing that the knight capture came with check (Qxe3 instead of Nxe3+). In 1/5 cases the player gave an imprecise check that let the king escape rather than the precise check leading to forced mate (Nc4+ instead of Nd7+). In 1/5 cases the player pushed a pawn instead of executing an available tactical combination. The average cp_loss of 2325 and average of only 1.8 good moves confirms these are extremely narrow positions where one wasted tempo is catastrophic.
analysis.move_pattern: Diverse piece types and directions, but all share the property of being non-maximally-forcing: king retreats instead of pawn advances, captures without check instead of captures with check, imprecise checks instead of mating checks
analysis.why_bad: In positions where tempo is the decisive factor (pawn races, forced mating nets, tactical sequences requiring intermediate checks), these moves squander one critical tempo by choosing a natural-looking but non-forcing continuation, allowing the opponent to activate (promote a pawn, escape a mating net, reposition a piece from liability to attacker)
sub_patterns: King moves instead of immediate passed pawn advances in pawn races
Capturing with wrong piece, missing that correct piece captures with check
Giving imprecise check that drives king to safety vs precise check leading to mate
Positional moves that miss available forcing tactical combinations

analysis.label: A piece (usually a knight) moves to a peripheral or tactically exposed square, abandoning coordination and creating immediate exploitable vulnerabilities.
analysis.description: This feature fires on moves where a piece relocates to a suboptimal square—often on the rim or an unprotected post—while abandoning a critical active or defensive role. In 4/7 positions, knights specifically move to rim squares (Nh3, Nxa5, Nb5) or away from key posts (Nf6 abandoning support for b4 knight). The resulting position consistently allows the opponent to exploit the misplaced piece through direct tactics: bishop captures the exposed knight (Position 4: Bxh3), diagonal pins against the misplaced piece (Position 7: Bc5 pins/attacks f2 after Nb5 leaves d4), pin of rook (Position 7: Bc5 after Rf2), or structural disruption while the piece is out of play (Position 6: dxc3 while knight is on a5). Tempo loss is cited in 5/7 analyses, and piece_activity issues appear in all 7. The common thread is that the piece's destination serves no urgent function while its departure creates an immediate tactical or structural hole.
analysis.move_pattern: Piece (usually knight) moves to rim file (a/b/h) or away from central/active post, often a capture or repositioning move to a square lacking support or purpose
analysis.why_bad: The move abandons a critical defensive or coordinative function (central post, piece protection, tension management) while placing the piece on a square where it either becomes a tactical target, loses tempo returning, or enables opponent's dormant pieces (especially bishops) to activate on newly-opened diagonals
sub_patterns: Knight retreats/jumps to rim square (h3, a5, b5) becoming target or losing time
Piece moves before resolving central tension (move-order error)
Piece placed on square creating pin/tactical vulnerability along diagonal
Active piece abandoned without addressing its needs first

analysis.label: Quiet or routine-looking moves played at critical decision points where only one specific concrete move maintains the position, allowing the opponent a forcing tactical punishment.
analysis.description: This feature fires on positions where the player chooses a 'natural-looking' quiet move (developing, retreating, or repositioning) when the position demands one specific forcing or concrete action. The average number of good moves available is only 1.6, indicating these are extremely narrow decision points. In 9/11 positions, the played move allows the opponent an immediate forcing sequence—often involving a check—that wins material: Ke7 removes a blocker allowing Rxh8 (Position 4), h4 removes the g4 guard allowing Qg4+ (Position 8), Be7 allows Ra6+ then Nxe7 (Position 12), Ke7 allows Qg7+ winning a rook (Position 14), Ra2 allows Rg4+ deflection (Position 9), Qd2 enables a Bxf3/Nd4 fork geometry (Position 10), Bd7 leaves c4 hanging (Position 1). The moves look reasonable on the surface—developing bishops, moving kings toward safety, connecting rooks—but they all miss the single critical tactical requirement of the position.
analysis.move_pattern: Quiet non-forcing moves (bishop developments, king walks, pawn pushes, rook repositioning) that are typically one-square adjustments or minor piece relocations rather than captures or checks
analysis.why_bad: These moves either remove a piece from a critical defensive function (blocking, guarding a square), place a piece on a square that becomes tactically vulnerable after a forcing reply (usually a check), or simply fail to address the position's one urgent requirement—allowing the opponent a concrete forcing sequence that wins material
sub_patterns: Removing a blocking/guarding piece that allows opponent access to a key rank or square
Placing a piece on an undefended square exploitable after a forcing intermediate move (check)
Choosing passive defense or consolidation when only one active/forcing move holds the position
Pawn moves that permanently weaken structure or remove critical square control

analysis.label: Natural-looking but non-urgent moves that waste a critical tempo when the position demands immediate, time-sensitive action.
analysis.description: This feature activates on moves that appear logical or positionally sensible (centralizing, developing, contesting files, pushing pawns) but fatally ignore a narrow window of opportunity requiring urgent action. In 6/6 analyzed positions, the tag 'tempo_loss' is explicitly identified as the core error. Position 1: Rf1 is a passive rook move when Nf5 was urgently needed before ...g6 restricts the knight. Position 3: Ra5 targets a defended pawn instead of restraining the opponent's king invasion. Position 7: Nc6 develops a piece instead of capturing the tactically vulnerable Nf7 before it retreats safely. Position 8: g4 pushes the pawn instead of advancing the king first (king before pawn principle). Position 10: Ke4 centralizes into a tempo-gaining check. Position 13: Ke5 goes the wrong direction, one critical square too far from the defensive post. Position 14: Rbc1 contests a file instead of executing the winning g4 break. In every case, the opponent uses the gifted tempo to consolidate, restrict, or execute a plan that was previously preventable.
analysis.move_pattern: Various piece types making non-forcing, non-capturing quiet moves in positions requiring immediate specific action
analysis.why_bad: Each move wastes a irreplaceable tempo in a time-critical position, allowing the opponent to execute a plan (restrict a piece, advance a king, consolidate material, create a passer) that could only have been prevented by acting immediately on the previous move
sub_patterns: Passive rook redeployment instead of urgent piece repositioning
Pawn advance before king advance in pawn endgames
King centralization walking into tempo-gaining checks or wrong defensive zone
Development/routine move ignoring a fleeting tactical capture window
Contesting a file when a forcing pawn break was available

analysis.label: Playing a quiet strategic or developmental move while an immediate queen checkmate-in-one exists or is enabled on a pawn adjacent to the king.
analysis.description: In all 6/6 positions, the played move allows an immediate checkmate-in-one by the opponent's queen capturing a pawn near the castled king (Qxg2# in 3/6, Qxh2# in 1/6, Qxb2# in 1/6, Qxg7# in 1/6). The blundering moves are all quiet, non-forcing moves pursuing strategic goals—queenside expansion (b4), piece centralization (Ne5, Ng5), rook development (Rad1, Rac8), or queen repositioning (Qg4)—while a lethal one-move mating threat demands immediate attention. In some cases (Ne5, Qg4, possibly Ng5), the move actively removes the sole defender of the mating square (3/6), while in others (b4, Rad1, Rac8) the threat already existed and is simply ignored (3/6). All positions feature a queen poised on an open diagonal or file targeting an under-defended pawn adjacent to the king, where the king's escape squares are sealed by its own pieces or pawns.
analysis.move_pattern: Quiet non-forcing moves (pawn pushes, knight centralizations, rook lifts to open files) that neither defend the threatened mating square nor block the attacking queen's path
analysis.why_bad: Each move either removes the sole piece defending a critical square near the king or completely ignores a pre-existing queen checkmate-in-one threat, allowing the opponent's queen to capture a pawn adjacent to the king with immediate checkmate
sub_patterns: Removing a knight from f3 that guards g2, enabling Qxg2#
Moving the queen away from a square where it guards h2/g2, enabling Qxh2#
Playing a development/expansion move while an open diagonal permits Qxg2# or Qxb2#
Ignoring a queen-bishop battery targeting a pawn next to the castled king

analysis.label: Endgame moves that pursue secondary plans while neglecting the position's most urgent concrete requirement—whether a hanging pawn, king safety issue, or mating threat.
analysis.description: This feature fires on endgame positions where the player makes a strategically plausible-looking move (piece repositioning, pawn advance, or attacking a secondary target) while completely overlooking the position's most critical immediate demand. In 5/7 positions, the best move addresses a specific tactical vulnerability (protecting h5 pawn in Position 1, blocking f4 square in Position 10, maintaining rook on cutting-off rank in Positions 5 and 7, securing king safety in Position 9), while the played move ignores this need entirely. In Position 4, the error is choosing slow piece maneuvering over a decisive king advance. In Position 5, a check is given that actually helps the opponent reach a superior square. The common thread is that each position has ONE urgent concrete need that dominates all strategic considerations, and the player instead pursues a slower, secondary objective—attacking a passed pawn (Rc2), advancing their own passer (d6), repositioning a piece (Ng3, Rb1, Rc8), or giving an ill-conceived check (f3+).
analysis.move_pattern: Non-forcing or weakly forcing moves (rook relocations, knight repositioning, pawn advances) that address secondary targets rather than the critical immediate need; often pieces move away from optimal active squares to pursue a different plan
analysis.why_bad: Each position has a single dominant tactical demand (protecting a hanging pawn, blocking a mating pattern, maintaining a piece's cutting-off function, or securing king safety) that must be addressed before anything else; ignoring this allows the opponent to immediately exploit the neglected vulnerability, often with devastating consequences
sub_patterns: Rook abandoning active rank to pursue secondary target (Rb1, Rc8, Rc2)
Advancing passed pawn before securing king safety (d6)
Slow piece repositioning when decisive king advance available (Ng3)
Check that creates permanent structural weakness and helps opponent (f3+)

analysis.label: Piece moves away from its critical defensive duty of blocking or controlling an advanced passed pawn within 1-2 squares of promotion.
analysis.description: In 8/9 positions, there is an enemy passed pawn on the 6th or 7th rank (one or two squares from queening), and the move played either removes a piece from its blockading post or fails to establish the necessary blockade. Specifically: Rf8 abandons the b8 blockade of b7 (Position 6), Be6 removes the bishop from the g8/f7 blockade of g7 (Position 9), Rd8+ pulls the rook off a8 blockading the a-pawn (Position 11), Rf7 leaves c7 unguarded allowing c6-c7 (Position 15), Rfb1 fails to blockade d2 with Rd1 (Position 8), Kg2 ignores the a2 pawn about to queen (Position 10), Ka5 fails to play Rh8 blockading the h-pawn (Position 3), and Rd2 allows tactical exploitation relating to the a3 passed pawn (Position 5). The refutations consistently feature immediate pawn promotion or unstoppable advancement once the defensive piece vacates.
analysis.move_pattern: Any piece (rook, bishop, king) moving away from the file or square that blockades/controls an advanced passed pawn, typically lateral or backward relative to the pawn's promotion path
analysis.why_bad: Removing the only piece preventing a 6th/7th rank passed pawn from promoting allows immediate or near-immediate queening, often with tempo (check/capture), converting a difficult but defensible position into a forced loss or mate
sub_patterns: Rook leaves blockading square on promotion file (Rf8, Rd8+, Rf7)
Bishop abandons blockading diagonal of passed pawn (Be6)
Failure to establish blockade when one is urgently needed (Rfb1, Kg2, Ka5)

analysis.label: King (or key piece) advances one rank forward toward the center when retreating to the back rank was essential for survival.
analysis.description: In 6/7 positions, the king advances forward (e2→e3, e2→d3, c8→c7, f7→e6) when the best moves all involve retreating to the back rank (Ke1, Kd1, Kf8, etc.). The 7th position (Rd3) follows the same geometric principle—a rook moves forward to the 3rd rank instead of retreating to d1 to control the promotion square. In every case, the advancing move places the piece on an exposed central square where it becomes vulnerable to checks on open files (especially the e-file and d-file, which are explicitly open in 5/7 positions), diagonal attacks, and coordinated piece assaults. The best moves consistently maintain the piece on the 1st/8th rank where it is sheltered from tactical exploitation. The refutations universally begin with checks exploiting the piece's exposed forward position (Re1+, Rxc3+, Qg5+, Nc5+).
analysis.move_pattern: King moves one rank forward toward center (rank 2→3 for White, rank 7/8→6/7 for Black); retreating to back rank was correct
analysis.why_bad: Advancing forward places the king on exposed central squares intersecting open files and diagonals, allowing enemy rooks, queens, and bishops to deliver devastating checking sequences, forks, or mating attacks that would be impossible against a back-rank king.
sub_patterns: White king e2/d2 advances to e3/d3 into open file
Black king leaves back rank into center (c8→c7, f7→e6)
Piece advances to 3rd rank instead of retreating to 1st rank for critical defensive duty

analysis.label: Playing natural-looking, non-forcing moves in positions that demand immediate tactical or forcing action.
analysis.description: This feature fires on positions where the player selects a routine, passive, or 'natural-looking' move when the position critically demands an immediate forcing continuation. In 6/7 positions, the best move was significantly more active (typically a queen activation like Qe5+, Qa4, Qg4, Qd4, or Qd5), while the player chose quiet development, passive retreats, or slow repositioning. The tagged motif is 'tempo_loss' in 5/7 positions, and 'missed_tactic' appears in all 7 analyses. The blunders share the characteristic of appearing reasonable on the surface (Bd3 develops, Be6 centralizes, Qd1 unclutters, h5 attacks a pawn) but fatally ignore the position's tactical urgency—giving the opponent time to consolidate defenses, create counterplay, or exploit newly-undefended pieces. The average cp_loss of 270 and average of only 1.9 good moves available indicate these arise in sharp positions with narrow paths to maintaining an advantage.
analysis.move_pattern: Non-forcing moves (no check, usually no capture) that retreat, develop passively, or reposition slowly; typically pieces moving to 'natural' squares (back rank, standard development diagonals) rather than aggressive central or attacking squares
analysis.why_bad: These moves waste a critical tempo in positions where the opponent's vulnerability (exposed king, hanging piece, tactical sequence) requires immediate exploitation; the quiet move allows the opponent to neutralize threats, consolidate, or generate counterplay that wasn't previously available.
sub_patterns: Passive queen retreats to back rank when active placement maintains initiative (Qd1, Qf1)
Routine piece development when a forcing tactical blow exists (Bd3, Be6)
Slow flank pawn push ignoring central/tactical opportunities (h5)
Piece move that creates self-inflicted coordination problems (Ndf3 blocking escape, Nxe4 leaving piece hanging)

analysis.label: Playing a non-forcing, non-urgent move (typically a pawn push) when the position demands immediate tactical action, gifting the opponent a decisive tempo.
analysis.description: This feature fires on positions where a player makes a 'reasonable-looking' but insufficiently urgent move—most commonly a flank pawn push (a5, b3, g5, f4 appear in 8/11 cases) or a non-optimal piece relocation—when the position is tactically critical and requires immediate forcing action. In every case, the position contained an urgent need: an undefended piece (positions 1, 10), a looming tactical break (positions 8, 12), a pawn race requiring precise timing (positions 5, 7, 15), or a forcing continuation that would end the game (positions 3, 6). Instead of addressing the critical threat, the player spends a tempo on a slow positional idea, allowing the opponent to execute a concrete tactical operation—whether that's a pin (position 8), capturing a hanging piece (positions 1, 10), a tempo-gaining check enabling a knight maneuver (position 5), a pawn break winning material (position 12), or escaping a mating net (position 6). The average cp_loss of 2036 and only 1.8 good moves available confirm these are high-stakes moments where precision is mandatory.
analysis.move_pattern: Non-forcing moves, predominantly pawn advances (a-file, b-file, f-file, g-file pushes) or king/piece moves that create no immediate threat, check, or capture
analysis.why_bad: The move wastes a critical tempo on a non-urgent operation, failing to address an immediate tactical vulnerability (hanging piece, imminent pawn break, forced mating sequence, or pawn race timing). The opponent exploits the gifted tempo to execute a concrete tactical operation that the correct move would have prevented or pre-empted.
sub_patterns: Flank pawn push ignoring central/tactical crisis
Quiet move allowing opponent's decisive pawn break
Non-optimal check/king move letting opponent escape mating net
Rook move offering exchange when material capture was available
King move to wrong square in pawn race/endgame timing

analysis.label: Playing a preparatory or secondary move when an immediate pawn breakthrough or forcing action was critically time-sensitive.
analysis.description: In 5/6 positions, the best available move was an immediate pawn advance or breakthrough (d5, g4, e6, e7, b4) that exploited a time-sensitive feature like an uncastled king or tactical vulnerability. Instead, the played moves were preparatory (Bf4, Bg4 developing bishops; a3 provoking an exchange; Rh1 repositioning a rook; g6 passively defending; g4 chasing a piece). In every case, the tempo wasted allowed the opponent to neutralize the critical threat: castling to safety (3/6), capturing an undefended pawn (2/6), or exploiting newly created weaknesses (1/6). The analyses label 5/6 positions with 'tempo_loss' as the primary tactical motif. The average cp_loss of 245 reflects that these positions were all at critical inflection points where one specific forcing continuation was demanded.
analysis.move_pattern: Non-forcing moves (bishop developments, rook repositions, edge pawn pushes, defensive pawn moves) played instead of central/advanced pawn breakthroughs
analysis.why_bad: The position demands an immediate concrete action (usually a pawn breakthrough exploiting an exposed king or tactical vulnerability), and the preparatory move gives the opponent exactly the tempo needed to neutralize the threat—castling to safety, capturing material, or launching counterplay against newly created weaknesses.
sub_patterns: Bishop development when pawn breakthrough available (Bf4, Bg4)
Slow prophylactic pawn push instead of attacking (a3, g6)
Piece repositioning into tactical vulnerability (Rh1)
Attacking wrong target when critical advance exists (g4 instead of e7)

analysis.label: Reasonable-looking moves that waste a critical tempo when the position demands one specific urgent action, allowing the opponent to execute a refutation that wouldn't otherwise be possible.
analysis.description: This feature fires on positions where there are very few good moves (avg 1.9) and the player selects a plausible-looking alternative that addresses a secondary concern while missing the position's urgent primary requirement. In 8/10 positions, the analysis explicitly tags 'tempo_loss' as a key factor. The moves look superficially active or logical—advancing pawns for attack (g5, g4, b4, e6 in 4/10), repositioning pieces to seemingly good squares (Nb4, Nc4, Rd8, Re8, Bb2 in 5/10), or capturing material the wrong way (dxc4 in 1/10)—but each wastes exactly the one tempo the opponent needs to execute their plan. The refutations consistently exploit the wasted move: pins become possible (positions 12, 13), forks emerge (position 6), pieces get trapped (position 2), king races are lost (position 5), or tactical shots are enabled (positions 8, 9). The average cp_loss of 324 reflects that these are narrow positions where only the critical move maintains the evaluation.
analysis.move_pattern: Mixed piece types and directions; no consistent geometric pattern. Includes pawn advances (4/10), knight moves (2/10), rook moves (2/10), bishop moves (1/10), and pawn captures (1/10). All are non-forcing moves that don't deliver check or create immediate threats.
analysis.why_bad: Each move wastes a tempo on a non-urgent task when the position has one narrow critical requirement. The opponent uses the gifted tempo to execute a concrete plan (pin, fork, pawn break, piece activation, king march) that the correct move would have prevented or pre-empted.
sub_patterns: Premature pawn advances ignoring development or king safety (g4, g5, b4, e6)
Passive piece repositioning when a concrete tactical shot exists (Rd8, Re8, Bb2)
Piece placement to vulnerable squares that lose tempi when attacked (Nb4, Nc4)
Wrong capture order that surrenders a critical structural element (dxc4 vs bxc4)

analysis.label: Moving a piece to the first/eighth rank in the endgame when active forward positioning is required.
analysis.description: All 7/7 positions involve a piece retreating to the back rank (rank 1 for White, rank 8 for Black) during the endgame, when the position demands active, forward placement. In 4/7 cases, this is a king retreating to the back rank instead of maintaining a blockade directly in front of an opponent's passed pawn (Positions 2, 4, 5, 10 — classic opposition/blockade failures in K+P endgames). In 3/7 cases, a piece moves to the back rank corner area (Bh8, Kh1, Rh8) either prematurely, passively wasting tempo, or walking into a tactical vulnerability. The common thread is that endgame positions punish passivity and back-rank placement severely — pieces need to be actively positioned forward (blockading, centralizing, or creating counterplay) rather than retreating to the edge where they lose tempo, abandon critical squares, or become tactically vulnerable.
analysis.move_pattern: Any piece (King, Bishop, or Rook) moving to the 1st or 8th rank, typically sideways or backward, in endgame positions
analysis.why_bad: In endgames, the back rank is passive and strategically irrelevant — kings must blockade passed pawns by standing directly in their path (not retreating behind), and pieces need active central posts rather than corner retreats that waste tempo or abandon critical squares.
sub_patterns: King retreats to back rank abandoning pawn blockade/opposition (K+P endgames)
Piece moves to h8/h1 corner prematurely, losing tempo or walking into discovered attacks
Passive king tuck to corner when active counterplay is needed

analysis.label: Playing a quiet non-forcing move (typically a king move) when the position demands an immediate forcing pawn break or piece activation as the sole path to hold or win.
analysis.description: In all 6 positions, the player chose a quiet, seemingly natural move instead of executing the one available concrete forcing action. In 4/6 cases the blunder was a king move (Kb6, Kf3, Kd6, plus Rb1's passive retreat), while the correct move was a specific pawn break (c4 in Position 1, f5+ in Position 13, g4 in Position 8) or piece activation (Re6 in Position 6, Bd1 in Position 7, Rd7 in Position 9). All 6 positions share the 'tempo_loss' tag—the quiet move surrenders the initiative, allowing the opponent to execute the critical break or seize the key square first. The positions are overwhelmingly endgames (5/6) with an average of only 1.2 good moves available, indicating razor-sharp moments where one and only one continuation preserves the evaluation. The average cp_loss of 321 reflects that these are 'now or never' moments where the window for the forcing move closes permanently after the passive alternative.
analysis.move_pattern: Single-square quiet moves (king retreats/shuffles, passive rook retreats, wrong pawn advances) - no checks, no captures, no direct threats created
analysis.why_bad: The quiet move wastes the critical tempo needed to execute a forcing pawn break or piece activation; the opponent then seizes that same tempo to execute their own breakthrough, occupy the key square, or neutralize the forcing resource that was available on the previous turn.
sub_patterns: King retreat allowing opponent's pawn break with tempo (Kb6, Kd6)
King blocking critical piece square (Kf3 blocking Bf3)
Wrong pawn push creating target instead of correct breakthrough (c4 instead of g4, a3 instead of Rd7)
Passive piece defense instead of active counterplay (Rb1 instead of Re6)

analysis.label: A check delivered from an intermediate square when a deeper check on the same file (usually to the back rank) would be far stronger.
analysis.description: In 8/9 positions, the player gives check from an intermediate rank (3rd or 6th) when the correct move was checking from the same file pushed to the back rank (1st or 8th). Specific pairings: Qa3+ instead of Qa1+ (positions 3, 4, 8), Qh6+ instead of Qh8+ (positions 5, 13), Qa6+ instead of Qa8+ (position 2), Qxh3+ instead of Qh1+ (position 12), and Rf6+ instead of Rh1+ (position 7). In every case, the back-rank check controls critical escape squares or enables decisive tactical follow-ups (deflection, fork, prevention of interposition) that the intermediate check does not. The average cp_loss of 1325 reflects that these positions are critical tactical moments where only one good move exists (avg 1.1 good moves), and choosing the wrong checking square completely squanders the tactical opportunity.
analysis.move_pattern: Queen (or Rook) check on an intermediate rank (3rd/6th) along a file, when the same piece checking from the back rank (1st/8th) on the same or adjacent file would be decisive
analysis.why_bad: The intermediate check fails to control a critical king escape square (e.g., g1, b1, e3) or allows a defensive interposition (e.g., Qg7 blocking Qh6+), whereas the back-rank check cuts off those resources and enables forcing continuations like deflection, fork, or perpetual
sub_patterns: Qa3+ instead of Qa1+ (fails to control b1 or access d4 diagonal)
Qh6+ instead of Qh8+ (allows queen interposition on g7 or fails to deflect a key defender)
Qa6+ instead of Qa8+ (allows king to escape to b8 instead of forcing it to d7 for a fork)
Qxh3+ instead of Qh1+ (fails to control g1, giving king a safe escape)
Rf6+ instead of Rh1+ (rook exposed to queen capture on open diagonal vs safe back-rank perpetual)

analysis.label: Moves that waste a critical tempo in positions where an advanced passed pawn creates extreme urgency, typically by making irrelevant pawn pushes, misdirected checks, or placing pieces on squares that will immediately be attacked.
analysis.description: This feature fires on moves that squander a vital tempo in time-sensitive positions dominated by advanced passed pawns or promotion threats. In 6/10 positions, there is a passed pawn within 1-3 squares of promotion (h6, f6, d6, e2, h5 pawns), and the mistake involves playing a move that fails to address this decisive threat. The most common error types are: irrelevant pawn pushes on the wrong flank (a3, a5, f5 in positions 2, 7, 8), misdirected checks that drive the opponent's king toward safety rather than addressing the promotion threat (Qc8+, Qh7+ in positions 3, 14), and piece placements to squares where they'll immediately be attacked or are inefficient (Ra2, Be7, Qg6, Ke5 in positions 4, 15, 12, 5). The 'tempo_loss' tag appears in 8/8 fully analyzed positions, and 'passed_pawn' appears in 6/8. The catastrophic average cp_loss of 1131 reflects that in races against promotion threats, a single wasted tempo is often the difference between drawing/defending and immediate loss.
analysis.move_pattern: Any piece type; non-forcing moves (pawn pushes, quiet moves, or checks in the wrong direction) that fail to address the board's most urgent geometric demand — typically a passed pawn's promotion path
analysis.why_bad: In positions where an advanced passed pawn creates a race condition, every tempo is critical. These moves waste that tempo on secondary objectives (wrong-side pawn advances, speculative checks that run out, pieces placed on immediately-attacked squares), allowing the opponent's pawn to promote or the conversion to become trivially easy.
sub_patterns: Pawn push on irrelevant flank while opponent's pawn races to promote
Check that drives king toward safety rather than keeping it exposed to the promotion threat
Piece placement on square immediately attacked by opponent's natural reply
King move away from critical passed pawn's promotion zone

analysis.label: Playing an aggressive or active-looking move instead of the required consolidating/retreating move in positions demanding narrow defensive precision.
analysis.description: This feature fires on moves where the player chooses an apparently active or ambitious option—advancing a piece, centralizing, or counterattacking—when the position demands a specific defensive or consolidating move. In 8/10 cases, the best move was a retreat or quiet consolidation (Be7, Kg6, Be6, Bc2, Kf1, Bf1, g4, Rd7) while the played move sought activity. The positions share extremely narrow margins (avg 1.5 good moves available), meaning the player had almost no room for creativity yet chose the ambitious path. In every case, the active move either abandoned a critical defensive duty (6/10: Qf7 abandoned bishop defense, Qe3 abandoned back-rank coverage, Qb4 ignored kingside tension, Qb6 abandoned dominant centralization, Nb5 abandoned restraining post, e5 ignored piece safety) or placed a piece on a tactically vulnerable square where it could be hit with tempo or exploited (4/10: Bc4 allowing Ne5+Bxc5+, Ke2 allowing Nc3+ fork, Kg4 allowing h3+ check, Nb5 allowing Ba6 tempo). The resulting tactical punishments span multiple motifs—forks, hanging pieces, tempo gains, back-rank threats—but all stem from the same root cause of prioritizing apparent activity over concrete defensive requirements.
analysis.move_pattern: Any piece type moving to an apparently active/forward square (advance, centralize, attack) instead of retreating or consolidating; no consistent geometric direction
analysis.why_bad: These moves either abandon a critical defensive responsibility (guarding a piece, covering back rank, restraining opponent's pieces) or place a piece on a square where it becomes a tactical target, creating concrete vulnerabilities (forks, hanging pieces, tempo gains, checks) that the opponent exploits immediately.
sub_patterns: Queen abandons defensive duty for counterplay (Qf7, Qb4, Qe3, Qb6)
Piece advances to exposed square allowing tempo gain or fork (Nb5, Bc4, Ke2, Kg4)
Aggressive pawn push ignoring existing piece vulnerability (e5, g3)

analysis.label: Moves that are thematically or geometrically adjacent to the winning continuation but miss by one critical square, piece, or pawn file.
analysis.description: This feature activates on moves that pursue the correct strategic idea but land on the wrong specific square or use the wrong unit. In 4/6 positions, the played move is literally one square or one file away from the winning move: Qa3 instead of Qc3 (missing the mate threat), Qa6 instead of Qc6 (failing to control the escape square c7), Kc5 instead of Kc6 (arriving one tempo too late for the stalemate trick), and f7 instead of e7 (pushing the wrong passed pawn). In 5/6 positions, the correct move was nearly identical in character to what was played—same piece type, same general direction, same strategic concept—but the precise geometric detail that made it decisive was missed. The remaining cases (Qh3 instead of Bxg3, b6 instead of Bb2) show the same pattern at a broader level: the right area of the board but the wrong execution. All positions feature very few good alternatives (avg 1.8), meaning the critical resource was narrow and specific.
analysis.move_pattern: Piece moves to a square adjacent to or thematically similar to the optimal square, typically same piece/same direction but wrong file or rank
analysis.why_bad: The moves miss a single critical geometric detail—control of a specific escape square, a one-tempo stalemate resource, a knight's ability to reach a capture square, or a forcing check/mate threat—that transforms the position from winning/drawn to significantly worse
sub_patterns: Queen placed one file away from the mating/dominant square (Qa3 vs Qc3, Qa6 vs Qc6)
King moved one square short of the drawing/winning square (Kc5 vs Kc6)
Wrong passed pawn advanced when the adjacent pawn was the winning push (f7 vs e7)
Superficially aggressive move near opponent's king that misses the concrete tactical blow (Qh3 vs Bxg3)

analysis.label: Playing a plausible-looking move that addresses a secondary concern while neglecting the single most urgent positional requirement in a narrow-margin position.
analysis.description: This feature fires on positions where the player makes a 'reasonable' move that completely misses the one critical action demanded by the position. In 4/4 cases, there were very few good moves (avg 1.5), and the played move addressed a secondary concern: Nxf2 captured material but with the wrong piece (queen was needed, 1/4); Kd7 centralized the king but moved away from the critical queenside sector (1/4); a4 expanded on the queenside when only immediate kingside queen action preserved the advantage (1/4); Re3 repositioned the rook 'actively' while ignoring the urgent need for Kb7 to escape the c-file (1/4). In 3/4 cases, the best move involved a specific piece going to a specific square (Qxf2, Kb7, Qf3/Kb7), while the played move operated in a completely different direction or with a different piece. The refutations consistently exploit the unaddressed vulnerability: trapped pieces (1/4), pawn breakthroughs gaining tempo via checks (2/4), or attacking undefended material given the tempo gift (1/4).
analysis.move_pattern: Various piece types moving to plausible squares, but consistently in the wrong direction or wrong sector relative to where the critical action is needed
analysis.why_bad: These moves waste a critical tempo on secondary operations while the position demands one precise action; the opponent immediately exploits the unaddressed vulnerability (trapped pieces, pawn breaks with check, attacks on undefended material) because the narrow position tolerance (avg 1.5 good moves) means any deviation is catastrophic.
sub_patterns: Wrong capturing piece leaving piece trapped
King moving away from critical sector in endgame
Slow flank pawn push when immediate piece activity required
Rook repositioning instead of urgent king safety move

analysis.label: Playing a superficially logical but strategically misguided move that neglects the position's single most urgent demand (neutralizing an opponent's dominant piece, exploiting a tactical vulnerability, or addressing king safety).
analysis.description: In all 7 positions, the player had a position with one overriding critical demand—typically neutralizing the opponent's most dangerous/active piece or addressing an immediate tactical vulnerability—yet chose a move that pursued a secondary objective instead. In 5/7 cases, the best move involved directly confronting or eliminating the opponent's most active piece (Pos1: f3 challenges Bg4; Pos2: Rxc8 removes infiltrated Bc8; Pos3: Bxh3 eliminates attacking Rh3; Pos4: Ng5 challenges Be4; Pos5: f4 attacks Be3). In 2/7 cases, the priority was king safety (Pos6: Kd8 retreats to safety; Pos7: Qd2/Kg2 consolidates). The blunders instead pursued pawn grabs (3/7: Rxf2, axb4, g4), aggressive piece/pawn advances (3/7: Nb5, g5, Kd6), or passive file play (1/7: Rd1). The average cp_loss of 346 with only 1.6 good moves available confirms these are critical decision points where the position demanded exactly one correct plan.
analysis.move_pattern: Diverse piece types and directions (pawn pushes, piece moves, captures, king moves); no single geometric pattern—unified by choosing a move oriented toward a secondary sector/plan rather than the position's primary tactical/strategic flashpoint
analysis.why_bad: Each move ignores the position's most urgent issue (a dominant enemy piece, a ripe tactical shot, or immediate king safety), giving the opponent a free tempo to exploit the neglected vulnerability—typically resulting in the opponent's active piece/attack becoming decisive or a winning tactical sequence being unleashed
sub_patterns: Pawn grab on a quiet flank while opponent's attack crashes through on the other (axb4, Rxf2)
Generic pawn storm advance missing a specific tactical blow (g4 missing f4, g5 creating weaknesses)
Displacing a key piece from its functional post to pursue an irrelevant plan (Nb5 vacating c3, Rd1 inviting simplification)
Advancing the king toward danger rather than retreating to safety (Kd6 into open center)

analysis.label: Playing a passive, non-forcing move that wastes a critical tempo or removes a key piece from its optimal role when the position demanded immediate concrete action.
analysis.description: This feature fires on positions where a player had a significant advantage requiring immediate exploitation through a forcing continuation (sacrifice, pawn break, or precise capture order), but instead chose a quiet 'reasonable-looking' move that either retreated an active piece, made a slow pawn move, or developed without urgency. In 7/9 positions, the best move involved a concrete tactical strike or forcing sequence (Bxe6 sacrifice in positions 2 and 6, Bxc6 capture order in position 1, d4 break in position 3, h5 advance in position 7, g4 attacking a bishop in position 8). The played moves all share the characteristic of looking natural or logical in isolation—developing a rook (Rad8), retreating a bishop (Bh2), repositioning a knight (Nf3, Nb3), gaining space (b4, g4, e5, c6)—but each fundamentally misreads the position's concrete demands. In at least 5/9 cases, the move specifically removed a piece or pawn from a role that was essential for maintaining tactical pressure (knight leaving d4 in positions 2 and 6, b-pawn leaving defense of Bc4 in position 8, g-pawn abandoning h4 defense in position 7).
analysis.move_pattern: Non-forcing moves: piece retreats (knight from center, bishop to passive square), slow pawn advances, or developing moves when a sacrifice/break was available
analysis.why_bad: The moves fail because they surrender a critical tempo in positions where the opponent can immediately solve their problems, seize the initiative, or exploit a newly created weakness—the 'improving' move actually degrades the position by removing a key support or creating tactical vulnerabilities that didn't previously exist.
sub_patterns: Knight retreating from powerful d4 centralization (Nf3, Nb3) when Bxe6 sacrifice was winning
Pawn advances creating new weaknesses or removing defense of key pieces (b4, g4)
Slow preparatory moves when urgent central pawn break was required (Rad8, c6)
Piece retreat to passive square when active continuation maintained advantage (Bh2)
Wrong capture order forfeiting tactical follow-up (Nxc6 instead of Bxc6)

analysis.label: Seemingly natural 'improving' moves that create critical tactical vulnerabilities by ignoring the position's most urgent concrete demand.
analysis.description: This feature fires on moves that appear logical on the surface (solidifying pawns, centralizing pieces, improving king placement) but catastrophically ignore the position's concrete tactical requirements. In 5/9 positions, f-pawn or d-pawn advances create new structural weaknesses near the king (f6 opening the a2-g8 diagonal, f3 leaving g3 alive while weakening cover, f5 opening the 7th rank, d4 allowing e4! with tempo). In 2/9 positions, king moves walk directly into tactical shots (Kg8 into Ne7#, Kg3 into Rd3+ winning material). In 2/9 positions, piece moves to seemingly active squares either hang material (Be5 captured by rook on 5th rank) or misplace the piece while neglecting the real need (Bc3 instead of Nc3, Qc4 instead of Bg7). The average cp_loss of 1371 and only 2.2 good moves available confirm these are critical moments requiring precision where the player chose a generically reasonable move over the one concrete solution.
analysis.move_pattern: Quiet non-forcing moves (no checks, no captures) that weaken the player's own structure or expose their king - frequently pawn advances (f-pawn or center pawn) or king/piece moves to tactically vulnerable squares
analysis.why_bad: Each move prioritizes a general strategic goal (solidification, centralization, space) while either creating a new concrete vulnerability in the player's position or failing to address an existing urgent tactical threat, allowing the opponent an immediate tactical exploitation (check sequences, piece captures, mating patterns, or pawn breaks with tempo).
sub_patterns: F-pawn advances weakening king shelter or removing key diagonal/rank coverage (f6, f3, f5)
King moves stepping onto tactically exposed squares vulnerable to checks (Kg8, Kg3)
Piece placement on squares that are undefended or tactically exploitable (Be5 en prise, Bc3 wrong piece)
Premature pawn breaks releasing tension in opponent's favor (d4 allowing e4!)
Queen wandering from critical defensive sector (Qc4 abandoning h6 control)

analysis.label: Playing a non-urgent or misdirected move in a critical position where immediate concrete action is required, allowing the opponent to seize the initiative with a forcing response.
analysis.description: This feature fires on moves that waste a critical tempo in positions demanding immediate action. In 9/11 positions, the primary tactical motif or tag is 'tempo_loss' — the player makes a passive, greedy, or misdirected move while the position screams for concrete, forcing play. The consequences follow a consistent pattern: the opponent exploits the wasted move with a forcing response (check, capture, or unstoppable threat) that either wins material or permanently seizes the initiative. Key variants include: passive pawn pushes when pieces need activating (a4, g6, h4 — 3/11), king moves to squares inviting tempo-gaining checks that force retreat (Kb2, Kg3 — 2/11), piece relocations to vulnerable or inferior squares (Ra5, Qe8, Nf3 — 3/11), and wrong-order captures that allow the opponent favorable recaptures (Nxd2, Ne4, Qxc7 — 3/11). The positions average only 1.8 good moves available, indicating these are razor-sharp moments where one specific action was required and the player instead addressed a secondary concern.
analysis.move_pattern: Any piece type or direction; the common geometric thread is that the move is non-forcing (not a check, not capturing a key piece, not creating an immediate threat) in a position where forcing moves were available and necessary
analysis.why_bad: The move wastes a critical tempo in a position where the opponent has a forcing response (check, capture, or decisive threat) that exploits the inactivity — the player addresses a secondary concern while ignoring the position's primary demand for immediate concrete action
sub_patterns: Passive pawn push when king evacuation or piece activity is urgent (a4, g6, h4)
King steps to a square inviting a tempo-gaining check that forces retreat (Kb2, Kg3)
Piece relocation to a vulnerable or easily neutralized square (Ra5, Qe8, Nf3)
Wrong move-order capture that allows opponent to recapture favorably and eliminate key attacking potential (Nxd2, Ne4)
Material greed ignoring critical positional emergency like king safety (Qxc7)

analysis.label: Moves that expose the player's own king to immediate tactical punishment through checks, forks, or mating threats by prioritizing another goal over king safety.
analysis.description: This feature fires on moves where the player makes a seemingly natural or improving move (centralization, material grab, pawn advance) that critically exposes their king to a forcing tactical sequence. In 4/10 positions, the king itself moves to the vulnerable square (Kc2 onto open c-file allowing Rfc8+ mate, Ke2 into Nxd4+ fork, Kf4 into g5+ deflection, Kd3 retreating passively). In the remaining positions, a piece moves away from defensive duties or creates the vulnerability: Rxa4 leaves king on h3 exposed to Qd7+ winning the rook (3/10), Ne4 abandons king defense allowing Qa4+/Bb8 mating net (6/10), Nd5 becomes a target after e4 with Qh7# threats (2/10), d6 invites Nc6 fork (10/10), and Bc3 is a move-order error allowing king escape from a mating net (4/10). The best moves in these positions consistently prioritized king safety first—Kd1 instead of Kc2, Nf1 instead of Ke2, Kh2 before Rxa4, king retreat moves in Ne4 position—demonstrating that the feature detects moments where king safety was the critical factor but was overlooked.
analysis.move_pattern: King moves to exposed central/file squares (e2, c2, f4, d3), or piece moves (knight/rook/bishop/pawn) that leave the king tactically vulnerable to checks along files, diagonals, or knight-fork squares
analysis.why_bad: The move places the king on (or leaves it on) a square where the opponent has a forcing tactical sequence—typically a check that wins material, a fork exploiting the king's placement, or a file/diagonal check creating a mating attack. The player prioritized a secondary goal (centralization, material gain, pawn advance) over the urgent need for king safety.
sub_patterns: King walks onto open file allowing rook/queen checks (Kc2, Kd3)
King moves to square allowing knight fork winning material (Ke2→Nxd4+, Kf4→g5+)
Piece moves away from king defense enabling mating net (Ne4, Nd5)
Greedy capture leaving king on exposed diagonal for check-and-win (Rxa4→Qd7+)
Move-order error in position with exposed king (Bc3, d6 inviting fork)

analysis.label: Non-urgent moves (prophylactic pawns, rim knights, premature development) that ignore unresolved central pawn tension, typically leaving the e5 pawn hanging in Italian Game positions.
analysis.description: This feature fires on opening positions where critical central pawn tension (most commonly d4 vs e5 with a Bc4 aimed at f7) demands immediate resolution, but the player instead makes a quiet, non-urgent move. The most common sub-pattern is the Italian Game after 1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.Bc4 Nf6 4.d4, where the e5 pawn is attacked and requires immediate attention via exd4, d6, or Nxe4—but instead the player plays Na5 (3/15), h6 (3/15), a6 (1/15), Nf6 (1/15), or other non-addressing moves. In 10/15 positions, the e5 pawn is directly left en prise. In 14/15 positions, both kings remain in the center, amplifying the tactical consequences. The refutations consistently involve simple captures of the undefended central pawn (Nxe5, dxe5) often followed by Bxf7+ sacrifices or devastating forks. The remaining cases (g6 ignoring development urgency, c4 hanging a pawn, Kc6/Ke7 king walks, Bg4 exposing f7, g4 weakening the king) all share the same underlying error: prioritizing a secondary objective while an immediate tactical obligation goes unaddressed.
analysis.move_pattern: Diverse piece types and directions (flank pawn pushes h6/g6/a6, rim knight Na5, normal development Nf6/Bg4, king moves Ke7/Kc6) - unified by being non-forcing moves played when the center requires immediate action
analysis.why_bad: These moves waste a critical tempo in positions where unresolved central tension creates an immediate tactical obligation; the opponent simply captures the hanging central pawn (usually e5) and follows up with devastating tactics exploiting the Bc4-f7 diagonal, pins, or forks against the uncastled king.
sub_patterns: Na5 attacking Bc4 while e5 hangs (3 cases - leaves e5 undefended AND exposes f7 to sacrifice)
Prophylactic flank pawn pushes (h6/a6/g6) while d4xe5 tension is unresolved (5 cases)
Developing a piece (Nf6/Bg4) without first resolving central tension, enabling Nxe5 or Bxf7+ tactics
Premature captures (Nxd4/c4) that abandon defensive duties or hang material
King moves (Ke7/Kc6) that forfeit castling rights and create tactical targets

analysis.label: Playing non-urgent improving or repositioning moves while the king faces an immediate tactical vulnerability requiring specific defensive action.
analysis.description: This feature activates when a player makes a 'normal-looking' quiet move—developing a piece, repositioning, gaining space, or making a prophylactic pawn push—while their king faces an immediate or imminent tactical crisis that demands precise defensive attention. In 6/7 positions, king safety is the explicit issue: Re8 ignores Qg3+/Qg7# mate in 3, Na4 removes the only piece blocking a back-rank Qc8+ (leading to mate in 4), Kd8 walks into a Bg5+ double attack winning the queen, b4 allows Bxb4+ with check exploiting the uncastled king, g5 weakens the h5-e8 diagonal allowing Qh5+ against the uncastled king, and Qe2 fails to prevent the ...e4 break that rips open lines against the exposed Kf1. Even the positional case (h3) involves wasting a critical tempo when only active counterplay could hold the position. The average cp_loss of 3007 reflects how catastrophic these 'routine' moves are—they convert defensible positions into immediately lost ones. The positions share extremely low good-move counts (avg 1.6), indicating razor-sharp moments where only specific defensive moves work, yet the player defaults to a generic improving move instead.
analysis.move_pattern: Quiet non-forcing moves (rook development, queen repositioning, pawn pushes, knight maneuvers, king moves) that do not address an immediate tactical threat to the player's own king
analysis.why_bad: The position demands one specific defensive move to address an immediate king safety crisis (back-rank mate, mating attack, check-based tactic, or diagonal/file exploitation), but the player instead makes a general-purpose improving move that ignores the concrete threat, allowing a devastating tactical punishment
sub_patterns: Quiet rook/piece development while facing a forced mating sequence
Removing a key defensive piece from its critical guarding post
Pawn expansion that weakens the king's diagonal while uncastled
King move that walks into a discovered or double attack
Prophylactic pawn push wasting tempo in a critical position

analysis.label: Playing active-looking moves in positions where an exposed king demands immediate defensive attention, typically a king retreat or prophylactic measure.
analysis.description: This feature fires on positions where one side has a critically exposed king and the position demands precise defensive play (avg 1.4 good moves available), but the player instead makes a constructive-looking move that ignores the king's vulnerability. In 7/9 positions, the analysis explicitly notes an exposed king on the moving side. In 5/9 positions, the single best move was a king retreat (Kf7, Kh1/Kg1, Kd1, Kg2, Kc5). The played moves range from piece repositioning (Nc2, Nf4, Qf4, Qa5, Rbc1), to slow pawn moves (b3, f5), to misguided king moves (Kd7) or pointless checks (Nb2+), but all share the fatal flaw of ignoring an immediate tactical vulnerability created by the king's exposure. The consequences are catastrophic (avg 2270 cp loss), with opponents exploiting the neglected king via checks, forks, and forcing sequences that the 'active' move failed to prevent.
analysis.move_pattern: Any piece type; typically moving away from defensive coordination with the king, or moving a piece that was guarding key squares near the exposed king
analysis.why_bad: The position demands immediate attention to king safety (retreat, prophylaxis, or prevention of specific checks/forks), but the played move addresses a secondary concern, allowing the opponent to exploit the king's exposure with forcing tactical sequences (checks, forks, removal of defenders)
sub_patterns: Removing a piece guarding king-adjacent squares (Nf4, Nc2)
Moving queen away from king defense (Qa5, Qf4)
Delaying critical king retreat (b3 instead of Kg1, f5 instead of Bxg4)
Moving king TO exposed square (Kd7)
Pointless check abandoning strong outpost (Nb2+)

analysis.label: Moves that abandon defensive responsibility against an opponent's dangerous passed pawn near promotion, allowing it to advance or queen.
analysis.description: In 9/9 positions, the opponent has a dangerous advanced passed pawn (often on the 6th or 7th rank) threatening promotion, and the move played fails to address this threat. The errors take several forms: removing a piece from a critical blockading/restraining post (Rd8 vacates e8 enabling e6 breakthrough; Rxb8 vacates a8 allowing axb8=Q), placing pieces on passive squares unable to contest the pawn (Re4 abandons control of f8 promotion square; Ne8 becomes a spectator against the h-pawn; Nc5 doesn't threaten the supporting rook unlike Nd6), decentralizing the king away from the pawn's path (Ke5 goes to exposed square instead of Kc7 to recover material; Ke4 leaves d5 allowing a8=Q favorably), weakening structure to enable pawn advance (f5 drops the b6 pawn), or losing tempo that permits the pawn to progress (Ra6 is attacked by Kb7). The 'passed_pawn' tag appears in all 9 analyses, and promotion/near-promotion positions dominate (7/9 have pawns on the 6th-7th rank).
analysis.move_pattern: Any piece type moving away from or failing to engage with the opponent's advanced passed pawn; no consistent geometric direction, but consistently moving AWAY from the critical promotion axis
analysis.why_bad: The moves abandon the one defensive task that matters most—restraining the opponent's advanced passed pawn—by removing defenders from blocking squares, placing pieces on irrelevant squares, or losing tempo that allows the pawn to advance unopposed to promotion.
sub_patterns: Removing a piece from a square physically blocking promotion (Rxb8 from a8, Rd8 from e8)
Placing a piece on a passive square that cannot contest the passed pawn (Re4, Ne8, Nc5)
King decentralizing away from the pawn's advance path (Ke5, Ke4)
Structural/tempo errors enabling the pawn's support network (f5 weakens b6, Ra6 loses tempo)

analysis.label: Moves that create vulnerabilities in one's own position through passivity, retreat, or structural weakening when active play was required.
analysis.description: This feature fires on moves where the player weakens their own position by creating exploitable targets or wasting critical tempi. The pattern manifests in several ways: pawn advances that undermine the king's shelter (g4 in Position 6, g5 in Position 10 both shatter the kingside pawn shield), pieces retreating to passive rim/back-rank squares instead of maintaining active posts (Na7 in Position 1 goes to a vulnerable rim square, Ng6 in Position 5 abandons the crucial e5 square, Kc1 in Position 2 retreats to the back rank), the king walking into danger (O-O-O in Position 7 castles into a ready-made pawn storm, Kh4 in Position 9 allows tempo-gaining bishop checks), and passive developing moves when aggressive exploitation was available (Rcd1 in Position 8 when Qxb7 won material immediately). In 8/10 positions, the best alternatives involved either maintaining structural integrity or pursuing immediate aggressive action. The refutations consistently exploit the newly-created weakness: hanging pawns (6/10), exposed kings (7/10), or tempo gains from attacking misplaced pieces (5/10). The common thread is that each move hands the opponent a concrete target or free tempo that didn't exist before.
analysis.move_pattern: Diverse piece types; king/knight retreating to edge squares, pawn advances toward opponent weakening own shelter, or passive piece placement when active captures/attacks available
analysis.why_bad: Each move either creates a tactical vulnerability (hanging pawn, exposed king, targetable piece) or wastes a critical tempo in positions where the opponent can immediately exploit the new weakness through checks, captures, or pawn breaks against the self-inflicted target.
sub_patterns: Pawn advances that weaken own king shelter (g4, g5, creating hanging pawns or exposed squares)
Knight/piece retreating to passive rim square abandoning key central control (Na7, Ng6)
King moving to exposed square vulnerable to tempo-gaining checks (Kh4, O-O-O, Kc1)
Passive developing move when aggressive forcing move wins material (Rcd1 instead of Qxb7)

analysis.label: Quiet rook moves to non-forcing squares in won rook endgames where checks, captures, or immediate king activation were available.
analysis.description: All 5 positions feature rook moves in endgames (5/5) that reposition the rook to a 'natural-looking' but non-forcing square — no checks, no captures, no immediate threats. In 3/5 cases the better alternatives involved immediate checks (Rh3#, Rb3+, Rb7+, Rf1+), and in 4/5 the best moves either delivered check or directly attacked a critical pawn. The played moves (Rc4, Rc2, Rd1, Rc8, Rb4) all place the rook on open files or ranks that appear active but fail to create immediate tactical pressure. The most catastrophic examples (positions 5 and 8 with ~9000+ cp loss) show the rook moving to a quiet square when checkmate or decisive forcing sequences were available. Even in the 0-cp-loss cases (positions 1 and 14), the moves represent the indirect/repositioning approach rather than the most forcing continuation. The c-file is particularly common (3/5 moves go to the c-file), suggesting a habitual preference for centralized file control over concrete calculation.
analysis.move_pattern: Rook moves along a file to an unoccupied square, no check, no capture, typically to c-file or middle ranks (1st/2nd/4th/8th rank destinations)
analysis.why_bad: These moves waste tempo by repositioning the rook to a square that doesn't immediately constrain the enemy king, attack a critical pawn, or deliver check — allowing the opponent time to flee or create defensive resources in positions where forcing moves would have been decisive.
sub_patterns: Rook to c-file without creating threat
Rook to back rank instead of checking
Rook lateral move to 4th rank instead of king activation

analysis.label: Giving a purposeless check in a winning position instead of making a constructive move that restricts the opponent's king or advances the winning plan.
analysis.description: All 8/8 positions feature a check that accomplishes nothing concrete—or actively helps the opponent—when quiet constructive moves (pawn advances, piece repositioning, creating barriers, king activation) would convert faster. In 7/8 cases, the check allows the opponent's king to reach a better square than it occupied (e.g., Rb8+ lets king reach c3, Rf8+ frees king from h8 to g7, Qe5+ gives king access to safer g2, Re2+ fails to cut off the king with a rank barrier). The tagged motif across all positions is 'tempo_loss'—the checking piece must relocate afterward or the position is objectively worse because the king improved. Positions are overwhelmingly won (avg eval heavily positive/forced mate), making these technique failures rather than game-losing blunders. The average cp_loss of 1170 is inflated by one massive miss (Position 2: Be4+ instead of the mating Bf1+, a 9200cp swing), but typical activations represent 3-93cp inefficiencies that delay forced mates by 3-14 moves.
analysis.move_pattern: Any piece type delivering check (rook, bishop, or queen), typically moving to an open file or diagonal, where the check does not trap or meaningfully restrict the opposing king
analysis.why_bad: The check gives the opponent's king a free choice of escape square (often improving its position), wastes a tempo that could be spent on constructive moves (pawn advances, barriers, piece coordination), and frequently forces the checking piece to subsequently relocate to where it should have gone initially
sub_patterns: Rook check that abandons a superior rank/file barrier position
Queen check that gives king multiple escape routes vs. a more precise check that corners it
Check that can be blocked by interposition when an adjacent-square check would be unblockable
Check in R+minor piece vs K endgames that fails to restrict king to the edge

analysis.label: Moving a piece to a seemingly active but tactically vulnerable square where it becomes an immediate target for the opponent's forcing reply.
analysis.description: This feature detects moves where a piece (usually a bishop or queen) is placed on a square that appears natural or aggressive but is immediately exploitable through a tactical refutation. In 6/9 positions, the moved piece itself becomes directly capturable or attacked on its new square (Rf5 hanging to Rxd5, Bb2 hanging to Qxb2, Qd5+ allowing Qxd5, Bd3 opening the d5-g2 diagonal for Qd5+, Qd7 exposed to the d4 pawn break, Qb8+ stranded far from defensive duties). In 3/9 positions, the piece move creates a critical tactical weakness by vacating a defensive square or wasting tempo when forcing moves were required (g6 allowing Rb6+/e4+, Bb5 being slow when Ne4+ wins, Bd3 allowing f4 pawn break). The average cp_loss of 2328 reflects that these are catastrophic errors, often converting winning positions into losing ones or throwing away forced mates.
analysis.move_pattern: Piece (bishop, queen, or rook) relocated to an open file, rank, or diagonal where it lacks support and faces immediate tactical exploitation
analysis.why_bad: The piece lands on a square where it is either directly capturable by a forcing move, exposed on an open line to a discovered or direct attack, or has abandoned critical defensive duties that the opponent immediately exploits with a concrete tactical shot.
sub_patterns: Queen/bishop placed on undefended square immediately captured
Piece move opens critical diagonal or file for opponent's forcing check
Queen sent too far from king defense allowing mating attack
Slow developing move when immediate tactical strikes were mandatory

analysis.label: Playing a natural-looking improving move that ignores the single critical demand of a narrow position, resulting in catastrophic evaluation loss.
analysis.description: This feature fires on positions where only 1-2 good moves exist (avg 1.6 good moves available) and the player makes a 'reasonable' move that addresses a secondary concern instead of the one urgent requirement. In 7/7 positions, the played move has a clear justification—gaining material (Nxb7, Rgxh2), developing pieces (Rae1, O-O-O), gaining space (c5, f6), or improving a piece (Nd6)—yet each catastrophically fails because the position demanded one specific action: addressing king safety (3/7: O-O-O needed h3, Rae1 needed Kg1, f6 needed Qxf5), preserving a critical piece/advantage (2/7: c5 let the a2-bishop get challenged, Nd6 exposed both knights to pawn forks), capturing the correct target (1/7: Rgxh2 abandoned a dominant g2 infiltration), or avoiding piece diversion (1/7: Nxb7 removed the knight from defensive duties). The average cp_loss of 1631 reflects how narrow these positions are—one wrong priority and the position collapses entirely.
analysis.move_pattern: Various piece types and directions; no geometric commonality. Moves include pawn pushes, captures, castling, knight repositioning, and rook development—all appearing purposeful but misidentifying the critical sector.
analysis.why_bad: Each move addresses a secondary positional concern (development, material, space, piece activity) while ignoring the one critical tactical or safety requirement that the position demands, in situations where only 1-2 moves maintain the evaluation.
sub_patterns: Material grabs that divert pieces from defensive duties (Nxb7, Rgxh2)
Development/improvement moves that ignore immediate king safety crises (O-O-O, Rae1)
Passive pawn moves or piece repositioning instead of active decisive action (c5, f6, Nd6)

analysis.label: Unjustified aggressive pawn advances or piece lunges to g4/g5 that weaken the king position before development is complete.
analysis.description: This feature fires on positions where a player launches a premature aggressive action—most commonly a g-pawn advance (g4 or g5)—while fundamental positional requirements like development and king safety are unaddressed. In 4/5 positions, both kings remain in the center with pieces undeveloped, yet the player pushes the g-pawn or moves a piece aggressively instead of castling or completing development. In 3/5 cases the move is literally ...g5 or g4 (a g-pawn advance), and in 1/5 it's Ng5 (a piece lunge to g5 abandoning f3). The outlier Kc7 (1/5) shares the theme of an ill-conceived active move that ignores positional duty and exposes the king. All moves result in either hanging pawns (4/5 leave the g-pawn or key squares undefended), abandoned blockades (1/5), or fatal exposure of the uncastled king to checks and tactical exploitation. The refutations consistently involve either capturing the undefended g-pawn with tempo, exploiting the weakened king via checks on the opened diagonals, or punishing the loss of central control.
analysis.move_pattern: G-pawn advance (g4 or g5) or piece move to g5, typically in the opening with king still in center
analysis.why_bad: The g-pawn advance or piece lunge weakens the king's pawn shield, leaves material undefended, and wastes a critical tempo needed for development or castling—allowing opponents to exploit via direct captures, checks, or central counterstrikes.
sub_patterns: g-pawn advance to g4/g5 ignoring central tension
Knight lunge to g5 abandoning defensive f3 post
King move abandoning critical blockade duty

analysis.label: Moves that catastrophically ignore a piece (usually a major piece) being en prise—either failing to capture an opponent's hanging piece or leaving one's own piece undefended.
analysis.description: This feature fires on moves that overlook the single most critical tactical obligation in the position, almost always involving a hanging or soon-to-be-hanging major piece. In 5/10 positions, the move directly leaves the player's own queen undefended or capturable by a simple tactic (Kb7 leaves queen to Qxb5, Kg8 allows Bc4+ winning queen, Ng5 permits Rxe6+ winning queen, d3 allows c6 forking knight and queen, Rc1+ puts rook en prise to Bxc1). In 2/10 positions, the player fails to capture an opponent's hanging piece (Nc6 ignores a free rook on e6; Nxc3 captures a rook instead of the hanging queen on g3). In 1/10 cases the move removes a defender leaving a piece hanging (exf4 undefends the d4 knight). The remaining cases involve ignoring a forced mate (f5) or wasting tempo when the attack demands immediate action (Bb2). All positions share extremely narrow margins (avg 1.4 good moves) and catastrophic consequences (avg 1402 cp loss), indicating positions where one specific tactical action was demanded and the player made a 'normal-looking' alternative move instead.
analysis.move_pattern: Diverse piece types and directions; no geometric commonality. Moves appear 'reasonable' in isolation (developing, capturing, checking, advancing) but uniformly ignore the critical tactical relationship between undefended pieces.
analysis.why_bad: Each move wastes the one critical tempo needed to either capture a hanging enemy piece or protect/move one's own vulnerable piece, allowing the opponent to win decisive material (usually a queen or rook) through a simple one-move tactical operation.
sub_patterns: Leaving own queen undefended to simple capture along rank/file/diagonal
Capturing the wrong enemy piece when a more valuable one is available
Removing a pawn defender that was shielding a piece from capture
Playing passive/developmental moves when a forcing capture is available
Giving check that places the checking piece en prise

analysis.label: Playing a non-urgent or generic move in a narrow position that demands one specific concrete tactical action, wasting a critical tempo.
analysis.description: This feature activates on positions where the player makes a 'reasonable-looking' but ultimately slow move—typically a pawn advance or generic piece development—when the position demands immediate, precise tactical action. In 7/9 positions, the best move was a specific piece maneuver addressing the critical tactical feature (Rb4 preparing a combination, Bb7 blocking a diagonal, Ba5 attacking a rook, Bc5 enabling a tactical sequence, Nc5 saving a hanging piece). Instead, players chose pawn pushes (c6+, b4, a5, g3, c5 in 5/9 cases) or generic rook moves to open files (Re8, Rae8 in 2/9 cases) that address secondary concerns. The positions share extremely narrow best-move windows (avg 1.6 good moves), meaning only one or two moves maintain the evaluation. The common thread is that each position has a fleeting tactical vulnerability in the opponent's camp—an exposed king, an undefended piece, an overloaded defender—that requires immediate exploitation before the opponent can reorganize, and the played move gives exactly that reorganization tempo.
analysis.move_pattern: Pawn advances (5/9) or generic rook-to-open-file moves (2/9) or passive retreats (1/9) instead of the one concrete piece maneuver the position demands
analysis.why_bad: These moves waste the critical tempo needed to exploit a specific tactical vulnerability; the opponent uses that tempo to escape (king retreating to safety in 1, knight reaching defensive square in 11, pawn driving away blocker in 2) or to launch a counter-resource that equalizes or reverses the position.
sub_patterns: Pawn push instead of preparatory/attacking piece move
Generic rook doubling instead of concrete tactical sequence
Passive king retreat instead of active pawn break
Premature check before proper preparation

analysis.label: Moves that ignore an opponent's ability to capture a queen (or major piece) with check, resulting in irrecoverable material loss.
analysis.description: In 6/7 positions, the player's queen is left en prise to a capture that simultaneously gives check to the king, making the material loss unavoidable. Position 1: f6 allows Bxd4+ winning the queen along the diagonal. Position 3: Ke6 walks the king onto the c4-bishop's diagonal, enabling Bxd5+ capturing the queen with check. Position 4: Kd1 places the king directly behind the queen, allowing Qxd2# (capture with checkmate). Position 5: Nb4 leaves the e6 rook capturable via Bxe6+ with check to king on c8. Position 7: Qd2 places the queen on a square attacked by the f4-bishop, allowing Bxd2+. Position 8: Bh3 ignores Rxe5+ capturing the queen with check along the open e-file. Position 13: Bxa6 leaves the queen on d2 hanging to Bxd2+ along the h6-c1 diagonal.
