The unifying thread is that the opponent's capture delivers check, making the material win forced regardless of other considerations.
analysis.move_pattern: Any piece move that leaves a major piece (usually queen) capturable by an enemy piece that simultaneously gives check to the king along a file, rank, or diagonal
analysis.why_bad: The capture-with-check element means the material loss cannot be prevented by any defensive resource—the king must move or block, and the captured piece is simply gone. Players focus on their own plans while overlooking that their most valuable piece sits on a line connecting an enemy attacker to their king.
sub_patterns: Queen hanging on diagonal to bishop capture with check
Queen hanging on open file to rook/queen capture with check
King moving onto same line as queen enabling discovered/direct capture with check

analysis.label: Piece (usually queen) moved to an active-looking square that is immediately exploitable by an enemy knight attack, fork, or capture.
analysis.description: This feature fires on moves where a piece is repositioned to a square that appears active but is tactically vulnerable to an enemy knight. In 5/9 positions, the queen specifically moves to a square directly attackable by a knight (Qg6 punished by Ne5 in positions 1-2, Qg6 punished by Nh4 in position 6, Qd3 allowing Ng4 in position 7, Qd3 forked by Ne5 in position 13). The remaining positions share the broader pattern of pieces moved to seemingly active squares that are concretely refuted: Nf7 loses tempo as the knight must retrace (position 5), Ra4 places the rook where it lacks checking distance (position 4), Rg8 abandons defensive duties allowing c5 (position 11), and Kf4 marches the king the wrong direction losing critical tempo (position 12). The common thread is that all moves prioritize apparent activity over concrete calculation, overlooking that the destination square is tactically compromised—most frequently by a knight's unique L-shaped geometry reaching the piece immediately.
analysis.move_pattern: Piece (queen 5/9, rook 2/9, knight 1/9, king 1/9) repositioned to a square that is within one-move striking distance of an enemy knight, typically moving laterally or forward to an 'active' file or diagonal.
analysis.why_bad: The piece lands on a square directly controlled or reachable by an enemy knight, allowing an immediate knight jump that wins material (capturing the queen), creates a fork, or exploits the piece's absence from its defensive post. The player misjudges the destination as safe/active without calculating the knight's access.
sub_patterns: Queen to g6 vulnerable to Ne5 or Nh4 capture/attack
Queen to d3 vulnerable to knight fork from e5 or g4
Piece repositioned to active-looking but tactically refuted square (tempo loss)

analysis.label: Quiet moves (king steps or pawn pushes) that squander a critical tempo in positions where a single tempo determines the outcome between winning and drawing/losing.
analysis.description: This feature fires on positions where the player makes a seemingly reasonable quiet move—typically a king step to an adjacent square or a pawn advance—that wastes the one decisive tempo determining the game's result. In 7/11 positions these are pawn endgames where king positioning and opposition are everything: the player pushes the pawn before the king reaches its critical square (positions 3, 15), moves the king to the wrong square losing the race to a blockading position (positions 1, 2), or makes a cosmetic pawn push instead of the one urgent move (position 14). In opening/middlegame positions (positions 5, 7, 11), the same principle applies: a passive move wastes the tempo needed for concrete tactical action. The catastrophic evaluations (avg ~1963cp loss) reflect that these are razor-thin positions where one tempo is the entire margin between a won and drawn position, or between a lost position and immediate checkmate.
analysis.move_pattern: Quiet non-forcing moves: king steps to adjacent squares (6/11 positions) or single pawn pushes (4/11), typically without check or capture, in positions demanding immediate urgent action
analysis.why_bad: These moves waste the single critical tempo that determines the game's outcome—in pawn endgames, the king fails to reach the decisive square (opposition, blockade, or escort position) before the opponent, or the pawn advances before the king has secured the critical squares; in tactical positions, a slow move surrenders the initiative when concrete action is required
sub_patterns: Pawn pushed before king reaches critical escort/blockade square (king must lead the pawn)
King moves to wrong adjacent square losing the race to defensive/offensive perimeter
Cosmetic pawn push wasting tempo when only king activation saves the position
Passive development move when concrete tactical strike is urgently required
King walks into mating pattern by abandoning safe square

analysis.label: Moves that appear constructive (developing, centralizing, capturing threats, advancing) but fatally undermine the player's own defensive coordination, creating immediate tactical vulnerabilities.
analysis.description: This feature fires on moves where a player relocates a piece to a seemingly purposeful square—only to catastrophically compromise their own position's internal structure. In 3/8 cases, the move removes a piece from a critical defensive duty (Be3 abandons guarding b2, Rc3 abandons covering e2, Ke1→Ke3 walks into a knight fork zone). In 3/8 cases, the move physically obstructs the player's own pieces (Rd2 blocks the king's escape allowing back-rank mate, Rxf5 blocks the bishop's defensive diagonal leaving a knight hanging, b2 immobilizes the rook behind it). In 2/8 cases, the move trades into a catastrophically worse structure (Nxg2 enters a lost pawn endgame, Qh4 abandons concrete material gains for a neutralizable aggressive post). All moves share the quality of looking natural or logical to a human eye—development, centralization, threat removal, pawn advancement—while actually creating the very vulnerability the opponent exploits.
analysis.move_pattern: Any piece type moving to a square that appears active/useful; no consistent geometric direction. Pieces move forward, sideways, or capture—the commonality is relocation from a position of hidden defensive importance to a square of illusory activity.
analysis.why_bad: Each move disrupts a critical but non-obvious defensive relationship in the player's own position—whether guarding a square, maintaining an escape route, preserving a protective diagonal, or keeping a piece flexible—allowing the opponent an immediate tactical blow (fork, mate, hanging piece, or winning simplification).
sub_patterns: Removing sole defender of a pawn/square (Be3, Rc3)
Self-obstruction blocking own king's escape or piece's defensive line (Rd2, Rxf5, b2)
Walking king into fork/attack geometry (Ke3)
Trading into catastrophically worse simplified position (Nxg2)
Choosing flashy aggression over concrete material gain (Qh4)

analysis.label: Natural-looking piece repositioning moves that critically waste tempo or place pieces on tactically vulnerable squares, allowing the opponent an immediate concrete refutation.
analysis.description: This feature fires on moves that appear to improve piece placement or address secondary concerns but fatally neglect the position's most urgent tactical demand. In 8/11 positions, the played piece lands on a square where it becomes immediately exploitable: Rc4 is captured via deflection (Position 1), Ke4 walks into a rank skewer (Position 2), Rf2 allows a forced rook exchange (Position 8), Rd4 is attacked along the fourth rank by Rf4 (Position 14), Kf1 creates a knight fork geometry (Position 15), Bg4 abandons back-rank defense (Position 13), Qc4+ allows interposition forcing a losing queen trade (Position 6), and Rd6 allows a favorable rook exchange into a lost pawn endgame (Position 10). The remaining positions (3, 7, 12) involve pure tempo loss where the opponent gains a critical move to execute a breakthrough (h5 break, Rb7+ tempo, f7+ sacrifice). In all cases, 2-3 good alternatives existed involving immediate concrete action (capturing central pawns, delivering checks on safe diagonals, or placing rooks on squares covering critical entry points), but the player chose the one move that created a geometric or temporal vulnerability.
analysis.move_pattern: Non-capturing piece repositioning (rook, king, bishop, or queen) to a square that appears active or safe but is tactically exposed along a rank, file, or diagonal
analysis.why_bad: These moves prioritize apparent piece improvement over addressing the position's most urgent concrete need, placing pieces on squares where they become targets of skewers, forks, deflections, forced exchanges, or leaving critical squares undefended—granting the opponent a decisive tactical tempo they wouldn't otherwise have.
sub_patterns: Piece placed on square attackable along shared rank/file (Rc4, Ke4, Rd4, Rf2)
King move creating geometric vulnerability - fork or mating pattern (Kf1, Ke4)
Rook abandoning critical file/defensive duty (Rd6, Bg4, Rd2)
Check allowing forced interposition/trade into losing endgame (Qc4+)
Pawn/king move losing critical tempo when immediate action required (e5, Kf7)

analysis.label: Non-forcing piece moves that ignore an immediate tactical threat or abandon a critical defensive duty, allowing the opponent to exploit a concrete vulnerability.
analysis.description: This feature fires on quiet, non-forcing moves (no checks, no captures) played in positions that demand urgent concrete action. In 12/12 cases, the blundering move is a piece repositioning or development move that looks reasonable in isolation but ignores the position's most critical tactical requirement. The most common failure mode is leaving a piece or pawn undefended (Bb7 on an open b-file, Bc4 in the queen's line of fire, Qb3 abandoning the Bg5, Rb8 abandoning c7 defense, Bf6 leaving Ne4 hanging: ~6/12 cases), while the remainder involve abandoning king defense (Qb5 allowing Rxg3+/Qxh4#, Nd2 instead of castling, Qd8 allowing perpetual: ~4/12 cases) or losing critical tempo (Be5 allowing f4, h5 enabling Bxg6 sacrifice: ~2/12 cases). Positions average only 1.9 good moves available, indicating these are razor-sharp moments where only concrete responses work. The average cp_loss of 1114 reflects the catastrophic nature of choosing a 'general improvement' move over the one thing the position demands.
analysis.move_pattern: Non-capturing, non-checking piece moves (any piece type, any direction) that relocate away from a critical defensive square or onto an undefended/tactically vulnerable square
analysis.why_bad: The moves prioritize piece development, centralization, or creating threats over addressing the position's most urgent tactical need—typically an undefended piece, an exposed king, or an imminent forcing sequence that requires immediate concrete response rather than general improvement.
sub_patterns: Piece moves to undefended squares in enemy piece's line of fire (Bc4, Bb7, Bf6)
Queen moves abandoning critical defensive sectors allowing mating attacks or perpetual (Qb5, Qd8, Qb3)
Developing moves instead of addressing king safety (Nd2 instead of castling, h5 weakening shield)
Rook/piece repositioning abandoning defense of key pawns or squares (Rb8 leaving c7, Be5 losing tempo)

analysis.label: Aggressive pawn advances in king-and-pawn endgames that prematurely release structural tension or break interlocked pawn chains when patient king maneuvering was required.
analysis.description: All 5/5 positions are pure king-and-pawn endgames where the player pushes a pawn aggressively forward (c5, h5, d6, g5+, f4) instead of making the correct move, which was typically a king maneuver (4/5 cases: Kf7, Kd7, Kc4/Kc5, or a quiet prophylactic pawn move like a6/a4). In each case, the pawn advance irreversibly damages the pawn structure by allowing exchanges that either free the opponent's trapped king (Position 10: d6 allows cxd6 freeing Black's king), eliminate the weakness the opponent was tied to defending (Position 15: f4 removes the e5 weakness), liquidate into a losing pawn race (Position 13: g5+ leads to total kingside liquidation), create chain-capture sequences exploiting tempo (Position 4: c5 allows dxc5+ then cxb6), or commit a pawn to a square where it becomes a target (Position 8: h5 gives White additional passed-pawn creation methods). The average cp_loss of 2293 reflects the catastrophic and irreversible nature of structural errors in pawn endgames.
analysis.move_pattern: Single-step pawn advance toward center or opponent's position, typically into a capture/exchange, in pure pawn endgames
analysis.why_bad: These pawn advances irreversibly release tension that was either maintaining a draw or providing a winning advantage; in king-and-pawn endgames, the king should do the work while pawns maintain their structural integrity, since every pawn exchange or structural concession is permanent and can create decisive passed pawns for the opponent.
sub_patterns: Pawn push allowing chain-capture with tempo (check)
Pawn break freeing opponent's trapped king
Central tension release deflecting own king from key square
Breaking interlocked kingside pawns creating opponent's passed pawn
Advancing pawn when king invasion was the winning method

analysis.label: Executing a strategically logical move prematurely, skipping a critical preparatory step that leaves a tactical vulnerability unaddressed.
analysis.description: In 6/6 positions, the player makes a move with clear strategic logic (Ng4 attacks e5, Rd7 penetrates the 7th rank, Qa4 defends the b5 knight, d6 supports e5, Rb8 attacks the queen, Kd3 centralizes) but neglects an urgent intermediate requirement. In 5/6 cases the analyses explicitly identify the error as needing to do something else FIRST: save the h1 rook before Rd7 (Position 9), retreat the bishop before d6 (Position 7), castle with Qe2 before committing the queen (Position 5), play Ne4 to the stable outpost instead of the unstable Ng4 (Position 1), and keep the rook defending c7 before relocating (Position 14). The move-order/preparation theme is dominant, with 'tempo_loss' tagged in 5/6 positions and 'move_order' explicitly identified in 3/6. Average cp_loss of 1820 reflects that these premature moves create immediate tactical catastrophes (including one mate-in-1).
analysis.move_pattern: Any piece type moving to execute a known strategic plan without completing a necessary defensive/preparatory intermediate move first
analysis.why_bad: The move skips a critical preparatory step, leaving a piece undefended, a square unguarded, or the king exposed to an immediate tactical exploit that the preparation would have prevented.
sub_patterns: Piece moves to active square while leaving another piece hanging (Rd7 leaves Rh1, Rb8 leaves c7)
Piece moves to unstable/exposed square before securing a safe retreat (Ng4 with no retreat, Kd3 on open file)
Committal move played before necessary repositioning of another piece (d6 before Bb6, Qa4 before O-O)

analysis.label: Moves made by the losing side in positions that are already completely decided (typically 500+ centipawns against), especially simplified king-and-pawn endgames.
analysis.description: This feature fires on positions where the side to move is in a hopelessly lost or resignable position (eval 500+ centipawns against them). In 7/9 top-activating positions, the player was already losing by 500+ cp before moving, with the remaining 2 positions creating such a deficit through the blunder. The dominant position type is pure king-and-pawn endgames (6/9 positions), where minimal material remains and the outcome is theoretically determined regardless of move choice. In these endgame cases (positions 1-4), the cp_loss is negligible (0-2 cp) because multiple moves are equivalently hopeless — the feature fires on the POSITION STATE rather than the move quality. When the feature activates in middlegame/opening positions (3/9), it correlates with catastrophic blunders (355-9332 cp loss) that either create or cement a hopeless evaluation. The common positional elements include exposed kings (9/9), open or semi-open files, weak pawn shields on both sides, and very few good moves available (avg 2.8).
analysis.move_pattern: Any piece type or direction; predominantly king moves in endgames (4/9) or slow pawn/piece moves that don't change the position's decided nature
analysis.why_bad: In most cases these moves aren't meaningfully bad (4/9 have 0-2 cp loss) because the position is already lost. When actual blunders occur, the player makes a slow/structural move (h6, c3, g5, Bg4) ignoring an urgent tactical priority — the already-dire position collapses completely because there's no margin for tempo loss.
sub_patterns: King moves in decided K+P endgames (no winning chances regardless)
Tempo-losing pawn moves when king activity is paramount
Slow positional moves ignoring immediate tactical crises in already-lost positions

analysis.label: Playing a passive, non-forcing move when the position demands immediate dynamic action—either a tactical strike, urgent king march, or counterplay generation.
analysis.description: This feature fires on positions where the player chooses a quiet, 'natural-looking' move (prophylactic pawn push, slow development, king retreat, piece retreat) that squanders a time-sensitive opportunity. In 11/11 positions, the correct alternative was significantly more forcing or active: tactical combinations (Ng4/Bxg2+ in position 4, Bd5 winning the rook in position 8, c6 pawn sacrifice in position 13), urgent king marches toward passed pawns (Kf8/Kf7 in position 6, Kf6 in position 3, Ke5 in position 11), or counterplay-generating moves (h4/f5 in position 14). The tempo-wasting move consistently allows the opponent to execute their plan unimpeded—whether advancing passed pawns, invading with rooks on open files, or exploiting newly undefended pieces. The 'tempo_loss' tag appears in all 11 analyses, and the average 2.2 good moves available confirms these positions have limited correct options that all share the quality of urgency.
analysis.move_pattern: Non-forcing quiet moves: pawn pushes (h6, g5, c3), piece retreats (Nd6, Ke3, Kf3, Kh6), routine development (Bd7×2), or tension-releasing captures (cxb4)—all lacking checks, meaningful threats, or forcing character
analysis.why_bad: The position contains a time-critical element (tactical shot, pawn race, dynamic tension, counterplay window) that requires immediate action; the quiet move surrenders the initiative by giving the opponent the exact tempo needed to neutralize threats, advance passed pawns, invade on open files, or consolidate their position.
sub_patterns: Missing available tactical combination for a quiet move (cxb4, c3, Bd7-position13)
King retreating/moving wrong direction instead of advancing toward critical squares (Kh6, Ke3, Kf3)
Prophylactic pawn move when development/activation is urgent (h6, g5-opening)
Retreating well-placed piece that was restraining opponent's activity (Nd6)
Quiet development when dynamic counterplay (h4, f5) is needed to survive (Bd7-position14)
Starting a losing race instead of blockading/centralizing king (g5-endgame)

analysis.label: Moves that worsen an already-exposed king position by advancing the king forward or removing critical defensive resources, when retreating to safety was essential.
analysis.description: This feature fires on positions where the player's king is already exposed or inadequately sheltered, and instead of prioritizing king safety (retreating, castling, maintaining defensive pawns), the player makes the situation catastrophically worse. In 4/9 cases, the king literally advances forward into greater danger (Kf6 from g6, Kf5 from f6, Kg3 from h3, Kh4 from g5) — all walking toward enemy pieces or into mating nets. In 3/9 cases, pawn moves weaken the king's protection (d5 opens the center with king on e8, h3 wastes tempo with king on e1, f5 removes a critical defensive pawn shielding the back rank). In the remaining positions, moves neglect the urgent king safety priority (Rh7+ wastes tempo when the player's own king needed attention). The best moves in 7/9 positions explicitly involved retreating the king (Kh7, Ke7, Kf7, Kg6, Kh6) or developing toward castling (Nf3). Average cp_loss of 3371 reflects that many trigger forced checkmates.
analysis.move_pattern: King moves one square forward/toward center (Kf6, Kf5, Kg3, Kh4); pawn advances that open lines to own king (d5, f5, h3); checks/moves that waste tempo with exposed king
analysis.why_bad: The player's king is already exposed and the position demands retreating to safety or maintaining defensive structures, but the move increases exposure — walking into check corridors, mating diagonals, or enabling forced rook exchanges into lost endgames. The resulting positions allow immediate tactical exploitation via checks, forks, and mating attacks.
sub_patterns: King marches forward into mating nets (Kf6/Kf5/Kg3/Kh4)
Pawn push opens lines toward own vulnerable king (d5/f5)
Tempo waste with uncastled/exposed king (h3/Rh7+)
Removing defensive pawn that guards critical diagonal or back rank

analysis.label: Playing a non-confrontational, self-focused move when the position critically requires active engagement such as a capture or concrete counterplay.
analysis.description: In all 3/3 positions, the player chose a passive move (advancing own pawn, centralizing king, retreating queen) when the position had exactly one good move that involved active engagement with the opponent's threats. In Position 3, f4 advanced Black's own pawn instead of capturing White's dangerous passed pawn with gxh6 (the only hold). In Position 4, Kc3 pursued general king centralization instead of the precise defensive reposition Bc2 (the only equalizer). In Position 14, Qg8 retreated the queen passively to guard the back rank instead of actively capturing with Qxc3 (the only way to maintain counterplay). All three positions had only 1 good move available, and in each case the player pursued their own plan or safety rather than addressing the opponent's concrete threats. The blunders all carry the 'tempo_loss' tag (2/3 explicitly, 1/3 implicitly), reflecting that the non-engaging move wasted a critical tempo in positions where every move counted.
analysis.move_pattern: Non-capturing, non-confrontational moves (pawn push forward, king sidestep, queen retreat) that ignore the opponent's most dangerous threats
analysis.why_bad: These moves waste critical tempo by pursuing the player's own agenda (pawn race, king centralization, back-rank safety) instead of addressing the opponent's immediate concrete threats, which required active engagement—typically a capture or precise piece redeployment that was the sole saving resource.
sub_patterns: Advancing own passed pawn instead of capturing opponent's more dangerous passer
King move for general improvement instead of unique defensive piece maneuver
Queen retreat for safety instead of active material-winning capture

analysis.label: King moves to a square where it can be immediately checked, with the check winning material, deflecting the king from a critical task, or enabling a mating attack.
analysis.description: This feature fires on endgame king moves (8/10 are king moves) that place the king on a tactically exploitable square. In 7/10 positions, the refutation involves an immediate check that creates a fork/skewer (Positions 1-3: rook checks winning the other rook; Position 5: Nc3+ forking king and rook; Position 9: Ng3+ gaining tempo), deflects the king from a critical blockade square (Position 10: Re7+ pushing the king away from stopping a passed pawn), or enables a mating net (Position 8: Kc3 then d2#). In the remaining 3/10 cases, the king similarly moves to a wrong square but the punishment is positional—abandoning the defensive zone needed to stop an enemy passed pawn (Positions 4, 6, 7). The moves typically appear logical—centralizing, advancing toward passed pawns, or approaching enemy pieces—but ignore specific checking geometry that makes the chosen square catastrophically vulnerable.
analysis.move_pattern: King moves (occasionally rook) to a square within checking distance of an enemy piece (rook along rank/file, knight fork square), especially moving forward or laterally onto the same rank/file as own undefended rook
analysis.why_bad: The new king square allows a forcing check that either wins material through a fork/skewer (king aligned with own rook on same rank), deflects the king from a critical defensive duty (blocking passed pawn promotion), grants the opponent a crucial tempo to activate pieces, or walks into a mating cage
sub_patterns: King moves onto same rank as own rook, allowing enemy rook check that skewers/forks (Positions 1, 2, 3)
King moves to square within knight-fork range of own piece (Positions 5, 9)
King moves away from passed pawn blockade square, allowing unstoppable promotion (Positions 6, 7, 10)
King moves into mating net created by advanced passed pawns (Position 8)

analysis.label: White makes a natural-looking move that neglects a critical defensive requirement for the king, enabling immediate tactical punishment.
analysis.description: In all 4/4 positions, White's king is in a precarious state requiring a precise defensive response, but White instead plays a move that appears reasonable yet fatally ignores the king's vulnerability. In Position 1, Nc3 centralizes a knight instead of the queen (Qc3) that would provide counter-threats, allowing Be3+ invasion. In Position 2, h4 pushes a kingside pawn while the queen is stranded on e8, allowing Qd2 with forced mate. In Position 3, Rxf2 captures material but removes the sole back-rank defender, allowing Rd1+/Rxe1#. In Position 4, Kg2 moves the king to an adjacent square instead of the correct one (Kf2), exposing it to Qe2+ deflection winning a piece. All 4/4 positions had extremely few good moves (avg 1.5), indicating razor-thin defensive margins. All 4/4 refutations involve forcing sequences directly attacking White's king (checks, mates, or deflections). The common thread is that the played move has a plausible positional or material justification but catastrophically overlooks that king safety was the overriding priority.
analysis.move_pattern: Various piece types making moves that appear constructive (centralization, capture, pawn advance, king tuck) but fail to address back-rank, file, or diagonal vulnerabilities of White's king
analysis.why_bad: Each move either removes a critical king defender, weakens the king's pawn shield, or places the king on a square exposed to forcing sequences — when the position demanded a single precise defensive move to maintain king safety
sub_patterns: Removing back-rank defender via capture (Rxf2)
Wrong piece to correct square neglecting counterplay (Nc3 vs Qc3)
King stepping to wrong adjacent square enabling check (Kg2 vs Kf2)
Aggressive pawn push while queen is too far to defend king (h4)

analysis.chip: Critical Tempo Loss in Pawn Races
analysis.label: Non-urgent moves (especially aimless checks or misdirected king moves) that waste the decisive tempo in endgame positions where one specific concrete action is required to win or hold.
analysis.description: This feature fires on positions where a player makes a tempo-wasting move in a critical endgame (10/11 endgames) involving passed pawns (11/11 positions feature dangerous passers). The most common error types are pointless checks that accomplish nothing (Rd1+, Rh8+, Rd2+, Rxh3+, Re5+ — 5/11 positions) and king moves in the wrong direction (Kf2, Ke4, Ke3 — 3/11 positions), though passive quiet moves also appear (Rb8, h3 — 2/11). In every case, the position demanded one specific urgent action — advancing a passed pawn (a2!, b7!), delivering a precise check/mate (Rf4+ fork, Rf1#, Re4#), or reaching a critical defensive square (Kd2 to d1) — and the player instead made a move that superficially looks active or safe but squanders the one tempo that separates winning from drawing/losing. The average cp_loss of 1956 and average of only 1.9 good moves available confirm these are razor-sharp positions where concrete calculation, not general principles, determines the outcome.
analysis.move_pattern: Varied piece types (king moves, rook checks/captures, pawn pushes) that share the property of being non-forcing or misdirected — checks that drive the opponent's king to a better square, king moves away from the critical sector, or quiet moves when a forcing sequence wins immediately.
analysis.why_bad: These moves waste the single decisive tempo in positions where passed pawn races, mating threats, or fortress constructions demand immediate concrete action. The opponent uses the gifted tempo to advance their own passer, escape a mating net, reach a drawing setup, or neutralize the player's key threat.
sub_patterns: Pointless/wrong rook checks that drive the enemy king to a safer or more active square (5/11)
King moves in the wrong direction or to the wrong square in critical pawn races (3/11)
Passive prophylactic moves when a forced tactical sequence wins outright (2/11)
Captures with check that miss immediate checkmate on an adjacent square (2/11)

analysis.label: Playing a superficially active or attacking move that ignores the position's most urgent tactical vulnerability, allowing the opponent to exploit it with a forcing blow.
analysis.description: In 8/8 positions, the player chose a move that pursued a secondary objective (attacking an enemy piece, grabbing material, creating threats, or gaining space) while leaving the position's primary vulnerability completely unaddressed. The punishment in each case directly exploits the ignored weakness: Nc6 fork on the unguarded rook (Position 3), Rxf2+ mating attack after the f2 defender left (Position 5), Rxe7+ exploiting the uncastled king (Position 6), Bxf2+ deflection winning the unprotected rook (Position 7), Qxg6 exploiting the dissipated attack (Position 8), Rxd4! capturing the now-undefended bishop (Position 10), Nxd5+ fork after the f7/d5 guard left (Position 11), and f4 gaining tempo since the concrete Bc6 deflection was missed (Position 13). In 6/8 cases, the move played attacks or captures something (a piece, pawn, or square), creating the illusion of productivity. The average cp_loss of 2579 reflects that these moves are catastrophic precisely because the ignored vulnerability is immediately and forcefully exploitable.
analysis.move_pattern: Miscellaneous piece types and directions (knight jumps, pawn pushes, captures), all characterized by being directed toward a secondary target rather than addressing the position's critical point
analysis.why_bad: The move leaves the position's most critical vulnerability (an exposed king, an undefended piece, or a key defensive square) completely unaddressed, and the opponent can immediately exploit that vulnerability with a forcing tactical blow (fork, deflection, back-rank, mating attack) that was already latent in the position.
sub_patterns: Removing a key defensive piece to attack something less important (Nh4, Ng4 leave f2/f7 unguarded)
Slow pawn push while king is exposed to battery or file pressure (b5, g3, d6)
Aggressive knight sortie ignoring a critical f2/f7 weakness (Nb5)
Premature capture/exchange that leaves own piece undefended (Nxe4, fxg6)

analysis.label: A slow, non-forcing move is played while a piece is undefended or a free capture is available, allowing immediate material loss.
analysis.description: This feature activates on moves where the player chooses a quiet, positional, or preparatory move while ignoring an immediate tactical reality involving undefended pieces. In 5/9 positions, a specific piece is left directly en prise (Positions 2, 8: knight on c6 captured by dxc6; Position 3: opponent's knight on e5 free to capture; Position 7: rook on a1 accessible via check; Position 14: knight on d2 left hanging after its defender moves away). The remaining positions involve closely related errors: passive retreats ignoring forcing moves (Positions 1, 4), moving the king into tactical vulnerability (Position 6), or capturing with the wrong piece destroying coordination (Position 9). The unifying thread is choosing a plan-based or strategic-looking move without first verifying whether an immediate tactical obligation exists—essentially failing to ask 'what can my opponent do right now?' The average cp_loss of 297 reflects the severity of these oversights, and the average of only 1.9 good moves available confirms these are positions demanding one precise response.
analysis.move_pattern: Quiet non-forcing moves (pawn pushes, piece retreats, slow development) when a piece is undefended on the board or becomes undefended due to the move
analysis.why_bad: The move ignores an immediate material threat—either leaving one's own piece en prise to a simple capture, failing to take a free opponent piece, or removing a critical defender—allowing the opponent to win material with a straightforward tactical sequence (usually a capture or check-then-capture).
sub_patterns: Leaving own piece hanging while making a pawn push (e6 ignoring dxc6)
Missing a free capture of opponent's undefended piece (g3 instead of Nxe5)
Moving a defender away from a critical piece (Bc4 unguarding Nd2)
Non-developing flank move allowing forcing check that wins material (b4 allowing Qe5+)
Passive retreat giving opponent tempo to exploit structural weakness (Nce7, Na5)

analysis.label: Making a constructive-looking move while leaving a piece undefended on a square attacked along a diagonal by an opponent's bishop or queen.
analysis.description: This feature fires on positions where the player makes a natural 'improving' move (centralizing, developing, repositioning) while critically overlooking that one of their pieces is undefended on a square directly attacked along a diagonal. In 5/7 positions, the immediate punishment involves a bishop or queen capturing (or threatening to capture) a piece along an open diagonal: Positions 1 and 2 both feature a rook hanging on f5 to Bxf5 from c8; Position 4 has a bishop placed on d5 directly capturable by a queen on the h1-a8 diagonal; Position 11 leaves a rook on e1 vulnerable via Qh5+ deflection along the d1-h5 diagonal; Position 6 sees a rook vacate e4, enabling the opponent's Bxd5 capturing a free pawn. Notably, nearly all tactical vulnerabilities occur on light squares (f5, d5, e6, h5-d1 diagonal), suggesting the feature specifically detects overlooked light-square diagonal threats. The moves themselves appear reasonable (Rf5 looks active, Ne4 centralizes, Bd5 appears dominant) but each fatally ignores a one-move tactical capture.
analysis.move_pattern: Any piece type moving to an active-looking square while another own piece remains undefended on a light-square diagonal attacked by opponent's bishop or queen
analysis.why_bad: The player focuses on their own 'improving' plan while failing to notice that a piece is en prise along an open diagonal — typically capturable for free by an opponent's bishop or queen in a single move.
sub_patterns: Rook left/placed on undefended square capturable by bishop along diagonal (positions 1, 2)
Piece placed directly on a square attacked by queen along long diagonal (position 4)
Piece vacates defensive square enabling opponent's diagonal capture (positions 6, 11)
Wrong recapture creating passivity and enabling diagonal/knight exploitation (position 14)

analysis.label: Impulsive checks (overwhelmingly with the queen) that squander winning positions or drawing resources by failing to achieve any concrete objective.
analysis.description: This feature fires on positions where players deliver reflexive forcing moves—predominantly queen checks—instead of the correct, often quieter move. In 7/10 top positions, the blunder is a queen check (Qg1+, Qe3+, Qe3+, Qxg4+, Qe3+, Qd1+, Qe6+). The consequences are devastating: in 3/10 cases the check allows the opponent to interpose and force a winning queen trade (positions 2, 7, 8 with Qf4 blocking); in 2/10 cases the check from the wrong square lets the king escape a perpetual that a one-square-different check would have maintained (positions 12, 13); in 1/10 the check replaces an immediate checkmate (d7# missed for Qe6+); and in 1/10 a greedy capture-with-check allows a key defensive resource (Qxg4+ allowing ...f5). The remaining non-check blunders (Rg2, Rdg8, Nxe4) share the broader pattern of making an 'active-looking' move that abandons a critical strategic asset. The correct moves were frequently quiet pawn advances (f4+, h4+, c5, f5+, d7#) or geometrically precise alternatives.
analysis.move_pattern: Queen delivers check (or piece makes forcing move) typically along open files/diagonals to central squares, especially e3, g1, g4, d1, e6
analysis.why_bad: The checks are geometrically imprecise—they either allow the opponent to interpose with a simplifying queen trade, permit the king to escape to a safe square breaking a perpetual mechanism, or waste the critical tempo needed for a decisive quiet move (pawn break, promotion, or proper piece placement).
sub_patterns: Queen check allows opponent to interpose and force winning queen trade (Qf4 blocks)
Check from wrong square lets king escape perpetual check net
Flashy queen check instead of quiet pawn advance that delivers checkmate/wins material
Greedy capture-with-check that allows key defensive pawn resource
Active-looking piece move that abandons critical file control or defensive duty

analysis.label: King moves one square to a more exposed position, walking into checks or mating patterns while ignoring critical tactical needs.
analysis.description: This feature activates on positions where the player advances their king (5/7 are king moves) to a square that appears to offer escape or activity but actually increases exposure to tactical blows. In 4/7 positions, the king advances along the h-file (Kh1→h2, Kh2→h3, Kh6→h5), while Kb6 advances into a pawn-checkmate net. The moves waste a critical tempo when urgent action is required — exchanging queens (positions 1-2), saving a hanging piece (position 6/Kh3), or maintaining active defense against promotion (Kh5). In all cases, the king lands on a square vulnerable to diagonal/file checks that enable opponent coordination (Re2 invasions, Rd7 back-rank control, or Qf3+ tempo gains). The f5 pawn push (1/7) and Qc2 (0 cp_loss outlier) loosely share the 'quiet move ignoring critical threat' pattern. Average cp_loss of 5400 reflects that 4/7 positions transition directly to forced checkmate.
analysis.move_pattern: King advances one square forward (typically along h-file or toward board edge) to a more exposed square
analysis.why_bad: The king move wastes the critical tempo needed to address an urgent tactical threat (mating attack, hanging piece, unstoppable promotion), while placing the king on a square where it becomes a target for forcing checks that enable decisive piece coordination by the opponent.
sub_patterns: Kh1→h2 walking into Qg3+/Qf4+ diagonal checks enabling Re2 invasion
Kh2→h3 leaving rook en prise on d5
King advancing into pawn+rook mating cage (Kb6 into a5#)
King advancing to exposed square enabling tempo-gaining checks before promotion (Kh5)

analysis.label: Plausible-looking moves that waste decisive tempo in positions demanding one specific urgent action.
analysis.description: This feature activates on moves that appear reasonable or even active on the surface but catastrophically miss the position's singular critical demand. In 3/3 positions, the player had an extremely narrow window (avg 1.3 good moves) where one specific action was required: king advancement in a Q vs R endgame (Position 1), immediate central resolution to protect a hanging pawn (Position 11), or a precise queen check leading to forced mate (Position 14). Instead, each player chose a move with superficial appeal—a queen repositioning that looked active, a prophylactic pawn push that looked prudent, a forcing capture with check that looked strong—but all fundamentally wasted the critical tempo the position demanded. The tag 'tempo_loss' appears in 3/3 analyses, and 'missed_tactic' in 2/3. The extremely high average cp_loss (3356) reflects positions where the gap between the one right move and the next-best option is enormous.
analysis.move_pattern: Various piece types making seemingly active/useful moves (queen repositioning, prophylactic pawn push, forcing capture with check) that are NOT the position's one critical continuation
analysis.why_bad: Each move ignores the position's most urgent tactical or strategic demand in favor of a superficially appealing alternative, squandering a narrow window where only one move preserves the full advantage—resulting in massive evaluation drops because the opponent gains time to reorganize or escape.
sub_patterns: Queen repositioning when king activity is required
Prophylactic flank pawn move when central tension must be resolved immediately
Materialistic capture/check when a more geometric forcing sequence delivers checkmate

analysis.label: Playing a superficially reasonable move (material grab, prophylactic, or passive repositioning) that wastes a critical tempo when the position demands immediate action on the dominant factor.
analysis.description: All three positions share a pattern where the player ignores the most urgent element in the position in favor of a 'normal-looking' move. In Position 3 (3/3), Black plays Ra4 targeting material/defense rather than addressing White's imminent g4 pawn break with king activation or maintaining the rook on the critical second rank. In Position 5 (3/3), White plays the prophylactic h3 instead of exploiting a hanging knight on a6 that can be won immediately via Bxa6. In Position 9 (3/3), Black captures a rook with bxc5 without eliminating the dominant knight on d6, allowing a devastating Qxe6+ tactical sequence. Each move appears logical in isolation—defending material, preventing pins, or winning a piece—but catastrophically fails to address the single most critical factor (dynamic counterplay, a tactical win, or a dominant centralized piece). The tempo wasted gives the opponent time to either escape punishment or launch a decisive counter-blow.
analysis.move_pattern: Varied piece types (rook lateral, pawn push, pawn capture) sharing the quality of addressing a secondary concern rather than the position's critical tactical/strategic demand
analysis.why_bad: The move wastes a tempo on a secondary concern while the position has one critical factor (a hanging piece, a dominant enemy piece, or imminent dynamic counterplay) that demands immediate attention—the lost tempo allows the opponent to either save their problem piece, launch counterplay, or execute a tactical combination.
sub_patterns: Prophylactic pawn push ignoring a hanging piece
Rook repositioning ignoring king activation urgency
Material grab ignoring a dominant centralized piece that enables tactics

analysis.label: Playing a slow, passive, or peripheral move in a position demanding one specific urgent action, losing a critical tempo.
analysis.description: This feature fires on moves that squander a decisive tempo by choosing a quiet, preparatory, or peripheral action when the position demands immediate concrete play. In 12/13 positions the analysis identifies 'tempo_loss' as a core factor. The positions typically have very few good options (avg 1.8 good moves), indicating precision-demanding moments. The blunders share a common structure: the player defaults to a 'natural-looking' move—retreating a piece (Ba1, Bd8, Ke3), pushing a preparatory pawn (a6, h3, c3), capturing peripheral material (Kxg3, Kxf4, Rxc7), or making a slow positional maneuver (Kd6, Rd6)—while ignoring the single urgent requirement: an immediate pawn break (d4 in pos 2, b5 in pos 10), king activation toward the critical sector (Kd6 in pos 3, Kg5 in pos 14), advancing the correct passed pawn (e6 in pos 5), or prophylaxis before committing (Kf2 in pos 15). The average cp_loss of 225 reflects that these are not subtle inaccuracies but position-transforming errors where one wasted move allows the opponent to establish a fortress, promote a pawn, invade with the king, or execute a tactical blow.
analysis.move_pattern: Retreats, preparatory pawn pushes, or peripheral captures—moves directed away from or orthogonal to the critical zone of the position
analysis.why_bad: The position has exactly one urgent demand (a pawn break, king race, counterplay creation, or prophylaxis) and only 1-2 moves satisfy it; the played move addresses a secondary concern, granting the opponent a free tempo to establish a decisive advantage (fortress, promotion, king invasion, or tactical shot)
sub_patterns: Passive piece retreat to inactive square (Ba1, Bd8, Ke3, Rd6)
Preparatory/defensive pawn move instead of breakthrough (a6, h3, c3)
Capturing peripheral material while king deflects from critical pawn (Kxg3, Kxf4, Rxc7)
Advancing wrong passed pawn or wrong priority (a6 instead of e6, f5 instead of b5)

analysis.label: Playing a quiet, repositioning, or misdirected move in a critical position where only one precise forcing continuation maintains the evaluation.
analysis.description: This feature fires on positions where the player chose a plausible-looking but fundamentally wrong move in a position with very few good alternatives (avg 1.5 good moves). In 8/10 cases, the played move was a quiet or non-forcing alternative (king retreat, piece repositioning, slow pawn push) when the position demanded immediate tactical action—a precise capture, a check with the correct piece, or an urgent pawn advance. Several positions show the 'wrong piece' error: Qf4+ instead of Rf4+ (Position 2), b5 instead of Rb5 (Position 10), Bf2 instead of Rf2+ (Position 11)—where the player addressed the right concept but with the wrong executor. In other cases, the player pursued a secondary strategic idea while the position demanded immediate confrontation of the primary threat: Rfb1 abandoning kingside defense (Position 5), Ne7 blockading instead of capturing (Position 9), e3 advancing when Bxd5 was the critical tactical resource (Position 8). The catastrophic average cp_loss of 1174 reflects how unforgiving these positions are—they are 'one-move positions' where missing the single critical resource is devastating.
analysis.move_pattern: Quiet piece repositioning moves (king retreats, bishop/queen relocations, non-forcing pawn pushes) or checks/captures with the wrong piece, typically in positions requiring an immediate forcing tactical solution
analysis.why_bad: These moves surrender the critical tempo needed to address the position's primary tactical demand—whether that's a pawn race, a mating attack, a promotion threat, or a forcing combination—allowing the opponent to execute their plan unopposed while the played move addresses a secondary or irrelevant concern.
sub_patterns: Wrong piece delivers check/occupies key square (Qf4+ vs Rf4+, b5 vs Rb5, Bf2 vs Rf2+)
Passive retreat when immediate pawn advance creates decisive counterplay (Kf2 vs g5, Ke4 vs Kf5)
Slow repositioning when a forcing capture/combination exists (e3 vs Bxd5, Ne7 vs Bxg7, Qe3 vs Ne4)
Removing key defensive piece from critical sector (Rfb1 leaving kingside undefended)

analysis.label: Playing a seemingly natural or logical move one tempo too early, before the necessary preparatory forcing move or without considering the opponent's immediate tactical response.
analysis.description: This feature fires on moves that execute a reasonable plan at the wrong moment. In 4/9 positions, the player needed to play an intermediate forcing move first (Position 1: checks before Rxf8; Position 6: Re6+ before Kc2; Position 7: h4+ before Re3; Position 8: g2 before e1=Q). In 3/9 positions, the player ignored the opponent's devastating forcing reply (Position 7: f4+ forking king and rook; Position 9: Qd1+ winning the hanging rook on a4; Position 10: Nxe4 followed by Ng5 gaining tempo on the queen). The remaining positions involve passive/aimless moves when active forcing continuations were required (Position 3: Qf1 retreat losing initiative; Position 4: Rc5 abandoning a dominant square). The common thread is that all moves are motivated by general chess logic—capturing material (Rxf8, Rxa4), promoting (e1=Q), centralizing (Ne4, Re3, Rc5), seeking safety (Qf1, Kc2)—but ignore the specific tactical pulse of the position requiring precise calculation of forcing sequences.
analysis.move_pattern: Piece moves to apparently natural/active square (captures, promotions, centralizations, retreats) without regard for opponent's immediate forcing reply or without necessary preparatory intermediate move
analysis.why_bad: The moves are punished because they either skip a critical intermediate forcing move (check, pawn advance) that was needed to make the plan work, or they leave pieces/positions vulnerable to the opponent's immediate tactical response (forks, checks winning material, captures with tempo, promotional recaptures).
sub_patterns: Capturing/promoting before deflecting the opponent with an intermediate check
Placing pieces on squares vulnerable to pawn forks or discovery
Passive retreats surrendering initiative when forcing moves maintain advantage
Material captures leaving the capturing piece undefended to subsequent checks

analysis.label: Moves that pursue an active plan while leaving a rook (or major piece) undefended, allowing immediate tactical exploitation via capture, fork, or pin.
analysis.description: This feature fires on moves where the player focuses on their own goal (capturing, activating, or repositioning) while critically neglecting the safety of a piece—most often a rook. In 3/7 positions (Qxd3, Qd7, Qb6), the queen moves and leaves a rook on the a-file completely undefended, allowing the opponent's queen to capture it immediately. In 2/7 positions (Rxf2, Re3), a rook is placed on a square where it immediately falls to a knight fork exploiting its geometric relationship with the queen. In 1/7 positions (Qxg2), a queen captures a pawn but lands on a diagonal where it is pinned and lost. The outlier (h6) loses tempo allowing the opponent to win material with Nxd5. The common thread is that the player executes a 'natural-looking' or 'active' move while missing that a piece—predominantly a rook—is left tactically exploitable through elementary tactics the opponent can execute in one move.
analysis.move_pattern: Queen or rook moves to a seemingly active square (often a capture or centralization), leaving a rook undefended on its original square or placing a rook/queen where it becomes immediately exploitable
analysis.why_bad: The move neglects a critical defensive requirement—keeping a major piece defended—while pursuing an active idea that provides insufficient compensation for the material lost. The opponent exploits the hanging piece through simple capture, knight fork, or pin, typically winning a full exchange or more.
sub_patterns: Queen captures/moves leaving rook on a-file capturable by opponent's queen (3/7)
Rook placed on undefended square where knight fork wins it against the queen (2/7)
Piece captured/placed on diagonal creating pin vulnerability (1/7)
Tempo-wasting move allowing opponent to win material with gain of tempo (1/7)

analysis.label: Moving the king backward or away from a critical passed pawn instead of advancing to escort, blockade, or support it.
analysis.description: In 5/5 positions, there is a critical passed pawn that demands the king's active participation (either to promote it or blockade it). The mistake in each case involves retreating or misdirecting the king's energy: Kg3 retreats from f4 away from the e6 pawn (Position 1), Kf1 retreats from f2 away from the d5 pawn (Position 2), Rf2 physically blocks the king from advancing through f2 to escort its escape toward e3 (Position 3), Bg7 wastes a tempo on a pointless bishop move when Kd3 was needed to blockade the d4 pawn (Position 4), and Kh5 moves the king away from the f3 passed pawn instead of toward it via h3 or f4 (Position 5). In 4/5 cases the best move involved direct king advancement toward the passed pawn; in 1/5 the king needed to advance for safety but was blocked. All positions punish the error through tempo loss that allows the opponent to activate pieces or neutralize the pawn.
analysis.move_pattern: King (or piece blocking king) moves backward/laterally away from a passed pawn rather than toward it; typically one rank retreating or sideways instead of advancing toward the 8th/1st rank or toward the pawn
analysis.why_bad: In endgames and late middlegames with passed pawns, the king is the primary escort/blockader; retreating loses a critical tempo that allows the opponent to activate a rook behind the pawn, reposition a knight to a dominant outpost, or neutralize the pawn's promotion threat entirely
sub_patterns: King retreats one rank instead of advancing toward own passed pawn
Piece blocks king's forward escape/advance route
Tempo-wasting non-king move when king centralization is urgent

analysis.label: Playing a quiet, routine-looking developing or positional move that fatally ignores an immediate concrete tactical vulnerability in the position.
analysis.description: This feature fires on moves that appear reasonable from a general principles standpoint (piece development, pawn structure improvement, piece repositioning) but catastrophically overlook an urgent tactical demand. In 6/8 positions, at least one king remains in the center, and the ignored vulnerability is often exploitable on the very next move. The pattern spans quiet pawn pushes to the queenside (b3, b6, c5 in 3/8), natural-looking piece developments that block retreat squares or leave pieces/pawns hanging (Be7 twice in 2/8), piece relocations away from critical defensive duties (Nb6 in 1/8), and queen moves to exposed squares (Qf5, Qc6 in 2/8). In every case, multiple safe alternatives existed (avg 2.6 good moves), yet the player chose a move that follows long-term logic while ignoring that the opponent has an immediate tactical blow—discovered attacks (2/8), hanging pieces (1/8), trapped pieces (1/8), or exploitation of exposed kings (3/8).
analysis.move_pattern: Non-forcing, quiet moves (no checks/captures): pawn pushes to b/c-file, bishop developments to e7, knight relocations to queenside, queen moves to exposed central squares
analysis.why_bad: Each move ignores a concrete one-move tactical refutation the opponent has available—whether a discovered attack on an undefended diagonal, a piece capture exploiting removed defenders, a tempo-gaining developing move that attacks the misplaced piece, or a pawn advance that traps/exploits a badly placed queen. The player follows 'autopilot' positional logic instead of calculating the immediate tactical consequences.
sub_patterns: Quiet pawn push (b3/b6/c5) when king safety or piece defense demands immediate action
Bishop development (Be7) that blocks retreat squares or leaves key pawns/pieces undefended
Piece relocation to queenside (Nb6/Qc6) abandoning critical defensive duties or inviting tempo-gaining attacks
Queen placed on exposed square (Qf5/Qc6) vulnerable to discovered or direct attack

analysis.label: Natural-looking moves that catastrophically blunder in positions demanding concrete precision, where the player pursues a general idea while ignoring an immediate tactical vulnerability or missed opportunity.
analysis.description: This feature fires on positions where very few moves work (avg 1.8 good moves) and the player commits a large blunder (avg 408 cp_loss) by playing a move that looks strategically reasonable but has a concrete tactical flaw. In 9/9 positions, the played move pursues a 'self-improving' plan—attacking a piece (f5), supporting promotion (Kf2), normalizing the king (Ke1), sacrificing for attack (Rxg6+), centralizing (Re6, Ne5), chasing a piece (g3), developing (Bf4), or creating pressure (Qa3)—while ignoring the opponent's concrete counter-resources. The refutations are typically simple tactical responses: capturing newly-undefended material (4/9), exploiting tempo to establish forks or blockades (3/9), or counter-attacking exposed pieces (2/9). The critical commonality is the mismatch between a position demanding ONE precise move and the player defaulting to a 'plausible' alternative.
analysis.move_pattern: All piece types represented (pawn, king, rook, bishop, queen, knight); no geometric consistency. Moves are characterized by being proactive/improving rather than responsive to concrete threats.
analysis.why_bad: Each move prioritizes a general strategic goal (develop, centralize, attack, advance) over the specific concrete demand of the position, creating or failing to prevent an immediate tactical exploitation. The opponent's refutation is always a straightforward concrete response (capture, fork, advance, blockade) that the player's move either enabled or failed to prevent.
sub_patterns: Pawn advances that create immediate tactical weaknesses (f5 weakening g5, g3 opening own king)
King moves to natural-looking squares that allow forks or lose critical tempo (Ke1 allowing Nf3+, Kf2 enabling blockade)
Piece moves that ignore concrete winning/saving tactics in favor of generic improvement (Bf4 missing Bb5, Qa3 abandoning defense, Re6 misplacing rook)
Unsound sacrifices in positions where quiet moves are winning (Rxg6+ when e6 was crushing)
Knight centralization to unstable outpost immediately challenged by pawns (Ne5 met by d4)

analysis.label: Seemingly purposeful but non-constructive moves that waste critical tempo or create new weaknesses when the position demanded active, constructive play.
analysis.description: This feature fires on moves that appear to serve a logical purpose (gaining space, repositioning, prophylaxis) but actually squander tempo on secondary concerns while ignoring the position's primary demand. In 7/8 positions, tempo loss is explicitly identified as a key factor. The good alternatives consistently involve active piece play—development (positions 1, 6), piece centralization (positions 2, 7, 8), king activation (position 3), or advancing concrete plans (position 5). Instead, the played moves address imagined threats or secondary goals: g5 and f6 'reinforce' when development is needed, Kh8 and Kb8 retreat from phantom dangers, Ra4 abandons a dominant position for a superficially active one, Bg4 repositions to a useless square, e5 grabs space while creating permanent holes, and Qc6 centralizes into a tactical trap. In 6/8 cases, the blunder directly creates a new vulnerability that the opponent exploits (diagonal weakness, weakened squares, pin, corner entrapment). The average 2.2 good alternatives confirms these aren't forced situations—the player simply chose plausible-looking non-solutions over genuinely constructive moves.
analysis.move_pattern: Non-capturing, non-checking moves that don't improve piece coordination—pawn pushes to gain space (g5, f6, e5), piece repositioning sideways/backward (Bg4, Ra4, Qc6), or king retreats (Kb8, Kh8)
analysis.why_bad: These moves waste a critical tempo on a non-essential or counterproductive gesture, allowing the opponent to seize the initiative by exploiting either pre-existing vulnerabilities (uncastled king, passed pawn race) or new weaknesses created by the move itself (holes, pins, corner traps).
sub_patterns: Weakening pawn pushes instead of developing (g5, f6, e5 with king uncastled or when piece play is needed)
Passive king retreats when active play or plan execution is required (Kb8, Kh8)
Piece repositioning that abandons a strong post for a superficially active but actually passive square (Bg4, Ra4)
Queen placement that creates tactical vulnerability on shared diagonal with king (Qc6)

analysis.label: A piece voluntarily leaves a square where it performs an essential guarding or restraining function, moving to a nearby but less effective square.
analysis.description: In 6/7 positions, the moved piece was actively defending a critical square or pawn (Ng6 abandoned d7 control enabling Rd7+; Qb7 abandoned e5 defense enabling Nxe5; Be7 abandoned d4/central control enabling d4 break; Rb8 abandoned e8 defense of f8 knight enabling Bd6; Be3 placed bishop on a square vulnerable to d4 tempo; Bd3 lost tempo allowing knight activation via Ng3-Nh5-Nf4). In every case, the piece moved to a seemingly reasonable adjacent square—often looking active or purposeful—but the original square's function was far more important than whatever the new square offered. The opponent immediately exploited the abandoned function, typically within 1-2 moves. The average cp_loss of 1473 (inflated by the queen blunder) reflects how catastrophic it is to voluntarily surrender a critical post. All 7 positions featured alternatives that maintained the piece's key function while achieving equal or better coordination.
analysis.move_pattern: Short-range piece relocation (1-2 squares) away from a square that guards a critical pawn, controls an invasion square, or restrains opponent's pieces
analysis.why_bad: The piece was performing an irreplaceable defensive or restraining function on its original square; no other piece can substitute, so the opponent immediately exploits the newly unguarded point (capturing an undefended pawn, invading through an uncontrolled square, or gaining decisive tempo against the relocated piece)
sub_patterns: Queen leaves diagonal that defends a central pawn (Qb7 abandoning e5)
Knight leaves outpost that controls key invasion square (Ng6 abandoning d7)
Bishop retreats from active post enabling opponent's central break (Be7, Be3)
Rook shifts files abandoning back-rank defense of a piece (Rb8 leaving e8)
Bishop placed on wrong square losing critical tempo in endgame (Bd3 vs Be2)

analysis.label: Player repositions a piece to an apparently active square instead of executing the urgent pawn break, prophylactic defense, or forcing continuation the position demands.
analysis.description: In 8/10 positions, the player moved a piece (bishop, queen, or rook) to what appeared to be an active or developing square, when the position critically required a concrete action — most commonly a pawn break (d5 in positions 3 and 14, f5 in position 8, b6 in position 7) or development with tempo forcing the opponent's hand (Nc3 in positions 5 and 11). The played moves look 'natural' by general principles (Bg4 'attacks' a knight, Bc4 'develops actively,' Qe3 'centralizes,' Be6 'controls squares,' Rfc8 'seizes an open file') but each misses the position's specific urgent demand. In 7/10 cases the analyses explicitly tag 'tempo_loss' because the opponent gains initiative through a forcing response — whether a tempo-gaining check (Bf7+ after Qc5, Bb7+ after Be6, Qh5+ after Nxe4), a fork (Nd5 after Qe3), a piece leap with threats (Ng5 after Bg4), or simply capturing undefended material (Qxg2 after Bc4). The average cp_loss of 253 reflects how dramatically these 'reasonable-looking' moves squander positions that demanded precision.
analysis.move_pattern: Minor piece or queen developed/repositioned to an apparently active square (usually bishop to diagonal or queen to central/attacking square), rather than executing a pawn advance or concrete forcing move
analysis.why_bad: The piece move wastes critical tempo on illusory activity while the position demands a concrete action (pawn break, king safety move, or file seizure); the opponent exploits the wasted tempo with a forcing response — check, fork, or capture of newly-undefended material — seizing the initiative that should have belonged to the moving side.
sub_patterns: Bishop development that leaves a key square/diagonal undefended (Bc4 leaving g2, Be6 exposing a8-h1 diagonal or blocking e-file)
Queen repositioning that walks into a knight fork or removes defensive coverage (Qe3 allowing Nd5, Qc5 allowing Bf7+)
Piece 'attack' that gives opponent tempo via retreat-with-threats (Bg4 allowing Ng5 with initiative)
Moving the wrong rook or piece away from the critical file needed for the decisive pawn break (Rfc8 when f5 was needed)
Pawn capture/push that removes a key defender when pawn break was needed (Nxe4 removing f6-knight, c3 blocking Nc3)

analysis.label: Plausible-looking moves in positions with very few viable alternatives that create immediate tactical exploitation by the opponent.
analysis.description: This feature fires on positions where (1) very few moves maintain the evaluation (avg 1.8 good moves), creating a critical decision point, and (2) the player selects a 'natural' or 'principled-looking' move that immediately enables a forcing tactical refutation. In 7/9 positions, a piece is placed on a square where it becomes directly exploitable: Re3 allows a knight fork, Qg6 gets trapped by Nh4, Qd6 is attacked by Ne4 with tempo, Ne4 is captured exposing the queen, Nf3 enables capture-with-check plus discovered attack, a5 leaves the d5 knight trapped after c4, and Kf4 walks into Be5#. The remaining positions (f6 opening lines for the opponent, Rc1+ activating the opposing king) similarly follow the pattern of intuitive moves that fail against specific concrete threats. The average cp_loss of 1287 confirms these are catastrophic errors where general principles clash fatally with tactical reality.
analysis.move_pattern: Any piece type moving to a seemingly logical/active square; no consistent direction or piece, but all moves appear reasonable based on general principles (centralization, space gain, forcing moves, pawn breaks)
analysis.why_bad: The move places a piece (or exposes a piece) to an immediate forcing tactical refutation — the 'natural' square turns out to be tactically poisoned due to forks, trapping, discovered attacks, tempo-gaining attacks, or mating nets that the player failed to calculate.
sub_patterns: Piece placed on square immediately attacked by opponent's minor piece with tempo (Qg6/Nh4, Qd6/Ne4, Re3/Nxf4)
Piece moved to square enabling discovered attack or capture-with-check (Nf3, Ne4)
Aggressive-looking move that helps opponent (Rc1+ activating king, f6 opening lines)
Move ignoring critical positional threat to own piece (a5 ignoring c4 trapping knight)
King move into mating net (Kf4/Be5#)

analysis.label: Moving a bishop to h6 (or h3) to exchange the opponent's fianchettoed bishop, but prematurely abandoning a critical defensive role and allowing immediate tactical punishment.
analysis.description: In 8/9 positions, the player moves a bishop to the h-file (7x Bh6, 1x Bh3) attempting to exchange the opponent's fianchettoed bishop (g7 or g2), a thematically well-known positional idea but one executed with catastrophic timing. In every case, the bishop was previously performing a vital defensive function—guarding the d4 knight (positions 3, 4), maintaining a pin on the f6 knight that indirectly protected e4 (position 9), providing general central coordination (positions 7, 8, 11), or the bishop simply ends up undefended on its new square (positions 7, 11). The 2 Rd7 positions share the same abstract error: abandoning a piece's defensive post for an aggressive-looking but premature offensive maneuver. The refutations consistently exploit the vacated defensive role through knight forks (5/9), hanging pieces (3/9), or queen deflection tactics (1/9). Average cp_loss of 292 reflects that these moves convert equal or advantageous positions into losing ones.
analysis.move_pattern: Bishop moving diagonally to h6 (or h3) on the edge of the board, targeting an opponent's fianchettoed bishop on g7 (or g2), from a central/interior square where it was defending other pieces
analysis.why_bad: The bishop was defending a critical central piece or maintaining a pin; moving it to h6/h3 abandons that defensive function, allowing the opponent to exploit the unguarded piece or square with immediate tactical strikes (forks, captures with tempo, or discovered attacks along newly opened lines).
sub_patterns: Bh6 removes defender of d4 knight, allowing Nxd4 + Nxf3 fork
Bh6 releases pin on f6 knight, allowing Nxe4 + queen fork
Bh6 places bishop on undefended square exploitable via intermediate checks
Bh6 with king uncastled allows central pawn captures with tempo
Rd7 abandons back-rank defensive post for offensive 7th-rank adventure

analysis.label: Playing a natural-looking but non-urgent improving move when the position demands one specific immediate action.
analysis.description: This feature fires on moves that appear reasonable or generally improving but fatally waste tempo in positions with a single critical demand. In 7/8 positions, the analyses explicitly identify 'tempo_loss' as the core error. The pattern manifests as: developing a bishop when center action is needed (Bb7, Position 1), pushing cosmetic pawns when king activation is required (g5, Position 12), activating the king when a preparatory pawn move must come first (Kg4, Position 7), playing prophylactic pawn moves while a piece hangs (b3, Position 9), or repositioning a rook while abandoning its critical defensive duty (Rd3, Position 10). In 5/8 positions, only ONE good move existed within 50cp of optimal, indicating these are razor-sharp moments where the single correct response is obscured by the plausibility of the 'improving' alternative. The catastrophically high average cp_loss (1307) reflects that these positions punish inaccuracy exponentially—the moves aren't random blunders but seductive-looking alternatives that address a secondary concern while the position's primary demand goes unmet.
analysis.move_pattern: Any piece type, any direction - characteristically 'quiet' or 'improving' moves (pawn pushes, piece repositioning, king walks, development) rather than forcing moves
analysis.why_bad: The position has exactly one critical demand (defend a hanging piece, lock pawn structure before king activation, advance passed pawn immediately, exploit opponent's lag) and the played move addresses a different, non-urgent positional concern, giving the opponent a free tempo to exploit the unaddressed vulnerability.
sub_patterns: Pawn push when piece play needed (b3, g5)
King activation before necessary preparatory move (Kg4 before f5)
Quiet development ignoring tactical emergency (Bb7, Rd3)
Wrong recapture damaging critical structure (gxf3)

analysis.label: Moves that pursue seemingly active plans while abandoning a critical defensive or attacking function, allowing the opponent to exploit the vacated responsibility.
analysis.description: In all 4 positions, the played move redirects energy to a secondary concern while ignoring the position's primary demand. In Position 2 (Kg4), the king abandons safety to approach its own queen, walking into a g-file skewer (4/4 involve losing coordination). In Position 5 (Nc5), the knight leaves its powerful b3 blockade post, freeing White's b4 advance (4/4 involve releasing restraint). In Position 7 (c4), White plays a slow central break instead of exploiting concrete tactical pressure on f6 and the e-file pin (3/4 involve ignoring immediate tactical obligations). In Position 14 (a4), White pushes on the queenside while the kingside attack demands immediate prosecution (3/4 feature playing on the wrong flank). The 'tempo_loss' tag appears in 3/4 positions, and all 4 positions had multiple clearly better alternatives (avg 2.5 good moves), indicating these errors were avoidable misdirections rather than forced mistakes.
analysis.move_pattern: Piece or pawn moves to an apparently active square/direction that abandons its current critical function (blockade, restraint, or king safety)
analysis.why_bad: Each move releases tension or abandons a restraining/controlling function, gifting the opponent exactly the tempo or structural change they need to execute their primary plan (b4 break, piece exchanges, counterattack, or skewer)
sub_patterns: Abandoning a blockade square allowing opponent's pawn advance
Slow pawn push on wrong flank when immediate tactical action is available
Releasing central tension when piece pressure demands maintenance
Moving king into alignment with own piece creating skewer vulnerability

analysis.label: Moves that abandon a critical defensive function (blocking, shielding, guarding) to pursue apparent piece activity, creating an immediate tactical vulnerability exploited by forcing sequences.
analysis.description: This feature detects moves where a piece leaves a position where it was performing a crucial but non-obvious defensive role—blocking a file, shielding another piece, guarding a key square, or maintaining king safety—in favor of a move that appears active or natural. In 6/8 positions, the refutation begins with a check that leads to material gain (Kc2→Rh2+ skewer, Kh5→Rh2+ winning rook, a4→Qd2+ winning h2, Nf5→Qe5+ winning c7, Rh6+→Qxh6 winning exchange, Be6→Rxf3 winning queen). In 7/8 cases the analyses tag 'tempo_loss' because the move accomplishes nothing while the opponent gains a forcing initiative. The player typically had 2-3 good moves available that maintained the defensive function while still making progress, but chose a move that prioritized apparent centralization, checking, or pawn advances over positional integrity. The catastrophic average loss (1373cp) reflects how completely the defensive structure collapses once the critical guardian is removed.
analysis.move_pattern: Any piece type moving to a seemingly active square while vacating a critical defensive post (blocking file, guarding square, shielding from checks); king moves to exposed squares are especially common (3/8 are king moves to vulnerable files/ranks)
analysis.why_bad: The moved piece was performing a hidden defensive function (blocking a file, preventing a check sequence, guarding a hanging piece/pawn, or maintaining opposition), and its departure creates an immediate tactical vulnerability—typically an exploitable alignment along a rank, file, or diagonal that allows a forcing check sequence to win material.
sub_patterns: King moving to a square exposed to rook checks along a file/rank, enabling skewer or piece separation (Kc2, Kh5)
Piece leaving a blocking/shielding position, opening a file that exposes another piece to capture (Be6 unblocking f-file, Nf5 abandoning e7)
Queen/piece retreating from defense of a pawn or square, leaving it hanging (Qc8 abandoning d5)
Playing on the wrong side of the board while an urgent tactical threat exists (a4 ignoring h2 weakness)
Giving a superficial check that allows the opponent to simplify favorably (Rh6+ captured by queen)

analysis.label: Slow, non-forcing piece moves (usually rooks) that abandon active positions or critical functions when concrete aggressive action was required.
analysis.description: In 5/6 positions, the played move was tagged as 'tempo_loss' — the player moved a piece passively or away from a critical post instead of playing a concrete forcing move. In Position 5 (Rg2), the rook abandoned a dominant g7 attacking post. In Position 4 (Be4), the bishop left a powerful d5 outpost for a square challengeable by ...f5. In Position 1 (Rb8) and Position 6 (Re8), rooks moved to passive back-rank squares instead of seizing available tactics (Qxa4, Rg8+). In Position 3 (Rd2), the rook infiltrated prematurely allowing a tempo-gaining Ne4. In Position 15 (Nxf8), a piece was removed from a critical blocking function for material gain, opening a lethal diagonal. The common thread across all 6 positions: the player prioritized quiet repositioning or material over maintaining the critical pressure/function their pieces already provided, giving opponents a free tempo to neutralize or counterattack.
analysis.move_pattern: Major/minor piece (4/6 rooks) moving to a passive or unprotected square, typically non-forcing (5/6 no check, 5/6 no meaningful capture), often retreating or moving laterally away from the critical zone of action
analysis.why_bad: These moves surrender the initiative by abandoning a piece's critical function (attacking, blocking, or pressuring) in positions that demand concrete action, giving the opponent a free tempo to consolidate, escape threats, or launch counter-resources that neutralize the player's entire positional/tactical advantage.
sub_patterns: Retreating an attacking piece from a dominant post (Rg2 from g7, Be4 from d5)
Playing a passive rook move instead of an available concrete tactic (Rb8 instead of Qxa4, Re8 instead of Rg8+)
Moving a piece to a square where it can be challenged with tempo (Rd2 allowing Ne4, Be4 allowing ...f5)
Removing a critical blocking piece for material gain (Nxf8 opening fatal diagonal)

analysis.label: Playing a non-forcing or indirect move in a tempo-critical position where an immediate forcing action (often a pawn break with check or direct king approach) was required to maintain the initiative.
analysis.description: In 4/5 positions, the player chose a quiet repositioning or indirect move (b5 pawn push, Bd2 bishop shuffle, Rg7 rook maneuver, Nxe5 wrong-order capture) when the position demanded an urgent forcing move—typically a pawn advance with check (f4+ in position 1, g4+ in position 4) or a direct king approach to a critical square (Kf2 in position 5). The common thread is that these are endgame positions (4/5) where a tempo race is in progress: whoever executes the critical forcing move first wins the initiative permanently. All 5 positions had exactly 1 good move available, indicating razor-sharp moments. The 'tempo_loss' tag appears in 4/5 analyses, and every position features exposed kings where the race for initiative is paramount. The blunders allow the opponent to execute the very forcing continuation the player should have played first—White gets Ra6+ perpetual (pos 1), White plays g4+ seizing centralization (pos 4), Black advances unstoppable passed pawns (pos 5).
analysis.move_pattern: Quiet piece repositioning or non-forcing pawn/piece move (no check, no direct threat) when an immediate check or critical pawn break was available
analysis.why_bad: The opponent gains a decisive tempo to execute the critical forcing continuation first—seizing king centralization, initiating perpetual check, or advancing passed pawns—because the quiet move fails to disrupt the opponent's plan or claim the initiative in a tempo-sensitive race.
sub_patterns: Quiet pawn push instead of pawn break with check
Bishop/rook repositioning instead of forcing king advance
Wrong capture order allowing opponent's attacking sequence

analysis.label: Playing a non-forcing move (pawn push or pawn capture) when an immediate check initiates a forced mating sequence against an exposed king.
analysis.description: In all 3/3 positions, Black had a forced checkmate available starting with a check (Qb5+, Ng4+, Qf3+), but instead played a slow, non-checking move focused on material or positional considerations (d3 attacking a knight, c5 advancing a pawn, Qxf4 capturing a pawn). In each case, the White king was critically exposed (f1 with weak diagonal in position 3, h2 with minimal pawn cover in position 12, h1 on back rank in position 15), and the checking move exploited this vulnerability to force a mating net. The played moves all represent 'tunnel vision' on material targets rather than recognizing the king's fatal weakness. The average cp_loss of ~5923 reflects that 2/3 positions converted forced mates into merely winning positions, while the third delayed mate by 7 moves.
