analysis.move_pattern: Non-checking pawn advance or pawn capture (d-file push, c-file push, queen takes pawn) instead of a piece check toward the exposed king
analysis.why_bad: These moves waste critical tempo on material/positional goals when a forcing check initiates an unstoppable mating sequence; the opponent uses the gifted tempo to reorganize king defenses and escape the mating net.
sub_patterns: Pawn push attacking a piece instead of queen check on diagonal
Positional pawn advance instead of knight fork-check
Pawn capture instead of queen check on adjacent square

analysis.label: Moving a piece (often a knight) to a peripheral, back-rank, or otherwise non-functional square while ignoring the position's concrete tactical demands.
analysis.description: This feature fires on moves that appear purposeful or aggressive but actually misplace a piece on an idle square while critical tactical needs go unaddressed. The clearest sub-pattern involves knights moving to rim or back-rank squares: Nh6 to an exposed edge (1/8), Nh4 abandoning central support for a speculative f5 plan (1/8), Ng6+ giving a pointless check that strands the knight (1/8), and Nd8 retreating to the back rank blocking its own rook (1/8). Non-knight examples follow the same logic: Rab1 places a rook on a file irrelevant to the critical g4 threat (1/8), Rhc1 supports a pawn that doesn't need support while missing a b-file tactic (1/8), g4 advances a pawn aggressively while leaving d4 hanging (1/8), and Qf8+ gives a check that fails to deny a key escape square (1/8). In all 8 positions, the played move prioritizes a superficially appealing plan over concrete positional or tactical requirements, resulting in the moved piece becoming disconnected from the game's critical area. The average centipawn loss of 212 reflects that these aren't subtle inaccuracies but substantial misevaluations of what the position demands.
analysis.move_pattern: Piece (especially knight) moved to a peripheral, rim, or obstructive square, often with superficially active intent (check, attack, file occupation) but landing where it becomes passive or disconnected
analysis.why_bad: The piece ends up stranded on a non-functional square (rim, back rank, wrong file) while the position required addressing concrete threats, maintaining coordination, or exploiting tactical opportunities in the center or at the critical point of tension.
sub_patterns: Knight to rim square (h6, h4, g6) abandoning central coordination
Knight to back rank (d8) blocking own rook and abandoning dominant outpost
Rook to wrong file ignoring concrete tactical ideas on adjacent file
Aggressive pawn advance or check that ignores hanging material or key escape squares

analysis.label: Giving checks (usually along diagonals) that waste tempo, help the opponent's king, or create exploitable tactical vulnerabilities.
analysis.description: In 3/4 positions, the player delivers a check that is counterproductive: Qd3+ is a meaningless tempo-wasting check when forced mates via Qe6 or Nxe5+ exist (Position 2); Bb4+ is a classic 'patzer check' that drives White's king to the ideal centralizing square d3 (Position 3); Qf6+ fatally allows Qg5+ interposition-with-check forcing a lost queen trade (Position 4). The 4th position (d4) represents the flip side—ignoring the opponent's devastating diagonal check (Qh4+/Bxg3+) that wins material. All positions share the theme of mishandling check-related tactics on diagonals, either by giving premature checks that aid the opponent or by failing to prevent the opponent's checking threats. The analyses consistently identify 'tempo_loss' (3/4), 'patzer_check' (2/4), and 'check_not_best' as core tags.
analysis.move_pattern: Checks delivered along diagonals (queen or bishop) toward the opponent's king, or moves that ignore the opponent's diagonal checking resources
analysis.why_bad: The checks either drive the opponent's king to a better square, allow a winning interposition with counter-check, accomplish nothing the opponent wasn't already planning, or the aggressive-looking move ignores a concrete tactical refutation involving checks along exposed diagonals
sub_patterns: Queen check on diagonal that wastes tempo
Bishop check that centralizes opponent's king
Check that enables forced queen trade via interposition+check
Ignoring opponent's diagonal check threat

analysis.label: Speculative non-developing moves that waste critical tempo while the king remains uncastled and vulnerable to immediate tactical exploitation.
analysis.description: This feature fires on positions where the player makes an ambitious but misguided move—typically a pawn advance or speculative piece maneuver—while ignoring the urgent need for development and king safety. In 5/6 positions, the blundering side's king remains in the center (uncastled), and the move either further weakens the king's defenses (g5, f6, e5 opening diagonals or dark squares) or squanders a critical tempo on a slow repositioning idea (Ba2, Qd4). All 6 positions had multiple sound developing alternatives available (avg 2.7 good moves), yet the player chose a 'wish move' pursuing a speculative plan. The refutations consistently exploit the uncastled king via diagonal attacks (Qh5+, Qc8+, Nf6+), knight forks, or central pawn breaks that punish the wasted tempo. In 5/6 cases the punishment involves direct king-targeting tactics, and in 4/6 cases the blunder specifically opens or leaves open a critical diagonal to the king.
analysis.move_pattern: Non-developing pawn advances (especially kingside f/g pawns or central e-pawn) or speculative piece shuffles, not addressing checks or threats, with king still on original square
analysis.why_bad: These moves waste a critical tempo on speculative plans while the king is uncastled and vulnerable, allowing the opponent to exploit the exposed king via diagonal checks, knight forks, or forced queen invasions that win material immediately
sub_patterns: Kingside pawn advance (g5/f6) weakening king diagonals
Central pawn advance (e5) opening queen invasion diagonal
Speculative piece repositioning (Ba2/Qd4) ignoring tactical threats

analysis.label: Pawn moves or captures that remove critical defensive structure, ignoring the position's concrete tactical demands.
analysis.description: This feature fires on positions where the player makes a structurally self-damaging move—overwhelmingly a pawn advance or capture (7/9 positions)—that looks natural on the surface but fatally undermines their own position by opening lines, weakening key squares, or removing blocking pawns. In 9/9 cases, a more forcing or active alternative existed (often a piece move like Bd3, Ne7+, Nc5, Qa5, or castling preparation). The played moves consistently release tension in ways that benefit the opponent: g3 weakened f2 (1/9), gxh5 opened the g-file toward own king (1/9), dxc3 removed a d-file blocker enabling Qe6+ (1/9), f4 left e3 undefended (1/9), exd4 surrendered attacking tempo for a passive exchange (1/9), d4 and e5 advanced pawns prematurely abandoning square control (2/9). The non-pawn moves (Rc8, Qd6) share the same DNA: choosing a slow/routine-looking move at a moment demanding concrete tactical precision. The opponent's refutations typically involve immediate forcing shots—knight jumps to weakened squares, checks exploiting opened files, or forks on newly accessible outposts.
analysis.move_pattern: Predominantly pawn advances or captures (forward or diagonal), occasionally quiet piece moves; non-forcing, non-checking moves that alter pawn structure to the mover's detriment
analysis.why_bad: These moves remove a pawn or piece from a critical defensive role (blocking a file, defending a square, maintaining tension), creating an immediate tactical vulnerability the opponent exploits with forcing play—while simultaneously missing the player's own stronger forcing continuation that the position demanded.
sub_patterns: Pawn advance weakening own king shelter (g3, gxh5, f4)
Premature central pawn advance releasing tension (d4, e5, exd4)
Pawn capture removing a critical file-blocking defender (dxc3, exd4)
Quiet developing move ignoring immediate tactical threat (Rc8, Qd6)

analysis.label: Non-urgent pawn push or piece move played in a position demanding immediate tactical response to a concrete threat or opportunity.
analysis.description: This feature fires on moves that waste a critical tempo by addressing a secondary concern while the position requires immediate concrete action. In 10/12 positions, the move is a pawn push, predominantly on the a-file or h-file (8/12 involve rook-pawn or flank-pawn moves: h4, h4, a4, a4, h5, hxg5, hxg5, c5, c6). The remaining moves are slow piece repositionings (Na6, Nf5). In every case, the position has very few good moves available (avg 2.2), indicating a critical juncture where precision is required. The common thread is that an urgent tactical demand exists—an unresolved pin (3/12), a mating threat on the kingside (4/12), a winning capture available (2/12), or an opponent's imminent pawn break that must be stopped (3/12)—and the player instead plays a non-forcing move on a part of the board irrelevant to the crisis. The tempo loss is consistently identified as the primary tactical motif across the analyses.
analysis.move_pattern: Predominantly flank pawn advances (a- or h-file) or peripheral piece moves (knight to rim) that are non-forcing and do not address the critical sector of the board
analysis.why_bad: These moves squander a tempo in positions where the opponent has an immediate tactical threat or the player has a narrow window to exploit a concrete opportunity; the wasted move allows the opponent to execute their plan (open files, complete development, launch a decisive attack) unopposed, often resulting in catastrophic material loss or a mating attack.
sub_patterns: Flank pawn push ignoring central tension or pin
Opening h-file against own castled king via hxg5 capture
Queenside a-pawn advance while kingside is under immediate tactical threat
Slow knight development squandering existing tactical advantage
Pawn break that weakens own pawn chain enabling opponent's tactical shot

analysis.label: Voluntarily placing a piece on an exposed or peripheral square where it immediately becomes a tactical target for a simple opponent response.
analysis.description: This feature fires on moves that place pieces on unstable squares where they can be immediately exploited by straightforward opponent responses, typically pawn advances. The clearest sub-pattern is knights moving to rim squares (Nh5 appears 2/8 times, Na5 1/8) where they are trapped or won by g4, f4, or b4 pawn thrusts. King moves to exposed squares also appear (Ka2, Kc6, Kh8 = 3/8) where the king walks into tactical shots, hanging pieces, or mating attacks. The remaining cases (Qe7 blocking development 1/8, g4 weakening king position 1/8) share the pattern of creating an immediate tactical vulnerability that the opponent exploits with a simple forcing move. In 7/8 cases, the common tag is 'tempo_loss' - the moved piece must retreat or is captured, meaning the move accomplished nothing while giving the opponent a free attacking tempo. The average cp_loss of 1395 reflects that these self-weakening moves often cross critical thresholds from survivable to lost positions.
analysis.move_pattern: Piece (especially knight or king) moves to rim, edge, or exposed square away from safe central positioning; destination square is immediately attackable by opponent's pawn advance or tactical shot
analysis.why_bad: The destination square is immediately vulnerable to a simple forcing response (usually a pawn advance like g4, f4, b4, or a piece capturing/checking) that traps the piece, wins material, or creates decisive tactical threats against the now-exposed piece or king.
sub_patterns: Knight retreating to rim (h5, a5) where pawn advance traps it
King moving to exposed square walking into mating attack or allowing tactical shots
Piece blocking own development or creating self-obstruction on a tactically vulnerable square

analysis.label: Playing a slow, preparatory, or misdirected move in a narrow position that demands one precise, immediate action to maintain the advantage.
analysis.description: This feature fires on positions where the player wastes a decisive tempo by choosing a reasonable-looking but insufficiently urgent move when the position demands the single correct continuation. The hallmark is extremely narrow decision points (avg 1.4 good moves available) where only one precise action maintains the evaluation. In 11/11 cases, the move gifts the opponent time to consolidate, reorganize defenses, or launch counterattacks that neutralize the position. Examples include slow prophylactic pawn pushes instead of immediate tactical strikes (h3 instead of e5, f3 instead of Qh4+), knight rerouting maneuvers when devastating queen moves are available (Nh2 instead of Qe3), retreating strong pieces when king safety demands attention (Bb3 abandoning d5), wrong forcing moves that allow simple blocks (Qa6+ allowing c4 interposition vs Qb5+), premature captures that surrender move-order advantages (dxc6 instead of Qc8+ first, dxe6+ instead of perpetual with Qc6+), and king moves that abandon critical defensive squares (Kf7 abandoning g5 control, Kb2 failing to block queen infiltration via d2). The average cp_loss of 322 reflects positions swinging from winning/comfortable to equal or worse.
analysis.move_pattern: Any piece type; typically quiet/preparatory moves (pawn pushes, piece retreats, knight rerouting, king repositioning) OR forcing moves directed at the wrong target (checks that allow easy blocks or drive king to safety)
analysis.why_bad: The position has a single narrow path requiring immediate decisive action (tactical strike, precise check sequence, or critical square control), and the played move wastes the one tempo that separates advantage from equality, allowing the opponent to solve their problems—consolidating king safety, reorganizing pieces, or establishing counterplay.
sub_patterns: Slow prophylactic pawn moves instead of immediate tactical breaks (h3, f3)
Piece retreats/rerouting when immediate attacking continuation exists (Nh2, Bb3)
Wrong check square allowing easy interposition or king escape (Qa6+, Nh8+)
Premature captures disrupting optimal move order (dxc6, dxe6+)
King moves abandoning critical square control (Kf7, Kb2)

analysis.label: Playing a natural-looking developing, centralizing, or prophylactic move that ignores the position's most urgent concrete tactical demand.
analysis.description: This feature fires on moves that appear reasonable in isolation—developing a piece (Nc6, Bg5), centralizing a queen (Qd6×2, Qe3), repositioning a knight (Nc5, Nh4), making a prophylactic pawn push (h6), or adjusting the king (Kg3, Kh2)—but catastrophically fail to address the position's single critical requirement. In 8/10 positions, the best move involved a specific forced action: exchanging a dominant enemy piece (positions 6, 8), evacuating the king from a lethal file (position 7), blocking a critical pawn break (position 3), maintaining a piece's defensive coverage (positions 1, 3), creating immediate counterplay (position 4), or keeping the queen away from fork-vulnerable squares (position 9). The blundered moves all share the quality of addressing secondary positional concerns while the position screamed for one concrete action. Average cp_loss of 308 with only 2.1 good moves available confirms these are narrow critical moments where the player chose a 'general improvement' over the specific necessity.
analysis.move_pattern: Any piece type moved to a seemingly logical/active square (development, centralization, prophylaxis) rather than executing the one critical concrete action the position demands
analysis.why_bad: The move fails to address the position's most urgent tactical vulnerability—whether that's an undefended piece, a critical exchange that must happen now, a king needing to flee, a defensive post that must be maintained, or a fork/discovered attack that becomes possible. The opponent exploits the wasted tempo to execute the threat the player ignored.
sub_patterns: Queen centralization to tactically vulnerable square (Qd6 allowing fork/back-rank)
Knight move abandoning critical defensive square (Nc5 leaving f4, Nh4 hanging)
Prophylactic move when forced exchange is required (h6 instead of Rxe6)
King move creating new tactical vulnerability (Kg3 enabling discovered attack)
Piece development ignoring king safety emergency (Nc6 blocking escape, Bg5 leaving piece hanging)

analysis.label: A minor piece (usually a bishop) is placed on or left on an exposed square where it can be captured without adequate recapture, losing a full piece in the opening.
analysis.description: In 5/7 positions, a bishop is actively placed on g4 or g5 where it can be immediately captured, and the recapture either leaves the recapturing piece (usually a knight) itself hanging to the opponent's queen, or no recapture exists at all. In the remaining 2/7 positions, the player makes a developing or prophylactic move (Nf3, h3) while ignoring that an existing bishop is already hanging or tactically vulnerable. All 7 positions occur in the opening with kings still in or near the center, and all result in losing approximately a full piece (~400-530 cp loss). The unifying thread is that the player makes a 'natural-looking' move without noticing that a bishop is undefended and can be captured for free or that the recapture chain collapses.
analysis.move_pattern: Minor piece (predominantly bishop) moved to g4/g5, or another piece moved while a bishop remains undefended; no capture or check involved in the blundering move itself
analysis.why_bad: The bishop is placed on or left on a square where it can be captured, and the expected recapture either does not exist (wrong piece geometry) or leaves the recapturing piece itself undefended and capturable by the opponent's queen on the newly opened diagonal.
sub_patterns: Bishop to g5/g4 captured, knight recaptures but hangs to queen (Bxg5 Nxg5 Qxg5)
Bishop to g4 captured with no recapture available due to knight geometry
Developing move ignores own bishop already hanging on an open diagonal
Knight moves away from defending a bishop, leaving it en prise

analysis.label: Playing quiet, non-forcing moves (retreats, pawn pushes, castling) when immediate tactical captures of hanging or vulnerable material are available.
analysis.description: This feature fires on positions where the player chose a passive, routine, or preparatory move instead of seizing an immediate concrete tactical opportunity. In 5/7 positions, the best move was a direct capture of hanging material (Nxe3, Nxe7, Qxh5 appearing twice, and a forcing pawn advance). The actual moves played were universally quiet and non-forcing: bishop retreats from attacked pieces (Bb3, Bg3 in 2/7), slow queenside pawn preparation (b6 in 1/7), a pawn challenge that weakens rather than consolidates (f6 in 1/7), routine castling into danger (O-O in 1/7), a queen reposition ignoring a hanging pawn (Qe6 in 1/7), and a greedy pawn grab that trades a dominant piece for a pawn (Bxh7 in 1/7). The positions all have very few good options (avg 1.1), indicating the demanded move was specific and forcing, yet the player defaulted to general principles rather than calculating concrete tactics.
analysis.move_pattern: Various piece types; quiet non-forcing moves (bishop retreats, pawn pushes, castling, queen repositions) rather than the available captures or forcing attacks
analysis.why_bad: These moves waste critical tempo by ignoring hanging material or forcing tactical sequences, allowing the opponent to consolidate, retreat their vulnerable pieces to safety, or seize the initiative. The player responds to positional concerns (piece safety, preparation, routine development) rather than recognizing that the position demands immediate concrete action.
sub_patterns: Bishop retreats when the attacker itself is hanging (Bg3, Bb3)
Quiet preparatory pawn moves ignoring central/tactical tension (b6, f6)
Routine safety moves in sharp tactical positions (O-O, Qe6)
Material grab that trades dynamic attacking piece placement for a pawn (Bxh7)

analysis.label: Playing a seemingly logical but non-urgent move in a concrete position where only one or two moves maintain the evaluation, ignoring an immediate tactical requirement.
analysis.description: This feature fires on moves that appear strategically reasonable—developing a piece (Nd7, Qe7), centralizing (Qd4), repositioning (Bd2, Bh3, Rd8), consolidating (c6, Kh8, f3), creating threats (a5), or grabbing material (Nxb4, Qxd4)—but critically miss the ONE concrete demand of the position. In 10/12 positions, only 1-2 good moves existed (avg 1.5), yet players chose moves addressing secondary concerns. The mistakes frequently leave pieces hanging (Nd7 leaves Nf5 unprotected, Qe7 leaves b7/a8 undefended, Nxb4 leaves knight capturable, f3 leaves c4 hanging: 4/12), waste decisive tempo when the opponent has concrete threats (Kh8, Bh3, Qd4, a5, Qxd4: 5/12), or self-block critical coordination (Bd2 blocks the d-file rook, Rd8 abandons e-file pressure, c6 misses the urgent capture: 3/12). The common thread is that positions demand concrete precision but the player defaults to a 'looks good' general-purpose move.
analysis.move_pattern: Diverse piece types and directions; typically non-forcing moves (quiet retreats, slow pawn pushes, unmotivated repositioning, or greedy captures) rather than checks/forced sequences
analysis.why_bad: The position has very few correct moves (avg 1.5) due to a concrete tactical requirement—a hanging piece, an urgent capture, a critical tempo race, or a back-rank/king-safety issue—and the chosen move addresses a secondary strategic goal while ignoring the immediate tactical demand, allowing the opponent to exploit the oversight with material gain or decisive positional advantage.
sub_patterns: Developing/repositioning while leaving a piece en prise (Nd7, Qe7, Nxb4, f3)
Passive non-forcing moves surrendering tempo in sharp positions (Kh8, Bh3, Qd4, a5)
Self-blocking or abandoning critical file/diagonal control (Bd2, Rd8, c6)
Grabbing material at cost of initiative against exposed king (Qxd4)

analysis.label: Playing a quiet, preparatory, or secondary move when the position demands immediate concrete action, squandering the one tempo that matters.
analysis.description: In 7/7 positions, the player chose a natural-looking but non-urgent move (reinforcing a rook, developing a knight, advancing a pawn, retreating a king) when the position had an extremely narrow window requiring immediate tactical or concrete action. The best moves were consistently forcing: tactical sacrifices like Nxh2 (positions 9, 10), piece challenges like Nd7 winning material (position 2), prophylactic precision like b3 trapping a piece (position 1), or critical pawn races like h5/g5 (position 3). The blunders all share an average of only 1.4 good moves available, indicating positions where ONE specific action was required. In 6/7 cases the analyses tag 'tempo_loss' as the core motif - the wasted move gave the opponent the exact tempo needed to consolidate, escape, or seize the initiative. The moves appear reasonable in isolation (doubling rooks, developing, pushing pawns) but address secondary concerns while the position's true demand goes unanswered.
analysis.move_pattern: Diverse piece types (king, rook, knight, bishop, pawn) making quiet non-forcing moves - no checks, no critical captures, no direct threats to the opponent's key weakness
analysis.why_bad: The position has a narrow tactical or tempo-critical requirement (avg 1.4 good moves), and the quiet move wastes the one tempo needed for the critical action, allowing the opponent to neutralize threats, consolidate an advantage, or win the resulting race
sub_patterns: Passive king moves instead of tactical sacrifices (Ke8, Kd6)
Quiet pawn pushes instead of forcing play (b5, a4)
Building moves instead of addressing the critical problem (Rfe1 instead of b3)
Apparent tempo gains that backfire (Nf6 allowing Nc3 first)
Material grabs that surrender key piece activity (Bxb4 instead of Bxe3)

analysis.label: Moving a piece to a seemingly active but actually exposed or irrelevant square while ignoring the opponent's concrete tactical threats.
analysis.description: This feature fires on positions where a piece is repositioned for apparent activity but the new square creates tactical vulnerability or abandons critical duties. In 4/5 positions, the moved piece lands on a square where it becomes an immediate target on an open line: Re1 places an undefended rook on an e-file dominated by Black's Q+R (position 3), Kd3 puts the king on the open d-file where Rd5+ forces a losing exchange (position 11), Rg8 abandons the dominant 7th rank for a passive back-rank square creating no threats (position 14), and Ba5 sends a bishop offside where it's undefended while removing kingside defensive coverage (position 15). In all mistake cases, the player had concrete alternatives (Be2/h4/Bd3/Kb3) that addressed real positional needs, but instead chose a move that prioritized perceived piece activity over the opponent's forcing plans. The 'tempo_loss' tag appears in 4/5 positions, and 'piece_activity' appears in 5/5, confirming the pattern of misguided activation.
analysis.move_pattern: Non-forcing piece relocation to an open file/rank square, typically a major piece or king moving to what appears to be an active post
analysis.why_bad: The piece abandons its current functional role (defense or concrete plan execution) and lands on a square where the opponent can immediately exploit it via checks, captures, or uninterrupted execution of their primary threat, effectively giving the opponent a free tempo or winning material.
sub_patterns: Rook placed on open file already dominated by opponent's heavy pieces
King stepping onto open file where it is immediately checked
Rook abandoning active rank for passive repositioning without concrete threats
Bishop moved offside leaving key sector undefended and piece unprotected

analysis.label: Aggressive pawn advances to the 4th/5th rank challenging enemy structure when piece improvement or repositioning was required.
analysis.description: All 9 positions feature a pawn advancing to challenge an enemy pawn (f5, f4, g4, c5, b5, d5, c4) when the correct approach was piece repositioning or activation. In 8/9 cases, the best moves were piece moves (Qd7, Bb5, Rde1, O-O, Bb7, Rdg8, Qc7, Nh4) rather than pawn advances. The pawn breaks look thematic—challenging the center or attacking the opponent's king—but they are critically mistimed, giving the opponent free tempi to develop (Position 8: Nc3 develops), consolidate (Position 2: exf5 creates a passed pawn), exploit newly opened lines (Position 15: dxc4 isolates d4), or attack weakened squares (Position 4: knight reaches e5 outpost). In 7/9 positions, the pawn advance creates an immediate structural weakness or target. The common thread is that the player chose a committal structural change over patient piece improvement, prioritizing 'action' over coordination.
analysis.move_pattern: Single-step pawn advance to the 4th rank (White) or 5th rank (Black), attacking an enemy pawn to initiate a structural break
analysis.why_bad: The pawn break grants the opponent free tempo to develop dormant pieces, consolidate weaknesses, or exploit newly created structural targets (isolated pawns, outpost squares, open lines); meanwhile the player's own pieces are not yet positioned to benefit from the structural change.
sub_patterns: f5 challenging e4 pawn prematurely
c5/c4 challenging d4/d5 with king exposed
Kingside pawn storm (f4/g4) creating weaknesses before pieces are coordinated
Queenside pawn advance (b5) creating targets without piece support

analysis.label: Playing an attractive-looking but non-critical move in a position that demands one specific urgent action, wasting a decisive tempo.
analysis.description: This feature fires on positions where very few moves maintain the evaluation (avg 1.8 good moves) and the player chooses a move that appears active, aggressive, or purposeful but fails to address the position's single most urgent requirement. The pattern manifests as: speculative checks that don't win material or force favorable simplification (Qe5+, Qc6+ - 2/13), aggressive piece placements that walk into traps or get sidelined (Ne3, Qc3, Nc4, Qh5 - 4/13), pawn advances that weaken rather than strengthen (f5, b6, g5 - 3/13), and passive king/rook moves when immediate counteraction against passed pawns is required (Kh8, Rg8, Kd3 - 3/13). In nearly every case (10+/13), the position demanded one precise action - capturing a critical pawn (Rxa5 in positions 9, 11), delivering a forcing check sequence (Qg6+ in position 6, Qxc5+ in position 1), or retreating to a functional square (Qe7 in position 13). The 'tempo_loss' tag appears in 10/13 analyses, confirming the unifying thread: these moves surrender a tempo that proves decisive because the positions are on a knife's edge.
analysis.move_pattern: Diverse piece types moving to apparently active/aggressive squares (forward knight jumps, queen checks, pawn advances, file changes) rather than the one concrete action the position demands
analysis.why_bad: These moves waste a critical tempo in positions where only 1-2 moves work. The opponent gains time to consolidate defenses, advance passed pawns, activate dormant pieces, or execute concrete threats that the 'active' move failed to prevent or address.
sub_patterns: Speculative checks that allow the king to reach safety or force unfavorable simplification
Aggressive piece placements that get trapped or sidelined from the real fight
Pawn advances that irreversibly weaken king safety or remove key defenders
Passive king/rook moves when passed pawns demand immediate capture

analysis.label: Playing a non-forcing repositioning move in a position that demands a single specific concrete tactical action, resulting in catastrophic evaluation loss.
analysis.description: This feature fires on positions with extremely narrow margins (avg 1.6 good moves available) where the player makes a 'reasonable-looking' but non-urgent move instead of the one critical forcing action the position demands. In 7/9 cases, the played move is a passive piece repositioning (Re8, Qb8, Rf1, a6, Kd6, Rc8, Qf5) rather than the required concrete action—typically a capture (Qxa6, Bxf3, Nxd5 in 3/9), a fork (Nd4 in 1/9), or an active piece placement creating immediate threats (Kd4, Qd5, Qc8 in 3/9). The blunders share a common signature: the correct move addresses the single most urgent tactical demand of the position, while the played move addresses a secondary concern or pursues a vague plan. The average cp_loss of 2276 reflects catastrophic consequences—including two positions going from holdable to forced mate. In every case, the opponent has one clear tactical punishment that exploits the abandonment of the critical function.
analysis.move_pattern: Non-forcing piece repositioning (rook/queen/king to a new square without check or meaningful capture) when the position requires a specific capture, fork, or actively threatening placement
analysis.why_bad: These moves fail because they ignore the position's single most urgent demand—a specific tactical resource (capture, fork, active defense) that is the only way to maintain the evaluation—instead playing a generic 'improving' move that allows the opponent to execute a decisive tactical sequence (fork, intermediate check, mating attack, unstoppable pawn promotion) that was previously prevented by the piece's original position or by the unmade tactical action.
sub_patterns: Removing a piece from a critical defensive post, exposing a tactical vulnerability (Re8, Rc8, Qf5 - 3/9)
Playing a passive move instead of a game-changing tactical shot (a6 missing Nd4 fork, Kd6 missing Kd4 attack - 2/9)
Premature forcing move (check/capture) before the essential preparatory action (Qh1+ before Bxf3, Qxe5 before Nxd5 - 2/9)
Placing a piece on a similar-but-wrong square (Qb8 vs Qc8, Rf1 vs Bf1 - 2/9)

analysis.label: Non-forcing 'improving' moves played in positions that demand immediate concrete action, resulting in catastrophic tempo loss.
analysis.description: This feature fires on positions where the player chooses a quiet, non-forcing move (king walk, piece repositioning, preparatory pawn push) when the position urgently demands immediate, direct action. In 7/9 positions, the played move is explicitly tagged as 'tempo_loss' - the player wastes exactly the one tempo that the opponent needs to execute a decisive plan. The best moves are always more forcing or direct: immediate pawn races (b5 instead of a4 in Position 15), blockading critical pawns (Be7 vs Bb2 in Position 4), delivering mating threats in one move (Qc1/Qd2 to h6 vs Qe2 needing two moves in Position 9), or creating active counterplay (Rd2 vs Kh7 in Position 1). The positions typically have very few good alternatives (avg 1.6), meaning the critical nature of the position leaves no room for 'improving' moves. The catastrophic average cp_loss of 2276 reflects that these tempi are irreplaceable - the opponent immediately exploits the wasted move with passed pawn advances (5/9), mating attacks (2/9), or tactical strikes (2/9).
analysis.move_pattern: Quiet non-forcing moves (king steps, bishop retreats, queen repositioning, preparatory pawn pushes) - no checks, no captures, no direct threats
analysis.why_bad: The position demands immediate concrete action (promotion race, mating attack, blockade, active counterplay) and the quiet move gives the opponent exactly the tempo needed to execute their winning plan first
sub_patterns: King moves to 'safer' squares that are actually more vulnerable (Kh7, Kg7)
Piece attacks irrelevant targets instead of addressing critical threat (Bb2, Nd3)
Queen placed on suboptimal square requiring extra tempo to reach key diagonal (Qe2, Qf4, Qd2)
Preparatory pawn advance instead of immediate breakthrough (a4 vs b5)

analysis.label: Playing an ambitious or active move instead of urgently capturing/neutralizing the opponent's most dangerous piece that enables immediate tactical punishment.
analysis.description: In 6/6 positions, the player made an active-looking move (capture, development, pawn push, piece repositioning) while ignoring an enemy piece that was creating an immediate tactical crisis requiring urgent elimination. In 4/6 cases, the correct move was specifically capturing an enemy knight creating fork or discovered attack threats (hxg3, hxg6, hxg6, Bxd5). In 5/6 positions, the best move was a simple capture of the opponent's most dangerous piece. The positions averaged only 1.3 good moves available, indicating extremely narrow defensive paths. The blunders enabled devastating punishments: discovered attacks in 3/6 positions, hanging pieces in 2/6, and a knight fork in 1/6. All 6 positions share the characteristic that the opponent had a powerfully-placed piece (usually a knight on g6, d5, or g3, or a bishop on c4) that was one move away from executing a lethal tactic, and the player's move either removed a shielding piece (exf3 removing the e4 pawn shield) or simply ignored the threat entirely (Bg2, f5, Bc5, Bxf4 capturing the wrong piece, Nc4 creating a new vulnerability).
analysis.move_pattern: Various active moves (piece captures, developments, pawn pushes to aggressive squares) that are NOT captures of the most threatening enemy piece; the ignored piece is typically a knight or bishop on an attacking square enabling discovered checks or forks
analysis.why_bad: These moves fail because they leave the opponent's tactically critical piece alive and active, allowing it to execute a devastating combination (discovered check, fork, or capture of a now-unshielded piece) on the very next move. The player addresses a secondary concern while the primary tactical threat remains lethal.
sub_patterns: Capturing the wrong enemy piece while a more dangerous one remains (Bxf4 instead of hxg6, exf3 removing own shield)
Developing/repositioning own piece instead of capturing the critical threat (Bg2, Bc5, Nc4)
Positional pawn move ignoring immediate tactical crisis (f5 instead of hxg6)

analysis.label: Playing materially-motivated captures, forks, or aggressive moves that overlook the opponent's simple recapture or forcing tactical counter-blow.
analysis.description: This feature fires on positions where the player, typically holding a significant advantage (5/6 positions had the moving side better), plays an aggressive or greedy move that appears to win material but contains a tactical flaw. In 4/6 cases (Nc2, Bxb2, Nd3, Nxc2), a piece moves to a square targeting material gains but is immediately recaptured or trapped. In the remaining cases (d6, Kg2), the move creates a tactical vulnerability that enables a devastating fork. The common thread is that the correct approach required a preparatory move first—displacing the opponent's key defender (g6 before Nxc2 in position 10, Nd6 instead of d6 in position 3) or challenging the opponent's active piece (Bf6 in position 8, c6 in position 7, h6 in position 4, Kf3 in position 12)—before committing to tactical action. All 6/6 positions had very few good alternatives (avg 1.3), indicating critical moments requiring precision that the player squandered with impatience.
analysis.move_pattern: Minor piece or pawn moving aggressively to capture material or create forks, typically to b2/c2/d3 squares deep in opponent's territory, or king moving without accounting for forcing checks
analysis.why_bad: The move attempts a combination prematurely—the opponent has a direct recapture (Nxc2, Qxc2), counter-fork (Nc6, Nf2+), trapping resource (Rab1), or tactical exploitation of newly-undefended pieces (Nxf5/Bxf5) that the player overlooked. A preparatory move to displace the defending/recapturing piece was needed first.
sub_patterns: Knight captures on c2 where opponent's piece directly recaptures
Piece grabs pawn on b2 and becomes trapped or recovered with tempo
Knight moves to 'active' square leaving other pieces tactically undefended
Pawn push attacks a piece that jumps forward with a fork instead of retreating
King moves into a square allowing a forcing check sequence into a fork

analysis.label: Playing a non-urgent 'useful-looking' move when the position demands immediate action to address a critical vulnerability, allowing tactical exploitation.
analysis.description: In all 5 positions, the player chose a move that appears logical in isolation (seeking counterplay, prophylaxis, centralization, or flexibility) but fatally ignores the single most urgent demand of the position. In 5/5 cases, the move wastes exactly one critical tempo that the opponent exploits tactically. Position 3: Nb4 seeks counterplay instead of maintaining the knight's defensive guard of a7. Position 5: f6 prepares a future break instead of developing the knight to its natural f6 square. Position 7: h3 prevents a hypothetical Bg4 instead of castling to escape the e-file. Position 9: Qe7 is 'flexible' instead of the precise Qc7 enabling the crushing Nc3 combination. Position 12: Qe4 centralizes aggressively instead of maintaining the queen on a safe square away from knight forks. In 4/5 cases, king safety was the underlying urgent concern being ignored. In 5/5 cases, the opponent had a concrete tactical refutation exploiting the wasted tempo.

analysis.why_bad: The move wastes a critical tempo on a non-urgent aim while an immediate vulnerability exists, giving the opponent time to execute a tactical blow (e-file pin, sweeping rook checks, discovered attacks, knight forks, or winning combinations) that would have been impossible had the urgent issue been addressed first.
sub_patterns: Prophylactic pawn push (h3/f6) delaying development or castling
Piece relocation to aggressive but tactically vulnerable square (Qe4/Nb4)
Queen placed on passive/wrong square missing the only winning continuation (Qe7)

analysis.label: Tempting captures, aggressive advances, or apparently active moves that create tactical vulnerabilities by disrupting the player's own piece coordination.
analysis.description: This feature fires on moves that appear immediately attractive—capturing material, advancing pawns aggressively, or placing pieces on active-looking squares—but that create exploitable weaknesses in the player's position. In 4/7 positions, the move involves a capture or material grab (Rxd2, Qxd6, Qxd4, Ra4 attacking a piece). In 2/7 positions, f-pawn advances (f4, f5) appear aggressive but fatally weaken structure or surrender key squares. In 1/7, a developing move (Bc5) looks natural but blocks escape routes. The common thread is that each move prioritizes an apparent short-term gain while overlooking that it leaves the player's pieces uncoordinated or exposed—resulting in trapped pieces (2/7), hanging pieces (2/7), premature simplification (1/7), or tempo loss (4/7). All positions had 2-3 clearly better alternatives that maintained coordination.
analysis.move_pattern: Captures (especially on d-file), f-pawn advances, or piece moves to apparently active but exposed squares; typically materialistic moves toward the center or opponent's pieces
analysis.why_bad: The move disrupts the player's own piece coordination by committing to an immediate gain (material or activity) while overlooking that it creates a tactical vulnerability—whether by exposing the moved piece to trapping/attack, removing a key defensive piece from its duties, weakening king shelter, or allowing the opponent to simplify when the player's advantage requires maintaining complexity.
sub_patterns: Capturing with wrong piece or in wrong order, allowing tempo-gaining intermezzo (Rxd2, Qxd6)
Queen capture that enables unfavorable simplification when attacking advantage requires queens on board (Qxd4)
Aggressive f-pawn advance weakening own king or surrendering key squares (f4, f5)
Piece placed on exposed square where it can be trapped by opponent's minor pieces (Ra4, Bc5)

analysis.label: Pieces moved to active squares while abandoning their role of protecting other pieces or pawns, leaving material hanging.
analysis.description: This feature fires on moves where a piece relocates to an apparently active or aggressive square while neglecting its critical defensive coordination. In position 5 (Qc3), the queen left f3—the sole protector of the e4 knight—allowing Black to simply capture it with Qxe4 (2/3 positions involve hanging pieces). In position 4 (Nxe6), the knight abandoned d4 where it was guarding the e5 pawn, and after Black's Nxe5, White suffered decisive material loss (2/3 involve the e-file as the abandoned defensive target). Position 3 (Ne4) represents the feature's baseline activation: an aggressive knight centralization that happens to work in this simplified endgame, but structurally matches the same 'piece seeks activity' impulse that proves catastrophic in the other cases. The common geometry is pieces jumping to central or forward squares (e4, e6, c3) that look powerful but sever a critical defensive link.
analysis.move_pattern: Piece (knight or queen) moves to an active central/forward square, departing from a square where it was defending another piece or pawn
analysis.why_bad: The moved piece was the sole defender of another piece or pawn; relocating it leaves that target completely unprotected, allowing the opponent to win material with a simple capture
sub_patterns: Knight leaves defensive post for aggressive capture/centralization
Queen relocates from piece-protection square to target enemy pawns

analysis.label: Playing a routine quiet move instead of a pawn thrust (typically ...g5) to exploit a bishop with limited retreat squares on the h4-f4 diagonal.
analysis.description: In 3/3 positions, the player made a quiet developing or structural move (castling, bishop repositioning, central pawn break) when a concrete pawn or piece attack against a vulnerable bishop was available. In 2/3 cases, the missed winning move was specifically ...g5 attacking a bishop on h4 that had no safe retreat (g3 blocked by own pawn or unavailable). In the third case (Bf4), the player actively placed their own bishop on a square where it became vulnerable to Nxd3 with tempo. All positions featured a bishop on the h4-d8 or a1-h8 diagonal with restricted mobility, and the correct approach was an aggressive pawn thrust (g5 or d4) rather than a positional consolidation move. The played moves were all 'normal-looking' — castling for king safety, repositioning a bishop, challenging central pawns — but each squandered the critical tempo needed to exploit the trapped/exposed piece.
analysis.move_pattern: Quiet positional moves (castling, bishop retreat/development, pawn break) instead of aggressive pawn thrusts (g5, d4) targeting bishops on h4/f4 with limited escape squares
analysis.why_bad: The quiet move surrenders the tempo needed to trap or attack a bishop with restricted retreat squares, allowing the opponent to calmly exchange or reposition the vulnerable piece, eliminating the primary source of the player's advantage.
sub_patterns: Castling when ...g5 traps Bh4
Central pawn break ignoring Bh4 vulnerability
Bishop development to square where it becomes a tactical target

analysis.label: Playing a natural-looking improving or developing move when the position demanded an immediate concrete action (capture, pawn advance, or forcing move).
analysis.description: This feature fires on positions where the player chooses a routine 'improving' move—typically developing a rook to an open file, centralizing a piece, or repositioning the king—instead of executing an urgent concrete action that the position demands. In 9/9 positions, the best move was a forcing or concrete action: advancing a critical passed pawn (positions 1, 6), capturing an undefended piece or dangerous pawn (positions 10, 15), executing a tactical blow (positions 3, 5, 8), or evacuating from a tactical vulnerability (position 2, 7). Instead, the played moves were universally non-forcing: rook-to-open-file moves (Rfe1, Rad1, Rge8 in 3/9), queen repositions to natural-looking squares (Qd5, Qg3, Qe2 in 3/9), king centralization moves (Kg3, Kf6 in 2/9), and bishop centralization (Be5 in 1/9). The positions averaged only 1.4 good moves available, indicating razor-sharp critical moments where only one or very few moves maintained the evaluation. The average cp_loss of 1331 reflects catastrophic consequences of this pattern.
analysis.move_pattern: Non-forcing piece repositioning (rooks to open files, queens to central squares, kings centralizing, bishops to 'active' outposts) without delivering check, making a capture, or creating an immediate threat
analysis.why_bad: The position contains a concrete tactical demand (a hanging piece, an urgent pawn advance, a forcing sequence, or a piece that must flee) that expires in one tempo—playing a slow improving move wastes that critical tempo, allowing the opponent to neutralize the threat or execute their own tactic
sub_patterns: Rook development to open file instead of capturing hanging material
Queen repositioning to natural square instead of maintaining forcing pressure
King walk instead of critical passed pawn advance
Bishop centralization away from key defensive blockading square

analysis.label: Playing a non-forcing, slow, or misdirected move in a position that demands immediate concrete tactical action.
analysis.description: This feature fires on positions where the player ignores the most urgent tactical demand of the position—whether a critical capture, castling, or precise defensive move—in favor of a slow, passive, or misdirected alternative. In 9/9 positions, the correct move was concrete and forcing (e.g., capturing a free pawn in positions 1 and 15, castling in position 3, emergency king defense in positions 2 and 7, maintaining critical defensive coverage in positions 10 and 6). The average number of good moves was only 1.7, meaning these are narrow positions requiring precision. Instead, players chose purposeless pawn pushes (h4, g4, g5 in 4/9), queen moves abandoning defensive duties (Qg5, Qg5, Qb6 in 3/9), passive retreats (Ne8 in 1/9), or premature captures (Bxe6 in 1/9). The enormous average cp_loss of 2332 reflects that these positions are 'on fire'—the tactical situation is critical—and the played moves catastrophically fail to engage with reality.
analysis.move_pattern: Non-forcing moves (pawn pushes, passive retreats, piece relocations to inactive squares) when the position demands an immediate tactical response—capture, castle, or precise defense
analysis.why_bad: The position has one urgent tactical demand (a hanging piece, an exposed king, a critical defensive square to maintain) and only 1-2 moves address it; the played move ignores this demand entirely, giving the opponent a free tempo to execute devastating tactics—checkmates, captures of undefended pieces, or unstoppable attacks against the now-unaddressed vulnerability.
sub_patterns: Pawn push (g/h file) weakening own king or ignoring tactical crisis
Queen abandoning critical defensive square for illusory counterplay
Passive piece retreat when active central action was required
King walk ignoring a free capture or urgent tactical resource

analysis.label: Playing routine developing or quiet moves in positions where an enemy queen has deeply infiltrated and demands immediate concrete tactical response.
analysis.description: In 10/13 positions, an infiltrated queen (opponent's queen on squares like b2, a1, h1, or the player's own overextended queen on b7/h8 that needs exploitation) creates an urgent tactical demand. The player consistently responds with quiet, 'natural-looking' moves (castling, piece development, pawn pushes) instead of the ONE precise response that either attacks/traps the infiltrator or generates critical counterplay. The average of only 1.5 good moves available confirms these are narrow tactical positions demanding precision. Examples include: O-O instead of Ne5 threatening Nc4 to trap the queen (Position 3), Bb5 instead of Ne5 creating immediate threats (Position 5), Ne2 abandoning defensive duty on c3 (Position 4), and c5 when Rb8 would trap an overextended queen on b7 (Position 9). The common thread is a catastrophic tempo loss at a moment when every single move must carry a concrete threat or address the infiltrator's presence.
analysis.move_pattern: Quiet non-forcing moves (development, castling, pawn pushes) to squares that don't interact with the infiltrated enemy piece or create immediate threats
analysis.why_bad: These moves waste the one critical tempo needed to address an infiltrated queen - either by attacking/trapping it, creating counterplay against the opponent's exposed king, or generating forcing threats. The opponent then safely consolidates the infiltrated piece, grabs undefended material, or redirects the queen to an even stronger square without any pressure.

Castling when the position demands an immediate attacking move to exploit queen placement
Moving a defensive piece away from its critical guard duty
Slow pawn moves when forcing piece moves would exploit overextended enemy queen
Wrong rook / wrong piece choice leaving critical squares undefended

analysis.label: Playing a natural-looking improving or developing move while neglecting an immediate concrete tactical vulnerability or urgent positional prerequisite.
analysis.description: This feature fires on positions where the player makes a 'reasonable-looking' move—typically king centralization, castling, pawn expansion, or piece repositioning—that ignores the single most urgent concrete demand of the position. In 6/10 positions, the move is a king move (Ke8, Kc3, Kb4, Ke4, Kg2, O-O) that appears to improve king activity but either creates a new tactical vulnerability (skewer on rank in positions 3-4, hanging piece in position 7) or fails to prevent opponent infiltration (positions 2, 8). In the remaining cases, moves like h4, Ng4+, Be1, and b5 are similarly 'natural' improving actions that miss the critical priority—whether that's restraining the opponent's king (g4 before Kg2), securing a piece before centralizing (Bg2 before Ke4), targeting a key pawn (Bb6 instead of Be1), or defending a vulnerable pawn (e5 instead of b5). The correct moves universally address the concrete tactical/positional emergency FIRST, only then proceeding with the general improvement. The average cp_loss of 1150 reflects that these 'autopilot' moves often catastrophically mis-prioritize, turning winning positions into losing ones.
analysis.move_pattern: Mostly king moves (6/10) toward centralization or safety squares; also includes pawn advances and piece retreats/checks—all are 'improving' moves played one tempo too early
analysis.why_bad: The move neglects an urgent concrete prerequisite (securing a hanging piece, blocking an infiltration square, preventing a skewer alignment, or defending a targeted pawn), allowing the opponent to exploit the unaddressed vulnerability immediately
sub_patterns: King centralization creating rank/file alignment for skewer (Kc3, Kb4)
King improvement before restraining opponent's king infiltration (Kg2 before g4, Ke8 before a5)
King/piece move abandoning defense of hanging material (Ke4 leaving Bc6, O-O enabling Bxc3/Rxe2)
Peripheral pawn/piece move ignoring central tactical threat (b5 ignoring Rxe6, Be1 ignoring d-pawn)

analysis.label: Ambitious forward piece or pawn moves in underdeveloped opening positions that neglect piece safety and create immediate tactical vulnerabilities.
analysis.description: This feature fires on moves that prioritize aggressive ambition over fundamental soundness in underdeveloped positions. In 5/6 cases, at least one king remains uncastled. The blunders share a common structure: a piece or pawn lunges forward (f4 pawn pushes in 2/6, knight centralizations Ne4 in 2/6, a knight sortie Ndb5 in 1/6, a bishop placement on a rim square Ba5 in 1/6) while ignoring that this forward move either leaves another piece undefended (Ne4 abandoning the Bb4 in 2/6 cases), creates critical square weaknesses near an uncastled king (f4 weakening e3/f2/diagonals in 2/6), or places a piece on an unstable square easily challenged with tempo (Ndb5 kicked by ...a6, Ba5 trapped by b4 in 2/6). In all cases, the best alternatives were modest developing or consolidating moves (Nge2, O-O, Be7, Nb3, d5) that prioritized completing development and piece safety. The average cp_loss of 357 with 2.7 good moves available confirms these are severe, avoidable blunders born from impatience rather than necessity.
analysis.move_pattern: Piece or pawn moving forward aggressively (knight centralization, f-pawn push, knight sortie, bishop to rim) in underdeveloped positions with uncastled kings
analysis.why_bad: The forward move either abandons defense of another piece (creating hanging pieces), weakens critical squares near an uncastled king (enabling knight invasions and forks), or places a piece where it can be immediately challenged/trapped with simple pawn advances, while simpler developing moves maintained equality.
sub_patterns: f4 pawn push with uncastled king weakening e3/f2 squares enabling Ng4 invasions
Knight centralization (Ne4) leaving an undefended bishop on b4 to be captured
Knight sortie to aggressive but unstable square (Ndb5) kicked by pawn with tempo
Bishop retreat to rim square (Ba5) where it becomes trapped by advancing pawns

analysis.label: Moving a piece (usually the queen) to a peripheral or exposed square instead of consolidating/retreating, allowing the opponent to gain decisive tempo.
analysis.description: This feature fires when a player makes a move that places a piece on a vulnerable peripheral square (or wastes a critical tempo) when the position demands consolidation, retreat, or immediate action. In 7/10 positions, the played move is a queen move to a kingside rim square (Qh5, Qg5, Qh3, Qf5, Qh3, Qxf2) or a king advance to an exposed square (Kg4, Kh1 in 2/10). The remaining cases involve ignoring an exposed piece's vulnerability (Rfd1 when the queen on h7 needed relocation, g6 wasting tempo when a decisive tactic existed). In every case, the correct move was a consolidating retreat or repositioning to a safer/more functional square (Qe7, Qe3, Bd1, Ke2, Qd5, Ne7, Bg2, Rg8, Rxc4, Qd3). The refutations universally exploit the misplaced piece through tempo-gaining attacks—chasing the queen with rook lifts, bishop attacks, or intermezzos—neutralizing the player's advantage or creating decisive material gains.
analysis.move_pattern: Queen (or king) moves laterally or forward to g4/g5/h3/h5/f5/f2 on the kingside periphery, away from central safety; occasionally a non-urgent move that ignores an already-exposed piece
analysis.why_bad: The piece lands on a square where it has no concrete threats but is itself vulnerable to tempo-gaining attacks (Bf4 trapping, Rf4/Rh3 chasing, Bh5+ intermezzo, doubled rooks on g-file), allowing the opponent to gain multiple tempi and execute decisive plans while the misplaced piece is neutralized or lost.
sub_patterns: Queen to h3/h5 rim square with no real targets, opponent gains tempo with piece attacks
Queen to g5/f5 where bishop or rook drives it with tempo
King advances to exposed square (g4/h1) losing coordination and leaving pieces undefended
Non-urgent prophylactic move when a decisive tactic or critical consolidation is required
Queen captures on peripheral square vulnerable to intermezzo check

analysis.label: King moves toward the board edge or corner in a pawn endgame, losing opposition or critical defensive positioning.
analysis.description: This feature fires on endgame positions (10/10) where the king (9/10 moves are king moves) retreats toward the board edge, corner, or back rank instead of maintaining a more central or active stance. The critical blunders share a common thread: in drawn K+P positions, the king retreats one square too far toward the rim (e.g., Kc1 instead of Kc2 in position 6, Kb1 instead of Kb2/Kc2 in position 7, Kh8 instead of Kh7 in position 4, Kh1 instead of Kg1 in position 2), surrendering the opposition and turning a theoretical draw into a loss. In positions 3, 4, 6, and 7 (4/10), this single-square edge retreat converts a 0.00 drawn evaluation into a decisive loss (~550cp). The one non-king move (Rb1, position 9) follows the same geometric logic—placing a piece on the back rank where it gets trapped and exchanged. The milder activations (positions 1, 5, 8, 12) show the same directional tendency in already-decided positions.
analysis.move_pattern: King (or piece) moves toward the board edge: specifically retreating to the back rank, corner square, or rim file (h1, h8, b1, c1, d1, h6)
analysis.why_bad: In pawn endgames, the king on the edge loses opposition, gets confined with fewer escape squares, and cannot contest the critical squares needed to blockade or oppose the enemy passed pawn. One square closer to the center maintains drawing chances; one square toward the edge is fatal.
sub_patterns: King retreats to corner losing opposition (Kh1, Kh8, Kb1)
King steps to back rank one square too deep (Kc1 vs Kc2, Kd1)
King drifts to rim file abandoning central defense (Kh6, Kb4)
Piece retreats to back rank allowing forced exchange (Rb1)

analysis.label: Playing a preparatory or repositioning move when the position demanded an immediate, time-critical pawn advance or forcing continuation.
analysis.description: This feature fires on positions where the player chooses a 'reasonable-looking' quiet move (king centralization, piece repositioning, or wrong pawn selection) instead of the ONE critical forcing pawn advance that the position demands. In 6/8 actual blunders, the correct move was an immediate pawn push (a5, e4, h6, h6, e5, d5) but the player made a preparatory move instead. The positions share extreme narrowness (avg 1.6 good moves), mostly endgame phases (7/10), and exposed kings in pawn-race or tempo-critical situations. The errors consistently involve misjudging urgency: the player treats a razor-sharp timing position as one allowing gradual improvement. Key examples include pushing e4/e5 when h6 was the only winning move (positions 6, 8), playing Kc7 when a5 wins by the rule of the square (position 1), playing Kc5 when e5 with a bishop sacrifice wins the promotion race (position 7), and playing Bc3 when d5 wins the exchange tactically (position 15).
analysis.move_pattern: Quiet piece repositioning (king, bishop, queen, rook to nearby square) or wrong pawn push, typically non-forcing and non-capturing
analysis.why_bad: These moves lose a critical tempo in positions where the winning plan requires immediate forcing action—typically advancing the most dangerous passed pawn before the opponent can reposition defensively, enter the pawn's square, or neutralize a tactical window that exists for only one move.
sub_patterns: King march instead of immediate pawn push in pawn race
Advancing the wrong passed pawn (e-pawn instead of h-pawn)
Piece repositioning instead of decisive pawn break
Quiet positional move missing a one-move tactical window

analysis.label: Moving a well-placed piece away from a critical post to capture or target a peripheral pawn, losing tempo and allowing the opponent to seize the initiative.
analysis.description: This feature fires when a player displaces a piece from a strategically vital square to grab peripheral material or pursue seemingly active but actually inferior placement. In 4/6 cases, the move involves capturing or attacking a pawn (Nxc5 grabs c5 pawn, Qxa6 grabs a6 pawn, Nxa4 grabs a4 pawn, Nf3 targets h4 pawn). In 5/6 cases, the piece moves away from the critical zone of the position toward the flanks or edge. The common consequence is a tempo loss (tagged in 5/6 positions) that allows the opponent to seize a key square (Rd5 in Position 1), escape a mating net (Ke3 in Position 2), capture a strategic asset (Rxb6 in Position 3), push passed pawns (h5 in Position 5), reposition a trapped piece (Nf5 in Position 6), or win the displaced piece (Qh5+ in Position 9). All 6/6 positions cite piece activity deterioration as the core problem.
analysis.move_pattern: Piece (usually knight 4/6) moves away from a dominant central or active square, often capturing toward the rim or flank files (a4, a6, c5, h4, f3, f6)
analysis.why_bad: The piece was performing a critical function on its current square (controlling key squares, supporting mating nets, maintaining pressure), and moving it grants the opponent a free tempo to reorganize, escape tactical danger, or seize the vacated key square.
sub_patterns: Knight captures peripheral a-file pawn (Nxa4)
Knight/Queen captures flank pawn abandoning central dominance (Nxc5, Qxa6)
Knight moves to attack a pawn instead of pressing mating attack (Nf3)
Piece moves to exposed square with no support (Nh4)
King retreats passively relinquishing central control (Kf6)

analysis.label: Moving a piece that was the sole defender or blocker preventing the opponent's queen from delivering checkmate on a square adjacent to the king.
analysis.description: In all 3/3 positions, the move played allows the opponent's queen to deliver checkmate on the very next move by capturing a pawn or piece adjacent to the king. The mechanism varies: in one case (Position 7, Be2) the piece is placed directly on the mating square where the queen captures it for mate; in another (Position 11, Qxe2) the queen abandons defense of a critical pawn (c7) next to the king for a greedy capture; and in the third (Position 13, Nfd5) a knight blocking the queen's diagonal to g7 is centralized, unmasking the lethal battery. All 3/3 result in queen checkmates on squares immediately adjacent to the king (e2 near e1, c7 near b8, g7 near g8), and all 3/3 had available alternatives that simply required maintaining the defensive piece's position or addressing the king's safety first.
analysis.move_pattern: Various piece types (bishop, queen, knight) move away from critical defensive positions, unblocking or unguarding a square adjacent to the king where the opponent's queen delivers checkmate
analysis.why_bad: The moved piece was the sole obstacle (blocker on a file/diagonal or defender of a critical square) preventing the opponent's queen from accessing a mating square next to the king; removing it grants an immediate one-move checkmate.
sub_patterns: Piece placed on square where queen captures with mate (self-immolation)
Queen abandons defense of critical pawn near king for greedy capture
Knight/piece unblocks diagonal allowing queen-bishop battery to deliver mate

analysis.label: Natural-looking developing or improving moves that ignore concrete tactical demands such as hanging pieces, forcing sequences, or critical vulnerabilities.
analysis.description: This feature fires on positions where the player makes a 'textbook' or generic improving move—placing rooks on open files (Rc1, Re8, Rd8 in 3/9 positions), developing bishops to active-looking squares (Bg4, Be3 in 3/9 positions), or making standard development moves (Nf6 in 1/9)—while the position demands a specific concrete action. In 6/9 cases, the mistake involves ignoring undefended pieces: either the player's own pieces becoming vulnerable (Bg4 leaving f7/b7 undefended in positions 3 and 5; Re8 leaving Bb7 hanging in position 12) or failing to capture the opponent's hanging piece (Nf6 ignoring free Ng5 in position 6). The common thread is prioritizing general principles (control files, develop pieces, create pins) over calculation of forcing moves. The best moves consistently involve either capturing hanging material (Qxg5), executing tactical strikes (Nf4 fork, Nd8 winning pawns), or addressing concrete vulnerabilities (Bc8 protecting a hanging bishop). The played moves look reasonable to a principles-based player but represent a failure to engage with the position's specific tactical content.
analysis.move_pattern: Pieces moved to generically 'good' squares (rooks to open files, bishops to pins/diagonals, knights to central squares) without addressing the position's concrete tactical requirements
analysis.why_bad: These moves waste critical tempo on generic improvements while the position contains forcing tactical opportunities (captures of hanging pieces, dual-attack knight moves, pawn breaks) or urgent defensive necessities (protecting undefended pieces, addressing king safety). The opponent exploits the tempo loss by executing the tactic the player should have either played or prevented.
sub_patterns: Rook to open file ignoring hanging/vulnerable piece elsewhere
Bishop sortie creating undefended weaknesses (f7, b7) with king uncastled
Standard development move ignoring free material capture
Generic piece improvement when forcing tactical sequence available
Slow moves allowing opponent's clearance or combination tactics

analysis.label: Non-forcing, slow moves played when the position demands immediate concrete action to address a critical tactical vulnerability.
analysis.description: This feature activates on positions where players choose passive, non-urgent moves—typically quiet pawn advances or 'improving' piece repositions—while ignoring an immediate tactical crisis. In 4/6 positions, the moves are non-threatening pawn pushes (g6, h6, a3) or quiet repositioning (Ne4, Kh7) when concrete action was required. The critical vulnerabilities ignored include f7/f2 weaknesses (positions 1, 3, 7), an exposed king offering captures with check (position 4), and walking into a geometric pin (position 5). In 5/6 positions with meaningful cp_loss, the average loss is 2121cp. The refutations consistently exploit the tempo wasted: e5 breakthroughs against undeveloped armies (positions 1, 3), Bxf7+ sacrifices exploiting the unshielded f-pawn (position 3), Rxf2+ mating attacks against undefended pawns (position 7), and d-pawn advances enabled by the opponent's failure to capture immediately (position 4). The common thread is that all moves represent 'reasonable-looking' ideas in a vacuum (fianchetto preparation, prophylaxis against Bg5, knight centralization, king blockade) but catastrophically ignore the concrete demands of the position.
analysis.move_pattern: Non-forcing, non-capturing moves (predominantly quiet pawn advances to g6/h6/a3 or piece repositioning) with no check or immediate threat
analysis.why_bad: These moves waste a critical tempo when the position contains an urgent tactical vulnerability (typically f7/f2 weakness, exposed king, or concrete winning capture) that demands immediate attention, allowing the opponent to execute a decisive combination or seize the initiative irreversibly.
sub_patterns: Kingside pawn push ignoring central/developmental urgency
Prophylactic flank pawn move ignoring existing tactical threat
Quiet piece centralization missing concrete capture with check
King move walking into geometric vulnerability (pin/diagonal)

analysis.label: Playing a superficial check in an already-winning position instead of finding the quiet or more precise killer move.
analysis.description: This feature activates in positions where one side has a dominant, winning attack against an exposed enemy king with multiple forcing options available. In 3/4 positions, a check was played; in the two most costly cases (Bh4+ losing 479cp, Ng7+ losing 9138cp), the check was a tactical blunder that either hung material or removed a critical piece from its dominant post, while quiet moves (Rh7, Ne6+) delivered forced mate. Position 3 saw Bh4+ hanging the bishop to a rook on the open h-file when Ne6+ won decisively via fork. Position 4 saw Ng7+ vacating the knight from f5—the linchpin of every mating pattern—when quiet Rh7 forced mate in 3. The 0cp-loss positions (1 and 2) represent milder activations where the forcing move happened to be equivalent to alternatives. The pattern is the 'patzer sees a check' syndrome in already-won positions.
analysis.move_pattern: Various pieces delivering check to exposed/centralized kings, typically moving away from optimal squares to give check (bishop to h4, knight to g7, rook to f1)
analysis.why_bad: The checks are superficial—they either hang the checking piece (Bh4+ to an unnoticed rook), remove a critically-placed piece from its dominant square (Ng7+ vacating f5), or achieve nothing concrete, while quiet moves maintain the mating net or exploit the position more decisively.
sub_patterns: Knight check abandoning dominant outpost
Bishop check hanging to rook on open file
Capture-check when alternative wins more cleanly

analysis.label: Moves that voluntarily abandon a dominant piece position or critical resource for a tempting but inferior alternative, releasing pressure on the opponent.
analysis.description: This feature activates on moves where the player gives up a powerfully-placed piece or critical positional resource in favor of a tempting-looking alternative (capture, centralization, or repositioning) that actually surrenders the initiative. In 4/8 positions, a well-placed piece is voluntarily moved from a dominant outpost to a passive or vulnerable square (Nd5 from crushing e3, Be2 retreating from active c4, Nd1 from strong c3, Qc5 from flexible e7). In 3/8 positions, a greedy capture removes a piece from a critical role or destroys a key structural resource (Rxc2 abandons the attacking g-file, dxc3 grabs a pawn while ignoring king exposure, fxe6 captures with the wrong unit destroying the king's pawn shield). In all cases, the opponent gains the tempo or freedom needed to consolidate, develop, or launch a devastating counterattack that was previously impossible. The average cp_loss of 1486 reflects that these positions had significant built-up pressure or advantage that was catastrophically released by one move.
analysis.move_pattern: Any piece type; moves away from an active/disruptive square toward a passive, exposed, or structurally damaging alternative; often captures or apparent improvements
analysis.why_bad: These moves release built-up positional pressure or remove a critical resource from its optimal post, giving the opponent the time/freedom to consolidate development, exploit exposed kings, execute tactical strikes (forks, checks, sacrifices), or transition favorably—opportunities that were suppressed while the original piece placement or structure remained intact.
sub_patterns: Knight retreats from paralyzing outpost to challengeable square (Nd5 from e3, Nd1 from c3)
Bishop/piece retreat from active attacking diagonal to passive square (Be2 from c4)
Greedy pawn/piece captures removing attacker from critical file or duty (Rxc2, dxc3)
Capture with wrong unit destroying king's pawn shield (fxe6 instead of Bxe6)
Queen moving to exposed/tactically vulnerable square losing coordination (Qc5, Qxd5)

analysis.label: Playing a reasonable-looking move that follows a general plan while missing the position's most urgent concrete opportunity or requirement.
analysis.description: This feature fires on moves that appear logical on the surface—centralizing, capturing a piece, preparing development, attacking pawns—but miss a more forcing or precise alternative demanded by the position's concrete circumstances. In 3/6 positions, the best move was a specific capture that went unplayed (Nxf8 winning the exchange in Position 2, cxd6 cashing in positional pressure in Position 5, Nxg4 taking a hanging pawn in Position 7). In 2/6 positions, the piece was sent to a superficially active but actually suboptimal square (Kf3 instead of the more direct Kf4 in Position 1, Rb4 instead of the critical Re3 in Position 8). In 5/6 cases the player followed an understandable strategic rationale (doubling rooks, attacking targets, preparing fianchetto, racing the king) but the position required precise calculation rather than general planning. The average cp_loss of 251 reflects that these 'looks right' moves typically overlook a tactical priority that changes the position's evaluation dramatically.
analysis.move_pattern: Various piece types moved to squares that appear purposeful but are concretely suboptimal; often a quiet/repositioning move when a forcing capture was available
analysis.why_bad: The moves prioritize a general strategic idea over the position's specific tactical demand—whether that's capturing hanging/undefended material, maintaining a piece on a critical defensive post, or choosing the most efficient path in a racing endgame
sub_patterns: Quiet developing/repositioning move when a free capture exists
Capturing the wrong target when a stronger capture is available
Abandoning a piece's critical defensive role for an offensive plan
Choosing a less direct path in a tempo-critical endgame

analysis.label: Playing a non-forcing move (quiet development or material grab) while a forced checkmate pattern exists in the position, either to execute or to defend against.
analysis.description: In 6/6 analyzed positions, the player made a non-urgent move while an immediate or near-immediate checkmate existed. In 3/6 cases (Bxf6, Qxd3, Rfe1), the opponent had a mate-in-one available as punishment. In 2/6 cases (g6, g3), the player themselves had a forced mate-in-two but played a slow pawn push instead. In 1/6 cases (Na3), only perpetual check could save the game but a quiet developing move was chosen, allowing mate-in-4. The moves split between material-grabbing captures (Rxd3, Bxf6, Qxd3) that remove defensive pieces or ignore threats, and quiet positional moves (g6, g3, Rfe1, Na3) that treat the position as non-urgent. The common denominator is a complete failure to recognize that the position's critical feature is king safety requiring an immediate forcing response — either delivering mate, escaping mate, or forcing perpetual check.
analysis.move_pattern: Mixed piece types and directions; captures on d3/f6 (material grabs), quiet pawn pushes (g6, g3), rook/knight development (Rfe1, Na3) — all non-forcing moves that fail to address the first-rank/diagonal mating geometry
analysis.why_bad: The position has an immediate or near-immediate checkmate pattern active (queen+piece battery on diagonal, back-rank vulnerability, or exposed king), and the played move either ignores the opponent's mating threat or misses the player's own forced mate, treating a tactically critical position as if normal positional considerations apply.
sub_patterns: Material-grabbing capture that removes a key defensive piece, enabling opponent's immediate checkmate (Bxf6→Qh7#, Qxd3→Qg7#)
Quiet pawn push or development when own forced mate-in-two exists (g6 missing Qd1+/Qxe1#, g3 missing Rb8+/Rxe8#)
Positional developing move that completely overlooks opponent's one-move mate (Rfe1 allowing Qg2#)
Quiet move in mutual-attack position where only perpetual check saves (Na3 when Qc5+ draws)

analysis.label: Non-forcing moves to h-file squares (pieces or pawns) that create kingside liabilities by trapping pieces on the rim or weakening the king's pawn shelter.
analysis.description: This feature fires on moves that place pieces or advance pawns to h-file squares in ways that create kingside vulnerabilities. All 5/5 moves target h-file squares (Bh4, Bh5, Nh2, h4, h6). In 3/5 cases, a piece retreats or advances to an h-file square where it becomes trapped or a tactical target (Bh4 gets entombed by g5-h5-h4 pawns, Bh5 becomes an undefended target for ...Qh4, Nh2 becomes completely passive while abandoning the critical f3 defensive post). In 2/5 cases, an h-pawn advance creates structural weaknesses (h4 is a tempo-wasting move that ignores a critical tactical window, h6 weakens the kingside pawn cover allowing a Bxh6 sacrifice). The common thread is that these h-file moves appear superficially purposeful (maintaining pins, creating threats, preventing piece development) but are actually counterproductive—they either strand pieces on rim squares where they lose mobility (4/5 tagged with piece_activity issues) or weaken king safety (4/5 tagged with king_safety).
analysis.move_pattern: Piece (bishop/knight) or pawn moving to an h-file square (h2, h4, h5, h6); non-capturing, non-checking moves
analysis.why_bad: Pieces placed on the h-file rim become passive, trapped, or undefended targets (lacking retreat squares or support), while h-pawn advances weaken the castled king's structure, and in all cases better constructive or tactical alternatives exist that maintain piece coordination and king safety.
sub_patterns: Bishop advancing/retreating to h4/h5 where pawns or queen attacks trap it
Knight retreating to h2 abandoning key defensive duties
h-pawn advances weakening own king's shelter when tactical play was required

analysis.label: King moves to the 1st/8th rank in endgames, losing tempo by self-restricting mobility or blocking promotion.
analysis.description: This feature fires on king moves to the back rank (1st or 8th rank) in endgame positions involving passed pawns and promotion threats. In 10/12 positions, the king moves to the edge rank (Kg1, Kb1, Kg8, Kc8, Kb8, Kf1, Kc1) where it becomes restricted. The common error is moving the king directly to a seemingly logical destination (near a pawn, behind a promotion square) without first making an intermediate move that would force the opponent to waste tempo. In positions 1 and 2, Kg1 traps the king in a corner shuttle. In position 10, Kb8 physically blocks the b8 promotion square.
