In positions 11 and 15, going directly to the back rank gives the opponent a free tempo to advance their king. In position 8, Kg8 traps the king on the back rank enabling a forced mate. In position 13, Kf1 places the king on an open first-rank square where approaching king + queen create a mating net. The consistent thread is that the back rank limits escape routes and the opponent exploits the lost tempo or restricted geometry.
analysis.move_pattern: King moving to 1st or 8th rank (corners and edges), typically one square retreat/sideways to the board edge
analysis.why_bad: Back-rank king moves lose tempo by either blocking one's own pawn promotion, allowing the opponent a free move to advance/reposition, creating vulnerability to rank-based checks, or trapping the king in a corner oscillation pattern where opponents gain approach tempi
sub_patterns: King blocks own promotion square (Kb8 blocking b8=Q)
King enters corner shuttle trap (Kg1 bouncing g1-h1)
King moves directly to destination without forcing opponent to check first (Kg8 instead of Kf7)
King retreats to open first rank vulnerable to mating coordination (Kf1, Kc1)

analysis.label: Playing a non-forcing, slow positional move when the position demands immediate concrete action, allowing the opponent to exploit a tactical vulnerability or seize the initiative.
analysis.description: This feature activates on moves that waste a critical tempo in positions requiring immediate tactical attention. The blunders share a common pattern: the player opts for a slow, often queenside or peripheral action (a4 twice, Na2, Qb7) or places a piece on a tactically vulnerable square without checking consequences (Rf3 twice, Rf6, Kxf1, Ng5) when concrete forcing moves were available. In 8/10 positions, the side had a clear advantage or equality that demanded maintaining momentum. The opponent consistently punishes by exploiting the tempo loss — launching forks (Position 1: Ne5), creating pins (Position 7: Bg4), attacking undefended pieces (Position 12: f5 hitting Be4), exploiting exposed kings (Position 3: Qf6+), or seizing kingside initiative (Position 8: f4, Position 11: h5). The positions typically offer 2-3 good alternatives focused on immediate tactical engagement (captures like Qxd6, pawn breakthroughs like d6, or piece coordination like Ne2→Nf5), making these errors clearly avoidable failures of tactical prioritization.
analysis.move_pattern: Non-forcing moves: pieces/pawns moved to peripheral squares (a-file pushes, rim knight retreats) or rooks lifted to tactically exposed ranks without checking opponent's concrete responses
analysis.why_bad: The wasted tempo allows the opponent to execute a concrete tactical idea (fork, pin, piece attack, pawn break) that the position was already threatening, turning a favorable or equal position into a losing one because the moved piece either becomes a target itself or was needed for defense/attack elsewhere
sub_patterns: Queenside pawn push ignoring kingside crisis (a4×2)
Rook lift to tactically vulnerable square (Rf3×2, Rf6)
Knight retreat/advance to peripheral square losing tempo (Na2, Ng5)
Passive recapture exposing king (Kxf1)
Queen repositioning away from critical sector (Qb7)

analysis.label: Playing a quiet developing move (usually a knight move) instead of capturing a completely undefended enemy piece with the queen.
analysis.description: In all 8/8 positions, the player made a passive developing move while an enemy piece (almost always a knight) was completely undefended and could be captured for free by the queen. In 7/8 cases the blunder was specifically a knight development move (Nh6 x3, Nh3, Nc6, Na6, Nf6), and in 7/8 cases the missed capture was Qxg5 taking an undefended knight on g5 in Italian Game-type positions. The average centipawn loss was ~408, representing approximately a full piece squandered. In every case, only 1 good move existed (the queen capture), and the player instead chose generic positional development—often to a passive rim square—while completely overlooking the simple tactical reality that the opponent's aggressively-posted piece had no defenders.
analysis.move_pattern: Knight moved to a passive/natural development square (typically rim squares h6, h3, a6, or standard squares c6, f6); one case was a pawn push f5. All ignored an available queen capture of a hanging enemy knight.
analysis.why_bad: The player prioritized routine development or prophylactic defense (e.g., 'defending f7') over a simple free capture. They failed to recognize that the piece creating the threat was itself undefended and could be taken, making the threat illusory.
sub_patterns: Nh6 to defend f7 against a hanging Ng5 that Qxg5 wins for free
Natural knight development (Nc6, Nf6) ignoring hanging piece
Knight to rim square (Na6, Nh3) when queen capture wins material
Pawn advance for positional reasons when enemy piece is en prise

analysis.label: Superficially attractive moves that follow general principles but walk into a specific tactical punishment the opponent can exploit.
analysis.description: This feature fires on positions where the player makes a 'natural-looking' move that follows a general chess principle (castle for safety, capture material with check, gain space with pawns, advance a passed pawn) but ignores a concrete tactical refutation. In 3/5 cases the player chose a pawn advance or passive action when piece activation/development was the critical need (a3 instead of Rd7, g4 instead of Bg5, O-O instead of Nbd7). In 4/5 cases, the correct approach involved prioritizing piece activity or coordination over the superficially attractive goal pursued. The blunders share the trait of being 'autopilot' moves—ones that would be reasonable in a generic position but catastrophically fail because of a specific tactical vulnerability: Nh5 walks into g4 trapping the piece (1/5), O-O allows Bxc5/Qxd8 winning material on the queenside (1/5), Rxa4+ sacrifices the winning piece for a pawn (1/5), g4 invites h5 cracking open the king's shelter (1/5), and a3 creates a fixed target while wasting the tempo needed for rook activation (1/5).
analysis.move_pattern: Varied piece types and directions; no single geometric pattern. Includes knight to rim, kingside castling, pawn advances (a-file, g-file), and rook capture with check on the a-file.
analysis.why_bad: Each move prioritizes a secondary goal (safety, material, space, pawn advance) while ignoring that the opponent has a concrete tactical response that exploits the specific vulnerability the move creates or exposes, resulting in catastrophic material loss or positional collapse.
sub_patterns: Piece retreat to rim square allowing pawn trap (Nh5→g4)
Premature pawn advance when piece development needed (g4, a3)
Routine castling enabling tactical sequence on abandoned files (O-O)
Capturing material at the cost of the decisive attacking piece (Rxa4+)

analysis.label: Playing a non-forcing repositioning move when an immediate capture, check, or forcing combination wins decisive material or delivers checkmate.
analysis.description: This feature fires on positions where the player makes a quiet, positional-looking move (repositioning a piece to a seemingly useful square or making a prophylactic pawn push) while completely missing an immediately available forcing tactical blow. In 6/7 positions, the best move was a direct capture or check that won significant material (Qxa3 capturing a hanging piece, Qxc3+ winning a knight with check, Nf6+ winning the queen via sacrifice, Qc3+ delivering mate in 2, exf6 leading to discovered check winning an exchange, Nxd1+ capturing a rook with discovered check). The played moves instead include quiet rook repositioning (Rb1, Re8, R3b4), knight retreats to passive squares (Ng3), queen relocation to less active squares (Qg2), a flashy but materially unproductive check (Nh3+), and a prophylactic pawn push (h3). The positions are characterized by extremely few good moves available (avg 1.3), indicating sharp tactical moments demanding precision rather than general improvement. The average centipawn loss of ~2992 reflects that several positions involved missed checkmates or missed queen-winning combinations.
analysis.move_pattern: Non-capturing piece repositioning (rook to file, knight sideways/backward, queen to passive diagonal, pawn push) in positions where a forcing capture or check was immediately available
analysis.why_bad: These moves fail because they squander a critical tactical moment—the position demands an immediate forcing blow (capture with check, sacrifice, en passant, or simple hanging piece capture), but the player instead makes a slow improving move that gives the opponent time to defend, escape, or neutralize the threat. The forcing opportunity is typically a one-move window that disappears once the opponent gets a tempo.
sub_patterns: Quiet rook moves to files when a queen capture/check wins material (Rb1, Re8, R3b4)
Piece repositioning away from ideal attacking square when sacrifice/forcing move wins (Ng3, Qg2)
Wrong forcing move—choosing a flashy check over a material-winning capture (Nh3+ vs Nxd1+)
Passive pawn push when active pawn capture/advance solves the position (h3 vs h4/hxg3)

analysis.label: Piece moves to a seemingly aggressive or purposeful square while fatally abandoning a critical defensive duty or creating an immediate tactical vulnerability.
analysis.description: In 5/5 positions, the blunder involves moving a piece with a clear attacking or positional intent—threatening an enemy piece/pawn, contesting a file, or approaching a target—but the move either removes a key defender (Ng5 leaves Rc4 unguarded, 1/5; Rhd1 strips kingside defense, 1/5), wastes a critical tempo window on an inferior continuation (Nf6 misses Nf4 winning the exchange, Nh4 misses Nc3+ fork, 2/5), or walks into a geometric alignment that allows a devastating tactic (Kg6 creates a skewer on the g-file, 1/5). In all cases, there existed at least one clearly superior move (avg 2.0 good moves available) that either maintained the piece's defensive role or exploited the position's true tactical priority. The average cp loss of 2246 reflects that these moves consistently convert playable positions into lost or mated ones because the 'attack' created is far less significant than the vulnerability exposed.
analysis.move_pattern: Piece (often knight 3/5, also rook or king) moves to a forward or lateral square with apparent attacking purpose, away from its current defensive/functional position
analysis.why_bad: The piece was performing a critical defensive function (guarding another piece, shielding the king, maintaining a tactical fork possibility) that is instantly exploited once the piece leaves—resulting in hanging material, forced mates, skewers, or loss of a decisive tactical window
sub_patterns: Knight leaves defensive post exposing hanging piece
Knight moves to wrong square missing critical check/fork tempo
Rook abandons king defense for file control
King advances into tactical alignment with own piece

analysis.label: Capturing a pawn when the position demands addressing a more critical strategic or tactical need, resulting in self-deflection from a key role.
analysis.description: In all 3/3 positions, the player captures a pawn with a well-placed piece (Qxc4, Rxh6, Nxc3) instead of addressing the most urgent positional demand. In position 2, Black grabs the c4 pawn instead of securing the king with Kg7, allowing White's e5 pawn break to generate a devastating attack. In position 5, White captures the h6 pawn, deflecting the rook from f6 where it prevented the f5 counter-strike, allowing Black to win the unprotected g4 knight. In position 7, Black abandons a powerfully centralized knight on e4 to capture the c3 pawn, ignoring the critical need to neutralize White's crushing e6 pawn. All 3/3 positions feature the capturing piece leaving a superior post for material gain, and all 3/3 have a single devastating refutation that exploits the newly created vulnerability. The average cp loss is 233, indicating these are serious blunders masked as reasonable-looking captures.
analysis.move_pattern: Any piece captures an enemy pawn, moving away from a critical defensive/controlling square
analysis.why_bad: The pawn capture deflects the player's own piece from a more important role (defense, blockade, or central control) while ignoring the position's most urgent demand, allowing the opponent a single powerful counter-resource that exploits the resulting vulnerability.
sub_patterns: Queen leaves center to grab flank pawn, exposing king to counterplay
Rook deflects from critical file/rank for a pawn, enabling tactical counter-strike
Knight abandons strong outpost for peripheral pawn, ignoring dangerous enemy passed pawn

analysis.label: A piece (usually a rook) moves to a square on an unobstructed enemy bishop diagonal, allowing the bishop to simply capture it.
analysis.description: In all 7/7 positions, the blundering side moves a piece to a square that lies directly on an enemy bishop's active diagonal, allowing that bishop to capture the piece with no recourse. In 6/7 cases, a rook is moved to the hanging square (Rxh7 into a c2-bishop's diagonal, Rxd2 into a g5-bishop's diagonal, Rxh2 into an e5-bishop's diagonal, Rd2 into an f4-bishop's diagonal, Rc6 into an e4-bishop's diagonal, Rd3 into an h7-bishop's diagonal), and in 1/7 a knight is placed on a square controlled by a g1-bishop (Ne3). The bishop diagonals range from 2 squares to 5 squares in length, but all are completely unobstructed at the moment the piece arrives. The player typically has a plausible positional or material motivation for the move (centralizing, grabbing a pawn, activating on a rank) but catastrophically overlooks the geometric relationship between the destination square and the enemy bishop.
analysis.move_pattern: A piece (rook 6/7, knight 1/7) moves to a square along an unobstructed enemy bishop diagonal, typically 2-5 squares from the bishop
analysis.why_bad: The destination square is directly attacked by an enemy bishop along a clear diagonal, meaning the piece is immediately captured for free or near-free, resulting in catastrophic material loss
sub_patterns: Rook captures a pawn on a bishop-controlled square (Rxh7, Rxh2, Rxd2)
Rook moves to an active square on a bishop diagonal without capturing (Rd2, Rc6, Rd3)
Minor piece moves to a square on bishop's short diagonal (Ne3)

analysis.label: Suboptimal moves in decisive endgames that fail to directly address or exploit critical passed pawns.
analysis.description: This feature fires on endgame positions with extreme evaluations (400-800cp advantage) where the player makes a plausible-looking move that wastes tempo relative to the most critical positional element—almost always dangerous passed pawns. In 6/8 positions, connected or advanced passed pawns are the defining feature, and the move played fails to optimally engage with them: Qb6+ gives check but doesn't capture the d6 pawn when Qxd6+ was available (Position 6, -383cp); Ka7 moves the king to the wrong side of White's connected passers instead of blockading with Kb7 (Position 7, -242cp); Nf6 places the knight where it's immediately captured, removing the only piece fighting the e4/f5 passers (Position 8, -171cp); Rc3 fails to address Black's advanced g3/h3 duo urgently (Position 1, -50cp). Even in positions without pawns (Positions 3, 5), the same tempo-loss pattern appears—pieces placed on passive squares creating no immediate threats when forcing continuations were available. The moves look reasonable but miss the urgency of the tactical moment.
analysis.move_pattern: Any piece type moving to a passive or indirect square in a materially decisive endgame, typically failing to interact with the critical passed pawn(s) on the board
analysis.why_bad: The moves waste tempo in positions where the critical factor (usually advanced passed pawns) demands immediate action—either capturing, blockading, or repositioning to directly fight the pawns. The passive/indirect move allows the opponent to advance pawns, reposition their king optimally, or consolidate a defensive setup that was preventable with one forcing move.
sub_patterns: Check that doesn't capture the critical pawn when capture-with-check exists
King retreating to wrong side of advancing passed pawns
Piece moving to square where it's immediately captured, losing defense against passers
Queen placed on passive rank when diagonal/check creates immediate pressure
Rook placed near pawns rather than cutting off the supporting king

analysis.label: The player moves their king (or removes its shield) in the wrong direction, stepping onto a square that creates a new tactical vulnerability exploitable by checks or attacks along newly-opened lines.
analysis.description: In 8/9 positions, the player makes a king move that walks directly into tactical danger rather than choosing the one available safe square; in 1/9, a knight is moved away from a blockade square that was protecting the king from queen checks. In every case, the position demanded a precise king safety decision with very few good options (avg 1.4), and the player chose the wrong direction. The correct move was consistently available - Kb1 instead of Kd2 (Position 1), Kh8 instead of Kf7/Kf8 (Positions 3, 10), Kh2 instead of Kf2 (Position 8), Kb2 instead of Kc1 (Positions 5, 9), Kf8 instead of Kd7 (Position 11), Kb8 instead of Nc6 (Position 14) - but the player selected a square that exposed the king to immediate tactical punishment. The refutations consistently exploit the king's new position via checks on newly-accessible files or diagonals (Qh5+ after Kf7, Rxb3/Rc2+ after Kc1, e3+ after Kf2, Qa8+ after Nc6 removes the a7 blockade). The enormous average cp_loss (1503) reflects how catastrophic these directional errors are in sharp positions.
analysis.move_pattern: King moves (or shield piece moves away) to an adjacent square that places it on an open file, dangerous diagonal, or in the path of an advancing pawn - consistently choosing the wrong escape direction from a position requiring precise king safety
analysis.why_bad: The king lands on a square where it becomes immediately vulnerable to checks, discovered attacks, or piece invasions along lines (files/diagonals) that were not dangerous with the king on its previous square, while a safer alternative (usually a corner or sheltered square) was available
sub_patterns: King steps onto open/semi-open file where opponent has rook (Kc1 positions)
King steps onto diagonal allowing queen check (Kf7, Kf8 onto h5-f7 or h6-f8 diagonal)
King steps into path of advancing pawn with check (Kf2 into e3+)
King moves to exposed central square allowing perpetual check (Kd2)
Removing blockade piece from king's shield file enabling queen invasion (Nc6 unblocking a-file)

analysis.label: Making an active-looking move that ignores the position's most critical tactical requirement, allowing the opponent to exploit an unaddressed vulnerability.
analysis.description: In all 3/3 positions, the player chose a natural, aggressive-seeming move (centralizing a king, capturing a pawn to open lines, penetrating with a rook on the second rank) instead of addressing the single most urgent tactical demand of the position. In Position 1, Kd4 looks dominating but ignores the critical need to capture cxd3 before White resolves the tension. In Position 2, Bxg3 looks like a devastating kingside attack but is an unsound sacrifice without prior preparation (Ne5 or piece coordination first). In Position 3, Ra2 looks like profitable rook activity but abandons the c2 square where the rook provided a crucial defensive resource (Rc3+ check after Rxf6). All 3/3 moves are 'seductive' because they appear purposeful and aggressive, yet each one neglects the position's one true priority, allowing the opponent a single clear tactical punishment that transforms the evaluation.
analysis.move_pattern: Any piece type moving to a visually active/aggressive square (centralization, penetration, or capture) while abandoning a critical defensive or tactical function
analysis.why_bad: The moves prioritize apparent activity over the position's actual urgent requirement—whether that's a critical capture timing, piece safety, or maintaining a defensive resource—allowing the opponent to exploit the neglected vulnerability with one precise tactical blow.
sub_patterns: King centralization before critical pawn capture (move-order error)
Premature piece sacrifice without preparation
Rook relocation abandoning key defensive geometry

analysis.label: Choosing a passive repositioning or preparatory move when the position demands immediate forcing, concrete action (tactical strike, capture, or urgent piece activation).
analysis.description: This feature fires on moves that prioritize slow positional improvement over immediately necessary concrete action. In 7/10 positions, a forcing tactical opportunity existed (Ng5 gaining tempo on a queen in 2/10, Bxf7+ sacrifice in 1/10, Nxh5 free pawn in 1/10, active king safety moves in 2/10, correct recapture preserving structure in 1/10) but the player chose a repositioning or preparatory move instead. The played moves include knight repositioning to 'nice' squares (Nd4, Nb3, Nd2 - 5/10 involve knights), bishop retreats from active diagonals (Be2, Bf5 - 2/10), and passive pawn pushes (c5, g6, h4 - 3/10). In every case, the position had narrow margins (avg 1.5 good moves available) requiring precision, and the chosen move either abandoned a piece's critical function (Bf5 leaving dominant c2, Be2 retreating from f7-targeting c4, Ndxe2 removing key d4 knight) or wasted tempo on slow plans while opponents seized the initiative. The astronomical average cp_loss of 1188 reflects positions where one tempo of passivity allowed opponents to consolidate, generate unstoppable threats, or win material.
analysis.move_pattern: Piece retreats/repositions to passive square OR preparatory pawn push, typically moving away from the critical sector of the board; frequently knight relocations to seemingly central squares
analysis.why_bad: These moves abandon the piece's most effective post or miss a concrete tactical opportunity, giving the opponent time to neutralize threats, generate counterplay, or exploit newly created weaknesses — the position's urgency demanded forcing moves but received slow ones
sub_patterns: Knight repositioning away from coordination duty (Nd4, Nb3, Nd2, Ndxe2)
Bishop retreat from active attacking diagonal (Be2 from c4, Bf5 from c2)
Passive prophylactic pawn move instead of active piece play (g6, h4, c5)

analysis.label: Moving a piece away from a critical defensive function, creating an exploitable tactical vulnerability the opponent punishes with a tempo-gaining move.
analysis.description: This feature fires on moves where a piece that was serving a vital defensive role (blocking a line, guarding a square, protecting another piece, or maintaining a defensive stance) gets moved for 'active' purposes, instantly creating a fatal weakness. In 8/10 positions, the move directly abandoned defense of the king or a key piece: Qa2 left the king undefended against g5+ (Position 5), Nc4 vacated d2 opening the g5-c1 mating diagonal (Position 13), Nc3 ignored the Qh4# threat by failing to cover h4 or create an escape (Position 10), Kf5 abandoned protection of the f3-bishop (Position 7), and Rhc8 failed to contest the critical d-file against the exposed king (Position 6). In the remaining cases (Bb5, g6, Nc3 Position 11, Qd6), the move was a non-urgent 'improving' move that wasted a critical tempo when the position demanded immediate defensive action. The average cp_loss of 2132 reflects that these defensive lapses frequently lead to immediate tactical catastrophes including forced checkmates (2/10 positions).
analysis.move_pattern: Various piece types moving away from defensive squares toward seemingly active but irrelevant positions - typically away from the vulnerable king or away from a piece/square requiring protection
analysis.why_bad: The moved piece was performing a critical defensive function (blocking a diagonal, protecting a piece, contesting a file, or maintaining tempo priority), and its departure allows the opponent to exploit the resulting vulnerability with a forcing move - typically a check, capture, or unstoppable threat that gains decisive tempo or material.
sub_patterns: Queen retreating to a corner/edge far from an exposed king (Qa2, Qd6)
Knight leaving a square that blocked a critical attacking line (Nc4 from d2, Nc3 ignoring diagonal)
King moving away from a piece it was protecting (Kf5 abandoning bishop on f3)
Non-urgent piece improvement when immediate defensive action required (Bb5, g6, Rhc8)
Premature piece redeployment creating timing vulnerability (Nc3 move-order error)

analysis.label: Natural-looking moves that waste critical tempo in passed pawn endgames where promotion races or opposition determine the outcome.
analysis.description: This feature fires on simplified endgame positions (8/10 endgame) centered on passed pawn promotion where a single tempo determines whether a position is won or drawn. The typical mistake is a 'preparatory' or 'natural' move—usually a king move in the wrong direction (Kf4, Kf3, Kg3) or a premature pawn push before the king is optimally placed (b5, c5)—that violates fundamental endgame principles like 'king before pawn,' opposition, or immediate pawn advancement in promotion races. The blunders share enormous evaluation swings (avg 391cp loss, with 5/10 positions losing 500+ centipawns) because in these razor-sharp tempi positions, one wasted move converts a theoretical win into a theoretical draw. Even the 0cp-loss positions (2/10) represent the same critical position type where only one move maintains the advantage. The pattern of 'tags' confirms this: tempo_loss appears in 7/10 positions, passed_pawn in 8/10, and king_activity/pawn_endgame terminology dominates throughout.
analysis.move_pattern: King moves sideways or backward (away from the pawn's promotion path), or pawn advances made before king reaches optimal escort/opposition square; occasionally a piece move to a trapped/useless square
analysis.why_bad: These moves waste the single critical tempo that determines win vs. draw in simplified endgames—either allowing the opponent's king to seize the opposition/blockade square, or giving the opponent time to establish a defensive fortress or promote their own pawn
sub_patterns: King retreats behind its own passed pawn instead of advancing ahead (Kf3, Kf4)
Pawn pushed before king secures opposition/outflanking position (b5, c5)
King moves to support pawn when immediate pawn push wins the race (Kg3)
Piece moved to trapped/irrelevant square losing the critical asset (Na8+)
Defensive piece/pawn removed that was guarding a critical square (f5, O-O)

analysis.label: King moves to a tactically vulnerable square (usually along an open file, rank, or diagonal) when a safer square was available nearby.
analysis.description: In 9/11 positions, the blunder is a king move that places the king on a square where it becomes immediately exploitable by checks, forks, or mating attacks. The kings consistently move toward the center or toward open lines rather than away from danger: Kc7 walks onto the open c-file allowing Rc8# (Position 2), Kg4 walks into Qh3# (Position 3), Kc6 walks onto the 6th rank enabling Rf6+/Qxf6+/Rd5# (Position 6), Ke7 walks onto the d-file allowing Rd7+ fork (Position 5), Kb3 walks onto a diagonal for Qc2+ mating net (Position 9), Ke6 and Kf7 step onto diagonals allowing queen checks with material gain (Positions 8, 15), Ke3 walks into d-file check sequence (Position 1), and Ke5 centralizes but allows consolidation (Position 10). In nearly every case, a different king move just one square away (Kf3, Ka5, Kf5, Ka6, Kc6, Kb4, Kh7 respectively) would have avoided the tactical catastrophe. The 2/11 non-king moves (a6, Bd2) share the theme of placing a piece/pawn on a square already controlled by enemy pieces, losing tempo critically.
analysis.move_pattern: King moves (9/11) typically one square toward the center or toward an open file/diagonal/rank controlled by enemy heavy pieces; the destination square is geometrically aligned with enemy attacking lanes
analysis.why_bad: The king lands on a square that is tactically exposed to immediate checks, forks, or mating patterns along open files, ranks, or diagonals—typically when a safer square just one step in a different direction existed that would have avoided all forcing sequences
sub_patterns: King steps onto an open file where enemy rook/queen delivers immediate check or mate (Kc7→Rc8#, Ke7→Rd7+, Kc6→Rf6+)
King steps onto a diagonal where enemy queen delivers check with material gain (Kg4→Qh3#, Ke6→Qxg6+, Kf7→Qxd5+, Kb3→Qc2+)
King moves toward center when retreating to the flank was safer (Ke3 vs Kf3, Kc6 vs Ka6, Ke5 vs staying/advancing pawns)

analysis.label: Moves that waste a critical tempo by pursuing a superficially logical plan while ignoring the position's most urgent demand.
analysis.description: This feature fires on moves where the player makes a seemingly reasonable or natural-looking move that catastrophically misjudges what the position requires. In 4/5 positions, the analyses explicitly identify 'tempo_loss' as a key motif. The pattern includes: premature piece placement to a passive square (Bh8 to blockade but gets immediately driven away, 1/5), ignoring an immediate lethal threat in favor of a 'developing' move (Qe4 allowing Bg5#, 1/5), choosing a passive defensive pawn move when dynamic piece action was critical (f3 instead of Nf4/Re1, 1/5), moving a piece away from the critical zone of action (Ke4 retreating from the only defensive square Kf5, 1/5), and placing a piece on an undefended square where it's immediately captured (Ra3, 1/5). All positions featured clearly better alternatives that addressed the most urgent positional or tactical demand, and in 4/5 cases the move was punished by multiple equally strong refutations, suggesting the errors were not subtle.
analysis.move_pattern: Any piece type moving to a square that is either passive, exposed, or irrelevant to the position's critical demands; no consistent geometric direction
analysis.why_bad: The moves waste a tempo (or worse) by ignoring the position's most urgent requirement - whether that's an immediate mating threat, the need for active piece development, maintaining proximity to critical squares, or basic piece safety - in favor of a superficially logical but fundamentally misguided plan.
sub_patterns: Premature piece commitment to passive/corner squares
Ignoring immediate tactical threats for positional ideas
Passive pawn moves when dynamic piece play required
King moving away from critical defensive zone
Placing undefended piece on vulnerable square

analysis.label: Moving the king forward into a tactically vulnerable square when an immediate forcing move (check, capture, or promotion) was available.
analysis.description: In 3/4 positions, Black plays a king move forward (Kf7, Ke5, Ke3) that appears to centralize or activate the king but actually walks into a tactical vulnerability - a discovered check (Position 3: f4+ with rook discovery), piece coordination attacks (Position 1: Be5 + Rb8), or self-blocking of a critical promotion (Position 4: king blocks e2 pawn from queening with check). In 4/4 positions, the player chose a slow 'active-looking' move when an immediate forcing tactical solution existed (Qf7 trading the rook, Rf3+ winning a pawn, e1=Q+ with forced mate, Rc6 blockading). The pattern is strongest in endgames (3/4) where king centralization is generally correct strategically but here is tactically premature. The average cp_loss of 2600 reflects that these positions typically have one narrow winning/drawing move being squandered.
analysis.move_pattern: King moves forward/toward center (f7, e5, e3) exposing itself on open files/diagonals; variant includes piece moving to undefended square (Rxh2)
analysis.why_bad: The king walks onto a square where it becomes a tactical target (discovered checks, piece forks, pawn checks) while simultaneously missing an available forcing move that would have resolved the position immediately through checks or material gain.
sub_patterns: King centralizes into discovered check
King blocks own passed pawn promotion
King exposes itself on open file/diagonal
Piece grabs irrelevant material ignoring critical forcing moves

analysis.label: Catastrophic blunders where the player makes a quiet or "natural" move while ignoring an urgent tactical vulnerability, typically involving king safety with an uncastled king.
analysis.description: This feature fires on positions where the player commits a massive blunder (avg 1116 cp loss) by ignoring a critical tactical demand in the position. In 9/11 cases, both kings are still in the center, and the refutation exploits king safety—often via the f7 square, exposed diagonals, or forcing checks. The moves themselves appear superficially reasonable (prophylactic pawn moves like h6/g6, space-gaining moves like e5/g4, natural development like Nc6/Bg4/Na5) but catastrophically fail to address the position's most urgent requirement. In 8/11 positions, the refutation involves an immediate check, sacrifice, or forcing sequence that the blunder enables. The positions characteristically offer very few acceptable moves (avg 2.2), meaning these are critical decision points where one specific defensive or addressing move is mandatory. The blunders share the common thread of prioritizing a secondary plan (preventing Bg5, fianchettoing, gaining space, developing) over the position's most pressing tactical crisis.
analysis.move_pattern: Quiet non-forcing moves (pawn advances, piece development to natural-looking squares, or greedy captures) in positions requiring urgent defensive/tactical attention—no consistent piece type or direction, but consistently non-addressing of the critical threat
analysis.why_bad: Each move ignores the position's most critical tactical vulnerability (usually king safety/f7 weakness with uncastled king), allowing the opponent an immediate devastating forcing sequence—a sacrifice, check, or breakthrough—that the move did nothing to prevent or prepare against
sub_patterns: Prophylactic flank pawn moves (h6/g6) ignoring f7 or central threats
Natural piece development (Nc6/Bg4/Na5) to wrong square ignoring diagonal or square weakness
Aggressive pawn advances (e5/g4) creating holes while king is uncastled
Greedy captures (Nxe5) removing key defenders of critical squares
Bizarre decisions in won positions (c8=N underpromotion, Kf4 ignoring free queen)

analysis.label: Queen (or major piece) checks from the wrong square/direction, allowing the opponent's king to escape to safety and breaking the perpetual or attacking sequence.
analysis.description: In 7/8 positions, the player delivers a check (almost always with the queen) from a geometrically incorrect square. The correct move was typically ALSO a check, but from a different angle that would sustain a perpetual check pattern or maintain a winning/drawing attack. The played check allows the king to sidestep to a safe square where no further productive checks exist. In Position 2, Qh3+ fails where Qa8+ sustains perpetual; in Position 6, Qd1+ allows Kh3 escape where Qg1+ traps the king; in Position 7, Qc1+ allows Kf3 stability where Qf2+ forces Ke5 vulnerability; in Position 8, Qd7+ allows a queen trade where Qh4+ maintains tension; in Position 13, Qh4+ allows Ke6 escape where Qf8+ drives the king to g4; in Position 15, Qd8+ misplaces the queen where Qh4+ wins. The common thread (7/8 positions) is that the player's checking instinct is correct but the chosen direction/diagonal is wrong, typically because the target square gives the king access to a shelter the player's piece cannot reach from its new position.
analysis.move_pattern: Queen (or rook) check from the wrong diagonal/file/rank, typically choosing a longer-distance or less constraining angle instead of the geometrically optimal checking square
analysis.why_bad: The check allows the opponent's king to escape to a square where the perpetual check sequence breaks down—either no further checks exist, the queen becomes misplaced far from defensive duties, or the opponent can interpose with tempo (blocking + counter-check or forcing queen trade into a lost endgame)
sub_patterns: Failed perpetual - wrong diagonal allows king to safe square
Check that displaces own queen from critical defensive duties
Check allowing interposition that breaks the attacking sequence
Check from distance when adjacent check would corral the king

analysis.label: Moves that place a piece (usually the queen) on an exposed or unproductive square where the opponent immediately gains decisive tempo through attack, capture, or forced unfavorable trade.
analysis.description: This feature fires on moves that waste tempo by placing a piece on a square where it is immediately challenged, captured, or forced into an unfavorable exchange. In 5/7 positions, the queen is moved to a square where it can be directly attacked (Qh5 hit by Nf4, Qg4 chased by f3), captured (Qb5 taken by Qxb5), or forced into a losing trade (Qc8 offering queens off when compensation requires them on). The remaining 2/7 positions show the same tempo-loss pattern with other pieces: a pawn advance (d4) that ignores an immediate back-rank threat, and a king move (Kf3) that accomplishes nothing and must be reversed. All 7/7 positions are explicitly tagged with 'tempo_loss' in analysis. The average cp_loss of 1669 is extreme, and only 1.7 good moves were available on average, indicating these are critical moments where the wasted tempo is catastrophically punished. The common thread is that each move pursues an illusory goal (attack, simplification, centralization) without recognizing that the opponent has an immediate tactical response that exploits the piece's new vulnerability.
analysis.move_pattern: Queen (5/7) or other piece moved to an exposed square on an open rank/file/diagonal accessible to opponent's pieces, often to the 4th-5th rank or edge squares (h5, g4, b5, b1, c8)
analysis.why_bad: The moved piece lands on a square where it can be immediately attacked, captured, or forced into an unfavorable trade, giving the opponent a free tempo to seize the initiative, consolidate advantages, or execute decisive tactical threats that the wasted move left unaddressed.
sub_patterns: Queen to exposed square attacked by minor piece (Qh5/Nf4, Qg4/f3)
Queen offering unfavorable trade that eliminates dynamic compensation (Qc8, Qb5)
Wrong check square losing intermediate tactical resource (Qb1+ instead of Qd1+)
Pawn/king move ignoring immediate tactical vulnerability (d4 back-rank, Kf3 aimless)

analysis.label: A non-forcing piece repositioning move that wastes a critical tempo by addressing a secondary concern while the position demands a specific urgent action.
analysis.description: This feature fires on positions where the player makes a quiet, reasonable-looking move (piece development, repositioning, or king movement) that completely misidentifies the position's #1 priority. In 9/11 cases, the position had only 1-3 good moves available, indicating razor-sharp demands for precision. The played moves appear natural—bishop development (Ba4, Be2, Bc4, Bh5, Bc5 = 5/11), king repositioning (Kd8, Kg3, Kh5 = 3/11), quiet development (d3, Nh3, Qg6 = 3/11)—but all ignore an urgent positional or tactical requirement: defending against a passed pawn advance (3/11), resolving critical central tension (3/11), addressing king safety (3/11), or exploiting opponent weaknesses (2/11). The common result is the piece lands on a square where it either becomes tactically vulnerable, is disconnected from the critical theater of action, or simply loses the one tempo that made the difference between holding and collapsing. All positions tagged 'tempo_loss' in analysis (9/11).
analysis.move_pattern: Non-forcing piece move (usually bishop or king) to a plausible but strategically irrelevant square, no check, no capture, no direct threat
analysis.why_bad: The position has one specific urgent demand (challenge a dominant piece, activate king toward passed pawn, exploit tactical weakness, resolve central tension) and the played move addresses a secondary concern instead, giving the opponent a free tempo to execute their winning plan
sub_patterns: Bishop moved to wrong diagonal/passive square when position demands active defense (Ba4, Bh5, Bc5)
Routine piece development ignoring critical tactical vulnerabilities (Be2, Bc4, d3, Nh3)
King moved to exposed/wrong square when precise placement was essential (Kd8, Kg3, Kh5)
Queen retreated to tactically vulnerable square instead of only safe option (Qg6)

analysis.label: Slow, non-forcing piece moves played in tactically critical positions that demand immediate action on urgent threats.
analysis.description: This feature fires on positions where the player makes a 'natural-looking' quiet move (developing, repositioning, or consolidating a piece) while ignoring a critical tactical demand in the position. In 8/10 positions, the move is a non-forcing piece relocation (bishop or rook repositioning) that treats the position as calm when it's actually razor-sharp with only 1-3 good moves available. The common thread is tempo waste in critical moments: ignoring hanging pieces (a4 leaving d5 undefended, Bb5 leaving Nb1 hanging - 2/10), abandoning critical defensive duties (Bb4 leaving d2 unguarded, Bb1 burying the bishop - 2/10), ignoring king safety emergencies (Rd8, Be3 allowing perpetual, Qh3 walking into a fork - 3/10), or missing fleeting tactical opportunities (Nc6 instead of Rxf7, Re8 instead of counterplay - 2/10). The average cp_loss of 1160 and average of only 1.9 good moves confirms these are positions where one quiet move is catastrophic.
analysis.move_pattern: Non-forcing piece moves (especially bishops: 4/10) to quiet squares - no checks, no meaningful captures, no direct threats - typically sideways or backward repositioning
analysis.why_bad: The positions demand immediate tactical action (capturing hanging material, addressing perpetual check threats, fixing king safety, or seizing fleeting tactical opportunities), but the player spends a tempo on a slow positional move, allowing the opponent to execute a devastating tactical blow that was previously unavailable or contained.
sub_patterns: Bishop repositioned away from critical defensive square (Bb4, Bb1, Be3)
Piece development ignoring hanging material (a4, Bb5, Nc6)
Passive rook move ignoring king exposure (Rd8, Re8)
Queen misplacement creating tactical vulnerability (Qh3, Qxe6+)

analysis.label: Moving a piece to a peripheral or misplaced square where it is immediately captured, forked, or tactically exploited.
analysis.description: In 4/5 positions, the played move places a piece on a square where it is immediately won or forked by the opponent: Na5 hangs to Nxa5 (position 3), Na6 is captured by Bxa6 ruining pawn structure (position 6), Ra6 walks into a devastating Nc7 fork (position 15), and g4 allows a central pawn fork via cxd6/e5 winning material (position 1). The remaining case (Qb8, position 11) moves the queen to a passive back-rank square losing critical tempo. All 5 moves share the pattern of relocating a piece to a peripheral or edge square (a5, a6, a6, b8, g4-file) while ignoring the position's critical demands—central tension, king safety, or defensive needs. The moves are punished by immediate tactical exploitation of the newly-placed piece's vulnerability.
analysis.move_pattern: Piece (knight, rook, queen, or pawn) moves to an edge/rim square (predominantly a-file: a5, a6, a6; also b8, g4) where it becomes immediately tactically vulnerable
analysis.why_bad: The piece lands on a square where it can be immediately captured, forked by a knight, or taken by a bishop along an open diagonal—the player ignores that the destination square is controlled or attacked by opponent pieces, prioritizing an illusory goal over piece safety
sub_patterns: Knight to rim square where it hangs to capture (Na5, Na6)
Rook to square vulnerable to knight fork (Ra6 into Nc7)
Flank pawn advance enabling central fork/breakthrough (g4)
Queen retreat to passive square losing tempo in won position (Qb8)

analysis.label: Slow or retreating moves that ignore immediate tactical tension in the position, gifting the opponent a tempo to launch a devastating strike.
analysis.description: All four positions feature a critical tactical tension that demands immediate attention, yet the played move sidesteps the issue entirely with a passive, slow, or decentralizing choice. In Position 1 (Nb8), the knight retreats to its starting square while Ng5/Qh3+ tactics needed prevention (3/4 positions involve king safety). In Position 3 (Rd6), the rook ignores the hanging bishop on f4, placing itself on a vulnerable diagonal (4/4 positions have piece activity as a key theme). In Position 6 (Nh5), the knight abandons f6, leaving the h6 pawn undefended when the g5 tension needed resolving by capture. In Position 7 (e6), a passive pawn move ignores the d6 weakness and allows Ndb5-Nd6 invasion. The common thread is that each position had one clearly urgent issue (a pawn capture needed, a piece to relocate from danger, a threat to prevent), and the player chose a move with a different slow plan instead. The opponent then exploits the extra tempo ruthlessly, with refutations involving knight invasions (2/4), tactical captures (2/4), and king-targeting attacks (3/4).
analysis.move_pattern: Mixed piece types moving passively (retreating, going to rim, or making non-engaging pawn pushes) rather than addressing the board's critical contact point
analysis.why_bad: Each move ignores the position's most urgent tactical demand—an immediate capture, defense, or counter-threat was needed—and instead makes a slow move that gives the opponent a free tempo to execute a prepared tactical blow against exposed kings or hanging pieces.
sub_patterns: Knight retreating from active post to passive square (Nb8, Nh5 rim)
Piece moving to tactically vulnerable square while ignoring own hanging piece (Rd6)
Passive pawn move creating permanent structural weakness (e6 weakening d6)

analysis.label: Advancing a piece or pawn that appears progressive but lacks immediate forcing threats, squandering dynamic potential by giving the opponent a free tempo to consolidate or neutralize.
analysis.description: This feature fires on moves that look like natural progress—pushing passed pawns forward (d2, b2, a6 in 3/6 positions), making structural pawn moves (c6 in 1/6), repositioning the queen 'aggressively' (Qh3 in 1/6), or committing the king early (Kc6 in 1/6)—but all share the critical flaw of failing to create an immediate threat the opponent must answer. In every case, the best moves instead maintained dynamic tension (keeping a passed pawn as a restraining asset rather than pushing it into a blockade), exploited existing tactics (Ne3 fork, Qxe4 capture), or preserved flexibility (h5 prophylaxis, Ke5 centralization). The blundered moves uniformly gave the opponent a free tempo to execute their plan: blockading (Rd1 in position 2), capturing (Nxb2 in position 3), castling to safety (O-O in position 14), invading with the king (Ke4 in position 15), or consolidating piece coordination. All 6 positions tagged with 'tempo_loss' and 5/6 with 'piece_activity' confirm that the common thread is choosing apparent progress over maintaining pressure.
analysis.move_pattern: Non-capturing, non-checking forward advance (pawn push or piece move toward opponent's side) that does not attack any opponent piece or create a concrete tactical threat
analysis.why_bad: These moves eliminate dynamic tension by committing to a plan the opponent can easily neutralize—the advanced pawn gets blockaded or captured, the repositioned piece loses control of critical squares, or the committed king allows the opponent's king to invade elsewhere. The opponent gains a free tempo to consolidate because no immediate threat demands a response.
sub_patterns: Premature passed pawn advance into blockade/capture (d2, b2, a6)
Slow structural/positional move when forcing tactics exist (c6, Qh3)
Premature king commitment abandoning central/flexible positioning (Kc6)

analysis.label: Moves that prioritize aggression or secondary plans over addressing the position's most critical defensive need, fatally compromising king safety or piece security.
analysis.description: In 5/5 analyzed positions, king_safety is tagged as a primary concern, and in all cases the blunder creates a target the opponent exploits with a tempo-gaining move. The pattern manifests as: wrong recaptures that shatter pawn shelter (gxf6 in Position 2, Nxe5 in Position 11 where dxe5 was needed), pawn advances that weaken key defensive squares (e5 in Position 6 abandoning f7 coverage), king moves toward danger rather than safety (O-O-O castling into a pawn storm in Position 7, Kd3 walking into e4+ in Position 8), and ignoring a trapped piece to pursue centralization (Qd7 in Position 3 allowing Rc7 invasion). In every case, the refutation involves a forcing tempo-gaining move (Nh4, Rc7, Ng5, b5, e4+, f4) that the correct move would have prevented. Average good moves available is only 1.7, indicating these arise at critical junctures where the defensive move is essentially forced but the player opts for something superficially active instead.
analysis.move_pattern: Various piece types and directions, but consistently choosing the more aggressive/active option (advancing rather than retreating, capturing with the wrong piece to maintain 'activity', castling toward open files) when the position demands consolidation
analysis.why_bad: Each move creates or leaves a concrete vulnerability that the opponent exploits with an immediate tempo-gaining forcing move (check, attack on piece/queen, pawn advance with threats), converting the positional weakness into a tactical catastrophe before the 'active' plan can materialize.
sub_patterns: Wrong recapture weakening pawn structure around king (gxf6/Nxe5 vs piece capture)
King moving toward danger instead of retreating to safety (Kd3/O-O-O)
Pawn advance abandoning defensive coverage of critical squares (e5 weakening f7)
Ignoring urgent piece rescue to pursue vague centralization (Qd7 ignoring trapped Na7)

analysis.label: Moving a piece away from a square where it was performing an irreplaceable defensive or tactical function, allowing immediate concrete exploitation.
analysis.description: In 9/11 positions, the blundering move relocates a piece that was the sole guardian of a critical square, diagonal, or tactical possibility. In Position 1, the queen abandons h-file control enabling Nf3+/Rh1+. In Position 2, the bishop leaves f6 where it guarded d8, permitting Ke6+ discovered check and Rd8#. In Position 6, the queen leaves e6 where f4+ was winning. In Position 10 (Nxe3), the knight abandons f5 which controlled e7, allowing the e-pawn to promote. In Position 7, the knight leaves its powerful c4 outpost for a3 where it's trapped. In Position 8, the rook moves leaving a8 hanging on the bishop's diagonal. In Position 9, the fianchettoed bishop is traded away surrendering the long diagonal permanently. The remaining positions (b6, g5) involve ignoring urgent threats in favor of slow plans, which is a temporal version of the same error—abandoning defensive obligations. All positions share critically narrow margins (average 1.6 good moves available), meaning the abandoned function was uniquely essential.
analysis.move_pattern: Any piece type moving away from a square where it performed a sole defensive or tactical function; often retreats, captures that eliminate the defender, or lateral moves to the rim/corner away from the critical zone
analysis.why_bad: The moved piece was the single irreplaceable defender of a key square, line, or tactical resource. Its departure creates an immediate concrete refutation—typically a forcing sequence (check, discovered attack, promotion, or piece win) that was previously impossible because the moved piece was blocking or covering it.
sub_patterns: Queen retreats from critical file/diagonal enabling mating or winning combinations
Knight/Bishop leaves outpost allowing pawn promotion or discovered attack
Piece trades that eliminate sole guardian of key diagonal or square
Slow pawn moves ignoring urgent tactical tension requiring immediate piece action
Piece moves to vulnerable square where opponent gains tempo attacking it

analysis.label: Playing a plausible-looking but non-forcing move when the position demanded immediate concrete action, wasting a critical tempo.
analysis.description: This feature fires on moves that appear purposeful (centralizing a queen, developing, advancing the king, grabbing a pawn) but fatally waste tempo because the position required a more direct, forcing continuation. In 7/9 positions, the key tag is 'tempo_loss.' The pattern manifests as: attacking a piece with a slow mover when a faster piece could capture immediately (Kc6 instead of Rxc7, position 15; Kf8 instead of Rc4, position 14), developing the queen prematurely when a knight needed the square or the position demanded piece development first (Qd5 and Qd7 instead of Nf6, positions 7 and 10), choosing a passive consolidation when active counterplay was essential (Re8 instead of e3/Qe7, position 4), playing on the wrong flank when central tension demanded resolution (c4 instead of f4, position 13), and placing pieces on squares that look active but create exploitable vulnerabilities (Qe5 allowing unfavorable queen trade, position 1; Qxb7 walking into a queen trap, position 3). In all cases, 2-3 forcing alternatives existed that addressed the position's concrete demands.
analysis.move_pattern: Mixed piece types (queen, rook, king, pawn) moved to squares that appear active or purposeful but are indirect/non-forcing relative to the position's tactical demands
analysis.why_bad: Each move wastes a critical tempo by choosing an indirect approach when the position required immediate forcing action (capturing hanging material, resolving central tension, trading on favorable terms, or deploying the most efficient piece), allowing the opponent to execute threats, escape danger, or exploit newly-created vulnerabilities.
sub_patterns: Attacking/approaching a piece with the king when a rook could capture immediately
Premature queen development blocking needed knight development squares
Passive piece placement when active counterplay (pawn breaks, forcing trades) was essential
Playing on the wrong side of the board while ignoring urgent central tension
Pawn-grabbing with the queen creating trapped-piece vulnerabilities

analysis.label: A quiet, seemingly improving move played in a position that demands immediate concrete action to address a specific tactical vulnerability.
analysis.description: This feature fires on positions where the player makes a natural-looking 'improvement' move (centralizing a piece, gaining space, repositioning for activity, or addressing a perceived safety concern) while ignoring an urgent tactical obligation. In 5/5 positions, the correct move addressed a concrete, immediate threat or necessity: defending a critical square (Re8 abandoned f7 defense, Ne6 abandoned g2 defense), addressing an imminent kingside attack (b5 ignored the Qh5/Bxg6 threat), capturing a key pawn before it becomes a target (Bg3 instead of Bxa7), or saving a tactically vulnerable piece (Kc1 instead of Be4). The positions are characteristically narrow—averaging only 1.8 good moves—meaning the player is in a 'must-find-it' situation but treats it as a calm position. In 4/5 cases the opponent has one clearly devastating punishment, and in 2/5 the error specifically involves moving a piece away from a critical defensive square it was guarding.
analysis.move_pattern: Non-forcing, non-capturing quiet moves (piece repositioning, pawn advance, king walk) that appear to improve piece placement or address a non-urgent concern
analysis.why_bad: The moves ignore an immediate, concrete tactical obligation—either removing a key defender from a critical square (enabling forks, sacrifices, or perpetual checks) or wasting a tempo in a position where the opponent can execute a forcing sequence (double attacks, sacrificial breakthroughs, or material collection) on the very next move.
sub_patterns: Moving a piece away from a critical defensive square (removing guard of key pawn/square)
Queenside pawn push ignoring imminent kingside attack
Slow king move when a specific piece needs immediate rescue/repositioning
Bishop repositioning instead of capturing to eliminate opponent's target

analysis.label: Non-forcing, tempo-wasting moves in positions that demand immediate action, allowing the opponent to seize the initiative.
analysis.description: All 6/6 positions share the same fundamental error: the player makes a quiet, non-forcing move (retreat, repositioning, or preparatory) when the position urgently demands an immediate, forcing response. In each case, the best moves involve direct action—creating threats (Qb6 threatening mate in Position 1), capturing material (dxe5 in Position 2), developing with urgency (Nc3 in Position 3), clearing a critical path (Kc1 in Position 6), generating counterplay (Ne5 in Position 7), or preparing castling (d6 in Position 13). Instead, the played moves all look superficially reasonable—repositioning a rook, advancing a pawn, retreating a bishop—but accomplish nothing forcing, giving the opponent a free tempo to execute devastating plans. The average cp_loss of 380 and average of only 1.5 good moves available confirm these are high-stakes moments where timing is everything. Tags 'tempo_loss' and 'piece_activity' appear in 6/6 positions, and 'king_safety' in 6/6.
analysis.move_pattern: Non-forcing quiet moves (retreats, repositions, preparatory advances) with no check, capture, or direct threat
analysis.why_bad: The position demands immediate forcing action (a threat, a tactical blow, urgent development/castling), but the played move wastes a critical tempo on a passive or preparatory idea, giving the opponent time to execute their own plan—whether that's launching a pawn storm, creating mating threats, or exploiting exposed king position.
sub_patterns: Move-order errors: playing a preparatory move before the forcing move that makes it work (Ra1 before Qb6)
Premature piece sorties creating no real threat (Qh5 easily refuted by development with tempo)
Self-blocking: piece occupies a square needed by another piece (Rd2 blocking king's path)
Passive king moves when active counterplay is essential (Ka8 instead of Ne5)
Purposeless bishop retreats losing development time (Bb6 instead of castling preparation)

analysis.label: Moving a minor piece aggressively to an undefended square where it is immediately captured by the opponent for free or near-free.
analysis.description: All 4/4 positions involve White playing a minor piece (bishop or knight) forward to a square where it has no defensive support, and where an opponent's piece can immediately capture it, resulting in the loss of a full minor piece (avg 442cp loss). In Position 2, Bxc7 places the bishop where the queen recaptures instantly. In Position 6, Nd4 puts the knight where the e-pawn or c6-knight takes it. In Position 7, Nxe5 places the knight where the c6-knight recaptures for free. In Position 14, Ba6 drops the bishop on a square where two Black pieces can take it immediately. All occur in the opening (4/4) with both kings still in the center, and in every case 3/3+ good developing moves were available. The tactical motif is consistently 'hanging_piece' (4/4), and the blunder stems from the player perceiving an aggressive opportunity while overlooking that the destination square is fatally unguarded.
analysis.move_pattern: Minor piece (bishop or knight) moves forward aggressively—often a capture or central jump—to a square with no defensive support, where it is immediately recaptured or taken by an enemy piece
analysis.why_bad: The piece lands on a square where it has zero defensive coverage, and the opponent has an obvious and immediate recapture or free capture available, resulting in losing a full minor piece for at most a pawn
sub_patterns: Bishop captures pawn defended by queen
Knight jumps into pawn capture range
Knight captures pawn defended by another knight
Bishop advances to square capturable by multiple pieces

analysis.label: Advancing a piece (often the king) for apparent activity in endgames while neglecting a more urgent concrete positional or tactical requirement.
analysis.description: This feature fires on positions—predominantly endgames (8/10)—where the player makes a move that appears to follow sound general principles (centralizing the king, activating pieces, grabbing material) but misses a more critical concrete need. King moves account for 4/10 top activations (Ke4, Ke3, Kc5, Kf3), and in each case the king advances before establishing proper piece coordination: in KR vs K positions (2/10), the king moves without the rook first restricting the opponent; in Kc5 the king occupies the exact square the queen needed; in Kf3 the king advances before Re1 controls a critical file. The remaining moves share the same spirit: e4 advances a pawn destroying critical mutual protection, Ne5 centralizes a knight on the wrong outpost, Bg3 seeks king-attack when a promotion threat demands attention, Rh3 abandons a file cut-off, and Bxa6 captures a pawn while abandoning a defensive diagonal. The unifying thread is a move-order error where the played move would be reasonable in a different context but fails to address the position's most urgent demand first.
analysis.move_pattern: Piece or king advances toward center/active square (especially king moving 1 square forward/sideways in endgame), often without captures or checks
analysis.why_bad: The move addresses a secondary concern (activity, centralization, material) while neglecting the position's primary concrete requirement—typically piece coordination, file/rank restriction, or addressing an immediate tactical threat that needed to be handled first
sub_patterns: King advances in KR vs K without rook restriction first
King blocks optimal square for another piece
King advances before rook activation (move-order error)
Piece/pawn advances that abandon critical defensive or structural duties

analysis.label: Playing a non-forcing, natural-looking move in a position with open central files where concrete tactical action was immediately required.
analysis.description: This feature activates when players make passive or seemingly reasonable moves that ignore the concrete tactical demands of dynamically open positions. All 9/9 positions are middlegames featuring open or semi-open central files (d and/or e files) with active heavy pieces creating high tactical tension. The mistakes include slow pawn pushes when free captures existed (h4 and c3 missing hanging pawns in positions 5-6), piece moves that abandon critical defensive posts (Ng5 removing f2's guard in position 2, Nc5 removing a counter-tactic in position 4), pieces placed on exposed/trapped squares (Ba3 in position 3, Bf5 in position 8), ignoring imminent fork threats (Rfe1 in position 7), weakening king shelter unnecessarily (f6 in position 1), and walking into forced exchange sequences (Qd7 in position 9). In every case, the correct move required direct engagement with the tactical tension—capturing material, neutralizing a specific threat, or contesting the open files—with an average of only 1.3 good moves available, indicating critical moments demanding precision.
analysis.move_pattern: Various piece types and directions; no single geometric pattern—moves are united by being non-forcing (no checks, no captures, no direct threats) in positions with open d/e-file dynamics
analysis.why_bad: The open central files create immediate tactical tension requiring concrete action; these quiet moves waste tempo, allowing opponents to exploit hanging material, execute forks, trap misplaced pieces, or launch combinations along the open files that the non-forcing move failed to prevent or preempt.
sub_patterns: Slow pawn pushes when undefended material is available for capture
Moving a defender away from a critical square creating immediate tactical vulnerability
Placing a piece on an exposed square where it becomes trapped or won by force
Natural-looking development that ignores an imminent fork or combination
Weakening king position when the open-file dynamics demand active piece play

analysis.label: Natural-looking moves in the king's vicinity (f2-g3-f4-g7 zone) that waste critical tempo when the position demands urgent active play elsewhere.
analysis.description: All 5 positions share a common pattern: the player makes a seemingly reasonable move in the kingside area (f2/f4/g3/g7) that appears to address local concerns—developing a piece (Bf4), shoring up pawns (g3), capturing material (Kxg7, Kxg3), or improving king placement (Kf2)—but each move fatally wastes tempo at a moment when the position demands immediate forcing action. In 5/5 cases, the position had a critical tactical or strategic demand that required urgency: trapping a piece (Position 3), maintaining king shelter integrity (Position 5), keeping the king safe behind pawns (Position 7), winning a promotion race (Position 8), or pressing initiative with a passed pawn (Position 15). The tempo loss in all cases allowed the opponent to either launch a decisive attack or reorganize their defensive setup. The average cp_loss of 292 reflects that these positions were all at critical tipping points where one tempo made the difference between winning and equality/losing.
analysis.move_pattern: Moves to f2, f4, g3, or g7 squares—king moves (3/5), pawn pushes (1/5), or bishop development (1/5)—all on the kingside, typically non-forcing and without check or meaningful threat
analysis.why_bad: Each move prioritizes local kingside comfort or material over the position's urgent demand for active/forcing play, gifting the opponent a critical tempo to either launch an attack against the now-weakened king position or neutralize the player's initiative
sub_patterns: King captures pawn when a different recapture or move order was essential (Kxg7, Kxg3)
Passive king move wastes initiative when aggressive piece play is required (Kf2)
Kingside pawn/piece move weakens shelter or vacates key defensive square (g3, Bf4)

analysis.label: Quiet king or piece repositioning moves in endgames with passed pawns that sacrifice critical tempo for gradual improvement.
analysis.description: This feature activates on non-forcing positional moves—predominantly king walks and piece repositioning—in endgame positions featuring open centers and passed pawns. In 6/7 positions, the center files (d/e) are open. In 5/7 cases, the move is a king move (Kxe7, Kf1, Kg7, Ke7, Ke2); the others are a rook lateral shift (Rb3) and a bishop redeployment (Bb2). The critical pattern is choosing gradual piece improvement over concrete action. When this is actually punished (4/7 positions have significant cp_loss), the opponent gains time to advance a passed pawn (positions 2, 6 with g-pawn/c-pawn advancing), exploit a pawn break (position 3 with g4 trapping a piece), or activate their rook (position 1 with Rg8). When the feature fires on non-blunders (3/7 positions with 0 cp_loss: Kg7, Ke7, Bb2), the advantage is already overwhelming and no urgent demand exists. Both kings are exposed in 7/7 positions, and passed pawns feature in 6/7.
analysis.move_pattern: King steps (1 square, non-checking) or quiet piece slides to natural squares; no checks, no captures on most (6/7), predominantly in endgames
analysis.why_bad: Surrenders tempo in positions where an opponent's passed pawn, pawn break, or piece activation demands immediate concrete action (restraint, checks, captures, or prophylactic pawn moves); the gradual repositioning gives the opponent a free move to cross a critical threshold.
sub_patterns: King walking toward center ignoring passed pawn on opposite wing
Rook leaving active file for passive lateral position
Piece repositioning when prophylactic pawn move is urgent

analysis.label: Moves that squander a vital tempo in positions where timing is paramount, allowing the opponent to execute a decisive check, capture, or promotion sequence.
analysis.description: This feature fires on moves that ignore the critical time-sensitive demand of the position, wasting a tempo on something irrelevant or low-priority while the opponent has (or gains) a forcing sequence involving checks or captures. In 5/9 positions, the move directly allows the opponent to play a devastating move with check (Kd1 allows e2+, Ke8 allows f7+, Bb4 allows Qa4+ fork, b5 allows Rxe7+, Bc7 enables Qc1+ back-rank). In the remaining positions, the move wastes tempo when precise timing was needed: Rxb3+ enters a pawn endgame without first activating the king, Nb7 retreats passively instead of capturing an attacked pawn, g6 abandons the g5-pawn while trying to chase a queen, and Qf3 ignores a piece-winning tactical vulnerability on c3. The average position has only 2.0 good moves available, confirming these are critical junctures with razor-thin margins. The 'tempo_loss' tag appears in 7/9 analyses, and 'king_safety' in 6/9, reflecting how timing intersects with king vulnerability.
analysis.move_pattern: Any piece type; no consistent direction. The move either places own king/piece on a square vulnerable to check/fork, or addresses a non-urgent concern while an immediate tactical demand exists.
analysis.why_bad: The position demands an immediate response to a specific tactical threat or time-critical situation (exposed king, advancing passer, hanging piece), and the move instead addresses a secondary concern, granting the opponent a free tempo that enables a forcing sequence (check, capture, or promotion) that was previously not available or less effective.
sub_patterns: King walks into check/fork square (Kd1, Ke8, Bb4→Qa4+)
Ignoring immediate tactical threat to play irrelevant pawn push or retreat (b5, Nb7, g6)
Premature forcing move before necessary preparation (Rxb3+ before Kf2)
Abandoning critical defensive piece/square (Bc7 leaves king exposed, Qf3 abandons c3)

analysis.label: Non-developing flank pawn advances (a-file, g-file, h-file) played in the opening when urgent central, tactical, or developmental needs demand immediate attention.
analysis.description: This feature activates on opening moves that push pawns on the extreme flanks (a-file or g/h-file) or move pieces to irrelevant edge squares while critical tactical or developmental issues go unaddressed in the center. In 9/10 positions, the move is a flank pawn push (a6, g4, g5, a5, a4, h6); 1/10 is a bishop retreat to an irrelevant edge square (Bb4). In all 10/10 positions, there existed an urgent need—whether defending a hanging pawn (Position 15: e5 undefended), resolving a tactically pinned/attacked piece (Position 1: Bg4 under pressure), blocking a dangerous diagonal (Position 14: f7 attacked by Bc4), or simply developing pieces toward castling. In 8/10 positions, at least one king remains in the center uncastled, amplifying the cost of the wasted tempo. The average cp_loss of 274 reflects how severely these moves are punished: opponents exploit the tempo with central strikes (d4, e5), tactical sacrifices (Bxf7+, Nxe5), or direct captures of hanging material (Nxg4, Nxe5).
analysis.move_pattern: Pawn advances to rim files (a2-a4, a7-a6, a7-a5, g2-g4, g7-g5, h7-h6) or piece moves to edge squares (Bc5-b4), all non-essential and non-developing
analysis.why_bad: These moves waste a critical tempo in positions where central tension is unresolved, pieces are hanging, dangerous diagonals are open, or development is desperately needed—allowing opponents to seize the initiative with forcing central moves, tactical strikes, or simple captures of undefended material.
sub_patterns: a-file pawn pushes (a6/a5/a4) when central pawns or pieces need defense
g-file pawn pushes (g4/g5) weakening king position while undeveloped
h-file pawn push (h6) ignoring tactical vulnerability on f7
Edge piece placement (Bb4) abandoning active diagonal for irrelevant square

analysis.label: Piece (usually king) moves to a seemingly natural or active square that actually creates immediate tactical vulnerability through geometric alignment or exposure.
analysis.description: This feature fires on moves where a piece—predominantly the king (6/10 positions)—relocates to a square that appears to improve its placement but actually creates an exploitable tactical weakness. The most common pattern involves creating dangerous geometric alignments: king moves onto the same rank as an own rook enabling a skewer (Kc4, Position 7) or capture with check (Kf1, Position 14), king steps onto an open file inviting queen checks (Kg7, Position 11), king advances past a passed pawn allowing it to run (Kc5, Position 10), or king moves to an exposed central square enabling pawn breaks (Kd7, Position 4). Non-king instances follow the same logic: a knight moves to an unstable rim square where it gets trapped (Nh5, Position 1), a knight develops creating a fork target (Nc6, Position 3), or a queen relocates leaving defensive gaps while becoming a fork target itself (Qb6, Position 9). In 8/10 cases the move looks natural—centralizing, activating, or seeking counterplay—but each creates a concrete tactical shot the opponent can exploit immediately.
analysis.move_pattern: Piece (king 6/10, knight 2/10, queen 2/10) moves to a square that creates a line-based geometric vulnerability (rank/file/diagonal alignment) or positional exposure, typically 1-2 squares in any direction
analysis.why_bad: The destination square creates an immediate tactical vulnerability—typically a geometric alignment (skewer, fork, check along open line) or exposes the piece to attack with tempo—that the opponent can exploit in 1-2 moves to win material or decisive positional advantage
sub_patterns: King moves onto same rank/file as own piece, enabling skewer or capture-with-check
King steps onto open file or diagonal, inviting check-based attacks
King advances past critical defensive square (passed pawn blockade)
Piece moves to unstable square where it gets trapped or creates fork targets
Queen relocates away from defensive duties, creating multiple tactical weaknesses

analysis.label: Moves that place or expose high-value pieces (king/queen) on open files where enemy rooks can capture or deliver devastating checks.
analysis.description: In 7/8 positions, the blunder either directly places a king or queen onto an open file controlled by an enemy rook, or removes a defender that was shielding against such exploitation. Position 3: Queen goes to f6 on the open f-file → Rxf6+ wins queen with check. Position 6: King goes to f2 → Rxf3+ wins queen with check on the f-file. Position 8: King goes to g1 → Rg3+ delivers devastating check on the g-file. Position 10: Ne7 ignores the g-file x-ray → Rxg6 captures the queen. Position 11: Nf5 abandons d4 → exchange sequence allows Rxd6 winning a piece on the open d-file. Position 15: Queen goes to f2 → Rxf2+ captures queen with check. Position 9: Re1 removes the rook from f1 → f3 break exploits the now-unguarded f-file. The common thread is catastrophic misjudgment of open-file rook power, where the player either walks into or enables a rook capture/check along an unobstructed file.
analysis.move_pattern: King or queen moves to a square on an open file (especially f-file or g-file) where an enemy rook has direct line of attack, or a piece moves away from guarding such a file
analysis.why_bad: The move places a high-value piece directly in the firing line of an enemy rook on an open file, allowing capture with check or a devastating material-winning tactical blow that exploits the file geometry
sub_patterns: Queen placed on open file where rook captures with check (Qxf6, Qf2)
King steps onto open file enabling Rxf3+/Rg3+ type attacks (Kf2, Kg1)
Piece moves ignore existing rook x-ray on file allowing queen capture (Ne7→Rxg6)
Defender abandons file allowing pawn break or piece invasion (Re1, Nf5)

analysis.label: Playing a natural-looking move that ignores the one critical tactical or strategic demand in positions where essentially only a single good option exists.
analysis.description: This feature fires on moves that appear reasonable—developing a piece, capturing material, repositioning—but fatally miss the single urgent requirement of the position. In 8/10 positions, only 1 good move existed (avg 1.3), yet the chosen move addresses a secondary concern while the position's true crisis goes unattended. The pattern manifests as: grabbing a pawn while a passed pawn advances (Position 1, Bxh4 vs Nd2); developing a rook while a critical blockade is needed (Position 2, Rb8 vs Bd4); moving the queen to an 'active' square while freeing the opponent's constrained piece (Position 5, Qb7 vs Qxc5); blocking one's own key file (Position 6, Kf7 blocks Rf8); removing a critical defender from its file (Position 10, Rce8 abandons c-file); developing the wrong piece first (Position 15, Be3 vs Ne2). All positions feature a razor-sharp tactical situation where one specific move addresses the position's central tension, and the blunder is choosing something generically useful instead.
analysis.move_pattern: Various piece types making non-forcing moves (quiet development, passive retreats, secondary captures, lateral repositioning) in positions requiring one specific forcing action
analysis.why_bad: These moves fail because they address a secondary positional concern while ignoring the position's single most urgent tactical demand—whether that's blocking a passed pawn, executing the only forcing sequence, maintaining a critical constraint on the opponent, or keeping a key defender on its essential square. The resulting tempo loss allows the opponent to exploit the now-unaddressed vulnerability.
sub_patterns: Grabbing material while a critical positional task is ignored (Bxh4, Nb5 vs Qxf7)
Moving a piece away from the one square/file it must occupy (Rce8, Qb7, Qb6)
Passive retreat giving tempo in a position requiring active engagement (Bg3, Kf7)
Developing the wrong piece or in the wrong order (Be3, Nc6, Rb8)

analysis.label: Playing a non-urgent or secondary move in a position demanding immediate concrete action, squandering the one tempo needed to address the position's most pressing requirement.
analysis.description: This feature fires on moves that waste a critical tempo when the position is at a tipping point requiring precise, urgent action. In 7/9 positions, the analyses explicitly identify 'tempo_loss' as the primary tactical motif. The pattern manifests in several forms: releasing central tension prematurely when maintaining it was critical (exf5, exf4 in positions 3 and 13), quiet piece repositioning when tactical strikes or development were demanded (Qd3, Qb7, Nd6 in positions 2, 8, 15), irrelevant flank pawn moves when piece activation was urgent (a4 in position 9), weakening pawn moves that ignore the real threat (g3 in position 4), and superficially active checks instead of decisive captures (b5+ in position 11). The average good moves available is only 1.6, confirming these are razor-thin positions where one wasted tempo is catastrophic.
