In 8/9 cases, the best move addresses the single most pressing positional need—developing a dormant piece, capturing hanging material, or maintaining critical structural tension—while the played move addresses a secondary concern.
analysis.move_pattern: Diverse piece types and directions; no geometric commonality. Moves include quiet queen repositioning, pawn captures releasing tension, flank pawn pushes, knight retreats/advances, and pawn checks—all non-forcing or addressing secondary concerns.
analysis.why_bad: The position demands immediate concrete action (development, capturing free material, maintaining tension, or counterattacking a critical threat), but the played move spends a tempo on something non-urgent, giving the opponent the crucial extra move needed to execute their tactical plan, exploit a weakness, or consolidate a previously unstable position.
sub_patterns: Premature tension release (pawn captures opening position when undeveloped or releasing key squares with tempo)
Quiet piece repositioning when tactics or free material are available
Irrelevant flank pawn moves when piece activation is the urgent priority
Superficially active moves (checks, outposts) that ignore the position's concrete demands

analysis.label: Playing slow, non-forcing preparatory moves when the position demands immediate tactical action or concrete development.
analysis.description: This feature activates on quiet, positional-looking moves that waste critical tempo in positions containing urgent tactical demands. In 4/4 positions, the player chose a non-forcing move (pawn nudge or passive piece placement) that appeared to improve long-term prospects — fianchetto preparation (g6), outpost occupation (Nd5), prophylaxis (a3), or safe development (Nge7) — while the position actually required immediate concrete action. In 3/4 cases both kings remained in the center, and in 4/4 cases the refutation exploited a specific tactical vulnerability that the slow move failed to address: a central pawn break winning material (Position 1), an undefended pawn after removing its defender (Position 2), a trapped piece after pawn advance (Position 3), or a devastating queen-bishop battery enabled by blocking the d-pawn (Position 5). All positions featured closed or semi-closed centers that may have lulled the player into believing the position was slow enough for preparatory moves.
analysis.move_pattern: Non-forcing, non-developing moves: quiet pawn pushes (g6, a3) or piece placements to seemingly stable squares (Nd5, Nge7) — no checks, no captures, no direct threats
analysis.why_bad: The position contains concrete tactical vulnerabilities (hanging pawns, trappable pieces, exploitable batteries) that demand immediate action; the slow move wastes the tempo needed to either exploit an advantage or prevent a tactical blow, allowing the opponent to seize the initiative with forcing play.
sub_patterns: Prophylactic pawn moves (a3, g6) when center requires immediate action
Piece moves to 'impressive' squares while leaving material undefended (Nd5)
Passive piece development blocking critical pawns (Nge7)

analysis.label: Moves that waste a decisive tempo on secondary objectives in positions where only one immediate action maintains the evaluation.
analysis.description: This feature activates on positions where the player has essentially one critical move available (avg 1.4 good moves) and instead spends their turn on a secondary concern—often an apparently active or aggressive move that looks purposeful but fatally ignores the position's most urgent demand. In 5/7 positions, the best move involved an immediate concrete action (f7 promotion, Rg2+ with check, h4 pawn advance, Kd2 escaping the check file, Bg6 saving a piece), while the played move pursued a different plan that was 'one tempo too slow.' Queen moves to the kingside (Qg2, Qh2, Qg3) appeared in 3/7 cases as premature attacks that left critical squares undefended. In 6/7 positions, the analyses explicitly identify 'tempo_loss' as the primary tactical motif. The catastrophic average cp_loss of 330 reflects that these are positions at a razor's edge where a single wasted move flips the evaluation entirely—from winning to losing, or from equal to lost.
analysis.move_pattern: Various piece types (queen, rook, knight, king, pawn) moving to squares that appear active or aggressive but fail to address the single most urgent tactical demand of the position
analysis.why_bad: Each move wastes the one tempo that was critical for executing the position's urgent tactical requirement (promotion, check-based captures, pawn advances, escaping check lines, saving trapped pieces), allowing the opponent to seize the initiative or exploit newly undefended material.
sub_patterns: Premature queen raids to g/h files while pieces are undefended or undeveloped (Qg2, Qh2, Qg3)
Quiet improving moves when an immediate forcing sequence was the only winner (a4 instead of f7, Nc4 instead of h4)
Right idea wrong execution missing the check tempo (Rf2 instead of Rg2+, Kb2 instead of Kd2)

analysis.label: Playing a routine developing move or inferior capture while a more critical piece is hanging (either your own en prise piece or an opponent's undefended piece).
analysis.description: This feature fires when a player makes a move that ignores the most critical tactical element in the position—typically a hanging or attacked piece. In 3/6 positions, Black has a bishop on c5 attacked by White's b4 pawn and plays a knight development move (Nge7, Nf6, Nb7) instead of addressing the threat with Bxb4. In position 6, Black captures a pawn (Bxb3) while White's rook on g4 sits completely undefended and could be taken for free with Bxg4. In position 5, the knight moves to d4 where it itself becomes hanging to cxd4. In position 3, White grabs a pawn (Qxa7) while ignoring a lethal kingside attack. The common thread across all 6 positions is prioritizing a secondary goal (development, pawn capture, repositioning) over the position's most urgent tactical demand—typically involving undefended pieces worth far more than whatever the played move achieves.
analysis.move_pattern: Knight development or minor piece move (4/6 knight moves) or pawn-grabbing capture, ignoring an attacked/undefended piece elsewhere on the board
analysis.why_bad: The moves fail because they leave a piece en prise (own bishop captured for free in 3 cases, own knight captured in 1 case) or miss capturing an opponent's undefended piece (1 case) or abandon king safety for a pawn (1 case)—all losing far more material than any benefit the played move provides.
sub_patterns: Knight development ignoring b-pawn attack on own bishop (Bxb4 available)
Capturing a pawn while a higher-value piece hangs elsewhere
Moving piece to undefended square where it is immediately captured
Queen grabs distant pawn abandoning defensive duties

analysis.label: Making a superficially purposeful move that ignores the position's primary vulnerability (undefended piece or weakened king), when only quiet consolidation maintains the position.
analysis.description: This feature fires on positions where a critical tactical or structural vulnerability demands immediate attention, but the player makes a different 'natural-looking' move instead. In 3/8 positions (Positions 3, 4, 13), the player abandons the defense of a bishop on c4 (via Qe2, Nxe5, Neg5) when the quiet retreat Bd3 was the only good move. In 3/8 positions (Positions 6, 11, 15), the player pushes ...g6 weakening the kingside dark squares when consolidating moves like ...Qf6, ...Bf8, or ...c5 were needed to neutralize attacking pressure. In 2/8 positions (1, 12), a piece moves to a square where it immediately gets exploited with tempo (Qa6 hit by Bc8; Kg7 allowing Qg3+ perpetual). The unifying thread: with an average of only 1.5 good moves available, these positions require precise consolidation, but the player pursues a secondary plan (attack, 'defense,' development) that leaves the primary vulnerability unaddressed, allowing the opponent to exploit it with a tempo-gaining response.
analysis.move_pattern: Piece or pawn moves away from its defensive obligation or creates a new weakness; often knight/queen abandoning guard duty, or g-pawn advancing to g6 weakening king shelter
analysis.why_bad: The move ignores the position's most urgent requirement (protecting a hanging piece or maintaining king shelter integrity), allowing the opponent to exploit the neglected vulnerability immediately with a tempo-gaining capture, check, or fork that the correct consolidating move would have prevented.
sub_patterns: Knight leaves post exposing undefended bishop (Nxe5/Neg5 abandoning c4-bishop)
Pawn push ...g6 weakening dark squares when bishop/knight already pressures kingside
Queen/king moves to square where opponent gains tempo via attack on it (Qa6 hit by Bc8, Kg7 allowing Qg3+)
Quiet retreat or consolidation (Bd3, Bf8, Kf7, Qf6) was the only good move

analysis.label: Developing a piece to a textbook square while overlooking an immediate tactical vulnerability that the opponent exploits with a tempo-gaining forcing move.
analysis.description: This feature fires on moves that look like standard development or piece improvement but catastrophically ignore a concrete tactical demand in the position. In 6/8 cases the move is a knight move to a 'natural' square (Nc6, Nf6, Nb6, Nd4). The common punishment is that the opponent gains tempo with a forcing response: d4-d5 displacing a knight that just arrived (positions 1, 14), Ng5/Bxf7 attacking a newly-undefended f7 pawn after castling queenside (positions 3, 5), Ne5 occupying an outpost vacated by the moved knight (position 11), b4 attacking an exposed queen after a knight reroute (position 6), or Nxb4 winning material left hanging by a blocking knight (position 9). In all cases, 2-3 good alternatives existed that addressed the concrete threat first (e6 blocking d5 in 3/8 positions, simple developing moves in others), but the player chose the superficially logical move instead of the positionally/tactically necessary one. The average cp_loss of 207 reflects that these 'natural' moves consistently walk into one clear refutation.
analysis.move_pattern: Mostly knight moves (6/8) to standard development squares (c6, f6, b6, d4); also includes castling and rook centralization - all appearing routine but ignoring forcing replies
analysis.why_bad: The move neglects an immediate tactical vulnerability (undefended pawn, abandoned key square, exposed piece) that the opponent exploits with a tempo-gaining forcing move, typically a pawn advance or piece jump that simultaneously attacks the moved piece and creates a secondary threat.
sub_patterns: Knight to natural square allows d5 displacing it with tempo (Nc6, Nf6)
Knight leaves defensive post allowing opponent to occupy vacated outpost (Nf6 abandons e5 control)
Castling queenside leaves f7 undefended for Qxf7 or Ng5+Bxf7
Knight reroute creates tactical target while exposing another piece (Nb6, Nd4)

analysis.label: Playing a non-urgent, misdirected move when the position demands immediate concrete action toward the critical sector.
analysis.description: In all 7/7 positions, the player makes a move that appears purposeful but wastes a critical tempo by failing to address the position's most urgent demand. The blunders share a pattern of moving toward the wrong area or reaching a destination without necessary intermediate forcing moves: Qa5 retreats to the queenside ignoring kingside king safety (5/7), Bf6 repositions a bishop when king/pawn advancement was needed (6/7), Rb7 goes directly to blockade without first attacking the pawn on b5 (9/7), Kf3 walks toward the kingside when queenside passed pawns are the decisive factor (11/7), Kh8 tucks into a corner creating back-rank weakness (12/7), h5 pushes a flank pawn when Nfxe5 was the only move capturing a critical tactical window (13/7), and f3+ gives a structurally weakening check that invites the enemy king closer rather than displacing it with Ng5+ (15/7). The average 1.6 good moves available confirms these are narrow critical moments where only immediate, forcing, or correctly-directed action maintains the evaluation. The common tag across 6/7 positions is explicit 'tempo_loss.'
analysis.move_pattern: Any piece type moving to a peripheral, passive, or premature destination instead of playing the one forcing/concrete move the position demands
analysis.why_bad: The position has a narrow tactical or strategic window requiring immediate concrete action (a capture, a forcing check, or movement toward the critical sector), and the played move squanders that tempo on a secondary plan, allowing the opponent to seize the initiative or advance their own threats unopposed.
sub_patterns: Moving toward the wrong wing while passed pawns or threats exist on the opposite side
Reaching a correct blockading/defensive square via wrong move order, missing intermediate forcing moves
Playing a slow positional move when a one-move tactical window exists for a capture or exchange
Giving a check or pawn advance that structurally weakens own position while improving opponent's king placement

analysis.chip: King retreats one square too far
analysis.label: King (or piece) retreats passively to the back rank when maintaining position one rank forward was critical for opposition or activity.
analysis.description: This feature fires on positions where the player retreats their king one square too far backward—typically to the back rank (1st or 8th)—when staying one rank forward was essential. In pawn endgames, this manifests as losing the opposition by retreating to the 1st/8th rank instead of holding the 2nd/7th rank (positions 5, 7, 9 show Kc1/Kb1/Kh8 losing drawn positions where Kc2/Kb2/Kh7 held). In position 2 and 10, Ke1/Kc1 retreat to the back rank losing tempo compared to Kf2/Kc3. Position 14 shows Kf8 retreating to the back rank and walking into forced checkmate. Position 12 and 15 show the king retreating away from the critical sector (Kf7 toward the wing, Kc7 away from center) when staying centralized was required. The outlier Qg6 (position 6) also involves a piece retreating to a passive square when a more active retreat existed. In 8/9 positions the move is a king move, and in at least 7/9 the king moves toward or onto the back rank. The average cp_loss of 1336 reflects that many of these errors convert drawn positions into lost ones.
analysis.move_pattern: King moves backward one rank toward own back rank (rank 1 for White, rank 8 for Black), typically along the same file or an adjacent file
analysis.why_bad: In pawn endgames, retreating one square too far back surrenders the opposition—the precise king-facing-king relationship that determines whether the defender can blockade a passed pawn. On the back rank, the king lacks the option to step forward to contest the critical squares, giving the opponent a free tempo to outflank or advance. In tactical positions, the back rank creates mating vulnerabilities.
sub_patterns: King retreats to back rank losing opposition in drawn K+P endgame (Kc1 vs Kc2, Kh8 vs Kh7)
King retreats to back rank losing blockading tempo in lost endgame
King retreats to back rank walking into forced back-rank mate
King retreats away from center/critical sector allowing passed pawn breakthrough

analysis.label: Playing routine positional or preparatory moves (especially rook-to-file) when the position demands immediate concrete tactical action.
analysis.description: In 10/10 positions, the player chose a non-urgent, 'natural-looking' move instead of addressing a concrete tactical demand. The most common manifestation is placing a rook on an open file (5/10: Rfc8, Rac1, Re8, Rhf1, Rac1) when an immediate tactical strike or critical defensive move was required. The remaining moves include a wrong capture that opens a dangerous file (fxe5), a piece repositioning that abandons a defensive post (Be5, Nc2), a queen move to a vulnerable square (Qg6), and a waiting pawn push (h6). In every case, the position had only 1-3 good moves available (avg 1.7), indicating critical moments where tempo was paramount. The errors uniformly allowed the opponent to execute a decisive tactical operation: winning trapped/hanging pieces (3/10), exploiting king safety (4/10), advancing passed pawns (1/10), or invading with decisive effect after forced exchanges (2/10).
analysis.move_pattern: Non-forcing moves—typically rooks sliding to open files, pieces repositioning to 'active' squares, or prophylactic pawn pushes—that fail to address an immediate concrete threat or miss a winning tactical blow
analysis.why_bad: These moves waste a critical tempo in positions where the opponent has (or gains) a specific tactical threat that requires immediate resolution; by not capturing vulnerable material, delivering forcing checks, or maintaining essential defensive coverage, the player hands the initiative to the opponent who executes a concrete combination.
sub_patterns: Rook to open file missing immediate tactical win (Rac1, Rhf1, Re8)
Piece leaves critical defensive post exposing back-rank or invasion square (Be5, Nc2)
Wrong capture direction destroying own pawn shield (fxe5 vs dxe5)
Waiting/prophylactic move when concrete counteraction required (h6)
Rook trade on contested file loses control of adjacent critical file (Rac1)

analysis.label: Quiet, non-forcing moves (pawn advances or king walks) that create self-inflicted weaknesses when the position demands immediate concrete action like castling, tactical shots, or piece activation.
analysis.description: This feature fires on positions where players choose slow, seemingly purposeful moves that actually worsen their own position, while ignoring urgent tactical or safety demands. In 6/9 positions, the move directly weakens the player's own king (g5, f5, f6, f4 weakening pawn shields; Ke2, Kf7 exposing kings). In 4/9 cases, the correct move was castling or immediate piece activation that the player deferred (Positions 4 and 8 demanded O-O; Position 12 demanded Qa4+; Position 15 demanded queen activation). The played moves share the quality of feeling 'constructive' - expanding on the kingside, centralizing the king, fianchettoing a bishop, grabbing space - but actually create targets, waste critical tempo, or block own pieces (b6 blocking knight retreat in Position 11). The average cp_loss of 1332 reflects how severely positions punish this pattern when urgent concrete action was available (avg 1.9 good moves), indicating narrow positions where only forcing/active moves maintain the balance.
analysis.move_pattern: Quiet non-forcing moves: pawn advances (especially f-pawn and flank pawns), aimless king walks, or piece retreats - never checks, captures, or forcing moves
analysis.why_bad: These moves waste critical tempo or create structural/king-safety weaknesses in positions where the opponent can immediately exploit the self-inflicted damage through checks, invasions on weakened squares, tactical strikes on exposed kings, or winning trapped/undefended pieces - the position demanded concrete forcing action that the player replaced with a vague slow plan
sub_patterns: Pawn advances weakening own king shield (g5, f5, f6, f4) when king safety is already precarious
King moves wasting tempo or forfeiting castling (Ke2, Kf7, Kb2) when urgent active play was needed
Passive piece repositioning (Bg2) instead of addressing king safety via castling
Pawn advance blocking own piece retreat (b6) creating trapped piece vulnerability

analysis.label: Moves that fatally expose the player's own back rank to immediate checkmate by ignoring or removing the sole defender.
analysis.description: All 4/4 positions feature the same catastrophic pattern: the player makes a move that leaves their back rank completely undefended, allowing an immediate or near-immediate back-rank checkmate. In 3/4 cases (Re2, Rh3, Rxc5), the critical error involves moving or misusing a rook that was needed to guard the 8th (or 1st) rank, directly enabling an opposing rook to deliver mate along that rank. In 1/4 cases (f4), a non-defensive pawn move ignores the lethal back-rank threat entirely. In all positions, the king is entombed behind its own unmoved pawns (f2/g2/h2 or a7/b7 or f7/g7/h7) with zero escape squares, and the opponent has a rook poised to invade the back rank. The best moves in every case involve creating luft (h3, h5, h6, a6, b6), stepping the king off the back rank (Kf1, Kg1), or reinforcing the back rank with a piece (Rc8, Raa8). The average cp_loss of ~9832 reflects that these blunders convert holdable or losing positions into instant forced checkmate.
analysis.move_pattern: Piece (usually rook) moves away from back rank, or any non-defensive move when back rank is critically vulnerable
analysis.why_bad: The move removes or neglects the only piece defending the first/eighth rank while the king is completely trapped behind its own pawns, enabling an immediate back-rank checkmate sequence
sub_patterns: Rook leaves back rank to go forward (Re2, Rxc5)
Rook moves to wrong square instead of correct prophylaxis (Rh3 vs h3 pawn)
Non-defensive pawn advance ignoring back-rank threat (f4)

analysis.chip: King move instead of pawn push
analysis.label: In a critical pawn endgame, playing a king move when the only winning move is to immediately advance a passed pawn.
analysis.description: This feature fires on positions where a player has a winning (or nearly winning) king-and-pawn endgame with an advanced passed pawn ready to be pushed, but instead makes a king move that allows the opponent to establish a drawn blockade. In 11/12 positions, the move played is a king move while the only winning continuation is an immediate pawn advance (e2, e7, b2, g7, c7, f2, etc.) to the 7th rank or to force the defending king off a critical square. In 11/12 cases, exactly one good move existed. The positions cover the full range of textbook K+P vs K configurations: pawn on 6th rank with supporting king (Positions 2, 4, 6, 7, 8), pawn on 3rd/6th rank needing immediate advance with king already ideally placed (Positions 1, 3, 5, 9, 10, 11). The average centipawn loss is catastrophic (~6725), with many positions swinging from forced mate to dead draw.
analysis.move_pattern: King moves in any direction (no consistent geometric pattern) in pure pawn endgames; the critical feature is that a passed pawn one square from a decisive advance is NOT pushed
analysis.why_bad: Moving the king wastes a critical tempo, allowing the defending king to reach the blockading square directly in front of the passed pawn. Once the blockade is established (often with stalemate resources), the position becomes a theoretical draw regardless of the attacker's king position.
sub_patterns: King retreats from ideal pawn-supporting square (e.g., leaving f3 when e2 wins, leaving g3 when f2 wins)
King moves sideways/away from 6th-rank pawn when c7/e7/g7 push is the only winning technique
King moves away from passed b-pawn when b2 permanently imprisons the defending king

analysis.label: Knight captures a piece on a central square (d4/d5/e4/e5) where the pawn recapture creates a devastating fork or exchange sequence winning material.
analysis.description: In 8/10 top activating positions, a knight captures an opponent's piece on a central square (e5 in 5 cases, d5/d4/e4 in others), and the resulting pawn recapture (dxe5, exd5, fxe5, cxd4, or dxe4) creates a lethal pawn fork or triggers an unfavorable exchange chain that nets the opponent a full minor piece. In positions 3, 4, and 7, the pattern is identical: Nxe5 leaves a bishop on d6 and knight on f6 simultaneously vulnerable to dxe5, whereas Bxe5 would have preemptively removed one target. In positions 1, 5, and 9, the wrong capturing piece initiates a forced exchange sequence that loses additional material. The best alternatives (available in all cases: avg 2.4 good moves) consistently involve capturing with the bishop instead, or ignoring the tension entirely. Two outlier positions (8, 10) involve piece movements to/through central squares that create different tactical vulnerabilities.
analysis.move_pattern: Knight captures on central squares d4/d5/e4/e5, removing a well-placed opponent piece
analysis.why_bad: The pawn recapture (dxe5, exd5, fxe5, cxd4, dxe4) attacks pieces that were previously shielded by the now-departed knight or its former square, creating pawn forks on two minor pieces or initiating forced exchange sequences that net a full piece.
sub_patterns: Nxe5 where dxe5 forks bishop on d6 and knight on f6 simultaneously
Knight capture where pawn recapture exposes a bishop to a second pawn/piece capture in sequence
Wrong capturing piece (knight instead of bishop) leaving own bishop as a fork target
Exchange on central square where opponent's pawn chain realigns to attack multiple pieces

analysis.label: Moving a piece away from a non-obvious but critical defensive or tactical role, allowing an immediate exploitation of the vacated function.
analysis.description: In 9/11 positions, the blundering move repositions a piece that was performing an essential but hidden function—either defending a square, guarding against a breakthrough, or being capable of a key capture. Positions 1 and 2 show the king retreating (Kb2) instead of capturing a hanging rook, abandoning its offensive function as a piece. Positions 6 and 8 show the f-rook (Rfe1, Rfb8) leaving the f-file where it was the sole guard against a pawn breakthrough (f2 weakness or fxg6+). Position 15 shows the queen (Qc4) leaving d3 where it defended d4, and position 10 shows c6 removing the c-pawn's defense of b7. Position 9 (Rb8) leaves the queen undefended. Positions 4, 3, and 14 show the king moving to a vulnerable square (Ke7 into a check diagonal, Ke1 into a promotion path, Kf3 wasting tempo) when concrete forcing moves were required. All moves appear 'natural' or 'improving' but fatally ignore the immediate concrete demands of the position, with an average loss of 1153cp reflecting catastrophic tactical oversights.
analysis.move_pattern: Any piece moves away from a square where it performed a critical function (defending, capturing, blocking); often king retreats, rook redeploys to wrong file, or queen/pawn abandons a guard
analysis.why_bad: The moved piece was the sole guardian of a tactical vulnerability (hanging piece, breakthrough square, promotion path, or check diagonal); removing it creates an immediate tactical collapse that the opponent exploits with forcing moves
sub_patterns: King retreats instead of capturing a hanging piece (Kb2 instead of Kxa1)
F-rook leaves f-file removing defense against pawn breakthrough (Rfe1, Rfb8)
Queen/pawn abandons defense of a specific square leaving material hanging (Qc4, c6)
King walks into a tactical vulnerability (check diagonal, promotion path, open file)
Slow improving move when immediate concrete/forcing action is required (h3, Kf3)

analysis.label: Non-forcing moves that ignore immediate decisive tactical vulnerabilities (mate, discovered attacks, trapped pieces) while pursuing illusory or secondary goals.
analysis.description: This feature fires on moves that appear purposeful—attacking a piece, supporting a plan, or looking aggressive—but catastrophically ignore an immediate tactical refutation in the position. In 4/5 positions, the move directly worsens the player's tactical vulnerability: Rf8 self-blocks the queen's escape square enabling a winning pawn advance (Position 1), Bh3 blocks the queen's retreat allowing Rg1 to trap it (Position 5), Re8 places the rook on a file where a discovered attack wins it via Ng6+ (Position 3), and h4 ignores an immediate back-rank checkmate Rf8# (Position 4). In Position 2, Bh6 abandons critical central defense for a hollow kingside threat. The average cp_loss of 2177 reflects that these are not subtle positional errors but cases where the player completely missed a forced tactical sequence. All 5 moves are non-forcing (no check, no capture, no genuine threat) played in positions that demanded addressing an immediate concrete danger.
analysis.move_pattern: Non-forcing piece/pawn moves (bishops, rooks, pawns) to seemingly active squares, never checks or captures, typically to h-file or f-file squares
analysis.why_bad: The moves ignore an immediate decisive tactical refutation (back-rank mate, discovered attack, piece trapping) while often actively worsening the situation by self-blocking escape routes or abandoning critical defensive duties
sub_patterns: Self-blocking a friendly piece's escape square (Rf8 blocks queen, Bh3 blocks queen retreat)
Placing a piece on a file/diagonal where a discovered attack wins it (Re8 behind knight)
Ignoring immediate forced checkmate to pursue irrelevant plan (h4 allowing Rf8#)
Hollow aggressive bishop move that abandons defensive responsibilities (Bh6)

analysis.label: Non-forcing moves that pursue secondary plans while fatally neglecting the position's most urgent defensive or tactical requirement.
analysis.description: This feature fires on positions where a player makes a plausible-looking quiet move that completely ignores the position's primary demand. In 4/10 cases, the move wastes tempo on non-urgent pawn moves (a3, b3, g6, g6) when immediate action like castling, capturing, or advancing passed pawns is required. In 3/10 cases, the move physically removes a piece from a critical defensive post (R7d3 abandons the c7 blockade, Rh3 abandons back-rank defense on c1, Nf5 abandons f7 coverage from h6). In 2/10 cases, the move self-weakens while attempting to address a secondary concern (f3 weakens g3, Bf5 abandons h5 control). In 1/10 cases, the player moves a piece into danger rather than capturing free material (Ne6 walks into Rxe6 instead of taking the hanging rook). All 10/10 moves are quiet and non-forcing - no checks, captures, or direct threats - and all have a superficially logical intent that represents a catastrophic priority misjudgment. The average cp_loss of 2040 reflects that many lead to immediate mate or decisive material loss.
analysis.move_pattern: Quiet non-forcing moves (no check/capture/threat) - diverse piece types including pawns (f3, g6, a3, b3), knights (Nf5, Ne6), bishops (Bf5), and rooks (R7d3, Rh3) - typically moving away from where the piece is most needed or spending time on a flank/non-critical square
analysis.why_bad: Each move ignores the position's most urgent requirement - whether maintaining a critical blockade, defending a back rank, preserving a key square's integrity, or not wasting tempo when immediate tactical action is demanded - in favor of a secondary plan that looks purposeful but is catastrophically lower priority.
sub_patterns: Removing own piece from critical defensive square (R7d3, Rh3, Nf5 - allows mate or promotion)
Slow pawn moves wasting tempo when castling/development/pawn advance is urgent (b3, g6, a3)
Self-weakening pawn moves that create holes while trying to resolve tension (f3 weakening g3)
Placing pieces on seemingly active squares that are actually tactically vulnerable (Ne6 into Rxe6, Bf5 allowing ...h5)

analysis.label: King moves in endgames with advanced passed pawns where the immediate pawn advance was more urgent.
analysis.description: This feature activates on king moves in endgame positions featuring advanced passed pawns near promotion. In the critical blunders (6/14 positions with cp_loss > 30), the correct move was invariably an immediate pawn push: g7 instead of Kf7 (Position 2), c2 instead of Kd2 (Position 3), e3 instead of Kf3 (Position 10), d6 instead of Ke6 (Position 11), e2 instead of Kd2 (Position 14), and b5 instead of Ke2 (Position 7). Even in low-cp-loss positions (8/14 with cp_loss ≤ 9), the feature still fires because the structural pattern is identical: a king escorting move in a pawn promotion scenario where the pawn push was equally strong or marginally better. The consistent thread is players choosing king-escort technique (supporting the pawn from behind or beside) over the more forcing immediate pawn advance, losing critical tempo in pawn races.
analysis.move_pattern: King move (any direction, no capture, no check) in positions with an advanced passed pawn 1-3 squares from promotion
analysis.why_bad: In pawn races and promotion scenarios, immediate pawn pushes create unstoppable threats or maintain critical tempo advantages, while king moves waste time and allow the opponent to escape confinement, start counterplay, blockade, or advance their own passed pawns in the race.
sub_patterns: King steps behind own passed pawn instead of pushing it forward (Kf7/Kd7/Ke6/Kc6)
King retreats away from action instead of advancing the pawn (Ke2/Kf3/Kh2/Kd2)
King approaches pawn's promotion path redundantly when pawn can self-promote (Kb3/Kd3/Kc5)

analysis.label: Moving a piece away from its essential defensive post, leaving a key square or piece fatally unguarded and allowing immediate tactical exploitation.
analysis.description: In 7/7 analyzed positions, the blundering move removes a piece from (or fails to place it on) a square where it was the sole defender of a critical entry point or hanging piece. Position 4 (Rd2) abandons c1, allowing Qc1+ to win the rook. Position 8 (Rd6) abandons the first rank, allowing Rb1+ leading to back-rank mate. Position 14 (Kf1) places the king where it cannot capture a queen check on h1, losing the c1 rook. Position 10 (Qg4) places the queen in the path of a back-rank check sequence (Re8+-Rg8+-Rxg4) instead of returning to d8 to defend. Position 11 (h5) ignores the rook's need to defend g8, allowing Rg8+ to win the a8 bishop. Position 1 (Qe5) abandons coverage of g6, enabling Qg6+ invasion. Position 3 (Rxf6) removes the rook from f7, surrendering seventh-rank control to White's rooks. Position 12 (Qf3) abandons defense of b2, allowing simple capture. The consistent pattern: a seemingly active or natural move ignores that one piece was the sole guardian of a vulnerable square, and the opponent punishes instantly.
analysis.move_pattern: Any piece type moving away from a square where it was providing sole coverage of a critical defensive point (back rank, invasion square, or hanging piece)
analysis.why_bad: The moved piece was the only thing preventing an immediate tactical blow—typically a back-rank check sequence, rook invasion, or simple capture of an undefended piece. The 'active' repositioning gains nothing because the opponent's forcing reply (usually a check or capture) exploits the newly abandoned square before any benefit is realized.
sub_patterns: Rook leaves back rank allowing mating attack or piece capture via rank invasion
Queen moves off a defensive diagonal/file allowing enemy queen/rook invasion with check
Piece ignores need to guard a hanging piece on the 8th rank, allowing capture after a check
King moves to a square where it cannot deal with a check that forks another piece

analysis.label: Playing a slow, consolidating, or routine move in a position with very few acceptable continuations that demands immediate concrete action.
analysis.description: This feature fires on positions where the player makes a quiet, seemingly reasonable move—piece retreats, slow pawn pushes, or 'natural' development—while ignoring an urgent tactical or structural demand. In 10/11 positions, king safety is the critical theme being neglected; the player either fails to address threats to their own king or misses the chance to exploit the opponent's exposed king. The positions share extremely low availability of good moves (avg 1.6), meaning they are critical decision points where only one or two precise responses maintain the evaluation. The played moves look reasonable in a vacuum—developing a knight (Nc3), consolidating with a pawn (c3), castling (O-O-O)—but fatally ignore specific concrete needs like resolving pawn tension (positions 10, 11), defending against tactical shots (positions 3, 4, 8), or preserving king shelter (positions 7, 9). The average cp_loss of 1051 reflects that these are catastrophic oversights, not minor inaccuracies.
analysis.move_pattern: Quiet piece repositions (knight retreats to c3/d7), slow pawn pushes (c3, g5), or king moves (castling, Ke6) when the position demands a forcing response (pawn breaks, tension captures, or tactical counterattacks)
analysis.why_bad: The move ignores the one critical concrete demand of the position—whether resolving pawn tension, defending against an imminent tactical blow, or maintaining a key defensive piece—allowing the opponent to execute a devastating tactical or positional punishment that was only possible because of the passive move played.
sub_patterns: Knight retreating from active/defensive squares (Nc3 from e4, Nd7 from f6) abandoning critical control
Slow c3 pawn pushes blocking own development or ignoring kingside tension
Weakening pawn advances (g5) creating tactical targets near own king
Castling or moving king into the line of fire of opponent's active pieces
Natural-looking recaptures that allow discovered attacks or checks

analysis.label: King moves forward toward the center when it should retreat to the back rank for safety.
analysis.description: In all 12/12 positions, the player advances their king forward (toward the center or an exposed square) when the only good move was retreating the king to the back rank (1st rank for White, 8th rank for Black). The best moves were consistently Ke1/Kd1/Kb1 for White or Kf8/Ke8/Kd8/Kc8/Kg8 for Black, while the blunders walked the king onto exposed central squares (e3, f3, g3, d7, d6, c3, f6, e6, d3) where enemy pieces could immediately exploit it with checks, forks, discovered attacks, or mating nets. The positions share the common feature of active enemy pieces (queens, knights, rooks on open files) that can punish a centralized king with tempo-gaining tactics. The average centipawn loss of ~4188 reflects the catastrophic nature of these errors, with many resulting in forced checkmate.
analysis.move_pattern: King moves one square forward/toward center (away from back rank) instead of retreating toward the 1st/8th rank
analysis.why_bad: The king walks into the active zone where enemy pieces (queens, knights, rooks on open files, bishops on diagonals) can deliver immediate checks, forks, or construct mating nets; retreating to the back rank removes the king from all these tactical patterns by maximizing distance from enemy piece activity.
sub_patterns: King advances into knight fork squares (Ke3→Nd5+, Kd6→Nf7+, Kf6→Ne4+)
King walks onto open file where rook/queen delivers check (Ke6/Kd6 onto open e/d-file)
King advances into forced checkmate net (Kf6→Qd6#, Kg3→Qe3+...Qg5#)
King moves toward enemy piece concentration instead of away from it (Kf3 toward kingside attacking pieces)
King advances to exposed diagonal allowing tempo-gaining bishop/queen checks (Kd3→Qa6+)

analysis.label: Voluntarily moving the king (or key piece) forward to an exposed square where it becomes an immediate tactical target, when retreating to safety was required.
analysis.description: This feature fires on positions where the player advances their king toward the center or to an exposed square, creating catastrophic tactical vulnerabilities. In 8/12 positions, the blunder is a direct king move forward (Kf2, Kd7, Kd3×2, Ke6, Kd2, Kc6), walking into checkmate (3/12), forced mating nets (2/12), or enabling devastating checks/forks that win material. The remaining 4/12 positions involve slow or misplaced piece moves (Bf3, Qd7×2, d3, Nc6) that similarly fail to address king vulnerability or expose pieces on tactical lines. In every case, the best alternatives involved retreating the king to safety (Kd1, Kf1, Ke8, Kg8) or making active moves that addressed defensive urgency. The average cp_loss of 2602 reflects the catastrophic consequences—the king repeatedly lands on squares controlled by diagonals, files, or mating nets that the opponent immediately exploits.
analysis.move_pattern: King moving forward/toward center (ranks 2-6) to an exposed square, often on the d-file or adjacent central files; secondarily, slow piece moves when king safety demands urgency
analysis.why_bad: The king lands on a square where opponent pieces (rooks on open files, bishops on diagonals, knights covering escape squares) create immediate tactical threats—checkmates, forks with check, or captures along newly opened lines that the king's presence enables
sub_patterns: King advances to central square allowing immediate checkmate (Kd3, Kd2 into mating nets)
King moves forward abandoning defense of key pawns or enabling forced trades into lost endgames (Kf2, Ke6, Kc6)
King walks into open file/diagonal where opponent rook or queen delivers devastating checks (Kd7, Kc6)
Slow/passive move fails to address king exposure, allowing opponent tactical exploitation (Bf3, Qd7, d3, Nc6)

analysis.label: Playing a natural-looking or seemingly active move that wastes a critical tempo by ignoring the position's single most urgent demand.
analysis.description: This feature fires on positions where the player makes a 'reasonable-seeming' move that addresses a secondary concern while failing to deal with the one critical priority the position demands. In 11/13 positions, the move is explicitly tagged as a tempo loss. The positions are characteristically demanding (avg 1.8 good moves available), meaning there is typically only one correct plan. The blunders include passive pawn moves when tactical urgency exists (d6 ignoring king safety in positions 1,3), natural development ignoring hanging pieces (Nc6 in position 2), retreating active pieces from critical posts (Rf1 abandoning pressure in position 8), premature attacks easily refuted (Qh5 answered by g6, g5+ improving opponent's king), captures that abandon defensive duties (Nxd4 leaving e4 hanging), and queen moves abandoning critical coverage (Qe7 leaving back rank unguarded). The common punishment involves the opponent exploiting the wasted tempo to execute the very threat the move failed to address.
analysis.move_pattern: Any piece type or direction; no geometric consistency. Moves appear 'normal' (development, captures, checks, pawn pushes) but are non-forcing and fail to address the critical positional demand.
analysis.why_bad: The position has one urgent priority (king safety, hanging piece, advanced passed pawn, critical pressure to maintain) and the move ignores it, spending a tempo on something secondary. The opponent then exploits the gifted tempo to execute the threat that needed addressing, often with a forcing sequence (check, capture, or promotion).
sub_patterns: Passive pawn moves (d6, g5) when piece activity or king safety is urgent
Premature attacks/checks that improve opponent position (Qh5, g5+)
Piece retreats abandoning critical pressure (Rf1, Nd2)
Natural development that ignores tactical vulnerability (Nc6, Nxd4)
Queen moves abandoning defensive coverage (Qe7, Qh4)

analysis.label: Playing a natural-looking rook deployment (usually to an open file) when the position demands an immediate forcing continuation like a pawn thrust or knight jump.
analysis.description: This feature fires on positions where the player chose a slow, routine-looking move—overwhelmingly rook moves to open files (7/9 positions)—instead of the critical forcing continuation the position demanded. In positions 1, 4, and 7 (Rad1, Rad1, Re1), the correct move was a forcing central action (e5 or Nd5) that would gain tempo or disrupt the opponent, but the player defaulted to 'put rooks on open files.' In position 6 (Rfd1), the wrong rook was chosen, stranding the a-rook in passivity. In position 2 (Rf3), the rook abandoned a critical defensive duty. In position 3 (Rb8), the rook left a key file allowing queen infiltration. In positions 5 (exf5) and 8 (Qxf2), the player made a natural-seeming capture that released tension or grabbed material rather than maintaining dynamic pressure. In position 9 (Rd8+), a blockable rook check was played instead of unblockable knight checks delivering mate. The common thread across all 9 positions: choosing a 'looks-right' positional/developing move when concrete forcing play was essential, gifting the opponent a critical tempo to neutralize or counterattack.
analysis.move_pattern: Rook moves to open files (d-file or e-file primarily), or captures/checks that appear natural but are non-forcing; typically vertical rook deployment from the back ranks
analysis.why_bad: These moves are non-forcing and give the opponent a free tempo to neutralize the position's critical demands—the opponent can sidestep pressure, cover key squares, or launch counterplay that was previously impossible, turning winning or equal positions into losing ones.
sub_patterns: Rook to open d-file instead of e5/Nd5 pawn/knight thrust
Wrong rook to file stranding the other rook
Rook abandoning critical defensive file/square
Blockable rook check instead of unblockable knight check
Releasing central tension with a capture instead of maintaining it

analysis.label: Quiet, positionally-motivated moves played in tactically critical positions that demand immediate concrete or forcing action.
analysis.description: This feature fires on positions where the player chose a 'natural-looking' quiet move—development, consolidation, file-contesting, or king safety—when the position demanded urgent concrete action within a narrow window. In 8/8 positions, the correct move involved an immediate capture, tempo-gaining check, or critical defensive repositioning, while the played move was non-forcing and allowed the opponent to seize the initiative. Examples include: f3 (passive pawn push) instead of Bxf5 (winning material), Bd3 (developing) instead of Qxf5 (eliminating the critical pawn), Raf8 (contesting a file) instead of Rg7 (defending the king), Kf8 (king retreat) instead of Rd4 (tactical blow), and Qc2+ (purposeless check) instead of Qc4+ (forcing the king to stay exposed). The average cp_loss of 361 and average of only 1.6 good moves confirms these are positions with extremely narrow tactical demands where any non-forcing move collapses the position.
analysis.move_pattern: Various piece types making quiet, non-forcing moves (no meaningful captures or threats) to apparently-logical squares—pawns consolidating, rooks contesting files, bishops developing, kings retreating, knights centralizing—rather than the single concrete action required.
analysis.why_bad: These moves waste a critical tempo in positions where a temporary advantage (piece activity, exposed enemy king, tactical opportunity) must be exploited immediately. The quiet move allows the opponent to neutralize the position's key tension—whether by capturing an undefended piece, launching a pawn break, generating perpetual check, or redirecting an attack against a newly-created vulnerability.
sub_patterns: Quiet pawn/bishop development instead of immediate material-winning capture (f3 vs Bxf5, Bd3 vs Qxf5)
Rook doubling/file-contesting ignoring critical king safety needs (Rhe8, Raf8)
Moving a piece's sole defender away from protection duty (Qf7 leaving Bg4 hanging)
Purposeless check driving enemy king to safer square (Qc2+ allowing Ke1)
Passive king move instead of forcing tactical continuation (Kf8 vs Rd4)

analysis.label: Capturing material or playing passively while one's own king remains critically vulnerable, allowing tactical punishment via the exposed king.
analysis.description: In 5/5 positions, the blunderer's king is exposed or inadequately shielded (uncastled on e8 in 3/5, exposed on g7 in 1/5, weakened castled position in 1/5). The mistake in each case ignores this vulnerability: 3/5 moves capture pawns (Qxc2, Qxd4, Nxh5) prioritizing material over safety, while the other 2 (Bf4, h3) are slow/passive moves that fail to address the urgency. In every case, the refutation directly exploits the king's exposure—via checks along open diagonals (Qh5+ in position 3, Bb5+ in position 11, Qxe4+ in position 8), rook sacrifices to open files (Rxh5 in position 14), or bishop sacrifices to destroy pawn shields (Bxh3 in position 10). The common thread is that 5/5 positions demanded immediate attention to king safety or aggressive exploitation of the opponent's king, but the player chose a materialistic or prophylactic move instead, allowing a forcing tactical sequence that converts the king weakness into a decisive advantage.
analysis.move_pattern: Mixed piece types capturing pawns (3/5) or making slow non-forcing moves (2/5), all occurring in positions where the mover's king lacks adequate protection
analysis.why_bad: The moves ignore urgent king safety needs—removing defensive pieces, wasting tempo, or creating new weaknesses—while the opponent has forcing resources (checks, sacrifices, file-opening) ready to exploit the exposed king immediately
sub_patterns: Queen pawn-grabs pulling queen away from king defense (Qxc2, Qxd4)
Capturing pawns that remove key defensive pieces near the king (Nxh5)
Passive/prophylactic moves when aggressive central action was required (h3, Bf4)

analysis.label: King moves in critical King+Pawn vs King endgames that waste the decisive tempo, when an immediate pawn push or precise blockade placement was the only correct move.
analysis.description: This feature fires on king moves in pure King and Pawn versus King endgames at the critical moment where exactly one move maintains the evaluation. In 10/12 positions, the correct move was an immediate pawn push (advancing a passed pawn on the 6th or 7th rank) while the king was already optimally placed to support promotion - instead the player moved their king, allowing the opponent to establish an unbreakable blockade or stalemate fortress. In 2/12 positions, the correct move was a specific king placement directly in front of the opponent's passed pawn to maintain a blockade/opposition - instead the king moved to an adjacent square, surrendering the critical defensive position. All positions share the characteristic of having exactly 1 good move available (avg good moves: 1.0) with catastrophic consequences for any alternative (avg cp_loss: 7622), representing textbook theoretical endgame positions where precise technique is required.
analysis.move_pattern: King moves in any direction in K+P vs K endgames, moving away from or failing to reach the critical square (either beside a pawn that needs pushing, or directly in front of an enemy pawn that needs blocking)
analysis.why_bad: The king move wastes the critical tempo: when a passed pawn is on the 6th/7th rank with the king ideally supporting it, the pawn must advance immediately to displace the defending king from the blockade square. Any king move allows the opponent to occupy the blockade square (directly in front of the pawn), creating either an unbreakable stalemate fortress or drawn opposition. The technique requires pawn-first, king-second - not the reverse.
sub_patterns: King retreats from 6th rank when pawn push wins (Kd6->Ke5 instead of e7, Kf6->Kf5 instead of g7, Kb6->Kc5 instead of c7)
King advances away from pawn support when pawn push wins (Kf3->Ke4 instead of e2, Kg3->Kg4 instead of f2, Ke3->Kf4 instead of f2)
King moves sideways abandoning blockade square (Ke1->Kf1 instead of Ke2, Kf8->Ke8 instead of Kf7)

analysis.label: Choosing superficially active or aggressive-looking moves that actually undermine the player's own key positional assets, while missing a critical pawn break or concrete action.
analysis.description: This feature fires on positions where the player selects an apparently aggressive or active move that self-sabotages their position's core strength. In 3/4 cases, the best move was a decisive pawn break or central advance (f5+ in Position 2, e6 in Position 4, d4 in Position 15), but the player chose a piece move that looked active yet was counterproductive. In Position 2, Qxg4+ grabs a pawn but allows ...f5 which permanently blocks White's own critical f5 breakthrough. In Position 15, Bg4 'develops' the bishop but blocks White's own g-file rook—the whole point of the Rg1 setup. In Position 4, Nc4 centralizes the knight but removes it from a3 where it guarded the b4 square, enabling a devastating Bb4+ check. In Position 14, f5 looks thematic but opens lines against Black's own exposed king. All 4/4 positions share the 'piece_activity' tag, 3/4 feature 'tempo_loss', and 3/4 involve 'missed_tactic'. The average cp_loss of 294 reflects these as severe blunders where an objectively winning or equal position is compromised.
analysis.move_pattern: Piece or pawn moves to active-looking squares (captures, centralizations, aggressive advances) that block own pieces or remove key defenders
analysis.why_bad: These moves prioritize surface-level aggression or trivial gains while neglecting the position's true demand—typically a powerful pawn breakthrough (f5+, e6, d4) or maintaining a closed structure. They self-sabotage by blocking own files, removing defensive guardians, or opening lines against their own king.
sub_patterns: Material-grabbing captures that allow opponent's defensive resource on the same square/file
Knight centralization that removes a key defensive guardian
Premature pawn break that opens lines against own exposed king
Bishop 'development' that blocks own rook's file

analysis.label: Moving a piece or king to a central square that abandons king protection or walks into check-based tactics on open files.
analysis.description: All 5 positions share a common pattern: a piece or king voluntarily moves to a square (d3, d7, f2, f6) where it either removes critical king protection or exposes itself to immediate tactical exploitation along open lines. In 5/5 cases, the resulting punishment involves checks or forcing moves on open files/ranks. Specifically: Qd3 abandoned g2 defense allowing Qg5 (position 4), Qd7 placed the queen on the open d-file as a deflection target for Rd1 (position 7), Kf2 walked the king into a corridor of double-rook checks on the 2nd/3rd ranks (position 12), Kf6 stepped into a mating net from doubled rooks on the e-file (position 14), and Bd3 removed the bishop from e2 where it shielded the king, allowing Bg5+ (position 15). King safety is the tactical motif in 4/5 positions and tagged in 5/5. The average cp_loss of 2124 reflects how catastrophically these moves fail when open-file checks punish the newly created weakness.
analysis.move_pattern: Piece or king moves to d3/d7/f2/f6 — exposed central squares adjacent to open files — typically one step toward the center or along the file
analysis.why_bad: The moved piece was either defending the king from its original square or the king itself moves to a square where coordinated enemy pieces (especially rooks on open files) can deliver devastating checks, deflections, or immediate checkmate. The move creates or walks into a tactical vulnerability on an open line that didn't previously exist.
sub_patterns: Queen abandons king-shielding square to centralize on open file (Qd3, Qd7)
King voluntarily steps to rank/file where enemy rooks deliver forced checks or mate (Kf2, Kf6)
Bishop leaves defensive post, exposing king to diagonal/file checks (Bd3)

analysis.label: Playing a tempting check or capture that displaces a well-placed piece from its optimal square, when a quieter preparatory move would maintain or increase the advantage.
analysis.description: This feature fires on positions where players choose an 'obvious' forcing move—typically a check or capture—over a more precise alternative. In 4/7 positions, the move played is an actual check (Nd2+, Bc4+, Bxd5+, Kf6 enabling checks). In 5/7 cases, the piece leaves a strong centralized square (knight from f3 or e4, bishop from e4, rook from b-file) to execute the forcing move. The best moves in contrast are consistently quieter preparatory moves: Ke2 instead of Nd2+, Rd1 instead of Bc4+, Kc1 instead of Nd2, Rb6# instead of Bxd5+, Rxb6 instead of Rbc8. The recurring analysis tags across all positions include 'premature_check' and 'tempo_loss' (appearing in 6/7), confirming the pattern of choosing flashy forcing moves that alert the opponent or dissolve winning positions. The average cp_loss of 2897 is extreme, driven by Position 15 (missing mate-in-one for a check) and Position 8 (walking into forced mate), showing these impulsive moves can be catastrophic.
analysis.move_pattern: Piece moves from a strong/controlling square to deliver a check or make a capture, typically a minor piece (knight or bishop) or rook moving to give check or capture along a diagonal/file
analysis.why_bad: The forcing move reveals the attacking plan prematurely, displaces a well-coordinated piece from its ideal square, and gives the opponent defensive resources (escape squares, recaptures with tempo, counterplay) that wouldn't exist after proper preparation with a quiet move first.
sub_patterns: Knight leaving strong central square to give premature check (Nd2+ from f3, Nd2 from e4)
Bishop check/capture that dissolves a mating net or bypasses a stronger quiet move (Bxd5+, Bc4+)
Moving the wrong piece when the position demands preparation (Rbc8 abandoning b-file, Kf6 retreating into mating net)
Capture that enables opponent's recapture with check or tempo gain (Nxe6 allowing Qxe6+)

analysis.label: Rook (or king) moves to an irrelevant square in a critical endgame, wasting a decisive tempo while the opponent's concrete threats go unaddressed.
analysis.description: This feature fires on endgame positions where the player moves a rook (8/9 positions) to a passive or irrelevant square—most commonly the a-file or back rank (Ra8 appears 3/9, Ra7 1/9, Ra6 1/9)—when the position demands immediate concrete action against passed pawns, pawn breaks, or mating threats. In every case, the opponent has an urgent advancing threat (passed pawn in 7/9, mating attack in 2/9) that requires the rook to stay on or move to a specific critical file for blockading, restraining, or counterattacking. Instead, the piece redeploys to a square that looks 'active' but has no connection to the position's actual crisis. The consistent analytical tag across all positions is 'tempo_loss' (8/9 analyses), and the average cp_loss of 3237 reflects that these wasted tempi are often the difference between holdable and lost positions—or even between survival and immediate mate (positions 8, 12, 13 show forced mates after the move).
analysis.move_pattern: Rook sliding to the a-file, back rank, or wing file (away from the critical central/kingside sector); occasionally king retreating toward an irrelevant wing
analysis.why_bad: The move wastes a critical tempo in a position with concrete threats, allowing the opponent to execute an unstoppable plan (pawn advance, king invasion, or mating attack) that the rook could have prevented by remaining on or moving to the relevant file/rank
sub_patterns: Rook to a8/a7/a6 when passed pawns need blockading on another file
Rook to back rank when opponent's king is invading the center
Piece retreating toward an irrelevant wing while opponent's passed pawn advances

analysis.label: Playing a slow, non-forcing move in a time-critical position where the opponent needs just one tempo to consolidate or neutralize the player's advantage.
analysis.description: This feature activates when a player makes a quiet, passive, or preparatory move in a position that demands immediate tactical urgency. In 6/6 positions, the move played is entirely non-forcing (no check, no capture, no direct threat), while the best moves involve forcing continuations like checks (Qa5+, Bb4+), central breaks (d5), or precise king marches (Kf4). In 5/6 positions, the opponent needs exactly one tempo to consolidate—whether it's Rh1 to blockade a passed pawn (2 endgame positions), d5 to fork pieces, Bxc6/Nxe5 to win a central pawn, or Qe2 to neutralize an initiative. The average cp_loss of 295 reflects that these are positions with extreme urgency where a single wasted tempo collapses the evaluation entirely. In 4/6 cases, only 1 good move existed within 50cp of the best, showing these are narrow tactical moments disguised as quiet positions. The moves themselves look reasonable in isolation—developing a bishop, pushing a pawn, centralizing a king—but catastrophically ignore the position's time-sensitive demands.
analysis.move_pattern: Non-forcing quiet moves: bishop retreats to passive squares (Bd7), slow pawn advances (h5, c3), or king moves in the wrong direction (Kd6, Kf6)—all lacking check, capture, or direct threat
analysis.why_bad: Each move wastes a critical tempo in a position where the opponent needs exactly one move to consolidate, blockade, or seize the initiative—the quiet move allows the opponent to execute their key defensive/offensive resource (Rh1 blockade, central break, queen invasion, piece capture) that would have been prevented by an immediate forcing continuation
sub_patterns: Passive bishop retreat when active checks or pins exist
King moving away from the critical square in promotion races
Slow preparatory pawn moves ignoring urgent development needs
Breaking pins passively instead of exploiting opponent's exposed king

analysis.label: Natural-looking moves that fail to address a specific imminent tactical threat, enabling the opponent to execute a forcing sequence that was previously unavailable or preventable.
analysis.description: This feature activates on moves where the player makes a superficially reasonable decision—a capture (gxh3), a queen repositioning (Qd7, Qb7), a rook invasion (Rb7), a knight retreat (Nh8), or a king move (Ke8)—but critically ignores the opponent's most forcing tactical resource. In 6/6 positions, the played move either creates a new vulnerability or removes a key defensive piece/resource, enabling a specific tactical punishment: perpetual check via opened g-file (Position 1), queen double attack Qf6 (Position 2), Nxd6+ exploitation (Position 5), rook challenge forcing trade (Position 6), Nh7+ winning the exchange (Position 7), and Nf6+ knight fork winning the queen (Position 15). In 5/6 cases, only 1-2 good moves existed, indicating these are critical moments requiring precise responses. The common thread is that the position's tactical tension demanded a specific defensive or preparatory move, but the player played 'off-topic'—addressing a secondary concern while the opponent's forcing blow was one move away.
analysis.move_pattern: Diverse piece types (pawn capture, queen, rook, knight, king) moving to squares that appear reasonable but are functionally passive or misguided given the tactical demands
analysis.why_bad: Each move either removes a critical defender from a key square, opens a line for the opponent's attack, or places a piece on a square vulnerable to a forcing tactical shot (fork, perpetual, double attack), while failing to address the one defensive requirement the position demanded.
sub_patterns: Captures that open files toward own king (gxh3 enabling perpetual)
Queen moves to passive squares when counterplay was essential (Qd7, Qb7)
Premature piece activation without preparatory moves (Rb7 without Bf4)
Retreating pieces that abandon critical defensive squares (Nh8 leaving g6)
King moves walking into fork/forcing sequences (Ke8 into Nf6+)

analysis.label: Playing a non-forcing repositioning move in a position that demands a specific tactical solution, with very few good alternatives available.
analysis.description: This feature fires on positions where the player chooses a quiet, 'improving' or repositioning move while ignoring the concrete tactical demands of the position. In 8/10 cases, the correct move involved either an active capture (Nxe4, Bxd6, Nxd6), a forcing piece activation (Qa4, Nh7), or a precise approach move (Kf6 for mate). Instead, the played moves are universally non-forcing: passive king walks (Kh7, Kc5, Kf2 in 3/10), piece/queen repositioning to inferior squares (Bb3, Qh8, Qb2 in 3/10), generic development (Re8, Bc4 in 2/10), or premature advances (h2+, g5 in 2/10). The positions share a critically narrow solution space (avg 1.9 good moves), meaning the player faced a 'one right answer' situation but selected a plausible-looking alternative. The average cp_loss of 1195 reflects the catastrophic nature of these errors.
analysis.move_pattern: Non-forcing, non-capturing moves (piece repositions, king walks, generic development) in positions where a specific forcing move (often a capture or active piece engagement) is required
analysis.why_bad: These moves fail because they ignore the concrete tactical urgency of the position—either missing a critical capture that eliminates threats with tempo, allowing the opponent to execute a devastating tactical response (forks, attacks on exposed kings, unstoppable passed pawns), or voluntarily weakening one's own position by relocating pieces away from their defensive/offensive duties.
sub_patterns: King walks to exposed/irrelevant squares (Kh7, Kc5, Kf2) when active piece play was needed
Queen/piece repositioning that abandons key defensive duties (Bb3, Qh8, Qb2)
Generic developing moves missing concrete tactical captures (Re8 vs Nxe4, Bc4 vs Ne2)
Premature advances that create weaknesses or help the opponent (h2+, g5)

analysis.label: Playing an active/counterplay-seeking move while ignoring a critical threat to the player's own exposed king.
analysis.description: In all 4/4 positions, the player's own king is exposed or vulnerable (f7, c7, g2, f4), and the move played seeks piece activity or counterplay (rook to open file, knight to attacking square, pawn push for space) rather than addressing the immediate defensive need. The best moves in each case were prophylactic or defensive: h5 preventing g4 (pos 1), Nc6 defending d5 and shielding the king (pos 2), Rh1 defending h3 near the king (pos 3), Ke3 escaping a mating net (pos 4). The blunders allow the opponent to exploit the king's vulnerability immediately—via Rxh7+ and g4 (pos 1), Nc3-Nxd5+ fork near the king (pos 2), Bxh3+ check (pos 3), and Rd3 threatening Rd4# (pos 4). The average cp_loss of 2549 reflects how catastrophic it is to ignore king safety at critical moments, with 3/4 positions having only 1 good move available.
analysis.move_pattern: Non-defensive piece improvement (rook to file, knight to outpost, pawn advance) directed away from the player's own exposed king
analysis.why_bad: The player's own king is critically exposed and requires immediate prophylactic defense or escape; playing for activity elsewhere grants the opponent a tempo to execute a devastating tactical blow against the undefended king position.
sub_patterns: Rook activation on distant file while king is under attack
Pawn push ignoring adjacent king weakness
Knight relocation abandoning key defensive square near king

analysis.label: Black relocates a piece away from a critical defensive role on the kingside, allowing the opponent to exploit the suddenly unguarded h6 pawn or exposed king.
analysis.description: In 4/4 positions, Black plays a quiet repositioning move that removes a piece from a square where it was performing a vital kingside defensive function, specifically around the h6 pawn or king shelter. In 3/4 cases (Qf7, Kg7, Nb6), the h6 pawn becomes directly vulnerable to tactical exploitation (Nf5+Rxh6, g-file attacks after gxf5, or Bxh6 sacrifice). In 3/4 positions, the best moves involved immediate concrete action (f5 blocking Nf5, Rg8 preparing h5, Ne4 centralizing) rather than slow repositioning. The feature captures the pattern of a 'quiet' piece relocation in a tactically critical moment—typically involving queen, king, or knight moving to a seemingly reasonable square—when the position demands maintaining defensive coordination near the castled king. All 4 blunders are non-forcing moves that look positionally motivated but ignore the urgent tactical reality of kingside vulnerability.
analysis.move_pattern: Various pieces (Q/K/N) moving away from kingside defensive positions to passive or peripheral squares; non-forcing, non-capturing quiet moves
analysis.why_bad: The repositioned piece was the sole or primary defender of a kingside weakness (usually h6), and its departure allows an immediate tactical blow (sacrifice, knight jump, or file-opening) that cracks open the king's shelter before Black can compensate.
sub_patterns: Queen retreating from g-file squares that defended h6
Knight moving to queenside leaving h6 pawn tactically hanging
King moving to open file/diagonal creating a direct target

analysis.label: Black's king advances forward (typically f7→g6) into tactical vulnerability when retreating to safety was required.
analysis.description: In 3/4 positions, Black's king is displaced to f7 in the opening (typically in Two Knights Defense-type positions with a White knight on g5) and instead of retreating to safety (Kg8 or Ke8), the player advances the king to g6 where it becomes a target for pawn checks (f5+, h4-h5+) and piece attacks (Nh4+, Qh5). In all three Kg6 cases, Black held a significant advantage (-185 to -398) that was completely squandered, with the king walking into forced tactical sequences involving discovered checks and pawn storms. The 4th position (b4, 1/4) shares the broader theme of an unnecessary aggressive forward move that creates irreversible targets when quiet consolidation was correct. All positions featured Black having an existing advantage that demanded patience rather than aggression.
analysis.move_pattern: King advancing one square forward from f7 to g6 (toward opponent's side), or pawn pushing forward creating structural weakness
analysis.why_bad: The king on g6 is directly vulnerable to pawn advances (f5+, h4-h5+) that deliver checks or open lines, knight checks (Nh4+), and queen invasions (Qh5), transforming a safe advantage into a losing exposed-king position with no shelter.
sub_patterns: Kf7-g6 walking into f5+ pawn check
Kf7-g6 walking into h4-h5 pawn storm
Kf7-g6 allowing Nh4+ knight check with Qh5 follow-up
Aggressive pawn advance gifting passed pawn to opponent

analysis.label: Choosing an aggressive-looking or obvious move that misplaces a piece or wastes tempo, missing a quieter but concretely stronger continuation.
analysis.description: In 9/9 positions, the player chose a move that appeared active, aggressive, or natural on the surface but was concretely inferior to a less obvious alternative. The pattern manifests as piece misplacement to apparently active squares (Qa4, Bh4, Qh3, Bc5, Ra6 - 5/9), material grabs that enable counterplay or simplification (Qxe5, Qxg4+ - 2/9), or the 'obvious' tactical continuation over a deeper one (gxf8=Q+, c4 - 2/9). In all cases, the move prioritizes surface-level activity over concrete effectiveness: pieces land on squares where they're vulnerable (Bc5 gets captured with check), abandon critical defensive duties (Bh4 leaves kingside unguarded, Ra6 abandons passed pawn blockade), or miss devastatingly stronger tactical shots (Qxg4+ misses pawn mate, gxf8=Q+ misses deflection sacrifice into forced mate). The 'tempo_loss' tag appears in 7/9 analyses, confirming that the core error is squandering time through moves that look purposeful but accomplish less than the alternative.
analysis.move_pattern: Piece moves to an apparently active/aggressive square or makes an apparently strong capture, typically a queen/bishop moving to an exposed outpost or a capture that seems to combine multiple advantages
analysis.why_bad: The move prioritizes apparent activity over concrete calculation: it either places a piece where it becomes a target or must retreat (losing tempo), abandons a critical defensive function enabling opponent's tactics, or selects the 'obvious' tactical continuation while missing a quieter but forcing winning sequence.
sub_patterns: Queen/Bishop to aggressive-looking but exploitable outpost (Qa4, Bh4, Qh3, Bc5)
Rook/piece abandoning critical blockade or defensive post (Ra6, c4)
Material grab enabling unfavorable simplification (Qxe5)
Obvious tactical choice missing deeper forced win (Qxg4+, gxf8=Q+)

analysis.label: Playing a slow non-forcing flank move when an immediate central pawn capture would win material with both kings uncastled.
analysis.description: This feature fires on opening positions where critical central pawn tension exists and both kings remain in the center, yet the player makes a non-forcing peripheral move instead of the concrete central capture that wins material. In 8/9 positions, the best move was a central pawn capture (exd5, exd3, dxe5, Nxe4, exd4) that either won a clean pawn or gained decisive advantage through the opened lines against the opponent's uncastled king. Instead, the player chose flank pawn pushes (b5, b6, b6, h4, f6 in 5/9 cases) or peripheral piece moves to non-central squares (Ne5, Nh7, Bb4, Bb5 in 4/9 cases). Both kings were uncastled in 9/9 positions, making tempo absolutely critical. The average cp_loss of 268 reflects that these moves typically squander a winning tactical opportunity (pawn capture plus follow-up checks/forks exploiting the exposed king) in favor of a slow positional plan that gives the opponent time to consolidate.
analysis.move_pattern: Non-capturing moves to flank squares (b-pawn pushes, h-pawn pushes, pieces to rim/b-file) while central pawn captures (exd5, dxe5, exd3, Nxe4) are available
analysis.why_bad: The central pawn tension creates a narrow tactical window where capturing wins material (the captured pawn is underdefended because both sides lack full development), but the non-forcing flank move wastes the critical tempo, allowing the opponent to either defend the weakness or launch counterplay exploiting the still-open center and uncastled king.
sub_patterns: Flank pawn push (b5/b6/h4/f6) instead of central capture
Peripheral piece development (Bb4/Bb5/Ne5/Nh7) instead of resolving center
Slow fianchetto preparation (b6) when dxe5 wins material immediately
Aggressive-looking knight sortie (Ne5/Nh7) abandoning pressure on hanging center pawn

analysis.label: Moves that appear active or purposeful (checks, captures, advances, repositioning) but waste critical tempo by neglecting the position's most urgent requirement.
analysis.description: This feature fires on moves that look like they accomplish something—giving check, making a capture, advancing a passed pawn, or repositioning a piece to a seemingly active square—but actually ignore the position's primary demand. In 6/7 positions, the analyses highlight 'tempo_loss' as a core tag, and 'piece_activity' degradation appears in 6/7. The pattern manifests as: Qa6+ displaces the queen from a mating net for an aimless check (position 8); c5+ gives check but permanently eliminates the b5 counterplay break (position 5); Bxf2 captures with the wrong piece, exposing the queen (position 4); d6 overextends the passed pawn beyond support (position 15); Qc7 repositions the queen to an 'active' square while ignoring the tactically hanging bishop on g6 (position 12); Kd8 seeks apparent safety but walks onto the open d-file (position 3). In each case, the best moves addressed the actual critical factor: maintaining coordination (5/7), protecting a threatened piece (2/7), or keeping pieces on dominant squares (3/7). The played moves all sacrifice these fundamentals for cosmetic improvement.
analysis.move_pattern: Mixed piece types and directions; commonality is superficially purposeful actions (checks, captures, advances, repositioning) that move pieces away from where they're critically needed
analysis.why_bad: Each move neglects the position's primary requirement—whether that's piece safety, maintaining counterplay options, preserving coordination, or addressing an immediate tactical threat—in favor of a superficially attractive action, allowing the opponent to exploit the newly unaddressed vulnerability
sub_patterns: Aimless checks that displace own queen from the critical zone (Qa6+, c5+)
Wrong capture order that exposes a more valuable piece (Bxf2)
Pawn advances that overextend beyond support or eliminate counterplay (d6, c5+)
Piece repositioning that ignores immediate tactical threats (Qc7, Kd8)

analysis.label: Playing a natural-looking centralizing or checking move while missing the one specific tactical action (often a simple capture or precise prophylactic) that the position demands.
analysis.description: This feature fires on endgame positions where extreme precision is required (avg 1.6 good moves available) but the player chooses a superficially attractive move—centralizing a piece, giving a check, or advancing the king—over the one concrete action the position demands. In 3/7 positions (Ne6+, Ke5, and indirectly Qd5+), the player missed capturing or winning a hanging queen. In 2/7 positions (Bc6, Kb5), the player failed to execute a precise prophylactic move against an unstoppable pawn promotion. In 2/7 positions (Bd4, Qe7), the player made a centralizing move that allowed the opponent to execute a critical plan (pawn break or forced queen trade). The common thread is choosing moves that look purposeful by general chess principles—occupying central squares, giving checks, advancing pieces toward the action—while overlooking a simple concrete requirement that was the only way to maintain the position.
analysis.move_pattern: Pieces move to central or active-looking squares (d4, d5, e5, e6, e7, c6, b5) or give checks, rather than making captures, blockades, or retreats to specific required squares
analysis.why_bad: Each position had one critical tactical or prophylactic requirement (capture a hanging piece, blockade a passed pawn, avoid a forced trade, execute a skewer) that the 'natural-looking' move completely ignores, wasting the one tempo that was essential for survival or winning
sub_patterns: Giving check or centralizing instead of capturing a hanging queen (Ne6+, Ke5, Qd5+)
Placing a piece on a geometrically wrong square that appears to address a threat but doesn't (Bc6 not covering c8, Qd5 not creating skewer)
Advancing/centralizing king when a specific piece maneuver is urgently needed (Kb5 instead of Nc1 blockade)
Centralizing a piece that enables opponent's key break or forced simplification (Bd4 allowing b4, Qe7 allowing Qe5+ trade)

analysis.label: Advancing a passed pawn or making a committal forward move when the king (or another piece) needed to reach that square or provide preparation first.
analysis.description: This feature fires on moves that look aggressive or progressive—typically pawn advances—but catastrophically misorder the position's needs. The most striking sub-pattern appears in 3/14 positions where the player literally pushes a pawn to a square where the king should have gone instead (f6 instead of Kf6, c4 instead of Kc4, f3 instead of Kf3), violating the cardinal endgame principle that the king must lead its pawns. In 7/14 total positions, the error is a premature passed pawn advance (f6, c4, c7, f3, c7, g5, b6) that either self-blocks the king, removes a tactical threat protecting another piece, creates an easily-attacked target, or commits to a move-order that allows the opponent to neutralize the pawn. The remaining positions (2/14 captures removing key defenders: Bxg5, Bxc5; and piece moves abandoning duties: Qc7, Qe1, Ra1, Bf2) share the same underlying logic: choosing the 'obvious forward' move over the patient preparatory one. Nearly all positions are endgames (9/14) with very narrow margins (avg 1.9 good moves), making the committal error immediately fatal.
analysis.move_pattern: Pawn advances (especially c- and f-file passed pawns moving forward one rank), captures that remove defenders, or piece relocations away from critical defensive posts—all sharing the quality of 'forward/committal' action in positions requiring restraint.
