analysis.why_bad: These moves sacrifice flexibility, self-block the king from critical squares, remove tactical threats that were protecting other pieces, or strip defensive resources—all because the player prioritizes the appearance of progress (pawn closer to promotion, material gained, piece 'activated') over the actual positional requirement of preparation, coordination, or king activity.
sub_patterns: Pawn push to exact square where king should go (f6/Kf6, c4/Kc4, f3/Kf3)
Premature passed pawn advance removing a latent tactical threat (c7 unguarding bishop, b6 without c4 support)
Capture that removes a critical defensive piece for a peripheral gain (Bxg5 removing e3 defender, Bxc5 removing dark-square shield)
Piece relocation that abandons critical defensive duties (Ra1 ignoring g2, Qe1 allowing Ne7+ fork, Bf2 enabling Bxe1)

analysis.label: Playing a superficially natural or profitable move (passive development, pawn capture, material grab) that wastes a critical tempo while the position demands immediate attention to a concrete tactical vulnerability.
analysis.description: This feature fires on moves where the player prioritizes a secondary concern over the position's most urgent demand. The dominant sub-pattern (5/12) involves passive developing moves in Italian Game positions (Be7, Nge7, g6) that ignore the critical f7 vulnerability, allowing White's queen to exploit the a2-g8 diagonal with devastating effect. The second major sub-pattern (4/12) involves h-pawn captures on g5/g4 that open the h-file against the player's own castled king, gifting the opponent a lethal attacking highway (positions 5, 11, 12, 13). The remaining cases (3/12) involve capturing irrelevant material while ignoring urgent threats: Bxh8 captures an already-trapped piece while a passed pawn promotes, Rxg3 grabs a meaningless pawn while an a-pawn queens, and Qd7 vacates a critical defensive square. In every case, the player's move appears sensible in isolation—developing, capturing, winning material—but fundamentally loses a decisive tempo, allowing the opponent to execute their primary tactical plan unopposed.
analysis.move_pattern: Passive piece development to non-critical squares (especially e7), h-pawn captures on g4/g5, or captures of low-priority material on the wing while the center/king demands attention
analysis.why_bad: Each move wastes a critical tempo on a secondary concern while the opponent has an immediate tactical threat that goes uncontested—whether it's a queen invasion exploiting f7, an h-file ripped open against a castled king, or a passed pawn racing to promotion.
sub_patterns: Passive developing moves (Be7/Nge7/g6) ignoring f7 vulnerability in Italian Game structures
h-pawn captures (hxg5/hxg4) opening the h-file against own castled king
Capturing already-neutralized or irrelevant material while a critical threat goes unaddressed

analysis.label: Moves that neglect the critical factor of king exposure—either failing to defend one's own exposed king or failing to exploit the opponent's—in favor of some other goal.
analysis.description: Across all 11 positions, the dominant condition is a critically exposed king (own or opponent's), and the blunder is a move that ignores this factor to pursue something else. In 8/11 positions, the player's own king is directly vulnerable and they move a defender away (Qb2 abandons f2 king, Rd1 leaves h-file unguarded, Raf8 ignores h-file defense, Ke1 walks into perpetual check, Ne7 opens diagonal to uncastled king, fxe3 removes king shelter pawn). In 2/11 positions, the opponent's king is fatally exposed but the player fails to deliver the precise killing blow (Bf6+ checks on wrong diagonal letting king escape mating net, Bxa4 captures with wrong piece removing the attacking bishop). In 1/11 positions, the player walks their king directly into danger for material (Kxg6). The common thread is that all moves are 'natural-looking' (captures, checks, piece development, rook centralization) but fatally overlook that king safety is the overwhelmingly dominant positional factor.
analysis.move_pattern: Diverse piece types and directions; no single geometric pattern. Moves include piece retreats, queen repositioning, captures (both pawn and piece), king moves, and checks—all sharing the property of being directed AWAY from the critical king-safety task.
analysis.why_bad: These moves fail because they prioritize secondary goals (material gain, piece repositioning, file control, slow preparation, or inaccurate checks) while the position's dominant factor is king exposure—either needing to defend one's own vulnerable king or to exploit the opponent's. The punishment is always immediate: checks, mating attacks, or perpetual check sequences that exploit the unaddressed king vulnerability.
sub_patterns: Moving a defensive piece away from own exposed king (Qb2, Rd1, Raf8, Ne7, Qd7)
Removing a key pawn/structural defender of own king (fxe3 removes f2 shield)
King walking into exposed square for material or mispositioning (Kxg6, Ke1)
Inaccurate check/capture that lets opponent's exposed king escape (Bf6+ wrong diagonal, Bxa4 wrong piece)
Slow preparatory move when king-related action is urgent (g6 loses tempo)

analysis.label: A move that wastes a critical tempo when an opponent's pawn advance is one move away from trapping a bishop on a main diagonal.
analysis.description: In all 15 positions, a bishop sits on a key diagonal (typically b3/c4 for White or b6/c5 for Black) where an opposing pawn advance of one square (a4→a5, b2→b4, b7→b5, a5→a4, or g2→g4) can trap or win it. The moves played—whether passive pawn moves (d6 in 4/15), routine development (Nc6, Nc3, Bd7 in 3/15), castling (O-O in 2/15), prophylactic moves (h3 in 1/15), or other non-urgent actions (b3, Nf1, Bb6, e6, d5)—all share the critical property of failing to address the bishop's vulnerability before the opponent executes the pawn thrust. In every case, the best moves either prevent the pawn advance directly (playing ...a5 or ...a6 to block a5, or a4 to block ...b5 in ~10/15 positions), retreat the bishop to safety (Bb3, Ba4 in 3/15), or free an escape square (like ...c6 vacating c7 in 2/15). The refutations are strikingly uniform: a one-move pawn advance that attacks the bishop, which then has no safe retreat because its diagonal is blocked by its own pawns or pieces.
analysis.move_pattern: Any move type (pawn push, piece development, castling, piece retreat) that is NOT the bishop retreat, NOT blocking the threatening pawn advance, and NOT freeing an escape square for the endangered bishop
analysis.why_bad: The bishop on b3/c4/b6/c5 has restricted retreat squares (often blocked by own pawns on c7/d6/b3/a2), making it vulnerable to a single-step pawn advance that attacks it with tempo; the played move wastes the one remaining tempo needed to address this threat, allowing the opponent to trap and win a full piece for one or two pawns.
sub_patterns: Bishop on b6/c5 trapped by a4-a5 or b2-b4 advance (own d6 or c7 pawn blocks retreat)
Bishop on c4/b3 trapped by ...b7-b5 or ...a5-a4 advance (own b3 pawn or missing c4 defender blocks retreat)
Bishop on f5 trapped by g2-g4 advance (own e6 pawn blocks backward diagonal)
b3 pawn move self-blocking bishop's a2 retreat square before opponent plays ...b5

analysis.label: Active-looking moves that fatally open lines toward the player's own vulnerable king, allowing punishing checks or tactical sequences.
analysis.description: This feature fires on moves that appear aggressive or natural (piece redeployments, captures, pawn advances) but catastrophically expose the player's own king by opening critical diagonals or removing defensive pieces. In 4/5 positions, the moving side's king is uncastled or exposed. In 4/5 positions, the refutation involves an immediate check on a newly-opened diagonal (Bb4+ exploiting vacated d2 in Position 1, Qh5+ on the h5-e8 diagonal in Position 7, Qh4+ on the e1-h4 diagonal in Position 9, g4+ in Position 4). The moves share a common deceptive quality: Ndf3 looks like natural development, Nxd4 looks like winning material, h4 looks like creating kingside pressure, and f5 looks like gaining space—but each removes protection from a critical line pointing at the player's king. Multiple safe alternatives (averaging 3.0 good moves) existed in every case, typically involving quiet development or consolidation.
analysis.move_pattern: Piece moves or pawn advances that vacate squares/diagonals adjacent to own king (knight leaving guard duty, f-pawn advances opening e1-h4 or h5-e8 diagonals, h-pawn advances weakening king shelter)
analysis.why_bad: Each move removes a critical defensive element (a blocking piece or shielding pawn) from a diagonal or line pointing at the player's own uncastled/exposed king, enabling forcing checks that win material or permanently ruin king safety.
sub_patterns: Knight leaving a square that blocks a check diagonal (Ndf3 exposing b4-e1)
f-pawn advance opening diagonal to uncastled king (f5 opening h5-e8 or e1-h4)
Pawn advance weakening king shelter allowing forcing pawn break with check (h4 allowing g4+)
Premature capture ignoring tactical consequences of piece removal

analysis.label: Active-looking or centralizing moves that abandon the position's critical concrete requirement in favor of superficial piece improvement.
analysis.description: In 7/7 positions, the player makes a move that appears natural, active, or centralizing but fatally ignores the position's actual strategic or tactical demand. In Position 1, Nd6 places a knight on a central square where it gets trapped by pawn advances (d5+c5). In Position 9, Bd5 centralizes the bishop instead of eliminating the only asset giving Black winning chances (g4 pawn). In Position 14, Ne3 abandons the dominant d5 outpost to 'attack' a rook. In Position 13, Qd3+ gives a superficial check instead of the quiet a6+ that forces mate. In Position 15, Bd6 looks aggressive against the knight but blocks the d-pawn and creates a fork vulnerability. In Position 7, Nxg5 trades an active piece when positional pressure (cxb5) was decisive. In Position 5, f5 advances aggressively but surrenders the f6 square. In 6/7 cases, the move places a piece on a square that immediately becomes tactically vulnerable. The common thread is prioritizing appearance of activity over the position's concrete needs.
analysis.move_pattern: Pieces (especially minor pieces) moving to central/semi-central squares (d3, d5, d6, e3) or making aggressive-looking captures/advances that look natural but ignore concrete positional demands
analysis.why_bad: The moves abandon the position's critical priority (maintaining an outpost, eliminating a passed pawn, finding a forcing sequence, avoiding pawn forks) in favor of superficially attractive centralization or aggression, typically resulting in the piece landing on a tactically vulnerable square or the key positional factor being lost
sub_patterns: Piece moves to central square where it gets attacked by advancing pawns
Knight abandons dominant outpost for seemingly active but inferior square
Superficial check/capture that allows defensive interposition or relieves opponent's cramp
Bishop centralizes instead of addressing critical passed pawn
Pawn advance that surrenders control of key square to opponent's piece

analysis.label: Moves that appear to serve the same strategic purpose as the correct move but choose the wrong piece, direction, or timing in narrow positions where only 1-2 moves work.
analysis.description: This feature fires on moves that are 'near misses' - they pursue approximately the correct strategic goal but execute it with the wrong piece, wrong direction, or wrong move order, in positions where extreme precision is required (avg 1.6 good moves available). In 8/8 positions, the played move serves a similar apparent function to the best move: Qh8+ mimics the Bb4+ checking sequence (Position 1), Ke4 centralizes like Kc4 but goes the wrong way (Position 6), c4 advances a pawn like d5 but the wrong one (Position 9), Neg3 routes toward blockade like Nhf4 but takes an extra tempo (Position 10), Kd6 activates the king like Kf6 but toward danger (Position 12), and Nd3 repositions a knight like Nc3 but the wrong one retreats (Position 14). The critical shared thread is that each move loses a decisive tempo (tagged in 7/8 positions) because the 'twin' choice - the alternative piece, square, or direction - was the only option that addressed the position's concrete tactical demands. The average cp_loss of 2600 reflects that these near-miss decisions occur in razor-sharp positions where one tempo determines the outcome.
analysis.move_pattern: Mixed piece types (K, Q, N, pawns) moving to squares that mirror the correct move's apparent purpose but differ by one square, one piece choice, or one move in timing - no single geometric direction unifies them
analysis.why_bad: Each move wastes exactly one critical tempo by choosing the wrong 'twin' option (wrong knight, wrong direction, wrong pawn, wrong move order), and in these narrow positions that single tempo allows the opponent to execute a decisive tactical blow - whether a mating attack, rook invasion, pawn storm, or king escape from the net.
sub_patterns: Wrong piece delivers check/advances when sibling piece was required (Qh8+ vs Bb4+, Neg3 vs Nhf4, Nd3 vs Nc3, c4 vs d5)
King moves to wrong adjacent square - exposed instead of safe, passive instead of active (Kf6 vs Kf8, Ke4 vs Kc4, Kd6 vs Kf6)
Piece abandons critical defensive/controlling function for seemingly active square (Qc4 leaving f8 defense, Nd3 abandoning e5 control)

analysis.label: In rook endgames with a vulnerable back rank, the player moves a piece away from defensive duties toward illusory active play, allowing immediate or near-immediate corridor/back-rank checkmate or decisive rank invasion.
analysis.description: This feature fires on positions where the blundering side fatally prioritizes piece activity over critical rank defense in rook endgames. In 6/9 positions, the move directly allows back-rank checkmate (Re2 allowing Rb8+/Rxe8#, Rc2 allowing Rb8# or Rd8#, Rd4 allowing Ra8+ mating combination). In the remaining 3/9 positions, the move ignores analogous threats: a king move to an exposed rank allowing forced rook trade via check (Ke2 allowing Ra2+), a pawn push ignoring immediate mating threats (a6, f4), or placing a piece on an exposed square losing critical tempo (Rf4, Kg3). The positions share a consistent geometry: the king is trapped on an edge rank with opponent rooks dominating open files aimed at that rank, and the blundering piece was the sole guardian preventing invasion. The average cp_loss of 5182 reflects that most of these moves allow immediate checkmate (5/9 positions result in forced mate within 3 moves).
analysis.move_pattern: Piece (usually rook) moves laterally along a rank or forward along a file, AWAY from the back rank or critical defensive rank, in positions where the king is confined to the edge with opponent rooks on open files
analysis.why_bad: The move removes the last piece defending the critical rank (usually 8th/1st), allowing opponent rooks to deliver corridor checkmate or force devastating material-winning invasions. The 'active' destination (second rank pawn attacks, central squares, pawn pushes) provides zero value because the resulting mate/invasion is immediate.
sub_patterns: Rook moves to second rank for pawn attacks while abandoning 8th rank coverage (Re2, Rc2, Rc2)
Rook moves to central square abandoning back-rank interposition duty (Rf4, Rd4)
King or pawn move completely ignoring existing mating threat on open file (Ke2, a6, f4, Kg3)

analysis.label: Playing natural-looking 'improving' or repositioning moves at critical moments when the position urgently demands one specific precise action, allowing the opponent to seize decisive tempo.
analysis.description: This feature fires on positions where a player makes a plausible, routine-looking move (developing a piece, centralizing, gaining space, or seeking king safety) while ignoring the single most critical tactical or strategic demand of the position. In 6/7 positions, the analyses explicitly tag 'tempo_loss' as a key motif. The pattern manifests as: placing a rook on a natural-looking file instead of attacking a trapped piece (Position 2), retreating the king for safety instead of exploiting active counterplay (Position 3), checking on the wrong square that drives the opponent's king to safety (Position 10), placing the queen on a diagonal vulnerable to tempo-gaining development (Position 11), advancing a pawn that abandons control of a critical square (Position 12), developing a bishop while ignoring an unstoppable promotion threat (Position 13), and advancing the king to an apparently active square that's vulnerable to a tempo-gaining check (Position 14). In all cases, the positions had very few good moves available (avg 1.7), indicating narrow critical moments where precision was essential.
analysis.move_pattern: Any piece type making a short, non-capturing, 'improving' move (development, centralization, repositioning, or quiet pawn advance) rather than the one urgent tactical response the position demands
analysis.why_bad: These moves waste a critical tempo on a secondary objective, giving the opponent time to execute a decisive plan—whether invading with a rook, promoting a pawn, delivering a tempo-gaining check/attack, or seizing key central squares. The opponent exploits the wasted move to gain irreversible initiative.
sub_patterns: Quiet piece repositioning when a trapped/hanging piece needs immediate attention
King moves to squares vulnerable to tempo-gaining checks
Checking on the wrong square that drives the enemy king to safety
Placing pieces on squares where opponent gains development tempo by attacking them
Pawn advances that abandon control of critical squares needed for defense

analysis.label: Playing a non-urgent quiet move in a position with only one critical task, wasting an irreplaceable tempo.
analysis.description: This feature activates on positions where the player makes a normal-looking, quiet move (rook repositioning, prophylactic pawn push, passive king move) while ignoring the single most urgent demand of the position. In 5/8 cases the urgent task was king safety or king positioning (Kf2, Ke6, Kh2, Kd2, Kf8); in the remaining cases it was piece activation before an opponent's key break (Nf4 before c4, Qd8 for back-rank threats). The blunders share a strikingly low number of good alternatives (avg 1.2), indicating razor-sharp positions where only one plan was viable. The played moves all appear reasonable in isolation—contesting a file, preventing a pawn advance, improving a rook—but catastrophically fail because the position tolerates zero tempo waste. The average centipawn loss of ~1496 reflects that these positions sit on a knife-edge where a single wasted tempo allows the opponent to execute a decisive plan (king invasion, diagonal check sequence, pawn promotion, piece coordination breakthrough).
analysis.move_pattern: Quiet non-forcing moves (rook lifts to open files, king retreats to wrong square, prophylactic pawn advances) that don't address checks, captures, or immediate threats
analysis.why_bad: The position has exactly one critical need (usually king evacuation or piece relocation before opponent's key break), and the quiet move wastes the single tempo available to address it, allowing the opponent to execute a winning tactical or strategic sequence that was previously preventable
sub_patterns: Rook repositioning to a file when king needs immediate evacuation (Rb1, Rh1, Rab8)
King moving to wrong square allowing opponent queen check with tempo gain (Kc2 to square on check diagonal)
Passive king move squandering dynamic winning chances (Kg7 instead of Qd8/b4)
Prophylactic pawn move wasting critical tempo in pawn endgame (a6 instead of Ke6)
Piece move creating tactical vulnerability via deflection (Rg8 leaving piece hanging after check)

analysis.label: White makes a piece move that either abandons a dominant knight on e5, removes its defender, or places it on e5 unstably, allowing the opponent to exploit the resulting tactical void.
analysis.description: In 3/4 positions, the e5 square is directly central to the mistake: Position 1 removes a dominant knight FROM e5 (Nxg4), Position 7 retreats the queen from e2 leaving the e5 knight undefended (Qd1), and Position 13 places a knight ON e5 without stability (Ne5, punished by ...f6). The average cp_loss of 308 reflects how these moves convert advantageous or manageable positions into significantly worse ones. In every case, the opponent punishes by either capturing the now-undefended piece (3/4) or launching a central break that exploits the tempo loss (4/4 involve exposed kings or uncoordinated pieces).

analysis.why_bad: The move disrupts critical piece coordination by abandoning the defensive/supportive relationship between pieces (especially around the e5 outpost), leaving material hanging or creating an unstable piece that can be challenged with tempo, while the opponent exploits the resulting tactical hole with simple captures or central pawn breaks.

Aggressive piece placement that ignores undeveloped army and central vulnerability

Check with wrong piece or on wrong square, losing critical tactical resource

(2) In 2/6 positions (Be3), the opponent's dark-squared bishop captures on e3 forcing fxe3, saddling the player with crippled doubled isolated e-pawns and an exposed king on an opened f-file. All moves share the characteristic of appearing to be natural developing moves that challenge opponent's active pieces or control central squares, but each places the bishop on a square where the geometric alignment of pieces creates an immediate tactical vulnerability.

analysis.label: Seemingly active or natural moves that miss the one precise requirement of a position demanding narrow accuracy.

In each case, the position required one specific move—often quiet, prophylactic, or involving precise timing—that the player bypassed in favor of something that appeared more active or logical on the surface.
analysis.move_pattern: Mixed piece types moving to seemingly strong/active squares or pawn advances that appear purposeful; no consistent geometric direction but consistently choosing action over the one required precise response
analysis.why_bad: These moves fail because they address a secondary concern while ignoring the position's critical tactical or structural requirement—typically releasing tension prematurely, removing a key defensive element, exposing the king, or missing a forced tactical sequence that was the ONLY way to maintain the position's balance or advantage.
sub_patterns: Premature pawn advances that remove defensive barriers or release critical tension (c4, e4, c5, h4, cxb4)
Wrong-piece captures that miss superior tactical continuations (Rxe3 instead of Nc4, Kxg7 instead of Qxg7)
Piece repositioning to apparently active squares that creates tactical vulnerabilities (Nc5, Qe5, Kf2)

analysis.label: Seemingly purposeful moves that squander a critical tempo in positions demanding one specific precise action, enabling immediate tactical punishment.
analysis.description: This feature fires on positions where the player makes a natural-looking, constructive move (gaining space, giving checks, supporting pawns) that fatally ignores the ONE urgent requirement of the position. In 5/7 cases, the primary tagged motif involves tempo loss - the move appears proactive but actually hands the opponent a free tempo to exploit a newly created or existing vulnerability. The moves include flank pawn advances that seem space-gaining but create weaknesses (h4, g4, b3, g6 - 4/7 positions), and queen moves that appear aggressive but are geometrically imprecise (Qe3+, Qd2+, Qf4 - 3/7 positions). The positions are characteristically narrow, with only 1.7 good moves available on average, yet the blunders lose an average of 1635 centipawns - indicating these are critical junctures where precision was paramount. In every case, the opponent's refutation directly exploits what the move enabled: a cleared diagonal (b3 allows Bxa1), a blocked retreat (g6 traps the bishop), an exposed queen (Qf4 invites e5/g5 tempo attacks), or an escaped king (Qe3+ lets the king reach safety without restriction).
analysis.move_pattern: Mixed pawn advances (typically one-square flank pushes on g/h/b files) and queen moves to seemingly active squares; none are captures; 2/7 are checks
analysis.why_bad: Each move addresses a superficial concern (space, attack, pawn support) while ignoring the position's one critical tactical demand, wasting the crucial tempo that would have solved the real problem - enabling the opponent to immediately exploit the tempo loss with a concrete tactical blow
sub_patterns: Flank pawn pushes that weaken critical squares/diagonals or block own pieces (g6, h4, g4, b3)
Premature or geometrically wrong queen checks that drive the opponent's king to safety or miss the one correct attacking square (Qe3+, Qd2+)
Queen centralization to exposed square that abandons defensive duties (Qf4)

analysis.label: Natural-looking piece-improving moves that ignore an immediate tactical vulnerability, allowing the opponent a concrete exploitation (sacrifice, fork, or piece capture).
analysis.description: This feature fires on quiet, non-forcing moves that appear positionally reasonable—developing, centralizing, or repositioning pieces to active-looking squares—but fatally ignore a concrete tactical issue in the position. In 5/9 cases, a bishop is moved to a seemingly strong square (Bd6, Bd5, Bf4, Be7, Be5) where it either becomes a tactical target or abandons a critical defensive duty. In the remaining cases, a piece is similarly 'improved' (Nd7 developing, Kg7 connecting rooks, Rb2 preparing, Kd1 retreating) while an urgent tactical problem goes unaddressed. The best alternatives in these positions (avg 2.1 good moves available) all share the trait of addressing the concrete issue FIRST—whether that's attacking an opponent's piece to disrupt a battery (Position 9: Nb6 hitting Bc4), playing a prophylactic pawn move to secure a weakness (Position 4: h6 protecting g5), or choosing a stable defender over an unstable one (Position 7: Re1 instead of Bf4). The average cp_loss of 333 reflects that these are positions where the difference between 'looking good' and 'being correct' is enormous.
analysis.move_pattern: Non-forcing piece repositioning (primarily bishops 5/9) to central or active-looking squares; no checks, captures, or direct threats; all directions represented
analysis.why_bad: The move either places a piece on a square where it becomes a tactical target (exchange sacrifice, pawn kick, forced capture opening lines), removes a piece from a critical defensive post exposing king or material, or simply ignores an immediate concrete threat that the opponent can exploit on the very next move
sub_patterns: Bishop centralization creating a tactical target (Bd6/Bd5/Be5 - piece can be captured with devastating follow-up)
Piece placement on unstable square vulnerable to pawn attacks (Bf4 hit by g5, Be7 ignoring Nxf7)
King move to wrong square exposing it to tactical motifs (Kd1 allowing invasion, Kg7 exposing to diagonals)
Rook/piece displacement from critical defensive duty (Rb2 abandoning back rank, Be5 abandoning kingside guard)

analysis.label: Natural-looking moves that miss the single urgent requirement in narrow-path positions, causing catastrophic evaluation swings.
analysis.description: This feature fires on positions where the player makes a reasonable-looking move (centralizing a king, repositioning a piece, giving a check, pushing a pawn) but catastrophically misses the ONE specific action the position demands. The positions share extremely narrow best-move paths (avg 1.8 good moves available) and enormous centipawn losses (avg 3250). In 10/12 cases, the correct move addressed a specific urgent need: capturing a dominant piece (Kxe6 in pos 2), escorting passed pawns (Ke3/Kd3 in pos 3/6), initiating a pawn break (e4 in pos 8), starting a pawn race immediately (b4 in pos 9), maintaining a crushing pawn center (d6+ in pos 10), closing a mating net (Kf5 in pos 11), or eliminating a key attacker (Bxh4 in pos 14). The blundered moves all appear 'logical' on the surface—they centralize, develop, advance, or check—but address the WRONG priority, wasting the critical tempo that separates winning from losing in these razor-thin positions.
analysis.move_pattern: Any piece type moving to a plausible-looking square that fails to address the position's single critical tactical/strategic demand; no specific geometric direction
analysis.why_bad: These moves waste a decisive tempo in positions where only one (or very few) moves maintain the evaluation, because they pursue a secondary goal while ignoring the single urgent requirement—whether that's capturing a dominant piece, advancing a passed pawn in a race, closing a mating net, or neutralizing a lethal attacking piece.
sub_patterns: King moving to wrong adjacent square (Kg3/Kc3/Ke3/Kf7 - correct square was one step away)
Premature forcing move that dissolves own advantage (h2+/exf6+ - checking before setup is complete)
Piece repositioning that ignores urgent threat (Ra3/Qg6/Ne6 - quiet move when decisive action needed)
Weakening pawn advance in closed position (h4/e6 - structural concession that enables opponent's counterplay)

analysis.label: Playing impulsive major-piece checks (or passive moves) that accomplish nothing, while missing far stronger concrete tactical blows—typically knight forks or piece activations.
analysis.description: In 4/5 positions, the played move is a check with a rook or queen (Rh1+, Qf8+, Rc1+, Rh8+) that drives the opponent's king to a safer square without creating any lasting threats, while the remaining case (Qd2) is a passive queen repositioning that ignores immediate tactical danger. In all 5 positions, a much stronger concrete tactical move was available—often a knight fork or capture with check (Ne5+ in position 8, Nd3+ in position 6, Nxg4+ in position 15, Ne3+ in position 2) or a quiet piece activation (Rf1 in position 1, Rc8 in position 2). The played checks uniformly fail because the opponent's king simply sidesteps to a better square (Ke2→f3 in position 2, Kg1 in positions 6 and 15), after which the checking piece is misplaced far from the action (rook stranded on h8/h1/c1, queen passive on f8/d2). The average cp_loss of 2044 reflects that these positions demanded precision, and the instinctive 'check first' impulse squandered critical tactical resources.
analysis.move_pattern: Major piece (rook or queen) delivering a check or retreating passively, typically along a rank or file toward the opponent's king, without capturing material or creating a lasting threat
analysis.why_bad: The check drives the opponent's king to a safer square (often from an exposed position to a tucked one), wastes a critical tempo, misplaces the checking piece away from where it's needed, and squanders the one move that would have exploited a concrete tactical vulnerability (usually a knight fork or piece activation)
sub_patterns: Rook check along h-file that lets king escape to center/safety
Rook check along back rank that misplaces rook from active file
Queen check/retreat to passive square missing knight fork opportunity
Giving check 'because you can' without calculating the follow-up

analysis.label: Advancing pieces or pawns to seemingly active forward squares on the e-h files while abandoning critical defensive duties or ignoring urgent positional priorities.
analysis.description: This feature fires on moves that push pieces or pawns forward (typically to the 3rd-5th rank on the e-h files) that appear active or aggressive but catastrophically abandon the position's most critical requirement. In 5/7 positions, the move abandons a specific defensive function: Bf5 leaves the c8 blockade (Position 11), Qf4 abandons back-rank control on d1 (Position 13), h5 weakens the g5-recapture possibility and creates a mating square (Position 8), Be5 invites an immediate tempo-gaining f4 kick (Position 12), and g5 wastes a critical tempo in a king-race endgame (Position 1). In 1/7 positions (e3), the advance ignores a more urgent pawn tension. The typical activation shows a player choosing a 'proactive-looking' forward advance when the position demands patience, blockade maintenance, or addressing a more pressing threat—resulting in an average cp_loss of 5584 due to the opponent gaining a forcing tactical sequence.
analysis.move_pattern: Pieces or pawns advancing forward to squares on the e-h files (ranks 3-5), typically without creating immediate threats or captures
analysis.why_bad: The forward advance abandons a critical defensive function (blockade, king shelter pawn, back-rank coverage, square control) or ignores a more urgent positional priority (king race tempo, pawn tension resolution), allowing the opponent to exploit the abandoned weakness with a forcing sequence
sub_patterns: Kingside pawn pushes (g5/h5/h4) weakening king shelter or wasting tempo in pawn races
Bishop/Queen advances to 'active' central squares (Be5/Bf5/Qf4) abandoning blockade or defensive coverage
Passed pawn advances (e3) that are too slow compared to addressing critical tension elsewhere

analysis.label: Playing a slow strategic move when a bishop can simply capture an undefended knight.
analysis.description: In all 3/3 positions, the correct move was a bishop capturing an undefended or vulnerable knight (Bxd4, Bxa5, Bxc6), but the player instead made a positional/strategic move (pawn push or bishop retreat). The blundered moves—d5, Ba2, b4—are all thematically reasonable positional ideas (central breaks, piece preservation, queenside expansion) that completely overlook a one-move tactical opportunity. In each case there was exactly 1 good move available (avg good moves: 1.0), and the average cp_loss was 330, representing approximately a full piece's worth of advantage squandered. The feature captures the moment a player's strategic thinking completely overrides tactical awareness of an unprotected piece.
analysis.move_pattern: Player makes a quiet pawn push or bishop retreat instead of a bishop capturing an undefended knight (Bxd4/Bxa5/Bxc6 pattern)
analysis.why_bad: A completely undefended knight is available for capture by a bishop, but the player is thinking positionally/strategically and overlooks the simple tactical capture, allowing the opponent time to move the hanging piece to safety.
sub_patterns: Pawn push ignoring hanging knight
Bishop retreat when bishop should capture knight
Strategic move overriding one-move tactic

analysis.label: Playing an apparently productive move that ignores the position's most critical defensive requirement, allowing the opponent to exploit the neglected vulnerability.
analysis.description: In all 5 positions, the player chose a move that appeared active or purposeful (attacking a piece, capturing material, developing aggressively, defending a pawn) while ignoring the single most urgent positional demand. In 3/5 cases, the critical need was king safety (uncastled king exposed on an open file or facing tactical threats), while in the other 2/5 cases it was maintaining a critical defensive function (keeping a knight on its defensive post, preserving a bishop's retreat path). The blunder moves addressed secondary concerns: Nb4 attacked c2/d3 but abandoned defense of b6 (1/5); Bd3 aimed at h7 but blocked the Bf4's escape (1/5); Rb8 attacked the Nb6 but ignored the need to castle (1/5); Qd3 defended e4 but failed to address the lethal pin (1/5); dxc6 grabbed material but ignored discovered check threats on the e-file (1/5). All positions featured very few good alternatives (avg 1.6), indicating critical 'only-move' situations where the player failed to recognize what was truly urgent.
analysis.move_pattern: Various piece types moving to active-looking squares (attacks, captures, central development) while a critical vulnerability remains unaddressed
analysis.why_bad: The moves ignore the position's most pressing tactical or structural requirement—typically king safety or a critical defensive duty—allowing the opponent to exploit the neglected vulnerability with an immediate tactical blow (discovered attacks, trapped pieces, material-winning combinations).
sub_patterns: Abandoning a defensive piece from a critical square for apparent counterplay
Developing a piece to a seemingly aggressive square that blocks a friendly piece's escape
Attacking a secondary target instead of castling when the king is fatally exposed
Greedy captures that ignore discovered check or pin-based tactics

analysis.label: Player addresses a secondary concern (often a pawn advance or non-urgent repositioning) when the position demands immediate concrete action on its most critical element.
analysis.description: Across all positions, the player squanders a significant advantage by making a move that looks reasonable in general terms but ignores the position's #1 urgent demand. In 6/10 cases, the mistake is a pawn advance (h6, c5, c5, gxh5, gxf5, d5) when piece action was needed; in 4/10 cases it's a passive piece/king move (Be3, Nb2, Kc3, Kd8) when a concrete priority existed. The best moves consistently involve addressing the critical tactical factor: eliminating a key enemy piece (Ng4, Bxe4, fxg7 in positions 2/15/9), saving an endangered piece (Bd6/Be5 in position 10), defending vulnerable pawns (Rd7 in position 13), advancing a time-sensitive passed pawn (h4 in position 8), or maintaining structural tension (e4 in position 3, cxb5 in position 5). The common thread in 10/10 positions is that the played move gives the opponent a free tempo to neutralize the position's decisive factor—whether that's closing a pawn structure, capturing an undefended piece, activating a queen invasion, or starting a king march.
analysis.move_pattern: Varied: pawn advances (often 1-2 squares forward or diagonal captures), piece retreats, or king moves to non-critical squares—all sharing the property of being non-forcing and failing to interact with the position's critical element
analysis.why_bad: These moves waste the critical tempo needed to exploit the position's key factor, allowing the opponent to equalize by solving their primary problem (stabilizing their king, capturing an undefended piece, blockading a pawn, or activating dormant pieces) while the player addresses something secondary or irreversible.
sub_patterns: Premature pawn advance releasing critical tension (h6, c5, c5, d5)
Wrong capture priority—taking peripheral pawn instead of critical piece/pawn (gxh5, gxf5)
Passive piece/king repositioning when concrete forcing action needed (Be3, Nb2, Kc3, Kd8)

analysis.label: King (or piece) retreats or moves passively in an endgame when aggressive forward king activation is urgently required to maintain tempo in a race.
analysis.description: This feature fires on endgame positions where the player makes a retreating or passive move—overwhelmingly a king retreat—when the position demands immediate forward king activation to race for promotion, maintain opposition, or generate counterplay. In 9/11 positions the move is a king move that goes backward or laterally instead of advancing (Kd2 instead of Kf4, Kd3 instead of Kd5, Ke2 instead of active bishop moves, Kf1 instead of Kh3, Ke4 instead of Ke5). The remaining cases involve a piece retreating to a vulnerable square (Bc8, 1/11) or a passive pawn push when the king should activate (a6, 1/11). The tagged tactical motif is 'tempo_loss' in 9/11 positions. The catastrophic cases (positions 1, 5, 13 with cp_loss >9000) show how a single retreating move can convert a survivable position into forced mate by falling one crucial tempo behind in a pawn race or exposing pieces to tactical sequences.
analysis.move_pattern: King retreats one square toward the back rank or away from the critical theater of action (e.g., e3→d2, d4→d3, g2→f1, e3→e2, f4→e4 instead of e5); occasionally a piece retreat to a passive/vulnerable square
analysis.why_bad: In endgames, king activity is paramount—every tempo matters in promotion races, opposition battles, and pawn escort duties. Retreating the king loses a critical tempo, allowing the opponent's king to centralize, passed pawns to advance unchallenged, or tactical vulnerabilities to emerge on the retreat square/file. The single lost tempo often proves decisive in converting marginal positions into forced wins.
sub_patterns: King retreats one rank when it should advance toward a passed pawn to escort or blockade
King retreats away from kingside pawns that need physical blockading
King moves to same file/diagonal as own piece creating tactical vulnerability (skewer/hanging piece)
Passive pawn push wastes tempo when immediate king centralization is required
King doesn't advance far enough forward (e.g., one square short of optimal)

analysis.label: Choosing a natural-looking but non-forcing move when the position demands immediate decisive action, allowing the opponent to consolidate or counterplay.
analysis.description: In 7/7 positions, the played move looks purposeful (advancing a pawn, centralizing a king, preparing an attack, grabbing material) but critically wastes a tempo when the position demands an immediate forcing continuation. In 5/7 positions, the best move was a more direct forcing action (Rf7+ sacrifice, Qh3+ check, b4 pawn race, Kh6 infiltration, Nf6 attacking). In 4/7 cases, the tempo loss allows the opponent to blockade or consolidate (g7+ allows ...Kf7 blockade, Rf3 allows ...g6, g5 allows ...Kg7 blockade, Ke3 allows ...Kxh4 + counterplay). In 3/7 cases, a king move to a seemingly logical square actually exposes it to tactical exploitation (Kd6 to Rd1+ pin, Ke3 to Nc4+ fork, Kf6 abandoning blockade). The pattern represents choosing 'general principle' moves over concrete, position-specific demands.
analysis.move_pattern: Any piece type; moves that appear active or aggressive but are one tempo too slow compared to an available forcing alternative (check, capture, or immediate pawn race)
analysis.why_bad: The wasted tempo allows the opponent to consolidate defenses, establish blockades, escape to safety, or launch counterplay that neutralizes or reverses the position's demands - the position required immediate concrete action, not preparation or gradual improvement.
sub_patterns: Preparatory move when immediate check/sacrifice wins (Rf3 instead of Qh3+, g7+ instead of Rf7+)
Premature pawn advance before king infiltration enables blockade (g5 before Kh6)
King centralization when pawn race urgency demands immediate push (Ke3 instead of b4)
King walks to exposed square on open file/abandons critical post (Kd6, Kf6)
Greedy capture putting piece on vulnerable square with no safe retreat (Qxg2)

analysis.label: Playing a slow or positional move instead of a decisive knight fork that wins material (typically the exchange).
analysis.description: In all 10/10 positions, the strongest available move was a knight fork winning significant material—usually forking two rooks or a queen and rook to win the exchange. The missed forks include: Nc3 (fork Q+R), Ng5→Nd7 (fork Q+R), Nc6 (fork R+R), Nxb2 (fork Q+R), Nxc6 (fork R+R), Nd3 (fork R+R), Nf2 (fork R+R), Nxf7 (fork R+R), Nb3 (fork Q+R), and Nf7 (fork R+R). Instead of executing these decisive tactical blows, the player chose superficially reasonable but non-forcing alternatives: quiet development (Bg4, Ba6), piece rerouting to passive squares (Na4, Na2, Nc5, Nc6), slow pawn moves (a4, c5), a prophylactic rook move (Rac1), or the wrong capture (Nxe4 instead of Nxf7). The average cp_loss of 311 reflects that these knight forks were typically the only path to maintaining a winning or significantly better position.
analysis.move_pattern: Any non-forcing move (piece development, pawn push, quiet rook lift, wrong capture) played instead of a knight jump to a square forking two major pieces
analysis.why_bad: The played moves waste a critical tempo on a non-forcing idea while a concrete knight fork is available that wins the exchange or more; once the tempo is lost, the opponent reorganizes and the fork opportunity disappears permanently.
sub_patterns: Knight to rim instead of fork (Na4, Na2, Nc6)
Bishop development instead of knight fork (Bg4, Ba6)
Slow pawn move instead of knight fork (a4, c5)
Wrong piece captures instead of fork (Nxe4 vs Nxf7)
Quiet rook move instead of knight fork (Rac1)

analysis.label: Moving a key piece to a distant or peripheral square pursuing a secondary objective while the king desperately needs immediate defensive support.
analysis.description: In all 5 positions, the player moves a piece away from the zone where king safety is critically threatened, toward a peripheral or distant square to pursue material or counterplay. In 5/5 cases, king_safety is the primary tactical motif exploited by the refutation. Qb2 abandons kingside defense for queenside counterplay against f2 (position 3). Re3 addresses the f3 pawn but leaves the g-file fatally unguarded (position 4). Kh6 advances the king into a rank-alignment trap (position 5). Ka3 moves the king toward the a-file for a pawn while the opponent's king invades the kingside (position 8). Rxa7 captures a distant pawn while the king on g3 is exposed to diagonal checks (position 13). In 4/5 cases, the piece moves explicitly toward the a/b-file area or to a square far from the king, and the refutation immediately exploits the absence of defensive coverage with checks, discovered attacks, or mating patterns. The average cp_loss of 2501 reflects the catastrophic nature of neglecting king safety at critical moments.
analysis.move_pattern: Any piece type moving toward a peripheral file (a/b) or distant square, away from the player's exposed king, often capturing or targeting material
analysis.why_bad: The move removes a critical defender or piece from the king's vicinity, allowing the opponent to exploit the exposed king with checks, lateral attacks, or mating combinations that the displaced piece can no longer prevent or interrupt
sub_patterns: Queen retreating to queenside while kingside is under attack
Rook capturing distant pawn while king is exposed to diagonal/file attacks
King wandering to wing while central/kingside defense collapses
Piece addressing secondary threat while primary king-safety threat is lethal

analysis.label: Playing a slow, preparatory, or prematurely committing move in a razor-sharp position that demands immediate concrete action, gifting the opponent a decisive tempo.
analysis.description: This feature fires on moves that waste a critical tempo in positions with extremely narrow margins (average only 1.8 good moves available). The pattern manifests predominantly in endgames (10/13) where a single tempo often determines the outcome. The blundered moves include premature pawn advances that create fixed targets or allow the opponent to lock the structure (h4 allowing ...h5 lockout, a4 allowing ...a5 freeze, g5 abandoning e5 control, f4 creating an attackable target - at least 8/13 positions), passive king/piece moves when urgent action was needed (Kd7 instead of ...e4, Kc2 instead of b5, Rfb1 instead of f3 - 3/13), and a routine developing move ignoring a tactical opportunity (O-O instead of ...c4 - 1/13). In every case, the correct move involved either an immediate pawn breakthrough (f3/e4, b4, c4), a restraining advance (a4 to prevent ...b5), or urgent counterplay creation. The blunder gave the opponent precisely the one tempo needed to either lock pawns favorably, activate their king, or launch an unstoppable plan.
analysis.move_pattern: Quiet pawn advances (especially flank pawns h4/a4/g3/g5/h5/f4/b3), passive king moves (Kd7/Kc2), or piece retreats/repositioning in positions requiring immediate forcing action
analysis.why_bad: These moves waste an irreplaceable tempo in positions where timing is everything—allowing the opponent to either permanently lock the pawn structure (making the player's majority useless), seize a critical square or breakthrough, or activate their king/pieces to a dominating position one move before the player can execute their own plan.
sub_patterns: Premature pawn advance that gets locked by opponent's reply (h4/h5, a4/a5)
Wrong pawn advance order abandoning key square control (g5 before f6, a4 before b4)
Preparatory pawn move instead of immediate breakthrough (g3 instead of f3/e4)
Passive king/piece move when urgent pawn action needed (Kc2 instead of b5, Kd7 instead of e4)
Routine developing move missing concrete tactical shot (O-O instead of c4/Bxe3+)

analysis.label: Playing a superficially reasonable move that fatally ignores the position's single most critical tactical demand, resulting in catastrophic tempo loss.
analysis.description: This feature fires on positions where very few good moves exist (avg 1.7) and the player chooses a 'natural-looking' move that addresses a secondary concern while missing the one critical tactical priority. The evidence shows: leaving a piece hanging by ignoring a knight capture (1/7), playing a flashy check instead of quiet mate-in-one (1/7), making a passive development move while allowing a devastating fork sequence (1/7), advancing a pawn that can be recaptured with tempo (1/7), capturing an irrelevant pawn while a passed pawn promotes (1/7), walking the king into a mating net instead of staying on safe squares (1/7), and retreating the king for safety while leaving a bishop completely undefended (1/7). In all 7/7 cases, the move grants the opponent a decisive tempo to execute their primary threat. The tag 'tempo_loss' appears in all 7 positions, and 'missed_tactic' in 6/7, confirming the pattern of wasting the critical tempo in razor-sharp positions.
analysis.move_pattern: Any piece type or direction; the common geometric thread is that the move goes AWAY from or ignores the critical square/threat rather than engaging it directly
analysis.why_bad: The move addresses a secondary positional or tactical concern (king safety, pawn capture, piece repositioning, giving check) while the position demands engaging with one specific critical threat - this grants the opponent the decisive tempo to execute their winning plan (promotion, mating attack, piece capture, fork)
sub_patterns: King retreats for safety while leaving pieces hanging
Capturing irrelevant material while a passed pawn promotes
Playing a check when a quiet move wins immediately
Passive piece moves ignoring tactical vulnerabilities
Pawn advances that lose material to tempo-gaining recaptures
King walks toward danger instead of maintaining defensive posture

analysis.label: Moves that fatally ignore or worsen back-rank mating vulnerabilities by removing defensive coverage or walking the king into a corridor.
analysis.description: In 9/10 positions, the blundering move either removes the last piece defending against a back-rank mate or places the king on a square where opponent rooks deliver corridor checkmate. The most common sub-pattern (6/10: Rd4, Rc2, Rg5, Rc2, Re2, and implicitly b3) involves moving a rook away from the file or rank where it could interpose against a back-rank check, typically to a 'more active' square (second rank, fifth rank) that pursues illusory counterplay. The second sub-pattern (3/10: Kd8, Kc1, Kf8) involves the king stepping to a square where opponent rooks already control all adjacent ranks, creating an instant mating box. In nearly all cases, the opponent has two coordinated rooks—one sealing the 7th rank as a 'lid' and one delivering the fatal check on the 8th rank. The average cp_loss of ~7700 reflects that most activations convert playable (though often losing) positions into immediate or near-immediate forced checkmate.
analysis.move_pattern: Any piece (rook, king, or pawn) moves away from back-rank defense—rooks leave the critical file/rank, kings step to squares boxed in by opponent rooks, or pawns waste the last available tempo
analysis.why_bad: The move removes the sole remaining back-rank defender (or places the king on a fatally sealed rank), enabling opponent's coordinated rooks to deliver corridor/back-rank checkmate—typically one rook seals the 7th rank while the other checks on the 8th
sub_patterns: Rook moves laterally to an active square (2nd or 5th rank) abandoning interposition duty on the back rank
King steps to a square where both adjacent ranks are controlled by opponent rooks (corridor mate)
Quiet pawn move wastes critical tempo while opponent has immediate back-rank threats

analysis.label: A natural-looking improving move (developing, centralizing, or capturing) that ignores the position's single most critical concrete demand, allowing the opponent to consolidate or create a tactical refutation.
analysis.description: This feature fires on moves that appear reasonable on the surface—centralizing a piece, gaining space, or capturing material—but fatally miss the one concrete action the position demands. In 6/9 cases, the player had a specific tactical or strategic priority (winning material via Rxa6, exploiting an exposed king via Nxf7, defending f4 with a bishop move, evacuating the queen from an exposed file) but instead played a 'general improvement' move. The positions typically offer very few good alternatives (avg 2.0 good moves), meaning precision was essential. The blundered moves include piece centralizations (Bd4, Bd2), queen repositioning to seemingly active squares (Qc7, Qh4), space-gaining pawn pushes (d4, f6), king moves toward perceived targets (Ka3, Ke2), and greedy material captures (Qxb5). In every case, the move looks like it follows sound general principles but fails to address the position's critical vulnerability or opportunity, resulting in an average loss of 308 centipawns.
analysis.move_pattern: Mixed piece types (Queen 4/9, Bishop 2/9, King 2/9, Pawn 1/9) moving to squares that appear active or purposeful but don't address the position's primary tactical demand
analysis.why_bad: The moves prioritize a secondary objective (general piece improvement, material gain, space) while the position has one urgent concrete need—either a tactical shot to execute, a critical piece to reposition defensively, or a specific threat to address. The wasted tempo or newly created vulnerability gives the opponent time to neutralize the advantage or launch a devastating counterattack.
sub_patterns: Queen moves to 'active' squares that create no real threats while abandoning defensive duties (Qc7, Qh4, Qxb5)
Piece development/centralization that blocks critical lines or allows tactical refutation (Bd2, Bd4)
King/pawn moves pursuing peripheral goals while the critical sector is elsewhere (Ka3, Ke2, d4, f6)

analysis.label: Moving a piece to a seemingly safe but passive square when exactly one engaging/confrontational move was needed to address the critical tactical obligation.
analysis.description: This feature fires on positions where the player makes a retreating, consolidating, or misdirected move that abandons the most critical sector of the board, when the position demanded direct engagement with an immediate tactical obligation. In 6/8 positions, the move is a retreat or passive repositioning (Qg8, Qg1, Kg8, Ke7, Nd8, Kd6) to a back-rank or seemingly safe square. In 2/8, the move ignores a hanging piece or creates a fatal weakness (Rd3 leaves Ra8 hanging, g3 weakens the king). The best moves consistently required confrontation: capturing a hanging piece (Kxf7 in position 9), active centralization (Qd2 in position 5, Qxc3 in position 3), staying near the critical threat zone (Kf6 in position 15, Kf7 in position 7), or evacuating the actually endangered piece (Re8 in position 13, Kh1 in position 2). These positions average only 1.5 good moves, indicating the player faced a narrow critical decision and chose avoidance over engagement.
analysis.move_pattern: Piece moves to passive/back-rank square or retreats away from the critical sector; often king retreats, queen retreats to g1/g8, or wrong piece moves while another is left en prise
analysis.why_bad: By avoiding direct engagement with the position's critical tactical element (a hanging piece, an invasion square, or proximity to threats), the player cedes tempo and allows the opponent to exploit the abandoned sector—capturing hanging material, invading with checks, or advancing pawns unopposed.
sub_patterns: King retreats instead of capturing an en prise piece
King moves in wrong direction away from critical pawn mass or threat
Queen retreats to passive back-rank square instead of active centralization or capture
Wrong piece moves while the actually threatened piece remains hanging
Defensive pawn push that weakens own king when king evacuation was needed

analysis.label: Advancing king/pieces forward or making passive moves in open-file rook positions when king safety or piece coordination demands retreat/flexibility.
analysis.description: This feature fires on moves that ignore critical tactical requirements in positions dominated by rooks on open files. The most severe sub-pattern involves king advances into mating nets (Kf5, Kf4, Kg4 - 3/6 positions), where the king walks forward into squares surrounded by enemy pawns and rook coverage. The remaining moves (b6, Ra1, Rf5) share the same fundamental error: prioritizing a 'logical-looking' improvement while ignoring the dynamic threats posed by active rooks. In 5/6 positions, the player's king is explicitly noted as exposed, yet the chosen move either advances toward greater danger or neglects the king's vulnerability. All 6 positions feature rooks on open files as the primary tactical element, and all refutations exploit the open-file dynamics (rook checks, rook invasions to the 2nd/6th/7th rank, or mating nets using rook + pawn coordination). The average cp_loss of 3325 is heavily skewed by two immediate mates, but even the smaller errors (30-255cp) follow the same principle of misjudging urgency.
analysis.move_pattern: Piece advances (especially king forward one rank toward center/enemy territory) or committal rook/pawn moves in positions with rooks on open files and exposed kings
analysis.why_bad: The moves ignore the tactical danger created by rooks on open files combined with exposed kings - either walking the king into a mating cage formed by pawns and rook coverage, or surrendering critical tempo/activity that allows the opponent's rook to exploit open lines for invasion, checks, or material gain.
sub_patterns: King advances forward into pawn-enclosed mating nets (Kf5, Kg4, Kf4)
Passive rook placement surrendering open-file control (Ra1)
Slow pawn moves ignoring exposed king and active enemy rook (b6)
Premature piece commitment giving opponent redeployment tempo (Rf5)

analysis.label: Playing an active-looking positional/pressure move (often to the 7th rank) instead of simply capturing an undefended hanging piece.
analysis.description: In all 3/3 positions, the player chose an aggressive-looking move targeting the 7th rank or creating pins, while completely overlooking a trivially available capture of an undefended piece. Position 1: Rc7 (7th rank penetration) missed Qxd4+ capturing a hanging bishop with check. Position 10: Qe2 (creating a pin on f3) missed Qxb3 capturing an undefended queen. Position 11: Qc7 (7th rank pressure) missed Qxf5+ capturing an undefended queen with check. The common thread is tactical blindness to hanging pieces, caused by fixation on 'active' piece placement and indirect pressure rather than direct material gain. The moves played all look purposeful and aggressive but ignore the most basic tactical principle: take free pieces.
analysis.move_pattern: Queen or rook moved to an active/aggressive square (often 7th rank or creating pins) while a simple capture of an undefended piece existed elsewhere
analysis.why_bad: The player prioritizes impressive-looking positional pressure (7th rank penetration, pins) over simple captures of hanging pieces, suffering tactical blindness to undefended material that could be taken immediately—often with check.
sub_patterns: 7th-rank rook/queen penetration ignoring hanging piece
Creating pins instead of taking free material
Positional pressure move when capture-with-check available

analysis.label: Quiet preparatory or repositioning moves played in positions that demand immediate concrete action to address a critical tactical vulnerability.
analysis.description: This feature fires on positions where the player makes a non-forcing move (development, pawn push, piece repositioning) while ignoring the single most urgent demand of the position. In 11/12 cases, the move addresses a secondary concern—fianchetto preparation (b6 in positions 6, 8), prophylaxis (h3 in position 13, f6 in position 10), expansion (c4 in position 11, h4 in position 12), repositioning (Bc8 in position 9, Bg3 in position 7), or premature aggression (Qf3 in position 3, Nb4 in position 4)—while leaving a piece hanging, abandoning a critical defensive duty, or failing to resolve central tension. The positions average only 1.5 good moves available, indicating razor-sharp moments where only one concrete response maintains the position. In every case, the correct move involved immediate material interaction: capturing a central pawn (dxe5, exd5, Nxe3, Qxd5, fxe5), challenging a key piece directly, or resolving critical tension. The blunders universally occur because the player prioritizes their own plan over the position's objective demands.
analysis.move_pattern: Quiet non-forcing moves (no checks, no captures, no direct threats): piece repositioning, pawn pushes to secondary flanks, or development moves that abandon a defensive task
analysis.why_bad: These moves waste a critical tempo in positions where the opponent can immediately exploit an undefended piece, open diagonal, or unresolved central tension—the position demands one specific concrete action and any preparatory move allows the opponent to seize a decisive advantage
sub_patterns: Removing a defender from its post (Bd7 abandons b7, Nb4 abandons c6 diagonal)
Slow flank pawn moves ignoring central crisis (b6, h3, h4, c4)
Placing pieces on attacked/capturable squares (Nf3 to bishop-attacked square, Bg3 to rook-captured square, Bc8 undefended)
Weakening king position with unnecessary pawn moves (f6, h4)

analysis.label: Playing slow, positionally-motivated repositioning moves in positions that demand immediate forcing action to maintain a winning advantage or avoid disaster.
analysis.description: In 8/8 positions, the played move is a non-capturing, non-forcing 'improvement' move (piece repositioning, centralization, prophylaxis, or wrong-angle check) when the position demanded an urgent, concrete continuation—typically a capture, a critical pawn advance, or a precisely-aimed forcing move. The best moves were captures (dxc5, Rxe5, dxc4) in 3/8 cases, urgent pawn advances (e6, f5) in 2/8 cases, a king evacuation (Kf7) in 1/8, a precise check direction (Qd8+) in 1/8, and a consolidating pawn move (b5) in 1/8. In all cases the played move looks 'reasonable' by positional standards—centralizing a knight to d5/d6, repositioning a rook to the 7th rank, placing a bishop on an active diagonal—but squanders a narrow tactical window (avg 1.2 good moves available). The average loss of 3700cp reflects that many of these positions convert winning/drawn evaluations into forced mates against the player.
analysis.move_pattern: Non-capturing quiet moves (piece relocations, pawn pushes to non-critical squares, wrong-direction checks) rather than captures or precisely-aimed forcing continuations
analysis.why_bad: Each move wastes a critical tempo in positions with extreme urgency—pawn races about to be lost, mating threats about to be delivered, hanging material about to be defended, or tactical windows about to close. The opponent uses the gifted tempo to consolidate, escape a mating net, promote a pawn, or activate pieces for decisive counterplay.
sub_patterns: Knight centralization ignoring immediate mating threats (Nd6, Nd5)
Rook repositioning abandoning winning formations or pawn advances (Ra7, Rf1)
Prophylactic pawn moves when concrete tactics win (a6)
Bishop relocation leaving key pawns/squares undefended (Ba3)
King move in pawn race when pawn push was critical (Kd6)
Check on wrong square allowing defensive interposition (Qe6+)

analysis.label: King moves to rank 1 or 8 in pawn promotion endgames, losing critical tempo, flexibility, or self-trapping near the promotion square.
analysis.description: In 12/14 positions, the king retreats to the absolute back rank (rank 1 or rank 8) during a passed-pawn endgame where the key pawn is on the 7th rank or near promotion. This back-rank retreat consistently fails because it either: blocks the pawn's own promotion square (positions 8, 12, 14 — costing 129-9331cp), traps the king in a corner shuttle pattern allowing the opponent free tempi (positions 1, 4, 9, 11), or abandons a theoretical drawing zone by leaving the correct fortress squares (positions 5, 7 — converting draws into forced mates). The remaining two non-king moves follow the same structural logic: Rd2 (position 10) traps the king on e1 enabling Qg1#, and Bc5 (position 15) wastes the tempo needed for Kc7 to support promotion. In every case, the correct alternative kept the king on an interior rank (2nd-7th) maintaining mobility, avoiding self-obstruction, or preserving stalemate resources.
analysis.move_pattern: King moves to rank 1 (g1/f1/b1/c1) or rank 8 (g8/c8/b8/a8) — always retreating to the board's edge in positions with advanced passed pawns
analysis.why_bad: Back-rank king placement in promotion endgames creates self-obstruction (blocking promotion squares), confinement (corner trapping allows opponent's king to approach freely), or abandonment of defensive fortresses (leaving stalemate zones), all costing critical tempo that the opponent exploits to promote, deliver mate, or win the pawn race.
sub_patterns: King occupies own pawn's promotion square, requiring extra tempo to unblock
King retreats to corner creating predictable check-shuttle while opponent's king approaches
King leaves theoretical drawing zone (h-file stalemate fortress) for exposed f/e-file squares
Self-obstruction of escape square enabling back-rank mate

analysis.label: Avoiding a favorable queen exchange or capture that would decisively convert an advantage, opting instead for a seemingly active but ultimately passive or vulnerable piece placement.
analysis.description: In 3/4 positions, the best move was a queen exchange or capture (Qxd2+ in Position 1, Qxd5 in Position 8, Qxe5 in Position 14) that would have converted a structural, material, or positional advantage into a winning simplified position. In the 4th case (Rb1), the correct approach was to first challenge/simplify the opponent's active piece (Ned2 attacking the bishop) before committing to the file. Instead, all four moves played were 'developing' or 'active-looking' placements (Qc7, Qf4, Rb1, Qd2) that maintained or increased complexity when the position demanded simplification. The common result: the opponent gains tempo or counterplay against the misplaced piece (knight activation hitting Qf4, bishop diagonal exploiting Rb1, ...g5 hitting the knight after Qd2), transforming advantages averaging +134 into positions averaging +74 for the opponent.
analysis.move_pattern: Queen (or major piece) moves to a neutral/seemingly active square instead of capturing or exchanging on the critical contested square where pieces directly confront each other
analysis.why_bad: By avoiding the winning exchange, the player leaves their piece on a tactically vulnerable square where the opponent gains tempo through attacks, while simultaneously forfeiting the structural or material advantage that simplification would have locked in permanently.
sub_patterns: Queen retreats to passive square avoiding direct capture (Qd2, Qc7)
Queen repositions to active-looking but exposed square instead of trading (Qf4)
Premature rook activation without first neutralizing opponent's active piece (Rb1)

analysis.label: Ambitious-looking piece moves that leave own material undefended, allowing simple captures or forks.
analysis.description: This feature fires when a player makes a move that appears to improve piece activity or development but fatally ignores a material vulnerability. In 5/8 positions, the moved piece (or a piece it was coordinating with) becomes directly hanging after the move (Ng3 leaves rook on a8 undefended, Nc3 puts knight on undefended square, Ng6 abandons defense of bishop on d4, Qg6 leaves bishop on f4 unguardable via fork, Nc4 leaves the outpost and becomes targetable with tempo). In 2/8 positions the move blocks or traps a friendly piece (Qd7 blocks bishop retreat allowing d5 to win it). In 1/8 positions (Nf6) the player develops naturally while missing a tactical capture exploiting opponent's loose pieces. The positions typically have very few good alternatives (avg 1.4), meaning precision is required, yet the player opts for a 'natural' or 'ambitious' move instead of addressing the concrete tactical obligation.
analysis.move_pattern: Mostly knight moves (5/8) or queen moves (2/8) to seemingly active squares, typically moving a piece that was defending another piece or moving to an unprotected square
analysis.why_bad: The moves prioritize piece activity, development, or attack over immediate material safety, leaving a piece (either the moved piece or one it was guarding) undefended and capturable by the opponent through simple takes or short tactical sequences (forks, removal of defender)
sub_patterns: Knight moves away from defense leaving piece hanging (Ng3, Ng6)
Knight moves to undefended invasion square and gets captured (Nc3, Nc4)
Queen/piece move allows fork winning undefended piece (Qg6, b3)
Queen self-blocks friendly piece creating trap (Qd7)
Development move misses capture of opponent's loose pieces (Nf6)

analysis.label: Quiet, non-forcing repositioning moves played in positions that demand immediate concrete action (tactical strikes, critical defenses, or urgent pawn locks).
analysis.description: This feature fires on moves that are passive, non-forcing piece or pawn repositions chosen in positions where the clock is ticking on a concrete opportunity or threat. In 6/6 positions, the played move is neither a check nor a capture—it's a 'quiet improvement' move (Nb5, Rc2, Qc2, Bd1, Rf8, d3) that ignores an immediate tactical necessity. In positions 2 and 3, a clear material-winning tactic existed (capturing an undefended pawn or executing a tactical combination like Bxb6/Nxd6), but the player chose a repositioning move instead. In positions 9 and 12, the move abandoned a critical defensive function (the queen guarding the bishop in position 9, the rook defending the bishop in position 12), leaving pieces hanging. In positions 11 and 14, urgent pawn actions or prophylactic moves were needed to prevent the opponent from seizing initiative through pawn breaks or tempo-gaining development. All 6/6 moves share the common thread of wasting a critical tempo on a non-threatening maneuver.
analysis.move_pattern: Any piece type moving to a passive/neutral square without creating a direct threat—no checks, no captures, no attacks on hanging pieces. Typically lateral repositioning (Rc2, Qc2), retreats (Bd1), or non-urgent advances (d3, Nb5, Rf8).
analysis.why_bad: These moves squander a critical tempo in positions where the opponent can immediately exploit the lost time—either by defending a previously winning tactic, executing a pawn break that was previously harmless, or capitalizing on a piece left undefended when its guardian was redeployed.
sub_patterns: Repositioning a piece away from a winning tactical continuation (missing concrete material gain)
Moving a defender away from a critical defensive assignment, leaving pieces hanging
Playing a slow preparatory move when an urgent pawn fix or prophylactic is required to prevent opponent's breakthrough

analysis.chip: Critical Tempo Wasted on Secondary Goals
analysis.label: Playing a plausible but non-urgent move that wastes a critical tempo when the position demands immediate attention to the primary strategic/tactical priority.
analysis.description: In all 4/4 positions, the player makes a reasonable-looking move that addresses a secondary concern while ignoring the single most urgent demand of the position. In Position 1, dxc6 grabs material while the king remains fatally exposed on the e-file (should be Be2 + castle). In Position 8, g6 tinkers with pawn structure instead of the immediately decisive Ke4 king centralization. In Position 9, Kd3 retreats the king away from the critical d5 blockade square, allowing White's passed pawn to advance freely. In Position 15, Qc2 repositions the queen before activating the stranded a2-rook (Raf2), giving Black a free tempo to organize a lethal rook battery. The tag 'tempo_loss' appears in 4/4 positions, and 'piece_activity' in 3/4. In each case, only 1-2 good moves existed (avg 1.5), meaning positions were relatively demanding with one clear priority that was ignored.
analysis.move_pattern: Quiet, non-forcing moves (pawn captures/pushes, king retreats, queen repositioning) that fail to address the critical sector or activate the key piece
analysis.why_bad: Each move wastes a tempo on a secondary objective while the opponent gains time to execute their primary plan—whether that's exploiting an exposed king, advancing a passed pawn, or organizing a mating attack. The position had one urgent task and the player chose something else.
sub_patterns: Material-greedy capture ignoring king safety
Wrong king direction in endgame (retreat vs. centralize/blockade)
Move-order error: repositioning secondary piece before activating the critical one
Pawn play when king activity is paramount

analysis.label: Playing a non-forcing, seemingly constructive move that wastes a critical tempo in a position demanding immediate concrete action.
analysis.description: This feature fires on moves that appear purposeful (developing a piece, pushing a pawn, repositioning) but catastrophically ignore the most urgent tactical demand of the position. In 11/11 positions, the player chose a slow 'improving' move when the position screamed for immediate concrete action—whether capturing a hanging piece (Rxf1 instead of Qxd7, Position 13), executing a forcing combination (Rf6 instead of Bxg6, Position 1), defending against mate (Nc3 ignoring Qf3+/Rh1#, Position 6), maintaining attack coordination (d4 allowing f5 winning the knight, Position 8), or addressing critical defensive needs (Qc6 abandoning kingside defense against doubled h-file rooks, Position 10). The 'tempo_loss' tag appears in all analyzed positions. The average cp_loss of 2050 reflects that these positions were tactically critical (avg 1.8 good moves available), and the wasted tempo is immediately and severely punished.
analysis.move_pattern: Any piece type, any direction; characteristically NON-capturing and non-checking moves in positions where a forcing move (capture, check, or critical defensive move) was required
analysis.why_bad: The position has one urgent tactical demand (a threat to parry, a piece to capture, an attack to maintain, a combination to execute) and the move played addresses a secondary concern instead, giving the opponent a critical tempo to execute their threat, activate a piece, or neutralize the player's advantage.
sub_patterns: Developing/repositioning a piece while ignoring immediate mating threats
Positional pawn push that releases critical tension or abandons piece coordination
Moving a piece away from its essential defensive role
Capturing the wrong target when a bigger prize hangs
Passive king move when active piece play is demanded

analysis.label: Playing a slow positional/repositioning move that ignores an urgent tactical requirement—either a hanging piece, a fork threat, or an immediate capturing opportunity.
analysis.description: In all 8 positions, the player makes a non-forcing, non-capturing 'developing' or repositioning move to a seemingly logical square while the position demands immediate tactical action. In 3/8 cases the player ignores their own vulnerable/undefended piece (Na5 abandons the f3-bishop to Nxf3; c5 ignores the Bg5-Ne7-Rd8 alignment allowing Bxe7/Bxd8; Bb2 leaves Ne2 hanging to Qh5+/Qxe2). In 2/8 cases the player misses a free capture of opponent's material (Qc7 ignores the hanging d4-pawn; Bf4 when Ba6/Nxb2 won material). In 2/8 cases the player moves to a square allowing a devastating fork (Kc3 allows Nb5+ winning d4; Bf4 enables Nc4-b6 fork). In 1/8 cases a passive king move (Kh8) wastes a critical tempo allowing a breakthrough. The average cp_loss of 293 reflects how severely these 'do-nothing' moves are punished when concrete threats exist. Typically only 1-2 good moves were available (avg 1.8), indicating positions where precision was mandatory.
analysis.move_pattern: Non-forcing, non-capturing piece repositioning or development move to a 'reasonable-looking' square; no checks, no captures, no direct threats
analysis.why_bad: The position contains an urgent tactical element (a hanging piece, an undefended piece, a fork vulnerability, or a forcing capture) that requires immediate concrete action; the quiet move wastes a critical tempo, allowing the opponent to execute or consolidate against the tactical vulnerability that should have been addressed first.
sub_patterns: Leaving own piece undefended while making a different 'developing' move (Bb2/Na5/c5)
Missing an immediate free capture in favor of repositioning (Qc7/Bf4)
Moving to a square that creates a new tactical vulnerability like a fork (Kc3/Bf4)
Passive king move wasting tempo when active counterplay was essential (Kh8)
Removing a key defender from its post to a seemingly better square (Nd4 from f3)

analysis.label: Moving a piece or pawn away from an essential defensive function, creating an immediately exploitable tactical vulnerability.
analysis.description: This feature fires on moves that remove a piece or pawn from a critical defensive role—whether blocking a passed pawn, shielding the king on a diagonal, or covering a back rank—to pursue seemingly active play. In 3/6 positions, the move specifically opens a line toward the player's own king (fxe5 opens e1-h4 diagonal, e5 opens a2-g8 diagonal, Ka5 exposes the king to Qb5#). In 2/6 positions, the move removes a blockader or key defender enabling an immediate tactical blow (Nxc4 removes the e5 knight blocking a passed pawn, Bd2 creates structural collapse on c3). In 1/6 positions, the move ignores an immediate back-rank threat for irrelevant flank play (h5). All moves share the characteristic of looking natural or active on the surface—captures, pawn pushes, development—while catastrophically neglecting the position's primary defensive requirement. The extremely high average cp_loss (1771) and low number of good alternatives (2.2) confirm these are critical positions where one specific defensive duty dominates all other considerations.
analysis.move_pattern: Piece or pawn moves away from a square where it performs an essential shielding/blocking/covering function; captures and pawn advances predominate (4/6 are captures or pawn pushes)
