analysis.why_bad: Removes the one element (blockading piece, shielding pawn, defensive post) that was preventing the opponent from executing a decisive tactical blow along a newly opened line, diagonal, or square—typically enabling passed pawn promotion, king-targeting checks, or mating attacks.
sub_patterns: Pawn advance removing diagonal shield from own king (e5, fxe5)
Knight capture abandoning blockade of advanced passed pawn (Nxc4)
King move walking into undefended square/mating net (Ka5)
Ignoring immediate back-rank/tactical threat for flank play (h5)
Pseudo-defensive move that creates structural collapse (Bd2)

analysis.label: Moves that pursue a secondary objective while overlooking the opponent's immediate tactical exploitation of an abandoned defensive duty or newly created vulnerability.
analysis.description: This feature fires on moves where the player prioritizes their own plan (centralization, checking, passed pawn creation, flank expansion) while failing to account for the opponent's strongest forcing response. In 4/7 positions, the move directly leaves a piece undefended or abandons a critical defensive function: Qa7 abandons defense of the e7-bishop (Position 14), Bf3 ignores the knight attacking the d1 rook (Position 4), Bg5+ places the bishop where it's captured by the queen (Position 5), and Ne4 places the knight where it's captured by the b7-bishop enabling simplification (Position 1). In the remaining positions, the move wastes a critical tempo: a5 pushes a flank pawn when development is urgently needed (Position 9), Rb1 abandons 7th-rank activity allowing king infiltration (Position 8), and dxc3 trades structural dominance for a blockadable passed pawn (Position 2). The consistent thread across all 7 positions is 'hope chess'—playing what looks good without verifying the opponent's concrete response. The tag 'tempo_loss' appears in 6/7 positions and 'piece_activity' in 6/7, confirming the pattern of wasting time while degrading piece coordination.
analysis.move_pattern: Any piece type moving to a plausible-looking square while leaving another piece undefended, abandoning a critical defensive assignment, or ignoring an urgent positional demand
analysis.why_bad: The opponent has a simple forcing response (capture of a hanging piece, exploitation of an abandoned square, or decisive infiltration) that the player failed to check before committing to their plan
sub_patterns: Piece repositioned while another piece left en prise (Bf3, Qa7, Bg5+)
Piece centralized on capturable square enabling unwanted simplification (Ne4)
Active piece retreated to passive square losing critical activity (Rb1)
Non-developing flank move when piece coordination is urgently needed (a5, dxc3)

analysis.label: Playing seemingly logical repositioning or improving moves that waste a critical tempo when the position demands immediate, concrete action.
analysis.description: This feature fires on positions where the player chose a quiet, indirect, or 'improving' move instead of the most urgent concrete action the position demanded. In 7/9 positions, the analyses explicitly tag 'tempo_loss' as a key factor. The positions typically involve time-critical elements—passed pawns needing immediate advancement or blockade (6/9 positions involve passed pawn dynamics), or tactical shots requiring immediate execution (Nf1 missing Nxe5, Nd5 allowing a fork). The moves look reasonable on the surface—advancing a pawn (b2, e5), centralizing a king (Kd3, Ke7), repositioning a knight to a seemingly strong square (Nc5, Nc2, Nd5, Nf1), or retreating a queen (Qc8)—but all sacrifice the one tempo needed to execute the position's most critical plan. The correct moves across positions share the quality of directness: immediate pawn advances (a4), direct piece placement on optimal squares (Ne2 instead of Nc2, Bf6 instead of Ke7), or concrete tactical strikes (Nxe5).
analysis.move_pattern: Quiet piece repositioning (especially knights 4/9) or non-forcing advances to seemingly logical squares, without capturing or checking
analysis.why_bad: The position contains a time-critical demand (passed pawn race, blockade requirement, hanging piece, or forcing sequence) that punishes any loss of tempo. The chosen move follows a reasonable-looking plan but arrives one move too late, allowing the opponent to execute their threat first or neutralize the player's advantage.
sub_patterns: Knight rerouting through intermediate square instead of direct placement (Nf1, Nc2)
Abandoning a restraining/blockading post for a seemingly active square (Nc5 leaving b3)
Passive king support instead of active piece play (Ke7 instead of Bf6)
Premature/misguided pawn advance when piece action needed (e5 instead of rook blockade)
Piece retreat leaving key pawn undefended (Qc8 abandoning d5)

analysis.label: Natural-looking moves that pursue secondary goals (captures, development, repositioning) while ignoring the position's most urgent tactical or structural requirement.
analysis.description: This feature fires on moves that appear reasonable in isolation but miss a critical positional demand. In 2/7 cases, pawn captures on f5 remove a structurally important pawn—one opens lines against an uncastled king (Position 1), the other eliminates a pawn guarding a critical diagonal/square enabling perpetual check (Position 8). In 3/7 cases, the queen is placed on or moves to a square where it becomes tactically exploitable: Qc7 creates a target for Nb5 with tempo (Position 3), Qd2 allows a forced unfavorable queen exchange via Qf4+ (Position 9), and Qxg4 puts the queen on a knight-defended square (Position 12). In 2/7 cases, knight moves to natural-looking squares create catastrophic consequences: Ndf3 blocks the h4-knight's only retreat, trapping it after ...g5 (Position 14), and Nf6 develops while ignoring that the queen on d5 is hanging to Nxd5 (Position 15). The common thread is a player making a 'default' or 'tempting' move rather than addressing the single most critical demand of the position.
analysis.move_pattern: Mixed piece types moving to seemingly natural or productive squares (captures, central squares, development squares) that are actually tactically compromised or leave a critical vulnerability unaddressed
analysis.why_bad: Each move prioritizes a secondary goal (material gain, development, repositioning) over the position's most urgent need, and the resulting vulnerability is immediately exploitable—whether through piece trapping, forced unfavorable exchanges, opened lines against the king, or simple captures of hanging pieces.
sub_patterns: Pawn captures that remove defensive structure (exf5 opening lines/diagonals)
Queen placed on square exploitable by tempo-gaining piece jumps (Qc7→Nb5, Qd2→Qf4+)
Queen moving to a defended square (Qxg4 captured by knight)
Knight blocking own piece's retreat (Ndf3 trapping Nh4)
Developing while a major piece hangs (Nf6 ignoring queen attacked)

analysis.label: Playing a natural-looking or routine developing move in a critical position that demands one specific concrete response, surrendering decisive tempo to the opponent.
analysis.description: This feature activates on positions where a player makes a move that follows general chess principles (develop a piece, castle, place a rook on the 7th rank, fianchetto) but catastrophically ignores the single most urgent demand of the position. In 7/8 cases, the position had only 1-2 good moves available, indicating a critical juncture requiring precision. The played moves all appear reasonable in a generic sense—Re7 aims for classic 7th-rank pressure, Qh4 looks aggressive, b6 prepares a fianchetto, O-O-O seeks king safety, Na6 heads toward c5, Nf6 develops naturally—but each ignores a specific concrete threat or opportunity (Rc5+ creating an unstoppable passed pawn, attacking the vulnerable e5 rook, preventing d5-d6, staying centralized against a rook, avoiding the open d-file, capturing a free pawn, routing via d7 to avoid Bxa6, preventing e5 tempo gain). The average cp_loss of 1410 reflects that these 'autopilot' decisions allow the opponent to execute devastating plans unopposed.
analysis.move_pattern: Diverse piece types moving to natural/thematic-looking squares (7th rank, development squares, castling, flanks) rather than the single critical square demanded by the position
analysis.why_bad: Each move surrenders a critical tempo in a position with extremely narrow margins (avg 1.5 good moves), allowing the opponent to execute a specific devastating plan—typically a forcing pawn advance (d6, e5), a capture with structural damage (Bxa6), a tempo-gaining attack (Rh5), or a mating construction—that the correct move would have prevented or preempted.
sub_patterns: Natural development walking into a tempo-gaining pawn push (Nf6 into e5, b6 allowing d6)
King moving to wrong side/edge instead of addressing the concrete threat (Ka6 toward rim, Kd1 wrong direction, O-O-O into open file)
Piece placement following general principle over specific calculation (Re7 seventh-rank cliché over Rc5+ forcing line, Qh4 aggression over Bd4 attacking the vulnerable piece)
Knight routing via rim instead of safe central path (Na6 allowing Bxa6 vs Nd7)

analysis.label: Non-forcing moves (king moves, pawn pushes, passive retreats) played in positions with extremely narrow margins where only 1-2 good moves exist, wasting the critical tempo needed to address an urgent tactical vulnerability.
analysis.description: This feature fires on positions where the player makes a quiet, non-forcing move—typically a king move (Kh2, Kb8, Kf2, Ka6, O-O in 5/11 cases), a pawn advance (g6, g5, g4, a3 in 4/11 cases), or a passive piece retreat (Bd5, Ne2 in 2/11 cases)—in a position that demands immediate concrete action. The defining characteristic is the extremely narrow margin: the average number of good moves available is only 1.5, meaning most positions had just one acceptable continuation. The played moves are all non-checking, non-capturing, and non-threatening, yet the positions contain latent tactical vulnerabilities (hanging pieces in 4/11, exposed king geometries in 5/11, critical passed pawns in 2/11) that the opponent exploits with the gifted tempo. The resulting punishments are devastating (avg cp_loss of 1973), ranging from simple piece captures (Qxd5, Qxf2, Rxd5, Qxd6+) to forced checkmates (positions 2 and 13) to complete positional collapse. The common thread is that one precise move would have maintained the position, but the player defaulted to a 'natural-looking' quiet move that catastrophically failed to address the concrete demands of the position.
analysis.move_pattern: Quiet non-forcing moves: king relocations (5/11), pawn advances (4/11), or passive piece retreats (2/11)—never checks, captures, or direct threats
analysis.why_bad: Each move wastes a critical tempo in a position with only 1-2 acceptable continuations, allowing the opponent to exploit a specific latent vulnerability (undefended piece, geometric alignment, passed pawn breakthrough, mating net) that the one correct move would have addressed or prevented.
sub_patterns: King moves that abandon defense of a piece or walk onto a vulnerable geometry (Kh2, Kb8, Kf2, Ka6, O-O)
Slow pawn advances that ignore concrete tactical needs or create targets (g6, g5, g4, a3)
Passive piece retreats that surrender initiative when aggressive play was required (Ne2, Bd5)

analysis.label: Non-forcing moves played in critical positions where the wasted tempo allows the opponent to execute a decisive tactical or strategic plan.
analysis.description: This feature fires on positions where the player makes a quiet, non-forcing move (repositioning, peripheral pawn push, or natural development) when the position urgently demands immediate active play. In 6/9 cases the tactical motif is explicitly 'tempo_loss' - the move creates no threat and allows the opponent to seize the initiative. In 3/9 cases (Kh7, Ke3, d5) the move additionally walks into a concrete tactical vulnerability (knight fork or material loss). The common thread across all positions is that good alternatives existed (avg 2.1 good moves) involving active, threatening play - aggressive queen deployment (positions 1, 9, 10), immediate threat creation (position 4), addressing tactical motifs (positions 3, 6, 12), or solid development (position 7). Instead, the played moves address secondary concerns (rook development in position 3, king prophylaxis in positions 6/12, pawn expansion in positions 2/10) while the primary tactical/strategic demand goes unmet for one critical tempo.
analysis.move_pattern: Quiet non-forcing moves (retreats, pawn pushes, piece repositioning to intermediate squares) - no checks, no captures, no direct threats to opponent's key pieces
analysis.why_bad: The wasted tempo gives the opponent time to execute their primary plan: advancing passed pawns (positions 1, 4, 10), activating knight forks (positions 3, 6, 12), capturing undefended material (positions 4, 7), or forcing unfavorable exchanges (position 9). The position's sharpness means one tempo is the difference between maintaining advantage and losing it.
sub_patterns: Passive queen retreat when kingside attack demands aggressive queen deployment
Peripheral pawn push (h4, h5) ignoring central/piece-based urgency
King move walking into knight fork square
Natural development (Rad1) ignoring imminent tactical threat
Bishop/piece to intermediate square losing tempo for immediate threat creation

analysis.label: A knight advances aggressively to an unsupported square where it is immediately challenged and trapped or driven back by a simple pawn advance.
analysis.description: In all 11 positions, a knight makes an aggressive forward jump to an attacking square (g4, e5, b4, b5, g5, e4, h5, d4) without adequate pawn or piece support, and is immediately punished by a one-square pawn advance that challenges it (h3 in 4/11, a3/a6 in 2/11, c3/d3/f6/g4 in 5/11). The knight invariably has no safe retreat: either it is outright trapped and lost (6/11 positions tagged 'trapped_piece'), or it must retreat to its starting square having wasted two full tempi while the opponent gains central space or wins hanging pawns (5/11 tagged primarily 'tempo_loss'). These occur overwhelmingly in the opening (10/11) when development is incomplete, meaning the wasted tempi are especially costly. The average cp_loss of 235 reflects that these moves frequently lose the equivalent of a full piece or more in practical value.
analysis.move_pattern: Knight advances forward (typically 2 squares) to an aggressive/attacking square lacking pawn support, usually toward the opponent's side of the board
analysis.why_bad: The knight lands on a square where a simple one-move pawn advance (h3, a3, c3, d3, g4, f6) challenges it with no safe retreat available, resulting in the knight being trapped, losing critical tempi returning to its original square, or abandoning key defensive duties
sub_patterns: Ng4 challenged by h3 with no retreat (f6 controlled or occupied)
Knight to b4/b5 challenged by a3/a6 forcing retreat to rim (a6/a3)
Knight to central outpost (e4/e5/d4) challenged by adjacent pawn (d3/c3/f6)
Knight to rim (h5/g5) trapped by g4/h6 pawn advance
Knight abandons defensive duty of key pawn to attack, allowing capture of undefended pawn

analysis.label: Moves that remove a piece or pawn from an essential defensive role, leaving a critical square, rank, or piece immediately exploitable.
analysis.description: This feature activates on moves where a player relocates a piece or pawn that was performing a vital (often hidden) defensive function, creating an immediate tactical vulnerability. In 8/10 positions, the moved piece was the sole defender of a critical square or piece: b3 removed the b-pawn's defense of c3 enabling a knight fork; dxc6 removed d7's coverage of e6 enabling knight invasion; dxc3 left the queen on d1 undefended after Bxf2+; Rff8 and Rg8 both abandoned rooks from defending the 7th rank or back rank enabling immediate invasion; Nc5 moved the knight away leaving the h5-bishop hanging to Nxe5/Qxh5; f3 weakened the king's diagonal enabling a discovered check; and Kxe4 placed the king on a promotion-check diagonal. The moves typically look active or natural (attacking something, capturing material, challenging a file) but fatally ignore their piece's current defensive responsibility.
analysis.move_pattern: Any piece type moving away from a square where it was defending a critical point - often pawn pushes (b3, f3, d6, dxc6, dxc3), rook repositions (Rff8, Rg8), or knight jumps (Nc5, Nd5) that abandon guardianship of adjacent squares/pieces
analysis.why_bad: The move prioritizes an active-looking plan (attacking an enemy piece, grabbing material, contesting a file, centralizing) while being blind to the piece's current essential defensive function, allowing the opponent to immediately exploit the newly undefended target with tactics (forks, invasions, sacrificial combinations, discovered attacks).
sub_patterns: Pawn push that unguards an adjacent square allowing piece invasion or fork
Rook leaving a rank/file that was the sole barrier to enemy invasion
Knight relocating while leaving a piece tactically hanging
Pawn capture that removes structural defense of queen or key square
King moving to a square creating fatal alignment with promotion/check

analysis.label: Endgame moves that advance king or pawn in the wrong direction or without proper preparation, when a more patient or differently-directed move was critical.
analysis.description: This feature fires on endgame positions where the player makes an intuitive-looking advancing move (king march or pawn push) that is either misdirected or premature. In 5/8 positions, the king moves to the wrong square—typically away from the flank requiring defense (Positions 2, 8: Kd1 instead of Kf1 abandoning kingside pawn defense; Position 5: Kg7 instead of Kf8 losing tempo toward center; Position 14: Kc4 walking into a rank-skewer). In 3/8 positions, a passed pawn is pushed prematurely without coordination (Position 4: b2 before placing rook behind it; Position 9: c7 before rook redeployment to 7th rank; Position 12: b6 before c4 creates connected passers). The unifying thread is that the move appears logical and progressive—advancing the most advanced pawn or marching the king forward—but neglects a critical preparatory requirement that only becomes apparent through precise calculation. All positions have very few good alternatives (avg 2.2), making these narrow decision points where the 'obvious' move fails.
analysis.move_pattern: King or pawn advances forward/toward the wrong flank in endgames, typically one square moves that seem natural but go the wrong direction or commit too early
analysis.why_bad: The moves neglect a critical defensive or preparatory requirement: king moves abandon the flank where a pawn needs protection or walk into tactical alignments, while pawn advances commit before coordination (rook placement, supporting pawn, or piece activity) makes them effective—allowing the opponent to exploit the premature commitment with counterattacks, skewers, or pawn races.
sub_patterns: King retreating/moving toward wrong flank away from critical pawn defense (Kd1 instead of Kf1)
Premature passed pawn push before rook is optimally placed behind it
Pawn advance without supporting structure (b6 before c4 creates isolated target)
King advancing into geometric alignment with own piece (Kc4 allowing rank-skewer)

analysis.label: Playing a superficially reasonable but tempo-losing move in a razor-thin position where only one concrete action (capture, king march, or piece activation) maintains the advantage.
analysis.description: This feature fires on positions with extremely narrow winning margins (avg 1.2 good moves available) where the player wastes a decisive tempo on a 'natural-looking' move instead of the ONE required concrete action. In 5/8 positions the tagged tactical motif is explicitly 'tempo_loss.' The pattern manifests as: king shuffles instead of piece activation (Kb2 × 2 when Bg2 wins immediately, 2/8), king moves to wrong square allowing opponent tempo-gaining checks/advances (Ke6 allowing f5+, 1/8), passive piece repositioning when aggressive king advance is needed (Re8 instead of Kd4, 1/8), premature pawn advances ignoring concrete captures (f5 missing Nxe5, h2+ missing king march, 2/8), and abandoning critical defensive duties for 'active' piece placement (Qxb2 abandoning e5 control, Nd3 abandoning c3 control, 2/8). All positions share exposed kings and high tactical tension where one precise move resolves everything but the chosen move gives the opponent time to consolidate, blockade, or launch a counterattack.
analysis.move_pattern: Mixed piece types (king moves, piece repositioning, pawn advances, captures) that all share the quality of being one tempo too slow - choosing a visually logical but non-forcing move over the single concrete winning continuation
analysis.why_bad: These moves waste the critical tempo in positions where the margin is razor-thin (only ~1 good move exists), allowing the opponent to either find shelter for their exposed king, establish a blockade, launch a counterattack with checks, or consolidate a previously untenable position. The concrete winning move always involves immediate tactical action (capturing material, advancing the king into a mating net, or activating a piece decisively) that the played move delays by exactly one fatal tempo.
sub_patterns: King shuffle instead of decisive piece activation (Kb2 instead of Bg2)
King walks into opponent's tempo-gaining pawn advances or checks (Ke6 into f5+)
Passive rook/piece repositioning when aggressive king advance wins (Re8 instead of Kd4)
Premature pawn advance missing concrete capture (f5 missing Nxe5, h2+ missing king march)
Abandoning critical square control for material/activity (Qxb2 leaving e5 unguarded, Nd3 leaving c3 unguarded)

analysis.label: Capturing a piece (usually a bishop) that isn't escaping, when a more urgent tactical move should be played first.
analysis.description: In all 10/10 positions, the player captures an enemy piece that is already en prise and 'not going anywhere' — it could safely be taken on a subsequent move. In 9/10 cases, the captured piece is specifically a bishop that has infiltrated deep into the player's position (Bxf3 capturing Bf3, Bxf8 capturing Bf8, bxc3 capturing Bc3, Nxc6 capturing Bc6, bxc6 capturing Bc6, cxb3 capturing Bb3, Qxd7 capturing Bd7, gxf3 capturing Bf3, Qxe2 capturing Be2, axb6 capturing Bb6). In every case, a stronger intermediate move exists — typically a different capture, a check, a pin exploitation, or a pawn advance — that should be played FIRST because it creates a tactical threat, exploits a vulnerability, or generates a tempo advantage that will not be available after the 'obvious' recapture. The analyses consistently identify move-order errors (tagged in 6/10 positions) where the urgency hierarchy of captures was misjudged. Average cp_loss of 1172 reflects how catastrophic this reflexive capture habit can be.
analysis.move_pattern: Any piece or pawn capturing an enemy piece (predominantly bishops) that has infiltrated into one's own position and is currently static/undefended with no escape route
analysis.why_bad: The captured piece wasn't escaping, so taking it immediately wastes a critical tempo. A more urgent tactical move (zwischenzug, different capture order, pin exploitation, or interposing move) should precede this capture, after which the static piece can still be collected.
sub_patterns: Recapturing intruder bishop before playing forcing intermediate move
Taking hanging piece with wrong piece/pawn when check-first wins more
Capturing obvious target before exploiting pin or fork opportunity
Removing nuisance piece reflexively instead of recognizing it as trapped

analysis.label: Natural-looking moves played at critical junctures where only 1-2 specific continuations maintain the evaluation, resulting in massive cp loss.
analysis.description: This feature fires on positions where the player chooses a superficially reasonable move—a developing move, a 'logical' check, a space-gaining pawn push—but the position actually demands one precise concrete continuation. The average number of good moves available is only 1.5, indicating razor-thin margins. In 3/11 cases, the mistake is a purposeless or premature check (Qe4+, Qc5+, Bb3+) that helps the opponent's king find safety or disrupts a winning sequence. In 3/11 cases, it's a pawn push (c6, d4, h4) that ignores immediate tactical requirements or weakens the position. In 5/11 cases, it's a piece move to a 'natural' square (Rh4, Qe2, Bf5, Bd3, Kd1) that abandons a dominant position or misses a concrete winning opportunity like a capture or forcing pawn break. The correct moves are often counterintuitive (h3+, g3+, g4!, Qg3 offering a queen trade, Qxb7 grabbing material) while the played moves follow general chess principles rather than calculating the specific demands of the position.
analysis.move_pattern: Various piece types moved to seemingly logical squares; often checks, developing moves, or pawn advances that appear active but lack concrete forcing value
analysis.why_bad: The position demands one specific concrete action (a forcing pawn break, a precise capture, a queen trade, or a correctly-ordered forcing sequence) but the player substitutes a generic 'good-looking' move based on general principles, ignoring that only 1-2 continuations maintain the evaluation in these critical moments
sub_patterns: Premature or purposeless checks that help opponent's king escape (Qe4+, Qc5+, Bb3+)
Passive developing moves that miss concrete wins like hanging pawns (Qe2 missing Qxb7, Bd3 missing g4!)
Pawn advances that weaken defensive structure or ignore immediate threats (h4 removing g4 defense, d4 opening fatal diagonal, c6 clearing fork square)

analysis.label: Non-forcing moves that waste a crucial tempo in positions demanding immediate concrete action, ignoring the position's most urgent tactical or defensive requirement.
analysis.description: This feature fires on positions where the player makes a quiet, non-forcing move that appears reasonable (active-looking piece placement or 'safe' king repositioning) but catastrophically wastes tempo in a position with very narrow requirements (avg 1.8 good moves available). In 6/8 cases, the move ignores an urgent tactical demand: abandoning a critical defensive post (Bd3 leaves e2 unguarded for Bxf3 recapture; Nd4 leaves c6 unguarding a6), making passive king moves instead of active ones (Kf8 instead of Kd8 which wins a piece; Kh8 instead of Ra7 addressing dual vulnerabilities), or placing pieces on unstable squares where they're immediately challenged (Ng4 gets chased by h5; Ng6 gets forced into an unfavorable exchange). In 7/8 cases the analyses tag 'tempo_loss' and 'piece_activity' as key factors. The average cp_loss of 318 reflects how these positions are at critical junctures where one wrong tempo decisively shifts the evaluation.
analysis.move_pattern: Quiet, non-forcing moves (no checks, no captures) - typically piece or king moves to squares that appear active or safe but don't address the position's concrete demands
analysis.why_bad: These moves waste an irreplaceable tempo in positions with narrow tactical paths, allowing the opponent to execute threats (pawn attacks chasing pieces, exploiting abandoned defensive duties, seizing open files/diagonals) that would have been preventable with the correct concrete response
sub_patterns: Piece moved to exposed square immediately challenged by pawns or forced into retreat (Ng4, Ng6)
Passive king move instead of active king move that wins material or addresses threats (Kf8 x2, Kh8)
Piece abandons critical defensive post for apparently active placement (Bd3, Nd4)
Rook/piece placed on vulnerable square creating tactical targets (Rd5)

analysis.label: Choosing an indirect, preparatory, or passive move in a critical position where one specific immediate concrete action was required to maintain the evaluation.
analysis.description: This feature fires on moves where the player selects a 'reasonable-looking' but fatally slow or indirect continuation in a position that demands precise, immediate action. In 7/9 positions, the best move involved an urgent concrete step (immediate king activation in endgames like Ke5/Kd3, immediate captures like Rxh6/Rxb7/Rxc3, or specific check directions like Qh4+), but the player instead chose a preparatory, repositioning, or peripheral move that squanders the critical tempo. The positions share extremely narrow margins (avg 1.7 good moves available), meaning timing is everything. Whether it's repositioning a bishop when the king must march immediately (Bc8, Bb5), grabbing a peripheral pawn while ignoring the opponent's most active piece (Nxf7), doubling rooks instead of capturing now (Rdh1), retreating passively instead of creating threats (Qf1), or walking the king instead of capturing the decisive pawn (Ke3), the pattern is consistent: the indirect move would be fine with one extra tempo, but the position doesn't grant it.
analysis.move_pattern: Mixed piece types and directions; typically quiet non-forcing moves (repositioning, preparation, peripheral captures) when the position required a specific forcing move (direct capture, correct check direction, or urgent king march)
analysis.why_bad: The position has a narrow window requiring one specific immediate action; the chosen indirect move gives the opponent a free tempo to execute their counterplan (activate pieces, advance passed pawns, neutralize the attack, or force favorable trades), permanently collapsing the advantage.
sub_patterns: Piece repositioning instead of urgent king activation in endgames (Bc8, Bb5, Ke3)
Slow buildup/preparation instead of immediate capture or strike (Rdh1, Qf1)
Peripheral pawn grab abandoning critical piece coordination (Nxf7)
Wrong recapture creating indefensible structural weakness (bxc3)
Check on wrong geometric line allowing devastating interposition (Qe4+)
Aggressive pawn advance ignoring developmental urgency (g5)

analysis.label: Playing a non-urgent structural or material move when the position demands immediate dynamic/forcing action, wasting a critical tempo.
analysis.description: This feature activates when a player makes a move that addresses a secondary concern (resolving pawn tension, retreating a piece, advancing a passed pawn, grabbing material) while ignoring the primary urgent demand of the position. In 4/5 positions, the move is explicitly tagged as 'tempo_loss' — the player spends a tempo on something non-critical, allowing the opponent to solve their main problem. In Position 1, White recaptures cxd4 instead of launching a decisive kingside attack with Rg1. In Position 4, Black retreats Bg6 instead of capturing a free hanging piece on b1. In Position 5, White plays Qc3 (creating overload vulnerability) instead of addressing the bishop's tactical exposure on b2. In Position 12, Black grabs a pawn with Nxe5 but removes a crucial defensive piece from c6. In Position 15, Black pushes b3 into the rook's path instead of centralizing the king. All 5/5 moves are non-forcing (no checks, no immediate threats), and all allow the opponent to resolve their critical weakness on the very next move.
analysis.move_pattern: Non-forcing moves (captures of non-critical material, piece retreats, quiet pawn pushes) that fail to address the position's primary tactical or dynamic demand
analysis.why_bad: The moves waste a critical tempo on a secondary concern, allowing the opponent to consolidate, escape danger, or develop a key piece — squandering dynamic advantages that required immediate concrete action to exploit
sub_patterns: Structural recapture instead of attacking (cxd4)
Piece retreat instead of capturing hanging material (Bg6)
Pawn grab that removes a key defensive piece (Nxe5)
Premature pawn advance instead of king centralization (b3)
Queen centralization creating tactical overload (Qc3)

analysis.label: Natural-looking piece improvement moves played when the position demands addressing an immediate concrete tactical threat or vulnerability.
analysis.description: This feature fires on positions where a player makes a quiet, seemingly reasonable improving move (developing, centralizing, or repositioning a piece) while ignoring an urgent tactical requirement. In 8/11 cases, the move places a piece on a square where it is immediately capturable or tactically exploitable (Be3 hung to Nxe3, Ng4 captured by Bxg4, Ne5 undermined by c5/Bxe5, Ba1 trapped, Nd5 allowed Nxd6). In 3/11 cases, the move ignores a specific opponent threat that required immediate attention (a3 ignored Nxc4 winning e4 pawn + Ng3+ fork, Be4 ignored Na4-Nb6+ fork, Bh6 abandoned defensive fianchetto). The positions characteristically have very few good moves available (avg 1.5), meaning they demand precision over general improvement. The moves all share the quality of being non-forcing (no checks, only 1 capture) in positions where concrete calculation was essential. The average cp_loss of 251 reflects the severe punishment for prioritizing vague positional goals over immediate tactical necessity.
analysis.move_pattern: Quiet non-forcing piece moves (primarily minor pieces and king) to seemingly natural squares; no checks, rarely captures, typically centralization or development moves
analysis.why_bad: The position demands addressing a specific concrete threat or tactical vulnerability, but the player makes a general-purpose improving move instead, allowing the opponent to execute an immediate tactical blow (capture, fork, pin, or exploitation of an abandoned defensive square)
sub_patterns: Piece moves to a square directly attacked by opponent's piece (Be3, Ng4, Ne5)
Slow pawn/king moves ignoring opponent's imminent tactical combination (a3, Kg1, fxg5)
Bishop abandoning critical defensive diagonal/fianchetto (Bh6, Ba1)
Piece improvement ignoring opponent's knight fork maneuver (Be4, Nd5)

analysis.label: Playing a non-forcing piece repositioning move when the position demands an immediate concrete action such as a capture, trade, or forcing tactical blow.
analysis.description: In all 8/8 positions, the player chose a quiet, non-capturing, non-checking piece move that repositioned a piece to a seemingly useful square, while ignoring a critical tactical demand that required an immediate concrete action. The best moves were consistently forcing: captures (Qxd5 in Position 1, Bxa6 in Position 7), queen trades or challenges (Qe1 in Position 3, Qe7 in Position 4, Qf7 in Position 6, Qc3 in Position 12), or forcing rook activations (Rae1 in Position 8). In 7/8 cases, only 1-2 good moves existed, indicating positions with razor-thin margins where general 'improvement' moves are catastrophically wrong. The average cp_loss of 301 reflects how these aesthetically reasonable but concretely flawed moves squander decisive advantages or collapse tenable defenses. The blunders variously allow hanging pieces to be captured (Position 5: Bb7 leaves Nc3 hanging), expose kings to forcing sequences (Positions 3, 4, 6: removing defenders or walking into attacks), self-interfere with piece coordination (Position 12: Ke4 blocks queen's retreat), or chase opponent pieces to superior squares (Position 7: Ba4 drives queen to c3).
analysis.move_pattern: Non-capturing, non-checking piece moves (knights, bishops, or kings) repositioning to apparently useful squares; no specific geometric direction but universally quiet/non-forcing
analysis.why_bad: The position has one specific concrete demand (a capture, trade, or forcing move) that must be addressed immediately; the quiet repositioning ignores this urgency, allowing the opponent to exploit the unaddressed tactical vulnerability with a forcing response
sub_patterns: Bishop repositioning while own piece is hanging or key square abandoned (Be1, Bb7, Ba4)
King advancing/retreating when a queen trade or queen challenge was essential (Kd6, Kd8, Ke4)
Knight move for activity ignoring material capture or forcing rook activation (Nf4, Nc1)

analysis.label: Natural-looking repositioning moves that waste a critical tempo by leaving a pawn or square undefended against an immediate tactical exploitation.
analysis.description: In all 5 positions, the player makes a move that appears positionally reasonable (centralizing a knight, developing a rook, advancing a pawn for space, or repositioning the king) but fatally ignores an immediate concrete vulnerability—typically an undefended pawn. In 5/5 cases, the refutation involves directly exploiting the neglected weakness: Rxg7 captures the unguarded g7 pawn (Position 11), Nxc6 wins the now-undefended c6 pawn (Position 3), Nd3-Nxf2 forks exploit the abandoned f2 square (Position 8), Qc4 targets the exposed f7 (Position 9), and queen checks harvest the exposed h4 pawn (Position 1). The best moves in each position instead address the tactical urgency first—castling to defend g7, playing Bc7 to eliminate the threatening rook, placing the knight on f4 covering d3, activating the queen toward e3, or retreating the king behind pawns. The common error is prioritizing 'general improvement' over a specific defensive requirement when the position demands immediate concrete action.
analysis.move_pattern: Diverse piece types (K, N, R, pawn) making repositioning moves away from or unrelated to the critical defensive point, typically moving toward the queenside or center while the vulnerability exists on a specific undefended square
analysis.why_bad: Each move wastes the one tempo needed to defend a concrete tactical vulnerability (usually an undefended pawn), allowing the opponent to immediately exploit with a capture, fork, or decisive attack on the neglected point
sub_patterns: King moving toward exposed squares instead of shelter
Knight/piece abandoning defense of a critical pawn
Slow pawn advance releasing tension when active piece play is required
Rook development ignoring an immediate hanging pawn

analysis.label: Moving the king (or piece) to a square already covered by enemy attacking pieces, creating immediate tactical catastrophe via checks, mates, or captures.
analysis.description: In 3/4 positions, the king moves one square to a tactically fatal destination: Kh3 walks into Qf5+/Qh5+ check sequences leading to forced mate (Position 1), Kc8 walks into Be6+ discovered check winning the queen (Position 4), and Kg4 walks directly into Qh3# immediate checkmate (Position 6). The outlier Ba6 (Position 5) shares the same structural error—placing a piece on a square already controlled by the opponent where it is immediately captured or exploited. All 4 moves place the moved piece on a square where the opponent's existing pieces (especially queens on diagonals) already have lethal influence. The average cp_loss of 4871 reflects that these moves transform defensible positions into immediate tactical disasters. In every case, safer alternatives existed (3/4 positions had 1-3 good moves) that moved the king/piece toward safety rather than toward enemy-controlled squares.
analysis.move_pattern: King (3/4) or bishop moving one square toward the board edge or corner, landing on a square already in the firing line of enemy queen diagonals/files
analysis.why_bad: The destination square is already tactically controlled by enemy pieces (especially queens), enabling immediate forcing sequences (checks, discovered attacks, or checkmate) that the player failed to calculate before committing the move.
sub_patterns: King walks into immediate checkmate (Kg4 → Qh3#)
King walks into check sequence leading to forced mate or queen loss (Kh3 → Qf5+/Rd2+)
King walks into discovered check winning material (Kc8 → Be6+ then Nd3+)
Piece placed on undefended square in enemy's tactical zone (Ba6 → bxa6)

analysis.label: Playing a plausible-looking move that neglects to block or address an open attacking line against the player's exposed king.
analysis.description: This feature fires on positions where the player's king is critically exposed along an open file or diagonal, and the correct move involves shielding/blocking that line (often with a specific piece), but instead the player makes a superficially reasonable move that ignores the defensive priority. In 3/4 positions, the king faces an immediate geometric threat along an open line: Position 1's king on f8 is exposed on the a3-f8 diagonal (Nxe5→Nf7 would shield, but Qxe5 doesn't); Position 4's king on g8 faces a fully open g-file (only Bg7 can block, but Qe7 cannot); Position 3's queenside-castled king is weakened by a6 which enables a Bxa6 sacrifice blowing open the b-file. Position 2 (weakest activation at only 26cp loss) involves failing to neutralize counterplay against the king's zone. The common thread is choosing a move that appears active or purposeful while catastrophically failing to address the primary attacking lane aimed at the king.
analysis.move_pattern: Various piece types (queen captures/moves, pawn pushes) that fail to interpose on or protect a critical file/diagonal targeting the player's king
analysis.why_bad: The moves fail because they leave open attacking lines (files or diagonals) aimed directly at the king unblocked, allowing the opponent to exploit these lanes with checks, sacrifices, or rook lifts that create irresistible mating threats or win decisive material
sub_patterns: Capturing with wrong piece that doesn't shield king (Qxe5 vs Nxe5)
Moving queen for 'defense' when only a bishop/knight can physically block the attacking lane
Weakening pawns near castled king enabling sacrifice to open lines
Premature offensive push ignoring counterplay against own king position

analysis.label: Choosing a passive, retreating, or non-critical move when the position demands immediate active/forcing play to address an urgent tactical or strategic need.
analysis.description: In 7/8 positions, the played move is either a piece retreat to a passive square (Na3, Nb3, Qc1), a purposeless king move (Kg6, Kh7), or a materialistic capture of a secondary target (Rxf5) when the position desperately requires forcing, active play. The best moves in these positions are consistently checks (Rg8+, Rb1+, Nxa4+), active captures that address the root problem (Nxa4), development moves (Qe3, Ne2), or concrete counterplay (cxb4, f3). The positions all share time-critical elements—promotion races (3/8), attacking opportunities against exposed kings (4/8), or development advantages that must be exploited immediately (2/8). The played moves waste the critical tempo that separates a tenable or winning position from a lost one, allowing the opponent to execute their plan (promote, consolidate, launch an attack) unopposed.
analysis.move_pattern: Piece retreats to rim/back-rank squares (Na3, Nb3, Qc1), passive king moves to non-functional squares (Kg6, Kh7), or captures of non-critical material (Rxf5) — all non-forcing moves that fail to interact with the opponent's primary threats.
analysis.why_bad: These moves squander critical tempo in positions where urgent action is required. They address secondary concerns (material, prophylaxis, piece rerouting) while ignoring the position's primary demand—whether stopping a promotion, maintaining a mating attack, or preventing the opponent from consolidating. The opponent then executes their plan uncontested.
sub_patterns: Knight retreating to rim squares (a3/b3) instead of active centralization or capture
King moves creating targets or wasting tempo instead of active counterplay
Capturing secondary pawns while losing a promotion race
Queen retreating to passive squares when piece exchanges or active defense is required
Wrong forcing move (check that can be neutralized) when a superior forcing move exists

analysis.label: Moving a piece to a plausible-looking square instead of making the one urgent forcing move the position demands, losing a decisive tempo.
analysis.description: This feature fires on moves where the player selects a 'reasonable' or 'natural-looking' move that fails to address the position's most urgent priority, resulting in a catastrophic tempo loss in time-critical positions. In 6/7 positions, the analyses explicitly tag 'tempo_loss' as a key factor. The pattern spans king moves to wrong squares (Kf3 instead of pushing e3; Kg8 instead of Kh7; Ka6 instead of Kb6), wrong pawn push order (d3 instead of c3), and pieces abandoning critical defensive posts (Rf4 vacating f3 where it blocked checks; Nh2 removing the knight from f3 where it guarded key squares; Nd7 blocking the king's escape route). In every case, the position contained a razor-sharp timing element—pawn races (3/7), exposed king requiring immediate action (4/7), or forcing sequences that must begin on the exact correct move—and the played move squanders the one tempo that made the difference between winning/drawing and losing.
analysis.move_pattern: Any piece type moving to a plausible square; no consistent geometric direction. Often a quiet/improving move (king repositioning, piece rerouting, non-forcing pawn push) when the position demanded an immediate forcing continuation.
analysis.why_bad: The move addresses a secondary concern (king centralization, piece repositioning, wrong pawn advance) while ignoring the position's primary urgent demand (pushing the correct passed pawn, fleeing to the exact right square, maintaining a critical defender). The lost tempo allows the opponent to seize the initiative through checks, pawn advances to penultimate squares, or exploitation of newly created tactical vulnerabilities.
sub_patterns: King moves to adjacent-but-wrong square in time-critical endgame (Kf3/Kg8/Ka6 vs correct Ke4/Kh7/Kb6)
Piece abandons critical defensive post creating immediate tactical vulnerability (Rf4/Nh2 vacating f3)
Wrong move order in pawn race or forcing sequence (d3 before c3, Nd7 instead of king escape)

analysis.label: Active-looking moves (checks, pawn advances, forward king moves) that squander a critical tempo needed for the position's truly urgent action.
analysis.description: This feature fires on moves that appear aggressive or purposeful but fundamentally waste the one tempo the position demands for something specific. In 5/7 positions, the blunder is a forward pawn advance (c5, f5, e5) or forward piece/king move (Ke3, Bg7+) that looks forcing but misses the critical action. In Position 3, Rc1+ gives pointless checks that escort White's king from a passive back-rank prison to an ideal centralized square (h1→g2→g3→f4). In Position 1, Bg7+ delivers check on a long diagonal that permits interposition (Ne5), when the adjacent Bc5+ couldn't be blocked. In Position 2, c5 advances a pawn when Kf4 was essential to remove the king from a check-vulnerable square. In Position 5, Ke3 moves the king before the prophylactic h4 that prevents Black's connected passers. In Positions 7 and 10, premature pawn pushes (f5, e5) block own tactical resources or weaken the king. The unifying thread across 6/7 positions is that the opponent immediately exploits the gifted tempo for a specific devastating action (creating connected passers, activating a king, delivering Qh4+, capturing with check, or consolidating).
analysis.move_pattern: Forward-moving aggressive actions: pawn advances (typically one or two squares forward on central/kingside files), checks on long diagonals or files that can be blocked/evaded constructively, or king advances that misordering critical pawn moves
analysis.why_bad: The move prioritizes an apparently active continuation over the position's one critical demand, gifting the opponent a tempo to execute a specific tactic or positional transformation (interpose on a check, create connected passers, activate their king through forced checks, exploit a newly-weakened diagonal, or consolidate a vulnerable position)
sub_patterns: Pointless/blockable checks that improve opponent's king or allow interposition (Bg7+, Rc1+)
Premature pawn advances that weaken own position or block own tactics (f5, e5, c5)
Move-order errors where king moves before essential prophylactic pawn advances (Ke3 before h4)

analysis.label: Impatient pawn advances or piece lunges that create structural weaknesses in the player's own position while ignoring the position's actual strategic or tactical demands.
analysis.description: This feature fires on moves that appear aggressive or active but actually damage the player's own position. The dominant pattern is premature pawn advances that weaken the player's king shelter or pawn structure (f4, f6, f5, g4, d5, c3 — 6/10 positions), but it also captures piece moves to exposed squares that abandon critical defensive functions or invite tactical punishment (Ng4 removes a key defender from f6, Rh4/Rh5 move rooks to inferior or tactically vulnerable squares, Qa4+ wastes a tempo on a premature check). In nearly all cases (8/10), the position demanded something fundamentally different: patient prophylaxis (h6 in position 4), piece activation (Be7 in positions 5 and 9), concrete tactical execution (b3+ in position 8, f5 in position 2), or resolving central tension before flank play (dxc5 in position 10, cxb4 in position 3). The average of 2.3 good alternatives confirms these were avoidable errors where superior options existed.
analysis.move_pattern: Pawn advances (especially f-pawn, g-pawn pushes) or piece moves toward the opponent's side that abandon defensive duties; typically one or two squares forward into territory that creates new vulnerabilities
analysis.why_bad: These moves create concrete weaknesses (opened diagonals, undefended pawns, exposed kings, pieces on tactically vulnerable squares) while generating no real threats, giving the opponent time and targets to exploit. The position's actual requirements — whether prophylaxis, piece activation, concrete tactics, or resolving central tension — are left unaddressed.
sub_patterns: Kingside pawn advances weakening own king shelter (f4, f6, f5, g4)
Premature central pawn breaks that leave pieces/pawns tactically loose (d5, c3)
Piece moves to aggressive but exposed squares inviting forks or displacement (Ng4, Rh5)
Premature checks that alert opponent and waste attacking tempo (Qa4+)
Rook retreats from dominant positions to passive squares (Rh4)

analysis.label: Moving a piece to a passive peripheral square (back rank, rim file) when the position demands one precise active/forcing move.
analysis.description: In all 5 positions, the player chose a move that places a piece on a passive square at the board's edge or back rank: Nb6 (rim), Ke8 (back rank), Bxh6 (h-file rim), Rxf1 (back rank), Bb8 (back rank corner). In every case, there was essentially only one good alternative (avg 1.6 good moves), and that alternative was significantly more active or forcing: Ne4 seizing a central outpost (Position 1), Be7 maintaining flexibility (Position 2), a3 advancing the critical passed pawn (Position 3), Qxd7 capturing an undefended piece (Position 4), Bc7 winning material (Position 5). The chosen moves appear reasonable on the surface—they attack something, capture something, or move away from danger—but they all surrender the initiative by misidentifying the position's primary demand. In 5/5 cases the move resulted in the piece being passive or misplaced, enabling the opponent to seize the initiative with tempo-gaining responses (c5 kicking the knight, Rxe6+ exploiting the open file, e7 promoting, Nf6 seizing an outpost, Ne2 invading).
analysis.move_pattern: Any piece type moving to back rank (1st/8th) or rim file (a/h/b), often appearing as a retreat, sideways capture, or edge development
analysis.why_bad: The move addresses a secondary concern while missing the one forcing/active continuation the position requires, resulting in tempo loss and allowing the opponent to seize the initiative with a gaining move that exploits the piece's new passivity
sub_patterns: Back-rank retreat when forward play needed
Rim capture that displaces piece from key diagonal/file
Wrong capture choosing lesser target over hanging piece
Passive bishop retreat when active bishop wins material

analysis.label: Moves that directly capture, check, or advance against opponent's forces when precise piece repositioning or regrouping was required.
analysis.description: This feature fires on positions where the player chooses an 'obvious' engaging move—typically a capture, check, or pawn advance—over a more subtle piece repositioning that the position demanded. In 7/10 positions, the blunder involves a capture or pawn push (exd5, dxe5, Rxd6, Bxd4+, d6, f6, Ne5+), while the best moves overwhelmingly involve piece maneuvers to superior squares: Na5/Ne5 in Position 1, Nh5/Nd5 in Position 2, Rdd8 in Position 4, Nd4+ in Position 6, Nf3 in Position 7, Ng6 in Position 9. The remaining moves (Kb5, Ka6, Rb2) similarly choose an 'active-looking' direction over optimal placement (Kd5, Ka5, g5). In 8/10 cases, the correct move involves repositioning a piece (especially a knight) to a functionally superior square rather than immediately grabbing material or delivering forcing moves. The positions average only 2.2 good moves, indicating high precision demands where the 'natural' looking move is a trap.
analysis.move_pattern: Captures (pawn or piece), checks, or pawn advances directed at opponent's material, typically on central files (d/e) or diagonals, when a repositioning move to a different square was needed
analysis.why_bad: The engaging move either opens lines against the player's own vulnerable king, allows the moved piece to be recaptured with devastating effect, removes a piece from a critical defensive post, or wastes tempo pursuing a secondary goal while the opponent gains decisive positional/tactical advantages through the newly created weaknesses or freed coordination.
sub_patterns: Pawn captures (exd5, dxe5) that open files/diagonals against own uncastled or exposed king
Piece captures/checks (Bxd4+, Rxd6, Ne5+) where the piece is immediately recaptured or enters a losing trade
Pawn advances (d6, f6) that ignore hanging pieces or allow mating constructions
King/piece moves to wrong squares (Kb5, Ka6, Rb2) that lose critical tempo compared to direct approach

analysis.label: Moving a well-placed piece away from its most effective square, forgoing the concrete tactical opportunities that its current position enables.
analysis.description: In 5/5 positions, the played move relocates a piece from a strong square or abandons its current coordination, missing a more concrete tactical blow available from the piece's current placement. In Position 2, the Queen leaves g4 (where it coordinated with Nh6 for the crushing Nxf7) to go to g5 where it's refuted by ...f6. In Position 3, the Rook abandons the dominant d-file to capture on b7, trading itself for pawns and drawing. In Position 6, the Knight goes to the passive d2 instead of the optimal c3 (or the central break cxd5 that exploits existing piece placement). In Position 10, the King moves to d8 prematurely instead of utilizing the h7 pawn's promotion potential from its current setup. In Position 11, the Knight leaves the powerful f5 outpost for d6 where it becomes tactically vulnerable to ...Ke7. In 4/5 cases, the best move was a concrete forcing action (capture, promotion, or break) enabled by the piece's CURRENT position, while the played move instead repositioned a piece, losing the tactical window.
analysis.move_pattern: Piece (any type) moves away from an effective square to a seemingly active but less precise square, often when a tactical capture/promotion was available from the original configuration
analysis.why_bad: The piece's current position enables a specific concrete tactic (capture with tempo, promotion with check, central break), but by moving it elsewhere the player loses that tactical window and gives the opponent time to consolidate or exploit the new piece placement's vulnerabilities
sub_patterns: Knight abandoning outpost for check (Nd6+, moving from f5)
Queen leaving coordination square for aggressive-looking post (Qg5, moving from g4)
Rook trading itself off active file for material (Rxb7+)
Piece retreating passively when concrete break exists (Nd2)

analysis.label: Playing a natural-looking move that pursues a secondary objective while ignoring the position's single most critical and urgent demand.
analysis.description: In 9/9 positions, the player had very few good options (avg 1.9) indicating a critical decision point with a narrow correct path. The blunder in each case was choosing a move that looks purposeful—advancing a passed pawn (d6, Position 1), centralizing a queen (Qe6, Position 3), pushing for space (c4, d4, Positions 7 & 11), activating a king (Kf4, Position 10), relocating a knight aggressively (Ng5, Position 12), or defending a pawn with a piece (Bf4, Position 13)—but which fatally ignores the ONE thing the position demands. In 7/9 cases, the correct move was defensive or prophylactic (securing king safety, defending a pawn, maintaining a piece on its dominant square), yet the player chose an offensive-looking alternative. The average centipawn loss of 1301 reflects how punishing these errors are: the narrow correct path existed, the position was critical, and the 'reasonable-looking' alternative allowed a devastating tactical or strategic punishment.
analysis.move_pattern: Diverse piece types and directions (pawn advances, piece relocations, king moves), all characterized by pursuing a forward/active plan rather than addressing an immediate concrete vulnerability
analysis.why_bad: Each move leaves a specific critical vulnerability unaddressed—an exposed king (Positions 1, 7), an undefended piece (Positions 10, 11), a back-rank weakness (Position 3), an exchangeable defender (Positions 4, 13), a dominant piece abandoned (Position 12), or a tempo wasted when immediate counterplay was required (Position 5)—allowing the opponent a concrete tactical punishment that the 'plan move' completely overlooked.
sub_patterns: Advancing passed pawns before securing king safety
Relocating pieces from dominant squares to pursue peripheral targets
Pushing central pawns that remove key defensive duties
Playing passive moves when one specific counterplay break was essential
Defending with exchangeable pieces instead of structural solutions

analysis.label: Moving a piece to an apparently active square while neglecting the position's most critical concrete demand, resulting in severe tempo loss or tactical vulnerability.
analysis.description: This feature fires on moves that pursue a secondary objective (attacking a pawn, 'centralizing,' gaining space) while ignoring the one urgent action the position demands. In 8/9 positions, the blunder involves a piece moving to a seemingly purposeful square that is actually irrelevant to the critical need: Qc5 abandons support of the f6-knight (Position 2), Qg4 leaves b1 hanging (Position 8), Qc2 misses the decisive Qxf3 capture (Position 6), Nf4 abandons the c3 guard (Position 1), Nf6 removes a king shield allowing mate (Position 3), Qa6 ignores central tension resolution (Position 9). In all cases, the best moves address a concrete, urgent need—capturing a key piece (Qxf3, Rxb7), maintaining a critical defensive post (Rc1, Kg7), resolving dangerous tension (exf5), or completing development (Ng6). The common thread across all 9 positions is that the player chose what 'looks active' over what concretely matters, losing an average of 1405cp. Tags of 'tempo_loss' (8/9) and 'piece_activity' (8/9) confirm the pattern of wasted time on misdirected activity.
analysis.move_pattern: Piece (often queen 4/9, knight 3/9) moves to an apparently active but strategically irrelevant square, typically away from the critical sector of the board
analysis.why_bad: The move ignores the position's single most urgent concrete demand (a forced capture, maintaining a critical defensive guard, resolving dangerous pawn tension, or completing king safety), giving the opponent time to exploit the neglected vulnerability with a decisive tactical or positional blow
sub_patterns: Queen moves to peripheral square ignoring central urgency (Qc5, Qc2, Qg4, Qa6)
Knight moves to 'outpost' abandoning critical defensive duty (Nf4, Nf6)
Passive/premature moves wasting development tempo (Rb8, O-O-O, e5)

analysis.label: Playing seemingly purposeful moves that completely bypass a critical concrete tactical necessity in the position.
analysis.description: This feature fires on positions where a specific, concrete tactical action is urgently required—yet the player makes a move motivated by a vague strategic idea instead. In 5/6 positions, there was a piece that was either hanging, trappable, or capturable through a forcing sequence that the player ignored. Position 5: f4 ignores the need to reposition the h4 knight, creating a fatal e3 weakness exploitable by fork. Position 7: e3 blocks the g5 bishop's only retreat square, trapping it. Position 11: Qa2 misses the forced Nxc8 sequence winning the exchange. Position 12: Rxe3 captures with the wrong piece, missing the superior Nc4 knight fork with check. Position 13: Bd7 ignores the e5 bishop's tactical vulnerability to Rxe5. Position 15: Qg1 overextends the queen where Be3 traps it, instead of first challenging the g5 knight. In all cases, the position demanded addressing a specific piece interaction (a capture, a rescue, a fork), but the player chose a move that appeared active or useful—space-gaining pawn pushes (2/6), passive development (1/6), queen repositioning (2/6), or incorrect capture method (1/6)—while the critical tactical element went unaddressed.
analysis.move_pattern: Various piece types (pawns, queens, bishops, rooks) making non-forcing or misdirected moves when a specific forcing tactical sequence involving a vulnerable piece was available
analysis.why_bad: Each move ignores the position's tactical focal point—a concrete piece vulnerability (hanging, trappable, or forkable)—in favor of a vague strategic idea, allowing the opponent to either exploit the created weakness or escape from a critical threat that should have been resolved immediately.
sub_patterns: Self-weakening pawn advances that create exploitable squares (f4, e3 blocking retreat)
Queen moves to irrelevant or overextended squares ignoring concrete captures (Qa2, Qg1)
Wrong piece captures or passive development when a forcing tactical sequence was available (Rxe3 instead of Nc4, Bd7 instead of Bb8)

analysis.label: Quiet, natural-looking moves that waste a crucial tempo in positions demanding immediate concrete action, allowing the opponent to seize the initiative.
analysis.description: This feature fires on positions where the player chooses a slow, passive, or preparatory move when the position urgently demands forcing, active play. In 5/7 positions, the game is in the endgame phase where every tempo is magnified. The common thread is consistent: correct moves involve immediate piece activity (Rxe5, f5, Rd8, Kh4, Rxg7+, gxh4) while the blunders are quiet pawn pushes (c6, g6, h5 in 3/7), passive retreats (Be7, Rd7 in 2/7), or captures that passivize pieces (Rxh4 in 1/7). In 6/7 cases, the opponent exploits the free tempo to advance passed pawns, deliver rook checks, or seize open files. The analyses repeatedly identify 'tempo_loss' as the primary tactical motif (4/7 explicitly), and 'piece_activity' appears as a tag in all 7 positions. The average of only 1.4 good moves available confirms these are razor-sharp moments where one precise active move is required.
analysis.move_pattern: Mixed piece types; typically non-forcing moves (pawn pushes, piece retreats, or captures to passive squares) that don't create immediate threats or checks
analysis.why_bad: The opponent uses the gifted tempo to execute concrete threats—advancing passed pawns, delivering rook checks on exposed kings, or invading with active pieces—that the slow move failed to preempt or counter
sub_patterns: Unnecessary kingside pawn pushes in rook endgames (g6, h5, c6)
Passive piece retreats abandoning active squares (Be7, Rd7)
Capturing with wrong piece creating passivity (Rxh4)
King walking into tactical vulnerability instead of supporting counterplay (Kf5)

analysis.label: Playing non-capturing repositioning or prophylactic moves in positions where the only good continuation is a concrete capture.
analysis.description: In 5/6 positions with actual mistakes, the best move was a capture (Nxd4, Nxe4, Nxe4, hxg5, Bxh7+) but the player instead chose a non-capturing move — either a prophylactic pawn push (a6 in 2/7 positions), a piece repositioning (Ne5, Qc3, Qe1 in 3/7), or a structural pawn advance with check (f6+ in 1/7). The positions share extremely low counts of good alternatives (avg 1.4), indicating critical moments demanding precise tactical calculation. The played moves all have superficial logic (centralization, prophylaxis, checking) but ignore the concrete tactical requirement. Positions 4 and 5 show an identical sub-pattern: Italian Game structures where 5...Nxe4 wins a pawn but 5...a6 is played instead. Position 6 (0 cp loss) appears to be an outlier where the feature fires on a lost endgame position.
analysis.move_pattern: Non-capturing moves (quiet piece repositioning, flank pawn pushes, or structural pawn advances) played instead of forcing captures on central/kingside squares
analysis.why_bad: The positions demand concrete tactical action — specifically a capture that resolves critical tension, wins material, or forces a necessary exchange. The non-capturing alternatives waste tempo or abandon key defensive duties, allowing the opponent to seize the initiative through central breaks (d4), piece invasions, or unstoppable passed pawns.
sub_patterns: Playing prophylactic a6 instead of tactical Nxe4 in Italian Game positions
Repositioning queen to passive/wrong square instead of forcing capture-sacrifice
Playing flashy check/centralization instead of resolving pawn tension via capture

analysis.label: Moves that address a secondary concern while ignoring the position's single most critical tactical demand, squandering a decisive tempo.
analysis.description: This feature fires on positions where the player makes a purposeful-looking move that addresses a non-urgent goal while the position demands immediate action on one specific critical factor. In 9/11 positions, the move is tagged as 'tempo_loss' — the player spends their turn on something plausible (pawn grab on a4, attacking a knight with h6, defending a pawn with Ra8, aggressive queen centralization with Qg6/Qf5/Qd3) but fails to address the ONE thing the position requires right now. The positions are extremely demanding (avg only 1.4 good moves), meaning there is essentially a single correct priority. Common patterns include: queen moves to aggressive-looking squares that abandon defensive coordination (5/11 are queen moves: Qf5, Qxa4, Qg6, Qd3, Qd2), rook moves that abandon critical defensive posts for peripheral concerns (Ra8, Rc7), pawn pushes that waste tempo in critical races (h5, h6), and captures/retreats that resolve non-urgent tension while allowing the opponent a free tempo for a devastating response (Bxb5, Kd2). The critical ignored demands include: back-rank defense (3/11), pawn promotion races (2/11), hanging material (3/11), and piece coordination maintenance (3/11).
analysis.move_pattern: Any piece type moving to address a secondary goal; often queen moves to aggressive but miscoordinated squares, rook retreats from active posts, or tempo-wasting pawn pushes in sharp positions
analysis.why_bad: The move gives the opponent a free tempo to execute their critical threat — whether that's a back-rank invasion, winning hanging material, completing a promotion race, or launching a decisive attack against an undefended king. The position required the player to address exactly one urgent factor, and they spent their move on something else.
sub_patterns: Queen moves to aggressive squares abandoning defensive duties (Qf5, Qg6, Qd2, Qd3)
Pawn grabs or peripheral captures ignoring king safety (Qxa4, Bxb5)
Rook/piece retreats abandoning critical posts (Ra8, Rc7)
Defensive king moves wasting tempo in pawn races (Kd2)
Pawn pushes that ignore hanging material or wrong move order (h5, h6)

analysis.label: A slow, preparatory, or self-blocking move that ignores or enables a devastating central pawn advance (d5/d4/e5) attacking multiple pieces simultaneously.
analysis.description: In 9/11 positions, the played move allows the opponent to execute a central pawn thrust (d5, d4, or e5) that attacks two or more pieces simultaneously—typically a knight and bishop pair. The mechanism falls into two categories: (1) tempo-wasting moves (f6, g6, Bg7, O-O-O) that fail to prevent an imminent pawn advance that was already the critical threat (positions 1, 2, 4, 6), and (2) self-blocking moves (Qd2, Qe2, Ne7, e6) that obstruct a piece's retreat square, turning the pawn advance from merely annoying into materially decisive because the attacked piece has no escape (positions 3, 5, 8, 10). In position 9 (Be3), the piece voluntarily places itself on the fork square. The refutations consistently feature d5 hitting Nc6+Be6 (positions 1, 2, 4, 13), d4 hitting Nc3+Be3 (positions 3, 6, 9), e4/e5 hitting bishop+knight (positions 5, 8). The remaining 2/11 positions (Kh7, Rb7) share the tempo-loss / abandoning-key-square theme but manifest as endgame inaccuracies rather than central pawn breaks.
analysis.move_pattern: Any piece or pawn move (non-forcing, non-developing or self-obstructing) that leaves two friendly minor pieces aligned on squares attacked by a single opponent pawn advance on the d or e file
analysis.why_bad: The move wastes a critical tempo or blocks a retreat square, allowing the opponent's central pawn advance to simultaneously attack two pieces (typically knight + bishop), winning material through a fork or piece-trapping mechanism that would have been preventable with one correct move.
sub_patterns: Slow kingside prep (f6/g6/Bg7) ignoring imminent d5 attacking Nc6+Be6
Queen blocking bishop retreat (Qd2/Qe2) enabling pawn fork to win trapped piece
Knight/pawn blocking bishop escape (Ne7/e6) enabling e5 or d5 to trap bishop
Piece placed on fork-vulnerable square (Be3/O-O-O) enabling d4 fork of Nc3+Be3

analysis.label: Seemingly reasonable piece placements that catastrophically compromise king safety by enabling forcing sequences (mates, perpetuals, or decisive attacks).
analysis.description: This feature fires on moves that appear natural or centralizing on the surface but fatally expose the player's own king to tactical exploitation. In 5/10 positions, the king itself moves to a square that enables perpetual check or forced mate (Ka6 to the edge enabling R+K mate, Kd2 twice enabling perpetual via Qa2+/Qc4+, Kf6 enabling Qf8+ perpetual, Kc1 enabling back-rank Re1+). In the remaining 5/10 cases, a piece moves to a 'natural' square but either becomes a target in a mating net (Nf6 enables Rh7+/Qxf6/Qg7#), blocks a critical defensive file (Bd6 blocks the rook's d-file pressure), removes defensive coverage from the king (Qd7 removes e7 interposition against e-file checks), loses crucial attacking tempo when the opponent's king is exposed (Qf6 instead of Qh4), or chooses a passive outpost over an immediately threatening one (Nd6 instead of Ne5 with fork). The common denominator across all positions is that the player prioritizes a superficially reasonable positional goal (centralization, development, apparent safety) while ignoring an urgent, concrete king safety vulnerability that the opponent can exploit with forcing moves.
analysis.move_pattern: Piece (often king) moves to a seemingly natural/central square; typically moves toward the center or an 'active' post rather than addressing immediate tactical king safety needs
analysis.why_bad: The moves ignore urgent king safety concerns—enabling perpetual checks (4/10), forced mates (3/10), back-rank tactics (1/10), or decisive tempo gains against the exposed king (2/10)—because the player was drawn to a 'natural-looking' placement instead of calculating the concrete forcing sequences available to the opponent.
sub_patterns: King moves to exposed square enabling perpetual check draw
King moves toward edge/back-rank enabling forced mate
Piece placement on natural square enables mating pattern against own king
Piece blocks own defensive file or removes defensive coverage from king
Passive piece placement loses tempo when immediate tactical threats existed

analysis.label: Promoting a pawn to queen immediately when the promotion square is controlled by an enemy piece, instead of first playing a preparatory move to make the promotion safe.
analysis.description: All 14/14 positions involve a pawn promoting to a queen that is immediately captured or creates a fatal vulnerability. In the vast majority of cases (at least 11/14), the promoted queen lands on a square directly controlled by an enemy rook along an open file (e.g., rook on e7/e8 capturing a queen promoted on e1, rook on f5/f6 capturing on f1, rook on a8 capturing on a1). In each case, better alternatives existed: playing an intermediate check to deflect the opponent's king or rook (4/14 positions like Re1+, Rd1+, Ra4+), advancing a second pawn first to change the calculation (3/14 like g2, g5), deflecting/eliminating the piece controlling the promotion square (3/14 like Na4, Bf3, Nc3), blocking the file before promoting (1/14 like Ba6), or simply keeping the pawn as a positional restraint rather than promoting (1/14 like position 8 with Bxd4). One position (6/14) features promotion blocking the promoting side's own king escape square, allowing back-rank mate.
analysis.move_pattern: Pawn advances to 1st or 8th rank and promotes to Queen on a square directly attacked by an enemy piece (usually a rook on the same file)
analysis.why_bad: The newly created queen is immediately captured by the piece controlling the promotion square (typically a rook on the same file), resulting in a massive material or positional loss. A preparatory intermediate move—check, deflection, file-blocking, or advancing a second pawn—was needed to first neutralize the enemy piece's control of the promotion square.
sub_patterns: Promoting into a rook's open-file control (queen immediately captured by rook)
Promoting on a square geometrically covered by an enemy minor piece (knight/bishop captures)
Promoting blocks own king's escape square enabling back-rank mate
Promoting destroys a pawn's restraining function (pawn was more valuable as a threat than as a captured queen)

analysis.label: Quiet or plan-based moves that ignore immediate tactical demands, allowing the opponent to gain decisive tempo against undefended material.
analysis.description: This feature fires on moves that appear strategically motivated but fatally ignore an immediate tactical vulnerability requiring attention. In 4/5 positions, the move is explicitly tagged as causing tempo loss. The pattern manifests in several ways: placing a piece on a square where it becomes a target (Qe3 allows Bh6 winning the c1 bishop, 462cp; Bxe4 allows f3 gaining tempo, 231cp), moving the king away from a critical defensive task (Ka7 leaves f5 fatally undefended, 409cp), or spending time on a slow preparatory plan when forced tactics are imminent (g3 ignores Bxc3+Nxe4 winning a pawn, 223cp). In 4/5 positions with significant losses, there was essentially one clearly correct move (avg 1.8 good moves), indicating these are critical decision points where precision is demanded but the player chose a 'logical-looking' quiet alternative. The refutations consistently involve the opponent gaining material by attacking the misplaced piece or capturing now-undefended pawns.
analysis.move_pattern: Quiet moves (retreats, preparations, wrong captures) that are non-forcing and non-confrontational, placed on squares where they either become targets or fail to address an immediate threat
analysis.why_bad: The moves waste a critical tempo in positions where the opponent has a concrete tactical idea ready. Either the moved piece becomes a target (allowing opponent to gain tempo attacking it), or the move ignores an undefended piece/pawn that the opponent can immediately exploit. The opponent converts the tempo advantage into material.
sub_patterns: Piece placed on diagonal where it can be attacked with tempo (Qe3, Bxe4)
King moves away from critical defensive zone allowing pawn capture (Ka7)
Slow pawn preparation ignoring imminent tactical break (g3)

analysis.label: Playing a routine developing move or recapture instead of a devastating queen check (Qh5+/Qh4+) exploiting the opponent's missing f-pawn diagonal.
analysis.description: In 5/6 positions, the best move was a queen check along the e8-h5 (or e1-h4) diagonal made possible by the opponent's absent f-pawn, typically winning material via a fork on king and rook. Instead, the player chose quiet developing moves (Nf3 in 3 cases, Ne2, Be2, or dxe5 recapture). The missed tactic follows a consistent pattern: the f-pawn is gone, the king sits exposed in the center, and Qh5+/Qh4+ forces g6/g3, followed by Qxe5+ forking king and rook. In Position 10, the pattern is slightly different (Ndb5 exploitation instead of queen check), but the core error remains identical: a passive developing move replaces an aggressive tactical strike. Average cp_loss of 310 reflects the enormous gap between routine development and the winning tactic.
analysis.move_pattern: Minor piece or pawn moved to quiet developing square (Nf3, Ne2, Be2, dxe5) instead of queen deploying to h5/h4 with check along the opened diagonal
analysis.why_bad: The routine move ignores a forcing queen check that exploits the absent f-pawn's diagonal, typically winning a full rook via Qh5+ g6 Qxe5+ forking king and h8-rook, or gaining decisive attacking advantage
sub_patterns: Nf3 blocking queen's path to h5
Be2/Ne2 developing while Qh5+ wins immediately
Routine recapture instead of Qh4+ with exposed king

analysis.label: Endgame moves that pursue material or "active" repositioning while fatally abandoning the position's most critical defensive requirement.
analysis.description: This feature fires on endgame moves where the player makes a natural-looking improvement (capturing pawns, advancing passers, repositioning pieces) but neglects the one thing the position urgently demands. In 9/9 positions the move is an endgame mistake. In at least 5/9 cases the move directly captures or targets material (Rxg4, Rxa7, fxg3, Ke4 chasing f-pawn twice). In the remaining cases, pieces are repositioned to seemingly active squares while abandoning critical functions (Ba4 abandons f3 control, Bh5 walks into a fork, Ke7 enters a promotion corridor, h6 pushes prematurely). The common thread is a mismatch between what the player pursues (secondary gain) and what the position requires (specific defensive coordination). The refutations consistently exploit the exact weakness created: back-rank mates, knight forks on unguarded squares, king exposure from pawn captures, promotion enabled by abandoned blockade, or checking sequences through opened files.
analysis.move_pattern: Any piece type moving toward material targets or 'active' squares, typically captures on wing pawns, king advances toward enemy pawns, or bishop/piece repositioning away from defensive duties
