analysis.why_bad: The move abandons a critical defensive function (back-rank coverage, fork prevention, blockade duty, key-square control, king shelter) to pursue a secondary objective, allowing the opponent to exploit the resulting positional vacuum with an immediate tactical shot or unstoppable strategic threat.
sub_patterns: Rook captures wing pawn abandoning back-rank or king protection
King marches toward enemy pawns instead of challenging active opponent pieces
Minor piece repositions to undefended square allowing fork or tactical exploitation
Pawn advance/capture that opens critical lines to own king

analysis.label: Aggressive-looking moves that create immediate tactical vulnerabilities by neglecting what they leave behind.
analysis.description: This feature fires on moves that appear purposeful or aggressive but actually squander an existing advantage by creating exploitable tactical weaknesses. In 5/7 positions, the moved piece (usually a queen - 5/7 cases) lands on a square where it becomes a target or enables a forcing response: Nh4 is immediately harassed by Qh5 losing two tempi (Position 6), Qe2 enables Nxd4 fork (Position 7), Qc3 allows d4 tempo-gain exposing a hanging bishop (Position 3), e5 leaves the b4-e1 diagonal open for Qb4+ winning a bishop (Position 1). In 2/7 cases the piece abandons a critical post: Bc3 leaves the back rank exposed to Rd8+ (Position 9), Qh3 surrenders the only attacking compensation (Position 8). In 1/7, premature capture (Qxb7+) trades away the winning piece. The common thread is that each move prioritizes an apparent goal while overlooking the opponent's concrete tactical exploitation of the resulting vulnerability.
analysis.move_pattern: Piece (usually queen 5/7) moves to an apparently active or purposeful square that is actually unstable, exposed to tempo gain, or abandons a critical defensive/attacking function
analysis.why_bad: Each move enables the opponent to exploit the newly-created vulnerability through a forcing response (check, tempo-gaining attack, fork, back-rank invasion, or simple recapture), resulting in lost material, lost tempo, or surrendered compensation that was previously sustaining the position.
sub_patterns: Queen placed on square vulnerable to tempo-gaining pawn/piece attack (Qc3/d4, Qe2/Nxd4)
Piece moves to unstable rim/edge square immediately challenged (Nh4/Qh5)
Piece abandons critical defensive post exposing king (Bc3 leaves back rank, Qh3 surrenders attack)
Premature capture that trades away the winning piece (Qxb7+ allows recapture)
Pawn advance that opens critical diagonal/file for opponent (e5 opens b4-e1)

analysis.label: Catastrophic blunders in positions with exposed/centralized kings where the player chooses an obvious king-related move (check, castling, king walk) that misses the truly winning tactical continuation.
analysis.description: In all 5 positions, kings are exposed or in the center (White king on e1 in 4/5 positions), creating a 'king safety' context that dominates the player's thinking. The player responds with a superficially logical king-safety-related move: giving check (3/5: Bxf7+, d2+, Qxa1+), castling (1/5: O-O), or manually repositioning the king (1/5: Ke2). In every case, the move appears forcing or prudent but catastrophically misses the actual best continuation. In Position 1, Bxf7+ gives check with the wrong piece when Qxf7# was mate. In Position 2, d2+ advances with check but the pawn was stronger as a stationary threat. In Position 3, Ke2 addresses king safety manually when Bg5+ or O-O-O was correct. In Position 4, O-O castles for safety when Bc2 addressed the real tactical vulnerability. In Position 5, Qxa1+ grabs material with check when Nxb3+ led to mate in 2. The average of only 2.0 good moves confirms these are razor-sharp positions where only precise play works, yet players default to king-centric instincts.
analysis.move_pattern: Checks (captures or pawn advances giving check) or king-safety moves (castling, king walks) in positions with centralized/exposed kings
analysis.why_bad: The player recognizes that king vulnerability is the dominant theme but addresses it with the most obvious or instinctive move rather than the precise tactical solution; checks, captures with check, and castling feel 'forcing' or 'safe' but bypass the specific winning combination the position demands.
sub_patterns: Wrong piece/square check missing forced mate
Premature pawn check when threat-in-place was stronger
Castling or king walk ignoring tactical emergency
Material grab with check missing shorter mate

analysis.label: Moves that invite or enable the opponent to force an exchange (usually rook-for-rook) that transitions into a structurally lost or significantly worse simplified position.
analysis.description: This feature fires on moves that allow the opponent to force a simplifying exchange leading to a position where the player's structural deficiencies become decisive. The clearest sub-pattern involves rook moves to files or ranks where the opponent can immediately capture: Rg5 allows Rxg5 into a theoretically drawn wrong-colored-bishop endgame (position 5), Re1 allows Rxe1 into a lost pawn endgame (position 6), Re7 allows Rxe7+ into a lost minor piece endgame (position 7), and Rf7 allows Rxf7 into a lost bishop-vs-knight endgame (position 9) — that's 4/10 positions with identical rook-exchange-into-worse-endgame structure. Additionally, Kf3 allows Qxe2+ forcing a queen trade on unfavorable terms (position 2), Bxa6 removes a defensive piece enabling a decisive passed pawn (position 1), Nxc3 is the wrong capture allowing material recoupment via Bxb7 (position 4), and bxc4 creates connected passed pawns for the opponent (position 10) — all 8/10 share the theme of enabling unfavorable simplification. The positions consistently had very few good moves available (avg 2.0), indicating critical decision points where the player chose an active-looking or materialistically appealing move without calculating the resulting simplified position.
analysis.move_pattern: Diverse piece types (predominantly rooks), typically moving to a square on an open file/rank where the opponent's corresponding piece can immediately capture, or making captures that enable the opponent's forcing recapture sequence
analysis.why_bad: The moves allow the opponent to force an exchange that transitions into an endgame where the player has a decisive structural disadvantage (wrong-colored bishop, inferior king position, opponent's connected passed pawns, or lost pawn ending) that wasn't exploitable before the exchange
sub_patterns: Rook moves to a file where opponent's rook can immediately capture, entering a worse endgame
Captures that remove a key defender or abandon a dominant outpost, allowing tactical punishment
Pawn exchanges that create connected passed pawns for the opponent
Tempo-losing moves that allow opponent to dictate favorable exchange terms

analysis.label: Playing a natural-looking but tempo-wasting move in a position where few alternatives are acceptable and concrete/forcing play is demanded.
analysis.description: This feature fires on positions with very few good moves (avg 1.9) where the critical factor is timing and tempo. The played moves are typically 'natural' or 'reasonable-looking' — king centralizations (Kd5, Kf4, Ke5), defensive pawn moves (b3, a3), quiet developing moves (Bd7), or checks/captures that appear active (Qg6+, Nh7+, Bxg7) — but all share the trait of being slower or less precise than the position demands. In 9/14 positions, the primary error is explicitly identified as tempo loss: choosing a preparatory or indirect path when immediate concrete action was available. The punishment consistently involves the opponent gaining time to execute a plan (Positions 2, 6, 12, 15), escaping a mating net (Positions 7, 10), or exploiting a newly-created tactical vulnerability (Positions 8, 9, 14). Even positions with near-zero cp_loss (Positions 1, 5) share the structural characteristic of narrow decision points where timing between king moves and pawn advances is paramount.
analysis.move_pattern: Diverse piece types; typically a quiet/preparatory move (king walk, defensive pawn push, piece retreat) or a misdirected forcing move (wrong check/capture) when a more concrete alternative exists
analysis.why_bad: The moves waste a critical tempo — either defending something that should be sacrificed, moving a piece before establishing a forcing threat, removing a piece from a key defensive/attacking duty, or allowing the opponent time to execute their plan or escape danger.
sub_patterns: King moves before pawn advances in endgames (Kd5, Kf4, Kf4)
Defensive pawn moves instead of active piece play (b3, a3)
Wrong forcing move that releases pressure (Qg6+, Nh7+, Bxg7)
Piece retreats to passive squares (Qa7, Bd7)
Self-blocking own pieces (Ng6 blocking bishop retreat)

analysis.label: Moving a piece (usually the king) toward an exposed central square when the position demands urgent defensive retreat or addressing immediate tactical threats.
analysis.description: This feature fires on positions where the player advances a piece—most commonly the king—into an exposed or central zone, rather than retreating to safety or addressing a critical tactical vulnerability. In 5/8 positions, the king directly moves to a more exposed square (Kd2, Ke7, Kc3, Kc7, and the neutral Rd2). In 4/8 cases (Kd2→checks on c2/a2, Ke7→Nxd6+ fork, Kc3→Qxe3+ mating net, Kc7→Nc5/Rxd7+ combination), the king walks forward into a square where it becomes immediately vulnerable to checks, forks, or mating attacks. The non-king blunders share the same 'ignoring defensive urgency' logic: Qd7 blocks the f6-knight's retreat (2/8), Rc8 delays castling when b7 hangs (6/8), and Bc4 moves the wrong piece while another bishop hangs (8/8). In 6/8 positions the result is forced mate or near-mate, with average cp_loss of 4723. The common thread is choosing an apparently active or centralizing move when only defensive retreat/addressing the immediate threat could save the position.
analysis.move_pattern: Piece (predominantly king) moves toward center or forward along c/d files to ranks 2-7, typically one step toward enemy forces rather than retreating toward safety
analysis.why_bad: The moved piece (especially the king) lands on an exposed square where it faces immediate tactical exploitation—queen checks, knight forks, discovered attacks, or mating nets—while the player ignores that only a specific defensive move (retreat, castling, or addressing a hanging piece) could prevent catastrophe.
sub_patterns: King advances from back rank into center where queen checks create mating net (Kd2, Ke7, Kc3, Kc7)
Piece occupies square needed by another piece for retreat, creating trapped piece (Qd7 blocking Nf6-d7)
Slow developing move ignoring immediate tactical threat to undefended piece (Rc8, Bc4)

analysis.label: Moves that look active or purposeful (checks, centralizations, advances) but fail to create a concrete threat, giving the opponent a free tempo to exploit the position.
analysis.description: This feature fires on moves that appear natural or aggressive—queen centralizations (Qf5, Qf6, Qg6+), piece advances (Rc8, Nf6, g5), king marches (Kb4, Kd6, Ke5, Ke7), and checks (Rh8+, Qg6+)—but share the critical flaw of being non-forcing. In 8/11 positions the move fails to address the concrete tactical or strategic demand: maintaining piece coordination (Qf5 in pos 1), executing an available tactic (Rh8+ missing Nxg4+ in pos 5), protecting a piece (Kb4 abandoning the knight in pos 6), avoiding unfavorable trades (Qg6+/Qf6 allowing queen captures in pos 9-10), or creating immediate threats before the opponent improves (Rc8 vs Rc7+ in pos 2, g5 vs f4 in pos 14). The common thread is that these moves prioritize superficial activity over the position's concrete requirement, and because they don't force the opponent to respond to a specific threat, the opponent gains a free tempo to execute their own plan—whether that's completing development, promoting a pawn, trading into a winning endgame, or capturing an undefended piece.
analysis.move_pattern: Piece or king moves forward/toward center or gives check, typically to a natural-looking square, without creating an immediate forcing threat that demands a specific response
analysis.why_bad: The move doesn't force the opponent to react to a concrete threat, effectively wasting a tempo and allowing the opponent to improve their position, exploit a newly created vulnerability (undefended piece, exposed king, unfavorable trade), or execute their own plan unimpeded
sub_patterns: Pointless checks that drive opponent's king to safety (Rh8+, Qg6+)
Queen/piece centralization that allows unfavorable capture or trade (Qf5, Qf6, Qg6+)
King moves that abandon critical defensive duties (Kb4, Ke7)
Non-forcing advances when forcing alternatives exist (g5 vs f4, Rc8 vs Rc7+)
Natural development that ignores a specific tactical vulnerability (Nf6 walking into e5)

analysis.label: Making natural-looking improving or advancing moves in critical positions that demand a single specific forced response, typically capturing a dangerous enemy piece.
analysis.description: This feature fires on positions where very few good moves exist (avg 1.8) and the player chooses an active-looking or 'natural' move instead of the one required concrete response. In 4/8 positions (Kg5, Ne5, Kg4, and partially Nd5), the correct move was capturing a dangerous enemy knight that enabled mating threats, but the player instead advanced their own piece to a seemingly strong square. In 2/8 positions (dxe5, exd5), the player made a premature central pawn capture before necessary preparation (eliminating an attacker first or playing prophylaxis). The blunders share a common thread: the position demands tactical precision with essentially one correct move, but the player defaults to a positionally appealing or active-looking choice—king advances toward the center, knight centralizations to d5/e5, or 'obvious' pawn captures—while a specific enemy piece (typically a knight) goes uncaptured and proceeds to deliver devastating tactical blows (discovered checks, mating nets, or piece-winning sequences).
analysis.move_pattern: Advancing king/knight to central or forward squares (g4, g5, e5, d5), or making premature central pawn captures (dxe5, exd5), when the position demands a specific capture or prophylactic move
analysis.why_bad: These moves fail because they ignore the one critical tactical element in the position—usually a dangerous enemy piece enabling mating threats or discoveries. By advancing instead of capturing/neutralizing the threat, the player allows devastating forced sequences (mate in 2-3, discovered checks, piece-winning combinations) that the one correct move would have prevented.
sub_patterns: King advancing into mating net instead of capturing the piece enabling mate (Kg5, Kg4)
Knight centralizing away from critical defensive duty, enabling discovered attacks (Ne5, Nd5)
Premature central pawn capture before eliminating attacker or playing prophylaxis (dxe5, exd5)
Pawn push to wrong square missing defensive geometry (h3 instead of h4)

analysis.label: Playing a natural-looking active piece move (usually a rook to an open file/rank or a check) that wastes a critical tempo when the position demands a more precise tactical or strategic action.
analysis.description: In 5/7 positions the move involves a rook (Re1+, Re1+, Rb8, Rb2, Rf3), and in 4/7 the move delivers or seeks a check. The common error across all positions is choosing a superficially logical 'active' move—placing a piece on an open file, giving a check, or repositioning for general pressure—when the position's concrete demands require something far more specific. In Position 1 and Position 6, premature Re1+ checks allow the opponent to interpose with a developing piece (Ne5 or Be7), neutralizing the attack in one move. In Position 2, Qf8+ is a move-order error that fails to deny a key escape square. In Position 4, Bb5 is a slow positional idea when immediate Nxb6 exploits doomed material. In Position 7, Rb8 passively repositions while leaving c7 tactically vulnerable to a knight fork. In Position 9, Rb2 repositions the rook while the king urgently needs evacuation from h5. In Position 14, Rf3 lifts the rook but creates a target for Nd4 while stripping back-rank defense. The average cp_loss of 2845 reflects how severely these seemingly reasonable moves misread positional urgency.
analysis.move_pattern: Piece (predominantly rook) moved to an open file, rank, or checking square that appears active but lacks concrete purpose in the specific position
analysis.why_bad: These moves prioritize general piece activity over the position's specific tactical demands—they waste a critical tempo by allowing opponents to block with development, escape to uncontrolled squares, exploit newly undefended material, or advance unstoppable threats while the 'active' piece achieves nothing concrete.
sub_patterns: Premature rook check on open file allowing interposition with development
Rook repositioning that ignores urgent king safety needs
Rook lift that creates tactical vulnerabilities (fork/hanging piece)
Check in wrong move order failing to deny key escape square
Slow piece maneuver when immediate tactical strike is available

analysis.label: Seemingly active or aggressive moves that abandon a critical defensive duty (usually king safety), allowing the opponent to exploit the vacated defense with a forcing tactical blow.
analysis.description: This feature fires on moves where a piece is relocated to an apparently better/more active square but critically abandons defense of a key square near the king. In 8/10 positions, the resulting exploitation involves direct king safety threats (back-rank invasions, checks along diagonals, perpetual check opportunities, or pawn-storm attacks against an exposed king). The queen is the most frequently misplaced piece (Qf6 twice, Qf5, Qxf7, Qe2 = 5/10), typically moving to a square that looks centralized or attacking but leaves e8, g7, or the back rank unguarded. The moves share a common pattern of prioritizing offense over defense in positions where defensive coordination was the higher priority. The opponent consistently punishes with forcing moves (checks, captures with check, or invasion of the abandoned square) that gain tempo. The average cp_loss of 324 and only 1.8 good moves available indicates these are critical decision points where the defensive requirement was non-obvious but essential.
analysis.move_pattern: Piece (usually queen) moves laterally or diagonally toward seemingly active square (often f5, f6, f7, or e2-e3), away from back rank or key defensive diagonal/file
analysis.why_bad: The moved piece was performing a hidden defensive function (guarding a back-rank square, covering a key diagonal, or blocking an invasion route), and its removal allows the opponent to immediately exploit the undefended position with tempo-gaining checks, invasions, or tactical strikes against the exposed king.
sub_patterns: Queen leaves back-rank defense allowing Re8+ or Qe8+ invasion (positions 4, 15)
Queen/piece moves to square where it is immediately captured or forked with check (positions 8, 10, 12)
Queen abandons diagonal coverage allowing perpetual check (position 9)
Premature piece repositioning before securing defensive prerequisites (positions 1, 14)
King/pawn advances to exposed square inviting forcing pawn-check sequences (positions 5, 6)

analysis.label: Quiet, non-forcing moves that waste tempo while ignoring the position's critical defensive or strategic demand.
analysis.description: In all 3/3 positions, the player made a quiet, non-forcing move (pawn push or piece relocation) that appeared consolidating or prophylactic but completely ignored the position's most urgent priority. In Position 1, b3 ignored back-rank vulnerability when Rg1 was needed to prevent Rd1+ mating. In Position 3, f5 was a superfluous pawn push when the queen needed to vacate d5 to avoid a lethal queen exchange into a lost pawn endgame. In Position 6, Nd7 decentralized a perfectly-placed knight from e5 when king activation (Ke2/Ke1) was needed to contain a passed a-pawn. All 3/3 moves share the quality of being 'reasonable-looking' positional ideas that fatally misjudge the position's tempo requirements, allowing the opponent to execute a decisive plan (mating attack 1/3, unstoppable passed pawn 2/3).
analysis.move_pattern: Quiet non-forcing moves (pawn pushes or piece relocations away from the critical sector) that don't address checks, captures, or threats
analysis.why_bad: These moves waste a critical tempo on a non-urgent plan while the opponent has an immediate tactical or strategic resource (back-rank invasion, forced queen exchange into won endgame, or passed pawn advance) that needed to be addressed this move.
sub_patterns: Pawn push weakening king shelter when back-rank defense needed
Non-urgent pawn advance when piece relocation is critical
Knight decentralization when king activation required to contain passed pawn

analysis.label: Moves that pursue secondary goals (pawn grabs, repositioning, slow improvement) while neglecting the position's single most urgent requirement, resulting in pieces becoming vulnerable or decisive tempo loss.
analysis.description: This feature fires on moves where the player ignores the position's critical priority in favor of a tangential plan that looks active but is strategically misguided. In 5/7 positions, the move either abandons a piece's critical role (Rh3 leaves the c-file, Rxg2 abandons f2 leaving the b7 bishop undefended, Nxf2 quits the d3 outpost, Ra5 enters a bishop's diagonal) or ignores an urgent tactical necessity (Kd6 fails to capture the passed d-pawn, g4 wastes tempo instead of centralizing the king). The consistent punishment involves either a piece left hanging (3/7: Rxg2, Nxf2, Ra5 all create immediately capturable material) or critical tempo loss (3/7: g4, Rh3, Kd6 allow the opponent to advance plans unchecked). The moves share a psychological profile: they address a secondary concern (winning a pawn, pressuring a file, centralizing) while the position screams for one specific action that the player overlooks.
analysis.move_pattern: Mixed piece types moving to squares that abandon their current critical function or enter a tactical danger zone; no single geometric direction but moves tend toward the opponent's territory or flanks rather than addressing central/immediate concerns
analysis.why_bad: Each move neglects the position's #1 priority (capturing a dangerous passed pawn, maintaining piece defense, keeping active file control) to pursue a secondary plan, allowing the opponent to exploit the newly-created vulnerability (hanging piece, unstoppable pawn, lost coordination) within 1-2 moves
sub_patterns: Piece captures a pawn while leaving another piece undefended (Rxg2, Nxf2)
Rook/piece repositions away from its critical file/duty into a passive or vulnerable square (Rh3, Ra5)
King or pawn advances for long-term improvement while ignoring an urgent immediate threat (Kd6, g4)

analysis.label: Forward moves to central e4/e5/e6 squares that prioritize aggression over addressing critical defensive or tempo requirements.
analysis.description: This feature fires on moves where a piece or pawn advances to the e4, e5, or e6 squares (4/5 positions explicitly target these squares) in an aggressive-looking centralization or attack, but the move fundamentally ignores the position's critical needs. In Position 6, Ne6 hangs the knight to a rook on the e-file while ignoring mate threats. In Position 9, Ke5 takes a longer route in a pawn race, losing a crucial tempo. In Position 12, Qe4 centralizes the queen but abandons defense of the d7 bishop, allowing Qd8+ winning material. In Position 14, Ndxf7 removes the dominant outpost knight rather than keeping it, leaving the remaining piece trapped. In Position 15, e6 pushes a pawn forward but wastes a tempo when Black's e3 breakthrough is the real threat. All 5/5 positions share the theme of choosing an apparently active forward move over addressing the position's actual critical requirement (defense, tempo, or piece safety).
analysis.move_pattern: Various piece types (Knight, King, Queen, pawn) moving forward to e4, e5, or e6 squares (or adjacent f7), typically advancing toward the opponent's territory
analysis.why_bad: These moves waste critical tempo or abandon defensive duties by prioritizing aggressive-looking centralization/advancement when the position demands addressing immediate threats, protecting hanging pieces, or racing efficiently with the shortest path
sub_patterns: Knight jumping to e6 hanging to a rook on the e-file
King centralizing to e5 when a shorter path to the target exists
Queen centralizing to e4 abandoning protection of a back-rank piece
Pawn pushing to e6 wasting tempo in a critical endgame race

analysis.label: Choosing a slow, non-forcing move (development, castling, repositioning) when the position demands immediate concrete tactical action.
analysis.description: This feature fires on positions where players make quiet, 'improving' moves—developing pieces, castling, or repositioning—when the position contains a specific tactical opportunity that must be exploited immediately or will evaporate. In 8/10 positions, a concrete forcing move (capture, sacrifice, or aggressive piece placement) was required: capturing a hanging pawn (position 2: Nxg4), taking an undefended piece (position 6: Qxh4), executing a tactical knight jump (positions 8, 10: Nb5), launching a kingside demolition (position 5: Nxg5 with forced mate), maintaining an attacking queen on its dominant post (positions 4, 9: keeping queen on f7/h5 rather than retreating), or choosing active queen squares over passive ones (position 3: Qg5 over Qe7). The moves played instead—Qe2, b6, Qe7, Qf4, O-O-O (×2), Rfe1, Qf3, Bc7—are all non-capturing, non-checking moves that look reasonable in isolation but waste the critical tempo needed to strike. The average position had only 1.7 good moves available, confirming these are high-precision moments where generic play is catastrophically punished.
analysis.move_pattern: Non-forcing moves (no check, no capture, no direct threat): quiet queen retreats/repositioning, castling, rook development to open file, pawn pushes, bishop relocation
analysis.why_bad: These moves waste a critical tempo when the position contains a concrete tactical opportunity (hanging piece, forced combination, dominant piece placement) that evaporates if not seized immediately, allowing the opponent to consolidate, simplify, or counter-attack.
sub_patterns: Castling or king safety moves when forced tactics exist (O-O-O ignoring mate-in-12, O-O-O ignoring hanging knight)
Queen retreats from dominant attacking posts (Qf4 leaving f7, Qf3 leaving h5 area)
Generic development (Rfe1, Qe2) when specific tactical strikes (Nb5, Bb5) are required
Slow piece repositioning (Bc7, b6) when captures or active attacking moves maintain advantage

analysis.label: Rook moves to a square where the opponent can profitably capture or exchange it, leading to a simplified position that is much worse.
analysis.description: In 5/7 positions, the blundering rook moves to a square where the opponent's rook can immediately capture it (Rd2→Rxd2, Rb4→Rxb4, Rd3→Rxd3, Rf7→Rxf7, Re8→Rxe8/Bxg7+), and the resulting simplified endgame is catastrophically worse because the rook was the primary source of dynamic counterplay or positional advantage. In Position 9 (Re3), the rook lands on a square vulnerable to a pawn fork (f4+). In Position 6 (Rh4), the rook abandons a critical file, allowing the opponent to seize it and neutralize a winning advantage. The common thread across all 7 positions is that the rook leaves an active or safe post and moves to a square where it becomes capturable or exchangeable on the opponent's terms, destroying the player's dynamic compensation or converting advantages into drawn/lost simplified positions.
analysis.move_pattern: Rook moves to an open file or rank square already controlled or contested by the opponent's major piece, typically a lateral or forward move to a central square (d2, b4, h4, e8, e3, d3, f7)
analysis.why_bad: The rook abandons its active/safe post and lands on a square where the opponent can force a favorable exchange or tactical capture, eliminating the critical dynamic counterplay that the rook was providing and entering a simplified position where structural or material disadvantages become decisive.
sub_patterns: Rook moves to a square directly capturable by opponent's rook, enabling winning simplification (5/7)
Rook moves to a tactically vulnerable square allowing fork or deflection (2/7)
Rook abandons critical file control, allowing opponent to seize key lines (3/7)

analysis.label: Passive or non-forcing moves that waste a critical tempo when the opponent's king is stuck in the center, allowing it to castle to safety and neutralizing a dynamic advantage.
analysis.description: This feature fires on positions where one side has a significant but temporary advantage based on the opponent's uncastled king being stuck in the center. In 10/12 positions, the opponent's king is explicitly on e8 or e1 (uncastled), and the dynamic advantage demands immediate forcing action. The most striking sub-pattern is that in 6/12 positions (Positions 1, 2, 3, 5, 9, 12), the #1 best move is specifically Ba3 on the a3-f8 diagonal to prevent kingside castling. Instead, players chose quiet moves (h3, a3, Bd3, Qe2, Ne5, Bb5, Qd2, Qd7, c5, Bb7) that create no concrete threats against the exposed king, allowing the opponent to simply castle on the next move and equalize. The refutations consistently show the opponent castling (O-O appears as a top refutation in 8/12 positions). The average cp_loss of 308 reflects how completely these dynamic advantages evaporate once the king reaches safety.
analysis.move_pattern: Non-forcing moves (quiet pawn pushes, passive piece development, retreats, or wrong-direction bishop moves) that fail to target the opponent's uncastled king
analysis.why_bad: The advantage in these positions is entirely dynamic and time-sensitive—based on the opponent's king being temporarily stuck in the center. Any non-forcing move gives the opponent a free tempo to castle, instantly neutralizing the advantage. The position demands immediate concrete action (typically Ba3 preventing castling, or forcing checks/threats against the exposed king) rather than generic development or prophylaxis.
sub_patterns: Missing Ba3 on the a3-f8 diagonal to prevent kingside castling (6/12 positions)
Prophylactic pawn moves (h3, a3, c5) when the position requires forcing play
Developing the wrong piece to a passive square (Bd3, Bb5, Qe2, Qd2, Qd7) while the critical diagonal or square goes unused
Placing a piece where it becomes trapped or exposed to counterattack after the opponent consolidates (Bb7, Ne5, Qxc3)

analysis.label: Moves that ignore critical king vulnerability in positions demanding precise defensive or attacking play around exposed kings.
analysis.description: This feature fires on positions where king safety is the decisive factor—either the player's own king is critically exposed or the opponent's king is vulnerable to a precise attack—and the player makes a move that fails to address this. In 9/11 positions, king_safety is explicitly tagged as the primary concern. The mistakes include decentralizing attackers away from an exposed enemy king (Nh6 instead of Ng7 in 2/11), moving one's own king onto a tactical vulnerability (Kg7 onto a deadly diagonal, Kh2 onto a check-enabling diagonal, Kf5 into open space—4/11 are king moves to exposed squares), ignoring an immediate mating threat (Re5 allowing Qb5#, Qg6 allowing Re1#—2/11), choosing the wrong piece for a critical defensive square (Ne2 instead of Re2 leaving f2 unguarded), and prioritizing material over development when the king is uncastled (Qxc3 with king on e8). The positions average only 1.6 good moves available, indicating razor-thin margins where only very specific moves address the king safety crisis.
analysis.move_pattern: Various piece types moving to squares that are either exposed to tactical exploitation (diagonals, open files) or away from squares needed to address king vulnerability; often king moves to adjacent-but-wrong squares (Kh2 vs Kh1, Kb4 vs Kb2, Kf5 vs Ke3)
analysis.why_bad: Each move either places a piece/king on a tactically vulnerable square (enabling checks, pins, or mates), decentralizes from a position needed to attack/defend the critical king, or wastes a tempo in a position where immediate forcing play was required to exploit or address king exposure.
sub_patterns: King stepping onto dangerous diagonal (Kg7, Kh2)
Knight decentralizing from dominant outpost away from exposed enemy king (Nh6×2)
Non-forcing move allowing immediate mate (Qg6, Re5)
Wrong piece to defensive square leaving king exposed (Ne2)
Greedy capture ignoring uncastled king vulnerability (Qxc3)
King moving to open/wrong square in endgame (Kf5, Kb4)

analysis.label: Playing an active-looking but irrelevant move in a critical position where only one specific move prevents immediate catastrophe, typically involving king safety.
analysis.description: This feature fires on positions where the player faces an immediate tactical crisis (almost always involving king safety, 9/10 positions) and there exists essentially only ONE move that prevents disaster (average good moves: 1.2), but the player instead makes a move that looks active or purposeful in isolation while completely failing to address the urgent threat. In 6/10 cases the moved piece is a queen relocating to a seemingly aggressive square (Qf5, Qg3, Qf4, Qc3, Qxe8+, with Rd8 being a rook equivalent); in the remaining cases, pieces move to vulnerable squares (Bd6, Bxf3) or the king walks into danger (Kh6, Kd7). The catastrophic consequence (average cp_loss: 3940, with 5/10 positions resulting in forced checkmate) stems from abandoning a critical defensive function—guarding a mating square, blocking an open file, defending a hanging piece, or preventing a discovered check mechanism. The positions share extreme tactical tension where the opponent's pieces are already coordinated for a decisive blow that only one precise defensive resource can prevent.
analysis.move_pattern: Piece (usually queen 6/10, also bishop, rook, or king) moves to an active-looking square while vacating a critical defensive post; no consistent direction but typically away from the immediate danger zone around one's own king
analysis.why_bad: The move abandons the one piece or square that was preventing an immediate tactical catastrophe (checkmate, discovered check, capture of undefended piece), in positions where only a single specific defensive resource could hold the position together
sub_patterns: Queen leaves defensive post near king, allowing mating attack (Qf5, Qf4, Qc3, Qg3)
King walks into immediate checkmate or mating net (Kd7, Kh6)
Piece moves to tactically vulnerable square enabling forcing sequence (Bd6 allowing Nxd6+)
Piece leaves critical file/diagonal, collapsing defensive structure (Rd8, Bxf3)
Trade initiated without calculating recapture tempo (Qxe8+)

analysis.label: Playing non-forcing or insufficiently forcing moves in razor-sharp positions where only immediate checks or direct tactical blows maintain the evaluation.
analysis.description: This feature fires on positions where the player makes a natural-looking but non-forcing move (development, pawn advance, capture without check) when the position critically demands an immediate forcing continuation—almost always a check. In 5/8 positions, the correct move was a check (Qc6+, Qd8+, Qe1+, Qg5+, Nf4+), and in the remaining cases it was a direct tactical blow that couldn't be ignored (Rad8 winning the queen, Nxh6 immediate capture, Qxe7 removing a key piece). The positions all feature extremely narrow best paths (avg 1.2 good moves), meaning these are critical decision points requiring precise calculation. The blunders share the pattern of choosing a 'logical' move—developing a piece (Nd2, Nc6), placing a rook on a 'good' file (Rf8, Rab8), making a preparatory attack (g5, Qg4), or grabbing material (Nxe5, Bxg7)—while missing that only forcing continuations prevent catastrophic counterplay. The average centipawn loss of ~3950 reflects the devastating consequences of surrendering the initiative in these positions.
analysis.move_pattern: Diverse piece types (knights, rooks, queens, pawns, bishops) making non-checking moves—either quiet development, wrong-file placement, preparatory advances, or captures that don't force a response—when the position requires an immediate check or unavoidable tactical blow
analysis.why_bad: These moves surrender the critical tempo needed to maintain a forcing sequence; the opponent uses that tempo to either escape danger, launch a decisive counterattack against the player's own vulnerable king, or neutralize all threats. In sharp positions with only 1-2 good moves, any non-forcing move allows the opponent to seize the initiative.
sub_patterns: Knight moves that look active but disrupt winning coordination (Nc6, Nd2, Nxe5)
Rook moves to wrong squares when one specific file/square is critical (Rf8, Rab8)
Move-order errors playing the second move first without the required intermediate check (Qg4 before Nf4+)
Slow pawn advances when immediate captures/checks win (g5 instead of Nxh6/Ng5+)
Attacking the opponent's king when own king is fatally exposed (Bxg7)

analysis.label: Quiet, positionally-motivated moves that create critical tactical vulnerabilities by abandoning key defensive functions or exposing pieces/king to concrete exploitation.
analysis.description: This feature fires on moves that appear to consolidate or improve the player's position through general positional logic—centralizing a king (Ke4, Kg7), repositioning a piece to an 'ideal' square (Nh4 toward f5, Bb3 for a diagonal battery, Rb7 to contest a file, Rf6 to pressure a pawn), or strengthening pawn structure (f3×2, f5)—but actually create a new concrete vulnerability that didn't previously exist. In 7/9 positions, the move directly weakens the player's king safety or removes a critical defender. In 6/9 cases, the opponent punishes with an immediate tactical blow (fork, discovered attack, trapped piece, or hanging material). In 8/9 positions, multiple good alternatives existed (avg 2.3) that maintained the status quo, indicating these weren't forced errors but voluntary self-inflicted wounds. The common thread is prioritizing a vague positional objective over concrete tactical reality—applying general principles when the position demanded specific calculation.
analysis.move_pattern: Mixed piece types (king, knight, bishop, rook, f-pawn) making non-forcing, non-capturing moves to squares that appear strategically logical but create immediate tactical liabilities
analysis.why_bad: Each move either abandons a critical defensive function (piece leaves a key post), creates a static target the opponent exploits, or walks into the opponent's tactical range—all while safe alternatives existed that maintained the position without creating new weaknesses
sub_patterns: Piece abandons defensive post enabling opponent's tactical blow (Nh4, Bb3, Kg7)
f-pawn advance weakens king or creates exploitable target (f3, f3, f5)
Piece/king moves to square within opponent's tactical striking range (Ke4, Rb7, Kg7)

analysis.label: Pushing the h-pawn (h4/h5) to "support" a bishop on g4/g5 that is challenged by the opponent's h-pawn, but the pawn cannot actually defend the bishop and material is lost after capture.
analysis.description: In 9/10 positions, the player has a bishop on the g-file (g4 for Black, g5 for White) that is being challenged by the opponent's h-pawn (h3 or h6). Instead of retreating the bishop (Bh5/Bh4), exchanging it (Bxf3/Bxf6), or relocating it (Be6/Bf4), the player pushes their own h-pawn (h5 or h4) believing it anchors or supports the bishop. This is a fundamental tactical error: the h-pawn cannot protect the bishop diagonally backward, so after the opponent captures (hxg4 or hxg5), the bishop is simply taken and only a pawn is recovered. In 7/10 cases, the king remains uncastled in the center, which compounds the error because after hxg4 hxg4, the knight leaps to g5 creating devastating attacks on f7 (seen in positions 2, 4, 5, 7, 8). The average cp_loss of 248 reflects that this typically costs a full minor piece or enables a crushing tactical sequence.
analysis.move_pattern: h-pawn advance one square (h4 or h5) on the same side as a friendly bishop sitting on g4/g5 that is under challenge from the opponent's h-pawn
analysis.why_bad: The h-pawn cannot defend a piece diagonally behind/beside it - after hxg4/hxg5, the bishop is captured for free (only a pawn is recovered). The opened h-file and displaced g-pawn then create further tactical vulnerabilities, especially Ng5 attacking f7 when the king is uncastled.
sub_patterns: Black Bg4 + h5 after White h3: hxg4 hxg4 Ng5 exploiting f7 weakness with uncastled king
White Bg5 + h4 after Black h6: hxg5 captures bishop outright, winning a full piece for a pawn
h-pawn advance when bishop should simply retreat along diagonal (Bh5/Bh4) or exchange (Bxf3/Bxf6)

analysis.label: Playing a slow non-capturing king move or pawn push when an enemy piece is hanging and can be captured for free.
analysis.description: In all 8/8 positions, an enemy piece (rook, knight, or bishop) sits completely undefended and within direct capture range of one of the player's pieces. Instead of taking the free material, the player makes a quiet, non-forcing move—either a king walk (Kg7, Kf5, Kc7, Kd7 in 4/8 cases) or a pawn push (a4, a6, g5, g7 in 4/8 cases). The hanging pieces include: rook on e6 capturable by queen (pos 2), rook on d8 capturable by bishop (pos 3), knight on g5 capturable by pawn (pos 6), bishop on f4 capturable by knight (pos 8), rook on d1 capturable by queen (pos 9), rook on e4 capturable by bishop (pos 12), rook on a3 capturable by bishop (pos 13), and rook on d2 capturable by bishop or rook (pos 14). In every case, the wasted tempo allows the opponent to move the hanging piece to safety, converting forced mates or overwhelming advantages into merely large advantages requiring technique.
analysis.move_pattern: Non-capturing quiet moves (king steps to adjacent squares or single pawn advances) with no check or threat, when a simple one-move capture of an undefended piece exists
analysis.why_bad: An undefended enemy piece is freely capturable in one move, but the player makes a purposeless quiet move instead, gifting the opponent a tempo to rescue the hanging piece and dramatically extending or degrading the winning process.
sub_patterns: King walks ignoring hanging pieces (Kg7, Kf5, Kc7, Kd7)
Passed pawn fixation over free captures (a6, g7)
Slow flank pawn pushes missing central tactics (a4, g5)

analysis.label: Playing a slow peripheral move (often a b-pawn push) when the position demands an immediate central pawn break or aggressive forward action.
analysis.description: In 5/6 positions, the player chose a secondary or peripheral operation while ignoring the primary tactical/strategic demand of the position, which was nearly always a central pawn break or aggressive forward piece advance. The pattern is most striking in positions 5 and 7, where b4 and b5 were played when d4 and d5 respectively were clearly best—identical flank-vs-center errors. In position 1, Nc3 moved the knight sideways/backward toward the queenside instead of the winning Nf4 forward toward the kingside. In position 3, Ke7 was a passive king shuffle instead of the active f5 counter-strike. In position 2, Rxf8 prematurely exchanged active attacking pieces instead of maintaining pressure with f3. Across all blunders (5/5 mistakes), the best move involved direct central action (d4, d5, f5, f3, or Nf4), while the played move addressed a secondary concern—queenside expansion, simplification, or king placement—that the position did not require or reward.
analysis.move_pattern: Flank pawn advances (especially b-file) or lateral/backward piece moves instead of central pawn breaks (d4/d5/f-file) or forward attacking moves
analysis.why_bad: These moves waste a critical tempo on a peripheral goal while the position demands urgent central action; the opponent exploits the lost tempo to seize the initiative, execute tactical strikes on the unaddressed central/kingside vulnerabilities, or consolidate a position that would otherwise be under pressure.
sub_patterns: b-pawn push instead of d-pawn central break (b4 vs d4, b5 vs d5)
Knight retreat/sideways when forward attack wins (Nc3 vs Nf4)
Premature exchange dissipating attack when pawn break maintains pressure (Rxf8 vs f3)
Passive king move instead of active counter-strike (Ke7 vs f5)

analysis.label: Moving the queen to a square where the opponent can immediately capture it, resulting in an unfavorable queen exchange that dissipates the player's dynamic advantages.
analysis.description: In 8/11 positions, the blunder is a queen move, and in at least 6 of those, the primary refutation is the opponent simply capturing the queen with their own queen (Qxh4 in pos 2, Qxe2+ in pos 4, Qxh6 in pos 7, Qxg5 in pos 9, forced Qxh6+ in pos 12, Qxg5 in pos 15). The player typically has a dynamic advantage or attacking position that requires queens on the board, yet voluntarily offers a trade that eliminates their attacking potential. Critically, in several positions (7, 12, 15) the correct move was actually to ATTACK the opponent's queen with a pawn or knight (g6 or Ne7), gaining tempo rather than offering one's own queen. The rook moves (3/11) share a related pattern of abandoning a critical defensive post or inviting simplification. The average cp_loss of 1184 reflects how dramatically these positions collapse once queens are traded under unfavorable circumstances - structural weaknesses get exposed, hanging pieces become capturable, and dynamic compensation evaporates.
analysis.move_pattern: Queen moves to squares within immediate capture range of the opponent's queen, typically sideways or forward to an unprotected square on the 4th-7th ranks
analysis.why_bad: The queen exchange dissipates dynamic advantages (attacking potential, piece coordination, initiative) that only existed with queens on the board, while exposing tactical vulnerabilities (hanging pieces, weak pawns, exposed kings) that emerge in the simplified position
sub_patterns: Queen offered adjacent to opponent's queen allowing immediate Qx capture
Queen moved away from defending a piece, leaving material hanging after trade
Rook moved from critical defensive post, enabling tactical exploitation of exposed king
Active position simplified when concrete attacking moves (pawn pushes attacking opponent's queen) were available

analysis.label: Black makes a seemingly constructive move (repositioning, capturing, centralizing) while neglecting an urgent threat to their own king that the opponent immediately exploits.
analysis.description: In all 4/4 positions, Black plays a move that appears reasonable in isolation—repositioning a rook (Ra5), centralizing a king for the endgame (Kf7), creating a passed pawn (fxg2), or retreating to perceived safety (Ka6)—but catastrophically ignores a concrete tactical threat against their own king. In 3/4 cases the primary tactical motif is king_safety, where the opponent exploits checking sequences or diagonal/rank attacks that the played move either enables or fails to prevent. In 4/4 cases, the best moves available involved either generating immediate counterplay (h4 creating threats against White's king), keeping the king on its safe square (Bd5 maintaining king on g8), addressing the lethal threat directly (Qf8 blocking the diagonal), or centralizing the king rather than cornering it (Kb4). The common failure is prioritizing a 'positional improvement' or material gain over addressing the position's most critical concrete demand.
analysis.move_pattern: Various piece types (rook, king, pawn) moving to passive or exposed squares; no consistent geometric direction, but all are non-forcing moves that fail to address existing checking/mating lines
analysis.why_bad: These moves allow the opponent to exploit immediate tactical threats—particularly queen checks along diagonals/ranks, or rook coordination—that the player's move either ignores or actively worsens by placing the king on vulnerable squares or wasting critical tempo
sub_patterns: King walking into check/attack vulnerability (Kf7, Ka6)
Passive piece repositioning when counterplay is mandatory (Ra5)
Greedy capture ignoring mating threat (fxg2)

analysis.label: Quiet, non-forcing moves that squander a critical tempo in positions demanding immediate dynamic action, allowing the opponent to execute a decisive threat or plan.
analysis.description: This feature fires on moves that appear reasonable (prophylactic, improving, or repositioning) but catastrophically waste time in positions where only one or two precise moves maintain the balance. In 8/9 positions, the analyses tag 'tempo_loss' as a key factor. The positions share a common structure: an urgent dynamic requirement exists (piece coordination in Position 1, counterplay via g5 in Position 7, piece safety in Position 2, king defense in Positions 6/8/13) but the player chooses a slower, non-forcing alternative. The average of only 1.9 good moves available confirms these are razor-sharp positions with narrow correct paths. In 6/9 cases, the refutation involves the opponent simply executing the obvious plan that the wasted tempo failed to prevent (f6 hitting two pieces, Nxc5 capturing the undefended pawn, Nd7 trapping the rook, Qe4+ exploiting the open file, Rc8 exploiting the c-file, Nxd6 sacrificing into the exposed king).
analysis.move_pattern: Non-forcing, non-capturing, non-checking quiet moves of any piece type; often pawn pushes (a3, a6, c4), piece repositionings to peripheral or suboptimal squares (Rh8, Bh5, Nc4, Qh3, Rb6), or king walks (Kc2)
analysis.why_bad: The position contains an urgent tactical or dynamic requirement (defending a threat, maintaining piece coordination, creating counterplay before the opponent acts) that permits no tempo waste, and the quiet move allows the opponent to execute their primary plan unimpeded—whether that's a double attack, piece capture, pawn promotion, or exploiting an exposed king.
sub_patterns: Prophylactic pawn moves (a3, a6) when piece action is urgent
Piece repositioning to worse squares abandoning critical coordination (Rh8, Bh5, Rb6)
Slow piece maneuvers when only pawn breaks create counterplay (Nc4 instead of g5)
King moves to seemingly safer squares that create new tactical vulnerabilities (Kc2)
Queen/piece overextension to squares with easily-parried threats (Qh3, c4)

analysis.label: Moves that voluntarily abandon or destroy the single critical structural/tactical feature holding the position together, while appearing superficially constructive.
analysis.description: In 8/8 positions, the played move removes the ONE key element that was sustaining the position's viability. In Position 1, Nh5 abandons the dominant f6 outpost that enabled Qxh6+ combinations. In Position 2, N4xf5+ destroys the coordinated knight pair needed for the Ne6+ discovered check mechanism. In Position 3, Kc2 leaves the d5 knight undefended (the piece holding the position together). In Position 4, Qe2 vacates control of c3, the exact square Black needs for a tactical invasion. In Position 5, Bg4 blocks the queen's access to g4—the only counter-resource against Ng3 fork. In Position 6, Rc2 places the rook where it gets trapped in the Bxb2/cxb2 sequence, enabling back-rank mate. In Position 7, g5 shatters the locked pawn structure that was the sole foundation of the drawing fortress. In Position 8, b3 wastes the critical tempo needed to play a4, allowing Black's knight to activate devastatingly. All moves look constructive (repositioning, capturing, breaking pawns) but fundamentally misidentify what matters most in the position.
analysis.move_pattern: Any piece type moving to a seemingly reasonable square; no consistent geometric direction—the commonality is functional (abandoning the critical positional requirement) rather than geometric
analysis.why_bad: Each move voluntarily removes the one factor (outpost, piece coordination, key defender, prophylactic control, structural fortress) that was holding the position together, gifting the opponent the exact tempo or square they need to execute a winning tactical sequence
sub_patterns: Abandoning a dominant piece from its optimal outpost (Nh5 from f6, N4xf5 destroying coordination)
Moving a defender away from the critical square it controls (Qe2 abandoning c3 control, Kc2 leaving knight hanging)
Self-obstruction blocking own piece's vital escape/counter-resource (Bg4 blocking Qg4)
Breaking a defensive fortress structure that guaranteed the draw (g5 in locked pawn endgame)
Tempo-losing moves that allow opponent's decisive piece activation (b3 instead of a4, Rc2 walking into a trap)

analysis.label: Choosing a slow preparatory or repositioning move when an immediate concrete tactical blow (capture, sacrifice, or forcing break) was available and required.
analysis.description: This feature fires on positions where the player selects a non-forcing, 'improving' move—a piece regrouping, passive retreat, preparatory pawn push, or developmental move—in a position that demands immediate concrete action. In 11/11 cases, the best move was a direct tactical strike: Bxh6 exchanges destroying the fianchetto (4/11), immediate captures of hanging/weak material like Bxa6 or Bxh3 (2/11), tactical forks like Nf7 (1/11), or forcing central breaks like e5/d4/exd4 (4/11). Instead, the players chose knight redeployments to inferior squares (Ng5, Ne2, Na4, Ng4), passive bishop retreats (Bh4, Bg3), premature flank pawn advances (g4, h4, g5, a4), or slow development (O-O-O). The positions share an average of only 1.1 good moves available, indicating narrow tactical windows where the concrete action was the ONLY way to maintain the advantage. A fianchettoed bishop on g7 appears in 10/11 positions, and in many cases the missed tactical blow specifically targeted this structure via Bxh6. The common thread is prioritizing abstract piece improvement over available forcing continuations.
analysis.move_pattern: Non-forcing moves (piece retreats, knight redeployments to rim/passive squares, slow pawn advances, castling) that create no immediate threat—none are checks or captures
analysis.why_bad: These moves waste a critical tempo in positions where a concrete forcing action (capture, sacrifice, central break) was immediately available; the opponent uses the gifted tempo to neutralize the tactical opportunity, escape danger, or launch counterplay that didn't previously exist
sub_patterns: Passive bishop retreat (Bg3, Bh4) instead of Bxh6 exchange sacrifice destroying fianchetto
Premature flank pawn advance (g4, h4, g5, a4) instead of immediate central break or capture
Slow knight redeployment (Ne2, Na4, Ng4, Ng5) instead of decisive tactical fork or break
Strategic development move (O-O-O) instead of capturing hanging material

analysis.label: King voluntarily moves to a square where it becomes immediately vulnerable to checks, pins, or forcing tactical sequences.
analysis.description: In 7/10 positions, the blunder is a king move that places the king on an exposed square inviting immediate tactical exploitation. Kc2 (pos 1) walks onto the c-file allowing Rxb2+ with check. Kc8 (pos 6) creates a fatal queen-king alignment on the c-file enabling a winning pin. Ke5 (pos 9) walks into d4+ pawn check initiating a forcing king hunt. Kf8 (pos 10) steps onto the h6-f8 diagonal allowing Qh6+. Kd5 (pos 13) marches into the open where c4+ starts a forced mate. Kc8 (pos 4) passively retreats allowing coordination of two passed pawns. Even the non-king moves share the theme of passive/self-weakening choices when active play was demanded: Ne3 abandons a winning capture, f3 blocks king centralization, Re8 creates a back-rank alignment. The common thread is choosing a move that appears reasonable but creates a new geometric vulnerability (file, diagonal, or rank) that the opponent exploits with tempo-gaining forcing moves, typically checks.
analysis.move_pattern: King moves (7/10) to adjacent squares that land on exposed files, diagonals, or ranks; remaining moves are passive piece/pawn moves creating similar alignments
analysis.why_bad: The king lands on a square where it faces immediate checks, pins, or mating threats along newly-created geometric alignments (files, diagonals), giving the opponent forcing moves with tempo that convert into decisive material or positional gains
sub_patterns: King steps onto open file creating queen-king or rook-king alignment (Kc2, Kc8)
King advances into center where pawn checks initiate king hunt (Ke5, Kd5)
King moves to diagonal where queen check becomes possible (Kf8)
Passive king retreat when active piece play was required (Kc8 endgame, Kh7)
Non-king passive move when tactical opportunity exists (Ne3, Re8, f3)

analysis.label: Playing a seemingly progressive or active move (pawn advance, piece advance, capture) that wastes a critical tempo by neglecting the position's most urgent defensive or positional need.
analysis.description: This feature activates on moves where the player pushes forward with a pawn or piece that appears active or constructive, but fundamentally ignores the one thing the position demands. In 5/11 positions, the blunder is a premature pawn advance (a3, e6+, h4, c6, a3) when king activation or piece repositioning is the critical priority. In 3/11 positions, a bishop is moved to a seemingly active but exposed/vulnerable square (Bf5, Bg5, Ba4) when maintaining existing piece placement or retreating to safety is correct. In 2/11 positions, a piece abandons its optimal square for a 'progressive' but inferior one (Rd3 leaving the dominant 2nd rank, Bxf6 recapturing instead of launching counterplay). The unifying theme is that the correct move in every case is quieter—a king walk, a piece retreat, maintaining a defensive function—while the blunder prioritizes apparent activity over true positional necessity. The tag 'tempo_loss' appears in virtually all analyses (10/11), confirming that the lost tempo on the wrong plan is the fundamental cost.
analysis.move_pattern: Forward-moving pieces or pawn advances (pushes toward opponent's side, captures, checks) when the position requires backward repositioning, king activation, or maintaining defensive piece placement
analysis.why_bad: The move wastes the critical tempo needed to address the position's true priority (activating the king in pawn endgames, saving a hanging piece, maintaining a blockade, keeping a piece on its optimal square), allowing the opponent to exploit the neglected vulnerability before the player's 'active' plan generates any benefit.
sub_patterns: Premature passed pawn advance when king activation is needed (e6+, h4, c6)
Pawn push that destroys a critical structural resource (a3 removing axb3 recapture)
Bishop placed on exposed square where it gets trapped or leaves something hanging (Ba4, Bf5, Bg5)
Piece abandons dominant position for seemingly active but inferior square (Rd3 from d2)
Reactive capture instead of launching concrete counterplay (Bxf6 instead of Nb4)

analysis.label: Playing an aimless or misdirected move that wastes a critical tempo when the position demands immediate piece activation or addressing a concrete threat.
analysis.description: This feature fires on moves where the player ignores the position's primary demand—typically urgent piece activation or addressing a specific threat—in favor of a move that looks purposeful but achieves nothing concrete. In 9/9 positions, the correct moves involved immediate piece activity (rook activation to open files/ranks, bishop improvements, or maintaining critical blockades), while the played moves wasted time on speculative pawn advances (f5, f4, g4 in 3/9), aimless rook relocations to tactically vulnerable or irrelevant squares (Rd8, Rc4, Rc6, Rb7, Rh2 in 5/9), or an exposed king advance (Kf4). The tempo loss is devastating because opponents punish by seizing the initiative—activating their own pieces, advancing passed pawns, or executing tactical combinations that exploit the newly created vulnerability. The average cp_loss of 2304 (including two mate-forcing blunders) reflects how these seemingly quiet mistakes often prove immediately fatal in positions where concrete action was required.
analysis.move_pattern: Any piece type; no consistent direction. Pawn advances (f/g file), rook moves to passive/vulnerable squares, or king advances to exposed squares—all sharing the trait of being non-forcing moves in positions demanding urgency.
analysis.why_bad: The move surrenders a critical tempo, allowing the opponent to seize initiative through piece activation, passed pawn advancement, or tactical exploitation of the piece's new vulnerable placement—while the position's primary demand (piece activity, blockade maintenance, or threat neutralization) goes unaddressed.
sub_patterns: Speculative pawn advance instead of rook activation (f5, f4, g4)
Rook placed on tactically vulnerable square enabling opponent's combination (Rd8, Rc4, Rc6)
Rook/King abandons critical defensive post for illusory counterplay (Rh2, Kf4, Rb7)

analysis.label: White places a piece on or near the a7-g1 diagonal where Black's active dark-squared bishop immediately exploits it.
analysis.description: In 3/4 positions, White moves a piece directly onto the a7-g1 diagonal (Rg1 to g1, Be3 to e3 twice) where Black's dark-squared bishop on c5 or a7 immediately captures it, winning material or triggering devastating tactical sequences (fxe3 opening the diagonal further, enabling knight forks). In position 8, Bb3 is a quiet bishop repositioning that gives Black time to activate their dark-squared bishop (Bd6) to neutralize White's advantage. All four moves are passive developing/repositioning moves that ignore the opponent's active piece pressure along key diagonals, particularly when Black has a bishop aiming at g1 through c5/a7. The common tactical punishment involves the opponent's dark-squared bishop either directly capturing the misplaced piece (3/4) or being activated to dominate the position (4/4).
analysis.move_pattern: Quiet piece development (bishop or rook) to squares on the a7-g1 diagonal (g1, e3, e3) or adjacent long diagonal (b3), typically non-capturing and non-checking
analysis.why_bad: The piece is placed on a square controlled by Black's active dark-squared bishop (on c5 or a7), allowing immediate capture or tactical exploitation via the open a7-g1 diagonal, often winning an exchange or creating knight forks after pawn recaptures open lines
sub_patterns: Rook to g1 captured by bishop on a7
Bishop to e3 captured by Bc5 enabling Nxe3 fork after fxe3
Slow bishop retreat allowing opponent's dark-squared bishop activation

analysis.label: Playing a seemingly purposeful move (development, centralization, or check) while catastrophically ignoring that a piece is hanging or will become hanging.
analysis.description: This feature fires on positions where players choose an 'active-looking' move over addressing a critical material situation. The strongest sub-pattern involves placing pieces on e6 (5/10 positions: Be6 x3, Qe6, Ne6+), particularly in openings where Be6 walks into a devastating d5 pawn fork hitting both the bishop and a knight on c6 (3/10 positions). The remaining positions share the same decision-making flaw: Kf2 escapes check instead of capturing the hanging checking knight (Position 3), Nd4 moves from a protected square to one hanging on the bishop's diagonal (Position 4), Ka7 marches the king away leaving pawns defenseless (Position 8), Bc5 abandons defense of c3 pawn (Position 12), Ne6+ gives check instead of capturing the opponent's queen with Nxh5 (Position 13), and Ra2+ gives check instead of capturing the opponent's rook (Position 15). In all cases, the moves appear purposeful but ignore a straightforward material consideration.
analysis.move_pattern: Piece moves to an apparently active central/forward square (especially e6, d4, c5) or gives check, while a simple capture or defensive necessity exists
analysis.why_bad: The player prioritizes apparent activity (development, centralization, giving check) over concrete material tactics—either leaving their own piece undefended on the new square, self-blocking critical pawns that allow forks, or failing to capture an opponent's hanging piece. The opponent punishes with simple captures or pawn forks (especially d5).
sub_patterns: Be6/Qe6 in opening allowing d4-d5 pawn fork against piece on c6
Giving check (Ne6+, Ra2+) instead of capturing a hanging piece
Moving piece from protected to unprotected square where it is immediately captured
Abandoning defense of a pawn by moving its protector to an 'active' square

analysis.label: Playing a natural-looking but non-urgent move when the position demands one specific immediate action, squandering an irreplaceable tempo.
analysis.description: This feature fires on positions where the player makes a reasonable-looking, routine move (development, structural pawn push, simplifying exchange, or prophylaxis) while the position demands one precise urgent action. In 8/9 positions, the analyses explicitly identify 'tempo_loss' as the core motif. The positions share extremely narrow margins (avg 1.6 good moves available) where typically only ONE move maintains the advantage. Common scenarios include: failing to block an open e-file toward an uncastled king when Be2/Qe2/O-O was critical (4/9 positions), playing a slow pawn move (a5, h3, d6) when an immediate tactical strike or breakthrough was time-sensitive (3/9), choosing the wrong piece or square for a tactical operation like a capture or check (3/9 - Bxe5, Rxg3, Nf7+). In all cases, the opponent gains a specific concrete resource (occupying a blockade square, executing a fork, challenging a key piece, escaping a mating net) that was only possible because the player squandered the one tempo needed to prevent it.
analysis.move_pattern: Quiet developing moves (Nf3, Bf4), structural pawn pushes (d6, a5, h3), or simplifying exchanges (Bxe5, Rxg3) played when a specific forcing or preventive move was required
analysis.why_bad: Each move wastes the single critical tempo needed to address an urgent positional demand (blocking a file, executing a breakthrough, choosing the correct tactical continuation), giving the opponent time to neutralize the advantage with a concrete tactical resource that wasn't previously available.
sub_patterns: Failing to block the e-file with a piece on e2 or castling when opponent's queen targets uncastled king
Playing a slow flank pawn move when a central/kingside breakthrough is time-critical
Capturing with the wrong piece or on the wrong square, losing coordination or allowing counterplay
Making prophylactic moves that ignore an active enemy piece's concrete tactical shot

analysis.label: Moving a piece away from a key defensive role, immediately leaving a pawn, piece, or square complex unguarded and tactically exploitable.
analysis.description: In all 6/6 positions, the player moves a piece that was performing a critical defensive function—guarding a pawn, protecting a square, or maintaining piece coordination—to a square where it serves no immediate defensive purpose, creating an instant tactical vulnerability. In 2/6 cases (Bf3 abandoning c4 pawn defense, Rad1 abandoning a2 pawn defense), the piece was the sole guardian of a specific pawn that gets immediately captured. In 2/6 cases (Nd7 removing the f6-knight guarding g5/h7, Na4 removing the c5-knight that controlled the kingside dark squares), a knight leaves a strong central/defensive outpost for a passive or rim square, collapsing king safety. In 1/6 cases (Nxb4), a centralized knight leaves its safe d5 post for an exposed square where it falls to a double attack. In 1/6 cases (h3), a tempo-wasting move fails to address an existing alignment vulnerability. The moves all appear superficially purposeful—prophylaxis, piece activation, material gain, rook doubling—but fatally neglect the defensive duty the piece was performing.
analysis.move_pattern: A piece (knight, bishop, or rook) moves away from a square where it was defending a pawn, guarding key squares around the king, or maintaining piece coordination; often to the rim, to capture a peripheral pawn, or to a 'more active' diagonal/file
analysis.why_bad: The piece was the sole or primary defender of a critical point (pawn, square complex, or coordination); removing it creates an immediate tactical vulnerability—hanging pawns, undefended pieces, king safety collapse, or exposed piece on the new square—that the opponent exploits in one move.
sub_patterns: Knight leaves central outpost for rim/passive square, collapsing defensive coverage (Nd7, Na4, Nxb4)
Bishop/rook moves off defensive square leaving pawn immediately hanging (Bf3 undefends c4, Rad1 undefends a2)
Tempo-wasting pawn push ignores existing tactical alignment requiring immediate attention (h3)

analysis.label: Moving a piece to a seemingly purposeful but actually irrelevant square, abandoning its critical defensive or offensive role and wasting a key tempo.
analysis.description: This feature fires on moves where a player voluntarily repositions a piece to a square that appears active or natural but actually serves no critical function in the position, while the piece's departure from its current role (or failure to reach the correct square) gives the opponent a free tempo to execute their plan. In 8/8 analyzed positions, the blunder is explicitly tagged as 'tempo_loss' — the piece moves somewhere that looks reasonable but doesn't address the position's most urgent demand. Examples include: a queen going to h7 targeting irrelevant pawns while the king is exposed (Position 1), a knight jumping to g6 abandoning defense of a hanging rook (Position 3), a king marching to h4 toward the edge instead of centralizing (Position 7), a rook going to g7 blocking its own king's escape (Position 9), a rook moving to a6 abandoning its critical f6 defensive post (Position 12), and a queen landing on e2 when three other squares (Qc2/Qd3/Qg4) all enable a decisive sacrifice (Position 13). The punishment consistently involves the opponent exploiting the tempo to advance passed pawns, infiltrate with the king, or execute tactical blows the misplaced piece can no longer prevent.
analysis.move_pattern: Any piece type moving to a square that appears active but is functionally irrelevant — often sideways, backward, or to the rim — abandoning the piece's critical role in the current position
analysis.why_bad: The piece abandons its most important function (defending a key square, enabling a tactic, blocking infiltration, or maintaining escape routes) to land on a square where it neither attacks anything meaningful nor prevents the opponent's primary plan, effectively gifting the opponent a free tempo to execute their strategy.
sub_patterns: Queen moving to offside square targeting irrelevant material while king is exposed
Piece retreating to passive back-rank square when forward action is needed
Rook abandoning a critical defensive file/rank for an apparently active but useless square
King walking toward the board edge when centralization is required
Piece developing to a natural-looking square that doesn't enable the position's key tactical idea

analysis.label: Pieces moved aggressively to g4 or g5 that abandon critical defensive or tactical duties for non-forcing kingside pressure.
analysis.description: This feature fires on moves that relocate pieces to the g4 or g5 squares (5/7 positions explicitly: Qg5, Ng4, Rg4, Rg5, Qg5) or make similarly aggressive-looking but non-forcing flank advances (a4, h5 in the remaining 2/7). In all cases, the move appears to create kingside attacking potential but is actually a tempo loss that abandons something more urgent. In Position 1, Qg5 abandons protection of c3/d4/f2. In Position 2, Ng4 removes the critical f6 defender, allowing Rxb7. In Position 3, Rg4 is a slow activation missing Qxh4 capturing a hanging piece. In Position 11, Rg5 wastes the crucial tempo needed to play Rd1 attacking the bishop (missing mate-in-8). In Position 13, Qg5 undefends the e4 pawn, allowing Rxe4. The pattern extends to pawn moves (a4 missing mate, h5 leaving g6 undefended) that share the same 'looks aggressive but misses the point' quality. Average cp_loss is 2802, reflecting that these positions often had narrow best-move paths (avg 1.9 good moves).
analysis.move_pattern: Piece (Queen, Rook, or Knight) moves to g4 or g5; occasionally a flank pawn advance (a-file or h-file) with the same aggressive-but-non-forcing character
analysis.why_bad: The move creates no concrete forcing threat, giving the opponent a free tempo to either exploit newly undefended squares/pieces, escape a mating net, or reposition defensively. The piece on g4/g5 attacks something non-critical while abandoning protection of something essential.
sub_patterns: Queen to g5 abandoning central/pawn defense
Knight/Rook to g4 leaving critical defensive post
Rook to g5 missing a more forcing rook move (Rd1)
Flank pawn push missing forced tactical sequence

analysis.label: Playing a plausible but non-urgent move in a position where one specific time-critical action is required, resulting in catastrophic tempo loss.
analysis.description: This feature fires on positions where the player chooses a 'natural-looking' or 'reasonable' move that addresses a secondary concern while ignoring the single most urgent priority. In 9/11 positions, the analysis explicitly tags 'tempo_loss' as the core issue. The critical pattern: positions with very few good moves (avg 1.7) where timing is everything - advancing a passed pawn (positions 1,3,5,6,8), maintaining forcing checks (position 4), capturing hanging material (positions 7,15), or resolving tactical tension (position 9). Instead, players chose centralizing moves (Ne5, Qc4), rerouting pieces (Ng5, Ne8), supporting secondary targets (Rc2, Ra4, Rf7), or prophylactic pawn pushes (a6, d5). The endgame dominance (8/11 positions) confirms that tempo sensitivity is the key trigger, as endgames are where single-tempo errors most dramatically swing evaluations. The moves themselves span all piece types and directions, but uniformly share the property of being non-forcing and non-addressing of the position's critical demand.
analysis.move_pattern: Any piece type moving to a plausible but non-forcing square; typically not a check or tactically necessary capture; diverse directions but uniformly 'slow' moves that don't execute the position's one critical action
analysis.why_bad: These moves waste an irreplaceable tempo in positions where only one specific urgent action maintains the advantage - whether advancing a passed pawn, capturing hanging material, maintaining a forcing check sequence, or resolving tactical tension. The opponent then seizes the initiative with the gained tempo, either creating counterplay (perpetual checks, passed pawn races) or consolidating a defensive setup.
sub_patterns: Failing to advance a passed pawn when tempo is critical in a pawn race
Quiet centralizing move instead of maintaining forcing check sequence
Removing a critical defensive piece to 'improve' it positionally
Prophylactic pawn move ignoring concrete hanging material
Repositioning a well-placed piece to address a secondary threat

analysis.label: Playing a quiet repositioning move when the position urgently demands an immediate tactical engagement (usually a capture or direct confrontation).
analysis.description: In all 6 positions, the player chose a non-forcing piece or pawn repositioning move while ignoring a critical tactical demand. In 3/6 cases (h6, Rdf8, Rb8), the best move was a pawn capture resolving central tension or eliminating a dangerous enemy piece (fxg4, dxe4, dxe5). In 2/6 cases (Ba5 x2), the piece abandoned a critical defensive post (c3 guarding the a3 check square) to chase a secondary target. In 1/6 cases (Qf6), a piece was placed on a square creating a new tactical target (Nd5 fork). The common thread is that each move treats the position as having time for preparatory play when in reality an immediate concrete tactical response was essential. All 6 moves are quiet (no checks, no captures, no direct threats), yet 5/6 positions had forcing tactical sequences available to the opponent that the move either enabled or failed to prevent.
analysis.move_pattern: Quiet piece/pawn repositioning (no capture, no check) to a secondary square while a critical capture, tension resolution, or defensive duty is ignored
analysis.why_bad: These moves waste a critical tempo in positions with urgent tactical demands—either abandoning a defensive post that enabled opponent tactics (Ba3+ check sequences, Qd6 invasion, Nc6 fork), failing to capture a dangerous enemy piece that then executes threats (Ne5+, Nxf7), or placing a piece on a newly vulnerable square (Nd5 fork).
sub_patterns: Piece abandons critical defensive post, enabling opponent check/invasion (Ba5 x2, Rdf8)
Slow pawn/piece move instead of capturing dangerous enemy piece (h6 instead of fxg4, Rb8 instead of dxe5)
Piece repositioned to square where it becomes a tactical target (Qf6 allowing Nd5 fork)

analysis.label: Playing an attractive-looking developing, centralizing, or aggressive move when the position demands the single specific prophylactic or concrete response.
analysis.description: This feature fires on positions where there is essentially only one good move (avg 1.4 good moves available) and the player instead chooses a natural-looking 'active' alternative. In 7/9 positions, the played move is a piece move to a seemingly attractive square (Nf5 to an outpost, Ne4 centralizing, Bc6 activating, Nh5 attacking a bishop, Bd6 developing) or an aggressive pawn push (h4, g6) while the position critically demanded something specific: a prophylactic pawn break (c4 in position 6, d5 in position 9, f6 in position 4), retreating a piece to safety (Bg6 in position 10, Kf2 in position 13), or a precise tactical sequence (g4 in position 14, Nc4 in position 2). The moves all look purposeful but fatally ignore the one urgent concrete need the position demands.
analysis.move_pattern: Piece moves to active/central squares or pawn advances that appear to improve the position, diverse piece types (knights, bishops, pawns, rooks), no consistent geometric direction
analysis.why_bad: These moves fail because the position has a single critical demand (stopping a threat, executing a specific break, saving a vulnerable piece, or maintaining a defensive resource) and the 'active' move wastes the one tempo available to address it, allowing the opponent to execute their threat or exploit the neglected vulnerability with devastating tactical effect.
sub_patterns: Centralizing a piece instead of addressing an exposed king (Rd1, g6, Nf5)
Developing/activating a piece while another piece hangs tactically (Bd6, Bc6)
Slow piece maneuver instead of a critical pawn break (Nh5 vs c4, g6 vs d5)
Pawn advance removing a defensive resource (h4 removing hxg3 recapture)
