Capturing/trading when quiet reorganization was required (Nxd5)

analysis.label: Moves that appear active or purposeful but squander tempo by ignoring the position's single most critical demand.
analysis.description: In 5/5 positions, the player chose a move that looked productive—a check (h4+), a capture (Nxe5), an aggressive pawn push (h4), a defensive rook move (Re2), or an active queen reposition (Qc7)—but each fundamentally ignored the one thing the position demanded. In Position 15, h4+ gave a flashy check but surrendered the crucial reserve h-pawn when d2 was winning (5/5 tagged tempo_loss). In Position 7, Re2 used the wrong piece to address the h2 threat when only the king (Kg3/Kh3) could properly contain promotion. In Position 12, Nxe5 grabbed a pawn greedily when quiet development (b3/Nc3) was essential. In Position 2, Qc7 repositioned the queen when Bd7 was the only move creating a forcing threat. In Position 5, h4 initiated an exchange that weakened f3 rather than centralizing the king. All 5/5 positions had very few good moves available (avg 2.0), indicating critical junctures where one specific action was required, and the blunder represents choosing 'activity' over 'accuracy' at precisely the wrong moment.
analysis.move_pattern: Varied piece types making seemingly active moves (checks, captures, attacks, repositions) that fail to address the position's primary tactical or strategic demand
analysis.why_bad: Each move wastes a critical tempo on a secondary concern—a check that gives away a key pawn, a capture that loses material, a rook move that allows check+promotion, a queen move that allows a tempo-gaining pawn advance—when the position required one specific urgent action that the player overlooked in favor of something superficially attractive.
sub_patterns: Giving check that surrenders a vital passed pawn resource
Using the wrong piece to address a threat (rook vs king for promotion defense)
Premature capture/tactical strike when quiet development maintains advantage
Queen repositioning that creates a target instead of developing the critical piece

analysis.label: Playing a superficially purposeful but non-critical move in a position where only one or two precise continuations maintain a large advantage.
analysis.description: This feature fires on moves where the player holds a significant advantage but wastes it by choosing a 'reasonable-looking' move that fails to address the position's concrete tactical demand. In 6/8 positions, the player had a winning or large advantage that was squandered to near-equality or a draw. The critical thread is that only ~1.5 good moves existed on average, meaning the position demanded precision, yet the player substituted vague activity for the one specific action required. Examples include: giving a check that helps the opponent's king escape to safety (Rf8+, Qg2+), retreating a piece when a capture wins material (Bc8 instead of Bxb2), playing a slow pawn move when a decisive exchange exists (g6 instead of Rxc4), ignoring hanging material (a3 with g5 en prise), creating tactical vulnerabilities with an aggressive-looking push (d4 allowing a fork), weakening protective pawn structure (b5 abandoning c6), and placing a piece passively when an attacking move traps material (Rc2 instead of Ra1). All 8 moves are tagged with tempo_loss in analysis.
analysis.move_pattern: Diverse piece types and directions; no geometric commonality. Moves include quiet pawn pushes (a3, g6, b5, d4), piece retreats (Bc8, Rc2), and forcing moves that backfire (Rf8+, Qg2+). The unifying pattern is non-optimal action in a low-optionality position.
analysis.why_bad: Each move wastes the one critical tempo needed to execute the winning idea, allowing the opponent to reorganize, escape danger, or neutralize the advantage. The position required a specific concrete action (capture, exchange, precise king move, or attacking move) and the chosen move gave the opponent breathing room to equalize.
sub_patterns: Giving a check that improves the opponent's king position rather than worsening it
Playing a slow/preparatory move when an immediate tactical shot wins material
Advancing a pawn that undermines the protection of one's own pieces/pawns
Placing a piece passively when an aggressive placement exploits a trapped/hanging target

analysis.label: King or piece moves in decisively won pawn endgames where the player prioritizes repositioning over immediate pawn advancement, often losing a tempo.
analysis.description: This feature fires on piece repositioning moves (predominantly king moves, 7/8 positions) in clearly won endgame positions with passed pawns. All 8 positions are endgames with evaluations ranging from +531 to +1177 (or equivalent for Black). The characteristic pattern is choosing to move the king (or occasionally a bishop, 1/8) rather than immediately advancing a passed pawn. In the clearest error cases (positions 6, 12), the optimal move was an immediate pawn push (Ke5 capturing toward the enemy pawn, or a6 advancing the passed pawn), while the player moved a piece to a 'natural-looking' but less urgent square. Even in positions where the king move was correct or near-optimal (positions 1, 2, 15 with 0-28cp loss), the common context is a won pawn race where the player must choose between king activity and pawn advancement. The dominant tactical motif across all analyses is 'tempo_loss' (tagged in 7/8 positions).
analysis.move_pattern: King moves (or piece moves) to central/advanced squares in endgame positions, not capturing, not checking - repositioning moves that don't directly advance a passed pawn
analysis.why_bad: In won pawn endgames, every tempo matters for the pawn race; repositioning pieces when the pawn should advance immediately allows the defending king to get closer to the promotion square or capture material, reducing the advantage through pure tempo loss.
sub_patterns: King retreats or moves sideways when pawn should push forward (Ke3, Kb3)
King overextends past optimal square, requiring later retreat (Kg7, Kh7)
Bishop repositions when passed pawn needs immediate advancement (Bg7)
King centralizes correctly but pawn push was equally or more urgent (Ke5, Kf7)

analysis.label: Quiet, non-forcing moves played in positions that demanded immediate active or tactical play, wasting critical tempo.
analysis.description: This feature fires on moves that are passive, prophylactic, or inefficiently forcing in positions where a concrete, active continuation was urgently required. In 9/11 positions, the primary tag is 'tempo_loss' - the played move addresses a secondary concern or looks superficially useful while missing the position's most critical demand. Examples include prophylactic pawn moves (h6, h3) played while central pawns hang, passive piece retreats (Qe8, Re2, Rh7) when active counterplay or forcing lines exist, king moves (Kh7, Kg8) that accomplish nothing constructive, premature quiet moves (a4, Na4) that ignore preparation or leave pieces undefended, and even checks (Qf5+, Bf6+) that are less efficient than available captures that deliver forced mate. In 8/11 positions, 'piece_activity' is a key tag - the best moves consistently involve activating pieces forcefully (Rf1, e6, Nxe5, Qxh6+, Qxe6+, Ng6, Qd4). The average 2.4 good moves available confirms these are narrow positions demanding precision, and the average 1906cp loss reflects catastrophic consequences of choosing passivity over action.
analysis.move_pattern: Mixed piece types (kings, rooks, queens, bishops, knights, pawns); typically short-range or retreating moves; non-capturing and non-threatening; occasionally inefficient checks that miss winning captures
analysis.why_bad: These moves waste a critical tempo by addressing a secondary concern (prophylaxis against future threats, passive defense, blocking a pawn) while ignoring the position's primary demand - whether that's capturing hanging material, delivering forced checkmate, generating essential counterplay, or contesting critical files/squares. The opponent then exploits the gifted tempo to execute their plan, escape danger, or consolidate an advantage.
sub_patterns: Prophylactic pawn moves (h3, h6) ignoring hanging central pawns
Passive piece retreats (Qe8, Re2, Rh7) abandoning active squares
King moves (Kh7, Kg8) that waste tempo without creating counterplay
Inefficient checks (Qf5+, Bf6+) missing winning captures with check
Premature pawn/piece advances (a4, Na4) without proper preparation

analysis.label: Pieces move to address a secondary target or plan while ignoring the position's most critical urgent requirement.
analysis.description: This feature fires on moves that look purposeful—attacking a pawn, centralizing, blockading, defending a piece—but fundamentally misidentify the position's priority. In 7/10 positions, the played move addresses a visible but secondary concern while neglecting a more urgent need: Rd5 attacks the d4-pawn instead of activating the king (Position 2); Rg2 attacks h2/g3 pawns instead of maintaining promotion-square control (Position 10); Kc5/Kb7 target specific pawns while abandoning critical defensive zones (Positions 12, 15); Re1 targets the e5-bishop while removing the d-file defender that kept h2 safe (Position 13); Bd4 centralizes instead of launching the decisive Ng4/Qh4+ attack (Position 5); Rge8 defends e7 instead of playing the dynamic a3 break (Position 11). The moves share the trait of being explainable and logical-looking—addressing something real on the board—but catastrophically wrong because they give the opponent a free tempo to execute a more important plan. Average cp_loss of 1124 with only 1.9 good moves available confirms these are critical positions with narrow paths where choosing the wrong priority is severely punished.
analysis.move_pattern: Any piece type moving to a seemingly purposeful square (attacking, defending, or centralizing) that commits it away from the position's primary demand; no consistent direction or piece type.
analysis.why_bad: The move gives the opponent a critical tempo to execute their primary threat (promotion, king advance, piece redeployment, simplification) because the moving piece has abandoned its most important function or the player has chosen activity on the wrong part of the board.
sub_patterns: Rook abandons defensive file/rank to attack secondary target
King marches toward one flank while opponent creates unstoppable threat on the other
Piece centralizes slowly when a concrete tactical solution was available
Piece commits to a square prematurely, allowing opponent a key regrouping tempo

analysis.label: Playing a slow, non-forcing move when immediate passed pawn advancement (or a tempo-gaining action) was the only way to maintain the position's advantage.
analysis.description: In 10/10 positions, the player had a critical time-sensitive plan available—almost always advancing a passed pawn or creating an immediate tactical threat—but instead played a quiet, non-urgent move addressing a secondary concern. The best moves consistently involved advancing a passed pawn (g6, h4, f3, c4, a4, b6, f5) or gaining tempo via check (Rg2+), while the blunders were slow pawn pushes on the wrong wing (a3, h5, a6, h4, c4 in 5/10), piece relocations away from the critical sector (Nc4, Nd6 in 2/10), or rook moves to passive squares (Rf2, Rb7, Rh8 in 3/10). Tagged as 'tempo_loss' in 9/9 analyzed positions and 'passed_pawn' in 8/9. The positions are overwhelmingly endgames (8/10) with very few good alternatives (avg 1.3), meaning one wasted tempo was catastrophic—typically allowing the opponent's king to reach a blockading square or enabling decisive counterplay that didn't exist one move earlier.
analysis.move_pattern: Quiet, non-forcing moves (pawn pushes, piece relocations, rook lifts) that don't create immediate threats, typically on the opposite wing or sector from where the decisive action is needed
analysis.why_bad: In race-type positions (especially endgames with passed pawns), one tempo determines whether the pawn promotes or gets blockaded. These moves waste the critical tempo on a non-urgent plan, allowing the opponent to reorganize defensively (king reaches blockade square, counterplay materializes, or pieces activate with tempo).
sub_patterns: Quiet pawn push on wrong wing instead of advancing passed pawn
Knight relocation away from critical sector when pawn push wins
Rook move to passive square when check or pawn advance was decisive
Preparatory move when immediate execution was required

analysis.label: Moves that catastrophically compromise the player's own king safety in positions where exactly one defensive resource exists.
analysis.description: This feature activates on moves that fatally worsen the player's king safety in positions demanding a single precise defensive move. In 5/5 positions, exactly one good move was available, and the chosen move instead created or exacerbated a lethal vulnerability around the player's king. The punishments include immediate checkmate (3/5 positions: Kd1 allows #-2, Ne5 allows #+1, c4 allows #-2) and severe material/positional collapse (2/5: h4 loses 159cp via central breaks exploiting undeveloped king, Kh2 loses 194cp via Qf4+ winning a piece). The moves take various forms—king retreating to a back rank (Kd1), king stepping onto a check-vulnerable diagonal (Kh2), removing a critical shielding pawn (c4), relocating a defensive piece (Ne5), or wasting tempo on a flank push while the king remains exposed (h4)—but all share the pattern of actively dismantling one's own king defenses in positions of extreme fragility.
analysis.move_pattern: Various piece types moving to squares that remove defensive coverage around the player's own king (king retreats to vulnerable ranks/diagonals, pawns advance away from king shelter, pieces relocate from defensive posts)
analysis.why_bad: Each move actively removes a critical element of the player's king defense (pawn shield, piece guard, or safe square) in positions where exactly one move preserves defensive integrity, allowing immediate forced mates or devastating tactical sequences exploiting the newly-created king vulnerability.
sub_patterns: King retreats to back rank allowing mating patterns (Kd1)
King steps onto check-exposed diagonal/file (Kh2)
Pawn advances removing king shelter, enabling infiltration mates (c4)
Piece relocates from defensive duty allowing smothered/support mate (Ne5)
Tempo-wasting flank pawn push while king remains dangerously uncastled (h4)

analysis.chip: Premature Pawn Push in Rook Endgame
analysis.label: Advancing a passed pawn prematurely in a rook endgame instead of first preparing with king activation, rook repositioning, or addressing the opponent's counterplay.
analysis.description: This feature fires on rook endgame positions where a player pushes a passed pawn one square closer to promotion without adequate preparation, when a preparatory move (king activation, rook redeployment, or neutralizing the opponent's threats) was required first. In 9/11 positions, the blunder is a literal pawn advance toward the promotion square (b2, c2, c7, h2, d2, d7, f7); the remaining cases involve passive moves that prioritize the pawn over piece activity (Ra1 supporting the pawn, Kh7 instead of a decisive rook maneuver). The consistent punishment mechanism is that the premature advance either paralyzes the player's rook into babysitting the pawn (5/11 cases: both b2 pushes, c2, Ra1, and the c7 push), loses a critical tempo in a promotion race allowing the opponent to counter-promote or create mating threats (4/11: h2, both d2 pushes, f7), or leaves the pawn unsupported and capturable because the king hasn't arrived to escort it (2/11: c7, d7). All 11 positions are rook endgames, and in every case the correct approach involved prioritizing piece activity or king centralization before committing to the pawn advance.
analysis.move_pattern: Pawn push one square forward toward promotion (typically to 2nd or 7th rank), or passive piece move to support a passed pawn, in rook endgames
analysis.why_bad: The pawn advance either immobilizes the rook (which must now defend the pawn from behind), loses a critical tempo in a promotion race, or pushes without king support allowing the opponent to blockade/capture. In all cases, a preparatory move (king march, rook reposition, or addressing opponent's threats) was needed first to make the advance effective.
sub_patterns: Pawn to 2nd/7th rank paralyzing own rook as passive defender
Pawn push losing promotion race tempo (opponent promotes with check or creates mating threats)
Pawn advance without king escort allowing blockade or capture
Missing a tactical rook capture/reposition that the premature push forfeits

analysis.label: Playing a seemingly purposeful move that neglects the position's single most urgent defensive requirement, typically abandoning key squares or pieces needed for king safety.
analysis.description: This feature fires on moves where the player ignores the most critical defensive need in the position in favor of a move that appears active or constructive but fails to address the primary vulnerability. In 5/5 positions, king safety is a central concern that the played move fails to address. In 3/5 cases (Re8, Nxc3, Ba3), a piece moves away from or fails to reach a critical defensive post (the f-file/f6 square specifically in positions 1, 3, and 4). In 2/5 cases (g6, c3), the move either weakens the king position or wastes tempo when immediate king safety measures are required. The key connecting thread is that each move looks superficially reasonable—activating a bishop, challenging a file, grabbing material, advancing a passed pawn—but catastrophically misidentifies the position's #1 priority. With an average of only 2.0 good moves available, these are narrow decision points demanding specific defensive precision that the player fails to find.
analysis.move_pattern: Any piece type; moves directed away from the critical defensive zone (typically kingside/f-file area) or structurally weakening the king position; includes captures, pawn pushes, and piece relocations
analysis.why_bad: The move abandons, removes, or fails to establish a critical defensive resource (blocking a file, guarding a key square, maintaining a key defender, or securing king safety), allowing the opponent to exploit the now-unaddressed vulnerability with immediate tactical or positional punishment.
sub_patterns: Removing a key defensive piece from its post for material gain (Nxc3, Re8)
Misplacing a piece on an irrelevant square instead of the one critical defensive square (Ba3 instead of Bf4)
Creating structural king weaknesses when active defense is needed (g6)
Wasting tempo on an irrelevant advance when castling is urgent (c3)

analysis.label: Piece repositioning that inadvertently removes a critical indirect defense, enabling an immediate tactical exploitation (fork, discovered attack, or capture).
analysis.description: In all 4/4 positions, the player moves a piece to a seemingly active or natural square while failing to recognize that the move eliminates a crucial defensive resource. In Position 4, Nf3 removes the knight from g5 where its Nxe6 fork threat was indirectly shielding the e4 pawn from capture. In Position 9, Nf3 blocks the f1 rook's defense of the f4 pawn, creating self-interference that allows Qxf4+ with check. In Position 13, Qf7 abandons the queen's coverage of c7, enabling Nxc7+ forking king and rook. In Position 2, Ra5 ignores the lethal queen-king alignment on the c5-e7 diagonal, allowing the blocking knight to leap away with Nb5+ as a discovered attack. Each move appears purposeful (attacking an opponent's piece, developing, defending a square) but fatally overlooks that the piece's prior placement was performing an invisible but essential tactical function.
analysis.move_pattern: Piece repositioned to an ostensibly useful square (knight to f3, rook to 5th rank, queen to f7) that disrupts own defensive coordination
analysis.why_bad: The moved piece was serving a hidden defensive role—either indirectly protecting a pawn through a latent counter-threat, blocking an attacking line, or covering a critical fork square—and its relocation exposes an immediate tactical vulnerability that the opponent exploits with a forcing move (check, fork, or discovered attack).
sub_patterns: Knight retreat that removes indirect pawn protection via eliminated counter-threat
Piece placement that blocks own rook's defensive file coverage (self-interference)
Queen/piece move that abandons coverage of a fork square
Active-looking move that ignores a discovered attack alignment

analysis.label: Playing a non-urgent or slow move in a time-critical position where an immediate forcing continuation (passed pawn advance, tactical strike, or checkmate) was essential.
analysis.description: This feature fires on positions where the player squanders a decisive tempo advantage by choosing a passive, preparatory, or non-forcing move when the position demands immediate decisive action. The most common pattern involves failing to advance a passed pawn at the critical moment (positions 1, 2, 5, 9, 10 — 5/11 positions explicitly required d5, d6, or c7 pawn advances), choosing slow wing pawn pushes over active piece play (positions 1, 3), moving the king when a pawn advance was urgent (positions 5, 9, 10), or selecting a superficially attractive check/capture over an immediately winning tactical blow (position 12). In 9/11 positions, 'tempo_loss' was explicitly identified as the tactical motif or primary tag. The consistent punishment is that the opponent uses the gifted tempo to establish a blockade (position 1: a4 fixing pawns), activate counterplay with a passed pawn (position 3: b7 advance), gain a key check (positions 9, 10: Rc4+), or simplify into a drawn endgame (position 13: Qxg5). The positions almost universally feature exposed kings and pawn-race dynamics where a single tempo determines the outcome.
analysis.move_pattern: Quiet non-forcing moves (pawn side-pushes, king retreats, piece repositioning) played instead of the required decisive advancing move (passed pawn push, forcing check, or checkmate)
analysis.why_bad: The position has a narrow time-critical window where one specific forcing move creates an irreversible advantage (unstoppable pawn, checkmate, winning tactical sequence), and the slow move allows the opponent to establish a blockade, gain a tempo-check, simplify favorably, or neutralize the time-sensitive threat.
sub_patterns: Failing to advance a passed pawn when king race timing is critical
Premature king activation walking into tempo-gaining checks on open files
Passive wing pawn pushes instead of active tactical blows exploiting exposed kings
Offering/allowing piece trades that eliminate the attacking side's dominant piece
Playing superficially attractive checks/captures while missing immediate checkmate

analysis.label: Quiet, non-forcing moves played in positions with unresolved tactical tension, allowing the opponent a concrete forcing refutation.
analysis.description: This feature fires on moves that pursue seemingly logical strategic goals (maintaining pins, activating pieces, gaining space, castling) while ignoring an immediate concrete tactical demand in the position. In 7/9 cases, the refutation begins with a forcing move (check, capture, fork, or discovered attack) that exploits a vulnerability the played move either created or failed to address. The played moves are uniformly non-forcing (no checks, captures, or direct threats) and tend to be 'one move too slow'—the position demanded resolving tactical tension first. Examples include Bh4 allowing g5 trapping the bishop (1/9), Qb7 walking onto a diagonal enabling Nf6+ discovered attack (2/9), O-O ignoring that exf3 wins a knight (6/9), Qe2 allowing Nxd4 fork (7/9), and Bh6 enabling Nxd5 discovered check (9/9). In every case, 2-3 good alternatives existed that addressed the concrete tactical situation—whether by resolving tension (Bxf6, dxe4, Nxe5), completing development safely (Ne2, Be3, Rf1), or consolidating (c3, Rd8).
analysis.move_pattern: Non-forcing piece repositions, pawn pushes, or routine developing moves (no checks/captures) in tactically charged positions with unresolved tension
analysis.why_bad: These moves ignore the position's most urgent tactical demand—whether that's a hanging piece, an exposed king, a vulnerable alignment on a file/diagonal, or a piece that can be trapped—giving the opponent time to execute a forcing sequence (fork, discovered attack, piece trap, or direct attack) that wins material or creates a decisive advantage.
sub_patterns: Piece moves to rim/vulnerable squares creating hanging or trappable pieces (Bh4, Nh4, Qb7, Qe2)
Premature pawn pushes that overextend or weaken key squares while ignoring development (c4, c4)
Slow positional moves that ignore opponent's impending forcing attack (Rb7, Bh6, O-O)

analysis.label: Developing a piece or making a preparatory move while ignoring critical central pawn tension (typically f-pawn vs e-pawn), allowing the opponent to capture the undefended center pawn with tempo.
analysis.description: This feature fires on opening positions where critical central pawn tension (most commonly f4 vs e5 or f5 vs e4 in King's Gambit/Vienna structures) demands immediate resolution, but the player instead makes a non-urgent developing or preparatory move. In 8/10 positions, the tension specifically involves the f-pawn attacking the e-pawn, and the blunder is addressed by the opponent simply capturing the undefended e-pawn (fxe5 or fxe4) with devastating tempo gains. The three Bc5 positions (1, 4, 6) and Bb4 (position 8) all develop bishops to flanks while leaving e5 hanging to fxe5. Positions 2, 3, and 5 (Bc4, c3, Nc3) similarly ignore Black's f5 tension against e4, allowing fxe4 to win material. Position 7 (g6) prepares a fianchetto instead of addressing the e5 tension. Position 9 (e5) closes the center rather than capturing to resolve tension favorably, and position 10 (Nxe5) miscalculates the tactical resolution. The average cp_loss of 308 reflects the catastrophic nature of leaving central pawns undefended.
analysis.move_pattern: Minor piece development to flank squares (c5, c4, b4) or slow preparatory moves (c3, g6, Nc3) when center pawns are directly attacked and undefended
analysis.why_bad: The unresolved f-vs-e pawn tension means the central pawn is hanging; once captured, the opponent gains a pawn AND tempo (typically attacking the knight on f6/f3), leading to forced retreats that compound the material loss with catastrophic development collapse.
sub_patterns: Bishop development to c5/b4 ignoring fxe5 threat in King's Gambit structures
White developing pieces (Bc4/Nc3/c3) instead of resolving f5xe4 tension
Flank pawn moves (g6) before addressing central pawn threats
Advancing e5 to close center instead of capturing to resolve tension

analysis.label: Playing a passive repositioning or prophylactic move in a position demanding immediate concrete action, allowing the opponent to seize the initiative or exploit an unaddressed tactical vulnerability.
analysis.description: In 7/7 analyzed positions, the player chose a quiet, non-forcing move (piece retreat, pawn push, or repositioning) at a moment when the position demanded either continuing a concrete attack or addressing an immediate tactical threat. The moves include queen sorties away from the critical sector (Qa4 abandoning kingside attack, Qd7 x2 leaving active squares), piece retreats from dominant posts (Nef3 abandoning e5 outpost, Bc7 passive bishop retreat), slow prophylactic pawn moves (a3 instead of Ne5), and piece placements ignoring tactical dangers (Bb3 allowing a trap, Qe7 allowing a sacrifice, Kh7 worsening king exposure). In all cases, the position had only 1-3 good alternatives (avg 1.8), indicating these were critical decision points requiring precise play. The average cp_loss of 1415 reflects that these tempo losses typically convert winning positions to losing ones or equal positions to hopeless ones, as the opponent gains time to execute central breaks, exploit weaknesses, or launch tactical combinations.
analysis.move_pattern: Non-forcing piece moves (queen repositioning, minor piece retreats, quiet pawn pushes, king walks) typically moving away from the critical sector of the board where immediate action is required
analysis.why_bad: Each move wastes a tempo that the position cannot afford, either allowing the opponent to execute a decisive central break (e5, c4), exploit a piece vulnerability (trapped bishop, hanging piece), launch a mating attack against an exposed king, or consolidate an advantage that the played move should have been preventing or punishing
sub_patterns: Queen moves to irrelevant flank instead of pursuing concrete attack
Piece retreats from dominant outpost enabling opponent's central break
Passive repositioning ignores immediate king safety threats
Quiet pawn move when concrete piece action (occupation of key square) is urgent
Piece placed on square vulnerable to trapping or tactical exploitation

analysis.label: Advancing a piece or pawn toward the opponent's side when the position demands addressing an immediate structural, tactical, or defensive priority.
analysis.description: In 5/6 positions, the player advances a piece or pawn forward (toward the opponent's king or territory) in a way that appears active but fatally ignores the position's critical demands. The moves include queen advances to h6 (positions 1, 5), a kingside pawn push g5 (position 3), a king advance Kg4/Kf7 (positions 5, 6), and a queen centralization Qe6 (position 4). In all cases, the correct moves involved addressing urgent priorities: resolving central tension (1/6), blockading a passed pawn (1/6), giving the king luft (1/6), keeping pieces on tactically safe squares (3/6), or supporting one's own pawns (1/6). The forward moves created vulnerabilities: trapped pieces via g4 (position 1), undefended pawns grabbed (position 3), tempo loss requiring the piece to return (positions 3, 6), back-rank mate enablement (position 4), and unfavorable simplification (position 5). The common thread is that these moves prioritize apparent aggression over the position's actual critical need.
analysis.move_pattern: Piece or pawn advances forward (toward opponent's territory/king), typically moving a queen to h6/e6, a king forward one rank, or a g-pawn push - all toward the kingside or central opponent-facing squares
analysis.why_bad: The forward move ignores the position's most urgent demand (resolving tension, defending critical squares, blockading, or maintaining coordination), resulting in exploitable tactical vulnerabilities, tempo loss, trapped pieces, or fatal simplification that dissipates existing advantages.
sub_patterns: Queen advancing to rim squares (h6) abandoning control of critical central squares
King advancing forward when it will need to return or blocks own pawns
Aggressive pawn push ignoring urgent central tension or defensive needs
Queen centralizing to a square that creates tactical vulnerability (back-rank interposition)

analysis.label: Black plays the visually obvious non-forcing move addressing the primary positional concern, missing a more precise forcing alternative (often an intermediate check or subtly better square).
analysis.description: In open positions with exposed kings and tactical tension, this feature fires when Black selects the most straightforward move to address the obvious goal—pushing toward promotion (g2), attacking a visible target (Bh6 hitting Ng5), centralizing (Kd4), developing to an active-looking square (Bf5), or directly covering a threat (Qf7)—without first inserting a more forcing intermediate move. In 3/5 positions, the best move involved a check (Nf3+, Qf2+) or direct attack on a key piece (Be6 hitting Rd5), while the played move was quiet. In 2/5 positions (Kd4 vs Kd5, Bf5 vs Be6), the error was choosing a square that looked equally good but was subtly worse due to concrete tactical vulnerabilities. All 5 positions feature open centers (4/5 explicitly noted) and king safety issues on both sides, creating environments where the tempo difference between a forcing and non-forcing move is magnified enormously. The cp_loss varies wildly (0 to 9620), suggesting the feature identifies the move TYPE rather than guaranteed blunder quality.
analysis.move_pattern: Non-checking, non-capturing Black move to an apparently active/logical square, typically along an open file or diagonal toward the center or opponent's side
analysis.why_bad: In tactically sharp open positions, the 'obvious' direct approach surrenders tempo or exposes the moved piece to tactics; an intermediate forcing move (check, capture, or attack on a key piece) would have maintained initiative or avoided vulnerability on the chosen square
sub_patterns: Missing intermediate check before a quiet advance (g2 without Nf3+, Qf7 without Qf2+)
Bishop developed to an exposed square one rank off from the correct square (Bf5 vs Be6, Bh6 vs Bb5)
King stepping to a square that allows immediate restriction (Kd4 allowing Rh5 cutting off ranks)

analysis.label: Playing natural-looking but non-urgent improving moves in positions where one specific concrete action is time-critical.
analysis.description: This feature activates on moves that appear positionally reasonable—prophylactic pawn pushes, piece repositioning, king centralization—but fatally waste tempo in positions where a single concrete action is urgently demanded. In 7/9 positions, the primary tactical motif is 'tempo_loss,' and the average number of good moves available is only 1.9, indicating extremely narrow positions where precision is mandatory. The moves tend to be quiet (non-forcing, non-capturing) retreats or sideways maneuvers: a6 (prophylactic pawn push), Ne1/Bc1/Bf4 (piece retreats from active squares), Kc6/Ke6 (slow king moves), Nf1+ (premature check without preparation). In each case, the opponent uses the gifted tempo to either consolidate a defense (5/9 positions: establishing blockades, centralizing kings, developing pieces), or advance their own concrete threats past a critical threshold. The positions share exposed kings on both sides (8/9) and open/semi-open files, creating time-sensitive races where a single wasted move is decisive.
analysis.move_pattern: Quiet non-forcing moves: piece retreats to back rank, slow king steps, prophylactic pawn pushes, or premature checks without preparation—generally moving away from or failing to engage in the critical sector
analysis.why_bad: These moves gift the opponent a crucial tempo to either establish a defensive blockade, centralize their king past a critical threshold, or neutralize the player's active piece coordination—converting winning/balanced positions into draws or losses because the position's narrow tactical window closes in exactly one move
sub_patterns: Prophylactic pawn moves ignoring king marches in pawn races
Piece retreats abandoning dominant central posts
King centralization when immediate pawn breaks are available
Premature checks without preparatory forcing moves
Bishop/knight repositioning when castling or development is urgent

analysis.label: Moving a piece away from a square or file where it was performing an essential (often hidden) tactical or strategic function, breaking position coordination.
analysis.description: In 8/8 positions, the blunder involves relocating a piece that was performing a critical duty—controlling a key file, defending a piece, maintaining a mating net, or enabling a tactical resource—to a square that appears active or purposeful but fundamentally undermines the position. Rooks abandon critical files in 5/8 cases (Rce2 leaves c-file losing Rc1+ resource; Rcd2 moves to a deflection-vulnerable square; Rbb7 creates forced exchange; Rd2 is passive when king safety is urgent; Rd1 abandons g-file mating net control). Knights leave essential posts in 2/8 cases (Nh4 leaves g6 area making Bg5 hang; Ng5 leaves f3 abandoning e3 control). A pawn move (c3) wastes the critical tempo needed for immediate Rf3 rook-lift attack in 1/8 cases. The common thread is that each piece was performing a 'hidden' function—not immediately obvious but tactically essential—and the player chose to redeploy it for a seemingly logical purpose (doubling rooks, attacking, centralizing) without recognizing the invisible duty being abandoned.
analysis.move_pattern: Piece (usually rook or knight) moves away from a key file, rank, or square to a seemingly active but tactically counterproductive destination
analysis.why_bad: The moved piece was the linchpin holding the position together—it was defending another piece, controlling a critical escape/invasion file, enabling a back-rank tactic, or maintaining a mating net—and its relocation creates an immediate exploitable tactical vulnerability (hanging pieces, deflection, king escape routes, lost tempi).
sub_patterns: Rook leaves critical file, losing key tactical resource (back-rank, mating net, deflection defense)
Knight leaves post, undefending adjacent piece or critical square
Slow/passive move when position demands immediate forcing action (tempo loss)

analysis.label: Superficially attractive moves (captures, promotions, development, activations) that catastrophically ignore the position's critical tactical demands in narrow positions with very few correct options.
analysis.description: This feature fires on positions where the player faces a razor-sharp situation with very few good moves (avg 2.0) and plays an instinctively appealing move that misses the critical tactical requirement. The moves all share a 'constructive' surface appeal: capturing material (Kxh2, cxb5), promoting with check (a1=Q+), developing a piece (Nh3), activating a rook (Rd6), or improving king position (Kf7, Ka5). In 5/7 positions, the correct alternative was more defensive or restrained (Kg1 retreating, Qa7 repositioning defensively, Qe4 creating an escape square, Kb3/Kc3 retreating toward center, Ra6 keeping the rook safe). In 6/7 cases the blunder walks into a forced mating attack or loses massive material, while the correct moves would have maintained survivable positions. The positions share exposed kings (7/7 have king safety issues noted) and narrow tactical corridors where the obvious/greedy choice is catastrophically wrong. The one exception (a1=Q+ missing Qb1#) still fits: the player chose the flashy move over the precise one.
analysis.move_pattern: Diverse piece types moving to 'active-looking' squares - captures, promotions, development moves, or piece activations that appear constructive but land on tactically vulnerable squares or ignore immediate threats
analysis.why_bad: The moves prioritize secondary goals (winning material, promoting, developing, attacking pawns) while ignoring the position's single most critical factor - typically an immediate mating threat, a hanging piece, or a forced tactical sequence that punishes the move. In these narrow positions with only 1-3 correct options, the 'obvious' choice is precisely the wrong one.
sub_patterns: King moves to exposed/edge squares (Kxh2, Kf7, Ka5) walking into mating nets
Piece moves ignoring back-rank/mating threats (Nh3, Rd6)
Flashy promotions/captures missing simpler wins (a1=Q+, cxb5)

analysis.label: Quiet or seemingly natural moves played in positions that demand immediate concrete action to address a critical tactical vulnerability.
analysis.description: This feature activates on moves that appear positionally reasonable but fatally ignore an urgent tactical requirement in the position. In 8/10 cases, the move leaves a key piece undefended or removes critical protection: Ne2 abandons defense of Nd3 (position 1), Qf3 leaves Nd4's sole defender attackable (position 3), e4 removes pawn protection from Nf3 (position 10), Kh1 makes gxf3 recapture impossible leaving Nf3 indefensible (position 8), Rg1 vacates e1 opening a fatal diagonal (position 5), fxe5 strips the e1-h4 diagonal of protection (position 4), Ba7 places the bishop where b6+ forces a losing exchange (position 6), and Be1 allows a forced trade into a lost endgame (position 7). The correct moves (averaging only 2.1 good alternatives) consistently involve either active concrete play (captures, checks, piece centralization) or directly addressing the specific defensive need. The blundered moves all prioritize general improvement, repositioning, or seemingly prophylactic ideas over the one thing the position urgently requires.
analysis.move_pattern: Mixed piece types and directions; all are non-forcing moves (no checks, mostly no captures) that fail to address the single most critical tactical obligation in the position
analysis.why_bad: Each move removes protection from a key piece or creates a fatal vulnerability (open line, pin, undefended piece), allowing the opponent to exploit the resulting tactical flaw through removing-the-guard, pins, diagonal attacks, or simple captures of hanging pieces
sub_patterns: Retreating an active piece to a passive square when the position demands maintaining or increasing aggression
Making a pawn move that removes protection from a piece on an open file
Placing a piece on a square where a forced exchange leads to a losing simplification
Moving the king to a square that makes recapture on a defended piece tactically impossible

analysis.label: Passive or non-forcing moves played in positions where advanced passed pawns demand immediate tactical action (checks, captures, or perpetuals).
analysis.description: This feature fires on positions where one or both sides have dangerously advanced passed pawns (typically on the 6th-7th rank) creating extreme tactical urgency, and the player chooses a quiet, non-forcing move instead of the required immediate tactical resource. In the significant blunders (9/13 positions), the correct move was a forcing check or capture: perpetual check resources were missed in 3/13 positions (Rg7+, Rf8+, Qe4+), tempo-critical checks before opponent promotion in 3/13 (Rh4+, Rd1+, Rb3+), immediate captures in 2/13 (Rxa7, Ra4), and tactical defense of vulnerable pieces in 1/13 (Bf4). The remaining 4/13 positions show near-zero cp_loss, indicating the feature also activates on quiet moves in promotion-heavy positions that happen to be acceptable. Virtually all positions (12/13) feature passed pawns on the 6th or 7th rank, and 11/13 are endgames with exposed kings.
analysis.move_pattern: Non-capturing, non-checking piece moves (king retreats, rook repositions to quiet squares, bishop development, queen to corner) in positions with advanced passed pawns on 6th/7th rank
analysis.why_bad: These moves squander critical tempo in positions where promotion threats create razor-thin timing margins. By playing quietly, the opponent gains the tempo needed to promote, advance a second pawn, or coordinate pieces for an unstoppable attack — whereas an immediate check or capture would have disrupted their coordination, forced a perpetual, or won decisive material.
sub_patterns: Passive king move instead of perpetual check drawing resource (Kd2, Ke6, Ke7 vs Rg7+/Rf8+/Rb3+)
Quiet rook reposition instead of tempo-gaining check before opponent promotes (Rh1, Rc1, Re1 vs Rh4+/Rd1+/Ra4)
Wrong capture/move order allowing opponent's pawn to advance with tempo (Rb7 vs Rxa7, Qa1 vs Qe4+)

analysis.label: Playing a seemingly natural move that fails to address the king's critical vulnerability to checks or tactical exploitation along open lines.
analysis.description: This feature activates when a player makes a move that ignores an urgent king safety issue in positions with exposed monarchs and open files/diagonals. In 7/9 positions, both kings are explicitly noted as exposed with weak or absent pawn shields. The played moves are diverse in type (knight retreats, pawn pushes, bishop moves, king moves) but share the common failing of not addressing the most critical tactical vulnerability. In 7/9 positions, the refutation directly exploits the exposed king through checks (Qe5+, Ra8+, Re2+, g4+ discovered check, Rxf8+, Qe7+, Qa5+). The best moves in each position specifically address the king's vulnerability: blocking critical check lines (Ne3/Ne5 blocking the e-file in positions 1-2), moving the king to safety (Kc7 in position 5, Kd1 in position 12), or activating the king (Kg3 in position 3). The played moves instead pursue secondary goals—piece development, pawn advances, or seemingly safe retreats—that look natural but catastrophically ignore the immediate tactical emergency.
analysis.move_pattern: Any piece type moving to a square that does not shield the king or address open-line vulnerability; often retreating/passive placement or a pawn advance when king action is needed
analysis.why_bad: The move fails to address the king's exposure on open files/diagonals/ranks, allowing the opponent to exploit this vulnerability with immediate checks, discovered attacks, back-rank threats, or forcing tactical sequences that either win material or deliver checkmate.
sub_patterns: Knight placed on wrong square failing to block check file (e1 vs e3, e3 vs e5)
Pawn advance ignoring back-rank or king exposure (d4, a4)
Piece retreat to back rank where it's captured or enables mating attack (Bf8, Bg7)
King stepping into a square with converging tactical lines (Kf2 into discovered check)

analysis.label: In pawn endgames, moving the king or pawns away from the opponent's critical passed pawn to pursue one's own offensive plan instead of addressing the urgent defensive task.
analysis.description: All 7/7 positions are pawn endgames (or one bishop endgame) where the opponent has a dangerous advanced passed pawn requiring immediate attention. In every case, the player makes a move that ignores this threat—either advancing their own pawns (e5, a4, g5, f4 in 4/7), moving the king in the wrong direction (Ke4, Kc5 in 2/7), or capturing a non-critical pawn that pulls the king away (Kxf3 in 1/7). The correct move in each position was to use the king to race toward the opponent's passed pawn to blockade it (Kd6, Ke7, Kd3, Kc4, Ke5, Ke3) or to capture/eliminate the threat directly (gxh6). The average cp_loss of 450 reflects how in pawn endgames, a single tempo in the wrong direction is often the difference between drawing/holding and losing, since these positions have only 1.3 good moves on average—razor-thin margins where only one plan works.
analysis.move_pattern: King or pawn moves directed away from the opponent's most advanced passed pawn; moves toward one's own side of the board or toward one's own passed pawns rather than toward the critical defensive square
analysis.why_bad: In pawn endgames, king proximity to the opponent's passed pawn is the decisive factor in promotion races. Moving away—even to capture material or advance one's own pawns—loses the tempo race by exactly the margin needed, allowing the opponent's pawn to promote or reach an unstoppable position.
sub_patterns: King moving toward own counterplay instead of blockading opponent's passer
Advancing own pawns while opponent's passed pawn is closer to promotion
Greedy captures that pull king away from the critical defensive zone
Starting a pawn race with inferior king placement

analysis.label: Playing a routine developing move instead of a winning bishop capture on the d-file (Bxd6 or Bxd3) that wins material or creates decisive positional damage.
analysis.description: In 12/13 positions, the clearly best move was a bishop capturing an opposing bishop on d3 or d6 (Bxd6 in 8 positions, Bxd3 in 4 positions), where the capture wins material because recapture is impossible or unfavorable—typically because a knight blocks the queen's recapture path, or the capturing bishop escapes to a3 preventing castling. Instead, players chose routine developing moves (Nf3, Ne7, Nbd2, Ne5, Bg3×2, h3, h4, e6, O-O-O, Bd6) or wrong-piece captures (Bxf7+ instead of Qxf7#, Be8+ instead of Qe8# in 2/13 cases). The positions nearly always feature a Slav/Semi-Slav structure with closed center, both kings in center, and mutual bishop tension along the d-file diagonal that demands immediate resolution. The average centipawn loss of ~1854 reflects that these captures are often the ONLY winning move (good moves available averages 1.0), and delaying even one tempo allows the opponent to resolve the tension on their own terms.
analysis.move_pattern: Any non-capture (development, pawn push, castling, or retreat) played when a bishop-takes-bishop on d3 or d6 wins decisively; occasionally wrong-piece-to-same-square (bishop instead of queen)
analysis.why_bad: The player prioritizes routine development or prophylaxis over an urgent, time-sensitive tactical capture where the opposing bishop on d3/d6 is undefended or cannot be adequately recaptured due to geometric blocking (own pieces obstructing recapture paths) or post-capture escape routes (Ba3 preventing castling). One tempo of delay allows the opponent to fix the vulnerability permanently.
sub_patterns: Bxd6 winning a piece because queen is blocked by own Nd7 from recapturing
Bxd6 followed by Ba3 retreat preventing castling and maintaining material gain
Bxd3 exploiting White's vulnerable light-squared bishop with tactical follow-ups
Wrong piece to same square (Be8+ instead of Qe8#, Bxf7+ instead of Qxf7#)

analysis.label: Playing a non-urgent or misdirected move in a sharp position that demands one specific immediate action, causing catastrophic evaluation swings.
analysis.description: This feature fires on moves that squander a critical tempo in positions where exactly one tactical priority dominates. In 8/11 positions, the player made a slow, peripheral, or misdirected move while ignoring the position's singular urgent demand: blockading a passed pawn (Ra2 instead of Rc8), exploiting an uncastled king immediately (b5, a6 instead of dxc4), preventing a devastating fork (Bc6 ignoring Nc7), sealing escape routes (Bd4 instead of Bh6), defending against an imminent mating threat (Qa4 ignoring Rxh7+), or maintaining an attacking initiative (Nh6 retreating instead of Nxh2 sacrifice). In 2/11 cases the blunder was a greedy capture that ignored a back-rank vulnerability (Rxf2, Rxc6). The positions share extremely low numbers of good alternatives (avg 1.7), indicating narrow tactical paths where any deviation is catastrophic. The average cp_loss of 2059 reflects that these tempo losses typically allow forced mates, decisive material wins, or complete positional collapses.
analysis.move_pattern: Varied piece types making quiet/peripheral moves (often to a-file, edge squares, or passive retreats) or greedy captures, in positions requiring one precise tactical response
analysis.why_bad: Each move ignores the position's single most urgent tactical demand—whether defensive (blocking a mate, preventing a fork, stopping a promotion) or offensive (exploiting an exposed king, maintaining attack momentum)—giving the opponent exactly the one tempo needed to execute a decisive threat.
sub_patterns: Queen/piece drifts to queenside ignoring kingside emergency (Qa6, Qa4, Ra2)
Slow pawn moves in sharp positions requiring concrete captures (b5, a6)
Greedy captures removing critical defenders (Rxf2, Rxc6)
Piece retreats abandoning active positions (Nh6, Nd3)
Piece placement to wrong square missing key geometry (Bd4 vs Bh6, Bc6 ignoring Nc7)

analysis.label: Active-looking moves that ignore critical king safety vulnerabilities, allowing devastating tactical refutations targeting the exposed monarch.
analysis.description: This feature fires on positions where the player makes a natural-looking, aggressive, or active move while their king faces an urgent and specific threat that demands immediate defensive attention. In 5/6 positions, the tactical motif is explicitly king_safety, and all 6 positions have tempo_loss as a tag. The average number of good moves is only 1.3, meaning these are razor-sharp positions requiring a single precise defensive response. In Position 1, Ng4 abandons a critical defensive knight allowing Rxb5+ sacrifice. In Position 4, Qc5 ignores the Rh8+ sacrifice on the open h-file. In Position 8, c5 ignores kingside dark-square collapse from g5 weakness. In Position 9, Nf6 allows e5+Ba3 preventing castling permanently. In Position 10, Qd2 loses tempo when urgent development/castling was needed. In Position 12, Ne4 allows capture leading to Ng5 tempo gain and e6 king attack. The common thread across all 6/6 positions is that each move pursues an offensive or positional idea that appears logical in isolation but catastrophically ignores the one critical defensive requirement of the position.
analysis.move_pattern: Various pieces (knights, queens, pawns) making forward/active moves to seemingly useful squares, ignoring defensive requirements
analysis.why_bad: The position demands a single precise defensive move addressing king safety, but the player instead makes an active-looking move that either removes a key defender, loses critical tempo, or allows the opponent to execute a tactical blow (often a sacrifice) against the vulnerable king.
sub_patterns: Knight moves away from key defensive square enabling king sacrifice
Queen repositions to irrelevant square while kingside attack is imminent
Queenside pawn advance ignoring kingside pawn structure collapse
Natural development to square that allows tempo-gaining pawn advance preventing castling
Centralization move that allows forced capture + exposed piece + king breakthrough

analysis.label: Moves that waste a critical tempo by addressing a secondary concern while the opponent's primary passed pawn threat goes unchecked.
analysis.description: This feature fires on positions—predominantly endgames (6/7)—where dangerous passed pawns create urgent promotion threats, but the player makes a 'natural-looking' move that fails to address the most pressing danger. In 6/7 positions, the blunder involves losing decisive tempo against passed pawn threats through various mechanisms: blocking the wrong pawn (Bg6 targets g-pawn while d6 promotes), pushing a slow pawn instead of a forcing move (b6 ignores back-rank/c2 promotion; h5 misses decisive Nd8), moving the king away from the required blockade square (Kf8 retreats from h8; Ke4 abandons f3), grabbing material while abandoning defensive duties (Nxd4 removes f3 knight-guardian), or placing the wrong piece on the correct square (Be5 when Ke5 was needed). All 7 positions share the pattern of a tempo-critical moment where one wasted move allows the opponent to advance/promote unstoppably. Tags confirm: tempo_loss appears in 6/7 analyses, passed_pawn in 6/7.
analysis.move_pattern: Any piece type moving to address a secondary positional concern—often a bishop or king repositioning passively, a non-forcing pawn push, or a material-grabbing capture—when the position demands immediate action against the primary threat
analysis.why_bad: In positions with advanced passed pawns, a single wasted tempo is often the difference between holding and losing; these moves address the wrong threat or make non-forcing plays, giving the opponent time to advance the critical pawn to promotion or achieve a decisive positional breakthrough
sub_patterns: Blocking/targeting the wrong passed pawn while the more dangerous one advances
Slow pawn pushes when a forcing piece move solves the position
King moving away from the required blockade or defensive square
Material-grabbing capture that removes a key defensive piece
Placing the wrong piece on the correct square (bishop vs king)

analysis.label: Moving a piece away from its essential defensive or controlling role for an active-looking but misguided purpose, leaving a key asset immediately exploitable.
analysis.description: In 5/6 positions, the blundering move directly removes a piece from a square where it was performing a critical function—defending another piece, blockading a pawn, or controlling a key invasion square. Position 1: Nd5 abandons the c3-knight's defense of the e2-knight, allowing Rf2+/Rxe2. Position 3: Ke8 abandons the f7 blockade of White's passed f-pawn, enabling forced promotion. Position 7: Bxb5 leaves the c3-knight 'defended' only by a pinned b2-pawn, allowing Rxc3. Position 11: Na5 abandons c6's control over b5/d4, permitting the devastating Nb5-Nd6+ fork. Position 13: Rac1 removes the only defender of the a2-pawn, which is immediately captured. Position 12 (Qa5) fits a related pattern: the player makes an active-looking queen move instead of executing the urgent dxc3 capture, allowing White time to eliminate the d4 pawn with Qxd4. All moves appear purposeful (centralization, file control, pressure, captures) but fatally neglect the piece's current defensive obligation.
analysis.move_pattern: Any piece type moving away from its current square where it defends/blockades/controls something critical, typically toward a more 'active' or aggressive-looking destination
analysis.why_bad: The moved piece was the sole or critical defender of an important asset (piece, pawn, or key square), and its departure creates an immediate tactical vulnerability—a hanging piece, unstoppable passed pawn, or invasion opportunity—that the opponent can exploit with one forcing move.
sub_patterns: Knight leaves defense of another piece for 'active' centralization
Rook/king leaves defense of a pawn for file contest or retreat
Piece leaves control of key invasion square allowing fork/infiltration
Wrong piece captures, leaving the critical piece still on its vulnerable square
Tempo wasted on non-urgent activity instead of executing critical tactical blow

analysis.label: Premature pawn advance in king-and-pawn endgames that offers an exchange destroying White's winning structural advantage.
analysis.description: All 5/5 positions are pure king-and-pawn endgames where White plays an aggressive-looking pawn advance that directly confronts an enemy pawn, allowing the opponent to capture and eliminate the very tension or structural advantage that underpinned White's winning position. In Position 1 (e5), the exchange destroys connected pawns creating a theoretical draw; in Position 4 (f4), it releases central tension and deflects the king; in Position 5 (h4), it opens a king highway for Black through f5-e4; in Position 6 (b5), it weakens c4 allowing a zwischenzug; in Position 10 (d6), it frees Black's trapped king from its cage. In all cases (5/5), the correct approach was either a king move or a pawn advance on a different flank, maintaining the tension that was the source of the advantage.
analysis.move_pattern: Single-step pawn advance pushing directly toward or adjacent to an enemy pawn, creating an immediate recapture opportunity for the opponent
analysis.why_bad: The pawn exchange eliminates the structural tension, connected pawn duo, or positional bind that constituted White's entire winning advantage, often also granting the opponent's king critical activity or simplifying to a theoretical draw.
sub_patterns: Destroying connected pawn pair via exchange (e5/fxe5)
Releasing central tension that freed opponent's king (f4/exf4)
Opening king invasion paths through captured pawn's square (h4/gxh4)
Freeing trapped king from geometric cage (d6/cxd6)
Creating tactical vulnerability on vacated square (b5 weakening c4)

analysis.label: Natural-looking moves that miss the one precise continuation required in critical positions where only 1-2 moves maintain the evaluation.
analysis.description: This feature fires on moves that pursue a reasonable strategic concept (centralization, space gain, king safety, attacking the 7th rank) but execute it imprecisely—wrong square, wrong piece, or wrong move order—in positions where extreme precision is demanded (avg 2.0 good moves available). In 6/8 positions, a much more forcing alternative existed (Ba3+, Re7, Nd5, Rg6, Qf6+, Kf2) while the played move was the 'quiet' or 'general' version of the same idea. Examples include Ke2 instead of Kf2 (one square difference between winning and drawing via perpetual check), f5 instead of e5 (wrong pawn fails to restrict the enemy king), Rcc7 instead of Re7 (doubling on 7th rank looks natural but is pure tempo loss when a tactical blow existed), and Re5 instead of Rg6 (correct plan executed in wrong move order). The positions uniformly punish the lack of concreteness: 6/8 feature 'missed tactic' in their tags, and 6/8 feature 'tempo loss' as the opponent exploits the non-forcing nature of the move.
analysis.move_pattern: Quiet piece/pawn moves to plausible-looking squares, typically one square off from optimal or pursuing the right plan with the wrong execution order; no checks or forcing moves played when available
analysis.why_bad: The positions demanded concrete, forcing play (checks, direct attacks, precise square selection) but the player defaulted to a superficially reasonable alternative that either allows the opponent to consolidate, creates tactical vulnerabilities, or wastes the critical tempo needed to maintain advantage
sub_patterns: Wrong adjacent square for king safety (Ke2 vs Kf2)
Wrong pawn advance (f5 vs e5, e5 vs Nd5)
Wrong rook destination or move order (Rcc7 vs Re7, Re5 vs Rg6)
Queen to vulnerable square instead of forcing move (Qe6 vs Ba3+, Qxd5 vs Qf6+)

analysis.label: Playing a passive piece move (king walk or bishop repositioning) when the position demands an immediate pawn advance or concrete tactical action.
analysis.description: In all 4 positions, the player chose a quiet, non-forcing piece move instead of executing a critical pawn advance or tactical strike that the position demanded. In 3/4 cases the best move was a decisive pawn push (e6 in position 11, b5 in position 12, Rb8 enabling b6 in position 7), while position 10 required Nb5 with immediate tactical threats. The played moves were passive: king retreats (Kf2, Kc1) or bishop repositioning (Be2, Bb5+) that wasted the critical tempo needed to execute the winning plan. In position 12, the pointless check Bb5+ actually enabled ...c6 permanently blocking the b5 pawn advance. In position 7, Kf2 abandoned defense of h4. In position 11, Kc1 gave Black time for the crushing ...b2. In position 10, Be2 allowed Black to consolidate with natural development. The common thread (4/4) is prioritizing 'piece improvement' over the concrete forcing continuation that the position required.
analysis.move_pattern: Quiet king retreat or bishop development/check (non-forcing piece moves to passive squares) when a pawn advance or active piece jump was available
analysis.why_bad: Wastes the critical tempo needed to execute a winning pawn advance or tactical strike, allowing the opponent to either create counterplay, consolidate their position, or permanently prevent the intended breakthrough
sub_patterns: King retreat instead of pawn push (Kf2, Kc1)
Passive bishop move instead of pawn advance (Be2, Bb5+)
Pointless check that enables opponent's defensive resource

analysis.label: Moves that waste a vital tempo in positions with exposed kings, allowing the opponent to escape or neutralize the attack.
analysis.description: All three positions feature exposed kings where the timing of each move is paramount, yet the played moves squander a critical tempo. In 3/3 cases, the analyses identify 'tempo_loss' as a core error. In Position 1, Rg6+ is a hollow check that shortens White's survival by 5 moves instead of the constructive Re8+ plan. In Position 2, Nc3 is a superficially forcing fork easily sidestepped by Qe1, wasting Black's initiative when Qa5 created unstoppable threats. In Position 3, Be3 voluntarily abandons the d4 bishop's control of g7, giving the exposed king an escape square and dissolving a forced mate-in-9. The narrow average of 1.7 good moves confirms these are positions demanding precise concrete action, where one wasted tempo collapses the position. The common thread is playing moves that appear purposeful (check, fork, development) but fail to address the single most critical factor—maintaining pressure on the vulnerable king.
analysis.move_pattern: Various piece moves (rook check, knight fork, bishop retreat) that appear active or forcing but waste tempo in king-attack positions
analysis.why_bad: Each move loses a critical tempo that allows the opponent's vulnerable king to escape, find safety, or neutralize the attack, converting winning/defending positions into significantly worse outcomes
sub_patterns: Hollow checks that achieve nothing constructive (Rg6+)
Superficially forcing forks easily sidestepped (Nc3)
Quiet retreats abandoning control of key king escape squares (Be3)

analysis.label: Playing a non-forcing major piece centralization when an immediate check or checkmate was available against an exposed king.
analysis.description: In all 3/3 positions, Black plays a major piece (queen or rook) to a central or 'active-looking' square (Qf5, Rc2, Qc5) instead of delivering an available immediate check or checkmate against White's exposed king. In position 4, Rh3# was a one-move checkmate; in positions 1 and 7, checks (Qf4+ and Qe2+) would force the enemy king into worse squares and maintain maximum pressure. The moves played all share the characteristic of being positional centralizations—placing the piece on a 'nice' square that controls space—but without the forcing tempo of a check. In 3/3 cases, the opponent's king was exposed (h2, h5, e4), and the strongest continuation exploited that exposure with an immediate forcing move. The cp_loss ranges from trivial (4cp) to catastrophic (9402cp for missing mate-in-one), but the underlying decision pattern is identical.
analysis.move_pattern: Major piece (queen/rook) moves to a central square (c5, f5, c2) without giving check, when a check or checkmate was available on a different square along a rank or diagonal
analysis.why_bad: Non-forcing centralizing moves surrender tempo to an exposed king, allowing it to escape to safety or improve its position, when an immediate check would either deliver mate or force the king into a progressively worse box
sub_patterns: Queen centralizes instead of checking exposed king
Rook moves laterally instead of delivering back-rank/file mate
Positional placement when forcing sequence wins

analysis.label: Moving a piece or pawn that was silently protecting the king, opening a line that allows the opponent's queen to deliver devastating checks or captures.
analysis.description: This feature fires on moves that look constructive (centralizing, advancing, developing) but fatally remove a piece or pawn performing a hidden defensive function—usually king protection. In 7/9 positions, the moved piece/pawn was directly shielding the king from queen checks: g5 and g6 remove g-pawn shelter (2/9), f3 opens the second rank (1/9), Nf6 unblocks a check diagonal (1/9), Kc3 walks into a mating zone (1/9), Rc3 allows king deflection (1/9), and Qd7 ignores immediate king threats (1/9). The remaining 2/9 (Bd4, Bd5) involve placing pieces on squares that appear protected but are tactically hanging due to pins or open diagonals. The unifying mechanism is that the refutation in 8/9 cases involves the opponent's queen immediately exploiting the newly-created vulnerability via checks (Qh8+, Qf7+, Qg2+, Qe2+, Qa4+, Qd4+) or captures on the opened line (Qxd4, Qxd5).
analysis.move_pattern: Any piece or pawn moving away from a square where it blocked or shielded the king from queen access along a file, rank, or diagonal
analysis.why_bad: The moved piece/pawn was performing a crucial but non-obvious defensive function (blocking a check diagonal, shielding the king from perpetual, preventing queen infiltration on an open rank), and removing it gives the opponent's queen immediate forcing moves (checks, captures, deflections) that exploit the newly-opened geometry.
sub_patterns: Pawn advance removing king shelter (g5, g6, f3) allowing queen perpetual or invasion
Knight/piece move unblocking a dangerous diagonal to the king (Nf6 opening a4-e8)
King walking into exposed position where queen+pieces coordinate mating net (Kc3)
Piece placed on apparently-protected square that hangs due to pin or open line (Bd4, Bd5)
Ignoring immediate king danger to make a developing move (Qd7, Rc3)

analysis.label: Making committal or aggressive moves while the king remains dangerously uncastled in the center, allowing immediate tactical exploitation of king vulnerability.
analysis.description: In 5/6 positions, the player's king sits uncastled in the center, and rather than addressing this urgent weakness through castling or quiet development, the player makes a committal move that creates new vulnerabilities. The specific moves vary—aggressive kingside pawn pushes (g4 appears in 2/6 positions), slow flank pawn advances (b3 in 1/6, c4 in 1/6), a self-blocking knight development (Nc3 in 1/6), or a recapture that exposes the king to e-file tactics (Qxe7 in 1/6). The refutations consistently exploit the centralized king through checks along the a5-e1 diagonal (Bb4+ appears in 3/6 positions), pins, forks with tempo against exposed pieces, or direct file pressure. The best moves across all positions overwhelmingly prioritized castling (O-O appears as best in 2/6), development (Nd2, d4, Rc1), or consolidation. With an average cp_loss of 241 and an average of 2 safe alternatives available, these represent cases where obvious sound moves existed but the player chose premature commitments instead.
analysis.move_pattern: Various piece types - pawn flank advances (g4, b3, c4), piece moves blocking defensive pawns (Nc3), captures exposing own king (Qxe7) - all made before the king is properly secured or when the move creates immediate structural/tactical holes
analysis.why_bad: These moves ignore the urgent priority of king safety, creating tactical vulnerabilities (checks on weakened diagonals, pins, forks, open-file pressure) that opponents exploit immediately against the exposed central king
sub_patterns: Aggressive kingside pawn pushes (g4) with king still on e1
Quiet flank pawn moves (b3) weakening critical diagonals toward the central king
Piece placement blocking critical defensive pawn advances (Nc3 preventing c3)
Recaptures that place pieces on squares exposed to tempo-gaining attacks (Qxe7 allowing Nxd5)

analysis.label: Bishop moves to pin an opponent's knight in the opening but creates a greater tactical vulnerability (typically on f7/f2) that is exploited by a sacrifice or check-based fork.
analysis.description: In all 12/12 positions, the player moves a bishop to pin an opponent's knight (Bg4 pinning Nf3 to Qd1 in 8 cases, Bg5 pinning Nf6 to Qd8 in 2 cases, Bb4/Bb5 pinning Nc3/Nc6 to the king in 2 cases) while both kings remain uncastled in the center. The critical error is that this superficially active pin abandons defense of a critical square or places the bishop on an undefended square. In 8/12 positions, the refutation is a classic Bxf7+ (or Bxf2+) sacrifice followed by a knight fork (Ne5+, Ng5+, or Ne4+) that wins the pinning bishop back with interest. In 3/12 positions, the bishop lands on an undefended square and is won outright by a queen check (Qa4+ or Qa5+). All positions occur in the opening phase with both kings in the center, and in every case multiple safe developing moves were available (avg 2.8 good alternatives).
analysis.move_pattern: Bishop develops to 4th/5th rank on g-file or b-file to create a pin against an opponent's knight, while own king remains uncastled in center
analysis.why_bad: The pin abandons defensive coverage of f7/f2 (enabling a classic bishop sacrifice + knight fork) or places the bishop on an undefended square exploitable by a check, while the uncastled king provides the geometric conditions for the fork/winning combination to work.
sub_patterns: Bg4 abandons f7 defense → Bxf7+ Kxf7 Ne5+/Ng5+ fork wins bishop
Bg5 abandons f2 defense → Bxf2+ Kxf2 Ne4+ fork wins bishop
Bb4/Bb5 lands undefended → Qa4+/Qa5+ check wins hanging bishop
Knight leaves pin square enabling Qxg4/Qxg5 capture of now-hanging bishop

analysis.label: Moves that waste the decisive tempo in razor-thin positions where only one immediate forcing resource (check, pawn break, or piece doubling) draws or wins.
analysis.description: This feature fires on positions where the player had typically only 1-2 good moves (avg 1.7) and chose a 'reasonable-looking' alternative that squanders the critical tempo. In 7/9 positions, the correct move was a specific immediate forcing action: a perpetual check (Rg7+ in pos 5, Rd1+ in pos 14), doubling rooks on the 2nd rank (Ree2 in pos 8), an immediate pawn break (b4 in pos 9), a tempo-gaining check (Rf8+ in pos 4), or a precise piece placement controlling key squares (Bd3 in pos 13, Kg7 in pos 10). In 2/9 positions, the player gave checks that actually gifted the opponent the tempo (g5+ driving the king to e5, Qf5+ allowing Qd5+ counter-check). In all cases, the opponent then executes their own plan one tempo faster—promoting a pawn (3/9), centralizing/escaping the king (3/9), or activating a passed pawn (3/9)—resulting in a catastrophic evaluation swing averaging 367cp.
analysis.move_pattern: Mixed piece types and directions; the common geometric thread is that the played move does NOT interact forcingly with the opponent's king or critical pawn, while the correct move always does (delivers check, blocks a promotion path, or controls a key promotion/escape square)
analysis.why_bad: These moves give the opponent one free tempo to execute their winning/drawing/escaping plan—whether that's promoting a passed pawn, centralizing a king to safety, or advancing connected passers. The position's razor-thin nature (typically only 1 good move) means any non-forcing alternative immediately crosses a critical threshold.
sub_patterns: Passive king moves instead of immediate forcing checks or pawn breaks (Ke6, Kd2, Kg3)
Premature checks that drive the opponent's king to a superior square (g5+, Qf5+)
Rook repositioning that abandons a critical defensive/attacking duty (Rd8, Rg8, Rc1)
Bishop placement that fails to control the one critical square complex (Be6 instead of Bd3)

analysis.label: Playing a natural-looking or active move that addresses a secondary concern while catastrophically ignoring the single most critical requirement of the position.
analysis.description: This feature fires on positions where the player makes a plausible-looking move (centralization, development, pawn capture, active piece placement) that fatally neglects the position's most urgent priority. In 9/9 positions, the critical issue was clearly identifiable: a vulnerable king needing defense (positions 1, 2, 9, 11, 14), a passed pawn demanding attention (positions 5, 12), a pawn structure that must be preserved (position 3), or a piece placed on an unstable square ignoring concrete tactical obligations (position 7). The played moves uniformly look reasonable in isolation—knight to e5 for centralization, bishop development to b2/a3, king 'centralization,' pawn captures for material—but each ignores the one thing the position demands. The average of only 1.8 good moves available confirms these are narrow critical moments requiring precise action, and the average 2400cp loss shows the punishment is catastrophic when the priority is misidentified.
analysis.move_pattern: Any piece type or direction; the common geometric thread is that the move goes AWAY from where the critical action is (pieces leave defensive posts, kings move toward the wrong flank, captures occur on secondary sectors)
analysis.why_bad: The position has one overwhelming priority (defending the king, stopping a passed pawn, maintaining a critical blockade, addressing an immediate threat) and the played move addresses something else entirely, giving the opponent a free tempo to execute a devastating tactical blow or achieve a winning structural transformation.
sub_patterns: Removing a piece from a critical defensive post (Ne5 abandoning f3 diagonal block, Ne5 abandoning d3 file block)
King marching toward the wrong flank in endgames (Kd3 toward queenside, Kc5 missing pawn break)
Developing a piece to an unstable/irrelevant square while ignoring urgent needs (Ba3, Bb2)
Materialistic pawn captures ignoring attacking threats against own king (cxd4, e5)

analysis.label: Advancing an already-advanced pawn one more square, breaking a strong pawn formation or releasing tension, when piece improvement was needed.
analysis.description: All 6/6 positions feature a pawn that is already advanced (4th or 5th rank) being pushed one square further into enemy territory, destroying a stable pawn duo or chain that was providing long-term positional pressure. In every case, the best moves involved piece development, repositioning, or castling (6/6 had piece moves as alternatives), while the pawn thrust attempts an immediate tactical breakthrough that backfires. Position 1: g6 shatters the f5/g5 duo; Position 3 and 11: e6 sacrifices a strong e5 outpost pawn; Position 6: g5 overextends while the king remains uncastled; Position 2: d4 breaks the protective d3/c3 chain; Position 8: e4 releases central tension to the opponent's benefit. The analyses consistently identify 'premature attack' (4/6 explicit), 'releasing tension' or 'pawn structure destruction' as the core error, with opponents exploiting the weakened squares and material left behind.
analysis.move_pattern: Pawn advance (one square forward) of an already-advanced pawn (typically from 4th/5th rank to 5th/6th rank), pushing into opponent's territory
analysis.why_bad: The advancing pawn breaks apart a strong pawn formation that was exerting long-term pressure, releases tension that favored the player, creates tactical vulnerabilities (hanging pieces, exposed king), and gains nothing concrete because the opponent can capture or decline and consolidate with extra material or superior structure.
sub_patterns: Breaking a pawn duo by advancing one of the pair (g6 from g5/f5, g5 from g4/f4)
Premature e-pawn sacrifice pushing e5-e6 without supporting pieces
Central pawn advance releasing tension when piece development is incomplete
Attacking a piece with a pawn when the pawn's departure leaves other pieces undefended

analysis.label: Black plays a superficially active developing move (usually a bishop) while the king is vulnerable, allowing a forcing tactical blow that exploits king safety.
analysis.description: In 9/9 positions, Black's king is either uncastled (7/9) or dangerously exposed (2/9), and the player makes a natural-looking developing or repositioning move—predominantly bishop moves (6/9: Bd6, Bd6, Bc3, Be6, Bb4, Ba6)—that appears to contribute to piece activity but fatally ignores an immediate tactical threat against the king. The best moves consistently prioritize king safety: blocking dangerous diagonals (Nf6 in positions 1-2), castling (position 6), or keeping defensive coordination (positions 4, 8, 9). Instead, the chosen moves develop pieces to 'outward-facing' aggressive squares that neither shield the king nor prevent the critical tactical shot. The punishment typically involves queen checks along open diagonals (Qh5+ in 3/9), knight forks exploiting the exposed king (Nc7+ in position 7, Nf6+ in position 4), or winning undefended material now left hanging by the queen/piece displacement (Qxb7 in position 9). The average cp_loss of 1355 reflects how catastrophic it is to ignore king safety for cosmetic development.
analysis.move_pattern: Piece (usually bishop) moves to an apparently active square, directed away from the king's defensive needs, neither blocking a critical diagonal/file nor preparing immediate castling
