analysis.why_bad: The moves address piece development or activity while the king faces a concrete, immediate tactical threat (open diagonals, undefended squares, fork possibilities) that the chosen move does nothing to neutralize, allowing a forcing sequence that wins material or delivers checkmate
sub_patterns: Bishop develops to active diagonal while h5-e8 diagonal is open to queen check
Piece blocks king escape square enabling mating attack
Bishop repositions aggressively while allowing knight sacrifice destroying king cover
Non-developing flank move when f7/b7 is tactically vulnerable
Queen leaves defensive post exposing hanging pawns to double attack

analysis.label: Moves that pursue a superficially logical objective while fatally ignoring the single most urgent demand of the position.
analysis.description: This feature activates on moves that look reasonable in isolation—centralizing pieces, advancing pawns, capturing material, improving king position—but catastrophically miss the one thing the position demands. In 7/7 positions, exactly one critical task exists (defending a key square, addressing a passed pawn, exploiting a tactical window), and the player does something else entirely. The positions are narrow (avg 1.7 good moves), meaning there's little margin for error. In 3/7 cases a passed pawn needed urgent attention (positions 3, 6, 7). In 2/7 cases a defensive piece was moved from a critical guard duty (positions 1, 2). In 2/7 cases the player retreated or repositioned when concrete action was required (positions 4, 5). The average cp_loss of 3003 reflects that ignoring the #1 priority in these narrow positions leads to catastrophic consequences—including two forced mates.
analysis.move_pattern: Mixed piece types and directions; typically 'improving' moves (centralizing knight/king, advancing pawns, capturing material) rather than the required concrete action
analysis.why_bad: The position has exactly one critical demand (guard a square, stop a passed pawn, execute a forcing sequence) and the move addresses a secondary concern instead, giving the opponent a tempo to execute their decisive threat
sub_patterns: Abandoning guard duty of critical square (Nd5 leaving f1, Kb5 leaving b6)
Ignoring opponent's advanced passed pawn (h4 ignoring d6, Be1 ignoring d4)
Capturing poisoned material (Rxa8 walking into pawn promotion)
Making 'improving' moves when concrete forcing action wins (Kd2 instead of Rhd1)
Weakening pawn advance in position requiring development (f5 exposing bishop)

analysis.label: Moves that place a piece or king on a square that falls on an opponent's active attack line (diagonal, file, or rank), enabling an immediate tactical exploitation.
analysis.description: In 9/11 positions, the moved piece or king lands on a square that creates a critical geometric alignment with an opponent's piece, enabling a forcing response: Bxd5 opens the g5-c1 diagonal for a queen fork (position 1); Kc7 places the king on the c-file where White's rook delivers mate via Rc8# (position 3); Bd5 puts the bishop directly on the h1-a8 diagonal where the queen captures it (position 5); Be3 offers the bishop to the opponent's queen for free (position 7); Kg7 exposes the king to the Rg3+ rook lift (position 8); Rxc2 removes the rook from its attacking post enabling Nd5+ fork (position 9); Rf6 places the rook on the same diagonal as its own king, enabling a bishop fork via Be5+ (position 10); Kh2 steps onto the g1-h2 diagonal enabling Qg1+ perpetual (position 11). In each case, the move pursues a visible goal (capture, centralization, apparent safety, material gain) while overlooking that the destination square is tactically compromised by an opponent's line of attack. The remaining positions (Qxa7, Rc6, Bf5) involve a slightly softer version where the piece moves away from its critical defensive duty, enabling a positional or tactical break.
analysis.move_pattern: Any piece type moving to a square that falls on an opponent's active diagonal, file, or rank—often appearing natural (captures, centralizations, king retreats) but creating geometric vulnerability
analysis.why_bad: The destination square sits on an active attack line of an opponent's piece, enabling an immediate tactical exploitation (fork, capture, check sequence, or mate) that wasn't possible before the move. The player focuses on the apparent benefit of the move while failing to check the opponent's forcing replies along the relevant lines.
sub_patterns: Piece moves onto diagonal controlled by opponent's queen/bishop, getting captured or forked
King steps onto open file or diagonal enabling check-based tactics (mate, perpetual, fork)
Piece leaves critical defensive post to grab material, allowing opponent's forcing sequence
Wrong piece captures, removing the interposer needed against a subsequent check on a specific line

analysis.label: Queen delivers check from a suboptimal square, missing a more precise check or non-checking move that would have maintained critical geometric control.
analysis.description: In all 10/10 positions, the player delivers a Queen check that appears forcing but is tactically inferior. The common failure is choosing the wrong square for the check: in 7/10 cases a check from a nearby square (Qa8 vs Qa6, Qa1 vs Qa3, Qe1 vs Qe3, Qh6 vs Qf6, Qd5 vs Qe3, Rb1+ vs Qd1+, Qh5+ vs Qe4+) would have controlled a critical escape square or enabled a winning combination, while in 3/10 cases a non-checking move was superior. The checks consistently fail because: they don't control the key escape square the king needs to be denied (5/10), they drive the king to a safer square (4/10), or they displace the queen from a dominant post without concrete compensation (3/10). The average cp_loss of 2256 reflects that these positions are razor-sharp (avg 1.2 good moves available), where one-square differences in queen placement determine whether a forced mate, material recovery, perpetual, or positional advantage is achieved or squandered.
analysis.move_pattern: Queen check (often with capture) to any square, typically one square away from the optimal checking square, in positions where the king is exposed
analysis.why_bad: The check fails to control a critical square (usually the king's best escape route), allowing the opponent's king to reach safety or a better square, while a check from a different square or a non-checking move would have maintained geometric dominance over the king's flight path
sub_patterns: Check from wrong square misses fork/winning combination (Qa6 vs Qa8, Qf6 vs Qh6)
Check drives king toward safety rather than danger (Qb5+, Qf6+ in endgame)
Queen check loses perpetual by failing to control key escape square (Qe3 vs Qe1)
Check displaces queen from active central post for worthless tempo (Qxa3+, Qe4+)
Wrong piece checks first, ruining coordination (Qd1+ vs Rb1+)

analysis.label: Choosing an aggressive-looking or forward move that ignores the position's single most urgent tactical or strategic demand.
analysis.description: This feature fires on positions where the player has very few good options (avg 1.9) and selects a move that appears active or purposeful but completely misses the position's #1 priority. In 2/9 cases, the player missed checkmate in one (Qc7+ instead of Qc6#, Bb4+ instead of Bc1#). In 2/9 cases, the player captured with the wrong piece—using a pawn instead of the queen (gxf2+ vs Qxf2+, exd3+ vs Qxd3+)—sacrificing critical piece activity for a static pawn. In 3/9 cases (Nd2, dxe7, d5), the player advanced material or developed when king safety was the overwhelmingly urgent need (castling, breaking a pin, or defensive retreat). In 2/9 cases (a5, Kd5), the player pushed a pawn or moved the king away from material when king centralization or captures were required. The connecting thread is that the played moves all look reasonable or 'active' (giving check, advancing pawns, developing) but catastrophically miss the one thing the position demands.
analysis.move_pattern: Forward-moving or checking moves (pawn advances, captures with wrong piece, checks on wrong square, development moves) when the position demands one precise action
analysis.why_bad: These moves prioritize secondary objectives (giving check, pawn advancement, development, aggression) over the position's actual critical need—typically delivering immediate checkmate, maintaining piece activity on a key square, castling for king safety, or capturing available material. The positions allow almost no margin for error (avg 1.9 good moves), making any deviation from the critical action catastrophic.
sub_patterns: Capturing with wrong piece (pawn instead of queen) losing critical piece activity
Giving check on wrong square when immediate checkmate exists
Advancing pawns or developing pieces when king safety is the sole priority
Moving king away from capturable material or optimal centralization

analysis.label: Aggressive-looking moves (checks, advances, attacks) that fatally abandon a critical defensive or positional requirement the position demands.
analysis.description: This feature fires on moves that appear active or natural but catastrophically ignore the position's primary requirement. In 4/9 positions, a key defender is moved away from a critical square (Ne3 abandons d5 guarding the queenside; Ng4 removes f6 guarding f7 allowing mate; Bd2 leaves the a1-h8 diagonal enabling promotion; gxf4+ opens f4 for the opponent's king). In 3/9 positions, checks or pawn advances are played prematurely without proper preparation (h4 before the king reaches g3; g5+ before Re4+ reposition; Qf4+ giving escape squares instead of Qh8#). In 2/9 cases, tempo is wasted on purposeless moves when the position demands immediate action (h3 ignoring development crisis; Qc7 missing decisive checks). The average cp_loss of 2387 reflects that these positions typically have very few good moves (avg 1.9), making the 'obvious-looking' wrong choice catastrophic.
analysis.move_pattern: Mixed piece types and directions; typically moves toward the opponent (advances, attacks, checks) or retreats away from a critical defensive station
analysis.why_bad: Each move sacrifices a critical defensive function (guarding a key square, maintaining a crucial diagonal, keeping proper move order) for an illusory tactical gain; the opponent's refutation directly exploits the abandoned defensive requirement
sub_patterns: Removing a defender from a critical square allowing immediate tactics
Premature pawn breaks/checks before positioning pieces correctly
Pointless checks that give the opponent better squares or counter-tempo
Abandoning a critical file/diagonal allowing promotion or invasion

analysis.label: Moving pieces/pawns to ineffective edge squares instead of addressing critical king safety or coordination needs.
analysis.description: In all 3/3 positions, the player made a move to a peripheral or rim square (b4, Ng4, Na6) that ignored the most pressing positional demand—typically king safety or piece coordination. In 3/3 cases, the best moves involved improving existing piece harmony (king centralization in Position 6, knight centralization in Position 8, king escape in Position 11) rather than developing/advancing on the wing. In 3/3 cases, the played move resulted in the piece being immediately captured, chased back with tempo loss, or left completely disconnected from the critical battle zone. The common thread is a 'constructive-looking' peripheral action that wastes a crucial tempo while the opponent exploits the real vulnerability—whether that's an undefended pawn (b4 captured by Rxb4), a knight kicked by advancing pawns (h5 attacking Ng4), or a king left exposed while the knight sits uselessly on the rim (Na6 while Rf4/Qg8+ decides).
analysis.move_pattern: Piece or pawn moving to edge/rim squares (a-file, b-file 4th rank, g4) away from the critical zone of action
analysis.why_bad: These moves waste a critical tempo on non-urgent peripheral improvements while ignoring the position's most pressing need (king safety, piece coordination, or defending against immediate tactical threats), allowing the opponent to exploit the real weakness with tempo-gaining attacks.
sub_patterns: Knight to rim square disconnected from battle
Wing pawn push leaving material en prise
Knight to exposed square immediately chased by pawns

analysis.label: Plausible-looking moves that pursue a secondary goal while neglecting the position's most critical tactical or defensive requirement.
analysis.description: This feature fires on positions where the player makes a move that looks reasonable in isolation—developing a piece, attacking a target, moving the king—but catastrophically ignores the one thing the position truly demands. In 8/10 cases, there were only 1-3 good moves available, indicating critical junctures with razor-thin margins. The played moves typically address secondary considerations: Na5 attacks c6 but ignores central tension; Bd3 develops but leaves Nh4 tactically exposed; g3 challenges Black's h-pawn but neglects the stranded Nh1; c4 pushes a pawn but fails to prevent White's castling; Ne4 centralizes but goes to the wrong square versus Nc4; Bc4 develops toward f7 but walks into b5; Ra5 targets d5 but fails to restrain Black's king. In every case, the best move addressed the URGENT priority (activating trapped pieces 2/10, defending hanging pieces 2/10, avoiding exposed-king checks 3/10, resolving critical tension 2/10, preventing opponent's plan 1/10) while the played move pursued something plausible but non-critical.
analysis.move_pattern: Various piece types moving to squares that appear active or purposeful but are either exposed to immediate attack, leave critical vulnerabilities undefended, or fail to address the position's dominant tactical theme
analysis.why_bad: The position has one clear urgent need (defending a piece, blocking a file, activating a trapped piece, preventing a breakthrough) and the move ignores it entirely, allowing the opponent to immediately exploit the unaddressed vulnerability—often winning material, exposing the king, or creating an unstoppable passed pawn.
sub_patterns: Piece develops/moves to a square where it becomes an immediate target (Bc4→b5, Bd3→g5 attacks Nh4)
King walks into an open file or check pattern (Ke2→Re8+, Kg7→Qg6+, Kf8 abandons defense)
Pawn push weakens own structure or wastes critical tempo (g3 opens kingside, c4 loses tempo)
Piece decentralizes or goes to wrong square when central action is required (Na5 rim, Ne4 vs Nc4, Ra5 passive)

analysis.label: Plausible-looking developing or active moves that ignore urgent king safety demands in critical positions with very few good options.
analysis.description: This feature fires on moves that look natural or purposeful (piece development, rook activation, attacking moves, pawn advances) but fatally neglect the single most urgent tactical demand of the position—almost always involving king safety. In 5/7 positions, the player's own king is exposed or uncastled (Kb3 walks into mating attacks, Rb8 and Be6 delay castling, Rb5 abandons back-rank defense, f5 strips king cover). In 2/7 positions (Qg5+ and Bh6), the player misses a decisive forcing blow against the opponent's vulnerable king, playing a slow or counterproductive move instead. The positions share extremely narrow margins (avg 1.7 good moves available), meaning precision is required, yet the player consistently chooses a secondary strategic goal (development, piece activity, space) over the critical primary need. The best moves in these positions are typically either immediate king safety (castling, Kb1 retreat) or precise forcing sequences (Qxg6 with mate threat, Rg6+ exchange sacrifice, Qd8 back-rank invasion).
analysis.move_pattern: Diverse piece types (R, K, R, p, Q, B, B) moving to natural-looking squares; no geometric unity, but all are non-forcing or ineffectively-forcing moves that address secondary concerns rather than the critical tactical demand
analysis.why_bad: These moves ignore the position's most urgent tactical requirement (securing own king or delivering a decisive forcing blow) in favor of generic piece activity, development, or slow attacking plans, allowing the opponent to exploit the neglected king safety crisis with checks, sacrifices, or infiltrations
sub_patterns: Abandoning back-rank defense for piece activity (Rb5, Bh6 missing Qd8)
Delaying castling for development or rook moves (Rb8, Be6)
King moving to more exposed square instead of safer one (Kb3 vs Kb1)
Pawn push weakening own king cover (f5)
Superficial check that helps opponent's king escape (Qg5+ instead of Rg6+ sacrifice)

analysis.label: Playing a non-urgent repositioning or routine move in a razor-sharp position that demands immediate concrete action on one specific threat or opportunity.
analysis.description: This feature fires on moves that address a secondary concern while catastrophically ignoring the position's single most critical demand. In 7/9 positions, the player moves a piece away from or fails to engage with the urgent tactical sector: Na5 removes a knight from kingside defense during a mating attack, Bd7 removes a bishop from its critical b-file blocking duty, Ngf1 removes the wrong knight from a key defensive/offensive post, O-O ignores a hanging rook, c3 ignores immediate Qh4+/Rxg2 threats, Rxa2 captures the wrong target (h2 needed to free the passed pawn), b4 advances the wrong pawn allowing a double blockade. The positions share extremely low good-move counts (avg 1.8) meaning they are 'one correct answer' positions, yet the played moves are plausible-looking in a vacuum—repositioning pieces, castling, advancing pawns, or capturing material—making them seductive but fatally misprioritized.
analysis.move_pattern: Piece repositioning, routine development, or material capture directed away from the position's critical tactical sector
analysis.why_bad: The position demands immediate concrete engagement with ONE critical issue (defending against mate, capturing the right target, blocking a specific file, advancing a specific pawn first), but the player addresses a secondary concern, allowing the opponent to execute a devastating tactical blow (mating attack, fork, piece trap, pawn breakthrough, or passed pawn advance) that was only possible because the critical piece/resource was redirected elsewhere.
sub_patterns: Moving a defensive piece away from the threatened king (Na5, Ngf1, Bd7)
Making a slow positional move ignoring immediate tactical threats (c3, O-O)
Capturing the wrong target / wrong move order in critical races (Rxa2, b4)
Overcommitting an attacking piece to a vulnerable square (Qh6, Qd6)

analysis.label: Placing a bishop on an undefended b4/b5 square while the king remains uncastled, allowing a queen fork with check.
analysis.description: In 5/6 positions, the player moves a bishop to b4 or b5 where it has no protection, while their king sits uncastled on the e-file. This creates a devastating queen fork opportunity: the opponent plays Qa4+, Qb5+, or Qa5+ delivering check along the a4-e8 (or a5-e1) diagonal while simultaneously attacking the hanging bishop. After the check is blocked (typically with ...Bd7), the queen captures the undefended bishop, winning a full piece. In 5/6 cases the refutation is exactly this pattern - a queen check that double-attacks the bishop. The 6th position (g4) shares the broader theme of creating an undefended target while the king remains exposed in the center, inviting tactical punishment. All positions occur in the opening phase with both kings still centralized, and in every case multiple safe developing moves (within 50cp) were available that addressed central tensions or prepared castling.
analysis.move_pattern: Bishop moving diagonally to b4 or b5 (rank 4-5, b-file), landing on an undefended square with the king still on e1/e8
analysis.why_bad: The bishop lands on an unprotected square along the same geometric corridor (a4-e8 or a5-e1 diagonal) as the uncastled king, enabling the opponent's queen to fork both targets with a single check move.
sub_patterns: Bb4 with king on e8 allowing Qa4+ fork
Bb5 with king on e1 allowing Qa5+ fork
Premature aggressive move creating hanging target with king uncastled

analysis.label: Moves that voluntarily worsen the player's own king safety by exposing it to tactical exploitation.
analysis.description: In 5/5 positions, the played move directly worsened the moving side's king safety, allowing the opponent to gain tempo or launch attacks against the exposed monarch. In 3/5 cases (Kxh6, Kc5, Kc6), the king itself moved to a more exposed square where it became a direct tactical target for checks and forcing sequences. In 1/5 cases (g6), a pawn move weakened the king's shelter, creating light-square holes exploitable by Qh3/Ng4. In 1/5 cases (Re1), an irrelevant developing move ignored the urgent need to address an already-exposed king on e2. The refutations universally involve direct exploitation of the weakened king: Bxf7 attacking the stripped king on h6, Kf5 exploiting the king's distance on c5, Qd5+ checking the exposed king on c6, Ng4/Rae8+ targeting the unshielded king on e2, and Qh3/Ng4 assaulting the weakened kingside after g6. In all cases, superior alternatives existed that maintained king safety (gxh6 keeping shelter, Kc8 tucking away, Ke7 staying near kingside, Nxd6 gaining material, Bb6 playing queenside).
analysis.move_pattern: King moves to exposed squares (3/5), or weakening moves near own king (pawn advance, passive rook) that leave the king tactically vulnerable
analysis.why_bad: These moves voluntarily place the king on squares where the opponent gains tempo through checks, sacrifices, or forcing sequences, or they create structural weaknesses (light-square holes, open files) that the opponent immediately exploits to attack the king.
sub_patterns: King captures/advances to tactically exploitable square (Kxh6, Kc6)
King marches away from critical defensive zone (Kc5)
Pawn move weakening own king shelter in closed position (g6)
Developing move ignoring exposed king's urgent needs (Re1)

analysis.label: Voluntarily moving a piece away from a critical defensive function, allowing the opponent to exploit the newly created vulnerability with an immediate tactical or strategic blow.
analysis.description: This feature fires on moves that remove a key defensive piece from its post in positions where tempo is critical. In 7/9 positions, the moved piece was performing an essential defensive role: the bishop on g2 defended d5 (Bf1), the knight on f6 guarded the back rank (Nd7), the king on g1 was safe from forks (Kf2), the queen on e2 avoided geometric alignment (Qd2), the king needed to retreat to safety (Kh5), the king needed to blockade a passed pawn (Kd6), and the knight on f3 shielded the exposed king (Ng5). In the remaining positions (Ne6, Kc1), the move wasted a critical tempo on a non-urgent objective while an immediate threat demanded attention. All moves share the characteristic of being motivated by a superficially reasonable plan (repositioning, centralizing, attacking) but fatally misjudging that the position's urgency required maintaining the current defensive setup. The resulting punishments include knight forks (3/9), passed pawn breakthroughs (3/9), back-rank exploitation (1/9), and piece captures via exposed alignments (2/9).
analysis.move_pattern: Any piece type moving away from a square where it performs a critical defensive function (blocking, guarding, or shielding), often a retreat to passive square or an advance to pseudo-aggressive square
analysis.why_bad: The position contains an urgent latent threat that the piece was containing by its current placement; removing it gives the opponent a decisive tempo to execute a tactical combination (fork, promotion, back-rank attack) or win material through the newly created geometric vulnerability.
sub_patterns: King advancing into fork vulnerability (Kf2, Kh5, Kd6)
Knight/bishop retreating from key defensive diagonal or rank (Bf1, Nd7)
Pseudo-aggressive piece move ignoring urgent defensive need (Ne6, Ng5)
Wrong piece moved when specific piece needed immediate action (Kc1, Qd2)

analysis.label: Moves that pursue a secondary objective while failing to address the single most urgent tactical or positional vulnerability in the position.
analysis.description: This feature fires on positions where very few good moves exist (avg 1.8) and the player chooses a move that completely ignores the one critical threat demanding immediate attention. In 6/8 positions, the played move either removes a piece/pawn from a vital defensive function or fails to neutralize the opponent's most dangerous attacking resource: Be5 abandons d4 restraint enabling White's d4 advance; Ba5 removes the dark-squared bishop from kingside defense against a pawn storm; fxe6 removes the f-pawn enabling Bxg7+ winning the exchange; Nb4 abandons the diagonal allowing Bxg7 winning the rook; f4 ignores a discovered attack geometry on the c-file; c3 wastes the one tempo needed for h4 against an e-file invasion; Ke7 walks into d-file exploitation; Rab2 allows a simplifying queen trade eliminating counterplay. In every case, the correct move(s) directly address the primary vulnerability first, while the played move pursues counterplay, captures, or development that is irrelevant given the tactical emergency.
analysis.move_pattern: Mixed piece types and directions; no geometric consistency. Moves are quiet or secondary-objective moves (retreats, pawn pushes, captures of non-critical material, piece repositioning) in positions requiring one specific defensive action.
analysis.why_bad: The position has exactly one critical vulnerability (open file, undefended piece, dangerous diagonal, discovered attack) that demands immediate attention, and the played move addresses something else entirely, allowing the opponent to execute the primary tactical threat with devastating effect.
sub_patterns: Removing a piece from a critical defensive role (Ba5, Be5, Nb4, fxe6)
Wasting tempo on irrelevant plans when one saving move exists (c3, f4)
Walking into the primary threat rather than away from it (Ke7, Rab2)

analysis.label: Playing a plausible-looking move in a critical position where exactly one precise move was required to maintain the evaluation.
analysis.description: This feature activates on positions where exactly one move works (avg good moves = 1.0 across all 7 positions) and the player instead chooses an intuitive, natural-looking, or superficially aggressive alternative. In 6/7 cases, the played move appears reasonable by general principles—developing a rook (Rac8), centralizing a queen (Qf6, Qd7), attacking the kingside (Nh4, Bxh6, Bxh3), or pushing a seemingly decisive pawn (cxb7)—but each ignores a specific tactical or positional requirement that only the single correct move addresses. The refutations exploit precisely what the correct move would have prevented: an unguarded piece (2/7), an exposed king square (2/7), a forced queen exchange defusing an attack (2/7), or a missed preparatory move that enables a decisive combination (1/7). The positions are characteristically sharp middlegame moments (6/7 middlegame) where calculation must override pattern-matching intuition.
analysis.move_pattern: Various piece types and directions; no single geometric pattern. Moves include rook development, queen relocation, knight lunges, bishop sacrifices, and pawn captures—all appearing active or natural.
analysis.why_bad: Each move fails because it defaults to a general principle (activity, development, attack, material gain) while overlooking the one specific tactical requirement of the position—whether that's maintaining control of a critical square, keeping a piece performing a vital defensive/constraining function, or preparing a combination with correct move order.
sub_patterns: Premature sacrifices without concrete follow-up (Bxh6, Bxh3, Nh4)
Natural developing moves that leave a critical weakness unaddressed (Rac8, Qf6)
Moving a piece that was performing a hidden essential function (Qd7 releasing trapped piece, Rac8 not unblocking diagonal)
Obvious-looking forcing move that misses superior move order (cxb7 vs Qa4 preparation)

analysis.label: Playing a plausible-looking but non-forcing move in a narrow position that demands one specific urgent action, catastrophically squandering the initiative.
analysis.description: This feature detects positions with extremely narrow margins (avg 1.7 good moves available) where the player chooses a reasonable-looking but insufficiently forcing move instead of the one required precise continuation. In 10/12 positions, the correct move was more forcing than what was played: an intermediate check (Bxf2+ in position 10, Bb5+ in position 5), a mating check (Qf5+ in position 4), a critical capture (axb6 in position 14), or a move addressing the actual tactical threat (Nd3 in position 1, Rbd1 in position 13). The played moves share the characteristic of addressing a secondary concern or a vague positional idea—king escape (Kf1, Ka6), premature attack (Qh5, Qf8+), space-gaining (g4, g5), consolidation (c6, Rf2, Qe2)—while missing the position's single critical demand. The catastrophic average cp_loss of 2627 reflects that these are 'point of no return' positions where one wasted tempo allows the opponent to consolidate defenses, escape mating nets, or launch decisive counterattacks.
analysis.move_pattern: Any piece type moving to a plausible square that fails to be the ONE forcing/precise continuation the position demands; no consistent geometric direction
analysis.why_bad: These moves waste the critical tempo needed to execute the position's tactical requirement (delivering a specific check, making an intermediate move, capturing a key piece/pawn, or defending the actual weakness), allowing the opponent to escape, consolidate, or counter-attack decisively
sub_patterns: Wrong check square allowing king escape (Qe8+ vs Qf5+, Qf8+ losing queen)
Passive move when forcing check/capture exists (Qe2 vs Bb5+, Qxd1+ vs Bxf2+ first)
Weakening pawn push when position requires piece moves (g4, g5)
Addressing wrong defensive priority (Rf2 defends king not d3-pawn, c6 consolidates instead of capturing)
King move toward edge/exposure rather than center/safety (Kf1, Ka6)

analysis.label: Playing a slow positional or preparatory move in a closed position when a concrete capture wins undefended or weakly-defended material.
analysis.description: In all 7 positions, the best move was a concrete capture or forcing sequence that wins material outright (Bxd6 winning a pawn in 2/7, Nxe4/Nxb3/Nxb5 winning material in 3/7, Bxg5 capturing a hanging pawn in 1/7, g4 leading to a winning exchange in 1/7), but the player instead chose a quiet non-forcing move — pawn pushes (e4, h3, d5, h4), piece repositioning (Bd1, Ng6), or slow development (Bg2). All positions feature closed or semi-closed centers (7/7), which likely triggered a 'maneuvering' mindset rather than tactical alertness. The average cp_loss of 267 reflects how costly it is to miss free material. Critically, only ~1 good move existed on average (1.1), meaning the tactical capture was essentially the only way to maintain the position's potential.
analysis.move_pattern: Non-capturing, non-forcing moves (pawn advances, piece retreats, fianchettoes, knight repositioning) when an immediate piece or pawn capture was available on an undefended target
analysis.why_bad: The closed center creates an illusion that the position is slow and strategic, causing the player to choose building/prophylactic moves when a concrete tactical capture of undefended material exists — the one-tempo delay allows the opponent to defend the weakness or equalize.
sub_patterns: Prophylactic h-pawn push ignoring hanging pawn (h3, h4)
Piece repositioning instead of material-winning capture (Bd1, Ng6, Bg2)
Premature central break instead of completing prior tactical idea (d5, e4)

analysis.label: Playing a natural-looking but non-forcing developing/repositioning move in a position that demands one specific urgent action, typically castling for king safety.
analysis.description: This feature fires when a player makes a quiet, non-forcing 'improving' move (development, repositioning, or a slow pawn push) in a position where only ~1 good move exists and the position demands immediate concrete action. In 4/7 positions, the best move was castling or urgently moving the king, and the player instead made a plausible-looking developing move (Qc7, Bf4, Qe7, a4). In 5/7 positions, the king was still in the center or critically exposed. In all 7 cases, the moves are quiet (no checks, no captures, no direct threats) and appear 'useful' on the surface—developing a bishop (Bg4, Bf4), repositioning a queen (Qc7, Qb5, Qe7), shifting a rook (Rdg8), or advancing a pawn (a4)—but they fatally ignore the one critical demand of the position. The average cp_loss of 1559 and average of only 1.4 good moves confirms these are narrow, critical moments where tempo is everything.
analysis.move_pattern: Quiet non-forcing moves (bishop developments, lateral queen repositions, rook shifts, pawn pushes) with no check or capture—typically moving away from the critical sector
analysis.why_bad: These moves waste a critical tempo in positions where only one action (usually castling or addressing an immediate tactical vulnerability) maintains the position, allowing the opponent to exploit the unresolved weakness—most commonly an uncastled king exposed to checks, pins, or pawn breaks
sub_patterns: Developing a bishop instead of castling (Bf4, Bg4)
Repositioning queen sideways instead of castling (Qc7, Qe7)
Moving pieces to a flank while abandoning central control (Rdg8)
Quiet queen move missing concrete material win (Qb5 instead of Qxa7)
Pawn push when king race demands king movement (a4)

analysis.label: Moving a piece or pawn away from a critical defensive post that was shielding the king from checks or invasions along a now-unguarded line.
analysis.description: In 3/4 positions, the played move removes a piece or pawn from a square where it was performing an essential king-guarding function, enabling the opponent to deliver devastating checks or invasions along the vacated line. In Position 1, Rce8 abandons the c-file, allowing Rc7+ to invade with check against the exposed king on c6. In Position 7, Bc3 removes the bishop from f6 where it guarded the back rank, enabling Rd8+ with a crushing follow-up. In Position 9, g3 advances the g-pawn off g2, leaving f2 completely undefended and allowing Ne4 + Qxf2+ with a mating attack. The common thread is that each move appears active or purposeful (doubling rooks, attacking a pawn, creating luft) but fatally neglects the piece's invisible defensive duty of preventing opponent piece infiltration toward the king. The refutations consistently begin with immediate checks or invasions along the newly unguarded file/square.
analysis.move_pattern: Piece or pawn moves laterally or forward away from a file/square adjacent to own king, vacating a critical defensive post
analysis.why_bad: The moved piece was the sole defender against an opponent invasion route (open file, back rank, or weak square near king); its departure allows immediate checks or penetrations that win material or create mating attacks
sub_patterns: Rook abandons file that opponent can use for check invasion
Bishop abandons diagonal/rank defending back rank from rook infiltration
Pawn advance removes protection of adjacent square enabling knight+queen combination

analysis.label: Playing a routine or superficially reasonable move while ignoring a critical piece vulnerability, defensive obligation, or immediate tactical threat that demands specific action.
analysis.description: This feature fires on positions where the player makes a 'normal-looking' move while the position actually demands an immediate, specific response to a piece crisis. In 7/9 cases, a piece or pawn is performing a critical function (blocking a diagonal, guarding key squares, or needing immediate rescue) that gets either ignored or voluntarily abandoned. Positions 1-3 all feature a knight stranded on h3 that urgently needs f3 to reroute, but the player instead plays routine moves (Rd1, O-O, Qe1). Positions 4, 6, and 8 involve voluntarily moving a piece/pawn off a critical defensive post (e5 pawn blocking a diagonal, knight on d5 blocking the a4-e8 diagonal, knight on e6 guarding c7/f7). Position 5 involves moving the f7 pawn that defended e6. Position 7 ignores an immediate fork threat. Position 9 weakens the king's diagonal instead of castling. The deceptive element is that 6/9 positions have closed centers making them appear quiet, yet all contain urgent hidden priorities. The average of only 2.3 good moves available confirms these are positions demanding precise, non-obvious action.
analysis.move_pattern: Varied piece types and directions; no geometric consistency. Moves are typically developing moves, pawn pushes, or captures that appear constructive but miss the critical demand.
analysis.why_bad: The move ignores the position's single most urgent priority—whether rescuing a trapped/vulnerable piece, maintaining a critical blocker on a diagonal, or addressing an immediate tactical threat—allowing the opponent to exploit the neglected vulnerability with checks, forks, or piece infiltration on newly-opened lines.
sub_patterns: Ignoring a stranded/trapped knight that needs immediate pawn support to retreat (positions 1-3)
Voluntarily moving a piece/pawn off a critical diagonal-blocking or square-guarding post for material gain (positions 4, 6, 8)
Playing slow pawn moves while ignoring immediate tactical threats to own pieces (positions 7, 9)
Weakening king position with pawn moves instead of prioritizing castling (position 9)

analysis.label: Quiet repositioning moves that appear purposeful but waste critical tempo in positions demanding concrete urgent action, often exposing the moved piece to tactical exploitation.
analysis.description: This feature fires on moves that superficially look active or developmental but fundamentally waste tempo in positions requiring immediate concrete action. In 6/6 analyzed positions, 'tempo_loss' was identified as a primary tag. The moves share a pattern of appearing reasonable—gaining space (h4), repositioning (Qc3, Kf2), developing (Bg4, Bf5), or centralizing (Nh4, Re4)—but each ignores an urgent tactical demand. In 5/6 cases, there was only 1 good move available within 50cp, indicating critical-precision positions where the tempo waste is immediately punishable. The moved piece consistently ends up on a vulnerable square: Re4 falls to Bb7 diagonal attack, Nh4 becomes stranded and capturable, Bg4 creates no real threat while e5/b6 breaks arrive, Bf5 walks into an e4 fork, Kf2 allows Rc2+ invasion, Qc3 abandons f2 defense, and h4 creates a fixed target for the king march. The average cp_loss of 225 reflects how severely these pseudo-active moves are punished.
analysis.move_pattern: Non-forcing quiet piece repositioning (any piece type) to seemingly active but tactically vulnerable squares; no captures or checks
analysis.why_bad: The position demands one specific concrete action (a tactical strike, a defensive necessity, or a forcing sequence), but the player makes a 'reasonable-looking' move that addresses no urgent need, giving the opponent a free tempo to execute their primary threat while often placing the moved piece on an exposed square that creates new tactical vulnerabilities.
sub_patterns: Piece moves to undefended/exposed square creating tactical target (Re4→Bb7, Nh4→capture, Bf5→e4 fork)
Defensive piece abandons critical guard duty (Qc3 leaves f2, Kf2 leaves tactical operations)
Premature advance creating fixed structural weakness (h4 target)
Development to wrong square ignoring opponent's concrete threats (Bg4 vs Bh3)

analysis.label: Playing an active-looking move that pursues a secondary objective while completely ignoring the position's single most critical priority, typically a king safety threat or dangerous passed pawn.
analysis.description: In all 6/6 analyzed positions, the player makes a purposeful-seeming move (attacking a piece, grabbing a pawn, expanding on the queenside, developing, or launching an attack) while ignoring the one urgent priority that dominates the position. In 4/6 cases, the critical priority involves direct king safety (Bxb2 removes the fianchettoed kingside defender, O-O-O castles into open lines, Bxh3 launches an unsound sacrifice with own king uncastled, Nc3 ignores an immediate checkmate). In 2/6 cases (Bc6 and b5), the priority is neutralizing a devastating g6 passed pawn that becomes unstoppable once ignored. The positions typically have very few good moves (avg 2.1), and the punishment is a concrete tactical exploitation of the neglected weakness — usually Bh6/Bxg7 unblocking the passer, Nxf7 exploiting the stripped king, d5 opening lines against the castled queenside king, or immediate checkmate. The moves span all piece types and directions but share the functional error of addressing a secondary concern while the house is burning.
analysis.move_pattern: Diverse piece types and directions (bishop moves, knight jumps, pawn pushes, castling) — no single geometric pattern; functionally these are moves directed at secondary targets away from the critical zone of the position
analysis.why_bad: Each move ignores the single most urgent threat or priority in the position (king safety vulnerability, dangerous passed pawn, or checkmate threat), allowing the opponent to execute a concrete tactical punishment that exploits the neglected weakness with tempo
sub_patterns: Queenside pawn/piece moves ignoring a critical kingside passed pawn (Bc6, b5)
Removing a key defensive piece for material gain (Bxb2 strips fianchetto, Bxh3 sacrifices unsoundly)
Developing or castling while ignoring immediate tactical threats to the king (Nc3, O-O-O, Ne5)

analysis.label: Moves that waste a critical tempo by addressing a secondary concern while ignoring the position's most urgent tactical or strategic requirement.
analysis.description: In all 7 positions, the player makes a move that appears purposeful but catastrophically ignores what the position demands most urgently. In 2/7 cases (c3 moves), a passive pawn push is played when a passed pawn must be advanced or a piece needs active deployment. In 2/7 cases (Qf4, Qe2), the queen is repositioned to a square that abandons a critical function or walks into tactical vulnerability. In Position 4 (Rf3), a piece is moved to an undefended square where it hangs. In Position 7 (Nd8), a knight abandons an essential blockading post. In Position 1 (g5), a pawn weakens the king when queenside counterplay is urgent. The unifying thread is that each position had a clear 'must-do' task (advance d6, maintain the c6 blockade, break a pin, preserve king safety, keep piece coordination) and the player instead made a plausible-looking but fundamentally irrelevant move, gifting the opponent a tempo to execute their primary plan. All positions feature exposed or vulnerable kings (7/7), amplifying the cost of the wasted tempo.
analysis.move_pattern: Mixed piece types (pawns, queens, rooks, knights) making repositioning or advancing moves that abandon their current critical function or ignore the position's most urgent requirement
analysis.why_bad: Each move wastes a tempo that the position cannot afford to lose - the opponent has an immediate threat, breakthrough, or tactical opportunity that requires addressing NOW, and the played move either abandons a vital defensive duty, creates a new vulnerability, or makes a non-urgent 'improvement' while the opponent gains a decisive initiative.
sub_patterns: Passive pawn moves (c3) when passed pawn advancement is critical
Queen repositioning that abandons key defensive coverage
Knight/piece retreat from essential blockading or controlling post
Pawn advance that weakens own king's safety net

analysis.label: Playing a slow, non-forcing move (typically a flank pawn push or passive retreat) when a specific concrete tactical opportunity demands immediate action.
analysis.description: This feature fires on positions where the player chooses a speculative or prophylactic move instead of executing the one critical tactical strike available. In 5/7 positions, the played move is a pawn advance (mostly on the g or h files: g3, h4, g5+, h3, e6+), with the remaining two being passive piece relocations (Bh4, Kb2). In every case (7/7), the position demanded immediate concrete action—typically a piece-based tactical strike—that the player missed: Bxd6 winning an undefended pawn (positions 7 and 10), Qb5+ saving a hanging piece with tempo (position 5), Bf4 maintaining coordination (position 6), Re4+ correcting move order (position 9), Bg2 forcing a won simplification (position 15), or Kf5/f3 maintaining pawn coordination (position 2). In 5/7 positions, only one move was within 50cp of optimal, making these critical-precision moments. The average cp_loss of 261 reflects how devastating a single wasted tempo can be when the opponent uses it to consolidate, equalize, or find counterplay.
analysis.move_pattern: Non-forcing moves, predominantly flank pawn advances (g/h file) or passive king/piece retreats, in positions requiring immediate tactical resolution
analysis.why_bad: These moves waste the critical tempo that the position demands for a concrete tactical strike—allowing the opponent to fix weaknesses, escape danger, or generate counterplay that erases the advantage
sub_patterns: Prophylactic h-pawn push instead of capturing undefended pawn (h3, h4)
Premature flank pawn advance with wrong move order (g3, g5+)
Passive piece relocation ignoring hanging material or mating threats (Bh4, Kb2, e6+)

analysis.label: Moving a well-placed piece (knight or queen) away from its critical positional function to a superficially attractive but inferior or vulnerable square.
analysis.description: In all 5 positions, the blunder involves relocating a piece that was performing an essential role—blockading, controlling key squares, or maintaining pressure—to a square where it becomes exposed, passive, or irrelevant. In 4/5 cases, the piece moves to the kingside f- or g-file (Ng5, Qf5, Nf5, Nf3, Qxh2). In 3/5 cases, the piece specifically leaves a dominant central post (e4→g5, d6→f5, g5→f3 retreating from attack). In 2/5 cases the queen abandons coordination for a peripheral square. The common consequence is that the opponent exploits the piece's absence—whether by invading the vacated square (Rd7 after Nf5), forcing a favorable exchange (Bxg5 after Ng5), punishing the exposed king (Qb4+ after Nf3), attacking undefended pawns (Qxd6 after Qxh2), or consolidating when pressure drops (Re1 after Qf5). Average cp_loss of 248 with only 1.4 good alternatives confirms these are critical moments where maintaining the piece's current function was paramount.
analysis.move_pattern: Knight or queen moves laterally/backward from a central or critical square to f3/f5/g5/h2, typically toward the kingside wing
analysis.why_bad: The piece was performing an irreplaceable positional function (blockading, outposting, attacking, controlling key squares) and its departure allows the opponent to exploit the vacuum—whether through file invasion, favorable exchanges, checks on newly-opened diagonals, or recapturing the initiative
sub_patterns: Knight leaves outpost/blockade for exposed kingside square (Nf5, Ng5)
Knight retreats from active attacking square leaving king exposed (Nf3)
Queen wanders to peripheral square abandoning coordination (Qxh2, Qf5)

analysis.label: Playing self-improving quiet moves while an enemy passed pawn is one tempo from promotion or a critical one-tempo tactical window exists.
analysis.description: In all three positions, the player chose a 'positionally desirable' quiet move (pawn advance, castling, king activation) instead of addressing the single most urgent threat in the position. In 2/3 cases, the ignored threat is an advanced passed pawn one or two moves from promotion (Position 5: Black's d3 pawn; Position 10: White's e7 pawn). In 3/3 cases, the move wastes the final tempo available to address the critical threat. The played moves (c5 advancing queenside pawns, O-O tucking the king away, Kg3 activating the king) all represent reasonable ideas in a vacuum but are catastrophically mistimed given the immediate tactical emergency. All three analyses tag 'tempo_loss' and 'passed_pawn' as key motifs, and all refutations exploit the free tempo granted by simply executing the threat the player ignored.
analysis.move_pattern: Quiet self-improving moves (pawn push, castling, king walk) that neither capture, check, nor address the opponent's most advanced threat
analysis.why_bad: Each move wastes the single critical tempo needed to neutralize or slow an existential threat (usually an advanced passed pawn), allowing the opponent to promote or execute a decisive tactical sequence unimpeded
sub_patterns: Pawn push ignoring enemy promotion
Castling when tactical exploitation is required
King walk ignoring enemy passed pawn

analysis.label: Materialistic or superficially logical moves that ignore an urgent positional or tactical demand (king safety, development, structural integrity), allowing the opponent to exploit the neglected priority.
analysis.description: This feature fires on positions where the player makes a tempting but misguided move—most often a pawn capture or material grab—while the position urgently demands something else entirely. In 6/9 cases, the move is a direct capture of material (Nxd4, exf5, Bxd3, Nxa3, exf6+, Nxd5), while the remaining moves (a4, f6, Ba5) are superficially logical but address the wrong priority. The common thread is that each position has a narrow set of correct moves (avg 2.0 good alternatives) that address a critical need—usually king safety (positions 1, 2, 8), development (positions 1, 6, 9), or structural integrity (positions 4, 5, 7)—but the player is seduced by immediate material gain or a seemingly attractive-looking move. The punishments consistently exploit the neglected factor: open diagonals to exposed kings (5/9), pins on open files, exchange sequences winning back more material, or dissolved pawn structures surrendering forced mates. The extremely high average cp_loss (1186) reflects that these positions are critically poised moments where choosing the wrong priority has catastrophic consequences.
analysis.move_pattern: Captures of central/advanced pawns (knight or pawn captures on d4/d5/f5/f6/d3/a3) or slow flank moves (a4, f6, Ba5) in positions requiring urgent action elsewhere
analysis.why_bad: The moves address a secondary concern (material gain, space, piece relocation) while ignoring the position's primary demand (king safety, development, or maintaining critical tension/structure), allowing the opponent to exploit the neglected vulnerability with forcing moves
sub_patterns: Capturing a pawn that places the piece on a tactically vulnerable square (pinned, hanging, or trapped)
Making slow flank moves while king safety demands immediate development
Dissolving favorable pawn tension for material when maintaining it was stronger
Grabbing material that removes a key defender of another target

analysis.label: Playing a natural-looking but misdirected move in positions where essentially only one precise continuation maintains the evaluation.
analysis.description: This feature fires on positions with extremely narrow margins (average 1.4 good moves available) where the player selects a plausible-seeming alternative instead of the single critical continuation. In 9/10 positions, only 1-2 moves were within 50cp of optimal, yet the chosen move addresses a secondary concern while missing the primary urgent demand. The pattern manifests as: abandoning a critical defensive post (Qb8 leaves the diagonal 1/10, Kg8 abandons blockade 1/10), choosing passivity over required counterattack (Rd2 instead of Rxe6, O-O-O instead of Bxc4), making non-forcing moves when concrete action is needed (g6 giving tempo, Ke3 delaying the winning capture, b4 weakening structure when Kb5 invaded), or delivering the wrong forcing move (Rdb1+ abandoning the d-file resource vs Rd5+). The average cp_loss of 234 reflects that these are not subtle inaccuracies but critical missed moments where the one correct move was qualitatively different from all alternatives.
analysis.move_pattern: Mixed piece types and directions; typically a reasonable-looking consolidating, retreating, or seemingly active move chosen over the single forced/concrete continuation
analysis.why_bad: The moves abandon a critical resource (key square, file, diagonal, or pawn capture) or give the opponent a free tempo, failing to address the position's primary demand in favor of a secondary concern. The opponent then exploits the missed opportunity—often by occupying the abandoned square, advancing pawns unopposed, or executing the tactic that the correct move would have prevented.
sub_patterns: Abandoning a critical blockade or defensive square (Kg8/f6, Qb8/f7 diagonal)
Passive defense when counterattack was the only resource (Rd2 vs Rxe6, O-O-O vs Bxc4)
Delaying the one winning/drawing pawn capture for a king move (Ke3 vs cxd5, b4 vs Kb5)
Wrong forcing move that drives opponent to safety (Rdb1+ vs Rd5+)
Non-forcing pawn push giving opponent tempo for infiltration (g6, g4)

analysis.label: White's bishop makes a premature aggressive sortie deep into Black's position (ranks 6-7) where it is immediately captured with no recapture available, losing a full piece.
analysis.description: In all 7/7 positions, White moves a bishop aggressively to the opponent's side of the board (6th or 7th rank) where it is immediately captured or recaptured by an adjacent enemy piece, resulting in catastrophic material loss. The targets include h6 (2/7, captured by knight or fianchettoed bishop), a6 (2/7, captured by c8-bishop along its natural diagonal), g7 (1/7, recaptured by f8-bishop), c7 (1/7, recaptured by queen), and b7 (1/7, recaptured by c8-bishop). In every case, the bishop arrives at its destination square completely undefended with no possibility of recapture, and White had multiple simple developing moves available (Nf3, e4, d4, c4, Nc3) that maintained a normal opening advantage. The players appear to see a seemingly undefended target on Black's side and lunge for it, failing to check whether the destination square is actually safe—a fundamental tactical oversight repeated across different diagonal directions.
analysis.move_pattern: Bishop moves diagonally to opponent's 6th or 7th rank (h6, a6, g7, c7, b7) where it lands undefended and immediately capturable
analysis.why_bad: The bishop arrives on an undefended square deep in enemy territory where an adjacent piece (fianchettoed bishop, knight, queen, or undeveloped bishop) can immediately capture it with no recapture possible, netting the opponent a full piece for nothing or for just a pawn.
sub_patterns: Bishop to h6 captured by fianchettoed g7-bishop or g8-knight
Bishop to a6 captured by c8-bishop along its home diagonal
Bishop captures pawn on 7th rank (g7/c7/b7) but immediately recaptured by bishop or queen

analysis.label: Non-forcing, routine-looking moves played in critical positions that demand one specific urgent action.
analysis.description: In all 4/4 positions, the player chose a slow, non-forcing move (no check, no capture, no direct threat) in a position with very few good options (avg 1.8). In Position 6, Qd2 looks like natural development but ignores the gaping light-square weaknesses around the king. In Position 7, Kf2 appears to centralize the king but misses the crushing c6+ forcing sequence. In Position 11, h5 attempts prophylactic pawn play but wastes the single tempo needed to establish a life-saving Nc7 blockade. In Position 13, b6 tries to solidify pawn structure but ignores the exposed king and rook activity needs. All 4/4 positions required concrete, specific action—either patching a defensive crisis or executing a forcing tactical sequence—but the player defaulted to a generic positional improvement move that looked reasonable in isolation but was catastrophic in context.
analysis.move_pattern: Quiet non-forcing moves (king steps, queen repositioning, pawn advances) with no check, capture, or direct threat
analysis.why_bad: These moves waste a critical tempo in positions demanding immediate concrete action—either defending against an imminent threat or executing the one forcing sequence that maintains the advantage. The positions had extremely narrow margins (1-3 good moves) making any non-optimal choice devastating.
sub_patterns: Slow pawn advances (h5, b6) creating targets instead of addressing piece placement
Quiet piece repositioning (Qd2, Kf2) that ignores tactical urgency
Defensive-looking moves in positions requiring offensive precision

analysis.label: Playing purposeful-looking but irrelevant moves while the king faces an immediate tactical crisis requiring a specific defensive response.
analysis.description: This feature fires on positions where the player's king faces an urgent, often lethal threat (back-rank mate, pawn promotion, open file attack) but the player makes a move pursuing a different agenda entirely. In 4/4 positions, the king was already in danger with weak pawn shields or exposed placement. In 3/4 positions, an advanced h-pawn or h-file attack was the critical threat being ignored. The played moves look 'reasonable' in isolation — a space-gaining pawn push (a4), piece activation (Ng6), queen centralization (Qf7), pawn solidification (f6) — but all catastrophically fail to address the one thing the position demands. The average good moves available was only 2.0, indicating these are positions where the defensive requirement is extremely narrow and specific (e.g., Kg1 to escape the back rank, Qh8 to blockade a promotion square, queen repositioning to enable interposition).
analysis.move_pattern: Mixed piece types and directions; no geometric commonality. Moves are diverse (pawn pushes, knight development, queen repositioning) but all fail to move toward or address the critical threat axis.
analysis.why_bad: The position demands a specific defensive move to prevent immediate checkmate or pawn promotion, but the player plays a constructive-looking move that addresses a secondary concern, leaving the primary threat completely uncontested.
sub_patterns: Irrelevant pawn pushes while under mating attack (a4 ignoring back-rank, f6 weakening king shelter)
Piece moves that abandon critical defensive squares (Qf7 abandoning h8 blockade, Ng6 into a capture that destroys pawn cover)
Pursuing positional goals when only tactical defense survives

analysis.label: Playing a slow, non-forcing move when the position urgently requires attacking or challenging a key enemy piece to gain tempo.
analysis.description: In 5/7 positions, the best move directly attacks or challenges a dominant enemy bishop (b5 attacking Bc4 in positions 2 and 10, g4 attacking Bh5 in position 8, c5 challenging Bd4 in position 12, h6 challenging Bg5 in position 14), while the blunder is a passive or routine move that fails to disturb this piece. In 6/7 positions, 'tempo_loss' or 'missed_tactic' is explicitly tagged. The played moves include passive retreats (Bf8), routine development (Nc3), wrong move-order pawn advances (c5 before b5), quiet queen repositioning (Qd7, Qe7), and premature central breaks (d5, cxd4). In all cases, the opponent's key piece remains unchallenged, allowing them to execute their plan — whether that's a kingside attack via Ng5/Bf6, maintaining a dominant outpost, or exploiting newly-created tactical vulnerabilities. The common thread is ignoring the position's forcing requirements in favor of a 'reasonable-looking' move.
analysis.move_pattern: Non-forcing moves (retreats, quiet development, slow pawn advances, queen repositioning) instead of tempo-gaining attacks on opponent's active pieces
analysis.why_bad: By failing to challenge the opponent's key active piece immediately, the player gives the opponent a free tempo to execute threats, maintain dominant piece placement, or exploit tactical vulnerabilities that the passive move creates or fails to address.
sub_patterns: Retreating a defensive piece when a pawn advance attacks an enemy bishop
Routine development ignoring a forcing tactical shot
Wrong pawn move order losing tempo against a well-placed bishop
Quiet queen moves leaving key pieces unchallenged

analysis.label: Playing a reasonable-looking move that addresses a secondary concern while missing the single narrow tactical continuation that maintains a winning advantage.
analysis.description: This feature fires on positions where the player makes a 'logical' or 'natural' move—often addressing a perceived threat, repositioning a piece, or creating counterplay—when the position demands one specific concrete action. In 7/9 positions, a direct tactical blow was available (capturing material, delivering mate, or creating an unstoppable threat) but the player chose an indirect alternative: Qe7 instead of winning Qc7/Ng6 (2/9), queen captures eliminating a threat instead of maintaining the queen with checks (2/9), passive pawn pushes instead of winning captures like Bxc3/Bxg5 (2/9), wrong pawn break f3 instead of crushing e3 (1/9), queenside pawn push instead of addressing a promotion (1/9), and premature castling creating a hanging piece (1/9). The average good moves available is only 1.9, meaning these are razor-thin positions where nearly every alternative loses the advantage. The catastrophic average cp_loss of 2251 reflects that these are often decisive moments squandered.
analysis.move_pattern: Varied piece types making non-forcing or incorrectly-directed moves (passive queen retreats to e7, pawn pushes on wrong flank/file, bishop retreats, captures of secondary targets) when a forcing tactical blow exists
analysis.why_bad: The moves spend a critical tempo on a secondary concern (threat elimination, repositioning, counterplay on the wrong flank) while the position's true winning resource—usually a specific capture, check, or pawn break—evaporates because the opponent gets one free move to consolidate or counterattack
sub_patterns: Queen placed passively when active square wins tactically
Queen sacrificed to eliminate pawn threat when checks maintain it
Pawn pushed on wrong flank ignoring critical passed pawn or capture
Piece repositioned away from its attacking target
Wrong pawn break chosen among multiple advancing candidates

analysis.label: Playing a plausible but non-forcing move in a tactically critical position where only one precise continuation maintains the evaluation.
analysis.description: This feature fires on positions where very few good moves exist (avg 1.7 good alternatives) and the player makes a natural-looking repositioning or non-forcing move instead of the one critical tactical continuation. In 8/10 positions, the played move is a quiet piece redeployment (Ba6, Qc7, Qd2, Qf5), prophylaxis (h3, Kh8), premature simplification (Qxd4), or wrong forcing move (Rb8+) that ignores the position's immediate tactical demands. The pattern spans all piece types and both colors, but consistently involves choosing a move that would be reasonable in a generic context while missing that the specific position requires precise, often forcing play—whether that's a defensive retreat (Ne7 in pos 1), active development (Nc4 in pos 3), a forcing exchange sequence (Nxe6/Rxd1+/Nxd1 in pos 14), or maintaining a critical defensive function (queen guarding f2 in pos 5). The high average cp_loss (301) reflects that these are make-or-break moments where imprecision is severely punished.
analysis.move_pattern: Diverse piece types making quiet repositioning moves (non-captures, non-checks) or misdirected forcing moves, typically moving a piece AWAY from the critical sector of the board
analysis.why_bad: The position has extreme tactical tension requiring one specific continuation; the played move wastes a critical tempo, abandons a key defensive/attacking function, or allows the opponent to execute a concrete tactical blow (fork, skewer, promotion, king attack) that the one correct move would have prevented or preempted.
sub_patterns: Piece repositioned away from critical defensive duty (Ba6 leaving b7, Qxe6 leaving f7 defense)
Prophylactic/slow move when immediate forcing sequence exists (h3, Kh8, Qd2)
Queen placed on tactically vulnerable square enabling deflection/skewer (Qf5 on king's file, Qc7 enabling b-file skewer)
Premature simplification surrendering dynamic advantage (Qxd4 trading queens)
Wrong forcing move that helps opponent rather than self (Rb8+ allowing Kc7)

analysis.label: Playing visually appealing aggressive moves that squander winning positions by ignoring more forcing tactical continuations.
analysis.description: This feature fires on positions where the player has a significant or winning advantage but chooses an 'impressive-looking' or 'natural' active move instead of the most forcing tactical solution. In 4/4 positions, the player had a clearly winning position (including forced mates in positions 2 and 15). The played moves all appear aggressive or purposeful—a natural recapture (Bxf6, position 2), a dominant centralization (Nd5, position 8), an ambitious pawn break (e4, position 9), and a rook check (Rf3+, position 15)—yet each one fails to find the truly winning line. In 3/4 cases, the best move involved a more precise forcing sequence (dxc2+ leading to promotion mate, Re8+ exploiting back rank, Qh3+ with correct piece delivering check). The errors share the trait of prioritizing visual appeal or positional intuition over concrete calculation of the most forcing moves available.
analysis.move_pattern: Diverse piece types making active-looking moves (captures, centralizations, pawn pushes, checks) that appear aggressive but miss the most forcing continuation
analysis.why_bad: These moves allow the opponent defensive resources that wouldn't exist after the correct forcing move—interpositions (Rf2 blocking Rf3+), time to regroup (after Bxf6 or e4), or exploitation of abandoned defensive duties (after Nd5). The played moves are seductive because they 'look strong' but they're less forcing than the available alternatives, giving the opponent options they shouldn't have.
sub_patterns: Natural recaptures that ignore promotion/mating tactics
Knight centralization that abandons defensive duties
Premature pawn breaks without piece support
Check with wrong piece/square allowing interposition

analysis.label: Moves that remove a piece or pawn from an essential defensive role, leaving a specific target immediately exploitable by the opponent.
analysis.description: This feature fires on moves where a player abandons a critical defensive function—whether by moving a piece away from a vital defensive post, advancing a pawn that was serving a key structural role, or relocating a defender that was the sole guardian of an important square or piece. In 11/11 positions, the played move created or exposed a concrete undefended target that the opponent could immediately exploit: Rac8 left a7 hanging (Position 15), Ne4 removed the king's sole defender enabling a mating attack (Position 11), Rxf1 removed the only barrier to pawn promotion (Position 14), Na4 abandoned support for the queen on d4 (Position 4), Ng3 moved a critical defensive knight from f5 where it could be captured for nothing (Position 8), d6 removed the d-pawn's ability to recapture on c6 (Position 13), Bg4 left b7/f7 undefended (Position 3), and e5/d3 created immediately hangable pawns (Positions 9, 6). These positions typically had very few good alternatives (avg 1.8), indicating critical moments demanding specific action where the player chose a 'natural-looking' move that ignored tactical urgency.
analysis.move_pattern: Diverse piece types and directions; the common geometric thread is a piece/pawn MOVING AWAY from a square where it performed an essential defensive or structural function, typically toward the periphery or forward without support
analysis.why_bad: Each move creates or exposes an immediate concrete vulnerability—an undefended pawn, an unguarded square, or a removed defender—that the opponent can exploit with a forcing tactical response. The player prioritizes a secondary plan (development, attack, space) over the primary defensive or tactical requirement of the position.
sub_patterns: Piece moves away from defensive post leaving king or queen vulnerable (Ne4, Na4, Ng3, Rxf1)
Pawn advances that remove critical structural/defensive functions (d6, d3, e5, b5)
Rook/piece relocations that leave material hanging (Rac8 abandoning a7, Bg4 abandoning b7/f7)
Tempo-losing moves in positions demanding immediate forcing action (Rf2 instead of f5)

analysis.label: Moves that pursue a superficially attractive secondary objective while ignoring the position's most urgent tactical or strategic demand.
analysis.description: This feature fires on positions where the player makes a plausible-looking move that wastes a critical tempo by addressing a non-urgent concern. In 7/9 positions, the analyses identify 'tempo_loss' as a primary tag. The pattern manifests in three sub-types: unnecessary pawn pushes (f5, b6, g6, a5, h5 — 5/9 positions) that create weaknesses or ignore the true priority; queen repositioning to apparently active but exposed/misplaced squares (Qc2, Qe6 — 2/9); and greedy material grabs that neglect defensive necessities (Qxa7, Bxd4 — 2/9). In every case, the position demanded a specific urgent action — advancing a passed pawn (positions 5, 11), developing pieces (positions 7, 15), maintaining defensive control of a diagonal (positions 1, 3), defending against perpetual check (position 13), or retreating for precise defense (position 8) — and the player instead chose a move that looked reasonable but was decisively off-topic. The average cp_loss of 271 with only 2.1 good moves available confirms these are precision-demanding positions where the wrong plan is severely punished.
analysis.move_pattern: Predominantly pawn pushes (5/9) or piece moves to seemingly active squares (4/9), typically directed toward flanks or non-critical sectors of the board while the position's demands lie elsewhere
analysis.why_bad: These moves waste the one available tempo needed to address the position's critical requirement — whether defending a key diagonal, centralizing a king, advancing a passed pawn, or completing development — allowing the opponent to seize the initiative, exploit a newly created weakness, or execute a tactic that was previously impossible.
sub_patterns: Flank pawn pushes ignoring central/positional urgency (f5, b6, g6, a5, h5)
Queen repositioning to exposed squares abandoning defensive duties (Qc2, Qe6)
Greedy captures on peripheral squares leaving king undefended (Qxa7, Bxd4)

analysis.label: Playing a non-forcing, constructive-looking move that fails to address an immediate critical tactical vulnerability, allowing the opponent a decisive blow.
analysis.description: This feature fires on positions where the player makes a natural-seeming 'improving' move (developing a rook, pushing a pawn, repositioning the king) while ignoring the single most urgent tactical demand in the position. In 7/9 cases, the position had very few good moves (avg 2.3), indicating narrow tactical corridors where only specific moves address the critical vulnerability. The mistakes include: removing a pawn that defended a key square (e5 exposing f7, f5 destroying king shield - 2/9), moving a piece that was defending a critical square or shielding another piece (Rf2 blocking king escape, Rd2 abandoning back rank, Nxf7 removing queen's shield - 3/9), and wasting tempo with quiet moves when the opponent has an immediate tactical shot available (Rac8 leaving d7 hanging, Kc1 ignoring bishop vulnerability, Rg8 ignoring king safety, b4 giving free development time - 4/9). The punishments are typically singular and devastating (7/9 have 'one clear best punishment'), and the average cp loss of 3296 reflects that these moves transform survivable positions into immediately lost ones.
analysis.move_pattern: Diverse piece types and directions (pawns forward, rooks to files/ranks, king sideways, knight capture); no geometric commonality - the pattern is functional rather than geometric: non-forcing moves in positions demanding immediate tactical response
analysis.why_bad: Each move fails to address the single most critical tactical vulnerability in the position - whether that's an undefended piece, a king escape route, a defensive pawn, or an overloaded defender - allowing the opponent to execute a forcing sequence (check, capture, or mating attack) that decisively exploits the neglected weakness.
sub_patterns: Removing a pawn/piece that defended a critical square (e5, f5, Nxf7)
Moving a defender off a critical file/rank creating back-rank or invasion threats (Rf2, Rd2)
Quiet developing/improving moves when an immediate tactical threat exists (Rac8, Kc1, Rg8, b4)

analysis.label: Moves that prioritize an aggressive or active-looking idea while leaving a critical target undefended, allowing the opponent an immediate tactical exploitation.
analysis.description: These moves share a common pattern: the player makes a superficially attractive move (attacking a piece, grabbing material, centralizing, advancing a pawn) that specifically removes protection from a critical target, which the opponent can then exploit immediately. In 11/13 positions, the refutation directly captures or attacks something that was defended before the blunder: Re6 abandons f7 (Nxf7), f4 removes e4's support (Bxe4), f3 unguards the queen on g3 (Qc5+/Nxg3), Qb5 abandons b2 (Qxb2), Qc3 abandons a2 (Nxa2), exf5 releases the c7 pawn's grip (Rxc7), Bxe4 leaves the c5 knight unprotected (Bxc5), Bxg2 wastes a tempo allowing king attacks (Bf7+), Nc4 places a piece on an undefended square while the king is exposed (Qa4+), Kd5 walks onto the same file as its own knight (Rd7+ skewer), and c4/Rb8/e5 squander tempo on non-urgent actions while critical threats go unaddressed. The average cp_loss of 323 and average of only 1.8 good moves available suggest these are positions demanding precision where the player is seduced by one attractive-looking option that happens to create a concrete vulnerability.
analysis.move_pattern: Any piece type moving away from a defensive post or toward an aggressive square, creating an immediate undefended target (piece, pawn, or square) that the opponent exploits tactically
analysis.why_bad: Each move removes a specific defensive function (guarding a pawn, protecting a piece, covering a diagonal/file, or maintaining positional pressure) in exchange for a superficially appealing but less urgent goal, allowing the opponent an immediate tactical refutation that exploits the newly created vulnerability.
sub_patterns: Pawn advances that remove support from other pawns or open critical lines (f4, f3, e5, exf5, c4)
Queen displacements that abandon defense of key pawns (Qb5 leaves b2, Qc3 leaves a2)
Piece captures/moves that abandon defensive posts (Re6 leaves f7, Bxg2/Bxe4 waste tempo when king safety is urgent)
King/piece moves into tactical alignments on open files (Kd5 into skewer, Nc4 into check-based refutation)

analysis.label: Forward pawn advances or piece moves to seemingly active squares that create immediate tactical vulnerabilities the opponent can exploit.
analysis.description: This feature fires on moves that appear purposeful and aggressive but fatally overlook the opponent's immediate tactical response. In 7/10 positions, the move is a pawn advance (d4, e5, d5, a5, c5, bxc6) or piece placement to an exposed square (Bb4, Rfe8, Re8, Kf6) that creates a concrete target. The common mechanism: the move either places a piece/pawn on a square immediately attackable by the opponent (a5 captured by Nxa5 in Position 8, Bb4 captured by Nxb4 in Position 3, Rfe8 captured by Nxe8+ in Position 13), opens a critical line toward the player's own king (d4 opens the c4-f7 diagonal in Position 1, e5 opens the a4-e8 diagonal in Position 5), or creates structural damage that invites exploitation (bxc6 doubling pawns in Position 14). In every case, at least one patient alternative existed (quiet development, piece repositioning, or correct move order) that maintained the player's advantage. The average cp_loss of 1091 confirms these are catastrophic errors where the player's ambitious intent completely misfires.
analysis.move_pattern: Pawn advances (typically 1-2 squares forward) or piece moves to apparently active but tactically exposed squares; predominantly Black moves (9/10) in positions with unresolved central tension or exposed kings
analysis.why_bad: The moves prioritize executing the player's own plan (challenging the center, opening files, creating passed pawns, pinning) without first checking whether the destination square is safe or whether moving the piece/pawn removes critical defensive protection, giving the opponent a free tactical shot (capture, check, fork, or line-opening) that wasn't available before the move.
sub_patterns: Pawn advance to square capturable by enemy knight (a5, Rfe8 landing on knight's square)
Pawn push removing diagonal guard from own king (d4, e5, d5 opening bishop diagonals)
Piece placed on square attackable by the piece it supposedly threatens (Bb4 captured by 'pinned' knight)
Wrong move order giving opponent time to stabilize (Re8 before d2, c5 before c6)
Structural self-damage from wrong recapture method (bxc6 creating doubled pawns)

analysis.label: In pawn endgames with active kings, the player advances a flank pawn when the position demands prioritizing king activity or precise move order.
analysis.description: This feature fires on pawn endgame positions where the critical decision is between advancing a pawn and making a king move. All 12/12 positions are endgames, and 9/12 moves played are pawn advances (mostly on flank files: a, b, c, or h). The positions consistently feature exposed kings on both sides, passed pawns or pawn majorities, and razor-thin tempo margins. In the serious blunders (positions 6, 10, 13, 14 with 500+ cp_loss), the player pushed a pawn when the only winning/drawing move was a king march — e.g., b4 instead of Kd4 (position 6), h3 instead of Ke6 (position 10), c5 instead of Kc6 (position 13), b4 instead of Kb2 (position 14). Even the moderate errors (positions 11, 12, 15) share this pattern: a pawn advance wastes a critical tempo that should have gone to king activation. The 0 cp_loss positions (1, 3, 7, 9) represent the same structural archetype — pawn endgames at the king-vs-pawn-push decision point — but where the move happened to be acceptable.
analysis.move_pattern: Single-step pawn advances on flank files (a, b, c, h) in pure pawn or minimal-piece endgames; occasionally king moves to suboptimal squares
analysis.why_bad: In pawn endgames where tempi decide the outcome, advancing a pawn wastes the move on something that could wait, while the king needed to reach a critical square (blockade, opposition, capture, or escort) immediately. The pawn push either allows the opponent's king to centralize, enables a blockade, or loses a crucial tempo in a king race.
sub_patterns: Premature pawn advance before king captures enemy pawn (h3, b4, a3)
Pawn exchange that simplifies away the advantage (c5, b4)
Pawn push that allows opponent king to establish opposition or blockade (b5, h4)
