analysis.label: Moves that appear purposeful or aggressive but address a secondary concern while ignoring the position's primary tactical or strategic demand.
analysis.description: This feature fires on moves that look natural, active, or purposeful but fundamentally misdirect resources away from the position's critical need. In 9/11 positions, the move chosen addresses a secondary objective (giving check, attacking a piece, creating counterplay, centralizing) while ignoring the urgent primary demand—usually king safety (positions 3, 7, 9, 10, 15), handling a passed pawn (positions 1, 6), executing the correct tactic (position 2), or resolving critical pawn tension (positions 8, 13). The common thread is a tempo wasted on the wrong plan: Kg2 activates the king the wrong direction; Re3+ gives check to a passive square; Rb8 attacks a distant piece while the king burns; Qb4+ gives a pointless check when Qxf4+ wins material; Rfe1 centralizes but abandons a critical guard square; g4 advances aggressively but weakens the king shelter. All 11 moves appear plausibly motivated but catastrophically misread the position's hierarchy of priorities.
analysis.move_pattern: A piece or pawn moves to an apparently active/purposeful square (often giving check, attacking a target, or centralizing) but in the wrong direction or to the wrong destination relative to the position's primary demand
analysis.why_bad: These moves waste a critical tempo addressing a secondary concern while the position's true demand (king safety, blocking a passed pawn, executing the precise tactic, maintaining a defensive guard) goes unmet, allowing the opponent to exploit the primary vulnerability with devastating effect
sub_patterns: Piece moves in wrong direction away from where it's urgently needed (Kg2 instead of Ke2, Rb8 away from defensive duties)
Pointless or inferior check when a constructive alternative exists (Qb4+ instead of Qxf4+, Re3+ instead of Rd6+)
Attacking a secondary target while ignoring immediate king danger (Rb8 vs knight while king on d6 is under fire)
Pawn advance that weakens position or fixes targets (f6, g4, b5 creating vulnerabilities)
Abandoning critical defensive post for an attractive-looking destination (Rfe1 leaving f2 unguarded)

analysis.label: Playing a quiet, non-forcing move in a critical position where only immediate concrete action maintains the advantage, allowing the opponent to exploit a tactical vulnerability.
analysis.description: All four positions share a critical feature: they demand precise, concrete action (only 1-2 good moves available on average), yet the player chose a slow, non-forcing move that appears logical on the surface but wastes a crucial tempo. In 4/4 cases, the moves are quiet (no checks, no captures, no direct threats) while the position contains an immediate tactical vulnerability. Rab1 looks like the right plan but uses the wrong rook, leaving a2 hanging (1/4). a6 is a prophylactic pawn push while the king on f4 is vulnerable to a devastating knight fork sequence (2/4). Kc3 retreats the king for safety when b4 creates a winning passed pawn, and the retreat allows axb4+ with check gaining tempo (3/4). Qe7 appears developmental but blocks the f8-bishop and leaves the g8-knight trapped for capture (4/4). In every case, the opponent punishes the tempo loss with a concrete tactical blow: winning material via undefended pieces (2/4), fork sequences (1/4), or trapped pieces (1/4). The feature detects the specific error pattern of choosing plausible-looking quiet moves in positions where the margin for error is razor-thin.
analysis.move_pattern: Non-forcing quiet moves (no check, no capture, no direct threat) of any piece type, often appearing to address a secondary concern (safety, prophylaxis, development)
analysis.why_bad: Wastes a critical tempo in a position with only one or two viable options, allowing the opponent to execute an immediate tactical blow exploiting an undefended piece, fork, or trapped piece that the slow move fails to address
sub_patterns: Wrong rook choice leaving pawns undefended
Prophylactic pawn push ignoring king exposure to forks
King retreat abandoning active pawn breakthrough
Queen development blocking own pieces and leaving material trapped

analysis.label: Playing a superficially reasonable move in critical positions where exactly one narrow tactical resource was required.
analysis.description: This feature fires on positions where only ONE good move exists (avg good moves = 1.0 across all 6 positions) and the player chooses a plausible-looking alternative that misses the concrete tactical resource. In 4/6 positions, the correct move was a forceful central pawn action (d5, e5, d7+, dxe4) that the player failed to find. Instead, the played moves look purposeful on the surface - centralizing a knight (Nce5, Na5), playing a 'safe' pawn move (e6), giving a check (Qe6+), advancing a flank pawn (h6), or centralizing the king (Ke2) - but each catastrophically fails to address the one critical element. The positions share a common structure: extreme tactical tension requiring immediate concrete resolution, where the 'natural' or 'routine' move allows the opponent to consolidate or counterattack. The enormous average cp_loss (1898) reflects how punishing these narrow positions are when the single correct continuation is missed.
analysis.move_pattern: Various piece types moving to seemingly active/logical squares; no single geometric pattern but all are non-forcing alternatives to a concrete tactical shot
analysis.why_bad: Each move ignores the ONE critical tactical resource in the position (usually a central pawn break or precise forcing sequence), choosing instead a superficially reasonable but non-forcing alternative that allows the opponent to neutralize or exploit the resulting loss of tempo/initiative
sub_patterns: Passive pawn move (e6) instead of active pawn break (e5)
Premature flank attack (h6) ignoring critical central tension (dxe4)
Self-blocking check (Qe6+) preventing own passed pawn advance (d7+)
Knight to wrong square (Nce5/Na5) missing the correct outpost/tactic
King to vulnerable square (Ke2) one square away from the safe one (Ke1)

analysis.label: Bishop moves that attack or defend a knight but enable the opponent's tactical refutation through that very knight interaction.
analysis.description: In all 3/3 positions, the player makes a bishop move that directly interacts with a knight—either placing the bishop where an enemy knight can capture it (Be5 allows Nxe5 leading to Qxe3+ fork), attacking an opponent's knight that can improve by jumping away (Bf4 allows Ne3→Nc4→Nb6 fork), or attempting to defend their own knight inadequately (Bd2 fails to hold c3 and the bishop itself becomes capturable with check). In each case, the bishop move appears logical on the surface—occupying a central outpost, attacking a piece, or adding a defender—but the tactical reality is that the knight-related consequences are devastating. All three positions had clearly superior alternatives (3/3 had multiple good moves available) that either addressed the real positional priority (development, piece activation) or avoided creating the tactical vulnerability. The average cp_loss of 277 reflects how these seemingly reasonable bishop placements catastrophically misread the knight dynamics.
analysis.move_pattern: Bishop development/repositioning to squares that interact with knights (attacking enemy knight or defending own knight), typically to central or semi-central squares (e5, f4, d2)
analysis.why_bad: The bishop-knight interaction backfires: the target knight can capture the bishop profitably, jump away to a superior square with tactical threats (forks), or the defense of the knight is illusory, while the bishop move itself creates new vulnerabilities (hanging pieces, check sequences, structural collapse)
sub_patterns: Bishop placed on capturable central square near enemy knight (Nxe5 type)
Bishop attacks knight that improves with tempo/fork (knight relocation type)
Bishop passively defends own knight but defense is insufficient and bishop becomes target

analysis.label: Playing a natural-looking but tempo-wasting move that ignores the position's critical concrete demand, allowing the opponent to execute a decisive tactical or positional threat.
analysis.description: This feature fires on moves that appear reasonable on general principles (king centralization, development, defense, space-gaining) but fatally waste a tempo in positions requiring immediate precision. In 7/8 positions, 'tempo_loss' is explicitly identified as a key theme. The pattern manifests as: abandoning a critical blockading square (Ke2 in Position 1 leaves d3, allowing d3+ with check), retreating an active piece to a passive square (Qd2 in Position 15 abandons the dominant d8 post; Qc2 in Position 3 allows forced simplification), making routine developing moves when tactical needs are urgent (Be3 in Position 8 ignores the unprotected Ng5), advancing pawns that weaken key squares (f6 in Position 11 opens the a2-g8 diagonal for Qd5+; c5 in Position 10 creates a target for the enemy king), and making lateral detours that accomplish nothing (Rh3 in Position 12). In every case, 2-3 good alternatives existed that addressed the actual critical need, and the punishment involved a concrete tactical blow that the 'slow' move failed to prevent.
analysis.move_pattern: Diverse piece types (king, queen, bishop, rook, pawn) making moves that appear purposeful but address secondary goals—typically retreats, lateral shifts, routine developments, or premature pawn advances—rather than the one critical action the position demands.
analysis.why_bad: Each move wastes a crucial tempo pursuing a secondary objective (defense, centralization, development, space) while the position has one specific urgent tactical or structural need. The opponent exploits the lost tempo to execute a concrete threat: a pawn fork with check, a forced simplification, an invasion on a newly-opened diagonal, capturing an advanced pawn, or advancing an unstoppable passer.
sub_patterns: King retreating from an ideal blockading/central square to a seemingly safer but tactically vulnerable one (Ke2, Ke1)
Queen retreating from an active post to a passive defensive square that allows forced exchanges or pawn advances (Qc2, Qd2)
Pawn advances that weaken key diagonals or create targets for the opponent's pieces (f6, c5)
Routine developing moves that create tactical vulnerabilities rather than addressing urgent positional needs (Be3)
Piece excursions targeting secondary pawns when the winning plan requires immediate pawn advances or king activity (Rh3)

analysis.label: Moves that pursue a plausible secondary objective while ignoring the position's most critical demand, effectively wasting a crucial tempo.
analysis.description: This feature fires on moves that appear purposeful—giving check, activating a piece, making a prophylactic pawn push, or attacking a secondary target—but fundamentally miss what the position urgently requires. In 6/8 positions, the move directly allows the opponent to exploit an unaddressed tactical vulnerability (hanging piece, advancing passed pawn, undefended key square). The tempo loss tag appears in 7/8 analyses. Examples include: Ng6 abandoning d5-pawn defense for 'activation' (Position 11), Qd7 abandoning e5-knight defense for 'infiltration' (Position 10), h6/g6 playing prophylactic pawn moves while immediate central action or piece defense is required (Positions 12, 5), Nd5+ giving a check that actually improves the opponent's king position (Position 1), Rab8 using the wrong rook and vacating the a-file (Position 4), and Rc6 attacking a peripheral pawn while a passed pawn advances to e2 (Position 14). The common thread is a mismatch between the move's apparent purpose and the position's actual priority.
analysis.move_pattern: Mixed piece types and directions; typically quiet or semi-forcing moves (1 check, 0 captures) that relocate a piece to a square addressing a non-critical concern
analysis.why_bad: Each move wastes a tempo on a secondary objective while the position has one critical demand (defending a key piece, resolving central tension, stopping a passed pawn, maintaining a defensive guardian) that goes unaddressed, allowing the opponent to exploit the neglected vulnerability immediately.
sub_patterns: Piece leaves critical defensive post for 'activation' (Ng6, Qd7)
Slow prophylactic pawn moves when immediate tactical action required (h6, g6)
Apparently tempo-gaining moves that actually lose it (Nd5+ activates opponent's king, Rab8 gives queen safe retreat)
Rook targets secondary pawns while ignoring the main threat axis (Rc6, Rf7)

analysis.label: Giving a forcing check with a major piece (usually queen) that is suboptimal because it either displaces the piece from a superior role, improves the opponent's king position, or misses a stronger alternative move.
analysis.description: All 6/6 positions involve delivering check with a major piece (5/6 queen, 1/6 rook) when a different move would have been significantly stronger. In 3/6 cases the better move was a different check with a different piece (Rd1+ instead of Qf8+, Re1+ instead of Qe7+, Rg1# instead of Rg7+), in 2/6 cases the better move was a quiet/tactical move (Rad1 deflection instead of Qxf6+, Qxd5+ material capture instead of Qe3+), and in 1/6 cases it was a slightly more efficient check (Qxc4+ instead of Qd2+). The common thread is that the player selected the most visually obvious check available, prioritizing 'giving check' over evaluating which forcing move actually maximizes positional or tactical advantage. The average cp_loss of 3230 reflects catastrophic consequences in several cases, and only 1.5 good moves were available on average, meaning precision was critical.
analysis.move_pattern: Major piece (usually queen) delivering check by moving to an open file, rank, or diagonal targeting the opponent's king
analysis.why_bad: The check either displaces the piece from a superior defensive/attacking post, drives the opponent's king to a safer square, blocks friendly piece coordination, or misses a stronger quiet/tactical move that exploits the position more deeply (deflection, mate-in-one with different piece, material win with tempo)
sub_patterns: Queen check that improves opponent's king position
Wrong piece delivering check (blocking friendly lines)
Premature check missing quiet deflection/winning tactic
Check that removes queen from dominant central square

analysis.label: Moving a piece (especially the king) away from a square where it performs an essential function, missing the narrow set of precise moves that maintain the position.
analysis.description: This feature fires on positions where the player makes a natural-looking or seemingly active move that abandons a critical post, in positions with extremely few good options (avg 1.7). King moves dominate (6/11 positions), typically leaving blockade squares (Ke5 abandons d6 blockade, Ke8 abandons f7 blockade, Kd6 abandons c7 support) or blocking own pieces (Kf3 blocks bishop's needed f3 square, Ne7 blocks king's escape). Non-king moves follow the same logic: Qa4 abandons pressure on f2 when Qxf2 was the only holding move, Qc7 abandons attack on a6 when Rxa6 was winning, Rb6 leaves the d5 knight unprotected. In every case, the correct move was a specific concrete action (a pawn push like a5, a bishop reroute like Bg1, a capture like Qxf2/Rxa6, or simply staying put) rather than the played 'improving' move. The average cp_loss of 1089 reflects how catastrophic these abandonments are in positions demanding precision.
analysis.move_pattern: Piece (predominantly king) moves away from a functionally critical square to a seemingly reasonable but purposeless square; no consistent direction or capture/check pattern
analysis.why_bad: The piece was performing an irreplaceable function at its current location (blockading a passed pawn, supporting a pawn break, pressuring a weakness, shielding own pieces) and the position had only 1-2 moves that worked - the 'active' alternative abandons this duty, giving the opponent a critical tempo or tactical opportunity that immediately exploits the vacated square
sub_patterns: King abandons passed pawn blockade allowing promotion/infiltration
King/piece blocks own piece's critical maneuver square
Queen/rook moves to active-looking square instead of making the one concrete capture
King moves to square allowing opponent's pawn advance with check (tempo gift)
Piece leaves support of a critical break or defensive structure

analysis.label: Moves that waste a decisive tempo in endgame positions with passed pawns, typically through pointless checks or moves that fail to address the critical positional requirement.
analysis.description: This feature fires on moves that appear active but squander a critical tempo in positions where every move counts—predominantly endgames with passed pawns (10/13 endgame, 12/13 involve passed pawns). The most common manifestation is giving checks that accomplish nothing: Re1+ (positions 3,4) forces the rook to immediately return to blockading duty while gifting the opponent's king a free advance to g3; Qa6+ and Qa8+ (positions 8,13) are pointless checks allowing the opponent to improve; Qd3+ (position 2) checks from the wrong square letting the king escape a mating net. King moves going the wrong direction form another cluster: Kf7 (position 7) allows Kd4 when c5 was needed first; Ke6 (position 9) fails to reach the blockading square d8; Kc5 (position 12) abandons defensive coverage of the e-pawn's path. The remaining cases (b4, Qg3, Rf1) all similarly sacrifice critical tempi—committing a pawn prematurely, allowing a kingside pawn storm with tempo, or abandoning a blockade. Average cp_loss of 1669 reflects how catastrophic single-tempo errors become in these racing/promotion positions.
analysis.move_pattern: Various piece types (queen/rook checks, king retreats, pawn pushes) that appear active but fail to address a time-critical positional requirement—7/13 are checks, 3/13 are misdirected king moves
analysis.why_bad: These moves waste a critical tempo in positions where passed pawn races, king marches, or promotion threats make every single move count—the opponent uses the gifted tempo to advance a passed pawn, infiltrate with their king, or promote, turning equal/winning positions into lost ones.
sub_patterns: Pointless checks requiring piece to return to original duty (Re1+, Qa6+)
King moving away from critical blockading/intercepting square (Ke6, Kc5, Kf7)
Checks from wrong square allowing king escape (Qd3+, Qa8+ enabling interposition)
Abandoning critical defensive post for apparent activity (Rf1, b4)

analysis.label: Natural-looking moves that appear active or purposeful but squander the position's advantage by ignoring its most urgent tactical or strategic requirement.
analysis.description: This feature fires on positions where the player makes a superficially logical move—a check, a piece development, a centralization, or an attack on a piece—that actually helps the opponent or abandons a critical resource. In 5/7 positions, the move looks 'active' (a check in positions 1 and 3, attacking a queen in position 5, centralizing in positions 4 and 7) but concretely fails because it either enables the opponent's escape/counterplay or misses a forcing tactical shot. The positions typically have very few good moves (avg 1.6), demanding precise calculation over general principles. In position 1, Rf8+ helps the enemy king escape to safety; in position 7, Rge4 abandons the critical g-file attacking highway; in position 6, Qe2 is passive when Bxc7 wins material; in position 5, Bd7 attacks the queen but leaves c4 hanging; in position 8, Kf3 goes the wrong direction enabling the opponent's decisive pawn break. The common thread is choosing a move that satisfies a general principle (checks are good, centralization is good, attacking pieces gains tempo) while missing the ONE specific concrete demand of the position.
analysis.move_pattern: Diverse piece types and directions; no single geometric pattern. Moves include checks, piece development, king moves, pawn pushes, and rook transfers—all appearing purposeful but misdirected relative to the position's critical factor.
analysis.why_bad: These moves prioritize surface-level logic (give a check, attack a piece, centralize) over the position's concrete demands, either enabling the opponent's escape/counterplay, abandoning a key attacking resource (file, diagonal, initiative), or missing a forcing tactical sequence that was the only way to maintain the advantage.
sub_patterns: Checks that improve the opponent's king position (Rf8+, g5+ vs Nd5+)
Passive centralizing moves that miss concrete winning tactics (Qe2 missing Bxc7)
Piece moves that appear to gain tempo but leave material hanging (Bd7 leaving c4 undefended)
Abandoning a critical file or attacking conduit for generic centralization (Rge4 leaving g-file)
King or pawn moves in wrong direction enabling opponent's key break (Kf3 enabling ...f5, f3 weakening g3)

analysis.label: Moves that pursue superficially attractive goals (captures, checks, centralization) while wasting a critical tempo the position cannot afford.
analysis.description: This feature fires on moves that look appealing—capturing seemingly free material, placing a piece on an impressive central square, or delivering a check—but critically waste a tempo when the position demands urgency. In 7/9 positions, the analysis explicitly identifies 'tempo_loss' as the tactical motif. The pattern manifests in several forms: greedy pawn captures that ignore development needs (Nxd5, Nxe4, bxa5, Bxb3 in 4/9 positions), piece repositioning to attractive-looking squares when king activation or concrete action is required (Bd4, Bb5, Nfe7 in 3/9 positions), and a premature check that shatters a mating net (Re4+ in 1/9 positions). The common thread is that the player is distracted by a short-term enticement while the opponent gains the tempo needed to execute their real plan—whether that's a queenside pawn break, a tactical refutation via check/pin, or king infiltration. The average 2.2 good moves available confirms these are positions where better alternatives existed, typically involving development, king activation, or prophylactic play.
analysis.move_pattern: Diverse piece types (bishops, knights, rooks, king, pawns); typically captures or piece placements to central/active-looking squares; includes checks that are premature
analysis.why_bad: Each move wastes a crucial tempo on something superficially attractive, allowing the opponent to execute their primary plan (pawn breaks, tactical shots exploiting exposed kings, or king infiltration) one move faster than would otherwise be possible
sub_patterns: Pawn captures that ignore development urgency or tactical vulnerabilities (Nxd5, Nxe4, bxa5, Bxb3)
Piece repositioning to attractive squares when king activity or concrete threats are more urgent (Bd4, Bb5, Nfe7)
Premature checks that release tension or free the opponent's king from a trap (Re4+)

analysis.label: Playing a natural-looking, non-forcing move in a critical position that demands immediate concrete action on a single urgent issue.
analysis.description: This feature fires on positions where the player makes a plausible 'improving' move (rook repositioning, natural development, passed pawn push, king tuck) while ignoring the one critical demand of the position. In 5/7 cases, the move is tagged as a tempo loss; in 5/7 cases a concrete tactic was missed. The positions share extremely narrow paths to success (avg 1.4 good moves available) yet the played moves address secondary concerns: e7 advances a pawn ignoring Rxg2+ mate (Position 1), Rb8/Rab8 contest the b-file instead of advancing a critical passed pawn or resolving central tension (Positions 2, 7), Nc6 develops naturally instead of enabling urgent castling (Position 6), Rc7 improves rook placement while leaving king exposed to forks (Position 9), Kh8 tucks the king into a worse square enabling discovered attacks (Position 12), and Rd5 centralizes a rook onto a square where it becomes a tempo-gaining target (Position 15). The average cp_loss of 1787 reflects that these 'autopilot' moves are catastrophic precisely because the positions demand one specific concrete response.
analysis.move_pattern: Non-forcing piece moves (often rook repositioning or piece development) to seemingly active squares, without delivering check or making captures
analysis.why_bad: The position has a single critical demand (defensive threat, tactical opportunity, or urgent pawn break) requiring immediate concrete action, and the played move wastes a tempo on a secondary concern, allowing the opponent to execute a decisive tactical blow (mate, fork, breakthrough, or tempo-gaining attack on the misplaced piece)
sub_patterns: Rook moves to contest a file while ignoring a critical passed pawn or pawn tension (Rb8, Rab8, Rc7, Rd5)
Advancing a passed pawn while ignoring an immediate mating threat (e7)
Natural piece development ignoring urgent king safety needs (Nc6, Kh8)

analysis.label: Playing slow developing or repositioning moves when the position demands immediate forcing action, wasting a critical tempo.
analysis.description: In 6/6 positions, the player chose a quiet, non-forcing move (piece development, repositioning, or non-optimal capture) when the position required urgent tactical or strategic action. In 4/6 cases the best move involved either castling to address king safety (positions 2, 5 with O-O-O and O-O) or aggressive piece activation creating immediate threats (positions 1, 3 with Rh2/Qd4). In 5/6 cases the played move created zero immediate threats, giving the opponent a free tempo to exploit weaknesses created by the move itself (b2 hanging after Qe3, d4 hanging after Be2/Nc3, exchange won after Kh6, queen trade forced after Qd3). The positions share a common characteristic: they appear to allow 'normal' development or improvement, but a concrete tactical need (defending a specific pawn, forcing a check, creating an unstoppable threat) makes tempo absolutely critical. The average cp_loss of 222 reflects how devastating a single wasted tempo can be in these sharp, critical positions.
analysis.move_pattern: Non-forcing piece moves to central/semi-central squares (e2, e3, c3, d3, h6, d4) that improve piece placement without creating threats
analysis.why_bad: These moves waste a critical tempo in positions demanding immediate forcing action, either leaving key pawns/pieces undefended (b2, d4), allowing favorable exchanges (Qxd3), or giving the opponent time to execute decisive tactical blows (Bb5 winning exchange, advancing passed pawns unopposed).
sub_patterns: Passive development leaving central pawns undefended (Be2/Nc3 allowing Bxd4/dxe5)
Queen repositioning abandoning pawn defense (Qe3 leaving b2, Qd3 inviting trade)
King walk losing tempo when piece activation critical (Kh6 vs Qc7/Qd6)
Material capture instead of more forcing mating continuation (Bxd4 vs Qc3)

analysis.label: Failing to immediately advance a critical passed pawn in a time-sensitive endgame pawn race, instead making a preparatory king move, rook repositioning, or wrong pawn push that loses the decisive tempo.
analysis.description: This feature fires on endgame positions where a passed pawn must be pushed immediately but the player makes a slower 'preparatory' move instead. In 7/10 positions, the correct move was an immediate pawn advance (e6, b6, a6, f5, h6, a3, g4) but the player chose a king move (Kf5, Kb4, Kh4, Kxh5), rook repositioning (Ra8, Rh8, Rf7), or wrong pawn push (g6, c5, c4). The common thread is that all positions involve mutual passed pawns creating a race where a single tempo is decisive. The mistakes share the logic of 'preparing' to push (escorting with the king, improving the rook, consolidating the pawn chain) rather than pushing immediately. In every case, the opponent exploits the lost tempo by either advancing their own counter-threats, delivering checks on the exposed piece, or setting up defensive fortresses that would have been impossible one move earlier. The average cp_loss of 300 reflects how a single wasted tempo in these razor-thin pawn races transforms winning positions into draws or draws into losses.
analysis.move_pattern: King moves forward (4/10), rook moves to back rank or passive square (3/10), or non-critical pawn pushes (3/10) — all in lieu of advancing the decisive passed pawn
analysis.why_bad: In critical pawn race endgames, a single tempo determines the outcome; preparatory moves give the opponent time to create counter-threats (checks on the exposed king, launching their own passed pawn, establishing defensive blockades) that would have been impossible had the pawn been pushed immediately.
sub_patterns: King 'escorts' passed pawn instead of pushing it immediately (Kf5, Kb4, Kh4)
Rook repositions to irrelevant square instead of supporting immediate pawn advance (Ra8, Rh8, Rf7)
Wrong pawn pushed — consolidation move or wrong flank instead of critical passer (g6, c5, c4)
Capturing material (Kxh5) that allows simplification and neutralizes the pawn race advantage

analysis.label: Active-looking or forcing moves (especially checks) that accomplish nothing concrete and waste critical tempo while missing the position's true demands.
analysis.description: This feature fires on moves that appear aggressive or purposeful but actually squander tempo without achieving concrete objectives. The clearest sub-pattern involves giving pointless checks that either drive the opponent's king to a better square or fail to coordinate with other pieces (g5+ allows Kf5 invasion, c4+ gifts Kd4, Re2+ fails to restrict, Qf3+ breaks mating coordination) — 4/10 positions. Another sub-pattern involves repositioning pieces to 'active-looking' squares while missing immediate tactical shots (Bh6 ignores a hanging rook, b4 misses Qxg7, Ng6 abandons d5 defense for speculative knight activity, c5 abandons d5 pawn defense) — 4/10 positions. The remaining cases involve passive/purposeless moves when the position demanded concrete action (Kh1 wastes tempo when Bxa7 was urgent, Kf5 blocks the rook's needed square) — 2/10 positions. In all cases, the player chose a move that 'felt active' over the position's concrete requirement, resulting in an average 245cp loss.
analysis.move_pattern: Various piece types moving to seemingly active squares or giving checks; no single geometric direction, but characterized by the move being forcing-looking (check) or repositioning without concrete purpose
analysis.why_bad: These moves waste a critical tempo by prioritizing apparent activity over the position's concrete demands — checks that improve the opponent's king placement, piece moves that abandon defensive duties or miss immediate tactical wins, and king moves that block own piece coordination or ignore urgent tasks.
sub_patterns: Checks that drive opponent's king to a superior square (g5+, c4+)
Checks that fail to maintain attacking coordination (Re2+, Qf3+)
Piece repositioning that misses hanging material or immediate tactics (Bh6, b4, Ng6)
Moves abandoning critical defensive control for speculative activity (Ng6, c5)
Passive moves when active material-gaining play was required (Kh1, Kf5)

analysis.label: Playing a superficially attractive move (centralization, material gain) that neglects the position's true strategic priority, resulting in tempo loss or misplacement.
analysis.description: This feature fires when a player selects a move that appears active or materially advantageous but actually misplaces a piece relative to the position's critical demand. In 4/5 positions, the analyses explicitly tag 'tempo_loss' as a motif, and in 4/5 the tag 'piece_activity' appears—highlighting the irony that moves chosen FOR activity actually reduce effective coordination. The true priority was typically king activation/safety (positions 7, 9, 10) or central structural integrity (positions 14, 15), but the player instead chose a cosmetically appealing alternative: centralizing to e5 (positions 9, 14), attacking a distant pawn (position 7), advancing the king without preparation (position 10), or grabbing material in a corner (position 15). In each case, the refutation exploits the specific resource the move neglected—the opponent's king invades (pos 7, 9), checks cascade against the exposed king (pos 10), structural collapse follows (pos 14), or the initiative surges against the displaced piece (pos 15). The average cp_loss of 253 with 2.0 good alternatives available confirms these are positions where correct moves existed but the player was lured by the apparently active option.
analysis.move_pattern: A piece or king moves to a visually impressive or materially tempting square (often centralization to 5th rank/e5, or a capture on a distant square) while the true priority lies elsewhere
analysis.why_bad: The move addresses a secondary concern (centralization, material gain, piece activity) while ignoring the position's primary strategic demand (king safety, king centralization, structural integrity, or dynamic initiative), allowing the opponent to exploit the neglected priority with tempo-gaining threats
sub_patterns: Piece centralizes to e5/5th rank but blocks own king's critical path
Bishop captures distant material but removes itself from key attacking diagonal
King advances without first securing piece coverage, exposing to checks
Knight centralizes to outpost but allows recapture that destroys pawn structure defending another piece
Rook moves to active-looking but peripheral square while opponent's king infiltrates

analysis.label: Playing a natural-looking strategic or repositioning move when the position demands a specific forcing continuation or precise move order.
analysis.description: In 6/7 positions analyzed, the player executes a plausible positional plan (repositioning a piece, developing to an 'active' square, advancing a passed pawn, rerouting a knight) while ignoring the position's most critical concrete requirement. In Position 1, Rf1 is a quiet rook improvement when g7 forces immediate promotion. In Position 5, Bh3 aggressively posts the bishop but leaves it hanging to checks. In Position 6, c6 advances the passer without the preparatory Kb6 for king support. In Position 8, Bf4 develops to an undefended square capturable by the queen. In Position 9, Kf3 'centralizes' but creates fatal fork vulnerability. In Position 10, Nd7 reroutes for a strategic outpost but removes the critical defender of d5. In Position 14, Bxd5 captures in the wrong order, allowing removal of the key attacking piece. All 7 moves have a clear strategic rationale but fail because they substitute general improvement for the one precise move the position demands. The correct moves were consistently more forcing (5/7 involved immediate tactical threats, pawn advances to the 7th, or captures in correct order).
analysis.move_pattern: Quiet piece repositioning, development, or pawn advance that is non-forcing and ignores the most critical tactical element of the position
analysis.why_bad: The position requires one specific forcing or precisely-ordered move, but the player substitutes a general strategic improvement, allowing the opponent to exploit a hanging piece, establish a blockade, remove a key attacker, or create a decisive tactical sequence that the 'quiet' move failed to prevent or preempt.
sub_patterns: Piece repositioning when a forcing pawn advance wins (Rf1 instead of g7, c6 instead of Kb6)
Developing/posting piece to undefended square within capture range (Bf4, Bh3)
Moving a piece away from critical defensive duty (Nd7 removing d5 guard)
Executing captures in wrong order allowing counter-removal (Bxd5 before Nxf5)
King move to tactically exposed square ignoring fork geometry (Kf3)

analysis.label: Aggressive or active-looking moves in positions where the player's own king is critically exposed, when defensive precision was urgently required.
analysis.description: This feature fires on positions where the player's king is vulnerable (exposed, uncastled, or weakly shielded) and very few good moves exist (avg 2.1), yet the player makes a forward, aggressive, or materialistic move that ignores the king's peril. In 7/9 positions, the player's own king is explicitly described as exposed. The correct moves consistently involve king retreat (Kf2/Ke2/Kg2 in Position 1, Kf1/Ke1 in Position 5), maintaining defensive file control (keeping rook on c4 in Positions 2-3), or addressing the critical diagonal/threat (Bg2/h4 in Position 8). Instead, players chose advancing moves (Kg4, Kf3, Ne4), speculative attacks (Rf4 twice), material grabs (Bxd4, fxe4), or passive retreats that surrender active defensive pressure (Raa8). The catastrophic average cp_loss of 2320 reflects that these positions are knife-edge moments where one wrong step triggers immediate tactical punishment—often checkmate (Positions 1, 8) or loss of critical positional assets (Positions 2-3, 12, 14).
analysis.move_pattern: Pieces advancing forward (to 3rd-4th rank) or capturing material, when the position demands king retreat, defensive piece placement, or threat-addressing moves
analysis.why_bad: The moves fail because they ignore the critical vulnerability of the player's own king position, allowing opponents to exploit exposed kings with checks, mating patterns, central pawn breaks (d5!), or decisive infiltration that was previously restrained by the piece now misplaced
sub_patterns: King advancing into mating net (Kg4, Kf3)
Rook abandoning critical defensive file for speculative attack (Rf4)
Pawn/capture opening key squares near own king (fxe4, h3)
Active piece voluntarily retreating to passive square (Raa8)

analysis.label: Moves that compromise the player's own king safety by stepping into or opening lines for immediate checks and tactical exploitation.
analysis.description: In 6/7 positions, the played move directly exposes the player's king to immediate checks or captures with tempo. King moves place the monarch on vulnerable squares along open files or diagonals (Ke1 allows Ra1+, Kxf1 allows Bb5+, Kd8 allows Rb8+/Rd3+), while pawn advances (g4 twice, h3) remove defensive shields enabling captures-with-check (Rxh3+, Bxg4+). The remaining position (Rb4) similarly neglects urgent counterplay, allowing a simplification that exploits the exposed king. In all cases, the best move was a more forcing/active option—a capture (Bxg4, Rxf1), a counterattacking break (d4), or a king move to a genuinely safe square (Kg1). The common error is playing a slow, natural-looking, or routine move that creates tactical vulnerability to checks, when the position demanded immediate action. Tags across positions confirm: king_safety (6/7), tempo_loss (6/7), missed_tactic (5/7).
analysis.move_pattern: King moves to squares on open files/diagonals (1st rank, f1, d8), or kingside pawn advances (g4, h3) that remove defensive cover—all creating lines for opponent checks
analysis.why_bad: Each move creates an immediate tactical vulnerability (usually a check or capture-with-check) that the opponent exploits to win material or gain decisive tempo, when instead an active forcing move (capture, counterplay, or king-to-safe-square) would have maintained or increased the advantage
sub_patterns: King stepping onto open file/diagonal allowing discovered or direct check
Kingside pawn advance removing shield pawn and allowing Rx-pawn+ with check
Routine/passive move when an immediate capture or forcing move wins material
Recapturing with the wrong piece (king instead of rook) exposing to diagonal check

analysis.label: Moving a piece (usually the king) to an exposed square that allows the opponent a tempo-gaining check, deflection, or attack that converts into a decisive advantage.
analysis.description: In 6/7 positions, the blundering move places a piece (king in 4/7, queen in 2/7) on a square where it becomes immediately vulnerable to a forcing response—typically a check or attack that gains a critical tempo. In Position 7 (Kf4), the king walks into Rg4+ deflection; in Position 15 (Kg3), the king allows Rd3+ gaining tempo to win b3; in Position 4 (Kh6), the king enables Rh8+ deflection enabling promotion; in Position 1 (Qf5+), the queen lands where Qd5+ counter-checks and forces a fatal trade; in Position 6 (Qb6), the queen reaches an exposed square trapped by Ra6; in Position 9 (Kd7), the king abandons a critical defensive post allowing Ra8. Even the pawn move h5 (Position 11) shares the core flaw: it wastes a tempo when immediate rook activation was required, gifting the opponent one move to centralize the king to a defensive post. The consistent pattern is choosing an 'active-looking' move over the position's actual requirement (safety, patience, or immediate concrete action), with the punishment being a forcing response that exploits the new vulnerability.
analysis.move_pattern: King or queen moves forward/sideways to an unprotected or exposed square, typically toward the opponent's forces or away from a critical defensive zone
analysis.why_bad: The piece lands on a square where the opponent can deliver a check, deflection sacrifice, or trapping attack with tempo, converting the exposure into material gain or decisive positional advantage—the 'active' move actually hands the opponent the initiative at a critical moment
sub_patterns: King walks into a check that enables deflection/removal of guard (Kf4→Rg4+, Kh6→Rh8+, Kg3→Rd3+)
Queen moves to an exposed rank/file where it can be counter-checked or trapped (Qf5+→Qd5+, Qb6→Ra6)
King abandons critical defensive post allowing opponent's passed pawn or rook invasion (Kd7 allows Ra8)
Non-forcing move wastes tempo when immediate concrete action was required (h5 instead of Rf3)

analysis.label: Moves that appear active or aggressive but place pieces on squares where they become vulnerable, trapped, or waste critical tempo against concrete tactical responses.
analysis.description: This feature fires on moves that look proactively good—centralizing pieces, grabbing material, or targeting weaknesses—but are concretely refutable because they ignore the opponent's forcing responses. In 3/9 cases the moved piece becomes literally trapped (Bxh2, Nb6, Ba4). In 4/9 cases the move wastes a critical tempo allowing the opponent to seize a dominant position (Qa5, Rf8, d4, Bd4). In 2/9 cases the move is a natural-looking capture or centralization that misses a far stronger tactical resource (Nxd4 missing Nb5 with Nc7+ fork, Nd5 hanging the e4 pawn). The consistent thread is that each move appears plausible or even strong on superficial assessment—queens go to 'active' squares, pieces centralize on 'outposts,' pawns advance 'aggressively'—but careful calculation reveals the piece ends up worse off than before, either driven back, trapped, or creating new tactical weaknesses that the opponent exploits with forcing moves.
analysis.move_pattern: Pieces (especially minor pieces and queens) moving to apparently strong or active squares; also includes pawn breaks and captures that seem natural but prove premature
analysis.why_bad: The moves prioritize visual activity or intuitive 'good placement' over concrete calculation, failing to account for the opponent's forcing responses (tempo-gaining attacks, trapping sequences, or tactical shots) that exploit the piece's new vulnerability on its seemingly attractive square.
sub_patterns: Piece moves to active square but gets trapped by pawn advances (Bxh2, Ba4, Nb6)
Natural-looking capture or centralization that misses a stronger tactical alternative (Nxd4, Nd5, Bd4)
Premature activation that wastes tempo and allows opponent consolidation (Qa5, Rf8, d4)

analysis.label: Moves that pursue superficially active or aggressive goals while abandoning the piece's critical positional function or ignoring the position's true strategic priority.
analysis.description: This feature fires on moves where a piece leaves a critical role—guarding a key asset, occupying a dominant outpost, or fulfilling a developmental need—to make a move that appears active or materially rewarding but fundamentally misunderstands the position's demands. In 8/8 analyzed positions, the move involves tempo loss as a core tag. The pattern manifests as: a rook abandoning guard duty of a passed pawn (Rb1, Position 1), a knight jumping to an aggressive but unstable rim square instead of addressing the real problem (Ng4, Nh5, Positions 3-4), a piece making a superficial 'developing' move while ignoring urgent castling/development needs (Rc1 Position 6, Rh7 Position 13), capturing material at the cost of dominant positioning (Rxg6 Position 7, Nxc6 Position 15), choosing wrong recapture that ruins structure for illusory file-opening (fxe3 Position 9), attacking a piece that trivially sidesteps (Bb4 Position 8), or walking the king into danger seeking activity (Kg5 Position 10). In all cases, the player was seduced by a move that LOOKS purposeful but sacrifices something far more important than what it gains.
analysis.move_pattern: Any piece type moving to an apparently active square or making an apparently useful capture/attack, typically forward or sideways, while vacating a square or role where it was performing an essential function
analysis.why_bad: The move abandons a critical function (defending a key asset, occupying a dominant outpost, completing development, maintaining king safety) in exchange for a superficially attractive but strategically hollow goal that the opponent easily refutes by exploiting the newly-created vulnerability left behind.
sub_patterns: Piece leaves defensive post exposing key pawn/square (Rb1, Nxc6)
Knight jumps to aggressive rim/forward square that becomes unstable target (Ng4, Nh5)
Rook/piece develops to contested file while ignoring urgent castling/bishop development (Rc1, Rh7)
Captures material at cost of dominant positional pressure (Rxg6, Nxc6)
King/piece advances into exposed position seeking false activity (Kg5, Bb4)

analysis.label: Moves that create a fatal diagonal alignment allowing an opponent's bishop to win the queen through pin, skewer, or trap.
analysis.description: In 9/9 positions, the move played creates or fails to prevent a lethal diagonal vulnerability that an opponent's bishop exploits to win the queen. The most common sub-pattern (7/9) is a pin or skewer along a diagonal: the queen aligns with the king on b5-e8 (positions 4, 7 via Bb5), on a7-g1 (positions 3, 5, 6 via Bc5), or on a6-f1 (position 8 via Ba6). In other cases, the bishop directly attacks a queen with no safe retreat (positions 1, 9 via Bc4/Bg4) or creates a double attack trapping the queen (position 2 via Bg5+Ne5). The triggering moves themselves are diverse—queen moves to bad squares (Qe6, Qc6, Qxd7), king moves that create the alignment (O-O, O-O-O, Kd1), pawn moves that open the critical diagonal (e5), rook moves that place themselves behind the queen on the diagonal (Re2), or tempo-wasting moves that allow the opponent to execute the diagonal tactic (a3). The unifying error is blindness to how a bishop can exploit the geometric alignment being created.
analysis.move_pattern: Any piece type or direction; the move creates an alignment of the player's queen with another friendly piece (usually king) on a diagonal, or places the queen on an unprotected diagonal square
analysis.why_bad: The move creates a geometric alignment on a diagonal that the opponent's bishop can exploit through pin, skewer, or direct attack to win the queen
sub_patterns: Queen placed on same diagonal as own king, enabling bishop pin (Qc6/Bb5, Qxd7/Bb5, O-O then Qe3/Bc5)
King moves to square that creates queen-king diagonal alignment (O-O creating a7-g1 diagonal pin, O-O-O enabling double attack)
Pawn advance opening critical diagonal to queen (e5 opening c5 for bishop to attack Qe3)
Piece placed behind queen on same diagonal enabling skewer (Re2 behind Qd3 on a6-f1 diagonal)
Tempo-wasting move allowing opponent to execute existing diagonal threat (a3 allowing Bc5 pin)

analysis.label: Playing a non-forcing, indirect move in a sharp position where an immediate concrete tactical continuation was available, gifting the opponent a crucial tempo to consolidate or counterattack.
analysis.description: This feature fires on positions where the player chooses a slow, non-urgent move instead of an immediately available forcing tactical opportunity. In 8/8 positions, the best move involved a concrete, forcing action (queen infiltration to h3 in positions 1,8,15; piece capture/exchange in positions 5,12; piece coordination attacks in positions 6,7,13), while the played move was indirect or peripheral. The blunders include quiet pawn advances on the flank (a6, b5, g5 in 3/8 cases), piece relocations that appear aggressive but create no real threats (Ng4, Nh5 in 2/8), greedy captures away from the critical sector (Qxf6 in 1/8), and queen centralization moves ignoring immediate tactical obligations (Qd4, Qe5 in 2/8). In every case, the tempo loss allowed the opponent to either execute a tactical strike (d5 fork, hxg5/gxf6, Qb4+ check), consolidate defensive coordination (Nd2 development, Rc1 defense), or neutralize the position's dynamic potential. The average cp_loss of 294 reflects positions at critical tactical turning points where one tempo made the difference between winning and losing.
analysis.move_pattern: Non-forcing moves (quiet pawn pushes, piece relocations without immediate threats, captures away from key sector) replacing available forcing moves (queen infiltrations, piece captures, discovered attacks)
analysis.why_bad: The positions all demand immediate tactical execution because the opponent has a specific consolidating resource available on the next move; the slow move hands them exactly the tempo needed to neutralize threats, develop a key piece, or launch a counterattack that exploits the newly-created positional weakness.
sub_patterns: Quiet flank pawn advance (a6, b5, g5) ignoring central/kingside tactical opportunity
Knight relocation to seemingly aggressive square (Ng4, Nh5) abandoning a crucial defensive/attacking post
Queen move to 'active' square (Qd4, Qe5, Qxf6) that actually removes it from the critical sector

analysis.label: Quiet, natural-looking moves played in narrow critical positions where the one urgent tactical or safety requirement is completely ignored.
analysis.description: This feature fires on positions where the player makes a 'routine' or 'natural-looking' quiet move (no captures, no checks) while the position demands one very specific response to an urgent crisis. The positions share extremely narrow margins (avg 1.6 good moves available) and catastrophic consequences (avg 1334 cp loss). In 7/9 positions, exposed or uncastled kings create the primary crisis. The best moves typically address an urgent specific need: rescue a trapped/exposed queen (Qc6 in position 12), enable castling (Be2 in position 11, Nd2 in position 5), place a defensive piece on a critical square (Ne7 instead of Be7 in position 13), or find the only safe king square (Kf8 in position 15). Instead, players chose generic development (Nf3, Nc3), consolidating pawn moves (g3, c3), passive retreats (Bg1), or wrong-square king moves (Kf2, Ke7). In 3/9 cases, the played move specifically blocks a friendly piece from its optimal square (c3 blocks knight retreat, Be7 blocks Ne7 which was the best move, Bg1 entombs the bishop). The common cognitive error is treating a tactically critical moment as a normal positional one.
analysis.move_pattern: Quiet non-forcing moves (no check, no capture) - typically short-range piece development, pawn pushes to 3rd rank, retreats to back rank, or king steps to adjacent square
analysis.why_bad: The position has only 1-2 viable moves addressing an urgent tactical or safety crisis (usually king exposure, piece trapping, or forced sequences), and the played move ignores this crisis entirely, allowing the opponent to exploit the unaddressed vulnerability with devastating force
sub_patterns: Self-blocking: piece occupies square needed by another piece (c3 blocks knight, Be7 blocks Ne7)
Passive retreat to dead square when active defense needed (Bg1)
Generic development ignoring piece in danger (Nf3 ignoring trapped queen)
King moves to exposed square instead of safe haven (Kf2 to diagonal, Ke7 into mate)
Weakening pawn push near own king (g3 opening lines for opponent)

analysis.label: Non-forcing moves that squander a vital tempo in time-critical positions where the opponent has an advancing unstoppable threat (passed pawn or mating attack).
analysis.description: This feature fires on moves that waste a critical tempo in positions demanding maximum urgency. In 11/11 positions, the played move creates no immediate threat (no check, no capture, no attack on a piece) while the opponent has an advancing plan requiring instant counteraction. In pawn race endgames (6/11 positions: Kc5, Kb4, Kf3, Ke6, both Rh5 moves), the piece moves toward a goal but either takes an indirect path, moves in the wrong direction entirely, or goes to a square vulnerable to check that forces retreat. In middlegame positions (4/11: Kg2, Kh3, Qb7, Bd3), the move abandons defensive coordination or exposes the king to tactical exploitation. The common punishment across all positions is that the opponent gains a free tempo to advance their plan—pushing a passed pawn, delivering an intermediate check, or tightening a mating net—converting manageable disadvantages into hopeless ones. King moves predominate (8/11), typically moving to squares that appear logical but are tactically vulnerable.
analysis.move_pattern: Non-capturing, non-checking piece moves (predominantly king moves) that move toward a positional goal but land on tactically vulnerable squares or fail to address the most urgent threat
analysis.why_bad: The move grants the opponent a free tempo in a time-critical race or attack—either by allowing an intermediate check that forces the piece back, by moving in the wrong direction away from the critical sector, or by addressing a secondary concern when the position demands maximum urgency against an unstoppable advancing threat.
sub_patterns: King moves to checkable squares allowing opponent to gain tempo (Ke6→Nf4+, Kf7→Bg6+, Kg2→forks/checks, Kh3→diagonal mate)
King moves wrong direction in pawn races, abandoning counterplay (Kc5, Kb4, Kf3 away from promotion support)
Rook/piece moves to passive squares creating no threats while passed pawns advance (Rh5×2, Bd3 wrong move order)
Queen/piece abandons defensive post allowing mating attack to proceed unchallenged (Qb7)

analysis.label: Aggressive-looking piece moves that prioritize activity or attacks while ignoring a critical positional vulnerability that the opponent immediately exploits.
analysis.description: All 5 positions feature a piece move to an ostensibly active or attacking square (Bg4 pins a knight, Bb3 activates on a diagonal, Rxa5 grabs a pawn, Ba3 develops aggressively, Ng5 threatens the king) while neglecting the most urgent need in the position. In 3/5 cases, king safety is the ignored priority (uncastled king in positions 2 and 13, exposed king in position 5). In 4/5 cases, the analyses flag 'tempo_loss' because the aggressive piece either must retreat (Bg4 forced back to d7, Ng5 forced back to f3) or becomes a target on its new square (Bb3 captured via Rf3xb3, Rxa5 captured by Nxa5). In all 5 cases, the best available moves addressed the critical vulnerability (e6/c6 challenge the center, Kg2 secures the king, Nb3 maintains piece dominance, Ne5 centralizes with tempo, Qe3 targets the passed pawn). The common error is choosing offense or activity when the position demands consolidation or defense, giving the opponent free tempi to exploit the neglected weakness.
analysis.move_pattern: Minor piece or rook moved to an aggressive/active square (attacking, pinning, or capturing) away from the area of critical vulnerability
analysis.why_bad: The moves waste tempo on optically aggressive ideas while leaving a critical vulnerability unaddressed (hanging piece, uncastled king, exposed king, or unstoppable passed pawn), allowing the opponent to immediately exploit the neglected weakness with decisive force.
sub_patterns: Bishop develops to active diagonal ignoring king safety (Ba3, Bb3, Bg4)
Knight sortie to attacking square while critical defensive task is urgent (Ng5)
Greedy pawn capture placing piece on vulnerable square (Rxa5)

analysis.label: Non-forcing piece repositioning moves to seemingly active squares that ignore the position's urgent concrete demands, wasting a critical tempo.
analysis.description: This feature fires on moves that appear to improve piece placement or activity but actually waste a crucial tempo by not addressing the position's most pressing need. In 7/7 positions, the played move is a non-forcing repositioning (no check, no capture, no direct threat) to an 'active-looking' square while a concrete tactical or structural issue demands immediate attention. The tempo loss tag appears in all 7 positions. Specifically: Re4 centralizes the rook while ignoring d5 pawn tension (Position 1), Be4 places the bishop centrally but walks into ...f5 trapping it (Position 2), Qd3 centralizes the queen but abandons b2's defense (Position 3), c6 consolidates but ignores urgent kingside tension (Position 4), Kg5 advances the king without first restricting the opponent's king with Be7 (Position 5), Rh3 targets a pawn but must immediately return to a3 (Position 6), and Bg5 'develops' to a square where it's immediately captured for free (Position 7). In 5/7 cases the evaluation swung 116+ centipawns; in 6/7 cases only 1-2 good moves existed, showing these were critical decision points where the 'natural' improving move was fatally wrong.
analysis.move_pattern: Non-forcing piece repositioning (rook, bishop, queen, or king) to central or advanced squares without delivering check, making a capture, or creating a concrete threat
analysis.why_bad: The move wastes a critical tempo on cosmetic piece improvement while the position demands addressing an urgent concrete issue (pawn tension, piece defense, king restriction, or development), allowing the opponent to execute their plan unchallenged—whether winning material, opening attacking files, or seizing key squares.
sub_patterns: Piece centralization that ignores hanging/undefended pawns (Qd3, Re4)
Piece placement on tactically vulnerable central squares (Be4 trapped by f5, Bg5 captured immediately)
Premature king/piece advance without preparatory restriction of opponent (Kg5, Rh3)
Quiet consolidation move when kingside/tactical urgency demands action (c6)

analysis.label: Natural-looking constructive moves (development, pawn breaks, centralization) that ignore a critical concrete vulnerability requiring immediate attention.
analysis.description: This feature fires on moves that appear superficially reasonable—developing pieces (Be7, Bb7, Nf6, Ne4), making pawn breaks (g4, g5, c6), or capturing material (Bxb3)—but fatally ignore an urgent tactical or structural requirement in the position. In 6/8 cases, the player's move creates or exposes an immediate exploitable weakness: a piece placed on an undefended square (Ne4 captured by Bxe4), a pawn move removing a critical defender (c6 allowing Qxb6), pawn advances destroying king shelter (g4, g5 both shredding pawn shields), and pieces developed into tempo-gaining attacks (Be7 allowing d6, Nf6 walking into e5 fork). In 7/8 positions, the opponent has one clearly strongest punishment that exploits the specific vulnerability created. The average position had 2.6 good alternatives available, indicating these were not forced errors but voluntary choices of attractive-seeming plans over concrete necessities. The common thread is prioritizing a 'constructive idea' over the position's actual tactical demands.
analysis.move_pattern: Mixed piece types (pawns, bishops, knights) moving forward to seemingly active/natural squares or making apparently constructive captures/breaks, typically on the kingside or center
analysis.why_bad: Each move ignores a single critical tactical or structural vulnerability in the current position—whether an undefended piece, an exposed king, a critical defender being removed, or a tempo-gaining response available to the opponent—in favor of pursuing a superficially logical plan that the position does not support
sub_patterns: Pawn advances weakening own king shelter (g4, g5)
Development to square immediately exploitable with tempo (Be7 hit by d6, Nf6 hit by e5)
Slow moves ignoring critical central tension (Bb7 allowing dxe6 wedge)
Piece placed on undefended square (Ne4 captured by bishop)
Pawn move removing defender of another piece/pawn (c6 unguarding b6)

analysis.label: Playing a non-pawn move instead of immediately pushing a passed pawn to the penultimate rank (7th/2nd) in a time-critical endgame.
analysis.description: In all 6/6 positions, the sole winning (or drawing) move was to push a passed pawn to the penultimate rank before promotion (h2, g2, b2, c7, a2, g2 respectively). Instead, the player made a 'preparatory' or 'improving' move with another piece—king moves (3/6: Kh6, Kd4, Ka5), a bishop move (1/6: Bh6), a rook move (1/6: Rb2), or a secondary pawn push (1/6: h4). In every case, the one-tempo delay allowed the opponent's rook to seize control of the promotion file, establish a blockade on the first/eighth rank, or deliver intermediate checks that permanently neutralize the passed pawn. The positions are all razor-sharp (avg 1.2 good moves), and the average cp_loss of 525 reflects the catastrophic consequence of losing this single critical tempo in a promotion race.
analysis.move_pattern: Non-pawn move (king, rook, or bishop repositioning, or wrong pawn) when the critical passed pawn needed to advance one square to the 7th/2nd rank
analysis.why_bad: The one-tempo delay allows the opponent's rook to reach the promotion file or first rank, establishing an unbreakable blockade or gaining check-based tempi that permanently prevent promotion.
sub_patterns: King move toward the passed pawn instead of pushing it (Kh6, Kd4, Ka5)
Bishop repositioning before the decisive pawn push (Bh6)
Rook repositioning instead of immediate pawn advance (Rb2)
Advancing a secondary pawn instead of the critical one (h4 instead of g2)

analysis.label: Quiet, positionally-motivated moves played at critical tactical crossroads where only a specific forcing move (often a sacrifice or check) could maintain the position.
analysis.description: This feature fires on positions where the player makes a 'reasonable-looking' quiet move that catastrophically ignores immediate tactical demands. In 7/9 positions, the correct move involved a forcing tactic (Bxf2+ check, cxd5 sacrifice, Qxe5 exchange sacrifice, Bxd4+ capture) or precise defensive retreat, while the played move was a passive development, pawn push, or piece maneuver. The positions share extremely narrow correct paths (avg 1.9 good moves), and the blunders typically expose diagonal weaknesses (f6/f4/exd5 opening critical diagonals in 4/9 cases), leave pieces hanging or trapped (Nb6/Be4/Qf1 in 3/9 cases), or walk into checkmate (Ke6). The average cp_loss of 1310 reflects game-ending severity. In 6/9 positions, king safety was the primary tactical theme exploited by the refutation.
analysis.move_pattern: Non-forcing moves (no checks, mostly non-captures) - pawn advances (b3, f6, f4, exd5), piece retreats/developments (Nbd7, Be4, Nb6, Qf1), and king moves (Ke6) - all lacking immediate tactical purpose
analysis.why_bad: Each move ignores that the position has reached a critical tactical inflection point where only one or two forcing moves maintain viability; the quiet move either opens a fatal diagonal, places a piece on an undefended/trapped square, misses a time-sensitive sacrifice, or walks into a mating net - allowing the opponent to execute a decisive tactical blow (fork, pin, diagonal check, piece capture, or checkmate).
sub_patterns: Pawn moves weakening king diagonals (f6, f4, exd5, b3)
Passive development missing critical forcing moves with check (Nbd7, Be4)
Pieces placed on vulnerable/trapped squares (Nb6 hanging, Qf1 trapped)
King walking into mating patterns (Ke6)

analysis.label: Quiet king or rook moves that appear safe or consolidating but catastrophically compromise the position by self-blocking escape routes, walking into mating nets, or abandoning critical tactical resources.
analysis.description: This feature fires on positions where the player makes a non-forcing king or rook move that seems natural or defensive but fails to address the position's primary tactical demand. In 3/5 positions, the move directly worsens king safety: Re7 self-blocks the king's only escape square allowing immediate Qf5# (position 3), Kh4 walks the king into a g5+/Bf6+ mating net (position 4), and Kc4 exposes the king to Ne5+ forks while abandoning the center (position 1). In the remaining cases, the move passively retreats an active piece when concrete action is required: Rf8 removes the rook from f5 where it enabled a decisive Qd3 queen sacrifice creating an unstoppable passed pawn (position 5). The common thread is choosing a 'quiet consolidation' move when the position demanded either aggressive pawn advances, tactical combinations, or precise retreats toward safety rather than sideways/forward into danger. The average cp_loss of ~3947 reflects that these seemingly innocuous moves often convert playable positions into immediate forced mates or completely lost positions.
analysis.move_pattern: King or rook moves to a seemingly natural square; non-capturing, non-checking quiet relocations. Kings tend to move sideways/forward (Kc4, Kh4, Kh7) while rooks retreat or self-block (Re7, Rf8).
analysis.why_bad: These moves prioritize perceived safety or piece improvement over urgent tactical demands—they either self-block critical escape squares, walk into mating patterns enabled by opponent's piece coordination, or abandon active piece placements that were enabling decisive tactical shots.
sub_patterns: King walks toward edge/exposed square into mating net (Kh4, Kc4)
Rook self-blocks king escape square allowing immediate checkmate (Re7)
Rook retreats from active tactical position surrendering decisive combination (Rf8)
Quiet king repositioning when pawn advances or concrete action required

analysis.label: Playing a plausible-looking but non-urgent move in a tactically sharp position where the exposed king or concrete threats demand immediate precise action.
analysis.description: This feature fires on moves that squander a critical tempo in positions with extreme urgency—typically involving exposed or uncastled kings (10/10 positions feature at least one exposed king), where very few good moves exist (avg 1.8). The played moves appear superficially active or purposeful (rook 'activations' to g5/g8/h2/a4, pawn 'attacks' like f6/c4/g5, knight 'improvements' like Nh6/Nb5, or material grabs like Qxd5) but fundamentally fail to address the position's most critical demand. In every case, the position required either forcing moves (checks/perpetuals in 1/10), immediate castling/king safety (4/10), maintaining tactical pressure (3/10), or not leaving pieces hanging (2/10). The refutations consistently exploit the wasted tempo through passed pawn advances (4/10), center breaks opening lines against the exposed king (3/10), or simply capturing undefended pieces (3/10). The high average cp_loss of 294 reflects that these are narrow positions where one wrong tempo is catastrophic.
analysis.move_pattern: Any piece type or pawn; moves to seemingly active but strategically irrelevant squares; non-forcing moves (no checks, no captures of defended pieces) in positions demanding forcing play
analysis.why_bad: The position has a critical tactical or strategic demand (perpetual check, castling, attack continuation, piece defense) with an extremely narrow window—wasting one tempo allows the opponent to exploit the exposed king via center breaks, passed pawn advances, or piece captures that were previously impossible.
sub_patterns: Purposeless rook moves to 'active' files that ignore central urgency (Rh2, Rg5, Rg8, Ra4)
Weakening pawn pushes when piece development is critical (f6, c4, g5)
Knight repositioning away from tactically critical squares (Nh6 from g4, Nb5 from c7)
Pawn grabs that surrender attacking momentum against exposed king (Qxd5)

analysis.label: King moves or pawn pushes in endgame pawn races that lose a critical tempo by choosing the wrong direction or wrong unit to advance.
analysis.description: This feature fires on endgame positions with exposed kings and active pawn races where the player makes a one-square move (overwhelmingly king moves: 11/13 positions) that wastes a decisive tempo. The errors fall into clear sub-types: stepping the king to an inefficient square requiring extra moves to reach the ideal destination (Kg6 needing Kg6-Kh7-Kg8 vs direct Kh7-Kg8 in Position 4; Ke3 instead of Ke4 in Position 7; Ka1 cornering instead of staying active in Position 10; Ke8 allowing tempo-losing checks in Position 11), or advancing the wrong passed pawn (h6/h5 instead of the king-supported b6 in Positions 1 and 3). The tactical motif 'tempo_loss' appears explicitly in 10/13 analyses. The feature also fires on correct moves in identical contexts (Positions 6, 13, 15 with 0cp loss), confirming it detects the structural pattern—endgame pawn races requiring precise king routing—rather than only mistakes. High-activation positions show catastrophic losses (avg 1617cp) because in razor-sharp races, one wasted tempo converts draws to losses or losses to forced mates.
analysis.move_pattern: One-square king moves (or h-pawn advances) in open endgame positions with passed pawns on both sides, typically moving away from or perpendicular to the optimal racing path toward a promotion-support square
analysis.why_bad: In endgame pawn races, every tempo is critical—the king must take the shortest path to support its own pawn's promotion or blockade the opponent's. These moves choose a suboptimal adjacent square that adds one extra move to the racing sequence, or advance an unsupported pawn while the correctly-supported one should advance first, allowing the opponent to win the tempo race or generate decisive counterplay.
sub_patterns: King steps to wrong adjacent square adding extra move to reach ideal support square (Kg6/Ke3/Ka1/Ke8)
Pushing unsupported h-pawn instead of king-supported b-pawn in rook endgames (h6/h5 vs b6)
King moves exposing to check sequences that waste further tempi (Kb7/Ke8)

analysis.label: King moves toward the board's edge or corner in endgames where centralization is critical for survival or winning.
analysis.description: In 7/9 positions, the blunder is a king move toward the rim or corner (Ka1×3, Kh1, Ka3, Kg4, Ka4) when the position demands active king centralization. The remaining 2 positions (f4, Qf6) share the theme of failing to prioritize king activity—f4 was played instead of the centralizing Kc3, and Qf6 ignored an urgent tactical need. In nearly every case (8/9 endgame), the best move involved directing the king toward the center (Kb3, Ka3→b4, Kc1, Kg3, Kc3×3, Kg5), while the blunder sent it to passive squares where it becomes trapped, vulnerable to checks, or too distant from critical pawn battles. The average cp_loss of ~1191 reflects catastrophic consequences, including multiple forced mates, because cornered kings in endgames cannot contribute to defense or support passed pawns.
analysis.move_pattern: King moving toward a1/h1 corners or a/h-file edge squares, retreating away from the center of the board
analysis.why_bad: The king becomes passive and trapped on the edge/corner, where it is vulnerable to back-rank checks, cannot contest passed pawns, cannot support its own pawns, and loses critical tempi returning to useful squares—violating the cardinal endgame principle of king centralization.
sub_patterns: King to a1/h1 corner fleeing checks
King to a-file edge instead of centralizing via c-file
King to rim square when passed pawns demand central king support

analysis.label: Playing a reasonable-looking move in a position where essentially only one specific continuation maintains the evaluation, resulting in a catastrophic blunder.
analysis.description: This feature activates on positions where there is typically only ONE correct move (avg 1.3 good moves available) and the player instead makes a move that appears constructive or natural but catastrophically misses the critical tactical requirement. The moves all 'look like chess' — developing pieces (Nc3, Nf6, Bd7), centralizing (Be4, Kf7), attacking (Qg4, Qe8+), doubling rooks (Rda1), advancing the king (Ka6), or capturing material (Nxh8) — yet each ignores the single forcing or precise continuation that the position demands. In 7/8 analyzed positions, the move fails because it doesn't address a concrete tactical vulnerability: a hanging piece goes uncaptured (Qg4 missed Qxd7, 2/8), a forcing sequence is played in wrong order (Qe8+ before Rxg7+), a pawn is left undefended (Be4 allows Nxd4), the wrong piece is captured in a fork (Nxh8 instead of Nxd8), or a self-block creates a tactical vulnerability (Bd7 blocks queen's guard of d5). The average cp_loss of 1221 reflects positions of extreme criticality where precision was non-negotiable.
analysis.move_pattern: Varied piece types moving to plausible-looking squares (development squares, attacking squares, centralization) rather than the one specific forcing/capturing move required
analysis.why_bad: Each move ignores the single concrete tactical demand of the position — whether that's capturing an undefended piece, playing moves in the correct forcing order, protecting a critical square, or choosing the correct geometric path — in favor of a general-purpose 'improving' move that allows the opponent to exploit the unaddressed vulnerability
sub_patterns: Missed capture of undefended material (Qg4/Nxh8/Be4)
Wrong move order in forcing sequence (Qe8+ before Rxg7+)
King moves to wrong square allowing mating net or losing opposition (Kf7/Ka6)
Self-blocking or tempo-losing piece placement enabling opponent tactics (Bd7/Nf6)
Passive piece placement when active counterplay was the only defense (Rda1)

analysis.label: Moves that worsen or neglect a critical king safety emergency when a king is dangerously exposed in the center, on an open file, or with a compromised pawn shield.
analysis.description: This feature fires on moves played in positions where a king (own or opponent's) is critically vulnerable—typically uncastled/centralized (5/9 positions have an uncastled king in center), on a weak back rank (3/9), or with a shredded pawn shield—and the player makes a move that either directly worsens the king's exposure (Ke7, Kd7 walking into mating nets; f5, g4 weakening pawn cover; Qxc7 blocking escape), removes a defensive piece from the king zone (Qxh5 abandoning back-rank defense), or wastes a critical tempo on something unrelated to the king emergency (Qxd6 greedy capture instead of attacking exposed king; Nc3 retreat from dominant outpost; Qd6 non-developing move). In all 9 positions, the refutations exploit the exposed king through open files, ranks, knight infiltrations, or back-rank patterns. The average cp_loss of 2343 and only 1.6 good moves available confirm these are positions where king safety is THE dominant concern and only one or two moves properly address it.
analysis.move_pattern: Varied piece types (K, Q, N, pawns) moving in directions that either place own king on exposed squares, block king escape routes, weaken king pawn cover, or move pieces away from defending/attacking an exposed king
analysis.why_bad: The moves fail because they ignore the overwhelmingly dominant positional factor—a critically exposed king—in favor of material gain, passive consolidation, or irrelevant plans, allowing the opponent to exploit open files, diagonals, and weak squares around the vulnerable king with immediate tactical force (mating attacks, back-rank combinations, knight forks).
sub_patterns: King voluntarily walks into danger (Ke7, Kd7)
Pawn push weakening own king shelter (f5, g4)
Queen capture that exposes own back rank or blocks king escape (Qxh5, Qxc7)
Greedy/passive move ignoring opponent's exposed king (Qxd6, Nc3)
Non-developing queen move when castling is urgent (Qd6)

analysis.label: Playing a quiet developing move when an enemy piece must be captured or recaptured immediately.
analysis.description: This feature fires on positions where a player makes a routine developing move (typically a bishop development, castling, or pawn push) while completely ignoring an urgent capture that must be made NOW. In 4/11 positions, an enemy bishop has infiltrated to f3 attacking g2/e2 and must be eliminated immediately (Bxf3 or gxf3), but the player castles or pushes a pawn instead. In 3/11 positions, the opponent just captured a piece (on c3 or f3) and the player fails to recapture, instead developing a bishop (Bd3, Be2, Bd2). In 2/11 positions, an enemy piece is completely undefended/hanging and can be captured for free, but the player develops instead (Be7 instead of capturing a hanging Bf6). In 1/11 positions, the player moves the sole defender away from a threatened piece (Ng5 removing the guard of Rg1). The common thread across all cases is that the position demands an immediate, forced capture—either to eliminate an infiltrator, complete a recapture, or collect a hanging piece—and the player instead makes a 'normal-looking' move that ignores this obligation, allowing the opponent to escape with material or make exchanges on their own favorable terms.
analysis.move_pattern: Quiet developing moves (bishop placements, castling, pawn pushes) played instead of capturing/recapturing an enemy piece that is hanging, infiltrating, or freshly arrived from an exchange
analysis.why_bad: By ignoring the mandatory capture, the opponent either escapes with their hanging/infiltrating piece intact, completes a favorable exchange on their own terms (often with check), or exploits the unresolved tactical tension to win material—typically resulting in a net loss of a full minor piece worth of value.
sub_patterns: Ignoring an infiltrating enemy bishop on f3 that attacks g2 and e2 (castling or pushing pawns instead of Bxf3/gxf3)
Failing to recapture after opponent took a piece on c3 or f3 (developing a bishop instead of completing the exchange)
Missing a free capture of a completely undefended enemy piece (developing instead of simply taking a hanging piece)
Wrong capture order when two enemy pieces are en prise (taking the less dangerous one, letting the more threatening piece escape)

analysis.label: Moves that pursue a secondary goal (development, material, pawn advance) while overlooking the position's single most urgent tactical requirement.
analysis.description: This feature fires on positions where the player makes a plausible-looking, apparently useful move that completely neglects the one critical demand of the position, resulting in a simple tactical punishment. In 4/10 cases (Positions 1, 2, 4, and the opening Bf5/Nc6 examples), the player develops a piece or makes a natural move while leaving the d5-pawn fatally undefended against cxd5. In 3/10 cases (Positions 3, 9, 12), the player captures material (Bxe4 twice, captures a pawn) while ignoring lethal king-safety threats (pins, discovered checks, mates).
