In 3/10 cases (Positions 5, 8, 10), the player makes a reasonable king move or pawn advance while allowing a devastating fork, check+capture, or promotion. The common thread is an extremely narrow position (avg 1.8 good moves available) where only one specific move addresses the critical need, and the player instead pursues a secondary but logical-seeming plan. The opponent's refutation is typically embarrassingly simple—a basic capture, check, or pin that exploits the newly-created/ignored vulnerability.
analysis.move_pattern: Diverse piece types (bishops, kings, queens, rooks, pawns, knights) making moves that look active or purposeful but move toward/capture on squares that neglect a critical defensive or tactical obligation
analysis.why_bad: These moves abandon defense of a critical point or ignore an immediate tactical vulnerability to pursue a secondary goal (piece development, material gain, pawn advance, king repositioning), allowing the opponent a simple forcing sequence (capture of undefended material, pin, fork, discovered check, or promotion) that devastates the position.
sub_patterns: Premature bishop development (Bf5) leaving central pawn undefended against cxd5
Material captures (Bxe4) creating pins or allowing discovered checks against exposed king
King moves to squares allowing forks or forced simplification
Pawn advances leaving the pawn undefended after opponent's check
Attacking secondary targets while ignoring critical promotion or mating threats

analysis.label: Playing a quiet, seemingly purposeful move that wastes a critical tempo while ignoring the position's most urgent concrete demand.
analysis.description: This feature fires on positions where the player makes a non-forcing move (typically a pawn advance or piece relocation) that looks reasonable in isolation but fatally ignores the position's single most critical priority. In 8/10 positions, the analyses explicitly tag 'tempo_loss' as the primary issue. The pattern manifests as: quiet pawn advances when concrete action is needed (h5 instead of fxe4, g4 instead of h4, f6 instead of b4, f4 instead of Nb3, g6+ instead of Rf6+ perpetual); piece/king moves to the wrong sector (Rfc1 to queenside when Nh4 attacks kingside, Kb5 to queenside when Kd5 centralizes, Rb8 for 'activity' while ignoring Bd5 threat, Bg3 'improving' while allowing ...f6 break); or development to a vulnerable square (Na6 to the rim). In every case, the opponent exploits the gifted tempo to execute a concrete plan that was previously impossible or less effective — whether a kingside king march (5/10), a pawn break (4/10), or a tactical shot (3/10).
analysis.move_pattern: Non-forcing quiet moves: pawn advances (6/10) or piece/king relocations to irrelevant squares (4/10), all non-captures, addressing the wrong sector or concern
analysis.why_bad: The position has one critical demand (resolve tension, prevent a break, execute an attack, take a draw) that requires immediate action; the played move addresses a secondary concern, giving the opponent a free tempo to execute their critical plan — whether infiltrating with the king, breaking the pawn structure, or landing a tactical blow.
sub_patterns: Pawn advance on wrong wing while critical tension exists elsewhere
Piece relocation to wrong sector while attack/defense is urgent on the other side
Solidifying/reinforcing when concrete resolution is demanded
Overambitious pawn push when drawing resource exists
Development to tactically vulnerable square ignoring opponent's threats

analysis.label: Playing a quiet positional/developmental move while ignoring an immediate tactical crisis that demands concrete attention.
analysis.description: In all 4/4 positions, the player chose a non-forcing 'improving' move (castling, bishop development, pawn advance) that would be reasonable in a quieter position but catastrophically ignores an urgent tactical need. In Position 2, O-O ignores a ready d6 pawn advance smashing the e7 bishop. In Position 5, Bb2 develops a dormant bishop while the king is about to be mated along the a8-g2 diagonal via Bxf3+. In Position 9, b4 pursues queenside pawn play while the f4 knight hangs to Bxf4 with gxf4 unplayable due to king exposure. In Position 13, c5 challenges the center but allows dxc6 en passant shattering the pawn structure. All 4/4 positions feature a specific concrete opponent resource that was 'loaded' and needed to be neutralized before any other plan could be pursued. The average cp_loss of 2530 and average of only 1.8 good moves reflects how narrow these positions were — demanding precise calculation rather than routine improvement.
analysis.move_pattern: Quiet non-forcing moves (no checks, no captures, no direct threats) — pawn pushes, piece development, castling — that do not address the critical sector of the board
analysis.why_bad: The opponent has a concrete tactical resource already 'loaded' in the position (pawn advance, piece capture, mating attack) that only needed one tempo to execute; the slow move hands them that tempo instead of neutralizing the threat first
sub_patterns: Castling while ignoring a ready pawn breakthrough
Developing a piece while ignoring a mating attack on the king
Queenside pawn push ignoring a hanging piece elsewhere
Pawn advance allowing en passant or structural destruction

analysis.label: Playing a reasonable-looking move that squanders a narrow tactical window requiring immediate concrete action.
analysis.description: This feature fires on positions where the player wastes a critical tempo in a position demanding immediate, concrete action. In 10/10 positions, the analysis identifies 'tempo_loss' as a key tag. The positions share extremely narrow tactical windows (avg 1.9 good moves available), meaning the position demanded one specific action NOW. The played moves look superficially reasonable—castling (O-O), structural pawns (c3, g3), material captures (Bxg4, Qxg7, gxh2+), checks (Re8+), piece repositioning (Bd1, Re6), or pawn breaks (f6)—but all fail to address the position's critical demand. In 4/10 cases (O-O, c3, g3, Bd1), a slow positional move is played instead of a forcing tactical strike. In 3/10 cases (gxh2+, Bxg4, Qxg7), the wrong target is captured when a more precise capture or approach maintains maximum pressure. In 2/10 cases (Re8+, Re6), a piece is moved to an active-looking square that actually achieves nothing concrete. The average cp_loss of 1128 reflects how punishing these errors are in positions that brook no delay.
analysis.move_pattern: Diverse piece types and directions; the commonality is playing a natural-looking move (capture, check, development, structure) that fails to address the one urgent concrete demand of the position
analysis.why_bad: The opponent gains a crucial tempo to solve their defensive problems, consolidate, organize counterplay, or exploit a tactical vulnerability that the played move failed to address—turning a winning/equal position into a significantly worse one.
sub_patterns: Slow positional moves ignoring hanging material (O-O, c3 instead of Qxb7)
Capturing the wrong target when a more precise capture wins more (gxh2+ vs gxf2+, Bxg4 removing key attacker)
Pawn grabs allowing tempo-gaining counterplay (Qxg7 refuted by Nf5 with tempo)
Pointless checks that displace nothing (Re8+ when Qe7+ forces favorable interposition)
Passive retreats in critical positions (Bd1, g3 ignoring imminent tactical threats)

analysis.label: Aggressive pawn advances or piece relocations that destroy the player's own positional advantage by acting before necessary preparation is complete.
analysis.description: This feature fires on moves that impatiently push forward (pawn advances or piece movements seeking activity) when the position requires a quiet, preparatory, or restraining move. In 6/10 positions, the correct move was a patient preparatory action (Kc3, Kf2, h4 as a restraint, fxe4 to resolve tension correctly) while the blunder was a premature aggressive break (b5, g4, g4, d4, h5). In 4/10 positions, pieces were moved to ambitious but misguided squares (Qa2, Be5, Rcb8, Qh6) abandoning critical defensive functions. The common thread is that the player had an advantage (7/10 positions show the blundering side was winning or significantly better) and squandered it by 'overreaching'—choosing an aggressive-looking move that either destroys a sound pawn structure, abandons control of a critical file/square, or allows a tempo-gaining refutation. The correct alternatives consistently maintained the existing positional pressure through patience, proper move ordering, or defensive consolidation.
analysis.move_pattern: Primarily pawn advances (6/10: b5, g4, g4, h5, d4, plus partial h5) pushing 1-2 squares forward, often on flanks; also piece relocations away from defensive posts to aggressive but vulnerable squares
analysis.why_bad: These moves destroy the structural or positional foundation of the player's advantage—breaking solid pawn formations that generated long-term pressure, abandoning control of critical files that restrained the opponent's pieces, or placing pieces on squares where they can be attacked with tempo. The correct move almost always involved preparation first (fixing the opponent's structure, maintaining file control, or improving king position before breaking).
sub_patterns: Premature kingside pawn breaks (g4, h5) that shatter own pawn chain
Central pawn advances without necessary preparatory moves (d4 before h4, b5 before Kc3)
Piece relocations abandoning critical file control (Rcb8 leaving c-file, Rb6 leaving attack on f2)
Queen/piece moves to aggressive squares that allow tempo-gaining refutations (Qh6 allowing Ng4, Qa2 allowing Na6)

analysis.label: Playing a plausible move addressing a secondary concern while missing the single most forcing tactical blow that resolves the position's critical issue.
analysis.description: In all 4/4 positions, the player chose a move with clear logical intent (eliminating a threatening pawn, giving check, supporting promotion, developing a passive piece) but missed the ONE decisive action that directly solved the position's most urgent problem. In each case, the best move was more forcing and direct: a winning capture (Qxf3 in pos 1, Nxf4 in pos 4), a capture-with-check (Qxd6+ in pos 5), or immediate promotion to forced mate (b8=Q in pos 6). The played moves all waste a critical tempo on a secondary concern, and the refutations in all 4/4 cases exploit this lost tempo to seize the initiative. These positions uniformly had very few good options (avg 1.2 good moves), meaning they were precision-critical moments where only the most direct action worked.
analysis.move_pattern: Diverse piece types moving to plausible squares; the commonality is choosing a less-forcing action (quiet development, preparatory support, non-optimal capture/check) when a maximally forcing move (best capture, capture-with-check, immediate promotion) was available
analysis.why_bad: Each move wastes a tempo on a secondary goal, allowing the opponent to exploit the lost time—whether by capturing an undefended piece (pos 1, 4), advancing a king to support a passed pawn (pos 5), or generating discovered check counterplay (pos 6). The direct tactical solution would have resolved the position's tension before the opponent could act.
sub_patterns: Capturing on a secondary target instead of the critical capture (Bxe6 vs Qxf3, Na3 vs Nxf4)
Giving a non-capturing check when a capturing check exists (Qb6+ vs Qxd6+)
Playing a preparatory move when the decisive blow is immediately available (Ra8 vs b8=Q)

analysis.label: Quiet, non-forcing moves that create new tactical or structural vulnerabilities in the player's own position while ignoring concrete alternatives.
analysis.description: This feature fires on positions where a player chooses a slow, preparatory, or repositioning move in a position demanding immediate concrete action, and critically, the chosen move introduces a NEW exploitable weakness that didn't previously exist. In 8/8 positions, the refutation specifically targets a vulnerability created by the move itself: Qd2 creates a Bb4 pin target on the Nc3-Qd2 alignment (2/8), b3 blocks the bishop's retreat allowing ...b5 to trap it (1/8), g3 entombs the h2-bishop and exposes the g-file (1/8), f6 abandons control of g6 allowing Qg6 infiltration (1/8), Nh5 leaves h6 undefended for gxh6 (1/8), Rab1 abandons e-file tension allowing Re8 counterplay (1/8), and Qb6+ displaces the queen from defending both rooks (1/8). The positions typically have very few good moves available (avg 1.9), indicating critical moments requiring precision, yet the player chose natural-looking but objectively terrible moves that prioritize vague improvement over urgent tactical demands.
analysis.move_pattern: Non-forcing moves (quiet repositioning of queens, rooks, knights, or pawn pushes) that are neither captures nor meaningful checks, typically moving pieces away from where tactical action is needed
analysis.why_bad: These moves waste critical tempo in positions requiring concrete action, while simultaneously creating new tactical targets (pin alignments, trapped pieces, weakened squares, undefended material) that the opponent can immediately exploit with simple developing or forcing moves
sub_patterns: Queen moves creating pin vulnerabilities (Qd2 allowing Bb4 pins)
Pawn pushes weakening own king or trapping own pieces (f6, b3, g3)
Piece repositioning abandoning defensive duties or critical squares (Rab1, Nh5, Qb6+)

analysis.label: Playing a quiet positional move when a bishop on the long diagonal can capture an undefended pawn to win the exchange (rook for bishop).
analysis.description: In all 3/3 positions, a bishop sits on the long diagonal (a1-h8 or a8-h1) with a completely unobstructed path to an underdefended pawn that, once captured, also attacks the rook behind it—winning the exchange. The correct move in each case is a bishop capture along this diagonal (Bxg7, Bxb2, or Bxg2), each winning a rook for a bishop. Instead, the player makes a routine, non-forcing move: f4 (positional pawn push), e6 (which actually blocks the bishop's own diagonal), or Be7 (passive development). All 3/3 blunders occur in the opening with both kings still in the center, and all have exactly 1 good move available. The average loss is ~288cp, reflecting the massive material opportunity squandered. The shared error is 'autopilot' play—prioritizing structure or development over a concrete, forcing tactical sequence that exploits diagonal geometry.
analysis.move_pattern: Quiet non-capturing move (pawn push or minor piece development to passive square) instead of a bishop capture along the open long diagonal targeting a pawn + rook
analysis.why_bad: The played moves ignore a concrete tactical capture on the long diagonal that wins the exchange (rook for bishop), settling for routine development while the opponent can then secure the diagonal weakness on their next turn, permanently eliminating the tactical opportunity.
sub_patterns: Pawn push that blocks own bishop's active diagonal (e6)
Positional pawn push ignoring opponent's diagonal weakness (f4)
Passive bishop development ignoring own bishop's tactical capture (Be7)

analysis.label: Quiet, non-forcing moves played in tactically demanding positions where only 1-2 precise forcing continuations maintain the evaluation.
analysis.description: This feature activates when a player makes a routine, passive, or non-engaging move in a position that demands immediate concrete action. In 7/9 positions, the correct move was a forcing continuation (tactical capture like Nxf6+, simplifying exchange like Qxd5, or precise piece placement like Kg4/Nh5), while the played move was a quiet repositioning, routine capture, or piece retreat. The played moves include rook shuffles to wrong files (Rf1, Rhg8), king tucks to vulnerable squares (Kg2, Kh7), routine pawn captures (dxc5), weakening pawn advances (g4), and voluntary retreats from dominant outposts (Ne3). In all cases, the position had very few good alternatives (avg 1.9), signaling a critical decision point where the player failed to recognize the urgency. The common thread is that the position's key tactical tension required immediate resolution through forcing moves, but the player instead made a 'natural-looking' move that either ignored the tactic entirely or abandoned the source of their advantage.
analysis.move_pattern: Quiet piece repositioning (king moves, rook shuffles, knight retreats) or routine pawn captures, typically non-checking and non-capturing, in positions demanding sharp tactical solutions
analysis.why_bad: These moves waste critical tempo or abandon key piece placements in positions with razor-thin margins (1-2 good moves), allowing the opponent to exploit the newly created vulnerability—whether through intermediate checks, diagonal attacks on exposed kings, or winning hanging pieces that were previously defended by the moved piece's prior position.
sub_patterns: King moved to square vulnerable to discovered/intermediate check (Kg2, Kh7)
Piece retreated from dominant outpost without extracting concession (Ne3 from f5, Nxe7+ from d5)
Routine pawn capture ignoring decisive tactical blow (dxc5 missing Nb5-Nd6+-Nxf7+)
Rook placed on wrong file away from critical defensive task (Rf1, Rhg8)
Weakening pawn advance instead of development (g4 exposing diagonal)

analysis.label: Playing a non-capturing developing or prophylactic move when the position demands an immediate central pawn capture to resolve existing pawn tension.
analysis.description: In all 13/13 positions, the best move was a central pawn capture (exd4, dxe5, cxd5, dxe4, fxe5, etc.) that would resolve critical pawn tension favorably, but the player instead made a quiet non-capturing move—developing a piece (Be7, Nf6, Nf3, Ne2, Bc5), retreating a piece (Bg3, Bb3, Bb6), playing a prophylactic move (a6, Be2), or making a non-central pawn push (c5, e5, Na5). In every case, the central pawns were in direct mutual tension (e.g., d4 vs e5, e4 vs d5) where one pawn was inadequately defended, and the correct approach was to capture immediately. By deferring the capture for one tempo, the opponent seized the initiative to resolve the tension on their terms—typically winning a clean pawn (11/13 positions) or gaining a devastating positional advantage through tactics like pins, forks, or sacrifices exploiting the now-undefended central pawn.
analysis.move_pattern: Any non-capture move (piece development, retreat, or flank pawn push) played instead of a required central pawn exchange (pxp on d4/d5/e4/e5 files)
analysis.why_bad: Central pawn tension with an inadequately defended pawn creates a one-move tactical window; by not capturing immediately, the player gives the opponent the chance to capture first (or advance with tempo), winning material because the central pawn is left hanging or the resulting position creates tactical motifs (forks, pins, sacrifices) against the uncastled king.
sub_patterns: Passive piece development while e5 pawn hangs to Nxe5/dxe5
Bishop retreat releasing pressure on the tension point
Prophylactic flank move while central pawn is under-defended
Piece placed on square that blocks retreat or is itself captured by the tension pawn
Knight development to square immediately kicked by advancing tension pawn (e4/e5)

analysis.label: Black plays a natural-looking or plan-based move while ignoring urgent tactical threats to their vulnerable king, in positions where very few moves survive.
analysis.description: This feature fires on positions where Black's king is exposed or vulnerable and Black plays a move that fails to address the immediate concrete danger. In 5/6 positions, Black's king is explicitly noted as exposed or lacking pawn shelter (c7, e8, h6, c8, e8). The played moves look superficially reasonable—pawn pushes for space (e4, g6, f4), piece moves to active squares (Rd6, Qd7), or king moves toward apparent safety (Kc7)—but all ignore the critical tactical requirement of the position. The average number of good moves is only 1.8, indicating these are narrow positions demanding precision. In 4/6 cases the primary refutation exploits king exposure directly (Qa5+ checking the c7 king, Rh1 threatening Rh8+ with king on e8, Qxb7+ checking the c7 king, Bb5 pinning against the queen). The average cp_loss of 1794 (inflated by one forced-mate case) confirms these are catastrophic oversights, not minor inaccuracies.
analysis.move_pattern: Various piece types (pawns, rooks, queens, kings) moving to seemingly natural or active squares; no single geometric direction but consistently non-defensive moves in defensive positions
analysis.why_bad: The moves fail because they prioritize slow plans, space-gaining, or piece repositioning while the position demands immediate concrete defensive action to address king vulnerability—the opponent punishes by exploiting the exposed king with checks, pins, back-rank threats, or queen invasions that the played move did nothing to prevent.
sub_patterns: Pawn pushes ignoring king exposure (e4, g6, f4)
Piece moves abandoning critical defensive duties (Rd6 leaving back rank)
Queen/King moves walking into tactical motifs (Qd7 into pin, Kc7 onto open file)

analysis.label: Playing a natural-looking active move (often a check) in a position where exactly one precise tactical move exists, missing the critical resource.
analysis.description: In all 5/5 positions, exactly one good move was available (avg good moves = 1.0), making these razor-sharp moments demanding extreme precision. The played moves are universally 'active-looking' — 3/5 are checks (Qg7+, Qc1+, Rd1+) and 2/5 are purposeful piece mobilizations (Rc8, Qf5). In each case, the correct move exploited a specific geometric relationship the played move fails to achieve: a rook perpetual instead of a queen check (Position 1), capturing a hanging piece instead of developing (Position 3), a double-attack check on e6 instead of a simple check (Position 5), maintaining critical defensive coverage on c6 (Position 13), or an intermediate bishop check before the rook check to drive the king to a worse square (Position 15). The common thread is that the played move appears aggressive or constructive but fundamentally misses the one precise tactical shot, with catastrophic consequences (avg 4076 cp loss).
analysis.move_pattern: Active piece moves (queen checks to peripheral squares, rook moves to files, queen relocations) that bypass the single critical tactical move in the position
analysis.why_bad: The active-looking move fails to exploit the specific geometric/tactical relationship that makes the one correct move work — whether that's a perpetual check pattern, a hanging piece capture, a double-attack check, critical square coverage, or a forcing move-order requirement. By choosing the 'obvious' active move, the player allows the opponent to escape, defend, or counterattack.
sub_patterns: Wrong piece giving check when different piece forces perpetual or mate
Move-order error: giving check with piece A before piece B loses the critical square
Queen relocation to 'active' square abandoning critical defensive coverage
Positional rook move ignoring free material capture

analysis.label: Passive or slow moves in critical endgame positions that ignore the position's most urgent defensive or structural requirement, wasting a decisive tempo.
analysis.description: This feature fires on endgame positions (9/10 cases) where the player makes a quiet, non-forcing move that appears purposeful—pushing a pawn (h6, h3, h5, a3 in 4/10), repositioning a king (Kd7, Kf5, Ke7 in 3/10), or moving a rook laterally (Ra2, Ra7 in 2/10)—but critically ignores the position's most pressing need. In every case, the position demanded immediate specific action: defending a critical pawn (Ra2 abandoned h4), keeping a defensive piece in place (Nf3 removed a mate-blocking knight), retreating an exposed king (h3 instead of Kb3), or improving piece coordination before advancing (h5 instead of knight relocation). The played moves all have some superficial logic—activating a rook, pushing a passed pawn, centralizing—but the refutations consistently show the opponent exploiting the specific vulnerability left unaddressed, typically within 1-2 moves. The average cp_loss of 2899 is extreme because in time-critical endgames, a single wasted tempo often converts a holdable position into immediate catastrophe.
analysis.move_pattern: Quiet non-forcing moves (pawn pushes, lateral rook moves, king wandering) that don't address an immediate tactical or structural requirement
analysis.why_bad: In tempo-critical endgame positions, these moves waste the one tempo needed to address the position's most urgent requirement—whether that's defending a specific pawn, maintaining a defensive piece on a critical square, or retreating an exposed king—allowing the opponent to exploit the unaddressed vulnerability immediately.
sub_patterns: Premature pawn pushes that create targets or allow blockade (h6, h3, h5, a3)
King moves that walk into danger zones or away from critical duties (Kd7, Kf5, Ke7)
Rook moves that abandon defensive files for illusory activity (Ra2, Ra7)
Piece moves that remove critical defensive resources (Nf3)

analysis.label: Moves that appear active or improving but fatally abandon control of a key square, blockade, or defensive function.
analysis.description: This feature fires on moves where a player chooses an apparently constructive or aggressive-looking continuation that actually relinquishes a critical defensive responsibility. In 5/6 positions, the move directly abandons control of a specific vital square: Bd3 abandons g2 (allowing Bg2 trapping the rook), Ng4 wastes tempo when e5 was the only way to exploit a concrete tactical window, Kc4 loses a critical tempo in a pawn race (vs Kc2 supporting from behind), Bf5 abandons the c8 blockade square (allowing unstoppable promotion), g4 overextends creating a target on a square the king can attack, and f4 surrenders e4 control enabling decisive king infiltration via d5-e4-f3. The common deception is that each move looks like it's 'doing something' — centralizing, gaining space, activating a piece — but the abandoned defensive function was irreplaceable. The average cp_loss of 1823 reflects how catastrophic these seemingly reasonable moves are, and the low average of 2.5 good alternatives suggests these are positions where maintaining the defensive function was critical and few moves preserved it.
analysis.move_pattern: Piece or pawn moves to an apparently active/aggressive square (forward or centralizing), typically along a diagonal or toward the center, while vacating a square that performed an essential guard, blockade, or control function
analysis.why_bad: The moved piece/pawn was performing an irreplaceable defensive function (guarding a key square, maintaining a blockade, or preserving tempo efficiency) that no other piece could fulfill, and abandoning it allows the opponent to immediately exploit the unguarded weakness — whether through infiltration, promotion, or piece trapping
sub_patterns: Bishop abandons guard of critical square allowing piece trap or infiltration (Bd3, Bf5)
Pawn advance relinquishes control of key square enabling king penetration (f4, g4)
Piece/king moves to suboptimal square losing critical tempo in a race (Kc4, Ng4)

analysis.label: Player makes a passive or redirecting move instead of capturing or eliminating a dangerous enemy passed pawn that demands immediate attention.
analysis.description: In all 7/7 positions, the opponent has a dangerous advanced passed pawn (e6, e3, e3, g6, c7, c3, f7) that the best move eliminates by capture (fxe6, fxe3, Rxe3, Rxg6, Bxc7, Qxc3, Rxf7). Instead, the player makes a move that either uses the same piece/pawn in a non-capturing direction (f6 instead of fxe6, f3 instead of fxe3), moves the critical blockading/defending piece away from the pawn (Rc2 abandoning the e2 blockade, Qd7 leaving the e-file), or develops/repositions a piece ignoring the passed pawn entirely (Be5, Ba7, Qc2). The average cp_loss of ~2990 reflects that many of these errors allow unstoppable promotion sequences or expose critical defensive weaknesses. The positions typically have only 1-2 good moves available, indicating these are 'must-find' captures where the passed pawn is an existential threat.
analysis.move_pattern: Any piece type; moves laterally, forward, or retreats instead of capturing toward the enemy passed pawn; non-capture moves when a pawn capture or piece capture of the passed pawn is required
analysis.why_bad: The enemy passed pawn is an existential threat (often 1-2 squares from promotion or creating decisive tactical motifs), and failing to capture it immediately allows promotion, back-rank mates, or loss of the piece that was defending against promotion. The played moves look reasonable in isolation but catastrophically misjudge the urgency of the passed pawn threat.
sub_patterns: Pawn advances adjacent to but not capturing the passed pawn (f6 vs fxe6, f3 vs fxe3)
Critical blockader/defender moves away, allowing pawn advance (Rc2 off e2, Qd7 off e-file)
Bishop/Queen repositions to 'active' square instead of capturing the pawn (Ba7 vs Bxc7, Qc2 vs Qxc3)

analysis.label: Pursuing a secondary objective on the wrong side of the board while the opponent's critical strategic threat goes unaddressed.
analysis.description: In all 3/3 positions, the player makes a move that pursues a secondary or peripheral goal (capturing a flank pawn, pushing a pawn to create activity on the wrong wing, or prematurely resolving pawn tension) while the position's critical strategic priority demands immediate attention. In position 1, Kxa4 grabs a meaningless a-pawn while abandoning defense of the c3/b2 chain against a devastating passed pawn. In position 2, e6 resolves central tension that should be maintained, surrendering king centralization advantage. In position 3, f5 chases kingside pawn play while White's queenside passed pawns required immediate blockade. All 3/3 positions are simplified (endgame or late middlegame), all 3/3 have very few good moves (avg 1.3), and in all cases the opponent punishes by advancing their primary plan unopposed—typically a passed pawn or king centralization that becomes unstoppable.
analysis.move_pattern: Pawn advances or king captures directed toward a flank/peripheral square, moving away from the board sector containing the critical strategic threat
analysis.why_bad: By investing a tempo on a secondary objective, the player gives the opponent a free move to execute their primary plan (advancing a passed pawn, centralizing the king), and the resulting threat becomes unstoppable because the player's pieces are now misplaced on the wrong side of the board.
sub_patterns: King capture moving away from critical pawn chain
Flank pawn push while opponent has advanced passers on opposite wing
Premature tension resolution allowing opponent king activation

analysis.label: Playing a non-forcing preparatory or repositioning move when the position demands immediate concrete action, wasting a critical tempo.
analysis.description: This feature fires on moves that appear strategically reasonable but fatally mistime their execution by choosing slow, non-forcing moves when the position demands immediate action. In 7/9 positions, the primary tag is 'tempo_loss.' The pattern manifests as: king marches when passed pawns need pushing (Kf6 instead of c3, Kc5 instead of e5), piece repositioning when forcing moves exist (Qh4 instead of Bf5, Qa2 instead of Re1), premature blockade placement (Bh8 when Kd6 was needed first), and pawn advances that address long-term concerns while ignoring urgent tactical demands (g3 allowing Bxg3, b6 enabling c6!, c5 dropping material). The common thread is a player who identifies a correct strategic idea (king activation, blockading, queen repositioning, pawn structure) but executes it at the wrong moment, ceding the opponent a free tempo to advance their own concrete threats—typically a pawn promotion race, a tactical shot, or a consolidating regrouping move.
analysis.move_pattern: Various piece types (K, Q, B, pawns) moving to apparently logical squares; typically non-capturing, non-checking moves that reposition rather than create immediate threats
analysis.why_bad: The position has concrete urgency (pawn races, tactical shots, forcing sequences) where one tempo determines the evaluation, and the played move wastes that tempo on a preparatory idea that allows the opponent to execute their threat first
sub_patterns: King maneuvers instead of immediate pawn advances in endgames
Queen/piece repositioning to passive squares missing forcing continuations
Pawn advances that weaken structure or enable opponent's breakthrough
Premature blockade placement before extracting positional concessions

analysis.label: Natural-looking developing or improving moves played in positions demanding immediate tactical action, allowing the opponent to exploit the wasted tempo with a concrete tactical blow.
analysis.description: This feature fires on moves that appear positionally reasonable—developing a piece, centralizing, or making a 'useful' advance—but catastrophically ignore the position's urgent tactical demands. In 7/9 positions, the blunder places a piece on a seemingly active square (Re3, Bd6, Qe6, Bd3, Qd8, Qd6, d5) while overlooking an immediate tactical vulnerability: forks exploiting undefended pieces (positions 1, 11), trapped/attacked pieces (position 3), removal of key support for own pieces (position 4), enabling forced mating patterns (position 8), allowing the opponent to strike with tempo-gaining centralization (position 13), or permitting devastating sacrifices (position 12). In 9/9 cases, the player had at least 1-3 good alternatives that addressed the concrete tactical situation, yet chose a move oriented toward long-term improvement over immediate necessity. The refutations consistently exploit the single tempo wasted—knight jumps to fork squares, pawn advances trapping pieces, back-rank combinations, or piece centralization with tempo. The average cp_loss of 1306 reflects how severely these 'reasonable-looking' moves are punished when the position's tactical tension is at its peak.
analysis.move_pattern: Piece development or repositioning to central/active-looking squares (d3, d6, e3, e6, d8) or positional pawn advances (d5, h4, c4) — non-forcing moves that don't address an immediate threat
analysis.why_bad: Each move wastes a critical tempo in a position where the opponent has a concrete tactical resource (fork, trap, sacrifice, mating pattern, or tempo-gaining attack) that punishes the lack of urgency, turning the position from manageable to lost.
sub_patterns: Developing a piece to an undefended square allowing a fork (Re3/Ng4, Bd3/Ng4-f2+)
Centralizing the queen on a square that enables a tactical combination against it (Qe6 back-rank, Qd6 Ne4 tempo)
Slow pawn moves ignoring king safety or attack urgency (h4 with uncastled king, c4 wasting attacking tempo)
Piece placement that fails to address a vulnerable piece or key defender (Bd6 ignoring trapped knight, Qd8 abandoning g7 defense)
Pawn advance that removes support from own key piece (d5 undermining knight on e5)

analysis.label: Pieces moved to ostensibly active or aggressive squares while ignoring concrete tactical demands of the position.
analysis.description: This feature fires on moves where a piece (most often a bishop, 5/8 cases) is placed on an apparently aggressive or active square—pinning (Bg5, Bg4 x2), centralizing (Be5), maintaining diagonal pressure (Bb6), or attacking (Neg5, Qa4, Rb8)—while ignoring a more critical concrete requirement. In 3/8 positions, the move leaves f7 or a critical pawn undefended, enabling a forcing sacrifice or combination. In 2/8 positions (Be5, Rb8), the player misses the identical winning idea Bc7 attacking a knight on b6. In 2/8 positions (Qa4, Bb6), the piece lands on a square where it becomes irrelevant to the position's true demands or is directly trapped. In 1/8 (Neg5), a well-placed piece is voluntarily moved from its ideal square to a 'flashy' but tactically refutable one. The common thread is that all moves are motivated by general positional principles (pins, activity, centralization) rather than concrete calculation, and each one either creates a new tactical vulnerability or misses an existing tactical opportunity that the opponent can exploit within 1-2 moves.
analysis.move_pattern: Pieces (predominantly bishops) moved to active-looking squares on ranks 4-8, often creating pins or targeting enemy pieces, without addressing concrete tactical obligations
analysis.why_bad: These moves prioritize superficial piece activity or general principles over the position's concrete tactical demands—leaving critical squares/pieces undefended, placing pieces where they can be trapped or attacked with tempo, or missing stronger forcing continuations that the position required.
sub_patterns: Bishop developing to pin but leaving f7 undefended (Bxf7+ sacrifice)
Piece centralizing while missing a winning tactical combination (Bc7 motif)
Queen/piece moving to queenside while kingside defense is critical
Piece moving to active square where it becomes trapped by pawn advance
Knight leaving ideal centralized square for aggressive but tactically flawed outpost

analysis.label: Moves that squander a vital tempo on an irrelevant or counterproductive action when the position demands one specific urgent response.
analysis.description: This feature fires on positions where the player makes a move that ignores the single most pressing demand of the position, wasting a critical tempo. In 7/9 positions, the analysis explicitly identifies 'tempo_loss' as the core tactical motif. The positions share extremely narrow defensive or offensive paths (avg 1.9 good moves available), meaning one wasted move is catastrophic. Examples include: king retreating indecisively instead of committing to a pawn race (Kc6, Kd4), knights abandoning dominant posts or blocking own pawns (Ng5 leaves e6 outpost, Nf3 blocks g4), irrelevant pawn pushes when the king must immediately flee (h6 with king exposed on d7, f6 blocking bishop's retreat), checks that drive the enemy king to safety (Qb4+ allows Ke3-Kd2), pawn grabs that decentralize the queen from defensive duties (Qxb2), and developing the wrong piece while a smothered mate looms (Bc6 instead of Bg7). The average cp_loss of 3330 reflects how punishing these tempo wastes are in positions that demand immediate precision.
analysis.move_pattern: Any piece type moving to a square that does not address the position's most urgent tactical or strategic demand; typically sideways/backward/peripheral moves when forward/committed moves are required
analysis.why_bad: The position has only 1-2 viable moves addressing an urgent threat (mate, pawn race, piece restriction, king safety), and the played move wastes the one tempo needed to stay in the game, allowing the opponent to execute their plan unopposed or reach a winning configuration one move faster
sub_patterns: King retreating/wandering instead of committing to a pawn race or fleeing direction
Knight relocating away from dominant outpost or blocking own critical pawn advance
Irrelevant pawn push when king relocation is the only defense against forced mate
Check that drives enemy king toward safety rather than keeping it exposed
Queen pawn-grab that decentralizes it far from critical defensive zone

analysis.label: Playing natural-looking or "improving" moves in narrow positions that demand one specific concrete action.
analysis.description: This feature fires on positions where the player makes a move that looks reasonable by general chess principles (developing a piece, centralizing, advancing a pawn for counterplay, moving the king toward a target) but ignores the single most critical demand of the position. In 6/7 actual mistakes, there were only 1-3 good moves available (avg 1.8), indicating extremely narrow positions requiring precise calculation. The correct moves were often counterintuitive: an en passant capture (Position 10), a pawn sacrifice to force exchanges (Position 11's c6), keeping a pawn stationary for defense (Position 13's g5 guarding a square), maintaining piece placement rather than 'improving' it (Position 15's Kg3 over Nd3), or addressing a pawn tension before developing (Position 1's e5). The blundered moves instead follow general improvement logic—Nf6 develops, Be4 centralizes, g4 advances for counterplay, Ke3 approaches a pawn, Nd3 targets b4—all ignoring the position's specific tactical or structural emergency.
analysis.move_pattern: Piece/pawn moves to apparently active or natural squares (development squares, central squares, advanced squares) rather than addressing the position's most urgent concrete issue
analysis.why_bad: These moves ignore the position's primary tactical or structural demand—whether that's neutralizing a dangerous pawn (f5, h6), capturing via en passant, sacrificing to simplify, or maintaining a defensive piece/pawn on a critical square—resulting in the opponent exploiting the unaddressed threat (mating attacks, tempo-gaining advances, passed pawn races, piece infiltration).
sub_patterns: Developing or centralizing a piece when a specific pawn move is required to defuse tension
Advancing a pawn for 'counterplay' that vacates a critical defensive square
Moving a well-placed piece away from its optimal post, losing tempo
Pursuing an obvious-looking plan while missing a counterintuitive saving resource
Ignoring an immediate mating or tactical threat to play a 'general improvement' move

analysis.label: Playing a non-forcing, quiet, or peripheral move in an overwhelmingly winning position where an immediate decisive tactical blow (usually forced mate) was available.
analysis.description: This feature fires on moves that waste a critical tempo in positions demanding immediate tactical execution. In 5/7 positions, forced checkmate was available but the player chose a quiet or suboptimal move instead. The errors manifest as: quiet pawn pushes when piece activity wins (c4 instead of Rb2, a6 instead of h3, g3 instead of Qd6), pointless king moves when mates exist (Kh3 instead of Qd6), wrong checks that let the king escape (Ra4+ instead of Rb6# in 2), captures of peripheral material instead of attacking the king (Rxa4 instead of Rxf4 forcing mate in 6), and wrong recaptures that block the winning piece (Nxe3 instead of Qxe3 enabling mate). All 6 analyzed positions share the 'missed_tactic' tag, 5/6 share 'tempo_loss', and the average cp_loss of 6642 reflects converting forced wins into merely large advantages. The unifying thread is a player who recognizes they are winning but fails to find or execute the precise forcing continuation, defaulting to a 'reasonable-looking' move that grants the opponent a crucial defensive tempo.
analysis.move_pattern: Diverse piece types (pawns, kings, rooks, knights); all are non-forcing or suboptimally forcing moves - quiet pushes, peripheral captures, wrong checks, wrong recaptures - when a specific forcing sequence delivers immediate mate or decisive material gain
analysis.why_bad: These moves waste a critical tempo in positions where the opponent's king is trapped or vulnerable and every move counts for maintaining the mating net; the gifted tempo allows the opponent to trade pieces, reposition their king, or disrupt the attacking coordination, converting forced mates into merely winning positions
sub_patterns: Quiet pawn push instead of forcing piece activation (c4, a6, g3)
Pointless king move when mating attack exists (Kh3)
Wrong check that pushes king toward safety (Ra4+ vs Rb6+)
Peripheral material grab instead of king attack (Rxa4 vs Rxf4)
Wrong recapture blocking the winning piece (Nxe3 vs Qxe3)

analysis.label: Playing a slow prophylactic or consolidating move when the position demands immediate aggressive or forcing action.
analysis.description: In all 4/4 positions, the player chose a non-forcing move that addressed a secondary concern (recapturing an intruder on c3, defending the a2-pawn, centralizing the queen, or activating the king) while the position demanded urgent dynamic play. In position 2, bxc3 eliminates a bishop that was already trapped instead of winning it via the forcing exf6. In position 8, Kf3 'activates' the king but blocks its own rook's tactical resource while leaving b2 hanging. In position 9, a3 defends a pawn that should have been sacrificed for a decisive kingside pawn storm. In position 15, Qd6 centralizes but places the queen on a square where Nf5 hits it with tempo, enabling a forced combination. All 4/4 positions feature the common tag of 'tempo_loss' and 'missed_tactic', with the player consistently choosing positional tidying over the position's true demand for immediate action. The average cp_loss of 232 reflects that these slow moves allow the opponent to reorganize or exploit the gifted time.
analysis.move_pattern: Quiet non-forcing moves (pawn captures, pawn advances, king moves, queen centralization) that address local concerns rather than creating threats
analysis.why_bad: The position requires immediate forcing play (pawn breaks, sacrifices, or preventing opponent counterplay), but the player spends a tempo on a non-urgent concern, allowing the opponent to reorganize, create counterplay, or exploit the time wasted on an irrelevant or counterproductive move.
sub_patterns: Recapturing material when an intermediate forcing move wins more
Defending a pawn that should be sacrificed for tempo
King/piece move that blocks own tactical resources
Piece centralization that creates a target for opponent's forcing reply

analysis.label: Playing a slow, routine, or passive move that wastes a critical tempo when the position demands immediate concrete action to address a tactical vulnerability.
analysis.description: In 7/7 positions, the player chose a 'natural-looking' quiet move (a capture, retreat, pawn move, or developing move) instead of addressing the position's most urgent tactical demand. In 3/7 cases (Rad8, Rf1, Kg1), the move was a slow rook or king repositioning that ignored a specific hanging piece or back-rank vulnerability. In 2/7 cases (g3, g6), a pawn move created new weaknesses while failing to generate counterplay. In 2/7 cases (Be7, Bxg4), a bishop move was either a passive retreat into the opponent's threats or a material grab that removed a key piece from its dominant square. In all cases, the best moves shared the theme of immediately addressing the position's most critical dynamic element—whether maintaining a mating attack (Position 1), seizing central space first (Position 7), creating piece counterplay (Position 9), or evacuating from a tactical alignment (Positions 11, 14). The average cp_loss of 1633 reflects how catastrophically these tempo losses are punished.
analysis.move_pattern: Quiet non-forcing moves (retreats, slow development, passive pawn moves, premature captures) that fail to address an immediate tactical alignment or dynamic crisis
analysis.why_bad: The opponent exploits the wasted tempo with a devastating tactical blow—either seizing the initiative (d4, d6 pawn advances), executing a combination (Rxd2+, Rd1+, Rxh3), or opening lines against the vulnerable king (fxg6). The 'natural' move ignores that the position has one critical demand that must be addressed NOW.

Slow rook/king move ignoring hanging piece or back-rank vulnerability (Rf1, Kg1, Rad8)
Defensive pawn move that weakens own king shelter or leaves pieces hanging (g3, g6)

analysis.label: Player misses an aggressive pawn advance (usually g4/g5) that attacks an exposed enemy bishop, instead making a routine developing or exchanging move.
analysis.description: In 5/6 positions, the best move was a g-pawn advance (g4 or g5) attacking an enemy bishop sitting on the h-file (h4 or h5), while the 6th position required b5 attacking a bishop on a4 — the same concept mirrored to the queenside. Instead of these forcing pawn thrusts, players chose passive alternatives: routine captures (fxe4, cxd4 in positions 1,5), quiet developing moves (Bd7, Qe2, Bg4 in positions 3,4,6), or positional knight maneuvers (Na4 in position 2). The enemy bishop is consistently on an exposed square where a pawn advance both gains tempo and disrupts opponent coordination. The missed pawn advances are not merely good — they are critical timing moves that exploit the bishop's vulnerability before the opponent can consolidate, averaging 321cp loss when missed.
analysis.move_pattern: Any piece type or capture; the ERROR is choosing routine development/exchanges instead of an available g-pawn (or b-pawn) advance attacking an exposed enemy bishop on the h-file or a-file
analysis.why_bad: The routine move fails because it squanders a narrow timing window to attack an exposed enemy bishop with a pawn advance; without this forcing move, the opponent stabilizes their piece placement, and the player's passive alternative often creates new tactical vulnerabilities (hanging pawns, overloaded defenders, exposed pieces) that the opponent immediately exploits.
sub_patterns: g4/g5 missed against bishop on h5/h4
b5 missed against bishop on a4
pawn capture releasing tension instead of pawn advance creating it
quiet development instead of tempo-gaining pawn thrust

analysis.label: Playing a slow, non-forcing move when the position urgently demanded an immediate threat (check, capture, or attack on a piece), surrendering a critical tempo that allows the opponent to consolidate or seize the initiative.
analysis.description: All 5/5 positions share a common thread: the player chose a move that looks natural or purposeful on the surface but creates no immediate threat, when forcing alternatives (checks, captures, attacks on pieces) were available and necessary. In Position 1, Rcc7 'doubles rooks' but creates no threat and the rook is forced back (tempo loss). In Position 4, Kh8 is a prophylactic king tuck that ignores the urgent c6 tension. In Position 5, Kxc7 captures with the wrong piece, exposing the king when Qxc7 maintained safety. In Position 7, c5 is a premature pawn break that gives White time to regroup (Bc1). In Position 12, Rd6 is a passive rook placement when Rd2+ invaded with check. The analyses confirm 'tempo_loss' is tagged in 5/5 positions, 'piece_activity' in 5/5, and 'missed_tactic' in 5/5. In every case, the opponent exploited the gifted tempo to either create a passed pawn (4/5), centralize their king (3/5), or launch a kingside attack (2/5).
analysis.move_pattern: Any piece type; non-forcing repositioning moves (no check, no capture of active material, no direct attack on a piece) when forcing alternatives existed
analysis.why_bad: The position required immediate action—a check, a capture, or a direct attack on an enemy piece—to maintain the initiative. The passive move gives the opponent a free tempo to execute their plan (advance a passed pawn, centralize the king, or redirect pieces to attack), transforming the position's character irreversibly.
sub_patterns: Passive rook placement when rook invasion with check was available (Rcc7, Rd6)
Purposeless king moves when urgent pawn tension or tactical issues demand resolution (Kh8, Kxc7)
Premature pawn breaks that relieve tension and gift opponent a reorganizing tempo (c5)

The positions share extremely limited margin for error (avg 1.8 good moves available), meaning only precise responses to the critical threat maintain the position. In 4/5 cases, the player's move would be perfectly reasonable in a calmer position but here it grants the opponent a decisive tempo to exploit a specific vulnerability: a discovered check (Nf3), a pawn advance with check exploiting blocking vs. guarding (Bb3), a knight fork on unprotected rooks (d6), a forced mating net via pawn check (Kf5), or advanced pawn breakthroughs (Ne7). The extremely high average cp_loss (2138) reflects that these 'calm' moves in 'sharp' positions typically convert slight disadvantages into catastrophic losses or forced mates.
analysis.move_pattern: Mixed piece types (bishop, knight, pawn, king) moving to squares that appear constructive or natural but fail to address the critical forcing line in the position
analysis.why_bad: The move ignores the position's most urgent tactical demand—often a single forcing sequence (discovered check, fork, mating net, promotion threat)—in favor of a generically improving move, granting the opponent the exact tempo needed to execute a decisive combination.
sub_patterns: Piece repositions to guarding square instead of blocking square (Bb3 vs Ba2)
Development to natural square ignoring discovered attack geometry (Nf3)
Premature pawn advance neglecting back-rank piece vulnerability (d6)
King advances into pawn-storm mating zone (Kf5)
Regrouping move conceding critical tempo for opponent's pawn advance (Ne7)

analysis.label: Quiet, non-forcing moves that pursue secondary goals while ignoring the position's critical tactical demand, resulting in catastrophic tempo loss.

In 7/9 positions, the move either ignores a direct tactical threat (Nd4 ignores f7 attack, Rac1 ignores Ne6-Nf4+, Ke8 ignores Qxa8) or creates a self-inflicted problem by obstructing friendly pieces (Be3 blocks rook escape allowing Nd3, Bd3 blocks bishop retreat allowing e5 trapping it). The average cp_loss of 1243 reflects the catastrophic nature of wasting tempo in positions with high tactical tension, where opponents can execute decisive operations in a single move.
analysis.move_pattern: Quiet non-forcing moves (no captures, mostly non-checks) of any piece type, typically repositioning or developing to squares that don't address the critical tactical axis
analysis.why_bad: These moves waste a critical tempo in tactically demanding positions, allowing the opponent to execute a winning operation (trapping a piece, winning material, launching a mating attack) that the best moves would have prevented or preempted
sub_patterns: Self-blocking moves that trap own pieces (Be3, Bd3)
Unnecessary prophylaxis ignoring concrete threats (b3, Rac1)
Passive retreats when active defense was required (Ke8, Rb6)
Pointless checks that improve opponent's position (Rb2+)
Speculative activity ignoring immediate tactical threats (Nd4)

analysis.label: Positionally-motivated moves that ignore the critical need to reposition the queen, creating or exposing tactical vulnerabilities in major pieces.
