Instead, the player made a seemingly reasonable move—often a quiet pawn push (g3, h5, d4, b5 in 4/9 cases), a piece centralization (Be5 in 1/9), or a queen move to the WRONG square (Qg4, Qa6, Qd7 in 3/9). In every case, the move played prioritized secondary positional aims (space, centralization, prophylaxis) over the urgent tactical requirement of proper queen placement. The resulting positions invariably exposed a hanging or inadequately defended major piece (rook in 5/9 cases, queen in 3/9 cases) to a tactical shot—typically a diagonal/file exploitation that won material. The average cp_loss of 307 reflects how catastrophically these 'reasonable-looking' moves fail when the position's true demand is ignored.
analysis.move_pattern: Quiet pawn advances, piece centralizations, or queen moves to wrong squares—all non-forcing moves played instead of the required queen repositioning to a specific safe/active square
analysis.why_bad: Each move ignores the position's critical tactical demand (correct queen placement) and instead creates or exposes an undefended major piece to a concrete exploitation—typically via a diagonal attack, file pin, or deflection tactic that wins material
sub_patterns: Quiet pawn push (g3/h5/d4/b5) when queen needs immediate repositioning
Queen moved to wrong square (Qg4/Qa6/Qd7) leaving it passive or undefended
Piece move (Be5/Qxe5) that removes a critical defender or interposer from a diagonal

analysis.label: Moves that relocate a piece or pawn from a square where it was performing an essential (often non-obvious) defensive function, creating an immediate tactical vulnerability.
analysis.description: In all 6 positions, the player moves a piece/pawn that appears to serve a constructive purpose (centralizing, activating, gaining space) but critically abandons a latent defensive duty. In Position 7, f5 removes the f7-pawn from the d5-g8 diagonal, enabling Qd5+ and forced back-rank mate (6/6 abandon defense). In Position 8, Qc8 places the queen where a rook belongs—unlike a rook, the queen cannot safely trade on d8, enabling a devastating battery (5/6 create back-rank or piece-capture vulnerability). In Position 12, Qe7 removes the queen from f6 where it provided the counter-threat Qxf1+, leaving the e6-bishop hanging to Nxe6 (4/6 remove indirect tactical counter-threats). In Position 2, Bd5 leaves the bishop en prise to cxd5 with no compensation. In Position 5, f4 abandons control of e3/f2 while the king remains uncastled. In Position 6, Qe2 blocks the e2 development square and creates e-file pin vulnerability. All moves (6/6) appear superficially constructive but ignore that the moved piece was the sole guardian of a tactical vulnerability.
analysis.move_pattern: Piece or pawn moves to a seemingly active/central square, away from a square where it was passively defending a critical weakness (diagonal, file, or providing counter-threat)
analysis.why_bad: The moved piece/pawn was the sole defender of a critical tactical weakness (back-rank, diagonal, hanging piece, or counter-threat); removing it creates an immediate forced tactical punishment that the opponent can exploit with checks, captures, or batteries.
sub_patterns: f-pawn advance exposes king diagonal or back rank (f4, f5)
Queen relocates from square providing key counter-threat, leaving pieces hanging (Qe7, Qc8)
Piece moves to unprotected central square where it is simply captured (Bd5)
Queen/piece self-blocks development creating file vulnerability (Qe2)

analysis.label: Making a constructive-looking piece move (capture or development) that fatally ignores an immediate checkmate threat against the player's own exposed king.
analysis.description: In all 5/5 positions, the player's king is severely exposed and under imminent mating attack. Instead of addressing the lethal threat with the only viable defensive moves, the player makes a 'normal' looking move—capturing material (Qxe2, Qxd3), developing/repositioning a piece (Bc4, Bd1), or attempting a prophylactic block (Bg7). In 5/5 cases, the position was already losing (avg eval ~600cp against), with only 1-2 survivable moves available, indicating extreme desperation. The blunders all result in immediate or short forced checkmate (mate-in-1 in 2/5 cases, mate-in-7 or shorter in 4/5). The critical failure is identical across all positions: the player prioritizes piece activity or material concerns over the single most important factor—their king's survival against an imminent mating attack.
analysis.move_pattern: Bishop or Queen moves (3 bishop, 2 queen) that either retreat/develop away from king defense or capture on a tactically compromised square, all while the player's king faces immediate checkmate threats on adjacent squares or short diagonals
analysis.why_bad: The moves fail because they completely ignore immediate checkmate threats (often mate-in-1) against the player's own exposed king—either removing a piece that was the sole defender of a critical square near the king, or making a move that does nothing to block/prevent the unstoppable mating attack
sub_patterns: Removing sole defender of king's critical square (Bc4 abandons g2, allowing Qg2#)
Ignoring one-move mate threat entirely (Bd1 ignores Qxh3#)
Placing queen on square where it's recaptured with check leading to mating attack (Qxe2, Qxd3)
Providing tactical target that accelerates opponent's mating sequence (Bg7 allows Bxg7 cascade)

analysis.label: Natural-looking or principled moves that ignore an immediate tactical vulnerability, allowing the opponent a tempo-gaining or material-winning response.
analysis.description: This feature fires on positions where the player makes a move that appears to follow sound general principles (developing a piece to its natural square, capturing material, improving piece placement) but critically overlooks a concrete tactical shot available to the opponent. In 3/9 positions, the move is Nf6 allowing e5 with devastating tempo gain against the uncastled king. In 3/9 positions, the player moves their king or a piece to a square directly vulnerable to a forcing attack (Kc2 allows Rxb2+ leading to mate, Kxc7 allows d5 with tempo, Bc5 allows Qc4+ fork). In 2/9 positions, the player wastes a tempo on a non-urgent move while leaving an existing piece or vulnerability unaddressed (Rhg8 leaves bishop on d5 capturable, Rhh5 abandons the critical 6th rank). In 1/9, a slow positional pawn push (c4) misses an immediate material-winning queen invasion. The common thread across all positions is that concrete tactical calculation was required but the player instead followed autopilot principles, and the opponent's refutation typically gains a tempo or exploits a newly-created vulnerability with a forcing move.
analysis.move_pattern: Varied piece types moving to seemingly natural/logical squares; no single geometric direction but all involve placing pieces or making moves that create or ignore an immediate tactical target
analysis.why_bad: Each move ignores that the opponent has an immediate forcing response (pawn advance with tempo, check, fork, capture of undefended piece) that exploits either the moved piece's new vulnerability or an existing tactical weakness left unaddressed by the tempo-wasting move
sub_patterns: Nf6 allowing e5 with tempo against uncastled king (3/9)
King/piece moves to square vulnerable to forcing check or fork (3/9)
Non-urgent rook or pawn move leaving existing piece/square undefended (3/9)

analysis.label: Natural-looking or thematic moves that neglect an urgent concrete tactical demand in the position, either removing a critical defender, wasting tempo, or addressing a secondary concern.
analysis.description: This feature fires on moves that appear strategically reasonable—contesting a file (Rac1), capturing material (Rxf4), advancing pawns (g4, g5, a4), castling (O-O), repositioning pieces (Bh8, Rfd8), or chasing threats (Ncb5 x2)—but critically ignore the position's primary tactical requirement. In 7/11 cases, a concrete tactic was available (queen trap, knight fork, discovered check, pawn break) that the player missed in favor of the 'natural' move. In 6/11 cases, the move specifically removes a piece from a critical defensive function (Ncb5 removes c3 knight defending diagonal/e4/d4; Rac1 abandons a2 defense; Rxf4 dismantles attacking battery; Bh8 abandons d4 blockade). In 5/11 cases, slow pawn moves or routine development waste tempo when forcing play is essential. The average cp_loss of 253 reflects positions demanding precision where 'autopilot' play is severely punished.
analysis.move_pattern: Various piece types making non-forcing moves (quiet repositioning, pawn advances, routine development) rather than the demanded forcing/tactical continuation
analysis.why_bad: The position requires concrete calculation—either exploiting a tactic (fork, trap, pawn break) or maintaining a critical defensive function—but the player defaults to a 'reasonable-looking' move based on general principles, either removing a key defender, wasting a tempo the opponent exploits, or missing a one-move tactical shot.
sub_patterns: Moving the wrong piece when two similar options exist (Ncb5 vs Ndb5, Rxf4 vs Bxf4)
Removing the sole defender of a pawn or square (Rac1 abandons a2, Ncb5 abandons diagonal/e4)
Slow pawn pushes ignoring hanging pieces or concrete tactics (g4, g5, a4)
Routine developing moves when forcing play is available (O-O ignoring fork, Rd1 ignoring active counterplay)
Voluntarily relocating a piece from a critical post to a passive square (Bh8 from d4)

analysis.label: Player chooses a natural-looking piece activation or repositioning move when a concrete forcing continuation (check, capture, or sacrifice) was immediately available and much stronger.
analysis.description: In 8/10 positions, the player selects a 'reasonable' non-forcing move—typically centralizing a piece, activating a dormant piece, or making a natural-looking capture—when a specific forcing tactical sequence would have been far superior. Position 3 (Nb6 instead of capturing a hanging knight with Qxf4), Position 5 (Ne5 centralizing instead of Ng5+ sacrifice with check), Position 9 (Rg5 aimlessly repositioning instead of Rh8+ into a skewer), and Position 10 (Nc4 activating the knight instead of maintaining it on defensive duty) all share this pattern clearly. Position 2 (Nxd4 wrong recapture leaving e5 hanging), Position 4 (Bxg5 wrong capture order), and Position 6 (Rf1 passive move when forcing queen moves prevent mate) follow the same logic. The average cp_loss of 1116 with only 1.5 good moves available confirms these are narrow positions where one forcing move dominates and the 'natural' alternative is catastrophic.
analysis.move_pattern: Piece repositioning or activation move (knight/rook centralization, natural capture, king advance) to seemingly active squares, without delivering check or exploiting immediate tactical features
analysis.why_bad: The non-forcing nature of the move gives the opponent a free tempo to address the critical vulnerability (defend hanging material, consolidate king safety, neutralize threats), whereas the missed forcing move would have exploited the position's concrete features—undefended pieces, exposed kings, or back-rank weaknesses—before the opponent could react.
sub_patterns: Knight centralization when forcing knight check/sacrifice wins material
Wrong piece captures (recapture or pawn capture order) leaving key squares/pieces undefended
Rook repositioning to natural file when forcing check leads to skewer/deflection
Piece activation that abandons critical defensive duty of guarding a pawn or square

analysis.label: Playing a non-forcing repositioning move when the position urgently demands an immediate capture, check, or concrete tactical action.
analysis.description: This feature activates on moves where a player chooses a slow, quiet piece repositioning over an available forcing continuation (capture, check, or urgent pawn push). In 7/10 positions, the best move was either a capture (Bxh6, Nxh7, Bxf3) or a check (Rd3+), while the played move was a quiet piece placement to a natural-looking square (Bf6, Ng7, Bd5, Rc5, Bd4, Ne4). In the endgame cases (3/10), the best move was an urgent pawn push (f4) or active king move creating a pawn race, while the played move was a passive king retreat (Ke7, Kc8) or quiet rook move. The common thread is that the blundered moves look positionally reasonable — centralizing, repositioning, or targeting something — but they lack forcing power, giving the opponent the tempo needed to execute devastating plans (perpetual checks, pawn promotion races, or crushing attacks). The average cp_loss of 335 with only 1.7 good moves available confirms these are narrow positions where only concrete action maintains the evaluation.
analysis.move_pattern: Piece moves to a natural/central square without delivering check, making a capture, or creating an immediate forced threat — typically one square away from where the tactical action is required
analysis.why_bad: The quiet move surrenders a critical tempo, allowing the opponent to seize the initiative through checks, captures, pawn advances with check, or forcing sequences that the player could have preempted with their own forcing move first
sub_patterns: Approaching a target instead of capturing it (Bf6 vs Bxh6, Ng7 vs Nxh7)
Wrong piece to the right square (Bd5 vs Nd5, Ne4 vs Nd5)
Passive king/rook move instead of urgent pawn push in endgame races (Kc8/Ke7 vs f4)
Removing a key defender for a non-forcing exchange (Bd4 abandoning kingside)
Non-forcing exchange when order of captures matters (Nxe5 vs Bxf3 first)

analysis.label: Moving a piece away from its essential defensive role (or wasting tempo) in a position where king safety demands immediate attention, allowing the opponent to exploit the newly unguarded squares.
analysis.description: In all 6 positions, the player makes a move that removes a piece from a critical defensive function or squanders a tempo on a non-urgent goal while the king is vulnerable. In 5/6 positions, king safety is the primary issue being ignored (king in center or exposed). In 5/6 positions, the move creates or worsens a tempo deficit. The blunders look 'reasonable' on the surface—natural development (Nf6), prophylactic retreat (Ba7, Bc8), quiet pawn move (b3), material grab (Bxd5), or seemingly safe recapture (Kxc7)—but each fatally neglects the position's urgent tactical demands. The opponent's refutations consistently exploit the vacated defensive coverage: diagonal control lost (4/6), key squares abandoned (5/6), or king exposure created (5/6). All positions were extremely critical with only 1-2 good moves available, indicating the player failed to recognize the position's sharpness.
analysis.move_pattern: Piece retreats to passive square, captures material away from defensive post, or makes quiet non-forcing move; typically bishop/knight moving away from center or key defensive diagonal
analysis.why_bad: The piece was performing a critical defensive function (guarding key squares, controlling diagonals, shielding the king) and its removal or displacement allows the opponent an immediate tactical or positional blow exploiting the newly undefended zone—usually against a vulnerable king
sub_patterns: Bishop retreating to passive square abandoning active defense (Ba7, Bc8)
Materialistic capture removing piece from defensive duty (Bxd5, Kxc7)
Quiet prophylactic move ignoring urgent tactical crisis (b3, Nf6)

analysis.label: Moving the king (or its key defender) to a square that creates a new geometric alignment exploitable by opponent's pieces for a mating attack.
analysis.description: In 4/5 positions, a king voluntarily moves to a square that opens a new line of attack (rank, file, or diagonal) that was previously unavailable. In Position 2, Kh6 steps onto the 6th rank enabling Rxd6+ lateral mating attack. In Position 6, Ka7 leaves c7 undefended and exposes the king to Qxc7+ with a back-rank skewer. In Position 14, Kb7 steps onto the a8-h1 diagonal allowing Bf3+ to activate a bishop-rook mating net. In Position 10, Ra5 removes the only defensive piece from the king's vicinity, creating identical mating geometry. Position 15 (88cp loss) is a milder case where Rc4 allows queen infiltration to e2. The common thread across 4/5 high-activation examples: the move creates a new exploitable geometric line (rank/diagonal/file) connecting the opponent's attacking piece to the king, enabling a forcing sequence leading to mate.
analysis.move_pattern: King moves one square (typically forward toward center or along edge) to an adjacent square that places it on a new rank, file, or diagonal shared with opponent's heavy pieces/bishop; or rook moves away from king's defensive perimeter
analysis.why_bad: The move creates a new geometric alignment (rank, file, or diagonal) between the king and an opponent's attacking piece that didn't exist on the previous square, enabling a check or capture that initiates a forced mating sequence. The previous square was safe precisely because it didn't share these critical lines.
sub_patterns: King steps onto rank shared with opponent's rook (Kh6 onto 6th rank)
King steps onto diagonal shared with opponent's bishop (Kb7 onto a8-h1 diagonal)
King moves exposing key pawn to queen capture with check (Ka7 undefending c7)
Defensive rook abandons king zone enabling mating construction (Ra5 leaving e-file)

analysis.label: Playing superficially active checks, captures, or aggressive-looking moves that squander a decisive advantage by missing the precise forcing continuation.
analysis.description: This feature fires on positions where the player has a large or decisive advantage but throws it away by choosing a move that looks active or aggressive rather than finding the truly winning continuation. In 5/9 positions, the blunder is a check or capture (Ne5+, Ng3+, Ba6+, dxe4, Nxe5) that feels forcing but is tactically hollow. In 3/9 cases (Ne5+, Ng3+, Ba6+), the player gives an aimless check that either removes a key piece from a dominant square or places it en prise—classic 'checking addiction.' In 2/9 cases (dxe4, Nxe5), the player makes a routine pawn/piece capture when Qh4+ exploiting an open diagonal would win a full rook. The remaining moves (e5, Bb2, h5, Kc7) are active-looking moves that waste critical tempo or walk into tactical patterns. The average cp_loss of 3316 and average of only 1.6 good moves available confirm these are positions at critical decision points with narrow correct paths and enormous advantages being squandered.
analysis.move_pattern: Checks (knight or bishop), pawn/piece captures, or active-looking advances—moves that appear forcing or purposeful but lack genuine tactical teeth
analysis.why_bad: The moves remove key pieces from dominant squares, waste tempo the opponent needs to escape, place pieces on vulnerable squares where they hang, or consume reserve tempi—all while the correct move (usually a different forcing sequence, often a queen check on an open diagonal) delivers a decisive blow
sub_patterns: Aimless checks that let the king escape or remove attacking pieces from key squares (Ne5+, Ng3+, Ba6+)
Routine captures that miss a devastating queen check on an open diagonal (dxe4, Nxe5 both miss Qh4+)
Active-looking pawn advances that weaken pawn structure or waste critical tempo (e5, h5)
Developing moves that miss concrete tactical shots (Bb2 misses Nxe5)

analysis.label: Aggressive knight (or piece) move that abandons coordination, leaving another piece tactically vulnerable or the knight itself hanging.
analysis.description: In 7/9 positions, a knight is moved to an aggressive-looking square (g5, g4, f6, e5, c3) when the position demands quiet consolidation. In 4/9 cases, the identical opening position appears (Ne4+Nf3+Bc4 vs d5+e5+Nc6) where the correct move is always 6.Bd3, but instead the e4-knight is moved away (to g5, c3, e5, or sacrificed on f6), leaving the bishop on c4 tactically exploitable via dxc4. In 2/9 cases, a knight on f6 jumps to g4 for speculative f2-attacks, either becoming hanging itself (Qxg4) or abandoning its defensive role (allowing Nxc6 forks). The remaining cases (h4, Ba6) represent tempo losses that ignore critical central tension requiring immediate piece trades. The tagged tactical motifs are predominantly 'hanging_piece' (5/9) with 'tempo_loss' appearing in 7/9 analyses. All positions occur in the opening with an average cp_loss of 314.
analysis.move_pattern: Knight (occasionally bishop) moves to an aggressive square (g4, g5, f6, e5, c3) away from a coordination role, typically toward the enemy king or an attacked pawn
analysis.why_bad: The piece movement breaks coordination: either it leaves another piece undefended (most commonly a bishop that becomes capturable by a pawn), the moved piece itself becomes hanging on its new square, or it abandons a defensive post allowing devastating forks/tactics. The correct move is almost always a quiet consolidating move (Bd3, O-O, capturing a strong enemy piece).
sub_patterns: Knight leaves e4 exposing bishop on c4 to pawn capture (4/9 positions, same opening)
Knight moves from f6 to g4 becoming hanging or abandoning defensive duties (2/9)
Knight jumps to g5 for f7 attack when target is adequately defended or bishop hangs (2/9)
Tempo-wasting move ignoring central tension that demands immediate piece trade (2/9)

analysis.label: Non-forcing moves that appear purposeful but waste critical tempo in positions demanding immediate tactical precision.
analysis.description: This feature fires on moves where a player chooses a slow, positionally-motivated action—piece 'improvement,' king centralization, pawn advance, or apparent defense—while ignoring the position's concrete tactical demands. In 11/11 positions, the move played looks superficially logical (centralizing a king in Ke3/Kc6/Kg3, attacking a piece with Bc7/Nf5, defending with Qe7, blocking with d3, improving with Bd6) but creates or ignores a specific tactical vulnerability exploitable by forcing moves. The common punishment involves the opponent gaining tempo through checks, captures, or forks that the 'improving' move failed to prevent: Nb6-Nc4 forking the rook (Position 3), f5+ driving back the king (Position 11), exf7+ bypassing the 'defender' (Position 12), Bc5 targeting f2 (Position 6), and g5/gxf4+ winning material (Position 4). In 8/11 cases, king safety is the primary factor ignored. The average 1.9 good moves available confirms these are narrow positions where only immediate, forcing continuations preserve the evaluation—any slow alternative collapses.
analysis.move_pattern: Quiet piece repositioning (king walk, bishop slide, knight hop, pawn push) to an apparently useful square, non-capturing and non-checking, in positions with exposed kings and tactical tension
analysis.why_bad: The move wastes a critical tempo on a non-forcing 'improvement' while the position demands either an immediate tactical blow (g2+, Rb3, Nb5) or concrete prophylaxis; the tempo loss allows the opponent to execute a forcing sequence (check, fork, pawn break with check) that exploits the vulnerability the slow move either created or failed to address.
sub_patterns: King advancing into tactical danger (Ke3, Kg3, Kc6, g4)
Piece relocating to a capturable or self-blocking square (Bc7, Bd6, Nf5, Nxd5)
Passive retreat/defense when forcing tactics win (Qc1, Qe7, d3)

analysis.label: Standard-looking developing moves (especially bishop pins like ...Bg4) played in positions demanding concrete tactical responses, leaving critical squares or pieces undefended.
analysis.description: This feature fires on positions where a player makes a 'textbook' developing move instead of addressing an urgent tactical demand. The dominant sub-pattern (4/7 positions) involves bishop pins on knights: ...Bg4 pinning Nf3 to the queen appears in 3/7 positions, and Bg5 pinning Nf6 appears in 1/7—in all four cases, the bishop move leaves a critical square undefended (f7 in the Bg4 cases, e4 in the Bg5 case), enabling a tactical refutation. The Bg4 positions specifically allow the classic Bxf7+ sacrifice followed by Ne5+ forking king and bishop (3/7). The remaining moves (Nc3, Nf3, Qd2) are similarly routine developing moves that ignore concrete threats: Nc3 ignores Ng4 attacking f2 (1/7), Nf3 ignores a dominant enemy knight on e4 (1/7), and Qd2 allows a simplifying queen trade that neutralizes a tactical advantage (1/7). All 7 positions feature both kings in the center during the opening phase, and in every case the position demanded specific, forcing play rather than general development.
analysis.move_pattern: Piece development to natural/standard squares (especially bishops to g4/g5 for knight pins), non-forcing, non-capturing moves in the opening
analysis.why_bad: These moves ignore immediate tactical vulnerabilities—most commonly, placing a bishop on g4 removes it from defending f7, enabling a Bxf7+ sacrifice + knight fork. More broadly, choosing routine development over concrete responses gives the opponent time to exploit hanging pieces, undefended squares, or execute forcing tactical sequences.
sub_patterns: ...Bg4 pin exposing f7 to Bxf7+/Ne5+ fork combination
Bg5 pin leaving a central pawn/piece undefended
Generic knight/queen development ignoring an opponent's centralized piece or tactical threat

analysis.label: Giving a check that wastes tempo, leaves pieces hanging, or squanders a critical move-order opportunity by checking before proper preparation.
analysis.description: All 9/9 positions feature the player delivering a check (+) that is either premature, on the wrong square, or leaves a piece undefended. In 3/9 cases (Bg5+, Ne6+, Ng4+), the checking piece lands on an unprotected square where it can simply be captured, often with devastating counter-check or tempo gain. In 4/9 cases (Ba3+, Ng4+, Qe6+, Qd6+), the check is a move-order error where the same check appears in the best line but at a later move—played too early, it allows the king to escape to a square that should have been denied first. In 2/9 cases (Qe3+ vs Qe1+, Qb6+ vs Qb1+), the check is delivered from the wrong square, failing to control a critical escape route that the correct check would have covered. The average cp_loss of 1519 reflects the catastrophic nature of these impulsive checks, and the average of only 1.7 good moves available shows these were narrow tactical moments requiring precision rather than any check.
analysis.move_pattern: Any piece type (bishop, queen, knight) delivering check, often moving to an undefended square or checking before a preparatory move repositions other pieces
analysis.why_bad: The check either (1) places the piece on an unprotected square where it is captured for free, (2) allows the enemy king to reach a safe square that a preparatory move would have denied, or (3) wastes the critical tempo needed to execute a stronger tactical sequence that may include the same check later
sub_patterns: Hanging piece check - piece lands undefended and is captured
Premature check - correct thematic idea but wrong move order
Wrong-square check - check from adjacent square fails to control key escape route
Purposeless tempo-wasting check - king simply sidesteps to equivalent or better square

analysis.label: Making a plausible-looking active or material-gaining move that critically ignores the opponent's immediate simple tactical refutation.
analysis.description: This feature fires on positions where a player pursues a superficially attractive goal—capturing a pawn, centralizing a piece, giving a check, or gaining space—while critically failing to address the most urgent tactical vulnerability in the position. In 6/6 analyzed positions, the move had a clear logical intent (winning material on e5 in positions 1, 5, 8; developing in position 2; defending in position 3; attacking in position 4) but overlooked a devastating opponent response that exploited an undefended piece, open diagonal, or tactical motif. The refutations are consistently simple (recaptures, checks, forks, captures of hanging pieces) rather than deep multi-move combinations. The moves span captures (3/8), piece development/centralization (3/8), a check (1/8), and a pawn push (1/8), unified by the pattern of the player being 'too focused on their own idea' to calculate the opponent's concrete response. All positions had 1-3 clearly better alternatives that addressed the critical vulnerability first.
analysis.move_pattern: Piece or pawn moves to active-looking squares (frequently e5/f5 area: 5/8 moves), including captures, centralizations, and checks that leave critical vulnerabilities unaddressed
analysis.why_bad: The move pursues a secondary objective (material gain, development, aggression, defense of wrong threat) while leaving a simple tactical shot available to the opponent—typically a recapture of a hanging piece, a check on an unblocked diagonal, or a fork exploiting the exposed king
sub_patterns: Capturing a defended pawn with a piece that becomes hanging (Nxe5 x2)
Centralizing/developing while ignoring an opponent's check or fork (Bf5, h5, Ne5)
Capturing material without first blocking a critical check diagonal (exf5)
Choosing the wrong square for a forcing move when a better square enables a winning tactic (Qf2+ vs Qb2+)
Defensive move that leaves another piece undefended (Bb2)

analysis.label: Playing a passive, peripheral, or non-urgent move when the position demands immediate decisive action, wasting a critical tempo.
analysis.description: All 10/10 positions share the defining characteristic of a player choosing a slow, repositioning, or peripheral move at precisely the moment when the position demanded immediate forceful action. In 10/10 cases, the analyses explicitly tag 'tempo_loss' as a key factor. The moves include retreating/repositioning pieces away from the critical sector (Nd2, Ne2 - 2/10), slow flank pawn pushes ignoring urgent threats (g3, a3, f4 - 3/10), capturing peripheral material while abandoning a decisive tactical position (Qxa6, Ra1 - 2/10), and premature or misordered moves that squander a concrete advantage (g3+, Qf6, dxe5 - 3/10). The average cp_loss of 331 reflects the severity: these are positions with narrow windows where one specific plan works, and the player instead pursues a secondary goal. The opponent's refutations consistently exploit the gifted tempo to resolve critical tension, escape danger, challenge key files, or blockade passed pawns.
analysis.move_pattern: Any piece type; typically moves toward the periphery, retreats from active squares, or addresses a secondary sector rather than the critical one; includes quiet knight retreats, flank pawn pushes, peripheral captures, and premature advances
analysis.why_bad: These moves waste the critical tempo needed to execute a winning plan or maintain pressure, allowing the opponent to resolve tension favorably, escape danger, challenge key lines, or establish defensive coordination that neutralizes the player's advantage
sub_patterns: Piece retreat/repositioning when attack demands continuation (Nd2, Ne2)
Slow flank pawn push ignoring urgent kingside/central demands (g3, a3, f4)
Capturing peripheral material while abandoning decisive tactical setup (Qxa6, Ra1)
Premature forcing move before necessary preparation (g3+, Qf6, dxe5)

analysis.label: Passive, non-forcing moves that ignore the most critical immediate threat, gifting the opponent a decisive tempo.
analysis.description: This feature fires on positions where the player makes a quiet, natural-looking move (development, repositioning, luft) instead of the one concrete action demanded by the position's urgency. In 6/6 cases, the played move is non-forcing (no check, no capture, no direct threat) while the best move directly confronts the opponent's most dangerous asset: Rd6 attacks the queen (Position 2), Re3/Ke3 blockades the advancing e-pawn (Position 4), Rgf1/Rg2 defend the king (Position 6), Bg6 attacks the queen (Position 10), Nb3/Qc3 immediately contain the passed pawn (Position 13), and Bxe6 eliminates the deadly passed pawn (Position 14). In all cases, the blunder grants the opponent one free tempo that enables a devastating tactical execution—typically back-rank invasions (4/6), pawn promotions (3/6), or mating nets (3/6). The average cp loss of ~4700 reflects the catastrophic nature of losing tempo in critical positions.
analysis.move_pattern: Non-forcing quiet moves (piece retreats, pawn pushes, development moves) with no check, capture, or direct threat—typically repositioning away from the critical sector
analysis.why_bad: These moves waste a critical tempo by failing to address the most urgent threat (back-rank weakness, advanced passed pawn, or attacking piece coordination), allowing the opponent to execute a decisive tactical blow that was previously preventable
sub_patterns: Piece retreat/repositioning instead of counter-attacking (Rd7, Nd3, Bb7)
Quiet king/pawn move instead of concrete defense (Ke2, h6)
Wrong piece activation ignoring king safety (Rab1)

analysis.label: Quiet, non-forcing moves that ignore the position's most critical demand, gifting the opponent a decisive tempo to execute their primary plan.
analysis.description: In all 7 analyzed positions, the played move fails to address the single most urgent requirement of the position—whether that's king safety (Bxd5 ignoring mate threats, Bc1 ignoring need to castle), active counterplay (Nc2 retreating when Nb5/Nc6 create threats, b3 when a4 attacks the pawn chain), maintaining a dominant piece (Nb4 abandoning d5 outpost), avoiding a passed pawn's advance path (Re7 walking into d6), or preserving attacking potential (Qc1 offering simplification when Qb3 maintains pressure). The 'tempo_loss' tag appears in 7/7 analyzed cases. In every instance, the best moves involve concrete, forcing, or directly relevant actions (king evacuation, captures of hanging material like Nxf4, aggressive piece placement creating dual threats), while the blunders are quiet moves addressing secondary concerns. The average cp_loss of 1325 (inflated by one extreme case) reflects how catastrophically a wasted tempo compounds when the opponent has a concrete plan ready to execute.
analysis.move_pattern: Non-forcing moves (retreats to back rank, passive repositioning, non-critical pawn pushes) when the position demands immediate concrete action—pieces moving backward/sideways rather than engaging the critical sector
analysis.why_bad: Each move gives the opponent a free tempo to execute their primary threatening plan (mating attack, passed pawn advance, piece invasion, structural breakthrough), because the played move addresses a secondary or non-existent concern instead of the position's #1 priority
sub_patterns: Piece retreats to passive back-rank squares (Nc2, Qc1, Bc1)
Premature/misdirected pawn breaks when piece play is needed (d5, b3)
Decentralizing active pieces away from optimal posts (Nb4 from d5)
Greedy captures ignoring existential king threats (Bxd5)
Placing pieces in the path of opponent's advancing passed pawn (Re7)

analysis.label: Playing a slow, non-forcing move in a position that demands immediate tactical action or concrete resolution of critical tension.
analysis.description: Across all 11 positions, the played moves share a common character: they are 'improving' or 'natural-looking' quiet moves (developing a bishop, pushing a pawn, repositioning a piece, doubling rooks) made in positions where the tactical tension has reached a critical threshold demanding forced play. In 8/11 positions, the primary tag is tempo_loss - the move wastes a tempo that allows the opponent to execute a devastating tactical operation (Bxe5 leading to a fork, Rxd5 exchange sacrifice, e5 central break, Qxa4 exploiting a pin, etc.). The best moves in these positions were overwhelmingly forcing: captures (Nxe4, Rxe5, Nxc6), threats (Re5 threatening mate, Nh4 threatening Nf5+, Nc5 attacking), or counterattacks (b5, e4 central breaks). The average cp_loss of 1121 and average of only 2.2 good moves confirms these are narrow critical moments where only concrete solutions work. In 9/11 cases, the opponent had a clear tactical refutation exploiting the wasted tempo - typically involving a capture, fork, or breakthrough that wouldn't have been possible had the player chosen the forcing continuation instead.
analysis.move_pattern: Varied piece types (knights, bishops, pawns, rooks, king, queen) making non-capturing, non-checking repositioning or pawn advances - universally non-forcing moves
analysis.why_bad: The moves fail because they ignore the position's tactical demands: either missing a winning tactical opportunity (forced mate, tactical capture, crushing break) or allowing the opponent a free tempo to execute a devastating tactical blow (exchange sacrifice, fork, pin exploitation, central breakthrough) that was previously prevented by the tension in the position.
sub_patterns: Slow pawn pushes that create weaknesses (f3, b3, b4, e5) allowing tactical exploitation of new holes or undefended squares
Passive piece repositioning (Nh5, Bd7, Bd5, Kf7) missing concrete forcing continuations
Positional moves (Rfc1 doubling, Nh4 maneuvering, Qf6 pressuring) that are too slow given the opponent's concrete tactical resources

analysis.label: King centralization or quiet maneuver in simplified endgames instead of an immediate concrete action (capture, pawn advance, or forcing move).
analysis.description: This feature fires on positions in simplified endgames (11/12 endgame) where the player makes a slow, positional move—overwhelmingly a king march (9/12 are king moves)—when a more concrete, forcing alternative exists. The positions share open centers (10/12), exposed kings on both sides, and minimal material (pawn endgames or near-pawn endgames). When the move IS a mistake, the pattern is consistently a tempo/move-order issue: the player prioritizes 'improving the king' or making a preparatory move over an immediate capture or pawn advance that would be more forcing. For example, Position 3 plays Kf4 instead of f4 (pawn advance first), Position 7 plays g4 instead of Kxe4 (capture first), Position 8 plays Rb5 instead of cxb4 (capture to create passed pawn), Position 10 plays Kf4 instead of Bd5/f4 (creating threats first), and Position 12 plays Kc3 walking into a fork instead of Nc3 blockading. Even the 0-cp-loss positions (5/12) show the same structural pattern—king advances in simplified positions with multiple equivalent options—suggesting the feature detects the positional archetype rather than strictly the error magnitude.
analysis.move_pattern: King moves (or quiet pawn/piece moves) advancing toward center or toward a target pawn in simplified endgame positions with open files and exposed kings
analysis.why_bad: The king march (or quiet move) wastes a tempo that should be spent on an immediate concrete action—a capture, a forcing pawn advance creating a passed pawn, or a piece redeployment—allowing the opponent to improve their king position, generate counterplay, or (in extreme cases) exploit the king's new square tactically.
sub_patterns: King advance before pawn capture/advance (move-order tempo loss)
King blockade attempt walking into tactical vulnerability (fork/check)
Passive piece move instead of immediate pawn capture creating passed pawn
Quiet pawn push allowing opponent to lock structure (g6 allowing g4)

analysis.label: Active-looking moves (centralizations, captures, checks, attacks) that squander advantage by missing the single critical move the position demands.
analysis.description: This feature fires on positions where the player chooses a superficially attractive, active-looking move over the one precise continuation required. In 5/8 positions, the move centralizes a piece or makes a tempting capture (Ke6, Nxd4, Nxe5, Qe5, Ne4), while the remaining cases involve aggressive actions like checks (Rf4+), piece attacks (Rb8), or pawn advances (a4). The critical shared factor is that only ~1.4 good moves existed on average, yet the player selected something that appears productive but wastes the crucial tempo. In 6/8 cases, 'tempo_loss' is explicitly identified as the primary failing. The positions uniformly punish general activity: Ne4 abandons the crushing Nb5-Nxc7+ fork; Ke6 walks into the center instead of retreating to safety; Nxe5 captures a pawn but leaves the piece hanging; Rb8 attacks the queen but leaves its own queen en prise; Qe5 centralizes but creates an overloaded defense; a4 pushes a pawn when piece pressure was essential; Rf4+ gives a flashy check when simply advancing a passed pawn was unstoppable.
analysis.move_pattern: Piece moves toward center, makes captures, or gives checks that appear active but fail to address the position's concrete tactical demand
analysis.why_bad: These moves give the opponent the critical tempo needed to consolidate, counter-attack, or exploit a newly-created vulnerability, in positions where only one precise move maintained the advantage or held the position together.
sub_patterns: Centralizing a piece that abandons a stronger concrete threat (Ne4, Ke6, Qe5)
Captures that miscalculate the resulting material exchange (Nxe5, Nxd4)
Aggressive moves (checks, attacks, pawn pushes) that ignore defensive obligations or simpler winning plans (Rf4+, Rb8, a4)

analysis.label: Capturing a rook on the back rank with a minor piece while ignoring a more urgent tactical threat from an enemy knight.
analysis.description: In all 6/6 positions, the player uses a minor piece (bishop in 5/6 cases, knight in 1/6) to capture a rook sitting on the first or eighth rank, lured by the seemingly large material gain. However, in every case, an enemy knight poses a more critical immediate threat that is left unaddressed: a fork opportunity (2/6), a hanging piece that should be captured first (2/6), or an attack on a now-undefended piece (2/6). The best moves in all 6/6 positions involve dealing with the dangerous knight first—either capturing it, blocking its threats, or moving the attacked piece to safety. The back-rank rook capture appears to be a 'tunnel vision' mistake where the obviously valuable target on the back rank draws attention away from the more dynamic and immediate tactical reality of the position.
analysis.move_pattern: Minor piece (usually bishop) captures a rook on the opponent's back rank (1st or 8th rank) via diagonal or knight jump
analysis.why_bad: The rook capture ignores a more urgent tactical threat from an active enemy knight, which immediately exploits the neglect through forks, captures of undefended pieces, or sacrificial attacks that recover equal or greater material.
sub_patterns: Bishop captures rook on 8th rank ignoring knight fork
Bishop captures rook ignoring hanging piece elsewhere
Minor piece captures rook while own piece left en prise to knight

analysis.label: King (or piece) moves in endgames that lose a critical tempo by heading toward the wrong sector or to a peripheral square, allowing the opponent to seize dominant positioning.
analysis.description: This feature fires on endgame positions where the player moves their king (8/9 cases) or piece (1/9) in a direction that appears active or purposeful but actually surrenders control of the critical squares or loses a decisive tempo race. In 8/9 positions, the key error is moving the king toward the rim or wrong flank when centralization or approaching the critical sector was required: Kh4 instead of Kf4 (Position 1), Ke6 instead of the c6 breakthrough (Position 4), Ke3 retreating instead of Kg5 advancing (Position 6), Kh5 instead of Kg6/Kf6 (Position 11), Ke6 toward the center when the kingside was critical (Position 9), and Ke6 surrendering f4 control (Position 10). The consistent tactical consequence is that the opponent's king immediately claims the dominant square (g6, c6, e5, f4) that determines the endgame outcome. The average cp_loss of 283 and the fact that typically only 1-2 good moves exist confirms these are critical decision points where a single tempo determines the result.
analysis.move_pattern: King moves (rarely bishop) in endgames, often toward the board edge (h-file) or wrong flank, when a centralized or sector-appropriate king move was required
analysis.why_bad: The king abandons control of a critical square (f4, e5, g6, c6) or moves away from the decisive sector of the board, giving the opponent one free tempo to seize dominant king positioning or execute a breakthrough that cannot be contested
sub_patterns: King to rim (h-file) instead of center
King advances to wrong flank when other wing is critical
King moves when a pawn break was the only winning move
King retreats when counterattacking advance was required

analysis.label: Plausible-looking active moves (checks, captures, advances) that waste the one critical tempo the position demands, allowing opponents to execute saving or winning resources.
analysis.description: This feature fires on positions where a player makes an apparently active or natural move—a check, capture, pawn advance, or developing move—that fatally wastes the most critical tempo in the position. In 8/10 positions, the analyses explicitly identify 'tempo_loss' as the core error. The positions share extreme time-sensitivity: there is typically only 1-2 good moves available (avg 1.6), and the position requires addressing one specific urgent need (blocking an escape route, threatening a piece directly, activating the king before advancing a pawn, or exploiting a tactical window). Instead, the player chooses a move that LOOKS productive—Qc3+ drives a king but toward safety (1/10), Kg3 approaches a rook without threatening it (2/10), a7/c6 advance pawns before preparatory moves (4-5/10), Qg4+ checks before cutting off escape squares (8/10), Nxd5 captures but gives development tempo (10/10)—but gives the opponent exactly the tempo needed to neutralize the threat (Rh1 blockade, Rg4 swing, Ra1 behind pawn, Kd3-c3 escape, Ngf6 development). The catastrophic average cp_loss of 3054 reflects that these positions are knife-edge moments where a single wasted tempo transforms forced wins into draws or draws into losses.
analysis.move_pattern: Diverse piece types and directions (checks, captures, advances, quiet moves) that share the quality of being superficially active but failing to address the position's most urgent tactical demand
analysis.why_bad: Each move gives the opponent exactly one critical tempo to execute a saving/winning resource—an escape route, a blockade, a counterattack, or a development solution—that would have been impossible had the correct (often quieter or more precise) move been played first
sub_patterns: Premature checks that drive the king toward safety rather than keeping it trapped
Premature pawn advances before preparatory piece moves (king activation or file control)
Captures that remove well-placed pieces or expose back-rank weaknesses
King moves in the wrong direction, missing the precise square that creates a direct threat
Developing moves that miss a unique one-move tactical window

analysis.label: Superficially active or material-grabbing moves that squander a critical advantage by ignoring the position's concrete, often more forcing demand.
analysis.description: This feature fires on positions where a player makes a plausible-looking move—a capture, piece activation, or seemingly useful repositioning—but fails to find the one or two precise moves the position demands. In 7/7 analyzed positions, the correct move was more forcing or addressed a more urgent need: advancing a passed pawn with tempo before capturing (Position 4: e3 before Bxc4), maintaining a mating net rather than grabbing material (Position 1: f4 instead of Nxf7), exploiting an open file for queen infiltration rather than a bishop maneuver (Position 14: Qd3 instead of Bg4), or addressing king safety before centralizing (Position 11: Kb2 instead of Qe2). The average number of good moves was only 1.8, indicating these are narrow critical moments where only precise play preserves the advantage. The played moves all appear reasonable—they target weaknesses, capture material, or place pieces on active-looking squares—but they address secondary concerns while the position's primary demand goes unmet, resulting in catastrophic evaluation drops (avg 1468cp loss). Tempo loss is a recurring theme in 7/7 positions, as the moves either waste time on non-essential actions or create new vulnerabilities that opponents exploit.
analysis.move_pattern: Pieces moved to apparently active squares (captures on f7/c4, queen/knight/bishop repositioning to central or attacking squares) that address secondary targets rather than the position's primary tactical or strategic demand
analysis.why_bad: These moves ignore the concrete, forcing continuation the position requires—whether that's tightening a mating net, advancing a passed pawn with tempo, infiltrating via an open file, or addressing king safety—and instead pursue a secondary objective (material, apparent activity) that either removes a critical piece from its optimal post, wastes tempo that gets punished, or creates new tactical vulnerabilities (skewers, forks, counterplay).
sub_patterns: Material capture that removes key attacking piece from dominant square
Piece repositioning to active-looking square that creates tactical vulnerability
Premature capture without proper preparation (wrong move order)
Tempo-losing bishop/queen maneuver when immediate infiltration was available
Pawn push that weakens structure when development/reinforcement was needed

analysis.label: Playing a natural-looking or active piece move in a position that demands a single specific defensive resource, ignoring an immediate tactical obligation.
analysis.description: This feature fires on positions where essentially only one good move exists (avg 1.3 good moves) and the player instead makes a 'reasonable-looking' piece move—typically a queen or rook going to a centralized or active-seeming square—while completely ignoring an immediate concrete threat. In 9/11 cases the move is a queen or rook relocation that appears purposeful (centralizing, contesting a file, grabbing material, challenging an opponent's piece) but catastrophically fails to address the position's critical tactical demand. Examples include: Re5 abandoning back-rank defense (Pos 11), Qxd4 grabbing a pawn while leaving the king fatally exposed (Pos 5), Qf7 stepping into a discovered attack (Pos 2), Re3 leaving f2 undefended (Pos 14), Rh4 surrendering a check tempo in a drawn endgame (Pos 15), and Ng3 ignoring a mate-in-one threat (Pos 1). In every case, the correct move was a non-obvious defensive resource (Kf2, Qe8, Qxd6, Bg6, Re6, Qf2, Ra2, d5, Bf6, Ke2, Rh3+) that specifically neutralized the threat the played move ignored.
analysis.move_pattern: Major piece (queen or rook, occasionally minor piece) relocated to an active-looking or seemingly purposeful square, typically moving laterally or forward rather than addressing a defensive obligation on a different axis
analysis.why_bad: The position contains an immediate tactical vulnerability (mate threat, discovered attack, back-rank weakness, fork, pawn break gaining tempo) that demands one specific antidote; the played move fails to address this threat, giving the opponent a devastating tactical blow that exploits the unresolved vulnerability
sub_patterns: Queen moves to active square while abandoning critical defensive coverage of king
Rook lifts or relocates while leaving back rank or key pawn undefended
Pawn-grabbing queen move that removes it from essential defensive post
Piece moves to square that is itself tactically vulnerable (discovered attack, tempo gain)
Rook move that surrenders a critical checking tempo in endgame

analysis.label: Aggressive or greedy pawn advances and king moves that ignore critical king safety vulnerabilities, when precise defensive or tension-resolving play was demanded.
analysis.description: This feature fires on positions where the player makes a forward-looking move (pawn advance or king step) while their own king is already vulnerable or in the center, and the position demands addressing that vulnerability with precision. In 8/9 positions, the player's king is explicitly noted as exposed, in the center, or having a weak pawn shield. The moves played are uniformly non-defensive: pawn advances (f4, f3, g5, e5, h4, c4 — 6/9) or king moves toward exposed squares (Kxa5, Kg3, Kf3 — 3/9). In every case, only ~1 good move existed (avg 1.4), meaning these are critical-precision moments where the player chose an imprecise, often aggressive-looking alternative. The refutations consistently exploit king safety: perpetual checks (Kf3), diagonal/file attacks against uncastled kings (f4, f3, g5, e5), hanging pieces due to exposed king alignment (Kg3), or tempo for passed pawns while the king is displaced (Kxa5, h4).
analysis.move_pattern: Pawn advances (typically one square forward on the f/g/h/c/e files) or king moves forward/sideways — never retreating or consolidating. All moves are either pawn pushes or king steps, never piece development or captures (except Kxa5).
analysis.why_bad: These moves ignore the position's primary demand — addressing king vulnerability — in favor of pursuing an unrelated plan (attacking, grabbing material, advancing pawns, building pawn chains). With the king already exposed or uncastled, the forward move either creates new weaknesses around the king, wastes a critical tempo needed for defense, removes a key defender, or walks the king into tactical patterns (checks, forks, perpetuals).
sub_patterns: Kingside pawn advances (f4, f3, g5, h4) weakening king shelter with king still in center
King moves to worse squares (Kg3, Kf3) allowing checks or hanging pieces
Greedy king captures (Kxa5) ignoring urgent positional threats
Central/queenside pawn advances (e5, c4) opening lines or removing guards near the king

analysis.label: Moving a piece away from its sole defensive duty guarding a critical square, enabling an opponent's tactical invasion or promotion.
analysis.description: In 4/6 positions, the played move removes the only piece controlling a critical square, immediately allowing the opponent to exploit it: f3 vacates f2 enabling Nf2+ discovered attack; Bb3 abandons d3 control enabling Nd3+ fork; Re4 leaves the d-file/back rank enabling unstoppable a1=Q promotion; Rxd4 (wrong recapture) places the rook where it's vulnerable to an e5 pawn fork that the queen would have dodged. Position 6 (Rg8+) shares the theme of ignoring the critical defensive need by wasting tempo on a pointless check. Position 14 (Bf2) is actually the best move with only 10cp loss, suggesting the feature also fires on positions with this defensive pressure pattern even when handled correctly. The positions share extremely limited good options (avg 1.7) and catastrophic consequences for missteps (avg 1624cp loss).
analysis.move_pattern: A piece or pawn moves away from a square where it was the sole guardian of a critical defensive point (f2, d3, d1/a1, d4), typically moving laterally or forward in a way that appears constructive but leaves the key square undefended.
analysis.why_bad: The moved piece was performing an irreplaceable defensive function (blocking an invasion square, controlling a promotion path, or preventing a fork), and once removed, the opponent immediately exploits the unguarded square with a knight invasion+check, pawn promotion, or pawn fork that wins decisive material.
sub_patterns: Pawn advance vacating king-adjacent square (f2→f3) enabling knight invasion
Bishop retreat abandoning sole control of invasion square (Bc4→Bb3 loses d3)
Rook leaving critical file enabling unstoppable promotion (Rd4→Re4 loses a1)
Wrong recapture placing piece on tactically vulnerable square (Rxd4 vs Qxd4)

analysis.label: Moving a well-placed piece away from its critical post to a passive, peripheral, or self-blocking square, surrendering control and allowing immediate opponent counterplay.
analysis.description: This feature fires on moves where a piece voluntarily abandons a dominant or functionally critical position for a clearly inferior square. In 4/11 cases, knights leave powerful outposts (e5→d3, e4→g5, e6→d8, f3→h4) for rim squares or squares that block own pieces. In 4/11 cases, rooks abandon critical open files for peripheral squares (e8→d8, d8→a8, a8→b8) or take on passive duties (Rxg7 instead of Kxg7). In 2/11 cases, queens or pawns abandon key defensive/structural roles (Qf5→d7 removing diagonal guard, d3→d4 breaking protective structure). The common thread is that the moved piece was performing an irreplaceable function—restraining an opponent's piece, controlling a critical file, blockading a passed pawn, or defending against tactical threats—and its relocation immediately enables opponent invasions, forks, or material gain.
analysis.move_pattern: Active piece (typically knight or rook) moves away from a central/dominant square to a back-rank, rim, or self-blocking square, usually backward or laterally toward the board edge
analysis.why_bad: The piece was performing a critical restraining or controlling function (containing opponent's rook, guarding key squares, blockading pawns, defending tactical vulnerabilities), and its voluntary departure immediately grants the opponent tactical exploitation—typically rook invasions on the abandoned file, forks on undefended pieces, or checks against the now-exposed king.
sub_patterns: Knight retreats from dominant outpost to rim or back-rank square (Nh4, Nd3, Ng5, Nd8)
Rook abandons critical open file for peripheral target (Rd8, Ra8, Rab8)
Piece leaves defensive post enabling immediate check or invasion (Qd7, Nh4, Rd8)
Piece moves to square that blocks own forces (Nd8 blocks rook, Nd3 blocks bishop)

analysis.label: Playing a natural-looking but misdirected move when the position demands one specific urgent concrete action.
analysis.description: In all 3/3 positions, the player chose a move that appears reasonable on the surface (capturing material, retreating defensively, centralizing) but fundamentally fails to address the single most urgent dynamic demand of the position. In position 1, Nxf4 captures a pawn but abandons the knight's critical duty guarding c1 against promotion. In position 2, Qg1 retreats passively when Qd2 was needed to contest the second rank before Black's queen invades. In position 3, Kd6 centralizes when the immediate ...f5 break was the only way to disrupt White's advancing kingside pawn chain. All 3/3 positions had very few good moves available (avg 1.7), indicating critical decision points where the position demanded precise, concrete action rather than generic improvement. The common error is misjudging urgency: treating a dynamic, time-sensitive position as though it allows leisurely improvement.
analysis.move_pattern: Various pieces making seemingly logical moves (captures, retreats, centralization) that address secondary concerns rather than the primary urgent threat
analysis.why_bad: The position demands one specific concrete action to address an imminent threat (promotion, invasion, pawn advance), and instead the player makes a plausible but misdirected move that allows the opponent to execute their plan unimpeded.
sub_patterns: Abandoning defensive duty for material gain
Passive retreat when active placement needed
Generic king centralization instead of critical pawn break

analysis.label: Playing a natural-looking but non-urgent 'improving' move in a position that demands immediate concrete/forcing action, gifting the opponent a decisive tempo.
analysis.description: This feature fires on moves that appear reasonable—centralizing pieces, repositioning, activating—but fatally waste a critical tempo when the position demands immediate forcing action. In 11/13 positions, the analyses explicitly identify 'tempo_loss' as the core error. The pattern manifests as: pushing the wrong pawn instead of the critical passed pawn (Position 1: e4 instead of advancing c3), repositioning a piece passively when a decisive pawn break exists (Position 2: Rb2 instead of b5), moving a queen to a 'natural' square while abandoning defensive duty (Positions 5, 7, 10: Qc4/Qd7/Qa4 leaving pieces unguarded or king undefended), making a king move in the wrong order allowing the opponent to execute a counter-plan (Positions 11, 13: Kd4 before a3, Kg7 before Kg6), or relocating a defensive piece to an 'active' post that creates tactical vulnerabilities (Positions 4, 12: Ne6 abandoning f8, Ne4 opening the diagonal). In all 13/13 cases, the position had very few good alternatives (avg 1.7), meaning precision was paramount, and the opponent immediately exploits the gifted tempo for a specific concrete plan: establishing a blockade, invading with a rook, launching a pawn storm, or executing a tactical shot.
analysis.move_pattern: Any piece type moving to a plausible but non-forcing square; no checks, no captures, no immediate threats created; typically centralizing or repositioning moves
analysis.why_bad: The position demands immediate concrete action (a forcing move, critical pawn break, addressing an urgent threat, or precise move order), but the played move wastes a tempo on general improvement, allowing the opponent to execute a specific plan that neutralizes or reverses the evaluation—whether establishing a blockade, launching an attack, trapping a piece, or achieving a critical prophylactic advance.
sub_patterns: Wrong pawn/wrong piece advanced instead of critical passed pawn or pawn break
Queen repositioned to active-looking square while abandoning defensive duty
King move in wrong order allowing opponent critical counter-tempo
Defensive piece moved to active post exposing king or creating tactical vulnerability
Piece repositioned passively when forcing continuation was required

analysis.label: In endgames with passed pawn races, the player moves toward the wrong flank or wastes a critical tempo instead of racing the king toward the decisive theater.
analysis.description: This feature fires on endgame positions where passed pawns create a racing dynamic and the player makes a move that goes in the wrong direction or wastes a critical tempo. In 10/10 positions, the game is in the endgame with passed pawns or imminent pawn races. The key error is misidentifying the critical sector: instead of rushing the king toward blockade duty or active counterplay (Ke3/Kf3 to blockade in positions 5, 9, 12, 13; Kf7/Ke6 to centralize in positions 3, 11; Kf6/Kg6 toward the action in positions 2, 7), players move toward the edge/wrong flank (Kh7, Kh6, Kg7, Kg4, Kc3) or push irrelevant pawns (g5, h4, c5). In 7/10 cases, the best move was king centralization or moving toward the opponent's passed pawns, while the played move went sideways or backward. The average cp_loss of 1046 (skewed by one mate) reflects how devastating even a single wasted tempo can be in racing endgames.
analysis.move_pattern: King moves toward the board edge or wrong flank; pawn pushes or piece moves when the king urgently needs to race toward the critical sector (passed pawns or center)
analysis.why_bad: In pawn race endgames, every tempo is decisive. Moving toward the wrong flank or wasting a move on irrelevant pawn pushes means the opponent's passed pawn advances one square further unopposed, often crossing the point of no return where the king can no longer catch it or where counterplay evaporates entirely.
sub_patterns: King retreats toward corner/edge instead of centralizing (Kh7, Kh6, Kg7, Kc3)
King advances toward wrong flank while opponent's passed pawn is on the other side (Kg4)
Pawn push wastes tempo when king activation is urgent (g5, h4, c5)
Piece move to address passed pawn when only king blockade works (Nb6)

analysis.label: Playing a preparatory, threatening, or positional move when an immediately available forcing check (usually a rook check) delivers a decisive tactical blow.
analysis.description: In all 6/6 positions, the best move was an immediate check that either delivered checkmate or won decisive material, yet the player chose a non-forcing alternative. In 5/6 cases the winning check was specifically a rook check (Rhg7+, Rh1#, Rh8+, Rh8+, Rh2+, Rf4+). The played moves often look thematically related to the correct idea—doubling rooks on the h-file when Rh1# already mates (Rah8), moving the queen to h3 to threaten mate when Rh8+ forces it (Qh3), moving the king to f4 when Rf4+ wins a rook via skewer (Kf4), moving the rook to d2 when Rh2+ forces mate in 2 (Rd2). The average cp_loss of ~4847 reflects that these are catastrophic missed opportunities, and the average of only 1.5 good moves available confirms these were narrow tactical moments demanding precision rather than general play.
analysis.move_pattern: Various pieces (R, Q, K) making non-checking moves to seemingly active squares when a rook check (or queen check after rook sacrifice) on a nearby file/rank delivers immediate decisive tactics
analysis.why_bad: By failing to deliver the forcing check, the player gives the opponent a crucial tempo to defend, escape, counterattack, or neutralize the threat—converting forced wins (often checkmates) into merely better positions or even allowing tactical counterblows along exposed lines
sub_patterns: Preparing/doubling when the single piece already delivers mate (Rah8 instead of Rh1#)
Threatening mate in one tempo when a sacrifice-check forces it immediately (Qh3 instead of Rh8+)
Moving the king when the rook should occupy that square with check (Kf4 instead of Rf4+)
Moving the rook to the wrong file when the h-file check wins (Rd2 instead of Rh2+)
Passive rook improvement instead of forcing checks that exploit king exposure (Rhe7 instead of Rhg7+)

analysis.label: Playing a superficially reasonable but non-urgent move when the position demands immediate action on king safety or a decisive tactical opportunity.
analysis.description: This feature fires on moves that address secondary objectives while ignoring the critical demand of the position. In 4/6 positions, king safety is the dominant tactical motif being neglected. In 5/6 positions, the move constitutes a clear tempo loss at a moment when timing is decisive. The moves span all piece types (knight capture, pawn pushes, queen moves, bishop retreat) but share the trait of being 'plausible-looking' operations—a natural recapture (Nxg3), a pawn grab (Qxb3), gaining space (c4), fixing a weakness (h5), giving check (Qb1+), repositioning (Be2)—that catastrophically ignore what the position actually demands. The positions typically offer very few good alternatives (avg 1.7), indicating razor-sharp moments where only specific moves maintain the balance or advantage. The average cp_loss of 2018 reflects how severely punished these tempo-wasting moves are.
analysis.move_pattern: Diverse piece types and directions; no single geometric pattern. Moves include captures, pawn pushes, quiet retreats, and checks—unified by being non-critical operations in critical moments.
analysis.why_bad: Each move squanders a vital tempo on a secondary objective (material, space, repositioning, checking) while the position's primary demand—usually addressing king vulnerability, maintaining piece activity on the critical sector, or delivering an immediate tactical blow—goes unmet, allowing the opponent to seize the initiative or escape danger.
sub_patterns: Pawn grab abandoning defensive duties (Qxb3)
Wrong recapture missing file-opening (Nxg3 instead of hxg3)
Non-prophylactic pawn push ignoring opponent's threat (c4, h5)
Passive piece retreat surrendering key square control (Be2)
Wrong forcing move missing the decisive blow (Qb1+ instead of Qc2#)

analysis.label: Quiet piece repositioning or improvement moves that waste a critical tempo when the position demands immediate concrete action, typically against or involving passed pawns.
analysis.description: This feature fires on positions where the player makes a non-forcing 'improving' move—repositioning a piece to a seemingly better square or centralizing the king—when the position has reached a critical inflection point demanding immediate concrete action. In 7/8 positions, tempo_loss is explicitly tagged as the core error. In 7/8 positions, a passed pawn (either the opponent's dangerous passer or the player's own promotion threats) creates the urgency that makes the slow move fatal. The moves look reasonable in isolation (centralizing a bishop to e4, doubling rooks on an open file, advancing the king toward the center) but ignore that the opponent has a concrete, time-sensitive threat that will become unstoppable with one more move. The average cp_loss of 1524 and average of only 1.5 good moves available confirms these are razor-sharp positions where a single wasted tempo is catastrophic. Typical examples include moving the king the wrong direction when a passed pawn needs immediate attention (Kd3, Kf3), repositioning a piece when it should be blockading (Rb3, Be4), or choosing slow preparation over forced winning sequences (Kb4, Rfa8).
analysis.move_pattern: Quiet (non-capturing, non-checking) piece moves—kings, rooks, or bishops—repositioning to seemingly active squares rather than making the one forcing/concrete move the position requires
analysis.why_bad: These moves waste a critical tempo in positions where the opponent has an imminent concrete threat (usually a passed pawn one push from promotion, or a forced tactical sequence). The 'improved' piece placement is irrelevant because in one tempo the opponent creates an unstoppable threat, transforms the pawn structure decisively, or activates pieces against the now-misplaced pieces.
sub_patterns: King moves toward wrong flank while opponent's passed pawn advances (Kd3, Kf3)
Piece repositioning that blocks own piece's escape route (Rf7 blocking knight, Bb3 inviting tempo-gaining Nc5)
Attacking a passed pawn instead of blockading its promotion square (Rb3 vs Ra2)
King improvement when rook action was needed for forced promotion/mating (Kb4)
Doubling pieces on open file when immediate tactical strike was required (Rfa8)

analysis.label: Moves that address secondary concerns while ignoring the most urgent positional demand in time-critical positions.
analysis.description: This feature fires on moves where a player wastes a critical tempo by attending to a secondary concern—such as a prophylactic pawn push, a non-essential capture, or an aimless repositioning—when the position urgently demands direct, aggressive action toward the primary goal. In 5/7 positions, the best move involved either advancing toward the opponent's king (Kc3 in position 14), pushing a critical passed pawn (a4 in position 6), targeting critical files (Rab1 in position 13), evacuating the king (Kd7 in position 3), or developing meaningfully (Qd7 in position 5). The played moves instead went sideways or backward: Kc5 retreated when Kc3 was needed (867cp loss in pawn race), a6 was a prophylactic flank push when development was critical (239cp), Ra2 repositioned aimlessly allowing rook invasion (296cp), and Qf6 moved the queen decoratively when king evacuation was paramount (269cp). All 7/7 positions feature time-sensitive elements—passed pawn races, attacking urgency, or development demands—where every tempo counts.
analysis.move_pattern: Diverse piece types moving sideways, backward, or to secondary squares instead of directly toward the critical sector of the board
analysis.why_bad: In positions with urgent time-sensitive demands (pawn races, attacks, development crises), these moves waste a critical tempo on secondary concerns, allowing the opponent to execute their primary plan or gain a decisive tempo advantage in the race
sub_patterns: King moving away from critical sector instead of advancing aggressively
Prophylactic pawn moves when immediate action is required
Rook repositioning to passive squares instead of active files
Queen moves that appear active but ignore the position's primary demand

analysis.label: Natural-looking moves that fatally weaken the position in critical situations where only one or two alternatives maintain the balance.
analysis.description: This feature fires on positions requiring precise, narrow solutions (avg 1.8 good moves available) where the player instead makes a move that appears purposeful but creates an exploitable tactical vulnerability. In 6/8 cases, the move directly or indirectly compromises king safety. In 4/8 cases, the move blocks or interferes with the player's own piece coordination (f6 removes e6 coverage, c5 blocks bishop's best square, Qd7 blocks knight retreat, Nf5 places knight on capturable square enabling removal-of-defender). In 3/8 cases, the move places a piece/king on a square immediately exploitable by the opponent (Kh5 walks into knight check range, Bb2 places piece on undefended square along king diagonal, O-O-O puts king in path of pawn storm). The refutations are typically one clear best punishment (6/8 positions), suggesting these positions have a single sharp tactical exploitation that the blundering move enables.
analysis.move_pattern: Various piece types making seemingly logical moves (developing, attacking, defending, castling) that inadvertently create a specific square weakness, self-block, or tactical exposure
analysis.why_bad: Each move prioritizes an apparent goal (kicking a piece, developing, attacking the queen, castling for safety, fixing structure) while ignoring or creating a more severe tactical vulnerability that the opponent immediately exploits—typically an outpost on a vacated square, a check/fork on the chosen square, a removal-of-defender, or opening lines against the king.
sub_patterns: Pawn advances vacating critical squares for opponent outposts (f6→Ne6, g3→Bd5)
Piece/king moves to squares within opponent's tactical attack range (Kh5→Nf4+, Nf5→Bxf5+Ng5, Bb2→Qb6+)
Self-blocking own piece retreat or activation (Qd7 blocks Nd7, c5 blocks Bc5)
Castling into opponent's prepared pawn storm (O-O-O→a4-a5)

analysis.label: Choosing an aggressive-looking move that releases tension or creates tactical vulnerabilities when quiet, patient alternatives would maintain or increase the advantage.
analysis.description: This feature fires on moves that appear active or threatening on the surface but are strategically or tactically flawed. In 4/7 positions, the played move prematurely releases critical tension (d5 releasing central pawn tension, e3 dissolving the exf3 threat, Qc4 allowing unfavorable simplification, Kxg7 exposing the king when pieces could capture safely). In 3/7 positions, a piece is placed on an aggressive-looking square where it immediately hangs or becomes vulnerable (Bb4 to a Qa4+ fork, Bg5 hanging to fxg5, Ng4 allowing d4/Bxf7+ punishments). The correct alternatives across all positions are consistently quieter: maintaining tension (Bc3, Rfe7), safe development (Be6, Be7), piece improvement (Bf4), or challenging structure patiently (f5, d5, O-O). The average cp_loss of 228 reflects these moves as significant errors where impatience transforms advantageous or equal positions into clearly worse ones.
analysis.move_pattern: Pieces or pawns advancing aggressively toward the opponent (forward pawn pushes, piece jumps to attacking squares, captures toward the enemy) rather than consolidating or maintaining pressure
analysis.why_bad: The aggressive move either dissolves a strategic threat that was the player's primary weapon (tension release), places a piece on a tactically vulnerable square where it can be won or exploited, or invites simplification that favors the opponent—while the quiet alternative maintained genuine, sustained pressure.
sub_patterns: Premature pawn advance releasing central tension (d5, e3)
Piece placed on square where it hangs to a simple tactic (Bb4, Bg5)
Premature attack neglecting king safety or development (Ng4, Kxg7)
Offering simplification that eliminates own dynamic compensation (Qc4)

analysis.label: A piece retreats to a passive square (usually minor piece to back ranks) when concrete forcing moves were available, abandoning critical defensive duties or dynamic potential.

In 4/5 cases, a knight or bishop retreated toward the player's own back rank (Nd7, Bd7, Nc1, Nf1), and in 1/5 a slow pawn consolidation was chosen (e6). Each time, the retreating piece either abandoned a critical guarding function (Nd7 left the back rank exposed in 1/5, Nf1 abandoned e4 control in 1/5, Bd7 self-blocked the d-file in 1/5) or simply wasted tempo when a forcing sequence existed (Nc1 missed Rae1 winning the queen in 1/5, e6 missed Rc3 tactical combination in 1/5). analysis.why_bad: The retreat abandons a critical defensive/offensive duty (guarding key squares, maintaining file control, supporting passed pawns) or wastes tempo when concrete forcing sequences would have won material or maintained decisive dynamic advantages
sub_patterns: Knight retreat to back rank abandoning guard duty (Nc1, Nf1)
Piece move to d7 creating self-block or back-rank weakness (Nd7, Bd7)
Slow consolidation pawn move missing tactical combination (e6)

analysis.label: Playing a preparatory, reorganizing, or passive move in a time-critical position where only one immediate decisive action (king advance, correct capture, or critical pawn push) maintains the advantage.
analysis.description: This feature fires on positions—predominantly endgames (7/10)—where the player makes a plausible-looking but non-urgent move that squanders a critical tempo. In the majority of cases, the correct move was an immediate king advance to a dominant square (Kd5 in positions 9, 12; Kf2/Kh3 in positions 13, 5) or capturing with the correct pawn to create a passed pawn (gxf4 in position 7; fxe5 in position 11). The unifying thread is that each position had extreme urgency (a king race, a forced mating net, or a critical pawn promotion sequence) that demanded the single forcing move, and the player instead chose a 'useful-looking' preparatory action.
analysis.move_pattern: Diverse piece types (king, pawn, bishop, rook); typically non-forcing, non-checking moves that reorganize or prepare rather than execute the critical action; often directed sideways or backward rather than toward the opponent's position

The lost tempo allows the opponent to either win a critical king race, establish a drawing fortress, achieve perpetual check, or neutralize a passed pawn that was about to become unstoppable.

Wrong capture direction failing to create passed pawn (exf4 instead of gxf4, Kxe5 instead of fxe5)
Piece repositioning when king activation is the urgent priority (Bb6, Rc7, Ra7 when Kd5/Kf2 wins)
King move exposing to tactical refutation instead of precise defense (Kg1 allowing perpetual, fxe3 ruining structure)

Trading pieces with check instead of delivering intermediate check that wins bigger material

Preparatory pawn moves ignoring central tension (b6)

Prophylactic king/rook moves ignoring urgent development (Kh1, Re1)

Kg7 moves the king to safety but picks the wrong square—Kh8 was needed to avoid Nf5+ fork (Position 5). Rfe1 centralizes the correct piece to the correct square but uses the wrong rook—Rbe1 was needed to keep f1-rook guarding f3 (Position 10). Correct pawn push without prerequisite defensive move (opens invasion square)
Correct piece deployment without prerequisite queen relocation (enables unfavorable exchange)
