The rook leaving f7 for e7 (Position 3) abandoned f-file defense allowing a mating attack; the rook leaving c8 for e8 (Position 5) abandoned c-file coverage enabling a checking cascade; the rook leaving the g-file for c6 (Position 13) abandoned kingside defense against lethal passed pawns; the rook moving to c5 (Position 1) left it undefended where checks won it; the queen moving to c6 (Position 6) abandoned the diagonal guarding a hanging piece from capture-with-check; and the bishop moving to f4 (Position 7) left it tactically vulnerable to pawn attacks. In all cases, the opponent immediately exploited the defensive vacuum with forcing moves (checks, captures with check, or pawn advances) against the now-exposed king.
analysis.move_pattern: Piece (typically rook/queen) moves laterally or to a centralized square, away from guarding own king's file, rank, or diagonal

sub_patterns: Rook leaves defensive file allowing mating attack on exposed king
Queen/piece moves to active square leaving hanging piece capturable with check
Rook moves to distant file abandoning defense against advancing passed pawns

In 3/3 cases, the refutation involves the opponent exploiting open files (g-file rooks trapping the queen in Position 10, a/b-file pawn breaks exposing the king in Position 11, and Qb2 consolidating along the second rank in Position 3). King castling into unresolved pawn tension on open files (O-O-O)
Slow rook redeployment missing a forcing tactical blow (Rc4)

analysis.label: Playing aesthetically pleasing or intuitively reasonable moves that squander a time-critical advantage by missing more forcing alternatives.

In 7/7 positions, the played move looks like a natural improving move (Qg4+ giving check, Nf5 occupying an outpost, Re5 centralizing a rook, Qe7 consolidating, Bc5 activating a bishop, Ne7 developing, g3 creating luft) but fails because the position urgently required a more forcing tactical solution. In 6/7 cases, the opponent's exposed king or a concrete tactical vulnerability needed immediate exploitation. In 7/7 cases, the tempo wasted allowed the opponent to consolidate, escape, or launch a counterattack that neutralized the advantage. The common thread across all analyses is 'tempo_loss'—these moves choose appearance over calculation, prioritizing piece placement aesthetics over the concrete demands of the position.

analysis.why_bad: They waste a tempo in positions requiring urgent tactical action, allowing the opponent to resolve their vulnerable king position, neutralize threats, or exploit newly-created weaknesses—transforming winning advantages into equal or lost positions.

Placing the wrong piece type on a strong square when another piece would be irremovable (Re5 instead of Ne5)
Passive consolidation when sharp tactics demand immediate strikes against an exposed king (Qe7, g3)
Repositioning a piece while ignoring an urgent tactical vulnerability on the position (Bc5 allowing skewer)

analysis.label: Moving a piece to the kingside wing (or away from its critical post) for a speculative attack that abandons a vital defensive or positional duty.
analysis.description: This feature fires on moves that redeploy pieces toward the h/g-file area (or away from key files) in pursuit of illusory attacking ideas while abandoning critical responsibilities. The dominant sub-pattern is Bh6 targeting g7 without concrete follow-through (3/9 positions), which in each case leaves something undefended—a piece on e2 (Position 5), the d3 pawn (Position 13), or the knight on d4 (Position 14). Rook redeployments to the c-file or h-file (Rc1×2, Rh1) similarly abandon open-file control (d-file, f-file) for slower plans that give opponents counterplay. Queen moves to wing squares (Qh2, Qg4) leave central influence while creating no forced threats. In 8/9 positions, the move generates no immediate concrete threat, allowing the opponent a tactical refutation (hanging piece, knight outpost, tempo-gaining counterattack). Positions average only 1.2 good moves available, indicating critical junctures demanding precision rather than speculative redirection.
analysis.move_pattern: Piece (bishop, queen, or rook) moves laterally or diagonally toward the h-file/g-file wing (or from a central file to a lateral file), typically non-capturing and non-checking
analysis.why_bad: The moves abandon a critical defensive duty or positional responsibility (guarding a piece, controlling a key file/square, restraining opponent's pieces) in favor of a speculative attacking idea that either generates no forced threats, is easily neutralized by the opponent, or places the piece on a vulnerable/passive square where it can be challenged with tempo.

Rook leaving open d-file for c-file/h-file, surrendering control of key central square like d5 (3/9)
Queen moving to wing square (h2/g4) abandoning central influence for an h-file battery that is easily neutralized (2/9)
Slow positional move when immediate tactical strike is required (1/9)

In 7/9 cases, the correct move was a defensive or precise move addressing the king's vulnerability (Rd8 keeping back-rank defense, Rh8 guarding the h-file, h6 preventing a mating pawn advance, Rc1 covering the back rank, Kg1 retreating to safety, staying near the king). The average cp_loss of 5491 and average of only 1.4 good moves available confirm these are razor-thin positions where the single critical defensive resource was overlooked in favor of a tempting but irrelevant active idea. The pattern is especially visible in the rook placements (4/9 positions) where the rook goes to the wrong file—choosing apparent activity over the one defensive file that prevents mate.

Queen displaced far from king for material gain or repositioning (Qxa4, Qa6)
King walking into exposed position instead of retreating to safety (Kh3, O-O-O)
Wrong check direction allowing king to escape toward safety (Bf5+ vs Bd1+)

analysis.label: Natural-looking developing moves played when the position demands addressing a specific tactical vulnerability, typically an undefended pawn or a forcing opponent breakthrough.

In 5/7 positions, the move is a minor piece development to a classical square (Nf6 x2, Nf3, Nge7, Be3) that ignores an immediate tactical vulnerability. The punishments consistently involve the opponent exploiting an undefended pawn or weak square that the 'natural' move failed to protect: e5 advances attacking newly-placed knights (positions 1, 2), Ng5 lunges exploiting unguarded f7 (position 4), Nxe4 capturing a hanging pawn with tempo (position 7), and dxe4 winning material by attacking an unguarded piece (position 6). In position 5, Be3 is slow development that misses a forcing tactical sequence (Nh4-Ng6). The common thread is prioritizing general principles ('develop your pieces') over the specific demands of the position, where one critical vulnerability requires immediate attention.

analysis.why_bad: The move leaves a critical pawn (usually e4) undefended or fails to prevent a forcing opponent breakthrough (usually e5 or Ng5), allowing the opponent to win material with tempo by exploiting the specific vulnerability that the routine move ignored

Pawn push (c4) that abandons defense of a key central pawn

analysis.label: Playing a plausible-looking improving move in a position with essentially one correct option, fatally wasting the critical tempo the position demands.

In 4/6 cases the move is tagged as tempo_loss where immediate specific action was required: Be5 centralizes a bishop instead of attacking the opponent's piece with Kd6 (Position 1); b5 pushes a pawn for space instead of exploiting kingside weakness with Nh5 (Position 3); Ke3 centralizes the king instead of urgently pushing b4 in a pawn race (Position 4); Kb2 chases a decoy pawn instead of playing the drawing h4 (Position 5). In 2/6 cases the move captures/recaptures material while leaving a critical piece undefended: Qxd4 wins a pawn but leaves the bishop on c4 hanging (Position 2); Nxd4 recaptures centrally but removes the sole defender of the e5 pawn (Position 6). Slow positional pawn push when immediate tactical exploitation is needed
King move toward a decoy when a counter-pawn-push is the only drawing resource

In at least 5/9 cases the best move was a direct pawn capture winning material (Qxg2 in positions 8 and 9, Qxb7 in positions 10 and 13, Qxb2 in position 3). Passive rook development when active counterplay required

Knight repositioning allowing opponent to castle to safety

analysis.label: Unnecessary forward pawn advance (typically f-pawn or e-pawn) when the position urgently demands piece development, king safety, or defensive measures.
analysis.description: This feature fires on positions where a player makes a gratuitous advancing move—overwhelmingly a pawn push (7/9 positions)—instead of addressing the most critical positional demand. The dominant sub-pattern (4/9: positions 1, 3, 5, 6) involves f-pawn advances (f4 or f5) in the opening that catastrophically weaken the king along the h4-e1 or h5-e8 diagonal, typically allowing queen checks that win material. A secondary sub-pattern (2/9: positions 2, 4) involves e6 in Sicilian Dragon positions, creating an irremediable d6 weakness that allows knight invasions and loss of castling rights. The remaining cases (3/9) involve tempo-wasting advances in critical moments—h5 instead of blocking a promotion, Kg2 instead of centralizing, and Nc5 instead of addressing a rook invasion. In all cases (9/9), multiple natural moves (averaging 2.4 good alternatives) were available that addressed the actual positional needs, making these errors of prioritization rather than difficult positions.
analysis.move_pattern: Pawn advance (f-pawn or e-pawn most commonly) moving one or two squares forward; occasionally a piece move forward that abandons defensive duties
analysis.why_bad: The advance ignores the position's most critical demand (typically piece development or king safety in the opening), simultaneously creating tactical vulnerabilities—most commonly exposing the king on an open diagonal that allows forcing checks winning material, or creating permanent structural weaknesses that invite piece invasions.
sub_patterns: f-pawn advance (f4/f5) in opening exposing king on h4-e1/h5-e8 diagonal, allowing Qh4+/Qh5+ winning material
e6 in Sicilian Dragon creating permanent d6 weakness enabling Ndb5-Nd6 invasion and loss of castling rights
Pawn advance in endgame wasting critical tempo when immediate king action is required

analysis.label: Playing a non-forcing move (retreat, repositioning, or non-urgent capture) in a razor-sharp position that demands an immediate forcing action, wasting the one tempo that holds the position together.
analysis.description: In all 6 positions, the player had very few good moves available (avg 1.7) and chose a quiet, non-forcing alternative when the position demanded immediate tactical action. The best moves were consistently forcing: a check (Qg4+ in position 4), a tactical capture (Nxe5 in position 5), an immediate pawn break (b4 in position 6), creating an instant promotion threat (h7 in position 3), a critical defensive move (f3 in position 1), or natural development (Nf6 in position 2). Instead, the played moves were passive retreats (Qd8, Ne1), self-blocking repositioning (Qe2), aimless shuffles (Qb3), non-urgent captures (Qxg5 grabbing a pawn instead of giving check), or move-order errors (h5 instead of h7). The 'tempo_loss' tag appears in 6/6 positions and 'missed_tactic' in 6/6, confirming the pattern. The positions are all critical moments where one wasted tempo allows the opponent to either execute their plan or neutralize the player's key resource.
analysis.move_pattern: Piece (usually queen) moves to a passive, non-threatening square - retreats, lateral shuffles, or non-urgent captures - rather than moving forward with a check, forcing capture, or immediate threat
analysis.why_bad: The non-forcing move surrenders the critical tempo needed to maintain the position's tactical balance, allowing the opponent to execute their own plan (rook lift to mating attack, capturing a key piece, king march, consolidation) that the forcing move would have prevented or preempted
sub_patterns: Queen retreat/shuffle abandoning defensive or offensive duty (Qd8, Qb3, Qe2)
Knight retreat removing key tactical resource (Ne1 instead of Nxe5)
Greedy pawn capture instead of check (Qxg5 instead of Qg4+)
Wrong move order in pawn race failing to create immediate threat (h5 instead of h7)

analysis.label: Piece leaves its critical role restraining or blockading a dangerous passed pawn to capture or target a peripheral, less important pawn.
analysis.description: This feature fires when a player moves a piece away from a critical restraining duty—typically blockading, attacking, or indirectly controlling an advanced passed pawn—to chase an irrelevant or low-priority pawn elsewhere. In 8/9 non-trivial positions, the blunder involves abandoning control over a dangerous passed pawn: Ne4 leaves the d2 blockade of Black's c3 passer (Position 13); Nxh5 removes the knight from g3 where it attacked the rook guarding c3 (Position 14); Rxe5 captures an irrelevant e5 pawn while a6/c7 pawns promote (Position 7); Ra1 targets the a3 pawn instead of checking, allowing b4 connected passers (Position 9); Bxf8 trades the only piece that could stop Black's c3 passer (Position 3); Rh3 telegraphs an attack on a3, allowing a4 to create a passed pawn (Position 4); Ke4 retreats from h6 leaving Black with two connected passers (Position 12); Kd4 walks away from the kingside where the h4 pawn structure was critical (Position 1). The consistent punishment is the opponent's passed pawn advancing freely to promotion or creating decisive threats.
analysis.move_pattern: Any piece type moves away from a square where it restrains/blockades an advanced passed pawn, often toward the opponent's wing to capture or target a peripheral pawn
analysis.why_bad: The piece was performing an irreplaceable restraining function against a dangerous passed pawn; once it moves, the opponent's passer advances unopposed to promotion or forces catastrophic material commitments to stop it, far outweighing the value of the captured/targeted pawn.
sub_patterns: Knight abandons blockade square to centralize or capture (Ne4, Nxh5)
Rook captures irrelevant pawn instead of contesting promotion file (Rxe5, Ra1)
King walks away from critical pawn sector toward the other wing (Kd4, Ke4)
Piece trades that remove the only restrainer of a passed pawn (Bxf8)
Rook commits to attacking a defended pawn, giving opponent tempo to advance passers (Rh3)

analysis.label: Superficially attractive moves (captures, checks, active-looking placements) that critically lose tempo or displace pieces from essential duties, allowing the opponent a decisive tactical response.
analysis.description: This feature fires on moves where the player chooses a superficially appealing option—typically a material grab, a check, or a seemingly active piece placement—while ignoring the position's true tactical demand. In 5/8 positions, the blunder involves a capture or check (Nxh2+, Nxf2, Rd7+, Rxg3, Qxc4) that appears to win material or gain tempo but actually allows a crushing counter-tactic. In the remaining cases (Qe2, Be3, Ng1), the move looks developmental but misses the one concrete solution the position demands. The common thread across all positions is tempo loss: 7/8 positions are explicitly tagged with 'tempo_loss' in analysis. The good moves available average only 1.8, indicating these are critical-moment positions where only one or two specific moves maintain the position, yet the player is seduced by a more obvious-looking but fundamentally flawed alternative. The average cp_loss of 283 reflects that these aren't subtle positional errors but dramatic miscalculations where the opponent gains a full move's worth of initiative to execute a winning tactic.
analysis.move_pattern: Diverse piece types; predominantly captures (especially knight/rook captures on flanks) and checks that appear to gain material or tempo but displace the moving piece from a critical defensive or offensive duty
analysis.why_bad: The move addresses a secondary concern (winning a pawn, giving check, placing a piece on an 'active' square) while ignoring the position's primary tactical requirement—typically defending a critical square, maintaining piece coordination, or preventing an opponent's forcing sequence that the displaced piece was uniquely positioned to stop.
sub_patterns: Greedy pawn grabs that clear lines for opponent's discovered attacks (Nxf2, Nxh2+)
Checks that improve the opponent's king position rather than degrading it (Rd7+)
Captures that remove a piece from a critical defensive post (Rxg3, Qxc4)
Slow or retreating moves when one concrete forcing move was required (Qe2, Ng1, Be3)

analysis.label: Playing a natural-looking but slow consolidating or prophylactic move when the position demands immediate concrete action, wasting a critical tempo.
analysis.description: This feature fires on moves that appear reasonable from general principles (developing a piece, supporting a pawn, prophylaxis) but fatally neglect the position's concrete tactical demands. In 6/7 positions, the move is explicitly tagged as 'tempo_loss' - the player spends time on a secondary concern while the opponent gains a free move to execute a specific tactical blow. The pattern manifests as: quiet bishop developments that get kicked with tempo (Be6 hit by f5, position 1; Ng6 forced back by f5, position 2), piece moves that abandon defensive duties (Be3 leaving b2 unguarded, position 5; dxc4 removing e4 control, position 12), enabling opponent tactics through unnecessary pawn moves (b6 allowing b4 trapping a bishop, position 13; b6 allowing Nxe5, position 15), or consolidating retreats that create new vulnerabilities (Qe2 allowing Nf4 fork, position 4). In all cases, 2-3 good alternatives existed that addressed the position's primary demand.
analysis.move_pattern: Mixed piece types and directions; typically quiet non-forcing moves (piece development to natural square, one-square pawn advance, queen retreat) that lack immediate tactical purpose
analysis.why_bad: The move addresses a secondary positional concern (development, prophylaxis, consolidation) while ignoring the position's primary concrete demand, granting the opponent a free tempo to exploit a specific tactical or structural vulnerability that the move either creates or fails to prevent.
sub_patterns: Piece development to a square where it immediately becomes a target with tempo (Be6/f5, Ng6/f5)
Moving a piece away from a critical defensive duty, leaving a weakness unguarded (Be3 abandons b2, dxc4 abandons e4 control)
Prophylactic pawn move that enables opponent's tactical shot (b6 allowing b4 piece trap)
Passive consolidation when dynamic central action or piece activation was required (b6 instead of Nc6/e4/Qd5)

analysis.label: King (or piece) positioned exactly one square away from the critical optimal square, losing opposition, tempo, or blockade in simplified positions.
analysis.description: This feature fires on moves that are geometrically close to correct but fatally imprecise—typically placing the king one square too far back or one square short of the drawing/winning square. In 8/11 positions, this occurs in endgames, and 6/11 moves are king moves (Ke1, Kc1, Kd6, Kd6, Kd1, Kh8). The signature pattern is retreating the king to the back rank when staying one rank more advanced is essential: Ke1 instead of Kf2 (Position 1), Kc1 instead of Kc2 (Position 4), Kh8 instead of Kh7 (Position 12). In other cases, the king advances to the wrong adjacent square: Kd6 instead of Kd5 (Position 9) or Kd6 instead of Kd4 (Position 5). The non-king-move examples share the 'almost right' quality: Rc8 instead of Kc8 (Position 2, correct square wrong piece), b5 instead of b6 (Position 8, one square too far forward). The average cp_loss of 280 with only 2.1 good moves available confirms these are narrow positions where a single square determines the outcome.
analysis.move_pattern: King retreating along file/rank to back rank (1st/8th) when 2nd/7th rank is critical; or king advancing one square short of the key blockade/opposition square
analysis.why_bad: These moves lose the opposition, abandon a critical blockade square, or surrender a decisive tempo in positions where exact king placement determines whether the game is drawn or lost. The one-square difference allows the opponent's king to outflank, a passed pawn to advance unstoppably, or lines to open fatally against the misplaced king.
sub_patterns: King retreats to back rank losing opposition (Ke1, Kc1, Kh8)
King one square short of critical drawing/blockading square (Kd6x2)
Wrong piece to correct square neglecting king safety (Rc8 vs Kc8)
Pawn over-advance removing critical defender (b5)

analysis.label: Choosing a slow, consolidating or preparatory move when the position's dynamic tension demands immediate active play, squandering a significant advantage.
analysis.description: All three positions share a striking pattern: the player held a substantial advantage (averaging +235cp better before the move) but chose a quiet, non-forcing move—a reinforcing pawn push (e6, b3) or passive bishop retreat (Be2)—when the position urgently demanded dynamic action. In 3/3 cases, the position featured exposed kings (uncastled kings on open files or a king on d2) and concrete tactical opportunities (attacking an overextended center, castling immediately, or capturing material). In 3/3 cases, the chosen move was a 'preparatory' move—reinforcing structure, preparing a fianchetto, or retreating a piece—that would be reasonable in a quiet position but catastrophically wastes tempo in a sharp one. The refutations in all three cases show the opponent exploiting the gifted tempo to seize initiative against the now-vulnerable king or consolidate their own position. The common thread tagged across all positions is 'tempo_loss'—these moves hand the opponent exactly the time they need to equalize or take over.
analysis.move_pattern: Quiet non-forcing moves (pawn pushes to 3rd/6th rank or minor piece retreats) with no check, capture, or direct threat
analysis.why_bad: The position contains urgent dynamic demands (open files against uncastled kings, capturable material, overextended opponent structures) that require immediate exploitation; the quiet move gifts a critical tempo allowing the opponent to neutralize weaknesses or seize the initiative
sub_patterns: Reinforcing pawn push (e6/b3) instead of challenging opponent's center or castling
Passive bishop retreat instead of active capture or simplification

analysis.label: White plays a quiet developing or positional move in a position where an immediate concrete action (pawn break, tactical shot, or prophylactic) was demanded.
analysis.description: This feature activates when White makes a non-forcing 'autopilot' move—typically piece development or centralization—in positions that require immediate concrete action. In 4/6 positions, a Bc4 is present and the critical issue involves d-pawn dynamics (either pushing d5-d6 or preventing ...d5). In 2/6 cases (positions 7, 8), White should push an advanced d5 pawn to d6 immediately but instead develops a bishop passively. In 2/6 cases (positions 2, 4), White needs to prevent/address Black's ...d5 central break but plays a routine developing move that walks into a fork or tactical refutation. In 1/6 (position 12), White misses a tactical Ng5 shot exploiting f7 weakness for a generic Rad1. All 6 moves are quiet and non-forcing (no checks, captures, or direct threats), and in each case the opponent gains a free tempo to execute their plan—either stabilizing with ...d6 blockade, breaking with ...d5, or neutralizing tactical pressure.
analysis.move_pattern: Quiet non-forcing moves (bishop development to natural squares, queen repositioning, rook centralization, or pawn advance) with no check, capture, or direct threat
analysis.why_bad: They waste a critical tempo in positions where one specific concrete action was required—either an immediate pawn advance (d6), a prophylactic measure (a4/Bb3), or a tactical strike (Ng5). The opponent uses the free tempo to solve their key positional problem (blockading, breaking through, or defusing threats).
sub_patterns: Passive bishop development instead of crushing d5-d6 pawn advance (Bf4, Be2)
Routine development creating fork vulnerability after opponent's ...d5 break (Be3, Qd2)
Generic rook centralization missing immediate tactical combination (Rad1)
Premature pawn advance exposing king when consolidation needed (f5)

analysis.label: Moving the king (or opening lines toward it) to a square immediately vulnerable to a forcing check or discovered attack.
analysis.description: This feature fires on moves that voluntarily expose the player's own king to an immediate forcing check or discovered attack. In 6/8 positions, the move is either a direct king move to a tactically vulnerable square (Kf6 allowing Qf3+, Kf7 allowing Qf6+, Kd2 allowing Qe3+ mate, Kf2 allowing Rh2+) or a pawn/piece move that opens a critical line toward the king (e5 opening the f-file for fxe5+ discovered check, g4 weakening the king's shield). The remaining cases involve related forcing-move errors: Ng4+ gives the wrong check allowing the enemy king to escape a mating net, and Rb7 places a piece one square short of preventing the opponent's defensive resource. The common thread is that each move ignores an immediate tactical vulnerability on an open file, rank, or diagonal pointed at the player's king, allowing the opponent a check that wins material, gains decisive tempi, or delivers checkmate.
analysis.move_pattern: King moves forward/sideways onto open lines (files, ranks, diagonals) or pawn advances that open files toward own king; predominantly king moves to f6/f7/f2/d2 landing on squares controlled by opponent's queen or rook
analysis.why_bad: The destination square sits on an open line (file, rank, or diagonal) where the opponent has an immediate forcing check or discovered attack, leading to material loss, king exposure, or checkmate. The player fails to recognize that the square is tactically unsafe despite appearing active or centralizing.
sub_patterns: King advances onto diagonal allowing queen check (Kf6/Kf7/Kd2)
King moves onto open file allowing rook check (Kf2 -> Rh2+)
Pawn push opens file for discovered check against own king (e5 -> fxe5+)
Weakening pawn advance exposing king position prematurely (g4)
Wrong forcing move allowing opponent's king to escape (Ng4+ instead of Bd4+)

analysis.label: Moving a piece laterally away from its essential defensive responsibility, leaving a specific target or line fatally unguarded.
analysis.description: In 5/6 positions, a major piece (rook or queen) or king relocates from one sector of the board to another, abandoning a specific defensive function that the opponent immediately exploits. Rfb8 removes the rook from the f-file allowing fxg6+ breakthrough (Position 3). Rag8 removes the rook from guarding the a5 pawn, enabling Nxa5 (Position 6). Qg6 abandons queenside pawn defense, allowing Qxa7 (Position 4). Rg1 vacates the e-file, enabling Qe4+ on the diagonal leading to back-rank mate (Position 5). Kd2 places the king in alignment with the queen on b2, enabling discovered checks (Position 6). Qd7 places the queen on a target square vulnerable to Nc5 rather than generating counterplay (Position 1). In all cases, the player prioritizes an apparently active plan (attacking, repositioning, contesting a file) over maintaining a piece's critical but unglamorous defensive duty, and the punishment is immediate exploitation of the exact weakness left behind.
analysis.move_pattern: Major piece (rook/queen) or king moving laterally across files/ranks to a different board sector, typically non-capturing and non-checking repositioning moves
analysis.why_bad: The piece was performing an irreplaceable defensive function (guarding a pawn, blocking a file/diagonal, or maintaining king safety) and its departure creates an immediate tactical vulnerability that the opponent exploits in one move, often winning material or delivering checkmate.
sub_patterns: Rook leaving kingside f-file to pursue queenside counterplay while king is under pawn-storm attack
Rook leaving queenside a-file to pursue kingside attack while queenside pawns are undefended
Rook vacating a key file that was blocking diagonal/file-based mating threats
Queen repositioning that abandons protection of specific pawns near the king
King stepping into alignment with enemy attacking piece enabling discovered attacks

analysis.label: Quiet, non-forcing moves in positions where available checks or captures were needed to maintain tempo and initiative.
analysis.description: This feature fires on moves that are passive or slow (no check, no capture, no direct threat) in positions where forcing moves—especially checks—were critically available and necessary. In 4/6 positions, the best move involved giving check (g5+, bxa3+, g5+, h4+), yet the played moves were all quiet (Re2, Ng8, Kh6, Rb1, Kf3, g3). In 5/6 positions, the refutation involved the opponent immediately seizing the initiative with their own forcing move (Ra8+, Ng5+, Qf4+, Qxa2+, Rxd6). The common thread is surrendering a critical tempo: the player makes a consolidating, repositioning, or structural move when the position's tension demands immediate action. These moves often simultaneously abandon a defensive duty (Re2 leaves back rank, Rb1 leaves 2nd rank defense) or walk into tactical vulnerabilities (Kh6 into Qf4+), because the lack of forcing play gives the opponent a free move to exploit the newly created weakness.
analysis.move_pattern: Any piece type; quiet non-checking non-capturing moves; often retreats, passive repositions, or structural pawn pushes in positions where check-giving alternatives existed
analysis.why_bad: They surrender critical tempo in urgent positions—the opponent exploits the free move to launch forcing sequences (checks, captures, promotions) that the missed forcing move would have prevented or preempted.
sub_patterns: Passive piece retreat when check-first move order was available (Ng8, Kf3, g3)
Abandoning defensive post for non-urgent repositioning (Re2, Rb1)
King walking into tactical vulnerability instead of staying safe (Kh6)

analysis.label: Playing Qe7 (or similar passive piece moves) in the opening that block the f8-bishop and create e-file vulnerabilities against the uncastled king.
analysis.description: The dominant pattern is Black playing Qe7 in the opening (7/11 positions) when the king remains on e8, typically intending to pressure White's e5 pawn or 'defend' the position. In every case, this move catastrophically blocks the f8-bishop's development, prevents timely castling, and aligns the queen with the king on the semi-open e-file, allowing White to castle (O-O) and follow with Re1 creating devastating pin/pressure motifs. The remaining positions share the broader theme of choosing seemingly logical but ultimately passive/reactive moves (Ng4 attacking a queen that escapes with check, 2/11; Qe2 wasting tempo when Ng5 attacks, 1/11; Rf7 blockading instead of pushing a passed pawn, 1/11; cxd4 capturing a knight while ignoring a hanging queen, 1/11) when a more forcing tactical continuation was available. All 11 positions feature critical tempo loss where the played move allows the opponent to consolidate or counterattack.
analysis.move_pattern: Queen (or piece) moves to e-file squares (especially e7/e2) in opening positions with both kings in center; broader pattern includes any piece moving to a seemingly active square that fails to address the most forcing tactical need
analysis.why_bad: The move wastes a critical tempo in a sharp position: Qe7 specifically blocks the f8-bishop (preventing castling), creates a queen-king alignment on the e-file exploitable by Re1 after castling, and fails to solve the actual tactical problem (e.g., dealing with e5 threat via d5/Ne4). The opponent gains time to consolidate, castle, or escape threats with tempo.
sub_patterns: Qe7 blocking f8-bishop and creating e-file pin after O-O + Re1
Ng4 attacking queen that escapes with check on g5 (missing Bf4 which covers escape)
Passive queen development (Qe2) when sharp tactical blow (Ng5) was available
Reactive defensive move (Rf7) when offensive pawn push (a3) was winning

analysis.label: Slow, non-forcing moves that ignore the critical need to contest an open file where the opponent has or threatens dangerous rook activity.
analysis.description: In all 8/8 positions, the opponent has an active rook on an open file (e-file in 6 cases, d-file and a-file in others), and the best move involves contesting that file with a rook (Rfe1, Rae1, Re1, Rfe8, Ra8) or addressing the resulting tactical threats. Instead, the blundering side plays a slow, non-urgent move—typically a pawn push (b4, c4, h3, e5, c5 in 5/8 cases) or a piece move that doesn't address file control (Nc5, Rc2, Qb7). The punishment consistently involves the opponent exploiting unopposed file control via 7th-rank invasion (Ra7 in Position 12, Re7 in Position 14), tactical combinations enabled by the tempo loss (Rg6/Rxg2+ in Position 1, Ne2+ in Position 10), or simply consolidating an overwhelming activity advantage. The average cp_loss of 260 reflects how severely open-file negligence is punished in the middlegame.
analysis.move_pattern: Non-forcing pawn advances or passive piece moves (any direction) that fail to place a rook on the critical open file
analysis.why_bad: The opponent's rook on the open file creates imminent threats (7th-rank penetration, tactical combinations, or piece coordination). Each tempo wasted on a non-urgent move allows the opponent to convert file control into decisive material or positional gains.
sub_patterns: Queenside pawn pushes ignoring e-file (b4, c4, c5)
Prophylactic pawn moves missing tactical shots (h3)
Queen/piece leaving sentry duty over invasion squares (Qb7, Rc2)
Central pawn advance weakening pawn chain cohesion (e5)

analysis.label: Player chooses a superficially active or aggressive move while missing the single concrete tactical shot that the position demands.
analysis.description: This feature fires on positions where exactly ONE good move exists (avg 1.0 good moves across all 9 positions) — typically a forcing capture exploiting a concrete vulnerability — and the player instead plays something that appears purposeful but squanders the narrow tactical window. In 7/9 cases, the correct move was a specific capture (Nxe4, Bxg4, Nxe5, Nxg6, Rxe8, Bxf2+, Be6 saving a piece), while the played move was either a non-forcing alternative (Ng4, Qe7, Bb2, h4, Rc8), a greedy distraction (Qxb2, d2), or the wrong forcing move (Nxe8 wrong capture order, Bh2+ wrong check). The common thread is that these are razor-sharp moments requiring precise calculation where the position offers exactly one path to maintain the evaluation, and the player gets seduced by a move that looks active, aggressive, or natural but fails to address the position's concrete tactical demand. The average centipawn loss is 267, reflecting that missing the sole good move in these critical positions is severely punished.
analysis.move_pattern: Varied piece types and directions; the played moves are non-forcing or imprecise alternatives (quiet development, wrong captures, purposeless checks, greedy grabs) when the position demands one specific forcing capture or tactical strike
analysis.why_bad: Each position has exactly one narrow tactical solution (usually a concrete capture exploiting a pin, hanging piece, or forcing sequence), and the chosen move wastes the critical tempo needed to execute it, allowing the opponent to stabilize, escape, or counterattack — turning winning/equal positions into losing ones.
sub_patterns: Quiet development/pawn push instead of decisive tactical capture (Bb2/h4/Qe7 instead of Nxe5/Nxg6/Nxe4)
Wrong check or capture that misses material (Bh2+ instead of Bxf2+, Nxe8 instead of Rxe8)
Greedy pawn grab ignoring piece vulnerability (Qxb2 leaving bishop hanging, d2 premature advance)
Piece retreats to aggressive-looking square instead of exploiting pin (Ng4 instead of Nxe4)
Activating the wrong piece instead of addressing king safety (Rc8 instead of Kc7)

analysis.label: Materialistic moves pursuing secondary gains while ignoring devastating immediate tactical threats in positions with razor-thin margins for error.
analysis.description: In all 4/4 positions, the player makes a move with a clear materialistic or piece-exchange motivation (c3 attacks b2, Bxf3 captures a knight, Rb8 attacks the b5 pawn, Be4 tries to trade off a dangerous bishop) while catastrophically ignoring a far more urgent tactical reality. In 4/4 cases, only 1-2 good moves existed (avg 1.5), meaning the positions were critical moments demanding the single correct defensive resource. In 3/4 positions, the ignored threat involved a devastating piece tactic (queen capturing undefended rook, knight fork/mating sequence, bishop capturing along a diagonal). In 4/4 cases, the move either wasted a critical tempo on material pursuit (positions 1, 7), moved a piece into an immediate capture (position 11), or removed a key defender from its post (position 14). The common thread is tunnel-vision on a materialistic goal while the position demands immediate prophylaxis.
analysis.move_pattern: Various piece types (pawn, bishop, rook) making captures or moving toward opponent material, typically lateral or diagonal moves aimed at winning/trading material on secondary targets
analysis.why_bad: Each move pursues a secondary material objective while the position contains a single critical tactical threat that requires immediate attention—the materialistic move either wastes the one available tempo, moves a piece to a square where it hangs, or removes a defender that was holding the position together
sub_patterns: Capturing a piece while ignoring a mating/forking threat
Moving a piece to attack a pawn while placing it en prise on a diagonal
Removing a defending piece from a critical square to pursue an exchange

analysis.label: Playing a natural-looking quiet move that wastes the decisive tempo in a position where only one specific action maintains the evaluation.
analysis.description: This feature fires on positions with extremely narrow solutions (avg 1.6 good moves) where the player makes a reasonable-appearing move that ignores the single most urgent positional demand. In pawn endgames (5/9 positions), this manifests as king moves to the wrong square—particularly opposition errors where Ke6 is played instead of the only winning Kf5 (2/9), or Kd4 instead of the critical Kc5 (2/9), or Kc8 retreating when only an immediate pawn break saves the game (1/9). In openings/middlegames (4/9), this manifests as piece moves that look developmental but miss the critical need—Nc3 blocking the essential d3 pawn break (1/9), Na6 developing to the rim while the king is under attack (1/9), Ne5 advancing a piece into a tactical refutation (1/9), and Rh1 ignoring an urgent king evacuation (1/9). All positions share the defining trait that the played move appears active or logical by general principles but catastrophically wastes the one tempo that the position demanded for a specific action.
analysis.move_pattern: Quiet non-forcing moves (king repositioning, knight development, rook lift) that move away from or fail to address the critical zone of tension
analysis.why_bad: These moves waste the single available tempo in positions with only one correct plan—in endgames they surrender opposition or allow opponent breakthrough, in earlier phases they ignore the one structural/safety requirement that the position demands
sub_patterns: King moves to wrong square giving away opposition in pawn endgames
Knight development that blocks critical pawn advances or goes to irrelevant squares
Quiet piece moves that ignore urgent king safety emergencies
King retreats away from the critical zone when immediate counterplay was required

analysis.label: Playing slow, non-forcing moves in positions demanding immediate tactical action, leaving pieces hanging or vulnerable to exploitation.
analysis.description: This feature fires on positions where the player makes a passive, non-threatening move while the position urgently requires tactical precision to maintain piece safety or coordination. In 4/6 cases (Ke2, g3, Rc7, Nh6), the quiet move directly results in material loss: a piece is left undefended (g3 leaves knight on d7 hanging; Rc7 removes the defender of the d8-rook), a piece self-blocks creating a trap (Nh6 blocks the h8-rook's escape), or the king walks into a fork (Ke2 allows Bc4+ winning the b5-knight). In the remaining 2/6 cases (Kh1, Rd5), the wasted tempo allows the opponent to consolidate or counterattack, collapsing a winning position. All 6 moves share the characteristic of being non-forcing (no checks, captures, or direct threats) in positions where only 1-2 good moves existed, with an average cp_loss of 386.
analysis.move_pattern: Non-forcing moves (king shuffles, pawn pushes, piece retreats/repositions) that neither attack nor defend critical squares/pieces
analysis.why_bad: The moves waste a critical tempo in sharp positions, leaving pieces undefended or creating tactical vulnerabilities (discovered attacks, forks, traps) that the opponent immediately exploits to win material
sub_patterns: Removing a piece from its defensive duty, leaving another piece hanging (Rc7, g3)
King moves that walk into or enable forks/discoveries (Ke2, Kh1)
Retreating an active piece to a passive square that self-blocks or creates traps (Nh6)
Placing a piece on an exposed square attackable with tempo (Rd5)

analysis.label: Wasting a decisive tempo in positions where both kings are vulnerable and immediate action is required.
analysis.description: This feature fires on positions where both kings are exposed or weakly shielded (10/11 positions feature at least one 'king exposed' notation, 7/11 have both kings vulnerable), creating time-critical situations where every move matters enormously. The played moves are typically natural-looking but slow—passive bishop retreats (Bg7, Bb4), pointless checks that improve the opponent's king (Bc5+, b4+), prophylactic pawn moves when a king march is urgent (a6), king moves to wrong squares (Kg2, Kd7), or captures that surrender key square control (fxe4). The average number of good moves is only 1.9, confirming these are narrow positions demanding precision. In 6/11 cases the tagged tactical motif is 'tempo_loss' and in 4/11 it's 'king_safety'—but both themes appear together in nearly every position. The common thread is that the best move always involves immediate active play (king marches, 7th-rank invasions, direct threats) while the played move defers action by one critical tempo.
analysis.move_pattern: Various piece types (king, bishop, pawn, rook) making passive repositions, slow prophylactic moves, or superficially forcing moves (checks/captures) that fail to address the most urgent threat in a time-critical position
analysis.why_bad: In positions with mutual king vulnerability and very few good options (~2), wasting even one tempo allows the opponent to establish a defensive blockade, escape a mating net, improve their king position, or neutralize a decisive advantage. The positions are 'races' where the first player to act decisively wins.
sub_patterns: Passive bishop retreats when active attack is available (Bg7, Bb4)
Pointless checks that let opponent's king improve (Bc5+, b4+ allowing Ka4 blockade)
Slow prophylactic pawn moves when king march is urgent (a6 instead of Ke4)
King moves to vulnerable squares ignoring tactical threats (Kg2, Kd7)
Near-miss forcing moves that allow king escape (Rf8 instead of Rf7)

analysis.label: Moves that voluntarily weaken the player's own king safety by advancing shield pawns, castling into danger, or placing the king on exposed squares.
analysis.description: This feature fires on moves that catastrophically compromise the player's own king safety. The dominant sub-pattern involves advancing pawns in front of the king (g6, g5, g4, g4 — 4/11 positions), which tears open lines and weakens critical squares around the castled or exposed king. A second sub-pattern involves castling into the wrong direction where the opponent has ready-made attacking levers (O-O-O in positions 1 and 13 — 2/11), placing the king directly in the path of pawn storms or open files. A third sub-pattern involves moving the king to a tactically vulnerable square (Ke1 in position 2). In 8/11 positions, 'king_safety' is explicitly identified as the primary tactical motif. The remaining positions (Nh6, Qc5, Nxd5) share the theme of ignoring the king's existing vulnerability to pursue other goals. The average cp_loss of 1875 reflects the catastrophic nature of these errors — several result in forced checkmate.
analysis.move_pattern: Pawn advances on the g-file (g4/g5/g6) in front of own king, or king placement moves (O-O-O, Ke1) toward exposed squares/dangerous flanks
analysis.why_bad: These moves remove critical pawn defenders from the king's shelter or place the king where opponent pieces can immediately exploit open files, weakened diagonals, or invasion squares — often enabling forced mating attacks or devastating material-winning combinations against the exposed king.
sub_patterns: Advancing g-pawn in front of castled/exposed king (g4/g5/g6) creating immediate tactical weaknesses
Castling queenside into opponent's ready pawn lever (a4) or open file pressure
Moving king to square where open files and diagonals converge for forced tactics
Passive development moves that ignore urgent king safety demands

analysis.label: Moves that address the most visible threat or opportunity while missing the deeper tactical or strategic priority of the position.
analysis.description: This feature fires on moves that react to the most salient tactical element in the position—capturing an attacker (hxg4 taking the bishop, Nxd2 taking the bishop), chasing a threatening piece (h6 attacking the knight), giving a check (b5+), moving a piece to apparent safety (Bc5), or placing a piece on an aggressive-looking square (Qh5, Qg3)—while missing the correct underlying priority. In 5/7 cases, the correct move involved addressing a different, less obvious problem first: a preparatory exchange sacrifice before capturing (Nxd2 needed Rxf3 first), blocking a diagonal before chasing a piece (h6 needed d5 first), maintaining a defensive function rather than seeking activity (Qh5 abandoned the queen's role on g6), or finding the decisive tactical square over the merely aggressive one (Qg3 missed Qe3's winning threats). The average cp_loss of 1584 and only 1.1 good moves available confirms these are razor-sharp positions where the superficially natural move catastrophically fails. In 4/7 positions the refutation involves a fork or combination exploiting what the mistaken move left unaddressed.
analysis.move_pattern: Diverse piece types (pawns, knights, bishops, queens); moves typically capture an attacker, attack a threatening piece, give check, or relocate to a seemingly active square—always the most visually obvious action available
analysis.why_bad: These moves address the symptom (a visible threat, an obvious target, an apparent opportunity for activity) rather than the root cause of the position's tension, allowing the opponent to exploit the deeper unaddressed vulnerability—whether that's a move-order dependent combination, an exposed back rank, uncoordinated pieces, or a critical square left uncontested.
sub_patterns: Capturing an attacking piece instead of neutralizing the more dangerous positional threat
Wrong move order: taking the obvious target before the necessary preparatory move
Relocating a piece for superficial activity while abandoning a crucial defensive function
Choosing a forcing check or attack over a quiet decisive move

analysis.label: Moving pieces away from optimal attacking positions or choosing material/checks over maintaining decisive coordination in winning positions.
analysis.description: This feature fires on moves that dissipate a winning attack by breaking piece coordination or losing critical tempo. In 8/10 positions, the player had a large advantage or forced mate but chose a move that reduced attacking pressure. The pattern manifests in three sub-types: (1) repositioning active pieces to passive squares (Qc2 instead of Qh4, Ndc6 retreating from dominant d4, Qa5 leaving central e5, Nd3 instead of Ne4), seen in 5/10 cases; (2) choosing checks/captures over stronger quiet moves that maintain the mating net (Rg8+ driving king to safety, Nxf2+ fork instead of Qb3#, fxg2 removing the key attacking pawn), seen in 3/10 cases; and (3) making captures/advances that remove critical positional assets (fxe5 opening a diagonal to own king, Kg5 abandoning g3 pawn), seen in 2/10 cases. The average cp_loss of 2891 reflects that these moves typically occur in already-winning positions where precision was needed to convert.
analysis.move_pattern: Any piece type moving away from the critical zone of attack (queen/knight retreating from center/kingside, rook giving unhelpful check, pawn capturing away from key file, king advancing prematurely)
analysis.why_bad: The moves break the coordination between attacking pieces needed to deliver the finishing blow, giving the opponent critical tempi to reorganize defenses, escape mating nets, or exploit newly created weaknesses. The moved piece typically ends up on a less active square than where it started.
sub_patterns: Queen/knight retreating from dominant central or attacking square to peripheral/passive position
Giving premature check that drives opponent's king to safety instead of maintaining quiet mating threats
Capturing material that removes a key attacking asset (pawn structure, piece placement) critical for the continuation
King advancing into territory that abandons defense of critical pawns or structure

analysis.label: Playing a slow, non-forcing move in a tactically critical position where only 1-2 precise moves maintain the evaluation, wasting a crucial tempo.
analysis.description: This feature fires on positions where the player makes a passive, non-urgent move when the position demands immediate tactical or strategic action. The common thread across all 11 positions is tempo waste: the played move addresses a secondary concern (pawn grabs on the wing, passive piece repositioning, slow pawn pushes) while ignoring the position's most critical demand. The 'tempo_loss' tag appears in 10/11 positions, and 'missed_tactic' in 11/11. The average number of good moves is only 1.6, confirming these are razor-sharp positions with narrow solutions. In 8/11 cases, the best move was either forcing (checks, captures, direct threats to key pieces like Nh4 attacking a critical defender, Rc8+ winning material, Nd4 with counterplay) or urgently defensive (Kd2 addressing king safety, Bd3 blockading a passed pawn, Qf6 guarding critical squares). The blunder moves instead drift to irrelevant sectors of the board or make positional gestures (Ba2 repositioning, b3 on the queenside, g5 pushing a pawn, a4 expanding) that give the opponent a free tempo to execute their plan.
analysis.move_pattern: Non-forcing moves (passive retreats, slow pawn pushes, wing operations) in positions requiring immediate central/tactical action; diverse piece types but consistently non-checking, non-threatening moves
analysis.why_bad: The position has an urgent tactical or strategic demand (exposed king, hanging piece, dangerous passed pawn, critical defender to target) with only 1-2 correct responses, and the played move wastes a tempo on an irrelevant plan, allowing the opponent to execute a winning sequence that was previously one tempo short of working.
sub_patterns: Pawn pushes ignoring urgent piece play (e6, e4, g5, b3, a4)
Piece retreats/repositions abandoning defensive duties (Qf1, Qe8, Re7, Ba2)
Pawn grab removing a key defender from critical zone (Bxb2)
Development to wrong square ignoring king vulnerability (Bb4)

analysis.label: Giving an impulsive check on the wrong square or with the wrong piece when a more precise check (often closer to the king) would deliver checkmate or maintain a decisive advantage.
analysis.description: In all 6/6 positions, the player gives check but chooses the WRONG check — either the wrong square, wrong piece, or wrong capture. In 4/6 cases, checkmate in 1-3 moves was available but missed (positions 2, 3, 5, 14). The correct move was typically a check delivered from a square adjacent to or more restrictive of the enemy king: Qf3# instead of Re8+ (position 2), Qxc7+ instead of Qg6+ (position 3), Qxb2# instead of Qxc4+ (position 5), Qf2+ instead of Qg4+ (position 7), Qxf6+/Rae1+ instead of Rfe1+ (position 11), Qe3+ instead of Qe5+ (position 14). In 5/6 cases, the wrong check allows the enemy king access to escape squares that the correct check would have sealed. In 2/6 cases (positions 7, 11), the wrong check allows interposition or removes a critical piece from its optimal file. The average cp_loss of 8248 and only 1.2 good moves available confirm these are positions where only one precise check works.
analysis.move_pattern: Queen or rook delivering check from a suboptimal square or with the wrong piece, typically checking from greater distance or a less restrictive angle than the winning alternative
analysis.why_bad: The chosen check fails to control critical escape squares adjacent to the enemy king, or allows defensive resources (interposition, king flight to uncontrolled squares) that the correct check would have prevented — classic 'seeing a check and playing it' without verifying it's the RIGHT check
sub_patterns: Queen check on wrong square misses mate (e5 vs e3, g6 vs c7, xc4 vs xb2)
Distant check allows interposition (Qg4+ allows Qg3 block)
Wrong rook check removes critical piece from mating file (Rfe1+ vs Rae1+)
Attractive capture-check over simple checkmate (Qxc4+ vs Qxb2#)

analysis.label: Pieces moved to e2/e7 (or enabling threats via that square) that obstruct development, prevent castling, or create tactical vulnerabilities.
analysis.description: In 4/4 positions, the e2 square (for White) or e7 square (for Black) is central to the mistake. Three moves literally place a piece on e2/e7: Ne2 puts an undefended knight there allowing Bg4 to win it with tempo (Position 1), Be2 passively develops the bishop there instead of addressing the hanging Bf4 (Position 6), and Qe7 blocks the f8-bishop preventing kingside castling (Position 13). The fourth move (dxe4) ignores the opponent's devastating Ne2+ fork that wins the queen (Position 10). In all cases, the player chose a routine-looking move involving the e2/e7 square while ignoring concrete tactical threats. The common punishment involves the opponent exploiting the self-obstruction or the vulnerability of that square with tempo-gaining attacks (Bg4 in Position 1, Qf6 in Position 6, Ne2+ in Position 10, d5 in Position 13).
analysis.move_pattern: Piece (knight, bishop, or queen) placed on e2/e7, or pawn capture that leaves e2 tactically exploitable; all involve the second-rank e-square for the moving side
analysis.why_bad: These moves either block development of the kingside bishop (preventing castling), place an undefended piece on an exposed square vulnerable to tempo attacks, or ignore immediate tactical threats involving e2/e7 (forks, pins, invasions)
sub_patterns: Knight to e2 leaving piece undefended against tempo-gaining bishop attack
Bishop to e2 passively ignoring threats to other pieces
Queen to e7 blocking own bishop and delaying castling
Pawn capture ignoring Ne2+ fork geometry

analysis.label: Moving a bishop or queen to a peripheral edge square (especially h-file or a-file) where it becomes exposed, trapped, or disconnected from critical duties.
analysis.description: This feature fires on moves that reposition a piece (predominantly bishops or queens) to the edge of the board where it becomes tactically vulnerable. In 8/10 positions, the piece moves to the a-file or h-file. The most common sub-pattern is bishops going to h4 or h5 (4/10) where they get trapped or chased by pawn advances (g5-h5-h4 or g4-f4), followed by queens going to h3 (2/10) where they land on exploitable diagonals (c8-h3). In every case, the moved piece simultaneously abandons a critical defensive function: guarding d5 (Bh5 positions), protecting e4 (Rf1, Qh3), or maintaining counterattacking potential (Qa7, Qe5). The opponent consistently punishes by either trapping the piece with pawns (4/10 positions), winning material through tactical exploitation of the now-undefended squares (3/10), or gaining multiple tempi against the exposed piece while building a dominant position (3/10).
analysis.move_pattern: Bishop or queen moving 1-2 squares diagonally/laterally to the a-file or h-file (rim squares), typically as a 'retreat' when challenged
analysis.why_bad: The piece lands on an exposed peripheral square where it can be trapped by pawn advances, exploited via discovered attacks on newly-opened diagonals, or rendered passive while simultaneously abandoning defense of critical central pawns or squares
sub_patterns: Bishop to h4/h5 getting trapped or chased by g5/g4 pawn storms
Queen to h3 landing on the c8-h3 diagonal exploitable by ...d5
Queen to a7 becoming boxed in by own pawns
Bishop to a4 left undefended and won tactically

analysis.label: Moves that address a legitimate positional concern but use the wrong piece, wrong square, or wrong timing, losing critical tempo to the opponent.
analysis.description: This feature fires on moves that have a plausible strategic intent but execute it suboptimally, allowing the opponent to gain decisive tempo. In 4/4 positions, the played move addresses a real concern (king activation, pawn control, blockading a passed pawn) but does so inefficiently: Kg7 instead of Kg8 walks into Re7+ with check (one square difference allows tempo-gaining attack); Ke8 instead of Kd8 loses a triangulation tempo in a critical pawn endgame; f4 attempts to strengthen the center when castling was the urgent priority, leaving e3 undefended; Na6 uses the knight to attack a passed pawn when only the king's direct march (Ka4) could neutralize it. In 3/4 positions the opponent gains a tempo through immediate threats (check, attack on undefended piece/pawn), and in all cases the evaluation swing stems from the opponent using that tempo to execute their primary plan (7th rank penetration, passed pawn advance, tactical exploitation of exposed king).
analysis.move_pattern: Various piece types moving to plausible but subtly incorrect squares; often one square off from optimal or using wrong piece entirely for the task
analysis.why_bad: These moves give the opponent a critical free tempo by failing to address the position's most urgent demand directly, allowing immediate tactical exploitation (checks, attacks on undefended material, decisive pawn advances) that the 'correct' move would have prevented or preempted
sub_patterns: King to wrong adjacent square allowing check (Kg7 vs Kg8)
Piece decentralization when king action was required (Na6 vs Ka4)
Pawn advance when king safety needed immediate attention (f4 vs O-O-O)
Imprecise king route losing triangulation tempo (Ke8 vs Kd8)

analysis.label: Rook pawn advances (a3/a6/h3/h6) to "put the question" to an active enemy piece when urgent tactical or developmental needs exist.
analysis.description: All 7/7 positions feature a rook pawn advance (a-file or h-file, one square) intended to challenge an enemy minor piece that's exerting pressure — a bishop on g4/g5 (5/7 positions) or a knight/bishop on b4/b5 (2/7 positions). In every case, the player expected the piece to passively retreat, but instead the opponent has a devastating tactical response: the 'kicked' piece captures profitably rather than retreating (6/7 cases), the pawn advance itself becomes a target (h3 captured in 2/7, h6 captured in 1/7), or the tempo loss allows a forcing combination exploiting undeveloped pieces or undefended squares. The positions overwhelmingly occur in the opening (5/7) where development tempo is critical, and the average cp_loss of 224 reflects how severely these waste time in tactically loaded positions. All positions featured better moves that either developed pieces, challenged the center, or addressed the real tactical threats rather than chasing an active piece with a pawn.
analysis.move_pattern: Rook pawn advance one square (a3, a6, h3, or h6) toward an enemy minor piece on the 4th/5th rank
analysis.why_bad: The enemy piece has a stronger response than retreating — typically capturing a pinned/pressured piece to shatter pawn structure, or ignoring the threat to execute a tactical combination that the wasted tempo now enables. The pawn advance often weakens the very squares it touches and creates new targets.
sub_patterns: h6/h3 to kick a bishop pinning a knight on f3/f6, allowing devastating capture on f3/f6
a6/a3 to kick a knight or bishop, enabling tactical combinations on the newly weakened square
h3 creating a target pawn that gets won after deflection of the g-pawn defender

analysis.label: Passive piece repositioning or centralization that wastes a critical tempo when an immediate forcing move (capture, check, or direct attack) was required.
analysis.description: In 5/6 positions, the player chose a slow centralizing or repositioning move—placing a piece on a 'good-looking' square—when the position demanded immediate concrete action. In Position 1, Qxd5 captured toward the center with the wrong piece instead of the forcing Rxd5. In Position 3, Be5 centralized the bishop when Bxa5+ delivered check and won material. In Position 6, Ke1 passively centralized the king when Nb5 actively threatened the opponent's rook. In Position 11, Be5 again centralized the bishop when Kf4 directly attacked a pawn and advanced the king. In Position 14, Rf7 passively repositioned the rook when Rxc4 captured a critical pawn. The common thread is choosing an aesthetically pleasing but non-forcing move that grants the opponent the tempo to consolidate, escape, or launch their own plans. The average cp_loss of 322 reflects positions with typically only ~1 good move, making these critical tempo-sensitive decisions.
analysis.move_pattern: Piece moves toward center or dominant-looking square (e5, d5, e1, f5, f7) without creating an immediate threat, when a capture or check was available
analysis.why_bad: The slow move surrenders a critical tempo, allowing the opponent to consolidate their king, activate pieces, or advance passed pawns—exactly the threats that the available forcing move (capture/check) would have prevented or exploited
sub_patterns: Bishop centralization to e5 blocking own king's path
Capturing with wrong piece on contested file
Passive king move when knight/piece attack was available
Rook repositioning instead of capturing vulnerable pawn

analysis.label: Seemingly improving moves that abandon a critical defensive function, allowing the opponent a devastating forcing response (check, fork, or tactical blow).
analysis.description: This feature fires on moves that appear active, centralizing, or 'improving' but fatally neglect an immediate tactical vulnerability—typically by removing a piece from a key defensive square or placing it where it becomes a tactical target. In 7/10 positions, the refutation begins with a check or fork exploiting the exact weakness created by the move (Nc6+ fork after Re5, Ng3+ after Ke2, Ng6+ after Nxd5, Qa5+ after Qc3 and Qc2, Qh6+ after Rb7, Qf8+ after g5). In 6/10 cases, the blunder specifically removes a piece from guarding a critical square (Nxd5 unguards g6, Kb5 unguards b6, g5 removes pawn shield from king, Qc3/Qc2 removes queen from anti-check diagonal). The moves all share a greedy or forward-looking intent (centralizing, capturing, gaining space, activating) that ignores the opponent's concrete tactical resources. The average centipawn loss of 1109 with only 2.0 good alternatives indicates these are narrow positions requiring defensive precision where the natural-looking move is catastrophically wrong.
analysis.move_pattern: Piece/king/pawn moves to an apparently useful square while vacating or abandoning a defensive post, creating a target or unguarding a critical square
analysis.why_bad: The move removes a piece from a defensive duty or creates a new tactical target, allowing the opponent a forcing response (check, fork, or combination) that exploits the exact square/diagonal/geometry left undefended—the seemingly improving move gives the opponent exactly one extra tempo or one unguarded square needed for a devastating blow.
sub_patterns: Piece moves to forkable square alongside existing piece/king (Re5 with king on b4)
King/queen moves to square attackable by opponent knight check (Ke2 allows Ng3+)
Capture removes key defender of a square (Nxd5 unguards g6 for Ng6+)
Queen repositions away from anti-check diagonal (Qc3/Qc2 allowing Qa5+)
Pawn advance removes critical king shield (g5 opens f8-h6 diagonal and vacates g6)
King abandons pawn defense for greedy counterattack (Kb5 abandons b6 defense)

analysis.label: Seemingly logical moves that pursue a secondary objective while abandoning a critical defensive duty or missing a forced tactical sequence, resulting in catastrophic material or positional loss.
analysis.description: In 6/6 analyzed positions, the played move appears to follow a reasonable plan—piece centralization (Ne5, Nc6), repositioning (Qf2, Be6, Qf8+), passive blockade (Rc1), or aggressive pawn breaks (f4, c4)—but fatally ignores the position's most urgent tactical reality. In 3/6 cases (Qf2, Be6, Nc6), the move directly abandons defense of a piece or pawn, leaving it hanging for the opponent to capture. In 2/6 cases (f4, c4), aggressive pawn advances create immediate tactical vulnerabilities (forks, exposed pieces). In 2/6 cases (Qf8+, Ne5), the player plays a passive or 'improving' move when the position demanded a specific forced tactical response (Nd3+ fork, or Ka4/Ka6 to escape mate). The unifying thread is that each move would be reasonable in a quieter context, but the concrete tactical situation demanded addressing one specific urgent problem—and the player's 'plan' blinded them to it.
analysis.move_pattern: Various piece types moving to ostensibly reasonable squares (centralization, repositioning, pawn breaks) while leaving a critical square, piece, or mating net unaddressed
analysis.why_bad: Each move abandons a defensive obligation or wastes a critical tempo, allowing the opponent to exploit an immediate tactical vulnerability (hanging piece, fork, undefended pawn, checkmate) that the move fails to prevent or even creates
sub_patterns: Piece repositioning that leaves another piece undefended (Qf2, Be6, Nc6)
Aggressive pawn pushes creating tactical vulnerabilities in own position (f4, c4)
Passive or 'improving' moves when forced tactical sequences were available (Qf8+, Ne5, Rc1)

analysis.label: Non-urgent moves played in critical positions where only 1-2 specific responses address the primary tactical threat.
analysis.description: This feature fires on positions where the player makes a plausible-looking move addressing a secondary concern (king repositioning, pawn expansion, material capture, piece centralization) while ignoring the position's single most critical demand. In 8/8 analyzed positions, the correct move required addressing a specific concrete threat (e.g., blockading a passed pawn, gaining a tempo with a forcing move, or maintaining critical structural tension), but the player chose a slower alternative. King moves pursuing 'safety' that walk into tactical vulnerabilities appear in 4/8 cases (Kc7, Ke7, Kf7, Kd2). Pawn moves addressing the wrong flank or releasing beneficial tension appear in 4/8 cases (b4, b3, f4, fxe4). Material greed ignoring a lethal passed pawn (Rxa3) and self-blocking a key defender (Be5) round out the set. The positions universally feature very few good options (avg 1.9), meaning the critical moment demanded precision, and the resulting punishments are catastrophic (avg 2122 cp loss). In 7/8 cases, the move loses a critical tempo that allows the opponent to execute a forcing sequence (fork, promotion, mating attack, or pawn advance) that wasn't possible one move earlier.
analysis.move_pattern: Quiet non-forcing moves (king retreats/walks, slow pawn pushes, passive captures/repositionings) in positions demanding a single specific forcing response
analysis.why_bad: The position demands one concrete response to the primary threat (passed pawn, mating attack, forcing sequence), but the move addresses a secondary concern, gifting the opponent a critical tempo to execute a winning tactical sequence that the correct move would have prevented
sub_patterns: King walks into tactical vulnerability (diagonal/file exposure)
Slow pawn push ignoring opponent's active kingside/central attack
Material greed abandoning critical defensive duty
Releasing pawn tension that was the source of advantage

analysis.label: Moving a piece or pawn away from a square where it performs an essential defensive or controlling function, enabling the opponent to exploit the vacated squares with a breakthrough or tactic.
analysis.description: In all 4/4 positions, the blunder involves moving a piece or pawn that was performing a critical defensive duty—controlling key squares, blocking advancing pawns, or preventing tactical motifs. In Position 3 (Ne5), the knight leaves f3, which was blocking Black's f4-pawn advance and defending the kingside. In Position 13 (Na4), the knight leaves c3, which controlled e4 and supported kingside defense, allowing f4 and king invasion. In Position 5 (c6), the pawn vacates the c7 square's protection, enabling a Nc7+ fork after dxe5. In Position 2 (Bf6), the bishop moves to a square where it becomes a tactical target for Nd5 (threatening Ne7+ fork), rather than addressing the actual primary threat. The common thread is prioritizing a secondary objective (attacking a piece, repositioning, chasing a threat) over maintaining the piece's current essential defensive function. The result in all cases is an immediate tactical or strategic exploitation by the opponent through the newly weakened squares.
analysis.move_pattern: A piece (usually a knight, 2/4) or pawn moves away from a central/functional square to a peripheral or less relevant square, vacating control of critical squares in the player's own camp
analysis.why_bad: The moved piece/pawn was performing an invisible but essential defensive function—controlling key squares, blocking pawn advances, or preventing forks. By removing it, the player opens a hole that the opponent immediately exploits with a forcing sequence (fork, pawn breakthrough, or king invasion).
sub_patterns: Knight decentralization from c3/f3 to rim squares, allowing pawn breakthroughs
Pawn move vacating a critical guard square, enabling knight forks
Piece relocation that creates a tactical target on its new square while ignoring the primary threat

analysis.label: Choosing a superficially active move (check, capture, or centralization) that has an immediate tactical refutation, when only one or two precise continuations maintain the position.
analysis.description: This feature fires on positions where the player selects a move that appears aggressive or natural—often a check, capture, or piece centralization—but lands on exactly the wrong square or abandons a critical defensive function, allowing a devastating tactical refutation. In 7/8 analyzed positions, the correct move was nearly unique (avg 1.7 good moves available), meaning these are positions demanding extreme precision. The blunders frequently involve choosing the 'almost right' move: Qe5+ instead of Qe1+ (wrong check square allowing counter-interposition), Qd7+ instead of Qc8+ (queen capturable on d-file), Rb3 instead of Rb1 (same file, wrong rank missing forced exchange), Rf5 instead of Rf8 (active-looking but abandons back rank), Ne5 instead of Nh2 (removes key defender), Ne7+ instead of keeping knight on f5 (allows fork after recapture). The average centipawn loss of 2323 reflects that these positions sit on a knife's edge where the difference between the correct and chosen move is often just one square or one tempo.
analysis.move_pattern: Various piece types moving to apparently active squares (often giving check or attacking something), frequently one square away from the correct destination or in the same direction as the best move but to the wrong rank/file
analysis.why_bad: The chosen square has a specific tactical vulnerability: the piece can be immediately captured (Qd7+, Bd2, Ne7+), a critical defensive function is abandoned (Rf5 leaves back rank, Ne5 removes h-file guard), or the opponent gains a counter-tactic (Qe5+ allows interposition-with-check, Kc6 allows perpetual check setup). The correct move was typically quieter, more precise, or forcing in a different way.
sub_patterns: Check on wrong square allowing counter-check or capture (Qe5+, Qd7+, Ne7+)
Piece moves to square where it's immediately capturable (Bd2, Qxh1 leaving pieces hanging)
Active rook move abandoning critical rank defense (Rf5, Rb3 vs Rb1)
King retreating/sideways when only advance maintains winning chances (Kc6, Ke6)

analysis.label: Playing a slow, non-forcing move when a simple material-winning capture is available on the board.
analysis.description: In all 13/13 positions, the best move was a capture (Bxc4, Rxd5, Rxe5, Rxb5, Bxc5, Rdxd3, Rxe4, Bxe6, Qxd4, Nxe5, etc.) that won material or eliminated a critical threat, yet the player chose a quiet repositioning move instead. The blundered moves are uniformly non-forcing: piece retreats (Nc1, Qe2), pawn advances (h4, b4, g6, b5), piece repositioning (Nf6, Re3, Bf4, Ba4), king walks (Kg3, Ka2), or passive development (Qe7). The pattern is remarkably consistent: the player's attention is drawn to slow improvement or prophylaxis while a concrete, often simple, capture sits available that resolves the position's central tension. The average cp_loss of 1751 reflects that these captures were typically decisive—hanging pieces, undefended pawns, or tactically justified takes that the opponent cannot properly recapture.
analysis.move_pattern: Any quiet non-capture move (retreat, pawn push, king move, piece reposition) when a winning capture exists on a central or enemy pawn/piece
analysis.why_bad: The player ignores an immediately available material-winning capture—often of a hanging or inadequately defended piece/pawn—in favor of a slow positional idea, gifting the opponent a crucial tempo to consolidate, defend, or launch counterplay that eliminates the tactical window.
sub_patterns: Piece retreat instead of capturing hanging material (Nc1, Qe2, Bf4)
Irrelevant pawn push instead of capturing a critical pawn (h4, b4, g6, b5)
King move instead of tactical capture (Kg3, Ka2)
Piece development/repositioning instead of winning capture (Nf6, Re3, Ba4, Qe7)

analysis.label: Player makes a non-forcing or misdirected move in a critical middlegame position where king vulnerability (own or opponent's) demands an urgent, specific response.
analysis.description: In all 6 positions, king safety is the overwhelmingly dominant positional factor - either the opponent's king is dangerously exposed and demands an immediate attacking continuation (positions 1, 3, 5: Rxc8 instead of Qf6, cxb3 instead of Rxe4, Nxd8 instead of Rh7), or the player's own king is critically vulnerable and requires urgent defensive attention (positions 4, 6: Rh7 and Rah8 both ignore fatal threats to own king on e7/d7), or the move actively creates king exposure (position 5: Kg2 allows Qxf3+ with check). All 6/6 positions feature prominently exposed kings, all 6/6 involve tempo loss as a key tag, and 5/6 feature missed tactics. The average of only 1.2 good moves available confirms these are razor-sharp positions where only one precise response maintains the evaluation. The blunders uniformly pursue secondary objectives (material gain via exchanges, file doubling, prophylaxis) while the position's life-or-death dynamic—centered on king vulnerability—goes unaddressed.
analysis.move_pattern: Various piece types; captures that simplify prematurely (3/6) or quiet moves that waste tempo (3/6); no consistent geometric direction but all are non-forcing relative to the king-safety critical demands of the position
analysis.why_bad: The move fails to address the position's most urgent dynamic—king vulnerability—either by exchanging a key attacking piece for material, playing a slow move that grants the opponent tempo for a decisive kingside/queenside breakthrough, or actively exposing one's own king to tactical exploitation.
sub_patterns: Exchanging a dominant attacking piece for material when the opponent's king is exposed (Rxc8, Nxd8)
Passive rook/king moves ignoring mating threats against own exposed king (Rh7, Kg2, Rah8)
Slow pawn capture ignoring hanging piece and giving opponent attacking tempo (cxb3)

analysis.label: Moves that appear active or purposeful but catastrophically ignore the position's single most urgent tactical requirement, creating or exposing decisive vulnerabilities.
analysis.description: This feature fires on moves where the player makes a 'natural-looking' choice—advancing a passed pawn (e7), activating a piece (Qc5, Nf5, Qf5), developing (Bd2), giving check (Qf4+), defending the second rank (Rf2), or tucking the king away (Kh8)—while completely missing the one critical tactical or defensive requirement of the position. In 4/8 positions, only one good move existed (avg 1.9 good moves), indicating extreme tactical narrowness. In 6/8 cases, the move specifically abandons defense of a critical square or creates a new tactical vulnerability: Nf5 vacates d6 allowing Rd7 invasion, Qf5 abandons c7 allowing immediate mate, Rf2 enables a knight fork after Rxf2/Nd3+, Kh8 makes Nxf7+ a check, Qf4+ fails to control f2 letting the king escape, and Qc5 exposes the queen to tempo-gaining e5/Be3. The moves share the characteristic of looking reasonable to a player focused on their own plan while being oblivious to the opponent's concrete tactical opportunities.
analysis.move_pattern: Various piece types moving to apparently active/useful squares; no consistent geometric direction; typically non-captures that prioritize the player's agenda over positional demands
analysis.why_bad: Each move either abandons a critical defensive duty (guarding a key square like c7, d6, f2), creates a new tactical vulnerability (fork, check pattern, tempo-gaining attack), or wastes the tempo needed to execute the only winning continuation—all in positions where the correct choice was extremely narrow
sub_patterns: Queen abandons defense of mating square (Qf5 leaving c7)
Piece vacates blocking/controlling post allowing invasion (Nf5 from d6)
Move creates fork or check vulnerability (Rf2 enabling Nd3+, Kh8 enabling Nxf7+)
Slow development when crushing tactic available (Bd2 instead of Nh7)
Check on wrong square missing mating construction (Qf4+ instead of Qf2+)

analysis.label: Playing a plausible but non-urgent move in a critical position where only one precise action addresses the primary tactical necessity.
