analysis.description: This feature fires on positions with extremely narrow margins (avg 1.4 good moves available) where the player makes a reasonable-looking move that fails to address the single most pressing tactical issue. In 6/8 positions, the best move required a specific concrete action (capturing a critical pawn, exploiting a hanging piece, resolving central tension, choosing the exact correct square) while the played move addressed a secondary concern or made a 'close but wrong' choice. Common patterns include: retreating when counterplay is the only defense (Nb8 instead of Nc5, Position 5), quiet king moves when material capture is urgent (Kh7 instead of Bxb2, Position 6), moving the wrong piece to the right square (Rd2 instead of Nd2, Position 8), moving the right piece to the wrong square (Kc1 instead of Ke1, Position 3; Rg2 instead of Rh2, Position 7), and self-weakening pawn moves that create new vulnerabilities (fxg6 opening the diagonal, g6 blocking escape). The extremely high average cp_loss (2428) reflects that these one-move-puzzle positions punish imprecision catastrophically.
analysis.move_pattern: Quiet, passive, or misdirected moves (retreats, consolidation, wrong-square choices) when a single forcing or precise action is required
analysis.why_bad: The moves fail to address the position's single most urgent tactical demand—whether that's capturing a critical piece/pawn, resolving forced tension, or choosing the exact correct square for a defensive task—allowing the opponent to exploit the unaddressed vulnerability with a clear refutation.
sub_patterns: Wrong square for correct piece (Kc1/Ke1, Rg2/Rh2)
Wrong piece to correct square (Rd2/Nd2)
Passive retreat when active counterplay required (Nb8/Nc5, Kh7/Bxb2)
Self-weakening pawn move opening critical lines (fxg6, g6)
Piece repositioning before resolving central tension (Bd3 before exd5)

analysis.label: Plausible-looking moves that catastrophically ignore the position's single most urgent tactical demand, in positions with very few correct options.
analysis.description: This feature fires on positions where only 1-2 moves maintain the evaluation (avg 1.8 good moves) and the player makes a natural-seeming alternative that misreads the position's top priority. In 7/11 cases the move involves material gain or piece 'improvement' (bxa5 wins a bishop, exd6 wins material, Rxc7 wins a pawn, Qxd3 wins a pawn, Nd5 centralizes, Nc6 develops, b4 expands) while ignoring a dominant threat—typically king safety (tagged in 9/11 positions). The remaining cases involve tempo-wasting moves (Kh8, h4, Qe2) or wrong forcing moves (Re8+ instead of Re5+). The common thread is that each position has ONE critical demand (stop a promotion, maintain a key defender, exploit an exposed king, prevent a mating net) and the player addresses something else entirely, resulting in catastrophic evaluation swings (avg 2040cp loss). These are 'narrow path' positions where the correct move is often counter-intuitive or defensive.
analysis.move_pattern: Diverse piece types and directions (captures, retreats, advances, checks); no single geometric pattern. Typically a materialistic capture, a piece repositioning, or a non-urgent pawn push played when concrete tactical action addressing king safety or a critical threat was required.
analysis.why_bad: Each move fails because it addresses a secondary concern (winning material, centralizing a piece, gaining space) while the position's true demand is singular and urgent—usually defending against a mating threat, maintaining a critical defender, stopping a promotion, or delivering a precise forcing sequence against an exposed king. The one-tempo error allows the opponent to execute a decisive tactical blow.
sub_patterns: Material grabs that ignore a bigger tactical threat (bxa5, exd6, Rxc7, Qxd3)
Moving a critical defender away from its post (Nd5 unguards f1, Nc6 abandons f7 defense)
Tempo-wasting moves in critical positions (Kh8, h4, Qe2 when concrete action needed)
Wrong forcing move when a specific check/sequence wins (Re8+ instead of Re5+)
Pawn advances creating tactical vulnerabilities in sharp positions (b4 allows en passant deflection)

analysis.label: Giving check with a heavy piece that wastes tempo and fails to address the critical threat (usually an advancing passed pawn).
analysis.description: This feature fires on positions where a player delivers check with a rook or queen that accomplishes nothing concrete. In 6/6 positions the move played is a check, and in 5/6 the opponent's king simply sidesteps to an equal or better square. The common context is endgames (4/6) or middlegames (2/6) with dangerous passed pawns where tempo is critical — the check wastes time that should be spent blockading or addressing the pawn. In 5/6 positions, the analyses explicitly identify 'tempo_loss' as the tactical motif or tag. The checks often actively help the opponent: driving the king to a safer/more active square (4→Kh2, 6→Kf5, 10→Kg2), abandoning a critical defensive post like a blockade square (10), or landing on a square where the piece is immediately captured (15→Bxf2). The catastrophic outliers (positions 12 and 15 with ~9400cp loss) show the extreme consequence: one squanders a critical defensive tempo enabling forced mate, the other places the rook en prise to a bishop.
analysis.move_pattern: Rook or Queen delivering check along a rank or file, typically moving away from a critical defensive square toward the opponent's king
analysis.why_bad: The checks waste tempo without creating any concrete threat, allowing the opponent's king to reach a better square or the opponent to advance a passed pawn one step closer to promotion; meanwhile the checking piece abandons its defensive duties (blockade, control of key files).
sub_patterns: Rook check abandoning passed pawn blockade
Check driving king to safer square
Check landing piece on en-prise square
Back-rank check with easy king escape

analysis.label: Playing an indirect or preparatory move when the position demanded an immediate concrete action—usually a capture or forcing advance—resulting in critical tempo loss.
analysis.description: In 7/8 positions, the best move was a direct concrete action (capture or forcing advance): Rxg2 captures the deadly pawn (Position 1), f5+ checks the exposed king (Position 2), c3 advances the counter-threat (Position 3), Qxf4 takes the hanging pawn (Position 4), Kxg3 captures the knight (Position 8), Qc5/Bxc4 exploits queenside targets (Position 9), Be4 wins material on the diagonal (Position 10). Instead, the players chose slower alternatives that merely 'approached' or 'prepared'—Kf2 walks toward g2 instead of capturing with the rook, Qf5 hovers near f4 without taking it, Kh3 moves near the knight without capturing it, Kc6 blockades passively instead of advancing. The average cp_loss of 1357 and average of only 1.5 good moves confirm these are critical moments where the single forcing action had to be found immediately. In 6/8 cases, the opponent punished by gaining a tempo (check, threat, or pawn advance) that wouldn't have been available had the player executed the concrete action one move earlier.
analysis.move_pattern: Non-forcing moves (king repositions, quiet pawn pushes, or piece relocations) that approach or hover near a target rather than immediately capturing/forcing; 4/8 are king moves, 2/8 are pawn pushes, all avoid the available direct capture or check
analysis.why_bad: By choosing a preparatory move instead of the immediate concrete action, the player gifts the opponent one critical tempo to either create counter-threats (h3 creating connected passers, Bxc5+ with check, Nf5 repositioning), consolidate a weak position, or seize the initiative—the opponent's response exploits the extra tempo in a way that wouldn't have been possible had the forcing move been played first
sub_patterns: King approaching a piece/pawn without capturing it (Kf2 toward g2, Kh3 near Ng3, Kc6 near b6-pawn)
Queen/piece repositioning near a hanging pawn without taking it (Qf5 near f4)
Quiet pawn push when a tactical capture/check wins immediately (c4, g5, dxc5 instead of f5+)
King moving to exposed square instead of safe haven (Kd7 instead of Kb6)

analysis.label: Playing quiet developing or positional moves when the position demands immediate tactical action or concrete responses to urgent threats.
analysis.description: In all 4/4 positions, the player chose a 'textbook' quiet developing move (d3, Nd3, Bc5, Nf6) that would be perfectly reasonable in a normal position but catastrophically ignores the specific tactical demands of the current situation. In Position 1, d3 ignores a hanging g5 pawn and Nxf7 fork opportunity. In Position 2, Nd3 centralizes a knight while ignoring a lethal g4-h4 pawn storm requiring Nxh4. In Position 3, Bc5 develops the bishop while the king on f7 faces an imminent g5 break. In Position 4, Nf6 develops naturally while a completely undefended knight on g5 can be captured for free with Qxg5. All 4/4 positions had concrete forcing moves available (captures, king safety moves, or counterattacks) that addressed the tactical reality, while the played moves prioritized long-term positional goals over immediate necessity.
analysis.move_pattern: Non-forcing quiet moves (pawn pushes, knight/bishop development to natural squares) with no check, no capture, and no direct threat to opponent
analysis.why_bad: These moves ignore urgent concrete tactical features (hanging pieces, advancing pawn storms, exposed kings, fork opportunities) in favor of general positional improvement, allowing the opponent to consolidate advantages or execute devastating attacks that were previously preventable or exploitable.
sub_patterns: Quiet pawn moves missing piece captures (d3 missing Nxe5)
Piece centralization ignoring kingside pawn storms (Nd3 missing Nxh4)
Development moves ignoring king safety crises (Bc5 with king on f7)
Natural development missing free hanging pieces (Nf6 missing Qxg5)

analysis.label: Playing a reflexive check that disperses attacking coordination when a much stronger forcing move (often immediate checkmate or a superior check) was available.
analysis.description: All 5/5 positions feature a check (queen or rook) that catastrophically squanders a winning or mating position. In 3/5 cases (positions 9, 12, 13), immediate checkmate or forced mate in 1-3 was available but the player chose an inferior check instead. In position 6, the check removed a rook from its dominant 7th-rank coordination, leaving its partner hanging. In position 5, the check allowed a simple queen interposition that neutralized the attack. The common thread is 'patzer sees a check' syndrome: the player reflexively plays a visible check without scanning for a more decisive continuation. The played checks typically move pieces AWAY from optimal attacking squares (e.g., Rg5 leaves g6 for Rg6#, queen leaves e1 where Qg3# was available, rook leaves e7 where Re8+ forced mate). Average cp_loss of 6168 confirms these are among the most costly possible errors.
analysis.move_pattern: Queen or rook delivering check (often to back rank or board edge) that moves the piece away from a more lethal square
analysis.why_bad: The check allows the opponent's king to escape to a new square, permits an interposition, or removes the checking piece from a position where it coordinated with other attackers for immediate checkmate or decisive material gain
sub_patterns: Queen check to edge/corner missing Qg3# or similar short mate
Rook check to back rank abandoning 7th-rank dominance
Check that allows defensive interposition neutralizing the attack
Wrong piece check when the other piece's check forces removal of defender

analysis.chip: Ignoring King Danger for Peripheral Move
analysis.label: Moving a piece (usually a knight) to a rim/peripheral square or advancing the king while ignoring an immediate mating or tactical crisis.
analysis.description: This feature fires on positions where the player makes a seemingly purposeful move—often a knight maneuver to the edge of the board or a king advance—while completely overlooking an urgent king safety emergency. In 5/7 positions, a knight is moved to a rim or edge square (Nh3 twice, Na5, Nxc7, Nc6) pursuing development, material gain, or repositioning goals. In 2/7 positions, the king itself advances into a mating net (Kf5, Kh6). The common thread across all 7 positions is that the player's king (or opponent's attacking potential against it) is under immediate tactical pressure, yet the chosen move addresses a secondary concern instead. All 7 positions feature exposed kings with weak pawn shields, and in every case the refutation involves a check, fork, or forced checkmate that exploits the neglected king safety. The average cp_loss of 4419 reflects catastrophic consequences—4/7 positions result in immediate checkmate or mate-in-few.
analysis.move_pattern: Knight moved to rim square (h-file or a-file) or piece/king moved to peripheral/exposed square away from defensive duties; non-capturing development moves or greedy captures ignoring king zone
analysis.why_bad: The move completely ignores an immediate tactical crisis involving king safety—typically a mating threat, devastating check sequence, or fork—pursuing instead a secondary goal like development, material gain, or piece repositioning that is irrelevant given the urgency of the position.
sub_patterns: Knight retreats to h3 rim while king is under mating attack
Knight moves to rim (a5/c7) chasing material while own king faces tactical emergency on exposed square
King advances to exposed square walking directly into forced checkmate pattern
Natural-looking developing move (Nc6) that ignores an imminent positional/tactical catastrophe

analysis.label: Playing greedy, active, or positional moves while one's own king faces a critical vulnerability requiring immediate defensive attention.
analysis.description: This feature activates in positions where the moving side's king is seriously exposed or vulnerable, demanding precise defensive play, but the player instead chooses a move motivated by other considerations (material gain, piece activity, pawn advances). In 5/7 positions, the player's own king is explicitly described as exposed, weak-shielded, or on the back rank. The errors include capturing peripheral material while a back-rank mate looms (Nxb5, Position 6), taking the wrong pawn and leaving a critical attacker alive near the exposed king (gxh3, Position 4), advancing a pawn that destroys the king's remaining shelter (b5, Position 7), placing a piece on a square that blocks a needed defensive retreat (Rd3, Position 5), moving the queen to a tactically vulnerable square when only one safe square existed (Qe3, Position 3), and placing a knight where it's immediately kicked with tempo (Ne4, Position 10). The one non-blunder (Qf7+, Position 14) is the mirror case: correctly EXPLOITING the opponent's king vulnerability. The average of only 1.7 good moves available confirms these are razor-thin defensive situations requiring precision.
analysis.move_pattern: Diverse piece types and directions; no single geometric pattern — the commonality is choosing non-defensive moves (captures, advances, piece placements) when the player's king requires immediate protective action
analysis.why_bad: The moves fail because they neglect an urgent king-safety crisis — either allowing a forcing tactical sequence against the exposed king (back-rank mate, mating net, check sequences gaining material) or actively worsening the king's pawn shield, while the position demanded the one or two specific defensive moves that address the vulnerability.
sub_patterns: Material greed while back-rank mate threat exists
Weakening own king's pawn shield with a pawn advance
Self-blocking a piece's defensive retreat path
Capturing the wrong target while a critical attacker survives near exposed king
Placing a piece on an unstable square easily kicked with tempo

analysis.label: Premature f-pawn captures toward the center in the opening that fatally expose the uncastled king's diagonal to a queen check winning the rook.
analysis.description: The dominant pattern (7/11 positions) involves the f-pawn capturing on e4 or e5 in the opening while the king remains uncastled, stripping away the last pawn defender of the h4-e1 diagonal (for White) or h5-e8 diagonal (for Black). This allows a devastating queen check (Qh4+ or Qh5+) followed by a double attack winning the corner rook. Positions 1, 3, 7, 8 show White playing fxe5 and getting hit by Qh4+ g3 Qxe4+ Qe2 Qxh1; Positions 2 and 11 show Black playing fxe4/fxe5 and getting hit by Qh5+ g6 Qxe5+ Qe7 Qxh8. Position 4 shows a d-pawn capture (dxe4) that leaves a piece hanging. The remaining positions (5, 8/Na5, 10/Be7, 11/c6) share the broader pattern of wasting tempo or making non-urgent moves in the opening with an uncastled king, giving the opponent a decisive central breakthrough. All 11 positions feature uncastled kings (11/11) and nearly all involve pawn-structure-weakening moves that prioritize material gain or peripheral activity over king safety and development.
analysis.move_pattern: F-pawn capturing toward center (fxe5 or fxe4), or other tempo-losing moves, with king uncastled on original square
analysis.why_bad: Removing the f-pawn eliminates the only shield on the king's diagonal (h4-e1 or h5-e8), allowing a queen check that forks the king and corner rook, winning decisive material. More broadly, these moves prioritize material gain or peripheral activity over the urgent need to develop and castle.
sub_patterns: White fxe5 allowing Qh4+ g3 Qxe4+ Qxh1
Black fxe4/fxe5 allowing Qh5+ g6 Qxe5+ Qxh8
Pawn capture leaving piece undefended (dxe4 with Ng4 hanging)
Peripheral knight moves abandoning central control (Nh4, Na5)
Slow non-developing moves allowing central breakthrough (Be7, c6)

analysis.label: Ambitious central pawn advances or aggressive piece forays that are fatally mistimed due to incomplete development or positional unreadiness.
analysis.description: This feature fires on moves that represent thematic aggression executed at the wrong moment. In 5/7 positions, the blunder is a central pawn advance (e4, e5, e5, c4, d4) that opens the position when the player's king is uncastled (4/7 positions), pieces are undeveloped, or defensive obligations are unmet. The remaining 2/7 are piece moves to exposed forward squares (Ba4, Nb4) that lose critical tempo and abandon defensive duties. In every case, multiple patient alternatives existed (averaging 2.6 good moves) focused on development, consolidation, or king safety. The common thread is that each move appears natural or 'thematic' for the pawn structure but ignores concrete tactical consequences: undefended pieces become hanging (Position 7: Bxh4), key pawns lose defenders (Positions 2,3: d5 collapses after e6 vacates), exposed kings face diagonal attacks (Position 1: Qa5 on a5-e1), and pieces on forward squares get expelled with tempo (Positions 5,6: Ba4 chased by b5, Nb4 kicked by a3). The average cp_loss of 248 reflects how severely these 'one move too early' decisions are punished.
analysis.move_pattern: Forward pawn pushes (d4, e4, e5, c4) to the 4th/5th rank in the center, or piece advances (Ba4, Nb4) to exposed squares on the 4th rank
analysis.why_bad: The aggressive advance is mistimed because prerequisites aren't met (king uncastled, pieces undeveloped, defensive square abandoned), creating immediate tactical vulnerabilities that opponents exploit via tempo gains, hanging pieces, or open lines against the exposed king.
sub_patterns: Central pawn break with king uncastled (e4/e5/d4 in open center)
Piece move to exposed square losing tempo (Ba4/Nb4 easily kicked)
Structural pawn break abandoning key defender of another pawn (e5 removing e6 support of d5)
Aggressive move when concrete tactics demand immediate exploitation instead

analysis.label: Playing a non-defensive move (king walk, rook repositioning) while the player's own king faces an imminent mating attack requiring immediate attention.
analysis.description: In all 3/3 positions, the player's king is under acute kingside attack (h-file pressure, queen invasion threats, weak pawn shields), yet the move played either removes a critical defender from the king's vicinity (Rfe8 abandons f8 leaving f7/h8 undefended; Kf8 walks into forced checks), or invests a crucial tempo on an irrelevant plan (Rb1 pursues queenside play while kingside collapses). In every case, exactly 1 good move existed (avg good moves: 1.0) that addressed the defensive emergency directly—Bf7 to enable queen exchanges, Kf2 to evacuate the king preemptively, or f6 to challenge the attacking structure. The average cp_loss of 3778 reflects that these positions are on a knife's edge where one wasted tempo converts a defensible position into a lost or mated one. All 3/3 positions feature open or semi-open files aimed at the player's king with enemy heavy pieces poised to deliver checkmate.
analysis.move_pattern: Piece (king or rook) moves laterally away from own kingside, typically toward center or queenside (f8, e8, b1), vacating a defensive post or wasting the one available defensive tempo
analysis.why_bad: The king is under immediate mating threat and the position demands the single precise defensive move; instead, the player pursues a non-urgent plan or misidentifies the escape route, allowing the opponent's attack to crash through with checks, piece infiltration, or removal of key defenders.
sub_patterns: King walking into forced check sequences
Rook abandoning kingside leaving mating squares unguarded
Investing tempo on queenside plan while kingside attack breaks through

analysis.label: Playing a superficially aggressive or purposeful-looking move in a critical position where only one specific forcing continuation (usually a concrete capture or check) maintains the evaluation.
analysis.description: This feature fires on positions with extremely narrow best play (avg 1.2 good moves) where the player chooses a plausible-looking active move but misses the one critical forcing continuation. In 8/10 positions, the best move was a specific capture or check that addressed the position's tactical demands (Qxe6+, Bxg6, Qxd5, Bxh6, Qc6+, Nxd6+, g4 attacking a piece, Qb3 attacking a piece), while the played move pursued a different agenda—typically an aggressive-looking idea directed at the wrong target. The played moves look purposeful to a casual observer (Ng6 threatens a fork, Qh6 threatens mating squares, a7 advances a passed pawn, Na3+ gives check, Qg4 targets g7), but each fatally ignores the position's actual critical element. The average centipawn loss of 1269 reflects that these are decisive moments where the single correct move often involves a non-obvious tactical shot (sacrifice, exchange, or precise capture) that solves multiple positional problems simultaneously.
analysis.move_pattern: Various piece types moving to aggressive-looking or active squares, often forward/toward the opponent's king, when the required move is a specific capture, check, or forcing move directed elsewhere
analysis.why_bad: The moves ignore the position's one critical tactical demand—typically a specific forcing continuation (capture with check, key exchange, or precise threat to a vulnerable piece)—in favor of a superficially attractive but non-forcing idea that gives the opponent time to exploit the actual tactical vulnerability in the position
sub_patterns: Queen moving to aggressive kingside squares (Qh6, Qg4) when it should be making a specific tactical capture or targeting a concrete weakness
Giving check or making a capture on the wrong target (Na3+, Qxb4) when a different check/capture solves the position
Non-forcing pawn pushes or piece retreats (a7, Bh8, f3) when a concrete tactical blow is required
Piece moving to an attacking-looking square that abandons a critical defensive or tactical function (Ng6 leaving f4, Qh6 leaving h3)

analysis.label: Quiet, seemingly purposeful moves made from winning positions that create immediate tactical vulnerabilities the opponent can exploit.
analysis.description: This feature fires on positions where a player holds a significant advantage (avg eval ~300cp in their favor) but plays a non-forcing, cosmetically reasonable move that creates a concrete tactical weakness. In 4/4 cases, the player had multiple strong alternatives (avg 2.5 good moves) but instead chose a move that looked logical yet enabled a specific tactical punishment. Position 1: Nf5 places a knight on an undefended square capturable by Bxf5. Position 2: f5 weakens the e6 square enabling a devastating Ng5-Ne6 fork. Position 3: Ke8 places the king on the h5-e8 diagonal enabling Qh5+/Bxg6+ sacrifice. Position 4: Qe2 wastes a critical tempo and blocks Rhe1, allowing f4 counterplay. All moves share the pattern of appearing purposeful (aggressive outpost, space-gaining push, safety retreat, queen repositioning) while actually creating specific exploitable weaknesses.
analysis.move_pattern: Quiet non-forcing moves (no check, no capture, no direct threat) - piece repositioning, pawn advances, or retreats that inadvertently weaken a specific square, diagonal, or piece coordination
analysis.why_bad: Each move ignores the concrete tactical demands of the position while creating a specific new vulnerability - an undefended piece, a weakened square enabling forks, a king walking into a dangerous diagonal, or a tempo loss allowing opponent counterplay. The player 'relaxes' when precise action was required to maintain the advantage.
sub_patterns: Piece moved to undefended square enabling simple capture
Pawn advance weakening key defensive square enabling knight outpost/fork
King retreat to worse diagonal enabling sacrifice combination
Queen repositioning that blocks own rook activation and loses critical tempo

analysis.label: Moves that look aggressive or active but abandon critical positional duties, resulting in significant tempo loss when the opponent exploits the vacated function.
analysis.description: This feature fires on moves where a player chooses a superficially attractive or aggressive-looking continuation while ignoring the actual strategic/tactical demand of the position. In 8/11 positions, the blunder involves moving a piece away from a critical central or defensive function toward the flank or an exposed square: Ng3 and Nf4 abandon dominant central knight posts (e4, e6); both Rc1 moves abandon the critical d-file for a slower c-file plan; Qg5 and Qb5 place the queen on exposed flank squares where it gets attacked with tempo; Bh6 voluntarily moves to an edge square for a trade that loses development; Kg6 moves toward the flank instead of centralizing in a tempo-critical endgame; g5 pushes a flank pawn while ignoring urgent central tension. In 9/11 cases the analyses explicitly tag 'tempo_loss' as a key factor. The common refutation pattern involves the opponent exploiting the vacated square/function (Nd5 exploiting the abandoned d-file in 2/11, Nc3+ exploiting the discovered check in 1/11, Nd7 fork after knight leaves defensive post in 1/11) or gaining tempo attacking the misplaced piece (Qe1 hitting the queen after Ng3 in 1/11, Nb4 hitting the exposed queen in 1/11). The average cp_loss of 301 reflects that these are positions where the actual priority was narrow (avg 1.6 good moves), making the misdirected move especially costly.
analysis.move_pattern: Piece moves away from center or key defensive square toward flank/edge, often to g3/g5/h6/f4/b5 squares; includes lateral rook moves abandoning critical open files and king/pawn moves toward the wing
analysis.why_bad: The move abandons a critical function (file control, defensive coverage, central dominance, tempo in a race) for an objective that either doesn't exist, is easily parried, or is far less important than what was given up, allowing the opponent to exploit the vacated duty with tactical or positional gains.
sub_patterns: Knight abandons dominant central outpost (e4/e6) for flank square (g3/f4) creating fork or losing initiative
Rook leaves critical open file for adjacent closed/semi-open file, allowing opponent piece centralization
Queen moves to exposed flank square where it gets attacked with tempo or traded unfavorably
Piece/king moves toward wing when central action or king race demands direct approach
Reactive capture/trade when dynamic counterattack was required

analysis.label: Playing a passive, non-forcing preparatory move in a position that demands immediate concrete action to address a hanging pawn, development crisis, or tactical vulnerability.
analysis.description: This feature fires on positions where a player chooses a slow, quiet move (typically a preparatory pawn push or modest piece development) when the position has a specific urgent concrete need. In 3/9 positions (1-3), the identical error occurs: developing a piece (Nge7, Be6, Bf5) instead of playing g5 to support a hanging f4-pawn that is immediately capturable. In 5/9 positions (4, 5, 6, 8, 9), passive pawn moves (f6, b6, g6, b6, h6) are played when immediate piece development or castling is critical to survive a tactical threat (passed pawn advance, central break, piece attack). In 1/9 (position 7), a slow piece rerouting (N1d2) leaves a piece tactically undefended. All 9 positions share the pattern that the opponent has ONE specific punishing response that the tempo loss enables—whether capturing a hanging pawn (6/9), advancing a passed pawn, or executing a central break. The average cp_loss of 238 reflects how these single wasted tempi transform the position from defensible to losing.
analysis.move_pattern: Non-capturing, non-checking quiet moves—predominantly rim/flank pawn advances (h6, g6, b6, f6) or piece moves to modest squares (Nge7, Be6, Bf5, N1d2)—that do not address the position's most pressing tactical or structural need.
analysis.why_bad: Each position contains a specific time-critical vulnerability (an undefended pawn, an exposed king on an open file, or an impending decisive pawn advance) that demands immediate concrete action. The slow move wastes the one tempo needed to neutralize the threat, allowing the opponent to execute their plan (capture the hanging pawn, push d6 winning material, break with e5, or win a piece via tactical exploitation).
sub_patterns: Developing a piece instead of supporting a hanging advanced pawn with another pawn (g5 needed to protect f4)
Playing a preparatory queenside pawn push (b6) when kingside development and castling are desperately urgent
Making a prophylactic rim pawn move (h6, g6, f6) when central tension demands immediate resolution or piece activity

analysis.label: Playing a slow or misdirected move that abandons a critical defensive/offensive duty, giving the opponent time to advance passed pawns or execute tactical threats.
analysis.description: This feature fires on moves that waste a crucial tempo by abandoning a piece's essential role (usually restraining or attacking a passed pawn) or ignoring an urgent positional/tactical demand. In 5/7 positions, a rook is moved to a square that looks superficially active but leaves a critical target unaddressed (Ra8 abandons c-file support, Rab8 frees the a5 passer, Rg8 misses the d5 pawn, Rd3 abandons d6 pawn support, Rc3 'attacks' a knight that happily relocates to a dominant outpost). In 2/7 positions, a slow pawn move (b3, a4) is played when the position demands immediate tactical action. The common thread across all 7 positions is that exactly one tempo is critical—the opponent's passed pawn is one move from becoming unstoppable, or a tactical threat needs immediate attention—and the played move does nothing to address this urgency. Average cp_loss of 1573 reflects that these tempo losses are catastrophic precisely because the positions are at tipping points.
analysis.move_pattern: Rook relocation to a non-critical file/rank or slow pawn push, typically moving away from the square where the piece was performing a restraining or attacking function
analysis.why_bad: The move abandons restraint of an opponent's passed pawn or ignores the position's single most urgent demand (a tactical threat, a vulnerable target, or a time-critical attack), giving the opponent exactly the one tempo needed to cross a decisive threshold.
sub_patterns: Rook abandons restraint of opponent's passed pawn (Ra8, Rab8, Rd3)
Rook targets wrong piece/file instead of the critical pawn weakness (Rg8, Rc3)
Slow prophylactic pawn move when immediate tactical action is required (b3, a4)

analysis.label: Moves that pursue a plausible secondary objective while ignoring the position's most urgent tactical or strategic demand, typically directing a piece toward the wrong target or side of the board.
analysis.description: This feature identifies moves where a piece is deployed toward a logical-looking but ultimately peripheral target while the critical need of the position goes unaddressed. In 7/9 positions, the played move targets a secondary concern (pressuring a pawn, attacking a file, grabbing material) while the best moves address an immediate tactical vulnerability or maintain critical piece coordination. For example, Rc1 attacks the c-file while the g3 knight hangs to ...Bh4; Qc4 eyes queenside targets while exf2+ delivers check; Qa5 seeks queenside counterplay while abandoning the crucial f3 rook; Ba4 maintains queenside pressure while the attack demands Bd3; Qxh3 grabs a pawn while breaking the decisive queen-rook coordination. In 8/9 positions, the analyses tag 'tempo_loss' as a key factor, confirming that these moves waste a critical tempo at a moment of maximum urgency. The average cp_loss of 249 reflects that these mistakes occur at critical decision points where the position's true demand is specific and the misdirection proves costly.
analysis.move_pattern: Various piece types (Q, R, B, K) moving toward a secondary target—often toward the queenside, a peripheral pawn, or a less critical file—rather than toward the board sector where the primary threat or opportunity exists.
analysis.why_bad: The position has one urgent demand (defending a tactical threat, maintaining piece coordination on the critical file, or exploiting a time-sensitive weakness), and the played move wastes the critical tempo addressing a secondary concern, allowing the opponent to execute their key tactical or positional plan unopposed.
sub_patterns: Queen/rook moves to wrong file (Rc1 to c-file, Rad8 to d-file, Qa5 to a-file) when e/f-file is critical
Bishop placed on exposed square vulnerable to tempo-gaining pawn attacks (Bf4 to ...g5, Ba4 to ...a5/b5)
Queen abandons coordination post to grab peripheral material (Qxh3, Qa5)
Piece develops toward a logical but non-urgent target while ignoring an immediate tactical threat (Qc4 ignoring exf2+, Rc1 ignoring Bh4)
King/piece moves toward wrong sector in endgame (Ke3 toward center instead of bishop reroute to blockade)

analysis.label: Playing a routine piece or pawn move in a position where only one specific urgent action (usually a king move or simple capture) addresses the existential threat.
analysis.description: This feature activates on positions where the player makes a 'natural-looking' improving move while completely missing the one critical action the position demands. In 4/7 positions, the best move was a king move (Kd8 evacuating an open file, Kg3 approaching a promotion square, Ke5 blockading a passed pawn, Kxf7 eliminating a promotion threat) but the player instead moved a piece (Rf8, Re2, Bxf5, Ng3). In 2/7 positions, an undefended piece was hanging and capturable (Bxc6, Bxg8) but the player made a positional pawn move instead (d5, cxb5). In 1/7, a forced mate required a specific blocking move (Nf3) but the player played a rook move (Rc3). The average cp_loss of 2923 and average of only 1.3 good moves confirms these are razor-sharp positions with essentially one correct response that the player ignores in favor of something superficially reasonable.
analysis.move_pattern: Mixed piece types (rooks, knights, pawns, bishops) making developing/capturing/repositioning moves; no specific geometric direction, but consistently choosing a secondary piece action over the uniquely correct move
analysis.why_bad: The played move addresses a secondary concern (piece activity, material gain, general improvement) while ignoring the one existential priority in the position—typically the king needing to personally address a threat (evacuation, pawn capture, blockade) or a free capture that must be taken immediately before the opportunity vanishes
sub_patterns: King must evacuate/approach but player moves a rook instead (Rf8, Re2)
King must capture a pawn to eliminate promotion threat but player attacks elsewhere (Bxf5, Ng3)
Hanging piece is available but player makes a positional pawn move (d5, cxb5)
Forced mate requires specific restraining move but player plays a general activating move (Rc3)

analysis.label: Playing a non-urgent move in a pawn endgame where a single time-critical pawn advance was required to lock the structure or execute a breakthrough.
analysis.description: This feature activates on positions—overwhelmingly pure king-and-pawn endgames (7/9)—where exactly one precise pawn advance was needed to either lock the opponent's pawn structure (preventing a breakthrough) or execute a decisive breakthrough, but the player instead made a different, seemingly reasonable move that lost the critical tempo. In 6/9 positions, the correct move was a specific pawn advance (b5, h5, g4, h4, c5+/g5, g5) that the player missed in favor of a wrong pawn push (a4, g6, g3, h4, c4) or an unnecessary king move (Kd7, Kc3). The average good moves available was only 1.6, confirming these are razor-sharp positions with essentially one correct choice. The common punishment is that the opponent then gets to play their own critical pawn move first—either locking White's breakthrough (e.g., ...f6 preventing g5) or activating their own majority (e.g., ...c5, ...h5-h4). Tags like 'tempo_loss' appear in 8/9 analyses.
analysis.move_pattern: Any move type (pawn advance, king move, or piece move) that is NOT the one urgent pawn advance needed; often a different pawn pushed one square or a king repositioning
analysis.why_bad: In critical pawn endgame positions, the opponent has a single-tempo window to neutralize or execute a pawn structure fix; the played move wastes that tempo, allowing the opponent to play their critical pawn move first, permanently altering the structure in their favor
sub_patterns: Wrong pawn advanced instead of the critical one (a4/g6/h4/c4 instead of b5/h5/c5+/b4)
Pawn advanced one square instead of two (g3 instead of g4)
King moved when a pawn advance was urgently required (Kd7/Kc3 instead of h4/g5)

analysis.label: Natural-looking moves that miss the single critical tactical requirement in positions where very few moves work.
analysis.description: This feature fires on positions where the player chooses a reasonable-seeming move—development, piece improvement, attacking a secondary target, or generic defense—while the position demands one specific precise action. In 7/9 cases, only 1-2 moves were acceptable (avg good moves: 1.6), making these razor-thin tactical moments. The played moves address plausible but non-critical concerns: chasing a knight with c3 instead of capturing an undefended bishop (Position 1), doubling rooks with Rde1 instead of securing a hanging bishop (Position 4), developing with Bd2 instead of the only equalizing Bf4 (Position 9), repositioning the queen to f7 instead of preventing Nf5 (Position 8), and moving the king (Kd6) instead of maintaining a critical blockade (Position 3). In 6/9 cases, the correct move was counter-intuitive or less 'natural' than the played one (Na8 retreat, g5 prophylaxis, Bf4 with hidden tactical point, Nc5 patience over Qa3 aggression).
analysis.move_pattern: Non-forcing piece moves (quiet development, repositioning, pawn pushes) in positions demanding immediate forcing or precise tactical action; no consistent piece type or direction
analysis.why_bad: Each move addresses a secondary positional or tactical concern while ignoring the ONE critical requirement of the position—whether that's capturing a hanging piece, preventing a specific tactical blow, maintaining a blockade, or executing a precise forcing sequence. The position collapses because the wasted tempo allows the opponent's primary threat to execute.
sub_patterns: Positional move ignoring tactical urgency (c3, Bd2, Kd6)
Piece placement walking into tactical vulnerability (Rd7 discovered attack, Rf6 deflection)
Premature/wrong attacking move when patience needed (Qa3, Qc7+)
Abandoning defensive duty for repositioning (Qf7 leaving h6 undefended)
Removing tactical resource for generic improvement (Rde1 unguarding bishop)

analysis.label: Moves that directly create or expose the specific vulnerability the opponent immediately exploits for a decisive tactical response.
analysis.description: This feature fires on catastrophic blunders where the played move itself directly enables the opponent's winning tactical response. In 2/6 cases, checks (Qc4+, Rf3+) are given on squares where the opponent can interpose a piece, forcing a simplifying trade that kills the attacker's position. In 1/6 cases (b6), a pawn self-blocks the king's escape route, enabling a mating attack. In 1/6 cases (Ke5), the king walks directly into a mating net. In 1/6 cases (Ba4), a piece abandons a critical defensive duty (guarding e6), allowing immediate material gain. In 1/6 cases (Ne2), passive development fails to address a critical vulnerability (f2), enabling a tactical strike. The positions share extremely narrow margins (avg 1.7 good moves) and catastrophic punishment (avg 5061 cp_loss), indicating critical decision points where the played move is the precise trigger for the opponent's refutation.
analysis.move_pattern: Various piece types moving to squares that specifically enable an opponent interposition, capture of undefended material, simplifying trade, or mating pattern - often checks or piece repositions that create the very vulnerability exploited
analysis.why_bad: Each move directly creates or exposes the specific tactical vulnerability that the opponent exploits: checks allow winning interpositions/trades, piece moves abandon critical defensive duties, king moves enter mating nets, and pawn moves self-block escape routes
sub_patterns: Checks that allow opponent to interpose with a winning trade/simplification (Qc4+, Rf3+)
Piece moves that abandon defense of a critical pawn or square (Ba4 leaving e6 undefended)
King or pawn moves that create self-inflicted mating vulnerabilities (Ke5 into f4#, b6 blocking escape)

analysis.label: Playing a structurally-committing pawn move (push or capture) that opens lines or squares for the opponent when the position demands a piece move for development, activation, or safety.
analysis.description: In 7/8 positions, the blunder is a pawn move (push or capture) that changes the pawn structure when the best moves are piece moves addressing urgent tactical or developmental needs. The played moves include space-gaining pushes (c5, g5, d5, e5) and materialistic captures (dxc3, exf5, dxe5), all appearing 'logical' but fatally premature. In every case, the top alternatives are piece moves: Rhe8/Qe5/Qe7 in position 1, Nc5 in positions 2 and 4, Qd3/Bc2 in position 5, Kg2/Rg1 in position 6, Ngf3/Bb2 in position 7, and Bc5/Qh4 in position 8. The pawn moves consistently open files against the player's own king (dxe5 opening the f-file, 6/8), create outpost squares for opponent pieces (exf5 granting Nf5, 5/8), expose hanging pieces on newly-opened lines (d5 exposing Ra1, dxc3 exposing Bd6, 4/8), or weaken pawn structure without compensation (g5, e5). The average cp_loss of 287 reflects that these are serious blunders with multiple good alternatives available (avg 2.8), suggesting the player defaulted to a 'natural-looking' pawn move rather than calculating concrete piece requirements.
analysis.move_pattern: Pawn push or pawn capture (mostly central d/e/c pawns) that alters the structure, typically forward or exchanging toward the center
analysis.why_bad: The pawn move removes a critical structural element (blocking pawn, defended square, closed file) that was restraining the opponent's pieces, instantly granting the opponent open lines, outpost squares, or tactical targets - while the player's pieces remain uncoordinated and unable to exploit the changed structure.
sub_patterns: Pawn capture that opens a file directly against own exposed/uncastled king (dxe5, dxc3)
Pawn capture that vacates a square becoming a dominant outpost for opponent's piece (exf5 → Nf5)
Pawn push that opens a diagonal exposing an undefended piece (d5 → Bxa1)
Prophylactic/space-gaining pawn push that weakens squares and allows opponent to consolidate (g5 → h6 wedge, e5 → f4 target, c5 → ignoring queen trap)

analysis.label: Moves that superficially attack or chase an opponent's piece (usually the queen) but backfire by creating a worse weakness, abandoning a critical defensive function, or missing a stronger tactical continuation.
analysis.description: This feature fires on moves that prioritize attacking or displacing an opponent's piece—most often the queen—over addressing the position's true demands. In 8/10 positions, the blunder directly attacks or chases the opponent's queen (c4 attacks queen on d5, Bg4 attacks queen on f3, a3 chases queen from b4, h6 chases queen from g5, Rfd1 pressures queen on d4, Re1 challenges queen on e5, Rh4 chases queen on h5, Ng4 attacks queen on e3). The remaining moves (Rxe6 captures with wrong piece, Be6 retreats passively) share the pattern of choosing a superficially logical but strategically misguided move over the position's true requirement. In every case, the opponent's piece (queen) either moves to a superior square (a3→Qd4, Re1→Qd4+), or the attacking move creates a vulnerability worse than what it gains (c4 unguards d3, h6 enables Rxh6 sacrifice, Rfd1/Re1 abandon kingside defense, Rh4 leaves g5 hanging). The average cp_loss of 243 and only 1.6 good moves available indicates these are critical positions where the natural-looking 'attack something' instinct leads to disaster.
analysis.move_pattern: Various piece types moving toward an opponent's piece (especially the queen) in an attacking gesture—pawn pushes toward queen's square, rook/bishop/knight moves targeting queen's position, or captures directed at the opponent's camp.
analysis.why_bad: The move prioritizes a superficial tempo gain or piece attack while ignoring the position's critical requirement—whether that's maintaining a defensive piece on its post (Re1, Rfd1, Rh4), preserving pawn structure integrity (c4, h6, a3), executing a stronger concrete tactic (Ng4 vs Nxe4, Rxe6 vs Nxe6), or developing toward safety (Bg4 vs castling). The opponent's queen happily relocates to a superior square or the created weakness proves more damaging than the tempo gained.
sub_patterns: Pawn push chasing queen weakens key defensive pawn (c4→d3, a3→d4 access, h6→sacrifice target)
Rook move to attack queen abandons critical defensive post (Re1 leaves f2, Rfd1 leaves kingside, Rh4 leaves center)
Minor piece attack on queen misses stronger concrete tactic (Ng4 vs Nxe4, Bg4 vs development/castling)
Wrong piece captures when the alternative creates unstoppable secondary threats (Rxe6 vs Nxe6 fork)

analysis.label: Non-forcing, routine-looking moves played in positions with critical tactical demands, catastrophically missing either a winning/saving resource or allowing a devastating opponent combination.
analysis.description: This feature fires on moves where the player makes a seemingly reasonable positional or materialistic choice—a pawn push (f6, a4), a quiet development (Bf3), a greedy capture (Qxa2), a queen repositioning (Qb4, Qc7, Qd6), or a passive rook move (Ra6)—while completely missing that the position contains a critical tactical element requiring immediate attention. In 9/10 positions, king safety is the central issue: either the move creates a fatal king weakness enabling a sacrifice (f6 moves in positions 1-2 enabling Bxh7+ Greek Gifts; Qc7 enabling Bxf7+; Qd6 enabling Nh5 with fork), or the move ignores the player's own king danger (a4 missing the only defense against mate; Ra6 missing the only perpetual check drawing resource). In 9/10 positions, a concrete tactic is missed—either by the moving side (Nd6# mate-in-one, Bb5 deflection, Rxb2+ perpetual) or the opponent's impending combination goes unaddressed. The average cp_loss of 2153 reflects that these are catastrophic positional collapses, with the common thread being that tempo is absolutely critical and the player burns it on a move that addresses nothing urgent.
analysis.move_pattern: Various piece types and directions—no single geometric pattern; typically non-forcing moves (no check, no immediate threat) including quiet pawn pushes, passive piece retreats, greedy captures away from the action, or slow development
analysis.why_bad: These moves squander a critical tempo in positions where tactical urgency demands immediate action—either exploiting a forced win/draw or addressing an opponent's impending combination, typically a king-targeted sacrifice (Bxh7+, Bxf7+, Nh5 forks) or a mating threat
sub_patterns: f6 pawn advance weakening kingside enabling Greek Gift Bxh7+ sacrifice
Queen retreat/repositioning abandoning control of critical defensive squares
Greedy pawn capture with queen ignoring development and king exposure
Irrelevant pawn push ignoring immediate mating threats requiring precise defense
Slow positional move missing a forcing tactical shot (mate, deflection, perpetual)

analysis.label: Playing a quiet, non-forcing positional or repositioning move when the position demands immediate concrete action, most often capturing undefended material.
analysis.description: This feature fires on positions where players choose slow, preparatory moves (pawn pushes, piece repositionings, prophylactic maneuvers) while ignoring urgent tactical requirements. In 4/8 positions, the best move was a direct capture of hanging material (Qxg5, Qxg4, Bxb5, Bxh6) that the player bypassed for a quiet alternative (b3, Nb3, g5, Bh8). In the remaining cases, the best moves were concrete tactical operations (Qb4 winning the exchange, gxf4 resolving tension, f3 sealing kingside, Be6 controlling a critical square) that were similarly ignored in favor of slow, non-forcing moves. The average cp_loss of 310 and only 1.5 good moves available per position confirm these are critical moments where one specific concrete action is demanded, but the player defaults to a 'developing' or 'improving' move that gives the opponent a crucial tempo to strike first or consolidate.
analysis.move_pattern: Quiet non-capturing, non-checking moves (pawn advances, piece retreats, knight repositions, bishop developments) that carry no immediate threat
analysis.why_bad: These moves waste a critical tempo in positions where concrete action (usually a capture of free material or an urgent tactical strike) is required NOW; the opponent exploits the lost tempo to launch attacks, infiltrate with pieces, or advance dangerous pawns that were previously containable
sub_patterns: Quiet pawn advance ignoring hanging enemy pawn (g5, b3, f6)
Piece repositioning to passive square instead of capturing (Bh8, Nb3, Bd7)
King march toward peripheral goal ignoring critical prophylaxis (Kb3)
Knight development to rim abandoning defensive duties (Nh6)

analysis.label: Materialistic captures (usually with check) that look forcing but miss a much stronger continuation, often checkmate.
analysis.description: In 5/5 positions, the player makes a capture of a piece, and in 4/5 cases the capture gives check, making it feel forcing and strong. However, in 3/5 cases (positions 2, 4, 5), the capture misses an immediate checkmate in 1-2 moves (Qh8#, Qxf2+/Qxg2#, Qe8#). In the remaining 2/5 cases (positions 1, 3), the capture prematurely trades away a dominant piece that was enabling a stronger tactical idea (a pin winning the exchange, or simply maintaining crushing pressure). The common thread is that the player is seduced by the most 'obvious' forcing move—capturing material, especially with check—rather than looking for the geometrically precise move that delivers a decisive blow. The average cp_loss of 5646 reflects that these positions overwhelmingly featured missed mates converted into merely winning positions.
analysis.move_pattern: Piece captures another piece (bishop takes knight, queen takes rook/bishop, rook takes rook), usually with check, targeting material rather than the optimal square
analysis.why_bad: The capture removes a key attacking piece from the board or redirects it to the wrong square, abandoning a mating net or dominant positional configuration in exchange for mere material gain. The 'check' aspect creates tunnel vision, making the move feel like it must be best.
sub_patterns: Capture with check misses back-rank mate in 1
Trading dominant piece relieves opponent's defensive bind
Removing the piece that enables a mating combination

analysis.label: Playing a natural-looking move that wastes a decisive tempo by prioritizing the wrong piece or square in time-sensitive positions.
analysis.description: This feature fires on moves that represent tempo losses in positions where move order is critical. In 5/7 positions, the player advanced a pawn or moved a secondary piece when the king or primary piece needed immediate repositioning (c5 instead of Kd6, a5 instead of Nd7, g5 instead of Kg4, Rhe8 instead of Qxd5). In 2/7 positions, the correct piece was chosen but sent to the wrong square (Kf6 instead of Ke6, Kg3 instead of Kh1). In 1/7, the wrong piece captured on the same square (Qxc6+ instead of Rxc6+). All 7 positions share the 'tempo_loss' tag in their analyses. The played moves are typically part of the eventual plan but executed one move too early or represent 'general improvement' moves that ignore the position's specific tactical demand, costing anywhere from 4cp to 9215cp depending on the sharpness of the position.
analysis.move_pattern: Pawn advances or secondary piece moves to reasonable-looking squares when a different piece (usually king or queen) requires immediate priority repositioning; or king/queen moves to a nearby-but-suboptimal square
analysis.why_bad: These moves waste a critical tempo in positions where the sequence of actions matters enormously - typically in pawn races, mating attacks, or positions with imminent tactical threats. By addressing a secondary concern first, the opponent gains time to advance counter-threats, escape mating nets, or exploit newly-created vulnerabilities.
sub_patterns: Pawn advance before king optimization (c5, g5, a5)
King to wrong adjacent square (Kf6→should be Ke6, Kg3→should be Kh1)
Wrong capturing piece displacing key attacker (Qxc6+ vs Rxc6+)
General rook development ignoring urgent queen safety (Rhe8)

analysis.label: Playing a natural-looking move when a bishop-delivered tactic (pin, diagonal attack) would have won the opponent's queen.
analysis.description: In 7/9 positions, the missed best move specifically involves a bishop delivering a decisive blow that wins the opponent's queen—via absolute pins along diagonals (Bb5 pinning queen to king, Bg5 pinning queen to king, Bd5 pinning queen to king), direct attacks (Be3 attacking queen then winning via Bxf2+, Bb4 attacking exposed queen, Be6 attacking queen), or tactical combinations (Bf4 enabling a queen-winning sequence). Instead, players chose routine-looking alternatives: captures (exd5, Bxc5, Nxf3), centralizations (Nd5, Ne6, Re4, Qf5), invasions (Re2), or generic development (Bf6). The common thread is that a bishop sat ready to exploit a diagonal toward the opponent's queen, but the player was drawn to a 'natural' or 'obvious' move that squandered this geometric relationship. Average cp_loss of 358 reflects these are devastating oversights in positions with very few good alternatives (avg 1.4 good moves).
analysis.move_pattern: Various piece types (captures, centralizations, developments) played INSTEAD of a bishop move exploiting a diagonal pin/attack on the opposing queen
analysis.why_bad: These moves ignore a concrete forcing bishop tactic (pin or diagonal attack) that would win the opponent's queen; by playing something natural-looking but non-forcing, the opponent escapes the deadly diagonal geometry and the queen-winning opportunity vanishes permanently.
sub_patterns: Pawn capture instead of bishop pin (exd5 vs Bb5)
Knight centralization instead of bishop diagonal attack (Ne6/Nd5 vs Be6/Rf7)
Knight capture removing the piece that enabled the pin (Nxf3 vs Bg5)
Rook move instead of bishop combination (Re2/Re4 vs Be3/Rxf8+Bd5)
Queen relocation away from enabling square (Qf5 vs Bf4 combination)

analysis.label: Moving a piece to an unprotected central/kingside square for illusory aggression while ignoring the position's concrete demands.
analysis.description: In all 3/3 positions, the player moves a piece to an exposed square in the e-g file, rank 4-5 area (Ke5, Rg4, Qg5), motivated by vague notions of 'activity' or kingside pressure rather than addressing the position's concrete requirements. In each case, the piece lands on a square where it can be immediately exploited—via fork (Ne5 hitting Rg4 and Qf3), queen trade (Qc1 forcing the misplaced Qg5 off), or pawn advance/tempo attack (Ra4 exploiting Ke5's exposure). All 3/3 positions had specific concrete demands (Rh2 attacking f2, dxc6 trading material, Nc8 challenging a dominant knight) that were ignored in favor of speculative piece placement. The common refutation pattern involves the opponent punishing the exposed piece's position through tactical exploitation or forced simplification that renders the piece's 'activity' meaningless.
analysis.move_pattern: Any piece moving to an unprotected square on files e-g, ranks 4-5, without creating a concrete threat
analysis.why_bad: The piece lands on a tactically vulnerable exposed square where it can be forked, captured, forced to trade unfavorably, or driven back with tempo—meanwhile the position's real concrete demands (material exchanges, challenging key pieces, attacking specific weaknesses) go unaddressed.
sub_patterns: King centralizing to exposed square ignoring rook activity
Rook lunging to undefended attacking square creating fork targets
Queen deployed to aggressive square with no real threats, inviting favorable trades

analysis.label: Moves that place the king (or ignore the threat of placement) on a line where an enemy piece screened by another can deliver a devastating discovered check.
analysis.description: In 10/11 positions, the move enables a discovered attack/check by placing the king on a diagonal or file where an enemy long-range piece (bishop or queen) is blocked by an intervening piece (typically a rook or knight). When that screening piece moves—often capturing material simultaneously—it unmasks the check, winning significant material or delivering checkmate. The king moves (7/11 are literal king moves: Kg2, Kg7, Kg6, Kf1, Kc8, Kf7, Kg8) walk directly onto the fatal alignment. The non-king moves (h6, Rc1, Nf5, Rd1) either waste tempo ignoring an existing discovered check threat or remove a critical defender. In nearly every case, the best alternative involved moving the king to a square OFF the dangerous diagonal (e.g., Kh1 instead of Kg2/Kf1, Ke8 instead of Kg8/Kf7/Kc8, Ke6 instead of Kg6). The average cp_loss of 1305 reflects the catastrophic nature of enabling discovered checks, which typically win queen-for-nothing or deliver checkmate.
analysis.move_pattern: King moves (predominantly) stepping onto a diagonal or file controlled by a screened long-range piece; occasionally non-king moves that ignore the latent discovery or remove defenders
analysis.why_bad: The move places the king on a line where an enemy bishop or queen is blocked by a movable piece (rook/knight), enabling a discovered check that simultaneously captures material or creates a double attack, winning decisive material with tempo
sub_patterns: King walks onto bishop diagonal blocked by rook (Kg6, Kf1, Kf7, Kg2, Kc8)
King moves to square where capture comes with check costing critical tempo (Kg7, Kg8)
Tempo-wasting move ignoring existing discovered check geometry (h6, Rc1, Nf5)
Removing back-rank defender enabling mate (Rd1)

analysis.chip: Aimless Tempo Loss in Won Positions
analysis.label: Non-forcing moves in winning endgame positions that waste tempo instead of executing the most efficient winning technique.
analysis.description: This feature activates on moves that represent tempo losses in overwhelmingly won positions, typically endgames. In 7/8 positions, the game is in the endgame phase with a decisive advantage for the moving side (or forced mate). The moves share a common pattern: they are quiet, non-forcing moves (no checks, captures, or immediate threats) that fail to execute the most direct winning plan. In 6/8 cases, the analyses explicitly tag 'tempo_loss' as the tactical motif. The moves allow the defending side to gain freedom - whether escaping toward open space in KR vs K endgames (positions 2, 3, 8), avoiding promotion threats (positions 1, 5), or exploiting the moved piece's placement for counterplay (position 4 where Kf4 allowed Ne2+ with tempo). The positions typically had very few good alternatives (avg 2.2), meaning precision was required even in won positions.
analysis.move_pattern: Quiet non-forcing moves (predominantly king moves - 5/8 are king moves), no checks or captures, often sideways or backward, in positions where forcing continuations (checks, clearance moves, rank/file cut-offs) were available
analysis.why_bad: These moves squander tempo in positions demanding immediate execution of a winning plan - they allow the opponent to reposition their king, escape restrictive cut-offs, or gain defensive resources through tempo-gaining replies (checks, counterattacks), prolonging or even compromising the win
sub_patterns: King moves in elementary checkmate endgames (KR vs K, KQ vs K) that fail to restrict the opposing king
Quiet king retreats or advances that walk into defensive tempo-gaining checks or forks
Pawn pushes or piece repositioning that delay execution of an imminent promotion plan
Queen/rook moves that abandon optimal cut-off positions or delay forcing continuations

analysis.label: Quiet piece moves to suboptimal squares that squander a critical tempo when the position demands urgent active play or addressing immediate threats.
analysis.description: This feature fires on positions where a player makes a seemingly reasonable but tempo-wasting piece move—typically a minor piece retreat, repositioning, or misdirected placement—instead of addressing the position's most urgent tactical or strategic demand. In 8/11 cases, the move involves a bishop or knight going to a passive square (Bc8, Bd8, Nd2, Nbd2, Ra8) or a tactically irrelevant one (Nc5, Bc4, Bd6) when active alternatives were clearly available. In 2/11 cases, a king steps to an exposed square (Kg6, Kg7) when piece activity was needed instead. The best moves in every case prioritize either active centralization (Nd4, Nc3, Bc5 appear repeatedly as correct alternatives), urgent development, or directly confronting the opponent's threats. The common thread is that the played moves look 'natural' or 'safe' but actually waste the one tempo the player couldn't afford to lose—allowing the opponent to seize initiative through tactical strikes, pawn advances, or piece activation that the passive move fails to prevent.
analysis.move_pattern: Minor piece (bishop/knight) or king moving to a passive, back-rank, or strategically irrelevant square; non-forcing quiet repositioning moves
analysis.why_bad: The position demands immediate active play (development, counterattack, addressing a specific threat) but the player wastes a tempo on a quiet piece move that doesn't address the critical need, giving the opponent time to execute decisive tactical or positional plans
sub_patterns: Bishop retreating to back rank (Bc8, Bd8) instead of active development
Knight placed on d2 instead of more active c3 (Nd2, Nbd2 vs Nc3)
King stepping to exposed square instead of generating piece activity (Kg6, Kg7)
Piece placed on seemingly active but strategically wrong square ignoring defense (Bc4, Nc5, Bd6)

analysis.label: Playing a natural-looking, non-forcing piece repositioning move that wastes a critical tempo when the position demands immediate concrete action.
analysis.description: This feature fires on positions where a player makes a quiet 'improving' move—typically centralizing a piece or repositioning to an apparently active square—when the position urgently requires a specific concrete action (a pawn break, a capture, a forcing defensive resource, or an immediate advance). In 11/12 positions, the blunder is tagged as a tempo loss. The correct moves were typically concrete: pawn breaks (f5, d5, d6, g4, h4 in positions 2, 4, 7, 8), captures (Qxb5 in position 3, Rxb4 in position 9), or precise defensive moves (Ng1 in position 5, Kb2 in position 12). Instead, players chose superficially logical quiet moves (Ne4, Nf4, Nd4, Nc3, Qa5, Qd7, Qg3, Qd2, Rd3, Rd8, Kc8, f5) that either created new tactical vulnerabilities (fork/pin/back-rank/hanging pieces in 7/12 positions) or simply ceded the initiative. The average good moves available was only 1.8, indicating these were narrow critical moments demanding precision rather than 'improving' moves.
analysis.move_pattern: Non-forcing piece move (no check, no capture, no direct threat) to a central or seemingly active square, typically knights to e4/f4/d4/c3, queens to lateral squares, or rooks to open files
analysis.why_bad: The position had an urgent concrete requirement (pawn break, capture, forced defense, or pawn advance) that, if not executed immediately, allowed the opponent to seize the initiative with a tactical blow or execute a strategic plan first. The quiet repositioning move wasted the one tempo needed to maintain the balance or advantage.
sub_patterns: Knight centralization that removes a critical defender or creates fork/pin vulnerability (Ne4, Nf4, Nd4, Nc3)
Queen repositioning to seemingly active square that accomplishes nothing concrete or creates pin/hanging-piece problems (Qa5, Qd7, Qg3, Qd2)
Rook repositioning that abandons a dominant square or wastes tempo when pawn advancement was needed (Rd3, Rd8)
King/pawn move to seemingly logical square that creates geometric vulnerability (Kc8 back-rank, f5 weakening)

analysis.label: King moves to a square that increases its exposure to enemy rooks on open files/ranks, resulting in back-rank mates, mating nets, or decisive tactical exploitation.
analysis.description: All 9/9 positions involve king moves that place the king on a more vulnerable square rather than a safer one, typically walking into the firing line of enemy rooks operating on open files or ranks. In 3/9 cases (Kc8→Rb8#, Kc6→Rc5#, Kd6→mate in 7), the king walks directly into immediate or near-immediate checkmate. In 2/9 cases (Kd1, Kf8), the king enters a back-rank or open-file vulnerability that allows devastating checks. In 2/9 cases (Ke4, Kg5), the king vacates a critical blocking square, allowing enemy pieces to penetrate with decisive effect. In 2/9 cases (Kd2 positions), the king moves to a subtly wrong adjacent square that either blocks its own defensive resources or strays too far from a critical defensive task. The average cp_loss of 4337 reflects the catastrophic nature of these errors, with 5/9 resulting in forced checkmate sequences. Open files with enemy rooks are present in all positions.
analysis.move_pattern: King moves one square (any direction) to an exposed square in positions with enemy rooks on open files/ranks
analysis.why_bad: The king moves to a square where it becomes vulnerable to enemy rook attacks along open files/ranks—either walking into immediate checkmate patterns, entering mating nets created by coordinated major pieces, vacating squares that blocked enemy piece penetration, or straying from critical defensive duties against passed pawns.
sub_patterns: King walks into back-rank or rank-based checkmate (Kc8→Rb8#, Kc6→Rc5#)
King enters mating net from coordinated rooks/queen (Ke4, Kd6)
King vacates critical blocking square allowing piece capture or penetration (Kg5, Kd2-blocks-interposition)
King moves away from defensive duty against passed pawn (Kd2 in rook endgame)
King walks into open file occupied by enemy rook (Kf8 into f-file)

analysis.label: Playing a quiet preparatory or threatening move when an immediate concrete action (capture or prophylaxis) was urgently required, gifting the opponent a critical tempo.
analysis.description: In all 3/3 positions, the player chose a non-forcing move (threat, retreat, or pawn advance) when the position demanded immediate decisive action. In Position 1, White threatened the b3-knight with Qc2 instead of capturing it outright with axb3, giving Black time to redeploy it to even stronger squares. In Position 2, Black retreated the bishop to g6 instead of capturing the hanging b1-knight with Bxb1, allowing White to develop it to safety on the very next move. In Position 3, White pushed c4 for space instead of consolidating with Be2/Kh1/Qd1, ignoring the latent ...Qh3 attacking threat and creating a tactical target. The common thread is prioritizing an indirect or 'improving' move over the position's most urgent concrete demand, with the consistent punishment being that the opponent uses the gifted tempo to resolve their critical problem (3/3 cases).
analysis.move_pattern: Non-forcing quiet moves (queen repositioning, bishop retreat, pawn advance) in positions requiring immediate captures or defensive prophylaxis
analysis.why_bad: Each move grants the opponent a free tempo to solve their most critical vulnerability—rescuing a hanging piece, completing development, or launching an attack—that should have been exploited or addressed immediately.
sub_patterns: Threatening a capturable piece instead of taking it immediately
Retreating a piece instead of capturing an undefended enemy piece
Expanding with pawns while ignoring an opponent's imminent tactical threat

analysis.label: Playing a slow, non-forcing move that leaves an immediately capturable piece or pawn undefended, allowing the opponent to win material or create a decisive attack.
analysis.description: In all 6 positions, Black plays a quiet preparatory move (development, pawn push, or king walk) that completely ignores an urgent tactical obligation. In 3/6 cases (b6, Nge7, Be6), a specific pawn is left hanging and the opponent simply captures it. In 2/6 cases (Kd7, e5), a critical tempo is squandered in a time-sensitive position, allowing the opponent to create an unstoppable threat. In 1/6 cases (f6), the move creates new weaknesses worse than the problem it tried to solve. The common thread is that each position demanded one specific concrete action (defend d5, support f4 with g5, play Ke7 not Kd7, play f5 not f6, move the king not the pawn), and instead the player chose a move that 'looks reasonable' by general principles but ignores the immediate tactical reality. The tag 'tempo_loss' and 'missed_tactic' appear across all positions, confirming this is fundamentally about wasting a critical tempo on a non-urgent task.
analysis.move_pattern: Quiet non-forcing move (no check, no capture, no direct threat) - typically a pawn advance, piece development, or king walk to a plausible but wrong square
analysis.why_bad: Each move ignores an immediately hanging or critically vulnerable piece/pawn, granting the opponent a free tempo to capture material, advance a decisive passed pawn, or construct a mating attack that the slow move does nothing to prevent
sub_patterns: Developing a piece while a pawn remains undefended (Nge7/Be6 leave f4 hanging, b6 leaves d5 hanging)
King moving to wrong square losing critical tempo in endgame (Kd7 instead of Ke7, e5 self-blocking king)
Attacking opponent's piece while creating worse weaknesses than the one addressed (f6 weakens e6 square)

analysis.label: Pieces voluntarily leave squares where they perform essential defensive or coordinating functions, allowing the opponent to exploit the newly unguarded responsibilities.
analysis.description: This feature fires on positions where a piece is moved away from a critical defensive duty or optimal functional square to a seemingly active but actually counterproductive location. In 7/9 positions, the moved piece was performing an essential task (guarding a square, protecting material, or maintaining coordination) that the player failed to recognize. Key examples: Qf6 abandons defense of f7 allowing Nf7+ (position 14), Ba4/Bh5 displace the bishop from the a8-h1 diagonal where it needed to reach c6 for defense (positions 3, 7), Kd2 moves the king before saving the hanging bishop on e5 (position 2), Ne7+ moves the knight from its powerful f5 outpost to a square where it's captured (position 8), Ke7 walks the king into a mating net (position 11), and Qd3 ignores the threatening knight on e4 (position 9). The common thread is prioritizing general principles (activity, centralization, giving checks) over the specific positional/tactical requirements of the moment.
analysis.move_pattern: Any piece type moving away from a square where it serves a critical defensive or coordinating function, often to the rim or to a square disconnected from the main battle
analysis.why_bad: The piece was performing an essential but non-obvious defensive function (guarding a square, protecting material, or maintaining coordination); its departure allows the opponent to exploit the now-unguarded responsibility through tactics, captures, or invasions
sub_patterns: Bishop displaced from critical diagonal loses tempo in defensive race
King moves before resolving hanging piece (move-order error)
Queen abandons guard of key square enabling knight invasion
Piece gives check but moves to vulnerable square where it's lost
King walks forward into tactical refutation zone

analysis.label: Making a natural-looking move that ignores or creates a critical geometric alignment allowing the opponent to fork pieces or exploit passivity.
analysis.description: This feature fires on moves that appear constructive on the surface (centralizing a king, developing a bishop, capturing material, gaining space) but fatally ignore or create tactical vulnerabilities—most commonly forks. In 3/6 positions, the move directly enables a fork: Kd4 walks into Nf3+ forking king and rook (Position 1), Be6 allows d5 forking bishop and knight (Position 3), and h4 leaves Be4+ forking king and rook intact (Position 5). In the remaining 3/6 positions, the move creates a passive/misplaced piece: Kxh5 abandons a dominant central king for an exposed h-file position vulnerable to tempo-gaining checks (Position 6), Rb3 makes a passive rook move while failing to protect the critical compensating piece (Position 8), and Rxh4 captures with the wrong piece leaving the rook sidelined on the rim (Position 15). The average cp_loss of 304 and average of only 1.8 good moves indicate high-stakes positions where the player chose an appealing-looking move while missing the one critical factor—typically a piece alignment enabling a fork or the need to keep a piece actively placed.
analysis.move_pattern: Various piece types moving to seemingly useful squares (centralizing, capturing, developing) while leaving or creating a diagonal/knight-hop alignment between two friendly pieces
analysis.why_bad: The moves prioritize superficial positional goals (material capture, centralization, development, space) while ignoring critical geometric alignments that allow the opponent to fork two pieces or exploit the newly passive/exposed placement of the moved piece
sub_patterns: King/piece moves to square enabling knight or bishop fork
Capturing material with piece that then becomes passive on rim file
Slow move ignoring existing fork alignment between own king and rook

analysis.label: Playing a plausible-looking quiet or repositioning move when the position demands a single critical forcing action, resulting in a catastrophic loss of tempo or initiative.
analysis.description: In 6/7 positions, the player chose a natural-looking move (piece repositioning, material capture, or pawn push) that addressed a secondary concern while ignoring the position's single most urgent requirement. In Position 1, Nf4 repositions the knight attractively but misses the forcing Nxg3 capture that wins material through tactical exchanges. In Position 3, Kf1 approaches the passed pawn but loses a tempo to Ra1+ compared to the precise Kf3 blockade. In Position 4, Nf4 looks aggressive but places the knight on an exposed square where it's profitably captured. In Position 7, Qxa5 grabs material but misses a forced mate in 3 with Qe5. In Position 8, Re1 repositions a rook but abandons d-file pressure, allowing unstoppable pawn advances. In Position 9, g3 pushes a pawn when Kg3 (king activation) was the critical tempo-saving move. The consistent pattern (5/7 positions tagged 'tempo_loss') is choosing aesthetically reasonable moves in positions where only 1-2 moves maintain the balance.
analysis.move_pattern: Quiet piece repositioning, non-forcing captures, or pawn pushes (no checks, no threats) when a forcing alternative exists
analysis.why_bad: These moves waste a critical tempo or fail to address the position's single urgent demand (a tactical shot, a forced mate, a precise blockade, or an undermining break), allowing the opponent to seize the initiative or advance unstoppable threats
sub_patterns: Piece repositioning instead of forcing capture (Nf4 vs Nxg3)
Material grab instead of mating attack (Qxa5 vs Qe5)
Pawn push instead of king activation (g3 vs Kg3)
Wrong king square losing tempo to check (Kf1 vs Kf3)
Abandoning critical file pressure (Re1 off d-file vs f4 break)

analysis.label: Catastrophic blunders in narrow positions (typically only 1 good move) where the player ignores an immediately available simple solution for an apparently reasonable but fatally flawed alternative.
analysis.description: This feature fires on positions where there is essentially one correct move (avg 1.6 good moves available) and the player catastrophically misses it, resulting in enormous evaluation swings (avg 2521 cp loss). In 6/8 actual blunders, the best move was a straightforward action: a simple capture (Kxh2 in pos 3, Kxh6 in pos 9, axb4 in pos 10), a forcing check that wins material (Qe4+ in pos 4, Qxf4+ in pos 15), or a precise one-square king placement (Kh1 vs Kh2 in pos 13). Instead, players chose moves that appear active or reasonable—checks that accomplish nothing (Rf2+, Qb4+), passive development (Bd7), slow pawn pushes (a3), repositioning moves that ignore threats (Rf5, Kg6), or captures that trade away dominant pieces (Bxf5). The positions span all phases but share the characteristic of having extremely narrow correct play where one simple, concrete move solves everything.
analysis.move_pattern: No single geometric pattern; diverse piece types and directions, but the WRONG move often looks 'active' (checks, advances, repositioning) while the RIGHT move is typically a simple capture or minimal king adjustment
