analysis.why_bad: These moves fail because they address a secondary concern (activity, development, pawn advancement, giving check) while completely ignoring the position's single critical demand—usually capturing free/dangerous material, giving the one check that wins material, or placing the king on the precisely correct square to avoid tactical vulnerabilities.
sub_patterns: Pointless check instead of winning capture (Rf2+, Qb4+)
Slow move ignoring forcing continuation (a3, Bd7)
King move into tactical vulnerability (Kg6, Kh2)
Trading dominant piece for insufficient return (Bxf5)
Repositioning when simple capture solves everything (Rf5)

analysis.label: Wasting a must-use tempo on a peripheral or secondary objective when the position demands immediate attention to the primary strategic/tactical necessity.
analysis.description: This feature fires on positions where the player has very few acceptable moves (avg 1.8 good moves) and spends their critical tempo on something non-essential. In 5/10 positions, the wasted move targets material (Kb2 chasing a2-pawn, Qb4 targeting a4-pawn, Kf7 defending f6-pawn, Kc6 attacking b6-pawn, c5 pushing a pawn while ignoring back-rank mate). In 3/10 positions, the move is a slow prophylactic/positional idea when sharp action is required (a3 preventing Nb4, h4 before king centralization, Bh6 attempting to trap the enemy king while own king is under attack). In 2/10, the move-order is wrong (Ra1+ before Re1+, Bxg5 removing a critical file-blocking piece). The 'tempo_loss' tag appears in all 10 positions. The positions share a common structure: one critical task demands immediate execution (supporting a passed pawn, addressing a mating threat, executing a forcing sequence in the right order), but the player diverts attention to a less important goal. The avg cp_loss of 3000 reflects that in critical-tempo positions, one wasted move can be catastrophic.
analysis.move_pattern: Varied piece types moving toward peripheral targets or secondary objectives; often directed away from the critical sector of the board (toward wing pawns, away from exposed kings, or capturing pieces that were actually serving a defensive function)
analysis.why_bad: The position has extremely narrow margins (avg 1.8 good moves) requiring the one available tempo be spent on the primary task—supporting a passed pawn, addressing a mating threat, or executing a forcing sequence in correct order. Diverting to secondary goals (pawn captures, prophylaxis, wrong-order checks) grants the opponent time to consolidate, escape, or counterattack in the critical zone.
sub_patterns: King moving toward a peripheral pawn instead of staying centralized/active (Kb2, Kf7, Kc6)
Slow prophylactic moves when sharp tactical action is demanded (a3, h4)
Move-order errors in forcing sequences that allow defensive resources (Ra1+ before Re1+)
Ignoring immediate lethal threats to pursue own attacking ideas (c5 ignoring Rf8+, Bh6 ignoring Qxf2+)
Removing a piece that was guarding a critical file or square (Bxg5 opening h-file)

analysis.label: King (or piece) moves toward an enemy passed pawn 1-2 squares from promotion that cannot be stopped, wasting a critical tempo instead of generating counterplay elsewhere.
analysis.description: In 12/12 positions, an enemy passed pawn sits 1-2 squares from promotion and is effectively unstoppable. The blundering move sends the king (11/12) or a piece (1/12) toward that pawn in a futile attempt to blockade or approach it, when the correct strategy is to create counterplay: capturing other pawns to generate counter-passed pawns (Positions 1, 4, 5), gaining tempo with checks (Position 11), fleeing away from the promotion square to complicate the post-promotion mating task (Positions 3, 9), or avoiding squares where promotion delivers check (Positions 7, 8). The approach move consistently wastes the last available tempo before promotion, leaving the player without compensation. In Position 2, Kc2 chases the a2 pawn instead of Ke4 attacking e5; in Position 5, Kd3 approaches a3 instead of capturing e5/f4; in Position 14, Kc6 blockades b6 instead of pushing c3 for a counter-race. The refutation is almost always the immediate pawn promotion, often with enhanced effect (check, better queen placement) because the king has moved into the promotion zone.
analysis.move_pattern: King moves toward an enemy passed pawn on the 7th rank (or piece moves toward promotion square), typically moving 1-2 squares in the direction of the pawn rather than away or laterally
analysis.why_bad: The pawn promotes regardless of the approach, so the move wastes a tempo that should be spent creating counterplay (capturing material, pushing own passed pawns, gaining tempo with checks, or fleeing to complicate the opponent's post-promotion task). Worse, approaching the promotion square often places the king where the new queen delivers check or creates immediate tactical threats.
sub_patterns: King approaches promotion square and gets checked by newly promoted queen
King chases passer instead of capturing free material to create counter-passed pawn
King moves toward passer instead of fleeing away to maximize distance from promoted piece
King attempts passive blockade when active counter-promotion race was required
Piece moves to watch promotion square, abandoning a critical defensive duty

analysis.label: Natural-looking moves (castling, attacking, advancing) that ignore the position's most urgent tactical demand, enabling an immediate refutation.
analysis.description: This feature fires on positions where the player makes a move that follows general chess principles or pursues a secondary goal—castling for safety (3/5: O-O, O-O-O), making aggressive piece moves (2/5: Ng5 attacking a bishop, Nb6+ forking rook), or advancing pawns for space (1/5: f5)—while the position urgently demands a specific, often counterintuitive response. In each case, the correct moves involve retreating or repositioning pieces defensively (Qc2/Bb2/Qe2 in position 2, Qb5/Qd3 in position 12), maintaining sustained pressure instead of grabbing material (Nc3+ in position 3), trading queens to neutralize threats (Qd6 in position 7), or improving passive pieces (Nhf6 in position 6). The blunders share the trait that they each specifically ENABLE a tactical shot that wasn't previously available: removing a knight from f3 unguards d4 allowing a queen fork, castling kingside makes Nxf6+ a check winning the queen, castling queenside puts the king on the d-file, f5 gives a free tempo for h7, and Nb6+ leads to a permanently trapped piece. All 5/5 positions had at least one clearly superior alternative (avg 2.0 good moves), suggesting the player defaulted to 'autopilot' rather than calculating concrete consequences.
analysis.move_pattern: Varied piece types and directions (knight advances, castling both sides, pawn pushes) - all are 'purposeful-looking' moves that address secondary concerns rather than the position's primary tactical demand
analysis.why_bad: Each move ignores the most urgent feature of the position (an undefended queen, a critical defensive piece, an open file aimed at the king, an unstoppable passed pawn) in favor of pursuing a natural-looking but lower-priority goal, directly enabling the opponent's tactical refutation
sub_patterns: Castling into an existing tactical vulnerability (O-O enabling Nxf6+ check, O-O-O walking into d-file pressure)
Aggressive knight moves abandoning critical defensive duties (Ng5 unguarding d4, Nb6+ leading to trapped piece)
Tempo-wasting pawn moves when forced action is required (f5 when queen trade was urgent)

analysis.label: Playing a quiet, non-urgent move in a razor-sharp position where one specific time-sensitive action is required to maintain the evaluation.
analysis.description: This feature fires on positions where the player makes a slow, passive, or preparatory move (typically a king retreat, quiet pawn push, or non-forcing piece move) when the position demands immediate, precise action due to urgent threats like advancing passed pawns, tactical vulnerabilities, or narrow drawing resources. In 8/10 positions, the correct move involved either advancing a critical passed pawn (h3 in positions 1-2), engaging pieces against enemy passed pawns (Ne5/Ra2 in position 3), making a unique prophylactic pawn fix (a4 in position 15, Bc6 in position 12), or addressing the center before the opponent can strike (e5 in position 9). The positions share extremely low good-move counts (avg 1.6), meaning there's essentially one correct action and everything else is a significant mistake. The blundered moves look 'reasonable' in isolation—king centralization, rook development, structural reinforcement—but catastrophically ignore the single critical demand of the position.
analysis.move_pattern: Quiet non-forcing moves (king retreats/repositions, slow pawn advances, passive piece shuffles) that neither capture, check, nor create immediate threats
analysis.why_bad: These moves waste a critical tempo in positions where timing is decisive—typically allowing the opponent to advance passed pawns one step closer to promotion, execute a tactical sequence exploiting underdevelopment/king exposure, or establish an unstoppable positional advantage that didn't exist one move prior
sub_patterns: King retreats/sidesteps away from critical zone (Ke7, Ke3, Ke2)
Slow pawn advances on wrong flank (h4, f3)
Preparatory piece moves ignoring urgent central/tactical demands (Rb8, Rg1)
Premature pawn advances creating weaknesses (d5, a7)

analysis.label: Seemingly constructive repositioning moves that inadvertently create a specific tactical vulnerability the opponent can immediately exploit.
analysis.description: This feature fires on moves where the player makes a 'natural' or 'improving' move—repositioning a piece to an apparently active square, contesting an open file, or advancing a pawn for space—but in doing so creates or exposes a concrete tactical vulnerability. In 7/7 positions, the played move abandons a critical defensive function or weakens a key square/line: Bh5 leaves the bishop undefended allowing Qb5+ (1/7), Rae8 self-blocks the f8-rook's escape enabling Ba3 trapping it (2/7), f5 opens the e-file against the uncastled king for Re1+ pins (3/7), b6 weakens a6 enabling an unstoppable Nb5 knight invasion (4/7), Qh4 abandons central control allowing a d5 breakthrough (5/7), Rae1 places a rook where forced exchanges with check give counterplay (6/7), and Ng3 removes the knight guarding d4/c2 allowing a devastating Nd4-Nxc2 fork (7/7). In all cases, the position was roughly equal before the move, multiple safe alternatives existed (avg 2.6 good moves), and the error stems from prioritizing a slow positional improvement over maintaining tactical integrity.
analysis.move_pattern: Piece or pawn moves to a seemingly active/constructive square, typically away from a defensive post or to a square where it becomes tactically exploitable; diverse piece types (bishop, rook, pawn, queen, knight) all moving toward 'improvement' rather than addressing concrete threats.
analysis.why_bad: Each move abandons a specific defensive responsibility or creates a new weakness (undefended piece, weakened square, opened line, blocked escape route) that grants the opponent an immediate tactical shot—a fork, pin, trapped piece, or breakthrough—that wasn't available before the move was played.
sub_patterns: Piece repositioned to undefended square while king position allows check-and-capture combination
Rook placed on file that blocks another piece's escape route, enabling trapping tactics
Pawn advance opens critical line against own uncastled king
Prophylactic pawn move weakens outpost-controlling square, enabling knight invasion
Queen sortie to flank abandons control of central tension, allowing pawn breakthrough
Piece removed from guarding square enables opponent's fork or invasion

analysis.label: Playing a natural-looking improving move instead of the most forcing or concrete continuation that exploits a time-sensitive tactical window.
analysis.description: All three positions share the critical theme of tempo loss through choosing plausible but suboptimal moves when the position demanded immediate, precise action. In Position 1 (Re1+), White gives a check but with the wrong piece, allowing the king more escape routes versus the tighter Qe6+ mating net. In Position 4 (Bf6), Black repositions a bishop 'improving' it positionally while missing the concrete exd3/Ne2+ combination that wins material immediately before the vulnerable rook escapes. In Position 6 (b5), Black pushes a pawn thinking it advances their winning position, but it gives White a crucial tempo for king centralization when direct king infiltration (Kb2) or flexible waiting (a6) maintained maximum pressure. In 3/3 cases, the move played looks constructive and thematic but fails to exploit a specific, time-sensitive vulnerability in the opponent's position. The common thread across all analyses is the 'tempo_loss' tag (3/3), and in each case the opponent uses the gifted tempo to improve their defensive resources.
analysis.move_pattern: Various piece types making seemingly constructive moves (checks, piece improvements, pawn advances) that are less forcing than the optimal continuation available
analysis.why_bad: These moves gift the opponent a tempo to escape a specific vulnerability - whether it's a king escaping a tighter mating net, a rook fleeing a tactical trap, or a king reaching a better defensive square. The position demands concrete action NOW, not general improvement.
sub_patterns: Giving check with wrong piece allowing king more room
Repositioning a piece when a capture/fork wins immediately
Pushing a pawn when king activity is more urgent in endgame

analysis.label: Moving the queen to a peripheral queenside square (a4/a5/c2) while the king faces imminent tactical threats from opponent's active pieces on open files.
analysis.description: In 5/6 positions, the queen is displaced to a far-flung square (a4 appears 3 times, a5 once, c2 once) abandoning its defensive coordination near the king. In all 6 positions, the opponent has rooks on open files aimed at the player's king, and the queen's departure enables devastating tactical exploitation—back-rank mates (3/6), rook invasions to the 7th rank (1/6), or tempo-gaining checks against the exposed monarch (2/6). The one non-queen move (c5) follows the same principle: pursuing a peripheral objective while the back rank crumbles. In every case, the best moves involved maintaining piece coordination near the king (Re8, Qf5, Qd2, Re2) rather than chasing material or creating illusory queenside threats.
analysis.move_pattern: Queen moving laterally to a-file or c-file peripheral squares (a4, a5, c2), away from the king's defensive zone
analysis.why_bad: Removing the queen from its defensive/coordinating role exposes the king to immediate tactical exploitation—typically back-rank sacrifices, rook invasions on open files, or forced checks that win material or deliver mate, because no other piece can compensate for the queen's absence.
sub_patterns: Queen to a4 abandoning king (3 instances)
Queen captures peripheral pawn on c-file
Queen to a5 abandoning kingside defense
Pawn advance ignoring back-rank weakness

analysis.label: Advancing the king or a pawn in a seemingly active but wrong direction in endgames, wasting critical tempo in positions where timing is paramount.
analysis.description: This feature fires on endgame positions where the player makes a forward-looking move (king advance or pawn push) that appears active but actually wastes a critical tempo or creates a fatal vulnerability. In 10/10 cases the position is an endgame, and in 8/10 cases the analysis explicitly identifies 'tempo_loss' as the core error. The moves share a geometric pattern of advancement—kings stepping forward toward the opponent (Kf5, Kg4, Kb5, Kg3, Kf4, Kh4) or pawns pushing aggressively (h3, g5, g5, c5)—but each goes in the wrong direction or at the wrong time. In pawn race positions (Positions 2, 5, 8, 13), the advancing move loses the exact tempo needed to intercept an opponent's passed pawn. In tactical positions (Positions 3, 11, 14), the advancing move walks the king into a mating net or leaves it fatally exposed. In move-order positions (Position 12), the advance is premature, allowing the opponent to gain a tempo with check. The unifying thread is that the position demanded either retreating, going to the opposite wing, or executing a specific prior move, but the player chose the instinctively 'active' forward option.
analysis.move_pattern: King advancing forward/sideways toward opponent's territory, or pawn pushing forward one square, in endgame positions where the king is already somewhat exposed
analysis.why_bad: These forward moves waste the one critical tempo needed to win a pawn race, intercept a passed pawn, escape a mating net, or execute the correct move-order—the position demands retreat, redirection, or a different priority, but the move's apparent activity masks its tempo cost
sub_patterns: King advancing toward wrong flank while opponent's pawn races on the other side
Pawn push that blocks own king's escape square or weakens critical squares
King stepping forward into a mating net created by opponent's pieces
Premature king advance before a critical pawn push that would gain tempo
Aggressive pawn advance instead of necessary king centralization

analysis.label: Quiet, non-forcing developing or preparatory moves played in positions where an urgent concrete tactic (fork, attack, or forced sequence) demanded immediate execution.
analysis.description: This feature fires on slow, natural-looking moves (Be3 ×3, Ne2, Nf3, pawn pushes like e4, c3, f3, e6) that prioritize generic development or consolidation in positions demanding immediate tactical action. In 7/9 positions, the best move involved a concrete forcing idea: Qe4 leading to Nf6+ queen fork (Position 7), Bxf6/Nb5 enabling Nc7+ fork (Position 8), Qa5+ with d4 fork (Position 3), Qg4/Qh5+ exploiting an uncastled king (Position 14), O-O-O addressing king safety (Position 15). The played moves are all non-forcing — no checks, no captures, no direct threats — making them appear reasonable to players focused on development principles rather than concrete calculation. The average cp_loss of 248 reflects how these missed tactical windows, once lost, allow opponents to consolidate (3/9), execute counter-forks (4/9), or exploit newly-created vulnerabilities like trapped pieces (1/9) or diagonal weaknesses (1/9).
analysis.move_pattern: Non-forcing minor piece development (especially Be3, Nf3, Ne2) or slow preparatory pawn pushes (e4, c3, f3, e6) — no checks, captures, or direct threats
analysis.why_bad: These moves surrender the tempo needed to execute a fleeting tactical opportunity (fork, forced sequence, or attack on exposed king), allowing the opponent to consolidate weaknesses or counter-exploit the passivity with their own tactical strikes
sub_patterns: Be3 development missing queen/knight fork opportunities
Knight moves retreating from dominant outpost when fork sequences exist
Preparatory pawn pushes blocking key squares or creating tactical vulnerabilities
Passive consolidation when opponent's king is exposed and forcing moves available

analysis.label: Moves that relocate pieces to seemingly reasonable but strategically irrelevant squares while ignoring the position's primary tactical or defensive requirement.
analysis.description: This feature fires on moves that abandon control of critical squares, diagonals, or areas to address a secondary concern (or no concern at all). In 6/7 positions, the move removes a piece from influence over the key tactical zone, allowing the opponent to exploit the newly unguarded territory. Specifically: Bh3 abandons the a8-h1 diagonal allowing Nc6 (Position 13), Kh6 walks onto the f8-h6 diagonal allowing Bf8+ mate (Position 9), Qe7 blocks development and enables Rxf7 sacrifice (Position 10), Rd8+ drives the king to safety wasting tempo (Position 8), a5 ignores kingside threats entirely (Position 15), Qe8 releases restriction on the opponent's king (Position 1), and Kf2 allows a check resource instead of improving coordination first (Position 7). The consistent punishment is tactical exploitation of the vacated influence zone. Tags like 'tempo_loss' appear in 6/7 positions and 'missed_tactic' in 5/7.
analysis.move_pattern: Various piece types moving to peripheral or less relevant squares, often toward board edges (h3, h6, e8, e7, a5) or away from the center of tactical tension
analysis.why_bad: The moves abandon control over the critical square, diagonal, or area that the position demands be guarded, allowing the opponent to immediately exploit the newly undefended zone with tactics (forks, checks on vacated diagonals, sacrifices on unguarded squares, or simply grabbing undefended material).
sub_patterns: Bishop leaving critical diagonal allowing knight invasion
King walking onto unguarded diagonal enabling mating attack
Premature check driving opponent's king to a safer square
Pawn push on inactive wing while ignoring immediate threats
Queen placement blocking own development or creating tactical vulnerabilities

analysis.label: Slow or seemingly defensive moves that waste critical tempo when the king faces urgent tactical threats requiring immediate precise action.
analysis.description: In all 5/5 positions, the player's king faces significant safety issues with opponent pieces converging on the kingside. The blundered moves are all 'quiet' or 'natural-looking' responses that appear to address the position (Rh8 targets a pawn, g3 attacks a knight, Kh6 tries to escape, exd5 resolves tension, Bg7 develops defensively) but fatally ignore the tactical urgency. In 5/5 cases, the position required one specific precise tactical response (Rg4 actively attacking, Nh4 counterattacking, Kg8 retreating to safety, Na6 developing, Bxe5 eliminating the key attacker) but the player chose a passive alternative that either worsened king exposure (3/5: g3, Kh6, exd5 opening lines) or squandered decisive tempo (4/5: Rh8, g3, Kh6, Bg7). The consistent result is that the opponent gains time to execute a devastating tactical blow—mating attacks in 2/5 cases, crushing forks or coordination in 3/5 cases.
analysis.move_pattern: Various piece types making quiet kingside moves (retreats, pawn pushes, captures) that are non-forcing and fail to engage tactically with the critical threat
analysis.why_bad: They waste the one crucial tempo needed to address an urgent king safety crisis, allowing the opponent to execute a concrete tactical strike (mate, fork, or decisive material gain) that the slow move fails to prevent or actively enables by weakening the position further
sub_patterns: Passive rook/bishop retreats losing tempo in tactical positions
Pawn moves weakening the king's pawn shield under attack
King moves walking into tactical nets (checks, forks)
Central captures opening diagonals toward own king

analysis.label: Choosing an active-looking or aggressive move that concretely backfires, when the position demanded patient consolidation or a simpler tactical solution.
analysis.description: This feature fires on positions where players select moves that appear purposeful—gaining space, giving checks, creating threats—but actually undermine their own position through overlooked tactical consequences. In 6/8 positions, the best alternative was either a quiet consolidating move (Bg3, Rb1, a3, O-O) or a simple precise tactic (Qxg7, Qxg5+, exd5), while the played move was superficially ambitious. The errors include pointless checks that waste tempo (Nf3+, Qd3+ missing mate-in-1), premature pawn advances that lose material (b4, e4), moving key pieces from critical defensive posts (Ne2 from c3, Nb6 from the d-file diagonal block), and placing pieces on tactically vulnerable squares (Qb3 allowing Na5 fork). In 5/8 positions, king safety is a central factor—either the blunder exposes the player's own king or fails to exploit the opponent's exposed king. The average cp_loss of 1432 with only 2.4 good moves available indicates these are critical decision points where precision was essential but the player opted for flash over substance.
analysis.move_pattern: Diverse piece types (knights, queens, pawns, king) moving to apparently active squares—forward pawn pushes, checks, piece redeployments—that look aggressive but create concrete tactical vulnerabilities
analysis.why_bad: The moves sacrifice existing positional/tactical assets (key piece placement, pawn structure integrity, king safety) for illusory activity, overlooking that the opponent has concrete tactical refutations exploiting the newly created weaknesses—forks, open files to exposed kings, hanging pieces, or missed immediate wins
sub_patterns: Pointless checks that waste tempo or miss stronger continuations (Qd3+, Nf3+)
Removing a piece from a critical defensive square (Ne2 from c3, Nb6 exposing diagonal)
Premature pawn advances creating tactical vulnerabilities (b4, e4)
Placing pieces on squares vulnerable to tactical exploitation (Qb3 allowing fork)
Capturing with the wrong piece exposing the king (Kxg7 instead of Qxg7)

analysis.label: King moves forward into an exposed position where it gets caught by checks or mating nets, when retreating would maintain safety or a draw.
analysis.description: In 11/12 positions, the king advances forward (away from its back rank or shelter) into an exposed square where it becomes vulnerable to devastating check sequences, pawn checks, or mating patterns. The remaining position (Bc7) shares the same logic by blocking the king's retreat path. The correct alternatives consistently involve retreating the king backward—to the back rank, a corner, or behind pawns—often maintaining perpetual check draws (positions 1, 4, 5, 9, 10) or simply avoiding tactical exploitation (positions 3, 11, 12, 13). The pattern is especially prevalent in queen endgames (8/12 positions) where the queen's long-range checking ability punishes exposed kings catastrophically. In every case, the forward king move creates geometric vulnerabilities—diagonal check corridors, file-based attacks, or pawn advance checks (f4+, f3+, g5#)—that the retreating alternatives avoid entirely. The average cp_loss of 4408 reflects that these forward king moves frequently convert drawn or winning positions into immediate losses or forced mates.
analysis.move_pattern: King moves forward (toward center or opponent's side), typically one square advancing along a rank or diagonal away from its own back rank; one case involves a bishop blocking the king's retreat square
analysis.why_bad: The forward king square is exposed to queen checks, pawn checks, or mating nets that force the king into progressively worse squares with no retreat, whereas backward/retreating moves maintain safety by keeping the king near shelter or within perpetual check drawing corridors
sub_patterns: King advances into diagonal mating corridor in queen endgame
King steps forward allowing pawn check (f4+, f3+, g5#) that traps it
King walks to square where check sequence wins material or forces mate
King abandons perpetual-check drawing zone by moving forward
King centralizes aggressively when it should retreat to back rank

analysis.label: King captures a less-critical pawn in the endgame, fatally abandoning control of a more dangerous enemy passed pawn that then races to promotion.
analysis.description: This feature fires on positions where a player's king (or pawn) captures material that appears attractive but critically moves away from the primary threat—an advanced enemy passed pawn. In 7/9 cases the move is a king capture (Kxg6, Kxb5, Kxg5, Kxf4, Kxc5), while the remaining cases involve king/pawn moves toward less important targets. In 8/9 positions, the immediate punishment involves an enemy passed pawn advancing to promotion (h4-h3-h2, d3-d2-d1=Q, a3-a2, h7-h8=Q, d7-d8=Q). The tactical motif is unanimously 'passed_pawn' across all analyzed positions. The core error is a tempo/distance miscalculation: the capturing king ends up one or more critical squares too far from the promotion path to intercept, while the captured pawn was either less dangerous or already contained. All positions are pawn endgames (8/9 endgame phase) where king proximity to passed pawns is the single most important factor.
analysis.move_pattern: King captures a pawn (usually sideways or forward), moving away from the critical file/diagonal where an enemy passed pawn needs blockading
analysis.why_bad: The king moves to the wrong side of a passed pawn or too far from its promotion square, creating an irrecoverable tempo deficit in the resulting pawn race—the captured pawn was a decoy compared to the lethal passed pawn that is now unstoppable
sub_patterns: King captures pawn and ends up on wrong side of remaining passed pawn (Kxg6 with h-pawn racing)
King captures away from a pawn 2-3 squares from promotion (Kxf4/Kxc5 allowing d-pawn queening)
King abandons blockade square to capture decoy pawn (Kxg5 releasing h6-h7-h8=Q)
Capturing with wrong unit dissolves critical structural restraint (dxc4 removing d5 anchor)

analysis.label: Moves that pursue a secondary plan or target while neglecting the position's most urgent requirement, allowing immediate devastating exploitation.
analysis.description: In 7/7 positions, the player makes a move that addresses a secondary concern (7th-rank penetration, pawn blockade, kingside attack, queenside pawn structure) while catastrophically ignoring the position's single most critical demand. In Position 2, Rd7 executes the correct plan one move too early, leaving h1 hanging (move-order error). In Position 5, Rh6 chases kingside pawns while the queenside collapses via a3+. In Position 4, Kf2 seeks king safety on the wrong square (f2 vs f1), exposing diagonals. In Position 3, Kh5 approaches the passed pawn instead of fleeing to the center. In Position 7, Kf5 blocks the rook's critical f5 square. In Position 6, a3 addresses a queenside pawn when kingside stabilization was urgent. In Position 1, Qf3 aggressively pressures Black but creates a target enabling Nxd4 fork. The common thread is that the best moves (available in all cases, avg 2.4 good alternatives) address the primary threat or need, while the played moves pursue tempting but secondary objectives.
analysis.move_pattern: Various piece types moved to attractive-looking but wrong squares or sectors, often one square or one tempo away from the correct choice
analysis.why_bad: Each move neglects the position's single most urgent requirement (protecting a hanging piece, stabilizing a critical sector, choosing the safe king square, keeping coordination) in favor of a plausible-looking alternative plan, giving the opponent an immediate tactical or positional exploitation of the neglected vulnerability
sub_patterns: Right plan wrong move-order (leaving pieces hanging)
King moving to exposed square instead of safe square
Piece pursuing target on wrong flank while critical flank collapses
Piece occupying square needed by another piece (self-obstruction)
Pawn advance creating target instead of addressing urgent need

analysis.label: Quiet repositioning moves that remove a piece from its essential defensive role, leaving a key piece or square tactically unguarded.
analysis.description: In 6/6 positions, the player makes a natural-looking quiet move (no check, no capture) that repositions a piece to a seemingly useful square while fatally abandoning a critical defensive responsibility. In 3/6 cases (Positions 1, 13, 15), the queen moves away from defending a specific piece (the e7 bishop in Positions 1 and 13, the c7 square in Position 15), allowing the opponent to capture it for free or execute a fork. In 2/6 cases (Positions 6 and 3), a rook repositions when the position demanded addressing king safety or piece geometry instead, enabling check sequences or pawn captures. In 1/6 cases (Position 8), a bishop develops to a logical square but ignores that a pawn will fall with a queen attack once its defender is driven away. The average cp_loss of 325 reflects how devastating these seemingly innocuous moves are — each enables a simple, forcing refutation (hanging piece in 3/6, fork in 2/6, overloaded defender in 1/6).
analysis.move_pattern: Non-capturing, non-checking piece repositioning (often Queen or Rook) moving away from a square where it was the sole defender of a critical piece or controlling a vital line
analysis.why_bad: The moved piece was the only defender of a tactically critical piece or square; relocating it creates an immediate tactical vulnerability (hanging piece, fork target, or forced winning sequence) that the opponent exploits with a simple one-move threat

Queen repositions abandoning control of key square enabling knight fork (Qf7)
Rook shifts along rank removing defense from critical file/king corridor (Rb7)
Quiet development ignoring that a key pawn becomes tactically loose (Rac8, Bd2)

analysis.label: Moves that fatally strip away a critical defensive resource (piece, pawn, or king position) when the opponent's pieces are already poised to attack the king.
analysis.description: In 8/8 positions, the played move removes the one element holding the king's defenses together while the opponent already has active attacking pieces in the vicinity. In 3/8 cases (Kf8, Kg8, Kg1), the king itself walks to a square where it faces a stronger attack or mating net. In 2/8 cases (fxg3, g3), a pawn shielding the king is pushed or captured away, opening lethal diagonals or files directly to the monarch. In 3/8 cases (Qxc2, Rc3, Nxb2), a piece that was defending the king area leaves for material or positional reasons, enabling immediate tactical exploitation (perpetual check, knight forks, mating attacks). The average cp_loss of ~3953 reflects that these moves consistently convert survivable positions into forced mates or catastrophic material loss, as the opponent's pre-existing attacking configuration needs only one defensive lapse to become lethal.
analysis.move_pattern: Any piece type moving away from king defense zone - king to worse square, pawn capture/push removing shield, or piece leaving for material on opposite wing
analysis.why_bad: The opponent already has active pieces aimed at the king; the move removes the single remaining defensive barrier (pawn shield, key defender, or safe king square), allowing an immediate decisive attack or forced mate that was previously just barely held at bay.

Shielding pawn removed by capture/advance, opening fatal lines (fxg3, g3)

analysis.label: Playing a plausible-looking move when only one precise, urgent action maintains the position in a critically narrow decision point.
analysis.description: These positions share an extremely narrow solution space (average 1.4 good moves available) where the player spends their one available tempo on a non-critical action—often an active-looking or 'reasonable' move—while missing the single urgent move that addresses the position's primary tension. In 9/11 positions, the core tag is tempo_loss: Qa4 threatens a knight instead of capturing it (Position 15), b6 prepares a fianchetto while the queen hangs (Position 8), a4 advances a pawn when only f3 buys critical time against a passed h-pawn (Position 13), Qb5 activates the queen while abandoning the promotion-blocking duty (Position 10), Rde1 doubles on the wrong file while leaving a piece hanging (Position 7), Nc3 retreats an aggressive knight surrendering the initiative (Position 6), and Kxd8 recaptures with the wrong piece exposing the king to tempo-gaining attacks (Position 11). The average centipawn loss of 1273 reflects that these are catastrophic one-move collapses where the single critical resource (perpetual, forcing capture, defensive key square) is missed in favor of a superficially active alternative.

Slow pawn advances ignoring immediate piece-level threats (b6, a4)

analysis.label: Playing a slow, non-forcing move when a critical tactical opportunity (usually a free capture of a hanging piece) demands immediate action.
analysis.description: This feature fires on positions where only ~1 good move exists (avg 1.2 good moves) and the player chooses a passive, non-urgent move instead. In 6/8 analyzed positions, there was a completely undefended piece that could be captured for free (e5 pawn in pos 1, c1 bishop in pos 2, b4 knight in pos 4, d3 knight in pos 6, d4 pawn in pos 8, e5 bishop via Nxe5 in pos 14). In the remaining cases, the player ignored a critical threat to their own hanging piece (double-attacked e6 bishop in pos 11, piece placed where it's recaptured with check in pos 10). The moves played are overwhelmingly quiet/non-contact (8/10): pawn pushes (b4, g6, c5, f3, fxe5), piece repositioning (Re2, Bd6, Rf8), or a king walk (Kf8). All share the characteristic of being 'normal-looking' positional moves that would be reasonable in quiet positions but are catastrophic here because they completely ignore the one critical tactical element.

analysis.why_bad: The position has exactly one critical tactical demand (a free capture available, or an immediate threat to address), and the move played does nothing to engage with it, allowing the opponent to consolidate, capture the hanging material, or execute a devastating tactical sequence on the next move.
sub_patterns: Pawn push ignoring capturable enemy piece
Piece repositioning while own piece is doubly attacked
Capturing with wrong unit leaving another piece hanging
King move that worsens exposure while ignoring central tension

analysis.label: Playing a superficially active or logical move that wastes the one critical tempo needed to address an urgent tactical obligation in the position.
analysis.description: In all 7 positions, the player faced a time-sensitive tactical demand (a hanging piece to capture, a promotion threat to neutralize, or a king exposure requiring immediate retreat) but chose a move that appeared reasonable—often a check, piece reposition, or greedy capture—that gave the opponent exactly one tempo to execute a devastating counter-plan. In 3/7 cases, the wasted move was a purposeless queen check (Qa4+, Qb4+, and the check-adjacent Qb6) that allowed the opponent's king to reach a critical square (Kb7 supporting promotion, Kxc8 capturing the rook, Nc6 escaping). In 2/7 cases, bishop moves to apparently active squares (Bg4, Bb3) abandoned critical defensive duties or chose the wrong diagonal. In 2/7 cases (Kd4, cxb5), the move addressed a secondary concern while ignoring the primary vulnerability. The common thread is that each position had essentially one urgent action (averaging 1.7 good moves available) and the player chose something else, conceding an average of 3016 centipawns.
analysis.move_pattern: Various piece types (mostly queen moves and bishop moves) that look active or forcing but fail to address the single most urgent tactical element; often checks or repositioning moves that don't capture/neutralize the critical threat
analysis.why_bad: Each move gives the opponent exactly one tempo to execute their tactical plan—whether escaping a trapped piece, promoting a pawn, capturing an undefended piece, or exploiting king exposure—transforming won or equal positions into draws or losses
sub_patterns: Aimless queen checks that allow the opponent's king to reach a perfect defensive square
Piece repositioning that abandons a critical defensive duty, leaving a piece unguarded
Greedy captures that ignore exposed king or time-critical threats
Bishop moves to wrong diagonals when one specific square was essential for defense

analysis.label: White plays a quiet non-forcing move instead of the critical pawn advance needed to challenge Black's powerfully centralized knight.
analysis.description: In all 5/5 positions, Black has a strongly posted knight (on d4, d4, e5, g4, e5 respectively) that dominates the position, and White has exactly one pawn advance available (c3, c3, f4, h3, f4) that would challenge, dislodge, or trap that knight. Instead of executing this urgent pawn challenge, White plays a quiet developing or repositioning move (Ne2, Be3, Qd2, Ng5, c3-as-structural) that gives Black a crucial tempo to consolidate the knight's position with moves like ...f5, ...c6, ...dxe5, or ...Nxe2. In 5/5 cases, only one move was within 50cp of optimal, and the average loss was 275cp. The refutations all exploit the extra tempo to either stabilize the knight permanently, trade it favorably, or undermine White's center now that the pawn challenge has been delayed.
analysis.move_pattern: Quiet piece development or passive pawn move by White instead of an aggressive pawn advance (f4, c3, h3) toward a centralized enemy knight
analysis.why_bad: The position demands an immediate pawn challenge to a dominant enemy knight, and any non-forcing move grants Black the tempo needed to consolidate the knight or neutralize the threat, squandering a large positional/tactical advantage.
sub_patterns: Developing piece instead of c3 vs Nd4
Quiet queen move instead of f4 vs Ne5
Speculative knight sortie instead of h3 vs Ng4
Structural pawn move instead of f4 vs Ne5

analysis.label: Playing a reasonable-looking but non-urgent quiet move when the position demands one specific immediate action, catastrophically wasting the critical tempo.
analysis.description: This feature fires on positions where only 1-2 moves work (avg 1.4 good moves) and the player chooses a superficially logical quiet move—piece repositioning, prophylactic pawn push, or positional improvement—while ignoring the position's single urgent demand. In 7/7 positions, the move played appears strategically motivated (Bb2 repositions to long diagonal, a4 prevents b5, Bd4 centralizes, Rb8 attacks b7, h5 restrains g4, Qf8 'defends' kingside, Kf3 'centralizes') but fatally wastes the one tempo needed for the critical action. The refutations in 5/7 cases exploit the specific defensive or offensive function abandoned by the tempo loss—White's king reaches a blockade square (Bb2→Kf2-e3), Black captures an undefended pawn (Rb8→Rxc4, Kf3→Rxg5), or the opponent exploits newly created weaknesses (h5→Ng5, Qf8→Bxf6/Rb8+). The positions share extremely narrow margins where the critical move was often non-obvious (e3 push, Bh6 not Bd4, Kg3 not Kf3, Ra1 not Rb8).
analysis.move_pattern: Quiet non-forcing moves (piece repositioning, flank pawn pushes, king walks to wrong square) in positions requiring one specific immediate action
analysis.why_bad: The single wasted tempo allows the opponent to establish a critical defense (blockade, king escape) or exploit a newly undefended target, because the position has razor-thin margins where only 1-2 moves maintain the evaluation
sub_patterns: Piece repositioning when a pawn must advance immediately (Bb2 vs e3)
Piece moving to wrong square when one specific square is critical (Bd4 vs Bh6, Kf3 vs Kg3)
Prophylactic flank pawn push ignoring urgent tactical vulnerability (a4, h5)
Rook/Queen moving to attack secondary target while abandoning key file or defensive duty (Rb8, Qf8)

analysis.label: Moves that appear constructive or prophylactic but ignore urgent tactical demands while creating new vulnerabilities in the player's own position.
analysis.description: This feature fires on moves where a player makes an apparently purposeful but ultimately non-constructive move that worsens their own position by creating tactical vulnerabilities or removing critical defensive resources. In 6/7 positions, the move ignored an urgent concrete need (defending a hanging piece, supporting a critical pawn, addressing an active enemy piece). In 5/7 cases, the move was tagged as tempo_loss—the player spent a move on something that either didn't help or actively hurt. The moves share a 'self-weakening' quality: f6 removed a critical defensive pawn, b3 allowed a stronger enemy pawn advance, Rb7+ drove the opponent's king to its ideal blockading square, Bh6 surrendered a bishop for nothing, Rf3 removed a tactical justification that previously kept an enemy capture in check, Ka2 exposed the king to an open file, and Kg2 walked into a mating net while leaving the queen hanging. In all cases, good alternatives existed (avg 2.3 good moves available) that addressed the position's concrete demands.
analysis.move_pattern: Mixed piece types (2 king moves, 2 pawn pushes, 2 rook moves, 1 bishop move); typically quiet non-forcing moves to squares that appear safe or useful but create tactical holes
analysis.why_bad: These moves ignore the position's most urgent tactical requirement—whether that's defending a piece, supporting a critical pawn structure, or addressing an active enemy threat—while simultaneously creating a new vulnerability (exposed king, hanging piece, structural weakness, or lost defensive resource) that the opponent can immediately exploit with a concrete refutation.
sub_patterns: King moves to exposed squares while ignoring hanging pieces (Kg2, Ka2)
Pawn advances that remove critical defensive structure (f6, b3)
Piece moves that eliminate their own tactical justification (Rf3, Bh6)
Pointless checks that improve opponent's piece placement (Rb7+)

analysis.label: Moves that waste a crucial tempo on non-forcing play when the position demands immediate concrete action.
analysis.description: In all 6/6 positions, the player makes a superficially reasonable move—a piece repositioning, a prophylactic king move, a defensive placement, or an 'improving' push—but fails to execute the one forcing continuation the position demands. In 4/6 cases, the correct move involved an immediate forcing action (capture Nxg7 with piece win, Rg2 threatening Rxg3+ with check, e5 grabbing space and restricting opponent, g4 driving away a piece). In 5/6 cases, the error gives the opponent a free tempo to contest a file (Kb8→Rfd1), advance passed pawns (Rh2→c5), capture an undefended pawn (e4→Nxe4), exploit structural weakness (g5→Rc1/Qxf5), or retreat a threatened piece (Ng3→Bf8). The positions share extremely narrow margins (avg 1.7 good moves) where a single wasted tempo converts a winning/equal position into one that is equal/losing.
analysis.move_pattern: Various piece types moved to non-threatening squares (retreats, sideways shuffles, or one-square-off placements) when a forcing alternative existed
analysis.why_bad: Each move fails to create an immediate threat, giving the opponent a free tempo to neutralize the player's positional trumps (passed pawns, file control, piece activity, structural integrity) or execute their own concrete plan unchallenged
sub_patterns: Piece retreat from dominant outpost (Ng3 from h5)
Unnecessary king shuffle when development is urgent (Kb8)
Passive rook placement when active queen play was needed (Rd1)
One-square-off rook placement missing tempo-gaining check (Rh2 vs Rg2)
Self-weakening pawn advance removing defensive duties (g5)
Pawn push to tactically vulnerable square (e4 capturable by knight)

analysis.label: Playing a quiet positional or preparatory move in a position that demands immediate concrete tactical action to address king safety or piece vulnerabilities.
analysis.description: This feature fires on moves where the player chooses a slow, non-urgent action (typically a pawn push or quiet piece repositioning) while ignoring an immediate tactical demand in the position. In 8/10 positions, king safety is the exploited weakness — either the player's own king is exposed/uncastled and needs urgent attention, or the opponent has hanging pieces requiring immediate capture. The blunders share a common quality: they would be reasonable in a calm position but catastrophically miss the tactical urgency of the moment. Examples include pawn pushes (g6, g4, a5, b6) when development or concrete piece action was critical, wrong recaptures (fxe6, fxe3) that weaken king shelter or bury pieces, and quiet piece placements (Rac8, Rf4, Bd3) that ignore immediate tactical shots. The average cp_loss of 1293 and only 1.8 good moves available confirm these are critical positions where precision was essential but the player chose long-term thinking over immediate necessity.
analysis.move_pattern: Predominantly pawn advances (6/10) or quiet non-forcing piece moves (4/10); no checks, no captures of attacked pieces, no moves addressing the most urgent threat in the position
analysis.why_bad: The position contains an immediate tactical vulnerability (exposed king, hanging piece, discovered attack threat, or forced sequence) that the opponent can exploit on the very next move, but the played move does nothing to address this concrete danger, giving the opponent a free tempo to execute the punishment.
sub_patterns: Slow pawn push while king remains uncastled/exposed (g6, g4, a5, b6)
Wrong recapture that weakens king shelter or buries pieces (fxe6, fxe3)
Quiet piece move ignoring an immediate tactical shot (Rac8, Rf4, Bd3)
King move walking into a tactical pattern (Kb7)

analysis.label: Natural-looking moves in critical positions that ignore the one specific tactical demand, resulting in major evaluation losses.
analysis.description: This feature activates on positions where the player makes a 'natural' or 'routine' move (developing a rook, centralizing a piece, castling, capturing material) while ignoring the position's primary tactical requirement. In 8/10 positions, there were very few good moves available (avg 1.7), indicating critical positions demanding precision. The moves appear logical in general chess terms — Re3 attacks a queen, Rad1 develops a rook, O-O secures the king, Nxe4 wins a pawn, Nd6 centralizes a knight — but each ignores a concrete tactical vulnerability: an undefended piece (Rad1 leaves Bg5 hanging, Rd3 leaves e4 undefended in 2/10), a fork opportunity for the opponent (O-O allows Ne7+ in 1/10), a discovered attack (Qd3 allows Nxb3+ in 1/10), or a forcing continuation that was the only way to maintain the position (Re3, Qc8, g5 in 3/10). The average cp_loss of 325 confirms these are serious blunders, and 7/10 positions involved missed tactics or tempo loss as tagged motifs.
analysis.move_pattern: Any piece type moving to a seemingly natural/active square; no consistent geometric direction; includes captures, development moves, castling, and pawn advances
analysis.why_bad: The moves prioritize secondary positional goals (developing, centralizing, capturing material, king safety) while failing to address the one critical tactical demand of the position — leaving a piece undefended, allowing a fork/discovered attack, or missing the only forcing continuation that maintains advantage
sub_patterns: Developing a piece while leaving another piece tactically vulnerable
Capturing material with an attacking piece that was more valuable in its current role
Making a routine positional move (castling, pawn push, rook lift) when only a specific forcing move maintains the evaluation
Placing a piece on a seemingly strong square that is immediately exploitable

analysis.label: Quiet, non-forcing moves in overwhelmingly won endgame positions that waste tempo instead of immediately executing the winning plan.
analysis.description: This feature fires on positions where one side has a massive material or positional advantage (often with forced mates available) but plays a slow, non-urgent move rather than directly advancing the winning plan. In 9/9 cases, the position is an endgame with a large advantage (avg eval ~+900cp or forced mate). The moves are consistently 'improving' or 'consolidating' rather than immediately decisive: pawn pushes that don't contribute to the main plan (f5, a6, b3, h3, c3 in 5/9 positions), piece relocations to attractive but non-critical squares (Nf3, Nf5 in 2/9), or king moves that are marginally less efficient than alternatives (Kf6, Kg7 in 2/9). The analyses overwhelmingly tag these as 'tempo_loss' (7/9 positions). The two catastrophic blunders (f5 losing 9010cp, Nf5 losing 9077cp) specifically removed critical constraints on the opponent's king, allowing it to escape a mating net or invade the queenside. Even the milder cases (b3, h3, c3) share the same DNA: treating a won position as needing preparation rather than execution.
analysis.move_pattern: Quiet (non-checking, non-capturing) moves in all directions—pawn advances, knight repositions, king walks—that don't create immediate threats or advance passed pawns toward promotion
analysis.why_bad: These moves waste critical tempo in positions where the opponent's king is exposed or the winning plan requires immediate execution. The tempo allows the opponent's king to centralize, escape a mating net, or capture material that dissolves the advantage. The correct moves almost always involve either advancing the key passed pawn, activating the king toward the critical zone, or maintaining piece placement that restricts the opponent's king.
sub_patterns: Wrong pawn advance that fails to restrict opponent's king (f5 instead of e5)
Prophylactic pawn moves when immediate action is needed (a6, b3, h3)
One-square pawn push instead of two-square push (c3 instead of c4)
Knight relocation to 'pretty' square abandoning critical defensive duties (Nf5)
Marginally less efficient king path in won K+P endgames (Kg7 vs Kg6)

analysis.label: Passive piece repositioning in positions demanding immediate concrete action (captures or pawn breaks), wasting a critical tempo.
analysis.description: This feature fires on quiet, non-forcing piece maneuvers played in positions where the concrete tactical or structural demands are urgent and narrow. In 8/10 positions, the correct move was a capture or direct confrontation (dxe5, cxb4, Nxe5, Nxh4, Nxb5, exd5, dxc4, Be6 challenging a piece), while the played move was a passive repositioning (Bh2, Bg3, Ne2, Bd3, Rb2, Be7) or a misguided activation (Qe5, Qe3, Qc2, Ne6) that ignored the critical tension. The positions typically feature unresolved pawn tension (7/10 cases), where one side must capture NOW or lose the opportunity. The average cp_loss of 1160 and only 1.8 good moves available confirm these are narrow critical moments where tempo is everything. The blunders all share the characteristic of being 'natural-looking' moves that would be reasonable in a slower position but are catastrophic when the position's tactical clock is ticking.
analysis.move_pattern: Non-capturing, non-checking piece moves (bishops, knights, queens, rooks) to seemingly reasonable squares, typically retreats or lateral repositioning rather than engaging the critical tension
analysis.why_bad: These moves waste a crucial tempo in positions with urgent concrete demands—unresolved pawn tension, imminent threats, or tactical opportunities that expire in one move—allowing the opponent to seize the initiative, break through, or consolidate an advantage that was previously exploitable
sub_patterns: Bishop retreats from active diagonal to passive square (Bh2, Bg3, Bd3, Be7)
Knight repositioning away from critical control square (Ne2, Ne6)
Queen centralization ignoring structural/defensive urgency (Qe3, Qe5, Qc2)
Rook move to quiet square while kingside burns (Rb2)

analysis.label: A passive, non-forcing move (usually a king move to an exposed square) in a position where only one urgent defensive resource exists, resulting in immediate tactical punishment.
analysis.description: This feature fires on positions where the player makes a quiet, non-forcing move while the position demands a single specific concrete response to a critical threat. In 7/9 cases, the move is a king move to a more exposed or tactically vulnerable square (Kh6, Kg7, Kh7, Kf3, Ke4). The remaining cases are quiet pawn or piece moves (a5, h6, Bb2) that similarly ignore urgent threats. The positions share extremely narrow margins—averaging only 1.6 good moves available—meaning essentially one correct answer exists. The threats being ignored include passed pawn promotion requiring blockade (3/9: a5, Kg7 needed Rd8/Bd8), immediate checkmate patterns (4/9: Kh6 into Rh7#, Ke4 into Qf5#, h6 allowing Qh5+ mate, Kh6 allowing Nf5+), and critical defensive requirements (2/9: Bb2 abandoning pin defense, Kf3 exposing to pawn checks). The average cp_loss of 4437 is extreme, with 5/9 positions resulting in immediate or near-immediate checkmate after the blunder.
analysis.move_pattern: Quiet non-capturing, non-checking moves; predominantly king moves (7/9) to forward or lateral squares that increase exposure; also includes passive pawn pushes and piece retreats to inactive squares
analysis.why_bad: These moves fail because they completely ignore the single most urgent demand of the position (blockading a promotion, avoiding a mating net, maintaining a critical defense). The king walks to squares controlled by opponent's pieces, or the quiet move wastes the one tempo needed to address an immediate lethal threat in positions with essentially no margin for error.
sub_patterns: King moves to squares attacked by opponent's rook/queen/knight creating immediate mate
Pawn or piece moves ignoring an advanced passed pawn requiring immediate blockade
King advances to exposed central square vulnerable to checks along diagonals/files
Prophylactic-looking moves in positions demanding concrete tactical responses

analysis.label: Making a superficially active or natural-looking move that abandons a critical defensive responsibility, allowing the opponent to exploit the newly created vulnerability.
analysis.description: In all 4/4 positions, the player makes a move that appears positionally motivated (centralizing a king, capturing a pawn, contesting an open file, advancing a pawn) but fatally neglects a concrete defensive need. In position 3, Kd4 centralizes the king but moves it away from blockading the a-pawn's promotion. In position 12, Re1 contests the e-file but leaves the f7-rook hanging to a simple king capture. In position 15, a4 advances the pawn but fixes it as a target while leaving Black's b4-pawn alive to become a passer. In position 4, exd4 grabs material but fails to address the king's urgent need to flee via queenside pawn breaks. All positions were already worse (4/4), and in each case the correct approach was more patient or defensive—maintaining a rook on its defensive file, keeping the king near the critical zone, or exchanging to neutralize threats. The common error is prioritizing apparent improvement over the position's most concrete defensive requirement.
analysis.move_pattern: Various piece types (king, pawn, rook) making forward or lateral moves that look naturally improving but vacate a critical defensive post or create a new target
analysis.why_bad: Each move abandons a specific defensive function (blockading a passer, protecting a piece, covering a promotion square, or eliminating an opponent's advanced pawn) in favor of apparent activity, allowing the opponent to immediately exploit the abandoned responsibility with tempo-gaining threats or simple captures
sub_patterns: King advancing away from critical defensive zone (passed pawn blockade)
Rook repositioning off a file where it defended another piece
Pawn advance creating a fixed target instead of exchanging to eliminate threats
Material capture ignoring urgent king safety needs

analysis.label: Moving a piece away from its critically needed defensive or blockading station when only one specific placement preserves the position.
analysis.description: In all 6 positions, the piece moves in the wrong direction—away from where it is critically needed—abandoning an essential defensive, blockading, or controlling function. In 5/6 cases, the correct move involved placing the piece on a specific square to maintain control of a vital area (Qf6 guarding g6, Nf8 heading to blockade on g6, Kh8 staying near g8 blockade, Ke6 blocking White's king penetration, Kb6 staying centralized). Instead, the played move retreats toward the periphery or a passive square (Qe8 to back rank, Nb6 to the edge, Kf8 away from blockade, Kf6 failing to control d6, Nh4 removing a critical f2 defender, Ka6 toward the board edge). In 6/6 positions, only 1-2 good moves existed (avg 1.2), indicating razor-thin margins where directional choice is decisive. The average cp_loss of 1961 reflects catastrophic consequences—4/6 positions swing from drawn/better to lost or mated.
analysis.move_pattern: Piece (King, Knight, or Queen) moves one square in the wrong direction—typically toward the edge, back rank, or away from a critical sector—when the only correct move was toward the center or toward the threatened area.
analysis.why_bad: The piece abandons its essential function (blockading a passed pawn, controlling a key invasion square, defending a critical pawn, or maintaining centralization), allowing the opponent immediate exploitation of the newly uncontrolled square or area with a forcing sequence.
sub_patterns: King retreats toward edge instead of centralizing in endgame
King moves away from pawn blockade square allowing promotion
Knight retreats to passive square abandoning critical defensive post
Queen retreats to back rank abandoning kingside defense

analysis.label: Playing a plausible-looking active move instead of the one uniquely precise continuation needed to exploit an exposed king.
analysis.description: This feature activates when a player faces a position with extremely narrow precision requirements (avg 1.2 good moves) involving a vulnerable opposing king, and chooses an 'almost right' active-looking move instead of the singular best continuation. In 4/4 positions, king safety is the central theme and the best move maximally exploits the opponent's king exposure. The errors include: blocking one's own mating piece by occupying its target square (Rf7+ blocking Bf7#, Position 1), placing a knight on the wrong square leaving a critical file unblocked (Nc5 vs Ne5, Position 2), playing a non-forcing queen centralization when immediate checks force mate (Qd2 vs Qh1+, Position 4), and making a slow pawn advance when an immediate rook invasion wins material before the king consolidates (c5 vs Rd3, Position 6). In all cases, the move played appears reasonable or aggressive on its face but catastrophically misses the precise tactical requirement, resulting in an average 4890cp loss.
analysis.move_pattern: Various piece types moving to plausible-looking active squares (checks, attacks on pieces, central placement, pawn breaks) that are NOT the uniquely correct forcing move against the exposed king
analysis.why_bad: Each move surrenders the critical tempo or square needed to exploit the opponent's king vulnerability—either blocking a mating piece, failing to block a checking file, missing forcing checks, or allowing the king to escape to safety before the decisive blow lands.
sub_patterns: Occupying the square another piece needs for checkmate
Knight to wrong square failing to block critical file
Non-forcing queen move when perpetual checks force mate
Slow pawn advance giving opponent king-consolidation tempo

analysis.label: Pieces move to seemingly active squares in endgames but abandon critical blockading or restraining duties, allowing opponent's king infiltration or passed pawn advance.
analysis.description: In 5/6 positions, the played move sends a piece (usually a knight or king) to a square that appears tactically or positionally appealing—targeting enemy pawns, centralizing, or attacking—but abandons the piece's essential restraining function. In Position 1, Nf6 looks centralized but leaves the knight hanging after a deflection check. In Position 4, Kxc6 captures material but moves the king two files from the critical kingside blockade zone (the correct Nxc6 keeps the king on d6). In Position 6, Nd7 moves the knight from its dominant e5 outpost toward apparent queenside targets but abandons restraint of the a-pawn. In Position 11, Nf2 targets g4 but ignores the imperative of challenging the dominant opposing knight with the king. In Position 15, Kg5 advances toward kingside pawns but abandons the f5 blockade, allowing White's king to seize e5. The punishment in 4/6 cases involves the opponent's king immediately infiltrating the abandoned key square or a passed pawn advancing unchecked.
analysis.move_pattern: Piece (knight or king) moves forward or sideways to an apparently active square, away from its current restraining/blockading post in the endgame
analysis.why_bad: The piece abandons its essential defensive or restraining role (blockading a passed pawn, controlling a key infiltration square, or maintaining coordination), allowing the opponent to exploit the abandoned responsibility through king penetration or pawn advance that the piece was specifically preventing
sub_patterns: Knight moves to 'active' outpost but becomes tactically vulnerable or offside (Nf6, Nd7, Nf2)
King moves toward apparent pawn targets but abandons critical blockade square (Kxc6, Kg5)
Piece targets enemy material instead of maintaining essential positional restraint

analysis.label: Playing an aggressive-looking or natural move that misses the single most forcing/concrete continuation in a critical position, wasting a decisive tempo.
analysis.description: This feature fires on positions where the player chooses a move that appears active or threatening but fails to address the most concrete tactical or defensive need. In 7/10 positions, there was only 1 good move available, indicating these are razor-sharp critical moments demanding precision. The pattern manifests in several ways: missing immediate captures in favor of threats (Qg7 threatening f7 instead of Qxh7 capturing it in position 3; fxe6 capturing a bishop instead of Rxb7 capturing the queen in position 6); missing forcing checks/forks for slow moves (f4 instead of Ng8+ check-fork in position 2); abandoning critical defensive duties for aggressive repositioning (Qg6 attacking the king instead of Qd2 covering g2 in position 7; Qd3 centralizing instead of Na3 concretely winning the e3 pawn in position 9); and placing pieces on natural-but-wrong squares (Rd7 attacking a7 instead of Rd8 with dual offensive/defensive purpose in positions 14-15; Kf7 exposing the king instead of Rf7 shielding it in position 10). The average cp_loss of 313 confirms these are severe mistakes where a single wasted tempo transforms winning or equal positions into lost ones.
analysis.move_pattern: Any piece moving to an aggressive or natural-looking square that fails to execute the most forcing available continuation (check, capture, or critical coordination), typically one rank/file away from the optimal square
analysis.why_bad: These moves waste a critical tempo in positions demanding immediate concrete action - the opponent uses the gifted tempo to either organize defenses against the missed tactic, launch a counterattack exploiting the piece's absence from its defensive post, or consolidate a position that was previously under existential pressure.
sub_patterns: Threatening a capture instead of making the winning capture (Qg7 vs Qxh7, fxe6 vs Rxb7)
Abandoning queen's defensive post for an aggressive foray (Qg6, Qd3 leaving g2/back-rank unguarded)
Placing rook on 7th rank targeting pawns instead of 8th rank for dual-purpose coordination (Rd7 vs Rd8)
Slow positional move missing a forcing check or fork (f4 vs Ng8+, Nb3 vs Nf3/Ne2)
King advance exposing itself when defensive regrouping was required (Kf7 vs Rf7)

analysis.label: Moves that pursue a secondary goal (attack, development, material) while ignoring the position's single most urgent demand.
analysis.description: This feature fires on positions where very few moves maintain the evaluation (avg 1.7 good moves), and the player selects a natural-looking, purposeful move that completely misses the critical task. In 4/6 cases, the urgent demand involves handling a passed pawn or blockade duty (Kd6 ignores Na8 blockade, Ra1 uses wrong piece as blockader, Rxa3 abandons d-file blockade, Bf4 misses Nd5 strike timing). In the remaining cases, pieces abandon critical defensive functions for offensive posturing (Ne5 removes the only h-file defender, Qb4 abandons protection of the d3 bishop). The moves all share surface plausibility—centralization, development, material gain, active appearance—but catastrophically fail to address the one thing the position demands. The extremely high average cp_loss (1838) reflects that these narrow positions punish misprioritization with devastating immediacy.
analysis.move_pattern: Various piece types move to plausible-looking squares (central, capturing, developing) while abandoning a critical defensive, blockading, or tactical function
analysis.why_bad: The position has one critical demand (blockade a passer, defend the king, strike tactically) with very few correct moves, and the chosen move pursues an attractive but non-urgent secondary goal, allowing the opponent's primary threat to become immediately decisive
sub_patterns: Piece abandons defensive post for offensive adventure (Ne5, Qb4)
Wrong piece assigned to blockade duty when superior blockader exists (Ra1)
Material greed over critical positional task (Rxa3)
Routine development when immediate tactical strike is required (Bf4)
King approaches danger instead of delegating to piece (Kd6)

analysis.label: Playing an obvious aggressive move (check, capture, or attack) that appears forcing but squanders a winning position by granting the opponent a critical defensive resource, when only one precise continuation maintained the advantage.
analysis.description: This feature fires on positions where the player chooses a superficially attractive aggressive move—typically a check, capture, or threatening centralization—over the single correct continuation in a critical, narrow position (avg 1.2 good moves available). In 5/9 positions, the blunder is a check or capture that looks forcing but actually allows the opponent an escape square (positions 1,2,4,5) or intermediate counter-tactic (position 6). In 2/9 positions, the error opens a line for the opponent (positions 3,7 - abandoning defense or opening a file). In 2/9 positions, the player makes a natural-looking positional move (centralization/repositioning) when a concrete tactical breakthrough was the only path (positions 8,9). The unifying thread is that all positions demanded exact calculation of a single narrow path, but the player defaulted to the most visually aggressive or natural-looking option. The correct moves are often more subtle: a discovered check instead of a direct one (position 5), capturing a different piece (position 6), keeping a file closed (position 7), or a quiet king move (position 8).
analysis.move_pattern: Queen checks/moves (4/9), knight captures/checks (3/9), pawn capture (1/9), knight centralization (1/9) — predominantly checks and captures that appear forcing
analysis.why_bad: The aggressive-looking move grants the opponent a critical resource: an escape square for the king (4/9), an intermediate check or tactic (2/9), an open file for counterattack (1/9), or simply wastes tempo when concrete action was required (2/9). In all cases, the position had only ~1 truly good move, and the player's instinct for 'most forcing' diverged from 'most precise.'
sub_patterns: Check that drives king toward safety instead of keeping it exposed (positions 1,2)
Material-gaining check/capture that lets king escape a mating net (positions 4,5)
Capture that enables opponent's intermediate tactical shot (position 6)
Recapture/move that opens a critical file for opponent's pieces (positions 3,7)
Natural positional move instead of the one concrete forcing breakthrough (positions 8,9)

analysis.label: Non-forcing preparatory or repositioning moves played in positions demanding one specific immediate concrete action.
analysis.description: This feature fires on positions where a player makes a non-forcing move (passive repositioning, slow preparation, or premature non-threatening advance) when the position urgently demanded one specific concrete action. In 6/8 positions, the primary tag is 'tempo_loss.' The average number of good moves available is only 1.6, indicating narrow critical positions where a single correct continuation existed. The correct moves were always more confrontational: immediate pawn breaks challenging key pieces (b4 in Position 1, c4 in Positions 5 and 12), direct tactical strikes (f4 in Position 8), prophylactic king safety (Kf7 in Position 9), piece activation (Bxa3 in Position 15), or developing moves (Nf6 in Position 6, e5 in Position 13). Instead, the played moves were all non-urgent alternatives—rook shuffles, queen repositioning, knight retreats, king walks, or structurally weakening pawn pushes—that gave the opponent time to neutralize the player's advantages or exploit newly created weaknesses.
analysis.move_pattern: Non-forcing moves of any piece type (rook, queen, knight, king, or pawn) that create no immediate threat, check, or capture in positions requiring concrete action
analysis.why_bad: These moves waste the critical tempo needed to execute the one available winning/equalizing plan, allowing the opponent to consolidate defenses, seize counterplay, or exploit tactical vulnerabilities that the slow move either created or failed to prevent.
sub_patterns: Passive piece repositioning instead of active counterplay (R1d2, Nb1, Qa5, Ka6)
Slow preparatory moves missing one-move tactical windows (Qd3 delaying c4)
Premature pawn advances creating structural/king-safety weaknesses without compensation (f4, g5)

analysis.label: King (or piece) moves to a seemingly natural adjacent square that wastes one critical tempo in a time-sensitive race or penetration attempt.
analysis.description: This feature fires on moves that lose exactly one critical tempo in positions where timing is paramount. In 6/8 positions, the move is a king move to a plausible-looking adjacent square that turns out to be the wrong direction or wrong timing. The pattern manifests as: Kb4 instead of Kb2 (longer path to pawn escort), Kg6 instead of Kh7 (extra move needed to reach g8), Kd4 instead of Kc5 (arrives at penetration square one tempo late), Ke5 instead of Kc7 (exposed central square instead of material recovery), Ke5 instead of Kc5 (wrong king direction). The non-king moves share the same logic: Rf2 wastes a move on an illusory attack when prophylaxis was needed (3/8), f4 advances the wrong pawn losing critical sequencing (5/8). In 6/8 positions, the tag 'tempo_loss' is explicitly identified as the primary motif, and the average cp_loss of 1338 reflects how in razor-thin endgame races, one wasted move transforms draws into losses or wins into draws.
analysis.move_pattern: King moves one square toward center or along a non-optimal path; occasionally a piece/pawn move that looks active but loses the critical tempo
analysis.why_bad: In time-critical positions (pawn races, king penetration attempts, promotion threats), one wasted tempo is the difference between success and failure—the opponent's counter-threats arrive exactly one move sooner than the player's plan completes
sub_patterns: King centralizes when it should take a more direct path toward a specific target square
King moves before a pawn push when the pawn should advance first (move order error)
Active-looking move chosen over essential prophylactic/direct move

analysis.label: Playing a non-urgent or tempo-wasting move in a critical position where only one or two precise responses address the position's most pressing tactical demand.
analysis.description: This feature fires on positions where the player makes a move that fundamentally ignores the most critical requirement of the position, opting instead for a passive, retreating, or tangential continuation when immediate precise action was demanded. In 9/9 positions, the move played either retreated a piece wastefully (Ng8, Bc8 back to starting squares), made a superficial/premature forcing move (Qg5+ driving the king to safety, Qxe6+ choosing the wrong check), pushed a pawn that weakened rather than helped (f3, b5, gxf5), or played a 'quiet improving' move when only forcing play maintained the position (Qd2, Ra8). The average number of good moves available was only 1.4, confirming these are razor-sharp positions requiring unique precision. All 9 positions involved either exposed kings or sharp tactical imbalances where initiative/tempo was paramount. The common thread across all analyses is that the played move surrendered the initiative or wasted a critical tempo, allowing the opponent to seize control of the position's key feature (an open file, a weak king, a tactical shot).
analysis.move_pattern: No single geometric pattern; includes backward piece retreats, irrelevant pawn pushes, passive queen repositions, and imprecise checks/captures - all sharing the quality of being non-critical in critical moments
analysis.why_bad: These moves waste a crucial tempo or surrender the initiative in positions that demand immediate precise action on the most critical issue (contesting an open file, executing a tactic, addressing king safety). With only ~1-2 good moves available, any deviation from the critical path causes catastrophic evaluation drops because the opponent seizes the initiative permanently.
sub_patterns: Piece retreating to starting square (Ng8, Bc8) when forward action needed
Superficial/imprecise check that helps opponent's king escape (Qg5+, Qxe6+)
Pawn move that weakens own king or ignores critical threat (f3, gxf5, b5)
Passive piece repositioning when only forcing moves maintain position (Qd2, Ra8)

analysis.label: Pieces or king move toward the board's rim/edge, abandoning critical central or defensive responsibilities at a moment when immediate active measures were required.
analysis.description: In 6/7 positions, the blundering move sends a piece toward the h-file or board edge (Kh6, Kg5, Kh1, Nh5, Rb1 toward corner, a6 on a-file) while the correct move demanded central activity or maintaining a key post (Ne5, Ra2+, Kf5/Ke5, Kg1, Bh3). In every case, the position had extremely narrow defensive requirements (avg 2.0 good moves), and the played move wasted the critical tempo needed to address an immediate tactical threat. The refutations consistently exploit the vacated central control: Qe3+ after Kh6 (2/7), Re1+ back-rank exploitation after Rb1 (4/7), Rf1 seizing the f-file after Kg5 (7/7), Qa4+ diagonal fork after Nxc4 (8/7), e5 pawn break after a6 (13/7), g3-g2 promotion after Kh1 (14/7), and Ne5 tempo attacks after Nh5 (15/7). The common thread is that plausible-looking peripheral moves hand the opponent a free tempo to execute their winning plan.
analysis.move_pattern: Piece or king moves toward the h-file, back rank corner, or board rim (laterally or diagonally away from center), typically non-forcing and non-capturing
analysis.why_bad: The move abandons the one critical defensive function the position demanded (blockading a pawn, controlling a key file/diagonal, maintaining central presence), giving the opponent a decisive tempo to execute a tactical strike or promotional advance that the correct move would have prevented.
sub_patterns: King retreats to h-file corner (Kh6, Kh1, Kg5) when it should stay centrally active or on a blockade square
Piece moves to rim (Nh5, Rb1) abandoning central defensive coordination
Slow flank pawn push (a6) wasting tempo when centralization was the only resource

analysis.label: Playing a slow, non-forcing move that ignores the position's most urgent demand, allowing the opponent to execute their primary threat unopposed.
