analysis.description: This feature fires on moves that catastrophically misjudge positional urgency by spending a tempo on a secondary concern while the position's critical demand goes unaddressed. In 5/7 positions, the blunder involved king safety being compromised (O-O-O castling into an attack, fxe3 opening the f-file toward own king, a3 ignoring diagonal threats to the king, Nfd7 removing a defender of kingside pawns, h4 ignoring a passed pawn racing toward promotion). In 6/7 cases, the analyses explicitly identify tempo_loss as the core mechanism. The moves range from passive retreats (Bb3 instead of forcing Bb5+), to irrelevant flank pawn pushes (h4, a3), to moving well-placed pieces to inferior squares (Ng5 abandoning the e6 outpost), but all share the characteristic of being non-forcing moves played in positions where only one or two moves were acceptable (avg good moves: 1.6). The extreme average cp_loss of 1521 reflects that these positions were at critical inflection points where a single wasted tempo proved decisive.
analysis.move_pattern: Non-forcing moves of varied piece types (pawn pushes, knight retreats/jumps, bishop retreats, castling) that fail to address the board's primary tension point
analysis.why_bad: Each position had one critical demand (stopping a passed pawn, maintaining a key defender, generating immediate counterplay, keeping lines closed) and the move spent the tempo on an irrelevant or secondary concern, granting the opponent the crucial tempo needed to execute their winning plan
sub_patterns: Passive piece retreats when forcing moves available (Bb3 vs Bb5+)
Flank pawn pushes ignoring central/major threats (h4, a3)
Moving the wrong piece or removing a key defender (Nfd7 vs Nbd7, Ng5 from e6)
Self-destructive pawn captures that open lines toward own king (fxe3)
Premature castling into opponent's prepared attack (O-O-O)

analysis.label: Playing a tempting-looking active or material-gaining move that abandons the one essential defensive task in a position with very few good options.
analysis.description: In 7/7 positions, the player faced a critical juncture where only 1-2 moves were acceptable (avg 1.6 good moves), and each position demanded a specific defensive action: maintaining a blockade (g6 abandoned king blockade of c-pawn), preserving king shelter (gxf5 removed the g4 shield, h4 wasted tempo to evacuate the king), keeping a piece on its critical defensive square (Qf5 left d3 where it covered b1/c3, Qxb2 removed the queen from back-rank defense, Rf2 went to the wrong file instead of challenging the enemy rook on g6), or finding the unique tactical save (d8=N+ instead of Rf8+ enabling perpetual). In every case, the chosen move appeared superficially reasonable—gaining material (Qxb2, gxf5), creating counterplay (g6, h4), or delivering check (d8=N+)—but fatally neglected the position's single overriding requirement. The astronomical average cp_loss of 6719 reflects that these positions have razor-thin margins where one wrong move converts a survivable position into forced mate or decisive material loss.
analysis.move_pattern: Diverse piece types and directions (pawn pushes, queen captures/repositioning, rook moves, promotions), but all move AWAY from the critical defensive task—either physically relocating a piece from its essential square or structurally removing a defensive element
analysis.why_bad: Each move abandons the single critical defensive requirement of the position in favor of an appealing but irrelevant alternative, and because only 1-2 moves are viable, any deviation is catastrophic—the opponent immediately exploits the unattended vulnerability (exposed king, unstoppable promotion, back-rank weakness)
sub_patterns: Pawn push abandoning blockade/shelter duty (h4, g6, gxf5)
Queen relocation away from critical defensive coordination (Qf5, Qxb2)
Piece placed on wrong square/wrong tactical choice when only one resource saves (Rf2 vs Rg2, d8=N+ vs Rf8+)

analysis.label: Quiet, natural-looking moves that fail to address the position's most urgent tactical requirement, when a forcing or active resolution was necessary.
analysis.description: This feature fires on positions where the player makes a seemingly logical but non-forcing move (king retreat, rook development, pawn advance, aimless check) while ignoring the critical tactical demand of the position. In 4/7 positions, the best move was a forcing action—typically a capture that eliminates a dangerous attacking piece (Rxf2 in positions 3 and 7) or an exchange that resolves unsustainable tension (dxc5 in position 14, Qb4+ forcing material gain in position 10). In 3/7 positions, the best moves maintained a critical defensive post or addressed an immediate threat (keeping the king on c6 in position 5, avoiding knight check squares in position 4, or countering a dangerous knight with g5 in position 15). The played moves all share the characteristic of being 'one move too slow'—they address secondary concerns (king safety appearance, piece placement, space) while the position's true urgency lies in an immediate tactical resolution that, once missed, allows the opponent to execute a devastating tactical blow (discovered attacks in 2/7, tempo-gaining checks in 2/7, central breakthroughs in 2/7, forced material gain in 1/7).
analysis.move_pattern: Quiet non-forcing moves (king retreats, rook lifts, pawn advances, non-gaining checks) when captures or precise forcing moves were required
analysis.why_bad: The position demands immediate forced play (capturing a key attacker, resolving central tension, or making a precisely calculated forcing check) but the player instead makes a 'consolidating' move that gives the opponent a free tempo to execute their tactical threat—whether a discovered attack, a fork, a central breakthrough, or a king invasion.
sub_patterns: King moves to tactically vulnerable squares (discovered check diagonals, knight-check squares)
Aimless checks that drive opponent's king to safety without material gain
Passive piece development ignoring unresolved central tension
Flank pawn advances ignoring critical central/king safety issues

analysis.label: Moving or leaving a bishop on a square where an enemy knight profitably captures it, typically causing structural damage upon the forced pawn recapture.
analysis.description: In all 8 positions, the key mistake involves a bishop being placed on or left on a square within an enemy knight's capture range. The knight captures are either the primary refutation (5/8 positions: Nxg6, Nxf4, Nxg3, Nxg6, Nxe6) or a strong secondary punishment (3/8: Nxg3, Nxb3 twice). The critical consequence is that the forced pawn recapture (fxg6, hxg3, exf4, fxe6, axb3) creates structural damage—doubled pawns, opened files toward the king, or removal of key pawn defenders. Specific instances include: Bg3 allowing Nxg3 damaging the kingside (2/8), Bb3 allowing Nxb3 creating doubled b-pawns (2/8), Bg6 allowing Nxg6 fxg6 opening lines against the king (2/8), Be6 allowing Nxe6 fxe6 with Qh5+ (1/8), and Ngf3 allowing Nxf4 exf4 Bxf2+ (1/8). The common error is treating the bishop retreat/placement as a quiet positional decision while overlooking that the knight capture fundamentally alters the pawn structure and creates tactical vulnerabilities.
analysis.move_pattern: Bishop (or piece) placed on a square within one knight-hop of an active enemy knight, where the capture forces a pawn recapture creating structural weakness
analysis.why_bad: The knight capture forces a pawn recapture that either doubles pawns, opens critical files/diagonals toward the king, or removes key pawn defenders—transforming what appears to be a simple piece trade into a structural catastrophe or tactical combination.
sub_patterns: Bishop retreats to g3 where Nh5 captures it (hxg3 damages kingside)
Bishop retreats to b3 where Na5 captures it (axb3 doubles pawns)
Bishop placed on g6/e6 where centralized knight captures with fxg6/fxe6 opening king position
Ignoring knight's ability to capture a bishop elsewhere (Nxf4 exf4 opening diagonal)

analysis.label: Aggressive-looking pawn advances or bishop developments that remove a critical defender from a pawn, leaving it hanging for the opponent's queen to capture.
analysis.description: In 6/7 positions, the player makes a move that appears natural and aggressive—gaining space, developing a piece, or attacking the opponent's queen—but fatally removes a piece or pawn from a critical defensive duty. The most common sub-pattern involves leaving the g2 pawn undefended (3/7: Bd3 removes bishop from f1's guard of g2, f4 removes f3 pawn's guard of g2, Bc4 removes bishop from f1's guard of g2), while other positions involve the c-pawn abandoning defense of d3 or d4 (3/7: c4 leaves d4 hanging, c4 leaves d3 hanging). In nearly every case, the opponent's actively-placed queen immediately exploits the undefended target, often with check or winning material. The player's intent is consistently to gain tempo by attacking the opponent's queen or seize space, but they overlook that the moved piece/pawn was performing an essential defensive function.
analysis.move_pattern: Pawn advances (c4, f4, c5) or bishop development from f1 (Bd3, Bc4) that vacate a square or diagonal previously defending a critical pawn, typically g2 or d3/d4
analysis.why_bad: The moved piece/pawn was the sole defender of a critical pawn (usually g2 or a central pawn), and removing it allows the opponent's queen to immediately capture the undefended target, often winning material or creating devastating threats against the exposed king
sub_patterns: Bishop leaves f1 exposing undefended g2 pawn to queen capture (Bd3, Bc4)
f-pawn advances from f2/f3 leaving g2 undefended or opening diagonal to hanging piece
c-pawn advances removing defense of adjacent d-pawn (c4 leaves d3/d4 hanging)

analysis.label: Moving a piece away from its essential defensive post to pursue a slower or irrelevant plan while the opponent has immediate threats.
analysis.description: In 3/4 positions, the blundering move explicitly removes a piece from a square where it was performing a vital defensive function: the f8 rook guarding against a kingside breakthrough via g6 (Position 1), the d6 bishop blockading a lethal e6 passed pawn from advancing to e7 (Position 10), and the king wasting tempo on f7 instead of activating the queen to maintain defensive coordination (Position 15). In Position 6, the rook 'activates' to d6 but lands on a square controlled by the opponent's dominant piece, fitting the broader pattern of prioritizing apparently active piece placement over concrete positional requirements. In all 4/4 cases, the player chose what appeared to be an improving or ambitious move while ignoring the opponent's primary, more urgent threat. The refutations in every case immediately exploit the abandoned responsibility: the kingside collapses (Position 1), the rook is captured (Position 6), the pawn promotes (Position 10), and the knight executes a winning maneuver (Position 15).
analysis.move_pattern: A major or minor piece (rook, bishop, or king) moves away from a critical square—typically laterally or diagonally—leaving an opponent's primary threat uncontested
analysis.why_bad: The piece was the sole guardian against the opponent's most dangerous threat; removing it grants the opponent a free tempo to execute their primary tactical or strategic plan without resistance, causing immediate and catastrophic evaluation drops.
sub_patterns: Rook leaves kingside file to double on queenside while king is under attack
Bishop abandons blockade square of advanced passed pawn for 'active' placement
King makes purposeless move instead of developing pieces to maintain defensive coordination
Rook advances to aggressive-looking rank but lands en prise to opponent's well-placed piece

analysis.label: Playing a natural-looking but non-critical move in a razor-thin position where only one or two precise moves maintain the evaluation.
analysis.description: This feature fires on positions where the margin for error is extremely narrow (avg 1.8 good moves available) and the player chooses a move that appears purposeful or reasonable but fatally ignores the single most urgent demand of the position. In 6/11 cases only one move was within 50cp of best play, and the average cp_loss of 2715 (including several instances of allowing forced mate) reflects catastrophic consequences. The played moves are diverse in type—king moves (4/11), queen moves (4/11), rook moves (2/11), bishop/pawn (1 each)—but all share the pattern of pursuing a secondary objective (grabbing material on a7/Position 9, attempting activity with Qc1/Position 5, passive development with Bd2/Position 11, roundabout checking with Rg8+/Position 4) while the position demanded a specific tactical resolution, defensive blockade, or precise piece placement. In 7/11 positions, tempo loss is explicitly identified as the core failing—the move either wastes time in a race or allows the opponent to seize initiative via the neglected threat.
analysis.move_pattern: Any piece type moving to a seemingly reasonable square that either abandons a critical defensive post, self-blocks a key retreat square, enters a tactically vulnerable location, or addresses a secondary concern in a position demanding one precise action
analysis.why_bad: The position has extremely narrow margins (often one correct move) and the played move ignores the single most urgent tactical or defensive requirement—whether that's blockading a passed pawn, staying off a dangerous diagonal/file, maintaining back-rank coverage, or executing the one forcing sequence that holds the position together. The move looks purposeful but addresses a lower-priority concern while the critical threat goes unanswered.
sub_patterns: Piece abandons critical defensive file/rank (Ra6, Qc1, Qxa7)
King steps onto dangerous square/diagonal (Kb7, Ke3, Kc5)
Piece self-blocks critical retreat square (Bd2, Rc2)
Inefficient route when direct path exists (Rg8+ vs Rh5+, h4 vs Kb2)

analysis.label: Playing forcing-looking moves (especially queen checks) that waste tempo or allow the opponent a critical defensive resource.
analysis.description: This feature fires on moves that appear aggressive or forcing—predominantly queen checks—but actually squander the position's advantage by granting the opponent time, better king placement, or critical interposition opportunities. Of the 13 top-activating positions, 8/13 are queen checks that fail tactically: some allow the opponent's king to walk to a safer square (Qf4+→Ke3, Qb4+→Ke3-Kd2, Qd6+→Kb7 breaking perpetual), others permit interpositions that break mating nets (Qe6+→Qc6 blocks, Qf6+→Nd6 blocks, Qe4+→Qe6+ counter-check interposition), and one simply results in the king returning to its original square (Qd8+→Kh3→Kh4). The remaining 5/13 positions share the same tempo-loss pathology without being checks: ignoring an immediate promotion threat (Nf4, Qe2 in positions 1 and 7), making a passive pawn move instead of a concrete breakthrough (f6), abandoning defensive coordination (Qb3), or repositioning a piece away from critical duties (Rf5). The average 1.7 good moves available confirms these are positions demanding precision where the 'natural-looking active move' is a trap.
analysis.move_pattern: Queen (or piece) moves that deliver check or appear forcing, typically along files/diagonals where the opponent can interpose or the king can improve its position
analysis.why_bad: The moves either (1) allow interpositions that neutralize attacks, (2) drive the opponent's king to safer squares, (3) waste critical tempo when an urgent concrete threat must be addressed, or (4) abandon defensive coordination for illusory activity—all cases where apparent forcing moves are actually the losing choice.
sub_patterns: Queen check allowing defensive interposition on the checking line
Queen check driving opponent king to a safer square
Ignoring critical promotion/mating threat for speculative activity
Purposeless check where king simply returns (tempo triangulation fails)

analysis.label: Superficially active or natural-looking moves that catastrophically fail to address the position's single most urgent requirement.
analysis.description: This feature fires on moves that appear plausible—checks, piece development, centralization, contesting files—but ignore what the position actually demands, resulting in massive evaluation collapses (avg 4375cp loss). In 3/9 cases, the king drifted toward the board edge in KR vs K endgames when centralization was essential. In 3/9 cases, bishops were moved to active-looking squares (Bf4, Be6, Bb4+) that removed critical defenders or walked into tactical motifs. In 2/9 cases, speculative checks (Qe8+, Bb4+) were played when quiet moves (perpetual check, Bc1#) were decisive. In 1/9 case, a 'normal' developing move (d4) was played while a queen on b1 threatened immediate checkmate. The best moves were typically quiet retreats (Kg1, Rc2, Bc1#), precise captures removing threats (Qxb1, Qxf8, Qxe6+), or centralizing moves—all addressing the ONE critical priority. The played moves consistently chose a secondary objective over the existential one.
analysis.move_pattern: Any piece type moving to an apparently active/natural square (checks, forward moves, file-contesting, development) when position demands specific quiet/defensive/tactical response
analysis.why_bad: The move fails to address the position's single most urgent need—whether that's staying centralized to avoid mating nets, maintaining a critical defender, securing a perpetual, or removing an immediate threat—causing a catastrophic tactical or strategic collapse.
sub_patterns: King drifting toward edge when centralization required (KR vs K)
Bishop leaving critical defensive post enabling invasion
Giving speculative check when quiet move wins/draws
Normal development ignoring immediate existential threat

analysis.label: Passive, non-urgent, or self-obstructing moves that waste a decisive tempo in positions requiring immediate concrete action.
analysis.description: This feature fires on positions where the player makes a move that fails to address the most urgent concrete demand, resulting in catastrophic tempo loss. The pattern manifests in several forms: retreating pieces to passive squares when active play is required (Bc8 retreating from d7, Qd8 returning to start square, Kh7 abandoning the dominant 6th rank - 3/10), pushing pawns on the wrong flank or at the wrong moment when the position demands immediate action elsewhere (h4 ignoring a passed pawn, b4 twice ignoring kingside pawn advancement or tactical exploitation - 3/10), self-obstructing own pieces by placing them on squares that block critical escape routes or counter-attack paths (c4 blocking Qc2 enabling a fork, Bg4 blocking Qg4 enabling a fork, Bd5 blocking the d-file rook - 3/10), and giving checks that drive the opponent's king toward safety rather than keeping it exposed (Qc3+ pushing the king toward c8 sanctuary - 1/10). In every case, the position had very few good moves available (avg 1.9), indicating razor-thin critical moments where a single wasted tempo proved fatal.
analysis.move_pattern: Mixed piece types and directions; predominantly retreats to back-rank/passive squares, wrong-flank pawn advances, or piece placements that obstruct friendly pieces' key squares
analysis.why_bad: The position demands one specific urgent action (exploiting a tactic, advancing a critical pawn, centralizing the king, or maintaining defensive coordination), and the played move ignores this demand entirely, gifting the opponent the tempo needed to execute their plan, consolidate a weakness, or begin an unstoppable threat.
sub_patterns: Piece retreats to passive back-rank squares (Bc8, Qd8, Kh7)
Irrelevant flank pawn pushes when center/other wing is critical (h4, b4, b4)
Self-obstructing moves that block own key escape/counter-attack squares (c4, Bg4, Bd5)
Checks that drive opponent's king toward safety rather than keeping it exposed (Qc3+)

analysis.label: Rook pawn advance (a- or h-pawn one square) that "asks the question" of an enemy piece when the position demands immediate central action or development.
analysis.description: All 4 positions feature a single-square rook pawn advance (h6, a6, a6, h3) intended to challenge an enemy minor piece on an active square (Bg5, Bb5, Bb5, Bg4). In every case (4/4), this tempo expenditure is punished because the challenged piece has a productive response: either a favorable capture that damages the defender's pawn structure (positions 7 and 15: Bxf6 wrecking kingside, Bxf3 creating doubled f-pawns) or a happy retreat to an equally good or better diagonal (position 12: Bd3 aiming at the king). In position 10, the a6 move chases the wrong piece entirely while Ng5 threatens a lethal f7 invasion. All analyses identify 'tempo_loss' as the primary motif (4/4), and in every case the correct move involved immediate central action (Bc7, e6, Bg4, d5) addressing the true positional or tactical priority rather than a prophylactic pawn push against a piece that doesn't mind being asked.
analysis.move_pattern: Rook pawn (a- or h-pawn) advancing one square to challenge an enemy minor piece on the 5th rank (or equivalent)
analysis.why_bad: The challenged piece has a favorable response (capture with structural damage, or retreat to a better square), while the tempo spent ignores a far more urgent positional or tactical priority in the center or regarding king safety.
sub_patterns: h-pawn push inviting a bishop capture on f3/f6 that wrecks pawn structure
a-pawn push chasing a bishop that retreats to an equally strong diagonal
Piece-kicking move that ignores an immediate tactical threat elsewhere

analysis.label: Aggressive piece moves to seemingly active squares instead of simply capturing an available central d-file pawn.
analysis.description: In 6/7 positions, the clearly best move was a queen capture on the d-file (Qxd5, Qxd4, or Qxd6), yet the player instead made an aggressive-looking piece sortie—typically to the b-file area (5/7 moves go to b4, b5, or b7). The played moves all prioritize apparent piece activity or attack over a straightforward material gain on the d-file. The resulting positions leave the aggressive piece tactically vulnerable: in Position 1, Nb4 falls to a Qa4+ fork; in Position 5, Nd4 is simply captured as a hanging piece; in Positions 7 and 12, Bb4 allows Qxg7 or Qb5+ queen forks; in Position 9, Qxb7 walks into Nd3+ knight forks. The common thread is that a simple, available central pawn capture was ignored in favor of a speculative attack that proves tactically unsound.
analysis.move_pattern: Minor piece or queen moving to b4/b5/b7 squares (or aggressive central advance), bypassing an uncontested d-file pawn capture
analysis.why_bad: The aggressive piece lands on an undefended or tactically vulnerable square, allowing the opponent to punish with forks (Qa4+, Qb5+, Nd3+), simple captures of the undefended piece, or exploitation of weaknesses the piece's departure creates—while the ignored d-pawn capture would have been safe and equalizing.
sub_patterns: Knight to b4/b5 allowing queen fork along a4-e8 diagonal
Bishop to b4 leaving it hanging to Qb5+ or abandoning kingside defense
Queen grabbing b7 pawn while underdeveloped, allowing knight forks
Pawn advance (e5) weakening f7 when Qxd6 was available

analysis.label: Non-forcing, secondary-objective moves played in positions where immediate decisive or forcing action was required.
analysis.description: This feature activates on moves that waste critical tempo by addressing secondary concerns when the position demands immediate, forcing play. In 7/7 analyzed positions, the played move was a quiet, non-forcing continuation (pawn capture of irrelevant material, piece repositioning, prophylactic pawn push, space-gaining advance) while the best moves were significantly more forcing - checks (Nc3+, Re1+), forcing pawn breaks (g5), critical captures resolving tension (Bxd3), or moves creating direct threats (Qa4 attacking a rook). The 'tempo_loss' tag appears in 6/7 analyses. The positions span endgames with passed pawns (where one specific advancing move was needed), middlegames with tactical tension (where resolving threats immediately was critical), and openings with piece tension (where exchanging/developing trumped prophylaxis). The common thread is that multiple good forcing continuations existed (avg 2.3 good moves), but the player chose a quiet alternative addressing a non-critical concern - capturing a side pawn during a mating attack, shuffling a bishop instead of breaking through, advancing the wrong pawn when a specific advance was decisive.
analysis.move_pattern: Quiet, non-forcing moves (pawn advances for space/prophylaxis, minor piece repositioning, captures of non-critical material) rather than checks, forcing captures, or direct threats
analysis.why_bad: These moves squander a critical tempo by pursuing secondary objectives (material cleanup, spatial gains, prophylaxis, piece repositioning) while the position's primary demand - advancing a decisive passed pawn, delivering forcing checks, resolving piece tension, or maintaining a critical defensive duty - goes unaddressed, allowing the opponent to consolidate or exploit the wasted time.
sub_patterns: Capturing irrelevant material during a mating/promotional attack
Passive piece repositioning instead of dynamic pawn breaks
Prophylactic pawn moves when immediate tactical resolution is required
Advancing the wrong pawn when a specific pawn must advance immediately
Moving a piece to an 'active' square while abandoning a critical defensive function

analysis.label: Non-forcing moves (typically queen repositions or slow pawn advances) played in positions where an immediate capture or forcing action was the only way to maintain the evaluation.
analysis.description: This feature activates on positions where the critical tempo is being squandered by playing a non-forcing move when an immediate concrete action (usually a capture) was required. In 5/7 mistake positions, the correct move was a capture (Qxg3, Qxe6, Nxd5) or a move forcing an immediate tactical resolution (f3 forcing Rxf3, b4 forcing cxb3), while the played move was a quieter repositioning move that gave the opponent a free tempo to execute their own threats. The played moves often look reasonable or even aggressive on the surface (Qd6 looks attacking, Qf3 looks centralizing, a4 creates a passed pawn) but fatally fail to address the position's most urgent tactical demand. The 'tempo_loss' tag appears in 7/8 positions, and 'missed_tactic' appears in 6/8 positions, confirming this is fundamentally about failing to play the most forcing move at the critical moment. Position 14 (Kg4, 0cp loss) represents the correct execution in a similar critical-tempo situation, validating that the feature recognizes these time-critical positions.
analysis.move_pattern: Non-capturing repositioning moves (queen to quiet/central squares, pawn advances one square, king walks) when a capture or two-square forcing advance was available
analysis.why_bad: These moves waste the critical tempo that the position demands, allowing the opponent to execute their own threats first—whether that's advancing a passed pawn to promotion, capturing an undefended piece, executing a tactical combination, or consolidating a defensive position.
sub_patterns: Queen retreats/repositions from active square to passive square (Qc7, Qf3 retreat)
Queen moves to seemingly active but tactically vulnerable square (Qb3, Qd6)
Slow pawn advance when immediate forcing advance available (a4 vs f3, b3 vs b4)
Non-capture when capture maintains critical tactical pressure (Qf3 vs Qxg3, Qf3 vs Qxe6)

analysis.label: Playing a natural-looking developing or repositioning move that ignores an immediate tactical vulnerability requiring urgent prophylaxis.
analysis.description: This feature fires on positions where the player makes a 'normal-looking' move (development, repositioning, or quiet improvement) while ignoring a concrete, exploitable tactical vulnerability in their position. In 7/10 positions, the correct move was a specific prophylactic action addressing an immediate threat (e.g., relocating a vulnerable piece, blocking a dangerous diagonal, or resolving critical tension). The blundered moves are diverse in piece type (bishops, knights, rooks, pawns, castling) but share the quality of being generically reasonable yet catastrophically ill-timed. Common refutation themes include diagonal exploitation via Ba3 (3/10 positions sharing nearly identical a3-f8 diagonal attacks), capturing undefended material along open lines (3/10), and exploiting pins or forks enabled by the passive move (2/10). The average cp_loss of 401 and average of only 1.8 good moves available indicate positions demanding extremely specific responses that the player treated as calm.
analysis.move_pattern: Any piece type moving to a seemingly natural square (development, retreat, repositioning, castling) rather than addressing a specific tactical vulnerability
analysis.why_bad: The moves treat the position as stable/calm when it contains an immediate tactical crisis—a vulnerable piece on an exploitable diagonal, an unresolved pin about to become absolute, an undefended point about to be captured, or a piece about to be trapped—allowing the opponent to execute a concrete tactic on the very next move.
sub_patterns: Ignoring a piece vulnerable on the a3-f8 diagonal (Ba7, b6, Rb8 all fail to move knight from d6)
Removing a defensive piece from a critical guarding duty (Rfe1 abandons f2, Bc5 abandons g7)
Developing to irrelevant square while leaving key square uncontrolled (Nh3 ignores d4, Nbd7 ignores Ng5xe6)
Failing to resolve central tension before committing king (O-O makes pin absolute, e5 opens lines while undeveloped)
Natural development failing to block critical diagonal (Nf6 instead of c6 blocking queen path to a8)

analysis.label: King (or piece) moves toward the board edge in an endgame when centralization or proximity to a critical pawn was required.
analysis.description: This feature activates on endgame positions with exposed kings and passed pawns where the critical decision involves king direction. The dominant pattern is a king moving toward the edge, wing, or corner when the position demanded centralization or defensive blockade duty. In 8/13 positions, the king moves away from the center (Kf7 toward mating corner, Kc6 toward edge in KR vs K, Kh5/Kg4 toward wing abandoning passed pawns, Kb4 abandoning a blockade). The catastrophic examples (positions 4, 10, 12 with 9000+ cp_loss) show kings walking directly into mating nets or allowing unstoppable promotions by leaving critical squares. The 0-cp-loss positions (2, 3, 7) share the same structural features—exposed kings, passed pawns, endgame—but happen to be correct moves in those specific positions, suggesting the feature partially encodes position type alongside move direction. Position 9 (Rc7) extends the pattern: a rook move when the king needed to advance (Kg6), representing the same tempo-loss/wrong-piece-moving concept.
analysis.move_pattern: King moves toward board edge (files a/h or ranks 1/8) rather than toward center squares (d4/d5/e4/e5 region); predominantly 1-square king retreats or advances in wrong direction
analysis.why_bad: Moving the king toward the edge in endgames either (1) allows the opponent's pieces to construct a mating box more quickly (KR vs K, KQ vs K), (2) abandons blockade of a critical passed pawn enabling promotion, or (3) leaves the king too far from the decisive theater to defend or support its own pawns, losing crucial tempi in a race.
sub_patterns: King walks toward corner in KR/KQ vs K (enabling faster checkmate)
King abandons passed pawn blockade allowing promotion
King marches to wing while opponent breaks through in center
Piece develops (rook/queen) when king advance was the only winning move

analysis.label: Non-forcing moves that address the wrong positional priority in razor-sharp positions demanding one specific urgent action.
analysis.description: In all 7 positions, the player chose a plausible-looking move that addressed a secondary concern while ignoring the ONE critical demand of the position. In 5/7 cases, the position had only 1-2 good moves available (avg 1.6), indicating extreme tactical sharpness where a single wasted tempo is catastrophic. The correct moves always addressed the true urgent need: king safety via Kg8 (position 3), defensive piece redeployment via Nf8 (positions 4-5), piece coordination with Qd6 (position 6), methodical attack-building with Rg6 (position 9), tactical exploitation with Bd5 (position 11), or forcing pawn action with g4 (position 12). Instead, the played moves were aesthetically reasonable repositioning moves (Ng6 'attacking', Kh7 'prophylaxis', Qf4 'centralizing', Bb3 'maintaining diagonal', Qg7 'preparing g-file') or a premature sacrifice (Bxh3). All 7 moves share the property of being non-forcing and failing to create threats or solve the actual problem, granting the opponent a free tempo to execute their plan. The average cp_loss of 347 reflects how punishing this error is in critical positions.
analysis.move_pattern: Various piece types making quiet repositioning moves (no checks, non-critical captures) - typically sideways or backward movements that don't interact with the opponent's threats
analysis.why_bad: These moves waste the one available tempo in positions where only 1-2 specific moves maintain the evaluation, allowing the opponent to execute a tactical plan (rook lifts, tempo-gaining attacks on misplaced pieces, capturing undefended material, or exploiting newly created weaknesses) that the correct move would have prevented or preempted.
sub_patterns: Ignoring king safety for piece activity (Ng6 instead of Kg8)
King move that increases exposure rather than decreasing it (Kh7 when Nf8 was needed)
Queen placement vulnerable to tempo-gaining pawn pushes (Qf4 hit by e5, Qg7 allowing Qe3xg5)
Bishop retreat removing critical tactical resource (Bb3 losing Bd5xa8 combination)
Premature sacrifice when patient buildup was winning (Bxh3 when Rg6 maintained attack)

analysis.label: Plausible-looking moves in narrow positions where only 1-2 specific moves address an urgent tactical/defensive requirement, resulting in catastrophic punishment.
analysis.description: This feature fires on positions where the player faces a critical juncture with extremely few viable options (avg 1.6 good moves) and makes a seemingly reasonable move that follows general chess principles—but catastrophically fails to address the position's one urgent necessity. In 5/8 cases the king is moved to an exposed or fatal square (Kf2 into a mating net, O-O before resolving a tactical vulnerability, Ke5 into knight forks instead of capturing the attacking rook, Ke3 into a diagonal mating pattern). In 2/8 cases the queen abandons defensive duty for the wrong side of the board (Qxg2 material greed leaving back rank undefended, Qg7 abandoning queenside king defense enabling discovered check mate). In 2/8 cases slow preparatory pawn moves are played when immediate piece action is required (f6 instead of developing/defending queenside pawns, b3 instead of urgent Kf1 to contest kingside threats). The unifying thread is that each position has ONE critical action demanded by concrete tactical circumstances, the player instead pursues a normal chess goal (centralization, castling, material gain, preparation), and the punishment is immediate and devastating (avg 3713 cp loss).
analysis.move_pattern: Any piece type moving to a plausible-looking square that fails to address the position's one critical tactical requirement; frequently king moves to exposed central/forward squares, or queen/pawn moves away from the critical defensive sector
analysis.why_bad: Each position has an extremely narrow margin (1-2 correct moves) where one specific action addresses an urgent threat—the played move ignores this requirement entirely, allowing the opponent to exploit the unaddressed vulnerability with forcing moves (checks, captures, mating attacks, discovered attacks) that immediately collapse the position
sub_patterns: King walking into mating net or exposed square (Kf2, Ke3, Ke5, O-O)
Queen/piece displaced far from critical defensive duty (Qxg2, Qg7)
Slow preparatory pawn move when immediate tactical action required (f6, b3)

analysis.label: Player captures or targets a secondary piece/pawn while ignoring the position's single critical priority (a different capture, threat, or defensive necessity).
analysis.description: In all 7/7 positions, the player makes a superficially logical move—usually a capture—that addresses a secondary tactical element while completely missing the one critical priority demanded by the position. In 5/7 cases, the move is an explicit capture of the wrong target: Rxb2 captures the b-pawn instead of the g2-pawn (which sets up a winning fork), Rxd3+ captures the bishop instead of using the discovered check mechanism to win the queen via Re5+, hxg4 captures the bishop instead of eliminating the dominant knight with Bxe5, Kxe6 captures the rook instead of eliminating the lethal passed pawn with bxc6, and Nxe4 grabs a pawn but activates White's rook on that square. In 2/7 cases, the move is a repositioning that abandons critical defensive duties: Qd8 passively retreats instead of maintaining active queen pressure on a5, and Ba4 moves the bishop to an 'active' diagonal but abandons coverage of f3, enabling a devastating knight fork. All positions share the characteristic of having exactly 1 good move (avg good moves = 1.0), meaning these are narrow decision points where the player chose the obvious-looking action over the only correct one.
analysis.move_pattern: Captures or piece movements targeting secondary material/squares while a different target (often nearby) represents the critical tactical priority
analysis.why_bad: The move addresses a secondary concern (winning a less-important piece/pawn, retreating to a 'safe' square, or repositioning) while ignoring the position's true priority—either a superior tactical combination involving a different target, an existential threat that must be neutralized, or a critical defensive function that must be maintained. The opponent then exploits the neglected priority (promotion, fork, discovered attack, or piece activation).
sub_patterns: Capturing wrong pawn/piece when a different capture yields a tactical combination (Rxb2 vs Rxg2, Rxd3+ vs Re5+, hxg4 vs Bxe5)
Taking material while ignoring an unstoppable passed pawn (Kxe6 vs bxc6)
Grabbing a pawn that activates opponent's pieces with tempo (Nxe4)
Moving a piece to a seemingly active square while abandoning a critical defensive duty (Ba4 leaving f3, Qd8 losing activity)

analysis.label: Moves that disrupt defensive relationships between the player's pieces, leaving material tactically vulnerable through abandonment of protection or creation of exploitable geometric alignments.
analysis.description: This feature fires on moves that break the protective coordination between a player's own pieces, creating immediate tactical vulnerabilities. In 6/9 positions, the moved piece either abandons the defense of another piece (Rc3 leaves bishop on c2 undefended, Qxd4 abandons rook on b7, Ng5 leaves knight on d2 hanging, Qa4 abandons back-rank defense) or creates a new exploitable geometric alignment (Rb2 aligns both rooks on the same diagonal enabling a Ba3 skewer, Rad1 places the rook on the queen's diagonal enabling Bg4 to win the exchange). In 2/9 positions, the piece moves to an exposed square where it can be attacked with tempo, simultaneously revealing other weaknesses (Qe4 on an open file, e3 self-blocks enabling Nd3+ fork). The common consequence is that the opponent gains a tempo-based tactical strike that wins material or creates a decisive positional advantage. Average cp_loss of 293 reflects the severity of leaving pieces undefended.
analysis.move_pattern: Any piece type moving to a new square that severs a defensive link to another friendly piece or creates a new line-based vulnerability between two friendly pieces
analysis.why_bad: The move breaks an existing defensive relationship (protection, coordination, or geometric safety) between the player's pieces, immediately creating a tactical target that the opponent exploits through tempo-gaining attacks, skewers, forks, or captures of the newly-undefended piece.
sub_patterns: Piece moves away from protecting another piece, leaving it hanging (Rc3/Qxd4/Ng5)
Piece placement creates exploitable diagonal/file alignment with another friendly piece (Rb2/Rad1)
Queen decentralizes away from critical defensive duties (Qa4/Qe4)
Self-blocking pawn move that enables opponent's piece invasion (e3)

analysis.label: King or Queen moves to the b-file seeking queenside activity while ignoring a critical tactical vulnerability.
analysis.description: All three positions (3/3) feature a piece (King or Queen) relocating to a b-file square (b3 or b6) that appears to create threats or attack queenside targets, but fatally abandons coverage of a critical square or ignores a decisive tactical threat. In Position 6, Kb6 overextends the king away from defending a2, allowing Bc4/Ra8 invasions. In Position 8, Qb3 abandons control of d1, permitting Qd1+ leading to a forced mating attack with Ne4+. In Position 13, Qb6 fails to prevent Nc7+, a devastating knight fork winning the exchange. In all cases (3/3), the opponent has a forcing reply (check or fork) that immediately exploits the misplaced piece, and strong alternative moves existed that addressed the actual positional demands rather than pursuing illusory queenside activity.
analysis.move_pattern: King or Queen moves laterally/diagonally to b3 or b6, non-capturing, non-checking
analysis.why_bad: The b-file placement appears active but abandons critical defensive duties, allowing the opponent to exploit the vacated squares or ignored tactical threats with immediate forcing moves (checks, forks, invasions).
sub_patterns: Queen to b3/b6 abandoning back-rank or central defense
King to b6 overextending away from pawn defense
Piece targets queenside while central/tactical threats go unaddressed

analysis.label: Playing a plausible-looking but non-urgent move when the position has exactly one critical requirement that must be addressed immediately.
analysis.description: This feature fires on moves that waste a decisive tempo by ignoring the single most urgent demand of the position. In 7/7 positions, the player had a narrow set of correct moves (avg 1.9 good options) centered on one critical task—blockading a passed pawn (positions 4, 7), executing a breakthrough (position 3), defending against a mating attack (position 1), exploiting an exposed king (position 8), capturing an available pawn (position 13), or trading precisely to limit damage (position 15)—and instead played something that looked purposeful but addressed the wrong priority entirely. The moves range across piece types (queens, rooks, bishops, king, pawn) but share the quality of being non-forcing in positions demanding immediate action. In 5/7 cases, the opponent's refutation directly exploits the gifted tempo by advancing their own plan (pushing passed pawns, launching kingside attacks, trapping pieces). The common thread of 'tempo_loss' appears in all analyzed positions.
analysis.move_pattern: Non-forcing move (any piece type) that addresses a secondary concern while the position's primary tactical/strategic demand goes unmet; typically moves toward the wrong sector or makes a quiet move when forcing play is required
analysis.why_bad: The position has one critical urgency (a mating attack, a passed pawn, a tactical opportunity, or a must-capture moment) that tolerates zero wasted moves; by playing something else, the opponent gains the single tempo needed to execute their winning plan unopposed
sub_patterns: Queen sortie to wrong flank while critical threat exists on the other side (Ba6, Qh4)
Slow/passive move when immediate forcing play is required (g3, Rb8)
Failing to capture or exchange when it's the only drawing resource (Kb7, Qxf6)
Positional queen repositioning instead of executing the decisive breakthrough (Qc3)

analysis.label: King moves to a seemingly logical square that actually increases tactical vulnerability to checks or mating patterns.
analysis.description: In all 4/4 positions, the player makes a king move that appears reasonable (centralizing, retreating, or tucking away) but places the king on a square where it is more exposed to tactical exploitation than the available alternative. In 3/4 cases the king moves toward the center or along a rank/file where it encounters checks (Nc3+ on d5, Bd5+ on f3, Ra1+ on g1). In 4/4 cases, a better king destination existed (Kf5 instead of Kd5, Kg3 instead of Ke3, a3 instead of Kf3, Kf1 instead of Kg1) that either avoided open lines of attack or fulfilled a critical defensive function. The blunders range from trivial (3-4cp in already-decided games) to catastrophic (9518cp enabling back-rank mate), but all share the core pattern of the king stepping onto a compromised square that enables enemy checks, discovered attacks, piece trapping, or mating nets.
analysis.move_pattern: King move (any direction) to a square on an open file, rank, or diagonal exploitable by enemy pieces
analysis.why_bad: The king lands on a square exposed to immediate checks or tactical motifs (open files, diagonals, back rank) when an alternative king destination provided better shelter or served a critical defensive purpose
sub_patterns: King enters open diagonal enabling bishop check
King retreats to back rank enabling mate
King moves away from critical defensive square
King centralizes into discovered/fork threats

analysis.label: Playing a slow prophylactic or repositioning move when an immediate concrete gain (usually a pawn capture or forcing action) is available.
analysis.description: In all 3/3 positions, the player chose a non-forcing, positional-looking move (b3, Nf5, a6) while a direct tactical opportunity sat on the board. In 2/3 cases, the best move was a simple pawn capture by the queen (Qxf4 in position 12, Qxa2 in position 14), and in position 6, the best move was a piece exchange (Bxh4) addressing an immediate promotion threat. The played moves all appear 'reasonable' at a glance—b3 shores up the queenside, Nf5 occupies an outpost, a6 chases a queen—but each wastes a critical tempo on prophylaxis or aesthetics while the opponent has the time to consolidate. In 3/3 cases, the opponent exploits the tempo by improving piece centralization (Qd5, g4 kicking the knight, Bxe1) or simplifying into a favorable endgame. The average cp_loss of 221 reflects positions where concrete action was essential and the slow move allowed the opponent to neutralize or reverse the initiative.
analysis.move_pattern: Non-capturing, non-checking quiet moves (pawn pushes or piece repositioning to visually appealing squares) when a direct capture or forcing move exists
analysis.why_bad: These moves waste a critical tempo on long-term or aesthetic goals while ignoring an available concrete material gain or urgent tactical demand, allowing the opponent to consolidate their position or seize the initiative.
sub_patterns: Pawn push ignoring hanging enemy pawn
Knight repositioning to unstable outpost instead of capturing
Prophylactic pawn move when rook/queen activity is urgent

analysis.label: Playing a quiet preparatory or developing move when an immediate forcing tactical strike (mate, sacrifice, perpetual) was critical and time-sensitive.
analysis.description: In all 5/5 positions, the player chose a non-forcing 'improving' move—developing a rook (Rgf8, Rae1), centralizing a knight (Nd4), or pushing a prophylactic/preparatory pawn (a3, h4)—when the position demanded an immediate tactical blow that would be neutralized after one tempo of delay. In 3/5 cases, a forced checkmate was available (positions 1, 4) or a perpetual check was the only drawing resource (position 12). In the remaining cases, a decisive sacrifice (Rxh7, position 7) or forcing bishop move (Bg5, position 3) exploited a narrow tactical window. The average good moves available was only 1.4, indicating extremely narrow positions where the critical line was unique. Once the slow move was played, opponents gained the tempo needed to consolidate defenses (blocking diagonals with ...e5, playing ...h5 to prevent sacrifices, grabbing hanging pieces, or simply organizing).
analysis.move_pattern: Quiet non-forcing moves (rook development, knight centralization, flank pawn pushes) with no check, capture, or immediate threat—played in positions requiring an immediate forcing blow
analysis.why_bad: These moves waste a critical tempo in positions with a narrow tactical window; the opponent uses that single extra move to block mating diagonals, consolidate defensive resources, grab unprotected material, or neutralize the attacking coordination that made the forcing blow possible
sub_patterns: Developing rook instead of delivering forced mate
Prophylactic pawn move instead of decisive sacrifice
Preparatory pawn advance instead of perpetual check (only resource)
Centralizing piece move that leaves material hanging

analysis.label: Playing a slow, passive, or misdirected move in a position that demands immediate urgent action to maintain the initiative.
analysis.description: In 10/10 positions, the player faced a critical moment where only 1-3 good moves existed (avg 1.5), yet chose a plausible-looking but tempo-wasting move. The pattern manifests as: premature pawn advances without piece support (a4, e6, b5, b5 — 4/10), prophylactic/defensive pawn moves when the position required attacking (h3, f3 — 2/10), pieces moving to squares where they're immediately driven back or displaced (Nf6, Qxa7, Rb6 — 3/10), or the king retreating in the wrong direction (Kd2 — 1/10). In every case, the position featured dynamic tension requiring urgent exploitation — connected passed pawns needing piece support, mating attacks to press, exposed enemy kings to target, or rook activity to generate — and the player instead addressed a secondary concern (prophylaxis, material, pawn expansion). The opponent then exploits the wasted tempo by either escaping a mating net, capturing undefended pawns, activating pieces, or simplifying into safety.
analysis.move_pattern: Diverse piece types and directions; predominantly forward pawn pushes (6/10) or piece moves to exposed/peripheral squares (4/10); never checks, rarely captures (1/10)
analysis.why_bad: The position demands immediate active play to maintain a dynamic advantage, but the move wastes the critical tempo needed, allowing the opponent to solve their defensive problems, escape danger, counterattack undefended material, or simplify away the attacker's coordination.
sub_patterns: Premature pawn advance without piece coordination (e6, b5, a4)
Prophylactic pawn move ignoring urgent tactical demands (h3, f3)
Piece/queen displaced to peripheral square losing coordination (Qxa7, Rb6)
Piece moving to square where it's immediately driven back (Nf6)
King retreating away from the critical sector (Kd2)

analysis.label: Moves that look purposeful but accidentally remove protection from the player's own pieces or critical squares, leaving material hanging or fatally exposed.
analysis.description: This feature fires on positions where a player makes a plausible-looking move (pawn break, piece reposition, prophylactic king move, capture) that inadvertently destroys a critical defensive relationship in their own position. In 7/10 cases, the move directly causes the player's own piece to become undefended or trapped: g3 removes the g-pawn's defense of the Nh3 (Position 12), Qxc3 abandons the queen's defense of Na4 (Position 7), Qd7 removes the queen's guard of f6 allowing mate (Position 3), f3 blocks the knight's only good retreat square (Position 1), Kg7 occupies the square the knight needs for defense (Position 6), Ng4 places the knight on a completely unguarded square (Position 14), and f4 creates a sequence where e3 becomes undefended (Position 8). The remaining positions involve walking into tactics (Kf3 into a knight fork, Position 4) or squandering tempo/initiative that allows the opponent to exploit newly created weaknesses (Kh8, Bh6). The common thread is that each move appears to serve a constructive purpose (attacking, defending, maneuvering) but fatally ignores the defensive function being abandoned.
analysis.move_pattern: Any piece type or pawn moving away from or blocking a square that was providing critical defense to the player's own piece; no consistent direction or piece type, but predominantly non-forcing moves (rarely checks/captures of value)
analysis.why_bad: Each move removes a protective relationship (pawn guarding piece, queen defending piece, square serving as retreat/access path) that the opponent immediately exploits to win material, deliver checkmate, or create decisive tactical threats against the now-undefended target.
sub_patterns: Pawn advance removing defense of own knight (f3/g3/f4 leaving knight hanging)
Queen move abandoning defense of own piece (Qd7/Qxc3 leaving piece or square unguarded)
King or piece occupying square needed by own piece for retreat/defense (Kg7/f3 blocking knight)
Piece moving to completely undefended square (Ng4 hanging to simple capture)
Tempo-wasting move ignoring critical positional tension (Kh8 allowing passed pawn creation)

analysis.label: Pawn advances that prematurely commit the structure, releasing critical dynamic tension or eliminating counterplay when maintaining flexibility or executing a more urgent action was essential.
analysis.description: This feature fires on positions where a player makes an irreversible pawn advance (7/8 positions) or slow consolidation move (1/8) that commits the pawn structure in a counterproductive way. The core error manifests in several related forms: releasing central tension that favored the player (e5 in Position 3 allowing d5; d4 in Position 5 giving White time to regroup; f4 in Position 8 giving White a free queenside break), self-eliminating critical pawn breaks (a5 in Position 11 permanently blocking the essential ...b5 break; g3 in Position 9 wasting the tempo needed for the winning b5 advance), overextending pawns that create weaknesses (c5 in Position 14 removing d4's defense of e5; c4 in Position 15 creating an undermining target for b3), and choosing slow consolidation over decisive tactical action (Bc3 in Position 12 missing the winning d5 break). In all 8 positions, the best moves either maintained dynamic tension, executed the correct break, or prioritized development/king safety. The blundered moves all look 'space-gaining' or 'prophylactic' on the surface but are strategically catastrophic because they hand the opponent either unlimited time to improve (5/8) or concrete tactical targets (3/8).
analysis.move_pattern: Pawn advances (forward one square), typically in the center or on the wing, that lock or commit the pawn structure; occasionally a slow piece consolidation move in lieu of a critical pawn break
analysis.why_bad: These moves release dynamic tension that was restraining the opponent, eliminate the player's own future pawn breaks or counterplay sources, or waste critical tempo when the position demanded immediate concrete action—granting the opponent either time to reorganize passive pieces or the ability to exploit newly created structural weaknesses.
sub_patterns: Central pawn advance releasing tension and allowing opponent's breakthrough (e5, d4, f4)
Wing pawn advance self-blocking critical counterplay break (a5, g3)
Overextending c-pawn creating targets or removing key defenders (c5, c4)
Slow consolidation move missing a one-move tactical window (Bc3)

analysis.label: Natural-looking moves that prioritize a secondary objective while missing the position's one critical tactical or tempo requirement.
analysis.description: This feature fires on positions where the player makes a plausible, principled move that catastrophically fails because it neglects the position's primary demand. In 5/7 cases, the correct move was narrowly specific (avg 2.1 good moves available), yet the played move followed a recognizable chess principle: capturing material (Nxe4, Qxe2+), developing pieces (Nf6, Bf4), activating the king (Kc7, Kb2), or attacking a target (Rh8). In each case, one concrete requirement trumped general logic: the right capture piece for a mating pattern (Pos 2), immediate pawn push in a tempo race (Pos 5), maintaining rook activity over passive blockade (Pos 9), queen safety before development (Pos 14), or one specific king square to neutralize a tactic (Pos 12). The moves are 'almost right' - close in concept but fatally imprecise, resulting in enormous evaluation swings (avg 2953cp loss).
analysis.move_pattern: Mixed piece types and directions; moves are typically one-square king moves, piece captures, or retreats/developments that look standard but land on the wrong square or use the wrong piece
analysis.why_bad: Each move pursues a reasonable secondary goal (material gain, development, king activity, pawn attack) while failing to address the single critical requirement of the position, allowing a concrete tactical refutation that the correct move would have prevented
sub_patterns: Wrong piece for capture when piece coordination matters (Qxe2+ vs Rxe2+)
King tempo loss in pawn race or geometric positions (Kc7, Kb2)
Passive piece placement when active defense required (Rh8)
Development/captures ignoring existing piece vulnerability (Nf6, Nxe4)
Piece retreat ignoring opponent's tactical access to weak squares (Bf4)

analysis.label: Non-forcing pawn advances that irreversibly squander a critical resource (tempo, defensive structure, or attacking potential).
analysis.description: All 4/4 positions feature a quiet, non-capturing pawn advance played at the wrong moment that permanently eliminates a valuable future option. In Position 5, d3 wastes a tempo when Bd5 could win material immediately (tempo loss). In Position 6, g5 allows en passant fxg6, destroying Black's defensive pawn chain and creating an unstoppable passed pawn (structural self-destruction). In Position 7, h5 prematurely commits Black's last spare tempo move, which was essential for winning the opposition in the king maneuver (reserve tempo eliminated). In Position 15, e6 pushes into an easy capture that dissolves White's threatening f5/e5 pawn duo without creating lasting threats (attacking potential squandered). In each case, the pawn move appears natural or proactive but is actually irreversible damage—the player fails to recognize that preserving the pawn's flexibility was more valuable than advancing it.
analysis.move_pattern: Single pawn advance (forward, non-capturing, non-checking) that is non-forcing and gives the opponent a free hand to respond optimally
analysis.why_bad: The pawn advance irreversibly eliminates a resource (spare tempo, defensive barrier, tactical threat, or attacking pawn duo) that was more valuable kept in reserve, allowing the opponent to consolidate or exploit the structural change
sub_patterns: Wasting tempo with slow pawn moves when concrete tactics exist
Destroying own defensive pawn chain via premature advance
Eliminating spare tempo needed for opposition battles
Dissolving an attacking pawn duo by pushing into a capture

analysis.label: King moves backward to the 1st/8th rank instead of stepping forward, creating back-rank vulnerabilities, diagonal exploits, or fatal passivity.
analysis.description: In all 8/8 positions, the king moves TO the back rank (1st rank for White, 8th rank for Black) when the correct move was to advance the king forward or to a more active square. The blundered moves (Ke1, Ke8, Kg8, Kd8, Kd1) all place the king on rank 1/8, while the best alternatives (Ke3, Kf2, Kg6, Kd7, Kd6, Kd2) step the king forward. This backward retreat creates a constellation of problems: back-rank mate vulnerabilities (explicit in positions 13 and 9 where Re1# and Qxh8+ exploit the back rank), diagonal tactical shots (position 3 where Bc3+ forks king and knight, position 4 where Qc3 threatens Qg7# without check), piece hanging (position 7 where Kd8 leaves h8 rook undefended vs Kd7 which creates counterplay), tempo loss allowing opponent to build attacks (position 10 where Nd5+Bxf6+ becomes crushing), and king passivity preventing defensive coordination (position 1 where Ke1 can't contest the second rank like Ke3 would).
analysis.move_pattern: King moves backward/laterally TO the first or eighth rank (the home rank), typically one square retreat from an already somewhat exposed position
analysis.why_bad: The back rank creates a geometric trap: the king has no retreat squares behind it, making it vulnerable to back-rank mates, file-based checks that gain tempo, and diagonal attacks that exploit the fixed rank. Moving forward instead gives the king escape squares and active defensive participation.
sub_patterns: King to back rank enabling back-rank checkmate (Kd1, Ke8 with Qxh8+)
King to back rank creating diagonal fork vulnerability (Ke1 allowing Bc3+)
King to back rank allowing mating threats without check (Kg8 allowing Qc3 threatening Qg7#)
King to back rank leaving pieces undefended (Kd8 hanging the h8 rook)
King to back rank becoming passive bystander (Ke1 unable to contest rook invasion)

analysis.label: Playing non-urgent moves (often peripheral pawn advances or seemingly-improving piece moves) while ignoring immediate tactical threats, particularly lethal king safety issues.
analysis.description: This feature fires on moves that fundamentally misjudge priorities, pursuing secondary strategic goals while the position demands an urgent tactical response. In 6/8 positions, king safety was the critical ignored factor: three cases involve literal a-file pawn pushes (a5, a5, a4) while the player's king faces immediate mating threats or devastating sacrifices (Greek Gift in position 14, mate-in-1 in position 15, exposed king on g5 in position 12). In position 2, Rh6 ignores a forced mating sequence. In position 6, Nc3 develops a piece instead of castling the endangered king. In position 9, Bxf5 grabs a pawn instead of eliminating a lethal attacking piece near the king. The two partial outliers (Be5 self-blocking the e-file in position 1, and Bb4 creating a hanging piece in position 4) still share the core pattern: choosing a move that looks reasonable in isolation but catastrophically ignores the position's most urgent demand. The average cp_loss of 2572 (including two instant-mate blunders) reflects how severely these priority failures are punished.
analysis.move_pattern: Diverse piece types but frequently a-file pawn advances (3/8); moves are consistently directed AWAY from the critical sector of the board where threats exist, often operating on the queenside while kingside dangers demand attention.
analysis.why_bad: The position demands an immediate concrete response to a tactical threat (usually a king safety crisis involving mating nets, sacrifices, or exposed kings), but the player instead pursues a long-term plan that is completely irrelevant given the urgency, effectively giving the opponent a free tempo to execute their threat.
sub_patterns: a-file pawn push while king is under direct mating threat
piece development/improvement move ignoring need to castle or address king exposure
material capture on peripheral square while lethal attacking piece remains unchallenged near king
seemingly-active piece move that self-blocks critical defensive lines

analysis.label: Forward-advancing moves (pawn pushes, piece advances, king moves) that remove a critical defensive element, creating an immediate exploitable tactical vulnerability.
analysis.description: This feature detects catastrophic blunders where the player makes an aggressive or 'improving' forward move while overlooking that it fatally compromises their position's defensive integrity. In 5/9 positions, a pawn advance removes a critical guard (d4 undefends e4 allowing Nxe4 fork; f3 opens the h4-e1 diagonal to an uncastled king; h4 removes the h5 pawn's control of g4, allowing Qg4+; d5 pushes to a square with no recapture; d6 pushes a passed pawn while the king is exposed to rook doubling). In 3/9 positions, a piece/king moves into immediate danger (Kf7 walks into Qh7#; Nc5+ places a piece on a square where it's captured for free; Ke1 moves the king away from the critical defensive zone). In 1/9 a check is delivered on the wrong square (Qe2+ instead of Qc4+), allowing the king to escape to safety. All share the pattern of prioritizing 'active' moves over maintaining existing defensive resources, with an average cp_loss of 1357 indicating these are position-destroying mistakes.
analysis.move_pattern: Forward moves (pawn advances, piece moves toward opponent, king steps forward/laterally) that vacate or weaken a critical defensive square or walk into tactical danger
analysis.why_bad: The advancing move removes a piece or pawn from a critical defensive duty (guarding a square, blocking a diagonal, shielding the king, maintaining material) or places itself on an immediately exploitable square, creating a one-move tactical refutation that the opponent can easily find.
sub_patterns: Pawn advance removes guard from key square (d4/f3/h4 undefending e4/diagonal/g4)
Pawn push to undefended or irrecoverable square (d5/d6 overextension)
King walks into mating net or away from needed defensive zone (Kf7/Ke1)
Piece advances to capturable undefended square (Nc5+ taken by bishop)
Check on wrong square allowing opponent's king escape (Qe2+ vs Qc4+)

analysis.label: Moves that pursue a plausible secondary objective while wasting the decisive tempo needed to address the position's most urgent requirement.
analysis.description: This feature fires on positions where the player makes a move with a reasonable-looking purpose but critically wastes a tempo in a position where time/initiative is the decisive factor. In 10/10 cases, the played move ignores the position's primary demand: development when underdeveloped (f5, b4, d3 - 3/10), king activation in endgames (Bb5, a7 - 2/10), maintaining a restraining piece position (Rd5, Qf3 - 2/10), retreating to safety over grabbing material (Bxa4 - 1/10), choosing the wrong piece for the right idea (Bd5 vs Nd5 - 1/10), or giving a premature check that helps the opponent (Qh3+ - 1/10). The common thread is that the correct move addresses the position's critical vulnerability while the played move looks constructive but allows immediate exploitation of the neglected priority. The opponent's refutation consistently exploits exactly the factor the wasted tempo failed to address—back-rank weakness, diagonal vulnerability, king escape, pawn capture with tempo, or counterplay on abandoned files.
analysis.move_pattern: Various pieces and pawns; moves directed toward seemingly useful squares or captures but failing to address the position's critical factor; no single geometric direction dominates
analysis.why_bad: Each move wastes the one tempo that was needed to address the position's most urgent tactical or strategic demand, allowing the opponent to immediately exploit the neglected vulnerability through checks, captures, or positional seizure that the correct move would have prevented
sub_patterns: Premature pawn advances ignoring development/king safety (f5, b4, d3, a7)
Piece moves to plausible but non-critical squares instead of addressing the key factor (Bb5, Qf3, Bd5)
Material greed exposing tactical vulnerability (Bxa4)
Abandoning a critical restraining post (Rd5)
Premature checking that releases opponent's king from confinement (Qh3+)

analysis.label: Rook (or piece) moves to an intermediate rank in a passed-pawn endgame, sacrificing the long-range flexibility needed to combat advancing pawns.
analysis.description: This feature fires on positions where the player moves a rook (or piece) to a middle-distance square—typically the 4th or 5th rank—in a rook endgame featuring dangerous passed pawns, when the correct defense required maintaining maximum checking distance or getting behind the pawn. In 6/9 positions, the rook moves specifically to rank 4 or 5 (Rb4, Ra4, Rb4, Rc4, Rf5, Re5), while the best moves consistently kept the rook on ranks 6-8 (Ra8, Ra6, Ra7, Rb8, Rb6, Rb7, Rg8, Re1). In 8/9 positions, the game is in an endgame phase with exposed kings and critical passed pawns. The common error is choosing a square that appears to directly confront the passed pawn but actually reduces the rook's ability to deliver lateral checks, swing to the back rank, or get behind the pawn—all fundamental rook endgame defensive techniques. The outlier positions (Bf7+ wasting tempo, Rg1 retreating passively, Kd3 moving away from the threatened flank) share the same strategic sin: spending a critical tempo on a move that fails to address the passed pawn's advance while reducing overall piece coordination.
analysis.move_pattern: Rook moves along a file to an intermediate rank (typically 4th or 5th), arriving at a square too close to the enemy king/pawns for effective checking distance but not behind the passed pawn either
analysis.why_bad: The rook on the intermediate rank loses the long-range flexibility needed to generate perpetual checks against the exposed enemy king, cannot swing to the back rank to prevent promotion, and cannot position behind the passed pawn—allowing the opponent's king to advance unopposed and the passed pawn(s) to become unstoppable
sub_patterns: Rook to 4th rank vs passed pawn on same rank (loses lateral checking distance)
Rook to 5th rank directly attacking passed pawn instead of getting behind it
Rook retreating to passive square disconnected from the critical file
Wasting tempo with pointless check instead of addressing passed pawn threat
King moving away from the flank where passed pawns will decide the game

analysis.label: Moving a well-placed piece away from a critical square to capture material or retreat, forfeiting the position's tactical/strategic integrity.
analysis.description: This feature fires on moves that displace a piece from a square where it was performing a crucial function—maintaining a mating net, defending key squares, controlling open files, or coordinating an attack. In 4/10 positions, the piece captures unimportant material (Rxb7 abandons a mating rook on g7, Nxh8 traps a dominant knight for a passive rook, Qxb4 grabs a pawn while abandoning king defense, Bxf6 trades the sole defensive piece for a pawn). In 4/10 positions, the piece retreats to a passive or vulnerable square (Qf1 allows deflection, Qg3 abandons d4 defense, Na3 leaves c3 hanging, Rb1 quits the c-file). The remaining cases involve suboptimal piece placement choices (Qb1+ instead of Qd1+ loses an intermediate check resource, e6 weakens the position instead of maintaining active piece pressure). The average cp_loss of 2130 reflects how catastrophic these displacements are—with only 1.3 good moves available on average, these positions demand that the critical piece stay exactly where it is.
analysis.move_pattern: Any piece type moving away from an active/central/attacking square to a passive, peripheral, or tactically vulnerable square—often captures on edge squares or retreats along files/diagonals away from the critical zone
analysis.why_bad: The displaced piece was the linchpin of the position's tactical or strategic foundation; removing it creates a void that the opponent immediately exploits—whether through capturing now-undefended pawns/pieces, infiltrating uncontrolled files/squares, executing deflection tactics, or launching attacks against the now-undefended king.
sub_patterns: Removing attacking piece to capture irrelevant material (Rxb7, Nxh8, Bxf6)
Queen retreating to passive/vulnerable square (Qf1, Qg3, Qxb4)
Knight/Rook abandoning central post for rim/passive square (Na3, Rb1)
Choosing wrong square for a check/move when precise placement is critical (Qb1+ vs Qd1+)

analysis.label: Playing a natural-looking or secondary-purpose move that completely ignores a decisive forced tactical sequence, resulting in massive evaluation collapse.
analysis.description: This feature fires on positions where the player makes a catastrophic tactical oversight by choosing a move that looks purposeful or reasonable in isolation but completely misses an immediate forced combination. In 6/9 positions, the correct move involved a forced checkmate or decisive material-winning sequence (Qg1+ promotion mate, Qb8+ back-rank mate, Nxd8 queen capture, Bd5+ skewer). Instead, players chose moves addressing secondary concerns: structural pawn pushes (g4, b3, f6 in 3/9), piece 'activation' (Re8, Rd6, Rxd1 in 3/9), or king centralization (Kd5, Kc6 in 2/9). The positions share extremely narrow correct paths (average 1.7 good moves available) with enormous punishment for deviation (average 6473cp loss). In every case, the chosen move either ignores an immediate winning combination the player could execute, fails to address an incoming mating threat, or walks directly into a tactical shot.
analysis.move_pattern: Various piece types making seemingly purposeful moves (pawn pushes, rook placements, king walks, captures of secondary targets) while a critical forced sequence involving checks exists
analysis.why_bad: They prioritize secondary objectives (development, structure, pawn activity, wrong capture target, king centralization) over immediate tactical imperatives - either a forced mate the player can deliver, a forced mate they must prevent, or a tactic they walk into
sub_patterns: Missing own forced checkmate by playing developing/activating moves (Re8, Rxd1)
Quiet pawn pushes ignoring immediate mating threats against own king (g4, b3, f6)
King moves walking into discovered checks, skewers, or diagonal attacks (Kd5, Kc6)
Capturing wrong target when a stronger capture exists (Qxd6, Rd6 hanging)

analysis.label: Playing a quiet king shuffle, piece retreat, or decentralization when one specific active move (typically attacking an enemy pawn) was the only way to hold the position.
analysis.description: This feature fires on positions where the player makes a non-constructive move—typically a king shuffle (Kf1, Kg2, Ke1 in 3/6 positions), a passive piece retreat (Bb8 in 1/6), or a piece decentralization (Na4 in 1/6)—in a critical-precision position where only one specific active counterattacking move maintains the balance. In 4/6 positions, the correct move was literally the same move (Bc7, attacking the a5 pawn) but the player instead chose a quiet move that accomplished nothing urgent, gifting the opponent a crucial tempo to consolidate piece superiority (knight on d5, king march, or f4 pawn break). The remaining positions follow the same logic: a seemingly purposeful move (Nf3+ giving check, Na4 targeting a pawn) wastes the critical tempo needed to maintain defensive coordination. The average of only 1.7 good moves available confirms these are narrow-margin positions where precision was essential.
analysis.move_pattern: Quiet king moves (Kf1/Kg2/Ke1), back-rank bishop retreat (Bb8), or knight moving to rim (Na4)—all non-forcing, non-threatening moves in positions requiring immediate active play
analysis.why_bad: These moves waste a critical tempo in positions where only one active continuation holds, allowing the opponent to achieve dominant piece placement (centralized knight on d5/e4, king invasion, or pawn breaks like f4) that cannot be subsequently contested because the counterplay window has closed.
sub_patterns: King shuffle instead of bishop activation (Kf1/Kg2/Ke1 when Bc7 needed)
Bishop retreat to passive back-rank square (Bb8 instead of Bc7)
Knight decentralization from critical defensive post (Na4 leaving c3 unguarded)
Flashy check that hangs a piece (Nf3+ into Nxf3)

analysis.label: Playing a slow, non-forcing move (quiet king move, routine castling, or premature pawn push) when the position urgently demands an immediate tactical response such as a check, capture, or direct threat.
analysis.description: This feature activates on positions where the player chooses a quiet, non-forcing move instead of addressing a critical tactical demand. In 6/6 positions, the best available move was a forcing action—a check (Rc8+ in Position 1, Rf8+ in Position 15), a capture (Kxe4 in Position 9), or an active tactical threat (Nb5 threatening Nc7 fork in Position 3, Qa4 creating counterplay in Position 7, Kc4 centralizing with purpose in Position 11)—yet the player opted for a passive alternative. The blunders include king retreats (Ke2, Kg8), routine development (O-O), passive rook relocation (Rg8), and premature pawn advances without support (a6, a5). In 5/6 cases, the analysis explicitly tags 'tempo_loss' as the core error. The average cp_loss of 3226 reflects that these tempo losses often prove fatal, particularly in positions where the opponent has advanced passed pawns (4/6 positions) or immediate tactical threats that exploit the wasted move.
analysis.move_pattern: Quiet, non-forcing moves: king retreats/sidesteps (Ke2, Kg8, O-O), passive rook relocation (Rg8), slow pawn advances (a5, a6) — all without delivering check, making a capture, or creating an immediate threat
analysis.why_bad: The position demanded an immediate forcing response (check, capture, or direct tactical threat) to maintain initiative or address an existential threat; the passive move wastes a critical tempo, allowing the opponent to execute their own plans — promote a pawn, activate their king, establish a blockade, or launch a tactical combination that was previously prevented.
sub_patterns: King retreat when active king capture was required (Ke2 instead of Kxe4)
Premature pawn advance ignoring opponent's imminent promotion (a5 ignoring f2=Q)
Passive rook relocation abandoning check-giving file (Rg8 instead of Rc8+)
Routine castling when sharp tactical strike was available (O-O instead of Nb5)
King walk into tactical vulnerability instead of active counterplay (Kg8 instead of Qa4)

analysis.label: Playing a reasonable-looking but non-urgent move in a position where only one specific response addresses a critical tactical or strategic demand.
analysis.description: This feature fires on positions with extremely narrow correct paths (avg 1.5 good moves) where the player chooses a 'natural-looking' move that catastrophically ignores the position's most urgent demand. In 5/10 positions, pawn advances or piece repositioning neglect a critical blockade or passed pawn threat (positions 3, 5, 8 involve failing to address a dangerous passed pawn; positions 5 and 8 are nearly identical - advancing b-pawns instead of playing Ke7 to maintain a blockade). In 4/10 positions, slow developing/positional moves miss immediate tactical shots (Bc4 misses exf5/Nf6+ fork; c4 misses Qd2/Nf6+ winning the exchange; Nxd2 removes a critical d4-defender; Re4 abandons f4 where the rook pressured a weak pawn). In 2/10 positions, king moves walk into devastating tactics (Kg8 allows Ne7#; Kh3 allows Qh7+ capturing g7 with check). The unifying thread is that each move would be reasonable in a generic context but is precisely wrong at the critical moment.
analysis.move_pattern: Mixed piece types (kings, bishops, pawns, rooks, knights) - no single geometric pattern; moves tend to be non-captures, non-checks, and positionally motivated rather than tactically sharp
