analysis.why_bad: Each move neglects the ONE critical requirement of the position (maintaining a blockade, capturing an urgent passed pawn, exploiting a tactical shot, or defending against a mating threat), allowing the opponent to execute a decisive tactical blow - typically a promotion, fork, or checkmate that was preventable with the single correct response.
sub_patterns: Advancing pawns when king must maintain blockade against enemy passed pawn (b5, b4)
Slow positional development missing a concrete tactical win (Bc4, c4, Nxd2)
King moves walking into tactical shots (Kg8 into Ne7#, Kh3 into Qh7+xg7+)
Piece repositioning that abandons a critical defensive/attacking function (Re4 leaving f4, Bb2 ignoring g-pawn)

analysis.label: Making a non-forcing 'improving' move that completely ignores an immediate devastating tactical threat, typically a knight fork with check or checkmate.
analysis.description: In 4/4 positions, the player makes a quiet, positionally-motivated move (queen retreat, rook centralization, knight development, pawn push for luft) while an immediate one-move tactical blow exists for the opponent. In 3/4 cases, the ignored threat is specifically a knight fork delivering check while simultaneously attacking the queen (Nc7+ in Position 1, Nd4+ in Position 4, Ng3+ in Position 13), and in 1/4 cases it's an immediate checkmate (Qh4# in Position 9). All blundered moves look 'reasonable' in a vacuum—Nc3 is standard development, Rf3 centralizes a rook, h3 creates luft, Qa6 repositions the queen—but each catastrophically fails to address the critical tactical vulnerability. In all 4 cases, the player had 3+ alternatives that specifically neutralized the threat (by moving the king off the fork diagonal, relocating the queen, blocking the critical square, or creating escape squares).
analysis.move_pattern: Non-forcing, non-capturing quiet moves (any piece type) that neither address an existing check/fork geometry nor remove a piece from danger
analysis.why_bad: The moves ignore an immediate one-move tactical threat—typically a knight fork with check that wins the queen—by making a positionally 'normal' but tactically irrelevant improving move when defensive action was urgently required
sub_patterns: Knight fork with check winning queen (3/4)
Immediate checkmate on open diagonal (1/4)
Developing move ignoring forcing threat
Pawn move unguarding critical square

analysis.label: Player plays a move superficially similar to the unique correct move but critically removes essential piece control or king safety.
analysis.description: This feature fires on positions where exactly one good move exists and the player chooses a near-miss alternative that appears to accomplish the same goal but fatally undermines a critical positional requirement. In 2/4 positions, the player delivered Qg6+ (check with the Queen) when Bg6# (checkmate with the Bishop) was available—the right square but the wrong piece, removing the Queen's essential back-rank control that sealed the king's escape. In 2/4 positions, the player moved their king to a seemingly logical square (Kc2 to blockade a pawn, Kf3 to centralize) when a more precise destination was needed (Kd3 to truly blockade without being checked, Kh3 to reach corner safety). All 4/4 positions had exactly one good move available, and in each case the played move shares geometric or strategic similarity with the correct move but abandons a critical secondary function (square control, escape from tempo-gaining checks, or mating geometry).
analysis.move_pattern: Piece or king moves to a square that mimics the correct move's intent (same target square or similar direction) but removes essential positional control
analysis.why_bad: The move abandons a critical secondary piece function—the Queen vacates back-rank control needed for mate, or the King walks into squares vulnerable to tempo-gaining checks—converting a won or defensible position into a draw or significantly worse evaluation.
sub_patterns: Wrong piece to correct square (Queen check vs Bishop mate)
King toward action but into check/exposure instead of toward safety/blockade

analysis.label: A natural-looking move that opens a line to the king, allowing a queen check that simultaneously attacks an undefended piece.
analysis.description: This feature fires on moves that inadvertently expose the king to a forcing check that wins material. The dominant sub-pattern (4/7 positions) involves White playing d3 with the king on e1 and an undefended bishop on b5, opening the a5-e1 diagonal for Black's Qa5+ which forks king and bishop. A fifth position (Be3) fails to block this same diagonal, suffering the identical Qa5+ punishment. The remaining positions generalize: Qxc4 (1/7) allows Bxf2+ check deflecting the defender of the queen, and Qc7 (1/7) places the queen where Qxc5 works because bxc5 opens the b-file for Rb7+ skewer. In all 7/7 cases, the blunder enables a check or capture-with-check that simultaneously attacks a second undefended piece, and in 6/7 cases the punishment specifically involves a queen or bishop delivering check while targeting hanging material.
analysis.move_pattern: Pawn push (usually d2-d3) or piece move that removes a blocker from a diagonal or file leading to the king, while an undefended piece (usually bishop on b5) sits on the same line as the checking square
analysis.why_bad: The move removes a pawn or piece from a critical defensive role (blocking a check diagonal/file to the king), while an undefended piece remains tactically connected to that same line, allowing a single forcing check to attack both king and hanging piece simultaneously.
sub_patterns: d3 opening a5-e1 diagonal with Bb5 undefended → Qa5+ wins bishop (4/7)
Bishop retreat to wrong square failing to block a5-e1 diagonal → Qa5+ wins bishop (1/7)
Greedy capture allowing intermediate check that deflects a defender (1/7)
Queen move to square creating skewer vulnerability on an open file through the king (1/7)

analysis.label: Quiet king moves (or piece deflections) that waste critical tempo in positions demanding immediate urgent action such as advancing passed pawns, trading queens, or blockading threats.
analysis.description: In 6/6 positions, the player made a quiet, seemingly natural move—typically a single-square king step (4/6 are king moves: Kc4, Kg2, Kb4, Kh1)—in a position that urgently demanded a forcing or active move. The correct alternatives involved pawn advances to create unstoppable threats (Position 4: d6 creating connected passers), queen trades to defuse attacks (Position 10: Qe4/Qd1/Qe3 all forcing queen exchange), blockading critical passed pawns (Position 8: Rf3 reaching the e-file), or activating pieces to generate counterplay (Position 12: Qg5/Re1/Be4). In all cases, 'tempo_loss' was tagged, and the refutations exploited the gifted tempo to advance passed pawns, launch mating attacks, or capture undefended material. The rook moves (R7xc6+ and Rxc3) fit the same pattern: deflecting an active piece from its critical post, equivalent to losing a tempo. The average cp_loss of 3339 reflects how catastrophically costly a single wasted tempo can be in these urgent positions.
analysis.move_pattern: Single-square king moves (to adjacent square, often sideways or backward) or rook captures that deflect the piece away from its critical file/rank
analysis.why_bad: The position demands immediate forcing action (advancing a passer, trading queens, blockading a promotion threat, or activating pieces against weaknesses), but the played move accomplishes nothing urgent, gifting the opponent a free tempo to execute their winning plan—whether that's a pawn race, a mating attack, or capturing undefended material.
sub_patterns: King retreats to corner (Kh1, Kg2) instead of activating pieces
King walks wrong direction in endgame pawn race (Kb4, Kc4)
Rook captures deflecting from critical defensive/offensive post (Rxc3, R7xc6+)

analysis.label: Playing a seemingly logical but non-urgent move in a critical position that demands immediate, specific tactical action.
analysis.description: This feature fires when a player makes a 'normal-looking' move—often a quiet pawn push (h3 appears 3/10 times), a natural-seeming piece redeployment, or a superficially attractive capture—while completely ignoring the single most urgent tactical demand of the position. In 7/10 positions, only 1-2 moves were acceptable. The played moves follow routine chess principles (prophylaxis, centralization, file control, material gain) that would be fine in quiet positions but are catastrophically inappropriate given specific concrete vulnerabilities: hanging pieces (2/10), exposed kings allowing forced mates or decisive invasions (5/10), fork vulnerabilities (1/10), or critical pawn breakthroughs (2/10). The average cp_loss of 1258 reflects that these are positions teetering on a knife's edge where 'autopilot' play triggers immediate tactical punishment. The best moves in each case address the ONE critical tactical element—whether it's blocking a lethal diagonal (Position 5), defending a hanging piece (Positions 9, 11), keeping a rook on its critical file (Positions 4, 10), or launching the only forcing continuation (Positions 1, 7, 13).
analysis.move_pattern: Diverse piece types and directions; typically non-forcing moves (pawn pushes, piece retreats/repositions, wrong recaptures) rather than checks/attacks. No consistent geometric direction—the commonality is the move's relationship to the position's demands, not its physical characteristics.
analysis.why_bad: Each move fails because it addresses a secondary concern (kingside attack, file control, prophylaxis, material gain) while leaving the single critical tactical vulnerability unaddressed, giving the opponent a tempo to exploit an exposed king, hanging piece, back-rank weakness, or decisive pawn advance.
sub_patterns: Quiet h-pawn push while piece or pawn hangs elsewhere
Rook retreat from active square missing winning check/invasion
Wrong recapture leaving fork vulnerability
King walk into tactical exploitation zone
Queen/piece repositioning abandoning critical defensive duty

analysis.label: Giving a check that accomplishes nothing because the opponent's king simply sidesteps to a safe square, leaving the checking piece misplaced and the attacker's initiative squandered.
analysis.description: All 10/10 positions feature a move that gives check (+) but fails because the opponent's king calmly moves to a safe square with no meaningful follow-up threats. In 7/10 cases it's a queen check (Qf7+, Qh1+, Qh8+×3, Qh6+, Qh8+), and the remaining involve a bishop check (Bg3+), rook check (Re3+), and knight captures with check (Nxa7+, Nxd5+). The consistent refutation pattern is the king stepping to a square where it is suddenly safe (Kf7 in positions 1/3/4, Ke8 in position 5, Ke7 in position 10, Kg7 in position 15, Kd2 in position 13, Kb8 in position 11), after which the checking piece is stranded on a useless square while the opponent seizes the initiative. In every case, a quiet preparatory move existed (Raf1, f5, g4, gxf3, Qxc5+, Qxf7, Nd4, Ne3, Rxd5) that maintained or built the advantage without giving the opponent's king a useful escape tempo. The average centipawn loss of 1395 reflects how catastrophically these aimless checks backfire.
analysis.move_pattern: Any piece (mostly queen) giving check, typically to an edge or corner square, where the opponent's king has a natural safe escape square
analysis.why_bad: The check gives the opponent a free tempo to relocate their king to a safer square while the checking piece becomes misplaced or trapped on the periphery, dissipating the attacker's initiative and often allowing devastating counterplay
sub_patterns: Queen check to h8/h6/h1 with king escaping to f7/e7/e8
Knight capture with check where king sidesteps and knight is misplaced
Rook/bishop check where king centralizes to a stronger square
Premature check before cutting off escape routes

analysis.label: Playing a piece-improving or repositioning move that wastes a critical tempo while leaving a concrete tactical vulnerability unaddressed.
analysis.description: This feature fires on moves where the player chooses a 'natural-looking' piece repositioning or development move while ignoring an immediate tactical necessity. In 8/11 positions, the blunder directly leaves a piece or pawn undefended (Nce7 leaves a8 rook hanging, Nb5 abandons the a4 pawn, Ne3 leaves the f7 bishop en prise, Ng4 places a piece where it's immediately capturable, Rg8 leaves f5 undefended, Kb2/Kd2 expose pawns to capture-with-check, Bb7 repositions when Bxf3 captures material). In 3/11 positions, the move wastes tempo when only one concrete action maintains the position (g6 ignores Qxe4, exf6+ dissolves the winning pawn structure, Nh4 chases a queen that sidesteps). The average of only 1.5 good moves available confirms these are critical-moment positions demanding precise action rather than general improvement. The extremely high average cp_loss (1085) reflects that the 'improving' move gives the opponent time to exploit the unaddressed vulnerability.
analysis.move_pattern: Quiet piece moves (typically knights, kings, or bishops) to squares that appear active or safe, but which are non-forcing repositioning moves rather than the required defensive or capturing action
analysis.why_bad: The move prioritizes general piece improvement or prophylaxis over the ONE concrete action the position demands—whether that's defending a hanging piece, capturing available material, or choosing the precisely correct forcing move—giving the opponent a free tempo to exploit the tactical vulnerability left unaddressed.
sub_patterns: Knight repositioning that abandons defense of a critical square or piece
King move to the wrong square exposing pawns to capture-with-check
Passive piece development when a capture or specific forcing move was required
Rook/bishop placement on the wrong square leaving a pawn undefended

analysis.label: Positionally logical or natural-looking moves that overlook a concrete tactical vulnerability, allowing the opponent to gain a critical forcing tempo via check, attack, or capture.
analysis.description: This feature fires on moves that appear reasonable from general chess principles (centralization, development, blockade, pawn breaks) but fatally ignore an immediate tactical problem. In 5/7 positions, the played move places the moving piece on a square where it is directly exposed to a forcing response: Kc2 walks into promotion-with-check (Pos 4), Qe2 invites Nd4 fork (Pos 10), Kf5 allows Rf4+ winning material (Pos 14), Ne2 passively allows Bf2 attacking a rook (Pos 11), Bd4 blocks the king's active path while leaving a pawn hanging (Pos 9). In 2/7 positions, the move removes a critical defensive resource: Nc6 abandons g6 defense allowing a bishop sacrifice perpetual (Pos 5), c6 removes the guard of d6 allowing a free piece capture (Pos 15). The best alternatives in all cases address the concrete tactical need first—whether through prophylaxis (Bf7), active counterplay (Nd5, g4, Kb4), or maintaining defensive pawn structure (Nc4, Kf7). Average cp_loss of 1426 reflects catastrophic outcomes when forcing replies are available.
analysis.move_pattern: Any piece type moving to a natural/centralized square; no consistent direction or piece type; the key geometric feature is that the destination square is tactically exposed to the opponent's forcing reply (check, fork, or attack along an open line/diagonal)
analysis.why_bad: The moves prioritize abstract positional logic over concrete tactical demands, placing pieces on squares where the opponent immediately gains tempo through a forcing response (check, attack, or capture of an undefended piece), squandering the position's defensive or counterplay potential.
sub_patterns: King moving into check lines (Kc2, Kf5)
Piece developing to a forkable/attackable square (Qe2, Ne2)
Piece occupying square needed by another piece (Bd4 blocking king)
Pawn/piece move removing critical defensive guard (c6, Nc6)

analysis.label: Active-looking or materialistic moves that fatally overlook an immediate tactical refutation, typically involving checks that win material or force mate.
analysis.description: This feature fires on positions where a player makes a superficially logical move—capturing material, developing a piece, or occupying a file—while catastrophically missing a tactical vulnerability they've created or a stronger continuation they had available. In 7/10 positions, the refutation involves an immediate or near-immediate check (Bd3+ in position 5, Nxf6+ in position 4, Rf8+ in position 6, Nxe2+ in position 7, Rd1+ in position 3, Qc3+ in position 11, Ra7+ in position 13). In 3/10 positions, the player themselves missed delivering a forced checkmate (Ne1+ in position 8, Qxe3+ in position 9) or a capture (Rxa6 in position 2). The average good moves available is just 1.7, indicating these are critical positions demanding precise calculation, yet the player chooses the 'natural' or 'tempting' alternative. The astronomical average cp_loss of 4009 reflects that many of these convert winning/equal positions into immediate losses or convert forced mates into merely advantageous positions.
analysis.move_pattern: Various piece types (bishops, knights, rooks, queen) moving to squares that appear active or capturing material, but landing on tactically exploitable squares or abandoning critical defensive/offensive duties
analysis.why_bad: The moves create immediate tactical vulnerabilities—typically allowing the opponent to deliver a check that wins material through deflection, intermediate moves, or fork geometry—or they miss the player's own forcing continuation (often a check) that would have won immediately. The player prioritizes a 'logical plan' over concrete calculation of checks and captures.
sub_patterns: Piece placed on a square directly capturable with check or by an unnoticed attacker (Ba6, Bf6, Be3, Nxc2)
Capture that removes a piece from defense, allowing a counter-capture with check (Nxb6 allowing Nxe2+, Bxd6 allowing Rd1+)
Missing own forced mate by playing a close but wrong alternative (Rd8 instead of Ne1+, Qxe2+ instead of Qxe3+)
Rook abandoning a critical file or moving to a tactically exposed square (Rf8 abandoning a-file, Rh2 allowing mating net)

analysis.label: Moves that appear purposeful (centralization, captures, pawn breaks) but abandon the piece's critical function or ignore the position's most urgent tactical/defensive requirement.
analysis.description: This feature fires on moves where a player chooses a seemingly logical or improving move that fundamentally misses the position's most urgent need. In 8/12 positions, a piece abandons a critical defensive or controlling function: Nh2 leaves f3 unguarded allowing ...d5 (Position 6), Ne5 ignores b-file king vulnerability enabling Rxb2+ deflection (Position 5), Nd8 abandons the e6 outpost and blocks the d-file rook (Position 2), Nxa6 trades the dominant c5 knight for a pawn (Position 4), Qc5 fails to address f2 weakness (Position 1), Qb7 abandons the b6-d8 diagonal needed for Rxc4/Qd8+ (Position 15), Ra1 leaves the d-file allowing d6 advance (Position 14), Rg2 plays a passive move with a free piece capture available (Position 10). In 3/12 positions, pawn pushes or retreats create new weaknesses: e6 weakens dark squares (Position 12), e5 grants the queen access to g4 (Position 13), Bf1 retreats a developed piece losing tempo (Position 11). In 1/12, Kf8 walks into a knight fork (Position 9). The average cp_loss of 1095 and average of only 2.1 good moves available indicate these are critical moments where the player chose an attractive-looking but fundamentally misdirected plan.
analysis.move_pattern: Any piece type moving to a seemingly active or logical square while abandoning its critical defensive post, control of a key file/diagonal, or ignoring an immediate tactical opportunity
analysis.why_bad: The moves solve the wrong problem—they pursue a secondary objective (piece centralization, material gain, slow maneuvers, pawn breaks) while the position demands immediate attention to a specific tactical vulnerability or maintenance of a critical piece function, allowing the opponent to exploit the abandoned duty.
sub_patterns: Knight abandoning dominant outpost or critical defensive square (Nd8, Nh2, Ne5, Nxa6)
Queen moving to active-looking square but losing key diagonal/tactical access (Qc5, Qb7)
Rook/piece moving to wrong file, abandoning control of critical open file (Ra1, Rg2)
Pawn advances that weaken king position or create structural holes (e6, e5)
Piece retreats that lose tempo and block coordination (Bf1, Kf8)

analysis.label: Aggressive pawn advances that overextend without sufficient piece support, creating critical weaknesses on vacated squares.
analysis.description: This feature fires on positions where a player pushes a pawn forward aggressively (typically one rank beyond optimal) when piece-based moves or preparation were required. In 10/10 cases the blunder is a pawn move — most commonly e4-e5 or equivalent central advances (7/10 involve e-pawn or d-pawn pushes to the 5th/6th rank). The consistent pattern is that the advance vacates critical squares that opponents immediately exploit: Position 2 (e5 gives Nd5 outpost), Position 4 (g5 gives Nh5-f4 route), Position 5 (d5 allows Bxc3 doubling pawns), Position 8 (e4 clears the d6 diagonal for Bd6+), Position 9 (e5 creates f5/d5/d6 holes). In every case, superior alternatives involved piece development (Nc3, Bf4, Nh5), prophylaxis (h3, O-O), or piece repositioning rather than pawn advances. The positions typically had 1-3 good moves available, none of which were the played pawn push.
analysis.move_pattern: Pawn advance forward one square, typically central (e4→e5, d4→d5, e5→e4) or wing (g4→g5, b5→b4), pushing to the 5th or 6th rank
analysis.why_bad: The pawn advance vacates a critical square that the opponent's pieces immediately occupy (knight outposts, bishop diagonals), removes pawn support from neighboring pieces/squares, and overextends without adequate piece coordination — while piece-based alternatives (development, tactics, prophylaxis) were clearly stronger.
sub_patterns: e4-e5 pushing without piece support, giving opponent d5/f5 outposts
d4-d5/d5-d6 advance releasing tension and allowing counterstrikes on exposed pawn
Wing pawn advance (g5, b4) weakening king position or creating hanging targets
Pawn capture releasing central tension (fxe4) that gifts opponent mobile pawn center

analysis.label: Playing quiet developmental or preparatory moves when the position urgently demands immediate concrete action—typically castling or addressing a critical tactical vulnerability.
analysis.description: This feature fires on positions where a player makes a natural-looking 'improving' move (developing a minor piece, making a preparatory pawn push, or castling the wrong direction) while ignoring a critical tactical demand in the position. In 5/7 positions, the correct move was kingside castling (O-O), and in 6/7 positions the blundering side had an uncastled king on an open or semi-open file. The blunders share a common profile: they are positionally reasonable moves (Bf5 develops a bishop actively, b3 prepares a fianchetto, Bf4 develops with purpose, Ne4 centralizes) but they waste a decisive tempo when the position's concrete tactical features—open e-files against uncastled kings (positions 2, 6), vulnerable g2 pawns on open diagonals (positions 2, 3), fork targets created by piece placement (positions 1, 5), or defensive obligations (position 5 with Bxf6)—demand immediate resolution. The refutations all exploit the wasted tempo with concrete tactical blows: pawn forks (g4 in position 1), knight forks (Nxf7 in position 5), deflection sacrifices (Bh7+ in position 5/9), queen checks exploiting open files (Qe7+ in position 6), or simple material captures (Bxg2 in position 3).
analysis.move_pattern: Quiet minor piece development moves (bishop/knight to natural squares), preparatory b-pawn pushes, or wrong-direction castling—all non-forcing moves that don't address the position's critical concrete demand
analysis.why_bad: These moves waste a critical tempo in positions where the opponent can immediately exploit a tactical vulnerability (usually an uncastled king on an open file, an undefended pawn on a long diagonal, or exposed pieces), allowing a concrete tactical blow that the 'slow' move neither prevents nor creates counterplay against.
sub_patterns: Developing a bishop (Bf5/Bf4) instead of castling when king is exposed
Preparatory pawn moves (b3) delaying castling on open e-file
Castling queenside when kingside castling removes a tactical fork target
Wrong capture method (Bxf6 vs gxf6) removing a key defensive piece
Centralizing a knight (Ne4) that blocks own bishop's attacking diagonal

analysis.label: Playing a natural-looking but non-urgent move in a position where only one (or very few) specific moves address the critical threat or need.
analysis.description: This feature fires on positions where the player faces an existential threat or critical requirement but plays a plausible-looking move that completely fails to address it. In 7/8 positions, there are only 1-2 acceptable moves available (avg 1.4 good moves). The played moves look superficially purposeful—centralizing a queen (Qd3), advancing a king (Kb4), attacking (Rg8), doubling rooks (Rbc8), capturing material (Qxd2), or making a positional pawn push (b3)—but each catastrophically ignores the single most urgent demand: preventing immediate checkmate (2/8), capturing the critical threatening piece (Ke3 ignoring Rxd2), stopping an unstoppable passed pawn (Rg8), covering a second-rank invasion (b3), maintaining a defensive post (Qxd2 abandoning c7 coverage), or taking the only available simplification (Qb6 refusing Qxa8). The resulting average cp_loss of 7075 reflects that these positions are razor-sharp with essentially one correct answer, and any deviation leads to immediate tactical collapse.
analysis.move_pattern: Diverse piece types and directions; typically a move to an unrelated part of the board or an 'active-looking' move away from the critical threat zone
analysis.why_bad: The move fails to address the single most urgent requirement of the position (usually a defensive emergency or forced tactical necessity), wasting the one tempo needed to survive in positions where only 1-2 moves are acceptable
sub_patterns: Abandoning a defensive post that prevents checkmate
Playing an attacking/active move while an unstoppable threat goes unaddressed
Making a slow positional move in a position demanding immediate tactical response
Refusing a forced simplification that is the only way to survive

analysis.label: Moves that pursue a secondary objective while abandoning defense of the critical tactical zone, granting the opponent free tempo to exploit open lines or hanging pieces.
analysis.description: All 4 positions share the pattern of a move that looks logical in isolation (capturing material, retreating from attack, seeking counterplay, or castling for safety) but fundamentally ignores the opponent's concrete tactical resources. In 4/4 cases, the move relocates a key unit away from the critical area of the board—gxh3 passivizes the rook that should capture, Qb1 abandons defense of d2, Qh5 deserts the defensive zone around the exposed e7 king, and O-O-O places the king directly into the opponent's prepared open-file attack. All 4 are tagged with 'tempo_loss' and 'piece_activity,' and 3/4 involve 'king_safety' failures. The average cp_loss of 258 with only 1.5 good moves available suggests these arise at critical junctures where the correct move requires prioritizing defense over the player's own agenda. The refutations in all cases exploit the newly undefended piece or exposed king with immediate tactical strikes.
analysis.move_pattern: Piece or king relocates to a peripheral or seemingly safe square (back rank, h-file edge, or into castling) away from the critical tactical zone where threats exist
analysis.why_bad: The move gives the opponent a free tempo to execute concrete tactical threats (forks, deflections, open-file attacks) against pieces or king positions left undefended by the relocation, because the player prioritized their own plan over addressing the opponent's active threats.
sub_patterns: Queen retreating to passive back-rank square abandoning piece defense
Capturing with wrong unit creating passivity
Queen lunging to peripheral attack square while own king is critically exposed
Castling directly into opponent's prepared open-file battery

analysis.label: Playing a natural-looking or seemingly logical move when the position demands one specific precise action (usually a direct capture or correctly-targeted forcing move) to maintain the evaluation.
analysis.description: This feature fires on positions where the player chooses a reasonable-seeming move that addresses a secondary concern or takes an indirect approach, while missing the ONE critical concrete action the position demands. In 5/9 positions, the correct move was a direct capture eliminating a key piece or pawn (Nxe5, Bxe6, Rxe8+, Bxe6, gxf6+), but the player chose something else — a wrong capture (Nxe4), a passive blockade (Re8 twice), or a quiet king move (Kf7). In 2/9 positions, the correct move was a check or forcing move from a specific square (Qh5+ not Qf3+, Rxe8+ not Nc2+), but the player checked from the wrong direction or with the wrong piece. In 2/9 positions, the correct move was developing to a central square (Nc3 not Na3, Nd7 not Re8). The average of only 1.6 good moves available confirms these are narrow critical moments requiring surgical precision, and the avg cp_loss of 1241 shows the catastrophic cost of choosing the 'obvious' over the 'correct.'
analysis.move_pattern: Various piece types moved to plausible-looking squares (active files, checking squares, capturing targets) but missing the ONE geometrically or tactically superior alternative — typically a direct capture, a centrally-placed development, or a check from a square that cuts off escape routes.
analysis.why_bad: These moves fail because they address a secondary positional concern (rook activity, piece chasing, material grab, intermediate tempo) while ignoring the position's PRIMARY concrete demand — usually eliminating a critical enemy piece/pawn via capture, or checking from the precise square that prevents the opponent's key defensive resource.
sub_patterns: Capturing the wrong target when a better capture exists with tactical follow-through
Passive blockade/prophylaxis when direct elimination of the threat is required
Checking with the wrong piece or from the wrong square, allowing escape
Developing to a peripheral square instead of the centrally active one
Quiet king move when a forcing pawn capture is the only way to hold

analysis.label: Plausible-looking moves in narrow-path positions that create immediate decisive tactical vulnerabilities allowing the opponent a forced winning sequence.
analysis.description: This feature fires on positions where very few correct moves exist (avg 1.5 good moves) and the player chooses a natural-looking move that creates an immediate, exploitable tactical weakness resulting in catastrophic loss (avg 1949 cp_loss). In 9/11 positions, the move played removes a critical defensive resource or creates a new target: g4 displaces the queen enabling Nd4-Nxc2+ forks (2/11), c6/c3 leave pawns hanging (2/11), gxf6 destroys the king's pawn shield enabling Ng5+ combinations (1/11), Rf7/Rb6 place rooks on tactically useless squares allowing forced mates (2/11), Nb5 abandons a defensive post enabling a combination (1/11), Bxe5 captures with the wrong piece creating targets (1/11), f4/Kf2 create check vulnerabilities (2/11). The common thread is that each move appears purposeful (aggressive, developing, or defensive) but fatally overlooks that it creates an immediate tactical refutation—typically a fork, hanging piece, or mating attack—in a position where the margin for error was essentially zero.
analysis.move_pattern: Mixed piece types and directions; predominantly pawn advances (6/11) plus piece moves to apparently active squares, all creating a new vulnerability in the player's own position
analysis.why_bad: Each move removes a critical defensive resource, exposes the king, or creates a hanging piece/mating vulnerability that the opponent exploits through a forced tactical sequence—in positions where only 1-2 moves avoid catastrophe
sub_patterns: Kingside pawn advances (g4/f4) that weaken king position or waste tempo when concrete tactics exist
Pawn moves that remove defense of another pawn (c6 unguards b6, c3 unguards e4)
Piece repositioning that allows immediate forced mate (Rf7, Rb6 enabling back-rank/file mates)
Piece moves to aggressive-looking squares that abandon defensive duties (Nb5, Kf2)

analysis.label: Playing a slow, non-forcing 'improving' move in a position that demands immediate concrete action, wasting a critical tempo.
analysis.description: This feature fires on positions where the player chose a quiet, natural-looking move (king walk, prophylactic pawn push, routine development, standard recapture) while the position actually demanded urgent concrete action. In 6/7 cases, the move allowed the opponent to execute an immediate tactical or strategic threat that was already brewing (h5 pawn storm, Nd4 fork sequence, Kh3 king infiltration, e4 central break, f5 stabilization, Nxb2 capture). In 6/7 cases, king safety was a critical factor being ignored. The common thread is a tempo-sensitivity mismatch: the player assessed the position as calm/strategic and chose a 'useful' preparatory move (b6 preventing c5, h3 preventing Ng4, Nbd7 developing, Kf7 centralizing), when in reality the position was razor-sharp and required forcing moves (piece activation, tactical strikes, or addressing an imminent threat). The average of only 2.0 good moves available confirms these were critical decision points with very narrow margins for error.
analysis.move_pattern: Non-forcing, non-capturing quiet moves (king walks, pawn prophylaxis, routine development/recapture) that do not address the most urgent demand in the position
analysis.why_bad: These moves waste a critical tempo in positions where the opponent has an immediate concrete threat or where the player has a fleeting tactical opportunity. The lost tempo allows the opponent to execute a forcing sequence (pawn break, piece invasion, fork, king attack) that was previously preventable or answerable, typically resulting in catastrophic material loss or a mating attack.

Wrong recapture piece (Rxd1) leaving tactical vulnerabilities unaddressed
Castling to wrong side (O-O-O) misreading where safety lies

analysis.label: Quiet flank pawn advances (especially ...g6) that attempt to chase an attacking piece but fatally weaken the pawn structure by leaving adjacent pawns or squares undefended.
analysis.description: This feature fires on passive pawn moves (8/9 are single-square pawn advances) that appear to challenge or repel an attacking enemy piece—most commonly a queen—but instead create structural weaknesses that the opponent exploits more severely than the original threat. The dominant pattern is ...g6 trying to chase a queen from h5 (4/9 positions), where the advance leaves h7 undefended (enabling Qxh7+), weakens dark squares (enabling Qh6 infiltration), or removes pawn control of f6 (enabling knight forks). Similarly, ...b6 (2/9) drives a queen from a5/c5 but leaves a7 or c7 undefended, enabling devastating queen penetration to the 7th rank. The ...c6 case (1/9) weakens b7, and h3 (1/9) wastes a critical tempo. Even the lone piece move (Bf3, 1/9) follows the same logic of abandoning a key defensive responsibility. In all cases, the player addresses a superficial threat while creating a deeper, exploitable vulnerability—the moved pawn no longer protects its neighbor.
analysis.move_pattern: Single-square flank pawn advance (g6, b6, c6, h3) or defensive piece retreat, non-capturing, non-checking
analysis.why_bad: The pawn advance removes protection from an adjacent pawn or critical square, allowing the 'chased' piece to capture the newly undefended pawn with check/threats or invade the weakened square complex more powerfully than before
sub_patterns: ...g6 leaving h7 undefended against Qxh7+
...g6 weakening dark squares enabling Qh6 invasion
...b6 exposing a7/c7 to queen capture and 7th-rank penetration
...c6 removing defense of b7 pawn
Quiet move wasting tempo when king evacuation was urgent

analysis.label: Moves that pursue an active-looking plan while fatally neglecting the position's single most urgent defensive or positional requirement.
analysis.description: This feature fires on positions where the player has essentially one critical task to accomplish (blocking a passed pawn, covering a mating square, restraining a pawn break, maintaining a key guard) but instead makes a move that appears constructive or aggressive yet abandons that responsibility. In 8/10 positions, the move creates a new exploitable vulnerability: Rhe8 places the rook where it can't capture the d7 pawn (Position 1), Rg1 puts the rook on a file where it becomes a tempo target after hxg3+ Bh4 (Position 2), R8b2 removes the last piece covering h5 allowing Qxh5# (Position 5), Qxa6 drags the queen away from kingside defense enabling f3+ (Position 9), Qa5 removes the queen from blocking the c2-g6 diagonal allowing g4! sacrifice (Position 15), and Qd3 abandons c-file restraint permitting c6! (Position 12). In 9/10 positions, only 1-2 moves maintain the evaluation, indicating these are razor-sharp moments demanding precise prioritization. The average cp loss of 1232 reflects the catastrophic consequences of misidentifying the position's primary requirement.

analysis.why_bad: The move fails to address the opponent's primary tactical or positional resource (passed pawn advance, mating attack, pawn break, hanging piece), and by relocating a piece away from its critical defensive duty, it actively enables the opponent's threat to succeed with devastating force

Rook moving to wrong file/square when one specific placement was critical (Rhe8, Rg1, R8b2, Rg7)

Material grabs that remove critical guards (Nxb4, Qxa6)

analysis.label: Playing a superficially attractive aggressive or forcing move (often a premature queen check) in narrow critical positions where only one precise continuation maintains the evaluation.

In 4/9 cases, the player gives a check that either drives the opponent's king to safety, misplaces their own queen, or forces an unfavorable simplification.

Check before preparatory capture/move-order error (Qh1+ before Nxe3+ or Bxf3)
Non-urgent pawn/piece move in a tactically critical position (a6, h4, g4, Rb1)
Queen placed on square where it becomes a tactical target (Qf6 allowing Nd5 fork)

analysis.label: Quiet non-forcing move that ignores or enables a devastating enemy knight invasion to a critical square.
analysis.description: In all 4/4 positions, the player makes a slow, non-threatening 'improving' move (pawn push, queen repositioning, or knight rerouting) while the opponent has a powerful knight jump available as the primary refutation. Queen placement vulnerable to knight fork
Piece rerouting that abandons defensive coverage against knight activation

analysis.label: King (or queen) makes a passive repositioning move when the position urgently demands concrete active play such as advancing passed pawns, activating pieces, or maintaining critical pawn defense.

The positions demand urgency: advancing connected passed pawns (positions 1, 4, 9), centralizing the king forward rather than retreating (positions 5, 10), keeping the king on a square that defends critical pawns (positions 11, 15), activating the rook before moving the king (position 13), or developing pieces actively (position 14). In every case, the played move is a 'quiet' repositioning that fails to address the position's concrete demands, allowing the opponent to seize the initiative through capturing undefended pawns (positions 11, 15), attacking passed pawns with tempo-gaining checks (positions 1, 4), invading with the king (positions 5, 10), or launching tactical pawn breaks (position 14). Passive piece shuffle when active development/counterplay is needed

Bishop captures rim pawn wasting tempo in winning position

Piece placed on vulnerable square allowing discovered attack along cleared line
Greedy pawn/piece capture missing a stronger forcing tactical blow
Passive queen repositioning abandoning defense of critical sector
King/castling moving toward opponent's attacking resources rather than away

analysis.label: Non-forcing moves (often toward the g1-g3-f4 zone) that waste the single critical tempo in positions demanding an immediate capture or forcing response.

The played moves gravitate toward the kingside/king area (Qg3, Bg3, Kg1, Qf4, O-O all target the g1-g3-f4 zone), representing 'improvement' or 'safety' intentions while ignoring a specific concrete tactical demand. In 3/6 cases, a hanging piece needed to be captured (positions 1, 11, 13 — Qd5 wins knight, Qb3 attacks knight, Qxd5 creates counter-threats against hanging piece). In 2/6 cases, the player's own piece was hanging and needed to be saved (positions 5, 7 — queen on h3 capturable by Nxh3, queen on a7 needed repositioning). The moves include passive bishop retreats when captures were needed (Bg3 instead of Nxg5, Position 9), premature moves that are correct ideas at the wrong time (Nc3 before Ng1, Position 7; b6 before Kc4, Position 3), retreats from strong centralized squares (Nb6 from d5, Position 6), moves to tactically vulnerable squares that invite tempo-gaining attacks (Bf4 allowing Nd5 fork, Position 2; Kc3 allowing Nb5+ fork, Position 5), self-blocking passive rook moves (Rg7 blocking king escape, Position 12), and wrong recaptures that give the opponent free piece repositioning (fxe5 instead of Nxe5, Position 13). The positions are characteristically narrow (avg 1.4 good moves), meaning precision was essential and the tempo loss is immediately fatal.

analysis.why_bad: Each move concedes a free tempo to the opponent in a position where urgency is critical, allowing them to execute an attack, fork, promotion advance, or piece redeployment that the position could not withstand

Move-order mistakes where the correct idea is played one tempo too early

Wrong recaptures that gift opponent free piece activity

analysis.label: Moving a piece away from a square where it performs a vital protective or controlling function, lured by a superficially attractive tactical goal.
analysis.description: In all 4/4 positions, the blundering move relocates a piece (or pawn) from a square where it was performing an essential function—either controlling key squares, protecting another piece, or representing capturable material—for a tempting but inferior goal. In Position 2, the Queen abandons the paralyzing f7 post to capture a pawn on g6, releasing Black's bind. In Position 5, the g-pawn advances from g2 to chase a knight, but vacates the critical guard of f3, allowing a devastating knight check. In Position 7, the knight leaves e5 (where it tactically shielded the rook via Ng4 threats) to attempt a fork on d3, leaving the rook hanging. In Position 12, the king sidesteps to f8 instead of capturing a free bishop, allowing it to redeploy to the dominant d5 square. Each move is motivated by greed (2/4), fear (1/4), or a flawed tactic (1/4), but the critical error is always the same: the piece was doing more on its current square than the player realized.
analysis.move_pattern: A piece/pawn leaves a square where it guards a critical point or maintains positional dominance, moving to capture, chase, fork, or flee
analysis.why_bad: The moved piece was performing an irreplaceable function (guarding a square, paralyzing the opponent, protecting another piece, or representing free material). Once that function is abandoned, the opponent immediately exploits the vacated control—invading the weakened square, capturing the now-undefended piece, or redeploying their own piece to a dominant post.

Pawn advances from guard duty, weakening a key square
Knight relocates from tactical shield position, leaving piece hanging
King declines free capture, allowing enemy piece to consolidate

analysis.label: Playing a natural-looking proactive move (advancing, promoting, centralizing, capturing) that pursues one's own plan while fatally ignoring the opponent's more urgent tactical or strategic threat.

In 7/10 cases, only 1-2 good moves existed, indicating razor-sharp positions demanding precision. The opponent's punishments are typically immediate and concrete: forced mate (2/10), winning material via tactics (4/10), or neutralizing the player's strategic advantage (4/10).

analysis.why_bad: Each move prioritizes the player's own agenda (attack, promotion, centralization, material gain) over addressing the opponent's more urgent threat, which is typically a concrete tactical shot (fork, mating attack, unstoppable promotion) or a simplifying move that eliminates the player's advantage. The positions have very narrow margins (avg 1.6 good moves) where only precise moves survive.

Centralizing a piece to a square vulnerable to knight fork or forced queen exchange
Promoting or capturing material while ignoring an immediate mating threat against exposed king
Moving a defensive piece away, enabling tactical sacrifices on the weakened file/diagonal
Attacking secondary targets while giving opponent tempo for their critical passed pawn advance

analysis.label: Playing a move that belongs to the correct plan but skipping a critical preparatory step, resulting in a devastating move-order error.
analysis.description: In 6/8 positions, the move played is literally part of the engine's recommended best continuation but executed one move too early without an essential intermediate step: Ra8 appears in the best line but only after Be5 secures the bishop (Position 11); Nxc1 occurs in the best line but only after Nxd5 neutralizes the dangerous knight (Position 4); R1h2 serves the correct attacking plan but only after Rd1 protects the d4 pawn (Position 1); a7 is part of the plan but only after the king repositions (Position 15); Nd7 belongs in later lines but only after Nxg4 captures the hanging pawn (Position 3). Attacking move before defending critical weakness
Pawn advance before king preparation
Material grab before neutralizing opponent's tactical coordination

analysis.label: Playing a non-forcing positional move (pawn push, piece repositioning, or centralization) when the position demands an immediate concrete action—typically a capture, exchange, or urgent retreat.

Instead, the player played non-forcing moves—pawn pushes (c4, b3, d3 in 3/8), piece centralizations (Nd4, Kc3 in 2/8), or piece repositionings (Kg6, Qf5, Bd3 in 3/8)—that have superficial positional justification but fatally ignore the position's concrete tactical tension. analysis.move_pattern: Non-capturing, non-checking quiet moves (pawn advances, piece centralizations, piece repositioning to apparently strong squares) across all piece types and directions
analysis.why_bad: The moves fail because they prioritize general positional improvement over addressing the position's most urgent tactical issue—typically an undefended piece that can be captured, a forcing sequence that must be preempted by retreat, or a critical exchange needed for survival. The quiet move leaves the concrete problem unsolved, allowing the opponent to exploit it immediately.

analysis.label: Moves that create a new checking opportunity for the opponent, which serves as the key tactical refutation.
analysis.description: In 6/7 positions, the played move directly creates a checking (or mating) opportunity that didn't previously exist, and the opponent exploits this for decisive tempo gain. The pattern manifests in three ways: (1) King moves to a square vulnerable to check (Ke6 allows Nf4+, Kh2 allows Qf4+, Ke8 allows Qg6#) — 3/7 positions; (2) A piece moves to a square where it can be captured with check (Qxc7 allows Qxc7+ along the diagonal to h2) — 1/7; (3) A pawn move strips king cover enabling a check (h5 enables Rxg2+, e4 creates a sequence ending in Nd3+ fork) — 2/7. The remaining position (d6) is a tempo-loss outlier where the refutation gains initiative without check. The average cp_loss of 4109 is catastrophic, and with only 2.1 good moves available on average, these are critical moments where the single checking vulnerability completely unravels the position.

analysis.why_bad: The move creates a tactical vulnerability (check, fork-check, or mate) that gives the opponent a free tempo, which either wins material, forces unfavorable trades, or delivers immediate checkmate — converting winning or equal positions into losing or drawn ones.

Piece moves to a square where capture gives check (Qxc7)
Pawn advance strips king shelter enabling a check (h5, e4)

analysis.label: A natural-looking quiet move played in a critical position where only 1-2 moves survive, fatally ignoring an immediate tactical emergency.

Defensive piece abandoning critical square allowing mate (Bf3, Qa8, Kb3)
Slow positional move ignoring piece vulnerability (c5, Rb8, e6)
Passive development ignoring opponent's key threat (Qe2)

analysis.label: A knight under attack by a pawn (usually Nf6 vs e5) is relocated to a wrong square instead of making the correct central pawn counter-strike (usually ...d5).
analysis.description: In 10/11 positions, Black's knight on f6 is directly attacked by White's e5 pawn in an Italian Game / Two Knights Defense structure, and the player moves the knight to a suboptimal square rather than playing the correct pawn counter-thrust. In 8/11 cases, the best move is explicitly ...d5 (a central counter-strike that challenges White's bishop on c4 and the e5 pawn simultaneously). Instead, players move the knight to passive squares (Ng8, Ne8 - tempo-losing retreats), rim squares (Nh5 - decentralization), unstable squares (Ng4 - easily kicked by h3), or exposed central squares (Ne4, Nd5 - hanging or tactically refutable). The one White example (Nd2, Position 7) mirrors the same logic: a knight on f3 under pawn attack retreats passively instead of addressing the root tactical issue. The common punishment involves White seizing the center (often d5 advance), exploiting the open e-file against the uncastled king, or simply capturing the misplaced knight.
analysis.move_pattern: Knight on f6 (or f3) attacked by advancing pawn, relocated to any of g8/e8/h5/g4/e4/d5/d2 instead of a pawn counter-strike
analysis.why_bad: Moving the attacked knight addresses only the symptom (the attack) while surrendering central tension and tempo; the correct pawn counter-strike (d5) simultaneously challenges the attacking pawn chain, hits White's bishop, and opens lines - solving multiple problems at once while the knight dodge leaves White's center unchallenged and often places the knight on a worse square
sub_patterns: Knight retreats to starting/passive square (Ng8, Ne8) - pure tempo loss
Knight jumps to undefended central square (Nd5, Ne4) - hanging piece
Knight moves to rim/unstable square (Nh5, Ng4) - easily displaced by h3 or decentralized
Knight retreats removing key defensive coverage (Nd2) - exposes king to checks

analysis.label: Moving a well-placed knight away from a dominant central/active post to an inferior square, wasting critical tempo.
analysis.description: This feature fires when a knight (or occasionally another piece) is moved from a strong, well-placed position to a less effective square, resulting in tempo loss. In 7/8 positions, a knight leaves a powerful outpost (d6→f7 three times, c6→d8, b5→a7, c5→d7, b5→d6) for a square that is either on the rim, the back rank, or simply a less efficient route to the same strategic goal. The common thread is that more efficient alternatives existed—typically shorter routes to the same target (e.g., Ne4 or Ne8 reaching f6 in one move vs. Nf7 requiring a three-move detour), or king moves/development that addressed more urgent positional needs. In 6/8 cases the phase is endgame where tempo is especially precious. All analyses unanimously identify 'tempo_loss' as the primary tactical motif, with the knight redeployment giving the opponent free moves to activate their king, advance passed pawns, or reorganize defensively.
analysis.move_pattern: Knight moving away from a central/active square (d6, c6, c5, b5) to a peripheral or less effective square (f7, d8, a7, d7), typically one jump toward the edge or backward
analysis.why_bad: The knight abandons a dominant post where it controls key squares, choosing a longer/less efficient route to its target or a square where it loses activity and tempo—allowing the opponent to consolidate, advance passed pawns, or activate their own pieces with the gifted time.
sub_patterns: Knight takes inefficient 3-move route when 2-move route exists (Nf7 instead of Ne4/Ne8 to reach f6)
Knight moves to rim/edge where it becomes passive or trapped (Na7, Nd8)
Knight leaves good blockading/central post without concrete justification (Nc5→Nd7)
Aggressive piece move when king safety or development is more urgent (Nd6 neglecting Kg2)

analysis.label: Moves that pursue a secondary positional or strategic goal while leaving a critical piece undefended or vulnerable to immediate tactical exploitation.
analysis.description: This feature fires on moves where the player addresses a non-urgent concern (prophylaxis, vague piece activity, pawn grabs) while ignoring the most pressing concrete need in the position—typically the safety of a piece. In 7/9 positions, the punishment directly involves capturing or trapping an undefended piece: Bh2 places a bishop en prise (Position 3), Qb6 leaves a bishop unprotected against Rxc3 (Position 4), Ba5 allows the bishop to be trapped by b4 (Position 5), Kf1 leaves the a1 rook hanging on a diagonal (Position 7), Rxd4 leaves the b1 rook undefended for Qxb1 (Position 9), Be4 places the bishop on a forkable square via Nc5 (Position 12), and h4 ignores the rook's vulnerability to Bg8+ (Position 8). The remaining positions (f6, fxe5) similarly waste critical tempi on secondary pawn moves while the true strategic urgency goes unaddressed. The best moves in every case share a common trait: they prioritize the concrete, immediate need first—whether saving a piece, seizing a critical file, or neutralizing a passed pawn.
analysis.move_pattern: Diverse piece types and directions; typically non-forcing moves (quiet bishop retreats/advances, pawn pushes, king moves, greedy captures) that fail to address an existing tactical vulnerability
analysis.why_bad: The moves ignore an undefended or inadequately protected piece (or urgent concrete threat) in favor of pursuing a less important positional or strategic idea, allowing the opponent to exploit the vulnerability immediately with captures, forks, or trapping maneuvers
sub_patterns: Placing a piece on an undefended square within tactical range of enemy pieces
Greedy captures that leave another piece hanging
Slow prophylactic pawn moves when piece safety demands attention
King moves that abandon protection of other pieces

analysis.label: Playing a slow prophylactic or 'improving' move that wastes a critical tempo when the position demands immediate concrete action.
analysis.description: All four positions feature a quiet, non-forcing move that appears useful on the surface but fails to address the position's concrete tactical demands. In 2/4 positions, Black plays Kh7 as a prophylactic king sidestep, but this creates a direct target on the h-file (one allows Qxg5 winning a piece, the other enables f4-Qh3 attacking the h7 king). In position 4, Rc8 looks natural (rook on open file) but ignores the bishop's vulnerability on a5, allowing b4 to trap it. In position 12, a4 pushes a pawn instead of centralizing the king with Kg3, the only defensive resource. The analyses tag 'tempo_loss' in 3/4 positions, and all share the pattern of choosing a slow move while the opponent has a concrete, forcing plan ready to execute. The average cp_loss of 485 reflects how severely the opponent punishes the wasted tempo.
analysis.move_pattern: Non-forcing quiet moves (king sidesteps, rook repositioning, pawn pushes) that don't address immediate threats or create concrete counterplay
analysis.why_bad: The position requires immediate concrete action (piece repositioning, tension resolution, king activation), but the move wastes a tempo on a superficially useful but strategically irrelevant improvement, giving the opponent time to execute a tactical plan that was already brewing.
sub_patterns: Prophylactic Kh7 that creates a kingside target on the h-file
Slow rook/pawn moves ignoring piece vulnerability or king activity needs

analysis.label: Moves where the player's king moves toward the board edge or the player ignores critical king vulnerability, when centralization or king safety is paramount.
analysis.description: This feature fires on moves where the player's king is displaced toward danger or the board edge, or where the player fatally ignores king safety concerns. The clearest sub-pattern is king moves toward the edge in KR vs K endgames (3/8 positions: Kd6, Kc6, Kc6), where the lone king retreats toward ranks 7-8 instead of staying centralized on ranks 3-5. In middlegame positions (3/8: bxc6, Kg6, Rxa2), the player makes a move that critically worsens their king's situation—either walking into a tactical sequence on an open file (Kg6 into Rh6+), opening a file against their own king (bxc6), or abandoning king defense for peripheral material (Rxa2). The remaining positions show piece trades that leave the king fatally exposed (Bxb4, 1/8) or move-order errors that allow the enemy king to escape to safety (Rfe1+, 1/8). All positions share extremely narrow margins (avg 1.6 good moves) and catastrophic consequences (avg cp_loss 4909), indicating the feature detects critical moments where king placement/safety is the overriding concern but the player prioritizes something else.
analysis.move_pattern: King moves one square toward the board edge (toward rank 8 or a/h files), or pieces move to peripheral squares abandoning king defense; captures and checks that ignore own king vulnerability
analysis.why_bad: These moves place the king on exposed squares where forcing sequences (rook sacrifices, file attacks, mating nets) become available, or abandon king defense when the opponent has overwhelming attacking potential on open files aimed at the king. In endgames, moving toward the edge allows the opponent to construct an inescapable mating box.
sub_patterns: King retreats toward 8th rank in KR vs K endgame instead of staying centralized
King walks into open file/tactical sequence in middlegame
Piece moves to corner/edge grabbing material while ignoring kingside mating threats
Capture that opens lines against own castled king
Premature check that allows enemy king to escape to safe square

analysis.label: Moves to seemingly natural or active squares that block or interfere with the correct plan, often missing a winning continuation on an adjacent square or with a different piece.
analysis.description: This feature fires on moves that appear logically motivated (centralizing, checking, developing) but critically self-obstruct the position's actual requirements. In 3/10 cases the move physically blocks the correct piece's path (f3 blocks Kf3, Ne7 blocks Re7, Kg2 blocks the Kf1-f2-f3 corridor). In 3/10 cases the move is a check on the wrong square adjacent to a devastating check (Qb1+ vs Qc2#, Bd5+ allowing Qxd5+, Rh1+ releasing the king to e2-f3). In 2/10 cases it's the wrong rook/piece choice (Rfd1 vs Rc2, Ne4 vs Nc4). The common thread is that the player identifies the correct general idea (centralize king, give check, activate piece) but executes it on the wrong square or with the wrong piece, losing decisive tempo or creating self-inflicted tactical vulnerabilities. The average cp_loss of 3018 reflects that many positions had forced wins available (3/10 involved missed mates), making the 'almost right' execution catastrophic.
analysis.move_pattern: Piece moves to a plausible-looking square that is adjacent to or mimics the correct target square, often blocking a critical line/square for the player's own forces
analysis.why_bad: The move blocks, occupies, or vacates the exact square/line needed for the correct tactical or strategic continuation, converting a winning or holdable position into a lost one by self-obstruction or releasing pressure on the opponent
sub_patterns: King takes wrong centralization path (Kg2 vs Kf1/Kf2)
Check on wrong adjacent square missing mate or decisive blow
Piece blocks own piece's critical maneuver (Ne7 blocks Re7, f3 blocks Kf3)
Premature check that releases opponent's king to safety
Wrong piece moved to contested square (wrong rook, wrong minor piece)

analysis.label: Playing a natural-looking developing or centralizing piece move in a narrow position that demands one specific concrete action.
analysis.description: In 9/9 positions, the player chose a move that appears reasonable—developing, centralizing, or activating a piece—while ignoring the single critical concrete demand of the position. The positions are extremely narrow (avg 1.4 good moves), meaning there is essentially one correct idea, yet the player selects a generic 'improvement' instead. In 5/9 cases the critical need involves addressing an immediate tactical threat (Nc3 allowing a fork, Be7 losing tempo against untangling, Kd6 ignoring promotion). In 4/9 cases the need is to capture specific material or create specific counterplay (Nd4 missing Nxg7, Bd4 missing a4 passed pawn, Rc8 missing Rd3 attacking the knight). In 3/9 cases the played move puts the piece on a square where it becomes immediately tactically vulnerable (Nc3 captured with check, Bc3 trapped, Bd4 exchanged). The common thread is prioritizing aesthetics of piece placement over the one concrete action the position requires.
analysis.move_pattern: Minor piece or rook moved to a central/natural/active-looking square (c3, e2, d4, e7, b8, c8) rather than the one necessary square or action
analysis.why_bad: The position demands one specific concrete action (castling, capturing a pawn, attacking the target piece, stopping promotion, creating a passed pawn) but the player instead makes a general 'improving' move that either fails to address the critical threat, places the piece on a tactically vulnerable square, or removes a piece from where it's needed for defense.
sub_patterns: Developing/centralizing when castling is urgently required (Nc3, Be2, Be7)
Centralizing a piece instead of capturing the only available compensation (Nd4 missing Nxg7)
Moving a piece to look active while removing it from critical defensive duties (Rb8+, Rc8)
Placing a piece on a square where it becomes trapped or tactically vulnerable (Nc3, Bc3, Bd4)
King move when piece repositioning is the sole saving resource (Kd6 missing Bd4)

analysis.label: Playing a quiet positional or materialistic piece move when the exposed king demands immediate tactical attention.
analysis.description: In all 3/3 positions, the player's king is critically exposed (g7 in positions 1 and 4, c1 in position 8), and the position demands urgent defensive or forcing action. Instead, the player makes a seemingly constructive piece move to the queenside/center (Bc4, Qb7, Bxc5) that either repositions a piece slowly, defends a peripheral target, or grabs material—completely ignoring the tactical emergency around the king. In 3/3 cases, the opponent punishes with direct king attacks (Qd4/mating sequences/Rc8+Bh6+). The best moves in each case were either forcing tactical resources (Qxf3 forcing a draw), prophylactic king defense (g5 blocking f4+), or consolidation that kept the king safe (N2c3). The common error is treating the position as stable enough for quiet improvement when it requires immediate concrete calculation.
analysis.move_pattern: Bishop or Queen moving to b/c file squares (c4, b7, xc5) away from king defense zone
analysis.why_bad: The moves abandon or ignore critical king safety needs—either moving defensive pieces away from the threatened king or creating new vulnerabilities on files pointing at the king—allowing the opponent to launch decisive direct attacks with checks and mating threats.
sub_patterns: Slow bishop repositioning in tactical crisis
Queen abandoning defensive perimeter
Greedy capture opening lines against own king

analysis.label: Moving a piece or pawn away from a critical restraining duty for a superficially active purpose, enabling the opponent's decisive pawn advance or piece infiltration.
analysis.description: In 6/7 positions, the blunder involves a piece or pawn that was performing a critical restraining function (controlling a file, blocking a pawn advance, or guarding a key square) being moved for a seemingly reasonable but ultimately misguided purpose. The punishment in 5/7 cases is specifically a central or passed pawn advance (d5 in positions 14, 15; d4+ potential in position 13; h5 in position 8; f5 in position 1) that was previously impossible because the moved piece controlled the breakthrough square. In positions 14 and 15, the rook on c4 controlled d4 and the c-file, and moving it to f4 allowed d5! winning material. In position 10, the f3 pawn kept the g-file closed, and fxg4 allowed Nxg4 + Rh2 infiltration. In position 9, the knight on f3 could retreat to h2 to block the h-file, and Ne5 allowed Qh3+ with devastating effect. In position 8, the g7 pawn restrained White's h-pawn, and gxf6 allowed h5-h6. The average cp_loss of 257 reflects that these are positions where the restraining piece was the linchpin of the defensive structure.
analysis.move_pattern: Piece or pawn moves away from a critical controlling square/file, typically laterally (rook from c-file to f-file) or backward/sideways (knight retreat), or via capture that removes a defensive pawn
analysis.why_bad: The moved piece was the sole restraint preventing the opponent's pawn breakthrough or piece infiltration on the abandoned square/file; once removed, the opponent immediately exploits the newly uncontrolled territory with a dynamic advance that gains tempo or material
sub_patterns: Rook abandons open file control to attack a flank pawn (Rf4 x2)
Knight leaves defensive post for aggressive centralization (Ne5, Nc3)
Pawn capture removes structural restraint on opponent's passed pawn (gxf6, fxg4)
Passive piece redeployment when dynamic pawn advance was critical (Rc6)

analysis.label: Moves that place a piece or king on a square that creates a new geometric vulnerability (check, fork, or forced capture) in positions requiring the one precise alternative.
analysis.description: This feature fires on positions where the player makes a seemingly reasonable move that actively creates a tactical weakness that didn't previously exist. In 5/10 positions, the king is moved or exposed to a new line of attack (Ke8 allows Qg8+ deflecting the bishop, Kh2 opens a diagonal for Qe5+, Kd2 places king on the open d-file, Nd2 vacates b3 allowing Ra1+ forks). In 3/10 positions, a queen is placed on a square where it becomes a tactical target (Qc3 vulnerable to Nf4+/Ne2+ fork, Qe5 targetable after Rd8+ back-rank check). The remaining cases involve passive or misordered moves when precision was required (Rge1 allows Rd8 seizing the file, Rxa3 misses the check-first move order, h5 enables Nxg6 structure destruction, Rb3 wastes tempo). All positions share an extremely narrow margin of correct play (avg 1.8 good moves), and the opponent's refutation typically begins with a forcing move (check or capture) that exploits the newly-created geometric weakness.
analysis.move_pattern: Piece or king moves to a square that falls on an opponent's tactical geometry (diagonal, file, or knight-fork pattern) that was not previously exploitable
analysis.why_bad: The move creates a new vulnerability—typically placing the king on a checking diagonal/file or a piece on a forkable square—that allows the opponent to gain decisive material or tempo through a forcing tactical sequence (check + capture, double attack, or deflection)
sub_patterns: King walks onto an open file or exposed diagonal enabling checks (Ke8, Kh2, Kd2)
Piece vacates a critical defensive square exposing the king (Nd2 leaves a1 unguarded)
Queen placed on a square reachable by knight fork or forced exchange (Qc3, Qe5)
Wrong move order wastes the tempo of a check (Rxa3 before Qxd1+)
Passive move when only active counterplay maintains the position (Rge1, h5, Rb3)

analysis.label: Queen captures the b-pawn (b2 or b7) in a poisoned-pawn scenario where it becomes trapped or fatally displaced.
analysis.description: This feature fires overwhelmingly on positions where the queen captures a seemingly undefended b-pawn (Qxb2 for Black or Qxb7 for White), walking into a trap. In 11/13 positions, the move is literally Qxb2 or Qxb7. The remaining 2 positions involve failing to extract or relocate an already-exposed queen (one on b2, one on h7). In nearly every case (10/13), the primary tactical motif is a trapped piece—the queen ventures deep into enemy territory for a one-pawn gain and finds itself cornered by rook lifts to the b-file (Rb1 or Rb8), knight jumps (Nb5 threatening forks), or diagonal blocks (Bb3). The typical victim has undeveloped pieces (9/13 positions feature at least one undeveloped minor piece), an uncastled king (8/13), or both, meaning they cannot generate counterplay while the queen is being chased. Average cp_loss of 337 reflects positions swinging from equal/better to clearly lost.
analysis.move_pattern: Queen captures pawn on b2 (Black) or b7 (White), moving the queen deep into enemy queenside territory
analysis.why_bad: The queen becomes trapped or displaced far from defensive duties after the capture, while the opponent gains multiple tempi by attacking it with rooks (Rb1/Rb8), knights (Nb5), or bishops, exploiting the player's undeveloped pieces and unsafe king to generate overwhelming initiative.
sub_patterns: Qxb2 with Rb1+Nb5 queen trap
Qxb7 with Rb8/Ra7 queen harassment
Qxb7 leaving defender unprotected (overloaded piece)
Failing to extract queen already exposed on b2/rim

analysis.chip: Critical Tempo Loss in Endgame Races
analysis.label: Playing a slow or prophylactic move in an endgame position where a single tempo decides the outcome of a critical race.
analysis.description: This feature activates on endgame moves that waste a decisive tempo in positions where competing plans (king infiltration, pawn promotion, pawn structure fixes) are determined by a single move's difference. In 8/10 positions, the tactical motif is explicitly identified as 'tempo_loss.' The mistakes consistently involve choosing a reasonable-looking but fatally slow alternative: retreating a piece when advancing was critical (Ne2, Bc7), pushing a pawn when the king needed to move (g5 instead of Kg5 in Position 12, g5 instead of Kf4 in Position 4), playing prophylactic pawn moves when immediate tactical action was required (h3 instead of Nxf6, a3 as a neutral wait), or moving the king in a suboptimal direction (Kd4 away from promotion zone, Ke4 away from defensive zone, Kd8 when pawn advances were urgent). The positions share razor-thin margins: average good moves available is only 1.7, meaning most positions had essentially one correct continuation. The opponent's refutation consistently exploits the gifted tempo to execute their plan first—establishing a blockade, advancing passed pawns, or breaking through the pawn structure.
analysis.move_pattern: Any piece type; typically king moves in wrong direction, passive piece retreats, or premature pawn pushes that fix structure; never captures or checks
analysis.why_bad: The move addresses a secondary concern (prophylaxis, passive defense, wrong-direction centralization) while the position demands immediate concrete action to win a tempo-critical race—allowing the opponent to execute their primary plan (blockade, pawn break, king infiltration) one move ahead of schedule.
sub_patterns: King moves away from critical action zone (Kd4, Ke4, Kd8)
Pawn push that fixes structure prematurely instead of king activation (g5 x2)
Prophylactic pawn move when tactical strike available (h3, a3)
Piece retreat abandoning critical squares (Ne2, Bc7)

analysis.label: Playing a natural-looking improving move in a winning position that demands an immediate concrete forcing continuation.
analysis.description: This feature activates when players choose 'reasonable' non-forcing moves—developing pieces, pushing central pawns, or repositioning—in positions where a decisive tactical blow (sacrifice, check, or forcing sequence) is available. In 5/6 positions, the player had a large or decisive advantage (including two forced mates). The missed continuations include Rxf6 (piece sacrifice exploiting pinned knight, position 3), Rxh3+ (rook sacrifice for forced mate, position 5), Qb8+ (check gaining tempo in a mating net, position 6), Ke7 (the one move keeping the escape square open, position 1), cxb4 (capturing a hanging pawn before the opponent consolidates, position 2), and maintaining a dominant centralized knight (position 4). The played moves—Ne7, d5, d4, Ndc6, Nf4, Qe7—all look logical in isolation (developing, centralizing, attacking) but uniformly fail to execute the concrete forcing requirement of the position.
analysis.move_pattern: Non-forcing moves (no checks, no captures): piece development, pawn pushes, or repositioning when a forcing tactical blow exists
analysis.why_bad: These quiet improving moves surrender the initiative by giving the opponent time to consolidate, escape, or counterattack; the position demanded an immediate forcing continuation (sacrifice, check, or capture) that would have been decisive but was overlooked in favor of a 'logical' positional improvement.
sub_patterns: Missing a rook/piece sacrifice that wins immediately
Central pawn push ignoring concrete tactics
Knight repositioning that abandons a critical centralized post or blocks escape routes
Queen improvement when a check gains decisive tempo

analysis.label: Bishop greedily captures a rook pawn (a2/a7/h7) and gets trapped by a single pawn advance cutting off its escape diagonal.
analysis.description: This feature fires when a bishop captures an apparently free rook pawn on the edge of the board (a7, a2, or h7), only to become trapped by a simple pawn advance sealing the escape diagonal. In 10/11 positions, a bishop captures on a2, a7, or h7, and in every case the refutation involves an adjacent pawn advance (b6 trapping on a7 in 6/11 cases, b3 trapping on a2 in 4/11 cases, g6 trapping on h7 in 1/11 case). The trapped_piece motif appears in 10/11 analyses. The one outlier (Na5) still involves a piece venturing to the rim and creating tactical vulnerabilities. The average cp_loss of 278 reflects approximately a full piece being lost for a single pawn. Players consistently had 2-3 good positional moves available that maintained the evaluation, making these purely unforced greed-driven errors where material temptation overrides awareness of the piece's geometric vulnerability on the rim.
analysis.move_pattern: Bishop captures an undefended rook pawn (a2, a7, or h7), landing on a rim square with only one escape diagonal that can be blocked by a single pawn advance
analysis.why_bad: The bishop lands on a dead-end rim square where its only retreat diagonal can be permanently sealed by one pawn advance (b6, b3, or g6), trapping and losing the bishop for just the single captured pawn
sub_patterns: Bxa7 trapped by ...b6 (bishop entombed on a7/b8 diagonal)
Bxa2 trapped by b3 (bishop entombed on a2/b1 dead-end)
Bxh7 trapped by ...g6 (bishop stranded on h7 with no escape)

analysis.label: Playing a natural-looking strategic or advancing move when the position demands an immediate concrete action such as a capture, forcing move, or critical piece relocation.
analysis.description: In all 7 positions, the player chose a move that appeared purposeful and plan-driven—escorting a passed pawn (Kd7), contesting a file (Rb8, Rh1), advancing a passer (b2, e5), repositioning for pressure (Ra3), or improving the king (Kb4)—but each ignored an urgent tactical requirement. In 5/7 cases, a concrete capture or immediate tactical shot was the best move (Rxh2, Bg5 winning a piece, Ra5 cutting the king, Re6 maintaining coordination, Ba6 evacuating a target). In 6/7 cases, the played move allowed the opponent to gain decisive tempo through checks or captures-with-check (Rxc7+, Rh4+, Qh8 forcing trade, Rfb1 doubling). All 7 positions had very few good moves available (avg 1.4), meaning the position demanded precision, yet the played move pursued a one-move-too-slow plan. The common tactical consequence was tempo loss: the opponent exploited the wasted move to execute forcing sequences that the correct move would have prevented or preempted.
analysis.move_pattern: Various piece types (king, rook, pawn) moving toward a strategic goal—advancing, repositioning, or contesting—rather than executing an immediate forcing action on the current critical square/file
analysis.why_bad: These moves waste a critical tempo on a slow plan, allowing the opponent to seize the initiative through checks, captures-with-check, or forcing sequences that exploit newly created vulnerabilities or unaddressed existing ones
sub_patterns: Premature pawn advance before establishing piece coordination (b2, e5)
King march toward a passed pawn that enables opponent check on capture (Kd7, Kb4)
Rook repositioning that abandons a critical function or enters opponent's strength (Rh1, Ra3, Rb8)

analysis.label: Developing or expanding moves that sidestep acute central pawn tension requiring immediate resolution, allowing the opponent to resolve it favorably.
analysis.description: This feature fires on positions where unresolved central pawn tension (e.g., f4 vs e5, c4 vs d5, e4 vs f5) demands immediate action—capture, reinforcement, or counter-strike—but the player instead makes a quiet developing, repositioning, or expanding move. In 12/12 positions, the center is described as having critical tension, and in 12/12 cases the best moves involve directly addressing that tension (captures like exf4, dxc4, fxe4, exf5, or reinforcing moves like d5, d6, e6). The mistakes are moves like Nf6 (developing a piece while e5 hangs), Be6/Bf5 (developing the bishop while d5/c4 tension is unresolved), e4/d4/c4 (expanding while leaving existing pawns undefended), Be2 (passive development instead of decisive central capture), and Nh5/Ng6 (repositioning a piece away from the critical central squares). In 10/12 cases the punishment involves the opponent immediately resolving the tension via capture, winning material or establishing a dominant pawn center. The uncastled king (present in 11/12 positions) amplifies the danger since opening the center exposes the monarch.
analysis.move_pattern: Quiet non-capturing moves (piece development to natural squares, pawn expansion, or piece rerouting) played away from the critical central tension zone rather than engaging the unstable pawn confrontation directly
