analysis.why_bad: By ignoring the acute central tension, the player allows the opponent to resolve it on their own terms—typically winning a pawn outright (the undefended tension pawn), establishing a dominant pawn center with tempo gains, or opening lines against the uncastled king. The 'developing' move wastes the narrow tactical window where the tension must be addressed.
sub_patterns: Piece development to natural square while own central pawn hangs (Nf6, Qf6 with e5 undefended)
Bishop development blocking own e-pawn advance while d5/c4 tension unresolved (Be6, Bf5)
Premature pawn expansion creating new tension while existing tension leaves pawns en prise (c4, d4 leaving e4 undefended)
Premature central break before castling, allowing opponent to dissolve center with tactical sequences (e4 with king on e1)
Knight repositioning to rim/passive square instead of engaging central battle (Nh5, Ng6)

analysis.label: Moving the king defensively instead of capturing an undefended piece on g5/g4 with the queen.
analysis.description: In all 11 positions, the correct move was a queen capture on the g-file (Qxg5 in 9/11, Qxg4 in 2/11), targeting an undefended or vulnerable piece (almost always a knight aggressively posted on g5 threatening the king). Instead, the player moved their king to a retreat square (Ke8, Kg8, Kg6, Kg1, Kf1, Ke7), prioritizing passive king safety over the active tactical solution of simply capturing the threatening piece. The exposed king on f7 (9/11 Black positions) creates panic that leads to flight rather than counterattack. The king moves invariably leave other pieces hanging (typically a bishop on g4 becomes undefended after the king retreats), compounding the error by both missing material gain AND losing material.
analysis.move_pattern: King move to any square (retreating/sideways) when queen can capture undefended piece on g5 or g4
analysis.why_bad: The king move is purely defensive and fails to address the tactical reality that the threatening piece (Ng5) is itself undefended. Moving the king wastes tempo, often exposes other pieces (especially a bishop on g4 left hanging), and surrenders a winning or equal position by choosing passive defense over a simple winning capture.
sub_patterns: Ke8 retreating from f7 instead of Qxg5
Kg8/Kg6 retreating from f7 instead of Qxg5
White Kg1/Kf1 instead of Qxg4 leaving Bg5 hanging

analysis.label: Playing a quiet preparatory move instead of the most forcing continuation in time-critical positions with promotion races or hanging material.
analysis.description: This feature fires on positions where the player makes a non-forcing, supportive move (typically a king step or quiet pawn push) when an immediate forcing move was required. In 5/6 positions, the critical context is a promotion race or advanced passed pawn situation where every tempo is decisive. The errors include: king moves intended to 'escort' a pawn when the pawn should push immediately (Ka6 instead of b7, Kb3 instead of d2, Kf3 instead of e2), pawn pushes that ignore a more urgent defensive/offensive task (g3 ignoring Bh6 blockade setup, g4 as a slight move-order imprecision), and a rook repositioning that abandons a defensive duty (Rd1 leaving the a3 bishop undefended). In 5/6 cases the analysis tags 'tempo_loss' as the primary tactical motif, and in 5/6 cases passed pawns and promotion threats are central to the position.
analysis.move_pattern: Quiet one-square king moves, pawn pushes, or piece repositioning—no checks, no captures, no immediate threats to opponent material
analysis.why_bad: These moves waste a critical tempo in time-sensitive positions where the most forcing move (usually an immediate pawn advance toward promotion or a direct tactical strike) was required. The opponent exploits the lost tempo by advancing their own promotion threats, capturing undefended material, or establishing coordination that would have been impossible one move earlier.
sub_patterns: King escort moves when pawn should push immediately (Ka6, Kb3, Kf3)
Pawn pushes ignoring defensive urgency or move-order precision (g3, g4)
Piece repositioning abandoning critical defensive function (Rd1)

analysis.label: Playing a strategically logical move prematurely without essential preparatory steps, creating immediate tactical vulnerabilities.
analysis.description: This feature fires on positions where the player executes a move that is part of the correct plan but critically out of sequence — skipping a necessary preparatory move (typically a check, piece activation, or king safety move) that should come first. In at least 4/9 positions, the exact move played literally appears 1-2 moves later in the engine's best line: e5 is move 2 of the Nd3+/e5+ combination (Position 1), Ka3 follows a4 in the best line (Position 2), a4 follows Nd3/Nc5 (Position 6), and Ke2 follows Bb3 (Position 13). The remaining positions show the broader pattern: d5 is a standard break needing development first (Position 11), h4 opens lines near an exposed king without first retreating it (Position 15), Re2 abandons back-rank defense without securing it (Position 5), Rg8 places the rook where it becomes a tactical target (Position 8), and Qd8 blockades without accounting for the pin (Position 3). All 9/9 moves are non-forcing (no checks, captures, or immediate threats), and in every case the top alternative involves either a forcing move or a safety/development step first.
analysis.move_pattern: Non-forcing moves (pawn advances, piece repositions, king moves) that appear logical in isolation but skip a critical forcing or preparatory intermediate move
analysis.why_bad: By skipping the essential preparatory step (a check, piece activation, or safety move), the player creates an immediate tactical vulnerability — exposed king, undefended piece, back-rank weakness, or trapped piece — that the opponent exploits through forcing sequences the preparation would have prevented or rendered harmless.
sub_patterns: Exact move appears later in best line but played too early (4/9 cases)
Premature pawn breaks without sufficient development or piece coordination
King moves to active squares before piece preparation neutralizes tactical motifs
Piece repositioning that abandons critical defensive duties

analysis.label: Playing a quiet developing or repositioning move when the position demands an immediate forcing tactical action (capture, prophylaxis, or concrete threat exploitation).
analysis.description: Across all 7 positions, the player chose a 'natural-looking' quiet move—piece development, repositioning, or a standard pawn break—while ignoring a concrete tactical demand. In 3/7 cases (Nf3, Nc3, e6), the player missed capturing a hanging or tactically vulnerable piece (undefended rook on h5, blocked-defender knight on e5, d5-pawn with diagonal consequences). In 3/7 cases (Rb1, Rh1, Bf4), the player made a slow repositioning move while an urgent threat needed addressing (centralized knight threatening forks, knight invasion on d3, bishop sacrifice on f2). In 1/7 cases (Bd6), the piece was placed on a square inviting tempo-gaining advances. The common thread is that all moves would be reasonable in a quiet position but catastrophically ignore the specific tactical reality—averaging 301cp loss with typically only 1-2 good moves available, indicating positions requiring precision rather than general play.
analysis.move_pattern: Non-forcing quiet moves (piece development, rook lifts, bishop repositioning, standard pawn breaks) to natural-looking squares—no checks, no captures, no direct threats
analysis.why_bad: The position demands concrete tactical action (capturing undefended pieces, neutralizing immediate threats, or exploiting forced sequences) but the player defaults to general positional principles, missing that the position's tactical tension requires immediate resolution rather than slow improvement
sub_patterns: Quiet development when opponent piece is hanging or inadequately defended
Slow rook repositioning when enemy knight fork/invasion is imminent
Bishop retreat/repositioning that abandons critical square control
Standard pawn break that opens lines favorably for the opponent's tactics

analysis.label: Quiet positional moves that ignore or enable a bishop's direct diagonal capture of the queen.
analysis.description: In 6/6 positions, the player makes a quiet developing or positional move (pawn push, piece development, or piece rerouting) while a bishop has a direct, unobstructed diagonal line to capture the queen. In 5/6 cases, the bishop on g4 attacks the queen on d1 along the g4-f3-e2-d1 diagonal, and the move either ignores this existing threat (c3, d3, Be3 in positions 3, 4, 9, 11) or removes the sole blocking piece from the diagonal (Nd2 in position 12, moving the knight off f3). In 1/6 cases (position 2), Black's Bd6 ignores White's Bg5 threatening Bxd8. All positions feature closed centers with kings still centralized, and the blunder consistently costs approximately 550-600 centipawns—precisely the value of queen minus bishop. The correct moves in every case either block the diagonal (Ne2, f3, Nf3), chase the attacking bishop (h3, f3), trade it off (Be2), or move the queen itself (Qd3).
analysis.move_pattern: Quiet non-forcing moves (pawn pushes c3/d3, piece development Be3/Bd6, knight reroute Nd2) while a bishop has an unobstructed diagonal to the queen
analysis.why_bad: The moves completely ignore an immediate one-move threat where an enemy bishop can capture the queen along an open diagonal, either by failing to notice the threat exists or by removing the only piece blocking that diagonal.
sub_patterns: Ignoring existing Bg4xQd1 threat with quiet pawn push
Moving blocking knight off diagonal (Nf3-d2 uncovers Bg4-d1)
Ignoring Bg5xQd8 threat with irrelevant piece development

analysis.label: Superficially aggressive moves (checks, captures, attacks) that squander a concrete tactical opportunity by choosing the wrong piece, target, or move order.
analysis.description: This feature fires on positions where the player selects an aggressive-looking move—a check, capture, or attack—that appears to maintain pressure but critically misses a more precise winning continuation. In 6/8 positions, a concrete tactic was available (forced mate, hanging piece, decisive combination) that required a specific move order or target selection. Instead, the player chose: pointless checks that abandon strong outposts (Ng7+ leaving f5, Rg6+ wasting a discovered check resource), captures of the wrong target (Bxe5 taking a knight while a free rook hangs on b4, Bxd4 capturing material instead of delivering faster mate), attacks with the wrong piece (Qf7 going where the bishop should land), or aggressive piece repositioning that destroys the enabling conditions for a combination (Ng5 leaving e4 where it supported Bxg2). The common thread is that all moves LOOK active but fail to respect the precise tactical demands of the position, resulting in an average 309cp loss. The refutations are typically straightforward (7/8 have clear punishments), confirming these are failures of calculation/prioritization rather than genuinely complex decisions.
analysis.move_pattern: Active piece moves (checks, captures, knight jumps, queen attacks) to aggressive-looking squares, often abandoning a key square or choosing the wrong target/sequence
analysis.why_bad: These moves waste the critical tempo needed for the precise winning combination—by checking without purpose, capturing the wrong target, or moving the wrong piece first, they give the opponent time to consolidate, escape, or counterattack, transforming winning positions into equal or lost ones.
sub_patterns: Pointless checks that abandon strong outposts (Ng7+, Rg6+)
Wrong capture target when a hanging piece exists elsewhere (Bxe5, Bxd4)
Wrong piece to the critical square / premature queen attack (Qf7)
Aggressive piece relocation that destroys combination prerequisites (Ng5)
Premature pawn aggression weakening own king (g4)
Defensive king move walking into perpetual check (Kf8)

analysis.label: Black plays a move that abandons critical defensive coverage of their own exposed king, allowing the opponent to exploit open lines with checks, forks, or invasions.
analysis.description: In all 5 positions, Black's king is already somewhat exposed or vulnerable, and the played move fatally worsens the situation by either: moving a key defender away from the king's vicinity (Qa2+ and Qb2 both relocate the queen far from the king, 2/5), stepping the king itself onto a tactically vulnerable square (Kc7, 1/5), destroying the pawn shield protecting the king (gxf6, 1/5), or failing to contest the critical invasion file leading to the king (Re8 instead of Rc8, 1/5). In every case, the refutations involve immediate tactical exploitation via checks, discovered attacks, or piece invasions on the newly undefended lines—Ng5+ forks, Qc3+ winning material, Bxf5+ combinations, Rc7 invasions, and Queen+Rook mating batteries. The best moves in each position consistently prioritize king safety: trading off attacking pieces (Qxd7), keeping the king tucked safely (staying on b8/a8), maintaining counterplay that doubles as defense (Rhh5 keeping queen on h2), preserving pawn structure (Qxf6 instead of gxf6), or contesting invasion files (Rc8).
analysis.move_pattern: Diverse piece types (queen, king, pawn, rook) but all move in a direction AWAY from defending the player's own vulnerable king or open critical lines toward it
analysis.why_bad: Each move removes defensive coverage from the player's exposed king—whether by relocating a defender, advancing the king into check-prone squares, opening files/diagonals toward the king, or failing to contest invasion routes—allowing the opponent to exploit with immediate tactical blows (checks, forks, rook invasions on 7th rank)
sub_patterns: Queen abandons king defense for ineffective queenside activity (Qa2+, Qb2)
King steps onto exposed file vulnerable to queen checks (Kc7)
Pawn capture destroys own king shelter opening tactical lines (gxf6)
Rook placed on wrong file leaving critical invasion route uncontested (Re8 vs Rc8)

analysis.label: Superficially active or aggressive moves (checks, captures, pawn advances) that waste tempo by ignoring the position's actual critical demand.
analysis.description: This feature fires on moves that appear purposeful—delivering checks, grabbing material, gaining space, or centralizing pieces—but actually miss the position's true priority. In 4/11 cases, pointless or counterproductive checks are given (Rc1+, Qxe6+, Rd7+, Re1+) that either help the opponent's king reach a better square or miss a stronger preparatory move. In 4/11 cases, pawn moves are played (a5, a4, c5, and the pawn-grab Nxe4) when urgent piece development or king safety is needed with the king still in the center. In 3/11 cases, pieces are moved to apparently active but tactically vulnerable squares (Be5 blocking own pawn, Bb4 hanging to Qa4+, Qg5 missing a mate-in-2). The common thread is a player drawn to 'doing something visible' rather than addressing what the position actually requires—be it castling, quiet rook repositioning, maintaining a well-placed piece, or a simple winning capture.
analysis.move_pattern: Diverse piece types and directions; typically checks, captures, or forward pawn/piece advances that appear aggressive but serve no constructive purpose relative to the position's demands
analysis.why_bad: The moves waste critical tempo on superficial activity while ignoring the position's actual priority (development, king safety, maintaining strong piece placement, or a simple tactical win), allowing the opponent to exploit the newly created vulnerability or reach a better configuration
sub_patterns: Counterproductive checks that help opponent's king (Rd7+, Re1+, Rc1+, Qxe6+ move-order)
Pawn advances before development with king in center (a5, a4, c5)
Piece moves to tactically vulnerable squares (Bb4 hanging, Be5 self-blocking, Nxe4 forkable)
Missing simple winning captures for flashier-looking alternatives (Qg5 instead of Qxg4+ mate)

analysis.label: A piece or pawn moves away from a critical defensive role, leaving another piece or pawn immediately hanging or tactically vulnerable.
analysis.description: Across all examined positions, the blundering move involves relocating a piece/pawn that was performing an essential guarding function, instantly creating an undefended target the opponent exploits. In 8/10 positions, a specific piece was the sole defender of something: Nd2 removed the f3-knight defending against ...d4 (Position 1), Qc6 abandoned defense of e5 (Position 2), Ng4 left e7 bishop unguarded (Position 3), Rb1 ignored the hanging c3 knight (Position 8), e5 removed the e6 pawn's support of d5 (Position 10), Ke7 left g6 undefended (Position 13), Be3 left e5 pawn unguarded (Position 14), and Ne4 abandoned coverage of f4 (Position 15). The remaining positions (Qd3, d5) similarly create immediate tactical targets through the departure. The consistent refutation is a simple capture of the now-undefended material, often followed by a positional collapse. The avg cp_loss of 270 reflects that these are clean material losses from a single defensive lapse.
analysis.move_pattern: A non-capturing, non-checking piece relocation (knight, queen, bishop, king, rook, or pawn advance) that moves AWAY from the square or diagonal it was using to defend another piece/pawn
analysis.why_bad: The moved piece was the sole or critical defender of another target; by relocating it, that target becomes immediately capturable or tactically exploitable, typically resulting in clean material loss within 1-2 moves.
sub_patterns: Knight leaves guarding post, exposing adjacent pawn or piece (Nd2, Ng4, Ne4)
Queen relocates from defensive square, leaving pawn hanging (Qc6)
Pawn advance breaks support chain, leaving sister pawn undefended (d5, e5)
Piece moves to seemingly active square while ignoring existing hanging material (Rb1, Qd3)
King or bishop repositions without addressing the critical defensive need (Ke7, Be3)

analysis.label: Quiet piece moves that reposition away from the urgent tactical zone, wasting critical tempo while the opponent's primary threat becomes unstoppable.
analysis.description: In all 5 positions, the player makes a purposeful-looking quiet move (no check, no capture) that repositions a piece toward a secondary objective while completely ignoring the most urgent issue on the board. In 5/5 cases, the piece moves away from the critical sector: Rd1 places the rook behind its own vulnerable bishop instead of evacuating it; Ng1 retreats the knight to a corner abandoning f4-control needed to stop mate; Qg6 slides the queen laterally missing a forced mate-in-2 via Qxh2+; Nc2 moves the knight to the queenside abandoning kingside defense against a mating net; Rb6 attacks a secondary b-pawn instead of addressing the immediate h7 promotion threat. In 4/5 cases the opponent has either a mating threat or a promotion threat that the move fails to address. The average cp_loss of 4014 reflects that these 'reasonable-looking' repositioning moves create catastrophic tempo deficits on the truly decisive element of the position.
analysis.move_pattern: Any piece type, moved to a quiet (non-checking, non-capturing) square directed away from the board sector containing the critical threat or opportunity
analysis.why_bad: The piece abandons the zone where its presence is urgently required—either defensively to prevent mate/promotion, or offensively to deliver a decisive blow—creating a fatal tempo deficit that allows the opponent's primary threat to become unstoppable
sub_patterns: Knight retreats to back rank abandoning king defense (Ng1, Nc2)
Rook/Queen moves laterally to wrong file ignoring critical threat (Rb6, Qg6)
Rook placed passively behind own piece on contested file (Rd1)

analysis.label: Playing a standard-looking developing or improving move while ignoring a critical concrete tactical or central pawn action that the position demands.
analysis.description: This feature activates when a player makes a 'reasonable-looking' move—typically developing a piece (Bb4, Bc4, Be7, Qe2, Qb3), castling (O-O), or pushing a pawn for pressure (c5)—while ignoring the position's most urgent concrete need. In 6/6 analyzed positions, the best move involved either a central pawn action (d5, d6, d3, exf4, dxe4) or a direct tactical capture/forcing move (Nxg5, Nc6 with tempo). The punishments follow a consistent pattern: in 3/6 cases the opponent exploits the wasted tempo with a fork (Qd5, Nd4), in 2/6 cases a hanging piece or square is captured (Bxg7, Nxg5 no longer available), and in 1/6 a pawn advance gains tempo on the developed piece (d5-d6 hitting Be7). All positions feature both kings still in or near the center (7/8 opening phase), creating tactical volatility that demands concrete action over routine development. The average cp_loss of 278 reflects how severely these 'autopilot' moves are punished when the position contains unresolved central tension or direct threats.
analysis.move_pattern: Non-forcing developing move (bishop development, queen relocation, castling, or space-gaining pawn push) played when a forcing central action was required
analysis.why_bad: By ignoring the position's urgent concrete demand (typically central pawn tension, a direct threat, or a hanging piece), the player gives the opponent a free tempo to execute a forcing tactical blow—usually a fork, a pawn advance with tempo, or capturing something left undefended by the misplaced development.
sub_patterns: Bishop develops to pin (Bb4) while central pawn tension requires resolution
Piece develops to square that becomes immediately targetable by pawn advance (Be7 hit by d6)
Queen relocates to 'active' square that becomes fork target (Qe2/Qb3 hit by Nd4)
Castling when central tactical demands require pawn breaks first
Developing move ignores hanging material (Bc4 instead of Nxg5)

analysis.label: Piece development or repositioning to b-file squares that ignores critical tactical vulnerabilities, typically punished by queen forks or captures of hanging material.
analysis.description: This feature fires on moves that place pieces on queenside squares (especially the b-file) while ignoring immediate tactical refutations. In 4/6 positions, the move places a piece on b2, b4, or b5. In 4/6 cases, the punishment involves a queen fork or check exploiting an exposed king or undefended piece (Qa5+ in Position 1, Qa4+ in Position 2, Nd3 forking queen+rook in Position 6, Bh3 double attack in Position 5). The moves all appear to pursue reasonable developmental or active goals (pinning a knight, attacking along a diagonal, capturing material, pressuring a file) but fatally ignore a more urgent tactical reality in the position. The common thread is prioritizing an attractive-looking piece placement over addressing a critical vulnerability - whether that's an uncastled king on an open diagonal (3/6), a hanging piece (1/6), or a square vulnerable to a knight fork (1/6). All positions had 1-3 good alternatives clearly available.
analysis.move_pattern: Piece (especially bishop) moves to b-file squares (b2/b4/b5), or captures that ignore b-file/queenside tactical vulnerabilities
analysis.why_bad: The moves ignore critical tactical vulnerabilities (open diagonals to uncastled kings, hanging pieces, fork squares) by prioritizing development or activity over addressing immediate threats, allowing queen forks, double attacks, or simple captures of undefended material.
sub_patterns: Bishop to b5/b4 ignoring queen fork check on open diagonal
Queen/piece to b2 creating knight fork vulnerability
Greedy capture ignoring hanging piece elsewhere
Piece development blocking king escape from open file pressure

analysis.label: Making a king move (or non-critical pawn move) instead of immediately advancing a passed pawn in a pawn endgame race, losing a decisive tempo.
analysis.description: This feature fires on positions where a player loses a critical tempo in a pawn endgame by making a king move when the urgent requirement is to push a passed pawn immediately. In 8/10 positions, the correct move was an immediate pawn advance (g4, f4, b4, a5, c4) but the player made a king move instead (Ke7, Kc8, Ke6, Kf2, etc.). The remaining positions involve the king moving in the wrong direction or making a structurally committal pawn move (g3) instead of advancing the key passed pawn. All 10 positions are pure pawn endgames where the evaluation swing (avg 343cp) comes entirely from a single lost tempo in a razor-sharp pawn race. The analyses unanimously identify 'tempo_loss' as the tactical motif, and in most cases only 1-2 moves maintain the advantage, highlighting how narrow these critical moments are. The typical scenario is a king stranded far from the opponent's passed pawn, where every single move of the race determines whether one side promotes first or both promote simultaneously.
analysis.move_pattern: King moves (any direction) in pawn endgames when a pawn push was required; occasionally a non-critical pawn move instead of advancing the key passed pawn
analysis.why_bad: In pawn races, a single tempo determines whether you promote first, simultaneously, or last. A king move that doesn't directly contribute to stopping the opponent's pawn or doesn't outperform simply pushing your own pawn wastes the one tempo that decides the entire game. The king move appears natural (centralize, approach, blockade) but the arithmetic of the race demands immediate pawn advancement.
sub_patterns: King move instead of pushing passed pawn in active race
Capturing a pawn before advancing your own (wrong move order)
King retreating when it should advance toward opponent's pawn
Defensive/restrictive pawn move instead of advancing passed pawn
King overshooting by one square (e7 vs e6) losing opposition tempo

analysis.label: A piece (usually a rook) moves to target or defend material but abandons a critical defensive duty, creating an immediate tactical catastrophe.
analysis.description: In 5/5 positions, the blundering move prioritizes a material consideration (attacking a piece/pawn or passively defending one) while the moving piece was silently performing a vital defensive function. In 3/5 cases (Rd6, Rd1, Re8), the piece vacates a rank or square that guards against back-rank threats or promotion with check. In 4/5 cases the blundering piece is a rook. The key signature is that the move looks natural and purposeful—attacking the g6 bishop (Rd6), targeting f5 (Rf6), defending e4 (Re8), pressuring d4 (Rd1), grabbing b6 (Nxb6)—but ignores that the piece's departure opens a devastating one-move tactical shot: back-rank promotion (3/5), bishop fork discovering check (5/5 position), or knight capturing queen with check (Nxb6). The average cp_loss of 2251 reflects that these create immediate, often game-ending tactical refutations.
analysis.move_pattern: Piece (predominantly rook, 4/5) moves laterally along a rank or file to a square targeting enemy material, departing from a critical defensive post
analysis.why_bad: The piece's departure exposes a critical vulnerability (unguarded back rank, diagonal alignment with king, or unprotected high-value piece) that the opponent exploits with a tempo-gaining response (check, fork, or promotion with check)
sub_patterns: Rook leaves back rank allowing promotion or invasion with check
Rook lands on square sharing diagonal with own king, enabling bishop fork
Piece leaves post guarding key square, enabling opponent's piece to deliver check while capturing
Knight captures material but removes guard from critical square near own king/queen

analysis.label: Superficially strong attacking moves that ignore concrete tactical vulnerabilities or simpler winning continuations.
analysis.description: In all 3/3 positions, the player chose an aggressive-looking move (centralizing a knight to an outpost, pushing a pawn to attack a queen, or capturing a piece) that appears tactically or positionally motivated but misses the actual concrete demands of the position. In Position 1, Ne5 attacks the queen but ignores a lethal kingside attack against White's own king. In Position 3, f4 attacks the queen but fatally opens the c5-g1 diagonal allowing Qc5+ winning a piece. In Position 5, Nxe4 captures an undefended bishop but with the wrong piece—dxe4 wins it for free with a pawn. Each move has a 'this looks powerful' quality (centralized knight, space-gaining tempo, taking a piece) but the player failed to calculate the concrete tactical consequences, instead relying on general positional impressions. The average cp_loss of 331 and only 1.7 good moves available suggest these arise in positions requiring precise calculation rather than intuitive play.
analysis.move_pattern: Forward/aggressive piece or pawn moves toward center—knight centralization, pawn push attacking enemy piece, or knight capture on central square
analysis.why_bad: These moves prioritize the appearance of activity and aggression over concrete calculation, causing the player to miss either critical defensive needs, newly created tactical vulnerabilities (opened lines/diagonals), or simpler winning alternatives that require less flashy but more accurate play.
sub_patterns: Knight centralizes aggressively while own king is under attack
Pawn push gains tempo but opens fatal diagonal/line
Capturing with wrong piece (minor piece instead of pawn) throws away free material

analysis.label: Moving a piece away from the position's critical area to a superficially purposeful but functionally disconnected square, enabling immediate tactical exploitation.
analysis.description: In 9/9 positions, the blundering move relocates a piece (queens 4x, knights 3x, rook 1x, bishop 1x) to a square that appears to serve some strategic goal—attacking (Ng5 targeting h7), developing (Nbd2), repositioning (Qa2, Qh5, Bb6, Ra1), or checking (Qb8+)—but in reality abandons a critical function. The common thread is that each move either vacates a key defensive/controlling post (Ng5 leaves f3 unguarding the e3-bishop in 1/9; Nxd4 abandons the dominant f5 outpost in 1/9; Ra1 abandons the c-file and second-rank defense in 1/9), blocks a crucial retreat path (Qd2 blocks the f4-bishop's escape in 1/9; Nbd2 clogs the d-file in 1/9), or displaces a piece to a peripheral square while urgent concrete threats go unaddressed (Qa2, Qh5, Bb6 in 3/9). In every case, the opponent exploits the resulting disconnection through pawn breaks (f4, g5, f5), piece invasions (Qh4-f2), or direct tactical strikes against now-undefended pieces/squares.
analysis.move_pattern: Any piece type moving to a square that looks active or purposeful but is disconnected from the position's primary tactical/defensive requirements; often toward a wing or peripheral square, away from the center or critical sector
analysis.why_bad: The piece abandons a critical function (defending a piece, controlling a key file, restraining an opponent's pawn break, or maintaining an outpost) without the position's concrete threats being neutralized first, creating an immediate tactical vulnerability that the opponent exploits through forcing moves
sub_patterns: Knight leaves key defensive post for aggressive-looking but refutable lunge (Ng5, Nxd4)
Queen displaced to peripheral square disconnected from center/kingside defense (Qa2, Qh5, Qd2)
Piece blocks retreat path of another piece creating trapping vulnerability (Qd2, Nbd2)
Rook retreats to passive square abandoning active file/rank (Ra1)
Slow repositioning move ignoring immediate tactical threats (Bb6, Nbd2)
Premature forcing move (check) that allows escape before decisive blow (Qb8+)

analysis.label: Playing a superficially logical or aggressive-looking move that catastrophically overlooks a concrete tactical refutation or misses a critical tactical opportunity.
analysis.description: This feature fires on positions where players make moves that appear intuitively strong—centralizing pieces (Be5, Ne5 in 2/9), launching pawn breaks (f5, h6 in 2/9), making captures or checks (Rxe7+, Nxd4 in 2/9), or improving piece placement (Kg1, Rg1, Rae8 in 3/9)—but which catastrophically ignore concrete tactical realities. In every case, the move follows a recognizable strategic principle (centralization, attacking, file control, king safety) but misses a forcing tactical sequence that either punishes the move directly or was available as a much stronger alternative. The average cp_loss of 1354 reflects the catastrophic gap between intuitive plausibility and tactical truth. Common sub-themes include missing immediate checkmate (1/9), allowing forced tactical sequences exploiting uncastled kings (2/9), removing pieces from squares where they performed critical tactical functions (2/9), and creating tactical vulnerabilities by ignoring opponent's forcing replies (4/9).
analysis.move_pattern: No consistent geometric pattern; varied piece types and directions including piece centralization to e5, pawn advances, captures with check, king retreats, and rook repositioning
analysis.why_bad: Each move follows a general strategic heuristic (centralize, attack, double rooks, seek king safety) while ignoring the specific forcing tactical sequence that either refutes the move or represents a vastly superior alternative—the player trusts intuition over calculation in positions demanding precise tactics.
sub_patterns: Centralizing a piece to a square where it can be captured with a forcing follow-up
Premature pawn break that opens position to opponent's advantage
Flashy capture/check that misses a more decisive tactical blow
Repositioning a piece away from where it performs a critical tactical function
Move-order error that activates opponent's dormant piece

analysis.chip: Quiet King Move, Miss Pawn Action
analysis.label: Passive king or piece repositioning moves played when an urgent pawn advance, capture, or break was the time-critical action needed.
analysis.description: This feature fires on positions where a quiet, non-forcing move (usually a king move — 7/9 cases) is played instead of an urgent pawn action in endgame positions with critical pawn tensions or passed pawn races. In the high-loss cases, the correct move was consistently a pawn advance or capture: Position 1 needed d4/h6+ instead of Kf3, Position 5 needed gxf6+ instead of Kd2, Position 9 needed c3 instead of Ke1, and Position 2 needed centralization (Kd7) rather than committing to the wrong flank (Kb7). The positions share exposed kings (9/9), weak pawn shields (9/9), and endgame phase (7/9). The feature also fires at lower intensity on positions where king moves are essentially correct but the position contains the same structural signature of time-critical pawn dynamics (Positions 4, 7, 8 with cp_loss of 1-20).
analysis.move_pattern: King moves (7/9) or quiet piece moves to non-attacking squares; all non-capturing, non-checking repositioning moves in positions with advanced/passed pawns
analysis.why_bad: These moves waste a critical tempo in time-sensitive endgame positions, allowing the opponent to advance passed pawns, execute pawn breaks, or lock pawn structures favorably — actions that the correct move was specifically designed to preempt or prevent
sub_patterns: King retreats/sidesteps missing urgent pawn capture (gxf6+, d4)
King commits to wrong flank allowing passed pawn creation on other side
King move instead of essential pawn advance blocking promotion (c3)
Piece repositioning allowing opponent's pawn break (b4, f5)

analysis.label: Quiet, non-forcing repositioning moves played in positions that demanded immediate concrete tactical or forcing action, surrendering a significant advantage.
analysis.description: This feature activates when players choose slow, non-threatening moves—typically piece repositions, pawn pushes, or king shuffles—in positions where only 1-2 good moves exist and all of them are forcing (captures, sacrifices, checks, or threats). In 9/9 positions, the best move involved immediate concrete action: tactical strikes like Bxf2+ (Position 3), discovered check setups like Qg3→Ne6+ (Position 4), centralizing knight captures like Nxf5 (Position 5), file seizures like Rd1 (Position 9), or simplifying captures like Qxc5 (Position 7). Instead, players chose quiet moves: queen retreats to d2/e1 (3/9), slow h5 pawn pushes (2/9), or piece placements that looked natural but created no threats (Bg7, Kb2, Rd4, Re2). The average cp_loss of 298 and average of only 1.6 good moves confirms these are critical moments where precision was mandatory. The common punishment is that the opponent gains a free tempo to develop (Positions 1, 3, 7, 14), consolidate defenses (Positions 4, 6), or exploit newly created tactical vulnerabilities on the moved piece (Positions 5, 9, 15).
analysis.move_pattern: Quiet non-capture, non-check piece repositioning or pawn push to a seemingly natural square; often queen to d-file, rook to central file, or h-pawn advance
analysis.why_bad: These moves waste a critical tempo in positions where the advantage is transient and requires immediate forcing action to convert; the opponent uses the gifted tempo to develop, consolidate, generate counterplay, or exploit tactical vulnerabilities created by the piece's new placement
sub_patterns: Passive queen retreat when attack should be pressed (Qd2, Qe1)
Slow pawn push when forcing sacrifice/strike available (h5 twice)
Piece repositioning that creates fork/deflection vulnerability (Rd4, Re2)
King move when open-file seizure demanded (Kb2)
Bishop relocation weakening attacking coordination (Bg7)

analysis.label: Player makes a plausible-looking move addressing a secondary objective while ignoring the position's single most urgent tactical or strategic demand.
analysis.description: In all 9 positions, the player faces a critical moment with very few acceptable moves (avg 1.8 good moves) and selects a move that pursues an irrelevant or secondary plan instead of addressing the one thing the position demands. In 5/9 cases, a piece or queen moves AWAY from the critical sector (Rc3 abandons kingside defense, Qc1 abandons king protection, Qc7 abandons counterplay, Ng4 goes peripheral instead of central, Nf3 retreats from dominant outpost). In 2/9 cases, a pawn advance addresses the wrong wing (b5 when king must move, h3 when active capture is needed). In 2/9 cases, a move creates self-imposed vulnerabilities (e5 overextends losing material, Qe2 places queen on a vulnerable diagonal). The common thread is that each move appears constructive—attacking something, preventing something, developing—but fatally neglects the position's single critical need, whether that's occupying a central outpost, maintaining king safety, or preserving active piece placement.
analysis.move_pattern: Non-forcing quiet moves (no checks/captures) that redirect a piece away from the critical sector or advance a pawn on the wrong wing
analysis.why_bad: The position demands addressing one specific urgent need (central occupation, king defense, active counterplay, or material preservation) with very few acceptable alternatives, and the chosen move pursues an irrelevant secondary plan, giving the opponent time to execute their primary threat unchallenged.
sub_patterns: Piece retreats from dominant outpost to passive square (Nf3 from e5, Rc3 from f-file)
Queen repositions away from defensive/counterplay duties (Qc1, Qc7, Qe2)
Pawn advance on wrong wing when king safety or central action is critical (b5, h3, e5)
Knight goes to rim/periphery instead of strong central square (Ng4 vs Ne4)

analysis.label: Positions with essentially one good move where the player chooses a plausible-looking alternative, resulting in catastrophic evaluation loss.
analysis.description: This feature activates on positions with extremely narrow margins (avg 1.2 good moves available) where a single precise move is required but the player instead makes a natural-seeming alternative. In 6/7 error positions, the best move involved activating or advancing a specific piece to a critical square (Kh3 to support a pawn breakthrough in positions 1-2, Kc5 for king centralization in position 3, Ng6 for piece activity in position 4, Nxd3 to eliminate a key attacking piece in position 5, O-O for king safety in position 7, Nc7 to unblock a tactical diagonal in position 8). The played moves instead chose retreat (Kg1 x2), secondary piece repositioning (Bc2, Rac8), passive consolidation (d6), or material grabs that ignore positional requirements (Qxd2, Nxf3). The catastrophic average cp_loss of 1309 reflects that these are knife-edge positions where the one correct move addresses the single critical priority while every alternative collapses the position.
analysis.move_pattern: Diverse piece types moving to plausible but wrong squares; typically retreating, developing passively, or capturing material when the position demands one specific active/advancing move by a particular piece
analysis.why_bad: These moves address secondary concerns (safety, development, material gain) while ignoring the ONE critical positional or tactical requirement—usually king advancement to support a breakthrough, king safety via castling, or removing/repositioning a specific piece to enable a tactic or prevent a devastating response.
sub_patterns: King retreating instead of advancing to support passed pawn breakthrough
Moving wrong piece when king activation is the only priority
Capturing material while neglecting back-rank/king safety vulnerability
Passive development missing a unique tactical resource requiring specific piece repositioning

analysis.label: King moves to the wrong adjacent square, landing on a diagonal or check-vulnerable square when a neighboring square avoids the tactic.
analysis.description: In all 3/3 positions, the player made a king move when the best move was ALSO a king move to a different adjacent square. The critical error is choosing the wrong direction: in Position 1, Kc2 lands on a light-square diagonal exposed to Qxe4+ (Kc1 was correct); in Position 2, Kh6 places the king on a square controlled by Nf5+ (Kh7 was correct); in Position 3, Kf8 walks onto the a3-f8 diagonal allowing Bd6+ (Kg8 was correct). Each time, the one-square difference transforms the position catastrophically—the wrong square allows a tempo-gaining check that dismantles the defense. All three positions had exactly 1 good move available (avg good moves: 1.0), highlighting how razor-sharp these king-direction decisions are. The average cp_loss of 6570 reflects that these are not minor inaccuracies but position-destroying errors stemming from a single misdirected king step.
analysis.move_pattern: King moves one square to a square that falls on an enemy piece's attack line (diagonal or knight-range), when an alternative adjacent square avoids the check
analysis.why_bad: The chosen square allows an immediate tempo-gaining check (by bishop, queen, or knight) that either forces the king into a worse position or enables a mating/winning combination, while the alternative king square would have sidestepped this tactical resource entirely.
sub_patterns: King steps onto diagonal vulnerable to bishop/queen check
King steps into knight-check range
King moves toward attacker instead of away from attack lines

analysis.label: Playing a routine or positionally-motivated move in a critical position where a specific concrete capture (often with the queen) wins or preserves material.
analysis.description: This feature fires on positions where the player makes a 'natural-looking' move—developing a piece, castling, pushing a pawn, or recapturing with the wrong piece—while missing an available concrete tactical opportunity. In 4/8 positions, the best move was specifically a queen capture winning free material (Qxd5, Qxd5, Qxd4, Qxe4). In 2/8 positions (1 and 9), the player captured on the correct square but with the wrong piece (knight instead of queen), constituting a 'wrong recapture' that allowed counterplay. In the remaining positions, the move created an undefended piece or opened a critical line for the opponent. The common thread is that these are narrow positions (avg 1.8 good moves) demanding precise concrete calculation, but the player defaulted to a general positional instinct—developing, centralizing, castling, or eliminating a threat—rather than identifying the specific tactical solution. The high average centipawn loss (362) reflects that these instinct-over-calculation errors occur at critical moments where one wrong choice dramatically shifts the evaluation.
analysis.move_pattern: Diverse piece types making developing/centralizing/routine moves (captures with wrong piece, bishop development, queen repositioning, castling, pawn pushes) instead of the precise capture or queen move that wins material
analysis.why_bad: The player prioritizes general principles (development, king safety, centralization, eliminating threats) over calculating the specific tactical reality—typically a free or near-free capture, an undefended piece, or a forced winning sequence that demands immediate attention before any other plan.
sub_patterns: Wrong recapture: knight captures instead of queen (leaves queen exposed to tempo)
Piece development to tactically vulnerable square (creates fork/discovery target)
Slow positional move when free material capture available
Queen leaves defensive post (hangs an undefended piece)

analysis.label: Playing a plausible-looking but non-urgent move in a tactically critical position where only one or two precise responses maintain the evaluation.
analysis.description: This feature fires on moves that appear reasonable in isolation but catastrophically ignore the single most urgent concrete demand of the position. In 6/8 cases, the correct move was a specific forcing action (capture, development addressing a threat, or precise check) while the played move was a slow pawn advance or passive repositioning (f6, Kg1, d3, a5, g6, Qg4). In 2/8 cases (Rxb7, Re7+), the move was forcing but targeted the wrong objective entirely. The positions share an extremely narrow margin for correct play (avg 1.6 good moves available), meaning they are tactical bottlenecks where almost every alternative fails. The average cp_loss of 1465 reflects that these positions punish imprecision catastrophically—the evaluation often swings from winning to losing or from drawn to hopeless. The best moves typically involve addressing an immediate concrete threat (promotion on e2, mating net, hanging piece, king diagonal weakness) that the played move completely ignores in favor of a 'logical' but irrelevant plan.
analysis.move_pattern: Varied piece types and directions; predominantly quiet pawn advances (5/8) or misdirected piece moves, chosen over the single required forcing move (capture, development, or precise check)
analysis.why_bad: The position has one critical tactical demand (an immediate threat to address, a piece to capture, a mating sequence to execute) that requires a specific forcing response, and the played move ignores this demand in favor of a slower plan that gives the opponent time to exploit the overlooked vulnerability.
sub_patterns: Weakening pawn moves near own king when defensive piece moves were needed (f6, g6, d3)
Slow queenside pawn advances ignoring an immediate promotion or tactical threat (a5, Rxb7)
Passive king/queen repositioning when material capture was available (Kg1, Qg4)
Wrong forcing move (check with wrong piece/sequence) missing a forced mate (Re7+ instead of Rf6+)

analysis.label: Plausible-looking moves that fatally ignore the position's single most urgent requirement, in positions where only 1-2 moves are acceptable.
analysis.description: This feature fires on positions with extremely few correct options (avg 1.5 good moves) where the player makes a natural-looking move that catastrophically misses the one thing the position demands. In 6/11 cases, the king moves to the wrong square (Kd6, Kh5, Kc8, Kc5, Kd8, and implicitly f3 weakening the king), often advancing into danger when retreat is required (Kd6 into Bf4#, Kh5 forward instead of back to g8, Kc5 into b6+ mating attack) or moving away from the critical sector (Kc8/Kd8 losing tempo in pawn races). The remaining moves place pieces on tactically vulnerable squares (Nd3 allowing deflection, R3d2 allowing Nf3+ fork, Ne4 allowing d3 challenge) or abandon the critical zone entirely (Bxh2 leaving queenside undefended, Be1 passively retreating when Bb6 attacks the key pawn). In every case, the opponent has one clear primary plan (advancing a passed pawn 4/11, delivering checkmate 3/11, or executing a tactical sequence 4/11) that the played move completely fails to address.
analysis.move_pattern: Piece or king moving to a plausible but wrong square, typically away from the position's critical sector or into a tactically exploitable location, in positions with essentially one correct continuation
analysis.why_bad: The move spends a crucial tempo on a secondary concern (material gain, passive repositioning, wrong-direction king march) while the opponent's primary plan—whether a mating attack, passed pawn advance, or tactical sequence—proceeds unimpeded, resulting in catastrophic evaluation swings
sub_patterns: King advancing into tactical vulnerability instead of retreating to safety
King moving wrong direction in tempo-critical pawn races
Piece placed on square immediately exploitable by fork/deflection/exchange
Piece retreating passively when active engagement with opponent's threat is required
Pawn move weakening king shelter while ignoring infiltration threats

analysis.label: Moves on the f/g files near the player's own king that appear defensive but fatally remove or block critical defensive resources.
analysis.description: This feature activates on moves played in the immediate vicinity of the player's own king (f and g files) that superficially appear to reinforce the king's position but actually create catastrophic tactical vulnerabilities. In 3/4 positions, the move is on the g-file or f-file directly adjacent to the player's king. Position 1: R8g7 moves a rook near the king on h7 but leaves the g5 rook undefended for Nxg5+ (hanging piece). Position 2: Rg1 appears to bolster the g-file near the king on h2 but blocks the king's sole escape square, enabling Bf1# (self-block). Position 3: f6 appears to challenge attackers near the king on g8 but opens the diagonal for Bxe6+ leading to a devastating knight fork. Position 4 (Kf5, 16cp) is negligible and likely represents weak/borderline activation. In the 3 significant cases (3/4), the moves look intuitively defensive but actually dismantle the king's safety infrastructure.
analysis.move_pattern: Piece or pawn moves to f or g file squares adjacent to own king, typically appearing to add defense near the king
analysis.why_bad: These moves remove critical defensive elements (unguard pieces, block escape squares, open diagonals) that were holding the king position together, enabling immediate tactical exploitation via forks, discovered attacks, or mating patterns
sub_patterns: Rook to g-file blocking king escape (self-block enabling mate)
Wrong piece moved to defensive square leaving sibling piece hanging
f-pawn advance opening diagonal to own king

analysis.label: King moves to a natural-looking central square (or pawn pushes) that waste a critical tempo in pawn endgames where precise timing determines the outcome.
analysis.description: This feature fires on moves in pawn endgames (8/10 positions) where the player makes a seemingly reasonable centralizing king move or pawn advance that loses a crucial tempo. The king moves are typically to central squares like e5, d4, d6, f6 (7/10 are king moves, with 3 being a-pawn pushes), but they fail because they don't address the most urgent positional need—usually directly supporting a passed pawn's promotion, maintaining a blockade, or defending a critical pawn. In 9/10 positions the analysis explicitly identifies 'tempo_loss' as the tactical motif. The opponent exploits the wasted tempo to achieve a key resource: establishing a blockade (Position 3: Kd2), delivering checks that drive the king back (Position 4: Re2+), capturing an abandoned pawn (Position 14: Kxf6), advancing counterplay pawns (Position 1: b5), or neutralizing the player's pawn advance (Position 5: a4). The average cp_loss of 106 reflects that while these moves aren't always catastrophic, they represent significant precision failures in positions where every single tempo matters.
analysis.move_pattern: King moves to central squares (d4, e5, d6, f6) or a-pawn advances, typically lateral/indirect rather than toward the critical zone of action
analysis.why_bad: Wastes a critical tempo in a pawn endgame by choosing an indirect route or premature pawn push, allowing the opponent to achieve a blockade, deliver a driving check, capture an undefended pawn, or advance counterplay one move faster
sub_patterns: King moves laterally/backward instead of directly toward passed pawn promotion zone
King abandons defense of a critical pawn to centralize
Pawn push when king repositioning was the urgent priority (move order error)
King moves to exposed square allowing tempo-gaining checks
categories: king activity inaccuracy in pawn endings

analysis.label: Moves that prioritize material gain or natural-looking activity while fatally neglecting a critical defensive obligation, enabling severe tactical punishment.
analysis.description: This feature fires on positions where a player makes a tempting-looking move—most often capturing a pawn (5/9 positions involve pawn captures, with 3/9 specifically grabbing b2/a2 pawns)—while ignoring a critical defensive requirement. In Position 4 (Qxa2) and Position 13 (Qxb2), queens grab edge pawns and become trapped. In Position 15 (Bxb2), the fianchettoed bishop abandons kingside defense for a pawn, allowing queen infiltration. In Position 7 (Bxd4), the only defensive minor piece is traded for a pawn, unleashing the opponent's bishop. In Position 14 (Rxd5), a rook grabs a pawn while the king is exposed, allowing counterattack. Even non-captures share this theme: Position 1 (Qg4) moves the queen to an aggressive square leaving pieces undefended (7/9 tagged for piece_activity/tempo_loss); Position 2 (Nc6) develops to a natural square instead of the only one blocking a lethal file; Position 8 (Nc3) blocks the critical c2-c3 pawn support; Position 9 (Kg6) steps to a square allowing a tempo-gaining check. The unifying thread is that each move looks reasonable in isolation but catastrophically ignores the position's specific defensive demands.
analysis.move_pattern: Piece moves to capture pawns (especially on a2/b2/d4/d5) or relocates to natural-looking squares, moving away from critical defensive posts or coordination duties
analysis.why_bad: The moved piece either becomes trapped/displaced far from the action, or its departure from its previous role leaves critical squares, files, or pieces fatally unguarded, allowing the opponent to exploit the resulting tactical vulnerability (trapped pieces, discovered attacks, queen infiltrations, or hanging pieces)
sub_patterns: Queen captures edge pawn (a2/b2) and gets trapped
Defensive bishop captures pawn and abandons king protection
Piece develops to natural square while blocking critical defensive resource
Rook/piece captures bait pawn while own king is exposed to counterattack

analysis.label: Black plays a structurally-motivated pawn move when the position demands immediate piece activity to address tactical threats or maintain attacking pressure.
analysis.description: In all 3/3 positions, Black chose a pawn move (h5, cxd4, f6) attempting to address a positional or prophylactic concern—preventing a pawn advance, opening lines, or solidifying structure—when the position urgently required piece moves. In 3/3 cases, the best moves were piece relocations (Rg8/Na6, Nxf2, Qd7/Qc8) that improved coordination or executed tactics. In 2/3 positions (h5 and f6), the pawn move directly weakened the king's pawn shield or light-square complex, creating hooks or infiltration squares the opponent immediately exploited. In 1/3 (cxd4), the pawn capture squandered a critical tempo needed for a knight tactic. All positions featured Black's king in a vulnerable state (h7, h8, e7) where piece coordination was the defensive/offensive priority, yet Black chose the 'slow' structural fix over the 'fast' piece solution.
analysis.move_pattern: Pawn advance or capture (various files) by Black, typically one-square pushes or central captures, replacing needed piece moves
analysis.why_bad: The pawn moves create new weaknesses (light-square holes, pawn hooks, exposed king) or waste tempo in tactically critical positions where piece activity was required to maintain the balance of attack/defense—allowing the opponent to seize the initiative with forcing moves targeting the newly-created vulnerabilities.
sub_patterns: Kingside pawn advance creating hook for opponent's pawn lever (h5 enabling g4, f6 enabling Qg4+h6)
Premature pawn capture losing tempo on key attacking piece (cxd4 before Nxf2)

analysis.label: Quiet, retreating, or consolidating moves in dynamic positions where immediate active play was required, typically allowing the opponent to execute a knight fork or seize decisive initiative.
analysis.description: This feature fires on positions where the player makes a passive, retreating, or misdirected move instead of the one urgent dynamic action the position demands. In 5/8 positions, the blunder specifically enables a devastating knight fork or check (Nf2+ after Bd1, Ne4 after Qd6, Nd5+ after Ke3, Nd7+ after Kf8, Nb5+ after Kc7). In the remaining cases, the tempo loss allows the opponent to execute a winning strategic operation (king centralization after Rc6, rook invasion after h5, recapture sequence after Bxd4). The correct moves consistently involve active play—king advances toward the center (Kc4, Kf3, Kd6), dynamic pawn breaks (d5), piece activation (Rd8, Qb4), or development (Rc1)—while the blunders are characterized by retreats (Bd1, Kf8), defensive repositioning (Rc6), moves to tactically vulnerable squares (Qd6, Ke3, Kc7), irrelevant pawn pushes (h5), or premature captures (Bxd4). All 8/8 positions feature exposed kings and open lines creating tactical tension that punishes passivity.
analysis.move_pattern: Various piece types moving to passive, retreating, or tactically vulnerable squares instead of forward/active alternatives; typically king retreats, bishop retreats, defensive rook moves, or quiet pawn pushes
analysis.why_bad: The move wastes a critical tempo in a position where the opponent has an imminent tactical resource (usually a knight fork or check) or strategic operation (passed pawn advance, king centralization) that can only be prevented by immediate active counterplay; the passive move hands the initiative to the opponent who exploits exposed pieces/king positions.
sub_patterns: King retreating to back rank allowing knight fork (Kf8→Nd7+, Kc7→Nb5+)
King advancing to square controlled by enemy knight (Ke3→Nd5+)
Bishop/piece retreat ignoring imminent knight fork (Bd1 ignoring Nf2+)
Passive defensive rook move instead of critical pawn advance (Rc6 instead of d5)
Irrelevant wing pawn push when rook activation is urgent (h5 instead of Rd8)

analysis.label: Playing a non-forcing 'improving' move that wastes a critical tempo when the position demands urgent concrete or prophylactic action.
analysis.description: In all 4/4 positions, the player chose a quiet, seemingly reasonable move—either a queen centralization (Qe3, Qd2) or a speculative flank pawn push (h4, h4)—when the position contained a critical, time-sensitive demand. In 4/4 cases the best move addressed an urgent tactical or prophylactic need (Rce1 threatening Re8+, f4 solidifying structure, Qh6 activating before pushing, Kc2 preventing knight invasion), while the played move addressed nothing urgent. In 4/4 positions the opponent immediately exploited the wasted tempo: 7th-rank invasion (2/4), piece invasion to dominant outpost (2/4), tactical combination exploiting newly-created geometric weaknesses (2/4). The average good moves available was only 1.5, indicating these are 'one right answer' positions where the natural-looking move is a trap. The common thread is that the position appeared to allow a 'consolidating' or 'improving' move, but the opponent had concrete resources that demanded immediate attention.
analysis.move_pattern: Non-forcing quiet moves: queen centralization to natural squares (e3, d2) or h-pawn one-square advances, none creating checks, captures, or concrete threats
analysis.why_bad: Wastes a critical tempo in positions where the opponent has an immediate concrete plan (knight invasion, 7th-rank penetration, tactical combination), allowing them to execute their threat unopposed while the 'improving' move addresses nothing urgent
sub_patterns: Queen centralization to seemingly logical square (Qe3/Qd2) that creates new tactical vulnerabilities
Speculative h-pawn advance ignoring opponent's imminent piece invasion or positional breakthrough

analysis.label: Moving a piece already on an optimal square to a seemingly active but counterproductive square, losing critical tempo or coordination with the position's demands.
analysis.description: This feature fires when a player moves a piece that is already well-positioned to a square that appears attractive (often giving a check or targeting something) but actually abandons the piece's critical coordination. In 5/6 positions, the piece was already on or near its optimal square and moved laterally or to the periphery. In 3/6 cases (Qh7+, Qc4+, Qd3), the queen is displaced from a square where it coordinated with tactical motifs (stopping promotion, enabling a knight fork, delivering forced mate via checks). In 2/6 cases (Nh5, Rg5), a piece leaves a critical post for a speculative rim/lateral square. In 1/6 (Ba1), a piece retreats deeper into the corner ignoring the real problem. All 6/6 positions feature tempo loss as the core punishment mechanism—the opponent exploits the wasted move to execute their plan (promote a pawn, escape the king, win material, or extend a mating sequence).
analysis.move_pattern: Piece (especially Queen) moves laterally, to the rim, or one square away from its current optimal post—often giving a check or appearing aggressive—while abandoning coordination with the critical zone
analysis.why_bad: The piece was already optimally placed for the position's key demands (stopping promotion, enabling forks, maintaining mating threats, defending critical squares). The move wastes a tempo by displacing the piece from where it needs to be, giving the opponent time to execute their counterplan or escape danger.
sub_patterns: Pointless checks that displace the queen from its coordinating square (Qh7+, Qc4+)
Quiet repositioning when forcing moves are required (Qd3 instead of immediate check)
Knight/Rook moving to rim/lateral square abandoning critical defensive or attacking duty (Nh5, Rg5)
Passive retreat of a piece not under real threat while ignoring urgent problems (Ba1)

analysis.label: Moving a piece away from critical defensive duties or the main tactical zone to pursue a peripheral or illusory secondary objective.
analysis.description: In 7/7 analyzed positions, the blundering move relocates a piece away from where it is critically needed—typically king defense or the primary theater of operations—to chase a secondary goal (pawn grab, speculative attack, or slow positional idea). In 5/7 cases the queen or major piece moves far from the king, directly enabling mating attacks or decisive checks (Qa6 abandoning g2 defense, Qf8 abandoning h2, Rf6 leaving defensive coverage, Rh1 leaving the active f-file, Kf7 walking into check corridors). In 2/7 cases a pawn or minor piece pursues material at the rim (Nxa4 grabbing a wing pawn while the h4 knight escapes; h4 chasing a slow pawn break when Rxf6 won immediately). The punishment consistently involves the opponent exploiting the now-unguarded critical zone—usually via checks, queen infiltration, or capture of suddenly undefended material. The average cp_loss of 3275 reflects that these self-deflections create catastrophic vulnerabilities in positions where only 1.9 good moves existed on average.
analysis.move_pattern: Any piece type moving away from the critical defensive zone or active central post toward a peripheral square (rim files, far flanks, or non-threatening positions)
analysis.why_bad: The piece was needed where it was (or needed to go to a specific urgent square); by pursuing a secondary objective, the player leaves the king or critical squares fatally undefended, allowing the opponent to exploit the vacated zone with checks, infiltrations, or material captures.
sub_patterns: Queen abandons king defense for rim/attacking square (Qa6, Qf8, Qh5)
Rook leaves active file for peripheral pawn chase (Rh1, Rf6)
Pawn/piece move weakens own king shelter (b3, h4, Kf7)
Knight/piece captures peripheral pawn while opponent's trapped piece escapes (Nxa4)

analysis.label: Playing a natural-looking plan move (pawn advance, development, king move) before addressing an immediate critical precondition such as king safety, move order, or a tactical threat.
analysis.description: This feature fires on positions where the player executes the 'next logical step' of their plan without first establishing necessary preconditions. The most common sub-pattern is premature passed pawn advances (4/9 positions: both d7 moves, d2, and b2), where the pawn push is indeed the correct strategic idea but fails because king support or an intermediate check must come first. In 3/9 positions (Kf1, Re8, Re1), the player makes a developing or repositioning move while ignoring an immediate forced-mate threat that required addressing king safety first. In 2/9 positions (Kc2, Kb4), king moves pursue a natural improvement but miss that a tactical issue (hanging piece, edge placement) takes priority. The unifying thread is that the correct move in every case involves addressing an urgent prerequisite BEFORE executing the plan: giving check first (Rc1+ before d2), activating the king first (Ke5 before d7, Kc5 before b2), fleeing the correct direction (Kd1 not Kf1), or defending a hanging piece (Nd3 not Kc2). The average cp_loss of 4511 reflects that many of these errors convert winning/drawing positions into immediate checkmates or catastrophic material loss.
analysis.move_pattern: Advancing a passed pawn, developing a rook to a central file, or making a king move in the 'natural' direction - all forward-looking moves that pursue a visible plan
analysis.why_bad: The position demands addressing an immediate tactical precondition first (intermediate check, king safety, piece defense, king activation for pawn support) before executing the plan; skipping this preparation allows the opponent to exploit the unaddressed threat with mate, piece capture, or pawn elimination
sub_patterns: Premature passed pawn push without king support or intermediate check (d7, d2, b2, d7)
Developing/repositioning move ignoring immediate forced mate (Re8, Re1, Kf1)
King improvement ignoring hanging piece or positional requirement (Kc2, Kb4)

analysis.label: Active-looking moves that catastrophically fail to address the position's single most critical requirement in sharp, narrow positions.
analysis.description: This feature fires on positions where very few moves are acceptable (avg 1.7 good moves) and the player chooses a plausible, often active-looking move that entirely misses the position's dominant tactical or safety requirement. In 6/10 cases, the critical issue involves king safety—either the player's own king stepping into danger (Kc7 walking into queen checks, Kg7 walking into discovered attack, Rf7 ignoring king on open g-file) or failing to secure king safety before taking action (Bxe6 before castling). In 4/10 cases, the error is addressing the wrong piece or wrong target—Nd6 centralizes the wrong knight instead of challenging the opponent's dominant piece, Re2 prepares passively when immediate Rxe7 capture was essential, Nc4+ delivers a hollow check while abandoning the piece critical for a mating pattern, and Qf4 attacks a secondary target while ignoring the vulnerable g5 knight. The connecting thread is that these positions all have ONE overwhelmingly important action, and the played move substitutes a secondary (but superficially appealing) goal.
analysis.move_pattern: Diverse piece types moving to apparently active/purposeful squares; no single geometric pattern—the commonality is moves that look reasonable but address a secondary concern rather than the critical one
analysis.why_bad: Each position has a single critical requirement (securing king from tactical shot, capturing immediately before opponent consolidates, maintaining piece on critical tactical square) and the played move prioritizes a less important goal, allowing the opponent to exploit the neglected vulnerability with often devastating tactical punishment
sub_patterns: King moving to exposed square (Kc7, Kg7)
Premature capture before securing safety (Bxe6)
Supporting a threat when prophylaxis needed first (Rf7)
Superficial check that abandons critical tactical setup (Nc4+)
Passive preparation when forcing action required (Re2, g4)
Wrong piece moved while key problem ignored (Nd6, Qf4)

analysis.label: Natural-looking moves that ignore the single most urgent tactical or positional requirement in positions with very few correct options.
analysis.description: This feature fires on positions where the player makes a move with clear, logical intent but catastrophically fails to address the one critical demand of the position. In 9/11 cases, there were only 1-2 good moves available (avg 1.8), indicating razor-thin positions requiring precise play. The moves all have obvious purposes: g5 chases a knight, axb5 captures a piece, O-O seeks king safety, Qxh2 grabs material, Nd7 attacks a bishop, Nf5 attacks a queen, b4 attacks a knight, Kd3 centralizes—yet each ignores a prerequisite: securing a hanging piece first (g5, axb5 with wrong piece), protecting a vulnerable piece before acting (b4 before Bg6), maintaining a critical defender (Nd7 removing f6 knight, Nf5 abandoning d4), or resolving urgent tactics before routine play (O-O instead of Ngxe4). The average cp_loss of 1098 reflects that these 'one move too early' or 'wrong priority' errors occur at critical junctures where the position collapses if the single correct action isn't taken first.
analysis.move_pattern: Mixed piece types and directions; no geometric commonality. Moves are functionally 'purposeful actions' (attacks, captures, development, castling) executed without prerequisite safety measures.
analysis.why_bad: Each move pursues a secondary objective (attack, material, development, king safety) while the position demands addressing one specific urgent tactical vulnerability first—a hanging piece, a critical defender's role, a forcing sequence available to the opponent, or a precise positional requirement like opposition.
sub_patterns: Advancing/attacking before securing a vulnerable piece (g5 with bishop on c4, b4 with bishop on f5)
Removing a critical defensive piece to pursue offense (Nd7 abandoning h7, Nf5 abandoning d4/d8)
Capturing with the wrong piece, leaving development unsolved (axb5 instead of Bxb5)
Routine development when urgent tactics demand immediate resolution (O-O instead of Ngxe4)
Pawn-grabbing or queen wandering while fundamentally underdeveloped (Qxh2 with unmoved knights)

analysis.label: Non-developing pawn moves (especially f-pawn advances) that weaken the king's diagonal protection while the king remains in the center.
analysis.description: This feature fires on positions where a player makes a non-developing pawn move in the opening with their king still in the center, most commonly advancing the f-pawn (f6 for Black or f4 for White, seen in 5/8 positions). The critical shared consequence is weakening the diagonal leading to the king (e8-h5 for Black after ...f6, e1-h4 for White after g4/f4), which enables immediate tactical exploitation via queen checks (Qh5+ appears in 4/8 refutations, Qh4+ in 1/8). The remaining positions (b3, c5, g4) share the same structural error: wasting a tempo on a non-developing pawn move when the king is uncastled (8/8 positions have the moving side's king in the center), allowing the opponent's already-developed pieces to launch decisive attacks against the exposed monarch. In all cases, simple developing moves (Nc6, Nf3, d6, etc.) were available as alternatives.
analysis.move_pattern: Pawn advance (predominantly f-pawn one square forward) that removes diagonal protection from the uncastled king; no capture, no check
analysis.why_bad: The f-pawn advance (or similar weakening pawn move) removes critical diagonal shielding from the king while it still sits in the center, and wastes a developing tempo, allowing the opponent's pieces to exploit the newly opened diagonal with forcing checks (typically Qh5+ or Qh4+) that win material or permanently displace the king.
sub_patterns: ...f6 weakening e8-h5 diagonal allowing Qh5+
f4/g4 weakening e1-h4 diagonal allowing Qh4+
Non-developing queenside pawn move (b3/c5) when critically behind in development with king in center

analysis.label: Moves that waste a critical tempo, allowing an opponent's passed pawn to advance/promote (often by checking in a direction that permits pawn interposition).
analysis.description: This feature fires on positions where a player makes a natural-looking move—frequently a queen check or piece-improving move—that critically fails to address the most urgent threat in the position, typically an advanced passed pawn about to promote. In 8/11 positions, a passed pawn within 1-2 squares of promotion is the dominant tactical element. The most distinctive sub-pattern (positions 1, 2, 3, 10, 14 = 5/11) involves giving a queen check along a rank/file/diagonal where the enemy pawn can INTERPOSE by advancing or promoting, simultaneously blocking the check AND making progress toward queening. In other cases (positions 4, 5, 9 = 3/11), the player makes a piece-improving or king move that ignores the one-move promotion threat. The remaining positions (6, 7, 8, 11) share the broader pattern of spending a tempo on a non-critical action while a devastating tactical reply exists. The average cp_loss of ~2026 reflects that these tempo errors frequently convert winning positions into draws or losses.
analysis.move_pattern: Any piece type; often queen checks along ranks/files/diagonals that pass through the promotion square, or piece-improving moves that ignore an imminent promotion or tactical shot
analysis.why_bad: The move gives the opponent a free tempo to advance/promote a passed pawn (often with interposition that blocks a check), or to execute an immediate tactical threat that the 'active-looking' move failed to prevent. The correct moves either check in directions where no interposition is possible, or directly address the promotion square/pawn before doing anything else.
sub_patterns: Queen check along line where pawn interposes by promoting (positions 1, 2, 3)
Piece improvement move ignoring immediate promotion threat (positions 4, 9, 10)
Non-critical pawn/piece move ignoring opponent's tactical shot (positions 5, 6, 11)
Premature capture missing more forcing intermediate move (positions 7, 8)

analysis.label: Playing a slow, non-forcing 'improving' move when the position demands an immediate concrete/forcing action, wasting the one tempo that determines the outcome.
analysis.description: This feature fires on positions where the player chooses a quiet, natural-looking move (development, repositioning, centralization, or slow pawn advance) in a critical moment that demands precise, forcing action. In 9/11 positions, the best move was a concrete tactical or forcing move (Bxd5 capturing a key pawn, Rxg3+ sacrificing with check, Rf8 immediately trapping a piece, Nh5 blockading, Rf2 enabling perpetual checks) while the blunder was a generic 'improving' move (Bb1 retreating, Rad8/Rae1 centralizing rooks without threats, a5/e3/b4 advancing pawns slowly, Ng2/Qd7 passively repositioning). The average good moves available was only 1.5, confirming these are narrow-path positions where one specific idea works. In every case, the non-forcing move gifts the opponent a free tempo to consolidate, execute their plan, or exploit a newly undefended piece/square. The tag 'tempo_loss' appears in 10/11 analyses.
analysis.move_pattern: Diverse piece types and directions; characteristically non-capturing, non-checking, non-threatening moves—quiet retreats, non-forcing rook lifts, slow pawn pushes, and passive piece repositioning
analysis.why_bad: The positions all have a narrow window for concrete action (avg 1.5 good moves); the quiet move wastes the critical tempo, allowing the opponent to fix their vulnerability, advance their plans (passed pawns, piece activation), or exploit newly undefended pieces/squares that the moving piece previously controlled
sub_patterns: Passive piece retreat to inactive square (Bb1, Ng2, Qd7)
Non-forcing rook centralization missing immediate threats (Rad8, Rae1, Rh2)
Slow pawn advance missing forcing tactic (a5, e3, b4)
Move-order error choosing wrong pawn/capture (fxg6, b4)
Queen repositioning abandoning defensive duty (Qb3, Qd7)

analysis.label: Moving a piece to an active-looking or greedy square while abandoning its essential defensive function, allowing immediate tactical exploitation of the vacated responsibility.
analysis.description: In 6/7 positions, the played move sends a piece (or pawn) toward what appears to be a purposeful square—centralizing (Ke6, Qe4), grabbing material (Qxa4, Bxh3), seeking activity (Nd7, Rd3), or gaining space (b5)—while fatally neglecting an urgent defensive task. The knight abandons a-pawn blockade duty (Pos 3), the king walks away from safety into checkmate (Pos 4), the rook leaves second-rank coverage exposing the king (Pos 5), the bishop captures with the wrong piece leaving a knight hanging (Pos 6), the queen grabs a pawn far from the king under attack (Pos 9), the pawn commits prematurely fixing targets (Pos 11), and the queen centralizes while abandoning protection of e3 (Pos 12). In all cases, exactly 1-3 good moves existed (avg 1.6), indicating positions requiring precise defensive awareness. The punishment is typically immediate and severe (avg 1552cp loss), exploiting the specific square or function that was abandoned.
analysis.move_pattern: Various piece types moving to apparently active/central/material-gaining squares, typically moving AWAY from the critical sector or abandoning a specific defensive function
analysis.why_bad: The moves prioritize superficial piece activity, centralization, or material gain while ignoring an urgent positional or tactical requirement—a specific defensive task (blockade, king coverage, piece protection, square control) that, once abandoned, allows the opponent to execute an immediate tactical blow or strategic breakthrough.
sub_patterns: Queen leaving king defense to grab distant pawn
Piece moving to wrong sector while opponent's threat demands presence
Capturing with wrong piece, leaving another piece undefended
King walking into tactical vulnerability while seeking activity
Premature pawn advance creating fixed targets
