analysis.label: Playing a plausible-looking move that fails to address the position's single most urgent defensive or structural requirement, allowing a concrete tactical exploitation.
analysis.description: This feature fires on positions where the player chooses a 'reasonable-seeming' move—often a capture, development, or repositioning—while the position demands one specific action to prevent a concrete tactical threat. In 5/7 positions, a piece or pawn was performing a critical defensive function (controlling a key square, defending a weakness, or maintaining structural integrity) and the player moved it or failed to reinforce it. In Position 1, Rxd5 captures the wrong target (should address the a4 passed pawn). In Position 2, b6 ignores the immediate e5 threat to the knight. In Position 4, Bf4 places the bishop where e5 creates a pawn fork. In Position 8, Bh4 abandons control of f4, allowing a knight fork. In Position 11, Nf6 abandons defense of f7 against a triple battery. In Position 15, dxe5 captures with the wrong unit, destroying the d6 pawn's structural defense. These moves all look logical in isolation but miss the position's critical requirement, typically with only 1-3 good alternatives available (avg 1.9), indicating high-precision positions where inattention to the key threat is immediately punished.
analysis.move_pattern: Varied piece types and directions; the common thread is moving a piece away from its critical defensive post or executing a capture/plan that neglects the position's most urgent vulnerability
analysis.why_bad: Each move abandons or fails to address a critical defensive responsibility (controlling a key square, defending a weak point, or maintaining pawn structure), allowing the opponent an immediate concrete tactical exploitation—typically a fork, invasion, or unstoppable pawn advance.
sub_patterns: Capturing the wrong target when a more dangerous threat exists elsewhere
Moving a piece from a square that was preventing a tactical shot (fork/invasion)
Slow positional move (flank pawn push, fianchetto prep) when immediate central/tactical action is required
Capturing with the wrong piece/pawn, destroying critical structural defense

analysis.label: Moving a piece away from an essential defensive duty, leaving a key square or pawn tactically exploitable.
analysis.description: This feature fires on moves where a piece is relocated away from a critical defensive function—whether guarding a specific square, shielding the king, or maintaining positional tension—to pursue an apparently active but strategically irrelevant goal. In 3/11 positions, a rook or knight abandons defense of f7/g7 (Re8 leaves f8, Re6 leaves f6, Nxe4 removes the f6 knight), enabling immediate Nxf7 or Nxg7 tactical strikes. In 2/11 positions, a knight vacates a powerful central outpost (Ng3 from e4, Nc4 from e5), leaving critical central pawns undefended and inviting forks or exchanges. In 4/11 positions, the move ignores an urgent defensive requirement—typically king safety or file control—in favor of irrelevant piece repositioning (Ba6 ignores kingside mating attack, Nd7 delays castling, Rh2 ignores c-file infiltration, b5 exposes king to check). The average cp_loss of 1150 with only 2.2 good moves available confirms these are positions where the defensive function was paramount and nearly unique.
analysis.move_pattern: Any piece type moving away from a defended square or protective post; often sideways/backward retreats or captures away from the critical sector of the board
analysis.why_bad: The moved piece was performing an irreplaceable defensive function (guarding f7, g7, a central pawn, or shielding the king from checks), and its departure immediately enables a concrete tactical blow—typically a knight fork, discovered attack, or mating sequence targeting the now-undefended square.
sub_patterns: Rook leaves f-file abandoning f7 defense (Re8, Re6)
Knight captures away from kingside guard duty (Nxe4 removing g7 defender)
Knight abandons central outpost leaving pawn hanging (Ng3, Nc4)
Piece develops to irrelevant flank while king is under attack (Ba6, Nd7)
Passive retreat ignoring primary positional threat (Rh2, Rfb1, b5)

analysis.label: Aggressive or active moves that remove a piece or pawn from a critical defensive role, immediately allowing the opponent to exploit the unguarded weakness.
analysis.description: In 5/6 positions, the blundering move removes a specific defender from its post to pursue an attractive but non-essential offensive idea. In Position 2, Ne4 moves the c3-knight that was the sole recapture piece on a3 after bxa3. In Position 6, Nd4 moves the c6-knight that was the sole defender of the a6 pawn, allowing Nxd4/Rxa6. In Position 3, a5 removes the a-pawn's ability to later play ...a6, the only resource to prevent Bb5 exploiting the d7-bishop. In Position 4, c5 dissolves the c6-d5 pawn chain, leaving an isolated d5 pawn vulnerable to White's king. In Position 1, g4 wastes a critical tempo needed to address the c3-knight's vulnerability to b4. Position 5 (Rd6) fits as an 'active' rook move that overlooks a basic diagonal defense. All moves share the quality of looking superficially strong (centralizing, space-gaining, attacking) while catastrophically neglecting a specific defensive requirement.
analysis.move_pattern: Piece or pawn moves away from a square where it performs a unique defensive function—typically knights leaving guard posts (c3→e4, c6→d4) or pawns advancing past squares they needed to control (a5 past a6, c5 past c6)
analysis.why_bad: Each move removes the sole defender of a specific weakness (usually a pawn on the a-file or a critical structural support pawn), allowing the opponent to immediately win material or create a decisive structural advantage through the now-unguarded point.
sub_patterns: Knight leaves defensive post allowing pawn capture (Ne4/Nd4 abandoning a-file pawn defense)
Pawn advance removes future defensive resource (a5 preventing ...a6, c5 dissolving pawn chain)
Aggressive pawn thrust ignoring critical queenside tension (g4 while b4 threatens)
Active piece placement on controlled square (Rd6 into bishop diagonal)

analysis.label: Quiet piece-improving moves that fatally neglect an immediate tactical threat, typically exposing the king to checks, forks, or checkmate.
analysis.description: This feature fires on moves where the player prioritizes piece activity, development, or repositioning while ignoring a critical, often immediate tactical threat—usually to king safety. In 6/8 positions, the refutation involves a check or checkmate (Nxe7+ check, Rg1+ back-rank mate, Ne4# checkmate, Nf6+ fork, Qh1+ infiltration, Ra8→Ra1# mating pattern). The blundered moves are typically quiet and non-forcing—bishops centralizing (Bd5, Bf4), knights repositioning to 'active' squares (Ne5, Nb4), rooks lifting or shifting (Rf2, Rb1), queens retreating (Qd1), or kings moving (Kg8)—that look purposeful in isolation but abandon critical defensive duties. In 5/8 cases, the move directly removes a piece from guarding a key square (Rf2 abandons back rank, Rb1 abandons g1 coverage, Qd1 leaves f3 unguarding g2/h1, Ne5 blocks the king's escape while enabling mate, Kg8 walks into knight-check range). The average cp_loss of 3741 with 3 positions resulting in forced mate underscores the catastrophic nature of these oversights.
analysis.move_pattern: Non-forcing piece moves (any piece type) to apparently active or purposeful squares, typically without capturing or giving check
analysis.why_bad: The move abandons a critical defensive function or ignores an imminent tactical blow—usually a check, fork, or back-rank invasion—by prioritizing piece improvement over addressing the most urgent threat to king safety
sub_patterns: Rook lifts off back rank allowing back-rank mate (Rf2, Rb1)
Queen/piece abandons guard of key square enabling infiltration (Qd1 leaves g2/h1, Rb1 leaves g1)
King walks into square attacked by opponent's piece (Kg8 into Ne7+ range)
Piece blocks own king's escape enabling checkmate (Ne5 blocks e5 for Ne4#)
Slow repositioning ignoring opponent's immediate tactical shot (Nb4 ignoring Nf6+, Bf4 ignoring d4)

analysis.label: Playing a plausible-looking but tactically catastrophic move in a position where only 1-2 specific moves prevent disaster.
analysis.description: This feature fires on positions where the player makes a 'reasonable' or 'instinctive' move that catastrophically fails because the position demanded one very specific response. The positions share extremely narrow margins (avg 1.7 good moves available) and enormous consequences for imprecision (avg 1941 cp_loss). In 7/11 cases, the move either removes a piece from a critical defensive duty (Bf8 abandons g7 diagonal, Bd2 abandons a1-h8 diagonal, Qc7 removes queen from c8→e8 defensive route, Kh8 eliminates escape via f8) or places a piece on a tactically vulnerable square (Qe7 creates pin target on h4-e7 diagonal, Rd1 enables Ne4-Nf2+ fork, Nc7 hangs to queen). In 4/11 cases, the move is a slow/prophylactic pawn push or development move (a3, h6, g6, Nxd4 capture) that ignores an immediate tactical demand. The common thread across all examples is that each move appears purposeful (developing, defending, attacking) but fundamentally misreads the position's single most critical requirement.
analysis.move_pattern: Diverse piece types and directions; predominantly quiet non-forcing moves (8/11 non-captures/non-checks); pieces frequently moved backward, laterally, or to seemingly safe squares; several involve retreating to the back rank or corner
analysis.why_bad: Each move fails to address the position's one critical tactical or defensive requirement, allowing the opponent an immediate forcing sequence (pin, fork, sacrifice, mating attack, or piece capture) that the 'natural' move did nothing to prevent or made possible
sub_patterns: Removing a piece from a critical defensive diagonal/file (Bf8, Bd2, Qc7)
Moving the king to a trapped/matable square instead of an escape square (Kh8 vs Kf8)
Placing a piece on a tactically exploitable square enabling pins/forks (Qe7, Rd1, Nc7)
Playing slow prophylactic moves when immediate tactical action is required (a3, h6, g6)
Making captures based on optical illusions like apparent pins (Nxd4 missing zwischenzug)

analysis.label: Moves that pursue an apparently attractive secondary goal (material, activity, centralization) while fatally ignoring the position's most critical tactical or strategic priority.
analysis.description: This feature fires on positions where the player makes a superficially logical move—capturing material (Nxh8, Qxa2: 2/8), placing pieces on active-looking squares (Bg4, Rag8: 2/8), or centralizing/activating the king (Kd3, Kf7, Kg4: 3/8)—but ignores the one thing the position truly demands. In each case, a specific critical priority exists: addressing a pawn break (d5 in position 1, bxc6 in position 7), blockading a passed pawn (e2 in position 5), avoiding a diagonal vulnerability (position 10), taking urgent tactical action before a hanging piece is captured (position 12), or keeping the queen near the exposed king to prevent perpetual check (position 15). The played moves would often be reasonable in other contexts, but here they allow the opponent a concrete tactical resource (tempo-gaining pawn advance, promotion, perpetual check, trapping a piece) that the correct alternatives would have neutralized. The average 2.0 good moves available confirms these are narrow positions requiring precise prioritization.
analysis.move_pattern: Mixed piece types (king moves 4/8, captures 2/8, piece development/repositioning 2/8); no consistent geometric direction; moves tend toward seemingly active or rewarding squares (captures, centralization, open files) rather than defensive or prophylactic positions
analysis.why_bad: Each move ignores an urgent tactical resource the opponent possesses—a pawn break gaining tempo, a promotion threat, a perpetual check drawing mechanism, or a piece-trapping pattern—because the player prioritized a tempting secondary goal (material gain, king activity, piece development) over the position's one critical demand.
sub_patterns: King moves to exposed/wrong squares abandoning defensive duties (Kd3, Kf7, Kg4)
Material-grabbing moves that displace pieces from defensive positions (Nxh8, Qxa2)
Active-looking piece moves that ignore critical pawn tension or threats (Bg4, Rag8)

analysis.label: Moving a piece from a critical defensive post to a seemingly more active or natural square, unaware it was the sole protector of a key vulnerability.
analysis.description: In 6/8 positions, the blundering piece was performing a vital defensive function (guarding a square, blocking a line, maintaining pawn tension) that the player failed to recognize. The bishop on c6 guarded d7 against a knight fork (Bb7), the knight on f6 controlled h5 against a pawn storm (Ne8), the c6 pawn pressured d5 keeping White's center constrained (c5), the d5 pawn supported a future c4 knight-winning blow (d4), the queen on e7 flexibly covered the c4 knight (Qc5), and the rook staying on a8 kept it off the vulnerable diagonal (Re8). In all cases, the player chose a move that appeared to improve piece placement—centralizing, developing, activating—while failing to recognize the concrete tactical consequence of abandoning the defensive duty. The average cp_loss of 240 with only 1.8 good moves available confirms these are positions where the one critical requirement was maintaining a specific guard, and the played move violated it for an illusory improvement.
analysis.move_pattern: Any piece type moving away from a square where it performs a latent defensive function (guarding a square, blocking a line, maintaining tension) to a more 'active-looking' destination
analysis.why_bad: The moved piece was the sole guardian of a critical square, line, or tension point; removing it allows an immediate tactical blow (fork, discovered attack, breakthrough, material win) that the 'active' destination cannot compensate for.
sub_patterns: Piece leaves square that blocked a fork or check (Bb7 allows Nd7+, Ne8 allows h5)
Pawn advances release critical tension prematurely (c5 frees d5, d4 activates opponent bishop)
Piece moves to exposed square creating new vulnerability (Qc5, Qd3, Kd3 on open files/diagonals)
Developing move ignores undefended piece on long diagonal (Re8 leaves Ra8 hanging)

analysis.label: Quiet piece/king moves to seemingly logical squares that waste a critical tempo by failing to address the position's most urgent concrete demands.
analysis.description: All 6 positions share the pattern of a non-forcing, non-capturing quiet move that appears purposeful but is concretely ineffective. In 6/6 cases the move is tagged as 'tempo_loss'. The moves include: a bishop going to a decent but suboptimal diagonal (Bd3, Position 1), a bishop creating a superficial pin on an undefended square (Bb4, Position 2), a bishop attempting to block a pawn on the wrong color complex (Bb6, Position 3), a knight retreating to a passive rim square (Nh7, Position 5), a king moving sideways away from the action (Kh2, Position 6), and a king centralizing onto an exposed square where it becomes a checking target (Kd5, Position 15). In all cases, the best moves were more concrete and forcing—captures (Rxc7), checks (Rb2+), castling (O-O), or precise piece placement on optimal squares (Bg6, Nbd7, Bc7). The player in each case appears to follow a general principle (pin, block, centralize, develop) but misapplies it to the specific position's concrete demands.
analysis.move_pattern: Quiet non-capturing, non-checking piece or king moves to squares that look active or purposeful but are concretely suboptimal
analysis.why_bad: Each move wastes a critical tempo on a superficially logical but concretely ineffective idea, allowing the opponent to execute forcing plans (promotions, checks, invasions, forks) that exploit the time gifted by the passive move
sub_patterns: Bishop moved to seemingly active but tactically vulnerable or wrong-colored square (3/6)
King moved in wrong direction or to exposed square becoming a target (2/6)
Knight retreated to passive rim square abandoning central control (1/6)

analysis.label: Capturing a central pawn with an active piece (usually Bxd4) when a different piece should capture a more valuable target first, allowing the opponent's queen to recapture with devastating centralization.
analysis.move_pattern: Bishop captures pawn on d4 from c5 (5/10), or more broadly, capturing on a central square (d4/d7) with the wrong piece when another piece should take a different, higher-value target first
analysis.why_bad: The player greedily captures a pawn with an active piece, leaving that piece en prise to the queen, when the correct move order involves a different piece capturing the opponent's bishop (Nxc4) first. The queen recaptures centrally with tempo, and the opponent's piece coordination collapses — trading a well-placed piece for a mere pawn while surrendering all initiative.
analysis.description: This feature fires most strongly on Italian Game positions (5/10) where Black has Bc5 and Ne5 attacking White's d4 pawn and Bc4, and Black plays Bxd4 instead of the correct Nxc4. In all five cases, the best move was capturing White's bishop on c4 with the knight first (Nxc4), which wins a full piece or exploits the center collapse, while Bxd4 allows Qxd4 centralizing the queen with tempo on the e5-knight. The pattern extends to Qxd7 (1/10) where the queen captures instead of the knight, leaving a piece vulnerable on an open file. The remaining positions (4/10) share the broader theme of surrendering an active piece's defensive/offensive function for inadequate compensation — removing a key file-blocker (Nc4, position 7), placing a piece passively (Rd2, position 12), walking into a fork geometry (Kc2, position 8), or dissolving critical structural tension (h4, position 6). Average cp_loss of 290 confirms these are severe errors at critical decision points with typically only 1-2 good alternatives.
sub_patterns: Bxd4 instead of Nxc4 in Italian Game/Two Knights (greedy pawn grab)
Qxd7 instead of Nxd7 leaving pieces vulnerable on open files
Removing a key defensive piece from its post for illusory activity
Passive piece placement surrendering initiative when active play was required

analysis.label: Natural-looking moves that squander urgency when the position demands immediate concrete action.
analysis.description: This feature activates on moves that appear reasonable on the surface—routine development (Nc3, Nbc6), natural king centralization (Ke6, Kd2, Kc7), queen repositioning (Qe2, Qa4), or space-gaining pawn pushes (b5)—but fatally waste a critical tempo when the position demands immediate, forcing action. In 7/8 positions, the analysis explicitly tags 'tempo_loss' as a key theme. The positions consistently feature one urgent requirement (converting a passed pawn in 2/8, defending against a tactical threat in 3/8, generating counterplay in 3/8) that the played move completely ignores in favor of a 'generic good move.' The best alternatives are always concrete and specific: capturing a pawn (Kxf6, cxb7), advancing toward a key square (Kb5, Ke4), or playing prophylaxis against an imminent threat (Qf1 guarding g1, Ng6/h6 preventing Ng5). The average of only 2.0 good moves available confirms these are narrow decision points where precision matters enormously.
analysis.move_pattern: Various piece types moving to natural-looking but non-urgent squares; typically moving away from or perpendicular to the critical sector of the board
analysis.why_bad: Each move ignores the position's single most urgent demand (converting a tactical asset, defending a specific threat, or racing to a critical square), giving the opponent a free tempo to execute their plan or neutralize the player's fleeting advantage
sub_patterns: King moving in wrong direction in pawn endgame
Queen decentralizing when king safety demands central presence
Routine development when an immediate tactical strike exists
Pawn push ignoring development/tactical emergency

analysis.label: Non-forcing moves that squander critical tempo when the position demands immediate concrete action.
analysis.description: This feature fires on moves that appear purposeful (prophylactic king moves, bishop repositioning, pawn preparation, decorative checks) but waste a decisive tempo in positions requiring urgency. In 7/7 analyzed positions, the blunder is explicitly tagged as 'tempo_loss.' The moves include pointless checks that drive the enemy king to better squares (Qh5+, Qh3+ in positions 1, 3), passive retreats to back-rank squares (Bc1 in positions 7, 12), queen relocations to irrelevant squares abandoning key defensive duties (Qb2, Qh3 in positions 4, 8), slow pawn moves when development is critical (g6, b6 in positions 2, 13), and prophylactic king moves when material is hanging (Kh1 in position 14). In every case, the correct moves were concrete and forcing — capturing material, creating real threats, or maintaining defensive control of critical squares — while the blunder allows the opponent to execute their plan one move sooner than necessary.
analysis.move_pattern: Quiet non-forcing moves: retreats to back rank (Bc1), lateral queen shuffles to passive squares (Qb2, Qh3), non-developing flank pawn pushes (g6, b6), prophylactic king moves (Kh1), or checks that improve the opponent's king position (Qh5+, Qh3+)
analysis.why_bad: These moves give the opponent a free tempo to execute their concrete threat — whether that's king infiltration in endgames, a tactical fork/capture in middlegames, or a developmental lead in openings. The moved piece ends up on a passive or irrelevant square while the opponent's plan succeeds unimpeded.
sub_patterns: Pointless checks that improve opponent's king (Qh5+, Qh3+)
Bishop retreats to passive back rank losing control of critical diagonal (Bc1 x2)
Queen relocations abandoning defense of key squares (Qb2, Qh3)
Slow flank pawn moves ignoring developmental urgency (g6, b6)
Prophylactic king moves when forcing captures are available (Kh1)

analysis.label: Active-looking moves that waste a critical tempo by ignoring the single urgent tactical or strategic obligation of the position.
analysis.description: This feature fires on positions where the player makes a seemingly purposeful move (a check, an attack on a pawn, a piece improvement, a king centralization) while the position demanded ONE specific response to an urgent need. In 6/8 positions, only 1 good move existed, confirming these are critical-decision moments. The blunders share the pattern of choosing a 'natural-looking' alternative over the mandatory response: d4+ gives check but drives the king to safety when Re7+ wins a piece (1/8); Rfc8 doubles rooks but misses Ncxd4 capturing a hanging pawn (2/8); Ra5 attacks a pawn but leaves a rook en prise requiring Rxg7+ (3/8); Ka4 appears to escape but walks into a mating net when Ka3 was the only survival (4/8); Kf1 prophylactically improves the king but ignores a hanging d4 pawn needing Rd1 (5/8); Bh5 relocates the bishop but to the wrong diagonal, losing the tempo race (6/8); Ke6 centralizes but walks into Re1+ on the open file (7/8); Kb5 attacks c5 but loses the kingside pawn race requiring Kb3 toward center (8/8). All moves appear active but constitute pure tempo losses against the position's ONE critical demand.
analysis.move_pattern: Mixed pieces (kings, rooks, bishops, pawns) making active-looking moves (checks, attacks, improvements) in random directions - no geometric unity
analysis.why_bad: Each position has exactly one urgent obligation (defending a hanging piece, executing a winning tactic, racing the king to the right sector, controlling a critical file) and the blunder spends a tempo on a secondary plan, allowing the opponent to exploit the neglected vulnerability immediately
sub_patterns: Pointless checks that drive the opponent's king to a better square
Slow positional improvements when an immediate tactical capture is available
King moves toward material targets while losing a pawn/piece race elsewhere
Piece relocations to wrong squares when specific defensive geometry is required

analysis.label: Natural-looking quiet piece moves that block own pieces' critical paths or abandon urgent tactical necessities in positions with very few good options.
analysis.description: This feature fires on positions where the player makes a plausible-looking quiet developing or repositioning move that catastrophically misses the one critical action the position demands (avg 1.8 good moves available). The most prominent mechanism is self-obstruction: Ne3 blocks own rook's e-file attack (1/10), Rd7 blocks the king's escape square allowing Qa8+ (2/10), Nbd7 blocks the f6-knight from its critical Ng4 tactical strike (3/10), Qd2 blocks the b1-knight's natural development square (4/10), and Kg3 places the king on the square the queen needed (5/10). The remaining positions share the pattern of routine-looking moves that abandon critical pressure: Rd2 leaves the c-file giving a passed pawn tempo (6/10), Bd2 abandons active placement when back-rank threats demanded immediate rook action (7/10), Bd6 develops the wrong bishop while leaving another piece hanging (8/10), h5 pushes a pawn when only king penetration wins (9/10), and f5 opens lines prematurely against own uncastled king (10/10). All moves are quiet (no checks or captures) and appear purposeful on the surface.
analysis.move_pattern: Quiet piece/pawn moves (no checks, no captures) to seemingly natural squares, often moving a piece TO a square that interferes with own piece coordination or AWAY from a square providing critical pressure
analysis.why_bad: These moves obstruct own pieces' tactical resources (blocking files, escape squares, or tactical paths) or waste the single critical tempo in razor-thin positions where only one specific move maintains the advantage, allowing opponents to neutralize threats, escape danger, or launch counterattacks
sub_patterns: Piece moves to square blocking own rook's file or king's escape
Developing the wrong piece while another piece needs immediate tactical attention
Pawn advance when king activity or piece action is the only winning plan
Passive repositioning that surrenders tempo in positions requiring immediate action

analysis.label: A piece leaves its essential restraining or defensive function for a tempting but peripheral goal, allowing the opponent to exploit the newly unguarded vulnerability.
analysis.description: Across all 11 positions, the blundering move removes a piece from a critical defensive or restraining role—typically to capture a wing pawn or reposition to a seemingly active square. In 5/11 cases the move is a capture of a peripheral pawn (Qxg5, Bxh6, Qxg2, Rxf5, and effectively Bf6 enabling exf6). In 4/11 cases a rook abandons file control allowing invasion (Rd8, Ra8, Rab8 all leave the king on c2 exposed to Re2+ checks; Rxf5 abandons the c-file). In 3/11 cases a piece leaves a square that was preventing enemy piece activation (Bd7 abandons coverage of h5 enabling Nh5; Qe7 places the queen where Nf5 gains tempo; Kc5 abandons defense of f6). The common thread is that each piece was performing an 'invisible' but vital function—pinning down an enemy piece, guarding a key square, or preventing invasion along a file—and the player was seduced by a tangible but insufficient alternative (material gain, apparent activity). The refutations consistently exploit the exact weakness the departed piece was covering, typically within one move.
analysis.move_pattern: Any piece type moving away from a critical axis (file, diagonal, or key square) toward the periphery or toward a capture, typically lateral rook moves along back ranks, queen captures on wing squares, or bishop/king moves away from defensive zones
analysis.why_bad: The moved piece was performing a crucial but non-obvious defensive function (restraining enemy piece invasion, protecting a hanging piece, or guarding a key square); removing it grants the opponent an immediate tactical exploitation of the abandoned weakness—typically file invasion with check, tempo-gaining attacks on undefended pieces, or pawn captures that destroy the position.
sub_patterns: Rook abandons central file control allowing enemy rook invasion with check (positions 1, 4, 7)
Queen/Rook captures peripheral pawn while own king is exposed or pieces are undefended (positions 2, 6, 9, 10)
Piece retreats from a square that was preventing enemy piece activation via tempo (positions 3, 5)
King or piece advances abandoning defense of a critical pawn (positions 8, 11)

analysis.label: Player makes a repositioning move (usually a king move) instead of capturing an undefended enemy piece for free.
analysis.description: In 4/4 positions, the player had a simple, immediately available capture of a hanging or inadequately defended enemy piece (Bxe8 capturing a rook, Nxf3 capturing an intruding knight, Bxd4 capturing a knight, gxf5 capturing a rook) but instead played a quiet repositioning move that ignored the free material. In 3/4 cases the blunder was specifically a king move (Ka7, Kd1, Kd5) to an adjacent square, while 1/4 was a rook activation move (Rd2). All positions had exactly 1 good move available (the capture), and the average centipawn loss was 606, reflecting catastrophic evaluation swings from winning to equal or losing. The players appeared focused on positional goals—escaping perceived threats, centralizing, or activating pieces—while being completely blind to the simple tactical capture that dominated the position.
analysis.move_pattern: Single-square king move (3/4) or piece repositioning move (1/4), always a non-capture quiet move to a nearby square, ignoring an available free capture of a major or minor piece
analysis.why_bad: A free capture of an enemy piece exists (hanging piece or piece en prise to a pawn/minor piece), and by playing a quiet move instead, the player allows the opponent to save or reposition that piece, converting a winning position into an equal or losing one
sub_patterns: King retreat/sidestep ignoring bishop-captures-piece
King move ignoring knight capture
Rook activation ignoring pawn-captures-rook

analysis.label: Playing a slow, non-forcing move (usually a pawn push) when the position demands immediate concrete tactical action.
analysis.description: This feature fires on positions where a player chooses a quiet, preparatory, or routine move while a specific forcing tactical opportunity exists. In 8/10 cases the played move is a non-critical pawn push (f5, c3, d6, f4, h5, b6, g6) or a passive/routine move (O-O, Qd3), while the best move involves a concrete tactical sequence—a capture (Nxc6 winning the exchange in position 12, Nxg4 winning a pawn with a fork in position 13, R6xb5 grabbing material in position 9), a forcing developing move (Bd2 unpinning in positions 2 and 15), or an active king/piece move addressing an urgent threat (Kg7 in position 7, Qe6 in position 11). The 'tempo_loss' tag appears in 9/10 positions and 'missed_tactic' in 7/10. The average cp_loss of 342 with only 1.3 good moves available confirms these are critical moments where one tempo makes the difference between exploiting or surrendering a concrete advantage. The pattern captures the classic amateur error of 'improving' the position slowly when it's time to calculate and strike.
analysis.move_pattern: Non-forcing pawn pushes (typically to 3rd-6th rank) or routine quiet moves (castling, queen repositioning) that neither check, capture material, nor create immediate threats
analysis.why_bad: These moves waste a critical tempo in positions with narrow tactical windows, allowing the opponent to neutralize threats, consolidate weaknesses, or seize the initiative—the concrete forcing opportunity that existed disappears after giving the opponent one free move to respond.
sub_patterns: Slow pawn push ignoring available tactical capture (b6, g6, d6, f4)
Routine developing move when a forcing combination wins material (O-O, Qd3)
Premature kingside pawn advance weakening own king (f5, h5)
Self-blocking pawn move removing tactical resources (c3)
Wrong capture order losing piece coordination (Nxg4)

analysis.label: In rook endgames with passed pawns, the player moves the rook too close to the pawn (attacking, blocking, or approaching it directly) instead of maintaining optimal checking distance or positioning behind/far from the pawn.
analysis.description: This feature fires in rook endgames where a critical passed pawn exists and the player makes a rook move (11/13 positions) that approaches or directly engages the passed pawn at short range, violating fundamental rook endgame principles. The key error manifests in several forms: placing the rook IN FRONT of advancing passed pawns (Rc8, Rf7, Rg8 in positions 12, 14, 11), moving the rook to directly attack a pawn while losing checking distance (Ra4, Rf5, Rc4 in positions 8, 3, 4), or committing the rook to a blockading file without proper preparation (Ra7, Ra8 in positions 6, 10). In every case, the correct moves involved maintaining maximum rook distance for perpetual checks (position 8: Ra8/Ra6/Ra7 for checking distance), placing the rook behind pawns rather than in front (position 12: Rg8 reaching the 5th rank behind pawns), staying on active files to force favorable exchanges (position 14: Rg4/Rg2/Rg3 keeping g-file pressure), or forcing the opponent's pieces to suboptimal squares before committing (position 6: Rb7+ first, then Ra7). All 13/13 positions are endgames, and the passed_pawn tactical motif dominates every analysis.
analysis.move_pattern: Rook moves toward or onto the file/rank of a passed pawn at close range (typically within 1-2 squares), often landing on the same rank as the pawn or directly in front of it on its promotion file
analysis.why_bad: The rook sacrifices its primary endgame asset—long-range activity and checking distance—for illusory direct engagement with the pawn; at close range the rook becomes passive, loses tempo when the pawn advances past it, cannot generate perpetual checks against the opponent's exposed king, and often ends up trapped or exchanged, allowing the passed pawn(s) to promote uncontested.
sub_patterns: Rook placed in front of advancing passed pawn (violating Tarrasch rule)
Rook attacks passed pawn directly but loses critical checking distance
Rook commits to blockading file without first deflecting opponent's king/rook
Rook exchanges made possible by moving onto opponent's active file

analysis.label: Moves that address a secondary objective while completely ignoring the position's most critical tactical or strategic priority.
analysis.description: This feature fires on moves where the player makes a superficially reasonable-looking operation (a capture, centralization, pawn push, or retreat) that fails to address the single most urgent demand of the position. In 8/10 positions, there was a specific critical priority being ignored: advancing a decisive passed pawn (positions 6, 12, 13 - bxa5 ignoring h6, b5 ignoring Be8 to deal with g6 passer), exploiting or defending against an exposed king (positions 1, 10, 11 - Nxe4 abandoning the attack, Qc8 removing counterplay, Rd8 ignoring Kg7), capturing clearly available material (position 5 - Kd7 instead of Kxf7), or executing the one tactical resource that justifies the position (position 14 - h4 blocking the critical Bh4 pin). The moves often look productive in isolation but represent catastrophic tempo losses because they allow the opponent to execute their primary plan unopposed. Average cp_loss of 315 with only 2.1 good alternatives confirms these are positions demanding specific, urgent action where any deviation is severely punished.
analysis.move_pattern: Diverse piece types and directions; the commonality is choosing a 'natural' or routine operation (capture, centralization, flank pawn push, retreat) instead of the position's one critical move
analysis.why_bad: These moves waste the critical tempo needed to address the position's primary demand—whether pushing a decisive passed pawn, attacking an exposed king, capturing hanging material, or executing a key tactical resource—allowing the opponent to consolidate or seize the initiative
sub_patterns: Capturing/pushing on wrong wing while passed pawn needs advancing
Centralizing a piece while king safety is urgent
Choosing routine development over a specific tactical shot
Failing to capture free/hanging material
Blocking a key square with a pawn that a piece needs

analysis.label: Playing a secondary/peripheral move instead of advancing the primary winning plan in a time-sensitive position, allowing the opponent to neutralize the advantage.
analysis.description: In all 5/5 positions, Black held a decisive advantage (avg ~450cp) based on a time-sensitive winning plan—typically a passed pawn needing to advance or an attack requiring sustained pressure. In each case, the played move pursued a tangential objective (pawn grab on a2, attacking a rook with Nc2, aimless king moves with Kb2/Kg3, premature pawn break with c4) instead of the critical winning action. The correct moves were consistently direct: push the passed pawn immediately (positions 6, 9), centralize the king to dominate (position 2), address a critical pawn vulnerability (position 11), or maintain the queen's attacking coordination (position 13). All 5/5 mistakes gave the opponent exactly the tempo needed to organize a defense—whether blockading a pawn, capturing an undefended asset, or launching a counter-check. The tag 'tempo_loss' appears in 5/5 analyses and 'passed_pawn' in 4/5, confirming the pattern is fundamentally about squandering initiative in time-critical endgames/attacks.
analysis.move_pattern: A piece (king, knight, queen, or pawn) moves toward a peripheral target or secondary square instead of advancing directly along the primary winning plan's path
analysis.why_bad: The move wastes a critical tempo in a position where the opponent is one move away from organizing a defense (blockade, check, capture), converting a won position into a draw by allowing the opponent to neutralize the time-sensitive advantage
sub_patterns: King moves away from a critical square before pushing a passed pawn (Kg3, Kb2)
Piece relocates to attack a peripheral target instead of advancing the main threat (Nc2, Qxa2)
Premature pawn break that freezes the structure when patient piece play was winning (c4)

analysis.label: Piece moves to an active-looking but unsupported square, leaving the moved piece or something it was defending tactically vulnerable.
analysis.description: In 6/8 positions, the moved piece either becomes directly capturable (Nf5 taken by queen, Na5 trapped by b4, Ng5 enables Bh2+/Nxf2+) or its departure leaves a critical piece/pawn undefended (Ngf7 leaves b3 hanging, Qc3 leaves Nc6 unprotected due to blocked c-file, Bc3 abandons e2 defense). In 2/8 cases (Qg4, Rd7), the move is a premature aggressive sortie that wastes tempo while a simple defensive or capturing move was required. The common thread is choosing a forward-looking, aggressive-appearing move over a quieter one that maintains material integrity. The average cp_loss of 1453 reflects that these are severe oversights where the tactical refutation (simple capture or exploitation of the vacated defensive role) is typically one move deep.
analysis.move_pattern: Piece (knight, bishop, queen, or rook) moves forward/aggressively to an undefended or tactically exploitable square, often away from a critical defensive post
analysis.why_bad: The piece either lands on an unprotected square where it can be immediately captured or trapped, or its departure from the previous square leaves another piece/pawn hanging that the opponent exploits with a simple one-move tactic
sub_patterns: Piece placed en prise on the destination square (Nf5, Ng5 enabling fork)
Piece moves away from critical defensive duty leaving something hanging (Ngf7 abandons b3, Bc3 abandons e2, Ng5 abandons h2/f2)
Piece moves to rim/edge where it gets trapped by a pawn advance (Na5 trapped by b4)
Premature aggressive sortie that gets refuted by tempo-gaining responses (Qg4 chased by f3/h3)
Flashy attacking move ignoring a free capture available (Rd7 instead of Qxf3)

analysis.label: Quiet repositioning moves that neglect the single critical defensive priority, giving the opponent a free tempo to execute their winning plan.
analysis.description: In all 7/7 positions, the player makes a slow, non-forcing repositioning move (pawn advance, piece retreat, or king walk) that ignores the one urgent defensive task in the position. In Position 2, c4 ignores the need for h4 to prevent king infiltration on g5. In Position 3, Kd1 abandons the only safe repetition zone (Kb1-a1 corridor). In Position 4, f6 reinforces the center while ignoring the critical queenside tension requiring b4/bxc4 before White plays cxb5+a4. In Position 6, Ra6 places the rook where Kb7 hits it with tempo, losing a critical move. In Position 7, Nd2 removes the knight from b3 where it guarded a1, enabling a devastating check+fork sequence. In Position 8, Rdd8 withdraws the rook from the 7th rank, abandoning the one piece preventing Rc7 invasion. In Position 12, Kb7 places the king one square too far from b6, forfeiting the tempo-gaining Bb5+ check. All 7/7 positions feature the common tag 'tempo_loss' in their analysis, and all punishments involve the opponent freely executing the plan that was previously restrained.
analysis.move_pattern: Quiet non-forcing move (any piece type) that moves away from or fails to address the critical defensive square/task; no checks or captures
analysis.why_bad: The position has exactly one critical defensive priority (blocking infiltration, maintaining repetition, resolving tension, guarding a key square), and the move addresses a secondary concern instead, giving the opponent a free tempo to execute the plan that was being held at bay
sub_patterns: Pawn advance ignoring opponent's infiltration route (c4, f6)
Piece retreating from critical defensive post (Nd2, Rdd8, Kd1)
Piece placed on unprotected square attackable with tempo (Ra6)
King placed one square off from optimal tactical coordination (Kb7)

analysis.label: Bishop sacrifices on h3 or h6 to rip open the g-file against the castled king, but the attack lacks sufficient supporting pieces to generate compensation.
analysis.description: All 8 positions feature a bishop capturing the h-pawn (h3 for Black, h6 for White) that shields the opponent's castled king, intending to follow up with Qxh3/Qxh6 after gxh3/gxh6 opens the g-file. In every case (8/8), the sacrifice is premature and unsound because the attacker lacks sufficient supporting pieces to sustain the assault. The defender consistently finds adequate resources: in Position 4, Bf1 blocks the queen's infiltration; in Position 8, Kh1 sidesteps to safety; in Position 1, f6 closes the position; in Position 12, the undeveloped f1-bishop means no reinforcements exist. All positions (8/8) featured same-side kingside castling, and in 7/8 cases the center was closed or stable, meaning the attacker couldn't generate open lines elsewhere to support the kingside assault. The average cp_loss of 249 reflects that these are significant material investments (full bishop for 1-2 pawns) yielding no compensation. In every case, 3 patient positional alternatives existed that maintained the evaluation.
analysis.move_pattern: Bishop captures the h-pawn (h3 or h6) adjacent to the opponent's castled king, sacrificing a piece to open the g-file
analysis.why_bad: The attacking side has insufficient pieces coordinated for a kingside assault—the queen alone on h3/h6 cannot create mating threats when the defender has adequate defensive resources (bishop retreats blocking infiltration, king escaping to the corner, counterattacks exploiting abandoned central duties, or simply consolidating with an extra piece)
sub_patterns: Bxh3 gxh3 Qxh3 met by Bf1/Kh1 defensive resource
Bxh6 gxh6 Qxh6 met by Bf8/f6 shutting down the attack
Sacrifice in closed center where no supporting pieces can join the attack

analysis.label: Plausible-looking moves that actively create an exploitable weakness in one's own position during critical moments with very few good alternatives.
analysis.description: This feature fires on positions where the player makes a move that appears constructive or natural but actively introduces a concrete structural or positional weakness that wasn't previously present. The damage is self-inflicted: trapping own pieces (g6 traps bishop, 1/13), abandoning critical defensive posts (Rc8 abandons back rank, Rg1 abandons b-file, 2/13), blocking own king's mobility or path (Be5 blocks Kf4, g5 locks cage around king, Rg1 blocks king escape, 3/13), placing the king on an exposed file or square (Kd2 on open d-file, Kd7 into discovered attacks, 2/13), prematurely locking pawn structures that help the opponent (d5 closes center, g5 creates prison, 2/13), choosing the wrong piece for a critical task (Qxc1 instead of Rxc1, Nf4+ instead of Nc4#, 2/13), or wasting the critical tempo that allows an opponent's tactical blow (c5 enables Ng5, 1/13). These positions average only 1.8 good moves, indicating the player faced a narrow decision point requiring precise play but chose the one 'reasonable' option that catastrophically backfires.
analysis.move_pattern: No single geometric pattern; moves span all piece types and directions. They are united by being 'locally sensible' actions (checks, captures, developments, advances) that happen to create a specific concrete vulnerability in the player's own camp.
analysis.why_bad: Each move actively creates or exposes a specific exploitable weakness (trapped piece, exposed king on open file, abandoned defensive post, locked structure) that the opponent can immediately punish with a concrete tactical or positional blow, in positions where maintaining the status quo or finding one precise alternative was essential.
sub_patterns: Pawn advances that trap own pieces or lock structure into a cage (g6, g5, d5, e4)
Piece/king moves to exposed squares on open files (Kd2, Kd7, Rg1)
Abandoning critical defensive posts for seemingly active play (Rc8, Rg1, Qxc1)
Piece moves that obstruct own king's mobility or path (Be5, g5, Rg1)
Checks or captures that enable devastating forced simplification or miss stronger continuations (Qc3+, Nf4+, Qxc1)

analysis.chip: Tempo-losing piece placement near passed pawns
analysis.label: Moving a piece (usually king) to a square that allows a tempo-gaining forcing move (check, capture, or pawn advance), critically losing time in endgame positions with dangerous passed pawns.
analysis.description: This feature fires on moves that lose decisive tempo in endgame positions involving passed pawns. In 9/11 positions, dangerous passed pawns create time-critical situations where every tempo matters. The common error is placing a piece on a square that allows the opponent an immediate forcing response: the king walks into a check (Kf5 allows Rb5+ in position 6; Kc7 allows Nb5+ in position 15; Ke8 allows Qc6+ in position 2), a piece abandons its blockading duty against a passed pawn (Rc8 abandons a8 blockade in position 3; Ng6 allows e7 liquidation in position 12; Bc8 freezes passively in position 14), the king takes an indirect route losing a critical tempo in a king race (Kg4 instead of Kf4 in position 8; Kc5 walks away from kingside pawns in position 4), or a tempo is wasted when immediate forcing action is needed (Kb4 instead of Rxa7 in position 13). The average cp_loss of 1157 reflects how catastrophic a single tempo loss is in these razor-sharp endgame positions.
analysis.move_pattern: Piece (predominantly king, 7/11) moves to a square on a rank, file, or diagonal where it can be immediately attacked by a check, capture, or pawn advance; typically moving laterally or away from the critical sector
analysis.why_bad: In positions with advanced passed pawns, a single tempo is often the difference between winning and losing. These moves either expose the piece to an immediate forcing response (check/capture) that gains the opponent a free move, or abandon a critical restraining role against a passed pawn, allowing it to advance or liquidate favorably.
sub_patterns: King moves to square allowing rook/queen/knight check (positions 2,6,15)
Piece abandons blockade of passed pawn (positions 3,12,14)
King takes indirect route in critical king race (positions 4,8)
Slow move when immediate forcing action required (position 13)
Piece moves to square where it's immediately captured (position 5)

analysis.label: Quiet, preparatory moves (pawn pushes or passive piece placements) played in positions that demand immediate active piece play or forcing moves.
analysis.description: This feature fires on positions where the player chooses a slow, non-forcing, preparatory move when the position urgently requires concrete action. In 6/8 positions, the move played is either a quiet pawn push (b6, c6, g6) or passive piece development (Be2, Nbd7, Nh2) that prepares a future plan but ignores the critical tactical or developmental demand of the moment. The best alternatives in nearly all cases involve immediate piece activity—developing to active squares (Nc6 appears as best in 4/8 positions), forcing exchanges that resolve tension, or precise tactical strikes. The analyses repeatedly identify 'tempo_loss' as the core motif (tagged in 7/8 positions), with the opponent's refutations consistently exploiting the wasted tempo to organize counterplay, seize the initiative, or launch attacks that the preparatory move did nothing to prevent. The average cp_loss of 186 reflects positions where the difference between 'good' and 'slow' is substantial—these aren't subtle inaccuracies but meaningful squanderings of dynamic advantages.
analysis.move_pattern: Quiet non-forcing moves: pawn pushes to passive squares (b6, c6, g6), piece retreats/maneuvers to rim or passive squares (Nh2, Be2), or blocking developments (Nbd7). No captures, no checks, no direct threats.
analysis.why_bad: The position has a concrete, time-sensitive demand (development lead to exploit, tactical tension to resolve, king safety to address, or a forcing blow available) but the move chosen is a slow preparatory step that neither threatens nor defends anything critical, giving the opponent one free tempo to consolidate, develop, or launch their own initiative.
sub_patterns: Preparatory pawn moves (b6/c6/g6) when piece development is urgent
Passive piece development (Be2/Nbd7) blocking own plans or ignoring key tension
Slow knight maneuvers (Nh2) abandoning critical defensive duties
Choosing a non-optimal forcing move when a precise tactical blow exists (Nh4+ vs Nf4+)

analysis.label: Non-forcing moves (especially king moves) in positions with narrow tactical windows requiring immediate piece coordination or exchanges.
analysis.description: This feature fires on positions where the player makes a natural-looking but non-urgent move while the position demands a specific forcing continuation. In 4/10 cases the error is a king move (Kg3, Kb7, Kh2, Kh2) when piece activation or queen exchange was critical. In 4/10 cases it's a queen move (Qf6+, Qc7, Qe5, Qxc6) that ignores the position's tactical demands—centralizing instead of exchanging, or capturing material while leaving a critical weakness. The remaining 2/10 (Bb4, Rc8) similarly prioritize secondary concerns over the urgent requirement. The positions share extremely narrow margins (avg 1.7 good moves available) and high punishment (avg 2938 cp_loss), indicating razor-sharp tactical moments where only forcing moves maintain the position. Best moves consistently involve immediate exchanges (Qxe3+, Qxf4+), tactical strikes (Nf5+, Rf5-Rc5), or piece blockades (Na6-Nb3), while the played moves drift into passive territory.
analysis.move_pattern: King or queen moves to non-forcing squares (often forward/sideways) when the position requires captures, exchanges, or knight/rook activation
analysis.why_bad: The positions have a single critical path requiring immediate forcing action (exchange, fork, piece activation), and the played move wastes the tempo needed to execute it—allowing the opponent to advance threats, invade with rooks, or construct mating nets unchecked.
sub_patterns: King moves forward when queen exchange needed (Kh2 x2)
King walks when knight/rook blockade needed (Kg3, Kb7)
Queen centralizes instead of trading to defuse attack (Qe5, Qc7)
Queen captures material while leaving tactical weakness (Qxc6)

analysis.label: Quiet repositioning moves played in positions demanding immediate forcing action, surrendering the initiative through tempo loss.
analysis.description: This feature fires on positions where the player chooses a non-forcing, slow, or 'improving' move (piece repositioning, quiet development, or even a counterproductive check) when the position urgently demands concrete tactical action. In 5/7 positions, the tagged tactical motif is 'tempo_loss.' The blunders include centralizing a queen that can be challenged with tempo (Qd5, Qc7), a check that helps the opponent's king advance to a superior square (Bc4+ allowing Ke7), passive knight maneuvering instead of a forcing tactical combination (Nc2 missing Nxc4-Nxd6+-Nxc8+), slow development when only immediate counterplay with checks saves the position (Nd7 instead of Qb1+), and walking the king into the open abandoning pawn defense (Kd2). In 5/7 cases only 1-2 good moves existed, confirming these are critical-decision moments where the narrow forcing path was missed in favor of a superficially reasonable but fatally slow alternative.
analysis.move_pattern: Various pieces (Q, B, N, K) making quiet repositioning or non-forcing moves to seemingly 'good' squares, rather than capturing, checking with purpose, or executing forced tactical sequences
analysis.why_bad: These moves waste a critical tempo in sharp/urgent positions, allowing the opponent to execute tactical threats (sacrifices on undefended pawns, king advances to superior squares, checks along opened files/diagonals) that were only being held at bay by the need for immediate concrete action
sub_patterns: Queen moves to 'active' central square but abandons defense of key pawn (Qd5, Qc7)
Check that drives opponent's king to a superior square (Bc4+ enabling Ke7)
Passive piece regrouping when a forcing tactical combination exists (Nc2 missing Nxc4 fork sequence)
Slow development when only immediate counterplay with checks holds (Nd7 instead of Qb1+)
King walk abandoning pawn shelter and walking into check patterns (Kd2)

analysis.label: Playing a non-forcing 'improving' move in a tactically critical position that demands one specific concrete action.
analysis.description: This feature activates when a player chooses a quiet, natural-looking move (piece repositioning, development, or pawn push) in a position where essentially only ONE forcing continuation maintains the evaluation (avg 1.3 good moves available). In 7/7 positions, the move played was non-forcing (no check, no capture, no immediate threat), while the best move involved a concrete tactical operation: a knight sacrifice with discovered check (Position 1), an urgent capture of a vulnerable piece (Position 3), maintaining a critical blockade (Position 4), a pawn sacrifice exploiting a geometric pin (Position 5), essential development before the opponent strikes (Position 9), a precise defensive rook placement (Position 10), or infiltrating with the queen rather than the rook (Position 15). The positions share extreme tactical tension where tempo is the decisive factor, and the 'reasonable-looking' alternative costs an average of 323 centipawns.
analysis.move_pattern: Non-forcing quiet moves (rook slides, knight development, pawn pushes, queen repositioning) that don't deliver check, capture, or create an immediate concrete threat
analysis.why_bad: The position demands a specific forcing sequence (sacrifice, capture, or concrete threat) and the quiet move squanders a critical tempo, allowing the opponent to consolidate, escape tactical danger, or launch their own threats. The narrow tactical window closes permanently once the tempo is wasted.
sub_patterns: Quiet piece improvement when a tactical sacrifice/combination exists
Slow pawn push when concrete forcing play is required
Piece repositioning that abandons a critical defensive function
Moving the wrong piece to the right square (losing a hanging piece)

analysis.label: Purposeless piece moves in endgames that waste a critical tempo by failing to address the position's most urgent requirement.
analysis.description: This feature fires on endgame positions (12/13) where the player makes a move that appears superficially reasonable but fundamentally wastes tempo by not addressing the critical positional need. The most common manifestation is king moves toward the board edge that either block a friendly knight's needed square (Kg7 in positions 1, 2, 4; Kh7 in position 14 — 4/13 positions) or abandon coordination with a piece that needs support. Another manifestation involves placing knights or rooks on squares that are immediately exploitable — either undefended (Nd5, Ne2, Nf7 — 3/13), disconnected from the critical battle zone (Nb4, Nd7 — 2/13), or abandoning a key defensive post (Rf1, Ra6 — 2/13). In nearly every case, the opponent punishes by immediately exploiting the created vulnerability: winning an undefended piece, breaking through with an unstoppable pawn advance, or gaining a decisive tempo for king centralization. The tagged tactical motif of 'tempo_loss' appears across virtually all positions.
analysis.move_pattern: King, knight, or rook moves to passive/edge squares in endgames — typically sideways or backward moves that don't address the critical threat or coordination need
analysis.why_bad: The move wastes a tempo in positions where precise coordination is essential — the piece either blocks a friendly piece's critical square, abandons a defensive duty, or lands on a square where it's immediately attacked, giving the opponent a free move to execute their winning plan (pawn advance, piece capture, or king march).
sub_patterns: King moves to g7/h7 blocking knight's escape square in R+PP vs N endgames
Knight moves to undefended squares exploitable via open files or queen attacks
Piece abandons critical defensive post allowing opponent to penetrate
Purposeless move ignoring immediate mating or material threats

analysis.label: Plausible-looking moves that waste a critical tempo by addressing a secondary concern while the position demands one specific urgent action.
analysis.description: This feature fires on positions where a clear strategic priority exists (such as castling, preventing a key break, or maintaining piece coordination) but the player makes a purposeful-looking move that addresses something else entirely. In 8/12 positions, the best moves involved either getting the king to safety (Positions 3, 5, 8: castling/d5 to lock center), preventing a specific enemy break (Position 4: a4 to stop ...a4; Position 9: f4 to shore up kingside), or repositioning a piece BEFORE committing (Position 10: Bb3 before Kd5). Instead, the played moves look active—queen sorties (Qh3, Qh8, Qh5, Qa6 in 4/12), piece development (Bd2, Rd1), pawn advances (b5, f3, f6), or king walks (Kf2, Kd5)—but all ignore the one thing the position demanded. The common punishment is that the opponent immediately exploits the wasted tempo: 7/12 positions feature the opponent seizing the initiative with the exact break or tactic that the correct move would have prevented.
analysis.move_pattern: Any piece type moving to a plausible-looking but strategically misguided square; no consistent geometric direction—includes queen advances to exposed squares, rook centralizations that abandon key files, pawn pushes ignoring development, and king moves into danger or away from critical sectors
analysis.why_bad: The position is at a critical juncture with one clear urgent need (king safety, prophylaxis against a specific break, or piece coordination), and the move squanders the one available tempo on a secondary concern, allowing the opponent to execute the very plan that needed to be prevented or to exploit the newly created vulnerability
sub_patterns: Queen overextension to exposed squares enabling unfavorable trades (Qh3, Qh8, Qh5, Qa6)
Pawn/piece moves ignoring uncastled king when center is about to open (Bd2, f3, b5)
Abandoning control of the critical file or sector (Rd1 leaving a-file, Kd5 leaving kingside, R8b5 blocking own escape)
King moves creating new tactical vulnerabilities (Kf2 enabling checks, Kd5 losing pawn race)

analysis.label: Moves that pursue a reasonable secondary objective while ignoring the single most critical threat or task demanding immediate attention.
analysis.description: This feature fires on positions where players choose a move addressing a secondary concern while neglecting the ONE urgent priority in the position. In 3/6 cases, the urgent task involves neutralizing a dangerous passed pawn (Positions 2, 3, 6: the d6, g7, and c3 pawns respectively demanded direct action via Nf6/Bxg7/Rc7, but players chose Qg5 attacking a pawn, Ne7 blockading instead of capturing, and Rxb7 grabbing material). In 2/6 cases, the priority was king safety that was violated by the move itself (Position 4: O-O walked into Bxg7; Position 5: Kg7 walked into Nh5+ discovered attack). In 1/6 cases, a critical defender was removed for a secondary repositioning goal (Position 1: Ne2 displaced the c3 knight guarding e4). All positions share extremely narrow decision points (avg 1.5 good moves), indicating critical moments where only one idea works. The chosen moves all appear superficially reasonable—developing, attacking, grabbing material, castling—but each fundamentally misidentifies the position's primary demand.
analysis.move_pattern: Various piece types moving to apparently useful squares (development, attack, material gain, king safety) while the position's single critical concrete task goes unaddressed
analysis.why_bad: Each position has one overriding concrete priority (eliminating a passed pawn, maintaining a key defender, avoiding a tactical vulnerability) and the chosen move ignores it entirely, allowing the opponent to exploit the neglected threat with a forcing sequence that reverses the evaluation.
sub_patterns: Grabbing wing material while ignoring a central passed pawn
Blockading a passed pawn instead of capturing it directly
Moving the king into a tactical vulnerability while pursuing general safety
Removing a critical defensive piece for a secondary repositioning plan
Pursuing aggressive piece placement while a concrete structural threat demands attention

analysis.label: Piece repositioning moves in endgame pawn races that waste critical tempo instead of advancing immediate counterplay.
analysis.description: This feature fires on endgame positions (6/7) with dangerous passed pawns where the player makes a piece move (king, queen, or rook) aimed at the opponent's threats rather than creating immediate counterplay. The catastrophic blunders (Ke7, Kd6 with ~9100cp loss each; Rc7 with 423cp loss) all involve moving a piece toward the opponent's passed pawn or territory when advancing one's own pawn or placing a piece more aggressively was essential. In 5/7 positions, the move results in a fatal tempo loss in a pawn promotion race - e.g., Ke7 tries to intercept the h-pawn but allows it to advance unopposed, Kd6 retreats passively instead of Kd4 which harasses the rook, and Rc7 activates the rook on the 7th rank but wastes the critical tempo needed for Kg6. The 2/7 positions where the move was correct (Qh3, 0-1cp loss) show the feature also fires when stopping the opponent's promotion IS the priority, confirming the feature detects the general pattern of piece-vs-pawn tension in promotion races.
analysis.move_pattern: King, queen, or rook repositioned toward opponent's pawns/territory in open endgame positions with advanced passed pawns
analysis.why_bad: The piece move wastes a critical tempo in a pawn race - the opponent's passed pawn advances unopposed or the player loses the precise coordination needed to maintain winning chances, often converting wins to draws or draws to forced mates
sub_patterns: King moving toward opponent's passed pawn instead of advancing own counterplay (Ke7, Ke6)
King retreating passively instead of harassing opponent's pieces (Kd6 vs Kd4)
Rook/queen repositioning when king advance was the only winning move (Rc7 vs Kg6)
Queen targeting opponent's promotion threat (Qh3 - sometimes correct)

analysis.label: Natural-looking moves that waste a critical tempo in positions with very few good options, failing to address the one urgent tactical or strategic demand.
analysis.description: This feature fires on moves that appear reasonable or constructive on the surface but catastrophically ignore the single most critical requirement of the position. The positions share an extremely narrow margin (avg 1.9 good moves available) meaning precision is mandatory, yet the player chooses generic 'improving' moves instead. In 8/10 cases the analyses tag 'tempo_loss' as the core issue. The pattern manifests as: slow pawn pushes when prophylaxis is needed (b6, a3 in 2/10), checks that drive the opponent's king toward safety rather than into a mating net (Rc1+, Bd6+ in 2/10), moving a critical defensive piece to 'attack' (Nh4 removing f2's guardian in 1/10), generic development to the wrong square ignoring a hanging pawn (Bd3 instead of Be3 in 1/10), occupying an open file when a tactical vulnerability demands immediate attention (Rad1 in 1/10), and passive king moves when urgent counterplay is required (Kf2 in 1/10). All share the fatal flaw of spending the one available tempo on something that looks constructive but is strategically irrelevant to the position's critical demand.
analysis.move_pattern: Any piece type or direction; no geometric consistency. Moves are typically non-forcing (quiet development, pawn pushes, king moves) or forcing but misdirected (checks that drive the target to safety).
analysis.why_bad: Each position has a single critical demand (defend a key square, deliver a precise check sequence, generate urgent counterplay, or prophylactically address an imminent threat) and the played move addresses a secondary concern instead, allowing the opponent to execute the one decisive idea that the correct move would have prevented.
sub_patterns: Wrong check: giving check that drives the king toward safety instead of into a mating corridor (Rc1+, Bd6+)
Removing a critical defender: moving a piece that guards a key square to 'attack' something less important (Nh4 abandoning f2)
Slow pawn push: spending tempo on a pawn move when the position demands immediate piece action (a3, b6)
Generic development: placing a piece on a natural-looking square that fails to address the actual tactical tension (Rad1, Bd3)
Passive king move: improving king position when urgent counterplay or active measures are needed (Kf2)

analysis.label: Quiet, natural-looking piece repositioning moves that waste a critical tempo in positions demanding immediate concrete action.
analysis.description: In all 5/5 positions, Black plays a move that appears positionally reasonable (centralizing a king, placing a knight on an 'outpost,' developing a queen to a natural square) but critically ignores the most urgent tactical demand in the position. In 4/5 cases the analyses tag 'tempo_loss' as the primary motif. The best alternatives consistently involve concrete actions: pawn thrusts to create threats (f4, h4, f6), rook activations to open files (Rb8, Rd8), or moves that directly address a tactical vulnerability (Ng6 defending, h6 challenging a bishop). Instead, the played moves are 'improving' moves that give the opponent time to either consolidate (Ke5 allows g3+Nc3), exploit exposed pieces (Ndf6 blocks knight retreat allowing h3, Qc7 allows f3 trapping Ng4, Nc4 invites b3 with Ba3+ coming), or launch decisive tactics (Kh8 enables Ng5+Rf8+ back-rank). The common thread is prioritizing abstract positional goals over concrete tactical requirements.
analysis.move_pattern: Various piece types (knight, king, queen) moving to apparently natural/strong squares (central, corner-safe, outpost, developing) without captures or checks
analysis.why_bad: The moves waste a tempo on repositioning when the position requires immediate concrete action; the opponent exploits the lost tempo to challenge/trap pieces, consolidate weaknesses, or launch tactical sequences that the 'natural' move fails to prevent
sub_patterns: Knight moves to seemingly strong square but gets immediately challenged, losing two tempi (Ndf6 blocks retreat, Nc4 hit by b3)
King moves to 'safe' or 'active' square but walks into tactical motifs (Kh8 back-rank, Ke5 allows consolidation)
Queen develops to natural square ignoring piece vulnerability that opponent exploits with tempo (Qc7 ignores Ng4 hanging to f3)

analysis.label: King moves away from the critical sector of the board in endgames, losing decisive tempo while the opponent's main threat advances uncontested.
analysis.description: All 9/9 positions are endgames where the player moves their king in a direction that takes it further from the most critical action on the board. In 9/9 cases the move is a king move, and in every analysis the primary tactical motif identified is 'tempo_loss.' The pattern manifests as the king heading toward the wrong wing (Kg4 moving kingside while queenside pawns roll, 1/9), retreating passively to back rank or corner (Kb1, Ke1, Ke2 at 3/9), chasing irrelevant material while passed pawns advance (Ka3 chasing the a2-pawn while c-pawn promotes, 1/9), or overshooting past the optimal central square (Kd7 instead of Kd6, Kb3 instead of Kd2, at 2/9). In every case, the best alternatives involve moving the king toward the center or toward the opponent's most dangerous passed pawn. The consequences range from trivial 1-6cp losses in already-decided positions to catastrophic 8913-9551cp losses that convert drawn/slow losses into forced checkmates.
analysis.move_pattern: King move in any direction, but specifically AWAY from the board sector containing the opponent's most dangerous advancing pawn(s) or primary threat; often toward edges, corners, or back rank
analysis.why_bad: In endgames, every tempo is critical in pawn races. Moving the king away from the key theater (usually where passed pawns are advancing) means the king must later return, wasting two or more tempi. This allows the opponent's passed pawns to advance unimpeded, the opponent's king to centralize unopposed, or mating nets to be constructed without resistance.
sub_patterns: King retreats to back rank/corner instead of centralizing (Kb1, Ke1, Ke2)
King goes to wrong wing opposite from critical passed pawns (Kg4, Kb3)
King chases unimportant material while main threat advances (Ka3, Kf3)
King overshoots optimal square by one step (Kd7 instead of Kd6)

analysis.label: Moves that pursue an attractive positional or material goal while ignoring an immediate tactical vulnerability—usually of one's own exposed king.
analysis.description: This feature fires on positions where the player makes a natural-looking move (centralization, capture, development, or king repositioning) that ignores a concrete, urgent tactical problem. In 6/8 positions, the player's king is exposed or insufficiently defended, and the move either removes a key defender (Position 1: Nxd5 removes the f6 knight guarding f7; Position 6: Re1 undermines the f2 bishop's defensive role), worsens king exposure (Position 4: Kc5 walks into a knight fork; Position 15: Kb1 makes a2 attackable with check), blocks the king's own escape (Position 9: Bd6 blocks the d6 retreat square while discovered check exists), or ignores the need to address king safety entirely (Position 3: Nd5 centralizes instead of developing and castling). The moves share a geometric tendency toward 'attractive' central squares (5/8 moves target the c5/d5/d6/f5 zone), but the unifying thread is prioritizing a non-urgent goal over addressing an immediate tactical crisis. The extremely high average cp_loss (1489) and very low good-move count (1.6) confirm these are positions demanding precise defensive action where the player instead chose a 'wishful thinking' alternative.
analysis.move_pattern: Piece moves toward the center or to seemingly active/safe squares (especially d5, c5, d6, f5, e1, b1) — captures, centralizations, developments, or king walks that look positionally motivated
analysis.why_bad: The moves ignore an immediate tactical threat (fork, discovered check, sacrifice, overloaded defender) targeting the player's vulnerable king, prioritizing a non-urgent strategic goal over addressing the concrete danger that the opponent can exploit on the very next move
sub_patterns: Removing a key defensive piece for material gain (Nxd5 removing f7 guard)
Centralizing a piece instead of castling/developing when king is exposed (Nd5, Bd6)
King walking into a tactical motif (Kc5 into fork, Kb1 enabling Qa2+ check)
Natural-looking rook/queen move that fails to address critical defender vulnerability (Re1, Qf5)
King targeting wrong objective in endgame (Kc5 toward d5 instead of a6)

analysis.label: Playing a general-principles developing or improving move while ignoring urgent central pawn tension or concrete tactical demands.
analysis.description: This feature fires when a player makes a move that follows conventional chess wisdom (piece development, active diagonals, rook doubling, castling) but critically fails to address an immediate, concrete positional or tactical demand—most often unresolved central pawn tension. In 5/9 positions, the move is a bishop or queen development to an 'active' square (Bc5 x3, Bc4, Qb6, Qd6) while a critical pawn capture (typically fxe5 or fxe4) is available to the opponent that wins material or creates devastating tempo gains. The remaining cases (O-O-O, g3, Rhd8) similarly prioritize general improvement over the position's specific concrete requirement (castling into an attack, prophylaxis instead of final development, doubling rooks instead of an exchange sacrifice). The refutations consistently exploit the wasted tempo: the opponent captures the undefended central pawn, gains tempo attacking the prematurely developed piece, or exploits the piece's new vulnerability on its 'active' square. Average cp_loss of 293 and only 1.8 good moves available confirm these are critical moments demanding precision over generality.
analysis.move_pattern: Minor piece or queen development to an apparently active square (typically bishop to c4/c5 diagonal, queen to b6/d6), or a non-urgent improving move (castling, pawn push, rook doubling), all ignoring an immediate central pawn tension or tactical shot
analysis.why_bad: The position contains an unresolved critical tension (usually f-pawn vs e-pawn) or a concrete tactical opportunity that demands an immediate specific response; the 'natural' move leaves key pawns undefended or pieces on vulnerable squares, allowing the opponent to capture with tempo, create forks/skewers, or build an overwhelming center while driving back the prematurely deployed pieces.
sub_patterns: Bc5 in King's Gambit ignoring fxe5 winning the e-pawn with tempo (3/9)
Queen displacement to flank/center square creating fork or skewer vulnerability (Qb6→Nd5 fork, Qd6→Ba3 skewer)
Quiet improving move (g3, O-O-O, Rhd8) instead of completing development or executing concrete tactic

analysis.label: Playing a passive, non-forcing move that addresses a secondary concern while ignoring the position's critical demand—whether king safety, development, or a concrete tactical opportunity.
analysis.description: In all 5 positions, the player chose a quiet, non-forcing move (3/5 pawn pushes, 2/5 passive piece repositions) that pursued a secondary strategic goal while the position demanded immediate concrete action. In Position 4, Qd6 centralizes the queen instead of executing the winning Rdg3 rook lift. In Position 5, Rf8 passively repositions instead of playing e5 to prevent the opponent's Bf4. In Position 8, e4 pushes a pawn instead of activating the king. In Position 11, b6 pursues queenside pawn play instead of creating king escape squares with h6. In Position 15, b5 bolsters material instead of developing with Ne7 and preparing king evacuation. All 5/5 positions share the 'tempo_loss' tag—the opponent exploits the wasted move to execute their primary plan (pawn thrusts, piece activation, file seizure, or tactical combinations). The average cp_loss of 261 reflects how severely punished these 'do-nothing' moves are in positions with concrete demands.
analysis.move_pattern: Quiet non-forcing moves (pawn pushes to b5/b6/e4, passive Rf8/Qd6) that don't check, capture, or create immediate threats—typically directed away from the critical sector of the board
analysis.why_bad: The move wastes a critical tempo on a secondary concern, giving the opponent a free move to execute their key tactical or strategic idea (pawn thrusts exploiting piece placement, doubling rooks on open files, activating dormant pieces with tempo) that the correct move would have prevented or preempted.
sub_patterns: Queenside pawn pushes ignoring kingside urgency (b5, b6)
Passive piece repositioning instead of preventing opponent's key idea (Rf8)
Pawn push instead of king activation in endgame (e4)
Positional centralization missing concrete tactic (Qd6)

analysis.label: Playing a non-urgent, non-forcing move in a tactically critical position that demands immediate concrete action.
analysis.description: This feature fires when a player wastes a critical tempo by choosing a quiet, natural-looking move in a position where very few good moves exist (avg 1.5 good moves). In 12/12 positions, the blunder involves ignoring an urgent tactical or positional demand: pawn pushes addressing secondary concerns (h5, f5, e4, b4, g6 = 5/12), passive piece retreats (Be8, Bc8, Nf6 = 3/12), or piece displacements away from the critical zone (Qh4, Qxa7, Rc1, Be5 = 4/12). In every case, the position was at a tipping point where one specific forcing or active move was required—exploiting an open file (Qd4 in pos 1), preparing an attack (Rf3 in pos 2), activating the queen (Qf5 in pos 3), deploying defensive pieces (Bc3 in pos 4), maintaining central pressure (Qb3 in pos 5), or capturing hanging material (Qxc3 in pos 14). The tempo wasted allows the opponent to consolidate, reorganize, or launch counterplay that wasn't previously available. All 12 positions are tagged with tempo_loss, 11/12 with piece_activity issues, and 10/12 with missed_tactic.
analysis.move_pattern: Any piece or pawn; typically a non-capturing, non-checking move directed away from the critical sector of the board or toward a passive/blocked square
analysis.why_bad: The position has only 1-2 good moves (a narrow tactical demand), and the chosen move wastes the one tempo needed to exploit a concrete opportunity or address an urgent threat, giving the opponent time to neutralize the position's critical imbalance
sub_patterns: Pawn push addressing secondary kingside/queenside concern
Bishop retreat to passive starting square
Queen displacement to peripheral square away from action
Piece repositioning to blocked or undefended square
