analysis.label: Playing a non-urgent, preparatory, or tangential move in a position that demands immediate tactical resolution.
analysis.description: This feature fires on positions where the player makes a move that would be reasonable in a calm position but is catastrophic because it ignores a burning tactical need. In 9/9 cases, the position had very few good moves (avg 1.6), indicating critical-precision moments. The actual moves vary widely in type (retreats like Ne8, captures like dxc3, centralizations like Qd4/Nc5, preparatory moves like g6/b6, passive moves like Rd2, or superficial checks like Qc8+), but all share the quality of being non-urgent when the position screams for immediate action. In 7/9 positions, there was a specific tactic to either execute or defend against—a fork (b6 missed Nxg4), a hanging piece (Qd4 ignored Ne3xf1), a back-rank sacrifice (Qc8+ missed Rh8+), or a critical exchange (Rd2 missed Nxg4). The blunders transform playable positions into lost or near-lost ones because the opponent gets a free tempo to resolve their problems or execute their threats.
analysis.move_pattern: Any piece type or direction; the unifying factor is that the move addresses a non-critical concern while a concrete tactical obligation exists elsewhere on the board
analysis.why_bad: These moves waste a critical tempo in positions where the opponent has immediate tactical threats or the player has a narrow-window tactical opportunity, allowing the opponent to either consolidate their weakness (e.g., castle to safety) or execute a devastating blow (e.g., capture a hanging piece, launch a mating attack) that was previously preventable or answerable.
sub_patterns: Passive piece retreats when active counterplay is required (Ne8)
Irrelevant pawn captures while facing a mating attack (dxc3)
Offensive piece maneuvers when defensive emergency exists (Nc5, Qd4)
Slow preparatory moves when a concrete tactic is available (g6, b6, Rd2)
Superficial checks instead of precise tactical strikes (Qc8+, Qg4)

analysis.label: Moves with plausible positional intent that catastrophically overlook the player's own king vulnerability, allowing immediate tactical punishment.
analysis.description: This feature fires on moves where the player pursues a seemingly reasonable plan (centralizing a king, developing a piece, capturing a pawn, activating a rook) but fatally ignores that their own king is exposed or becomes exposed by the move. In 7/7 positions, the player's king is on a weak or exposed square, and the move either worsens that exposure or fails to address it while creating a new tactical vulnerability. The punishments exploit the exposed king through queen checks/perpetuals (2/7), knight forks involving the king (3/7), discovered attacks toward the king (1/7), or back-rank invasions targeting the king (1/7). The average cp_loss of 3044 reflects that these are catastrophic oversights—the moves look natural but miss that the king's precarious position is the dominant factor requiring immediate attention. In every case, the best moves either directly improve king safety or at minimum avoid creating new tactical relationships between the king and enemy pieces.
analysis.move_pattern: Various piece types (king, rook, bishop, pawn) moved to squares that create or worsen tactical geometry between the player's own exposed king and opponent's attacking forces
analysis.why_bad: The moves create or ignore a tactical relationship between the player's exposed king and another piece/square, allowing the opponent to exploit that king exposure through forks, checks, discovered attacks, or mating nets that the natural-looking move failed to foresee.
sub_patterns: King actively walks into check/perpetual corridors (Kd2, Kf6)
Pieces move to squares forkable with the exposed king (Rf7, Bd7)
Defensive pawns/pieces abandon king protection creating immediate tactical holes (Re3, fxg4, f4)

analysis.label: Playing a slow positional move instead of capturing an enemy knight with the rook to enter a trivially won pawn endgame.
analysis.description: In 10/10 positions, the strongest move was to capture the opponent's knight with the rook (Rxf6+, Rxf5+, Rxe4, Rxf8, Rxf3+, Rxd6, Rxc6+, Rxf3), transitioning into a pure king-and-pawn endgame that is trivially won due to connected passed pawns or decisive pawn majorities. Instead, the player chose a slow continuation—king marches (Kf4, Kh3, Ka4, Kf5 in 5/10), rook repositions (Rf4, Ra2, Rh8 in 3/10), or pawn pushes (a5, e4 in 2/10)—that kept the knight alive, allowing it to serve as a blockader, deliver checks/forks, or reach active defensive squares. The positions share a common structure: rook vs knight endgame with passed pawns, where the knight is the sole defender preventing a trivially won conversion, yet the player defaulted to generic endgame improvement rather than the concrete tactical liquidation.
analysis.move_pattern: Any non-capturing move (king walk, rook relocation, pawn push) when Rook x Knight was available, often with check
analysis.why_bad: Keeping the opponent's knight alive preserves their only defensive resource—the knight can blockade passed pawns, deliver forks/checks against the exposed king, and create counterplay, whereas eliminating it via Rx(knight) produces a trivially won pawn endgame with unstoppable passers.
sub_patterns: King march instead of Rx capture (5/10)
Rook repositioning instead of Rx capture (3/10)
Pawn advance instead of Rx capture (2/10)

analysis.label: Moving a piece away from a critical defensive square, allowing an immediate tactical exploitation of the abandoned position.
analysis.description: In all 4 positions, the player voluntarily moves a piece that was performing an essential (often non-obvious) defensive function, creating an immediate tactical vulnerability. In Position 2, the queen leaves f5 where it blocked Qe4+ checks on the exposed king (4/4 involve king safety). In Position 3, f4 abandons pawn coverage of e3, enabling a decisive Ne3 fork (4/4 create exploitable weak squares). In Position 9, the knight leaves c6 where it protected the a8 rook, allowing Qb7 to win it with check (4/4 leave pieces or squares hanging). In Position 11, the knight leaves g7 where it blocked back-rank mate ideas, allowing Rf8+ Nxf8 Qxf8# (4/4 are punished by forcing sequences). The common thread is that 4/4 moves appear constructive (centralizing, gaining space, attacking) but fatally abandon a defensive responsibility that the opponent immediately exploits with a check, fork, or mate.
analysis.move_pattern: Piece (typically knight or queen) moves away from a square where it defended against checks, forks, or mate; pawn advance that unguards a critical square
analysis.why_bad: The moved piece was the sole or primary defender of a critical square, diagonal, or back rank; its departure creates an immediate tactical vulnerability (check, fork, mate) that the opponent exploits with forcing moves before the piece can contribute from its new square.
sub_patterns: Knight abandons king defense for centralization (Ne6, Na7)
Queen retreats from active defensive post (Qd7)
Pawn advance weakens critical square behind it (f4)

analysis.label: Playing a quiet prophylactic or preparatory move in a position that demands the single concrete winning continuation, wasting a critical tempo.
analysis.description: In all 4/4 positions, the player had a commanding advantage (avg +306 eval) with exactly one good move available, but instead chose a non-forcing, non-threatening quiet move that addressed a minor positional concern. Position 2: Kh1 was a king tuck when Bxf7+ was a forcing tactical blow against Black's uncastled king. Position 6: Ra5 placed the rook on the wrong rank when Ra7 created an unstoppable passed pawn. Position 7: g3 defended h4 prophylactically when Ra7 was immediately decisive. Position 12: Be7 retreated an active bishop when O-O was needed to maintain the developmental advantage. In all cases, the closed center (4/4) created an illusion that the position was slow and positional, masking the urgency of the one winning continuation. The opponent's punishment in each case was simple: 4/4 positions allowed the defender to neutralize the advantage through exchanges or consolidation during the gifted tempo.
analysis.move_pattern: Quiet non-forcing moves (king tucks, pawn pushes, piece retreats, rook to wrong square) - no checks, no captures, no direct threats
analysis.why_bad: The position requires immediate concrete action (the single winning move) but the player treats it as slow/positional due to the closed center, gifting the opponent a tempo to exchange key pieces, castle, or neutralize the winning mechanism entirely.
sub_patterns: King prophylactic tuck (Kh1) missing tactical shot
Rook to wrong invasion square (a5 vs a7)
Defensive pawn push (g3) ignoring breakthrough
Bishop retreat from active diagonal losing development tempo

analysis.label: Aggressive-looking moves directed toward a weakened enemy king that actually compromise the attacker's coordination or ignore critical tactical needs.
analysis.description: This feature fires on moves that advance or capture toward an opponent's exposed or weakened king position, appearing to intensify attacking pressure but actually misfiring tactically. In 8/9 positions, the move physically targets the area around the enemy king (Nxg6 near king on h6, Bg8 near king on f8, g6 toward king on g7, Bxh6 near king on h7, a7 toward king on a8, Qg3 toward kingside, Bxh2 near king on h1, Qe4 centralizing aggressively). In 7/9 positions, the opponent's king explicitly has a 'weak pawn shield' or is 'exposed.' The core failure mechanism varies but centers on sacrificing piece coordination for apparent gains: in 3/9 cases the move captures a pawn near the king but trades/strands a key attacking piece (Nxg6, Bxh6, Bxh2); in 3/9 cases it misplaces a piece in the attacking zone (Bg8, Qe4, Qg3); and in 2/9 cases it pushes a pawn prematurely (g6, a7). All positions had forcing alternatives that maintained coordination—often quiet repositioning moves (Qg2, Bh5, Ne5, Qh2) that were far stronger than the flashy 'finishing blow' attempted.
analysis.move_pattern: Pieces or pawns moving toward/capturing near the enemy king's weakened position (often capturing kingside pawns or advancing toward a cornered king), typically on ranks 6-8 or the h/g files
analysis.why_bad: The move prioritizes a superficially threatening gain near the enemy king over maintaining piece coordination, allowing the opponent to exploit tactical flaws—whether hanging pieces left behind, counterattacks against the player's own exposed king, the stranding of the moved piece, or the loss of a more precise forced winning sequence.
sub_patterns: Capturing a pawn near the enemy king that trades/strands a key attacking piece
Misplacing a piece in the attacking zone when a retreat or redeployment creates stronger threats
Premature pawn pushes toward the enemy king that block own pieces or lack support
Non-forcing moves toward the enemy king when checks or immediate tactics are required

analysis.label: Playing a natural-looking or automatic move that wastes the one decisive tempo needed to exploit or survive the position's critical tactical demand.
analysis.description: This feature fires on positions where the player makes a move that appears productive on the surface—a capture (Rxc5, fxe5), a check (Qa5+, Qg4+), a development move (Bg7), a prophylactic pawn move (b3), or a king retreat (Kh3)—but critically wastes the single tempo that determines whether the position is won, drawn, or lost. In 7/7 positions, the correct move required using that exact tempo for a specific, often less obvious purpose: finding a tactical shot (Nxd4 in position 5, Bd5# in position 10), placing a piece on a precise square (Qc5+ not Qa5+ in position 7), fleeing the king immediately (Kh6 in position 14, Kf2 in position 15), or maintaining dynamic initiative (Bg5 in position 13). In 5/7 cases, the opponent punishes by exploiting the lost tempo through forcing sequences—check chains, piece activations, or capturing undefended material. The average cp_loss of 4111 and average of only 1.7 good moves confirms these are razor-thin critical moments where one wasted tempo collapses the position entirely.
analysis.move_pattern: Any piece type; typically captures, checks, or quiet moves that address secondary concerns rather than the position's primary tactical demand
analysis.why_bad: The move spends the one available tempo on something non-essential (grabbing material, giving a non-optimal check, passive regrouping) while the position demands an immediate, specific action—the opponent then exploits the tempo gap through forcing sequences that were preventable one move earlier.
sub_patterns: Giving check on the wrong square when a specific square creates the decisive coordination
Capturing material while the king is fatally exposed and needs to flee
Making passive/prophylactic moves in positions requiring immediate tactical action
Developing a piece to a blocked or dysfunctional square instead of finding the critical tactic

analysis.label: Playing a non-forcing material grab or piece repositioning move instead of executing an available forced checkmate or immediate decisive attack against an exposed king.
analysis.description: This feature fires when a player, in a completely winning position with forced mate or an overwhelming tactical blow available, chooses instead a 'sensible-looking' move that either captures non-critical material or repositions a piece away from the attack. In 4/6 positions, a forced checkmate was on the board (#+3, #-2, #+6, #+3). In 5/6 positions, the opponent's king was critically exposed. The chosen moves include greedy pawn captures (Rxa2 abandoning a mating net, Qxd5 missing Bg6 mate-in-3, Kxh4 displacing a centralized king for a rim pawn) and piece repositioning away from the decisive action (Rf1 leaving the e-file where Re6# was possible, Ne4 centralizing instead of pushing the winning e7 pawn). The common thread is that all moves are non-forcing—they don't deliver check, don't create an unstoppable threat, and thus grant the opponent time to escape or reorganize their defense.
analysis.move_pattern: Non-checking, non-forcing moves: captures of peripheral pawns (rim/center) or piece relocations away from the opponent's exposed king zone
analysis.why_bad: These moves abandon the forcing sequence (checks, mating threats, promotion pushes) that would end the game immediately, granting the opponent critical tempi to evacuate their exposed king or neutralize the mating configuration
sub_patterns: Greedy pawn capture that displaces an attacking piece from its mating configuration (Rxa2, Qxd5, Kxh4)
Piece repositioning/centralization when an immediate forcing continuation exists (Rf1, Ne4, Rc8)
Abandoning a critical file or diagonal needed for the mating net

analysis.label: Reasonable-looking moves that waste a critical tempo in sharp positions where only one precise continuation maintains the advantage.
analysis.description: This feature fires on positions where the player faces a critical moment with very few good options (average 1.4 good moves available) and chooses a move that appears active, aggressive, or purposeful—but fundamentally wastes the tempo needed to execute the position's one key resource. In 8/10 cases, the move played looks superficially appealing (checks like Qxe6+, Qf6+, Bb4+; aggressive piece jumps like Ng4, Ng5; active development like Bf4, Bc5, Bd4; or prophylactic moves like h3, g6) while a single precise forcing move was required. The tempo loss tag appears in 9/10 analyses. In 7/10 positions both kings are still in the center (opening phase), creating tactical tension where one wasted move is catastrophic. The critical missed opportunities include: winning checks on different squares (Qc3+ instead of Qf6+, Qa5+ instead of Bb4+, Qxc6+ instead of Qxe6+), simple captures winning material (Nxe5, Rxc4), and essential structural support moves (e3 instead of h3, Qe2 instead of Bf4).
analysis.move_pattern: Diverse piece types and directions (bishop development, knight jumps, queen checks, pawn pushes) - no single geometric pattern; the commonality is that each move appears purposeful/active but addresses the wrong priority
analysis.why_bad: These moves waste the one critical tempo in positions with essentially only one correct continuation, allowing the opponent to either consolidate (neutralizing a tactical threat), exploit exposed/undefended pieces, or escape from a forcing sequence that would have been decisive
sub_patterns: Wrong checking square when a different check sets up a winning combination
Piece development to exposed square when a concrete tactic wins material
Prophylactic pawn move when a decisive tactical blow exists
Aggressive knight jump that abandons coordination of other pieces

analysis.label: Playing a natural-looking or material-gaining move instead of addressing the position's most critical and urgent demand.
analysis.description: This feature fires on positions where the player makes a move that appears reasonable—capturing material, giving check, attacking a piece, or placing a piece on a 'natural' square—but fatally ignores the position's most pressing requirement. In 8/9 cases, the move loses critical tempo: Bf6 looks defensive but loses time for back-rank coordination; Ra5 seems active but allows f4-f5; Qg4 appears aggressive but exposes g2; Kg1 seems logical but wastes the tempo needed for Rd6; Kxf7 captures the checking piece but steps onto a dangerous file; Qxa2+ wins a pawn with check but misses immediate mate; Kb7 approaches a passed pawn but neglects knight blockade; Rxb2 grabs a pawn but abandons a critical active square; Re6 attacks a piece but releases kingside pressure. In 6/9 cases the best move was something non-obvious and specific (Qb8, Rd8, Qe5, Rd6, Nd4#, h3). The positions typically feature urgent threats (passed pawns in 6/9, king safety issues in 8/9) that demand immediate concrete action rather than general improvement.
analysis.move_pattern: Short-range moves to apparently useful squares; often captures (Kxf7, Qxa2+, Rxb2), attacks on pieces (Re6, Ra5), or repositioning to natural-looking squares (Bf6, Qg4, Kg1, Kb7)
analysis.why_bad: These moves waste a critical tempo on something non-essential (material gain, attacking a piece, natural development) while the position demands a specific urgent action—typically establishing a blockade, maintaining piece coordination against a decisive threat, or delivering an immediate tactical blow.
sub_patterns: Reflexive captures/checks instead of finding the strongest non-forcing move (Kxf7, Qxa2+, Rxb2)
Slow piece repositioning when a concrete pawn break or piece sacrifice is needed (Bf6, Ra5, Qg4, Re6)
King moves that waste tempo in positions requiring immediate piece activity (Kg1, Kb7)

analysis.label: Moving a piece or pawn that was the sole guardian of a critical square, line, or escape route, immediately enabling a tactical punishment.
analysis.description: This feature fires on moves that remove the one piece or pawn performing an irreplaceable defensive function, instantly exposing a fatal tactical vulnerability. In 6/8 positions, the moved piece was the sole protector against a specific threat: Bh1 removed the e4 bishop blocking a discovered check on the e-file; Nf4 removed the knight from e6 which was the only piece preventing Re8+ back-rank mate; Bg2 removed the f1 bishop that was the only piece preventing Qh4+ check; Kd7 blocked the bishop's only retreat square on d7, letting d5 win the piece; h5 advanced the pawn shield creating an irrecoverable king weakness enabling forced mate; Qc3 placed the queen where it became the overloaded sole defender of two pieces simultaneously. In all cases, the positions demanded precise defensive awareness (avg 1.8 good moves available), and the players instead chose moves that appeared developing or active but fatally ignored their piece's indispensable guardian role. The catastrophic average cp_loss of 2668 reflects that removing the sole defender typically allows an immediate forcing sequence (check, discovered attack, or mate).
analysis.move_pattern: Any piece type moving away from a square where it was the unique defender of a critical line, square, or escape route; no consistent direction but always vacating a defensive post
analysis.why_bad: The moved piece was performing an irreplaceable defensive function (blocking a file, guarding a mating square, preventing a check, or providing a retreat path), and no other piece could substitute; removing it allows an immediate forcing tactical blow
sub_patterns: Piece vacates file-blocking duty enabling discovered check/attack (Bh1)
Knight leaves critical back-rank guarding square enabling mate (Nf4)
Bishop leaves diagonal enabling queen check that ruins castling (Bg2)
King blocks own piece retreat square enabling pawn break winning material (Kd7)
Pawn advance weakens king shelter enabling mating attack (h5, h4)
Queen repositions to overloaded square where it cannot defend everything (Qc3)

analysis.label: Natural-looking moves that inadvertently create a concrete tactical vulnerability the opponent can immediately exploit.
analysis.description: This feature fires on moves that appear positionally reasonable or principled on the surface but introduce a new, exploitable tactical weakness. In 11/11 positions, the played move looks logical (developing a piece, defending a pawn, castling, pushing a central pawn) yet creates a specific tactical flaw: pieces placed en prise to forks or captures (Bd3 captured by Nxd3+, Rh3 taken by Bxh3, Ba4 hit by ...b5), defensive functions removed (d6 eliminating dxc6 recapture, Qf3 undefending the c1 rook, Rd7 exposing king to Re8+ checks), or king safety compromised (f3 opening the h4-e1 diagonal, f6 allowing Qc8 invasion, O-O enabling Bc5+Re1 combination). The average cp_loss of 292 reflects that these aren't subtle inaccuracies but serious blunders, yet the average of 2.4 good alternatives confirms that concrete improvements were available. The common thread is a disconnect between the player's strategic intention and the position's tactical reality—they play 'on principle' rather than calculating the immediate consequences.
analysis.move_pattern: Diverse piece types and directions; typically quiet/non-forcing moves (no checks or captures) that place own pieces on tactically vulnerable squares or remove pieces from critical defensive duties
analysis.why_bad: Each move introduces a specific new tactical vulnerability that didn't previously exist—a hanging piece, an exposed king diagonal, a removed defensive function, or a tempo gift—allowing the opponent a concrete refutation that was impossible on the previous move.
sub_patterns: Pawn moves that weaken king diagonals or remove recapture options (f3, f6, d6)
Pieces moved to squares where they are immediately captured or trapped (Bd3, Rh3, Ba4)
Moves that abandon a critical defensive task leaving material hanging (Qf3, Rd7)
Tempo-wasting moves allowing opponent to seal tactical opportunities shut (a3, Nd5)
Routine developing moves that activate opponent's tactical combinations (O-O)

analysis.label: Playing a quiet, non-urgent move when your own king is still stuck in the center and the position demands immediate castling or king safety measures.
analysis.description: In all 10/10 positions, the blunderer's own king remains uncastled in the center (e1 or e8), and the move played is a slow, non-forcing action (piece repositioning, prophylactic pawn push, or passive development) that ignores the critical urgency of king safety. The best moves in 8/10 cases directly involve castling (O-O or O-O-O) or actively challenging the center to compensate for the king's location. The opponent's punishment consistently involves opening the center with pawn breaks (e5, e4, cxd4) or launching piece attacks along open files and diagonals that exploit the exposed king. The blunders span various move types—knight retreats (Ne7, Nd2, Nbd7), pawn pushes (c6, g6, b3, h3), bishop repositioning (Bf2), queen moves (Qd7), rook moves (Rc8)—but they are unified by being one tempo too slow in a position where the central king creates a ticking tactical clock.
analysis.move_pattern: Any quiet non-forcing move (piece retreat, pawn push, repositioning) played by the side whose king remains on e1/e8 uncastled
analysis.why_bad: Each wasted tempo allows the opponent to blast open the center or launch a piece attack against the exposed king, exploiting the open e-file, central diagonals, or knight outposts that arise when lines open before the king escapes
sub_patterns: Prophylactic pawn moves instead of castling (h3, b3, c6, g6)
Piece repositioning when castling was available (Bf2, Ne7, Nd2)
Quiet development ignoring tactical vulnerability (Nbd7, Rc8, Qd7)

analysis.label: Black plays a superficially purposeful move while overlooking a straightforward tactical resource, usually a capture or critical piece placement that should take absolute priority.
analysis.description: This feature fires when Black makes a 'reasonable-looking' move in positions with very few good alternatives (avg 1.4 good moves). In the strongest activations, 2/5 positions involve Black missing that a knight can capture a hanging queen (Ke5 instead of Nxb6; Ne6+ instead of Nxh5) — identical tactical blindness in Q-vs-N endgames. In 2/5 other positions, the piece moves away from a powerful square where it provides critical coordination or defense (Nd1 abandoning the dominant f2 outpost; Bxa3 removing the bishop from the b2-e5 diagonal needed to prevent Nd6+ fork). In 1/5 cases, a subtle move-order error loses tempo. The common thread across all 5/5 positions: Black makes a move that appears active, strategic, or acquisitive (giving check, capturing a pawn, centralizing) while ignoring the single most concrete tactical demand of the position. The moves succeed at a 'secondary objective' while catastrophically failing at the primary one.
analysis.move_pattern: Minor piece (knight or bishop) or king moves to an apparently purposeful square, ignoring that the piece (or another piece) should instead make a concrete capture or hold a critical square
analysis.why_bad: The moves prioritize superficial activity (checks, pawn captures, repositioning) over the position's primary tactical demand — typically a hanging piece capture or critical defensive duty. With only ~1 good move available, any deviation from the one correct action results in massive evaluation loss.
sub_patterns: Knight misses capturing a hanging queen in Q-vs-N endgame (positions 4, 5)
Piece abandons a critical outpost/diagonal for a passive or greedy alternative (positions 3, 6)
Move-order inaccuracy losing key tempo in piece coordination (position 1)

analysis.label: Playing a thematically correct or plan-consistent move prematurely, skipping an essential preparatory move that addresses the most urgent tactical need.
analysis.description: In 3/5 positions, the move played literally appears later in the engine's best line but is executed one move too early: Ra7 is move 2 of the best sequence (after Rb7+ first), Bb5 is move 2 (after Ke8 first), and c4 appears in the third-best variation (after Qh7 first). In all 5/5 cases, the player selects a quiet, non-forcing move that advances a reasonable strategic idea (blockading a pawn, exchanging bishops, rerouting a knight, maintaining centralization, gaining queenside space) while failing to address the single most urgent concrete need in the position. The skipped preparatory moves are typically forcing (a check in Position 1), prophylactic (king safety in Positions 2, 4, 5), or defender-preserving (keeping the knight on f6 in Position 3). All 5/5 positions are tagged with 'tempo_loss' and involve gifting the opponent a free move to execute their primary threat unchallenged.
analysis.move_pattern: Quiet non-forcing move (no check, no capture, no direct threat) of any piece type, typically a repositioning or pawn advance that addresses a secondary positional concern
analysis.why_bad: By skipping the critical preparatory move, the player grants the opponent a free tempo to execute their primary tactical threat (pawn advance, piece capture, rank-cutting technique, or kingside breakthrough) with devastating effect, often transforming the position from tenable to lost
sub_patterns: Premature execution of a move from the correct plan sequence
Quiet positional move ignoring immediate concrete threat
Removing or misplacing a key piece that provided latent defensive resources

analysis.label: Playing an active-looking or preparatory move (especially bishop moves/checks) when the position demanded immediate sharp tactical execution.
analysis.description: This feature fires on positions where the player chose a 'natural' or 'logical-looking' move that wastes a critical tempo, when the position demanded immediate concrete action. The dominant sub-pattern is pointless bishop checks (4/9 positions: Bd5+, Bb5+, Bd4+, Bd5+) that look forcing but allow the opponent to organize defenses, often representing move-order errors where a stronger tactical blow should have preceded the check. Other activations involve bishop development to seemingly active squares that backfire (Be4 allowing capture, Be3 allowing structural damage: 2/9), or slow positional regrouping moves (Rfc8, Rbb1, Qe3: 3/9) when hanging material or mating attacks were available immediately. In all 9/9 cases, the position had a narrow window of opportunity (avg 1.8 good moves) that the played move squandered by giving the opponent time to neutralize the threat. The astronomical average cp_loss (3355) reflects how many of these converted forced mates or winning attacks into merely advantageous positions.
analysis.move_pattern: Primarily bishop moves (6/9) to central or checking squares (d5, b5, e4, d4, e3), often delivering check; also queen/rook moves to 'active' squares that block own pieces or retreat from optimal positions
analysis.why_bad: The move looks purposeful (check, centralization, development, doubling) but wastes the critical tempo needed to execute an immediate tactical blow (sacrifice, capture of hanging material, mating combination), allowing the opponent to consolidate defenses or neutralize the position's tactical tension
sub_patterns: Premature/wrong bishop check before the killing tactical blow (move-order error)
Bishop development to a square where it can be immediately captured with structural damage
Slow positional preparation (rook doubling, regrouping) when concrete material wins exist
Blocking own pieces from key files/diagonals with centralizing moves

analysis.label: Moves that ignore or worsen an urgent king safety crisis by pursuing a secondary objective when the position demands immediate, direct action to address the king's vulnerability.
analysis.description: This feature fires on positions where the player's king faces an immediate safety crisis (exposed king in center, weak pawn shield, or tactical threats exploiting king position), yet the player chooses a move that either further weakens the king's cover, passively retreats without confronting the core threat, or prioritizes an unrelated objective. King safety is the primary issue in 11/13 positions, with 'king in center' or 'king exposed' appearing as position features in nearly every case. The average number of good moves is just 2.0, indicating these are precision-demanding positions with narrow correct paths. In 3/13 cases the player chose Kd1 instead of Kd2 (failing to directly attack an invading knight), in 4/13 cases a pawn push (f5, f3, f6, g5+) fatally weakened the king's pawn cover, and in the remaining cases pieces were moved to secondary objectives (Qh2, Rh1, Qd4, c4, Bd8, Bh3) while the critical king vulnerability went unaddressed. The catastrophic average cp_loss of 1654 reflects that ignoring king safety at these critical moments often leads to forced mates or decisive material loss.
analysis.move_pattern: Varied piece types (king, pawns, queen, rook, bishop) but typically a move near or on the same wing as the king that looks constructive yet fails to directly address the king's specific vulnerability - often one square or one tempo away from the correct defensive action
analysis.why_bad: These moves fail because the position has ONE critical urgency (usually securing the king or neutralizing an immediate threat to it), and the chosen move either worsens the king's exposure (pawn pushes opening lines/diagonals), wastes a crucial tempo (passive retreats when direct confrontation was needed), or removes a key defensive piece from its post - allowing the opponent to exploit the king's vulnerability with checks, discovered attacks, or mating nets.
sub_patterns: Pawn push weakening own king cover (f5/f3/f6/g5+ opening lines or diagonals against own king)
Slow king retreat instead of direct confrontation (Kd1 instead of Kd2 attacking invading piece)
Piece development/repositioning ignoring king in center (Bh3/Bd8/Rh1 when king urgently needs to move)
Queen displacement abandoning critical defensive square (Qh2 leaving f3-pawn unaddressed, Qd4 ignoring hanging material)

analysis.label: Making a superficially reasonable but fatally passive or misdirected move in narrow-margin positions where only one precise active continuation maintains the evaluation.
analysis.description: This feature fires on positions where the evaluation demands exactly one specific move (avg 1.3 good moves available) and the player instead makes a natural-looking but catastrophically wrong choice. In 2/7 positions, the player shuffles the king (Kb2) when a piece activation (Bg2) was required to convert a winning advantage. In 3/7 positions, the player captures with the wrong piece—knight instead of rook (Nxc3+, Nxd7) or knight instead of maintaining counter-threats (Nxe2)—placing the knight on a tactically vulnerable square. In 2/7 positions, a passive rook move (Rd1, Rg8) is played when an active capture or counter-strike was the only way to maintain the position. The common thread is that the correct move always involves a more forceful piece action (bishop activation, rook recapture, queen counter-attack) while the blunder is a 'softer' alternative that appears safe or natural but fatally squanders tempo in a position with zero margin for error.
analysis.move_pattern: Passive king shuffles, wrong-piece captures (especially knight captures), or defensive rook repositioning when an active piece improvement or specific capture was required
analysis.why_bad: These moves waste the critical tempo needed to address the position's primary tactical demand—they either abandon a dominant piece from its outpost, place a piece on a tactically vulnerable square (forks/pins), create self-pins, or allow the opponent to seize the initiative through checks, attacks on newly-created weaknesses, or forced sequences that exploit the misplaced piece
sub_patterns: Purposeless king moves when piece activation converts the position (Kb2 x2)
Knight captures that abandon strong outposts or land on forkable squares (Nxc3+, Nxd7, Nxe2)
Passive rook development when an active capture or counter-strike is essential (Rd1, Rg8)

analysis.label: King moves forward (away from the back rank) into an exposed position when retreat to safety was required.
analysis.description: In 7/8 positions, the blunder is a king move that advances toward the center or edge of the board rather than retreating toward the back rank, while the 8th position (h4) weakens the king's pawn shelter achieving the same effect. In every case, the correct move was a king retreat: Kf2 (Position 2), Kg7/Kh7 (Position 4), Kg8 (Position 7), Kf1/Kh1/Kg1 (Position 8), Kg1 (Position 10), Ke2 (Position 11), maintaining structure (Position 12), and Kc8/Kd8 (Position 15). The forward king moves walk into immediate or near-immediate checkmate patterns (6/8 result in forced mate), typically because the king becomes trapped by its own pawns, exposed to queen checks along diagonals/files, or caught in coordination between enemy pieces. These positions are extremely narrow (avg 1.8 good moves), and the player consistently chose the psychologically tempting 'active' or 'escaping' direction rather than the counterintuitive retreat.
analysis.move_pattern: King moves forward/laterally away from the back rank (or pawn advance weakening king shelter), typically one square toward center or board edge
analysis.why_bad: The king walks into tactical refutations (checks, mating nets, piece coordination) because advancing exposes it to enemy forces, while retreating toward the back rank provides escape squares and pawn shelter that prevent immediate tactical exploitation
sub_patterns: King advances into self-entombment by own pawns (Kh5, Ke6)
King advances into direct mating square (Ke8, Kh3)
King advances into pawn check/deflection (Kg3, Ke4)
Pawn advance removes critical king shelter (h4)

analysis.label: Moves that leave a piece or critical pawn completely unprotected and immediately capturable by the opponent.
analysis.description: In all 7/7 positions, the played move results in (or fails to address) a piece or critical pawn being completely undefended and immediately capturable. The pattern manifests in two sub-types: (1) Moving a piece to a square where it is directly en prise (Rxc6 captured by 3 pieces, Bd5 hanging to exd5, Nc7 hanging to Nxc7, Nxh5 hanging to Rxh5 - 4/7 cases), and (2) Making an irrelevant quiet move while a high-value piece or critical pawn sits unprotected (h3 and g3 both leaving the d5 pawn capturable by rooks, Nh3 leaving a rook on f5 capturable by a bishop - 3/7 cases). The average cp_loss of 463 closely matches the value of a full minor piece, consistent with losing material through simple hanging pieces. In every case, the opponent's refutation is a straightforward capture of the undefended piece/pawn, often requiring no complex calculation.
analysis.move_pattern: Any piece type; move places own piece on undefended square capturable by opponent, or quiet pawn move ignoring already-hanging piece
analysis.why_bad: The move ignores that a piece or critical pawn is completely unprotected and can be captured immediately, resulting in material loss equivalent to roughly a full piece on average
sub_patterns: Piece moves to a square where it is immediately capturable (Rxc6, Bd5, Nc7, Nxh5)
Quiet pawn move played while own piece/pawn already hangs undefended (h3, g3, Nh3)

analysis.label: Aggressive-looking moves (checks, attacks, central placements) that miss the one precise tactical continuation in narrow positions.
analysis.description: This feature fires on positions where the player chooses a superficially active or threatening move over the single correct continuation. In 5/5 cases, there were very few good moves available (avg 1.4), and the player opted for something that LOOKS aggressive—a check (Rf6+, Rxh3+), an attacking piece placement (Ne4, Bf3), or a space-gaining advance (e5)—while missing a more concrete tactical solution. The best moves were often less obviously flashy: a check in a different direction (Rh1+ maintaining perpetual), an immediate mate (Rf1#), a quiet developing move (Nc6/Bh3), or a pawn grab (Qxh3). In 4/5 positions the played move gained apparent tempo or material but left a piece misplaced or allowed the opponent a critical escape. The common thread is prioritizing visible aggression over precise calculation in positions demanding exactness.
analysis.move_pattern: Active-looking moves (checks, captures, attacks on enemy pieces, central placements) that appear to create threats but are concretely imprecise
analysis.why_bad: The moves trade precision for apparent activity—they give checks along the wrong axis (allowing escape), place pieces on undefended aggressive squares (allowing capture), or grab material while missing forced wins (mate or perpetual). In each case, the correct move required seeing a less obvious but more concrete continuation.
sub_patterns: Check along wrong rank/file missing perpetual or mate
Aggressive piece placement leaving piece hanging to forcing sequence
Pawn advance creating permanent weaknesses while missing developing alternatives
Pawn capture with check missing immediate checkmate

analysis.label: Playing a non-essential or misdirected move in a razor-sharp position where only 1-2 specific moves maintain the evaluation, squandering a decisive tempo.
analysis.description: This feature fires on positions at a tactical tipping point where extremely few moves (avg 1.8) are acceptable, and the player wastes a critical tempo on a seemingly reasonable but ultimately irrelevant or misdirected action. The errors take several forms: quiet flank pawn moves ignoring central emergencies (b3 in positions 1 and 6, g5 in position 11), passive piece retreats removing active pressure (Be7 in position 2), piece relocations that abandon defensive duties (Nf5 in position 5), king moves that expose the monarch or miss urgent captures (Kh7 in position 14, Kg7 in position 15), and wrong forcing moves that squander the initiative (Bf6+ in position 3, Qh3+ in position 4). In 7/8 genuine blunders, the analyses explicitly tag 'tempo_loss' as a contributing factor. The positions share the characteristic that ONE specific concrete action was required—controlling a critical square (d4), capturing a key piece first (Rxf4+, Rxd8), or addressing an immediate tactical vulnerability—and any non-optimal use of tempo proved catastrophic.
analysis.move_pattern: Diverse move types (pawn pushes, piece retreats, king moves, checks) that are non-critical or misdirected relative to the position's ONE urgent demand; typically non-capturing, non-threatening moves in positions requiring immediate concrete action
analysis.why_bad: These moves waste an irreplaceable tempo at the exact moment the position's tactical balance depends on finding the single precise action; the opponent gains a free move to execute a devastating tactical sequence (fork, discovered attack, mating net, or infiltration) that the correct move would have prevented or preempted.
sub_patterns: Quiet flank pawn moves (b3, g5) ignoring central/tactical emergencies
Passive piece retreats from active squares removing counterplay pressure
Wrong forcing move (premature or inefficient check) when a different forcing move was required
King moves that expose the monarch to diagonals or mating nets when a capture/exchange was essential first
Piece relocations to seemingly strong squares that abandon critical defensive coverage

analysis.label: King moves to suboptimal squares in endgame positions, losing critical tempo for centralization or allowing the opponent's king to penetrate.
analysis.description: This feature fires on king moves (7/9 positions) predominantly in endgame positions (6/9) where the king needs to reach a specific critical square but takes an indirect or wrong-direction path. The clearest examples are the two Kg2 positions (3,4) where the king should go Kf1/Kf2 toward the center but instead steps sideways to g2, losing a tempo that allows Black's king to penetrate to e4 and the rook to cut off along the f-file. Similarly, Kf4 (position 9) advances toward the kingside when Kd2/Ke2 was needed to maintain central control, and Kf2 (position 13) retreats passively when aggressive piece play was demanded. The feature also activates on positions with 0 cp loss (3/9) that share surface-level characteristics: exposed kings in open endgame positions making king moves in the f/g file zone. The consistent error in true blunders is choosing a natural-looking king square that fails to account for the opponent's concrete tactical response (rook cut-offs, king penetration, passed pawn advances).
analysis.move_pattern: King moves (occasionally other pieces) to squares on the f/g files in ranks 2-5, typically one step in the wrong direction relative to the critical area of the board
analysis.why_bad: The king loses a critical tempo by moving sideways or toward the kingside instead of directly centralizing, allowing the opponent to penetrate with their king, cut off the White king with a rook along a file, or advance a passed pawn unopposed
sub_patterns: Kg2 instead of Kf1/Kf2 in rook endgames (king gets cut off)
Kf4/Kf2 retreating/advancing toward wrong flank when center/queenside matters
Passive king safety moves when aggressive play maintains initiative

analysis.label: Moves that pursue a seemingly purposeful secondary plan while neglecting the position's most critical tactical or structural vulnerability.
analysis.description: This feature fires on positions where the player makes a 'reasonable-looking' move—activating a piece, gaining space, or challenging an opponent's piece—while ignoring the single most urgent demand of the position. In 8/10 cases, a specific concrete vulnerability existed (a pin needing neutralization, an undefended pawn under file pressure, a piece heading to a trap square, or a king shelter about to be exploited) and the player's move either failed to address it or actively worsened it. The moves span pawn pushes that weaken king shelter (h3, h6, g5 in 3/10), slow piece repositioning when immediate action was needed (Rd3, Nd3, Bd3 in 3/10), premature captures disturbing defensive coordination (Nxf4 twice, 2/10), and pieces moving to tactically vulnerable squares (Nb4, Rd6 in 2/10). The common thread is that the best moves in each position directly addressed the critical issue (neutralizing a pin, defending f7, challenging dominant pieces, maintaining defensive coordination) while the played moves pursued a plausible alternative that left the critical problem unresolved, resulting in an average 240cp loss.
analysis.move_pattern: Mixed piece types and directions; typically a developing/repositioning/space-gaining move to a natural-looking square that fails to address the position's key tension point
analysis.why_bad: The move leaves a critical tactical vulnerability unresolved—whether a pin, an open-file weakness, a piece coordination gap, or a king safety issue—allowing the opponent a concrete exploitation (deflection, exchange sacrifice, pawn storm, trapped piece, or discovered attack) that the player's secondary plan does nothing to prevent.
sub_patterns: Pawn pushes (h3/h6/g5) weakening king shelter while ignoring active tactical threats
Piece repositioning (Nd3/Rd3/Bd3) blocking key squares or being too slow for the position's demands
Premature captures (Nxf4) removing defensive pieces from critical squares
Aggressive piece placement (Nb4/Rd6) to unstable squares vulnerable to tempo-gaining attacks

analysis.label: Playing a routine or superficially logical move in a position that demands one specific, urgent action, resulting in catastrophic evaluation loss.
analysis.description: This feature fires on moves where the position has a single critical requirement (capture a hanging piece, evacuate a king, maintain a key defender, use the correct piece for a capture) but the player instead makes a 'normal-looking' move that completely misses the urgent tactical demand. In 6/8 positions, only 1 good move existed (avg 1.8), yet the player chose routine alternatives: wrong-piece captures (Bxb2 instead of Rxb2, fxe4 instead of Rxe4 in 2/8), slow pawn pushes ignoring king emergencies (b6, h6 in 2/8), pointless checks over winning captures (Rc2+ in 1/8), moving critical defenders away from their duty (Nf2, Nd2 in 2/8), or routine development ignoring king safety (Nc6 in 1/8). The average cp_loss of 2602 reflects positions where one precise move preserves a winning/drawn position while the chosen move catastrophically collapses it. The common thread is a player defaulting to general chess reasoning (captures, checks, development, prophylaxis) rather than calculating the concrete demands of the specific position.
analysis.move_pattern: Varied piece types and directions; moves are captures with wrong piece, passive retreats, routine pawn pushes, or purposeless checks - all 'reasonable-looking' moves that ignore a singular critical tactical requirement
analysis.why_bad: The position demands one specific urgent action (correct recapture piece, king evacuation, winning capture, maintaining a key defender) and the chosen move ignores this demand entirely, allowing the opponent to exploit the neglected tactical element with devastating force
sub_patterns: Wrong piece captures on same square (bishop/pawn instead of rook)
Slow pawn moves (h6, b6) ignoring king safety or tactical emergencies
Moving critical defenders away from guarded squares (Nf2, Nd2)
Pointless checks instead of concrete winning captures
Routine development ignoring exposed king on open file

analysis.label: A key defensive piece moves to a peripheral or tactically exploitable square, leaving critical points (f7, e7, central pawns) undefended against the opponent's existing threats.
analysis.description: In all 6/6 positions, the blundering side moves a piece that was needed for defense to a square that is either peripheral (a3, a5, h5, h7) or tactically exploitable (c3), while urgent threats against the king or critical pawns demanded attention. In 3/6 cases (Qa5, Qh5, Bxa3), the piece explicitly abandons defense of the king's vulnerable zone (exposed kings on f8, e7, g8), allowing mating attacks or decisive material gains against f7/e7. In 2/6 cases (both Bc3 moves), the bishop is placed on a square where it becomes a tactical target rather than an asset, enabling the opponent to win material through piece captures along the diagonal. In 1/6 cases (Rh7), a passive retreat wastes tempo when urgent development was required to contest the opponent's crushing initiative. The common thread is choosing a move that 'looks active' or grabs material while the real battle is happening elsewhere on the board.
analysis.move_pattern: Piece (bishop, queen, or rook) moves to a peripheral square (a-file, h-file, or edges) or to a square away from the critical defensive zone around the king/weaknesses
analysis.why_bad: The moved piece was the key defender of a critical point (f7, e7, e4-pawn, or king escape squares); by relocating it to an irrelevant square, the opponent can immediately exploit the undefended weakness with sacrifices, forks, or mating combinations that weren't possible before
sub_patterns: Queen abandons back-rank/king defense for peripheral activity (Qa5, Qh5)
Bishop captures pawn on wrong flank while kingside is under attack (Bxa3)
Bishop misplaced to tactically vulnerable square where it becomes a target (Bc3 x2)
Rook makes passive retreat instead of urgently developing defenders (Rh7)

analysis.label: Critical positions with exactly one good move available where the player makes a routine or natural-looking move instead of the singular defensive resource, leading to catastrophic material loss or mate.
analysis.description: This feature fires on positions where exactly one move maintains the evaluation (avg good moves = 1.0 across all 8 positions) and the player fails to find it, resulting in enormous evaluation swings (avg 2738 cp loss). The most prominent sub-pattern involves Ke7 walking into Qf7+/Qf7# when g6 was the only saving move (3/8 positions). In 5/8 cases, the correct saving move was a pawn push (g6 three times, c6 once, g3 once) that blocks a critical diagonal or drives back an attacking queen. The played moves are diverse (Nf6, Kd1, Ke7×3, Nd7, Qe8, a4) but share the characteristic of being 'plausible' or 'routine' choices—development moves, king relocations, or strategic pawn pushes—that completely ignore the singular urgent tactical requirement. Positions are predominantly in the opening (6/8) with exposed or centralized kings, and the refutations typically exploit undefended pieces (3/8 hanging piece), devastating check sequences (3/8 king safety/fork), or immediate checkmate (2/8).
analysis.move_pattern: Any non-critical move (development, king relocation, quiet pawn push, piece retreat) in a position demanding one specific saving resource—no consistent piece type or direction
analysis.why_bad: These moves ignore the single critical tactical requirement of the position (blocking a deadly diagonal, preventing a fork/mate, defending a hanging piece) in favor of a natural-looking but fatally irrelevant alternative, allowing the opponent's existing tactical threats to execute unopposed.
sub_patterns: Ke7 walking into Qf7+/Qf7# when g6 was the only defense (3/8 positions)
Routine development (Nf6, Qe8) leaving major pieces hanging on open lines
Moving a critical blocking/defending piece (Nd7 unmasking diagonal, Kd1 enabling fork)
Slow strategic moves (a4) when immediate tactical defense was required

analysis.label: Playing a plausible-looking repositioning move that wastes the critical tempo needed to address an immediate tactical vulnerability, allowing a decisive refutation.
analysis.description: This feature fires on moves that appear reasonable (centralizing a king, advancing a passed pawn, defending a square, developing a queen, giving a check) but fatally ignore the single most urgent concrete demand of the position. In 6/6 positions, the played move wasted a critical tempo: Ke1 ignored a hanging b2 pawn (Position 3), b6 ignored a deflection tactic against an undefended rook (Position 5), g6 weakened the exact squares it intended to defend (Position 7), Bb3 guarded rather than blocked a deadly pawn advance (Position 8), Qe2 made a passive queen move instead of the one tactical knight maneuver that neutralized a g-file threat (Position 13), and Rg3+ gave a purposeless check that trapped the rook (Position 14). All positions featured very few good moves (avg 2.0), indicating razor-sharp situations where only specific concrete actions maintained the position. The tempo_loss tag appears in all 6 positions, and missed_tactic appears in 5/6.
analysis.move_pattern: Any piece type making a non-forcing repositioning move (or purposeless check) that fails to address the position's single most critical tactical requirement
analysis.why_bad: The position demands exactly one or two specific urgent actions (saving material, blocking a threat, executing a tactical operation), and the played move wastes the one available tempo on something indirect or superficially useful, allowing the opponent to execute a concrete tactical blow (capturing hanging material, delivering checkmate, winning an exchange through deflection/trapping).
sub_patterns: King centralization ignoring hanging material
Pawn advance leaving pieces undefended to deflection
Defensive pawn move that weakens the squares it intends to cover
Piece repositioning that guards rather than blocks a critical threat
Passive development when only one forcing move maintains the position
Purposeless check that worsens own piece placement

analysis.label: Playing a natural-looking but passive or premature move when the position demands one specific active continuation to maintain the evaluation.
analysis.description: This feature fires on positions where the player chose an instinctive, natural-looking, or reactive move instead of the single precise active continuation required. In 4/5 positions, the blunder involved a tempo loss (Na4 decentralizing, Kd2 retreating, Rb1 wrong move order, c6 premature push). In 4/5 positions, the correct move involved superior piece activity (Bg5 activating bishop, Rh1 repositioning rook, f5 keeping files closed while winning material, Rxc7 forcing a specific sequence). All positions had extremely narrow margins with only ~1.4 good moves available on average, meaning these are critical junctures demanding precision. The played moves all appear reasonable at surface level—attacking a queen (Na4), advancing a passed pawn (c6), recapturing material (fxg6), placing a rook on an open file (Rb1), defending pawns (Kd2)—but each fundamentally fails to address the position's most urgent demand, surrendering the initiative and allowing the opponent to consolidate or counterattack.
analysis.move_pattern: Geometrically diverse (knight to rim, pawn push, pawn capture, rook to back rank, king retreat) but all share the quality of being non-forcing or sub-optimally sequenced when a forcing/precise alternative exists
analysis.why_bad: These moves waste a critical tempo or execute the correct plan in the wrong order, allowing the opponent to activate counterplay (back-rank invasion, rook-behind-passer defense, file opening, king march) that neutralizes or reverses the position's evaluation. The positions demand one precise action first, and any delay is severely punished.
sub_patterns: Decentralizing a piece when defensive coordination is needed
Premature pawn advance before rook repositioning
Automatic recapture that opens a critical file for the opponent
Correct tactical idea executed in wrong move order
Passive king retreat when pawn advance maintains initiative

analysis.label: Knight moves attempting material-winning forks that fail because they are non-forcing, move to defended squares, or abandon critical positional duties.
analysis.description: All 9/9 positions involve knight moves that attempt to fork two or more enemy pieces (typically rooks, or king+rook), appearing to win material but actually being severe blunders. The most common sub-pattern is Nf2 forking two rooks (3/9 positions), where the knight abandons a powerful centralized square (e4) and the fork is non-forcing, allowing the opponent to play the faster Bxf7+ check. Other instances include Nxf7/Nf7 attempting king-rook forks where the king simply captures (2/9), Nc2/Nxc2 attempting rook forks while abandoning dominant central knights (2/9), and Nd7/Nxc7 attempting rook or queen-rook forks that fail to defended squares or superior counterplay (2/9). The average cp_loss of 434 reflects catastrophic evaluation swings, as these moves consistently trade powerful, well-placed knights for illusory material gains while exposing critical weaknesses (especially f7) or allowing the opponent's faster forcing moves.
analysis.move_pattern: Knight jump to fork two or more pieces (typically rooks on first rank, or king+rook on f7/c7), moving away from a central square (e4, d4, e5, g4) to the second rank (f2, c2) or seventh rank (f7, c7, d7)
analysis.why_bad: The fork is non-forcing (not a check), so the opponent can ignore the material threat and execute a faster tactical response (commonly Bxf7+ check), or the forking square is defended and the knight is simply captured, or the knight abandons critical central/defensive duties that were more valuable than the material it wins.
sub_patterns: Nf2 forking two rooks while abandoning e4 centralization, allowing Bxf7+ in return
Nxf7/Nf7 fork on king+rook where king captures and retreats safely, losing a piece for nothing
Nc2/Nxc2 forking rook on a1 while abandoning dominant d4 knight, exposing king or allowing escape
Nd7/Nxc7 forking rooks or queen+rook on a defended square, allowing powerful counterplay

analysis.label: Pieces move to h-file squares (h6/h3/h5/h2) pursuing speculative kingside threats while leaving critical pieces or pawns undefended elsewhere.
analysis.description: This feature fires on moves directed predominantly toward the h-file (7/9 positions: Bh6×3, Bh3, Qh5, Kh2, h6) where the player pursues an aggressive-looking kingside idea but critically abandons defensive duties. In Position 1, Bh6 leaves the e2 bishop undefended (exploited by Rxe2). In Position 6, Bh6 removes the e3 bishop's protection of the d4 knight (exploited by cxd4). In Position 12, Bh3 removes the bishop's coverage of c6 (exploited by Bxc6+). In Position 14, Qd2 moves the queen away from tactical justification for the f7 bishop (exploited by Qxf7). In Position 15, h6 ignores the tactical vulnerability on f2 (exploited by Qxf2). The consistent pattern across 8/9 positions is that the moved piece was performing a hidden defensive function—protecting another piece or providing tactical counter-threats—and its relocation creates an immediate hanging piece or exploitable weakness. The remaining case (Position 2, Qh5) similarly directs the queen to an irrelevant h-file square while ignoring a forced mating sequence.
analysis.move_pattern: Piece (especially bishop) or pawn moves to h-file squares (h2, h3, h5, h6), typically aimed at opponent's kingside castled position
analysis.why_bad: The moved piece was silently defending another piece or providing tactical counter-threats; its relocation leaves a piece hanging or a critical square unguarded, allowing the opponent to win material immediately through capture of the now-undefended piece
sub_patterns: Bh6 abandoning protection of central knight or bishop (3/9)
Bishop to h3/h6 removing defense of a knight (Nc6, Nd4) exploited by capture with check
Queen repositioning that removes tactical justification for a deep-penetrating piece
H-pawn push ignoring immediate tactical vulnerability on f-file

analysis.label: Making aggressive or advancing moves in positions where an exposed king demands consolidation or retreat, creating exploitable tactical vulnerabilities.
analysis.description: This feature fires on moves that prioritize activity, advancement, or superficially logical play while ignoring the critical need to address king vulnerability. In 10/12 positions, an exposed king (either the player's or opponent's) is the dominant positional factor, yet the move played either worsens the king's safety or fails to exploit/address it correctly. The best moves in these positions are typically retreats or consolidating moves (Kf1, Ke2, Kf3, Ng6, Nf6, Be6 appear as top alternatives in 8/12 cases), while the played moves advance pieces forward or capture material. The resulting vulnerability is then punished via checks (Qg4+, Bh5+, Bf5+, Qh5+, Rxd5+ appear as refutations in 7/12 cases) that exploit the newly created weakness. The average cp_loss of 1746 reflects how catastrophic it is to ignore king exposure in tactically charged positions.
analysis.move_pattern: Forward advances (pawn pushes, knight hops to edge/aggressive squares, king marching toward center) when position demands backward/consolidating moves (king retreats, piece withdrawals to safe squares)
analysis.why_bad: The move creates or exposes a concrete tactical vulnerability (hanging piece, opened diagonal/file to king, vacated defensive square) that the opponent immediately exploits via forcing moves (checks, captures with check, discovered attacks) targeting the already-exposed king.
sub_patterns: Pawn advances that open lines toward own king (d5, g6, cxb4, e4)
Knight moves from safe/defensive squares to exposed/hanging squares (Nh3, Nh4, Nf6)
King advancing toward center when retreat is required (Kd3)
Choosing flashy checks over concrete material-winning continuations (Ng5+)

analysis.label: Moves with a clear logical intent that catastrophically abandon the position's most critical demand, allowing a forcing tactical punishment.
analysis.description: This feature fires on moves that look purposeful and reasonable—attacking a piece, giving check, repositioning, or addressing a concern—but fundamentally misread the position's priorities, abandoning a critical function and allowing devastating punishment. In 8/10 positions, the move played had an obvious intent (h3 to challenge a pin, Nd7 to centralize, Nd5+/Nd6+ to give check, Bd1 to reposition, Nf2 to attack a bishop, Bb4 to hit a rook, Rb3 to pressure a pawn) yet each ignored a more urgent positional or tactical demand. The average cp_loss of 1316 is enormous, and with only 2.0 good moves available on average, these are critical decision points requiring precision. In 7/10 cases the opponent punished with a forcing response (check, capture, or zwischenzug) that exploited exactly what was abandoned. Tags across all positions consistently include 'tempo_loss' (9/10), 'missed_tactic' (8/10), and 'piece_activity' (8/10), confirming that these moves squander tempo on secondary goals while the opponent seizes the initiative on the primary battleground.
analysis.move_pattern: Diverse piece types and directions; no single geometric pattern. Moves include piece repositioning (Nd7, Bd1, Rb3, Rd4), checks (Nd5+, Nd6+), attacks on opponent pieces (Bb4, Nf2, h3), and king moves (Kg8).
analysis.why_bad: Each move pursues a secondary objective (attacking, repositioning, checking) while abandoning the position's critical element—whether that's a defensive piece guarding a key pawn, king safety, a forcing simplification, or piece coordination—allowing the opponent a tactical blow (check, zwischenzug, or capture) that exploits the newly created vulnerability.
sub_patterns: Pointless checks that abandon defensive duties (Nd5+, Nd6+)
Piece repositioning that self-blocks or leaves critical squares unguarded (Nd7, Bd1, Rd4, Rb3)
Aggressive gestures ignoring opponent's stronger forcing moves (Nf2, Bb4, h3)
King moves into tactical danger zones (Kg8)

analysis.label: Tempting material captures in the opening that ignore the vulnerability of an uncastled or exposed king, allowing tactical punishment through forks, checks, or hanging pieces.
analysis.description: This feature fires on opening moves where a player makes a greedy or tempting capture (or aggressive move) while their king remains dangerously exposed in the center or on an open file. In 8/9 positions, the move is a capture (usually of a central pawn on e4, e5, d4, or g6), and in 9/9 positions, the blundering side's king is either uncastled or exposed. The punishment consistently exploits the king's vulnerability: queen checks that fork pieces (positions 4, 6, 8 via Qd5/Qh5+), queens captured because the king can't recapture (positions 1, 5), pieces left hanging because the capture ignored a more urgent threat (positions 7, 9), or unsound sacrifices that leave insufficient compensation (positions 2, 3). The average cp_loss of 292 reflects that these are serious blunders where safe developing moves or castling were readily available (avg 2.1 good alternatives).
analysis.move_pattern: Captures (usually by knight or pawn) toward central squares (e4, e5, d4) or aggressive piece moves, while the player's king remains on its starting square or is exposed on an open file
analysis.why_bad: The capture prioritizes immediate material gain but ignores that the exposed/central king creates a tactical vulnerability—typically allowing the opponent to exploit open lines with queen checks, double attacks, or simply winning undefended pieces that the king cannot support
sub_patterns: Knight captures e4 pawn leaving knight exposed to queen fork (3 instances)
Captures that leave queen undefended on open file due to king misplacement (2 instances)
Unsound knight sacrifices on e5 with insufficient central compensation (2 instances)
Pawn/piece captures that leave another piece hanging on a diagonal (2 instances)

analysis.label: Quiet, natural-looking piece placements that ignore the position's immediate tactical or strategic demand, resulting in critical tempo loss.
analysis.description: All 5 positions feature moves that appear reasonable in isolation—developing a bishop (Be2), targeting a pawn (Ra1), preparing fianchetto (g6), attacking a passed pawn (Nb6), or occupying an 'outpost' (Nc5)—but each fatally ignores the position's most urgent requirement. In 4/5 cases the move is tagged as tempo_loss; in 4/5 cases piece_activity is central; in 4/5 cases king_safety is a factor. The critical thread is that each position had a concrete, urgent demand (castling immediately to cover c2 in Position 1; maintaining f-file defensive coordination in Position 5; addressing the f6 knight's tactical vulnerability in Position 8; preserving the c8 blockade in Position 9; developing/exchanging to reduce cramping in Position 12), and the player instead chose a cosmetically appealing but strategically irrelevant move. The piece ends up either captured (Nb6 by Rb3), driven back with tempo lost (Nc5 after b4), tactically exploited (Be2 allowing Nd4 fork), stranded out of play (Ra1 while kingside collapses), or simply wasted while the opponent strikes (g6 allowing Ne4).
analysis.move_pattern: Non-forcing quiet moves (no check, no capture) placing pieces/pawns on seemingly natural or active squares away from the position's critical sector
analysis.why_bad: Each move addresses a secondary concern while the position demands immediate concrete action on its most critical issue—whether that's king safety, maintaining a blockade, or preserving defensive coordination. The resulting tempo loss allows the opponent to execute their primary threat unchallenged.
sub_patterns: Piece moves to natural-looking square that becomes a tactical target (Be2, Nb6, Nc5)
Piece repositions away from the critical file/sector toward a peripheral target (Ra1)
Slow pawn move for future preparation when immediate piece action is required (g6)

analysis.label: King or piece moves toward an unimportant target while ignoring the opponent's critical passed pawn racing toward promotion.
analysis.description: This feature fires on endgame positions where the player makes a move—almost always a king move (7/9 positions)—that pursues a secondary target (typically an unimportant enemy pawn) while neglecting the opponent's advanced or racing passed pawn. In Position 1, Kf3 chases f2/g3 pawns while the h5 passer advances. In Position 2, Kd4 abandons blockade of the d5 passer to attack c4. In Position 4, Kg6 attacks f6 while d2 promotes. In Position 5, Kf1 approaches h2 but walks into a promotion check. In Position 6, Ka3 targets a2 while the c-pawn runs. In Position 8, Kh5 hunts the g5 pawn while the e-pawn queens. In Position 9, a4 wastes the critical tempo on a meaningless pawn challenge while b3 promotes. The remaining positions (3, 7) show analogous misdirection where pieces abandon key defensive duties for inferior goals. Across all 9 positions, the tag 'tempo_loss' and 'passed_pawn' appear universally, and average cp_loss is enormous (3213), reflecting how catastrophic misallocation of tempo is in promotion races.
analysis.move_pattern: King (or piece) moves toward a secondary pawn target, typically 1-2 squares in the direction of an unimportant pawn and away from the opponent's critical passed pawn or key defensive post
analysis.why_bad: Every tempo is critical in endgame pawn races; moving toward an irrelevant target gives the opponent a free move to advance their passed pawn, which often reaches promotion unstoppably because the king/piece is now too far away to intercept
sub_patterns: King abandons blockade of passed pawn to capture a static pawn
King marches toward secondary kingside/queenside pawn while center/opposite-wing passer promotes
Piece (rook/pawn move) wastes tempo on secondary goal while opponent's pawn races

analysis.label: King moves to an exposed square vulnerable to checks when a safer (often counterintuitive) king move was the only good option.
analysis.description: In all 9/9 positions, the player needed to move their king but chose a square that sits on a vulnerable line (file, diagonal, or rank) exploitable by the opponent's forcing checks, rather than the single safe square available. The correct moves were often counterintuitive: corners or edges (Ka1, Kh8, Ka5, Kb2, Kh7 in 5/9 cases) or paradoxical forward advances (Kc4, Kd5, Kh4 in 4/9 cases). The blundered moves consistently went toward the center or retreated 'safely' backward, but landed on intersections of the opponent's checking lanes. In every position, exactly 1 good move existed (avg good moves: 1.0), making these razor-thin king placement decisions. The catastrophic average cp_loss of 3499 reflects that several resulted in immediate checkmate (Kc7 allowing Rc8#, Kd2 allowing Qe1+/Qe3#) or loss of forced mates (Kd6 losing mate-in-5).
analysis.move_pattern: King move to a square on an opponent's checking diagonal, file, or rank; correct square was typically toward the board edge, corner, or counterintuitively forward
analysis.why_bad: The chosen king square sits at the intersection of the opponent's checking lanes (diagonals for queens, files for rooks), enabling tempo-gaining check sequences that win material, force perpetual, or deliver checkmate, while the alternative square breaks all checking geometry.
sub_patterns: King retreats toward center instead of escaping to corner/edge (5/9)
King retreats backward when counterintuitive forward advance escapes checking geometry (4/9)
King enters file controlled by enemy rook allowing back-rank mate (2/9)
King enters diagonal allowing queen check sequence with material gain (5/9)

analysis.label: Moving a piece away from its vital defensive role (or into a tactically exploitable square), enabling an immediate forcing sequence that wasn't possible before.
analysis.description: In 7/7 positions, the player makes a move that actively creates a new tactical vulnerability by displacing a piece from its critical defensive function. In 3/7 cases, a king steps to a square where it becomes vulnerable to immediate checks, forks, or mating patterns (Kf7 into Re7+/Qg7#, Kh3 into h5/hxg4#, Kh2 into Ng4+ fork). In 3/7 cases, a non-king piece abandons its defensive post (Nd7 removes the f6 knight that could interpose on e8; Rd1 removes the f1 rook that supported f2-f3 against bishop-trapping; Nxf4 removes the d3 knight protecting b1 from a fork). In 1/7 cases (d4), a 'developing' move ignores an immediate hanging piece. The common thread across all positions is that the player makes a move that appears purposeful—contesting a file, capturing material, fleeing to apparent safety—but fatally overlooks that the moved piece (or its former square) was the linchpin preventing a concrete tactical blow. The resulting punishments are severe (avg 2950cp loss) because the moves don't just worsen the position gradually but instead unlock specific forced sequences.
analysis.move_pattern: Various piece types (king, knight, rook, pawn) moving away from a square where they performed critical defensive work, or moving TO a square that is tactically compromised by opponent's forcing moves (checks, forks, mating nets)
analysis.why_bad: Each move removes the one piece or resource that was preventing a specific tactical blow—whether blocking a check, defending against a fork, supporting a key pawn push, or simply staying off a controlled square—enabling an immediate forced sequence that wins material or delivers checkmate.
sub_patterns: King walks into check/fork/mating square (Kf7, Kh3, Kh2)
Knight/Rook abandons defensive post enabling tactical shot (Nd7, Nxf4, Rd1)
Constructive-looking move ignores immediate en prise threat (d4)

analysis.label: Quiet, routine moves played in positions where a forcing bishop sacrifice on f7 (or f2) with check would exploit the opponent's uncastled king.
analysis.description: In all 10 positions, the best move involved a tactical strike against the f7-pawn (or f2-pawn) exploiting the opponent's uncastled king — specifically Bxf7+ was the top or second-best move in 8/10 positions, and Bxf2+ featured in the remaining 2/10. Instead, players chose non-forcing, routine moves: castling (3/10), quiet bishop development like Be3/Bg5/Bd7 (3/10), pawn pushes like d5/h3/e6 (3/10), or an autopilot recapture cxd4 (1/10). In every case, the opponent's king was still in the center with f7 (or f2) vulnerable to a bishop sacrifice with check that would either win material through a subsequent fork/discovered attack, permanently displace the king, or strip castling rights. The played moves all gave the opponent a critical tempo to play ...e6 (blocking the diagonal), castle to safety, or otherwise consolidate — completely closing the tactical window.
analysis.move_pattern: Any non-forcing move (castling, quiet development, pawn push, recapture) when a bishop sacrifice Bxf7+ or Bxf2+ with check is available against an uncastled king
analysis.why_bad: These routine moves waste a critical tempo, allowing the opponent to block the a2-g8/a7-g1 diagonal (usually with ...e6) or castle, permanently eliminating the forcing Bxf7+/Bxf2+ tactical opportunity that was the entire basis of the position's advantage.
sub_patterns: Castling instead of Bxf7+ (king safety over tactics)
Quiet bishop development (Be3/Bg5/Bd7) missing Bxf7+ fork setup
Prophylactic pawn move (h3) instead of tactical sacrifice
Autopilot recapture (cxd4) ignoring classical Bxf7+ sacrifice
Positional pawn advance (d5/e6) missing Bxf2+ combination

analysis.label: Moves that appear aggressive or purposeful (checks, captures, piece repositionings) but actually squander a critical tempo by failing to address the position's true demands.
analysis.description: This feature fires on moves that look active or forcing on the surface—giving checks, making captures, or 'improving' piece placement—but in reality waste a crucial tempo in positions where timing is decisive. In 7/8 positions, the analysis explicitly identifies 'tempo_loss' as the core tactical motif. The pattern manifests in several sub-forms: premature checks that let the king escape to safety (Rc6+ in position 5, c5+ in position 10, Re7+ in position 9), piece repositionings that abandon important duties (Be5 abandoning a4-pawn coverage in position 3, Nf7 leaving a dominant d6 outpost in position 7, Ng4 wasting time when king centralization was urgent in position 4), captures in the wrong order (Nxe5 allowing a bishop to escape in position 1), and 'attacking' pawn moves that weaken structure without gaining real time (c4 in position 2). In all cases, the position demanded either a specific move order, immediate king activation, or maintenance of positional tension, but the player chose a cosmetically appealing move instead. The average cp_loss of 1332 reflects how punishing these tempo losses are—in many cases transforming winning positions into drawn or lost ones.
analysis.move_pattern: Various piece types and directions; often checks (3/8), captures, or piece centralization moves that appear forcing but don't actually constrain the opponent's best response
analysis.why_bad: The move wastes a tempo in a position where timing is critical—it either allows the opponent to escape a tactic, advance pawns in a race, reach a key square first, or eliminate a tactical vulnerability that existed only for one move
sub_patterns: Purposeless checks that allow king escape from a tactical net
Piece moves abandoning dominant squares for cosmetically active but inferior ones
Wrong capture/move order that allows opponent's piece to escape
Premature pawn advances that fix structure and lose defensive flexibility
Piece repositioning when king activation or pawn advances were urgent

analysis.label: Pawn captures in closed positions that prematurely release structural tension, opening lines or squares that benefit the opponent.
analysis.description: All 6/6 positions feature closed centers where the player makes a pawn capture (exd4, dxc5, dxe6, exd5, hxg4, dxe5) that resolves critical pawn tension. In every case, the better alternatives maintain the tension while improving pieces or making prophylactic moves (6/6). The captures consistently open lines for the opponent's pieces: opening the h-file for an opponent's rook (2/6 - positions 13, 15), creating unstoppable connected passers by removing a blockading pawn (1/6 - position 9), surrendering a space-gaining pawn wedge (1/6 - position 8), gifting the opponent a dominant pawn center (1/6 - position 6), or opening the position when critically underdeveloped (1/6 - position 7).
