The average cp_loss of 248 reflects how transformative these seemingly routine exchanges are—each fundamentally alters the strategic balance by unlocking the opponent's latent advantages that the closed structure was suppressing.
analysis.move_pattern: Pawn captures pawn (any direction), resolving a point of tension in a closed or semi-closed pawn structure
analysis.why_bad: The closed pawn structure was actively restraining the opponent's pieces, blocking dangerous files, or maintaining a space advantage; the capture removes this structural barrier, immediately activating the opponent's dormant forces (rooks gaining open files, knights finding outposts, connected passers forming) while yielding no compensating benefit.
sub_patterns: Opening files toward own castled king (hxg4, dxe5)
Surrendering a central pawn wedge/blockade (dxe6, exd5)
Opening position when underdeveloped or uncastled (dxc5)
Creating dominant pawn center for opponent (exd4)

analysis.label: Advancing a piece to an apparently active square where it immediately becomes a target for tempo-gaining checks or captures by the opponent.
analysis.description: In all 3/3 positions, the player moves a piece forward/aggressively when the correct approach is to retreat, consolidate, or execute a different plan entirely. In Position 2, the king advances from e2 to f2 instead of retreating (or capturing the active knight), walking into a Qd2+ checking sequence. In Position 6, the knight jumps to f3 with check but hangs to Nxf3, a capture the player apparently overlooked. In Position 10, the king advances from f3 to e4 instead of retreating to e2, landing on a square where f5+ hits it with tempo, ruining a won pawn race. The common thread is choosing the 'active-looking' forward move over the objectively superior quiet/retreating move, with the advanced piece immediately punished by a tempo-gaining response (check or capture). In 2/3 cases the blundering piece is the king; in 3/3 cases the refutation exploits the moved piece directly with tempo.
analysis.move_pattern: Piece (usually king) advances one square toward center/kingside to a square vulnerable to immediate check or capture
analysis.why_bad: The advanced piece lands on a square where the opponent can immediately gain tempo via check or capture, squandering the initiative and either losing material outright or allowing a devastating checking sequence that dissipates a large advantage.
sub_patterns: King advances into pawn check (e4 hit by f5+)
King advances into queen check sequence (f2 hit by Qd2+)
Knight gives check but hangs to opponent's piece capture

analysis.label: Playing a slow, non-forcing move in a critically urgent position where only 1-2 moves address an immediate tactical demand.
analysis.description: This feature fires on positions where the player makes a 'normal-looking' quiet move (king repositioning, pawn push, piece maneuver, or peripheral capture) while ignoring an immediate tactical crisis that demands concrete action NOW. In 7/9 positions, there were only 1-2 good moves available, indicating extremely narrow tactical positions. The urgent demands varied: eliminating a promotion threat (Position 1: Rxg2 needed), keeping a defender on its post (Position 2: rook needed on f4), removing a lethal infiltrator (Position 3: Qxf3/Nxf3 needed), offering a queen trade to avoid mate (Position 5: Qg6 needed), avoiding a check-enabling square (Position 7: Kh7 needed), saving a hanging piece (Position 8: Kd8/Ba4 needed), creating immediate pawn counterplay (Position 12: g5 needed), avoiding a forced simplification (Position 14: Qa8 needed), and neutralizing a discovered check (Position 15: Bc4/Bxa2/Kg8 needed). In every case, the player instead made a move that would be reasonable in a quieter position but catastrophically ignores the single critical requirement.
analysis.move_pattern: Diverse piece types (king moves 4/9, pawn pushes 2/9, piece moves 3/9); all non-forcing, non-checking quiet moves that fail to address the position's tactical demand
analysis.why_bad: The position requires one specific concrete action (capturing a threat, offering a trade, creating counterplay, or fleeing a tactical pattern), but the player makes a slow positional or developmental move that wastes the single tempo needed to survive, allowing the opponent's threat to execute unopposed.
sub_patterns: King walks into mating/checking patterns (Ke2, Kg2, Kf7, Kg7)
Slow pawn pushes ignoring tactical threats (a4, a5)
Piece repositioning when immediate counterplay is required (Nc4, Qe7)
Peripheral capture abandoning critical defensive post (Rxb4)

analysis.label: Pieces moved to seemingly active squares where they are immediately attacked, forced back, or block critical coordination, giving the opponent a decisive free tempo.
analysis.description: This feature fires on moves that appear purposeful or active but catastrophically waste a tempo, allowing the opponent to execute a decisive tactical or strategic blow. In 7/7 positions, the moved piece lands on a square where it is immediately challenged: Kf7 walks into a mating net and must retreat (1/7), Bd2 blocks its own rook on the critical d-file (1/7), Qf5 abandons a key diagonal and gets attacked by g4 or allows Ba3 with tempo (1/7), Nxd4 removes a critical defender giving White tempo via Bf4 (1/7), g3 wastes development time allowing e4 with discovered check (1/7), Qg3 places the queen where it's forced into an unfavorable trade via Qc6+ (1/7), and Kd6 moves the king where f5 immediately pushes it back (1/7). The common thread is that all moves look natural or active on the surface but ignore an urgent concrete threat, effectively gifting the opponent a free move to execute their plan. Positions average only 1.7 good alternatives, indicating narrow tactical demands where precise move selection was critical.
analysis.move_pattern: Piece (any type) moves to a seemingly logical square that is immediately exploitable - either attacked by opponent's pawn advance, blocking own piece, or abandoned a defensive duty
analysis.why_bad: The move gives the opponent a crucial tempo by placing the piece on a square where it will be immediately driven back, exchanged unfavorably, or where it blocks critical coordination - the opponent uses this free tempo to execute a decisive tactical blow (mating attack, pawn break, file seizure, or forced simplification).
sub_patterns: King advancing into opponent's attacking zone instead of retreating to safety (Kf7, Kd6)
Piece blocking own rook's access to a critical open file (Bd2)
Queen abandoning defensive control of a key diagonal for apparent activity (Qf5, Qg3)
Capturing material that removes a key defensive piece, giving opponent tempo (Nxd4)
Slow preparatory pawn move when urgent development is needed (g3)

analysis.label: Moves that remove a piece or pawn from an essential defensive function, catastrophically collapsing the position.
analysis.description: This feature fires on moves where the player voluntarily withdraws, captures with, or displaces a piece/pawn that was performing an irreplaceable defensive duty, instantly allowing the opponent to exploit the now-unguarded weakness. In 5/11 positions, the king retreats toward the edge or back rank instead of maintaining centrality (Kc6, Kc6, Kd6, Ke8, Kd6), directly enabling mating nets or tactical combinations along newly opened lines. In 2/11 positions, the wrong piece is moved/captured with, removing a critical blocker (Nxg5 removes the e4-knight enabling Qxc3+ fork; Nfd7 removes the f6-knight that blocked the a1-h8 diagonal). In 2/11 positions, a key back-rank or king-shield defender is removed (Rxf2 removes the f1-rook enabling Rd1+/Rxe1#; g3 removes the g2-pawn shield enabling mate). The remaining cases involve abandoning active piece placement (Rc6 abandons the 2nd rank) or wasting tempo on an unstable post (Nd5). The extremely high average cp_loss (4510) and low number of good alternatives (avg 2.1) confirm these are narrow decision points where the defensive function was the sole thing holding the position together.
analysis.move_pattern: Any piece type moving away from its current square where it performed an essential defensive or blocking function — typically retreating, capturing with the wrong piece, or pushing a shielding pawn forward
analysis.why_bad: The moved piece/pawn was the sole element preventing a concrete threat (mating attack, pawn capture, tactical combination, or edge-driving technique), and its removal instantly allows the opponent to execute the previously-blocked winning plan
sub_patterns: King retreating toward board edge in KR vs K endgames, abandoning centrality
Removing back-rank or king-shield defender (rook or pawn) allowing mating combinations
Moving/capturing with wrong piece, removing a critical diagonal or square blocker
Abandoning an active piece post (2nd rank, center) for a passive square
Wasting critical tempo on unstable placement in time-sensitive positions

analysis.label: A Queen or Rook captures a dangerous passed pawn with check adjacent to the enemy king, which simply recaptures, trading a major piece for a pawn and ruining a winning endgame.
analysis.description: In 13/13 positions, a major piece (Queen in 7 cases, Rook in 6 cases) captures a pawn with check in an endgame, only for the opponent's king (or in one case a bishop) to recapture the piece, catastrophically simplifying the position. In nearly all cases (12/13), the captured pawn was an advanced passed pawn 1-2 squares from promotion, creating urgency that seduced the player into the trade. The opponent's king sat directly adjacent to the capture square, making recapture trivial. The resulting positions typically transform from forced mates or decisive advantages into drawn or barely-winning pawn endgames. Better alternatives consistently involved either advancing one's own passed pawn first (creating counter-threats before capturing), delivering checks from safe squares to dominate the enemy king without trading, or improving king position before committing to the exchange. The average cp_loss of 3112 reflects multiple positions where forced checkmates were converted into mere pawn advantages.
analysis.move_pattern: Queen or Rook captures a pawn on a square adjacent to the enemy king, delivering check; the king recaptures the major piece
analysis.why_bad: Trading a Queen or Rook (the decisive winning piece) for a mere pawn enters a drastically simplified endgame where the winning advantage evaporates. The passed pawn being captured was typically already controlled/blockaded and could have been won later while preserving the major piece, or the player's own counter-threats (their own passed pawns, mating attacks) were stronger than the promotion threat.
sub_patterns: Queen captures near-promoting pawn with check, king recaptures queen → draw
Rook captures near-promoting pawn with check, king recaptures rook → drawn K+P endgame
Premature capture before advancing own passed pawn (move-order error)
Capture with check when distant checking sequence would dominate without trading
Fear-driven capture of promotion threat when forced mate existed via checks

analysis.label: Playing a non-forcing, non-critical move when the position demands immediate action on the most urgent tactical or strategic issue.
analysis.description: This feature fires on positions where players waste a critical tempo by choosing a superficially reasonable but ultimately irrelevant or misdirected move while ignoring the position's single most important demand. In 8/10 positions, the analyses explicitly tag 'tempo_loss' as the core error. The pattern manifests as: decentralizing well-placed pieces to inferior squares (Nh6 instead of forcing Ng7 in positions 1 and 3; Nd3 retreating from dominant e5 in position 8; Ke5 going the wrong direction in position 15), playing slow flank pawn moves when dynamic central action is required (a4 instead of f5 break in position 9; b5 ignoring the d6 passed pawn in position 12; h6 creating a target in position 5), or choosing passive/misdirected piece moves when forcing continuations exist (Rc6 instead of advancing d5 in position 6; Nc3 as a premature move-order error in position 10; Qc3 creating illusory defense in position 13). The average of only 1.8 good moves available confirms these are narrow, critical positions where precision is mandatory. In every case, the opponent exploits the wasted tempo to either activate their own king (Ke4-d5), advance a decisive passed pawn (d7), or consolidate a vulnerable position that one more forcing move would have cracked.
analysis.move_pattern: Varied piece types moving to non-forcing, peripheral, or strategically irrelevant squares when a forcing central/attacking move exists; often rim knight moves, flank pawn pushes, retreats, or lateral rook moves
analysis.why_bad: The position has one critical demand (a forcing tactic, a passed pawn to advance/stop, or a piece to keep centralized) and the move ignores it, giving the opponent a free tempo to consolidate, activate their king, or advance a decisive threat
sub_patterns: Decentralizing a dominant knight to the rim (Nh6 instead of forcing Ng7, Nd3 retreating from e5)
Slow flank pawn push when central/dynamic break is required (a4 instead of f5, b5 ignoring d6 pawn)
King moving wrong direction in endgame (Ke5 abandoning queenside counterplay)
Premature move-order error playing correct move too early (Nc3 before deflecting king with Ng1)
Passive defense instead of advancing passed pawn (Rc6 instead of d5)

analysis.label: Quiet repositioning or advancing moves that look like natural improvements but create specific exploitable weaknesses (tactical alignments, hanging pieces, abandoned key squares, or lost tempo).
analysis.description: This feature fires on positions where a player selects a non-forcing 'improvement' move—typically a king step, knight reposition, pawn advance, or rook relocation—that appears to improve piece placement but actually introduces a concrete tactical or structural vulnerability. In 12/12 positions, the played move was quiet and non-forcing (no checks, no captures, no immediate threats), while the best alternatives involved concrete action: immediate checks (Rh3+ in position 8), tactical threats (Nb5 threatening Nxc7+ in position 5), tension resolution (fxe5/d5 in positions 10/4), or precise king routing (Ke7 in position 6). The blunders create diverse vulnerabilities: skewers (Kc5 aligning king with bishop, position 15), trapped pieces (Nc6 blocking bishop retreat, position 7), hanging pieces (Nb4, position 12), exposed kings (f4/Ke6/g4, positions 4/6/11), abandoned files (Rf5 leaving e-file, position 9), and lost tempo (Rh4/Kh7, positions 8/2). The common thread is choosing superficially attractive quiet moves in positions demanding precision or forcing play.
analysis.move_pattern: Quiet non-forcing moves (king steps, knight hops, pawn pushes, rook slides to adjacent files/ranks) with no check or capture, typically appearing to centralize or advance
analysis.why_bad: The position demands concrete action (immediate forcing moves, tactical threats, or precise prophylaxis), but the player chooses a 'nice-looking' quiet move that either creates a direct tactical vulnerability (alignment, hanging piece, exposed king) or wastes the critical tempo needed to maintain the position's equilibrium
sub_patterns: King moves to squares creating piece alignments (skewers/pins) or exposed to perpetual checks
Knight repositioning to squares where it blocks own pieces or becomes tactically vulnerable
Pawn advances that create targets or expose the king's defenses
Rook moves that abandon critical open files or lose forcing check tempo

analysis.label: Playing a routine-looking developing or repositioning move that ignores the position's urgent concrete demand, enabling tactical punishment.
analysis.description: In all 6 positions, the player makes a move that appears to improve piece placement or pursue standard development (Be7 developing, Nf6 to a natural square, Qd2/Qc5/Qf5 repositioning the queen, e5 grabbing space), but each ignores a critical positional urgency - typically king safety or maintaining a key defensive piece configuration. In 5/6 positions, the king is exposed (uncastled or weak pawn shield), creating latent tactical issues that demand precise responses. In 4/6 cases, the moved piece lands on a square where it becomes a direct tactical target (Be7 hit by Ba3, Qf5 hit by Bd3, Qd2 hit by Ne4, Nf6 enabling Nc4 vs queen). The correct moves are often non-obvious urgent actions (Kf8, f3, Rc8, Qd8) that address the position's most critical demand. The average 1.7 good moves confirms these are narrow positions requiring concrete precision over general improvement.
analysis.move_pattern: Piece (usually queen, knight, or bishop) moves to a standard/natural development square, typically not a capture or check, often along a central file or to a 'textbook' square
analysis.why_bad: The natural-looking destination square either becomes a tactical target (enabling tempo-gaining attacks against it) or abandons a critical defensive function, while the position's urgent concrete need (king safety, maintaining key piece placements, dynamic counterplay) goes unaddressed
sub_patterns: Queen repositioned to active-looking square becomes exposed to tempo-gaining minor piece attacks (Qd2→Ne4, Qf5→Bd3, Qc5→Rd1)
Piece developed to natural square enables opponent's tactical combination exploiting uncastled/exposed king
Premature pawn advance creates static target when resolving tension or developing was required

analysis.label: Natural-looking moves that waste a critical tempo by executing the plan in the wrong move order, giving the opponent time to save or turn the position.
analysis.description: This feature fires on positions where the player makes a direct, seemingly aggressive or logical move but loses a critical tempo that the opponent exploits. In 3/8 positions (f3, b4, and partly Kd7), the player advances a pawn prematurely instead of repositioning the king first, violating the 'king before pawn' principle and allowing a blockade or tempo-gaining check. In 3/8 positions (Qxf2, Qxa6, Kb5), the player prioritizes a peripheral material grab or centralizing move while ignoring a more urgent positional demand (maintaining queen activity, neutralizing a threat, or keeping the king on the critical file). In 2/8 positions (Qf7+, Ra1), the player plays a superficially forcing move (pointless check or slow preparation) when an immediate concrete threat was required. All positions share extremely low good-move counts (avg 1.8) indicating critical moments where precision is essential, and the common thread is that the 'obvious' direct action gives the opponent exactly the tempo needed to establish a blockade, reach a drawing fortress, execute a breakthrough, or find a defensive interposition.
analysis.move_pattern: Mixed piece types (pawns, kings, queens, rooks) all executing what appears to be the 'next logical step' in a plan — pawn advances toward promotion, captures of available material, checks, or piece redeployments — but in the wrong move order
analysis.why_bad: Each move gives the opponent a critical free tempo to execute their defensive or counterattacking resource — establishing a blockade (f3, b4), reaching a drawing square (Kb5, Kd7), creating an unstoppable threat (Ra1, Qxa6), interposing with tempo (Qf7+), or launching a central break (Qxf2). The correct moves all involve a less obvious preparatory step that denies the opponent this single saving tempo.
sub_patterns: Premature pawn push in K+P endgame allowing blockade (f3, b4)
Pawn grab/peripheral capture ignoring urgent positional threat (Qxf2, Qxa6)
King move to tactically vulnerable square allowing tempo-gaining response (Kd7, Kb5)
Superficial check or slow maneuver when immediate forcing move exists (Qf7+, Ra1)

analysis.label: Moves that appear constructive but fatally remove a piece/pawn from a critical defensive or initiative-maintaining role, enabling immediate tactical exploitation.
analysis.description: This feature fires on moves where the player relocates a piece or pawn that was performing an essential function (defending a key square, maintaining checking initiative, guarding a pawn, or blocking an infiltration path) in pursuit of an illusory goal. In 5/8 positions, the moved piece was directly defending against a specific threat: f4 removed the f2 pawn guarding the second rank from rook infiltration; Qd6 removed the queen from f4 where it could interpose on g4; Bxb4 removed the dark-squared bishop from defending g7; Kf3 abandoned defense of the f5 pawn. In 3/8 positions, the move surrendered the initiative by playing a non-forcing move when continuous pressure was required: Rg7 attacked a pawn instead of delivering checks in a forced mate; Qe6+ allowed the king to escape to a safe square breaking a checking pattern; a4 played a slow flank move when piece development was urgent. In all 8/8 cases, the opponent immediately exploited the abandoned function with a concrete tactical blow (Rd2+ check, Kxf5 capture, Re8 tempo gain, Rg4+ without interposition, e4 advance enabling fork, Qg4 exploiting g7 weakness).
analysis.move_pattern: Any piece type moving away from a square where it performs a critical defensive or tempo-maintaining function; includes pawns advancing from shield positions, queens retreating from interposition squares, bishops captured off defensive diagonals, kings stepping off pawn-guarding squares, and rooks making non-checking moves in mating positions
analysis.why_bad: The move abandons a critical function (defending a key square, maintaining checking initiative, or guarding material) for a secondary objective (pawn capture, centralization, structural improvement), and the opponent immediately exploits the newly created vulnerability with a forcing tactical sequence that was previously impossible
sub_patterns: Removing own pawn from king shelter (f4 opening second rank)
Queen retreating from critical interposition/defensive square
Capturing material that removes piece from defensive diagonal
Playing non-forcing move when continuous checks deliver mate
King stepping off guard duty of a pawn

analysis.label: Playing a natural-looking or superficially attractive move (development, check, capture, attack) when the position demands one specific tactical or defensive solution.
analysis.description: This feature fires on positions where only 1-2 good moves exist (avg 1.7) and the player defaults to a 'general principles' move instead. In 3/11 positions, the same missed tactic appears: Black should play e5 attacking White's Nd4+Bf4, followed by Qa5+ winning material, but instead plays routine development (d5, Nf6, Be7). In 2/11 positions, a check or attack backfires by driving the opponent's piece to its ideal square or allowing simple capture (Rg2+ drives king to h6; Na7+ allows Rxa7). In 3/11 positions, a piece is moved to an apparently active square but abandons a critical defensive duty (Qh8 leaves king undefended; Qd6 leaves a-pawn hanging; Be6 leaves b7 undefended). In 2/11, aggressive knight sorties waste tempo without concrete threats (Nb3 attacks queen but allows Qc2 targeting g6; Ng4 abandons d4-pawn support). In 1/11, a pawn grab (Qxd4) surrenders decisive initiative against an uncastled king. The average cp_loss of 2065 reflects that these are positions with extremely narrow margins where the 'obvious' move is catastrophically wrong.
analysis.move_pattern: Mixed piece types moving to superficially logical squares (developing, checking, attacking, capturing) - no single geometric pattern; the commonality is choosing a default/routine action over the position's specific demand
analysis.why_bad: The position requires one precise move (tactical strike, quiet defense, or maintaining pressure), but the player defaults to a move that follows general principles rather than the specific tactical demands, squandering a narrow window of opportunity or exposing a fatal weakness
sub_patterns: Missing e5/Qa5+ combination against Nd4+Bf4 alignment (3/11 positions)
Giving checks that drive opponent's piece to its ideal square or allow capture
Knight sorties that waste tempo while abandoning critical pawn support
Queen/bishop moves that abandon defense of key squares or pawns
Material grabs that surrender decisive initiative

analysis.label: Playing a natural-looking quiet or routine move when a concrete forcing opportunity (winning material, delivering checkmate, or essential prophylaxis) demands immediate attention.
analysis.description: This feature fires on positions where the player chose a 'reasonable-looking' move following general principles—development (Bg5, Bd7, Nef6), castling (O-O), structural reinforcement (c3, b3), pawn captures (Qxd5, Qxc7), or king repositioning (Kg6)—while a specific concrete tactical opportunity existed that required immediate exploitation. In 10/10 positions, the correct move was a forcing or precise action: capturing a hanging pawn (Qxb7 in positions 1 and 2), delivering forced checkmate (Rxh6+ in position 13), preventing a tactical shot (d4 blocking Nd4 in position 6), keeping a defensive piece on its critical square (maintaining Nh2 in position 4), exchanging a vulnerable piece first (Bxe2 in position 9), or seizing a concrete pawn break (c5 in position 10, cxb4 in position 15). The average number of good moves was only 1.4, indicating these were narrow critical moments with typically just one correct choice. The catastrophic average cp_loss of 2276 reflects that these 'natural' moves squandered forced wins, allowed defensive consolidation, or exposed fatal tactical vulnerabilities.
analysis.move_pattern: Mixed piece types and directions; characteristically non-forcing moves (quiet pawn pushes, piece development to natural squares, routine captures, castling) rather than checks, forcing captures, or essential prophylactic moves
analysis.why_bad: These moves waste a critical tempo in positions where only one (or very few) concrete forcing moves maintain the advantage; the quiet move allows the opponent to organize defenses, consolidate, create counterplay, or exploit a newly-created tactical vulnerability that the routine move failed to address
sub_patterns: Quiet structural pawn moves instead of winning material (c3, b3 when Qxb7 or d4 was needed)
Routine piece development leaving tactical vulnerabilities unaddressed (Bg5, Bd7, Nef6)
Pawn-grabbing instead of forcing checkmate or winning combination (Qxc7, Qxd5)
General principle moves (O-O, Kg6) when a specific concrete line was required
Moving a critical defensive piece to a 'natural' square (Nf3 abandoning h2 defense)

analysis.label: Playing a natural developing move while ignoring an imminent knight fork that wins major material.
analysis.description: This feature fires when a player makes a routine, positionally-motivated opening move (fianchetto, castling, pawn push, knight development) while completely ignoring a concrete knight fork threat that wins significant material. In 7/7 positions, the punishment involves a knight delivering a devastating fork (Nxc7+ forking king/rook in 3 positions, Nxf7 forking queen/rook in 2 positions, Nd3/Nxd4 forks in 2 positions). The blundering moves are all 'natural' opening moves - e6 (standard pawn development), c5 (central counterstrike), Bg7 (fianchetto), Ne7 (kingside development), Na6 (knight development), O-O (castling), Nbc3 (centralization) - that would be perfectly reasonable in other contexts but catastrophically ignore the immediate tactical crisis. In 5/7 cases the move either fails to address an already-existing fork threat, while in 2/7 cases the move actively enables the fork by removing a defender or blocking an escape square.
analysis.move_pattern: Any piece moved to a natural developing square (not addressing the critical threat square), ignoring an enemy knight's access to a fork square (c7, f7, d3, d4)
analysis.why_bad: The player prioritizes general opening principles (development, castling, fianchetto, central control) over the urgent concrete tactical requirement of preventing a knight fork that wins at minimum an exchange, often more.
sub_patterns: Ignoring Nb5 threatening Nxc7+ fork on king and rook (c7 undefended or vacated)
Ignoring Ng5+Bc4 battery enabling Nxf7 fork on queen and rook
Leaving c2 undefended allowing knight invasion with subsequent fork

analysis.label: Quiet, non-forcing moves that inadvertently remove a piece or pawn from a critical defensive function, enabling the opponent to execute a winning tactical shot.
analysis.description: This feature fires on positions where a player makes a slow, positional-looking move that fatally removes a key defensive element from the position. In 6/6 cases, the move played is non-forcing (no check, no capture, no direct threat) and each one either blocks an escape route, removes a guardian piece, or vacates a critical defensive square/line. Specifically: pawn pushes that block own piece retreat squares (b6 blocking knight's b6 escape, 1/6), pawn pushes that remove protection from key diagonals (b3 exposing rook on a1-h8 diagonal, 1/6), pawn pushes that abandon active pieces needing immediate attention (a4 ignoring the h4 knight, 1/6), pieces moved to tactically vulnerable squares (Ra4 placed on queen's undefended diagonal, 1/6), king moves into fork geometry (Kd8 into Ne6+ range, 1/6), and defenders abandoning their post (Ng4 removing knight from king defense, 1/6). The average cp_loss of 1820 reflects catastrophic consequences, and with only 2.3 good moves available on average, these positions demanded precise calculation rather than slow positional play.
analysis.move_pattern: Non-forcing moves (no check/capture) of various piece types, typically quiet pawn pushes or piece relocations away from defensive duties
analysis.why_bad: Each move removes a piece or pawn from a square/line where it was serving a critical (often hidden) defensive function—blocking a diagonal, providing an escape route, guarding against forks, or defending another piece—allowing the opponent to execute a concrete tactic that was previously prevented by that exact piece placement.
sub_patterns: Pawn blocks own piece retreat square (self-obstruction)
Pawn vacates critical defensive diagonal (unblocking for opponent)
Piece moved to undefended square on opponent's attack line
King walks into knight fork geometry
Defender abandoned for aggressive but refutable sortie

analysis.label: Natural-looking developing moves played while the player's own piece is critically vulnerable to capture or trapping.
analysis.description: In all 3/3 positions, the player makes a quiet, structurally appealing move (bishop development, central pawn reinforcement, or bishop diagonal preparation) while ignoring an urgent tactical vulnerability of their own piece. In 2/3 cases (e6, e3), the pawn advance specifically blocks the retreat path of the player's own vulnerable piece—e6 blocks the Bg4's retreat along the c8-h3 diagonal, and e3 blocks the Qc3's escape to e3. In 1/3 cases (Bg4), the player simply ignores a directly attacked piece (Bb4 after a3) to make an unrelated development move. The moves all appear natural and principled in isolation—pinning a knight, reinforcing the center, opening a bishop diagonal—but catastrophically fail to address the most urgent demand of the position: saving an endangered piece. Average cp_loss of 372 confirms these are severe blunders, not subtle inaccuracies.
analysis.move_pattern: Quiet non-forcing moves (pawn pushes to 3rd/6th rank, or bishop development) that do not address an existing threat to the player's own piece
analysis.why_bad: The moves ignore an immediate tactical emergency (a hanging or soon-to-be-trapped piece), and in most cases actively worsen the situation by blocking the endangered piece's retreat square, allowing the opponent to win material with simple tactics.
sub_patterns: Pawn advance blocks own piece retreat (e3/e6 self-obstruction)
Developing move ignores piece under direct attack
Natural-looking move in position requiring urgent tactical response

analysis.label: Playing a non-forcing repositioning move while ignoring that a piece is or becomes undefended, allowing a simple one-move capture.
analysis.description: In all 5/5 positions, the player makes a quiet, seemingly purposeful move (king tuck, bishop reposition, knight centralization, rook activation) while completely overlooking that a piece is left en prise to a trivial one-move capture. In Position 1, Kh1 wastes tempo while Bd2 hangs to Qxd2. In Position 2, Bb5 places the bishop on an undefended square capturable by Qxb5. In Position 4, Nc4 allows Bxc4 which removes the defender of the hanging Bg5. In Position 6, Bf3 places the bishop where Qxf3 wins it immediately. In Position 12, Rc8 ignores the undefended Ba2, allowing Qxa2. The average cp_loss of 386 reflects roughly a full piece being lost each time. All refutations are simple captures requiring no deep calculation—just awareness that a piece lacks defenders.
analysis.move_pattern: Quiet non-forcing piece move (any piece type, any direction, no check or capture) while another piece on the board is undefended
analysis.why_bad: The player pursues a secondary objective (king safety, piece centralization, file activation) while failing to notice the most urgent tactical issue in the position: a piece that is or becomes capturable in one move with no adequate compensation.
sub_patterns: Moving a piece to an undefended square directly capturable by opponent queen
Making a purposeless tempo move while an existing piece hangs elsewhere
Exchanging or removing a key defender, leaving another piece unprotected

analysis.label: Giving a check (usually on the wrong square) that dissipates a winning advantage by misplacing the attacker's piece or allowing the opponent's king to escape.
analysis.description: This feature fires on positions where the player holds a significant advantage and delivers a forcing move—almost always a check (7/9 positions)—that squanders the winning potential. The dominant sub-pattern is choosing the WRONG check square: Qf8+ instead of Qe8+ (2/9), Qa6+ instead of Qa8+ (1/9), Qe6+ instead of Qe8+ first (1/9), Rc6+ instead of Re7+ (1/9). In each case, a cosmetically similar check exists on an adjacent square that would enable devastating follow-ups (knight forks, mating pivots like Qc6, discovered attacks), but the chosen square strands the piece far from the action. Secondary sub-patterns include abandoning a dominant piece position for a pointless check (Qg4+ leaving h5, Nb2+ leaving c4: 2/9) and offering premature simplification when a mating attack exists (Qe4 instead of Qe1: 1/9). The average cp_loss of 1227 reflects how these moves convert clearly winning positions into draws or much reduced advantages. In all cases, the opponent's best punishment involves the king calmly stepping to a safe square that the correct move would have denied.
analysis.move_pattern: Queen (or piece) delivers check on wrong/suboptimal square, typically one file or rank away from the correct check square; overwhelmingly checks (+) with queen moves dominating (6/9)
analysis.why_bad: The check misplaces the attacking piece on a square with no powerful follow-up, while allowing the opponent's king to reach a safe square that the correct check would have denied—effectively wasting a tempo and dismantling the coordination needed for the tactical payoff (fork, mate threat, or discovered attack).
sub_patterns: Wrong check square: adjacent square enables devastating follow-up (Qf8+ vs Qe8+, Qa6+ vs Qa8+)
Pointless check abandoning dominant outpost (Qg4+ from h5, Nb2+ from c4, Rc6+ instead of Re7+)
Move-order inaccuracy: correct check must come first to deny escape square
Premature simplification when forced mate exists on the board

analysis.label: In closed-center positions facing an urgent flank attack, the player makes a move that fails to address the opponent's most threatening plan—either by playing on the wrong side, withdrawing a key defender, or inadvertently helping open lines for the attacker.
analysis.description: All 5/5 positions share a closed or locked center where the critical battle is on one flank, with the opponent already possessing a dangerous pawn storm or space advantage on that flank. In each case, the best moves directly confront the opponent's most urgent threat (e.g., capturing the threatening pawn like hxg5 or fxg5, placing a piece on a defensive square like Nf5, or prophylactically containing the pressure like a3). Instead, the played move either pursues irrelevant activity on the wrong side (Position 1: g5 ignoring queenside crisis), misplaces a piece away from the critical flank (Position 2: Nd5 instead of Nf5 for kingside defense; Position 5: Nd7 abandoning f6's kingside coverage), or actively assists the opponent's attack by opening lines (Position 6: a4 opening the a-file for Black's pieces; Position 12: h6 inviting gxh6 to rip open the king's shelter). The average cp_loss of 206 reflects how punishing these errors are in closed positions where tempo and piece placement on the critical flank are decisive.
analysis.move_pattern: Various piece types (pawns, knights) moving away from the critical flank or pushing into the opponent's pawn chain in a way that creates favorable captures/line-openings for the attacker
analysis.why_bad: In closed-center positions, the flank battle is everything—these moves either abandon the critical defensive sector, create weaknesses that the opponent's already-prepared pieces exploit immediately, or waste tempo on irrelevant plans while the opponent's attack plays itself
sub_patterns: Pawn push colliding with opponent's storm, helping open attacking files (g5, h6)
Knight retreating/centralizing away from the flank needing defense (Nd5, Nd7)
Pawn advance opening lines where opponent's pieces are already optimally placed (a4)

analysis.label: Active-looking moves that ignore critical king safety or defensive needs, allowing immediate tactical exploitation of the already-vulnerable king.
analysis.description: This feature fires on positions where the player's king is already vulnerable or under pressure, and instead of addressing that vulnerability, the player makes an 'ambitious' or 'improving' move that either exposes the king further or removes a critical defender. In 6/8 positions, the king was explicitly exposed or uncastled; in nearly all cases, the best moves involved prophylactic king evacuation (Kf1/Kh1/Kh2 in positions 1, 10, 11), maintaining key defenders (Rf2 in position 1, Qc3 in position 10), or continuing an already-safe plan (Ka5 in position 3). Instead, the played moves pursued centralization (Ne4, Nd6), file control (Rd1), counterplay (Qb5, Qg5), pawn challenges (f3), or 'active' king moves (Kf2, O-O-O) that looked positionally desirable but catastrophically ignored the tactical reality. The refutations consistently exploited the newly-created vulnerability with checks (Rb8+, Bc4+, Qxf4+), forks (Nf3+, Nxd3+), or material capture of abandoned pieces/pawns (Qxb2, Bxd5, Qxf7+/Bc7#).
analysis.move_pattern: Various piece types making 'improving' moves (centralization, file occupation, attacking repositions) that ignore the king's existing tactical vulnerability on exposed squares or diagonals
analysis.why_bad: The moves prioritize positional goals (outposts, open files, pawn challenges, counterplay) over the critical defensive requirement of the position—typically king safety—allowing the opponent to immediately exploit the abandoned defensive function with forcing moves (checks, forks, captures of undefended material)
sub_patterns: King walks into tactical shots (Kf2, O-O-O entering knight fork range)
Key defender relocated from defensive duty (Nd6 leaving king exposed to check, Ne4 abandoning d5 pawn, Qg5 abandoning f7 defense)
Pawn move weakening king shelter under attack (f3 opening lines toward own king)
Queen displacement from critical defensive post to peripheral target (Qb5 leaving b2 hanging)
Rook development ignoring existing diagonal/check vulnerability (Rd1 allowing Bc4+)

analysis.label: Moving a well-placed piece (usually a knight) away from its optimal square to pursue a tempting but inferior target, forfeiting a superior tactical continuation.
analysis.description: In 6/8 positions, a knight is moved from a square where it was performing a crucial function—supporting a mating attack (Nxe5 leaving f3 where Nxg5 was forced mate), maintaining a stranglehold on the enemy king (Nexc2 abandoning e3), defending key squares (Nc3 leaving kingside unguarded), or enabling a critical combination (Ne2 instead of Nd5). The remaining cases follow the same logic: a rook gives a purposeless check (Rc6+) instead of the setup move Re7+ for a fork, and a bishop goes to an undefended square (Ba6) where it's immediately forked. In all 8/8 cases, the piece leaves its post to pursue something visually attractive—a pawn capture, a check, or an attack on a higher-value piece—but this self-deflection removes the piece from where it was essential for the position's primary tactical or strategic demand.
analysis.move_pattern: Piece (predominantly knight) moves away from a central or functionally critical square to capture a pawn, give check, or attack an enemy piece on a peripheral square
analysis.why_bad: The piece was performing an irreplaceable function on its current square (enabling a combination, controlling escape routes, maintaining attack coordination), and its departure grants the opponent time to reorganize defenses, escape mating nets, promote pawns, or launch counterplay that the piece's presence previously prevented.
sub_patterns: Knight captures meaningless pawn while abandoning attacking/blocking post (Nexc2, Nxe5)
Knight/piece attacks enemy rook or gives check but loses key square control (Nc3, Ng3, Rc6+)
Piece retreats passively when only an active centralizing move maintained the advantage (Ne2 instead of Nd5)
Piece moves to undefended square creating immediate tactical vulnerability (Ba6, Nf4)

analysis.label: Black plays a non-urgent piece-harassing or repositioning move that wastes a critical tempo, allowing White to execute a devastating tactical combination.
analysis.description: This feature fires when Black plays a slow, non-forcing move—typically chasing or harassing an opponent's piece—instead of addressing an urgent tactical need in the position. In 4/6 positions, the move directly targets an opponent's piece (h6 chasing Ng5, h6 chasing Bg5, a6 chasing Bb5, Na7 attacking Qb5), while the remaining moves (Rf6, Qb7) are premature repositioning moves that also waste a critical tempo. In all 6/6 cases, the opponent exploits the wasted tempo with a devastating tactical blow—typically involving king safety exploitation (5/6 positions feature exposed or uncastled kings) through forks, discovered attacks, or mating combinations. The correct moves in each case involve concrete, forcing responses: capturing attacking pieces (fxg5), developing urgently (Nd7, Nc6), resolving critical pawn tension (bxc5), or maintaining defensive coordination (g5, Nd8). The common thread is that Black sees a 'natural' move that seemingly gains time against an opponent's piece but fails to recognize that the opponent's piece doesn't need to stay where it is—the real threat is a tactical combination that the lost tempo now enables.
analysis.move_pattern: Non-capturing, non-checking quiet moves—often pawns to h6/a6 or pieces to rim squares (Na7)—that target an opponent's piece without addressing the critical tactical situation
analysis.why_bad: The moves waste a critical tempo on a non-urgent piece-harassment when the position demands immediate concrete action; the opponent's piece being 'chased' either doesn't need to retreat (it has a stronger square to go to) or the extra tempo allows execution of a devastating combination exploiting existing vulnerabilities (uncastled king, open files, undefended pieces)
sub_patterns: h-pawn push chasing kingside piece (Ng5/Bg5) while king is unsafe
a-pawn push chasing queenside piece (Bb5) while ignoring central pawn break
Knight retreat to rim square abandoning defensive duties
Premature piece repositioning without supporting coordination

analysis.label: Superficially active or aggressive moves that catastrophically ignore the position's critical tactical or defensive requirement.
analysis.description: This feature fires on moves that look purposeful—attacks, checks, development, captures—but fundamentally miss the position's defining demand. In 8/10 positions, the player chose a 'natural' active move (usually a piece deployment to an aggressive-looking square) while only ~1.6 good alternatives existed on average. The pattern manifests as: queens moving to active squares while leaving pawns/king undefended (Qa2, Qf6, Qa4, Qc3 in 6/10 cases); knights jumping to aggressive targets while abandoning dominant outposts (Nf7 leaving e5, Nb4 leaving d5 in 2/10); or captures/moves that open critical lines against one's own king (fxe5 opening the f-file, R4f2 choosing passive defense over active counterplay). In every case, the position demanded a specific response—a winning combination (Ne4 discovered attack), a prophylactic move (g5 preventing a breakthrough), a critical pawn break (e4), or maintaining a piece's dominance—and the player instead pursued a secondary objective that the position didn't support.
analysis.move_pattern: Piece (predominantly queen, also knight/rook) moves to a seemingly active or aggressive square, or a capture that appears purposeful; the destination looks logical in isolation but misaddresses the position's actual priority
analysis.why_bad: The moved piece becomes misplaced relative to the position's critical battle—either too far from defensive duties, abandoning a dominant station, or opening lines that benefit the opponent. The move addresses a secondary concern while the position has one urgent requirement (a winning tactic, a defensive necessity, or maintaining a key structural advantage) that goes unmet.
sub_patterns: Queen sorties to distant/active squares that neglect king safety or pawn defense (Qa2, Qa4, Qf6, Qc3)
Knight jumps to aggressive-looking squares abandoning superior centralized outposts (Nf7 from e5, Nb4 from d5)
Captures or pawn moves that fatally open lines against one's own king (fxe5 opening f-file)
Checks that drive the opponent's king toward safety rather than keeping it exposed (Qc3+ allowing Kd7-c8)
Passive defensive moves when active counterplay was the only way to survive (R4f2 instead of Qd4)

analysis.label: Playing a superficially natural or improving move that ignores the position's most critical concrete demand, wasting a decisive tempo.
analysis.description: This feature fires on moves that look plausible or 'improving' but fail to address the position's most urgent requirement, squandering a critical tempo. In 4/11 cases, the blunder is a non-urgent pawn push (b5, h5, c5, h5) when piece activity or forcing moves were required. In 5/11 cases, a piece is repositioned to a seemingly active square (Qc7, Qa7, Ra7, Nc3, Qd7) that either abandons a critical defensive duty, creates a tactical vulnerability, or simply doesn't address the real threat. In 2/11 cases, a capture or development (Bxc5, Bc4) targets a secondary concern while ignoring the primary tactical demand. The common thread is that the position demanded immediate concrete action—whether a forcing winning sequence (Kd7 in pos 4, b4 in pos 2, Re1 in pos 5), removal of a tactical threat (cxb4 in pos 8), or urgent defensive repositioning (Qg8 in pos 7, Qd6 in pos 11-12). Instead, the player chose a move that appears constructive but gives the opponent one free tempo to execute their plan, whether that's capturing a critical pawn (6/11), launching a tactical combination (3/11), or advancing a passed pawn (2/11).
analysis.move_pattern: Any piece type; typically non-forcing (no check, no immediate threat); often a one-square pawn advance or a piece sliding to a 'natural' square away from the critical sector
analysis.why_bad: The position is at a critical inflection point requiring immediate concrete action (forcing move, defensive priority, or tactical execution), and the tempo wasted on a non-urgent 'improving' move allows the opponent to execute their winning plan—capturing an undefended pawn, launching a tactical combination, advancing a passed pawn, or neutralizing the player's advantage.
sub_patterns: Non-urgent pawn pushes when piece activation is critical (b5, h5, c5)
Piece repositioning that abandons a defensive duty (Qc7 leaving b4, Ra7 leaving c1)
Natural-looking development that ignores an immediate tactical threat (Bxc5 ignoring Nc2+, Bc4 ignoring cxd4/Qc5)
Queen moves to plausible squares that create geometric vulnerabilities (Qa7 allowing skewer, Qd7 removing e7 block)

analysis.label: Black plays a preparatory king move in the endgame instead of immediately advancing a passed pawn or playing a forcing move, wasting a critical tempo.
analysis.description: In 5/6 positions, Black plays a king move (Kf4, Ke4, Kg4, Kg4, Kd3) when the optimal move was an immediate pawn advance (f4, h5, g5, g4, a4) or a forcing piece move (Nb8, Bb8, Ra1+). The 6th position (h5) follows the same logic in reverse: a slow pawn move instead of a forcing rook check. In all cases, the player's move appears to 'prepare' the winning plan by improving king position, but the concrete action was already available and more efficient. The analyses unanimously identify 'tempo_loss' as the tactical motif (6/6 positions), with the king move either requiring the king to return to its original square (positions 8, 9: Kg4 then ...Kf5/Kf4), or simply granting the opponent a free tempo to activate their own king or advance counterplay (positions 1, 5, 10, 12). The average cp_loss is moderate (44cp) because these positions are typically very winning/losing, making the tempo waste non-fatal but technically imprecise.
analysis.move_pattern: King moves one square forward/sideways (usually toward a passed pawn) in endgame positions where the king's current square was already adequate
analysis.why_bad: The king move wastes a tempo that the opponent uses to activate their own king or advance counterplay; the immediate pawn push or forcing move would have created concrete threats one tempo sooner, often making the difference between a clean conversion and giving the opponent unnecessary counterplay.
sub_patterns: King approaches own passed pawn instead of pushing it immediately
King moves to escort square when pawn can self-advance
Preparatory move when forcing move available

analysis.label: Moving a well-placed piece away from its essential positional or defensive function, lured by captures, checks, or seemingly more active squares.
analysis.description: This feature fires on moves where a piece voluntarily leaves a square where it performs an irreplaceable function—blockading, guarding key diagonals, maintaining mating nets, or restraining passed pawns—to pursue superficially attractive continuations. In 4/8 cases, knights leave dominant outposts or critical coordination squares (Nxf7 abandons d6 dominance, Nxg5 unblocks a deadly diagonal, Nf7+ trades away the piece enabling perpetual, Nf4+ dismantles a mating net). In 3/8 cases, kings or queens move away from essential posts (Qc7 abandons b4's defense, Kc7 abandons blockade for material, Kf3 retreats when Kg5 wins). In 1/8 cases a rook abandons a critical file (Rg8 leaves h-file pressure). The common thread: the moved piece was the linchpin of the position's evaluation, and its departure—however attractive the destination—collapses the entire positional or tactical foundation. The extremely high average cp_loss (1542) and narrow average good moves (1.5) confirm these are positions where the correct piece placement is uniquely important.
analysis.move_pattern: Any piece (most often knight: 4/8) moves away from its current ideal square, frequently via capture or check, to a square that appears more active or materially rewarding
analysis.why_bad: The piece being moved was performing a critical, often invisible function (blocking a diagonal, maintaining a blockade, covering escape squares, enabling perpetual). Its departure allows the opponent to exploit the newly created weakness—whether through counterattack on the exposed king, winning back material, activating pieces, or advancing passed pawns unchallenged.
sub_patterns: Knight captures pawn but abandons dominant outpost (Nxf7, Nxg5)
Knight gives check/fork when staying put was essential for attack or defense (Nf7+, Nf4+)
King moves wrong direction abandoning blockade or advancing position (Kc7, Kf3)
Queen/Rook repositions to seemingly better square while losing critical coverage (Qc7, Rg8)

analysis.label: King (or key defender) moves to an apparently safe but actually vulnerable square, abandoning a critical tactical or defensive function.
analysis.description: In 5/5 positions, the player chose a move that prioritized apparent shelter over necessary activity. In 4/5 cases this was a direct king move (Ka1 to corner, Kf6 away from critical d-file, Kd7 backward instead of Kd6, Kg1 to back rank), while in 1/5 (Rxb6) the rook abandoned king defense to grab material. The common thread is that the correct move in each case was counterintuitive—keeping the king more central (Kc2, Ke3), maintaining tactical proximity (Ke8 staying adjacent to enemy rook), or blocking a critical square (Kd6 controlling d5). The blunder square looked safer (corner, back rank, retreated) but actually exposed the king to diagonal checks (3/5), back-rank mates (2/5), or allowed opponent's pieces to seize critical squares (3/5). Average cp_loss of ~3992 reflects positions with very narrow correct choices (avg 1.6 good moves).
analysis.move_pattern: King moves toward corner/edge/back rank (retreating or passive direction), or defensive piece moves away from king protection duty
analysis.why_bad: Abandons a critical tactical function (square control, indirect piece defense, back-rank coverage) in exchange for illusory shelter, allowing opponent to exploit the newly unguarded squares or lines with checks, pins, or mating attacks
sub_patterns: King retreats to corner allowing rook/bishop checks on open files/diagonals
King moves away from piece it was indirectly defending
King retreats one rank losing control of critical blocking square
Defensive piece captures distant pawn abandoning back-rank duty

analysis.label: Quiet minor piece development moves in positions demanding immediate concrete action, where the placed piece becomes a target for tempo-gaining attacks.
analysis.description: In all 3/3 positions, the player makes a natural-looking minor piece development move (bishop or knight to a standard square) while ignoring an urgent tactical requirement in the position. Each position features an uncastled king (3/3) and volatile central tension demanding concrete resolution. In Position 8, Bg4 is a bishop repositioning that gets punished by f3 driving it back with tempo loss. In Position 14, Bd2 is a 'connecting' bishop move that fatally blocks the queen's retreat square, enabling a knight fork. In Position 15, Nf3 is a textbook knight development that walks directly into Black's advanced g-pawn attacking it with g4. All three moves share the characteristic of looking like reasonable developing moves but failing to address the position's concrete demands—queen infiltration via an open file, prophylaxis against tactical forks, or resolving central tension before piece placement.
analysis.move_pattern: Minor piece (bishop or knight) developed to a natural-looking square (g4, d2, f3) in the opening or early middlegame
analysis.why_bad: The piece is placed on a square where it immediately becomes a target for a tempo-gaining pawn advance or tactical blow, while the position's urgent concrete requirements (exploiting open files, resolving central tension, avoiding forks) are ignored entirely
sub_patterns: Bishop developed to square vulnerable to pawn thrust (Bg4 met by f3)
Bishop developed to square blocking critical queen retreat (Bd2 enabling fork)
Knight developed to square attacked by advanced enemy pawn (Nf3 met by g4)

analysis.label: Active-looking or improving moves that ignore an immediate tactical vulnerability or urgent positional priority in the position.
analysis.description: This feature fires on moves where the player pursues a seemingly reasonable plan—activating a piece, launching an attack, or following general principles—while the position demands specific concrete action to address a critical vulnerability. In 7/9 positions, the move wastes a critical tempo (tagged tempo_loss); in 7/9 positions, the player misses a tactic that was available or that the opponent can now execute. The moves look varied superficially (Qf3, Ba4, g3, Bxf6, Rf6, Qh6, O-O, Qg3, Rhg1) but share the pattern of being 'luxury' moves in positions of urgency: Position 1 needed exd5 to eliminate a dominant knight; Position 2 needed d4/Bf4 development instead of exposing the bishop; Position 5 needed to maintain piece tension; Position 6 needed to resolve the e5 knight before committing the rook; Position 9 needed the concrete Bxg6 sacrifice; Position 12 needed Re3 to defend the back rank; Position 13 needed immediate bishop retreat to avoid being trapped. In 8/9 cases, the punishment exploits the specific weakness the move left unaddressed.
analysis.move_pattern: Any piece type moving to an ostensibly active or improving square while a concrete defensive/tactical priority goes unaddressed; no single geometric direction dominates
analysis.why_bad: The position requires immediate concrete action (resolving central tension, retreating a vulnerable piece, defending a critical square, or finding a tactical counter-blow), but the player makes a 'general improvement' move that gives the opponent time to exploit the unaddressed vulnerability—resulting in trapped pieces, back-rank mates, forks, or devastating counterattacks.
sub_patterns: Speculative attacking queen moves abandoning defensive duties (Qf3, Qh6, Qg3)
Piece moves to exposed/irrelevant squares while critical piece needs retreating (Ba4, Rhg1)
Premature exchanges or commitments that release the tension sustaining one's advantage (Bxf6, Rf6)
Routine moves (O-O, g3) played on autopilot in positions demanding specific concrete action

analysis.label: Quiet, non-forcing piece moves that waste a critical tempo in positions demanding immediate concrete action.
analysis.description: This feature fires on positions where the player makes a slow, non-threatening repositioning move (no check, no capture, no direct threat) when the position urgently requires a forcing continuation. In 8/8 positions, the blunder is a quiet piece relocation that either abandons a critical function (Ra1 leaves e5 undefended, Qb6 abandons the a5-e1 diagonal, Nc3 ignores a free capture) or walks into a tactical vulnerability (Bh5 into a knight fork, Qh4 into Nf5 attack, Kg3 into Ra3+ check). The common refutation exploits the gifted tempo: the opponent either executes a tactical combination that was previously impossible (6/8 positions), or repositions to a dominant square unopposed (Rd8 allowing ...Rh5, Rg6 allowing ...g4). All moves share the characteristic of appearing positionally logical (centralizing, defending, activating) while ignoring that the position's concrete demands make such luxury moves catastrophic. The average 330cp loss reflects how severely one wasted tempo compounds in sharp or critical positions.
analysis.move_pattern: Non-capturing, non-checking piece relocation to a seemingly improved square; includes knight/queen/rook/bishop/king repositioning moves with no immediate threat
analysis.why_bad: The position demands an immediate forcing move (capture, check, or direct threat), but the player makes a slow developmental/repositioning move that either abandons a critical defensive or offensive function, or places the piece on a tactically vulnerable square, giving the opponent a free tempo to seize the initiative or execute a winning combination.
sub_patterns: Piece moves away from critical defensive post (Ra1 abandoning e5, Nc3 ignoring capture)
Piece moves to a square vulnerable to fork or check (Bh5 into Nf4+, Qh4 into Nf5, Kg3 into Ra3+)
Queen repositioning that abandons a key attacking diagonal or line (Qb6 leaving a5-e1 diagonal)
Rook move that creates no threat when checks/tempo-gaining moves are available (Rd8, Rg6)

analysis.label: Moves that fail to challenge or neutralize a powerfully centralized opponent knight, instead pursuing secondary plans that create new weaknesses.
analysis.description: In 12/12 positions, the opponent possesses a dominant centralized knight (on e4, e5, c4, d3, or d4) that anchors their positional/tactical advantage. The best moves consistently involve directly confronting this knight—usually by bringing one's own knight to challenge it (Nd7 vs Ne5 in positions 1,4,6; Nc3 vs Ne4 in positions 2,8; Nd2 vs Nc4 in position 9; Ne2 vs Nd4 in position 10) or exchanging it (Bxe5 in position 12). Instead, the played moves pursue secondary objectives—bishop repositioning (Bf6, Bc1, Bd5, Bf5, Bc2), pawn advances (f4, g6, e4, g4, h4), queen excursions (Qa5), or knight moves to the rim (Nh4)—that ignore the critical centralized piece. These secondary moves typically create a new tactical vulnerability (weakened king cover, hanging pieces, abandoned defensive duties) that the opponent exploits precisely because the dominant knight remains unchallenged, amplifying its influence in the resulting tactics.
analysis.move_pattern: Diverse piece types and directions (bishop retreats/advances, pawn pushes, queen sidesteps, knight to rim), but uniformly NOT directed at challenging the opponent's centralized knight
analysis.why_bad: The dominant centralized knight is the engine of the opponent's advantage; by leaving it unchallenged, the player allows it to support devastating tactical combinations while their secondary move typically creates a new weakness (abandoned defense, hanging piece, weakened king) that the still-dominant knight helps exploit
sub_patterns: Bishop repositioning that abandons a defensive duty (Bf6, Bc1, Bd5, Bf5, Bc2)
Pawn advances that weaken structure while ignoring the knight (f4, g4, h4, e4, g6)
Queen displacement away from where defense is needed (Qa5)
Knight move to rim instead of central action (Nh4)

analysis.label: Playing a generic principled move (capture, develop, castle, activate) when the position demands immediate specific tactical action.
analysis.description: In all 4/4 positions, the player chose a move that appears sensible by general chess principles—a pawn exchange (exf6), bishop development (Bc5), castling (O-O), or rook activation (Rc6)—but catastrophically ignores an urgent tactical demand. In 3/4 positions, the critical tactical element involves the f7 square or f-pawn: Position 1 missed Nxg5 threatening f7, Position 2 allowed f7+ with a queen fork, Position 3 missed Nxf7 winning material from a fork, and Position 4 allowed f3 creating an unstoppable mating net. The average cp_loss of 2600 reflects that these autopilot decisions occur in positions with extremely sharp tactical requirements (avg 1.8 good moves available), where one specific action is demanded. In each case, the player's move would be perfectly reasonable in a quieter position but represents a fundamental failure to recognize that the position has crossed a threshold into tactical emergency.
analysis.move_pattern: Various piece types making generic positional moves (pawn captures, bishop development, castling, rook to open file) rather than concrete tactical strikes
analysis.why_bad: The position demands immediate tactical exploitation or critical defensive maintenance, but the player defaults to routine strategic moves, giving the opponent time to neutralize threats or advance winning plans—particularly around the vulnerable f7 square and exposed kings.
sub_patterns: Routine pawn exchange when a piece sacrifice exploits king weaknesses
Developing a piece to an undefended square while ignoring an advanced passer threat
Castling when a fork/capture wins immediate material
Moving a defensive piece away from its critical post allowing a mating attack

analysis.label: Piece moves that vacate or fail to establish control over a critical square, allowing the opponent to immediately invade or exploit the undefended point.
analysis.description: This feature fires on moves that look purposeful (developing, centralizing, or attacking) but fatally abandon control over a key square or line. In 5/7 positions, the moved piece was directly guarding the critical square: Ne2 removed the knight from f4 allowing Ng4 invasion; Bh6 released the pin on g5 enabling Nxe4; f4 abandoned pawn control of e5 allowing Ne5; Nfd5 vacated f4 opening the a7-g1 diagonal for Bc5+; Qb6 moved the queen away from e3 where it restrained the passed e-pawn. In 2/7 positions, the player chose development that ignored the critical square: Nc6 failed to cover f6 (allowing Qf6 winning the rook) and Nh3 failed to address the h4-e1 diagonal (allowing Bh4/Bxf2+ winning the queen). The common thread across all positions is that each move creates or leaves an undefended critical square that the opponent can immediately exploit with a forcing move (check, capture, or invasion), resulting in catastrophic material or positional losses averaging 453cp.
analysis.move_pattern: Piece (often knight: 4/7) relocated away from a square where it performed a critical defensive function - either guarding a key square, maintaining a pin, or blocking a dangerous line
analysis.why_bad: The piece being moved was performing a hidden but essential defensive function (guarding a square, maintaining a pin, blocking a diagonal/file, or restraining a passed pawn), and its removal allows an immediate tactical exploitation of the now-undefended point
sub_patterns: Knight retreating from outpost that controlled key invasion square (Ne2, Nfd5)
Bishop/Queen abandoning pin or restraining duty (Bh6, Qb6)
Pawn advance surrendering control of critical square (f4 giving up e5)
Development move ignoring urgent need to cover weak square (Nc6, Nh3)

analysis.label: Moving a piece (usually knight) to e6 or a similar seemingly active square while ignoring critical tactical threats or abandoning a superior position.
analysis.description: In 3/4 positions the move is specifically to e6 (Rxe6, Ne6, Ne6), while the fourth (Ng3) shares the same conceptual error. In all cases, the player moves a piece to what appears to be a strong, active central square—capturing a pawn (Position 5), centralizing a knight (Positions 7, 11), or attacking a rook (Position 9)—but the piece was better placed before or there were far more urgent needs. In 3/4 cases the piece becomes a tactical target on its new square (exposed on the a2-g8 diagonal in Position 7, subject to counterattack in Position 5, irrelevant in Positions 9 and 11). In 4/4 cases the move ignores existential threats: a stronger winning combination (Position 5), mating attacks on the player's own king (Position 11), imminent pawn promotions (Position 9), or abandons a dominant outpost that was winning the game (Position 7).
analysis.move_pattern: Knight (3/4) or rook (1/4) moving to e6 (3/4) or similar central/attacking square, typically a forward jump that appears to gain activity or material
analysis.why_bad: The piece abandons a critical function (defense, outpost dominance, or threat prevention) for a superficially attractive square where it becomes tactically vulnerable, irrelevant to the real fight, or allows the opponent's concrete threats to become unstoppable
sub_patterns: Knight abandoning dominant outpost (f4/e4) for exposed e6/g3
Rook capture on e6 grabbing material but becoming a target
Counterattacking move that ignores mating threats against own king
Piece relocation that allows opponent's passed pawns to promote

analysis.label: Natural-looking moves (centralizing, capturing, developing) that ignore the position's most critical concrete tactical demand, creating or allowing devastating vulnerabilities.
analysis.description: This feature fires on moves that appear reasonable based on general chess principles but catastrophically miss the specific tactical or strategic urgency of the position. In 4/7 cases, queen moves to 'natural' squares (Qe2, Qc6, Qe7, plus Qf8 being the only saving move missed via Kg7) either block own development, unguard critical pieces, or expose the piece/king to tactical exploitation. In 2/7 cases, premature piece centralization (Ne5, Ke4) ignores forced tactical sequences or pawn race urgency. In 1/7 cases (hxg4), a routine peripheral capture misses a far more decisive tactical blow. The common thread is choosing a 'second-order improvement' — centralization, development, material grab — when the position demands one specific concrete action. All positions had at least 1-3 clearly superior alternatives (avg 2.3 good moves), indicating the positions weren't impossibly difficult but required reading the tactical pulse correctly.
analysis.move_pattern: Piece moved to a seemingly natural/active square (centralization, development, simple capture) rather than addressing the position's concrete tactical demand
analysis.why_bad: The moves create or fail to prevent a specific tactical vulnerability — forks exploiting unguarded pieces (3/7), tempo-gaining attacks on exposed kings/queens (3/7), or missed pawn promotion races (1/7) — because the player defaults to general positional reasoning instead of calculating the concrete consequences of their move and alternatives.
sub_patterns: Queen moved to square that unguards a piece or self-targets on a file
Piece centralized prematurely allowing forced exchanges into fork/pin
Peripheral/routine capture when a decisive tactical blow exists
King moved to exposed square enabling rook lifts or discovered attacks

analysis.label: Non-forcing piece repositioning to an aesthetically pleasing square when the position demands immediate concrete action (capture, pawn advance, or forcing placement).
analysis.description: In all 7 positions, the player moved a piece to a square that appears active or purposeful but creates no immediate concrete threat, when the position critically demanded a forcing move. In 6/7 cases, 'tempo_loss' is explicitly identified as the key failing. The best moves were always forcing: a material-winning capture (Nxe1 in Position 1), a rook placed behind a passed pawn (Ra1/Rd1 in Position 9), an exchange-forcing rook move (Rd8 in Position 10), a pawn advance creating unstoppable threats (b4 in Position 12), or a queen placement with multiple concrete threats (Qd4 in Position 13). Instead, the played moves were quiet repositioning (queen to c4/d2, rook to f1/b4/e8, bishop to c4, knight to e4) that gave the opponent a free tempo to either execute a tactical counter-blow (Nxf5 sacrifice, Bxb2+ back-rank attack, Nh5 kingside assault) or resolve their defensive problems (dissolving the center with ...e6, generating counterplay with ...h4). The average number of good moves available was only 1.9, confirming these are critical-moment positions where the tempo spent on non-forcing play was irretrievable.
analysis.move_pattern: Any piece type moved to an open/central/active-looking square without delivering check, capture, or concrete tactical threat; typically one square of displacement from the optimal forcing square or direction
analysis.why_bad: The positions all contained a narrow tactical window requiring immediate forcing action; the slow repositioning move surrendered a critical tempo, allowing the opponent to execute counterplay (kingside attacks, back-rank threats, pawn advances, center dissolution) that was previously impossible or ineffective.
sub_patterns: Queen repositioned to attacking square instead of capturing hanging material
Rook moved to active file while abandoning critical defensive/supporting duty
Piece centralized to strong-looking square that is tactically refutable
Bishop/Queen relocated when a pawn advance creates unstoppable threats
Natural developing move instead of specific forcing placement with multiple threats

analysis.label: Playing a non-urgent or secondary move when the position demands immediate concrete action, wasting a critical tempo.
analysis.description: This feature fires on moves that ignore the single most urgent demand of the position in favor of something slower or less relevant. In 5/8 positions, the tactical motif is explicitly 'tempo_loss.' The pattern manifests as: slow preparatory pawn moves ignoring central tension (g6, a6 in positions 2 and 8), king moves that waste time in pawn races instead of pushing passers (Ke3, Ka4 in positions 1 and 4), removing a key defensive piece for 'active' play (Ne4 in position 3 abandons d7 guard), move-order errors that release an opponent's trapped piece (dxc5 in position 7 gives the b4-bishop escape to c5), greedy captures that ignore king safety threats (Qxd5 in position 6 allows recapture with check), and king centralization into a mating net instead of fleeing (Ke4 in position 7). In every case, one specific action was critically time-sensitive - whether pushing a passed pawn, resolving central tension, maintaining a guard, or executing captures in the right order - and the player chose something else that looked reasonable in isolation but catastrophically failed given the position's concrete demands.
analysis.move_pattern: Any piece type or direction; moves are geometrically diverse (king moves, pawn pushes, knight jumps, captures) but share the trait of being non-forcing or addressing a secondary concern
analysis.why_bad: The position has one urgent concrete demand (pawn race timing, central tension resolution, defensive obligation, or precise tactical sequence), and the played move wastes the one tempo needed, allowing the opponent to seize the initiative through an unstoppable pawn advance, tactical exploitation of an unguarded square, or escape from a trap
sub_patterns: Slow prophylactic pawn moves ignoring unresolved central tension (g6, a6)
King repositioning moves that waste tempo in pawn races (Ke3, Ka4)
Moving a piece that was guarding a critical square, enabling a fork (Ne4)
Wrong capture order releasing a trapped piece (dxc5 before Nxc8+)
Greedy capture allowing recapture with check or counterattack (Qxd5)
King walking toward danger instead of fleeing to safety (Ke4)

analysis.label: Moves that look naturally active or purposeful but abandon a critical defensive function, creating a concrete tactical vulnerability.
analysis.description: This feature fires on positions where the player chooses a 'natural-looking' activating move over a more precise alternative, overlooking a specific tactical or positional vulnerability they create. In 6/8 positions, the move sends a piece to a seemingly reasonable active square while a nearby or analogous alternative was clearly superior (Rae1 vs Rad1, Qa5+ vs Qc2+, Kf3 vs e3, Nf4 vs f2, Ke4 vs Kc4, Rad1 vs staying on the a-file). In 5/8 cases, the move explicitly abandons a defensive responsibility: leaving a rook undefended on f1, allowing a king to escape toward safety, abandoning passed pawn support, destroying the king's pawn shield, or vacating the a-file where a pawn needed protection. The resulting punishments are diverse but concrete: knight forks (Kf3→Nd4+), piece captures (Nf4→Bxf4, Rad1→Rxa4), diagonal exploitation (Rae1→Bh3, gxf3→Qh4+), and strategic collapse (Ke4→blockade, Qa5+→king escapes). The shared thread is choosing a move motivated by general principles (centralization, activation, development) over one demanded by the specific tactical requirements of the position.
analysis.move_pattern: Piece moved to an active-looking square (central file, aggressive post, forward king move) when it should address a concrete defensive or positional need nearby
analysis.why_bad: The move abandons a critical defensive function or creates a tactical vulnerability that the opponent can immediately exploit with a forcing sequence (check, capture, fork, or pawn break), turning a favorable or equal position into a losing one.
sub_patterns: Rook placed on wrong open file, leaving another rook or pawn undefended
King centralized toward wrong flank, abandoning passed pawn support or walking into tactical shots
Piece moved to capturable/forkable square when a pawn advance or quieter move was decisive
Pawn recapture that destroys king safety when a developing recapture was available
Check given in wrong direction, allowing king to escape toward safety

analysis.label: Playing a quiet strategic move (rerouting a piece, pushing a pawn, or activating a rook) while ignoring an urgent king safety crisis that demands immediate attention.
analysis.description: This feature fires on moves where the player pursues a secondary positional goal — challenging a centralized piece, gaining queenside space, activating a rook on an open file, or preparing a fianchetto — while their king faces imminent tactical danger. In 7/10 positions, the king is either uncastled in the center (5 cases: positions 3, 6, 14, 15, and position 2 pre-move) or under direct kingside attack with pieces already aimed at h7/the king's shelter (positions 1, 4, 9). In 6/10 cases, castling or a defensive king move was the clear best alternative. The refutations typically involve piece sacrifices on h7 (Greek Gift in positions 1, 9), pawn breaks tearing open lines to the king (positions 2, 3, 6, 14), or tactical strikes exploiting the king's exposure (positions 4, 8, 15). The common thread is a mismatch between the position's urgency level and the tempo cost of the chosen move — these moves would be perfectly reasonable in calmer positions but are catastrophic given the latent attacking energy already aimed at the king.
analysis.move_pattern: Non-forcing, non-defensive moves: knight reroutes away from defensive posts (Nd7, Nbd7), quiet pawn advances (c5, a3, b6, f6), positional rook placement (Rc8), or king movement toward the wrong flank (O-O-O, Kb3)
analysis.why_bad: Each move wastes a critical tempo on a secondary goal while the king is vulnerable — either leaving it uncastled in the center where it can be attacked along open files/diagonals, removing a key defensive piece from guarding the king's shelter, or ignoring an opponent's attacking buildup that requires immediate defensive response.
sub_patterns: Removing the f6 knight (h7 guardian) to challenge a centralized piece, enabling Greek Gift sacrifice
Delaying castling with a slow positional move (pawn break, rook lift, fianchetto prep) while opponent's pieces are poised to exploit the central king
Playing a slow queenside pawn advance while kingside is under direct tactical assault
Moving the king toward a strategic target while opponent's king infiltrates unguarded territory

analysis.label: Seemingly active or developing moves that self-obstruct, block retreat squares, or create immediate tactical targets in positions demanding precise/counterintuitive play.
analysis.description: This feature fires on moves that appear natural or improving (centralizing, developing, activating) but actually create concrete tactical vulnerabilities. In 3/6 positions, the move blocks a critical square needed by another piece (Qf6 blocks Ng8-f6 development, Ndf6 blocks Ng4's retreat square causing it to be trapped, Ke7 steps into the c-pawn's promotion corridor).
