In 2/6 positions, the move creates an immediate target or weakness that the opponent exploits tactically (g3 creates a capturable pawn for the f5 knight, Ng6 places the knight where Bxg6 wins it due to fxg6 failing to Qxe6+). In 1/6, the king abandons its defensive post to a seemingly active square where it's exposed to checks and infiltration (Kd3). All positions featured very narrow paths (avg 1.7 good moves), and the correct alternatives were typically counterintuitive: quiet prophylaxis (Kh8), central pawn strikes (d5, e5), or queenside activity (Qa4) rather than the natural-looking piece improvements chosen.
analysis.move_pattern: Piece or pawn moves to an apparently active square (often on the f/g files, ranks 3-7) that blocks friendly pieces or creates immediate tactical targets
analysis.why_bad: The destination square either blocks a critical retreat/development path for another friendly piece, steps into an immediate tactical motif (fork, capture, promotion corridor), or creates a concrete structural weakness that is instantly exploitable—all in positions where only 1-2 precise moves maintain the evaluation.
sub_patterns: Piece blocks retreat square of another piece (Ndf6 traps Ng4, Qf6 blocks Nf6)
King steps into tactical danger zone (Ke7 into promotion path, Kd3 into check diagonal)
Pawn/piece move creates immediate capture target (g3 for knight, Ng6 for bishop)

analysis.label: Moving a piece or pawn away from a critical defensive function, instantly exposing another piece to capture or trapping.
analysis.description: In all 3/3 positions, the blundering side moved a piece or pawn that was serving a crucial but non-obvious defensive role—shielding another piece from attack along a line. In Position 2, Bxc5 moved the bishop off e7, leaving the e4 knight completely undefended against Re1 along the open e-file. In Position 4, Rf3 placed the rook on the bishop's only retreat square, trapping the bishop after f5 and resulting in exchange loss. In Position 7, g3 advanced the g2 pawn that was blocking the h3-f1 diagonal, allowing the opponent's bishop to capture the f1 rook. Each move had a plausible forward-looking intent (capturing material, challenging an enemy piece, creating king luft), but the player failed to recognize that the piece/pawn being moved was performing a vital hidden defensive function for another piece. The result in every case was immediate material loss through tactical exploitation of the newly exposed piece.
analysis.move_pattern: Any piece/pawn moves off a square where it was shielding a friendly piece from attack along a file or diagonal
analysis.why_bad: The moved piece/pawn was inadvertently blocking an attack line (file or diagonal) targeting another friendly piece; removing it instantly exposes that piece to capture or trapping with no time to compensate.
sub_patterns: Pawn shield removal exposing piece on diagonal
Piece capture vacating defensive post on open file
Rook blocking own bishop's retreat square

analysis.label: Black fails to eliminate or neutralize a dangerously placed enemy piece (typically a knight on f7) when it is the sole correct defensive action, enabling 7th-rank invasions or discovered attacks.
analysis.description: This feature activates when Black faces a critical 'only-move' situation requiring the immediate neutralization of a dominant enemy piece or threat, but instead plays a seemingly active or natural alternative. In 3/6 positions, the sole good move was literally Rxf7 capturing a deeply embedded knight on f7; in a 4th position (Position 8), a knight on c7 demanded urgent attention via Ke7. In 5/6 positions, the punishment involved either a 7th-rank rook invasion (Rc7/Re7 in positions 5, 8, 9, 15) or a discovered attack exploiting the unchallenged piece (positions 1, 5). The average number of good moves was only 1.2, confirming these are positions with essentially zero margin for error. The played moves (Qe8, Rb6, Bxc7, Qf6, Kxe3, Rd2) all look reasonable—attacking something, capturing material, or repositioning actively—but fatally ignore the single critical defensive obligation, resulting in an average 480cp loss.
analysis.move_pattern: Various piece types moving to active-looking squares or making captures, while a dangerous embedded enemy piece (usually knight on f7/c7) remains uncaptured and the 7th rank is left unguarded
analysis.why_bad: The moves leave a dominant enemy piece (typically a knight on f7) alive and unchallenged, which then enables devastating discovered attacks or allows rooks to invade the 7th rank with decisive tactical threats against the exposed Black king
sub_patterns: Failing to capture knight on f7 with Rxf7 (3/6 positions)
Abandoning rook coverage that prevents 7th-rank invasion
Greedy captures or move-order errors when one critical defensive move exists
Queen repositioning that loses control of key invasion squares

analysis.label: Knight delivers a tempting but counterproductive check that wastes tempo, displaces the knight from a superior square, or misses a much stronger continuation.
analysis.description: All 7/7 positions feature a knight giving check that turns out to be a significant mistake. In every case, the knight check is superficially attractive (forcing the opponent's king to move) but concretely inferior to quieter or differently-forcing alternatives. The common failure mode is that the check either: (1) displaces the knight from a dominant square where it coordinated with other pieces (5/7 positions—Nc3+ leaving e4, Nc5+ leaving e4, Ne2+ leaving g1, Ng4+ leaving e3, Nd2+ leaving f3), (2) allows the opponent's king to actually improve its position after the check (6/7—king escapes to d3, c2, e2, g6, Ke2, Kd3), or (3) misses immediately decisive moves including forced checkmates (4/7 positions had mate available). The average cp_loss of 4053 reflects that these include catastrophic blunders (missing mate-in-1, mate-in-3) alongside smaller inaccuracies, all united by the same psychological impulse to give check with the knight rather than calculate the position's true demands.
analysis.move_pattern: Knight move giving check (any direction), often moving away from a centralized or well-coordinated square
analysis.why_bad: The knight check wastes a tempo because the opponent's king finds an equal or better square after moving, while the knight itself lands on an inferior square where it loses coordination with friendly pieces—meanwhile, stronger moves (quiet rook invasions, different piece checks, or immediate checkmates) are missed.
sub_patterns: Knight leaves dominant central outpost to give check
Knight check misses forced checkmate with another piece
Knight check allows opponent's king to centralize/escape
Premature knight check that appears later in the best line but under better circumstances

analysis.label: Piece moves toward a secondary objective while abandoning its essential strategic responsibility in the position.
analysis.description: In 6/6 detailed positions, the blunder involves moving a piece (king, queen, rook, or bishop) away from the single most critical task demanded by the position. In positions 1 and 3, the king drifts toward a flank instead of blockading/staying near a dangerous passed pawn. In position 8, the queen retreats from the a5-e1 diagonal that was the foundation of a winning tactical combination against White's uncastled king. In position 11, the rook leaves d1—the only piece restraining a lethal passed d-pawn. In position 14, the bishop occupies e5 blocking the king's critical path to f4. In position 15, a pawn advance ignores the urgent need to cover the a8-h1 diagonal. Each move appears purposeful (centralization, 'active' placement, attacking a pawn) but fatally neglects the ONE responsibility that holds the position together, allowing the opponent to exploit the now-unguarded critical factor.
analysis.move_pattern: Piece moves laterally or toward a secondary flank/square, away from the primary strategic axis (typically a file, diagonal, or square requiring blockade/restraint)
analysis.why_bad: The move abandons the piece's essential function (blockading a passed pawn, restraining an advance, controlling a critical diagonal, or enabling king activation), allowing the opponent to immediately exploit the unguarded vulnerability with a breakthrough, passed pawn advance, or tactical strike.
sub_patterns: King drifts to wrong flank instead of blockading a passed pawn
Queen relocates to seemingly active square but abandons attacking/defensive diagonal
Rook leaves the file restraining a dangerous passed pawn
Piece occupies a 'good' square that blocks own king's critical advance

analysis.label: Moves that neglect urgent king safety concerns to pursue unrelated plans, allowing tactical exploitation of the exposed king.
analysis.description: This feature activates on positions where king safety is the dominant concern but the player makes a move addressing something else entirely. In 6/8 positions, the move either creates new king weakness (g5 weakening dark squares, Kg6 walking into open lines) or ignores existing vulnerability (both Bg4 moves abandon f7 defense enabling Bxf7+ sacrifice-fork combinations, O-O ignores a trapped piece crisis near the enemy king, c5 pushes a pawn without securing the king with g3 first). The positions consistently feature exposed kings with weak pawn shields (7/8 positions list explicit king exposure). The common punishment pattern involves forcing tactical sequences - typically sacrifices, forks, or checks exploiting the neglected king weakness. The moves themselves appear natural or purposeful in isolation (developing a bishop, pushing a passed pawn, castling) but fatally misjudge positional priorities. Position 3 (Nf6, 0cp loss) fires because it shares the same positional fingerprint - critically exposed kings with weak pawn shields - even though the move happens to be correct.
analysis.move_pattern: Various piece types and directions; no single geometric pattern - includes bishop development to g4, pawn advances (g5, c5), king moves, rook lifts, and castling
analysis.why_bad: The moves ignore an urgent king safety crisis - either removing a key defender from the king's vicinity, advancing pawns that weaken the king's shelter, or spending tempo on irrelevant plans while the opponent has forcing tactical resources targeting the exposed king
sub_patterns: Bishop to g4 abandoning f7 defense, punished by Bxf7+ sacrifice into knight fork (2/8)
Premature pawn advance weakening own king's pawn shield (g5, c5) allowing tactical exploitation (2/8)
Routine developing move (O-O, Rac1) ignoring urgent tactical crisis involving exposed/trapped pieces near kings (2/8)
King voluntarily walking into exposed position (Kg6) where queen-rook coordination creates mating threats (1/8)

analysis.label: King moves away from an enemy bishop it should capture, declining a free piece out of misplaced fear of king exposure.
analysis.description: In all 13/13 positions, an enemy bishop sits on a square adjacent to the king (typically giving check or recently landed via sacrifice), and the only good move is for the king to capture it (Kxf7, Kxf2, or Kxh7). Instead, the player moves the king to a different square (Kf8, Kh8, Kd2, Kf1, or even plays a non-king move like d6), declining the free piece. This allows the opponent to retreat the bishop to safety on the next move (to squares like Bb3, Bc4, Bd5, Bh5), preserving material that should have been lost. The positions arise overwhelmingly in the opening (10/13), predominantly as Black (11/13), and almost always involve a bishop on f7 that the king on e8/f8 should capture (9/13 are specifically Kf8 instead of Kxf7). The average cp_loss of 338 reflects that this is essentially refusing a free piece worth ~300cp. In every case, exactly 1 good move existed.
analysis.move_pattern: King moves one square sideways/diagonally AWAY from an adjacent enemy bishop instead of capturing it; most commonly Kf8 instead of Kxf7, also Kh8 instead of Kxh7 or Kf1/Kd2 instead of Kxf2
analysis.why_bad: The player fears king exposure after the capture (e.g., Ng5+ checks, queen discoveries), but these continuations are manageable; by declining the capture, they gift the opponent a full piece when the bishop safely retreats to an active diagonal on the next move.
sub_patterns: Kf8 declining Kxf7 in Italian/Two Knights openings
Kh8 declining Kxh7 in Greek Gift-style middlegames
Kf1/Kd2 declining Kxf2 after ...Bxf2+ sacrifices

analysis.label: King (or piece) retreats toward the edge of the board instead of maintaining active centralization in endgames, surrendering critical tempo.
analysis.description: In 4/4 positions, the played move retreats or steps toward the board's periphery instead of maintaining central presence. In 3/4 cases the king specifically moves toward the edge (Kc7 toward queenside, Kg7 backward, Kh2 toward h-file) when centralization was essential (Ke6 was best in positions 1 and 3, Kf2 in position 4). In position 2, a4 is a peripheral pawn push missing the critical central c3 that sealed a mating net. All 4/4 positions are endgames where tempo and king activity are paramount. The common consequence is that the retreating move either exposes the king to checks along ranks/files (3/4 positions feature immediate check refutations: Qg7+, Rh8+, Kd4-e5-f6 march), or allows the opponent's king to advance unchallenged through the center. The 'tempo_loss' tag applies to all four positions.
analysis.move_pattern: King moves toward the edge (h-file, g-file, or c-file) retreating from center; or pawn push to rim square instead of critical central pawn move
analysis.why_bad: Retreating to the periphery exposes the king to rook/queen checks along open files and ranks, and cedes the center to the opponent's king, which then advances unopposed to dominate the position or complete a mating net
sub_patterns: King retreats to file exposed to rook checks
King retreats allowing opponent king march through center
Peripheral pawn push missing critical central tactical move

analysis.label: Positions with a passed pawn or clear conversion task where the player loses tempo by choosing a peripheral or premature action instead of the most direct path.
analysis.description: This feature fires on positions—predominantly simplified endgames (6/11) but also middlegames (4/11)—where there is a clear advantage to convert, almost always involving a passed pawn or concrete winning plan. The critical decision revolves around TIMING: whether to advance the king first (escorting the pawn), push the pawn directly, or address an urgent tactical need. When the feature fires on blunders, the common error is a tempo loss: premature pawn advances without king support (a5 in positions 7 and 12, costing 532cp and shortening mate from 18 to 3), passive piece retreats ignoring active threats (Bb1 costing 449cp), peripheral captures diverting from the main task (cxb4 at 184cp, Qxc4 at 223cp), or king moves to wrong squares (Kd7 at 227cp). When it fires on optimal moves (3/11 positions at 0cp), these are correct king-escort moves in KP endgames (Kf4, Kb5, Kd3). The positions share extremely narrow decision trees (avg 2.3 good moves), heavily one-sided evaluations, and open/simplified structures where precise move order determines whether the advantage converts or evaporates.
analysis.move_pattern: Mixed piece types but predominantly king moves (5/11) and pawn pushes (3/11); typically non-capturing, non-checking moves that advance toward or along a passed pawn's promotion corridor, or peripheral moves away from it
analysis.why_bad: The moves lose critical tempo in positions where timing is everything—either advancing a pawn before the king is properly positioned ahead of it (allowing stalemate/drawing resources), making passive retreats that gift the opponent tactical opportunities, or capturing peripheral material while ignoring the most urgent concrete action in the position
sub_patterns: Premature rook-pawn advance without king ahead (stalemate draw resource)
Passive piece retreat gifting tempo for opponent's tactics
Peripheral pawn capture ignoring central/urgent threats
King move to wrong square losing development tempo
Capturing the wrong hanging piece

analysis.label: Natural-looking or routine moves played in positions with extremely narrow margins where only 1-2 specific concrete actions maintain the evaluation.
analysis.description: This feature fires on positions where the player chose a reasonable-seeming move—often developing, centralizing, capturing material, or improving piece placement—but missed the one critical concrete requirement of the position. In 10/12 positions, only 1-2 good moves existed (avg 1.8), yet the played moves all appear superficially logical: routine development (O-O, Be7), active-looking piece moves (Nb4, Ng6, Qf4, Be3), seemingly correct captures (fxe4, dxc5, Rxh6), or natural pawn advances (e4, Kf4). The best moves consistently demanded precise calculation—tactical shots (Nc5 winning material in positions 4 and 5), forcing intermediate moves (Rd7+ in position 12), critical defensive maintenance (Qc7 in position 1, Ke5 in position 2), or attacking the correct target (Qxd4 in position 3, c4 in position 10). The average centipawn loss of 1092 reflects that these 'second instinct' moves catastrophically fail in positions where only one narrow path works.
analysis.move_pattern: Diverse piece types and directions—no geometric constant. Moves include piece repositioning, routine development, pawn captures, castling, and king moves. United by appearing 'normal' or 'improving' rather than forcing/concrete.
analysis.why_bad: Each move addresses the wrong priority—choosing general improvement (development, centralization, material capture, space gain) over the one specific concrete action the position demands (exploiting a tactic, maintaining a critical defender, forcing an intermediate move, or addressing an urgent threat).
sub_patterns: Routine developing moves when immediate tactics are available (O-O, Be7 missing Nc5 fork)
Active-looking moves abandoning critical defensive duties (Nb4 leaving d5, Kf4 undefending knight, Be3 allowing deflection)
Capturing wrong target or in wrong move order (fxe4 leaving dangerous bishop, dxc5 removing blockader, Rxh6 missing intermediate check)
Slow piece repositioning when forcing moves are urgent (Ng6 instead of Qxf3, Qf4 ignoring passed pawns)

analysis.label: Making constructive-looking moves that fail to address the position's single most urgent tactical vulnerability, allowing immediate exploitation.
analysis.description: This feature fires on moves where the player pursues a secondary objective (piece development, activation, pawn advancement) while completely ignoring the one critical tactical demand of the position. In 9/12 positions, the best moves all share a common urgent theme the blunder ignores: moving a bishop off a vulnerable square (Positions 9, 12 - Bg3/Bd2 needed), creating king luft (Position 11 - g6/h5/h6 needed), defending a critical pawn (Positions 6, 13 - f2 defense needed), or avoiding placing pieces on tactically exploitable squares (Positions 2, 14 - Bc5 hangs to Qh5+ geometry). In 10/12 cases, the refutation exploits exactly the vulnerability the move failed to address. The average of only 2.2 good moves available confirms these are high-urgency positions demanding specific responses, yet the played moves address a completely different part of the board or plan (Na3 developing queenside during kingside mate, a5 pushing a pawn during kingside collapse, Rb1/Rad1 activating rooks while leaving pieces hanging).
analysis.move_pattern: Diverse piece types moving toward secondary objectives (queenside development, file activation, pawn advances) rather than toward the critical defensive zone or away from tactical vulnerability
analysis.why_bad: Each position has one overriding tactical necessity (defend a key square, relocate a tactically exposed piece, create king escape squares, or block a passed pawn), and ignoring it for even one tempo allows the opponent to execute a decisive combination exploiting that exact weakness
sub_patterns: Piece moved away from critical defensive duty (Bg4, Rdd3, Rf5)
Development/activation on wrong flank while mating threats exist (Na3, a5, Rb1)
Piece placed on undefended square creating geometric vulnerability (Bc5×2, Be6)
Slow repositioning when specific urgent piece maneuver required (Kd2, Ng2)

analysis.label: Playing a seemingly active but non-urgent move in a position that demands immediate attention to one specific critical task.
analysis.description: This feature fires on positions where there is typically only ONE correct approach (avg 1.8 good moves available) and the player invests a tempo on a move that addresses the wrong priority. In 6/8 positions, the move ignores an immediate tactical or positional demand: Rab1 ignores a g-file battery aimed at the king (Position 8), h5 misses a decisive Nd8 exploiting an overloaded queen (Position 10), g5 launches a flank attack while central passed pawns break through (Position 12), f3 kicks a knight but creates a worse fork square (Position 14), Ne4 abandons the only piece blockading a lethal passed pawn (Position 6), and e5 permanently weakens key squares in a minor piece endgame (Position 4). The blundered moves often look logical in isolation—centralizing, gaining space, creating threats—but they universally fail to address the ONE thing the position demands. In 7/8 positions, king safety is a critical factor being ignored, and in 6/8 positions the move constitutes a clear tempo loss that allows the opponent to seize the initiative.
analysis.move_pattern: Diverse piece types and directions (pawn pushes, piece repositioning, piece centralization); no single geometric pattern—the commonality is choosing a non-forcing move when one forcing/critical move is required
analysis.why_bad: The position has exactly one critical demand (address king safety, capture a key pawn, exploit a tactical shot, or challenge a dominant piece) with very few good alternatives, and the chosen move wastes a crucial tempo on an irrelevant objective, allowing the opponent to execute their primary threat unchallenged
sub_patterns: Flank pawn push ignoring central crisis (g5, h5, e5)
Piece repositioning away from critical defensive duty (Ne4, Rab1)
Pawn advance creating new weaknesses while ignoring existing threats (f3, e5)
Aggressive-looking queen/piece move to a tactically vulnerable square (Qg4)

analysis.label: Moving a piece toward the edge or back rank when centralization or active play in the opposite direction was required.
analysis.description: All three moves share the geometric trait of directing a piece toward the board's periphery—Qb8 retreats the queen to the back rank, Kf7 walks the king toward the kingside corner, and Na5 places the knight on the a-file rim. In 2/3 positions this results in catastrophic evaluation drops: Kf7 walks into a forced mate by heading toward the corner instead of the center/queenside (9585 cp loss), and Na5 creates a passive, nearly trapped knight on the rim instead of the powerful central Ne5 square (299 cp loss). The 1/3 case (Qb8) incurred 0 cp loss only because the position was already a forced mate regardless of move choice. The common strategic error is choosing the wrong direction—moving away from where the piece would have maximum influence—resulting in reduced mobility, vulnerability to being trapped or cornered, and loss of tempo while the opponent seizes the initiative.
analysis.move_pattern: Any piece moving toward the board edge (a/h files, 1st/8th ranks, or corner direction) rather than toward the center or active squares
analysis.why_bad: Pieces on the periphery have drastically reduced mobility and influence, allowing the opponent to dominate the center, trap the misplaced piece, or execute mating patterns against a cornered king
sub_patterns: Knight retreat to rim (a5/h5 etc.) instead of central outpost
King walking toward corner in K+R+N vs K endgame
Queen retreat to back rank when forward activity needed

analysis.label: Playing a non-urgent move (often a pawn push or passive repositioning) that wastes a critical tempo while the opponent has an imminent tactical threat, usually involving a knight invasion or fork.
analysis.description: This feature fires on positions where the player makes a slow, off-point move—frequently a flank pawn push (a4, h4, h6 in 3/8 cases), passive piece retreat (Qc1, Qh4 in 2/8), or wrong capture (Rxf6, fxg5 in 2/8)—in positions demanding immediate concrete action. In 6/8 positions, the opponent's refutation involves a devastating knight maneuver: Ne5 centralizing with tempo (pos 1), Nb4 forking queen/pawn (pos 5), Nxc2 winning material (pos 6), Nd5-Ne7+ forking king/rook (pos 8), or a rook lift exploiting the wasted tempo (pos 4). The common thread is that exactly one or two precise moves existed to maintain the position (avg 1.8 good moves), yet the player chose something that addressed a non-existent or low-priority concern while leaving a concrete tactical vulnerability unattended. The average cp loss of 289 reflects how devastating a single wasted tempo can be when the opponent has a forcing sequence ready to execute.
analysis.move_pattern: Diverse piece types; predominantly slow pawn advances (a4, h4, h6, fxg5) or queen/king moves to passive or exposed squares, all characterized by being non-forcing and non-defensive
analysis.why_bad: These moves waste a critical tempo in tactically demanding positions, allowing the opponent to execute a concrete knight invasion, piece coordination strike, or forcing sequence that was already threatened and needed immediate prevention
sub_patterns: Unnecessary flank pawn push (a4/h4/h6) ignoring central tactical threats
Queen repositioned to wrong square abandoning key defensive duties
Wrong recapture that misplaces a piece and enables opponent's knight invasion
King moved to vulnerable square enabling rook lift or fork patterns

analysis.label: Positions with large advantages where the player makes an active-looking move to press or convert, ranging from optimal technique to tempo-wasting inaccuracies.
analysis.description: This feature fires on positions where one side holds a significant advantage (typically +200 to +700 cp) and plays a move aimed at converting or pressing that advantage. In 5/9 positions, these are endgames involving passed pawn escort (especially king marches like Kb5, Kf4). In 4/9 positions, the player squanders their advantage with a move that appears active or safe but wastes a critical tempo (e5, Qe6, Kb1, Ng2). The common positional signature includes exposed/active kings on both sides (7/9), passed pawns or potential for them (7/9), and open/semi-open positions. The feature captures the decision point where a winning side must choose between multiple 'reasonable-looking' continuations, whether the choice is correct (cp_loss 0-4 in 5 cases) or catastrophically wrong (cp_loss 161-377 in 4 cases).
analysis.move_pattern: Active-looking piece repositioning (king advances, piece centralization, pawn pushes) in positions with large material or positional advantages; no consistent piece type or direction
analysis.why_bad: In the blunder cases, the player chooses a 'natural' or 'safe' move that wastes a tempo when the position demands immediate concrete/forcing action—blocking own passed pawn (Qe6), premature advance (e5), unnecessary prophylaxis (Kb1), or retreating from an active post (Ng2)
sub_patterns: King marching to escort passed pawn in KP endgame
Tempo-wasting move squandering opening advantage
Piece placement that blocks own counterplay asset
Passive retreat abandoning tactical resources

analysis.label: Natural-looking quiet repositioning moves chosen over concrete active responses that address critical threats or opportunities.
analysis.description: In all 3/3 positions, the player chose a quiet, 'building' move (Kg8 tucking the king away, Kf3 advancing the king suboptimally, Raf1 doubling rooks passively) instead of the required concrete action (Nf6 challenging a dominant piece, Kf4 taking the most efficient racing path, Rxg4 eliminating a dangerous attacker). Each move looks logical on the surface—improving safety or coordination—but fails to address the critical dynamic of the position. In 3/3 cases, the position demanded immediate, concrete engagement (a capture, an active challenge, or a more direct path) rather than slow improvement. The common thread across all analyses is 'tempo_loss' and 'piece_activity' tags, reflecting that these moves waste time in positions where the opponent can exploit the passivity.
analysis.move_pattern: Quiet non-capture repositioning moves (king retreats, king lateral shifts, rook lifts to open files) that avoid confrontation
analysis.why_bad: These moves lose critical tempo by choosing passive repositioning over concrete action (captures, challenges to dominant pieces, or most efficient paths), allowing the opponent to exploit the delay—whether through back-rank infiltration, winning a pawn race, or launching a decisive kingside break.
sub_patterns: King retreating to apparently safe square that creates back-rank vulnerability
King taking suboptimal path in racing endgame
Rook doubling passively instead of decisive exchange or counterplay

analysis.label: King moves to a seemingly natural square that immediately exposes it to checks along ranks, files, or diagonals, whereas a counterintuitive alternative (often a corner or advanced square) was safe.
analysis.description: In 6/7 positions, the king moves to a square that appears normal or centralizing but is immediately punished by a check along a rank, file, or diagonal. In 4/7 cases (Kf2, Kh2, Kd2, Kg7), the king specifically steps onto the 2nd/7th rank where an enemy queen or rook delivers check along that rank (Qa2+, Ra2+, Qe7+). In 5/7 cases, the correct move was a counterintuitive king move to a seemingly worse square (Kh5 instead of Kg7, Kh2 instead of Kf2, Kh1 instead of Kh2, Kh6 instead of Kg8) that avoided the check pattern. The Rf7 outlier fits because the correct move was Kh8 to sidestep a Qf7+ check. The tempo gained by the checking move consistently allows the opponent to either win material, penetrate decisively, or dissolve a winning advantage completely.
analysis.move_pattern: King moves from edge/corner square to a more central or rank-adjacent square (typically onto the 2nd/7th rank or an open file), where opponent's major piece delivers immediate check
analysis.why_bad: The new king square sits on an open rank, file, or diagonal where the opponent's queen or rook can deliver an immediate tempo-gaining check, enabling forced sequences that win material, eliminate key advantages (passed pawns), or destroy coordination that held the position together
sub_patterns: King steps onto 2nd/7th rank allowing rank check (Qa2+/Ra2+)
King moves to open file square allowing file check (Rg3+)
King retreats to 'safe' square instead of advancing to tactically immune square (Kh5/Kh6)
Piece moves to f7 instead of king sidestepping the check threat

analysis.label: Apparently logical moves in tactically critical positions where only one precise response avoids catastrophe.
analysis.description: This feature fires on positions of extreme tactical tension (avg 1.6 good moves available) where the player makes a move that looks natural or purposeful but catastrophically misses the one essential response. In 6/8 positions, the played move either gives a seemingly useful check (Ne1+, gxf4+), pursues a strategic plan (a4 for queenside attack, Kc5 toward the a-pawn), retreats to apparent safety (Kd7, Ke2), or centralizes a piece (Qf5) - all plausible-looking ideas. However, the position demanded a very specific counterintuitive move: Nb4+ instead of Ne1+ (better check geometry, 1/8), Rh8 to defend a hanging pawn rather than attack (1/8), Qe4 queen sacrifice rather than king flight (1/8), Kc4 advancing toward danger rather than retreating (1/8), gxh6 capturing the attacker rather than repositioning (1/8), and knight repositioning rather than pawn capture with check (1/8). The catastrophic average cp_loss of 1457 reflects that these positions have razor-thin margins where the 'obvious' move leads to disaster.
analysis.move_pattern: Diverse piece types making apparently purposeful moves (checks, captures, king retreats, pawn advances, piece centralization) that address secondary concerns rather than the position's critical requirement
analysis.why_bad: The moves fail because they address a secondary concern while ignoring the position's single most urgent tactical demand - whether that's blocking a mating file, maintaining a geometric defensive resource, defending a hanging pawn, or eliminating an attacking piece. The correct move typically requires seeing a non-obvious defensive or positional priority.
sub_patterns: Checks/captures that improve opponent's position (Ne1+, gxf4+)
King moves that walk into tactical exploitation (Kc5, Kd7, Ke2)
Pursuing strategic plans while ignoring immediate tactical threats (a4, Qf5)

analysis.label: Playing a routine-looking or natural move instead of the most direct, forcing continuation available in the position.
analysis.description: This feature fires on positions where a player selects a seemingly reasonable or 'natural' move while overlooking a more concrete, forcing, or direct action. In 6/6 positions, the played move appears logical on the surface (developing a piece, giving a check, advancing a pawn, approaching a target) but fails to execute the most precise continuation. The missed opportunities range from immediate captures (positions 1, 3 where Kxa2/Kxe4 were more direct), to eliminating tactical threats (position 5 where Bxe4/Be3 addressed the diagonal), to delivering checkmate (position 9 where Qe3# was available vs the played Qd3+), to maintaining dynamic piece play (position 12 where Ra3 kept rooks active vs Re3 inviting exchange), to addressing piece coordination urgency (position 14 where b4/Nc2 rescued the knight vs Bd2 blocking retreats). The cp losses range wildly (0 to 9465) because the feature detects the behavioral pattern regardless of how forgiving the position is.
analysis.move_pattern: Various piece types moving to seemingly natural squares; no single geometric direction, but moves tend toward quiet/preparatory rather than capturing, mating, or eliminating threats
analysis.why_bad: These moves prioritize general positional logic (development, approaching targets, gaining space) over specific tactical necessities—failing to calculate the most forcing line first, which leaves opponent's tactical resources intact or misses immediately winning continuations.
sub_patterns: Quiet developing move ignoring concrete tactical threat
Wrong check square (adjacent to winning check/mate)
Preparatory move before available immediate capture
Centralizing move that invites unfavorable simplification
Blocking own piece retreat with passive development

analysis.label: Playing a routine developing move (castling, bishop development, or pawn push) instead of immediately capturing or recapturing an undefended enemy bishop.
analysis.description: In all 11 positions, there is an undefended bishop that demands immediate capture (either an enemy bishop sitting en prise in the player's territory, or an enemy bishop that just took one of the player's pieces requiring recapture). Instead of making the obvious capture, the player plays a 'normal-looking' developing move: castling kingside (3/11), fianchettoing a bishop to g7 (3/11), developing a bishop to e7 or e2 (3/11), or making a pawn move (2/11). In every case, the correct move was a simple capture—Bxf3, Nxh6, Bxh6, Qxf6, gxf6, gxf3, or Qxf3—resolving an immediate tactical obligation. The blunder moves are all quiet, non-forcing moves that ignore the urgency, allowing the opponent to either save their hanging piece, trade it under favorable circumstances, or execute a tactical sequence exploiting the missed capture. The average cp_loss of 604 reflects that these positions typically involve losing a full minor piece's worth of value.
analysis.move_pattern: Quiet non-capturing moves (O-O, bishop development to natural squares like g7/e7/e2, pawn pushes) played when a bishop capture was required on f3/h3/h6/f6
analysis.why_bad: An undefended enemy bishop (or one that just captured material) sits on the board demanding immediate recapture/capture, but the player treats the position as routine and plays a standard developing move, allowing the opponent to either escape with the piece, trade it favorably, or exploit the resulting tactical vulnerability (often the unprotected g2/e2 bishop or exposed rook).
sub_patterns: Castling O-O while opponent's bishop attacks g2/e2 unaddressed (positions 1, 2, 15)
Fianchettoing Bg7 into a square controlled by opponent's bishop on h6, losing exchange (positions 4, 7, 14)
Developing Be7 instead of recapturing opponent's bishop on f6 (positions 5, 11)
Developing Be2 or playing d3/dxe5 instead of recapturing bishop on f3 (positions 3, 12, 13)

analysis.label: Moves that relocate a well-placed major piece from a critical controlling square to pursue an attractive-looking but strategically inferior plan, surrendering the position's key advantage.
analysis.description: This feature fires on moves where a player abandons a dominant or critical piece placement—usually a queen or rook on a controlling square—to pursue a tempting but ineffective plan, typically involving aggression toward the opponent's king or a pawn capture. In 4/8 positions, the queen leaves a paralyzing post (Qf6 abandons g6's kingside threats exposing d5; Qg5 ignores the passed d-pawn; Qd8 leaves the king unshielded from perpetual; Qxg6 vacates f7's bind on Black's pieces). In 3/8 positions, a rook is misredirected (Rh1 abandons the f-file for a doomed h-file battery; Rxd1 reflexively captures instead of delivering checkmate; Rgh3 moves the wrong rook, leaving a knight hanging). In 1/8, a pawn capture (gxh5) opens files that benefit the opponent. The common thread is that the original piece placement was performing an irreplaceable function—maintaining a bind, defending a weakness, controlling key squares that prevented the opponent's counterplay—and the chosen move removes that function for an illusion of increased activity.
analysis.move_pattern: Major piece (queen or rook) relocated away from a dominant controlling square/file, typically toward the opponent's kingside or toward a pawn capture, or a pawn capture opening files toward one's own king
analysis.why_bad: The piece was performing a critical function (maintaining a bind, preventing counterplay, defending a key square) and its relocation grants the opponent a concrete tactical resource: hanging pieces become capturable, perpetual check becomes available, passed pawns advance decisively, or newly opened files are seized by the opponent's better-positioned pieces.
sub_patterns: Queen vacates dominant 7th-rank or central post for a pawn capture or repositioning
Rook abandons critical open file for an ineffective doubling on another file
Pawn capture that opens lines benefiting the opponent's better-coordinated pieces
Reflexive defensive capture that misses a forcing tactical sequence

analysis.label: Moves that appear to gain tempo, simplify, or improve safety but actually create a worse tactical vulnerability than the problem they attempt to solve.
analysis.description: This feature fires on moves where the player prioritizes a superficial improvement (delivering check, escaping perceived pressure, simplifying via exchange) while missing that the move itself exposes them to a more damaging tactical shot. In 3/6 positions, the king moves to a seemingly safer square that is actually tactically vulnerable: Kg7 walks onto the g-file enabling a discovered attack (Position 6), Kh3 abandons counterplay and allows queen infiltration (Position 8), Kg3 steps onto a diagonal allowing Bd6+ winning an exchange (Position 14). In 2/6 positions, a check is delivered that appears to gain tempo but actually loses material: Bxg4+ removes a key defensive bishop allowing king infiltration (Position 2), and c5+ drops two pawns to Bxc5+ followed by Bxa7 (Position 9). In 1/6 positions, a natural-looking capture (exd4) removes a structural barrier that was preventing the opponent's pawn break (Position 12). The common refutation pattern involves the opponent immediately exploiting the newly created vulnerability—typically within 1-2 moves—via diagonal checks, discovered attacks, or material capture on the weakened square.
analysis.move_pattern: King moves to adjacent squares (especially g3, h3, g7) or captures/checks that remove own defensive resources; typically single-square king moves or forcing moves (checks/captures) that seem to improve the position
analysis.why_bad: The move solves an imagined or lesser problem while creating a real and greater one—exposing the king to a discovered attack, placing it on a vulnerable diagonal or file, removing a defensive piece that was preventing infiltration, or pushing a pawn into a square where it can be captured with devastating follow-up
sub_patterns: King moves to 'safer' squares that are actually tactically exposed (discovered attacks, diagonal checks)
Checks that appear to gain tempo but lose material (pawn or piece lands on capturable square)
Exchanges that remove key defensive pieces, enabling opponent's king/piece activation
Captures that open lines for the opponent's pawn breaks or piece coordination

analysis.label: Piece moves to grab material or reposition ambitiously, abandoning a critical defensive duty and allowing the opponent to win material through simple tactics.
analysis.description: In all 4/4 positions, the player makes a tempting-looking move that prioritizes immediate material gain or piece activity while fatally neglecting the moved piece's current role in the position's tactical balance. In 3/4 cases, the move is a pawn capture (Nxc7, Qxc5, Rxg3) that looks free but creates a larger tactical vulnerability. The refutations are all straightforward: a hanging piece is captured (3/4 - Rxh6 captures undefended bishop, Rc8 attacks trapped knight, Bxc6 exploits abandoned coordination), or a fork/discovered attack wins decisive material (1/4 - e4 forks bishop and knight then wins the queen). In every case, 1-2 good alternatives existed that addressed the position's actual demands (defensive coordination, resolving pins, protecting vulnerable pieces), but the player chose the superficially attractive option instead.
analysis.move_pattern: Any piece type moves to capture a pawn or reposition to a seemingly active square, traveling away from its current defensive assignment
analysis.why_bad: The moved piece was performing a critical defensive function (guarding another piece, contesting a file, maintaining coordination) that becomes exploitable the moment it leaves; the pawn or positional gain is far outweighed by the material lost to the resulting tactic
sub_patterns: Pawn capture removes defender from critical square, leaving another piece hanging
Piece captures on a square where it becomes trapped or immediately attacked
Piece repositions to a square that blocks own major piece and creates fork vulnerability
Queen/piece leaves coordinating post to grab material, allowing opponent tactical breakthrough

analysis.label: Playing a superficially active or natural-looking move instead of addressing a concrete preparatory, prophylactic, or defensive requirement demanded by the position.
analysis.description: This feature fires on positions where the player chooses an apparently attractive 'active' move—advancing a passed pawn, centralizing a piece on an open file, giving a check, or capturing material—while neglecting the one critical preparatory step the position requires. In 8/8 cases, the correct move involved preparation or prophylaxis (h5 preventing g4, Rg2 placing the rook behind the passer before advancing it, Qb2+ choosing the right check direction, Na4 removing a tactical vulnerability, Qd7 maintaining a key defensive connection). The blunders share the trait of looking natural to a human eye: Re8 seizes an open file (1/8), g7 and g6 push a passer toward promotion (2/8), Qg5+ gives check (1/8), f5 activates a pawn (1/8), Bxc5 captures a pawn (1/8), Rae1 occupies an open file (1/8), and Qg6 attacks a target (1/8)—all appearing purposeful but all fatally premature. The positions typically have only 1-2 good moves available (avg 1.5), indicating high-precision moments where the concrete demands of the position override general principles of activity.
analysis.move_pattern: Forward-looking moves: pawn advances (especially passed pawns), piece moves to apparently active squares (open files, attacking positions), captures, and checks—all directed at aggressive objectives rather than defensive/preparatory needs
analysis.why_bad: These moves fail because they skip a necessary intermediate step: the position contains a specific concrete requirement (blocking an opponent's plan, supporting a pawn before advancing it, maintaining a defensive connection, avoiding self-blocking) that must be addressed first. The 'active' move either creates a new vulnerability (hanging piece, trapped piece, unsupported pawn) or allows the opponent to execute a plan that the preparatory move would have prevented.
sub_patterns: Premature passed pawn advance without establishing rook support behind it (g7, g6)
Piece centralization on an open file that ignores a concrete tactical vulnerability (Re8, Rae1)
Moving a defensive piece to an 'active' square, abandoning its protective duty (Qg6, Bxc5)
Giving a check that allows the opponent to improve piece placement via interposition (Qg5+)
Committing a pawn advance before extracting maximum value from an existing asset (f5)

analysis.label: Quiet king moves (especially Kh7) to squares that create immediate tactical vulnerabilities, when the position demanded urgent concrete action.
analysis.description: This feature fires on positions where a player makes a non-forcing 'improving' move—most characteristically stepping the king one square forward—that creates fresh tactical vulnerabilities the opponent can immediately exploit. In 5/8 positions, the move is a king step (4× Kh7, 1× Ke7) that places the monarch on a square where it becomes a direct target for queen checks, queen-bishop batteries, or knight forks. The remaining cases (Ne5, Re7, Nf3) share the same structural error: a quiet piece repositioning that ignores the position's urgent tactical demands, either missing a forcing opportunity (5/8 positions had a clearly superior forcing move like Bc4+ or Nf8) or abandoning critical defensive duties (Re7 leaving the king undefended, leading to mate in 5). All 8 moves are non-forcing (no checks, captures, or threats), all have devastating concrete refutations available, and the average centipawn loss of 1449 reflects positions where one tempo of misdirection proves catastrophic.
analysis.move_pattern: King steps one square forward (h8→h7, e8→e7) or piece repositions to a 'natural' square without creating any threat; never a check or capture
analysis.why_bad: The move wastes a critical tempo on a non-forcing action while the position demands immediate tactical response—the king walks onto a square (especially light squares like h7/e7) where opponent queen-bishop batteries, knight forks, or mating attacks become instantly available, and the player's actual defensive resources (like Nf8, Bc4+, f3) go unused.
sub_patterns: Kh7 exposing king to Qh5/Qf5+ and b1-h7 diagonal batteries
King stepping forward into knight check/fork range (Ke7 vs Ng6+)
Piece leaving a strong post to a tactically vulnerable square (Nf3, Ne5)
Rook abandoning king defense allowing back-rank/first-rank mating coordination

analysis.label: Moving a piece to an active-looking but unstable square where it is immediately challenged, losing tempo and abandoning critical positional needs.
analysis.description: In 6/7 positions, the played move relocates a piece to a seemingly purposeful square that is immediately counter-attacked or kicked with tempo by the opponent. Bb3 repositions to a diagonal but ignores the urgent c3 challenge to Black's queen. Bh6 targets the fianchettoed bishop but leaves the c4 bishop undefended to ...Nb6 (gaining tempo). Bg5 attacks the queen with a piece instead of a pawn, allowing Qg3 to counter-attack the bishop. Ba4 attacks the c2 rook but is immediately kicked by b3, enabling a devastating Bc4+ and Rxe3. Rxd6 captures a pawn but lands the rook on a square vulnerable to Nc4 attacking the queen then winning the rook. Qd1 retreats from f3's critical defensive post, exposing g2 and h1 to immediate exploitation. Nf7 abandons the dominant e5 outpost for a superficial pawn attack, allowing Black's knight to activate via Nb5. The consistent thread is that each move prioritizes a secondary objective while placing the moving piece (or leaving a related piece) tactically vulnerable to an immediate tempo-gaining response.
analysis.move_pattern: Piece (bishop, knight, rook, or queen) relocated to a square that appears active but is immediately counter-attacked, kicked by a pawn, or left tactically undefended
analysis.why_bad: The piece lands on an unstable square where the opponent gains tempo by attacking it (or an undefended piece left behind), allowing the opponent to consolidate, activate their own pieces, or execute a tactical combination that was only possible because of the tempo gift.
sub_patterns: Bishop moves to a square immediately kicked by a pawn (Ba4→b3, Bh6→Nb6 hits vacated c4)
Piece attacks opponent's queen but gets counter-attacked on the same move (Bg5→Qg3 hits bishop back)
Piece abandons critical defensive post enabling immediate tactical exploitation (Qd1 leaves g2/h1; Nf7 leaves e5)
Capture with wrong piece leaves capturer vulnerable to tempo-gaining fork (Rxd6→Nc4 attacks queen then rook)

analysis.label: King moves to a square on an open file or back rank where opponent's heavy pieces can exploit it tactically.
analysis.description: In all 5/5 positions, the player made a king move that placed the monarch on a square directly vulnerable to the opponent's heavy pieces (queens and rooks) operating on open lines. In 4/5 cases (Kf1, Kg1, Ke8, Kg8), the king moved to or along the back rank, enabling back-rank tactics, checks with tempo, or mating nets. In the remaining case (Kf6), the king stepped directly into an open e-file where a queen-rook battery delivered forced mate. In each position, safer king squares existed (Kh1 instead of Kf1, Kh6/Kg7 instead of Kg8, staying on e7 instead of Ke8) or non-king moves (Qf2, Qg2, Qf7, Qg6, Qd6) were superior. The common thread is that the chosen king square falls on a rank or file dominated by the opponent's major pieces, turning what seemed like a routine king tuck or repositioning into a catastrophic exposure.
analysis.move_pattern: King move (any direction) landing on a square aligned with opponent's heavy pieces on open files or back rank
analysis.why_bad: The king lands on a square that is tactically exploitable by the opponent's queens/rooks on open lines, allowing checks with tempo, captures with check, back-rank threats, or forced mating sequences that would not exist on the alternative king square.
sub_patterns: King retreats to back rank enabling captures-with-check
King steps onto open file occupied by opponent's queen-rook battery
King moves along back rank toward exposed file instead of toward corner safety

analysis.label: King (or piece) advances forward toward the opponent's forces when defensive retreat was required, walking into immediate tactical punishment.
analysis.description: In 5/5 positions, the player moves a piece forward in an attempt to centralize or actively engage, but the chosen square is tactically compromised. In 4/5 cases it's a king move advancing toward the center or opponent's pieces (Kg6, Kc6, Kf4, Kc6), and in 1/5 it's a knight moving toward advancing enemy pawns (Ng7). In every case, the forward placement enables an immediate tactical refutation: pawn advances with tempo (3/5: h6 attacking Ng7, g5 attacking structure around Kg6, e5# checkmating Kf4), lateral checks forcing unfavorable exchanges (1/5: Rc4+ after Kc6), or queen captures with check along newly-exposed diagonals (1/5: Qxe6+ after Kc6). All 5 positions had at least one safe retreat available (Nd6, Kg7, Kc5, Kg2, Ke8) that maintained the position. The average cp_loss of 2193 reflects the catastrophic nature of these forward lunges.
analysis.move_pattern: King (or minor piece) advances one square forward/centrally, typically toward opponent's pawns or pieces, moving along a rank or diagonal into an exposed square
analysis.why_bad: The advancing piece reaches a square where it is immediately exploited by the opponent's forces—either attacked by advancing pawns, checked along newly-opened lines forcing material loss or exchange, or trapped in a mating net. Retreat would have maintained defensive integrity.
sub_patterns: King advances into pawn storm (g5, h6 breaks become devastating)
King steps onto file/diagonal enabling checks that force losing exchanges
King walks into checkmate net created by pawns and pieces
Piece advances to square immediately attacked and displaced by enemy pawns

analysis.label: Playing a plausible-looking move that abandons the one critical defensive or tactical requirement the position demands.
analysis.description: This feature activates when a player makes a move that appears reasonable (a capture, development, prophylaxis, or centralization) but fatally ignores the single most urgent demand of the position. In 4/6 cases, the move directly removes a piece from a critical defensive post: Bxh3 abandons the e6 bishop's shield of the g8 rook, Na6 removes the knight from guarding d5, g3 removes the pawn's control of h3, and Bd6 blocks the rook's pressure on the open d-file. In 2/6 cases (g6 and Qe4), the move is a slow/misdirected action when the position demands immediate tactical counterplay. All positions share extremely narrow best play (avg 1.5 good moves), meaning only one precise response held the position together. The common thread is that each move addresses a secondary concern while catastrophically neglecting the position's primary tactical reality, resulting in high material loss (avg 378cp).
analysis.move_pattern: Any piece type moving away from a critical defensive square or function; includes pawn moves weakening king shelter, piece retreats to rim, self-blocking moves, and tempo-wasting captures/advances
analysis.why_bad: Each move abandons the ONE thing holding the position together—whether a defensive guard, a critical file's pressure, or the tempo needed to address an urgent threat—allowing the opponent an immediate tactical exploitation (fork, file seizure, passed pawn advance, or knight invasion).
sub_patterns: Moving a defender away from a guarded piece or square (removal of guard)
Blocking one's own active piece on a critical file or diagonal (self-block)
Making a slow prophylactic move when the position demands immediate counteraction
Weakening king shelter by advancing a guarding pawn

analysis.label: Playing slow 'improving' or developing moves (especially rooks to open files) when the position demands an immediate concrete forcing move.
analysis.description: This feature fires on positions where players choose natural-looking, positionally-motivated moves instead of executing critical tactical blows that the position demands. In 5/9 cases, the move involves placing a rook on an open file (Rae1, Rad8, Rc8, Rb8+, Rd8) which appears logical but wastes the tempo needed for a forcing continuation. In 2/9 cases, a queen goes to an 'active' square (Qg4) missing a winning tactical shot. In 2/9 cases, pieces are repositioned to seemingly reasonable posts (Bg4 attacking a knight, Ng1 planning rerouting). The missed best moves are consistently concrete and forcing: pawn breaks (e4 in 3/9 positions), decisive penetrations (Rf2, Qxc1+), or precise defensive retreats (Qd1). The positions share extremely low good-move counts (avg 1.4), meaning only one or two moves maintain the evaluation—the position is on a knife-edge demanding precision, not general improvement. The opponent consistently gains a tempo to consolidate, block a tactical mechanism, or launch a faster counter-attack.
analysis.move_pattern: Pieces (especially rooks and queens) moved to 'natural' or seemingly active squares—open files, attacking posts, centralization—rather than executing an immediate forcing capture, check, or pawn break
analysis.why_bad: These moves waste a critical tempo in positions where a concrete forcing move would exploit a fleeting tactical vulnerability (exposed king, discovered attack, back-rank weakness, undefended pawn). The opponent uses the gifted tempo to consolidate defenses, block key files, or launch counter-threats that are now faster than the player's slow plan.
sub_patterns: Rook to open file instead of immediate pawn break or penetration (Rae1, Rad8, Rc8, Rd8)
Queen to 'active' square missing a winning capture or forced mate (Qg4 x2)
Piece repositioning when direct action required (Bg4, Ng1)
Pointless check that misplaces a piece away from defense (Rb8+)

analysis.label: Playing a passive or misdirected move instead of the urgent central pawn advance (typically e4) that creates necessary counterplay or a winning threat.
analysis.description: In 3/6 analyzed positions (Positions 1, 3, 6), the literal best move was the pawn push e4, and the player instead chose a passive king move (Kc7, Kd7) or wrong pawn advance (b4). In Position 5, the e4 pawn was central to the defensive formation. In Position 9, the player advanced the wrong pawn (h4 instead of maintaining tension). In Positions 2 and 11, the error was choosing a 'natural' simplifying capture instead of a dynamic alternative that maintained attacking pressure. The unifying thread is that all moves are slow, passive, or misdirected alternatives that squander a critical tempo—particularly devastating in endgames (5/7 positions) where the opponent's king immediately activates (often via Kf3-Ke4) to dominate the center and win the unsupported pawns.
analysis.move_pattern: Passive king retreats (Kc7, Kd7, Kg1), wrong pawn advances (b4, h4), or simplifying captures (cxd6, Nxe4) played instead of a critical central pawn advance
analysis.why_bad: These moves waste a crucial tempo in positions where an immediate pawn advance (usually e4) would create an unstoppable threat or necessary counterplay; the lost tempo allows the opponent's king to activate (typically reaching e4/f3) and dominate the resulting pawn race or structure.
sub_patterns: King retreat instead of e4 push in pawn endgames
Wrong pawn advance (flank instead of center)
Passive simplification instead of dynamic continuation
Moving king away from supporting critical pawns

analysis.label: Piece moves to a seemingly improved or active square while abandoning a critical defensive function or ignoring an immediate tactical vulnerability in the position.
analysis.description: In all 8 positions, the player chose a piece-repositioning move that appeared constructive—developing, activating, or capturing material—but fatally neglected an urgent tactical demand. In 6/8 cases, the piece moved away from a square where it was fulfilling an irreplaceable defensive function (Nb6 abandoned e7 defense, Nd2 abandoned kingside guard, Bg4 abandoned d3 coverage, Rh6 abandoned f-file pressure, Nxa7+ abandoned the dominant b5 outpost, Kg8 moved away from the flexible e7 escape). In 7/8 cases, the opponent punished by exploiting the specific vacancy or vulnerability created (Nf5 hitting undefended e7, Nxg4 winning the exposed h4 knight, Bb4 pinning the misplaced queen, Kf1 escaping all h-file threats, Kb8 trapping the displaced knight). The positions typically had very few good alternatives (avg 1.8), meaning the tactical situation demanded a specific response, but the player chose a 'plan' move in a 'tactics' position. The common evaluation swing (~282cp) reflects how these seemingly reasonable moves catastrophically misread positional priorities.
analysis.move_pattern: Any piece type moving to a square that appears more active, developed, or materially productive (captures included), generally moving AWAY from the critical sector where immediate threats exist
analysis.why_bad: The position demanded addressing an immediate tactical vulnerability (defending a hanging piece, blocking an invasion, maintaining pressure), but the player chose a constructive-looking repositioning move that was fatally too slow or actively abandoned the piece's essential current function, allowing the opponent to exploit the resulting gap.
sub_patterns: Knight rerouting away from defensive post (Nb6, Nd2, Nxa7+)
Piece repositioning to passive/misplaced square (Bg4, Kg8, Rh6)
Piece developing to tactically vulnerable square (Qc3, Bb5)

analysis.label: Moving a well-placed piece away from its optimal active square, surrendering critical positional pressure for a superficially attractive but inferior continuation.
analysis.description: This feature fires on moves that voluntarily displace a piece from a square where it was exerting maximum influence. In 4/6 positions, a bishop is moved from a powerful diagonal (c6→d7 losing long diagonal control, h3→g4 losing kingside paralysis, c6→d5 landing on a tactically vulnerable square, bishop capture on d4 prioritizing material over mating tempo). In the remaining cases, a pawn advance (c4) removes defensive coverage that was holding the position together, and a rook capture (R7xc6+) removes the critical 7th-rank rook from its dominant post. All 6 positions share the pattern that the piece's CURRENT function was more valuable than whatever the move achieved. The refutations consistently exploit the vacuum left by the piece's departure—opponents immediately capitalize on the abandoned diagonal, file, or rank within 1-2 moves.
analysis.move_pattern: Piece (usually bishop) moves away from a square where it controlled a critical diagonal/file, often to a square that appears active (check, capture, centralization) but is tactically inferior
analysis.why_bad: The piece was performing an irreplaceable function on its current square (paralyzing enemy pieces, defending key squares, maintaining coordination, or cutting off the king), and no amount of material gain, checking tempo, or repositioning compensates for losing that function—opponents immediately exploit the positional vacuum.
sub_patterns: Bishop retreating from active diagonal to passive square (Bd7, Bg4)
Giving check/capture that removes piece from dominant position (Bd5+, R7xc6+)
Pawn advance that removes critical defensive coverage (c4)
Capturing material when maintaining pressure yields more (Bxd4)

analysis.label: Moves that abandon a critical defensive responsibility to pursue superficially active or ambitious play while a concrete threat goes unaddressed.
analysis.description: In all 7/7 positions, the player made a move that looked active or purposeful (centralizing a piece, capturing material, attacking something) but catastrophically ignored the single most critical threat in the position. In 5/7 cases, the ignored threat involved invasion on an open file or rank (Ba3 ignoring f-file invasion, Be5 ignoring Rd8# back-rank mate, Ka3 walking into a mating net on the open c-file/third rank, Qh5 abandoning second-rank control allowing Rd2, Qxe6 abandoning f2 defense allowing Qxf2). In 6/7 positions there were only 1-3 good moves available, indicating extremely narrow critical moments where the one correct idea was defensive. The average cp_loss of 2873 reflects how punishing it is to ignore the primary threat: two positions resulted in immediate checkmate, and all others saw decisive material or positional collapse.
analysis.move_pattern: Diverse piece types (B, K, N, Q, pawn) moving to squares that appear active but are functionally disconnected from the position's critical vulnerability - typically moving AWAY from the threatened file/rank/square
analysis.why_bad: Each move abandons the one critical defensive duty (blocking an open file, addressing a back-rank threat, protecting a hanging piece, guarding an invasion square) in favor of a secondary objective, allowing the opponent to exploit the undefended vulnerability with decisive force
sub_patterns: Piece moves to irrelevant diagonal/square while open file invasion is imminent
Greedy capture that removes queen from key defensive post
Slow prophylactic move while immediate tactical threat exists
King move into mating geometry instead of toward safety

analysis.label: Pawn advances or pawn grabs that waste critical tempo in positions (especially endgames) where king activation or direct piece action is required.
analysis.description: This feature fires on moves where the player chooses a pawn advance or material-grabbing capture instead of the required active king/piece play. In 8/10 positions, the phase is endgame, and in 7/10 cases, the move played is a pure pawn advance (c6, e4, f5, b5, h5, a6, g4). Critically, in at least 6/8 positions where the move is suboptimal, the correct alternative was a king move (Kd4, Ke3, Ke5, Kd6, Ke6, or Rxe5 simplification). The remaining errors (Qxg4+ instead of fxg4#, Qxb3 pawn grab, Bd2 ignoring threats) share the same underlying principle: addressing a secondary concern (structure, material) while neglecting the primary positional demand. The 'tempo_loss' tag appears in 8/10 analyses, confirming the unifying theme of wasted tempi through irreversible pawn commitments or misdirected captures.
analysis.move_pattern: Pawn advances (any file, typically one square forward) or queen captures of pawns, played instead of king centralization moves or direct tactical solutions
analysis.why_bad: These moves waste irreplaceable tempo in positions where king activity is the decisive factor. Pawn advances permanently commit structure (eliminating spare tempos, fixing targets, or shortening king-race distances), while pawn grabs pull pieces away from critical defensive/attacking duties. The opponent exploits the tempo loss through king penetration, pawn breaks with check, or immediate tactical threats on the neglected sector.
sub_patterns: Premature pawn push that eliminates a crucial spare tempo in opposition battles (h5, f5)
Pawn move on the wrong flank while the other side requires immediate attention (a6, c6)
Pawn advance instead of king centralization in pure pawn endgames (e4 vs Kd4, f5 vs Ke3)
Queen pawn-grab that abandons critical defensive duties (Qxb3)
Capturing with wrong unit when simpler move wins instantly (Qxg4+ vs fxg4#)

analysis.label: Playing a natural-looking but non-forcing move in a critical position where essentially only one specific move maintains the evaluation.
analysis.description: This feature fires on positions with extremely narrow margins (average 1.4 good moves available) where the player catastrophically fails to find the single critical move. In 8/8 cases, the position demanded one specific concrete action—whether advancing a passed pawn (b2 in position 5), exploiting an exposed king (Bb5+ in position 7), defending a critical square (Kh6 in position 8), or consolidating material (Qc8 in position 4)—but the player instead chose a 'reasonable-looking' alternative that completely ignored the position's most urgent demand. The blunders include premature pawn breaks (e5, g4×2), queen repositions that abandon critical duties (Qe3, Qc5), king moves toward apparent safety that walk into tactical disasters (Kg8, Kf8), and piece retreats from dominant outposts (Nf3). The average cp_loss of 1509 reflects truly catastrophic outcomes: equal positions become lost, winning positions become equal or lost, and defensible positions become forced mates.
analysis.move_pattern: Diverse piece types (pawns, queens, kings, knights) making non-forcing moves that appear constructive (centralizing, gaining space, seeking safety, retreating) but fail to address the position's single critical tactical demand
analysis.why_bad: Each move ignores the ONE concrete action the position demands—whether capturing hanging material, delivering a critical check, pushing a promotion-threatening pawn, or maintaining a piece on its only useful square—allowing the opponent to seize the initiative or exploit the newly created vulnerability
sub_patterns: Premature/unnecessary pawn advances (e5, g4) weakening structure or giving free material
Queen repositioning that abandons support for critical passed pawns or defensive duties
King moves toward apparent safety that walk into mating nets or abandon pawn defense
Piece retreats from dominant outposts that surrender all tactical pressure

analysis.label: Piece moves to an active-looking square but leaves material undefended or creates a tactical vulnerability the opponent immediately exploits.
analysis.description: This feature fires on moves where a player repositions a piece to an apparently active or aggressive square (centralization, activation, attacking a target) but in doing so creates or exposes hanging material. In 7/10 positions, the move directly results in an undefended piece or pawn being captured: Bb2 leaves the bishop hanging after Rd2+ (pos 2), Re7 leaves Ra8 hanging (pos 6), Na4 exposes Ra7 (pos 7), Bf6 abandons defense of d6 pawn (pos 15), Nd4 leaves bishop undefended after exchange (pos 10), and multiple Ne4 moves create exposed recapture pieces (pos 1, 3). In 8/10 positions the player had multiple safe alternatives maintaining the evaluation. The average cp_loss of 240 reflects that these 'improving' moves typically hand the opponent a full piece or pawn advantage through simple captures or short tactical sequences.
analysis.move_pattern: Piece (often knight) moves to a central or active-looking square, typically 1-2 squares toward the center or an attacking diagonal, non-capturing, non-checking
analysis.why_bad: The move prioritizes superficial piece activity over concrete material safety, either abandoning a defensive duty (guarding a piece/pawn), placing the moved piece where it can be captured profitably, or creating a geometric alignment (fork target, check+capture) that allows the opponent to win material in 1-2 moves.
sub_patterns: Knight centralizes to a square where exchange forces recapture onto an exposed/attackable square (Ne4 positions 1, 3)
Piece activates to undefended square while king position allows check+capture combination (Bb2 position 2)
Piece repositions abandoning sole defense of a pawn or piece the opponent immediately captures (Bf6, Re7)
Knight jumps create fork target alongside another piece on the same rank/diagonal (Ne4 pos 4, Nd4 pos 10)
Piece decentralizes to attack peripheral target while leaving major piece undefended (Na4 position 7)

analysis.label: Playing a plausible-looking but non-urgent move in a position that demands one specific critical action, wasting an irreplaceable tempo.
analysis.description: This feature fires on positions where the evaluation is razor-sharp (avg 1.5 good moves available) and the player makes a natural-looking, seemingly purposeful move that fails to address the single most critical demand of the position. The moves include pointless checks that accomplish nothing (Nb2+ returning the knight to its original square, 1/10), passive piece repositioning that ignores threats (Rb1 ignoring a centralized knight, Rc3 placing a rook on a capturable square, Rfc8 removing a rook from the critical file, 3/10), premature or unnecessary king moves that waste tempo (Ke2, Kh6, Kh1, 3/10), wrong captures or pawn moves that leave pieces hanging (dxe4 wrong pawn, d6 ignoring bishop en prise, 2/10), and greedy queen moves that abandon critical defense (Qd4, 1/10). In every case, 'tempo_loss' is identified as a primary tag (8/8 analyzed positions), and the critical thread is that each move LOOKS constructive—developing, repositioning, checking, or capturing—but addresses a secondary concern while the position screams for one specific action that only 1-2 moves can provide.
analysis.move_pattern: Mixed piece types making quiet repositioning moves, wrong captures, purposeless checks, or unnecessary king moves—all sharing the property of consuming a tempo without addressing the position's primary tactical/dynamic requirement
analysis.why_bad: These moves waste an irreplaceable tempo in positions where the evaluation is extremely sensitive to timing—the position demands ONE specific action (neutralizing a threat, maintaining an attack, or executing a critical break), and the chosen move addresses a secondary concern, allowing the opponent to seize the initiative, win material, or consolidate a defense that would otherwise have been impossible
sub_patterns: Purposeless checks that achieve nothing structural (Nb2+ returning to c4)
Passive rook repositioning ignoring active threats (Rb1, Rc3, Rfc8)
Unnecessary king moves in positions demanding piece action (Ke2, Kh6, Kh1)
Wrong capture or supporting move leaving pieces en prise (dxe4, d6)
Greedy queen excursion abandoning critical defensive duties (Qd4)

analysis.label: Playing a strategically-motivated piece move that overlooks an immediate concrete tactical reality in the position.
analysis.description: This feature fires on positions where the player chooses a move with a logical strategic rationale (grabbing material, repositioning a piece, attacking a target) but critically misses an urgent tactical element. In 4/7 positions, the player ignored a hanging piece - either leaving their own piece en prise (Qxb7 walking into capture, Nf4 allowing Ne1+ fork on rook) or failing to capture an opponent's undefended piece (Be7 instead of Rxc8). In 5/7 positions, the move involved a 'tempo_loss' where a seemingly purposeful piece maneuver (Bg3 retreating from dominant c7, Kh2 retreating passively, Ne4 advancing to an unsustainable square) actually squandered the position's concrete demands. In 4/7 cases, the better alternative was a forcing/concrete move (Qxd5 with interposition available, Rxc8 free capture, Kf4 active centralization, Bd6 direct attack). The common thread is that positions demanded immediate tactical precision but the player defaulted to a general-purpose 'improving' move.
analysis.move_pattern: Any piece type moving to a square that appears active/purposeful but ignores a critical tactical relationship (capture, fork, check) in the position
analysis.why_bad: The move addresses a strategic concern (piece placement, material gain, repositioning) while overlooking a concrete tactical reality - a hanging piece, an available fork, a forced sequence, or a critical tempo requirement that the position demands be addressed immediately.
sub_patterns: Retreating active pieces to passive squares when aggression was needed (Bg3, Kh2)
Greedy captures that walk into tactical punishment (Qxb7 into queen capture, Bxd5 allowing fork)
Slow repositioning ignoring free material or forcing moves (Be7 missing Rxc8)
Moving a strong piece away from dominant post enabling opponent tactics (Nf4 allowing Ne1+ fork)
Advancing pieces to unsustainable outposts that waste critical tempo (Ne4)

analysis.label: Quiet, non-forcing moves played in positions that demand immediate concrete action, resulting in catastrophic tempo loss.
analysis.description: This feature activates on moves that are passive, non-threatening, and seemingly 'safe' or 'routine' but critically waste tempo in positions requiring immediate dynamic engagement. In 4/5 positions, the move is explicitly tagged as a tempo loss. The moves include king retreats (Kg1, Ke8), a quiet development (Nc3), and slow pawn moves (a3, b6) — all chosen when the position demanded confrontational play like challenging a dominant piece (f6 vs Ne5 in position 13), addressing center tension (c3 in position 10), centralizing actively (Be5 in position 8), gaining space (h5 in position 3), or defending a critical weakness (f3 in position 2). In each case, the player chose a 'housekeeping' move that appeared safe but gifted the opponent time to execute decisive tactical or strategic plans. The average cp_loss of 340 and average of only 1.8 good moves available confirms these are razor-thin positions where only active/forcing play survives.
analysis.move_pattern: Varied piece types (kings, knights, pawns); all are non-capturing, non-checking, non-forcing moves to passive or routine squares; typically retreats or prophylactic shuffles
analysis.why_bad: These moves waste a critical tempo in positions where the opponent has immediate tactical resources (forks, central breaks, penetration on open files) that can only be prevented by forcing or confrontational play; the quiet move hands the initiative to the opponent who then exploits the time gift decisively.
sub_patterns: King retreat to seemingly safe but tactically vulnerable square (Kg1, Ke8)
Prophylactic pawn push when center tension demands immediate resolution (a3, b6)
Routine development ignoring urgent need for active piece play (Nc3)

analysis.label: Moves by the losing side in decisively evaluated king-and-pawn endgames where passed pawn promotion is unstoppable.
analysis.description: This feature fires on moves in pawn endgames (13/13 endgame) where the evaluation is already decisive (typically ±500+ centipawns) and the position revolves around an unstoppable passed pawn. The vast majority are king moves (10/13) with occasional quiet pawn moves (3/13), almost always played by the losing side attempting futile resistance. In 6/13 positions the move has 0 or near-0 cp loss (the position is equally hopeless regardless), while in the remaining cases the error involves a tempo loss—either moving a pawn when the king should move (positions 3, 11, 14: a3, g5, h6), or moving the king in the wrong direction away from the critical defensive square (positions 5, 8, 9). The common thread is that these are quiet, non-forcing moves in positions where the passed pawn dynamics have already decided the game and king activity/tempo is the only remaining question.
analysis.move_pattern: King moves (or quiet pawn pushes) by the losing side in K+P endgames, typically non-forcing, moving toward or away from a passed pawn's promotion path
analysis.why_bad: When these moves are actual errors, they waste a critical tempo in a pawn race—either pushing a pawn when the king should march, or placing the king on a square where opponent gains tempo (via check or uncontested infiltration). In decisive positions, even one lost tempo transforms 'lost but resistant' into 'immediately collapsing'.
sub_patterns: Pawn push instead of king activation (a3, g5, h6 tempo losses)
King moves to wrong direction abandoning critical defensive square
Optimal defensive king moves in theoretically lost K+P positions (0 cp loss)

analysis.label: Moves that pursue secondary positional goals while neglecting a critical defensive duty or immediate tactical necessity.
analysis.description: This feature fires on middlegame moves where a player makes a seemingly reasonable or 'improving' move that fatally neglects the most urgent demand of the position. In 4/6 positions, the moved piece was either currently performing a defensive function or needed to go to a specific square for defense (Qxc3 abandons defense of Na4, Nb2 removes a central defender from d5/e3, Bf6 wastes a tempo when a rook needed to reach b8, Qf6 walks into a discovered attack on the f-file).
