In the remaining 2/6 positions, the player ignores an existing lethal threat to pursue a secondary plan (h5 ignores back-rank Rd8+ deflection, Qe3 misses a forced mate in 2). All moves share the characteristic of being 'reasonable-looking' from a positional perspective - centralizing, capturing a pawn, repositioning a piece, pushing for kingside play - while the position demanded specific tactical accuracy to address an immediate vulnerability.
analysis.move_pattern: Various piece types move to 'improving' or 'active' squares, typically away from critical defensive posts or toward positions that create new vulnerabilities; no single geometric direction dominates
analysis.why_bad: Each move breaks or fails to establish a critical defensive connection, allowing the opponent to exploit a specific tactical vulnerability (discovered attack, back-rank mate, hanging piece, fork) that the correct moves would have neutralized
sub_patterns: Moving a defender away from a piece it protects, leaving it hanging (Qxc3, Nb2, Bf6)
Ignoring back-rank or mating threats to pursue flank/positional play (h5, Qe3)
Walking a piece into a tactically vulnerable square (Qf6)

analysis.label: Playing a non-urgent move in a simplified endgame instead of the one decisive pawn-restraining or king-penetration move, giving the opponent a critical tempo to equalize.
analysis.description: All 6/6 positions are simplified endgames (mostly pure pawn endings) where only 1-2 good moves exist and the player wastes a decisive tempo. The core pattern: in each case, there was one 'now-or-never' move to either restrain the opponent's key pawn advance or achieve decisive king penetration, but the player chose a different logical-looking move that gave the opponent exactly one tempo to neutralize the advantage. In Position 2, Kf5 allowed ...b5 (should have played b5 first); in Position 4, g3 allowed ...h5 (should have played g4 to freeze the kingside); in Position 7, Kd3 allowed ...f5 equalization (should have played Ke5 for immediate penetration); in Position 8, ...c4 allowed c3 blockade (should have advanced d4 first); in Position 9, ...a5 allowed bxa5+a4 blockade (should have played ...b5 to lock the queenside); in Position 12, e4 allowed ...a4 passed pawn (should have played a4 to restrain it). In every case (6/6), the opponent's equalizing resource was a specific pawn move that the correct move would have prevented.
analysis.move_pattern: Any non-forcing move (pawn advance or king move) that fails to address the board's most critical structural urgency - typically ignoring the need to fix/restrain the opponent's pawn structure
analysis.why_bad: In razor-sharp pawn endgames with minimal margin for error, one tempo is the difference between winning and drawing; these moves allow the opponent to execute their one saving pawn advance (creating a blockade, generating a passed pawn, or fixing the structure favorably) that the correct move would have permanently prevented.
sub_patterns: Advancing own pawn that allows opponent's blockade (c4/a5/e4 enabling opponent's c3/bxa5+a4/a4)
Insufficient pawn advance giving opponent counterplay tempo (g3 instead of g4)
King move ignoring critical pawn-fixing priority (Kf5 instead of b5, Kd3 instead of Ke5)

analysis.label: Aimless piece repositioning in positions where exactly one concrete action (pawn advance, check, or capture) was required to maintain the evaluation.
analysis.description: This feature fires on moves that reposition a piece to a seemingly purposeful square but waste the single critical tempo available in a position with very narrow margins (avg 1.4 good moves). In 8/9 positions, the analyses explicitly tag 'tempo_loss' as the tactical motif. The pattern is consistent: the best move creates an immediate concrete threat (passed pawn advance in 7/9, tempo-gaining check in 2/9, material capture in 2/9), while the played move is a non-forcing 'improvement' that allows the opponent to establish a defensive setup or launch counterplay that would have been impossible one move later. The positions are overwhelmingly endgames (8/9) where a single tempo often determines whether a passed pawn decides or a king reaches a critical square. The average cp_loss of 233 reflects that these are positions at a tipping point where the concrete action wins/draws but any delay catastrophically shifts the evaluation.
analysis.move_pattern: Non-forcing piece repositioning (rook to new rank, king centralization, bishop relocation, or quiet pawn push) that does not create an immediate check, winning capture, or unstoppable pawn promotion threat
analysis.why_bad: In positions with exactly one winning/drawing plan, these moves waste the critical tempo needed to execute it, allowing the opponent to establish blockades, capture undefended pawns, create counterplay, or reach defensive squares that would have been impossible had the concrete action been played immediately.
sub_patterns: Rook moving to seemingly active rank (7th/8th) while abandoning pressure on key pawns (Rg7, Rg8, Rb7)
King advancing to 'active' square but abandoning defensive duties or walking into tempo-gaining checks (Kg7, Kf4)
Bishop repositioning away from a square where it creates concrete pressure (Be6 x2)
Quiet pawn push instead of decisive king centralization (c4)
Capturing with the wrong piece, making the capturing piece passive (Rxh4)

analysis.label: Playing a natural-looking but non-urgent move in a position where exactly one time-critical action is required to maintain a winning advantage.
analysis.description: In all 4/4 positions, the player makes a 'reasonable' move that addresses a secondary concern while ignoring the one urgent action the position demands. In Position 1, Rf7 supports the g-pawn but ignores the king's g-file vulnerability (needed Kg2). In Position 3, Kb6 evacuates the c-file but walks into Nd7+ (needed Kd8). In Position 5, Bxe6 launches an unsound attack when quiet consolidation with Nf5 was required. In Position 9, Ke2 centralizes the king but loses the pawn race where b6 was the only winning push. All 4/4 positions have extremely few good moves (avg 1.2), meaning the correct path is razor-thin. The average cp_loss of 2841 reflects that these tempo losses are catastrophic because the opponent's refutation exploits the exact tempo wasted — whether to blockade a pawn (Position 9), deliver a check (Position 1), fork with a knight check (Position 3), or consolidate material advantage (Position 5).
analysis.move_pattern: Quiet, non-forcing moves (king walks, rook repositions, piece captures without follow-up) that fail to address the position's single most urgent tactical demand
analysis.why_bad: Each move wastes exactly the critical tempo the opponent needs to neutralize the player's advantage — whether by reaching a blockade square, delivering a back-rank/file check, exploiting a discovered tactical motif, or simply consolidating extra material
sub_patterns: King move when pawn push wins the race
Piece repositioning when king must escape a tactical vulnerability
King move to a square vulnerable to forcing checks/forks
Unsound sacrifice instead of quiet consolidation

analysis.label: Playing a routine-looking move (capture, development, or pawn push) that leaves one's own piece undefended or ignores a critical hanging piece, when a tactically aware alternative was required.
analysis.description: This feature fires on moves that appear natural or structurally motivated but catastrophically fail to address an immediate hanging-piece situation. In 5/7 positions, the tactical motif is explicitly 'hanging_piece': Position 3 (d5 opens the a1-h8 diagonal leaving Ra1 undefended), Position 5 (Bxd4 removes the sole defender of Nf4), Position 10 (Bf6 ignores capturing opponent's hanging Be8), Position 14 (cxd4 removes the blocking pawn on c3, exposing Re1 on the a5-e1 diagonal), and Position 8 (g3 ignores Ne2+ fork winning the exchange). The remaining positions (6, 12) share the broader pattern of choosing a positional/structural move over addressing the position's most urgent tactical demand. The average cp_loss of 242 and only 2.1 good moves available confirm these are critical moments where concrete tactical calculation was needed but the player defaulted to a 'reasonable-looking' move.
analysis.move_pattern: Pawn pushes/captures or piece moves to natural squares that remove a defending piece/pawn from a critical line or square, or ignore an opponent's undefended piece
analysis.why_bad: The move removes a piece or pawn that was performing a critical defensive function (blocking a diagonal, defending another piece) or wastes a tempo on a non-urgent concern while an opponent's piece hangs or a tactical threat demands immediate attention, resulting in material loss.
sub_patterns: Pawn capture/push that opens a line to own undefended piece (d5, cxd4, bxc6)
Piece move that removes a critical defender of another piece (Bxd4)
Developing/repositioning move that ignores opponent's hanging piece (Bf6)
Quiet prophylactic move that ignores an imminent tactical threat (g3, Ngf6)

analysis.label: Playing an ambitious or active-looking move that ignores an imminent tactical threat requiring immediate attention.
analysis.description: In all 5/5 positions, the player made a move pursuing their own agenda—rook activation (Rd2, Ra3), counterplay (Qc7), a greedy capture (dxe7), or slow preparation (g6)—while the position demanded addressing a concrete, imminent tactical threat. In each case, the opponent had a forcing response available (check, combination, or double attack) that the move completely failed to prevent: Rc6 winning a queen (Position 3), d6 winning material via a pawn fork (Position 4), Bxf2+ deflection winning the queen (Position 7), Qf5+ check exploiting the abandoned defensive coverage (Position 8), and Qh5 creating an unstoppable double attack on f3 (Position 14). All 5/5 positions are tagged with both 'missed_tactic' and 'tempo_loss', and 5/5 feature 'piece_activity' as a tag—indicating the player chose an active-looking move when only precise defensive play could hold. The average good moves available was just 1.8, meaning these were tactically demanding positions with narrow saving paths that the player ignored in favor of their own plans.
analysis.move_pattern: Various piece types (rook, queen, pawn) moved to seemingly active squares or made captures, ignoring opponent's forcing replies (checks, double attacks, combinations)
analysis.why_bad: The moves waste a critical tempo on non-urgent plans while the opponent has a concrete forcing sequence (check, deflection, double attack, or pawn advance) that immediately wins material or creates a decisive attack.
sub_patterns: Rook activation to active-looking squares while leaving pieces undefended (Rd2, Ra3)
Queen seeking counterplay while abandoning critical defensive coverage (Qc7)
Greedy capture opening lines for opponent's tactical shot (dxe7)
Slow preparatory pawn move ignoring opponent's imminent pawn advance (g6)

analysis.label: Natural-looking moves (development, simple captures, quiet pawn pushes) played in positions with extremely narrow margins where only one specific continuation works.
analysis.description: This feature fires on positions where the player makes a 'plausible' or 'routine-looking' move—a piece development, a simple capture, or a preparatory pawn push—while the position actually demands one very specific response. The critical evidence: average good moves available is only 1.6, meaning these positions have almost no margin for error, yet the average cp_loss is 1267, indicating catastrophic punishment for the generic choice. In 6/10 cases the move is in the opening where standard development instincts conflict with concrete tactical demands. Common failures include: routine bishop development that removes a key defender (Bd3 unguards g2, Bc4 creates a fork vulnerability in 2/10), simple captures that overlook recaptures with check or counterattacks (Nxe4 allows Qxe4+, Rxh2 allows Qxh2+, Rxa3 hangs to Kxa3 in 3/10), passive pawn moves instead of the critical active alternative (d6 instead of d5, c6 instead of Nc6 in 2/10), and queen moves that waste tempo when a single precise tactical shot exists (Qxb6 misses c6, Qf3 misses b4/Rxg7+ in 2/10). The unifying thread is that every position has a 'hidden' critical requirement—exploiting a pin, preventing a diagonal attack, maintaining piece coordination—that the player's generic move completely ignores.
analysis.move_pattern: Mixed piece types and directions; typically development moves (Bc4, Bd3, Nc3), simple captures (Qxb6, Rxa3, Nxe4, Rxh2), passive pawn pushes (d6, c6), or purposeless repositioning (Qf3) that ignore the position's one critical path
analysis.why_bad: The position has extremely few good options (avg 1.6) demanding one specific precise move, but the player defaults to a generic 'normal-looking' alternative that either creates a tactical vulnerability, wastes a critical tempo, removes a key defender, or misses the only winning continuation
sub_patterns: Captures that allow devastating recaptures with check or counterattack (Nxe4→Qxe4+, Rxh2→Qxh2+, Rxa3→Kxa3)
Bishop development that removes a critical defender or creates fork vulnerability (Bd3 unguards g2, Bc4 allows cxd4/Qc5 fork)
Passive pawn moves blocking own pieces instead of the active alternative (d6 vs d5, c6 blocking Nc6)
Piece repositioning that wastes the one tempo needed for the critical tactic (Qf3 missing b4, Nc3 missing castling)

analysis.label: Voluntarily exchanging your most powerfully centralized or active piece for a less important enemy piece, surrendering positional dominance.
analysis.description: This feature fires when a player captures an opponent's piece using their own most dominant, centralized, or active piece—typically a knight on a powerful outpost (e5, d5, d4, d6) or an active bishop—when the position demanded maintaining that piece's influence. In 8/10 positions, the captured-with piece was explicitly described as the player's strongest or most centralized piece. In 7/10 cases, the capture was made by a knight; in 3/10 by a bishop. The better alternatives consistently involved either (a) maintaining the dominant piece while improving other pieces (e.g., preparatory rook moves, pawn advances to gain tempo), or (b) redirecting the strong piece to an even more devastating square. The average cp_loss of 239 reflects that these trades consistently convert winning or clearly better positions into equal or worse ones, as removing the key attacking piece allows the opponent to consolidate, castle, or neutralize pressure.
analysis.move_pattern: Knight or bishop captures an enemy piece (usually minor piece), where the capturing piece occupied a dominant central outpost or controlled critical squares
analysis.why_bad: The player's most active/centralized piece was the linchpin of their positional or tactical advantage; removing it from the board eliminates attacking pressure, grants the opponent time to consolidate (often castling or reorganizing), and typically gains no material since the trade is roughly equal in piece value but vastly unequal in positional value.
sub_patterns: Centralized knight on e5/d5/d4/d6 captures passive enemy piece instead of being maintained or redeployed
Premature capture before preparatory moves that would make the exchange far more favorable (move-order error)
Bishop captures a piece that could be driven away with a tempo-gaining pawn advance
Active piece exchanges into opponent's recapture that activates their dormant pieces

analysis.label: Natural-looking non-forcing moves (king walks, piece repositioning) that ignore an immediate tactical vulnerability in the position.
analysis.description: This feature fires on positions where the player makes a plausible, quiet repositioning move while a critical tactical obligation goes unaddressed. In 5/5 positions, the move played was non-forcing (no check, no capture, no direct threat) - typically a king safety move or piece relocation that would be reasonable in a calmer position. In 4/5 cases, only 1 good move existed within 50cp of optimal, indicating razor-sharp positions demanding concrete precision rather than general improvement. The resulting errors leave pieces hanging (Kg7 with queen en prise on e5, Rab1 leaving a2 undefended - 2/5), allow deflection/forcing sequences (Qf8 allowing Rxb6+ deflection - 1/5), permit tempo-gaining checks to key squares (Kh6 allowing Nf5+ - 1/5), or enable unwanted simplification (Qf6 allowing Qxf6+ trade - 1/5). In several cases the correct move was strikingly similar to the blunder (Rfb1 vs Rab1, Kh7 vs Kh6), suggesting the player had the right strategic intuition but failed the concrete calculation.
analysis.move_pattern: Non-forcing piece repositioning (king steps, queen relocations, rook shuffles) to nearby/natural-looking squares, without delivering check or making a capture
analysis.why_bad: The position demands an immediate concrete response to a tactical vulnerability (hanging piece, deflection opportunity, knight fork square), but the player makes a 'general improvement' move that either creates or fails to address the critical tactical problem, allowing the opponent a forcing blow (check, capture, or deflection sacrifice)
sub_patterns: Wrong rook choice leaving pawn undefended
King stepping to knight-controlled square
Queen repositioning allowing deflection/trade
Prophylactic king move ignoring hanging piece

analysis.label: Seemingly constructive forward moves that waste a critical tempo by failing to address the position's most urgent concrete requirement.
analysis.description: This feature fires on positions where the player makes a move that appears active, purposeful, or constructive—advancing a pawn (c5, h6, f5, c6), placing a rook aggressively (Re3+, Rc7, Ra7), or capturing material (Nxc6)—but which fundamentally misses the position's single most critical concrete demand. In 6/8 positions, only 1 good move existed (avg 1.9 good moves), indicating razor-sharp moments requiring precise action. The tempo-loss tag appears in 4/8 positions directly, and the broader theme of wasted time pervades nearly all examples: Rc7 wastes the king-advance tempo needed for Kg6 to win the endgame; h6 wastes a move when Rd8 was the only way to address a passed pawn; Ra7 blockades prophylactically when Kxf4 captures free material immediately; Re3+ looks forcing but allows the opponent to trade off the critical attacking piece; c5 releases tension prematurely instead of exploiting it with d5; f5 pushes into a capture that hands the opponent a free pawn and outpost; Nxc6 grabs material but abandons a dominant outpost leaving f4 hanging. The positions are predominantly endgames (4/8) with exposed kings where one tempo determines the outcome.
analysis.move_pattern: Forward-advancing moves (pawns pushed forward, rooks to 7th rank or toward opponent, knight capturing forward) that appear to make progress toward the opponent's position
analysis.why_bad: These moves prioritize a secondary goal (space, prophylaxis, material, forcing checks) while missing the ONE concrete action the position demands—typically a specific king advance, a forced tactical combination, or an immediate capture that the position's urgency requires RIGHT NOW before the window closes.
sub_patterns: Cosmetic pawn advances in time-critical endgames (h6, c5, f5)
Natural rook improvements missing critical king advances (Rc7, Ra7)
Superficial forcing moves that lose attacking material (Re3+)
Material-grabbing captures that abandon dominant piece placement (Nxc6)

analysis.label: A piece relocates to an apparently active or purposeful square, but abandons its critical role defending a specific target that the opponent immediately exploits.
analysis.description: In 4/5 positions, a piece moves to what looks like a strong or active square but leaves behind undefended material that is immediately captured or exploited. In Position 4, Na5 abandons c6 where the knight guarded against the Greek Gift sacrifice on h7, allowing Bxh7+. In Position 5, Bd6 places the bishop on a 'dominating' outpost but it hangs directly to Rxd6. In Position 10, Rb6 advances the rook from b5 (where it was indirectly defended by the queen) to b6 (where it becomes undefended after the forced Nxd3/Qxd3 sequence), allowing Qxb6 to win it. In Position 12, Nc4 leaves b6 where it protected the d5 pawn, allowing the immediate Qxd5 capturing the hanging pawn with devastating effect. In Position 14, Ke8 moves the king away from the g5 pawn threat, wasting a critical tempo. The consistent theme (5/5) is that the move is strategically motivated—seeking an outpost, centralization, or activation—but tactically negligent, ignoring the piece's existing defensive responsibility.
analysis.move_pattern: Piece (knight, bishop, rook, or king) relocates from a square where it defends something to a square that appears more active but leaves the defended target en prise
analysis.why_bad: The relocated piece was performing a critical dual function (active + defensive), and once it leaves, a specific target (pawn, piece, or square) becomes immediately capturable through a simple tactic or short combination that the opponent executes with tempo
sub_patterns: Knight leaves defensive square, unguarding a pawn or key square (Na5 abandoning h7 defense, Nc4 abandoning d5)
Piece moves to an undefended square where it can be directly captured (Bd6 hangs to rook, Rb6 hangs after deflection)
King/piece moves in wrong direction, wasting tempo when immediate defensive action is required

analysis.label: Playing slow or passive moves (especially piece blockades) in endgames with passed pawns where urgent active counterplay or immediate tactical resolution is required.
analysis.description: This feature fires on endgame positions (11/12) where both sides have passed pawns or critical pawn threats, creating a time-sensitive race dynamic. The blundering moves consistently choose passive defense—typically relocating a piece to blockade or restrain the opponent's pawn—over the urgently needed active play. Key examples: Bh2 passively blockades when Ke3 activates the king (Position 14); Nb2 passively blockades when h4 pushes the decisive pawn (Position 15); Ba8 commits to a static blockade when Rxh5 eliminates a passed pawn actively (Position 9); Bg6 blockades the wrong pawn while the real threat goes unaddressed (Position 5); b3 makes a slow prophylactic move while an e2 promotion threat demands immediate attention (Position 3). In 10/12 positions, the correct alternative involved either king activation, advancing one's own passed pawn, or resolving an immediate tactical vulnerability. The consistent thread is that the player identifies a valid defensive concern but addresses it in a tempo-wasteful manner, failing to recognize that the position's racing character demands immediate counteraction rather than consolidation.
analysis.move_pattern: Piece (usually bishop/knight) relocating to a passive square on back ranks or rim, or slow pawn moves; typically lateral or retreating piece movements to defensive/blockading positions
analysis.why_bad: In pawn-race endgames, tempo is paramount. These moves waste a critical tempo on passive defense (blockading, prophylaxis) when the position demands immediate active counterplay—either advancing one's own passed pawn, activating the king, or resolving an urgent tactical threat. The opponent exploits the wasted tempo to advance their own plans faster or win material from tactical vulnerabilities left unaddressed.
sub_patterns: Bishop/knight placed on passive blockading square instead of king activation or pawn push
Slow prophylactic pawn move ignoring immediate tactical crisis (hanging piece or promotion threat)
Piece trade or capture that removes active potential when restraint from distance was superior
Addressing secondary threat while ignoring the primary one in a multi-pawn-threat position

analysis.label: Moving a piece away from its essential defensive post, immediately leaving a key target or square undefended for tactical exploitation.
analysis.description: This feature fires when a player voluntarily relocates a piece that was performing a critical defensive function—guarding a piece, covering key squares, or shielding the king—to a passive or irrelevant square, allowing immediate punishment. In 6/8 positions, the moved piece was the sole defender of a specific target that gets exploited within one move (Qa7 abandons e7 bishop defense, Qd2 abandons kingside squares g3/g4/f2, Kh2 exposes f2 to check, Kb7/Kb6 leave c2 pawn undefended, Ne8 abandons d6 outpost leaving central control). In 7/8 cases, better alternatives involved either maintaining the defensive function or addressing the threat before relocating. The positions consistently feature pieces that appear to have reasonable destinations but whose departure creates an immediate tactical or positional hole that outweighs any benefit of the new square.
analysis.move_pattern: Any piece type moving away from a defended target/critical square, typically retreating or moving toward the board edge, without being forced to move
analysis.why_bad: The piece was the critical (often sole) defender of a target, square, or king shield; removing it immediately exposes that target to capture, check, or invasion that the opponent exploits within 1-2 moves
sub_patterns: Queen leaving defended piece/kingside squares (Qa7, Qd2)
King moving away from pawns it should protect (Kb7, Kb6, Kh2)
Knight retreating from dominant outpost to rim/passive square (Ng3, Ne8)
Pawn capture removing own king's shield (fxe3)

analysis.label: A piece (usually knight) captures an advanced wing pawn on the b- or g-file that is defended by an adjacent pawn, resulting in losing the piece for just one pawn after the simple pawn recapture.
analysis.description: In all 10/10 positions, a piece captures a pawn on b4/b5 or g4/g5 that is defended by an adjacent pawn (a-pawn, c-pawn, f-pawn, or h-pawn). The refutation in every case is a simple pawn recapture (axb4/axb5/cxb5/hxg5/fxg4), winning the capturing piece for just one pawn. The player appears to see the wing pawn as a free or weakly-defended target, miscalculating that after the recapture sequence they will have adequate compensation (threats, pins, or forks), but in reality they end up losing approximately a full piece. In 9/10 cases the capturing piece is a knight, and 9/10 occur in the opening phase when both sides are still developing. The positions consistently feature uncastled kings (both sides in center) and the erroneous belief that the resulting piece placement or tactical follow-up justifies the material investment.
analysis.move_pattern: Knight (or bishop) captures a pawn on the 4th or 5th rank of the b-file or g-file (wing squares b4, b5, g4, g5), where an adjacent pawn can immediately recapture
analysis.why_bad: The captured pawn is defended by an adjacent file pawn (a/c for b-file, f/h for g-file) that simply recaptures, winning the piece for a single pawn with no adequate compensation in the resulting position
sub_patterns: Nxb4 recaptured by axb4 on queenside
Nxb5 recaptured by axb5 or cxb5 on queenside
Nxg5/Bxg5 recaptured by hxg5 on kingside
Nxg4 recaptured by fxg4 on kingside

analysis.label: Quiet or aimless moves that waste critical tempo in positions where passed pawn dynamics demand immediate concrete action.
analysis.description: In all 5/5 positions, the player chose a move that appears superficially useful (developing a bishop, giving a check, centralizing a king, attacking a piece) but fatally ignores the time-critical nature of passed pawn races. In 3/5 cases, the opponent had dangerous advanced passed pawns requiring immediate attention (Bb2 ignoring g4, Rg1+ ignoring h-pawn race, Kf2 ignoring c6+ opportunity). In 2/5 cases, the player had winning passed pawns they failed to advance (Qg8+ instead of c5, Na5 instead of gxh4). The positions all share extremely high urgency where a single wasted tempo is catastrophic—average cp_loss of 2243 confirms these are among the most devastating possible errors. The best moves in each position were concrete and direct: capturing threatening pawns (Kxg4, gxh4), advancing passed pawns (c6+, c5), or marching the king purposefully (Kb6). Instead, the played moves are either purposeless checks that improve the opponent's king (2/5: Rg1+, Qg8+) or slow positional maneuvers in tactically critical moments (3/5: Bb2, Na5, Kf2).
analysis.move_pattern: Various piece types making quiet repositioning moves or non-productive checks, away from the critical sector where passed pawns demand attention
analysis.why_bad: These moves waste irreplaceable tempo in positions where passed pawn races make time the decisive factor—either failing to stop an opponent's runner or failing to advance one's own, allowing the opponent to reach a critical threshold (promotion, drawing fortress, counterattack) one move too soon.
sub_patterns: Pointless checks that improve opponent's king position (Rg1+, Qg8+)
Quiet piece maneuvers ignoring urgent pawn threats (Bb2, Na5)
Passive king moves missing forcing pawn advances (Kf2 instead of c6+)

analysis.label: Playing a plausible-looking but non-forcing move in a narrow position where essentially only one concrete action (tactical strike, precise centralization, or forcing sequence) maintains the advantage.
analysis.description: This feature fires on moves that waste critical tempo in positions demanding immediate concrete action. The hallmark is extremely narrow positions (avg 1.5 good moves) where the player chooses something superficially reasonable—a prophylactic pawn push (a6, g3: 2/12), a passive retreat or repositioning (Qd8, Qg2, Kf8: 3/12), a premature/misdirected aggressive gesture (Qh3, Qg4, Nh3+: 3/12), or a plausible but wrong piece interaction (Ndf3, Bxf4, Kc7: 3/12)—while missing the one specific forcing move the position requires. In nearly every case, the correct move involves an immediate tactical exploitation (Nf3+ fork in Position 2, Nf1+ fork in Position 12, Nxd6 capture in Position 10, Qxe4 hanging piece in Position 2) or a precise piece centralization that prevents the opponent from consolidating (Ne5 in Position 5, Nd5 in Position 14, Nc6 in Position 15). The played moves uniformly surrender tempo, allowing the opponent to stabilize, reorganize, or seize initiative.
analysis.move_pattern: Diverse piece types and directions; no single geometric pattern. Moves include queen repositionings, slow pawn advances, defensive king moves, purposeless checks, and wrong-order captures—all sharing the trait of being non-forcing in positions requiring forcing play.
analysis.why_bad: These moves address secondary concerns or create superficial threats while ignoring the position's single critical requirement. The resulting tempo loss allows the opponent to neutralize the player's advantage through consolidation (Qg2 allows reorganization), counterattack (g3 leaves e4 hanging), reaching a key defensive square (Re1+ allows Kf2 blockade), or simplifying exchanges (Bxf4 allows recapture that neutralizes pressure).
sub_patterns: Prophylactic pawn moves when tactical shots exist (a6, g3)
Passive queen retreats/repositionings instead of active centralization (Qd8, Qg2)
Counterproductive checks that improve the opponent's piece placement (Re1+, Nh3+)
Premature queen adventures instead of development (Qg4, Qh3)
Wrong capture order allowing opponent's best piece to survive (Bxf4)

analysis.label: Playing a routine developing move instead of capturing an undefended pawn (g2, g7, or b7) that wins the exchange or major material via a long diagonal.
analysis.description: In all 10/10 positions, the player made a natural-looking quiet developing move (Re1, Ngf6, Be7, Nc3, Bb2, Be2, d3, Qb6, Bg7) when an immediate capture of an undefended pawn was available that would win decisive material. The missed tactic follows a consistent pattern: capturing an undefended wing pawn (g2 in 4/10, g7 in 3/10, b7 in 3/10) with a long-range piece (bishop or queen) that then threatens the corner rook (h1, h8, or a8) behind it on the same diagonal. The tactical window is extremely narrow (avg 1.1 good moves), and in every case the opponent can neutralize the threat with a single developing tempo—typically by moving a knight to block the diagonal (Nf3 covering g2/h1, castling covering g7, or playing c6/Nc6 covering b7). The positions all occur in the opening phase with both kings typically in the center, where the attacking diagonal is temporarily unobstructed and the defending piece (usually a knight on g1/g8 or an undeveloped piece) has not yet moved to cover the weakness.
analysis.move_pattern: Any quiet non-capturing developing move (piece placement, pawn push, or repositioning) played instead of a diagonal capture on g2/g7/b7
analysis.why_bad: The move wastes a critical tempo in a position where one specific undefended pawn can be captured immediately to win the exchange (rook for bishop/nothing) via a long diagonal. The opponent needs exactly one move to neutralize the threat (develop a blocking piece, castle, or shore up the pawn), so any non-capturing move permanently surrenders the tactical opportunity.
sub_patterns: Missed Bxg2 winning h1 rook via a8-h1 diagonal
Missed Bxg7 winning h8 rook via a1-h8 diagonal
Missed Qxb7 winning a8 rook via queen invasion
Missed Qxg2 winning undefended g-pawn

analysis.label: Playing a natural-looking developing or improving move in a position that demands immediate concrete action to address a critical tactical or structural urgency.
analysis.description: In all 9/9 positions, the player makes a 'reasonable-looking' move (developing a piece, supporting a pawn, pushing a pawn to attack) that would be perfectly fine in a calm position, but catastrophically ignores the single most urgent demand. In 2/9 cases (Nc6, e6), a piece is left hanging to a simple capture or check. In 4/9 cases (Nbc6, Nc5, c3, b3), critical pawn tension demands immediate resolution—either capturing, reinforcing, or counter-breaking—before the opponent exploits it. In 3/9 cases (h5, Qb8, Bb4), the player misallocates a tempo to a peripheral concern while ignoring a dominant enemy threat or squandering a concrete opportunity. The positions share extremely low good-move counts (avg 1.9), confirming these are critical junctures where only specific urgent responses work. The blundered moves are uniformly non-forcing and address secondary concerns while the position's primary demand goes unmet.
analysis.move_pattern: Non-forcing developing or prophylactic moves (knight development, pawn pushes, piece repositioning) that do not capture, check, or address the immediate tactical flashpoint
analysis.why_bad: Each move wastes a critical tempo on a secondary objective while an urgent concrete demand (hanging piece, pawn tension requiring resolution, dominant enemy piece, forced break timing) goes unaddressed, allowing the opponent to exploit the neglected issue with a forcing sequence
sub_patterns: Developing a piece while leaving another piece tactically hanging (Nc6 with Nf6 en prise, e6 with Bg4 undefended)
Slow pawn/prophylactic move instead of resolving critical central pawn tension (c3 ignoring f4, b3 ignoring gxf3, Nbc6 ignoring d5)
Piece move to apparently strong square but wrong timing enables opponent's break (Nc5 enables e5, h5 enables Bg5, Bb4 enables Ne5)

analysis.label: Playing a quiet move targeting or reacting to a pawn concern while the position urgently demands piece coordination, king safety, or active piece repositioning.
analysis.description: In all 4/4 positions, the player chose a non-forcing move addressing a secondary pawn-related concern (blocking a passed pawn with a6, targeting a weak pawn with Kd5, repositioning a piece aimlessly with Be6, attacking a pawn with Rf1) while the position's primary demand was piece-level: active piece repositioning (Bc4 in position 9), king retreat to safety (Kc3 in position 13), defensive piece placement near the king (Bc6 in position 14), or king activation toward the relevant sector (Kd7 in position 15). In 4/4 cases, the played move was quiet and non-forcing, creating no immediate threats the opponent must address, thereby gifting the opponent a free tempo to solve their problems. The resulting punishment in all cases involved the opponent exploiting the wasted tempo to activate previously constrained pieces, escape with their king, or launch a devastating attack along newly undefended lines. The common evaluation swing averaging ~2570cp reflects how these seemingly innocuous moves catastrophically alter the position's dynamics.
analysis.move_pattern: Quiet non-forcing move (no check, no capture, no direct threat) directed at a pawn target or prophylactic pawn concern rather than the critical piece/king deployment
analysis.why_bad: The position demands urgent action on its primary strategic axis (piece pressure, king safety, or king activation), but the player wastes a critical tempo on a secondary pawn-level concern, giving the opponent time to untangle, escape, or launch a decisive counterattack
sub_patterns: Prophylactic pawn push when piece pressure is critical
King advance toward a pawn target when king safety demands retreat
Piece relocation away from defensive duty when king is under attack
Rook redeployment to attack a pawn when king activation is paramount

analysis.label: Playing aggressive, forward-looking, or greedy moves when the position critically demands addressing the opponent's immediate threats or defensive requirements.
analysis.description: This feature fires on positions where the player makes an active-looking or ambitious move while ignoring a critical defensive requirement, resulting in catastrophic evaluation swings. In 6/6 positions, the best move involved addressing the opponent's most dangerous threat (e4 central break exploiting uncastled king, Bg3 shoring up dark squares, Qd8 retreating to defend mate, forcing trades to prevent Re1#, Nxe4 eliminating a strong piece, Kd2 retreating toward safety), while the played move instead pursued the player's own 'plan' — aggressive piece placement (Nc5, Ra7), irrelevant counterplay (b4), non-forcing queen maneuvers (Qg6, Qxb5), or moving toward danger (Kc3). In 4/6 positions only 1 good move existed, with average cp_loss of 1743, indicating these are critical moments where ignoring the opponent's threats is immediately punished. The refutations exploit exactly what was left unaddressed: hanging pieces (1/6), back-rank mates (1/6), trapped queens (1/6), king exposure (2/6), and mating nets (1/6).
analysis.move_pattern: Varied piece types moving to active/forward squares (or capturing material) when the position demands retreat, defense, or addressing opponent's threats
analysis.why_bad: The moves ignore the opponent's most critical threat — whether it's a mating attack, piece trapping, tactical shot, or positional dominance — in favor of pursuing the player's own plans, and with so few good alternatives (avg 1.7), the resulting punishment is immediate and devastating.
sub_patterns: Greedy captures displacing pieces to vulnerable squares (Qxb5)
Aggressive piece placement ignoring opponent's tactical resources (Nc5, Ra7)
Irrelevant counterplay when under mating attack (b4)
Non-forcing moves when immediate threats require forcing responses (Qg6)
King moving toward danger instead of toward safety (Kc3)

analysis.label: Playing a natural-looking improving move while ignoring an immediate tactical vulnerability that allows the opponent a forcing combination.
analysis.description: This feature fires on quiet, non-forcing moves (piece development, rook activation, king repositioning, pawn advances) that pursue a reasonable long-term plan but fatally ignore an urgent tactical problem. In 8/8 positions, the played move leaves a specific piece or pawn tactically undefended or creates a combinative vulnerability that the opponent can exploit on the very next move. The refutations involve immediate captures or sacrifices: hanging pawns taken (Bxd5 in position 3, Bxh3 in position 7, Nxc6 in position 8), piece captures enabled by newly-created tactical motifs (Rxc3 in position 5, Nxb4 fork in position 6), sacrificial breakthroughs (Bxh6 in position 14), and deflection/back-rank combinations (Rxh6+Rxg8+ in position 15, Bxd4 exploiting e-file pin in position 1). In all cases, the best moves instead addressed the concrete vulnerability first — reinforcing the hanging point, prophylactically removing the king from danger, or closing critical lines.
analysis.move_pattern: Quiet non-forcing moves (no check, no capture, no direct threat) of any piece type — developing bishops, rooks to open files, queen repositioning, king walks, pawn advances — all played when immediate defensive action was required
analysis.why_bad: The moves spend a tempo on general improvement while a specific piece, pawn, or square is tactically undefended, allowing the opponent an immediate forcing combination (capture, sacrifice, or fork) that wins material or creates a decisive attack
sub_patterns: Rook to c-file while a central pawn is hanging (positions 3, 8)
Queen repositioning while a kingside pawn is left undefended (positions 7, 6)
King move that places it on a file dominated by enemy rooks (position 5)
Piece development ignoring that a recapture is impossible due to pin/back-rank (positions 1, 15)
Pawn advance for long-term plan while a piece is under immediate tactical attack (position 8, 14)

analysis.label: Superficially active or forcing moves (especially checks) that miss the precise tactical solution in positions requiring exactness.
analysis.description: This feature fires on catastrophic blunders where the player selects a 'close but wrong' active-looking move instead of the one correct continuation. In 5/11 positions, the blunder is a check that either helps the opponent's king escape (Rh3+ letting Kg7 escape back-rank threats, Qh4+ letting Ke6 reach safety, Rb2+ squandering queen-check wins) or misses a superior check by one square (Bg5+ instead of Bg7#, Rf2+ instead of Rg3+). In the remaining cases, pieces are developed to natural-seeming squares that create tactical vulnerabilities (Bd3 twice allowing tempo-gaining pawn advances, Rd3 falling into knight forks, Be3 ignoring Nxb4). The average good moves available is only 1.9, confirming these are precision-demanding positions where one specific move works and alternatives collapse. The average cp_loss of 3687 reflects that most are game-deciding errors, including 4 positions where mate-in-one or forced mate is missed.
analysis.move_pattern: Piece moves (bishops, rooks, queens) to active-looking squares, frequently delivering checks; often the move is geometrically adjacent to or conceptually similar to the correct forcing move
analysis.why_bad: The move addresses the wrong tactical priority: checks drive kings to safer squares, developments place pieces on vulnerable diagonals, and queen moves abandon critical defensive duties—all while the position demanded one specific precise continuation
sub_patterns: Check on wrong square when checkmate or winning check exists nearby
Check with wrong piece when queen checks maintain winning attack
Bishop/rook development to third rank creating tempo-gain vulnerability
Queen relocation abandoning critical defensive square

analysis.label: Wasting a tempo on an irrelevant or misguided action when the position demands immediate attention to a dangerous passed pawn (own or opponent's).
analysis.description: In all 5/5 positions, there is at least one advanced passed pawn (within 1-3 squares of promotion) that dominates the strategic landscape, and the move played fatally ignores or mishandles it. In Position 6, Black abandons the blockade of White's e7 pawn with Ra8. In Position 9, White uses the rook (Rg7) instead of the king to address the g2 pawn, losing a critical tempo. In Position 10, Black plays b3 ignoring White's a6 passer. In Position 12, Black prematurely advances the c-pawn (c3) without piece support, moving it out of the king's protective radius. In Position 13, White captures material with Kxe4 while Black's a2 pawn is one square from queening. All 5/5 positions are tagged with 'passed_pawn' as the tactical motif, and 5/5 are tagged with 'tempo_loss'. The refutations universally exploit the passed pawn advancing or promoting (often with check), confirming that the single wasted tempo was the decisive error.
analysis.move_pattern: Diverse piece types (rook, pawn, king); the unifying geometric feature is movement AWAY from the critical promotion square or file, redirecting attention elsewhere
analysis.why_bad: In passed-pawn endgames near the promotion zone, a single tempo is often the difference between holding and losing. These moves all squander that tempo on seemingly active but strategically irrelevant actions (material grabs, speculative attacks, premature advances), allowing the passed pawn to advance or the opponent to execute a decisive tactical sequence involving promotion.
sub_patterns: Abandoning blockade of opponent's advanced passed pawn
Capturing material while ignoring imminent promotion threat
Advancing own passed pawn without sufficient piece coordination
Using the wrong piece to address the passed pawn (rook instead of king)

analysis.label: Positions with only one good move where the player makes a superficially reasonable move that catastrophically ignores the position's most urgent tactical requirement.
analysis.description: This feature fires on positions with extremely narrow margins (avg 1.4 good moves available) where the player commits a devastating blunder (avg 2159 cp loss). In 8/10 positions, only one move maintained the evaluation. The common thread is that each blunder appears 'reasonable' in isolation—defending a square (Bf6, 1/10), advancing a passer (d6, 1/10), capturing material (Nxf7, Rxc5, 2/10), giving check (f3+, 1/10), repositioning pieces (Qd2, Qf8, Rc8, 3/10)—but completely ignores the position's single critical demand. The correct moves across all positions share the trait of addressing the ONE urgent tactical issue: blocking an invasion file (Ra8, Ra7), retreating to the only safe square (Kf2), capturing with the correct piece (Qxc5), challenging the opponent's center (c4), or winning material with tempo (Qxe4+). Several blunders allow forced mate (3/10: Ke3, Qf8, f3+ enabling king escape).
analysis.move_pattern: No consistent geometric pattern; diverse piece types and directions (king, rook, pawn, bishop, queen, knight moves in various directions including checks and captures). The unifying factor is decision-making: choosing a plausible but non-critical move when only one precise response exists.
analysis.why_bad: Each move addresses a secondary concern (own plans, development, material gain, prophylaxis) while the position demanded addressing a single urgent tactical issue—an opponent's mating threat, a back-rank weakness, a trapped piece opportunity, or a forcing sequence. The resulting punishment is immediate and severe because the position's narrow tactical margins tolerate zero deviation from the critical path.
sub_patterns: Greedy captures ignoring defensive requirements (Nxf7 ignoring back rank, Rxc5 enabling Ba3)
Pieces abandoning critical defensive duties (Qf8 abandoning a7, Ke3 walking into checks)
Passive/slow moves in positions demanding immediate action (Qd2, g3 when center challenge or active play required)
Checks/advances that help the opponent's king (f3+ enabling Ke3-d3 escape route)
Missing opponent's one forcing resource (Rc8 allowing Nxa8 exchange equalization, d6 enabling Qxb2 infiltration)

analysis.label: Advancing a passed pawn prematurely in endgames without proper preparation, allowing blockade or giving the opponent a critical tempo.
analysis.description: In 6/7 positions, the move played is a one-square pawn advance (d4, d3, g4, b5, b3, e5) in an endgame centered around passed pawn dynamics. The remaining case (Rd2) is a functionally equivalent tempo loss in a passed-pawn race. The common error is pushing a pawn forward when the THREAT of advancing was more valuable than the advance itself. In Position 3, d4 left h5 hanging and could be blockaded. In Position 9, b5 without king escort allowed Kc5 to attack it. In Position 12, b3 walked into a permanent king blockade on b1. In Position 13, e5 gifted the bishop the exact diagonal needed to blockade f7. In Positions 4 and 6, the wasted tempo allowed the opponent's passed pawn to surge forward (c6 and e6 respectively). All 7/7 positions involve passed pawn tension where the critical error is mismanaging tempo in the race.
analysis.move_pattern: Single-square pawn advance (or rook lateral shuffle), typically a central or queenside pawn push, non-capturing, non-checking
analysis.why_bad: The advance either walks the pawn into a blockade (king or bishop reaching the stopping square), leaves other material undefended by committing prematurely, or wastes the critical tempo needed to address the opponent's own passed pawn threats—violating the endgame principle that passed pawns need piece support before advancing.
sub_patterns: Pawn advance into king/bishop blockade square (b3→Kb1, b5→Kc5, e5→Bg7)
Tempo loss allowing opponent's passer to advance one critical rank (g4 allows e6, Rd2 allows c6)
Premature advance abandoning defensive resource (d4 uncovers h5 hanging)

analysis.label: Playing a quiet, non-forcing move (typically a flank pawn push or routine development) when the position demands immediate tactical resolution of central tension or an urgent threat.
analysis.description: This feature fires on positions where the player makes a passive, non-urgent move while ignoring a critical tactical demand. In 7/11 cases, a piece is hanging or a concrete tactical strike is available (Nxe4, fxe5, Nf6+) but the player plays a slow move instead. Flank pawn moves (b6, h6, a6, a6, b4) account for 5/11 positions, while quiet piece development (Nge7, Nf6, Nc3) accounts for 3/11. In 8/11 positions the phase is the opening with unresolved central tension, and in 7/11 cases the blundering side's king remains uncastled, making tempo critically precious. The average number of good moves available is only 1.5, indicating these are narrow positions demanding precision rather than general moves. The common punishment is that the opponent exploits the wasted tempo by capturing undefended material (5/11), executing a central pawn break with tempo (4/11), or launching a direct attack against the exposed king.
analysis.move_pattern: Non-forcing, non-capturing quiet moves - typically flank pawn advances (a6, b6, h6, b4) or routine piece development to safe squares (Nge7, Nf6, Nc3, Ra3, Qd1) - played without addressing the critical tactical tension in the center
analysis.why_bad: The position contains an immediate tactical obligation (defending a hanging piece, exploiting unresolved central tension, or seizing a forcing opportunity) that demands concrete action, but the player instead plays a slow move that wastes a critical tempo, allowing the opponent to either capture undefended material for free or execute a powerful central/kingside break with extra time
sub_patterns: Flank pawn push (a6/b6/h6) with king uncastled and center tense
Routine development ignoring en prise piece
Passive piece retreat abandoning critical defensive duty
Slow positional move missing a forcing tactical blow

analysis.label: Superficially attractive moves (checks, captures, centralizations) that waste critical tempo in positions demanding one precise action.
analysis.description: This feature fires on positions where very few good moves exist (avg 1.6) and the player chooses a move that appears active or forcing but catastrophically fails to address the position's singular critical demand. In 4/8 positions, the blunder is a check or capture-with-check (Nxh3+, Re1+, f6+, Qd8+) that looks forcing but actually helps the opponent (improving their king placement, allowing escape, or trapping the checking piece). In 2/8 positions, the blunder is an 'active' piece centralization (Nd4, Qf5) that abandons a critical defensive duty or walks into a tactical refutation. In 2/8 positions, the blunder is a slow positional move (g3, a4) that ignores an urgent concrete problem. The unifying thread is that all positions had one narrow path requiring precise calculation, and the player was seduced by a move that appears productive on the surface—gaining material, giving check, centralizing, gaining space—while the position's actual critical issue (a trapped piece, back-rank weakness, king vulnerability, or promotion threat) goes unaddressed. The tempo_loss theme appears in 7/7 analyzed positions.
analysis.move_pattern: Mixed piece types and directions; predominately checks (4/8), piece centralizations to active-looking squares (2/8), and slow pawn moves (2/8) — all in positions with very few good alternatives
analysis.why_bad: Each move squanders the one critical tempo needed to address the position's concrete demand — whether that's defending a trapped piece, contesting a file, maintaining a key defender's placement, or executing a precise move order — resulting in the opponent gaining time to exploit the ignored vulnerability
sub_patterns: Pointless or harmful checks that improve opponent's king or trap the checking piece (Re1+, f6+, Qd8+, Nxh3+)
Active-looking centralizations that abandon a critical defensive function (Nd4 unguards g5, Qf5 walks into Re5 battery)
Slow positional moves that ignore an urgent tactical vulnerability (g3 ignores back-rank, a4 ignores Bxh3+)

analysis.label: Non-developing a-pawn or h-pawn advances played as prophylaxis when urgent central tension demands immediate attention.
analysis.description: This feature fires on positions where a player advances a rook pawn (a- or h-file) as a seemingly useful prophylactic or space-gaining move, while critical central pawn tension or tactical obligations go unaddressed. In 12/13 positions, the move is literally a rook pawn advance (h3, h6, h5, a6, a5, a3), with the lone exception (Qh5) being a queen move to the h-file edge that similarly abandons central duties. The refutation in virtually every case involves the opponent exploiting the center: capturing an undefended e5/d5 pawn (positions 1, 4, 8, 10), winning the d5 pawn via cxd5 (positions 2, 5), advancing e5 with tempo (positions 6, 12), or gaining a central tempo against a piece (position 15). The positions are overwhelmingly in the opening (11/13) with the king still in the center (11/13 for the blundering side), making the tempo loss particularly catastrophic.
analysis.move_pattern: Pawn advance on the a-file (a3, a5, a6) or h-file (h3, h5, h6) — always a rook pawn moving one square forward, never a capture or check
analysis.why_bad: These moves waste a critical tempo on a flank pawn when the center has unresolved tactical tension (hanging pawns, pawn breaks available, or pieces needing development/castling), allowing the opponent to exploit the center with material-winning captures or space-gaining advances.
sub_patterns: h6/h3 leaving e-pawn undefended in Italian Game
a6/a5 ignoring cxd5 tension in Queen's Gambit structures
a6/a5 weakening key squares while undeveloped
h5/h6 weakening kingside while king remains uncastled

analysis.label: Playing a non-urgent or peripheral move when the position demands immediate attention to a critical tactical or structural crisis.
analysis.description: This feature fires on moves that ignore the most pressing requirement of the position in favor of a secondary, prophylactic, or peripheral concern. In 8/12 positions the move is made during the opening phase where unresolved central tension demands immediate action. The Na5 moves (3/12) decentralize a knight to attack a bishop while ignoring critical central pawn tension and f7 vulnerabilities. The h6 moves (2/12) make prophylactic wing pawn pushes against hypothetical Bg5/Ng5 while the e5 pawn is already hanging. The queen moves (Qd3, Qa4, Qf3 — 3/12) sortie the queen to seemingly active squares while neglecting development, leaving pieces vulnerable, or even allowing immediate checkmate. The rook moves (Rg8, Rg5 — 2/12) reposition to suboptimal squares while abandoning critical files or missing crushing invasions. The g3 move weakens the king's pawn shield prophylactically while ignoring a hanging knight. In all cases, the player's chosen move would be reasonable in a different context but is catastrophically wrong because the position contains an IMMEDIATE concrete obligation that, when ignored, gifts the opponent a decisive tactical blow.
analysis.move_pattern: Various piece types moving to peripheral/non-critical squares (knights to rim, pawns on wings, queens to exposed squares, rooks to passive files) rather than addressing the critical sector of the board
analysis.why_bad: Each position has a concrete, time-sensitive requirement (resolve central pawn tension, complete development, defend a hanging piece, invade on the 2nd/7th rank, prevent checkmate) that the chosen move completely ignores, gifting the opponent a free tempo to exploit the true vulnerability with captures, forks, sacrifices, or mates.
sub_patterns: Na5 in Italian Game positions: decentralizing knight to rim while f7 and center are tactically critical
Prophylactic h6/g3 pawn pushes while center is under immediate siege or pieces are hanging
Queen sorties to misplaced squares (Qa4, Qd3, Qf3) instead of addressing development or defensive needs
Rook repositioning to inferior files/ranks instead of occupying the decisive invasion square

analysis.label: Playing a non-forcing positional or prophylactic move when the position demands an immediate concrete tactical action, typically a capture or aggressive piece leap.
analysis.description: In 6/7 positions, the player chose a quiet, non-forcing move (pawn push, routine development, or queen repositioning) when a concrete tactical opportunity was available. In 4/7 cases, the best move was a capture winning material (Nxg5, Nxe4, exd5, or equivalent), and in 5/7 cases the best move involved a knight action (Ne1, Nxe4, Nd5, Nxg5, Nd5). The blundered moves share the trait of being 'autopilot' positional choices—h3 as prophylaxis (2/7), e5 for space (2/7), Nc6 for development (1/7), or queen centralization (2/7)—that prioritize general principles over the specific tactical demands of the position. Critically, in several cases the quiet move not only missed a tactic but also created a new vulnerability: h3 became a pawn target for g4, e5 created overextension, and Qe3/Qe2 placed the queen on squares where knight forks (Ng4, Nd4) punished it immediately.
analysis.move_pattern: Non-capturing, non-checking quiet moves (pawn advances to h3/e5, piece development Nc6, queen repositioning Qe2/Qe3) when forcing moves are available
analysis.why_bad: These moves waste a critical tempo in tactically demanding positions, missing available captures or powerful piece leaps that win material or seize dominance, while often creating new tactical vulnerabilities (exposed queens, weakened pawn structures) that the opponent exploits immediately.
sub_patterns: Prophylactic h3 missing a free capture (Nxg5/Nxe4)
Pawn advance e5 missing a tactical capture or knight leap (exd5/Nd5)
Queen development to a square vulnerable to knight attack (Qe2→Nd4, Qe3→Ng4)
Routine piece development ignoring hanging material (Nc6 vs Nxe4)

analysis.label: Moves that voluntarily remove (via capture, trade, or retreat) the one piece or pawn that was holding the position together, allowing the opponent's threats to become unstoppable.
analysis.description: This feature fires on moves where the player abandons their key positional resource to address a seemingly urgent but actually secondary concern. In 4/6 positions, a rook is moved from an active post to a passive one or traded off (Rg2 abandoning pressure on d-pawn, Rdd1 retreating from dominant d5 outpost, Rxb2 and Rxa2 both enabling rook trades into lost pawn endgames). In 1/6, a pawn shield is removed (exd4 eliminates the e5-pawn protecting the queen from Rxe7). In 1/6, a queen retreats to a vulnerable square (Qd3 leaving active b5 for a tempo-losing centralization). The common thread across all positions: the player had one critical element maintaining positional integrity (an active rook, a shielding pawn, or piece coordination), and the blunder specifically removes that element. In 5/6 cases, the best alternatives all preserved this anchor piece/pawn in its active role.
analysis.move_pattern: Piece (usually rook) moving to second rank or back rank via capture or retreat, abandoning an active file or outpost; also pawn captures that open critical lines against own pieces
analysis.why_bad: Each move removes the single piece or pawn that was maintaining the player's position—either enabling a fatal rook trade into a lost pawn endgame (3/6), self-blocking the king or surrendering counterplay (2/6), or opening a file that exposes a hanging piece (1/6). The opponent immediately exploits the absence of the removed resource.
sub_patterns: Rook captures passed pawn allowing trade into lost pawn endgame
Rook retreats from active outpost to passive back-rank square
Pawn capture that opens file exposing own major piece
Piece moves to square that self-blocks king escape routes

analysis.label: Moving a piece away from its essential duty—defensive coverage, pawn escorting, or active outpost—to a passive or irrelevant square, wasting a critical tempo.
analysis.description: In 7/7 positions, the played move redirects a piece away from the position's most urgent demand. In 5/7 cases, the piece physically retreats or moves to a less active square (Ng1 to the corner, Ng3 off a dominant outpost, Rh3 retreating from an aggressive rank, Qxb2 leaving the defensive zone, Kb4 abandoning the passed pawn). In 6/7 positions, the critical consequence is that the opponent gains a free tempo to execute their primary threat—whether that's advancing a passed pawn (2/7), exploiting an exposed king (4/7), or winning undefended material (2/7). All positions share the 'tempo_loss' and 'piece_activity' tags. The moves superficially serve some purpose (capturing a pawn, attacking a piece, repositioning) but fundamentally misread the position's priorities, treating secondary objectives as primary while the opponent's concrete threats go unanswered.
analysis.move_pattern: Piece (typically knight or major piece) moves backward, sideways, or to a peripheral square, away from the critical sector where threats are concentrated
analysis.why_bad: These moves waste an irreplaceable tempo in positions where the opponent has concrete, immediate threats (king attacks, promotion races, tactical shots). By addressing secondary concerns or passively retreating, the player grants the opponent time to execute their primary plan unimpeded, often converting a survivable position into a lost one.
sub_patterns: Knight retreating to passive back-rank square (Ng1, Ng3)
Queen/King moving away from critical defensive zone for pawn grab (Qxb2, Kb4)
Rook retreating when aggressive placement was required (Rh3)
Prophylactic pawn push addressing symptom not cause (h6)
Piece jumping to undefended square ignoring tactical refutation (Nd4)

analysis.label: Making an active-looking move that leaves a piece (often the moved piece itself or another piece) immediately capturable through a simple tactical oversight.
analysis.description: This feature fires on positions where the player makes a seemingly purposeful move—centralizing, developing, attacking, or capturing—but overlooks that the move either places a piece on an attacked square or removes a critical defender, allowing the opponent to win material with a simple one-move or short forcing sequence. The most striking recurring sub-pattern involves pieces placed on squares controlled by a bishop along an open diagonal (positions 3, 5, 14 all feature a rook landing on b8 captured by a distant bishop; position 11 features a pawn advancing to f5 captured by a bishop). Other instances include a bishop captured by a queen after landing on an exposed square (position 7), a knight left hanging to a queen (position 8), a queen abandoning pawn defense (position 6), a queen placement creating a fork vulnerability (position 13), and a king walking into a knight check (position 10). In 11/13 positions the refutation involves a direct material capture or simple 1-2 move forcing sequence. The average cp_loss of 974 reflects that these are catastrophic material blunders, not subtle positional errors.
analysis.move_pattern: Piece moves to an active-looking square (centralization, development, capture) while a friendly piece remains or is placed en prise to an opponent's long-range piece (bishop diagonal, queen line, or knight fork square)
analysis.why_bad: The move ignores that either the moved piece lands on a square directly attacked by an opponent's piece (especially along a long diagonal), or the move removes defense from another piece/pawn, allowing immediate material capture. The player focuses on their own plan while failing a basic safety check.
sub_patterns: Rook placed on b8 square attacked by bishop along open diagonal (3 cases)
Piece lands on square immediately capturable by queen
Move abandons defense of a pawn or piece elsewhere
Pawn advances to undefended square captured by bishop
King/queen moves to square creating fork geometry for opponent's knight

analysis.label: Moving a piece to a passive, peripheral, or exposed square when active centralization was required, creating an exploitable tactical vulnerability.
analysis.description: This feature fires on moves that voluntarily displace pieces from useful positions to passive, rim, or tactically vulnerable squares, ignoring the position's demand for active centralization or concrete action. Knights moving to the rim (Ng5→h3 trapped, Nxh7 offside, Nh4 creating overload, Nh2 dead-end retreat) appear in 5/11 positions. Bishops placed on tactically vulnerable squares (Bb5 hanging to Nc7, Bc4 creating fork target, Bf4 creating pawn fork with Nh4) appear in 3/11 positions. Tempo-wasting moves ignoring urgent piece vulnerability (a3, Kd7, Kc3) appear in 3/11 positions. In nearly every case, the best move involved either active centralization (Ne5, Nd4, Nf5 appear repeatedly as best alternatives) or removing a piece from a vulnerable configuration (Bg3, Bc4). The common consequence is that the opponent gains a concrete tactical shot—a pawn fork (g5 in 3/11), trapped piece (3/11), skewer, or hanging piece—that didn't exist before the move was played. The average cp_loss of 275 reflects positions where one precise move maintained the evaluation but the chosen passive alternative created an immediate exploitable target.
analysis.move_pattern: Minor piece (usually knight) or bishop moving away from active central square toward rim, backward, or exposed square; occasionally a tempo-wasting pawn/king move when pieces need urgent repositioning
analysis.why_bad: The moves place pieces on squares where they become immediate tactical targets (forkable by pawns, trappable, or creating overloaded defenders) while simultaneously wasting the tempo needed to address existing positional vulnerabilities, allowing opponents to exploit the newly created weakness with concrete tactics.
sub_patterns: Knight retreat/advance to rim square (h2, h4, h7, g5) when central outpost available
Bishop placement on square controlled by opponent's piece or creating fork geometry
Quiet move ignoring piece pair vulnerable to advancing pawn fork (g5 hitting Bf4+Nh4)
Tempo-wasting king/pawn move when trapped piece or tactical urgency demands immediate action

analysis.label: Playing a slow, non-forcing move (no check, no capture, no immediate threat) when the position demands immediate tactical action.
analysis.description: This feature fires on positions where players choose quiet, preparatory, or positionally-motivated moves instead of the available forcing continuation that the position demands. In 10/12 positions, the played move was explicitly tagged as 'tempo_loss' — the player had a concrete forcing option (capturing an undefended piece in positions 2 and 11, giving check to gain time in positions 10 and 13, playing an intermediate forcing move before retreating in position 12, or executing a pawn break/advance before White consolidates in positions 3, 4, 7, and 15) but instead chose a move with a reasonable long-term idea that was simply too slow. The pattern spans all piece types and game phases, but the common thread is always: a non-forcing move is played when an immediate tactical strike, capture, or check was necessary to maintain or exploit the position's dynamic demands.
analysis.move_pattern: Any piece type making a quiet (non-checking, non-capturing) developing, retreating, or advancing move when a forcing alternative exists
analysis.why_bad: These moves waste a critical tempo, allowing the opponent to execute their own plan (advance passed pawns, consolidate a dominant piece, escape tactical threats, or initiate a forcing sequence) that the correct move would have prevented or pre-empted through immediate action.
sub_patterns: Failing to capture an undefended piece (retreating/repositioning instead)
Slow pawn push when active piece play or immediate threats are needed
Move-order error: playing the second move of a sequence first, missing intermediate forcing move
Non-forcing attack when check or back-rank invasion wins immediately
Passive development instead of directly challenging opponent's dominant piece

analysis.label: Seemingly purposeful moves that inadvertently leave a piece undefended or create a tactical vulnerability exploitable by forks, deflections, or tempo attacks.
analysis.description: This feature fires on moves that appear constructive—activating rooks on open files, repositioning queens, advancing pawns aggressively, developing bishops—but critically overlook that the move leaves a friendly piece undefended or creates a geometric vulnerability. In 6/9 positions, the move directly results in a hanging or forkable piece: Qb3 places queen where Na5 forks it with the Bc4; Bb5 leaves Nh3 undefended after e4 deflects the queen; d4 allows exd4 forking Nc3 and Be3; Qc2 abandons defense of Nb6 allowing Bxb6; Rd6 places the rook where Ne8+ forks it with the king; Rd2 places the rook on a square directly attacked by Be3 losing a tempo. The remaining positions (Bh6+, h3, b3) share the same underlying error of choosing a superficially logical move while missing that the position demands addressing an immediate concrete tactical requirement. The low average of 1.9 good moves available confirms these are critical moments where precision was essential.
analysis.move_pattern: Any piece type moving to a seemingly active square (open file, attacking diagonal, advanced rank) while leaving itself or another friendly piece tactically unprotected
analysis.why_bad: The move ignores that a friendly piece is left without adequate protection, or places the moved piece itself on a square where it becomes a tactical target via fork, deflection, or tempo-gaining attack by the opponent
sub_patterns: Queen/rook moves to active square creating fork geometry with another undefended piece
Piece development that abandons defensive duty over another piece
Aggressive pawn advance that exposes supporting pieces to capture/fork
Placing piece on wrong square when a nearby alternative avoids the tactical vulnerability

analysis.label: A natural-looking developing or improving move played in a position that demands addressing one specific immediate tactical threat.
analysis.description: In 6/7 positions analyzed, the player chose a quiet, non-forcing move (bishop development, pawn advance, castling, or knight development) that would be reasonable in many contexts but catastrophically ignores the single most urgent requirement of the position. The positions share an extremely low average of good moves available (1.4), meaning there was essentially ONE thing that had to be addressed immediately. In Position 1, Bh6 ignores the need to blockade passed pawns with Kb4; in Position 2, f5 ignores king vulnerability on the e1-h4 diagonal; in Position 4, Bc5 ignores the f6 pawn's threat of f7+; in Position 5, Bf4 ignores a hanging knight on a3; in Position 9, O-O ignores the need to capture on e4 before Black exploits the d-file; in Position 12, Nc3 ignores the e3 pawn's threat of exf2+ check. All moves appear in or resemble moves from 'ideal' plans but are played one critical tempo too early or without prerequisite preparation.
analysis.move_pattern: Quiet non-forcing moves (piece development, repositioning, castling, pawn advances) - no checks, no captures - in positions requiring an immediate tactical response
analysis.why_bad: Each move wastes the one available tempo needed to address a concrete threat (hanging piece, advanced passed pawn, check, or piece invasion), allowing the opponent to execute a tactical blow that was preventable with the single correct alternative
sub_patterns: Bishop development ignoring hanging/threatened pieces
Pawn advance exposing king to immediate queen check
Piece improvement ignoring advanced passed pawn threats
Castling when a forcing capture was required first
Move-order error where the played move appears in the best line but one tempo later

analysis.label: Player makes a plausible-looking move in a critical position where exactly one move works, resulting in catastrophic evaluation collapse.
analysis.description: This feature activates on positions where exactly ONE good move exists (1.0 avg across all 6 positions) and the player instead plays a superficially reasonable alternative that catastrophically fails. The played moves include instinctive checks that help the opponent (Rf5+ driving king off a skewer diagonal in 1/6, Qd4+ giving a pointless check missing a dual-purpose Qe5+ in 1/6), king moves to the wrong square exposing critical geometry (Kh2 landing on a fork diagonal instead of Kh1 in 1/6, Kd7 walking into a discovered attack instead of Kf8 in 1/6), a passive pawn push (f3) instead of the winning active queen move in 1/6, and removing a critical defender (Rfc1) instead of blocking with Nf3 in 1/6. The average centipawn loss is an extraordinary 6566, with 4/6 positions converting winning/mating positions into losing ones or vice versa.
analysis.move_pattern: Diverse piece types and directions - king moves, queen checks, rook moves, pawn pushes - all sharing the quality of being 'instinctive' or 'natural-looking' alternatives to the single correct move
analysis.why_bad: Each move fails because it ignores the ONE critical geometric or tactical requirement of the position - whether that's avoiding a specific diagonal (Kh2), keeping an enemy piece on an exploitable square (Rf5+), maintaining tempo pressure on a passed pawn (f3), targeting the right piece with a check (Qd4+), fleeing in the correct direction (Kd7), or keeping a defender on a critical file (Rfc1)
sub_patterns: Pointless checks that drive opponent's king to safety (Rf5+, Qd4+)
King moves to wrong adjacent square exposing to tactics (Kh2, Kd7)
Passive/developing moves ignoring urgent tactical demands (f3, Rfc1)

analysis.label: A piece performing an essential (often hidden) defensive function is moved to a seemingly reasonable square, fatally leaving its critical duty unattended or creating self-interference.
analysis.description: This feature fires on moves where a piece abandons a vital defensive role—blockading passed pawns, defending key squares, or keeping escape routes clear—to relocate to a square that appears logical but is actually catastrophic. The pattern manifests in three main ways: (1) Self-blocking, where a piece occupies a square needed by another friendly piece (Rd2 and Nd2 both block the king's path to d2; Bd7 blocks the queen's defense of d5)—3/9 positions; (2) Abandoning defense of a passed pawn or allowing its exploitation (Ng6 removes blockade of two promotion squares; Reb1 allows exchange leading to passive rook vs. passed pawn; Rb1 moves the wrong rook leaving c2 undefended)—3/9 positions; (3) Abandoning king defense or moving to a tactically vulnerable square (Qh6 deserts the queenside king; Kg1 walks into a diagonal check; f6 advances while leaving a bishop en prise)—3/9 positions. In all cases, the moved piece looked reasonable (centralizing, contesting a file, advancing aggressively) but was already performing an indispensable function that only becomes apparent when the opponent immediately exploits its absence.
analysis.move_pattern: Non-capture, non-check piece relocation; typically moves to a 'logical' square (centralized, active-looking, or seemingly safe) that in reality abandons or obstructs a critical defensive function
analysis.why_bad: The piece was performing an essential but non-obvious defensive role (blockading, guarding, keeping a square available for a friendly piece), and its relocation allows the opponent to immediately exploit the abandoned function—whether promoting pawns, capturing undefended material, delivering decisive checks, or creating unstoppable threats.
sub_patterns: Self-blocking: piece occupies a square needed by the king or another piece (Rd2, Nd2, Bd7)
Removing blockade/guard of passed pawn allowing promotion or capture (Ng6, Reb1, Rb1)
Queen/king abandoning critical defensive zone enabling tactical exploitation (Qh6, Kg1)
Aggressive advance ignoring hanging piece left behind (f6)

analysis.label: Moving a well-placed piece away from its effective square to a peripheral or passive location, wasting critical tempo when the position demands immediate action.
analysis.description: This feature activates on moves where a piece voluntarily leaves a strong or necessary post and relocates to a less effective square—typically on the rim or periphery of the board. In 5/8 positions, the piece moves to a clear rim square (Kh3, Ng4, Ka7, Ng5, Ba7). In 3/8 positions involving knights specifically (Ng4 from f6, Ng5 from e6, Nxe7+ from d5), the knight abandons a dominant central outpost to chase a peripheral target. The common consequence is tempo loss (explicitly tagged in 5/8 positions), where the opponent immediately exploits the wasted move—either through checks that drive the piece back (Position 1: Qg2+), advancing a pawn that was being targeted (Position 10: ...h5), closing a window for counterplay (Position 12: d5), or executing the very threat the piece relocation failed to address (Position 14: Qg8+). The positions demanded either maintaining the piece on its current strong square or taking immediate concrete action (like 19...exd4 or 35...d3), but instead the player chose a repositioning move that proved too slow.
analysis.move_pattern: Piece (any type) moves away from a central or functionally critical square toward the rim (h-file, g-file, a-file) or to a square where it becomes tactically vulnerable or strategically irrelevant
analysis.why_bad: The piece relocation wastes a critical tempo, allowing the opponent to either force the piece back (nullifying the move entirely), advance threats that the piece was previously restraining, or exploit the vacated square/diagonal. The position typically required maintaining tension or taking immediate tactical action rather than 'improving' piece placement.
sub_patterns: Knight abandons central outpost (e6, d5, f6) to chase peripheral target on g4/g5/e7
