King walks toward rim/corner when it should stay in contact with critical pawns or threats
Bishop/Queen retreats passively when the position demands an immediate pawn break or tactical strike

analysis.label: Player delivers a queen check on a square where a bishop check was the correct move, abandoning the queen's critical coverage.
analysis.description: In all 7/7 positions, the player moved their Queen to deliver check on a specific square, when the correct move was to use the Bishop to check on that exact same square. The Queen needed to remain on its original post to maintain control of critical escape squares (covering back ranks, providing discovered check potential, or supporting mating nets). By checking with the Queen instead of the Bishop, the player destroyed the attacking geometry: in positions 1-2, Qg6+ was played instead of Bg6# (immediate checkmate); in position 4, Qh2+ replaced Bh2+ (losing a discovered check mechanism); in position 5, Qf6+ replaced Bf6+ (losing a mating net); in positions 6 and 11, Qxh7+/Qh7+ replaced Bxh7+/Bh7+ (destroying discovered check sequences via Bg6+); and in position 14, Qe6+ replaced Be6+ (abandoning the queen's dominant f7 post). The average cp_loss of 8608 reflects that these are catastrophic errors, typically converting forced mates into draws or losses.
analysis.move_pattern: Queen delivers check (moving to the exact square where the Bishop should go instead), typically toward the opponent's king on the h-file or kingside diagonals
analysis.why_bad: The Queen abandons its critical post (controlling escape squares, back ranks, or serving as the hidden piece behind a discovered check), while the Bishop on that square would have maintained the Queen's coverage and preserved the complete tactical geometry
sub_patterns: Qg6+ instead of Bg6# — Queen vacates e8 control allowing king escape
Qh7+/Qxh7+ instead of Bh7+ — Queen leaves h5 destroying discovered check via Bg6+
Qh2+ instead of Bh2+ — Queen moves first losing discovered check mechanism
Qf6+ instead of Bf6+ — Queen abandons d8 post losing mating net
Qe6+ instead of Be6+ — Queen abandons f7 post losing attacking coordination

analysis.label: Choosing a superficially attractive forcing move (capture, check, or pawn advance) that catastrophically undermines the player's own critical structural or tactical asset in a position requiring precise quiet play.
analysis.description: This feature fires on positions where the player makes a 'natural-looking' active move that destroys their own winning/defensive resource. In 5/9 positions the blunder is a pawn capture or advance (exf5, exf6+, c6, h5, Bxd3+) that dissolves a critical pawn structure. In Position 2, exf5 removes the e4 pawn that was blocking Black's attack. In Position 6, exf6+ dissolves the winning pawn duo. In Position 3, Bd7 blocks the king's escape square (d7) that was the ONLY path to avoid forced mate. In Position 7, Nb5 moves the knight to an irrelevant target when it needed to support the passed f6-pawn via Ne6. In Position 8, Nf6 walks into Bxf6 where gxf6 allows Qg7#. In Position 11, h5 creates the exact weakness the opponent's queen-knight battery exploits. The common thread across 8/9 positions is that only 1-2 good moves existed (avg 1.7), the best moves were quieter/less forcing (consolidating rook moves, king retreats, queen repositioning), and the blunder was the 'obvious' forcing option that seemed to gain tempo or material but actually handed the opponent exactly what they needed.
analysis.move_pattern: Captures, checks, pawn advances, or piece moves toward 'obvious' targets — moves that appear forcing or active but move away from the position's critical requirement
analysis.why_bad: Each move destroys the player's own critical asset (a defensive pawn barrier, an escape square, a dominant attacking piece, a winning passed pawn structure, or kingside pawn integrity) in exchange for something superficial (a pawn, a check, development, attacking a peripheral target), and the position required quiet precision rather than forcing play.
sub_patterns: Pawn captures that dissolve critical defensive/offensive pawn structures (exf5, exf6+)
Piece moves that block own king's escape route in tactical emergencies (Bd7)
Trading key attacking pieces for checks/material when maintaining pressure wins (Bxd3+)
Moving pieces toward peripheral targets away from the decisive zone (Nb5, Nf6)
Pawn advances that create new weaknesses or help opponent's passed pawns (c6, h5)

analysis.label: Choosing slow, retreating, or non-forcing moves when the position demands immediate active piece play, centralization, or tactical forcing sequences.
analysis.description: This feature fires on moves that prioritize passivity—retreats, slow pawn pushes, or structural concessions—over active alternatives that maintain initiative or exploit concrete tactical opportunities. In 3/8 positions, pieces retreat to passive squares (Nb8 to starting square, Bg8 to irrelevant corner, Kd8 to back rank) when centralization or counterattacking moves were critical. In 3/8 positions, pawn advances (a6 missing forced mate, h5 when king centralization was needed, d2 creating an easily blockaded target) were chosen over piece activity. In 1/8, a wrong recapture (fxe3 instead of Qxe3) damaged structure and surrendered initiative. In 1/8, a piece developed to a square that enabled opponent's tactics (Be6 becoming a stepping stone). The consistent thread: every best alternative involves active piece play—queen centralization, knight attacks, king centralization, forcing checks—while every blunder chooses something slow or retreating that squanders the position's dynamic demands.
analysis.move_pattern: Retreating pieces to back rank/corner squares, or pushing pawns slowly, instead of centralizing kings, activating pieces, or playing forcing moves (checks/attacks)
analysis.why_bad: These moves waste critical tempo in positions demanding urgency, allowing opponents to seize the initiative, execute tactical strikes, blockade passed pawns, or escape mating nets—the slow move gives the opponent time to consolidate or attack.
sub_patterns: Piece retreat to passive/starting square (Nb8, Bg8, Kd8)
Slow pawn push missing forcing tactical continuation (a6, h5)
Premature pawn advance creating blockade target (d2)
Wrong recapture damaging structure over active alternative (fxe3)
Developing piece to tactically exploitable square (Be6)

analysis.label: Moves that appear to achieve the same objective as the best move but use the wrong piece, square, or approach, squandering a winning advantage.
analysis.description: This feature fires on positions where the player has a clearly winning or advantageous position and makes a move that superficially accomplishes the same goal as the best move but through the wrong method. In 3/5 cases, this manifests as capturing with the wrong piece (Nxf7 instead of gxf7, Qxe4 instead of Nxe4, Rf6 abandoning the e8 rook that could be captured). In 2/5 cases, it's choosing a wrong square or plan that looks equivalent (Kd4 instead of Kd5, g4 instead of Nb7). The positions typically have very few good moves available (avg 1.8), meaning the margin for error is extremely narrow despite the position appearing comfortable. The player sees the right idea—capture the piece, centralize, gain activity—but executes with the wrong tool, failing to recognize the critical qualitative difference between seemingly equivalent options.
analysis.move_pattern: Captures or piece moves that mirror the best move's target/direction but use the wrong piece or land on the wrong square; often one square off or one piece substitution away from optimal
analysis.why_bad: These moves fail because they sacrifice a hidden critical resource—whether it's a passed pawn on the 7th rank (gxf7 vs Nxf7), attacking flexibility of the queen (Nxe4 vs Qxe4), defensive coordination (Rf6 leaving e8 undefended), centralization advantage (Kd5 vs Kd4), or the primary winning plan (knight activity vs pawn push). The player evaluates the moves as equivalent when they are qualitatively different.
sub_patterns: Wrong capture piece (correct square, wrong capturer)
Wrong square by one step (correct piece, adjacent square)
Active-looking move that abandons a critical defensive duty

analysis.label: Moves that create or fail to break a geometric alignment between the player's own king and rook, allowing the opponent to win the rook via a check-based tactic.
analysis.description: In all 4/4 positions, the played move results in the player's king and rook sitting on the same exploitable line (diagonal or rank), which the opponent punishes with a check that simultaneously attacks or wins the rook. In Position 1, Rb5 places the rook on the f1-b5 diagonal with the king, allowing Qd3+ to fork both. In Position 3, Ka6 walks the king onto the d3-a6 diagonal while the rook sits on c2, also attackable from d3, enabling Qd3+ to fork. In Position 5, Kd3 places the king on the b1-d3 diagonal with its own rook on b1, allowing Be4+ to fork both. In Position 13, g3 wastes a critical tempo while the king on g4 remains aligned with the rook on c7 along the 4th rank, permitting a discovered check that wins the rook. All four blunders result in losing a full rook to the tactical exploitation.
analysis.move_pattern: Various pieces/pawns; the common geometric thread is that after the move, the player's king and rook share a diagonal or rank with no adequate interposition, enabling a check-based attack on both
analysis.why_bad: The move creates or preserves a geometric alignment between the player's own king and rook on the same line, allowing the opponent to deliver check while simultaneously attacking the rook (via fork or discovered attack), winning material by force
sub_patterns: King and rook aligned on diagonal enabling bishop/queen fork with check
King and rook on same rank enabling discovered check that wins the rook
Tempo-wasting move that fails to break an existing dangerous alignment

analysis.label: Moving a king or knight away from its crucial safe/defensive square to a seemingly active but actually exposed or purposeless one, allowing immediate tactical exploitation.
analysis.description: In 6/6 positions, the blundering move involves either a king advancing to an exposed square (Ka5, Kf5, Kc6 - 3/6) or a knight relocating away from a critical post or defensive role (Ngf7, Ng4, Nxh7 - 3/6). The king moves all walk into check/mate patterns: Ka5 allows Re5+ lateral checks, Kf5 walks into Qd5#, and Kc6 enables perpetual queen checks. The knight moves all abandon essential duties: Ngf7 leaves b3 undefended when Nc4 was the only saving move, Ng4 abandons support of the e4 pawn allowing Nxe4/Nf4 exploitation, and Nxh7 voluntarily removes the dominant f6 knight for a mere pawn. In 5/6 positions, the correct alternative was a patient/consolidating move rather than an ambitious advance. The average cp_loss of 1823 reflects that these self-inflicted exposures create catastrophic vulnerabilities.
analysis.move_pattern: King or knight moves forward/sideways to exposed square, abandoning a safe or defensively critical position
analysis.why_bad: The piece leaves a square where it performed essential defensive or positional duties (shielding from checks, supporting pawns, maintaining coordination) and moves to a square where it is immediately exploitable via checks, forks, captures, or where its absence allows the opponent to win material or deliver mate.
sub_patterns: King advances into rank-based check or mating patterns (Ka5, Kf5, Kc6)
Knight abandons dominant outpost or defensive post for a greedy/speculative move (Ngf7, Ng4, Nxh7)
Piece moves toward opponent territory but creates self-inflicted tactical vulnerability

analysis.label: Premature queen moves (or moves leaving the queen exposed) to aggressive-looking but tactically vulnerable squares where the queen becomes a target for minor piece attacks, forks, or traps.
analysis.description: This feature fires on moves where the queen (9/11 cases) is placed on or left on an exposed square that invites immediate tactical punishment. The most common sub-pattern involves queen moves to b-file squares (Qb3, Qb5, Qb6 appearing in 7/11 positions) where knights can jump to attack the queen with tempo while simultaneously threatening forks on the uncastled king (Nd4 in positions 1-2, Na4 in position 4, Nb4 in position 11). In other cases, the queen overextends to the h-file (Qh5 getting trapped in position 13, Qh3+ being a purposeless check in position 14) or retreats to a passive square abandoning a key defensive function (Qc7 in position 6 allowing Bxf7+ sacrifice). The non-queen moves (fxe6, Bb4) share the same underlying pattern: they create or leave a tactical vulnerability where a piece becomes a target. All 11 positions occur with at least one king still in the center (11/11), amplifying the fork/safety motifs. The average cp_loss of 292 reflects how severely these exposed placements are punished.
analysis.move_pattern: Queen (or piece) moves to an aggressive but unprotected square, typically on the b-file (b3/b5/b6) or h-file (h3/h5), often in the opening with king still in center
analysis.why_bad: The queen lands on a square where it can be immediately attacked by minor pieces (especially knights) with tempo, creating forks against the uncastled king, trapping the queen, or forcing the queen to abandon critical defensive duties that allow tactical breakthroughs
sub_patterns: Queen to b3/b5 vulnerable to Nd4/Nb4 fork of queen and king/rook
Queen to b6 vulnerable to Na4 trap or allowing Qa4+ removing castling rights
Queen to h-file overextension leading to queen trap or purposeless check
Queen retreat to passive square abandoning control of key tactical squares
Pawn/piece move leaving queen on exposed square vulnerable to knight fork

analysis.label: Playing a passive or non-forcing move in a razor-sharp position where only immediate forcing play (checks, attacks, maintaining critical defenders) preserves the evaluation.
analysis.description: This feature fires on moves that surrender critical tempo in positions with extremely narrow best-move windows (avg 1.2 good moves available). In 6/6 positions, the player chose a slow, non-forcing alternative when the position demanded immediate tactical urgency. The blunders take various forms—passive pawn pushes instead of checks (b5 instead of Re5+, Rg8 instead of Rc8+), quiet moves instead of piece activation (h4 instead of Ne5, Kd8 instead of Kd7), and wrong captures that remove critical defenders from key squares (Bxc6 instead of dxc6, Nxc6 abandoning the e5 outpost). In every case, the position was balanced or winning but required one specific forcing continuation, and the slow move gave the opponent exactly the tempo needed to consolidate, escape checks, advance passed pawns, or launch a decisive counter-attack. The catastrophic average cp_loss of ~2000 reflects that these are positions on a knife's edge where one lost tempo means the difference between winning and losing.
analysis.move_pattern: Diverse piece types moving to passive squares; pawn pushes, retreating/sideways king moves, rook repositioning to non-checking files, captures that remove own pieces from dominant posts
analysis.why_bad: Each move surrenders a critical tempo in a position where the opponent needs exactly one move to consolidate, escape, or counter-attack—the played move allows the opponent to reach safety or activate threats that the forcing alternative would have prevented.
sub_patterns: Slow pawn advances instead of immediate checks (b5, h4)
Passive piece repositioning instead of tempo-gaining checks (Rg8, Kd8)
Wrong captures that remove critical defensive/positional pieces from key squares (Bxc6, Nxc6)

analysis.label: Playing a non-forcing piece repositioning move in a sharp position that demands immediate concrete action, typically allowing the opponent to exploit an exposed king.
analysis.description: This feature fires on positions where the player makes a 'normal-looking' quiet piece move (development, repositioning, or king walk) instead of the required forcing continuation. In 7/7 cases, the position demanded immediate tactical precision with very few good options available (avg 1.4). In 6/7 positions, the exposed king of the moving side was the critical vulnerability exploited after the quiet move—the opponent punished with checking sequences, back-rank invasions, or queen infiltrations. The blunders share the pattern of ignoring an urgent need (attacking the opponent's weak king in positions 1, 7, 12; defending one's own exposed king in positions 3, 8, 14; stopping a passed pawn in position 9) in favor of a move that would be reasonable in a calmer position. The catastrophic average cp_loss of 3026 reflects that these positions sit on a knife's edge where a single wasted tempo transforms the evaluation completely.
analysis.move_pattern: Non-forcing piece move (no check, no capture, no direct threat) — typically a minor piece or rook repositioning to a square that appears active but addresses the wrong problem
analysis.why_bad: These moves waste a critical tempo in razor-sharp positions, allowing the opponent to execute a winning tactical combination (usually a series of checks against an exposed king, a back-rank attack, or an unstoppable pawn promotion) that was only possible because the player failed to force the issue first
sub_patterns: Rook moves away from a critical defensive file, exposing king to checking sequences (Rb8, Rg8)
Minor piece development to unprotected/blocked square ignoring immediate tactical crisis (Bb7, Bf5)
Knight repositioning in wrong move order or to speculative square (Ng3, Nh5)
Passive king walk when forcing attack was available (Kc7)

analysis.label: Moves that follow general endgame principles (centralize king, activate rooks on ranks, create passed pawns, give checks) but ignore concrete tactical refutations.
analysis.description: This feature fires on moves that apply well-known strategic endgame principles without verifying tactical safety. In 5/7 positions, the move follows a recognized guideline: Rb2 and Re2 activate rooks on the 2nd rank, Rdb7 doubles rooks on the 7th rank, Ke5 centralizes the king, R1e5 'supports' a passed pawn, Qc4+ delivers a forcing check, and e4 creates passed pawns. The actual mistakes (5/7) are punished because the 'principled' move neglects a concrete vulnerability—Rb2 abandons back-rank defense allowing Qe8+ invasion, Rdb7 leaves g2 undefended for a double-rook kingside attack, R1e5 allows Rxf5 capturing with tempo, Qc4+ allows Qxc4 when a deflection sacrifice forced mate, and Ke5 walks into Qf4#. The 2/7 positions with 0cp loss (e4, Re2) represent cases where the aggressive principled approach happens to be tactically sound, confirming the feature detects the move PATTERN rather than strictly the error.
analysis.move_pattern: Pieces moving to classically 'active' squares in endgames: rooks to 2nd/5th/7th ranks, king advancing to center, queen giving check, pawns pushing forward
analysis.why_bad: The moves apply general strategic principles (rook activity, king centralization, checking) while ignoring specific tactical vulnerabilities—the piece either lands on a square where it can be captured/attacked with tempo, or it abandons a critical defensive duty that allows the opponent an immediate tactical blow against the king or undefended pawns.
sub_patterns: Rook to 2nd/7th rank abandoning king defense
King centralization walking into mating net
Purposeless check allowing piece capture
Rook 'supporting' passed pawn but actually blocking it

analysis.label: Plausible-looking developing or improving moves that lose a critical tempo by failing to address the opponent's most forcing tactical response (usually a check, fork, or pawn advance).
analysis.description: This feature fires on moves that appear logical—developing a piece (Nf3, Nc6), retreating to safety (Bb6, Kc1), pushing a prophylactic pawn (f6), or giving a check (Qe6+)—but all critically ignore the opponent's most forcing reply. In 5/7 positions, the punishment involves a check or capture-with-check (Bh3+, Rdc2+, Rdc2+, Nxd4+, Bb4+). In 6/7 positions, king safety is the primary vulnerability exploited. The correct moves in every case address the forcing threat first: moving the bishop off d4 before it's forked (Position 9), retreating to Ka1 to control the checking geometry (Positions 4-5), exchanging on c6 or playing Kg2 to neutralize the diagonal check (Position 1), castling preparation via d6 (Position 8), sacrificing the queen to dismantle the mating net (Position 12), or checking on d8/b8 to maintain a perpetual harassment pattern (Position 15). The average cp_loss of 239 reflects serious tactical oversights, and the low average of 2.1 good moves confirms these are narrow positions where prioritization is critical.
analysis.move_pattern: Various piece types moving to natural/central squares or giving non-optimal checks; no single geometric direction but all are 'routine-looking' moves that ignore a specific tactical geometry (diagonal check, rook check on file, knight fork)
analysis.why_bad: Each move prioritizes a secondary positional goal (development, centralization, prophylaxis, checking) over the concrete most-forcing opponent reply, granting the opponent a tempo to execute a tactical sequence—typically a check, fork, or forcing advance—that the correct move would have preempted or neutralized.
sub_patterns: King moves walking into forcing check sequences (Kc1 allowing Rdc2+)
Piece development ignoring diagonal/file-based check threats (Nf3 allowing Bh3+, Nc6 removing guard)
Pawn moves leaving pieces hanging to forks (f6 allowing Nxd4+)
Imprecise checks that allow the opponent's king to escape to safe squares (Qe6+ allowing Ka5)
Bishop retreats losing tempo when castling/king safety is urgent (Bb6 allowing e5)

analysis.label: Playing a routine non-capturing move in positions where the only good continuation was a specific capture.
analysis.description: In all 5/5 positions, the best move was a capture (cxd4, Qxc5, axb6, dxe5/Bxe5/Nxe5, Nxh5), but the player instead made a quiet, non-forcing 'autopilot' move (Be7 developing, Qf3 repositioning, a6 pushing a pawn, O-O castling, e4 gaining space). The played moves look like natural positional continuations that one might make without examining the concrete tactical demands of the position. In 3/5 cases the capture would win or remove hanging/en-prise material (Qxc5 wins free bishop, axb6 captures a queen, Nxh5 trades favorably), while in 2/5 cases the capture was necessary to neutralize the opponent's dominant centralized piece before it became too dangerous (cxd4 removing White's d4 knight, dxe5 removing Black's e5 knight before castling). The average cp_loss of 471 and average of only 1.8 good moves confirms these are critical moments where the capture was essentially forced.
analysis.move_pattern: Any quiet non-capture (development, castling, pawn push, piece repositioning) in positions where a pawn or piece capture was the only viable continuation
analysis.why_bad: The player defaults to routine positional play (developing, castling, gaining space) while completely overlooking that the position's concrete tactical features demand an immediate capture—either to win free/hanging material or to eliminate a dangerous opponent piece before it becomes overwhelming.
sub_patterns: Missed capture of hanging piece (Qxc5, axb6)
Missed exchange of dominant centralized piece (cxd4, dxe5)
Missed favorable trade to maintain structure (Nxh5)

analysis.label: Moving the king or a key piece to a square that creates immediate tactical vulnerability, often motivated by superficially reasonable goals like centralization or material gain.
analysis.description: This feature fires on moves where a player voluntarily places their king or a major piece on a square that is immediately exploitable by the opponent through concrete tactics. The most catastrophic cases (5/11) involve kings walking into tactical danger: Kd7 walks into a discovered check leading to mate (Position 8), Kd4 walks into checkmate-in-one (Position 9), Kd6 walks into a knight fork winning the queen (Position 5), and O-O-O castles directly into a pre-existing pawn storm (Position 6). Other cases involve pieces abandoning critical duties: Qxc2 grabs a pawn while the king on d6 is hopelessly exposed (Position 4), Bc3 leaves the e4 pawn completely undefended (Position 2), and Qg5 places the queen on a square where Nf3 traps it (Position 13). The common denominator is that the move serves a seemingly logical purpose—centralizing, gaining material, developing—but ignores an immediate tactical refutation that the opponent can execute. The average cp_loss of 1888 reflects that these positions often feature multiple move options that avoid disaster (avg 2.5 good moves available), making the choice to self-expose particularly costly.
analysis.move_pattern: King or major piece moves to a central/active-looking square that is directly vulnerable to forks, discovered attacks, traps, or mating patterns
analysis.why_bad: The piece lands on a square where it can be immediately exploited through concrete tactics (discovered checks, knight forks, queen traps, back-rank/central mates), while the player's actual goal (centralization, material gain, development) could have been achieved safely by alternative means
sub_patterns: King walks into discovered attack or fork on d-file (Kd6, Kd7, Kd4)
Queen grabs material while ignoring king exposure (Qxc2, Qb4)
Piece moves to a square where it gets trapped or creates a hanging piece (Qg5, Bc3)
Castling into an existing pawn storm or attack (O-O-O)

analysis.label: Constructive-looking moves that pursue a secondary objective while ignoring the position's most urgent tactical or defensive requirement, typically leaving a piece or pawn undefended.
analysis.description: This feature fires on moves that appear natural and purposeful—captures (Rxe6), castling (O-O-O), checks (Qa4+), prophylaxis (Kh2), development (Qd7, b6), pawn advances (a5)—but critically neglect the position's primary demand. In 5/7 cases, the move directly creates or exposes a hanging piece/pawn: a5 unguards b5 (2/7), Qd7 leaves Nc5 en prise (3/7), Rxe6 leaves b2 undefended (1/7), Qa4+ allows Bd7 trapping the queen (4/7), Kh2 leaves Nd7 and f4 unprotected (5/7). In 6/7 cases, one or more good alternatives existed that addressed the actual urgent need (centralizing, defending, or neutralizing a specific threat), but the player chose a move addressing a peripheral concern. The average cp_loss of 303 reflects that these aren't random blunders but systematically wrong priorities in critical positions.
analysis.move_pattern: Mixed piece types and directions; no geometric unity. Moves include pawn pushes, king moves, queen moves, captures, checks, and castling—all appearing constructive on the surface.
analysis.why_bad: Each move spends a crucial tempo on a secondary plan while the position's most urgent tactical requirement goes unaddressed, typically resulting in a piece or pawn becoming undefended, a critical square being abandoned, or giving the opponent time to exploit a vulnerability that the correct move would have neutralized.
sub_patterns: Pawn advance that removes protection from a neighboring pawn (a5 leaves b5, b6 ignores h5-g6 crisis)
Piece move that abandons defense of a critical square or piece (Qd7 leaves Nc5, Kh2 leaves Nd7/f4)
Premature check or capture that misplaces the attacking piece (Qa4+ gets trapped, Rxe6 captures wrong target)
Castling or king move into danger when quiet development was needed (O-O-O into open c-file, Kh2 instead of Qe4)

analysis.label: In endgames with a pawn on the 6th rank ready to advance to the 7th, the player moves the king instead of immediately pushing the pawn toward promotion.
analysis.description: This feature fires on endgame positions where an advanced passed pawn (typically on the 6th rank) can and should be pushed immediately to the 7th rank or promoted, but instead the player makes a king move. In the high-activation examples, 9/12 positions have a pawn on the 6th rank that should be pushed to f7 or g7 (Positions 1, 3, 6, 11, 13, 15) or a pawn on the 3rd rank that should advance toward promotion (Positions 4, 5, 10). The king moves are intended to 'escort' or 'support' the pawn, but the pawn can actually advance on its own because the opponent's king cannot reach the promotion square in time. The tempo wasted on the king move allows the opponent to establish a blockade (8/12 positions show the opponent's king reaching a blocking square), capture the pawn (3/12), or gain critical counterplay. The catastrophic examples (Positions 3, 10, 11 with 8000-9000+ cp_loss) show forced mates converted into merely winning positions, while milder activations (Positions 2, 5, 6, 12 with 0-4 cp_loss) represent positions where the king move happens to transpose or is barely suboptimal.
analysis.move_pattern: King moves in any direction (all 8 squares) in endgames; 11/12 examples are king moves, typically moving forward or sideways near an advanced passed pawn
analysis.why_bad: The king move wastes a critical tempo when the passed pawn can advance immediately and unstoppably; the lost tempo allows the opponent's king to reach a blockading square, capture the pawn, or escape a trapped position, converting a forced promotion or mate into a slower technical win
sub_patterns: King moves forward alongside pawn instead of pushing pawn (Kf7/Kf3/Kg3 instead of f7/g7)
King retreats behind passed pawn to 'support' instead of pushing immediately (Kd2/Ke2/Kf2 instead of c2/e2)
Wrong pawn advance when promotion push is available (e5 instead of f7)

analysis.label: Queen delivers check on a square where the opponent's queen can simply capture it, allowing an unwanted queen trade that dissolves a winning attack.
analysis.description: In all 6/6 positions, the player delivers a queen check that lands on a square directly accessible to the opponent's queen, enabling a simple queen capture/trade that devastates the attacker's position. In 5/6 cases, a forced checkmate was available (mate in 1, 2, 4, 7, and 4 respectively), making the queen trade catastrophic. The refutation in every case is identical: the opponent's queen captures the checking queen (Qxd2, Qxe5, Qxe6, Qxc1, Qxe4, Qxc4), transforming decisive mating attacks into merely advantageous or even losing endgames. This represents the classic 'patzer sees a check, patzer gives a check' syndrome, where the instinct to deliver check overrides calculation of whether the check actually accomplishes anything or whether the queen is safe on its destination square.
analysis.move_pattern: Queen moves to give check, landing on a square along a line (diagonal, file, or rank) where the opponent's queen has an unobstructed path to capture it
analysis.why_bad: The queen check places the queen en prise to the opponent's queen, allowing a simplifying trade that removes the attacker's most powerful piece and dissolves the mating attack or decisive advantage that depended on queen coordination with other pieces
sub_patterns: Queen check allows capture along diagonal by opponent's queen
Queen check allows capture along file/rank by opponent's queen
Missed forced mate due to impulsive check offering queen trade

analysis.label: Moves that prioritize non-urgent goals (centralization, material, development) while the player's own king faces immediate tactical exploitation via checks or mating attacks.
analysis.description: This feature fires on moves where the player neglects an urgent king safety crisis in favor of a seemingly reasonable but non-critical improvement. In 10/12 positions, the player's king is already exposed or about to be exploited, yet the move either worsens king vulnerability (king walks to an exposed square in 5/12: Kf8, Kxa5, Kd2, Ke3, Kd4), removes a critical defender (Nf6 leaving e5 undefended, Qg3 abandoning back-rank coverage), weakens the pawn shield (h6, f6), or simply ignores the threat (Qd3 not addressing h-file attack). The punishment in nearly all cases involves forcing checks or mating sequences: perpetual checks (Kf8 allows Qf6+/Qh8+ perpetual), back-rank infiltration (h6 allows Qc8+, Qg3 allows Qa8+), rook checks on open files (Kxa5/Kd4 allow Ra8+/Rxb4+), or discovered/diagonal checks (Kd2 allows Qxd4+, Ke3 allows captures on f3 with check, f6 allows Qg6+). The average cp_loss of 310 reflects that these moves typically convert playable positions into lost ones or throw away winning advantages entirely.
analysis.move_pattern: Diverse piece types (king moves to exposed squares, queen moves away from defensive duties, weakening pawn pushes, knight departing defensive post) - all sharing the property of being non-forcing moves made when the position demands immediate attention to king safety
analysis.why_bad: The moves allow the opponent to initiate forcing sequences (checks, perpetual checks, mating attacks) against the player's exposed king that were previously impossible or preventable, because the move either placed the king on a vulnerable square, removed a key defender, or wasted the critical tempo needed to address the threat
sub_patterns: King voluntarily walking to exposed squares (Kxa5, Kd2, Ke3, Kd4, Kf8) where it becomes a target for check sequences
Queen/piece moving away from defensive duty, enabling back-rank or infiltration tactics (Qg3, Nf6, Qd3)
Pawn moves that weaken the king's shield or waste tempo when castling/defense is urgent (h6, f6)
Choosing an aggressive/attacking move over addressing one's own king vulnerability (Qg2+ instead of Rh2+)

analysis.label: Moves that create or ignore a critical diagonal vulnerability toward the king, enabling a forcing check that wins material.
analysis.description: All 7 positions share a common thread: the played move either places the king on a dangerous diagonal, opens a diagonal by removing a shielding pawn, or fails to block/address an existing diagonal threat toward the king. In 7/7 positions, the primary refutation involves a diagonal check (bishop or queen) that gains decisive tempo or material. Specifically: Ka2 exposes the king to Qf7+/Qd5+ on the a2-g8 diagonal (1/7); Kh2 allows Bf4+ on the f4-h2 diagonal (2/7); fxg6 removes the f7 pawn opening h3-c8 for Be6+ (3/7); Qg7 allows Bf5+ saving a bishop with tempo (4/7); Bd2 fails to block b6-g1 diagonal allowing Qb6+ winning b2 (5/7); f4 ignores Bd5+ discovered attack on a2-g8 diagonal (6/7); Rf8 ignores Qb3+ on b3-f7 diagonal with follow-up exd6+ discovered check (7/7). The common 'diagonal_weakness' and 'king_safety' tags appear in all positions.
analysis.move_pattern: Various piece types; the commonality is not the moving piece but the resulting geometry — all moves leave the king sitting on or exposed to an unblocked diagonal where opponent's bishop or queen delivers check
analysis.why_bad: These moves fail because they leave the king vulnerable on a diagonal, allowing the opponent to deliver a forcing check (usually with a bishop) that wins material through tempo, discovered attack, or tactical combination — the check itself is not the damage but the consequence (winning a piece, queen, or achieving mate).
sub_patterns: King voluntarily steps onto dangerous diagonal (Ka2, Kh2)
Pawn capture removes diagonal shield exposing king to bishop check (fxg6)
Passive move ignores opponent's diagonal escape/attack with tempo check (Qg7, f4, Rf8)
Piece development fails to block critical checking diagonal (Bd2)

analysis.label: Playing a passive, non-forcing move in a position that demands immediate concrete tactical or strategic action.
analysis.description: In all 4/4 positions, the player chose a quiet, non-threatening move (piece retreat, sideways rook shift, or slow pawn push) precisely when the position demanded immediate forcing action. In Position 2, a rook retreated from a powerful central square (e4→e7) when c5 or Rxh4 created needed counterplay. In Position 5, a quiet a6 pawn push was played when axb6 literally captured the opponent's queen. In Position 6, the queen retreated to a passive back-rank square (Qe8) instead of activating the bishop (Bd6) which controlled the critical f5 square. In Position 13, a slow Rc1 was played instead of g5 or Ng5 which directly addressed the critical pawn tension. All 4/4 positions had very few good moves available (avg 1.2), meaning the position was at a critical decision point where only concrete, forcing moves maintained the balance. The average cp_loss of 390 reflects how severely these tempo losses are punished.
analysis.move_pattern: Quiet non-forcing moves: piece retreats to back ranks, lateral rook repositioning, or slow pawn pushes with no immediate threat or capture
analysis.why_bad: These moves waste a critical tempo in positions where the opponent can immediately execute tactical threats, resolve tension favorably, or activate pieces decisively. The positions all have a 'now or never' quality where one specific forcing action is required, and any quiet move allows the opponent to seize the initiative permanently.
sub_patterns: Retreating active piece from strong central square to passive position
Quiet pawn push ignoring an available capture or tactical necessity
Slow rook repositioning when immediate pawn breaks or piece sacrifices are required

analysis.label: Playing a natural-looking but concretely flawed move in a position where only one specific forcing continuation was correct, allowing a clear tactical refutation.
analysis.description: This feature fires on moves that appear reasonable or even attractive on the surface but fail in positions demanding extreme precision (avg 1.3 good moves available). The moves share a common thread: the player chooses something 'tempting'—a material grab (Nc2 grabbing a rook, Nxe6 winning a pawn), a repositioning move (Bf5, Kf7, Ke3), a space-gaining pawn push (c5, b6), a check (Rc1+), or a similar-looking alternative to the best move (Nc7 vs Nb6, Kf7 vs Kf6)—while ignoring the one critical concrete requirement of the position. In 7/10 cases the refutation involves a specific tactical motif (trapped piece in 2/10, knight fork in 3/10, released pressure allowing castling/coordination in 2/10). The positions are overwhelmingly critical junctures where only 1-2 moves maintain the evaluation, yet the chosen move looks plausible enough that a player might not calculate deeply enough to see the concrete flaw.
analysis.move_pattern: Diverse piece types (knights, bishops, kings, rooks, pawns) moving to squares that look purposeful but have a specific tactical vulnerability—often a piece going to a similar but wrong square compared to the best move, or a slow move when forcing play was required.
analysis.why_bad: Each move ignores the one concrete tactical requirement of the position—whether that's avoiding a square vulnerable to forks (Ke3, Kf7), not abandoning a critical outpost (Bf5 leaving c2), not allowing the opponent to solve their problems (Rc1+ letting the king escape, c5 ignoring Bf7+), or choosing the wrong piece/square for an otherwise correct idea (Nc7 vs Nb6, Nxe6 vs Bxe6). The opponent has a clear forcing refutation that exploits the specific defect.
sub_patterns: Piece moves to a square where it becomes trapped or loses coordination (Nc7, Nc2)
King walks to a square vulnerable to knight forks (Ke3, Kf7)
Slow non-forcing move ignoring an imminent tactical threat (c5, b6, h3)
Abandoning a powerfully-placed piece for a passive alternative (Bf5 leaving c2)
Pointless check that improves opponent's piece placement (Rc1+)
Wrong capture order losing material unnecessarily (Nxe6 vs Bxe6)

analysis.label: King or piece moves away from a critical defensive post, leaving a pawn or piece undefended and immediately exploitable.
analysis.description: This feature fires on endgame positions (7/8) where the player moves their king or a key piece one step away from a square that was performing a crucial defensive function, leaving a pawn or piece hanging. In Position 4, Ke1 abandons g2 (immediately captured by Rxg2). In Position 10, Ke8 abandons the g7 bishop (immediately captured by Rxg7). In Position 14, Kc4 abandons the b2 pawn (immediately captured by Rxb2 or gxh5+Rxb2). In Position 5, Bd7 abandons the bishop's protective influence over c4 and the queenside (allowing Rd4 penetration and Rxc4). In Position 6, Kb2 blocks the king's own passed pawn while abandoning the active c3 post, allowing Rc7 to seize the 7th rank and win g7. In Position 9, g5 removes the g7 pawn from its critical role as a tempo-giving sacrifice for perpetual check. Nearly all positions (6/8) are rook endgames where the defensive connection was subtle but essential, and the moves appear natural or improving but sever a hidden tactical link.
analysis.move_pattern: King or piece moves one square (or short relocation) away from a pawn/piece it was defending; predominantly king moves in endgame positions
analysis.why_bad: The moved piece was the sole defender of a specific pawn or piece; by relocating, the target becomes immediately capturable or the opponent gains a decisive tempo to exploit the undefended material, typically via rook capture or penetration to a key rank/file.
sub_patterns: King moves away from adjacent pawn it was guarding (Ke1/g2, Ke8/g7, Kc4/b2)
Bishop/piece relocates abandoning positional control over key squares (Bd7 leaving c4)
King blocks own passed pawn while abandoning active post (Kb2)
Pawn advance removes critical defensive tactical resource (g5 eliminating perpetual check mechanism)

analysis.label: Passive repositioning or retreat move played in a critical position where only one or two concrete/forcing moves maintain the evaluation.
analysis.description: This feature fires on positions where the player chooses a quiet, non-forcing piece move (often a retreat, consolidation, or seemingly 'improving' repositioning) when the position demands immediate concrete action. In 8/11 positions, the best move was a forcing action: a capture (Qxe5, Qxf5, Rxf6), a fork/check (Nf1+), a pawn break (d4/h6+), or a precise defensive resource (Bf8 for blockade, Qd4 covering diagonal). Instead, the player chose moves that look natural but waste the critical tempo: king retreats (Kg8, Kg5, Kf8, Kf3 appearing in 5/11), queen placements to seemingly active squares that block own pieces (Qe3, Qe7, Qf3 in 3/11), or piece repositioning away from dominant posts (Nb5, Rff1). The average cp_loss of 287 and only 1.6 good moves available confirm these are narrow positions where the single correct concrete move must be found.
analysis.move_pattern: Any piece type moving to a non-forcing, non-capturing square (no check, no capture, no direct threat) — predominantly king retreats/sidesteps and queen repositioning to central squares
analysis.why_bad: These moves waste the critical tempo in positions where only 1-2 specific forcing/concrete moves maintain the evaluation. The opponent exploits the free tempo to execute a tactical strike (fork, passed pawn advance, piece activation, or attack on a now-undefended target) that was previously prevented by time pressure or the moved piece's former position.
sub_patterns: King retreat/sidestep when aggressive king advance or piece action is needed (5/11 positions)
Queen placed on square that blocks own piece retreat or abandons critical defensive duty (3/11)
Piece voluntarily leaves dominant outpost or active square for seemingly safer but actually weaker post (Nb5, Rff1)

analysis.label: Advancing a piece (usually the king) toward opponent's material when the position demands retreating or redirecting to safety.
analysis.description: In 6/6 positions, the player makes a move that advances toward the opponent's material or captures something tempting, when the correct approach is to retreat, stay put, or move in a completely different direction. King advances dominate the pattern (4/6 moves are king moves forward: Kb4, Kxd6, Kf5, Kg4), while the remaining 2 are captures that open dangerous lines (hxg5 opens h-file, Rxc3 leaves rook hanging). In every case, the player prioritizes material targets over safety: Kb4 heads toward the a6 pawn instead of infiltrating the kingside (Position 1); Kxd6 grabs a bishop but exposes the king (Position 2); hxg5 wins a bishop but opens a devastating h-file attack (Position 5); Rxc3 grabs a pawn but hangs the rook (Position 6); Kf5 approaches enemy pawns but blocks the rook's critical square (Position 7); Kg4 approaches the opponent's knight but walks into checks and forks (Position 9). The correct moves in all cases are either retreats (Ke2, Kf2) or moves toward a completely different sector of the board (Kd4, Qxd6, Nxe5, dxe4, Rf5).
analysis.move_pattern: Piece (predominantly king) moves forward/toward opponent's material, often a capture or approach to a target piece/pawn
analysis.why_bad: The advancing piece becomes tactically vulnerable—exposed to checks, forks, discovered attacks, or simple recapture—while abandoning its defensive responsibilities or blocking allied pieces from critical squares
sub_patterns: King advances toward distant material instead of heading to the critical sector of the board
King captures a piece and becomes exposed in the center with no pawn shelter
Pawn capture opens a file directly toward own king where opponent has attacking pieces pre-positioned
Piece captures material on a square where it is immediately recaptured at a loss
King advances to a square needed by its own rook, destroying defensive coordination

analysis.label: Moves that look natural or active but directly enable a specific devastating opponent response (check, trade, or capture) that was previously impossible or ineffective.
analysis.description: In all 8/8 positions, the played move directly unlocks a specific opponent resource that transforms the evaluation catastrophically. In 5/8 cases (Kf6→Bd4+, Kh3→Qf5+, Kh1→Bxf3+ becoming check, Qf6→Nxh8, Nxe7+→dissolving mating net), the move places a piece on a square where a forcing check or capture becomes newly available. In 3/8 cases (Qxd4→unfavorable queen trade, Rxd3+→drawn pawn endgame, a5→Qxb6 into lost endgame), the move enables a simplification that eliminates the player's advantage. The common thread is that in each case the best move is typically quieter or more subtle (Kd7, Nxf6+, Kd1, Kf7, Qxf6, a6, Qd1, Qh4) while the played move appears more natural/active/obvious but critically overlooks that it gives the opponent precisely what they need. The average cp_loss of 2622 with only 2.0 good alternatives shows these are critical positions where one natural-looking move has a hidden catastrophic flaw.
analysis.move_pattern: Diverse piece types (kings, queens, rooks, knights, pawns) moving to squares that appear active or safe but geometrically align with opponent's tactical resources - diagonals, files, or exchange sequences
analysis.why_bad: Each move creates a new vulnerability (king on attackable square, piece enabling a check/discovered attack, or structural weakness enabling forced trade) that the opponent immediately exploits with a forcing sequence that was impossible before the move was played
sub_patterns: King moves to squares enabling check sequences (Kf6, Kh3, Kh1)
Captures/trades that voluntarily enter losing or drawn simplified positions (Rxd3+, Qxd4, Nxe7+)
Moves that fail to create sufficient counter-threats while enabling opponent's main plan (Qf6, a5)

analysis.label: Playing a slow, non-forcing move in a position that demands one specific urgent concrete action, wasting the critical tempo needed to exploit or maintain an advantage.
analysis.description: This feature fires on positions where the player makes a quiet, non-threatening move (developing, prophylactic, or repositioning) when the position narrowly demands immediate concrete action. In 13/13 cases, the move played was non-forcing (no check, no capture, no direct threat), while the best move was typically a sharp central break or tactical shot. The positions consistently had very few good alternatives (avg 1.4), indicating 'narrow' critical moments. In 5/13 cases (positions 1, 7, 9, 4, 11), the missed best move was a specific central pawn break (e5 or d5/f4) that exploited piece geometry or an uncastled king. In 6/13 cases, the opponent's king was still in the center and the wasted tempo allowed them to castle or consolidate. The blunders often involved choosing 'natural-looking' moves (Be7 developing, Nf6 developing, O-O castling, Kb8 improving king, a6/a3 prophylaxis) that would be reasonable in less critical positions but catastrophically squander a fleeting window of opportunity.
analysis.move_pattern: Non-forcing moves (no check, no capture, no immediate threat) to safe/natural squares - quiet piece development, prophylactic pawn moves, king safety moves, or passive repositioning
analysis.why_bad: The position has a narrow tactical or dynamic window (avg 1.4 good moves) demanding one specific concrete action; the quiet move wastes the critical tempo, allowing the opponent to solve their problems (castle to safety, seize the center, execute their own break, or invade on open lines)
sub_patterns: Missing a tactical combination (e5/Qa5+ fork) by playing routine development instead
Playing prophylactic pawn moves (a6, a3, Kb8) when an urgent central break (d4, d5) is needed
Castling or repositioning when the position demands an immediate pawn storm or attack
Passive piece moves (Rb8, Ne5) ignoring an immediate positional emergency (trapped piece, file domination)
Flank pawn advance (c4) when central action is the only way to maintain advantage

analysis.label: Natural-looking moves that waste a decisive tempo in narrow positions where only 1-2 moves maintain the evaluation.
analysis.description: This feature fires on moves that appear constructive based on general principles but fatally waste a critical tempo in positions with extremely narrow margins (average only 1.4 good moves available). The played moves follow intuitive ideas—giving checks (4/14: Rf7+, Qa7+, Ne3+, Bb4+), centralizing pieces (Kg1, Re4, Ke3, Qc4), advancing pawns (a4, g4), or capturing material (Rxc7, gxh5)—but in each case the position demanded ONE specific precise move addressing an urgent concrete tactical requirement. The best moves across all positions share a common quality of addressing the position's single most critical need (maintaining perpetual check, prophylactic king safety, correct piece geometry, seizing the initiative with forcing play), while the played moves accomplish secondary objectives that the opponent immediately exploits. The feature overwhelmingly fires in endgames (9/14) where single-tempo precision is paramount, and the average cp_loss of 943 reflects how catastrophically a single wasted tempo compounds in these razor-thin positions.
analysis.move_pattern: Diverse piece types and directions—no single geometric pattern. The connecting thread is moves that look purposeful (checks, captures, centralization, advances) but fail to execute the position's one concrete tactical demand.
analysis.why_bad: Each move surrenders a critical tempo in a position where the margin is razor-thin, allowing the opponent to achieve a specific concrete goal (promote a pawn, seize a dominant file, activate king to center, launch a decisive attack) that was previously preventable with the one precise alternative.
sub_patterns: Purposeless or premature checks that displace own pieces or give opponent useful king moves (Rf7+, Qa7+, Ne3+, Bb4+)
Passive piece placement when a specific active square is required for counterplay (Re4 vs Rc4, Kg1 vs Ra4+, Ke3 vs Ng1)
Greedy captures or pawn moves that create structural weaknesses or ignore prophylaxis (Rxc7, gxh5, f3)
Slow positional plans in positions demanding immediate forcing play (a4 vs Rf3+, g4 vs Rc4, Qc4 vs Qd8+, Bg5 vs Bf2)

analysis.label: Plausible-looking moves that catastrophically miss the one narrow tactical requirement in critically demanding positions with very few correct options.
analysis.description: This feature activates on positions where the tactical demands are extremely narrow (avg 1.8 good moves) and the player makes a move that appears purposeful but ignores the single critical requirement of the position, resulting in massive evaluation swings (avg 2380 cp_loss). In 9/9 positions, the chosen move had clear strategic intent—developing (Rc8), centralizing (Ne6, Nd4), fleeing (Kf8 x2, Kh5), repositioning (Qe1), challenging the center (f6), or recapturing (Bxe5)—but in each case that intent was catastrophically wrong given the specific tactical demands. The positions all share a 'one right answer' character where the correct move addresses an immediate tactical crisis (exploiting an attack 3/9, choosing the correct king square 3/9, capturing hanging material 2/9, or preserving pawn structure 1/9), and the blunder instead creates new decisive vulnerabilities: queen invasions, skewers, hanging pieces, or lost initiative that the opponent immediately exploits.
analysis.move_pattern: Diverse piece types and directions; moves appear purposeful (developing, centralizing, retreating, capturing) but voluntarily abandon a critical defensive duty or miss a concrete winning/saving tactical shot
analysis.why_bad: These moves ignore the single critical tactical demand of an extremely narrow position—either missing the one concrete opportunity (attacking, capturing) or creating a new decisive vulnerability (exposing king to skewer/invasion, hanging a piece, weakening key squares) that immediately collapses the position
sub_patterns: King moves to squares creating skewer/invasion vulnerability (Kf8, Kh5)
Slow positional moves when immediate tactical action required (Rc8, Qe1, f6)
Piece placement on undefended squares allowing simple capture (Ne6, Nd4)
Wrong recapture that fails to address king safety or piece vulnerability (Bxe5)

analysis.label: Playing quiet prophylactic or repositioning moves in critical positions that demand an immediate forcing response (capture, sacrifice, or active check).
analysis.description: In all 5 positions, the player chose a non-forcing, quiet, or aimless move when the position critically demanded one specific concrete action. In 5/5 cases, the best move was a capture or a purposeful check that directly addressed an immediate tactical crisis (Bxf5+ capturing with check, Nd7 addressing Nxf7 threat, Rxe6 eliminating a dominant piece, Rf3 sacrificing to block a mating attack, Bb4+ developing with tempo). Instead, the played moves were either passive retreats (Kb8, Nce7), slow positional preparations (g6), misguided king walks (Kg4), or purposeless checks that misplace pieces (Ba4+). The average number of good moves was only 1.6, indicating these are high-precision moments where only concrete action saves the position. The average cp_loss of 2031 reflects the catastrophic cost of passivity when urgency is paramount.
analysis.move_pattern: Quiet piece repositioning (king tucks, knight retreats, pawn pushes, bishop to inactive square) instead of required captures or forcing moves
analysis.why_bad: Each position contains an immediate tactical crisis (dominant enemy piece, mating threat, fork threat, advanced passed pawn) that requires a specific forcing response; the quiet move wastes the critical tempo, allowing the opponent to execute their threat or consolidate their advantage unchallenged.
sub_patterns: King safety moves ignoring tactical captures (Kb8, Kg4)
Passive retreats instead of active development with checks (Nce7 vs Bb4+)
Slow pawn moves ignoring piece-level threats (g6 vs addressing Nxf7)
Wrong check that misplaces a piece vs correct capture-check (Ba4+ vs Bxf5+)

analysis.label: Non-urgent pawn pushes or secondary development in the opening that waste critical tempo while the king remains dangerously in the center.
analysis.description: This feature fires on opening moves that ignore the position's most urgent demand—typically development, castling, or addressing a tactical vulnerability—in favor of 'luxury' moves like prophylactic pawn pushes (h3 in 2/5 positions), overambitious expansion (c4 in 1/5), structurally damaging recaptures (gxf3 in 1/5), or developing a new piece while an existing one hangs (Bg4 in 1/5). In all 5/5 cases, the player's king remains in the center (e1 or e8), and the tempo loss is punished by tactical exploitation of the uncastled king—via queen checks on open diagonals (Qh4+, Qa4+), attacks on f2, piece invasions, or knight forks. The best moves in each position consistently involve completing development (Nxf3, Nf3, Bb3, Nd7, c3) to enable castling or stabilize piece coordination. The pattern represents a fundamental misjudgment of positional urgency, treating a critical moment as calm.
analysis.move_pattern: Mostly pawn advances (h3, gxf3, c4) or non-forcing piece moves (Bg4) that neither develop toward castling nor address immediate tactical threats
analysis.why_bad: Wasting a tempo in an underdeveloped position with a centralized king allows the opponent to exploit open lines, weak squares (especially f2/f7), and piece activity advantages through checks, forks, or sacrificial attacks against the exposed king
sub_patterns: Prophylactic h3 when development is critical
Pawn recapture that damages king shield (gxf3 vs Nxf3)
Pawn expansion (c4) that creates tactical weaknesses with undeveloped pieces
Developing a new piece while an existing one is undefended

analysis.label: Forward-moving pieces or pawns seeking activity/threats while neglecting defensive needs, particularly when the player's own king is exposed to tactical exploitation.
analysis.description: This feature fires on aggressive forward moves (pawn pushes to the 5th rank, rook advances to the 5th/6th rank, king advances, queen lunges) in positions where one or both kings are exposed. In 7/8 positions, the analysis explicitly notes an exposed or weakly shielded king for the side making the move. The critical error pattern is that the forward advance creates a new tactical vulnerability—typically a checking line or open file—that didn't previously exist: e5 opens c3 for a rook check (1/8), d5 allows Nxf6+ with check (2/8), Rg6 allows g4 opening the h-file toward the king (4/8), Kg4 steps onto a diagonal enabling Qf3+ (5/8), g5 opens the f-file after fxg5 (6/8), and Qa5 abandons king defense allowing Bh4 along the e1 diagonal (7/8). In the two non-blunder positions (3/8 and 8/8), the side was already decisively winning, making the aggressive approach harmless. The correct alternatives consistently prioritized king safety (Kg2, Kg5), piece trades to reduce attacking potential (Qg3, Nxe4), or consolidation (Be6).
analysis.move_pattern: Diverse piece types (pawns, rooks, king, queen) all moving forward aggressively, typically to the 5th or 6th rank, in positions with open files/diagonals and exposed kings
analysis.why_bad: The aggressive advance creates or reveals a new tactical vulnerability (check square, open file, exposed diagonal) toward the player's own king that the opponent exploits with checks, forced trades, or mating attacks—the position demanded defensive attention first.
sub_patterns: Pawn advance to 5th rank opening lines against own king (e5, d5, g5)
Rook placed on wrong rank/file allowing counterattack with tempo (Rg6, Rf5)
King advance stepping onto tactically vulnerable square (Kg4)
Queen moving away from critical defensive zone (Qa5)

analysis.label: Plausible-looking moves (usually advancing pieces/pawns) that ignore the position's most urgent tactical or safety requirement in narrow positions with very few good options.
analysis.description: This feature fires on critical decision points where only 1-2 moves are correct (avg 1.6 good moves) and the player makes a natural-looking but fundamentally wrong choice. In 7/9 positions, the played move involves advancing a piece or pawn into seemingly active territory (Ne5, Ke5, Kxd6, b7, Nb5, Na5, c5) while ignoring the position's primary concrete demand. The ignored demands include: king safety vulnerabilities (5/9 positions explicitly involve king exposure - Ke5 walks into bishop diagonals, Kxd6 exposes to coordinated attacks, b7 ignores a mating net, c5 ignores back-rank weakness), tactical opportunities that require precise calculation (Na5 misses a queen-winning d5 break, Nb5 abandons a critical central post allowing pawn capture), and structural integrity (Ne5 allows favorable exchanges collapsing the center, b4 creates hanging pawns). The best moves in these positions consistently address the concrete need first - safe king moves (Kd6, Kf5), structural defense (Bb1, Qc7), or precise tactical strikes (Qg4, d4, d5) - rather than pursuing the attractive but wrong plan.
analysis.move_pattern: Piece or pawn advances (especially knights to 5th rank or beyond, king captures toward center, pawn breaks) that look strategically motivated but miss the position's tactical reality
analysis.why_bad: These moves prioritize a secondary goal (centralization, promotion, attack, pawn break) over the position's single most critical demand - typically addressing king safety, exploiting a specific tactical vulnerability, or maintaining structural integrity. With so few good moves available, any deviation from the concrete need is catastrophic.
sub_patterns: Knights advancing to aggressive but tactically refutable squares (Ne5, Nb5, Na5)
King captures/advances into exposed central squares (Ke5, Kxd6)
Pawn advances that ignore immediate threats to own king (b7 ignores mate, c5 ignores back rank)
Passive retreats when only aggressive exploitation maintains advantage (Ne2)

analysis.label: Slow developing moves that fail to address a direct tactical threat against the f7 pawn when White's bishop sits on the a2-g8 diagonal.
analysis.description: In 8/9 positions, White has a bishop actively placed on c4 or b3 targeting the f7 pawn along the a2-g8 diagonal, and Black plays a passive or irrelevant developing move (Bd7, Nd7, Be7, Nge7, Bg4, h6) instead of addressing this threat. The refutations consistently exploit f7: Bxf7+ sacrifices (positions 6, 8, 10, 11), Ng5 attacking f7 (positions 5, 6, 8), Qh5 targeting f7 (position 1), or Qb3 hitting both b7 and f7 (position 2). In every case, the top recommended move is Nf6 (appearing as best or second-best in 8/9 positions), which simultaneously develops, prepares castling, and provides crucial defensive resources near f7. The White-side example (position 4, f3) mirrors the pattern by blocking Nf3 and weakening f2. The average cp_loss of 254 reflects how these positions typically allow forcing tactical sequences that win material through sacrifices and forks.
analysis.move_pattern: Minor piece or pawn moves to passive squares (d7, e7, g4, h6) when the natural Nf6 development is available and urgently needed to defend f7
analysis.why_bad: They leave f7 defended only by the king while White's bishop on the a2-g8 diagonal (c4/b3) enables devastating tactical combinations (Bxf7+, Ng5, Qh5, Ne6 forks) that win material or destroy castling rights
sub_patterns: Bd7/Nd7 leaving f7 undefended against Bc4 (5/9 positions)
Be7/Nge7 developing kingside piece to wrong square instead of Nf6 (2/9)
Bg4 bishop sortie abandoning c8 defense of f7 diagonal (1/9)
Prophylactic pawn moves (h6/f3) wasting tempo when development is critical (2/9)

analysis.label: Natural-looking quiet piece repositioning that abandons critical restraints or defensive obligations in narrow, tactically demanding positions with exposed kings.
analysis.description: This feature activates on quiet, non-forcing moves (no checks, no captures) that appear positionally motivated—centralizing a bishop (Be5), repositioning a queen (Qg6), developing the king (Kd7), pushing a pawn (f3), or advancing the king (Kh6)—in positions with very few good options (avg 1.6) and exposed kings on both sides. In 4/5 cases, the move is a mistake because it releases pressure on a critical piece or square: Be5 abandons blockade duty on the b2/a3 passed pawns; Qg6 stops attacking the e5 rook, freeing it to capture a hanging knight; Kd7 allows the crushing e5 pawn break; f3 creates a fork target for the d4-knight. The one correct activation (Kh6, 0cp loss) confirms the pattern—it's the rare case where the 'quiet advance' IS the precise move. All positions share narrow decision points where concrete tactical demands override general positional principles.
analysis.move_pattern: Quiet piece/pawn moves (king steps, bishop retreats, queen repositioning, pawn pushes) that are non-forcing—no captures, no checks—typically moving toward seemingly active squares
analysis.why_bad: The moves abandon a critical restraining function (pressure on an enemy piece, blockade of passed pawns, control of a key square) in positions where the opponent has a specific tactical resource that was previously prevented, allowing forks, pawn breakthroughs, or piece captures
sub_patterns: Bishop abandoning blockade of passed pawns
Queen releasing pressure on an attacked piece (hanging piece exposed)
King walking into a pawn break zone
Pawn push creating a fork target

analysis.label: Player makes a passive, non-forcing piece move (repositioning or blockading) when a direct capture or concrete tactical action was critically required.
analysis.description: This feature fires on positions where the player chooses a quiet piece development/repositioning move while overlooking a direct tactical necessity. In 3/6 positions (Bd2, Rc1, Qb3), the best move was a straightforward capture of undefended material (Qxd5, Rxd3, Qxf5 respectively) that the player simply missed in favor of a 'logical-looking' piece move. In the remaining positions, the quiet move either places a piece on a tactically vulnerable square where it can be captured with devastating consequences (Bf6 allowing Nxf6+ shattering the king's pawn shield, Re8 leaving the e7-bishop hanging to Rxe7), or targets something that simply moves away (Ra8 attacking a pawn that advances with tempo). All 6/6 moves played are non-capturing, non-checking piece moves in positions that demanded forcing, concrete play. The average cp_loss of 240 and average of only 1.7 good moves available confirms these are critical decision points where the indirect approach catastrophically fails.
analysis.move_pattern: Non-capturing, non-checking piece move (any piece type) to a square that does not directly interact with the critical tactical element of the position
analysis.why_bad: The position demands concrete tactical action (usually a capture of hanging material or evacuation from a tactical threat), but the player instead makes an indirect repositioning move that either abandons a critical defensive duty, places a piece on a vulnerable square, or wastes tempo targeting something that escapes
sub_patterns: Missing a free capture of undefended material (Qxd5/Rxd3/Qxf5 missed)
Placing piece on square where it becomes tactically capturable with secondary damage (Bf6 allows Nxf6+ wrecking kingside; Re8 leaves bishop hanging)
Passive blockade or targeting of mobile material that simply advances away (Rc1 blockading while other pawn runs; Ra8 attacking pawn that pushes forward)

analysis.label: Playing a natural plan-continuation move before completing the critical preparatory step that makes it work.
analysis.description: This feature fires on positions where the player executes a move that belongs to the winning plan but skips the essential enabling step. In pawn endgames (4/8 positions), this manifests as advancing pawns before the king has penetrated to its critical square—positions 1, 2, 3, and 14 all show pawn pushes (h5, g4, g5, c4) when king infiltration (Kh3, Kh6, Kh3, Kc5) was the mandatory prerequisite, burning reserve tempi needed for zugzwang or fixing structures prematurely. In middlegame positions (4/8), this manifests as slow positional/prophylactic moves (Rc7, Bc5, Rc1, Nf3) when an immediate forcing move (capture, sacrifice, or tempo-gaining pawn thrust) was required first. The common thread across all 8 positions is a move-order error where the played move would often appear later in the best line, but executing it NOW gives the opponent the crucial tempo to neutralize the position—whether by establishing defensive coordination, exchanging critical pieces, or reaching a fortress.
analysis.move_pattern: Non-forcing moves (pawn advances without check/capture, quiet piece repositioning) that skip a prerequisite forcing move (king penetration, capture, sacrifice, or tempo-gaining attack)
analysis.why_bad: These moves surrender the critical tempo or flexibility needed to execute the full winning plan—the opponent uses that tempo to equalize (reach opposition, exchange attacking pieces, set up a fortress, or contest key files/squares that the prerequisite move would have denied them).
sub_patterns: Premature pawn advance before king penetration in pawn endgames
Positional piece move ignoring immediate tactical shot in middlegame
Burning reserve tempo needed for future zugzwang
Invading before removing the defender that contests the invasion

analysis.label: Plausible-looking moves that ignore the single critical requirement in positions where only one move avoids catastrophe.
analysis.description: This feature fires on positions with extremely narrow margins (avg 1.4 good moves available) where the player makes a reasonable-seeming move that completely misses the ONE urgent defensive or tactical priority. In 8/8 positions, the blunder involves pursuing a secondary goal—grabbing material (Bxh2), advancing pawns (a4), developing (Nh3), activating pieces (Rg7), seeking counterplay (Qg5), or repositioning (Rg8, Kc3, Kf3)—while the position demands a single specific move to prevent disaster. King safety is the ignored priority in 6/8 cases. In two striking examples, the WRONG piece goes to the correct square: Rg8 when Kg8 was needed (position 12), and Kc3 when Nc3 was critical (position 15). The average cp_loss of 3792 reflects how these narrow positions punish any deviation from the one correct path with catastrophic tactical consequences including checkmate, piece loss, or decisive material advantage.
analysis.move_pattern: Any piece type moving in any direction; no single geometric pattern—the commonality is a move that looks active/constructive but addresses a non-critical concern while the one saving move goes unplayed
analysis.why_bad: The position has essentially one correct move addressing an immediate tactical emergency (trapped piece, mating threat, hanging material, fork vulnerability), and the played move ignores this emergency to pursue something else, allowing a devastating refutation
sub_patterns: Wrong piece to correct square (Rg8 vs Kg8, Kc3 vs Nc3)
Active piece abandons critical defensive duty (Qg5 leaving f7)
Greedy capture ignoring positional urgency (Bxh2)
Quiet move ignoring immediate tactical shot (a4, Nh3)
King walks into tactical pattern (Kf3 into mating net, Kc3 into fork)

analysis.label: Natural-looking moves that fail to address critical king safety demands in positions where one or both kings are dangerously exposed.
analysis.description: This feature fires on positions where exposed or vulnerable kings create acute tactical tension, and the player makes a plausible but imprecise (or catastrophic) move rather than the most accurate continuation. In 8/9 positions, at least one king is explicitly described as exposed or in the center. The errors range from walking one's own king into danger (O-O-O castling into Qxc7#, Kd5 walking into Nc3+ sacrifice, Kh3 allowing Rg3+ check) to failing to exploit the opponent's exposed king with maximum precision (Qxf6+ premature check missing Rad1 deflection, Qd1 non-forcing when checks deliver faster mate) to placing pieces on vulnerable squares in tactical positions (Rf7 where it's captured with check, Qc7 where it becomes a tempo target). The average good moves available was only 2.1, confirming these are razor-sharp positions demanding precise calculation. The common thread is choosing the 'natural' or 'active-looking' move over the tactically critical one.
analysis.move_pattern: Various piece types moving to squares that appear active but are tactically compromised; includes king moves to exposed squares, pieces to capturable squares, and premature forcing moves
analysis.why_bad: In positions with critical king safety tension, these moves either place the player's own king/pieces on tactically vulnerable squares, or surrender the initiative by failing to exploit the opponent's exposed king with the most forcing/precise continuation, allowing the opponent to organize defense or deliver punishment.
sub_patterns: King walks into tactical danger (O-O-O, Kd5, Kh3)
Piece placed on capturable/targetable square (Rf7, Qc7)
Premature or non-forcing move when decisive checks/tactics exist (Qxf6+, Qd1)
Passive move ignoring critical threat (f4 ignoring passed pawn)

analysis.label: Playing a plausible-looking but non-critical move in a narrow position where essentially only one continuation maintained the evaluation.
analysis.description: This feature fires on positions with extremely limited correct options (avg 1.2 good moves) where the player selects a reasonable-seeming alternative that fails to address the position's single critical tactical or structural requirement. In 6/6 positions, there was one specific demand the position imposed—consolidating rooks on the back rank (Pos 1), capturing with the correct pawn to maintain king cover (Pos 3), directly attacking a knight to force repetition (Pos 9), developing a piece to defend a hanging pawn (Pos 13), exploiting a trapped queen with an open-file attack (Pos 14), or advancing a critical pawn before the opponent neutralizes the initiative (Pos 15)—and the player chose a move addressing a secondary concern instead. The played moves all appear purposeful (retreating the king to safety, fianchettoing, regrouping a knight, placing the queen aggressively) but each grants the opponent exactly the tempo needed to execute a decisive tactical operation.
analysis.move_pattern: Diverse piece types and directions (king retreats, pawn captures, knight retreats, queen advances); no single geometric pattern but all are non-forcing moves that fail to interact with the position's critical element
analysis.why_bad: Each move ignores the one urgent tactical requirement of the position, granting the opponent a crucial tempo to exploit an unaddressed vulnerability (exposed king, hanging piece, trapped queen, dominant outpost seizure)
sub_patterns: Slow regrouping move when immediate tactical strike available
Wrong pawn recapture direction exposing king
King move one tempo too slow to attack enemy piece
Prophylactic pawn move ignoring hanging material
Aggressive piece placement onto tactically vulnerable square

analysis.label: Playing a plausible-looking move that addresses a secondary concern while ignoring the position's single most critical defensive requirement.
analysis.description: In 6/6 positions, the player makes a move with logical-seeming intent (structural reinforcement, piece 'improvement', attacking a peripheral target) but fatally ignores the position's most urgent demand. In 5/6 cases only 1 truly good move existed, indicating positions requiring precise prioritization. The critical need varied—blockading a passed pawn (positions 1, 6), eliminating a dangerous intruding piece (position 2), preventing queen infiltration to a key square (position 5), maintaining a piece's defensive function (position 4), or preserving the bishop's active diagonal (position 3)—but in every case the player chose a different, less important objective. The 'tempo_loss' tag appears in 5/6 positions, and the average cp_loss of 338 reflects that one wasted tempo against an urgent threat is catastrophic. The moves look reasonable in isolation but represent a fundamental misidentification of the position's priorities.
analysis.move_pattern: Any piece type moving to a square that serves a secondary purpose (structural pawn pushes, lateral rook swings, piece repositioning) while the critical sector of the board is elsewhere
analysis.why_bad: The move wastes a critical tempo on a secondary concern, allowing the opponent's primary threat (passed pawn advance, piece infiltration, mating attack) to proceed unopposed, with the moved piece often becoming misplaced or blocking its own forces from reaching the truly important squares.
sub_patterns: Structural pawn push that blocks own piece's critical defensive access (f6, d6)
Piece relocating away from center/critical file to an irrelevant square (Bb4, Ra2)
King walking toward danger instead of addressing a tactical threat (Kb4)
Piece abandoning a critical defensive duty for an aggressive but unsound purpose (Nf4)

analysis.label: Apparently reasonable moves (especially king moves) that catastrophically ignore the ONE specific tactical or strategic requirement in positions demanding extreme precision.
analysis.description: This feature fires on positions where very few moves work (avg 1.6 good moves) and the player chooses a natural-looking move that misses the critical demand. King moves dominate (7/12 positions), typically retreating to 'safe' squares that are actually wrong: Kg1 retreats to the back rank when Kh3 was needed to support a pawn breakthrough (2/12), Kd8 walks into back-rank mating patterns when Kb8 was the only defense (2/12), Kxh5 and Kxg3 greedily capture pawns but lose decisive tempo in promotion races (2/12), and Kd3 centralizes but walks into a check sequence winning the queen (1/12). The remaining moves share the same character: Ra8 (1/12) repositions a rook to an irrelevant square ignoring a passed pawn crisis, Rb4 (1/12) attacks a knight but enables its devastating jump to e5, h4 (1/12) attempts the wrong pawn break, Qd3 (1/12) repositions before addressing king safety, and Bc3 (1/12) places a bishop on a tactically exploitable square. All positions feature exposed kings on both sides and demand a single precise response.
analysis.move_pattern: Predominantly king moves (7/12) to apparently safe/natural squares (retreating, capturing material, or centralizing); remaining moves are piece/pawn repositioning to reasonable-looking but critically wrong squares
analysis.why_bad: Each move fails to address the position's single urgent tactical requirement—whether supporting a critical pawn advance, preventing back-rank exploitation, maintaining tempo in a promotion race, or avoiding a forcing check sequence—because the player prioritizes general safety, material gain, or positional improvement over the one specific concrete demand
sub_patterns: King retreats to back rank when forward move supports decisive pawn advance (Kg1 vs Kh3)
King walks into back-rank tactics when sideways escape was needed (Kd8 vs Kb8)
King captures material losing critical tempo in pawn race (Kxh5, Kxg3)
King advances into check sequence (Kd3 into Re3+)
Piece repositioning before addressing king safety (Qd3 before Ke1)
Piece moves to tactically vulnerable squares enabling opponent combinations (Bc3, Rb4)

analysis.label: Playing a slow, non-forcing move that wastes a critical tempo when the position demands immediate active play, allowing the opponent to seize the initiative with a concrete tactical blow.
analysis.description: This feature fires on moves that squander tempo in positions requiring urgent action.
