In 10/10 positions, the played move was significantly less forcing than the best alternative: slow pawn pushes (a4, a5, f3, d5, g4) when piece activity was paramount (5/10), piece moves to squares where they get hit with tempo or abandon critical duties (Qd6 hit by Bg3, Qf8 abandoning c5, Be3 instead of Qe3), and king moves to vulnerable squares (Ke2 walking into checks). The best moves in every case were more active, more forcing, or addressed the most urgent positional demand—Rfc1 creating tactical threats, Qg5 attacking the exposed king, Ne2 developing, Bc1# delivering mate. The common thread is that each blunder gives the opponent a free tempo to execute a concrete plan (diagonal attack, sacrifice, fork, pin) that was previously unavailable or unsound. Average cp_loss of 1166 (inflated by a missed mate-in-one) with only 2.3 good moves available confirms these are high-tension positions where tempo is decisive.
analysis.move_pattern: Any piece type; typically non-capturing, non-checking moves to squares that either invite tempo-gaining responses or abandon critical defensive/attacking duties
analysis.why_bad: The position demands immediate forcing play (development, threats, contesting key files/diagonals), but the move wastes a tempo on a slow or misdirected idea, giving the opponent time to execute a tactical shot—whether a tempo-gaining bishop activation, a sacrifice exploiting an overloaded defender, a fork on newly weakened squares, or a check exploiting an opened diagonal.
sub_patterns: Slow pawn push ignoring concrete tactical threats (a4, a5, d5, f3)
Piece placed on square where it gets hit with tempo (Qd6 hit by Bg3)
Queen retreating from critical defensive post (Qf8 abandoning c5 defense)
Wrong piece to correct square (Be3 instead of Qe3)
Premature pawn advance before king/piece coordination (g4 before Kf4, d5 before Ne2)
Flashy check instead of quiet winning move (Bb4+ instead of Bc1#)

analysis.label: Moves that displace a piece from a tactically essential square, fatally disrupting coordination and creating king safety vulnerabilities.
analysis.description: This feature fires on moves where a piece leaves (or blocks) a square critical to the position's tactical demands, prioritizing a superficially attractive goal over the urgent need. In 6/7 positions, the moved piece was either defending the player's king or coordinating an attack on the opponent's exposed king. Re1 self-blocks the king's escape route enabling perpetual check (1/7). Kh6 walks the king into h-file check tactics (1/7). Nh2 retreats the f3-knight to a passive rim square where it becomes a target via Qxh2+ (1/7). Nxd4 removes the f3-knight that guarded g2, allowing Qxg2 invasion (1/7). Qg8+ and Qxh8 both displace the queen from a commanding central square, destroying the winning tactical coordination (2/7). b6 wastes a critical tempo with the king in the center, allowing f5 to blow the position open (1/7). In every case, the piece was needed exactly where it was or needed to go to a specific square, and its displacement allows immediate tactical punishment centered on king safety.
analysis.move_pattern: Any piece type moving away from a square where it provided critical defensive or attacking coordination; no consistent direction - includes retreats (Nh2), captures (Nxd4, Qxh8), checks (Qg8+), advances (Kh6, b6), and lateral moves (Re1)
analysis.why_bad: The moved piece was fulfilling an essential tactical function (guarding escape squares, defending key points, coordinating attacks) that becomes immediately exploitable once removed, always resulting in king safety catastrophes - perpetual checks, mating attacks, or winning material with check against the exposed king.
sub_patterns: Self-blocking king escape route (Re1 blocks e1 escape)
Removing defensive knight allowing queen invasion (Nxd4/Nh2 abandon f3 guard duties)
Displacing attacking queen from coordination square (Qg8+/Qxh8 leave critical diagonals)
King walking into check-vulnerable square (Kh6 onto open h-file)
Tempo waste with king unsafe in center (b6 ignoring f5 break)

analysis.chip: Defender Seeks Activity, Leaves Piece Hanging
analysis.label: A piece performing a critical defensive role is moved to an aggressive-looking square, immediately leaving another piece or pawn undefended and tactically exploitable.
analysis.description: In all 4 positions, the player moves a piece that was performing a vital protective function to a square that appears more active or attacking, but in doing so leaves something concretely hanging. In Position 2 (Qf4), the queen abandons defense of the e2 bishop, allowing immediate capture Qxe2 (4/4 hanging piece theme). In Position 8 (Qe3), the queen leaves c3 where it guarded b2, allowing Qxb2 winning a pawn plus attacking the rook and knight (3/4 queen moves). In Position 14 (Qf2), the queen infiltrates to f2 for a speculative g2 attack but abandons defense of d5 and the entire queenside, allowing Qd7 invasion. In Position 5 (Rc8), the rook moves to a seemingly active c-file but leaves the a8 rook permanently stranded on the bishop's diagonal with no recapture possible. The common thread is prioritizing apparent piece activity over maintaining an existing defensive responsibility, resulting in immediate material loss or decisive positional collapse (avg cp_loss: 238).
analysis.move_pattern: Piece (usually queen, 3/4) moves laterally or forward to an active-looking square, vacating a square where it was the sole defender of another piece or pawn
analysis.why_bad: The moved piece was the sole guardian of a specific piece/pawn/square; relocating it creates an immediately exploitable hanging piece or undefended sector that the opponent captures or invades with tempo
sub_patterns: Queen moves from defensive post to aggressive square, hanging a minor piece or pawn (Positions 2, 8)
Queen infiltrates opponent's position but abandons critical sector defense (Position 14)
Rook moves to active file but breaks back-rank connectivity, stranding another rook (Position 5)

analysis.label: Playing a reasonable-looking or intuitive move in a position that demands the single precise forcing continuation, resulting in catastrophic evaluation swings.
analysis.description: This feature fires on positions where very few good moves exist (avg 1.6) and the player chooses a natural-looking alternative instead of the one critical forcing sequence. In 6/9 meaningful positions, the player either moved the wrong piece (Qd3+ instead of Bd3+ in Position 1, Bb3 instead of Nxd8 in Position 15), placed a piece on the wrong square (Rg2 instead of Rg3 in Position 12), or defaulted to routine development when a concrete tactical capture was essential (Nf3 instead of fxe5 in Position 10, Nf6 instead of fxe4 in Position 13, Bg6 instead of Qd7 in Position 9). The remaining cases involve aggressive-looking moves that ignore a critical vulnerability (Nc5 ignoring back-rank mate in Position 8, Qe5 leaving the queen undefended in Position 3). The common thread is that the player identifies the general strategic direction but fails the precise calculation required, often being 'one step off' from the correct execution in positions with zero margin for error.
analysis.move_pattern: Mixed piece types and directions; no single geometric signature. Moves tend to be developing, centralizing, or repositioning pieces to natural-looking squares.
analysis.why_bad: These positions have extremely narrow solution sets where only one specific forcing move works. The played moves follow general principles (develop, centralize, attack) but ignore concrete tactical details—a hanging piece, a back-rank threat, a specific capture order, or a one-square difference that determines whether the opponent can neutralize the attack.
sub_patterns: Wrong piece to same/similar square (Qd3 vs Bd3, Bb3 vs Nxd8)
Wrong square for correct idea (Rg2 vs Rg3)
Routine development instead of concrete tactical capture (Nf3/Nf6 vs pawn captures)
Aggressive move ignoring critical defensive requirement (Nc5, Qe5)
Passive retreat losing critical tempo (Bg6)

analysis.label: Choosing materially tempting or superficially logical moves that waste critical tempo, sacrifice piece coordination, or ignore urgent positional demands.
analysis.description: This feature fires on moves that prioritize small material gains or routine-looking operations while ignoring the position's urgent tactical or strategic demands. In 4/9 positions, the player grabbed a pawn (Rxf2, Bxh2, Nexc2, b6 preparing Bb7) at the cost of piece activity or attack continuity. In 5/9 positions, the player made a 'normal-looking' move (Bc2, Nd2, Bg5, Rf1, b6) that ignored a critical positional urgency—whether that was advancing a passed pawn, relocating a queen to avoid an unfavorable trade, or maintaining a stranglehold on the opponent's king. The common thread is tempo loss (tagged in 7/9 positions) and piece activity degradation (tagged in 8/9 positions). The best moves consistently required maintaining maximum piece coordination or exploiting existing pressure rather than collecting material or making preparatory moves. The positions all punished the player for treating an urgent, dynamic position as though it were calm enough for routine operations.
analysis.move_pattern: Mixed piece types making captures of low-value targets (usually pawns) or making slow positional moves (retreats, development, pawn pushes) when immediate tactical action is required
analysis.why_bad: These moves sacrifice critical tempo, remove well-placed pieces from dominant posts, or ignore urgent positional demands (imminent attacks, favorable exchanges, passed pawn advancement) in exchange for trivial material gains or routine development that the position cannot afford.
sub_patterns: Capturing with wrong piece order (rook before knight on same square)
Removing attacking piece from dominant post to grab a pawn
Slow pawn/bishop moves ignoring imminent kingside attack
Developing into an unfavorable forced exchange
Ignoring queen relocation when favorable trade is threatened

analysis.label: Playing a non-urgent positional or improving move when the position demands immediate attention to a concrete tactical threat or vulnerability.
analysis.description: This feature fires on positions where the player makes a 'quiet' move—typically a king walk, pawn advance, or piece repositioning—that pursues a long-term plan while ignoring an immediate tactical crisis. In 8/8 analyzed positions, the move fails because an opponent's concrete tactical resource (check, fork, breakthrough, file penetration) goes unaddressed. The blundered moves include king centralizations that expose the king (Ke4, Kd2, Kf3, Kh4 — 4/8), flank/center pawn advances that ignore threats (a5, g4, c4, e5 — 4/8), and piece moves that abandon critical defensive duties (Na4, Rhe8). All share the characteristic of being 'slow' moves (no checks, captures, or direct threats) in positions where the narrow margin of good alternatives (avg 1.7 good moves) demanded tactical precision. The tempo wasted allows the opponent to execute a devastating tactical blow: Qh5+ exploiting an open diagonal (2/8), Ng4+ king attacks (1/8), Rg7 penetration (1/8), rook sacrifice enabling promotion (1/8), or piece removal exposing hanging material (2/8).
analysis.move_pattern: Quiet non-forcing move (king walk, pawn push, or piece retreat/repositioning) with no check, capture, or direct threat—typically moving away from the critical sector of the board
analysis.why_bad: The move wastes a critical tempo on a non-urgent improvement while the opponent has an immediate concrete tactical resource (check, fork, penetration, or breakthrough) that the move neither prevents nor addresses, allowing the opponent to seize the initiative with a forcing sequence
sub_patterns: King centralizing into exposed square while pieces need attention
Flank pawn advance ignoring central/king safety crisis
Piece relocation abandoning key defensive square
Positional pawn advance ignoring opponent's advanced passed pawns

analysis.label: Playing a natural-looking but indirect move in a position demanding immediate precise action, resulting in a critical tempo loss that the opponent exploits.
analysis.description: This feature fires on positions where the player chooses a reasonable-seeming move that follows a logical plan but executes it inefficiently, when the position demanded one of very few precise alternatives (avg 1.6 good moves). In 3/8 top positions, the knight goes to f7 when Ne4 or Ne8 reaches the target square f6 more efficiently—a pure routing inefficiency in the same endgame. In 1/8 positions, castling prioritizes unnecessary king safety over urgent queen infiltration (Qa7). In 1/8, Be7 blocks a check passively instead of the precise Qe7 that offers a simplifying trade. In 1/8, Qh5 places the queen aggressively on a square immediately exploitable by Nf4. In 1/8, c4 advances on the wrong flank when g5 was the critical breakthrough. In 1/8, b3 removes the defensive pawn cover from a knight. All 8/8 positions share the tag 'tempo_loss'—the move is never random but rather a plausible idea that costs the one tempo the position cannot afford to waste.
analysis.move_pattern: Varied piece types and directions, but all are non-forcing moves (no checks, no captures) that pursue an indirect plan when a more direct alternative exists
analysis.why_bad: The position requires immediate precise action with very few acceptable alternatives; the played move wastes a critical tempo that allows the opponent to either consolidate defensively (shutting down the winning plan) or execute a tactical exploitation (fork, pin, capturing undefended material)
sub_patterns: Knight taking inefficient route to target square (Nf7 vs Ne4/Ne8→Nf6)
Passive/preparatory move when aggressive concrete action is urgent
Quiet pawn move that removes a key defensive function (b3 unguarding Nc3, c4 allowing h4)

analysis.label: Playing a constructive-looking but non-urgent move while a central pawn is tactically undefended, allowing the opponent to capture it cleanly.
analysis.description: In 4/5 positions, the player made a reasonable-seeming developing, prophylactic, or improving move while a critical central pawn (d4, e4, or e5) was attacked more times than it was defended, allowing the opponent to simply capture it. Position 1: Bd2 left d4 attacked twice (Nc6+Bg7) and defended once. Position 3: h3 left e4 attacked twice (Nf6+Bb7) and defended once. Position 4: Rad8 (wrong rook) left e5 completely undefended for Nxe5. Position 6: Qxe2 moved the queen away from d3, the only defender of d4, allowing Nxd4. Position 5 is a related variant where g6 created a new tactical target (Nxg6 winning the exchange). The common thread is prioritizing general chess principles—development, prophylaxis, rook activation—over the concrete tactical necessity of defending material that is about to be captured for free.
analysis.move_pattern: Varied piece types (bishop, pawn, rook, queen) making non-defensive moves away from or unrelated to the threatened central pawn
analysis.why_bad: The move ignores a concrete counting problem on a central pawn (attackers > defenders), allowing the opponent to win material with a simple capture that requires no deep calculation
sub_patterns: Quiet developing move while center pawn is attacked twice, defended once
Recapturing with the wrong piece, removing the sole defender of another pawn
Developing the wrong rook, leaving a pawn without coverage
Pawn push creating a new tactical target near the king

analysis.label: Playing a natural-looking quiet move in a position demanding precise tactical calculation, leaving material or key squares immediately vulnerable.
analysis.description: This feature fires on positions where a player makes a routine, non-forcing move that appears to address a positional need (king safety, development, piece pressure) but overlooks that the position has only 1-2 correct options (avg 1.3 good moves across all examples). In 4/6 positions, the move directly leaves material hanging or undefended (Ke2 hangs the e3 knight to Bxe3, O-O leaves the e5 pawn undefended, Be7 leaves b5 pawn exposed to Rxb5, Qe1 allows a winning queen trade). In the remaining cases, the move self-blocks a critical tactical resource (Nf3 blocks Qf3 hitting an undefended rook, 1/6) or creates a new vulnerability (c6 opens the a6-c8 diagonal for Ba6+, 1/6). All moves share the quality of being 'the kind of move you'd play if you hadn't deeply calculated' — they follow general principles (address threats, develop, castle, chase pieces, simplify) but fail because the position demands one specific tactical solution.
analysis.move_pattern: Quiet, non-forcing moves (no checks, no captures): king moves, piece development, castling, pawn pushes, piece retreats — all appearing routine/consolidating
analysis.why_bad: The position has essentially one correct move, and these natural-looking alternatives either leave existing material undefended, block critical tactical resources, or create new vulnerabilities that the opponent can immediately exploit for material gain or decisive positional advantage.
sub_patterns: Quiet move leaves existing piece/pawn hanging (Ke2, O-O, Be7)
Natural development blocks key tactical square (Nf3 blocks Qf3)
Piece-chasing pawn push opens dangerous line (c6 opens diagonal)
Premature simplification enters lost endgame (Qe1)

analysis.label: Moving the king (or key defensive piece) to an apparently useful but tactically exposed square on an open line, enabling devastating checks or tempo-gaining attacks.
analysis.description: This feature fires on moves where a piece—most often the king (6/8 positions)—moves to a square that appears active or purposeful but sits vulnerably on an open file, rank, or diagonal. In 6/8 cases the king walks forward or sideways to a square where it can be immediately checked by the opponent's queen or rook along an open line, allowing the opponent to gain decisive tempo (winning material or delivering checkmate). Position 5 (Rd8) and Position 1 (Rf2) show the related pattern of a rook abandoning a critical defensive post, exposing the king to the same open-line exploitation. The moved piece's destination intersects with the opponent's major piece attacking corridors—the e-file (Ke3), h-file (Kg2), 6th rank (Kg6), f-file (Kf4), or d-file (Qd7). The average cp_loss of 3721 and multiple forced mates confirm these are catastrophic misjudgments where the player saw an 'active' purpose (capturing a pawn, blockading, centralizing, attacking) but overlooked that the destination square falls on a lethal geometric line already controlled by the opponent's pieces.
analysis.move_pattern: King (or major piece) moves to an adjacent square that sits on an open file, rank, or diagonal controlled by opponent's queen/rook
analysis.why_bad: The destination square is exposed to immediate tempo-gaining checks or attacks along open lines, allowing the opponent to win material, force the piece back with tempo lost, or deliver checkmate through a sequence of forcing moves
sub_patterns: King advances/sidesteps onto open file where opponent's queen delivers check (Ke3, Kg2, Kf4, Kg6, Kxh4)
Rook abandons defensive post on a key file/rank, exposing king to back-rank or file-based mating threats (Rf2, Rd8)
Queen moves to exposed square on open file where pawn break attacks it with tempo (Qd7)

analysis.label: Moves that pursue a secondary objective (material, space, repositioning) while ignoring the position's single most urgent defensive or dynamic requirement.
analysis.description: This feature fires on positions where the player chooses a seemingly purposeful move—capturing material, pushing pawns for space, or repositioning pieces—while completely neglecting the one critical requirement of the position. In 5/10 cases, a piece or pawn performing a vital defensive function was moved away (Nxb4 abandoned queen defense, c4 removed a rank-blocking pawn, Nh5 left a dominant outpost, Na4 removed back-rank coverage, fxg3 opened lines against own king). In 5/10 cases, a non-urgent pawn push or tempo-wasting maneuver was played when the position demanded immediate development or prophylaxis (h4, f3, b3, d4, Ne4+). These positions averaged only 1.7 good moves available, indicating critical junctures with razor-thin margins where only precise play sufficed. The moves all have plausible intent—gaining material, space, or piece activity—but fundamentally misread the position's true priority, resulting in catastrophic punishment (avg 2233cp loss) via tactics the opponent's response immediately unleashes.
analysis.move_pattern: Mixed piece types and directions; often pawn pushes (h4, f3, b3, c4, d4, fxg3) or knight relocations to peripheral squares (Nh5, Na4, Nxb4, Ne4+); moves directed away from the critical sector of the board
analysis.why_bad: Each move either removes a piece/pawn from a critical defensive function (enabling immediate tactical refutation like forks, back-rank mates, or mating nets) or wastes the single available tempo in a position where only one narrow defensive/developing move maintains the position, allowing the opponent to execute a decisive tactical blow.
sub_patterns: Removing a piece from critical guard duty (Nxb4, Na4, Nh5, c4)
Non-developing pawn push when behind in development (h4, f3, b3)
Releasing tension or opening lines that benefit opponent (d4, fxg3, c4)
Tempo-wasting check/maneuver when direct action was required (Ne4+)

analysis.label: Playing a seemingly constructive or active move that ignores the ONE most urgent positional or tactical requirement (usually castling or neutralizing an immediate threat).
analysis.description: This feature detects positions where exactly one critical task dominates the position's requirements, yet the player makes a 'normal-looking' move that addresses a secondary concern. In 5/9 positions, the urgent requirement was castling or securing king safety (positions 1, 2, 7, 8, 9), while in 2/9 positions it was capturing/neutralizing a dangerous attacking pawn (positions 3, 5). The remaining cases involve advancing a winning passed pawn (position 4) or maintaining a piece on its critical defensive square (position 6). The blunders are diverse in piece type and direction—queen moves, pawn pushes, knight repositioning, rook checks, captures—but all share the characteristic of looking reasonable in isolation while catastrophically failing to address the single thing the position demands. The low average of 1.9 good moves confirms these are narrow positions where only one plan works.
analysis.move_pattern: No single geometric pattern; diverse piece types and directions (queen development, pawn advances, knight moves, rook checks, captures) that share the trait of being secondary or tangential actions rather than the one critical move demanded
analysis.why_bad: The position has ONE dominant requirement (castle, neutralize a threat, advance a passed pawn, or maintain a critical defender), and ignoring it allows the opponent to exploit the unaddressed vulnerability—typically via a tactical shot (fork, discovered attack, pawn advance with check) that punishes the wasted tempo
sub_patterns: Developing/attacking instead of castling when king safety is critical (5/9 cases)
Grabbing material or gaining space instead of neutralizing a dangerous pawn aimed at the king (2/9 cases)
Playing an aimless active move (check, piece repositioning) instead of the one winning continuation (2/9 cases)

analysis.label: Moves that pursue a secondary objective while neglecting the position's single most urgent requirement (piece safety, king safety, or passed pawn), in narrow positions where only ~2 moves are acceptable.
analysis.description: This feature fires on positions where the player makes a move that ignores the most critical vulnerability in their position to chase a peripheral goal. In 5/11 cases, the player neglected king safety to pursue counterplay (Qa2 abandoning kingside, b5 ignoring mate-in-2, Qxh4 grabbing a flank pawn, Qa3 leaving the defense, f6 weakening the diagonal). In 4/11 cases, a piece was moved to a tactically vulnerable square or away from its critical duty (Na6 placing a piece en prise, Nd3 walking into a trapped-piece motif, Nh2 retreating from central control, Rd2 failing to go behind a passed pawn). In 2/11 cases, a pawn move ignored a piece's immediate vulnerability (a5 blocking the knight's escape while it hangs on the file, e6 allowing Qa4+ winning a hanging bishop). The average good moves available was only 2.0, meaning these were critically narrow positions demanding a specific response, yet the player pursued their own agenda instead. The average cp_loss of 1127 reflects catastrophic consequences.
analysis.move_pattern: Any piece or pawn move directed toward a secondary objective (flank, peripheral square, counterattack) while a critical vulnerability on a different axis remains unaddressed
analysis.why_bad: The position demanded addressing a single urgent issue (defending a vulnerable piece, securing king safety, or stopping a passed pawn), but the player pursued a secondary goal (counterplay, material, space, rerouting), allowing the opponent to exploit the unaddressed vulnerability with a forcing tactical sequence (fork, mating attack, piece capture, or promotion threat).
sub_patterns: Queen displacement from defensive duties to pursue queenside counterplay (Qa2, Qa3, Qxh4)
Pawn moves that ignore piece or king vulnerability (a5, b5, e6, f6)
Piece moves to wrong squares ignoring positional/tactical demands (Rd2, Nh2, Nd3, Na6)

analysis.label: Quiet, non-forcing moves played in critical positions where only one specific saving move exists, resulting in catastrophic tactical punishment.
analysis.description: This feature fires on positions where the player faces a severe tactical crisis with only 1-2 viable defensive moves, but instead plays a quiet, routine, or 'improving' move that ignores the emergency. In 5/5 positions, the average number of good moves was just 1.2, indicating razor-thin survival margins. The played moves are all non-forcing (no checks, captures, or direct threats): pawn pushes (f6, e4, b6) or passive queen moves (Qc7, Qc8). In each case, the position demanded a specific defensive resource—bringing a piece back to defend (Qf8 in Position 1, Re1 in Position 4), offering a simplifying trade (Qf3 in Position 2), or a prophylactic move to maintain a critical defensive structure (Ra7 in Position 3, a6 in Position 5). The catastrophic consequence is consistent: the routine move allows an immediate tactical exploitation—back-rank mate (1/5), fork (1/5), mating attack (2/5), or decisive material loss (1/5). All 5 positions were already losing before the blunder, suggesting players under pressure resort to 'normal-looking' moves rather than finding the one precise defensive resource.
analysis.move_pattern: Quiet, non-forcing moves (pawn pushes or queen retreats/developments) with no check, capture, or direct threat
analysis.why_bad: The position demands one specific defensive resource to prevent immediate tactical catastrophe, but the played move ignores the critical threat entirely, allowing the opponent a devastating tactical blow (mate, fork, or winning material through removing a key defender)
sub_patterns: Pawn push weakening own king or removing key defensive pawn support (f6, e4, b6)
Passive queen placement abandoning critical defensive duties (Qc7, Qc8)
Failing to address back-rank/mating net vulnerability

analysis.label: Moves that voluntarily weaken one's own king position by either advancing the f-pawn or walking the king to an exposed square, allowing immediate tactical punishment via checks on open lines.
analysis.description: This feature fires on moves that actively create king vulnerability where none previously existed (or dramatically worsen existing exposure). The dominant pattern involves f-pawn advances (3/9 positions: f4 and f5 pushes) that strip diagonal protection from the king (opening the e1-h4 or e8-h5 diagonal), and king moves to exposed squares (5/9 positions: Ke7, Kf6, Ka2, Kg1, Kf4) that place the king on vulnerable lines. In 7/9 cases, the tactical punishment involves immediate queen or rook checks exploiting newly created diagonal or file weaknesses. The refutations consistently feature Qh4+/Qh5+ patterns (positions 1, 3, 11), infiltration checks like Qg7 or Rf7+ (positions 4, 5), or diagonal checks against the misplaced king (positions 7, 10). The average cp_loss of 1295 is heavily driven by catastrophic cases where the king exposure leads to forced material loss or checkmate. Position 6 (Nf3, 39cp) and Position 8 (Kf4, 16cp) are mild outliers representing the lower activation range.
analysis.move_pattern: F-pawn forward pushes (f4/f5) without development, or king moves to open/exposed squares (typically one step toward the center or away from shelter)
analysis.why_bad: These moves remove critical defensive cover (f-pawn departing its home rank opens the diagonal to the king) or place the king directly on unprotected squares/lines, enabling immediate tactical exploitation through forcing checks that win material or deliver checkmate
sub_patterns: f-pawn advance opening diagonal to uncastled king
king walking into open file or diagonal exposure
king moving without defensive piece coordination
premature pawn thrust before development completed

analysis.label: Non-forcing moves in positions where king safety is the critical tactical factor, either failing to exploit an opponent's exposed king or worsening one's own king vulnerability.
analysis.description: This feature fires on positions where king safety is the overwhelmingly dominant factor (tagged in 7/7 positions) and the player chooses a non-forcing move—pawn pushes (f4, g4), king moves (Kc5, Kf7, Kf2), castling (O-O), or a non-capturing queen repositioning (Qg7)—instead of precise tactical action. In 3/7 cases, the player fails to exploit the opponent's already-exposed king with available forcing moves (Ng8+ fork, Qxh7 capture, c5 attacking White's king on c3). In 4/7 cases, the player actively worsens their own king's safety by walking it into mating nets (Kf2 into Qg2+/Nd5#), exposed positions (Kc5 into Qe3+ cascading checks), or squares that block critical defensive resources (Kf7 blocking the e-file while enabling Rh7+). The common thread is tempo loss (tagged 6/7) in razor-sharp positions where only 1-3 good moves existed, with the chosen move neither creating a concrete threat nor addressing the urgent king-safety tension.
analysis.move_pattern: Non-forcing moves (king moves, kingside pawn pushes, castling, non-capturing queen moves) in positions with exposed kings on both sides; predominantly kingside-directed (6/7 on f/g files or kingside castling)
analysis.why_bad: These moves waste a critical tempo in positions where king exposure demands immediate tactical resolution—either the opponent's exposed king escapes danger, the opponent seizes the initiative against the player's newly-weakened king, or the king walks directly into a mating pattern that the opponent's already-active pieces can immediately exploit.
sub_patterns: Missing forcing tactics against opponent's exposed king (Ng8+, Qxh7, c5 counterplay) in favor of slow improvements
Walking own king into mating nets or exposed squares (Kf2, Kc5, Kf7)
Weakening own king shelter with pawn pushes (f4, g4) when piece activity was needed
Castling away from where counterplay pressure exists against opponent's vulnerable king

analysis.label: Playing a passive repositioning or preparatory move when an immediate tactical capture or forcing strike is available.
analysis.description: In all 5 positions, the player chose a quiet, non-forcing move that repositions a piece or prepares future plans, while missing a concrete tactical opportunity (usually a capture) that was immediately available. In 5/5 cases, the best move involved a direct capture or forcing attack: Nxc5 winning a pawn (Position 1), Ncxe4 winning a central pawn (Position 7), Bg5 attacking a bishop with tempo to enable Bc1 winning b2 (Position 11), Nd3 invading to create a passed pawn (Position 12), and Bxc6+ capturing a piece with check (Position 13). Instead, the played moves were all non-capturing repositioning moves (b3 supporting, Ncd7 retreating, Bf6 passive placement, Re5 centralizing, Qb3 developing) that failed to capitalize on a concrete vulnerability in the opponent's position. The average cp_loss of 343 reflects how costly it is to give the opponent a free tempo to consolidate when a tactical strike was available.
analysis.move_pattern: Non-capturing piece/pawn repositioning move (any piece type, any direction) that is preparatory or 'improving' rather than forcing
analysis.why_bad: These moves waste a critical tempo on passive improvement when a concrete capture or forcing move would exploit a tactical vulnerability (hanging/underdefended piece, vulnerable pawn, or overloaded defender) that disappears once the opponent gets a free move to consolidate.
sub_patterns: Supporting a piece with a pawn when the piece itself should capture (b3 instead of Nxc5)
Retreating an active piece from its ideal square when it should capture immediately (Ncd7 instead of Ncxe4)
Placing a piece on a passive square instead of an aggressive one that creates threats (Bf6 instead of Bg5)
Moving the wrong piece entirely when another has a concrete tactical shot (Re5/Qb3 instead of Nd3/Bxc6+)

analysis.label: Playing a slow, seemingly purposeful move in a sharp position where only one precise continuation maintains the evaluation.
analysis.description: This feature fires on positions where the player makes a quiet, non-forcing move that appears to serve a logical purpose (targeting a square, centralizing, controlling a key point) but catastrophically misreads the position's urgent demands. In all 3/3 positions, there were very few good moves available (avg 1.3), meaning the position demanded extreme precision. In 3/3 cases, the played move gave the opponent a critical tempo to execute a devastating plan—whether invading with a queen (Qa4 allowing Black to consolidate, Kd8 allowing Qe3 winning pawns) or delivering forced mate (f6 allowing Ne5+ and Qxg7+). Each move addressed a secondary concern (queenside pressure, king centralization, e5 control) while ignoring the primary tactical demand of the position. The feature captures the moment a player makes a 'reasonable-looking' quiet move in a position that is actually tactically critical and unforgiving.
analysis.move_pattern: Quiet non-forcing moves (queen retreat/sortie, king walk, pawn push) in positions requiring the single precise continuation
analysis.why_bad: These moves waste a critical tempo in sharp positions where only one precise move works, allowing the opponent to execute a decisive tactical operation (queen invasion, pawn capture chain, or forced mating attack) that was previously preventable.
sub_patterns: Queen sortie to wrong flank abandoning initiative
King move when piece defense needed
Pawn push self-blocking escape squares

analysis.label: Aggressive-looking moves that abandon critical defensive responsibilities, allowing opponents to immediately exploit what's left unprotected.
analysis.description: This feature fires on moves that appear active or purposeful—attacking a target, seeking counterplay, or placing pieces on seemingly active squares—but fatally neglect the position's actual defensive demands. In 4/4 positions, the played move prioritized an offensive goal while leaving something critical exposed: e4 removed a pawn that defended a knight (2/4 involve removed defenders), Bd6 placed the bishop on a square directly attacked by an opponent's knight allowing capture with check (1/4), Qh6 abandoned the queenside while leaving b4 hanging (1/4), and Rb6 gave up f-file control and checking ability to passively target a pawn (1/4). In all cases, quieter alternatives (h5/Be7/b5/Rc6+) that maintained defensive integrity were available (avg 2.2 good moves). The common refutation pattern is the opponent immediately exploiting the abandoned defensive function—winning material, seizing initiative, or creating decisive threats—with tempo_loss appearing in 3/4 positions and piece_activity concerns in 3/4.
analysis.move_pattern: Any piece type moving toward an apparent target (center push, active diagonal, kingside attack, pawn attack) while leaving a critical square, file, or piece undefended
analysis.why_bad: Each move abandons a specific defensive duty (protecting a piece, controlling a key file, defending a pawn, avoiding a tactical square) in pursuit of an offensive plan that the position doesn't support, giving the opponent an immediate concrete exploitation.
sub_patterns: Pawn advance removing protection from a piece
Piece placed on square attacked by opponent's minor piece
Queen/major piece redeployed to wrong flank leaving material hanging
Rook abandoning active file for passive pawn targeting

analysis.label: Making a natural-looking move that wastes a decisive tempo, allowing the opponent's latent threat (usually a passed pawn advance or piece invasion) to become unstoppable.
analysis.description: This feature fires on moves that appear purposeful or active but fatally misjudge the position's timing requirements, gifting the opponent a crucial tempo for their own plan. In 6/7 positions, the analyses explicitly tag 'tempo_loss' as a key factor. The pattern manifests as: abandoning support of one's own passed pawn (Position 4: Ke5 leaves g7 unguarded, allowing Rg4; Position 8: Kd3 wastes time while a3-a2 creates unstoppable passers), removing a piece from a critical defensive post (Position 14: Nc6 vacates e7, releasing the rook along the 7th rank), or executing the right plan in the wrong move order (Position 5: e4 before fxg4 allows gxf3+ intermediate check; Position 2: cxb5 instead of dxc5 opens the a-file for opponent's counterplay). In 5/7 cases, the opponent exploits the tempo to advance passed pawns or deliver tactical blows through newly opened lines. The positions are already tense—often promotion races or positions with dynamic balance—where a single wasted tempo is the difference between winning/drawing and losing.
analysis.move_pattern: Piece (often king) moves in an apparently purposeful direction that abandons its most critical current function; or pawn push/capture executed one move too early before a necessary preparatory move
analysis.why_bad: The move neglects the position's most time-critical requirement—supporting a passed pawn, blocking an invasion route, or eliminating an intermediate tactical resource—giving the opponent exactly one tempo to convert a latent threat into a decisive one
sub_patterns: King moves away from its own passed pawn in a promotion race
Knight/piece leaves critical blockade square releasing opponent's pieces
Premature pawn push before eliminating opponent's intermediate check/capture
Wrong capture direction opening files toward own king

analysis.label: Non-urgent pawn moves or peripheral pawn captures that squander a critical tempo in dynamically tense positions requiring immediate action.
analysis.description: This feature fires on moves that waste a decisive tempo when the position demands urgent action—typically involving passed pawn races, active piece coordination, or defensive emergencies. The most common manifestation is prophylactic h-pawn pushes (h3, h6, h6 in 3/9 positions) or greedy captures of rim pawns (Kxh5, Rxh6, Qxb6 in 3/9 positions) when the position requires maintaining dynamic tension. In 7/9 positions, a critical passed pawn (either the player's own needing advancement or the opponent's needing restraint) is the key dynamic element being neglected. The quiet move gives the opponent time to either promote (positions 2, 5), execute a devastating exchange combination (positions 12, 14), exploit a hanging piece (position 3), or launch a kingside attack (position 15). Position 10 (Bd3+, 0cp loss) appears to be a control activation showing the same positional pattern where only one precise move works. The average cp_loss of 385 and average of only 1.3 good moves confirms these are critical-precision moments where a single wasted tempo is catastrophic.
analysis.move_pattern: Pawn advances to h3/h6/a5 (rim files), pawn captures by major pieces on wing squares (h5, h6, b6), or piece retreats abandoning critical blockade squares—all non-urgent moves peripheral to the board's dynamic center of gravity
analysis.why_bad: The position contains a time-critical dynamic element (passed pawn race, piece coordination advantage, or tactical vulnerability) that evaporates with one lost tempo, allowing the opponent to promote, execute exchange combinations, or launch decisive attacks that the 'quiet' move fails to prevent.
sub_patterns: Prophylactic h-pawn pushes (h3/h6) ignoring tactical urgency
Greedy pawn captures deflecting pieces from critical duties
Slow flank pawn pushes while center demands immediate attention
Piece retreat abandoning blockade of enemy passed pawn

analysis.label: Moving a piece (usually king or queen) to a square where it becomes immediately vulnerable to the opponent's already-active forces on open lines.
analysis.description: This feature fires on moves that voluntarily place a piece on a tactically compromised square, giving the opponent a decisive tempo or tactical opportunity. In 4/6 positions, the king moves to a square aligned on an open file with enemy rooks or queens (Kb6 walks into Qb3+ winning the queen, Ke2 places king on the open e-file as a permanent target, Ke7 creates a catastrophic pin between king and queen on the e-file). In 1/6, the queen captures a poisoned pawn and becomes trapped on a2 with no escape squares. In 1/6, the queen abandons a dominant central post (d5) for g2, directly in the path of an advancing f-pawn that gains a crushing tempo. In 1/6, a knight passively retreats to a natural-looking square that blocks its own counterplay and surrenders all initiative. The common thread is that each move looks plausible (centralizing, developing, or grabbing material) but places the piece precisely where the opponent's already-coordinated forces can exploit it immediately.
analysis.move_pattern: Piece (King, Queen, or Knight) moves to a square on an open file, diagonal, or restricted zone controlled by opponent's active pieces
analysis.why_bad: The piece lands on a square where it becomes an immediate tactical target—subject to pins, trapping, checks, or tempo-gaining attacks by the opponent's already-positioned forces—transforming a manageable position into a critical vulnerability.
sub_patterns: King walks onto open file aligned with enemy rooks/queen (3/6 positions)
Queen moves to restricted corner/edge square and becomes trapped or attacked (2/6 positions)
Piece retreats passively, surrendering active post and giving opponent free tempi (1/6 positions)

analysis.label: Playing a routine developing, repositioning, or prophylactic move in a critical position that demands immediate concrete action to address a single urgent problem.
analysis.description: This feature activates when players ignore the most pressing demand of the position in favor of a 'normal-looking' move. In 9/9 positions, there was one specific urgent issue requiring attention: an exposed king needing defensive coverage (positions 1, 7, 9), a piece needing immediate repositioning to avoid tactical exploitation (positions 2, 3, 8), a passed pawn requiring containment (position 5), a critical tempo needed to maintain central tension (positions 4, 6). Instead, players chose moves that addressed secondary concerns—bishop development (Bb2, Bc1 in 2/9), queen repositioning (Qd2, Qc6 in 2/9), prophylactic pawn moves (f5, g6, g6 in 3/9), or seemingly active piece play (Nb5, Re1 in 2/9). The positions average only 1.4 good moves, confirming these are narrow critical moments where only precise responses maintain the evaluation. The average cp_loss of 252 reflects how catastrophically these non-urgent moves fail when the position's single most important problem goes unaddressed.
analysis.move_pattern: Diverse piece types and directions—queen repositioning, bishop development/retreat, pawn advances, knight jumps, rook redeployment—all sharing the quality of being non-forcing and addressing a secondary concern
analysis.why_bad: Each move fails to address the single most urgent problem in the position (an immediate tactical threat, a critical weakness needing coverage, or a concrete forcing sequence requiring a response), giving the opponent a free tempo to execute their primary plan with decisive effect.
sub_patterns: Quiet bishop development/retreat while king faces immediate tactical danger (Bb2, Bc1)
Prophylactic kingside pawn moves that weaken rather than strengthen (g6, f5)
Queen repositioning that abandons critical defensive duties (Qd2, Qc6)
Active-looking piece moves that ignore the opponent's most threatening plan (Nb5, Re1)

analysis.label: Playing a natural-looking or superficially active move that wastes a critical tempo while the position demands one specific urgent concrete action.
analysis.description: This feature fires on positions where the player chose a plausible-looking aggressive or 'useful' move—attacking a pawn (a5, f6), giving a check (Bh2+), threatening a square (Ng4, Nb4), asking a question of a piece (h3), or 'improving' placement (Rcf5)—but missed the position's single urgent requirement. In 5/7 positions, only 1 good move existed within 50cp of best, indicating razor-sharp critical moments. The blunders all share a pattern of appearing active while actually wasting tempo: the pawn pushes (a5, f6, h3) ignore development or tactical shots; the piece moves (Ng4, Nb4) abandon control of critical central squares; the check (Bh2+) strands a piece; and the rook move (Rcf5) creates redundancy. In every case, the opponent punishes the wasted tempo with a concrete forcing sequence—breakthrough pawns (d6, b5), piece invasions, forks, or traps—that exploits the newly created weakness. The correct moves in 6/7 positions involved either concrete tactical exploitation (Nxe5, Bxf2+, Nf5+), urgent development (Nh6, Nd4, Nh5), or targeted counterplay on the correct sector.
analysis.move_pattern: Mixed piece types and directions; all are non-forcing moves (or purposeless forcing moves like checks) that appear active but serve a secondary goal rather than the position's primary demand
analysis.why_bad: Each move wastes a critical tempo pursuing a secondary plan while ignoring an urgent positional or tactical requirement (development, king safety, concrete tactical shot), allowing the opponent to seize initiative with forcing moves that exploit the newly undefended squares or stranded pieces.
sub_patterns: Flank pawn pushes ignoring urgent development needs
Purposeless checks that strand attacking pieces
Knight moves to aggressive squares that abandon control of key central squares
Slow prophylactic pawn moves missing concrete tactical shots
Redundant piece regrouping when forcing action is available

analysis.label: Playing a non-urgent positional move that fails to address an immediate tactical vulnerability of a specific piece or square, allowing the opponent to win material through a forcing sequence.
analysis.description: In all 6 positions, the player makes a quiet, positionally-motivated move (flank pawn push, rook activation, piece redeployment) while ignoring an urgent tactical problem that demands immediate attention. In 3/6 cases, the move itself actively removes a critical defense (b3 removes the b2-pawn's guard of Nc3, Nd7 removes the f6-knight's guard of h7, dxc3 removes the d4-pawn blocking queen diagonals to the king). In the other 3/6 cases, the move simply wastes tempo while an existing vulnerability goes unaddressed (Rhe8 ignores the undefended a6 pawn, g3 ignores the b2-bishop's exposure after e4+, a5 ignores the c6-knight's tactical weakness on the open file). The average cp_loss of 366 reflects that in each case, the opponent can immediately exploit the vulnerability through a forcing tactical sequence—sacrifices, checks, or simple captures—winning at least a full piece worth of material. The common thread is prioritizing a slow plan over addressing the single most critical tactical issue.
analysis.move_pattern: Quiet pawn pushes (especially flank: b3, g3, a5) or non-forcing piece moves (Rhe8, Nd7, dxc3) that neither defend the vulnerable piece nor neutralize the tactical threat
analysis.why_bad: Each move ignores an immediate tactical vulnerability—either actively removing a key defender or wasting tempo while a piece/square is already inadequately protected—allowing the opponent to exploit the hanging/exposed piece through a forcing sequence that wins material
sub_patterns: Self-unguarding: moving a pawn or piece that was the sole defender of another piece (b3 unguards Nc3, Nd7 unguards h7)
Line-opening self-harm: capturing/moving a pawn that was blocking dangerous lines to own king (dxc3 opens diagonals)
Ignoring existing vulnerability: playing elsewhere while a piece is already tactically exposed (Rhe8 ignores a6, g3 ignores Bb2, a5 ignores Nc6)

analysis.label: Playing a passive, non-forcing move when the position demanded immediate concrete action, wasting a decisive tempo.
analysis.description: This feature activates on moves that are superficially natural or 'improving' but catastrophically waste a tempo in positions at a critical tipping point. In 11/12 positions, the analyses explicitly tag 'tempo_loss' as a key motif. The played moves are universally non-forcing (no checks, captures, or direct threats), while the best alternatives involve concrete actions: checks (f5+ in positions 7, 9), captures (Nxg5 in position 1), urgent pawn breaks (d4 in position 12, e5 in position 10), or directly addressing the opponent's most pressing threat (Kf3 blocking a passed pawn in position 3, g3 creating king shelter in position 14). The blunders often look reasonable—centralizing a king (Kd5, Kh8, Kf7, Kg1), developing a rook (Re8, Rh3, Rad8), or a prophylactic flank move (a6)—but they all fail to interact with the position's critical tension, allowing the opponent one free tempo to execute a winning plan (a knight outpost, a pawn break, a mating net, or a perpetual check escape).
analysis.move_pattern: Non-forcing moves of any piece type (king retreats/sidesteps, rook repositioning, slow pawn advances, knight maneuvers) that do not deliver check, capture material, or create an immediate threat
analysis.why_bad: The opponent is one tempo away from executing a concrete winning plan (breakthrough, fork, promotion threat, mating net, or seizing the center), and the passive move gives them exactly the time needed to achieve it, transforming the position's evaluation by 200-9000+ centipawns
sub_patterns: King moves to wrong square when pawn advance or active centralization was needed (Kg3/Kd5/Kh8/Kf7/Kg1)
Rook repositioning that abandons critical defensive duties (Re8/Rh3/Rad8)
Quiet pawn/piece moves ignoring tactical urgency (a6/f6/Ndf6/Nd5)

analysis.label: Moving a piece to merely approach or threaten a target when an immediate capture or more forcing action was available.
analysis.description: In 5/5 positions, Black played a move that approached or indirectly threatened an enemy piece/pawn rather than executing a direct capture or decisive action that was immediately available. In 2/5 cases (Kc6 and Kf5), the king moved toward a knight that could have been captured outright by another piece (Rxc7 or dxe4). In 1/5 (Ba3), a bishop attacked a rook indirectly when the other bishop could infiltrate to d3 winning material immediately. In 1/5 (Kb5), the king approached a pawn on the queenside when centralization to d5 was required. In 1/5 (Rb4), the rook passively approached targets when the forcing d4 pawn break was available. The common thread is choosing a slow, 'threatening' move over an immediately decisive one — seeing the right target but using the wrong piece or wrong tempo to address it. All 5/5 positions feature tempo loss as the critical failure, giving the opponent time to escape or consolidate.
analysis.move_pattern: Piece (often king) moves toward an enemy piece/pawn without capturing, typically 1-2 squares, when a direct capture or forcing move by a different piece existed
analysis.why_bad: These moves give the opponent a full tempo to escape, reposition, or consolidate, turning what should be an immediate material gain or decisive action into a mere threat that can be parried — the target escapes and often becomes actively dangerous
sub_patterns: King approaches capturable piece instead of taking with rook/pawn
Bishop threatens from wrong angle when immediate infiltration wins
Piece approaches peripheral target when central action is decisive

analysis.label: Non-forcing 'improving' moves that waste a critical tempo when the position demands specific tactical or defensive precision.
analysis.description: This feature fires on positions where the player makes a plausible-looking quiet move (no check, no capture, no forcing threat) that misses the position's concrete tactical demand. In 12/12 positions, the played move was a non-forcing 'improvement' (developing, centralizing, repositioning) while either a critical tactical shot existed (Re7 missing Rd8+ back-rank mate pattern, Position 15; Rd4 missing Bxd5/Rxc5 combination, Position 9), or a specific defensive resource was required (Bd2 ignoring Nxg3, Position 1; h4 removing hxg3 recapture, Position 10). The moves consistently address the WRONG aspect of the position—pursuing general activity, development, or attacking ideas in positions that demanded concrete precision. In 9/12 cases the 'tempo_loss' tag appears, and in 10/12 cases 'missed_tactic' is relevant. The average cp_loss of 235 with only 1.9 good moves available confirms these are critical moments where the quiet approach catastrophically fails. The punished player essentially played 'a move' rather than 'the move.'
analysis.move_pattern: Non-forcing quiet moves (no checks, no captures): piece repositioning, development, pawn advances, or king walks that lack immediate threats
analysis.why_bad: The position required either a specific forcing continuation (tactical shot, back-rank combination, concrete defense) or prophylactic action against an imminent threat, but the player chose a general 'improving' move that gives the opponent a free tempo to execute their tactical plan or consolidate an advantage.
sub_patterns: Piece repositioning to seemingly active square that's actually passive or vulnerable (Nf6, Rd4, Re7, Rg8, Qe3, Qb6)
Development or king move that ignores a hanging/tactical weakness (Bd2, Na3, Ke3, Kg5)
Pawn advance that removes a critical defensive resource (h4, c6)

analysis.label: Passive, non-forcing repositioning moves played in positions that demand one specific concrete tactical action, resulting in catastrophic evaluation drops.
analysis.description: This feature fires on positions where players choose a slow, 'natural-looking' improving move (developing, centralizing, or repositioning a piece) when the position is tactically critical and demands immediate concrete action. In 7/11 positions, the move was a quiet non-forcing piece repositioning (Be7 x3, Ne6, Na4, Nh6, Nf6). In 3/11, it was a king move to the wrong square (Kg8, Kf1, Kc6). The positions share extremely narrow margins (avg 1.9 good moves available) where only one or two specific forcing moves maintain the position, yet the player defaults to a generic positional move. The consequences are catastrophic (avg 2811cp loss), with 3/11 resulting in forced mate. The common thread is that each move addresses a vague positional concern (development, centralization, king safety) while completely ignoring an urgent tactical demand: defending f7 (3/11), capturing hanging material (1/11), forcing a saving exchange (2/11), avoiding skewers/mate patterns (3/11), or maintaining perpetual check (1/11).
analysis.move_pattern: Non-capturing, non-forcing piece repositioning (knights, bishops, kings) to seemingly natural/improving squares; occasionally an ineffective check
analysis.why_bad: Each move ignores the one critical tactical requirement of the position—whether defending a weakness, capturing material, forcing a trade, or avoiding a geometric vulnerability—in favor of a slow improving move that gives the opponent a free tempo to execute a devastating tactical blow (skewer, fork, mate, material win).
sub_patterns: Passive bishop development (Be7) ignoring f7 vulnerability in Italian Game positions
Knight repositioning to undefended or self-blocking squares (Na4, Nh6, Ne6, Nf6)
King moves to wrong square missing only saving tactical resource (Kg8, Kf1, Kc6)
Ineffective check when only one specific check angle maintains survival (Qh4+ vs Qf8+)

analysis.label: Advancing a passed pawn to the 7th/2nd rank without adequate piece support, allowing blockade, capture, or tactical refutation.
analysis.description: This feature fires on moves that push a passed pawn to the penultimate rank (7th for White, 2nd for Black) prematurely, before establishing the necessary piece coordination to support promotion. In 13/13 positions, the move advances a passed pawn one square from queening—d7 (4x), c7 (2x), a2 (2x), d2 (2x), f7, f2, b2, e7—without the king or other pieces properly positioned to escort it. The correct alternatives consistently involve king activation first (Kh5, Kb5, Kd4, Kf5, etc.) before the final pawn push, ensuring the pawn advances with support rather than becoming an unsupported target. In at least 10/13 cases the refutation involves blockading the pawn with the opposing king (Kd7, Ke2, Ke7), attacking it from behind with a rook (Rf7, Rd8, Ra6), or simply capturing the undefended pawn/promoted piece. The average cp_loss of 3138 reflects that these positions are often decisive moments where the pawn represents the player's last significant asset.
analysis.move_pattern: Pawn push forward one square to the 7th rank (White) or 2nd rank (Black), always a passed pawn advancing to the penultimate promotion square
analysis.why_bad: Without king escort or piece support, the pawn on the 7th/2nd rank becomes a static target rather than a dynamic threat—it can be blockaded by the opposing king, attacked from behind by a rook, or the resulting promotion immediately neutralized, while the premature advance squanders the pawn's potential as a supported promotion threat.
sub_patterns: Pawn to 7th without king on adjacent supporting square, allowing king blockade (d7/e7/f7/c7 without king on e6/d6/g6/b6)
Pawn to 2nd rank with rook in front rather than behind, allowing opponent's rook to blockade from the first rank (a2/d2 with rook on wrong file)
Pawn to 7th enabling opponent's rook-behind-pawn technique to capture the pawn or newly promoted queen
Pawn to penultimate rank ignoring immediate king safety threats (allowing back-rank mate or tactical shots)

analysis.label: Advancing a pawn break in a closed position that loses material or dangerously opens lines against the player's own position.
analysis.description: This feature fires on positions where a player makes a pawn advance (typically a central or semi-central break) in a closed position, when maintaining the closed structure was essential. In 5/6 positions the center is explicitly closed, and in 5/6 cases the advancing pawn is immediately captured by an enemy pawn that was already controlling that square (exf5, fxe4, bxc5, fxe5/dxe5, exd5/cxd5). The common thread is that the closed structure was actually protecting the player—often shielding an exposed or uncastled king (4/6 positions involve king safety concerns) or preserving a positional advantage. The blundered pawn advance either drops material directly because the pawn is insufficiently supported (4/6), opens lines that expose the player's own king (3/6), or wastes a critical tempo when tactical threats demanded immediate attention (2/6). In every case, patient alternatives maintaining the closed structure (Bf4, a5, Qb6, e6, dxc4) were clearly superior.
analysis.move_pattern: Single-step pawn advance (typically d, e, f, or c-pawn) pushing into the center or toward the opponent's pawn chain, where enemy pawns already control the target square
analysis.why_bad: The advancing pawn enters a square already attacked by enemy pawns, allowing simple capture that either wins the pawn outright or opens critical lines against the player's vulnerable king—the closed structure that was protecting the player's position gets destroyed for nothing.
sub_patterns: Pawn push into double-attacked square loses pawn immediately (f5/e5/c5/e4)
Central break opens files against own uncastled/exposed king (d5/e5/b6)
Choosing a speculative pawn break over an available winning tactic (f5 instead of Bxg4)

analysis.label: Moves that place or leave the queen on the same open file as the player's own uncastled king, enabling a devastating rook pin.
analysis.description: In 10/11 positions, the blundering move creates or fails to resolve a fatal geometric alignment between the player's queen and their own uncastled king on the same open file. The most common pattern (9/11) involves the e-file, where moves like Qxe4, Qe2, or Qe6 place the queen directly in line with the king on e1/e8, while two positions involve the c-file (cxd5 opening it toward king on c8, Qxc5 placing queen on it). In every case, the opponent already has their king safely castled while the blundering side's king remains in the center. The punishment is almost universally a rook swing to the file (Re1, Re8, or Rc1), creating an absolute or near-absolute pin that wins the queen or forces catastrophic material loss. Position 9 (N2f3) is a subtle variant where the knight blocks the queen's only escape square from the vulnerable file. Position 12 (Bd3) wastes the critical tempo needed to castle, leaving the existing queen-king alignment exploitable.
analysis.move_pattern: Queen placed/captured onto same open file (usually e-file) as own king, or move that traps queen on that file; king always uncastled on e1/e8/c8
analysis.why_bad: The opponent exploits the queen-king alignment with a rook move to that file, creating a pin that wins the queen for a rook (or less), typically a 4+ point material swing. The uncastled king cannot escape the file quickly enough.
sub_patterns: Queen captures pawn on e4 with king on e1/e8 (Qxe4 - 4 positions)
Queen develops to e2/e6 on same file as king (Qe2/Qe6 - 3 positions)
Pawn capture opens file toward own castled king (cxd5/Qxc5 on c-file - 2 positions)
Move blocks queen escape from dangerous file (N2f3, Bd3 - 2 positions)

analysis.label: Player fails to capture an undefended central d-pawn (d4 or d5) in the opening, instead making a developing or repositioning move.
analysis.description: In all 12/12 positions, the best move was to capture a hanging d-pawn (d4 or d5) that was undefended or insufficiently protected, but the player made a different move instead. In 8/12 cases the best capture was specifically Qxd4 or Qxd5 with the queen; in 2/12 cases the player captured the d-pawn but with the wrong piece (Nxd5 or Nxd4 instead of using the queen), creating tactical vulnerabilities. In the remaining cases, players made quiet developing moves (Be3, Bf5, e6, f5) or repositioned their queen to unproductive squares (Qa5, Qc3, Qd8, Qc4) while a free central pawn sat uncaptured. All positions occurred in the opening (11/12) with both kings still in the center, and the average cp_loss was 291, reflecting the enormous cost of missing material. The average of only 1.2 good moves available confirms these were critical decision points where the hanging d-pawn capture was essentially the only correct choice.
analysis.move_pattern: Any piece move that is NOT capturing the hanging d4 or d5 pawn; often queen moves to side squares (a5, c3, c4, d8) or minor piece development (Bf5, Be3) or wrong-piece captures (Nxd4/Nxd5 instead of Qxd4/Qxd5)
analysis.why_bad: The player ignores a free central pawn capture, either failing to notice d4/d5 is undefended or instinctively making a 'natural' developing/repositioning move, thereby forfeiting material while allowing the opponent to consolidate their center or gain tempo with counterattacks.
sub_patterns: Queen retreats/sidesteps while d4 hangs (Qa5, Qd8, Qc4)
Knight captures d-pawn instead of queen, creating tactical vulnerability (Nxd5, Nxd4)
Quiet developing move ignoring hanging d-pawn (Be3, Bf5, e6, f5)
Autopilot theoretical moves in Scandinavian positions where d4 is actually undefended

analysis.label: Moving a rook to an open file to oppose the opponent's heavy pieces when a more forcing tactical move was required.
analysis.description: In all 4/4 positions, the player moves a rook to an open file (e-file in 3 cases, b-file in 1 case) where the opponent's queen already sits, intending to 'contest' the file through the general principle of placing rooks on open files. However, in each case the opponent already dominates that file with superior heavy-piece coordination, making the rook move ineffective or tactically vulnerable. The positions all demanded concrete, forcing alternatives instead: a centralizing knight leap (Nd5 in position 2), a piece attack on a hanging rook (Nf4 in position 3), challenging an invasive knight (b3 in position 11), or prophylactic king safety moves avoiding back-rank issues (h4 in position 12). The rook moves lose tempo (3/4 positions tagged tempo_loss) and allow the opponent to consolidate, block the file (position 11: Ne5 blocks), or exploit tactical vulnerabilities created by the rook's placement (position 12: back-rank combination). Average cp_loss of 221 reflects how the 'principled' but generic file-contesting move catastrophically misses position-specific tactical demands.
analysis.move_pattern: Rook moves along the back rank (1st or 8th) to an open file where the opponent's queen is already placed, opposing heavy pieces
analysis.why_bad: The opponent already dominates the contested file with better-coordinated heavy pieces, making the rook move either a wasted tempo (allowing opponent to consolidate/block), or tactically exploitable via forcing captures with check along that very file. A concrete forcing move was always available instead.
sub_patterns: Rook to e1 opposing queen on e-file (most common)
Rook to back rank opposing queen on b-file
Rook enters file that gets immediately blocked by opponent's knight

analysis.label: Making a strategic-looking move while a rook is hanging or being placed where it can be immediately captured by a minor piece.
analysis.description: This feature fires on moves that overlook a simple one-move tactical threat involving a rook being captured. In 6/8 positions, the blunder directly allows a minor piece (knight or bishop) to capture an undefended rook: Position 1 (b3 ignores Nxf1), Position 3 (c5 ignores Nxb6 winning the rook), Position 4 (Ra8 places rook on square attacked by Nb6), Position 5 (Re3 places rook on square attacked by Bg5), Position 12 (Nd5 ignores Nxf8), and Position 15 (Bxc2 leaves Rc1 undefended for Nxc1). The remaining positions follow the same template of overlooking immediate material-winning captures. The moves themselves look purposeful—pawn structure improvements, piece centralizations, active-looking deployments—but all fatally ignore a concrete one-move threat that wins the exchange or a full rook. The player appears to be thinking strategically while a simple tactical reality goes unnoticed.
analysis.move_pattern: Any piece type; move ignores or enables an opponent minor piece capturing a rook in one move
analysis.why_bad: The move ignores an immediate one-move tactic where an opponent's knight or bishop can capture an undefended or inadequately defended rook, winning the exchange or a full piece.
sub_patterns: Pawn/knight move ignores existing attack on own rook (b3, c5, Nd5)
Rook moves to a square controlled by opponent minor piece (Ra8, Re3)
Capturing with wrong piece leaves rook undefended (Bxc2, Rxg3)

analysis.label: Playing a natural-looking move in a critical position where exactly one move was required, enabling the opponent to deliver a forcing check that wins material.
analysis.description: In all 5/5 positions, there was exactly one good move available (avg good moves = 1.0), creating razor-thin tactical obligations. The blunder in each case was a seemingly reasonable move (king retreats, piece centralization, rook development) that ignored the single critical tactical requirement. In 4/5 cases, the punishment was an immediate forcing check (Qd2+ winning Rh6, Qxg7+ winning the b2 pawn, Nxf5+ winning the exchange, Ng5+ winning the d5 knight) that the correct move would have prevented. The correct moves varied—capturing an attacking piece (Kxf7, Nxe5 in 2/5), moving to the one safe square (Kg4, Kd5 in 2/5), or repositioning a tactically vulnerable piece (Nf6 in 1/5)—but all shared the property of being the unique response to the position's critical constraint. The blunders typically placed the king or pieces on squares that fell on checking diagonals/lines, giving the opponent tempo to execute material-winning combinations.
analysis.move_pattern: King moves to vulnerable squares (3/5) or piece moves ignoring captures/defensive duties (2/5); all moves place pieces on tactically exploitable squares along checking lines
analysis.why_bad: The moves ignore the position's single critical tactical constraint, placing the king or pieces on squares where the opponent gains decisive tempo through forcing checks, enabling material wins (hanging pieces captured, forks executed, passed pawns eliminated)
sub_patterns: King moves to a square allowing check + material capture (Kg2→Qd2+, Kd7→Qxg7+, Kd6→Nxf5+)
Piece development/centralization ignoring a hanging piece or defensive duty (Nd4 missing Nxe5, Rf8 ignoring Ng5+ vulnerability)
Failing to capture an attacking piece when that capture is the only good move (Kd6 instead of Kxf7)

analysis.label: Quiet, non-forcing flank pawn moves (or routine development) played in tactically critical positions that demand immediate concrete action.
analysis.description: This feature fires on positions where the player makes a passive, non-forcing move—overwhelmingly a one-square flank pawn advance (g6, g3, h6, b6, a5 account for 10/12 positions)—when the position urgently demands a concrete tactical response. In every case, the position contains an immediate tactical vulnerability (Nxf7 fork in 2/12, hanging piece in 2/12, open file/diagonal exploitation in 3/12) or requires urgent development/piece coordination (3/12), yet the player treats the moment as quiet and prophylactic. The blundered moves typically address imaginary future threats (preventing Bg5 pins, creating luft, claiming queenside space) while ignoring present dangers. The best moves in these positions are invariably forcing or concrete: capturing a powerful piece (Bxe5), retreating an attacked piece (Ne8, Bg6), making a tactical pawn break (g4), or playing a deflection (Nh4). The average cp_loss of 1033 and the low average of 1.9 good moves available confirm these are critical decision points where slow play is catastrophically punished.
analysis.move_pattern: One-square flank pawn advances (g3/g6/h6/b6/a5) or routine non-forcing development, almost never involving captures, checks, or direct threats
analysis.why_bad: These moves waste a critical tempo in positions where an immediate tactical threat exists or concrete action is needed—the opponent exploits the time gift with sacrifices, piece invasions, or positional seizures that the passive move fails to prevent or address
sub_patterns: g-pawn/h-pawn push weakening king shelter when dark squares are already under pressure
Prophylactic h6/a5 ignoring immediate knight sacrifice on f7 or central tactical blow
Flank pawn move (b6/a5) when urgent development or piece coordination is needed
g3 push opening critical diagonal or wasting tempo when forcing moves win material
Routine piece development ignoring immediate tactical vulnerability of existing pieces

analysis.label: Playing a superficially aggressive move (bishop pin, pawn thrust, or check) when the position demanded a more precise concrete winning continuation.
analysis.description: This feature activates when players choose optically aggressive moves that waste a critical tempo. In 4/9 positions (3, 8, 9, 10), the best move was a knight jump to g5 or g4 creating concrete tactical threats against f7, but instead a bishop was moved to a similar attacking square (Bb5, Bg4, Bg5) or the wrong knight was centralized (Nd5)—choosing the wrong piece for the right idea. In 3/9 positions (1, 2, 5), the player pushed a kingside pawn (g4, h5, g5) in a pawn endgame when king infiltration (Kh3, Kh6) was the only winning plan—squandering reserve tempo needed for zugzwang. In 2/9 positions (11, 15), a bishop was moved aggressively (Bf4+ check, Bh6 exchange attempt) when a quiet positional move or central break was required. The common thread is that all moves LOOK aggressive but fail to create sufficient concrete threats, giving the opponent one critical tempo to neutralize the position.
analysis.move_pattern: Bishop moves to attacking squares (pins, checks, exchanges) or premature kingside pawn advances, typically to squares on the 4th-6th ranks on the g/h files
analysis.why_bad: These moves waste a critical tempo on a superficially threatening action that the opponent can easily neutralize, when the position required either a more precise tactical strike (typically Ng5/Ng4 exploiting f7) or patient preparation (king infiltration, quiet repositioning) to maintain a winning advantage.
sub_patterns: Bishop to pin/attack square when knight jump to same wing was winning (Bg4/Bg5/Bb5 instead of Ng4/Ng5)
Premature pawn advance in endgame when king infiltration was the winning plan
Flashy check or exchange attempt when quiet positional move was required

analysis.label: Playing a non-capturing repositioning move when an enemy piece (usually a bishop) is hanging and can be won immediately.
analysis.description: In all 7/7 positions, the best move was a direct capture of an enemy piece that was en prise or could be taken with decisive material gain (Rxe7, Qxf6, Qxe3, Qxe3, Bxc3, Rxb2, Qxa6), yet White instead played a non-capturing move—a piece retreat (Nd3, Bd2), king move (Kh1 x2), queen repositioning (Qc2), pawn advance (b5), or seemingly flashy fork (Nc6). In 6/7 cases the hanging piece was specifically a bishop. The average good moves available was only 1.4, meaning the capture was typically the sole correct option and any delay was punished. These moves look purposeful (attacking, prophylactic, space-gaining) but fatally ignore the most concrete opportunity on the board.
analysis.move_pattern: Non-capturing moves (retreats, king moves, pawn pushes, piece repositions) when an immediate piece capture was available
analysis.why_bad: By failing to take the free material, White surrenders the initiative and gives Black time to either save the hanging piece, initiate favorable trade sequences on their own terms, or exploit new tactical vulnerabilities created by the non-capturing move (forks, discovered attacks, counter-captures).
sub_patterns: Piece retreat instead of material-winning capture
Prophylactic king move ignoring hanging piece
Pawn advance/queen reposition missing a simple take

analysis.label: Moves that address a secondary concern while ignoring the one urgent requirement of the position, in situations where only 1-2 moves maintain the evaluation.
analysis.description: This feature activates on moves made in narrow, critical positions (avg 1.5 good moves available) where the player chooses a seemingly purposeful action—a check (Qg2+), a capture (axb4), a pawn advance (a5, a3), or a piece reposition (Rg2, Qd3, Qb4, Kf8)—that completely fails to address the position's single most urgent demand. In 7/8 cases king safety was the critical factor being ignored, and in 7/8 cases a concrete tactic was missed. In 6/8 cases the move constituted a tempo loss by either helping the opponent improve their pieces (a5 driving a bishop to a superior diagonal, a3 provoking a favorable exchange, axb4 leaving a deadly pawn alive) or placing one's own piece on an inferior/vulnerable square (Kf8 walking into checks, Rg2 allowing a knight fork, Qb4 abandoning king defense). The positions all feature a single narrow correct path that demands addressing the primary threat, and the blundering move instead pursues a secondary objective that the position simply cannot afford.
analysis.move_pattern: Various piece types and directions; typically quiet-looking moves (non-forcing pawn pushes, piece repositioning) or superficially forcing moves (checks that allow strong interpositions) that don't engage with the position's critical axis
analysis.why_bad: Each move wastes a critical tempo in a position where only 1-2 specific moves hold things together, failing to address the primary tactical or king-safety requirement while the opponent's most dangerous threats go unanswered
sub_patterns: Pawn advances that drive enemy pieces to better squares (a5, a3)
Checks that allow favorable interpositions or improve defender coordination (Qg2+)
Piece moves to squares creating new tactical vulnerabilities (Rg2, Kf8)
Queen moves abandoning critical defensive duties (Qb4, Qd3)

analysis.label: Pushing the pawn (or misplacing the king) in KP vs K endgames instead of advancing the king first to escort the pawn to promotion.
analysis.description: This feature fires on King and Pawn vs King endgames where the player violates the fundamental principle that the king must lead the pawn. In 9/14 positions, the mistake is a premature pawn advance (b5, a5, g5, b4, g5, f5, f3, g4) that allows the defending king to establish a blockade or gain opposition in front of the pawn. In 3/14 positions, the mistake is a king move in the wrong direction (Kf3 retreating behind pawn, Kf4 moving sideways, Kg5 moving sideways) that abandons control of critical escort squares. The remaining 2-3 positions show near-zero cp_loss moves that still match the pattern context (KP vs K with king-escort dynamics). Every position is a pure pawn endgame with a single passed pawn, completely open board, and the entire fight centered on opposition, outflanking, and whether the stronger side's king occupies squares ahead of the pawn. The average cp_loss of ~394 reflects that these mistakes typically convert won positions into theoretical draws.
analysis.move_pattern: Single pawn push forward (any file) without king support ahead, OR king move retreating/sideways away from the pawn's promotion corridor, in pure KP vs K positions
analysis.why_bad: Advancing the pawn before the king reaches escort position (or moving the king away from the critical squares) gives the defending king time to reach the blockade square directly in front of the pawn, establish opposition, or invoke stalemate resources (especially with rook pawns), converting a theoretically won position into a draw.
sub_patterns: Premature pawn push allowing frontal blockade (g5, f5, f3, g4 on central/bishop files)
Premature pawn push allowing stalemate draw (a5, b5, b4 on rook/knight files)
King retreat behind own pawn losing escort position (Kf3 behind g-pawn)
King moving sideways losing critical tempo for escort (Kf4, Kg5 abandoning blocking squares)
