analysis.label: Non-forcing forward-pushing moves (typically pawn advances) that waste critical tempo when a concrete tactical action was required in the position.
analysis.description: This feature activates on positions where players choose aggressive-looking advancing moves—predominantly kingside pawn pushes (5/7: f6, gxh2+, h4, g7, h5) but also forward piece/king moves (2/7: Rhc1, Ke3)—instead of executing the concrete tactical solution demanded by the position. The tag 'tempo_loss' appears in 6/7 analyses, confirming the unifying thread: each move looks proactive but fails to create a forcing threat, granting the opponent exactly the tempo needed to solve their problems. In Position 11, h5 gives Black one tempo to march Kd5-e6 defending f7 (cost: 220cp). In Position 6, h4 allows Black's freeing ...d5 break (cost: 229cp). In Position 14, Ke3 walks into d5 opening the center (cost: 420cp). In Position 1, f6 blocks the bishop's retreat allowing h3-g4 trapping it (cost: 245cp). In each case, a more forcing alternative existed—often a piece move (Rf3, Nb5, Kg1, Ne1) rather than a pawn push—that would have maintained the advantage by creating immediate concrete threats.
analysis.move_pattern: Forward-advancing moves, predominantly pawn pushes on the f/g/h files, occasionally piece or king advances toward active-looking but vulnerable squares
analysis.why_bad: These non-forcing advances grant the opponent a crucial tempo to execute a defensive resource (king march, central break, piece activation, or tactical counter) that was not possible on the previous move, squandering positions where a concrete forcing action would have maintained decisive advantage
sub_patterns: Kingside pawn advances (h4/h5/g7/f6) when piece action like Rf3/Nb5 was needed
King/piece advancing into danger instead of retreating to safety (Ke3, Rhc1)
Capturing the wrong target with a pawn check (gxh2+ vs gxf2+)

analysis.label: Moves that address a secondary concern while ignoring the single most urgent positional or tactical demand, wasting the one available tempo.
analysis.description: All 5 positions share the pattern of having exactly one viable move (avg good moves = 1.0) that directly addresses an existential threat, while the played move pursues a secondary objective. In 5/5 cases, the analyses identify 'tempo_loss' as a key tag, and the best move always directly confronts the most critical issue: Bd4 centralizes for defense (pos 5), Re4 addresses the passed a-pawn (pos 8), Kg6 avoids tactical geometry (pos 11), g2 pushes the passer directly (pos 12), and Ke7 resolves king exposure (pos 13). The played moves instead attack enemy pieces (Qd2, Nh5, Rf2), block indirectly (Ng7), or retreat to the wrong square (Kg8)—all logical-seeming but fatally misguided given the position's singular critical demand. The average cp_loss of 3853 reflects that these one-tempo delays frequently turn defensible positions into forced mates or decisive material loss.
analysis.move_pattern: Various piece types (Q, N, K, R) moving to squares that address secondary tactical or positional concerns rather than the critical threat vector
analysis.why_bad: The positions each have exactly one move that addresses an existential threat (passed pawn promotion, king safety collapse, forced mating patterns); the played moves waste the single available tempo on lower-priority goals, giving the opponent time to execute their decisive tactical idea.
sub_patterns: Offensive piece sortie ignoring own king vulnerability
Attacking a blockading pawn indirectly instead of pushing the passer directly
Passive piece placement as shield instead of moving the exposed king itself
Speculative attack on wrong side of board while critical threat advances

analysis.label: Non-forcing moves (passive retreats, greedy captures, or vulnerable placements) that gift the opponent a decisive tempo for a concrete pawn break or tactical blow.
analysis.description: This feature fires on positions where the player makes a slow, non-urgent move in a position demanding immediate concrete action, allowing the opponent to execute a tempo-gaining pawn advance or tactical sequence. In 7/10 positions, the refutation involves a pawn advance (fxe5, e5, f5, h4, hxg3+) that strikes with tempo against a piece or king. The blunder moves are predominantly passive bishop retreats to back-rank or rim squares (Bc7, Be7, Bf8, Bh6 — 4/10), greedy captures that abandon defensive duties (Bxg4, Qxc2 — 2/10), or king moves that create new tactical vulnerabilities (Kf2, Kc1 — 2/10). In nearly every case (8/10), the best move was an active, concrete option — typically a central pawn break (d4, e5) or a piece move contesting the opponent's key line of attack. The average cp_loss of 1183 and only 1.6 good moves available confirms these are critical moments where the position is on a knife's edge and the slow move catastrophically tips the balance.
analysis.move_pattern: Piece (especially bishop) retreats/repositions to passive or back-rank squares, greedy captures away from the critical sector, or king moves that increase exposure — all non-forcing moves in tactically critical positions
analysis.why_bad: The non-forcing move gives the opponent a free tempo to execute a concrete pawn advance or forcing sequence (check, fork, deflection) that exploits the position's key vulnerability — typically an exposed king, an overloaded defender, or uncontested control of an open file/diagonal
sub_patterns: Bishop retreats to passive back-rank square (Bc7, Be7, Bf8, Bh6) abandoning control of critical central squares
Greedy captures far from the action (Bxg4, Qxc2) leaving king defenseless against tempo-gaining attacks
King moves that create new tactical vulnerabilities to checks/forks (Kf2, Kc1)
Piece moves to tactically vulnerable squares in the path of pawn advances (Qd6, Nh5)

analysis.label: Superficially reasonable moves in narrow positions where only one precise continuation maintains the advantage, chosen because they look similar to the correct idea but miss the key tactical detail.
analysis.description: This feature fires on positions requiring extreme precision (avg 1.7 good moves available) where the player selects a move that appears natural or thematically correct but fatally misses the specific tactical requirement. In 5/7 positions, the move involves placing the king on the wrong square or allowing the opponent's king to reach safety (Kg2 instead of Ke2, Ke2 instead of Kd1, Kb5 instead of Nd7+, O-O removing tactical threats, Qxh3+ letting the king reach g1 instead of Qh1+ which controls it). In 2/7 positions, a greedy queen capture on h3 ignores a back-rank or mating-net vulnerability. The common computational signature is a position with one clearly correct forcing move where the played move scores 2nd or 3rd but with a catastrophic evaluation gap (avg 4348cp loss), suggesting the player recognized the general theme (attack, king safety, material) but chose the wrong execution.
analysis.move_pattern: King moves to the wrong square (3/7), queen captures a pawn on h-file (2/7), castling/knight moves that remove or ignore critical tactical tension (2/7) — all are 'one square off' or 'one tempo too slow' relative to the correct forcing continuation
analysis.why_bad: Each move fails because it does not address the ONE specific tactical requirement of the position — typically controlling a critical escape square, maintaining a tactical threat that restrains the opponent, or executing an immediate forcing sequence. The move chosen satisfies a general strategic goal (king safety, material gain, piece activity) but misses the precise geometric or temporal detail that the position demands.
sub_patterns: King moves to exposed square instead of safe square (Kg2/Ke2/Kb5 vs Ke2/Kd1/Nd7+)
Queen captures pawn while losing control of critical mating square (Qxh3 vs Qh1+, Qxh3 allowing Qxc7#)
Routine developing moves that remove tactical threats protecting own pieces (O-O removing Nf3+ ideas)
Premature piece lunges to outposts that can be immediately challenged (Ne5 vs Nc3)

analysis.label: Playing a natural-looking move that squanders a decisive tempo in a position demanding one specific urgent action.
analysis.description: This feature fires on positions where the player makes a plausible-looking move that fundamentally fails to address the position's most urgent requirement, allowing the opponent a critical tempo to execute a winning plan. In 7/10 positions, a piece is moved away from where it's critically needed: Nb6 abandons kingside defense enabling h5-h6 (Position 5), Rh7 abandons the a-file enabling a3-axb4+ (Position 7), Rcd8 abandons the c-file enabling c5 breakthrough (Position 8), Bh6 abandons passed-pawn restraint enabling f7 (Position 2), Qa3 loses coordination with embedded pieces (Position 3), Kd1 retreats passively allowing a blockade (Position 1), and Nf3 develops routinely instead of checking the exposed king (Position 14). The remaining cases involve wrong execution: Bxf3 uses the wrong piece leaving fork vulnerability (Position 9), Qxb2 grabs material while the king is uncastled (Position 4), and Nd5 jumps to an unstable square kickable with tempo (Position 13). All 10 positions are narrow (avg 1.8 good moves) and demand a specific concrete action, making the tempo waste catastrophic.
analysis.move_pattern: Any piece type moving to a plausible square that fails to address the position's singular urgent demand; no consistent geometric direction
analysis.why_bad: The move wastes the one tempo needed to maintain a critical function (restraining a passed pawn, defending a vulnerable file/flank, continuing an attack, or maintaining piece coordination), allowing the opponent to execute a concrete plan that was previously restrained.
sub_patterns: Abandoning a critical defensive file or square (Rh7, Rcd8, Nb6)
Retreating/repositioning when active play is demanded (Kd1, Qa3, Bh6)
Routine development ignoring tactical urgency (Nf3, Nd5)
Material grab over king safety/coordination (Qxb2)
Wrong piece selection for recapture (Bxf3)

analysis.label: Active-looking moves (pawn pushes, bishop development, queen repositioning) that place a piece or pawn on a square directly capturable by an opponent's diagonally-attacking piece, or abandon diagonal defense of another piece.
analysis.description: This feature fires on moves that appear constructive (gaining space, developing, or repositioning) but fatally ignore diagonal threats from enemy bishops or pawns. In 4/7 positions, the moved piece/pawn lands on a square immediately capturable along a diagonal: Position 2 pushes c4 into the path of White's bishop on a6; Position 10 pushes b4 where Black's Bd6 captures it; Position 12 places Bc4 directly en prise to the d5 pawn; Position 4's Qf3 removes the queen from e3's diagonal defense of the d4 rook, allowing ...exd4 (a diagonal pawn capture). In Position 15, Bb3 places the bishop on the wrong diagonal, failing to cover the critical g6-c2 line needed to intercept Black's racing c-pawn. The common thread is that players choose forward-looking moves while being blind to the opponent's diagonal control of the target or vacated square.
analysis.move_pattern: Piece or pawn moved to a square on a diagonal controlled by opponent's bishop or pawn; or piece moved OFF a diagonal where it was defending another piece
analysis.why_bad: The target square (or the newly-undefended square) is directly attacked by an opponent's diagonally-moving piece (bishop or pawn), resulting in immediate free material capture or loss of a critical defender
sub_patterns: Pawn pushed to square capturable by opponent's bishop (c4, b4)
Bishop developed to square attacked by opponent's pawn (Bc4)
Queen/piece moved off defensive diagonal leaving hanging piece (Qf3)
Bishop placed on wrong diagonal failing to cover passed pawn (Bb3)

analysis.label: Player loses a decisive tempo against an opponent's advanced passed pawn or critical threat by capturing irrelevant material, giving hollow checks, or pursuing non-urgent goals.
analysis.description: This feature fires on moves where the player ignores or under-prioritizes an opponent's most dangerous advancing threat—almost always an advanced passed pawn—in favor of a less urgent objective. In 7/11 positions, the opponent has a concrete passed pawn that gains a critical tempo from the mistake. The errors include capturing pawns that aren't the real threat (Nxg6, Kxg3, Kxg6 in positions 1, 12, 14), moving the king away from a blockading or controlling square (Kf8 in position 2, Ke5 in position 4), giving a flashy but hollow check that displaces one's own piece (Nf6+ in position 3), making a move-order error that gifts the opponent a free tempo to advance (Ke1 in position 9), moving a piece away from controlling the promotion path (Rhh2 in position 10), or abandoning defensive responsibilities for vague activity (Qb5 in position 15). In every case, the correct move either addresses the passed pawn directly (blockading, intercepting, racing back) or executes the correct move order so no tempo is gifted. The average centipawn loss of 1163 reflects that these single-tempo errors are frequently decisive in positions with razor-thin timing margins.
analysis.move_pattern: Any piece type moving toward a secondary objective (capture, check, centralization, doubling) while directed AWAY from controlling or blockading the opponent's most advanced passed pawn or critical threat
analysis.why_bad: Each move gifts the opponent one critical tempo to advance their passed pawn (or execute their primary threat), and in these sharp timing-dependent positions, a single tempo is the difference between drawing/winning and losing—the opponent's pawn reaches the 7th rank or promotion square before the player can recover defensive control.
sub_patterns: Capturing an irrelevant pawn while opponent's passed pawn advances unchecked
King moving away from blockading square of a passed pawn
Move-order error: correct plan but wrong sequence gives opponent a free tempo
Giving a premature check that displaces own piece from a critical controlling square
Piece repositioning that abandons control of the promotion path

analysis.label: Routine-looking moves (castling, pawn pushes, piece development) that neglect an urgent tactical or structural problem near the king, when a specific defensive move (often f3) was critically needed.
analysis.description: This feature fires on positions where the player makes a 'natural' or 'routine' move—castling (3/8), advancing a g-pawn (3/8), or developing a piece (2/8)—while ignoring a critical vulnerability near their king that demands immediate attention. In 4/8 positions, the correct move was specifically f3 to either rescue a stranded knight on h3 (positions 2, 5, 6) or solidify the kingside pawn structure (position 14). In 3/8 positions, the player castled directly into an existing attacking configuration (Greek Gift in position 7, bishop diagonals in position 1, trapping their own piece in position 2). In 2/8 positions, g-pawn advances (g4, g3) fatally weakened the king shelter when the opponent's queen was already actively targeting the kingside. The common thread is that each position contained a specific, identifiable threat or structural weakness requiring urgent action, but the player chose a move that either worsened king safety or wasted a critical tempo, allowing the opponent's existing piece coordination to deliver devastating tactical blows.
analysis.move_pattern: King commitments (castling), g-pawn advances weakening king shelter, or developing moves ignoring king-area vulnerabilities—all when defensive pawn moves (especially f3) were urgently needed
analysis.why_bad: The moves ignore an urgent tactical vulnerability (trapped piece, attacking battery aimed at king, exposed pawn shelter) in favor of routine development or general improvement, allowing the opponent to exploit the pre-existing threat with devastating effect—often winning material or delivering checkmate.
sub_patterns: Castling into pre-aimed attacking pieces (bishops on diagonals, Greek Gift setup)
Ignoring stranded knight on h3 when f3 was needed for rescue
Advancing g-pawn weakening king shelter when opponent's queen targets kingside
Routine piece development while critical tactical problem festers

analysis.label: Moves that voluntarily remove the sole defender of a critical square, pawn, or piece, enabling the opponent to exploit the newly unguarded weakness.
analysis.description: This feature fires on moves where a piece or pawn performing an essential defensive function is moved away, creating a fatal vulnerability. The pattern manifests in several forms: pawns abandoning key square control (e5 removes e6's defense of f7 in Position 4; h5 removes h6's control of g5 in Position 10; 2/11), queens leaving critical guard posts (Qg5 abandons f7 defense enabling mate in Position 9; Qxf8 abandons e5 knight defense in Position 11; 2/11), kings/bishops abandoning pawn protection (Ke1 leaves g2 hanging in Position 2; Bc3 abandons kingside pawn integrity in Position 12; Bb2 fails to control c5 in Position 8; 3/11), and using the wrong piece to capture thereby removing a needed defender (Rxg4 instead of Kxg4 in Position 3; 1/11). In nearly every case, the moved unit was the SOLE guardian of the critical element, and the opponent's refutation immediately targets the newly undefended weakness. The moves often appear superficially reasonable—captures, development, centralization, space-gaining—which explains why players are drawn to them despite their catastrophic consequences.
analysis.move_pattern: Any piece type moving away from a square where it uniquely defended a critical point; includes captures with the wrong piece, pawn advances that relinquish key square control, and piece relocations that abandon guard duties
analysis.why_bad: Each move removes the only piece or pawn defending a critical square, pawn, or piece, immediately enabling the opponent to exploit the newly unguarded weakness through tactics (discovered attacks, captures, mating nets, or decisive invasions)
sub_patterns: Queen abandons defense of f7 or key piece, enabling mate or decisive material win
Pawn advance removes sole control of critical square (g5, f7), allowing king advance or attack
King/bishop moves away from sole pawn defense, leaving hanging material
Capturing with wrong piece removes defender from critical file or rank
Piece moves to seemingly active square but wrong diagonal/file, failing to control the key point

analysis.label: Natural-looking moves in positions demanding narrow precision, where only 1-2 moves maintain the evaluation and the chosen move allows a specific tactical punishment.
analysis.description: This feature fires on positions where the player chooses a reasonable-looking, thematic move (developing a piece, making a pawn break, occupying an outpost, doubling rooks) while ignoring the ONE critical requirement of the position. In all 7/7 cases, the position had very few good moves (avg 1.4), meaning the situation demanded surgical precision, not general chess principles. The moves are all 'second-best ideas' that look attractive: Be7 looks like natural development (but Bc5 was the only move controlling d4), Rfd1 looks logical for d-file pressure (but f4 was essential), d3 looks like advancing a passed pawn (but c5 was needed to protect the back rank), b4 looks like a standard pawn break (but allows en passant deflection), g5 looks like a kingside attack (but f5 was the only correct break), Nf5 looks like occupying an outpost (but Be8 was the only defense), and a4 looks like queenside expansion (but Rfc1 with concrete tactics was required). In every case, the opponent has a specific tactical shot (fork 2/7, deflection 2/7, back-rank exploitation 1/7, pawn storm 1/7, piece capture 1/7) that punishes the tempo spent on the 'natural' move.
analysis.move_pattern: Quiet, non-forcing moves (piece development, pawn pushes, rook lifts) that appear thematic but are not the position's critical move
analysis.why_bad: Each move wastes a critical tempo in a position where only 1-2 specific moves maintain the evaluation, allowing the opponent a concrete tactical refutation that exploits the newly-created or newly-unaddressed vulnerability
sub_patterns: Passive piece placement when only an active square works (Be7 vs Bc5, Rfd1 vs f4)
Wrong pawn advance when a specific one was mandatory (g5 vs f5, d3 vs c5)
Slow flank pawn push ignoring concrete tactical requirements (a4, b4)
Piece occupying an outpost that invites a pawn attack (Nf5 allowing g4)

analysis.label: Plausible-looking but non-urgent moves played in positions demanding immediate concrete action, wasting critical tempo when only 1-2 moves maintain the evaluation.
analysis.description: This feature fires on positions where the player chooses a superficially reasonable move—developing a piece, activating a rook, centralizing a king, or giving check—while ignoring the single urgent demand of the position. In 9/11 cases, the analyses explicitly identify 'tempo_loss' as a core tag. The positions share extremely narrow margins (average 1.8 good moves available), meaning they require specific concrete action: constructing a mating net (Position 1), resolving central tension with e4 (Position 2), preventing a central break by maintaining piece placement (Position 3), attacking from the correct direction with Re5 (Position 4), blockading a passed pawn (Position 5), executing an immediate tactical shot like Ng6 (Position 6), or freeing a trapped piece with Nf4 (Position 14). Instead, the player selects a move addressing a secondary concern—repositioning to the rim (Ba3, Nh2, Na5 in 3/11 cases), moving to a passive square (Qc2, Ra1, Be7), or walking into tactical vulnerability (Kf7, Ke5 in 2/11 cases). The catastrophic average cp_loss of 1978 reflects that these positions punish inaccuracy severely because the opponent can immediately exploit the wasted tempo.
analysis.move_pattern: Mixed piece types moving to non-critical squares (often rim/edge or passive positions), sometimes with check; direction is typically lateral or backward rather than toward the critical area of tension
analysis.why_bad: Each move wastes the one tempo needed to address the position's primary demand—whether that's a concrete tactic, preventing an opponent's break, saving a trapped piece, or avoiding a tactical vulnerability—allowing the opponent to seize the initiative or execute a punishing combination
sub_patterns: Piece retreat/redeployment to rim when center demands attention (Ba3, Nh2, Na5)
Slow developing move ignoring trapped/hanging piece (Be7, Ra1, Rc8)
King move walking into tactical shot on open line/diagonal (Kf7, Ke5)
Premature check or attack on secondary target when primary threat exists (Qh1+, Qc2, Rg6)

analysis.label: King passively retreats toward the back rank or corner in endgames instead of maintaining central activity or fleeing toward open space.
analysis.description: In 5/7 positions, the played move is a king retreat directly toward the player's own back rank or corner (Ka7 toward a8, Ka8 into the corner, Ke8 to back rank, Kf7 retreating from g6, Kc1 to first rank). In 1/7 (Rb5), the error is failing to activate the king forward when king centralization was essential. The middlegame outlier (Qd2+) involves a speculative check that misplaces the queen, sharing the theme of a purposeless move toward the edge. In every case, the best moves involve either centralizing the king (Kb5, Ka6, Kb3, Ke7/Kd7/Kf7) or repositioning another piece to maintain active control. The common thread is choosing a passive retreat when the position demands forward king activity, violating the fundamental endgame principle that the king must be an active fighting piece.
analysis.move_pattern: King moving one square toward the player's own back rank (rank 8 for Black, rank 1 for White) or toward a corner, retreating from a more active square
analysis.why_bad: Retreating the king toward the edge reduces its mobility, allows the opponent to create mating nets or advance passed pawns unopposed, and wastes critical tempo in positions where king centralization is the primary defensive or competitive resource.
sub_patterns: King walks into corner where mating net forms (Ka7, Ka8)
King retreats to back rank away from passed pawn fight (Ke8, Kf7, Kc1)
Failure to activate king forward when piece moves accomplish nothing (Rb5)

analysis.label: In rook endgames, the player makes a move that fatally passivizes their rook or enables its exchange into a losing pawn endgame.
analysis.description: This feature fires on endgame positions (9/9) where the player's move destroys their piece activity—the single most critical resource for defense or resistance. The pattern manifests in two main ways: (1) placing the rook on a passive square (Ra6 in front of passed pawns, Rf7 blocking a passer, Ra1 passively blockading, Rh4 statically attacking one pawn) seen in 4/9 positions; or (2) enabling/forcing an exchange into a losing pawn endgame (Kg3 allowing Rxf3+, Rc1 allowing Rxc1+, Rxf4 triggering gxf4+ with check, Bxa5 removing the last piece) seen in 4/9 positions. The remaining case (Kg6) blocks the player's own rook creating a skewer. In every case, better alternatives maintained piece flexibility—rooks on active ranks/files (Re3, Rg8, Rh6), kings blockading while rooks stay free, or bishops staying alive to control diagonals. The 'piece_activity' tag appears in 9/9 analyses and 'passed_pawn' in 7/9, confirming the connection between lost activity and unstoppable promotion threats.
analysis.move_pattern: Rook (or supporting piece) moves to a passive, static, or exchangeable square—often in front of passed pawns, adjacent to own pieces enabling captures, or onto files where it can be immediately traded
analysis.why_bad: In rook endgames, the weaker side's survival depends on rook activity (checks, lateral mobility, behind-the-pawn placement). These moves eliminate that activity—either by passivizing the rook where it cannot reposition, or by enabling an exchange that transitions into a pawn endgame where the opponent's passed pawns or superior king position is decisive.
sub_patterns: Rook placed passively in front of advancing passed pawns (Ra6, Rf7, Ra1)
King move enables forced rook exchange into lost pawn endgame (Kg3, Rc1)
Voluntary piece exchange transitions into hopeless pawn endgame (Rxf4, Bxa5)
Rook commits to attacking one pawn, losing flexibility to reposition (Rh4)
King blocks own rook's active file creating tactical vulnerability (Kg6)

analysis.label: A piece captures a seemingly free pawn on the a- or b-file edge, becoming trapped or fatally displaced from the critical action.
analysis.description: All 4/4 positions involve a piece (bishop, knight, or queen) capturing an apparently undefended pawn on the queenside rim (a7, a2, a7, b2). In 2/4 cases the capturing piece is immediately trapped by a simple pawn advance (Bxa7 trapped by ...b6; Bxa2 trapped by b3). In 1/4 cases the knight becomes completely offside on a7 while a central passed pawn surges forward unchecked. In 1/4 cases the queen leaves the kingside to grab a b-pawn, enabling a classic Greek Gift sacrifice on h7. The common thread is that the pawn appears free but is actually 'poisoned'—the cost of displacing the piece to the board's edge vastly exceeds the one-pawn material gain. Average cp_loss of 288 confirms these are severe mistakes, typically turning equal or advantageous positions into losing ones.
analysis.move_pattern: A piece (B/N/Q) captures a pawn on the a-file (a2/a7) or b-file (b2), moving to the queenside edge on ranks 1-2 or 7-8
analysis.why_bad: The capturing piece becomes trapped, offside, or removed from critical defensive duties, allowing the opponent to exploit the displacement via piece trapping (b3/b6), central pawn advances, or kingside attacks against the now-undefended king.
sub_patterns: Bishop trapped on a-file after opponent's pawn cage (b3 or ...b6)
Knight stranded on a7/a2 while central threats go unanswered
Queen lured to b2 exposing kingside to sacrificial attack

analysis.label: Natural-looking moves (captures, checks, advances) chosen over the one precise move demanded by a narrow critical position.
analysis.description: This feature activates on positions where very few good moves exist (avg 1.8) and the player selects an 'obvious' or 'active-looking' alternative that catastrophically fails. In 7/8 positions, the chosen move involves a concrete action—capturing material (Nxe8, Nxc3, Kxc6), giving check (Qg4+), or advancing a pawn (g4, c5)—that appears purposeful but ignores the one critical requirement of the position. The correct moves are typically more subtle: a quiet king march instead of a pawn push (Position 1), the right piece to a square instead of the wrong one (Position 2), retreating a knight rather than advancing the king (Position 3), exploiting a tactical fork instead of pushing a pawn (Position 4), trading queens to defuse an attack instead of grabbing material (Position 6), or activating a rook with check instead of a queen check (Position 8). In 6/8 cases, the blunder is explicitly tagged as a 'tempo_loss'—the move squanders the critical tempo needed for the only plan that works. The enormous average cp_loss (2505) reflects that these narrow positions punish imprecision ruthlessly.
analysis.move_pattern: Mixed piece types performing captures, checks, or pawn advances—all 'active' moves chosen over a quieter or differently-directed precise alternative
analysis.why_bad: Each move prioritizes an obvious concrete action (material gain, check, advance) while ignoring the position's true critical requirement—whether maintaining a blocking piece, proper sequencing, avoiding a diagonal alignment, or preserving piece coordination—resulting in catastrophic tactical or structural collapse.
sub_patterns: Premature pawn advances before necessary king preparation
Captures that remove critical defensive pieces or abandon key squares
Pointless checks that waste tempo and allow opponent consolidation
Wrong piece to the correct square
Captures in wrong order (sequencing errors)

analysis.label: Non-forcing 'improving' moves that waste a critical tempo while the opponent has an immediate tactical exploitation available.
analysis.description: This feature fires on quiet, non-forcing moves that appear logically motivated but fatally ignore the opponent's concrete tactical response. In 7/7 positions, the player chose a slow move (piece repositioning, pawn push, or king walk) when the position demanded urgent concrete action. The punishments involve forcing tactical themes: discovered attacks (2/7: g3 allowing Bxg3+d4+, Kd7 allowing Ne5+ with d-file discovery), forks (1/7: a6 allowing c6 pawn fork), skewers (1/7: Qh3 creating alignment with own Bh6), piece decentralization to passive squares (1/7: Bh3 off the strong f5 diagonal), fixing targets (1/7: a6 in pawn endgame), and walking into pawn tempo gains (1/7: Bd3 into e4). In each case, 2-3 concrete alternatives existed that addressed the position's tactical demands, but the player chose a superficially useful quiet move instead.
analysis.move_pattern: Quiet non-capturing, non-checking moves - piece repositions, pawn pushes, or king moves - typically to seemingly useful squares but ignoring forcing opponent responses
analysis.why_bad: These moves waste a critical tempo on a slow plan while the position contains an urgent tactical element requiring immediate attention; the opponent responds with a forcing sequence (fork, discovered attack, skewer, or pawn advance) that exploits the newly-created or pre-existing vulnerability before the quiet move's 'plan' can materialize.
sub_patterns: Piece moves that create self-alignment vulnerabilities (Qh3 skewer with own Bh6, Kd7 discovered check on d-file)
Developing pieces to squares immediately targeted by opponent pawn advances (Bd3 into e4, Bh3 to passive square)
Slow pawn moves that ignore critical pawn tension or tactical urgency (a6 ignoring c6 fork, g3 allowing Bxg3 + discovery, a6 fixing target in endgame)

analysis.label: Playing slow, non-forcing repositioning moves in tactically critical positions where immediate captures, checks, or concrete threats were essential.
analysis.description: This feature fires on positions where the player chooses a quiet piece repositioning move—often to a seemingly attractive square—while the position urgently demands forcing play. In 6/8 positions, the primary tag is 'tempo_loss,' and all positions share the characteristic of having very few good moves available (avg 1.8), indicating tactical criticality. The blunders include passive bishop fianchettoes to g7 (2/8), rook repositioning to seemingly active files (Rh8, Rb1, Rh4 — 3/8), king moves seeking safety that wasn't needed (Kh2, Kg4 — 2/8), and a non-urgent pawn push (e5 — 1/8). In every case, the best moves involved immediate captures (Bxd4, Rc3/Rxc4), active piece jumps (Ne5), or forcing sequences (Re2 for mate-in-8). The played moves all appear positionally reasonable in isolation—putting pieces on long diagonals, challenging files, or improving king position—but catastrophically ignore concrete tactical demands of the position.
analysis.move_pattern: Non-forcing quiet moves (piece repositioning, fianchettoes, king walks, pawn pushes) to squares that appear positionally desirable but create no immediate threat
analysis.why_bad: These moves waste critical tempo in positions where only immediate forcing play (captures, checks, direct threats) maintains the evaluation. The opponent gains a free move to consolidate, activate pieces, or execute tactical sequences that the slow move fails to prevent.
sub_patterns: Bishop fianchetto to g7 ignoring active piece play
Rook repositioning to edge files when captures are available
King safety moves when forced mating sequences or concrete tactics exist
Non-urgent pawn pushes surrendering initiative

analysis.label: Moves that pursue a secondary plan while neglecting the single most critical tactical requirement of the position.
analysis.description: This feature fires on moves where the player addresses a non-urgent concern (rerouting a piece, advancing a pawn, pursuing a long-term plan) while the position demands one specific, immediate action. In 9/9 positions, the correct move addresses a single critical vulnerability or creates a decisive dual-threat, but the played move ignores it entirely. Examples: Bb8 retreats passively when d2 must advance immediately (position 2); Na5 reroutes a knight while a bishop on f3 desperately needs saving (position 14); Qe1 repositions the queen while the f3 square requires immediate occupation (position 15); h4 advances a pawn when the queen must return to defend (position 10); Kf1 passively shifts the king when only g5! (a tactical sacrifice to eliminate a key defender) holds the position (position 13). The average good moves available is only 1.7, confirming these are positions with narrow paths where only the one urgent action works. The refutations consistently exploit the exact element the player neglected - the undefended piece, unblocked square, or unchallenged threat.
analysis.move_pattern: Any piece type moving to an irrelevant square/direction, typically away from the critical sector of the board where the urgent tactical demand exists
analysis.why_bad: The move leaves a critical vulnerability unaddressed (hanging piece, key square uncontrolled, passed pawn unsupported, king shelter weakened), and the opponent immediately exploits that specific neglected element with forcing moves
sub_patterns: Passive piece retreat when an aggressive forcing move is required
Piece rerouting to rim/back rank while a tactical threat goes unmet
Pawn advance weakening structure when a piece must defend
Piece development to wrong square/diagonal ignoring the critical sector

analysis.label: Moves that inadvertently allow the opponent's knight to jump to a dominant square with tempo or tactical threats.
analysis.description: In all 4/4 positions, the played move directly enables a devastating knight invasion by the opponent as the primary punishment mechanism. Position 1 (Bc4) allows Black's Ng4 to attack the undefended f2 square. Position 4 (Rd2) allows White's Ne4 to hit the rook with tempo, then redirect to capture the key f5-knight. Position 6 (Bxd8) allows White's Nd4-Nxe6 to exploit the now-undefendable e6 pawn after the bishop self-obstructs on d8. Position 14 (h5) abandons the h6 square, enabling Nh6+ as a tactical resource and more broadly allowing piece invasions on weakened dark squares. Each move appears purposeful (developing, attacking, capturing, defending a pawn) but fundamentally misjudges the position by creating or failing to prevent the opponent's knight from reaching a dominating square where it coordinates with other pieces for decisive tactical threats.
analysis.move_pattern: Various piece types (bishop development, rook penetration, bishop capture, pawn advance) that leave a key square uncontrolled or a piece vulnerable to knight tempo
analysis.why_bad: Each move creates or ignores a square vulnerability that the opponent's knight immediately exploits—either gaining tempo on a piece, accessing a fork/outpost, or coordinating with other pieces for a mating/material-winning attack
sub_patterns: Developing piece ignores knight jump to weak square (Bc4 allows Ng4)
Rook penetration without support allows knight tempo (Rd2 allows Ne4)
Wrong recapture creates passive piece enabling knight invasion (Bxd8 allows Nd4)
Pawn advance abandons square control for knight access (h5 allows Nh6+)

analysis.label: Plausible-looking moves that fail to address the position's single most urgent tactical or strategic requirement.
analysis.description: This feature fires on positions where the player makes a 'normal-looking' move—a pawn push, piece development, capture, or repositioning—that completely ignores the position's concrete demands. In 8/13 positions, the error involves a tempo loss where the player plays something non-forcing while the position requires immediate action. In 7/13 cases, the move creates or fails to address a king safety vulnerability. The positions share a critical characteristic: very few good moves exist (avg 2.4), meaning the position demands a specific response, yet the player opts for a generically reasonable but ultimately irrelevant alternative. Examples include pushing b4 while a skewer exists on the diagonal (Position 2), capturing Qxc6 while a piece hangs on e2 (Position 3), playing the slow h6 when only Rf7 defends (Position 12), and placing a rook on c1 allowing a forced exchange (Position 13). The unifying thread is choosing a plan-based or routine move over the position's concrete tactical necessity.
analysis.move_pattern: Diverse piece types and directions; no single geometric pattern—features quiet moves, pawn pushes, captures, and repositionings that share the trait of being non-forcing or failing to address the critical square/diagonal/file
analysis.why_bad: The position demands a specific concrete response (preventing a tactic, forcing an exchange, addressing a vulnerability, or executing immediately), but the player makes a generically reasonable move that ignores this urgency, allowing the opponent to exploit the unaddressed threat or newly created weakness
sub_patterns: Weakening pawn pushes that create king vulnerabilities (f4, f5, f6, h6)
Greedy captures that leave pieces undefended (Qxc6, Bxe6)
Quiet piece moves that ignore diagonal/file threats (b4, Bd2, Bf4, Rc1)
Tempo-wasting moves in won positions (f6, a1=B, Rdd6)

analysis.label: Advancing the g-pawn one square (g3/g6) as a seemingly defensive move that permanently weakens the king's pawn shelter when active alternatives were required.
analysis.description: In 6/8 top-activating positions, the blunder is a one-square g-pawn advance (g6 for Black in 4 cases, g3 for White in 2 cases) played during the middlegame with same-side castling. These moves are intended as prophylactic (preventing piece infiltration, creating luft, or restricting enemy pieces), but they permanently compromise the pawn structure around the king. In positions 2, 7, and 11, Black plays ...g6 and immediately creates dark-square holes (f6, h6) that enemy knights exploit via Ng4-f6+ motifs, or weakens f7 on the light-square diagonal. In positions 1 and 3, White plays g3 passively when forcing tactical moves (Nf3, Nh4) were available, wasting a critical tempo. The remaining positions (Ke7, Bd3, Qe4+) share the broader pattern of making a passive or structurally weakening move when the position demanded immediate active play. Across all positions, the average cp_loss is extreme (~1413) and few good alternatives existed (avg 1.6), indicating these are critical moments where the passive pawn push was particularly catastrophic.
analysis.move_pattern: g-pawn advance one square (g2-g3 for White or g7-g6 for Black), non-capture, non-check, typically in front of or near the castled king
analysis.why_bad: The g-pawn advance permanently weakens the king's pawn shield (creating dark-square holes around the king and exposing light-square diagonals), while simultaneously wasting a tempo that was critically needed for active piece play, forcing moves, or addressing immediate tactical threats. Enemy pieces immediately exploit the new weaknesses (knight forks via weakened f6, bishop pressure on opened diagonals, h-file pawn storms targeting g6).
sub_patterns: ...g6 creating dark-square weakness with enemy bishop on h6
g3 wasting tempo when forcing piece moves win material
...g6 weakening f7 on the a2-g8 diagonal
Defensive pawn push instead of piece consolidation

analysis.label: Non-forcing or dead-end moves in positions that demand immediate decisive action, resulting in critical tempo loss.
analysis.description: This feature fires on moves that appear purposeful but are fundamentally non-forcing in positions requiring urgent tactical or strategic action. The most common sub-pattern is a knight jumping to h4 to 'attack' a queen that simply sidesteps (3/11 positions), leaving the knight stranded and losing two tempi retreating. Other activations involve passive piece/pawn moves (Re2, Rf7, Kg7, h4, h3, Ke2) when the position demands an immediate forcing blow—such as a capture of an undefended piece (Position 3: Qxf6 available), a tactical combination (Positions 1-2: Ne5/Qa4+ winning the queen via pin), or an urgent king relocation (Position 10: king must flee checks). In 9/11 positions, the move gives the opponent a critical tempo to consolidate, counter-attack, or execute a tactical resource (discovered checks in Positions 5-6, counter-tempo with f5 in Position 14). The average cp_loss of 325 reflects that these are not subtle inaccuracies but catastrophic time-wasting in sharp positions where one tempo determines the outcome.
analysis.move_pattern: Piece or pawn moves to a non-forcing square (often rim/passive), particularly knight to h4, pawn pushes (h3/h4), or king/rook moves to squares lacking follow-up threats
analysis.why_bad: The move fails to create an immediate concrete threat that the opponent must address, gifting them a tempo to consolidate defenses, generate counterplay, escape danger, or execute a tactical resource that was previously unavailable
sub_patterns: Knight to h4 attacking queen that sidesteps (forced retreat loses 2 tempi)
Passive pawn/piece move missing available forcing capture or combination
Piece repositioning to dead-end square when position demands checks/captures
King/rook move ignoring geometric vulnerability (discovered checks, promotions)

analysis.label: Black moves a piece away from the critical square or file where it was needed to contain the opponent's primary threat.
analysis.description: In 4/4 positions, Black's move drifts a piece away from the key defensive station—typically a blockading square in front of a passed pawn or a square controlling a critical invasion point. In positions 5 and 8 (pawn endgames), the king moves laterally (Kc6, Kf6) instead of maintaining blockade of White's passed pawn on the d/e-file (correct: Ke6, Kd6/Kd7). In position 7, the knight captures on c3, abandoning its critical post on d5 that guarded f6 against queen invasion, enabling immediate checkmate threats. In position 2, the queen retreats to e7 (passive, seemingly preparing castling) instead of actively addressing the tactical situation, leaving f7 fatally weak. All 4 moves appear superficially reasonable (material gain, king activity, natural development) but ignore the single most important strategic/tactical demand of the position.
analysis.move_pattern: Piece (king, queen, or knight) moves laterally or captures away from the central d/e-file or critical defensive square, typically toward a flank
analysis.why_bad: The piece abandons its role containing the opponent's primary threat (passed pawn, mating attack, or tactical vulnerability), allowing the opponent to immediately exploit the undefended critical square or advance the threat unopposed
sub_patterns: King drifts to flank instead of blockading passed pawn
Knight captures on flank removing key defensive coverage
Queen retreats passively instead of addressing main tactical threat

analysis.label: Playing a non-forcing prophylactic move (usually a short pawn advance) when the position demands an immediate capture or forcing tactical sequence.
analysis.description: In 7/7 positions, the player chose a quiet, non-forcing move—typically a one-square pawn advance (f3, g6, g3, h3, a3 in 5/7 cases) or a passive king shuffle (Kf1, Kf8 in 2/7)—when an immediate tactical opportunity existed. In 4/7 cases, a piece was literally hanging and could be captured (often with check): Rxb5+ capturing an undefended knight (Position 7), Qxc3 capturing a hanging knight (Position 9), Qxd5+ sacrificing into unstoppable promotion (Position 4), and Rxf6 resolving critical pawn tension (Position 11). The moves share a geometric profile: they are all short-range, non-capturing moves that address peripheral concerns (king luft, prophylaxis against phantom threats, pawn structure tidying) rather than the critical tactical feature of the position. The average cp_loss of 307 reflects the severity of ignoring winning tactics for 'improving' moves.
analysis.move_pattern: One-square pawn advance (typically to 3rd/6th rank: f3, g3, h3, a3, g6) or single-square king retreat, always non-capturing and non-threatening
analysis.why_bad: These moves waste a critical tempo in positions where immediate forcing action is required—typically capturing an undefended piece or executing a tactical sequence—allowing the opponent to save hanging material, neutralize threats, or generate counterplay that erases the advantage.
sub_patterns: Pawn to 3rd rank as 'luft' when piece is hanging
King shuffle instead of piece activation
Prophylactic pawn move abandoning defense of key square/pawn

analysis.label: King retreats or commits to the kingside (f/g files) when centralization or queenside positioning is critically needed.
analysis.description: In 7/7 positions, the played move involves the king moving to or staying on the kingside f/g file area (Kf2, Kf6, Kf3, Kg2, O-O) or kingside pawn moves that entrench the king there (f3, g3). In every case, the best moves involved centralizing the king toward the d-file or queenside (Kd3 was best in 3/7 positions; Ke4, Kf1, c5 in others). The critical action — passed pawn battles, piece coordination, defense of queenside pawns — required king proximity to the center or queenside. By committing to the kingside, the king becomes passive, exposed to rook checks along ranks/files, cut off from the critical sector, or blocks its own escape squares. In 5/7 positions this occurs in endgames where king activity is paramount, and in 2/7 middlegame positions the king commits to a flank where it loses tempo or counterplay potential.
analysis.move_pattern: King moves to f2/f3/g2/g8/f6 squares (or f/g pawn advances blocking those squares), always toward the kingside rather than centralizing toward d-file
analysis.why_bad: The king ends up on the wrong side of the board — passive, exposed to checks along ranks, cut off from critical pawn battles (usually queenside), and often loses a full tempo returning to where it should have gone, granting the opponent time to create decisive threats or passed pawns.
sub_patterns: King moves to f2/f3 instead of d2/d3 in rook endgames, losing tempo when forced back
Kingside pawn advances (f3/g3) that block king escape squares and create dark-square weaknesses
Castling kingside when counterplay against opponent's exposed king requires keeping the king central
King to g2 instead of f1 allowing opponent a critical tempo to attack undefended pieces

analysis.label: Moves that fatally compromise the player's own king safety by removing defensive resources, opening critical lines, or ignoring imminent danger to the king.
analysis.description: This feature fires on moves that catastrophically weaken the player's own king position. The pattern manifests in several ways: removing a piece or pawn that was shielding the king from attack (dxe4 opening the a2-g8 diagonal in position 6, Ndf3 vacating the b4-e1 diagonal blocker in position 10, Nh7 retreating a key kingside defender in position 12), moving the queen far from defensive duties when the king is under threat (Qxc2 grabbing material while the king is exposed in position 8, Qg5 leaving the queen trapped and defenseless in position 2), castling into structural weakness (O-O-O behind a porous queenside in position 1), or wasting critical tempo when the king demands urgent attention (a4 ignoring a time-sensitive attack in position 11, Qf3 committing the queen prematurely in position 13). In 6/8 positions the primary tactical motif is explicitly 'king_safety,' and all 8 positions share the tag. The average centipawn loss of 338 reflects the catastrophic nature of these errors - once the king's safety is compromised, the resulting punishment is typically decisive.
analysis.move_pattern: Various piece types and directions; the connecting geometry is that each move either vacates a square/line that was blocking an attack path to the player's own king, or wastes tempo while the king remains in or moves into danger
analysis.why_bad: Each move allows the opponent to launch a devastating attack against the exposed king - either by opening lines (diagonals/files) that point at the king, removing key defensive pieces from their posts, or giving the opponent free tempi to organize an overwhelming assault against the undefended monarch
sub_patterns: Removing a pawn or piece that blocks a critical line to own king (dxe4, Ndf3)
Retreating or misplacing a key defensive piece away from king protection (Nh7, Qg5)
Material greed with queen far from vulnerable king (Qxc2)
Castling into a structurally weak wing (O-O-O)
Slow non-forcing moves when king safety demands immediate action (a4, Qf3)

analysis.label: Playing a natural-looking developing or aggressive move while leaving a friendly piece completely undefended and capturable.
analysis.description: This feature fires on opening moves by White that appear active or developing but critically ignore that a friendly piece is undefended. In 5/7 positions, the played move directly leaves a bishop or knight hanging for simple capture (Qf3 leaves Bd3 undefended in position 1; Nc3 ignores hanging Bf4 in position 2; Qg4 allows exf5 winning the knight in position 6; Bxh6 moves away leaving Bc4 unprotected in position 11; Be5 places the bishop on an undefended square where fxe5 wins it in position 12). In 7/7 cases, all best moves involve resolving piece tensions or defending vulnerable pieces before developing further. The remaining positions share the pattern of creating exploitable tactical vulnerabilities (pin in position 14, king exposure in position 4) through moves that prioritize activity over safety. All positions feature mutual piece tensions that demanded resolution before any other action.
analysis.move_pattern: Diverse piece types (Q, N, B, f-pawn) moved to active-looking squares while another friendly piece remains undefended on an open line or diagonal
analysis.why_bad: The move ignores that a friendly piece is en prise or becomes capturable after the move, allowing the opponent to win material with a simple one-move capture (or capture-with-check/pin). The best moves all resolve existing piece tensions or defend vulnerable pieces first.
sub_patterns: Queen moves to active square leaving bishop undefended (Qf3, Qg4, Qe2)
Bishop captures/moves away from protective proximity, leaving another piece hanging (Bxh6, Be5)
Developing a new piece while an existing piece is already attacked (Nc3)
Pawn advance creating tactical vulnerability on weakened squares (f4)

analysis.label: Quiet consolidating moves played in critical positions where only one specific forcing continuation (usually a pawn break or piece attack) maintains the evaluation.
analysis.description: In all 6 positions, the player chose a quiet, non-forcing move (piece repositioning, defensive consolidation, or wrong pawn break) when the position demanded immediate tactical action with an extremely narrow window of correct moves (avg 1.3 good moves available). In 5/6 cases, the best move was a forcing pawn break or direct piece attack (c5, b3, Be4, e3, Ng5, e4) that created immediate threats, while the played moves (Re2, Ne6, Bg2, f3, Kf2, Qc8) surrendered a critical tempo. This tempo loss consistently allowed the opponent to execute a tactical idea that wasn't previously possible: doubling rooks for mate (1/6), capturing without punishment (2/6), exploiting newly-exposed king with checks/forks (2/6), or repositioning pieces to neutralize the player's tactical resource (1/6). The positions share the characteristic that they appear stable enough for consolidation but actually sit at a tactical inflection point where one forcing move is essential.
analysis.move_pattern: Non-forcing moves (no checks, no captures, no direct attacks) - piece retreats, passive repositioning, or wrong-direction pawn advances in positions demanding immediate tactical action
analysis.why_bad: Each move surrenders the one critical tempo needed to execute (or maintain) a forcing tactical sequence, allowing the opponent to either deliver a decisive blow or neutralize the player's only winning resource
sub_patterns: Piece retreat/repositioning when counterplay pawn break is required (Re2, Ne6, Bg2, Qc8)
King move to 'solve' local problem while missing tactical shot (Kf2)
Wrong pawn break direction when correct one creates unstoppable passed pawn (f3 instead of e3)

analysis.label: Playing a natural-looking passive or consolidating move when the position demands immediate, precise forcing action, squandering a narrow window of opportunity.
analysis.description: This feature detects positions where a player makes a plausible-looking 'normal' move—castling, developing a piece, defending a weakness, grabbing material—when the position actually demands one specific forcing continuation. In 5/6 positions, 'tempo_loss' is tagged as the primary motif. The key signature is extremely narrow decision points (avg 1.3 good moves available) with high cost (avg 347cp loss). In Position 8, Black retreats the queen from its dominant a2 post to 'centralize' on e6 instead of the forcing Nd4-Ne2+ sequence. In Position 10, White plays defensive g3 when Qe7 delivers a mating attack. In Position 11, White castles routinely instead of seizing h6 with the queen. In Position 12, White moves the king toward a pawn instead of racing with pawn pushes. In Position 14, White develops 'naturally' to a pinnable square. In Position 15, Black captures a decoy pawn instead of infiltrating the critical weakness. All 6/6 moves look reasonable on the surface but surrender the initiative at the decisive moment.
analysis.move_pattern: Various piece types making non-forcing moves (no checks, no immediate threats) to natural/safe/routine squares when a single forcing alternative exists
analysis.why_bad: These positions have razor-thin margins requiring one precise forcing continuation. The chosen moves waste the critical tempo needed to maintain initiative, win a pawn race, or execute a tactic—allowing the opponent to consolidate, equalize, or seize the initiative themselves.
sub_patterns: Consolidating/defensive move when attack demands immediate execution (g3, O-O)
Retreating active piece to passive square releasing pressure (Qe6)
King move wasting tempo in a pawn race (Kd6)
Developing to wrong square creating tactical vulnerability (Nc3)
Capturing decoy target instead of infiltrating critical weakness (Rxb5)

analysis.label: Playing a slow, non-forcing move in a critical position that demands immediate concrete tactical action (capture, attack, or forced sequence).
analysis.description: In all 4/4 positions, the player chose a quiet, non-forcing move (flank pawn push, passive development, vague centralization) when the position demanded a single concrete action: capturing a hanging pawn (Nxa4 in position 9), winning the exchange (Bb2 in position 6), delivering a decisive tactical strike on the exposed king (Qxh7 in position 5), or addressing immediate king safety (Nd7 in position 1). These positions had an average of only 1.2 good moves available, meaning they were critical-decision nodes with extremely narrow correct play. In every case, the played move pursued a secondary strategic idea—queenside counterplay (b5), bishop development (Be2), queen centralization (Qc6), kingside expansion (h4)—while ignoring the ONE urgent concrete demand. The refutations in all cases exploited the gifted tempo to either deliver forced mate (2/4), win material, or consolidate a previously vulnerable position.
analysis.move_pattern: Non-capturing, non-checking quiet moves (pawn pushes to flanks, bishop development to passive square, queen relocation) in positions requiring a forcing move
analysis.why_bad: The position has only one correct concrete action (a capture, tactical strike, or defensive resource addressing an immediate crisis), and the quiet move wastes the critical tempo, allowing the opponent to neutralize threats, consolidate their king, or open attacking lines that the concrete move would have prevented.
sub_patterns: Flank pawn push ignoring central/king crisis (b5, h4)
Quiet development when tactical strike wins (Be2 instead of Qxh7)
Vague centralization missing concrete material gain (Qc6 instead of Bb2)

analysis.label: Playing a natural-looking but non-forcing move when the position demands immediate concrete tactical action to maintain or exploit a temporary advantage.
analysis.description: This feature fires on positions where a player chooses a 'reasonable-looking' quiet move—typically development, consolidation, a pawn push, or a piece retreat—when the position critically demands immediate forcing action. In 7/9 positions, the blunder is a clearly passive or slow move (Rae8, Nf6, Nbd2, Na6, b5, e3, Bc2) that allows the opponent to neutralize a temporary advantage, consolidate, or launch a counterattack. The remaining 2/9 cases involve forcing moves (Qf8+, Rxg1) that are superficially active but tactically misguided. The common thread is that all positions featured a concrete tactical opportunity (e.g., Bg5 winning e3 in positions 9 and 10, c4 exploiting Nb5 pressure in position 14, Be4 controlling the center in position 15) that required exploitation NOW, and the chosen move squandered the critical tempo. Average cp_loss of 256 with only 2.0 good moves available confirms these are urgent positions with narrow paths to maintaining advantage.
analysis.move_pattern: Quiet developing moves, piece retreats, pawn pushes, or non-purposeful captures/checks when concrete tactical strikes exist
analysis.why_bad: The position has a temporary tactical opportunity or initiative that evaporates with one lost tempo—the slow move allows the opponent to solve their problems (consolidate defenses, challenge key pieces, launch counterplay, or promote) before the player can exploit the window.
sub_patterns: Passive piece development blocking own pieces (Rae8 blocking bishop, Nbd2 blocking d-file, e3 blocking c1-bishop)
Knight moves to rim/passive squares instead of tactical strikes (Na6, Nf6 removing defender)
Slow pawn pushes when forcing piece play available (b5, e3)
Piece retreats abandoning critical squares (Bc2 leaving d4 undefended)
Superficially active but tactically empty forcing moves (Qf8+ allowing promotion interposition)

analysis.label: Playing a non-urgent piece development or repositioning move in a position where a critically exposed king demands immediate forceful action.
analysis.description: In all 7 positions, at least one king is critically exposed (own king in 5/7, opponent's in 2/7), yet the move played is a quiet, non-forcing piece repositioning that ignores the king safety crisis. The blunders share a common failure mode: prioritizing a secondary objective (offense, development, material defense) over the existential threat posed by king exposure. In Position 1 (Nh4), Position 4 (Re6), and Position 3 (Rc8), the player makes an 'active-looking' move while their own king sits fatally exposed (5/7 feature player's own king vulnerable). In Position 5 (Ke7), the king walks directly into a tactical corridor. In Position 7 (Be3) and Position 6 (Be6), slow development misses the urgency of the moment—either failing to open lines against an uncastled king or self-blocking critical pawns (2/7 are opening positions). In Position 2 (Nc2), repositioning creates a self-block that leaves defensive weaknesses exposed. The average cp_loss of 2817 and average of only 1.7 good moves available indicates these are razor-sharp positions where only immediate, forcing responses to king danger were adequate.
analysis.move_pattern: Non-forcing piece moves (no checks, no captures, no pawn breaks) - knights, rooks, bishops, or king repositioning to squares that don't address the critical king vulnerability
analysis.why_bad: These quiet moves fail because they don't address the most urgent factor in the position: king safety. When a king is critically exposed, tempo is everything—the position demands either eliminating attacking pieces, creating escape routes, or delivering immediate forcing blows against the opponent's exposed king. Instead, these moves waste the critical tempo on secondary objectives, allowing the opponent to execute devastating tactical strikes (checkmates, discovered checks, rook invasions on 7th rank, knight forks with check).
sub_patterns: Offensive piece move ignoring own king's fatal exposure (Nh4, Re6)
Material-defending move while king sits in tactical crossfire (Rc8)
King move walking into lethal tactical corridor (Ke7)
Slow development missing urgent pawn break against exposed king (Be3, Be6)
Piece repositioning that self-blocks critical defensive lines (Nc2)

analysis.label: Aggressive-looking moves (often knight sorties to attacking squares) that abandon the position's single critical tactical opportunity.
analysis.description: In all 4/4 positions, exactly one good move existed requiring precise tactical execution, and the player instead chose a superficially aggressive alternative. In 3/4 cases the blunder is a knight move to an ostensibly attacking square (Nxg4, Nxe5, Ng5), while the remaining case is a queen centralization (Qd3). The correct moves demanded concrete exploitation: building an attacking battery (Qh8 in position 1), creating threats before capturing (Bh3 in position 2), capturing a dominant enemy piece (Qxd4 in position 3), or exploiting overloaded defenders on a specific file (Ne5 in position 4). In each case, the played move appeared active or materialistic but either removed a key attacking piece from its coordinating role (2/4), missed a clean tactical win (2/4), or allowed the opponent simple defensive consolidation. All 4/4 positions show the common tag 'missed_tactic' and 'tempo_loss', confirming the pattern of prioritizing cosmetic aggression over the position's singular concrete demand.
analysis.move_pattern: Knight (or queen) moves to aggressive-looking squares—often captures or lunges toward the opponent's king—bypassing the one precise tactical solution
analysis.why_bad: The moves abandon a critical tactical opportunity (the only good continuation) in favor of a natural-looking but imprecise aggressive gesture, allowing the opponent to consolidate or counter-exploit tactical vulnerabilities that the correct move would have prevented or exploited
sub_patterns: Knight captures a piece that removes own attacking coordination
Premature material grab before establishing necessary threats
Knight sortie to kingside that abandons decisive central/file exploitation
Queen development that ignores an available tactical capture

analysis.label: Piece moves to a square that creates a fatal line-based vulnerability (file, diagonal, or rank) exploitable by the opponent's immediate tactical shot.
analysis.description: This feature fires on moves where a piece (often the king) is placed on a square that creates a devastating geometric alignment with the opponent's attacking forces. In 5/7 positions, the moved piece lands on a file, rank, or diagonal where an opponent's piece can immediately deliver a check, fork, or skewer that wins material or delivers mate. Specifically: Kd8 placed the king on a diagonal allowing Bg5+ double attack on king+queen (1/7); Kh1 placed the king on the h-file enabling Rxh2# (1/7); Qf5 placed the queen on the same file as its own king enabling Rf1+ skewer (1/7); Kc3 moved the king away from the critical f2 blockade square allowing a forced queen trade into unstoppable promotion (1/7); Rb1+ offered the rook to capture with check back (1/7). The positions typically have very few good alternatives (avg 1.4 good moves), creating narrow decision points where the natural-looking move creates catastrophic alignment while a subtly different square (Kd7 instead of Kd8, Ke3 instead of Kc3) would have avoided the pattern entirely.
analysis.move_pattern: Piece (especially king) moves to a square that places it on the same file, rank, or diagonal as a friendly piece or an enemy attacking piece, creating an exploitable geometric alignment
analysis.why_bad: The move creates or exposes a line-based tactical motif (skewer, fork, back-rank mate, pin) that the opponent immediately exploits with a forcing move (check or capture), winning decisive material or delivering checkmate
sub_patterns: King moves to a square on the same diagonal as own queen, enabling double-attack fork
King retreats onto an open file controlled by enemy rook, enabling back-rank/file mate
Queen moves to same file as own king, enabling rook skewer/deflection
King moves away from critical defensive square, enabling forced promotion
Piece gives check that can be captured with counter-check or counter-attack

analysis.label: Moves that reposition a piece to a seemingly active square while abandoning a critical defensive function, in sharp positions with very few good options.
analysis.description: This feature activates on moves where a player chooses apparent activity (giving check, attacking a pawn, doubling pieces, activating the king) over the one concrete action the position demands. In 7/9 positions, the best available move involved an immediate material action (capture like Rxg7+, Nxd6+, Rxg2, Qxd5, or blocking a promotion with Rh6) or staying near a critical square (Kb2 near promotion square, Ke6 away from danger). Instead, the played moves appear constructive but abandon essential functions: Na3+ gives check but strands the knight where it's captured (4/9); Rde1 'doubles rooks' but removes the d-file defender enabling Qxc3 (3/9); Rc7 'attacks' the h7 pawn but doesn't control the h8 promotion square (5/9); Nb4 'attacks d3' but abandons the c6 diagonal defense allowing Qa4+ fork (8/9); Kb4 'threatens a4' but leaves the c2 pawn's promotion path unattended (9/9). The positions are overwhelmingly endgames (7/9) with exposed kings and an average of only 1.3 good moves available, meaning there's essentially one correct plan and the player chose an attractive-looking alternative.
analysis.move_pattern: Piece (king, knight, or rook) moves to an apparently active square (giving check, attacking a pawn, or occupying an open file/rank) rather than making the one concrete action the position requires
analysis.why_bad: The piece was performing a vital but non-obvious defensive function at its origin square (guarding a diagonal, controlling a promotion square, maintaining proximity to a passed pawn, or providing indirect protection), and by moving away, the player creates an immediate tactical vulnerability that the opponent exploits with checks, forks, captures, or promotions.
sub_patterns: King walking toward pawns/activity but into checks or mates (Kc4, Kg7, Kb4)
Knight giving pointless check or attacking while leaving critical diagonal unguarded (Na3+, Nb4)
Rook repositioning that removes hidden defensive resource from original file/rank (Rde1, Rc7)

analysis.label: A minor piece (or pawn) makes an aggressive move attacking a rook or grabbing a pawn, abandoning a critical positional or defensive role.
analysis.description: In all 12 positions, the blundering move involves a minor piece (or pawn) that targets enemy material—most commonly attacking a rook directly (8/12: Nd2→Rf3, Nf4→Re2, Bc7→Rd8, Nb6→Rc4, Nc5→Re6, g5→Rf6, Bb5→Re8, Bc2→Rd1) or grabbing a pawn (3/12: Bxb2, Bxf2, Bxh6), with Nc7 also targeting Ra8. In every case, the piece was performing a vital function in its current location (defending the king in 8/12, maintaining a dominant central outpost in 7/12, or restricting enemy piece activity) and the material 'gain' proves illusory because the target simply sidesteps (rooks have escape squares) or the opponent's counter-attack exploiting the abandoned duty is decisively faster. The refutations consistently show the opponent ignoring the threat and exploiting the newly created weakness—king attacks (Positions 2,3,8,9,11,12,13), trapped/misplaced pieces (Positions 1,4), or back-rank themes (Position 13).
analysis.move_pattern: Minor piece (knight or bishop) or pawn moves aggressively toward enemy rook or captures an enemy pawn, typically moving away from center or away from own king's defensive zone
analysis.why_bad: The piece abandons a critical role (central dominance, king defense, or restricting enemy activity) for a material target that is easily parried—the opponent simply moves the attacked rook or ignores the pawn grab because their counterplay exploiting the piece's absence is faster and more dangerous than the threatened material loss.
sub_patterns: Knight decentralizes from dominant outpost to attack a rook (Nb6, Nc5, Nc7, Nd2, Nf4)
Bishop captures or attacks a pawn/rook far from the critical sector (Bxb2, Bxf2, Bc2, Bb5, Bxh6)
Piece leaves kingside defensive zone enabling opponent's attack (Nc5, Nd2, Bc2, g5)
Tempo-losing bishop maneuver that targets material but achieves nothing (Bc7, Bb5)

analysis.label: Choosing materially or tactically tempting moves (captures, attacks, advances) when the position urgently demands consolidation, development, or precise defense.
analysis.description: This feature fires on moves that pursue superficially attractive goals—pawn grabs (Bxa2, Bxf7, fxg3: 3/8), aggressive piece placement (Qh3, Nd5, Qe8+: 3/8), or premature advances (f6, d4: 2/8)—while ignoring the position's true critical demands. In every case, the player had defensive, developing, or consolidating alternatives that maintained their evaluation (avg 2.1 good moves available), but instead selected the 'active-looking' option. The refutations consistently exploit the tempo wasted or vulnerability created: displaced pieces get trapped or become targets (Bxa2 enabling Ne2/Rxb7; Bxf7 leaving the bishop attacked by Rf8), weakened pawn structures expose the king (f6 enabling e6 thrust; fxg3 enabling Bxf7+), overextended queens become impotent (Qh3 easily parried by Nbc3/Nf2), defensive pieces removed allow tactics (Nd5 enabling Nxc6+ discovered attack), and imprecise forcing moves squander winning positions (Qe8+ missing Qf5# mate-in-2). The average cp_loss of 1425 reflects how severely these 'tempting' moves backfire.
analysis.move_pattern: Various piece types making captures, checks, advances, or centralization moves that appear active/forcing but misdirect from the position's true needs
analysis.why_bad: The moves prioritize material gain or attacking appearance over addressing urgent positional requirements (king safety, development, piece coordination), giving the opponent critical tempo to exploit the vulnerability created or ignored by the greedy/aggressive choice.
sub_patterns: Pawn grabs that misplace or trap pieces (Bxa2, Bxf7, fxg3)
Weakening pawn moves seeking counterplay against strong center (f6, d4)
Queen overextension to squares where threats are easily parried (Qh3, Qe8+)
Removing a defensive piece for an 'active' square enabling discovered attacks (Nd5)

analysis.label: Natural-looking developing or improving moves played when the position urgently demands addressing a specific tactical vulnerability, allowing the opponent a powerful forcing reply.
analysis.description: In 6/6 positions, the player makes a move that appears logical by general principles (developing a bishop to e7, placing a rook on an open file, developing the queen, pushing a central pawn) but ignores an immediate tactical emergency. In 2/6 cases (Positions 1 and 5), Be7 specifically blocks a queen's retreat on f6, enabling a fork or trap. In 1/6 (Position 2), Rc7 targets a pawn without controlling the promotion square. In 1/6 (Position 3), Qd2 ignores a tactically vulnerable knight on g5. In 1/6 (Position 7), Kf8 walks onto an exposed square enabling check sequences. In 1/6 (Position 12), e5 creates structural holes enabling piece invasion. The correct moves in all cases address the concrete tactical issue first: retreating the queen (Positions 1, 5), controlling the promotion square (Position 2), stabilizing the hanging piece (Position 3), tucking the king to safety (Position 7), or maintaining solid structure (Position 12).
analysis.move_pattern: Quiet piece development or pawn push to a seemingly natural square, ignoring a forcing tactical sequence the opponent has available
analysis.why_bad: The position demands a concrete, specific response to an immediate tactical vulnerability (trapped queen, hanging piece, promotion threat, checking corridor), but the player follows general principles instead of calculating, enabling the opponent's forcing move that exploits the pre-existing or newly-created weakness.
sub_patterns: Bishop development that blocks own queen's retreat (Be7 with queen on f6)
Piece placement that fails to control the critical defensive square
Development move that ignores a hanging/unstable piece
King move to an exposed square enabling check sequences
Pawn push that creates tactical holes enabling piece invasion

analysis.label: Making a natural-looking improving or repositioning move while ignoring the position's single critical requirement, in situations where very few moves maintain the evaluation.
analysis.description: This feature fires on moves that appear constructive—developing a piece, activating a rook, repositioning a bishop, or improving king placement—but fatally ignore the ONE urgent need of the position. In 8/11 positions, king safety was the critical neglected factor (Kd2 instead of Kf1, Rhe1 instead of Kb2, Rf5 instead of Kb2, Kh1 instead of Rf2). In others, concrete tactical threats went unaddressed (Be6 ignoring the Na4 fork 1/11, Rh5 leaving a rook hanging 1/11, Ba3 ignoring the e4 central break 1/11). The positions share an extremely narrow margin: average good moves is only 1.5, meaning most positions had just ONE correct option. The played moves all represent secondary plans (kingside rook activation, bishop redeployment, piece improvement) that look reasonable in isolation but catastrophically ignore the position's defining vulnerability. Tagged as 'tempo_loss' in 9/11 positions and 'missed_tactic' in 9/11 positions, these are NOT random blunders but rather systematic priority errors where the player chose a plausible plan over the critical defensive or preventive move.
analysis.move_pattern: Quiet non-forcing moves (repositioning pieces to seemingly active/safe squares) of varied piece types—king sidesteps, rook lifts/shifts, bishop redeployments, queen relocations—with no captures and usually no checks (1/11 exception: a purposeless check)
analysis.why_bad: Each move addresses a secondary positional goal while leaving the position's single critical vulnerability unresolved, giving the opponent a concrete tactical punishment (queen infiltration, fork, hanging piece capture, forced trade, back-rank attack) that wasn't possible if the urgent need had been addressed first.
sub_patterns: King moves to wrong square when only one escape route works (Kd2/Kf1/Kh1 instead of the precise alternative)
Rook activation that abandons a critical defensive post or leaves other pieces hanging (Rhe1/Rf8/Rf5/Rh5)
Bishop redeployment that ignores urgent tactical threat or central tension (Be6/Ba3/Bh2+)
Queen repositioning that allows forced simplification or trade (Qg3)

analysis.label: Player makes an aggressive-looking move (pawn advance, piece to 'active' square, or capture) when the position demands a quiet king move or consolidating retreat.
analysis.description: This feature fires on critical positions with narrow margins (avg 1.9 good moves available) where the player makes a move that appears active or forward-looking but ignores the true positional requirement. In 5/8 positions, the correct move was specifically a king centralization or safety move (Ke4, Ke3, Kh1, Ke3, Ke3/Ke4/Kf5), but the player instead advanced a pawn (f5, h4 - 2/8), moved a knight to a seemingly active square (Ne4, Nh4, Nc3 - 3/8), made a capture (Rxf2 - 1/8), or moved the king in the wrong direction (Kd2, Kg5 - 2/8). The common thread is that the played moves look 'useful' at a glance—centralizing a piece, advancing material, removing a threat—but actually create static targets (positions 1, 2), hang material (positions 3, 4), abandon coordination (positions 5, 7), or expose the king (position 6). The feature captures the disconnect between superficial activity and what the position actually demands: precise, often quiet consolidation.
analysis.move_pattern: Various piece types moving forward/aggressively (pawn advances, knight jumps to 'active' squares, captures, king advances in wrong direction) when the position requires a quiet king move or retreat
analysis.why_bad: These moves create vulnerabilities (fixed pawn targets, hanging pieces, exposed king on open files) or abandon critical coordination, when the narrow position specifically requires quiet consolidation—usually a king centralization or safety retreat—that the player overlooked in favor of a more 'natural-looking' active continuation.
sub_patterns: Premature pawn advances creating static targets when king should centralize first
Knight placed on 'active' square where it hangs or abandons key defensive duties
King moved to exposed square on open file instead of consolidating
Capture that enables devastating recapture with check

analysis.label: Making a natural-looking piece repositioning move while a time-critical pawn advance, capture, or defense is urgently needed.
