analysis.description: This feature fires when a player makes what appears to be an active or purposeful piece move (king centralization, bishop development, queen repositioning, knight activation) but fatally ignores a concrete, time-sensitive pawn-related action that the position demands. In 7/8 positions, the correct move involved a direct pawn action—advancing a critical pawn (b5, f6, g5, a6), capturing a dangerous pawn (Kxg4, Qxf3, cxd6), or defending a key pawn (Kc4 for c5)—while the blunder was a non-forcing piece move that gave the opponent the tempo to execute their own plan first. The common thread is that positions with passed pawns or critical pawn races (6/8 feature passed pawns prominently) demand concrete immediate action over 'natural' piece improvements. The tempo lost allows the opponent to play the critical pawn move themselves (Position 1: a4; Position 6: Kxc5), unleash a pawn advance (Position 13: g3; Position 9: f2+), or exploit the abandoned defensive function (Position 12: d7+ discovered check). Average cp_loss of 283 confirms these are consequential errors at critical junctures.
analysis.move_pattern: Any piece (K, Q, B, N) moves to a seemingly active or natural square rather than executing a concrete pawn-related action (advance, capture, or defense); no consistent direction or piece type, but moves are characteristically non-forcing.
analysis.why_bad: The piece move wastes a critical tempo in positions where pawn timing is paramount—the opponent uses that tempo to advance/capture a key pawn, neutralize a pawn majority, execute a discovered attack, or promote an unstoppable passed pawn. The 'active-looking' piece placement provides no concrete benefit that compensates for losing the pawn race or allowing the opponent's pawn break.
sub_patterns: King centralizes aggressively but abandons defense of a critical passed pawn (Ke5, Kd6)
Bishop repositions to a 'nice' diagonal while an enemy passed pawn advances unchallenged (Bb2, Bb3)
Queen retreats or redeploys when capturing/blocking a dangerous pawn was essential (Qh2, Qf6)
Knight jumps to 'active' outpost inviting a structurally ruinous exchange (Nf5)

analysis.label: Black's queen captures an undefended pawn on the b2/c2 square while the king is exposed, abandoning critical defensive duties.
analysis.description: In 3/4 positions, Black's queen captures a seemingly free pawn on the second rank (c2 or b2) on the queenside while Black's king is dangerously exposed (d8 in 2/4, c7 in 1/4, open center in 1/4). The common thread is the queen relocating far from the vulnerable king to grab material, creating a fatal disconnect between Black's defensive needs and the queen's position. In all three queen-capture cases, White exploits the queen's absence with tactical strikes involving open files, checks, and piece coordination against the exposed king. The queen on b2/c2 becomes either a target (attacked by Rb1 or Nd4) or simply irrelevant to the king's defense. Position 4 (Kd4, 0 cp loss) appears to be a weaker/edge-case activation sharing the exposed-king geometry but not the blunder pattern.
analysis.move_pattern: Queen captures undefended pawn on b2 or c2 (second rank, queenside), moving laterally away from exposed king
analysis.why_bad: The queen abandons its defensive role near the exposed king to capture a distant pawn, allowing White to exploit the king's vulnerability with tempo-gaining attacks (checks, open file invasions, piece forks) while the queen is too far away to return in time.
sub_patterns: Qxc2 with king on back rank d8
Qxb2 with king exposed on c7
Queen trapped on second rank after pawn grab

analysis.label: Aimless king moves (or other slow repositioning moves) in endgames when an urgent concrete tactical operation with another piece was required.
analysis.description: This feature fires on positions where the player makes a 'natural-looking' slow move—predominantly king moves (8/11 positions)—that wastes a critical tempo when the position demanded immediate tactical action with a different piece. In Position 1, Kc3 was played instead of Rh5 (rook reposition before king). In Position 5, Kh5 chased a pawn instead of Ra5 winning material. In Position 10, Kc3 was played instead of Bb4 blocking the rook's path. In Position 12, Kb2 was played instead of Na4 deflecting the rook. In Position 7, Bf2 repositioned passively instead of Bb4 sacrificing. The non-king-move outliers (f3, h4) follow the same principle: making a slow positional move when concrete tactical urgency existed. The average cp_loss of 341 reflects that these tempo-wasting moves frequently transform winning positions into draws or drawn positions into losses, with most positions (8/11) having only 1-2 good moves available, indicating narrow tactical moments that demanded precision rather than general principles.
analysis.move_pattern: King move (or quiet piece/pawn repositioning) to a seemingly reasonable square, typically sideways or advancing, without immediate tactical purpose
analysis.why_bad: These moves waste a critical tempo in positions where an immediate tactical operation (piece sacrifice, deflection, interposition, or capturing a vulnerable target) was urgently needed—the opponent uses the gifted tempo to consolidate, execute their own plan, or neutralize the player's winning resource
sub_patterns: King moves when rook should capture/reposition first (Positions 1, 5)
King moves instead of piece sacrifice or interposition (Positions 7, 10, 12)
King wanders to wrong square losing tempo in pawn race (Positions 3, 4, 6)
Quiet pawn push wastes tempo when king activation or piece play was needed (Positions 8, 14)

analysis.label: Moving a piece to an apparently active or threatening square that actually wastes tempo by abandoning the piece's essential function or ignoring the position's true demands.
analysis.description: All 4/4 positions feature moves that prioritize cosmetic activity—checks, threats, centralization—over genuinely constructive play. In Position 1, Qf3 targets Black's king instead of developing with Nf3 (the piece the square was actually meant for). In Position 2, Qe1+ gives a pointless check that improves White's king instead of Qd1 which forces a drawing repetition. In Position 3, Nb5 leaves its powerful central post for a superficial d6/Nc7+ threat instead of playing d4 which leverages the knight's central control. In Position 4, Re5 centralizes the rook aesthetically but abandons the a-file counterplay, allowing a forced winning exchange. All 4/4 are tagged 'tempo_loss' because each move squanders time on an attractive-looking but strategically hollow idea while the opponent gains the initiative. The correct moves in each case were less flashy but addressed the position's true requirements: development, forcing mechanisms, maintaining piece function.
analysis.move_pattern: Any piece moved to a square that appears aggressive or active (threatening, checking, central) but abandons its current critical function or duty
analysis.why_bad: The moves waste tempo on superficial threats that are easily parried, while simultaneously removing the piece from where it was needed most—whether controlling key squares (Nc3), maintaining drawing mechanisms (Qa-file pressure), or supporting development. The opponent exploits the abandoned function.
sub_patterns: Pointless check that improves opponent's king
Knight abandoning central anchor for peripheral attack
Queen repositioning that duplicates another piece's ideal square
Rook abandoning active file for cosmetic centralization

analysis.label: Moves to seemingly active kingside squares that create immediate tactical vulnerabilities by neglecting defensive priorities.
analysis.description: This feature activates on moves that appear to create threats or improve piece activity on the kingside (f/g/h files) but actually generate exploitable weaknesses. In 5/6 positions, the move targets a kingside square (Kg4, Kh8, Qg5, f6, Nf6), with Bc5 being a partial outlier that still shares the 'looks active but hangs' theme. The punishments exploit hanging pieces (3/6: Qg5 leaves d5 undefended, Bc5 hangs to Qh5+ check, Nf6 hangs to Rxf6), king safety failures (4/6: Kg4 allows gxh5+ with check, Kh8 enables Rf8+ back-rank, Bc5/f6 exploit central king exposure), and trapped pieces (1/6: f6 blocks bishop retreat). All positions had 2-3 good alternatives available, and the average cp_loss of 281 reflects moves that fundamentally misjudge which sector of the board requires attention.
analysis.move_pattern: Pieces or pawns moving to f6/g4/g5/h8 (kingside squares, ranks 4-8), appearing to create activity or threats but landing on undefended or tactically exploitable squares
analysis.why_bad: These moves prioritize apparent aggression or prophylaxis over fundamental needs (defending critical pawns, maintaining piece safety, avoiding exposed king vulnerabilities), creating immediate tactical refutations that exploit the newly undefended piece or worsened king position.
sub_patterns: Placing a piece on an undefended kingside square within capture range of opponent's pieces
Moving the king toward the kingside when the critical theater is elsewhere or corner creates back-rank weakness
Abandoning defense of a critical central pawn for a superficially active queen/piece placement
Advancing a kingside pawn that blocks own piece's retreat route

analysis.label: Natural-looking active moves that place a piece on a tactically exploitable square, when a quieter prophylactic move was required.
analysis.description: This feature activates on moves that appear logical or active—centralizing a king, capturing an annoying piece, pushing in the center, or castling—but fatally place a piece onto a square where it becomes a tactical target. In 4/6 positions, the king or a major piece moves to a square that creates an immediate geometric vulnerability (diagonal, fork square, or file). In 5/6 cases, the correct move was a quiet or prophylactic alternative (Ka6 retreat, Kh2 sidestep, f6 pawn consolidation, h3 prophylaxis, Bh5 addressing a threat). The blunders share a common DNA: the player follows intuition or general principles (centralize, capture threats, develop) rather than calculating the opponent's concrete tactical response. The refutations exploit forks (2/6), diagonal attacks (3/6), and pawn breaks enabled by abandoned restraint (1/6). Average cp_loss of 286 indicates these are serious mistakes with typically only 1-2 good alternatives available.
analysis.move_pattern: Any piece type moving to an apparently active/natural square that creates a geometric vulnerability (diagonal, fork square, or abandons key restraining duty)
analysis.why_bad: The move looks reasonable by general principles but walks into a specific tactical refutation—a fork, diagonal check, or breakthrough—that the quiet alternative would have prevented.
sub_patterns: King advancing into center where checks/forks become available
Capturing a piece but placing own piece on exploitable line
Castling or moving king onto a vulnerable diagonal
Abandoning a restraining post allowing opponent's pawn break

analysis.label: Non-urgent repositioning or pawn advances that ignore immediate tactical demands, either squandering concrete opportunities or creating fresh vulnerabilities.
analysis.description: This feature fires on positions where players make natural-looking, quiet moves (piece repositioning, pawn advances, or incautious captures) when the position demands immediate concrete action. In 6/8 positions, the played move either places a piece/pawn on a tactically vulnerable square (Rd2 and Qd2 both land on the d-file where they're exploited via checks/deflections; c4 places a pawn on a capturable diagonal; Nxd5 opens the d-file for opponent's doubled rooks; b5 creates a permanent c5 weakness) or abandons the critical sector entirely (Bb3 retreats instead of exploiting a knight fork; Qb2 abandons kingside mating attack; Re4 moves away from the queenside where passed pawn defense was urgent). The average cp_loss of 306 with 2.8 good alternatives available shows these are positions where multiple safe continuations existed, yet the player chose a move that looks reasonable on the surface but fatally misjudges the tactical urgency of the position.
analysis.move_pattern: Quiet piece moves or pawn advances, predominantly to the queenside/center (b2, b3, b5, c4, d2, d5, e4), non-capturing or premature captures
analysis.why_bad: They prioritize secondary positional objectives (centralization, space, development) over the position's critical tactical demand—either exploiting an existing opportunity, preventing an opponent's concrete threat, or maintaining pressure in the key sector—resulting in either a squandered advantage or a newly created vulnerability that the opponent exploits with forcing moves.
sub_patterns: Piece retreats/repositions away from active duty when a concrete tactic is available (Bb3, Re4)
Queen moves to tactically exposed squares on open files (Qd2 x2, Qb2)
Pawn advances creating capture targets or permanent weaknesses (b5, c4)
Premature captures that open lines for the opponent's pieces (Nxd5)

analysis.label: Playing a natural-looking or routine move in a position that demands one specific precise action, thereby squandering a critical opportunity or allowing a tactical refutation.
analysis.description: This feature fires on positions where the player makes a plausible-seeming move (developing a piece, castling, advancing a pawn, centralizing) while ignoring the position's specific urgent demand. The positions share an extremely narrow set of good options (avg 1.6 good moves), meaning precision is critical. In 8/11 cases, the played move follows a general chess principle (develop: Be6, Ng5, Nc3; castle: O-O twice; advance pawns: c7, c4, g4; centralize king: Ke6) but fails to address the ONE thing the position requires—whether that's defusing a tactical threat (3/11 castling into attacks or leaving pieces hanging), exploiting a fleeting opportunity (2/11 missing Nd6 or h6), maintaining a strategic bind (2/11 releasing pressure with c4 or c7 without support), or finding the correct square in a critical endgame (2/11 Ke6 losing opposition, b8=R underpromotion). The refutations consistently exploit the specific vulnerability the 'routine' move failed to address.
analysis.move_pattern: Various piece types and directions; no geometric consistency. Moves are developing moves, castling, pawn pushes, or king moves that appear generically reasonable.
analysis.why_bad: Each move prioritizes a general chess principle (development, king safety, pawn advancement, activation) over the position's specific tactical or strategic demand, which required a narrow, often counterintuitive response. The 'natural' move either leaves a piece hanging, castles into an attack, pushes a pawn without support, releases a strategic bind, or chooses the wrong square in a precise endgame.
sub_patterns: Castling into a prepared kingside attack when defusing the threat was critical
Developing or activating one piece while leaving another piece tactically vulnerable
Premature pawn advance without proper piece support or preparation
Moving the wrong piece when a specific piece needed to act (e.g., Qd3 instead of Rd3)
Wrong king square in pawn endgame losing opposition or tempo

analysis.label: Non-forcing piece repositioning moves that ignore an immediate concrete tactical obligation, allowing simple refutations.
analysis.description: All 5 positions share a common pattern: the player makes a quiet, non-forcing move aimed at improving piece activity or placement (king activation, bishop repositioning, rook to open file) while ignoring a critical tactical necessity. In 5/5 cases, the position demanded addressing a specific concrete threat rather than a cosmetic improvement. Kb3 abandoned defense of c5 allowing Nxc5+ (3/5 involve leaving a piece undefended). Bh3 placed the bishop on an undefended square capturable by Kxh3 or after Rxg6+ checks. Kg2 walked into a Nxe1+ fork instead of capturing the dangerous c2 knight. Rd8 activated the rook while leaving the b5 knight hanging to Rxb5+. Bg3 repositioned the bishop while ignoring the critical Rxb2+ threat. In 4/5 cases the refutation involves a capture with check or a fork, exploiting the tempo wasted on the quiet move. Average cp_loss of 344 confirms these are severe blunders. The positions averaged only 1.6 good moves, indicating high tactical urgency that was ignored.
analysis.move_pattern: Quiet non-capturing, non-checking piece moves (kings, bishops, rooks) that reposition to seemingly active squares without addressing immediate board tension
analysis.why_bad: Each move wastes a critical tempo on piece improvement while a concrete tactical vulnerability (hanging piece, exposed king, undefended square) exists that the opponent can immediately exploit with checks, captures, or forks
sub_patterns: King moves abandoning defensive duty of key piece/pawn
Bishop placed on undefended square near enemy king, becoming capturable
Rook activation to open file while own piece hangs elsewhere
Piece repositioning ignoring back-rank or king-shield vulnerability

analysis.label: Plausibly active or aggressive moves that neglect the single most critical tactical/defensive requirement in the position, allowing immediate catastrophic punishment.
analysis.description: In 7/8 positions, the player made a move that appeared purposeful—centralizing a queen (Qd4, Qb3, Qb7), doubling rooks (Rcc6), capturing material (bxc5, Bxe5+), or developing (Nge7, f3)—while ignoring an immediate critical vulnerability that demanded specific attention. In 6/8 cases the correct move involved deploying a particular piece to a specific defensive square (Nf6 to guard g4, Ndf3 to route toward c2, Bd6 to clear king escape, Qf3 to cover kingside, Nh7 to prepare for Nf5, Nf1 to defend e3). In 5/8 positions the king (either side's) was directly at risk. The average cp_loss of 2677 reflects that these positions had razor-thin margins—averaging only 1.8 good moves available—where the one correct defensive/prophylactic idea was bypassed in favor of something that looked productive but was tactically irrelevant to the position's most pressing demand. The refutations consistently exploit the exact weakness the player's move failed to address: unguarded pieces, mating nets, tempo-gaining attacks on exposed queens, or immediate tactical sequences.
analysis.move_pattern: Diverse piece types moving to apparently active squares (centralizing, capturing, developing) that are directionally away from or irrelevant to the critical defensive zone; no single geometric motif but consistently moves that fail to address the board's most urgent square/piece
analysis.why_bad: Each move ignores the position's single most critical tactical requirement—typically a specific piece needing to defend a specific square—in favor of apparent activity elsewhere, allowing the opponent an immediate decisive tactical exploitation (mate, winning material via fork/pin, or stripping king cover)
sub_patterns: Queen moving to exposed/remote square abandoning key defensive duty (Qb3, Qb7, Qd4)
Choosing the wrong piece or square for a necessary function (f3 pawn instead of Ndf3 knight, Nge7 instead of Nf6)
Aggressive piece play while own king faces immediate mating threat (Rcc6 allowing Rxg2#)
Material capture wasting the critical tempo needed for a saving maneuver (bxc5 instead of Ne7-Nf5-Ng3+)
Flashy tactical shot missing a simpler decisive blow (Bxe5+ missing Ne4#)

analysis.label: Natural-looking positional or preparatory moves that ignore immediate concrete tactical vulnerabilities, allowing the opponent to exploit with forcing shots.
analysis.description: This feature fires on moves that appear strategically reasonable (centralizing, developing, preparing plans) but catastrophically overlook concrete tactical realities. In 7/8 positions, the analyses explicitly tag 'missed_tactic' as a key theme, and 7/8 also identify 'tempo_loss'. The played moves include preparing a fianchetto while a pawn hangs (b6), advancing a pawn before centralizing the king (f5), passively repositioning a rook when a concrete prophylactic was needed (Rf8 ignoring Bf4), moving a king into a check corridor (Kh2), centralizing a queen onto a fork square (Qe6), placing a rook on an attacked diagonal (Rh8), aggressively pushing a rook while leaving another undefended (Rg5), and choosing the wrong rook for a natural-looking move while missing a tactical exchange (Rfd1). The common thread is that each move prioritizes a vague or long-term idea over an urgent, calculable requirement. The average of only 1.9 good moves available confirms these were critical moments demanding precision, and the average 1390cp loss shows the tactical punishments were devastating.
analysis.move_pattern: Varied piece types and directions; all are non-forcing moves (no checks, no captures, no direct threats) played in positions requiring concrete tactical responses
analysis.why_bad: Each move ignores an immediate tactical reality—whether a hanging piece to capture, a check sequence to prevent, a fork to avoid, or a key opponent resource to neutralize—allowing the opponent to execute a concrete forcing sequence (check, capture, fork, or deflection) that wins material or creates decisive threats.
sub_patterns: Piece placed on tactically vulnerable square (Qe6 into fork, Rh8 onto attacked diagonal, Kh2 into check corridor)
Preparatory move ignoring free material (b6 ignoring hanging g4 pawn)
Wrong move order losing tempo in critical race (f5 before king centralization)
Passive rook move failing to prevent opponent's key consolidation (Rf8 allowing Bf4, Rfd1 missing Rc2 tactic)
Aggressive piece displacement leaving other pieces undefended (Rg5 leaving Rh1 hanging)

analysis.label: Moving a heavy piece to double on a rank or file where another piece already sits, neglecting more urgent tactical or defensive needs.
analysis.description: All 5 positions share the same pattern: the player moves a heavy piece (rook or queen) to a square that 'doubles' it with another friendly heavy piece on the same rank or file — Rcc7 doubles rooks on the 7th rank (3/5), Rdb7 doubles rooks on the 7th/b-file (4/5), Ree4 doubles rooks on the 4th rank (5/5), Rae8 doubles rooks on the e-file (5/5), and Qb2 places the queen on the 2nd rank alongside a rook on c2 (2/5). In every case, the 'doubling' follows standard positional principles but ignores urgent concrete needs: defending their own exposed king (4/5 positions involve king safety failures), preventing immediate tactical shots, or maintaining pieces on critical defensive squares. The punishment consistently exploits what was abandoned — perpetual check (position 2), an advanced passed pawn (position 3), checkmate in 2 (position 4), a devastating g-file attack (position 5), and a knight fork winning the exchange (position 6).
analysis.move_pattern: Heavy piece (rook or queen) moving to a rank or file already occupied by another friendly heavy piece, creating a doubled formation
analysis.why_bad: The doubling creates no immediate forcing threats while abandoning critical defensive duties or allowing concrete tactical refutations — the 'standard positional concept' is too slow when urgent tactical needs exist
sub_patterns: Doubling rooks on the 7th rank while own king is exposed
Doubling rooks on a file creating tactical vulnerability to a piece fork/block
Queen joining rook on a rank while abandoning king cover

analysis.label: Moving a piece away from its essential offensive or defensive role in a tactically demanding position, allowing the opponent an immediate decisive tactical blow.
analysis.description: In all 4/4 positions, the player moved a piece that was either performing a critical function or needed to execute a forcing sequence, instead making a 'natural-looking' but non-urgent move that fatally abandoned a key responsibility. In Position 2, Re8 abandoned queenside pressure when Nb4+ (a forcing check) was required, allowing Qxb7. In Position 7, Rxb2 grabbed a pawn but removed the rook from the f-file where it was simultaneously attacking AND preventing Rf7+/Qc8# back-rank mate. In Position 12, Ke1 retreated the king backward onto the open e-file where it remained vulnerable to Nxf3+ knight forks, rather than escaping forward toward g3. In Position 13, Kf2 moved the king to a square that exposed the queen to a forced trade via Qc5, transitioning into a lost endgame. All 4/4 positions demanded specific, often forcing play, but the player chose a reasonable-seeming alternative that ignored the position's concrete tactical requirements.
analysis.move_pattern: Any piece (king, rook) moved to a seemingly logical square that abandons control of a critical file, diagonal, or removes a tactical threat
analysis.why_bad: The move removes a piece from where it performs an essential function (defending against mate, maintaining forcing threats, or covering tactical squares), allowing the opponent to immediately exploit the vacated responsibility with checks, forks, forced trades, or mating attacks.
sub_patterns: Rook leaves critical file allowing back-rank or material threats
King retreats to vulnerable file instead of advancing to safety
Passive move played when position demands immediate forcing continuation
King walks into forced unfavorable exchange along newly-opened line

analysis.label: Player makes a superficially reasonable move when the position urgently demands a specific rook activation, repositioning, or capture.
analysis.description: In 6/8 positions, the objectively best move was a rook move (Re7, Rxc7, Rf4, Re8, Rc8, Rf8), but the player chose a different piece or the wrong square instead. In Position 2, Qe7 was played instead of Re7, exposing the queen to a pin. In Position 5, Kf1 was played instead of Rxc7, missing a free pawn capture. In Position 6, Qf6 was played instead of Rf4, leaving the rook on f8 to block the king's escape. In Position 7, Qf5 was played instead of Re8, abandoning critical g7 coverage. In Position 13, Re8 was played instead of Rc8, leaving the c-file uncontested. In Position 14, f4 was played instead of Rf8, choosing a weakening pawn push over rook activation. The common error is reaching for a 'natural-looking' queen move, king move, or pawn push when the rook's unique properties (expendability for blocking, file control, lower tactical vulnerability) make it the correct tool for the position's demands.
analysis.move_pattern: Various pieces (often queen) move to e/f file squares, when the correct move was a rook relocation to a specific file or rank
analysis.why_bad: The rook's lower value makes it ideal for blocking duties and sacrificial positions (vs queen getting pinned/trapped), and the rook's file-controlling ability means only it can contest critical open files; choosing another piece fails to address the position's concrete tactical requirement.
sub_patterns: Queen occupies square meant for rook, gets pinned or enables mating pattern (Qe7, Qf6)
Passive king/pawn move instead of active rook capture or activation (Kf1, f4)
Rook moves to wrong file, leaving critical file uncontested (Re8 vs Rc8)
Piece blocks own army's coordination instead of rook solving the problem (Nd2)

analysis.label: Voluntarily displacing a well-placed piece from its optimal square, disrupting winning coordination for a superficially logical but position-worsening alternative.
analysis.description: This feature fires on moves where the player removes a piece from a square where it was exerting maximum influence, often for a 'tempting' reason like giving check, making a capture, or centralizing. In 6/8 positions, the error directly involves moving a piece away from its dominant post: the queen leaves d6 for d3+ (Position 12), h5 for g4+ (Position 13), f4 for f2 (Position 11); the king retreats from f4 to e3 (Position 2); the bishop leaves f7 for d5 (Position 4); and the rook captures off e1, removing a critical pin (Position 6). The remaining 2/8 cases involve moves that disrupt coordination indirectly: Nc3 blocks the c-pawn needed to support a bishop (Position 5), and Rf1 commits the rook before addressing the prerequisite back-rank weakness (Position 3). In every case, the position was strong or winning, and the piece's prior placement was the foundation of that advantage.
analysis.move_pattern: A piece moves away from its zone of maximum influence - queens/kings retreat or shift laterally off dominant squares, bishops/rooks displace from key diagonals/files, or checks/captures remove a piece from a coordination role
analysis.why_bad: The moved piece was the linchpin of the position's strength - its placement created threats, pins, restrictions, or mating nets. By displacing it, the player dissolves their own attacking coordination, gives the opponent time to regroup or equalize, and often enables specific tactical refutations (perpetual checks, counter-forks, back-rank threats) that exploit the newly created weaknesses.
sub_patterns: Pointless checks that force the queen off a dominant square (Qd3+, Qg4+)
Queen/piece retreats that surrender control of critical squares (Qf2, Ke3)
Captures that remove a piece from a more valuable coordination role (Rxe7+ removing the e-file pin)
Seemingly improving moves that block or displace structural support (Nc3 blocking c-pawn, Bd5 inviting tempo attacks)

analysis.label: Moving a piece away from a critical defensive, controlling, or attacking role to pursue a seemingly attractive but tactically fatal goal.
analysis.description: This feature fires on moves where a piece abandons a vital function—defending another piece, controlling a key square, or enabling a forced tactic—in favor of something that appears active or purposeful. In 3/11 positions, a bishop leaves e3 (or goes to e3 to be captured), removing the defense of a centralized knight and enabling forks (Bh6 x2, Be3). In 2/11 positions, a center pawn capture (exd4) opens lines/squares against the player's own uncastled king. In 2/11 positions, a piece leaves a central square (e5 abandons f5 control, Nc5 abandons e4) allowing opponent exploitation. In 1/11, a knight leaves g4 where it enabled forced mate (Nxe3). In 1/11, a bishop develops ignoring f7 vulnerability (Bf5). The moved pieces typically go to squares that look active (attacking, capturing, developing) while the abandoned function is immediately punished with forks, line-opening, or piece wins. King safety concerns appear in 9/11 positions, and the average cp_loss of 1204 reflects catastrophic exploitation of the abandoned responsibility.
analysis.move_pattern: A piece (bishop, pawn, knight, or king) moves away from a square where it defended another piece, controlled a critical square, or was positioned for a key tactic—typically toward an apparently active destination (capture, attack, development)
analysis.why_bad: The moved piece was performing a critical hidden function (defending a piece from capture/fork, controlling a square that prevents enemy penetration, or enabling a forced tactical sequence), and its departure allows immediate tactical punishment—usually forks, exploitation of undefended pieces, or opening lines against an exposed king.
sub_patterns: Bishop leaving e3 removes defense of centralized knight, allowing Nxd4 + fork on f3 (Bh6 x2, Be3)
Center pawn capture opens lines/squares against own uncastled king (exd4 x2)
Piece leaves key central square, abandoning square control that prevented enemy piece activity (e5, Nc5)
Piece moves from critical attacking position, missing forced tactical continuation (Nxe3 missing mate)
Developing a piece while ignoring immediate tactical vulnerability of f7 or king position (Bf5, Qc7)

analysis.label: Moves that abandon a piece's essential defensive function in positions with exposed kings requiring precise defense, allowing immediate tactical exploitation.
analysis.description: In all 8 positions, the player makes a plausible-looking move that fatally abandons a critical defensive responsibility in a position with very few good options (avg 1.4). In 6/8 cases, king safety is the primary concern with already-exposed kings. The pattern manifests as: king moving away from defending a key piece (Kh2 abandons Rf2 defense, Position 13), king retreating to a trapped corner (Ka1 in Position 14, Kh8 in Position 2), a piece leaving its dominant defensive outpost for a seemingly aggressive but toothless square (Ng4 abandoning f2 in Positions 5-6, Qb4 abandoning kingside defense in Position 8), pawn shield self-destruction (f5 in Position 1), or passive retreat when active counterplay was the only resource (Qh3 in Position 15). In every case, the position demanded the one precise defensive move that maintained a specific function, and the player chose a natural-looking alternative that collapsed the entire defensive structure.
analysis.move_pattern: Any piece type moving away from a square where it performs a critical defensive function (guarding a piece, shielding the king, controlling an escape route, or maintaining active counterplay)
analysis.why_bad: Each move removes the one element holding the position together—whether it's a piece defending another piece, a knight on a dominant restrictive outpost, a pawn shielding the king, or a queen providing active counterplay—allowing the opponent to exploit the newly created vulnerability with forcing moves (checks, captures, mating attacks).
sub_patterns: King moves away from defending a key piece (Kh2 unguards Rf2)
King retreats to trapped corner square (Ka1, Kh8)
Piece abandons dominant outpost for aggressive-looking but empty square (Ng4 leaving f2)
Queen moves far from king when defensive coverage is essential (Qb4)
Pawn push destroys own king shield under pressure (f5)
Passive queen retreat when only active counterplay holds equality (Qh3)

analysis.label: Moves that actively worsen one's own position by blocking escape routes, removing defenders from critical posts, or creating self-blocking pawn structures in narrow positions where only 1-2 moves maintain the evaluation.
analysis.description: This feature fires on moves where the player makes a seemingly purposeful move that catastrophically fails to address the single most critical requirement of the position, often by actively self-restricting. In 4/11 cases, a pawn push creates a fatal self-block (g5 wastes tempo in a drawn endgame, g3 blocks the king's escape route allowing perpetual check, h2 self-blocks the promotion square against the opponent's king, b3 gifts connected passed pawns). In 5/11 cases, a piece or rook is moved away from a critical defensive post (Rd7 abandons b8 guard allowing promotion+mate, Rh2 abandons the first rank allowing queen infiltration, Rh4 removes the rook from its defensive third-rank position, Rfc1 blocks the queen's retreat trapping it, Kh4 moves the king away from its pawn losing the drawing connection). The positions are characterized by extremely narrow margins (avg 1.9 good moves available) and catastrophic consequences (avg 4499 cp loss), predominantly in endgames (7/11). The common thread is that the played move addresses a secondary concern while neglecting the ONE thing that matters.
analysis.move_pattern: No single geometric direction; mix of pawn pushes (forward), rook lifts (vertical), and king moves (lateral/diagonal) - all moving AWAY from the critical square or zone where the piece/pawn was needed
analysis.why_bad: Each move abandons the single critical defensive function or creates an irreversible self-restriction (blocking escape squares, removing guards from promotion/invasion squares, pushing pawns that self-block) in positions where only 1-2 precise moves maintain the position, and the opponent can immediately exploit the newly created weakness with forcing moves.
sub_patterns: Pawn pushes that block own king escape squares or self-block promotion (g3, h2, g5)
Rook moves that abandon critical defensive rank/file (Rh2, Rh4, Rd7, Rfc1)
King moves to adjacent wrong square losing critical connection (Kh4, Kb3)
Quiet moves that miss the single forcing/capturing continuation (Qd2, b3)

analysis.label: Playing a non-forcing 'improving' move in a position where only one concrete tactical shot maintains the evaluation.
analysis.description: In all 4/4 positions, exactly one good move existed (avg good moves = 1.0), and that move was a concrete, forcing tactical operation—typically a capture or attack with immediate consequences (Nf3 attacking the queen, Nxc6 exploiting a pin, Bxd2 cashing in a threat, Nxf7 as a tactical strike). Instead, the played moves addressed secondary positional concerns: Nb3 and a3 attacked bishops that weren't the priority (2/4), dxc5 grabbed a pawn in the wrong move order (1/4), and Ne4 attempted centralization onto a capturable square while abandoning a crushing attacking post (1/4). In all cases, the position demanded precise concrete action but the player chose a 'logical-looking' move that pursued a lesser goal. The catastrophic average cp_loss of 419 reflects how narrow these critical windows were—once the forcing move was missed, the opponent's counterplay or simple material gain closed the tactical opportunity permanently.
analysis.move_pattern: Knight or pawn moves to non-forcing squares (peripheral or captures of secondary targets) when a piece capture/attack on the primary tactical target was required
analysis.why_bad: These moves address secondary positional concerns (attacking a bishop, grabbing a pawn, centralizing) while ignoring the one forcing tactical operation that the position demands, allowing the opponent to neutralize the threat or win material
sub_patterns: Moving a piece away from defense to attack a peripheral target while king is exposed
Slow pawn push when a decisive capture exploiting a pin/fork exists
Wrong move-order: capturing secondary target before cashing in the primary threat
Centralizing a piece onto a square where it is immediately captured

analysis.label: Natural-looking moves that fail to address the single most critical tactical demand in positions requiring concrete precision.
analysis.description: This feature fires on positions where very few moves are acceptable (avg 2.1 good moves) and the player makes a plausible-looking 'improving' move that overlooks the position's most urgent concrete requirement. In 6/8 cases, the critical factor involves an immediate tactical vulnerability: leaving a pawn undefended (Ke1 abandoning g2, 1/8), wrong capture order giving opponent higher-value recapture (Rxd3 instead of exd3, 1/8), allowing promotion with check by failing to capture the threatening piece (Kd7 instead of Kxe8, 1/8), placing a piece on a tactically vulnerable square (Rd4 attacked by Rf4, 1/8), moving a key piece away before addressing pawn tension (Qc4 before g5/h5, 1/8), and king leaving the critical sector (Kd4 abandoning kingside support, 1/8). The moves all appear natural—centralizing, activating, or repositioning—but each ignores the one concrete issue that demands immediate attention, resulting in catastrophic evaluation swings (avg 1359 cp loss).
analysis.move_pattern: Quiet non-forcing moves (mostly king moves or piece repositions, no checks) in positions with open files, exposed kings, and immediate tactical tension requiring resolution
analysis.why_bad: Each move prioritizes a secondary strategic goal (centralization, piece improvement, general activity) over addressing the position's single most urgent tactical requirement—whether that's defending a hanging piece, preventing a tempo-gaining promotion, stabilizing critical pawn tension, or avoiding a vulnerable square
sub_patterns: King retreating to wrong square that abandons a defensive duty
Piece repositioning that places it on a tactically vulnerable square
Move-order error where a preparatory move must precede the played move
Failing to capture an immediately threatening piece

analysis.label: King (or piece) moves to a square immediately exploitable by a check, fork, or forcing sequence that wins material or forces mate.
analysis.description: This feature fires on moves where a piece—most often the king (6/11 positions)—is placed on a square that falls directly in the attack range of an opponent's piece, enabling an immediate tactical punishment via check or fork. In Position 1, Kb2 steps onto the a-file where Ra2+ deflects the king from defending the bishop. In Position 2, Kc8 allows Ra8+ winning the rook. In Position 6, Ke8 steps into the knight's fork range (Nxd6+). In Position 10, Kf7 enables Qc7+ driving the king into a mating net. The non-king moves share the same mechanism: Ra6 (Position 4) abandons the f6 post allowing Qe5+ check; c3 (Position 9) blocks the queen's interposition path enabling Qa7+ winning the bishop; Rb1 (Position 8) abandons the 7th rank allowing king infiltration via Kh5. In 8/11 cases, the opponent's primary refutation involves a check that exploits the new piece placement. The average cp_loss of 2612 reflects that these moves frequently convert difficult but holdable positions into immediately lost ones.
analysis.move_pattern: King moves to adjacent squares (usually lateral or retreating) that land on files/ranks/diagonals controlled by opponent pieces; secondary pattern of rooks/bishops abandoning squares that shield the king from checks
analysis.why_bad: The destination square is in the direct attack line of an opponent's piece, enabling an immediate check, fork, or forcing sequence that was impossible before the move—the piece was safe on its previous square but walks into a tactical shot
sub_patterns: King moves onto open file where opponent rook delivers check (Kb2, Kc8, Kc2)
King moves onto square controlled by knight fork (Ke8→Nxd6+)
King retreats toward back rank enabling queen check on 7th rank (Kf7→Qc7+)
Piece abandons defensive post exposing king to diagonal/file check (Ra6, c3)
Piece retreats from active position allowing king infiltration (Rb1, Bb3)

analysis.label: Retreating a piece from an active/controlling square to the player's second rank, surrendering critical square control and enabling opponent breakthroughs.
analysis.description: In all 3/3 positions, the player moves a piece backward to their own second rank (Qd2 for White; Qe7 and Nh7 on Black's 7th rank) when active alternatives were essential. In each case, the retreated piece was either already on or needed to reach a square that restrained a critical opponent plan: in Position 2 (Qe7), the queen abandoned b4 where it prevented c4-c5; in Position 3 (Nh7), the knight left f6 where it controlled e4/g4/d5 and prevented g4-g5; in Position 1 (Qd2), the queen went to an unambitious square instead of the aggressive Bg5 that would have exploited a pin. All three moves share the characteristic of prioritizing perceived safety or regrouping over maintaining dynamic tension, and all immediately allow the opponent a pawn breakthrough or tactical sequence (c5, g4-g5, Bxf3/Nd4 fork) that was previously impossible.
analysis.move_pattern: Queen or knight retreating to the player's second rank (d2/e7/h7), moving away from the center or from an active outpost
analysis.why_bad: The piece abandons control of critical squares that were restraining the opponent's key plan, granting a tempo-free breakthrough (pawn advance or tactical sequence) that was previously impossible
sub_patterns: Queen retreating from active outpost to passive second-rank square
Knight retreating from central post to rim/back rank

analysis.label: Seemingly active or purposeful moves that directly create a new tactical weakness the opponent immediately exploits for a devastating blow.
analysis.description: This feature fires on moves that actively enable the opponent's winning tactic — the player's own move is the final ingredient that makes a combination or exploitation work. The played moves look superficially reasonable (a check, a piece 'activation', a development move, a pawn push) but each one specifically creates the tactical condition the opponent exploits: pointless checks that centralize the opponent's king (3/11: Rb3+, Rd5+, and the check-inducing Qg3), king moves that walk into mating patterns or opponent piece diagonals (4/11: Kh5 into Qg4#, Kh3 onto Bd7+ diagonal, Kd6 ignoring promotion, Kd3 retreating passively), pieces abandoning critical defensive posts (2/11: Rd6 leaving back rank, Ne2 uncovering e3 fork), and moves that open fatal lines (2/11: f3 opening a7-g1 diagonal, Qh3 overextending). In every case, the position BEFORE the move lacked the tactical vulnerability that exists AFTER it — the player's own action is what 'turns on' the opponent's combination.
analysis.move_pattern: Various piece types moving to tactically exploitable squares or away from critical defensive posts; often king moves to vulnerable squares, rook/queen moves that look active but abandon key duties, or pawn/piece moves that open lines for the opponent
analysis.why_bad: Each move creates a specific new tactical vulnerability that didn't previously exist — whether placing the king on a matable/checkable square, removing a piece from a critical defensive function, or opening a line that the opponent's pieces immediately exploit for a decisive combination
sub_patterns: Pointless checks that improve opponent's king position
King walking onto opponent's piece diagonal or into mating net
Piece abandoning critical defensive post (back rank, key square control)
Pawn/piece move opening fatal line for opponent's bishop/queen
Active-looking queen moves to exploitable squares

analysis.label: Moves that catastrophically weaken the player's own position by destroying king pawn shelter or ignoring the single most urgent positional/tactical demand.
analysis.description: This feature fires on moves that appear superficially reasonable but catastrophically compromise the player's position. The dominant sub-pattern (5/8 positions: f6, f4, fxe3, g3, and Kf2) involves moves that weaken the king's protective pawn structure, typically by advancing or capturing with f/g pawns that open critical diagonals (a2-g8, a7-g1, a8-h1) directly toward one's own king. In positions 1, 2, and 12, the f or g pawn's departure immediately exposed a lethal diagonal for the opponent's bishop or queen check. The remaining positions (b3, Qe8, Qh6) share the broader pattern of making a 'normal-looking' move that completely ignores the position's most urgent single requirement—addressing a fork threat, blockading a passed pawn, or executing a winning tactical idea. All 8 positions share critically low good-move counts (avg 2.0), meaning these were narrow decision points requiring precision, and in every case the player chose a move that allowed the opponent an immediate, concrete, devastating response.
analysis.move_pattern: Primarily kingside pawn advances (f or g pawns) moving away from the king, plus passive piece moves (queen retreats, king steps) that ignore the critical threat; all are non-forcing, self-weakening moves
analysis.why_bad: These moves destroy the player's own defensive structure (usually the king's pawn shield) or waste a critical tempo, allowing the opponent an immediate tactical blow—typically a diagonal check/attack, a fork, or a decisive pawn advance that was previously prevented
sub_patterns: f-pawn or g-pawn advance opening diagonal toward own king (f6, f4, fxe3, g3)
Passive move ignoring the position's single most urgent tactical threat (b3, Qe8, Kf2)
Queen relocation to peripheral square abandoning critical central/tactical role (Qe8, Qh6)

analysis.label: Non-urgent quiet moves played when the position demands immediate concrete action to address central tension or tactical opportunities.
analysis.description: This feature activates on positions where a player makes a quiet, non-forcing move (or wrong forcing move) while the position has an urgent concrete demand that goes unaddressed. In 5/7 positions, the center is closed or semi-closed with critical unresolved tension. The most common pattern is flank pawn pushes (h3, h6) or piece repositioning moves (Bf4, Rb8) when the position requires stabilizing the center (positions 1, 2, 6), capturing free material (position 3), or executing the precise tactical sequence (position 4). The punishments consistently exploit the lost tempo: opponents strike at the unresolved tension (c4 breaks, f6 winning a knight, dxc5 grabbing a pawn, Bxg2 counterattack). Position 5 (dxc4) is a variant where the player makes a pawn capture that actively destroys their own central support structure. In 4/7 positions, a king remains uncastled in the center, amplifying the cost of tempo loss. The feature captures the pattern of playing 'looks useful' moves that serve secondary purposes (preventing Bg5, activating a rook on a quiet file, repositioning a bishop) while missing that the position's concrete demands are time-critical.
analysis.move_pattern: Quiet non-forcing moves (pawn pushes to h-file, piece retreats/repositioning, passive rook development) or imprecise forcing moves in positions with unresolved central tension
analysis.why_bad: The lost tempo allows the opponent to exploit unresolved central tension or tactical vulnerabilities—typically via pawn breaks (c4, f6, dxc5, dxe4) that either win material, destroy the player's center, or open lines against an uncastled king
sub_patterns: Flank pawn pushes (h3/h6) instead of central development
Piece repositioning instead of stabilizing center or grabbing material
Wrong check/capture direction missing the precise tactical solution
Pawn capture that undermines own central pawn structure

analysis.label: Passive pawn or piece moves on the g/h-file when the position demands immediate forcing action elsewhere.
analysis.description: All three positions feature quiet, non-forcing moves on the kingside (h6, Ng3, g3) when the position urgently demanded tactical solutions. In 3/3 cases, the best move was a forcing/capturing option: counterattacking pawn advances (c5/b5 in position 8), a piece-eliminating capture (exf4 in position 9), or winning a hanging piece (Bxc5 in position 12). Instead, the player chose a slow move on the g/h-file area—two of which literally involve the g3 square—that addressed no immediate threat and allowed the opponent to consolidate or seize the initiative. The average cp_loss of 331 reflects how catastrophic a single tempo loss can be when the position is tactically critical.
analysis.move_pattern: Quiet pawn push or piece placement on g3/h6 (kingside g/h-file area), non-capture, non-check
analysis.why_bad: These moves waste critical tempo on slow prophylactic or repositioning ideas when the position demands immediate forcing action (captures, counterattacks, or addressing hanging pieces), allowing the opponent to resolve threats or seize the initiative.
sub_patterns: Prophylactic h6/g3 pawn push ignoring counterplay urgency
Passive piece retreat to g3 when captures eliminate threats
Positional pawn move missing a hanging piece capture

analysis.label: Executing the correct plan one move too early—before a necessary preparatory/prophylactic move—allowing the opponent a tempo-gaining tactical response.
analysis.description: In 5/6 positions, the played move is explicitly part of the best continuation but executed in the wrong sequence, skipping a crucial preparatory step. The analyses tag 'tempo_loss' in 5/6 cases and 'move_order' in 3/6. Position 1: c5 before b4 lets the rook capture on b4. Position 2: f5 before Kf5 creates an intermediate check after gxf6+. Position 7: Ke4 before Ke2 allows f5+ with tempo. Position 11: Rxb6 before Kf2 leaves the king exposed to Rxe3+ after d4. Position 14: cxb5 removes a structural pawn before securing king safety, opening the c-file. Position 6: Ke5 instead of Ke4 allows Rc5+ or free capture of h2. In each case, the player identified the correct strategic goal (advance pawns, centralize king, capture material) but failed to first complete a quiet prophylactic move that would deny the opponent a tempo-gaining reply (check, capture, or breakthrough).
analysis.move_pattern: Forward-moving actions (pawn advances, king centralization toward center, captures of enemy pawns) that skip a quiet preparatory king retreat or different move-order sequence
analysis.why_bad: By acting aggressively before completing a necessary preparatory step, the player gifts the opponent a tempo-gaining response—typically a check, a capture with check, or a pawn break with check—that accelerates the opponent's counterplay by exactly the one tempo that the preparatory move would have denied.
sub_patterns: Pawn advance before king relocation (f5/c5 before Kf5/Kf2)
King centralization into check (Ke4/Ke5 walking into f5+/Rc5+)
Material capture before securing king safety (Rxb6/cxb5 before prophylaxis)

analysis.label: Black plays a non-forcing, peripheral move (usually a pawn push) when the position demands immediate tactical or developmental action.
analysis.description: In 6/6 positions, Black plays a quiet, non-urgent move while a critical threat or opportunity demands immediate attention. In 4/6 cases the move is a slow pawn push (a6, b6, d6, a5), and the remaining cases involve peripheral actions (Rxb2 pawn grab, Bd4 to wrong square). The consistent pattern is that Black's position requires urgency—whether exploiting an exposed enemy king (position 1), developing pieces before castling (positions 3, 11), controlling a critical square in a pawn race (position 7), defending against a kingside attack (positions 12, 13)—yet Black instead plays a preparatory or non-forcing move that wastes a critical tempo. The tag 'tempo_loss' appears in all 6 analyses, and 'development' or 'piece_activity' appears in 5/6. The refutations consistently show the opponent exploiting the wasted tempo to execute a concrete plan: capturing a now-trapped piece (position 1), launching a king attack (positions 3, 12, 13), advancing passed pawns (position 7), or winning material via fork (position 11).
analysis.move_pattern: Non-forcing moves, predominantly queenside pawn advances (a- and b-file) or peripheral captures, played when central/kingside action is critical
analysis.why_bad: Wastes a decisive tempo in positions requiring immediate action—allowing opponents to execute tactical strikes, consolidate against threats, advance passed pawns, or exploit undefended pieces that the slow move fails to address
sub_patterns: Preparatory pawn push (a6/b6/a5) when piece development or king safety is urgent
Peripheral pawn grab (Rxb2) abandoning defensive duties around the king
Piece placement to suboptimal square (Bd4) losing critical tempo in a race
Passive central pawn move (d6) leaving hanging piece undefended

analysis.label: Playing a plausible-looking move that addresses a secondary concern while ignoring the single most urgent tactical or strategic demand of the position.
analysis.description: In all 9 positions, the player chose a move that has a reasonable strategic justification on the surface but completely fails to address the position's most pressing, concrete need. In 7/9 cases, the position had only 1-2 good moves available (avg 1.7), signaling that the position was demanding a very specific response. The blunders include: attacking a piece when development was critical (h6, g4, b5), playing a flank pawn when king activity was the sole priority (a3), weakening the king when active defense was required (g3), blockading a pawn passively when captures were urgent (Rd8), capturing in the center while ignoring an embedded enemy piece (dxe5), developing a bishop instead of the only correct capture (Bd2), and giving a flashy check instead of delivering mate (Nd4+). In 8/9 cases the 'ignored demand' relates to king safety, development, or an immediate tactical threat. The average centipawn loss of 2350 reflects catastrophic consequences from a single tempo wasted on the wrong priority.
analysis.move_pattern: No single geometric pattern; moves span pawn pushes (5/9 flank pawns), piece development, captures, and checks — all 'reasonable-looking' but addressing a non-critical target
analysis.why_bad: Each move wastes the one critical tempo the position affords by addressing a secondary concern (chasing a piece, attacking a pawn, developing passively) while the position has exactly one urgent demand — typically an immediate mating threat, a forced tactical sequence, or a race-critical tempo that cannot be deferred.
sub_patterns: Flank pawn push ignoring development/king safety (h6, g4, b5, a3, g3)
Passive piece placement ignoring concrete tactical urgency (Rd8, Bd2)
Tempting capture that ignores the real positional crisis (dxe5)
Flashy check that misses forced checkmate (Nd4+)

analysis.label: Quiet piece repositioning that removes a key defender from its post, leaving material or the king tactically vulnerable to immediate exploitation.
analysis.description: In 5/5 positions, the player makes a non-forcing 'improving' move that appears to reposition a piece to a better square, but catastrophically overlooks an immediate tactical consequence. In 3/5 cases (Qd8, Ne4, Kg8), the moved piece was the sole defender of a critical target: Qd8 abandoned defense of c6, Ne4 left d5 unguarded, and Kg8 exposed the d7 bishop to a check sequence. In 1/5 cases (Ba4), the piece moved directly to a square where it hangs to a knight capture. In 1/5 cases (Qc2), the queen retreated passively when an immediate tactical strike was the only way to maintain the advantage, surrendering the initiative. All moves share the characteristic of being quiet repositioning attempts in positions requiring tactical alertness, with the opponent punishing via simple captures or forcing check sequences (4/5 involve hanging_piece or tempo_loss motifs). The average cp_loss of 233 and average of only 1.8 good alternatives confirm these are critical positions with narrow defensive paths where 'improving' moves prove fatal.
analysis.move_pattern: Any piece type moving to a new square in a non-capturing, non-checking repositioning move (retreat or sideways shift), typically away from the piece's current defensive responsibilities
analysis.why_bad: The moved piece was the sole or critical defender of a target (pawn, piece, or king square), and the quiet repositioning allows the opponent to immediately exploit the undefended material with captures, tempo-gaining attacks, or forcing check sequences that win material.
sub_patterns: Queen retreats from defending a weak pawn, allowing immediate capture
Knight moves to aggressive square, abandoning pawn it was guarding
Bishop repositions to undefended square capturable by enemy piece
King moves into tactical vulnerability instead of offering simplifying trade
Queen plays passive move when only an immediate tactical strike maintains advantage

analysis.label: Moving a piece away from an essential defensive duty to a superficially attractive square, allowing the opponent to immediately exploit the vacated function.
analysis.description: In all 5 positions, the blunder involves relocating a piece (or pawn) that was performing an irreplaceable structural or defensive role. In Position 2, Bh3 removes the bishop from f1, exposing e2/f1 squares and enabling a mating attack (5/5 abandon a function). In Position 4, Ne4 moves the knight from c3, the only piece that could recapture on a3, leaving a pawn hanging (5/5 opponent exploits immediately). In Position 10, f5 advances the pawn that was shielding the king and dark squares, allowing Nd6+ with check (5/5 weakens own position). In Position 11, Bc5 abandons the d6 blockade of a passed pawn, permitting the crushing d6 advance (5/5 cosmetic improvement over necessity). In Position 14, Qc2 retreats the queen to a passive square where it becomes a target for Bf5 tempo gains, abandoning active central duty (5/5 opponent gains tempo). All moves share the pattern of prioritizing superficial piece improvement while ignoring an essential positional responsibility.
analysis.move_pattern: Any piece type moving away from a square where it performs a critical guard/blockade/shield function, typically toward a seemingly active but ultimately ineffective square
analysis.why_bad: The piece was performing an irreplaceable defensive function (blockading a passed pawn, guarding a weak square, shielding the king, covering a recapture), and its relocation allows the opponent to immediately exploit the newly undefended weakness or advance a now-unblocked threat.
sub_patterns: Bishop abandoning king cover to an open diagonal (Bh3)
Knight leaving a guard square for a central post without resolving tension first (Ne4)
Pawn advance weakening own king to attack an enemy piece that has a superior destination (f5)
Bishop vacating a blockade square for superficial diagonal activity (Bc5)
Queen retreating from active duty to a passive square that becomes a tempo target (Qc2)

analysis.label: Piece relocated to a plausible square while ignoring an immediate tactical vulnerability that the opponent can exploit with checks, pins, or invasions.
analysis.description: This feature fires on moves where a player makes a 'reasonable-looking' piece relocation—developing, centralizing, capturing material, or consolidating—that fatally neglects an urgent tactical reality. In 6/8 positions, the refutation involves a concrete tactical blow (pin on an open file/diagonal in positions 1 and 2, pawn capture with check in position 5, knight attack on f7 in position 8, mating attack via Re6+ in position 14, and rook invasion in position 7). In 7/8 cases, the best moves shared a common theme of addressing the concrete defensive need BEFORE or INSTEAD of the 'logical' piece improvement. The positions all feature very few good moves available (avg 1.8), indicating high tactical tension requiring precise calculation rather than general principles. The moved piece either ends up creating a new geometric vulnerability (self-pin, self-block, diagonal alignment) or abandons a critical defensive role, allowing the opponent's already-existing tactical threats to materialize.
analysis.move_pattern: Various piece types (knight 4x, queen 3x, king 1x) moved to seemingly logical squares (development, centralization, material capture) that either block own pieces' defensive lines, create pin alignments, or abandon critical defensive coordination
analysis.why_bad: The move prioritizes general chess logic (development, centralization, material gain) over addressing an urgent concrete tactical threat, either creating a new exploitable alignment (pin, self-block) or removing a piece from a critical defensive function while the opponent has immediate tactical resources available
sub_patterns: Knight moved to natural square ignoring opponent's tactical strike (Nc6, Nf3)
Piece placed on line creating pin vulnerability (Qd2, Kf8)
Piece moved away from defensive zone allowing invasion (Nb6, Na7)
Material captured while king is tactically exposed (Qxf7)

analysis.label: Choosing a plausible-looking active piece move while missing the one critical tactical requirement of the position.
analysis.description: This feature fires on positions where very few good moves exist (avg 1.6) and the player selects a superficially active or purposeful move instead of the one concrete tactical solution. In 5/7 cases, the correct move involved a specific capture or check that exploited a tactical feature (pin exploitation in Nxe4, check sequence in Qa5+, correct capture direction in dxe4, tempo-gaining check in the endgame, knight maneuver threatening the king in Ne4). The played moves instead reposition pieces to 'active-looking' squares (Qf6 centralizing, Qd5 centralizing without check, Rd4 'controlling' the open file, Ng4 looking aggressive, Qb4 seeking queenside counterplay) while completely ignoring the critical tactical requirement. The result is catastrophic: 6/7 positions show enormous eval swings (avg 1518cp), with the common thread being that the position demanded one precise tactical response but the player was seduced by a move that appeared purposeful on general principles.
analysis.move_pattern: Piece repositioning to apparently active central or attacking squares (especially queen moves to open files/diagonals or knight/rook to central squares) instead of making the critical capture or check
analysis.why_bad: These moves waste the critical tempo needed to exploit a specific tactical feature (pin, exposed king, check sequence, or hanging material), allowing the opponent to consolidate, reposition defensively, or launch their own devastating tactical response
sub_patterns: Queen moving away from critical defensive duties (Qf6, Qb4)
Piece retreating/repositioning when a tactical capture was available (Ng4 instead of Nxe4, dxc4 instead of dxe4)
Centralizing without check when checks win material (Qd5 instead of Qa5+)
Placing piece on target square giving opponent tempo (Rd4 allowing c5)

analysis.label: Pieces or kings placed on apparently logical squares that are immediately exploitable through open files, diagonals, or pawn breaks.
analysis.description: This feature fires on moves that appear strategically sound—occupying a central outpost, retreating toward safety, capturing material—but actually place a piece or king on a square where the opponent can immediately exploit open lines or create them. In 5/7 positions, the moved piece lands on or near the d-file (Kd7, Kd6, Nd5, exd4, Qxe5) where open or easily-opened lines create devastating tactical targets. In 6/7 cases, the refutation involves exploiting an open file, diagonal, or pawn break that the move either created or failed to address (e5 break against Kd7, Rxe6+/Rd1+ against Kd6, Bxb7 along the long diagonal against Nb7, f4 break after exd4). The positions are extremely demanding with an average of only 1.9 good moves available, and the played moves represent natural-looking but imprecise choices where calculation of concrete open-line tactics was required.
analysis.move_pattern: Piece or king moves to central or semi-central square (especially d-file: d4-d7 range), captures in center, or pawn moves that open/fail to block critical lines
analysis.why_bad: The target square sits on an open file, unguarded diagonal, or line that becomes opened by a forcing pawn break, allowing the opponent to immediately exploit the placement with tactical blows (checks, captures, deflections) along those lines
sub_patterns: King walking into open d-file (Kd7, Kd6)
Knight/piece jumping to square immediately captured along open line (Nd5, Nb7)
Pawn capture removing structural barrier enabling opponent's pawn break (exd4, c3)
Queen capture in center enabling forced simplification (Qxe5)

analysis.label: Moving a piece to a seemingly attractive square while abandoning its sole responsibility for defending against the opponent's primary threat.
analysis.description: This feature fires when a player moves a piece away from a square where it was performing a critical (often sole) defensive function—guarding a passed pawn's advance path, defending a hanging piece, or covering mating squares—to a square that appears active or centralized but is functionally irrelevant to the position's main threat. In 5/8 positions, the abandoned duty involved stopping a passed pawn from promoting (Nd3×2 left h-pawn unguarded, Kc5 moved past the c-pawn, Bd3 blocked the king's path to intercept g/f pawns, Kd7 overshot the optimal blockade zone). In 1/8 positions (Nf1), the piece was the sole defender of a pawn that immediately hung. In 1/8 positions (Qb4), the queen was the sole kingside defensive piece and its departure allowed immediate checkmate. The moved piece typically lands on a square that looks centralized, active, or thematic (d3 appears three times as a 'strong central post'), but the concrete calculation reveals the original square's defensive function was irreplaceable.
analysis.move_pattern: Piece (any type) moves away from a square controlling/blockading the opponent's primary threat, typically toward the center or an apparently active square, without capture or check
analysis.why_bad: The piece was the sole defender against the position's dominant threat (usually a passed pawn advance or mating attack). Its departure allows the threat to proceed unchecked, typically resulting in unstoppable promotion or immediate checkmate because no other piece can substitute for the defensive function in time.
sub_patterns: Knight retreats from pawn-blockading square to 'active' central square (Nd3 from f4)
King advances past a passed pawn instead of maintaining blockade (Kc5 past c4-pawn)
Piece moves away from sole defense of a hanging pawn or mating zone (Nf1 from d2, Qb4 from d6)
Bishop/King placed on square that blocks own escape routes while creating tactical targets (Bd3, Kd7)

analysis.label: Moving a major piece to an a/b-file square that abandons king defense or walks into a tactical vulnerability.
analysis.description: In all 3/3 positions, the player moves a major piece (queen or rook) to the a-file or b-file in the queenside area (Qb6, Qa8, Rb2) while the king is exposed and under threat. In 2/3 cases the queen relocates to a remote queenside square (a8, b6) far from where defensive action is needed, leaving the king fatally unprotected. In 3/3 cases the piece ends up either hanging directly (Qa8 hangs to a rook, Rb2 hangs to a knight on d3) or becomes strategically useless (Qb6 can no longer cover f6 or the d-file). All positions feature an exposed king (h2 or e8) that requires immediate defensive attention, and all moves ignore this urgency in favor of perceived queenside activity or counterplay that never materializes.
analysis.move_pattern: Major piece (Queen or Rook) moves laterally or diagonally to a-file or b-file square on the rim, away from king and central action
analysis.why_bad: The piece abandons critical defensive duties around the exposed king and/or lands on a square that is tactically controlled by enemy pieces, allowing immediate material gain or mating attacks against the undefended king.
sub_patterns: Queen relocates to far queenside corner abandoning king defense
Rook moves to b-file square attacked by enemy knight
Major piece leaves critical file/diagonal unguarded

analysis.label: King (or key defender) moves to a square that creates an immediate tactical vulnerability—check, fork, or mating pattern—that didn't exist on the previous square.
analysis.description: In 8/10 positions the played move is a king move, and in the remaining 2 cases the move either exposes the king (fxe5 opening the f-file) or abandons its defense (Qc3 leaving king unshielded). The universal pattern is that the player has exactly 1 good option (avg good moves = 1.0) but chooses a square that looks safe yet is immediately punishable by a tactical shot: Kh2 allows Ng4+ (3/10 involve knight checks/forks on the new king square), Kc1/Ke1 walk into back-rank or mating nets (3/10), Kb7/Ke7 place the king on a diagonal or file allowing queen checks with tempo gain (2/10), and Kh8/Qc3 forfeit critical tempo allowing the opponent to consolidate or force perpetual (2/10). The consistently enormous cp_loss (avg 3050) reflects that these positions sit on a knife's edge where only one precise move survives, and the chosen square introduces a concrete, often forcing tactical refutation.
analysis.move_pattern: King move (or king-exposing move) to an adjacent square that places it on a line, diagonal, or knight-attack square where an immediate check or fork is available
analysis.why_bad: The destination square is directly attacked or exploitable by an opponent's piece (especially knights delivering check-forks, or queens/rooks delivering checks along newly opened or exposed lines), creating forced sequences that win material or deliver mate—the previous square did not have this vulnerability.
sub_patterns: King moves to square in knight-check range, allowing fork winning material (Kh2/Ng4+, Kf2/Nh3+, Ke1/Nxf3+)
King moves to back rank or mating corridor, enabling mating nets (Kc1, Ke1, Ke7)
King moves onto diagonal or file allowing queen check with tempo/material gain (Kb7/Qxe4+, Ke7/Qxd7+)
Move exposes king by opening lines or abandoning defensive coverage, enabling perpetual or mate (fxe5 opens f-file, Qc3 abandons e-file shield)
Passive king retreat wastes tempo in critical position, allowing opponent to capture key pieces (Kh8 loses bishop)

analysis.label: Natural-looking moves that catastrophically ignore the position's central king safety crisis, whether defending one's own king or exploiting the opponent's exposed king.
analysis.description: This feature fires on moves that appear reasonable on the surface (rook repositioning, pawn captures, material gains, defensive placements) but critically fail to address the most urgent tactical element in the position—always related to king safety. In 6/6 positions, king vulnerability is explicitly flagged (weak pawn shields, exposed kings, back rank issues). The blunders share a pattern of choosing secondary objectives over the primary king safety imperative: Ra1 and Rf2 are passive rook moves when immediate forcing attacks were available (2/6); Nxb3 and exd4 grab material while ignoring tactical threats to the king or from the king's exposure (2/6); e4 removes a critical defensive pawn shield opening a check diagonal (1/6); Bg7 self-blocks the king's escape route creating a mating net (1/6). All positions had very few good moves available (avg 2.2), indicating critical moments where only precise king-safety-aware play survived. The refutations in 5/6 cases directly exploit king exposure (checks, forks targeting king, mating nets).
analysis.move_pattern: Various piece types and directions; no geometric consistency. Moves include rook-to-corner, pawn captures, knight captures on rim, central pawn advances, rook-to-second-rank, bishop-to-fianchetto.
analysis.why_bad: Each move ignores the position's dominant tactical theme (king safety) in favor of a secondary goal—material gain, slow improvement, or seemingly solid defense—giving the opponent time or means to exploit the exposed king via checks, forks, pawn storms, or mating nets.
sub_patterns: Passive rook repositioning when immediate forcing counterplay is required against own vulnerable king
Material-grabbing captures that ignore tactical threats exploiting king exposure (forks, double attacks)
Pawn advances that remove critical defensive shields, opening diagonals for checks
Piece placement that self-blocks the king's escape squares, enabling mating nets

analysis.label: Playing a non-forcing preparatory or repositioning move when the position demands immediate, direct action (typically a pawn advance, correct attacking continuation, or maintaining a well-placed piece).
analysis.description: This feature fires on positions where a player chooses a quiet, indirect move—often a king repositioning, piece retreat, or non-urgent action—when the position requires an immediate forcing move. The 'tempo_loss' tag appears in 10/11 positions analyzed. In endgame cases (5/11), the error typically involves moving the king when a pawn push was urgent (positions 1, 5, 6, 9—where e3, h5, or Ra3 were needed before king movement). In middlegame/opening cases (6/11), the error involves repositioning a piece away from its optimal post (Qd3 abandoning e2's defensive duties, Qe6+ using the wrong piece, Qf5+ leaving the winning h7 square, Ne2 abandoning d5 control, Bxg6 removing a paralyzing piece from f7, f3 blocking Nf3 development). The common thread is choosing a move that appears reasonable or preparatory but surrenders a critical tempo that the opponent exploits to equalize, defend, or seize the initiative.
analysis.move_pattern: Diverse piece types (king moves 5/11, queen moves 3/11, knight/bishop/pawn 1 each) making non-forcing repositioning moves—typically sideways, backward, or to a less effective square—instead of advancing pawns or maintaining attacking piece placement.
analysis.why_bad: The move wastes a tempo that the opponent uses to either (1) gain checking/forcing opportunities that negate the move (e.g., Rh7+ after Kh2), (2) undermine the position with counterplay (e.g., ...c6 after f3, ...Qg5 after Qd3), or (3) escape tactical threats that were imminent (e.g., Kd8 escaping after Qe6+ instead of Be6+). The position demanded urgency but received passivity.
sub_patterns: King move before critical pawn advance in endgames
Queen/piece repositioning that abandons defensive or attacking duties
Capture that removes a well-placed piece from a dominant post
Non-developing pawn move that blocks piece coordination

analysis.label: Moves that displace a piece away from the vulnerable king or place the king in an exposed position, allowing immediate tactical punishment against the undefended monarch.
analysis.description: This feature fires on moves where a player neglects their king's safety in favor of some other goal (material gain, piece repositioning, or passive defense). In 9/11 positions, king_safety is the primary tactical motif exploited. The most common pattern involves moving a major piece (especially the queen) far from the king to grab material (Qxa7, Qxb6) or to pursue misguided positional goals (Qc3, Rf7×3), while the opponent's pieces are already aimed at the exposed monarch. Two positions feature castling directly into an opponent's prepared attack (O-O-O×2), one features walking the king to a tactically vulnerable square (Kf5 allowing Rb5+ skewer), and one features a passive developing move instead of urgently evacuating the king (Rh1 instead of Kg2). The punishment typically involves immediate checks, mating attacks, or tactical shots exploiting undefended squares that the displaced piece previously covered.
analysis.move_pattern: Major piece (queen or rook) moves to distant file (a/b/f-file) away from king, OR king moves/castles to exposed position lacking defenders
analysis.why_bad: The moves abandon defensive coverage of the king at a critical moment when the opponent's pieces are already positioned to attack; the opponent immediately exploits the unguarded squares, open files, or check opportunities that the displaced defender previously prevented.
sub_patterns: Queen captures distant pawn on a/b-file, stranding it far from kingside defense (Qxa7, Qxb6)
Queen or rook moves away from kingside, unguarding critical squares/pawns near the king (Qc3 unguards h5, Rf7 loses tempo)
Castling into the opponent's prepared pawn-break attack on that wing (O-O-O into ...c5 or Rc1 attacks)
King walks to exposed square allowing check+skewer or mating net (Kf5 allowing Rb5+)
Passive piece move instead of urgently addressing king exposure (Rh1 instead of Kg2)

analysis.label: Playing consolidating or aimless moves in positions requiring immediate tactical exploitation, wasting a critical tempo.
analysis.description: All three positions feature White possessing a dynamic, time-sensitive advantage (active pieces, exposed enemy king, or tactical opportunities) but choosing a move that looks strategically reasonable while ignoring the concrete tactical demands. In 3/3 cases, the position had a narrow window for exploitation: Position 1 required capturing material with Bxf5 before the Bd7 could be challenged; Position 4 required activating via the h3-c8 diagonal before Black's king reached safety; Position 6 required Nc2 to prepare Ke3 winning the knight. Instead, the played moves (f3 consolidating structure, Qc6+ a purposeless check, Kc3 'centralizing' the king) all waste the critical tempo.
