In 3/3 cases the opponent immediately seizes the initiative: Black targets the Bd7 in Position 1, forces favorable simplification in Position 4, and executes a knight fork in Position 6. All three are tagged with 'tempo_loss' and 'missed_tactic.'
analysis.move_pattern: Various piece types (pawn, queen, king); non-engaging moves that don't directly attack opponent's key pieces or exploit concrete tactical shots
analysis.why_bad: The position demands immediate tactical action to cash in on a fleeting advantage, but the move wastes the crucial tempo, allowing the opponent to neutralize threats or create counterplay that permanently swings the evaluation
sub_patterns: Passive pawn pushes ignoring active piece captures
Speculative checks that improve opponent's king placement
King centralizations walking into tactical vulnerabilities

analysis.label: Playing routine-looking moves (captures, development, checks) that fatally ignore the position's one urgent tactical priority.
analysis.description: This feature activates on moves that appear natural or automatic but catastrophically miss the position's critical tactical requirement. In 4/7 positions, the move is a reflexive pawn capture on the kingside (hxg5, gxh4, hxg4) that opens files or diagonals against the player's own king, directly enabling devastating attacks (queen sacrifices with discovered checks, rook invasions on the h-file). In 2/7 positions, the move is a slow 'developing' move (Rac8, Bg7) played when the position screamed for immediate tactical action (defending a hanging piece, striking at g2 with Bh3). In 1/7 positions, a purposeless check (Ra2+) gifts the opponent tempo to execute a crushing knight maneuver. The common thread across all positions is that the player chose the 'obvious' or 'automatic' response without recognizing that the position had one specific critical demand—whether defensive (protect the d7 bishop, block the b1-h7 diagonal) or offensive (attack g2 immediately)—and the best moves were always concrete, position-specific solutions addressing that exact demand.
analysis.move_pattern: Mixed piece types: predominantly h/g-pawn captures toward the kingside, plus quiet piece moves (rook lifts, bishop development) when forcing moves were required
analysis.why_bad: These moves ignore the position's single most urgent tactical requirement—whether it's a hanging piece, an open diagonal enabling a sacrifice, or a time-critical attacking window—allowing the opponent to execute a concrete punishment that was only possible because the critical demand went unaddressed.
sub_patterns: Reflexive kingside pawn captures that open files/diagonals against own king (hxg5, gxh4, hxg4)
Slow development or rook moves when immediate tactical strikes are available (Rac8, Bg7)
Pointless checks that gift the opponent a crucial tempo for regrouping (Ra2+)

analysis.label: Knight captures a centralized piece on d4/d5/e4/e5, allowing a pawn recapture that forks or double-attacks two remaining pieces.
analysis.description: In 12/12 positions, the player captures a well-placed enemy piece on a central square (e5, d5, e4, or d4) with a knight, but the resulting pawn recapture creates a devastating fork or double attack on two other pieces still on the board. The most common sub-pattern (seen in 9/12 cases) involves Nxe5 or Nxd5 where the recapturing d-pawn or e-pawn simultaneously attacks a bishop on d6/e6/e7 and a knight on f6/c6. In virtually every case (10/12), the correct alternative was to capture with a BISHOP instead of the knight—because the bishop capture removes one of the fork targets from the board before the pawn advances—or to avoid the capture entirely. The positions typically feature closed centers in the opening phase with both players having multiple minor pieces developed around the central squares, creating the geometric conditions for the pawn fork to hit two targets at once.
analysis.move_pattern: Knight captures inward onto a central square (e4/e5/d4/d5), always a capture, replacing the taken piece on that square where a pawn recapture radiates diagonally to hit two adjacent pieces.
analysis.why_bad: The knight capture vacates a supporting square and leaves two other friendly pieces (typically a bishop on an adjacent diagonal and a knight on a neighboring file) simultaneously vulnerable to the recapturing pawn's dual attack. Capturing with the bishop instead would remove one fork target from the board before the pawn advances.
sub_patterns: Nc6xe5 allowing dxe5 forking Bd6 and Nf6 (6 positions)
Nf6xd5 allowing exd5 attacking Be6 and Nc6 (3 positions)
Nd2xe4 allowing dxe4/fxe4 attacking Bd3 and Nf3 (2 positions)
Nf3xd4 allowing exd4 winning material through advancing pawn (1 position)

analysis.label: Moves that closely resemble the best available move but differ in one critical dimension—wrong piece, wrong square, or wrong timing—turning a winning idea into a blunder.
analysis.description: In 5/7 positions, the move played shares a key attribute with the best move: same destination square but wrong piece (Ra6 vs Qa6, Rxb4+ vs Qxb4+), same piece but wrong target square (Qe2+ vs Qh1#, Rxg3 vs Rxe7), or same file involvement but preparation instead of execution (Rdh1 vs Rxh4). The remaining cases (f4 vs e5, Be7 vs Re1) show a thematically adjacent but fatally flawed variation of the correct plan. The player consistently identifies the correct idea—the right square to target, the right piece to use, or the right file to contest—but makes one critical selection error in execution. These are not random blunders; they represent positions where the player is cognitively 'adjacent' to the solution but picks the wrong variant from a set of similar-looking candidates.
analysis.move_pattern: Diverse piece types and directions, but each move mirrors the best move's geometry with one critical substitution (wrong piece for same capture/square, wrong square for same piece, preparation instead of immediate execution)
analysis.why_bad: The move fails because the one dimension that differs from the best move is precisely what makes the tactic work—the queen covers escape squares that the rook doesn't (Rxb4+ vs Qxb4#), the correct square delivers mate while the played square merely checks (Qe2+ vs Qh1#), or immediate action was required rather than preparation (Rdh1 vs Rxh4). The 'almost right' quality makes these especially costly because the player was on the right track but chose the wrong fork at the critical decision point.
sub_patterns: Wrong piece to correct square (Ra6/Qa6, Rxb4+/Qxb4+)
Correct piece to wrong square (Qe2+/Qh1#)
Correct piece captures wrong target (Rxg3/Rxe7)
Preparation instead of immediate execution (Rdh1/Rxh4, f4/e5)
Aggressive placement ignoring forcing check-then-capture refutation (Be7)

analysis.label: Moves that neglect the player's own critically exposed king, when the position demands immediate attention to king safety.
analysis.description: In all 8/8 positions, the player's king is explicitly marked as exposed or vulnerable, and the move played addresses some other positional concern (centralizing a queen, advancing a pawn, placing a rook aggressively) instead of the urgent king safety issue. In 5/8 cases, the best move was literally a king move to a safer square (Ke2, Kh1/Kg1, Ke7, Ke4, Ka3), but the player chose a non-king move. The refutations consistently exploit the exposed king through checks, mating attacks, or perpetual check (positions 2, 6, 7, 10, 12, 13). Several moves actively worsen the king situation: g3 blocks escape squares (pos 7), Rd8 self-obstructs the king's flight (pos 10), Qc3 removes a key defensive interposition (pos 2), Rf4 abandons back-rank coverage (pos 12). The extremely high average cp_loss of 2551 reflects how catastrophically these king safety oversights are punished—often leading to forced mate or perpetual check.
analysis.move_pattern: Non-king moves (queen retreats, pawn pushes, rook relocations) made when the player's king is centrally exposed or lacks pawn shelter, typically ignoring the need for king flight or defensive consolidation
analysis.why_bad: The moves fail to address the most urgent problem in the position—the player's own king vulnerability—allowing the opponent to launch devastating tactical sequences (checks, mating nets, perpetuals) that the exposed king cannot survive
sub_patterns: Blocking own king escape squares with pawns (g3, Rd8)
Removing defensive pieces from critical squares (Qc3 loses d1 interposition, Rf4 abandons back rank)
Premature pawn advances that create new targets near the exposed king (d6, d5)
Choosing passive or irrelevant moves when king relocation was required (Rf1, Ke7)

analysis.label: Playing a natural-looking or seemingly purposeful move that squanders a critical tempo in a position demanding one specific concrete action.
analysis.description: This feature fires on positions where a player makes a move that appears reasonable by general principles (aggressive piece development, repositioning, castling, giving check) but catastrophically wastes tempo in a position that demanded precise, concrete action. In 7/9 positions, the analyses explicitly tag 'tempo_loss' as the core issue. The average cp_loss is extremely high (1392) and the average number of good moves is very low (1.7), indicating these are critical decision points where only narrow, forcing continuations maintained the advantage. The played moves share a conceptual thread: they prioritize appearance over calculation—Ng5 looks attacking but gives Black ...Bg7 with tempo; Rg8 targets the g-file but abandons the critical h-file; d5 advances but removes e5 support; Kf6 retreats from where it threatens a capture; Bg4 'develops' but ignores f7; Qe7 repositions but doesn't counter the kingside storm; Bc4 relocates but releases b5 pressure; O-O follows principle but walks into a tactical pattern; Bb3+ gives a check that helps the opponent's king escape a mating net.
analysis.move_pattern: Diverse piece types moved to apparently active/safe squares (no single geometric direction); the commonality is non-forcing piece relocations when a forcing/concrete move was required
analysis.why_bad: Each move gives the opponent a free tempo to solve their critical problem—whether escaping a mating net, capturing an undefended piece, launching a pawn break, or neutralizing an attack—because the played move doesn't address the position's concrete tactical demands
sub_patterns: Aggressive piece sortie that gives opponent counterplay with tempo
Piece relocation that abandons a critical pressure point or defensive duty
Routine/principled move (castling, development) that ignores specific tactical vulnerability
Purposeless check that improves opponent's king position

analysis.label: Playing a material-grabbing or active-looking move that abandons the critical defensive duty of preventing an enemy pawn from promoting.
analysis.description: In all 6/6 positions, an enemy pawn sits one square from promotion, and exactly one (or very few) moves exist to blockade or eliminate that threat. Instead of addressing the promotion, the player makes a tempting but irrelevant move—usually a capture (Bxe3, Nxc5, Bxh3 in 3/6) or an active-looking piece maneuver (Rd7, Rb6, b4 in 3/6). In each case, the moved piece was either the sole blockader of the promotion square (bishop abandoning the a3-f8 or a2-g8 diagonal in 2/6, rook failing to reach the back rank in 2/6) or the only piece capable of capturing the threatening pawn (knight leaving d2 unguarded in 1/6), or the move simply wastes a tempo while the pawn queens (b4 in 1/6). The average cp_loss of 7814 reflects that these are typically game-ending errors, converting survivable positions into forced mates.
analysis.move_pattern: A piece (often bishop or knight) captures material on a square away from the promotion file/diagonal, or a rook moves laterally instead of to the back rank blockade square
analysis.why_bad: The moved piece was the sole defender against an unstoppable pawn promotion one square away; removing it from its critical blockading role allows immediate queening with devastating tactical consequences (mating attacks, queen forks, skewers)
sub_patterns: Bishop captures material, abandoning the diagonal that blockades the promotion square (Bxe3, Bxh3)
Rook attacks laterally or on wrong rank instead of occupying the actual promotion square (Rd7 instead of Rd8, Rb6 instead of Rb8)
Knight captures irrelevant material while being the only piece able to eliminate the promoting pawn (Nxc5 instead of Nxd2)
Completely irrelevant pawn push while opponent promotes next move (b4 ignoring d2-d1=Q)

analysis.label: Wasting a crucial tempo on a non-urgent or misdirected move when the opponent has an imminent concrete threat (usually a dangerous passed pawn) that demands immediate attention.
analysis.description: This feature fires on positions where the player makes a move that looks superficially reasonable—a pawn push, king centralization, a check, or a piece reposition—but fatally ignores an urgent concrete threat, typically a dangerous passed pawn in a rook endgame. In 7/9 positions, a passed pawn was the dominant strategic factor requiring immediate action. In 7/9 positions, the blunder occurred in an endgame (mostly rook endgames). The lost tempo allowed the opponent's threat to cross a critical threshold: the passed pawn advances to the 7th rank (positions 1, 4, 8, 9), a rook invades decisively (positions 8, 10, 13), or a tactical vulnerability becomes exploitable (positions 2, 4). The moves include speculative pawn pushes that self-weaken (h4, f5, e3 in 3/9), passive or misdirected king moves (Ke2, Ke6, Kh2 in 3/9), and rook moves that abandon critical posts (Rg4+, Rb1, Rb4 in 3/9). All share the fundamental error of treating an urgent, concrete position as if time were not the decisive factor.
analysis.move_pattern: Mixed piece types (pawns, kings, rooks) moving to non-critical squares; no single geometric direction but all are slow/non-forcing moves that fail to address the board's most pressing sector
analysis.why_bad: The one wasted tempo allows an opponent's near-decisive threat (usually a passed pawn supported by an active rook) to cross the tipping point from 'manageable' to 'unstoppable,' because the position required immediate concrete countermeasures (blockading, capturing, or generating forcing counterplay) rather than any slow improvement.
sub_patterns: Speculative pawn pushes weakening own structure instead of addressing a passed pawn (h4, f5)
Passive king moves when active rook play was required (Kh2, Ke2)
King moves abandoning defense of a critical pawn (Ke6, f5 removing f7 shield)
Rook abandoning critical file/rank for a pointless check or passive square (Rg4+, Rb1)
Indirect rook maneuver losing one tempo vs direct route (Rb4 instead of Ra4)

analysis.label: King moves backward or away from the critical passed pawn when advancing the king toward it was essential for tempo.
analysis.description: This feature fires on positions where the player retreats the king (or plays passively) in endgames with passed pawns, when the best move was to advance the king aggressively toward the critical square. In 8/10 positions, the played move was a king move that went backward or sideways, while the best move advanced the king toward a blockading, attacking, or counterplay-generating square. The consistent error is losing a critical tempo in a pawn race: Kd7 instead of Kd5 (failing to blockade, 1/10), Kf7 instead of Kf5 (failing to attack the f4 pawn, 2/10), Kc3 instead of Kc5 (failing to threaten c6, 3/10), Ke7 instead of Kf5 (passive retreat, 4/10), Kc2 instead of Kc4 (stepping onto a check diagonal, 5/10), Kc2 instead of Kd3 (failing to blockade, 6/10), Kc8 instead of Ka7 (retreating from the a-pawn, 8/10). The non-king moves (Bd3, g5, Rad8) share the same underlying principle: passivity or misplaced resources when active play toward the critical target was required. All analyses consistently tag 'tempo_loss' as the core issue, with passed pawns as the dominant strategic theme.
analysis.move_pattern: King moves one square backward (toward own back rank) or laterally away from the critical passed pawn, typically along a file or diagonal that allows the opponent's pawn to advance with tempo (check)
analysis.why_bad: The retreating king loses a critical tempo in the pawn race, failing to blockade, attack, or contest the passed pawn directly, which allows the opponent to advance pawns with check, capture counterplay assets, or achieve an unstoppable promotion configuration one move sooner.
sub_patterns: King retreats when blockade square was available one rank forward
King steps onto pawn's checking diagonal enabling advance with tempo
King moves toward wrong wing abandoning the critical pawn

analysis.label: Moving a piece away from its essential defensive role, instantly allowing a devastating tactical exploitation.
analysis.description: In 5/5 positions, the player moves a piece that was performing a critical defensive function—guarding a key square, protecting a piece, or maintaining a tactical threat—to a seemingly reasonable but tactically irrelevant square. In Position 1, Ke4 abandons defense of the Nd6, allowing Qd5+ fork. In Position 2, Ba1 removes the sole guard of d8, enabling Ke6+ discovered check into Rd8#. In Position 4, Qd6 abandons both the attack on f7 and the guard of f5, allowing Qxf5+ mating attack. In Position 5, Ke2 places the king on a fork-vulnerable square on the open e-file, enabling Nc3+ fork. In Position 3, Kc7 ignores the urgent promotion (the pawn's 'defensive' role of becoming a queen), allowing perpetual check. All 5 positions had very few good alternatives (avg 1.6 good moves), and the blunders enabled immediate, often forcing tactical punishment.
analysis.move_pattern: A defending piece (king, queen, or bishop) makes a short quiet move away from its current square, neither capturing nor giving check, relocating to a square that loses contact with the critical defensive assignment.
analysis.why_bad: The moved piece was the sole guardian of a critical square or piece, and its departure instantly exposes a tactical vulnerability—fork, discovered check, back-rank mate, or perpetual check—that the opponent exploits with forcing moves.
sub_patterns: King stepping off the defense line of a hanging piece (Ke4, Kc7)
Piece leaving guard of a mating square (Ba1 unguarding d8, Qd6 unguarding f5)
King moving onto a tactically vulnerable square (Ke2 enabling fork)

analysis.label: Playing a non-urgent or misguided move while a critical piece (own or opponent's) is undefended and requires immediate tactical attention.
analysis.description: This feature activates when a player makes a plausible-looking move—often a quiet developing move (Nd7, d3, h6, g6), a prophylactic pawn push, or an aggressive but unsound piece placement (Ne6, Nxf7+, Be4)—while ignoring the most pressing tactical obligation in the position, which almost always involves an undefended piece. In 5/9 positions the explicit motif is 'hanging_piece' where either the player's own piece is en prise (positions 1, 3, 6, 8: knight on e4, knight on b5, bishop on h4, knight on e6 are all capturable) or the player places a piece where it's immediately taken. In 2/9 positions king safety weaknesses are created or exploited incorrectly (f3 opening a diagonal, Qxf1+ abandoning an attack). In position 2, a discovered attack winning the queen is missed. The unifying thread is that positions demand one specific concrete action (avg good moves: 1.8) but the player instead makes a move that would be reasonable in a quieter position, failing to recognize the tactical emergency.
analysis.move_pattern: Quiet piece/pawn moves (developing, retreating, prophylactic pushes) or aggressive piece placements to undefended squares, all ignoring an immediate capture/tactical threat
analysis.why_bad: The move wastes a critical tempo when a piece is hanging or a forcing tactical sequence demands immediate attention—either the player's own piece gets captured for free, their aggressive piece lands undefended, or they miss a winning tactic, resulting in significant material loss (avg 326cp).
sub_patterns: Prophylactic pawn push (h6, g6) while own piece is en prise
Developing move (Nd7, d3) exposing or ignoring a hanging piece
Aggressive piece placement to undefended square (Ne6, Nxf7+, Be4)
Premature simplification abandoning a winning attack (Qxf1+)
Pawn move creating king weakness when concrete tactic was required (f3)

analysis.label: Major piece moves in endgames that enable an unfavorable exchange into a lost simplified position (typically a pawn endgame) where the piece was the sole source of counterplay.
analysis.description: This feature fires on endgame moves where a player's queen or rook moves to a square that allows or invites an exchange leading to a hopelessly lost simplified position. In 6/9 positions, the move directly enables a major piece exchange resulting in a losing pawn endgame (Qe1→Qxe1+, Qe6→Qxe6+, Qd2→forced Qf1+ exchange, Qf6→Qxf6+, Rc3→Rxc3+, Rxb4→Rxb4+ Kxb4). In the remaining positions, the piece moves to a square that fatally compromises coordination or abandons critical defensive duties (Qg2 abandons e3 defense, Qxa3 breaks queen-rook coordination allowing a fork, Qe5 leaves the king exposed without adequate checking resources). The consistent thread is that the player's active major piece was the sole source of counterplay or defensive balance, and the move eliminates or neutralizes it. Correct play in all cases involved maintaining the piece actively (often through quiet king moves like Kf2, Kd4, Kg5, Kf7) rather than moving it to a vulnerable or exchange-enabling square.
analysis.move_pattern: Queen or rook moves to a square where it can be captured/exchanged or loses critical defensive function; typically queen centralizations (e1, e5, e6, f6, d2, g2) or rook captures/challenges (Rc3, Rxb4)
analysis.why_bad: The major piece was the player's only source of counterplay or defensive resources in the endgame; exchanging it or moving it off its critical function transitions into a simplified position (usually pawn endgame) that is technically lost due to structural inferiority, passed pawn advantages, or superior enemy king activity.
sub_patterns: Direct queen exchange offer into lost pawn endgame (Qe1, Qe6, Qf6)
Enabling forced queen exchange via tactical vulnerability (Qd2 allowing back-rank check)
Rook exchange offer into lost pawn endgame (Rc3, Rxb4)
Queen moves off critical defensive square allowing material loss (Qg2, Qxa3, Qe5)

analysis.label: Non-forcing, natural-looking moves played in critical positions where only one or two precise tactical solutions maintain the evaluation.
analysis.description: This feature fires on positions where the player makes a quiet, non-forcing move (retreat, development, centralization, or king tuck) instead of addressing the single most urgent tactical demand. In 7/8 positions, there was only 1-2 good moves available, indicating razor-thin defensive requirements. The blundered moves all appear 'reasonable' on the surface—Kg8 tucks the king (Position 1), Bf8 tries to shore up dark squares (Position 2), Nf6 centralizes a knight (Position 5), Qf2 supports pawns (Position 6), Nf3 targets an enemy rook (Position 12), Bc6 develops a bishop (Position 13), Kd3 centralizes the king (Position 14)—but each ignores the one critical action the position demands. In multiple cases (3/8), the required move was a different piece addressing the SAME square or threat (e.g., Bg7 instead of Bc6 to prevent Nf6#; Bf8 instead of Kg8 to escape the knight; Kf7 instead of Nf6 to leave the g-file). The average cp_loss of 1457 reflects that these 'one right answer' positions punish passive play catastrophically.
analysis.move_pattern: Any piece type, non-capturing, non-checking move to a seemingly natural square; often retreats or short-range repositioning moves
analysis.why_bad: These moves waste a critical tempo in positions demanding immediate precise action—either failing to neutralize an opponent's threat (mate, capture, passed pawn advance) or moving the wrong piece when only one specific piece addresses the urgent problem, allowing the opponent to execute their tactical idea with full force.
sub_patterns: King retreat when a different piece needs to move (Kg8, Kd3)
Piece development that ignores a mating/tactical threat (Bc6, Nf6)
Retreat to a square where the piece becomes a tactical target (Bf8 hanging to knight, Nf3 attacked by rook)
Queen displacement abandoning critical defensive duties (Qf2)

analysis.label: Moves directed toward a secondary flank target (often a pawn) instead of addressing the position's primary strategic demand, wasting a critical tempo.
analysis.description: This feature fires on moves that pursue a tempting but secondary objective—typically capturing or approaching a flank pawn—while the position urgently demands action on the primary strategic front. In 7/8 positions, the best move involved central action, counterplay on the correct wing, or precise pawn promotion support, while the blunder drifted toward the wrong target. Rxh2 grabbed an h-pawn but left the rook on a trapped diagonal (1/8); Kf3 went to capture g3 when c4 created an unstoppable passed pawn (1/8); Ke2 headed kingside when queenside counterplay via c3/Kc4 was critical (1/8); Kg2 moved to the wrong side of the f-pawn instead of Ke1 supporting promotion (1/8); a6 prematurely pushed a pawn instead of centralizing the king (1/8); h4 opened lines near an exposed king instead of creating counterplay elsewhere (1/8). The tag 'tempo_loss' appears in 7/8 analyses, and 'piece_activity' in 6/8, confirming the core pattern: these moves squander a tempo on a peripheral concern while the opponent gains time to execute the dominant plan.
analysis.move_pattern: Piece or pawn moves toward the board edge (h-file, a-file, back rank) or toward a secondary pawn target, away from the critical zone of action
analysis.why_bad: The move wastes a crucial tempo pursuing a secondary target, allowing the opponent to execute their primary plan (exploit a diagonal, seize an open file, advance a passed pawn, blockade a promotion square) uncontested. The peripheral target provides insufficient compensation for the time lost.
sub_patterns: King walks toward a flank pawn to capture it instead of supporting central/passed pawn play (Kf3, Ke2, Kg2)
Rook/piece moves to the rim to grab a pawn but lands on a vulnerable square (Rxh2, Rg8, Bh3)
Pawn advance on the wrong flank that either weakens the king position or wastes tempo (a6, h4)

analysis.label: Choosing superficially aggressive or active-looking moves (checks, attacks, piece activations) in critical positions where only one precise move addresses the true positional demand.
analysis.description: This feature fires on positions where the player selects an apparently active move—often a check, capture, or piece 'activation'—while missing the single critical move the position demands. In 5/6 positions, only 1 good move existed (avg 1.2), yet the chosen move looked natural or aggressive: Rf1+ abandoned a dominant d-file for a wrong-file check (1/6), Rh3+ delivered a purposeless check blocked by e3 with tempo (1/6), Rb1 sought speculative counterplay while ignoring a mating threat (1/6), Bg5 developed to a targetless square to be chased (1/6), Qf5 centralized the queen while breaking piece coordination (1/6), and fxg4 captured a pawn while opening invasion lines for the opponent (1/6). In every case, the correct move was more subtle—a quiet repositioning (Qc1, Qh2), a precise penetration on the correct file (Rd7+), or a counter-intuitive pawn thrust (g5). The blundered moves average 1922cp loss, indicating these pseudo-active choices often convert winning positions into losing ones or losing positions into immediate checkmates.
analysis.move_pattern: Piece moved to apparently active square (check, attack, development), typically a rook or queen relocating to a new file/rank or a piece developing to an 'aggressive' square without a concrete target
analysis.why_bad: The moves prioritize superficial activity or aggression over the position's single critical requirement (defending a key square, maintaining piece coordination, or exploiting the correct tactical line), wasting tempo in positions where only one narrow path succeeds
sub_patterns: Checks that allow king escape or enable blocking with tempo
Rook moves to wrong file abandoning critical pressure
Piece development to squares with no real target, losing tempo when chased
Queen relocation breaking existing coordination

analysis.label: Passive, non-forcing moves (often flank pawn pushes or piece drifts) that waste a critical tempo while the opponent has an exploitable tactical vulnerability.
analysis.description: This feature fires on positions where players make slow, non-urgent moves that fail to address the most critical demand of the position. In 4/6 cases, the moves involve the edge files (a6, h4, h4, Rh7 on the h-file), and in 5/6 cases the moves are clearly non-forcing (no checks, captures, or threats). The common thread is that each move ignores an immediate tactical vulnerability: abandoning back-rank defense (Re3, 1/6), allowing a skewer along a rank (Rh7, 1/6), permitting a central pawn break against an uncastled king (h4, 1/6), leaving a piece unguarded against a fork (Qf6, 1/6), or wasting tempo when forced mates are approaching (a6, h4). In every case, the opponent punishes with a concrete forcing sequence—checks, forks, skewers, or decisive pawn advances—that the quiet move did nothing to prevent.
analysis.move_pattern: Quiet non-forcing moves: flank pawn advances (a/h file) or piece repositioning away from the critical zone, with no check/capture/direct threat
analysis.why_bad: They squander a critical tempo on a slow move while the opponent has a concrete forcing sequence available (back-rank check, skewer, fork, central break), and the played move neither defends the vulnerability nor creates sufficient counterplay to distract from it.
sub_patterns: Flank pawn push (h4/a6) when king safety or development is urgent
Piece drift to wrong side of board (Rh7) allowing geometric tactic
Piece abandons critical defensive post (Re3 leaves back rank)
Queen placement fails to cover key piece (Qf6 leaves bishop hanging to fork)

analysis.label: Moving the king or key piece away from the critical flank in an endgame, wasting decisive tempo.
analysis.description: This feature fires on endgame positions where the player directs their king (or key piece) toward the wrong side of the board, abandoning the flank where the decisive action is occurring. In 8/12 positions, the mistake is a king move toward the queenside (Kc5, Kc4, Ka7, Kc6) or away from center when the critical pawn battle is on the kingside. In 3/12 cases, a rook abandons a critical defensive/blockading post (Rc7 leaving the active 2nd rank, Rc6 abandoning a blockade, Rf5 leaving the back rank). In 2/12 cases, a pawn push wastes the tempo that should have been spent on king activation. The consistent punishment across all positions is that the opponent gains free tempi to advance pawns (especially connected passers), activate their own king, or execute tactical strikes in the undefended sector. The average cp_loss of 953 reflects that endgame tempo errors are often catastrophic.
analysis.move_pattern: King (or rook) moves laterally/backward away from the board sector containing the critical pawn tension or defensive responsibility, typically toward the a/b/c files when kingside pawns decide the game
analysis.why_bad: In endgames, every tempo is critical - moving the king or key piece away from the decisive theater gives the opponent free moves to advance passed pawns, infiltrate with their king, or exploit undefended weaknesses, often turning holdable positions into lost ones
sub_patterns: King marches to queenside while kingside pawns are the decisive factor
Rook abandons critical defensive post (back rank, blockade, active rank) for a passive or irrelevant square
Pawn push wastes tempo needed for king centralization

analysis.label: Choosing a passive, aesthetically pleasing, or 'obvious' move instead of the one precise concrete action required in a narrow critical position.
analysis.description: This feature fires on positions where only ~1 good move exists (avg 1.1 good moves available) and the player selects a 'natural-looking' move that wastes critical tempo. In 6/7 positions, the primary tag is tempo_loss. The played moves look reasonable—centralizing a knight (Nd5), approaching a target with the king (Kg7 x2, Ka4), placing a rook on a 'logical' file (Rf1), creating apparent shelter (g6), or winning material (Bxc7)—but each squanders the initiative in a position demanding one specific concrete action. The correct moves are consistently more forcing or counterintuitive: a concrete attacking maneuver (Na4 targeting b2), a retreat away from perceived danger (Ke7), a dynamic exchange sacrifice (Nf6), a back-rank threatening placement (Re1), challenging the opponent's key piece (Bf8/Be5), or an immediate pawn advance (a4). The average cp_loss of 305 reflects how punishing these tempo-wasting moves are in positions with razor-thin margins.
analysis.move_pattern: Non-forcing, non-challenging moves (piece improvements, king shuffles, pawn weakeners, or minor captures) in positions requiring one specific concrete action
analysis.why_bad: They waste a critical tempo in positions where only one precise move works, allowing the opponent to activate key resources, neutralize threats, or launch counterplay that could not have materialized had the forcing move been played immediately.
sub_patterns: Aesthetic piece centralization instead of concrete target attack (Nd5 vs Na4)
King approaching passively instead of dynamic sacrifice or retreat (Kg7 vs Nf6/Ke7)
Rook/piece on wrong file missing key tactical resource (Rf1 vs Re1)
Pawn weakness instead of challenging opponent's key piece (g6 vs Bf8)
Material grab sacrificing piece activity and tempo (Bxc7 vs Be5)
King maneuvering instead of immediate pawn advance in pawn race (Ka4 vs a4)

analysis.label: Playing a seemingly constructive but non-forcing move that squanders a critical tempo in a position demanding immediate tactical action.
analysis.description: This feature fires on moves that appear reasonable (piece development, centralization, or material gain) but fatally waste tempo in positions requiring urgent forcing play. In 4/5 positions, the move is explicitly tagged as 'tempo_loss' — Ne7 repositions a knight only to be forced back by Qb5+ check; d6 is one tempo too slow when the immediate d5 delivers a winning double attack; Bg7 fianchettoes a bishop only to be driven back by Bc5; Qxc7 grabs a pawn while a forced mate in 3 exists via Rxh6+. Even Ne5 (position 7) wastes a 'tempo equivalent' by making an aggressive move that leaves Ba4 hanging after the forced exchange. All 5 positions share the feature that a much more forcing/concrete continuation existed (5/5), the played move looks constructive at surface level (5/5), the opponent immediately exploits the wasted time with a punishing forcing sequence (5/5), and king safety concerns are present (4/5). The average centipawn loss of 2144 reflects that these tempo losses occur at critical tactical junctures where precision is rewarded exponentially.
analysis.move_pattern: Any piece type moving to a seemingly constructive square (development, centralization, or capture) that is non-forcing when the position demands an immediate tactical continuation
analysis.why_bad: The position contains a concrete tactical demand (double attack, mating sequence, urgent castling need, piece coordination requirement) that punishes any delay — the 'improving' move gives the opponent a free tempo to resolve their vulnerability, execute a forcing sequence, or seize the initiative with checks/captures.
sub_patterns: Piece repositioning that opens a checking diagonal or file for the opponent (Ne7, Bg7)
Greedy capture/material grab when a forcing mating or winning sequence exists (Qxc7)
Slow pawn advance when an immediate pawn thrust creates a decisive double attack (d6 vs d5)
Aggressive centralization that leaves another piece tactically undefended (Ne5 leaving Ba4 hanging)

analysis.label: Playing a slow, non-forcing move when the position demands an immediate concrete tactical strike that will become unavailable on the next turn.
analysis.description: This feature fires on positions where a narrow tactical window exists—typically a hanging piece, a forcing check, a perpetual check resource, or a pawn breakthrough—and the player instead makes a quiet preparatory move (development, repositioning, a flank pawn push, or a non-optimal capture). In 7/8 positions, the best move was a direct forcing action: capturing an undefended pawn (Nxe4 in positions 2 and 13), attacking a concrete weakness (N7g6 targeting f4 in position 3), delivering check on an exposed diagonal (Bh5+ in position 5), executing a pawn breakthrough (a6 in position 7), initiating a perpetual check sequence (Rxb2+ in position 9), gaining immediate tempo on a piece (g4 in position 12), or simply castling to prevent exploitation (O-O in position 11). The average number of good moves was only 1.6, indicating extremely narrow positions where only one or two precise continuations maintained the advantage. After the quiet moves were played, in every case the opponent was able to close the window: defending the hanging pawn with d3, castling to safety, playing e3 to create king escape routes, or consolidating piece coordination.
analysis.move_pattern: Non-capturing, non-checking quiet moves (piece development, knight retreats, rook lifts, flank pawn pushes) when forcing captures, checks, or direct attacks on concrete weaknesses are available
analysis.why_bad: These moves surrender a critical tempo, allowing the opponent to fix the specific vulnerability (defend a hanging piece, castle to safety, block a diagonal, or create an escape route) that could have been exploited immediately with a forcing move—the tactical window permanently closes.
sub_patterns: Passive piece development when an undefended central pawn can be captured (Be7/h5 missing Nxe4)
Knight repositioning away from attacking targets when forcing checks or attacks on weaknesses exist (Nc4, Nb3)
Slow rook maneuver when immediate tempo-gaining moves are available (Rf3, Ra6)
Greedy non-forcing capture when a superior pawn breakthrough maintains full attacking coordination (Qxd6)
Structural pawn advance that removes a critical defensive barrier (e5 opening the diagonal to an undefended piece)

analysis.label: Black plays an irrelevant or diversionary move while their key piece is left en prise or undefended, resulting in catastrophic material loss.
analysis.description: In all 4 positions, Black is already significantly losing (avg eval +768 before the blunder) and has very few pieces remaining. The critical shared pattern is that Black's most important remaining piece is either already under attack or placed on an undefended square, yet Black plays a move that fails to address this immediate tactical crisis. In 3/4 positions, the tactical motif is explicitly 'hanging_piece' (Nxf2 leaves the knight capturable by queen/rook, Bb7 places the bishop directly on the rook's file for free capture, h4 ignores the double attack on the bishop from Rf7+Nd5). In 1/4 (Rd8), the move removes the only defender of f7, which amounts to the same result—a piece/pawn is captured for free. All moves appear 'active' (capturing a pawn, activating on an open file, pushing toward promotion) but ignore the most urgent defensive requirement. The feature fires strongest when the ignored threat leads to total collapse—typically forced mate—because the lost piece was Black's last defensive resource.
analysis.move_pattern: Any piece type or pawn move that ignores an immediately capturable/threatened friendly piece; no specific geometric direction—captures, retreats, and pawn pushes all appear
analysis.why_bad: The move fails to address an immediate tactical threat to a key piece (either already attacked or placed on an undefended square), allowing the opponent to win it for free and convert overwhelming material advantage into forced mate
sub_patterns: Moving a piece to a square where it hangs to an obvious capture
Pushing a pawn while a piece is under double attack
Removing a defender from a critical square while the defended piece/pawn is the only thing preventing a breakthrough

analysis.label: Quiet repositioning moves that waste a critical tempo in positions where passed pawns or forcing threats demand immediate action.
analysis.description: This feature fires on non-forcing moves (king walks, rook repositions, prophylactic pawn pushes) played in tempo-critical positions where the opponent has an advancing passed pawn or a forcing tactical sequence available. In 7/8 positions, the analysis explicitly identifies 'tempo_loss' as the core issue. In 6/8 positions, passed pawns are the urgent threat that gets ignored. The moves typically look purposeful—Kb2 heads toward the promotion square, Rb1 seeks back-rank activity, Ra7 occupies the 7th rank, h3 prevents g4—but each wastes an irreplaceable tempo in a position where one move determines whether a pawn promotes, a queen trade is forced, or a blockade is maintained. The common result is that the opponent's passed pawn advances with decisive tempo (d6! in Position 8, c6! in Position 5) or the player falls fatally behind in a pawn race (Positions 1, 6). King moves to seemingly active but misplaced squares appear in 5/8 cases (Kb2, Kd4, Kd6, Ka6, and the retreat Kb4 being the correct alternative in Position 13).
analysis.move_pattern: King or rook moves to seemingly natural/active squares (rim, 7th rank, back rank, center) or slow prophylactic pawn pushes; all non-forcing, no checks or captures
analysis.why_bad: The position demands immediate forcing action (pushing a passed pawn, forcing a queen trade, maintaining a blockade) but the move spends a tempo on piece repositioning, allowing the opponent's passed pawn to advance decisively or seize the initiative with forcing moves
sub_patterns: King walking to wrong square in pawn race endgames (Kb2, Kd4, Ka6)
Rook abandoning restraining duty allowing passed pawn advance (Rb1, Re7)
Rook overextending to active-looking square becoming vulnerable (Ra7)
Slow prophylactic pawn move when forcing continuation wins (h3)

analysis.label: Moves that appear to activate a piece or create threats but actually place it on a vulnerable square where the opponent gains decisive tempo or tactical exploitation.
analysis.description: This feature fires on moves that prioritize apparent activity over concrete positional needs, placing pieces on squares that look aggressive but create tactical vulnerabilities. In 5/7 positions, the moved piece becomes a target for tempo-gaining responses (Ke4 exposed to Rf4+ check, Qb5 kicked by ...c6, a4 opening lines for the better-developed side, Rf4 trapped by Bd3, Bg2 becoming passive and allowing Rb2+ with tempo). In 6/7 positions, quieter and more patient alternatives were available that maintained piece coordination and defensive integrity. The best moves consistently involve careful repositioning (Rd6 instead of Rf4, Bg4 instead of Bg2, Ra7/Bb7 instead of aggressive breaks) rather than the superficially active choices that trigger the feature. The common thread is choosing aggressive-looking moves that lack concrete forcing threats while simultaneously weakening the player's position.
analysis.move_pattern: Various piece types (rook, king, pawn, bishop, queen) moving forward or to ostensibly active squares - typically toward the center or the opponent's position - without creating concrete threats
analysis.why_bad: The pieces land on squares where they become targets for tempo-gaining attacks (pawn kicks, checks, bishop redeployments), abandon critical defensive functions (guarding ranks/diagonals), or open lines that favor the opponent's better-developed or more active forces, allowing decisive tactical exploitation.
sub_patterns: Piece moves to open rank/file where it's exposed to checks or attacks (Ke4, Rf4)
Premature pawn break when underdeveloped opens lines for opponent (a4, c5)
Queen/piece placed on square immediately kickable by pawns (Qb5)
Piece retreats to passive square blocked by own pawns (Bg2)

analysis.label: Playing a non-forcing, seemingly reasonable move in a critical position where only one specific concrete continuation maintains the evaluation.
analysis.description: This feature fires on positions where players choose quiet, plausible-looking moves when the position demands one precise forcing continuation. In 8/8 cases, the position had essentially only one good move (avg 1.1 good moves available), yet the player chose a non-forcing alternative that appeared constructive on the surface. The moves include tempo-wasting flank pawn pushes when sharp tactics existed (a6 played twice in Italian Game positions where Nxe4 won material), piece placement on cosmetically active but functionally wrong squares (Nc4 instead of Nd3 which would trap a bishop; Qh4 abandoning critical d-file control of a passed pawn; Qc2 instead of Bf4 winning the e5 pawn), and coordination failures from seemingly logical moves (Kd6 blocking own bishop's needed square; Kd2 without preparatory Rb4+ check allowing perpetual). The average cp_loss of 340 reflects positions with razor-thin margins where 'autopilot' play is catastrophic.
analysis.move_pattern: Quiet non-forcing moves (pawn pushes to flanks, piece repositioning, king walks) - no checks, no captures, no direct threats - in positions requiring one precise forcing move
analysis.why_bad: The position demanded one specific concrete or forcing move, but the player chose a 'reasonable-looking' quiet move that ignores the critical tactical requirement, wasting a tempo that the opponent immediately exploits to seize the initiative or advance a decisive plan
sub_patterns: Prophylactic flank pawn pushes ignoring available central tactics (a6, f6)
Piece/queen moves to cosmetically active but functionally wrong squares (Nc4, Qh4, Qc2)
King moves without necessary preparatory forcing play (Kd6, Kd2)

analysis.label: Non-forcing piece repositioning moves that inadvertently create immediate tactical vulnerabilities by removing defenders, placing pieces on targetable squares, or leaving material unprotected.
analysis.description: This feature activates on quiet 'improving' moves where the player repositions a piece without addressing a concrete tactical need, resulting in immediate exploitation. The pattern manifests in several sub-types: removing a key defender (Ng3 abandons f2 defense in Position 1; Kb5 abandons b7/d6 coverage in Position 14; Ra8 leaves knight hanging in Position 15 — 3/10 positions), placing a piece on a square vulnerable to forks or sacrifices (Be6 and Be3 both enable d5 pawn forks in Positions 12 and 3; Rac8 allows Nd6 attacking the rook in Position 11; Rf4 enables Rxe6+ exchange sacrifice in Position 10 — 4/10 positions), and abandoning a well-placed piece for a seemingly active but actually inferior square (Nc5 leaves powerful e6 outpost in Position 13). The average cp_loss of 239 (~full piece) reflects that these moves typically allow concrete material wins. The unifying thread is a player focused on positional improvement or development rather than recognizing the position demands tactical attention.
analysis.move_pattern: Non-forcing piece repositioning (any piece type) to a seemingly active square, without check or capture, that creates or exposes an undefended target
analysis.why_bad: The move either removes a piece from a critical defensive role, places it on a square where it becomes a tactical target (fork, attack, exchange sacrifice), or abandons protection of another piece — all while the opponent has forcing moves available to immediately exploit the vulnerability.
sub_patterns: Defender removal exposes hanging pawn or piece
Piece placed on square enabling pawn fork (d5 against bishop+knight)
Rook placed on square attacked by incoming knight jump
Non-forcing rook move leaves friendly piece undefended
King march abandons defensive responsibilities allowing rook invasion

analysis.label: Quiet, reasonable-looking piece moves that overlook critical tactical vulnerabilities such as hanging pieces, back-rank weaknesses, or forcing sequences.
analysis.description: This feature fires on moves that appear natural or strategically sound—repositioning a bishop (Bh5, Bh4, Bf7), centralizing a queen (Qd5, Qd2), penetrating with a rook (Re7, Rf1), or capturing material (Bxf4, Nxe4, Rxg1)—but critically ignore the position's most urgent tactical demand. In 6/12 positions, a piece is hanging or becomes hanging that should be captured or defended (positions 1, 2, 5, 9, 11, 14). In 3/12 positions, the move wastes a decisive tempo when a forcing continuation exists (positions 7, 10, 15). In 3/12 positions, the move abandons a critical defensive function or tactical resource (positions 4, 8, 13). The average cp_loss of 1000 and only 1.8 good moves available confirm these are sharp positions demanding concrete calculation where the player defaulted to 'looks reasonable' over 'what does the position require right now.' The played moves consistently represent the player seeing an attractive surface-level idea while being blind to the one critical tactical element.
analysis.move_pattern: Mostly non-capture piece moves (9/12) to plausible-looking squares—bishops to rim squares (h5, h4, f7), queens to central posts (d5, d2, h5), rooks to open files (e7, f1)—or captures of secondary targets when a primary target is available
analysis.why_bad: Each move ignores the single most critical tactical feature of the position (a hanging piece, a forcing sequence, a back-rank weakness, a trapping pawn advance, or a must-push passed pawn) in favor of a move that looks strategically reasonable but fails to address the concrete demand of the moment
sub_patterns: Bishop repositioning to rim squares while leaving pieces or pawns undefended
Capturing a secondary target while a more valuable hanging piece exists
Queen centralization that abandons critical defensive or tactical coordination
Rook moves that waste tempo when decisive forcing sequences are available
Pawn-grabbing captures before completing development with king in center

analysis.label: Moves pursuing attractive but secondary objectives while ignoring the position's single critical requirement, often leaving pieces undefended or missequencing a tactical idea.
analysis.description: This feature activates on positions with very few good options (avg 1.9) where the player selects a natural-looking or tempting move instead of the one action the position demands. In 5/9 positions, the move directly leaves a piece undefended or creates a target (Nxg2 leaves Bh3 hanging, Rad1 leaves Nc3 hanging, Bh3 leaves Ne6 en prise, f4 leaves e3 undefended, Nc8 creates a back-rank target). In 3/9 positions, the error involves using the wrong piece for a capture or incorrect move order (Nxg5 instead of Bxg5 trades away the dominant piece, Qxe4 instead of Bxe4 displaces the queen, Bh3 before Nxf8 reverses the winning sequence). In 1/9 cases (Kxh3), material is grabbed at the cost of abandoning a critical defensive zone. The unifying thread is that positions demand ONE specific action, but a 'reasonable-looking' alternative exists that ignores the critical tactical or positional requirement, resulting in catastrophic evaluation losses (avg 1241cp).
analysis.move_pattern: Diverse piece types and directions—captures (often of pawns/pieces that appear free), pawn pushes, developing moves, and retreats—but all are moves toward seemingly attractive targets or standard positional goals
analysis.why_bad: The move pursues a secondary objective (grabbing material, developing, activating a piece, following a plan) while ignoring that it either leaves a piece undefended for the opponent to capture, missequences a tactical combination, or abandons a critical defensive obligation—exploitable because the position offered very few viable alternatives
sub_patterns: Wrong piece capture/recapture trading superior piece
Move-order error executing tactical sequence out of order
Pawn grab moving king/piece away from critical defensive zone
Developing move ignoring hanging piece
Retreat creating back-rank or geometric vulnerability

analysis.label: Moving the wrong piece/pawn when a different unit delivers the position's strongest tactical blow.
analysis.description: In all 6/6 positions, the player moves a different piece or pawn than the one that should execute the critical action: Position 1 moves the wrong knight (Nxe7+ instead of Nxf6+), Position 10 moves the queen (Qa2) when the rook should capture (Rxc8), Position 11 moves the rook (Rdg1) when the knight should jump (Ng5), Position 12 moves the king (Kh7) when the pawn should advance (g5), Position 13 checks with the bishop (Bb4+) when the queen should check (Qa5+), and Position 15 pushes the wrong pawn (f3 instead of d4). The positions typically have very few good moves available (avg 1.7), meaning only the correct piece choice works. The played moves often look actively motivated—checks, captures, or piece improvements—but fundamentally misidentify which unit holds the key to the position's tactical solution.
analysis.move_pattern: Various piece types moved to active-looking squares, but always the wrong piece—the correct move invariably involves a different piece or pawn delivering the decisive action
analysis.why_bad: The moved piece either abandons a critical function (defending key squares, maintaining pressure on a file), or its action is simply less forcing than what the correct piece achieves. The wrong piece choice typically dissolves tactical coordination, allows the opponent to consolidate, or creates unnecessary weaknesses.
sub_patterns: Wrong knight/piece captures (Nxe7+ vs Nxf6+)
Queen retreats when rook should capture
Slow rook lift when knight jump creates immediate threats
King advances when pawn should advance first (tempo)
Check with wrong piece missing a fork
Wrong pawn push creating weaknesses instead of developing
